stem: You are a hospital medical officer in the early pregnancy assessment clinic. Sarah Nguyen, 25, was referred yesterday with light vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was eight weeks ago. She has had an ultrasound this morning and has come back for the result. She is on her own.

Information you have been given: observations BP 112/70, HR 76, T 36.6, she is well. Speculum yesterday: os closed, scant old blood, cervix healthy. Bimanual yesterday: uterus consistent with dates, non-tender, no cervical motion tenderness, adnexae normal. Transvaginal ultrasound today: single intrauterine gestational sac, crown–rump length consistent with 8 weeks, no fetal cardiac activity, no adnexal mass, no free fluid. Blood group A negative. Her own words at reception: 'Is everything all right? Nobody would tell me anything.'
tasks: Explain the ultrasound findings to the patient
Counsel her about further management
Answer any questions she has

dx: **Missed miscarriage at 8 weeks** — sac of 8 weeks' size with **no fetal cardiac activity**. Also called early fetal demise or silent miscarriage, but **never say those words to her**.

**Non-viability is a measurement, not an impression**: **mean sac diameter ≥ 25 mm with no embryo**, or **crown–rump length ≥ 7 mm with no heartbeat**. At 8 weeks the CRL is well past 7 mm, so the diagnosis is **secure on a single scan**. VERIFY

If the numbers were borderline — a small sac, or a pole **under 7 mm** — the correct action is a **repeat scan in 7 to 10 days** and you do **not** use the word miscarriage today. Saying this shows you know the thresholds rather than the label.

The sequence, and it fails in two opposite directions: **warning shot → one plain sentence → ten seconds of silence → and still reach the three options**. Some candidates break the news beautifully and run out of time with no management; others rush to the options and never let her react. You must do both.

The sentence itself, no hedging: **'The scan shows that the pregnancy has stopped growing. I'm very sorry — you have had a miscarriage.'** Then stop. No 'unfortunately the sonographic appearances are consistent with'.

Volunteer the blame answer before she asks it: **'there is nothing you did that caused this. It isn't the gym, it isn't your work, it isn't coffee, and it isn't anything you ate.'** Most early miscarriages happen because the pregnancy did not develop as it should from the very beginning. She still feels pregnant **because the hormones take a while to fall**.

The three options, **none more correct than the others**: **expectant** (no drugs, no surgery, at home — but no one can say when) · **medical** (**mifepristone, then misoprostol a day or two later**) · **surgical** (day-case **suction curettage** under anaesthetic — planned, least bleeding, tissue to the laboratory). If she asks which you would choose, **decline**, then help her weigh it: **'what matters more to you — knowing when, or avoiding an anaesthetic?'**

CORRECTION — medical management does **not** fail 5% of the time. Roughly **15–25% go on to need surgical evacuation**. Quote a range, and tell her that needing the operation afterwards is **common, not a complication**. CORRECTION — curettage does **not** meaningfully cause later ectopic pregnancy or placenta praevia; the real risks are **uterine perforation, cervical injury, infection, retained tissue and rarely intrauterine adhesions**.

CORRECTION — the **nine-week / 63-day limit is the MS-2 Step registration limit for medical TERMINATION**, not a ceiling for managing a miscarriage. Gestation affects how much bleeding and pain to warn her about, not her eligibility.

**Anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours** — she is **A NEGATIVE**, so it is needed **if managed medically or surgically**. VERIFY. Then: **histology on any tissue obtained** (which also excludes a molar pregnancy) · red flags · **no medical need to wait beyond one normal period** before trying again, and that is only to make dating easier · **about one in five pregnancies ends this way**, and after one miscarriage the next is essentially the same as anyone else's · continue folic acid. SA: **PATS** for travel to EPAS at TQEH, RAH, FMC or the WCH; **Sands**, **Red Nose Grief and Loss**, **Miscarriage Australia**; Country Health Connect; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: There is **no history to take** — do not spend the station taking one. Set up instead: **'Sarah, come and sit down. We won't be interrupted.'** Then **'before we start, is there anyone you'd like me to call to be with you?'**
Find out what she already knows: **'can you tell me what you understand so far about why you came in?'** She says the closed os was called a good sign.

**Give the normal findings first** — **'that's right, the neck of the womb was closed, and the pregnancy is in exactly the right place, inside the womb.'** It is true, and it makes the next sentence land as information rather than ambush.
**Warning shot: 'I'm afraid I don't have good news for you today.'** Then pause. Let her brace — two seconds is enough.
**One plain sentence: 'The scan shows that the pregnancy has stopped growing. I'm very sorry — you have had a miscarriage.'** Then stop talking.
**Ten seconds of silence.** Offer tissues if she is crying. **Do not fill the gap.** If she puts a hand up, wait longer.
**'I'm so sorry, Sarah. Take whatever time you need.'** Then volunteer the blame answer **without being asked** — the gym, work, coffee, food — and explain why she still feels pregnant.
Ask permission before pivoting: **'when you're ready, I'll explain what happens from here. Would that be all right?'**
Frame the choice: **'there are three ways this can be managed, and none of them is more correct than the others. It is your choice, and you don't have to decide today.'**
**Expectant** — wait and let your body pass the pregnancy; no drugs, no surgery, at home; **the difficulty is we can't tell you when**, and there will be bleeding and cramping.

**Medical** — **one tablet, then a second medicine a day or two later** which brings the bleeding on; avoids an anaesthetic, can be at home; causes **cramping, heavy bleeding and often nausea**, and **a proportion still need a small operation afterwards**.

**Surgical** — a **small operation under anaesthetic as a day case**; planned and predictable, least bleeding, **tissue goes to the laboratory**; downsides are the anaesthetic, and small risks of **infection, injury to the womb and rarely scarring inside it**.
If she asks which you would choose: **decline honestly**, then **'what matters more to you — knowing when, or avoiding an anaesthetic?'** Reflect her answer back without deciding for her.

**Anti-D: 'your blood group is A negative, so if we manage this with tablets or with an operation you'll need an anti-D injection within 72 hours — I'll organise that.'** Then **histology** on any tissue obtained.
Red flags: **soaking a pad within an hour · severe pain · fever · offensive discharge** — come straight back.

Answer the two questions she will ask: **can we try again** — no medical need to wait beyond one normal period, and that is only for dating; wait until you both feel ready. **Will it happen again** — about one in five, and after one the next is the same as anyone's. **Keep taking the folic acid.**
**'I'll write all of this down, and I'd like to see you again next week — not because anything is wrong, but because this is a great deal to take in on your own.'** Offer **Sands** and **Red Nose**.
pefe: **No examination task and no history task** — everything is handed to you on the door. The work is entirely in interpreting the scan and counselling.

The scan, read properly: **single intrauterine gestational sac · CRL consistent with 8 weeks · NO fetal cardiac activity · no adnexal mass · no free fluid**. The intrauterine sac is what excludes an ectopic; the absent cardiac activity at this CRL is what makes it a miscarriage.
**Non-viability thresholds: MSD ≥ 25 mm with no embryo, or CRL ≥ 7 mm with no heartbeat.** Below those, the answer is a **repeat scan in 7–10 days**, not a diagnosis. VERIFY

Yesterday's examination, already given: **os closed, scant old blood, cervix healthy; uterus consistent with dates, non-tender, no cervical motion tenderness, adnexae normal**. A closed os with a uterus at dates and no tissue is what makes this **missed** rather than incomplete or complete.

**Blood group and antibody screen** is the anti-D decision and it is already done — **A negative**. **Anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours if managed medically or surgically**; not required for expectant management of a **threatened** miscarriage before 12 weeks, but this is a confirmed miscarriage. VERIFY with the receiving unit.
**Histopathology on any tissue obtained** — it also excludes a molar pregnancy. Say it as part of the plan for the medical and surgical options.
**No serial βhCG** — this is a confirmed intrauterine miscarriage, not a pregnancy of unknown location. Serial levels would add nothing.
If challenged on a **5 mm CRL**: **'then I could not call it a miscarriage. Below 7 mm with no heartbeat the correct action is a repeat scan in 7 to 10 days, and I would not use the word today.'**

If she chooses expectant management and goes home to think — **that is entirely acceptable**. There is no urgency in a woman who is well and not bleeding heavily. Written information, red flags, and a review appointment.
ddx: **Missed miscarriage**
Little or no bleeding, **no pain**, pregnancy symptoms often persisting
**Os closed**, uterus at or below dates; sac present with **no cardiac activity**
**CRL ≥ 7 mm with no heartbeat confirms it on a single scan.** This is the diagnosis. Prompt
Viable pregnancy, dated too early
Uncertain LMP, irregular cycles, a small sac or a pole **under 7 mm**

**Repeat scan in 7–10 days before anyone uses the word miscarriage.** Not the case here at 8 weeks
Anembryonic pregnancy
Sac present with **no embryo at all**
**MSD ≥ 25 mm with no embryo**
Same three management options. Prompt
Threatened miscarriage
Bleeding with the pregnancy intact
Os closed, uterus = dates, **cardiac activity PRESENT**
**Excluded here** — there is no cardiac activity. Routine
Incomplete miscarriage
Heavy **worsening** bleeding, tissue passed, cramping in waves
**Os open, tissue at the os**, uterus smaller than dates
**Excluded here** — os closed, no tissue, uterus at dates. Urgent if present
**Ectopic pregnancy**
Constant pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness
Empty uterus, **CMT positive**, adnexal mass or free fluid
**Excluded here** — the sac is intrauterine, no adnexal mass, no free fluid. Immediate if present

**Hyperemesis**, grape-like tissue, very high βhCG
**Uterus larger than dates**; snowstorm with no fetus
**Histology on any tissue obtained excludes it** — one more reason to send it. Urgent if present

stem: You are the medical officer in the emergency department of a country hospital. Chloe Barrett, 24, has presented with vaginal bleeding that started early this morning and is getting heavier. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and a home pregnancy test was positive.
tasks: Take a focused history (approximately four minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain the diagnosis and your immediate management

dx: **Incomplete miscarriage with shock at 6 weeks** — **open os with products visible**, uterus **five weeks and contracting**, heavy worsening bleeding. The marks are not in the history; they are in the examination and **the first thing you do about it**.

CORRECTION — **what kind of shock is this?** The classic teaching is that tissue distending the cervical canal causes a **vagal discharge**, so cervical shock gives **bradycardia** with hypotension. This card gives a pulse of **110** — that is **hypovolaemia from ongoing blood loss**. **Say both**: the dominant cause is blood loss, but the tissue in the canal can also cause a vagal bradycardia, and **removing it treats both**.

Reciting 'cervical shock causes bradycardia' at a woman with a tachycardia is describing a textbook rather than the patient. Never mentioning cervical shock at all misses **why the tissue must come out immediately**. Name both mechanisms.

The line that passes the station, said **at the speculum, before your next question**: **'I would remove that tissue now with sponge forceps and send it for histopathology. Removing it will reduce the bleeding and relieve the vagal stimulation from the cervical canal.'**

Why removal reduces rather than increases bleeding: **tissue sitting in the cervical canal keeps the uterus from contracting down**, so it keeps her bleeding. It is both **diagnostic and therapeutic**, and no volume of fluid substitutes for it.

Why the uterus is **five weeks at six weeks by dates**: part of the pregnancy has already been expelled, so it is **smaller than dates and contracting down**. A uterus **equal to dates with a closed os** would be a threatened miscarriage instead.

Immediate management in order: **resuscitation area · two large-bore cannulae · bloods for FBE, group and cross-match, βhCG, coagulation · crystalloid, blood if she does not respond · REMOVE THE PRODUCTS AT THE OS · analgesia and antiemetic · repeat observations · anti-D · gynaecology · ultrasound once stable**.
**Anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours** — she is **O negative** and this is a miscarriage requiring intervention. VERIFY. **Histopathology on the tissue** — it also excludes a molar pregnancy.

**Septic miscarriage** is the one thing worse than this: **fever, offensive vaginal discharge, a tender uterus**. If present, the sepsis pathway with **blood cultures and IV antibiotics**, and **evacuation becomes urgent**. Screen for it in the history — it costs one question.

SA: a shocked woman in a Yorke and Northern ED is a **retrieval** conversation, not a transfer-by-car one. **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** or **RFDS** early, and speak to the on-call gynaecologist while you resuscitate. **Removing the tissue at the os is something you do before anyone is retrieved** — it does not wait for a specialist. Check what **O negative red cells** are held on site before you need them. **Sands**, **Red Nose Grief and Loss**, Country Health Connect, **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: Before you sit: **'Examiner, could I have her blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature?'** **This is the station** — ask now, or you will take a history from a shocked woman without knowing it.

One sentence, out loud, then go back to your task: **'Examiner, those observations concern me. I would move her to the resuscitation area now, insert two large-bore cannulae, take bloods including a cross-match, and start fluids while I continue.'** Do **not** spend two minutes resuscitating out loud.
WIPE, confirm identity, acknowledge what you can see: **'I can see that, and we're going to look after you.'**
The bleeding: **when did it start · is it getting worse or settling · have you passed any tissue, anything solid apart from blood · any clots · how many pads, and are they soaking through**.

Pain and haemodynamic symptoms: **are you having pain · out of ten · is it constant or does it come and go in waves · have you felt faint or dizzy · any pain at the tip of your shoulder**. Waves = a uterus contracting to expel. Pre-syncope confirms the shock is clinical, not just a number.
The **compressed 5 Ps** — at four minutes you keep **P1 and P3 only**: **when was your last period · is this your first pregnancy · any previous miscarriage or termination**.
Septic screen, one question: **any fever, or any offensive discharge?** Then **do you know your blood group · any medications or allergies**. The blood group is the anti-D decision.

**Drop** cervical screening, the partner and STI questions, the smoking and alcohol screen and the full past history. If challenged: **'I prioritised the bleeding, the haemodynamic symptoms and the rhesus status because she is shocked. I would complete the history once she was stable.'**

Examination: **general inspection — pale, distressed, alert?** → **abdomen — tenderness, guarding, rebound, uterus palpable?** → **'a pelvic examination with her consent and a chaperone'** → **'is the os open or closed?'**

**The moment you are told there is tissue at the os, say it — before the bimanual, before anything else**: remove it now with sponge forceps, send it for histopathology, and give both reasons. Then continue: active bleeding, lesions, **bimanual for uterine size, tenderness and contractions, adnexae**.
**'May I have repeat observations after removing the tissue?'** BP 104/68, HR 96. Asking is scored, and the improvement is your evidence for the vagal contribution.

Name it plainly: **'Chloe, I'm sorry. You are having a miscarriage. Some of the pregnancy tissue has already come away, and some was still sitting in the neck of the womb. That is why you were bleeding so heavily and why you felt faint.'**

Volunteer the blame answer **before she asks**: **'there is nothing you did that caused this.'** Most early miscarriages happen because the pregnancy was not developing as it should from the beginning.

The plan: fluids running, bloods taken and **cross-matched in case she needs a transfusion**; **'your group is O negative, so you'll need an anti-D injection within 72 hours — I'll organise that today'**; gynaecology referral and a **scan once stable** to check for retained tissue; then **tablets or a small operation** if there is.

**Refuse to send her home while she is still bleeding** — 'I want you here until we're both happy.' Then red flags for when she does go: **soaking a pad within an hour · severe pain · feeling faint · fever or offensive discharge**.
pefe: **Observations before you sit down**, including whether there is a postural drop. In this station they are the whole point.

Order: **general inspection (pale, distressed, alert) → abdomen (tenderness, guarding, rebound, uterus palpable) → consent and chaperone → speculum: THE OS FIRST, then tissue or active bleeding at the os, then any lesion on the cervix or vaginal walls → bimanual: uterine size, tenderness, contractions, adnexae**.

**Tissue at the os is removed at the moment you are told about it**, with **sponge forceps**, and **sent for histopathology**. Not afterwards, not in the management summary. Candidates who describe the finding and move on to the bimanual have failed even if everything else is correct.
**Ask for repeat observations after removal.** A rise in blood pressure and a fall in pulse is your evidence that a vagal component was operating.
Bloods: **FBE, group and antibody screen and CROSS-MATCH, quantitative βhCG, coagulation screen**. Two **large-bore** cannulae. Crystalloid first; **blood if she does not respond**.
**Do not scan her first.** She is shocked with visible tissue at the os — resuscitation and removal come first, and the **ultrasound follows once she is stable**, to look for retained products.
If she does not respond to fluids: **cross-matched blood, gynaecology and anaesthetics involved, and she goes to theatre for surgical evacuation rather than waiting for imaging**.

Surgical evacuation is indicated for **continued heavy bleeding, ongoing instability, sepsis, retained tissue on scan, or her preference**. **Misoprostol** is a reasonable alternative once she is stable. VERIFY regimens.
**Anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours** — O negative, managed miscarriage. Check on-site **O negative red cell** stock before you need it.
Septic miscarriage screen: **fever, offensive discharge, tender uterus** → **blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics**, and evacuation becomes urgent.

Heavy **worsening** bleeding, tissue passed an hour ago, cramping **in waves**, pre-syncope
**Os OPEN with tissue at the os**; uterus **smaller than dates**, tender, contracting
**This is the diagnosis.** Remove the tissue now; scan once stable to confirm the uterus is empty. Urgent
Cervical shock
Hypotension **with a relative bradycardia** from tissue distending the cervical canal
Tissue at the os; pulse **lower** than the blood loss would predict
**Removal is the treatment.** Here the pulse of 110 says hypovolaemia dominates — **name both mechanisms**
**Septic miscarriage**
**Fever, offensive discharge**, tender uterus with retained tissue
**Temperature, the smell of the discharge**, uterine tenderness
**Blood cultures and IV antibiotics; evacuation becomes urgent.** Screened for and negative here. Immediate
Complete miscarriage
Tissue passed, then pain and bleeding **settled**
**Os closed**, uterus **small and contracted**
**Excluded** — her os is open and she is still bleeding heavily. Ongoing bleeding means it is not complete
Threatened miscarriage
Bleeding with the pregnancy intact
**Os closed**, uterus **exactly the size of the dates**
**Excluded** — open os, uterus smaller than dates. Routine if present
**Ectopic pregnancy**
**Constant** pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness; IUD, IVF, prior ectopic or STI
Empty uterus of normal size, **CMT positive**, adnexal tenderness
**Only a sac inside the uterus excludes it** — but tissue at the os with a contracting uterus is not an ectopic picture. Immediate if suspected
Molar pregnancy
Hyperemesis, grape-like tissue, very high βhCG
**Uterus LARGER than dates**
**Histology on the tissue you remove excludes it** — one more reason to send it. Urgent if present
Cervical or vaginal source
Post-coital bleeding, overdue screening
**Ectropion, polyp, cervicitis, lesion, laceration**
Look at the cervix and vaginal walls on every speculum — none here. Routine

stem: You are the medical officer in a country emergency department. Amy Coulthard, 25, has vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago.
tasks: Focused history
Ask for examination findings and investigations
Explain the diagnosis and your management

dx: **Pregnancy of unknown location at 6 weeks by dates** — positive pregnancy test, **empty uterus of normal size**, βhCG **900**. Uncertainty is **not a failure to diagnose — it IS the diagnosis**, and it has to be stated, justified and converted into a plan.

The four marks: **1.** say plainly you cannot separate the possibilities today · **2.** name each possibility with the finding that supports it · **3.** name the must-not-miss one explicitly · **4.** give a plan **with dates on it** that will resolve the uncertainty.

**A very early intrauterine pregnancy — the most likely.** βhCG 900 is **below** the discriminatory zone, so an empty uterus is exactly what you would expect. Her cycles run **28 to 40 days**, so she may be less far along than the dates suggest. **Nothing is against it.**

**A complete miscarriage — less likely.** For it: bleeding, pain, empty uterus, os now closed. Against it: **she has passed no tissue**, and the uterus is **normal in size rather than small and contracted**.

**An ectopic pregnancy — the one to rule out.** For it: empty uterus with a positive test, and pain. Against it: no CMT, no adnexal mass or tenderness, no free fluid — **and none of that excludes it**. Say the sentence: **treat as an ectopic until proven otherwise**.

**The corpus luteum is a distractor.** A 1.5 cm corpus luteum cyst is an **expected** finding — it maintains the pregnancy until the placenta takes over. It tells you she has **ovulated**. It does not tell you **where the pregnancy is**, and it is **never the diagnosis**.

The numbers: **urine hCG threshold 20–25 IU/L** (a negative test excludes nothing) · **transvaginal discriminatory zone 1500–2000 IU/L** · transabdominal about **6000** (rarely relevant — scan transvaginally) · **normal 48-hour rise at least about two thirds** · **sac visible from about 5 weeks** · **cardiac activity from about 6 weeks or CRL ≥ 7 mm**. VERIFY the zone your local service uses.

The plan, with dates in it: **quantitative βhCG today and again at 48 hours**. **Rises normally → rescan in a week** and you should see it. **Falls → the pregnancy has ended.** **Plateaus or rises slowly → points to the tube, and you act on it.** **Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 7–10 days**, or sooner if the βhCG crosses the zone.
**Anti-D** if she is rhesus negative and bleeds significantly or is treated — **she is O positive here**, so it does not arise. Group and antibody screen regardless. VERIFY

SA: **follow-up is the part that fails in the country.** Before she leaves, **book** the 48-hour βhCG with **SA Pathology** and confirm the collection centre's opening hours, and **book** the repeat scan rather than telling her to arrange it. Referral to the **EPAS at TQEH, RAH, FMC or the WCH** with a named appointment; **PATS** for the travel; a written red-flag sheet and **a number that is answered after hours**. Deterioration on the Yorke Peninsula is **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** or RFDS, not a two-hour drive. **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: Before you sit: **'Examiner, could I have her blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature, and is there a postural drop?'**
WIPE, confirm identity, open question. Acknowledge in one sentence, then **'was this a planned pregnancy?'** — you do not yet know whether it is wanted.

The bleeding: **is it getting worse or settling · have you passed any tissue, anything solid · any clots · how many pads · bright red or darker**. Light and dark, no tissue — and **the no-tissue answer is what weakens complete miscarriage**.
The pain: **where is it · out of ten · is it constant or does it come and go in waves**. Then **'any pain at the tip of your shoulder?'** and **'have you felt faint or dizzy?'**

**'When was your last period, and are your cycles regular?'** — 28 to 40 days. **Say out loud that this matters**: long cycles mean she may be less far along than her dates suggest, which is half the reason the uterus is empty.

The ectopic risk sweep, one at a time: **is this your first pregnancy · any previous ectopic · any miscarriage or termination · any surgery on the tubes or womb · any coil or IVF · ever been told you had a sexually transmitted infection**. Then **do you smoke** and **do you know your blood group**.

Examination and investigations together: **abdomen → 'a pelvic examination with her consent and a chaperone' → is the os open or closed → tissue or bleeding at the os, any lesion → bimanual for CMT, uterine size and whether it is empty or full, adnexae → transvaginal ultrasound → serum βhCG → blood group**.
**State the uncertainty first**: **'Amy, I have to be honest with you. The scan hasn't given us a clear answer today, and I'd rather tell you that than guess.'**

**Possibility one, and the most likely** — it is simply very early. **'Your hormone level is 900, and below about 1500 to 2000 a pregnancy can be too small for the scan to see even when it's in exactly the right place — and your cycles being long means you may be less far along than the dates suggest.'**
**Possibility two** — a complete miscarriage, **'less likely, because you haven't passed any tissue and the womb isn't small and contracted, which is what we'd usually see.'**

**Possibility three, named as the must-not-miss** — **'a pregnancy growing outside the womb, in the tube. That is the one I have to rule out, because it can become dangerous, and it's the reason I'm not simply sending you home to see what happens.'**

When she says **'can't you just tell me which one it is?'** — do **not** invent an answer: **'not today, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Giving you a wrong answer now would be worse than telling you exactly how we're going to find out.'**

The plan with dates: **a blood test today and the same blood test in 48 hours · rises by at least two thirds means normal, and we rescan in a week · a fall means the pregnancy has ended · a slow rise or a plateau points to the tube**.

Safety-net, **specific not generic**: **'come straight back, day or night, if you get severe or one-sided pain, pain at the tip of your shoulder, if you feel faint or black out, or if the bleeding becomes heavy. Do not wait for the blood test.'** Written down, with a number and a booked EPAS appointment.
pefe: Observations before you sit, including the postural drop. She is stable, which is what makes an **actively managed outpatient plan** the right answer rather than admission.

Order: **abdomen → consent and chaperone → speculum: the os first, then tissue or bleeding at the os, then lesions → bimanual: CMT, uterine size and whether the uterus is empty or full, adnexae → then the investigations**.
**Transvaginal ultrasound**, not transabdominal. Report it as: **no intrauterine sac, no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, a corpus luteum cyst, no adnexal mass**.

**Quantitative serum βhCG now and at 48 hours.** A normal early intrauterine pregnancy rises by **at least about two thirds** over 48 hours. A slow rise or plateau points to an ectopic; a fall suggests the pregnancy has ended.

**βhCG 900 is below the transvaginal discriminatory zone (1500–2000).** An empty uterus at that level is **uninformative** — it neither confirms nor excludes anything. **Above** the zone with an empty uterus is **suspicious rather than diagnostic**. The zone guides **when to image**, never the diagnosis itself.
**Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 7–10 days**, or sooner if the βhCG crosses the zone. **Book it before she leaves** rather than telling her to arrange it.

tasks: Focused history
Explain the findings and the diagnosis

dx: **A viable intrauterine pregnancy — today — with two concerning features.** A threatened miscarriage, and the pass is **'viable now, with concerns, and a scan that will tell us'**. Neither 'everything is fine' nor 'you will miscarry' is acceptable.

**Concern one — size–date discrepancy.** The sac measures **6 weeks** and she is **8 by dates**. That can mean **late ovulation with uncertain dates** — and her **35-day cycles** make that quite possible — or it can mean the pregnancy is **growing slowly**.

**Concern two — embryonic bradycardia.** At 8 weeks the embryonic heart rate should be roughly **110–160 bpm**. **About 80 is slow**, and a slow embryonic heart rate carries a **materially higher chance of subsequent loss**.

CORRECTION — **the βhCG is not the problem here.** The source suggests a βhCG of at least **10 000** is needed before cardiac activity can be seen. **There is no such rule.** Viability is judged on **measurements**, not on a hormone level — cardiac activity by about **6 weeks or a CRL of 7 mm**. **70 000 is within the normal range for 8–12 weeks.**

The honest explanation, in this order: **'there is a heartbeat, and the pregnancy is in the right place. That is genuinely good news and I don't want to take it away from you. But I'm not going to tell you everything is fine, because there are two things I'm not happy about.'**

What you will and will not promise: **'I can't tell you today which way this will go, and I'm not going to guess. Some pregnancies with these findings go on completely normally, particularly when the dates turn out to be wrong. Others don't. The only thing that will answer it is a second scan.'**
**Repeat scan in about 7–10 days**, sooner if anything changes, to **compare the growth and the heart rate**. **Book it before she leaves.**
**No serial βhCG.** Once cardiac activity has been seen, serial levels add nothing — **ultrasound is the better test**. Serial βhCG is for a pregnancy of unknown location.

**No bed rest** — no evidence it changes the outcome, and **'it just gives people something to blame themselves for afterwards'**. **No progesterone** — vaginal micronised progesterone has a role only in a woman with bleeding **and at least one previous miscarriage**, once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed. This is her first. **'Nothing you have done caused this.'**

**Lead with the good news, and mean it**: **'there is a heartbeat, and the pregnancy is in exactly the right place, inside the womb. That is genuinely good news.'** Let her have the relief.

**Then the pivot, before she settles into false reassurance**: **'I do need to be straight with you though, because there are two things I'm not completely happy about, and I'd rather you heard them from me now.'**

stem: You are the medical officer in a country emergency department. Priya Ramanathan, 28, has vaginal bleeding and has been vomiting persistently. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago.
tasks: Focused history
Ask for examination findings
Explain the most likely diagnosis

dx: **Complete molar pregnancy** — uterus **ten weeks at six weeks by dates**, vomiting **eight to ten times a day**, grape-like tissue passed, **no fetal pole and no cardiac activity** with a cavity full of small cystic spaces, βhCG markedly elevated.

**Read the uterine size before you open your mouth.** In this block it is the single finding that changes the answer most often, and the examiner **always** gives it to you if you ask. Large for dates has three answers: **molar pregnancy · multiple pregnancy · wrong dates**.

**Commit on the uterine size plus the hyperemesis** — do not wait for the grape-like tissue. She mentions it **only if asked directly about tissue**, is slightly embarrassed by it, and in the real exam often will not volunteer it at all, **which is why the uterine size has to carry the diagnosis**.

Why the two extra symptom screens mark you out: very high βhCG causes **early pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks** (otherwise almost unheard of) — hence **headaches, blurred vision, swelling of hands and face** — and **biochemical hyperthyroidism**, because **βhCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor** — hence **tremor, palpitations, feeling hot**. She reports a racing heart and blames the vomiting.

In plain words, and then stop: **'at conception something went wrong, and instead of a baby developing, the tissue that would have become the placenta has overgrown into a mass of small fluid-filled sacs. That is what you saw yesterday. I'm very sorry — there is no baby, and there was never going to be.'**

Management: **rehydrate with IV fluids and antiemetics** · bloods — **FBE, quantitative βhCG, UEC, LFTs, THYROID FUNCTION, group and antibody screen, cross-match** · **blood pressure and urinalysis** for early pre-eclampsia · **chest X-ray as a baseline**, because the lung is the commonest site of metastatic gestational trophoblastic disease.

**Suction curettage under gynaecological care — NOT medical management**, because the tissue must go to histopathology to confirm the diagnosis and to distinguish **complete from partial mole**. All tissue to histology.

**Serial βhCG surveillance until it normalises and then for a defined period afterwards**, with registration to a **gestational trophoblastic disease service**. VERIFY the surveillance duration and the current SA referral pathway. **Reliable contraception and no pregnancy until she is cleared** — a new pregnancy makes the levels uninterpretable. **Avoid an intrauterine device until the βhCG has normalised.**

The part she must understand, and the word said by you rather than read later: **'in a small number of women some of this tissue can persist, and very occasionally it can behave like a cancer. It is very treatable when it is picked up early, and that is exactly what the blood tests are for.'** Then: **most women go on to have entirely normal pregnancies afterwards.**

**Anti-D** — she is **AB negative**. A complete mole contains **no fetal rhesus D antigen** so it is arguably unnecessary, but a **partial mole does**, and histology has not come back. **Give it and discuss with the receiving unit.** VERIFY. SA: not managed in a Yorke and Northern hospital — **rehydrate and stabilise locally, then ring the on-call gynaecologist** at TQEH, RAH, FMC or the WCH; **PATS** for planned travel, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** or RFDS if she is bleeding heavily. **Someone must own the βhCG follow-up — write it into the discharge summary and the practice recall system, because surveillance is what fails in the country.** **SHINE SA** for contraception; **TIS National 131 450**.

**Quantify the vomiting — 'how many times a day are you vomiting? Are you able to keep any fluids down?'** Eight to ten times, nothing since Tuesday. **A number, not an impression.**

The bleeding: **when did it start · getting worse or settling · what colour**. Then the question that makes the diagnosis if she answers it: **'have you passed any tissue — anything solid?'** — *'it looked like little grapes. I thought I was imagining it.'* **She says this only if asked directly.**

**'Do you feel more pregnant than you would expect at six weeks — very sore breasts, very sick?'** *'Yes. My sister was never this bad and she had twins.'* **Symptoms out of proportion to the dates.**

Thyroid screen: **any tremor, palpitations, or feeling unusually hot?** She reports a racing heart and blames the vomiting. **βhCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor.**
**Last period · is this your first pregnancy · any previous miscarriage or termination · do you know your blood group.** AB negative.

**Commit**: **'Priya, I think the most likely explanation for all of this is something called a molar pregnancy.'** Then explain it in plain words, ending with **'there is no baby, and I'm afraid there was never going to be one.'** **Then stop and let her react.**

stem: Georgia Falzon, 24, six weeks by dates, has vaginal bleeding that started today, with right-sided lower abdominal pain. She still has pregnancy symptoms.
tasks: Focused history
Ask for examination findings
Explain the diagnosis and your differentials

dx: **A normal intrauterine pregnancy with separate right adnexal pathology** — not an ectopic. **The uterus is full and exactly six weeks in size, which is what you would expect if the pregnancy is in the right place. In an ectopic the uterus is empty.**

The sentence that separates you from the field, said to the examiner before anything else: **'the uterus is full and exactly six weeks in size, which is what I'd expect if the pregnancy is in the right place. In an ectopic pregnancy the uterus is empty. So my working diagnosis is a normal intrauterine pregnancy with a separate problem in the right ovary or tube.'**

Why candidates fail it: they hear **bleeding, pain, adnexal tenderness, six weeks** and say ectopic because that is the pattern they have drilled. **Read the uterine size before you open your mouth.**

The differential **in order of likelihood**: **1. haemorrhagic or ruptured ovarian cyst** — commonest, and a corpus luteum cyst is present in **every** early pregnancy · **2. ovarian torsion** — severe colicky pain with vomiting, **a surgical emergency** · **3. pelvic inflammatory disease** — but **CMT is negative**, which is against it · **4. another ovarian mass** · **5. appendicitis** — never forget it in a pregnant woman with right iliac fossa pain · **6. heterotopic pregnancy**.

**Heterotopic pregnancy is roughly 1 in 30 000 spontaneously**, so it goes **last** unless she has had assisted reproduction — after IVF it becomes a real differential rather than a curiosity. **Leading with it is showing off with a rarity, and is marked as a failure.**

You cannot **exclude** an ectopic without a scan, and you should not claim to: **'a full uterus of exactly the right size makes it much less likely, which is why the ovary is the more probable source. The scan is still mandatory.'**

What would make you think **torsion**: **severe colicky pain, vomiting, a tender adnexal mass, and pain out of proportion to the findings**. That is a **same-day surgical transfer**, not an outpatient scan — escalate immediately rather than wait.

Management: **analgesia, IV access if the pain is significant** · **FBE, quantitative βhCG, group and antibody screen**, plus **chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing** if PID is a possibility · **transvaginal ultrasound looking at the uterus AND both adnexae, with Doppler if torsion is suspected** · **gynaecology review, urgent if torsion is possible**.
**Anti-D** if rhesus negative and she bleeds significantly — **she is O positive here**, so it does not arise. Ask for the group anyway.

To her, good news first then the honest gap: **'the pregnancy appears to be in the right place. Your womb is exactly the size I'd expect at six weeks, and that makes a pregnancy in the tube much less likely.'** Then: **'what I can't explain yet is the pain and tenderness on your right side.'** Do not promise more about the baby than **'there's nothing so far to suggest a problem with the pregnancy itself'**. SA: suspected torsion is a same-day surgical transfer — **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** or RFDS; **PATS** for planned travel; **SHINE SA** for sexual health follow-up; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: Before you sit: **'Examiner, could I have her observations, including a postural drop?'**
WIPE, confirm identity, open question. She is anxious and well informed — **a friend had an ectopic and she is frightened this is the same thing**, and she will raise it early.

**'Which came first — the pain or the bleeding?'** The pain, late last night; the spotting this morning. **Pain preceding the bleeding is the ectopic pattern, which is exactly why the uterine size has to be the tie-breaker.**
The bleeding: **is it heavy · have you passed any tissue, or any clots**. Just spotting, no tissue.
The pain: **where exactly · is it constant or does it come and go · out of ten · anything make it worse**. Low right, fairly constant, five out of ten, **worse if she twists**.

**'Any nausea or vomiting with it?'** — queasy in the mornings, no vomiting. **Vomiting with severe colicky pain would push you toward torsion.** Then **'any shoulder-tip pain, or dizziness?'** — both no.

**'Are you still getting your pregnancy symptoms — sore breasts, tiredness?'** Yes, both, definitely. Then **when was your last period, and are your cycles regular** — six weeks, regular 28 days, so the dates are solid.

Risk sweep: **is this your first pregnancy · any previous ectopic, miscarriage or termination · was it conceived naturally or with IVF · any coil · any history of a sexually transmitted infection or pelvic infection**. All negative — **and the IVF answer is what keeps heterotopic at the bottom of your list**.
**'Any fever, or discharge with an unpleasant smell?'** — screening for PID. Then **'do you know your blood group?'** — O positive.
Examination: **abdomen → speculum: the os, blood or tissue, lesions → bimanual: cervical motion tenderness → THE UTERINE SIZE, and is the uterus empty or full → the adnexae**.

**Say it to the examiner the moment you have the uterine size**, before you turn to the patient: full, exactly six weeks, **so an ectopic is much less likely — in an ectopic I'd expect an empty uterus. Working diagnosis: a normal intrauterine pregnancy with separate right adnexal pathology.**

Give the differential **in order**: haemorrhagic or ruptured ovarian cyst · ovarian torsion · pelvic inflammatory disease · another ovarian mass · appendicitis · **and heterotopic pregnancy last, with the reason it is last**.

To her, **good news first**: **'the pregnancy appears to be in the right place. Your womb is exactly the size I'd expect at six weeks, and that makes a pregnancy in the tube much less likely.'** She will say her friend had one — acknowledge it.

**The honest gap**: **'what I can't explain yet is the pain and tenderness on your right side. The most likely cause is the ovary itself — a small cyst is normal in every early pregnancy, and sometimes one bleeds or bursts, which hurts. Less commonly the ovary can twist, which would need an operation, or there can be an infection.'**

The plan: **an internal ultrasound today looking at both the pregnancy and the ovary**, blood tests **including a pregnancy hormone level**, and **'I'm keeping you here until we have those.'** Refuse the go-home-and-come-back-tomorrow request.

**'Is the baby going to be all right?'** — **'there's nothing so far to suggest a problem with the pregnancy itself. I'd rather not promise you more than that until we've done the scan.'** Then escalation: **severe pain · vomiting · feeling faint · heavy bleeding — tell the nurse immediately.**
pefe: **Ask for the uterine size, and ask whether the uterus is empty or full.** It is the one finding that changes the answer, and the examiner gives it to you if you ask.

Order: **observations → abdomen (site of tenderness, guarding, rebound) → consent and chaperone → speculum: the os, blood or tissue, any lesion → bimanual: CMT first, then uterine size and whether it is empty or full, then adnexal mass or tenderness**.
**Cervical motion tenderness is negative here**, which argues against both ectopic and PID — but **CMT is not specific enough to decide anything on its own**.
**No definite adnexal mass is not reassurance.** Most ectopics are neither palpable nor visible on the first scan; here it is the **tenderness**, not a mass, that localises the problem.

**Transvaginal ultrasound is mandatory**, looking at **the uterus and BOTH adnexae**, with **Doppler if torsion is suspected**. A full uterus of the right size makes ectopic unlikely; **only a sac seen inside the uterus excludes it**.
Bloods: **FBE · quantitative βhCG · group and antibody screen**. Add **chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing** if PID is a possibility.
**Analgesia, and IV access if the pain is significant.**
**Gynaecology review — urgent if torsion is a possibility.** Suspected torsion is a **same-day surgical transfer**, not an outpatient scan.
**Do not send her home before the scan.** The go-home-and-come-back-tomorrow request is part of the station.
**Anti-D** if rhesus negative and she bleeds significantly — she is **O positive**, so it does not arise. Ask for the group anyway.

stem: Jenny, 21 years old, a primary school teacher. She has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 14. She takes insulin aspart (NovoRapid) before meals and insulin glargine (Lantus) at night.
Recorded today. BMI 24. BP 118/72. HbA1c 9.0% (75 mmol/mol), taken last week. No other medical history, no allergies, non-smoker.
Reason for attending. She and her partner are planning to start a family.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient, exploring the reasons for her poor blood sugar control
Counsel her regarding your management plan — before pregnancy, during pregnancy, at the birth, and after the birth

dx: **Poorly controlled pre-existing type 1 diabetes in a woman planning pregnancy — HbA1c 9.0% (75 mmol/mol).** The station is not a knowledge test. It is whether you can tell a young woman who wants a baby that she should **not conceive right now**, give her a number, and offer contraception — **warmly, without moralising, and without retreating when she pushes back**.

**The reason for the 9% is fixable, and finding it is the task.** Six months ago she had a **severe hypo in front of her class and an ambulance was called**; since then she deliberately takes **less Lantus** than prescribed. She also injects into **one lumpy spot on her abdomen** — **lipohypertrophy** makes absorption unpredictable and drives the dose up. She discloses neither unless you ask openly and without judgement.

**Targets: HbA1c under 7% before conception in type 1, under 6% in type 2.** VERIFY. Say the number **and the word postpone** in the first two sentences of your counselling: **'this isn't a no. It's let's do this properly.'** Then **offer reliable contraception** — a long-acting implant or device, rapidly reversible.
**Folic acid 5 mg daily** (not 500 microgram) from at least one month before conception to 12 weeks. **Iodine 150 microgram** through pregnancy and breastfeeding.

**Medication housekeeping before conception** — a whole mark on its own. **Stop ACE inhibitors and ARBs** (fetotoxic; switch to labetalol, methyldopa or nifedipine), **stop statins**, and **stop every glucose-lowering agent except insulin and metformin** — sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists all go. **Say it even though the stem lists no other drugs.** VERIFY

**During pregnancy: aspirin 100–150 mg nocte from 12–16 weeks to about 36 weeks** (pre-existing diabetes is a high-risk factor on its own) · **BGL four times daily**, targets **fasting ≤5.0–5.3, 1 h ≤7.4, 2 h ≤6.7 mmol/L** · **HbA1c every 4–6 weeks** · **insulin requirements rise steeply from about 20 weeks and roughly double by term** · **eyes each trimester**, because retinopathy progresses fast when control is tightened quickly. VERIFY

**Scans: NT 11–13+6 or NIPT · morphology 18–20 weeks · FETAL ECHOCARDIOGRAM 22–24 weeks · growth scans four-weekly from 28 weeks.** Congenital heart disease is the commonest malformation linked to peri-conception hyperglycaemia — that is why the heart gets its own scan.

**The birth: 38–39 weeks** for pre-existing or medication-treated diabetes (diet-controlled GDM can go to 40–41) · **vaginal unless the estimated weight is high; caesarean usually discussed at about 4500 g** · **a tertiary unit with obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal cover** · **hourly glucose in labour, often an insulin and dextrose infusion**. VERIFY. CORRECTION — the source's **'metamethasone' is betamethasone, 11.4 mg IM × 2, 24 hours apart**, for birth anticipated before about 35 weeks. **Give steroids and cover the hyperglycaemia — do not withhold them.**

**After the birth — explicitly in the task. Her insulin need drops the moment the placenta is out** — cut back to roughly the pre-pregnancy dose immediately, and breastfeeding lowers it further. **The baby's glucose is checked in the first hours and he is fed early**; watch for hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress, jaundice, polycythaemia and hypocalcaemia. **Encourage breastfeeding.** Antenatal colostrum expression from 36 weeks reduces formula supplementation. Then contraception, and pre-conception care again before the next one.

Two answers she will ask for: **'will he be born with diabetes?' — no; a small increase in lifetime risk, but he is not born with it.** **'Will he be taken away?' — usually not; most babies stay with their mother and are simply monitored, and early feeding is what keeps them together.** SA: high-risk clinic at the **WCH, FMC or Lyell McEwin**, endocrinology and educator by telehealth through **Country Health Connect**; birth planned in a metropolitan unit **early, not at 37 weeks**; **PATS** offered, not waited for; **NDSS registration** for subsidised strips; **Closing the Gap PBS**; **SHINE SA** for contraception; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for ketoacidosis or preterm labour; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: WIPE, sit at an angle. **'Can I just say — coming in to talk about this before you fall pregnant is exactly the right thing to do, and it genuinely makes a difference. Tell me what's been on your mind.'** **Do not open with the HbA1c** — if your first sentence is the number, she becomes a problem rather than a person and she will not tell you about the hypoglycaemia she is hiding.

Diabetes history, blocks 1, 2 and 4, fast: **when were you first told you had diabetes · what are you taking, which insulins and what doses · do you see a specialist as well as your GP · when was your last HbA1c and do you know the number**. Let her tell you the 9% herself.

**Block 3 — the stated task.** Ask all four, gently, one at a time: **'are there days you miss a dose, or is it pretty consistent?' · 'have you ever had your sugar drop too low? Tell me about that.' · 'has anyone gone through the injection technique with you — where you inject, and moving the sites around?' · 'is there anything that gets in the way — cost, work, remembering, or just being sick of it?'**

**When the hypo comes out, respond to the disclosure before moving on**: **'that sounds genuinely awful, and it makes complete sense that you'd want to avoid it. Running high is a really understandable response — and it's something we can fix properly rather than just asking you to try harder.'**

Complications and safety: **any blurring of vision, when were your eyes last checked · any numbness, burning or pins and needles in your feet · any chest pain or breathlessness · any kidney problems or protein in your urine · when your sugar drops, do you get warning symptoms · do you have ketone strips at home**. **Do not accept 'all fine' as a screen** — say aloud that none of it has been formally checked.

The antenatal sweep, **60 seconds, no more**: **last period and cycles · ever been pregnant · stable relationship and supportive partner · cervical screening up to date · any other medical problems · ANY OTHER MEDICINES OR SUPPLEMENTS AT ALL, INCLUDING OVER THE COUNTER · family history of diabetes or high blood pressure · talk me through a normal day's eating · any exercise · how has your mood been**.
**Summarise back, then signpost the four parts** — before pregnancy, during, the birth, afterwards. Twenty seconds that buy you the whole counselling block.

**Frame the risk before you list it**: diabetes does increase the risks, **but control before conception brings most of it back down**. If she asks for the list, keep it to **two lines for her and three for the baby**, then return immediately to what control achieves. **Do not recite the complication avalanche.**

**The discriminating issue, almost word for word**: **'your HbA1c is nine and I want it under seven before you conceive. The baby's organs form in the first few weeks, often before you even know you're pregnant, so the control has to already be right. This isn't a no. It's let's do this properly.'** Then **offer contraception** — an implant or device, removable the moment she is ready.

**Hold the line when she pushes back** (her sister is due in June): **'I really do understand, and I'm not trying to take this away from you. But fixing it afterwards doesn't work, because the important weeks have already happened. Let's review in four weeks and look at the numbers together.'**

The rest of 'before': **fix what you found** — educator for technique and site rotation, a plan to come down safely without hypos, consider premixed, a pump or CGM · **screen for complications** — dilated retinal exam, eGFR and urine ACR, feet, thyroid · **folic acid 5 mg and iodine 150 microgram today** · **the routine pre-pregnancy screen today**, and vaccinate for rubella now if not immune.

**During pregnancy, six items at pace**: the **team** (obstetrician, endocrinologist, **diabetes educator**, dietitian, midwife, GP) · **four-times-daily monitoring and HbA1c every 4–6 weeks** · **insulin needs rising** · **aspirin from 12 weeks** · **the extra scans including the heart scan at 22–24 weeks** · **eyes each trimester**. Plus everything routine — no smoking, no alcohol, vaccinations, weight, dental, mood.

**The birth**: not past the due date, **38–39 weeks**, aiming for a normal birth; a planned caesarean discussed if the baby is very big; **a bigger Adelaide hospital with a special care nursery**, with **PATS** for travel; **hourly sugars in labour, usually an insulin drip**. **Do not promise a normal vaginal birth or a local birth.**

**After the birth, three things**: **her insulin drops sharply the moment the baby is born** — cut the dose straight away; **the baby's sugar is checked in the first hours and he is fed early**, with breathing and jaundice watched; **encourage breastfeeding** — it helps his sugars and lowers both their later diabetes risk. Then contraception, and come back before the next pregnancy.

Close: **written information · refer today to the diabetes educator, dietitian and high-risk clinic · review in four weeks**. Safety-net: **vomiting and unable to keep fluids down · ketones up · a severe low that someone else had to help with**. Then the teach-back — **'what will you tell Sam when you get home?'**
pefe: **No examination task and no results card** — BMI 24, BP 118/72 and HbA1c 9.0% are given in the stem. The work is in the history and the counselling, and the investigations are what you **arrange**, not what you are handed.
**Bedside today: blood pressure, weight and BMI, urine dipstick for protein and ketones.** Then a **repeat HbA1c**.

**Complication screen, and say out loud that none of it has been done**: **dilated retinal examination** by optometrist or ophthalmologist · **eGFR, electrolytes and urine albumin–creatinine ratio** · **foot and neuropathy assessment** · **thyroid function** (autoimmune conditions cluster) · **ECG if any cardiac symptoms** · **lipids**, pre-conception only.

**Routine pre-pregnancy and antenatal screen today**: **FBE, ferritin, blood group and antibodies, rubella and varicella IgG, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and C, urine MCS, cervical screening if due.** **Vaccinate for rubella now if she is not immune — it cannot be given once she is pregnant.**
**Once pregnant, imaging**: dating scan · **NT 11–13+6 or NIPT** · **morphology 18–20 weeks** · **fetal echocardiogram 22–24 weeks** · **growth scans four-weekly from 28 weeks**.
**HbA1c every 4–6 weeks in pregnancy.** It falls physiologically — a pre-pregnancy 7% is roughly a first-trimester 6.5%. **It is a trend tool, not a diagnostic one** in pregnancy. VERIFY
**Home glucose four times daily** — fasting plus one or two hours after each meal. **Register with the NDSS** for subsidised strips.

**Treatment ladder when the barrier is the injections themselves**, worked down in order rather than jumping to a new drug: **review technique and sites** → **premixed insulin twice daily** → **insulin pump** → **continuous glucose monitoring**; **metformin** as a tablet option alongside insulin. VERIFY

**Ketones and a sick-day plan.** **Diabetic ketoacidosis in pregnancy can occur at near-normal glucose** (euglycaemic DKA) and carries a high rate of fetal loss. **Vomiting plus diabetes means ketone testing, whatever the glucose reads** — it is not gastroenteritis and it is not morning sickness.
**Not useful**: the glucose challenge test, no longer used in Australia; **HbA1c to diagnose gestational diabetes**.
ddx: **Fear of hypoglycaemia after a severe event**
Deliberately taking **less basal insulin**; a humiliating public hypo six months ago with an ambulance called
**'Have you ever had your sugar drop too low? Tell me about that.' · 'What made you start doing that?'**
**This is the answer here.** Educator review, a plan to come down safely without hypos, CGM. Validate before you problem-solve
**Lipohypertrophy from not rotating sites**
Injecting into **one spot**, a lumpy area, erratic absorption driving the dose up
**'Has anyone watched your technique — where you inject and rotating the sites?'**
**Also present here.** Diabetes educator to review technique and rotate sites
Needle fatigue and regimen burden
**'I'm sick of four injections a day'**; skipped doses without a specific trigger
**'Is there anything that gets in the way — cost, work, remembering, or just being sick of it?'**
**Offer real alternatives, never abandon the target**: premixed twice daily, a pump, CGM, metformin alongside insulin
Loss of hypoglycaemia awareness
No warning symptoms before a low; **worsens in the first trimester**
**'When your sugar drops, do you get warning symptoms?'**
CGM, temporarily relaxed targets, specialist referral. **A driving risk — ask about it**
Erratic eating and shift patterns
Skipped breakfast, eating at school, takeaway several nights
**'Talk me through a normal day's eating.'** Diet is **clinical** history here, asked early, not social history asked last
Dietitian; regular carbohydrate distribution across three meals and two to three snacks
Cost, access, refrigeration and distance
Rural, insulin storage, strip cost, distance to clinic
Ask directly — **these are clinical facts, not background**
**NDSS registration**, **Closing the Gap PBS** co-payment, **PATS** for repeated metropolitan appointments
Depression or diabetes distress
Low mood, disengagement, missed appointments, 'sick of it'
**'How has your mood been?'**
Mental health assessment; psychology; treating this often fixes the glucose
Infrequent specialist follow-up
**Annual video review only**; eyes last checked two years ago; no formal complication screening
**'Do you see your specialist and your GP regularly?'**
Endocrinologist, diabetes educator, dietitian; complete the complication screen now
Intercurrent illness or drug effect
**Corticosteroids**, some antipsychotics, tacrolimus, beta-agonists; infection or hyperemesis at the time of testing
The **full** medication list including a recent steroid course
Timing of the rise against the drug; recheck when well. **Do not use it to explain away a clear result**

stem: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, 12 weeks pregnant, has come to discuss her antenatal screening results. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated so far.
Recorded today. BP 112/70. Weight 82 kg, height 1.62 m, BMI 31. Urine dipstick negative.

Results available to you: Full blood examination normal. Blood group / antibody screen A positive / negative. Urine MCS no growth. Rubella IgG positive (immune). Syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and C negative. Chlamydia PCR negative. 75 g OGTT — fasting 5.6 mmol/L (reference <5.1); 1 hour 7.8 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 6.9 mmol/L (<8.5).
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
(Harder reported version adds) Outline your management plan

dx: **Gestational diabetes, diagnosed early, on an isolated raised fasting glucose of 5.6 mmol/L.** One- and two-hour values are normal. **One value above the line is enough** — you do not need two.

**The two questions that win the station.** A 12-week OGTT is **not routine**, so something prompted it — **previous gestational diabetes with Jack, diet-controlled, and a 4.1 kg baby**. And **the postpartum test was never done**, so her glucose has not been rechecked in two years.

**Say the uncertainty out loud — it is a distinction mark and it is honest**: **'because that follow-up test was never done, I can't be certain whether this is the pregnancy diabetes coming back, or whether your sugar has been running high since then. Either way today's plan is the same, and we'll sort out which it is with a test after the baby is born.'**

**Diagnostic thresholds: 75 g OGTT fasting ≥5.1 · 1 h ≥10.0 · 2 h ≥8.5 mmol/L — any one value.** CORRECTION — the **5.5 and 8.0** figures still taught are the **historical pre-2014 Australian criteria**. Current use is **ADIPS 2014**, adopted by RANZCOG. If challenged: **'I've quoted 5.1, 10.0 and 8.5, which is what my laboratory reports against, and I'd follow the reference range printed on the report in front of me.'** VERIFY

**Overt diabetes in pregnancy is a different box: fasting ≥7.0, random or 2 h ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%.** That is almost always **undiagnosed type 2**, is managed like pre-existing disease, and **does** carry the malformation counselling, complication screen, aspirin and fetal echo. **Classify her before you manage her.**

CORRECTION — **screening is at 24–28 weeks, not 26–28**; at the **first visit** if there is previous gestational diabetes, obesity, strong family history or a higher-risk background, **repeated at 24–28 weeks if the early test is normal**. **The glucose challenge test is no longer used in Australia**, and **HbA1c does not diagnose gestational diabetes** — red cell turnover and haemodilution make it unreliable.

**What it does NOT mean, and this is the commonest communication fail**: gestational diabetes **does not cause birth defects**. Hyperglycaemia develops in the second half of pregnancy, **after organogenesis**. **What it affects is growth** — a bigger baby, a harder birth, and neonatal hypoglycaemia for a day or two. Both are prevented by keeping levels in range.

**It is not her fault and not what she ate**: the placenta makes hormones that block her own insulin. She has **three risk factors** — previous GDM, a first-degree family history, and **BMI 31** — which is exactly why the early test was reasonable.

**Management: lifestyle first, not medication.** Dietitian for **timing and type of carbohydrate rather than cutting things out** · moderate activity about **30 minutes most days** · a meter and a **diabetes educator** · **four readings a day — fasting and after each meal**. Targets **fasting ≤5.0–5.3, 1 h ≤7.4, 2 h ≤6.7 mmol/L**. VERIFY. **Review in 1–2 weeks**; if targets are missed, **insulin is first line, metformin an accepted alternative or addition**. **Roughly one in four to one in three eventually need medication — say so now, so it doesn't feel like a failure later.** Register with the **NDSS** for subsidised strips.

**Birth and afterwards: diet-controlled with normal growth can go to 40–41 weeks; on medication or with macrosomia, 38–39 weeks.** Caesarean discussed at an estimated weight of about **4500 g**. **75 g OGTT at 6–12 weeks postpartum — booked before she leaves hospital this time** — then **HbA1c or fasting glucose every 1–3 years for life**, and an **OGTT at the first visit of the next pregnancy**. **Recurrence 30–70%; lifetime type 2 risk roughly 50%.** VERIFY. SA: diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic at the **WCH, FMC or Lyell McEwin**, endocrinology and educator by telehealth through **Country Health Connect**; **PATS** for metropolitan appointments; **SA Pathology** — tell her she must fast and **stay the full two hours** or she will not complete it; **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: WIPE, results held **but not shown yet**. **'I've got your pregnancy blood tests here and we'll go through them all together. First though — congratulations. Was this a planned pregnancy, and how have you been feeling in yourself?'** **Do not lead with the abnormal result.**

If she asks whether something is wrong, **park it honestly**: **'there is one result I do want to talk about, and I'll come to it properly in a moment — it is manageable and I'll explain it fully. First, can I ask you a few questions?'**

This pregnancy, 45 seconds: **when was your last normal period, are your cycles regular · how many weeks does that make you · any bleeding, pain or vomiting · are you keeping food and fluids down · have you started any pregnancy vitamins**.

**The previous pregnancy — the block that decides the station. Five questions, one at a time, do not batch them**: **'you've been pregnant before — tell me about that pregnancy' · 'were there any problems during it, high blood pressure or high blood sugar?' · 'had you ever had high blood sugar BEFORE that pregnancy?' · 'what treatment did they give you for it?' · 'how was the birth — a long labour, a big baby, any problems?'**

**The two questions that win it**: **'can I ask — do you know why they arranged the sugar test this early? Normally we do it at around six months.'** and **'after Jack was born, did anyone arrange a repeat sugar test for you, about six weeks afterwards?'** When she says no: **'it's very commonly missed — you're not the first. We'll make sure it happens this time.'**

The rest of the history, fast but not skipped: **any excessive thirst, passing more urine, or thrush · any other medical problems, blood pressure, thyroid, polycystic ovaries · any medicines including over the counter or herbal · allergies · anyone in the family with diabetes · cervical screening up to date · talk me through a normal day's eating and any activity · smoking, alcohol, anything else · partner supportive, how's your mood · do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander**.

**Summarise back and signpost.** You have now collected two things without noticing — a **first-degree family history of type 2** and a **BMI of 31**. Both belong in the summary, and both are why the early test was reasonable regardless of the previous GDM.

**Ask before you tell, and give the good news first**: **'what do you already know about the tests we do at this stage?'** Then: blood count, blood group, urine, **rubella immune**, infection screen all clear — **'there is one result I do need to talk about, and it's the sugar test.'**

**Explain the test, then the number, then the name, in that order**: fasting, then a sugary drink, then one and two hours. **'Your one-hour and two-hour readings were both normal. Your fasting reading was 5.6, and in pregnancy we want it under 5.1. That one reading on its own is enough to make the diagnosis.'**

Answer **'it's only a little bit over'**: **'you're right, and that's actually good news — it should be easier to control. But the cut-offs in pregnancy are deliberately tighter, because even small rises affect the baby's growth.'**

**What it means, and what it does not.** The placenta makes hormones that block her insulin — **not what she ate, not her fault**. Three risk factors, all present. **'It does not mean your baby will be born with anything wrong. The baby's organs formed in the first few weeks, before any of this.'** What it **does** affect: **growth, and low sugars for a day or two after birth**.

**The two forward statements.** It usually settles after the birth — **but we prove that with a repeat test at six to twelve weeks, the one that got missed last time**. And having had it raises her lifetime type 2 risk, so **a sugar check every one to three years from now on** — **'that's not a threat, it's the thing that lets us catch it early.'**

**Management, if the third task is present**: **food, activity and measuring — not medication** · dietitian, educator, meter, **four readings a day** · the **team** and the diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic · **extra growth scans** later on and blood pressure at every visit · **if readings stay high, insulin first line, metformin an alternative — and that is not a failure, it happens to a quarter to a third of women**.

Safety-net: **very thirsty or passing lots of urine · any bleeding or severe abdominal pain · headache with visual disturbance or sudden swelling · reduced fetal movements later on**. Review in **one to two weeks with her glucose diary**. **Book the postpartum test now.** Then the teach-back — **'what will you tell Dan when you get home?'**
pefe: **No examination task.** BP 112/70, BMI 31 and a negative dipstick are given, and the full screening panel is already on the results sheet. The work is the history and the explanation — but **know what each result was for**.

**Read the panel and say what is normal before you say what is not**: FBE normal · blood group **A positive, antibody screen negative** · urine MCS no growth · **rubella IgG positive, so she is immune** · syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and C negative · chlamydia PCR negative.
**The 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.6 (≥5.1 is diagnostic) · 1 hour 7.8 (normal) · 2 hour 6.9 (normal).** **One abnormal value is enough.** The abnormality is in the **fasting** line.

**Check she does not meet overt-diabetes criteria** — fasting ≥7.0, random or 2 h ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%. She does not. **Classification comes before management**, because the overt box brings malformation counselling, a complication screen, aspirin and a fetal echo that this box does not.

**Home glucose monitoring four times daily** — fasting plus one or two hours after each meal — with a meter and **diabetes educator** teaching. Targets **fasting ≤5.0–5.3, 1 h ≤7.4, 2 h ≤6.7 mmol/L**. VERIFY. **NDSS registration** for subsidised strips.

**Review after one to two weeks of lifestyle measures.** If readings stay above target, **escalate — do not give diet another month**. **Insulin is first-line pharmacological treatment**; **metformin** is an accepted alternative or addition, crosses the placenta, and many women still need insulin added. VERIFY
**Extra growth scans in the last few months** on top of the routine **morphology scan at 18–20 weeks**. **Blood pressure at every visit** — the risk of pre-eclampsia is higher.
**No fetal echocardiogram and no aspirin for straightforward gestational diabetes** — those belong to pre-existing and overt diabetes. Adding them here is as much an error as omitting them there.

**75 g OGTT at 6–12 weeks postpartum** — **book it before she leaves hospital**, because it is the single most commonly forgotten item in gestational diabetes and it is the one that was missed last time. Then **HbA1c or fasting glucose every 1–3 years for life**, and an **OGTT at the first visit of the next pregnancy**.

**Not used**: the glucose challenge test, and **HbA1c to diagnose gestational diabetes**. If the examiner asks why not HbA1c: **red cell turnover and haemodilution make it unreliable in pregnancy — but ≥6.5% early indicates overt diabetes.**
