stem: James Doherty, a 66-year-old man, presents complaining of nervousness.
Background. He is a known case of atrial fibrillation. He was taking flecainide; his cardiologist changed him to amiodarone four weeks ago. He has come today for his blood test results.
Results handed to you in the room: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (normal, 0.4–4.0) · Free T4 28 pmol/L (high, 10–20) · Free T3 8.9 pmol/L (high, 3.5–6.5).
tasks: Take a focused history
Interpret the investigation results for the patient
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses

dx: **Thyrotoxicosis with inappropriate (non-suppressed) TSH secretion** — lead with a **TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma**, amiodarone second. Two diagnoses, each with its reason.
His numbers: **TSH 1.8 mIU/L (normal 0.4–4.0) · free T4 28 pmol/L (high 10–20) · free T3 8.9 pmol/L (high 3.5–6.5)**. VERIFY ranges against the printed report, not from memory.

Thyrotoxicosis = raised circulating hormone whatever the source; hyperthyroidism = the gland itself overproducing. **Both are normally accompanied by a suppressed TSH.** The single exception is secondary (pituitary) disease.
The five causes of a **normal TSH with a high free T4**: **assay artefact including biotin · sampling error · amiodarone in its late phase · TSH-secreting adenoma · thyroid hormone resistance**.

Why the adenoma leads: it is the only cause that reliably produces a **non-suppressed TSH with a raised free T4**. And **four weeks is early** — amiodarone thyrotoxicosis usually develops after months.

CORRECTION — amiodarone is a sequence, not an event: **hyper → hypo → normal**, over months. Transcripts mis-state the third phase as a second hyperthyroid one. **Type 1** = iodine-induced synthesis in an abnormal gland; **type 2** = destructive thyroiditis leaking stored hormone; **colour-flow Doppler separates them**. Thionamide for type 1, corticosteroid for type 2. VERIFY

Four rungs to the patient, then stop: **the gland in the neck makes hormones → yours are high → a second hormone, TSH, made in the brain, controls it → normally TSH should come down, and yours has not**. No axis, no arrows, never the words **brain tumour**.
**'Please do not stop the amiodarone — I will speak to your cardiologist myself.'** It is holding his rhythm, and the half-life runs to **weeks or months**, so stopping is slow to help anyway. VERIFY

No carbimazole today: in an adenoma a thionamide lowers T4 and **drives the TSH higher** without treating the cause; in type 2 the gland is not overproducing at all. **Check cortisol before any thyroid-directed treatment** in pituitary disease.

SA — SA Pathology locally; ask the laboratory about **repeating on an alternative platform** and biotin interference before imaging. Endocrinology and neurosurgery via **Country Health Connect** to **RAH / FMC / TQEH**; MRI and formal perimetry need transfer, subsidised through **PATS**. Storm or instability: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**. **TIS National 131 450** · **healthdirect 1800 022 222**.
plan: WIPE, confirm name and date of birth, **results face down**. **'I do have your blood results and we will go through them together — but first I would like to understand what has been happening.'**

Block 1, explore the complaint: **what do you mean by feeling nervous — stressed and on edge, shaking in your hands, or your heart racing? · how long · constant or comes and goes · is it getting worse · anything that makes it better or worse · how is it affecting your day-to-day life?**

Block 2, the AF anchor: **how long have you had the irregular heartbeat · are you taking the amiodarone regularly, exactly as prescribed · why was the flecainide changed · any side effects since you started · are you having regular follow-up?** The switch is scored — flecainide stops when rhythm control fails or structural or ischaemic disease emerges, so his answer tells you how sick his heart is.

Block 3, AF complications: **are you still getting racing of the heart · any chest pain · short of breath on exertion, ankle swelling, waking at night · any weakness or numbness down one side, trouble speaking, or brief loss of vision · are you on a blood thinner?** TIA questions, not stroke questions — he is sitting in front of you talking.

Block 4, the two tracks. Thyroid: **can you not stand the heat · looser or more frequent bowel motions · any weight loss · do you sweat a lot · any shaking of your hands.** Pituitary: **do you get headaches · any blurred vision or difficulty seeing to the sides · any weakness or numbness anywhere.**

If he asks why you are asking about his head: **'one of the glands that controls the thyroid sits in the brain, and if there is a problem there it can press on the nerves to the eyes. It takes ten seconds to ask and it changes what I do next.'**

Block 5, psychiatry and stimulants — **the block that fails people**: **how has your mood been · how has your sleep been · I ask everybody this, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else · who is at home, any stresses · how much tea or coffee · how much alcohol · any other substances or cold and flu tablets · do you take any supplements, particularly biotin?**

Task 2, the results in **four rungs** and no more, then **'does that make sense so far?'** If he says 'so is it overactive or not' — **the hormones are too high, but the controller in your brain has not responded the way it should, and that is the unusual part.**

Task 3, **two diagnoses in order, each with its reason** — the adenoma first because it explains the pattern, amiodarone second with the honest caveat that it would usually give a **low** TSH. Then the rest of the list: assay artefact, anxiety or panic, phaeochromocytoma, stimulants, and the other thyroid causes that all give a low TSH.

The three answers he will demand. **'Is it cancer?'** — usually benign, treatable, not what worries me today. **'Should I stop the tablet?'** — please don't, I will speak to your cardiologist. **'What happens now?'** — repeat the blood test first.

Plan and safety net: **repeat assay on a different platform · cortisol and a full pituitary profile · formal visual fields · pituitary MRI · ECG · endocrinology referral**. Come back or go to hospital for **a bad headache, any change in vision, chest pain, breathlessness at rest, or feeling feverish and confused**. Offer to phone with the repeat result yourself.
pefe: Given in the room, not requested: **TSH 1.8 mIU/L normal · free T4 28 pmol/L high · free T3 8.9 pmol/L high**. Read the TSH first — **TSH tells you which way, free T4 tells you how far**.
Bedside: **confrontation visual fields**, pulse for rate and rhythm, tremor, sweating, goitre and its tenderness, eye signs.

**First investigation is a repeat TSH and free T4 on a different assay platform** — having asked about high-dose **biotin**. Not the MRI. Discordant results are commonly artefactual, and it is cheaper and faster than imaging.
Then **TSH alpha subunit and its molar ratio · SHBG · full pituitary profile including cortisol · formal perimetry · pituitary MRI**.
**ECG** for rate and rhythm; echocardiogram if the flecainide switch suggests structural or ischaemic disease.
If the TSH were low instead: **colour-flow Doppler** to separate type 1 from type 2, **TPO and TSH-receptor antibodies**, radionuclide uptake scan.
Episodic palpitations with headache and sweating: **plasma or 24-hour urinary metanephrines**.
Amiodarone monitoring worth naming: **TFTs · LFTs · chest X-ray and lung function for new cough or breathlessness · eyes · skin**. VERIFY intervals against Therapeutic Guidelines.
ddx: **TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma**
**Normal or raised TSH with a high free T4** — the only cause that truly explains this pattern
Headache, blurred vision, **bitemporal field loss**, other pituitary failure
Repeat TFTs; **alpha subunit and molar ratio**; SHBG; full pituitary profile; formal fields; **pituitary MRI** — urgent
**Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis**
The drug is in the stem; iodine load and direct thyrocyte toxicity. **Four weeks is early**
Duration of therapy, prior thyroid disease, goitre, tenderness
**Colour-flow Doppler** separates type 1 from type 2; TPO antibodies; **do not stop the drug without cardiology**
Assay interference or sampling error
An implausible combination of results in a patient who looks well
**Biotin supplements**, heterophile antibodies, blood taken soon after a levothyroxine dose
**Repeat on a different assay platform** — the cheapest step, and the first
Thyroid hormone resistance
High hormones with **few thyrotoxic symptoms**; family history; goitre
Family history, goitre, symptom–biochemistry mismatch
Alpha subunit ratio, TRH testing, THRB genetic testing — specialist
Graves · toxic adenoma · toxic multinodular goitre
All produce thyrotoxicosis — but **all give a low TSH**
Eye signs, diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, single or lumpy nodules
TSH-receptor antibodies; radionuclide uptake scan
Thyroiditis · exogenous thyroxine
Painful neck after a viral illness; or thyroxine taken for weight loss
Tender gland; impalpable gland with no eye signs
ESR and CRP; low uptake; **low thyroglobulin** in exogenous intake
Phaeochromocytoma
Nervousness, palpitations, sweating and AF in one patient
**Episodic** headache with palpitations and sweating; labile hypertension
**Plasma or 24-hour urinary metanephrines**
Anxiety · panic · adjustment disorder
Situational triggers, worry, poor sleep, recent stressor
Mood, sleep, stressors, **risk**; place, person or situation
Clinical assessment — but a **diagnosis of exclusion** while the T4 is high
Stimulants — caffeine, alcohol, decongestants
Heavy tea or coffee, binge drinking, pseudoephedrine
Quantify intake; over-the-counter cold and flu preparations
History; trial of withdrawal
Poorly controlled AF itself
Palpitations reported as 'nervousness'
Rate, exertional breathlessness, chest pain
ECG, examination, echocardiogram
Malignancy or chronic infection
Weight loss with sweats but a plausible alternative explanation
Night sweats, anorexia, lumps, cough
Directed by history; FBE, ESR, imaging

FAIL — One diagnosis. Two, in order, each with its reason.
FAIL — No psychiatric screen. Mood, sleep, and the risk question.
FAIL — Stopping the amiodarone yourself. Speak to the cardiologist.
ASK — What do you mean by nervous: on edge, shaking, or racing heart?
ASK — Headaches? Trouble seeing to the sides? That earns the adenoma.

stem: You are a GP. Jenny Alderton, 37, has come in with palpitations and dizziness for three days.
(Version A — shorter stem.)
tasks: Take a focused history (4–5 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient

dx: **Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response**, and in this version **secondary to ischaemic heart disease**. Every recall hands you a cause — a label with no cause is a listed fail.

AF is disorganised atrial electrical activity replacing coordinated contraction: **an irregularly irregular ventricular response and loss of the P wave**. Atrial flutter is managed identically, so an uncertain read does not change the answer.

To the patient: **'your heart is beating irregularly because the electrical signals that normally set a steady rhythm have become disorganised — the top chambers quiver instead of squeezing properly, and that is the fluttering you feel.'**

The cause here: **exertional chest tightness and breathlessness for a few months, settling within a minute of stopping**. Contributing — **four to five coffees a day, two to three wines most nights, ten cigarettes a day**; father had an MI in his fifties.

Differentials are delivered **as causes**, by system: thyrotoxicosis, hypertension, valvular disease, pericarditis or myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, electrolytes, anaemia — then close the palpitations list with **SVT, VT, ectopics, panic disorder, hypoglycaemia**.

**CHA₂DS₂-VA** — Australia omits the sex category: **C 1 · H 1 · A₂ age ≥75 = 2 · D 1 · S₂ prior stroke or TIA = 2 · V vascular disease 1 · A age 65–74 = 1**. **0 none · 1 consider · ≥2 anticoagulate.** She is **37 with none of these, so her score is 0 and she gets no anticoagulant today** — reassess when the results return.
Duration: **three days, continuous — beyond 48 hours**. **Unknown duration counts as beyond it too.**

Rate control first: **metoprolol 25–50 mg BD** or bisoprolol. **Diltiazem and verapamil are contraindicated in reduced ejection fraction**, and **AV nodal blockers are dangerous in pre-excited AF**. VERIFY

ECG numbers: **one large square 0.2 s · 10 seconds = 50 large squares · QRS count × 6 · normal QRS under 3 small squares (<120 ms)**. ST elevation **≥1 mm in two contiguous leads**; V2–V3 **≥2 mm men ≥40, ≥2.5 mm men <40, ≥1.5 mm women**. **Paroxysmal = self-terminating, usually within 7 days; persistent = beyond 7 days** — a separate box from the 48-hour rule.

SA — in MM5 the **echo and cardioversion need transfer**: **PATS**, cardiology telehealth in the interim, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if she destabilises. **Quitline 13 7848** · ambulance **000** · opportunistic AF screening **from age 65** · Closing the Gap PBS co-payment where eligible.
plan: To the examiner before you touch anything: **'could I please have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation?'** Then name it back — **tachycardic with an irregular pulse, but haemodynamically stable**.

WIPE, name, open question, empathy line. **'Tell me more about what's been happening.'** … **'I'm sorry you've been feeling like this. I'll do my best to work out what's causing it and help you today.'**

Characterise the palpitations: **can you tap out on the desk what the beat feels like · did it come on suddenly or build up · has it been there constantly for the three days or does it come and go · does anything set it off — coffee, alcohol, exercise, stress?** Irregular tapping is close to diagnostic.

Associated symptoms and stability: **with the palpitations do you get chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, or feel like you might black out · and the dizziness — is it a spinning feeling or more like you're about to faint · have you actually fainted?** Dizziness gets **one clarifying question, not its own structure**.

Cause sweep, fast, by system. CVS: **that chest tightness on the hill, how long has it been happening · breathless lying flat, waking at night, ankle swelling · ever been told you have a murmur, high blood pressure, or a heart problem.** RS: **cough, fever, sharp pain on breathing, calf swelling, long travel · do you snore or feel sleepy in the day.** Endocrine: **weight loss, feeling hot when others don't, tremor, loose bowels, a lump in the neck.**

SADMA and family: **how much coffee · how much alcohol · do you smoke · any other drugs · any other medical problems, medications, allergies · any heart problems in the family?** The examiner is scoring the sweep, not the guess.
**'Thank you Jenny. Examiner, may I now interpret the ECG?'** Seven steps in order, about 30 seconds, no pauses — and the **rate bypass line first**, then rhythm, which hands you the diagnosis.

Hold the read at essential level and commit. If challenged on V2–V3: **up-sloping, the trace ramping into the T wave at a fast rate, not a horizontal or convex injury pattern** — and the thresholds there are age- and sex-dependent.

Diagnosis in plain words, then **the cause named out loud**: **'I'm concerned this may relate to narrowing of the arteries supplying your heart, because of the chest tightness and breathlessness you get walking uphill. The caffeine, alcohol and smoking are contributing as well.'** Then **'does that make sense?'**

The rest of the differentials, **given as causes**: an overactive thyroid, high blood pressure, a valve problem, inflammation around the heart, a clot on the lung — and rarely a hormone-producing tumour; plus anxiety, low blood sugar and anaemia.

Safety net and close: **chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, or weakness or drooping on one side of the face or body → call an ambulance on triple zero**. Summarise, then invite questions — if her concerns were never elicited she will ask **'is this what my dad had?'**
pefe: Ask the examiner for **vital signs before you begin** — the irregular pulse is named before you ever touch the ECG.
**12-lead ECG**, read in **seven steps: rate → rhythm → P waves → PR → QRS → ST → T**, then commit to an impression.

**The bypass line, verbatim**: **'as the rhythm is irregular, the correct method is to count the QRS complexes across a 10-second strip and multiply by six. Rather than count fifty large squares now, may I proceed and return to the exact rate?'**
If you name only two investigations, name these: **TSH and echocardiogram**. TSH is mandatory in every new AF.
The echo answers three management questions at once: **ejection fraction (which drugs are safe), valve status (warfarin or a DOAC), and structural disease**.
**A transthoracic echo cannot reliably exclude left atrial appendage thrombus** — early cardioversion needs a **transoesophageal echo**.

Also: **FBC · EUC and creatinine · LFT · coagulation profile · magnesium · fasting glucose or HbA1c · lipids · CXR**. **Troponin only if there are ischaemic symptoms.** Holter or extended monitoring if paroxysmal.
Stress testing and a BP series where ischaemic heart disease or hypertension is the suspected cause.

dx: **Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response**, **secondary to untreated hypertension** with caffeine, alcohol and smoking adding to it. **Management is the predominant assessment area — brevity fails this station.**
Say the cause back to her: **'high blood pressure over years stretches the heart and makes this rhythm much more likely, and the coffee and alcohol are adding to it.'**

**Pillar 1 — find and treat the cause.** If you name only two investigations, name **TSH and echocardiogram**. The echo answers three questions at once: **pumping strength, valve status, and whether there is clot inside**.

Alongside it, because **AF is itself cardiovascular disease**: cut back the **coffee and alcohol**, **stop smoking — Quitline 13 7848**, diet, exercise, and treat the **blood pressure, sugar and sleep apnoea** if present.

**Pillar 2 — stroke risk. Name the score.** **CHA₂DS₂-VA**, the Australian version with the sex category removed: **C 1 · H 1 · A₂ age ≥75 = 2 · D 1 · S₂ prior stroke or TIA = 2 · V 1 · A age 65–74 = 1**. **0 none · 1 consider · ≥2 anticoagulate, no further debate.**

She scores **1 for hypertension — age does not score until 65 — so: consider, and in practice give**, because the stroke prevented outweighs the bleeding risk. Under the older CHA₂DS₂-VASc she would also have scored for being female, which is exactly why you name the score you are using.

Which anticoagulant, and **the echo answers it**: **moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve = valvular AF → warfarin, INR 2.0–3.0**, DOACs contraindicated. Everything else → **apixaban 5 mg BD** (2.5 mg BD if two of: **age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥133 micromol/L**), rivaroxaban 20 mg daily with food, or dabigatran 150 mg BD. VERIFY

**Pillar 3 — rate first: metoprolol 25–50 mg BD** or bisoprolol; target a resting rate **under about 100**. Diltiazem or verapamil as alternatives but **not in reduced ejection fraction**; digoxin only as an adjunct in sedentary patients or heart failure. VERIFY

**The 48-hour rule, with its reason said out loud**: fibrillating atria do not empty, clot forms in the left atrial appendage, and restoring coordinated contraction ejects it. **Under 48 h → cardiovert. ≥48 h or unknown → rate control, then either TOE to exclude thrombus or 3 weeks of anticoagulation first — and 4 weeks afterwards regardless.** **Give both pathways even though only one applies.**

SA — **PATS** for echo and cardioversion transfer from MM5, cardiology telehealth in the interim, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for retrieval. Warfarin needs reliable INR access in the country, which is a real argument for a **DOAC**. **Ambulance 000**; syncope from arrhythmia triggers a **non-driving period under the Austroads standard** (Registrar of Motor Vehicles).
plan: To the examiner: **'could I please have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation?'** **Unstable — hypotension, ischaemic chest pain, acute heart failure, syncope — and this is no longer a counselling station**: ED, oxygen if hypoxic, IV access, bloods including troponin, EUC, magnesium and FBC, monitoring, **urgent synchronised DC cardioversion**.

**'Examiner, may I interpret the ECG?'** Seven steps in order, about 30 seconds: **rate (bypass line) → rhythm, irregularly irregular → no discrete P waves → PR not measurable → QRS borderline → up-sloping ST in V2–V3, not pathological → T waves unremarkable.** Impression: **AF with a rapid ventricular response.**

Diagnosis to the patient in plain words, **then the cause**: the electrical signals have become disorganised so the top chambers quiver; and **'the main driver here is your blood pressure, which hasn't been treated or followed up'**, with the coffee and alcohol adding to it.

**Signpost the plan before you give it**: **'there are three parts — first, some tests to find out why this has happened; second, protecting you from a stroke; and third, treating the irregular beat itself. Is it alright if I go through them in turn?'**

Pillar 1. **'The two most important tests are a blood test for your thyroid and an ultrasound scan of your heart'** — the echo shows **how strongly it pumps, whether any valve is damaged, and whether there is clot inside**. Plus **FBC, kidney function and salts, LFT, coagulation, magnesium, fasting sugar and cholesterol, CXR**. Then the risk factors: **coffee, alcohol, smoking with a Quitline referral, diet, exercise, and treating the blood pressure**.

Pillar 2, **and name the score out loud**: **'when the heart beats irregularly the blood doesn't empty properly from the upper chambers and can form a clot; if it travels it causes a stroke. We use a scoring tool called the CHA₂DS₂-VA score'** — then the thresholds, then **her score of 1 for the blood pressure, and the recommendation to start one**. Warfarin versus a newer tablet, **and the echo decides which**.

Pillar 3. **Rate control now — a beta blocker, metoprolol 25–50 mg BD — to settle the palpitations and the dizziness.** Then **both duration pathways**: **'if it had been present less than two days we could correct the rhythm straight away; because it has been longer — or when we simply don't know — a clot may already have formed, and correcting the rhythm then could push it out and cause a stroke.'**

So the order is: **rate control now → anticoagulate → either a transoesophageal echo to look directly for clot, or three weeks on the blood thinner → then correct the rhythm → and four weeks of anticoagulation afterwards regardless.** Correction is **electrical, briefly asleep under sedation, or medication — flecainide if no structural disease and the EF is preserved, amiodarone if not**.

Safety net, in her words: **'if you get chest pain, severe breathlessness, if you faint, or if you notice weakness or drooping on one side of your face or body — call an ambulance on triple zero straight away. Those last ones are stroke symptoms and time matters enormously.'**

Summarise all three pillars in one breath, offer to **write it down**, say you will **involve a heart specialist** and see her with the results, then **'what questions do you have for me?'** If she refuses the blood thinner: acknowledge, offer the DOAC, respect the decision, and **offer to go through the actual numbers and decide together**.
pefe: **Vital signs from the examiner before anything else** — this is the step that separates a counselling station from an emergency one.
**12-lead ECG** read in **seven steps**, then commit. Keep it at essential level: **irregularly irregular with absent P waves cannot be anything except AF**.
**TSH and echocardiogram** head the workup — name these two if you name no others.

**FBC · EUC and creatinine · LFT · coagulation profile · magnesium · fasting glucose or HbA1c · lipid profile · CXR.** **Troponin only if ischaemic symptoms.**
**Renal function before a DOAC** — apixaban drops to 2.5 mg BD on two of age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥133 micromol/L. VERIFY
Blood pressure series to confirm the untreated hypertension, and a full **cardiovascular risk assessment** — AF is cardiovascular disease.

If asked about bleeding risk: **HAS-BLED identifies and corrects modifiable risks — uncontrolled hypertension, alcohol, NSAIDs, labile INR — it does not withhold anticoagulation.** A high score means closer review, not no treatment.

stem: You are the doctor in a general practice. Ray Docherty, 62, has come in with chest pain for the past two to three months. It comes on when he walks up the hill to the shops and settles when he stops.
Vitals: T 36.6 · HR 96 · BP 132/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · BMI 27.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
Outline your investigations and initial management

dx: **Stable angina secondary to iron deficiency anaemia, caused by an NSAID-induced bleeding peptic ulcer.** 'Stable angina' on its own is a third of the answer.

The chain, said out loud: **anti-inflammatory → peptic ulcer → chronic gastrointestinal blood loss → iron deficiency anaemia → less oxygen delivered and more cardiac work → angina.** Every part of the management follows from a different link.

Mechanism: angina is a **supply–demand mismatch**. Usually the supply falls because a coronary artery is narrowed; here **there is not enough haemoglobin to carry the oxygen**, and the heart compensates by beating faster and harder, raising demand at the same time. **Coronary disease may coexist and must still be assessed.**

Typical and **stable**: central, heavy, radiating to the left arm and jaw, **brought on by exertion and relieved by rest within minutes** — and, the graded question, **no rest pain, no night pain, no crescendo pattern**.

Three links, three treatments: **stop the ibuprofen** (paracetamol, a topical anti-inflammatory, physiotherapy, weight management for his knees) → **proton pump inhibitor at a standard healing dose** → **iron replacement**, oral once bleeding is controlled or IV if not tolerated → **eradicate Helicobacter pylori if positive**.

**Transfuse only if he is symptomatic at rest, haemodynamically compromised, or the haemoglobin is very low.** Restrictive threshold around **70 g/L**, around **80 g/L** with cardiovascular disease — safe wording is 'a restrictive threshold, a slightly higher one given his cardiac symptoms, discussed with the senior clinician'. VERIFY

**The antiplatelet conflict — raise it, never resolve it silently.** Aspirin protects the heart and harms the ulcer: **'aspirin thins the blood and irritates the stomach, and right now you're bleeding from your stomach, so I'm not going to start it today.'** Treat the ulcer, correct the count, then decide **jointly with cardiology and gastroenterology, with PPI cover**.

**Cardiac assessment after the haemoglobin recovers** — a stress test in a profoundly anaemic man is uninterpretable and carries risk. Meanwhile: **short-acting nitrate spray for episodes**, consider a beta-blocker, plus statin and blood pressure management.

**Say cancer aloud, calmly, with the plan attached.** **Iron deficiency anaemia in an older adult is scoped regardless of a plausible cause** — no weight loss and no change in bowel habit is reassuring, not exclusionary. 'I'd rather know than guess.'

SA — gastroscopy and colonoscopy from MM5 need **Country Health Connect** referral and **PATS**; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**; acute rebleed or haemodynamic compromise is **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: To the examiner: **'before I begin, may I have his vital signs, including a postural blood pressure?'**

WIPE, open question, acknowledge — then **signpost the odd questions before you ask them**: **'I'll ask about the pain first, then some questions that might seem unrelated to your chest — they matter, I promise.'**

Characterise the pain: **where exactly, and does it go anywhere · what's it like, heavy, tight, sharp, burning · what brings it on and what makes it go away · how long does it last · do you ever get it at rest, or at night, or does it wake you · has it changed, coming on with less effort than it used to · any sweating, nausea, breathlessness or palpitations with it?**

Cardiovascular risk factors: **do you smoke, or have you ever · any high blood pressure, diabetes or high cholesterol · any heart attacks or strokes in the family, and at what age · how active are you · how much alcohol?**

The other chest pain groups, one fast sweep: **any fever or recent viral illness, is it better leaning forward · any long travel or calf swelling · coughing up blood · any injury to the chest, or pain on pressing · any rash · any heartburn or acid taste?** If the history runs long, shorten **this** — **never the two bolt-on blocks**.

**Bolt-on 1 — the anaemia screen**, twenty seconds and it opens the case: **have you been more tired than usual · more breathless doing things you used to manage easily · any dizziness or light-headedness · any palpitations · has anyone said you look pale · any craving to chew ice?**

**Bolt-on 2 — the upper gastrointestinal screen, the pivot**: **any indigestion, burning or gnawing pain in the upper tummy, and is it related to eating · have you noticed your bowel motions turning black or tarry · have you ever vomited blood, or anything like coffee grounds · any difficulty swallowing · any weight loss or loss of appetite · any change in bowel habit or fresh blood · any bowel or stomach cancer in the family?**

Do not hear 'black stools' and move on. **Characterise it: how long, how often, are they sticky and offensive-smelling** — and **exclude iron tablets and bismuth, which also darken stool**. Then say out loud what it means.

Medications, **asked twice**. 'What medications are you on?' gets 'nothing really'. Then: **'are you taking anything at all for pain or for your joints — including anything you buy yourself at the chemist or the supermarket? Ibuprofen, Nurofen, Voltaren or aspirin? How much, and for how long?'** Then **previous ulcer or Helicobacter treatment**, allergies, and **'is there anything in particular you're worried about?'**

Examination from the examiner — **name each box and wait**, and **request the rectal examination explicitly, with consent and a chaperone**. Interpret the murmur rather than labelling it: in an anaemic patient a soft systolic murmur is usually a **flow murmur**.

Diagnosis as **three linked steps** in plain English — the pain is angina · the reason is that you are anaemic · the reason for that is slow blood loss from the stomach, most likely an ulcer from the anti-inflammatory tablets. Then the differentials, **naming malignancy honestly, with the reassuring features and the plan attached**.

Investigations and management by link: **bloods and cross-match · ECG · gastroscopy with H. pylori testing · colonoscopy · stop the NSAID with alternative analgesia · PPI · iron**. Then **defer the cardiac testing and the aspirin decision, and say why**.

Safety net and summarise: **chest pain at rest or that doesn't settle, vomiting blood, the black motions getting worse, or feeling faint → come straight back or go to the emergency department.** 'Does that all make sense?'
pefe: Ask for **vital signs including a postural blood pressure** before you begin.
Name each box and wait: **general appearance and anaemia signs · pulse and postural BP · heart sounds, murmurs, JVP, oedema · chest · abdomen · rectal examination · office tests**.

stem: Alan Prosser, 58, presents to the Emergency Department with central chest pain worse lying flat and better sitting forward, with a flu-like illness a week ago.
Vitals: T 37.2 · HR 88 · BP 128/76 · RR 18 · SpO2 97%.
ECG handed to you: ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No PR depression, no widespread concave elevation.
tasks: Take a history (4–6 minutes)
Interpret the ECG
Explain the diagnosis and immediate management

dx: **Acute inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.** The pericarditic history is a **mimic, not the diagnosis** — and this is precisely why an ECG and a troponin are part of the pericarditis workup.

The read, aloud and in order: **rate 88, sinus rhythm, normal axis. ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF — the inferior leads — with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No widespread elevation and no PR depression. That is a territorial pattern with reciprocal change.**

The discriminator: **pericarditis = widespread concave elevation crossing territories, PR depression (PR elevation in aVR), no reciprocal change, troponin normal or mildly raised, positional pleuritic pain relieved by leaning forward.** **Infarction = territorial, often convex, reciprocal change present, troponin substantially raised and rising.**

Name the mismatch to the examiner rather than explaining it away: **'the history was suggestive of pericarditis — positional pain relieved by leaning forward, after a viral illness. But the ECG overrides it. I am treating this as an infarct.'**

To the patient: **'your heart tracing shows something more serious than the story first suggested. One of the arteries supplying your heart muscle is blocked — that's a heart attack. I know the pain didn't feel typical, but the tracing is clear, and we need to act now to open that artery.'**

Immediate: **resuscitation area, continuous monitoring, IV access, aspirin 300 mg chewed, a second antiplatelet and anticoagulation per protocol, and analgesia. Oxygen only if he is hypoxic.** VERIFY doses against current protocol.

**Reperfusion is the priority: primary percutaneous coronary intervention if it can be delivered promptly, otherwise thrombolysis and urgent transfer.** **ST elevation with a consistent story is enough — do not wait for the troponin.**

**Right-sided leads (V4R): up to a third of inferior infarcts involve the right ventricle.** If they do, he is **preload dependent — avoid nitrates, which can cause profound hypotension, and give fluid instead**.
**Continuous monitoring for arrhythmia and heart block**, both of which inferior infarcts produce. Senior and cardiology involvement now, not later.

SA — in rural South Australia primary angioplasty is usually not immediately available: **thrombolysis here after checking contraindications, plus MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 retrieval** to a PCI-capable centre, **discussing the case with the receiving cardiologist while treatment is being given**.

stem: Jenny Hollis, 58, presents to your general practice with palpitations.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 150 · BP 124/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · alert and comfortable.
The ECG you will be handed: rate 150 · regular R-R intervals · no visible P waves · PR not measurable · narrow QRS · ST segments normal.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 6 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient

dx: **Supraventricular tachycardia** — a **fast, regular, narrow-complex rhythm arising above the ventricles**, in a patient with a heavy stimulant load.

Strictly SVT is an umbrella term covering atrial fibrillation, flutter, AVNRT and AVRT. **For this strip the answer they want is 'supraventricular tachycardia'; AVNRT is also acceptable.** **'PSVT' simply means paroxysmal — do not get drawn into the distinction.**

To the patient in three parts: **name it → 'your heart is beating faster than usual, but still regularly' → 'because of abnormal electrical signalling: your heart has its own wiring that sets the pace, and here an extra circuit takes over and drives it much faster than it should.'**

Then the contributing factor you found: **eight cups of coffee a day is very likely provoking it.** And **the planted hidden finding — a blood pressure she was told was raised once and never followed up** — which needs **its own line in the plan**, not a dismissal because 'it's just an SVT'.

**Address the stated fear before she asks again**: **'this is not a heart attack. There's nothing on your tracing to suggest one, and you don't have the symptoms that go with it — no chest pain, no sweating, no nausea. It's a rhythm problem, and it's very treatable.'**

**Unstable** = hypotension, altered conscious state, ischaemic chest pain or ECG change, breathlessness at rest or pulmonary oedema, syncope, a rate that will not settle, **a broad-complex tachycardia**, or known structural or ischaemic disease → **senior help and synchronised DC cardioversion**, not a leisurely history.

Stable: **continuous monitoring, IV access, 12-lead ECG → vagal manoeuvres first.** The **modified Valsalva** — blow against resistance, then lie flat with the legs raised — is **more effective than the standard technique**. **Carotid sinus massage only with care, and never with a bruit or a previous stroke.**

**Adenosine if vagal manoeuvres fail: rapid intravenous push through a large proximal vein with an immediate saline flush, 6 mg then 12 mg.** Warn her it causes **brief, very unpleasant flushing and chest tightness that passes within seconds**. **Avoid in severe asthma.** VERIFY against local protocol, with senior involvement.

Long term: **reduce or stop the stimulants · teach her to perform the vagal manoeuvres herself · refer for electrophysiology assessment, since catheter ablation is curative for recurrent SVT.** And **recheck the blood pressure, arrange follow-up, and assess absolute cardiovascular risk**.

SA — **adenosine only where resuscitation facilities and monitoring are available**; discuss early with the receiving cardiology service; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if she is unstable or needs repeated cardioversion. **Electrophysiology and ablation are metropolitan** — referral means a trip to Adelaide, so raise travel, **PATS** and support when counselling a country patient.
plan: To the examiner: **'before I begin, may I have her vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, and the rhythm if it's available, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** If told you don't have the rhythm yet, **accept it without fluster** — the mark is for asking, and the ECG is coming.
WIPE, open question, acknowledge: **'I understand how concerning this must be. Let me ask you some questions and look at your heart tracing, and we'll find the cause together. Is that all right?'**

**Box 1 — describe it**: **can you describe what you mean by palpitations — is your heart beating fast, does it feel irregular, or does it feel like it's missing or skipping a beat? · could you tap out on the desk what the rhythm feels like?** **Expect the refusal. Ask once, accept it, move on** — role-players have declined to tap since 2019.

**Box 2 — timing and course**: **when did it start · is it there all the time or does it come and go · how long does an episode last, and how does it stop · is this the first time, or have you had episodes before · is it getting worse or more frequent?**

**Box 3 — triggers**: **is there anything that makes it better or worse · do you notice it more when you stand up, bend forward or lie down · is it worse on exertion, and do you get it at rest as well · is there a particular place or situation that brings it on?** The positional trigger is classic for SVT; **exertion-only points to ischaemia and changes the case.**

**Group 1 — the full cardiovascular block, five sub-blocks, not one**: **any chest pain with the palpitations, any breathlessness, nausea or sweating · do you feel dizzy, have you ever fainted or blacked out · any swelling in your legs, any breathlessness lying flat, how many pillows · ever been told you have a murmur or valve problem, or had a heart attack · any family history of heart attack or stroke, any high blood pressure, high blood sugar or cholesterol, do you smoke, how much alcohol · any fever or recent flu-like illness?**

Groups 2 to 4: **any cough, noisy breathing or wheeze · any swelling or pain in your calves, recent long travel, previous clots in you or the family · any weather preference, do you find hot weather hard to tolerate, any weight loss, diarrhoea or tremor · how much coffee, tea or energy drink in a day · any recreational drugs · any asthma puffers or nasal decongestant sprays · any Chinese takeaway or very salty food before it started?**

Groups 5 to 8, compressed to one question each if the clock is tight — **but never at the expense of the cardiovascular block or the stimulant count**: **any stress at home or work · how has your mood been · during an episode did you ever feel you were going to die · unusually tired, or more breathless on exertion · any headaches, sweating episodes or tremor · did you miss any meals before it started, any diabetes treatment · when was your last period, and any hot flushes?**

Close the history — almost everything is already done: **any allergies · any other medical conditions or medications I haven't asked about · and is there anything in particular you're worried about?**
ECG to the examiner, **seven steps aloud in order**, landing on **one clean impression**. If your nerve goes, **describe rather than label**.
**Name it, define it, explain it** in plain words — then **address the heart-attack fear with your reasons, before she raises it again**.

**Differentials as the causes of palpitations, by system** — cardiovascular, respiratory, thyroid, stimulants, psychogenic, anaemia, phaeochromocytoma, hypoglycaemia — with **the negatives said out loud** so the examiner hears the sweep. **Never a catalogue of arrhythmias.**

Plan and close: **monitoring and IV access · vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine · bloods including thyroid function · cut the coffee down substantially · recheck and follow up the blood pressure · electrophysiology referral given recurrent episodes.** Safety net: **chest pain, feeling faint, blacking out, or breathlessness with it → come back straight away.**
pefe: **Ask for the rhythm in the vital signs.** The mark is for asking, even when the examiner withholds it.
**12-lead ECG read in seven steps: rate → regular? → P waves? → PR interval → QRS duration → ST segments → impression.**

**The rule at step 3: a P wave and a T wave must both be present and separate.** If there is only one deflection between QRS complexes at 150, **it is the T wave** and there is no P — the commonest error on this strip.
If you are unsure of the rhythm name, **describe what you see**: 'a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 without visible P waves' earns most of the mark before you attach any label.
**ECG during symptoms wherever possible** — the single most useful test. **Holter or event monitor** for paroxysmal symptoms with a normal resting tracing.
Bloods: **FBC · electrolytes including magnesium and calcium · thyroid function in every palpitations case · glucose**.
**Echocardiogram** if there is a murmur, a structural concern or an abnormal ECG.
**Troponin only if ischaemia is suspected. Metanephrines only if the phaeochromocytoma triad is present. Exercise testing where the symptoms are exertional.**

stem: Raymond Doyle, 68, attends your general practice with three days of palpitations and increasing breathlessness on exertion. He describes his heart 'racing steadily, not jumping about'. He has hypertension on perindopril, BMI 33, and drinks around 30 standard drinks a week. An ECG has been performed and is available.
Observations: BP 128/76 · PR 148 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 96% RA · Temp 36.5 °C · no chest pain, alert and well perfused.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Give your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Outline your management

dx: **Typical atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block**, ventricular rate 150, in a stable 68-year-old. **A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at or near 150 is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise** — say that sentence and you have already separated yourself from the field.

The read: **atrial rate about 300 · a continuous sawtooth baseline with no isoelectric segment · negative in II, III and aVF, positive in V1 · two flutter waves per QRS · narrow QRS.** **2:1 gives 150 · 3:1 gives 100 · 4:1 gives 75.** At 2:1 **one flutter wave hides in the QRS and the other in the T wave**, which is why it looks like sinus.

Why not sinus: **sinus tachycardia is a response and requires a driver** — pain, fever, hypovolaemia, sepsis, anaemia, PE, thyrotoxicosis, drugs — and he is afebrile, comfortable and well perfused at rest. **Sinus rates also vary with respiration; this is metronomically regular.**
**Adenosine unmasks flutter; it does not terminate it.** It terminates AVNRT and AVRT. Say this unprompted — it is the discriminator an examiner listens for.

Keep **two separate lists**. Differentials **of the rhythm**: sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia, and AF with a very rapid response that can look deceptively regular. Causes **of the flutter**: by system. Candidates who blur them sound muddled.

Rate control: **a beta-blocker first line, or verapamil or diltiazem where a beta-blocker is unsuitable — never both together**, because of profound bradycardia and heart block. **Expect it to work less well than in AF**; a rate stuck near 150 is the nature of flutter, not your failure, and it is the argument for a rhythm strategy sooner.

Stroke prevention is **identical to AF**. **CHA₂DS₂-VA: he scores for hypertension and age 65–74 — that is 2, so anticoagulate**, with a **DOAC preferred** over warfarin (warfarin for mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis). **Aspirin is not stroke prevention in flutter or AF**, and saying so unprompted is worth a mark. VERIFY which score is current.

**Three days is outside the 48-hour window.** Either **three weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation beforehand, or a transoesophageal echo to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus** — then cardiovert, then **at least four weeks afterwards**, because the atrium remains mechanically stunned even once the rhythm looks normal. **Instability overrides the rule.**

**Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is curative in typical flutter** — high success, low complication rate, considerably better than AF ablation — so **raise it early, not as a last resort**. But **a substantial proportion go on to develop AF**, so anticoagulation follows **the stroke score, not the rhythm on the day**. And **never flecainide without an AV nodal blocker on board** — a slower atrial rate can conduct **1:1 at over 200**.

The drivers are sitting in the stem, and naming them turns a rhythm diagnosis into a management plan: **hypertension · 30 standard drinks a week against the NHMRC limit of 10 a week and 4 in a day · BMI 33 with likely undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea** — plus **thyroid function in every tachyarrhythmia**. SA: sleep study and cardiology via **Country Health Connect** and **PATS**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if he destabilises.
plan: To the examiner, before touching the tracing: **'I would confirm his haemodynamic stability — blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, saturations and temperature — and ask specifically about chest pain, syncope and breathlessness at rest.'** Then **say it**: **'he is stable, which means I can work through this properly rather than proceeding to immediate cardioversion.'**

The ECG in seven steps: **rate ~150 · regular · no discrete P waves, a continuous sawtooth baseline negative in II, III and aVF and positive in V1 · atrial rate ~300 · two flutter waves per QRS, so 2:1 block · narrow QRS · no acute ischaemic change.** Impression: **typical atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction.**

Defend the call when challenged: **sinus needs a driver and he has none; sinus varies with respiration and this does not; and if I were uncertain I would increase AV block with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine under continuous ECG recording — in flutter that is diagnostic, not therapeutic.**
Diagnosis, then **the two lists kept apart**: the rhythm differentials, then the causes by system — **cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine, drugs and lifestyle**.

To the patient — **loop and filter, never the bare number**: **'the electrical signal gets caught in a loop, going round and round the top chamber about 300 times a minute. Your heart has a natural filter that only lets some of those through, which is why your pulse is 150 and not 300.'** If he says that sounds like he should be dead: **'that is the top chamber — the filter is doing its job, which is why you walked in here talking to me.'**

The two things that matter, in his words: **a heart running at 150 for three days gets tired, which is why you are breathless**; and **when the top chamber flutters rather than squeezing, blood can sit still and form a clot — if that travels to the brain it causes a stroke.** So **a blood thinner is a major part of the treatment.**

His three questions. **'Am I going to have a stroke?'** — higher than it should be, which is exactly why the tablet starts today. **'Can you shock it back today?'** — the highest-value thirty seconds in the station: **explain that a clot may already have formed, and cardioverting now could push it out and cause the very stroke we are preventing.** **'Is this from the drinking?'** — **be honest with a number: thirty a week against a recommended ten.**

Management, five headings out loud: **rate · rhythm · anticoagulation · ablation · the drivers.** Rate first with a beta-blocker and the warning not to combine agents; anticoagulate on the named score; defer cardioversion with the reason; raise CTI ablation early; then blood pressure, alcohol, weight and sleep apnoea.

Investigations: **FBC, electrolytes including magnesium, renal and thyroid function, glucose and lipids · chest X-ray · transthoracic echocardiogram** — and **a repeat ECG once the rate is controlled**, because the sawtooth is far clearer at a slower rate.
pefe: **Vital signs before you interpret anything** — plus **chest pain, syncope and breathlessness at rest** asked by name.
**12-lead ECG in seven steps: rate → rhythm → P waves → atrial rate → conduction ratio → QRS → ST and T.**
**Look at the inferior leads for the sawtooth and count the atrial rate.** At 2:1 one flutter wave sits inside the QRS and the other inside the T wave, which is exactly why it is missed.
**To unmask it: vagal manoeuvres — modified Valsalva or carotid sinus massage — or IV adenosine under continuous ECG recording.** **Diagnostic, not therapeutic.**
**Repeat the ECG after rate control** — the sawtooth is often much clearer at a slower ventricular rate.
Bloods: **FBC · electrolytes including magnesium · renal function · thyroid function in every tachyarrhythmia · glucose and lipids.** **Troponin only if ischaemia is suspected.**
**Chest X-ray** for heart size, pulmonary oedema and lung pathology. **Transthoracic echocardiogram** for chamber size, valves and ventricular function.
**Transoesophageal echo only if cardioversion is planned beyond 48 hours without adequate prior anticoagulation**, to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus.
**Holter or ambulatory monitoring** for paroxysmal cases and to assess rate control. **Sleep study** where obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected — and here it should be.

BP history, murmur, orthopnoea, oedema, recent CABG
**Echocardiogram**; treat the underlying disease

Pulmonary embolism · COPD and cor pulmonale · **obstructive sleep apnoea** · pneumonia
Calf swelling and travel; **snoring and witnessed apnoeas**; cough and wheeze
CTPA if suspected; CXR; **sleep study**

**Thyrotoxicosis** · diabetes · phaeochromocytoma

**Drugs and lifestyle**
**Alcohol — 30 standard drinks a week here** · caffeine and energy drinks · nicotine · stimulants · salbutamol · nasal decongestants · **obesity, BMI 33**
**Quantify each in standard drinks and cups; take the BMI seriously**
History; **reduce and reassess — these are the modifiable drivers in this stem**

stem: Your next patient is a 35-year-old woman who has presented to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath and chest pain.
Vitals: T 37.4 °C · HR 104 · BP 118/74 · RR 22 · SpO2 94% on room air · alert.
tasks: Take a relevant history — six minutes
You will be given the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
State your investigations

dx: **Pulmonary embolism arising from a left leg deep vein thrombosis**, provoked by **immobility on a long road journey and oestrogen exposure**. **Name the source in the leg**, not just the lung.

The chain: **clot forms in the leg → embolises to the pulmonary arteries → pulmonary vascular resistance rises sharply → right ventricular strain → pleuritic pain, breathlessness, tachycardia, hypoxia, and sometimes infarction of the lung.**

To the patient, plain and short: **'most likely you have a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood vessels of your lungs. The clot most likely formed in your leg during that long drive, when you were sitting still for a long time, and then a piece of it travelled up to your lung.'**

**Three reasons, every time**: **your left calf is swollen and painful, which is where the clot started · your chest pain is sharp and worse when you breathe in, and you're short of breath · the examination shows changes in your heart sounds that happen when a clot strains the right side of the heart.** The pill and the journey both add to the risk.

**The features that fool candidates and still fit PE**: **fever — both DVT and PE cause it · wheeze — reflex bronchoconstriction · haemoptysis — pulmonary infarction · orthopnoea · raised JVP — clot burden straining the right heart · basal dullness — infarction with a small effusion.** None of these is a reason to switch diagnosis.

**Wells** awards points for: **clinical signs of DVT · PE as likely as or more likely than an alternative · heart rate over 100 · immobilisation or surgery within 4 weeks · previous VTE · haemoptysis · malignancy.** **Two-level: above 4 means PE likely → image.** She scores on leg signs, tachycardia and immobility, so **straight to CTPA**. VERIFY — versions use different cut-offs.

**PERC applies only where suspicion is already low, and all eight must be negative**: **age under 50 · HR under 100 · SpO2 at least 95% · no haemoptysis · no oestrogen · no previous VTE · no unilateral leg swelling · no surgery or trauma needing hospitalisation in 4 weeks.** **She fails several.** **D-dimer is a rule-out test only** — it rises in pregnancy, infection, malignancy, surgery and older age.

Treatment: **apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily**, or **rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days, then 20 mg daily**. **Start anticoagulation before imaging if clinical suspicion is high and there is no bleeding contraindication.** Duration **at least 3 months for a provoked event**, longer or indefinite if unprovoked or recurrent. VERIFY

**Pregnancy: V/Q or perfusion scanning rather than CTPA, and low molecular weight heparin — not a DOAC, not warfarin**, with the obstetric team involved. **Massive PE — systolic under 90, syncope, arrest: resuscitation area, senior and intensive care help, bedside echo for right ventricular strain, and thrombolysis**, with embolectomy where thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated.

**Stop the combined pill — and give her an alternative contraceptive plan, not just an instruction to stop.** SA: **in a rural hospital without CT, treat on clinical suspicion and arrange MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 retrieval rather than waiting for confirmation**; on-call haematology for dosing and duration; Aboriginal Liaison Officer and **Closing the Gap PBS** for ongoing anticoagulant costs.
plan: To the examiner: **'may I have her vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** Name it back: **stable, but tachycardic, tachypnoeic and mildly hypoxic.**

WIPE, open question, acknowledge — then **signpost the decision out loud**: **'I'd like to start with the chest pain, then come back to your breathing.'** Two complaints, one structure: **chest pain wins, because its differential list already contains the respiratory one.**

Full pain analysis: **where exactly · when did it start and did it come on suddenly or gradually · what's it like, sharp, dull, heavy, burning · does it travel anywhere · how bad out of ten · anything that makes it better or worse — breathing, moving, position, or pressing on it · has anything like this happened before?** The better-or-worse question is **the highest-yield question in any chest pain history**.

Fold the breathlessness in, **three questions only**: **what do you mean by shortness of breath — difficulty getting air in, not getting enough, or tightness · anything that makes it better or worse · any cough, any noisy breathing or wheeze?** Then **have you coughed up any blood, and have you felt dizzy or faint?**

Cardiovascular group: **any sweating, nausea, racing heart or dizziness with the pain · do you smoke, any high blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol or family heart disease · any fever or flu-like illness, and is the pain better sitting up and leaning forward · any breathlessness lying flat, how many pillows, any leg swelling · ever blacked out, especially with exertion?**

Respiratory group — **where the case turns**: **any injury or trauma to your chest · have you had any long travel or long periods sitting still recently · any swelling, pain or redness in your legs, especially the calf · any fevers, chills or coughing up phlegm · any weight loss, loss of appetite, or lumps and bumps?** **Ask the open version of the travel question** — it is the immobility, not the aircraft.

**COST-VMPF, triggered the moment travel or leg symptoms appear**: **Contraception — are you on any pill, and do you know its name · Obesity · Surgery, injuries or hospital admissions recently · Travel and immobility · Varicose veins · Malignancy · Pregnancy and last menstrual period · Family history of clots — and have you ever had one yourself?**

**Finish the sweep — do not stop because you have the answer.** **Any acid or bitter taste, heartburn, related to eating · worse when you move or press on the chest wall · any rash on your chest or back · how have things been for stress** — then **SADMA, past history, medications and allergies**. The marks for those groups are still on the sheet.

**Interpret the findings out loud, do not recite them**: the tachycardia, tachypnoea and hypoxia fit an acute pulmonary problem; **the loud P2 and the parasternal murmur mean raised pulmonary pressures with tricuspid regurgitation from right ventricular strain**; **the basal dullness is infarction with a small effusion, not consolidation**; **and the swollen tender calf gives you the source.**

Diagnosis in plain English **with the three reasons**, then answer the fear honestly: **'it is a serious condition and we treat it seriously — but it's very treatable, and you've come in at the right time. The treatment is blood-thinning medication, not surgery.'**

Differentials: **two explained properly, the rest named.** Heart attack — the pain is sharp and breathing-related. Pneumonia — no proper fever, no chills, no phlegm, **and a clot itself raises the temperature**. Then name pneumothorax, pericarditis, reflux, a chest wall cause and anxiety. **At eight minutes, switch to naming.**

Investigations in **priority order, thirty seconds**: **CTPA first** — the confirmatory test; **V/Q if CTPA is contraindicated**; D-dimer only where suspicion is low; **ECG and bloods including renal function, which guides the anticoagulant**; **β-hCG**; chest X-ray; leg Doppler. **Cut from the bottom, never the top.**

Close: **'we'll scan you to confirm, start a blood thinner, and admit you — and you'll need to stop the combined pill, but I won't leave you without contraception; we'll sort out an alternative before you go home.'** Safety net: **worse pain, more breathless, or feeling faint — tell us straight away.**
pefe: **Vital signs before you begin** — the hypoxia and tachypnoea are half the diagnosis.

Face-to-face, ask in this order: **general appearance and work of breathing · vitals with saturations and temperature · trachea · chest expansion, percussion and auscultation · heart sounds including the pulmonary second sound and any murmur · JVP · and both calves for swelling, tenderness and asymmetry.** **The calves are the request candidates forget.**
**CTPA is the confirmatory test — lead with it.** **V/Q scan** where CTPA is contraindicated: contrast allergy, significant renal impairment, or pregnancy.
**D-dimer only where PE is unlikely and you need to rule out.** High negative predictive value; a positive result proves nothing.
**ECG** — **sinus tachycardia is the commonest finding**; look for right heart strain, right bundle branch block, T inversion in V1–V4. **S1Q3T3 is uncommon.**
Bloods: **FBC · renal function, needed before a DOAC · LFT if warfarin is being considered · coagulation profile · troponin**. **β-hCG in any woman of reproductive age.**
**Chest X-ray** — often normal, but it excludes pneumothorax and consolidation.
**Doppler ultrasound of the leg** confirms the source — **but do not delay the CTPA for it**.

stem: You are the doctor in the emergency department. James Okafor, 22, has presented with sudden onset chest pain that started while he was exercising today. He is already on oxygen when you enter the cubicle.
Information available: HR 98 · BP 122/74 · RR 22 · SpO2 94% · T 36.8 °C · alert and orientated.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Version A: at about five minutes a chest X-ray is provided — explain the X-ray to the patient. Version B: ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you require
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **Primary spontaneous pneumothorax** in a tall, thin 22-year-old who vapes — **rupture of a subpleural bleb**, air in the pleural space with no underlying lung disease.

**Say the conclusion out loud — this is a marked moment**: **'that's a sharp, well-localised pain that came on suddenly and is worse when you breathe in. We call that pleuritic, and it points me towards your lungs and the lining around them rather than your heart. I still need to check both properly.'**

**The conclusion does not change the structure.** You have narrowed your suspicion; **you have not earned the right to skip the cardiac block.** Run CVS first, in full, **exactly as you would for a 60-year-old with central crushing pain** — that is what would have caught pericarditis, myocarditis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy if the case had been one of those.

**The new question in a young person with exertional chest pain: family history of sudden cardiac death** — **anyone who died suddenly and young, or unexpectedly during sport or in their sleep.** Ask it **inside the cardiac block, not at the end with family history**, because the end of the station is where you run out of time.

**The X-ray script, six steps**: **'this is the X-ray of your chest' → three colours, white is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air → landmarks: heart, spine, and the windpipe, and say you are checking it sits centrally → the normal side, markings running to the edge and a sharp angle at the base → the abnormal side, lung edge visible with no markings beyond it → name it.** **Comment on the trachea even when it is normal** — that is how you demonstrate you were looking for tension.

**No radiology language to the patient.** 'A lucency with absent peripheral vascular markings and a visible visceral pleural line' is a correct description and **a failed communication task**. If the film is genuinely poor: **say what you can see, lean on the history, and ask to review the digital image** — that is what a safe doctor does, not a weakness.

**Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: hypotension, trachea deviated away, distended neck veins, hypoxia not correcting on oxygen.** **Immediate needle decompression with a large-bore cannula — 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line, with the 2nd space midclavicular line as the traditional alternative — then an intercostal catheter straight away, because decompression is only temporising. Do not wait for an X-ray.** VERIFY against local protocol.

**Intervention rule: symptomatic or unstable → pleural intervention** — aspiration, or a **small-bore 8–14 French catheter by Seldinger technique in the safe triangle, 5th intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line**. Minimally symptomatic and stable → **conservative or ambulatory care with review**. **Led by symptoms and stability rather than size alone — but still measure it and factor it into the conversation.**

**The counselling is where a 22-year-old's life is actually affected**: **stopping the vaping is the single most effective way to prevent recurrence · recurrence is about 30%, mostly in the first one to two years · no flying until fully resolved on imaging and typically a week beyond · and no scuba diving ever, without definitive surgery.** **Surgical referral** after a second ipsilateral event, a first contralateral event, bilateral disease, a persistent air leak, or a high-risk occupation. **High-flow oxygen speeds reabsorption** in conservative management.

**The clock is the second discriminator.** **Diagnosis in 30–40 seconds, three differentials with one reason each, then the rest as a rapid list.** **A beautiful forty-second explanation of pleural physiology eats the time the list needed — and the examiner cannot award marks for differentials you did not say.** Safety net: **more breathless, worse pain, feeling faint or a racing heart, or blue lips or fingers → come back or call an ambulance.**
plan: Face-to-face: **'may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?'** Online, a closed statement instead: **'I'll take you through to the treatment area and put you on the monitor to check you're stable while we talk.'** **A gate you walk through, not a place to spend thirty seconds.**

WIPE, confirm identity, open question — then **empathy once, properly**: **'I understand, and I can see this is worrying you. Let me ask you some questions and get you examined; we'll find the cause, and you're in safe hands. I'll come back to your concerns as soon as I know more.'** **Once, then work** — and again only if he becomes newly distressed, which role-players do when the X-ray appears.

SOCRATES in full: **where exactly — is it an area, or can you point to one spot · when did it start and what were you doing, sudden or gradual · sharp, dull, heavy, tight or burning · does it go anywhere · out of ten · constant or in waves, and getting worse?**

**The three named modifiers — patients rarely volunteer them, and the open question alone gets 'not that I've noticed'**: **does taking a deep breath make it worse · does it change with rest or activity · does leaning forward help at all?**
**Say 'pleuritic' out loud**, and say what it points you towards and away from.

**The cardiovascular block, in full, despite his age**: **any breathlessness, sweating or nausea with it · blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol, smoking, family history of heart disease · any recreational drugs, particularly cocaine or amphetamines · any fever or flu-like illness in the last week or two, and is it better sitting forward · breathless walking or lying flat, waking at night, ankle swelling, any condition you were born with · ever fainted or felt faint, especially during exercise · and any family history of sudden cardiac death?**

Respiratory: **any calf swelling or pain, long flights or car trips, recent surgery or immobility, clotting problems in the family, coughing up blood · what exercise were you actually doing, and did you take any knock or tackle to the chest · ever had a collapsed lung, or anyone in your family · do you smoke, vape or use cannabis · any fever, cough or coloured phlegm · and though it's unlikely at your age, any weight loss, lumps or bumps, night sweats?**

The rest of the sweep, briskly: **any tummy pain, vomiting, heartburn or sour fluid coming up, related to food · any rash on the chest, worse on pressing or twisting · any stress at home or uni, and how's your mood** — then **SADMA, past history, allergies**, and **'is there anything you were particularly worried this might be?'**

The bell. **Version A — the six-step X-ray script, 60–75 seconds, trachea named.** **Version B — the ten-step examination request**, opening with your reasoning: **'given the pleuritic character I'll go into more detail on the respiratory examination, with a relevant cardiovascular examination alongside it'**, then **expansion, trachea, percussion, auscultation and vocal resonance by name**.

**Diagnosis in 30–40 seconds, no more**: **'a pneumothorax — air collected in your chest cavity, outside the lung, usually because small bubbles on the surface of the lung burst and let air leak out.'** Then **three reasons**: sharp not heavy · worse on deep breathing, which is pleuritic · and the X-ray shows air around the lung with the lung edge visible.

**Differentials — three with reasons, then the rest as a list.** Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but no family history of sudden death · a clot on the lung, but no travel, immobility or calf symptoms · a chest infection, but no fever or cough. Then name **valve narrowing, heart failure, heart attack, pericarditis, a tear in the main artery, a growth in the lung, shingles, costochondritis, reflux or ulcer, and panic attack** in one sweep.

Plan and counselling: **oxygen, analgesia, monitoring · drainage by needle or a small tube between the ribs under local anaesthetic · admission and a repeat film.** Then the three that matter to him: **stop the vaping · no flying until cleared · no diving, ever, without an operation.** Safety net, summarise, check understanding.
pefe: **Four vital signs before the history** — and ask for **saturations on air as well as on oxygen**, since he is already receiving it.
**Ask for the trachea by name, in inspection and palpation.** 'Is the trachea midline or deviated?' If you ask only for 'a respiratory examination' you will not be told.

**If you get one positive, complete the system.** 'Air entry reduced on the left' is a **prompt, not an answer** — expansion, trachea, percussion, auscultation and vocal resonance are **four separate marks**.

**Interpret the card aloud**: reduced expansion, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance on the left with a midline trachea = **a left pneumothorax without tension physiology**. **Hyper-resonance rather than dullness rules out effusion or consolidation.**

**Erect chest X-ray** — and **trace the whole periphery of both lungs, apices included**. Two things that fool you: **a skin fold has lung markings crossing it**, and **bullous emphysema has an edge concave towards the chest wall**, which is dangerous to drain.
**ECG and troponin if there is any doubt about the cardiac differentials** — and ask for the ECG even when told it is pending.
**Lower limbs for oedema and calf asymmetry** — pulmonary embolism stays on the list of every pleuritic chest pain.

**In the traumatic variant**: large-bore IV access, **group and hold with crossmatch**, FBE and coagulation, erect CXR and consider **CT chest**, a **larger-bore drain rather than a small-bore catheter**, and surgical involvement early.
