stem: Your next patient is a 25-year-old man brought to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset chest tightness and shortness of breath that began while watching a movie at home. He has had similar episodes before and was told nothing was wrong. His parents are separated, he lives alone, works as an accountant, and has been under stress.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 96 · BP 126/78 · RR 18 · SpO2 99% RA · alert, anxious.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the pathophysiology of the condition

dx: **Panic attack occurring within a panic disorder**, with **early agoraphobic avoidance**, in a 25-year-old under psychosocial stress.

**The trap the whole station is built on: the psychosocial detail in the stem is bait.** Candidates who recognise the recall walk in and take a full psychiatric history — mood, sleep, appetite, psychosis screen — **and fail**. **This is a chest pain and shortness of breath presentation. You approach a case from the complaint, not from the diagnosis you remember**, and **psychogenic causes sit at the END of the chest pain list**, which is where you reach them legitimately.

**Panic attack: an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort peaking within minutes — typically under ten — with four or more of thirteen physical symptoms, characteristically including a fear of dying or of losing control.** Name the cluster and the fear of dying; **you are not expected to recite thirteen items**.

**Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks PLUS, for at least one month, persistent worry about further attacks OR a maladaptive change in behaviour to avoid them.** **Agoraphobia: fear or avoidance of two or more of — public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, queues or crowds, being outside the home alone — typically six months or more.**

**The three key questions, word for word**: **'During the attack, did you feel that you were going to die — were you afraid of dying?' · 'Since then, have you been worried about having another attack?' · 'Have you changed any of your routines or your behaviour because of that worry?'** **Question 1 names the attack; questions 2 and 3 convert it into the disorder.** Without them you cannot justify the diagnosis you are about to give.

**Do not convert to GAD on 'I'm generally an anxious person.'** **GAD requires excessive, hard-to-control worry about multiple everyday matters for at least six months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension or sleep disturbance — and prominent discrete physical attacks are NOT a core feature.** The two can coexist; **the attacks define this presentation**.

**When asked for differentials, give the differentials of the COMPLAINT** — cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal — **not a list of anxiety disorders**. Listing GAD, OCD, PTSD and adjustment disorder is the wrong answer; one or two psychiatric alternatives at the end are fine.

**The pathophysiology task is the one nobody rehearses.** Patient version: **your body has an alarm system — fight or flight. When it fires you release adrenaline: heart pounding, breathing faster, muscles tense, sweating. In a panic attack the alarm goes off when there is no danger. Then, because you feel you can't breathe, you over-breathe, which blows off carbon dioxide and causes the tingling in your fingers and around your mouth, the dizziness and the unreal feeling. And those sensations feel so much like a heart attack that your brain reads them as proof something terrible is happening — which fires the alarm again. That's the vicious cycle.** **It is real, not imagined — and it is not dangerous.**

Examiner version if asked technically: **a perceived threat activates the amygdala and sympathetic nervous system, producing a catecholamine surge with tachycardia, raised cardiac output, sweating and tremor. Hyperventilation causes hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis; cerebral vasoconstriction produces light-headedness and derealisation, and the fall in ionised calcium produces perioral and peripheral paraesthesiae and, if severe, carpopedal spasm. Catastrophic misinterpretation amplifies fear in a positive feedback loop, and repeated attacks produce conditioned anticipatory anxiety and avoidance.**

Management: **validate and explain — that is itself therapeutic → CBT is first line, with breathing retraining, cognitive work on the catastrophic interpretation, and graded exposure to avoided situations → a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan for subsidised sessions → an SSRI if needed, started low and increased slowly, warning that anxiety can briefly worsen in the first week or two and benefit takes several weeks → AVOID benzodiazepines beyond very short-term use, because of dependence and because they become a safety behaviour that reinforces avoidance → cut caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol and stimulants → GP follow-up and safety-net.** **NEVER say 'there's nothing wrong with you', 'it's all in your head', 'it's just stress, try to relax', or 'your tests are normal so you can go home'** — each is a marked communication failure. SA: **telehealth CBT and online programs matter more where psychology access is limited**; Aboriginal Liaison Officer or a local Aboriginal health service; **Closing the Gap PBS** if an SSRI is started. VERIFY
plan: To the examiner: **'may I have his vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** Then **say he is stable with a mild tachycardia**.

Open question, then **acknowledge the frustration explicitly — it buys the rapport you need for the diagnosis later**: **'I can hear how worrying this is, especially as it's happened before and you were told nothing was wrong. That's a frustrating place to be. Let's go through it properly and find the cause.'** Then signpost: **chest tightness first, then the breathing, then questions to rule out the important causes.**

Full pain analysis — **and do not skip the trajectory question**: **where exactly · when did it start and how quickly did it come on · HOW LONG DID IT TAKE TO REACH ITS WORST · tight, sharp, heavy or burning · does it go anywhere · out of ten · anything that makes it better or worse, breathing, moving, position, pressing · how long did it last and how did it settle?**

Breathlessness folded in, **three questions only — do not re-time it**: **what do you mean by shortness of breath — difficulty getting air in, not getting enough, or tightness · anything that made it better or worse · any cough or noisy breathing?**

Cardiovascular and respiratory sweep: **any sweating, nausea, racing heart or dizziness with it · smoking, blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol, family heart disease · any fever or recent flu-like illness, and is it better sitting up and leaning forward · breathless lying flat, how many pillows, leg swelling, ever fainted especially on exertion · any long travel or sitting still, calf swelling or pain, coughing up blood · any injury to your chest · any fevers, chills, phlegm, weight loss or lumps?** **Note the perioral and finger tingling — it is the fingerprint of hyperventilation, and you will use it in the mechanism.**

GI, musculoskeletal, drugs and endocrine — **the rows candidates drop because 'it's obviously anxiety'**: **any abdominal pain or vomiting, acid or bitter taste, heartburn, relation to eating · worse on moving or pressing, any rash · how much coffee or energy drink in a day, any recreational drugs, how much alcohol, have you recently stopped anything · any weight loss, feeling hot all the time, tremor or loose bowels?**

**Announce the negative organic screen out loud — this is the transition that earns the diagnosis honestly**: **'I've asked about your heart, your lungs, your stomach and your chest wall, and I haven't found anything pointing that way, which is reassuring. Now I'd like to ask about the episodes themselves.'** Then: **how many, over what period · out of the blue or always a trigger · what was happening in the film · any trembling, choking, or a sense things aren't real?**
**The three key questions, verbatim and in sequence.** Ask all three. **Question 1 names the attack; 2 and 3 name the disorder.**

**The agoraphobia screen** — places you now avoid, public transport, crowds, queues, being far from home alone, **and whether the avoidance is because you fear an attack there**. Then **the GAD criteria asked properly rather than assumed**, the stressors in one or two questions, mood, and **a brief, calm risk question** — fifteen seconds, matter-of-factly, with a response if positive.

Diagnosis, at **both levels**: **'what you've had is a panic attack'** — then the worry and avoidance — **'when that whole pattern is present, we call it panic disorder.'** Then **validate**: **'your symptoms are real. The tests being normal doesn't mean nothing happened.'** If he asks **'is it all in my head?'** — **'no, it's in your body.'**

**Differentials of the complaint, with why each is less likely**: heart attack or angina — 25, no risk factors, not exertional, no radiation, but we'll still do a tracing · clot on the lung — no travel, no leg symptoms, normal oxygen · collapsed lung — no injury · pericarditis — no viral illness, no positional change · **a rhythm disturbance, which is another reason for the tracing** · reflux or ulcer — no heartburn, no meal relation · chest wall — pressing doesn't reproduce it · and **two to check on bloods: thyrotoxicosis, and the caffeine.**

**The pathophysiology, in the patient version** — alarm, adrenaline, over-breathing, the tingling and unreality, then the catastrophic misinterpretation that fires the alarm again. **Check understanding once in the middle, not only at the end**, and draw it if you can.

Management and close: **CBT first line with a mental health plan · an SSRI if needed, low and slow · avoid sedatives · cut the coffee right down · ECG and bloods today, and say why you will stop there.** Safety net: **come back if the pattern changes, or you get pain with exercise, faint, or cough up blood.**
pefe: **Vital signs first** — and note that normal saturations and observations are part of your evidence, not just a formality.
**ECG in every chest pain presentation** — it is also a genuine differential test here, because **an arrhythmia such as SVT mimics panic closely and is easy to miss**.
**Bloods: FBC, electrolytes and renal function, thyroid function, glucose.** **Thyrotoxicosis is the classic organic mimic of anxiety** and must be excluded before you settle.
**Troponin only if the story or the ECG warrants it.**
**Urine drug screen where stimulant use is suspected** — asked non-judgementally, and disclosure handled without moralising.
**Chest X-ray only if a respiratory cause is genuinely in play.**
**Holter or ambulatory monitoring** if the palpitations are abrupt in onset and offset and an arrhythmia stays on your list.

**Then stop — and say why out loud.** **'I don't want to keep repeating tests, because that tends to feed the worry rather than settle it.'** Ordering a CT, echocardiogram and Holter 'to be safe' is a listed fail.

**The discriminating issue is diagnostic overshadowing, not the angina.** People with severe mental illness die **15 to 20 years earlier**, mostly of cardiovascular disease. Treat his chest pain exactly as you would anyone's.
The stem names schizophrenia for two reasons: **antipsychotic cardiometabolic risk explaining coronary disease at 40**, and the **three-question psychiatric screen** the examiner is waiting for.

Three reasons to give him, in plain words: **the character of the pain — central, heavy, to the neck, worse on exertion, better with rest · his risk factors — father's MI at 50, a pack a day, weight, diet, no exercise · the medication that keeps him well raises his heart risk.**

**Because it is new within 48 hours, do not discharge without excluding ACS.** Classically, new-onset angina within two months sits in the unstable category whatever the pattern — say so and you satisfy either examiner.

The test that makes the diagnosis is **functional: exercise stress ECG (Bruce protocol, steps every 3 minutes) or stress echo**. **ST depression of 1 mm or more, horizontal or downsloping, is positive.** Add that **CTCA is increasingly first-line**.

plan: **'Before I start, could I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?'** Then WIPE and the psych habit: **'everything we discuss stays between you and me, unless there's a risk of harm to you or someone else.'** Four seconds, and it unlocks the risk question later.

**'Jack, tell me more about this pain'** — then stay quiet. Follow with the empathy line: **'I'm sorry to hear that, and I understand your concern. I'll do my best to find the cause today.'** Both are separately scored.

Signpost, then the four questions for any known condition: **'I noticed you have schizophrenia — can I ask a few quick questions, because it may be relevant to your chest pain?'** → **when were you diagnosed · what treatment, and can you take it regularly · any side effects — weight gain, dizziness on standing, shakiness, dry mouth · do you see your GP and psychiatrist regularly?**

**Three questions, not thirty.** **'I ask everyone this — have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else?'** → **'do you ever hear, see or feel things that other people don't?'** → **'do you ever feel anyone is trying to harm you, or that someone is controlling you?'** Then get out.

Cardiovascular risk factors in one continuous run — **this case was built around them**: **family history of heart attack or stroke · ever told you have high blood pressure, cholesterol or diabetes · smoking, how much and how long · alcohol · recreational drugs · what do you usually eat in a day · any regular exercise?**

FAIL — Saying calcium lowers the potassium. It protects; it does not lower.
FAIL — Treating acutely and leaving him on ramipril and spironolactone.

dx: **Severe hyperkalaemia, K 7.2, WITH ECG changes** — acute-on-chronic kidney injury in stage 4 CKD. **The number is not the emergency; the ECG is.**
**Severity: mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe 6.5 or more · ANY level with ECG change is severe.** That last row overrides every row above it.
ECG progression: **tall peaked T waves → flat P and long PR → wide QRS → P waves lost → sine wave → VF or asystole**. A normal ECG at 7.2 is **not reassurance**.

**Four mechanisms at once, and saying all four is what separates a good answer from a list**: **stage 4 CKD sets the baseline · gastroenteritis and poor intake have caused an AKI on top · ramipril and spironolactone together are additive · the acidosis (HCO3 16) shifts potassium out of cells.**
**Three jobs, and know which drug does which. PROTECT · SHIFT · REMOVE.** The follow-up question is asked almost every time.

**PROTECT: calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL IV over 2–3 minutes** on the monitor, **repeat at 5 minutes if the ECG has not improved**. **It does not lower the potassium** — it stabilises the myocardium for **30 to 60 minutes**.

**SHIFT: 10 units of short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% glucose IV over 15–30 minutes** — onset 15–30 min, lasts 4–6 h. **Hourly BGL for at least 6 hours, said unprompted** — delayed hypoglycaemia is the commonest complication. Plus **salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised**, additive. **Bicarbonate only if acidotic**, and the evidence is weak.

**REMOVE: haemodialysis is definitive here** — oliguric, eGFR 16. **Involve renal and retrieval NOW, not after two failed rounds** — transfer time is the rate-limiting step. Loop diuretic only if passing urine and not volume deplete. **Modern binders, not resonium, and never as the acute answer.**

**Withhold ramipril and spironolactone**, and sweep the class list: **ACEi/ARB · potassium-sparing diuretics · NSAIDs · trimethoprim · heparin · beta-blockers · ciclosporin and tacrolimus · digoxin in toxicity · supplements and salt substitutes.** **Recheck K at 1–2 hours** on continuous monitoring.

To the patient, **explain the effect, never the number**: **'a salt called potassium is much higher than it should be · when it gets too high it upsets the electrical rhythm of your heart · the calcium does not lower it, it protects your heart while the rest works · two of your tablets hold potassium in, I am stopping both today, please do not restart them until you are reviewed.'**
plan: **The single highest-scoring sentence in the station, before you read the rest of the panel: 'Examiner, before I go through these results in full — the potassium is 7.2, which is in the severe range. I would attach cardiac monitoring and obtain a 12-lead ECG immediately, and I would check whether the sample was reported as haemolysed.'**

Read the ECG **in order — rate · P · PR · QRS · T — then conclude**. A short ordered read-out beats a list of adjectives. If challenged on ischaemia: **hyperacute T waves are broad-based and asymmetrical; it is the company they keep — flat P, long PR, wide QRS — that makes the diagnosis.**

The biochemistry: **severe hyperkalaemia · creatinine 312 and eGFR 16 = advanced renal impairment · urea 24 with that creatinine suggests a prerenal component, so AKI on CKD · bicarbonate 16 is a metabolic acidosis, which itself shifts potassium out of cells · mild hyponatraemia fits volume depletion.**

**The causes — all four, not one.** Then add the three questions you must ask by name: **over-the-counter anti-inflammatories · recent trimethoprim · potassium-based salt substitutes.** He is taking ibuprofen for his knee and will not mention it unless asked.
Management as **three jobs, naming which drug does which**. Protect, then shift, then remove — and say **'this does not lower the potassium'** as you say calcium, before the examiner can ask.

Say unprompted: **hourly BGL for 6 hours · recheck K at 1–2 hours · continuous monitoring · withhold ramipril and spironolactone · cautious volume replacement · renal referral and retrieval now.** Rurally, a **point-of-care blood gas** gives a potassium in minutes — treat on the ECG while awaiting the formal result. **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
Explain to the patient in plain words. **Never quote 7.2** — he will look blank and say 'is that bad?'. Effect, then what you are doing, then the two tablets you are stopping.

His three questions, in order. **'Am I going to have a heart attack?'** → not in the usual sense, this affects the rhythm rather than blocking an artery, **but do not understate it**. **'Is it something I did?'** → **'you have not done anything wrong.'** **'Do I have to go to Adelaide?'** → possibly, and **'I am arranging that conversation now rather than waiting. Is there someone you would like me to call?'**
pefe: **ECG and cardiac monitoring in your first sentence** — before you finish reading the panel. Not asking for an ECG is a fail on its own regardless of the total.

**Ask whether the sample was haemolysed**, whether processing was delayed, and what the platelet and white cell counts were — **but only as an exclusion after the ECG, never as an opening assumption**.

Three questions to ask every time: **was it haemolysed · is the patient passing urine** (anuria removes your safest route and moves dialysis up) **· is anything still making it worse** — rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, or a drug still in the system.
**Point-of-care blood gas** for a potassium in minutes where you are. **Recheck the potassium at 1–2 hours.** **Hourly BGL for at least 6 hours** after insulin.

Causes of a **falsely high** result: **haemolysis** (red cells hold potassium at about 25 times plasma) **· tight tourniquet or fist clenching · delayed processing or a cold sample · marked thrombocytosis or leucocytosis — a plasma rather than serum sample resolves it · contamination from a drip upstream**.

**Version B: ECG first, repeat the sample second, conclude third.** Repeat with a **wider-bore needle, no prolonged tourniquet, no fist clenching, straight to the laboratory**. Do not treat and do not cancel her procedure until a clean result is back.

**Always consider it first.** A well patient, an implausible result, a lab haemolysis comment

**ECG first, then repeat the sample properly.** Exclusion is a conclusion, not an opening assumption
**Reduced excretion — CKD and AKI**
**Creatinine 312, eGFR 16, urea 24** with a prerenal pattern; gastroenteritis and poor intake
Urine output, volume state, recent illness, nephrotoxins
**Volume replacement, stop contributors, dialysis if refractory or anuric**

Tasks are the same in both versions — interpret the results and any further investigation to the examiner → state the likely causes → outline immediate management → explain the situation to the patient. The two versions land on DIFFERENT answers.
rows: A · the sick one

68-year-old man, CKD stage 4, rural ED, two days of lethargy and generalised muscle weakness after gastroenteritis last week, drinking little. On ramipril, spironolactone, metformin, atorvastatin. BP 104/62, PR 52. K⁺ 7.2, urea 24.1, creatinine 312, eGFR 16, bicarbonate 16. ECG: bradycardic, flat P, long PR, broad QRS, peaked T.

SEVERE HYPERKALAEMIA with ECG changes — MULTIFACTORIAL: CKD sets the floor, acute illness and dehydration precipitate, ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone are additive, acidosis shifts K⁺ out of cells. Treat now.
B · the well one

44-year-old woman, entirely well, routine bloods before a minor procedure. Lab phones K⁺ 6.1. No symptoms, no relevant medications, normal renal function, lab comments 'specimen haemolysed'. ECG normal.
PSEUDOHYPERKALAEMIA — repeat the sample properly. But get the ECG FIRST and confirm it is normal before concluding the result is spurious, not after.
versions.note: The trap in version B splits candidates two ways and both fail: treating a haemolysed sample with insulin–dextrose in a well patient, or dismissing it as artefact with no ECG and no repeat. ECG first, repeat second, treat only if confirmed. Severity: mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe ≥6.5 · ANY level with ECG change = severe, and that row overrides the rest. A normal ECG at 7.2 is not reassurance. Practice cards in the source (crush injury/rhabdomyolysis, Addison, trimethoprim interaction, tumour lysis, dialysis patient with broad-complex tachycardia) are partner drills, not recalls.

stem: A 52-year-old man has presented complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath that started one hour ago. The pain began while he was chopping wood.
Vital signs: BP 135/85 · pulse 78 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 97% on room air · T 36.8°C. He has no history of bleeding disorders.
The ECG is handed to you with the stem.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your management plan to the patient

dx: **Acute anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction, proximal LAD territory.** **The declared predominant assessment area is management — task 1 will not fail you, task 2 will.** Most candidates finish early; **that is a warning sign, not a comfort**.
**Six numbers, and only six: 300 · 600 · 400 micrograms · 2.5–5 · 4–8 · 92%.** Say **drug, dose, route and when you would repeat it**, every time. The examiner is holding a checklist of numbers.
**Notify the cardiac team first — before any drug**, and say so out loud. **'The first thing I've already done is let the cardiac team know, so they're getting ready for you.'**

**Aspirin 300 mg chewed** rather than swallowed — faster buccal and gastric absorption — dissolved in water if he cannot chew. **Clopidogrel 600 mg as a single load before PCI**; **ticagrelor 180 mg is the more commonly preferred agent in Australian practice**, and is **never given with fibrinolysis**. VERIFY

**GTN spray 400 MICROGRAMS sublingual, repeatable every 5 minutes up to three doses** — micrograms, not milligrams; **one wrong unit undoes an otherwise specific answer**. Withhold for **right ventricular infarction, hypotension, bradycardia or extreme tachycardia, severe aortic stenosis, HOCM, or a PDE-5 inhibitor within 24–48 hours**. CORRECTION — the danger is profound **hypotension**, not hypertension, because the right ventricle is preload dependent.

**IV access ×2 · troponin plus FBE, UEC, glucose, lipids and coagulation · morphine 2.5–5 mg IV for pain · ondansetron 4–8 mg IV for nausea.** And the sentence that matters: **'we are not waiting for the blood test — the tracing is enough to act on, and waiting would cost you heart muscle.'**

**Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92% — say the threshold instead of giving it.** Routine oxygen in a normoxic patient **causes coronary vasoconstriction** and offered no benefit in randomised trials. Some Australian guidance uses 93%; quote 92% and say 'per Therapeutic Guidelines'. VERIFY

**The reperfusion decision must be spoken, not assumed. PCI if achievable within 120 minutes of first medical contact, with a target first-medical-contact-to-device time of 90 minutes or less.** In lay words: **a very fine tube passed from the wrist, sometimes the groin, dye injected to see which tube is blocked, then opened with a balloon — 'ballooning' — or a stent, 'a tiny metal scaffold that props the tube open'.** **Awake but comfortable**, and cardiology takes consent.

**'Am I going to die?' is answered with action, never with 'no': 'I'm not going to pretend this isn't serious — it is. But you got here fast, we've caught it early, and the treatment works well. I'm going to stay with you.'** Then **support, family — 'is there anyone you'd like me to call?' — concerns, and a one-line summary.**

Long term, **SAVA**: **Statin high-intensity and lifelong — atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg** (CORRECTION — simvastatin is not a high-intensity option) · **ACE inhibitor lifelong unless contraindicated** · **beta blocker once euvolaemic and haemodynamically stable** · **dual antiplatelets for 12 months, then aspirin 100 mg lifelong**, adding **pantoprazole or rabeprazole** if a PPI is needed, because **omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 and reduce clopidogrel activation**. **Cardiac rehabilitation for everyone.** **No private driving for about 2 weeks after an ACS.** VERIFY
plan: **Park the patient in one sentence, then turn away**: **'Hello James, I'm one of the doctors looking after you. I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly. I've been asked to look at your heart tracing with my examiner first — give me one minute and I'll come straight back with the plan.'** **No full WIPE and no stability ritual — every vital sign is printed in the stem.**

The ECG to the examiner, **one minute, fixed order**: **patient details, date and calibration · rate · rhythm · axis · PR · QRS · ST segments naming every lead · reciprocal change · Q waves · territory.** End on **acute anterolateral STEMI, most likely proximal LAD, time-critical.** **Three minutes here cannot pass you — it only steals the time management needs.**

Turn back and **give the diagnosis before the plan, in the words 'heart attack'**: **'one of the blood tubes supplying the muscle of your heart has become blocked by a clot, so part of that muscle isn't getting the blood and oxygen it needs — and that's what's causing this pain. It is serious. It is also very treatable, and we're starting right now.'** Then: **the cardiac team already knows.**

**'There are six things I'm going to do in the next few minutes. Let me take them one at a time.'** Steps 1 and 2: **aspirin 300 mg chewed, and clopidogrel 600 mg as a single dose — 'between them, these stop the clot from getting any bigger while we work on opening it.'**

Step 3, **the nitrate with the question attached so they are one action, not two**: **'a spray under your tongue called glyceryl trinitrate, 400 micrograms — it widens the blood tubes and should take the edge off the pain, and I can repeat it every five minutes up to three doses. Before I give it, one quick question I have to ask everybody: have you taken Viagra, Cialis or anything similar in the last 24 hours?'** If yes — **withhold it, say why, and use morphine instead.**

Steps 4 and 5: **a small drip in the arm · bloods through it, the important one a troponin, 'a chemical released when heart muscle is injured' · morphine 2.5 to 5 mg as a starting dose · ondansetron 4 to 8 mg for the nausea.** When he asks how long the blood test takes: **'an hour or so — but we are not waiting for it.'**

Step 6, **oxygen as a threshold, not a reflex**: **'it's 97 per cent at the moment, which is good, so you don't need oxygen — but if it falls below 92 per cent I will start it.'** Plus **repeat tracings every hour or two.**

**Reperfusion — the sentence the station is built around, then translated.** **'Because we're in a hospital with a catheter laboratory, the right treatment is to physically reopen the artery, and we aim to do that within 90 minutes.'** Then the lay explanation, and answer **'is that surgery, are you cutting my chest open?'** with **'no cut to the chest at all — a small needle puncture at the wrist, and most people go home within a couple of days.'**

**Support, family, concerns — do not leave these out.** **'I'm going to stay with you, and you are in the safest place you could be right now. Is there anyone you'd like me to call?'** Then **'do you have any questions or concerns about anything I've said?'**

**Say the decision out loud with the numbers**: **'the nearest hospital that can reopen the artery mechanically is 400 kilometres away — about four hours. The cut-off is two hours, and we cannot meet it. So the right treatment here is a clot-dissolving medicine, and I want to give it within the next 30 minutes.'**

**The four bleeding questions before you name the drug** — ten seconds, and all the examiner needs to see. **Absolute contraindications**: any previous intracranial haemorrhage · ischaemic stroke within 6 months · cerebral vascular malformation or intracranial tumour · **suspected aortic dissection** · active bleeding or bleeding diathesis · significant closed head or facial trauma within 3 months · recent major, intracranial or spinal surgery.

**The lytic, plus what goes with it — never instead of it.** **Tenecteplase**, a single weight-based IV bolus, is the agent used in most Australian rural STEMI pathways because it is far easier and safer to give in a small hospital. **Alteplase** is the accelerated alternative: **15 mg IV bolus, then 0.75 mg/kg over 30 minutes, then 0.5 mg/kg over 60 minutes.** Either is given **with enoxaparin (or unfractionated heparin) and with dual antiplatelets**. **CORRECTION — clopidogrel is not one dose for both versions. With fibrinolysis: 300 mg load if 75 or younger, and 75 mg with NO load if over 75**, because the loading dose increases intracranial bleeding in the elderly. **Ticagrelor and prasugrel are not given with fibrinolysis.** VERIFY

tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
You will be shown an ECG — give the examiner your overall impression and the key features that support it
Explain your likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **Acute pericarditis, most likely viral** — and **never diagnosed without excluding infarction**. Pericarditis and MI are genuinely easy to confuse, which is exactly why you always do **an ECG and always send a troponin**.

**The three-clue signature: better leaning forward · worse lying flat · a recent flu-like illness.** Absent cardiovascular risk factors are **supportive only — their presence does not exclude pericarditis**. A 55-year-old smoker with hypertension can absolutely have viral pericarditis.

**The ECG in four words: widespread · concave · no reciprocal change · PR depression.** Widespread means it **crosses territories** — **no single coronary artery supplies I, II and V2 to V6 together**. **Disregard aVR**, where ST depression and PR elevation are expected, not reciprocal.
**Voltage criteria: more than 1 mm in the limb leads, more than 2 mm in the chest leads.** Saying the numbers earns marks, and it explains why elevation looks more obvious in the chest leads.

Pericarditis versus MI: **posture changes pericarditic pain and never changes MI pain** · pericarditic pain is **often pleuritic, which is expected rather than exclusionary** · a viral prodrome with fever and fatigue · **concave and widespread versus convex 'tombstone' and territorial with reciprocal depression** · a **friction rub** · troponin normal, **or raised in myopericarditis**.

To the patient: **'the heart sits inside a thin covering, a bit like a sac. In pericarditis that covering becomes inflamed, and that inflammation is what causes the pain.'** Then **the three reasons — the mark-earning sentence**: the posture, the recent flu, and the tracing.

**Never over-reassure.** **'It looks much more like pericarditis than a heart attack — but I want to be honest with you: the two can look very similar, and I'm not going to tell you a heart attack is excluded until I have a blood test back.'** That troponin is **why he is managed in hospital rather than general practice**.

Treatment in two words: **colchicine plus an NSAID**. **Ibuprofen 400–600 mg three times daily with food**, continued until symptoms settle and CRP normalises, then tapered — **aspirin 600–900 mg three times daily if the pericarditis is post-MI**. **Colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily, or once daily under about 70 kg, for 3 months** — it substantially reduces recurrence. **Corticosteroids are not first line; they increase recurrence.** VERIFY

**Restrict strenuous exercise until symptoms resolve and inflammatory markers normalise**, longer for athletes and for myopericarditis. Causes to know: **viral, the commonest · autoimmune (SLE, rheumatoid) · bacterial and TB · post-MI and Dressler · uraemia · malignancy · radiotherapy · post-cardiac surgery · trauma · drugs**.

**Tamponade is the emergency: hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds — Beck's triad — with pulsus paradoxus and rising distress.** Say it out loud: **stop the history, MET call, IV fluids, urgent bedside echocardiogram, cardiology for pericardiocentesis.** SA: as a GP, **refer to the emergency department — you need the troponin now**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for retrieval.
plan: To the examiner, before a word to the patient: **'may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** It is a scoring point in its own right, and it is how you detect tamponade.

WIPE, introduce, confirm identity. Open question, then **acknowledge the fear and park it**: **'I understand why that's on your mind — I'll come back to that. First, let me ask you some questions about the pain.'** Signpost and gain consent.

**SOCRATES, finished before you commit — treat it as a sealed box.** **Where exactly, can you point to it · when did it start, sudden or gradual · what does it feel like, sharp, dull, crushing, tight · does it move anywhere · any shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, palpitations, dizziness, cough or fever · constant or does it come and go · out of ten.** Everything so far screams MI.

**The question the station turns on — and the acted clue**: **'is there anything that makes it worse? Anything that makes it better? I notice you're sitting forward and holding your chest — is it easier like that? And what happens if you lie flat? Does it change with a deep breath or a cough?'** Register it, thank him, **and keep going without announcing the diagnosis**.
The aetiology question: **'have you been unwell at all in the last week or two — any cold or flu-like symptoms? Have you felt feverish or unusually tired since?'**

The life-threatening screen, one efficient block: **exertional pain before today, sweating, nausea, a sense of doom · was it ever tearing or going through to your back, any difference between the arms · sudden breathlessness, coughing up blood, calf pain or swelling, long flights or car trips, recent surgery or immobility · fever, productive cough, night sweats, weight loss · any forceful vomiting before the pain started · any injury or heavy lifting, tender to press · any rash or blistering on the chest wall · burning pain related to meals or acid coming up.**

Excuse yourself to the patient, then the ECG in **seven steps**: rate → rhythm → P waves → PR → QRS → ST → impression, **with the voltage criteria stated**, ending on **widespread, concave, no reciprocal change, PR depression**.

Diagnosis in plain English, then **the three reasons**: the pain is better leaning forward and worse flat; there was a flu-like illness ten days ago and most of these are viral; and the tracing shows the changes we see in this condition rather than the pattern of a heart attack.
**'So it's definitely not a heart attack?'** — the honest answer, and the troponin as the reason for admission rather than discharge.

Differentials to the patient: **long, specific, one clause each, delivered quickly, life-threatening first.** MI, PE, dissection, pneumothorax, oesophageal rupture — then name heart failure, aortic stenosis, pneumonia, lung cancer, reflux, peptic ulcer, shingles, costochondritis and a psychogenic cause in one sweep.

Plan and safety net: **troponin, chest X-ray, inflammatory markers, echocardiogram · colchicine and an NSAID · avoid strenuous exercise.** Return immediately for **much worse or different pain, increasing breathlessness, feeling faint or blacking out, palpitations, high fever, or swelling of the legs or abdomen.** Summarise and check understanding.

**When the bell sounds, stop the history immediately and move on.** Candidates lose whole marked tasks by talking over it.

**The three-clue signature: better leaning forward · worse lying flat · a recent flu-like illness.** The role-player **sits leaning forward clutching his chest** — he is acting the answer, so name the observation and ask directly.

**Asking the examiner is its own marked task here.** Excuse yourself first — **'thank you for answering the questions, James. My apologies, I'll just talk to my examiner for a second'** — then ask for **every finding by name**, with no chit-chat.

**The friction rub must survive any compression of that request.** It is a **superficial scratching or creaking sound at the left sternal edge, with the patient sitting forward in end-expiration, and it is evanescent**. **Never over-reassure**: **'it looks much more like pericarditis than a heart attack, but the two can look very similar and I won't tell you a heart attack is excluded until I have a blood test back.'** Treatment is **colchicine plus an NSAID** — **ibuprofen 400–600 mg three times daily with food**, **colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily for 3 months**; **steroids are not first line and increase recurrence**. stem: Lily, a 50-year-old woman, presents with on-and-off chest pain. Her father had a heart attack recently. She is worried she is having a heart attack too.
An ECG has already been done — it will be handed to you approximately 4–5 minutes into the station. Vital signs are provided on request.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Interpret the ECG to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses, including an explicit response to her concern about a heart attack

dx: **Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease** — chronic, on and off, **burning, retrosternal with an epigastric component**, worse lying flat, better leaning forward, **with acid brash and water brash**, on a background of **coffee, alcohol and regular NSAID use**.

**The planted red herring: 'better leaning forward, worse lying down' is the classic pericarditis descriptor and it is here on purpose.** It is also entirely consistent with reflux — **lying flat abolishes gravity's protection against acid moving up the oesophagus**. Acknowledge it and keep going rather than announcing a diagnosis.

**'I'm not sure if it's related to food' is also deliberate** — the case protecting its own difficulty. **Ambiguity is a signal to keep asking.** Probe all three axes: **activity and rest · position · food**.

**Acid brash and water brash are the two questions that make the diagnosis.** **'Do you get an acidic or bitter taste at the back of your mouth?'** and **'have you noticed your mouth suddenly filling with saliva?'** Both yes.

**The two-axis rule: pain that tracks with meals and posture is oesophageal; pain that tracks with exertion and rest is cardiac.** On radiation — **cardiac characteristically goes to the arm; oesophageal sits in the epigastrium and may reach the jaw but not the arm.**

**A normal ECG does not exclude ischaemia** — say it explicitly, to the examiner and in plain words to her. What lets you settle on GORD is **the combination**: chronic non-exertional burning pain, no arm radiation, no cardiac associated symptoms, minimal personal risk factors, positive reflux features and clear triggers — **plus** the normal tracing. **Never let the ECG do the work alone.**

**Two reasons, always**, when you address her fear: **the tracing is normal, and — more importantly — the character of the pain doesn't fit heart pain**, which is heavy and crushing, exertional, eased by rest and radiating to arm or jaw. Then **offer the cardiovascular risk assessment anyway** — that converts reassurance into partnership.

**Premature cardiovascular disease means an event before 55 in men and 65 in women.** Her father was **78**, so the family history carries much less weight for her own risk — and **asking the age is the question most candidates forget**. A father who had one at 40–45 would change your threshold considerably.

Management: **stop the ibuprofen and substitute paracetamol** — the highest-yield step, because prescribing a PPI while she continues the NSAID **treats the smoke and leaves the fire**. Then **cut coffee and alcohol · smaller, more frequent meals · nothing within 3 hours of lying down · elevate the head of the bed 15–20 cm with blocks, not extra pillows · avoid tight clothing**. **A PPI once daily for 4–8 weeks** — esomeprazole 20 mg, pantoprazole 20–40 mg or omeprazole 20 mg, **30–60 minutes before breakfast** — then review and step down to the lowest effective dose. VERIFY

**Screen the alarm features before you label anything benign: dysphagia · odynophagia · weight loss · melaena · haematemesis · persistent vomiting · anaemia · new onset over 50.** Safety net: **exertional pain, radiation to arm or jaw, sweating, breathlessness or collapse → call 000, don't drive.** Food sticking, vomiting blood, or black tarry stools → urgent review. **Review in 4–6 weeks — failure to respond is itself an indication for endoscopy.**
plan: To the examiner: **'before I begin, may I please have the patient's vital signs?'** — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, saturations, temperature. **Verbalise stability even when the stem says vitals are stable.** Every chest pain station earns this.

WIPE, confirm name and date of birth, permission and purpose, check she is comfortable — then **the structured reassuring statement, which is a scoring moment**: **'Lily, I completely understand how frightening chest pain can be, especially after what happened to your dad. Let me ask you a few questions, then I'll look at your heart tracing. We'll work out the cause together, and I promise I'll address your concerns and come up with the best plan for you.'**

Block 1, the pain analysis: **where exactly, point with one finger · when did it start, sudden or gradual · what does it feel like, burning, crushing, tight, sharp, tearing · does it travel anywhere, arm, jaw, neck, back · constant or on and off, getting worse · out of ten** — and, because the pain is months old, **does it ever wake you from sleep?**

**Do not accept one answer on aggravating and relieving factors — push all three axes**: **does it come on walking uphill or climbing stairs, and settle with rest · lying flat, bending over, leaning forward · after meals, before meals, large meals, late at night?** Also ask **what she has tried — antacids, peppermint**.

Cardiac symptom screen, asked even though the pain sounds benign: **shortness of breath · nausea or vomiting · sweating or clamminess · palpitations · dizziness, blackouts or collapse · ankle swelling · orthopnoea · waking at night gasping · exercise tolerance.** Their absence is part of your evidence.

Cardiovascular risk factors, **every one**: **blood pressure · blood sugar · cholesterol · smoking · alcohol · weight · activity · family history** — and then the question most candidates forget: **'you mentioned your dad — how old was he when it happened?'**

Other cardiac and respiratory causes in one block: **recent viral illness or fever, sharp pain worse on deep breath or coughing** (pericarditis) · **exertional breathlessness or blackouts, known murmur** (aortic stenosis) · **sudden maximal tearing pain through to the back** (dissection) · **sudden breathlessness, haemoptysis, calf pain, long travel, surgery, immobility, the pill or HRT, previous clot, active cancer** (PE) · **fever, cough, sputum** (pneumonia) · **weight loss, appetite, night sweats, hoarse voice, neck lumps** — which also covers your oesophageal and gastric cancer red flags.

**Block 6 — where the case is decided.** **Any tummy pain, nausea or vomiting · do you get an acidic or bitter taste at the back of your mouth · has your mouth suddenly filled with saliva · does food or fluid come back up when you bend over or lie down · any chronic dry cough, hoarse voice in the morning, sore throat, night wheeze or dental problems?**

**Alarm features before any reassurance**: **does food stick when you swallow · does it hurt to swallow · any unintentional weight loss · have your bowel motions been black, tarry and sticky** — say it in those words, not 'melaena' and not 'dark stools' — **any vomiting of blood · persistent vomiting · any family history of stomach or oesophageal cancer?** Then the ulcer discriminators: **does it go through to your back, is it a deep dull ache rather than burning, does it wake you at night?**

Triggers and the medication question, which earns marks twice: **do you drink a lot of tea or coffee · spicy, fatty or fried food, chocolate, large meals late at night · are you taking any medications at all, including anything over the counter or from the pharmacy?** **NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, calcium channel blockers, nitrates, anticholinergics, doxycycline and potassium supplements** all cause or worsen reflux.

Sweep-up with the time left: **any rash or blistering on your chest or back · is it worse when you move, twist or press on your chest · how has your mood been, any stress at home or work** — then **SADMA, past history, family history, and confirm there is nothing else worrying her**.

The ECG: read it **systematically and out loud** — details and calibration, rate, rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS, ST, T, QTc — then **have the courage to call it normal**. Then **explain it to her, not to the examiner**: the headline first, each finding in everyday language, and **honest about the limits** — one normal tracing today does not rule out heart disease forever.

Diagnosis: **name it → explain it simply → give your reasons.** **'Normally there's a valve between your food pipe and your stomach that keeps the acid where it belongs. When it doesn't close properly, acid comes back up, and because the food pipe isn't built to handle acid it gets irritated — that irritation is the burning.'** Reasons: the burning quality, the posture relationship, the acid and water brash, and the coffee, alcohol and ibuprofen.

**Address the heart-attack concern head-on with two named reasons**, then: **'because your dad had a heart attack, I do want to check your overall heart risk properly with some blood tests and a blood pressure check, so we're looking after that side of things too.'**

**Differentials briskly — coverage beats depth with the clock running.** Heart, pericarditis, stomach ulcer, clot on the lung, collapsed lung, chest infection, gallbladder, chest wall, shingles, stress — one clause each, and keep going until the bell.

Plan and safety net: **stop the ibuprofen · lifestyle and bed elevation · a 4–8 week PPI trial · FBC, H. pylori, lipids and glucose · review in 4–6 weeks.** **000 for exertional or radiating pain with sweating, breathlessness or collapse; urgent review for food sticking, vomiting blood or black tarry stools.** Summarise and **check understanding**.
pefe: **Vital signs first**, and say the word stable out loud.

Examination to request: **cardiovascular and respiratory · abdominal including epigastric tenderness · chest wall palpation for reproducible tenderness · skin inspection for a zoster rash · BMI and blood pressure**.
**ECG read systematically**: details and calibration → rate → rhythm → P waves → PR → QRS → ST → T → QTc. **Then have the courage to call a normal ECG normal.**

**Mild concave ST elevation in the lateral and precordial leads is benign early repolarisation**, not pericarditis — which needs widespread elevation across territories, usually PR depression, and a compatible history.
**A single normal ECG in a pain-free patient does not exclude coronary disease or an evolving ACS.** Say so explicitly.
**FBC** for iron deficiency anaemia from occult upper GI blood loss — anaemia means endoscopy regardless of other features.
**H. pylori urea breath test or stool antigen** — withhold the PPI for 2 weeks beforehand to avoid a false negative.
**Fasting lipids, HbA1c or fasting glucose and U&E** for absolute cardiovascular risk, justified by the family history. **LFTs and upper abdominal ultrasound** only if biliary features.

**Troponin and serial ECG only if any feature raises suspicion of ACS.** **Upper endoscopy is not first line** — reserve it for alarm features, new onset over 50 with persistent symptoms, or failure of an adequate PPI trial.

**Oesophageal pain can radiate to the jaw. It is the ARM that discriminates towards cardiac.** That single fact rescues this station.

**Acid brash, water brash and relief with peppermint tea are all positive** — and peppermint is itself a reflux trigger as well as a smooth-muscle relaxant, so its effect is not reassurance about the heart.

**Overlap is real, in both directions.** Reflux and ischaemia genuinely overlap, and **both can be relieved by glyceryl trinitrate**, which relaxes oesophageal smooth muscle as well as coronary arteries. **Never use 'the antacid helped' or 'the GTN helped' as proof that pain is not cardiac.**

**A 28-year-old is not automatically low risk.** In a young person with genuinely ischaemic-sounding chest pain, actively consider **cocaine or amphetamine use · familial hypercholesterolaemia · myocarditis and pericarditis · spontaneous pneumothorax · pulmonary embolism · connective tissue disorders with aortic dissection.** **Ask the recreational drug question, non-judgementally, as part of SADMA.**

**Yes, you still ask every cardiovascular risk factor even when you think you know the recall.** Two practical reasons: **the role-player may have been changed, and the examiner is marking your process, not your recall memory.**

dx: **Acute inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction** — ST elevation in **II, III and aVF** with **reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL**.

**The station in one line: typical exertional chest pain plus cardiovascular risk factors plus an ECG read in seven steps → name the diagnosis early, justify it with three reasons, then fire out a long differential list, life-threatening first.**

**The key point of every chest pain station is the cardiovascular risk factor block**, asked as a fixed set of five: **family history of heart attack or stroke · diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol · smoking, how much and for how long · alcohol · weight.** **Candidates fail this station far more often for skipping risk factors than for missing an exotic differential.**

**Bradycardia at about 50 is a clue, not noise.** The **right coronary artery usually supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes**, so inferior infarcts commonly cause **bradycardia and heart block**. Saying so shows you understand the anatomy rather than reading numbers.

**The prompt that rescues the pain history**: when he answers 'I haven't noticed' to aggravating and relieving factors, **do not move on** — follow immediately with **'does activity or exercise make it worse, and does rest make it better?'** then **'and do you have pain at rest right now?'** Those two questions convert a vague story into a typical anginal one, and **pain at rest means acute coronary syndrome, not stable angina**.

**Three reasons — and reasoning scores more than explanation**: **the pain is typical, central, radiating to jaw and shoulder and worse with activity · you have risk factors, including a strong family history, blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking · and the ECG shows the changes of a heart attack.** Then **reason one or two differentials and list the rest**.

**Do now**: resuscitation area, **continuous cardiac monitoring, defibrillator to the bedside, two IV lines**, **a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival**, **aspirin 300 mg chewed or dispersed** unless genuinely allergic, and **titrated IV opioid with an antiemetic**. **Oxygen only if hypoxic — routine oxygen in a normoxic patient is not beneficial.** VERIFY

**Nitrate only for ongoing ischaemic pain and only if the systolic pressure is adequate.** **Withhold in suspected right ventricular infarction, in hypotension, and after a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor in the last 24–48 hours** — which is why you **ask about sildenafil in every chest pain history**.

**Activate the STEMI pathway and call cardiology now — do not wait for troponin. In a STEMI a normal troponin does not change the plan.** **Primary PCI where it can be delivered within the time targets from first medical contact; otherwise fibrinolysis, then transfer to a PCI-capable centre.** **Exclude aortic dissection before giving antiplatelets and anticoagulation.**

Longer term: **dual antiplatelet therapy, statin, beta-blocker and an ACE inhibitor or ARB as tolerated · smoking cessation, blood pressure, lipids, diabetes, weight and activity · cardiac rehabilitation and GP follow-up · screen family members given the strong family history.** **Coronary care unit — this patient is not for discharge under any circumstances.** Safety net: recurrent chest pain, breathlessness, fainting or palpitations → **call 000**.
plan: To the examiner: **'before I begin I would like the patient's vital signs please — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation.'** Then name the bradycardia out loud.

WIPE, confirm identity, consent and comfort — then **the acknowledgement line, memorised**: **'I understand how concerning chest pain can be, James. Let me ask you a few questions, I'll try to find the cause and make the best management plan for you, and I'll address your concerns as quickly as I can.'** Eight seconds, and it buys you permission to go fast.

**SICORA**: **where is it — a point you can put a finger on, or an area · out of ten · crushing or sharp · when exactly did it start, constant or on and off, getting worse · does it travel anywhere · does anything make it better or worse.**

**The four discriminating questions, every time**: **is it related to breathing, does a deep breath make it worse · does leaning forward make it better · does eating have any relation to it · is it worse on movement or pressing on your chest?** Four noes here, and that is what makes the pain **typical** — say the word.

**The systems screen in fixed group order**, one or two questions each: **MI associated symptoms — breathlessness, sweating, nausea, palpitations · pericarditis — fever, chills, recent flu-like illness · heart failure — flat, pillows, ankle swelling · aortic stenosis — fainting on exertion · PE — calf swelling or pain, long travel, family history of clots · pneumothorax — chest trauma · pneumonia — fever, cough, noisy breathing · lung cancer — weight loss, appetite, lumps, haemoptysis · GI — abdominal pain, vomiting, acid or bitter taste, water brash, relation to eating · musculoskeletal and skin — pressing, movement, rash · psychogenic — stress and mood.**

**THE KEY POINT — the five risk factor questions, never omitted**: **any family history of heart attacks or strokes · any history of high sugar, high blood pressure or high fats in your blood · do you smoke, how much and for how long · how much alcohol · are you currently overweight?**

Close the history: **any recreational drugs** — cocaine and amphetamines cause coronary spasm — **any medications, and specifically anything like Viagra**, which contraindicates nitrates, **any allergies**, and **'is there anything else you'd like to tell me today?'**

Bell. **The ECG in seven steps, out loud, in a fixed order**: **rate → rhythm → P waves → PR → QRS → ST elevation, naming every lead and the territory → ST depression and reciprocal changes, looking deliberately at the opposite leads.** Then, because this is inferior, **the extra step: check V1**.

Impression, then to the patient: **'most likely you have a myocardial infarction — the same as a heart attack. This usually happens when one of the blood tubes of your heart becomes blocked, so the muscle stops getting enough oxygen, and that is what causes the chest pain.'** Then **the three reasons**.

Differentials: **reason the first one or two — pericarditis, no fever or flu-like illness; PE, no travel or leg swelling; pneumothorax, no injury — then drop the reasons and list the rest, life-threatening first**: dissection, oesophageal rupture, heart failure, aortic stenosis, pneumonia, lung cancer, reflux, peptic ulcer, costochondritis, shingles, and last, panic attack.

Plan and close: **aspirin and analgesia given, monitor on, cardiology called, catheter laboratory, coronary care unit — you will not be going home today.** Safety net: **tell us immediately if the pain worsens or you feel faint.** Summarise, offer to call his wife. **When the bell goes mid-sentence, finish the phrase and stop.**

**After naming a territory, deliberately look at the opposite leads and say what you see.** Inferior (II, III, aVF) → look at I and aVL. Anterolateral (I, aVL, V1–V6) → look at II, III and aVF.
**In an inferior infarct, check V1 for right ventricular involvement** — and confirm formally with **right-sided leads, especially V4R**, because these patients are preload dependent.

stem: James, a 49-year-old man, presented to the emergency department with chest pain that started 30 minutes ago.
Vital signs available on request. An ECG will be provided after the history — it may be small and low contrast on screen.
tasks: Take a focused history — 5 minutes. A warning bell sounds at 5 minutes
Interpret the ECG to the examiner — step by step, out loud, in a fixed order
Explain your likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **Acute anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction** — elevation in **I, aVL and V2 to V6**, with **reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF**. The tracing is deliberately unclear and **at first glance looks like pericarditis**.

**The discriminator, in one sentence: widespread ST elevation WITH reciprocal ST depression is an infarct; widespread ST elevation with NO reciprocal change is pericarditis.** That single question — **'have I looked at the opposite leads?'** — is what this station tests.

**The biggest mistake is going straight for an overall impression.** Most candidates glance at elevation everywhere and announce pericarditis, **and that is exactly how the station is designed to catch you**. Walk the steps and you always land on an answer; lead with the impression and you get it wrong.

How the reasoning actually runs: **the tracing is unclear, but rate, rhythm, P waves, PR and QRS are all readable and normal → elevation in the lateral leads → check I and aVL, about one small square, real → so elevation in I, aVL and V2–V6 → widespread means pericarditis or anterolateral infarct → look at the inferior leads → III and aVF show about a millimetre of depression → reciprocal change present → therefore not pericarditis.**

**Technique for a poor image: zoom in and say out loud that you are doing so. Compare the ST segment with the isoelectric line — the TP segment — not with your expectation.** **One small square counts**: a single small square of deviation, named in a lead, is a real finding. **Never invent a finding to fit a pattern. Describe, then interpret.**

**The key point remains the cardiovascular risk factor block** — here loaded with positives: **hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia, and a pack a day for twenty years**, with a father who had an MI at 60. **Miss this block and a flawless pain history still fails.**

**Carry your formulation into the ECG**: *typical chest pain plus cardiovascular risk factors*. Say it to yourself before you look at the tracing — **it stops a messy ECG from talking you out of an infarct**.

**Three reasons to the patient**: **the pain is typical — squeezing, central, radiating to the left arm, worse with activity · you have risk factors — blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol and smoking · and the ECG confirms it.** Then **reason two or three differentials and list the rest, life-threatening first**.

**Do now**: resuscitation area, **monitoring, defibrillator at the bedside, two IV lines**, **ECG within 10 minutes**, **aspirin 300 mg chewed**, titrated IV opioid and antiemetic, **oxygen only if hypoxic**, **nitrate only if the pressure allows and no phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor in 24–48 hours**. **Activate the STEMI pathway and call cardiology — do not wait for troponin.** VERIFY

**Anterolateral territory means proximal LAD** — a large infarct. **Primary PCI where it can be delivered within the time targets; otherwise fibrinolysis then transfer.** **Exclude aortic dissection before antiplatelets and anticoagulation.** Disposition is **the catheter laboratory and then coronary care** — not discharge. Safety net: **recurrent pain, breathlessness, fainting or palpitations → 000.**
plan: To the examiner: **'may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation?'** State stability out loud.

WIPE, confirm identity, consent — then **the acknowledgement line**: **'I understand how concerning chest pain can be, James. Let me ask a few questions so I can find the cause and make the best plan for you.'**

**SICORA**: **where exactly — a point or an area · out of ten · crushing or sharp · constant since it started · does it travel anywhere · anything make it better or worse** — and when he hasn't noticed, **'does activity make it worse and rest make it better?'** then **'do you have pain at rest right now?'**
**The four discriminators**: **related to breathing · to position, does leaning forward help · to eating · worse on movement or pressing.** Four noes, and the pain is **typical**.

**The systems screen in fixed group order**: **breathlessness, sweating, nausea, palpitations · fever, chills, recent flu-like illness · flat breathlessness, pillows, leg swelling · fainting on exertion · calf pain or swelling, long travel, family history of clots · chest trauma · cough, coughing blood · weight loss, appetite, lumps · abdominal pain, vomiting, acid or bitter taste · pressing or movement, any rash · stress and mood.**

**THE KEY POINT — the five risk factor questions**: **family history of heart attacks or strokes · high sugar, high blood pressure or high fats · smoking, how much and how long · alcohol · are you currently overweight?** In this version the answers are loaded: **hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia, a pack a day for twenty years.**
Close: **any medications, including anything like Viagra · any recreational drugs · any allergies · anything else you'd like to tell me?**
Bell. **Announce that you are zooming in**, then steps 1 to 5 — **rate, rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS, all normal** — even on a poor tracing these are readable.

**The ST segments, named lead by lead against the isoelectric line**: **about one small square of elevation in I and aVL, and elevation across V2 to V6.** Say the two options out loud: **pericarditis versus anterolateral infarct.**

**Then the step that decides it**: **'because the elevation is widespread, I'll look specifically at the inferior leads for reciprocal change. Lead II looks acceptable, but there is about one millimetre of ST depression in III and aVF. Reciprocal changes are present, which argues against pericarditis.'** Impression: **acute anterolateral STEMI.**

To the patient: **'James, you're having a myocardial infarction — a heart attack. One of the blood tubes of your heart is blocked, so the muscle isn't getting enough blood.'** When he asks **'are you sure?'** — acknowledge the shock, then **the three reasons**.

Differentials: **reason dissection, PE and pneumothorax briefly — not likely here, no travel or leg swelling, no injury — then list the rest**: oesophageal rupture, pericarditis, heart failure, aortic stenosis, pneumonia, lung cancer, reflux, peptic ulcer, costochondritis, shingles, panic attack.

Plan and close: **aspirin and pain relief, monitor, cardiology called, catheter laboratory, then coronary care.** **'If your pain worsens or you feel faint, tell us straight away.'** Summarise. **If the bell goes mid-sentence, finish the phrase — 'that's my list of differentials' — and stop.**

**Zoom in on a poor tracing and say that you are doing so.** Compare each ST segment with **the isoelectric line, the TP segment** — not with what you expect to see.

**Name every elevated lead. One small square, named in a lead, is a real finding** — say it rather than dismissing it because it is not dramatic.
**Then look deliberately at the opposite territory before committing.** Anterolateral elevation (I, aVL, V1–V6) → **check II, III and aVF**.

**FBC, UEC, glucose, lipids, coagulation** as a baseline before anticoagulation and contrast. **CXR** for a widened mediastinum or pneumothorax — must not delay the catheter laboratory. **Bedside echocardiogram** for wall motion and mechanical complications.

dx: **Herpes zoster of the right T4 dermatome** — reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in the dorsal root ganglion. **Name the dermatome: T4 is the nipple line.**

**The co-diagnosis is the station.** Why is a 40-year-old reactivating varicella? Weight loss, night sweats, exhaustion and a **firm right axillary node** → **lymphoma or leukaemia**. Also diabetes, steroids, HIV.
Discriminators: **a unilateral band from nipple to back that stops dead at the midline · sharp and stabbing · ALLODYNIA, the bedsheet hurts · burning or tingling for a day or two beforehand**.
**No rash does not exclude it.** The neuropathic pain precedes the eruption by **2 to 3 days, up to about a week**. This is what wrecked the 2019 face-to-face candidates.
Clinical diagnosis. A **dry swab from the base of a de-roofed vesicle for VZV PCR** confirms it — **never delay antivirals waiting for the result**.

**72 hours from rash onset** is the antiviral window in the immunocompetent. **Immunocompromised: treat regardless of duration.** Pre-eruptive: the window has not opened — review promptly and start when the rash appears.

**Famciclovir 500 mg 8-hourly for 7 days**, or **valaciclovir 1 g 8-hourly for 7 days**, or **aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days**. Reduce the dose in renal impairment; IV aciclovir and admission if disseminated or immunocompromised.

Analgesia must be adequate: **regular paracetamol plus an NSAID**, stepping up to a **paracetamol-codeine combination** for breakthrough with constipation advice, and **amitriptyline, gabapentin or pregabalin** if it stays severe. Cool compresses, calamine, loose clothing, do not scratch. **No routine oral steroids, no topical antivirals.**

Contacts — **until every blister has crusted over**, avoid **pregnant women who have not had chickenpox, newborns, young children, and anyone immunosuppressed**. The blister fluid gives them **chickenpox, not shingles**. Off childcare work while lesions cannot be covered. **Notifiable in all jurisdictions except NSW.**

Do not miss: **zoster ophthalmicus — forehead, eyelid or tip of nose, Hutchinson's sign · Ramsay Hunt — ear vesicles with facial palsy · disseminated zoster — crossing the midline or over 20 lesions outside the dermatome · post-herpetic neuralgia**, and warn him the pain can outlast the rash.
plan: **'Before I begin, may I have the blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** Then WIPE, confirm **full name and date of birth**, agenda, and empathy — this is 8 or 9 out of 10 pain.

SOCRATES: **where exactly, can you point to it · when did it start, sudden or gradual · what is it like, tight or sharp · does it travel anywhere · DOES IT EVER CROSS TO THE OTHER SIDE · constant or coming and going · out of ten, and what has it stopped you doing?**

The discriminating question: **'anything make it worse — moving, breathing, exertion, lying flat, touching the skin?'** → the bedsheet. Follow it: **'is the skin there also tingling, burning or numb?'**

Exclude the killers, out loud, even though you have spotted it. **ACS — exertional, central, crushing, jaw or arm, sweating, nausea, risk factors. PE — sudden breathlessness, haemoptysis, calf swelling, travel, surgery, immobility. Pericarditis — WORSE LYING FLAT, BETTER SITTING FORWARD, recent viral illness. Pneumothorax. Pneumonia. Reflux. Dissection — tearing to the back, maximal at onset.**

The shingles layer: **what do you do for work — do you work with children or in healthcare?** and **do you have contact with anyone pregnant, any newborns or young children, or anyone with a weak immune system?** You cannot give the advice later if you did not ask now.

**Why now — the critical block.** **Have you lost weight without trying · drenching night sweats · lumps in the neck, armpits or groin · unusual bruising or bleeding · persistent fevers · more tired than usual?** Then **diabetes — thirst, passing more urine**; **steroids, chemotherapy, arthritis or bowel medicines, injections affecting the immune system**; and with a preface, **'I ask everyone this — anything that might affect your immune system, such as risk of blood-borne viruses?'**

**Any rash near the eye, forehead or tip of the nose? Any eye pain or change in vision? Any ear pain, hearing change, dizziness or facial weakness?** Then **did you have chickenpox as a child, ever had shingles, any vaccination?**

**SADMA** — medications matter twice, as a cause and for renal dosing. Past history, family history, home and who is there, then **'what were you most worried this might be?'** → a heart attack. Name it.
Consent and drape before exposing the chest, offer a chaperone, then **request the examination in order** and finish with **the ECG**.

Explain, and **answer his fear first**: the heart examination and the ECG are normal and this is not the pattern of a heart attack. Then shingles in plain English — **the chickenpox virus went to sleep in the nerve roots and has woken up along one nerve**, which is why the band stops in the middle and why the sheet hurts. Then the differentials, and why each is less likely.

**The second conversation** — say it straight: shingles at 40 with weight loss, night sweats and that lump means **I want to look for a reason your immune system is under strain**. To **'is it cancer?'**: you cannot say today, some causes are straightforward, and **finding it early genuinely matters**.

Antiviral with the **72-hour rationale said aloud**, combination analgesia, skin care, **contact and work advice**, notification, **review in 2 to 3 days**, the **post-herpetic neuralgia warning**, safety-net, summary, teach-back, written information.
pefe: Ask in this order, framed as **'my examination is still aimed at a patient with chest pain, so I'd like to start generally and then focus'**: **general appearance including CACHEXIA · full vitals including BGL · lymph nodes, cervical, supraclavicular, axillary and inguinal, plus hepatosplenomegaly · full cardiovascular including JVP and a PERICARDIAL RUB · brief respiratory · chest wall — IS THERE A RASH AND DOES IT CROSS THE MIDLINE, and tenderness to light touch · DERMATOMAL SENSORY TESTING across the painful band · abdomen · ECG, blood glucose and urinalysis.**
**The ECG is mandatory** — it excludes ischaemia and pericarditis. **Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression** would be pericarditis.
Confirmatory: a **dry swab from the base of a de-roofed vesicle for VZV PCR**, only possible if a rash is present, and it **rarely changes management**.

The underlying-cause screen, and say this purpose out loud: **FBE and film** for lymphocytosis, blasts or cytopenias · **BGL and HbA1c** · **HIV serology with consent and pre-test discussion** · **ESR/CRP, LDH, U&E, LFT and a chest X-ray** for mediastinal nodes.
**Renal function before dosing the antiviral.** **Troponin and CXR only if the history or the ECG raises ischaemic suspicion.**

Rash features to name if present: **unilateral, band-like, one dermatome, stopping abruptly at the midline · grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, becoming pustules then crusts over 7 to 10 days · marked allodynia and hyperaesthesia**.

Red-flag distributions: **ophthalmic division — forehead, eyelid, tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) · ear canal with facial weakness (Ramsay Hunt) · over 20 lesions outside the dermatome or crossing the midline (disseminated)**.

Two chest X-rays are available: the admission film and a repeat film taken this week.

Take a relevant focused history
Counsel her about the risks of travelling and advise her accordingly

NOT REQUIRED in this station. The films and the history are the whole of it

The area that was white is BLACK AGAIN. Heart border SHARP again. COMPLETE RADIOGRAPHIC RESOLUTION. Same pacemaker, unchanged
VERSION — the film has not cleared
Right mid-zone shadow persists and she has a lingering dry cough → DEFER TRAVEL, bloods and CT chest. She is 65 and smokes
Two episodes of FRESH HAEMOPTYSIS and 4 kg WEIGHT LOSS → this is now a suspected lung cancer station. Urgent CT chest and respiratory referral; travel is not the priority
Two episodes of NEAR-FAINTING while shopping since discharge → ECG and URGENT PACEMAKER INTERROGATION before she flies. Driving advice changes too

FAIL — Describing the two films as separate events. Say 'compared with the first film' out loud.
FAIL — Never asking how many nights she actually uses the CPAP, or dropping the smoking.
FAIL — Forbidding travel with no basis, or a safety net with nothing written in it.
