dx: **Community-acquired pneumonia, fully resolved**, in a 65-year-old with **obstructive sleep apnoea and poor CPAP adherence**, a **pacemaker for bradyarrhythmia**, and **ongoing smoking** — seeking pre-travel advice.
**There is no validated risk score for travel after pneumonia. Say so, then show a system.** CURB-65 and SMART-COP assess severity in acute disease, not fitness to travel.
**The four boxes, named aloud**: **has the pneumonia truly resolved · are her comorbidities controlled · what makes another infection likely · what does the trip involve?**

**Radiographic clearance normally lags clinical recovery by 4 to 6 weeks; hers has cleared at two.** Say that is genuinely reassuring. The usual **6-week film in a smoker over 50** is not needed because this one is already normal.

**Two modifiable risks are buried in the brief and she will not volunteer either: CPAP two nights a week because the mask digs in, and ten cigarettes a day for forty years.** Find both, manage both, and you pass.
**Somac is pantoprazole**, a proton pump inhibitor — say so without hesitating. **Long-term PPI use is itself a modest risk factor for pneumonia.**

**The verdict, plainly: yes, she can go** — symptoms settled, saturation normal, film clear. **There is no rule that you must wait a set time after a pneumonia**, and forbidding travel without a basis is a hard fail.
**Steer her off the scuba dive**: pressure change so soon after a pneumonia risks lung injury. **Snorkelling on the surface is fine; a real dive needs a formal dive medical first.**

Safety net must be **written**: a **letter** covering the admission, the organism, the antibiotics, the pacemaker model and the CPAP settings; **red flags** — cough returning or worsening, more breathless, fever or chills, chest pain, haemoptysis, feeling faint — **see a doctor, call 000 if severe**; and **tell the sister so she can act if Margaret can't**.

Before she goes: **influenza vaccine today**, check **pneumococcal and COVID-19** status. Up north: **no untreated creek or river water · cover cuts and avoid mud in the wet season (melioidosis) · repellent for dengue, Ross River, Barmah Forest · hydrate and walk the aisle in flight.** **Quitline 13 7848 · healthdirect 1800 022 222.**
plan: WIPE, confirm **name and date of birth**, then **acknowledge and signpost to buy your time**: **'I can already tell you the X-rays look encouraging. Let me go through both films, ask about your recovery, your heart and sleep apnoea and the trip, then give you a clear answer and something in writing.'**

The films, **in five steps**: **details — this one on admission, this one this week · three colours — white is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air · landmarks — heart, spine, windpipe · THE NORMAL SIDE FIRST — your left lung is uniformly black, that is normal · then the right**.

The abnormal side, then **name the pacemaker**, then **the comparison out loud**: **'compared with the first film, the area that was white is black again, and the heart edge is sharp again. Your pneumonia has cleared completely.'**
**Promise the answer, do not give it yet** — **'I think the answer will be yes. Before I commit, let me ask a few things.'** Once she has her answer she stops giving you information.

**Box 1, the pneumonia itself**: **when admitted and when home · how many days of antibiotics, did you finish the course · still coughing, bringing anything up · ANY BLOOD IN IT · short of breath walking or lying flat · fever, chills or night sweats since · chest pain on breathing in · energy, appetite, WEIGHT.**

**Box 2, her two known diseases** — for each: when diagnosed, treatment, compliance, follow-up, complications. **Pacemaker: when put in, when last checked, any heart tablets and do you take them, any racing or fluttering, any dizzy spells or blackouts.** **Then the question that decides the station: 'how many nights a week do you actually use the CPAP?'** plus daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, concentration.

**Box 3, why she got a pneumonia at all**: **asthma, emphysema, scarring · steroid tablets or inhalers, regular medications · diabetes, kidney or liver trouble, cancer · stroke, memory problems, choking on food · flu and pneumococcal vaccination.** Then **SADMA — and quantify the cigarettes.**

**Box 4, the trip**: **where, when, how long · flying or driving, how long a flight · who with and who are you staying with · WHAT ARE YOU PLANNING TO DO WHILE YOU'RE UP THERE · diving, boating, bushwalking, camping · travel insurance and enough medication · is there anything in particular that worries you?**
**The verdict, plainly, with the reasons.** Then **the letter**, **the red flags with 000**, **tell the sister**, and **steer her off the dive**.

**Return to the CPAP as promised**: **'two nights a week gives you the discomfort without the benefit'** — oxygen dips overnight, blood pressure runs higher, strain on a heart that already needs a pacemaker, more chest infections. **Fix the mask, not the machine**: different size, nasal pillows, humidifier, sleep-service refit. **Take it on the plane — airlines carry it as medical equipment.**

**Smoking, brief and structured — ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange. Ninety seconds, never moralise.** **Quitline 13 7848**, combination nicotine replacement, and a review in a fortnight. Then **flu vaccine today**, the travel advice, and summarise: **'have I missed anything you were worried about?'**
pefe: **No physical examination is required.** The observations are handed to you at the door and the two films are on the desk.
**Compare the films, never describe them separately.** The mark is for the comparison — say **'compared with the first film'** before every observation on the second.
**Name the pacemaker on the film** and say it is correctly sited with intact wires.

For the examiner, not the patient: **radiographic clearance normally takes 4 to 6 weeks** and **a repeat film at 6 weeks is standard in a smoker over 50** to exclude a lesion behind the pneumonia. Hers is already clear, so the six-week film is not needed — **but keep a low threshold given the smoking**.

stem: Jenny Alcott, 60, has been brought to your practice. She has been breathless for two months and has been coughing up red / pink sputum.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 5 minutes)
A chest X-ray is provided at 5 minutes — explain it to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient

dx: **Pleural effusion secondary to lung cancer.** **'Pleural effusion' is a sign, not a diagnosis** — the examiner is waiting for you to name the finding on the film **and then name what is causing it**. Candidates who stop at 'fluid around your lung' **fail a case they had already solved**.

**The calibrated phrase**: **'Breathlessness can have a number of different causes. But in your case, I do have a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung.'** Honest — you have not concealed the word; accurate — you do not have tissue; and it does not convert an eight-minute station into a breaking-bad-news case you were not asked to run.

**Then justify it immediately from her own findings**: **'you've been losing weight without trying, you've been coughing up what I believe is blood in your phlegm, and your X-ray shows fluid collecting around the lung. Those three things together mean I need to look for a cancer and rule it out properly. I can't tell you today that that's what it is — but I'm not going to wait either.'**

**Hold the moment before moving on**: **'I can see that's a shock, and I'm sorry to be telling you this today. Take a moment. Is there someone you'd like with you while we go through what happens next? I'll write everything down for you as well.'** **Two sentences of acknowledgement cost almost nothing and are visibly scored.**

**The four-step film script — 30 to 40 seconds, one minute at the absolute most**: **three colours (white is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air) → three landmarks (heart, spine, and the main airway, sitting centrally) → the NORMAL side FIRST, with its sharp angle where lung meets chest wall → the abnormal side, where that angle is missing and filled in → and NAME IT.** **Say both the plain description and the medical name** — 'fluid collecting around the lung — we call that a pleural effusion'.

**Speak in her sides, not the film's.** The patient's left is on the right of the image. **Reversing this in front of an examiner is small, avoidable and very memorable.** And **no jargon**: 'costophrenic angle obliterated' and 'homogeneous opacification' are correct descriptions and failed communication.

**The white-out discriminator, which is why the trachea is one of the three landmarks**: a completely opacified hemithorax is not automatically an effusion. **Mediastinum pushed AWAY from the white side = effusion or a large mass · pulled TOWARDS = collapse or pneumonectomy · central with no shift = consolidation.**

**Exudate versus transudate.** **Exudate — unilateral, high protein: cancer · infection or empyema · TB · pulmonary infarct · connective tissue disease. Transudate — often bilateral, low protein: heart failure · liver failure · nephrotic syndrome · hypothyroidism.** **Light's criteria — any one makes it an exudate: pleural/serum protein ratio >0.5 · LDH ratio >0.6 · pleural LDH more than two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH.** VERIFY

**Still deliver the differential list — Task 3 asks for diagnosis AND differentials**, and it is therapeutic, because it shows her you have not simply jumped to the worst answer: **infection including tuberculosis, though no fevers, sweats or travel · heart failure, though one pillow and no ankle swelling · liver or kidney disease · an underactive thyroid · asthma · smoking-related lung damage · occupational dust scarring · repeated chest infections · and anaemia.**

Plan: **bloods including paired serum protein and LDH · CT chest with contrast · an ULTRASOUND-GUIDED diagnostic pleural aspiration for cytology, microbiology and biochemistry — cytology yield improves with up to three samples · therapeutic drainage for breathlessness, no more than 1–1.5 L at a sitting to avoid re-expansion pulmonary oedema · urgent respiratory referral.** Safety net: **much more breathless, more blood, chest pain or fever → straight to hospital**, and review in a few days regardless. SA: CT locally where possible, **telehealth respiratory and oncology clinics, a cancer nurse coordinator early**, **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20**, **PATS** for travel.
plan: **'Examiner, before I begin, may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** Then **react to the 91%**: keep the oxygen on. WIPE, open question — then **address the fear without reassuring before you know anything**: **'I'm so sorry to hear that, and I understand how worrying it must be. Let me ask you a few questions, then I'll go through your chest X-ray with you, find the cause and make the best plan for you.'** **Signpost the film** — it prepares her and reminds you of the clock.

Explore the breathlessness: **is it difficulty getting the breath in, tightness in the chest, or not getting enough air · how long · constant or on and off · getting worse · anything that makes it better or worse?**
**The rest question — the severity marker, and one sentence**: **'you've said it's worse when you walk. Does rest make it better? And are you ever breathless at rest, just sitting still?'**

**Characterise the second complaint yourself**: **how many times has the pink phlegm happened · what colour exactly, pink or frankly red · any streaks or clots · and how much — a few drops, a teaspoonful, or more?**

**The cancer block — FIRST, not last.** **Have you lost any weight without trying, and if so how much over what period · any loss of appetite · any lumps or bumps · have you ever coughed up blood · have you ever had cancer anywhere in the past · what's your occupation now, AND what did you do before that · any asbestos exposure · and any numbness or weakness in your arm, or anyone commenting on your eyelid or face looking different?** **The moment weight loss is positive, your provisional diagnosis has changed** — and you want that early enough to shape the rest of the history.

Infection, heart failure and the tail of the list: **any fevers or chills · sore throat or runny nose · any night sweats, travel overseas or contact with anyone with tuberculosis · are you breathless lying flat, how many pillows · any swelling in your legs · any rashes or joint pains · and have you been unusually tired?**
SADMA and background **only if genuinely spare** — and let it go without anxiety if not. **Never let the history run into the three minutes that belong to the film and the diagnosis.**

**The film, four steps, uninterrupted, under a minute.** If she interrupts: **'it can come from a few different things, and that's exactly what I want to talk about next — let me just finish showing you the film.'** Do not abandon the structure, and do not ignore her.

**The differential list — deliver it, do not skip it.** Infection and TB · heart failure · liver, kidney and thyroid · asthma, COPD, occupational scarring, repeated infections · anaemia — each with the reassuring negative attached.

**The plan and the safety-net**: bloods, CT chest, **an ultrasound-guided sample of the fluid which also helps her breathing**, urgent respiratory referral. **'If you become much more breathless, cough up more blood, get chest pain, or develop a fever, go straight to hospital.'** Review in a few days regardless, and check understanding.

FAIL — Accepting 'I don't smoke' and 'I'm retired' at face value.

stem: Gerald Munro, 60, presents with shortness of breath for three months. The previous doctor has already requested a full blood count, thyroid, liver and renal function — all normal. Spirometry has also been requested and will be given to you.
Spirometry: FEV1 predicted 2.60 L, pre-bronchodilator 1.35 (52%), post 1.37 (53%) · FVC predicted 3.35, pre 2.50, post 2.54 · FEV1/FVC predicted 0.83, measured 0.54.
tasks: Take a history and rule out your differentials
Interpret the spirometry — to the examiner face-to-face, to the patient online
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
findings: BP 138/82 · P 84 · RR 18 · T 36.6 · SpO2 95% on room air. Ask for them even with a 3-month history — chronic disease presents acutely
PRE- and POST-bronchodilator columns, predicted values, and % predicted in brackets. TAKE FIVE SECONDS OF SILENCE and name the columns before interpreting
Predicted 2.60 · PRE 1.35 (52%) · POST 1.37 (53%) — a change of 0.02 L = 20 mL, about 1.5%
Predicted 0.83 · MEASURED 0.54 — DECREASED, so OBSTRUCTION IS CERTAIN. Post-BD ratio stays BELOW 0.70, which formally confirms COPD
OBSTRUCTIVE with NON-SIGNIFICANT REVERSIBILITY — under 200 mL and under 12%. COPD, not asthma. Post-BD FEV1 53% predicted = MODERATE airflow limitation
Ratio 0.90 against predicted 0.79 — INCREASED. FEV1 and FVC BOTH around half predicted → RESTRICTIVE PATTERN. Stonemason cutting engineered benchtops → silicosis
Ratio 0.67 against predicted 0.71 — decreased. FEV1 3.00 → 3.70 = +700 mL and +23%, OVER BOTH THRESHOLDS → ASTHMA

The examiner blocks it and hands you a CHEST X-RAY: FLATTENED HEMIDIAPHRAGMS · HYPERLUCENT lung fields from air trapping · LONG NARROW TUBULAR HEART that hangs rather than sits · more than 6 anterior ribs. Describe it feature by feature BEFORE naming COPD
Ratio normal, FEV1 and FVC at or above predicted. A NORMAL test — marks are for not forcing a diagnosis onto it. Normal spirometry does NOT exclude asthma
findingsLabel: Vitals and the spirometry chart · open when you would ask for it
must: FAIL — An answer with no workings. 'This is COPD', then silence when asked how.
FAIL — Comparing the ratio pre and post. Once the ratio shows obstruction, only FEV1 matters.
FAIL — Giving the pattern as the diagnosis. 'Restrictive pattern' is a chart, not a disease.
FAIL — Using one threshold, or confusing litres and millilitres. Both are needed: 200 mL AND 12%.
ASK — You don't smoke now — did you ever? How much, and for how long? Then pack-years aloud.
ASK — Any blood in the phlegm? Weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats — and the occupation.

dx: **COPD — moderate airflow limitation** in a 60-year-old ex-smoker with **40 pack-years** and three months of progressive exertional dyspnoea with a productive morning cough.
**The mark is the workings, not the answer.** 'Ratio 0.54, FEV1 1.35, FVC 2.5, I think this is COPD' tells the examiner you cannot interpret anything. **Narrate every comparison.**

**Three numbers only: FEV1 · FVC · FEV1/FVC (FER).** **% predicted = measured ÷ predicted × 100.** Labels vary — predicted may print as normal range or LLN, measured as best, actual, baseline or pre-bronchodilator.
**Step 1 is always the ratio, measured against the PREDICTED ratio** — not a memorised cut-off. **Decreased → obstructive, left branch. Normal or increased → right branch.**

**Step 2 left: FEV1 pre versus post bronchodilator.** Predicted values and the ratio are now irrelevant. **200 mL AND 12% or more → asthma; under both → COPD.** **Step 2 right: FEV1 and FVC against predicted — both down with a preserved ratio = restrictive pattern.**
**Charts are in litres. 0.02 L is 20 mL; 200 mL is 0.2 L.** Say the conversion out loud. **True reversibility = (post − pre) ÷ pre × 100** — subtracting % predicted is a screen, not the calculation.

**Spirometry cannot diagnose restriction.** A reduced FVC with a preserved ratio also comes from poor effort, obesity, neuromuscular weakness or a large effusion. Say: **'I would confirm true restriction with formal lung volumes and gas transfer, and arrange an HRCT chest.'**

**Convert the pattern into a named disease with two reasons.** COPD: **a pack a day for forty years**, and **narrowing that barely improved with the puffer**. ILD: **a high-risk occupation**, and **a restriction in how the lungs move and exchange gas**.

**COPD severity on post-BD FEV1 % predicted: 80 or more mild · 50–79 moderate · 30–49 severe · under 30 very severe.** The ratio makes the diagnosis and **never grades it**. Chronic respiratory failure: **PaO2 under 60 mmHg ± PaCO2 over 50 mmHg**.

Plan: **chest X-ray, and HRCT given the asbestos history · reinforce abstinence · inhaled bronchodilator · pulmonary rehabilitation · influenza, pneumococcal and COVID vaccination · a written COPD action plan and review.** **Silicosis is notifiable** — SafeWork SA, a ReturnToWorkSA claim, and screening of co-workers.
plan: **'Before I start, could I have the vital signs?'** Then WIPE and set the agenda: **'let me ask some questions, then we'll look at your breathing test together and I'll explain what it shows.'**

Character first — **heart or lung**: **'is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in?'** Then **how long · constant or coming and going · getting worse · better or worse with what · ARE YOU SHORT OF BREATH AT REST · cough, wheeze, noisy breathing, phlegm?**

**The cancer questions, which are separately marked and which the normal bloods do not excuse you from**: **weight loss without trying · appetite · lumps or bumps · night sweats · HAVE YOU COUGHED UP ANY BLOOD · any previous cancer?**

**The two questions that carry this station.** **'Do you smoke?'** → 'no, gave it up' → **'did you ever? How much, and for how long?'** → **say the pack-years out loud**. Then **'what is your occupation, and what did you do before? Have you worked with dust, fumes, stone or asbestos? Did you use a mask or respirator?'** → asbestos in the old sheds, mentioned only if asked.

Cardiac, **asked even though the stem says cardiac causes were excluded — you are marked on your history**: **chest pain on exertion · palpitations · dizziness · worse lying flat, how many pillows · ankle swelling.**

The rest of the sweep: **childhood chest infections or repeated pneumonias · hay fever, eczema, asthma in the family · fevers, sweats, travel, TB contact · joint pains or rashes · tiredness or bleeding · medications including anything long-term, allergies, family history.**

**Take the chart. Five seconds of silence.** Then **orientate before interpreting**: **'I can see pre- and post-bronchodilator columns, with predicted values and the percentage predicted in brackets, and I have all three values I need.'**
**Step one, spoken**: **'the measured ratio is 0.54 against a predicted of 0.83. That is decreased, so there is an obstructive pattern, and obstruction is now certain.'**

**Step two, spoken**: **'because the ratio is decreased, I compare FEV1 before and after the bronchodilator — 1.35 to 1.37 litres, 0.02 litres, that is 20 millilitres, about one and a half per cent. Under 200 millilitres and under 12 per cent, so no significant reversibility — COPD rather than asthma.'** Then **the post-BD ratio under 0.70 confirms it, and 53% predicted makes it moderate.**

**The disease, with two reasons**, in plain words. Then answer **'is it going to get worse?'** honestly: **COPD does not reverse, but how fast it progresses is in our hands, and stopping smoking changes the slope more than any tablet.**

**Differentials — scored separately. Name eight or so with one reason each**: lung cancer, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, asthma, interstitial lung disease from the asbestos, bronchiectasis, infection including TB, sarcoidosis, anaemia. Then the plan and the summary.
pefe: **The two investigations you always name in chronic breathlessness: chest X-ray and spirometry.** If one is blocked, ask for the other — Version C turns entirely on having the second answer ready.

**Orientate to the chart layout before interpreting.** Predicted may be printed as predicted, normal range or LLN; measured as measured, best, actual, baseline or pre-bronchodilator. **This, not the algorithm, is the commonest cause of panic in the room.**

**Bronchodilator response is measured 10 to 15 minutes after a rapid-acting bronchodilator.** Australian criteria (National Asthma Council): **FEV1 up by 12% AND 200 mL**. The 2022 ATS/ERS standard proposes more than 10% of predicted instead — acknowledge it and say you applied the Australian criteria.

**A normal spirometry does not exclude asthma** — airflow is often normal between episodes. If the history is convincing, offer **FeNO (40 ppb or more supports asthma) or a bronchial challenge test**. FeNO is mainly in accredited labs, so quote it as an adjunct.
Restrictive pattern → **formal lung volumes (TLC) and gas transfer (DLCO), plus HRCT chest**, and an occupational physician.
**Flow-volume loops** if shown instead of the table: **the obstructive loop is scooped out on the descending limb; the restrictive loop is a tall thin version of normal**, shifted to lower volumes.

**Hyperinflation on the film**: **flattened hemidiaphragms · hyperlucent lung fields · long narrow tubular heart · more than 6 anterior or 10 posterior ribs above the diaphragm** (the least reliable — lead with the diaphragms and the lucency) **· increased retrosternal airspace on the lateral**.
Then the rest: **FBE and iron studies, TSH, ECG and echocardiogram** where the cardiac questions raise it, sputum culture and AFB for TB, diagnostic tap for an effusion.

Variable and episodic, night and early morning, triggers, atopy, family history
Diurnal variation, wheeze, hay fever, eczema
**12% AND 200 mL reversibility**; FeNO; bronchial challenge
**Occupational ILD — silicosis, asbestosis, coal worker's pneumoconiosis**
**Mining, boilermaking, engineered stone benchtops, dry cutting without a respirator**
**Exact job, materials, years, protective equipment**, fine crackles, clubbing
**Restrictive pattern → HRCT, lung volumes and DLCO; occupational physician. Silicosis is NOTIFIABLE** — high urgency
**Mesothelioma or lung cancer**
**Asbestos exposure with a 20–40 year latency**; smoking; haemoptysis, weight loss
Weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats, pleuritic pain, clubbing
**CXR then CT chest; urgent referral** — immediate
Bronchiectasis · TB · pleural effusion
Large-volume sputum, childhood infections; fevers, sweats, travel or contact; unilateral dullness
Sputum volume and colour, fevers, TB contact
HRCT; sputum culture and AFB; CXR then diagnostic tap — high

Orthopnoea, ankle swelling, exertional chest tightness, palpitations
**Pillows, PND, oedema, murmur — ask even if the stem says cardiac causes are excluded**
ECG, echocardiogram, CXR — high
Drug-induced lung disease
**Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin** — a restrictive chart with no occupational story
Full medication history **including duration**

stem: Mrs Margaret Ellis, 72, presents with shortness of breath and cough.
A chest X-ray will be provided. Observations available from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a history (5 minutes)
Interpret and explain the chest X-ray to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differentials

dx: **Lung cancer presenting as a mass on the chest X-ray.** **This is a breaking-bad-news station wearing a respiratory costume.** Weight loss plus haemoptysis plus smoking plus a mass gives you the answer in thirty seconds — **what separates candidates is the last ninety seconds.**

**Two complaints in the stem — explore BREATHLESSNESS, not cough.** Cough alone drifts towards post-nasal drip, sinusitis and ACE inhibitors, **none of which cause breathlessness** — whereas **essentially every cause of breathlessness also causes cough**. Run breathlessness as the spine and pick the cough up inside it.

**The sputum question that turns the case**: **'what colour exactly — and have you ever seen any blood in it, even streaks or specks, even once?'** **'Yellowish phlegm' sounds like a chest infection and is offered to see whether you stop there.** **Never accept a sputum description without asking about blood.**

**Quantify, or it is not a finding.** **'A bit of weight' → seven to eight kilos over four months. 'I used to smoke' → a pack a day for thirty years = thirty pack-years**, said out loud, because it demonstrates you calculated rather than noted.

**The X-ray script, in lay terms**: **'there are really only three colours on it: white is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air. On this side — the normal side — I can see the normal dark shadow of your lung, and a nice sharp angle at the bottom where the lung meets the chest wall. But on this side I can see something that shouldn't be there: an abnormal mass, a growth, in the lung. And that raises the possibility of a cancer.'**

**If there is no effusion, go hunting for a mass** — grey soft tissue against grey soft tissue, easily missed **behind the heart, at the apices and in the hila**. And the converse: **a normal-looking film does not change your diagnosis when there is weight loss and haemoptysis** — **say so to her explicitly**, so she does not leave falsely reassured.

**The warning shot, then the word, then the silence.** **'Before I go on — is there anyone you'd like with you for this, or would you rather I go ahead?' … 'I'm afraid what I've found is more serious than a simple chest infection.' [pause] … 'my main concern is that this could be a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that.' [pause — DO NOT FILL THE SILENCE]** Then **'that's a lot to take in. What's going through your mind?'**

**The two opposite failures.** **Bluntness**: 'you've got lung cancer', no warning shot, no pause. **Evasion**: 'there's a shadow we need to look into', and she leaves not knowing. **Warning shot → the word → apology → silence → check in.** And: **'this isn't a diagnosis yet — we need a scan and a sample. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I didn't tell you honestly what I'm thinking.'**

**'How long have I got?'** — **'I understand why you're asking, and I'm not going to give you a number I can't stand behind. We don't yet know what this is, and if it is a cancer, what matters is the type and whether it has spread — and those are exactly what the scan and the sample will tell us. What I can promise is that I won't keep anything from you.'** **Giving a number is marked down.**

Plan: **urgent CT chest with contrast, extending through liver and adrenals · urgent respiratory referral and lung cancer MDT · tissue diagnosis by bronchoscopy with EBUS or CT-guided biopsy · PET-CT and brain imaging for staging.** **'I'll ring you personally with the result rather than leaving you waiting.'** Safety net: **more than a small amount of blood, worsening breathing, chest pain, or swelling of the face or arms.** **Offer a longer appointment this week and a support person.** SA: **arrange the CT locally in parallel with the referral, not sequentially**; **PATS**; **Cancer Council 13 11 20**; **Quitline 13 7848** — cessation is worthwhile at any stage. **She is symptomatic, so she is NOT a screening candidate.**
plan: **To the examiner before you sit down**: **'may I have her observations — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'**

WIPE, confirm name and date of birth — **and check she can talk**: **'are you comfortable, and are you short of breath sitting here now?'** Open question, then acknowledge: **'that sounds like it's been wearing you down, and I'm glad you've come in.'** Signpost: history, then the X-ray together, then what happens next.

**Box 1 — describe it**: **what does the breathlessness feel like · when did you first notice it · constant or does it come and go · WHAT CAN'T YOU DO NOW THAT YOU COULD SIX MONTHS AGO · how far can you walk on the flat before you stop · can you lie flat · do you wake at night short of breath · any noisy or wheezy breathing?**

**Box 2 — time it**: **sudden or gradual · getting worse, staying the same, or improving · has it ever been this bad before** — and the same for the cough: **how long, dry or productive, worse at any particular time of day.**
**Box 3 — what changes it**: **worse with exertion, lying down, cold air, dust, pets, anything at work · what makes it better, rest, sitting up · have you tried any puffers or medications?**

**The sputum, in two questions and not one**: **'are you bringing anything up? What colour exactly?'** … then **'and have you ever seen any blood in it, even streaks or specks, even once?'** Thank her for telling you.

Systems screen: **fevers, chills, night sweats that soak the sheets, TB contact or travel · any chest pain or tightness, ankle swelling, how many pillows, palpitations · calf pain or swelling, recent surgery, immobility, long flights · heartburn, post-nasal drip, change in your voice · tiredness, dizziness, black or bloody stools.**

**The red-flag block — the one the examiner is waiting for**: **have you lost weight without trying, how much and over how long · any night sweats · has your voice changed or become hoarse · any trouble swallowing · any new bone pain, or pain in the shoulder or arm · any headaches, morning vomiting or weakness · any swelling of your face or arms, or veins standing out on your chest?**

**Smoking and exposure, both quantified**: **'do you smoke, or have you ever — how many a day, for how many years?'** Then say the pack-year figure aloud. **'And what work have you done over your life — any exposure to asbestos, dust or fumes?'**

Close the history: **other conditions · medications including puffers and anything bought over the counter · allergies · anyone in the family with lung problems or cancer · who's at home and how are you managing · and is there anything you were particularly worried this might be?**

**The X-ray, described to her in lay terms** — three colours, the normal side first, then the mass. **Scan both fields deliberately before you commit**, and do not use the word 'shadow' as a hiding place.
**The warning shot, the word, the apology — then stop talking.** Let the silence run. Then **'what's going through your mind?'** and the clarification that this is not yet a diagnosis.

**Differentials, briskly, after the news has landed**: heart problem — no chest pain, normal examination · COPD · asthma, unlikely with no wheeze · infection including TB · lung abscess · lung scarring · mesothelioma if asbestos · heart failure · a low blood count. **'We'll work through them — but today's finding is the one I want to act on straight away.'**

**Plan, safety net and close**: urgent CT, urgent specialist referral, MDT discussion, **'I'll ring you personally with the result.'** Return sooner for **more than a small amount of blood, worse breathing, chest pain, or facial or arm swelling.** **'Shall we book a longer appointment later this week, and would you like to bring your husband?'** Finish with **an open question, not 'is that alright?'**
pefe: **Observations including oxygen saturation before you begin**, and oxygen if hypoxic.
**Examine fully — including supraclavicular nodes, finger clubbing, and the face and neck for SVC obstruction.**
**Chest X-ray if not already done.** **No effusion → deliberately scan both lung fields for a mass**, behind the heart, at the apices and in the hila.
**Bloods: FBE, UEC, LFT, CALCIUM — hypercalcaemia of malignancy — CRP and a coagulation profile.** Sputum for microscopy, culture and acid-fast bacilli if infection or TB is possible.
**Urgent CT chest with contrast, extending through liver and adrenals.**
**Tissue diagnosis: bronchoscopy with EBUS, or CT-guided biopsy.** **PET-CT and brain imaging for staging.** **Spirometry and lung function before any treatment decision.**
**Urgent respiratory referral and lung cancer multidisciplinary team** — the Optimal Care Pathway sets the expected timeframes.

**The National Lung Cancer Screening Program does not apply**: it is for **asymptomatic** people aged 50–70 with **≥30 pack-years** who smoke or quit within 10 years, low-dose CT every 2 years, commenced 1 July 2025. **A symptomatic patient needs a diagnostic CT, not screening** — offering screening here is a visible error.

stem: Mr James Doherty, 50, presents with breathing difficulty.
Observations available from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes online / 4 minutes face-to-face)
Request the physical examination findings from your examiner (online: they appear on screen)
Explain your diagnosis and differentials

dx: **A left pleural effusion secondary to lung cancer — say BOTH parts.** 'Pleural effusion' alone is the sign; the station wants the sign **and** the reason there is fluid there.

**The face-to-face hand-over is itself being marked.** The examiner sits behind you while you face the role-player, so asking for findings means physically turning away mid-consultation. **One short line, turn, fixed sequence, turn back**: **'James, just give me one moment — I'm going to speak with my examiner and I'll be right back with you. Apologies.'** **Three ways to lose marks: turning away silently, holding a long conversation with your back to the patient, or forgetting to re-engage.**

**Ask for vocal resonance by name.** **Effusion and lower-lobe pneumonia both give reduced expansion and dullness** — the discriminators are the two candidates skip: **breath sounds (ABSENT in effusion, BRONCHIAL in consolidation) and vocal resonance (REDUCED in effusion, INCREASED in consolidation).**

**The chest-signs grid worth having cold**: **effusion — reduced expansion, stony dull, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance, trachea pushed away if large · consolidation — dull, bronchial breathing, crackles, increased vocal resonance · pneumothorax — hyper-resonant, reduced breath sounds, trachea pushed away if tension · collapse — dull, reduced breath sounds, TRACHEA PULLED TOWARDS.**
**Interpret the findings aloud BEFORE you turn back** — that is what shows you reasoned past the sign to the cause, rather than reciting a list.

**The sputum question that turns the case**: **'what colour exactly — and have you ever seen any blood in it, even streaks or specks, even once?'** He will say 'yellowish' and stop. **The blood is disclosed only to the second, specific question.**

**Quantify, or it is not a finding**: **seven to eight kilos over four months · a pack a day for thirty years = thirty pack-years, said out loud · builder all his life, so ask about asbestos directly** and keep **mesothelioma** live.

**The warning shot, the word, the apology, then the silence.** **'Before I go on — is there anyone you'd like with you for this?' … 'I'm afraid what I've found is more serious than a simple chest infection.' [pause] … 'the examination shows there's fluid collected around the bottom of your left lung, and that's why you're breathless. What concerns me is WHY that fluid is there. Together with the weight loss, the blood in your phlegm and your smoking history, my main concern is that this could be a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that.' [pause — do not fill it]**

**'How long have I got?'** — **'I'm not going to give you a number I can't stand behind. The sentence that passes: **'You do have COPD, and we will treat it — and there are things here that COPD does not explain, so I am also concerned about a cancer.'** **Two diagnoses, neither buried, neither trivialised.**

**Clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD.** Bucketed: **RS — lung cancer, bronchiectasis, ILD, empyema and abscess, cystic fibrosis, mesothelioma, TB · CVS — infective endocarditis, cyanotic congenital heart disease, atrial myxoma · GI — IBD, cirrhosis, coeliac · thyroid acropachy · familial and idiopathic.**
**Localised added sounds mean a localised lesion** — tumour with distal collapse or infection, bronchiectasis, or fibrosis. **In COPD you expect them generalised.**

**Weight loss argues against heart failure**: decompensation is a fluid-retaining state, so the expected trajectory is **weight GAIN**, and daily weights are how we monitor it. **Cardiac cachexia is real but late and in established disease.**

**Reversibility is 12% AND 200 mL from the measured baseline** — both, calculated on baseline, not by subtracting percentages of predicted. **COPD is confirmed by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC under 0.7.**
**Give the spirometry 90 seconds, not four minutes.** Five minutes covers the spirometry and the history together, and **the history is where the weight loss lives**.

Plan: **chest X-ray and bloods today · CT chest and upper abdomen this week · then tissue — bronchoscopy, EBUS or CT-guided biopsy · PET-CT for staging · lung cancer MDT.** Alongside: **smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation, a written COPD action plan.**
**Do not invent a prognosis**: **'I'm not going to give you a number I can't stand behind.'** Offer to have someone with him, and **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 — he can ring without giving his name.**

plan: Greeting, then the spirometry in plain words: **it measures how much air you can blow out in total and how much comes out in the first second · the proportion in the first second is reduced, so the air is meeting resistance on the way out — an OBSTRUCTIVE PATTERN · we gave a reliever and repeated it · it improved by 3% and 120 mL, and we look for at least 12% AND 200 mL · so the narrowing did not reverse, and narrowing that does not reverse in someone who has smoked is COPD.**

**The pivot that keeps the station open: 'even though that test points to COPD, I don't want to assume it explains everything.'** Then explore: **how long · constant or coming and going · getting worse · how far could you walk a year ago and how far now · WORSE LYING FLAT, HOW MANY PILLOWS · waking at night gasping · ankle swelling.**

**The cancer block, where this case is won. 'There are questions I ask everybody with these symptoms.'** **HAVE YOU LOST ANY WEIGHT WITHOUT TRYING — how much, over how long · appetite · lumps or bumps, especially neck and above the collarbones · unusually tired · night sweats or fevers · bone pain · has your voice changed · what is your job NOW and what did you do BEFORE · HAVE YOU EVER WORKED WITH ASBESTOS, or in mining, welding or construction · any cancer of any kind?**

**The four signs of an effusion: reduced expansion · stony dullness · absent breath sounds · reduced vocal resonance.** Say **'those four findings together are a pleural effusion'** before you turn back.

Compare: **consolidation — dull, BRONCHIAL BREATHING, INCREASED vocal resonance · pneumothorax — hyper-resonant, absent breath sounds, trachea pushed away if tension · collapse — dull, trachea PULLED TOWARDS.**

**Weight loss is not compatible with decompensated heart failure**, which is a fluid-retaining state causing weight GAIN. **Cardiac cachexia is late and in established disease — not the explanation for new weight loss in an undiagnosed smoker.**

**Rank three out loud, with reasons: 'My first diagnosis is X because… my second is Y, which I have not excluded because… and I am also considering Z.'** Structure said aloud beats a correct single answer said silently.
**Light's criteria — an exudate if ANY ONE is true: pleural/serum protein ratio over 0.5 · pleural/serum LDH ratio over 0.6 · pleural LDH over two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.**

**Transudates** (pressure-driven): **heart failure · cirrhosis · nephrotic syndrome · hypothyroidism · constrictive pericarditis · peritoneal dialysis.** **Exudates**: **parapneumonic and empyema · malignancy · TB · PE · rheumatoid and SLE · pancreatitis · chylothorax.**

**Diagnostic tap always. Therapeutic drainage if symptomatic — but do not remove too much at once, because of re-expansion pulmonary oedema.** Recurrent malignant effusion: **indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis.**

Heart failure management: **echocardiogram for ejection fraction · diuretic for congestion · then ACE inhibitor or ARNI, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor.** **Beta-blocker up-titration is DEFERRED until euvolaemic** — starting one in a congested patient makes them worse. Daily weights, fluid and salt advice, cardiac rehabilitation.

Say cancer properly even in Version 1: **'whenever there is fluid like this in someone who has smoked, I must rule out a cancer — so I'm going to take a sample of the fluid and arrange a scan.'** **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · Quitline 13 7848 · PATS · TIS 131 450.**

dx: **Congestive heart failure from ischaemic cardiomyopathy after a thrombolysed MI**, in a man on no secondary prevention who has had no follow-up for a year.

**A patient one year post-MI who takes nothing and sees nobody has TWO complications waiting: heart failure, and RECURRENT ISCHAEMIC HEART DISEASE.** Ask about both — the second is the one candidates forget.

**The discriminating issue is the differential list you give after you already know the answer.** You can score six of seven on history, score one on differentials, and fail. **Name eight to ten, one reason each.**
**The question that splits heart from lung, asked first: 'is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in?'** In a man with known IHD, tightness reopens another coronary event.
The stock AMC line is **six months, worse on walking, better with rest, walking less far** — **do not stop there. 'Are you short of breath when you're resting as well?'**

Heart failure signs: **raised JVP over 3 cm · displaced apex · S3 gallop · bibasal creps · hepatomegaly with positive hepatojugular reflux · bilateral pitting oedema.** **Definitive test: echocardiogram.**

**Four pillars of HFrEF: ACE inhibitor (or ARB or sacubitril–valsartan) · a beta-blocker licensed for heart failure — bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol CR, nebivolol · a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist · an SGLT2 inhibitor.** Start low, titrate slowly, monitor potassium and renal function. **Frusemide relieves congestion but does not change prognosis.**

Self-management: **daily weights with an action plan for a gain over 2 kg in 2 days · fluid restriction around 1.5 L daily if congested · salt reduction · cardiac rehabilitation · influenza, pneumococcal and COVID vaccination.** Plus the **secondary prevention he has been missing — aspirin, a high-intensity statin, blood pressure control.**

The rural exposures the stem plants: **wheat, hay and birds → hypersensitivity pneumonitis · cattle, sheep and goats → Q fever, and the vaccine needs PRE-VACCINATION SKIN TESTING AND SEROLOGY because vaccinating someone already exposed can cause a severe reaction · old sheds → asbestos and mesothelioma.**

**Reframe the name when he reacts to it**: it does not mean the heart is about to stop, it means it is not pumping as strongly as it should, and treatment makes people feel better and live longer. **Ask what he drives** — Austroads: symptoms at rest or on minimal exertion means not fit for an unconditional licence. **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **'Before I start, could I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation?'** Then introduce, open question, and your own fixed acknowledgement line: **'thank you for coming in to get this assessed today. Let me ask some questions and examine you, and we'll find the cause together.'**

**Character first: 'is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in?'** Then **how long · constant or coming and going · getting worse · what makes it worse and better · how far could you walk six months ago and how far now · AND ARE YOU SHORT OF BREATH AT REST AS WELL?**
**Cough and noisy breathing** — cough, wheeze, phlegm and colour. Cheap, and it closes off asthma and COPD before you open the clue.

**The stem's clue — the heart of this station.** **When did you have your heart attack · what treatment did you have at the time · what medications are you on for it NOW · ARE YOU MANAGING TO TAKE THEM EVERY DAY · have you had regular follow-up with a GP?** → ran out at three or four months, never got a new script, three-hour round trip. **Thank him and normalise it; do not judge.**

**Both post-MI complications.** Recurrent IHD: **any chest pain with the breathlessness, especially on exertion · racing of the heart · dizziness or blackouts?** Heart failure: **worse lying down · HOW MANY PILLOWS · waking at night gasping · swelling in the legs or ankles?**
**The cancer block, done anyway**: **weight loss without trying · appetite · lumps or bumps · night sweats · HAVE YOU COUGHED UP ANY BLOOD · any previous cancer?**

**Occupation and exposures**: **what's your occupation · do you work with hay, grain or birds · ever exposed to ASBESTOS · contact with cattle, sheep or goats — and HAVE YOU HAD THE Q FEVER VACCINATION?**

The remaining sweep: **childhood chest infections or repeated pneumonias · fevers or chills · recent cold or flu · travel or TB contact · joint pains or rashes · bruising, tiredness, bowel change or black stools.** Then **SADMA with pack-years and quit date, past history, family history.**

**'Given the history, I'd like to start with the cardiovascular examination'** — say why. Then **JVP · apex and parasternal heave · heart sounds, murmurs, GALLOP OR THIRD HEART SOUND** → respiratory → **hepatomegaly and hepatojugular reflux** → **oedema, and is it pitting** → **ECG and spirometry.**

**Diagnosis with THREE reasons**: the pattern of the breathlessness and the three pillows · the swelling in both legs · the examination findings named one by one. Then reframe the term if he reacts to it.

**'I was also thinking about…' — said once per differential.** Recurrent IHD, arrhythmia, valve disease; then lung cancer, COPD, asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis from the grain, ILD, bronchiectasis, pneumonia and Q fever, TB, and anaemia. **If you realise you forgot to ask something, name it as a differential anyway — do not go back and re-take history.**
pefe: **Vitals before you sit down**, then **cardiovascular FIRST and say why** — changing the order signals you are adapting to the case rather than reciting a template.

The order: **general appearance — distress, cyanosis, drowsiness · JVP · apex beat and parasternal heave · heart sounds, murmurs, GALLOP AND THIRD HEART SOUND · respiratory — symmetrical movement, percussion, breath sounds and added sounds, vocal resonance · abdomen — hepatomegaly and HEPATOJUGULAR REFLUX · lower limbs — oedema, AND IS IT PITTING · office tests — ECG and spirometry.**

**ECG always, even when heart failure is obvious** — prior infarction, LVH, atrial fibrillation, bundle branch block. **A pathological Q wave is at least 40 ms wide or deeper than 25% of the following R wave, in two or more contiguous leads**, and is permanent. **Small narrow septal Q waves under 40 ms in I, aVL, V5 and V6 are normal — do not call those an old infarct.**
**Echocardiogram is the definitive test** — ejection fraction, regional wall motion abnormality, valves, chamber sizes.

**Chest X-ray**, read as **A B C D E — Alveolar oedema (bat-wing) · Kerley B lines · Cardiomegaly · Dilated upper lobe vessels · Effusions.** **The cardiothoracic ratio over 0.5 is only valid on a PA film at full inspiration** — on an AP or portable film say the ratio cannot be assessed reliably. **And screen the lungs while you are there.**

**Spirometry** for obstructive versus restrictive. Bloods: **FBE for anaemia, UEC and eGFR, LFT, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, TSH, iron studies.** **24-hour ambulatory BP** where hypertension is part of the picture.

**A natriuretic peptide 'if available to me'** — BNP and NT-proBNP are guideline tests to rule out heart failure but community access in Australia is limited and they are not universally MBS-rebated. **Echocardiography is definitive regardless.**
**Avoid the shotgun list.** Relevance scores, not length — and do not stop at 'chest X-ray' as an entire investigation answer.

dx: **Cardiovascular disease — and that is the answer.** Months of exertional breathlessness, chest heaviness, ankle swelling and long-standing hypertension, in a man in his seventies with **no previous MI**.
**The vagueness is the design.** The sparse findings exist so that the investigation task has something to do. **Refusing to over-call it is what is being marked.**

Say it as a range within cardiovascular disease: **narrowing of the heart's arteries · heart failure · a problem with the heart muscle itself · a rhythm disturbance — the heart is running fast today. 'I don't yet have enough to tell you which, and I'd rather test than guess.'**

**Bilateral oedema alone is not heart failure.** With **no raised JVP, no gallop, no crepitations and no hepatomegaly**, the commonest innocent explanation is a **calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine** — so take the medication list seriously.

**Long-standing hypertension is the thread**: it drives ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease with diastolic dysfunction, and atrial fibrillation. **24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring earns its place here.**
A murmur with tachycardia keeps **valvular disease — especially aortic stenosis in this age group — and arrhythmia** live. **Echocardiogram answers both.**
**The lung list still has to be said**: **lung cancer at the top, then COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis and interstitial lung disease.** History and differentials are separately scored.

Investigations, with a reason attached to each: **ECG because this could still be ischaemic heart disease · echocardiogram for heart failure and the murmur · 24-hour ambulatory BP given the hypertension · chest X-ray, which may show cardiomegaly or an effusion and screens the lungs · spirometry · FBE for anaemia.**
**Avoid the shotgun list** — 'FBE, ESR, CRP, LFT, TFT, renal function and an echo'. **Relevance is what scores, not length.**

If the tests confirm HFrEF, the **four pillars** follow: **ACE inhibitor or ARNI · a beta-blocker licensed for heart failure · a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist · an SGLT2 inhibitor**, with **frusemide for congestion only**. Until then, **investigate rather than commit**.

stem: Lily, 28, presents with shortness of breath since last night, which began while she was sitting on the couch and has not settled.
tasks: Take a complete history (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
findings: BP 118/74 · PULSE 104 · RR 22 · SpO2 95% on room air · T 37.1. Say it back: MILDLY TACHYCARDIC AND TACHYPNOEIC BUT NOT SHOCKED. TACHYPNOEA AND TACHYCARDIA ARE THE COMMONEST SIGNS OF PE
NOT PART OF THIS VERSION — six minutes of history, then diagnosis and differentials. Every finding that makes the diagnosis is disclosed ONLY if you ask the specific question
EXAMINATION IS OFTEN ENTIRELY NORMAL IN PE. A normal examination, a normal ECG and a normal chest X-ray DO NOT EXCLUDE IT
AT LEAST 7.5 — DVT signs and symptoms 3 · PE the most likely diagnosis 3 · immobilisation 3 or more days 1.5. Over 4 = PE LIKELY → IMAGE. NO D-DIMER
PERC, if the examiner raises it
SHE FAILS ON AT LEAST THREE COUNTS — oestrogen use, unilateral leg swelling, heart rate over 100. PERC only applies when PE is unlikely and suspicion is low

BP 84/52 · HR 128 · SpO2 87%. HIGH-RISK (MASSIVE) PE — this is a resuscitation. Priority-one ambulance, high-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, CAUTIOUS fluid (over-filling worsens right ventricular failure), monitoring with a defibrillator, ECG, and discuss THROMBOLYSIS. MedSTAR in parallel, not afterwards. DO NOT DELAY TRANSFER FOR IMAGING
findingsLabel: Observations and the scoring · open when you would ask
must: FAIL — Never asking about the legs. The swollen calf is the entire case.
FAIL — No clotting risk sweep. Run COST VMPF as a named block, under 60 seconds.
FAIL — Sending her home, or arranging an outpatient scan. Ambulance, ED, today.
FAIL — Settling on a panic attack before PE is excluded in a woman on the pill.
ASK — Which pill, and do you know its name? The risk is the oestrogen.
ASK — What did you do during the flight? That is what converts travel into immobility.

dx: **Pulmonary embolism, provoked** — prolonged immobilisation on a long-haul flight plus an **oestrogen-containing pill**, on a background family history of clotting.

**This is the highest-failure case in the breathlessness cluster**, because there is no image and no examination — **the calf, the flight, the sleeping tablet, the pill and the family history are each disclosed only if you ask a specific question.**
**If you could say only one phrase in this station it would be 'DVT signs and symptoms.'** The leg is the source, it is a Wells criterion worth three points, and here it is positive.

**Since last night is neither acute nor chronic — do not deliberate.** Run the same breathlessness structure you always run, and add **'what were you doing exactly before it started?'** as your open hunt for a trigger.
**COST VMPF, as a named block: Contraception · Obesity · Surgery · Travel and immobility · Varicose veins · Malignancy · Pregnancy · Family history.** Under 60 seconds.

**The oestrogen is the risk.** Combined pills, patches and rings count; **progestogen-only pills, implants and hormonal IUDs do not.** And **it is the immobility, not the aeroplane** — a long bus or car trip, bed rest or a leg cast all count.

**Wells, two-tier: DVT signs 3 · PE most likely 3 · HR over 100 1.5 · immobilisation 3 or more days or surgery within 4 weeks 1.5 · previous VTE 1.5 · haemoptysis 1 · malignancy 1. Over 4 = likely → image. 4 or less → D-dimer.** **Do not order a D-dimer when PE is already likely** — a positive changes nothing and a negative will not reassure you.
**CTPA is the investigation of choice. V/Q if pregnant**, in contrast allergy or significant renal impairment. **Check a β-hCG in any woman of childbearing age before imaging.**

**Stable, non-pregnant adult: rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily, or apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily.** Alternative **enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily or 1 mg/kg twice daily** bridging to warfarin, **target INR 2–3**. **In pregnancy LMWH only — DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated.** **At least 3 months when provoked.**

**Stop the combined pill and arrange the replacement — do not leave her uncovered.** Condoms now; mini-pill, implant or IUD at follow-up. **Disposition is worth as much as the diagnosis: ambulance, emergency department, today, not driving herself.** **000 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS for metropolitan follow-up.**
plan: **'Before I begin, may I have her observations — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** Then WIPE, **confirm name and date of birth**, **'are you comfortable, and are you short of breath just sitting here?'**, open question, and **'I understand how stressful that must be — let me ask you some questions and we'll find the cause together.'**

Explore it: **is it tightness in the chest, difficulty getting the breath in, or not getting enough air · constant or coming and going · is it getting worse · is this the first time · worse on exertion, AND IS IT THERE AT REST · worse lying flat · AND WHAT WERE YOU DOING EXACTLY BEFORE IT STARTED?**
Cough and chest: **any cough · bringing anything up, what colour · HAVE YOU SEEN ANY BLOOD IN IT · any noisy or wheezy breathing · any chest pain, and is it worse when you breathe in deeply?**

**The question that decides the station: 'have you had any swelling or pain in your calves or legs?'** Then chase it — **which leg · when did you first notice it · is it painful, red or warm · is it sore to squeeze the calf, or when you walk?**

**COST VMPF, under 60 seconds.** **C — are you taking any contraceptive pill, and do you know which one? · O — would you say you're currently overweight? · S — any surgery or hospital stay in the last month or two? · T — any long travel recently, AND WHAT DID YOU DO DURING THE TRIP, any period off your feet for days? · V — any prominent or dilated veins in your legs? · M — any previous cancer, or weight loss you didn't intend? · P — when was your last period, and is there any chance you could be pregnant? · F — have you or anyone in your family ever had a clot in the leg or lung?**

Rule out the rest: **any injury or blow to the chest, do you smoke · any wheeze, night cough, hay fever, eczema or asthma in the family · any fever, chills, sweats or unwell contacts · any chest tightness, palpitations, ankle swelling or fainting, any sudden death in the family under 40 · any rash, itch or swelling of the lips or tongue, any new food or medication · any tiredness, dizziness, heavy periods or black stools · any weight loss or night sweats.**

Mood and close: **how have things been generally, any unusual stress, any episodes of panic with a racing heart and a feeling of dread** → then **other conditions, medications including over the counter, allergies, smoking and alcohol, who's at home, and WAS THERE ANYTHING YOU WERE PARTICULARLY WORRIED THIS MIGHT BE?** → she offers the panic attack. **Keep it on the list, explicitly last, pending exclusion.**

**The diagnosis in plain words, linked to the leg**: a clot in one of the blood vessels of the lung, which **almost certainly formed in your leg and travelled up** — the flight, having slept through it, the combined pill, and her mother's clot. **'None of this is something you did wrong — it's a set of things stacking up.'**

**The differentials, briskly, each with one reason**: collapsed lung, asthma, chest infection, a heart problem, severe allergic reaction, low blood count, panic attack — **only settled on once the clot is excluded** — and cancer at the far end.

**Disposition, which is the other half of the marks: 'this needs dealing with today, not next week. I'm calling an ambulance — I don't want you driving.'** CTPA at the hospital, blood thinner for at least three months, **stop the combined pill and arrange the alternative**, safety-net, **'is there someone I can call to meet you there?'**, summary.
pefe: **Stability first: blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature.** If no examiner is available, say it to the patient — the observations are still your first move.

**Examination is often entirely normal in PE.** When signs are present: **tachypnoea and tachycardia (commonest) · DVT signs in one leg · LOUD P2 from acute pulmonary hypertension · raised JVP · S3 gallop and hypotension in massive PE · a systolic murmur at the tricuspid area · low-grade fever · pleural rub, and dullness where infarction or a small effusion has occurred.**
**Calculate the Wells score out loud**, then **CTPA — the investigation of choice. V/Q if pregnant, contrast allergy or significant renal impairment.** **D-dimer only where PE is unlikely.**

**ECG: tachycardia with non-specific ST and T change is by far the commonest.** Also **right bundle branch block, right axis deviation, T-wave inversion V1–V4, atrial fibrillation**. **S1Q3T3 is classic, genuinely uncommon, and neither sensitive nor specific.** **A normal ECG does not exclude PE.**
**CTPA description to say aloud: 'filling defects within the contrast-opacified pulmonary arteries, consistent with pulmonary emboli.'** An accompanying pleural effusion is not evidence against it.

dx: **Pulmonary embolism, provoked** — and the whole of this version is whether **one examination finding can overturn a history that points elsewhere. It cannot.**

**Dullness at a lung base reads as pneumonia.** But **consolidation gives dullness WITH bronchial breathing and INCREASED vocal resonance** — neither is offered here. **Dullness in PE means pulmonary infarction, possibly with a small effusion.**

**Loud P2 = acute pulmonary hypertension. Left parasternal systolic murmur = tricuspid regurgitation from right ventricular strain.** Both are recognised PE findings — **say what each one means out loud.**
**Haemoptysis is a feature of PE, not only a cancer red flag — and it is a Wells point worth 1.** Ask for it inside the sputum question and again in the cancer block.

**COST VMPF as a named block: Contraception · Obesity · Surgery · Travel and immobility · Varicose veins · Malignancy · Pregnancy · Family history.** **The oestrogen is the risk; the immobility, not the aeroplane.**

**Wells, two-tier: DVT signs 3 · PE most likely 3 · HR over 100 1.5 · immobilisation or recent surgery 1.5 · previous VTE 1.5 · haemoptysis 1 · malignancy 1. Over 4 → image. 4 or less → D-dimer.** She is well over. **A D-dimer here adds nothing.**
**CTPA is the investigation of choice. V/Q if pregnant, contrast allergy or renal impairment. β-hCG before imaging in any woman of childbearing age.**

**Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily, or apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily. Enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily or 1 mg/kg twice daily — the only option in pregnancy. Warfarin target INR 2–3. At least 3 months when provoked. Thrombolysis only for haemodynamic instability.**

**Red flags making this high-risk: hypotension, syncope, heart rate over 110, saturation under 92%, cyanosis, raised JVP with an S3, altered conscious state, pregnancy, massive haemoptysis.** That is resuscitation and thrombolysis, not an outpatient pathway.

**Stop the combined pill and arrange the replacement.** **Ambulance, emergency department, today — she does not drive herself.** Future long journeys: **walk hourly, calf exercises, hydration, and discuss compression stockings with her treating team.** **000 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**

stem: A 68-year-old man with tachypnoea. History of hypercholesterolaemia, hypertension and previous myocardial infarction.

SpO2 89% RA · BP 132/84 · HR 112 · RR 28 · T 36.8 °C. Distended neck veins; apex not displaced; systolic murmur at the apex; S1 and S2 muffled with an S3 gallop; bibasal dullness and crepitations; pitting oedema to the knees.
tasks: Explain your diagnosis to the medical student
Explain your immediate management plan
findings: SpO2 89% ON ROOM AIR · BP 132/84 · HR 112 · RR 28 · T 36.8. Tachypnoeic, tachycardic and hypoxic — and NORMOTENSIVE, which is the finding that settles the tamponade question
DISTENDED — the systemic venous side of the same raised pressure
FIRST AND SECOND HEART SOUNDS MUFFLED, with a THIRD HEART SOUND PRESENT — GALLOP RHYTHM. The S3 is rapid filling into a stiff, dilated ventricle
SYSTOLIC MURMUR AT THE APEX — expect radiation to the axilla. FUNCTIONAL (SECONDARY) MITRAL REGURGITATION from a dilated ischaemic ventricle, NOT mitral valve prolapse
DULLNESS TO PERCUSSION AT BOTH BASES with BIBASAL CREPITATIONS. Fine, bibasal and SYMMETRICAL — the dullness is transudative pleural effusion
HYPOTENSION · RAISED JVP · MUFFLED HEART SOUNDS. He has TWO OF THREE — but at 132/84 he is NORMOTENSIVE, so THIS IS NOT TAMPONADE. Order the echocardiogram anyway to answer the pericardium

BP 78/50, cool peripheries, lactate 4.2, oliguric. NO NITRATE — it will drop him further. Oxygen and non-invasive ventilation, cautious or withheld diuretic until perfusion improves, INOTROPE OR VASOPRESSOR, urgent bedside echo, cardiology and intensive care now. SAY THE WORDS CARDIOGENIC SHOCK

Two hours of severe breathlessness, BP 210/120, lungs clear yesterday, NEW LOUD PANSYSTOLIC MURMUR three days after an inferior infarct → PAPILLARY MUSCLE RUPTURE with acute severe mitral regurgitation. Urgent echo and cardiothoracic surgery
findingsLabel: Findings given in the stem · open before you teach
must: FAIL — Half a diagnosis. 'Heart failure' alone, or 'pulmonary oedema' alone.
FAIL — Calling tamponade in a normotensive man. Beck's triad is HYPOTENSION.
FAIL — Leaving him flat, or a management list that opens with oxygen or frusemide.
FAIL — No ECG and no troponin after a previous infarct; or starting a beta-blocker today.
ASK — the student first: what did you make of him? Then teach, don't recite.
ASK — at the end: does that hang together? Anything you want me to go back over?

dx: **Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, secondary to decompensated heart failure.** **Say the whole phrase** — 'heart failure' alone misses the emergency, 'pulmonary oedema' alone misses the cause.

**The chain, six links, not a list**: hypertension, cholesterol and a previous infarct are the substrate → **the left ventricle cannot eject enough** → pressure backs into the left atrium and the pulmonary veins → **pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure exceeds the oncotic pressure holding fluid in the vessel** → fluid crosses into the interstitium and then the alveoli → **gas exchange fails**.

**Hang every sign on a link.** Raised JVP and pitting oedema = the systemic venous side of the same pressure. **S3 = rapid filling into a stiff dilated ventricle.** Crepitations = alveoli opening against fluid. Basal dullness = **transudative effusion**.
**Crackles are not pneumonia when they are fine, bibasal and symmetrical and sit beside a raised JVP, an S3 and oedema.** Consolidation is focal, with bronchial breathing and a fever.

**CORRECTION — the murmur is functional mitral regurgitation, not mitral valve prolapse**: annular dilatation and papillary muscle displacement in a dilated ischaemic ventricle. **Prolapse gives a mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur, usually in a younger patient.**

**CORRECTION — Beck's triad is HYPOTENSION, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds** (plus **pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg** and electrical alternans). **Reversing it to hypertension is a hard fail.** Muffled sounds are far more often obesity, hyperinflation or crackles drowning them.

**Seven ordered steps, numbered aloud: 1 sit him upright with legs dependent · 2 oxygen to 92–96% (88–92% if CO2 retention is a risk) · 3 IV access, cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG · 4 GTN 300–600 microg sublingual or 400 microg spray, repeated while systolic stays above 100 · 5 IV frusemide 20–40 mg or the usual daily oral dose, with a catheter to chart output · 6 STOP ANY IV FLUIDS · 7 CPAP 5–10 cmH2O if still hypoxic, and call cardiology.**

**Nitrate before diuretic when the pressure allows** — much of the acute picture is **redistribution rather than total body overload**, and nitrates drop preload and afterload within minutes while the diuretic only addresses volume.

**Deliberately not doing: no IV fluids · no NSAIDs · no beta-blocker today.** **CORRECTION — morphine is no longer routine**; observational data associate it with worse outcomes, more ventilation and longer stay. Reserve it for severe distress or ischaemic pain.

**Four pillars of HFrEF once euvolaemic: ACE inhibitor or ARNI · a beta-blocker with heart failure evidence — bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol CR, nebivolol, started low and slow · a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist · an SGLT2 inhibitor.** A loop diuretic sits alongside for congestion, **not as disease-modifying therapy**. **Action plan: 2 kg in 2 days. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **Frame it in fifteen seconds**: **'let's take two minutes on this gentleman before we go back in. I'll tell you what I think is going on and why, then what I want done in the next ten minutes. Stop me at any point. WHAT DID YOU MAKE OF HIM?'**

**Name it in full: acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, secondary to decompensated heart failure.** He will say he thought it was pneumonia because of the crackles — **praise the thought, then answer it with what goes WITH the crackles.**

**The chain, six links, cause to consequence** — substrate, failing ejection, backward pressure, hydrostatic exceeding oncotic, fluid into interstitium then alveoli, gas exchange failing. **'That is his respiratory rate of 28 and his saturation of 89%.'**
**Map the signs onto the links, one at a time**, and say the framing sentence: **'each sign is a link in the chain, not a separate finding.'**

**The murmur and the muffled sounds.** Systolic, apex, radiating to the axilla → **functional mitral regurgitation**. Then **test tamponade properly out loud**: recite Beck's triad, **say which element is absent**, and **order the echo anyway**.

**Investigations with reasons attached**: **ECG and SERIAL TROPONIN** for the precipitant · **FBE, UEC before diuresis, LFT, TFT, glucose** · **blood gas and lactate** · **chest film — Alveolar oedema, Kerley B lines, Cardiomegaly, upper lobe Diversion, Effusions** · **echocardiogram: ejection fraction, regional wall motion, severity of the mitral regurgitation, and pericardial fluid.**
**The seven steps, numbered as a sequence**, with **sitting upright as step one — free, immediate, and it reduces preload.** Then say what you are **deliberately not doing** and why.

**The four pillars, once he is stable and euvolaemic** — and **'the beta-blocker does not go in today, while he is wet.'** Plus cardiac rehabilitation, daily weights with the 2 kg in 2 days trigger, vaccination, device assessment later.

**Summarise and check understanding: 'does that hang together? Anything you want me to go back over?'** If asked to explain it to the patient instead, **switch register completely** — no hydrostatic pressure, no ejection fraction.
pefe: **The examination has already been performed for you** — this station is the explanation and the management, not the examining.
**ECG and serial troponin in every acute pulmonary oedema.** A mild rise occurs in any decompensation; **a rising trend means ACS**, the commonest precipitant, and he has infarcted before.

**Echocardiogram is the key investigation — and never order it without saying what for: ejection fraction · regional wall motion · the severity of the mitral regurgitation · pericardial fluid**, which is what answers the muffled sounds.
**Chest X-ray: A B C D E — Alveolar bat-wing oedema · Kerley B lines · Cardiomegaly · upper lobe Diversion · Effusions.** **Do not delay escalation waiting for the film.**
**FBE, UEC, LFT, TFT, glucose** — anaemia and thyroid as precipitants, **renal function before you diurese**. **Venous or arterial gas with lactate** before non-invasive ventilation.
**BNP or NT-proBNP is most useful for its negative predictive value when the diagnosis is uncertain.** VERIFY Medicare access is restricted.

**Avoid: lying him flat even briefly for a procedure · IV fluids · NSAIDs · introducing or up-titrating a beta-blocker while congested** (continue an established dose unless shocked) **· routine morphine · delaying escalation for imaging.**
ddx: **Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema** — the answer
Orthopnoea, risk factors, **S3, raised JVP, bibasal creps, oedema**
Gallop rhythm, hepatojugular reflux, positive fluid balance
**CXR, BNP or NT-proBNP, echocardiogram** — immediate
**Acute coronary syndrome as the trigger**
Prior infarct, risk factors, **may be entirely painless**
New ECG changes, arrhythmia
**ECG and troponin in every case** — immediate
**Acute severe mitral regurgitation**
**Flash oedema, new loud pansystolic murmur, recent MI**
Thrill, hyperdynamic apex, cardiogenic shock
**Urgent echocardiogram, cardiothoracic referral** — immediate
**Cardiac tamponade**
**Muffled sounds, raised JVP** — the bait in this stem
**Beck's triad, pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg**, quiet precordium
**Echocardiogram; pericardiocentesis if positive. He is NORMOTENSIVE, so not tamponade** — immediate
Arrhythmia, commonly atrial fibrillation
Irregular pulse, abrupt decompensation
Rate, rhythm, apex-radial deficit
ECG; rate or rhythm control — urgent
Progressive pneumonia or parapneumonic effusion
Fever, purulent sputum, focal signs
**Unilateral dullness with bronchial breathing** — not what he has
Repeat CXR, ultrasound, inflammatory markers — urgent
**Pulmonary embolism**
Hypoxia out of proportion, immobility, malignancy
Pleuritic pain, calf signs, loud P2
**Wells score, CTPA. Prophylactic enoxaparin does not exclude it** — immediate
**ARDS — non-cardiogenic oedema**
Sepsis, aspiration, no cardiac history
**Bilateral infiltrates with a NORMAL JVP**
**Echocardiogram showing normal filling pressures** — immediate
Sepsis with septic cardiomyopathy
Fever, a source, warm peripheries then shock
Lactate, source of infection
Cultures, lactate, sepsis pathway — immediate
Anaemia · thyrotoxicosis · renal failure
Precipitants of decompensation
Pallor, tremor, uraemia, oliguria
FBE, TFT, UEC — urgent
