dx: **Post-operative atelectasis on day 1.** Splinting from wound pain → shallow tidal volumes → alveolar collapse, basal or mid-zone, with fever, tachypnoea and desaturation. **Loss of lung volume from collapse of alveoli that are no longer being inflated — not an infection, though it predisposes to one.**

**Nobody is marked on knowing the answer.** You are marked on **a differential list generated by the post-operative TIMELINE**, on including **the two things that kill — myocardial infarction and venous thromboembolism** — and on **asking for the one finding that separates collapse from consolidation**.

**Say the list in this shape: in the first few hours — the inflammatory response itself, drug or transfusion reaction, malignant hyperthermia, or an infection he brought in with him. In the first three days — atelectasis and pneumonia, myocardial infarction, UTI, early wound infection, VTE. After day three — wound infection, a surgery-specific complication such as a collection or bile leak, thrombophlebitis, hospital-acquired infection, drug fever. He is on day one, so my list narrows to the middle group.**
**Vocal resonance is the discriminator. NORMAL OR REDUCED = atelectasis. INCREASED = consolidation.** Air entry, crepitations and a dull percussion note are **identical in both**.

**Pain is a respiratory question.** A painful abdominal wound means no deep breath, and shallow breathing without periodic sighs collapses dependent alveoli within hours — **which is why analgesia is the first line of treatment, not physiotherapy.**

Management, in this order: **1 optimised multimodal analgesia — paracetamol 1 g every 6 h, max 4 g in 24 h, an NSAID if renal function and the surgical team allow, an opioid or PCA for breakthrough · 2 paracetamol also treats the fever · 3 continuous saturation, oxygen to 92–96% · 4 chest physiotherapy TODAY — deep breathing and effective cough with wound support · 5 sit up and mobilise, which is also VTE prophylaxis · 6 smoking cessation now, Quitline 13 7848 · 7 review in a few hours.**
**ANTIBIOTICS ARE NOT INDICATED FOR ATELECTASIS.** Say it deliberately — prescribing them is the reasoning error the examiner is watching for.

**CORRECTION — it is malignant HYPERthermia**, a pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile agents and suxamethonium, treated with **dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV**. **CORRECTION — ask for FBE and CRP, not ESR**: ESR rises non-specifically after any surgery and lags by days, and CRP is raised by the operation itself on day 1, so use the trend.

**The Five Ws are second-best**: Wind d1–2 · Water d3–5 · Walking d4–6 · Wound d5–7 · Wonder drugs d7+. **They omit myocardial infarction and anastomotic or bile leak entirely** — the two things that will actually fail you. Use the timeline, keep the Ws as a cross-check.

**Escalate tonight for: systolic under 90 · heart rate over 130 · respiratory rate over 25 despite oxygen · new confusion · lactate 2 or more · bilious drain output · generalised abdominal tenderness.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450.**
plan: **To the examiner first: 'before I begin I'd like this patient on continuous observations, and I'd move him to a monitored bed if he deteriorates. I have the chart, so I'll proceed.'** Six seconds, and it is a scored line. Then gel, introduce, open question.

**The concern statement — do not skip it**: **'I completely understand why a temperature after an operation is worrying. Let me ask you some questions and examine you, then we'll work out the cause together and I'll tell you exactly what we're going to do.'**

**Box 1, the fever itself: do you feel feverish? any shivering or shaking chills? when did it start? DID YOU HAVE ANY FEVER BEFORE THE OPERATION? is it getting worse?** Rigors point to bacteraemia rather than collapse; fever before the list means the infection came in with him.

**Box 2, the post-operative review — the block everyone skips: any nausea or vomiting? have your bowels worked, have you passed wind? any tummy pain apart from the wound? any dizziness? have you started eating and drinking? HAVE YOU BEEN OUT OF BED? ARE YOU IN PAIN RIGHT NOW — AND ARE THE PAINKILLERS HELPING?** When he says it hurts to breathe in, **react to it in the room**: 'that's really important — I think the pain is part of what's causing this.'
**Box 3, chest: any cough — dry or bringing anything up, what colour? any shortness of breath? any noisy breathing? ever had a lung condition? do you smoke, or have you ever?**

**Box 4, heart — the box that decides Version B and the single most dangerous omission: ANY CHEST PAIN OR TIGHTNESS, EVEN BRIEFLY? have you noticed your heart racing or thumping? any previous heart trouble, heart attack or angina?** If he has known ischaemic disease, **which cardiac medicines were withheld for surgery** — abrupt beta-blocker cessation causes rebound ischaemia.
**Box 5, urine: any burning or pain passing urine? going more often? cloudy or offensive? any back or loin pain? HAVE YOU HAD A CATHETER?**

**Box 6, the wound: any discharge or weeping? any redness or swelling? is it more painful than yesterday?** Discharge is the discriminating symptom — some redness after a fresh incision is normal, **escalating pain is not**.
**Box 7, legs: any swelling or pain in the calves? any sharp chest pain on breathing in, or coughed up blood? have you had the blood-thinning injection each day?**

**Box 8, travel — and say why: 'did you travel anywhere in the weeks before the operation? I ask because an infection picked up before surgery can present like this'** — not because you are chasing a clot.

**Box 9, lines, drugs and blood: any redness or pain around the drip site — AND WHEN WAS IT PUT IN? have you ever had a fever after an operation before, after a blood transfusion, or after starting a new medicine?** That last sentence ticks off drug fever, transfusion reaction and a family history of malignant hyperthermia at once.
**Closure: any other medical conditions, regular medicines, allergies, anything in the family? And is there anything you were hoping I'd ask that I haven't?**

**The examination request, specific not generic**: general appearance · 'I have the vital signs, so I'll move on' — **say it, don't silently skip it** · **respiratory in full ending with VOCAL RESONANCE** · cardiovascular · **abdomen with the four asks — wound, suprapubic, renal angle, masses, plus distension and drain** · **cannula site, I'm looking for thrombophlebitis** · **lower limbs for oedema, calf size difference and tenderness** · **urine dipstick**.

**Say 'I've grouped my differentials by how long it is since the operation'**, deliver the timeline list, **then** name atelectasis in plain English — **'because of the pain you haven't been breathing deeply, and a small part of your lung has collapsed down'** — and **name the differentials to the patient** so he could repeat them back.

**Management with ANALGESIA FIRST**, then paracetamol for the fever, chest X-ray and bloods, urine to the lab, monitoring and oxygen, **physiotherapy today**, sitting up and out of bed, no smoking, **'antibiotics don't treat a collapsed lung'**, review this afternoon, and the safety-net: **breathing worse, chest pain, racing heart, wound leaking or much more painful, feeling faint — tell the nurses immediately.**
pefe: Request it in this order: **general appearance — respiratory distress, cyanosis, IS HE IN PAIN · vital signs (say you have them) · respiratory — symmetrical movements, tracheal position, percussion note, breath sounds and added sounds, AND VOCAL RESONANCE · cardiovascular — S1, S2, murmurs, gallop · abdomen — the surgical site, SUPRAPUBIC tenderness, RENAL ANGLE tenderness, masses, distension and what is in the drain · cannula site for erythema, tenderness or discharge · lower limbs for oedema, calf size difference and calf tenderness · and a urine dipstick.**

**Do now, before you leave the room: full observations with a repeat temperature · urine dipstick · 12-lead ECG if any chest pain, palpitations, tachycardia or hypertension · inspect the wound, cannula and drain yourself · oxygen to 92–96% · and FIX THE ANALGESIA NOW rather than deferring it to the plan.**

**Do next: CHEST X-RAY — the single most useful test, separating collapse from consolidation · FBE and CRP · urine MCS, because a UTI can be present with a negative dipstick · two sets of blood cultures if septic or rigoring · serial troponin if the ECG or history raises cardiac concern · U&E, LFT and lipase with abdominal signs, and CT abdomen with contrast if a collection or bile leak is suspected · venous lactate if any sepsis features.**
**Do not order more than this** — a scattergun panel reads as absent reasoning, and you still have to talk about management.
**D-dimer is unreliable post-operatively** — go to compression ultrasound or CTPA. **Dipstick alone misses infection and is unreliable with a catheter.**

**Cannulae are reviewed daily and generally resited by 72 hours** unless clinically indicated sooner. VERIFY against local SA Health policy — some sites work to 72–96 hours or replace on clinical indication only.
**Avoid: diagnosing atelectasis without a chest X-ray · antibiotics 'just in case' · treating the fever and ignoring the pain · 'the physio will sort it out' as your whole plan.**

dx: **A cardiac event until proven otherwise — post-operative myocardial infarction.** Fever, tachycardia and hypertension **with a normal respiratory rate, normal saturation and no chest findings is not atelectasis.**

**This version was piloted once and almost nobody diagnosed it**, because candidate differential lists for post-operative fever traditionally contain **no cardiac entry at all**. **Keep MI on the list in every post-operative fever station you ever sit.**

**Surgery is a major physiological stressor, and post-operative MI is frequently silent or atypical.** In a 45-year-old with cardiovascular risk it is **the single most dangerous omission in this station**.
**ECG and serial troponin before anything else**, cardiac monitoring, and involve the medical team. **Do not wait to be asked.**
**Ask which cardiac and antihypertensive medicines were withheld peri-operatively** — **abrupt beta-blocker cessation causes rebound ischaemia**.

**The same observations also fit a surgery-specific complication** — **bile leak or subhepatic collection** — and that must be voiced in an abdominal case, alongside **pulmonary embolism**, which fever does not exclude.

**The honest caveat scores**: 'with normal respiratory observations and no chest signs I cannot call this atelectasis. My working diagnosis is a cardiac event until the ECG and troponin say otherwise, and I would also want to exclude an intra-abdominal complication.' **Do not invent a final diagnosis.**

**Say it to the patient without frightening him**: **'I'm concerned the operation may have put strain on your heart. I want to rule out a heart attack first, because that's the one that can't wait — so I'm doing a heart tracing and a blood test right now, and asking the medical team to see you.'**

**Escalation triggers: systolic under 90 · heart rate over 130 · respiratory rate over 25 · new confusion · lactate 2 or more · bilious drain output · generalised abdominal tenderness.** **Never keep taking a history through a deteriorating patient** — name the change, name the pathway, name who you are calling.

**The timeline still drives the list: day 2–3 is the EARLY group** — atelectasis and pneumonia, **myocardial infarction**, UTI, early wound infection, VTE. **The Five Ws omit MI and anastomotic leak entirely.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**

setting: General practice. You are the GP. The patient's relative (cousin) gives the history; the patient is beside her, awake but not really talking.
stem: A 40-year-old woman has been brought to the clinic feeling unwell. Her relative is with her and will speak to you.
Vital signs: BP 85/55 · pulse 122 · respiratory rate 18 · SpO2 93% on room air · temperature 36.8°C.
tasks: Take a history from the relative
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials
time: 8 minutes. Stability + flat positioning 0:00 · consent gate · unpack 'unwell' · timing · 'what was she doing just before?' (the sting) → treatment sentence and keep going · four anaphylaxis systems · mimic sweep · background · examination airway-first · diagnosis with three reasons + six lay differentials + after-care.

back.dx: Anaphylaxis to an insect sting (Marie Whitcombe, 40; history from cousin Dawn): sudden onset within minutes of a sting, hypotension with tachycardia (warm shock, CRT 3 s), widespread expiratory wheeze, flushing/pruritus, presyncope, nausea — no upper airway involvement, no stridor, no retained sting, glucose 6.2, ECG sinus tachycardia. Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis; adrenaline IM outer mid-thigh now, flat, ambulance. Differentials swept and named in lay terms with a reason each: septicaemia/meningococcaemia (no fever, blanching rash), cardiac event/arrhythmia (no chest pain, ECG sinus tach), stroke/SAH (normal neuro), ruptured ectopic/AAA/GI bleed (no pain, no bleeding, abdomen soft), hypoglycaemia (6.2), drug reaction (no medicines). Discriminating behaviours: the consent gate before disclosure, asking tongue/throat/voice by name, and airway + sting FIRST in the examination.
plan: Gel; ★ to examiner: 'treatment room, lie her flat, continuous monitoring, a colleague stays with her while I take the history'; intro; 'I can see you're both worried — what has happened?'; concern statement; ★ consent gate: 'has she agreed to my discussing her condition with you?'
Unpack 'unwell' (confused/sleepy, weak, feverish, struggling to breathe) · onset · worsening · ever before · ★ 'what was she doing just before this started?' → sting on the neck
★ Treatment sentence, then keep going: 'I want her lying flat, I'm giving adrenaline into her thigh now, and I'm calling an ambulance.'

Four systems: skin (rash/hives/welts, itch, lip/face/eye swelling) · lower airway (noisy breathing — what sound, SOB, cough) · ★ upper airway by name (tongue swollen? throat tight? voice changed?) · CVS (dizzy, faint, collapse) · GI (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain)

Mimic sweep, signposted: fever/chills, rash blanches?, headache/neck stiffness/photophobia, recent flu-like illness · chest pain/palpitations · weakness/numbness/slurred speech/gait/thunderclap headache · abdominal/back pain, bleeding, ★ LMP · asthma, allergies, EpiPen, medicines (diabetes, BP)

Examination airway-first: general (distress, cyanosis, rash, conscious state) → ★ lip/tongue swelling, ★ stridor, ★ visible sting — may I remove it? → chest (air entry, added sounds) → CVS (S1 S2, murmurs, CRT, peripheral temperature) → abdomen incl. expansile pulsatile mass → neuro (cranial nerves, fundoscopy, limbs) → bedside ★ glucose, dipstick, 12-lead ECG. Read the findings back before interpreting.

Diagnosis with three reasons (minutes after the sting; low BP + fast heart = circulation; wheeze = tightened airways); adrenaline given, repeatable; ambulance; ≥4 h observation in hospital because of biphasic reactions; six differentials in lay language with why each is less likely

Replies: 'is she going to be alright?' · 'never allergic before' (sensitisation) · after-care: two autoinjectors, action plan, training, allergy referral, venom immunotherapy; 'can she go home?' → not before 4 h; 'any questions or concerns?' (hidden agenda: cousin's guilt — reassure, no delay caused harm); summary
ask: ★ 'With those observations I'd take her to the treatment room, lie her flat and put her on continuous monitoring.'

★ 'Has she agreed to my discussing her condition with you?' (if 'only her cousin': 'she isn't well enough to consent right now, so I'll share what I need to in order to treat her, and speak to her directly as soon as she's able')
'Can you describe what you mean by unwell — confused, weak, feverish, or struggling to breathe?' / ★ 'What was she doing just before this started?'
★ 'That changes what I think is going on. I want her lying flat and not standing up, I'm giving adrenaline into the muscle of her thigh now, and I'm calling an ambulance.'
★ 'Is her tongue swollen? Does she say her throat feels tight? Has her voice changed?'
'I'm confident this is an allergic reaction, but I want to be sure I'm not missing an infection, a cardiac problem or a bleed.' / 'Does the rash fade when you press on it?'

★ To examiner: 'Before the systems — is there swelling of the lips or tongue? Is there stridor? Do I see a sting — if so, may I remove it?' / 'Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis — I'm not waiting for a test.'

'It's a severe allergic reaction — the sting has made her blood vessels open up and her airways tighten. The treatment is adrenaline into the thigh muscle, which I've given; it works within minutes and we can repeat it.'

'She needs at least four hours of observation, because occasionally these reactions come back.' / 'She'll go home with two adrenaline pens, a written action plan and training, and a specialist referral — venom immunotherapy can substantially reduce the risk.'
'Should I walk her through?' → ★ 'No — please keep her lying flat; standing up can drop her blood pressure further.'
Summary: sudden collapse ten minutes after an insect sting with low BP, fast heart and wheeze — anaphylaxis; adrenaline given, flat, ambulance, hospital observation, specialist follow-up
pefe: Given: pale, distressed, no cyanosis, mild chest flushing, alert. No lip/tongue swelling, no stridor. Insect bite on the neck, no retained sting. Air entry equal, widespread expiratory wheeze. Heart sounds dual, no murmur, CRT 3 s, peripheries warm. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no masses. Neuro normal. BSL 6.2. Dipstick negative. ECG sinus tachycardia.

Variant — airway (stridor, tongue swelling, croaky voice, 'throat closing'): highest-risk anaphylaxis — IM adrenaline now, repeat at 5 min, nebulised adrenaline, high-flow O2, 000 + anaesthetic support, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 early; do NOT examine the throat; sit with legs out if flat worsens breathing VERIFY

Variant — mimic (fever, shivering, non-blanching purpura, headache, photophobia, no sting): meningococcaemia until proven otherwise — adrenaline is NOT the treatment; immediate IM/IV benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone before transfer, cultures if no delay, fluids, ambulance/retrieval; notifiable — public health for contact prophylaxis VERIFY

Variant — drug trigger (amoxicillin this morning; card says penicillin allergy, nobody looked): stop the drug, adrenaline IM, flat, O2, fluids, ambulance; then ★ open disclosure — apologise for the event, state known facts, no blame or speculation, commit to incident report, allergy flag, and to coming back ADDED

Variant — teaching the autoinjector: 'blue to the sky, orange to the thigh' — pull blue cap, orange end firmly into outer thigh until it clicks (through clothing), hold 3 s (EpiPen; Anapen 10 s — CORRECTION to the teaching source's 5 s; check the device), rub 10 s, call 000 and say 'anaphylaxis', keep flat, second pen at 5 min if no better VERIFY

Post-event: tryptase 15 min–3 h + later baseline; ≥4 h observation (longer if severe, required repeat adrenaline, or asthma); discharge with 2 autoinjectors, ASCIA action plan, allergy referral, venom immunotherapy; TIS 131 450; healthdirect 1800 022 222
fails: Disclosing to the relative without the consent gate ★
Not asking 'what was she doing just before this started?' — the sting is volunteered only on that question ★
Not naming adrenaline with dose, IM route and outer thigh, or not keeping her flat / letting the cousin stand her up ★
Asking only about wheeze — omitting tongue swelling, throat tightness and voice change ★
Examining in textbook order and never reaching the airway/stridor/sting first
Racing to the diagnosis on 'stung' and dropping the mimic sweep and bedside glucose
Diagnosis without differentials, or no after-care (4 h observation, two pens, action plan, referral)
numbers: Stem obs: BP 85/55 · HR 122 · RR 18 · SpO2 93% · T 36.8°C
Adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 IM outer mid-thigh, max 0.5 mg (adult 0.5 mg = 0.5 mL), repeat every 5 min if no improvement
Autoinjectors: 150 mcg (7.5–20 kg) · 300 mcg (>20 kg / adult) · 500 mcg Anapen (>50 kg where supplied) · EpiPen hold 3 s · Anapen hold 10 s VERIFY
Fluid bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline if hypotensive · high-flow O2 · observation minimum 4 h · tryptase 15 min–3 h + baseline
Six lay differentials: blood infection · heart · stroke · bleed inside (ectopic/AAA) · low sugar · medicine reaction

stem: Jane Sotiris, a 35-year-old woman, presents to your general practice complaining of tiredness. Nothing else is given in the stem.

tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
You will then be given the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Exploration is five questions, not a conversation; the marks are in the M probe, the four node words, the word cancer, one feelings check, and excision biopsy.

back.dx: Lymphoma — four months of constant, worsening lack of energy (not sleepiness); 5 kg unintentional weight loss over a few months, appetite fine; two lumps in the LEFT axilla for two months, slightly bigger, painless; drenching night sweats (changes her nightie); no fever, no itch, no alcohol-induced pain; no breast lumps; no family cancer; screening two years ago; one cat, no scratches; safe sex; no travel. Examination: two 2 cm HARD, FIXED, NON-TENDER left axillary nodes, no other chain, breasts normal, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bone tenderness, afebrile, office tests and pregnancy test normal. Hidden agenda: a friend had lumps that were cancer. Must say 'lymphoma, which is a type of cancer of the lymph glands'; excision of a whole node, not a needle. Automatic fails: never saying cancer/lymphoma · never characterising the nodes · no malignancy screen · prognosis or cure rate · FNA as the test · false reassurance.
plan: Intro, open, ★ acknowledge the worry she volunteers, contract, 'some questions will sound unrelated'
Five questions: lack of energy vs sleepy vs feverish · how long · constant · worse · better/worse · impact
H and E in ten seconds each (all no)

★ M: weight → YES 5 kg → PROBE, do not move on: appetite, lumps → two in the armpit → how long, bigger, painful; night sweats — change the sheets?; fevers; itching without rash; alcohol pain; breast lumps/dimpling/discharge; cancer in you/family; last cervical screen
I: fever/chills, sore throat/flu-like, sexually active + safe sex (HIV can present exactly like this — ask everyone), travel, pets — cat scratches on that arm, TB contact
A, AD, D, C, O, P in one run; alcohol/allergies/PMHx/FHx; ★ 'was there anything you were worried this might be?' → friend → 'thank you — I'll examine you and be straight with you'

Examination: general (pallor, jaundice, cachexia, bruising/petechiae, scratch marks) · temperature · thyroid · ★ full lymph node examination by chain → 'two enlarged in the left axilla' → ★ immediately: size, stony hard or rubbery, fixed or mobile, tender → breasts + axillary tail, skin of the arm → CVS, resp → abdomen hepatosplenomegaly → bone tenderness sternum/spine → BSL, dipstick, urine pregnancy test

Name it → ★ one feelings check → three reasons from her findings → differentials reasoned (breast cancer; infections incl. HIV — offer the test; pregnancy excluded) then rapid list → plan: bloods today, CXR, urgent haematology referral in Adelaide for excision biopsy, phoned today; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 + travel → safety-net → support person → questions → 'is it curable?' → no numbers before type/stage
ask: 'Good morning, my name is Dr —, one of the doctors here. What has brought you in today?' → 'I am sorry to hear that, and I can understand why it is worrying you. Let me ask a number of questions to find the cause, then examine you and explain what I think. Some questions will sound unrelated; I ask everyone.'

Can you describe what you mean by tired — a lack of energy, feeling sleepy, or feeling feverish? How long? Constant or coming and going? Getting worse? Anything making it better or worse? How is it affecting your life?

★ Have you lost weight recently? → 'That is important, let me ask more. Has your appetite changed? Have you noticed any lumps or bumps anywhere in your body? How long have they been there, are they getting bigger, are they painful? Any night sweats — do you have to change the sheets or your nightclothes? Any fevers? Any itching all over without a rash? Do the lumps ache after alcohol? Any breast lumps, skin dimpling or nipple discharge? Any cancer in you or your family? When did you last have a cervical screening test?'

Any fevers or chills, sore throat or flu-like illness? Are you sexually active — do you practise safe sex? Any recent travel? Any pets — any cat scratches or bites on that arm? Anyone around you with tuberculosis?

Short of breath or heart racing on exertion? Stiffness in your shoulders or hips? Headaches, joint pains, rashes? Any medicines at all? Mood — still enjoying things, any stress? Greasy stools or blood in the stool? Chest pain? How many pillows? Ankle swelling? Cough, do you smoke? Has anyone said you snore or gasp? Occupation? Last period — regular, heavy, any chance of pregnancy? Alcohol, allergies, other medical problems, family history? ★ Was there anything you were worried this might be?

★ Examiner: 'On general appearance — pallor, jaundice, cachexia, bruising or petechiae, scratch marks? Vital signs, the temperature particularly. A thyroid examination. Then a full lymph node examination of every chain: occipital, pre- and post-auricular, submental, submandibular, anterior and posterior cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal and popliteal.' → ★ 'How large are they? Stony hard, or rubbery? Fixed or mobile? Tender? I would also like to examine both breasts and the axillary tail and inspect the skin of that arm. Cardiovascular — heart sounds and murmurs. Respiratory — air entry and added sounds. Abdomen — hepatomegaly or splenomegaly? Bone tenderness over the sternum or spine? Office tests — blood sugar, urine dipstick, and a urine pregnancy test.'

★ 'Jane, tiredness can have many different causes. In your case, I am concerned about the possibility of lymphoma, which is a type of cancer of the lymph glands. I am not certain yet — a biopsy is what confirms it — but I would not be honest if I said anything less. How are you feeling about what I have just said?' [one check-in, then continue] 'The reasons I am concerned: you have lost about five kilograms without trying; the two lumps in your armpit are hard and not moving when I examine them; and you have drenching night sweats. Those three things together point that way.'

'Because the lumps are in your armpit and you are 35, I also have to think about other cancers, particularly breast cancer — your examination was normal, but I will still arrange imaging. Then infections: glandular fever, HIV, toxoplasmosis, tuberculosis and cat-scratch disease — less likely because you have no fever, no travel and no unsafe sexual practice, but I would like to include an HIV test. Then pregnancy — excluded today. Beyond those: underactive thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, hepatitis, haemochromatosis, coeliac disease, autoimmune conditions such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, medications, depression, sleep apnoea and heart failure.' → 'Which do you think?' → 'The lymphoma is the one I am acting on today.' ★ 'Blood tests today, a chest x-ray, and an urgent referral to a blood specialist in Adelaide for a small operation to remove one gland whole and look at it under the microscope — a needle sample is not enough. I will phone the referral through today. Cancer Council SA on 13 11 20 can help with information and the travel. Come straight back or to hospital if you get a fever, your face or neck swells, you become breathless lying flat, or you start bruising or bleeding. Is there someone who can come with you? What questions do you have?' → 'Is it curable?' → 'I cannot give you numbers before we know which type this is, and many lymphomas respond very well to treatment. Let me get the biopsy done.'

SA: urgent haematology at RAH/FMC; PATS (>100 km); Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if SVC obstruction; TIS 131 450

Never characterising the nodes — accepting 'two enlarged nodes' and going to the diagnosis ★
No malignancy screen; hearing 'weight loss' and moving to the next letter ★

setting: General practice. You are the GP. The patient attends alone and yawns repeatedly throughout — scripted behaviour.
stem: Lily, 22, a university student, presents with tiredness. She is worried because it is not getting better.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6–7 minutes)
Physical examination findings will be provided
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Open and address the concern · 'low in energy, sleepy, or feverish?' decides the station · timing and impact in 40 s · sleep history in three phases (bedtime AND sleep-onset time separately; quantify caffeine AND time the last dose; weekend/holiday pattern) · mood, narcolepsy, pregnancy, ★ driving · rapid general sweep · interpret the normal examination out loud · sleep restriction with BOTH reasons · prioritised, specific differentials · sleep hygiene, diary, caffeine taper, driving advice; no hypnotic.

back.dx: Chronic sleep restriction (sleep deprivation) with behavioural sleep-onset insomnia: sleepy — not low-energy — for months; bed at 10 pm but asleep at 3 am (five hours lying awake on her phone in a noisy share house), ~5 h/night, unrefreshing, 4–5 coffees plus energy drinks with the last at 9 pm, feels better after sleeping in to midday at weekends; no snoring/gasping, no cataplexy or sleep paralysis, mood normal now, not pregnant; entirely normal examination, BMI 22. Two reasons: the sleep history, and the completely normal remainder of history and examination. Prioritised differentials: other sleep disorders — OSA (no snoring/gasping), narcolepsy (no cataplexy, sleep paralysis or hallucinations), delayed sleep–wake phase disorder (holiday pattern doesn't fully fit); psychological — major depression, adjustment disorder, GAD (onset with exams, mood normal now); pregnancy (excluded); anaemia (periods not heavy, no exertional symptoms); then thyroid, diabetes, EBV/infection, leukaemia/lymphoma, coeliac, autoimmune, medications. Discriminating behaviour: asking sleep-onset time separately from bedtime, and asking about driving.
plan: Intro, name, 'how can I help?'; acknowledge the worry ('especially when the exams are over and it hasn't settled'); contract
★ 'Do you feel low in energy, sleepy, or feverish?' → sleepy · duration, constant, worsening, modifiers, impact (concentration, falling behind, stopped going out) — 40 s only
★ 'I've noticed you've been yawning — can you tell me more about your sleep?' Phase 1: bedtime → ★ 'and what time do you actually fall asleep?' → 3 am · phone/TV in bed · room quiet and dark · pets

Phase 2–3: hours per night · refreshing? · initiation vs maintenance · nightmares · snoring/gasping · restless legs · hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations · drugs, medications, alcohol · ★ caffeine quantified AND timing of last · ★ weekend/holiday pattern (longer? better?)

Mood: 'started around exams — how has your mood been? still enjoying things? appetite? stressors?' · narcolepsy: ★ 'ever woken unable to move or speak? sudden weakness with strong emotion?' · LMP, pregnancy risk, heavy periods · ★ 'Do you drive? Ever felt sleepy at the wheel?' → near-miss → 'I'm glad you told me, we'll come back to that'

Rapid HEMI-AD-COP sweep with red flags: tanning/jaundice, polyuria/thirst, heat/cold intolerance, weight/appetite/lumps/night sweats, fever/sore throat/travel, exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, bowel symptoms, joints/rash, PMH/meds/allergies/smoking
Examination: read it back and ★ interpret it aloud as a positive finding; confirm no pallor, no goitre, normal BMI

★ Diagnosis with both reasons · 'there is something wrong — you're about three hours short every night, and it's fixable without a tablet' · hidden agenda (friend's glandular fever) answered honestly · prioritised, named differentials each with the excluding finding · plan: 2-week sleep diary, fixed bed/wake time 7 days, no phone for an hour before bed, caffeine taper with none after ~2 pm, daytime exercise, earplugs, CBT-i if still not falling asleep, Sleep Health Foundation, uni counselling; ★ driving advice; baseline bloods; review 3–4 weeks; red flags; summary

'How many hours do you get on an average night? Is your sleep refreshing?' / 'Has anyone told you that you snore or gasp during sleep?' / 'Any pain or restlessness in your legs at night? Ever seen anything frightening as you fell asleep or woke up?'
★ 'How many caffeinated drinks a day — and how late is the last one?' / ★ 'On weekends or holidays, do you sleep longer, and do you feel better?'
★ 'Have you ever had sudden weakness with a strong emotion? Have you ever woken unable to move or speak?'
★ 'Do you drive? Have you ever felt sleepy at the wheel?'

★ 'Most likely you have sleep restriction — you're not getting enough good-quality sleep. Two reasons: your sleep history — bed at ten, asleep at three, five hours, phone in bed, four or five caffeinated drinks with the last at nine at night; and, just as important, the rest of your history and your whole examination are completely normal.'

'So there's nothing actually wrong with me?' → ★ 'There is something wrong — you're running about three hours short every night, and that has real effects on concentration, mood and driving safety. The difference is it's completely fixable, and it doesn't need a tablet.'

dx: **Iron deficiency anaemia from occult gastrointestinal blood loss — and gastrointestinal malignancy until proven otherwise**, with a bleeding NSAID-related peptic ulcer alongside it.

**The discriminating issue is whether ruling out cancer is the first thing out of your mouth in the management task, before iron is mentioned at all.** **'I will start you on iron and then arrange a scope' fails the station in that order.**

**If you can say only one sentence, say this one: 'The first and most important step is to find and treat the cause, which means referring you for both an endoscopy and a colonoscopy.'** That sentence alone passes the management domain.

**Four causes of iron deficiency: LOW INTAKE · MALABSORPTION · BLOOD LOSS · INCREASED DEMAND.** Every one of those blocks is a scored item, and **vague differentials do not score** — say **'a diet low in iron, for example a vegetarian diet without red meat'**, not 'diet'.
**The rule: iron deficiency in ANY man or ANY post-menopausal woman with no obvious cause is investigated with BOTH scopes, even when a plausible alternative cause exists.**

**Explicitly wrong: a therapeutic trial of oral or parenteral iron in place of full investigation · deferring investigation until the haemoglobin responds · FOBT in a symptomatic patient · transfusion in a stable outpatient.** **Acceptable: starting oral iron alongside, provided the priority is stated clearly.**

**Name the cancer concern with the formula: 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer in the bowel or the stomach' — then immediately the reasons: the weight loss, and the dark stools, which mean you are bleeding somewhere.** To 'are you sure?': **'I am not sure, and that is exactly why I want the tests.'** Never deny it.

**Stop the NSAID and substitute something safer.** **A GASTRIC ulcer is biopsied and re-scoped to confirm healing, because it can be malignant; a DUODENAL ulcer is not.** **H. pylori positive → eradication therapy.**

**Iron replacement after the cause: oral iron on an empty stomach with vitamin C, away from tea, calcium and antacids; alternate-day dosing improves absorption. IV iron if oral is not tolerated, not absorbed, or replacement must be rapid.** **Recheck FBE and ferritin at about four weeks; continue iron about three months after the haemoglobin normalises.** VERIFY doses.

**Ferritin is an acute phase reactant — a normal ferritin with a transferrin saturation under about 16% is still iron deficiency.** **Both scopes normal → coeliac serology, then capsule endoscopy or CT enterography.** **PATS for metropolitan travel · Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · TIS 131 450.**
plan: **Open before you read out a single number**: **'good morning, my name is Dr [name]. Am I speaking with Margaret? How can I help you today?'** Twenty seconds of ordinary conversation is a scored item — **opening with 'your haemoglobin is low' reads as cold.**

**The results in SIX LINES and under ninety seconds.** **Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, and haemoglobin is made of iron · your total haemoglobin is low · your red cells are smaller than they should be · there is less haemoglobin in each cell and it is less concentrated · your ferritin, your body's iron store, is low · the cells vary in size, ANISOCYTOSIS, and some have abnormal shapes, POIKILOCYTOSIS.** Then: **'all of these findings together confirm iron deficiency anaemia.'** **Do not explain white cells, platelets or how blood is made.**
**'Is it all right if I ask you a few questions to work out why your iron is low?'** Then the tiredness, briefly: **low energy or feeling sleepy? how long, and is it getting worse?**
**1. Diet — 'DO YOU EAT RED MEAT?'** Never 'how is your diet?' — a vegetarian also has a healthy balanced diet, and the bland answer loses the mark.

**2. Obvious blood loss — any recent surgery? any bleeding episodes? any blood donations? WHEN WAS YOUR LAST PERIOD — and BEFORE THEY STOPPED, were they heavy or irregular?** Late anovulatory cycles are often heavy, so do not stop at 'menopause'.

**3. Gut blood loss — 'HAVE YOU SEEN ANY BLOOD IN YOUR STOOLS, OR HAD ANY DARK OR BLACK STOOLS?'** Never 'how are your bowels?' — that gets 'fine'. **Say the answer back: 'that tells me you may be losing blood somewhere in your stomach or bowel.'**

**4. Peptic ulcer — are you taking any anti-inflammatory painkillers, ibuprofen, Nurofen, Voltaren, ANYTHING YOU BUY YOURSELF? any indigestion, heartburn or tummy pain? any vomiting?** Asked as 'any medications?' she says none.

**5. Bowel cancer — ANY WEIGHT LOSS, HOW MUCH AND OVER HOW LONG? any loss of appetite? any lumps or bumps? any change in your bowel habit? have you done your national bowel cancer screening test? any family history of bowel cancer?** Six kilos in two months is significant; six kilos in two years is not.
**6. Malabsorption — any long-term diarrhoea? any greasy pale stools that float or stick to the pan? any mouth ulcers, joint pains or rashes on your shins?**

**Ask for the examination by name**: **conjunctival pallor · koilonychia · angular cheilitis and glossitis · pulse and POSTURAL blood pressure · an ejection systolic flow murmur · abdominal masses and epigastric tenderness · lymph nodes INCLUDING THE LEFT SUPRACLAVICULAR NODE · and a RECTAL EXAMINATION with consent and a chaperone**.

**The cancer conversation, in order — gentle opening, concern, THEN reasons.** **'Iron deficiency can have several different causes. But in your case, I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer in the bowel or the stomach. The reasons are that you have been losing weight, and that you have dark stools, which means you are bleeding somewhere.'** **Then sit with the silence.**

**The differentials, specific not vague**: **a bleeding peptic ulcer, made more likely by the anti-inflammatories · a diet low in iron, for example a vegetarian diet without red meat · blood loss from heavy periods, surgery, a bleeding episode or frequent donation · poor absorption, as in coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease.** **'But the weight loss and the dark stools are the two things I cannot ignore.'**

**Management, and the first sentence is the one that passes: 'the first and most important step is to find the cause and treat the cause. That means referring you for BOTH an endoscopy AND a colonoscopy.'** Then what each camera does and that they will biopsy anything abnormal.

**Stop the Nurofen and substitute something safer · coeliac serology, UEC, LFT, thyroid function and a repeat FBE · then replace the iron, tablets or an infusion, and recheck the blood in a few weeks.** Mark the referral **urgent**, and offer **PATS** for the travel.

**Safety-net verbatim: come back straight away or go to the emergency department if you vomit blood, if your stools become black and tarry, or if you get chest pain, breathlessness or dizziness at rest.** Then **teach-back: 'what will you tell your husband tonight about what we are doing?'**

stem: Your next patient is John Brennan, 45, complaining of tiredness. He told the receptionist he has been tired for about three weeks and it is getting worse.
His record notes that he was told as a child that he had a heart murmur. He has no regular medications and has not attended the practice for several years.

back.dx: Subacute infective endocarditis on a rheumatic mitral valve (mitral stenosis): childhood murmur with years of antibiotics/injections and constant sore throats and no follow-up (rheumatic fever → RHD), three weeks of worsening fatigue starting at the time of a root canal with no prophylaxis, feverish, splinter haemorrhages; T 38.5, mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at the apex, dipstick blood 1+. Four reasons to the patient: murmur as a child and a murmur today; fever; dental work three weeks ago matching the three weeks of tiredness; marks under the nails. Differentials, grouped with reasons: heart failure on the stenotic valve (less likely — no chest pain, oedema, orthopnoea, PND); blood cancers — leukaemia/lymphoma (no weight loss, lumps, night sweats); other infections — TB, EBV, HIV, hepatitis; thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, autoimmune, medications and mood, coeliac/IBD, OSA. Plan: three sets of blood cultures before any antibiotic, bloods, urine, ECG, CXR, hospital today for echocardiography and IV antibiotics. Discriminating behaviours: changing tack on the murmur, asking about dental work, naming the peripheral stigmata to the examiner.

'I believe you have infective endocarditis. One of your heart valves is narrowed — that's the murmur from childhood. When you had the root canal, bacteria from the mouth got into the bloodstream and settled on that damaged valve. Four reasons: the murmur then and now; a fever; dental work three weeks ago, the same three weeks you've been tired; and the marks under your fingernails.'

'The main alternative is heart failure from the long-standing valve problem — less likely because no chest pain, no leg swelling, one pillow, not waking breathless. I also thought about blood cancers like leukaemia and lymphoma — less likely, no weight loss, lumps or night sweats; other infections such as TB, glandular fever, HIV and hepatitis; thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, autoimmune conditions, medications and mood, coeliac and bowel disease, and sleep apnoea.'

'I can't go — I'm driving to Adelaide Monday. Give me tablets.' → 'I can't make you go, but this infection sits on a heart valve; untreated it can destroy the valve or throw clots to the brain. stem: Samantha (Sam) Doyle, 60, was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica four months ago (some versions: giant cell arteritis; Version 3: sarcoidosis). She attends today concerned about tiredness and, separately, loss of weight.
tasks: Take a relevant history (7 minutes)

findings: This is SEVEN MINUTES OF HISTORY and ONE MINUTE for diagnosis and differentials. The longest history in the tiredness cluster and the shortest closing. SET AN INTERNAL ALARM AT SIX MINUTES — stop asking, whatever is uncovered
The two numbers that make malignancy compulsory
5 TO 6 KILOGRAMS, OVER ABOUT SIX WEEKS, UNINTENTIONAL. 'I've lost weight' is not a finding. Ask the amount AND the interval

'I JUST STOPPED. NOBODY SAID ANYTHING ABOUT REDUCING IT.' She volunteers that she stopped ONLY when asked whether she is taking it regularly — and she does NOT volunteer that it was abrupt unless you ask HOW
HER DOG BARNEY DIED, fifteen years old. Mentioned only when you ask why. It explains the non-adherence AND opens the mood block — 'sorry to hear that' and moving on loses both
NAUSEA, ABDOMINAL PAIN and LOOSE BOWELS — all three positive. LIGHT-HEADED ON STANDING. No salt craving. These become part of your stated reasons
What is NOT there — and it matters

NO PIGMENTATION and NORMAL POTASSIUM. This is SECONDARY insufficiency: ACTH is low, so no pigmentation; aldosterone is preserved, so potassium is normal. PIGMENTATION AND A HIGH POTASSIUM WOULD BE PRIMARY ADDISON DISEASE, not steroid withdrawal

Appetite POOR. No lumps, no night sweats, no family history. MAMMOGRAM last year · CERVICAL SCREENING two years ago · BOWEL KIT done and normal. In the harder variant she has NEVER done the bowel kit — then arranging it becomes part of your management
Stopped at 52, NO BLEEDING SINCE. You are not asking about menopause — ANY postmenopausal bleeding is ENDOMETRIAL CANCER until proven otherwise

Memory fine. LIVES ALONE — husband died three years ago, son in Perth, the dog was her company. No falls. 'I cook, but lately just toast' — MALNUTRITION and SOCIAL ISOLATION are live differentials for the weight loss

SHE IS AFRAID IT IS CANCER — 'my sister went like this. It was cancer.' Volunteered only if you ask what worries her, otherwise said straight after you name the diagnosis. She will also ask: 'SO IT'S MY FAULT FOR STOPPING THE TABLETS?'
findingsLabel: What she withholds, and what she gives only if asked
must: FAIL — Finding the diagnosis at three minutes and abandoning the differentials.
FAIL — Not pursuing malignancy: four red flags AND the three screening programs.
FAIL — Never quantifying the weight loss. Two numbers: how many kilograms, over what period.
FAIL — Calling it adrenal crisis, Conn syndrome, or 'steroid cessation syndrome'.
ASK — Did you stop it abruptly, or did you reduce the dose gradually? The hinge.

dx: **Secondary adrenal insufficiency from abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal.** **NOT an adrenal crisis** — she is haemodynamically stable and holding a conversation. **Not Conn syndrome. And 'steroid cessation syndrome' is not a recognised term — do not say it.**

**The discriminating issue is the differentials, not the diagnosis.** Candidates who know the recall still fail: they ask two questions, hear 'yes I stopped it', and spend the remaining five minutes on the steroid. **Seven minutes was allotted so that you would exclude cancer in a 60-year-old who has lost 5–6 kg in six weeks.**

**The four probes on any condition handed to you in a stem: when diagnosed · what treatment, are you taking it regularly, any side effects · are you still having follow-up · have the original symptoms come back.** **For a steroid, add the fifth: ABRUPTLY OR TAPERED?**

**CORRECTION — the relapse symptoms are commonly taught inverted. POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA is shoulder and hip GIRDLE pain with morning stiffness. GIANT CELL ARTERITIS is headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual loss.** Ask both sets — up to a fifth of PMR patients develop GCA.

**CORRECTION — the treatments are NOT the same and it does matter.** **PMR: prednisolone about 12.5–25 mg daily. GCA: 40–60 mg daily, and pulsed IV methylprednisolone if there is visual loss, because the risk is irreversible blindness.** VERIFY doses.

**Primary vs secondary: PRIMARY (Addison) has high ACTH, pigmentation, high potassium and salt craving. SECONDARY (steroid withdrawal) has low ACTH, NO pigmentation and NORMAL potassium.** If an examiner offers pigmentation and a high potassium, you are being shown primary disease.
**HPA suppression is expected after roughly three weeks or more of supraphysiological glucocorticoid, and recovery takes weeks to months.** VERIFY.

**Investigations: 8 am serum cortisol; short Synacthen test if equivocal, with endocrinology. EUC for sodium and potassium, glucose or HbA1c, calcium. FBE and film, ESR, CRP, LFT, TSH, iron studies, B12 and folate, LDH. Coeliac serology; ferritin and transferrin saturation. DEXA and vitamin D — four months of steroid is a bone risk.** VERIFY.

**Management: RESTART the steroid and TAPER it — do not simply reassure and review. Sick-day rules — double the dose during intercurrent illness, parenteral hydrocortisone if vomiting. Steroid emergency card and MedicAlert bracelet. Bone protection — calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, DEXA (treatment threshold T-score −2.5 or below).** **Adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately plus fluids — DO NOT WAIT FOR THE CORTISOL.** VERIFY.

back.dx: Atypical (community-acquired) pneumonia after four weeks in Far North Queensland: three weeks of dry cough, low-grade fever 37.8, night sweats, back/body aches, exhaustion; two failed beta-lactam courses (amoxicillin then amoxicillin-clavulanate — neither covers Mycoplasma, Chlamydia or Legionella); right middle-zone dullness with crackles, RR 18, SpO2 96%. Four reasons: dry cough for three weeks; low-grade rather than high fever; aches, night sweats and exhaustion; and the antibiotic failure points towards, not away from, this — plus right-sided chest signs. Differentials in two announced groups. Group 1, other causes of persistent cough: typical bacterial pneumonia (chesty cough, high fever, would have responded), tuberculosis (taken seriously — three weeks of cough with night sweats; no weight loss or haemoptysis; CXR and sputum settle it), lung cancer (CXR in any adult with cough >3 weeks, never-smoker or not). Group 2, travel-acquired infections: Q fever, leptospirosis, melioidosis, mosquito-borne viruses — Ross River fits the aches. Then the negative screen: anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, hepatitis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications, mood, OSA. Do not blame the previous doctor. Plan: CXR today, bloods, sputum, atypical PCR swab, travel serology; doxycycline 100 mg bd 5–7 days (macrolide if pregnant or <8 y); review 48 h; named red flags.

back.dx: Obstructive sleep apnoea in a treated hypertensive commercial driver: months of worsening daytime sleepiness (nodding off at his desk), wife reports chainsaw snoring and witnessed apnoeas, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, poor morning concentration, dry mouth, 6 kg weight gain with tighter collar, 4–5 beers nightly up to bed, brief nocturnal arousals that settle in seconds (not PND), grain-haulage truck driver with one or two episodes of sleepiness at the wheel; BP 135/85 on perindopril — close to target, not 'fine'. Reasons drawn from his own answers. BP link: OSA is a recognised cause of hypertension resistant to tablets (nocturnal sympathetic surges); treating the OSA may do more than another tablet. Differentials reasoned: heart failure (no chest pain, one pillow, no oedema — the arousals settle in seconds), lymphoma/leukaemia (no weight loss, lumps, sweats), infections — EBV, COVID, hepatitis, HIV (no fever, travel, risk); then hypothyroidism, diabetes, anaemia, haemochromatosis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications/alcohol, depression, shift work. Driving: no blanket ban, no blanket reassurance — 'I am not taking anything off you today'; do not drive sleepy; sleep study; commercial standards stricter (Austroads), specialist opinion and evidence of treatment; hidden worry is his father's MI at 58.

setting: Your general practice. Face-to-face station. The role-player is in the room even though there is no history-taking task. Notice on the door: findings are given only if you ask for them specifically.
stem: Mary Whitfield, a 40-year-old woman, has presented complaining of feeling tired, weight loss over the last few months, night sweats and loss of appetite.

back.dx: Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) presenting with B symptoms: four months of fatigue, ~7 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats, anorexia, generalised pruritus; examination — pallor, thin and unwell, T 37.8, HR 96, scratch marks, ecchymoses, conjunctival pallor, two to three rubbery, fixed, non-tender cervical nodes (largest ~3 cm, skin normal), bone tenderness, splenomegaly 4 cm, thyroid normal, chest clear. Clubbing is present but is NOT a lymphoma sign — it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on the list (say so). Reasons to the patient led by your findings: rubbery, fixed, non-tender neck glands (infection glands are tender and mobile), enlarged spleen, scratch marks from the itch — plus her B symptoms. Differentials by group: other cancers — leukaemia (ecchymoses, bone tenderness), lung/bowel/breast; infections — TB, HIV, syphilis, EBV, CMV, toxoplasmosis (some need consent); hyperthyroidism (explains fatigue, sweats, weight loss; thyroid normal today). Investigations in order of priority: FBE, blood film today, excisional node biopsy (architecture, not FNA cells), PET-CT staging (or CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis); then LDH, ESR/CRP, HIV and syphilis serology with consent, EBV/CMV/toxoplasma serology, IGRA + CXR, TSH. Febrile neutropenia = emergency: cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour.

stem: You are the HMO. Blood results have returned on Mr Arthur Nolan, 78, a resident of a nearby aged-care facility, currently an inpatient. Sodium 118 mmol/L (135–145), chloride low, serum osmolality low. Nothing else is given.
tasks: Report and explain the investigation results to the nurse
Take a history from the nurse
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the nurse
findings: Conscious state — ASKED BEFORE THE RESULTS
ALERT AND ORIENTED TO HIS USUAL LEVEL. NO FITTING. A sodium of 118 can seize — discussing the number before you know he is awake fails the safety domain however good the rest is
BP 128/76 · PULSE 78 · RR 16 · SpO2 97% on air · T 36.6. Stable
Admitted THREE DAYS AGO after a FALL at his aged-care facility, no fracture. History: HYPERTENSION, osteoarthritis, mild memory impairment. NO recent surgery. CT head on admission CLEAR
The medication chart — read in full

HYDROCHLOROTHIAZIDE · paracetamol · atorvastatin. Nothing changed since admission. SHE NEVER VOLUNTEERS THE THIAZIDE AS A CAUSE — and if you ask only about NEW medications she says 'nothing new since admission' and lets you miss it
NO change from his baseline confusion. No drowsiness, headache, dizziness, nausea or vomiting. Unsteady — but that is what brought him in. NO seizure
GLUCOSE 5.4 · TRIGLYCERIDES NORMAL · TOTAL PROTEIN NORMAL. Say the conclusion out loud: 'then this is a TRUE HYPOTONIC hyponatraemia, not an artefact and not glucose-driven'
NO vomiting or diarrhoea. Eating and drinking normally. No burns or large wounds
NO breathlessness, ONE pillow, no ankle swelling. No jaundice, dark urine or pale stools. Urine output normal — FLUID CHART ROUGHLY BALANCED, about 1400 in and 1300 out
VOLUME STATUS — the question that decides the station

'CAN I ASK YOU TO LOOK AT HIM FOR ME?' → MOUTH MOIST, NO POSTURAL DROP, NO OEDEMA, CHEST CLEAR, WEIGHT STABLE = EUVOLAEMIC. SHE WILL NOT OFFER THIS. Volume status is an EXAMINATION finding, and on the telephone the only way to get it is to ask her to examine him

INFECTION: no fever, chills, cough, breathlessness, headache or neck stiffness. MALIGNANCY: no weight loss, lumps, night sweats or cancer history. INTRACRANIAL: did not hit his head, CT clear. POLYDIPSIA: drinking normal for him

FAIL — Asking only about NEW medications, so the long-standing thiazide is missed.

ASK — Is he alert and oriented, or drowsy? Has he had any fitting?

dx: **Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia due to SIADH, most likely drug-induced — the hydrochlorothiazide.** **Almost every AMC hyponatraemia recall lands on SIADH caused by a medication: thiazide, SSRI or carbamazepine.**

**Pseudo → volume → group.** Rule out pseudohyponatraemia, establish volume status, then run the three volume groups as three labelled blocks. **Volume status is an examination finding, not a history answer** — on the telephone you must ask the nurse for it; in clinic you must say out loud that you would look for it.

**Explain in THREE LAYERS, not one word. LAYER 1: SIADH, and the drug that triggered it. LAYER 2: the other causes of SIADH — malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma) · infection (pneumonia, TB, meningitis) · intracranial pathology (bleed, head injury). LAYER 3: the other causes of hyponatraemia — hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, the hypovolaemic group, the hypervolaemic group.** **Saying 'it's SIADH' and stopping is the commonest reason this station scores poorly.**

**SIADH diagnostic criteria: hyponatraemia with SERUM osmolality under 275 mOsm/kg · URINE osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg · urine sodium over 30–40 mmol/L · clinical euvolaemia · normal thyroid, adrenal and renal function · no diuretic on board.** **Serum low, urine high** is the memory hook.

**CORRECTION — hyperglycaemia is NOT pseudohyponatraemia.** **High triglycerides and high protein cause a laboratory artefact with a NORMAL serum osmolality. Hyperglycaemia causes a real dilutional hyponatraemia with a HIGH serum osmolality**, because glucose pulls water out of cells. Same screen, different boxes on the algorithm.

**Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia has a urine sodium UNDER 20** — the kidney is holding on to sodium. **In SIADH the urine sodium is HIGH because the patient is volume replete and there is no stimulus to conserve it.** That contrast separates the two.

**Register: you are talking to a senior colleague. Use ISBAR and clinical language — hyponatraemia, serum osmolality, euvolaemic, SIADH.** **Translating 'sodium' into 'a salt in your blood' for a registered nurse costs communication marks.**

**Drugs to name first: THIAZIDES · SSRIs · CARBAMAZEPINE.** Then **ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, chemotherapy, MDMA, desmopressin.** **Review the chart with the pharmacist; discuss substitution with the prescriber rather than stopping unilaterally.**

**Correction: no faster than about 8 mmol/L in 24 hours**, and less in the malnourished, alcohol-dependent, hypokalaemic or those with liver disease. **Faster risks OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME — dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis or a locked-in state, appearing days later and usually irreversible.** VERIFY.

**Management is NOT a task here — one sentence if asked, then return to the diagnosis.** **Never give normal saline in SIADH: the kidney concentrates the urine above the tonicity of the saline, so salt is excreted and water retained and the sodium falls further.** **Severe and symptomatic: 3% sodium chloride in small boluses to lift by 4–6 mmol/L, then stop.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **Pick up the phone: 'Hello, this is Dr [name], the HMO covering the ward this evening. WHO AM I SPEAKING WITH, and WHICH WARD are you calling from?'**

**Before the numbers — the scored safety behaviour: 'IS HE ALERT AND ORIENTED, OR IS HE DROWSY OR MORE CONFUSED THAN USUAL? HAS HE HAD ANY FITTING? And can you give me his latest observations — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, saturations and temperature?'** Fifteen seconds, and it banks the domain.

**Report the results in colleague register**: sodium 118 against 135–145, a significant hyponatraemia · chloride low, which tends to track the sodium · **and the serum osmolality is low, which tells me this is a TRUE HYPOTONIC hyponatraemia rather than a laboratory artefact.** Then ask permission to work through the causes.

**Orient: can you tell me more about him · WHAT IS HE ADMITTED WITH · what does his past medical history include · CAN YOU READ ME HIS MEDICATION CHART, EVERYTHING ON IT INCLUDING ANYTHING STARTED OR CHANGED IN THE LAST FEW WEEKS · and has he had any recent surgery?** Note the thiazide and **deliberately keep going**.
**Symptoms: is he confused or more confused than his baseline · any drowsiness · any headache, dizziness, nausea or vomiting · any unsteadiness or falls since admission · HAS HE HAD ANY SEIZURE?**

**The pseudohyponatraemia screen: can you check whether there are recent results for his BLOOD GLUCOSE, his TRIGLYCERIDES and his TOTAL PROTEIN?** Then **say the conclusion aloud** — it converts a silent thought into scored reasoning.
**Block one, losing fluid — announce it: any vomiting or diarrhoea · is he eating and drinking as usual · any burns or large wounds · is he on a fluid tablet?**

**Block two, retaining it: any chest pain or breathlessness, worse lying flat, HOW MANY PILLOWS · any swelling in the legs · any yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or pale stools · has he been passing less urine · DOES HE HAVE A FLUID BALANCE CHART, what are the intake and output?**
**Block three, euvolaemic: any weather preference, is he intolerant of the cold · any constipation or weight gain?**

**The question candidates never ask: 'CAN I ASK YOU TO LOOK AT HIM FOR ME, and tell me what his fluid state looks like? dx: **Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia due to SIADH, drug-induced — CITALOPRAM and CARBAMAZEPINE are both recognised causes.**

**Pseudo → volume → group.** Rule out pseudohyponatraemia, establish volume status, then run the three volume groups as three labelled blocks. **Examination is not a task here, so say out loud that you would still assess volume status and why.**

**Explain in FIVE MOVES, patient register: 'your blood test shows a low sodium level · sodium is a mineral, or a salt, that your body keeps in careful balance · the most likely cause is SIADH, the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH · ADH is a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, and in this condition your body makes more than it should, so you hold extra water and that dilutes the salt · in your case the most likely trigger is your medication, and that is a side effect rather than anything you have done wrong.'**

**Then the layers: other causes of SIADH — certain cancers, particularly lung and lymphoma (your chest X-ray is normal) · infections of the chest or the lining of the brain · problems inside the head such as a bleed or injury (your brain scan is normal).** **Then outside SIADH — losses, fluid tablets, an underactive thyroid (your test rules it out), and heart, liver or kidney problems.**

**CORRECTION — hyperglycaemia is not pseudohyponatraemia.** **Triglycerides and protein give an artefact with a NORMAL serum osmolality; hyperglycaemia gives a real dilutional hyponatraemia with a HIGH serum osmolality.** His glucose is normal, so neither applies.

**Do NOT stop an SSRI or an anticonvulsant abruptly.** **Abrupt SSRI cessation causes discontinuation symptoms; abrupt carbamazepine cessation risks seizures.** **Confirm, then plan a substitution with the prescriber — and say that out loud.**
**Drugs to name first: thiazides · SSRIs · carbamazepine.** Then **ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, chemotherapy, MDMA, desmopressin.**

**Register matters both ways.** To a patient: 'a mineral, or salt, in your blood', 'a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water'. **To a nurse or examiner: hyponatraemia, serum osmolality, euvolaemic, SIADH.** Using the wrong one costs marks in both directions.

**Do not alarm a well patient.** Not 'your sodium is dangerously low' but **'it is low enough to need sorting out, and here is exactly how.'** He came for a routine check — **ask his ideas, concerns and expectations.**

**Correction no faster than about 8 mmol/L in 24 hours** — faster risks **osmotic demyelination syndrome**, appearing days later with dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis, usually irreversible. **SIADH fluid restriction is commonly 800–1000 mL/day.** VERIFY.

**Finish the spine: SADMA including ALCOHOL (beer potomania) and recreational drugs (MDMA) · past history of cancer, lung, kidney or adrenal disease, previous low sodium, long-term steroids recently stopped · family history · and his IDEAS, CONCERNS AND EXPECTATIONS**, because he came for a routine check.

**Say the volume line even though examination is not a task**, then **name each normal result in the stem and what it excludes**: chest X-ray — lung malignancy; CT brain — intracranial cause; thyroid function — hypothyroidism; eGFR — renal.
**The five-move explanation in patient register**, then **the layers** — other causes of SIADH, then the causes of hyponatraemia outside SIADH.

**The next step said plainly: confirm it, and then talk to whoever prescribes your medicines, BECAUSE WE DO NOT STOP AN ANTIDEPRESSANT OR AN ANTICONVULSANT ABRUPTLY — we plan the change.** Safety-net for drowsiness, confusion, vomiting or fitting.

'You have hyperkalaemia' is a laboratory state, not a diagnosis — the commonest fail. back.dx: Mild hypokalaemia (K 3.1) from thiazide-induced renal potassium wasting — the dose was doubled four weeks ago for creeping readings, which fits the timing exactly; bicarbonate 30 at the top of range is consistent. Normal renal function (say so — interpreting creatinine/eGFR is part of 'explain the results'). Four differential buckets, numbered, in plain English: (1) not enough in — restricted diet; (2) losing it through the bowel — vomiting, diarrhoea, laxatives (name tablets, powders, teas); (3) losing extra through the kidneys — a tablet like his, or 'a small gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone that dumps potassium' (primary aldosteronism: cramps, weakness, polyuria, resistant BP); (4) shift into cells — some asthma puffers, insulin, and 'a rare adrenaline-producing tumour' (phaeo triad: headache + sweating + palpitations, patients go pale, not flushed). Plan: repeat U&E to confirm, ECG today (arrhythmia is the consequence that matters 10 days from a GA), magnesium (thiazides waste Mg; low Mg makes K replacement ineffective), oral KCl supplement, review the antihypertensive for a potassium-sparing option, write to surgeon and anaesthetist, recheck in 3–7 days and again before theatre. The operation most likely proceeds — mild, asymptomatic; if it stays low a short delay is for anaesthetic safety. Never tell him to stop the antihypertensive himself. Hidden agenda: daughter's wedding in six weeks — ask an open concerns question early.

back.dx: Excessive vitamin D supplementation (4 × 1000 IU = 4000 IU/day for six weeks, started because his mother has osteoporosis with two fractures this year) → probable hypercalcaemia → polydipsia. Ten days of constant worsening thirst, 4–5 L/day up from 2, no polyuria, nocturnal drinking not voiding, bowels sluggish this last week; no weight loss, vision change, infections; no bone pain, fatigue, sweats, bruising; no headache/vision loss; no heat intolerance, loose bowels, palpitations, tremor; no stones, nausea; lifestyle unremarkable. Four-link chain in plain words: vitamin D helps you absorb calcium → too much pushes blood calcium up → high calcium makes the kidneys pass out more water → your body feels that as thirst; the word is hypercalcaemia. Differentials, each with why less likely: diabetes (no polyuria/weight loss; finger-prick today anyway), overactive thyroid, a brain problem with the water-balance hormone (DI), a bone-marrow condition that raises calcium (myeloma — asked bone pain, tiredness, infections), everyday causes (coffee, alcohol, salt, heat). Honest uncertainty: no blood test yet, so no declared 'vitamin D poisoning'. Plan: stop the capsules today, bring the bottle in, BSL now, bloods for calcium, UEC, 25-OH vitamin D, glucose, TSH; drink to thirst 2–3 L; review when results back, phone sooner if needed. Separate him from his mother: her dose was worked out for her bones and her blood test — his wasn't; do not change her treatment.

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Results-discussion station; the examiner interrupts to hand you further results after your investigation list.

back.dx: Primary hyperparathyroidism (single adenoma ~85%) — PTH elevated with corrected calcium 2.78, vitamin D normal, phosphate low-normal, eGFR 88, examination normal. Total calcium 2.56 reads 'normal' only because albumin is 31: corrected = 2.56 + 0.02 × (40 − 31) = 2.74 ≈ 2.78 per report — a station-ending false reassurance if you read the total line. Calcium was 'high last year'; she was told to stop her multivitamin and cut dairy — chronicity makes malignancy less likely but does not exclude it, and diet was never the driver (correct the science kindly without attacking the colleague). Only positive symptom: 'a bit more thirsty, I keep a bottle on my desk'. Malignancy screen clean (weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, breast/mammogram clear last year, cough, smoking, haematuria); mother had breast cancer at 60 — the hidden agenda; ask ICE before you explain. Investigations ranked with BECAUSE: 1 serum PTH (commonest cause; the one test that splits the differential in two) · 2 25-OH vitamin D with phosphate (read as a set; low phosphate supports PTH) · 3 UEC/eGFR (renal function, hypercalcaemic nephropathy) · then CXR (lung Ca, TB, sarcoid), FBE/ESR/SPEP + free light chains (myeloma, lymphoma), 24-h urine calcium (exclude FHH before any surgery), full examination incl. breasts and nodes. Explain: four tiny glands behind the thyroid, different job — keep blood calcium right; one is overworking, pulling calcium from bone; the hormone is raised, which confirms it; not cancer, not the thyroid tablets, not diet. Differentials named: cancers (blood, breast, lung, kidney), vitamin D/calcium antacid excess, fluid tablets, lithium, overactive thyroid (excluded), sarcoid/TB. Refer endocrinology (age <50 → surgery will be discussed, their decision with her); hydrate; do not restrict dairy; safety-net.

But a few cancers can also raise calcium, so I check for them in everybody — not because I suspect it in you. Nothing you've told me so far points that way.'

'Apart from the thyroid tablet, any other regular medicine — anything for blood pressure or fluid, or any tablet for your mood?' (thiazide, lithium by use) / 'Any vitamin D, multivitamins or calcium tablets? Anything for indigestion — antacid tablets or liquid?'

★ 'Calcium travels in the blood two ways — some floats free, some is carried by a protein called albumin. Your albumin is low, so the raw number looks normal; once we adjust for it, the true level is high.' / 'Calcium isn't really controlled by what you eat — your body controls it with a hormone.'

★ 'My first priority is serum parathyroid hormone, because primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the community and PTH is the single test that splits the differential in two.' / 'Calcium, phosphate and vitamin D are read as a set.'

★ 'Behind your thyroid gland sit four tiny glands called the parathyroid glands — different glands, different job. Their only job is keeping your blood calcium right. One of them appears to be overworking, and that pulls extra calcium out of your bones into your blood.' / ★ 'It is not a cancer, and it is not caused by your thyroid tablets or by what you eat.'

'Is it cancer?' → 'On everything I have so far, no. Your hormone result points to a gland problem, not a cancer. I'm still completing a chest x-ray and a couple of blood tests so that I'm certain rather than nearly certain.' / 'Should I stop dairy?' → 'No — diet isn't the driver, and cutting calcium hard can be bad for your bones. Drink plenty of water.' / 'Will I need an operation?' → 'Possibly — the only definitive treatment, but not everyone needs one; because you're forty-five the specialist will talk it through seriously.'

★ 'If you become very thirsty and pass a lot of urine, start vomiting, feel drowsy or confused, or get severe tummy, back or loin pain, I want you seen the same day.' / 'To summarise — is there anything I've missed, or anything you'd like me to write down?'

setting: Suburban general practice; you are the GP. Vitals (including BSL) on request. 9-minute station. RECALL NOTE: the source recording verifies the stem and history; later tasks follow the standard three-task shape.
stem: Marianne Kovac, 50, presents with two days of nausea and vomiting on a week of feeling weak, tired and lethargic. She is holding a vomit bag. Known hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Current medications: perindopril 5 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the examination findings and investigations you want
Explain the most likely diagnosis and outline your immediate management
time: 9 minutes: 40 s opening · 4 min history · 1.5 min examination/investigations · 2 min explanation · 45 s safety-net and close. The diagnosis is on the medication list — the marks are for what you ask AFTER you've worked it out: ★ obs incl. BSL · acknowledge the bag, offer water · vomit content · ★ 'when did you start the PAINKILLER, who started it' + OTC/chemist separately · ★ cardiac screen unprompted · abdomen/melaena · ★ urine output, uraemic symptoms · fluid status FIRST · investigations by analyte incl. ECG and troponin · ★ diagnosis by name · triple whammy in plain English · stop, hold, ★ transfer today, no driving · teach-back.

back.dx: Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (stage 2 — eGFR 45 → 22, creatinine roughly doubled) with hyperkalaemia (K 6.3 + peaked T waves, narrow QRS → treat as severe) and metabolic acidosis (HCO3 18) — the 'triple whammy': NSAID (constricts the afferent arteriole) + ACE inhibitor (dilates the efferent) + thiazide (lowers circulating volume), in a woman with baseline CKD. Ibuprofen 400 mg tds for three weeks for a knee — self-bought at the chemist, then scripted by a locum who didn't have her record; she doesn't call it a medication. Uraemic symptoms: much less urine, postural dizziness, metallic taste; examination — dry mucosa, postural drop 20 systolic, JVP not visible, abdomen soft, no bladder, no asterixis. BSL 5.4 removes DKA at the door; troponin normal and cardiac screen negative (nausea + lethargy without chest pain is a recognised MI presentation in women and CKD). Explain: 'your kidneys were working at about half strength and have taken a sudden extra hit — an acute injury on chronic kidney disease; waste products build up and cause the sickness and exhaustion'; mechanism of the three drugs in plain words; 'you can buy it anywhere' → 'that's exactly why it catches people out'. Plan: ibuprofen stops today and never again without checking; hold (not stop forever) perindopril and the thiazide while unwell; ★ ED today for fluids and potassium treatment — ring ahead, results with her, don't drive; repeat UEC 48–72 h; paracetamol + physiotherapy for the knee; letter to usual GP, flag on file. Hidden agenda: mother died on dialysis — 'not today, and in most cases like yours this is reversible once we take the pressure off'.
plan: ★ 'Examiner — BP, pulse, RR, saturations, temperature AND blood sugar?' → 142/86, 72 reg, 16, 98%, afebrile, BSL 5.4 → 'stable, afebrile, normal sugar — a diabetic emergency is unlikely from the outset'
WIPE, 'how would you like me to address you?' · open · ★ 'I'm sorry — that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first?' (the vomit bag is marked)

Symptom package in one block: onset (tiredness 1 week, vomiting 2 days), worse, better/worse · 'tired — low energy, sleepy, or breathless?' · frequency 4–5/day · ★ 'what does the vomit look like — any blood, or anything green?' (UGI bleed vs obstruction; she's on an NSAID) · keeping anything down?

Background: when diagnosed CKD (5 y, 'about half') and HTN (10 y), what for them → perindopril + 'a fluid tablet' · adherence · ★ 'and when did you start the PAINKILLER — who started it, and what was it for?' → ibuprofen ~3 weeks, knee, self-bought then locum script · ★ 'did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?' → 'it's only ibuprofen' (don't correct now; save it) · 'anything from the chemist, or herbal?'

★ Cardiac screen, unprompted, 10 s: 'a few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious — chest/arm/jaw/back discomfort, exertional SOB, cold sweats (clammy yesterday), palpitations, blackouts'
Abdomen: pain/where, bowels, ★ black/tarry stools, fevers, jaundice · ★ urine output 'more, less or the same?' → much less · dizzy standing (yes) · confusion, hiccups, itch, ★ metallic taste (yes)

★ Examination — fluid status FIRST: postural BP, mucosa, JVP, cap refill; abdomen (tenderness, guarding, organomegaly, palpable bladder); cardiorespiratory; pallor, pigmentation, oedema, asterixis → dry, postural drop 20, JVP not seen, soft abdomen, no bladder, no asterixis

★ Investigations by name: ECG now (hyperkalaemia AND ischaemia) · UEC/eGFR vs baseline — specifically K, Na, bicarbonate · VBG · troponin · FBE, Ca, PO4, Mg, LFT, lipase, urinalysis → eGFR 22 (baseline 45), creatinine ×2, K 6.3, HCO3 18, troponin normal, peaked T narrow QRS · 'why a troponin with no chest pain?' answered · read back: stage 2 AKI on CKD; K moderate by number, severe by ECG; acidosis shifts K out of cells

★ Diagnosis by name · 'will I need dialysis? my mother died on dialysis' → pause, acknowledge, honest answer · mechanism: three medicines, three directions — painkiller narrows the vessel in, perindopril widens the vessel out, fluid tablet lowers the circulating volume — 'the triple whammy' · 'you can buy it anywhere' → exactly why it catches people out · 'the locum's fault?' → missing record, not the person; letter to usual GP

Plan: 1 ibuprofen stops today, never that class without checking · 2 hold perindopril and the fluid tablet — temporary, don't stop anything else alone · 3 ★ ED today (K affects the heart's rhythm; can't keep fluids down) — ring ahead, results with her · ★ don't drive · red flags en route: chest pain, palpitations, faint, weak muscles → ambulance · repeat UEC 2–3 days · paracetamol + physio for the knee · ★ teach-back · 'anything still worrying you?'
