'When you say tired — low in energy, sleepy, or breathless when you move about?' / ★ 'What does the vomit look like — any blood, or anything green?'
★ 'When did you start the painkiller, and who started it for you?' / 'Anything from the chemist, or anything herbal?' / 'Did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?'
★ 'A few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious. Any discomfort or tightness in the chest, arm, jaw or back?'
★ 'How much urine have you passed in the last day — more, less, or the same?' / 'Any confusion, hiccups, itch or a metallic taste?'

★ 'I'd like her fluid status first — postural blood pressure, mucous membranes, JVP and capillary refill.' / 'Why a troponin with no chest pain?' → 'Because nausea and lethargy without chest pain is a recognised presentation of infarction in women and in chronic kidney disease.'
★ 'Her eGFR has halved from 45 to 22, which meets criteria for a stage 2 acute kidney injury.' / ★ 'The potassium is 6.3, and with ECG changes I treat that as severe regardless of the number.'

★ 'Your kidneys have taken a sudden extra hit on top of the long-standing damage — an acute kidney injury on top of chronic kidney disease.' / 'Will I need dialysis?' → 'Not today, and in most cases like yours this is reversible once we take the pressure off — that's exactly why we're acting now.'

★ 'Each of these medicines is sensible on its own. Together, with kidneys like yours, they're too much — in Australia we call it the triple whammy.' / 'But it's only ibuprofen — you can buy it anywhere' → 'You can — and that's exactly why it catches people out. Being sold without a prescription doesn't make it harmless for your kidneys.'

★ 'The painkiller stops today. The other two we hold while you're unwell — that's temporary.' / ★ 'I'm sending you to the emergency department today. Please don't drive.' / 'Could you tell me back what you'll say when you get to the hospital?'

setting: General practice in Kadina, regional South Australia; you are the GP registrar. A results card is handed to you. Expect a prompt at 5 minutes covering tasks 1 and 2.
stem: Mr Colin Whitfield, 58, semi-retired farm contractor, returns for the results of blood tests taken a fortnight ago when he attended feeling tired. Hypothyroidism for six years on levothyroxine 100 µg daily; no other regular medication recorded. BP 138/82, HR 76 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98%, T 36.7; he looks well. Results: TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0), free T4 15 (10–20), total calcium 2.58 (2.15–2.60), albumin 28 (low), corrected calcium 2.82 (HIGH), phosphate 0.68 (low, 0.75–1.50), creatinine 88/eGFR >60, FBE and LFT normal, PTH sent — result not yet available.
tasks: Explain these blood results in language he can understand
Take a focused, relevant history
Give your most likely diagnosis and your differentials
Explain what happens next
time: 8 minutes: results 90 s MAXIMUM (signpost → thyroid in one breath → ★ calcium in four sentences: straight reading normal, stuck to a protein, protein low, corrected is high → check understanding → permission) · history 3½ min in seven blocks: tiredness · ★ stones · bones · groans · moans · ★ cancer · drugs incl. OTC · family/alcohol · ★ ICE before the diagnosis · transition line · four glands, one overactive, usually benign, 'I'm not going to promise you that today' · ★ say the word PTH and what high and low each mean · rest of workup, referral, PATS · fluids, don't cut dairy, avoid diuretics/supplements · safety-net · summary · 'have I missed anything?'

back.dx: Primary hyperparathyroidism with end-organ disease — corrected calcium 2.82 (total 2.58 + 0.02 × (40 − 28)), phosphate 0.68 low (PTH wastes phosphate — read the whole panel), TSH/T4 normal (dose right, no change), FBE/LFT normal; PTH pending — 'I've already sent that sample, so we won't lose any time'. History: six months of tiredness; ★ renal colic three years ago (overnight at Wallaroo) + nocturia ×2 + thirst; hip ache ('forty years on tractors'); constipation new this year; 'I've been flat' — name low mood as part of the illness, not a weakness; malignancy block clean (weight steady, never smoked, no sweats/lumps/cough); thyroxine only, 'doesn't hold with vitamins'; no FHx of calcium/stones/neck surgery (FHH, MEN 1); beers Friday, more at harvest (explains the low albumin); diet plenty of milk and cheese. Hidden agenda: brother Wayne died of bowel cancer at 55 last year — ask ICE before you explain, then build the explanation around it. Explain: one of four small neck glands behind the thyroid, different job, slightly overactive, pushing calcium out of bone — fits the stone, constipation, thirst, feeling flat; usually benign and treatable; honest middle — 'a couple of other things can raise calcium, one is a cancer somewhere else, which I know you've worried about since your brother'; what makes it less likely: weight steady, never smoked, normal FBE/LFT, no bone pain or lumps. ★ PTH: high → the gland, common, treatable; low → calcium from somewhere else → CXR and further bloods. Workup: vitamin D, magnesium, renal function, 24-h urine calcium, DXA, renal ultrasound (stone history); PTH confirms → endocrinology in Adelaide, PATS via the practice nurse; neck scan only to plan surgery, not to diagnose; some need the gland out, some are watched — decided with the specialist on calcium, kidneys, bone scan. Meanwhile 2–3 L fluids, more in the heat; don't cut dairy; avoid fluid tablets and calcium/vitamin D supplements; safety-net; ring him with the PTH; review two weeks.
plan: WIPE, DOB · ★ signpost: 'Most of them are reassuring, but there is one I want to go through properly with you — and then I'll need to ask you some questions. Is that alright?' · 'the wife reckoned you'd only get me back in if something was up' → one sentence of acknowledgement, then proceed

Thyroid in one breath: 'the TSH tells us whether you're on the right dose — normal, well controlled, T4 normal too, no change to your thyroxine' · 'what's TSH stand for?' → do not take the invitation; one line and move

★ Calcium in four sentences: 'we measured a mineral called calcium; the straight reading came back normal — but it isn't reliable on its own, because a large part of the calcium is stuck to a protein, and your protein is low, so the reading understates it; we do a calculation that corrects for the protein — and once we do, your calcium is high' · 'so is it normal or isn't it?' → 'the corrected number is the one we go on' · ★ 'is that making sense so far?' · 'not an emergency, you look well, but it needs explaining — may I ask some questions?'

Tiredness — two sentences, not two minutes (6 months, done by lunchtime) · ★ stones: 'ever passed a kidney stone, severe back/side pain?' (3 y ago, Wallaroo) · 'passing more urine, up at night?' (×2, thirsty) · bones: aches, fragility fracture, height loss (hips) · groans: constipation (new this year), indigestion/ulcer, nausea/vomiting · moans: mood, memory, concentration, sleep ('flat') → 'that can be part of this picture — not you being difficult'

★ Cancer block: 'questions I ask everyone with a high calcium' — weight, night sweats/fevers/lumps, cough/haemoptysis, smoking → all clean · drugs incl. OTC: fluid tablets, lithium, calcium/vitamin D, antacids, vitamin A/multivitamins → thyroxine only · FHx: high calcium, stones, parathyroid/neck operation, pituitary/pancreas tumour → no · alcohol (Friday beers, more at harvest) · home/work

★ ICE before the diagnosis: 'what did you think might be causing the tiredness? anything you've been particularly worried about?' → brother, bowel cancer, 55 → 'I'm sorry about your brother — and I'm glad you told me, because it changes how I explain the next bit' · ★ transition line: 'I've got what I need. Let me tell you what I think is going on and what I'd like to do about it'

Diagnosis: 'one of four small glands in your neck — the parathyroid glands, behind your thyroid but a completely different job — has become slightly overactive and is pushing calcium out of your bones into your blood; that fits the kidney stone, the constipation, the thirst and feeling flat; usually a benign growth, not a cancer, treatable' · 'but you can't be sure' → ★ 'not today, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise' — the honest middle; why cancer is less likely (weight, never smoked, FBE/LFT normal, no bone pain/lumps); 'I want to prove it rather than assume it'

★ 'There is one blood test that separates those two possibilities, and it's called PTH. If it's high, it's the gland — common and treatable. If it's low, the calcium is coming from somewhere else and I'd look for a cause in the chest and the bones with a chest x-ray and further blood tests. I've already sent that sample' · alongside: vitamin D, magnesium, kidney function, 24-h urine calcium, bone density scan, renal ultrasound (stone) · PTH confirms → endocrinologist in Adelaide, PATS via the practice nurse · 'an operation?' → some do, some are watched; decided with the specialist on calcium, kidneys, bones; neck scan is for surgical planning, not diagnosis

pefe: Role-player: Colin, 58, property 20 min outside Kadina, wife Denise, two adult children in Adelaide; seeding/harvest for three neighbours; understated, dry, minimising, watches your face. Levothyroxine only, no supplements ('don't hold with vitamins'), never smoked, 4–5 beers Friday/more at harvest, plenty of milk and cheese. Father MI at 70, mother 84 arthritis, brother Wayne died at 55 of bowel cancer last year. Does not hand over the stone unless asked about stones/urine; constipation only if asked about bowels. setting: General practice. No physical examination and no results — history substitutes for examination. Six minutes of history, two of explanation.
stem: Mrs Jane Halloran, 47, presents having found a lump in her neck. She noticed it while touching her neck and has been reading about it online. She is very worried.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (approximately 6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 0:00 open + empathy line · 0:30 the lump — number, ★ 'show me exactly where', 'when did you first notice it', growth, four features (hard/tender/skin/mobile) · 1:30 thyroid box (ask despite lateral site) · 2:00 lymphoma + B symptoms · ★ 2:40 top-down cancer screen scalp → stomach — where all four positives live; do NOT stop at the cough · 4:20 infection box (★ toothache/dentist) · 5:10 travel, animals, sexual health, SADMA · 5:40 ICE · 6:00 'several conditions, not one' — ranked, each with its reason, benign and infective included · plan, timeframe, safety-net.

back.dx: Right lateral, hard, fixed, painless, enlarging cervical lymph node (~2 weeks) in a 47-year-old smoker (15/day × 30 years) — four buried positives found only by a systematic top-down screen: (1) dry cough for months (lung cancer), (2) non-healing buccal ulcer for two months (oral SCC), (3) food sticking on swallowing, not painful (oesophageal cancer — ask dysphagia and odynophagia separately), (4) aching back tooth, no dentist for years (dental infection with a reactive node — genuinely on the list, but a hard fixed node is not explained by it). Thyroid box negative (no movement on swallowing/tongue protrusion, no thermal intolerance); B symptoms negative — recite as relevant negatives. Explanation: 'I've been thinking about several conditions and I can't tell you today which it is' → most concerned about a cancer, and why: a gland reacting to a cancer in the lung (cough + smoking), the mouth (the ulcer), or the food pipe (food sticking) → the bad tooth as a real alternative → thyroid, other cancers that travel to the neck (skin, nose, stomach, salivary), throat/sinus/skin infections. Plan: examine properly, bloods, neck ultrasound, urgent specialist referral (ENT); organised today, hear within the week; safety-net — rapid growth, trouble breathing or swallowing → straight back. No false reassurance (she is briefed to push 'but you can't actually know that').
plan: WIPE · 'tell me about it in your own words' · 'it's cancer, isn't it?' → ★ 'I can imagine how frightening that's been, and I'm not going to guess. I'm going to ask quite a lot of questions, because a lump here can come from several different places — then I'll tell you honestly what I'm thinking.'

The lump: one or more · ★ 'show me exactly where' (right lateral, below the jaw angle — midline vs lateral vs supraclavicular is the only substitute for examination) · ★ 'when did you first notice it?' (not 'how long has it been there') · ever before · bigger · hard/soft · tender · skin · mobile/fixed → rock hard, painless, stuck

Thyroid box despite the lateral site: moves on swallowing? on tongue protrusion? heat/cold intolerance, bowels, weight, voice, family thyroid → all no · lymphoma box: weight loss, appetite, lumps elsewhere (axilla, groin), tiredness, drenching night sweats, fevers, cancer in you/family → all no

★ Top-down, signposted: 'I'm going to ask about things that might seem unrelated — they help me work out where the lump has come from': changing moles/sun · nosebleeds/one blocked nostril/one blocked ear · ★ mouth ulcer that hasn't healed → YES · sore throat/hoarseness · ★ 'does food stick? and separately, is swallowing painful?' → sticks, not painful · abdominal pain/melaena · ★ cough — dry or productive, haemoptysis, smoking → dry cough months, 15/day 30 y — KEEP GOING · hand numbness/ptosis · cheek swelling/facial weakness
Infection box: fevers/chills · ★ toothache, pain chewing, last dentist → bad back tooth, years since a dentist · sore throat/runny nose/ear pain · rashes, cuts, boils on head/neck
Travel · animals/pets · 'a confidential question I ask everyone — sexually active, protection?' · alcohol · medications
ICE: 'what were you most worried this might be, and what were you hoping we'd do today?' → cancer; hasn't told her husband

★ 'I've been thinking about several different conditions, and I want to be honest about all of them — I can't tell you today which it is.' Cancer first with reasons: lung (cough + 30 years' smoking), mouth (ulcer), food pipe (food sticking) · ★ the bad tooth — a dental infection alone can swell a gland · thyroid; skin/nose/stomach/salivary cancers; throat/sinus/skin infections · plan: examination, bloods, neck ultrasound, urgent specialist referral · 'how long?' → organised today, hear within the week · safety-net: grows quickly, trouble breathing or swallowing → straight back

'The one I'm most concerned about is the possibility of a cancer, and I'll tell you why rather than leave you guessing: the lump could be a gland reacting to a cancer in the lung — you've had a cough for months and smoked for thirty years; it could relate to a cancer in the mouth, because of that ulcer; or the food pipe, because food is sticking. But you also told me about the bad tooth — a dental infection on its own can cause a swollen gland, so that's genuinely on my list too.'

'But you can't actually know that, can you?' → 'No — and I won't pretend to. What I can do is examine you properly, take bloods, get an ultrasound of your neck and have a specialist see you quickly. I'll organise it today and you'll hear from me within the week. If it grows quickly or you have trouble breathing or swallowing before then, come straight back.'
pefe: Role-player: Jane, 47, office at a fruit-packing company near Berri; married, two teenagers; smoker 15/day × 30 y; 2–3 wines/week; no meds/allergies/PMHx; no FHx cancer or thyroid. Lump found two nights ago, right side below the jaw angle, ~2 weeks, rock hard, non-tender, skin normal, stuck, maybe bigger, no movement on swallowing. Four buried positives given ONLY to the specific question — 'any other symptoms?' gets 'not really'. Frightened, slightly tearful, calmer once there's a plan; false reassurance makes her more anxious: 'but you can't actually know that, can you?'. Hasn't told her husband

Referral thresholds: node persisting >4–6 weeks, >2 cm, hard, fixed or supraclavicular; age >40 with smoking or alcohol · hoarseness or mouth ulcer >3 weeks → urgent ENT · first imaging neck ultrasound · FNA does not diagnose lymphoma — core or excisional biopsy · no open node biopsy before ENT assessment · reactive node must be re-checked and resolved in 2–4 weeks

Variant 1 — two findings only (smoker with dry cough + toothache): 'two things on my mind — a gland reacting to a lung cancer, or the bad tooth; hard and fixed concerns me, so I investigate properly rather than treat the tooth and wait'

Variant 2 — midline, years, lifts on swallowing AND tongue protrusion: thyroglossal duct cyst — 'a remnant from the way the thyroid forms before birth; not a cancer'; TFTs, ultrasound, surgical referral (usually removed to prevent infection). Discriminator: thyroid moves on swallowing but NOT on tongue protrusion

Variant 3 — 34-year-old, tender node, red warm skin, fever, painful back tooth, 3 days: reactive lymphadenitis from a dental source → urgent dental + antibiotics ★ AND book the 2–4 week review — the node must be proven to resolve · Variant 4 — 61M, painless left supraclavicular lump 3 weeks, indigestion, weight loss: Virchow's node (Troisier's sign) → below the diaphragm (stomach, oesophagus, pancreas) or lung; gastroscopy + neck US with guided FNA + CT staging

setting: General practice, Kadina, Yorke Peninsula. Examination findings supplied in the stem. Counselling station — two minutes of history restricted to treatments, then five minutes of talking.
stem: James Whitlock, 27: runny nose for two weeks, getting worse. Known hay fever; mother has asthma. Examination: afebrile, clear watery discharge, enlarged swollen inferior turbinates, respiratory examination normal.
tasks: Take a history for two minutes, to inquire about the treatments taken
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Counsel the patient about your immediate and long-term management
time: 8 minutes: 2 min treatment-only history (signpost it; he opens with a symptom list — redirect) → five questions: what now · how long/how often · is it helping · what before and did each help · concerns → 45 s diagnosis (name BOTH: rhinitis medicamentosa + hay fever; rebound; reversible) → ★ 'STOP the Otrivin' first, alone, then a pause; warn 1–2 weeks worse → saline/steroid/antihistamine, cost solved → ladder by name → 5-step technique → non-drug → testing THEN immunotherapy 3–5 years → 2-week review, safety-net, summary repeating the stop.

back.dx: Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion from two weeks of xylometazoline — Otrivin — 3–4 times a day, both nostrils) on a background of allergic rhinitis. Pattern: brilliant for the first few days, now lasts an hour, nose worse than before he started. Treatment history: antihistamine tablets helped eyes not nose; a steroid spray WORKED but he stopped it because of cost (saving for a house) and switched to Otrivin — so the plan is to restart that drug cheaply, not invent a new one. Concerns: cost; 'have I wrecked my nose?' (mate said so) — answer both explicitly: completely reversible. Explain: decongestant squeezes the vessels in the lining — beautiful for 3–5 days, then the lining becomes reliant, each dose wears off into more swelling; three reasons — two weeks, helped then stopped, swollen with clear discharge and no fever (not infection). Immediate: STOP Otrivin outright (tapering prolongs it; one-nostril-at-a-time compromise only if he can't cope), warn 1–2 weeks worse, saline before a daily steroid spray (prescribed, cheaper brand in class), cetirizine 10 mg to cover. Long-term ladder by name: saline → antihistamine (oral cetirizine/loratadine/fexofenadine for eyes, or intranasal azelastine for the nose) → ★ mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily, preventer not rescue, no immediate relief, up to 2 weeks → Dymista 1 spray bd (bitter) → montelukast if asthma. Five-step technique. Allergen measures. Allergy testing (specific IgE or skin prick) BEFORE immunotherapy (SC or SL, 3–5 years, allergy clinic in Adelaide, PATS). Review 2 weeks not 6, bring the spray.
plan: WIPE briskly · he launches into sneezing/itchy eyes → ★ 'I can see from your notes you have hay fever, so rather than go back over that, I'd like to spend the next couple of minutes on the treatments you've been using — I suspect that's where the answer is. Is that all right?'

★ 'What medication are you using now?' → Otrivin · ★ 'how long, and how often?' → 2 weeks, both nostrils, 3–4×/day · 'is it helping?' → brilliant then worse ('a telling pattern — I'll come back to it')

'What did you try before? Did those help?' → antihistamine tablets: eyes yes, nose no · steroid spray: worked, too expensive, stopped · ★ 'any concerns about the treatments?' → cost; 'have I damaged something?' · 10 s: other meds incl. BP/pain, decongestant tablets?

'Have you heard of nasal sprays causing a rebound effect?' · name both: hay fever hasn't gone away + rhinitis medicamentosa ('inflammation of the nose caused by a medicine') · rebound mechanism · three reasons · ★ 'completely reversible — you haven't done permanent damage'

★ 'The most important thing, starting today: stop using the Otrivin altogether. Not cut down — stop.' [pause] · ★ 'Your nose will feel worse for one to two weeks — that's the lining recovering; it's why most people give up, so please don't.' · 'wean off?' → no; one-nostril compromise if needed · saline before steroid · daily steroid spray · cetirizine 10 mg daily
Cost: 'it's the reason the steroid stopped working — you stopped taking it; I'll write a prescription and pick a cheaper option in the same class; tell me if it's still a problem'

Ladder by name: 1 saline · 2 antihistamine — oral (cetirizine/loratadine/fexofenadine; fast, good for eyes) or intranasal azelastine (better nose, worse eyes) · 3 ★ mometasone 2 sprays each nostril once daily — preventer not rescue, days to start, 2 weeks for full effect · 4 Dymista 1 spray each nostril bd, bitter · 5 montelukast if asthma emerges

★ Technique, taught: shake · blow nose/saline · look DOWN · opposite hand · aim OUT towards the ear · sniff gently, mouth closed — 'if you taste it you sniffed too hard' (he's been head back, sniffing hard, nosebleeds) · non-drug: pets out of bedroom, mite covers, bedding weekly ≥55 °C, smoke-free house, mask for dust/grain, windows shut and car on recirculate on high-pollen days

Testing first (allergen-specific IgE panel or skin prick) → then immunotherapy: purified allergen in increasing doses, injections or sublingual tablets, ~6-month build-up, ★ 3–5 years, allergy clinic in Adelaide, PATS paperwork · safety-net: fever, facial pain, thick/coloured/bloody discharge, nosebleeds, one-sided blockage, loss of smell, wheeze/SOB · ★ review 2 weeks, bring the spray · summary — ★ repeat 'stop the Otrivin'
ask: ★ 'I can see you have hay fever, so rather than go back over all of that, I'd like to spend the next couple of minutes on the treatments you've been using. Is that all right?'

★ 'Can I ask what medication you are using now? … How long, and how often? … And is it helping?' / 'What did you try before this? … And did those help?' / ★ 'Do you have any concerns about the treatments you've been taking?'

Can't name it → 'Is it a spray or a tablet? Describe the box — is it on your phone? Does the name start with Otri-, Drix- or Sud-? Does it unblock you within a minute or two?' → instant = decongestant; a steroid spray never works that fast
'We already know you have hay fever — but there's a second problem on top of it, caused by the spray. It's called rhinitis medicamentosa — inflammation of the nose caused by a medicine.'

dx: **Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)** — **pus between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor**, usually complicating acute tonsillitis. The commonest deep neck space infection of young adults, typically **polymicrobial — Group A Streptococcus plus oral anaerobes**.
**The sentence that passes this station: A ONE-SIDED THROAT IS A DRAINAGE PROBLEM, NOT AN ANTIBIOTIC PROBLEM.** **Antibiotics do not treat a collection — it has to be drained.**
**Read the photograph in two words: UNILATERAL SWELLING and UVULAR DEVIATION.** Add the bedside triad you elicited — **trismus, muffled voice, ipsilateral otalgia.**

**Odynophagia is painful swallowing — that is the sore throat. DYSPHAGIA means food will not pass, which means obstruction.** Candidates lose the station by hearing 'I can't swallow' and recording it as ordinary throat pain.

**Do now: 1 assess the airway — upright, oxygen if hypoxic, NIL BY MOUTH · 2 refer the SAME VISIT by ambulance to ED for ENT — do not send her home with a script · 3 analgesia — paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly, max 4 g/day, plus ibuprofen 400 mg 8-hourly with food · 4 IV access and fluids · 5 IV antibiotics after cultures.** VERIFY.

**IV antibiotics: benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly PLUS metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly**, or IV amoxicillin–clavulanate. **Severe penicillin hypersensitivity: clindamycin 600 mg IV 8-hourly.** **Step down to oral amoxicillin–clavulanate 875+125 mg 12-hourly to complete 5–7 days.** VERIFY.

**DRAINAGE is the definitive step** — needle aspiration or incision and drainage under local anaesthetic by ENT or an experienced emergency physician. **Either is accepted; the choice is the ENT team's. The principle you must not get wrong is that the collection has to be drained.**

**A single dose of dexamethasone is often given in practice for oedema and pain but is NOT a firm guideline recommendation — do not lead with it.** **Discuss tonsillectomy with ENT if abscesses recur.** **GP review within 48–72 hours of discharge.**

**Answer the request in the stem**: **'you came in for better pain relief, and you will get it — regular paracetamol and an anti-inflammatory now, and stronger relief in hospital. But the pain will not settle properly until the pus is drained, which is why I am not just writing a script.'**

**Safety net, then ask her to repeat it back**: **cannot swallow saliva or drooling · noisy breathing · voice change · neck swelling or stiffness · climbing fever · rash · not improving by 5–7 days · pain up under the left ribs.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS for metropolitan ENT.**
plan: WIPE, introduce, **and get the agenda on the table in the first minute: 'was there something in particular you were hoping we'd do today?'** The request is written into the stem — surfacing it at seven minutes means you fail. Then **signpost the whole station.**

**Lead with the side — the single most discriminating question: IS THE PAIN ON ONE SIDE OF YOUR THROAT, BOTH SIDES, OR ALL THE WAY ACROSS?** Then **how long · sudden or gradual · getting worse · out of ten · burning or dull · DOES IT TRAVEL ANYWHERE, UP INTO YOUR EAR · what makes it better or worse and what have you tried?**

**ENT screen in one breath: any fevers, chills or sweats · any ear pain or discharge · runny or blocked nose, and WHAT COLOUR, thin and watery or thick · any pain over the cheeks or forehead · any dripping down the back of the throat · any change in smell · any lumps or bumps in the neck?**

**The red-flag block — the marks live here:** **can you swallow your own saliva, or are you drooling at all · IS IT TOO PAINFUL TO SWALLOW, OR DOES FOOD PHYSICALLY NOT GO DOWN · has your voice changed, does it sound muffled · any noisy breathing or whistling when you breathe in · CAN YOU OPEN YOUR MOUTH FULLY · any swelling or stiffness in your neck · any headache, dislike of bright light, or a rash?**

**The lower respiratory block, which people forget: any cough — bringing anything up, what colour · any shortness of breath, wheeze or chest pain?** **Cough drives the diagnosis both ways: its presence supports viral, its absence is a Centor feature.**

**Gut and spleen: any nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea · any tummy pain, PARTICULARLY UP UNDER THE LEFT RIBS · appetite and fluid intake?** Then **permission and two sexual health questions only: are you sexually active, do you use condoms, any oral sex?**

**Rheumatic fever risk — asked as its own named question, never folded into 'any past medical history':** **have you ever been told you had rheumatic fever or rheumatic heart disease · has anyone in your FAMILY, or anyone living in your HOUSEHOLD · and do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander?**

**Background in one sweep: any medical problems · regular medications, ANYTHING FOR YOUR THYROID OR MENTAL HEALTH · allergies, particularly penicillin · vaccinations including influenza and COVID · smoking and alcohol · work · anyone around you unwell, any travel?** Then **ideas, concerns and expectations — and stop.**

**Request the examination by component, naming what you seek from each:** **general appearance — alert or drowsy, dehydrated, ANY DROOLING OR STRIDOR, any rash · vital signs, particularly TEMPERATURE, plus pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and saturations · ears — otoscopy for redness, bulging or discharge · throat — tonsillar size and exudate, SYMMETRY, THE POSITION OF THE UVULA, any palatal bulge, and HOW FAR SHE CAN OPEN HER MOUTH · nose and sinuses — discharge and its character, sinus tenderness · neck — cervical nodes anterior AND posterior, swelling, stiffness · chest — air entry and added sounds · heart — sounds and murmurs · abdomen — AND SPECIFICALLY, IS THERE SPLENOMEGALY?**

**Describe the photograph before you diagnose:** **1 SYMMETRY FIRST — 'there is a unilateral swelling of the left soft palate above the tonsil', or 'the tonsils are symmetrically enlarged' · 2 UVULA — deviated, or midline · 3 SURFACE — exudate, white spots, a grey confluent membrane, ulceration, or clean erythema only · 4 SURROUNDING MUCOSA — palatal petechiae, erythema, vesicles · 5 THEN COMMIT. Do NOT open with 'the throat looks red and infected' — DESCRIBE, THEN DIAGNOSE.**

**Explain in plain English WITH THE THREE REASONS: 'the infection in your tonsil has formed a pocket of pus behind it — an abscess is a sac full of pus — and that pocket is pushing your tonsil across. I think that for three reasons: the pain is only on the right, you cannot swallow solids, and there is a swelling on one side pushing the little tag at the back across.'**

**Lead management with the definitive step**: antibiotics alone will not clear an abscess, so **ambulance to ED today for ENT drainage** — then **explain the procedure simply**, answer **'an ambulance? is it that bad?'** proportionately, and **answer the pain request explicitly.**
**Safety net with named red flags**, review in a couple of days, tonsillectomy discussion if recurrent, then **check-back: 'how would you describe this to your mum?'**

**Fever and sore throat on carbimazole, clozapine, methotrexate, sulfasalazine or chemotherapy is AGRANULOCYTOSIS until proven otherwise** — cease the drug, same-day FBC, discuss with the prescribing team.

back.dx: Allergic rhinitis (hay fever) — perennial (cat on the bed, dust mite in an older fully carpeted house, grain dust at the depot, partner smoking indoors) with a spring pollen flare; persistent and moderate–severe by ARIA (sleep, work, taste, embarrassment). Six months, intermittent weeks, ★ bilateral, clear watery copious discharge, no smell, no blood; worse in spring, worse at home in the mornings and in bed; chemist antihistamines help for hours. Atopic package: itchy nose, sneezing fits, red streaming eyes, itchy throat, no chest symptoms (harder version: night cough, puffed at netball → asthma), childhood eczema, sister asthma, mother hay fever. Occasional decongestant spray ('not really a medication') — a week here and there: counsel the 5-day limit, stop it. Two exclusions signposted and clean: chronic rhinosinusitis (no facial pain/pressure, fever, PND, upper toothache, smell loss) and sinonasal/nasopharyngeal malignancy (no epistaxis, weight loss, neck lumps, unilateral ear blockage, diplopia, facial numbness). Hidden agenda: aunt had 'a growth in her nose' — surfaces at the red-flag questions; reassure with the specific negatives, after the screen. PEFE normal → 'a normal examination doesn't change my diagnosis — it reassures me there's no infection, polyp or growth; hay fever is diagnosed on the story'. Three reasons: clear watery bilateral discharge; the travelling symptoms (sneeze, itch, eyes); trigger exposure + family atopy. 'Why all year?' → perennial (mite, cat) plus seasonal (pollen). Mechanism: allergen → mast cell → histamine → inflammation and leaky dilated vessels → blockage and watery discharge (two waves: early histamine = itch/sneeze/run, antihistamines work; late inflammatory cells = blockage, needs the steroid, 1–2 weeks). Plan: cat out of the bedroom, mite covers, hot-wash bedding, lift/vacuum the carpet, recirculate on pollen days; mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily (technique, 2 weeks); cetirizine 10 mg; eye drops; stop the decongestant; smoke-free home, Quitline; review 4–6 weeks with the spray; escalate to combination spray or testing/immunotherapy if uncontrolled.

back.dx: Version A — acute viral hepatitis (A or E) after falling chest-deep into sewage five days ago while sampling for the water utility (full PPE; doesn't know if fluid entered mouth/eyes; incident report filed; no head injury): five days of fever, aches, night sweats, anorexia, RUQ pain, mild nausea, no diarrhoea; card — no jaundice yet, T 38.1, tender hepatomegaly, RUQ tenderness, no splenomegaly, no rash, no calf tenderness, ★ urine dipstick bilirubin positive (bilirubinuria precedes visible jaundice — the point of the card). Explain: 'acute hepatitis — inflammation of the liver — most probably hepatitis A or a close relative, hepatitis E; both picked up by swallowing something contaminated with sewage; not yellow yet but the pigment is already building up in the urine'; settles over weeks, doesn't become chronic; infectious via the bowel — handwashing, household vaccination. Version B card (no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, mild lower abdominal tenderness, dipstick normal; history of loose stools 4–5/day, lower abdominal pain) → gastroenteritis, said cleanly: 'not hepatitis' — no hedging with 'might be early hepatitis'. Plan: LFTs, clotting, hepatitis and leptospirosis serology, liver ultrasound; rest, fluids, no alcohol; notify hepatitis A; vaccinate household (3-year-old son); employer letter — off work while infectious; ReturnToWorkSA; safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, can't keep fluids down, turning yellow; review 2 days, talk about the dreams properly then.

back.dx: HIV seroconversion illness ± secondary syphilis. Eight days of fever, chills, aches, headaches, exhaustion (sick twice), mild early sore throat; two days of a flat red blotchy non-itchy non-painful ★ blanching rash chest → back and upper arms; lumps in neck and axillae, night sweats, appetite down, weight steady. Findings: febrile, generalised lymphadenopathy, ★ lesions on the palms (ask), no splenomegaly, mouth clear. To Ben: 'I'm concerned about a sexually transmitted infection — specifically HIV, or syphilis, or possibly both'; reasons from history (MSM, no condoms, casual partners; eight days of fever/aches/headache/exhaustion, spreading rash) and examination (fever, glands everywhere, rash on the palms — characteristic of syphilis; the painless sore fits); 'they look identical at this stage, which is exactly why we test for both'. (uncle died of AIDS in the 90s) → HIV today is not that illness: treatment, normal lifespan, undetectable = untransmissible; syphilis cured with an injection; don't promise a result you don't have. setting: General practice. Examination card at six minutes — three versions: (1) hepatitis card, (2) HIV seroconversion card (scripted here), (3) endocarditis card. Six minutes of history.
stem: Gary, 26, attends alone feeling unwell. He has recently returned from an overseas trip in South-East Asia, and used heroin while he was away.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6 minutes)
You will be given a physical examination card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the fear in one sentence · ★ signpost three blocks: the unwellness, the trip, the heroin · define, time, impact · ★ full travel history A B C D E F G S (don't accept 'just fun with mates'); write down 'no sex overseas' · ★ heroin in three steps IN ORDER: open question → route → shared needles · ★ three BBV boxes every time: hepatitis · HIV · injection/endocarditis · ★ go BACK for the sexual history ('ever been sexually active?') · ★ guilt ×3 → mood, anhedonia, self-harm, use since · card — interrogate for jaundice, organomegaly, murmur, injection sites, dipstick · name the version's diagnosis with reasons · grouped differentials · ★ HIV test named, consent · malaria films · harm reduction · confidentiality with the notification caveat · safety-net.

back.dx: Version 2 — HIV seroconversion illness: a week of no energy and fever, constant, worsening, bed-bound two days; three weeks in Indonesia, back two weeks; one night injected heroin — first ever use — one needle shared between the group, none since; street food nightly; pre-travel GP gave a hepatitis shot; no bites, sick contacts, animals, tattoos, transfusion; 'no sex overseas' — but ever sexually active: yes, never condoms, multiple partners at times, women. HIV box positive: sore throat, chest rash, fever/chills, drenching night sweats, some weight loss, neck lumps; hepatitis box negative; injection box negative. Card: T 38.2, morbilliform rash, generalised lymphadenopathy, exudative tonsillitis; on request — no jaundice, no hepatosplenomegaly, no murmur, injection sites unremarkable, dipstick negative. EBV is the trap answer — say it is the closest mimic. Explain: 'I'm concerned you contracted HIV when you shared that needle — the first stage, seroconversion illness, causes exactly this: fever, sore throat, rash, glands, night sweats, exhaustion — it looks like flu and is very commonly missed'; reasons — the route, the symptoms, the findings. 'I've ruined my life over one stupid night' → pause, 'what's going through your mind?' → concern not result; treatment today — normal lifespan, undetectable = untransmissible. Differentials: EBV/CMV/toxoplasma · hepatitis B and C ('your shot covers A and B; no vaccine for C — curable with tablets 8–12 weeks') · infective endocarditis (no murmur, reassuring) · malaria, dengue, typhoid (films) · syphilis · leukaemia/lymphoma · depression/anxiety. Plan: ★ HIV test with specific permission (4th-gen Ag/Ab ± RNA, repeat 6 weeks), HBV/HCV, syphilis, EBV, LFT, FBE, thick/thin films ×3; sexual health referral; confidentiality honest — notifiable, contacts traced sensitively, name not given; NSP and take-home naloxone 'not because I assume you'll use again'; mood review next week; safety-net confusion/drowsiness, jaundice, chest pain/SOB → ED/000.

Have you EVER been sexually active?' → yes · condoms (never) · multiple (at times) · ★ male/female/both (women)

'Thank you for being honest, that helps me a lot. Sharing a needle can pass on infections carried in blood, so I need to check for those.' → hepatitis box, HIV box, injection box
★ 'These infections are also passed on sexually, so I need to come back to this. Have you ever been sexually active? Do you use condoms? Ever had multiple partners? Male, female, or both?'

'You've said a few times that you feel guilty. How are you coping with it? How's your mood been? Still enjoying the things you normally enjoy? — I ask everyone this — any thoughts of harming yourself? Any use since you got back?'
'May I have the examination findings? ★ And can I confirm: any jaundice? Any hepatosplenomegaly? Any murmur? Anything at the injection sites? And the urine dipstick?'

'Gary, I'm concerned about the possibility that you contracted HIV when you shared that needle. The very first stage is called seroconversion illness, and it causes exactly this picture: fever, sore throat, a rash, swollen glands, night sweats and exhaustion. It looks so like the flu that it's very commonly missed.' → 'I've ruined my life' → (pause) 'That's a hard thing to hear. What's going through your mind?' → 'First, we don't know yet — this is a concern, not a result. Second, if it is HIV, treatment today is extremely effective: a normal life span and, on treatment, cannot pass it on.'

★ 'The hepatitis shot covers A and B. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C' — 'but it is now curable with tablets, usually over two to three months.' / ★ 'One of these is an HIV test — I need your permission for that specifically.' / 'Also hepatitis B and C, syphilis, glandular fever, liver tests, a blood count and malaria films.'

'What you tell me is confidential, though some infections have to be reported to public health so contacts can be traced — that's done sensitively and your name isn't given to your contacts.' (never 'everything is completely confidential') / 'I'll give you information about free needle and syringe services and take-home naloxone — not because I assume you'll use again, but because it costs nothing to have.'

setting: General practice, Kadina. Nine-minute station. He coughs harshly and repeatedly throughout — the acting is data. Observations from the examiner include the fifth vital sign. Two headings: infection, and malignancy.
stem: Jack Mullins, 30, has come in feeling unwell and feverish. He is a known case of HIV and stopped his antiretroviral medication six months ago.
tasks: Take a history from the patient (about 6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings, or read them from the card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 9 minutes: 0:00 ★ all five observations incl. SpO2 · one empathic sentence · ★ 'I can hear that cough' · unwell and fever explored separately · 1:30 HIV history — diagnosed when, ★ why stopped (no moralising), follow-up, complications · 2:15 ★ signposted whole-body infection screen (breadth not depth; characterise the cough in three questions) incl. sexual history despite HIV, injecting, chest pain · 4:45 ★ open the malignancy heading — weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, mouth ulcers/patches, purple marks, haemoptysis, smoking, asbestos, moles · mood · 5:45 examination in one run incl. vocal resonance and a full node survey · ★ the white patch — painful? scrapes off? colour? where? · ★ 'normal chest but febrile, tachypnoeic, hypoxic — in advanced HIV a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia' · 7:00 pneumonia named and reasoned · opportunistic infection as a concern not a diagnosis · ★ the cancers named honestly, reaction contained · other infections individually · restart ART · safety-net.

back.dx: Pneumonia in a man with untreated HIV (ART stopped six months ago — felt well, tablets nauseated him, long trip to Adelaide; no specialist review for a year; no prior complications), with opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis, TB) and malignancy on the list. Three to four days feverish with rigors, worsening, paracetamol useless; dry cough; new exertional breathlessness on stairs; everything else negative; smokes 10/day; mood flat. Examiner: alert, no rash/jaundice, mildly dehydrated; T 38.0, HR 104, BP 118/74, RR 24, ★ SpO2 92% RA; ★ a white patch in the mouth — scrapes off, on tongue and buccal mucosa (candidiasis — but describe before naming: Kaposi = violaceous, raised, hard palate, doesn't scrape; OHL = white, corrugated, lateral tongue, doesn't scrape); no lymphadenopathy; ★ respiratory examination entirely normal; HS dual; abdomen and dipstick normal. To the examiner: 'although the chest is normal he is febrile, tachypnoeic and hypoxic — in advanced HIV there isn't enough immune function to produce consolidation, crackles or an effusion, so a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia — the same principle as febrile neutropenia'. To Jack: 'the most likely thing is a pneumonia — fever, cough, unwell, Panadol not helping; on examination your oxygen is low and you're breathing fast — your lungs aren't picking up oxygen properly, even though listening sounded normal'; 'but my chest sounded fine?' → 'the low oxygen tells me more than my stethoscope does'. Opportunistic concern named (Pneumocystis, TB) alongside common causes (COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcus, Legionella, Mycoplasma) — don't call it Pneumocystis with no CD4, viral load, white cells or film. ★ 'HIV also raises the risk of certain cancers, and I have to be honest with you': lung cancer (cough, smoker), Kaposi sarcoma (the patch — exclude), lymphoma, leukaemia → he is shaken → contain: 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer; I'm telling you what I have to rule out; the most likely explanation today is still an infection'. Other infections named individually (tonsillitis, pharyngitis, sinusitis; gastroenteritis; hepatitis; syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea; meningitis; cellulitis); then low mood/adjustment, anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, OSA. Plan: send in today — CXR, bloods incl. CD4/viral load, start treatment; reconnect with the HIV team; ★ restarting ART is one of the most important things we do — and look at what made it hard last time. 'Is this because I stopped my tablets?' — hidden agenda at ~7 min.
plan: ★ 'Before I begin, could I have his observations — BP, pulse, RR, temperature AND oxygen saturation?' → 118/74, 104, 24, 38.0, 92% · 'Hello Jack, I'm sorry to hear you've not been well — let's work out what's going on together' · ★ 'I can hear that cough — we'll come to it'
Unwell: sleepy/low energy/feverish? duration (3–4 days), constant, worse, better/worse · fever block: measured? chills? (yes) taken anything, helped? (Panadol, nothing)

HIV: 'when were you diagnosed? (5 y) I know you've stopped your medication — can you tell me what led to that? (felt fine, nausea, long trip to Adelaide) — no judgement here · regular follow-up? (not for a year) · any complications before? (never)'

★ 'I'm going to run through the whole body fairly quickly, area by area — most of these will be a simple no, and that's what I'm hoping for': sore throat/coryza/facial/ear pain · ★ cough — dry or chesty? SOB? noisy breathing? (dry; puffed on the stairs — three questions, keep going) · nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain/diarrhoea · dysuria/frequency · headache/stiff neck/photophobia · ★ sexual health (active in 3 months? condoms? discharge/rash/ulcers/scrotal pain) — despite HIV · jaundice/dark urine/pale stools · rash, hot painful skin · travel · ★ recreational drugs, ever injected? chest pain/palpitations (endocarditis) · animals

★ Malignancy heading: 'a few more — weight loss without trying? appetite? lumps or bumps? night sweats? ulcers or patches in your mouth? new purple or red marks on your skin? ever coughed up blood? do you smoke? (10/day) what work — asbestos? new or changing moles?' · if time: 'how has your mood been?' (flat)

★ Examination in one run: general — alert/drowsy, rash, jaundice, dehydration · all five vitals · throat — swelling/redness, ★ any lesion in the mouth · full lymph node survey, thyroid · respiratory — expansion, percussion both sides, added sounds, ★ vocal resonance ('I'm looking for consolidation') · CVS — S1 S2, murmurs · abdomen — tenderness, splenomegaly · dipstick → 'there is a white patch in his mouth'; respiratory entirely normal

★ The patch, two questions: 'is it painful to touch with a tongue depressor? can it be scraped off? colour? where?' → white, scrapes off, tongue and buccal mucosa → describe first, name second · ★ the normal-chest sentence to the examiner

To Jack: pneumonia named + reasons (fever, cough, unwell, Panadol failed; low oxygen, fast breathing) · 'but my chest sounded fine?' answered · opportunistic concern — Pneumocystis, TB — alongside common viruses/bacteria · ★ 'HIV also raises the risk of certain cancers, and I have to be honest with you about that' — lung, Kaposi (the patch), lymphoma/leukaemia → shaken → ★ 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer; I'm telling you what I have to rule out' · other infections named individually · then low mood, anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, OSA

'Is this because I stopped my tablets?' → honest, not blaming · plan: send in today — CXR, bloods incl. a check of the immune system, treatment started · ★ 'restarting your HIV treatment is one of the most important things we can do — and we can look at what made it hard last time' · safety-net: more short of breath, confused/drowsy, severe headache/stiff neck, haemoptysis → ambulance · confidentiality/Adelaide follow-up if he prefers · questions
ask: ★ 'All five observations, including oxygen saturation.' / ★ 'I can hear that cough — tell me about it.' / 'I'm sorry you're feeling like this, Jack. Let me ask you a few questions, and we'll work out what's going on together.'
'When were you diagnosed? Can you tell me what led to stopping?' / 'Are you still having regular follow-up with your specialist?' / 'Thank you for telling me that, and there's no judgement here.'

★ 'I'm going to run through the whole body quickly — most of these will be a simple no.' / 'Is the cough dry or chesty? Short of breath? Coughed up blood?' / 'Can I ask about sexual health? Sexually active now or in the last three months? Condoms? Any discharge, rash or ulcers?' / 'Any recreational drugs — have you ever injected? Any chest pain or racing of the heart?'
★ 'Any weight loss, appetite change, lumps, night sweats, mouth ulcers or patches, new purple or red marks on your skin, coughed-up blood? Do you smoke? Any asbestos at work?'

'Is vocal resonance increased anywhere — I'm looking for consolidation.' / ★ 'Is the patch painful to touch with a tongue depressor, and can it be scraped off? What colour is it, and where in the mouth?'

★ 'Examiner, although the respiratory examination is normal, he is febrile, tachypnoeic and hypoxic. In advanced HIV there isn't enough immune function to produce consolidation, crackles or an effusion, so a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia here — the same principle as febrile neutropenia in a child on chemotherapy.'

★ 'Jack, the most likely thing is a pneumonia — an infection in your lung. Fever, cough, feeling unwell, Panadol not helping — and on examination the oxygen level in your blood is low and you're breathing faster than normal.' / 'But you said my chest sounded fine?' → 'When the immune system is weakened the body can't mount the response I'd normally hear. The low oxygen is telling me more than my stethoscope is.'

'Because you have HIV there's a higher chance of unusual infections — we call them opportunistic — things like Pneumocystis and tuberculosis. But it could still be a common virus such as COVID-19 or influenza, or a common bacterial pneumonia — pneumococcus, Legionella or Mycoplasma.' / Examiner: 'why not just say Pneumocystis?' → 'Because I have no CD4 count, viral load, white cell count or chest film. I'm calling it a pneumonia, and Pneumocystis is at the top of the list of causes.'

★ 'I also have to be honest that HIV raises the risk of certain cancers. Because you have a cough I'm thinking about lung cancer. Because of the white patch in your mouth I want to exclude a cancer that occurs specifically in HIV called Kaposi sarcoma. Lymphoma and leukaemia are also more common.' → (shaken) ★ 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer. I'm telling you what I have to rule out, because ruling it out properly is how we make sure nothing is missed. The most likely explanation today is still an infection.'

★ 'Restarting your HIV treatment is one of the most important things we can do — and we can look at what made it difficult last time.' / 'Am I dying?' → 'I can't answer that today and I'm not going to guess. setting: General practice, Moonta. EXAMINATION-FIRST station — no history taking. Findings from the examiner for four minutes; the results card is handed over at exactly four minutes; then you explain results, diagnosis and differentials to Jane.
stem: Jane Whitmore, 40, has come in feeling unwell — tired and nauseated, no fever. She has recently returned from a trip to the Philippines. No sexual activity overseas, no mosquito bites, no needle exposures. Appendicectomy ten years ago.
tasks: Begin with a physical examination, asking the examiner for the findings — there is no history taking
At four minutes you are given the investigation results; explain them to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: ★ 0:00 GREET JANE FIRST — name, role, what will happen, when I'll be back, is that all right (15 s) · 0:20 examination as one run across the differentials, not at the liver: general (jaundice) · four vitals · throat, ears · thyroid, full node survey · chest · heart · abdomen → 'hepatomegaly' → ★ don't accept it: span, tender?, border, shifting dullness, scratch marks, bruising, bowel sounds · DRE · ★ 'with the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone' pelvic · ★ two office tests: dipstick (bilirubin) and ★ pregnancy test · 4:00 turn back to Jane, acknowledge the wait · results in three sentences (test → plain English → meaning), under a minute, no numbers, no abbreviations · 5:30 'most likely' hepatitis A + reasons incl. bilirubin in the urine · 6:30 differentials — ★ TRAVEL FIRST, then liver/abdominal incl. cancer, then pregnancy, then the generic tiredness list · plan, notification, hygiene, alcohol, safety-net.

back.dx: Acute hepatitis A (most likely — confirmatory anti-HAV IgM pending): three weeks in the Philippines with relatives, home cooking and street food, back a fortnight; a week tired, nauseated, off food, afebrile; husband noticed yellow eyes two days ago. Examination: alert, ★ jaundiced, no rash/pallor, mildly dehydrated; BP 120/80, HR 88, RR 12, T 36.9; throat/ears/thyroid/nodes normal; chest clear; HS dual; abdomen not distended, ★ hepatomegaly 3 cm, non-tender, smooth regular border, no splenomegaly, no ascites, no scratch marks/bruising, bowel sounds normal; DRE and pelvic normal; ★ dipstick bilirubin positive, urobilinogen raised; ★ pregnancy test negative. Results card: WCC 13.2, bilirubin 68, ALT 780, AST 640, ALP 130, GGT 110, INR 1.1, albumin 38, HBV and HCV negative — hepatocellular pattern (to the examiner). Explain in three beats each: FBC — white cells, immune cells, raised = fighting infection/inflammation · liver test — enzymes raised = inflammation in the liver · hepatitis B and C negative. 'Damaged?' → 'inflamed rather than damaged; the two numbers that measure how well it's doing its job are normal today'. Diagnosis 'most likely', never certain: enlarged liver, jaundice, bilirubin in the urine ('made by the liver, normally never reaches the urine — finding it there tells me the problem is in your liver'), raised enzymes, B and C negative, recent travel, nausea; spreads via contaminated food/water. Settles over 2–8 weeks, no specific treatment, never chronic, lifelong immunity. Differentials in the order the case demands: (1) travel — malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis, hepatitis E, EBV, HIV, TB; (2) liver/abdominal — hepatitis B/C (negative), autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, gallstones/cholangitis, ★ cancer of the liver or pancreas ('particularly because your liver was not tender'); (3) pregnancy (tested, negative); (4) anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, haemochromatosis, lymphoma/leukaemia, autoimmune, depression, heart failure, OSA. Plan: anti-HAV IgM, liver ultrasound, review this week; no alcohol, check before any medication (paracetamol at reduced dose VERIFY); handwashing, don't prepare food for others, don't share towels; notify — household vaccinated (within 14 days VERIFY); safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, worsening jaundice, can't keep fluids down. Hidden agenda: sister died of pancreatic cancer — tearful at the word cancer; name it, proportion it, say what resolves it.
plan: ★ 'No questions, thank you. — Hello Jane, I'm Dr [name], one of the doctors here, and I'll be looking after you today. I'm going to speak with my colleague for a few minutes and go through an examination, then I'll come straight back to you and explain everything I've found. Is that all right?'

One continuous run: general — alert/drowsy, ★ jaundice, rash, pallor, dehydration · all four vitals · throat (swelling, redness, exudate), ears (red bulging TM) · thyroid, ★ full lymph node examination every chain · respiratory — air entry, added sounds · CVS — S1 S2, murmurs · abdomen — inspection (distension, redness, bruising), palpation (tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly)

'Hepatomegaly' → ★ 'what is the span? is it tender? border regular or irregular? shifting dullness? scratch marks? bruising? bowel sounds?' → 3 cm, non-tender, smooth, no ascites, no scratch marks/bruises, BS normal

'I would like a digital rectal examination. ★ And with the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone, a pelvic examination — inspection for discharge or rash, speculum for cervical discharge, bimanual for cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, and the adnexae' → all normal (there IS time here — judge by the clock you're given)
★ 'Two office tests: a urine dipstick — I'm looking particularly for bilirubin — and a urine pregnancy test' → bilirubin positive, urobilinogen raised; pregnancy negative → results card handed over

★ Turn back: 'thank you for waiting, Jane — I've examined you and I have your results; let me talk you through them, then tell you what I think' · three sentences, test → plain English → meaning: white cells raised · liver enzymes raised · hepatitis B and C negative · 'is my liver damaged?' → inflamed, not damaged; the job-numbers (INR, albumin) are normal

'Most likely hepatitis — your liver is inflamed — most likely caused by a virus called hepatitis A' + reasons (enlarged liver, jaundice, bilirubin in the urine, raised enzymes, B and C negative, recent travel, nausea) · 'from the food?' → most likely · 'will I get better?' → 2–8 weeks, no specific medicine, never long-term, immune for life · 'can I pass it on?' → hands, food, towels; notification → household vaccine

★ Differentials, travel FIRST: malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis, hepatitis E, EBV, HIV, TB · liver/abdomen: B/C negative, autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced (antibiotics), gallstones/cholangitis, ★ cancer of the liver or pancreas — 'particularly because your liver was not tender' → tearful, sister → name it, proportion it (travel, pattern, bilirubinuria point to a virus), what resolves it · pregnancy — tested · the generic list

Plan: confirmatory blood test, liver ultrasound, review this week · no alcohol, check before any medication ('Panadol for headaches?' → reduced dose, ask me) · handwashing, no food preparation for others, no shared towels · notification, household vaccination · work certificate · safety-net: confused/unusually sleepy, bruising/bleeding, yellowing much worse, can't keep fluids down → hospital · questions
ask: ★ 'Hello Jane, I am Doctor [name] — give me a few minutes with my colleague and I will come straight back to you.'
'Examiner, on general appearance: is she alert or drowsy? Any jaundice? Any rash? Any pallor? Any dehydration?' — findings, not regions
★ 'What is the span? Is the liver tender? Is the border regular or irregular?' / ★ 'Is there shifting dullness? Any scratch marks? Any bruising?'
★ 'With the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone…' / ★ 'Two office tests: a urine dipstick, looking particularly for bilirubin, and a urine pregnancy test.'

'The first test is a full blood count. The white blood cells are the cells of your immune system, and they're higher than normal — your body is fighting an infection or inflammation.' / 'Your liver enzymes are raised — that means there is inflammation in your liver.' / 'We tested for two viruses that commonly cause liver inflammation, and both are negative.'
'Is my liver damaged?' → ★ 'Inflamed rather than damaged. The liver is a remarkably good healer. There are two numbers that tell me how well it's doing its job, and both are normal today.'

But the whole picture — you've just come back from overseas, the pattern of your blood tests, the bilirubin in your urine — points much more strongly to a viral infection. The blood test I'm arranging should settle it, and the ultrasound looks directly at the liver.'

'We notify this routinely, which means your household can be offered a vaccine.' / 'Avoid alcohol completely, and check with me before any medication.' / 'Come back straight away, or go to hospital, if you become confused or unusually sleepy, if you start bruising or bleeding easily, if the yellowing gets much worse, or if you cannot keep fluids down.'

setting: General practice. Vitals in the stem. Examination findings on screen/card when asked. Five minutes of history. No management task — but a plan and a safety-net still earn marks.
stem: Ben Alderton, 25, has come in feeling unwell. He attends a sauna regularly with friends, and his friends have similar symptoms. He is currently taking PrEP. T 38.4, HR 96, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.

You will be given the examination findings on screen or card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the worry · 'unwell' in four questions · ★ open the sauna: how often, ★ 'what do your friends have?', what do you do there (sex) · ★ three water infections: Legionella (cough, SOB, fever, diarrhoea, confusion) · hepatitis A (abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice, dark urine/pale stools) · Pseudomonas (itchy spots under swimwear) · ★ PrEP block, three separate marks: adherence · 3-monthly screening · hepatitis A/B vaccination · ★ normalise once, then the full sexual history (partners, number, gender, condoms, practices, previous STI, alcohol/drugs) — don't stop to counsel · STI symptoms incl. ulcers, discharge, scrotum, back passage · the rest · examination by name incl. throat, nodes, palms/soles, genitals, dipstick · acute viral hepatitis WITHOUT guessing the subtype · differentials by exposure: sauna ×3 + crypto, STIs with ★ HIV high on the list despite PrEP · ★ three-site swabs · confidentiality accurately · vaccinate · 3-monthly reviews · safety-net.

back.dx: Acute viral hepatitis (subtype deliberately not guessed — A via faecal-oral including sexual transmission between men, or B/C via sex) in an MSM on PrEP: a week of fever, anorexia, upper abdominal pain, vomiting, partner says he looks yellow, urine darker; no cough/SOB/diarrhoea/confusion (Legionella less likely), no rash (Pseudomonas less likely). Sauna 2–3×/week, same group, a couple of friends off work with unknown symptoms; 'we have sex there as well' (say it back: both a water exposure and a sexual exposure). PrEP: misses the odd dose when he stays out; last review two months ago but ★ never screened for STIs; doesn't know if he's had hepatitis A/B vaccines. Sexual history: no stable partner, several partners, all men, no condoms, oral and anal, never diagnosed, sometimes after drinks. No STI symptoms. Card: jaundiced, T 38.4, tender hepatomegaly span >13 cm, no splenomegaly, chest clear, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no genital/perianal lesions or discharge, dipstick bilirubin positive. Differentials grouped by exposure: sauna — Legionella (warm-water spray; no cough/SOB), Pseudomonas folliculitis (no rash), cryptosporidium (chlorine-resistant; no diarrhoea); STIs — ★ HIV high on the list ('PrEP is very effective but not absolute, and it depends on taking it consistently — you miss doses; one blood test'), syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea and chlamydia (throat and rectum often asymptomatic — urine alone misses them); then EBV/CMV, travel, lymphoma/leukaemia, depression, thyroid/diabetes/anaemia/coeliac. stem: Mary Ellis, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has come in because she has been feeling unwell for the past few days. First pregnancy; antenatal care so far uncomplicated.

back.dx: Acute pyelonephritis at 20 weeks: 3–4 days hot and shivery with rigors last night, worsening, paracetamol useless; dysuria and frequency, no visible haematuria; vomited 3–4 times; right flank/back pain radiating to the groin (Version B: low central suprapubic pain — the diagnosis is unchanged when renal angle tenderness is positive). Examiner: alert, flushed, mildly dehydrated; BP 110/70, HR 108, RR 18, ★ T 38.7; throat/chest/heart normal; mild suprapubic tenderness, no RUQ tenderness, no organomegaly; ★ fundal height 20 cm consistent with dates, uterus non-tender, FHR 145; ★ right renal angle tenderness POSITIVE; dipstick leucocytes +++, nitrites +, blood ++, protein trace. Your completed assessment: recent examinations with considerable stress; bed after 1 am, up at 6:30; easy-going personality; mood normal, no anxiety disorder; three to four cups of coffee every night while studying. No weight loss, fever, night sweats, lumps or travel; no snoring or witnessed apnoeas; no medications, alcohol or drugs; periods regular and not heavy. Examination and vital signs normal.

(the temazepam line — park it explicitly), ★ 'is it all right if I explain what I think, then we make a plan together?' · Task 1, four blocks, three minutes: NAME it (sleep restriction) · DEFINE it (8–10 h needed; she gets ~5) · REASON it (exam trigger, pattern persisting, caffeine) · SAY WHAT YOU EXCLUDED · teach-back · Task 2, eight headings one sentence each: hygiene · diary · ★ CBT-I first line · caffeine · relaxation · lifestyle · named organisation · review 4 weeks + conditional bloods/sleep study · Task 3, ★ VALIDATE → DECLINE with ≥2 reasons → SUBSTITUTE (not second best) → CONTRACT (four weeks, a date) · safety-net incl. mood/self-harm · driving.

back.dx: Chronic insufficient sleep — behaviourally induced sleep restriction — in a 17-year-old: ~5 hours on school nights (bed 1–2 am, up 6:30), studies and scrolls in bed, 3–4 instant coffees each evening (last ~11 pm, ~380 mg, half still circulating at bedtime), set off by exam stress and persisting after it; catches up to midday at weekends and feels much better (the pattern that says 'not enough sleep', not blood or thyroid); mood normal, no self-harm, no snoring/apnoeas/sleep attacks. 'Nothing wrong with me?' → 'there is something wrong — it just isn't a disease'. Management aim: improve quantity and quality of sleep — (1) sleep hygiene: fixed bed and wake time seven days, bed for sleep only (no phone/laptop/study/TV), dark quiet cool, out of bed if not asleep in 20–30 min, warm shower/milk; (2) sleep diary two weeks (bedtime, sleep onset, hours, quality/10); (3) ★ CBT-I — first line in Australia, more effective than hypnotics and durable — psychologist referral or Australian online programmes; cognitive half (the 'if I don't sleep I'll fail' worry) + behavioural half (stimulus control, relaxation, time-in-bed matching); (4) caffeine: half-life ~5 h, nothing after early afternoon, cut the total, expect a headache; (5) relaxation — mindfulness, breathing, PMR, yoga; (6) lifestyle — daytime exercise, regular meals, no alcohol/smoking/vaping, screens off; (7) named: Sleep Health Foundation fact sheets, headspace (12–25); (8) review 4 weeks with the diary → if no better TSH, FBE, ferritin → sleep study if another disorder is suggested. Temazepam: validate (exhausted, worked for a friend) → decline with reasons (dependence/tolerance/withdrawal, next-day drowsiness for driving and study, not recommended under 18, doesn't fix the cause) → substitute (CBT-I works better and lasts) → contract (four weeks, then we look together). 'Just a few for exams?' → exam time is when grogginess costs most; two weeks is enough to start dependence. 'So you're not going to help me?' → 'I'm not doing the thing that helps for two weeks and causes a problem for two years — everything else starts today.' Safety-net: mood drops, hopelessness, self-harm thoughts, sudden daytime sleep attacks, snoring/apnoeas → sooner. Driving: don't drive sleepy, pull over (P-plater).

★ 'In your case I think it's sleep restriction — your sleep is fine, there just isn't enough of it.' / 'Someone your age needs eight to ten hours.' / 'These problems are often triggered by stress and then keep going after the stress has passed.'

★ 'I've looked for the other causes and not found them — that's what lets me be confident.' / 'So there's nothing wrong with me?' → 'There is something wrong — it just isn't a disease. Not getting enough sleep is a real problem with real effects and a real treatment. I'm not dismissing it.'
'Bed for sleep only. If you're not asleep in twenty to thirty minutes, get up, do something boring in dim light, and come back when you feel sleepy.'

★ 'CBT for insomnia is first line — more effective than sleeping tablets, and it keeps working after you stop.' / 'What will the psychologist actually do?' → 'Two halves. The cognitive half works on the thoughts that keep it going — the "if I don't sleep I'll fail" worry that itself keeps you awake. The behavioural half teaches stimulus control, relaxation, and matching your time in bed to the sleep you're actually getting.'
'Caffeine hangs around about five hours, so four cups in the evening is half still circulating at bedtime. Nothing with caffeine after early afternoon.'

★ 'I can see why you're asking — you're exhausted and you've heard it worked for someone else. But I don't think a sleeping tablet is the right answer for you. It helps for a short time, but it comes with real problems. The main one is dependence — your body gets used to it, it stops working at the same dose, we end up increasing it, and if you try to stop you get withdrawal: worse sleep than before, anxiety, shakiness. There's next-day drowsiness, which matters for driving and study, and these tablets aren't recommended at your age. And most importantly — it doesn't fix the cause.'

★ 'What I'm offering instead isn't second best. The psychological treatment works better than the tablets do, and it keeps working after you finish.' / ★ 'Give me four weeks with the diary and the plan. Come back and we'll look at it together — and if it hasn't worked we think again, properly, not by reaching for a tablet.'

'Just a few, to get through exams?' → 'Exam time is exactly when the next-day grogginess would cost you most, and two weeks is long enough to start the dependence problem. What I can do this week is get the diary going, fix the coffee, and get you a psychology appointment quickly.' / 'So you're not going to help me?' → 'I am helping you — I'm just not doing the thing that would help for two weeks and cause a problem for two years. Everything else on that list I will start today.'

'Come back sooner if your mood drops, if you feel hopeless or have thoughts of harming yourself, if you start falling asleep suddenly during the day, or if anyone tells you that you snore or stop breathing at night.' / ★ 'And please — don't drive when you feel sleepy. Pull over.'

back.dx: Cardiac (exertional) syncope from aortic stenosis. 'Out cold', <1 min, witnessed by his wife, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, not confused after (shaken only), grazed elbow, no head strike. ★ Walking up the driveway with the shopping (exertion), ★ no warning at all, prior light-headedness twice on the golf course walking uphill, months of chest tightness and breathlessness on hills 'put down to age' — the AS triad. No meds, none stopped; no FHx sudden death. PEFE: no postural drop, pulse regular slow-rising (ask: low volume? heave? thrill?), ESM RUSE radiating to the carotids, soft S2, neuro normal, glucose 5.6, ECG SR with LVH. To Bill: 'not a trip — a blackout from the heart rather than a simple faint: no warning (faints almost always give a few seconds of dizziness or sweating), and it happened on exertion; a murmur — a narrowed, stiff valve, the door blood leaves the heart through; on exertion the body asks for more blood, the valve can't let enough through, the brain briefly goes short'. Differentials: arrhythmia (still needs excluding), cardiomyopathy, PE, stroke/seizure. Plan: admit to a monitored bed, bloods, echo, cardiology; if severe → valve replacement, works very well. ★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you' (Austroads; SA Registrar of Motor Vehicles; notification duty) · no heights, machinery, swimming alone · 000 if recurrent, chest pain, palpitations, severe SOB. Hidden agenda: brother-in-law's stroke; 'can I drive home and come back tomorrow?' — always asked.

★ 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?' / 'Did anyone see it happen?' / ★ 'Did you have any jerky movements of your arms or legs? Did you bite your tongue? Did you wet or soil yourself?'

'How long were you unconscious? Is this the first time? Can you describe each episode for me?' / ★ 'What were you doing when it happened?' / ★ 'Did you have any warning at all — did you know you were about to go down?'

'Had you missed any meals, and were you drinking normally that day?' / ★ 'When you came round, were you confused, or just tired?' / 'Did you injure your head, or any other part of you, when you fell?'

'For the next few questions, tell me whether you had it before this happened, after it, or not at all — I won't ask you everything twice.' / ★ 'Do you take any medications regularly, or have you recently stopped any?' / ★ 'Has anyone in your family died suddenly and unexpectedly, especially at a young age?'

★ 'Examiner, I have the blood pressure and pulse rate — may I have the postural blood pressure and the pulse rhythm?' / 'That murmur is very significant. Is the pulse volume low as well as slow-rising, and is there a heave or thrill?'

'What you had wasn't a trip — you blacked out, and I think the blackout came from your heart rather than being a simple faint. Two things point me there: you had no warning at all — simple faints almost always give a few seconds of dizziness or sweating first — and it happened while you were exerting yourself.'

'There's a murmur — an extra sound — which suggests one of the valves has become narrowed and stiff. That valve is the door blood leaves your heart through. When you exert yourself your body asks for more blood, the narrowed valve can't let enough through, your brain briefly goes short, and you black out. It also explains the chest tightness and breathlessness on hills.'

'Is it serious?' → 'I want to be straight with you: blacking out with this kind of valve problem is serious, and it's treatable. I'd like to admit you today to a bed with heart monitoring, do bloods, and arrange an echo to see exactly how narrow that valve is. If it's significantly narrowed the treatment is to repair or replace it, which works very well.'

★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you — and don't work at heights, use machinery, or swim alone.' / Examiner on driving: 'Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive — the non-driving period depends on cause, treatment and licence type; commercial stricter; I'd check the current standard rather than quote from memory; in SA the Registrar of Motor Vehicles, and doctors carry a duty to notify where a patient is unfit and continues to drive.'

back.dx: Vasovagal (reflex) syncope — third episode, each with a textbook trigger and a prodrome: (1) jumped out of bed to answer the phone, (2) the sight of blood, (3) today after 1–2 hours standing still in a hot, packed, exciting parade — blurry vision and light-headedness first, 30 s LOC, went floppy (no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence), tired but oriented after, 'white as a sheet', hip bruise. Chronic headaches on Nurofen (distractor): no morning vomiting, weight loss, nocturnal/positional worsening; fundoscopy normal → refer to GP, medication-overuse flagged. No palpitations, chest pain, SOB; periods regular; no alcohol/drugs; no FHx sudden death. PEFE: BP 120/80 sitting → 94/62 standing (drop 26/18 — name it), pulse 82 reg, neuro/fundi/CVS/RS/abdo normal. Explain: nerves overactive → vessels in the legs widen → blood pools → brain short for seconds → lying flat fixes it. Three reasons: setting (hot, prolonged standing, crowd, excitement); earlier episodes fit classic triggers; clear prodrome. Postural drop = supporting evidence, not the diagnosis (postural hypotension causes dizziness/near-fainting more than true LOC; reflex syncope produces a transient drop). Differentials by system: cardiac (arrhythmia — no palpitations; HOCM — no chest pain/SOB/FHx, had a warning; valve/ischaemia), brain (seizure — friends' account; SOL, bleed, meningitis), chemistry (glucose, sodium), blood (anaemia — periods), drugs/alcohol/medications, panic. Management: lie down legs up or head between knees at the warning; counter-pressure; fluids in heat; don't skip meals; keep calves moving; FBC + pregnancy test today; caution heights/swimming alone; GP 1–2 weeks (headaches, ibuprofen frequency); driving — a triggered, prodromal, standing faint generally doesn't restrict; tell the GP if the pattern changes; return if no warning, supine, exertional, or chest pain/palpitations first. Hidden agenda: brain tumour fear from googling the headaches; the licence.
