time: 8 minutes: 0:00 vitals, WIPE, ★ confidentiality statement, open question, empathy, ★ declare neutrality on the allegation · 0:40 ★ 'complete LOC or aware?' → aware; witnessed; seizure screen → ★ jerking + awareness — RECONFIRM THE CONTRADICTION OUT LOUD · timing (20–30 s), first, context (mid-argument) — don't announce the diagnosis at two minutes · 2:30 BEFORE ×4 incl. ★ 'did you hit your head, or did anything happen physically?' · AFTER ×3 (★ confusion vs embarrassment) · 3:30 organic exclusion signposted — CNS, CVS, GI, drugs/meds/cessations, travel/jaundice/thermal — negatives are your reasoning · 4:45 hyperventilation, ★ 'did you feel frightened you were about to die?', mood/sleep/appetite/anhedonia, home and work, ★ RISK — self-harm and harm to others, PMHx/epilepsy/FHx · explanation: functional seizure named, ★ 'what happened to you was real', three reasons, honest differentials with EEG/ECG/glucose, no antiepileptics, driving, safety-net, crisis numbers.

back.dx: Psychogenic (functional) non-epileptic seizure — provisional, diagnosis of exclusion. Collapse mid-argument after being accused of shoplifting; 20–30 s; bilateral arm and leg shaking WITH retained awareness (heard people talking, the ambulance being called, remembers all of it) — incompatible with a generalised epileptic seizure; no tongue bite, no incontinence, no warning, clear-headed immediately (mortified, not confused), no injury, first episode; nobody touched her — shouting only; organic sweep entirely negative; no alcohol/drugs/meds/cessations; not breathing fast; ★ did not feel she was about to die (panic screened); mood stressed, sleep poor, appetite fine, still enjoys things, home fine with partner, work hard — manager 'on at me for months'; ★ no thoughts of self-harm or harming others (if positive — stop, explore ideation/plan/intent/means/previous/protective, same-day mental health); no PMHx/epilepsy/FHx. Explain: 'a psychogenic seizure — also called a functional seizure; looks very like an epileptic seizure and your arms and legs really were shaking, but it doesn't come from abnormal electrical activity in the brain'; ★ 'what happened to you was real — you weren't putting it on, and you couldn't have stopped it; under intense emotional stress the body can respond physically, outside your control'. 'So you think I faked it — that's what he said too' (scripted) → ★ 'No — I'm saying the opposite. I believe what happened, and I don't think you had any control over it. A recognised condition with a name and a treatment — the treatment isn't epilepsy tablets, it's working with someone on the stress.' Three reasons: aware throughout; clear-headed after; the exact moment of confrontation. Differentials, honestly: true epileptic seizure — frontal lobe type can mimic → EEG (video-EEG telemetry definitive); brain bleed/infection/growth (no headache, focal signs, fever); arrhythmia → ECG; glucose/electrolytes → bloods; alcohol/drugs/cessation (none); panic (didn't feel she was dying). Plan: ECG, finger-prick glucose, bloods; neurology + psychology (talking therapy is the most effective treatment); no antiepileptics; ★ no driving until assessed — after any blackout, whatever the cause; no heights/machinery/swimming alone; return if recurrent, injured, prolonged; crisis numbers. Words to avoid: 'not a real seizure', 'nothing wrong', 'all in your head', 'pseudoseizure', 'faking'. Medical certificate offered; nothing written about the allegation; anything written is hers to share.
plan: Vitals → normal · WIPE · ★ 'everything we talk about today stays between you and me, unless there's a risk of harm to you or someone else — is that alright?' · 'tell me more about what happened' → accused, argued, went down, 'I didn't take anything' · empathy · ★ 'my job here isn't to work out what happened at the shop — it's to work out why you collapsed'

★ 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?' → aware, heard everything · witnessed (manager + colleagues) · 'jerky movements? tongue? wet or soil?' → shaking all over; no; no · ★ 'Can I just check something, because it's important — your arms and legs were shaking, but you were aware the whole time and you remember it. Is that right?' → yes
Duration 20–30 s · ever before (never) · doing (mid-argument) · hot/stuffy, standing long, position change → no — keep excluding for another three minutes

BEFORE: warning (not really) · meals/fluids (normal) · ★ 'did you hit your head at all, or did anything happen physically during the argument?' → nobody touched me, just shouting · fever/rash · AFTER: ★ 'confused, or clear-headed straight away?' → clear-headed, just embarrassed · pale (no) · injured (no)

Signpost 'before, after, or not at all': CNS (headache, vision, speech, weakness, numbness) · CVS (chest pain, palpitations, SOB, cough, leg swelling) · GI · alcohol, drugs, ★ medications or recently stopped · travel, jaundice, thermal intolerance → all negative = organic excluded on history

'Breathing fast just before?' · ★ 'during the episode — did you feel frightened that you were about to die?' → no · mood, sleep, appetite, enjoyment · 'who do you live with, stresses at home?' · 'tell me about work generally — difficulties with anyone?' → months of it

★ 'Jane, I ask everyone this and I'd like to check with you too — with everything that's happened today, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else?' → no (positive → stop and explore) · PMHx, epilepsy/fits, FHx similar episodes or sudden death

★ Name it — psychogenic/functional seizure, looks like epilepsy, not electrical · ★ 'what happened to you was real; you weren't putting it on; you couldn't have stopped it' · scripted challenge 'so you think I faked it' → pause, ★ deny explicitly, restate belief · three reasons

Differentials honestly: epileptic seizure (a type that mimics — EEG), bleed/infection/growth, rhythm (ECG), sugar/salts (bloods), alcohol/drugs/cessation (none), panic (no fear of dying) · plan: ECG, glucose, bloods today; neurology (EEG) + psychology; no epilepsy medication · ★ 'please don't drive until you've been assessed — that applies after any blackout, whatever the cause' · no heights/machinery/swimming alone · return if recurrent, injured, prolonged · crisis numbers written down · 'is it going to happen again?' → may, especially under stress; very treatable · summary · questions ('nobody believes me' → answered)
ask: ★ 'Everything we talk about today stays between you and me, unless there's a risk of harm to you or someone else.' / ★ 'My job here isn't to work out what happened at the shop — it's to work out why you collapsed.'

★ 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?' / 'Did you have any jerky movements? Did you bite your tongue? Did you wet or soil yourself?' / ★ 'Can I just check — your arms and legs were shaking, but you were aware the whole time and you remember it?'
★ 'Did you hit your head at all, or did anything happen physically during the argument?' / 'When it stopped, were you confused, or clear-headed straight away?'
★ 'During the episode itself — did you feel frightened that you were about to die?' / 'Tell me about work — how have things been there generally?'

★ 'I ask everyone this — have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else?' → positive: 'Thank you for trusting me with that. When you say there wouldn't be much point, have you had thoughts of ending your life? How? Any plans or preparations? Ever tried before? What keeps you going? I'm not going to leave you on your own with this — I'd like our mental health team to see you today.'

★ 'I think this is a psychogenic, or functional, seizure. It looks like an epileptic seizure, but it doesn't come from abnormal electrical activity in the brain.' / ★ 'What happened to you was real. You weren't putting it on, and you couldn't have stopped it.'

'So you think I faked it. That's what he said too.' → (pause) ★ 'No — I'm saying the opposite, and I can see why it might sound that way, so let me say it plainly. I believe what happened to you, and I don't think you had any control over it at all. This is a recognised condition with a name and a treatment. The only difference is the treatment isn't epilepsy tablets — it's working with someone on the stress that set it off. Take your time.'

★ 'In an epileptic seizure that makes all your limbs shake, you'd be unconscious — and you weren't.' / 'Afterwards you were completely clear-headed; after a true seizure people are usually confused for a while.' / 'It happened at the exact moment of a very stressful confrontation.'

'A true epileptic seizure — there's a type that can look a lot like this, so I'd like a brain wave test, an EEG… a heart rhythm problem — so I'll do a heart tracing… a low blood sugar or salt imbalance — bloods… and a panic attack — but you didn't feel you were going to die.' / 'I'm not going to start you on epilepsy medication, because it wouldn't help and could cause side effects.'

★ 'Please don't drive until you've been assessed — that applies after any blackout, whatever the cause.' / 'Can you write something for my boss?' → 'A certificate covering today and the time you need, stating you were seen after a collapse and are under investigation — yes. Anything about the allegation itself — no, that isn't a medical question. And anything I write about your health is yours; you decide what to share.'
pefe: Role-player: Jane, 25, retail, lives with partner, no PMHx. Answers 'aware' and 'shaking' separately — never spells out the contradiction. Flat and defensive, close to tears; defensive if you comment on the shoplifting either way ('why does everyone keep going on about that?'). ALWAYS delivers 'so you think I faked it — that's what he said too' whatever your wording; 'it's not a real seizure'/'nothing wrong with you' → goes cold: 'right, can I go then'. If never asked about self-harm, says nothing — the omission costs. Hidden agenda: losing the job and nobody believing her — 'nobody believes me about any of it' near the end. Jargon (psychogenic, functional, conversion, dissociative) → 'what does that mean?'

Features: bilateral jerking with retained awareness (the crux) · no tongue bite/incontinence/postictal confusion · 20–30 s · emotional trigger · full memory · further PNES features: asynchronous limb movements, side-to-side head shaking, waxing and waning, eyes closed resisting opening, ictal crying · frontal lobe seizure = classic mimic (preserved awareness, brief, no postictal) · definitive test video-EEG telemetry · treatment CBT/psychological therapy; no AEDs · bedside in every collapse: glucose + 12-lead ECG with QTc; then EUC, Ca, Mg, FBC, β-hCG

Variant 1 — angry ('first I'm a thief, now I put on a fit, I'm going home'): don't defend, re-state plainly — 'I am not saying you put it on; I'm saying the opposite'; offer to write it down; 'two more minutes?' · Variant 2 — risk positive: stop everything else, explore, same-day mental health — the seizure work-up continues but is no longer the priority · Variant 3 — findings shift (side-of-tongue bite, incontinence, 20 min confused): change track and say so — glucose, EUC + Ca/Mg, FBC, drug/alcohol/withdrawal history, CT brain, urgent neurology/EEG, driving advice

Examiner 'why not conversion disorder?' → 'psychogenic/functional non-epileptic seizure sits within DSM-5 functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder, with attacks or seizures) — not competing labels; but conversion disorder requires clinical findings demonstrating incompatibility, and I have no examination here; neuro examination and ideally video-EEG before formalising; functional seizure is the term I'd use with the patient' · 'a psychiatric diagnosis on a first presentation with no examination — safe?' → provisional; strongly suggestive history; video-EEG definitive; epileptic and psychogenic seizures coexist in a meaningful minority so a functional diagnosis doesn't stop the epilepsy work-up; would not start an AED or discharge without glucose and ECG

SA: driving — not until assessed; Austroads; Registrar of Motor Vehicles; neurology (RAH/FMC) for video-EEG; psychology via MHTP; Mental Health Triage 13 14 65; Lifeline 13 11 14; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 not needed
Words to avoid: 'not a real seizure' · 'nothing wrong' · 'all in your head' · 'pseudoseizure' · 'faking'

'It's not a real seizure' / 'there's nothing wrong with you' / 'pseudoseizure' to the patient ★
Recovering badly from 'so you think I faked it' — defending instead of denying explicitly and restating belief ★
Commenting on the shoplifting allegation, sympathetically or sceptically; skipping the confidentiality statement (you need it for the risk question)
Recording 'aware' and 'shaking' as two independent answers without reconfirming the contradiction out loud
Announcing the diagnosis at two minutes — finishing the history at three; treating the all-negative organic sweep as wasted; skipping the head-injury/touched question
No glucose/ECG/EEG; starting an antiepileptic; no driving advice; no crisis numbers

must: FAIL — Not asking about self-harm — the single most commonly failed item: a distressed young woman who may lose her job over an accusation of theft; 'I ask everyone this — with everything that's happened today, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or anyone else?'; if positive, stop and explore ideation, plan, intent, means, previous attempts, protective factors, and arrange same-day mental health assessment; the confidentiality statement at the start is what earns you this question (★)

FAIL — 'It's not a real seizure' or 'there's nothing wrong with you' — she has spent the day being told she is lying; she goes cold and withdraws ('right, can I go then'); say 'not an epileptic seizure', and explicitly: 'what happened to you was real; you weren't putting it on, and you couldn't have stopped it'; when she says 'so you think I faked it — that's what he said too' (always scripted), pause, deny it plainly, restate belief; never 'pseudoseizure' in the room (★)

FAIL — Being drawn into the allegation — sympathetic or sceptical, any comment costs you; 'my job here isn't to work out what happened at the shop — it's to work out why you collapsed', said once, then move on (★)

FAIL — Recording 'aware the whole time' and 'arms and legs shaking' as two independent answers — reconfirm the contradiction out loud: 'your arms and legs were shaking, but you were aware the whole time and you remember it — is that right?'; generalised jerking with preserved consciousness is incompatible with an epileptic seizure, and reconfirming it is the strongest evidence you gather; and 'clear-headed straight away, or confused?' — embarrassment is not postictal confusion (★)

FAIL — Announcing the diagnosis at the two-minute mark because of the emotional trigger — psychogenic is a diagnosis of exclusion and the AMC gave you six minutes deliberately; the organic sweep (CNS, CVS, GI, drugs, cessations, the added three), head injury and 'did anything happen physically during the argument?', hyperventilation and 'did you feel you were about to die?', mood, sleep, appetite, anhedonia, home and work — the all-negative sweep is your reasoning, not wasted time

DO — Three reasons (aware throughout, clear-headed afterwards, at the exact moment of confrontation); differentials honestly with the frontal-lobe mimic acknowledged → EEG; glucose and ECG today, bloods; neurology and psychology ('talking therapy is the most effective treatment'), no antiepileptics; driving advice applies after any blackout whatever the cause; heights, machinery, swimming; crisis numbers written down

setting: Emergency Department. Examination findings on a card after the history (~6 minutes): BP normal, ★ pulse 42 regular, T 36.5, CVS normal, neuro normal, BSL normal. Vitals may be deferred by the examiner to the card.
stem: Gary, 52, has presented after two episodes of falls. He is concerned about the reason for these falls.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Examination findings will be provided on screen or on a card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes, ~6 history. Vitals · WIPE · ★ name and answer his concern ('what if nobody's there?') · ★ reconfirm LOC despite the stem · witnessed · ★ seizure screen ×3 · duration, not first time, ★ 'describe each episode' (episode 2: seated on the couch, a thump in the chest, then out) · environment ×4 anyway · BEFORE ×4 — ★ no warning · AFTER ×3 (pale after the first — non-specific) · signpost → CNS → CVS: ★ palpitations → ★ 'fast or irregular? tap it out?' (he can't — the mark is asking; it's why you stay at bradyarrhythmia) → RS, GI, ★ meds/cessations (rate-slowing drugs), psychogenic last, travel/jaundice/thermal, PMHx, ★ FHx sudden death · ★ card: say '42, regular — a significant bradycardia, the key finding' aloud; ask for ECG + monitoring · ★ diagnose BRADYCARDIA, don't name a rhythm; rhythms and reversible causes as 'we don't know yet' · differentials across systems · admit, monitor, ECG, bloods, echo, cardiology · close his loop · ★ driving.

back.dx: Bradyarrhythmia causing cardiac syncope — pulse 42 regular; rhythm deliberately not named (sinus bradycardia, sinus node dysfunction, second/third-degree AV block, ischaemic conduction disease all compatible; if pushed: palpitations preceding syncope + resting 42 favour sinus node dysfunction with a tachy–brady pattern — but telemetry before saying so; measure the QT — pause-dependent torsades). Two witnessed blackouts (daughter), 1–2 min each, complete LOC, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, back to normal immediately, no injuries: episode 1 getting out of bed, looked very pale (non-specific — don't build vasovagal on it); ★ episode 2 sitting on the couch — 'a thump in my chest, one big heavy beat' — then out; ★ heart racing before the second (can't say fast vs irregular, can't tap it); ★ no warning either time. No chest pain/SOB/oedema, no meds and none stopped (drugs are the commonest reversible cause — beta blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin), no PMHx/FHx. Card: BP normal, ★ pulse 42 regular, T 36.5, CVS/neuro normal, BSL normal (hypoglycaemia excluded, <4.0 the adult threshold). To Gary: 'genuine blackouts, not trips — bradycardia, the heart beating more slowly than it should; normal 60–100, yours 42; too slow to push enough blood to the brain'; two things: no warning; a thump in the chest while seated (not standing up too quickly). Cause 'we don't know yet from a pulse alone': the natural pacemaker running slow; a block in the wiring; blood supply; medication, underactive thyroid, salt imbalance (the fixable ones) → ECG + monitoring over time. Differentials: seizure (no jerking/tongue/confusion), brain (no headache/focal/fever, normal neuro), PE (no travel/leg swelling/SOB), hypoglycaemia (excluded), vasovagal/orthostatic (no warning; seated), anxiety (no fast breathing; last resort). Plan: admit on a monitor, ECG, TSH, electrolytes, troponin, echo, cardiology; pacemaker if intrinsic. ★ Close his loop: 'you asked what happens if you're alone — that's exactly why I don't want you at home tonight; on a monitor we capture it and know what to fix'. 'Can I go home?' → no; ★ driving — not until assessed; no ladders/machinery/swimming alone.
plan: Vitals (may be deferred — 'he is stable at present') · WIPE · 'tell me more about the falls' → 'what if it happens when nobody's around?' → ★ 'I completely understand how concerning that must be. I'll do my best to find the cause today so we can prevent it. Is it alright if I ask some questions?'

★ 'Can you just confirm — did you lose consciousness, or were you aware of your surroundings?' → completely out · witnessed (daughter, both) · ★ 'jerky movements? bite your tongue? wet or soil yourself?' → no ×3

Duration (1–2 min) · first time? (twice) · ★ 'can you please describe each of the previous episodes for me?' → 1: getting out of bed, went down, very pale · 2: sitting on the couch, a thump in the chest — one big heavy beat — then out · environment anyway: hot/humid, emotion, position change, prolonged standing → no (the first was getting out of bed — orthostatic still live)

★ BEFORE: 'any warning at all — dizziness, sweating, nausea, blurred vision?' → 'none, that's what bothers me' (react) · meals/fluids · head injury · fever/rash · AFTER: confused or tired? (neither — back to normal) · injuries (none) · pale (after the first — take it, move on)

Signpost · CNS: headache, vision, speech, weakness, numbness → no · CVS: chest pain (no) · ★ 'any racing of your heart?' → yes, before the second → ★ 'describe that — beating fast, or irregularly? could you tap the rhythm out on the desk?' → 'I don't know', declines → 'that's fine' · SOB, leg swelling, cough → no

GI · alcohol (couple/week), drugs · ★ 'medications regularly, or recently stopped any?' → nothing · breathing fast/stress · travel, thermal intolerance, jaundice · PMHx · ★ FHx similar episodes or sudden death, especially young

★ Card, aloud: 'BP, temperature, CVS and neurological examination normal; glucose normal — hypoglycaemia excluded, threshold <4 in an adult; ★ but the pulse is 42 and regular, a significant bradycardia — I think that's the key finding. Could I have a 12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring?'

★ To Gary: genuine blackouts; bradycardia named at the right level; 60–100 vs 42; too slow to push blood to the brain · two things: no warning; the thump while seated · 'what's making it slow?' → ★ 'I can't tell you which one it is yet from a pulse alone' — pacemaker/wiring/blood supply/medication/thyroid/salts; ECG + monitoring will tell · differentials across systems

'Can I go home and see how it goes?' → no · admit on a monitor, ECG, bloods (thyroid, salts, heart enzymes), echo, cardiology; pacemaker if the heart is running too slowly on its own — works very well · ★ 'you asked what happens if you're on your own — that's exactly why I don't want you at home tonight' · ★ driving — not until assessed, national rules, notification · no ladders/machinery/swimming alone · summary · questions
ask: ★ 'I completely understand how concerning that must be. I'll do my best to find the cause today so we can prevent this happening again.' / ★ 'Can you just confirm for me — did you lose consciousness, or were you aware of your surroundings?'
'Did you have any jerky movements of your arms or legs? Did you bite your tongue? Did you wet or soil yourself?' / ★ 'Can you describe each of the previous episodes for me?'

★ 'Did you have any warning at all — did you know you were about to go down?' / 'When you came round, were you confused, or just tired?' / 'For the next questions, tell me whether you had it before this happened, after it, or not at all.'

★ 'Can you describe that racing — was it beating fast, or beating irregularly? Could you tap the rhythm out for me?' / ★ 'Do you take any medications regularly, or have you recently stopped any?' / 'Has anyone in your family died suddenly and unexpectedly, especially at a young age?'
★ 'His pulse is 42 and regular, which is a significant bradycardia — I think that's the key finding. Could I have a 12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring?'

★ 'You have a condition called bradycardia, which means your heart is beating more slowly than it should. A normal resting rate is 60 to 100; yours is 42.' / 'When the heart beats too slowly it can't push enough blood up to the brain, and that's why you blacked out.' / 'Two things fit: no warning at all — a simple faint almost always gives a few seconds of dizziness or sweating first — and the thump in your chest while you were sitting down, so it wasn't a matter of standing up too quickly.'

★ 'I can't tell you which one it is yet from a pulse alone — that's why I want a heart tracing and monitoring.' / 'It can be the heart's own natural pacemaker running slow; a block in the electrical wiring between the top and bottom chambers; a problem with the blood supply; or a medication, an underactive thyroid, or a salt imbalance — and those we can simply fix.'

'How do you know that?' (if you name a rhythm) — don't. Examiner 'bradycardia isn't a diagnosis': 'I'd call it a bradyarrhythmia causing cardiac syncope. A regular 42 is compatible with sinus bradycardia, sinus node dysfunction, second- or third-degree AV block, or ischaemic conduction disease, and he couldn't characterise the palpitations. If pressed, palpitations preceding syncope with a resting 42 would make me favour sinus node dysfunction with a tachy–brady pattern — but I'd want the ECG and telemetry before telling a patient that. I'd also measure the QT.'

★ 'You asked what happens if you're on your own — that's exactly why I want you here on a monitor tonight. If it happens again we capture it, and then we know precisely what to fix.' / 'If your heart is running too slowly on its own, the usual treatment is a pacemaker — a small device that stops it dropping below a safe rate — and it works very well.'

★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you — and no ladders, machinery, or swimming alone.' / Refuses admission: 'It's your decision and I won't keep you against your will — but you've blacked out twice with no warning and your heart is running at 42; my worry isn't another fall, it's a pause long enough that someone needs to be there with the equipment. Whatever you decide — no driving, no heights or machinery; ambulance if it happens again, chest pain or severe breathlessness. Can I ask what's making you want to leave?'
pefe: Role-player: Gary, 52, logistics, lives with his adult daughter (witnessed both). 'What if nobody's there?' in the opening line (part of the stem) — raises it again in the last minute if never answered. FAIL — Naming a specific rhythm from a pulse rate — 'you have complete heart block' or 'this is long QT' is a guess dressed as a diagnosis, and he asks 'how do you know that?'; diagnose bradycardia, offer the rhythms as causes (sinus node, AV block, ischaemic conduction disease) plus the reversible ones (medication, thyroid, salts): 'I can't tell you which one it is yet from a pulse alone' (★)

FAIL — A generic 'so what happened?' — he answers 'I just went down, both times'; 'can you describe each of the previous episodes for me?' opens the whole case: episode 1 getting out of bed, pale; episode 2 SITTING on the couch, a thump in the chest, then out — gravity is not the explanation (★)

FAIL — Recording 'yes, my heart was racing' and moving on — the palpitations cluster: 'fast, or irregular? could you tap the rhythm out?' — he cannot help you and declines to tap; the mark is for asking, and his inability to characterise it is exactly why the final diagnosis stays at bradyarrhythmia (★)

FAIL — Sending him home ('can I go home and see how it goes?' is always asked), or finishing without driving advice — admit today on a monitor, ECG, thyroid, salts, troponin, echo, cardiology; a pacemaker if the heart is running slow on its own; 'you asked what happens if you're on your own — that's exactly why I don't want you at home tonight'; no driving pending specialist assessment, no ladders, machinery or swimming alone (★)

DO — Name his fear in the first sentence and close the loop at the end; reconfirm loss of consciousness despite the stem; seizure screen; 'any warning at all?' and react to the absence (never volunteered — 'that's what bothers me'); confusion vs tiredness; don't build a vasovagal case on the pallor; 'medications regularly, or recently stopped any?' — drugs are the commonest reversible cause and a documented negative is worth as much as a positive; family sudden death; differentials across more than one system

setting: Emergency Department. Mother on the way. An ECG has already been done — laminated tracing handed over for task 2. The examiner gives the QTc (0.54 s) ONLY if you ask for it. Vitals: BP normal, ★ pulse 50, RR and temperature normal.
stem: Lily, 15, brought in by ambulance after fainting at school. Her mother is on the way. She has had two previous similar episodes, and an ECG has already been done.
tasks: Take a history (5 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: 8 minutes: 5 history · ECG · explanation. Register 'pulse 50' at the vitals · speak to Lily, plainly, permission first · ★ confirm LOC · ★ seizure screen ×3 · duration, ★ each episode, ★ 'what were you doing?' → sitting, three times — no reflex/orthostatic explanation · context ×4 · ★ BEFORE — no warning (positive 1) · AFTER ×3 · sweep: CNS, CVS, GI, ★ all medications (acne, allergies, nausea, mood), alcohol/drugs, stress · ★ protect the last 30 s for FAMILY HISTORY — similar episodes (mum faints — positive 2), sudden death, drowning, cot death, congenital deafness · ★ ECG in seven steps aloud → step 7: 'examiner, could you tell me what the QTc is?' → 0.54 → commit · LQTS + three reasons · honest about 'could I die?' · differentials across systems · admit, monitor, K/Mg/Ca/TSH, paediatric cardiology, beta blocker, drugs to avoid · ★ ECG the mother and first-degree relatives · defer sport; no swimming alone.

back.dx: Congenital long QT syndrome: three syncopal episodes over months, each while seated doing nothing (class, home, class), ~1 min, complete LOC, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, ★ never any warning ('I'm fine, then I'm on the floor'), not confused after, not pale, no injury; everything else negative — no chest pain/palpitations/SOB, no medications (none for acne/allergies/nausea/mood), no alcohol/drugs, no stress, no PMHx; ★ mother used to faint when younger and still does sometimes; no sudden deaths, drownings, cot deaths or congenital deafness. Vitals: pulse 50 (bradycardia — note it). ECG in seven steps: rate ~50 (six large squares), regular, P before every QRS → sinus bradycardia, PR normal, QRS normal, ST no elevation/depression, T waves and QT → ★ 'examiner, could you tell me what the QTc is?' → 0.54 s = 540 ms — markedly prolonged (expect <~460 in a girl; >500 high risk) → sinus bradycardia with a significantly prolonged QTc — long QT syndrome. Never try to measure it silently on a laminated tracing (paper-folding unavailable, Bazett under time pressure unrealistic — candidates default to sinus bradycardia/sick sinus and fail; a correct differential does not rescue a wrong primary diagnosis). To Lily: 'after each beat the electrical system takes longer than it should to reset; sometimes it tips the heart into a fast, disorganised rhythm — the heart can't pump, blood doesn't reach the brain, you black out, then it settles, which is why you wake up fine'. Three reasons: the QT on the tracing; mum's fainting (a version runs in families); no warning (cause in the heart, not a simple faint). 'Could I die?' → honest: taken seriously, occasionally dangerous — hence not home; very treatable; finding it today is good news; a tablet (beta blocker) greatly reduces the chance; a list of medicines to avoid. Differentials across systems: other rhythms (too slow, block), muscle/valve, seizure, brain, glucose/salts, PE, reflex/orthostatic (seated, no warning), panic last. Plan: admit on a monitor, K/Mg/Ca/TSH/glucose, paediatric cardiology today, beta blocker likely, QT-prolonging drug list (antibiotics, antiemetics); ★ when mum arrives — with Lily's permission — mum needs an ECG today; screen parents and siblings; sport — defer to the specialists (type-dependent), hold competitive sport, no swimming (some forms triggered by exercise and swimming).
plan: 'Vital signs?' → BP normal, pulse 50, RR/temp normal → 'I'll note the bradycardia' · 'Hi Lily, I'm Dr —; I hear your mum's on her way. How can I help?' → third faint, everyone staring, scared · 'I'm so sorry that happened again — that must have been frightening, especially in front of everyone. Is it okay if I ask a few questions so we can find the reason?'
★ 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware?' → completely · witnessed (whole class, teacher) · ★ 'jerky movements? bite your tongue? wet or soil yourself?' → no ×3

Duration (~1 min) · first time? (third) · ★ 'describe each episode' → class / home / class · ★ 'what were you actually doing?' → just sitting, listening → register it · hot? stressed? standing long? just stood up? → no ×4

★ BEFORE: 'any warning at all — dizzy, sick, sweating, vision going?' → 'never any warning — I'm fine, then I'm on the floor' (positive 1, make a clear note) · meals/fluids (had lunch) · head knock · fever/rash · AFTER: confused or tired (neither) · pale (no) · injured (no — sitting down)

Signpost · CNS: headache, vision, speech, weakness, numbness · CVS: chest pain, ★ racing/fluttering, SOB · GI · alcohol/drugs · ★ 'any medications at all — including anything for acne, allergies, nausea or your mood?' → none · breathing fast/stress → no

★ Protected family history: 'has anyone else in your family had episodes like this?' → mum used to faint, still does (positive 2 — pause on it) · 'anyone died suddenly and unexpectedly, or drowned, or an unexplained accident? cot deaths?' · 'is anyone deaf from birth?' → no · PMHx none

★ ECG, seven steps aloud: rate ~50 (six large squares) · regular · P before every QRS → sinus bradycardia · PR normal (<5 small squares) · QRS normal (<3) · ST — no elevation/depression · ★ 'T waves and QT interval — examiner, I'd like to check the T waves and calculate the corrected QT. Could you tell me what the QTc is?' → 0.54 → '540 ms — markedly prolonged; expect under ~460 in a girl her age; above 500 is high risk — sinus bradycardia with a significantly prolonged QTc: long QT syndrome'
To Lily: LQTS named; mechanism in her words · ★ three reasons · 'is it serious? could I die?' → honest, then the good news · differentials across systems

Plan: monitor, bloods (salts, thyroid), children's heart specialists today, beta blocker likely, medicines to avoid (some antibiotics, anti-sickness) · ★ 'when your mum gets here I'd like to talk to you both — if she's been fainting too she needs a heart tracing herself today; this runs in families, so we'd check parents, brothers and sisters — is that alright with you?' · netball/swimming → defer to the specialists; hold competitive sport, no swimming, especially alone · summary · questions
ask: 'I'm so sorry that happened again today — that must have been really frightening. Is it okay if I ask you a few questions so we can find the reason for these faints?' / 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of what was going on around you?'
'Can you describe each of the episodes for me?' / ★ 'What were you actually doing when it happened?' / ★ 'Did you get any warning at all — did you know it was about to happen?'
'Do you take any medications at all — including anything for acne, allergies, nausea or your mood?'
★ 'Has anyone else in your family had episodes like this? Has anyone died suddenly and unexpectedly, or drowned? Is anyone deaf from birth?'

'Counting large squares between R waves — about six, so a rate of roughly 50.' / 'P waves present and normal before every QRS, so this is sinus bradycardia.' / ★ 'Examiner, I'd like to check the T waves and calculate the corrected QT interval. Could you tell me what the QTc is?' / ★ '0.54 seconds is 540 milliseconds, which is markedly prolonged.'

Examiner won't give it: 'The QT runs from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave, measured in lead II. At normal rates the QT should be less than half the RR — here the T wave extends beyond the halfway point, so it's prolonged. At a rate of 50 the raw QT overstates it, so it must be rate-corrected with Bazett — QT ÷ √RR. My assessment: the corrected QT is prolonged; with recurrent syncope without prodrome and a family history, long QT syndrome.'

★ 'After each beat, the electrical system takes longer than it should to reset — and that can tip the heart into a fast, disorganised rhythm, so blood doesn't reach the brain and you black out.' / ★ 'Three reasons: the QT measurement on your tracing, your mum's history of fainting, and the fact you faint with no warning.'

'Is it serious? Could I die from it?' → 'You asked me straight, so I'll answer you straight. It is something we take seriously — occasionally that rhythm can be dangerous, and that's why I don't want you going home while we sort it out. But it's very treatable once we know about it, and finding it today is genuinely good news, because now we can protect you.' (never 'don't worry, it's nothing' → 'then why am I here for the third time?')

★ 'If your mum's been fainting too, she needs a heart tracing herself today. This runs in families, so we'd usually check parents and any brothers or sisters.' / Mother arrives: 'Lily, is it alright with you if I go through what I've found with your mum here?' — first

'Netball trials, swimming?' → 'A fair question and I don't want to guess. It depends on which type you have, and the specialists will work that out. Until they've seen you, hold off competitive sport and please don't swim — especially not alone; some forms are triggered by exercise and by swimming in particular. Not a permanent ban — until we know what we're dealing with.'
pefe: Role-player: Lily, 15, Year 10, mum and younger brother, netball, healthy; never volunteers the absent warning or the family history — the only two positives. Articulate, deadpan, teenage-blunt; engages with a doctor who talks TO her. Always asks 'is it serious? could I die?'; 'don't worry, it's nothing' → 'then why am I here for the third time?'. Jargon (syncope, prodrome, repolarisation, QT interval) → 'what does that mean?'. If mum's screening never mentioned: 'Mum faints too — does that mean she's got it?'. Asks about netball

Findings: BP normal · pulse 50 · RR/temp normal · ECG sinus bradycardia; normal P, PR, QRS, ST · QTc 0.54 s — only if you ask · bloods to request: K, Mg, Ca, TSH, glucose · ECG all first-degree relatives

Variant 2 — acquired: erythromycin for a chest infection + days of vomiting: macrolide + hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia prolong the QT → check and replace K/Mg/Ca urgently, cease the macrolide, repeat ECG; may be fully reversible — still monitor; still take the family history (drugs unmask predisposition) · Variant 5 — you said 'sinus bradycardia' and the examiner offers 'anything else?': take the lifeline — go back to the T waves and QT, ask for the QTc, revise; a correct differential does not rescue a wrong primary diagnosis

Measuring it yourself (if asked): QRS onset to T-wave end, lead II or V5; Bazett QTc = QT ÷ √RR (seconds); eyeball QT < half the RR at normal rates — unreliable at 50, which is why you ask for the corrected value · Horner-free ECG checklist: rate = 300 ÷ large squares; PR 3–5 small squares (120–200 ms); QRS <3 small squares

Treatment: beta blocker (propranolol/nadolol) first line; ICD after arrest or breakthrough syncope on treatment · torsades with a pulse: IV magnesium sulfate, correct K, overdrive pacing or isoprenaline VERIFY · QT-prolonging drugs to avoid: macrolides, some antiemetics (ondansetron, domperidone), antipsychotics, some antihistamines, etc. — give the list · LQT1 exercise/swimming trigger; LQT2 auditory/emotional; LQT3 sleep/rest ADDED VERIFY

SA: admit paediatric ward on telemetry → WCH paediatric cardiology; ECG the mother in ED today; family screening/genetics via WCH; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval from a regional site; mature-minor consent — check with Lily before talking to mum

SINUS BRADYCARDIA; normal P wave, PR interval, QRS and ST segments
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Trying to measure the QTc yourself on a laminated tracing — candidates lose ninety seconds, panic, and default to 'sinus bradycardia' or 'sick sinus syndrome': plausible and wrong; 'examiner, I'd like to check the T waves and calculate the corrected QT — could you tell me what the QTc is?' — the single decisive act of the station; 0.54 s = 540 ms, markedly prolonged, above 500 is high risk (★)

FAIL — Blurting 'this is long QT' the moment you see the tracing, or stopping at sinus bradycardia — the seven-step interpretation is scored separately from the diagnosis: rate (six large squares, ~50), rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS, ST, then T waves and QT; and a correct differential does not rescue a wrong primary diagnosis — if the examiner offers a second look, take the lifeline and ask for the QTc (★)

FAIL — Dropping the family history because you ran out of time — it is half the diagnostic evidence and the reason her mother needs an ECG today: 'has anyone else in your family had episodes like this?' (mum used to faint — never volunteered) → sudden death, drowning, unexplained accident, cot death, congenital deafness; protect the last thirty seconds of the history for it (★)

FAIL — Not asking about warning, or not registering 'just sitting in class' — an almost entirely negative history has two positives, and the absence of a prodrome is one of them; syncope while seated, three times, with no trigger excludes reflex and orthostatic causes before you have seen a tracing; note the pulse of 50 in the vitals as a finding (★)

FAIL — 'Don't worry, it's nothing serious' when she asks 'could I die?' — she replies 'then why am I here for the third time?'; honest then framed: 'it is something we take seriously — that rhythm can occasionally be dangerous, which is why you're not going home — but it's very treatable, and finding it today is genuinely good news' (★)

DO — Speak to the 15-year-old directly with permission, not over her; seizure screen despite 'obviously a faint'; diagnosis with three reasons (the QT on the tracing, mum's fainting, no warning); mechanism in her language ('the electrical system takes longer to reset and can tip into a fast disorganised rhythm'); admit on a monitor, K/Mg/Ca/TSH, paediatric cardiology, beta blocker, QT-prolonging drugs to avoid; ECG the mother and siblings today — check with Lily first before talking to her mother; defer the sport question but no swimming alone meanwhile (★)

setting: Regional South Australian ED; you are the resident. Vitals on arrival in the stem. Findings given only if requested specifically — the examiner answers only the question asked ('any added sounds?' → 'no'). Five variants share this stem and differ only in the findings.
stem: Gary, 40, brought in by his tennis partners after he collapsed on court this morning. BP 110/70, PR 84 regular, RR 12, T 36.5, SpO2 98% RA, GCS 15.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you want — given only if requested specifically
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: 4 history · 2 examination · 15 s diagnosis · 15 s reasons · 35 s differentials · 25 s plan. Vitals/stability · WIPE, acknowledge · ★ complete LOC, duration, first time · ★ seizure screen ×3 · ★ 'any warning at all?' → none — say the deduction aloud · ★ 'mid-point, or had you just stopped?' → mid-rally · heat/meals/fluids (the decoy) · emotion, head injury, fever/rash · after ×3 incl. injuries · signposted CNS · ★ 'any chest pain?' → yes — site, radiation, quality one at a time · ★ SOB · palpitations, oedema, cough/haemoptysis/pleuritic/calf/travel · GI · hyperventilation/stress · SADMA · BP/sugar/lipids in one sentence · murmur/rheumatic fever · ★ FHx sudden death · examination: general, postural BP, pulse character (slow-rising, low volume, narrow PP), neuro; CVS inspection/palpation (JVP, apex displaced/heaving, thrill, heave); ★ 'are there any MURMURS or added sounds?' → site · timing · radiation · A2 · ★ carotid bruits; RS, abdo, limbs; ECG, BSL, dipstick · aortic stenosis in 15 s · trio + murmur · differentials across ≥4 systems · admit, monitor, troponin/serial ECG, echo, cardiology · no tennis, ★ no driving + SA notification · return if recurrent, chest pain, SOB at rest.

back.dx: Aortic stenosis (commonest cause at 40: bicuspid valve) — exertional syncope with the triad: collapsed mid-rally chasing a ball, complete LOC 2–3 min, first ever, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, ★ no warning at all, warm day but drinking between games and had breakfast (the decoy), clear-headed on waking, looked washed out, grazed elbow; ★ chest pain while playing — left/central, radiating down the left arm and up the neck, heavy 'like a weight' (exertional angina — hold both ACS and AS; you haven't listened yet); ★ more puffed on court this season; no palpitations/oedema/PE features; non-smoker, 6–8 SD/week, no meds; cholesterol high-normal 3–4 years ago, BP normal, no diabetes, no known murmur/rheumatic fever, no FHx sudden death. Examination: no postural drop; pulse 84 regular (ask character — slow-rising/low volume/narrow pulse pressure); neuro normal; JVP not raised; ★ prominent but undisplaced LV impulse (pressure overload, concentric hypertrophy — say so), no thrill; S1 S2 normal; ★ murmur — aortic area (R 2nd ICS), systolic, radiating to the carotids, no separate carotid bruit; chest clear; abdomen normal; no oedema/calf tenderness; ECG, BSL normal (a normal ECG doesn't exclude structural disease → echo). 15-second diagnosis: 'the aortic valve is the gateway between your heart and the main blood tube carrying blood to your body — in your case that gateway has become narrowed'; two reasons: the trio with exercise, the murmur. Differentials by system: heart — MI/blocked artery (ECG normal, troponin), arrhythmia (no palpitations), HOCM, pericarditis, PE; brain — seizure, stroke, bleed, meningitis, SOL; chemistry — glucose, salts; simple — dehydration, heat, standing faint; drugs/alcohol/panic. Plan: admit on a monitor, bloods + serial ECGs (exclude MI), echo, cardiology today; valve replacement if tight — results very good; no tennis or heavy exertion; ★ no driving until cleared — SA notification, done together; return if recurrent, chest pain, SOB at rest; letter for the employer, social work. Hidden agenda: 'am I going to drop dead?' (a colleague's brother); 'will I lose my licence — I drive for work?'.
plan: 'Vital signs — BP, pulse, RR, sats, temperature; is he haemodynamically stable?' → stable · WIPE, 'is it alright if I call you Gary?' · 'I know how stressful and concerning this must be — let's go through it together'

★ 'Complete LOC, or aware?' → completely · duration (a few minutes) · ever before (never) · ★ 'your friends were with you — jerky movements? tongue? wet or soil?' → no ×3 → 'that makes a fit much less likely'

★ 'Did you get any warning at all — dizziness, light-headedness, sweating, nausea, ringing, vision going dark?' → none → 'that's important' (deduction aloud) · ★ 'mid-point, or had you just stopped?' → mid-rally · hot/humid (warm, usual) · standing long · meals (breakfast) · fluids (water between games) · emotion · head injury, fever, rash → no
After: confused/drowsy or normal straight away (normal) · pale (washed out) · ★ injuries (elbow graze)

Signpost 'before or after the collapse' · CNS → no · ★ 'any chest pain?' → yes → 'where exactly? does it travel? what does it feel like?' one at a time → left/central, arm and neck, heavy · ★ SOB — exercise, flat, night? → more puffed this season · palpitations, ankle swelling, cough/haemoptysis/pleuritic/calf/flights/surgery, GI incl. melaena, fast breathing/tingling/stress → no

SADMA: smoke (no), alcohol (6–8/week), drugs (no), meds started/stopped (none), allergies · 'ever been told high BP, high sugar, or high fats?' (one sentence) → cholesterol high-normal · 'a murmur, or rheumatic fever as a child?' · ★ 'family history of heart attacks or strokes — anyone died suddenly at a young age?'

Examination: general — alert, pallor, dehydration, rash, injuries · postural drop · pulse rate, rhythm, ★ character — slow-rising? low volume? narrow pulse pressure? · neuro — cranial nerves, fundoscopy, limbs → all normal, no drop

CVS: inspection — JVP raised? visible apex? scars/stigmata? · palpation — apex displaced? heaving? thrill in the aortic area? parasternal heave? → prominent LV impulse, undisplaced, no thrill → 'pressure overload with concentric hypertrophy' · ★ auscultation: 'S1 and S2 normal? are there any MURMURS or added sounds?' → murmur → ★ 'where best heard? timing — systolic or diastolic? radiate? is A2 soft or absent? ★ any carotid bruits?' → aortic area, systolic, to the carotids → 'an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids' · RS, abdomen, limbs (oedema, calves) · ECG, BSL, dipstick

★ 15 s: 'most likely aortic stenosis — the aortic valve is the gateway… narrowed' · 15 s reasons: the trio with exercise; the murmur · 'serious?' → 'we take it seriously, but it's very treatable, and you've come to the right place' · 35 s differentials across heart, brain, chemistry, simple, drugs/psych

Plan: admit on a monitor, bloods and repeat tracings (not a heart attack), echo, cardiologist today; valve replacement if tight, results very good · no tennis/heavy exertion · ★ 'please don't drive until the specialist has cleared you — in SA I'm also required to notify the licensing authority, and I'd rather we do that together' · return if blackout, chest pain, SOB at rest · 'will I play again?' → very often, after treatment; the cardiologist's call · summary · questions
ask: 'Examiner, before I start, may I have the vital signs?' / 'I know how stressful and concerning this must be, Gary. Let's go through it together.' / 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?'
'Did your friends mention any jerky movements, tongue biting, or wetting yourself?' / ★ 'Did you get any warning at all before you fell?' / ★ 'Were you mid-point, or had you just stopped playing?'

'For each symptom, tell me whether it was before or after the collapse.' / ★ 'Any chest pain?' → 'Where exactly? Does it travel anywhere? What does it feel like?' / ★ 'Have you been short of breath — with exercise, lying flat, or at night?'

'Have you ever been told you have high blood pressure, high blood sugar, or high fats in your blood?' / 'Ever a heart murmur, or rheumatic fever as a child?' / 'Has anyone in your family died suddenly at a young age?'

'Pulse — rate, rhythm, and its character: is it slow-rising or low volume, and is the pulse pressure narrow?' / 'On palpation — is the apex beat displaced? Is it heaving? Is there a thrill in the aortic area?' → 'prominent but undisplaced — pressure overload with concentric hypertrophy'

★ 'On auscultation — are S1 and S2 normal? Are there any murmurs or added sounds?' → ★ 'Where is it best heard? What is its timing? Does it radiate anywhere? Is A2 soft or absent? And are there any carotid bruits?' (the published critical error is failing to ask for both carotid and cardiac bruits)

★ 'Most likely you have a condition called aortic stenosis. The aortic valve is the gateway between your heart and the main blood tube that carries blood and oxygen to your body — and in your case that gateway has become narrowed.' (15 seconds — no chambers, no great vessels)

★ 'Two reasons: you have the well-known trio — chest pain, breathlessness and blacking out, all with exercise — and when I listened to your heart I heard an abnormal sound that fits with that narrowing.' / 'It's serious, but it's very treatable, and you've come to the right place.'

★ 'No tennis, no heavy exertion, and please don't drive until the specialist has cleared you — here in South Australia I'm also required to notify the licensing authority, and I'd rather we do that together.'

'Am I going to drop dead?' → 'A fair worry. This condition can be dangerous if left alone — exactly why we're admitting you today. But it's one of the most fixable heart problems there is: once the valve is replaced, most people go back to a normal life and life expectancy. The risky thing would be carrying on playing without knowing.' / 'My licence — I drive for work' → 'You can't drive for now — not until the cause is treated and a specialist clears you. Once the valve is fixed, driving is usually restored. A letter for your employer, and our social worker if the time off is a problem.'
pefe: Role-player: Gary Whitfield, 40, building project manager, Port Pirie; wife, children 9 and 12; social tennis twice a week; non-smoker; 6–7 beers/week; no meds/allergies; cholesterol 'high normal' 3–4 y ago, BP normal, no diabetes/murmur/rheumatic fever; no FHx. Does NOT volunteer chest pain or breathlessness — 'any other symptoms?' → 'not really'; gives one element per question for site/radiation/quality. Over-explained anatomy >20 s → 'sorry doctor, what does that actually mean for me?'; 'nothing to worry about' → 'oh good, so I can play on Thursday?'; no plan → 'so what happens now?'. Examiner: alert, no pallor/dehydration/rash/injuries · no postural drop · pulse 84 regular (character often 'normal/not assessed' — ask anyway; severe variant → slow-rising) · neuro normal · JVP not raised · prominent LV impulse, apex not displaced, no thrill · S1 S2 normal · murmur: aortic area R 2nd ICS, systolic, radiates to the carotids, no separate carotid bruit · chest clear · abdomen normal · no oedema/calf tenderness · ECG normal · BSL normal · dipstick not available

Variant B — BP 158/94 + six months exertional dyspnoea: one sentence — 'your blood pressure is also up, adding strain on a heart already working against the valve; we'll treat it — but the valve is the priority' (don't run a hypertension counselling station) · Variant C — 28-year-old, brother died suddenly at 32: HOCM — ★ ask if the murmur changes with manoeuvres (louder on standing/Valsalva, softer on squatting/handgrip — the OPPOSITE of AS, which softens with Valsalva); jerky/bisferiens carotid upstroke; family screening (children, brother); same echo + ECG

ask: 'Before I begin, may I have the vital signs, including lying and standing blood pressure?' / 'I'm so sorry to hear that — let's find out what's happening together.' / ★ 'Did you black out completely, or did you go down but stay aware?'
'Did it happen while you were passing urine or opening your bowels, or straining? Was the bathroom hot?' / ★ 'Did you get any warning?' / ★ 'Did you hit your head?'

★ 'Have you had a blood-thinning injection since the operation — do you know which one, and have any doses been missed?' / 'What have they been giving you for pain — anything strong like morphine or oxycodone, or a nerve tablet such as pregabalin? Were your usual blood-pressure tablets restarted this morning?'

'Have you ever had a clot in the leg or the lung? Any cancer? Long flights or drives? Anyone in the family with clotting problems, or died suddenly and young?' / ★ 'Is there anything you have been particularly worried about?'

★ 'Everything you've told me is reassuring, and I want to be honest about where that leaves us. The thing I am most concerned about is a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood tubes of your lungs. The reason I am concerned is not your symptoms — it is your situation. You had major knee surgery yesterday and you have hardly been able to move that leg; when the legs stay still, blood can clot in the deep veins, and a piece can travel to the lungs. That can cause exactly this sort of blackout, sometimes with no chest symptoms at all. So even though your breathing is fine, I am not prepared to leave that untested.'

'But I feel fine — how can it be a clot?' → 'I know, and that's a good sign. But a clot in the lung doesn't always announce itself — sometimes a blackout is the only thing it does. It is treatable, and very treatable when we find it early, which is exactly what I'm trying to do. The scan takes about twenty minutes and we'll know today.'

'A simple faint — a vasovagal faint — is common when people are in pain, or straining on the toilet, or standing up for the first time after an operation, and that may well be what happened. Heart attacks are more common in the first few days after a big operation and can be surprisingly quiet, so I want to check that. Low blood pressure from blood loss during surgery, together with the strong painkillers, can also drop you when you stand.' / 'A simple faint is a diagnosis I can only make after ruling out the dangerous ones.'

★ 'For pulmonary embolism, which is my leading diagnosis: an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram, after checking renal function and contrast allergy — a V/Q scan if contrast is contraindicated.' / ★ 'I would not order a D-dimer, because it is elevated in virtually every patient a day after major surgery and would not change my management either way.'

'For myocardial infarction: the ECG plus serial troponin. For bleeding and anaemia: full blood examination, coagulation profile, group and hold, and inspection of the wound and drains. For metabolic causes: urea, electrolytes and creatinine — which I also need before contrast — plus calcium and magnesium. A chest X-ray; a CT head if he struck his head or remains confused; a bedside echo looking for right ventricular strain if he becomes hypotensive.' / 'I'd discuss empirical anticoagulation with the orthopaedic team while awaiting the scan, escalate to my registrar now, and call a MET if he deteriorates.'

'Am I still getting home Friday? My wife's not well' → 'Thank you for telling me — I can hear how much it matters. I can't promise, but I'll make sure the team knows about your wife and that social work is involved either way.' / ★ 'Please press the buzzer before you get up — do not walk to the toilet on your own.'

back.dx: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (posterior canal) — Version A. True spinning ('like six beers'), bursts of 20–30 s, completely normal between, ★ set off by rolling over in bed, getting up, looking up to the top shelf; settles lying still; no LOC, no falls (grabbed the bedpost); all five ear questions negative; all nine brain questions negative; no CVS symptoms; perindopril 5 mg × 6 y unchanged, 2–3 beers Friday, ex-smoker at 40; widowed, lives alone, drives grandson to school Thursdays. ask: 'Before I begin, may I confirm the patient is haemodynamically stable?' / 'Was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'

★ 'Dizziness means different things to different people. Do you mean a spinning sensation — the room going round, or you going round? Or light-headed as if you're about to faint? Or off-balance and unsteady on your feet?' / 'Any fainting or blacking out, even for a second? … And any falls?'
'When you get an episode, how long does it last? Is it there all the time or does it come and go?' / ★ 'Does a change of position — for instance rolling over in bed — set it off?'

★ 'A few questions about your ears: any change in your hearing on either side? Any nausea or vomiting with the spells? Any ringing, buzzing or roaring? Any pain or discharge? A cold or flu-like illness in the last few weeks?'

'Any slurred speech? Double or blurred vision? Weakness in the arms or legs? Numbness or pins and needles? Trouble with balance or walking between the spells? Any recent knocks to the head or falls? Any headache — particularly vomiting first thing in the morning — or weight loss? Flashing lights or sensitivity to light? Any fever?'
★ To examiner: 'specifically, is there any nystagmus — present or absent, in which direction, and does it fatigue?' / 'As a special test I'd like to perform the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre.'

★ 'You have a condition called benign positional vertigo. It happens because of a disruption of the normal fluid circulation in the balance organ of your inner ear, so when you move your head your brain briefly gets a false signal that you're spinning.' / ★ 'There are two reasons I'm saying that. First, true spinning brought on by changing position and lasting under a minute is very characteristic. Second — and just as important — I've looked specifically for the serious causes and they aren't there.'

'A stroke affecting the balance centres almost always causes constant dizziness rather than short bursts, and nearly always brings something else with it — slurred speech, double vision, weakness, or being unable to walk. You have none of those.' / scan: 'this is diagnosed by the story and the positional test, not by a scan — where I would arrange one is if you developed hearing loss on one side, any of the warning signs, or didn't improve as expected.'

★ 'The main treatment isn't a tablet — it's a manoeuvre I can do right now. I need to warn you it will make you feel very dizzy for a few seconds and possibly a bit sick — that's expected and it passes. It fixes it in about eight out of ten people. Are you happy for me to go ahead?' / 'Only a couple of days of the anti-sickness tablet — taking it longer actually slows your recovery.'

★ 'While you're still having attacks you shouldn't drive — including the school run. Don't drive straight home after the manoeuvre today. Here in South Australia doctors have a legal duty to notify the licensing authority about anyone who isn't safe to drive, so I'd much rather we sort this out together and get you back behind the wheel quickly.' / ★ 'Come back straight away, or call an ambulance, if you get slurred speech, weakness or numbness down one side, double vision, trouble swallowing, a severe headache or new neck pain, hearing loss or ringing in one ear, if the dizziness becomes constant instead of coming in bursts, or you can't walk without help.' / 'What will you do if you get any of those warning signs?'

back.dx: Multifactorial acute falls — FOUR causes, numbered: (1) symptomatic UTI (48 h frequency, urgency, nocturia, dysuria; suprapubic tenderness; nitrites + leucocytes) — the reason he is rushing at night; (2) postural hypotension 120/80 → 94/60 (26 systolic), likely from reduced intake + infection, no meds; (3) hypoglycaemia border — capillary glucose exactly 4.0 after skipping dinner ('cooking for one's a nuisance, I go to bed early'); (4) the situation — woken from sleep, drowsy, dark hallway, toilet at the far end, hurrying because he can't hold on. Nothing points to stroke: never blacked out, awake the whole way down, speech/vision/strength/sensation normal. Hidden agenda: brother's stroke at 68 — if never asked he interrupts the explanation with 'is this a stroke?'. Naming only the UTI is the single commonest fail.

Diagnosis is clinical: endemic exposure + characteristic rash; serology often negative in the first weeks (two-tier ELISA → Western blot) — do not withhold treatment for it. Doxycycline 100 mg bd for 10–21 days VERIFY; treat now to prevent disseminated disease (arthritis, carditis/heart block, facial palsy/meningitis).

back.dx: Discharge planning after NOF fracture — a negotiation, not a report. Ross's mental model is 'the hip is fixed, so she can go home'; correct it (repaired, not recovered) before the OT findings so the conclusion lands as a consequence. In technical terms: independent in personal ADLs, dependent in instrumental ADLs (cooking, shopping, cleaning, getting about) — say it once, translate, never again. Third path offered unprompted: rehabilitation → transition care → home with services; respite is short-term and she comes home. Two medical items the cohort drops: osteoporosis (minimal-trauma hip fracture → treat regardless of DEXA) and VTE prophylaxis continuing after discharge (enoxaparin up to ~35 days). Mrs Hartnett is alert and competent — she decides; nothing is decided in this room.

★ 'That's the practical side. There are two medical things I don't want to miss. The first is her bones: she broke her hip falling at standing height — that tells us the bone is more fragile than it should be. That's osteoporosis. We'll do a bone density scan, but because it was a hip fracture we start treatment regardless of what the scan shows. The second is clots — after a hip operation, and moving less than usual, there's a real risk of a clot in the leg travelling to the lungs. So she goes home on a blood-thinning injection for up to about five weeks.'

★ 'Can I just take her home today and sort the rest out later?' → 'I understand why you'd want that, and I won't pretend it's easy. But I can't recommend a discharge today, and I have to be honest with you about that. Can I put it another way? If she went home this afternoon, who would cook her dinner tonight?' [wait] 'That's the gap I'm trying to close, and it's fixable. Give me two weeks and I can close it properly.'

'I feel terrible about this' → ★ 'You've driven an hour to be here on a work day. That is not what a bad son looks like. There's support for you too — Carer Gateway, 1800 422 737.' / 'Rehabilitation for a couple of weeks, then transition care — short-term intensive support that can run up to about twelve weeks — then home with services. Every stage aims at home. Would you be able to live with that?'

★ 'Nothing gets decided in this room. I'd like to bring the three of us together with the therapist so your mum can tell us what she wants. I'll start the referrals this afternoon — I can't promise a date, but I can promise the referral goes in. She'll be seen in fracture clinic at six weeks and by her GP within a week of getting home. If she becomes more confused, or gets a fever, calf pain or breathlessness, tell the nurses straight away. What have I missed that you wanted to cover?'

We don't judge someone's ability to make decisions while they're delirious. If she does end up unable to decide and there's no advance care directive or enduring power of attorney, that goes to SACAT, not to next of kin automatically.'
