time: 8 minutes. Introduce, sit, ★ 'how's the pain out of ten?' · ★ 'anything worrying you about going home with this?' (first ask — she deflects; note the pause, re-ask before closing) · ★ signpost FIVE headings at 0:45: (1) what you've broken and what the plaster does (2) looking after it — swelling, dry, clean, moving (3) what brings you straight back (4) the plan — clinic 7 d with X-ray, cast off ~6 wk at clinic, then physio (5) why the bone broke and the scan · fracture explained on your own arm, thumb free (scaphoid = spica) · cast care by 4:45 · ★ two red-flag families with DESTINATIONS: tight cast → Emergency now; skin/infection → same day us or GP · plan with intervals, places, events; PATS if distance · ★ 'minimal-trauma fracture' → DEXA + bloods + GP letter, ask permission · mechanism check ('trip, or dizzy/faint first?') · no driving in plaster or on sedating analgesia · rings off · written sheet · ★ re-ask concerns → husband → social work · ★ teach-back: 'what are the two things that would bring you straight back?'

back.dx: Counselling: minimally displaced extra-articular Colles' fracture in POP — cast care, follow-up plan, and the minimal-trauma fracture conversation. Version A: straightforward trip on a hose, no presyncope; hidden agenda — husband Ray has Parkinson's, she does everything for him and is frightened she can't with one hand; deflects the first concern question ('not really, I just want to get home'), tells you on the second ask or a home-specific question, otherwise blurts it at 7:40. Her mother broke a hip in her eighties. 'Will it go back to normal?' → honest: most return to usual activities; some stiffness/cold-weather ache can persist and the physio is what changes that.
plan: 'I'm Dr —, one of the doctors here in Emergency. Are you Mrs Harper — Denise? Do you mind if I pull up a chair?' · ★ 'before we start on the plaster — how's the pain right now, out of ten?' (3/10) · ★ 'is there anything in particular worrying you about going home with this on?' → pause, 'not really' → note it

★ 'I'd like to cover five things: what you've actually broken, how to look after the plaster, the warning signs that would bring you straight back, the plan over the next six weeks, and one important thing about your bones. I'll stop at each so you can ask.'

(1) 'You've broken the end of the radius just above the wrist; the broken end has tipped slightly backwards — a Colles' fracture. The pieces are lined up well, so plaster rather than an operation. The plaster holds the ends still so the bone can knit, about six weeks. Thumb left out deliberately — a scaphoid would have the thumb wrapped in.'

(2) SWELLING: 'the plaster can't stretch, so we keep the swelling down three ways — arm up (sling by day; at night forearm on pillows, ★ hand above the heart), ice on top of the plaster in a bag/thin towel 15–20 min every 2–3 h for the first days, and ★ keep the fingers moving — full fist, straighten, every hour awake; moving them pumps the swelling out' · DRY: 'plaster of Paris goes soft if wet — two plastic bags taped to skin for showers, no baths/swimming for six weeks; if damp, hairdryer on ★ COOL only — never warm; you can burn skin you can't see' (sister's wet cast → 'hers may have been fibreglass; yours is plaster') · CLEAN: 'nothing down inside — no needles, pens, coat hangers; cool air for the itch; no powder/lotion/oil; don't trim the edges — ring us; rest it on something soft for a day or two while it hardens' · itch is normal — a fixed burning pain in one spot is a pressure sore · MOVING: 'fingers, elbow, shoulder all free and I want them used — the wrist is the only thing that stays still' · ★ 'let's get the rings off — if the fingers swell overnight a ring turns into a tourniquet'

(3) ★ 'Two things would make me want to see you straight away. First, if the plaster becomes too tight: pain getting worse rather than better, painkillers stop touching it, fingers numb or tingly, pale, blue or cold, can't move them or it hurts to straighten them — ★ come straight back here to Emergency, don't wait for the clinic; we can split the plaster in two minutes and that fixes it. Second, the skin underneath: fever, a bad smell, ooze or staining through the plaster, or a burning rubbing pain in one fixed spot — ★ same day, us or your GP. I'll write both lists down.' ('would I need a new one?' → 're-do once the swelling settles; splitting costs nothing, a tight plaster can cost you the use of your hand')

(4) Plan: ★ 'fracture clinic in one week with another X-ray — these occasionally slip in the first week or two and it's far easier to fix early; if it's holding, plaster stays until about six weeks and comes off at the clinic, not at home' · distance → PATS, coordinate the film locally VERIFY · ★ 'expect a stiff wrist and weaker arm when it comes off — normal, not a complication — I'll arrange physiotherapy / hand therapy; a couple of months of exercises to get movement and grip back' · 'will it go back to normal?' → honest

(5) ★ 'The most important part: you broke this bone falling from standing height, on the flat. A healthy bone at your age shouldn't break from a fall like that. We call that a minimal-trauma fracture — a signal the bone may be thinner than it should be: osteoporosis. I'd like to arrange a bone-density scan, a DEXA, and some blood tests, and your GP will go through the results. If the bones are thin there are very good treatments, and starting now substantially cuts the chance of the next fracture — which could be a hip. Is that something you'd be happy for me to organise?' ('my mother had a hip' → 'all the more worth doing — it runs in families')

★ 'Did you trip, or did you feel dizzy, faint or black out first?' → hose (presyncope → this becomes a syncope work-up) · 'I'll ask your GP to check BP and tablets' · ★ no driving in the plaster or on anything sedating (she drives Ray → transport plan) · written fact sheet + number · ★ re-ask: 'earlier I asked whether anything was worrying you — is there something at home you're not sure how you'll manage?' → husband → social worker before she goes, home support, transport; 'we won't send you home without a plan' · ★ teach-back: 'what are the two things that would bring you straight back?'
ask: ★ 'Before we start on the plaster — how's the pain right now, out of ten?' / ★ 'Is there anything in particular that's worrying you about going home with this on?' / ★ 'I'd like to cover five things … I'll stop at each one so you can ask.'

★ 'Some swelling over the next couple of days is completely normal, but the plaster can't stretch, so we work hard to keep it down. Keep the arm up — a sling during the day, and at night rest the forearm on a couple of pillows so the hand sits higher than your heart. Ice on top of the plaster, fifteen to twenty minutes every two or three hours for the first few days. And keep your fingers moving — a full fist, then straighten them right out, every hour or so while you're awake.'

★ 'Yours is a plaster-of-Paris cast, and if it gets wet it goes soft and stops holding the bone. Two plastic bags taped to your skin for showering; no baths, no swimming for the six weeks. If it does get damp, dry it with a hairdryer on the cool setting — never warm or hot, because you can burn skin you can't see.' / 'Hers may have been the fibreglass sort. Yours is plaster, and plaster goes soft.'

'Nothing goes down inside the plaster — no knitting needles, no pens, no coat hangers, however maddening the itch gets; people break the skin and end up with an infection under a cast we can't see into. An itch is normal; a fixed burning pain in one spot is a pressure sore — ring us.' / ★ 'Your fingers, elbow and shoulder are all free and I want all of them used. The wrist is the only thing that stays still. And let's get the rings off — if the fingers swell overnight a ring turns into a tourniquet.'

★ 'Two things would make me want to see you straightaway. The first is if the plaster becomes too tight: pain getting worse rather than better, painkillers stop touching it, fingers numb or tingly, pale or blue or cold, or you can't move them or it hurts to straighten them — come straight back here to Emergency, don't wait for the clinic. We can split the plaster in a couple of minutes and that fixes it. The second is the skin underneath: a fever, a bad smell, ooze or staining through it, or a burning, rubbing pain in one fixed spot — same day, us or your GP.'

★ 'We'll see you at the fracture clinic in one week, and they'll take another X-ray then, because these occasionally slip out of position in the first week or two and it's far easier to fix early than late. If the position is holding, the plaster stays on until about six weeks and comes off at the clinic — not at home.' / ★ 'When it comes off, expect a stiff wrist and a weaker arm — that's normal after six weeks in plaster, not a complication. I'll arrange physiotherapy for stretching and strengthening.'

★ 'There is one more thing and it's the most important part of this conversation. You broke this bone falling from standing height, on the flat. A healthy bone at your age shouldn't break from a fall like that. We call that a minimal-trauma fracture, and it's a signal the bone may be thinner than it should be — osteoporosis. So I'd like to arrange a bone-density scan, called a DEXA, and some blood tests, and your GP will go through the results. If the bones are thin there are very good treatments, and starting now cuts the chance of the next fracture — which could be a hip — substantially. Is that something you'd be happy for me to organise?'

Version B (refuses): 'That's completely your decision and I'm not going to push it. Can I just be straight about why I raised it? A broken wrist from a simple trip at your age is often the first sign the bones have thinned, and the next one is often a hip. I'll put it in the letter to your GP so it's there whenever you're ready, and leave you an information sheet — you don't need to see me, just ask your GP. And two things worth doing regardless: enough calcium, and staying active on your feet.'

★ 'Can I just check — did you trip, or did you feel dizzy or faint or black out at all first?' / 'You mustn't drive while you're in the plaster or on anything that makes you drowsy.' / ★ 'Earlier I asked whether anything was worrying you — is there something at home you're not sure how you'll manage?' / ★ 'Just so I know it has landed — what are the two things that would bring you straight back?'
pefe: Role-player: Denise Harper, 60, retired primary teacher, lives with husband Ray on a block outside town; practical, polite, slightly brisk, embarrassed; mild hypertension on one tablet; no previous fractures; non-smoker; a glass of wine most nights; mother broke her hip in her eighties and never recovered. Pain 3/10. Deflects the first concern question with a pause; tells you about Ray (Parkinson's — she does everything: showering, dressing, meals, tablets, driving) on the second ask or a home question; if never asked, at 7:40: 'how am I supposed to look after my husband like this?'. Prompts: 'won't moving them make it worse?', 'my sister got hers wet and it was fine', 'split it? would I need a new one?', 'will it go back to normal? I do the garden and play bowls', 'I haven't had that ring off in thirty years', 'but I drive Ray to all his appointments', jargon → 'sorry, what does that mean?'. Prompts once at 6:30 if no warning signs; NEVER prompts about bones

Facts: isolated R wrist injury, skin intact, NV normal pre- and post-cast; minimally displaced extra-articular Colles' (dorsal angulation), acceptable alignment; below-elbow POP, thumb free; paracetamol + ibuprofen given; no LOC, no head strike; obs normal

Version C — 8-year-old with a buckle (torus) fracture: drops DEXA, minimal-trauma talk, falls assessment, driving; keeps the four cast-care groups and both red-flag families; stable injury → removable wrist splint or short cast 3–4 weeks, often no routine repeat film VERIFY local paediatric ortho guideline; child red flags: stops using the hand, fingers pale/swollen/won't be touched, crying with pain paracetamol won't settle → Emergency; fever/smell → same day; school tomorrow with a note, no sport/bikes/monkey bars until cleared, keep out of the sandpit; a fall from height is NOT minimal trauma; ADDED: ask briefly whether this child fractures easily/repeatedly (paediatrician conversation). Paediatric buckle station also exists as its own pair

Numbers VERIFY: swelling peaks 24–48 h · ice 15–20 min q2–3h · POP hardens fully 24–72 h · ischaemic muscle tolerance ~4–6 h → split cast to skin, limb at heart level (not elevated) · fracture clinic day 7 with film; second film at 2 wk if reduced · cast ~6 wk · DEXA: normal ≥ −1.0, osteopenia −1.0 to −2.5, osteoporosis ≤ −2.5 · Ca 1300 mg/d · 25-OH vit D >50 nmol/L · paracetamol 1 g qid max 4 g/d · ibuprofen with food, caution in older patients

Never say 'compartment syndrome' or 'neurovascular compromise' to the patient — 'the plaster gets too tight and squeezes the nerves and blood vessels'. A red flag without a destination is not a safety-net. If she reports numb/tingling fingers mid-script — STOP the script, look at the hand, go to the red flags

SA: PATS for travel >100 km · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Quitline 13 7848 · TIS 131 450 · ReturnToWorkSA if at work · social work for carer strain; Carer Gateway 1800 422 737; My Aged Care for Ray's supports
fails: ★ Never saying the fracture was minimal trauma, or never arranging a bone-density scan (the commonest fail) — or delivering it as a decree at 7:50 without asking permission
★ No red flags, or red flags with no action/destination attached
★ No follow-up interval when Task 2 asks for a plan ('we'll keep an eye on it')
★ Telling her a warm or hot hairdryer is safe
★ Continuing the script after she reports numb or tingling fingers
'Keep it elevated' without the landmark (hand above the heart) or the night version; 'rest it and keep it still' (stiff fingers, frozen shoulder); arguing with the sister; rings left on

Stopping the plan at 'the cast comes off' — no physiotherapy, stiffness not normalised; 'yes, absolutely' to 'will it go back to normal?'; accepting 'not really' at 0:40 and never re-asking; skipping the mechanism question; no teach-back
numbers: Cast ~6 wk, below-elbow, thumb free (scaphoid = spica) · clinic day 7 + repeat film · second film 2 wk if reduced · physio after removal, ~2 months of exercises
Swelling peaks 24–48 h · ice 15–20 min q2–3h · POP hardens 24–72 h · ischaemia tolerance ~4–6 h · split to skin, limb at heart level
DEXA: ≥ −1.0 normal · −1.0 to −2.5 osteopenia · ≤ −2.5 osteoporosis · Ca 1300 mg/d · vit D >50 · paracetamol 1 g qid max 4 g VERIFY
Child buckle: splint 3–4 wk, no routine repeat film VERIFY · PATS >100 km · Carer Gateway 1800 422 737 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

source: Colles_Cast_Care_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf (Denise Harper, 60, Colles' fracture in POP after tripping on a hose — cast care, follow-up plan, minimal-trauma fracture, carer for a husband with Parkinson's)
drive: AMC Clinical Notability › Medicine AMC Clinical › Medicine MSK › Colles_Cast_Care_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf
must: FAIL — Never saying the fracture was minimal trauma, or never arranging a bone-density scan — the commonest fail; verbatim: 'you broke this bone falling from standing height, on the flat; a healthy bone at your age shouldn't break from a fall like that — we call that a minimal-trauma fracture, and it's a signal the bone may be thinner than it should be; I'd like to arrange a DEXA and some bloods, and your GP will go through the results — is that something you'd be happy for me to organise?'; the opposite fail is delivering it as a decree at 7:50 — ask permission, and if she refuses, name it once, give the reason, accept, 'I'll put it in the letter to your GP' — a third pitch fails too; she will not prompt you for this one (★)

FAIL — Red flags with no destination — two families, two actions: the tight cast (pain worse not better, painkillers not touching it, fingers numb or tingly, pale, blue, cold, can't move or hurts to straighten) → 'come straight back to Emergency — don't wait for the clinic; we can split the plaster in two minutes'; the skin underneath (fever, smell, ooze, a burning pain in one fixed spot — a pressure sore, not an itch) → same day, us or the GP; never 'compartment syndrome' or 'neurovascular' to her (★)

FAIL — 'We'll keep an eye on it' when Task 2 asks for a plan — a plan has intervals, places and events: seven days, fracture clinic, repeat X-ray ('these occasionally slip in the first week and it's far easier to fix early'); six weeks, cast off at the clinic not at home; then physiotherapy — say the word — with a stiff wrist normalised as expected, not a complication; PATS if the drive is long (★)

FAIL — Telling her a warm or hot hairdryer is safe — cool setting only: 'you can burn skin you can't see and you won't feel it until it has blistered'; plaster of Paris goes soft when wet — two bags taped for showering, no baths or swimming for six weeks; 'my sister got hers wet' → 'hers may have been fibreglass' in one line, don't argue (★)

FAIL — Continuing the script after she reports numb or tingling fingers, or 'it's already feeling tight' — stop, look at the hand, and go straight to the red flags; and 'rest it and keep it still' is wrong — fingers, elbow and shoulder all used, the wrist is the only part that stays still; rings off before she leaves ('a ring turns into a tourniquet') (★)

DO — Sit, ask about pain before starting, signpost five headings at 0:45 (what's broken and what the plaster does; swelling with hand above the heart by day and night, ice 15–20 min every 2–3 h, fist hourly; dry, clean — nothing down inside; the flags; the plan; why the bone broke); ask what's worrying her twice — she deflects the first time ('not really') and the husband with Parkinson's comes out the second (social work, home support, transport); ask the mechanism ('did you trip, or feel faint or dizzy first?' — presyncope turns this into a syncope station); no driving in plaster or on sedating analgesia; teach-back of the two things that bring her straight back

setting: Regional general practice. Results already back; follow the task order — explain results (0:40–2:00), focused history (2:00–5:00, seven questions), then contributing factors and plan (5:00–8:00). No examination. The line the station is built around: 'have you ever broken a bone — even years ago?' at 2:10; the plan branches on the answer. Falls plan must START by 6:40 whatever is unfinished.
stem: Ben Hartley, 55, known COPD, saw your colleague two weeks ago because of three falls in the past three months. Budesonide inhaler; prednisolone for eight days with every exacerbation. Results: DEXA — L1–L4 T −2.1, femoral neck T −1.4, total hip T −1.3. FBE, fasting glucose, UEC, LFT, TSH normal; corrected Ca 2.38; 25-OH vitamin D 30 nmol/L (normal >50).
tasks: Explain the results of the investigations to the patient
Take a further focused history from the patient
Explain the contributing factors and outline your management plan
time: 8 minutes. 0:00 WIPE, turn the results to him, ★ agenda ('what if I go down and no one's there?') → answer it at the end, signpost three areas · 0:40 results: what a DEXA is, three sites, T vs Z (★ 'I'm using your T-score, that's the one we diagnose on'), ★ name the range (−1 to −2.5) BEFORE the word osteopenia, ★ 'thinned' not 'soft', NOT osteoporosis, 'thin bones don't make you fall — they turn a fall into a fracture' · bloods: group the normals in one sentence, land on vitamin D 30 · 2:00 history: permission, one open falls question, ★ LOC screen · ★ 2:10 'ever broken a bone, even years ago?' → no · three bone-lifestyle questions BY NAME: dairy (milk/cheese/yoghurt), sun, exercise + breathing limit, alcohol · two COPD questions: smoking, adherence, exacerbations/admissions, ★ days of prednisolone (8 — planted) · falls risk list: vision, hearing, joints/balance, ★ light-headed on standing, sleeping/BP tablets (fluid tablet), home hazards (★ the hall rug) · 5:00 contributing factors: ★ BOTH steroids (puffer small, oral courses matter more), COPD itself (inflammation, inactivity), low vit D, little dairy, little exercise · ★ 'don't stop anything' · bone plan: no fracture + osteopenia → ★ risk calculator first, drug only if high; dentist before any drug; vit D 1–2 caps/d, 3–4 dairy serves (food first), weight-bearing + balance, sun, cut wine · chest: add LABA, review 3 mo, pulmonary rehab, vaccines, ★ prednisolone 5 days not 8 · ★ 6:40 falls: falls clinic, vision/hearing, physio, OT (★ the rug), medication review (★ fluid tablet, light-headedness), personal alarm · 7:30 recheck vit D 3 mo, DEXA 2 y, red flags, summary, his fear answered.

back.dx: Osteopenia (spine T −2.1; hip −1.3/−1.4) with vitamin D deficiency (30) in a 55-year-old with COPD, glucocorticoid exposure (ICS + repeated 8-day oral courses), low dairy, indoor, inactive — and three mechanical falls with no fracture. Version A: never broken a bone → no drug today; fracture-risk calculator (Garvan/FRAX) first, treat if high; correct vitamin D before any antiresorptive. Falls: hall rug, old glasses, wobbly turning, ★ light-headed on standing + fluid tablet → falls clinic, OT, physio, medication review, alarm. Hidden fear: mother had osteoporosis, broke her hip, nursing home, died — 'so I'm not going to end up in a home?' → 'that's the opposite of what I'm aiming for'.
plan: 'Hello Mr Hartley — Ben? My colleague arranged tests after the falls; they're back. I'd like to go through them, ask a few questions, then make a plan together.' · ★ 'anything in particular you were hoping we'd cover?' → 'what if there's no one around next time' → 'that's exactly what I want to prevent — three things: your results, some questions, then a plan for your bones, your chest and your falls'

★ 'We did a bone mineral densitometry — a DEXA. It measures how dense and strong the bones are at three places: spine, hip, top of the thigh bone. Two scores: the T-score compares you with a healthy young adult of the same sex; the Z-score with someone your own age. I'm using your T-score, because that's the one we make the diagnosis on.'

★ 'Your T-scores are −2.1 in the spine, −1.4 at the femoral neck, −1.3 at the hip. Because they sit between −1 and −2.5, you have osteopenia — your bones have thinned; there's less bone than we'd expect. It's the stage before osteoporosis, when bones become fragile and break easily. A warning, not a disaster.' · 'is that osteoporosis?' → 'not yet — and that's an important difference' · 'is that why I'm falling?' → ★ 'no — thin bones don't make you fall; they turn a fall into a broken bone, which is why we work on both'

'Your blood count, sugars, kidneys, liver and thyroid are all normal — that rules out most other causes of thinning bone. Calcium is normal too. The one thing that isn't: your vitamin D is low at 30, when it should be above 50 — it's what lets your body absorb calcium. Make sense so far?'

'Is it alright if I ask some questions, so I can work out why the bones have thinned and why you've been falling?' · 'tell me a bit about the falls' (acknowledge, then take control) · ★ 'when you fall, do you black out, or are you aware the whole time?' → aware, tripped on the hall rug
★ 'Have you ever broken a bone — even years ago, even if it seemed minor at the time?' → 'no, never — touch wood' → repeat it back; the plan branches here

★ By name: 'do you have dairy regularly — milk, cheese, yoghurt — how much in a day?' (milk in tea only) · 'time outdoors in the sun in a normal week?' (indoors) · 'what exercise, and does your breathing limit it?' (puffed to the letterbox) · 'alcohol per week?' (glass of wine most nights)

COPD: 'still smoking, or stopped?' (quit 5 y, 30 pack-years) · 'using the puffer every day as prescribed?' (most days, forgets) · 'flare-ups in 12 months, any admissions?' (3–4, none) · ★ 'how many days of prednisolone each time?' (8 — note it)

Falls list: eyesight/hearing (glasses 4 y old) · joint pain/balance (knees on stairs, wobbly turning) · ★ 'light-headed when you stand?' (yes, sometimes) · sleeping or BP tablets (★ fluid tablet) · home — steps, rugs, lighting (★ the hall rug, two front steps) · who's at home (Denise, works Tue/Thu)

★ 'The main cause is the steroid medication — two kinds: the steroid in your puffer, a small amount but not nothing, and more importantly the prednisolone tablets with every flare-up. COPD itself thins bone — inflammation and inactivity. Add low vitamin D, not much dairy, not much exercise.' · 'should I stop the puffer?' → ★ 'please don't stop anything — we manage the risk, we don't abandon the treatment; smallest amount that keeps your chest well — and ★ next flare-up, five days of prednisolone, not eight'

Bone: ★ 'because you've never broken a bone, and this is osteopenia not osteoporosis, I'm not starting a bone tablet today. I'll put your details into a fracture risk calculator — age, weight, steroids, family history, hip reading — and if it's high I'll recommend treatment: a weekly tablet or a six-monthly injection; either way dentist first.' · vitamin D 1–2 capsules/day, ★ 3–4 serves of dairy ('food first — tablets only if you can't manage that'), regular exercise with weight-bearing and balance, sun outside the middle of the day, cut the wine · chest: add a long-acting puffer, review 3 mo, pulmonary rehab, flu/pneumococcal/COVID vaccines

★ FALLS, regardless of what's unfinished: 'I'll refer you to a falls clinic — they'll check vision and hearing, a physio will work on balance and strength, an OT will come to the house — ★ starting with that hallway rug. We'll review your medications including the fluid tablet, since that light-headedness on standing may be part of it. And a personal alarm, so if you go down alone help is one button away.' · 'so I'm not going to end up in a home?' → ★ 'that's the opposite of what I'm aiming for — everything on this list is to keep you safe in your own house'

'Recheck vitamin D in 3 months, repeat the bone scan in 2 years. Come back sooner if you break anything, have a fall you can't get up from, hit your head, or get sudden severe back pain. Summary: thinned bones from the steroids and your chest condition, low vitamin D, and falls we can do something about. Anything I haven't covered?'
ask: 'I'd like to go through them with you, ask you a few questions, then we'll make a plan together.' / 'Before we start — is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd cover?'

★ 'It gives us two scores. The T-score compares your bone density with a healthy young adult of the same sex; the Z-score compares you with someone your own age. I'm going to use your T-score, because that's the one we make the diagnosis on.' / ★ 'Because they sit between minus one and minus two-and-a-half, you have a condition called osteopenia. That means your bones have thinned — it's the stage before osteoporosis, when bones become fragile and break easily. So it's a warning, not a disaster.'

★ 'Thin bones don't make you fall — but they turn a fall into a broken bone. That's why we're going to work on both.' / 'Your blood count, sugars, kidneys, liver and thyroid are all normal, which rules out most of the other causes of thinning bones. The one thing that isn't: your vitamin D is low, at 30, when it should be above 50.'

★ 'When you fall, do you black out completely, or are you aware the whole time?' / ★ 'Have you ever broken a bone — even years ago, and even if it seemed minor at the time?' (if yes: 'which bone, and was it a big injury or a simple trip?')

★ 'Do you have dairy products regularly — milk, cheese, yoghurt? Roughly how much in a day? How much time do you spend outdoors in the sun in a normal week? What sort of exercise do you manage — and does your breathing limit what you can do? And how much alcohol in a week?' / ★ 'How many flare-ups in the last twelve months, were you admitted, and how many days of prednisolone do you take each time?'

★ 'The main cause is the steroid medication. There are two kinds: the steroid in your puffer, which is a small amount but not nothing, and more importantly the prednisolone tablets you take with every flare-up. On top of that, COPD itself thins bones — through the inflammation, and because it stops you being as active.' / ★ 'Please don't stop anything. We manage the risk; we don't abandon the treatment.' / ★ 'Next flare-up, take the prednisolone for five days, not eight — five days is what the guidelines recommend.'

★ 'Because you've never broken a bone, and this is osteopenia rather than osteoporosis, I'm not starting a bone tablet today. I'll put your details into a fracture risk calculator, and if it comes back high I'll recommend treatment — a weekly tablet, or a six-monthly injection. Either way I'd send you to the dentist first.' / 'Injection? what sort?' → one sentence: 'a six-monthly injection under the skin — the important thing is having it on time.' / 'Food first — three to four serves of dairy; we only add tablets if you can't manage that.'

★ 'For the falls: I'll refer you to a falls clinic. They'll check your vision and hearing, a physiotherapist will work on your balance and strength, and an occupational therapist will come to the house — starting with that hallway rug. We'll review your medications, including the fluid tablet, since that light-headedness on standing may be part of it. And I'd suggest a personal alarm.' / 'So I'm not going to end up in a home?' → ★ 'That's the opposite of what I'm aiming for. Everything on this list is designed to keep you safe in your own house.'

Variant 1 (wrist from the dog lead): ★ 'That's important and it changes what I'd recommend. Breaking a wrist from a simple trip is a minimal trauma fracture — when someone's had one, we start treatment at −1.5 rather than waiting for −2.5. Your spine is −2.1, so I'd start treatment now, alongside the vitamin D, the calcium and the falls plan.' / Variant 2 (hip 18 months ago): 'A broken hip from a simple fall tells me more than the scan does — we treat whatever the reading, so I'd start now and I won't need a calculator.' / Variant 3 (mid-back pain, lost height): 'Losing height with new back pain can mean a small crack in a spine bone — I'd like an X-ray of your back; if it shows what I suspect, we treat regardless of the scan.'

FAIL — 'I'll refer you to a specialist' as the whole plan, or 'don't worry, that won't happen to you' about her mother — she goes quiet for the rest of the station; 'I'm not going to pretend the risk is nothing — but your mother's generation mostly wasn't offered treatment, and you are being offered it today; and a big part of the plan is making sure you don't have that fall' (★)

FAIL — Taking a history after being told not to ('but what does the x-ray show, doctor?') — one rapport line, one agenda question ('has anything in particular been on your mind?' — she says no, but it opens the door for the mother's hip at 3:50), then the film: three colours (white bone, grey soft tissue, black air) → blocks called vertebrae → 'in one of those blocks I can see a break' → 'is it actually broken?' → yes, then bound it (cord not involved, back wall intact, legs working, no operation or plaster) → wedge explained; you may respond to what she offers (reflux tablets, no milk) but not start asking (★)

DO — Use 'but I only picked up a bag of shopping' as the hinge: 'a healthy bone would not break doing that — the bone was already weak'; osteoporosis named and translated in the same breath (honeycomb), six causes in order (age, menopause, calcium, vitamin D, exercise, conditions and medicines — steroids, acid tablets); tests named (DEXA, vitamin D, calcium) but 'I'm not waiting for those before we start — the scan is a starting point, not permission to begin'; three drug routes and let her choose ('I already rattle with tablets' → the injection or the drip); dentist first; jaw risk sized not dodged; calcium as food, sun, supervised exercise, alcohol and coffee; falls clinic ('if you fall now, the next bone is likely your hip'); review 1–2 weeks, DEXA in two years; summary in five points

setting: ED, regional SA hospital. Prompt bell at 4:00 → examination request 4:00–6:00 (findings only for what you name), explanation 6:00–8:00. 27, female — pregnancy and pelvic causes live from the first second. Ask stability aloud even though the numbers are on the door.

time: 8 min. 'Examiner, is my patient haemodynamically stable, and could I have the vital signs?' · intro · open → four-part acknowledgement in one breath (sorry / concerning to me too / I'll ask questions / I'll take good care of you) · 'in pain now? want something?' → nurse, two questions and out · pain in order: where → ★ WHERE DID IT START (periumbilical → RIF) → /10 → sharp/dull → when → constant → worse → radiates → better/worse (car bumps) · four groups as headings: GI (N/V — order vs pain, bloating, flatus, D/C, fever) · red flags (weight, ★ appetite gone, lumps, dizziness, blood/melaena, habit, FHx CRC) · urinary · groin · gynae/sexual with permission (bleeding, discharge, LMP 3 wk regular, sexually active, condoms 'most of the time', STI) · ops/meds/allergies · bell → seven named steps: appearance, postural BP, inspection (respiration, distension, scars, hernia), palpation (max tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, mass), percussion, bowel sounds, inguinal, DRE with consent/chaperone, ★ Rovsing + psoas · ★ pelvic exam with consent + chaperone even though sure (inspection, speculum, bimanual: CMT, uterus, adnexa) · ★ dipstick, βhCG, BSL · name it, explain the appendix, ★ four reasons, grouped DDx with a reason each incl ectopic, plan (NBM, IV, fluids, analgesia, bloods, USS, surgical review), ★ answer 'will I need an operation?' yourself, safety-net.

back.dx: Acute appendicitis — pain migrated from periumbilical to RIF overnight, dull → sharp, 6/10, constant, worse, worse over bumps; nausea and one vomit AFTER the pain; anorexia since yesterday; bowels/urine normal; LMP 3 wk, regular, condoms most of the time. PEFE: RIF max tenderness with rebound and percussion tenderness, no guarding/rigidity/mass, BS normal, inguinal and DRE normal, Rovsing +, psoas +; pelvic normal (no CMT, no adnexal tenderness); dipstick negative, βhCG negative, BSL 5.4. Four reasons: migration, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, positive special tests. Version B: perforation with peritonitis and sepsis — 'the pain eased then became generalised' is the appendix perforating; say it aloud; resuscitate while taking the history.
plan: ★ 'Examiner, before I start — is my patient haemodynamically stable, and could I have the vital signs?' · 'Hello Jenna, I'm Dr —; is it all right if I ask some questions?' · 'what's brought you in?' → ★ 'I'm really sorry to hear that, Jenna. The pain you're describing is concerning to me too. I'll need to ask a few questions to get a better idea, and I promise I'll take good care of you.'
'Are you in pain right now? Would you like something for it?' → 'I'll ask the nurse to organise pain relief now and we'll keep going' (no drug/dose/allergy detour)

'Show me where' → ★ 'Where did it start — was it always there, or did it begin somewhere else?' → belly button, moved overnight (do not diagnose aloud) · /10 (6) · sharp/dull (dull → sharper) · when (yesterday late afternoon) · constant · worse · travel (no) · better/worse (nothing; every bump in the car)

GI as a heading: nausea/vomiting (sick once this morning, after the pain), bloating, wind, D/C, fever ('might have felt hot last night') · ★ 'a few questions I ask everybody with tummy pain': weight loss, ★ appetite (none since yesterday — couldn't face toast), lumps, dizziness, blood/black motions, habit, FHx bowel cancer

Waterworks: burning, frequency, blood · groin lump · ★ 'I need to ask a few personal questions about your periods and sexual health, because some causes of this pain start in that area — is that all right?' → bleeding, discharge, LMP + regular (3 wk, regular), sexually active/condoms (one partner, most of the time), STI ever · ops, meds, allergies

★ Bell → examiner: general appearance · postural BP · inspection — moves with respiration, distension, scars, hernia, bruising · superficial and deep palpation — site of maximal tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, mass · percussion tenderness · bowel sounds · inguinal region · DRE with consent and chaperone · ★ Rovsing and psoas

★ 'With the patient's consent and a chaperone present, I'd like to perform a pelvic examination: inspection — rash, lumps, bleeding, discharge; speculum — cervical discharge; bimanual — cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, adnexal tenderness or mass' · ★ 'bedside tests — urine dipstick, urinary βhCG, capillary glucose' (LMP unreliable in early pregnancy; a missed ectopic is a preventable death)

★ 'Jenna, most likely you have acute appendicitis. The appendix is a small finger-shaped pouch attached to the large bowel on the right lower side of your tummy, and at the moment it's inflamed.' · 'Is it serious? will I need an operation?' → ★ 'it is something we take seriously, and yes — very likely an operation to remove it; usually keyhole, home within a day or two' · ★ four reasons: pain moved, appetite gone, feeling sick/vomited, specific tests positive

DDx in groups with a reason each: pregnancy — ectopic (normal period 3 wk ago, βhCG negative) · gynae — PID/torsion (no discharge, internal exam normal) · urinary — UTI/ureteric stone (no burning/blood, dipstick clear) · bowel — gastroenteritis/mesenteric adenitis (bug gives vomiting first + diarrhoea; neither) · plan: NBM, IV, fluids, analgesia, bloods, USS, surgical team on their way · safety-net: 'if the pain suddenly gets much worse or spreads across your whole tummy, tell the nurse straight away' · questions
ask: ★ 'Examiner, before I start — is my patient haemodynamically stable, and could I have the vital signs, please?' / ★ 'I'm really sorry to hear that, Jenna. The pain you're describing is concerning to me too. I'll need to ask you a few questions to get a better idea of what's going on, and I promise I'll take good care of you. Is that all right?'

★ 'Where did the pain start? Was it always in that spot, or did it begin somewhere else?' / 'On a scale of one to ten, how bad is it? Sharp or a dull ache? There all the time? Getting better or worse? Does it travel anywhere? Anything that makes it better or worse — food, movement, position?'

'A few questions I ask everybody with tummy pain: any weight loss? How has your appetite been? Lumps or bumps? Dizziness? Blood in the motions or black tarry motions? Change in bowel habit? Anyone in the family with bowel cancer?'

★ 'I need to ask a few personal questions about your periods and your sexual health, because some causes of this pain start in that area. Is that all right? Any vaginal bleeding or discharge? When was your last period, and are they regular? Are you sexually active, and do you use condoms? Have you ever been told you had a sexually transmitted infection?'

★ To examiner: '…on superficial and deep palpation — where is the tenderness maximal, is there guarding, is there rigidity, is there rebound tenderness, any mass? … the inguinal region, and with consent and a chaperone a rectal examination? And I'd like Rovsing sign and the psoas sign.' / ★ 'With the patient's consent and with a chaperone present, I would like to perform a pelvic examination … is there cervical motion tenderness, is the uterus of normal size and non-tender, and is there any adnexal tenderness or mass?' / ★ 'Bedside tests — a urine dipstick, a urinary βhCG, and a capillary blood glucose.'

If pushed on βhCG: 'I would still request it. The last menstrual period is unreliable in early pregnancy, and a missed ectopic is a preventable death, so I test every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain.'

★ 'Jenna, most likely you have a condition we call acute appendicitis. The appendix is a small finger-shaped pouch attached to the large bowel, on the right lower side of your tummy. At the moment that pouch is inflamed. There are four reasons I think that: your pain moved — it started around your belly button and settled in the right lower side; your appetite has gone since yesterday; you've been feeling sick and vomited; and when I examined you, the specific tests we use for appendicitis were positive.'

★ 'It is something we take seriously, and yes — it's very likely you'll need an operation to take the appendix out. It's usually keyhole surgery and most people go home within a day or two. The surgical team will come and talk you through it.' / 'A pregnancy sitting outside the womb — but your period was normal three weeks ago and the pregnancy test is negative. An infection of the womb and tubes, or a twisted ovary — but no discharge and the internal examination was normal. A bladder infection or a stone in the kidney tube — no burning, no blood, urine clear. A stomach bug or inflamed glands — a bug usually gives vomiting first and diarrhoea, and you have neither.'

'We'll keep you nil by mouth, put a drip in, give you fluids and pain relief, take some blood tests, and arrange an ultrasound. I'm asking the surgical team to come and see you. If at any point the pain suddenly gets much worse or spreads across your whole tummy, tell the nurse straight away.'

Version B: 'Those observations concern me. I can see you're not well — I'm going to ask a few quick questions and start treatment at the same time.' → examiner: two large-bore cannulas, bloods incl cultures and βhCG, fluid bolus, IV antibiotics, antiemetic, analgesia, NBM, urgent surgical review; 'in a rural site I would be ringing MedSTAR now' · ★ 'the pain that eased and then became generalised — I'm concerned about a perforated appendix with peritonitis and sepsis. Is the abdomen rigid, are bowel sounds absent, is there generalised rebound?' · 'I think the appendix has burst and the infection has spread; fluids and antibiotics now, the surgical team is coming — you'll need an operation today.'

(colicky), onset, worse, radiation, better/worse · ★ obstruction block: vomiting — how many, ★ colour ('is any of it green?'), faeculent smell; distension; ★ 'when did you last pass WIND? when did you last open your bowels?' (absolute constipation — patients don't use the word) · ★ cause block: previous abdominal operation (appendicectomy in his 20s), groin lump/hernia, weight loss/PR blood/change in habit (tumour), chronic constipation · ischaemia block: palpitations/AF, MI/stroke/DVT, post-prandial pain and food fear · closure: urinary, rash/injury, smoking/alcohol/drugs/meds (anticoagulants, NSAIDs)/allergies, PMHx/FHx · examiner, seven steps named: appearance, four vitals, inspection (distension, scars, ★ visible peristalsis), palpation (tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, masses), percussion (tympanic/dull), ★ auscultation (present/absent/tinkling), ★ inguinal region and scrotum, ★ DRE — rectum full or empty, dipstick + BSL · dx + CAUSE + layman explanation · grouped DDx · management: drip and suck.

back.dx: Small bowel obstruction from adhesions (appendicectomy in his twenties) — colicky central pain 8/10, four vomits with the last two green and bitter, distended, no flatus for two days, no motion for three; no groin lump. Explain adhesions without sounding accusatory: 'bands of scar are normal healing, not a mistake; years later one can kink or squeeze a loop'. Management: drip and suck (NBM, IV fluids, NG tube), analgesia, antiemetic, IDC for fluid balance, bloods, AXR/CT, surgical team; most adhesive SBO settles in 1–2 days; operate if it doesn't or if any sign of strangulation.

Years later one of those bands can kink or squeeze a loop of bowel and nothing gets past. Four cardinal features: colicky pain · vomiting (bilious → faeculent) · distension · absolute constipation (no flatus). Four adult causes: adhesions · hernia · tumour · volvulus. Small bowel on AXR: valvulae conniventes, full width, central; large bowel: haustra, partial, peripheral; erect film for air-fluid levels. CT abdomen with contrast is the definitive test (transition point, closed loop, ischaemia). Gastrografin challenge: contrast reaching the colon within 24 h predicts non-operative resolution VERIFY

Eight-step resuscitation — imaging is step seven: NBM · IV access + bloods (FBE, UEC, VBG/lactate, lipase, G&H) · fluids · NG tube · analgesia · antiemetic · IDC · imaging · surgical referral. Strangulation signs: constant pain, peritonism, fever, tachycardia, leucocytosis, raised lactate → theatre. Harder variants: sigmoid volvulus (elderly, gross distension, coffee-bean loop from the pelvis → flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression, surgery if it fails/ischaemia) · ruptured AAA (older smoker, central/back pain, faint, pulsatile mass — stop the history and say so; recognising when to stop is scored) · ischaemic colitis (anticoagulated, crampy left pain, bloody diarrhoea settling — supportive care; thumbprinting is colonic)

Mortality high, rises with delay

pefe: Role-player (reconstructed): Elyse, 20; no motion for six days, bloated, hard pellets; hurt her back ten days ago, taking Panadeine Forte a few times a day; back pain now settled. Card: soft, mildly distended, palpable faecal loading LIF, bowel sounds present, rectum loaded with hard stool

Opioid-induced constipation: reduced motility, increased tone/sphincter, reduced secretions — dose-related, no tolerance. Panadeine Forte = paracetamol 500 mg + codeine 30 mg (S4; OTC codeine ended in Australia 2018). Management: stop/reduce opioid; osmotic laxative (macrogol) ± stimulant (senna/bisacodyl); suppository/enema for rectal loading; PAMORAs for chronic opioid use (specialist). Avoid bulk-forming alone in opioid constipation. Fibre 25–30 g/day, fluids, exercise VERIFY

Constipation red flags: age >50 new onset, blood, weight loss, anaemia, FHx CRC, nocturnal symptoms, obstruction (vomiting, absolute constipation, distension) — hospital. Secondary causes: opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, pregnancy, diabetes, Parkinson's, pelvic floor dysfunction. Always βhCG in a 20-year-old with lower abdominal pain
Codeine counselling: also drowsiness, dependence, not for chronic non-cancer pain; ultra-rapid metabolisers; not in breastfeeding · SA: healthdirect 1800 022 222

stem: Ron Falzon, 60, presents with alternating constipation and diarrhoea, 5 kg of unintentional weight loss and some rectal bleeding. His aunt had bowel cancer. He says his screening test last year was normal.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials

back.dx: Suspected colorectal cancer — age 60, persistent change in bowel habit (alternating), 5 kg unintentional weight loss, rectal bleeding, family history (aunt); a normal FOBT last year does not apply because he now has symptoms (screening ≠ diagnosis; FOBT sensitivity for cancer ~70–80%, less for polyps). Urgent colonoscopy is the investigation; bloods for iron-deficiency anaemia. Haemorrhoids may co-exist and must not be accepted as the explanation. Break the concern honestly: 'I am concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer' — concerned, not certain; the test gives the answer within weeks.

Findings to expect: ± pallor, ± abdominal mass/hepatomegaly, DRE ± rectal mass or blood; FBE — iron-deficiency anaemia

Red flags for CRC: age ≥50 (younger with FHx), change in habit >6 wk, rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss, abdominal/rectal mass, tenesmus. Referral: Category 1 colonoscopy within 30 days for suspected cancer VERIFY (Cancer Council Optimal Care Pathway). National Bowel Cancer Screening Program: iFOBT every 2 years 45–74 (from 2024) VERIFY; sensitivity for cancer ~70–80%, positive predictive value low — a negative test does not exclude cancer, and symptomatic patients need colonoscopy regardless. Family history categories: one first-degree relative >55 = slightly above average (screen from 45); first-degree <55 or two relatives → colonoscopy every 5 years from 40 or 10 y before youngest VERIFY; aunt = second-degree

Investigations: FBE, iron studies, UEC, LFT, CEA (baseline, not diagnostic), colonoscopy + biopsy; staging CT chest/abdo/pelvis; MRI rectum for rectal cancer; MDT. Lynch syndrome clues: young onset, endometrial/ovarian/gastric/urothelial cancers in the family

stem: Jenny Walker, 25, administration officer, complains of bloating. T 36.7 · P 72 · BP 112/70 · RR 14 · BMI 21. Well and comfortable.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Tell the examiner your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons
Give the examiner your differential diagnoses
time: 6 min history. Intro, acknowledge, consent (bowels and periods), ★ concerns in the first minute (aunt with bowel cancer) · ★ DEFINE 'bloated': burping / more wind / tummy actually swollen · timing: how long, constant vs comes and goes, worse time of day, ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' · triggers: better/worse, ★ 'worse after eating — any food that sets it off?' (A: eases after the toilet — Rome IV bait, don't close; B: pizza and bread — only when food is named) · GI screen: N/V, pain, ★ constipation or diarrhoea must be answered, fever · ★ red flags by 4:10: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness (B: 'anaemic — they said it's my heavy periods'), blood/dark stools, lasting habit change, FHx bowel/ovarian cancer · ★ ovarian and obstruction: early satiety, urinary frequency, FHx ovarian/breast, previous surgery, groin lump, ★ passing wind normally · ★ diet: dairy; ★ 'greasy, bulky, float, stick to the pan, hard to flush?' (B: yes to all, flushes twice, thought normal) · infection/motility: travel/camping, meds incl supplements (★ iron tablets), diabetes, cold intolerance · IBD/IBS: joints, mouth ulcers, eyes, ★ rashes (B: itchy blistery rash on elbows), alternating stools, relief with defecation · ★ periods by 5:00: LMP, regular, ★ pregnancy possible, home/work stress · stop at 6:00 → speak the diagnosis in full sentences → DDx by group, IBS last.

back.dx: Version A — irritable bowel syndrome: recurrent discomfort related to defecation with a change in stool form (Rome IV), a clear work stressor, and a positive diagnosis of exclusion — no weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, mass, family history, dietary trigger, travel, not pregnant. Version B — coeliac disease: gluten-related symptoms, steatorrhoea, iron-deficiency anaemia 'I do not accept as menstrual until malabsorption is excluded', itchy blistery elbow rash (dermatitis herpetiformis), sister with a gluten problem; second contributor — oral iron itself causes bloating, cramping and constipation. Discriminating behaviour in B: challenge the 'heavy periods' explanation and ask stool character directly.
plan: 'Am I speaking with Jenny? What's brought you along?' → 'that sounds uncomfortable and I'm glad you came in — I'll ask about your bowels and your periods, is that all right? ★ Before I start, was there anything in particular you were worried it might be?' (aunt — bowel cancer)

(no) · ★ 'anything that makes it better or worse — in particular worse after eating, any food that sets it off?' (A: eases after the toilet; B: 'not really' → name food → pizza and bread)

★ Aloud to the examiner — A: 'My most likely diagnosis is irritable bowel syndrome. She meets Rome IV criteria — recurrent abdominal discomfort related to defecation with a change in stool form — and there is a clear stressor. I say this as a positive diagnosis of exclusion: no weight loss, no bleeding, no anaemia, no nocturnal symptoms, no mass, no family history, no dietary trigger, no travel, and she is not pregnant.' B: 'coeliac disease — gluten-related symptoms, steatorrhoeic stools, an iron deficiency anaemia I do not accept as menstrual until malabsorption is excluded, an itchy elbow rash consistent with dermatitis herpetiformis, and a sister with a gluten problem; a second contributor is the oral iron.' · DDx by group: malignancy (bowel; ★ ovarian — presents exactly like this) · obstruction (adhesions, hernia, volvulus, constipation — normal flatus, no surgery) · dietary (coeliac, lactose) · infection (giardia, post-infectious) · motility (drugs, diabetic enteropathy, hypothyroidism) · IBD · functional — IBS last, a diagnosis of exclusion · exclude pregnancy

IBS placed below it (stools alternate, but a reproducible food trigger takes precedence and IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion). Still exclude coeliac (causes secondary lactose intolerance) and IBD (must-not-miss at 20). Explain: enzyme (lactase) shortage, not an allergy — depends on the amount. To patient: ★ 'Your bowel is short of an enzyme called lactase, which normally breaks down a sugar called lactose in dairy foods. Without enough of it, the sugar passes through undigested, pulls water into the bowel and is fermented by the bacteria there — that produces the gas, bloating, cramping and loose motions an hour or so after dairy.' / 'So I'm allergic to milk?' → ★ 'Not quite — an allergy is the immune system reacting, and even a tiny amount causes trouble. This is an enzyme shortage, so it depends on the amount: a milkshake floors you, a bit of cheese may be fine.'

'Blood tests — full blood count, iron, an inflammation marker and a coeliac screen, because coeliac disease can cause exactly this as a knock-on effect. Then cut lactose out completely for two to four weeks, and if it settles bring it back gradually to find your limit. A dietitian so you don't lose calcium — that matters for your bones at your age. Come back sooner if you see blood, lose weight, get fevers, or the pain wakes you at night.'

Examiner 'isn't this abdominal migraine?' → ★ 'I did consider it. Abdominal migraine requires discrete episodes of midline pain with complete wellness between them, usually with anorexia, nausea or pallor, and critically the final criterion is that the pain is not better accounted for by another disorder. Here it is — there is a reproducible dairy trigger. The family history of migraine is background rather than evidence.' / 'My mate said it's an ulcer' → 'ulcers give burning pain higher up, often at night or when hungry, linked to anti-inflammatories or Helicobacter — none of that fits; yours is tied to dairy.'

IBS Rome IV: pain ≥1 day/week over 3 months, onset ≥6 months, 2 of 3. Abdominal migraine (Rome IV): paroxysmal midline pain ≥1 h, complete wellness between, ≥2 of anorexia/nausea/vomiting/headache/photophobia/pallor, not better explained

stem: Steph Corrigan, 25, presents with severe epigastric pain since last night and repeated vomiting. Results: WCC raised · lipase markedly raised · AST and ALT 2–3× upper limit · bilirubin normal.

Explain the results and your diagnosis
Give your differentials and management

(yes), 'sitting forward or curling up help?' (a bit), 'what does food do?' (worse, not eating) · vomits ×5–6, bilious, blood?, bloating/wind/D/C/fever · ★ six cause questions in order: alcohol (standard drinks/week, heavy session?) · gallstones/gallbladder surgery (cholecystectomy 4 y) · medicines — NSAIDs, steroids, diuretics, ★ 'any injections for weight loss or diabetes — Ozempic, Wegovy, Trulicity?' · cholesterol/triglycerides/FHx, calcium · ERCP/trauma · viral illness · ★ cardiac: chest pain/tightness, SOB, sweating, jaw/arm — 'I would like an ECG' · red flags: weight loss → ★ 'was that on purpose?' (yes — the injection), appetite, dysphagia, haematemesis/melaena, lumps, FHx · urinary · SADMA · summarise · explain each result in plain words · dx + CAUSE · DDx · management spoken: admit, fluids (the single most important treatment), analgesia, antiemetic, USS, lipids + Ca, early feeding, no routine antibiotics, stop the GLP-1 and report the reaction.

back.dx: Acute pancreatitis — 9/10 epigastric pain boring through to the back, eased sitting forward, food makes it worse, bilious vomiting ×5–6, lipase markedly raised. Cause by version: A alcohol (twelve drinks Saturday); B1 severe hypertriglyceridaemia (inherited — father); B2 semaglutide — no alcohol, no lipid disorder, gallbladder out four years ago (choledocholithiasis still possible — look), pancreatitis is a recognised uncommon effect of GLP-1 agonists → stop it, report it, 'you haven't done anything wrong'. Mildly raised AST/ALT are expected with pancreatitis and prompt a gallstone look, not a second disease; normal bilirubin suggests the main duct isn't blocked. 3 kg loss was intentional — a therapeutic effect, not a red flag.

B2: ★ 'The two commonest causes are gallstones and alcohol, and neither fits you well — though stones can still form in the tube even after the gallbladder is removed, so we will look. I can't prove that today, but it is high on my list, and I think we should stop it while we sort this out.' / 'Have I done something wrong?' → ★ 'Not at all. A: 'The most likely cause is the alcohol, and I want to explain that without any judgement. A large amount at once can trigger the pancreas to digest itself. The single most useful thing for preventing this again is stopping alcohol, and I'd like to help you with that rather than just tell you to.' / B1: 'Your blood carries a fat called triglyceride — yours is extremely high, high enough to inflame the pancreas directly. FAIL — Accepting 'nothing makes it better or worse' — 'what about food — is it any different when you eat?' → 'now you say it, worse after I eat'; then both probing questions aloud: 'is there a particular food that sets it off — spicy, dairy, bread and pasta, fatty?' (food type separates coeliac, lactose and biliary colic) and 'how soon after eating — straight away or a few hours later?' (within the hour = gastric; 2–5 hours, nocturnal, relieved by food = duodenal, benign)

plan: 'Am I speaking with Susan? How can I help?' → 'food sticking, a few weeks, I'm worried' → 'that does sound worrying, and you were right to come in — I'd like to ask a number of questions to work out what's causing it'

★ 'Is it hard to swallow, or painful to swallow?' (hard) · ★ 'hard to start the swallow — cough or choke as you begin? or does it go down and then get stuck — in your throat or your chest?' (goes down, catches mid-sternum) · ★ 'solid food only, or liquids as well?' (solids only; bread and meat worst)

How long (6 wk) · first time · every day or on and off · ★ 'gradually getting worse?' (definitely) · better/worse, particular foods · impact: 'managing to eat enough?' (soft/mashed food, not enjoying eating)

(ever → 20/day, quit 10 y) · alcohol (2 glasses most nights) · spicy, coffee · other conditions, FHx (mother bowel cancer at 70) · ★ 'is there anything particular on your mind?' → sister-in-law

(B) Card: general/vitals normal, no lymphadenopathy, no goitre, chest clear, abdomen soft, neuro normal → ★ aloud: 'I note the examination is entirely normal. A normal examination does not exclude an oesophageal malignancy and my concern is unchanged.'

★ 'Susan, I've been thinking about a number of conditions that cause difficulty swallowing. In your case I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer in the food pipe. It is not confirmed, and that is exactly why I want to arrange a test. My reasons: reflux for a long time and the Mylanta that used to help has stopped working; it is getting worse; you have lost six kilograms without meaning to; and it happens only with solid food, which suggests something is physically blocking the way rather than a problem with the muscle movement.' · 'but the examination was normal?' → ★ 'you're right, and I want to be honest — I examined you and could not find anything abnormal, but a normal examination does not rule out a cancer; early tumours very often produce no physical signs. My concern comes from your symptoms, and it has not changed.' · DDx in groups, ~9 s each: other cancers pressing on the pipe — throat, thyroid, lung; narrowing from long-standing reflux — a stricture; infections in the throat; movement problems — nerve conditions (stroke, MS, myasthenia, diabetes), immune conditions (scleroderma), achalasia; medications. 'The camera test sorts between them.'

★ 'I'll arrange the camera test urgently and refer you to Adelaide today; our nurse will start the travel scheme paperwork. I'd like our dietitian to see you in the meantime. If you reach the point where you cannot swallow your own saliva, if food becomes completely stuck, or if you vomit blood, go straight to the emergency department.' · 'am I going to be alright?' → no false reassurance: 'I don't know yet — that's what the test is for, and I'm not waiting' · questions

Version C: 'The most likely cause is a narrowing of the food pipe — a stricture. These are scars caused by long-term inflammation from acid coming up, and they narrow the pipe so solid food catches. A cancer of the food pipe is still on my list and I haven't ruled it out; you don't have the warning signs, which is reassuring, but the camera test is what tells us for certain.' / 'Isn't it just GORD?' → 'GORD is the underlying condition but does not itself cause dysphagia — the swallowing difficulty is from a peptic stricture, a complication of years of reflux. pefe: Role-player: Susan Hartley, 57, front office at a Kadina transport yard, lives in Wallaroo with husband Ray; composed, practical, tense — frightened and covering it. Answers only what's asked. 'Do you smoke?' → flat 'No'; 'have you ever smoked?' → '20 a day, gave up 10 years ago'. The Mylanta line delivered with emphasis once — not repeated if missed. Version B: after 'cancer', 'but you said the examination was normal?' then waits in silence — soften = fail. 'Am I going to be alright?' once. Hidden: sister-in-law died of oesophageal cancer 4 years ago — only if asked concerns, else at the very end

Version B card: general appearance normal, vitals normal, neck — no lymphadenopathy, no goitre, chest clear, abdomen soft non-tender, neuro normal. Version C: no weight loss/appetite change/tiredness, not progressive, heartburn + metallic taste + water brash, lots of spicy food

Dysphagia logic: oropharyngeal (difficulty initiating, cough/choke, nasal regurgitation — neuro/muscular, pharyngeal pouch) vs oesophageal (sticks after swallowing — throat vs chest); solids only, progressive = mechanical obstruction (cancer, stricture, extrinsic compression); solids and liquids from the start, intermittent = motility (achalasia, spasm, scleroderma); odynophagia = infection (candida, HSV, CMV), pill oesophagitis, ulcerated tumour. Six differential groups: cancers (oesophageal, oropharyngeal, thyroid, lung/mediastinal) · strictures/reflux (peptic, Schatzki, eosinophilic oesophagitis in the young) · infection · neurological motility (stroke, MS, MND, myasthenia, Parkinson's, diabetic neuropathy) · autoimmune (scleroderma, Sjögren) · medications (bisphosphonates, doxycycline, NSAIDs, KCl; anticholinergics)

Oesophageal cancer risks: adenocarcinoma — GORD/Barrett's, obesity, male; SCC — smoking, alcohol, achalasia, caustic injury. First investigation: gastroscopy with biopsy (Category 1, urgent VERIFY timeframe); barium swallow first only for suspected pharyngeal pouch; CT/PET for staging after tissue; MDT. Peptic stricture: endoscopic dilatation + long-term PPI, biopsy the stricture

SA: Category 1 referral to an Adelaide upper GI unit · PATS travel/accommodation started at this visit · Country Health Connect · dietitian · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if she obstructs completely or aspirates · TIS 131 450

Six differential groups: cancers (gastric, oesophageal) · ulcer/reflux (PUD, oesophagitis, gastritis) · varices (liver block) · Mallory-Weiss (vomit count) · bleeding disorders/anticoagulants · swallowed blood (epistaxis)/haemoptysis (source questions). Dysphagia is the cardinal symptom of oesophageal cancer — its absence ranks it third

Four boxes for a vague complaint: describe it · time it · triggers and relief · impact. Triple loss: weight, appetite, colour (pallor). Weight loss three follow-ups: kilos, period, intentional? Red flags for dyspepsia: weight loss, anaemia/bleeding (melaena, haematemesis), dysphagia, persistent vomiting, epigastric mass, age ≥50–55 new onset, FHx. DDx order: gastric cancer, then PUD — never the reverse with weight loss and melaena at 50+. Task 4: endoscopy with biopsy → FBE + iron studies → stop; H. pylori from biopsies (UBT if delayed; test of cure); no FOBT; CEA/CA19-9 not diagnostic; staging CT after tissue; colonoscopy only if gastroscopy normal with IDA

Gastric adenocarcinoma risks: H. pylori, smoking, alcohol, salt/smoked/processed food, pernicious anaemia/atrophic gastritis, previous gastric surgery, FHx/CDH1; Virchow's node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg tumour = advanced. Category 1 endoscopy referral VERIFY timeframe; MDT; PATS

dx: **Biliary colic — transient obstruction of the cystic duct by a stone, causing pain without infection or inflammation. The stone falls back and the pain settles.**

**Explain the three as a PROGRESSION, not a list: a stone in the neck of the gallbladder that FALLS BACK gives biliary colic · a stone that STAYS gives cholecystitis · a stone that MOVES ON into the common bile duct and obstructs it gives cholangitis.** Said in that order the differences look inevitable rather than memorised.
**Biliary colic: episodes UNDER 6 HOURS · after fatty food · radiating to the RIGHT SHOULDER BLADE · no fever, no jaundice · normal bloods · normal examination between attacks.**

**The diagnosis is made on the history of the episodes, and a normal examination does not rule it out** — say that to the patient explicitly, because she will otherwise hear 'normal' as 'nothing wrong'.

**Ask the jaundice block in EVERY right upper quadrant station, whatever the vital signs say**: yellowing, dark urine, pale stools, itching. **Scleral icterus appears before skin jaundice, and in an examination-report format you never see the patient at all.**

**The layman explanation, one picture for three diseases**: **'your gallbladder is a small bag under the liver that stores bile, the fluid that helps digest fat. When you eat something fatty the bag squeezes. If there are stones in it, one can block the outlet — that gives pain for an hour or two until it falls back. If the stone stays stuck the bag becomes inflamed and infected. And if a stone escapes into the main drainage tube and blocks it, bile backs up into the blood, which turns you yellow, and the tube gets infected — that is the most dangerous of the three.'**

**Management: analgesia · reassurance · low-fat diet advice to reduce the frequency · ULTRASOUND to confirm the stones and LFTs to check the liver · then ELECTIVE LAPAROSCOPIC CHOLECYSTECTOMY, which is the only definitive treatment.**

**Her three questions, answered: dissolving tablets exist but work poorly, take a long time and the stones usually come back · she does not have to have surgery, it is her decision · but if she does nothing the attacks tend to continue and a stone may get properly stuck, which causes the more serious problems.** **You can live perfectly well without a gallbladder.**

**Courvoisier's law: in a jaundiced patient, a palpable but NON-TENDER gallbladder is unlikely to be gallstones** — chronic stone disease scars and shrinks the gallbladder. **Suspect malignant obstruction, typically carcinoma of the head of the pancreas or a periampullary tumour.** Say the law by name.

**A previous cholecystectomy does not close the biliary tree** — stones can remain in or form in the common bile duct, so **choledocholithiasis and cholangitis stay on the list.** **SA: elective cholecystectomy is a PATS-supported metropolitan referral; TIS National 131 450.**
plan: **'Examiner, may I confirm the patient is haemodynamically stable — blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?'** Then introduce, **offer analgesia if she is in pain**, and open.

**The pain, full SICORA with the biliary specifics: show me where · out of ten · DOES IT COME ON AFTER FATTY OR RICH FOOD, AND HOW LONG AFTER · HOW LONG DOES AN EPISODE LAST · DOES IT TRAVEL TO YOUR RIGHT SHOULDER BLADE or the tip of the shoulder · have you had EXACTLY this before · is it constant now, or does it come and go?**

**The jaundice block — four questions, never skipped:** **have you or anyone else noticed any YELLOWING OF YOUR EYES OR SKIN · has your URINE GONE DARK · have your STOOLS GONE PALE or clay-coloured · ANY ITCHING?**

**The infection block: any fevers · ANY SHAKING CHILLS OR RIGORS, the sort where your teeth chatter and you cannot stop shivering · any confusion or drowsiness · any dizziness on standing?** The last two take you from Charcot's triad to Reynolds' pentad.

**The liver risk block: how much alcohol in a usual week, in standard drinks · any blood transfusions, tattoos, piercings, injecting drug use or travel overseas · how much paracetamol, and any herbal or over-the-counter medicines · any liver disease in the family?**

**GI general and red flags: nausea, vomiting, bloating, wind, bowel habit · any WEIGHT LOSS and was it intentional · appetite · difficulty swallowing · vomiting blood · black tarry motions · any lumps?**

**The chest questions, because a RIGHT LOWER LOBE PNEUMONIA presents as RUQ pain: any cough, phlegm, breathlessness, or pain when you take a deep breath?** Then **SADMA**, past medical and surgical history, family history.

**Summarise back, then request the examination, naming every step:** **general appearance — alert, distressed, dehydrated, AND IS THERE SCLERAL ICTERUS OR JAUNDICE OF THE SKIN · all four vital signs including temperature · inspection for scars, distension, movement with respiration, scratch marks · palpation for tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, a palpable gallbladder or LIVER EDGE, AND IF ENLARGED IS IT SMOOTH OR NODULAR, TENDER OR NON-TENDER · MURPHY'S SIGN, named · percussion for tenderness, liver span and shifting dullness · auscultation, bowel sounds AND THE CHEST BASES · groin and rectal examination with STOOL COLOUR ON THE GLOVE · office tests — urine dipstick, blood sugar, and a PREGNANCY TEST in a woman of reproductive age**

**Murphy's sign, named and described:** **'I would perform Murphy's sign.' With the patient lying flat and the abdomen exposed, place your hand at the RIGHT COSTAL MARGIN in the MID-CLAVICULAR LINE. Ask her to BREATHE ALL THE WAY OUT, press your fingers DEEPLY IN UNDER THE COSTAL MARGIN, then ask her to TAKE A DEEP BREATH IN. As the diaphragm descends it pushes the inflamed gallbladder onto your fingers. POSITIVE if she CATCHES HER BREATH AND STOPS INSPIRATION — and to be valid, THE SAME MANOEUVRE ON THE LEFT SHOULD NOT DO THAT.**

**Diagnose on the story and say the normal examination changes nothing.** Then the layman explanation — one picture, three diseases — and the reasons: **pain an hour or two after fatty food, lasting a couple of hours then settling, radiating to the right shoulder blade, recurrent over months, no fever, no jaundice, normal examination between attacks.**

**Management: ultrasound and liver function tests · analgesia · low-fat diet · referral for ELECTIVE LAPAROSCOPIC CHOLECYSTECTOMY** — then answer the three questions she asks about dissolving, choice and doing nothing, and safety-net for **constant pain over six hours, fever with rigors, or yellow eyes.**

**The discriminating behaviour: ask about jaundice, dark urine and pale stools in EVERY right upper quadrant station, and do not let a positive Murphy's sign stop you asking.** **Murphy is positive in cholecystitis AND in cholangitis. Jaundice is what separates them — and jaundice is what changes the treatment from an operating list to an emergency ERCP.**

**The sentence that rescues the station: 'Examiner, you have told me Murphy's sign is positive, which tells me the gallbladder is inflamed. Before I commit to cholecystitis, may I ask — is there any scleral icterus or jaundice, and what is the bilirubin?'** Then: **'that changes my diagnosis. With right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors and jaundice, this is Charcot's triad and I am treating this as ascending cholangitis.'**
**CHARCOT'S TRIAD = pain + fever with rigors + jaundice. REYNOLDS' PENTAD adds hypotension and altered mental state** — suppurative cholangitis with septic shock.
**Treat it as sepsis: resuscitate · BLOOD CULTURES · IV ANTIBIOTICS WITHIN ONE HOUR · fluids · analgesia and an antiemetic · correct coagulopathy · VBG with lactate · HDU if unstable.**
**The definitive treatment is BILIARY DECOMPRESSION BY ERCP WITHIN 24 HOURS** — urgently if there is shock or failure to improve. **Cholecystectomy afterwards, on the same admission where possible.**
**The obstructive picture: bilirubin, ALP and GGT up, ALT mildly up.** **Lipase normal excludes pancreatitis.** **Ultrasound first, then MRCP if the duct is dilated but no stone is seen.**

**Say it to the patient straight without frightening him: 'you have an infection in the drainage tubes of your liver, which are blocked — almost certainly by a gallstone. It is serious, and you are already showing signs the infection is affecting your whole body. But it is very treatable and we are going to start straight away.'** To **'serious how?'**: **serious enough to be in hospital now and on antibiotics within the hour** — then name the three things that told you.

**SA: ERCP is not available on Yorke Peninsula. Suspected cholangitis is a TIME-CRITICAL RETRIEVAL — blood cultures and IV antibiotics within the hour at Wallaroo or Kadina, fluids, then MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 and the receiving unit at TQEH or the Royal Adelaide. DO NOT WAIT FOR LOCAL IMAGING BEFORE YOU MAKE THE CALL.** RFDS for fixed-wing transfer.

**Courvoisier's law: jaundice with a palpable NON-TENDER gallbladder is malignant obstruction until proven otherwise** — typically carcinoma of the head of the pancreas. **And a previous cholecystectomy does not close the biliary tree: stones remain in or form in the common bile duct.**
plan: **'Examiner, may I confirm he is haemodynamically stable — all four observations and saturations?'** → T 39.1, HR 112, BP 108/64. **Say it out loud: 'those observations concern me and I'll be moving quickly.'** Then **offer analgesia before you start.**

**The pain: show me where · out of ten · did it come on after a meal · DOES IT TRAVEL TO YOUR RIGHT SHOULDER BLADE or round to the back · is it constant now · HAVE YOU HAD EXACTLY THIS BEFORE?** → a couple of shorter episodes over the past year that settled — the colic that preceded it.

**The jaundice block, four questions, and he volunteers none of it:** **have you or anyone else noticed any YELLOWING OF YOUR EYES OR SKIN · has your URINE GONE DARK · have your STOOLS GONE PALE or clay-coloured · ANY ITCHING?**

**The infection block: any fevers · WAS THAT A PROPER RIGOR — teeth chattering, shaking the bed, couldn't stop · any confusion or drowsiness · any dizziness on standing?** The last two are what take you to Reynolds' pentad.

**The liver risk block: alcohol in standard drinks per week · blood transfusions, tattoos, piercings, injecting drug use, travel · paracetamol and any herbal or over-the-counter medicines · family history of liver disease.**

**GI red flags and the chest: nausea and vomiting, bowels, appetite · any weight loss, intentional or not · difficulty swallowing, vomiting blood, black motions, lumps · ANY COUGH, PHLEGM, BREATHLESSNESS OR PAIN ON DEEP BREATHING?** Then **SADMA**.

**Summarise back, then request the examination, naming every step:** **general appearance — alert, distressed, dehydrated, AND IS THERE SCLERAL ICTERUS OR JAUNDICE OF THE SKIN · all four vital signs including temperature · inspection for scars, distension, movement with respiration, scratch marks · palpation for tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, a palpable gallbladder or LIVER EDGE, AND IF ENLARGED IS IT SMOOTH OR NODULAR, TENDER OR NON-TENDER · MURPHY'S SIGN, named · percussion for tenderness, liver span and shifting dullness · auscultation, bowel sounds AND THE CHEST BASES · groin and rectal examination with STOOL COLOUR ON THE GLOVE · office tests — urine dipstick, blood sugar, and a PREGNANCY TEST in a woman of reproductive age**

**Murphy's sign, named and described in full:** **'I would perform Murphy's sign.' With the patient lying flat and the abdomen exposed, place your hand at the RIGHT COSTAL MARGIN in the MID-CLAVICULAR LINE. Ask her to BREATHE ALL THE WAY OUT, press your fingers DEEPLY IN UNDER THE COSTAL MARGIN, then ask her to TAKE A DEEP BREATH IN. As the diaphragm descends it pushes the inflamed gallbladder onto your fingers. POSITIVE if she CATCHES HER BREATH AND STOPS INSPIRATION — and to be valid, THE SAME MANOEUVRE ON THE LEFT SHOULD NOT DO THAT.** **Then, on being told it is positive, ASK THE FOLLOW-UP about scleral icterus and bilirubin rather than committing.**

**Reason out loud: Murphy positive tells me the gallbladder is inflamed — but that is true in cholecystitis and in cholangitis, so it is THE JAUNDICE AND THE OBSTRUCTIVE LIVER TESTS that decide this. This is Charcot's triad: ascending cholangitis.**

**Tell the patient plainly**, answer 'serious how?' with the three findings that told you, then **the differentials: cholecystitis alone, a duct stone without infection, and hepatitis — and why each is less likely.**

**Immediate management, in order: a drip in each arm · BLOOD CULTURES · IV ANTIBIOTICS WITHIN THE HOUR · fluids · analgesia and an antiemetic · correct coagulopathy · ULTRASOUND to confirm · then ERCP WITHIN 24 HOURS for biliary decompression, and cholecystectomy afterwards on the same admission.** **In a rural setting, MedSTAR is being phoned while that is happening.** Offer to call someone for him.
pefe: **Vital signs first, and visibly act on them.** A temperature of 39 with rigors and a heart rate of 112 is sepsis until proven otherwise.
**Ask for SCLERAL ICTERUS by name in the general-appearance step** — it appears before skin jaundice and it is the finding that converts cholecystitis into cholangitis.

**Imaging: ULTRASOUND FIRST — stones, wall thickness, pericholecystic fluid, and whether the COMMON BILE DUCT IS DILATED. MRCP if the duct is dilated but no stone is seen.** **Do not wait for imaging before starting antibiotics or making the retrieval call.**

**Ask for the chest bases** — right lower lobe pneumonia presents as RUQ pain with fever and is the differential nobody offers.
**Antibiotics within 1 hour. ERCP within 24 hours. Cholecystectomy within 72 hours is the CHOLECYSTITIS number — do not confuse them.** VERIFY local timing policy.

setting: Regional SA general practice. The master diarrhoea history: six minutes, then diagnosis and differentials to the patient. Duration is deliberately not on the door. The role-play version (David, 41) is the multiple-findings case — five days of watery diarrhoea, amoxicillin finished three days ago, Bali six weeks ago with street food, father with bowel cancer at 71. Name ONE most likely diagnosis with reasons, then the rest grouped, each justified from what he said.

time: 8 min.
