back.dx: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (amoxicillin 5 days for a sore throat, finished 3 days ago; diarrhoea began during the course) — five days of watery stools 6–7/day, no blood, no fever, low crampy pain, not nocturnal; the more serious version, pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile toxin), must be excluded with a stool test. Still considering a Bali-acquired infection (street food, ice, six weeks ago) and the travel group; bowel cancer stays on the list because of his father (diagnosed at 71) but is unlikely — no bleeding, no weight loss. Plan: stool MCS + C. difficile toxin PCR, oral rehydration (Hydralyte), avoid loperamide for now, safety-net, review 2–3 days.
plan: 'I'm Dr —; can I confirm your name and date of birth? What's brought you in?' → 'five days of bad diarrhoea, worried' → ★ 'that's exhausting, and I can understand the worry. I'd like to ask a series of questions about your bowels — some are personal — then tell you what I think. Is that all right?'

★ Timing: when (5 d), constant, worse?, ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' (no) · ★ CCCVO: 'how many times a day? watery, or soft and loose? any blood? large bulky amount? particularly offensive — floats, sticks to the pan, hard to flush?' (6–7, watery, no blood, not bulky) · better/worse (Gastro-Stop hasn't helped) · 'how is this affecting day to day?'

(amoxicillin, 5 d, sore throat; diarrhoea started while on it) · Gastro-Stop, Nurofen · thyroid: heat, racing heart

Sexual screen (married, wife) · IBS: settles after going? alternating? stress? · PMHx · ★ summarise back: 'five days of watery diarrhoea 6–7×/day, no blood, no fever, low crampy pain; amoxicillin finished a few days ago; Bali six weeks ago with street food; father bowel cancer at 71 — have I missed anything?' · 'was there anything you were particularly worried about?' → 'is this cancer? my dad…'

★ 'There are a few things that could be causing this, and I'd rather be honest about that than pick one and ignore the rest. The most likely is antibiotic-associated diarrhoea — antibiotics upset the balance of the normal bacteria in your bowel, and that causes loose stools.' · ★ 'There is a more serious version I need to make sure you don't have, called pseudomembranous colitis — one particular bug overgrows and produces a toxin. It's checked with a simple stool test.' · 'I'm also still considering an infection picked up in Bali, given the street food, along with the travel-related infections as a group. And because your father had bowel cancer I keep that on my list — unlikely, no bleeding, no weight loss, and he was diagnosed at 71, but I don't leave it off.' · 'which one?' → 'my money is on the antibiotics; the stool test tells us whether it's the serious version' · plan: fluids/Hydralyte, ★ avoid Gastro-Stop for now, stool test, ★ safety-net (fever, blood, severe pain, faint → ED), review 2–3 days with results; do the screening kit

★ 'Because you've been overseas I'd like to go through that trip in detail — where did you go, how long, what did you do? Any bushwalking or insect bites? Contact with anyone unwell, or with animals? Any drug use? Tattoos, piercings or medical treatment? Street food, ice, unbottled water? Did you see a GP before you went?'

★ 'Which antibiotic was it, how long for, and what was it for?' / ★ 'Have you lost any weight without meaning to — how much, and over how long?' / ★ 'Any family history of bowel cancer — and how old were they when they were diagnosed?' / 'Have you done the bowel screening test that comes in the post?'

★ 'Based on what you've told me, the most likely explanation is …' (never 'Bali belly' or 'traveller's diarrhoea' — neither is a diagnosis) / ★ 'Antibiotics upset the balance of the normal bacteria that live in your bowel.' / 'There are several possibilities and I'd rather be honest with you about that.'

★ 'I've specifically checked for the things that would worry me, and they're not there.' / ★ 'Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you develop a fever, blood in the stool, severe pain, or you feel faint.' / 'Was there anything you were particularly worried about today?'

Gastroenteritis version (recent travel, street food): 'Most likely you have a condition called gastroenteritis — an infection in your bowel. Three reasons: you've just come back from overseas; you ate street food, an important risk factor for a food-borne infection; and watery diarrhoea coming on over a few days with cramping fits an infection. I'm not going to guess the exact bug — knowing which doesn't change what we do first.' / DDx: 'because you've travelled — typhoid, malaria, bacterial infections, which is why I asked about mosquito bites; hepatitis A; inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, dairy intolerance, medication side effects, an overactive thyroid, irritable bowel — and I always think about bowel cancer in anyone with a change in their bowels.'
pefe: Role-player: David Bennett, 41, diesel mechanic (Kadina), Wallaroo, wife and two kids; 10 cigs/day, 6–8 SD Fridays; amoxicillin 500 mg tds × 5 d finished 3 d ago (sore throat) — gives 'I finished some antibiotics' and waits to be asked which; Gastro-Stop × 4 (no help), occasional Nurofen; father bowel cancer at 71 (age only if asked); never did the screening kit. Tired, embarrassed, cooperative; answers only the last part of a compound question; tense at 'cancer'. Hidden: frightened it's cancer — only if asked concerns/FHx; at ~6 min 'is this cancer? my dad had bowel cancer'. If reassured before weight/blood asked: 'but how do you know?'

No examination task. Versions: acute traveller (gastroenteritis), antibiotic-associated (this), Version F chronic coeliac (MED-137), norovirus cruise ship (MED-138); 'I'm gay and my partner has it too' converts to the PrEP station (MED-139)

Definitions: acute <14 d · persistent 14–30 d · chronic >4 wk. C. difficile onset during the course or up to 8 weeks after, most within 2 weeks. Coeliac serology: tTG-IgA + total IgA on a gluten-containing diet. iFOBT 2-yearly 45–74 (average risk); moderate risk (first-degree relative <60, or two relatives): colonoscopy 5-yearly from 10 years before the earliest diagnosis or 50, whichever earlier VERIFY — father at 71 = average/slightly above. Brand names: Nexium/Somac = PPI; Gastro-Stop = loperamide; Hydralyte/Gastrolyte = ORS

Investigations when indicated: stool MCS/PCR (bacterial, viral, parasitic), C. difficile toxin, ova/cysts/parasites (Giardia after travel), FBE/UEC/CRP, coeliac serology, TSH, faecal calprotectin for chronic; notifiable in SA: shigella, salmonella, campylobacter, giardia, hepatitis A, typhoid VERIFY. Loperamide avoided in bloody/febrile diarrhoea and suspected C. difficile. Travel DDx: typhoid, malaria (fever + travel = malaria until excluded), hepatitis A/E, amoebiasis, giardia, cholera

setting: Cruise ship berthed in Sydney after sailing from New Zealand; you are the ship's medical officer. stem: A 40-year-old man on a cruise ship berthed in Sydney has been diagnosed with norovirus gastroenteritis. He is insisting on being discharged home.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Perform an assessment, directed to the examiner, of whether this patient can be released home
time: 8 min. ★ Opening for the approach marks: 'I can hear how frustrating this is — I'd be frustrated too; can I ask what's making you so keen to get home? There may be something I can help with. Whatever you tell me stays between us.' (cat alone at home → 'we can almost certainly arrange for someone to look in on her') · ★ 'when did it start? is it still going? if it has stopped — when was the last symptom?' (the exclusion criterion is time since the last symptom) · count, consistency, ★ blood (would change the diagnosis) · fever/chills, abdominal pain, N/V, dizziness (must be asymptomatic, not just diarrhoea-free) · ★ 'eating and drinking normally and keeping it down?' · ★ immunocompromise: diabetes, cancer, steroids, chemo · ★ 'what treatment did you receive on board?' → IV fluids → the cannula · ★ occupation: food handler, childcare, healthcare (changes the exclusion period, public health duty) · to examiner: appearance/dehydration, vitals incl postural BP, full abdominal examination, ★ 'look at the cannula site' → photo: erythema, swelling, purulent discharge · ★ release criteria stated: no diarrhoea/vomiting for 48 h, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no dehydration, normal abdomen → release, remove cannula, oral flucloxacillin, mark the edge, GP 48 h / ED if fever or spreading.

back.dx: Resolved norovirus gastroenteritis meeting exclusion criteria for release (symptom-free ≥48 h, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no clinical dehydration, normal abdominal examination) — plus a peripheral cannula-site infection (erythema, swelling, purulent discharge at the insertion point) from the IV fluids given on board: remove the cannula, oral flucloxacillin as for a skin and soft tissue infection, mark the margin, GP review in 48 h, ED if fever, spreading redness or unwell. IV antibiotics only for systemic features (high fever, hypotension, tachycardia, drowsiness) — he has none. Not a reason to keep him on board.

stem: Michael Reid, 32, presents with diarrhoea for two weeks. 'I'm gay, and my boyfriend has exactly the same thing.'
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 min. Identity, open → disclosure → ★ 'thank you for telling me that so openly — it's directly relevant. I'd like to ask about your bowels, and also about your sexual health, because that may well be part of what's going on. Everything is confidential. Is that all right?' · ★ PrEP first: on it? every day, missed doses? since when, who prescribes? ★ 'last HIV/STI check and did you get the results?' (a month ago, never got them → 'I'll retrieve them today — not the same as a negative') · ★ three boxes — partners (stable? multiple? male/female/both), practices (condoms? oral/anal? receptive/insertive?), risk (previous STIs — chlamydia ×2, gonorrhoea, syphilis; sex under alcohol/drugs; sex work) · say it back · ★ seroconversion: fevers/night sweats, sore throat, glands, rash, mouth ulcers, myalgia · ★ anorectal: pain, discharge, tenesmus, bleeding · generic structure at pace: timing, CCCVO, general GI, travel/contacts, hepatitis + hep A/B vaccination, IBD/coeliac/lactose, other meds, thyroid, red flags · summarise · ★ name HIV as the condition to exclude, reasons, PrEP not absolute, grouped DDx (PrEP side effect, proctitis — chlamydia/gonorrhoea/LGV, enteric STIs — shigella/giardia, hepatitis A, general causes), ★ consent + pre-test discussion (window, repeat 6 and 12 weeks, result in person), three-site STI screen, ★ partner in for the same tests.

back.dx: Acute HIV infection to be excluded — two weeks of watery diarrhoea 4–5/day in a man on PrEP with ~fortnightly missed doses, a fluey illness with sore throat, fever, myalgia and a chest rash two weeks ago, persistent cervical lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers, some anal discharge; risk profile: open relationship, several male partners, condomless receptive anal sex, chlamydia ×2, gonorrhoea, syphilis, chemsex; last screen a month ago with results never seen. Most probable diagnoses are a PrEP side effect or a sexually transmitted enteric infection/proctitis — HIV is first as the diagnosis I most need to exclude because the consequence of missing it is greatest and the seroconversion picture fits. PrEP substantially reduces but does not eliminate risk; breakthrough is described.

Guarded if the doctor is uncomfortable/apologetic; warm if straightforward. Hidden: frightened it's HIV, feels foolish because of PrEP; if HIV named: 'but I'm on PrEP — I thought that meant I couldn't get it'; if never named, at ~7 min 'should I be worried about HIV?'; if told PrEP means he can't have HIV → 'oh good' and let them fail

back.dx: Pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile toxin-mediated colitis) 'may have' — three days of profuse watery diarrhoea 6–7/day with cramps starting ~10 days after a five-day amoxicillin course for bronchitis; no blood, no travel, mild dehydration, normal obs and abdomen. Second (and more common): plain antibiotic-associated diarrhoea — settles alone; a stool toxin test tells them apart, and only the first needs specific treatment. Recurrence ~1 in 5.
plan: 'I'm Dr —; can I confirm your name and date of birth? Before I tell you what I think is going on, talk me through what's been happening over the last few days.' → 'thank you — I've read your notes and I have a clear picture. I'll explain what I think this is, what tests I want, and what we'll do. Was there anything you were particularly worried about?' ('been reading online — it's not cancer, is it?')

★ 'I'm concerned you may have a condition called pseudomembranous colitis. Your bowel normally has a large population of harmless bacteria living in balance. When you take an antibiotic, it doesn't only kill the bug causing your chest infection — it disturbs that balance. One particular bug, Clostridioides difficile, can take over and overgrow. That bug produces a toxin — a poison — and it is the toxin that inflames the lining of the bowel and causes the diarrhoea and cramps. It's called pseudomembranous because with a camera we'd see whitish patches on the lining.' · 'is that serious? do I need hospital?' → non-severe form, treatable as an outpatient if the plan is followed

★ 'The other possibility — and the more common one — is simply that the antibiotic itself has loosened your bowels. That settles by itself. The difference matters, because the first needs specific treatment and the second doesn't, and a stool test tells us which it is.' · DDx with reasons from the stem: food/travel infection (no travel, no eating out, nobody unwell), IBD (no blood/mucus, not nocturnal, only 3 days), coeliac (not greasy/floating), dairy (no link), thyroid (no weight loss/heat), other medications (I'll check — Somac), bowel cancer (at 40 with no bleeding, weight loss or FHx — very unlikely; it stays on the list with any habit change)

★ Investigations, each with 'because': 'the most important test is a stool sample looking for that toxin — a PCR — that confirms or rules out this diagnosis · on the same sample, other bowel infections — viral, bacterial, parasitic · bloods: FBC and CRP for the degree of inflammation; kidney function and salts, because diarrhoea upsets those and you're a bit dry · faecal calprotectin — our best screening test for inflammatory bowel disease · coeliac antibodies — keep eating gluten normally until it's done · there's also a camera test, a sigmoidoscopy, because this condition has a characteristic appearance — I wouldn't do that first; the stool test is simpler and should give the answer'

stem: Mrs Margaret Harding, 67, presents with diarrhoea for two weeks. Gastro-Stop from the chemist is not helping — if anything it's worse. Lower abdominal ache.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 min. Identity, open → 'two weeks is worth sorting properly — and worsening despite treatment tells me we need the cause, not more symptom relief' · permission · timing, nocturnal, CCCVO (4–5/day, watery, no blood) · pain: where (low, no side), radiation, relation to bowels, ★ tenesmus ('feel you haven't fully emptied, or need to go and nothing comes?' — yes) · general GI · ★ 2:10 red-flag block 'I ask everybody with a change in their bowels': weight loss (how much/how long), appetite, lumps, tiredness, blood/black stools, ★ 'before this, had your bowels changed — more/less often, different shape?', FHx bowel cancer + age, ★ 'done the bowel screening kit?' (never sent it back) → all negative — do not change course · at speed: travel/contacts, meds incl chemist/antibiotics/anticoagulants, IBD ×4, coeliac/lactose, thyroid, alcohol · 3:50 hands off · ★ seven named PEFE steps: appearance (well/unwell, dehydration, pallor, jaundice, cachexia, rash) · vitals + postural BP · neck — thyroid, cervical + supraclavicular nodes · abdomen inspection · palpation (tenderness, masses, ★ organomegaly) → hepatomegaly 4 cm → ★ pursue: smooth or irregular/nodular? tender? pulsatile? · percussion (liver span, shifting dullness), auscultation, groins · ★ 'I would like to perform a digital rectal examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present' → perianal inspection; digital: mass → ★ pursue: cm from the verge, fixed/mobile, proportion of circumference, blood on the glove · dipstick · warning shot → findings → concern → ★ pause → her three questions → plan → DDx → stop loperamide → obstruction safety-net → support.

back.dx: Colorectal (rectal) carcinoma with hepatic metastases until proven otherwise — two weeks of worsening watery diarrhoea 4–5/day despite loperamide, dull lower abdominal ache, tenesmus, slightly dry, all red flags negative, never did the screening kit; PEFE: irregular non-tender hepatomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin, no splenomegaly/ascites, and on DRE a firm fixed rectal mass ~6 cm from the anal verge involving half the circumference with blood on the glove. Explain with a warning shot, name the findings, name the concern ('may be a cancer … may have spread to the liver'), pause, never give a prognosis; urgent colonoscopy + biopsy, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bloods (FBE, iron, UEC, LFT, coags, CEA baseline), referral today with a follow-up call, stop the Gastro-Stop, obstruction red flags, Cancer Council SA.
plan: Identity, open → ★ 'two weeks is worth sorting out properly, and it's getting worse despite what you've tried — so we need to find the cause rather than keep treating the symptom. I'll ask some questions, examine you, then tell you what I think. Some are personal — is that all right?'

Timing: 2 wk, constant, worse, not nocturnal · CCCVO: 4–5/day, watery, no blood, not bulky · pain: low, no side, no radiation, relation to defecation, ★ 'do you ever feel you haven't fully emptied, or need to go and nothing comes?' → yes (register, move on)

General GI: N/V, bloating (a bit), constipated before (no), fever · ★ 2:10 'there are some questions I ask everybody with a change in their bowels': weight loss — how much/how long (none), appetite (normal), lumps, tiredness (a bit), blood/black stools (no), ★ 'before this, had your bowels changed at all — more often, less often, a different shape?' (no), FHx bowel cancer + age (none), ★ 'have you done the bowel screening test that comes in the post?' (got it, never sent it back)

At speed: travel/contacts · meds incl chemist (perindopril, Gastro-Stop), antibiotics, blood thinners · IBD ×4 · greasy stools, dairy · thyroid · alcohol (glass most nights) · concerns ('I just want it to stop — granddaughter's wedding in three weeks') · 3:50 hands off

★ 'Examiner, I'd like specific findings — yes or no is fine. General appearance — well or unwell? dehydration — dry mucous membranes, skin turgor? pallor, jaundice, cachexia? rashes? · vital signs incl postural BP, RR, sats · neck — thyroid, cervical and supraclavicular nodes · abdomen inspection — moves with respiration, distension, scars, visible masses · palpation — tenderness, guarding, rebound, masses, ★ organomegaly' → 'hepatomegaly, 4 cm below the costal margin' → ★ 'is the edge smooth, or irregular and nodular? tender? pulsatile? splenomegaly, ascites, jaundice?' → irregular, non-tender, no spleen, no ascites · 'percussion — liver span, shifting dullness; bowel sounds; groins — hernias, nodes'

★ 'And I would like to perform a digital rectal examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present. On inspection of the perianal area — fissures, tags, piles, masses? On digital examination — is there a mass, how far from the anal verge, fixed or mobile, what proportion of the circumference, and is there blood on the glove?' → firm mass → ★ '~6 cm, fixed, half the circumference, blood on the glove' · dipstick (ketones)

★ Warning shot: 'Mrs Harding, I'd like to talk to you about what I found when I examined you. I'd rather be straight with you than vague — is that all right? Is there anyone you'd like to have with you?' → ★ 'I found two things. There is a lump in your back passage, and your liver is enlarged — I can feel it below your ribs, which I shouldn't normally be able to do.' [★ pause 2–3 s — do not fill it] → ★ 'I'm concerned that the lump may be a cancer in the bowel, and that the enlarged liver may mean it has spread there. I can't be certain today — I need tests to confirm it — but I don't want to tell you it's nothing when I'm worried that it isn't.' · 'but I feel fine, no weight loss' → 'that's true, and it's a good thing — but those symptoms don't always appear early; what I can feel on examination matters more than what the symptoms have shown so far' · 'are you sure?' → 'no, not yet — I'm sure of what I felt, and that it needs investigating quickly' · ★ 'how long have I got?' → 'I genuinely can't answer that, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I guessed — we don't yet know what it is, how big, or whether it has spread; once we have the camera test and the scan the specialist team can talk to you properly'

Plan: urgent colonoscopy with biopsy · CT chest/abdomen/pelvis · bloods today (FBE, iron, UEC, LFT, coags, CEA baseline) · ★ 'I'll do the referral this afternoon and ring you myself with the appointment' · DDx honestly: inflammation of the bowel, reduced blood supply, infection, a liver problem itself — 'the tests will sort them out; I'm telling you my main concern because I think you'd want to know' · ★ stop the Gastro-Stop · ★ safety-net: 'very painful or bloated tummy, vomiting, stop passing wind, or blood → sooner or ED' · review in a few days regardless · Cancer Council 13 11 20 — support and transport to Adelaide (PATS) · 'what questions do you have?'
ask: ★ 'It's getting worse despite treatment, so we need to find the cause rather than keep treating the symptom.' / ★ 'Do you ever feel you haven't fully emptied, or that you need to go and nothing comes?' / ★ 'There are some questions I ask everybody with a change in their bowels.' / ★ 'Before this, had your bowels changed at all — more often, less often, a different shape?' / ★ 'Have you done the bowel screening test that comes in the post?'

★ To examiner: 'I would like to perform a digital rectal examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present.' / ★ 'Is that liver edge smooth, or irregular and nodular? Is it tender? Is it pulsatile?' / ★ 'How far from the anal verge? Is it mobile or fixed to surrounding tissue? What proportion of the circumference? Is there blood on the glove?'

★ 'Mrs Harding, I'd like to talk to you about what I found when I examined you. I'd rather be straight with you than vague. Is that all right? Is there anyone you'd like to have with you?' / ★ 'I found two things. There is a lump in your back passage, and your liver is enlarged.' [pause] / ★ 'I'm concerned that the lump may be a cancer in the bowel, and that the enlarged liver may mean it has spread there. I can't be certain today — I need tests to confirm it — but I don't want to tell you it's nothing when I'm worried that it isn't.'

'But I haven't lost any weight' → ★ 'That's true, and it's a good thing. But those symptoms don't always appear early. What I can feel on examination is more important than what the symptoms have shown so far, and that's why I'm not letting it go.' / 'How long have I got?' → ★ 'I genuinely can't answer that, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I guessed. We don't yet know what it is, how big it is, or whether it has spread. Once we have the camera test and the scan, the specialist team will be able to talk to you properly about treatment. What I can tell you is that this is being taken seriously and it's being done quickly.'

'I'm going to arrange an urgent camera test of the bowel — a colonoscopy — and a CT scan of your chest, tummy and pelvis. Bloods today. I'll do the referral this afternoon and I'll ring you myself with the appointment. Please stop the Gastro-Stop. Come back sooner, or go to the emergency department, if your tummy becomes very painful or bloated, if you start vomiting, if you stop passing wind, or if you see blood.'

Examiner challenges: 'every red flag negative — still cancer?' → 'Yes. The examination findings outrank a negative symptom history — a palpable rectal mass with an irregular enlarged liver is metastatic colorectal cancer until proven otherwise; the absence of weight loss and bleeding means the disease has not yet produced those symptoms.' / 'could it be ovarian?' → 'an ovarian mass is felt in the iliac fossa or on bimanual examination, not within the rectum — staging CT would identify an ovarian primary if present.' / 'hepatomegaly unrelated?' → 'possibly — fatty liver, alcohol, right heart failure — but irregular and non-tender favours metastases; characterise on CT/MRI rather than assume.' / 'CEA to diagnose?' → 'No — not sensitive or specific; a baseline for monitoring. Diagnosis is colonoscopy and biopsy.' / obstruction variant (swollen, no wind since yesterday) → distension, bowel sounds, empty ballooned rectum; ED today, NBM, IV, surgical registrar, MedSTAR if deteriorating
pefe: Role-player: Margaret Harding, 67, retired school administrator, Moonta, husband, two children in Adelaide; perindopril; Gastro-Stop 10 days; glass of wine most nights. Brisk, pleasant, mildly impatient about the ineffective tablets; not worried — assumes a bug, wants something stronger; 'granddaughter's wedding in three weeks' if asked concerns; sheepish about the unreturned kit. Gives nothing unasked; every red flag negative. At the diagnosis: goes quiet, flat, disbelieving — 'but I feel fine, I haven't lost any weight', then 'are you sure?', then 'how long have I got?' (a prognosis or timeframe is marked down)

PEFE: looks well; mucous membranes slightly dry; no pallor/jaundice; obs normal, no postural drop; thyroid and nodes normal; abdomen soft, non-tender; ★ hepatomegaly 4 cm below costal margin — irregular, non-tender, no splenomegaly, no ascites; bowel sounds normal; groins normal; ★ DRE (only if requested): firm mass ~6 cm from the verge, fixed, ~half the circumference, blood on the glove. Release with consent/chaperone mark only if said aloud

Rectal cancer: tenesmus, altered habit (diarrhoea/overflow), bleeding, mass on DRE (~half of rectal cancers palpable); liver is the commonest metastatic site (irregular, hard, non-tender hepatomegaly). Work-up: colonoscopy + biopsy (Category 1, ~30 days VERIFY), CT chest/abdo/pelvis, MRI rectum (local staging), MRI liver, FBE/iron/UEC/LFT/coags/CEA baseline; MDT — neoadjuvant chemoradiation for rectal cancer, resection ± liver metastasectomy in selected cases; stoma counselling; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; PATS for travel to Adelaide; the wedding — honest that timing is uncertain

Screening: iFOBT 2-yearly 45–74 average risk; moderate risk colonoscopy 5-yearly from 10 y before earliest FHx diagnosis or 50 VERIFY · loperamide stopped — masking, obstruction risk with a stenosing lesion · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if obstruction from a rural site · TIS 131 450
Consent — The rectal finding is released only if consent and a chaperone are said aloud
fails: Skipping the red-flag block because the history is two weeks; hearing 'Gastro-Stop isn't working' as a minor detail
★ Stopping the abdominal examination at palpation — no DRE requested; consent and chaperone not said aloud; accepting 'hepatomegaly' and 'a mass' without characterising them
Explaining a big liver with no cause; a benign label ('a bug') after negative red flags
No warning shot; filling the silence; false certainty ('you have cancer') or false reassurance; ★ giving a prognosis or stage
No concrete plan/referral today/follow-up call; not stopping loperamide; no obstruction safety-net; not offering support (Cancer Council, someone with her)
numbers: History ~4 min · red flags 2:10 · hands off 3:50 · PEFE 4:00 · explain 6:00 · liver 4 cm, irregular, non-tender · rectal mass ~6 cm from verge, fixed, half circumference, blood on glove
Category 1 colonoscopy ~30 d VERIFY · CT C/A/P · MRI rectum + liver · CEA baseline only · iFOBT 45–74 2-yearly · moderate risk colonoscopy 5-yearly VERIFY
Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · PATS · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450

drive: AMC Clinical Notability › Medicine AMC Clinical › GI › Lower GI › 04_Colorectal_Cancer_Liver_Mets_2_Case_Tasks_Script_Notability.pdf
findings: Looks well; mucous membranes SLIGHTLY DRY; no pallor or jaundice
HEPATOMEGALY 4 cm BELOW THE COSTAL MARGIN — IRREGULAR, NON-TENDER; no splenomegaly, no ascites
A firm mass about 6 cm from the verge, fixed, occupying about half the circumference, with blood on the glove
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Stopping the abdominal examination at palpation with no digital rectal examination requested — you get hepatomegaly alone and spend the explanation talking about a big liver with no idea what caused it; the rectal mass is released only if a DRE is requested, and consent and chaperone must be said aloud ('I would like to perform a digital rectal examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present') (★)

FAIL — Skipping the red-flag block because the history is only two weeks — every recall of this case is silent on the red-flag answers, which strongly suggests the candidates never asked; every one is negative and she gives no prompt ('honestly, I just want it to stop — my granddaughter's wedding is in three weeks'); ask them out loud: weight quantified, appetite, lumps, tiredness, blood or black stools, habit change before this, family history with age, 'have you done the bowel screening kit?' (a year ago, never sent back) (★)

FAIL — Giving a prognosis or a timeframe — 'how long have I got?' → 'I genuinely can't answer that, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I guessed; we don't yet know what it is, how big, or whether it has spread; once we have the camera test and the scan the specialists will talk to you properly'; a stage or a timeframe goes beyond what you can know and is marked down (★)

DO — Hear 'Gastro-Stop isn't working' as the hinge ('getting worse despite treatment tells me we need to find the cause rather than keep treating the symptom'); the pain characterised and tenesmus asked ('do you ever feel you haven't fully emptied?'); the remaining blocks at speed; hands off the history at four minutes

DO — Pursue both findings, don't accept them: 'is the liver edge smooth or irregular and nodular? tender? pulsatile?' (irregular, non-tender) and 'how far from the anal verge? fixed or mobile? what proportion of the circumference? blood on the glove?' (six centimetres, fixed, half, blood); the seven examination steps by name incl. supraclavicular nodes, liver span, shifting dullness, groins, dipstick

SAY — Warning shot ('I'd rather be straight with you than vague — is that all right? is there anyone you'd like with you?'), the two findings, then a two-to-three-second pause you do not fill, then 'I'm concerned the lump may be a cancer in the bowel, and that the enlarged liver may mean it has spread there; I can't be certain today — but I don't want to tell you it's nothing when I'm worried that it isn't'; 'but I feel fine, I haven't lost weight' → 'those symptoms don't always come early; what I can feel matters more than what the symptoms have shown so far'; plan — urgent colonoscopy with biopsy, CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, FBE, iron, LFTs, 'I'll do the referral this afternoon and ring you myself'; differentials named (IBD, ischaemia, infection, a primary liver problem); stop the Gastro-Stop; obstruction safety-net (pain, bloating, vomiting, no wind); Cancer Council 13 11 20; CEA is a baseline, not a diagnostic test; to the examiner — examination findings outrank a negative symptom history

setting: General practice. Everyone knows the recall is haemorrhoids — that knowledge is why candidates fail: it is a RECTAL BLEEDING station, and you are assessed on your approach to rectal bleeding, not on haemorrhoid risk factors. 4-minute history (prompted), PEFE, diagnosis/differentials; 2025 added investigations and follow-up counselling. Proctoscopy must be requested by name — a normal digital examination does not exclude internal haemorrhoids. Father diagnosed at 52 → colonoscopy every 5 years from 42.
stem: Daniel Whelan, 34 (age varies by sitting from the twenties to the seventies), presents with bleeding from the back passage / blood in the stools / blood on the toilet paper.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (4 minutes — prompted)
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Request your further investigations
Counsel the patient regarding further follow-up
time: 8 min. Identity, open, ★ respond to the fear without 'I'm sure it's just piles' · ★ bleeding: when, first time, every time/intermittent, worse; ★ bright red or darker; ★ mixed through, on the outside, or on the paper (three separate parts); amount; brought on by constipation/straining · general GI + ★ dizziness/light-headedness (volume) · ★ 1:50 cancer block first: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, ★ change in habit (frequency/shape), ★ FHx bowel cancer + ★ 'how old were they when diagnosed?' (52), screening · fissure: ★ 'painful when you pass a motion?', constipated, hard stools, straining · haemorrhoids: ★ lump? push it back / goes back itself · IBD ×4 · infection: travel (Bali), contacts, ★ antibiotics — which/how long/what for · drugs/bleeding: ★ anticoagulants/aspirin, bruising, FHx · proctitis if time: sexual, discharge · examiner: appearance/pallor/cachexia, vitals + postural BP, abdomen (distension, masses, tenderness, hepatomegaly, BS, groins) · ★ 'rectal examination with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present' → perianal inspection in three categories (skin — fissure/tags/rash; lumps — external/prolapsed piles, abscess, warts, mass; discharge/bleeding) → digital if not in pain (masses, tenderness, tone, blood on glove) → ★ 'I would like to perform a proctoscopy — internal haemorrhoids often can't be felt digitally' → soft bulky masses · dx haemorrhoids with reasons · ★ cancer named with why unlikely · IBD, infection (Bali), C. difficile, diverticular, polyps, clotting · ★ colonoscopy argued ('I can see the piles but I can't see past them'), FBE/iron, stool sample incl C. difficile · ★ follow-up formula: category 1 iFOBT 45–74; father <60 = moderate risk → colonoscopy every 5 years from 10 years before his diagnosis or 50, whichever earlier → 42; symptoms any age → come back.

back.dx: Internal haemorrhoids (Version B) — three weeks of intermittent bright red blood on the outside of the stool and on the paper, a few drops, painless, worse with constipation, a lump on straining that he pushes back (grade III); proctoscopy: soft bulky masses in the anal canal; everything else normal. Colorectal cancer never off the list: bleeding is not explained by haemorrhoids until the colon has been seen, and his father was diagnosed at 52 → colonoscopy now (symptoms), FBE/iron, stool sample (Bali, unknown antibiotics — C. difficile). Follow-up: moderately increased risk → colonoscopy 5-yearly from 42. Version C (fissure): painful 'like passing glass', constipated, hard stools, no lump, refuses digital examination — inspect for a posterior midline tear and sentinel tag; stool softening, fibre, fluids, warm baths, topical GTN/diltiazem VERIFY; refer if not settled in 6–8 weeks; still discuss colonoscopy.
plan: Identity, open → 'blood is frightening to see, and you were right to come in — it's something we always look into properly. I'll ask some questions, examine you, then tell you what I think and what we'll do.'

★ 'When did it start? first time? every time you open your bowels, or on and off? getting worse? ★ Is the blood bright red and fresh, or darker? ★ Is it mixed through the stool? — on the outside of it? — on the paper when you wipe? Roughly how much — a few drops, or more? Does anything bring it on — constipation, straining?'
General GI: pain, N/V, bloating, D/C, fever · ★ 'felt dizzy or light-headed, especially standing?'

★ 'There are some questions I ask everybody who has bleeding from the back passage': weight loss (how much/how long), appetite, lumps, tiredness, ★ change in habit (more/less often, shape), ★ 'family history of bowel cancer — and how old were they when diagnosed?' (dad — 52), 'bowel screening test?'

Fissure: ★ 'is it painful when you pass a motion?' (no) · constipated, hard stools, straining · haemorrhoids: ★ 'felt any lumps around the back passage? can you push it back in, or does it go back by itself?' (lump; pushes back)

IBD ×4 · infection: ★ travel (Bali 2 wk ago — vomiting/diarrhoea, antibiotics there) → 'which, how long, what for?' (unknown, 5 d) · contacts · ★ 'medications — particularly blood thinners: warfarin, apixaban, clopidogrel, aspirin? bruise easily? FHx bleeding disorder?' · proctitis if time: sexually active, condoms, anal discharge · concerns

★ Examiner: appearance — well, pallor, cachexia · vitals incl postural BP, temperature · abdomen — distension, masses, tenderness, hepatomegaly, bowel sounds, inguinal nodes/hernias → all normal · ★ 'I would like to perform a rectal examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present. On inspection of the perianal area — skin changes: a visible fissure, skin tags, redness, rash? lumps or swellings: external or prolapsed haemorrhoids, abscess, warts, mass? discharge or bleeding?' → unremarkable · 'if not in pain, digital examination — masses, tenderness, anal tone, blood on the glove?' → normal · ★ 'and I would like to perform a proctoscopy — internal haemorrhoids often cannot be felt on digital examination' → soft bulky masses in the anal canal

★ 'Most likely you have haemorrhoids — piles. In the back passage we all have small blood vessels, like cushions; when they swell and enlarge they bleed easily as a stool passes over them. I'm saying that because the bleeding is bright red and on the outside of the stool, it isn't painful, you can feel a lump you can push back in, and when I looked with the small instrument I could see them.' · ★ 'I want to be clear about what else I've thought about. The most important is cancer of the bowel or the back passage. I don't think that's what this is — but bleeding from the back passage is never something I put down to piles without checking, and your father was diagnosed young, which matters.' · IBD; infection (unwell in Bali); a bowel infection that follows antibiotics; diverticular disease; polyps; clotting problems (no thinners)

★ Investigations: 'the main test is a colonoscopy — a camera through the back passage to look at the whole large bowel. I know I've said I think this is piles, and I do. But I can see the piles and I can't see past them — I can't tell you there isn't something further up also bleeding, and the only way to be sure is to look. With your father diagnosed at 52, I wouldn't do anything else.' ('is that because you think it's cancer?' → honest reasons) · FBE + iron (anaemia) · stool sample incl C. difficile (trip + antibiotics) · ★ follow-up formula: 'for most people with no family history — a stool test for hidden blood every two years from 45 to 74, posted automatically. Your situation is different: a first-degree relative diagnosed under 60 puts you in the moderately increased risk group — colonoscopy every five years, starting ten years before your father's diagnosis or at 50, whichever comes first. He was 52, so ten years before is 42, which is earlier than 50 — so from 42, every five years. You're 34; I'll put it in your record.' · 'and whatever your age — a change in bowels lasting more than a couple of weeks, unexplained weight loss, or different bleeding: come back' · haemorrhoid management: fibre, fluids, avoid straining, topical treatment, banding if persistent VERIFY
ask: ★ 'Blood is frightening to see, and you were right to come in.' / ★ 'Is it bright red and fresh, or darker? Is it mixed through the stool, on the outside of it, or on the paper when you wipe?' / 'Have you felt dizzy or light-headed at all, especially when you stand up?'

★ 'There are some questions I ask everybody who has bleeding from the back passage: weight loss without meaning to — how much, over how long? appetite? lumps or bumps? more tired? change in your bowel habit — more often, less often, a different shape? any family history of bowel cancer — and how old were they when they were diagnosed? have you done the bowel screening test?'

★ 'Is it painful when you pass a motion? Have you been constipated — are the stools hard, have you been straining?' / ★ 'Have you felt any lumps around your back passage? Can you push it back in, or does it go back by itself?' / 'Any medications — particularly blood thinners: warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, clopidogrel or aspirin?'

★ To examiner: 'I would like to perform a rectal examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present … and I would like to perform a proctoscopy. Internal haemorrhoids often cannot be felt on digital examination, so this is the test that will show them.'

★ 'Most likely you have haemorrhoids — most people call them piles … I'm saying that because the bleeding is bright red and on the outside of the stool, it isn't painful, you can feel a lump that you can push back in, and when I looked with the small instrument I could see them.' / ★ 'The most important thing I've also considered is cancer of the bowel or the back passage. I don't think that's what this is — but bleeding from the back passage is never something I put down to piles without checking, and in your case your father was diagnosed young, which matters.'

★ 'I can see the piles, but I can't see past them. I can't tell you there isn't something further up that's also bleeding, and the only way to be sure is to look. With your father having been diagnosed at 52, I wouldn't want to do anything else.' / ★ 'Ten years before your father's diagnosis, or 50, whichever comes first — he was 52, so from 42, a colonoscopy every five years.'

Fissure version (painful 'like passing glass', constipated, no lump; declines digital): 'That's absolutely your choice and I won't press it — a fissure is often too painful to examine digitally. Can I still ask for inspection of the perianal area, since a fissure is frequently visible? I'd be looking for a linear tear in the posterior midline and a sentinel skin tag.' / 'I think you have an anal fissure — a small tear in the lining, usually from a hard stool. Piles are usually painless and yours is painful; you've been constipated with hard stools; and there's no lump. Treatment aims at soft stools so the tear can heal — fibre and fluid, a stool softener, warm baths, and an ointment that relaxes the muscle and improves the blood supply. If it doesn't settle in six to eight weeks I'd refer you — and I'd still want to complete an examination once you're comfortable, and still discuss a colonoscopy given the bleeding.'

Examiner challenges: 'he's 22 and obviously piles — colonoscopy?' → 'Yes. Anorectal bleeding is not explained by haemorrhoids until the colon has been seen; youth alone is not a reliable reason to omit it — particularly with a first-degree relative under 60. I'd discuss it rather than simply order it, but my default is to look.' / 'FOBT?' → 'No — a screening test for asymptomatic people; once bleeding is visible it adds nothing and risks false reassurance.' / 'father at 63 instead?' → 'a single first-degree relative diagnosed at 60 or over is average/slightly increased risk — iFOBT two-yearly from 45 to 74 rather than five-yearly colonoscopy. He would still need a colonoscopy now, because he has symptoms.'
pefe: Role-player: Daniel Whelan, 34, electrician, Kadina, partner and toddler; three weeks of intermittent bright red blood on the outside/paper, a few drops, painless, worse when constipated; a lump on straining he pushes back; Bali 10 days two weeks ago — vomiting/diarrhoea, unknown antibiotics 5 d; father bowel cancer at 52 (age only if asked); no meds/thinners; all other red flags negative; never screened (too young). Awkward, embarrassed; relieved by a matter-of-fact manner; anxious at 'colonoscopy' ('is that because you think it's cancer?'). Hidden: frightened it's cancer, put it off three weeks — if never asked, at ~6:30 'my dad had bowel cancer — is that what this is?'. If you spend the history on heavy lifting/cough/liver disease, he answers briefly and lets the clock run

PEFE: well, no pallor, obs normal, abdomen normal, perianal inspection unremarkable, DRE normal, ★ proctoscopy (only if requested by name): soft bulky masses in the anal canal. Fissure variant: 'the patient declines a digital rectal examination'

Haemorrhoid grades: I bleed only · II prolapse, reduce spontaneously · III manual reduction · IV irreducible. Thrombosed external pile: excise within ~72 h. Fissure: posterior midline ~90%; treatment — stool softening (fibre, fluids, psyllium/docusate), warm baths, topical GTN 0.2% or diltiazem 2% VERIFY TG, refer if >6–8 weeks (botulinum toxin, lateral sphincterotomy). Haemorrhoid management: fibre/fluids/avoid straining, topical preparations short term, rubber band ligation for grade I–III, haemorrhoidectomy for grade IV/failures VERIFY

back.dx: Perianal abscess — three days of an increasingly painful, solid lump immediately lateral to the anal verge (left), 8/10 throbbing constant pain, worst sitting, hot and shivery since yesterday, no pus yet, first episode; T 38.1, HR 96, not septic; photo: erythematous indurated swelling immediately lateral to the anal verge with a fluctuant centre and surrounding cellulitis, no midline pit, no fissure, no thrombosed pile. Mechanism: infection of an anal gland tracking out under the skin. Needs incision and drainage under anaesthetic today — antibiotics cannot penetrate a collection; antibiotics as an adjunct only for cellulitis, diabetes, immunosuppression or valvular disease. Warn: fistula in about a third; recurrent perianal sepsis → think Crohn's. Hidden agenda: embarrassment and cancer fear; pushback 'can't you just give me antibiotics — we're in the middle of seeding'.
plan: Identity → ★ 'I can see you're in a lot of pain, Mr Keane — I'll be quick and I'll get you something for it straight away. What's been happening?' → 'I'll need to ask about a fairly private area and examine you afterwards — is that all right?'

★ 'Any fevers or chills?' (hot and shivery since yesterday) · nausea, bloating, D/C, tummy pain · cancer block: weight, appetite, lumps, tired, blood, habit, FHx → no

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — unwell or septic? vital signs including temperature; abdomen — tenderness, guarding, masses; groins — inguinal lymphadenopathy' → uncomfortable, not septic, T 38.1, HR 96, BP normal, abdomen soft, groins normal · ★ 'I would like to examine the perianal area, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present. On inspection — skin changes: redness, rash, a visible fissure, skin tags? lumps or swellings: their site relative to the anal verge and to the midline, colour, whether they look fluctuant, any punctum or opening? any discharge or bleeding?' → photo handed over → ★ 'Describing what I can see: an erythematous, indurated swelling immediately lateral to the anal verge, with what appears to be a fluctuant centre and surrounding cellulitis. No midline pit, no visible fissure, no purple thrombosed pile at the verge.' · ★ 'Given that appearance and the degree of pain, I would not proceed with a digital rectal examination — it would be extremely painful and would not change management; full assessment would be under anaesthesia.'

★ 'Mr Keane, most likely you have a perianal abscess — an infection right next to the back passage that has formed a pocket of pus. It starts in one of the tiny glands inside the back passage and tracks outwards to just under the skin — which is why it's so painful and why sitting is unbearable. I'm saying that because of where it is — immediately beside the back passage rather than up in the crease — because of the fever and shivers, and because of what I can see: red, swollen, and it looks like it has pus underneath.' · DDx with reasons: pilonidal abscess (crease, midline, ingrown hair — not midline); thrombosed pile (purple lump at the opening, no fever); anal fissure (pain specifically with motions); proctitis; Crohn's disease (if this ever recurs); anal cancer — always considered with any lump, nothing here suggests it

★ 'The important thing is that antibiotics on their own won't fix this — they can't get into a pocket of pus. It has to be opened and drained: a small operation, usually under a general anaesthetic, and it needs to happen today. I'm arranging for you to go to hospital and I'll speak to the surgical team myself. Strong pain relief now; nothing to eat or drink in case they take you to theatre. I'd add antibiotics if the redness is spreading, or if someone is diabetic or immune-suppressed.' · 'can't you just give me antibiotics? we're seeding' → hold firm, acknowledge · ★ 'one thing to know in advance: in around a third of people a small tunnel can form afterwards between the bowel and the skin — a fistula. If you notice ongoing discharge after it heals, come back — that's treatable too.' · smoking, hygiene, sitz baths after drainage, review

It starts in one of the tiny glands inside the back passage, and the infection tracks outwards to just under the skin.' / ★ 'Antibiotics on their own won't clear a pocket of pus — they can't get into it. This needs to be opened and drained, and that needs to happen today.' / ★ 'In about a third of people a small tunnel forms afterwards between the bowel and the skin. If you get ongoing discharge once this heals, come back — that's treatable too.'

Pilonidal version (midline, a pit that weeps for years, truck driver): 'Most likely a pilonidal abscess — some call it a hair cyst. In the crease between the cheeks a hair grows inwards and makes a small pit that traps hair and debris; when it gets infected and fills with pus we call it an abscess. It needs draining now; later you may need an operation to remove the pit, otherwise it tends to come back — hygiene and hair removal help. The wound is often left open to heal from the bottom up, so district nursing for a while.' / Fistula version (months of offensive expressible discharge, an abscess drained a year ago; photo — external opening with granulation tissue, induration, no cellulitis): 'A fistula is a small tunnel between the inside of the bowel and the skin near the back passage — what leaks out is bowel content, which is why it's offensive and keeps coming back; it very often follows an abscess. A surgeon maps the tunnel, usually under anaesthetic, sometimes with an MRI first, then lays it open or places a soft drainage stitch called a seton. I'd also check for Crohn's disease.'

Examiner challenges: 'oral antibiotics and review?' → 'Antibiotics do not penetrate a collection of pus; the definitive treatment is incision and drainage. Antibiotics as an adjunct for surrounding cellulitis, diabetes, immunosuppression or valvular heart disease.' / 'perianal vs pilonidal?' → 'Site. Perianal — immediately adjacent to the anal verge, from an infected anal gland at the dentate line. Pilonidal — midline of the natal cleft in hair-bearing skin, from a midline pit with ingrown hair, typically pointing slightly off the midline.' / 'three abscesses in two years?' → 'raises Crohn disease — ask about diarrhoea, blood, weight loss, mouth ulcers; colonoscopy and pelvic MRI with gastroenterology; check for diabetes and immunosuppression.' / 'diabetic, 39.5, tachycardic, dusky skin' → 'Fournier's gangrene — a surgical emergency: resuscitate, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately, cultures and lactate, urgent surgical debridement — immediate MedSTAR retrieval on 1300 13 12 33.' / 'irregular ulcerated bleeding lesion' → 'anal cancer — usually squamous cell, HPV-associated: urgent specialist referral for examination and biopsy, examine the inguinal nodes, offer HIV testing with consent.'

Examiner: uncomfortable, not septic; T 38.1, HR 96, BP normal; abdomen soft; groins normal. Photo on requesting inspection: perianal abscess (erythematous indurated fluctuant swelling lateral to the verge with cellulitis). If DRE requested: 'the patient will not tolerate it.' If inspection never requested: 'the examination is unremarkable' and nothing else. Variants: pilonidal (midline pit, Figures 4/5), fistula (external opening with granulation, Figure 6), thrombosed pile (36 h sudden severe pain, purple lump at the verge, years of painless bleeding, no fever, Figure 7)

(B: yes) · radiation · food/position · impact · GI general six: N/V, bloating, ★ wind, diarrhoea, ★ constipation, fever → 'constipated for years' → ★ probe: how long, hard stools, painful/difficult · ★ 3:30 'these next ones are the important warning-sign questions': weight loss → ★ how many kilos / over what period / on purpose? back.dx: Version A — diverticulitis: a month of constant dull LIF pain 5/10 in a 50-year-old with years of constipation and hard stools, no night pain, and every red flag negative (no weight loss, no bleeding, no habit change, no FHx). Version B — 'concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer': the same pain but it wakes him, 5 kg unintentional loss over two months, appetite down, bright red rectal bleeding he attributed to piles, age 50, a screening kit on the bench, pack-a-day smoker. Diverticulitis fits the constipation and site but not the weight loss or bleeding. Hidden agenda: brother-in-law died of bowel cancer three years ago.

Pain: 'show me where' (LIF) · ★ 'on a scale of one to ten, ten being the worst pain you've ever felt, one the least — how bad?' (5) · sharp or dull (dull ache) · when, first time, constant, worse · ★ 'has it ever woken you at night?' (A no / B a couple of times) · travel · food/position · 'how is it affecting day to day?' (still working)

(5 kg, ~2 months, no) · appetite (a bit down) · lumps · ★ 'blood in your bowel motions, or black tarry motions?' (bright red — 'thought it was piles') · change in habit · FHx bowel cancer (no) · ★ 'have you done your bowel screening test?' (kit on the bench)

B: ★ 'Gary, during our conversation I was thinking about a number of conditions, and I am concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer. Let me tell you why.' [pause — let it land] · 'cancer? are you serious?' → 'that's a frightening word and I'm sorry to raise it. I'm not saying you have it — I'm saying it must be ruled out, and there is a clear way to do that. My reasons: a month of pain that isn't settling; five kilos of weight loss you didn't intend; blood in your bowel motions; and your age' (+ the unreturned kit) · A: ★ negatives first: 'before I tell you what I think this is, I want to be clear about what I have ruled out — not losing weight, no blood, habit unchanged, no family history. Offer a script at any point → accepts happily, ends the call — automatic fail. 'You should go to hospital' without arranging it → 'yeah, I'll think about it' and hangs up — fail

No observations, no examination. Findings by history: bilious vomiting 2 d, no oral intake, cramping, distension, no flatus, no motion 3 d, anuria 2 d, postural light-headedness, continued metformin + antihypertensive

Version A (afebrile, 50 F, father with colon cancer): 'You have what we call obstructive jaundice. Something is blocking the tubes that drain bile from your liver, which is why your skin and eyes are yellow, your urine is dark and your stools are pale. Three reasons: that combination of findings; the six kilos you have lost without trying; and your father's bowel cancer. I am worried the blockage may be caused by a cancer — most likely the pancreas, possibly the bile ducts or the liver. I cannot tell which without a scan, and I want that urgently. You do not have a fever, which reassures me there is no infection in the tubes at the moment.'

Examiner challenges: 'post-cholecystectomy syndrome?' → 'a description, not a cause — surgical stricture, a retained or new duct stone, or a new obstructing tumour; with unintentional weight loss and anorexia I am most concerned about the third.' / 'no gallbladder, so cholangiocarcinoma is out?' → 'No — cholecystectomy excludes gallbladder carcinoma; cholangiocarcinoma arises from the bile-duct epithelium, which remains. It stays on my list with carcinoma of the head of the pancreas and a hepatic lesion.' / 'antibiotics and review?' → 'antibiotics alone do not treat an obstructed, infected biliary system — the pressure keeps driving bacteria into the bloodstream; the duct must be decompressed, usually by ERCP, and usually early. Antibiotics buy time; drainage is the treatment.' / antibiotics by name → 'IV empirical Gram-negative and anaerobic biliary cover per Therapeutic Guidelines after cultures, adjusted for renal function and local resistance — and drainage.'

Charcot's triad → Reynolds' pentad (+ hypotension, altered mental state). Malignant obstruction clues: painless or dull persistent jaundice, weight loss, anorexia, age, pain to the back (pancreatic head), new-onset diabetes, Courvoisier. Investigations: cultures, FBE, UEC, LFT (obstructive: bilirubin, ALP, GGT ↑↑, ALT mild), coags/INR (vitamin K), CRP, lipase, lactate; USS → CT pancreas protocol/MRCP → ERCP with stent/brush cytology; CA19-9 (not diagnostic); EUS-guided biopsy; staging CT; MDT. Can I ask a few questions to understand the situation?' · ★ 'what exactly do you mean — doesn't remember things, doesn't recognise you, or behaving oddly?' · onset, constant/intermittent, worse, better/worse · ★ four cirrhosis questions: treatment, ★ taking it as prescribed, follow-up GP/specialist (stopped a year ago) · complications in order — decompensation: jaundice, itch, bruising (yes), tiredness · ★ encephalopathy: sleep reversal (yes), weakness/numbness, balance/walking, vision · SBP/cancer/kidney/lung/bleeding: abdominal pain, N/V, fever, diarrhoea; weight/appetite/lumps; ★ urine output; SOB/cough; haematemesis/melaena → ★ 'her tummy has got bigger' (ascites — offered casually; collect it) · ★ six triggers: 'I know the notes say she stopped — can I just confirm, is she drinking any alcohol at all at the moment?' → beer cans hidden → 'thank you — that took some courage' · new medications, recent illness, ★ constipation (yes), vomiting/diarrhoea/dehydration, (bleeding already asked) · geriatric 30 s: falls, support, diet, ADLs, mood · dx hepatic encephalopathy, plain English, the trigger, ★ DDx in two named groups — cirrhosis complications first, then causes of confusion in an older person · 'is she losing her mind?' → treatable, reversible, not dementia · plan; 'she won't come' → home visit, community nursing, 'you're not doing this alone'.

back.dx: Hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by a return to alcohol (beer cans hidden in the cupboard) and constipation — a few weeks of fluctuating, worsening forgetfulness (glasses, whether she's eaten; recognises him), day–night sleep reversal, intermittent confusion, in a woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis who has stopped specialist follow-up and may not be taking her tablets; also easy bruising, an enlarging abdomen (ascites), poor intake; no fever, no jaundice, no bleeding, no oliguria. Two differential groups: (1) other cirrhosis complications — spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatorenal and hepatopulmonary syndromes, variceal bleeding; (2) other causes of confusion in an older person — infection (chest/urine), medications/withdrawal, intracranial (subdural after a fall, stroke, tumour), dementia (Alzheimer's, Lewy body), electrolytes/glucose. Usually treatable and often reversible once the trigger is corrected: lactulose, assessment (bloods, abdominal examination, ascitic tap to exclude SBP), alcohol support.

★ Results in plain words: 'as you know, you have cirrhosis — the tissue of your liver has been damaged by long-term alcohol. 'Each month an egg grows inside a small sac on the ovary. Around day 14 that sac bursts to release the egg, and a little fluid and blood escape into the tummy — in some women that stings for a day or two. That is mid-cycle pain. If the egg is fertilised it should travel down the tube and settle in the womb. If it settles in the tube instead, that is an ectopic pregnancy.'

But I want to be careful: the single most important thing in any woman with lower tummy pain is to be sure she is not pregnant, so if I could do one test today it would be a urine pregnancy test. pefe: Role-player: Mary, 19, retail assistant and part-time student; embarrassed, doesn't want to be judged; truthful when asked directly, volunteers nothing — except 'it hurts when we have sex, deep inside' when asked what makes the pain worse. 'Any discharge?' → 'yes, I have actually' and STOPS — colour/thickness/amount/smell each only when asked separately. Hesitates before partner questions; if the doctor pauses, frowns or sounds disapproving → 'a couple, I suppose' and vaguer. Once diagnosed: 'is that serious? will I still be able to have children?'; near the end: 'do I have to tell my partner?'; 'sorry, what does that mean?' to PID/adnexal/ectopic

Vitals 118/72 · 92 · 16 · 37.6 · 99%. V-B PEFE: uncomfortable, not septic, T 37.8; abdomen moves normally, lower tenderness worse right, no guarding/rigidity/mass, BS normal; vulva normal with discharge at the introitus; mucopurulent discharge from the os, contact bleeding; CMT +, uterus tender, right adnexal tenderness, no mass; βhCG −, dipstick clear

PID: ascending polymicrobial infection (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, Mycoplasma genitalium, anaerobes/BV organisms); clinical diagnosis — lower abdominal pain + any one of CMT/uterine/adnexal tenderness, after excluding pregnancy; low threshold to treat (sequelae: tubal factor infertility, ectopic, chronic pelvic pain, tubo-ovarian abscess, Fitz-Hugh–Curtis). Investigations: βhCG, endocervical/vaginal NAAT (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, M. genitalium), HVS (BV, trichomonas), HIV/syphilis/hep B serology, FBE/CRP if unwell, pelvic USS if mass/severe. Treatment VERIFY TG: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat + doxycycline 100 mg bd 14 d + metronidazole 400 mg bd 14 d (azithromycin alternative); IUD may usually remain if improving VERIFY; admit for IV therapy if febrile/septic, vomiting, pregnant, TOA, peritonitis, not improving at 48–72 h. Partner notification: contacts from 6 months (chlamydia) — Let Them Know; chlamydia and gonorrhoea notifiable; abstain 7 days post-treatment and until partners treated; retest 3 months; contraception review (pill + condoms); first cervical screening test from 25

stem: Jenny Marsden, 55, is worried that her tummy is getting bigger (also recalled as 'abdominal distension' / 'enlarged tummy'). Card: a mass is felt in the right iliac fossa; observations normal.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Physical examination findings will be given on a card — you do not examine
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 min. Intro, 'glad you came in rather than waiting' · ★ define by 1:20: 'bloated and full of wind, or has your tummy actually got bigger — waistband tighter, clothes not doing up?' (both — skirts stopped doing up) · timing (3–4 months), constant vs intermittent (constant now), worse, food, ★ better after bowels? (no) · pain, N/V, bowels → ★ 'constipated — is that new? how long? any blood?' · ★ red flags unconditional by 3:10: weight (put a couple of kilos ON — ascites), ★ appetite ('feel full really quickly' = early satiety), blood/black stools, lumps, tiredness, fever/sweats · ★ ovarian cluster by 4:30: early satiety confirmed, pelvic/dragging pain, urinary frequency/urgency + duration, ★ LMP/postmenopausal bleeding, post-coital bleeding/discharge, cervical screening + mammogram, ★ FHx bowel/ovarian/breast/uterine (mother breast cancer at 50) · rest of GI fast: groin lump, operations, ★ passing wind (obstruction), dairy/gluten, greasy stools, IBD ×4, travel · weight-gain sweep: cold intolerance, chest pain/SOB lying flat, leg swelling, jaundice, purple striae, medications incl OTC, diet/activity, mood · ★ 'what were YOU worried this might be?' (friend had ovarian cancer) · card → 'I would have examined with a chaperone — appearance/obs, inspection for distension and distended veins, palpation for tenderness/masses/organomegaly, percussion for shifting dullness and fluid thrill, bimanual pelvic' · ★ warning shot → 'a lump in the lower right' + 'I'm concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the ovary' → STOP, five seconds → three reasons → two lists → CA-125 + USS both urgent, phone the results, gynae-oncology, PATS, obstruction safety-net, support person.

back.dx: Ovarian cancer until proven otherwise — 3–4 months of progressive distension (wind AND girth — skirts stopped doing up), new constipation, early satiety, dragging pelvic ache, urinary frequency/urgency for two months, a couple of kilos gained (ascites), postmenopausal four years with no bleeding, mother with breast cancer at 50; card: RIF mass, observations normal. Three reasons: bloating/girth (wind and fluid), the persistent symptom cluster (early satiety, constipation, frequency — nothing alone, together and lasting this long they matter), and the lump. Two lists: bowel — bowel cancer (no bleeding), coeliac/lactose, IBD, obstruction (passing wind, no surgery), IBS ('a label I can't use when there's a lump'); other causes of a bigger tummy — fluid from heart/kidney/liver, hypothyroidism, hormonal (Cushing's), medications, ordinary weight gain. Plan: CA-125 and pelvic/abdominal ultrasound together, both urgent; phone the results; gynaecological oncology; PATS; obstruction safety-net; support person.

I would examine her with a chaperone present, starting with general appearance and vital signs, then inspection of the abdomen for distension and distended veins, palpation for tenderness, masses and organomegaly, percussion for shifting dullness and a fluid thrill, and then a bimanual pelvic examination.' → card: mass in the right iliac fossa; observations normal

Putting that together with everything you've told me, I'm concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the ovary.' [★ STOP — five seconds; 'that's what I was afraid of'] → 'I know. And I want to be clear — I don't know that yet. It's the thing I have to rule out first, and I don't want to waste any time doing it. Would it help if I explained why I'm thinking it?' → ★ three reasons: 'the bloating and your tummy getting bigger — this condition causes both, partly wind and partly fluid collecting; the pattern of the other symptoms — feeling full quickly, the constipation, passing urine more often — on their own each is nothing, together and lasting this long they matter; and the lump'

★ Two lists: 'in the bowel — a bowel cancer, less likely with no bleeding; food problems like coeliac or lactose intolerance, which don't fit; inflammation of the bowel; a blockage — no, you're passing wind normally and have had no surgery; and irritable bowel, a label people often get but which I can't use when there's a lump. Then the things that make a tummy bigger for other reasons — fluid from the heart, kidneys or liver; an underactive thyroid; hormone conditions; medications; and ordinary weight gain. None fit as well.' · plan: 'today a blood test called CA-125 and an ultrasound of your tummy and pelvis — both marked urgent — and I'll ring you as soon as they're back rather than waiting for you to book. Depending on what they show I'll refer you to a specialist team who deal specifically with cancers of the ovary; if you need to travel to Adelaide there's a scheme for travel and accommodation.' · ★ safety-net: 'straight to emergency if the pain becomes severe, you start vomiting, you stop passing wind or opening your bowels, or your tummy becomes hard and tender; ring me if any bleeding' · 'is there someone you'd like with you when we go through the results?' (daughter — video if needed) · 'am I going to be alright?' → speed and process, not outcome; written information

Variant B (ascites + weight loss on the card — shifting dullness and fluid thrill): 'before I go on — what's your understanding of why we did the examination today?' → 'I'm afraid the findings are more serious than I'd hoped, and I'd rather tell you properly than skate over it. As well as the lump, there is fluid collecting in your abdomen — that's what has made it swell so quickly, and it's also why you've lost weight elsewhere without noticing. Together, I'm concerned this is an ovarian cancer that has already spread within the abdomen. I'm arranging for you to be seen this week; the team will drain some of that fluid, which will make you more comfortable, and testing it tells them a lot. Would you like me to ring your daughter now?' (add ascitic tap for cytology/SAAG, VTE risk, nutrition, pain) / Variant C (came on over three days, vomiting, no wind since yesterday): 'thank you — that changes things. I'm going to stop the questions there. I'm concerned your bowel may be blocked, which needs looking at today. I'll examine you now, put a drip in, keep you nil by mouth and speak to the surgical team.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Marsden, 55, school administration officer in a country town, married to Peter, daughter in Adelaide; postmenopausal 4 y; practical, self-deprecating; put it off assuming 'just my age' — opens with it if given an opening (a weak candidate agrees). Does NOT volunteer early satiety — only 'I feel full really quickly' if appetite is asked (never the words 'early satiety'). Mother breast cancer at 50. Hidden: close friend's ovarian cancer started like this — only if asked what she's worried about, else ~7 min. At the news: 'that's what I was afraid of' then silent for a full five seconds — marks down talking through it. 'Am I going to be alright?' — mark down 'I'm sure it's nothing serious'. Asks about her daughter
Card: a mass is felt in the right iliac fossa; observations normal; no other abnormality recorded. Variant B: + shifting dullness and fluid thrill; weight loss

Six Fs of a big abdomen: fat, fluid, flatus, faeces, foetus, (fatal) growth. Ovarian cluster >12 times/month, persistent, new after 50 → CA-125 + TVUS together; RMI = U × M × CA-125 (refer >200 VERIFY); CA-125 normal in ~half of early ovarian cancer — never use it to exclude; shifting dullness needs ~1500 mL (roll 45°, wait 15–30 s). Screening status: CST 5-yearly 25–74; iFOBT 2-yearly 45–74 VERIFY; BreastScreen 2-yearly 50–74. Breast + ovarian FHx → BRCA — genetics referral. Obstruction from peritoneal disease is a real complication — flatus question and obstruction safety-net

DO — Red flags unconditionally by 3:10 (weight — 'if anything I've put a bit on'; appetite — 'I feel full really quickly' = early satiety, pick it up and say so later; blood; lumps; tiredness; fevers); the ovarian cluster by 4:30 ('full after only a small amount? pain low down or in the pelvis? passing urine more often, or a sudden urge? how long?' — two questions on frequency, not a UTI history; LMP four years ago, any bleeding since, discharge, screening status, family history of bowel, ovarian, breast or uterine cancer → mother's breast cancer at 50 — 'breast and ovarian can run together in families'); the rest of the GI list fast (groin, surgery, flatus, dairy and gluten, greasy stools, IBD, travel); the weight-gain sweep (cold intolerance, chest pain, orthopnoea, leg swelling, jaundice, purple striae, medications, diet, mood); 'what were you worried this might be?' → 'my friend had ovarian cancer — it started like this' (half the communication marks)

DO — Take the card aloud: 'I would examine her with a chaperone — general appearance and vitals, inspection for distension and distended veins, palpation for tenderness, masses and organomegaly, percussion for shifting dullness and a fluid thrill, and a bimanual pelvic examination'; the warning shot ('there is something in the findings I do need to explain — is it alright if we go through it now?'); three reasons (bloating and girth — wind and fluid; the symptom pattern — 'on their own each is nothing, together and lasting this long they matter'; the lump); CA-125 and ultrasound together, both urgent, 'I'll ring you as soon as they're back rather than waiting for you to book'; gynaecological oncology; PATS; obstruction safety-net (severe pain, vomiting, no wind or motion, hard tender tummy) and ring for bleeding; 'is there someone you'd like with you when we go through the results?' (her daughter — video if needed); Variant B (shifting dullness and a fluid thrill, weight loss): ascites — likely already spread, seen this week, drain and tap for cytology; Variant C (days, vomiting, no flatus): stop the history — 'obstruction', drip, NBM, surgical team

setting: General practice. Six-minute history (stops at 6:00), no examination, then diagnosis and differentials. Red flags first — malignancy and infection before the comfortable groups — because she looks fit and well. Ask intake and training load SEPARATELY (hours and days), and the consequences (periods, bones, performance). Automatic fails: stopping the history at 'athlete'; never asking purging or fear of weight gain in words; presenting the finding as good news; prescribing intake or training numbers across the desk.
stem: Anna Petrides, 35, is worried about losing weight.

No physical examination is performed or provided
