time: 8 min. Intro · ★ signpost the breadth: 'weight loss can come from a lot of directions, so I'm going to ask about quite a few areas — some will feel like they've come out of nowhere' · ★ quantify by 1:24: kilos, period, previous weight, ★ trying?, first noticed, impact (6 kg/4–5 mo, 58→52, not trying; tired, cold) · ★ malignancy first: appetite, lumps (neck/axilla/groin/breast), tiredness, night sweats/fevers, bleeding (bowel/urine/between periods/after sex), cervical screening, FHx cancer · ★ infection normalised: fevers/chills/sweats, travel, sexually active/condoms, IVDU/transfusion/tattoo, TB contact, cough >3 weeks, jaundice — 'why HIV?' → answer once, plainly, continue · endocrine/gut/autoimmune fast: heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, thirst/polyuria, postural dizziness; bowels, blood, greasy stools, pain, mouth ulcers; joints, rash, dry eyes · ★ psychiatric/eating screen in words: mood, sleep, enjoyment; 'questions I ask everyone about weight — nothing about you prompted them: intense fear of gaining weight? how do you feel about your body/shape? ever vomiting, laxatives, fluid tablets, appetite suppressants? exercise specifically to make up for eating?' · ★ energy in AND out: typical day's food, changed?, ★ 'who decides what you eat?' (dietitian + coach); ★ 'what does training look like — what, how many hours, how many days?' (~8 h/day, 6 days), changed? (up since February) · ★ consequences: periods (stopped 4 months), pregnancy, stress fractures (foot last year), infections, ★ performance (slower this season — the opening) · ★ one respiratory question: haemoptysis, cough, shoulder/inner-arm pain · 6:00 → explain the energy gap without making it good news; 2.5–5 h/week comparison; why it still needs treating; nine grouped DDx; bloods + CXR; sports physician + sports dietitian; DEXA; coach; safety-net; open door on eating.

back.dx: Low energy availability from excessive training with dietary restriction (relative energy deficiency in sport) — 6 kg (10%) unintentional loss over 4–5 months (58→52 kg), tired, cold, training ~8 h/day 6–7 days/week (up since February for trials) on reduced portions set by a programme dietitian and coach; amenorrhoea 4 months; stress fracture last year; performance slower this season (her real fear); no red flags for malignancy or infection; no fear of weight gain, no purging, no compensatory exercise ('I train because it's the job') — denial of intent excludes one criterion, not the spectrum. Explain the gap (adult guideline 2.5–5 h/WEEK), say clearly it is common in athletes and still harmful — the amenorrhoea is bone risk and the stress fracture is the evidence. Still exclude the serious causes: bloods (FBE, ESR/CRP, UEC, LFT, TSH, glucose/HbA1c, coeliac serology, iron, B12/folate, HIV/hepatitis/TB testing as indicated, βhCG), chest X-ray; sports physician + accredited sports dietitian (no numbers across the desk); DEXA after 6 months of amenorrhoea or any stress fracture; speak with the coach; open door on eating; Butterfly Foundation if the eating side surfaces.
plan: 'Am I speaking with Anna? Thanks for coming in — what's brought you along?' → 'losing weight, don't know why' → ★ 'I understand why that's worrying you, and I'm glad you came in to have it looked at properly. Weight loss can come from a lot of different directions, so I'm going to ask about quite a few areas — some will feel like they've come out of nowhere. Is that alright?'

★ Quantify: 'how many kilos, over what period? what did you weigh before? ★ have you been trying to lose weight? when did you first notice? how is it affecting you day to day?' → 6 kg, 4–5 months, 58→52, no, tired and cold

★ 'I'm going to start with the things I most want to rule out': appetite (fine — 'I eat what I'm given'), lumps — neck/armpits/groin/breast, tiredness, night sweats/fevers, bleeding — bowels/urine/between periods/after sex, cervical screening (up to date), FHx cancer (none)

★ 'Now some questions about infections — I ask these of everyone with unexplained weight loss': fevers/chills/sweats, travel, sexually active + condoms (one partner, both tested), IVDU/transfusion/tattoo, TB contact, cough >3 weeks, jaundice → 'why are you asking about HIV?' → ★ 'because infections are one of the groups I have to rule out when someone loses weight without meaning to — I ask everyone. Is that alright?' (no apology, continue)

Fast, one per group: heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor · thirst/polyuria · postural dizziness → 'no — I'm cold all the time' · bowels, diarrhoea/blood, greasy stools, tummy pain, mouth ulcers · joints, rash, dry eyes → all no

★ Psychiatric/eating in words: 'how has your mood been? sleep? still enjoying things?' (mood okay; sleep poor — early training) · ★ 'now some questions I ask everyone who comes in about their weight — nothing about you in particular has prompted them: do you have an intense fear of gaining weight? how do you feel about your body and your shape? have you ever tried to control your weight by making yourself vomit, or using laxatives, fluid tablets or appetite suppressants? do you ever exercise specifically to make up for something you've eaten?' → no ('I need the weight for power'; 'I train because it's the job')

★ Energy in: 'talk me through what you'd eat on a normal day — has that changed? ★ who decides what you eat?' (smaller portions; dietitian, part of the programme; dietitian + coach) · ★ energy out: 'what does your training look like — what do you do, how many hours, how many days a week? has that changed recently?' → ~8 h/day, 6 days, sometimes 7; up since February for trials (write it down — don't react, don't lecture) · ★ consequences: 'have your periods changed or stopped? any chance you're pregnant? stress fractures or bone injuries? more infections, or has your performance dropped?' → stopped 4 months ('just the training'); no; foot last year; ★ 'honestly, I've been slower this season' · ★ 'last thing — ever coughed up blood? any cough? shoulder or inner-arm pain?' → no · supplements (multivitamin, protein powder), alcohol, smoking

★ 'Anna, I think I know why you're losing weight, and I want to explain it properly rather than just reassure you. You're training around eight hours a day, six days a week — the general recommendation for adults is somewhere between two and a half and five hours a WEEK. At the same time your portions have come down. So you're taking in less energy than your body is using, and the weight loss is your body making up the difference from its own reserves.' · 'but I'm an athlete, that's normal' / 'my dietitian set the plan' → ★ 'it's common in athletes — and it's still a clinical problem; those are different statements' · ★ why it matters: 'when that gap goes on for months the body shuts down what it treats as optional. That's why your periods have stopped — and that isn't a side issue, because the hormone that drives your cycle is also what keeps your bones strong. That stress fracture last year fits the same picture. If this continues: more fractures, more infections, and — the part that usually gets athletes' attention — performance going backwards no matter how hard you train.' → 'I have been slower this season' → use the opening

★ DDx grouped, why less likely: cancers (no lumps/sweats/bleeding, screening current) · infections — HIV, TB, hepatitis (no risk factors; test anyway — can't afford to miss) · thyroid, diabetes · coeliac, IBD · autoimmune · depression and eating disorders ('I asked about those and I'll keep the door open') · medications/supplements · (respiratory screened) · plan: 'those blood tests and a chest X-ray, so the serious things are excluded rather than assumed; referral to a sports physician and an accredited sports dietitian so your intake is matched to your training by someone who does this properly — I don't want to hand you a number across the desk; a bone density scan because of the periods; ★ would you be willing for me to speak with your coach?' ('my coach won't like it' → 'that's exactly why I asked — this works far better as a conversation between all of us than as me telling you to train less') · safety-net: faint/near-faint on standing, palpitations, bone pain that doesn't settle, fevers/sweats, haemoptysis — 'and come back sooner if you find the eating side of this harder than you've told me today' · 'so I'm not sick?' → 'you haven't got the serious illnesses I was looking for — the tests confirm rather than assume — but I don't want you to hear "it's just the training" and go away, because the pattern is doing you harm; your periods and that fracture are the evidence'

Have you been trying to lose weight?' / 'That's helpful, thank you — I'll come back to it. First I want to rule out a few things.'

Do you have an intense fear of gaining weight? How do you feel about your body and your shape? Have you ever tried to control your weight by making yourself vomit, or by using laxatives or fluid tablets? Do you ever exercise specifically to make up for something you've eaten?'

I'm saying this pattern is doing you harm.' / ★ 'I don't want to hand you a number across the desk.' / ★ 'Would you be willing for me to speak with your coach?'

Can you tell me a bit more about what that's like?' → acknowledge, one open question, continue the screen; then: specialist eating-disorder assessment, check medical stability (postural BP and pulse, ECG for bradycardia/prolonged QT, electrolytes), psychology, Butterfly Foundation 1800 33 4673; no weight or intake targets from you; training not made conditional on a number
pefe: Role-player: Anna Petrides, 35, competitive athlete (swimmer/rower/dancer) training for national trials, part-time coach, lives with partner; articulate, disciplined, slightly impatient, doesn't see herself as a patient; multivitamin and protein powder, no alcohol in season, never smoked. Does NOT volunteer the training — 'do you exercise?' → 'yes, I'm an athlete' and stops; the eight hours only to 'how many hours and how many days'. Pushes back once on HIV ('why are you asking?') — apologising/backing off/skipping is marked down. Defends the programme ('normal for athletes', 'my dietitian set the plan'). Hidden: her performance has dropped and it frightens her more than the weight — only if asked directly about performance, or ~7 min with rapport; softens the moment it's connected. 'My coach won't like it' near the end — mark up offering to speak to the coach

No examination. Findings by history: 6 kg (10%) over 4–5 months unintentional; fatigue, cold intolerance; secondary amenorrhoea 4 months; stress fracture last year; performance decline; training ~48 h/week; reduced intake; all red-flag groups negative; eating screen negative (Variant C positive)

Significant weight loss: >5% in 6–12 months. Adult activity guideline 150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous per week. RED-S/low energy availability: energy availability <30 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day; consequences — hypothalamic amenorrhoea, low bone density/stress fractures, immune suppression, iron deficiency, low mood, performance decline, bradycardia/hypotension in severe cases; DEXA after 6 months of amenorrhoea or any stress fracture; management — increase energy availability (sports dietitian), reduce training load (sports physician + coach), consider transdermal oestrogen for bone in persistent amenorrhoea (specialist) VERIFY — the OCP masks the problem; monitor return of menses. Work-up for unintentional weight loss: FBE, ESR/CRP, UEC, LFT, Ca, TSH, glucose/HbA1c, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA on gluten), iron/B12/folate, βhCG, HIV/hepatitis serology, TB screening if risk, CXR (cough >3 weeks), urinalysis; targeted imaging by findings

Eating disorder screen (SCOFF-style, in plain words): fear of weight gain, body image, purging, laxatives/diuretics/appetite suppressants, compensatory exercise, binge/loss of control; medical instability — bradycardia <50, postural drop, hypothermia, electrolytes, QT; anorexia nervosa needs intent/fear — denial excludes one criterion, not the spectrum (atypical AN, ARFID, OSFED). Butterfly Foundation 1800 33 4673 · Sports Medicine Australia · TIS 131 450 · timing: quantify by 1:24 · malignancy + infection by 3:24 · psychiatric + lifestyle by 6:00
The station — NO physical examination is performed or provided — say what you would want, and why, then move on
What you would want — Weight and height for a BMI, and the TREND against previous weights · pulse and blood pressure, lying and standing · temperature
And — Thyroid examination · lymph nodes · abdomen for masses and organomegaly · signs of anaemia · dentition and parotids
Why the trend matters — Significant weight loss is MORE THAN 5% IN 6 TO 12 MONTHS — hers is 10% in four to five months
What you are screening for — Bradycardia, hypotension and hypothermia — the signs of an energy deficit, which is what makes this more than a lifestyle conversation

★ Presenting the finding as good news / 'normal for athletes'; ★ prescribing intake or training numbers across the desk; no bloods/CXR ('excluded rather than assumed'); no DEXA; no coach offer; no open door on eating; missing the performance opening

setting: General practice. He is here about weight gain; the bloods are already done (HbA1c 5.7%, AST/ALT mildly raised <2–3× ULN, triglycerides just over 2, everything else normal) — flag them in the first minute, explain them at the end. History to 5:00, examination request (BMI and waist FIRST), then a two-part explanation: lifestyle causes the weight gain; fatty liver explains the bloods — never inverted. Automatic fails: saying fatty liver causes weight gain; naming 'non-alcoholic' without an alcohol history; never asking BMI or waist; false reassurance.
stem: James Whitlock, 60, presents with progressive weight gain. Bloods: HbA1c 5.7% · AST and ALT mildly raised (<2–3× ULN) · triglycerides just over 2 mmol/L · FBE, UEC, ALP, bilirubin, albumin, TFT, other lipids normal.

PND?; leg swelling; frothy urine/passing less) · Cushing (purple striae, bruising, proximal weakness, ★ steroids — tablets/puffers/creams/injections) · ★ all medications incl OTC/herbal, started/changed · ★ eating screen even in a 60 M: fear of weight gain, vomiting/laxatives/diuretics, ★ binge/loss of control, mood · ★ lifestyle open then specific: a typical day of food; ★ 'what do you drink — soft drink, juice, energy drinks?' (2 L Coke/day — only if drinks asked separately); exercise; work (desk); ★ sleep — snoring/apnoea (wife moved out) · ★ liver group: jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch, tummy swelling; ★ 'do you drink alcohol at all? … not even socially, nothing on weekends?' (none — gave it away 15 y); transfusions/tattoos/IVDU/needle-stick; ever tested for hepatitis · joints; FHx diabetes (dad — lost toes) · 5:00 examiner: ★ BMI and waist first (38; 91 cm — 'discordant — I'd re-measure at the iliac crest at end-expiration'), four vitals esp BP, Cushingoid features, acanthosis nigricans, thyroid, CVS (JVP, HS, gallop, oedema), resp bases, abdomen (hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, shifting dullness), BSL, dipstick → normal · ★ two things, connected but not the same → bloods → DDx → plan.

back.dx: Lifestyle weight gain (6–7 kg over six months, 105→112 kg, BMI 38 class II obesity) with MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease — 'fatty liver'): skipped breakfast, servo lunch, takeaway 4–5 nights, ~2 L Coke a day, no exercise, desk job, loud snoring (probable OSA), father with type 2 diabetes; no alcohol for 15 years (asked twice); no thyroid, cardiac, renal, Cushingoid, medication or eating-disorder cause; examination normal apart from BMI. Bloods: mild transaminase rise (<3× — fatty-liver band, AST:ALT <1), triglycerides >2, HbA1c 5.7% (top of normal; 6.0–6.4 high risk). Two-part explanation — lifestyle causes the weight; fatty liver explains the bloods; 'it's not about fault'. Plan: liver ultrasound, hepatitis B/C serology, iron studies, FIB-4 (refer >2.67); 5–10% weight loss (6–11 kg) settles the enzymes; dietitian + exercise physiologist via a chronic disease plan; the two litres of Coke as the single win; sleep apnoea assessment; diabetes prevention (his hidden fear — 'am I turning diabetic like Dad?'); review 4–6 weeks; safety-net.

I can also see you've had blood tests done and there are one or two things in there I want to go through with you before you leave. Can I ask some questions first, then examine you, then we'll sit down and talk about it all together?'

★ 'James, I've got two things to tell you, and they're connected but they're not the same thing. The first is the weight itself. I went looking for a medical cause and I couldn't find one — your thyroid is normal, nothing suggests a heart, kidney or hormone problem, and none of your medications do this. What I did find is that you're having takeaway most nights, about two litres of soft drink a day, and you're not getting much movement. That combination is the most likely reason the weight is going up.' → 'so it's my fault then' → ★ 'It's not about fault. Weight is driven by a lot of things people don't choose — your job, your sleep, your genes. What I'm telling you is which parts we can actually change.'

★ 'The second thing is your blood tests. Three results are mildly off — two liver enzymes, your blood fats, and your sugar is sitting at the top of the normal range. Together that pattern points to something called fatty liver. When there's more fat around than the body can store in the usual places, some of it goes into the liver, and that irritates it — that irritation is what those enzymes are showing. The important part is that at this stage it is reversible.' → 'is my liver damaged? my uncle died of liver failure' → ★ 'It isn't damaged. There's fat in it, and at this stage that's reversible. What I want to know is whether there's any scarring — I can work that out from a score using bloods you've already had, plus an ultrasound; if it's up, a liver specialist; if not, we manage it here, together.' · DDx grouped: hormone — hypothyroidism (test normal), Cushing's (no signs); fluid — heart, kidneys, advanced liver disease (no swelling, no orthopnoea, normal exam); medications (none cause gain); eating patterns and mood (asked); ★ hepatitis — 'which is why I want a couple of blood tests' · 'am I turning diabetic like Dad?' → honest: HbA1c 5.7 is not diabetes; this is exactly the moment prevention works; recheck

Let's start the plan and get your results, then talk properly about whether medication or a surgical referral makes sense for you.'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitlock, 60, dispatch supervisor (desk) for a grain handler outside Port Pirie, married to Denise, two adult children; pleasant, blunt, mildly embarrassed; not anxious about the bloods (doesn't know they matter). Skips breakfast, servo lunch, takeaway 4–5 nights; Coke ~2 L/day ONLY if drinks asked separately ('do you eat healthily?' → 'not too bad'); no exercise; snores badly (Denise in the spare room), afternoon tiredness; no alcohol for 15 years — doesn't soften on re-asking; 10 cigs/day × 30 y; knees ache; pale old striae; one BP tablet. stem: James Whitmore, 40, storeman at the grain terminal, presents with sudden-onset abdominal pain this morning; the pain has now improved. T 36.8 · HR 88 · BP 128/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98%.
Version B: pain began in the right flank and now radiates to the groin. Dipstick: blood ++, nitrites −, leucocytes −. Non-contrast CT KUB done — film on the desk; no stone size reported.

Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings

(Version B) Explain the CT scan; explain the diagnosis; explain your management plan
time: 8 min. 'Am I speaking with James? before we start — comfortable enough to talk now? tell me what's been happening' → 'that sounds horrible, and you're not being silly at all' · 'may I have his vital signs, in particular his temperature?' · SICORA: ★ 'where exactly did it start — point with one finger? and where is it now?' (flank → groin), /10 (9), sharp, sudden, ★ 'all the time, or in waves?' (waves), travel (groin/testicles), better/worse (nothing — pacing), painkillers taken · GI: N/V (once), appetite, bowels, bloating/wind, ★ 'any fevers, chills or shaking episodes?' (no) · ★ the pivot aloud: 'one side, in waves, travelling to your groin — makes me want to ask about your waterworks next' → eight: burning (stinging), frequency (yes), ★ blood (pink this morning — goes tense), dribbling/hesitancy, urgency, nocturia, amounts, ★ 'you or anyone in your family ever had a kidney stone?' (dad, twice) · right-sided extras: jaundice, pale stools, fatty-meal pain; groin lump; testicular pain/swelling · background if time: smoking, alcohol, meds, gout/high calcium, kidney surgery/solitary kidney, ★ fluid intake (hardly any water — hot shed) · ★ 4:00 hard stop — 'was there something you were worried this might be?' (uncle died of bladder cancer at 58) → acknowledge, no false reassurance, commit to answering · ★ examiner: appearance, vitals (temperature first), full abdominal incl pulsatile mass, distended bladder, renal bruits, inguinal/genitalia/DRE, ★ 'as a special test — renal angle tenderness both sides; as an office test — a urine dipstick' · dx ureteric colic, three reasons · ★ the discriminating sentence: tender kidney + blood can suggest infection, but no fever, no nitrites, no leucocytes → not hospital today · cancer worry answered honestly · grouped DDx · three investigations with reasons: CT KUB non-contrast, urine MCS, UEC/eGFR · safety-net, summary.

back.dx: Ureteric colic — an obstructing stone (Version B: at the vesicoureteric junction, the last centimetre before the bladder): sudden 9/10 sharp right flank pain this morning, in waves, migrating to the groin, pacing, vomited once, now improved; stinging, frequency, pink urine, urgency, some dribbling; father had stones twice; hot shed, drinks almost no water; afebrile. PEFE: settled, T 36.8, mild right-sided tenderness, no peritonism/mass, BS normal, right renal angle tender, groin and scrotum normal, dipstick blood ++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace. Three reasons: flank-to-groin path, waves, blood in the urine. The fork: loin tenderness + haematuria could mean pyelonephritis — no fever, no nitrites, no leucocytes → no infection → not hospital today. Investigations: non-contrast CT KUB (site and size), urine MCS (no infection behind the block), UEC/eGFR (kidney function changes the plan). Management by size: ≤5 mm — home, NSAID first (± opioid), antiemetic, tamsulosin, strain the urine, normal fluids (don't force), review 2–3 days; >7 mm — urology (ureteroscopy + laser for a low stone, ESWL, PCNL for large renal stones, stent if the kidney needs relieving). Long term: 2.5–3 L/day, low salt, normal calcium/dairy, stone analysis, metabolic work-up. Hidden agenda: uncle died of bladder cancer at 58.
plan: 'I'm Dr —; am I speaking with James? Before we start — are you comfortable enough to talk to me now? … Tell me what's been happening.' → 'pain out of nowhere loading the truck, worst ever, pacing the yard; eased off now — feel a bit stupid coming in' → ★ 'that sounds horrible, and you're not being stupid at all — that kind of pain always deserves looking at. I'm glad it has eased. I'll ask a series of questions to work out what caused it.' · 'Examiner, may I have his vital signs, in particular his temperature?' → afebrile, stable

★ 'Where exactly did it start — point with one finger? … And where is it now?' (high right flank → right groin) · 'how bad at its worst, out of ten? (9) sharp, dull, cramping? (sharp, stabbing) when did it start — suddenly? (2 h ago, instant) ★ there all the time, or coming and going in waves? (waves) travel — back, groin, testicles? (groin, top of the leg) anything better or worse — moving, lying still, eating? painkillers?' (nothing; couldn't sit still; two Panadol did nothing)
GI: nausea/vomiting (once), appetite (off), bowels, bloating/wind · ★ 'and have you had any fevers, chills or shaking episodes?' → no → 'good — that matters more here than you'd think'

★ Pivot: 'the way you've described that — one side, coming in waves, travelling to your groin — makes me want to ask about your waterworks next.' → 'burning or stinging? (a bit) passing urine more often? (a lot) ★ any blood — pink, red or tea-coloured?' → 'pink this morning — that's really why I came' (tense) → 'thank you for telling me — important, we'll come back to it' · 'dribbling at the end, trouble starting? sudden urges you can't hold? up at night? passing normal amounts? ★ have you, or anyone in your family, ever had a kidney stone?' (dad, twice, about my age)

'Two quick ones — yellowing of the eyes or skin, pale stools, cramping after fatty food? any lump in your groin, or pain/swelling in your testicles?' (no) · if the clock allows: smoking (10/day), alcohol, meds/allergies, gout/high calcium, operations/kidney surgery, one kidney?, ★ 'how much fluid do you drink in a day?' ('hardly any water — hot in that shed') · ★ 4:00 HARD STOP: 'before I examine you — was there something in particular you were worried this might be?' → [pause] 'my uncle died of bladder cancer at 58 — when I saw the blood I thought, that's it' → ★ 'thank you for telling me. That must have been a frightening morning. I can't promise you anything before I've examined you and done a scan, but I will tell you honestly what I think, and we will not leave that question hanging.'

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — distress, restlessness, dehydration, pallor, jaundice · vital signs, temperature first · full abdominal examination — inspection for distension and scars; palpation superficial then deep for tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, organomegaly and any pulsatile mass; percussion for tenderness and a distended bladder; auscultation for bowel sounds and renal bruits · inguinal region, external genitalia, digital rectal examination · ★ as a special test — renal angle tenderness on both sides · ★ as an office test — a urine dipstick' → uncomfortable but settled; T 36.8; abdomen soft, mild right-sided tenderness, no guarding/rebound, no mass, BS normal; right renal angle tender; groin/scrotum normal; dipstick blood ++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace

★ 'James, I think you have what we call a ureteric colic — most people say a kidney stone. A small stone has formed in your kidney and started moving down the narrow tube that carries urine to your bladder. It presses on the wall of that tube and blocks it, and that is what causes the pain. Three things point to it: where the pain is — it started in your flank and travelled toward your groin, exactly the path that tube takes; it comes in waves, which is typical; and there's blood in your urine, which happens as the stone scrapes its way down.' · ★ discriminating sentence: 'I also want to be clear about something. You're tender over your kidney and there's blood in your urine, and those can suggest a kidney infection. But you have no fever, and your dipstick shows no nitrites and no white cells, so there's no sign of infection — and that's important, because a stone with an infection would mean hospital today.' · ★ the cancer worry: 'I can't rule anything out until the scan is back, and I won't pretend otherwise. But blood in the urine with this exact pattern of pain, at forty, with your father's history, points strongly to a stone. The scan will settle it.' · DDx by group: kidney/bladder — pyelonephritis, less likely a growth; liver/gallbladder (right-sided) — gallstones, inflammation, hepatitis; bowel — appendicitis, inflammation, rarely a growth; groin/testicle — hernia, torsion/epididymitis (excluded); the main abdominal blood vessel — very unlikely at forty

★ 'Three tests. One, a special CT scan of the kidneys, ureters and bladder without dye — the best test we have; it shows me where the stone is and how big. Two, your urine to the laboratory for culture, because I want to be certain there's no infection sitting behind the blockage. Three, a blood test — UEC — to check your kidney function, because if the kidney is struggling that changes what I recommend.' (pushed: FBE/CRP if infection suspected, cultures if febrile, calcium/urate if recurrent; ultrasound if pregnant) · ★ safety-net: 'come straight back, or go to the emergency department, if you get a fever or shakes, if the pain becomes uncontrollable despite the tablets, if you stop passing urine, or if you're vomiting so much you can't keep fluids down' · analgesia now (NSAID) · summary: 'sudden severe colicky right pain, flank to groin, blood in the urine, no fever — most likely a kidney stone on the move; scan, check for infection and kidney function, then decide together how to get it out. What questions do you have?' ('how long? work? will it happen again?')
V-B

'I have your scan here — let me take you through what it shows, then what it means, then what we do' · ★ orient: 'this is a slice through your lower tummy, looking from your feet upward; these bright white shapes either side are your hip bones; this big grey circle in the middle is your bladder' → 'two narrow tubes carry urine from your kidneys into the bladder — the ureters. This small bright dot is a stone, sitting in one of those tubes right where it joins your bladder — the vesicoureteric junction, or simply the last centimetre before the bladder' · dx: 'a kidney stone on the move — I can see it, and your story fits exactly' · ★ the fork before 4:15: 'what we do next depends on how big the stone is. But before any of that, two things: I need to be certain there's no infection sitting behind the blockage — urine for culture; a stone and an infection together is the one combination that means hospital the same day. And a blood test for kidney function, because that changes what I recommend.' · ★ small (≤5 mm): home — NSAID first (ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food / indometacin 100 mg PR), oxycodone 5 mg if inadequate, ondansetron, tamsulosin 400 mcg daily (light-headed on standing — get up slowly) VERIFY, ★ strain the urine and catch the stone, ★ drink normally — don't force water, review 2–3 days · ★ large (>7 mm): urology — ureteroscopy + laser (suits a low stone), ESWL, PCNL for large renal stones, stent if the kidney needs relieving; analgesia and tamsulosin meanwhile · long term: 2.5–3 L/day especially in the heat, low salt, ★ keep dairy/calcium normal ('cutting calcium out makes stones more likely'), stone analysis, blood/urine tests · safety-net · 'how big is it?' → 'the report doesn't give a measurement and I'm not going to guess from the picture — so here are both possibilities'

★ 'James, the most likely explanation is benign prostatic hyperplasia — benign prostate enlargement. The prostate is a small walnut-shaped gland just underneath the bladder, and the tube that carries urine out runs straight through the middle of it. As men get older it commonly enlarges. Benign means not a cancer. Two things follow: it squeezes the tube — which is why the stream is weak, you dribble, never feel empty, and you're up three or four times a night; and the surface of an enlarged prostate carries fragile blood vessels that bleed easily — which is where the blood is coming from.' · 'so it's not cancer? my father had prostate trouble' → ★ 'That's the most likely answer, and the examination today is reassuring — the gland felt smooth and even, which is what we expect with the benign kind. But I want to be straight with you: visible blood in the urine at your age always has to be properly investigated, because I cannot exclude a cancer of the bladder, kidney or prostate on examination alone. That's not because I think you have one — it's the one thing I'm not willing to guess about.'

Was it clear, cloudy, or yellow-green?' (yellowish, not much) · 'any deep pain in your pelvis, around your back passage? swelling or redness of the scrotum? pain in your testicles?' → no

★ 'James, from what you've told me I think you most likely have a condition called urethritis. That means inflammation of the urethra — the tube that carries urine out of your bladder. That's why it stings and why you're going more often. The most likely cause is a sexually transmitted infection. Three reasons: your symptoms; the discharge you had last week — the most important part, even though it settled; and the sexual history — more than one partner and not using condoms. This is common and it's very treatable.' · 'is it serious? will you have to tell anyone?' → ★ 'It's treatable, and treating it early prevents complications. Your care here is confidential. Infections like this are reported to the health department in a de-identified way for public health tracking, and we'd talk with you about letting recent partners know so they can be tested — that can be done anonymously. Nothing happens without us discussing it first.' · 'is it HIV?' → far more likely one of the common treatable infections; never tested → full screen incl HIV; PrEP discussion

★ DDx in four groups: 'the same infection a bit deeper — prostatitis, or epididymo-orchitis (no deep pelvic pain, no scrotal swelling); a bladder infection — cystitis — or a kidney infection (no suprapubic pain, no fever, no flank pain); a kidney stone (no colicky loin pain, no blood); and skin causes — balanitis or a contact dermatitis (no rash, nothing new)' · next steps (even without a management task): first-pass urine NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea/M. genitalium + pharyngeal and anorectal swabs, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B serology; empirical treatment today (ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg bd 7 days VERIFY TG); partners; abstain 7 days; retest; PrEP; hepatitis A/B vaccination · summary

pefe: Role-player: James Okafor, 24, hospitality, share house in a country town; fit, no meds/allergies; non-smoker, weekend drinks, no drugs. Opens vaguely ('a bit of trouble passing urine') and says nothing more until a second open question; single-word answers to a checklist. Discharge only if asked directly — adds 'it's gone now, so I figured it wasn't anything'. Says 'men' and watches your face — a pause, wince or tone change → closed for the rest. No preamble → 'do I have to answer that?' once. Hidden: worried it's HIV and who might find out in a small town. End: 'is it serious?' and 'will you have to tell anyone?'. 'You have an STI' bluntly → stung, 'right, okay' — marked down

No examination or investigation task. Positives: 5 d terminal dysuria, frequency, transient yellow discharge a week ago; ~3 male partners in 2 months, no condoms, oral + anal, never tested, never PrEP. Negatives: no fever, flank/suprapubic pain, N/V, haematuria, urgency, nocturia, scrotal/testicular symptoms, rash/ulcers/groin lumps, new products, stones, red flags

Urethritis: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, M. genitalium, (trichomonas, HSV, adenovirus); gonorrhoea — profuse purulent discharge, short incubation; chlamydia — scanty/clear or none. Testing: first-pass urine NAAT (first 20 mL, ≥20 min since last void) + pharyngeal and anorectal swabs (asymptomatic sites often missed), syphilis/HIV/hep B (± hep C) serology; empirical treatment: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg bd 7 d (or azithromycin) VERIFY TG; M. genitalium per resistance-guided therapy; abstain 7 days after treatment and until partners treated; test of cure for gonorrhoea; retest 3 months; contact tracing (last 6 months for chlamydia, 2 months for gonorrhoea) — Let Them Know; notifiable in SA: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV (de-identified/coded); PrEP eligibility (MSM, condomless anal sex) — refer; hepatitis A/B, HPV, meningococcal B vaccination for MSM VERIFY

Sterile pyuria: leucocytes + nitrites − → urethritis, TB, stones, partially treated UTI. Cystitis in young men is uncommon — always look for a cause · SA: SHINE SA · Clinic 275 · letthemknow.org.au · TIS 131 450

setting: Surgical ward, metropolitan teaching hospital; you are the ward MO. Three tasks — consent, explain the steps, select equipment from the trolley (you do NOT perform it). Clock: WIPE/agenda by 0:40 · consent done by 3:00 · steps by 5:45 · equipment by 7:15 · safety-net/summary. Five starred items: chaperone/privacy before exposure; contraindication screen (urethral injury, stricture, latex, cauda equina); urine BEFORE the balloon; foreskin replaced; explicit agreement + documentation. Jargon (meatus, urethra, Foley, aseptic field) is banned with the patient.
stem: James Whitfield, 55, right hemicolectomy 8 hours ago, morphine PCA running; has not passed urine since theatre, distressed with suprapubic discomfort. Bladder palpable; bedside scan 780 mL. HR 96 · BP 138/84 · T 36.8 · RR 16 · SpO2 97% · pain 6/10. The registrar has asked you to insert a urethral catheter. Equipment is laid out on the trolley.
tasks: Obtain informed consent for the procedure
Explain the steps you will take to perform the procedure
Select, from the equipment provided, the instruments you will use, explaining your choice
time: 8 min. Sanitise · 'Mr Whitfield — I'm Dr —, the ward MO. Would you like me to close the curtain? The nurses tell me you haven't passed urine since your operation. I'd like to explain what I think we need to do, go through the risks, and answer questions before you decide. Is anything worrying you in particular?' (brother's infection — park it, return at the risks) · 'just do whatever you have to' ≠ consent → 'I'd still like to explain it properly — a couple of minutes' · indication in his language: bladder full but can't empty — anaesthetic, morphine, lying flat switch off the signal; ~800 mL, three cups; stretch damage, pressure to the kidneys · what a catheter is: soft tube, drinking-straw thickness, in at the tip, along the water pipe, into the bladder, bag; tiny balloon filled with sterile water; awake; numbing jelly · ★ exposure/privacy/chaperone BEFORE: waist down for a minute or two, sheet, curtain and door closed, 'a nurse in the room — routine, for your comfort — male or female? anyone you'd like asked to step out?' (wife — 'I'll ask her myself') · ★ contraindication screen: pelvis/straddle injury, blood at the tip, previous catheter/prostate or water-pipe surgery, told the pipe is narrowed, allergies (latex), feeling around the bottom/legs changed · ★ risks named: stinging, a little blood, urge sensation; infection (rises daily — checked every morning), grazing the pipe, reaction to the material, won't pass → stop and ask urology; alternatives: better analgesia + privacy + try again (bounded), suprapubic by specialists; doing nothing unsafe at this volume · brother → validate, quantify, mitigate · ★ teach-back → explicit agreement → 'I'll document reasons, risks, alternatives, chaperone, agreement' · steps in three acts, plain English · ★ 'urine first, then the balloon' · ★ foreskin forward · equipment: ★ two-way Foley 14 Fr (green), not three-way; pack contents; 2% lignocaine gel; ★ 10 mL sterile water — not saline; closed bag, securing device; expiry/integrity checked · safety-net, 'say stop and I stop'.

back.dx: Acute post-operative urinary retention (780 mL) 8 h after right hemicolectomy — anaesthesia, morphine PCA, immobility, pain, ± underlying BPH (nocturia ×2, slow stream for a year) — needing urethral catheterisation with informed consent. Consent elements: indication in lay terms with the volume; what a catheter is; exposure, privacy, chaperone (choice of sex) before exposure; contraindication screen (urethral injury — pelvic/straddle trauma, blood at the meatus; stricture/previous urethral or prostate surgery; latex allergy; cauda equina — saddle numbness, leg weakness); risks (stinging, transient haematuria, bladder spasm/urge, CAUTI rising per catheter day, urethral trauma, material reaction, failure to pass → urology, not force); alternatives (analgesia + privacy + bounded retry; suprapubic catheter by urology; doing nothing unsafe); teach-back; explicit agreement; documentation. Equipment: two-way Foley 14 Fr, 2% lignocaine gel (dwell 3–5 min), 10 mL sterile water for the balloon (never saline — crystallises), closed drainage bag, securing device, sterile pack (drape, gallipot with 0.9% NaCl, gauze, forceps, fenestrated drape), sterile gloves/apron/eye protection; check expiry and integrity.
plan: Sanitise · 'Good afternoon — Mr Whitfield? I'm Dr —, the medical officer on the ward. Can I close this curtain for you? The nurses tell me you haven't passed water since your operation.' → 'bursting, nothing happens' → 'that is a horrible feeling and I'm sorry you've been sitting with it. Can I explain what I think is going on, go through the risks, and then you decide? ★ Is there anything worrying you before I start?' → brother's nursing-home catheter infection → 'thank you for telling me — I want to come back to that properly at the risks'

Indication: 'your bladder has filled up but can't empty. That's very common after bowel surgery — the anaesthetic, the strong pain relief you're pressing, and lying flat all switch off the signal that lets the bladder squeeze. The scan shows nearly 800 mL — about three cups. If we leave it, the bladder muscle can be stretched and damaged, and the pressure can back up to the kidneys.' · 'can I just have another go, standing?' → 'reasonable — standing genuinely helps some people. My honest view: at three cups and eight hours, waiting isn't safe, and the longer we leave it the harder it is for the bladder to recover. Better pain relief and fifteen minutes at the sink with the tap running — but if nothing comes, I'd want to drain it. Could you live with that?' → 'let's just do it'

'A catheter is a soft, thin, flexible tube — about the thickness of a drinking straw. It goes in through the opening at the tip of the penis, along the water pipe, and into the bladder, so the urine drains into a bag. A tiny balloon near the end is filled with a little sterile water once it's inside so it can't fall out. You stay awake; the only anaesthetic is a numbing jelly.' · ★ 'To do it I need to uncover you from the waist down — only for the minute or two it takes, with a sheet over you the rest of the time. Curtain and door closed. I'd also like one of the nurses in the room with us — routine for this, there for your comfort as much as mine. Would you prefer a male or a female nurse? Is there anyone you'd like asked to step out?' → male; wife outside → 'I'll ask her myself so it doesn't come from you'

★ Contraindication screen: 'a few quick safety questions. Any injury to your pelvis or the area between your legs — a fall, a straddle injury? Any blood at the tip? Ever had a catheter before, or an operation on the prostate or the water pipe? Ever told the water pipe is narrowed? Any allergies — latex in particular? And has anything changed in the feeling around your bottom or in your legs since the anaesthetic?' → no to all (excludes urethral injury and cauda equina aloud)

★ Risks and alternatives: 'the common things — it can sting going in, a little blood in the urine for a day, a feeling of needing to go even though the bladder is empty. The one I most want you to know about is infection — the risk climbs for every day the tube stays in, so we check every morning whether it can come out. Less commonly it can graze the water pipe. Rarely people react to the material. And occasionally it won't pass — then I stop and ask the urology team rather than force it. The alternatives are to wait a bit longer with better pain relief and privacy, or, if it can't go in, a tube through the skin above the pubic bone by the specialists. Doing nothing isn't safe at this volume.' · brother → ★ 'that's real, and it's the risk I'd worry about most too — nursing-home catheters stay in for months; yours: sterile insertion, a sealed drainage system, a review every morning, out the moment you're walking — a day or two, not weeks' · ★ teach-back: 'if you were telling your wife what we're about to do, what would you say?' → 'tube to drain the bladder, small infection risk, out in a day or two' → 'exactly. Any questions? ★ Are you happy for me to go ahead? Thank you — I'll write in your notes that we've discussed the reasons, the risks and the alternatives, that a nurse was present, and that you agreed.'

Steps — 'three parts: getting everything ready, passing the tube, finishing up; I'll talk you through and you can stop me' · (1) Ready: clean the trolley, collect, check every packet sealed and in date; clean hands, apron, gloves; open a sterile pack — 'the inside of that wrapper becomes a clean working surface nothing unsterile is allowed to touch'; drop in the tube, bag, syringe, cleaning fluid without touching; clean hands again, sterile gloves · paper sheet with a small opening; hold the penis with a swab, ease the foreskin back, clean around the opening with sterile salty water, fresh swab each time, working outwards; ★ numbing jelly into the opening, pinch closed, ★ wait three to five minutes — deliberate

(2) Passing: 'hold the penis upright at a right angle with a little stretch — straightens the water pipe; feed the tube in slowly. About two-thirds of the way there's a muscle ring guarding the bladder; when I reach it I lower the penis towards your toes with steady, gentle pressure until it slips past. Pressure, not pain. I never force it' ('if it doesn't go?' → 'I stop and ask urology — forcing is how the pipe gets damaged') · ★ 'I push the tube all the way in, right up to where it splits in two, even after urine starts coming — because the little balloon sits back from the tip, and if I blew it up too early it would be inside the water pipe. Once I can see urine draining, and only then, I fill the balloon with sterile water — the exact amount is printed on the tube, about two teaspoons. Then pull back gently until it sits snugly.' · (3) Finish: closed drainage bag below the bladder; ★ 'I make sure the foreskin is pulled back forward — if it's left back it can swell'; tape to the thigh with slack; clean up and cover; measure and chart the volume; daily review — out once walking and off the morphine, then a trial without it; safety-net: fever/shakes, back pain, no urine in the bag for four hours, heavy bleeding → nurses

★ Equipment: 'this one — a two-way Foley catheter: two ports at the funnel end, one to drain and one to fill the balloon. The three-way beside it has a third channel for washing the bladder out — only for heavy bleeding with clots or after prostate surgery; Mr Whitfield has simple retention with clear urine, so two-way. ★ Fourteen French — French is the circumference in millimetres, so a little under 5 mm across; 12–16 is the adult male range and 14 is the routine choice for clear urine — the smallest that drains reliably; bigger causes more urethral trauma without draining clear urine faster; the green funnel confirms the size. From the pack: sterile drape as the working surface, gallipot for sterile sodium chloride, gauze swabs and plastic forceps for cleaning, the fenestrated drape. I add sterile gloves, apron and eye protection, a 2% lignocaine gel syringe, ★ a 10 mL syringe of sterile water — not saline, which crystallises in the inflation channel so the balloon may not deflate — a closed drainage bag and a securing device. I confirm the balloon volume printed on the catheter, and check the expiry date and integrity of every package before opening.' · 'why not bigger?' → 'size is chosen by what has to pass through the lumen, not the size of the patient' · close: 'I'll get the nurse and the trolley. If at any point you want me to stop, say stop and I stop.'

pefe: Role-player: James Whitfield, 55; hemicolectomy this morning, PCA; heavy bursting suprapubic pressure 6/10, constant urge; polite, gruff, embarrassed, avoids eye contact at the genital mention; three agendas in order — fix the pressure, one more try on his own, brother's catheter infection. Jargon → 'sorry doc, you've lost me'; 'I'm going to put in a catheter' unexplained → 'and what does that actually involve?'; no privacy/chaperone by ~4 min → 'you're not doing this here with the curtain open, are you?'; no risks → 'is it going to get infected? my brother's did'; never volunteers agreement unless asked; digs in if the extra hour is refused without an offer. Background if asked: up twice a night, slow stream for a year; never catheterised; no prostate surgery; no stricture; no trauma; no blood at the tip; legs normal ('why — should they not?'); no latex allergy; BP tablet only. Asks: 'will it hurt? be straight', 'will I be knocked out?', 'how long am I stuck with it?', 'how soon will I feel better?'

Findings given: bladder palpable, scan 780 mL; HR 96, BP 138/84, afebrile; pain 6/10. Trolley: two-way and three-way Foley catheters of various sizes, catheter pack, lignocaine gel, syringes, sterile water and saline ampoules, drainage bags, securing device, gloves

Numbers: 14 Fr default adult male (12–16); funnel colours 12 white, 14 green, 16 orange, 18 red, 20 yellow, 22 purple; Fr ÷ 3 = mm outer diameter; male catheter 40–45 cm; three-way 20–22 Fr for irrigation; balloon 10 mL sterile water (volume printed); lignocaine 2% gel 6–11 mL, dwell 3–5 min VERIFY; hand rub 20–30 s, soap and water 40–60 s; residual 780 mL — >1000 mL → hourly output, U&E; post-obstructive diuresis >200 mL/h × 2 h or >3 L/24 h VERIFY. CAUTI risk ~3–7%/catheter day; contraindications — suspected urethral injury (blood at the meatus, perineal haematoma, high-riding prostate), known stricture/false passage; relative — recent urethral/prostate surgery (contact the surgeon); alternatives — suprapubic catheter (urology), intermittent catheterisation; post-op retention risk — anaesthesia, opioids, anticholinergics, pelvic/anorectal surgery, BPH, IV fluids

Aftercare: closed system below bladder level, secure, daily necessity review, TWOC when mobile and off opioids (consider tamsulosin before TWOC if BPH VERIFY), measure residual, document; safety-net — fever/rigors, loin pain, no drainage 4 h, frank haematuria/clots, bypassing, pain · TIS 131 450 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 (rural)

back.dx: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (catheterised 48 h ago for retention, removed yesterday — within the 48-hour definition) that has progressed to sepsis, possibly septic shock (T 39.5, BP 80/50 → MAP 60, HR 122, RR 26, SpO2 91% RA, vague/drowsy, no urine since morning — bladder scan 620 mL = retention again). Sepsis bundle by phone: oxygen 92–96%, two large-bore IVs, 500 mL crystalloid bolus over 15 min (repeat towards 20 mL/kg with reassessment), obs q15 min, bladder scan → recatheterise (aseptically) and take the urine from the new catheter's port; cultures (urine MCS, two sets blood cultures), FBE/UEC/CRP/LFT/coags/VBG+lactate/BSL/G&H, ECG, CXR; IV antibiotics within 60 min — gentamicin (weight/renal-dosed loading) + amoxicillin, or ceftriaxone if delayed-rash penicillin allergy; avoid all beta-lactams and seek advice if immediate hypersensitivity; escalate — walk down, call the registrar, ICU if not fluid-responsive. Long term: 7 days (10–14 if delayed response), IV→oral when afebrile, narrow at 48 h; treat the BPH (tamsulosin ± finasteride, urology/TURP) — fewer catheters is the single best prevention; no antibiotic prophylaxis at insertion/removal.
plan: Pick up, sit, pen ready: 'Hello, Dr —, medical officer on duty. Am I speaking with the nurse looking after Mr Nolan? May I take your name?' → Jane · 'I've read his notes — could you tell me in your own words what's happened, and give me his full observations, ★ including respiratory rate, conscious state, urine output and allergies?' → 39.5, 80/50, HR 122, RR 26, sats 91% air, 'a bit vague', little urine, penicillin allergy → 'thank you — particularly the respiratory rate and that he's vague'

★ 'Here is what I think is going on. Mr Nolan has a catheter-associated urinary tract infection — an infection seeded when he was catheterised two days ago — and that infection has progressed to sepsis. With a blood pressure of 80 over 50 he may already be in septic shock; I'll know that once we see whether he responds to fluid. Four things: instrumented 48 hours ago; temperature 39.5; hypotensive and tachycardic; hypoxic and drowsy — a systemic picture, not a bladder one.' · 'we've got oral trimethoprim — shall I start it?' → ★ 'No — oral is not enough and absorption is unreliable when someone is shocked.'

★ Sepsis door: 'Before we talk about tests, I am treating this as sepsis and I want a few things started now. One — oxygen, titrate to saturations of 92 to 96. Two — two large-bore cannulae. Three — 500 mL of balanced crystalloid over 15 minutes, then repeat his blood pressure and tell me the number (saline is fine if that's what you have). Four — observations every 15 minutes, and a bladder scan — I need to know whether he's in retention again. ★ Can you read those four back to me?'

★ Investigations, two buckets, before antibiotics: 'urine — a sample for microscopy, culture and sensitivity; midstream if he can, and if we recatheterise him, from the sampling port of the new catheter, never from the bag. Bloods — two sets of blood cultures from separate sites, FBE, UEC, CRP, LFT, coagulation, ★ a venous gas with a lactate, a blood sugar, and a group and hold. Bedside — an ECG and a chest X-ray, because I don't want to assume the urine is the only source' (cannula site, chest, wounds asked) · 'he hasn't passed urine since this morning' → 'then bladder scan first (620 mL). If there's urine he can't pass — catheterise, take the specimen from the new catheter; that also relieves the obstruction. Don't let the urine hold the antibiotics past about 45 minutes.'

★ 'Before I name a drug — the chart says penicillin allergy. What actually happened?' → 'a rash as a teenager' → 'that's a delayed rash, not an immediate reaction — a cephalosporin is reasonable: please prepare IV ceftriaxone at therapeutic dose; I'll confirm the choice and dose against the guideline when I'm with you. I want it in within the hour, and we'll narrow it when the cultures come back at about 48 hours.' (no allergy → gentamicin loading dose by weight/renal function + IV amoxicillin; 'lips swelled, couldn't breathe' → avoid all beta-lactams, gentamicin + on-call physician/ID advice, flag the allergy) · 'what dose?' → 'IV, empirical, therapeutic dosing, checked against the guideline' (never invent a number) · 'continuous monitoring, hourly observations, strict fluid balance and hourly urine measurement. ★ I am walking down now, and I will call the registrar myself. Ring me immediately if his blood pressure doesn't come up after that fluid, if he becomes more confused, or if he stops passing urine.' ('ICU?' → if not fluid-responsive — vasopressors; discuss with the registrar/ICU)

Long term, offered: 'once he's stable — two threads. The infection: seven days of antibiotics if he responds promptly, 10–14 if delayed; IV to oral once afebrile and tolerating intake; narrow when sensitivities return. The prostate — the part that stops it happening again: review anything worsening his outflow, an alpha blocker such as tamsulosin 400 mcg daily, finasteride or a combination if the gland is large; urology for a TURP or a newer endoscopic procedure if medical treatment fails or he re-obstructs. If we treat his prostate properly he shouldn't need catheterising again — and fewer catheters is the single best way to prevent this infection.' (no prophylactic antibiotics at insertion/removal/change) · ★ 'Thanks Jane. To summarise: oxygen, fluids, cultures, antibiotics within the hour, obs every 15 minutes. I'm on my way down and the registrar is being called. Anything you're worried about that I haven't covered?'

Anxious at 4 min if nothing started: 'is there anything you want me to start? he doesn't look well.' At 6 min if never asked: 'the notes say he's allergic to penicillin — does that matter?' 'A rash as a teenager' — or, if you've coped well, 'his lips swelled and he couldn't breathe'. Won't read back unless asked. Bladder scan if asked: 620 mL. Observations: T 39.5 · BP 80/50 (MAP 60; target ≥65) · HR 122 · RR 26 · SpO2 91% RA · vague · anuric since morning · bladder 620 mL. Catheter-associated = catheter in situ or removed within 48 h. Sepsis red flags: hypotension, RR ≥22, altered mentation (qSOFA ≥2), lactate >2, oliguria

Sepsis bundle (Sepsis Kills/SA Health VERIFY): oxygen to 92–96%, IV access, cultures (blood ×2 + urine + relevant sites) before antibiotics, lactate, IV antibiotics within 60 min, fluids 500 mL boluses to 20–30 mL/kg reassessing, hourly urine output, escalate (MET criteria); vasopressors (noradrenaline) if MAP <65 after fluid → ICU. Empirical urosepsis antibiotics VERIFY TG: gentamicin 4–7 mg/kg IV loading (renal/weight-adjusted, ideal body weight, single dose then review) + amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly; delayed non-severe penicillin rash → ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily acceptable; immediate hypersensitivity → no beta-lactams, gentamicin ± advice (e.g. ciprofloxacin); narrow at 48 h; duration 7 d (10–14 if slow/complicated); no post-treatment culture unless prostatitis; catheter removal if colonised; source control — relieve retention (recatheterise), exclude abscess/obstructing stone (USS/CT if not improving 48–72 h)

Long term BPH: tamsulosin 400 mcg daily; finasteride 5 mg daily (up to 6 months; halves PSA); combination; urology — TURP/laser/UroLift/Rezum; TWOC planning with alpha blocker; no antibiotic prophylaxis at catheter insertion/removal/change VERIFY. Telephone conduct: identify both ends, structured handover (ISBAR), closed-loop read-back, state you are attending and escalating, document · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 (rural)

★ Causes, without blame: 'James, erections depend on healthy blood vessels — blood has to flow in quickly and be held there; anything that damages small vessels affects it. First and biggest, your diabetes: your recent test was 8% where we aim for around 7, and missing doses will be part of that. Over years, high sugar damages the small blood vessels and later the nerves — the numbness in your feet tells me that damage has already started elsewhere. Second, one of your tablets — atenolol is known to cause this in some men. Third, your heart attack: the arteries that supply an erection are much smaller than the ones in the heart, so they often show trouble first. I also thought about hormones — a low testosterone level, which I'll test; thyroid; the penis itself — a curvature — or the prostate; nerve or spinal causes; and stress and mood, which are both a cause and a consequence. This is a physical, treatable problem — not a failing on your part.' · 'so it's my fault for skipping the tablets' → ★ 'No — the metformin upset your stomach, and that's a real side effect, not a character flaw. There are ways around it, and that's a problem we can solve together.'

★ Three boxes: (1) 'tests — a morning testosterone with a couple of related hormones, repeat sugar test, cholesterol, thyroid and kidney tests, and your blood pressure properly — at home over a week or a monitor for a day' · (2) ★ 'and this is the part that matters most: getting the diabetes and blood pressure under control. Tell me what makes the metformin hard to take — there are ways around the stomach upset. Then a second diabetes tablet from a group that also protects the heart and kidneys. Back to cardiac rehab, back to regular diabetes reviews; weight, exercise, cutting the beers back helps the diabetes, the heart and the erections all at once' · (3) ★ 'treatment for the erections themselves: sildenafil, taken when you need it, or tadalafil as a small daily dose — sildenafil is off patent, so cheaper. Before I prescribe either: ★ do you ever use a spray, or a tablet you put under your tongue, for chest pain?' → 'a little spray in the glovebox — never used it' → ★ 'that's exactly why I asked. That spray is a nitrate, and taken close together with these tablets it can drop your blood pressure dangerously. It doesn't necessarily mean you can't have the tablet, but we need clear rules and I want to discuss it with your cardiologist first. The rule: if you take one of these tablets, no spray for about a day afterwards — longer with the daily one. Chest pain in that window — call an ambulance and tell them you've taken this tablet. Can you tell me that back?' · 'the tablet needs sexual stimulation to work; headache, flushing, indigestion' · alternatives: vacuum device, injections, urologist · ★ 'I'd like to offer you and your wife a session with a counsellor — not because I think it's in your head, but because it affects both of you' · father at 62 → honest: risk factors treatable, the breathlessness gets checked · review 2 weeks with readings/results · ★ safety-net: chest pain/breathlessness at rest or during sex → stop, ambulance; erection >4 hours → hospital

pefe: Role-player: James Corrigan, 60, farm machinery mechanic near Kadina, married 32 y to Susan, two adult children; T2DM 5 y (metformin bd — skips 2–3×/week, stomach), MI 4 y (one stent, two rehab sessions then stopped), cholesterol tablet + aspirin (vague), GTN spray in the glovebox never used; ex-smoker (quit 5 y, pack/day), 3–4 beers most nights, little exercise, overweight, snores; no diabetes review >1 y; feet numb for months (unmentioned); father died of an MI at 62. ED: ≥3 months; organic clues — gradual onset, consistent, loss of morning erections, same with masturbation; psychogenic — sudden, situational, preserved nocturnal/morning erections. Causes: vascular (diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking, IHD — ED predicts CV events by 2–5 years), neurogenic (diabetic neuropathy, spinal, pelvic surgery), hormonal (hypogonadism — low libido, morning testosterone ×2 + LH/FSH/prolactin; thyroid), drugs (beta-blockers esp. non-selective/atenolol, thiazides, SSRIs, antiandrogens, alcohol), structural (Peyronie's), psychogenic (depression — cause and consequence; risk screen). PDE5 inhibitors: sildenafil 50 mg on demand 30–60 min before, once/24 h (100 mg max); tadalafil 10–20 mg on demand or 5 mg daily; need stimulation; side effects headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, visual disturbance; ★ absolute contraindication with nitrates (GTN spray/tablets, isosorbide, nicorandil VERIFY) — avoid GTN ~24 h after sildenafil, ~48 h after tadalafil VERIFY; caution recent MI/unstable angina/severe hypotension — cardiac risk stratification (Princeton) before resuming sexual activity; alpha-blocker interaction. Second line: vacuum device (band off within 30 min), intracavernosal alprostadil, urology (implant). Priapism >4 h — aspiration + intracavernosal phenylephrine (not adrenaline)

setting: General practice counselling station. The history and examination are done; the dipstick is in the stem. Four tasks: diagnosis with reasons (say cystitis, say bladder, name and exclude pyelonephritis, urethritis and prostatitis even though nobody asked), investigations (urine MCS before the first tablet — every man, every time — plus how to collect it), immediate management (nitrofurantoin SEVEN days, not three or five; the penicillin allergy is a distractor), long-term (reason first, stage one only). back.dx: Acute uncomplicated cystitis in a man — two days of dysuria and frequency, afebrile, no discharge, no flank/suprapubic pain, normal abdomen and DRE; dipstick nitrites positive + leucocytes + trace blood. Excluded aloud: pyelonephritis (no fever, vomiting, loin pain), urethritis (no discharge; one wife, fifteen years), prostatitis (DRE normal). Culture first (every man), treat today: nitrofurantoin 100 mg qid for 7 days (male regimen; not a penicillin — allergy irrelevant; trimethoprim 300 mg daily or cefalexin second line VERIFY), paracetamol, avoid urinary alkalinisers, normal fluids, review if no better at 48 h; same-day/ED for fever, rigors, vomiting, loin pain. Long term, staged: UEC + BSL today; renal/bladder/prostate ultrasound with post-void residual in 2–4 weeks; CT/urology only if abnormal or recurrent; no PSA during infection (falsely high). Hidden agenda: 'is this something I've caught? would I have to tell my wife?'
plan: 'Good morning, I'm Dr —. It's James, isn't it? Before I go through your results, could you tell me what's been happening?' → 2 d burning, running to the toilet; colleague did a urine test → 'that sounds uncomfortable — I have the result and can tell you what I think. ★ Before I do — is there anything in particular you're worried about?' → 'is this something I've caught? would I have to tell my wife?' → 'thank you for telling me — I'll come back to that properly in a moment'

★ 'The condition you have is called cystitis — a urine infection in the bladder. Bacteria have got into the bladder and inflamed the wall, and that inflammation causes the stinging and the need to go so often. Three reasons I'm confident: your symptoms; the urine test — leucocytes, white blood cells your immune system sends where there's infection, and nitrites, a chemical the bacteria themselves make — that's the important one; and the examination, which was normal.' · ★ 'I also considered and ruled out three things: pyelonephritis — infection travelled up to the kidney — you'd have a high temperature, vomiting, and pain in the back or side; urethritis — inflammation of the tube urine comes out through, usually sexually transmitted — the give-away is discharge, and you have none; and prostatitis — infection of the gland below the bladder — the internal examination was normal.'

★ The worry: 'which brings me to your question. What you have isn't usually sexually transmitted — but one condition can look similar, so with your permission I'd like to ask a few personal questions I ask everyone. Is that alright?' → 'just my wife, fifteen years; no discharge, no sores, never had an infection' → 'that, with no discharge, makes a sexually transmitted infection very unlikely — this isn't something you've caught. I'd rather have asked than assumed.'

★ 'One test I need today: another urine sample, to the laboratory for microscopy, culture and sensitivity — they look at it under the microscope, grow the bug to identify it, and tell us which antibiotic will kill it. In a man I do this every time, because urine infections are uncommon in men.' · 'another one? do I wait for the result?' → ★ 'No — you'll get the antibiotic today. But I need the sample before the first tablet, because once the antibiotic is in, the test can't tell us which bug it was.' · ★ how: 'a midstream sample — wash your hands; clean the tip of the penis, foreskin back if you have one; start passing urine into the toilet and let the first part go; then mid-stream hold the jar in the flow until about half full; finish in the toilet; close and label it; drop it at the pathology centre today. Does that make sense?'

★ 'I'm starting the antibiotic today — nitrofurantoin, four times a day for seven days; the seven days is the bit to remember, because men are treated longer than women. Take it with food; don't be alarmed if your urine goes brown — that's the drug, harmless. You mentioned a penicillin allergy — nitrofurantoin isn't a penicillin, so that's not a problem. If the culture shows the bug isn't sensitive, we'll change it. Paracetamol for the discomfort. ★ Leave the Ural-type sachets alone this week — they make the urine less acidic and that stops nitrofurantoin working properly. Drink normally, and don't hold on when you need to go.' ('can I drink on it?' — alcohol not contraindicated but sensible to limit; 'what if it doesn't work?' → next line) · ★ 'Two things bring you back sooner: no improvement after 48 hours; or fever, shakes, vomiting or pain in your back or side — that means it's gone up to the kidney, and I want you seen the same day or at the emergency department.'

★ Long term — reason before what: 'One more thing. Urine infections aren't common in men — in women they're routine; in men the plumbing normally protects you, so when one does happen it's worth a look, particularly if it happens again. I'm not expecting to find anything sinister. So, in stages: today, with the urine, your kidney function and blood sugar. Card → ★ 'Jane, we tested your urine with a dipstick — a strip that changes colour to show what's in the sample.
