must: FAIL — Clearing him for contact sport, or caving after two pushes — he pushes twice ('training's Tuesday, it's only social footy'); hold it with the reason and something constructive: 'this virus makes the spleen swell; enlarged, it's fragile, and a knock can rupture it — serious internal bleeding, emergency surgery; when it happens it's usually someone who felt better and went back early; no contact sport, no heavy lifting, nothing where you could take a hit to the abdomen, for at least four weeks from when this started; light running as you tolerate is fine'; the warning with teach-back — 'sudden severe pain in the upper left of your tummy or the tip of your left shoulder, or feeling faint — ambulance, don't drive; tell me back what you'd do' (★)

FAIL — Leaving 'penicillin allergy' on the record 'to be safe' — a lifelong harm and a scored discriminator; 'I don't think you're allergic; people with glandular fever who take amoxicillin come out in exactly this rash — it's the infection, not an allergy, so typical it can help make the diagnosis; if the label sits on your record you'd get second-choice antibiotics for the rest of your life; I'm recording it precisely as an amoxicillin rash in the setting of glandular fever; if a doctor ever asks, say that rather than just I'm allergic'; characterise the rash first and exclude true allergy (lip or facial swelling, wheeze) and SCARs (blistering, peeling, mouth or eye ulcers) before you say it (★)

FAIL — Never offering an HIV test — the sexual history is taken even though the EBV serology is positive ('I ask everyone who presents like this, because a few infections look exactly the same' → a new partner three weeks ago, no condoms — never volunteered); acute HIV seroconversion is clinically identical; offered as routine: 'one of the infections that looks exactly like this is early HIV — uncommon, very treatable when found early, a simple blood test I'd add when we recheck your liver; is that alright?'; STI screen given the new partner; 'can my parents find out?' → no — you're nineteen, it's your record (★)

FAIL — Omitting the airway question — tonsillar hypertrophy obstructing the airway is the one true emergency and the one indication for corticosteroids: 'can you swallow your own saliva and drink normally? any noisy breathing at night?'; drooling and sitting forward = hospital today, ENT, steroids; steroids otherwise only for severe haemolysis or thrombocytopenia — routine prescribing is a marked error; also LUQ and shoulder-tip pain, jaundice; and saying 'atypical lymphocytes' without immediately explaining it — he hears cancer ('that's not the word you want to hear')

DO — Acknowledge how unwell he looks, signpost, 'what's worrying you most?' (exams in three weeks, and the allergy label — not the fatigue); red flags (weight loss, drenching sweats, bruising, lumps), contacts (housemate's sore throat), alcohol (more than admitted if pressed), sport and training day, uni; diagnosis in plain English ('glandular fever — Epstein-Barr virus; catch it as a small child and you barely notice; catch it at nineteen and you get the throat, the fevers, the glands and the flattening exhaustion'); each result: lymphocytosis with atypical cells ('the classic appearance of fighting this virus, not anything sinister'), transaminitis ('the virus irritates the liver a bit — it settles, and it's why no alcohol'), serology ('three parts — two positive and EBNA negative; that negative is the most useful, because EBNA only appears six to twelve weeks after you catch it, so its absence tells us this is current')

DO — Honest fatigue timeline without promising a date ('throat and fevers settle in one to two weeks; the exhaustion drags — weeks for most, a few months for some; no treatment shortens it and pushing through prolongs it' — 'is that a promise?' catches over-confidence); no alcohol while the LFTs are up, recheck; transmission in saliva — no kissing or shared drinks while symptomatic, but no exclusion from uni ('it's shed for months, so isolating achieves nothing'); a medical certificate and support for special consideration or a deferred exam (visible relief — 'I didn't know I could defer'); review in a fortnight; teach-back at the end ('no footy for four weeks, and I'm not actually allergic to penicillin'); the athlete with a grand final — can't clear him, light non-contact conditioning, review at four weeks, write to the club, and the warning signs if he plays anyway; four months on and still exhausted — post-viral fatigue is recognised, normal bloods reassure, check iron and thyroid, screen mood, graded pacing not boom-and-bust, regular review

setting: Telehealth from general practice, Wallaroo; you cannot examine her and nobody else is in the house. The stem looks like a COPD exacerbation and tempts you into prednisolone + amoxicillin — it is not: the comorbidities make her eligible for an oral antiviral, and the ABSENCE of increased breathlessness removes the exacerbation treatment. Don't ask for vital signs she can't give. Time split: history to 4:35 · diagnosis · antiviral, reliever, sick-day rules by 7:35 · safety-net with teach-back.
stem: Mrs Barbara Quinn, 65, retired teacher aide, lives alone. Sore throat and productive cough for three days, worsening, more phlegm; no shortness of breath. COVID-19 test positive today. Known diabetes, COPD and hypertension.
tasks: Take a history
Explain your diagnosis
Explain your immediate management
time: 8 min. 'Is that Barbara Quinn? Dr — from the practice. Date of birth and address? Good time, somewhere you can talk? If we get cut off I'll ring you straight back. Tell me what's been happening' → ★ acknowledge the fear (positive test, alone) · cough ×6: when/worse, dry or chesty, ★ colour + changed?, blood, ★ more than usual?, smell · throat: ★ one side or both, ★ difficulty swallowing, ★ drooling/managing saliva, voice, mouth opening · ★ breathlessness — the disposition questions: SOB? ★ 'worse than your usual?', ★ normal daily activities (kitchen, shower), ★ breathless sitting still, wheeze/rattle, chest pain, haemoptysis · systems: N/V/D, keeping fluids down (off food, drinking tea), fever, aches, headache, dizziness, rash · COVID before? ★ vaccinations and date (~2 y) · ★ puffers (Seretide, Ventolin) · ★ 'what are you taking for the diabetes?' → metformin + ★ empagliflozin; BP — fluid tablet + another · reviews, control, checking sugars (not lately) · ★ who's at home / who could get to you tonight (nobody; Val next door; daughter in Adelaide) · concerns → 'I don't want to go into hospital — my Ron went in with his chest and never came home' · ★ two diagnoses in two sentences: COVID-19 lower respiratory tract infection + viral exacerbation of COPD · ★ antiviral FIRST: eligible (COPD + diabetes, 65), within 5 days (day 3), molnupiravir 4 capsules bd × 5 days, nausea, interaction check, script sent, delivery, subsidised · reliever: salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer q3–4h; continue Seretide · ★ the two refusals with reasons: no antibiotics (virus; trigger = breathing worse + phlegm change), no prednisolone (not more breathless; sugars) — 'if your breathing changes, both decisions change' · ★ sick-day rules: stop empagliflozin (ketoacidosis) and metformin until eating/drinking; test sugars more often; hold the diuretic if dry; no NSAIDs, paracetamol fine · ★ escalation: breathless at rest/worse than usual, can't do normal activities, chest pain, haemoptysis, confused/drowsy, can't keep fluids down → 000; healthdirect 1800 022 222 overnight; Val today; 'I'll ring you tomorrow'; ★ teach-back: 'tell me back the two things that would make you call an ambulance'.

back.dx: COVID-19 lower respiratory tract infection causing a viral exacerbation of COPD in a 65-year-old living alone with COPD, type 2 diabetes and hypertension — day 3 of sore throat (bilateral, swallowing ok, no drooling) and worsening productive cough with increased volume of whitish-yellow sputum (baseline colour), mild fever, off food but drinking, ★ no increase in breathlessness from baseline, no rest dyspnoea, no functional decline, no haemoptysis or chest pain; last COVID vaccine ~2 years ago; Seretide + Ventolin; metformin + empagliflozin; a diuretic + another antihypertensive; not checking sugars. Immediate management: oral antiviral today (eligible — 65 with two risk factors, within the five-day window): molnupiravir 800 mg (4 capsules) bd × 5 days (nausea; not in pregnancy) — or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir if no interactions VERIFY — script to the pharmacy with delivery; salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer every 3–4 h, continue the preventer; no antibiotics (confirmed viral; exacerbation antibiotic criteria not met — needs increased dyspnoea plus sputum volume/purulence), no corticosteroids (no increased dyspnoea; hyperglycaemia) — both decisions change if breathing changes; diabetes sick-day plan: withhold empagliflozin (euglycaemic ketoacidosis risk) and metformin until eating and drinking normally, monitor glucose more often, hold the diuretic if dehydrated, no NSAIDs; escalation criteria with 000/healthdirect, neighbour check today, GP phone review in 24 h; teach-back. Hidden agenda: husband Ron died of pneumonia in hospital — she fears admission.
plan: 'Good morning, is that Barbara Quinn? I'm Dr — from the practice. Can I confirm your date of birth and address? Is this a good time, and are you somewhere you can talk? If we get cut off I'll ring you straight back. Tell me what's been happening.' → cough 3 days, worse, more phlegm, test positive this morning, 'a bit frightened — on my own here' → ★ 'I can hear how worrying this is, especially with the test coming back positive today and you being on your own. Let me ask some questions so I can work out the safest plan, then I'll tell you exactly what we're going to do.'

Cough ×6: 'when did it start, is it getting worse? dry or bringing something up? what colour, and has the colour changed? any blood? bringing up more than usual? any bad smell?' → 3 d, worse each day; chesty; whitish/a bit yellow — always like that; no blood; definitely more; no smell · throat: ★ 'one side or both? any difficulty swallowing? any drooling or trouble managing your own saliva? voice changed? can you open your mouth normally?' → both; hurts but goes down; no drooling; croaky from coughing

★ Breathlessness: 'are you short of breath? ★ is it worse than your usual? ★ can you do your normal daily activities — getting to the kitchen, showering? ★ are you breathless sitting still? any wheezing or rattling? chest pain? blood coughed up?' → no more than usual (puffed on stairs, always); managing the same as last week; not at rest; a rattle when coughing; no pain/blood · systems: 'nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea — keeping fluids down? fever, aches, headache, dizziness? rash?' → off food, drinking tea; a bit hot yesterday; no rash

'Had COVID before? ★ vaccinations — when was the last one?' (once, 2 y ago; jab ~2 y) · ★ 'what puffers are you on for your chest, and are you using them?' (Seretide bd, Ventolin prn) · ★ 'what are you taking for the diabetes and the blood pressure?' → metformin and ★ 'one called empagliflozin'; a fluid tablet and another · 'seeing your GP/specialist regularly — sugar and BP usually well controlled? checking your sugars?' (not lately) · ★ 'who's at home with you? who could get to you quickly if you got worse tonight?' → nobody; Val next door looks in; daughter in Adelaide · 'anything worrying you?' → 'I don't want to go into hospital — my Ron went in with his chest and never came home' → acknowledge; honest: the plan is to keep her safe at home with clear triggers

★ 'Barbara, your test confirms COVID-19, and from what you've described it has gone down into your chest — a lower respiratory tract infection. COVID is a virus, and for most people it settles by itself. There's a second part: because you have COPD, your airways are already narrowed, and the inflammation this virus causes makes that narrowing worse — so you're also having a flare-up of your COPD. That's why the cough and phlegm have picked up. Does that make sense?' ('is it pneumonia? will I end up in hospital?' → no signs of that today; the plan is built to keep you out of hospital, and clear triggers if that changes)

★ Antiviral first: 'The most important thing today: because you have COPD and diabetes you're at higher risk of becoming seriously unwell with COVID, and that makes you eligible for an antiviral tablet. It works best started early — within the first five days — and you're on day three, so I want to start it today. Four capsules twice a day for five days; the commonest side effect is a bit of nausea. I'll check it against your other tablets, send the script to the pharmacy now and arrange delivery so you don't leave the house. It's subsidised because you qualify.' · 'Second — increase your blue Ventolin: four to eight puffs through a spacer, repeat every three to four hours if you need it. Keep the Seretide as normal.' · ★ 'Two things I'm deliberately not doing. I'm not giving antibiotics: we know this is a virus, and antibiotics do nothing to a virus — the trigger for antibiotics with your chest is when your breathing gets worse as well as the phlegm increasing or changing colour, and your breathing hasn't changed. And I'm not giving steroid tablets — those are for when a flare-up makes you significantly more breathless, and they push your sugars up, which with diabetes and an infection isn't a trade I want to make today. If your breathing changes, both of those decisions change.' ('my old doctor always gave me antibiotics' → hold; 'couldn't I have some in case?' → hold, promise the review)

★ Sick-day rules: 'Because you're on empagliflozin and metformin and you're off your food, stop both until you're eating and drinking normally — empagliflozin in particular can cause a dangerous build-up of acid if you're not eating. Keep your fluids up, and test your sugar more often than usual, not less — illness pushes it up even when you're not eating. If you get dehydrated, hold the fluid tablet too; no anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen — paracetamol is fine.' · ★ 'Now, when to worry: ring us straight away, or call an ambulance on 000, if you become breathless at rest or more breathless than your usual, if you can't do your normal activities, if you get chest pain, cough up blood, become confused or drowsy, or can't keep fluids down. Overnight, healthdirect is 1800 022 222. Can Val look in on you today? I'll ring you myself tomorrow.' · ★ 'Before we finish — tell me back the two things that would make you call an ambulance.' (correct the one she gets slightly wrong) · isolation: stay home, mask if anyone comes in, keep away from the elderly/immunosuppressed; Val leaves things at the door · booster when recovered
ask: ★ 'If we get cut off, I'll ring you straight back on this number.' / ★ 'I can hear how worrying this is, especially with you being on your own.' / ★ 'Has the colour changed, and are you bringing up more than usual?' / ★ 'Is the throat sore on one side or both? Any difficulty swallowing? Any drooling?'

★ 'Is the breathlessness worse than your usual?' / ★ 'Can you do today what you could do last week?' / ★ 'Can you finish a whole sentence without stopping for breath?' / 'What are you taking for the diabetes — which tablets exactly?' / 'Who's at home with you? Who could get to you quickly if you got worse tonight?'

★ 'You have COVID, and because of your COPD it has tipped you into a flare-up.' / ★ 'Because you have COPD and diabetes, you are eligible for an antiviral, and it works best within the first five days.' / ★ 'Antibiotics do nothing to a virus, and taking them when you don't need them stops them working when you do.' / ★ 'The trigger is when your breathing gets worse as well as the phlegm changing.'

★ 'Stop the empagliflozin and metformin until you're eating and drinking normally.' / ★ 'Test your sugar more often, not less — illness pushes it up.' / ★ 'Tell me back the two things that would make you call an ambulance.'

Variant A (day 7): 'Because you're a week in, the antiviral tablets have passed the window where they help — they only work in the first five days, when the virus is still multiplying. That doesn't leave us with nothing: it means we watch you more closely instead. I want to speak to you every day for the next three days, and I want you to be very clear about when to call an ambulance.' / Variant B (breathless at rest): stop counselling — 'your breathing has changed and I don't want to manage this over the phone. I'm arranging an ambulance to take you to hospital now to check your oxygen and your chest properly. I know that's not what you wanted to hear — can you tell me what worries you most about going in? … I'll ring the department myself and let them know you're coming and why.' / Variant C (one-sided throat, drooling): 'that pattern suggests a collection of pus behind the tonsil — antibiotics alone won't clear it, it needs to be drained; emergency department today.' / Variant D (third demand for antibiotics): 'Here's what I'll do instead: a script to hold, and you start it only if two things happen — your breathing gets worse AND the phlegm increases or changes colour. Write those two down. And I'm ringing you tomorrow. Does that feel fair?' / Variant E (grandchildren): 'not while you're infectious — stay home; mask and open windows if anyone must come in; keep away from the elderly or immunosuppressed; I'll give you the current SA Health advice on how long.'
pefe: Role-player: Barbara Quinn, 65, retired teacher aide, widowed, alone in Wallaroo; daughter Kylie in Adelaide; neighbour Val looks in most days; ex-smoker 15 y; COPD (Seretide bd, Ventolin prn), T2DM (metformin + empagliflozin), hypertension (a fluid tablet + one she can't name); COVID once 2 y ago; last vaccine ~2 y. Anxious, polite, short sentences (breathy from coughing but finishes them). Pushes twice on antibiotics ('my old doctor always gave me antibiotics' → 'couldn't I just have some in case?'). Withholds empagliflozin unless diabetes tablets are asked by name; 'I haven't got anything like that here' to BP/oxygen requests. Hidden: 'I don't want to go into hospital — my Ron went in with his chest and never came home' (~6 min if concerns not asked). Repeats the plan back with one thing slightly wrong so you correct it

No observations obtainable. History positives: day 3, increased sputum volume, baseline colour, bilateral sore throat without dysphagia/drooling, mild fever, off food but drinking; negatives: no increase in dyspnoea, no rest dyspnoea, no functional decline, no haemoptysis, chest pain, unilateral throat, vomiting → no red flags for emergency assessment

Antiviral eligibility (PBS, VERIFY current): ≥70; 50–69 with ≥2 risk factors; Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islander ≥30 with ≥1; ≥18 immunocompromised; within 5 days of symptom onset. Molnupiravir 800 mg (4 × 200 mg capsules) bd × 5 days (40 capsules) — nausea, not in pregnancy; nirmatrelvir/ritonavir 300/100 mg bd × 5 days — many interactions (statins, anticoagulants, some antihypertensives), renal dosing VERIFY. COPD exacerbation (Anthonisen): increased dyspnoea + sputum volume + sputum purulence — antibiotics if ≥2 including purulence, or ventilatory support: amoxicillin 500 mg tds × 5 d or doxycycline VERIFY; prednisolone 30–50 mg × 5 days for significant dyspnoea; salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer q3–4h; escalation — rest dyspnoea, SpO2 <92%, confusion, inability to complete sentences, cyanosis. Diabetes sick-day rules: withhold SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycaemic DKA), metformin (lactic acidosis), ACEi/ARB/diuretics if dehydrated, NSAIDs; check BGL 2–4-hourly, ketones if available; insulin adjusted not stopped. COVID booster: 65–74 recommended 12-monthly, eligible 6-monthly VERIFY; isolation per SA Health advice (stay home while symptomatic, mask if leaving, avoid high-risk settings ≥7 days VERIFY)

Telehealth conduct: identity + two identifiers, consent, call-back plan, don't request unobtainable observations, escalation criteria, teach-back, documented review · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · 000 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450
fails: Opening with 'can I have her vital signs?' on a phone to a woman alone at home

Hearing 'more phlegm' and starting antibiotics; accepting 'I do get short of breath' without 'worse than your usual?' (in COPD the answer is always yes); skipping the throat red flags (one side, drooling)
Not asking which diabetes medicines — missing empagliflozin; not asking who is at home
Naming only COVID or only the exacerbation; prednisolone + amoxicillin by reflex; caving on antibiotics; 'there's nothing I can give you'
Antiviral omitted or mentioned last; a lecture on how it works; no sick-day rules; no escalation criteria/review time; ending without teach-back; leaving the hospital fear unaddressed

FAIL — Opening with 'can I have her vital signs?' — she is at home, alone, on a phone ('I haven't got anything like that here'); telehealth conduct: confirm identity (DOB and address), 'is this a good time, are you somewhere you can talk? if we get cut off I'll ring you straight back'; acknowledge the fear of being on her own; and accepting 'I do get short of breath' without the follow-up — in COPD the answer is always yes; change from baseline is the only useful question: 'worse than your usual? can you do what you could last week — the kitchen, the shower? breathless sitting still? can you finish a whole sentence?' → no change, so no transfer; breathless at rest → stop counselling, ambulance

(one-sided with drooling = peritonsillar abscess, ED today); GI and fluids, fever, rash; previous COVID and last vaccination (two years ago — a booster once well); the inhalers by name; who's at home ('nobody — Val next door looks in') and who could reach her tonight; increase salbutamol to four to eight puffs via spacer every three to four hours, Seretide as normal

I'll ring you myself tomorrow'; teach-back — 'tell me back the two things that would make you call an ambulance' (she gets one slightly wrong so you correct it); her hidden fear — 'I don't want to go into hospital; my Ron went in with his chest and never came home' (volunteered at six minutes if never asked what's worrying her) — addressed kindly; isolation while infectious, grandchildren later; summary with the antiviral eligibility stated aloud (65 with two risk factors, within five days)

back.dx: Thyrotoxicosis, probably Graves' disease — three months of progressive 'nerves' with no situational trigger: wound up, tremor, palpitations worse at night, insomnia (waking at 3), irritability; heat intolerance (fan on in winter), loose stools 3–4/day, sweating through clothes, 5 kg weight loss despite increased appetite; mood preserved with no anhedonia, no suicidal ideation, no psychosocial stressors, no sedative use; no neck pain/fever/viral illness (thyroiditis less likely); periods stopped a year ago but no flushes (menopause doesn't cause weight loss or tachycardia); no syncope/chest pain; no episodic headache–sweating–palpitation triad or hypertension (phaeo); two coffees; mother had thyroid disease. Differentials with reasons: anxiety disorders/depression, thyroiditis, perimenopause, phaeochromocytoma, paroxysmal arrhythmia (AF/SVT), stimulants/withdrawal. Investigations: TSH + free T4 (T3 if TSH suppressed), FBC, EUC, glucose, ECG; examine thyroid, eyes, pulse, reflexes; then TRAb/uptake scan, endocrinology; beta-blocker for symptoms, carbimazole. Hidden agenda: a previous doctor said 'just stress'; privately afraid of cancer because of the weight loss.
plan: 'Hello Mrs Wilcox, I'm Dr —, one of the GPs. How can I help?' → 'something wrong with my nerves — wound up all the time, not like me, frightening' → 'I understand, Jenny, and I can see how overwhelming that must feel. Is it all right if I ask some questions so I can work out what's causing it and make the right plan?' → ★ 'Can you describe what you mean by something wrong with your nerves? Anxious and on edge, your heart racing, shaking, or something else again?' → all of it: can't settle, hands shake, heart goes at night

'When did this start? (3 months) all the time or comes and goes? (most of the time) getting worse? (yes) anything better or worse? ★ any particular situation or place that sets it off?' (no — that's what's odd) · 'how is it affecting your day-to-day life — work, sleep, the people around you?' (mistakes at work, exhausted, snapping at Ray)

★ Mini psych: 'how has your mood been in yourself? (all right — irritable) how are you sleeping — getting off, or waking? (awake at 3) ★ appetite, and has your weight changed? (eating more than ever — lost ~5 kg) still enjoying the things you normally enjoy?' (the garden) → ★ 'When people feel like this, they sometimes have thoughts of harming themselves. Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or anyone else?' (no) → 'thank you for answering that'

HEADSS: 'how are things at home? any stress — partner, family, money? work — anything stressful? alcohol in a week? (glass of wine most nights) other drugs? ★ anything to help you sleep or settle your nerves?' (no sleeping tablets)

★ Thyroid, as a run: 'a few questions about your thyroid gland. ★ Do you find hot weather or hot rooms harder than you used to? (can't bear it — fan on in winter) any change in your bowels — looser or more often? (3–4/day) heart racing or pounding? (yes, at night) sweating more than usual? (through my clothes) you mentioned the weight — is your appetite normal? (eating more) any lump, swelling or pain in your neck? any fever or flu-like illness in the last few weeks?' (no)

Menopause: 'when was your last period, and were they regular? (stopped a year ago) any hot flushes — sudden waves of heat over the face and chest? night sweats?' (warm, not flushes) · heart: 'do the palpitations come with dizziness, blackouts or chest pain?' (no) · phaeo: 'headaches with sweating and flushing together, in episodes? anyone told you your blood pressure is high?' (no) · stimulants: 'coffee, tea or energy drinks a day? smoke?' (two coffees; no)

Red flags: lumps or bumps, night sweats, unusual tiredness (very tired) · SADMA: allergies, medicines incl OTC, past history · ★ 'anything that runs in the family?' → 'my mother had something with her thyroid' · 'is there anything in particular you're worried about?' → 'the last doctor said it was just stress' → 'that must have been frustrating, especially when you can feel something has changed — what you've described is a pattern, not a vague feeling, and it points somewhere specific; I'm going to test for it rather than ask you to accept an explanation'

★ 'Jenny, thank you — that helps a lot, and I don't think this is just stress. The most likely explanation is a condition called hyperthyroidism. There's a small butterfly-shaped gland at the front of your neck called the thyroid, and its job is to set the pace your body runs at. Yours is producing too much hormone, so everything is running fast. That fits what you've told me: feeling anxious and on edge, not being able to bear the heat, looser bowels, sweating through your clothes, your heart racing, and — the one that convinces me most — losing weight even though you're eating more. Those together point to the thyroid rather than to nerves. Your mother having a thyroid problem fits too — it can run in families.' · 'so it's not all in my head? is it cancer?' → 'it's not in your head, and the great majority of the time it isn't cancer — usually the gland becoming overactive, which is very treatable. Let me tell you what else I considered, because I've not made up my mind on one thing alone.'

★ DDx, each with a because: 'anxiety conditions — generalised anxiety, panic attacks, phobias, post-traumatic stress — and low mood or an adjustment reaction: but no particular trigger, no panic attacks, your mood is reasonable and you're still enjoying your garden. Thyroiditis — inflammation of the same gland: but no neck pain, no fever, no recent viral illness. The menopause, which overlaps a lot at your age: but menopause doesn't usually cause weight loss or a racing heart. A rare adrenal tumour called a phaeochromocytoma — episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with high blood pressure: that pattern isn't there. Heart rhythm problems like atrial fibrillation or SVT — we'll check with a tracing. And stimulants — caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol, some medicines — two coffees wouldn't do this.' · ★ close the loop: 'a blood test for your thyroid, a full blood count and a heart tracing today, and I'll examine your neck, your eyes and your pulse before you go. I'll see you when they're back — and if your heart races with dizziness or chest pain before then, come back sooner. Anything I haven't covered?'

dx: **Acute inferior myocardial infarction** — territorial ST elevation in **II, III and aVF** with **reciprocal ST depression in aVL**.

**Part of the score is explicitly the reciprocal change.** Pointing out the elevation alone is not a passing interpretation, however confidently you name the territory — and **the reciprocal is also what distinguishes infarction from pericarditis, so naming it does two jobs at once.**

**Inferior = II, III, aVF — the triangle at the bottom. Lateral = I and aVL — the oblique pair at the top left. Anterolateral = V1–V6, taken as one group; you do not need to subdivide septal, anterior and lateral.** **Reciprocal rule: inferior elevation → look at I and aVL. Anterolateral elevation → look at II, III and aVF. IGNORE aVR.**

**Never pattern-recognise.** A formal step-by-step interpretation is expected every time — **recognising an inferior infarct at a glance is not the skill being tested; a reproducible method is, because that is what protects you on the tracing you cannot recognise.**

**Two extras worth naming in an inferior infarct: right ventricular involvement — request V4R — and bradycardia or heart block, which are common.** **If the right ventricle is involved, AVOID NITRATES: those patients are preload dependent and nitrates can drop the blood pressure profoundly. Give fluid instead.**

Management: **aspirin 300 mg CHEWED · a second antiplatelet and anticoagulation per protocol · analgesia · oxygen ONLY if hypoxic · reperfusion — primary angioplasty, or thrombolysis and urgent transfer if angioplasty is not promptly available · continuous monitoring for arrhythmia and heart block · urgent cardiology.**

**SA: in a rural or remote hospital there is no catheter laboratory. The STEMI pathway is thrombolysis locally PLUS MedSTAR retrieval to a PCI centre, with the receiving cardiologist involved WHILE treatment is being given.** Saying so shows you know where you are practising.

**Significant ST elevation: about 1 mm (one small square) in limb leads, about 2 mm in chest leads, in two contiguous leads.** If challenged: **'the formal criteria vary slightly by age and sex, but this degree of elevation is clearly significant.'**

To the patient, no lead names: **'your heart tracing shows that one of the arteries supplying your heart muscle is blocked — that is a heart attack. We need to act now to open that artery. I'm starting treatment immediately and calling the heart team.'**

To **'am I going to die?'**: **'this is serious and we're treating it as an emergency — but you are in the right place, we've found it early, and the treatments for this are very effective. I'll stay with you and keep you informed at every step.'**
plan: **Five seconds of silence first, in your head only: what is the most obvious abnormality, and does it map to a territory?** Then speak the steps. **Do not merge the two** — the examiner needs the structure, not your first impression. **No housekeeping: name, date, calibration and paper speed score nothing.**

**Step 1, rate: 'there are about X large squares between R waves, so the rate is around Y.'** Regular → **300 ÷ large squares** (1→300 · 2→150 · 3→100 · 4→75 · 5→60 · 6→50). Irregular → **count the complexes across the whole 10-second strip and multiply by 6**.
**Step 2, regularity: 'the R-R intervals are equal throughout, so the rhythm is regular.'** March them out with paper or fingers if you need to.

**Step 3, P waves: 'there is a P wave before every QRS, so this is sinus rhythm'** — or **'I cannot see P waves; the deflection after each QRS is the T wave.'** Look in **lead II and V1**. **A P and a T must both be present and separate.**
**Step 4, PR interval: 'about four small squares — normal.'** Normal **0.12–0.20 s = 3–5 small squares**. **If there is no P wave, say 'not measurable' — never invent a value.**
**Step 5, QRS duration: 'around two small squares — narrow.'** Normal **under 0.12 s = under 3 small squares**. Broad = bundle branch block or a ventricular origin.

**Step 6, ST segments — the block the marks sit in.** Compare with the isoelectric line, **then check the reciprocal territory**, then look at the T waves. **Significant elevation: about 1 mm in limb leads, 2 mm in chest leads, in two contiguous leads.**

**Step 7, one clean overall impression. Do not hedge across three diagnoses.** If the label will not come, **describe**: 'a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 with no visible P waves.' **The description earns most of the mark, and the label usually follows.**

**An ST-elevation infarct changes the station — do not wait to be asked.** Move straight to the pathway: **aspirin 300 mg chewed, second antiplatelet and anticoagulation, analgesia, oxygen only if hypoxic, reperfusion.**
**Right-sided leads, particularly V4R.** If the right ventricle is involved, **no nitrates — fluid instead.** Continuous monitoring for **arrhythmia and heart block**, given the bradycardia.
**To the patient, in plain English, no lead names**: a blocked artery, a heart attack, acting now, calling the heart team. Answer the fear honestly and **attach the plan to the answer**.
pefe: **Musts: the seven steps, the correct overall impression, and the reciprocal changes.** **Maybes: a sawtooth in V1, a bundle branch block, a hyperacute T wave.** **Don't-cares: the patient's name, the date, the calibration marks.**
**Request right-sided leads, particularly V4R**, in every inferior infarct.
**Troponin** — substantially raised and rising in infarction; normal or mildly raised in pericarditis.
**If the tracing quality is poor, say so once — 'the tracing quality is limited, but…' — then work with the leads you can read. Do not stall and do not invent findings.**

Do **not** narrate axis, R wave progression, or minor T inversion in a single lead unless asked. **'I can assess the axis — but I prioritised rate, rhythm, intervals and ST segments as the findings that change management here.'**

**When the history says pericarditis and the tracing says infarct, DIAGNOSE THE INFARCT.** Say the mismatch out loud, calmly: **'the history was suggestive of pericarditis. However, this tracing shows elevation confined to a single territory with reciprocal depression opposite, which is an infarct pattern. I am treating this as an acute myocardial infarction.'** **The history is a prior, not a verdict — an objective finding overrules a clinical impression.**

It's treatable, but it does raise the risk of stroke, so part of the plan is deciding whether you need a blood thinner.'**
**Name it → say what it means in one sentence → say what happens next.** No lead names, no jargon. **If she asks whether it is serious, answer honestly and attach the plan.**
plan: **Five seconds of silence first, in your head only: what is the most obvious abnormality, and does it map to a territory?** Then speak the steps. **Do not merge the two** — the examiner needs the structure, not your first impression. **No housekeeping: name, date, calibration and paper speed score nothing.**

**Step 1, rate: 'there are about X large squares between R waves, so the rate is around Y.'** Regular → **300 ÷ large squares** (1→300 · 2→150 · 3→100 · 4→75 · 5→60 · 6→50). Irregular → **count the complexes across the whole 10-second strip and multiply by 6**.
**Step 2, regularity: 'the R-R intervals are equal throughout, so the rhythm is regular.'** March them out with paper or fingers if you need to.

**Step 3, P waves: 'there is a P wave before every QRS, so this is sinus rhythm'** — or **'I cannot see P waves; the deflection after each QRS is the T wave.'** Look in **lead II and V1**. **A P and a T must both be present and separate.**
**Step 4, PR interval: 'about four small squares — normal.'** Normal **0.12–0.20 s = 3–5 small squares**. **If there is no P wave, say 'not measurable' — never invent a value.**
**Step 5, QRS duration: 'around two small squares — narrow.'** Normal **under 0.12 s = under 3 small squares**. Broad = bundle branch block or a ventricular origin.

**Step 6, ST segments — the block the marks sit in.** Compare with the isoelectric line, **then check the reciprocal territory**, then look at the T waves. **Significant elevation: about 1 mm in limb leads, 2 mm in chest leads, in two contiguous leads.**

**Step 7, one clean overall impression. Do not hedge across three diagnoses.** If the label will not come, **describe**: 'a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 with no visible P waves.' **The description earns most of the mark, and the label usually follows.**
**Land one clean impression: atrial fibrillation.** Do not hedge, and do not chase the sawtooth.
**Management: rate versus rhythm control · thyroid function and an echocardiogram · a stroke risk assessment for anticoagulation.**

**To the patient, plain English** — the top chambers firing off in a disorganised way, fast and irregular rather than steady, treatable, **and that it raises stroke risk, so part of the plan is deciding about a blood thinner.**
pefe: **Rate on an irregular rhythm: complexes across the whole ten-second strip × 6.** Never 300 ÷ large squares.
**Look for P waves in lead II and V1.** Baseline wobble is fibrillatory, not organised.
**Thyroid function and an echocardiogram**, plus **a formal stroke risk assessment** to decide anticoagulation.
**If challenged on flutter: the management of rate and stroke risk is the same either way** — say so and move on.
**Musts: the steps, one impression. Maybes: sawtooth, bundle branch block, T changes. Don't-cares: name, date, calibration.**
**Read it, then act.** An acute tracing changes the station — do not go back to history-taking.

dx: **Hyperkalaemia on the ECG — a medical emergency, treated before the level is repeated.** In a patient with **chronic kidney disease and a recently increased medication**, that is the whole story.
**Tall, peaked, narrow-based ‘tented’ T waves** across the leads are the earliest and most characteristic change.
Then in order as the potassium rises: **P waves flatten and disappear · the PR interval lengthens · the QRS widens progressively.** The late change is a **broad sine-wave pattern**.

The impression, in one sentence: **‘an ECG consistent with hyperkalaemia, which in this patient with chronic kidney disease and a recent medication increase I would treat as a medical emergency without waiting for a repeat level.’**

Management in three moves: **calcium (gluconate or chloride) to protect the myocardium → insulin with glucose ± nebulised salbutamol to shift it intracellularly → a potassium binder or dialysis to remove it.** VERIFY
**Stop the offending drug** — most often a **potassium-sparing diuretic, an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker**.

To the patient, no lead names: **‘the potassium level in your blood is too high, and I can see its effect on your heart tracing. At high levels it interferes with the heart’s electrical activity, which can be dangerous. We’re going to treat it straight away, and stop the tablet that is contributing.’**

The seven steps, always in this order: **rate → regular? → P waves? → PR interval → QRS duration → ST segments and T waves → one overall impression.** Two of the seven are rhythm, which is why some people count six.
Numbers: **small square 0.04 s (1 mm) · large square 0.20 s (5 mm) · full strip 10 seconds · normal rate 60–100 · PR 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares) · QRS under 0.12 s (under 3 small squares).**

If the label will not come, **describe before you label**: **‘a [regular/irregular], [narrow/broad] complex rhythm at [rate], with [P waves present / no visible P waves], and [ST changes described]’** — the description alone earns most of the mark.
plan: Five seconds silently first: **what is the most obvious abnormality, and does it map to a territory?** Here it does not — the abnormality is in the **T waves**. Then start the steps out loud. Do not merge the silent look with the spoken read.
**Rate**, with its method stated: **‘there are about X large squares between R waves, so the rate is around Y.’**
**Rhythm — regular?** ‘The R-R intervals are equal throughout.’ **Rhythm — P waves?** Here they are **flattened and difficult to identify**. Say that; do not invent one.
**PR interval — prolonged.** If the P waves have gone: **‘the PR interval is not measurable, as there is no P wave.’**
**QRS duration — widened.** Normal is **under 3 small squares (0.12 s)**.
**The T waves — tall, peaked and narrow-based, tented, seen across the leads.** This is the striking abnormality, and it is the step the whole tracing turns on.
**One overall impression, no hedging** — hyperkalaemia, **treated as an emergency without waiting for a repeat level**, in a patient with CKD and a recent medication increase.
Task 2 — to the patient. **Name it → say what it means in one sentence → say what happens next.** No lead names, no ‘ST elevation’, no ‘QRS’.

Task 3 — **‘what do you do first?’** → **calcium to protect**, then **shift**, then **remove**, then **stop the offending drug**. Reading the ECG and then carrying on with the history is a fail — an acute tracing changes the station.
pefe: **There is no physical examination task** — the tracing is handed over and the station is the readout. What must be requested is the **structured interpretation**, not findings.
**The ECG is the confirmation, not the screening test.** Treat on the tracing; **do not wait for a repeat potassium level.**
The history that belongs with this tracing is a **renal and medication history**, not a chest pain history: **chronic kidney disease, and which drug was recently increased.**
Housekeeping earns nothing and burns the time you need: **name, date, calibration, paper speed, axis, R wave progression.** Go straight to rate.
If the tracing is deliberately poor quality, say so **once** — **‘the tracing quality is limited, but in the leads I can read clearly…’** — then work with the readable leads and do not stall.
If challenged on what you left out: **‘I can assess the axis — but I prioritised rate, rhythm, intervals and ST segments as the findings that change management here.’**

Same STEMI pathway — primary angioplasty, or **thrombolysis plus MedSTAR retrieval** from a rural site

**No reciprocal depression** (ignore aVR). Does the elevation map to one territory? If not — pericarditis
Troponin and echocardiogram to exclude infarction and effusion; **NSAID plus colchicine**
Supraventricular tachycardia
**Regular, narrow-complex, 150**, no visible P waves
**A P and a T must both be present and separate** — the deflection after each QRS is the T wave
Stable: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine. Unstable: **synchronised cardioversion**
Atrial fibrillation
**Irregularly irregular**, no P waves
The baseline wobble is **fibrillatory activity, not organised P waves**. Rate = complexes across the strip **× 6**
Rate versus rhythm control, thyroid function and echocardiogram, and a **stroke risk assessment for anticoagulation**

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — the framework every CVS station is built on. Regional SA general practice; you are the resident. 8 minutes (2 reading): 1 min WIPE · 1½ min peripheral signs · 3½ min praecordium · 2 min presenting. Let me examine you properly first and then I'll tell you what I find.'

'Examiner, on general appearance no features of Marfan syndrome, no central cyanosis, no cachexia. — James, may I see your hands? — No splinter haemorrhages, no Osler nodes, no Janeway lesions, no clubbing.' → 'why are you doing the hands? skip it' → ★ 'Of course, Examiner. Moving to the pulse… regular, rate 84. May I check the blood pressure? Palpatory then auscultatory.' → 'auscultatory only' → 'thank you… 118 over 74' (no radio-radial delay — that is the hypertension station)

'James, turn your head and look to your left — Examiner, no raised JVP at 45 degrees. — James, I'm going to look at and feel your chest now, is that alright? On inspection, no visible apex beat, no pectus deformity, no scars. I cannot feel the apex beat. Heel of my hand at the left sternal edge — no parasternal heave. Pads of my fingers: mitral… tricuspid… pulmonary… aortic — no palpable thrills.' (no abdominojugular reflux; carotids later)

★ MITRAL: 'Bell on the mitral valve… now the diaphragm… S1 and S2 normal, no murmurs. I'd like to perform the mitral manoeuvre. James, roll onto your left side for me — and breathe out and hold — still no murmur. And into the axilla — nothing radiating to the axilla.' (stethoscope stays on the chest as he rolls)

★ TRICUSPID: 'Diaphragm at the tricuspid area… normal. I'd like to perform a Valsalva manoeuvre. James, pinch your nose and blow out with your mouth closed — like popping your ears on a plane.' → 'sorry, like what?' → [pinch your own nose, mime the effort] 'Like this — nose pinched, blow out with your mouth shut.' → 'Thank you. No murmur.'

★ PULMONARY, AORTIC, CAROTIDS: 'Pulmonary… normal. Aortic… normal. I'd like to perform the aortic manoeuvre — James, lean forward for me, breathe all the way out and hold — no murmur. And the carotids, right… left… no bruits.' · at 5:00 with one manoeuvre done → abandon the pulmonary valve, never the manoeuvres · bell before the aortic manoeuvre → 'I would complete by listening at the aortic area with the patient leaning forward in expiration, and auscultating both carotids'

★ 'James, the good news first — I listened very carefully today and I could not hear any murmur at all. The most likely explanation is the fever you had on the day of that check. When we have a fever the heart pumps faster and harder, and blood moving quickly through completely normal valves can make an extra sound — a flow murmur. It settles when the fever settles, and that fits exactly with what I found today. Even so, I'd like to arrange an echocardiogram — an ultrasound scan of the heart, painless, no needles — which looks directly at the valves so we can be certain there's nothing I can't hear. And if you develop fevers, night sweats, weight loss or any breathlessness before that scan, I want to see you straight away.' · 'so my heart's fine?' → yes on today's examination, echo to be certain · 'will this affect my insurance?' → 'I can't speak for the insurer, but I can write to them once the scan is back — a normal echo is the strongest thing you can give them' · 'do I need to stop working?' → 'nothing I found today gives me any reason to stop you working' · 'my dad had a valve replaced — is this that?' → 'worth knowing — one more reason to do the scan rather than just reassure you' · spare seconds → narrate the manoeuvres back (mitral valve when you rolled left, aortic when you leaned forward, heart muscle for the Valsalva) · close: 'normal examination today, most likely a harmless murmur from the fever, an echo to be certain, and back sooner if any warning signs — I'll write to you and the insurer once the scan is back'

pefe: Role-player: James Corrigan, 40, self-employed builder (no income protection if he stops); insurance medical six weeks ago with a cold and fever that week; 'the insurance doctor said he heard something in my heart'; completely well since; preoccupied with insurance and work. Never smoked, six beers a weekend, no meds; no sore throats/joint pains/rashes/dental work; father had a valve replaced in his sixties (doesn't know which). Nothing to find. Asks 'is it something serious?' early (marks counselling now); 'sorry — like what?' on the Valsalva (should be demonstrated, not explained); never asked to roll/lean/Valsalva → fail, says nothing; abdomen or ankles examined → marks it (excluded by the task). Three questions at the end in order: 'so my heart's fine?', 'will this affect my insurance?', 'my dad had a valve replaced — is this that?'. Second examiner: 'why are you doing the hands? skip it'; 'auscultatory only' → 118/74

Manoeuvre logic: left lateral + bell + expiration = mitral stenosis (and accentuates MR radiating to the axilla) · Valsalva — HOCM and MVP louder, everything else softer · lean forward + diaphragm + expiration = aortic regurgitation · handgrip — louder in regurgitant lesions, softer in AS and HOCM · AS radiates to the carotids, MR to the axilla · bell first at the mitral · pulse 15 s × 4 · 3 palpation steps · 5 auscultation spots · 3 manoeuvres. Flow murmur: soft, early/mid-systolic, no radiation, normal S2, disappears with resolution of fever/anaemia/pregnancy. Echo: TTE; TOE if endocarditis suspected. Endocarditis — Duke criteria; blood cultures ×3 from separate sites over ≥1 h before antibiotics VERIFY

Global rating: clear fail — fewer than two manoeuvres, or no explanation of the normal result; borderline — manoeuvres silent/hurried, or reassurance with no mechanism and no echo; pass — three manoeuvres named and performed, complete, honest explanation with mechanism, plan and safety net; excellent — plus absorbing the interruption and narrating the manoeuvres back
Left lateral, bell, expiration — No murmur
Leaning forward, expiration — No murmur
Valsalva and carotids — No murmur; no carotid bruits
fails: Counselling at 0:40 when he asks 'is it serious?' — costs a manoeuvre at 5:40
Jumping to the chest when the hands are skipped (pulse, BP, JVP still happen); attempting radio-radial delay ('stick to your task')
★ Fewer than two manoeuvres; manoeuvres performed silently or unannounced; explaining intrathoracic pressure instead of demonstrating the Valsalva
Examining the abdomen or lower limb — excluded by the task; wasting time on abdominojugular reflux
Reassuring with no mechanism, no echo and no safety net; saying it is 'cured'/'nothing' without the endocarditis/rheumatic caveat
numbers: WIPE 45 s · peripheries 60 s · inspect/palpate 75 s · auscultation + manoeuvres 3 min · explain 90 s · 45° · excludes abdomen and lower limb

Moving to the blood pressure', and nothing else — no explanation, no defence, no apology

DO — Announce each manoeuvre before performing it and keep the stethoscope on the chest as he moves — MITRAL: 'bell on the mitral valve… now the diaphragm… S1 and S2 normal, no murmurs. I'd like to perform the mitral manoeuvre. James, roll onto your left side for me — and breathe out and hold', then into the axilla; TRICUSPID: 'I'd like to perform a Valsalva manoeuvre. Pinch your nose and blow out with your mouth closed — like popping your ears on a plane'; AORTIC: 'lean forward for me, breathe all the way out and hold', then both carotids for bruits; if he cannot do the Valsalva, demonstrate it on yourself in two seconds rather than spending twenty explaining intrathoracic pressure; at 5:00 with one manoeuvre done, abandon the pulmonary valve, never the manoeuvres

DO — Warn about the positions inside the WIPE ('towards the end I'll ask you to move into a few different positions while I listen'), name Marfan and the endocarditis stigmata on general appearance, and take the skip at the hands without protest but still do pulse, blood pressure and JVP — that fifty seconds is exactly the margin the manoeuvres need; the task EXCLUDES the abdomen and the lower limb, and you deliberately leave out the abdominojugular reflux and hold the carotids back to the aortic step

SAY — The explanation needs mechanism, plan and safety net: 'the good news first — I listened very carefully today and I could not hear any murmur at all; the most likely explanation is the fever you had on the day of that check — when we have a fever the heart pumps faster and harder, and blood moving quickly through completely normal valves can make an extra sound, a flow murmur; even so I'd like to arrange an echocardiogram — an ultrasound of the heart, painless, no needles — so we can be certain'; safety net 'fevers, night sweats, weight loss or any breathlessness before that scan, I want to see you straight away'; insurance — 'I can't speak for the insurer, but I can write to them once the scan is back; a normal echo is the strongest thing you can give them'; work — 'nothing I found today gives me any reason to stop you working'; Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient → urgent rather than routine echo given background rheumatic heart disease rates, and ask about sore throats, skin sores and previous rheumatic fever; still febrile today → endocarditis station: three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before any antibiotics, plus urgent echo

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION + discharge conversation. Cardiology ward; you are the hospital MO. This is a HEART FAILURE examination — six places read for congestion; every negative is the evidence for task 2. Stop examining at 4:30 wherever you are and reserve 3½ minutes for a six-step conversation: bridge → state → ask → solve → risk → respect. Decide now that the answer is neither yes nor no. Automatic fails: telling a competent adult he is not allowed to leave; 'yes, you can go' with no examination-based reasoning; never bridging; letting him leave with no red flags/follow-up/medication plan.
stem: Ron Prescott, 70, admitted three days ago with decompensated heart failure. History: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, coronary artery bypass graft. He is insisting on being discharged today.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination with running commentary to the examiner
Advise the patient whether he can be discharged
time: 'Are you the one who can let me out?' → ★ 'I am, and I'll give you a proper answer in a few minutes once I've had a look at you' → WIPE (hands, eyes, pulse, heart, lungs, tummy, ankles; chest uncovered; any pain?) · general appearance: ★ alert/orientated, not drowsy, ★ 'not breathless at rest or on speaking', no cachexia/jaundice/cyanosis, no O2/infusion · hands: xanthomas, splinters, clubbing, peripheral cyanosis, ★ warm and well perfused · pulse 78 regular; ★ BP — 'what limits how far we push his heart-failure medications' · face: xanthelasma, arcus; ★ 'Examiner, I would like to perform fundoscopy' (hypertension) → skip · mouth; ★ JVP at 45° (sternal angle, vertical height); carotid bruits · praecordium: ★ midline sternotomy scar named + drain scars, ★ no device box, apex (unable to comment on displacement), heave, thrills; ★ bell at the apex for a THIRD HEART SOUND — 'no gallop rhythm'; ★ 'no murmur, so I'm deliberately not doing the manoeuvres' · lung bases (→ skip → name it: three points each side, bases to the anterior axillary line, bibasal crepitations) · abdomen without flattening the bed: liver from the RIF; ★ abdominojugular reflux — warn, 'breathe normally through an open mouth', hold 10 s, 'no SUSTAINED rise' · legs: press and hold 15 s, ★ long saphenous harvest scars · ★ offer sacral oedema, daily weights, fluid balance chart, electrolytes/creatinine · 4:30 summarise ('clinically euvolaemic and compensated') · six steps.

back.dx: Compensated (euvolaemic) heart failure on day 3 of treatment for decompensation — alert, not breathless at rest or on speaking, warm, pulse 78 regular, JVP not raised, no displaced apex, no S3, no bibasal crepitations, no hepatomegaly, no sustained abdominojugular reflux, no peripheral oedema; sternotomy + saphenous harvest scars (ischaemic cardiomyopathy the likely aetiology), no device. Discharge: clinically possible, not advised today — the oral diuretic dose and renal function are unconfirmed and the precipitant is unresolved (readmission within a month likely); if he chooses to go he has capacity and it is his right → discharge safely: written medication list, bloods, GP review within 7 days, red flags (more breathless, can't lie flat, PND, ankle swelling, weight up >2 kg in 2 days, chest pain, blackout), daily weights, door stays open. Hidden reason: wife Marg in a motel at $160/night, three hours from home → PATS.
plan: 'Are you the one who can let me out of here?' → ★ 'I am, and I'll give you a proper answer in a few minutes — I just want to have a look at you first so I'm telling you something useful rather than guessing. Good morning Mr Prescott, I'm Dr —. I'll look at your hands and eyes, feel your pulse, listen to your heart and lungs and press gently on your tummy and your ankles. I'll need your chest uncovered — is that all right? Any pain anywhere?' (gloves, sanitiser, blot; bed at 45° — never repositioned)

'Examiner, on general appearance Mr Prescott is ★ alert and orientated, not drowsy, comfortable at rest and ★ not breathless at rest or on speaking. No cachexia, no jaundice, no central cyanosis. Not on oxygen, no infusion running.' · 'may I see your palms… turn them over — no tendon xanthomas, no splinter haemorrhages, no clubbing, no peripheral cyanosis, and ★ the hands are warm and well perfused' → 'skip the peripheral signs' → 'Thank you — moving to the pulse and blood pressure. Rate 78, rhythm regular. ★ I'd also like his blood pressure, since it's what limits how far we can push his heart failure medications.'

'On the face no xanthelasma, no arcus. ★ Examiner, I would like to perform fundoscopy — he has hypertension in his history and the retina is the one place I can see end-organ damage.' → 'skip that' → take it (you've scored for asking) · 'open your mouth and lift your tongue — no central cyanosis, membranes moist. Turn your head to your left. ★ Examiner, at 45 degrees the JVP is not raised, and with the bell either side of the trachea there are no carotid bruits.' ('how do you measure it?' → 'vertical height of the top of the venous pulsation above the sternal angle at 45° — ≤3 cm normal')

'On inspection of the chest there is a ★ midline sternotomy scar consistent with the bypass grafting in his history, with drain scars below it. ★ I cannot see a device box beneath the left clavicle. No visible apex beat, no chest wall deformity.' → 'what does the scar tell you?' → ★ 'That he has established coronary disease, which makes an ischaemic cardiomyopathy the most likely reason he has heart failure at all — as opposed to what tipped him into this admission, which is a separate question.' · 'I cannot feel the apex beat, so I am unable to locate it or comment on displacement. No parasternal heave. No thrills at the mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary or aortic areas.' · ★ 'I'm starting with the bell at the apex specifically to listen for a third heart sound… S1 and S2 normal, no murmurs, no added sounds at each area. There is no gallop rhythm. There is no murmur, so I'm deliberately not performing the dynamic manoeuvres.'

'Examiner, I'd like to auscultate the lung bases' → 'skip the respiratory examination' → 'Thank you — I would have listened at three points each side with the bases out to the anterior axillary line, for bibasal crepitations. Moving to the abdomen.' · 'Mr Prescott, I'm going to press on your tummy — tell me if it's sore. I'm leaving you sitting up.' → 'no hepatomegaly, no liver tenderness. Now the ★ abdominojugular reflux — I'll press here for about ten seconds; ★ breathe normally through an open mouth, don't hold your breath' → 'there is ★ no sustained rise in the JVP'

'I'll look at your legs and press on your shin for about fifteen seconds — it may feel firm. Examiner, no peripheral oedema, and there are ★ long saphenous vein harvest scars on the medial calf and thigh, consistent with the graft. ★ I would also like to check for sacral oedema, and to review his daily weights, fluid balance chart and most recent electrolytes and creatinine.' → 'skip those — please summarise' → ★ 'A 70-year-old man on day three of an admission for decompensated heart failure. Alert, comfortable, not breathless at rest or on speaking, warm peripherally, pulse 78 regular. No features of ongoing decompensation: JVP not raised, no visible or displaced apex, no third heart sound, no bibasal crepitations, no hepatomegaly, no sustained abdominojugular reflux, no peripheral oedema. Sternotomy and vein-harvest scars consistent with his bypass; no device. He appears clinically euvolaemic and compensated on current treatment, which I'd confirm against his weights and renal function.' STOP.

★ 1 BRIDGE: 'Mr Prescott — can I tell you what I found? The blood tube in your neck, which stands up when there's too much fluid on board, is flat. Your lungs are clear at the bases — that's where fluid collects. Your liver isn't enlarged and your ankles aren't swollen. None of the signs that your heart failure is still overloaded are there today.' · ★ 2 STATE: 'So the treatment has worked. I do want to be straight with you though — the fluid has gone, but the heart condition hasn't. We've got you back under control; we haven't cured anything.' · ★ 3 ASK, then stop talking: 'Before I answer about home — can I ask what's pulling you home today? Something specific, or just three days of this place?' → 'the wife's in a motel at $160 a night, three hours from home — and I feel fine'

★ 4 SOLVE: 'That's a real problem and I'm glad you told me — there's a scheme that covers exactly that: travel and accommodation for country patients and an escort. I can get the paperwork started this morning. I can also ask the team to see you first on the round tomorrow.' (cigarettes → patch within the hour; somewhere to be → leave from the ward) · ★ 5 RISK, specific: 'What I'd want you to know is what isn't finished. Your fluid tablet has only just gone back to tablet form and we haven't checked your kidneys on the new dose. We haven't worked out what tipped you over this time — and if we don't find that, there's a fair chance you're back in here within a month.' · 'so can I go or not?' → ★ 'Clinically you're in good enough shape that going home is possible — so I'm not going to tell you that you can't. What I'm telling you is that it isn't what I'd advise today, and why. If you still want to go after that, we'll do it properly rather than have you walk out with nothing.'

★ 6 RESPECT: 'Having said all that — this is your decision, and you're entitled to make it. If you decide to go I'm not going to stand in your way. What I'll do is write your tablets down, get a blood test organised, ring your GP so you're seen within the week, and give you a list of things that mean come straight back: getting more breathless, not being able to lie flat, waking at night short of breath, your ankles swelling, or your weight going up more than two kilos in two days. Weigh yourself every morning. And if you change your mind tonight, come back — nobody will be annoyed with you. Does that sound fair?' · examiner 'yes or no?' → 'Clinically he is compensated, so discharge is possible. It is not what I would advise today, because his oral diuretic dose and renal function are unconfirmed and the precipitant is unresolved. If he chooses to go, he has capacity and that is his right — I would discharge him safely, with a written medication list, bloods arranged, GP review within seven days and red flags.'

pefe: Role-player: Ron Prescott, 70, retired grain farmer, Wallaroo, three hours from Adelaide; admitted 'full of fluid', much better since yesterday; hypertension, cholesterol, CABG eight years ago; not breathless, ankles fine, walking to the bathroom. Blunt, not hostile. Opens 'are you the one who can let me out of here?'; allows a few minutes if asked. Reason (ONLY if asked what's pulling him home): Marg in a motel at $160/night. 'So can I go or not?' at least once, presses if dodged. Told he can't leave or must sign something → irritated: 'you can't keep me here'. Examiner: skips at the peripheral signs (~1:20), fundoscopy, respiratory (~3:45), sacral oedema; asks 'what does that scar tell you?' (silence if you never mention it — marked), 'how do you measure the JVP?', 'please summarise' at 4:30, 'yes or no — can he be discharged?' at the end. Second run: Variant D findings

Heart-failure examination = six congestion sites: JVP · apex (displacement) · S3/gallop · lung bases · liver + abdominojugular reflux · peripheral/sacral oedema — plus 'not breathless on speaking' (most sensitive bedside marker), warm vs cool peripheries (perfusion), BP (limits therapy), daily weights and fluid balance, U&E/creatinine on the oral diuretic. Sternotomy + saphenous scars = CABG → ischaemic cardiomyopathy (aetiology) vs precipitant (ischaemia, arrhythmia/AF, infection, non-adherence, NSAIDs, salt/fluid, anaemia, thyroid, uncontrolled BP). Discharge readiness: euvolaemic, stable on oral diuretic ≥24–48 h, renal function checked on the oral dose, precipitant identified/addressed, GDMT titration plan, education (weights, 2 kg/2 days rule, fluid/salt), GP review within 7 days, HF nurse/telehealth. Capacity — Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 (SA): a competent adult may refuse/leave; document the discussion; discharge against advice done safely

SA: PATS (Patient Assistance Transport Scheme — travel and accommodation + escort for country patients) · Country Health Connect · heart failure nurse · GP within 7 days · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450
fails: ★ Telling a competent adult he is not allowed to leave / must sign something; fear or coercion ('you'll die if you walk out')
★ 'Yes, you can go' with no examination-based reasoning and no unfinished business named; ★ 'you can't' — indefensible
★ Never bridging — examining thoroughly then discussing discharge without reporting a finding to the patient in lay words; never asking why he wants to go

Generic general-appearance list (missing conscious level and breathless-on-speaking); not asking for fundoscopy; walking past the sternotomy; 'added sounds' instead of S3; flattening the bed for the liver; pressing the abdomen/exposing without warning
Still auscultating at 6:00 and improvising a verdict; ★ Variant D — still advising discharge is reasonable; no red flags/2-kg rule/GP follow-up/medication list
