setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — hospital ward. A normal screening examination with ONE finding that only appears if you actively test for it: hold both arms out, palms up, eyes closed, and WAIT A FULL TEN SECONDS. Miss the drift and you report a normal examination in a man who has had a TIA. 'Basic' means SCREENING — all four limbs, representative roots, gait at the end; it does not mean an exhaustive examination of one limb and it does not mean cranial nerves. The examiner interrupts three times with skip instructions and you must obey INSTANTLY and say what you are omitting. Automatic fails: examining one limb when the task said basic/screening; arguing with or ignoring a skip; unsafe gait assessment; silence — examining with no commentary.
stem: Hospital ward. A 54-year-old man admitted after a brief episode of feeling weak and clumsy down one side, which has now resolved. He is alert and comfortable; vital signs stable.
tasks: Perform a basic neurological physical examination with running commentary
State your findings and where you would localise any abnormality
time: DECLARE (15 s): 'I will perform a screening neurological examination of all four limbs · inspection, tone, power, reflexes, screening sensation and coordination · comparing both sides throughout, and I will assess gait at the end if it is safe' · WIPE 35 s + global look: alert and comfortable, speech fluent, face symmetrical, no tremor or involuntary movement, no mobility aid at the bedside · UPPER LIMBS 95 s: inspection, tone (let your arms go floppy), power C5 abduction / C5-6 elbow flexion / C7 extension / C8 grip / T1 finger abduction, biceps + supinator + triceps · THE TEST THAT MAKES THE STATION 15 s: 'hold both arms straight out in front, palms up, close your eyes' and WAIT TEN SECONDS → right arm pronates and sinks → 'there is a pronator drift of the right arm · an upper motor neuron sign, the only abnormality so far; I will pay particular attention to the right side' · LOWER LIMBS 95 s: inspection, tone + ankle clonus, power L2/3 hip flexion, L3/4 knee extension, L5/S1 knee flexion, L4/5 dorsiflexion, L5 great-toe extension, S1/2 plantarflexion, knee and ankle jerks, PLANTARS ('this may feel unpleasant') · SENSATION 60 s: cotton wool demonstrated on the sternum, C5/C6/C8 and L3/L5/S1 with the escalation rule stated · COORDINATION + GAIT 55 s: finger-nose, rapid alternating movements, heel-shin, ask about falls, walk BESIDE him, watch the turn · SUMMARISE 45 s with explicit negatives, then LOCALISE before diagnosing.

back.dx: Normal screening examination in all four limbs EXCEPT a pronator drift of the right arm — a subtle upper motor neuron sign that formal power testing at 5/5 misses. It localises to the LEFT cerebral hemisphere, most likely the corticospinal pathway, and in a man with a transient episode of right-sided weakness that has resolved, the leading diagnosis is a transient ischaemic attack. Say the localisation BEFORE the diagnosis — the localisation is the mark and the diagnosis follows from it. Plan: time-critical even though he looks well — immediate blood glucose, ECG for atrial fibrillation, urgent same-day assessment on the TIA/stroke pathway with brain and carotid imaging, vascular risk factor assessment (BP, lipids, glucose, smoking), antiplatelet or anticoagulant discussed with the stroke service, and do NOT drive until assessed, documented. Completion: cranial nerves, full sensory testing including vibration and proprioception, cardiovascular examination with pulse, heart sounds and BP in both arms, and cognition/speech. If the drift is ABSENT, do not manufacture a finding: 'this is a normal screening neurological examination — a normal examination does not exclude a TIA, because by definition the deficit has resolved, and the urgency of assessment is unchanged.' That sentence scores as well as finding the drift.
plan: Decode and declare: 'Examiner, I will perform a screening neurological examination of all four limbs — inspection, tone, power, reflexes, screening sensation and coordination — comparing both sides throughout, and I will assess gait at the end if it is safe.' (Silently choosing a scaffold means brevity later reads as omission rather than design.)

WIPE and exposure: 'Hello, I am Dr -, one of the doctors here. I have been asked to examine your nerves — I will look at you, check your arms and legs, test strength, reflexes, sensation and coordination, and then watch you walk. I will need your arms and legs exposed. Please tell me if anything is painful. Is that all right?' Then the global look, which produces no physical act but is free marks: 'alert and comfortable at rest, speech fluent, face symmetrical, no tremor or involuntary movement, no mobility aid at the bedside.'

Upper limbs, ITPR: 'no wasting, fasciculation, abnormal posture or tremor. Please let your arms go floppy — tone is normal and symmetrical at the wrist, elbow and shoulder. Copy me and don't let me move you — shoulder abduction C5, elbow flexion C5/6, elbow extension C7, grip C8, finger abduction T1. Power is 5 out of 5 and symmetrical from C5 to T1. Biceps, supinator and triceps reflexes are present and symmetrical.'

THE DRIFT: 'Please hold both arms straight out in front of you, palms facing up, and close your eyes. Hold them there for me.' WAIT THE FULL TEN SECONDS in silence. The right arm slowly pronates and sinks. 'Examiner, there is a pronator drift of the right arm. That is an upper motor neuron sign and it is the only abnormality I have found so far. I will pay particular attention to the right side for the remainder of the examination.' (Two or three seconds and the sign never appears — drift detects the pyramidal weakness that 5/5 power testing misses.)

Lower limbs: 'no wasting, fasciculation or deformity. Please let your legs go floppy — tone is normal, and I am testing for ankle clonus, of which there is none. Hip flexion L2/3, knee extension L3/4, knee flexion L5/S1, dorsiflexion L4/5, great-toe extension L5, plantarflexion S1/2 — power is 5 out of 5 and symmetrical. Knee jerks L3/4 and ankle jerks S1/2 present and symmetrical. Plantar responses — this may feel unpleasant — are downgoing bilaterally.' (Dropping the plantars in a possible pyramidal lesion throws away the most informative ten seconds available.)

Screening sensation with the escalation rule: 'This is cotton wool, and this is what it feels like on your breastbone. Now please close your eyes and say yes each time you feel it.' (C5 lateral upper arm, C6 thumb, C8 little finger; L3 medial knee, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral foot, each compared left with right.) 'Screening light touch is intact and symmetrical in representative dermatomes in all four limbs. Had any point been abnormal I would have mapped it fully — distal to proximal for a sensory level and root by root for a dermatomal pattern — and added vibration and proprioception.' (Never apologise for screening; state the plan and the escalation rule.)

Coordination and gait: 'Touch your nose, then my finger, as quickly and accurately as you can — keep your arm fully straight... now turn your hands over rapidly on your thighs... now the heel of one foot on the opposite knee and run it down the shin. Have you had any falls or dizziness? Good — if you feel safe, please walk to the wall, turn around and walk back; I will walk beside you.' → 'gait is normal, normal base and stride, preserved arm swing, normal turn, no ataxia, foot drop or circumduction.'

Summarise with explicit negatives, LOCALISE, then diagnose, then plan (see dx). Examiner: 'anything you would add to complete your examination?' → cranial nerves, full sensory testing, cardiovascular examination with BP in both arms, cognition and speech.
skips

The three interruptions — obey INSTANTLY, mid-movement if necessary, and state the omission. ~2 min: 'assume the reflexes are normal' → 'Thank you — I will move on to...' ~4 min: 'assume sensation is normal, move on' → 'Thank you — I will omit sensory testing and move to coordination and gait. For completeness I would have screened light touch in representative dermatomes in all four limbs and mapped fully if any point were abnormal.' ~5:30: 'tell me your findings now' → summarise what you have actually done, then say what remains: 'I had not yet assessed gait; I would want to before completing my assessment.' NEVER say 'can I just finish this?'

I will walk beside you.' / 'This localises to the left cerebral hemisphere.' / 'A normal examination does not exclude a transient ischaemic attack.' / 'I would complete my assessment with cranial nerves, full sensory testing, and a cardiovascular examination.'

Variant B — the GIDDINESS stem ('relevant neurological examination' in a 60-year-old): 'Examiner, given giddiness, the relevant components are cranial nerves with particular attention to nystagmus and eye movements, cerebellar testing in the upper and lower limbs, gait and Romberg, a screening limb examination for focal deficit, and a lying and standing blood pressure. I would also ask whether the giddiness is spinning or light-headedness, because that distinction changes the examination.' Trap: a rote four-limb screen with no coordination, gait or postural BP — 'relevant' is an instruction to CHOOSE, and choosing badly is worse than choosing narrowly.

Variant C — the CONSCIOUS-STATE stem (drowsy patient, formal power impossible): 'I will begin by assessing conscious state using the Glasgow Coma Scale, then pupils, then a limb examination adapted to a patient who cannot cooperate fully.' Score it aloud in components: 'eyes open to voice, E3; confused but using words, V4; localises to a central painful stimulus, M5 — total 12 out of 15, E3 V4 M5.' 'Because power cannot be formally tested I am relying on tone, reflexes, plantar responses and the symmetry of response to a painful stimulus; I would check pupils for size, equality and reaction, and the blood glucose immediately.' Traps: a bare GCS number, and a sternal rub — use a trapezius squeeze or supraorbital pressure and say which. Drift in someone who cannot lift their arms → observe asymmetry of resting posture and of response to a painful stimulus.
pefe: Role-player: Dennis Hale, 54, truck driver admitted overnight. Yesterday afternoon his right arm and leg felt weak and clumsy for about ten minutes, then normal; he feels completely fine and thinks the fuss is unnecessary. Smoker, blood pressure tablets taken 'most days'. Worried about his licence but raises it only if asked what is on his mind: 'Will this stop me driving my truck?' THE ONE ABNORMAL FINDING — if asked to hold both arms out, palms up, eyes closed, the right arm slowly pronates and sinks over about TEN seconds; held only two or three seconds, nothing happens; never asked, the sign never exists and is marked missed. No drift during any other test. The partner also plays the examiner and interrupts three times with skip instructions.

Numbers: MRC 0-5 — GCS 3-15 in three components — more than 3 beats of clonus is sustained — TEN SECONDS is how long you hold a drift — C5-T1 upper limb, L2-S2 lower limb power, L1-S1 lower limb sensation — 128 Hz for vibration — biceps C5/6, triceps C7, knee L3/4, ankle S1/2.

To the patient, never the jargon: 'when you held your arms out with your eyes closed, the right one drifted a little, which suggests the signal from the brain to that arm is not quite getting through as it should.' Avoid in front of the patient: pronator drift, upper motor neuron, pyramidal, dysmetria, plantar response. Licence question — do not promise: there are national medical standards for commercial drivers, you will go through them once he is assessed, and in the meantime he must not drive; VERIFY the commercial-vehicle standards in Austroads before quoting a timeframe.
Pronator drift — POSITIVE on the RIGHT — subtle, and appears only if you specifically test for it

FAIL — Arguing with or ignoring a skip instruction, or finishing the manoeuvre first — three interruptions come at roughly 2:00 ('assume the reflexes are normal'), 4:00 ('assume sensation is normal, move on') and 5:30 ('tell me your findings now'), and each is obeyed instantly, stopping mid-movement if necessary, with the omission stated: 'thank you — I will omit sensory testing and move to coordination and gait; for completeness I would have screened light touch in representative dermatomes in all four limbs and mapped fully if any point were abnormal'; never 'can I just finish this?' (★)

FAIL — Never testing pronator drift because power was 5/5, or holding it only two or three seconds so the sign never appears — drift detects subtle pyramidal weakness that formal power testing MISSES and it takes fifteen seconds, and the role-player only drifts if you hold the full TEN SECONDS: 'hold both arms straight out in front of you, palms facing up, and close your eyes — hold them there for me' → 'Examiner, there is a pronator drift of the right arm; that is an upper motor neuron sign and it is the only abnormality I have found so far, so I will pay particular attention to the right side for the remainder of the examination' (★)

FAIL — Unsafe gait assessment — no falls question, assessed from a chair or across the room, or no turn: 'have you had any falls or dizziness? … if you feel safe, please walk to the wall, turn around and walk back to me — I will walk beside you', then report base, stride, arm swing, the turn, and the absence of ataxia, foot drop or circumduction (★)

FAIL — Dropping the plantars in a screening examination — in a patient with a possible pyramidal lesion they are among the most informative ten seconds available ('this may feel a little unpleasant — the plantar responses are downgoing bilaterally'), alongside ankle clonus; and never test one whole arm and then the other, because asymmetry is invisible when the sides are ninety seconds apart — compare each movement left against right before moving on (power C5–T1 above, L2–S2 below)

SAY — Report the drift and then LOCALISE, because localisation is the mark and the diagnosis follows from it: 'the abnormality is a pronator drift of the right arm — a subtle upper motor neuron sign affecting the right side, which localises to the LEFT CEREBRAL HEMISPHERE, most likely the corticospinal pathway; in the context of a transient episode of right-sided weakness that has now resolved, my leading diagnosis is a TRANSIENT ISCHAEMIC ATTACK'; it is time-critical even though he looks well — immediate blood glucose, ECG for atrial fibrillation, urgent same-day assessment on the TIA or stroke pathway with brain and carotid imaging, vascular risk factors addressed, antiplatelet or anticoagulant discussed with the stroke service, and not to drive until assessed, documented; if the drift is ABSENT do not manufacture a finding — 'this is a normal screening neurological examination; a normal examination does not exclude a transient ischaemic attack, and the urgency of assessment is unchanged' scores as well as finding the drift; to the patient use plain words, never pronator drift, upper motor neuron, pyramidal, dysmetria or plantar response

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional general practice. The patient offers you 'my mate reckons it's carpal tunnel' in the first minute; candidates who take the bait start palpating the wrist and testing Tinel and never finish the examination they were asked for. Park it, examine, then explain why the findings do NOT fit a median nerve — naming the SPARED MIDDLE FINGER is the single highest-scoring negative available. Three agreeing findings (power, reflex, dermatome) assemble into one root. Automatic fails: performing carpal tunnel provocation tests instead of the neurological examination; testing sensation by peripheral nerve territory rather than by dermatome; silence; diagnosing without localising, or naming a diagnosis with no differentials.
stem: Regional general practice. A 61-year-old carpenter with six weeks of right-sided neck pain radiating down the arm, tingling in the thumb and index finger, and a grip that feels weaker. Worse looking up or turning his head. Vital signs normal.
tasks: Perform an upper limb neurological examination with running commentary
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: DECLARE (10 s): 'a full upper limb neurological examination · inspection, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination · comparing both sides at every step' · WIPE 30 s, BOTH arms exposed to the shoulders (you cannot compare through a sleeve) · the carpal tunnel line arrives: 'that is a very reasonable thought and I will come back to it properly once I have examined you · the examination is what will tell us' (do NOT palpate the wrist) · INSPECTION 35 s: thenar and hypothenar wasting, guttering between the metacarpals seen from the DORSUM, fasciculation, posture, tremor, scars · TONE 40 s in more than one plane (wrist flexion/extension AND supination/pronation, elbow, shoulder) + pronator drift held ten seconds · POWER 95 s, MRC graded, side by side movement by movement: C5 abduction 5/5, C5/6 elbow flexion 4/5 RIGHT, C6 wrist extension 4/5 RIGHT, C7 extension, C8 grip, T1 finger abduction all 5/5 · REFLEXES 40 s with both arms positioned identically: biceps and supinator REDUCED on the right, triceps symmetrical; REINFORCE ('clench your teeth when I say') before calling any reflex reduced · SENSATION 75 s BY DERMATOME: C5 lateral upper arm, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm → reduced at C6 right, MIDDLE FINGER SPARED · COORDINATION 35 s with the target a full arm's length away · offer to complete: lower limbs and plantars, cervical spine with Spurling, entrapment provocation tests if indicated · assemble three findings into one root, then explain in plain English.

back.dx: Right C6 cervical radiculopathy — three findings that agree with one another: weak elbow flexion and wrist extension at 4/5, reduced right biceps and supinator reflexes, and reduced light touch in the right C6 dermatome, with neck pain worse on looking up. Excluded, each with a reason: carpal tunnel syndrome — the sensory loss is dermatomal with a SPARED middle finger, there is neck pain, and a reflex is depressed; cervical myelopathy — no upper motor neuron signs; Pancoast tumour — no small-muscle wasting and no Horner syndrome. To the patient, no jargon: 'a nerve where it leaves your neck is being pinched; that single nerve supplies the thumb side of your arm and it explains all three things I found.' Plan: bloods for diabetes and thyroid, chest X-ray given forty years of smoking (Pancoast), keep moving and keep working with modified overhead work and heavy lifting, physiotherapy, a letter for the employer and a ReturnToWorkSA pathway if work-related; most settle in 6-12 weeks, surgery considered only if weakness progresses or pain does not settle. Safety-net: return or go to hospital if the weakness worsens, both hands become clumsy, he starts dropping things, or he becomes unsteady on his feet.
plan: 'Examiner, I will perform a full upper limb neurological examination — inspection, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination — comparing both sides at every step.' Then WIPE: 'Hello, I am Dr -, one of the doctors here. I have been asked to examine the nerves in both of your arms. I will look at your arms, move them gently, ask you to push against me, tap a few reflexes and check light touch. I will need BOTH arms exposed to the shoulders. Please tell me if anything is painful. Is that all right?' → 'Go ahead. My mate reckons it's carpal tunnel — he had the operation.' → 'That is a very reasonable thought and I will come back to it properly once I have examined you — the examination is what will tell us.' (Do not palpate the wrist. Do not do Tinel or Phalen now.)

Inspection: 'On inspection of both upper limbs I am looking for wasting, particularly of the thenar and hypothenar eminences and guttering between the metacarpals, and for fasciculation, abnormal posture, tremor and scars.' (Turn both hands over — guttering shows from the dorsum, thenar wasting from the side.) 'There is no wasting, no fasciculation and no abnormal posture.'

Tone and drift: 'Please let your arm go floppy and let me do the work.' (Wrist flexion, extension, SUPINATION and PRONATION, elbow, shoulder, both sides — cogwheeling and spasticity show up in rotation.) 'Tone is normal and symmetrical. Now hold both arms out in front, palms up, and close your eyes — hold it there. There is no pronator drift.'

Power C5-T1, MRC graded, comparing each movement side by side BEFORE moving on: 'Wings up, hold them — shoulder abduction C5 is 5/5 and symmetrical. Pull me towards you — elbow flexion C5/6 is 4 out of 5 on the right and 5/5 on the left. Cock your wrist back, stop me — wrist extension C6 is 4 out of 5 on the right. Push me away — elbow extension C7 5/5 both sides. Squeeze my two fingers — grip C8 5/5. Spread your fingers — finger abduction T1 5/5.' (Testing one whole arm and then the other makes a 4/5 invisible.)

Reflexes with reinforcement: 'Biceps C5/6 — my thumb on the tendon — is reduced on the right and normal on the left. Supinator C5/6 is also reduced on the right. Triceps C7 is present and symmetrical. Before I call a reflex reduced I will reinforce: please clench your teeth when I say... it remains reduced on the right.' (Position both arms identically or the asymmetry you find will be your own.)

Sensation BY DERMATOME: 'This is cotton wool — this is what it feels like on your breastbone. Now close your eyes and say yes each time you feel it.' (C5 lateral upper arm, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm, comparing sides.) → 'that one's duller on the right' at the thumb → 'There is reduced light touch over the right thumb and lateral forearm — the C6 dermatome. Sensation is intact at C5, C7, C8 and T1. Importantly, the loss follows a DERMATOME and not the median nerve territory, because the MIDDLE FINGER IS SPARED.'

Coordination and completion: 'Touch your nose, then my finger, as quickly and accurately as you can — keep your arm fully straight.' (Hold the target far enough away that the elbow fully extends.) 'Now turn your hands over rapidly on your thighs. Coordination is normal — no dysmetria, intention tremor or dysdiadochokinesia. Examiner, that completes my upper limb neurological examination. I would complete my assessment with a lower limb neurological examination and plantars, examination of the cervical spine including movements and the Spurling manoeuvre, and the provocation tests for median and ulnar entrapment if indicated.'

Summary to the examiner: three agreeing findings assembled into one root, with the relevant negatives (no UMN signs, no small-muscle wasting, no Horner syndrome, normal coordination) and the three excluded alternatives with reasons (see dx).

To the patient — ideas FIRST: 'Mr Cassidy, can I go through what I found? And first — what has been worrying you most about it?' → 'Whether I can keep working. I'm on the tools six days a week.' → plain-English explanation, why it is not carpal tunnel, the other possibilities (cord pressure, diabetes and thyroid, chest X-ray as a smoker), work advice and the safety-net (see dx).

The sentence that answers the mate: 'Carpal tunnel affects a nerve at the wrist and usually numbs the thumb, index and middle fingers. Your middle finger is completely normal, you have neck pain, and one of your reflexes is quieter on that side — that combination points to the neck, not the wrist.' To the patient use 'a pinched nerve in the neck', 'the strip of skin that one nerve supplies', 'pressure on the spinal cord itself' — never radiculopathy, dermatome, myotome, dysmetria, pronator drift, myelopathy.

Variant B — the NORMAL examination (58M, resolved deficit): 'this is a normal upper limb neurological examination — no wasting or fasciculation, normal symmetrical tone, no pronator drift, power 5/5 from C5 to T1, symmetrical reflexes, intact sensation C5 to T1, normal coordination. A normal examination does not exclude a transient ischaemic attack — by definition the deficit has resolved. This still requires same-day assessment on the stroke pathway with brain imaging, an ECG for atrial fibrillation, carotid imaging and vascular risk factor assessment.' To the patient: 'everything I have tested today is normal — genuinely good news, but it does not mean nothing happened.' Trap: hedging ('it all seemed okay I think') or letting the urgency evaporate.

Variant C — CERVICAL MYELOPATHY (66M, clumsy hands): increased tone, brisk reflexes, an INVERTED SUPINATOR JERK, positive Hoffmann, wasting of the small hand muscles, unsteadiness → 'there are upper motor neuron signs in the upper limbs with wasting of the small hand muscles. I would now examine the lower limbs and plantar responses, because that is what distinguishes a cervical cord lesion from a lesion above the foramen magnum... mixed signs with lower motor neuron findings at the level of the hands and upper motor neuron findings below make cervical myelopathy my leading diagnosis — urgent MRI cervical spine and a neurosurgical opinion, and I would advise against neck manipulation and heavy lifting.' Trap: diagnosing radiculopathy because there is neck pain and never examining the legs. Other turns: 'just check the hand, doctor' → 'I will examine the whole arm and compare both sides, because that is what tells us where the problem starts.' 'Show me how you test C7' → elbow extension, triceps reflex, middle finger, without hesitating. 'My arm is too painful to push against' → do not force it; grade against gravity, document pain-limited testing, address analgesia.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Cassidy, 61, self-employed carpenter in a country town. Six weeks of right neck pain radiating down the arm with tingling in the thumb and index finger; the grip gives way with the hammer; worse looking up or turning his head. Smokes fifteen a day for forty years. REAL WORRY: whether he can keep working — six days a week on the tools, no income protection — said only if asked what is worrying him. Offers 'my mate reckons it's carpal tunnel' in the first minute to see whether the doctor is pulled off course. Findings are given ONLY as each is tested and never volunteered; an untested root simply has no finding and is marked missed. If only the right arm is exposed he says nothing and marks it. If the candidate starts Tinel or Phalen at the wrist he lets them — and marks it a major error. Says 'in English, doc?' to any jargon.

Roots and numbers: C5 shoulder abduction / lateral upper arm — C6 elbow flexion and wrist extension / thumb — C7 elbow extension / middle finger — C8 grip / little finger — T1 finger abduction / medial forearm. Biceps and supinator C5/6, triceps C7. MRC 0-5. Drift held 10 seconds. A radiculopathy needs THREE agreeing findings. Most settle in 6-12 weeks.

Scored behaviours: declared the scaffold — both arms exposed — not pulled into carpal tunnel tests — inspected dorsum AND palms — tone in more than one plane — drift tested — power at all five roots with MRC grades, compared side by side — found the 4/5 elbow flexion and wrist extension — reinforced before calling reflexes reduced — sensation at all five dermatomes with the spared middle finger named — coordination with the arm fully extended — offered to complete (legs, neck, entrapment tests) — assembled three findings into one root — excluded three alternatives with reasons — elicited and addressed the work concern.

FAIL — Silence, or diagnosing without localising, or naming a diagnosis with no differentials — assemble the three agreeing findings into one root out loud: 'weakness of right elbow flexion and wrist extension at 4 out of 5, reduced right biceps and supinator reflexes, and reduced sensation in the right C6 dermatome — those three findings agree with one another and localise to the right C6 nerve root', then exclude three alternatives with reasons: carpal tunnel (dermatomal loss with a spared middle finger, neck pain, a depressed reflex), cervical myelopathy (no upper motor neuron signs), Pancoast tumour (no small-muscle wasting, no Horner syndrome) (★)

FAIL — Exposing only the affected arm, or testing one whole arm before the other so a 4/5 never stands out against its partner — the whole station is COMPARISON and you cannot compare through a sleeve; both arms exposed to the shoulders, each movement compared side by side, MRC grades and root names every time rather than 'power is normal' (shoulder abduction C5, elbow flexion C5/6, wrist extension C6, elbow extension C7, grip C8, finger abduction T1); and position both arms identically for reflexes, or the asymmetry you find will be your own

DO — Reinforce before you call a reflex reduced: 'before I call this reduced I will reinforce — please clench your teeth when I say… it remains reduced on the right' (biceps and supinator C5/6, triceps C7); inspect the DORSUM as well as the palms, because interosseous guttering shows from the back and thenar wasting from the side; move the joint through more than one plane for tone, since supination and pronation at the wrist is where cogwheeling and spasticity appear; hold your finger far enough away that a short reach cannot hide dysmetria; and close by offering to complete — lower limbs and plantars, the cervical spine including movements and the Spurling manoeuvre, and median and ulnar provocation tests if indicated

SAY — Ask what is worrying him before explaining (his livelihood — six days a week on the tools), then answer the carpal tunnel question in plain words, never 'radiculopathy', 'dermatome' or 'myelopathy' to a carpenter: 'a nerve where it leaves your neck is being pinched — that single nerve supplies the thumb side of your arm, and it explains all three things I found'; then 'CARPAL TUNNEL affects a nerve at the wrist and usually numbs the thumb, index and middle fingers; your middle finger is completely normal, you have neck pain, and one of your reflexes is quieter on that side — that combination points to the neck, not the wrist'; bloods for diabetes and thyroid, and a chest X-ray given forty years of smoking, because rarely a problem at the top of the lung presses on these nerves; most settle in SIX TO TWELVE WEEKS with modified overhead work and heavy lifting plus physiotherapy, a letter for the employer and the ReturnToWorkSA pathway; safety net — worsening weakness, both hands becoming clumsy, dropping things, or unsteadiness on the feet; Variant C (increased tone, brisk reflexes, an INVERTED SUPINATOR JERK, positive Hoffmann, small-muscle wasting) moves the marks to the LEGS, because upper motor neuron signs in the arms are meaningless until you know what the legs are doing — urgent cervical MRI and a neurosurgical opinion, and no neck manipulation or heavy lifting

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — Version A of the lower limb neuro document. The weakness is SUBTLE and grade 4: a candidate who is not actively looking for it records normal power and the station is already lost. Expect a firm press from a 40-year-old man — anything less than firm is a finding. Power gets two full minutes; the bell at six minutes stops you dead, mid-movement. Starred items in the source checklist: running commentary after EVERY movement, naming nerve ROOTS not movements, starting myotomes at L2 (not L1), and finishing power in both legs before the bell — missing any starred item is a fail regardless of the total.
stem: James Whitmore, 40, with a known diagnosis of sarcoidosis; regular medications prednisolone and atorvastatin. His legs have felt weak over recent weeks. Sensation is normal. BP 128/78 — HR 76 regular — RR 14 — SpO2 98% RA — T 36.7.
tasks: Perform a lower limb neurological examination with running commentary to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
time: TWO-MINUTE PLAN: write I T P R S C down the left margin, gait LAST; L2 L3 L4 L5 S1 = thigh, shin, calf, dorsum, sole; knee L3-L4 and ankle S1-S2, both supine; brain → cord → nerve → NMJ → muscle as the differential ladder; SARCOID, STEROID, STATIN in that order · WIPE 40 s: ID check and gloves BEFORE you speak, four steps explained, both legs fully exposed, 'I would wash my hands' · INSPECTION 10 s: no wasting, no fasciculations, no tremor, no abnormal posture, scars or skin changes · TONE 40 s: 'just relax and let me move your legs' · roll ankle, lift and drop the knee, roll the thigh, both sides; do NOT attach a nerve root to tone · POWER 2 min, where the case is won: L2 hands on both thighs 'press up' WEAK, L3 knees bent and hands on shins 'press forward' WEAK, L4 hands behind the calves 'pull your heels back' WEAK, L5 hands on the dorsum STRONG, S1 hands on the soles STRONG; commentate the root after every movement · REFLEXES 45 s: forearm under both thighs, knee L3/4; foot dorsiflexed, ankle S1/2; reinforce with Jendrassik before calling anything absent · SENSATION AND COORDINATION 20 s: VOLUNTEER both even though the stem says sensation is normal ('sensation is normal, please skip' is worth a mark; assuming it is not), heel-shin supine · GAIT: 'if time permits I would assess his gait including heel-to-toe walking, and I would ask about a Romberg test' · say it even after the bell · SUMMARISE the PATTERN before naming causes.

back.dx: Symmetrical proximal lower limb weakness — power reduced at L2, L3 and L4 bilaterally with L5 and S1 preserved, on a background of normal tone, normal reflexes and normal sensation and coordination. Three leading explanations, in order: a SARCOID-related polyradiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy; a CORTICOSTEROID-induced proximal myopathy; and a STATIN-associated myopathy — and they cannot be separated on examination alone. The full ladder for any motor deficit: upper motor neuron — stroke, haemorrhage, tumour, multiple sclerosis; cord and roots — compression, canal stenosis, lumbar radiculopathy; lower motor neuron — peripheral neuropathy, entrapment, traumatic nerve injury; neuromuscular junction — myasthenia; muscle — drug-induced, inflammatory or endocrine myopathy. Plan: bloods including CK and nerve conduction studies to separate neuropathic from myopathic; do NOT tell the patient to stop any medication in the station — 'please do not stop anything on your own; we will decide together.'
plan: ID and gloves BEFORE speaking. 'Hello James, I am Dr -. I have been asked to examine your legs. I will look at both legs, ask you to do some movements, gently tap your knee and ankle with this hammer, and check sensation with cotton wool. I will need both legs fully exposed. Is that alright?' → 'Yes doctor, that's fine.' → 'Thank you. I would wash my hands.'

Inspection, ten seconds: 'Examiner, on inspection of both lower limbs there is no muscle wasting, no fasciculations and no tremor. No abnormal posture, no scars and no skin changes.' → 'anything else on inspection?' → add 'no swelling, no deformity, and the patient is comfortable at rest.'

Tone: 'James, just relax completely and let me move your legs for you.' (Roll the ankle, lift the knee and let it drop, roll the thigh, both sides.) 'Tone at the ankle, knee and hip is normal on both sides.' → 'what would increased tone suggest?' → 'an upper motor neurone lesion.'

POWER — the decisive block: 'I am going to ask you to do some movements. I will place my hands on your leg, and I want you to press against them as hard as you can.' L2, hands on both thighs, 'press up against my hands' → the press is soft → 'Examiner, that press is weaker than I would expect. There is weakness of L2 bilaterally.' L3, knees bent and feet flat, hands on the shins, 'press forward' → 'L3 is also weak, bilaterally.' L4, hands behind the calves, 'pull your heels back towards you' → 'L4 is weak as well, on both sides.' L5, legs straight, hands on the dorsum, and S1 on the soles → 'L5 and S1 power are normal bilaterally.'

Reflexes: forearm under both thighs — 'I am checking the knee reflex, L3 and L4 — present and normal both sides.' Knee bent and foot held in dorsiflexion — 'ankle reflex, S1 and S2 — present and normal, both sides.' → 'what if you could not elicit it?' → 'I would reinforce with the Jendrassik manoeuvre — asking him to clench his teeth or interlock and pull his fingers — before calling it absent.'

Volunteer sensation and coordination: 'Examiner, I would now like to test light touch sensation with cotton wool in each dermatome from L1 to S2, comparing both sides.' → 'sensation is normal, please skip.' → 'Thank you. I would like to check coordination with the heel-shin test.' (Perform supine, both sides.) 'Coordination is normal. If time permits I would complete the examination by assessing his gait, including heel-to-toe walking, and I would ask about a Romberg test.'

BELL — stop dead. Summary: 'no wasting or fasciculation, tone normal, reflexes present and normal, sensation and coordination reported normal. Power is reduced symmetrically at L2, L3 and L4 bilaterally, with L5 and S1 preserved — a PROXIMAL pattern of lower limb weakness.' Then the three causes in order and the ladder (see dx).

To the patient: 'Some of the muscle groups in your hips and thighs are weaker than I would expect. This points either to the nerves supplying those muscles, or to the muscles themselves. I cannot tell you today which of the three it is.' → 'Is it the cholesterol tablet? My friend said those ruin your muscles.' → 'It may be, and that is one of three things on my list — but I do not want to blame it before I have checked. Your sarcoidosis can affect the nerves, the steroid tablets can weaken the big muscles around the hips, and yes, the cholesterol tablet can occasionally affect muscle. PLEASE DO NOT STOP ANYTHING ON YOUR OWN. I will arrange blood tests including a muscle enzyme, and nerve testing, and we will decide together.'

I would separate them with CK and nerve conduction studies.'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitmore, 40, lies on the bed with his legs on it and stays there; cooperative and polite. Sarcoidosis, on prednisolone and a cholesterol tablet; legs have felt heavy going upstairs for about two months. HOW HE PLAYS THE FINDINGS: hip flexion, knee extension and knee flexion — push only about half as hard as he could and let the hands win slowly; ankle up and down — push hard, normal; everything else completely normal; legs floppy for tone. If asked to walk he gets up very slowly and shuffles, taking a long time — deliberately, to burn the clock. Withholds that the weakness is worse going upstairs and does not volunteer the medications. At six minutes: 'Doctor, the examination time is up' — and stops the candidate dead, mid-movement. If the diagnosis is explained he asks: 'Is it the cholesterol tablet? Should I stop it?'

Timing: WIPE 40 s, inspection 10 s, tone 40 s, POWER 2 min, reflexes 45 s, sensory and coordination 20 s = 4 min 35 s, leaving 90 seconds of margin before the six-minute bell. Roots and levels: L2 thigh, L3 shin, L4 calf, L5 dorsum, S1 sole; knee jerk L3-L4, ankle jerk S1-S2, both tested supine; myotomes start at L2, sensation starts at L1.

Starred checklist items (a fail on their own): running commentary after every single movement — names nerve ROOTS, not movements — starts myotomes at L2, not L1 — detects the weakness at L2, L3 and L4. Also scored: ID and gloves before touching, resistance applied to every movement, states L5 and S1 normal, reflexes supine with no more than two taps per tendon, volunteers sensation and coordination, does not do gait first, does not examine the spine or hips, summarises the PATTERN before naming causes, gives all three causes, gives the UMN-to-muscle ladder, plain language, and tells him not to stop any medication alone. Pass guide 17/22 with all four starred items.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — Version B of the lower limb neuro document, the fall from a horse. EVERYTHING IS NORMAL and the examination runs identically to Version A (PE-19) — the only thing that changes is the ending. Do not freeze because there is no abnormality: a normal examination is the answer, and the marks are in naming the three injuries you were excluding, then safety-netting a head injury properly. The trap is treating normality as reassurance and letting the patient go without the return advice or checking who is at home tonight.
stem: Emergency department. A 17-year-old, Tom, after a fall from a horse. CT head has been done and is clear. Lower limb neurological examination requested; every finding is normal.
tasks: Perform a lower limb neurological examination with running commentary to your examiner
Explain your findings to the patient
time: Identical run to PE-19: ID and gloves before speaking, WIPE 40 s with both legs fully exposed, inspection 10 s, tone at ankle knee and hip both sides, power L2 through S1 both sides with the root named after every movement, knee and ankle reflexes supine with Jendrassik in reserve, volunteer sensation and coordination, heel-shin, then gait if time permits · the difference is entirely in the closing sequence: report the normal examination CONFIDENTLY, name the three injuries the examination was designed to exclude (brain, spinal cord, individual nerves), then state clearly what a normal NERVE examination does NOT exclude · a fracture or soft tissue injury · and offer to examine the neck, spine and limbs for tenderness; finish with head-injury safety-netting and 'is there someone at home with you tonight?'

back.dx: A completely normal lower limb neurological examination after a fall from a horse: inspection normal, tone normal at ankle, knee and hip, power normal L2 through S1 bilaterally, knee and ankle reflexes present and normal, sensation and coordination normal. Explain what that rules out, in order: first, an injury to the BRAIN — the CT was clear and the examination fits; second, an injury to the SPINAL CORD — the movements, reflexes and sensation controlled by each nerve level in the legs all work normally; third, injury to the INDIVIDUAL NERVES in the legs — also normal. Then the honest limit: a normal nerve examination does not rule out a broken bone or a soft tissue injury, so examine the neck, spine and limbs for tenderness. Head-injury safety-net: come straight back with a worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, new weakness or numbness, or problems passing urine — and ask whether someone is at home tonight.
plan: ID and gloves before speaking; WIPE with the four steps, both legs fully exposed, 'I would wash my hands.' Inspection: no wasting, fasciculations, tremor, abnormal posture, scars or skin changes.

Tone at the ankle, knee and hip, both sides — normal. Power with the root named after each movement: L2 'press up against my hands', L3 knees bent and hands on the shins 'press forward', L4 hands behind the calves 'pull your heels back', L5 hands on the dorsum, S1 hands on the soles — all normal bilaterally.

Knee reflex L3/4 and ankle reflex S1/2, supine, present and normal both sides; Jendrassik reinforcement offered if a reflex is hard to elicit. Volunteer sensation (L1 to S2 dermatomes with cotton wool, comparing sides) and coordination (heel-shin), and take the skip if offered.

Report the normal examination without hedging: 'Examiner — inspection normal, tone normal at ankle, knee and hip, power normal at L2 through S1 bilaterally, knee and ankle reflexes present and normal, sensation and coordination normal. This is a normal lower limb neurological examination.'

To the patient: 'The good news is that your neurological examination is completely normal. That matters after a fall from a horse, because I was looking for three things. First, an injury to the brain — your CT was clear and your examination fits that. Second, an injury to the spinal cord — I tested the movements, reflexes and sensation controlled by each nerve level in your legs and they all worked normally. Third, injury to the individual nerves in your legs — also normal.'

'So I can go home?' → 'Very likely — but a normal nerve examination does not rule out a broken bone or a soft tissue injury, so I would still examine your neck, spine and limbs for tenderness. And I want you to come straight back if you develop a worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, new weakness or numbness, or problems passing urine. Is there someone at home with you tonight?'

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional general practice. EVERY finding that makes the diagnosis lives in the BACK HALF of the examination: a candidate who does a beautiful motor examination and then dabs cotton wool at one foot will find nothing and call this normal. Two sensory runs and four modalities. The reflexes contradict each other on purpose — brisk knees with absent ankles cannot be one lesion, and saying that out loud is the whole case. Automatic fails: omitting sensation or coordination when the task named them; standing the patient up unsupervised for Romberg or gait; never asking about bladder, bowel or saddle sensation in a patient with bilateral leg signs; declaring the examination normal because only light touch was tested.

tasks: Perform a complete lower limb neurological examination, including sensation and coordination, with running commentary
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: DECLARE the full scaffold · WIPE 30 s with exposure FROM THE HIPS DOWN, underwear kept on, chaperone offered (you cannot test L1, L2 or L3 through trousers, and re-asking at four minutes costs you the sensory block) · INSPECTION AND TONE 55 s: no wasting, fasciculation, abnormal posture, deformity or ulceration; legs floppy; ANKLE CLONUS · four seconds and it is the difference between a vague comment and a documented pyramidal assessment · POWER L2-S2 80 s: it is normal here, get through it cleanly and move on · REFLEXES 45 s: knee jerks BRISK; ankle jerks · REINFORCE ('hook your fingers together and pull hard when I say') · still ABSENT; plantars UPGOING → THE SENTENCE THAT SCORES: 'brisk knee jerks with absent ankle jerks cannot be explained by a single lesion; that combination is important and I will look carefully at the sensory findings' · SENSATION 100 s, TWO RUNS AND FOUR MODALITIES: run one cotton wool L1 groin, L2 mid thigh, L3 medial knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral foot comparing sides; run two distal to proximal for a LEVEL; pinprick 'sharp or blunt?'; 128 Hz vibration great toe → medial malleolus → tibial tuberosity → iliac spine; proprioception with the toe held AT THE SIDES, eyes open then closed · COORDINATION, ROMBERG, GAIT 70 s: heel-shin; ask about falls; stand BESIDE him; Romberg positive = proprioceptive, NOT cerebellar; gait broad-based and stamping · OFFER TO COMPLETE: upper limb sensation, back and spine, peripheral pulses, and ASK about bladder, bowel and saddle sensation.

back.dx: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord due to vitamin B12 deficiency — a COMBINED upper and lower motor neuron picture with dorsal column loss: brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks (confirmed with reinforcement) and upgoing plantars, with loss of vibration to the knees, impaired joint position sense at the great toes, relative preservation of pinprick, a positive Romberg and a stamping gait, and NO sensory level. He is a long-term vegetarian on metformin — both deplete B12. Differentials, given honestly: diabetic neuropathy (would not give brisk knee jerks or upgoing plantars, and usually affects pinprick as much as vibration), hypothyroidism, alcohol, medications, and a lesion in the cord itself — made less likely by the absence of a sensory level, but red-flagged. Plan: bloods including B12 today and INJECTIONS STARTED IMMEDIATELY if low, because nerve recovery is better the earlier treatment starts; nerve conduction studies and neurology referral; honest caveat that some numbness may not fully reverse — which is exactly why treatment starts now. Red flags to return on: trouble passing urine, numbness between the legs, rapidly worsening weakness. A normal serum B12 does not exclude deficiency — check active B12 or methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, and never give folate alone.
plan: 'Examiner, I will run inspection, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination, comparing both sides throughout.' WIPE: 'Hello, I am Dr -, one of the doctors here. I have been asked to examine the nerves in both of your legs — I will look at them, move them gently, test your strength and reflexes, check different types of sensation, and then watch you walk. I will need your legs exposed FROM THE HIPS DOWN; you can keep your underwear on, and I can offer you a chaperone. Is that all right?'

Inspection and tone: 'No wasting, no fasciculation, no abnormal posture, no deformity, and the skin is intact with no ulceration. Please let your legs go completely floppy — tone is normal and symmetrical. I am now testing for ankle clonus — there is none.'

Power, briskly — it is normal: 'Lift your leg up and stop me pushing it down... kick out... pull your heel to your bottom... point your toes to your nose... big toe up, hold it... push down like an accelerator. Power is 5 out of 5 and symmetrical from L2 to S2.'

THE REFLEXES THAT DO NOT AGREE: 'Knee jerks, L3 and L4, are brisk bilaterally. Ankle jerks, S1 and S2 — I will reinforce: please hook your fingers together and pull hard when I say. They remain absent bilaterally. Plantar responses — this may feel unpleasant — are upgoing bilaterally.' Then react to them: 'Examiner, brisk knee jerks with absent ankle jerks cannot be explained by a single lesion. That combination is important and I will look carefully at the sensory findings.'

SENSATION — the scoring block, two runs and four modalities. Demonstrate first: 'This is cotton wool. This is what it feels like on your chest. Now please close your eyes and say yes each time you feel it.' Run one by dermatome: L1 groin, L2 mid thigh, L3 medial knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral foot, comparing sides. Run two: 'Now I am starting at the toes and working upwards to find where sensation becomes normal' → normalises at the mid-calf, NO sensory level on the trunk. Pinprick: 'this is a sharper tip — sharp or blunt?' Vibration: 'this is the buzzing on your breastbone — tell me the moment it stops' (great toe → medial malleolus → tibial tuberosity → iliac spine) → not felt until the tibial tuberosity. Proprioception: 'I am holding your big toe AT THE SIDES. Eyes open — this is up, this is down. Now eyes closed — up or down?' → wrong on two of four.

Report it as a pattern: 'There is mild distal reduction in light touch and pinprick, but the striking finding is loss of vibration sense to the level of the knees and impaired joint position sense at the great toes bilaterally, with relatively preserved pinprick — a selective dorsal column pattern. There is no sensory level on the trunk.'

Coordination, Romberg, gait: 'Put the heel of one foot on the opposite knee and run it smoothly down the shin... and the other side. Now, have you had any falls? Please stand with your feet together, arms by your side. I am standing right beside you and I won't let you fall. Now close your eyes.' → sways markedly → 'Heel-shin is accurate with the eyes open. Romberg's test is POSITIVE — steady with the eyes open and swaying with them closed, which indicates impaired PROPRIOCEPTION rather than cerebellar disease. The gait is broad-based and stamping.' Then offer to complete: upper limb sensation, back and spine, peripheral pulses, and ask about bladder, bowel and saddle sensation.

Summary and localisation to the examiner (see dx), then the patient — ideas FIRST: 'Mr Ellis, may I explain what I found? Before I do — what had you been thinking might be causing it?' → 'My brother said it sounded like the start of MS.' → acknowledge it, then explain in plain words: the nerves carrying vibration and joint position from the feet are affected while the ones carrying pain are relatively spared; the commonest cause of exactly that pattern is low vitamin B12; twenty years vegetarian plus metformin; B12 keeps the insulating coating around the nerves healthy, which is why balance is worse in the dark and the shower. Bloods today, injections started straight away if low, nerve conduction studies, neurology — and the honest caveat about incomplete recovery.

'Brisk knee jerks with absent ankle jerks cannot be explained by a single lesion.' / 'I am standing right beside you and I will not let you fall.' / 'Romberg is positive, indicating impaired proprioception rather than cerebellar disease.' / 'Have you had any trouble passing urine, any numbness between your legs, or any loss of bowel control?' / 'This localises to... and the most likely cause is...'

Variant B — CORD COMPRESSION (44F): spastic tone with sustained clonus, pyramidal weakness, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars, a SENSORY LEVEL at the umbilicus and new urinary urgency → 'sensation is reduced below a clear level at the umbilicus, at approximately T10. May I ask — have you had any trouble passing urine, any numbness between your legs, or any loss of bowel control?... This is a spastic paraparesis with a sensory level at T10 and new bladder symptoms — a spinal cord lesion until proven otherwise. Urgent MRI of the whole spine today and immediate discussion with neurosurgery; in a regional setting I would activate MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for transfer.' Trap: finding the level and then politely carrying on with heel-shin — the station has become an emergency and your commentary must say so.

Variant C — L5 RADICULOPATHY (36M): unilateral weak ankle dorsiflexion and great-toe extension, sensory loss over the dorsum and first web space, ankle jerk PRESERVED, positive straight-leg raise, back pain → 'the weakness is unilateral in an L5 distribution with matching dermatomal sensory loss and a preserved ankle jerk. I would like to test ankle INVERSION, which is weak in an L5 radiculopathy and spared in a common peroneal nerve palsy, and I would perform a straight-leg raise.' Harder turns: no tuning fork on the tray → say what you would have used and carry on, do not hunt. 'Is it MS, doctor?' mid-examination → 'that is exactly what I want to talk through with you — can I finish examining you first so that what I say is worth something?' 'Why not diabetic neuropathy?' → 'it would not give brisk knee jerks or upgoing plantars, and it usually affects pinprick as much as vibration.' 'He is anaemic with a normal B12' → 'a normal serum B12 does not exclude deficiency; I would check active B12 or methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, and I would not give folate alone.'
pefe: Role-player: Ray Ellis, 58, school groundsman in a country town. Six months of numb, tingly feet 'like thick socks', creeping up the shins; fingertips now tingling; unsteady, much worse in the dark and in the shower where he holds the wall; no falls. VEGETARIAN FOR TWENTY YEARS, type 2 diabetes on METFORMIN, rarely drinks. His brother told him it sounds like MS and it frightens him — he says so only if asked what he thinks is going on, or right at the end. No bladder, bowel or saddle symptoms, but only if asked directly. Findings are released ONE ROOT AT A TIME as tested and never volunteered; an untested modality simply has no finding. Ankle jerks: nothing, however well you tap, and nothing on reinforcement. Toe held TOP AND BOTTOM instead of at the sides — he gets them all right, and the technique is marked wrong.

Numbers: sensory run L1-S1, power L2-S2, knee jerk L3/4, ankle jerk S1/2, more than 3 beats of clonus is sustained, 128 Hz tuning fork for vibration (256 Hz is for hearing), MRC 0-5, TWO runs and FOUR modalities, 100 seconds is the target for the sensory block, medial malleolus = L4 in every reference. Romberg tests PROPRIOCEPTION, not the cerebellum — the single most commonly misquoted sign in the neurology stations.

Words to avoid in front of the patient: subacute combined degeneration, dorsal columns, proprioception, plantar response, Romberg, myelopathy. Say instead 'the nerves that tell your brain where your feet are' and 'the insulating coating around the nerves'. If the examiner skips you ahead ('please move to sensation'), obey instantly and state the omission — never negotiate and never finish the movement you were on.
Light touch and pinprick — Mildly reduced in the feet — relatively preserved
Vibration — ABSENT to the knees
fails: ★ Omitting sensation or coordination when the task named them; doing one modality or one run, so the dorsal column pattern — the entire diagnosis — is never separated from spinothalamic loss
★ Standing the patient up unsupervised for Romberg or gait — no falls question, candidate seated or across the room
Never asking about bladder, bowel or saddle sensation in a patient with bilateral leg signs
Calling a positive Romberg 'cerebellar'; reporting the reflexes without reacting to the brisk-knee/absent-ankle contradiction; calling ankle jerks absent without reinforcement
Leaving trousers on so L1-L3 cannot be tested; leading the explanation with 'subacute combined degeneration' instead of the vitamin, the nerve coating and the fact that treatment starts today
numbers: 2 sensory runs, 4 modalities, ~100 s · sensation L1-S1, power L2-S2 · knee L3/4, ankle S1/2 · >3 beats clonus = sustained · 128 Hz (not 256) · toe held AT THE SIDES · Romberg = proprioception

Brisk knees + absent ankles + upgoing plantars = combined UMN and LMN · vibration lost to the knees with preserved pinprick = dorsal column · no sensory level argues against cord compression · B12 injections started the same day; active B12/MMA if serum B12 normal; never folate alone

findings: No wasting or fasciculation; normal tone; no clonus
ABSENT — confirm with reinforcement before you report it
Romberg POSITIVE; unsteady, much worse in the dark
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Declaring the examination normal because only light touch was tested — every finding that makes the diagnosis lives in the BACK HALF of the examination, and a beautiful motor examination followed by a dab of cotton wool at one foot finds nothing at all; the sensory block is TWO RUNS and FOUR MODALITIES over about 100 seconds — run one L1 groin, L2 mid thigh, L3 medial knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral foot comparing sides; run two distal to proximal to find where sensation becomes normal; then pinprick ('sharp or blunt?'); then the 128 Hz fork from the great toe climbing to the medial malleolus and tibial tuberosity; then joint position sense with the toe held AT THE SIDES, eyes closed (★)

FAIL — Omitting sensation or coordination when the task named them, or reporting the reflexes without reacting to them — the examiner has built the case around the contradiction, so say it out loud: 'brisk knee jerks with absent ankle jerks and upgoing plantars is a combined upper and lower motor neuron picture; a single lesion does not explain it, so I will pay particular attention to the sensory modalities'; and REINFORCE before calling the ankle jerks absent — 'please hook your fingers together and pull hard when I say… still absent bilaterally, with reinforcement' — because without it 'absent' is an assertion rather than a finding (★)

FAIL — Standing the patient up unsupervised for Romberg or gait — no falls question, candidate seated or across the room: 'have you had any falls? … please stand with your feet together, arms by your side; I am standing right beside you and I won't let you fall — now close your eyes'; then walk with him, with a turn — the gait is broad-based and stamping, feet placed heavily, eyes on the floor (★)

FAIL — Never asking about bladder, bowel or saddle sensation in a patient with bilateral leg signs: 'have you had any trouble passing urine, any numbness between your legs, or any loss of bowel control?'; ask about the SYMPTOMS first and offer a rectal examination only if the answers warrant it and with a chaperone — never as your opening line (★)

FAIL — Calling a positive Romberg 'cerebellar' — the single most commonly misquoted sign in the neurology stations: 'Romberg's test is positive — he is steady with his eyes open and sways markedly with them closed, which indicates impaired PROPRIOCEPTION rather than cerebellar disease', and heel–shin is accurate with the eyes open, which is the point; also get the trousers off at the start, because you cannot test L1, L2 or L3 through clothing and re-asking at four minutes costs you the sensory block

SAY — Localise, then lead the explanation with the vitamin rather than the syndrome: 'brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks and upgoing plantars, with loss of vibration to the knees, impaired proprioception, relatively preserved pinprick, a positive Romberg and a stamping gait, and NO SENSORY LEVEL — a combined upper and lower motor neuron picture with dorsal column loss; my leading diagnosis is SUBACUTE COMBINED DEGENERATION from vitamin B12 deficiency', with twenty years vegetarian and metformin as the causes; ask what he has been thinking before explaining, because the MS fear is never volunteered; to the patient say 'the nerves that tell your brain where your feet are' and 'the insulating coating around the nerves', never subacute combined degeneration, dorsal columns, proprioception or Romberg; bloods including B12 with injections started TODAY because recovery is better the earlier you treat, plus nerve conduction studies and neurology referral, and the honest caveat that some numbness may not fully reverse; probes — diabetic neuropathy would not give brisk knee jerks or upgoing plantars and usually affects pinprick as much as vibration, and a normal serum B12 does not exclude deficiency (check active B12 or methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, and never give folate alone); Variant B — spastic tone with sustained clonus, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars, a sensory level at the umbilicus and new urinary urgency — is a spinal cord lesion until proven otherwise: urgent MRI of the whole spine TODAY, neurosurgery, and MedSTAR transfer from a regional site

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice. The script runs VERSION B, the cubital tunnel, because that is the version candidates lose. The finding only exists if you PULL YOUR FINGERS OUT of the grip, and the sensory loss is a SILENCE — he will not say 'no', he simply says nothing. The root you find chooses which tunnel you test first, and you say so out loud. No skips are given on ITPRSC in this station. Automatic fails: performing carpal tunnel provocation tests instead of the neurological examination; testing sensation by peripheral nerve territory rather than by dermatome; silence with no commentary; diagnosing without localising or with no differentials.
stem: General practice. James, a 35-year-old factory worker, with pins and needles in the right hand. Otherwise well, observations normal. 8 minutes, 2 minutes reading; expect a prompt around 6 minutes.
tasks: Perform an upper limb neurological examination, with a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: WIPE, patient stays SITTING, both arms fully exposed, hand hygiene verbalised (no sanitiser on the bench), gloves one size up · INSPECTION: no wasting of deltoids, forearms or small muscles, specifically NO thenar or hypothenar wasting, no fasciculations, no tremor, NO ULCERS on either surface, no abnormal posture (a claw hand or wrist drop is visible from the door) · TONE at wrist, elbow and shoulder both sides · POWER C5-T1 with the root named after EVERY movement: C5 'arms up like a chicken', C6 'bend your elbows, don't let me pull', C7 'straighten, then bend and push', C8 'squeeze my fingers' AND THEN PULL YOUR FINGERS OUT → they slide out of the RIGHT → 'reduced power at C8 on the right, approximately four out of five', T1 'spread your fingers' pressing GENTLY (the interossei are small) · REFLEXES: thumb over the biceps tendon, triceps tendon immediately above the olecranon with the forearm hanging; biceps C5/6 and triceps C7/8 present and symmetrical · SENSATION by dermatome, ONE modality, demonstrated on the sternum first: C5 deltoid, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger and ulnar border, T1 medial epicondyle → SILENCE at the right little finger → name it immediately and move on without repeating · COORDINATION with the target at full arm's length · THE SPECIAL TESTS, root first: 'my deficit is at C8 on the right, which points to the ulnar nerve, so I'll begin with the cubital tunnel tests' · elbow flexion test, then Tinel IN THE GROOVE between the olecranon and the medial epicondyle, asking about PINS AND NEEDLES (never 'does that hurt?'), then Phalen and wrist Tinel for completeness · then explain to the PATIENT, ideas first.

back.dx: Ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow — right cubital tunnel syndrome: reduced C8 power (4/5) and C8 sensory loss on the right, positive elbow flexion test and positive Tinel in the medial groove, with Phalen's and wrist Tinel's NEGATIVE, and no wasting yet. To complete: cervical spine examination and Froment's sign. Differentials ACROSS SYSTEMS, not six neuropathies: the same nerve trapped lower down at the wrist, or the neighbouring nerve — carpal tunnel; direct nerve injury given his work; a trapped nerve in the neck (worn disc); a generalised neuropathy — diabetes, low B12, hypothyroidism, alcohol, all checkable on bloods; and much less likely at his age with one hand affected, a central cause such as a small stroke or MS. Plan: nerve conduction studies to localise and grade; bloods for HbA1c, TSH, B12 and folate, U&E and eGFR, FBC, ESR/CRP; stop leaning on the elbow, avoid prolonged flexion including sleeping curled up, soft night splint at 30-45 degrees; workplace discussion and a work capacity certificate; conservative trial 6-12 weeks — unless there is wasting or motor loss, which goes straight to surgical referral. Safety-net: constant numbness, weaker grip, dropping things, hollowing between the fingers — and urgently if the other hand becomes clumsy or he is unsteady on his feet.
plan: WIPE: 'Hello James, my name is Dr -, I'm one of the doctors here. I've been asked to examine the nerves and muscles of both your arms. I'll look at your arms, gently move your wrists, elbows and shoulders, ask you to do some movements against my hand, tap your elbows with a reflex hammer, and check sensation with a piece of cotton wool. I'll need both arms fully exposed and I'd like you to stay sitting. It shouldn't hurt — tell me if anything is uncomfortable. Is that all right?' 'Examiner, I would wash my hands.' (Do not lie him down, do not fetch a pillow, do not spend forty seconds on gloves.)

Inspection and tone: 'no wasting of the deltoids, forearms or small muscles of the hand, and specifically no thenar or hypothenar wasting. No fasciculations, no tremor. No ulcers on either surface of the hands. Both limbs in a normal position and posture.' Then 'James, relax completely and let me do the work' — circumduct the wrist, flex and extend the elbow, rotate the shoulder, both sides — 'tone is normal at the wrist, elbow and shoulder bilaterally.'

POWER, and the finding: C5 'arms up like a chicken, don't let me push down' — normal; C6 'bend your elbows, don't let me pull' — normal; C7 'straighten them... now bend and push against my hands' — normal; C8 'squeeze my fingers as hard as you can, both hands' AND THEN PULL YOUR FINGERS OUT — the left grip holds, the fingers slide out of the right → 'Examiner, there is reduced power at C8 on the right — approximately four out of five'; T1 'spread your fingers apart and don't let me close them', pressing gently — normal. (Feeling the squeeze without pulling out misses the entire finding; crushing the abducted fingers at T1 invents bilateral weakness.)

Reflexes and sensation: thumb over the biceps tendon with the arm rested across your forearm, then the triceps tendon immediately above the olecranon with the forearm hanging — 'biceps C5 and C6 present and symmetrical, triceps C7 and C8 present and symmetrical.' Then 'James, this is cotton wool — it feels like this [sternum]. Now close your eyes and tell me when you feel it. I'm comparing both sides.' C5 deltoid, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger — 'yes' each time — then the RIGHT little finger and ulnar border → SILENCE → 'Examiner, there is loss of sensation at C8 on the right. Sensation at C5, C6, C7 and T1 is intact and symmetrical.' Move straight on; do not repeat it five times and do not prompt him.

Coordination, then the special tests in the right order: 'touch my finger, then touch your nose, and keep going' with the target at a FULL arm's length, then palm-and-back tapping — 'coordination is intact, no intention tremor, no past-pointing, no dysdiadochokinesia.' Then: 'Examiner, my deficit is at C8 on the right, which points to the ulnar nerve, so I'll begin with the cubital tunnel tests. James, bend both elbows right up, palms towards the ceiling — do you get any PINS AND NEEDLES in your hand?' → 'yes, my little finger's going numb.' Then find the olecranon and the medial epicondyle and tap IN THE GROOVE between them — 'any pins and needles?' → 'yes, that shoots straight down to my little finger.' Then for completeness: backs of the hands together and press (Phalen), and tap the wrist (Tinel) → both negative.

'Examiner, the elbow flexion test and Tinel's in the medial groove are positive on the right; Phalen's and Tinel's at the wrist are negative. My diagnosis is ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow — cubital tunnel syndrome on the right. To complete my assessment I would examine the cervical spine and check Froment's sign.'

TURN TO THE PATIENT, sit at eye level, change register: 'James, thank you — you can cover up. Can I explain what I think is going on? Before I do — what did you think might be causing it?' → 'I assumed it was carpal tunnel, my mate had that. I need my hands for the job.' → acknowledge the work worry and come back to it; then the funny-bone explanation, the differentials across systems, the plan, the work pathway and the safety-net (see dx). No 'C8', no dermatome, no myotome.

ask: 'I'll look at your arms, gently move your joints, ask you to do some movements against my hand, tap your elbows, and check sensation with cotton wool.' / 'Examiner, I would wash my hands.' / 'No wasting, no fasciculations, no tremor, no ulcers, and no abnormal position or posture.' / 'Relax completely and let me do the work — you don't need to help me at all.' / 'Copy my movement — and when I press, resist me.'

'Examiner, there is reduced power at C8 on the right, approximately four out of five.' / 'Close your eyes and tell me when you feel it. I'm comparing both sides.' / 'Examiner, there is loss of sensation at C8 on the right.' / 'My deficit is at C8, which points to the ulnar nerve, so I'll begin with the cubital tunnel tests.' / 'Do you get any pins and needles in your hand?' — at EVERY provocation test, never 'does that hurt?' / 'Tinel's sign is positive in the medial groove on the right; Phalen's and Tinel's at the wrist are negative.'

To the patient: 'Before I explain — what did you think might be causing it?' / 'It's the nerve you hit when you bang your funny bone, and it's being squeezed in a narrow tunnel on the inside of your elbow.' / 'It's common, it isn't dangerous, and it's very treatable — especially now, before any muscle wasting.' / 'Come back if the numbness becomes constant, the grip gets weaker, you start dropping things, or the muscles between your fingers start to hollow — and urgently if the other hand becomes clumsy or you feel unsteady on your feet.'

VARIANT A — the CARPAL TUNNEL version (C6): identical until power. Elbow flexion gives way on the right → 'reduced power at C6 on the right, approximately four out of five'; silence at the right THUMB → 'loss of sensation at C6 on the right'; the special tests REVERSE — 'my deficit is at C6, which points to the median nerve, so I'll begin with the carpal tunnel tests' — Phalen positive, wrist Tinel positive, elbow flexion test and medial groove Tinel negative. Explanation changes to the median nerve in the tunnel at the front of the wrist with the flexor tendons, tingling in thumb, index and middle fingers, waking him at night and shaking the hand out. Management: night wrist splint in neutral 4-6 weeks, then a steroid injection into the tunnel (methylprednisolone acetate 20-40 mg VERIFY — and NO injection at the elbow), then surgical release.

VARIANT B — the NORMAL examination: 'my examination of both upper limbs is entirely normal — tone, power at all five roots, reflexes, sensation and coordination — and both sets of provocation tests are negative. That does not exclude an early entrapment neuropathy, which remains my leading diagnosis on the history, and I would confirm it with nerve conduction studies.' Do not invent a finding and do not fall silent. VARIANT C — the task reads 'PERFORM A HAND EXAMINATION': this is musculoskeletal, not ITPRSC — look (both hands, dorsum and palm, nails, joints, thenar and hypothenar bulk, deformity), feel (temperature, pulses, joint lines, thickened tendons), move (active then passive, then function: 'undo this button', 'pick up this pen'), a brief neuro screen BY NERVE not root (median — thumb abduction and index pulp; ulnar — finger abduction and little finger; radial — wrist and finger extension and first dorsal web space), then the special tests including Froment's. Running full ITPRSC here is the fail. VARIANT D — RED FLAGS: pins and needles in BOTH hands, dropping things, unsteady on the stairs, pathologically brisk reflexes → 'that is an upper motor neuron pattern and takes me away from a peripheral entrapment towards cervical myelopathy. I would look for Hoffmann's sign and clonus, examine the lower limbs and gait, and arrange urgent MRI of the cervical spine with neurosurgical referral.'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitlock, 35, machine operator at a food-packaging plant in Murray Bridge, eleven years; married, two young children, the household earner. Four months of pins and needles in the right hand, mostly the little finger and the ulnar border, worse with the elbow bent — on the phone, driving, and in bed with the arm curled; leans on that elbow all shift on the packing bench; grip feels weaker and he dropped a mug last week. Smokes 10 a day, six standard drinks on a Friday, no medications, no diabetes or thyroid disease, father has type 2 diabetes. No neck pain, no left hand, leg or balance symptoms. HIDDEN AGENDA: frightened of losing his job — said only if asked what worries him, otherwise once near the end: 'Doc — am I going to be able to keep working?' THE GOLDEN RULE: he gives nothing that is not specifically asked for, in the specifically correct place. 'Does that hurt?' at any provocation test → 'no', truthfully. Tinel gives the finding ONLY if the fingers are in the groove between olecranon and medial epicondyle. At the right little finger he says NOTHING AT ALL — not 'no' — however many times it is repeated.

Numbers: myotomes C5 shoulder abduction, C6 elbow flexion, C7 elbow extension, C8 grip, T1 finger abduction. Dermatomes C5 deltoid, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger/ulnar border, T1 medial epicondyle. Reflexes biceps C5-C6, triceps C7-C8. MRC 0-5 (0 none, 1 flicker, 2 gravity eliminated, 3 against gravity, 4 against resistance, 5 normal). Provocation hold: reference 60 seconds, exam 1-2 seconds. Splints: wrist neutral at night 4-6 weeks; elbow 30-45 degrees at night. Conservative trial 6-12 weeks unless wasting or motor loss — then straight to surgery. Bloods: HbA1c, TSH, B12 and folate, U&E and eGFR, FBC, ESR/CRP. Confirm with nerve conduction studies plus or minus EMG.

Scored out of 20 with starred single-item fails: every component done bilaterally with comparison; running commentary naming the root at every myotome and dermatome; the special tests performed; differentials spanning at least three systems with investigations and a safety-net. Also scored: fingers pulled out of the grip at C8, gentle pressure at T1, one sensory modality demonstrated first with eyes closed, the cubital tests chosen FIRST with the reason said aloud, the medial groove tapped, and the diagnosis explained in plain language with ideas elicited and the work concern addressed.
fails: ★ Feeling the squeeze at C8 but never pulling your fingers out — the entire finding disappears
★ Doing the carpal tunnel tests first when the deficit is at C8, so the bell beats you to the one test that mattered
Asking 'does that hurt?' at a provocation test — he is briefed to answer the symptom you name, and the honest answer to pain is no; or tapping the epicondyle or forearm instead of the groove

SAY — Turn your body to the patient, change register, and ask first — 'before I explain, what did you think might be causing it?' — because the job fear is never volunteered; then plain words only, no C8, no dermatome, no myotome: 'there's a nerve called the ulnar nerve that runs down your arm to your little finger — it's the one you hit when you bang your funny bone; on its way past your elbow it passes through a narrow tunnel on the inside, right under the skin, and there it's being squeezed'; the differentials must SPAN SYSTEMS, since six causes of peripheral neuropathy score as one — the same nerve at the wrist or the neighbouring nerve (carpal tunnel), direct injury at work, a trapped nerve in the NECK, a general nerve problem (diabetes, B12, thyroid, alcohol, all checkable on bloods), and much less likely something central; plan — nerve conduction studies, bloods, stop leaning on the elbow, avoid prolonged flexion including in bed, a soft night splint at 30–45°, a work capacity certificate and workplace assessment, and a conservative trial of 6–12 weeks unless there is WASTING or motor loss, which goes straight to surgery; safety net — numbness becoming constant, grip weakening, dropping things, the muscles between the fingers hollowing out, and urgently if the other hand becomes clumsy or he feels unsteady on his feet (★)

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice. The task says SENSORY, so the run is I S R — Inspection, Sensation, Reflexes. No tone, no power, no coordination, no gait, no Romberg. Reading 'diabetes' and running a diabetic FOOT exam with pulses and ABI is a vascular assessment and is not what was asked. The role-player is briefed to offer you a walk at one minute to burn four of your eight; decline it in one sentence. On the tray: cotton wool, toothpick, 128 Hz tuning fork, 10 g monofilament, tendon hammer, gloves.
