back.dx: Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy secondary to diabetes, with LOSS OF PROTECTIVE SENSATION placing him at high risk of foot ulceration: callus over the metatarsal heads but no ulceration including the web spaces, no deformity, no infection; symmetrical loss of fine touch and pain to a level at the mid-calf in a stocking distribution; vibration absent at the first MTP; proprioception impaired at the hallux; monofilament absent at every site; ankle jerks absent with reduced knee jerks. Screen for reversible causes — B12, thyroid, liver, renal function, alcohol. To the patient, in plain words: high sugar damages the longest nerves first, which is why the numbness covers roughly the area a sock would cover; the damage already done usually does not reverse, but tight control of sugars, blood pressure and cholesterol slows it, and painful neuropathy responds well to tablets. The part that matters most: because he cannot feel his feet he can injure them without knowing — daily foot checks including between the toes, a mirror for the soles, never barefoot, test bathwater with the hand; podiatry referral and regular review. Return immediately for any break in the skin, redness, swelling or discharge, or a hot swollen foot.
plan: Gloves on, eyes over the tray during the WIPE. 'Hello, I'm Dr -, one of the doctors here. Am I speaking with James? I've been asked to examine the sensation in your legs. I'll look at both legs and feet first, then check the feeling with cotton wool, a toothpick, a tuning fork and this soft filament, and finish by tapping your knee and ankle. Nothing should hurt. I'll need both legs exposed to the thigh and BOTH SOCKS OFF. I'll just wash my hands — is that all right?' → 'Should I get up and walk for you, doctor?' → 'Not today, thank you — I'm checking the sensation rather than the strength, so I'd like you to stay lying down.' Then ask ONCE: 'Examiner, do I have a toothpick or neurotip available for pain sensation?'

INSPECTION, every element announced: 'no ulceration on the soles, dorsa, toe tips or heels. I AM NOW SPREADING EACH WEB SPACE — no ulceration or maceration between any of the toes on either foot. No hallux valgus and no midfoot deformity to suggest Charcot arthropathy. Skin dry with callus over the metatarsal heads bilaterally — a PRE-ULCERATIVE lesion. No redness, swelling, warmth or discharge, and no amputation scars.'

Fine touch, TWO runs. Run A by dermatome from L1: 'This is cotton wool. This is how it feels [sternum]. Now close your eyes and say yes every time you feel me touch you.' → 'L1 normal and symmetrical, L2 normal, L3 normal at the anterior knee. Examiner, sensation is reduced at L4 bilaterally — the patient does not report the touch. L5 absent bilaterally. S1 absent bilaterally. I will now look for a sensory level.' Run B distal to proximal — great toe tip, base, mid-foot, heel, medial malleolus, climbing a few centimetres at a time → 'sensation returns at approximately mid-calf, symmetrically, in a stocking distribution.'

Pain, vibration, proprioception, monofilament: 'I'm using a toothpick now — it won't break the skin. That was sharp, that was blunt. Eyes closed, and this time tell me SHARP OR BLUNT each time.' → matches the touch findings with the same level. 'This is a tuning fork — can you feel it buzzing on your breastbone? Eyes closed, tell me when the buzzing stops.' (1st MTP → medial malleolus) → 'vibration is absent at the first metatarsophalangeal joint and present from the medial malleolus proximally.' 'Now I'm holding your big toe AT THE SIDES. This is up, this is down. Eyes closed — which is it?' → half wrong at the hallux, correct at the ankle. Monofilament, perpendicular, bowed into a C, ~1.5 s, great toe and 1st, 3rd, 5th metatarsal heads → silence at every site → 'protective sensation is absent — THIS PATIENT IS AT HIGH RISK OF FOOT ULCERATION.'

Reflexes: externally rotate the leg, hold the foot in dorsiflexion, tap the Achilles firmly — nothing, repeat once; then forearm under the thigh, find the tibial tuberosity, tap the patellar tendon. 'Examiner, I am checking the ankle reflex — ankle jerks are absent bilaterally. Knee jerks are present but reduced, bilaterally.' (A reflex arc has a sensory limb, and the ankle jerk sits inside the Australian diabetes foot assessment — it is not 'motor'.)

Summary to the examiner, ending with the declared omission: '...my diagnosis is a distal symmetrical polyneuropathy secondary to diabetes, with loss of protective sensation placing him at high risk of ulceration. I would screen for reversible causes — B12, thyroid, liver, renal function and alcohol. I have not performed gait or Romberg; my task was a sensory examination.'

Change register completely for the patient: the sock analogy, the honest prognosis ('the nerve damage already done usually doesn't reverse — but we can slow it down'), then the part that matters most — daily foot checks including between the toes, a mirror for the soles, never barefoot, bathwater tested with the hand, podiatry referral. Answer the father-lost-a-toe fear directly: 'you don't have an ulcer today — that's genuinely good news. The people who run into trouble are usually the ones who don't know their feeling has gone. Now you know, and that changes the odds a great deal.' Then the differentials to be screened, and the same-day return advice.

pefe: Role-player: James Whitlock, 55, self-employed builder still working full days on site. Ex-smoker (quit four years ago, 25 pack-years), six to eight beers a week, steel-capped boots worn for years, never had a formal foot check, cannot see the soles of his own feet, walks barefoot at home. Metformin 1 g bd for nine years plus perindopril and atorvastatin, forgetting the evening metformin about twice a week. Father had type 2 diabetes, lost a toe, then died of a heart attack. HIDDEN AGENDA: frightened of amputation because of his father — volunteered late if never asked. Cheerful and minimising — 'it's only a bit of tingling'. AT OR BELOW THE MID-CALF HE SAYS NOTHING AT ALL — not 'no' — and stays still. Silent for every monofilament site. Guesses proprioception at the hallux and gets about half wrong; correct at the ankle. If the toe is held TOP AND BOTTOM he gets them all right and the technique is marked wrong. At about one minute he asks 'should I get up and walk for you, doctor?' — if the candidate accepts, he walks as slowly as physically possible and takes two full minutes.

Numbers: 10 g monofilament — 128 Hz tuning fork — sensation starts L1, power starts L2 — ankle jerk S1, knee jerk L3-L4 — HbA1c target <=53 mmol/mol (7%), individualised VERIFY — amitriptyline 10 mg nocte up to 25-75 mg, duloxetine 30 to 60 mg daily, pregabalin 25-75 mg nocte up to 150-300 mg/day with dose reduction in renal impairment, all VERIFY TG — analgesic trial 4-8 weeks, success is 30-50% pain reduction — foot review annual / 3-6 monthly / 1-3 monthly by risk — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.

The failing run, at the same timestamps: socks never removed and 'the feet look normal'; 'could you walk across the room for me' at 1:10 costing four minutes; cotton wool stroked in three random places; coaching the role-player with 'say no if you can't feel it'; vibration started at the ASIS and called normal; the bell at 5:30 with reflexes never reached; and 'you have a distal symmetrical polyneuropathy' said to the patient. Only one of those is a knowledge failure — the rest are sequencing, commentary and register. Scored 13 of 18 to pass, with the web-space announcement, the running commentary and interpreting the silence counting double.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED. A TIME-MANAGEMENT station: every finding is normal and the only real question is whether you finish BOTH limbs before the six-minute bell. The role-player's job is to cost you time — he interrupts at thirty seconds with 'is this a stroke? My father had one', and he takes fifteen to twenty seconds to lie down. Deflect in one sentence and keep examining. Do lower limb POWER before tone. Do NOT auscultate carotids or hunt for AF — not in the task unless the stem says 'relevant examination'. Starred items: deflecting the stroke question and continuing; running commentary after every root; lower limb power before tone; completing both limbs before the bell — failing to complete both limbs is a fail on its own.

time: TWO-MINUTE PLAN: inspect all four limbs ONCE; upper limb seated tone → power → reflexes, C5 C6 C7 C8 T1; LIE DOWN; lower limb POWER → reflexes → tone, L2 L3 L4 L5 S1; OFFER sensation and coordination and take the skip; TIA = temporary blockage, fully resolved, warning sign; ladder brain → cord → nerve → NMJ → muscle · OPENING under 30 s and FLAG THE LIE-DOWN ('I will start with you sitting and ask you to lie down part-way through') · the stroke question arrives: 'that is exactly what I need to work out · let me examine you first and I promise I will not leave without answering that' · INSPECTION of all four limbs in ten seconds · UL TONE wrist/elbow/shoulder both sides · UL POWER: C5 push the ELBOWS not the shoulders, C6 'don't let me pull', C7 'push against my hands', C8 'don't let me pull my fingers out', T1 press GENTLY · UL REFLEXES biceps and triceps only, TWO TAPS per tendon, no brachioradialis (say why if challenged) · LIE DOWN → LL POWER first: L2 thighs, L3 shins, L4 calves, L5 dorsum, S1 soles, commentating each root as you finish it · LL REFLEXES knee L3/4 and ankle S1/2 supine · LL TONE ankle, knee, hip · OFFER sensation (C4-T1 and L1-S2) and coordination → take the skip · normal examination IS the finding → TIA, defined plainly, framed as a WARNING, plus differentials and 'do not drive'.

back.dx: An entirely normal neurological examination — inspection, tone, power C5-T1 and L2-S1 bilaterally, reflexes, and (by report) sensation and coordination all normal. With a RESOLVED unilateral motor deficit, a normal examination and a normal glucose, the diagnosis is a transient ischaemic attack. To the patient: 'a temporary interruption to the blood supply to part of your brain — the blockage cleared on its own.' Then the framing that scores: it resolved, which is good news, BUT a TIA is a warning sign, the risk of a full stroke is highest in the next few days, so this is not something he goes home with — urgent brain and carotid imaging, an ECG for the heart rhythm, bloods, treatment started today, and no driving until reviewed. Differentials by ladder: brain — stroke or small bleed, tumour, multiple sclerosis; cord and nerve roots in the neck; individual nerves of the arm and leg; neuromuscular junction; muscle. Mimics named in patient words: hypoglycaemia ('a low blood sugar can mimic this exactly — we checked yours and it was normal') and Todd paresis after a seizure. Same-side arm AND leg with a normal examination points firmly to the brain.
plan: ID and gloves. 'Hello Gary, I am Dr -. I have been asked to examine your arms and legs. I will look at them, check the strength of your movements, tap them with this hammer and check sensation with cotton wool. I WILL START WITH YOU SITTING AND ASK YOU TO LIE DOWN PART-WAY THROUGH. Is that alright?' → 'Doctor, is this a stroke? My father had one.' → 'That is exactly what I need to work out. Let me examine you properly first and then I will explain everything — I promise I will not leave without answering that.'

Inspection of ALL FOUR limbs at once, ten seconds: 'no wasting, no fasciculations, no tremor, no abnormal posture or scars.' Then upper limb tone: 'Gary, relax completely and let me move your joints' — wrist, elbow, shoulder, both sides — 'tone at the wrist, elbow and shoulder is normal, and the same on the left.'

Upper limb power, root by root, commentating each: 'Copy my movement, arms out to the side — don't let me push your ELBOWS down. C5 normal both sides. Bend your elbows, don't let me pull — C6 normal. Straighten, now bend and push against my hands — C7 normal. Squeeze my fingers, don't let me pull them out — C8 normal. Spread your fingers, don't let me close them — T1 normal.' (Pushing the shoulders at C5 or pressing hard at T1 both produce false weakness.)

Upper limb reflexes, two taps per tendon: 'biceps and triceps reflexes are present and normal, both sides.' → 'you did not check brachioradialis' → 'I omitted it deliberately — it shares roots with biceps and I prioritised completing both limbs within the time.' (Re-tapping an absent reflex is the single biggest clock-killer in this station.)

'Gary, could you lie down for me now?' (he takes 15-20 seconds — do not fill it with counselling). LOWER LIMB POWER FIRST: 'I will put my hands on your leg and ask you to press against them. Press up — L2 normal. Bend your knees, feet flat, press forward — L3 normal. Pull your heels back — L4 normal. Straighten your legs, press up — L5 normal. Now press down — S1 normal. All bilateral.' Target: both limbs' power done by 5:00.

Lower limb reflexes then tone: forearm under both thighs — 'knee reflex L3 and L4, present and normal both sides'; foot dorsiflexed — 'ankle reflex S1 and S2, present and normal both sides'; then 'tone in the lower limbs is normal bilaterally.' If the bell goes first: 'I would complete the examination with lower limb tone and with gait' — say it regardless.

OFFER sensation and coordination by name — 'I would test sensation with cotton wool in each dermatome, C4 to T1 in the upper limbs and L1 to S2 in the lower limbs, and then coordination with finger-nose and heel-shin testing' → 'both normal — skip.' Never assume the skip; offer, then accept.

Bell. Summary: 'tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination are normal throughout. This is an entirely normal neurological examination. With a resolved unilateral motor deficit, a normal examination and a normal glucose, my diagnosis is a transient ischaemic attack.' Then to Gary: the plain definition, the warning-sign framing, the plan, no driving, and the differentials in patient words (see dx). 'So it wasn't a stroke — that's a relief?' → hold the frame: 'it is good news that it resolved, but I want to be straight with you: a TIA is a warning sign.'

Explaining: 'This is an entirely normal neurological examination.' / 'A temporary interruption to the blood supply to part of your brain.' / 'The blockage has cleared on its own — that is why the weakness has settled.' / 'It is good news that it resolved, but I want to be straight with you: this is a warning sign.' / 'The risk is highest in the next few days, which is why we act today.' / 'I need you not to drive until you have been reviewed.' / 'A low blood sugar can mimic this exactly — we checked yours and it was normal.' / 'A seizure can leave temporary weakness afterwards.'

Here is what I can tell you honestly: this was a warning, and it is a warning we can act on. Most of the risk is in the next few days, and the treatments we start today reduce it substantially. You have come in at exactly the right time.' Do not promise he will be fine.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Feldman, 58, sitting on the edge of the bed; right arm and leg weak for about ten minutes forty minutes ago, now completely resolved and he feels fine; his father died of a stroke at 66. EVERY FINDING IS NORMAL — push back firmly and equally on every movement, limbs floppy for tone, normal reflexes. HIS JOB IS TO COST TIME: at thirty seconds he interrupts once with 'Doctor, is this a stroke? My father had one' — if the candidate stops to counsel now, let them, and note it. Asked to lie down, he takes a genuine 15-20 seconds. He gives the skip for sensation and coordination ONLY if they are offered by name. After the explanation: 'so it wasn't a stroke — that's a relief?' (testing whether the warning frame survives) and 'what else could it have been?' (testing differentials). A stopwatch runs and at exactly six minutes: 'Doctor, time' — stopping them dead, mid-movement.

Sequence and pacing: opening under 30 s with the lie-down flagged; inspection of all four limbs at 0:40; UL tone by 1:35; five roots by 2:50; biceps and triceps by 3:25; lie down; LL power L2-S1 done by 4:55; LL reflexes and tone; offer sensation and coordination; bell at 6:00. C5 push the elbows, not the shoulders; T1 press gently; two taps per tendon maximum; lower limb power BEFORE tone; knee and ankle reflexes supine — do not sit him up.

Pass guide 17 or more of 22 with all four starred items, and failing to complete both limbs before the bell is a fail on its own. Also scored: warns about the lie-down, inspects all four limbs together naming wasting and fasciculation, starts UL power at C5 not C4 and LL power at L2 not L1, volunteers sensation and coordination by name, does NOT auscultate carotids or hunt for AF, states that the normal examination IS the finding, names TIA and defines it in plain words, frames it as a warning rather than reassurance, gives differentials across brain, cord, nerve and at least one mimic, and mentions urgent investigation and not driving.
Overall — AN ENTIRELY NORMAL EXAMINATION in a man whose deficit has resolved

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, often a REAL patient face to face. The tremor is obvious from the door and the trap is starting the Parkinson's tests: the first block of marks is the upper limb neurological examination you were literally asked to do, and the PIVOT LINE tells the examiner which half of the marking sheet you are on. Free marks sit on inspection before you touch anything — hypomimia, reduced blink, stooped posture. Automatic fails: omitting the upper limb neurological examination and going straight to the Parkinsonism tests; mobilising the patient unsafely (no falls question, candidate seated or across the room, or a pull test with nothing behind him); talking through the father's death without acknowledging it; diagnosing confidently and never mentioning a differential.
stem: General practice. A 68-year-old man whose family have noticed his right hand shakes; he has become slower over six months and his handwriting has become small. Vital signs stable.
tasks: Perform an upper limb neurological examination
Perform the relevant physical examination
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: DECLARE (10 s): 'I will complete a full upper limb neurological examination first, characterising the tremor as I go, and then perform the additional examination relevant to Parkinsonism' · WIPE 30 s + the GLOBAL LOOK that scores before you touch: reduced facial expression, reduced blink rate, stooped posture · ITPRSC at speed 140 s: inspection (tremor at rest named), tone with SUPINATION AND PRONATION and an ACTIVATION manoeuvre ('while I move this wrist, tap your other hand on your knee'), power 5/5 C5-T1, reflexes, sensation, coordination (finger-nose, rapid alternating · slow on the right) · THE PIVOT LINE: 'Examiner, that completes the upper limb neurological examination. I will now characterise the tremor' · TREMOR 60 s: REST with distraction ('rest your hands in your lap and count backwards from twenty'), POSTURAL (arms out, palms down, fingers spread, 15 s), ACTION (bring this cup up as if to drink), ASTERIXIS (wrists cocked back, 30 s) → '4 to 6 hertz pill-rolling tremor, present at rest, damping with voluntary movement, asymmetrical, more marked on the right; no asterixis' · BRADYKINESIA 45 s: finger tapping for AT LEAST TEN repetitions → decrement · FACE, SPEECH, WRITING, GLABELLAR 50 s ('British constitution'; write a sentence; tap from ABOVE AND BEHIND, not in front of the eyes) · GAIT 55 s: ask about falls first, walk beside him, and DEMAND THE TURN · then postural stability (pull test with a chair behind) and a lying and standing BP · then STOP after naming the diagnosis and let it land.

back.dx: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease: an asymmetrical 4-6 Hz pill-rolling REST tremor damping with movement, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist enhanced on activation, bradykinesia with DECREMENT on finger tapping, hypomimia, micrographia, and a stooped short-stepped gait with reduced right arm swing and an en-bloc turn — with the relevant negatives of no intention tremor, no cerebellar signs and no asterixis. Differentials given to the patient in plain English: essential tremor (a shake that runs in families), medications that cause the same picture, thyrotoxicosis, and problems with the balance part of the brain. Plan: bloods, a full medication review, neurology referral to confirm and start treatment, physiotherapy; then the driving conversation — raised by you, framed as rules you have to follow rather than a licence taken away today, with the offer to have his daughter present. Safety-net: return sooner for a fall, a faint, or confusion. Explain dopamine in one sentence, and never promise a course — 'Parkinson's varies enormously between people, and treatment today is far better than it was in your father's time.'
plan: Declare the plan, then WIPE: 'Hello, I am Dr -, one of the doctors here. I have been asked to examine your arms and look into the shakiness your family have noticed. I will look at your hands, move your joints gently, test your strength and reflexes, and then ask you to do a few simple tasks including walking. Tell me if anything hurts. Is that all right? Could I please expose both arms to the shoulders?'

The global look, before touching: 'On inspection there is no wasting, no fasciculation and no abnormal posture, but there is a tremor of the right hand present at rest. I also note REDUCED FACIAL EXPRESSION and a REDUCED BLINK RATE, and a slightly stooped posture.'

ITPRSC at speed. Tone: 'Please let your arms go floppy' — flex, extend, SUPINATE and PRONATE both wrists and elbows — 'there is increased tone at the right wrist with a cogwheel quality. I will confirm with an activation manoeuvre — while I move this wrist, could you tap your other hand on your knee? Yes, the cogwheeling is enhanced.' Then power 5/5 C5-T1, biceps/supinator/triceps symmetrical, sensation intact C5-T1, coordination: 'no dysmetria and no intention tremor; rapid alternating movements are performed but are slow on the right.'

THE PIVOT LINE, then the tremor: 'Examiner, that completes the upper limb neurological examination. I will now characterise the tremor. Please rest your hands in your lap and COUNT BACKWARDS FROM TWENTY for me' (the rest tremor becomes coarser) '... now hold both arms straight out in front, palms down, fingers spread ... now bring this cup up as if to drink ... and finally, arms out with your wrists cocked back like you are stopping traffic, and hold.' → 'This is a four to six hertz pill-rolling tremor, present at rest, damping with voluntary movement, and asymmetrical — more marked on the right. There is no asterixis.'

Bradykinesia and the face: 'Please tap your index finger and thumb together, as big and as fast as you can, and keep going until I say stop' — watch TEN or more repetitions — 'over ten repetitions there is progressive reduction in amplitude and speed on the right — that is bradykinesia with decrement.' Then 'say British constitution for me... now would you write this sentence out... and I am just going to tap gently on your forehead FROM ABOVE — please try to keep your eyes open': soft monotonous speech, micrographia shrinking along the line, blinking that fails to habituate.

Gait and postural stability: 'Before we do this — have you had any falls? Good. If you feel safe, please walk to the wall, turn around, and walk back to me. I will walk beside you.' → 'the gait is stooped and short-stepped with reduced right arm swing and an EN-BLOC turn. I would complete the assessment with a pull test for postural stability with a chair behind the patient, and with a lying and standing blood pressure.' (Omit the turn and you lose the most sensitive sign in the station.)

Summary to the examiner with the relevant negatives, then TO THE PATIENT, ideas first: 'Mr Doyle, may I share what I have found? First — what did you and your daughter think might be going on?' → 'She thinks it's Parkinson's. Is it?' → 'I think she may be right, and I am sorry to be confirming something you were worried about.' Then STOP. Let it land. → 'That's what my father had. He ended up in a wheelchair.' → acknowledge it before saying anything else: 'That must be a very frightening thing to have in your mind. Can I say something about that?' Then dopamine in a sentence, the honest differentials, the plan, the driving conversation with the daughter present, and the safety-net (see dx).

ask: 'I will complete a full upper limb neurological examination first, then perform the examination relevant to Parkinsonism.' / 'Examiner, that completes the upper limb neurological examination.' / 'Please let your arms go completely floppy.' / 'While I move this wrist, could you tap your other hand on your knee?' / 'Please rest your hands in your lap and count backwards from twenty.'

'Hold both arms straight out in front, palms down, fingers spread.' / 'Wrists cocked back, as if you are stopping traffic — hold it there.' / 'Tap your index finger and thumb together, as big and as fast as you can.' / 'There is progressive reduction in amplitude and speed — bradykinesia with decrement.' / 'This is a four to six hertz pill-rolling tremor, present at rest and damping with movement.' / 'Please walk to the wall, turn around, and walk back to me.'

To the patient: 'Before I explain — what did you think might be going on?' / 'The brain slowly loses cells that make a chemical called dopamine, which helps control movement.' / 'I would rather you heard about the driving rules from me than from a letter.' / 'Come back sooner if you have a fall, if you faint, or if you become confused.' Avoid in front of him: bradykinesia, cogwheeling, extrapyramidal, hypomimia, micrographia, dysdiadochokinesia.

Variant A — ESSENTIAL TREMOR (62M): tremor ABSENT at rest, appears with the arms outstretched and worsens through movement, symmetrical, no rigidity, no decrement, normal gait with full arm swing → 'this is a symmetrical postural and action tremor, absent at rest, with no cogwheel rigidity, no decrement on finger tapping, normal arm swing and a normal gait. The negatives are as important as the positives here: this is NOT Parkinsonism.' To the patient: often familial, often settles briefly with alcohol, and propranolol if it interferes with life. Trap: saying 'BENIGN essential tremor' — drop 'benign' and still ask how much it affects his work, his writing and his confidence.

Variant C — DRUG-INDUCED PARKINSONISM (28M on risperidone): SYMMETRICAL findings, rigidity and bradykinesia dominating over tremor, onset over weeks, a young patient, possibly akathisia → 'there is symmetrical bradykinesia and rigidity in a 28-year-old developing over weeks since a dose increase of risperidone. This is drug-induced parkinsonism rather than idiopathic Parkinson's disease, which is asymmetrical, insidious and a disease of later life.' To the patient: usually reversible; 'I will not change anything today on my own — I will speak with your psychiatrist about lowering the dose or switching, because stopping it suddenly could make you unwell again.' Trap: ceasing the antipsychotic yourself, or missing neuroleptic malignant syndrome — febrile, rigid, confused and unstable means stop examining and escalate. Harder turns: 'am I going to end up like my father?' → 'I can't promise you a course, and I won't pretend to. What I can tell you is that it varies enormously and that treatment now is much better than it was.' / 'don't tell them about my licence' → acknowledge what it means in a country town, explain the duty is not discretionary in South Australia, and offer to work through transport options together. / 'what if he were 34?' → screen for Wilson's disease with caeruloplasmin, urinary copper and a slit-lamp examination.
pefe: Role-player: Frank Doyle, 68, retired shearer in a country town; his daughter made the appointment because his right hand shakes and he has 'gone slow' over six months. Embarrassed rather than frightened. His father had Parkinson's disease and died in a nursing home — mentioned ONLY once the diagnosis is named. No regular medications except a fluid tablet; two beers most nights; still drives to the shops and the footy. HOW HE PLAYS IT: speaks softly and flatly, keeps his face still and blinks less than feels natural, right hand rolling gently in his lap and stopping the moment he reaches for anything; finger tapping starts big then gets smaller and slower with a stall around tap eight; writing small and shrinking; rises slowly, short steps, right arm hanging still, four or five little steps to turn — and if asked to walk with NO turn, he walks in a straight line only and never volunteers it. If the candidate talks over 'that's what my father had', he goes flat, stops answering, and marks it down.

Numbers: 4-6 Hz Parkinsonian rest tremor; 6-12 Hz essential tremor. At least TEN repetitions before you may call decrement. Postural tremor held 15 s; asterixis held 30 s. Normal glabellar habituation is 3-4 taps. More than 2 steps of retropulsion is an abnormal pull test. C5-T1 upper limb myotomes and dermatomes. Under 40 — screen for Wilson's disease. Weeks to months for drug-induced parkinsonism to resolve after the drug is stopped.

Three moments that carry the station: the PIVOT LINE, which tells the examiner exactly which half of the marking sheet you are on; counting backwards from twenty, fifteen seconds that turn an equivocal tremor into a diagnostic one; and the PAUSE after 'that's what my father had' — candidates who talk through that line lose the communication domain no matter how good the examination was. Also scored: tone tested including supination/pronation with an activation manoeuvre, asterixis tested, speech and handwriting assessed, falls asked about before mobilising, the walk AND the turn requested, a structured summary with relevant negatives, ideas elicited before naming the diagnosis, and three or more differentials in plain English.

setting: VIDEO / TEACHING STATION — your general practice, 8 minutes. A monitor plays a short clip of the patient and a MEDICAL STUDENT is in the room; there is no live patient. You watch the clip ONCE without talking, then teach head to foot in plain English. The two things that fail it: never saying the word BRADYKINESIA, and claiming a finding the video cannot show — tone, cogwheeling, power, or special tests being performed. The correct construction is 'if he were in front of us, I would expect...' and examiners specifically listen for it.

back.dx: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease: bradykinesia with decrement, an asymmetrical rest tremor, a mask-like face, hypophonic speech, a stooped shuffling festinating gait with reduced arm swing and an en-bloc turn, and a positive glabellar tap. Differentials IN GROUPS, drugs first because that group is reversible: DRUGS — antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, valproate; OTHER DEGENERATIVE — progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies; STRUCTURAL AND VASCULAR — vascular parkinsonism, normal-pressure hydrocephalus; OTHER TREMORS — essential tremor, thyrotoxicosis, and Wilson's disease if he were under forty. There is NO test that confirms Parkinson's disease — it is a clinical diagnosis; investigations exclude the mimics (TSH, UEC, LFT, FBE, B12, calcium; MRI) and a good response to levodopa supports it afterwards. Assess driving against Austroads with the SA reporting duty under the Motor Vehicles Act 1959, and refer to neurology. To the student's last question: treatment helps a lot with slowness and stiffness and often the tremor, but never promise the tremor will disappear — and much of what helps is not a tablet: physiotherapy for walking, speech pathology for the voice, and making the house safe.
plan: Set the structure before the clip: 'Before we watch this, let me tell you how I'm going to do it. I'll watch the whole clip once WITHOUT talking, because if I start commentating I'll miss things. Then I'll go through the patient from head to foot — face, posture, tremor, speech, the special tests, and the gait — and I'll tell you what each one means. Then we'll talk about what I still don't know and how I'd find out.' Start the clip; do not wait for permission. ONE viewing — rewatching loses the commentary time.

The four things before any special test: 'His POSTURE. Even sitting still, his trunk and neck are bent forward — a stooped posture. His FACE. Watch it for ten seconds — it barely changes; he's blinking far less than you or I would and his mouth sits slightly open. That's a mask-like face; it doesn't mean he feels nothing, it means the muscles of facial expression have become slow. His HANDS. There's a tremor of the right hand while it rests in his lap, with a pill-rolling quality, and crucially it's there AT REST and settles when he reaches — the opposite of the tremor you see in cerebellar disease. His SPEECH. Slow to get started, low volume, flat and all on one note — hypophonic and monotonous. Now — all four of those are the same thing underneath. They are all BRADYKINESIA: slowness in starting and in carrying out voluntary movement.'

The four tests, each taught: FINGER TAPPING — 'he starts reasonably, then slows, hesitates, and the fingers come closer and closer together. That shrinking is DECREMENT, and it is the single clearest demonstration of bradykinesia there is — the same reason his handwriting shrinks as he writes, micrographia.' HAND FLIPPING — 'he can do it, it's just very slow. That's still bradykinesia. If the movement were CLUMSY and IRREGULAR rather than slow, I'd call it dysdiadochokinesia and I'd be thinking about the cerebellum, not Parkinson's.' FINGER TO NOSE — 'he gets there, no overshooting, no past-pointing, and the tremor settles as he reaches — that confirms a rest tremor rather than an intention tremor.' GLABELLAR TAP — 'if I did that to you, you'd blink two or three times and stop. He keeps blinking every single tap — that failure to habituate is Myerson's sign; a feature of Parkinson's disease, though on its own not specific.'

The gait, six parts: 'One, he HESITATES before he starts. Two, the steps are SHORT. Three, he barely lifts his feet — REDUCED FOOT CLEARANCE, no heel strike, which is why it looks like shuffling. Four, once he's going the steps get quicker and shorter, as though he's chasing himself — FESTINATION, and that is different from shuffling; he has both. Five, his ARMS BARELY SWING. Six, the TURN — instead of pivoting he turns slowly and stiffly in several small steps, EN BLOC, like a statue rotating.'

What the video cannot show — the sentence examiners listen for: 'Now, what I can't tell from a video. I haven't touched him, so I can't comment on tone, power or reflexes, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If he were sitting in front of us, six things. One, tone at the wrist and elbow with slow passive movement — I would EXPECT increased tone, that's rigidity, and where the tremor is superimposed it feels like a ratchet, which is cogwheeling. Two, ask him to write his name and draw a spiral, looking for micrographia. Three, lying and standing blood pressure. Four, his eye movements, especially looking down. Five, a full medication list — particularly antipsychotics, metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, because those cause exactly this picture and it's reversible. Six, ask about falls, hallucinations, memory and acting out dreams.'

Diagnosis and the grouped differential, drugs first (see dx), and the closing honesty on treatment. Student probes to answer cleanly: 'what test confirms Parkinson's disease?' → 'none — it's a clinical diagnosis; investigations exclude mimics and a good levodopa response supports it afterwards.' 'Is it just his age?' → no; this is never normal ageing. 'Is that dysdiadochokinesia?' at the hand flip → no: slow but accurate is basal ganglia; irregular and uncoordinated is cerebellum, and it changes the whole differential.

Variants: ESSENTIAL TREMOR stem (tremor absent at rest, on posture and action, symmetrical, familial, settles with alcohol) → 'there is no bradykinesia and no rigidity. The tremor is absent at rest, symmetrical, and appears on posture and action. That makes essential tremor far more likely — the three findings that settle it are the absence of bradykinesia, rigidity and gait change.' / DRUG-INDUCED stem (onset over months, symmetrical signs, risperidone started four months ago) → 'the picture is parkinsonism, but it came on over months, the signs are symmetrical, and she was started on risperidone. My first diagnosis is drug-induced parkinsonism — potentially reversible. I would discuss reducing or switching the drug with the prescriber, NOT stop it myself, and reassess over several months.' / STUDENT PUSHES BACK ('my grandmother shakes too and she's fine') → 'plenty of older people have a benign tremor. This one isn't — it's at rest, one-sided, and comes with slowness, a still face and a changed walk.'
pefe: Partner brief: they play BOTH the medical student (Kate, second-year, keen, no jargon) and the video (acting out the signs, since there is no screen in practice). Patient portrayed: Ray Dolan, 68, retired shearer from Kadina, two years of a shaky right hand, wife says he has 'gone quiet', NO medications and no antipsychotics, no family history of tremor, two beers on a Saturday, handwriting has got smaller, wife says he thrashes about in his sleep, still drives into Kadina. Acting order: sit still 20 s slumped, face blank with slow rare blinking and mouth slightly open, right thumb rolling against the index finger and stopping whenever he reaches; one slow flat sentence with a pause before it starts; finger tapping starting wide then shrinking to almost nothing; hand flipping accurate but painfully slow, never clumsy; finger-to-nose accurate with the tremor dying as he reaches; blinking at EVERY glabellar tap; standing hesitantly, tiny shuffling steps speeding up, arms still, turning in five small steps.

Numbers: diagnosis rule — bradykinesia OBLIGATORY plus at least one of rigidity or rest tremor. Rest tremor 4-6 Hz, pill-rolling, asymmetrical. Glabellar tap: normal habituates after 2-3 taps. Parkinson-plus red flags: falls within one year, symmetrical onset, early dementia or hallucinations, early autonomic failure, restricted downgaze, poor levodopa response. Wilson's disease: consider under 40. Bloods: TSH, UEC, LFT, FBE, B12, calcium. Driving: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive, SA reporting duty under the Motor Vehicles Act 1959. Interpreter: TIS National 131 450.

Three mistakes the role-player makes that break the case: making the finger tapping CLUMSY instead of decrementing (that turns it into a cerebellar sign); blinking only a few times on the glabellar tap; and answering Kate's questions themselves — Kate asks, the candidate answers. Scored across recognition (all six gait components, decrement described rather than just slowness, Myerson named), reasoning and safety (bradykinesia said aloud AND defined, no claimed tone or cogwheeling, bradykinesia distinguished from dysdiadochokinesia, rest from intention tremor, six further bedside steps, medication history, driving) and communication (structure signposted, every sign in plain English, differentials in groups with drugs first, no inappropriate reassurance).

DO — Name DECREMENT rather than slowness at the finger tap ('he starts reasonably, then slows, hesitates, and the fingers come closer and closer together — the movement shrinks; that is decrement, the cleanest bradykinesia you'll see, and it's the same reason his handwriting shrinks — micrographia'), MYERSON'S SIGN at the glabellar tap (normal habituates after two or three taps; he keeps blinking every single tap), and all SIX gait components — hesitation starting, short steps, reduced foot clearance so there is no heel strike, FESTINATION (the steps speeding up and shortening, which is different from shuffling and he has both), reduced arm swing, and the EN-BLOC turn in several small steps

SAY — Offer the six bedside additions, then give the differentials in groups with DRUGS FIRST, because that signals you thought about the reversible cause before the incurable one: tone at the wrist and elbow, handwriting and a spiral, lying and standing blood pressure, eye movements especially downgaze, a full medication list (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, valproate), and falls, hallucinations, memory and acting out dreams; then 'idiopathic Parkinson's disease', with drugs, other degenerative (progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies), structural and vascular (vascular parkinsonism, normal-pressure hydrocephalus), and other tremors (essential tremor, thyrotoxicosis, Wilson's disease if under forty); 'there is no test that confirms it — it is a CLINICAL diagnosis; investigations exclude the mimics, and a good response to levodopa supports it afterwards', with TSH, UEC, LFT and B12, an MRI, an Austroads driving assessment and neurology referral; explain every sign to the student in plain English, and never promise the tremor will go — 'we manage this rather than cure it', with physiotherapy, speech pathology and home safety

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED. Two findings decide everything: a broad-based gait and LOSS OF BALANCE ON ROMBERG WITH THE EYES OPEN. That combination is cerebellar, not proprioceptive, and the COMMITMENT SENTENCE at about 1:50 converts them into a conclusion, justifies the cerebellar screen you are about to run, and disposes of the manoeuvre the examiner is waiting to see you handle. Candidates who never say it do a little of everything and complete nothing. The two things that fail this station: letting the patient fall or standing him up without guarding him, and examining in silence.
stem: Emergency department. Ben Whyte, 55, presents with an unsteady gait; long history of heavy daily alcohol intake. Blood glucose, B12 and thyroid function are NORMAL. Observations stable, alert and orientated, sitting on the bed.

back.dx: Alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration — ten positive cerebellar signs with no nystagmus: unsteady in sitting, broad-based gait, loss of balance on Romberg WITH THE EYES OPEN, dysdiadochokinesia bilaterally, intention tremor with past-pointing, upward drift, rebound, slurred staccato (scanning) speech, pendular knee jerk, abnormal heel-shin, and truncal ataxia — in a man with chronic heavy intake and gradual onset. Differentials IN SIX GROUPS: BRAIN — cerebellar stroke or TIA, posterior circulation ischaemia, tumour or metastasis, multiple sclerosis; NUTRITIONAL — Wernicke's encephalopathy, B12 deficiency; DRUGS — phenytoin, carbamazepine, lithium, sedatives; SENSORY — alcoholic or diabetic peripheral neuropathy causing sensory ataxia; VESTIBULAR — vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, Meniere's; LOWER LIMB — arthritis of hip or knee, lumbar radiculopathy, cauda equina. Plan: PARENTERAL THIAMINE BEFORE ANY GLUCOSE (a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's), bloods including LFTs, magnesium and B12, MRI brain, and referral for withdrawal management, falls prevention, physiotherapy and an OT home assessment. Raise driving. SA: DASSA ADIS 1300 13 1340, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, PATS, TIS National 131 450.
plan: 'Good morning Ben, I'm Dr -. I've been asked to examine you today. I'll look at your arms and legs, check your eyes, listen to your speech, and I'll ask you to stand and take a few steps. I'll be right beside you the whole time — if you feel like you're going, I've got you. Any pain anywhere? Happy for me to go ahead?' → 'Just don't let me go over.' Acknowledge the fear once, then move. 'No particular exposure or position is required for this examination.'

General appearance BEFORE the gait: 'Examiner, on general appearance my patient is alert and orientated. There is no obvious wasting or fasciculation. Notably, he is unable to maintain his balance even in a SITTING position — he is swaying from side to side as I speak to him.' (Do not call it truncal ataxia yet; that has a specific test at the end.)

GAIT, two or three steps only: 'Ben, I'd like you to stand up and take a few steps for me. I'm going to put my arms around you as you go — I won't hold you, but if you go I'll catch you. Ready?' (stand beside him, arms bracketing, walk backwards with him) 'That's plenty — let's sit you back down.' → 'On gait he places his feet wide apart from each other in order to maintain balance — a broad-based gait.'

ROMBERG, eyes OPEN: 'Now bring your feet together, side by side, and let your arms hang by your side. Stay just like that for me — I'm right here.' Count to five; he lurches at about two seconds — CATCH HIM. 'Got you. That's enough, sit yourself back down.' → 'On Romberg testing the patient lost his balance WITH THE EYES OPEN. I did not proceed to eye closure because he had already lost balance and I was concerned about a fall.'

THE COMMITMENT SENTENCE: 'Examiner, before I go on — a broad-based gait together with loss of balance on Romberg with the eyes open points to a CEREBELLAR cause rather than a proprioceptive one. I'm therefore going to focus the rest of my examination on a full cerebellar screen rather than a general neurological examination, and I'll call out each finding as I go. I'm also going to omit tandem gait, because he has already demonstrated loss of balance and I don't think it is safe.'

Hands and arms: 'Copy my movement — tap the palm of one hand with the palm and then the back of the other, as fast as you can. Now swap hands.' → 'dysdiadochokinesia, present on both sides.' 'Now touch your nose, then touch my finger, as quickly as you can' (finger at FULL arm's reach, two or three positions) → 'intention tremor that worsens as he approaches the target, and past-pointing — he does not reach my finger.' 'Stretch both arms out in front, palms facing up. Now close your eyes and hold them there.' → 'both arms show an UPWARD drift — the cerebellar pattern; a downward pronator drift would indicate an upper motor neurone lesion.' 'Arms out again. I'm going to press down and I want you to resist me' — press, then release suddenly → 'there is a rebound phenomenon — the arms overshoot well beyond their starting position.'

Face and lower limb: 'Keep your head still and follow my finger with your eyes only' (H-path, pausing at the extremes) → 'I can see no nystagmus on eye movements.' 'Can you repeat after me — West Register Street.' → broken syllable by syllable → 'his speech is slurred and staccato — scanning dysarthria.' Then SITTING with the legs hanging free, tap the patellar tendon → 'the knee jerk is PENDULAR — four or five swings before it settles, which reflects the hypotonia of cerebellar disease.' Lying: 'touch my finger with your big toe' → intention tremor and past-pointing; 'run your heel down your other shin in a straight line — now the other leg' → abnormal bilaterally; 'cross your arms and sit up without using your hands' → he cannot do it in one movement — TRUNCAL ATAXIA.

'Examiner, I have ten positive cerebellar signs and no nystagmus. Those localise to the cerebellum, and in a man with chronic heavy alcohol intake and a gradual onset my most likely diagnosis is alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration.' Then the six groups and the plan (see dx). 'Why thiamine before glucose?' → 'a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.'

Variants: SENSORY ATAXIA (2019 recall) — steady with the eyes open for five seconds, falls immediately on closing them, tandem gait normal, numb feet → 'he is steady with his eyes open and loses balance as soon as he closes them. That is a POSITIVE Romberg sign — proprioceptive loss, not cerebellar disease. I'll change direction and perform a lower limb sensory examination — light touch, pinprick, vibration and joint position sense — looking for a glove-and-stocking pattern. My diagnosis would be alcoholic sensory neuropathy causing sensory ataxia.' / RESTRICTED TASK (2023 recall) — 'perform a lower limb neurological examination' with power and sensation given as normal → 'that examination is inspection, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination. As power and sensation are given as normal I'll perform inspection, tone, reflexes and coordination — spending most of my time on coordination: heel-shin, toe-to-finger and the knee reflex sitting.'

The two hard questions: examiner 'is the Romberg positive or negative?' → 'strictly neither. A positive Romberg means steady with the eyes open and falling on closing them — proprioceptive loss. He is unsteady WITH HIS EYES OPEN, which points to the cerebellum.' / Ben: 'will it come good if I stop?' → 'some of it can improve with sustained abstinence — honestly, probably not all of it. But stopping is the most useful thing you can do, and I won't leave you to do it alone.'
pefe: Role-player: Ben Whyte, 55, former shearing-shed hand, lives alone in a unit in Kadina, divorced, two adult children in Adelaide he rarely sees, disability pension. A cask of wine and several beers most days for about twenty years, first drink around ten in the morning, never been to detox, eats one meal a day. Unsteadiness crept up over eighteen months, no sudden onset, no headache or vomiting; three falls in six months, no head injury; NO numbness or pins and needles in the feet (this keeps the case cerebellar rather than sensory); no spinning, no hearing loss or tinnitus; no medications. Flat, defensive about alcohol, embarrassed about falling. If the candidate is kind about the drinking he softens and asks 'will it come good if I stop?'; if judgemental he goes quiet and answers in single words.

How the signs are played: sways gently while seated the whole time; plants the feet very wide and lurches when walking; on Romberg starts to fall at about two seconds with the EYES STILL OPEN; hand tapping slow, irregular and messy on both sides; finger-nose steady at the nose then shaking more and more towards the target and missing it; arms drift UPWARD with eyes closed; arms fly up past the start on rebound; smooth eye movements with NO nystagmus; speech broken into syllables; knee jerk swinging four or five times; toe-to-finger shaking and missing; heel-shin wandering on both legs; cannot sit up with the arms crossed without two or three attempts. Three role-player mistakes that break the case: falling only once the eyes are closed (that is the sensory variant), making finger-nose merely slow rather than tremulous and missing (slow is Parkinson's), and volunteering the alcohol history before being asked.

Reference points: Romberg — falls with the eyes OPEN means cerebellar or vestibular; steady open then falling closed is a POSITIVE Romberg and means proprioceptive loss; count to five. Dysdiadochokinesia and heel-shin must be done on BOTH sides. Pendular reflex: knee jerk sitting with the legs hanging, 4-5 swings instead of 1-2. Drift: cerebellar is UPWARD with palms up; a downward pronator drift is UMN. DANISH — Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning speech, Hypotonia. Wernicke's triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia — thiamine before glucose, and correct magnesium.

must: FAIL — Letting the patient fall, or standing him up without guarding him — brace before he moves and take only two or three steps: 'I'm going to put my arms around you as you go — I won't hold you, but if you go I'll catch you', walking backwards with him; then omit tandem gait ALOUD with its reason — 'he has already demonstrated loss of balance and I don't think it is safe' — because walking him the length of the room is time you need and a fall you do not (★)
FAIL — Examining in silence — no running commentary means no marks for accuracy; each of the ten signs is named the moment you see it, and the commentary is what the accuracy domain is scored on (★)

FAIL — Never saying THE COMMITMENT SENTENCE at about 1:50 — it converts two findings into a conclusion, justifies the examination you are about to perform, and disposes of the manoeuvre the examiner is waiting to see you handle; candidates who never say it do a little of everything and complete nothing: 'a broad-based gait together with loss of balance on Romberg WITH THE EYES OPEN points to a cerebellar rather than a proprioceptive cause; I'm therefore going to focus the rest of my examination on a full cerebellar screen rather than a general neurological examination, and I'll call out each finding as I go' (★)

FAIL — Asking him to close his eyes after he has already lost balance with them open — it adds no information and it will put him on the floor: 'on Romberg testing the patient lost his balance WITH THE EYES OPEN; I did not proceed to eye closure because he had already lost balance and I was concerned about a fall'; and to 'is the Romberg positive or negative?' — 'strictly neither: a POSITIVE Romberg means steady with the eyes open and falling on closing them, which is proprioceptive loss; he is unsteady with his eyes open, which points to the cerebellum'

FAIL — Skipping general appearance and going straight to gait, so the swaying in sitting is never named — it is a free mark most candidates walk past: 'notably, he is unable to maintain his balance even in a SITTING position — he is swaying from side to side as I speak to him' (describe it now and save the term truncal ataxia until you have earned it with the arms-crossed sit-up at the end); and do not spend time on positioning or exposure — 'no particular exposure or position is required for this examination'

SAY — Name all ten signs in their own words, then give the differentials in SIX GROUPS rather than a flat list, which is the commonest reason candidates who examined well still fail the reasoning domain: dysdiadochokinesia BOTH SIDES, intention tremor worsening towards the target with past-pointing (finger held at full arm's reach), UPWARD drift with the palms up — the cerebellar pattern, where a downward pronator drift would be upper motor neuron — rebound overshooting well past the starting position, no nystagmus, slurred staccato SCANNING DYSARTHRIA, a PENDULAR knee jerk of four or five swings tested sitting with the legs hanging, abnormal heel–shin both sides, toe-to-finger, and truncal ataxia on sitting up with the arms crossed; then 'alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration', with brain (cerebellar stroke or TIA, posterior circulation ischaemia, tumour or metastasis, multiple sclerosis), nutritional (Wernicke's, B12), drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lithium, sedatives), sensory (alcoholic or diabetic neuropathy causing sensory ataxia), vestibular (neuritis, labyrinthitis, Ménière's) and lower limb (arthritis of the hip or knee, lumbar radiculopathy, cauda equina); parenteral THIAMINE BEFORE ANY GLUCOSE, because a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy, plus bloods with LFTs, magnesium and B12, an MRI brain, withdrawal management (DASSA ADIS 1300 13 1340), falls prevention and an occupational therapy home assessment; raise driving, and discuss the alcohol without shaming — 'some of it can improve with sustained abstinence; honestly, probably not all of it — but stopping is the most useful thing you can do, and I won't leave you to do it alone'

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, 8 minutes. He has ALREADY been told the biopsy shows metastatic squamous cell carcinoma; your job is to find where it came from, and the LINKING SENTENCE at about 4:30 is the station: a C8/T1 deficit, in a smoker, with a metastatic squamous node in the neck, points to the lung apex. The three things that fail it: finding C8 and T1 and never linking them to the node and the smoking history; claiming anhidrosis from a photograph card; and re-breaking the cancer diagnosis he already knows.
stem: General practice. Nick Farrell, 45, a long-term smoker, presented to your colleague with a lump in the LEFT side of his neck and tingling and numbness in the RIGHT upper limb. A lymph node biopsy has returned as metastatic squamous cell carcinoma and Nick has already been told the result. He is sitting on the couch in a singlet, arms already exposed.
tasks: Perform an upper limb neurological examination
Perform any further relevant examination
State your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
Explain your findings to the patient
time: 0:00-0:35 WIPE and NAME THE PURPOSE · acknowledge the biopsy result ONCE, then 'what I'd like to do today is examine you to work out where it has come from, because that's what decides the treatment' · 0:35-1:05 INSPECTION front AND back of both hands: WASTING of the small muscles of the right hand with DORSAL GUTTERING between the metacarpals and thenar/hypothenar wasting; no fasciculations, no tremor; left hand normal · 1:05-1:25 tone · 1:25-2:50 POWER C5-T1 both sides: C5, C6, C7 normal; C8 grip REDUCED on the right (offer two fingers of each hand so you can compare directly); T1 finger abduction REDUCED on the right · 2:50-3:20 reflexes biceps C5-6, supinator C6, triceps C7 with a C8 contribution · 3:20-4:30 SENSATION C5 lateral shoulder, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 MEDIAL FOREARM (the medial forearm is what separates a root lesion from an ulnar palsy) → loss at C8 and T1 on the right; offer coordination and skip it with a reason · 4:30 THE LINKING SENTENCE · 4:35-5:35 Horner's syndrome by name (photograph card: partial ptosis and miosis, and anhidrosis CANNOT be assessed from a photograph), skin survey of face, scalp and neck, oral cavity, then the neck and supraclavicular nodes · 5:35-6:40 respiratory findings BY REQUEST in order: expansion, trachea, percussion, breath sounds, vocal resonance → a right basal pleural effusion, which SUPPORTS the apical tumour rather than arguing against it · 6:40-8:00 diagnosis, three exclusions with reasons, five possible primaries, then the four-beat explanation to Nick.

back.dx: Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumour of the right lung — a squamous cell carcinoma involving the LOWER TRUNK of the brachial plexus and the cervical sympathetic chain, with a secondary pleural effusion and a metastatic cervical node: wasting of the small muscles of the right hand with dorsal guttering, reduced C8 and T1 power and C8/T1 sensory loss on the right with normal C5-C7 — a lower brachial plexus lesion, not a single peripheral nerve — plus partial ptosis and miosis (Horner's) and a hard, fixed, non-tender left supraclavicular node. Excluded with reasons: ULNAR neuropathy — the sensory loss extends onto the MEDIAL FOREARM, above ulnar territory, and an ulnar palsy never causes Horner's; C8 RADICULOPATHY — no neck pain, and a radiculopathy does not cause Horner's; thoracic outlet syndrome and radiation plexopathy — neither fits the history. Squamous primaries for a cervical node: skin of the head and neck, oral cavity, pharynx or larynx, lung, oesophagus — plus an occult primary. Imaging: CXR, CT chest and neck, MRI thoracic inlet for resectability, PET-CT, MRI brain, pleural tap with Light's criteria. Do NOT give a prognosis without staging. SA: RAH/FMC lung MDT, PATS, Cancer Council SA 13 11 20, Quitline 13 7848, TIS National 131 450.
plan: 'Good morning Nick, I'm Dr -. I understand you've had the result of the biopsy from your neck, and I'm sorry — that must have been a difficult thing to hear. What I'd like to do today is examine you to work out where it has come from, because that's what decides the treatment. I'll start with your arms — some movements, testing the feeling with cotton wool, and I may tap with a reflex hammer. Any pain? Happy for me to go ahead?' (washes hands) → 'They said it's cancer but nobody's told me where it started. And my right hand's been useless for a couple of months — is that part of it?' → 'That's exactly what I want to find out.' Do NOT deliver a warning shot or re-break the news.

INSPECTION, front and back — the finding most candidates walk past: 'On general appearance he is alert and comfortable at rest. On inspection of both arms and hands, front and back — there is WASTING OF THE SMALL MUSCLES OF THE RIGHT HAND with dorsal guttering between the metacarpals, and wasting of the thenar and hypothenar eminences. There are no fasciculations and no tremor. The left hand is normal.' Then tone, normal and symmetrical.

POWER and REFLEXES: 'Arms out to the side like a chicken, don't let me push down... bend your elbows, pull me towards you... now push me away' → C5, C6, C7 normal and symmetrical. 'Squeeze my fingers as hard as you can' (two fingers of each hand, compared directly) → the right is loose, 'that's all I've got, doc' → 'power of C8 is reduced on the right.' 'Spread your fingers apart and don't let me push them together' → right collapses → 'power of T1 is reduced on the right.' Biceps C5-C6, supinator C6, triceps C7 with a C8 contribution — present and symmetrical.

SENSATION, including the medial forearm: cotton wool demonstrated on the sternum, 'close your eyes and tell me if it feels the same on both sides' — C5 lateral shoulder, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 MEDIAL FOREARM, both sides at the same level → 'sensation is normal in C5, C6 and C7. There is sensory loss in C8 and T1 on the right.' Offer coordination and skip it with a reason: 'the findings already localise the lesion and I'd rather use the time on the relevant examination.'

THE LINKING SENTENCE: 'Examiner, to summarise task one: wasting of the small muscles of the right hand, with reduced power and sensory loss in C8 and T1 on the right, and normal C5 to C7. That is a LOWER BRACHIAL PLEXUS lesion, not a single peripheral nerve. A C8 and T1 lesion, in a smoker, with a metastatic squamous node in the neck, makes me think of a lesion at the LUNG APEX involving the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. For my further relevant examination I'd like to look for Horner's syndrome, examine the skin of the face, scalp and neck and the oral cavity for a primary, and then examine the respiratory system.'

The relevant examination: 'I'd like to look for Horner's syndrome — specifically ptosis and miosis' → photograph card → 'partial ptosis and miosis on the right. ANHIDROSIS CANNOT BE ASSESSED FROM A PHOTOGRAPH — I'd look for it clinically.' Then the skin survey said out loud ('suspicious moles, ulcers or non-healing lesions') over the face, behind the ears and the scalp; 'open your mouth and say ah' for masses or ulcers; then palpate the node groups and BOTH supraclavicular fossae → a hard, fixed, non-tender node in the left supraclavicular fossa.

Respiratory BY REQUEST, asked specifically and in order: 'Is chest expansion symmetrical?' → reduced right lower zone. 'Is the trachea central?' → central, so the effusion is not large enough to displace it. 'On percussion, both sides — any dullness?' → stony dullness at the right base. 'Is air entry equal? Any added or absent sounds?' → reduced at the right base. 'And vocal resonance?' → reduced. → 'The four together are a pleural effusion at the right base. The chest findings are at the base, but they are the signs of an EFFUSION rather than of the mass itself — a tumour large enough to compress the brachial plexus would not by itself produce them, and a secondary effusion is a recognised complication of an apical carcinoma. So the basal signs SUPPORT the diagnosis rather than argue against it.' Do not retract the apical diagnosis.

Diagnosis, the three exclusions and the five possible primaries (see dx). Then the four beats to Nick: WHERE — the top of your right lung; WHY YOUR SYMPTOMS FIT — it presses on the bundle of nerves running into your arm, which is the numbness, the weakness and the droopy eyelid, and there is fluid around the bottom of that lung; WHAT NEXT — CT chest and neck, MRI to see what it's touching, a whole-body scan, then a specialist team decides treatment, referral today; CHECK IN — 'I know that's a lot. What questions have you got?' If he asks how long he has: 'I'm not going to guess at that — I can't tell you until we have the scans. What I can promise is that I'll be straight with you at every step. Is there someone who can come with you to the next appointment?'
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute run sheet
ask: 'I want to examine you to work out where it has come from, because that's what decides the treatment.' / 'There is wasting of the small muscles of the right hand with dorsal guttering.' / 'Power of C8 and T1 is reduced on the right.' / 'There is sensory loss in the C8 and T1 dermatomes on the right.' / 'That is a lower brachial plexus lesion, not a single peripheral nerve.'

'A C8 and T1 lesion in a smoker with a metastatic squamous node makes me think of a lesion at the lung apex.' / 'There is partial ptosis and miosis — Horner's syndrome.' / 'Anhidrosis cannot be assessed from a photograph; I'd look for it clinically.' / 'The chest findings are the signs of a pleural effusion, not of the mass itself.' / 'The sensory loss extends onto the medial forearm, which is above the ulnar territory.' / To Nick: 'It presses on the bundle of nerves that runs down into your arm.'

Examiner challenge — 'why isn't this just an ulnar nerve palsy?' → three reasons: the sensory loss extends onto the medial forearm, above ulnar territory; there is a Horner's syndrome, which an ulnar palsy can never cause; and there is a metastatic node in the neck of a smoker.

Variants: REFLEXES TESTED and the right arm held stiff with no triceps jerk → 'the triceps reflex is depressed on the right, biceps and supinator preserved. Triceps is C7 with a C8 contribution, so that fits the same C8/T1 lower trunk lesion.' / HOARSENESS volunteered for six weeks → 'that matters. Hoarseness can mean involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which loops through the chest. I'd arrange ENT review with laryngoscopy, and it suggests mediastinal extension.' / FACIAL AND ARM SWELLING with distended non-pulsatile neck veins and morning headache → 'that is superior vena cava obstruction — an oncological emergency. Sit him up, oxygen, urgent CT with contrast, and discuss steroids and stenting with oncology and interventional radiology today.' / 'HOW LONG HAVE I GOT?' — the question this station is really marking → do not give a number with no staging; promise honesty and ask who can come with him. With thirty seconds left, ask about hoarseness and about facial or arm swelling with distended neck veins.
pefe: Role-player: Nick Farrell, 45, plant operator at the grain terminal, lives in Wallaroo with his partner Deb and two teenagers; 25 cigarettes a day since he was 17. Found a lump in the left neck two months ago, biopsied, ALREADY TOLD it is cancer spread to the gland with no known primary. Right hand weaker and number for three months — drops things, can't do up buttons. Deep nagging ache in the right shoulder for six months, treated as a frozen shoulder by a physio. Six kilos of weight loss, some night sweats, a smoker's cough, no haemoptysis. NO neck pain (keep saying no — neck pain would make a C8 radiculopathy the better answer). Matter-of-fact and blunt, wants information not sympathy. Asks early 'is the hand part of it?' and near the end 'how long have I got?' — that second question is the one being marked.

How the signs are played: the right hand rests with the fingers slightly clawed and the hollows between the bones show when it is turned over; C5, C6, C7 full both sides; the right grip barely closes — 'that's all I've got on that side, doc'; right finger abduction collapses as soon as pressure is applied; reflexes normal both sides (unless running the triceps variant); sensation 'same' at the shoulder, thumb and middle finger, but 'I can't feel that one at all' at the little finger AND THE MEDIAL FOREARM on the right — reporting numbness only in the little finger turns the case into an ulnar palsy and collapses the station.

Numbers: roots C5 shoulder abduction, C6 elbow flexion, C7 elbow extension, C8 grip, T1 finger abduction; reflexes biceps C5-C6, supinator C6, triceps C7 with a C8 contribution VERIFY; dermatome points C5 lateral shoulder, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm. Horner's: partial ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, apparent enophthalmos. Pancoast triad: shoulder and arm pain with a C8/T1 deficit, Horner's, small hand muscle wasting. Effusion signs: reduced expansion, stony dullness, reduced breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance. Imaging: CXR, CT chest and neck, MRI thoracic inlet for resectability, PET-CT, MRI brain, pleural tap with Light's criteria.

★ Claiming anhidrosis from a photograph card
Re-breaking the cancer diagnosis with a warning shot — he already knows; acknowledge once and move to purpose
Going straight to tone without turning the hands over, so the dorsal guttering is missed; testing sensation without the medial forearm, which leaves the case looking like an ulnar palsy
Retracting the apical diagnosis when the chest findings come back at the base; giving a prognosis with no staging

SAY — Exclude the alternatives with reasons, then explain in four beats and give NO PROGNOSIS: to 'why isn't this just an ulnar nerve palsy?' give three reasons — the sensory loss extends onto the MEDIAL FOREARM, above the ulnar territory; there is a HORNER'S SYNDROME, which an ulnar palsy can never cause; and there is a metastatic node in the neck of a smoker — while a C8 radiculopathy is out because there is no neck pain and it does not cause Horner's, and thoracic outlet syndrome and radiation plexopathy do not fit the history; name the five squamous primaries (skin of the head and neck, oral cavity, pharynx and larynx, lung, oesophagus, plus an occult primary); then to Nick — WHERE (the top of your right lung), WHY his symptoms fit (it presses on the bundle of nerves running into your arm: the numbness, the weakness, the droopy eyelid, with fluid around the bottom of that lung), WHAT HAPPENS NEXT (CT chest and neck, MRI of the thoracic inlet for resectability, whole-body scan, specialist team, referral today) and CHECK IN ('I know that's a lot — what questions have you got?'); to 'how long have I got?' — 'I'm not going to guess at that; I can't tell you until we have the scans, and what I can promise is that I'll be straight with you at every step. Is there someone who can come with you to the next appointment?'; in the last thirty seconds ask about HOARSENESS (recurrent laryngeal involvement — ENT review with laryngoscopy, suggesting mediastinal extension) and facial or arm swelling with distended neck veins (SVC obstruction, an oncological emergency: sit him up, oxygen, urgent CT with contrast, steroids and stenting discussed today)

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED, you are the HMO. The word is NEUROVASCULAR, not neurological: vascular and nerve supply DISTAL to the injury plus the compartments — and you declare the two omissions (reflexes and coordination) with a reason, which converts them from gaps into judgement. A tendon hammer and a tuning fork are left on the trolley as DISTRACTORS. He will refuse all active movement, and the mark is recording the motor component as UNASSESSABLE rather than normal. The three things that fail this station: running a neurological examination instead of a neurovascular one; claiming findings the prosthetic wound cannot show; and causing avoidable pain — an ankle jerk, or forcing movement after he has said stop.
stem: Emergency department. Jimmy Nowak, 24, came off a scooter. Radiographs confirm a comminuted, displaced, OPEN fracture of the right tibia and fibula. Primary survey complete, haemodynamically stable: HR 96, BP 124/78, RR 18, SpO2 98%, GCS 15. Analgesia has been given.

On the trolley: a moulded prosthetic over the mid-shin with exposed bone, dried blood and fragments of glass taped to the skin, no dressing — plus a tuning fork, cotton wool, a toothpick and a tendon hammer.
tasks: Perform a lower limb neurovascular examination
Give a running commentary of your findings to the examiner
State your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
time: 0:00-0:40 acknowledge the vitals in ONE line, WIPE, and OFFER ANALGESIA before touching (the offer is the mark, not the acceptance) · then DECLARE: 'the task is a neurovascular examination, so I'll assess the vascular and nerve supply distal to the injury, and the compartments · inspection, then temperature, capillary refill and pulses, then power and sensation by nerve, and a gentle passive stretch. I'm going to omit reflexes and coordination: they'd cause significant pain in a fractured tibia and wouldn't change my management' · 0:40-1:10 general appearance · 1:10-2:10 INSPECTION, PALLOR OF THE FOOT FIRST (pallor signals vascular injury and it is about the FOOT, not the wound), then the wound: open, bone visible, no active bleeding, dried blood, FOREIGN MATERIAL (glass), no dressing, deformed and swollen, left limb normal · 2:10-3:20 temperature with the BACKS of the hands on both feet together, capillary refill, dorsalis pedis LATERAL TO THE EHL TENDON and posterior tibial BEHIND THE MEDIAL MALLEOLUS, both sides · 3:20-3:50 compartment palpation (soft, not hard or woody) and say aloud why you are NOT testing bony tenderness · 3:50-4:50 power by NERVE: dorsiflexion (deep peroneal), plantarflexion (tibial), toe wriggle · all refused; stop immediately, never push against resistance · 4:50-6:10 sensation by nerve (first web space, dorsum, sole, both feet together), then dermatomes L1-S1 and a second modality if time · 6:10-6:40 PASSIVE STRETCH OF THE TOES ONLY, never the ankle · 6:40-8:00 diagnosis and FIVE concerns, each linked to what you did.

back.dx: An open, comminuted, displaced fracture of the right tibia and fibula, currently NEUROVASCULARLY INTACT. Concerns in order, each tied to the examination: VASCULAR INJURY — hence foot colour, temperature, capillary refill and both pedal pulses; NERVE INJURY to the peroneal or tibial nerve — hence power and sensation by nerve territory; COMPARTMENT SYNDROME — hence compartment palpation and passive stretch, and a present pulse does NOT exclude it; MUSCLE AND TENDON INJURY — unassessable today because he cannot move; CONTAMINATION AND INFECTION given visible foreign material. Management: IV antibiotics within one hour of injury (cefazolin VERIFY), check tetanus status, photograph the wound once and cover with a saline-moistened sterile dressing, splint the limb, keep him fasted, X-ray including the joint above and below, and urgent orthopaedic referral for debridement and fixation — from Wallaroo that is MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 and transfer to the Royal Adelaide. With thirty seconds left: examine the joint above and below and complete the secondary survey, palpating the whole fibula to the neck for a Maisonneuve pattern. To Jimmy in plain English: both bones of the lower leg are broken and the ends have torn through the skin from the inside — an open fracture; the blood supply and nerves to the foot are working normally; he needs an operation to clean it out and fix the bone, antibiotics now, and nothing to eat or drink.
plan: One line on the vitals, then the WIPE with the analgesia offer: 'Examiner, I note the primary survey is complete and he is haemodynamically stable — heart rate 96, blood pressure 124 over 78, saturations 98% on air, GCS 15. Hi Jimmy, I'm Dr -, one of the doctors here. That looks like a rough one. Before I examine you — how's your pain right now, and would you like me to organise something stronger? I'm going to look at your leg, gently feel both feet and check the pulses, then check the feeling in your foot and ask you to try a couple of small movements. I'll be as gentle as I can — if anything hurts, say stop and I'll stop.'

DECLARE the examination and the two omissions with their reason — fifteen seconds, said once, at the start: 'The task is a neurovascular examination, so I'll assess the vascular and nerve supply distal to the injury, and the compartments — inspection, then temperature, capillary refill and pulses, then power and sensation by nerve, and a gentle passive stretch. I'm going to omit reflexes and coordination: they'd cause significant pain in a fractured tibia and wouldn't change my management.'

INSPECTION — the FOOT before the wound: 'On general appearance he's alert, in pain but not distressed, and not pale. On inspection of both lower limbs — the RIGHT FOOT IS WELL PERFUSED, with no pallor. There is an open wound over the mid-shin with bone visible. There is no active bleeding. There is dried blood and I can see foreign material — fragments of glass — on the skin. There is no dressing in place. The limb is deformed and swollen. The left lower limb appears normal.' (Do not invent granulation tissue, muscle herniation or pulsatile bleeding — the prosthetic cannot show them.)

Vascular and compartments: 'Jimmy, I'm going to feel your feet now — tell me if it hurts. Backs of my hands, both feet together — warm and equal, no cold clammy foot. Capillary refill under two seconds bilaterally. Dorsalis pedis, lateral to the EHL tendon — present and equal. Posterior tibial, behind the medial malleolus — present and equal. The compartments do not feel hard or woody. I'm not testing bony tenderness, because he has a known fracture and it would be pain without information.'

Power by nerve — and the refusal: hand on the dorsum, 'pull your foot up against my hand' (deep peroneal); hand under the sole, 'push down like an accelerator' (tibial); 'can you just wriggle your toes for me?' → all three refused. Stop immediately each time. 'Examiner, I am unable to assess active movements because of pain. I would record the motor component of both the peroneal and tibial nerves as UNASSESSABLE rather than normal, and repeat it once analgesia has taken effect. I'm not going to push against resistance in a patient who has told me it hurts.'

Sensation by nerve, then use the spare time: cotton wool introduced on the sternum, 'close your eyes and tell me if it's the same on both sides' — first web space (deep peroneal), dorsum (superficial peroneal), sole (tibial), both feet at the same time → 'deep peroneal, superficial peroneal and tibial nerve sensation are intact and symmetrical.' Then, with time in hand, the dermatomes L1 groin, L2 mid thigh, L3 anterior knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 sole, repeated with the toothpick for pinprick → 'sensation is also intact in the L1 to S1 dermatomes, tested with light touch and pinprick.'

Passive stretch, TOES ONLY: 'I'm going to gently bend your toes — tell me the second it hurts.' → no pain → 'No pain on passive stretch of the toes — I've kept that to the toes rather than the ankle, because ankle movement would move the fracture itself. So at this moment there are no clinical features of compartment syndrome — but it is a SERIAL clinical diagnosis and I'd want regular documented neurovascular observations.'

Diagnosis and the five concerns, each linked to what you did (see dx), then the management sequence and the plain-English explanation to Jimmy. If he asks 'am I going to lose it?' — answer honestly on what you found: the blood supply and nerves to the foot are working normally today.
