pefe: Role-player: Jimmy Nowak, 24, apprentice fitter, lives in Moonta; came off his scooter about an hour ago on a gravel shoulder outside Kadina and the bike landed on his right leg. Helmet on, no head strike, no loss of consciousness, no other pain. Fit and well, no medications or allergies, smokes ten a day, last ate at midday, does NOT know when he last had a tetanus shot — make the candidate work for it, and for the fact he was riding home from work (ReturnToWorkSA / CTP). Shocked and sore, trying to be tough, grimacing whenever anyone comes near the leg. Baseline: foot warm, pink, well perfused; calf soft; sensation normal everywhere ('same both sides'); passive toe stretch does NOT hurt; ALL active movement refused — 'I can't, it hurts', and 'please stop' if pushed. If anyone tries to move the ankle or position it for a reflex: 'Ah — don't, please!' and it is marked down. Asks near the end: 'Am I going to lose it?' / 'Do I need an operation? Can you ring my mum?'

Numbers: capillary refill under 2 seconds. Antibiotics within 1 hour of injury — cefazolin VERIFY. Check tetanus. Deep peroneal = dorsiflexion plus the first web space; superficial peroneal = eversion plus the dorsum; tibial = plantarflexion plus the sole. Dermatomes L1 groin, L2 mid thigh, L3 anterior knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 sole. FOUR compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, deep posterior. Compartment syndrome: limb at heart level, not above; delta pressure below 30 mmHg supports fasciotomy VERIFY. Gustilo IIIC = arterial injury requiring repair, graded after debridement. SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, RFDS, RAH/FMC, PATS, ReturnToWorkSA, TIS 131 450.

Starred scoring items: saying the movements were UNASSESSABLE; using the spare time (dermatomes, a second modality); four or more differentials each linked to the examination. Also scored: named it a neurovascular examination, did not attempt reflexes or coordination, stopped the moment he said it hurt, offered analgesia before touching, acknowledged the vital signs, warned before every touch, announced each omission with a reason, did not invent wound detail, named pallor of the foot FIRST, both pulses both sides, compartments palpated, passive stretch kept to the toes, antibiotics within the hour, tetanus, fasted and referred, and explained it in plain English.
Radiographs — Comminuted, displaced, OPEN fracture of the right tibia and fibula
Compartments — Soft; NO pain on passive stretch of the toes; no pain out of proportion

SAY — Give four or more differentials, each LINKED to what you actually did rather than a list of words: 'an open, comminuted, displaced fracture of the right tibia and fibula, currently neurovascularly intact; my concerns in order — VASCULAR injury, hence the colour, temperature, capillary refill and both pulses; NERVE injury to the peroneal or tibial nerve, hence testing by nerve territory (deep peroneal = dorsiflexion and first web space, superficial peroneal = eversion and dorsum, tibial = plantarflexion and sole); COMPARTMENT SYNDROME, hence the compartment palpation and the passive stretch — and a present pulse does NOT exclude it, it is a serial clinical diagnosis; muscle and tendon injury, unassessable today; and contamination and infection, given visible foreign material'; plan — intravenous antibiotics within ONE HOUR of injury, tetanus status, photograph the wound once and cover it with a saline-moistened sterile dressing, splint, keep him fasted, X-ray including the knee and ankle, urgent orthopaedic referral for debridement and fixation, and from Wallaroo MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 to the Royal Adelaide; with thirty seconds left add the joint above and below and the secondary survey, palpating the whole fibula to the neck for a Maisonneuve pattern; a pale, cool foot with four-second refill and absent pedal pulses is a TIME-CRITICAL limb (realign and splint, immediately re-examine the pulses, orthopaedics and vascular surgery, CT angiography — an arterial injury requiring repair is a Gustilo IIIC), and pain out of proportion with a woody compartment and severe pain on passive toe extension despite present pulses is compartment syndrome — remove circumferential dressings, limb AT heart level and not elevated, and orthopaedics now for fasciotomy

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice. The core neck examination that every thyroid station is built on, and the station is lost in ONE sentence: palpating in silence and then saying 'the thyroid feels normal' — six separate marks thrown away. Say all SIX key points aloud and ASK about tenderness rather than declaring it. Two sips of water, not one (swallowing is assessed looking and feeling, and they are separate marks). Automatic fails: examining through the scarf; naming Pemberton's and then not performing it; unqualified reassurance that it is not cancer; never characterising the gland.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Jane Whitmore, 38, has noticed a swelling at the front of her neck over four months. She feels well in herself. T 36.8 — HR 78 regular — BP 118/74 — RR 14 — SpO2 99% RA. On the trolley: glass of water, stethoscope, tendon hammer, pen torch. She is wearing a scarf.
tasks: Perform a focused examination of the thyroid gland, with a running commentary to the examiner. Do not take a history
Report your findings to the examiner
Explain to the patient what you have found and what will happen next
time: WIPE with the four steps named (look, feel from behind, sip and swallow, tap and listen), the FRONT OF THE NECK UNCOVERED · ask her to remove the scarf, never reach for it, and offer the curtain and a chaperone · INSPECTION front then LATERAL: no visible swelling, no visible mass, no engorged veins, no scars; a normal straight line from the cricoid cartilage to the suprasternal notch · FIRST SIP: 'take a sip and HOLD it · don't swallow until I ask' → get your eyes into position → 'swallow now' → moves with swallowing · PALPATION from BEHIND, warning her first and asking about tenderness: displace the trachea to the left and palpate the RIGHT lobe, to the right for the LEFT lobe, then the isthmus below the cricoid → THE SIX KEY POINTS OUT LOUD: size, lower border, consistency, nodularity, tenderness, mobility · THRILLS with the finger pads over each lobe · SECOND SIP for mobility on palpation · EIGHT NODE GROUPS: submental, submandibular, pre-auricular, post-auricular, occipital, anterior cervical, posterior cervical, SUPRACLAVICULAR · back to the front for the TRACHEA in the suprasternal notch · PERCUSSION 3-4 taps SIDE TO SIDE across the manubrium for retrosternal extension · AUSCULTATION of each lobe for a bruit · PEMBERTON'S with the arms up beside the ears · then the 40-second summary WITH A PLAN, and the explanation.

back.dx: A clinically normal thyroid examination: no visible mass, engorged veins or scars, preserved lateral contour from cricoid to suprasternal notch, normal movement with swallowing; gland of normal size with a palpable lower border, normal consistency, no nodules, non-tender and mobile; no thrills, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, central trachea, resonant symmetrical percussion, no bruit, negative Pemberton's. Differential for the reported swelling: a small multinodular goitre or a benign solitary nodule, with thyroglossal cyst and thyroid carcinoma to be excluded. Plan: TSH (the screening test) and a NECK ULTRASOUND (first-line imaging), with ultrasound-guided FNA if a suspicious nodule is seen, and review with the results. Safety-net: return sooner if the swelling grows quickly, the voice becomes hoarse, or there is trouble swallowing or breathing, or a hard lump appears. If the clock beats you, drop the differentials — never the plan. Regional SA: check what imaging is available locally first, and PATS helps with travel and accommodation if she has to go to Adelaide.
plan: WIPE and exposure: '...I've been asked to examine your thyroid — that's a gland at the front of your neck. What I'll do is look at your neck, then feel it from behind you, ask you to sip some water and swallow a couple of times, gently tap on the top of your chest and listen with my stethoscope. It shouldn't hurt at all — will you tell me if anything is uncomfortable? I'll just need the front of your neck uncovered, and I'd like you to stay sitting as you are.' If she is wearing a scarf: 'Would you mind slipping that off for a couple of minutes so I can see the whole neck? I can pull the curtain across, and I'm happy to have a chaperone with us.' NEVER reach for her clothing.

Inspection front and lateral, then the FIRST sip: 'Could you tip your chin up a little for me? Examiner, on inspection from the front I can see no visible swelling and no visible mass, no engorged veins, and no scars to suggest previous thyroid surgery. I'll step to the side — from the lateral view there is a normal straight line from the cricoid cartilage to the suprasternal notch.' Then 'Jane, take a sip of water and HOLD it in your mouth — don't swallow until I ask you' → move in close → 'swallow now for me' → 'on inspection the thyroid moves with swallowing.'

Palpation from BEHIND, warned and consented: 'Jane, I'm going to come and stand behind you and feel your neck — is that all right? Please tell me if it's tender anywhere. Examiner, I'm displacing the trachea to the left and palpating the right lobe... displacing to the right and palpating the left lobe... and palpating the isthmus just below the cricoid. Examiner, THE KEY POINTS: the size is normal, I can feel the lower border, the consistency is normal, I cannot feel any nodules — Jane, is that painful at all? — no, so the gland is not tender.'

Thrills, second sip, nodes, trachea: 'I'm placing the pads of my fingers over each lobe — no palpable thrills. Jane, another sip, hold it... swallow now. On palpation the thyroid moves with swallowing, so it is mobile and not tethered. Cervical nodes: submental... submandibular... pre-auricular... post-auricular... occipital... anterior cervical or jugular chain... posterior cervical... and SUPRACLAVICULAR. No palpable lymphadenopathy.' Then back to the front, fingers into the suprasternal notch: 'the trachea is central.'

Percussion, auscultation, Pemberton's: 'Jane, I'm going to tap gently on the top of your chest' — three or four taps SIDE TO SIDE across the manubrium — 'percussion is resonant and symmetrical, no retrosternal extension.' Diaphragm on each lobe — 'no thyroid bruit.' 'Last thing — can you lift both arms straight up beside your ears and hold them there?... Arms down. Pemberton's sign is negative — no facial plethora, no cyanosis, no distended neck veins, no stridor.'

THE SCRIPTED CHALLENGE: 'Would you perform Pemberton's sign if you had found the thyroid to be of normal size?' → 'No, Examiner — in clinical practice I wouldn't, because the sign only becomes relevant when there is a goitre that may extend retrosternally. But FOR COMPLETENESS of my examination in this setting, I would still like to perform it.' Then DO IT. Naming a manoeuvre and skipping it is worse than never mentioning it.

The 40-second summary, ending with the plan (see dx). Then the patient explanation: the butterfly-shaped gland that sets the speed the body runs at, everything checkable at the bedside normal and reassuring, but an examination alone cannot tell everything and she has definitely noticed something — so a blood test and an ultrasound, FNA if the scan shows something to look at more closely, and review with both results, plus the red-flag safety-net.

The hidden agenda surfaces: 'Is it cancer?' → 'That's exactly the right question to ask, and I'd rather you asked it than worried on your own. The honest answer is that most neck lumps like this are not cancer — the great majority turn out to be a benign nodule or a slightly enlarged gland. What I can't do is promise you that from an examination alone, and I don't want to give you a reassurance I can't back up. That's exactly why we do the blood test and the ultrasound — so we're not guessing. Whatever the results show, I'll go through them with you and we'll decide what happens next together.' Also expect: 'my aunt had her thyroid out', 'will I need an operation?', 'do I have to go to Adelaide?' (PATS).

'Displacing the trachea to the left, palpating the right lobe... and the isthmus.' / 'Examiner, the key points: size, lower border, consistency, nodularity, tenderness, mobility.' / 'No palpable thrills... no bruit... percussion resonant and symmetrical.' / 'For completeness of my examination, I would still like to perform it.'

'Most lumps like this aren't cancer, but I can't promise you that from an examination alone — that's why we scan.' Red flags to safety-net: rapid growth, hoarseness, trouble swallowing or breathing, a hard lump.

Variant 1 — RETROSTERNAL GOITRE: 'visible swelling in the lower neck with distended superficial veins, and from the side the normal contour between cricoid and suprasternal notch is lost... the gland is diffusely enlarged, firm, non-tender, and critically I CANNOT FEEL THE LOWER BORDER — which raises retrosternal extension... percussion is DULL over the left manubrium and resonant on the right... Pemberton's sign is POSITIVE — after twenty seconds there is facial plethora and distended neck veins. Are you light-headed or short of breath? Examiner, this indicates thoracic inlet obstruction — CT neck and thorax, a flow-volume loop, an urgent endocrine surgical opinion, and I'd ask about orthopnoea and stridor.'

Variant 2 — HARD FIXED NODULE with hoarseness: 'a discrete nodule in the right lobe, about three centimetres, STONY HARD, non-tender, and it does not move freely with swallowing — it feels tethered. There is a hard, fixed node in the right supraclavicular fossa. With the reported hoarseness I am concerned about thyroid malignancy with possible recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement — urgent neck ultrasound with US-guided FNA, laryngoscopy to assess cord movement, and a same-week endocrine surgical referral.' Explaining without breaking bad news prematurely: 'I've found something I want to look into properly rather than wait on... I'm not able to tell you today what it is — that needs a scan and a small needle sample. What I can tell you is that I'm going to arrange it urgently, this week, and I'll ring you myself with a time. Is there someone who can come with you?' / Variant 3 — PAINFUL GLAND after a viral illness: 'diffusely enlarged and exquisitely tender — subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis. TSH, fT4 and inflammatory markers; expect an early thyrotoxic phase then a hypothyroid phase; simple analgesia and NSAIDs, corticosteroids reserved for severe pain' VERIFY TG. Tenderness is a finding you only obtain BY ASKING.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Whitmore, 38, primary teacher on the Yorke Peninsula, married with two children; non-smoker, two or three wines a week, no medications, allergies or previous surgery. Four months ago her neck looked fuller in a photograph; she feels completely well — energy, weight, bowels and periods normal, no tremor, palpitations, hoarseness or difficulty swallowing or breathing. Her AUNT had her thyroid removed fifteen years ago for 'a growth' that nobody explained, and that sits under everything she says. Composed, polite, slightly brisk, never volunteers worry — underneath she is frightened it is cancer, and says so only if invited or, failing that, quietly at the very end. She wears a scarf and keeps it on: removes it pleasantly if ASKED, lets them examine through it and marks them down, and pulls back with an 'oh -' if they reach for it. If told 'take a sip and swallow' in one breath she swallows immediately, before they are in position. Nothing hurts, and she says so only if asked. If given blanket reassurance she pushes once: 'how can you be sure without any tests?'

Numbers: SIX steps — inspect, sip/swallow, palpate, percuss, auscultate, Pemberton's. FOUR + 1 palpation parts — gland, thrills, sip/swallow and nodes from behind; trachea from the front. SIX key points — size, lower border, consistency, nodularity, tenderness, mobility. EIGHT node groups, ending at supraclavicular. 3-4 percussion taps side to side on the manubrium. TWO sips of water — one looking, one feeling. Arms up 10-20 s for Pemberton's in a timed station. TSH is the screening test; ultrasound is first-line imaging. Clock: 1:30 hands behind the patient, 3:45 percussion starts, 5:05 reporting starts.

Scored domains: approach (full WIPE, consent at each stage, exposure ASKED for rather than reached for, privacy or chaperone offered, warned before standing behind, tenderness asked about); technique (hands in the lower half of the neck, inspection front and lateral, sip-and-swallow used TWICE, both lobes and isthmus, thrills separately, all eight node groups, trachea from the front, 3-4 taps side to side, both lobes auscultated, Pemberton's attempted); commentary (continuous, specific rather than generic, all six key points aloud, negatives stated, the Pemberton's challenge answered without abandoning the manoeuvre); diagnosis and management (structured summary, sensible differential, TSH and ultrasound, FNA pathway, red-flag safety-net); communication (jargon-free, concerns invited, 'is it cancer' answered honestly without blanket reassurance and without frightening her, understanding checked, follow-up offered).
Swallowing and tongue protrusion — Moves normally on swallowing; does NOT move on tongue protrusion
Pemberton sign — Negative
Overall — A CLINICALLY NORMAL thyroid examination unless a variant is being run
fails: ★ Palpating in silence and reporting 'the thyroid feels normal' — six separate marks in one sentence; declaring the gland non-tender without ever asking
★ Examining through the scarf, reaching for her clothing unasked, or asking the EXAMINER for exposure instead of the patient
Naming Pemberton's and then not performing it after the scripted challenge
Using the water only once; stopping the node sweep at the jugular chain and never reaching supraclavicular; a single percussion tap, or percussing down the sternum instead of side to side
Unqualified reassurance ('don't worry, it's definitely nothing') before any imaging — the commonest way to lose Task 3 having done Tasks 1 and 2 perfectly; or reporting findings with no plan

FAIL — Unqualified reassurance that it is not cancer before anything has been imaged — the commonest way to lose task 3 having done tasks 1 and 2 perfectly, and she will push once ('how can you be sure without any tests?'): 'most neck lumps like this are not cancer — the great majority turn out to be a benign nodule or a slightly enlarged gland; what I can't do is promise you that from an examination alone, and I don't want to give you a reassurance I can't back up — that's exactly why we do the blood test and the ultrasound, so we're not guessing'; and do not swing the other way and frighten her either (★)

FAIL — The three technique errors that lose marks silently: saying 'take a sip and swallow' as ONE instruction, so she swallows while you are still straightening up and you see nothing (sip → hold → get your eyes into position → 'swallow now'); using the water only ONCE, when swallowing is assessed twice, looking and feeling, as separate marks; stopping the node sweep at the jugular chain and never reaching SUPRACLAVICULAR, the group that matters in malignancy (submental, submandibular, pre- and post-auricular, occipital, anterior cervical, posterior cervical, supraclavicular); and a single percussion tap, or percussing down the sternum instead of three or four taps SIDE TO SIDE across the manubrium

SAY — Be specific rather than generic on inspection — 'no visible swelling, no visible mass, no engorged veins, no scars to suggest previous thyroid surgery', and from the side 'a normal straight line from the cricoid cartilage to the suprasternal notch' — then report with a PLAN, because if the clock beats you, you drop the differentials and never the plan: 'a clinically normal thyroid examination; my differential for the reported swelling would be a small multinodular goitre or a benign solitary nodule, and I would want to exclude a thyroglossal cyst and thyroid carcinoma; my plan is a TSH and a neck ultrasound, with ultrasound-guided FNA if the ultrasound shows a suspicious nodule, and review with the results'; to the patient, the butterfly-shaped gland that 'sets the speed your body runs at', with the safety net — swelling growing quickly, a hoarse voice, trouble swallowing or breathing, or a hard lump — and PATS for travel if the scan means Adelaide; variants — a lost lateral contour with an IMPALPABLE LOWER BORDER, dullness over one side of the manubrium and a positive Pemberton's is retrosternal extension with thoracic inlet obstruction (CT neck and thorax, flow-volume loop, urgent endocrine surgical opinion, and ask about orthopnoea and stridor); a stony-hard tethered nodule with a fixed supraclavicular node and hoarseness is malignancy with possible recurrent laryngeal involvement (urgent ultrasound with ultrasound-guided FNA, laryngoscopy to assess cord movement, same-week endocrine surgical referral, and 'is there someone who can come with you?')

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice, with bloods already back (TSH suppressed, fT4 raised). Say 'I'm going to perform an examination for THYROTOXICOSIS' in the first fifteen seconds, or the wording of the stem drags you into a tremor or neurological examination. The eyes get FOUR separate manoeuvres and lid lag cannot be commented on from a motionless face. Automatic fails: performing a tremor or neurological examination instead of a thyroid one; naming carbimazole or propylthiouracil with NO agranulocytosis warning; prescribing in a woman of childbearing age without asking about pregnancy; reporting 'no lid lag' without ever moving the eye.

T 36.9 — HR 104 regular — BP 148/62 — RR 16 — SpO2 99% RA. On the trolley: sheet of paper, stethoscope, tendon hammer, pen torch, glass of water.

time: WIPE naming every part, and ASK FOR ARMS, NECK AND SHINS uncovered (no shins = no pretibial myxoedema) · then the sentence: 'given the blood results I'm going to perform an examination for thyrotoxicosis' · GENERAL APPEARANCE: anxious, restless, VISIBLE FACIAL SWEATING, thin for his frame · HANDS: onycholysis, thyroid acropachy, palmar erythema, then FEEL the palms (warm and sweaty) · TREMOR: arms out palms down, then the SHEET OF PAPER across the dorsum · PULSE: estimate the rate, then state the RHYTHM and the wide pulse pressure; no AF, confirm with ECG · PROXIMAL MYOPATHY against resistance at both elbows + ask about rising from a chair and stairs · ONE REFLEX, hammer in hand: biceps jerk BRISK · EYES, FOUR MANOEUVRES at 2:30: from the FRONT (lid retraction, chemosis, periorbital swelling), from ABOVE AND BEHIND (proptosis), H-PATTERN (ophthalmoplegia, diplopia, pain), and LID LAG on slow downgaze · NECK at 3:20, the FULL thyroid sequence including percussion, auscultation and Pemberton's · CHEST: gynaecomastia, heart sounds, flow murmur · SHINS: pretibial myxoedema, peripheral oedema · stop examining at 4:50, reporting done by 5:40 · then the three-tier plan and the CARBIMAZOLE SAFETY RULE with teach-back.

back.dx: Graves' disease — thyrotoxicosis with a DIFFUSE, smooth, symmetrical hypervascular goitre (palpable thrill, audible systolic bruit) plus ORBITOPATHY, which occurs in Graves' and not in the other causes: anxious and restless with facial sweating, fine tremor on paper, tachycardia ~105 regular with a wide pulse pressure, brisk biceps jerk, bilateral lid retraction, lid lag and mild proptosis with full movements. Negatives worth naming: no onycholysis or acropachy, no proximal myopathy, no ophthalmoplegia or diplopia, no lymphadenopathy, central trachea, resonant percussion, negative Pemberton's, no gynaecomastia, no pretibial myxoedema. Differentials: toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma (both less likely with a diffuse rather than nodular gland), thyroiditis (less likely with a non-tender gland). Plan: ECG for AF, TSH-receptor antibodies, baseline FBC and LFTs; beta-blocker for symptom control now; carbimazole after baselines WITH the agranulocytosis rule and teach-back; endocrinology referral for definitive treatment (radioiodine or surgery); ask about smoking, the single biggest modifiable factor for eye disease, and offer cessation; review in four weeks with repeat thyroid function.
plan: WIPE and exposure: '...I'll look at your hands and your eyes, feel your pulse, test the strength in your shoulders, tap your arm with this little hammer to check your reflexes, examine the gland in your neck, and have a look at your shins. I'll need your ARMS, NECK AND SHINS uncovered, and I'd like you sitting on the edge of the bed.' Then, out loud: 'Examiner, given the blood results I'm going to perform an examination for THYROTOXICOSIS, working from the general appearance through the hands, eyes and neck.'

Appearance, hands, tremor, pulse: 'From the end of the bed the patient is alert and orientated but appears anxious and restless. There is VISIBLE SWEATING OF THE FACE. He appears thin for his frame... no onycholysis — separation of the nail from the nail bed — and no thyroid acropachy... no palmar erythema, and the palms are warm and sweaty [FEEL them]. Could you hold both arms straight out in front, palms down, fingers spread? No coarse tremor. I'll now test for a fine tremor [lays the PAPER across the dorsum] — the paper is oscillating: there is a fine tremor. [radial pulse] The pulse is approximately 105, regular, normal character and volume, with a wide pulse pressure of 148 over 62. No evidence of atrial fibrillation — I would confirm with an ECG.'

Proximal myopathy and the reflex, straight on: 'Could you hold your arms out to the sides like wings, and stop me pushing them down? Shoulder abduction is 5 out of 5 bilaterally — no proximal myopathy. I would also ask whether he has difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs.' Then PICK UP THE HAMMER: 'Let your arm go floppy for me. Examiner, the biceps jerk is BRISK — hyperreflexia, consistent with thyrotoxicosis.' ('I would also check the reflexes' earns nothing; all four limbs burns the clock.)

THE EYES, four manoeuvres: FRONT — 'look straight ahead at the wall behind me. There is bilateral LID RETRACTION — sclera visible above the iris on both sides — with mild proptosis, no chemosis or conjunctival injection and no periorbital swelling.' ABOVE — 'may I stand behind you and look down over your forehead? From above there is mild bilateral proptosis, the globes protruding slightly beyond the orbital rim.' MOVEMENT — 'keep your head still and follow my finger with your eyes only — tell me if you see double or if it hurts. [H-pattern] Full movements, no ophthalmoplegia, no diplopia.' LID LAG — 'I'm bringing my finger down slowly from above; keep watching it. [pen above eye level, midline, lowered slowly] There is LID LAG bilaterally — the upper lid falls more slowly than the globe and upper sclera is transiently exposed.'

The neck IN FULL despite the obvious diagnosis, then chest and shins: 'the key points: the gland is diffusely and symmetrically enlarged, roughly twice normal size; lower border palpable; smooth and firm without discrete nodules; not tender; moves with swallowing. There is a palpable THRILL over both lobes and on auscultation a systolic BRUIT — a hypervascular gland. No lymphadenopathy, trachea central, percussion resonant, Pemberton's negative.' Then 'no gynaecomastia; heart sounds dual with no systolic flow murmur. Could I look at your shins? No pretibial myxoedema and no peripheral oedema. To complete I'd take a full set of observations including blood pressure, record the weight, and perform a full cardiovascular examination.'

The 45-second summary, committing to Graves' with reasons, plus the plan (see dx). Examiner: 'why Graves' rather than a toxic multinodular goitre?' → THREE reasons: the gland is diffuse and symmetrical rather than nodular; it is hypervascular with a thrill and a bruit; and there is orbitopathy, which occurs in Graves' and not in a toxic MNG — confirmed with TSH-receptor antibodies.

Explain in plain English: the thyroid as the accelerator pedal stuck too far down; Graves' disease as an autoimmune antibody that switches the gland on and won't let it switch off — common, very treatable, nobody's fault, and the cause of the eye changes. Three parts to treatment: a beta-blocker now for the racing heart and shakes (better within days), a tablet to turn the gland down, and later a permanent fix — radioiodine or surgery — which he does not decide today. Bloods for blood count and liver before the second tablet.

THE SAFETY COUNSELLING, said out loud: 'The tablet for the gland is called carbimazole. It works well, but it has one rare and serious side effect: in about one person in three hundred it can drop the white cells that fight infection. So this is the rule, and it matters more than anything else I've said today — if you develop a SORE THROAT, MOUTH ULCERS, A FEVER, or you just feel unwell and fluey, STOP THE TABLETS AND GET A BLOOD TEST THE SAME DAY. Don't wait to see if it settles. Ring the practice, or go to the hospital after hours. Can you tell me back what you'd do if you woke up with a sore throat?' Then smoking cessation offered, and review in four weeks.

ask: 'Examiner, I'm going to perform an examination for thyrotoxicosis.' / 'I'll need your arms, neck and shins uncovered.' / 'Anxious and restless, with visible sweating of the face.' / 'No onycholysis, no thyroid acropachy' — then FEEL the palms. / 'The paper is oscillating — there is a fine tremor.' / 'Pulse approximately 105, regular, wide pulse pressure.'

'Shoulder abduction 5 out of 5 bilaterally — no proximal myopathy.' / 'The biceps jerk is brisk — hyperreflexia.' / 'From the front... from above... on movement... and on downgaze.' / 'A palpable thrill over both lobes and a systolic bruit — a hypervascular gland.'

'Sore throat, mouth ulcers or fever — stop the tablets and get a blood test the same day.' / 'Can you tell me back what you'd do if you woke up with a sore throat?' / 'Smoking is the single biggest thing that makes the eye changes worse.'

Variant 1 — TOXIC MULTINODULAR GOITRE: 'the pulse is approximately 130 and IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR — this is atrial fibrillation... there are NO eye signs: no lid retraction, no proptosis, no lid lag... the gland is asymmetrically enlarged with multiple discrete nodules, non-tender, mobile on swallowing; there is no thrill and no bruit.' → 'thyrotoxicosis due to a toxic multinodular goitre rather than Graves' — nodular rather than diffuse, no bruit, no eye signs. I'd confirm with a radionuclide uptake scan showing patchy uptake. The AF changes my plan: rate control, stroke-risk assessment and anticoagulation, and radioiodine is usually the definitive treatment of choice.'

Variant 2 — SUBACUTE (de Quervain) THYROIDITIS: 'is that painful? Examiner, the gland is diffusely enlarged and exquisitely TENDER, with no thrill, no bruit and no eye signs. With a preceding viral illness this is subacute thyroiditis. The thyrotoxicosis is DESTRUCTIVE — stored hormone leaking out, so uptake is LOW not high, and inflammatory markers are raised. Critically a thionamide would not help, because the gland is not overproducing: simple analgesia and NSAIDs, a beta-blocker for symptoms, steroids for severe pain, and warn him to expect a hypothyroid phase before recovery' VERIFY. / Variant 3 — SIGHT-THREATENING ORBITOPATHY: marked proptosis with chemosis and injection, restricted upgaze with diplopia, and colours 'washed out' → 'loss of colour vision raises compressive optic neuropathy. I would check visual acuity and colour vision formally, look for a relative afferent pupillary defect, and make a SAME-DAY ophthalmology referral. High-dose corticosteroids after specialist discussion, and radioiodine is contraindicated while the eye disease is active. Smoking cessation is the single most important modifiable factor.'
pefe: Role-player: Daniel Okafor, 42, grain handler at the port, lives outside Kadina with his wife and two teenagers; ten cigarettes a day (mentioned only if asked), six or seven beers a week, no medications or allergies, 'my sister's always had something with her thyroid'. Six weeks of exhaustion while unable to sit still, racing heart, shaky hands noticed pouring tea, 4 kg weight loss while eating more, constant sweating and heat intolerance, gritty eyes and 'startled' in photographs, broken sleep, looser bowels three or four times a day. Restless and slightly wired, talks fast, fidgets, mildly irritable. Real fear — cancer, or an operation on his neck — voiced only if concerns are invited. WITHHOLDS unless asked: the smoking, the gritty eyes, the looser bowels, the 4 kg, his sister's thyroid. If the shins are never asked for, he does not offer — and marks it down. If a drug is named with no warning he pushes once: 'are there any side effects I should know about?' — and if still nothing is given, that is an automatic fail on safe prescribing.

Numbers: FOUR eye manoeuvres (front, from above, H-pattern, lid lag on downgaze). ONE reflex — the biceps jerk. Three P's and an R: Pemberton's, Proximal myopathy, Pretibial myxoedema, Reflexes. THREE Graves'-only signs: orbitopathy, acropachy, pretibial myxoedema. Agranulocytosis risk about 1 in 300 on carbimazole VERIFY. High uptake means overproduction; low uptake means a leak or exogenous hormone. Baselines before a thionamide: FBC, LFTs, pregnancy test. First trimester means propylthiouracil, not carbimazole VERIFY. Clock: eyes 2:30, neck 3:20, stop examining 4:50, reporting done 5:40.

Scored domains: approach (full WIPE, NAMED the examination as thyrotoxicosis rather than drifting into a tremor or neurological examination, asked for arms, neck and shins, consent at each stage, chaperone offered); technique (specific general-appearance comment including facial sweating, nails and fingers, FELT the palms, outstretched hands then paper, pulse rate AND rhythm, proximal myopathy against resistance, a reflex actually elicited, eyes examined four ways, complete thyroid examination including percussion, auscultation and Pemberton's, gynaecomastia and heart sounds, shins exposed); accuracy (lid retraction and lid lag distinguished correctly, reflex direction correct, no movement sign reported from a still face); diagnosis (committed to Graves' with at least three reasons, differentials with reasons for rejection, TRAb, ECG, FBC and LFTs); management (three-tier plan, beta-blocker, thionamide WITH the agranulocytosis rule, teach-back sought, pregnancy and contraception asked in a woman of childbearing age, smoking raised, follow-up arranged).
fails: ★ Naming carbimazole or propylthiouracil without the agranulocytosis rule in the same breath — an otherwise excellent plan is scored as unsafe prescribing; and no teach-back
★ Drifting into a tremor or upper-limb neurological examination because the stem said 'nervousness and tremor'
Reporting 'no lid lag' from a motionless face — retraction is an inspection sign, lag is a movement sign and needs the eye taken downwards

Never asking for the shins in the WIPE, which makes pretibial myxoedema unreportable; skipping the paper for the fine tremor; looking at the palms instead of feeling them; leaving the hammer on the trolley
Abandoning the neck because the diagnosis is obvious — percussion, auscultation and Pemberton's are marked in full whatever you have already worked out

FAIL — The four errors in the hands-and-pulse block: saying 'the patient looks unwell' instead of naming the visible FACIAL SWEATING; skipping the sheet of paper, which sits on the trolley precisely because a fine tremor is often invisible on the hands alone ('the paper is oscillating — there is a fine tremor'); LOOKING at the palms rather than feeling them with your own hand; and silently timing the pulse for thirty seconds instead of estimating the rate and stating the RHYTHM, which is the marked finding — and the hammer must leave the trolley, because 'I would also check the reflexes' earns nothing: elicit ONE, the biceps, and get the direction right (hyper → brisk, hypo → slow-relaxing)

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice in February, a warm room, and she is in a jacket, cardigan and scarf. The EXPOSURE CONVERSATION is the discriminating issue and the highest-weighted item: ask HER, inside the WIPE, with a reason, offering privacy and a chaperone, and let her uncover herself. The clothing is itself a clinical sign. The best peripheral sign is the DELAYED RELAXATION of the reflex, which you only see if you keep watching the limb. Automatic fails: examining through the scarf; asking the examiner for exposure instead of the patient; reaching for her clothing; dropping auscultation of the neck; describing her as 'sluggish', 'slow' or 'obese' in her hearing.

T 36.2 — HR 52 regular — BP 132/86 — RR 14 — SpO2 98% RA. She is wearing a jacket, a cardigan and a scarf.

I know it's not the warmest room. I can pull the curtain across, and I'm very happy to have a chaperone in with us' · if she hesitates, give a REASON, ask 'what would make this easier for you?', offer privacy, a chaperone or a female colleague; never reach, never repeat it louder · GENERAL APPEARANCE naming the CLOTHING as a sign, plus slow speech and a deep hoarse voice, dry coarse skin, dry thinning hair (never 'sluggish', 'slow' or 'obese' in her hearing) · HANDS: puffy oedematous fingers, peripheral cyanosis, PALE PALMAR CREASES, and FEEL them (cold and dry) · PULSE ~52 regular, low volume · PROXIMAL MYOPATHY against resistance + ask about chairs and stairs · THE REFLEX by 2:30: strike the biceps tendon and KEEP WATCHING THE LIMB FOR A FULL SECOND → delayed relaxation, the Woltman sign · THE FACE close up, deliberately at the LATERAL END of each eyebrow: loss of the outer third (sign of Hertoghe), periorbital oedema, malar flush, no xanthelasma, tongue not enlarged, full eye movements · NECK at 3:15: INSPECT FOR A THYROIDECTOMY SCAR BEFORE PALPATING, then the full sequence including percussion, auscultation and Pemberton's · HEART AND LUNGS for a pericardial or pleural effusion · ANKLES pressed over the tibia: non-pitting · stop examining 4:50, reporting done 5:40.

back.dx: Overt primary hypothyroidism, most likely HASHIMOTO THYROIDITIS given the family history and the firm rubbery goitre: clothing inappropriate for the weather (cold intolerance), slow speech and a deep hoarse voice, puffy fingers with peripheral cyanosis, cold dry palms, pale palmar creases, bradycardia ~52, a biceps jerk with a markedly delayed relaxation phase (Woltman sign), loss of the outer third of both eyebrows (sign of Hertoghe) with periorbital oedema and dry coarse skin, a firm rubbery lumpy goitre moving on swallowing, and non-pitting ankle oedema. Negatives: no thyroidectomy scar, no proximal myopathy, no xanthelasma, no macroglossia, no lymphadenopathy, central trachea, resonant percussion, no bruit, negative Pemberton's, normal-intensity heart sounds and clear bases — no clinical evidence of pericardial or pleural effusion. Differentials: a drug cause (amiodarone, lithium); post-ablative hypothyroidism, less likely with no scar; and a secondary pituitary cause had the TSH been low rather than high. Plan: TPO antibodies, FBC, lipids, sodium and an ECG, then LEVOTHYROXINE with a repeat TSH at 6-8 weeks; check for angina before starting and start low and go slow in the elderly or in ischaemic heart disease; if acutely unwell, exclude adrenal insufficiency and give hydrocortisone BEFORE thyroxine.
plan: WIPE with the exposure conversation inside it: name every part of the examination, then 'to do that properly I do need to see your neck, your arms and your lower legs — so I'll have to ask you to take the scarf and the jacket off for a few minutes. I know it's not the warmest room. I can pull the curtain across, and I'm very happy to have a chaperone in with us. Would that be all right?' → 'Do I have to? I'm freezing in here.' → give a reason, do not repeat it louder: 'I understand, and that's actually useful for me to know. Can I explain why I'm asking? The gland sits right at the front of the neck and I have to see it and feel it — through fabric I'd miss things that matter. I'll be quick, and you can put everything straight back on. Shall I turn the heater up first?' Let her uncover herself.

General appearance and hands: 'the patient is alert and orientated. She is dressed in a jacket, cardigan and scarf, which is NOT APPROPRIATE FOR THE WEATHER today — this suggests cold intolerance. Her speech is slow in rate and her voice is deep and slightly hoarse. She appears to have gained weight, the skin is dry and coarse and the hair is dry and thinning... the fingers are puffy and slightly oedematous with peripheral cyanosis of the nail beds; the palmar creases are pale, which may indicate anaemia; and the palms are COLD AND DRY [felt, not looked at]. The pulse is approximately 50 to 55, regular, of low volume — a bradycardia.'

Proximal myopathy, then THE REFLEX: 'hold your arms out to the sides like wings and stop me pushing them down — shoulder abduction is 5 out of 5 bilaterally, no proximal myopathy. I'd also ask about difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs. Now let your arm go completely floppy for me.' Strike the biceps tendon and KEEP WATCHING: 'Examiner, the biceps jerk contracts normally but there is a MARKEDLY DELAYED RELAXATION PHASE — the arm returns slowly. This is hyporeflexia in the hypothyroid pattern, the Woltman sign, and it is the single most useful peripheral sign in this examination.'

THE FACE, stepped in close and looking deliberately at the LATERAL END of each eyebrow: 'there is loss of the outer third of both eyebrows — the sign of Hertoghe — with periorbital oedema, dry coarse skin and a malar flush, and dry brittle hair with diffuse thinning. No xanthelasma; the tongue is not enlarged. Follow my finger with your eyes only — eye movements are full with no ophthalmoplegia.' (In the 2017 recall the eyebrow sign was simulated with skin-toned tape; candidates who glanced from a metre away reported 'no abnormality' and lost the diagnosis.)

The neck, INSPECTED BEFORE PALPATED: 'on inspection there is NO THYROIDECTOMY SCAR. The key points: the gland is moderately and symmetrically enlarged; lower border palpable; the consistency is FIRM, RUBBERY AND LUMPY, which fits Hashimoto thyroiditis; not tender; moves with swallowing. No thrills, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, trachea central, percussion resonant, NO BRUIT on auscultation, Pemberton's negative.'

Chest and legs: 'heart sounds are dual and of normal intensity — I was listening for muffled or distant sounds suggesting a pericardial effusion; the chest is clear with good air entry to both bases, listening for reduced breath sounds from a pleural effusion. Could I look at your ankles? [presses over the tibia] Mild NON-PITTING ankle swelling — myxoedema, not fluid overload. To complete, I'd take a full set of observations including temperature, weight and BMI, and check the ankle jerk for the delayed relaxation phase.'

The 45-second summary committing to overt primary hypothyroidism, likely Hashimoto's, with the differentials and plan (see dx). Examiner: 'if you could order one blood test, what would it be?' → 'TSH. A raised TSH with a low free T4 confirms overt primary hypothyroidism. TSH tells me which direction the gland is going; the free T4 tells me how far.'

Explain, and address the self-blame directly: 'you can put your jacket back on... your thyroid works like the thermostat and the accelerator for your body. Yours is underactive — that is why you're tired, why you're cold when everyone else isn't, why your bowels have slowed, why the weight has gone on and why your thinking has felt foggy. I want to be clear about something. THAT IS NOT LAZINESS AND IT IS NOT IN YOUR HEAD. There is a real, measurable, physical reason for how you've been feeling, and it's one of the most treatable conditions we see.' Then Hashimoto's — the same condition her mum has, nobody's fault — and levothyroxine: first thing in the morning on an empty stomach, FOUR HOURS apart from iron, calcium or indigestion tablets; repeat TSH at 6-8 weeks, not sooner; report chest pain or a racing heart; tell you early about pregnancy or planning one, because the dose needs to go up. On the weight: some is fluid and will settle, the rest gets easier as energy returns — do not promise it all comes off.

Variant 1 — THE HEADSCARF STATION ('I'd rather keep this on, if that's all right'): 'Of course — thank you for telling me, and I want to do this in a way you're comfortable with. He is also on amiodarone, which independently causes hypothyroidism, so both may contribute; I would not stop it without cardiology input. Given his age and the bradycardia I'd start levothyroxine LOW and increase slowly, check for angina first, and recheck TSH at six to eight weeks' VERIFY. pefe: Role-player: Helen Marchetti, 40, council administrator in Wallaroo, husband and two primary-school children; non-smoker, occasional wine, no medications or allergies, no previous surgery; her MOTHER has Hashimoto's (only if asked). Four months of exhaustion sleep doesn't fix, cold all the time in February, bowels every third day, 6 kg on without changing anything, rings don't fit, skin so dry she's been through three tubs of moisturiser, husband says she sounds different on the phone, rereads the same email four times, eyebrows gone sparse which she put down to age, periods heavier. She speaks at a noticeably reduced rate with a deeper croaky voice and pauses before answering — flat, a little defeated, telling herself she is lazy and useless and half-expecting to be told nothing is wrong. Wears layers and keeps them on until asked; RESISTS ONCE ('do I have to? I'm freezing') then agrees if given a reason, privacy or a chaperone; if no reason is given she keeps them on and makes them ask again; if they examine through the fabric she lets them and marks them down; if they reach for her clothing she pulls back. After the tendon strike she lets the arm come back down slowly — count one-and-two before it settles. If the diagnosis is delivered coldly she pushes once: 'so there really is something wrong with me? Everyone's been telling me I'm just busy.'

Numbers: FOUR signs you must not miss — the clothing, the eyebrows, the bradycardia, the delayed relaxation. TWO named signs — Hertoghe (eyebrows) and Woltman (delayed relaxation). ONE reflex, the biceps jerk, watched for a full second. Repeat TSH at 6-8 weeks VERIFY. FOUR hours between levothyroxine and iron, calcium or a PPI VERIFY. Start low and go slow in the elderly and in ischaemic heart disease. Hydrocortisone before thyroxine if adrenal insufficiency is possible. TSH tells you which way, free T4 tells you how far. setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice. The framework station for every MSK case, run on a chronic knee. Look, feel, move, SPECIAL TESTS — and the special tests are where candidates fail: if you are still palpating at 3:45, stop and move to them, because nothing else recovers those marks. Palpate with ONE hand, structure by structure, or the 'ow' cannot be localised and the finding is lost. STOP EXAMINING AT SIX MINUTES — the last two minutes are protected for the diagnosis and differentials. Automatic fails: no special tests performed; examining the normal knee first and running out of time; hurting the patient without warning or apology; treating a hot swollen joint as osteoarthritis; giving no diagnosis.
stem: General practice clinical skills station. Mr Peter Nolan, 50, has had pain in his left knee for eight months, worse after walking and after standing at work, eased by rest. No injury. Otherwise well. 8 minutes; no history required.
tasks: Perform a focused examination of the affected knee, giving a running commentary to the examiner
Ask the examiner for any finding you are unable to elicit
State your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 0:00-0:45 WIPE, consent, EXPOSE both knees and thighs, position on the couch, and ask about pain and a spot to avoid · 0:45-1:45 INSPECTION with NAMED findings (one generic sweep, then genu varum/valgum, fixed flexion deformity, quadriceps and vastus medialis wasting, popliteal swelling, effusion) then GAIT: antalgic, no Trendelenburg lurch · 1:45-3:15 PALPATION, four steps, ONE HAND: (1) temperature with the back of the hand above, over and below both knees, (2) capillary refill in both great toenails, (3) popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses both sides, (4) tenderness on the affected side only · quadriceps tendon, patella and borders, patellar tendon, tibial tuberosity, then flex to 90 degrees to open the joint lines: medial joint line TENDER, lateral joint line, collaterals, popliteal fossa · 3:15-3:45 ACTIVE movement with power, and SAY WHY you are omitting passive · 3:45-5:45 THE EIGHT SPECIAL TESTS, named, in order: patellar tap, bulge/sweep, anterior drawer at 90, Lachman at 30, posterior drawer with sag, valgus stress at 0 and 30, varus stress at 0 and 30, McMurray · 5:45-6:00 close, cover the patient, and ASK THE EXAMINER for observations, temperature and BMI · 6:00-8:00 diagnosis with reasons, then differentials EACH WITH THE REASON IT IS LESS LIKELY, then the plan.

back.dx: Osteoarthritis of the left knee — a 50-year-old with eight months of activity-related pain relieved by rest and no trauma; a varus deformity with vastus medialis wasting; medial joint-line tenderness with crepitus and flexion limited to 110 degrees; a COOL joint with no effusion, which argues against inflammation or infection; and a BMI of 32 as a strong risk factor. Differentials, each with the reason against: degenerate meniscal tear — McMurray negative, no locking, no effusion; inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid — monoarticular, brief morning stiffness, no warmth or synovial swelling; crystal arthropathy — no abrupt recurrent attacks; referred hip pain — normal hip examination; septic arthritis SPECIFICALLY EXCLUDED — afebrile, cool joint, preserved movement. Management: knee OA is a CLINICAL diagnosis — education, a supervised quadriceps strengthening programme, weight management and a topical NSAID, with a weight-bearing X-ray reserved for an atypical course; review at 4-6 weeks; safety-net to return urgently if the knee becomes hot, swollen or he becomes febrile.
plan: 'I've been asked to examine your left knee — I'll look, feel, ask you to move it, and then do some specific tests. I'll need you to roll your shorts up so I can see both knees and your thighs, and I'd like you to lie on the couch. Is that all right? Before I start, are you in any pain at the moment, and is there a particular spot I should be careful of?' → 'It's a bit sore on the inside of the knee, go easy there.' (You cannot see a varus deformity or wasting through clothing, and you cannot do Lachman on a seated patient.)

Inspection with NAMED findings, then gait: 'on general inspection he is comfortable at rest with no walking aid. From the front, side and behind there is no redness, rash, bruising or scar. More specifically: a mild genu varum on the left; no fixed flexion deformity; wasting of vastus medialis compared with the right; no popliteal swelling; no obvious effusion. Mr Nolan, could you walk to the door, turn and come back? Examiner, his gait is antalgic with a shortened stance phase on the left; there is no Trendelenburg lurch.'

PALPATION, four steps, ONE HAND: 'Tell me if anything is tender. One, temperature — the back of my hand above, over and below both knees: the left is not warm. Two, capillary refill — both great toenails, under two seconds. Three, pulses — popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis, both sides together: present and symmetrical. Four, tenderness, left knee only, supporting the leg with one hand and palpating with the other: quadriceps tendon, patella and borders, patellar tendon, tibial tuberosity — not tender. Flexing to 90 degrees to open the joint lines: the MEDIAL JOINT LINE -' 'Ooh, that's the spot.' '- tender here. Lateral joint line, collaterals, popliteal fossa — not tender, no swelling.' (Temperature, refill and pulses are your protection against the septic joint and the claudicant — do not drop them because the case 'is musculoskeletal'.)

Movement, and the justified omission: 'bend your knee up as far as it goes... now straighten it fully... now push out against my hand, and pull in. Examiner, active flexion is limited to approximately 110 degrees with palpable crepitus; extension is full with no fixed flexion deformity; power is 5 out of 5 and symmetrical. As active movement is not restricted by pain I would not expect passive range to add further information, and I'm moving to my special tests.' (A stated, justified omission is defensible; a silent one looks like forgetting.)

THE EIGHT SPECIAL TESTS, each named with its purpose and result: '1 patellar tap for a large effusion — negative. 2 bulge or sweep test for a small effusion — negative. 3 anterior drawer for the anterior cruciate at 90 degrees — negative with a firm endpoint. 4 Lachman's, the more sensitive test for the ACL at 30 degrees — negative. 5 posterior drawer with the posterior sag sign for the PCL — negative. 6 valgus stress at 0 and 30 degrees for the medial collateral — no laxity, no pain. 7 varus stress at 0 and 30 for the lateral collateral — no laxity. 8 McMurray's for a meniscal tear, medial and lateral — negative, no click, no pain.' Keep going to eight even when you are already sure — the examiner is scoring your knee examination, not your recall memory.

Close and harvest the free findings: 'Thank you, that's the examination finished — you can cover up. Examiner, to complete I would examine the joint above and below — the hip and the ankle — and I would ask for his observations, his body mass index, and whether he is febrile.' → 'Afebrile, observations normal, BMI 32, hip and ankle normal.'

Diagnosis with SIX reasons, then four differentials each with the reason against, then the plan and safety-net (see dx). If pushed: 'why didn't you examine the other knee?' → 'I compared both sides throughout inspection, temperature, capillary refill and pulses. The stem specified the left knee, so I confined tenderness, movement and the special tests to the affected side in order to complete them within the time.' To the patient: 'the smooth cushioning surface inside your knee has worn thinner, so the bones don't glide as easily. It's wear and tear, not the kind of arthritis that spreads through the body. Strengthening the muscles around the knee works better than any tablet I can give you.'

More specifically, I'm looking for...' / 'There is a mild genu varum on the left with wasting of vastus medialis.' / 'Could you walk to the door and back for me? — His gait is antalgic.'

'Palpation, four steps: temperature, capillary refill, pulses, then tenderness.' / 'I'm supporting the leg with one hand and palpating with the other — the quadriceps tendon, the patella, the patellar tendon, the tibial tuberosity...' / 'There is tenderness over the medial joint line.' / 'As active movement is full and pain-free I would not expect passive range to add information, so I'm moving to my special tests.' / 'Lachman's test for the anterior cruciate — negative' (name every test this way).

'Examiner, may I have his observations, his temperature and his BMI?' / 'My most likely diagnosis is osteoarthritis of the left knee, and my reasons are...' / 'My differentials are X — less likely because...' — the REASON is the mark, not the name. Do not hedge, do not run into the buzzer, and do not offer an X-ray as the answer: knee osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis.

Variant 1 — THE HOT KNEE: two days of pain, warm and tense. At step one of palpation: 'the left knee is warm compared with the right and there is a tense effusion. Before I go further — may I have his temperature and observations?' → 38.6, HR 108 → 'this is a hot, swollen, febrile joint and my primary concern is SEPTIC ARTHRITIS. I would limit my examination to avoid causing harm, keep him nil by mouth, take blood cultures, FBE and CRP, and arrange urgent joint aspiration BEFORE antibiotics with urgent orthopaedic review; in regional SA I would discuss transfer with the receiving orthopaedic unit and contact MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval were needed.' Continuing through eight ligament tests on a septic knee is an automatic fail.

Variant 2 — THE WRIST THAT WILL NOT MOVE (24, FOOSH): 'I won't force it and I won't move it for you. Examiner, the patient is unable to perform active movement because of pain, and I would not attempt passive movement in a suspected fracture as it risks harm and would not change my diagnosis. On palpation there is tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox with pain on axial compression of the thumb. My working diagnosis is a scaphoid fracture — thumb-spica splint, scaphoid-view X-rays, and because up to a quarter are not visible initially, re-image at 10-14 days or proceed to MRI, given the risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.' / Variant 3 — THE LEG THAT IS NOT MUSCULOSKELETAL (68, calf pain walking, worse uphill, relieved by rest): open by naming the system — a peripheral vascular examination; absent pedal pulses, refill 4 s, shiny hairless skin, positive Buerger's at 25 degrees with reactive hyperaemia; ABI and arterial duplex. Running a knee examination here fails the station — the stem told you the system. / Variant 4 — THE FOOT WITH TWO DIAGNOSES (45, heel pain worst on the first steps): point tenderness at the medial calcaneal tuberosity with a positive windlass test = plantar fasciitis — then KEEP GOING: Achilles palpation 2-6 cm above the insertion, Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze, and Mulder's click in the third intermetatarsal space = a coexisting Morton's neuroma. / Variant 5 — THE STEM THAT NAMES BOTH SIDES (62F, both hands): the only pattern where examining both sides in full is correct — Heberden's at the DIPs and Bouchard's at the PIPs, squaring of both thumb bases, and NO ulnar deviation or MCP synovial swelling, which argues for osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid; then grip, pinch and a button.
pefe: Role-player: Peter Nolan, 50, diesel and farm-machinery mechanic in the Riverland, on his feet on concrete all day; ex-smoker (15 pack-years, stopped 12 years ago), six to eight beers on the weekend, no regular exercise, BMI 32 crept up over ten years. Ramipril, plus supermarket ibuprofen 'a few days a week' — only mentioned if asked directly about medications. Twisted the same knee playing football at 22, no surgery. Mother had bad hand arthritis and a knee replacement. Stoic, understates pain, gruff, warms up if treated kindly. HIDDEN AGENDA: frightened of needing a knee replacement and months off work with the mortgage unpaid — given only if asked about concerns, otherwise once at the end: 'Doc — am I going to need a new knee? I can't afford to be off work.' He reacts ONLY at the medial joint line; if palpated with two hands he still says 'ow' but, asked where, says 'somewhere in there, I'm not sure' — make them work for it. Bends to about two-thirds and mentions the grinding. Every ligament and meniscal test is painless.

Numbers: 8-minute station, special tests start by 3:45, last 2:00 protected for diagnosis and differentials. EIGHT knee special tests. Capillary refill under 2 s. Lachman at 30 degrees, anterior drawer at 90, collateral stress at 0 and 30. This patient: flexion 110 degrees, BMI 32, eight months of symptoms, morning stiffness 10-15 minutes. Morning stiffness under 30 minutes = osteoarthritis; over 60 minutes = inflammatory. OTTAWA KNEE RULES: age 55 or over, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, cannot flex to 90, cannot take four steps. Doses VERIFY: diclofenac 1% gel 2-4 g QID, ibuprofen 200-400 mg TDS, celecoxib 100-200 mg daily, paracetamol max 4 g/24 h, intra-articular methylprednisolone 40 mg. Weight loss of 5-10% is clinically meaningful. Review 4-6 weeks after starting exercise therapy.

The consultation map to memorise: WIPE and consent → expose and position → ask about pain → LOOK with named findings → gait → FEEL: temperature, refill, pulses, tenderness → MOVE: active plus power → SPECIAL TESTS, all eight, named → thank and cover → ask the examiner for what you could not elicit → DIAGNOSIS with reasons → DIFFERENTIALS each excluded → plan and safety-net.
