must: FAIL — No special tests performed, running out of time before them, or stopping once you have found a positive — all single-item fails; announce each of the EIGHT by name with its result and keep going even when you are already sure, because the examiner is scoring your knee examination and not your recall: patellar tap (large effusion), bulge or sweep test (small effusion), anterior drawer at 90° (ACL), LACHMAN at 30° — more sensitive for the ACL, posterior drawer with the sag sign (PCL), valgus stress at 0° and 30° (MCL), varus stress at 0° and 30° (LCL), and McMurray medially and laterally; if you are still palpating at 3:45, stop and move on, because nothing else recovers those marks (★)

FAIL — Palpating with two hands, so the tender point cannot be localised and the commentary collapses — the role-player still says 'ow' but answers 'somewhere in there, I'm not sure' when you ask where; support the leg with one hand and palpate with the other, naming each structure aloud (quadriceps tendon, patella and its borders, patellar tendon, tibial tuberosity, then flex to 90° to open the joint lines — medial, lateral, both collaterals, popliteal fossa), and leave the sore medial line to last

FAIL — Dropping temperature, capillary refill and pulses because the case 'is musculoskeletal' — those three steps are what exclude the SEPTIC joint and the claudicant, and stating the negatives out loud is what shows you excluded them rather than forgot them; a hot, tense, febrile knee treated as osteoarthritis is an automatic fail, and so is continuing through eight ligament tests on a septic joint — stop at step one of palpation: 'the left knee is warm compared with the right and there is a tense effusion; before I go further, may I have his temperature and observations?' → nil by mouth, blood cultures, FBE and CRP, urgent joint aspiration BEFORE antibiotics, urgent orthopaedic review, and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval is needed (★)

FAIL — Examining over trousers or with the patient still in a chair — you cannot see a varus deformity or wasting through clothing, and you cannot perform Lachman's on a seated patient, so expose both knees and thighs and reposition before you touch; ask about pain first ('is there a particular spot I should be careful of?'), and never hurt him without warning or apology

DO — Earn the inspection marks with NAMED findings rather than a recited list — say the sweep once in a single sentence, then 'a mild GENU VARUM on the left, wasting of VASTUS MEDIALIS compared with the right, no fixed flexion deformity, no popliteal swelling'; do not skip gait because he is already lying down, because it costs fifteen seconds and it is scored ('antalgic, with a shortened stance phase on the left, no Trendelenburg lurch'); report the range with the finding ('active flexion limited to about 110 degrees with palpable CREPITUS, extension full, power 5 out of 5'), and justify omitting passive movement ALOUD rather than silently, because a stated omission is defensible and a silent one looks like forgetting

SAY — Stop examining at 6:00, ask the examiner for what you could not elicit, then COMMIT with reasons: 'may I have his observations, his temperature and his BMI?' — handed to you free, and they carry your exclusion of sepsis — then 'my most likely diagnosis is OSTEOARTHRITIS of the left knee, because he is 50 with eight months of activity-related pain relieved by rest and no trauma; because there is a varus deformity with vastus medialis wasting; because there is medial joint-line tenderness with crepitus and flexion limited to 110 degrees; because the joint is cool with no effusion, which argues against inflammation or infection; and because a BMI of 32 is a strong risk factor'; every differential needs the REASON AGAINST, because the reason is the mark and not the name — degenerate meniscal tear (negative McMurray, no locking, no effusion), inflammatory arthritis (monoarticular, morning stiffness 10–15 minutes rather than over 60, no warmth or synovial swelling), crystal arthropathy (no abrupt recurrent attacks), referred hip pain (normal hip examination), and septic arthritis specifically excluded; never hedge, and never offer an X-ray as the answer, because knee osteoarthritis is a CLINICAL diagnosis — education, supervised quadriceps strengthening, weight management (5–10% loss is clinically meaningful) and a topical NSAID, with a weight-bearing film reserved for an atypical course; elicit the hidden agenda about needing a new knee and time off work, and safety-net to return urgently if the knee becomes hot or swollen or he becomes febrile

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, acute twisted knee. Scored on the ACCURACY OF THE SPECIAL TESTS, not the diagnosis. She lies with TWO PILLOWS under the knee — leave them there; removing them takes away the positive finding and hurts her. Gloves from the door and no hand basin, so do not announce hand washing. Three starred items, each a fail on its own: comparing MOVEMENT with the normal side; ONE scream on McMurray with the leg lowered gently back to where it started; and differentials given with reasons plus a safety-net. Prompt bell at six minutes ends the examination.
stem: General practice. Samantha Reid, 40, with left knee pain: called from behind, turned around suddenly and twisted the knee two days ago. In shorts, semi-recumbent at 45 degrees with two pillows under the left knee, visibly in pain. Gloves are worn from the door.
tasks: Perform the relevant physical examination, giving a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 0:00-0:50 introduce, explain look/feel/move/special tests, promise to name each position, consent · and DO NOT announce hand washing or offer analgesia · general appearance: in pain and distress, protective posture, two pillows, no walking aids · 0:50-1:40 'are you able to stand up for me?' → 'ABLE TO BEAR WEIGHT' → TWO STEPS ONLY, then stop her → ANTALGIC gait (the only gait to name in a knee case) → inspection in THREE VIEWS while she stands, moving yourself: front (genu varum/valgum, supra- and infra-patellar pouches), side (FLEXION DEFORMITY, no hyperextension), back (popliteal fossa for a Baker's cyst), then the generic sweep · 1:40-3:05 lie her back leaving the pillows, note 'unable to fully extend', then palpation: temperature at three levels both sides, capillary refill, posterior tibial pulse (do not hunt for the popliteal), then SEVEN TENDERNESS STOPS with ONE hand · quadriceps, patella, MEDIAL JOINT LINE (ow), lateral joint line, patellar tendon, tibial tuberosity, fibular head, and reaching behind to the popliteal fossa · 3:05-3:35 active movement with a hand on the joint for crepitus, then THE CRITICAL ITEM: 'could you bend and straighten the OTHER knee for me?' · then signpost the omission of passive movement · 3:35-5:45 special tests: anterior and posterior drawer with the foot stabilised, varus and valgus at 15 degrees, then McMurray WITH A WARNING (expect 'not Apley's · do a different meniscal test'), ONE scream, lower the leg gently to where it started, then patellar tendon test, Clarke's, patellar tap, apprehension, sweep test · close before the bell.

back.dx: Medial meniscal tear — a twisting injury on a loaded leg with delayed (6-24 h) swelling, medial joint-line tenderness, a flexion deformity with inability to fully extend, catching or locking, and a positive McMurray, with all four ligaments stable. To the patient in plain words: two small C-shaped pieces of cartilage sit inside the knee as shock absorbers; turning suddenly with weight on that leg has most likely torn one, which is why it hurts along the inside line and why the knee will not fully straighten. Common and not dangerous — many settle with pain relief and physiotherapy over a few weeks, but because she cannot fully extend, a scan and an orthopaedic opinion are warranted; some tears do better with a small arthroscopic operation. Differentials EACH WITH A REASON: ligament tear — all four tested and stable; tibial plateau fracture — she could weight-bear, but still X-ray; osteoarthritis — builds over months rather than one twist and there was no crepitus; septic arthritis — not hot or red, no fever. Safety-net: come straight back or go to ED if the knee locks completely, becomes hot and swollen, she develops a fever, or the foot goes numb or cold.
plan: Gloves on as you walk in (do NOT say you would wash your hands — it reads as a memorised script): 'Hello Samantha, I'm Dr -. I've been asked to examine your knee today. I'll be looking at your knees, gently feeling them, asking you to do a few movements and take a couple of steps for me, and I'll finish with some special tests. I'll tell you the position I need at every step. Is that all right?' → 'Okay, but please be careful, it's really sore.' → 'Some of it may be uncomfortable, and I'll warn you before those parts. Tell me at any point and I'll stop.' Then: 'Examiner, on general appearance my patient is in pain and distress, with a protective posture. I can see two pillows supporting the left knee, and no walking aids.'

Weight-bearing, gait, three-view inspection: 'Samantha, are you able to stand up for me? Take your time... now just take two steps for me... that's enough, thank you.' → 'Examiner, my patient is ABLE TO BEAR WEIGHT. On walking I can see an antalgic gait.' Then walk around her: 'from the front I cannot see genu varum or genu valgum, and the supra- and infra-patellar pouches look normal with no obliteration. From the side, I can see a FLEXION DEFORMITY of the left knee; no hyperextension. From the back, looking at the popliteal fossa, there is no swelling suggestive of a Baker's cyst. In addition there is no swelling, redness, rash, bruising, scarring or quadriceps wasting.' (If you do not stop her she will walk a slow lap of the room — two steps is a gait.)

Lie her back WITHOUT moving the pillows: 'leave the pillows exactly where they are. Examiner, lying down, my patient is unable to fully extend the left knee.' Then 'I'm going to feel around the knee now. I'll be gentle, and if anything hurts, tell me and I'll stop. Examiner: no local rise of temperature at three levels both sides; capillary refill normal in the toes; the posterior tibial pulse is present and normal in volume bilaterally.' (Do not hunt for the popliteal pulse — a normal distal pulse makes it redundant and it costs a minute.)

SEVEN tenderness stops, ONE hand: 'quadriceps — no tenderness. Patella — no tenderness. Medial joint line -' 'Ow!' '- I'm sorry Samantha, I'll be gentler. Examiner, there is tenderness over the medial joint line. Continuing: lateral joint line, patellar tendon, tibial tuberosity, fibular head, and now reaching behind to the popliteal fossa — no further tenderness and no palpable mass.' (Stops 5, 6 and 7 are where Osgood-Schlatter, fibular head and Baker's cyst findings live.)

Movement, and the CRITICAL item: 'I'm going to rest my hand on your knee. Can you copy my movement and bend the knee as far as is comfortable?... and try to straighten it.' → a few degrees only → 'That's fine, don't push it. Examiner, active movement is severely restricted and painful in both flexion and extension, and I could not appreciate any crepitus. Samantha, could you bend and straighten the OTHER knee for me?... Thank you. Examiner, movement on the unaffected right knee is full and pain free, which contrasts with a severely restricted and painful range on the left. I'm going to omit passive movement, because active range is already severely limited by pain and passive testing would not change my management.' (Failure to test the normal side and compare is listed as a CRITICAL ERROR — and it is two sentences.)

Special tests in priority order: 'Samantha, I'm going to place your foot flat on the bed and sit lightly on it just to hold the ankle steady — is that okay? Examiner, anterior and posterior drawer, testing the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, thumbs either side of the tibial tuberosity — no laxity in either direction. Varus and valgus stress at about fifteen degrees of flexion, testing the lateral and medial collateral ligaments — no laxity and no pain. Examiner, I'd like to do a meniscal test.' → 'Not Apley's. Do something else.' → 'Thank you — I'll do a McMurray.'

McMURRAY, warned first: 'Samantha, this next one may be uncomfortable. I'll go slowly and stop the moment you tell me to, but I do need to do it to work out what's been injured.' → she screams → 'I'm stopping now — I'm sorry, Samantha.' LOWER THE LEG GENTLY BACK TO WHERE IT STARTED (she could not extend it at the start; do not extend it now) → 'Examiner, that is a positive McMurray test.' ONE positive is positive — repeating it in the other two rotations is three screams of unnecessary pain, and 2025 onwards has been unforgiving about that.

Finish the battery, then close: 'patellar tendon test, pressing the superior pole to expose the tendon — no tenderness. Clarke's test for chondromalacia — negative. Patellar tap for a large effusion — no floating patella. Apprehension test — no discomfort. And the sweep test for a small effusion — no bulge. Thank you Samantha, you can cover up and get comfortable. Examiner, that completes my examination.'

After the bell — diagnosis in plain words, then differentials EACH with the clause that makes it less likely, then the safety-net (see dx). Expect 'do I need an operation?' and, if concerns are never invited, 'will I need surgery? I can't afford to be off work' at the very end.
back.planNote: the source's six-minute run to the prompt bell
ask: 'I'll tell you the position I need at each step of my examination.' / 'Examiner, my patient is able to bear weight.' / 'That's enough, thank you — just stand still for me.' / 'Examiner, I can see an antalgic gait.' / 'From the front, no genu varum or genu valgum, and no obliteration of the supra- and infra-patellar pouches.' / 'From the side, a flexion deformity; no hyperextension.' / 'From the back, no swelling suggestive of a Baker's cyst.'

'Lying down, my patient is unable to fully extend the knee.' / 'I'm going to feel around the knee now — tell me if anything hurts and I'll stop.' / 'Examiner, tenderness over the medial joint line.' / 'Samantha, could you bend and straighten the other knee for me?' / 'I'm going to sit lightly on your foot just to hold the ankle steady — is that okay?'

'This may be uncomfortable. I'll stop the moment you tell me to, but I do need it to work out what's been injured.' / 'Examiner, that is a positive McMurray test' — then lower the leg gently. Examiner challenges: 'why didn't you do passive movements?' → 'active range was already severely limited by pain, so passive testing would not have changed my assessment or management and would have caused avoidable pain; I would reassess passively once she has adequate analgesia.' / 'shouldn't you examine the normal side first?' → 'inspection, temperature, capillary refill and pulses were all done bilaterally, and I compared movement directly; I confined tenderness and special tests to the symptomatic side to complete them within the time.'

Version A — 50M, six months, no trauma: gait may be normal and several stress tests may be painful WITHOUT laxity → 'in a fifty-year-old with six months of pain I read these as a diffusely painful arthritic joint rather than multiple ligamentous injuries.' If everything is normal: 'a normal examination is a finding — it excludes an effusion, ligamentous laxity and a meniscal injury; my leading diagnosis remains osteoarthritis, which is clinical and may have a normal examination early.' Do not offer Osgood-Schlatter in an adult. / Version B — PATELLAR TENDINITIS: the only positive is tenderness at the inferior pole with the patellar tendon test — 'that's a positive finding, but I'm going to complete my remaining special tests to make sure I'm not missing a coexisting ligamentous, meniscal or effusive problem.'

Version C — CHONDROMALACIA / patellofemoral syndrome: younger patient, pain worse after prolonged sitting (the theatre sign), the only positive is Clarke's — 'grasping the patella, displacing it towards the feet, pressing it down onto the joint, and asking her to squeeze the thigh muscles... that reproduces her pain — a positive Clarke's test.' / Version D — 13M BASKETBALLER, BILATERAL: the only bilateral case — palpation and special tests on both knees, many skips, and consent involving a minor: 'Alex, is it all right with you if I examine your knees? Thank you. I'll just check your parents are happy as well before we go on' — then START, do not stand waiting. Tenderness at both tibial tuberosities = Osgood-Schlatter, and still complete the special tests. Examiner challenges: 'skip that one but tell me how you'd do it' (Apley's: prone, knee to 90, thigh stabilised with your own knee, distract-and-rotate for ligament pain, compress-and-rotate for meniscal pain); 'how many special tests were you planning?' (all eight in priority order); 'the patient is in a lot of pain — should you continue?' ('the tests necessary to make the diagnosis, yes, with warning and consent — I would not add passive movement or repeat a test that has already given a clear positive').
pefe: Role-player: Samantha Reid, 40, office worker in a regional town, social netball on Wednesdays, otherwise well, occasional paracetamol, no allergies, non-smoker, mother has knee osteoarthritis. Two days ago someone called her name in a car park; she turned quickly with weight on the left leg and felt the knee twist, with sharp pain and having to sit on the kerb. It swelled BY THAT EVENING, not immediately. It will not straighten properly and has caught or locked once or twice. In real pain but polite; anxious about surgery because she is self-employed — not volunteered unless concerns are invited, otherwise at the very end. She says 'ow' ONLY at the medial joint line, moves the knee a few degrees only, moves the right knee fully and painlessly, screams when McMurray begins — and screams A SECOND TIME if the leg is straightened past where it started. If the pillows are removed she winces: 'please leave them.' If hurt without warning: 'you're hurting me.'

Numbers: 6-minute prompt bell; introduction 30-45 s maximum; 3 inspection views; 4 palpation steps; 7 tenderness stops; 8 special tests; drawer at 90 degrees, varus/valgus at 10-15 degrees, Lachman at 20-30 degrees; ONE side examined for tenderness and special tests; ONE scream. Swelling in under 30 minutes = haemarthrosis, think ACL; 6-24 h slower swelling = reactive effusion, think meniscus. OTTAWA KNEE RULES — X-ray if any one: age 55 or over, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, unable to flex to 90, unable to weight-bear four steps both at the time and in the room.

The six moments that carried it: 'able to bear weight' before the gait, a sentence almost nobody says; two steps then stop, controlling the room; naming the same sign twice — flexion deformity standing, unable to fully extend lying (the second phrasing is the Medicare MRI wording for a meniscal tear); seven-stop one-handed palpation so the tenderness could be localised; movement on the normal side, the handbook's critical error avoided in two sentences; and one scream, not four. What would have sunk it: removing the pillows, arguing for Apley's after being refused, repeating McMurray in all three rotations, adding passive range to a knee that could barely move actively, examining the right knee fully 'for comparison', and still testing when the bell went with no diagnosis given. Pass = 18 or more of 24 with all three starred items.
Everything else — Normal
fails: ★ Removing the pillows 'to examine properly' — you have taken away the positive finding and hurt her
★ Failing to test movement on the NORMAL side and compare — listed as a critical error
Repeating McMurray in all three rotations, or panicking and straightening the leg past where it started — the second scream
The two-handed sweep, so the site of tenderness (which IS the diagnosis here) cannot be named; stopping palpation at the joint line and missing stops 5, 6 and 7

Announcing hand washing when you are already gloved; walking her a full lap; naming every gait you know instead of just antalgic; arguing for Apley's after being refused; listing differentials with no reasons
numbers: 6-min prompt bell · 3 inspection views · 4 palpation steps · 7 tenderness stops · 8 special tests · drawer 90 degrees, varus/valgus 10-15 degrees, Lachman 20-30 degrees · 1 side, 1 scream

Swelling <30 min = haemarthrosis (ACL); 6-24 h = reactive effusion (meniscus) · Ottawa knee: age >=55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, cannot flex to 90, cannot weight-bear 4 steps · inability to fully extend drives the scan and orthopaedic referral

findings: FLEXION DEFORMITY of the affected knee
POSITIVE — one scream, so do it once and do it last
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Removing the pillows 'to examine properly' — you have taken away the positive finding and hurt her; leave them exactly where they are, and name the same sign twice, standing and lying: 'from the side I can see a FLEXION DEFORMITY of the left knee', then 'lying down, my patient is UNABLE TO FULLY EXTEND the left knee' — the second phrasing is the Medicare MRI wording for a meniscal tear

FAIL — Failing to test movement on the NORMAL side and compare — listed as a critical error, and it takes two sentences: 'Samantha, could you bend and straighten the other knee for me? … Examiner, movement on the unaffected right knee is full and pain free, which contrasts with a severely restricted and painful range on the left'; but do NOT then run tenderness and special tests on the normal side too — the handbook asks for movement only, and doing the whole examination twice is how candidates run out of time (★)

FAIL — Repeating McMurray in all three rotations, or panicking and straightening the leg past where it started — the second scream; ONE positive is positive, three screams is not three-plus positive, and she could not extend the knee at the start so do not extend it now: warn first ('this next one may be uncomfortable; I'll go slowly and stop the moment you tell me to, but I do need it to work out what's been injured'), then at the scream 'I'm stopping now — I'm sorry', lower the leg gently back to exactly where it began, and say 'Examiner, that is a positive McMurray test'; if the examiner refuses Apley's, do not argue — have McMurray ready (★)

FAIL — Palpating with a two-handed sweep, so you cannot say where the pain was, when in this station the SITE of tenderness is the diagnosis; and stopping at the joint line, when stops 5, 6 and 7 are where the Osgood-Schlatter, fibular head and Baker's cyst findings live — all SEVEN stops named aloud with one hand: quadriceps, patella, medial joint line, lateral joint line, patellar tendon, tibial tuberosity, fibular head, then reaching behind to the popliteal fossa; apologise immediately at the 'ow' and carry on, and do not hunt for the popliteal pulse, which costs a minute and is redundant once the posterior tibial is normal

FAIL — Losing the clock in the first two minutes — she will walk a slow lap of a large room if you let her, so TWO STEPS and 'that's enough, thank you — just stand still there for a moment'; say 'able to bear weight' before you name the gait, and name only ANTALGIC, because listing every gait you know loses marks here; inspect standing in THREE views by walking around her yourself rather than describing the popliteal fossa without moving; lead with the named findings (genu varum or valgum, the supra- and infra-patellar pouches, the flexion deformity, a Baker's cyst) and add the generic swelling-redness-rash-bruising list at the END; don't announce hand washing when the examiner has just handed you gloves, and don't offer analgesia — she will say she is not in pain right now, it scores nothing, and the task is an examination

SAY — Give the diagnosis in plain words and every differential with the clause that makes it less likely, because the reason is what is scored: 'you've most likely torn one of the cartilages inside your knee — a meniscus; there are two of them, small C-shaped shock absorbers inside the joint, and when you turned suddenly with your weight on that leg one of them has most likely torn — that's why it's sore along the inside line, why the knee is sitting slightly bent, and why you can't fully straighten it'; then a torn LIGAMENT (all four tested, the knee was stable), a FRACTURE of the top of the shin (she could stand on it, but still X-ray — Ottawa knee rules: age 55 or over, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, unable to flex to 90°, unable to weight-bear four steps), ARTHRITIS (builds over months rather than one twist, no grating) and INFECTION (not hot, not red, no fever); scan and orthopaedic opinion because she cannot fully extend, analgesia, and keep moving gently rather than resting completely; safety net — the knee locking completely, becoming hot and swollen, fever, or the foot going numb or cold; and signpost the omission of passive movement rather than leaving it silent: 'active range is already severely limited by pain and passive testing would not change my management' (★)

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — rural ED, Wallaroo. Acute shoulder after a fall, so dislocation and fracture stay alive out loud until you exclude them: name the DELTOID CONTOUR and the absence of bony tenderness explicitly. She REFUSES to stand — ask once, accept, tell the examiner, continue seated; asking twice, offering analgesia to get her up or apologising for thirty seconds has cost more candidates this station than any clinical error. Ten named palpation landmarks or nothing. One test per condition — empty can, full can, drop arm, Apley scratch, apprehension — and attach the MEANING to every result.
stem: Rural Emergency Department, Wallaroo, South Australia. Jane Whitford, 40, right-hand dominant, right shoulder pain after a fall two hours ago. BP 128/76, HR 82, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.8. Seated on the couch, simple analgesia in triage. Gloves available. 8 minutes.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination of the shoulder, giving a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 0:00-0:45 WIPE, hard ceiling · say 'I've washed my hands' even though gloved, and SAY THE WORDS 'expose both shoulders' (exposure is a marked item and is invisible unless said); do not ask her to stand · 0:45-2:00 general appearance, then THREE-DIMENSIONAL inspection, physically MOVING: from the front (swelling, redness, bruising, asymmetry, LOSS OF DELTOID BULK OR CONTOUR, biceps tendon deformity), from the side (tip of the shoulder), from behind (bruising, supraspinatus and infraspinatus wasting · not expected at two hours · scapular deformity); winging deferred with a reason · 2:00-3:40 PALPATION, four steps: temperature at two levels, capillary refill, radial pulse ('no evidence of proximal vascular injury'), then TEN LANDMARKS on the affected side only · sternoclavicular joint, whole clavicle, acromioclavicular joint, acromion, coracoid, head of humerus and biceps tendon in the groove, spine of scapula, borders of scapula, supraspinatus (TENDER), infraspinatus · 3:40-4:55 SIX active movements, both sides together, 'as far as you comfortably can': flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, external rotation, and internal rotation as HAND BEHIND THE BACK reaching up with the thumb · 4:55-7:00 FIVE special tests with the purpose said aloud: empty can, full can, drop arm, Apley scratch, apprehension (gentle) · close with the joint above and below and the neurovascular status · 7:00-8:00 diagnosis to the PATIENT with the reasoning from your own findings, differentials in lay terms, concerns elicited, plan and safety-net.

back.dx: Rotator cuff injury, most likely a supraspinatus tear — tenderness localised to supraspinatus and the greater tuberosity with NO bony tenderness, painful limited flexion and abduction to about 80 degrees, empty can AND full can both painful (which points to a cuff injury rather than isolated impingement), and a positive drop arm test, with a normal deltoid contour and a negative apprehension test. Differentials in lay terms, each excluded: dislocation — normal shoulder shape and she can move it; fractured clavicle or proximal humerus — no bony tenderness; acromioclavicular joint sprain — AC joint non-tender; labral tear — apprehension negative. Plan: X-ray in two views (AP plus axillary or scapular-Y) for the bones and then ULTRASOUND, first-line for the cuff, with MRI for the labrum or surgical planning; paracetamol and an NSAID if not contraindicated; physiotherapy — most cuff injuries settle and never need surgery, which is for the minority with a complete tear that is not recovering. Because it happened at work: notify ReturnToWorkSA and issue a work capacity certificate. Safety-net: return if the arm goes numb or weak, the hand gets cold or pale, the pain worsens markedly, or she develops a fever; review in 1-2 weeks with the scan.
plan: WIPE with the exposure words: 'Hello, I'm Dr -, one of the doctors here. Can I confirm your full name and date of birth? I understand you've hurt your right shoulder after a fall. I've washed my hands. I'd like to examine that shoulder — I'll look at both shoulders from the front, the side and the back, then feel around the joint, then ask you to do some movements. I'll need to EXPOSE BOTH SHOULDERS, so I'll ask you to lower the gown to your waist — is that all right? You can stay sitting exactly where you are. Tell me straight away if anything hurts and I'll stop.' Do not ask her to stand; if you do and she refuses, accept it once: 'Examiner, the patient is unable to stand, so I'll perform the examination seated; this does not limit any part of it.'

Three-view inspection, MOVING as you speak: 'on general appearance my patient is alert, in obvious discomfort, with a protective posture supporting the right elbow. No sling. From the front: bruising over the lateral right shoulder; no swelling or redness; no asymmetry of the shoulders; NO LOSS OF THE BULK OR CONTOUR OF THE DELTOID; no biceps tendon deformity. From the side: no swelling or redness over the tip of the shoulder. From behind: no bruising; no wasting of supraspinatus or infraspinatus — and I would not expect wasting at two hours; no scapular deformity. I would normally check for winging, but that needs her to stand and press against a wall, and serratus anterior is not my concern in this mechanism.' (Loss of deltoid contour with squaring IS dislocation — naming and excluding it shows you have not closed prematurely.)

PALPATION — the highest-yield 100 seconds. Warn her once, then commentate continuously: 'backs of my fingers at two levels — no local rise in temperature. Capillary refill under two seconds. The radial pulse is present, good volume and symmetrical, so no evidence of proximal vascular injury. Now tenderness, right side only: sternoclavicular joint... the whole clavicle... the acromioclavicular joint... the acromion... the coracoid process... the head of the humerus and the biceps tendon in the groove...' then step behind: '...the spine of the scapula... the borders of the scapula... and now supraspinatus -' 'Ow, that's exactly it.' '- tenderness localised to supraspinatus and the greater tuberosity, and NO bony tenderness anywhere.' (Pressing the tip of the shoulder twice and saying 'no tenderness on palpation' is the commonest single reason candidates fail this station.)

SIX active movements, demonstrated, both sides, 'as far as you comfortably can': 'arms forward and up — flexion. Back behind you — extension. Out to the side in a big arc — abduction. Across your body — adduction. Elbows tucked in at a right angle, turn the forearms outwards — external rotation. And last, put your hand behind your back and scratch as high as you can with your thumb — that's internal rotation.' → 'Examiner: active flexion and abduction are painful and limited to about 80 degrees on the right; extension, adduction and both rotations are preserved. I'm not proceeding to passive movement, because there is no global restriction to explain.' (Swinging the forearm across the stomach is NOT internal rotation of the shoulder.)

FIVE special tests, purpose said aloud, result AND meaning together: '1 empty can, which assesses for impingement — arms out and slightly forward, thumbs down, stop me pushing down — painful on the right, positive. 2 full can, same position, thumbs up — also painful; empty can and full can BOTH painful points to a rotator cuff injury rather than isolated impingement. 3 drop arm test, for supraspinatus — I'm supporting your arm; hold it there, then lower it slowly — the arm drops and it is painful, positive. 4 Apley scratch test, a rapid check of range — restricted on the right. 5 apprehension test, for instability and a labral tear — gentle and slow — negative, no apprehension and no pain.' One test per condition: 'Hawkins-Kennedy and Neer test the same thing as my empty can — I would replace, not add.'

Close, then explain TO THE PATIENT: 'Examiner, that completes my shoulder examination. To complete my assessment I would examine the joint above and below — the cervical spine and the elbow — and formally assess the neurovascular status of the whole limb. May I now explain my findings to the patient?' Then the diagnosis in plain words (the four cuff muscles, supraspinatus most likely torn or strained), THE REASONING FROM YOUR OWN TESTS ('the muscle at the back was tender and none of the bones were; it hurt when I pushed your arms down in both positions; and your arm dropped when I asked you to lower it slowly'), then the differentials in lay terms with each excluded (see dx).

Elicit the concern and act on it: 'Is there anything in particular you're worried about?' → 'It happened at work — I'm a carer, I lift people all day. If I can't use this arm I can't work. Am I going to need surgery?' → most settle with pain relief and physiotherapy and never need an operation; surgery is for the minority with a complete tear that isn't recovering. Notify ReturnToWorkSA, issue a work capacity certificate today, and safety-net (numbness, weakness, cold or pale hand, much worse pain, fever), review in 1-2 weeks with the scan.

ask: 'I'll look at both shoulders from three sides, then feel around the joint, then ask you to do some movements.' / 'I'll need to expose both shoulders — is that all right?' / 'You can stay sitting exactly where you are.' / 'Examiner, the patient is unable to stand, so I'll perform the examination seated; this does not limit any part of it.' / 'No asymmetry of the shoulders and no loss of the bulk or contour of the deltoid.'

'I'm looking for wasting of supraspinatus and infraspinatus — and I would not expect it at two hours.' / 'The radial pulse is present and of good volume, so no evidence of proximal vascular injury.' / The ten landmarks: 'sternoclavicular joint, clavicle, AC joint, acromion, coracoid, head of humerus and biceps tendon, spine of scapula, borders of scapula, supraspinatus and infraspinatus.'

'Copy my movement and take it as far as you comfortably can.' / 'For internal rotation, put your hand behind your back and scratch as high as you can with your thumb.' / 'Empty can and full can both painful points to a rotator cuff injury rather than isolated impingement.' / 'To complete my examination I would examine the joint above and below and assess the neurovascular status of the whole limb.' / 'Is there anything in particular you're worried about?' THE ONE TRANSFERABLE HABIT: result, then meaning, in the same sentence.

VERSION B — FROZEN SHOULDER (60M, fall one month ago): every active movement is minimally possible and painful in ALL directions → 'because the restriction is GLOBAL, I can't tell from active movement alone whether this is a muscle problem or a joint problem, so I'm going to proceed to passive movement.' Then report the capsular pattern: 'passively about 80 degrees of flexion, 15 of extension, 60 of abduction, and external rotation is the most restricted at around 20 degrees. Passive movement is restricted as well as active, and EXTERNAL ROTATION IS AFFECTED FIRST AND WORST — that is a capsular pattern and it places the problem in the joint, not the muscle.' Narrate what you cannot do rather than skipping it silently, and expect four spare minutes — slow down, do not invent things to do. To the patient: adhesive capsulitis, the capsule inflamed then tight and thickened, settles slowly over many months; physiotherapy, analgesia, an early intra-articular injection helps; check blood sugar and thyroid.

VERSION C — POST-DISLOCATION CLEARANCE (25M basketballer, three months on): everything normal PLUS the AXILLARY NERVE, which the handbook treats as a critical item: 'because anterior dislocation classically injures the axillary nerve, I'd like to examine that nerve specifically. Sensory: cotton wool over the lower deltoid, the regimental badge area, both sides — the SENSATION OF THE AXILLARY NERVE is intact and symmetrical. Motor: the axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor, so abduction against resistance and external rotation against resistance — power five out of five in both, so the axillary nerve is intact, motor and sensory.' The mark is for NAMING THE NERVE — 'sensation is normal' or 'C5 is normal' does not score. Return to sport: build up gradually over two or three weeks and keep up strengthening, because the main risk after a first dislocation is recurrence, highest in young athletes. / THE FLAT DELTOID: squaring with loss of contour and the arm held abducted and externally rotated → STOP the routine: 'this appearance is consistent with an anterior dislocation. I would not perform provocative special tests. I'd check the axillary nerve and the distal pulse now, give analgesia, and request an X-ray in two views before any attempt at reduction.' / SWAPPED FINDINGS — AC joint tenderness with pain in the last few degrees of abduction and a normal full can → 'that points away from a rotator cuff tear and towards an acromioclavicular joint injury' — do not force the recall.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Whitford, 40, right-handed, lives in Kadina with her husband and two children; personal care worker at an aged-care facility, lifting and transferring residents all day; ten cigarettes a day, four standard drinks a week, no regular medicines, no allergies, no previous shoulder problems. Slipped on a wet floor AT WORK two hours ago and landed on the point of the right shoulder; immediate deep pain radiating down the outer upper arm; cannot lift above shoulder height and it feels weak; no numbness, pins and needles, neck pain, head strike, chest pain or breathlessness. Stoic and anxious — winces and guards but does not cry. SHE REFUSES TO STAND: 'No, I'd rather stay sitting' — and repeats it if pressed. She does not volunteer the work worry unless concerns are invited, otherwise in the last twenty seconds: 'So can I still work?' If the doctor is rough or forces a movement: 'Ow — please stop', and pulls away; that is a marked event.

Numbers: 8 minutes, WIPE under 1:00, special tests by 4:30, last 55 s for task 2. FOUR rotator cuff muscles, THREE inspection views, FOUR palpation steps, TEN landmarks, SIX movements, FIVE special tests. Capillary refill under 2 s. Ranges: flexion 0-180, extension 0-50, abduction 0-180, adduction 0-45, external rotation 0-90, internal rotation to about T7-T10. Imaging: X-ray in two views (AP plus axillary or scapular-Y); ultrasound first-line for the cuff; MRI for labrum or surgical planning. Paracetamol 1 g orally, NSAID if no contraindication. Review 1-2 weeks. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.

Scored out of 20, pass at 14 with no automatic-fail item missed: introduces and confirms identity, explains look/feel/move, REQUESTS EXPOSURE of both shoulders, offers a position and accepts the refusal without fuss, general appearance with posture and sling, physically moves for three views, says asymmetry and deltoid contour, looks for supraspinatus/infraspinatus wasting, temperature/refill/radial pulse, palpates at least 8 of the 10 named landmarks ALOUD including supraspinatus and infraspinatus, examines the affected side only, all six movements active with 'as far as you can', internal rotation behind the back, empty can and full can WITH the interpretation, drop arm performed and interpreted, Apley and apprehension performed, gentle throughout with no forced movement, diagnosis with reasoning from the findings, and four or more differentials in lay terms plus concerns elicited and a safety-net.
Drop arm — Positive

★ Asking her to stand twice, offering analgesia to get her up, or apologising at length after the refusal
Examining through the gown, or never saying the words 'expose both shoulders' — exposure is invisible unless spoken

Announcing three views while standing still; saying 'wasting of the deltoid' two hours after a fall (the acute word is loss of CONTOUR); checking internal rotation by swinging the forearm across the stomach; going to passive movement in an acute injury

Bruising over the lateral shoulder with a NORMAL DELTOID CONTOUR

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Pressing the tip of the shoulder twice and reporting 'no tenderness on palpation' — the commonest single reason candidates fail this station, and the checklist demands at least EIGHT of the TEN named landmarks aloud: sternoclavicular joint, the whole clavicle, acromioclavicular joint, acromion, coracoid process, head of the humerus and the biceps tendon in the groove, then behind — spine of the scapula, borders of the scapula, SUPRASPINATUS and infraspinatus; palpate the affected side ONLY, because doing the normal side doubles the longest step and the marks are not there, and commentate continuously rather than reporting in a summary at the end, because the examiner cannot award anatomy marks for silence (★)

FAIL — Asking her to stand twice, offering analgesia to get her up, or apologising at length after the refusal — that sequence has cost more candidates this station than any clinical error; ask once, accept, tell the examiner and continue seated: 'Examiner, the patient is unable to stand, so I'll perform the examination seated; this does not limit any part of it' (★)

FAIL — Examining through the gown, or never saying the words 'expose both shoulders' — exposure is a marked item and it is invisible unless you say it, and inspection is comparative, so it is BOTH shoulders: 'I'll need to expose both shoulders, so I'll ask you to lower the gown to your waist — is that all right? You can stay sitting exactly where you are'; offer a chaperone if she hesitates (★)

FAIL — Announcing three views while standing still — the examiner is marking whether you physically MOVE for the front, the side and behind; and never say 'wasting of the deltoid' two hours after a fall, because muscle cannot atrophy in two hours — the acute word is LOSS OF CONTOUR, and naming it and excluding it aloud is how you show you have not closed prematurely, since loss of deltoid contour with squaring of the shoulder is a DISLOCATION and changes the station completely (if it is there, stop the routine: no provocative special tests, check the axillary nerve and the distal pulse, give analgesia, and request an X-ray in two views before any attempt at reduction)

FAIL — Forcing a movement, or a vigorous apprehension test — you are levering a shoulder towards dislocation, so go gentle and slow, watch her face and stop at the first flicker; take the six movements ACTIVE only and add 'as far as you comfortably can' rather than accepting a token fifteen degrees, and do not go to passive in an acute injury, because it adds pain and no information (Version B, the frozen shoulder with GLOBAL restriction, is the only exception, and there you say why first — passive restriction with EXTERNAL ROTATION affected first and worst is a capsular pattern, placing the problem in the joint rather than the muscle); internal rotation is the HAND BEHIND THE BACK reaching up with the thumb, not swinging the forearm across the stomach; and one test per condition — 'Hawkins–Kennedy and Neer test the same thing as my empty can; I would REPLACE, not add' (★)

SAY — Name each special test and what it is for, attach the meaning to the result in the same breath, then reason the diagnosis back from your own findings, which is what separates a five from a four: empty can (impingement) and full can both painful 'points to a rotator cuff injury rather than isolated impingement', drop arm for supraspinatus, Apley scratch as a rapid range check, apprehension for instability and a labral tear; then to the PATIENT in lay words rather than the medical list at the examiner — 'the rotator cuff is a group of four muscles around the shoulder that do most of the movement and hold the ball steady in the socket; when you fell, one of them, most likely supraspinatus, has been torn or strained… I think that because the muscle at the back was tender and none of the bones were, because it hurt when I pushed your arms down in both positions, and because your arm dropped when I asked you to lower it slowly'; differentials in lay terms, each with its exclusion (the shoulder coming out of joint — the shape is normal and she can move it; a broken collarbone or arm bone — no bony tenderness; a sprain of the small joint on top — not tender; a torn cartilage rim — the stability test was normal), then X-ray in two views and ultrasound as first-line for the cuff; ASK about her concerns before the bell so the work agenda surfaces, and offer ReturnToWorkSA notification and a work capacity certificate unprompted; safety net — numbness or weakness, a cold or pale hand, much worse pain, or fever; close with 'to complete my assessment I would examine the joint above and below — the cervical spine and the elbow — and formally assess the neurovascular status of the whole limb'; in Version C name the AXILLARY NERVE explicitly, because 'sensation is normal' and 'C5 is normal' score nothing — 'the sensation of the axillary nerve, over the regimental badge area, is intact and symmetrical', with abduction and external rotation against resistance for deltoid and teres minor

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice. Three hard rules: everything that needs the patient STANDING is done first in one block, so you lie them down ONCE; three special tests minimum (FABER, adductor squeeze, Thomas — drop FADIR before any of those); and STOP EXAMINING AT 6:10 whatever is left, because tasks 2 and 3 carry marks you cannot recover. Candidates lose 60-90 seconds either by moving the patient twice or by over-narrating palpation — seven quick landmark stops with ONE summary sentence, not seven sentences.
stem: Regional South Australian general practice; you are the GP registrar. Gary Nowak, 40, a shearer, with right hip pain. 8 minutes.
tasks: Perform a physical examination of the hip, giving a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 0:00-1:00 WIPE, exposure ('trousers off, underwear on'), OFFER A CHAPERONE, ask about a sore spot to leave until last, and announce the choreography: 'I will examine you standing first, then ask you to lie down for the rest' · 1:00-1:45 general appearance, gait (weight-bearing, antalgic, Trendelenburg lurch, pelvic tilt) then SQUAT · 1:45-2:15 TRENDELENBURG while still standing: stand behind, hands ready but not touching, lift the SOUND leg, watch the pelvis · 2:15-3:00 inspection in three views STILL STANDING: front (pelvic tilt, level iliac crests, scars, deformity), side (lumbar lordosis), behind (gluteal wasting, scoliosis, greater trochanter swelling or redness for bursitis) · 3:00-4:15 lie down ONCE: temperature with the backs of both hands, capillary refill and posterior tibial pulse, then SEVEN LANDMARKS · ASIS, iliac crest, PSIS (slide your hand under, do not roll him), the joint line at the outer half of the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral pulse, greater trochanter, quadriceps, adductor origin · one summary sentence · 4:15-5:30 SIX active movements DEMONSTRATED not described, with your HAND ON THE JOINT feeling for crepitus; offer a method for extension · 5:30-6:10 MEASUREMENT: true length ASIS to medial malleolus, apparent length umbilicus to medial malleolus, both legs · 6:10-7:00 FABER (and ask WHERE the pain is felt), adductor squeeze, Thomas · 7:00-8:00 close, then the diagnosis and the grouped differentials to the PATIENT.

back.dx: Osteoarthritis of the right hip — antalgic gait, an incomplete squat limited by groin pain, anterior joint-line tenderness, restricted movement with palpable CREPITUS worst in INTERNAL ROTATION (lost first and lost most in hip OA), a positive FABER reproducing GROIN pain (buttock pain would have pointed to the sacroiliac joint), and a positive Thomas test with a fixed flexion deformity — with equal leg lengths, which makes true shortening from fracture or avascular collapse less likely. He is young for it, so look for a secondary cause (childhood or developmental hip shape) with a plain X-ray. Differentials given to the patient IN GROUPS: inside the joint — OA, a torn labrum or an abnormally shaped joint, inflammatory arthritis (no other joints, no prolonged morning stiffness); soft tissues around the joint — adductor tendinopathy and greater trochanteric pain syndrome (those spots non-tender, squeeze negative); bone — fracture or avascular necrosis (no injury, weight-bearing, equal leg lengths); infection (afebrile, well); cancer (no night pain, no weight loss, no previous cancer); referred pain from the lumbar spine, kidneys or abdomen (pain reproduced by moving the hip, and in the groin rather than the buttock). Management message: THE MAIN TREATMENT IS EXERCISE, NOT REST — painkillers are there so he can exercise, not instead of it; most people never need a replacement; ReturnToWorkSA if work-related; review at 6 weeks. Safety-net: hot, red or swollen hip, fever, inability to weight-bear, numbness or weakness in the leg, night pain that wakes him, or unintended weight loss.
plan: WIPE with exposure, chaperone and choreography: '...I have been asked to examine your hip. That means looking at it, feeling it, and asking you to do some movements, and I will explain each position as we go. To examine the hip properly I need to see it, so I will need you to take your trousers off and keep your underwear on. WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE PRESENT? I will keep you covered whenever I am not actually examining. Are you sore anywhere in particular, so I can leave that until last? I will wash my hands. Examiner, I will examine Gary STANDING first and then ask him to lie down for the remainder.' (The chaperone offer and the sore-spot question are each scored present or absent and cost no time.)

Gait and squat, back to back while he is already on his feet: 'on general inspection he is comfortable, not in pain or distress, no protective posture, no walking aids. Gary, could you walk to the end of the room and back? Examiner, he fully weight-bears; there is a mild antalgic gait on the right — a shortened stance phase — with no Trendelenburg lurch and no pelvic tilt. Gary, still standing, could you squat down and stand back up?' → part way, wincing, 'it catches in the groin' → 'he cannot squat to full depth and is limited by groin pain. That tells me the extremes of hip range are restricted, and it also loads the proximal muscles.'

TRENDELENBURG, done while he is standing — the only special test that needs it: 'I will perform the Trendelenburg test, which assesses the hip abductors, gluteus medius and minimus. I am standing behind him with my hands ready but not touching. Gary, lift your LEFT leg off the floor and hold it. Examiner, there is no sagging and no tilting of the pelvis — the test is negative.' If told to skip: 'I would have asked him to stand on the affected side and lift the sound leg, and watched for the pelvis to sag on the unsupported side' — then move on immediately.

Inspection STILL STANDING (pelvic tilt and deformity disappear supine): 'from the front, no asymmetry or tilting of the pelvis, the iliac crests are level, no scars, no deformity. From the side, a normal lumbar lordosis, neither exaggerated nor flattened. From behind, no gluteal wasting, no scoliosis, and no swelling or redness over the greater trochanter to suggest bursitis.'

Lie him down ONCE, then palpation as landmarks with one summary: 'backs of both hands over the upper thigh and both hips — no local rise in temperature. Capillary refill under two seconds in the toes, and the posterior tibial pulse is present and normal. Tenderness: the anterior superior iliac spine... the iliac crest... Gary, I will slide my hand under your back, you do not need to move — the posterior superior iliac spine... the joint line, the outer half of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral pulse... the greater trochanter... the quadriceps... and the adductor origin. Examiner, there is tenderness over the right anterior joint line; everything else is non-tender.'

Movements DEMONSTRATED, with the hand on the joint: 'Gary, copy me. Knee up to your chest — flexion. Slide the leg out — abduction; as you do that I will rest my hand on your hip — EXAMINER, I AM FEELING FOR CREPITUS. Back across the other leg — adduction. Now hold your leg like mine, hip and knee bent to a right angle: ankle outwards — internal rotation; ankle inwards — external rotation. For extension I would roll Gary onto his left side or place him prone.' → 'skip extension' → 'thank you. Examiner, there is restriction of right hip movement with palpable crepitus, most marked in internal rotation; the left hip is full and pain free.' (If a movement is only described rather than demonstrated, the role-player will do it wrong.)

MEASUREMENT — the step most candidates lose, and it takes thirty seconds: 'true length, anterior superior iliac spine to medial malleolus, right... and left: equal. Apparent length, umbilicus to medial malleolus, right... and left: also equal. Examiner, there is no leg length discrepancy, which makes a hip pathology causing true shortening, such as a fracture or avascular necrosis with collapse, less likely.'

THREE special tests: FABER — 'right ankle on your left knee; one hand steadies the opposite pelvis, the other presses the knee gently down. WHERE EXACTLY do you feel that?' → 'in the groin' → 'the FABER test is positive and reproduces groin pain, localising to the hip joint; buttock or low back pain would have pointed to the sacroiliac joint.' ADDUCTOR SQUEEZE — fist between the knees, squeeze → no pain, negative, against adductor tendinopathy. THOMAS — 'my hand under the small of your back; I can feel the normal lumbar lordosis. Bring both knees to your chest — the lordosis has flattened. Now hold the left knee up and straighten the right leg down' → the right thigh will not reach the bed and the lordosis returns and exaggerates: a FIXED FLEXION DEFORMITY of the right hip.

Close and explain: 'Examiner, to complete I would examine the joint above and below — the lumbar spine and the knee — perform a neurovascular examination of the leg, examine the abdomen and groin for a hernia, and review the observation chart. In the interest of time I would also have performed a FADIR test and a log roll. Gary, may I explain what I have found?' Then the ball-and-socket explanation with the worn lining and the grating, 'you are a bit young for this so I want to check whether the hip is a slightly different shape — an X-ray answers that', and THE MAIN TREATMENT IS EXERCISE, NOT REST. Answer BOTH parts of the hidden agenda — 'am I going to need a new hip? And can I keep shearing?' — then the grouped differentials and the safety-net (see dx).
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute division
ask: 'I will examine you standing first, then ask you to lie down for the rest.' / 'Would you like a chaperone present?' / 'Are you sore anywhere in particular, so I can leave that until last?' / 'He fully weight-bears; there is a mild antalgic gait and no Trendelenburg lurch.' / 'The squat screens the extremes of hip range and proximal power in one movement.' / 'The Trendelenburg test assesses the hip abductors — gluteus medius and minimus.'

'The hip joint line is the outer half of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral pulse.' / 'As he moves I am resting my hand on the joint — I am feeling for crepitus.' / 'Internal rotation is lost first and lost most in hip osteoarthritis.' / 'True length ASIS to medial malleolus; apparent length umbilicus to medial malleolus; both legs.' / 'Where exactly do you feel that?' / 'Groin pain on FABER localises to the hip; buttock pain to the sacroiliac joint.' / 'In the interest of time I would also perform a FADIR test and a log roll.'

To the patient: 'your hip is a ball-and-socket joint, and both surfaces have a smooth, slippery lining... that lining has worn thin, so the joint grates and stiffens... that grating is what I could feel under my hand when you moved... the main treatment is EXERCISE, not rest — painkillers are there so you can exercise, not instead of it... most people never need a replacement... you are a little young for this, so I want to check whether the hip is a slightly different shape — an X-ray answers that.' Words to avoid in front of him: 'degenerative arthropathy', untranslated 'fixed flexion deformity', 'crepitus', 'bone on bone', 'nothing to worry about', 'you just need to rest it', 'you will need a replacement eventually'.

VERSION B — ADDUCTOR TENDINOPATHY: gait and squat normal, Trendelenburg negative, hip moves fully and painlessly with no crepitus, FABER and Thomas negative — the ONLY abnormalities are tenderness over the adductor origin and a positive adductor squeeze → 'because the joint itself moves normally, this is not an intra-articular problem. My diagnosis is adductor tendinopathy — an overload injury of the adductor tendons where they attach to the pubis.' To the patient: load management and graded strengthening rather than rest, over some weeks; no scan today because it would not change what we do. THE TRAP: an almost entirely normal examination tempts you to keep hunting, run over time and announce osteoarthritis anyway — a normal joint examination IS a finding; say 'full pain-free range with no crepitus' out loud and let it push you towards the soft tissues.

VERSION C — GREATER TROCHANTERIC PAIN SYNDROME: hip moves fully with no crepitus, FABER, squeeze and Thomas all negative, no leg length discrepancy, Trendelenburg MILDLY POSITIVE on the right, and exquisite point tenderness over the right greater trochanter → 'greater trochanteric pain syndrome — tendinopathy of the gluteus medius and minimus tendons with or without trochanteric bursitis. It is the hip's equivalent of rotator cuff disease at the shoulder, and the positive Trendelenburg fits, because those are the same abductor tendons.' To the patient: tendons attaching onto the bony bump with a bursa underneath, irritated — which is why it hurts exactly where you pressed, is worse on stairs and wakes him lying on that side; treatment is load management (avoid sitting cross-legged, avoid standing hanging on one hip, pillow between the knees at night) plus graded strengthening; an injection helps short term but does not beat exercise long term.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Nowak, 40, a shearer for 22 years, six days a week in season, bent over and loading the right leg; drives 60 km to the sheds; married with two children; ten cigarettes a day, four or five beers on a Friday; ibuprofen when bad, no regular medicines, no steroids; father had a hip replacement in his sixties; no childhood hip problems he knows of. Eight months of a deep right groin ache sometimes running to the front of the knee, worse at the end of a run and getting in and out of the ute, stiff for about fifteen minutes in the morning and after sitting; putting the right sock on has become awkward; no swelling, heat, injury, fever, weight loss or night pain. Practical and stoic — he winces briefly on the squat, on groin palpation and on FABER, and does NOT make a fuss, so the doctor must watch his face. He copies any movement he is SHOWN, but looks puzzled and does it wrong if a movement is only described. HIDDEN AGENDA, given once and quietly when concerns are invited or the explanation begins: 'Am I going to end up needing a new hip? And can I keep shearing?' — if the doctor brushes it aside or answers only one part, he goes flat and stops volunteering.

Numbers: ranges VERIFY — flexion 120, extension 30, abduction 45, adduction 30, internal rotation 40, external rotation 45. Trendelenburg: lift the SOUND leg, hold about 30 seconds, watch the pelvis — the sound side sags and the weakness is on the side being stood on. Rotation: ankle OUT = internal rotation, ankle IN = external rotation; FABER = Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation; FADIR = Flexion, ADduction, Internal Rotation. True length ASIS to medial malleolus, apparent length umbilicus to medial malleolus, both legs, and more than about 1 cm is significant. OA on X-ray = LOSS: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts. Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily, max 4 g in 24 h; ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food, shortest effective course VERIFY. Review at 6 weeks; ReturnToWorkSA if work-related; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.

The ten beats: frame (name, role, what the examination involves, exposure, chaperone, sore spot, choreography) — stand back for general appearance and aids — walk, then squat — stand on one leg for Trendelenburg — look front, side, back while still standing — lie down ONCE for temperature, pulses and seven landmarks — move, six active movements with the hand on the joint — measure true and apparent length — provoke with FABER, squeeze and Thomas — explain with grouped differentials, both parts of the concern answered, and a safety-net. If running late at 6:30: 'in the interest of time I would complete the Thomas test and add a FADIR and a log roll' — then give a compressed version rather than abandoning the differentials, because three named groups scores far better than none.
Squat — Cannot squat to full depth — limited by GROIN pain
Adductor squeeze — Negative
fails: ★ Moving the patient twice — lying them down after the gait and then asking them back up for inspection or Trendelenburg
★ Doing only one special test, or dropping FABER, adductor squeeze or Thomas in favour of FADIR
Never feeling for crepitus during movement, and never saying the words out loud
Skipping measurement of true and apparent leg length; forgetting the chaperone offer or the sore-spot question; describing movements instead of demonstrating them

DO — Offer a chaperone and ask about a sore spot before touching — each is a single scored line, neither costs time, and both are routinely forgotten under stress: 'to examine the hip properly I need to see it, so I'll need you to take your trousers off and keep your underwear on. Are you sore anywhere in particular, so I can leave that until last?'; DEMONSTRATE every movement rather than describing it, because he is briefed to look puzzled and do it wrong if you only describe (ankle OUT is internal rotation, ankle IN is external), take any skip gracefully with one sentence on what you would have done, and close by offering the lumbar spine and knee, a neurovascular examination of the leg, the abdomen and groin for a hernia, and the observation chart

back.dx: Acute right S1 radiculopathy from an L5/S1 disc protrusion — a lifting injury with radiating leg pain, lower lumbar and paraspinal tenderness, flexion grossly limited, a straight leg raise positive at about 45 degrees with a positive Bragard sign and a positive CROSSED straight leg raise (highly specific for a disc lesion), an ABSENT right ankle jerk against a normal left, and reduced sensation in the right S1 dermatome. Differentials in SIX GROUPS: MECHANICAL — radiculopathy from a disc (working diagnosis), non-specific mechanical back pain, facet arthropathy, spondylolisthesis, canal stenosis, vertebral fracture including osteoporotic and pathological; INFLAMMATORY — the spondyloarthropathies and sacroiliitis; MALIGNANCY — metastatic disease, myeloma, primary bone tumours; INFECTION — discitis, vertebral osteomyelitis, epidural abscess, and herpes zoster which can precede its rash by days; THE NEUROLOGICAL EMERGENCY — cauda equina syndrome, specifically screened for; REFERRED AND VISCERAL — pyelonephritis, renal colic, prostatitis, pancreatitis, and in an older patient a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm. Management: no imaging in the first six weeks without red flags; analgesia, keep moving, physiotherapy, review in a week; most are much better by six weeks, with leg pain taking 6-12 weeks.
plan: 'Hello, I'm Dr -. Is it James? I can see you're in a lot of pain — have you had something for it?' → 'Nurse gave me something.' → 'Good. I'm going to look at your back, gently feel it, ask you to try a couple of movements, and then do some tests on your legs. I'll stop the second you tell me to. I'll need your back uncovered — could you open the gown for me?' → 'Can you do it? I can't really let go.' → 'Of course — MAY I STEP BEHIND YOU AND OPEN IT? Thank you. I'll just clean my hands. Happy for me to start?' (Opening the gown unasked, or giving up and examining through fabric, are both fails — ask, get the yes, act, ten seconds.)

General appearance and the DEFERRED gait: 'on general appearance my patient is in obvious pain and distress, standing in a protective posture, leaning forward onto the desk for support with his hand over his lower back. He is not febrile and there is no obvious weight loss. I would normally assess gait, including heel walking for L4 and L5 and toe walking for S1. Given his pain and the fact that he can barely stand, I am DEFERRING gait — it would distress him without changing my management, and I would reassess once his pain is controlled.'

Inspection in TWO views: 'from behind, the spinous processes are in the midline with no scoliosis. There is no swelling, no redness and no rash, no scars and no muscle wasting. From the side, the lumbar lordosis is preserved — I'm looking for flattening, which would suggest paraspinal spasm.' Then palpation: 'James, I'm going to feel along your back now. Sing out the moment anything is sore. Backs of my fingers at three levels — no local rise in temperature. Now the spinous processes with my THUMBS, from the lower thoracic spine down to the sacrum — tenderness over the lower lumbar spinous processes, no step, no gap. Now the paraspinal muscles, both thumbs at the same level — bilateral spasm and tenderness, worse on the right. Finally the sacroiliac joints, pressing forward and outward — non-tender.'

ONE movement, then the declared omission: 'can you try bending forward for me, as far as is comfortable?' → about five degrees, 'ah — no' → 'flexion is grossly limited by pain. On that basis I am skipping extension, lateral flexion and rotation, because forcing further movement would distress my patient without adding information.' (Pushing him further is a fail; announcing the skip BEFORE attempting one movement tells the examiner you are running a recall.)

THE TRANSFER, narrated: 'James, I need you on the couch for the next part. There's no rush — would you like to take my arm? One step at a time. Sit down first... good... now I'll support your back while you lie down.' (The role-player is briefed to notice a candidate standing in silence, visibly impatient, for the forty seconds this takes — narrating it converts dead time into a communication mark.)

SLR, all THREE parts, with the ANGLE: 'let your right leg go completely floppy and let me do all the work. Tell me the moment you feel anything.' → 'Ah! — there' → 'straight leg raise POSITIVE on the right at approximately 45 degrees — within the 30 to 60 degree range suggesting root irritation. Backing off slightly and dorsiflexing the ankle reproduces the pain — BRAGARD'S sign is positive. Now the left: raising the LEFT leg reproduces the pain in the RIGHT leg — a positive CROSSED straight leg raise, which is highly specific for a disc lesion.' (Asking him to lift his own leg is not a straight leg raise, and 'positive' without a number is not an interpretation.)

THE SENTENCE THAT EARNS THE SECTION, then reflexes and sensation: 'I'd like to perform a lower limb neurological examination — I CANNOT CALL THIS A RADICULOPATHY WITHOUT DEMONSTRATING A ROOT DEFICIT. No wasting, no fasciculation. Tone and power...' → 'skip those' → 'thank you. Reflexes: the knee jerk, L3 and L4, is present and normal on the right. The ankle jerk, S1 and S2, is ABSENT on the right — and present on the left.' Then sensation with ONE tool: 'this is cotton wool — it feels like this on your chest. Now close your eyes, tell me when you feel it, and tell me whether it feels the SAME ON BOTH SIDES.' L1 groin, L2 mid thigh, L3 anterior knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral border of the foot and heel → 'sensation is intact from L1 to L5, with reduced sensation in the S1 dermatome on the right.'

The completion statement WITH the red-flag screen: 'to complete I would ask about saddle numbness, bladder and bowel function and bilateral leg symptoms; if present I would assess anal tone and perianal sensation and treat it as a CAUDA EQUINA EMERGENCY. I would check the plantar responses, and examine the hips and the abdomen including the aorta for referred causes.'

Diagnosis in plain English, thirty seconds: 'one of the nerves that comes out of your spine and runs down your leg is being squeezed. That's why you get pain in your back and pain shooting down your right leg, and why the feeling in the outer edge of your right foot is dulled. The usual reason is a tear in one of the discs — the cushions between the bones — with some of the softer centre pushing out onto the nerve.' → 'So it's a slipped disc? Am I going to need an operation? My dad had his back done and he was never right after.' → acknowledge it, then: 'the great majority settle without any operation — most people are much better within about six weeks, with the leg pain often taking a bit longer. We'll manage the pain, keep you moving, get physio going, and review you next week.' Then the six grouped differentials to the examiner (see dx).

back.dx: Left C6 cervical radiculopathy, most likely from a C5/6 posterolateral disc protrusion, with NO evidence of myelopathy, infection or malignancy: left paraspinal tenderness at C5-C6, restricted left lateral flexion and rotation with pain radiating to the thumb, a positive Spurling manoeuvre reproducing thumb paraesthesia, 4+/5 elbow flexion and wrist extension on the left, reduced left biceps and supinator reflexes, and reduced sensation over the left thumb and lateral forearm — motor, reflex and sensory findings ALL AGREE and localise to one root. The myelopathy screen (Hoffmann, inverted supinator jerk, Lhermitte, clonus) is negative. Differentials given to the PATIENT in groups: nerve — a pinched nerve (working diagnosis), pressure on the cord itself (tested for, normal), a trapped nerve lower down such as at the wrist; joint and bone — wear and tear, arthritis, fracture (no injury, no bony tenderness); muscle — postural strain, very common in her job; infection — spinal infection (afebrile, well); cancer — a growth or spread (no night pain, weight loss, systemic symptoms or bony tenderness); referred pain from the shoulder (her pain comes on moving the NECK). Management: conservative six-week trial, no imaging in the first six weeks without red flags, MRI rather than plain film if needed, simple analgesia, physiotherapy, stay active — rest and a collar make it slower, not faster; review in two weeks.

I will wash my hands, and I will talk the examiner through what I am doing as I go.' → 'It's the left side, and it goes down into my arm.'

THREE views: 'on general inspection Sarah is comfortable at rest, alert and orientated, not distressed, not febrile, and not holding her neck in a protective posture. FROM THE FRONT — no visible masses, no redness, no scars, no thyroid swelling, trachea central. FROM THE SIDE — the normal cervical lordosis is preserved, head not held forward. FROM BEHIND — no scoliosis, no step deformity, no muscle wasting, no swelling or redness.'

Palpation, temperature then tenderness: 'using the backs of both hands I am comparing temperature over the paraspinal regions at three levels — no increase. Now the spinous processes, from the base of the skull down to the upper thoracic spine — C7 is the vertebra prominens and I will go two levels below it. Sarah, tell me if anything is tender. Then the paraspinal muscles and trapezius on both sides. There is mild tenderness over the LEFT paraspinal muscles at C5 to C6, with NO midline bony tenderness and no step. No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and the thyroid is not enlarged.' (Midline bony tenderness suggests bone; paraspinal tenderness suggests soft tissue.)

ACTIVE movements only, demonstrated: 'Examiner, I will assess the spine with ACTIVE movements only — I will not move her neck for her. Sarah, copy me please. Tuck your chin to your chest... look up at the ceiling... right ear to right shoulder... and the left... look over your right shoulder... and the left.' → 'That's the one — it shoots down to my thumb.' → PICK IT UP IMMEDIATELY: 'thank you — pain radiating to the thumb corresponds to the C6 NERVE ROOT, and I will test that root specifically. Examiner: flexion and extension are full; left lateral flexion and left rotation are restricted by pain that travels into the left arm; right-sided movements are full and pain free.'

SPURLING, warned first: 'Sarah, I am going to do a test that may briefly bring on your arm symptoms — that is what tells me the diagnosis. I will stop as soon as you tell me to. Is that all right?' Then to the examiner: 'I am performing the Spurling manoeuvre: slight extension, then lateral flexion and rotation TOWARDS the symptomatic left side, then gentle axial compression of about seven kilograms through the vertex for up to ten seconds. This narrows the intervertebral foramen on that side.' → 'Stop — that's exactly the pain, down to my thumb.' → RELEASE IMMEDIATELY: 'thank you, I have my answer and I will stop there. It is positive on the left, reproducing pain and paraesthesia into the left thumb. Local neck pain alone would have been negative. It is highly SPECIFIC but poorly sensitive, so a negative result would not have excluded radiculopathy.'

THE SENTENCE THAT EARNS THE SECTION: 'because I suspect a nerve root problem, I CANNOT MAKE THAT DIAGNOSIS WITHOUT EXAMINING THE NERVE. I will now perform an upper limb neurological examination, comparing both sides.' Then ITPRSC condensed: 'inspection — no wasting, in particular of the small muscles of the hand, no fasciculation, no scars, no Horner syndrome. Tone normal and symmetrical, no spasticity, no clonus. Power — C5 shoulder abduction 5/5 both sides; C6 elbow flexion and wrist extension 4 plus out of 5 on the left, 5/5 right; C7 elbow extension 5/5; C8 grip 5/5; T1 finger abduction 5/5. Reflexes — left biceps and SUPINATOR reduced compared with the right; triceps equal. Sensation — light touch and pinprick reduced over the left thumb and lateral forearm, normal at the deltoid, middle finger, little finger and medial forearm. Coordination — I would complete with finger-nose testing.' THEN THE LOCALISATION SENTENCE: 'those three findings — motor, reflex and sensory — all agree, and localise to the left C6 nerve root.'

TASK 2 — the myelopathy screen, which is why task 2 exists: 'because radiculopathy and myelopathy present with the same complaint but are managed completely differently, I will now screen for upper motor neurone signs. Hoffmann sign — negative bilaterally. The supinator jerk is not inverted. Sarah, could you tuck your chin to your chest — any electric-shock feeling down your spine? No: Lhermitte sign is negative. There is no clonus.' Then the completion statement: 'to complete I would examine the lower limbs for tone, reflexes and plantar responses and assess gait; examine the shoulder and acromioclavicular joints, because rotator cuff disease refers pain to the neck; palpate the supraclavicular fossae and examine the LUNG APICES, because an apical tumour can produce a C8/T1 pattern with Horner syndrome; and check the peripheral pulses and blood pressure in both arms.' ('Nothing further, thank you' is a wasted mark.)

Tasks 3 and 4 to the patient: nerves leave the spine in the neck and travel into the arm, and one is being pinched where it leaves — usually a disc bulging slightly or wear-and-tear narrowing the tunnel; the nerve involved supplies the THUMB SIDE of the arm, exactly where her symptoms are; THE SPINAL CORD ITSELF IS NOT AFFECTED — checked specifically. Most are much better within six weeks with simple analgesia, physiotherapy and staying active, most never need an operation, and scans at her age nearly always show wear and tear that does not change treatment. Then, when she says 'my mum had a tumour in her spine, so I've been really scared it was that': acknowledge it directly, then give the grouped differentials naming what you looked for and what you found (see dx), and the safety-net: worsening weakness, CLUMSY HANDS (dropping things, trouble with buttons or coins), unsteadiness, bladder or bowel change, fever, or an electric-shock feeling down the spine on neck flexion.
