Also scored: introduced and consented, asked for full exposure of both legs, did NOT announce hand washing, general appearance covering pain AND fasciculation or tremor, named high-steppage gait and no other gait, heel walking, toe walking, looked for wasting and fasciculation, named the fibular head on inspection, temperature/capillary refill/distal pulse, palpated the fibular head and said why, knee movements only with no duplicated ankle range, dorsiflexion and eversion against resistance, plantarflexion and inversion tested and called normal, concluded with THE NERVE rather than a list of movements, cotton wool with eyes closed comparing sides, tested dorsum, first web space and sole, called the tap test positive out loud, named the diagnosis in plain words, and mentioned confirming with nerve conduction studies. 17 or more with all three stars = a pass.

FAIL — Testing power by copying only, with no resistance — copying demonstrates grade 3 at best, so always resist ('copy my movement… now push against my hand'); and do not list weak movements and stop, because naming the NERVE is the entire point of choosing a nerve-wise examination: 'I therefore have loss of the motor function of the COMMON PERONEAL nerve, with the motor function of the TIBIAL nerve intact' — PED, Peroneal = Eversion + Dorsiflexion; tibial = plantarflexion + inversion

FAIL — Running full dermatomes and myotomes when the task said 'relevant physical examination', or doing ankle movements twice — every ankle movement is about to be tested against resistance in the neurological block, so knee flexion and extension ONLY at the movement step, or you will have called weakness a restricted range before you called it weakness; and do not skip temperature, capillary refill and the posterior tibial pulse because 'it's a nerve case', since a limb examination includes a vascular assessment and it costs fifteen seconds; if the task DOES say 'lower limb neurological examination', run ITPRSC with myotomes L2–S1 and dermatomes L1–S1 and ADD the nerve-wise sweep and the tap test rather than replacing them

SAY — Name the FIBULAR HEAD twice, once on inspection ('I cannot see any swelling, redness or bruising over the lateral aspect of the knee at the fibular head') and again on palpation ('specifically palpating the fibular head, knowing this is where the common peroneal nerve can be entrapped'), because it shows you know a nerve entrapment at the knee causes symptoms in the foot, exactly as the cubital tunnel does for the hand; use the COTTON WOOL on the trolley rather than a finger, demonstrate it first, eyes closed, every territory both sides — 'close your eyes and tell me each time you feel it, and whether it's the same as the other side' → lost over the DORSUM (common peroneal) and the FIRST WEB SPACE (deep peroneal branch), normal over both SOLES, so the tibial nerve is intact; explain in four sentences — entrapment means a nerve under pressure, it is at the fibular head just below the knee on the outer side, most likely from hours of squatting, the muscles that lift the foot go weak and that is the foot drop, and the same nerve carries feeling from the top of the foot; most recover once the pressure comes off over weeks to a few months, with a change to the squatting (a kneeling stool, rotating tasks), a brace so he does not trip, physiotherapy, and nerve conduction studies at three to four weeks if it has not improved; the discriminator to keep in your mouth is that INVERSION IS PRESERVED in a common peroneal entrapment and WEAK in an L5 radiculopathy, because tibialis posterior is an L5 muscle supplied by the tibial nerve; do not get him up and down for a straight-leg raise with a minute left — offer it and move on; variants — increased tone, brisk reflexes and an upgoing plantar are upper motor neuron signs, so treat a sudden onset as a stroke until proven otherwise; bilateral symmetrical loss with numb hands is a peripheral neuropathy; a tense, tender anterior compartment with severe pain on passive plantarflexion is compartment syndrome needing urgent fasciotomy, not a pulseless foot to wait for; and bilateral foot drop with saddle numbness or bladder change is cauda equina

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — surgical ward, three hours post total thyroidectomy. THE ONE THING: reach TROUSSEAU'S SIGN with time to spare, and when the examiner asks what you are looking for, the scoring word is the FINDING — 'carpopedal spasm' with the posture described — not 'a positive Trousseau's', which is circular and scores nothing. The nerve examination will be entirely normal: that IS the result, so say what it excludes and move on rather than hunting. back.dx: HYPOCALCAEMIA from transient hypoparathyroidism after total thyroidectomy — paraesthesia in the hand with perioral tingling three hours post-operatively, an entirely normal hand neurological examination (which makes a compressive neuropathy unlikely), and POSITIVE Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs. Airway not compromised: clean flat dressing, no expanding swelling, no stridor, speaking in full sentences. Differentials, in plain words: carpal tunnel and cubital tunnel syndrome — power and feeling in every nerve were normal; cervical radiculopathy; hyperventilation from anxiety; hypomagnesaemia; and a positioning-related nerve stretch from how the arm lay during the operation. Plan: urgent CORRECTED CALCIUM, MAGNESIUM AND PHOSPHATE together, an ECG (looking for a long flat ST segment and a prolonged QT), calcium replacement guided by severity, and surgical and endocrine review. To her: four tiny glands behind the thyroid, each about the size of a grain of rice, keep the blood calcium steady; they are often bruised during the operation and go quiet for a while, and when calcium drops the nerves become irritable — common, expected and usually temporary. Safety-net: press the buzzer for worsening tingling, cramps or spasms, or ANY change in voice or breathing.
plan: WIPE with the airway screen built in: '...I understand you've got some pins and needles — I'd like to examine your hands. I'll look, gently feel, ask you to do some movements, check the feeling in your fingers, and finish with two quick tests — one with a blood pressure cuff, one where I tap gently on your cheek. Is that alright? Rest your hands on this pillow. ARE YOU HAVING ANY TROUBLE WITH YOUR BREATHING OR YOUR VOICE?' → 'breathing's fine, voice is a bit croaky but they warned me. It's my hand — and round my mouth, actually.' → 'around your mouth too — thank you, that's important. Let me examine you and then I'll explain what I think.' (Mild hoarseness on day zero is expected; stridor or worsening hoarseness is not.)

General appearance WITH the neck in one sentence: 'Examiner, on general appearance my patient is not in pain or distress, there is no protective posture, and she is alert and orientated. I can see a clean, flat neck dressing with no expanding swelling; she is speaking in full sentences with no stridor, so I have no concern about the airway. I WILL NOT DISTURB THE DRESSING.' (Removing it is an obvious fail; never mentioning the neck at all is subtler and, three hours post-thyroidectomy, worse clinically.)

Inspection and palpation: 'Marion, may I look at both hands, and turn them over? Examiner, on inspection of both hands, front and back, there is no THENAR or HYPOTHENAR wasting and no wasting of the small muscles, no fasciculation or tremor, and no swelling, redness, deformity or scars. On palpation: temperature is normal with no local rise, capillary refill is under two seconds, the radial pulse is present and of normal volume, and there is no tenderness over the hand, the wrist or THE ULNAR GROOVE at the elbow.' (Naming thenar and hypothenar shows you are actively excluding carpal and cubital tunnel — the two differentials the whole examination is built around.)

Movement then the nerve-wise examination: 'copy my movements. Make a fist and open... spread your fingers and close them... bend and straighten your wrist... and your elbow. Active movement is full and painless at the fingers, wrist and elbow. Now, palm flat, point your thumb at the ceiling; don't let me push it down — strong, MEDIAN motor intact. Pinch this paper and don't let me pull it — the thumb stays straight, Froment's is negative, ULNAR motor intact. Cock your wrist back — strong, RADIAL motor intact. Close your eyes and tell me when you feel me, and whether it's the same on both sides — sensation is intact and symmetrical over the index pulp, the little finger pulp and the snuffbox.' Then the interpretation: 'Examiner, THE NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION IS ENTIRELY NORMAL, WHICH MAKES A COMPRESSIVE NEUROPATHY UNLIKELY AND MOVES ME TOWARDS A METABOLIC CAUSE.' (Candidates who find nothing start hunting, repeat tests and run the clock down — a normal nerve examination IS the result. And do not run C5-T1: your differentials are compression at the wrist and elbow, so examine nerve-wise and say why.)

TROUSSEAU'S SIGN, warned and technically correct: 'Marion, I'm going to put a blood pressure cuff on your upper arm and pump it up. It will feel tight, and it may be uncomfortable for a couple of minutes — tell me if it's too much. Examiner, I am performing Trousseau's sign. I am inflating to TWENTY TO THIRTY MILLIMETRES OF MERCURY ABOVE THE PRESSURE AT WHICH THE RADIAL PULSE DISAPPEARS, and I will hold it for UP TO THREE MINUTES. I am looking for CARPOPEDAL SPASM.' → the examiner interrupts: 'what are you looking for?' → answer with the FINDING: 'carpopedal spasm — the wrist and knuckles flex, the fingers stay straight and held together, and the thumb is drawn across the palm.' → the hand adopts the posture → 'that's alright Marion, it will settle the moment I let the cuff down — and it actually tells me something useful. Examiner, this is a POSITIVE Trousseau's sign. Releasing the cuff now.'

CHVOSTEK'S SIGN: 'the last thing is that I'm going to tap gently on your cheek, just in front of your ear. It won't hurt. Examiner, I am performing Chvostek's sign, tapping over the FACIAL NERVE as it emerges anterior to the ear. I can see twitching of the facial muscles at the corner of the mouth — this is a POSITIVE Chvostek's sign.' Then her fear arrives: 'doctor, is this a stroke? My mum had a stroke at sixty.' → answer directly with the reason, then redirect: 'I don't think this is a stroke, and I can tell you why. A stroke usually affects one side of the body and often the face or speech, and everything I've tested in your nerves is normal. What I think is going on is different, and much more expected after this operation. May I explain?'

Diagnosis in plain words, then THREE differentials — do not skip them (see dx): the four grain-of-rice glands behind the thyroid, bruised at operation, calcium drops, nerves become irritable — which is the tingling in the hands and around the mouth; both tests point to a low calcium level; common, expected, usually temporary. Then the differentials she can follow: squeezed nerves at the wrist or elbow (power and feeling were normal), a trapped nerve in the neck, breathing quickly when anxious, and a nerve stretched by how the arm was positioned in theatre. → 'so what happens now? Do I need another operation?' → 'almost certainly not. I'll send a blood test now to check the calcium and a couple of related levels, do a quick heart tracing, and start you on calcium. We'll recheck it regularly. If the tingling gets worse, if you get cramps or spasms, or if your voice or breathing changes at all, press the buzzer straight away.'

she is speaking in full sentences with no stridor, so I have no concern about the airway; I will not disturb the dressing'; then the explanation in plain words — 'sitting behind your thyroid are four tiny glands, each about the size of a grain of rice, whose job is to keep the calcium in your blood at the right level; because they sit so close to the thyroid they often get bruised during the operation and go quiet for a while, and when the calcium drops the nerves become irritable, which is exactly what you're feeling — pins and needles in the hands, and often around the mouth… this is common, expected, and usually temporary'; answer the stroke fear DIRECTLY rather than dismissing it ('a stroke usually affects one side of the body and often the face or speech, and everything I've tested in your nerves is normal'); plan — an urgent CORRECTED CALCIUM with MAGNESIUM and PHOSPHATE sent together, an ECG looking for a long flat ST segment and a prolonged QT, calcium replacement guided by severity, and surgical and endocrine review; safety net — worsening tingling, cramps or spasms, or ANY change in voice or breathing, press the buzzer straight away; Version C — reduced sensation over the index pulp with weak thumb abduction and both special tests NEGATIVE — is a median nerve lesion rather than hypocalcaemia, raising positioning-related nerve injury as well as carpal tunnel, and you would still send a calcium, because the two can coexist

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, Kadina. Scored on EXAMINATION SKILL, not on the label, and the two accuracy points are OTOSCOPE DEPTH and the CLARITY OF YOUR TUNING FORK INSTRUCTIONS. The role-player is briefed to give you nothing on the fork until the instruction contains all THREE parts. Set the clock: fork in hand by 4:10, differentials starting by 6:40 — because the commonest way to fail with good technique is to score 7 on technique and 1 on differentials. Automatic fails: otoscope inserted into the canal; running the wrong branch when the task said otherwise; reporting a finding you never obtained; finishing with no differential list.
stem: General practice, Kadina, South Australia; you are the GP. James Whitmore, 24, previously well, with pain in the LEFT ear for three days. T 37.6, HR 78, BP 118/74, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA. In the room: a role-player on a chair, a HALF-HEAD MANNEQUIN with a left ear on the bench, an otoscope (possibly unassembled) with a box of specula, tuning forks, and gloves.
tasks: Perform a focused examination of the ear, giving a running commentary to the examiner
Report your findings and state your most likely diagnosis
Give your differential diagnoses
time: 0:00-0:40 WIPE with GLOVES (a direction, not an offer · do not start a discussion about alcohol rub), the whole route named in plain language, and 'everything I do, I'll tell you about first'; HOLD UP THE OTOSCOPE and name it, assembling it aloud if it is in pieces; no position, no exposure, and do NOT move him to the couch · 1:00-2:00 INSPECTION opening with the COMPARISON sentence (both ears symmetrical, no displaced earlobe), then the left external ear, THE MASTOID, and discharge; then PALPATION after a warning: helix, lobule, TRAGUS, mastoid, and movement of the pinna · 2:00-3:20 OTOSCOPY, the accuracy point: pencil grip, LEFT HAND FOR THE LEFT EAR, free fingers braced on the cheek, pinna UP AND BACK, and THE TIP STAYS AT THE ENTRANCE OF THE MEATUS · narrate before you describe, and never advance the speculum into the canal · 3:20-4:10 special tests: nine cervical node chains named while you announce stepping behind him, then the facial nerve (eyebrows, eyes shut, cheeks, teeth) · 4:10-6:40 HEARING: whisper 99 close and 66 at arm's length, standing BESIDE not in front, with the other ear blocked; then RINNE with the THREE-PART instruction, then WEBER; report the interpretation, not just the raw findings · 6:40-8:00 the ordered presentation, ONE committed diagnosis, then the differential list RECITED not composed, and a plain-language explanation with a specific safety-net.

back.dx: ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA of the left ear — a red, inflamed, BULGING tympanic membrane with loss of the cone of light, no perforation and no attic debris, on a background of a recent head cold and three days of deep constant ache; no mastoid swelling or tenderness, no lymphadenopathy, facial nerve intact, whisper heard at both distances with Rinne AC>BC and a central Weber. THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST, recited: wax impaction; otitis externa; foreign body; otitis media with effusion; chronic suppurative otitis media; cholesteatoma; mastoiditis; tympanic membrane perforation; herpes zoster oticus; and referred otalgia from the teeth, the temporomandibular joint, the tonsil or the cervical spine — plus labyrinthitis and Meniere disease, where fullness can be described as pain. Why not cholesteatoma: it gives WHITE KERATIN DEBRIS IN THE ATTIC with chronic offensive discharge and a conductive loss; here the drum is diffusely red and bulging with no attic debris and the history is three days — but it stays on the list. Management: regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, review at 48-72 hours, antibiotics per guideline VERIFY. Safety-net: swelling behind the ear, facial weakness, or a bad headache with a stiff neck.
plan: Gloves, WIPE, and NAME THE EQUIPMENT: '...I'd like to examine that ear now. I'll look at both ears, then feel around the ear, then I'll use this — (hold up the otoscope) — it's called an otoscope and it lets me look inside. At the end I'll check your hearing. You can stay sitting exactly as you are, and you won't need to take anything off. EVERYTHING I DO, I'LL TELL YOU ABOUT FIRST. Is that all right?' → 'will it hurt?' → 'I'll be gentle, and NOTHING GOES DEEP INTO THE EAR. If anything is uncomfortable, tell me and I'll stop straight away.' If the otoscope is in pieces, assemble it out loud: 'the head lines up with the notch, press down against the spring, and turn.'

Inspection led by the COMPARISON sentence, then palpation warned: 'on general appearance James is comfortable, alert, not in pain at rest, and holds his head in a normal position. COMPARING BOTH EARS, they are symmetrical with no displaced earlobe. Looking at the left external ear: no rash, no redness, no swelling, no scars or deformity. BEHIND THE EAR, OVER THE MASTOID, there is no swelling, redness or engorgement. There is no discharge or bleeding from the canal.' Then: 'James, I've finished looking. I'm going to feel around the ear now — tell me straight away if anything is tender' — helix, lobule, tragus, then the mastoid, then movement of the pinna → 'no tenderness over the helix, lobule or tragus, no mastoid tenderness, and no tenderness on movement of the pinna.'

OTOSCOPY — the accuracy point: 'James, I'm going to look inside your ear now with the otoscope. IT WON'T GO INTO YOUR EAR — I only hold it at the opening. Examiner, I'll perform otoscopy on the mannequin. I'm using a PENCIL GRIP in my LEFT hand for the LEFT ear, with my free fingers resting on the cheek as a stable point. I'm pulling the pinna UP AND BACK to straighten the canal, and holding THE TIP AT THE ENTRANCE OF THE MEATUS. The canal is clear, with no discharge or foreign body. The tympanic membrane is red, inflamed and bulging, with loss of the cone of light. There is no visible perforation and no attic debris.' (Advancing the speculum into the canal is described by examiners as the reason candidates fail this station outright — the TRACTION gives the view, the depth gives only pain. And ten seconds of silent peering is ten seconds the examiner cannot mark.)

Special tests, each move announced: 'James, I'm going to step behind you now and feel the glands in your neck with both hands. Tell me if anything is sore' — submental, submandibular, jugular, posterior cervical, posterior triangle, pre- and post-auricular, occipital, then round to the front for supraclavicular → 'no cervical lymphadenopathy.' Then 'coming round to the front. Raise your eyebrows... screw your eyes shut, don't let me open them... puff out your cheeks... and show me your teeth. The facial nerve is intact and symmetrical.' (A candidate was asked mid-station what he thought he was doing, having walked behind a seated patient unannounced.)

WHISPER, from beside not in front: 'now I'll check your hearing. Please block your right ear with your finger, like this. I'm going to whisper a number close to your left ear — just repeat it back to me' [whisper 'ninety-nine'] 'good — and one more from further away' [arm's length, about a metre, whisper 'sixty-six'] → 'the whisper is heard at both distances on the left.' (Standing in front lets him lip-read and gives you a false pass.)

RINNE, with the THREE-PART instruction that unlocks the findings: 'James, this is a tuning fork. When I ring it, it sounds like this — [ring it at a distance] — and I need you to tell me when you can hear that ringing. THREE THINGS for me. ONE, I'll put it on the bone behind your ear — tell me WHEN YOU START HEARING IT. TWO, tell me the moment YOU STOP HEARING IT. THREE, I'll hold it in front of your ear, and all I need is YES OR NO — can you hear it again? Is that clear?' Then WEBER: 'one more with the same fork — I'll place it in the middle of your forehead, and all I need to know is which side you hear it louder: left, right, or the same.' → 'Examiner, AIR CONDUCTION IS BETTER THAN BONE CONDUCTION on the left, and the Weber is central.' (Ring it by pinching the tips, hold it distally, base FLAT on the mastoid — not the sternocleidomastoid — and do not repeat a test because the answer surprised you.)

The ordered presentation and ONE committed diagnosis (see dx), then the differential list RECITED without hesitation — sort it afterwards, out loud, only if asked. 'Why not cholesteatoma?' has a scripted answer. Then to James: 'the eardrum is inflamed — a middle ear infection. Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, and I'd like to see you in two or three days. Come back sooner if you get swelling behind the ear, weakness of the face, or a bad headache with a stiff neck.' (His hidden agenda, raised late if concerns are never invited: a fishing trip in four days — can he go, and can he get in the water?)

ask: 'Everything I do, I'll tell you about first.' / 'Comparing both ears, they are symmetrical with no displaced earlobe.' / 'Behind the ear, over the mastoid, there is no swelling, redness or engorgement.' / 'No tenderness over the helix, lobule or tragus, no mastoid tenderness, and no tenderness on movement of the pinna.'

'Pencil grip, left hand for the left ear, free fingers on the cheek as a stable point.' / 'Pulling the pinna up and back, and the tip stays at the entrance of the canal.' / 'The tympanic membrane is red, inflamed and bulging, with loss of the cone of light.' / 'I'm going to step behind you now to feel the glands in your neck.'

'Tell me when you START hearing it... tell me when you STOP hearing it... then yes or no, can you hear it again?' / 'Which side do you hear it louder — left, right, or the same?' / 'Air conduction is better than bone conduction on the left; the Weber is central.' / 'The field is small and the appearances overlap, but the predominant colour is red, so on balance this is acute otitis media.' / 'I am unable to visualise the drum because of wax; I would soften and clear it and repeat otoscopy' — a finding and a plan, whereas inventing a drum you did not see is a claimed finding and a fail.

Variant 1 — THE TASK SAYS 'PERFORM A HEARING TEST' FIRST: open with the hearing tests in full (whisper, Rinne, Weber), then 'Examiner, I've completed the hearing tests. I'd now like to inspect and palpate the ear and perform otoscopy' — and expect 'skip inspection and palpation, go straight to otoscopy', which you take. Opening with inspection out of habit gets you stopped. / Variant 2 — THE ROLE-PLAYER WILL NOT GIVE FINDINGS ('hear what, sorry? I don't know what you want'): do NOT repeat the test — 'that's my fault, let me explain it again properly' and give all three parts, then test ONCE. He is briefed not to cooperate with an unclear instruction; nothing is wrong with the fork. / Variant 3 — DISCORDANT WEBER: 'the patient reports the sound lateralising to the right. I'll report that as found. MY DIAGNOSIS WAS MADE ON OTOSCOPY AND DOES NOT CHANGE, and my differentials are unaffected. May I move to those?' Candidates have repeated Weber four times and run out of clock before the only part they were still going to be marked on.

Variant 4 — HEARING LOSS STEM WITH WHITE ATTIC DEBRIS: 'the dominant appearance is a white, cheesy patch superiorly, in the attic — a CHOLESTEATOMA until proven otherwise. Bone conduction is better than air on the left and the Weber lateralises left, a conductive loss consistent with that. I'd want a CT of the temporal bones and an ENT opinion; the facial nerve is intact.' / Variant 5 — MASTOIDITIS: 'there is boggy redness behind the left ear with the auricle PUSHED FORWARD and mastoid tenderness. This is mastoiditis — admission, intravenous antibiotics and same-day ENT, with MedSTAR if he deteriorated.'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitmore, 24, diesel mechanic at a grain handling depot with a loud workshop (muffs 'mostly'). Three days ago a head cold; two days ago the left ear began a deep constant ache, worse lying down, about 6/10, with muffled sounds on that side; no discharge, bleeding, dizziness or measured fever; grommets as a small child; sometimes uses cotton buds (only if asked); paracetamol helped a little. Friendly and straightforward, mildly fed up, cooperative but NEVER volunteers. HOW HE PLAYS IT: no tenderness at helix, lobule, tragus or mastoid, and none on tugging the ear — 'it's deeper in that hurts'; OTOSCOPE INTO THE CANAL → 'ow! That really hurts', pulls away, and marks it; hand on the neck without warning → 'sorry, what are you doing back there?'; whisper repeated correctly at both distances, but if the candidate stands IN FRONT he repeats it and notes that he was allowed to lip-read; WITHHOLDS THE FORK FINDINGS until the instruction contains all three parts ('sorry — hear what? What do you want me to do?'); with a full instruction: 'yes, I hear it' ... five seconds ... 'it's stopped' ... 'yes, I can hear it again'; Weber 'about the same' (harder run: 'the right'). Hidden agenda raised at about seven minutes if concerns are never asked: a fishing trip on Saturday.

Numbers: 512 Hz fork (second choice 256 Hz; 128 Hz is for VIBRATION SENSE); far whisper at arm's length, about 1 m; the mannequin insert is about 5 mm; station 8 minutes; review at 48-72 hours; amoxicillin 15 mg/kg/dose to a maximum of 500 mg, 8-hourly for 5 days VERIFY; sudden sensorineural loss means onset within 72 hours; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; TIS 131 450. Clock: fork in hand by 4:10, differentials starting by 6:40.

Scored out of 4 in each domain: CHOICE AND TECHNIQUE — right order for the task, both ears compared, mastoid on inspection AND palpation, pinna tugged, both special tests, all three hearing tests. ACCURACY — correct hand and grip, pinna up and back, tip at the meatus, fork pinched and held distally and flat on the mastoid, Weber truly midline. COMMENTARY — a spoken conclusion after every block, and Rinne and Weber INTERPRETED out loud rather than reported raw. DIAGNOSIS AND DIFFERENTIALS — one committed diagnosis, and FEWER THAN SIX DIFFERENTIALS IS A FAIL. PATIENT INTERACTION — every movement announced including stepping behind him, pain acknowledged at the start, plain-language explanation and a specific safety-net in the last forty seconds.
fails: ★ Advancing the otoscope speculum into the canal — described by examiners as the reason candidates fail this station outright
★ Finishing with no differential list, or fewer than six — candidates score 7 on technique and 1 on differentials for exactly this
A vague tuning fork instruction, so the role-player gives you nothing — and then repeating the test instead of re-explaining it

Reporting a finding you never obtained (inventing a drum behind wax); re-testing a discordant Weber until the clock is gone; going straight to the sore ear without the comparison sentence; missing the mastoid on both inspection and palpation

Standing in front for the whisper so he lip-reads; walking behind him without warning; running the wrong branch when the task said hearing test first; moving him to the couch, which costs forty seconds you want back at 6:40
numbers: 512 Hz fork (256 Hz second choice; 128 Hz is vibration sense) · whisper close then at ~1 m · tip at the meatus, mannequin insert ~5 mm · pinna UP AND BACK · 3-part fork instruction · 9 node chains · fork in hand by 4:10, differentials by 6:40

Red, bulging drum with loss of the cone of light = acute otitis media · white attic keratin debris = cholesteatoma · auricle pushed forward with boggy mastoid = mastoiditis · review 48-72 h · amoxicillin 15 mg/kg/dose max 500 mg 8-hourly for 5 days VERIFY · >=6 differentials or it is a fail · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Advancing the otoscope speculum into the canal — described by examiners as the reason candidates fail this station outright, and the role-player is briefed to cry out and pull away; the TRACTION is what gives you the view and the depth gives you nothing but pain: 'it won't go into your ear — I only hold it at the opening', pencil grip in the LEFT hand for the LEFT ear, free fingers resting on the cheek as a stable point, pinna pulled UP AND BACK, tip at the entrance of the meatus (★)

FAIL — Finishing with no differential list, or fewer than six — candidates score 7 on technique and 1 on differentials for exactly this, because they stand at 7:20 wondering whether wax causes pain (it does, and so does cholesteatoma); RECITE the list rather than composing it, and sort it afterwards only if asked: wax impaction, otitis externa, foreign body, otitis media with effusion, chronic suppurative otitis media, cholesteatoma, mastoiditis, tympanic membrane perforation, herpes zoster oticus, and referred otalgia from the teeth, the temporomandibular joint, the tonsil or the cervical spine — plus labyrinthitis and Ménière disease, where fullness gets described as pain; say the list silently to yourself before you touch the door handle (★)

FAIL — Running the wrong branch after the task said otherwise — read the task TWICE, because 'examination' or 'hearing test first' sets the order of everything; if it says perform a hearing test, open with whisper, Rinne and Weber in full and then offer inspection, palpation and otoscopy, expecting to be told to skip straight to otoscopy — opening with inspection out of habit gets you stopped and told to stick to the task (★)

FAIL — A vague tuning fork instruction, so the role-player gives you nothing — he is briefed to withhold the findings until the instruction contains all THREE parts, and then repeating the test instead of RE-EXPLAINING is the error, because nothing is wrong with the fork: 'this is a tuning fork; when I ring it, it sounds like this — three things for me: one, I'll put it on the bone behind your ear, tell me when you START hearing it; two, tell me the moment you STOP hearing it; three, I'll hold it in front of your ear, and all I need is YES OR NO, can you hear it again'; then Weber — 'which side do you hear it louder: left, right, or the same?'; ring the fork by PINCHING the tips rather than tapping it on your palm, hold it distally so you do not damp it, and place the base flat on the MASTOID rather than the sternocleidomastoid (★)

FAIL — Reporting a finding you never obtained — inventing a drum behind wax is a claimed finding and a fail, when the honest version is both a finding and a plan: 'I am unable to visualise the tympanic membrane because the canal is obscured by wax; I would soften and clear the wax and repeat otoscopy'; if the mannequin is ambiguous, commit and move rather than burning thirty seconds — 'the field is small and the appearances overlap, but the predominant colour is red, so on balance this is acute otitis media'; and if the Weber lateralises the wrong way, report it as found and do NOT re-test — 'my diagnosis was made on otoscopy and does not change' — because candidates have repeated Weber four times and run out of clock before the differentials, which is the only part they were still going to be marked on (★)

SAY — 'Everything I do, I'll tell you about first' — then actually do it, announcing every move including stepping BEHIND him for the neck nodes, because a candidate was asked mid-station what he thought he was doing; compare BOTH ears in one sentence before narrowing to the left, and cover the MASTOID on inspection and again on palpation, because missing it twice looks like you do not know it is part of the ear; name the otoscope aloud and assemble it out loud if it is in pieces, which is a communication mark and an equipment-familiarity mark in one gesture; palpate helix, lobule, TRAGUS, mastoid and movement of the pinna, then the cervical node groups and the facial nerve (eyebrows, eyes screwed shut, cheeks puffed, teeth); whisper from BESIDE or slightly behind rather than in front, or he lip-reads and you get a false pass — 'ninety-nine' close, 'sixty-six' at about a metre; if redirected to the mannequin for palpation, do not report the finding as though it came from the patient ('palpating the mannequin as directed — I would be assessing for tenderness over the tragus, the mastoid and on movement of the pinna'); present in ORDER and commit to one diagnosis, with the answer to 'why not cholesteatoma?' ready — white keratin debris in the ATTIC with a chronic offensive discharge and a conductive loss, against a diffusely red bulging drum with no attic debris and a three-day history; close in plain words with the safety net — swelling behind the ear, weakness of the face, or a bad headache with a stiff neck — and review at 48 to 72 hours

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, Wallaroo. A sore throat AND an ear pain in one stem is the examiner telling you there are TWO DIAGNOSES. ENTS — the S is SINUSES — plus appearance, hands, neck, chest and heart, with the abdomen offered: name the whole route in the WIPE so arriving at the stethoscope is planned rather than remembered. DESCRIBE SYMMETRY AND THE UVULA BEFORE YOU NAME ANYTHING, because the quinsy photograph has been used in this station. And count the tasks: task 3 is spoken TO THE PATIENT and task 4 to the examiner — candidates deliver both to the examiner and lose task 3 entirely.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo, South Australia; you are the GP. Bill Nguyen, 20, university student home for the holidays, with sore throat and LEFT ear pain for three days. TEMPERATURE 39.0 — nothing else is given. In the room: a seated role-player, a pen torch, wooden tongue depressors, an otoscope, a stethoscope, gloves.
tasks: Ask the examiner for any further vital signs you require
Perform a relevant physical examination, giving a running commentary
Explain your findings and your diagnosis to the patient
Give your differential diagnoses to the examiner
time: 0:00-1:10 OBSERVATIONS FIRST, by name and with the reason ('in a febrile young adult with a sore throat I want to know whether he is septic or has a threatened airway'), then WIPE naming the WHOLE route including the chest · 1:10-2:00 GENERAL APPEARANCE spoken aloud: alert, NOT DROOLING, no dehydration (moist lips and tongue), no respiratory distress (no tracheal tug, accessory muscle use or recession), no rash, no stridor or wheeze, voice not muffled · then the HANDS: capillary refill, skin turgor, pulse volume · 2:00-4:30 E, N, T: otoscopy at the meatus with the pencil grip and pinna up and back; the nose by tipping the head back and LIFTING THE TIP WITH YOUR THUMB and a torch (there has been no nasal speculum since about 2017); then the throat with the blade ON THE ANTERIOR TONGUE and 'aah' · and describe SYMMETRY, PALATAL BULGE and UVULAR POSITION before naming anything · 4:30-6:00 S and NECK: frontal and maxillary sinus tenderness with transillumination offered, then NINE node chains named while stepping behind him announced, then chin-to-chest for meningism · 6:00-7:00 CHEST AND HEART: expansion, air entry front and back, then the FOUR VALVE AREAS with the reason said out loud, and OFFER the abdomen for splenomegaly · 7:00-8:00 explain BOTH diagnoses to BILL in plain English with understanding checked and a symptom-by-symptom safety-net, then the two-axis differential to the examiner.

back.dx: TWO diagnoses: ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA of the left ear AND EXUDATIVE TONSILLITIS, with reactive cervical lymphadenitis — the Eustachian tube opens into the back of the throat, which is how one led to the other. Differentials on TWO AXES. By condition: viral pharyngotonsillitis, group A streptococcal tonsillitis, glandular fever, acute otitis media, otitis externa, acute sinusitis and laryngitis — and the ones being ACTIVELY EXCLUDED: quinsy, epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess, Lemierre syndrome, pneumonia and meningitis. By organism: Epstein-Barr virus, adenovirus, influenza, COVID-19 and rhinovirus; group A Streptococcus and Fusobacterium necrophorum; and with a sexual history, gonococcal or chlamydial pharyngitis. On Centor criteria he scores 3 or 4, but in Australian practice swabbing and antibiotics are reserved for those at higher risk of acute rheumatic fever. AVOID AMOXICILLIN until glandular fever is excluded, because it causes a widespread rash. Management: regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, cold fluids, review at 48-72 hours, phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg twice daily for 10 days in adults when treatment is indicated VERIFY. Safety-net, symptom by symptom: drooling or inability to swallow saliva, a change in voice, noisy breathing, inability to open the mouth, or a bad headache with a stiff neck or a non-blanching rash.
plan: Observations by name, with the reason: 'Examiner, before I examine him, may I have his blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation? I have a temperature of 39 degrees, and IN A FEBRILE YOUNG ADULT WITH A SORE THROAT I WANT TO KNOW WHETHER HE IS SEPTIC OR HAS A THREATENED AIRWAY.' → 120/70, 84, 12, 98% → 'thank you — he is haemodynamically stable, not tachycardic, not tachypnoeic and not hypoxic.' Then WIPE naming the WHOLE route: 'I'll start by looking at you generally and checking your hands, then look in your ears, your nose and your throat, press over your sinuses, feel the glands in your neck, and then listen to your chest and your heart — so I'll need to get to your back at that point.'

General appearance SPOKEN — five sentences that exclude five emergencies: 'Bill is alert and orientated. He is NOT DROOLING and shows no evidence of DEHYDRATION — lips and tongue are moist. There is no RESPIRATORY DISTRESS: no tracheal tug, no accessory muscle use, no recession. There is no RASH on the exposed skin. I can hear no STRIDOR and no wheeze from where I stand, and his voice is hoarse but not muffled.' Then the hands: 'capillary refill under two seconds, skin turgor normal, radial pulse regular and of good volume, no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.' (If interrupted with 'why are you looking for drooling?': 'because a patient who cannot swallow his own saliva has either a peritonsillar abscess or epiglottitis until proven otherwise, and that changes this from a GP problem to an airway problem.')

E and N: 'looking at both ears: symmetrical, no discharge, no redness or swelling behind the ear over the mastoid. Bill, I'll look inside now — this only goes to the opening of your ear, it doesn't go inside. Examiner: pencil grip, left hand for the left ear, free fingers braced on the cheek, pinna up and back, tip at the entrance of the canal. On the left the tympanic membrane is red, inflamed and bulging with loss of the cone of light. The right drum is normal.' Then 'Bill, I'm going to look up your nose. Can you tip your head back and look at the ceiling? I'll lift the tip of your nose gently with my thumb and use this torch. — Mild mucosal swelling with clear discharge on both sides, the inferior turbinates are not obstructing, no polyps, septum midline.'

T — and the habit that saves you: 'now your throat. I'll use this wooden spatula ON THE FRONT of your tongue — it may feel odd but it shouldn't hurt. Open wide and say aah. — Examiner: the oral mucosa is moist; both tonsils are enlarged, erythematous and covered in white exudate; THE SWELLING IS SYMMETRICAL; THERE IS NO PALATAL BULGE; THE UVULA IS MIDLINE; the posterior pharyngeal wall is injected but not bulging; and he opens his mouth fully, so there is no trismus.' (Describe symmetry and uvular position BEFORE you name anything — that single habit is what saves you when the photograph is a quinsy. And the blade goes on the ANTERIOR tongue: too far back and he retches.)

S and the neck: 'I'm going to press over your sinuses — tell me if any of it is tender. Over both eyebrows, the frontal sinuses... and over both cheekbones, the maxillary sinuses. No sinus tenderness. I'd offer transillumination for completeness.' Then 'Bill, I'm going to step behind you now and feel the glands in your neck with both hands' — submental, submandibular, jugular chain, posterior cervical, posterior triangle, pre- and post-auricular, occipital, then round to the front for supraclavicular → 'two enlarged, tender nodes in the left jugular chain; the rest are clear.' Then meningism WHILE SEATED: 'one more with your neck — can you put your chin on your chest? And turn side to side? — The neck is supple with no meningism.'

CHEST AND HEART — the commonest omission: 'Bill, I'd like to listen to your chest. Would you mind lifting your shirt at the back? — Chest expansion is symmetrical, and I'm listening front and back. Air entry is equal with vesicular breath sounds and no added sounds. And the heart, in the FOUR VALVE AREAS — aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid, mitral. Heart sounds one and two are normal with no murmur. I LISTENED BECAUSE GROUP A STREPTOCOCCUS CAN BE FOLLOWED BY ACUTE RHEUMATIC FEVER. To complete the examination I'd like to lie him down and palpate for splenomegaly, as glandular fever is on my differential.' (Ask, adapt, listen through thin fabric if you must — and say that you have done so. 'You've got a shirt on so I'll skip the chest' is marked as abandoning the block.)

TASK 3, turned TOWARDS BILL and in his language: 'there are two things going on, and they're related. First, your tonsils — the two lumps at the back of your throat — are swollen and red with some white pus on them: a tonsil infection. Second, in your left ear the eardrum is red and bulging outwards, which means there's infected fluid trapped behind it — a middle ear infection. The tube that drains the middle ear opens into the back of your throat, which is how one led to the other. The glands in your neck are up and tender because your body is fighting the infection. Your chest is clear, your heart sounds normal and your neck isn't stiff, so there's nothing more serious going on today. Does that make sense? Anything you'd like me to go over?' → 'do I need antibiotics?' (his agenda — 'it worked last time, and I've got exams in ten days') → most sore throats like this are viral and settle without them; regular analgesia, cold fluids, review in two or three days; then the symptom-by-symptom safety-net. THEN task 4 to the examiner: the two-axis differential (see dx).

From Wallaroo that means discussion with the on-call ENT registrar and transfer.' / Variant 2 — SINUS TENDERNESS GIVEN: 'then there are THREE diagnoses: acute otitis media, exudative tonsillitis, and acute sinusitis given the maxillary tenderness with nasal mucosal swelling and discharge. I'd ask how long the nasal symptoms have run and whether he improved and then worsened, since that distinguishes bacterial from viral.' Every abnormal site is a diagnosis — count them, then say the number out loud.

Variant 3 — SUSPECTED EPIGLOTTITIS (sitting forward, drooling, soft stridor): STOP THE EXAMINATION — 'he is drooling, sitting forward, with a muffled voice and audible stridor. I am concerned about EPIGLOTTITIS. I WILL NOT EXAMINE HIS THROAT WITH A SPATULA. I'd keep him upright and undisturbed, give oxygen, not attempt cannulation, and call for immediate senior airway help — in Wallaroo, a call to MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval while I stay with him.' pefe: Role-player: Bill Nguyen, 20, second-year engineering student home for the holidays, works weekends at the pub; wearing a T-shirt with a light shirt over it. Three days of sore throat now 8/10 on swallowing, with a deep left ear ache worse since yesterday; hot and shivery, sleeping badly, eaten almost nothing for two days but still drinking. Voice HOARSE but not muffled, NOT drooling. Non-smoker, about ten standard drinks across a weekend, sexually active with one partner and condoms most of the time (only if asked directly), paracetamol helps a little, tonsillitis twice in two years that settled on its own, no allergies, no family history of rheumatic fever. Uncomfortable, flat, cooperative — answers what is asked and stops. HIDDEN AGENDA: he wants antibiotics because 'that's what fixed it last time' and he has exams in ten days — raised when the diagnosis is explained, and pressed once more if the answer is vague. THREE MOMENTS THE STATION IS DESIGNED TO TEST: otoscope in the canal ('ow — that hurts', pulls away); the blade too far back (retches, pulls back, hand up); a hand on the neck without warning ('whoa — what are you doing?'). If told 'you've got a shirt on so I'll skip the chest', he says nothing and marks it.

Numbers: observations to expect 120/70, HR 84, RR 12, SpO2 98% with T 39.0; station 8 minutes, OUT OF THE THROAT BY 4:30 and stethoscope in hand by 6:00; NINE cervical node chains; FOUR Centor criteria (fever above 38, exudate, tender anterior nodes, NO cough) VERIFY; phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg twice daily for 10 days in adults when treatment is indicated VERIFY; review at 48-72 hours; NO NASAL SPECULUM since about 2017; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; TIS National 131 450. The eight-to-eleven blocks: appearance, hands, E, N, T, S, neck nodes, neck stiffness, chest, heart, abdomen offered — most candidates get seven.

Scored out of 4 in each domain: CHOICE — how many blocks, did they ask for the observations, did they auscultate chest AND heart, did they offer the abdomen (seven or fewer blocks is a fail). TECHNIQUE — otoscope at the meatus, nasal tip lifted with a torch, blade on the anterior tongue, nine chains named aloud, neck stiffness screened. COMMENTARY — general appearance spoken with the two D's and two R's named, a conclusion after each block. DIAGNOSIS — both diagnoses stated, symmetry and uvula described before naming anything, differentials with the must-not-miss list named AS SUCH. COMMUNICATION — was task 3 delivered to the PATIENT, in his language, with understanding checked and a specific safety-net, or aimed at the examiner? Automatic fails: stopping at ear, nose and throat; one diagnosis when two are present; calling a unilateral swelling with a deviated uvula 'tonsillitis'; otoscope inserted into the canal; using a spatula in the airway-obstruction variant.

I have a temperature of 39 degrees, and in a febrile young adult with a sore throat I want to know whether he is septic or has a threatened airway'; then do general appearance ALOUD, because looking at a patient is not a mark while saying it is five marks and five excluded emergencies — the two D's and two R's: not DROOLING, no DEHYDRATION with lips and tongue moist, no RESPIRATORY DISTRESS (no tracheal tug, accessory muscle use or recession), no RASH, plus no audible stridor or wheeze and a voice that is hoarse but not muffled — and check the hands, the fastest objective test of the dehydration you have just called negative, since dehydration is the commonest reason a tonsillitis patient is admitted; lift the nasal TIP with your thumb and use a torch rather than hunting for a speculum, which has not been on the tray since about 2017; name all NINE node chains, stepping behind him with a warning, screen neck stiffness while he is seated, and say why you listened to the heart — 'because group A streptococcus can be followed by acute rheumatic fever'; safety net symptom by symptom — drooling or an inability to swallow saliva, a change in voice, noisy breathing, an inability to open the mouth, or a bad headache with a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade on pressure

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice. The framework for the whole eye block: EIGHT steps — inspection, acuity, fields, colour, movements, accommodation, pupils, fundoscopy — NOMINATED OUT LOUD, because a step you were not allowed to do still had to be named. The clock is the enemy and it is the FRONT of the station where candidates waste it: four verbs is the whole explanation. Automatic fails: reading only the bottom line and calling it a visual acuity; holding the pen beside your own head during confrontation fields; reporting fields, pupils or fundi as normal without attempting them; omitting a step without ever nominating it; reassuring the patient before the pinhole result is known.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Snellen chart on the wall with a cross taped to the floor; pen torch, ophthalmoscope, pinhole and red-topped pin on the tray. Gary Whitmore, 50, storeman, with six months of gradually blurred vision. No pain, redness, discharge or headache. BP 128/78, HR 74, afebrile, BGL 5.6, no medications, no glasses. 8 minutes, aim 5:30 / 1:30 / 1:00.
tasks: Perform an eye examination with a running commentary
Explain your findings and most likely diagnosis to the patient
Give the examiner your differentials
time: 0:00-0:40 WIPE in FOUR VERBS ('looking at your eyes, reading letters off that chart, following my pen, and shining a light'), nothing hurts, no touching the eyeball, hands washed · then NAME THE EIGHT STEPS to the examiner · INSPECTION in THREE named groups: lids (swelling, redness, discharge, ptosis), globe (exophthalmos, enophthalmos, redness, subconjunctival haemorrhage), pupils and anterior chamber (round, regular, symmetrical, no hyphaema or hypopyon) · ACUITY, the step that carries the finding: on the cross, ONE EYE AT A TIME with the palm and no pressing, STARTING AT THE TOP LINE, at least two letters per line, then BINOCULAR · and the acuity is THE LAST LINE READ, not the first line failed · PINHOLE only on the reduced eye, with the reason said before you use it · FIELDS: bring a chair, sit FACING at the same level about an arm's length away, cover your own matching eye, pen EQUIDISTANT between you, 'look at my nose and don't follow the pen', four quadrants per eye and SWAP HANDS while covering the same eye · then COLOUR, MOVEMENTS (head still, follow my finger, tell me if you see double), ACCOMMODATION, PUPILS (direct, consensual, swinging torch) and FUNDOSCOPY (right eye, right hand, dial at zero) run without pausing and taking every skip · then the explanation and GROUPED differentials.

back.dx: REFRACTIVE ERROR, most probably MYOPIA — a reduced monocular acuity FULLY CORRECTED BY PINHOLE, with normal inspection, fields, movements, pupils and fundi. The pinhole is the reasoning chain: if vision improves the problem is one of FOCUS; if it does not, the problem is the MEDIA, RETINA OR OPTIC NERVE. Differentials GROUPED, each with a reason for exclusion: in the eye — presbyopia, astigmatism, cataract, glaucoma, macular degeneration; vascular and metabolic — diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, retinal vascular occlusion; neurological — optic neuritis, and a compressive lesion at the chiasm or behind it; inflammatory or infective — uveitis, keratitis; drug-related — hydroxychloroquine, ethambutol, amiodarone, corticosteroids. Cataract and the retinal causes are less likely BECAUSE the pinhole fully corrected the acuity; the neurological causes are less likely BECAUSE fields, pupils and colour vision were normal. Plan: refer for formal refraction, and with a family history of eye disease ask the optometrist to check intraocular pressures and the optic nerve. Safety-net, same day: sudden worsening, eye pain, flashes or floaters, a curtain across the vision, or double vision. IF BOTH EYES ARE NORMAL: nothing about the technique changes — still do binocular acuity, still no pinhole — and the conclusion becomes 'the eye examination is normal; with persisting symptoms my differentials shift towards presbyopia, dry eye, early cataract, and a neurological cause with a normal fundus such as retrobulbar optic neuritis, and I would want formal refraction and a dilated fundus examination before reassuring him.'
plan: WIPE in four verbs and NAME THE EIGHT: '...I've been asked to examine your eyes today. That'll mean LOOKING at your eyes, asking you to READ letters off that chart, FOLLOWING my pen, and SHINING a light in your eyes. Nothing hurts and I won't touch the eyeball itself. I'll wash my hands. Happy for me to go ahead?' Then: 'Examiner, my eye examination has EIGHT parts: inspection, acuity, fields, colour vision, movements, accommodation, pupils and fundoscopy. I'll nominate each.' (Ninety seconds explaining all eight tests is how candidates lose the clock at the front of the station.)

INSPECTION in three named groups: 'general appearance: sitting comfortably, alert, not in pain or distress. On inspection — LIDS: no swelling, redness, discharge or ptosis. GLOBE: no exophthalmos, no enophthalmos, no redness, no subconjunctival haemorrhage. PUPILS AND ANTERIOR CHAMBER: both round, regular and symmetrical, with no hyphaema and no hypopyon.' ('Inspection is normal' as a single sentence scores nothing — the mark is in the three named groups. If asked what you look for in the anterior chamber: a HYPHAEMA, which is blood, or a HYPOPYON, which is pus.)

ACUITY: 'Gary, stand on the cross for me. Cover your left eye with your palm — don't press. START AT THE VERY TOP LINE and read across... and the next... and this one. Now swap: cover the right, same again from the top. Now both eyes together.' → 'Examiner, the right eye is 6/6, the left eye is 6/18, binocular 6/6.' THREE TRAPS: starting near the bottom; reporting the line he FAILED instead of the LAST LINE READ; and pinholing a normal eye, which shows you do not know what it is for.

THE PINHOLE, with the reason first: 'as the left is reduced I'd like to repeat it through a pinhole — because if the vision improves the problem is one of focus, and if it doesn't, the problem is further back in the eye. Cover the right, hold this over the left, and read from the top again.' → 'with the pinhole the left improves to 6/6.' Write the figures and READ THEM ALOUD as you hand them over: 'Left 6/18 uncorrected, 6/6 with pinhole. Right 6/6 uncorrected. Monocular figures only; binocular was 6/6.'

FIELDS — three ways to make the test meaningless, all visible from across the room: standing while he sits, sitting two metres away, or holding the pen beside your own head. 'I'll bring my chair across and sit facing you, about an arm's length away — sorry to be so close. Cover one eye. Now LOOK STRAIGHT AT MY NOSE and keep looking there, don't follow the pen. TELL ME THE MOMENT YOU SEE IT, THEN TELL ME IF IT DISAPPEARS.' Temporal upper and lower with one hand; then SWAP HANDS keeping the SAME eye covered for nasal upper and lower; then the other eye. → 'all four quadrants full in the right eye... and all four in the left. Fields are full to confrontation and comparable to my own.'

The remaining steps run without pausing, taking every skip: 'COLOUR VISION — I'd use an Ishihara chart, or failing that the red and green bands on the Snellen chart. MOVEMENTS — head still, follow my finger with your eyes only; tell me if you see double. Any double vision up? Down? Left? Right? — full range, no nystagmus, no diplopia. ACCOMMODATION — look at the far wall... now look at my pen. Convergence and constriction both present. PUPILS — direct and consensual on the right, direct and consensual on the left, and a swinging torch test: no relative afferent pupillary defect. FUNDOSCOPY — right eye, right hand, dial at zero. Gary, look past my ear at the wall behind me.' (A run of skips does not mean you have finished early — every step you were not allowed to do still had to be NAMED. And if a fundus photograph appears: DESCRIBE BEFORE YOU DIAGNOSE.)

Explain to Gary, then present: 'your right eye is normal. Your left eye can't see as far down the chart — but when I gave you that little card with the holes in it, your left eye read the whole chart. That tells me your eye itself is healthy, and the problem is simply that it isn't focusing light in the right place. That's called a refractive error — almost certainly short-sightedness. It's very common and completely correctable with glasses. I'd like an optometrist to measure it properly. Does that make sense so far?' → his hidden concern: 'so it's not something serious? My father went blind from something in his eyes' → 'that's an important thing to tell me... nothing I've found today points to anything serious — your side vision, your pupils and the back of your eyes were all normal. But a family history does matter, particularly for GLAUCOMA, so I'd like the optometrist to check your eye pressures and look at the nerve at the back when they do your glasses.' Then the same-day safety-net and the GROUPED differentials to the examiner (see dx).

'As that eye is reduced I'd like to repeat it through a pinhole.' / 'The pinhole improved it, so this is refractive rather than a media or retinal problem.' / 'Look straight at my nose and keep looking there — don't follow the pen.' / 'Tell me the moment you see it, and then tell me if it disappears.' / 'All four quadrants are full and comparable to my own.'

'Keep your head still and follow my finger — tell me if you ever see double.' / 'Direct and consensual present in both eyes, and no relative afferent pupillary defect.' / 'Right eye, right hand, dial at zero.' / 'To complete I'd check intraocular pressure and arrange a slit-lamp examination.' / 'Come back the same day for pain, flashes, floaters, a curtain, or double vision.'

Numbers behind the technique: 6/6 = 20/20 = normal, and 6/60 is the top line; at least TWO letters per line, starting at the top; the acuity is the LAST LINE READ; 6/18 means a normal eye reads it at 18 m and this eye at 6 m; the Snellen sits at 6 m (or 3 m) on the wall, handheld charts at about 1 m; fields are done sitting 1 m apart with the pen 50 cm from each face, four quadrants per eye and eight in total; three or four swings is enough for the swinging torch; the ophthalmoscope dial sits at 0 with the large round aperture; steps three to seven combined take about 90 seconds; WIPE is 40 seconds and no longer. All extraocular muscles are CN III except SO4 and LR6.

The differential discipline: GROUP them and attach ONE REASON to each exclusion — grouping is the difference between a candidate who memorised a list and one who examined a patient. And the scoring sheet's auto-fails are worth rehearsing as a checklist: bottom line only; pen beside your own head; reporting a step as normal without attempting it; omitting a step without nominating it; and reassuring before the pinhole result is known.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Whitmore, 50, storeman at a farm supplies depot in Kadina who drives a forklift. Distance vision blurring over about six months — road signs and the TV — with reading fine; no pain, redness, discharge, flashes, floaters, curtain, double vision, headaches or injury; never worn glasses; no diabetes and blood pressure fine two years ago; ten cigarettes a day for 25 years, four to six beers on a Friday. HIDDEN CONCERN: his father went blind in his sixties from what he was told was 'pressure in the eyes' — volunteered only if the candidate asks about family history, asks what is worrying him, or asks whether he has questions; otherwise raised at the very end as 'so it's not the thing my dad went blind from?' HOW HE PLAYS THE CHART: with the affected eye he reads down four lines and stops ('that next one's gone blurry'); with the other eye he reads the whole chart; through the pinhole he reads the whole chart. He does NOT read the bottom line unaided under any circumstances — and if asked to read the bottom line first, he says 'which one, the little ones?', reads it correctly, and lets the candidate mark themselves down.

Scored out of 20 across three domains. APPROACH AND COMMUNICATION: introduces, confirms identity, consents, washes hands; explains in four verbs rather than a lecture; instructs before each step; the commentary names FINDINGS, not movements; explains without jargon and checks understanding. TECHNIQUE: inspection in three named groups; acuity with the patient on the cross, one eye at a time, starting at the top, at least two letters per line, and binocular tested too; pinhole used because an eye was abnormal; fields done seated at the same level about a metre away, own opposite eye covered, pen equidistant, four quadrants each eye with hands swapped correctly; pupils in both eyes plus the swinging torch. COMPLETENESS AND REASONING: all eight steps nominated aloud; movements with the diplopia instruction; fundoscopy with the correct eye and hand; correct interpretation of the pinhole; differentials in groups with a reason for each exclusion.

Debrief prompts worth running on yourself: which line was the acuity, and why? How far away were you sitting, honestly? Where was the pen? Did you cover the correct eye after you swapped hands? Which of the eight did you forget to nominate? And what did the father's blindness turn out to matter for?

must: FAIL — Reading only the bottom line and calling it a visual acuity, or reporting the line he FAILED instead of the LAST LINE READ — start at the very TOP line, at least two letters per line, one eye at a time with the palm covering and not pressing, standing on the cross; then test BINOCULAR acuity as well, and use the pinhole ONLY on the abnormal eye, because using it on a normal eye shows you do not know what it is for: 'as that eye is reduced I'd like to repeat it through a pinhole… the pinhole improved it, so this is REFRACTIVE rather than a media or retinal problem' (6/18 means a normal eye reads at 18 m what this eye reads at 6 m) (★)

FAIL — Holding the pen beside your OWN head during confrontation fields, standing while he sits, or sitting two metres away — any of the three makes the test meaningless, and the examiner can see all three from across the room; bring a chair, sit facing him at about ONE METRE at the same level, cover your own opposite eye, hold the pen equidistant between the two of you, and instruct properly: 'look straight at my NOSE and keep looking there, don't follow the pen; tell me the moment you see it, then tell me if it disappears' — four quadrants per eye and eight in total, SWAPPING HANDS for the nasal quadrants while the same eye stays covered (★)

FAIL — Reporting fields, pupils or fundi as normal without having attempted them, or omitting a step entirely WITHOUT EVER NOMINATING IT — the eight steps are inspection, acuity, fields, colour vision, movements, accommodation, pupils and fundoscopy, and you nominate each aloud at the start and again as you reach it, so that a run of skips leaves you with the credit rather than the illusion you finished early: 'Examiner, my eye examination has eight parts — I'll nominate each one' (★)

FAIL — Reassuring him that nothing is wrong BEFORE the pinhole result is known — and when he says his father went blind, do not brush past it: 'that's an important thing to tell me, and I'm glad you did; nothing I've found today points to anything serious — your side vision, your pupils and the back of your eyes were all normal — but a family history of eye disease does matter, particularly for GLAUCOMA, so I'd like the optometrist to check your eye pressures and look at the nerve at the back when they do your glasses' (★)

DO — Keep the front of the station to FORTY SECONDS, because that is where the clock is lost — four verbs is the whole explanation ('looking at your eyes, reading some letters, following my pen, and shining a light'); split INSPECTION into its three named groups rather than announcing 'inspection is normal', because the mark is in the groups and not the verdict — LIDS (no swelling, redness, discharge or ptosis), GLOBE (no exophthalmos, enophthalmos, redness or subconjunctival haemorrhage) and PUPILS AND ANTERIOR CHAMBER (round, regular, symmetrical, no HYPHAEMA, which is blood, and no HYPOPYON, which is pus); then run colour vision, movements, accommodation, pupils and fundoscopy without pausing, about ninety seconds for the five — instructing him to report DIPLOPIA during movements, doing a swinging torch test for a relative afferent pupillary defect, and taking the correct eye and hand for fundoscopy with the dial at zero ('right eye, right hand, dial at zero; Gary, look past my ear at the wall behind me'); and if a fundus photograph appears, DESCRIBE before you diagnose

SAY — Explain the pinhole result in plain words rather than naming a condition at him: 'your right eye couldn't get as far down the chart, but through that card with the pinholes it read the whole thing — that tells me the eye itself is HEALTHY, and the problem is simply that it isn't focusing light in the right place; that's called a refractive error, almost certainly short-sightedness, and it's completely correctable with glasses'; then GROUP the differentials and attach ONE REASON to each exclusion, because grouping is the difference between a candidate who memorised a list and one who examined a patient — in the eye (presbyopia, astigmatism, cataract, glaucoma, macular degeneration), vascular and metabolic (diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, retinal vascular occlusion), neurological (optic neuritis, a compressive lesion at or behind the chiasm), inflammatory or infective (uveitis, keratitis) and drug-related (hydroxychloroquine, ethambutol, amiodarone, corticosteroids) — with 'cataract and the retinal causes are less likely because the pinhole FULLY CORRECTED the acuity, and the neurological causes are less likely because the fields, pupils and colour vision were all normal'; offer intraocular pressure and a slit-lamp examination to complete, and refer for formal refraction; safety net the same day for sudden worsening, eye PAIN, FLASHES or FLOATERS, a CURTAIN across the vision, or DOUBLE VISION; and if both eyes are normal nothing about your technique changes — you still perform the binocular acuity, you still do NOT use the pinhole, and the conclusion becomes 'the eye examination is normal; given a normal examination with persisting symptoms my differentials shift towards presbyopia, dry eye, early cataract, and a neurological cause with a normal fundus such as retrobulbar optic neuritis — and I would want formal refraction and a dilated fundus examination before reassuring him'

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice, and the task NOMINATES the acuity first. Four figures get written down and read aloud as you hand them over. The pinhole is a REASONING CHAIN, not a ritual: say the reason before you use it, use it only on the reduced eye, and follow where the result leads — if it does not improve, you are no longer looking at a refractive error. Automatic fails: testing both eyes together only; reading only the bottom line and calling it an acuity; finding a reduced acuity and never using the pinhole; ignoring a failed pinhole and diagnosing refractive error anyway; quoting a specific legal driving threshold as fact when unsure.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Snellen chart with a cross on the floor; pinhole, pen torch, ophthalmoscope and pen on the tray; BLANK PAPER on the desk. Raymond Pascoe, 50, forklift driver at a grain terminal, with several months of blurred vision. No pain, redness or discharge. BP 126/76, HR 72, afebrile, BGL 5.4, no medications, never worn glasses. 8 minutes, aim 2:30 / 2:30 / 3:00.
tasks: Check the visual acuity
Perform the rest of the eye examination with a running commentary
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: WIPE, and THE GLASSES QUESTION before anything else ('do you wear glasses or contact lenses at all?') · then THIRTY SECONDS OF INSPECTION even though the task nominated acuity first, in three named groups, because that is what tells you the eye is quiet · DISTANCE ACUITY on the cross, monocular then binocular, palm over the eye with no pressing and no peeking, starting at the TOP line, two letters minimum, and the acuity read OFF THE CHART rather than estimated · THE PINHOLE with its reason stated first, on the reduced eye ONLY · NEAR VISION offered given his age · THE WRITTEN RECORD: four figures, Right and Left in words, written and READ ALOUD as you hand it over · then fields, colour, movements, accommodation, pupils and fundoscopy run without pausing, taking every skip · then the explanation in TWO SENTENCES AND A REASSURANCE (he drives a forklift; do not explain axial length), understanding checked, the occupational concern answered honestly, and the same-day safety-net.

back.dx: REFRACTIVE ERROR, most likely MYOPIA — a right acuity of 6/12 FULLY CORRECTED BY PINHOLE, with normal inspection, near vision, fields, movements, pupils and fundi. Differentials, grouped with reasons: cataract and presbyopia first, then glaucoma, macular degeneration and retinopathy — each less likely because the pinhole fully corrected the acuity and the fields, pupils and fundi were normal. Plan: formal refraction by an optometrist, and address the occupational vision requirement honestly — there IS a legal vision standard for driving and a requirement for his forklift work, but a lens will correct him, so expect glasses to sort it out; do not quote a specific threshold as fact when unsure (the private driving standard is commonly quoted as binocular 6/12 VERIFY). Safety-net, same day: sudden worsening, eye pain, flashes or floaters, a curtain across the vision, or double vision. IF THE PINHOLE DOES NOT IMPROVE: 'that takes me away from a refractive error. I'd like to look at the RED REFLEX... it is dulled on the right. With full fields, normal colour vision and no relative afferent pupillary defect, my leading diagnosis is now a MEDIA OPACITY, most likely cataract, and I'd arrange slit-lamp examination and intraocular pressures rather than a refraction alone.' IF DISTANCE IS NORMAL BUT NEAR IS REDUCED: no pinhole is indicated; reduced near acuity with normal distance acuity at 50 is PRESBYOPIA — the lens stiffening with age, corrected by reading glasses.
plan: WIPE with the glasses question: '...I've been asked to check your vision and examine your eyes. I'll get you to read letters off that chart, follow my pen, and let me shine a light in your eyes — none of it hurts. BEFORE WE START, DO YOU WEAR GLASSES OR CONTACT LENSES AT ALL?' → 'never have' (or 'only some cheap readers from the chemist' — which hands you a presbyopia thread to follow). Then: 'Examiner, before the acuity I'll take thirty seconds on inspection' — lids, globe, pupils and anterior chamber, in three named groups. (The task says 'check the acuity', not 'do nothing else first'.)

DISTANCE ACUITY, monocular then binocular: 'stand on the cross for me. Cover your left eye with your palm — don't press, and DON'T PEEK THROUGH YOUR FINGERS. Start at the very top line and read across... and the next... and this one. Swap over — cover the right. Same again from the top. And now both eyes together.' → 'Examiner: right eye 6/12, left eye 6/6, binocular 6/6.' (Reporting 6/12 because that was the line he STRUGGLED on is the classic error — the acuity is the last line READ. Read the figure off the chart; do not estimate it.)

THE PINHOLE, reason first: 'as the right is reduced, I'd like to repeat that through a pinhole — BECAUSE IF THE VISION IMPROVES THE PROBLEM IS ONE OF FOCUS, AND IF IT DOESN'T, THE PROBLEM IS FURTHER BACK IN THE EYE. Cover the left, hold this over the right, and read from the top again.' → reads the whole chart → 'with the pinhole the right improves from 6/12 to 6/6. I'd also like to check near vision given his age.' (Pinholing the normal eye 'to be thorough' tells the examiner you are following a ritual rather than a reasoning chain — a 6/6 has nothing to improve.)

THE WRITTEN RECORD — four figures, written and read aloud as you hand it over: 'Right 6/12 uncorrected, 6/6 with pinhole. Left 6/6 uncorrected. Near vision normal both eyes. Monocular figures only; binocular was 6/6.' Expect the examiner probes: 'why the pinhole?' (give the REASON, not the name), 'what does that improvement tell you?' ('it is refractive'), 'what if it hadn't improved?' ('media, retina or optic nerve').

The rest, run without pausing and taking every skip: 'visual fields by confrontation — I'll bring my chair across... all four quadrants full in both eyes. Colour vision — Ishihara, or the red and green bands on the chart. Eye movements — head still, follow my finger, tell me if you see double... full range, no nystagmus, no diplopia. Accommodation — convergence and constriction present. Pupils — direct and consensual in both eyes, and a swinging torch test with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy — right eye, right hand, dial at zero.'

Explain in TWO SENTENCES AND A REASSURANCE — he drives a forklift, so no axial length and no focal points: 'the good news first: the back of your eyes, your side vision and your pupils are all normal. Your right eye couldn't read as far down the chart — but when you looked through that card with the tiny holes, it read the whole thing. That tells me your eye is healthy; it just isn't focusing the light in quite the right place. We call that a refractive error, and in your case almost certainly short-sightedness — close things stay clear, distant things blur. It's extremely common, it isn't a disease, and glasses correct it completely. I'd like an optometrist to measure it properly and make you a prescription. What questions do you have?' Then check understanding AND STOP TALKING.

The occupational concern, answered honestly: 'am I going to lose my forklift ticket over this?' → 'that's a fair thing to worry about, and I'm glad you raised it. There IS a legal vision standard for driving, and there will be a requirement for your forklift work too. But your vision came back to completely normal through the pinhole, which means a lens will correct it. So I'd expect a pair of glasses to sort this out entirely. The optometrist will measure it formally and we'll go through the paperwork for work together once you've got the prescription.' Then the same-day safety-net and the summary with grouped differentials (see dx).

'I'd like to repeat that through a pinhole — if it improves the problem is one of focus; if it doesn't, it's the media, retina or optic nerve.' / 'Right 6/6 uncorrected. Left 6/18 uncorrected, 6/6 with pinhole.' / 'I'd also like to check near vision, given his age.'

'Your eye is healthy — it just isn't focusing the light in the right place.' / 'It isn't a disease, and glasses correct it completely.' / 'There is a legal vision standard for driving; the optometrist will measure it formally.' / 'Come back the same day for pain, flashes, floaters, a curtain, or double vision.' / 'To complete, I'd want formal refraction, a slit lamp and intraocular pressures.'

Numbers: 20/20 = 6/6; top line 6/60; two letters per line from the top; the acuity is the LAST LINE READ. Below 6/60 the sequence is: closer distance, then counting fingers, then hand movements, then perception of light, then none. Near print is read at 30 cm. Presbyopia from the forties. Myopia takes a CONCAVE / minus lens; hypermetropia a CONVEX / plus lens; astigmatism a cylindrical lens. Private driving standard commonly quoted as binocular 6/12 VERIFY — and quoting a specific threshold as fact when unsure is an automatic fail.

The two variants that change the diagnosis: PINHOLE FAILS → check the RED REFLEX, and a dulled reflex with full fields, normal colour vision and no RAPD makes CATARACT the leading diagnosis — to the patient, 'the lens inside your eye works like the lens in a camera, and yours has become a little cloudy. It's part of ageing rather than a disease, glasses won't clear it, but it is very treatable with a short operation that replaces the lens.' DISTANCE NORMAL, NEAR REDUCED → no pinhole indicated; reduced near acuity with normal distance acuity at 50 is PRESBYOPIA, the lens stiffening with age, corrected by reading glasses.
pefe: Role-player: Raymond Pascoe, 50, forklift driver at a grain terminal near Wallaroo for 22 years, with a car licence and a workplace forklift ticket. Several months of worsening distance vision — road signs, the footy scoreboard, the TV from the couch — with reading fine; no pain, redness, discharge, flashes, floaters, curtain, diplopia, headaches, glare or haloes; never worn glasses; no diabetes (checked yearly at work), no eye injury or surgery, no steroids; ex-smoker (quit eight years ago after 20 years), six or seven beers over a weekend; mother had cataract surgery in her seventies. Matter-of-fact, a bit blunt, mildly embarrassed about needing glasses at 50. HIDDEN AGENDA: worried about his forklift ticket and licence, and he has not told anyone at work his vision is going — raised only if asked about concerns, work or questions, otherwise at the very end. HOW HE PLAYS THE CHART: right eye reads down to the 6/12 line and stops; left eye reads the whole chart; through the pinhole over the right eye he reads the whole chart and sounds mildly surprised ('oh — that's better'). If asked to start at the BOTTOM line he says 'the little ones?', reads them WRONG, and lets the candidate draw their own conclusion. If the pinhole is never used he says nothing. If each eye is never tested separately, he happily reads the whole chart with both eyes open.

Scored out of 20. ACUITY TECHNIQUE (8): asks about glasses or contacts BEFORE testing; patient at the mark; each eye separately; starts at the top; at least two letters per line; reports the last line read correctly; tests binocular acuity too; offers near acuity. PINHOLE AND INTERPRETATION (4): uses it because an eye was reduced; states the reason BEFORE using it; does not pinhole the normal eye; correctly concludes refractive error from the improvement. COMPLETION AND COMMUNICATION (8): inspection in three named groups; all remaining steps nominated aloud; pupils in both eyes plus swinging torch; a legible written record with four figures and Right and Left in words; explains myopia without jargon and checks understanding; differentials grouped with a reason for each exclusion; addresses the driving and occupational concern honestly; and safety-nets pain, flashes, floaters, curtain and double vision.

Debrief prompts: which line was the acuity, and why that one? Why did you pinhole, and what would you have concluded if it hadn't helped? Did you test near vision? What were the four figures you wrote? And when did the forklift come up — who raised it?
