setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — hospital outpatient clinic. DECODE THE BLOOD TEST IN THE READING TIME: a high T4 and T3 with a TSH that has NOT been suppressed means the pituitary is not obeying feedback, so the pituitary is the lesion — and the pituitary sits under the optic chiasm. Walk in already expecting a field defect, and say your structure out loud so you do not drift to the neck: THE THYROID IS A CONSEQUENCE HERE, NOT THE LESION. The station turns on the field technique and on a THREE-PART diagnosis. Automatic fails: performing a thyroid examination instead of an eye examination; reporting the fields as normal; never naming the defect; giving only one of the three parts; saying 'brain tumour' and leaving it there; proposing antithyroid drugs as the treatment.
stem: Hospital outpatient clinic, South Australia. Jim Corradi, 40, self-employed builder, with several months of visual disturbance — also nervous and shaky, sweating more, some weight loss. BP 132/80, HR 96 regular, afebrile. Thyroid function requested by a colleague: TSH 3.8 (NORMAL), free T4 32 (HIGH), free T3 9.6 (HIGH). 8 minutes, aim 5:00 / 2:00 / 1:00.

time: WIPE, flagging that you will bring a chair over partway through, then NAME YOUR STRUCTURE: 'the complaint is visual and the task is an eye examination, so that is my structure · the eight steps, with particular attention to the visual fields, given the thyroid function result' · INSPECTION with a SPECIFIC look for exophthalmos from above and from the side, and lid retraction: their ABSENCE supports a central rather than a Graves cause, because proptosis is autoimmune and not an effect of the hormone · ACUITY 6/6 both eyes, so NO pinhole (and do not let a normal acuity reassure you: chiasmal compression classically SPARES central acuity until late) · FIELDS, the step the station turns on: chair across, facing, same level, arm's length, cover your own matching eye, pen equidistant, 'look at my nose and don't follow the pen', and WHEN NO REPLY COMES, ASK · 'can you see the pen yet?' · because the absence of a reply IS the finding and you have to convert it into words · four quadrants each eye, SWAPPING HANDS while covering the SAME eye, then name it: BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA · then colour, movements (looking specifically for ophthalmoplegia, which would suggest cavernous sinus involvement), pupils and fundoscopy (looking specifically for optic atrophy), taking the skips · then the THREE-PART diagnosis, the pituitary screening questions, the plan and the driving advice.

back.dx: CHIASMAL COMPRESSION by a TSH-SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMA — a bitemporal hemianopia with 6/6 acuity, no exophthalmos, no ophthalmoplegia, no relative afferent pupillary defect and normal discs, in a man with thyrotoxic symptoms whose TSH is inappropriately non-suppressed against a high T4 and T3. THE THREE-PART DIAGNOSIS, all three said: (1) NAME THE FINDING in plain words — the outer half of vision is missing in both eyes, a bitemporal hemianopia; (2) LOCALISE IT — the nerves from each eye cross at one point behind the nose, the optic chiasm, and pressure there knocks out the outer half of vision in both eyes; (3) NAME THE CAUSE AND LINK IT — the commonest cause of pressure there is a growth in the pituitary sitting directly underneath, and that same gland controls the thyroid, so ONE growth explains the vision, the blood test and the shakes and sweats — delivered WITH the reassurance in the same breath: most are NOT cancer, they are benign and cause trouble by pressing, and they are treatable, usually through the nose. Differentials: craniopharyngioma, tuberculum sellae meningioma, carotid aneurysm and infiltrative causes; biochemically, assay interference and thyroid hormone resistance, NEITHER of which gives a field defect. Plan: MRI pituitary with contrast, formal perimetry, and a full anterior pituitary panel (TSH and free T4/T3, prolactin, 8 a.m. cortisol and ACTH, IGF-1, LH, FSH, testosterone or oestradiol), with urgent endocrine and neurosurgical referral and PATS for travel. Screen for apoplexy and the other pituitary effects: headaches, ring or shoe size, libido, thirst and polyuria. Same-day return for sudden severe headache, vomiting, double vision, a drooping eyelid or a sudden drop in vision — and no driving until the field is formally assessed, because there is a legal standard.
plan: WIPE and NAME YOUR STRUCTURE: '...I've been asked to examine your eyes. I'll look at your eyes, get you to read some letters, follow my pen, and shine a light in your eyes. Partway through I'll bring a chair over and sit quite close — I'll explain why then. Nothing hurts.' Then: 'Examiner, the complaint is visual and the task is an eye examination, so THAT is my structure. I'll run the eight steps with particular attention to the VISUAL FIELDS, given the thyroid function result.' If asked why: 'because a non-suppressed TSH with a high T4 points at the pituitary, and the pituitary sits under the optic chiasm.' (Reaching for the neck is the drift this sentence prevents.)

Inspection with a purpose, and acuity: 'given the thyrotoxic features I am specifically looking for EXOPHTHALMOS, from above and from the side — there is none, and no lid retraction. Lids: no swelling, redness, discharge or ptosis. Globe: no redness. Pupils: round, regular, symmetrical, no hyphaema or hypopyon.' (Why: thyroid eye disease — its ABSENCE supports a central rather than a Graves cause, because proptosis is autoimmune, not an effect of the hormone.) Then 'cover your left eye, read from the top... and swap... and both together. Examiner, 6/6 right, 6/6 left, 6/6 binocular — so NO PINHOLE IS INDICATED.' (Do not let a normal acuity reassure you: chiasmal compression spares central acuity until late, so normal acuity is exactly what you expect.)

FIELDS — the instruction, given in full: 'I'm bringing my chair across and sitting facing you, about an arm's length away — sorry to be close, but the test only works at that distance. Cover one eye with your palm — I'll cover the matching one of mine. Look straight at my nose and keep looking at it; don't follow the pen. Tell me the moment you see it, then tell me if it disappears.'

AS THE DEFECT EMERGES — convert silence into words: [pen well inside your own field] 'Jim, CAN YOU SEE THE PEN YET?... And now?... Examiner, the pen is clearly within my own temporal field and the patient does not see it — the temporal upper quadrant of the right eye is ABSENT. Temporal lower — also absent. Nasal upper, nasal lower — both full. Repeating on the left... temporal upper and lower absent, nasal quadrants full. EXAMINER, THIS IS A BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA.' (Carrying on in silence when he does not answer is the trap — the absence of a reply IS the finding. And swapping the covered eye when you swap hands puts the nasal quadrants on the wrong eye.)

The remaining steps, each with its reason: colour vision offered; 'eye movements — head still, follow my finger, tell me if you see double. Up? Down? Left? Right? — full range, no nystagmus, no diplopia, and importantly NO OPHTHALMOPLEGIA, which would have suggested cavernous sinus involvement. Pupils — direct and consensual both eyes, and on the swinging torch no relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy — right eye, right hand, dial at zero; I'M LOOKING SPECIFICALLY FOR OPTIC ATROPHY.'

THE THREE-PART DIAGNOSIS to Jim, all three parts: 'I found something definite. You're not seeing out to the side — the outer half of your vision is missing in the right eye, and in the left eye as well. That's called a bitemporal hemianopia.' → 'I've been clipping the door frames on site. Thought I was just tired.' → 'That fits exactly. Now — THAT PATTERN TELLS US WHERE THE PROBLEM IS. The nerves carrying vision from each eye cross over at one point inside your head, just behind your nose — the optic chiasm. Pressure on that one spot knocks out the outer half of vision in both eyes.' Then part three WITH the reassurance attached: 'the commonest cause of pressure there is a growth in a small gland sitting directly underneath — the pituitary... I know growth is a frightening word. Most of these are NOT cancer — they're benign and cause trouble by pressing. They're treatable, usually with an operation done through the nose.' Then the link: 'that same gland also controls your thyroid. Your blood test showed a high thyroid level with the control hormone that should have switched off — not switching off. So ONE growth explains your vision, your blood test, and the shakes and sweats.'

Screen the rest of the pituitary, then plan: 'any headaches? Any change in your ring or shoe size? Any problems with sex drive? Drinking or passing water much more than usual?' → daily headaches for two months, the rest negative. Numbers and rules: fields sitting 1 m apart, pen 50 cm from each face, four quadrants per eye and eight in total. THYROID FUNCTION — primary hyperthyroidism gives a LOW TSH; central hyperthyroidism gives a NORMAL OR HIGH TSH with a high T4. pefe: Role-player: Jim Corradi, 40, self-employed builder on domestic sites around the Yorke Peninsula, driving a ute daily for work. Vision has felt 'narrow' for a few months — he keeps clipping door frames and nearly reversed into a stack of timber he did not see. Also shaky hands, sweating more, 4 kg of unintended weight loss, and HEADACHES most days for two months. Non-smoker, six or so beers a week, no medications, supplements or biotin, no relevant past or family history. NOT present if asked: galactorrhoea, ring or shoe size change, libido change, thirst or polyuria, double vision, eye pain. Practical and a bit impatient at first; when the word 'growth' is used he goes quiet and worried and asks 'is that a brain tumour?' HIDDEN CONCERN: his business depends on driving and being on site, and he is afraid of being told to stop working — 'can I still drive? I've got jobs booked in.'

HOW THE FIELDS ARE PLAYED, exactly: he sits still, covers whichever eye is asked and looks at the candidate's nose. TEMPORAL quadrants (pen coming in from his outer side), BOTH eyes: HE SAYS NOTHING. If asked 'can you see it?' he says 'no, nothing yet', and only once the pen reaches roughly the midline in front of his nose does he say 'yes, there it is now'. NASAL quadrants: 'yep, I can see it' as soon as it appears, and 'no, it hasn't disappeared' when asked. IF THE CANDIDATE NEVER ASKS whether he can see it and simply moves on, HE STAYS SILENT AND LETS THEM MISS IT — that is the failure this station is designed to expose. Acuity: he reads the whole chart with each eye.

Scored out of 20. FIELD TECHNIQUE (8): brings a chair and sits at the same level; about one metre away; covers their own opposite eye; holds the pen equidistant IN FRONT rather than beside their head; moves it slowly without waving; gives the full instruction including 'tell me if it disappears'; four quadrants in each eye, eight in total; swaps hands for the nasal field while covering the SAME eye. FINDING AND NAMING (4): ASKS when no reply comes; states each absent quadrant out loud as it is found; names the defect as a bitemporal hemianopia; comments on the absence of exophthalmos and its significance. DIAGNOSIS AND REASONING (8): runs the EYE examination not a thyroid examination; nominates all eight steps; part 1 names the finding in plain words; part 2 localises to the chiasm and explains why; part 3 names the pituitary; explicitly links the tumour to the thyroid result; reassures (mostly benign, treatable, through the nose) IN THE SAME BREATH; and screens for apoplexy and the other pituitary hormone effects.

back.dx: VERSION B — BINOCULAR DIPLOPIA, leading diagnosis OCULAR MYASTHENIA GRAVIS: diplopia present with both eyes open and resolving with EITHER eye covered, horizontal and worst on left gaze, with full movements, 6/6 acuity, full fields, equal briskly reactive pupils with no RAPD and normal discs — plus fatigability (worse in the evening) and evening ptosis. Binocular means each eye is normal alone, so this is a disorder of MOVEMENT AND ALIGNMENT. DO NOT NAME A SINGLE CRANIAL NERVE from the gaze: left gaze requires the left lateral rectus (VI) AND the right medial rectus (III). Differentials BY LEVEL — brain: tumour, multiple sclerosis, stroke, raised intracranial pressure; cranial nerves III, IV and VI: microvascular mononeuropathy, compressive lesion, aneurysm; neuromuscular junction: myasthenia gravis; muscle: thyroid eye disease, and traumatic entrapment if there were injury; plus giant cell arteritis in an older patient. Give the MONOCULAR list as well whichever version you have — cataract, astigmatism, refractive error, corneal irregularity or keratoconus, dislocated lens, dry eye — excluded here because the diplopia cleared with either eye covered. Plan: acetylcholine receptor antibodies, MRI brain and orbits, thyroid function, CT chest for thymoma if antibodies positive, neurology referral, AND ADVICE NOT TO DRIVE. Safety-net: trouble swallowing, slurred speech, breathlessness, limb weakness, sudden severe headache, or a large painful pupil.
plan: WIPE with the cover test flagged: '...I'll look at your eyes, get you to follow my pen, read a few letters, and I'll shine a light in your eyes. AT A FEW POINTS I'LL ASK YOU TO COVER ONE EYE — that's part of the test. Nothing hurts.' Then inspection with two named targets: 'Examiner, on inspection I'm looking particularly for STRABISMUS and PTOSIS. The corneal light reflexes are symmetrical, so no obvious squint, and no ptosis. Lids clear. No exophthalmos or enophthalmos, no redness. Pupils round, regular, symmetrical, no hyphaema or hypopyon.' (Why ptosis: third nerve palsy and myasthenia both cause it, and both cause diplopia.)

THE INSTRUCTION, given before anything moves: 'keep your head still and follow my pen with your eyes only. This is the important bit: TELL ME STRAIGHT AWAY IF YOU SEE DOUBLE AT ANY POINT, AND TELL ME WHERE YOU'RE LOOKING WHEN IT HAPPENS.' Then CHECK ONE, both eyes open, full big H out to the extremes: 'any double vision looking left? Up there? Down there? To the right? Up? Down?' → 'yes, two of everything — worst when I look off to my left' → 'with both eyes open the patient reports diplopia, and the range of movement is full.'

CHECKS TWO AND THREE, each with the SAME full H: 'now cover your left eye with your palm and we'll do exactly the same again. Any double vision here? Here?' → 'no, that's single now.' 'And now cover your right eye, same again.' → 'also single.' (Shrinking the H for checks two and three because time is running out is the trap — the finding may only appear at the extremes. And ask the patient to use their own palm rather than covering with your hand while holding the pen.)

STATE THE CONCLUSION OUT LOUD before moving on: 'Examiner: diplopia is present with both eyes open and RESOLVES WITH EITHER EYE COVERED. That is BINOCULAR diplopia — each eye is normal alone, so this is a disorder of ocular movement and alignment. The separation is horizontal and worst on left gaze. I'll record that as an observation, but I WOULD NOT LOCALISE IT TO A SINGLE CRANIAL NERVE on clinical grounds, because left gaze requires both the left lateral rectus and the right medial rectus.'

The remaining steps, taking the skips: 'acuity — 6/6 both, no pinhole needed. Fields by confrontation — full in all eight quadrants. Colour vision — Ishihara or the chart bands. Accommodation — convergence and constriction present. PUPILS — and these matter a great deal here: direct and consensual in both eyes, and on the swinging torch both pupils are equal, briskly reactive, and there is no relative afferent pupillary defect. No ptosis and a normal pupil makes a compressive third nerve lesion much less likely. Fundoscopy — right eye, right hand, dial at zero; I'm looking specifically for PAPILLOEDEMA.' (Skipping the pupils because the movements were the interesting bit is the auto-fail that matters most: in a diplopia station THE PUPIL IS THE TRIAGE QUESTION.)

The fatigability and bulbar screen, which turns the case: 'is the double vision worse at any particular time of day? Any trouble with chewing or swallowing? Any weakness in your arms or legs, or getting short of breath? Any droopy eyelid, especially in the evening? Headaches?' → 'definitely worse by the evening. And my husband says my left eyelid droops at night.'

Explain, then the driving conversation: 'with both eyes open you see double, but the moment you cover either eye it goes. That means each eye is working fine on its own — the problem is the two eyes not moving together, so your brain gets two pictures. The control of eye movement runs along a chain: the brain, the nerves to the eye muscles, the junction where nerve meets muscle, and the muscles. Yours being worse in the evening, with the eyelid droop your husband noticed, makes me think particularly about that junction — a condition called myasthenia gravis. It's treatable. But I don't want to guess, so we'll do a scan and blood tests to sort it out properly.' → 'is it a stroke?' → 'it can be, and that's one of the things we'll rule out — but nothing in your examination points that way today.' → 'can I still drive? I've got a 30-minute run to school.' → 'I'm sorry, but no — not until this is sorted out. Double vision isn't safe at the wheel and there's a legal standard as well. I'll write you a letter for work today.' Then the safety-net and the level-by-level differential (see dx).

VERSION A, MONOCULAR: 'with both eyes open, diplopia. With the LEFT eye covered — so the right eye working alone — THE DIPLOPIA PERSISTS. With the right eye covered, it resolves. That is monocular diplopia, and the affected eye is the RIGHT. I'd now concentrate on the light path of that eye: acuity WITH A PINHOLE, the red reflex, and a request for slit-lamp examination.' The commonest cause is clouding of the lens — a cataract... it could also be the shape of the front window of the eye, or a focusing problem. Cataracts are very treatable.' The diabetes in the stem is a DECOY — do not diagnose a microvascular palsy from the history.

THE PUPIL-INVOLVING THIRD NERVE PALSY — ptosis, a down-and-out eye, PAIN and a DILATED, poorly reactive pupil: 'this changes the station. A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated, poorly reactive pupil is a POSTERIOR COMMUNICATING ARTERY ANEURYSM until proven otherwise. I would stop, escalate immediately, arrange urgent CT or MR angiography, and speak to neurosurgery. From a rural site that is a MedSTAR call on 1300 13 12 33. I WOULD NOT ATTRIBUTE THIS TO DIABETES even if the patient is diabetic — the pupil involvement is what removes that option.'

and finish the case properly — look for STRABISMUS and PTOSIS on inspection (corneal light reflexes symmetrical; twenty seconds, and two of the highest-yield findings in the station), nominate fundoscopy looking specifically for PAPILLOEDEMA, and screen the bulbar and respiratory symptoms that change the urgency (worse at a particular time of day, trouble chewing or swallowing, slurred speech, breathlessness, limb weakness, evening ptosis); to the patient — 'each eye is working perfectly well on its own; the problem is that the two eyes aren't moving together, so your brain gets two pictures instead of one' — with the chain named as BRAIN, NERVE, JUNCTION, MUSCLE and the evening worsening pointing at the junction, and no guessing which ('I can't tell you which it is from examining you, and I won't guess'); give differentials by LEVEL and give BOTH lists whichever version you have, because you are making a differential for diplopia rather than for the version you happened to find — monocular (cataract, astigmatism, refractive error, corneal irregularity or keratoconus, a dislocated lens, dry eye) and binocular (brain: tumour, multiple sclerosis, stroke, raised intracranial pressure; cranial nerves III, IV and VI: microvascular mononeuropathy, a compressive lesion, an aneurysm; junction: myasthenia gravis; muscle: thyroid eye disease, traumatic entrapment), plus giant cell arteritis in an older patient; plan for myasthenia — acetylcholine receptor antibodies, MRI brain and orbits, thyroid function, CT chest for thymoma if antibodies are positive, and neurology referral; safety net — trouble swallowing, slurred speech, breathlessness, limb weakness, a sudden severe headache, or a pupil becoming large with eye pain (★)

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED. THIS IS A TRAUMA STATION WEARING AN EYE STATION'S CLOTHES: general appearance, inspection, PALPATION, then the eye examination WITH MOVEMENTS FIRST, then cranial nerves V and VII. Fix that order before you go in, because the room will tempt you straight to the Snellen chart. Automatic fails: running a plain eye examination with no palpation and no cranial nerves; never asking about double vision; PRESSING ON THE GLOBE; 'inspection is normal' without naming the traumatic signs; a diagnosis with no supporting reasons; plain facial X-rays as the definitive imaging; discharging without nose-blowing and driving advice.
stem: Emergency department, regional South Australia. Kyle Brennan, 30, brought in two hours after a motor vehicle accident (some recalls: punched in the face), complaining of double vision. Primary survey complete, vital signs stable, GCS 15, BP 128/74, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 98%, afebrile. Cotton wool, pen torch, ophthalmoscope, Snellen chart and a pen available. 8 minutes.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination with a running commentary
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
time: 0:00-1:30 WIPE warning that the pressing may be tender and that you will not touch the eyeball, ONE sentence acknowledging the completed primary survey and C-spine precautions, general appearance INCLUDING conscious level · then INSPECTION with FIVE NAMED NEGATIVES: raccoon eyes, Battle sign (look behind both ears), CSF discharge from nose or ears, exophthalmos and enophthalmos from above and from the side, hyphaema at the anterior chamber · plus pupil SHAPE, because a teardrop pupil is a ruptured globe · 1:30-2:30 PALPATION, five regions, ONE SIDE AT A TIME, starting on the uninjured side: skull (temporal, parietal, occipital, vertex), orbital rims INCLUDING THE LATERAL WALL, nasal bones, zygomatic arches, mandible and TMJs with the bite · and say out loud that you are deliberately NOT palpating the globe · 2:30-5:00 EYE MOVEMENTS FIRST, given the complaint, with the diplopia instruction before you start and the question asked IN EACH DIRECTION · then acuity, fields, colour, pupils with the swinging torch (arguing against optic nerve compromise or retrobulbar haemorrhage) and fundoscopy for retinal detachment, commotio retinae or vitreous haemorrhage · 5:00-6:00 CRANIAL NERVES V AND VII as the special test in facial trauma: V motor (clench the teeth), V sensory in all three divisions BOTH SIDES with cotton wool, and VII (eyebrows, eyes shut, cheeks, teeth) · 6:00-8:00 the diagnosis with THREE REASONS, the reassurance about the eye, and the disposition with nose-blowing and driving advice.

back.dx: LEFT ORBITAL FLOOR FRACTURE with inferior muscle tethering and infraorbital nerve injury — THE FLOOR TRIAD: tenderness at the inferior orbital rim, DIPLOPIA ON UPGAZE (tethering of the INFERIOR RECTUS AND INFERIOR OBLIQUE), and NUMBNESS IN THE V2 INFRAORBITAL TERRITORY. Relevant negatives: normal conscious level, no raccoon eyes, no Battle sign, no CSF leak, no hyphaema, no enophthalmos, 6/6 acuity, no RAPD, normal seventh nerve. Plan: CT FACIAL BONES AND ORBITS WITH FINE CORONAL CUTS (not plain films), analgesia, ice, head elevation, NO NOSE-BLOWING (it can force sinus air into the orbit), ophthalmology and maxillofacial referral, review at 7-14 days, and immediate escalation for bradycardia, vomiting or any fall in acuity. Surgery for persistent diplopia in primary or downgaze, enophthalmos greater than 2 mm, or a large defect VERIFY. To the patient, THREE REASONS: there is a bruise and tenderness exactly where that bone runs; looking up gives double vision because small muscles sitting on the floor of the socket get caught in the break; and the cheek is numb because a nerve runs along that same bone. Reassure specifically: vision is 6/6 in both eyes, the pupils work, the eyeball is not damaged, and the double vision is MECHANICAL and usually settles as swelling goes down over a week or two — with an operation available if it does not. Also: no driving while seeing double.
plan: WIPE with the warning, and ONE sentence on the primary survey: '...I've been asked to examine your face and your eyes. That means looking closely at your face, gently feeling around the bones of your face and head, getting you to follow my pen, and shining a light in your eyes. THE PRESSING MAY BE TENDER — tell me the moment anything hurts and I'll stop. I WON'T TOUCH THE EYEBALL.' Then: 'Examiner, I note the primary survey is complete and he is haemodynamically stable; I'M ASSUMING CERVICAL SPINE PRECAUTIONS REMAIN IN PLACE. On general appearance he is sitting comfortably, ALERT AND ORIENTATED with an intact conscious level, not in obvious distress, and there is no airway concern.' (Re-running the primary survey to look thorough is how you fail to finish.)

INSPECTION with the five named negatives: 'I can see a bruise below the left eye with some lower lid swelling. Specifically: NO RACCOON EYES; looking behind both ears, NO BATTLE SIGN; no clear discharge from the nose or ears to suggest a CSF LEAK. Looking from above and from the side, no exophthalmos and NO ENOPHTHALMOS. At the anterior chamber, NO HYPHAEMA. On the sclera, no subconjunctival haemorrhage. No ptosis, no laceration. The pupils are equal, round, regular and symmetrical — PUPIL SHAPE MATTERS AFTER FACIAL TRAUMA.' (A teardrop pupil means a ruptured globe: stop, shield the eye, call ophthalmology.)

PALPATION, five regions, uninjured side first, one side at a time: 'Kyle, I'm going to gently feel around the bones of your face. Tell me the moment it hurts. I'll start on the side that wasn't hurt. Examiner: SKULL — temporal, parietal, occipital and vertex — no tenderness, no step, no boggy swelling. Right orbital rim — no tenderness anywhere. Left orbital rim — superior no tenderness, LATERAL WALL no tenderness, INFERIOR RIM: definite tenderness, and I think a small step. Nasal bones — no tenderness, no deviation. Zygomatic arches — no tenderness. Mandible and the temporomandibular joints — no tenderness, and the bite feels normal. I'm deliberately NOT palpating the globe, in case it is ruptured.' (Two hands on both sides at once looks neat and wrecks the comparison; and forgetting the LATERAL WALL is exactly where Version 2 hides its only positive.)

EYE MOVEMENTS FIRST, given the complaint: 'keep your head still and follow my pen with your eyes only. IMPORTANT: IF YOU SEE DOUBLE AT ANY POINT, TELL ME STRAIGHT AWAY. Any double vision looking up?' → 'yeah — two of everything when I look up' → 'looking down? To the left? To the right?' → 'no, all fine' → 'Examiner, the range of movement is full and there is no nystagmus, but the patient reports DIPLOPIA ON UPWARD GAZE — consistent with tethering of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique in an ORBITAL FLOOR FRACTURE.' (Not asking about diplopia means the single best finding in the station never appears — he is briefed never to volunteer it.)

The rest of the eye examination, each with its reason: acuity each eye and binocular ('6/6 — an important negative'); fields and colour offered and skipped; 'PUPILS — direct and consensual in both eyes, and a swinging torch test: equal, briskly reactive, NO relative afferent pupillary defect, WHICH ARGUES AGAINST OPTIC NERVE COMPROMISE OR A RETROBULBAR HAEMORRHAGE. Fundoscopy — right eye, right hand, dial at zero; I'm looking for retinal detachment, commotio retinae or vitreous haemorrhage.' IF A FUNDUS PHOTOGRAPH APPEARS, describe and then park it: 'this shows arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, copper wiring, hard exudates and a cotton-wool spot — HYPERTENSIVE RETINOPATHY. That tells me he has had raised blood pressure for some time and needs it followed up, BUT IT DOES NOT CHANGE TODAY'S DIAGNOSIS, WHICH IS TRAUMATIC.'

CRANIAL NERVES V AND VII — the special test in facial trauma: 'fifth, MOTOR — clench your teeth; temporalis and masseter bulky and symmetrical. Fifth, SENSORY — cotton wool, demonstrated on the hand, eyes closed: FOREHEAD, yes both sides; CHEEK, yes right, nothing on the left — REDUCED SENSATION IN THE LEFT V2, INFRAORBITAL TERRITORY; JAW, yes both. SEVENTH — eyebrows up, eyes shut tight, cheeks blown out, show me your teeth: full and symmetrical.' (Testing sensation only on the injured side leaves nothing to compare it with.)

The diagnosis with THREE reasons, then the reassurance and the disposition: 'I think you've got a break in one of the bones around your eye — the floor of the socket, just under your left eye. An orbital floor fracture. THREE THINGS point to it. One, there's a bruise there and it's tender exactly where that bone runs. Two, when you look up you see double — small muscles sitting on the floor of the socket get caught in the break. Three, your cheek is numb, because a nerve runs along that same bone.' → 'am I going to lose the eye? Will the double vision stay?' → 'No — and I understand why you'd ask. Your vision itself is completely normal, 6/6 in both eyes, your pupils are working properly, and the eyeball hasn't been damaged. The double vision is a MECHANICAL problem from the muscles being caught, and in most people it settles as the swelling goes down over a week or two. If it doesn't, there's an operation that frees the muscle and repairs the floor.' Then: CT facial bones, analgesia and ice, referrals to eye and face surgeons, DON'T BLOW YOUR NOSE and DON'T DRIVE while seeing double, and return for worsening pain, a bulging eye, worsening vision, fever, or feeling faint or sick.
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute split: 1:30 inspection, 1:00 palpation, 2:30 eyes, 1:00 nerves, 2:00 diagnosis
ask: 'Tell me the moment anything hurts and I'll stop.' / 'I'm assuming cervical spine precautions remain in place.' / 'No raccoon eyes, no Battle sign, no CSF discharge from the nose or ears.' / 'From above and from the side — no exophthalmos and no enophthalmos.' / 'At the anterior chamber, no hyphaema.'

'I'll start on the side that wasn't injured.' / 'Definite tenderness at the left inferior orbital rim.' / 'I'm deliberately not palpating the globe, in case it is ruptured.' / 'If you see double at any point, tell me straight away.' / 'Any double vision looking up?' / 'Reduced sensation in the left V2, the infraorbital territory.'

To the patient: 'a break in the bone in the floor of the socket that protects your eye.' / 'Small muscles on the floor of the socket get caught in the break.' / 'Don't blow your nose, and don't drive while you're seeing double.' / 'Come straight back for worsening pain, a bulging eye, worsening vision, fever, or feeling faint.'

VERSION 2, LATERAL WALL (2019 onward) — three moments change: inspection, 'there is no bruise and no swelling'; palpation, 'the inferior orbital rim is not tender; there is tenderness over the LEFT LATERAL ORBITAL WALL'; movements, 'no diplopia in any direction — but the patient reports PAIN ON LOOKING TOWARDS THE INJURED SIDE. V and VII are both normal.' To the patient: 'a break in the bone on the outer side of your eye socket. Two things point to it: that's exactly where it's tender, and it hurts when you look towards that side. Reassuringly, you're not seeing double, your cheek sensation is normal, and your vision is fine — so I don't think a muscle is trapped or a nerve damaged. Next is a CT scan of the facial bones.'

THE TWO EMERGENCIES. RETROBULBAR HAEMORRHAGE — proptosis with a tense globe, severe pain, acuity 6/60 and an RAPD: 'this is orbital compartment syndrome and a SIGHT-THREATENING EMERGENCY. I would stop examining, call for senior help, and proceed to LATERAL CANTHOTOMY AND CANTHOLYSIS immediately — this is a clinical diagnosis and I would NOT wait for a CT. In a rural site I'd do it here on telephone advice and call MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33.' RUPTURED GLOBE — a teardrop pupil or a soft eye: 'I would stop examining, NOT press on the eye, NOT measure intraocular pressure, and apply a RIGID SHIELD — never a pad. Nil by mouth, head up, analgesia and antiemetics, tetanus prophylaxis, intravenous antibiotics, and immediate ophthalmology.' And bradycardia with vomiting in a patient with entrapment is the OCULOCARDIAC REFLEX — escalate.
pefe: Role-player: Kyle Brennan, 30, self-employed fencing contractor who drives for work every day. Two hours ago his ute went off the road and he hit the LEFT side of his face on the door frame, seatbelt on, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting or fits, remembers everything. Face sore on the left, double vision looking UP, and the left cheek numb 'like after the dentist'. Smoker 15 a day, no alcohol before the crash, no medications, allergies or blood thinners, tetanus 'years ago, not sure'. Not present if asked: eye pain, flashes, floaters, curtain, fever, nausea, faintness, fluid from nose or ears, neck pain, headache. Sore and shaken but stoic. HIDDEN CONCERN: frightened he will lose the eye, and cannot afford time off work. HOW HE PLAYS THE FINDINGS, exactly: PALPATION — silent for the skull, the right orbital rim, the nose, the zygomatic arches, the mandible, AND the left superior rim and lateral wall; only the LEFT INFERIOR ORBITAL RIM gets 'ow — yeah, that's sore'. MOVEMENTS — he says NOTHING spontaneously; only if asked 'any double vision looking up?' does he say 'yeah, two of everything when I look up', and down/left/right are fine. IF THEY NEVER ASK, HE NEVER TELLS THEM — that is the failure this station exists to expose. COTTON WOOL — 'yes' for the forehead both sides, the right cheek and the jaw both sides; SILENCE over the left cheek. If they press on his eyeball: 'ow, don't push on my eye' — and it is an automatic fail.

Numbers: FIVE named inspection signs — raccoon eyes, Battle sign, hyphaema, enophthalmos, CSF leak. FIVE palpation regions — skull, orbital rims, nasal bones, zygomatic arch, mandible. THE FLOOR TRIAD — inferior rim tenderness, upgaze diplopia, V2 numbness. Muscles tethered: inferior rectus and inferior oblique. Nerve: infraorbital = V2. Imaging: CT facial bones and orbits with fine CORONAL cuts — plain films are an auto-fail as definitive imaging. Review 7-14 days. Operate for persistent diplopia in primary or downgaze, enophthalmos over 2 mm, or a large defect VERIFY. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS National 131 450, ReturnToWorkSA if work-related.

Scored out of 20. STRUCTURE AND INSPECTION (7): acknowledges the primary survey and C-spine; comments on conscious level; describes the bruise with the side; names raccoon eyes and Battle sign; names hyphaema at the anterior chamber; looks from above and the side for exophthalmos and enophthalmos; asks about or looks for CSF. PALPATION (5): warns and offers to stop; starts on the uninjured side; palpates one side at a time; covers all five regions INCLUDING the lateral wall; does not press on the globe. EYE EXAMINATION AND NERVES (8): does movements FIRST given the complaint; instructs the patient to report diplopia before starting; asks about diplopia in EACH direction including up; nominates the remaining eye tests; comments on acuity and pupils and why they matter here; tests V motor and V sensory in all three divisions BOTH sides; tests VII; and is not derailed by the fundus photograph.
fails: ★ Running a plain eye examination with no palpation and no cranial nerves — this is a trauma station wearing an eye station's clothes
★ Never asking about double vision, so the single best finding never appears; or PRESSING ON THE GLOBE, which would extrude intraocular contents if it were ruptured
'Inspection is normal apart from a bruise' — the marks are in the five named negatives
Forgetting the lateral orbital wall on palpation, which is exactly where Version 2 hides its only positive; palpating both sides at once; testing V2 only on the injured side

A diagnosis with no supporting reasons; plain facial X-rays as the definitive imaging; being derailed by the hypertensive-retinopathy photograph; discharging without the nose-blowing and driving advice

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Running a plain eye examination with no palpation and no cranial nerves — this is a TRAUMA station wearing an eye station's clothes, and the room will tempt you straight to the Snellen chart; fix the order before you enter — general appearance → inspection → palpation → eye examination with MOVEMENTS FIRST → cranial nerves V and VII; one sentence acknowledges the completed primary survey and C-spine precautions, and any more than that and you will not finish (★)

FAIL — Never asking about double vision, so the single best finding never appears — he says nothing spontaneously, and the station exists to expose that: instruct before you start ('keep your head still and follow my pen with your eyes only; important — if you see double at any point, tell me straight away'), then ask direction by direction, including UP — 'full range of movement, no nystagmus, but diplopia on UPWARD GAZE, consistent with tethering of the INFERIOR RECTUS and INFERIOR OBLIQUE in an orbital floor fracture' (★)

FAIL — Pressing on the globe, or palpating both sides at once with both hands, which looks neat and wrecks the comparison — say the omission aloud ('I'm deliberately not palpating the globe, in case it is ruptured', because pressure would extrude intraocular contents), start on the UNINJURED side, one side at a time, and cover all FIVE regions: skull (temporal, parietal, occipital and vertex, for step or boggy swelling), orbital rims, nasal bones, zygomatic arches, and the mandible with the bite — including the LATERAL WALL, which is precisely where Version 2 hides its only positive finding (★)

FAIL — 'Inspection is normal apart from a bruise' — the marks are in the FIVE named negatives: no RACCOON EYES, no BATTLE SIGN behind the ears, no HYPHAEMA at the anterior chamber, no ENOPHTHALMOS or exophthalmos looked for from above and from the side, and no CSF LEAK from the nose or ears; add pupil SHAPE, because a teardrop or peaked pupil after trauma raises a RUPTURED GLOBE — stop, do not press on the eye, do not measure intraocular pressure, apply a RIGID SHIELD and never a pad, nil by mouth, head up, analgesia and antiemetics, tetanus prophylaxis, intravenous antibiotics and immediate ophthalmology (★)

FAIL — Giving a diagnosis with no supporting reasons — name THREE, each tied to something you found: 'there's a bruise there and it's tender exactly where that bone runs; when you look up you see double, because small muscles sitting on the floor of the socket get caught in the break; and your cheek is numb, because a nerve runs along that same bone' — the FLOOR TRIAD is inferior rim tenderness, upgaze diplopia and V2 numbness; test cranial V in all three divisions on BOTH sides (motor with the teeth clenched for temporalis and masseter, then cotton wool at forehead, cheek and jaw, because testing only the injured side leaves nothing to compare with) and VII with eyebrows, eyes shut, cheeks blown and teeth; and do not be derailed if a fundus photograph appears — describe it, then say it does not change today's traumatic diagnosis (★)

FAIL — Ordering plain facial X-rays as the definitive imaging, or discharging without the NOSE-BLOWING and DRIVING advice — the imaging is a CT of the facial bones and orbits with fine CORONAL cuts, and 'don't blow your nose, because it can push air from your sinus into the eye socket, and don't drive while you're seeing double'; reassure properly, because he asks whether he will lose the eye — 'your vision itself is completely normal, 6/6 in both eyes, your pupils are working properly and the eyeball hasn't been damaged; the double vision is a MECHANICAL problem from the muscles being caught, and in most people it settles as the swelling goes down over a week or two — and if it doesn't, there's an operation that frees the muscle and repairs the floor'; plus analgesia, ice, head elevation, ophthalmology and maxillofacial referral, review at 7 to 14 days, and surgery for persistent diplopia in primary or downgaze, enophthalmos over 2 mm, or a large defect; safety net — worsening pain, a bulging eye, worsening vision, fever, or feeling faint or sick; and the two emergencies: PROPTOSIS with a tense globe, severe pain, acuity 6/60 and a relative afferent pupillary defect is a RETROBULBAR HAEMORRHAGE with orbital compartment syndrome, a sight-threatening CLINICAL diagnosis needing immediate LATERAL CANTHOTOMY AND CANTHOLYSIS without waiting for a CT (MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 and telephone advice from a rural site), and BRADYCARDIA with vomiting in entrapment is the OCULOCARDIAC REFLEX (★)

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, abdomen plus DRE on a mannequin. FLAG the back passage in ONE sentence at the start — front-loading the full sensitive-examination consent burns ninety seconds and you will still repeat it; saying nothing makes it an ambush. THE STATION'S FAIL IS STOPPING AT HAEMORRHOIDS: the word COLONOSCOPY must be spoken unconditionally, in the same breath as the diagnosis, never contingent on what you felt — and never offer a faecal occult blood test, because he is symptomatic and therefore on the DIAGNOSTIC pathway, not the screening one.
stem: VERSION A (the common recall): general practice. A 40-year-old with irregular bowel motions and rectal bleeding; a rectal examination mannequin is provided. 8 minutes. Patient in this script: John Whelan.

VERSION B (the old anaemia recall): a 45-year-old man with exertional chest pain radiating to the left arm and shoulder, palpitations, tiredness and bright red blood in the stools — iron deficiency anaemia from chronic blood loss, unmasking stable angina. You are still asked for an abdomen and a rectum.
tasks: Talk to the patient and gain consent
Perform an abdominal and rectal examination with a running commentary
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: OPENING WIPE for the abdomen plus ONE flagging sentence about the back passage · GENERAL APPEARANCE, HANDS AND FACE with the anaemia signs made explicitly relevant (he is bleeding): pallor, bruising and petechiae, pale palmar creases, koilonychia, capillary refill and pulse volume, conjunctival pallor, sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes · and ASK FOR A POSTURAL BLOOD PRESSURE, which separates a candidate who is examining from one who is performing · THE ABDOMEN run without stopping: inspection (Cullen and Grey Turner named), cough, superficial then deep palpation of all nine regions, liver, spleen and kidneys, percussion for organomegaly and shifting dullness with the reason for NOT percussing rebound said aloud, bowel sounds · THE SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION CONSENT, 30-40 seconds: steps, position (left side, knees up), exposure, privacy and a sheet, a STOP SIGNAL, and a CHAPERONE · then gloves ('I'll just get my gloves') · INSPECTION IN FOUR GROUPED BURSTS, then bearing down · THE DIGITAL EXAMINATION: pronate the forearm so the finger pad faces ANTERIORLY, sweep a full 360, ask about pain, say you are CHECKING the anal tone, offer the prostate in a man · WITHDRAW AND ACTUALLY LOOK AT THE GLOVE, naming blood, mucus AND melaena · then the diagnosis with COLONOSCOPY said unconditionally, the differential list and the safety-net.

back.dx: HAEMORRHOIDS as the most likely diagnosis — three soft, squishy, compressible lumps in the anal canal, a clean glove and a normal abdomen — BUT the station is about what you say next: a 40-year-old with rectal bleeding and a CHANGED BOWEL HABIT gets a COLONOSCOPY, said unconditionally, because you cannot see behind a haemorrhoid with your finger. Differentials in order: COLORECTAL CARCINOMA — the one that must be excluded and which the examination cannot exclude; haemorrhoids; anal fissure; inflammatory bowel disease; diverticular disease; polyps; anticoagulant or bleeding disorder; plus proctitis and a brisk upper GI bleed, which usually gives melaena but can present as fresh blood. Bloods today: FBC and iron studies. Never offer an iFOBT to a symptomatic patient — the NBCSP iFOBT is two-yearly, mailed 50-74 and requestable 45-49, for ASYMPTOMATIC people only VERIFY. Safety-net: heavy bleeding, feeling faint or dizzy, or severe abdominal pain means come straight back or go to ED rather than waiting for the appointment. VERSION B: two problems, one cause — chronic blood loss has caused iron deficiency anaemia, and the reduced oxygen delivery is what unmasks the exertional chest pain, so 'the chest pain is the alarm; the bleeding is the fire' — bloods, iron treatment and a colonoscopy.
plan: Opening WIPE plus ONE flagging sentence: '...for the first part I will be looking at your tummy, gently feeling it, gently tapping on it, and listening to your bowel sounds. I will need you lying flat with your tummy fully exposed. I will wash my hands before I forget. Are you happy for me to go ahead? THERE IS A SECOND PART WHERE I WILL NEED TO EXAMINE YOUR BACK PASSAGE — I will explain that part properly when we get there. Is that all right?'

General appearance, hands and face, with the anaemia made relevant, and the postural BP requested: 'on general appearance the patient is alert and orientated, comfortable at rest, not in pain and not cachectic. HE HAS BEEN BLEEDING, so I am specifically looking for pallor, and for bruising or petechiae. At the hands: pale palmar creases, koilonychia, capillary refill and pulse volume. At the face: conjunctival pallor, sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. MAY I HAVE A FULL SET OF OBSERVATIONS INCLUDING A POSTURAL BLOOD PRESSURE?' (Skipping the peripheries because 'it's a rectal case' throws away the diagnosis in Version B.)

The abdomen, run without stopping and with omissions NARRATED: 'the abdomen is not distended, moves symmetrically with respiration, no scars, no visible masses, no distended veins, no Cullen or Grey Turner sign. John, could you give me a cough? Any pain anywhere? — no pain on coughing. Superficial palpation of all nine regions, watching his face: no tenderness, no guarding, no rigidity. Deep palpation of all nine regions: no masses. Liver edge not palpable, spleen not palpable, kidneys not ballotable. THERE IS NO LOCALISED TENDERNESS, SO I AM NOT PERCUSSING FOR REBOUND; I will percuss for organomegaly and shifting dullness. Bowel sounds are present and normal in character.' (The task said perform an abdominal examination, not the relevant parts of one — a narrated omission is a clinical decision, a silent one is a missing mark.)

THE SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION CONSENT, 30-40 seconds and no longer: 'now for the second part I need to examine your back passage. What I will do: first I will LOOK at the back passage, then INSERT ONE GLOVED, LUBRICATED FINGER to feel inside. It will feel uncomfortable and a little strange, but it should not be painful, AND I WILL STOP IMMEDIATELY IF YOU ASK ME TO. Position: lying on your LEFT SIDE, with your knees bent up towards your chest. Exposure: trousers and underwear off. I WILL STEP OUT AND GIVE YOU PRIVACY, and a sheet to cover yourself. Are you happy for me to go ahead? WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE in the room with us?' Then: 'I'll just get my gloves' — now, not at the start — and say you would DOCUMENT the consent, the chaperone and the findings. If he pushes ('do you actually have to do that bit?'): 'I understand — nobody enjoys it. It is the only way for me to find where the bleeding is coming from, and it takes under a minute.'

INSPECTION IN FOUR GROUPED BURSTS, not one breathless list: 'one — no fissure, no haemorrhoids, no prolapse. Two — no skin tags and no external fistula openings. Three — no bleeding and no discharge. Four — no swelling, no redness and no abnormal mass.' Then: 'could you bear down for me as though you were opening your bowels? — on straining there is no prolapse and no faecal incontinence.'

THE DIGITAL EXAMINATION: 'John, I am going to insert my finger now. TAKE A BREATH IN FOR ME.' Small amount of lubricant; PRONATE THE FOREARM so the finger pad faces anteriorly; press on the posterior wall, then slide. '1. I am SWEEPING A FULL 360 DEGREES — anterior, right lateral, posterior, left lateral. Three soft, squishy, compressible lumps consistent with haemorrhoids; no hard or irregular mass, and the rectum is empty of hard stool. 2. John, any pain as I feel around? — no pain. 3. John, squeeze my finger for me. Examiner, I AM CHECKING the anal tone. 4. I would also palpate anteriorly for the prostate — size, consistency, surface and median sulcus.' (A supinated hand cannot sweep the circumference and the examiner can see it from your forearm. And never say 'anal tone is normal' — the mannequin cannot squeeze, so that is a finding you did not obtain.)

WITHDRAW AND LOOK AT THE GLOVE — the cheapest mark in the station and the most commonly dropped. Hold the finger up, give it a beat, actually look: 'Examiner, there is NO BLOOD, NO MUCUS AND NO MELAENA on my glove.' Then: 'all done, John. Please get dressed in your own time and I will talk you through what I found.'

THE EXPLANATION THAT PASSES THE STATION: 'the most likely cause of your bleeding is haemorrhoids — swollen, enlarged blood tubes in the back passage that bleed when you pass a motion. Very common, very treatable. BUT I WANT TO BE STRAIGHT WITH YOU. You are forty, you are bleeding, and your bowel habit has changed. I CANNOT SEE BEHIND A HAEMORRHOID WITH MY FINGER. So I am arranging a COLONOSCOPY — a camera test of the whole large bowel — to be certain we are not missing a growth or a cancer. Not because I think you have one, but because the only way to be sure is to look.' → 'cancer? You think I've got cancer?' → 'I do not think that is the most likely answer, and I am not trying to frighten you. But it is the one thing I am not willing to guess about. Most people who have this test are given the all-clear.' → 'my dad had bowel cancer, he was 61' → thank him, and say it makes you more certain you are doing the right thing and that you will ask about the rest of the family. Then the differential list, the FBC and iron studies, and the safety-net (see dx).

'One — no fissure, haemorrhoids or prolapse. Two — no tags or fistulae. Three — no bleeding or discharge. Four — no swelling, redness or mass.' / 'Take a breath in for me.' / 'I am pronating my forearm and sweeping a full 360 degrees.' / 'Examiner, I am checking the anal tone.' / 'There is no blood, no mucus and no melaena on my glove.'

'Haemorrhoids are swollen, enlarged blood tubes in the back passage.' / 'I cannot see behind a haemorrhoid with my finger.' / 'My most likely diagnosis is haemorrhoids; my primary concern is colorectal carcinoma.' / 'May I have a full set of observations including a postural blood pressure?'

VARIANT 1 — THE CANCER MANNEQUIN ('a hard, irregular, fixed mass at 5 cm, and fresh blood on your glove'): DO NOT SOFTEN IT — 'John, I would rather tell you straight than leave you guessing. I have felt a lump in the back passage, and there was blood on my glove. THAT LUMP IS NOT A HAEMORRHOID. It could be a growth, and I am concerned it could be a cancer. I cannot tell you for certain today. I am going to refer you urgently to the bowel surgeons for a camera test and a biopsy — a small sample — and take blood today. That will happen within a couple of weeks. I know that is a lot to hear. Is there someone you would like with you when we talk again?'

VARIANT 2 — VERSION B, ANAEMIA AND ANGINA (pale, pulse 104, postural drop 16 mmHg, fresh blood on the glove): 'two things are going on and they are connected. First, you have been losing blood from your back passage, so you have become anaemic — a low level of red cells and haemoglobin, the part of the blood that carries oxygen. Second, that is why your chest hurts when you walk: with less oxygen being delivered your heart works harder and faster, and complains. That is angina. THE CHEST PAIN IS THE ALARM; THE BLEEDING IS THE FIRE. So the question I care about is why you are bleeding — blood tests today, iron treatment, and a camera test of the bowel.' / VARIANT 3 — THE PAINFUL FISSURE (posterior midline tear with a sentinel tag, and he flinches): 'I can see a small tear — an anal fissure. Given how tender it is I WILL NOT FORCE a finger examination today. I would treat it and examine internally once you are comfortable.' Declining the DRE for a STATED reason is a pass behaviour, not an omission.
pefe: Role-player: John Whelan, 40, plumber, married with two children, ten cigarettes a day and about eight standard drinks a week, no medications or previous surgery. Three months of unpredictable bowels — some days loose, some constipated, going more often — and six weeks of BRIGHT RED blood, on the paper and in the bowl, not mixed in, and PAINLESS. A bit of slime sometimes, a few kilos of weight loss put down to work, always tired, often feels he has not fully emptied, and the motions are sometimes thinner. HIS FATHER HAD BOWEL CANCER AT 61 — not volunteered early, given only when asked about family history, or at seven minutes: 'doctor — my dad had bowel cancer. Is that what this is?' He came hoping for a cream. Flat and brusque at first, quietly reluctant about the back passage, and genuinely frightened and QUIET when cancer is mentioned. HE PUSHES ONCE on consent ('do you actually have to do that bit?') and agrees if the candidate explains why and offers to stop. IF THE CANDIDATE REASSURES TOO EASILY — 'it's just piles, nothing to worry about' — HE ACCEPTS IT CHEERFULLY AND SAYS 'great, so I don't need anything else?' That is the trap closing.

Numbers: station 8 min — abdomen 3 min, rectal wipe 40 s, rectal examination 1.5 min, diagnosis and differentials 1.75 min. Anal canal 3-4 cm; FOUR inspection groups; FOUR prostate characteristics; sweep 360 degrees. Sphincters: resting tone = INTERNAL; squeeze = EXTERNAL, S2-S4; anal wink = anocutaneous reflex, S2-S4. Haemorrhoid grades: I bleed only, II reduce spontaneously, III manual reduction, IV irreducible. NBCSP iFOBT two-yearly, mailed 50-74 and requestable 45-49, ASYMPTOMATIC ONLY VERIFY.

Scored out of 10: introduced and consented for the abdomen; FLAGGED the back passage in one sentence rather than front-loading or ambushing; ran a complete abdominal examination narrating any deliberate omission; full sensitive-examination consent covering steps, position, exposure, privacy, sheet, STOP SIGNAL and CHAPERONE; gloved at the right moment; inspection in FOUR grouped bursts; pronation with a full 360 sweep, pain checked, and said 'CHECKING' the anal tone; LOOKED at the glove and said so; SAID COLONOSCOPY UNCONDITIONALLY and named bowel cancer as the primary concern; and gave a plural differential list with a safety-net.

must: FAIL — Stopping at haemorrhoids — this is the fail the station exists for; the word COLONOSCOPY must be spoken unconditionally and in the same breath as the diagnosis, never offered as a maybe and never made contingent on what you felt: 'the most likely cause of your bleeding is haemorrhoids — swollen, enlarged blood tubes in the back passage that bleed when you pass a motion, very common and very treatable; but I want to be straight with you — you're forty, you're bleeding, and your bowel habit has changed, and I cannot see behind a haemorrhoid with my finger, so I'm arranging a colonoscopy, a camera test of the whole large bowel, to be certain we're not missing a growth or a cancer'; and never offer a faecal occult blood test, because he is symptomatic and therefore on the DIAGNOSTIC pathway rather than the screening one (★)

FAIL — Quiet self-editing of the abdominal examination — the task said perform an abdominal examination, not the relevant parts of one, so if you leave something out, say out loud why: a narrated omission is a clinical decision, a silent one is a missing mark ('there is no localised tenderness, so I am not percussing for rebound; I will percuss for organomegaly and shifting dullness') (★)

FAIL — Never looking at the glove — the cheapest mark in the station and the most commonly dropped; withdraw, hold the finger up, ACTUALLY look at it and give it a beat, then say all three negatives explicitly so the examiner knows you were looking for each one: 'there is no blood, no MUCUS and no MELAENA on my glove' — and dark, tarry stool changes the case to an upper gastrointestinal source (★)

FAIL — A supinated hand with the finger straight in and no rotation, so a full 360° sweep is physically impossible and an examiner watching your forearm can see it — PRONATE the forearm so the finger pad faces anteriorly, press on the posterior wall and then slide, and sweep anterior, right lateral, posterior, left lateral; and never say 'anal tone is normal', because the mannequin cannot squeeze and that is a finding you did not obtain — say you are CHECKING it ('John, squeeze my finger for me; Examiner, I am checking the anal tone'), then offer the prostate anteriorly for size, consistency, surface and median sulcus (★)

FAIL — Front-loading the whole sensitive-examination consent at the start, which burns ninety seconds and still has to be repeated, or saying nothing about the back passage at all, which makes it an ambush later — ONE flagging sentence early ('there is a second part where I'll need to examine your back passage; I'll explain that part properly when we get there'), then the full consent in 30 to 40 seconds when you arrive: what you will do (look first, then one gloved, lubricated finger), that it will feel uncomfortable and a little strange but should not be painful, THE STOP SIGNAL ('I will stop immediately if you ask me to'), the position (on the left side, knees bent up towards the chest), the exposure, privacy and a sheet, and the CHAPERONE offer — the chaperone box and the stop signal are single-line items with marks attached and both are routinely dropped; get the gloves at that point rather than at the start, and say you would document the consent, the chaperone and the findings

SAY — Do not skip the peripheries because 'it's a rectal case' — the stem hands you a bleeding patient, so every anaemia sign is directly relevant, and asking for a POSTURAL blood pressure is what separates a candidate who is examining from one who is performing: pallor, bruising and petechiae, pale palmar creases, koilonychia, capillary refill and pulse volume, then conjunctival pallor, sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes; deliver the perianal inspection in FOUR LABELLED BURSTS rather than one breathless list, because twelve findings fired off in a single breath sound like recall while four groups sound like a system — one, no fissure, haemorrhoids or prolapse; two, no skin tags or external fistula openings; three, no bleeding or discharge; four, no swelling, redness or abnormal mass — then ask him to BEAR DOWN for prolapse and faecal incontinence; give the differentials in order with COLORECTAL CARCINOMA as the primary concern the examination cannot exclude, then haemorrhoids as most likely, anal fissure, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticular disease, polyps, an anticoagulant or bleeding disorder, proctitis, and a brisk upper gastrointestinal bleed; FBC and iron studies today, ask about the rest of the family history, and safety-net heavy bleeding, faintness or dizziness, or severe abdominal pain as a same-day return; variants — a HARD, IRREGULAR, FIXED mass at 5 cm with fresh blood on the glove is not softened ('I have felt a lump in the back passage, and there was blood on my glove; that lump is not a haemorrhoid — it could be a growth, and I am concerned it could be a cancer… I'm referring you urgently to the bowel surgeons for a camera test and a biopsy within a couple of weeks. Is there someone you'd like with you when we talk again?'); pale with a pulse of 104 and a 16 mmHg postural drop is iron deficiency anaemia from chronic blood loss unmasking angina — 'the chest pain is the alarm; the bleeding is the fire'; and a tender posterior midline tear with a sentinel tag means DECLINING the digital examination for a stated reason, which is pass behaviour rather than an omission

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, abdomen plus DRE on a mannequin after an episode of urinary retention. THE TRAP IS IN THE FIRST SENTENCE: the word CATHETER is bait, and there is no management step here — the tasks are examination, examination, explanation. Three things decide it: a complete abdominal examination with AUDIBLE SUPRAPUBIC EMPHASIS; a correctly consented DRE with the FINGER PAD ANTERIOR; and ALL FOUR PROSTATE CHARACTERISTICS spoken out loud. And the last mark is honesty: a DRE cannot exclude cancer.
stem: General practice. A man who had an episode of URINARY RETENTION three days ago, resolved with a catheter, presenting today for further examination. Age recalled as 46 or 76 — it changes nothing. Patient in this script: Gary Nolan, 76. 8 minutes. Some recalls ask you to explain to the examiner rather than the patient.
tasks: Perform an abdominal examination
Perform a rectal examination on the mannequin
Explain your findings and your diagnosis to the patient
time: OPENING WIPE plus the one-sentence flag about the back passage · and if pushed to re-catheterise, ONE sentence back: 'you were catheterised three days ago and that has settled, so my job now is to work out why it happened' · GENERAL APPEARANCE AND HANDS with each item made relevant in a clause (alert and orientated, BECAUSE neurological causes are on the differential; not in pain at rest, BECAUSE retention and prostatitis both hurt), and observations INCLUDING TEMPERATURE · THE ABDOMEN with three 'SPECIFICALLY' lines: no visible suprapubic masses, swellings or distension; no suprapubic TENDERNESS on superficial palpation; no suprapubic MASS on deep palpation · plus kidneys and renal angles · PERCUSSION from just above the symphysis working UPWARDS (distended = DULL and you cannot get below it; empty pelvis = RESONANT) and bowel sounds, with the faecal-impaction reason ready · SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION CONSENT 30-45 seconds with stop signal and chaperone, then gloves · PERIANAL INSPECTION in four grouped bursts and bearing down, EVEN THOUGH none of it relates to retention · THE ANAL CANAL BEFORE THE GLAND: pronate, 360 sweep, pain checked, hard stool · THE FOUR CHARACTERISTICS in order every time · ANAL TONE and the ANAL WINK with the cauda equina reason ready · the glove looked at · then the explanation: gland, findings, name, and THE HONEST LIMIT.

back.dx: BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA — an enlarged gland (larger than a walnut, more than two finger-pads across) that is FIRM AND RUBBERY rather than hard, with a SMOOTH surface and no nodularity, a PRESERVED MEDIAN SULCUS and no tenderness, in a man with a poor stream, hesitancy, terminal dribbling, nocturia and incomplete emptying who went into retention. Explain it as: a walnut-shaped gland sitting just under the bladder with the urine pipe running THROUGH THE MIDDLE of it, so as it grows the flow gets squeezed. THEN THE HONEST LIMIT — a digital examination CANNOT rule out cancer: many tumours are impalpable and a smooth rubbery gland is compatible with an early carcinoma, so discuss PSA — deferred about SIX WEEKS after catheterisation, infection or retention, because all three push the number up (and finasteride halves it) VERIFY. Also today: urine test, bladder scan for post-void residual, renal function, and an alpha-blocker to relax the outlet (tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily; finasteride 5 mg daily with effect over 3-6 months VERIFY). Differentials for retention to keep visible: BPH, prostate carcinoma, prostatitis, urethral stricture, faecal impaction, DRUGS (he recently started a sedating antihistamine, and anticholinergics precipitate retention), and CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME. Safety-net: unable to pass urine at all, a painful swollen lower abdomen, fever and shakes, or numbness around the saddle area or leg weakness — straight back or to ED.
plan: WIPE, the flag, and the catheter question answered in ONE sentence: 'for the first part I will be looking at your tummy, feeling it, gently tapping on it, and I may listen to your bowel sounds at the end... there is a second part where I will need to examine your back passage — I will explain the steps when we get there.' → 'shouldn't you be putting that tube back in?' → 'Not today. You were catheterised three days ago and that has settled, so my job now is to examine you and work out why it happened in the first place.' If the examiner probes: 'I would never catheterise anyone without at least a brief history and an abdominal examination confirming a distended bladder — which is exactly the examination I am doing now.'

General appearance and hands, each made relevant in a clause: 'on general appearance Gary is ALERT AND ORIENTATED — relevant because neurological causes are on my differential list — and he is NOT IN PAIN AT REST, which matters because retention and prostatitis are both painful. At the hands I am looking for pale palmar creases. MAY I HAVE A FULL SET OF OBSERVATIONS, INCLUDING TEMPERATURE?' (In the prostatitis variant the answer is 38.8 and a pulse of 108.)

THE ABDOMEN with the suprapubic volume turned up — three 'specifically' lines: 'on inspection the abdomen is not distended, moves symmetrically, no scars or distended veins — AND SPECIFICALLY, IN THE SUPRAPUBIC AREA, no visible masses, swellings or distension. Gary, could you give me a cough? Any pain? — no pain. Superficial palpation of all nine regions: no tenderness, guarding or rigidity — AND SPECIFICALLY, NO SUPRAPUBIC TENDERNESS. Deep palpation of all nine: no masses — AND SPECIFICALLY, NO SUPRAPUBIC MASS. Kidneys not ballotable, no renal angle tenderness.' (What a suprapubic mass represents in retention is THE DISTENDED BLADDER — smooth, dull, tender, arising out of the pelvis and you cannot get below it. Bladder tumours are essentially never palpable abdominally.)

Percussion and auscultation, with both challenge answers ready: 'I will percuss from just above the symphysis pubis working UPWARDS. It is RESONANT — examiner, the bladder is not distended. Bowel sounds are present and normal in character.' → 'why not auscultatory percussion?' → 'stethoscope above the symphysis, direct percussion down the midline, a sudden increase in loudness at the upper border — but it only informs you when the bladder is ALREADY distended, which palpation has told me.' → 'why bowel sounds in a urinary case?' → 'faecal impaction is a genuine cause of retention, and the task asked for an abdominal examination, not part of one.' GET THE DIRECTION RIGHT: distended = DULL, empty pelvis = RESONANT.

SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION CONSENT, 30-45 seconds: steps (look, then one gloved lubricated finger to feel inside AND TO FEEL THE PROSTATE), 'uncomfortable but should not be painful, and I WILL STOP IMMEDIATELY IF YOU ASK', left side with knees to chest, trousers and underwear off, privacy and a sheet, 'are you happy for me to proceed? WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE with us? I will just get my gloves' — and document the consent, chaperone and findings. → 'is that the test for prostate cancer?' → 'it is part of assessing the prostate — it tells me the size, how it feels and whether the surface is smooth. It is not the whole answer on cancer; there is also a blood test we can talk about afterwards.'

Perianal inspection in four grouped bursts and bearing down — EVEN THOUGH none of it relates to retention, because skipping it tells the examiner you were pattern-matching the stem. Then THE ANAL CANAL BEFORE THE GLAND: 'take a breath in for me. Examiner, I am PRONATING MY FOREARM so the finger pad faces ANTERIORLY, and sweeping a full 360 degrees — anterior, right lateral, posterior, left lateral. No abnormal lumps, and the rectum is empty of hard stool. Gary, any pain as I feel around? — no pain.' (Supinated, the pad sits on the coccyx, and telling the examiner you are feeling the prostate while pointing at the sacrum is marked as an accuracy failure.)

THE FOUR CHARACTERISTICS — the scoring block, in this order every time and said aloud even when you can feel almost nothing: 'turning my finger anteriorly to the prostate. SIZE — larger than a walnut, spanning more than two finger-pads. CONSISTENCY — firm and rubbery, which is normal; not hard or stony. SURFACE — rubbing across the whole accessible surface, smooth, with no nodularity. MEDIAN SULCUS — the central groove is preserved. TENDERNESS — not tender.' Then: 'Gary, squeeze my finger for me. Examiner, I AM CHECKING the anal tone. May I have a cotton bud? I would like to check the ANAL WINK — if not I will stroke either side of the verge with my gloved finger: I am testing the anocutaneous reflex.' (Why bother: 'cauda equina syndrome causes painless retention with saddle anaesthesia and reduced anal tone, so tone and perianal sensation are how I screen for it. Resting tone is the internal sphincter; squeeze is the external, S2 to S4.') Withdraw, LOOK at the glove: 'no blood, no mucus and no melaena.'

THE EXPLANATION — gland first, then findings, then the name, then the LIMIT: 'today I was examining a gland called the prostate. It is a small walnut-shaped gland sitting just underneath the bladder, and the tube that carries urine out runs STRAIGHT THROUGH THE MIDDLE of it. I was checking four things. How big it is — yours is a little larger than we expect, common as men get older. How it feels — firm and rubbery, which is normal, not hard. The surface — smooth, no lumps. And a groove that normally runs down the middle — I could feel it clearly. Putting that together, I think you have BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA. Benign means not a cancer. The gland has grown, and because the pipe runs through it the flow gets squeezed — which is why you went into retention.' → 'so it's definitely not cancer then' → DO NOT AGREE: 'what I felt today is reassuring — nothing hard, no lumps, and the groove was normal. But I have to be straight with you: FEELING THE GLAND CANNOT RULE A CANCER OUT ON ITS OWN. So I would like to talk about a blood test called PSA. Because a catheter and the retention itself push that number up, the right time to check it is in about SIX WEEKS.' Then urine test, bladder scan for residual, renal function, an alpha-blocker, and the safety-net (see dx).

VARIANT 1 — THE CARCINOMA GLAND ('hard, craggy, nodular; you cannot feel the median sulcus'): to the examiner, 'the gland is enlarged, STONY HARD, with an irregular nodular surface and an OBLITERATED median sulcus — suspicious of prostate carcinoma.' To the patient, do not soften it: 'the gland felt harder and more irregular than I would expect, and the normal groove was not there. I cannot tell you today what that is, but it needs looking into urgently. I am referring you to a urologist and taking bloods including a PSA.'

VARIANT 2 — PAINLESS RETENTION WITH REDUCED TONE (younger man, back pain, numb when wiping, both legs heavy; 'anal tone is reduced'): THIS BECOMES AN EMERGENCY — 'I have painless retention with reduced anal tone. I would immediately test perianal sensation in the saddle distribution, lower limb power, reflexes and plantars. My primary concern is CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME, which requires an urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine and a same-day neurosurgical referral. This is time-critical and I would escalate before completing the examination.' / VARIANT 3 — 'EXPLAIN TO THE EXAMINER' rather than the patient: shorter and easier — 'the prostate is enlarged, of normal firm-rubbery consistency, with a smooth surface, no nodularity and a preserved median sulcus, and it is not tender. My diagnosis is benign prostatic hyperplasia. I WOULD NOT RELY ON THE DIGITAL EXAMINATION ALONE TO EXCLUDE CARCINOMA, and would discuss PSA testing in about six weeks.' Do not drop that last sentence just because you are talking to an examiner.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Nolan, 76, retired grain farmer, widowed and living alone, on amlodipine and a RECENTLY STARTED SEDATING ANTIHISTAMINE for hay fever (given only if asked directly — and it is the drug that precipitated the retention). Three days ago he could not pass urine at all, his lower abdomen swelled and became very painful, a catheter drained a great deal, the tube came out yesterday and he is passing urine again with a poor stream. Admits if asked: poor stream and terminal dribbling for a couple of years, hesitancy, up three or four times a night, never feels completely empty; NO burning, blood, fevers, back pain, saddle numbness, leg weakness or weight loss. HIS BROTHER HAD PROSTATE CANCER AT 70 — not volunteered early, given when asked about family or at seven minutes. Dry, understated, gruff; he minimises everything. HE OPENS WITH THE CATHETER QUESTION — 'shouldn't you be putting that tube back in?' — and if the candidate agrees to catheterise, that is the trap closing. He is mildly reluctant about the back passage and agrees if the steps are explained and a stop signal offered; if no chaperone is offered he does not help. WHEN THE DIAGNOSIS IS GIVEN HE PUSHES ONCE: 'so it's definitely not cancer then.' If the candidate says yes, he accepts it happily — the second trap closing.

Resting tone = internal sphincter; squeeze = external, S2-S4; anal wink = anocutaneous reflex, S2-S4. DISTENDED BLADDER = DULL and you cannot get below it; EMPTY PELVIS = RESONANT. Residual over 1000 mL risks post-obstructive diuresis. PSA deferred about SIX WEEKS after catheterisation, infection or retention; finasteride HALVES the PSA. Tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily; finasteride 5 mg daily with effect over 3-6 months VERIFY.

must: FAIL — Being pulled into management and agreeing to re-catheterise — the word CATHETER in the first sentence is bait, and the tasks are examination, examination, explanation with no management step in between; answer in one sentence and return to the examination: 'not today — you were catheterised three days ago and that has settled, so my job now is to examine you and work out why it happened in the first place', and if the examiner probes, 'I would never catheterise anyone without at least a brief history and an abdominal examination confirming a distended bladder — which is exactly the examination I am doing now' (★)

FAIL — Telling him the examination has ruled cancer out — he pushes once with 'so it's definitely not cancer then', and the digital examination has poor sensitivity, with many tumours impalpable and a smooth rubbery gland entirely compatible with an early cancer; give the finding, THEN the limit: 'what I felt today is reassuring — nothing hard, no lumps, and the groove was normal — but I have to be straight with you: feeling the gland cannot rule a cancer out on its own, so I'd like to talk about a blood test called PSA, and because a catheter and the retention itself push that number up, the right time to check it is in about SIX WEEKS' (★)

FAIL — Naming only two of the four prostate characteristics — the marks are for the COMMENTARY, not the findings, so say all four aloud even when you can feel almost nothing, in the same order every time: SIZE (larger than a walnut, spanning more than two finger-pads), CONSISTENCY (firm and rubbery, which is normal, not hard or stony), SURFACE (rubbing across the whole accessible surface, smooth with no nodularity) and MEDIAN SULCUS (the central groove preserved) — plus TENDERNESS (★)

FAIL — Skipping perianal inspection because 'this is a prostate examination' — none of those findings relate to retention, and saying them anyway is what shows you are not pattern-matching the stem: four labelled bursts (no fissure, haemorrhoids or prolapse; no skin tags or fistula openings; no bleeding or discharge; no swelling, redness or abnormal mass), then bear down for prolapse and faecal incontinence; and in the abdomen turn the SUPRAPUBIC volume up with the three 'specifically' lines — specifically no visible suprapubic masses, swellings or distension on inspection, specifically no suprapubic tenderness on superficial palpation, specifically no suprapubic mass on deep palpation — then percuss from just above the symphysis UPWARDS with the direction right (a distended bladder is DULL and you cannot get below it; an empty pelvis is RESONANT), and listen to the bowel sounds, because faecal impaction is a genuine cause of retention and the task asked for an abdominal examination, not part of one

SAY — Explain the GLAND first, then your findings, then the name: 'the prostate is a small walnut-shaped gland sitting just underneath the bladder, and the tube that carries urine out runs straight through the middle of it — I was checking four things: how big it is, and yours is a little larger than we expect, which is common as men get older; how it feels, firm and rubbery, which is normal, not hard; the surface, smooth with no lumps; and a groove that normally runs down the middle, which I could feel clearly — so I think you have BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA, and benign means not a cancer: the gland has grown, and because the pipe runs through it the flow gets squeezed, which is why you went into retention'; then urine testing, a bladder scan for the post-void residual, renal function, and a tablet to relax the outlet (tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily; finasteride 5 mg daily working over three to six months, and finasteride HALVES the PSA); ask the family history rather than waiting for it; safety net — unable to pass urine at all, a painful swollen lower abdomen, fever and shakes, or numbness around the saddle area or weakness in the legs; variants — a HARD, CRAGGY, NODULAR gland with an obliterated median sulcus is not softened ('the gland felt harder and more irregular than I would expect, and the normal groove was not there; I can't tell you today what that is, but it needs looking into urgently — I'm referring you to a urologist and taking bloods including a PSA'), and PAINLESS retention with REDUCED ANAL TONE in a younger man with back pain, saddle numbness and heavy legs is CAUDA EQUINA — test perianal sensation in the saddle distribution, lower limb power, reflexes and plantars, then urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine and a same-day neurosurgical referral, escalating BEFORE completing the examination
