Answer the examiner's questions on initial investigations
time: ONE GROUPED EXPLANATION plus the position warning (sitting first, then flat), then: GENERAL APPEARANCE (cachexia, scratch marks, pallor, jaundice, rash), HANDS (clubbing, koilonychia, Raynaud, digital infarcts, purpura) and the PULSE as a marker of anaemia · EPITROCHLEAR both sides, palm under the elbow and THUMB PROXIMAL AND ANTERIOR TO THE MEDIAL EPICONDYLE (not the ulnar groove, which is cubital tunnel) · AXILLAE both sides, arm supported on your forearm, FIVE named positions: apical, central, pectoral, subscapular, lateral · FACE AND MOUTH: conjunctivae, sclerae, gums, tongue for atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis, tonsils and WALDEYER'S RING · CERVICAL from behind, EIGHT chains ending at SUPRACLAVICULAR from the front with a shoulder shrug, and in the same movement PRESS THE CLAVICLES AND STERNUM for bone tenderness · ABDOMEN BY 5:30: inspection, then the SPLEEN two-handed starting in the RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA with the left hand lifting the posterolateral ribs, then ROLL HIM ONTO HIS RIGHT SIDE (the spleen is on the left, so you roll him towards you), then CASTELL'S percussion, then the liver EDGE only · INGUINAL NODES offered with permission and a chaperone · completion (legs, fundoscopy, obs chart, urine dipstick) · then the 40-second summary and the investigations.

back.dx: GENERALISED LYMPHADENOPATHY — LYMPHOMA UNTIL EXCLUDED, and in this case HODGKIN LYMPHOMA given his age and B symptoms: a six-week painless cervical swelling unchanged by antibiotics, with drenching night sweats, 6 kg weight loss and pruritus, and EXCORIATIONS as the single positive finding. Relevant negatives: no palpable nodes in the epitrochlear, axillary or cervical chains INCLUDING both supraclavicular fossae, no Waldeyer's ring enlargement, no nail, gum or tongue signs, no pallor or jaundice, no clavicular or sternal bone tenderness, no organomegaly and a normal Castell's. Considered and less likely: EBV, HIV and tuberculosis (painless node failing antibiotics over six weeks), and metastatic carcinoma (34 years old, no hard fixed node). INVESTIGATIONS: bedside — observations, temperature chart, urinalysis; bloods — FBC with film, LDH, urate, ESR, U&E, LFT, calcium, coagulation, EBV and CMV serology, HIV with consent; imaging — CHEST X-RAY for a mediastinal mass, then CT neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis; definitive — EXCISIONAL LYMPH NODE BIOPSY, because lymphoma is diagnosed on NODAL ARCHITECTURE and fine-needle aspiration gives cells without architecture. What would worry you most: FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA — antibiotics within an hour — and SUPERIOR VENA CAVA OBSTRUCTION from a mediastinal mass (facial swelling, distended neck veins, breathlessness). Rural: haematology at the Royal Adelaide or Flinders, surgical referral for the biopsy, PATS arranged EARLY, Country Health Connect for local nursing, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if he deteriorates.
plan: WIPE with ONE grouped explanation and the position warning: '...I've been asked to examine your blood and gland system today. That means I'll be looking at your hands, your face, inside your mouth and your tummy, and feeling for glands in your elbows, your armpits, your neck and your groin, and feeling your tummy for organs. At the end I'll gently tap on the left side of your tummy. I'll START WITH YOU SITTING and then ask you to LIE FLAT for the tummy part. I'll need your arms and tummy uncovered and I'll cover you again as soon as I can. Tell me if anything is uncomfortable and I'll stop.' (Twelve step-by-step explanations burn 90 seconds; skipping the position warning stalls you at both changes.)

General appearance, hands and pulse — and USE the positive when it comes: 'from the end of the bed Gary is alert and comfortable. I'm looking for cachexia, SCRATCH MARKS, pallor, jaundice and any rash.' → 'there are excoriations over the trunk and arms' → 'THANK YOU — excoriations fit the itch he described and are recognised in lymphoma.' Then 'nails for clubbing and koilonychia; fingers for Raynaud phenomenon and digital infarcts; skin for purpura. Pulse regular at about 88 — NO TACHYCARDIA TO SUGGEST SIGNIFICANT ANAEMIA.' (Saying 'okay' to a handed positive loses the interpretation mark.)

EPITROCHLEAR and AXILLAE: 'I'm placing my left palm under the left elbow and palpating with my thumb, JUST PROXIMAL AND SLIGHTLY ANTERIOR TO THE MEDIAL EPICONDYLE, in the groove between biceps and triceps — the epitrochlear node. Nothing on the left; same on the right with my right thumb. No epitrochlear lymphadenopathy.' Then 'supporting the right arm on my right forearm so the axillary muscles relax, palpating with my left hand: APICAL high into the apex, CENTRAL onto the chest wall, PECTORAL behind the anterior fold, SUBSCAPULAR under the edge of the scapula, LATERAL along the inner upper arm. No right axillary lymphadenopathy.' → 'you may skip the other side' → 'thank you — I'll take the left as normal.' (Palpating the ulnar groove and calling it epitrochlear is the wrong site named correctly, and scores as an inaccurate examination.)

FACE AND MOUTH: 'could you look up for me? Conjunctivae pink, no pallor. Look down — sclerae white, no jaundice. Open wide — gums for hypertrophy and bleeding: healthy. Tongue for ATROPHIC GLOSSITIS: papillae normal. Corners of the mouth for ANGULAR CHEILITIS: none. Say aah — no tonsillar enlargement and no enlargement elsewhere in WALDEYER'S RING.' (Not 'angular colitis'. The tonsils are lymphoid tissue and belong in this examination, not an ENT one.)

CERVICAL — eight chains from behind, then supraclavicular and BONE TENDERNESS as one movement: 'could you come and sit on the edge of the bed? I'm standing behind you with both hands under your chin. SUBMENTAL — SUBMANDIBULAR — anterior cervical or JUGULAR chain in front of sternocleidomastoid — POSTERIOR TRIANGLE behind it — PRE- and POST-AURICULAR — OCCIPITAL. Coming round to the front: could you SHRUG YOUR SHOULDERS up for me? Pressing above the collarbones for the SUPRACLAVICULAR nodes — none on either side. WHILE I'M HERE I'll press the clavicles and the sternum for bone tenderness — any pain, Gary? No bone tenderness.' (Supraclavicular is the eighth chain — candidates finish at occipital and walk away; and hands come off the clavicle without ever pressing the bone.)

ABDOMEN BY 5:30 — inspection and the spleen, two-handed: 'lie flat for me now and I'll uncover your tummy. No visible mass, no distension, the abdomen moves symmetrically with respiration. Standing on your right, MY LEFT HAND goes behind your lower left ribs, lifting forward. MY RIGHT HAND STARTS IN THE RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA, flat, parallel to the left costal margin. Big breath in and out — and again — moving diagonally up to the costal margin. I cannot feel a splenic edge. Gary, ROLL ONTO YOUR RIGHT SIDE TOWARDS ME — one more press under the costal margin. Examiner, there is no splenomegaly.' (One-handed palpation, or starting at the costal margin, slides past the edge; rolling him LEFT is backwards — the spleen is on the left, so you roll him right to bring it forward.)

PERCUSSION AND LIVER EDGE — do BOTH spleen methods: 'I'll also percuss using CASTELL'S METHOD — the lowest intercostal space in the anterior axillary line on the left. Percussing in expiration: resonant. Deep breath in and hold — still resonant. Castell's is normal.' → 'what would a dull note on inspiration mean?' → 'SPLENOMEGALY — inspiration pushes an enlarged spleen down across the percussion point, so a resonant note becomes dull.' Then 'palpating for the LIVER EDGE from the right iliac fossa towards the right costal margin — no liver edge, so no clinical hepatomegaly.' (Do not measure a liver span here — that belongs to the chronic liver disease station and costs you the closing minute.)

INGUINAL AND COMPLETION, then the 40-second summary: 'I would now like to examine the INGUINAL LYMPH NODES — the horizontal chain along the inguinal ligament and the vertical chain along the femoral vessels — with the patient's permission and a chaperone.' → 'you don't need to' → 'thank you. In the legs I'd look for ulcers, scratch marks and peripheral neuropathy. To complete I'd perform fundoscopy, check the observation and temperature chart and dipstick the urine.' (Skipping the groin is for HIS dignity, not your clock — if you never say the words you are marked as having missed a node group.) Then the summary: SUMMARY SENTENCE, POSITIVES, RELEVANT NEGATIVES, DIAGNOSIS, DIFFERENTIALS EACH WITH A REASON, PLAN, ESCALATION (see dx). His hidden agenda: 'my uncle had leukaemia. Is that what I've got?' → 'I can hear that's frightening, and I'm glad you told me. I don't know yet — the most useful next step is a small operation to take the whole gland out and look at it. I'll organise that and the blood tests today, and I'll ring you either way. If you get a fever above 38, breathlessness or swelling of your face, come straight back.'

ask: 'I'll be looking at your hands, face, mouth and tummy, and feeling for glands in your elbows, armpits, neck and groin.' / 'Start sitting as you are, then I'll ask you to lie flat for the tummy part.' / 'Left palm under the elbow, palpating with my thumb, proximal and anterior to the medial epicondyle — the epitrochlear node.' / 'Apical, central, pectoral, subscapular, lateral — no axillary lymphadenopathy.'

'No tonsillar enlargement and no enlargement elsewhere in Waldeyer's ring.' / 'Could you shrug your shoulders up for me?' / 'While I'm here I'll press the clavicles and sternum for bone tenderness.' / 'My left hand is behind the posterolateral lower ribs; my right hand starts in the right iliac fossa.' / 'Roll onto your right side towards me.' / 'Castell's method is normal — there is no splenomegaly.'

'I would examine the inguinal nodes with the patient's permission and a chaperone.' / 'Fine-needle aspiration cannot show nodal architecture, so I'd request an excisional biopsy.' / Commentary in THREE BEATS every time: REGION, then STRUCTURE, then FINDING — 'moving to the axilla, palpating the apical group, no lymphadenopathy.' Narrating intentions without ever stating a result, or reporting a region your hands never visited, both lose marks.

VARIANT B — IRON DEFICIENCY (52 F, tired, Hb 88, MCV 68, ferritin 6): the hands and mouth become the scored block — 'nails: I'm looking specifically for KOILONYCHIA, the spoon-shaped nail of longstanding iron deficiency. Pulse 104 and regular — a tachycardia consistent with significant anaemia... conjunctivae are pale; the tongue is smooth and shiny with loss of papillae — ATROPHIC GLOSSITIS; there is redness and fissuring at both angles — ANGULAR CHEILITIS. These three together are the classic triad.' The examiner's question: 'the single most important next step is TO FIND THE SOURCE OF BLOOD LOSS. In a woman of 52 I'd ask about menstrual and postmenopausal bleeding, and arrange gastroscopy and colonoscopy — IRON DEFICIENCY IN A MAN OR A POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMAN IS GASTROINTESTINAL CANCER UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. I'd also send coeliac serology.' Rescue line if the hands and mouth have eaten four minutes: 'I've covered the peripheral signs of anaemia; I'll now complete the lymph node survey and the spleen.'

VARIANT C — THROMBOCYTOPENIC PURPURA (28 F, easy bruising, platelets 18): 'there is a NON-BLANCHING rash over both shins — I'm pressing with a glass slide and it does not blanch. The pinpoint lesions are PETECHIAE and the larger confluent areas are ECCHYMOSES; together this is a purpuric rash.' Then: 'I'm checking the gums and palate for bleeding and petechiae, because WET PURPURA — mucosal bleeding — means a higher bleeding risk. THE SPLEEN IS THE DISCRIMINATOR: a palpable spleen argues AGAINST immune thrombocytopenia and points to hypersplenism, lymphoproliferative disease or marrow infiltration.' Four causes: IMMUNE (ITP); MARROW failure or infiltration (leukaemia, aplasia, drugs); CONSUMPTION (DIC, TTP, HUS); SEQUESTRATION (hypersplenism) — and exclude pseudothrombocytopenia by repeating the count in a citrate tube. The trap is describing the rash at length and forgetting the answer is in the left upper quadrant.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Whitfield, 34, storeman at the Wallaroo grain terminal, living in Kadina with his partner and two kids; ten cigarettes a day since 19, six to eight beers on a Friday; a Ventolin puffer twice a year; finished amoxicillin from another GP three weeks ago with no effect. UNCLE DIED OF LEUKAEMIA AT 51. Noticed the lump in the shower six weeks ago, painless and barely changed; soaks the sheets two or three nights a week; about 6 kg down so his trousers are loose; ITCHY ALL OVER, especially after a hot shower, scratching until he marks himself. Starts flat and cooperative, a practical bloke who doesn't make a fuss, follows every instruction promptly; around the neck he becomes quieter and points at the lump once. Winces at rough or unwarned pressure; asks 'what are you looking for?' once if explained nothing for two minutes. HIDDEN AGENDA: frightened this is his uncle's leukaemia — given if asked about concerns, otherwise at the very end: 'my uncle had leukaemia. Is that what I've got?' Only then does his voice tighten.

Numbers: 8 cervical chains, 5 axillary groups, 2 key points (the spleen done by BOTH palpation and percussion), 2 bones (clavicles and sternum). Node size thresholds: over 1 cm abnormal; over 1.5 cm inguinal; over 0.5 cm epitrochlear; ANY supraclavicular node is abnormal. Four node characteristics: size, consistency, tenderness, mobility. Over 10% weight loss defines a B symptom. Four to six weeks off contact sport after infectious mononucleosis. Under one hour to antibiotics in febrile neutropenia. HANDS ON THE ABDOMEN BY 5:30. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450, Cancer Council 13 11 20.

Scored in three columns, and THE MIDDLE ONE IS PASS/FAIL: approach and rapport (introduced, identified, consented; ONE grouped explanation; warned before each position change; redraped and washed hands; responded to the leukaemia question with empathy before facts); COMPLETENESS (epitrochlear both sides, axillae both sides with five positions each, all eight cervical chains named, supraclavicular done from the front, clavicle and sternum pressed, inguinal mentioned out loud); and accuracy and synthesis (thumb proximal and anterior to the medial epicondyle, two-handed spleen from the right iliac fossa, rolled the patient RIGHT, Castell's percussion done, commentary naming region-structure-finding, and a committed diagnosis with reasons). If the middle column is not complete, it is a fail no matter how good the rest was.

must: FAIL — An incomplete survey — the COMPLETENESS column is pass/fail no matter how good the rest was: EPITROCHLEAR both sides, FIVE axillary groups each side, ALL EIGHT cervical chains named, supraclavicular done FROM THE FRONT, the clavicles and sternum pressed for BONE TENDERNESS, and the inguinal nodes mentioned out loud (★)

FAIL — Never saying the words about the GROIN — it is skipped for HIS dignity, not to save your clock, and silence is marked as a missed lymph node group: 'I would now like to examine the inguinal lymph nodes — the horizontal chain along the inguinal ligament and the vertical chain along the femoral vessels — with the patient's permission and a chaperone'; the opposite error is worse, which is uncovering the groin without asking (★)

FAIL — Palpating the ULNAR GROOVE and calling it epitrochlear — that is where you tap for cubital tunnel syndrome, and the wrong site named correctly scores as an inaccurate examination; the epitrochlear node is found with your palm UNDER the elbow and your THUMB palpating just PROXIMAL AND SLIGHTLY ANTERIOR to the medial epicondyle, in the groove between biceps and triceps (★)

FAIL — One squeeze of the armpit followed by 'axillary nodes are normal', or reciting five names while one hand sits in one spot — SUPPORT the arm on your forearm so the axillary muscles relax, palpate with the opposite hand, and MOVE it five times, naming each: APICAL or infraclavicular high into the apex, CENTRAL down onto the chest wall, ANTERIOR or pectoral behind the pectoral fold, POSTERIOR or subscapular under the edge of the scapula, and LATERAL or humeral along the inner upper arm; if released from the second side, say so aloud — 'thank you, I'll take the left as normal'

FAIL — Doing only one of the two spleen methods, palpating one-handed, starting at the COSTAL MARGIN, or rolling the patient the wrong way — the spleen is a KEY POINT and you do BOTH: start in the RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA, because a big spleen reaches it and a hand that starts too high slides past the edge, with your left hand behind the posterolateral lower ribs lifting forward, moving diagonally on each breath; then roll him onto his RIGHT side TOWARDS you, because the spleen is on the left and rolling him left takes it away; then percuss with CASTELL'S method at the lowest intercostal space in the left anterior axillary line, resonant in expiration and again on held inspiration — and know what a dull note on inspiration means, because inspiration pushes an enlarged spleen down across the percussion point; palpate for the liver EDGE only, and avoid full liver percussion and span, which belong to the chronic liver disease station and will cost you the closing minute

SAY — Use a positive when the examiner hands you one rather than repeating it — 'thank you; excoriations fit the itch he described, and pruritus is recognised in lymphoma' — because 'okay' and moving on loses the interpretation mark; keep the commentary to THREE BEATS every time (region → structure → finding), and give ONE GROUPED explanation of the examination rather than narrating twelve steps, which burns ninety seconds you need for the spleen, while still warning about the TWO POSITION CHANGES; hands on the abdomen by 5:30; get the words right — ANGULAR CHEILITIS, WALDEYER'S RING — and do not skip the tonsils because they feel like ENT, since they are lymphoid tissue and belong here; then present in order (summary sentence, positives, relevant negatives, diagnosis, differentials each with a reason, plan, escalation) and COMMIT: 'my most likely diagnosis is LYMPHOMA, and Hodgkin lymphoma in particular given his age and B symptoms', with EBV, HIV and tuberculosis less likely for a painless node that failed antibiotics over six weeks, and metastatic carcinoma less likely at 34 with no hard fixed node; investigations — FBC with film, LDH, urate, ESR, U&E, LFT, calcium and coagulation; EBV and CMV serology, HIV with consent; a chest X-ray for a MEDIASTINAL MASS, then CT neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis; and an EXCISIONAL lymph node biopsy, never fine-needle aspiration, because lymphoma is diagnosed on NODAL ARCHITECTURE and FNA gives cells without architecture; attach an action to each red flag — FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA needs antibiotics within the hour, and SVC OBSTRUCTION means facial swelling, distended neck veins and breathlessness; raise the rural logistics at the first visit (haematology at the Royal Adelaide or Flinders, PATS travel support arranged early, Country Health Connect, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33); node thresholds — over 1 cm abnormal, over 1.5 cm inguinal, over 0.5 cm epitrochlear, and ANY supraclavicular node abnormal — with four characteristics (size, consistency, tenderness, mobility), and over 10% weight loss defining a B symptom; answer the leukaemia fear with empathy before facts; variants — iron deficiency makes the hands and mouth the scored block (koilonychia, tachycardia, conjunctival pallor, ATROPHIC GLOSSITIS and ANGULAR CHEILITIS as the classic triad), with the single most important next step being to FIND THE SOURCE OF BLOOD LOSS, since iron deficiency in a man or a postmenopausal woman is gastrointestinal cancer until proven otherwise; and thrombocytopenia makes the SPLEEN the discriminator, because a palpable spleen argues against ITP and points to hypersplenism, lymphoproliferative disease or marrow infiltration

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED, returning to a man you already examined. THIS STATION IS TWO EXAMINATIONS: a generalised node survey answers 'IS IT EVERYWHERE?', and a DRAINAGE-TERRITORY search — node characteristics, lower limbs, genitalia — answers 'OR IS IT JUST HERE?'. Most candidates deliver only the first. THE TRANSITION SENTENCE MUST ARRIVE AT 5:50 whatever is unfinished behind it; that is the whole skill of the station. Then say LYMPHOMA out loud, with reasons, to a frightened man.
stem: Emergency Department, regional South Australia. Gary Preston, 50, admitted with FEVER, NIGHT SWEATS AND WEIGHT LOSS. You examined him earlier and FOUND AN ENLARGED INGUINAL NODE, were called away, and have now returned. T 37.9 — HR 88 — BP 128/76 — RR 16 — SpO2 98% RA. 8 minutes.

Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: RE-INTRODUCE AND RE-CONSENT even though you have met him, and ASK FOR THE LEGS IN THE EXPOSURE (if you have not asked, you will not look) · general appearance, hands and pulse, then THE SKIN OF BOTH ARMS naming SCRATCH MARKS, which is the only way the positive is released · THE SURVEY: epitrochlear both sides with the corresponding thumb; axillae both sides, five groups; eyes and mouth including Waldeyer's ring; eight cervical chains from behind, then supraclavicular with a shoulder shrug and BONE TENDERNESS over clavicles and sternum · ABDOMEN AT 4:35 (ten seconds earlier than the general haematology station, because there is more to do afterwards): liver edge, two-handed spleen from the right iliac fossa, roll him onto his RIGHT side, Castell's · THE TRANSITION AT 5:50: 'that completes my general examination · I'd now like to come back to the node in the groin', then ASK FOR SIX FEATURES: number, size, consistency, tenderness, mobility, overlying skin · INTERPRET THE PATTERN · then THE TERRITORY: inspect both legs for cellulitis and for a melanoma or SCC, and OFFER a genital examination with permission and a chaperone, and when told not to, ANSWER IN DETAIL what you would look for · DIAGNOSIS FROM 6:40, then the differentials in TWO plain-English headings.

back.dx: LYMPHOMA — said out loud, with the reasons drawn from your own findings: fever, night sweats and weight loss, a SINGLE 3 cm HARD, NON-TENDER, FIXED inguinal node, and excoriations from pruritus. A single, large, hard, painless, fixed node is a MALIGNANT pattern rather than an infective one — infective nodes are typically small, tender and mobile (rubbery suggests lymphoma, stony hard suggests carcinoma). Admit the uncertainty without false comfort: the only way to know is an EXCISIONAL biopsy — architecture, not cytology. DIFFERENTIALS IN TWO PLAIN-ENGLISH HEADINGS: THINGS AFFECTING THE WHOLE BODY — another blood cancer such as leukaemia, long-running infections including HIV, glandular fever and tuberculosis, and occasionally medications or inflammatory conditions; THINGS IN THE AREA THAT DRAINS TO THE GROIN — the groin nodes drain the leg and the genitals, so a melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma of the leg, cellulitis, or an infection or skin cancer of the genitals. Anatomy to say out loud: THE SCROTAL SKIN AND PENIS DRAIN TO THE INGUINAL NODES, WHILE THE TESTIS DRAINS TO THE PARA-AORTIC NODES, so a testicular tumour would not typically present this way. Genital inspection would look for: an ulcer or rash — genital herpes gives painful vesicles with tender nodes, while the chancre of primary syphilis is a PAINLESS indurated ulcer with painless nodes; swelling or tenderness suggesting epididymo-orchitis; and any lesion suggesting SCC of the penis. Plan with a time frame: bloods today, chest X-ray, and haematology referral for an excisional biopsy THIS WEEK, not next month — and offer to call his wife.
plan: RE-INTRODUCE and ask for the legs: 'Gary, thanks for waiting — I'm sorry I had to dash off. My name is Dr -; I'd like to finish examining you now. I'll be looking at your arms, neck, tummy AND LEGS, and feeling your armpits, your neck, your tummy, and I'll need to come back to that lump in your groin. I'LL NEED YOUR TUMMY AND YOUR LEGS UNCOVERED. Stay sitting for now and I'll ask you to lie flat later. Happy for me to go ahead?' → 'no worries, doc. Do you know what it is yet?' → 'not yet — that's exactly what I want to work out, and I'll tell you honestly what I think once I've finished.' (Skipping the introduction because the stem says you have met him costs communication marks and gains nothing.)

Appearance, hands and THE ARMS — the sentence that releases the finding: 'from the end of the bed — cachexia, pallor, jaundice, any rash. Hands — clubbing, pale palmar creases, pulse regular with no tachycardia. Now the skin of both arms: I'm looking for a purpuric or petechial rash, AND FOR SCRATCH MARKS, which are excoriations from itching and a recognised feature of lymphoma.' → 'scratch marks are present' → INTERPRET IT: 'thank you — that is significant. PRURITUS WITH EXCORIATION IS A RECOGNISED SYMPTOM OF LYMPHOMA, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma. Gary, have you been itchy?' → 'driving me mad, especially at night.'

THE SURVEY, four regions, both sides: epitrochlear with the corresponding thumb, two to three centimetres proximal and anterior to the medial epicondyle; axillae with the arm supported — apical, central, pectoral, subscapular, lateral; eyes for pallor and jaundice with fundoscopy offered; mouth for gum hypertrophy, glossitis, angular cheilitis and Waldeyer's ring; then 'Gary, I need to stand behind you for your neck — alright?' and the eight chains, ending with the shoulder shrug for SUPRACLAVICULAR and, in the same movement, pressing both clavicles and the sternum for BONE TENDERNESS. (Doing only the cervical chains 'because he already has a groin node' answers the wrong question — the survey exists to establish whether the disease is generalised.)

ABDOMEN, on time: 'Gary, could you lie flat for me and let me see your tummy? Inspection — symmetrical movement with respiration, no visible masses. The liver from the right iliac fossa, lower border only — no hepatomegaly. The spleen bimanually — left hand around the posterolateral lower ribs, right hand from the right iliac fossa. Gary, roll towards me onto your RIGHT side... one further palpation. And Castell's percussion, lowest intercostal space in the left anterior axillary line — breathe in and hold, percuss; breathe out and hold, percuss.' (Hands on the abdomen by 4:35 here — earlier than the general station, because the territory search still has to happen.)

THE TRANSITION SENTENCE AND THE SIX FEATURES — the moment that decides the station: 'that completes my general examination. I'd now like to come back to the node in Gary's right groin. I would palpate along the inguinal ligament, with his permission and a chaperone. Examiner, whether or not I re-examine it, I'D LIKE TO KNOW SIX THINGS: how many nodes; the size; the consistency — soft, rubbery or hard; whether it is tender; whether it is mobile or fixed; and the overlying skin.' → 'a single node, about three centimetres, hard, non-tender, fixed to underlying tissue; overlying skin normal' → 'thank you. A SINGLE, LARGE, HARD, PAINLESS, FIXED NODE IS A MALIGNANT PATTERN RATHER THAN AN INFECTIVE ONE — infective nodes are typically small, tender and mobile.' (If told 'you already examined that node': 'understood — I'd still like its characteristics.')

THE DRAINAGE TERRITORY — legs, then the genital offer: 'Gary, could you let me see your legs? Examiner, I'm inspecting both lower limbs for TWO things. First, signs of infection — redness, warmth, swelling or an ulcer suggesting cellulitis. Second, ANY SUSPICIOUS MOLE OR SKIN LESION suggesting a melanoma or a squamous cell carcinoma, either of which drains to the inguinal nodes. I would also like to perform a genital examination, with permission and a chaperone.' → 'don't do it — tell me what you would be looking for' → ANSWER IN FULL (see dx): herpes versus the painless syphilitic chancre, epididymo-orchitis, SCC of the penis, and the scrotum-and-penis versus testis drainage. (Saying 'thank you' and moving on wastes the highest-yield question in the station.)

THE DIAGNOSIS, sitting down, covered up: 'Gary, let me cover you up. I want to be straight with you about what I've found, and I'm afraid some of it is concerning. You've had fevers, night sweats and weight loss, and I've found an enlarged gland in your groin. That gland is FIRM, IT DOESN'T MOVE, AND IT ISN'T PAINFUL — and I've also found scratch marks on your arms from itching, which fits the same picture. Putting all of that together, I'M CONCERNED ABOUT A CANCER OF THE LYMPH GLANDS CALLED LYMPHOMA. I can't be certain today — the only way to know is to take a sample of the gland and look at it under the microscope — but I don't want to give you false comfort.' → 'am I going to die?' → FOUR MOVES IN ORDER: acknowledge ('that's the fairest question you could ask, and I don't want to fob you off'), be honest about uncertainty ('it depends on exactly which type this is and how far it has spread, and we don't know that yet'), give a real anchor ('lymphomas are among the cancers we treat most successfully'), and commit to a next step with a time frame ('blood tests today, and I'll speak with the haematology team this morning about sampling that gland. Is there someone you'd like me to call?').

THE DIFFERENTIALS IN TWO HEADINGS, about 70 seconds and in plain English (see dx), ending with the plan and the time frame: 'blood tests today, a chest X-ray, and a referral to the blood specialists to take a sample of that gland. I'd like that to happen THIS WEEK, not in a month.' (Twelve diagnoses in medical language is the failure mode; 'whole body' and 'the area that drains here' shows you understand the anatomy without saying 'drainage territory'.)

ask: 'Gary, thanks for waiting — I'm sorry I had to dash off.' / 'I'll need your tummy and your legs uncovered.' / 'I'm looking for a purpuric rash, and for scratch marks.' / 'Pruritus with excoriation is a recognised symptom of lymphoma.'

'That completes my general examination — I'd now like to come back to the node in the groin.' / 'Number, size, consistency, tenderness, mobility, overlying skin.' / 'A single, large, hard, painless, fixed node is a malignant pattern rather than an infective one.' / 'I'm inspecting both lower limbs for cellulitis and for a melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma.' / 'I'd like to perform a genital examination, with permission and a chaperone.' / 'The scrotal skin and penis drain to the inguinal nodes; the testis drains to the para-aortic nodes.'

'I'm concerned about a cancer of the lymph glands called lymphoma.' / 'An excisional biopsy, not a needle sample — we need the architecture of the gland.' FOUR SENTENCES THAT LOSE MARKS, NEVER SAY THEM: 'there are some abnormalities we need to investigate' (evasion, and a missed disclosure); 'it's probably just an infection — try not to worry' (not honest with a hard fixed painless node and B symptoms); 'I'd do a fine-needle aspiration'; and 'I won't introduce myself — I've already met him'. IF BEHIND AT 5:40: 'I'll complete the remaining node groups verbally and move to the node and its drainage territory, which are the priority in this case.'

VARIANT A — A PIGMENTED LESION ON THE CALF ('a 9-millimetre irregular, asymmetrical, variably pigmented lesion on the left calf') → LET IT MOVE YOUR REASONING: 'thank you — that changes my leading diagnosis. An irregular, asymmetrical, variably pigmented lesion on the leg raises a MELANOMA, and the skin of the lower limb drains to exactly these nodes. So my leading diagnosis is now METASTATIC MELANOMA with lymphoma second. I'd want a full skin examination including the soles and between the toes, and an excision biopsy of the primary lesion as well as assessment of the node.' To Gary: 'I've found a mole on your calf that I'm not happy with. Skin cancers on the leg can spread to exactly the gland I've found in your groin, so I want both looked at together, and quickly.' / VARIANT B — CELLULITIS, the benign version ('the node is 1.5 cm, soft, tender and mobile; the right lower leg is red, warm and swollen with an ulcer over the shin') → 'a small, tender, mobile node with an obvious cellulitis in its drainage territory is a REACTIVE lymphadenopathy, not a malignant one. My leading diagnosis is now cellulitis with reactive inguinal lymphadenopathy. I would still take the B symptoms seriously, check a full blood count and film, and review the node once the infection has settled.' (Diagnosing lymphoma because that is what you revised is exactly what the six node features exist to prevent.)

VARIANT C — THE STEM ALREADY DESCRIBES THE NODE as 3 cm, hard, fixed and non-tender: interpret rather than ask — 'the stem describes a hard, fixed, non-tender node, which is a malignant pattern. So my examination has TWO AIMS: to establish whether the lymphadenopathy is generalised, and to search the drainage territory — the lower limb and the genitalia — for a primary.' The trap is assuming that because the node is described, the territory search is unnecessary; it is the opposite, because knowing the node is malignant makes finding a primary MORE urgent.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Preston, 50, shearing contractor from a South Australian country town, married to Deb with two adult children, worked outdoors all his life; smoked 20 a day for thirty years and gave up five years ago; six or seven beers on a weekend. Night sweats soaking the sheets four or five nights a week for two months; fevers mostly in the evenings; nine kilos down in three months without trying; ITCH driving him mad at night, scratching until it bleeds; noticed the lump in the shower six weeks ago, painless and no smaller. Legs: no rashes or sores, but 'I've got moles everywhere, mate, I've been in the sun my whole life.' No genital symptoms. Mother had breast cancer at 70. HIDDEN AGENDA: he has already looked it up and thinks it is cancer, and he has not told Deb how bad the sweats have been. He asks 'do you know what it is yet?' early and 'AM I GOING TO DIE?' after the diagnosis — and if the doctor is vague he asks again, more bluntly: 'doc, just tell me straight — is it cancer?' Practical, blunt, country, not tearful; goes very quiet for a few seconds when the word cancer is used, then asks a direct question; visibly frustrated by vague language, softens to 'fair enough' when the doctor is honest and specific. At the very end he asks them to ring his wife.

The partner also plays the examiner and RELEASES FINDINGS ONLY WHEN NAMED: cachexia/pallor/jaundice — 'he looks thin, no pallor, no jaundice'; scratch marks — 'scratch marks are present'; epitrochlear, axillary, mouth, cervical, supraclavicular, bone tenderness, liver, spleen and Castell's all normal; the node — 'a single node, three centimetres, hard, non-tender, fixed to underlying tissue, overlying skin normal', GIVING ONLY THE FEATURES ACTUALLY ASKED FOR; legs normal, or the calf lesion in the variant; on the genital offer, 'don't do it — tell me what you would be looking for'. If the candidate re-palpates without asking: 'you've already examined that node' — to see whether they ask anyway. At 3:00 a deliberate distraction: 'would you like to examine the chest?' Anything not named aloud: SAY NOTHING AT ALL. At 6:30 if not yet explaining: 'please explain your diagnosis to the patient.'

Numbers: 6 node features, 3 B symptoms, 8 cervical chains, 5 axillary groups, 2 spleen methods, 2 territory steps (legs and genitalia). Thresholds: over 1 cm abnormal, over 1.5 cm inguinal, over 0.5 cm epitrochlear VERIFY, and ANY supraclavicular node. RUBBERY = lymphoma; STONY HARD = carcinoma; TENDER AND MOBILE = infection. CLOCK: 4:35 abdomen, 5:50 groin, 6:40 diagnosis. Pass mark 17 of 24 AND ALL FOUR TERRITORY BOXES TICKED — the transition sentence by 5:50, all six node features, both lower limbs inspected for infection and skin cancer, and the genital examination offered with a description of what you would look for.

FAIL — The TRANSITION SENTENCE arriving late, or not at all, so the node is never characterised — set a timer for 5:50 and say it whatever is unfinished behind it, because that is the whole skill of the station: 'that completes my general examination; I'd now like to come back to the node in Gary's right groin — I'd palpate along the inguinal ligament, with his permission and a chaperone'; then ask for the SIX FEATURES — how many nodes, the size, the consistency (soft, rubbery or hard), tenderness, mobile or fixed, and the overlying skin — and if told 'you already examined that node', reply 'understood, I'd still like its characteristics'; then INTERPRET: 'a single, large, hard, painless, FIXED node is a MALIGNANT pattern rather than an infective one — infective nodes are typically small, tender and mobile' (rubbery suggests lymphoma, stony hard carcinoma, tender and mobile infection) (★)

FAIL — Offering the genital examination, being told not to do it, and saying 'thank you' — you have just been asked the highest-yield question in the station, so ANSWER IT IN DETAIL: any ulcer or rash (genital HERPES gives painful vesicles with tender nodes; the CHANCRE of primary syphilis is a painless indurated ulcer with painless nodes), swelling, redness or tenderness suggesting epididymo-orchitis, and any lesion suggesting squamous cell carcinoma of the penis — adding that the SCROTAL SKIN AND PENIS drain to the INGUINAL nodes while the TESTIS drains to the PARA-AORTIC nodes, so a testicular tumour would not typically present this way; and ASK FOR THE LEGS in your exposure, because if you have not asked you will not look — inspecting both lower limbs for cellulitis and for a suspicious mole suggesting MELANOMA or squamous cell carcinoma, either of which drains to these nodes (★)

FAIL — Saying 'no rash on the arms' and moving on — the examiner is holding a positive that is released only by the words SCRATCH MARKS, and it must then be USED rather than repeated: 'thank you, that is significant — pruritus with excoriation is a recognised symptom of lymphoma, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma'; and do the whole survey rather than only the cervical chains because he 'already has a groin node', since the point is to establish whether the disease is GENERALISED and one region cannot answer that — epitrochlear both sides with the corresponding thumb, five axillary groups both sides, eight cervical chains with supraclavicular from the front, bone tenderness over both clavicles and the sternum, then the abdomen with hands on by 4:35 (liver edge from the right iliac fossa, spleen bimanually with a roll onto the RIGHT side towards you, and Castell's percussion), because a survey that reaches the abdomen at 6:30 leaves no time for the territory search

FAIL — Vagueness ('there are some abnormalities we need to investigate'), which the patient hears as evasion and the examiner marks as a missed disclosure, or false reassurance ('it's probably nothing') with a hard, fixed, painless node and B symptoms — SAY THE WORD, give the reasons from your own findings, and admit the uncertainty: 'you've had fevers, night sweats and weight loss, and I've found an enlarged gland in your groin that's firm, doesn't move and isn't painful — and I've also found scratch marks on your arms from itching, which fits the same picture; putting all of that together, I'm concerned about a cancer of the lymph glands called LYMPHOMA. I can't be certain today, because the only way to know is to take a sample of the gland and look at it under the microscope — but I don't want to give you false comfort' (★)

FAIL — Answering 'am I going to die?' with statistics or 'let's not get ahead of ourselves' — FOUR MOVES IN ORDER: ACKNOWLEDGE ('that's the fairest question you could ask, and I don't want to fob you off'), be HONEST about the uncertainty ('I can't answer it today, because it depends on which type this is and how far it's spread, and we don't know that yet'), give a real ANCHOR ('lymphomas are among the cancers we treat most successfully'), and commit to a NEXT STEP with a TIME FRAME ('blood tests today, and I'll speak to the haematology team this morning about sampling that gland — is there someone you'd like me to call to be with you?'); then give the differentials to the PATIENT under TWO HEADINGS in plain English rather than reciting twelve diagnoses — things affecting the WHOLE BODY (another blood cancer such as leukaemia, long-running infections like HIV, glandular fever or tuberculosis, occasionally medications or inflammatory conditions) and things in THE AREA THAT DRAINS TO YOUR GROIN ('your groin glands drain your leg and your private parts, so a skin cancer or an infection in either place can do this — that's why I looked carefully at your legs and asked about examining you there'); plan — bloods today, a chest X-ray, and referral for an EXCISIONAL biopsy, never a fine-needle aspiration, because we need the ARCHITECTURE of the gland, and 'this week, not next month'; re-introduce yourself even though the stem says you have met him, because skipping it costs communication marks and gains nothing; variants — an irregular, asymmetrical, variably pigmented lesion on the calf CHANGES the leading diagnosis to metastatic melanoma with lymphoma second, needing a full skin examination including the soles and between the toes and an excision biopsy of the primary, and reporting it while continuing towards lymphoma anyway is exactly the failure it was planted to catch; while a small, tender, mobile node with an obvious cellulitis in its drainage territory is REACTIVE rather than malignant, and the six node features exist precisely to stop you diagnosing what you revised

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED, and THE SEROLOGY HAS ALREADY MADE THE DIAGNOSIS: you are examining for SEVERITY AND COMPLICATIONS. Structure: a haematological examination with an ENT INSERT at the face. The throat gets FIFTY SECONDS AND FIVE NAMED TARGETS; ears, nose and sinuses get NOTHING — and you announce that you are not doing them, which converts an omission into a decision. Liver and spleen are where the marks are and BOTH WILL BE HANDED TO YOU AS ENLARGED. LEAVE THE THROAT BY 3:35, HANDS ON THE ABDOMEN BY 4:45.

time: WIPE with the structure declared and THE MOUTH FLAGGED ('I'll also need to look inside your mouth and throat with a light' · it is the only step that goes inside the patient) · GENERAL APPEARANCE aimed at DEHYDRATION (a week of fever and a painful throat limits intake), pallor for haemolytic anaemia, jaundice for hepatitis, periorbital oedema · HANDS and pulse · THE SKIN OF ARMS, NECK AND FACE FOR TWO RASHES: the BLANCHING maculopapular eruption that follows amoxicillin in EBV, and separately PURPURA AND PETECHIAE because his platelets are 118 · and ASK ABOUT ANTIBIOTICS out loud, because that is why you were looking · EPITROCHLEAR both sides, AXILLAE both sides with five groups · THE THROAT, fifty seconds, FIVE TARGETS: tonsillar enlargement, exudate or membrane, pharyngeal erythema, PALATAL PETECHIAE, and uvular asymmetry or deviation, plus trismus and voice · THEN LEAVE, declining ears, nose and sinuses ALOUD · NECK: eight chains, noting POSTERIOR CHAIN involvement as favouring EBV over streptococcal pharyngitis, then NECK STIFFNESS, five seconds, naming meningitis and encephalitis · ABDOMEN AT 4:45: liver from the right iliac fossa, spleen bimanually rolled RIGHT, Castell's · SAY THE HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY BACK AND SAY WHAT IT CHANGES · inguinal offered, then the summary.

back.dx: INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS (EBV) WITH HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY — the diagnosis was serological before you entered, so the examination answers a different question: how severe, and what has it complicated into? Positives: exudative tonsillitis with grossly enlarged tonsils and palatal petechiae, tender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy MOST MARKED POSTERIORLY (which favours EBV over streptococcal pharyngitis), and a liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin with a spleen 2 cm below the left costal margin. Important negatives: no uvular deviation, trismus or drooling, so no quinsy and no airway compromise; NO NECK STIFFNESS, since meningitis and encephalitis are recognised complications; no rash of either type despite platelets of 118; mildly dry mucous membranes only. Management, in one closing sentence each: supportive analgesia and hydration, check liver function, NO CONTACT SPORT AND NO HEAVY LIFTING FOR AT LEAST FOUR WEEKS because an enlarged spleen can rupture VERIFY (published advice ranges four to eight weeks), and STOP THE AMOXICILLIN, since aminopenicillins cause a widespread rash in EBV — making clear THIS IS NOT A PENICILLIN ALLERGY. Escalate for stridor, drooling, or sudden left upper quadrant or SHOULDER-TIP pain. If serology is NOT given and there is a truncal rash with mouth ulcers and generalised nodes, say the word HIV out loud: acute seroconversion is the diagnosis that must not be missed, and it needs a sexual history in private plus an antigen/antibody test alongside EBV, CMV and toxoplasma serology.
plan: Open, consent, FLAG THE MOUTH, and declare the structure: '...I'm sorry you've been feeling so rough this week. I'd like to examine you — let me tell you what that involves. I'll be looking at your hands, arms, face and tummy, and feeling your armpits, which can be sensitive, your neck and your tummy. I'LL ALSO NEED TO LOOK INSIDE YOUR MOUTH AND THROAT WITH A LIGHT. For now stay sitting; a little later I'll ask you to lie flat.' Then to the examiner: 'THE DIAGNOSIS IS ESTABLISHED ON SEROLOGY, SO I'LL EXAMINE FOR SEVERITY AND COMPLICATIONS — a haematological examination with a focused throat examination.'

General appearance aimed at the right things, then hands: 'from the end of the bed, Daniel looks unwell but is alert and talking. I'm looking specifically for DEHYDRATION — dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor — because a week of fever and a painful throat limits intake; for PALLOR, since EBV can cause haemolytic anaemia; and for JAUNDICE, since it can cause hepatitis. I'd note any periorbital oedema. The hands — pale palmar creases, and the pulse, 96 and regular. I'd not expect clubbing in a one-week illness.' (Reciting the CLL triad in an acute febrile illness misses the finding that actually changes disposition.)

TWO RASHES, and the antibiotic question: 'looking at the skin of the arms, neck and face, I'm looking for two different things. A BLANCHING MACULOPAPULAR RASH, which occurs in EBV and characteristically follows amoxicillin or ampicillin — Daniel, HAVE YOU BEEN GIVEN ANY ANTIBIOTICS THIS WEEK? — and separately for PURPURA AND PETECHIAE, which are non-blanching, and which matter because his platelet count is 118.' → 'the GP gave me amoxicillin on Tuesday' → 'thank you — that's important and I'll come back to it.' Then epitrochlear both sides with the corresponding thumb, and axillae both sides: apical, central, pectoral, subscapular, lateral. (Naming only purpura, as in the CLL station, misses EBV's famous rash — the blanching one. And skipping the axillae 'because glandular fever is in the neck' scores as a failed survey.)

THE THROAT — fifty seconds, five targets, then LEAVE: 'Daniel, could you open wide and say ah? I'll use a light — I'll be as quick as I can. Examiner, I'm looking at the oropharynx for: ENLARGEMENT OF THE TONSILS; EXUDATE OR A MEMBRANE; PHARYNGEAL ERYTHEMA; PETECHIAE ON THE SOFT PALATE; and ANY ASYMMETRY OR DEVIATION OF THE UVULA, which would suggest a peritonsillar abscess. I'm also noting whether there is TRISMUS or a MUFFLED VOICE.' → grossly enlarged exudative tonsils, central uvula, no trismus → 'thank you — that is an exudative tonsillitis consistent with the confirmed EBV infection, and the absence of uvular deviation and trismus argues against a peritonsillar abscess. I WON'T EXAMINE THE EARS, NOSE OR SINUSES IN THIS CONTEXT. Moving to the neck.' (The whole station lives here: a complete ENT examination feels correct and costs you the abdomen.)

NECK — chains, then the five seconds most candidates never spend: 'Daniel, I need to stand behind you to feel the glands in your neck — alright? Submental, submandibular, anterior cervical or jugular chain, posterior cervical, pre-auricular, post-auricular, occipital, and — could you shrug your shoulders — supraclavicular. I'D NOTE IN PARTICULAR WHETHER THE POSTERIOR CHAIN IS INVOLVED, WHICH FAVOURS EBV OVER A STREPTOCOCCAL PHARYNGITIS.' → tender bilateral nodes, most marked posteriorly → 'Daniel, could you TUCK YOUR CHIN TO YOUR CHEST? There is no neck stiffness. I CHECK THAT BECAUSE MENINGITIS AND ENCEPHALITIS ARE RECOGNISED COMPLICATIONS OF EBV.'

THE ABDOMEN — both organs: 'Daniel, could you lie flat and let me see your tummy? On inspection, symmetrical movement with respiration, no distension or visible masses. THE LIVER — starting in the right iliac fossa with the radial border of my hand, moving up on each expiration towards the costal margin. THE SPLEEN — bimanually: left hand around the posterolateral aspect of the left lower ribs, right hand starting in the right iliac fossa parallel to the left costal margin. Daniel, could you ROLL TOWARDS ME ONTO YOUR RIGHT SIDE? One further palpation. And CASTELL'S PERCUSSION — the lowest intercostal space in the left anterior axillary line: breathe in and hold, percuss; breathe out and hold, percuss.'

SAY THE FINDING BACK AND SAY WHAT IT CHANGES — the highest-value moment in the station: 'liver edge three centimetres below the costal margin; spleen palpable two centimetres below the left costal margin' → 'THANK YOU — SO THERE IS HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY. That's consistent with EBV, AND IT MATTERS CLINICALLY BECAUSE AN ENLARGED SPLEEN CAN RUPTURE — so he must avoid contact sport and heavy lifting for at least four weeks.' (Answering 'thank you' and nothing else wastes the finding; and do not palpate an enlarged spleen deeply and repeatedly once you have been told it is enlarged.) Then: 'to complete the lymph node survey I'd examine the inguinal nodes along the inguinal ligament, with permission and a chaperone.'

Cover him, thank him, then the summary: positives (exudative tonsillitis with grossly enlarged tonsils, tender posterior-predominant cervical nodes, hepatosplenomegaly), important negatives (no uvular deviation, trismus or drooling; no neck stiffness; no rash despite platelets of 118; mildly dry mucous membranes only), then the plan and the escalation triggers (see dx). His hidden agenda, raised if you leave time: 'doc — I've got footy Saturday. I'll be right for that, yeah?' → ANSWER FIRMLY, this is the one point that demands a specific answer: 'no. Your spleen is palpable, and an enlarged spleen can rupture with relatively minor abdominal trauma, which can be catastrophic. No contact sport and no heavy lifting for at least four weeks from the onset of illness, and longer while the spleen remains palpable. Avoid sharing drink bottles and mouthguards. And seek help immediately for sudden left upper abdominal or left shoulder-tip pain.'
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute run: throat 2:45, leave it by 3:35, abdomen 4:45, summary 6:50
ask: 'The diagnosis is established on serology, so I'll examine for severity and complications.' / 'I'll also need to look inside your mouth and throat with a light.' / 'I'm looking for dehydration, pallor and jaundice.' / 'Two different rashes: a blanching maculopapular eruption, and purpura or petechiae.' / 'Have you been given any antibiotics this week?'

'Tonsillar enlargement, exudate, pharyngeal erythema, palatal petechiae, uvular deviation.' / 'The central uvula and absence of trismus argue against a peritonsillar abscess.' / 'I won't examine the ears, nose or sinuses in this context.' / 'Posterior cervical involvement favours EBV over streptococcal pharyngitis.' / 'Could you tuck your chin to your chest? — no neck stiffness.'

'So there is hepatosplenomegaly — and an enlarged spleen can rupture.' / 'No contact sport and no heavy lifting for at least four weeks, and no amoxicillin.' FOUR SENTENCES THAT LOSE MARKS: 'I'll just have a quick look in his ears and nose as well' (no mark, and it costs you the spleen); 'looking in the mouth — nothing abnormal' (no named targets means no findings released); 'thank you' as your ENTIRE response to hepatosplenomegaly; and 'the spleen is not enlarged' said before the examiner has spoken — an automatic fail. IF BEHIND AT 5:30: 'Examiner, in the interest of time I'll complete the remaining node groups verbally and move to the abdomen.'

VARIANT A — THE THREATENED AIRWAY ('he is drooling, sitting forward, and you can hear soft stridor') → STOP THE STATION: 'that changes my priorities entirely. This is a THREATENED AIRWAY. I would stop examining, call for senior help and ENT urgently, keep him sitting upright and undisturbed, give high-flow oxygen, avoid anything that distresses him, obtain intravenous access, and discuss corticosteroids — dexamethasone is used for impending obstruction from tonsillar hypertrophy VERIFY. I would not attempt to instrument the airway myself, and I'd ask for anaesthetic support to be present.' / VARIANT B — QUINSY ('unilateral swelling of the left peritonsillar region, uvula deviated to the right, mouth opens only two centimetres') → 'that is unilateral peritonsillar swelling with uvular deviation and trismus, which makes me concerned about a PERITONSILLAR ABSCESS. That is a different problem from glandular fever and needs urgent ENT review for aspiration or incision and drainage, with intravenous antibiotics and analgesia. I'd STILL COMPLETE THE ABDOMEN, because he may have both.' (Having a serological diagnosis and therefore not looking for a second one is exactly the premature closure this variant tests.)

VARIANT C — THE MONONUCLEOSIS-LIKE ILLNESS THAT IS NOT EBV (no serology given; truncal rash, mouth ulcers, generalised lymphadenopathy) → 'a mononucleosis-like illness with a truncal rash, mucosal ulceration and generalised lymphadenopathy raises ACUTE HIV SEROCONVERSION. I would take a sexual history in private and offer an HIV antigen/antibody test, along with EBV, CMV and toxoplasma serology. Acute HIV is the diagnosis that must not be missed here, because identifying it changes everything for the patient.' The word HIV must be said out loud. / PRACTICE DRILL: run the throat block against a stopwatch until FIVE NAMED TARGETS TAKE UNDER TWENTY SECONDS. That single drill is what buys you the abdomen.
pefe: Role-player: Daniel Okafor, 19, apprentice electrician playing senior colts football for a country club; two housemates, non-smoker, drinks socially, no regular medications; THE GP STARTED AMOXICILLIN ON TUESDAY for presumed tonsillitis. Sore throat a week, now agony to swallow even water, voice a bit muffled; sweats every night, worse in the evenings; 'I've never felt this tired in my life', sleeping fourteen hours; barely eating, sipping water only, urine darker than usual; glands in the neck up and sore; a bit of an ache under the left ribs, nothing severe; breathing fine, no stridor or drooling unless running the airway variant. Tired and flat, speaks in short sentences, swallows carefully before talking, not distressed; winces and pulls back slightly when the neck is palpated; opens wide slowly and says 'that hurts'; warms up slightly if the doctor is kind about the pain. HIDDEN AGENDA: he wants to be told he can play on Saturday — volunteered only if asked about work or activities, otherwise as they finish: 'doc — I've got footy Saturday. I'll be right for that, yeah?'

The partner also plays the examiner and RELEASES EACH FINDING ONLY WHEN THE SIGN IS NAMED: dehydration — 'mucous membranes slightly dry, turgor preserved'; pallor, jaundice, periorbital oedema — none; hands and pulse normal at 96; either rash — 'no rash of either type'; epitrochlear and axillary — nothing; tonsils and exudate — 'grossly enlarged with confluent white exudate, pharynx erythematous'; uvula and trismus — 'uvula central, no trismus, voice slightly muffled'; PALATAL PETECHIAE — 'there are petechiae on the soft palate'; EARS, NOSE OR SINUSES — 'not required, move on' AND MARK IT AS TIME LOST; cervical chains — 'tender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, most marked in the posterior chains'; neck stiffness — none; bone tenderness — none; liver — '3 cm below the costal margin'; spleen — '2 cm below the left costal margin'; Castell's — 'dullness on inspiration, consistent with splenomegaly'; inguinal — 'that's fine, don't do it, please summarise'; chest or heart — 'not required'. ANYTHING NOT NAMED ALOUD: SAY NOTHING AT ALL. At 7:00 if not yet summarising: 'please summarise your findings.'

Numbers: 5 throat targets, 4 node regions, 8 cervical chains, 5 axillary groups, 2 organs, 2 rash types. At least FOUR WEEKS without contact sport VERIFY. Posterior nodes favour EBV. Right iliac fossa start, roll RIGHT, Castell's in the left anterior axillary line. Platelets 118. CLOCK: leave the throat by 3:35, hands on the abdomen by 4:45. Pass mark 15 of 21, and ALL of: the throat targets named, liver AND spleen both examined, and NO INVENTED FINDINGS.
fails: ★ Doing a complete ENT examination because it feels correct — it costs you the abdomen, and the ears, nose and sinuses earn nothing here
★ Claiming a finding that was never given — 'the spleen is not enlarged' before the examiner has spoken is an automatic fail
Answering 'thank you' to hepatosplenomegaly instead of repeating it back and saying what it changes

Looking in the mouth without naming targets, so no findings are released; naming only purpura and missing EBV's blanching amoxicillin rash; skipping the axillae because 'glandular fever is in the neck'

Forgetting neck stiffness, which takes five seconds while you are already at the neck and names a complication most candidates never mention; not warning him about the mouth examination; hedging on the return-to-sport question, which is the one point that demands a firm, specific answer
numbers: 5 throat targets (tonsils, exudate, erythema, palatal petechiae, uvular deviation) + trismus and voice · 8 cervical chains · 5 axillary groups · 2 rash types (blanching maculopapular vs purpura) · CLOCK: leave the throat 3:35, abdomen 4:45

Platelets 118 · posterior cervical nodes favour EBV over strep · liver 3 cm, spleen 2 cm below the costal margins · NO contact sport or heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks VERIFY (published range 4-8) · STOP amoxicillin, and it is NOT a penicillin allergy · escalate for stridor, drooling, or left upper quadrant or shoulder-tip pain

Mucous membranes SLIGHTLY DRY; turgor preserved
NO rash of either type — no blanching maculopapular eruption, no purpura
TONSILS GROSSLY ENLARGED with CONFLUENT WHITE EXUDATE; pharynx erythematous; PALATAL PETECHIAE; uvula CENTRAL; no trismus; voice slightly muffled
TENDER and BILATERAL, MOST MARKED POSTERIORLY — which favours EBV over streptococcal pharyngitis
EDGE 3 cm BELOW the costal margin
PALPABLE 2 cm BELOW the left costal margin; Castell DULL on inspiration
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Doing a complete ENT examination because it feels correct — it costs you the abdomen, and the ears, nose and sinuses earn nothing here; ANNOUNCE the omission, which converts it into a decision: 'I won't examine the ears, nose or sinuses in this context'; leave the throat by 3:35 and have hands on the abdomen by 4:45, and if you are behind at 5:30, complete the remaining node groups VERBALLY rather than sacrificing the abdomen (★)

FAIL — Claiming a finding that was never given — 'the spleen is not enlarged' before the examiner has spoken is an automatic fail; findings are released only when you NAME the sign, and anything not named aloud gets silence (★)

FAIL — Looking in the mouth without naming targets, so no findings are released — the throat gets FIFTY SECONDS and FIVE NAMED TARGETS: tonsillar ENLARGEMENT, EXUDATE or membrane, pharyngeal ERYTHEMA, palatal PETECHIAE, and any ASYMMETRY or deviation of the UVULA suggesting a peritonsillar abscess — plus noting TRISMUS and voice quality; then interpret before you leave: 'that is an exudative tonsillitis consistent with the confirmed EBV infection, and the central uvula and absence of trismus argue against a peritonsillar abscess'; drill the five targets until they take under twenty seconds to say, because that single drill is what buys you the abdomen (★)

FAIL — Answering 'thank you' to hepatosplenomegaly instead of repeating it back and saying what it CHANGES — it is the highest-value finding in the station: 'thank you — so there is hepatosplenomegaly; that's consistent with EBV, and it matters clinically because AN ENLARGED SPLEEN CAN RUPTURE, so he must avoid contact sport and heavy lifting for at least FOUR WEEKS'; and do not palpate an enlarged spleen deeply and repeatedly once you have been told it is enlarged (★)

FAIL — Examining as though this were the CLL station — the diagnosis is ALREADY MADE on serology, so you are examining for SEVERITY AND COMPLICATIONS and the findings that matter are different: name DEHYDRATION in general appearance (dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor), because a week of fever and a painful throat limits intake and it is what changes disposition, rather than reciting cachexia-pallor-jaundice; name BOTH rash types, because EBV's famous rash is the BLANCHING maculopapular one that follows amoxicillin or ampicillin, as well as the non-blanching purpura and petechiae that matter with platelets of 118 — and ASK about recent antibiotics, saying so aloud, because it is why you were looking; do not skip the axillae because 'the nodes in glandular fever are in the neck', since a partial survey is scored as a failed survey; and TEST NECK STIFFNESS while you are already there, five seconds, because meningitis and encephalitis are recognised complications that most candidates never mention

SAY — Declare the structure at the start ('the diagnosis is established on serology, so I'll examine for severity and complications — a haematological examination with a focused throat examination') and WARN him about the mouth, the only step that goes inside the patient; interpret the neck finding rather than reporting it ('posterior cervical involvement favours EBV over a streptococcal pharyngitis'); do both abdominal organs properly — liver from the right iliac fossa with the radial border moving up on each expiration, spleen BIMANUALLY also starting in the right iliac fossa with a roll onto the RIGHT side towards you, and CASTELL'S percussion at the lowest intercostal space in the left anterior axillary line; OFFER the inguinal nodes to complete the survey and say a word to the patient before you finish, because both are free marks; summarise the positives (exudative tonsillitis, tender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy most marked posteriorly, hepatosplenomegaly) against the important negatives (no uvular deviation, trismus or drooling, no neck stiffness, no rash of either type, mildly dry mucous membranes only), then supportive management with analgesia and hydration, liver function tests, the four-week activity restriction, and STOPPING the amoxicillin — making clear that the rash aminopenicillins cause in EBV IS NOT A PENICILLIN ALLERGY; escalate for stridor, drooling, or sudden left upper quadrant or shoulder-tip pain; when he asks about Saturday's football, be FIRM and specific rather than hedging, because it is the one point in the station where a firm answer is required — no contact sport and no heavy lifting for at least four weeks from onset and longer while the spleen remains palpable, no sharing drink bottles or mouthguards, and immediate help for sudden left upper abdominal or left shoulder-tip pain (VERIFY the exact period, since published guidance ranges from four to eight weeks); variants — DROOLING, sitting forward and soft STRIDOR is a threatened airway, so stop examining, call senior help and ENT, keep him upright and undisturbed, high-flow oxygen, IV access, discuss dexamethasone, and do not instrument the airway yourself; UNILATERAL peritonsillar swelling with a deviated uvula and trismus is a QUINSY needing urgent ENT for aspiration or drainage, and having a serological diagnosis is not a reason to stop looking for a second one; and a mononucleosis-like illness with a truncal rash, mouth ulcers and generalised lymphadenopathy but NO serology raises ACUTE HIV SEROCONVERSION, which must be said out loud

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional medical clinic. CLL IS CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA, NOT CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE — the examination is haematological. EVERYTHING IS NORMAL AND THE DIAGNOSIS IS THE NEGATIVE, stated confidently and then qualified ONCE. Two things must happen: a COMPLETE BILATERAL NODE SURVEY with the chains named aloud, and A SPLEEN ASSESSED BY BOTH PALPATION AND PERCUSSION. Hands on the abdomen by 4:45, diagnosis started by 6:10.
stem: General medical clinic, regional South Australia; you are the HMO. Ben Whitfield, 34, with THREE MONTHS OF WEIGHT LOSS. Known CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA IN REMISSION under regular haematology follow-up. T 36.8 — HR 78 — BP 124/78 — RR 16 — SpO2 99% RA. Gloves are handed to you at the door. 8 minutes; the examiner will not prompt you.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination on the patient, giving a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: ONE ACKNOWLEDGING SENTENCE about the weight loss · that is all the history you are allowed · then the head-to-toe explanation with BOTH POSITIONS and consent; gloves are compulsory and REPLACE narrating hand washing, and DO NOT OFFER A CHAPERONE for mentioning the groin · GENERAL APPEARANCE (cachexia, pallor, jaundice), HANDS (clubbing, pale palmar creases, pulse), ARMS (scratch marks, purpura), then EPITROCHLEAR both sides with the corresponding thumb, elbow at ninety degrees, 2-3 cm proximal and anterior to the medial epicondyle · the single most commonly forgotten group, and it takes twelve seconds · AXILLAE with the arm resting on your forearm and FIVE GROUPS THE HAND ACTUALLY VISITS · FACE: eyes in one sentence, then the MOUTH as the key point, GIVING THE COMMAND AND WAITING before you comment · NECK: eight chains RUN AS CHAINS not four taps, ending supraclavicular, then BOTH CLAVICLES AND THE STERNUM for bone tenderness · ABDOMEN AT 4:45 WHATEVER IS UNFINISHED: liver from the right iliac fossa, spleen bimanually rolled RIGHT, then CASTELL'S WITH THE SPOT VISIBLY SEARCHED FOR · INGUINAL OFFERED even though you will be stopped · then the negative stated as the answer, and SIX DIFFERENTIAL BUCKETS in plain English.

back.dx: NO CLINICAL EVIDENCE OF RELAPSE — the negative IS the answer, and it must be stated as one: no palpable lymphadenopathy in any group, no splenomegaly by palpation or percussion, and no bone tenderness. Say it confidently, then QUALIFY IT ONCE: 'it makes relapse much less likely, and that's genuinely reassuring — but I can't say for certain from an examination alone. I'd want a blood test and a word with your haematologist before I promise you that.' SIX DIFFERENTIAL BUCKETS FOR THE WEIGHT LOSS, in plain English with one example each: OTHER CANCERS — lymphoma, or a cancer elsewhere such as bowel; INFECTIONS — long-running ones such as HIV or tuberculosis; HORMONE PROBLEMS — an overactive thyroid, or diabetes; BOWEL CONDITIONS — coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease, where food is not absorbed; MOOD AND APPETITE — low mood genuinely causes weight loss, and would be very understandable after what he has been through; and MEDICINES. Next step: blood tests, and questions about bowels, mood and medications. If NIGHT SWEATS are in the stem, name them: 'weight loss together with night sweats are what we call B SYMPTOMS — the pattern we watch for in blood cancers. Your examination is reassuring, but that combination means I don't want to just wait and see' — bloods today and haematology review THIS WEEK. If a node IS palpable: characterise it in fifteen seconds (site, size, consistency, tenderness, mobility, overlying skin, single or multiple), FINISH THE SURVEY to answer generalised versus localised, then tell him plainly that you are concerned the leukaemia has become active again and are arranging bloods and a haematology call today.
plan: Gloves on without commenting, then ONE acknowledging sentence: 'Good morning — my name is Dr -, one of the doctors here today. Are you Ben? I understand you've been worried about losing weight, and I'm sorry that's been on your mind. I'd like to examine you to look into that.' (The task says examine — one sentence about the concern is all the history you are allowed.) Then the explanation with BOTH positions: 'this is a fairly head-to-toe examination, so let me tell you what it involves. I'll be looking at your hands, your arms, your face and your tummy. I'll be feeling a few places — your armpits, which can be a bit sensitive, your neck, your tummy and your groin. For now, please stay sitting; a bit later I'll ask you to lie flat and let me see your tummy. Are you happy for me to go ahead?'

General appearance, hands, arms — and the group everyone forgets: 'I'll be performing a FOCUSED HAEMATOLOGICAL EXAMINATION. From the end of the bed, Ben is alert and comfortable. I'm looking for CACHEXIA, PALLOR AND JAUNDICE — none present. Taking the hands — no clubbing; turning them over, no pale palmar creases; and the pulse is regular with no tachycardia. The skin of both arms — no scratch marks, and no purpuric or petechial rash. Now the EPITROCHLEAR nodes: elbow at ninety degrees, finding the medial epicondyle, TWO TO THREE CENTIMETRES PROXIMAL AND ANTERIOR. Right side with my right thumb... left side with my left thumb. No epitrochlear lymphadenopathy on either side.' (Skipping from the hand straight to the axilla is the single most common omission in the whole examination.)

AXILLAE — five groups the hand actually visits: 'Ben, I'll just rest your right arm on my forearm — let it go completely floppy for me. Examiner, I'm supporting the right arm with my right forearm and examining with my left hand. High into the apex — APICAL or infraclavicular. Onto the chest wall in the mid-axillary line — CENTRAL. Under the border of pectoralis — PECTORAL. Behind, under the scapular muscles — SUBSCAPULAR. And on the inner upper arm — LATERAL. No lymphadenopathy on the right. Now the left.' → he laughs, 'ooh, that tickles' → 'I know, sorry — nearly done on this side.' (Reciting five names while one hand sits in one spot: accuracy is scored separately from completeness, and the examiner is watching your hand arrive at five different places.)

FACE — eyes in one sentence, MOUTH as the key point, command then wait: 'pulling down the lower lids — no conjunctival pallor; looking up — no scleral jaundice. To complete I'd perform fundoscopy. Ben, could you show me your teeth? — no gum hypertrophy and no gum bleeding. And poke your tongue out for me? — no glossitis, and no angular cheilitis at the corners. Last one — open wide and say ah. The tonsils are not enlarged, there is NO ENLARGEMENT OF WALDEYER'S RING, and no petechiae on the buccal mucosa.' (Commenting on the gums and tonsils of a closed mouth is marked — the role-player simply keeps it shut.)

NECK — eight chains RUN AS CHAINS, then bone: 'Ben, I need to feel the glands in your neck, so I'm going to STAND BEHIND YOU — is that alright? Under the chin, SUBMENTAL; along the jaw, SUBMANDIBULAR; in front of sternocleidomastoid, ANTERIOR CERVICAL, the jugular chain; behind it, POSTERIOR CERVICAL; in front of the ear, PRE-AURICULAR; behind the ear, POST-AURICULAR; at the hairline, OCCIPITAL. And Ben, could you shrug your shoulders? Above the collarbones, SUPRACLAVICULAR. No cervical lymphadenopathy. And while I'm here — I'm pressing on both collarbones, and on your breastbone. Any pain? Examiner, no bone tenderness.' (Four discrete taps with four names attached is not a chain examination; and walking behind without warning gets you 'whoa — what are you doing?')

THE ABDOMEN, ON TIME, WHATEVER IS UNFINISHED: 'Ben, could you lie flat for me now, and let me see your tummy? On inspection the abdomen moves symmetrically with respiration and there are no visible masses. Starting in the right iliac fossa with the radial border of my hand, moving up on each expiration — I cannot feel a liver edge. No hepatomegaly. Now the spleen. My left hand around the posterolateral lower ribs on the left; my right hand starting in the right iliac fossa, parallel to the left costal margin, palpating towards it — nothing felt. Ben, could you roll towards me onto your right side? One further palpation. No splenomegaly. And percussion by CASTELL'S METHOD: FINDING THE LEFT ANTERIOR AXILLARY LINE, RUNNING DOWN — rib, space, rib — until the abdomen, then back up to the lowest intercostal space. Ben, breathe in and hold — percuss. Breathe out and hold — percuss. Both resonant. Castell's method is normal.' (Three traps live here: arriving too late to do it; palpating without percussing; and percussing a remembered spot without visibly searching for it, which scores zero for accuracy. And it is the LEFT side.)

Inguinal offered, then THE DIAGNOSIS as a confident negative: 'to complete the lymph node survey I would examine the inguinal nodes along the inguinal ligament, with permission and a chaperone.' → 'that's fine, don't do it' → 'thank you. Ben, that completes my examination — let me cover you up. MY MAIN CONCERN TODAY — and the reason I examined you the way I did — WAS TO MAKE SURE YOUR LEUKAEMIA HASN'T COME BACK. The good news is that your examination is completely normal. I couldn't feel any enlarged glands anywhere — not in your neck, your armpits, your arms or your groin. Your spleen isn't enlarged. And there's no tenderness over your bones. SO THERE'S NO SIGN TODAY THAT YOUR LEUKAEMIA HAS RELAPSED.' → 'so it's definitely not back?' → QUALIFY ONCE, do not over-promise: 'it makes it much less likely, and that's genuinely reassuring — but I can't say for certain from an examination alone. I'd want a blood test and a word with your haematologist before I promise you that. What I can say is that everything I could feel today was normal.'

SIX BUCKETS IN PLAIN ENGLISH, about 60 seconds (see dx), ending: 'I haven't been able to examine for all of those today, so the next step is some blood tests and a few questions about your bowels, your mood and your medications.' → 'to be honest I have been feeling pretty flat since the treatment' → acknowledge in ONE sentence and do not start a psychiatric history: 'thank you for telling me that — it matters, and I'd like to come back to it properly.' (A flat list of twelve medical terms delivered to a patient is the failure mode; and do not manufacture reasoning from findings you do not have — inventing them is a bigger error than a plain list.)
