ask: 'I'll be performing a focused haematological examination.' / 'This is a fairly head-to-toe examination — for now stay sitting, later I'll ask you to lie flat.' / 'I'm looking for cachexia, pallor and jaundice.' / 'No clubbing, no pale palmar creases, and no tachycardia.' / 'Right epitrochlear with my right thumb, left with my left thumb.' / 'Same arm supports the same arm; the opposite hand goes in.'

'No enlargement of Waldeyer's ring.' / 'Ben, I need to stand behind you — is that alright?' / 'Could you shrug your shoulders? — supraclavicular. And any pain over the collarbones or breastbone?' / 'Breathe in and hold — percuss — breathe out and hold — percuss. Castell's method is normal.'

'My main concern today was to make sure your leukaemia hasn't come back — and I've found no sign of a relapse.' THREE SENTENCES THAT LOSE MARKS: 'everything is normal, so there's nothing wrong' (normal IS the finding, not the absence of a diagnosis); 'your leukaemia definitely hasn't come back' (you cannot know that from an examination); and 'I'll also do a quick cardiovascular and respiratory examination' (in six minutes you will not finish, and the spleen is what you will drop). IF BEHIND AT 4:30: 'I'll complete the remaining node groups verbally — I'd also palpate the left axilla and the occipital chain — and move to the abdomen now.' Naming what you skip earns partial credit; silently skipping earns none.

VARIANT A — NIGHT SWEATS IN THE STEM → name the pattern and commit to a timeframe: 'the weight loss together with the night sweats are what we call B SYMPTOMS — they're the pattern we watch for in blood cancers. Your examination is reassuring, but that combination means I don't want to just wait and see. I'd like blood tests today and I'll speak with your haematologist so you're reviewed this week.' / VARIANT B — A PALPABLE NODE → characterise it out loud in fifteen seconds ('a node in the right posterior cervical chain, approximately two centimetres, rubbery, non-tender and mobile, with normal overlying skin; it is a single node'), then 'I'll check whether the finding is generalised by completing the remaining groups' — and the diagnosis changes: 'Ben, I have found an enlarged gland in your neck. Given your history, I'm concerned this could mean your leukaemia has become active again, and I want to sort that out quickly rather than leave it.' (Finding a node and abandoning the survey to dwell on it answers the wrong question — generalised versus localised is next.)

VARIANT C — THE DISTRACTION at 3:00, 'would you like to examine the chest?' → DECLINE WITH A REASON: 'not in a focused haematological examination — I'd rather complete the spleen, which is the key point here. I would examine the chest if there were respiratory symptoms, or if I were looking for a mediastinal mass on imaging.' / VARIANT D — COEXISTENT THYROTOXIC FEATURES → sequence, then add: 'Examiner, I note a resting tachycardia and a fine tremor. I WILL COMPLETE THE HAEMATOLOGICAL EXAMINATION AS THE STEM DIRECTS, and I would then like to examine the thyroid — inspecting for a goitre, palpating from behind, and looking for lid lag — because thyrotoxicosis is a strong differential for the weight loss.' NEVER TRADE THE SPLEEN FOR A THYROID.
pefe: Role-player: Ben Whitfield, 34, diesel mechanic in a South Australian regional town, married with two young children; CLL diagnosed three years ago, treated, told he was in remission eighteen months ago; drives to Adelaide every four months for haematology review, next appointment in six weeks. About 7 kg lost over three months without trying, trousers looser, appetite 'not great, to be honest'; no night sweats (unless running that variant), no fevers, no lumps noticed; gave up smoking two years ago after 15 a day for 12 years, four or five beers on a Friday; no regular medications; father had bowel cancer at 68; MOOD FLAT SINCE FINISHING TREATMENT, and he does not raise it unprompted. Cooperative, polite, a little quiet, not tearful; TICKLISH IN THE AXILLAE — laughs once and apologises; if the candidate walks behind without warning he TURNS SHARPLY: 'whoa — what are you doing?'; if they comment on his gums or tonsils before he has opened, HE KEEPS HIS MOUTH SHUT. HIDDEN AGENDA: he is frightened the leukaemia is back and has told nobody, including his wife — if never asked about his concerns he volunteers it late, quietly: 'can I ask you something? Is it back?' When told the examination is normal he shows visible relief and IMMEDIATELY asks 'so it's definitely not back?' — which is a test, not a request for reassurance.

Numbers: 8 cervical chains, 5 axillary groups, 2 spleen methods, 2 bones (clavicle and sternum), 3 general-appearance items, 6 differential buckets. Epitrochlear: elbow at 90 degrees, 2-3 cm proximal and anterior to the medial epicondyle. Castell's: LOWEST INTERCOSTAL SPACE, LEFT ANTERIOR AXILLARY LINE, spot visibly located. CLOCK: hands on the abdomen by 4:45, diagnosis started by 6:10, finished inside 8:00.

Scored out of 20, pass at 14 AND ALL FOUR KEY-POINT BOXES: named it as a haematological examination; epitrochlear both sides with thumbs; axillary both sides with five groups named; cervical all eight chains named and run as chains; bone tenderness at clavicles and sternum; spleen palpated from the right iliac fossa; spleen percussed by Castell's with the spot visibly located; inguinal offered. Plus approach (introduced, confirmed name, acknowledged the concern, explained looking and feeling and both positions, consented before touching, warned before standing behind), timing, and the diagnosis block (stated 'no evidence of relapse' out loud, did NOT over-reassure, gave grouped differentials in lay language naming at least five of six buckets, and named MOOD without prompting).
Cervical and supraclavicular — None in any of the eight chains

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Reading CLL as chronic liver disease and examining the wrong system — it is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and the examination is HAEMATOLOGIC; the two things that must happen are a COMPLETE BILATERAL LYMPH NODE SURVEY with the chains named aloud, and a SPLEEN ASSESSED BY BOTH PALPATION AND PERCUSSION; everything is normal, and THE DIAGNOSIS IS THE NEGATIVE (★)

FAIL — Over-promising ('your leukaemia definitely hasn't come back') or freezing at the opposite pole with 'everything is normal, so there's nothing wrong' — normal IS the finding, not the absence of a diagnosis, and the pass sits between the two poles: state the negative confidently, then qualify it ONCE — 'my main concern today was to make sure your leukaemia hasn't come back, and the good news is that your examination is completely normal: no enlarged glands anywhere, your spleen isn't enlarged, and no tenderness over your bones, so there's no sign today that your leukaemia has relapsed' — then, when he asks 'so it's definitely not back?', which is the commonest reply and a test, 'it makes it much less likely, and that's genuinely reassuring, but I can't say for certain from an examination alone; I'd want a blood test and a word with your haematologist before I promise you that' (★)

FAIL — Skipping the EPITROCHLEAR group, the single most commonly forgotten in the whole examination, which takes twelve seconds — elbow at ninety degrees, find the medial epicondyle and move TWO TO THREE CENTIMETRES PROXIMAL AND SLIGHTLY ANTERIOR, right side with your right thumb and left side with your left thumb (★)

FAIL — Reciting five axillary names while one hand sits in one spot — accuracy is scored separately from completeness, and the examiner is watching your hand ARRIVE at five different places: support the same arm with your same forearm so the muscles relax, examine with the opposite hand, and move it high into the APEX (apical or infraclavicular), onto the chest wall in the mid-axillary line (CENTRAL), under the border of pectoralis (PECTORAL or anterior), behind under the scapular muscles (SUBSCAPULAR or posterior) and along the inner upper arm (LATERAL or humeral) — both sides; he is briefed to be ticklish and laugh, so acknowledge it and keep going (★)

FAIL — Arriving at the abdomen too late, palpating without percussing, or percussing a remembered spot without visibly SEARCHING for it, which scores zero for accuracy — hands on the abdomen at 4:45 no matter what is unfinished, and if you are behind at 4:30, NAME what you are skipping, because naming earns partial credit and silently skipping earns none; liver from the right iliac fossa with the radial border moving up on each expiration; spleen BIMANUALLY, left hand around the postero-lateral lower ribs and right hand starting in the RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA parallel to the left costal margin, then rolling him onto his RIGHT side towards you for one further palpation; then CASTELL'S — find the LEFT anterior axillary line and run down, rib, space, rib, to the abdomen and back up to the lowest intercostal space, percussing on held inspiration and held expiration; and decline the examiner's 3:00 distraction ('would you like to examine the chest?') with a reason rather than taking it: 'not in a focused haematological examination — I'd rather complete the spleen, which is the key point here; I would examine the chest if there were respiratory symptoms, or if I were looking for a mediastinal mass on imaging' (★)

SAY — Run the whole neck as CHAINS rather than four discrete taps with names attached, warning before you stand behind him because he turns sharply if you don't: submental, submandibular, anterior cervical (the jugular chain), posterior cervical, pre-auricular, post-auricular, occipital — and, shrugging the shoulders, SUPRACLAVICULAR, which is chain eight and routinely forgotten — then press BOTH CLAVICLES AND THE STERNUM for bone tenderness before you leave the neck; give the command and WAIT before commenting on gums and tonsils, because he keeps his mouth shut if you speak first, and keep the eyes to one sentence while the mouth is the key point (no gum hypertrophy or bleeding, no glossitis, no angular cheilitis, no enlargement of WALDEYER'S RING, no buccal petechiae); OFFER the inguinal nodes even knowing you will be stopped, because an unmentioned group is scored as an omitted group — eight seconds, one mark; do not narrate hand washing when gloves were handed to you at the door, and do not offer a chaperone for merely mentioning the groin; then give the differentials for the weight loss in SIX BUCKETS in plain English, naming the group and giving one example rather than reciting twelve medical terms — OTHER CANCERS (lymphoma, bowel), INFECTIONS (HIV, tuberculosis), HORMONE problems (an overactive thyroid, diabetes), BOWEL conditions (coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease), MOOD AND APPETITE ('low mood genuinely causes weight loss, and that would be very understandable after everything you've been through') and MEDICINES — then blood tests and a review of his tablets, bowels and mood; do not manufacture reasoning, because you have no findings to reason from and inventing them is a bigger error than a plain list; and ask what is worrying him, because he is frightened the leukaemia is back and has not told anyone, including his wife; variants — NIGHT SWEATS in the stem make this B SYMPTOMS, so name the pattern and commit to a timeframe ('that combination means I don't want to just wait and see — blood tests today, and I'll speak with your haematologist so you're reviewed this week'); a PALPABLE NODE gets characterised in fifteen seconds (size, consistency, tenderness, mobility, overlying skin, single or multiple) and then you FINISH THE SURVEY, because generalised versus localised is the next question; and coexistent thyrotoxic features are offered AFTER the haematological examination rather than traded for the spleen

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — shared-care antenatal clinic. HAEMATOLOGICAL, NOT OBSTETRIC: no fundal height, no Leopold's, no speculum — any of those is a single-item fail. Two other single-item fails: no hand washing, and no consent. THE STATION IS WON AT THE END: the differentials are THE CAUSES OF HER IRON DEFICIENCY in four groups with pregnancy first — answering 'thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, B12 deficiency' gives the differential of ANAEMIA, not of iron deficiency, and is the commonest reason candidates fail. Hands off the abdomen at 4:50, differentials start at 6:40.
stem: Shared-care antenatal clinic, regional South Australia. Julia Marsden, 25, G1P0, TEN WEEKS by dating scan, well apart from mild tiredness. Booking bloods: Hb 96 (115-165), MCV 72 (80-100), MCH 24 (27-32), FERRITIN 8 (30-200), white cells and platelets normal. 8 minutes; no history required.
tasks: Perform a focused haematological examination. No history required
Commentate to the examiner throughout — what you look for, what you find
Explain the most likely diagnosis to Julia in plain language
Give the examiner your differential diagnosis
time: WIPE ONCE, not region by region, with PAIN, CHAPERONE, AGENDA, CONSENT AND HANDS all inside 45 seconds · GENERAL INSPECTION naming the four things BEFORE answering them (pallor, jaundice, cachexia, and a rash thinking of DERMATITIS HERPETIFORMIS in coeliac disease) · HANDS: clubbing, pale palmar creases, and KOILONYCHIA named as the brittle spoon-shaped nail of iron deficiency, then the pulse for five to ten seconds · ARMS, then the EPITROCHLEAR NODE with the words MEDIAL EPICONDYLE said out loud, then AXILLAE with a one-line heads-up and five groups · EYES AND MOUTH AS THREE SEPARATE ASKS: look up, look down, big smile, tongue out, open and say ah · NECK CHAINS, then BONY TENDERNESS over STERNUM AND CLAVICLES (a named key point most candidates forget), then the JVP · HEART ADAPTED NOT ABANDONED: name the constraint, auscultate the four areas from below and laterally, and SAY WHY · listening for an EJECTION SYSTOLIC FLOW MURMUR of anaemia and for bibasal crepitations of high-output failure · ABDOMEN, the highest-value block, ending 4:50: at ten weeks THE UTERUS IS NOT PALPABLE ABDOMINALLY, so this is a standard abdominal examination · nine regions, spleen from the right iliac fossa rolled RIGHT, liver edge, Castell's · inguinal and legs offered, cover her up, then the 40-second summary, the explanation in three plain steps, and the four differential groups.

back.dx: IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA, most likely from the INCREASED IRON REQUIREMENT OF PREGNANCY — a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a ferritin of 8 and an entirely normal examination. The negatives that matter are the ones that exclude something: no lymphadenopathy in any region, no bony tenderness, no hepatosplenomegaly — together saying this is NOT a haematological malignancy. THE DIFFERENTIALS ARE THE CAUSES OF THE IRON DEFICIENCY, IN FOUR GROUPS, PREGNANCY FIRST: (1) INCREASED DEMAND — the pregnancy itself; (2) BLOOD LOSS — heavy periods before conception, gastrointestinal loss from peptic ulceration, oesophagitis, NSAIDs, haemorrhoids or inflammatory bowel disease, urinary loss, recent surgery, frequent blood donation; (3) MALABSORPTION — coeliac disease as the classic one at her age, plus H. pylori gastritis, inflammatory bowel disease, previous gastric or bariatric surgery, long-term proton pump inhibitors; (4) INADEQUATE INTAKE — a diet low in red meat, vegetarian or vegan. Only if asked or if time remains, the other causes of a MICROCYTIC anaemia: thalassaemia trait (argued against by a ferritin of 8 — and if present, test the partner), anaemia of chronic disease (ferritin normal or high with a raised CRP), rarely sideroblastic anaemia or lead. Management: oral iron 100-200 mg elemental daily or the same dose alternate days VERIFY, on an empty stomach or with orange juice, two hours away from tea, coffee, milk and antacids; black stools are harmless; repeat FBC and ferritin in 2-4 weeks and continue three months after the Hb normalises; IV iron is an option from about 13-14 weeks, avoided in the first trimester. ANSWER THE BABY QUESTION: treated properly, expect a normal pregnancy and a healthy baby; untreated, low iron can affect growth and leave her vulnerable to blood loss at delivery — which is why it is treated now, at ten weeks. Safety-net: breathlessness, dizziness, palpitations or any bleeding.
plan: WIPE ONCE, everything inside 45 seconds: '...I've been asked to examine you because of your blood test results. I'll look at your hands, eyes and mouth, feel for glands at your elbows, armpits, neck and the top of your legs, listen to your heart, and examine your tummy — SITTING FIRST, THEN LYING FLAT with your top lifted. IS THERE ANY PAIN ANYWHERE? WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE? Before I start — is there anything in particular you're worried about?' → 'is it something serious? Will it hurt the baby?' → BANK IT: 'that's exactly the right question and I'll come back to it properly once I've examined you. I'll just wash my hands. Are you happy for me to go ahead?' (Consenting region by region wastes 30-40 seconds; no handwashing or no consent is a single-item fail.)

GENERAL INSPECTION — name the four, then answer them: 'Examiner, from the end of the bed Julia is alert and comfortable. I'm looking for PALLOR — not clinically pale; JAUNDICE — none; CACHEXIA — none; and A RASH, THINKING OF DERMATITIS HERPETIFORMIS IN COELIAC DISEASE — none. No bruising or purpura.' Then hands: 'clubbing — nails together for me — none. Turning them over for pale palmar creases — well perfused. At the nails, looking specifically for KOILONYCHIA, THE BRITTLE SPOON-SHAPED NAIL OF IRON DEFICIENCY — none. Radial pulse regular, around 80, NO TACHYCARDIA TO SUGGEST SIGNIFICANT ANAEMIA.' → 'my nails have been a bit brittle, actually' → SAY IT BACK: 'thank you — brittle nails can go with low iron.' (Ignoring a handed clue is a reasoning fail.)

ARMS, EPITROCHLEAR, AXILLAE: 'along both arms — no scratch marks, no purpura. Now the EPITROCHLEAR node: supporting the right elbow in my right palm, feeling JUST ABOVE THE MEDIAL EPICONDYLE — none either side. Julia, I'm going to feel in your armpits; I'll press firmly, is that alright? Resting your forearm on mine so the armpit relaxes — palpating the APICAL, CENTRAL, PECTORAL, SUBSCAPULAR and HUMERAL groups, both sides. No axillary lymphadenopathy.' (Candidates skip the epitrochlear node because it feels obscure; it is a named key point, and the words medial epicondyle are what score.)

EYES AND MOUTH — three separate asks: 'Julia, LOOK UP for me — pulling the lower lid down, no conjunctival pallor. LOOK DOWN — no scleral jaundice. A BIG SMILE so I can see your gums — no gum bleeding or hypertrophy. TONGUE OUT — no atrophic glossitis, and no angular cheilitis at the corners. OPEN WIDE AND SAY AH — tonsils not enlarged, Waldeyer's ring normal.' → 'I did have a sore bit at the corner of my mouth last month' → 'thank you — that fits with angular cheilitis.'

NECK, BONE AND JVP: 'standing behind you, Julia — submental, submandibular, jugulodigastric and anterior cervical, posterior triangle, pre- and post-auricular, occipital. To the front — shrug your shoulders — supraclavicular. No lymphadenopathy. PRESSING OVER THE CLAVICLES AND STERNUM FOR BONY TENDERNESS — tell me if this is sore — none. Ideally I'd assess the JVP at 45 degrees; sitting up, looking left, no elevation.' (Bony tenderness is a named key point and is forgotten by most candidates — say the words sternum and clavicles while you press.)

HEART — ADAPTED, NOT ABANDONED: 'I'll keep Julia covered and only uncover what I need. I CAN'T INSPECT OR PALPATE THE APEX WITHOUT EXPOSING THE BREAST, SO I'LL AUSCULTATE AND ADAPT: aortic at the right second space, pulmonary at the left second space, then the lower left sternal edge and apex from below and laterally. Dual sounds, no murmur — I'M LISTENING FOR AN EJECTION SYSTOLIC FLOW MURMUR OF ANAEMIA — and no gallop. Stethoscope into both axillae and low on the back: no bibasal crepitations, so no high-output failure.' (Abandoning the heart silently reads as avoidance; naming the constraint and the reason makes it a deliberate examination.)

THE ABDOMEN, ending 4:50: 'Julia, could you lie flat with one pillow? I'll uncover your tummy from your ribs to just above your underwear. Tell me if anything is tender.' → 'is it safe to press on my tummy? I'm ten weeks' → 'COMPLETELY SAFE — AT TEN WEEKS THE WOMB IS STILL DOWN BEHIND THE PUBIC BONE.' Then: 'on inspection, moves with respiration, no distension, no mass, no scars — at ten weeks the uterus is not palpable abdominally, SO THIS IS A STANDARD ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION. Light palpation in all nine regions, watching your face — soft and non-tender. For the SPLEEN: from the right iliac fossa, left hand behind the lower left ribs, advancing to the left costal margin — deep breath in — no splenic edge; repeating with you ROLLED ONTO YOUR RIGHT SIDE — no splenomegaly. For the LIVER, right iliac fossa to the costal margin — no liver edge. And CASTELL'S POINT, lowest space in the anterior axillary line — deep breath in and hold — resonant, Castell's sign negative.'

CLOSURE AND THE 40-SECOND SUMMARY: offer the inguinal nodes and the legs, accept the skip without arguing, COVER HER UP AND HELP HER SIT FORWARD, and complete: 'I would check the vital signs including a POSTURAL blood pressure, review a peripheral blood film, dipstick the urine, and look at the antenatal record for her booking bloods and blood group.' Then the summary: a well 25-year-old at ten weeks with a microcytic hypochromic anaemia and a ferritin of 8; an entirely normal examination, with the negatives that exclude malignancy named; diagnosis IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA, most likely from the increased iron requirement of pregnancy.

EXPLAIN IN THREE PLAIN STEPS — cells, haemoglobin, stores — then WHY: 'in your blood you have red cells, and inside them a substance called haemoglobin, which carries oxygen around your body. Your haemoglobin is lower than it should be. Your red cells are also smaller than normal, and each one carries less haemoglobin. And your FERRITIN — that's the iron stored in your body — is low. Putting those together, you are low in iron. The commonest reason in pregnancy is simply that your body's demand for iron goes up a great deal when you're growing a baby, and the stores run down.' THEN ANSWER THE HIDDEN AGENDA: 'to answer what I think you're really asking — will this harm the baby? TREATED PROPERLY, WE EXPECT A NORMAL PREGNANCY AND A HEALTHY BABY.' Then the iron advice, the repeat bloods at 2-4 weeks, and the safety-net (see dx). If she asks for an infusion: 'we usually avoid intravenous iron in the first three months; from around thirteen or fourteen weeks it's an option if tablets don't suit you.'

THE DIFFERENTIALS — four groups, pregnancy first (see dx). This is where the station is won. If time remains, add the other causes of a MICROCYTIC anaemia briefly and last — never lead with them, and never drift into macrocytic anaemia, B12, folate or thyroid disease, which signals you have lost the thread of the case.

ask: 'Is there any pain anywhere, and would you like a chaperone?' / 'I'll keep you covered and only uncover what I need to.' / 'At ten weeks the womb is still behind the pubic bone, so examining your tummy is completely safe.' / 'I'm looking specifically for koilonychia — the brittle, spoon-shaped nail of iron deficiency.' / 'There is no tachycardia to suggest significant anaemia.'

'Feeling just above the medial epicondyle for the epitrochlear node.' / 'No atrophic glossitis and no angular cheilitis.' / 'Pressing over the sternum and clavicles for bony tenderness.' / 'I'm listening for an ejection systolic flow murmur, which anaemia can produce.' / 'Starting in the right iliac fossa and advancing to the left costal margin — deep breath in.' / 'Castell's point is resonant on full inspiration, so there is no splenomegaly.'

'Your haemoglobin is low, your red cells are small, and your iron stores are low.' / 'Treated properly, we expect a normal pregnancy and a healthy baby.' / 'My differentials are the causes of her iron deficiency — first, the increased demand of pregnancy.' / 'I'd repeat the full blood count and ferritin in two to four weeks.'

VARIANT B — THE EXAMINER SUPPLIES POSITIVES ('her conjunctivae are pale, she has koilonychia and angular cheilitis, and her pulse is 104') → 'thank you — that TRIAD tells me this deficiency is ESTABLISHED AND CHRONIC rather than something that has developed over a few weeks of pregnancy, so I would weight BLOOD LOSS AND MALABSORPTION higher, take a careful menstrual and gastrointestinal history, and send coeliac serology alongside starting iron.' If given a soft ejection systolic murmur: 'I'd interpret that as a FLOW MURMUR of anaemia rather than structural disease, and I'd expect it to resolve once the haemoglobin is corrected. I'd look for features of high-output failure — a raised JVP, a third sound, bibasal crackles and oedema — and there are none.'

VARIANT C — THE OLDER PATIENT (58-year-old man, same indices, 6 kg unexplained weight loss) → 'then my leading differential changes. In a man of 58 with iron deficiency and weight loss, this is OCCULT GASTROINTESTINAL BLOOD LOSS, and colorectal or gastric malignancy until proven otherwise. I would examine the abdomen for a mass and hepatomegaly, check for a supraclavicular node, and arrange BOTH gastroscopy and colonoscopy. Iron replacement alone would be inadequate management.' / VARIANT D — THE MIMIC (ferritin 145, MCV 63, RBC 6.1) → 'the ferritin is normal, so this is NOT iron deficiency. The MCV is disproportionately low with a high red cell count — a MENTZER INDEX BELOW 13 — which points to THALASSAEMIA TRAIT. I'd request haemoglobin HPLC, and if confirmed the priority becomes testing her partner and offering genetic counselling early.' / VARIANT E — NOT IRON AT ALL (cervical and axillary nodes, spleen 3 cm below the costal margin) → 'these findings are inconsistent with simple iron deficiency and raise a LYMPHOPROLIFERATIVE DISORDER. I would request an urgent blood film and full blood count, LDH, and refer urgently to haematology.'
pefe: Role-player: Julia Marsden, 25, primary school teacher in Kadina, living with her partner Dan; first pregnancy, ten weeks, dated on a scan two weeks ago; feels well, a little more tired than usual. Non-smoker, stopped alcohol the day the test was positive; MOSTLY VEGETARIAN with red meat maybe once a fortnight; two or three cups of TEA A DAY, USUALLY WITH MEALS; a pregnancy multivitamin most days, no NSAIDs or aspirin, no allergies. BEFORE THE PREGNANCY HER PERIODS WERE HEAVY — five to six days, changing every couple of hours on the worst day, occasional clots — and she never thought it a problem; ONLY MENTION IF ASKED. No bowel symptoms, no blood in the stool, no surgery, no blood donation, no travel, no family history of anaemia. Warm and cooperative, follows every instruction promptly, ALL FINDINGS NORMAL — does not act pale, does not wince, does not invent signs. PUSHES ONCE EARLY at about 30 seconds: 'is it something serious? Will it hurt the baby?' PUSHES AGAIN AT THE ABDOMEN: 'is it safe to press on my tummy? I'm ten weeks.' If never asked about concerns, volunteers at about six minutes: 'sorry — but is the baby going to be alright?' TWO CLUES to offer if the doctor is silent, one each: 'my nails have been brittle' and 'I had a sore crack at the corner of my mouth last month'. Never volunteers the periods, the vegetarian diet or the tea unless directly asked. If they are blunt about the baby with no reassurance she goes quiet: 'so it could hurt the baby?'

Numbers: Hb 96, MCV 72, MCH 24, ferritin 8. ANAEMIA IN PREGNANCY: under 110 in the first trimester, under 105 in the second and third, under 100 postpartum. Iron deficient: ferritin under 30; microcytic MCV under 80. Oral iron 100-200 mg elemental daily OR the same dose alternate days VERIFY; ferrous sulfate 325 mg = 105 mg elemental. Recheck at 2-4 weeks and continue three months after the Hb normalises. IV iron from about 13-14 weeks, avoided in the first trimester. THE UTERUS BECOMES PALPABLE ABDOMINALLY FROM ABOUT 12 WEEKS. CLOCK: hands off the abdomen at 4:50, differentials start at 6:40.

Marked on: introduced, confirmed name, gained consent, WASHED HANDS; explained the whole examination ONCE rather than region by region; kept her covered, did not ask her to remove her bra, re-covered her at the end; warned before the armpits and before the abdomen; named signs out loud throughout; SAID THE WORDS koilonychia, angular cheilitis, atrophic glossitis; PRESSED ON THE STERNUM AND CLAVICLES; examined for the spleen INCLUDING rolling her onto her right side, and percussed; DID NOT ATTEMPT a fundal height, Leopold's or any pelvic examination; ANSWERED THE BABY QUESTION clearly without dismissing it; explained in plain words — cells, haemoglobin, iron stores; gave practical iron advice; SAFETY-NETTED; and gave differentials AS THE CAUSES OF IRON DEFICIENCY, in groups, pregnancy first, finishing on time.
fails: ★ Giving the differential of ANAEMIA (thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, B12) instead of the causes of IRON DEFICIENCY in four groups with pregnancy first — the single commonest reason candidates fail this station
★ A fundal height, Leopold's manoeuvres or a speculum in a haematological station — a single-item fail, as are no handwashing and no consent
Naming the condition and stopping, instead of explaining the mechanism in three plain steps — cells, haemoglobin, stores — and then why
Not answering the baby question, and no safety-netting; using 'microcytic', 'hypochromic' and 'MCH' to a patient without translating them

Skipping the epitrochlear node because it feels obscure; forgetting bony tenderness over sternum and clavicles; abandoning the heart silently instead of naming the constraint and the reason; ignoring the brittle nails or the sore mouth corner when she hands them to you; arguing with a skip
numbers: Hb 96, MCV 72, MCH 24, ferritin 8 · anaemia in pregnancy <110 T1, <105 T2-3, <100 postpartum · ferritin <30 = iron deficient · uterus palpable abdominally from ~12 weeks · CLOCK: abdomen ends 4:50, differentials start 6:40

4 differential groups: increased demand (pregnancy), blood loss, malabsorption (coeliac the classic at her age), inadequate intake · oral iron 100-200 mg elemental daily or alternate days VERIFY · ferrous sulfate 325 mg = 105 mg elemental · recheck 2-4 weeks, continue 3 months after Hb normalises · IV iron from ~13-14 weeks, not first trimester

findings: Hb 96 · MCV 72 · MCH 24 · FERRITIN 8 — white cells and platelets normal
Well; not pale, no jaundice, no cachexia, no rash
NO koilonychia; palmar creases well perfused; pulse regular around 80 with NO tachycardia
NO angular cheilitis, NO atrophic glossitis; no gum bleeding
None — epitrochlear, axillary, cervical or inguinal
Dual heart sounds with NO flow murmur; no bibasal crepitations
No hepatosplenomegaly; Castell resonant; at ten weeks the uterus is NOT palpable abdominally
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Giving the differential of ANAEMIA (thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, B12) instead of THE CAUSES OF IRON DEFICIENCY — the single commonest reason candidates fail this station; FOUR GROUPS, pregnancy first: INCREASED DEMAND (the pregnancy itself — iron requirement rises several-fold and first-trimester deficiency is common), BLOOD LOSS (heavy periods before conception, gastrointestinal loss from peptic ulceration, oesophagitis, NSAIDs, haemorrhoids or inflammatory bowel disease, urinary loss, recent surgery, frequent blood donation), MALABSORPTION (coeliac disease is the classic one at her age, plus H. pylori gastritis, inflammatory bowel disease, previous gastric or bariatric surgery, long-term proton pump inhibitors) and INADEQUATE INTAKE (a diet low in red meat, vegetarian or vegan); the other causes of a microcytic anaemia come LAST and BRIEFLY if at all — thalassaemia trait, argued against by a ferritin of 8, and anaemia of chronic disease, where ferritin would be normal or high with a raised CRP (★)

FAIL — A fundal height, Leopold's manoeuvres or a speculum in a HAEMATOLOGICAL station — a single-item fail, as are no handwashing and no consent; at ten weeks the uterus is not palpable abdominally, so this is a standard abdominal examination, and you can say so to reassure her: 'completely safe — at ten weeks the womb is still down behind the pubic bone' (★)

FAIL — Naming the condition and stopping, instead of explaining the MECHANISM IN THREE PLAIN STEPS — cells, haemoglobin, stores — and then why: 'in your blood you have red cells, and inside them a substance called haemoglobin, which carries oxygen around your body; your haemoglobin is lower than it should be, your red cells are also smaller than normal and each one carries less haemoglobin, and your ferritin — that's the iron stored in your body — is low; putting those together, you are low in iron, and the commonest reason in pregnancy is simply that your body's demand for iron goes up a great deal when you're growing a baby, and the stores run down'; using MICROCYTIC, HYPOCHROMIC or MCH to a patient without translating them loses the mark (★)

FAIL — Not answering the baby question, and no safety-netting — the hidden agenda is asked at about thirty seconds ('is it something serious? Will it hurt the baby?') and must be BANKED and then RETURNED to: 'to answer what I think you're really asking — treated properly, we expect a normal pregnancy and a healthy baby; if it were left untreated, low iron can affect the baby's growth and make you more tired and more vulnerable to blood loss at delivery, which is exactly why we're treating it now, at ten weeks, with plenty of time'; then the practical iron advice (empty stomach or with orange juice, because vitamin C helps absorption; two hours away from tea, coffee, milk and antacids; stools will go black, which is harmless; constipation and nausea are common, so fibre and fluids; iron-rich foods), a repeat full blood count and ferritin at TWO TO FOUR WEEKS, continuing three months after the haemoglobin normalises, and a safety net of breathlessness, dizziness, palpitations or any bleeding; if she asks for an infusion, 'we usually avoid intravenous iron in the first three months; from around thirteen or fourteen weeks it's an option if tablets don't suit you' (★)

FAIL — Ignoring a handed clue — she offers BRITTLE NAILS and a SORE CRACK AT THE CORNER OF THE MOUTH one at a time if you are silent, and saying nothing back is a reasoning fail; say it back in one line and keep going without sliding into a history ('thank you — brittle nails can go with low iron', 'that fits with angular cheilitis'); and NAME the signs you are looking for rather than reporting bare negatives — KOILONYCHIA, the brittle spoon-shaped nail of iron deficiency; ATROPHIC GLOSSITIS; ANGULAR CHEILITIS; the EPITROCHLEAR node felt just above the MEDIAL EPICONDYLE, which candidates skip because it feels obscure but is a named key point; and BONY TENDERNESS over the STERNUM AND CLAVICLES, forgotten by most candidates and also a named key point

SAY — Explain the whole examination ONCE rather than consenting region by region, which wastes thirty to forty seconds, with a one-line heads-up before the axillae and the abdomen only; name the four general-inspection items BEFORE answering them (pallor, jaundice, cachexia, and a rash, thinking of dermatitis herpetiformis in coeliac disease), because a bare 'she looks well' scores nothing; ADAPT the cardiac examination rather than abandoning it silently, which reads as avoidance — 'I can't inspect or palpate the apex without exposing the breast, so I'll auscultate and adapt' — naming WHY you are listening (an EJECTION SYSTOLIC FLOW MURMUR of anaemia, and bibasal crepitations of high-output failure); the abdomen is the highest-value block: light palpation of all nine regions, spleen from the RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA advancing to the left costal margin and repeated with her rolled onto her RIGHT side, liver edge, and CASTELL'S POINT resonant on full inspiration; take skips without arguing, because accepting direction is itself assessed, and cover her up and help her sit forward, because forgetting costs professionalism marks; present the negatives that EXCLUDE something rather than reciting every normal finding — no nodes in any region, no bony tenderness, no hepatosplenomegaly — which together say 'this is not a haematological malignancy'; hands off the abdomen at 4:50 and differentials starting at 6:40; numbers — anaemia in pregnancy is under 110 in the first trimester, under 105 in the second and third and under 100 postpartum; iron deficient is a ferritin under 30; oral iron 100–200 mg elemental daily or the same dose on alternate days (VERIFY); variants — pale conjunctivae, koilonychia, angular cheilitis and a tachycardia of 104 make the deficiency ESTABLISHED AND CHRONIC rather than recent, so weight blood loss and malabsorption higher and send coeliac serology; a normal ferritin with a disproportionately low MCV and a high red cell count points to THALASSAEMIA TRAIT, where the priority becomes testing her partner and early genetic counselling; and lymphadenopathy with a palpable spleen is inconsistent with simple iron deficiency and raises a lymphoproliferative disorder needing an urgent film and haematology referral

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED, and THE MOTHER IS THE PERSON YOU SPEAK TO WHILE THE MANIKIN IS THE THING YOU EXAMINE. The rash explanation is FOUR FEATURES IN NINETY SECONDS, finishing on NON-BLANCHING. ANSWER THE MENINGITIS QUESTION WHEN SHE ASKS IT, not at the end. THE ARTHRITIS BLOCK MOVES EARLY, to about 3:20, because it is the only HSP-specific item on the mark sheet and the first casualty when a manikin station runs long. And never claim a finding you were not given — a stethoscope on plastic followed by 'his chest is clear' is an automatic fail.
stem: Emergency Department, regional South Australia. Liam Marsh, 5, brought by his mother Jenny, worried about a rash. URTI TWO WEEKS AGO. Rash on the legs and colicky abdominal pain. Neurological examination already done: NO NECK RIGIDITY, no meningism. T 37.2 — HR 96 — BP 98/60 — RR 22 — SpO2 99%. URINE DIPSTICK: BLOOD 4+, PROTEIN 1+. A photograph of the rash is on the desk. 8 minutes.
You are NOT asked for investigations, management or differentials.
tasks: Explain the rash to the mother
Perform a relevant physical examination on the manikin — the examiner will provide findings
Explain the diagnosis to the mother
time: WIPE TO JENNY, not to the manikin · she is the one who consents · THE RASH IN FOUR FEATURES, ninety seconds, holding the photograph so she can see it: WHAT KIND (purpuric · a small amount of bleeding under the skin), SYMMETRY (both legs, both buttocks), SITE (legs and bottom, nothing on tummy, chest or back), and NON-BLANCHING (the colour doesn't fade when pressed) · if she raises MENINGITIS, answer IMMEDIATELY with the evidence: no neck stiffness, alert and interacting, normal observations, and children with meningococcal infection get very unwell very quickly · CONSENT FOR THE EXAMINATION, then general appearance NAMING EACH SIGN because it is a manikin, with the blood pressure flagged as the marker of RENAL involvement · THE ARTHRITIS BLOCK AT 3:20: the ANKLE as the joint most typically involved, inspection for swelling and redness, palpation for tenderness and PERI-ARTICULAR swelling, range of movement, then the other joints named · NODE SURVEY with every chain named aloud · THE ABDOMEN IN FIVE NAMED STEPS, going beyond the spleen because THE GUT IS ONE OF THE FOUR INFLAMED ORGANS: inspection, superficial palpation of nine regions, DEEP palpation for masses AND SPECIFICALLY INTUSSUSCEPTION, organs, bowel sounds · OFFER the inguinal nodes AND THE SCROTUM, because scrotal involvement occurs and torsion must be excluded · STOP EXAMINING AT 7:10 and turn to Jenny.

back.dx: HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA (IgA vasculitis) — ONE PROCESS IN FOUR ORGANS, which is how you explain it: the small blood vessels become inflamed, usually set off by an infection (the cold a fortnight ago), and inflamed vessels in the SKIN leak a little blood (the rash), in the KIDNEYS give blood in the urine, in the BOWEL cause the colicky tummy pains, and in the JOINTS cause the puffy tender ankles. So it is NOT a bleeding disorder and NOT meningitis. THE PLATELET COUNT IS WHY: purpura with a LOW platelet count is a different disease, and normal platelets with normal clotting are what allow you to call this a vasculitis rather than ITP, leukaemia or DIC. Diagnostic criterion: PALPABLE PURPURA without thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy is mandatory, plus at least one of diffuse abdominal pain, arthritis or arthralgia, renal involvement, or biopsy showing IgA deposition VERIFY. Management is the FOLLOW-UP: most children settle in four to six weeks and recover completely, but urine and blood pressure are checked regularly for SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS VERIFY, plus bloods today to confirm it is not a bleeding problem. Admit for severe abdominal pain, vomiting or GI bleeding, hypertension, renal impairment, inability to walk, scrotal involvement, or a family too far from care to return easily. Home safety-net: severe or constant tummy pain, repeated vomiting or blood in the stool; much less urine, or urine like cola or blood; puffiness of the face or ankles; scrotal pain or swelling; not drinking, drowsiness or a new fever; a rash spreading to the trunk or new bruising elsewhere.
plan: WIPE TO JENNY: '...are you Jenny, Liam's mum? And this must be Liam. I can see you're worried about this rash. I'd like to go through it with you and then examine him. Before I start — I'll wash my hands.' → 'doctor, is it meningitis? I read about the glass test' → ANSWER NOW, WITH EVIDENCE: 'that's exactly the right thing to think about with this kind of rash, and I'm glad you asked. The good news is that Liam has NO NECK STIFFNESS, he's ALERT AND INTERACTING, and all his observations — temperature, heart rate and blood pressure — are NORMAL. Children with meningococcal infection are usually very unwell very quickly, and Liam isn't. So I don't think that's what this is — but I'll tell you what I do think once I've examined him.' (Addressing the manikin instead of Jenny, or deferring the meningitis question, both cost marks.)

THE RASH — FOUR FEATURES IN NINETY SECONDS, photograph turned towards her: 'FIRST, what kind of rash it is. These little red-purple spots are what we call a PURPURIC rash — in plain terms, there's a small amount of BLEEDING UNDER THE SKIN. It's not a simple red rash like a heat rash. SECOND, it's on BOTH SIDES — the same on both legs and both buttocks, a symmetrical rash, and that pattern is a clue. THIRD, WHERE IT IS — his legs and his bottom, and none on his tummy, chest or back. That distribution is quite characteristic. And FOURTH, the important one — WHEN I PRESS ON THIS RASH, THE COLOUR DOESN'T FADE. We call that NON-BLANCHING, and it tells us the colour is blood in the skin.' → 'bleeding under his skin? Is that dangerous?' → 'it sounds alarming, and I understand that. It's a small amount, and there are several possible reasons — I'd like to examine Liam now and then explain what I think is going on.' (Primary morphology, borders and secondary change score NOTHING here; and every sentence past ninety seconds is stolen from the abdomen.)

Consent from Jenny, then general appearance with EVERY SIGN NAMED: 'Examiner, I appreciate this is a manikin, so I'll NAME EACH SIGN I'm looking for as I go. On general appearance I'm assessing his LEVEL OF CONSCIOUSNESS — alert or drowsy; looking for PALLOR; and for CACHEXIA. I note the blood pressure is given and normal — IN THIS CONDITION I WOULD OTHERWISE MEASURE IT MYSELF, BECAUSE HYPERTENSION INDICATES RENAL INVOLVEMENT. Taking the hands — nails for clubbing, palms for pale palmar creases, and the pulse for tachycardia.' (Putting a stethoscope or hands on plastic and reporting a result you were not given is an automatic fail.)

THE ARTHRITIS BLOCK — here, not at the end: 'Examiner, I'd now like to examine for ARTHRITIS, which is one of the features of Henoch-Schonlein purpura. Taking the ANKLE, WHICH IS THE JOINT MOST TYPICALLY INVOLVED — on inspection, no swelling and no redness. On palpation I'm feeling for TENDERNESS and for PERI-ARTICULAR SWELLING. I'd like to take the joint through its range of movement. And I would examine the other joints in the same way — knees, wrists, elbows and hips.' → 'there is mild puffiness and tenderness around both ankles' → 'thank you — that's consistent with the joint involvement we see in this condition.' (It is the only HSP-specific item on the mark sheet and the first casualty when the station runs long. Do NOT describe deformity — that belongs to chronic arthritis and it sounds like recitation.)

THE NODE SURVEY, every chain named even though the plastic is unconvincing: arms for purpura and scratch marks; epitrochlear both sides with the corresponding thumb; axillae with the five groups named and the positions shown; mouth for gum hypertrophy and bleeding, glossitis, angular cheilitis, tonsils and Waldeyer's ring and PALATAL AND BUCCAL PETECHIAE, plus THE THROAT for redness or exudate given the infection two weeks ago; eyes for pallor and jaundice; the neck FROM THE FRONT since the manikin cannot sit, all eight chains, saying that normally you would stand behind; and pressing the clavicles and sternum for bone tenderness. (The mark is for NAMING the chains, not for the tactile quality of the plastic.)

THE ABDOMEN IN FIVE NAMED STEPS — and it goes beyond the spleen: 'on INSPECTION — whether it moves symmetrically with respiration, and any visible masses or distension. SUPERFICIAL PALPATION across all nine regions — tenderness, guarding, rigidity. DEEP PALPATION across all nine regions — masses, AND SPECIFICALLY A MASS THAT WOULD SUGGEST INTUSSUSCEPTION. ORGANS — the liver edge from the right iliac fossa; then the spleen, bimanually. I'd like to percuss with Castell's method. And BOWEL SOUNDS.' → 'soft, mildly tender centrally, no guarding, no masses, no organomegaly, bowel sounds present' → 'thank you — CENTRAL TENDERNESS WITHOUT GUARDING OR A MASS FITS THE ABDOMINAL INVOLVEMENT OF THIS CONDITION RATHER THAN A SURGICAL ABDOMEN.' (Examining the abdomen as though this were the CLL station — spleen only — misses the organ that puts a child in theatre.)

WHAT YOU OFFER RATHER THAN DO: 'to complete the survey I'd palpate the inguinal nodes along the inguinal ligament. AND IN A BOY WITH THIS CONDITION I'D WANT TO EXAMINE THE SCROTUM, BECAUSE SCROTAL INVOLVEMENT OCCURS IN HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA AND MUST BE DISTINGUISHED FROM TESTICULAR TORSION.' → 'that's fine, don't do it — the scrotum is normal.' (Eight seconds, and it is where the torsion mark lives.)

STOP EXAMINING AND TURN TO JENNY: 'I think Liam has a condition called HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA — it's a mouthful, and doctors also call it IgA vasculitis. It's the commonest condition of its type in children. What happens is that the SMALL BLOOD VESSELS BECOME INFLAMED — the tiny tubes that carry blood around the body — usually set off by an infection, which fits with the cold he had a fortnight ago. AND ONE THING EXPLAINS EVERYTHING YOU'VE NOTICED: inflamed vessels in the SKIN leak a little blood — that's the rash. Inflamed vessels in the KIDNEYS are why the urine test showed blood. Inflamed vessels in the BOWEL are causing his tummy pains. And it can affect the JOINTS, which is why I checked his ankles. So it ISN'T a bleeding disorder, and it ISN'T meningitis. In most children it settles by itself over a few weeks.' → 'will his kidneys be alright?' → 'most children recover completely. Because the kidneys can be involved, WE'LL CHECK HIS URINE AND BLOOD PRESSURE REGULARLY — FOR THE NEXT SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS — and that's how we make sure nothing is missed. I'll also send some blood tests today to confirm this isn't a bleeding problem.' (Blanket reassurance with no follow-up plan is a missed management point — THE RENAL FOLLOW-UP IS THE MANAGEMENT.)
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute run: rash 1:30, joints 3:20, stop examining 7:10
ask: 'These spots are a purpuric rash — a small amount of bleeding under the skin.' / 'It's the same on both legs and both buttocks — a symmetrical rash.' / 'It's on his legs and bottom, and nothing on his tummy, chest or back.' / 'When I press on it, the colour doesn't fade — that's a non-blanching rash.' / 'He has no neck stiffness, he's alert, and his observations are normal — so I don't think this is meningitis.'

'Examiner, I appreciate this is a manikin — I'll name each sign I'm looking for.' / 'I'd like to examine for arthritis — taking the ankle, the joint most typically involved.' / 'Inspection for swelling and redness; palpation for tenderness and peri-articular swelling.' / 'Deep palpation for masses, specifically anything suggesting intussusception.' / 'I'd want to examine the scrotum — scrotal involvement occurs, and torsion must be excluded.'

'The small blood vessels become inflamed — usually set off by an infection.' / 'We check his urine and blood pressure for the next six to twelve months.' FOUR SENTENCES THAT LOSE MARKS: 'the primary morphology is purpuric with well-demarcated borders' (noise, to a mother); 'his chest is clear and his pulse is 96' said with a stethoscope on plastic (automatic fail); 'he'll be completely fine' without the follow-up plan; and 'let me first exclude meningitis before I answer' — SHE ASKED NOW. Examiner extras: the platelet count matters because purpura with a LOW platelet count is a different disease; admission for severe pain, vomiting or GI bleeding, hypertension, renal impairment, inability to walk, scrotal involvement, or distance from care; the rash spares the trunk because the distribution follows gravity and hydrostatic pressure in dependent skin, which is why a non-ambulant infant gets it on the back and face instead.

VARIANT A — AN ABDOMINAL MASS ('tenderness in the right side of the abdomen, and you can feel a mass') → NAME IT AND CHANGE GEAR: 'a palpable mass with colicky abdominal pain in a child with HSP makes me concerned about INTUSSUSCEPTION. I'd stop examining, keep him nil by mouth, obtain intravenous access, give analgesia, and arrange an URGENT ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND and surgical review. In this condition the intussusception is typically ILEO-ILEAL, so ultrasound is the diagnostic test rather than an air enema.' And to Jenny: 'I've found something on Liam's tummy that I want a surgeon and a scan to look at straight away... I'm going to ask him not to eat or drink for now.' (Receiving that finding, saying 'thank you' and continuing unchanged means the station has told you the child is sick and you did not hear it.)

VARIANT B — SCROTAL PAIN reported mid-examination → 'scrotal pain and swelling in a boy with this condition CAN be part of the vasculitis — BUT I CANNOT ASSUME THAT. Testicular torsion must be excluded, so I'd request urgent surgical review and a Doppler ultrasound. Torsion is time-critical, so I would not wait for it to settle.' / VARIANT C — THE MOTHER'S REAL FEAR IS LEUKAEMIA ('my niece had leukaemia. She had bruises like this') → REASSURE WITH EVIDENCE, NOT TONE: 'that's part of what I was checking for when I examined him. In leukaemia we'd usually expect enlarged glands, an enlarged spleen, tenderness over the bones and often bleeding gums — and Liam has none of those. He's also not pale and not unwell. The blood test I'll send today will confirm it, and I'll make sure you get the result.' / VARIANT D — THE FEBRILE, UNWELL CHILD (drowsy, poorly perfused, non-blanching rash) → THE STATION STOPS BEING AN EXAMINATION: 'my immediate concern is MENINGOCOCCAL SEPSIS. I would call for senior help, give high-flow oxygen, obtain intravenous or intraosseous access, take blood cultures if it does not delay treatment, and give EMPIRICAL INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS IMMEDIATELY, with a fluid bolus. I would not continue a routine examination.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Marsh, 33, teacher's aide in a South Australian country town; Liam is 5, her youngest, and she has a daughter of 9; she drove forty minutes tonight while her husband stayed home. THE RASH appeared two days ago on his shins and is now up to his thighs and bottom, not itchy and not sore. THE COLD about two weeks ago — runny nose, sore throat, mild fever for three days, better on its own. TUMMY PAIN in waves that makes him curl up for a few minutes, started yesterday, no blood in his poo, vomited once this morning. JOINTS — 'he's been limping a bit', and his ankles look puffy to her. Urine — she hasn't noticed anything odd. No fever now, eating a bit less, drinking normally. Well child, immunisations up to date, no medications or allergies. HER NIECE HAD LEUKAEMIA AT SIX and is well now. TWO FEARS: MENINGITIS, raised in her first or second sentence ('is it meningitis? I read about the glass test'), and LEUKAEMIA, held back and raised only if asked about other worries or as the doctor wraps up. Anxious but articulate; not tearful unless the doctor is cold or dismissive, in which case she goes quiet and volunteers nothing; VISIBLY RELAXES when the meningitis question is answered properly. IF THE DOCTOR TALKS TO THE MANIKIN INSTEAD OF HER: 'sorry — are you talking to me?' If they use jargon: 'sorry — I don't understand what that means.'

Numbers: 4 rash features, 4 organs, 5 abdominal steps, 8 cervical chains, 5 axillary groups. Onset 1-3 weeks post-infection; peak age 3-10 years. PLATELETS NORMAL is the fact that excludes ITP, and clotting is normal. Ankles and knees are the typical joints. Intussusception here is ILEO-ILEAL, so ULTRASOUND is the test. Renal follow-up 6-12 months VERIFY; most settle in 4-6 weeks, with recurrence — usually milder — in a substantial minority, most often within the first few months VERIFY. CLOCK: rash 1:30, joints 3:20, stop examining 7:10.

Pass mark 17 of 24, and ALL of: ARTHRITIS EXAMINED, NON-BLANCHING NAMED, NO INVENTED FINDINGS, and A FOLLOW-UP PLAN GIVEN. Also scored: named the rash type, symmetry and site; plain English throughout; finished the rash inside 1:30; answered the meningitis question when asked; consent taken from HER, not the manikin; named every target before touching; inspection and palpation of the joint; all node groups named both sides; abdomen covering tenderness, guarding, masses, organs and bowel sounds; offered inguinal nodes and scrotum; named the condition; gave ONE mechanism — inflamed blood vessels — and linked skin, kidney, gut and joints to it; linked it to the infection two weeks ago; did not over-reassure; talked to her throughout, checked understanding and invited questions.
fails: ★ Claiming a finding you were not given — a stethoscope on plastic followed by 'his chest is clear and his pulse is 96' is an automatic fail
★ Leaving the joints until after the abdomen, so the only HSP-specific item on the mark sheet is the casualty when time runs out
Deferring the meningitis question until the end — she asked now, so answer now, with the evidence rather than the tone
Addressing the manikin instead of the mother, who is the person who consents; jargon in the rash explanation — primary morphology, borders and secondary change score nothing here

Running past ninety seconds on the rash, every extra sentence stolen from the abdomen; examining the abdomen as though it were the CLL station, spleen only; not offering the scrotum because you expect to be stopped; blanket reassurance with no renal follow-up plan, when the follow-up IS the management

must: FAIL — Claiming a finding you were not given — a stethoscope on plastic followed by 'his chest is clear and his pulse is 96' is an AUTOMATIC FAIL; declare the constraint instead and name every sign before you touch: 'Examiner, I appreciate this is a manikin, so I'll name each sign I'm looking for as I go' — if you were not given it, you do not have it (★)

FAIL — Leaving the joints until after the abdomen, so the only HSP-SPECIFIC item on the mark sheet is the first casualty when the station runs long — move the ARTHRITIS block to about 3:20: 'I'd now like to examine for arthritis, which is one of the features of Henoch–Schönlein purpura; taking the ANKLE, which is the joint most typically involved — on inspection, no swelling and no redness; on palpation I'm feeling for tenderness and PERI-ARTICULAR SWELLING; I'd take the joint through its range of movement, and I'd examine the knees, wrists, elbows and hips the same way'; and do not describe DEFORMITY, which belongs to chronic arthritis rather than an acute vasculitis and reads as recitation (★)

FAIL — Missing NON-BLANCHING, running past ninety seconds on the rash, or using jargon a mother cannot use — FOUR FEATURES in ninety seconds, holding the photograph so she can see it too: TYPE ('these little red-purple spots are a PURPURIC rash — in plain terms, there's a small amount of bleeding under the skin'), SYMMETRY ('the same on both legs and both buttocks'), SITE ('legs and bottom, and none on his tummy, chest or back — that distribution is quite characteristic') and, the important one, NON-BLANCHING ('when I press on it the colour doesn't fade, and that tells us the colour is blood in the skin'); primary morphology, borders and secondary change score nothing here, and every extra sentence is stolen from the abdomen (★)

FAIL — Deferring the MENINGITIS question until the end — she asks it in her first or second sentence, and you answer it THEN, with evidence rather than tone: 'that's exactly the right thing to think about with this kind of rash, and I'm glad you asked; the good news is that Liam has no neck stiffness, he's alert and interacting, and all his observations are normal — children with meningococcal infection are usually very unwell very quickly, and Liam isn't; so I don't think that's what this is, but I'll tell you what I do think once I've examined him'; the same applies if she raises LEUKAEMIA, which she holds back unless you ask about other worries — reassure with the findings ('in leukaemia we'd usually expect enlarged glands, an enlarged spleen, tenderness over the bones and often bleeding gums, and Liam has none of those'), never with a bare 'don't worry' (★)

FAIL — Examining the abdomen as though this were the CLL station, spleen only — the GUT is one of the four inflamed organs, and tenderness and masses are the findings that put a child in theatre: FIVE named steps — inspection; SUPERFICIAL palpation of all nine regions for tenderness, guarding and rigidity; DEEP palpation of all nine regions for masses and specifically anything suggesting INTUSSUSCEPTION; organs (liver edge from the right iliac fossa, then the spleen bimanually, with Castell's offered); and BOWEL SOUNDS; then OFFER what you will not be allowed to do, because it takes eight seconds and it is where the mark lives — the inguinal nodes, and the SCROTUM, 'because scrotal involvement occurs in Henoch–Schönlein purpura and must be distinguished from TESTICULAR TORSION'

SAY — Talk to JENNY, not the manikin, because she is the one who consents and she will ask 'sorry, are you talking to me?' if you drift; then give the diagnosis as ONE PROCESS IN FOUR ORGANS in plain English: 'Henoch–Schönlein purpura, which doctors also call IgA vasculitis — the commonest condition of its type in children; the small blood vessels become inflamed, the tiny tubes that carry blood around the body, usually set off by an infection, which fits with the cold he had a fortnight ago — and ONE THING EXPLAINS EVERYTHING you've noticed: inflamed vessels in the SKIN leak a little blood, and that's the rash; in the KIDNEYS, that's why the urine test showed blood; in the BOWEL, that's his tummy pains; and it can affect the JOINTS, which is why I checked his ankles — so it isn't a bleeding disorder, and it isn't meningitis'; never say 'he'll be completely fine' without the FOLLOW-UP PLAN, because the renal follow-up IS the management: 'most children recover completely, and because the kidneys can be involved we check his urine and blood pressure regularly for the next six to twelve months, which is how we make sure nothing is missed — and I'll send blood tests today to confirm this isn't a bleeding problem'; the PLATELET COUNT is the fact that excludes ITP, leukaemia and DIC, and palpable purpura WITHOUT thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy is the mandatory diagnostic criterion, plus at least one of diffuse abdominal pain, arthritis, renal involvement, or IgA on biopsy (VERIFY against the current classification); measure the BLOOD PRESSURE yourself if it is not given, because hypertension marks renal involvement; home safety net — severe or constant tummy pain, repeated vomiting or blood in the stool, much less urine or urine like cola, puffiness of the face or ankles, scrotal pain or swelling, not drinking or drowsiness or a new fever, or a rash spreading to the trunk; stop examining at 7:10 and turn to the mother; variants — a PALPABLE MASS with colicky pain raises INTUSSUSCEPTION, typically ILEO-ILEAL in this condition, so ULTRASOUND rather than an air enema, with nil by mouth, IV access, analgesia and surgical review; SCROTAL PAIN can be part of the vasculitis but torsion must still be excluded urgently, because assuming otherwise is premature closure; and a FEBRILE, DROWSY, POORLY PERFUSED child with a non-blanching rash is MENINGOCOCCAL SEPSIS — stop the routine examination, senior help, oxygen, IV or intraosseous access, cultures if they do not delay treatment, empirical IV antibiotics immediately and a fluid bolus

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — GP antenatal check. A PREGNANT WOMAN IS IN THE CHAIR AND A MANNEQUIN IS ON THE COUCH: consent HER, palpate IT — if you start on her abdomen she will let you once and then say 'wasn't there a model you were meant to use?'. TWO ACCURACY POINTS SEPARATE CANDIDATES — VISIBLY TURNING TO FACE THE FEET FOR GRIP FOUR, and ACTUALLY COUNTING THE FETAL HEART RATE, which half of candidates forget. back.dx: VERSION A — a normal late third-trimester examination: SFH 36 cm, appropriate for 37 weeks (gestation in weeks plus or minus 2-3 cm); LONGITUDINAL lie with the back on the LEFT; CEPHALIC presentation; head THREE-FIFTHS palpable, so engaging but not yet engaged; FHR 144, within 110-160; BP normal. Explain it as size, then position, then heartbeat, in plain words, then safety-net: reduced movements, bleeding, fluid loss, abdominal pain, or a bad headache with blurred vision. IF NOTHING IS PALPABLE, DO NOT CLAIM IT IS FINE — name what you did assess, name what you could not determine, and say a bedside ultrasound will resolve it. VERSION B — PROLONGED PREGNANCY at 40+4: causes are usually none, with inaccurate dates the commonest explanation (hers are certain), plus nulliparity, family history, previous post-dates, a male fetus, older age, obesity, and rarely a fetal hormonal cause. Implications — FOR HER: longer harder labour, more instrumental delivery and caesarean, more tearing and postpartum haemorrhage; FOR THE BABY: continued growth and macrosomia with shoulder dystocia, reducing liquor with cord compression, meconium aspiration, and rising risk beyond 41 weeks. Management in three parts: CHECK THE BABY (CTG plus ultrasound for liquor and growth); CHECK THE CERVIX with a speculum and A BISHOP SCORE — omitting it is how this station fails; and GET THINGS MOVING — offer a membrane sweep now, and INDUCTION FROM 41 WEEKS, ripening with gel or a balloon if the Bishop score is 6 or less, then ARM and oxytocin. IT IS HER DECISION: if she declines, twice-weekly CTG and liquor volume, and delivery by 42 weeks. TRANSVERSE LIE: scan for placental position and liquor, offer ECV from 37 weeks, caesarean around 39 weeks if it fails or is declined — and if her waters break or contractions start, COME IN IMMEDIATELY BY AMBULANCE because of the cord prolapse risk.
plan: OBSERVATIONS FIRST, then the missing BP noticed: 'Examiner, before I start, may I have Jenny's observations — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature? I notice the blood pressure hasn't been recorded — may I measure it?' Then hand hygiene and gloves, and the WIPE with a rapport line: '...can I confirm your full name and date of birth? How has the pregnancy been going so far — have you been enjoying it?' (The chit-chat is RAPPORT, NOT HISTORY — if she opens a symptom door, acknowledge, park it and come back: 'thank you for telling me — I'll come back to that properly once I've examined you.')

The explanation, exposure, chaperone and POSITION: 'today I've been asked to examine your tummy. I'll LOOK at your tummy first, then gently FEEL it to work out how the baby is lying, and at the end I'll LISTEN TO YOUR BABY'S HEARTBEAT with a stethoscope or a handheld Doppler. It shouldn't hurt at all, but if anything is uncomfortable please tell me straight away and I'll stop. I'll need to uncover your tummy from about the middle of your chest down to just above your pubic bone, and I'll keep you covered everywhere else. WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE PRESENT? I'd also like you lying back with your head supported and TILTED SLIGHTLY TO YOUR LEFT, which keeps the blood flowing well to the baby.' Then move to HER RIGHT SIDE — and to the mannequin.

PERIPHERIES IN 30 SECONDS, and accept the cut instantly: 'alert, comfortable at rest, not pale, not jaundiced. May I look at your hands? No palmar pallor, no swelling of the fingers, radial pulse regular at about 84. Blood pressure 118 over 76, normal. On the face there is NO PERIORBITAL OEDEMA, no chloasma, no conjunctival pallor and no scleral jaundice.' → 'skip the peripheral signs' → 'thank you, examiner — I'll move straight to the abdomen.' Then inspection: 'the abdomen is distended consistent with a term pregnancy, LONGITUDINALLY OVOID, no visible fetal movements, no surgical scars, no linea nigra and no striae gravidarum.' (Ninety seconds on peripheries and the grips get rushed; arguing with the redirection is worse.)

SYMPHYSIO-FUNDAL HEIGHT, landmarks located out loud: 'Jenny, I'm going to start feeling your tummy now. I'll be gentle — tell me if anything is uncomfortable. Examiner, I'm using the ULNAR BORDER of my hand from just below the xiphisternum to locate the top of the uterus... I have the fundus. I'm now identifying the UPPER BORDER OF THE SYMPHYSIS PUBIS... I have it. ZERO AT THE SYMPHYSIS, measuring in the midline, crossing the umbilicus, up to the highest point of the fundus. The symphysio-fundal height is 36 centimetres, APPROPRIATE FOR 37 WEEKS — I accept gestation in weeks plus or minus 2 to 3 centimetres. I'd plot this on her customised growth chart.' (If the number looks impossible, RE-MEASURE BEFORE YOU COMMENT: 'that's not what I expected — I'll re-check my landmarks.' One candidate read the inches side and reported 11 cm at 37 weeks. Re-checking is a mark, not a weakness.)

THE FOUR GRIPS, findings reported and conclusions saved for the end. GRIP 1, FUNDAL, facing her head: 'cupping both hands over the fundus, I'm checking which part of the baby occupies the fundus. A broad, softer, irregular pole that moves with the trunk — consistent with the BREECH.' GRIP 2, LATERAL: 'stabilising with my left hand and palpating with the palm of my right, then swapping. I'm assessing the LIE and the POSITION OF THE BACK. On the left, firm, flat, continuous resistance — the fetal back. On the right, small, irregular, mobile parts — the limbs. The lie is LONGITUDINAL.' GRIP 3, PELVIC: 'using the thumb and fingers of one hand suprapubically, checking the PRESENTING PART. A hard, round, smooth mass — the presentation is CEPHALIC.' (Both hands rubbing at once on the lateral grip is wrong — one hand stabilises. And do not announce a diagnosis at grip two.)

GRIP 4 — THE ACCURACY POINT: 'I'm NOW TURNING TO FACE JENNY'S FEET to assess engagement. Placing both hands on the lower abdomen and sliding them down towards the pelvic brim, I can feel about THREE-FIFTHS of the head above the brim, so the head is beginning to engage but is not yet engaged.' TURN YOUR BODY AND LET IT BE SEEN — doing grip four facing her head is the single accuracy point that separates candidates. IF YOU FEEL NOTHING AT ALL, do not press harder and do not invent: 'Examiner, I'm unable to define a fetal pole at the fundus. I'll continue — on the lateral grip I'm assessing the lie, on the pelvic grip the presenting part, and facing the feet, the degree of descent. I would confirm the lie and presentation with a bedside ultrasound.'

THE FETAL HEART — the step half of candidates forget: 'Jenny, last part — I'd like to listen to your baby's heartbeat. Examiner, DO I HAVE A HANDHELD DOPPLER, OR WOULD YOU LIKE ME TO USE MY STETHOSCOPE? I'm placing the diaphragm OVER THE FETAL BACK, below the umbilicus on the left. MAY I HAVE A TIMER? Counting for fifteen seconds... that is 36, giving a fetal heart rate of 144 beats per minute, within the normal range of 110 to 160. I'M PALPATING JENNY'S RADIAL PULSE AT THE SAME TIME to confirm this is the baby's heart rate and not hers.' (NEVER GUESS THE NUMBER — every candidate that day gets the same recording and the examiner already knows it. If you lose count: 'I lost count — may I have another fifteen seconds?' That costs nothing; inventing a plausible number costs the accuracy domain.)

Cover her, help her sit up, complete, then EXPLAIN IN PLAIN WORDS — size, position, heartbeat: 'your womb measured 36 centimetres and at 37 weeks we'd expect between 34 and 40, so your baby is growing exactly as we'd expect. Your baby is lying UP AND DOWN rather than across, with his HEAD DOWN at the bottom and his bottom at the top — the ideal position for a normal birth. His back is along your left side. His head has just started to settle down into your pelvis, which is exactly what we like to see at this stage. And his heartbeat is 144, right in the normal range. Your blood pressure is normal too.' Then questions, and the safety-net: reduced movements, bleeding, fluid loss, tummy pain, or a bad headache with blurred vision. Her hidden agenda if you leave a gap: 'my sister said I look small for 37 weeks — is the baby big enough?' → 'that's exactly what I was measuring... if it were ever more than about three centimetres off, we'd simply arrange a scan.'

VERSION B — THE POST-DATES CASE, four blocks: DIAGNOSIS ('the good news first: your baby is head-down, growing well, and the heartbeat is normal. My concern is how far along you are... once a pregnancy goes past 41 weeks we call it a PROLONGED PREGNANCY, and beyond that the risks slowly start to rise'); CAUSES (usually none, dates checked first because inaccurate dates are the commonest explanation, then first baby, family history, previous post-dates, a boy, older age, extra weight — 'none of these are anything you have done'); IMPLICATIONS (for her: longer labour, instruments or caesarean, tearing, heavier bleeding; for him: continued growth and a difficult shoulder delivery, reducing fluid pressing on the cord, meconium, and rising risk past 41 weeks); MANAGEMENT (CTG and ultrasound; SPECULUM AND A BISHOP SCORE; a membrane sweep now; induction from 41 weeks, ripening first if the Bishop score is 6 or less, then ARM and oxytocin — AND IT IS HER DECISION, with twice-weekly CTG and liquor if she waits, and delivery by 42 weeks). This station fails on OMISSION OF THE BISHOP SCORE and on STEAMROLLING THE INDUCTION.

VARIANTS: THE EMPTY MANNEQUIN — 'don't tell me what you're looking for, tell me what you feel' → 'Examiner, I'm not able to define a fetal pole here. I'll continue through the remaining grips and tell you anything I do feel, and I'd confirm the lie and presentation with a bedside ultrasound.' DO NOT PRESS HARDER AND DO NOT INVENT — candidates have passed feeling absolutely nothing. / TRANSVERSE LIE — 'the abdomen appears BROADER TRANSVERSELY than it is long. On the fundal grip I can't define a pole. On the lateral grip a hard, round, ballottable mass in the right flank — most likely the head... no presenting part at the brim. My conclusion is a TRANSVERSE LIE at 37 weeks.' To her: scan first, then ECV offered at about 37 weeks in hospital with monitoring, caesarean if it fails or she declines — and IF YOUR WATERS BREAK OR CONTRACTIONS START, COME IN IMMEDIATELY BY AMBULANCE, because the cord can come down first. / SHE DECLINES INDUCTION — never pressure, never simply agree and walk away: acknowledge the pain concern, give the reason the risks rise, then 'if that's your choice we'll support it and watch closely — twice a week for a CTG and a scan of the fluid, and I'd recommend we plan the birth by 42 weeks whatever happens.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Marsh, 31, primary school teacher on maternity leave, living with her partner Dave and children of 5 and 3, both born vaginally at term. Third pregnancy, 37+2 by an 8-week dating scan; routine care, all screening normal, no gestational diabetes or hypertension, blood group O positive; never smoked, no alcohol, pregnancy multivitamin taken reliably; mother had high blood pressure in her last pregnancy. Warm, chatty, a little tired, mildly anxious underneath — she wants to be told the baby is all right and a normal birth is still on the cards. HIDDEN AGENDA: her sister told her she 'looks small for 37 weeks' and she has been quietly worried since; not volunteered — given if asked about worries, or raised near the very end. HOW SHE PLAYS IT: SAY 'OW' LOUDLY if the doctor presses hard, digs fingertips in, or palpates roughly, then look at them and wait — THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING SHE DOES. If they go silent at the mannequin for more than about 30 seconds: 'is everything all right?' If they never explain what they are about to do: 'what are you doing now?' IF THEY START PALPATING HER ABDOMEN, allow it once, then: 'sorry — wasn't there a model you were meant to use?' Warm with a doctor who talks to her; quieter and more anxious with one who ignores her. When the heartbeat is heard: 'is that fast? It sounds fast.'

Numbers: FIVE steps — four grips plus the fetal heart. Grips 1-3 face the head; GRIP 4 FACES THE FEET. SFH = gestation in weeks plus or minus 2-3 cm, 34-40 cm at 37 weeks, plotted from 24 weeks. Engagement 5/5 free to 2/5 or less = engaged, to 0/5. FHR 110-160, counted for 15 seconds and multiplied by four. Tilt 15-30 degrees left lateral. GBS swab at 35-37 weeks. ECV offered from 37 weeks, caesarean around 39 weeks if it fails. PROLONGED PREGNANCY 41+0, POST-TERM 42+0. Induction offered from 41+0, delivery by 42 weeks. BISHOP SCORE 6 or less means ripen first; 7 or more means ARM plus oxytocin. If she declines: twice-weekly CTG and liquor volume.

Score out of 10, one point each: asked for observations before starting; introduced, confirmed identity, took consent, offered a chaperone; explained each step before doing it; stood on the RIGHT and worked on the MANNEQUIN, not on her; located the landmarks before measuring the fundal height; did all four grips in order with commentary; TURNED TO FACE THE FEET for the fourth grip; LISTENED TO AND COUNTED the fetal heart rate; stayed gentle throughout and responded properly to 'ow'; explained findings in plain words, asked for questions, and safety-netted.
Grip 1 — fundal — A BROAD, SOFTER, IRREGULAR pole moving with the trunk — the BREECH
Grip 2 — lateral — Firm flat continuous resistance on the LEFT (the back), small mobile parts on the right — lie LONGITUDINAL
Grip 4 — engagement — THREE-FIFTHS palpable above the brim — ENGAGING but NOT engaged
