findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Missing any of the FIVE STARRED ITEMS — RED REFLEX through the ophthalmoscope in BOTH eyes; the PHRASE 'dysmorphic features' with three or four named; hips INSPECTED (creases and limb length) then BARLOW then ORTOLANI, all named; both testes PALPATED with 'undescended testis' said aloud; and the MORO performed and described as SYMMETRICAL (★)

FAIL — Silence — more than about three pauses over five seconds is the commonest reason candidates fail this station; the sentence shape that carries it is 'I am looking for [named condition] — I do not find it', and when the model cannot cooperate, 'the model doesn't allow this; on a baby I would [do X], looking for [named condition]', and when you are behind, 'for time I will state rather than perform the following, and I'm happy to demonstrate any of them' (★)

FAIL — Naming the swelling without first asking whether it CROSSES THE SUTURE LINE — the discriminator between a routine finding and an emergency is a single anatomical question, and asking it IS the mark: 'does the swelling cross the suture line, or does it stop at it?'; name all three scalp swellings and the rule — CAPUT is oedema ABOVE the periosteum, present at birth, soft, pits, CROSSES sutures, resolving in 24 to 48 hours; CEPHALOHAEMATOMA is SUBPERIOSTEAL blood, appearing hours after birth, firm then fluctuant, LIMITED BY sutures, two weeks to three months; and SUBGALEAL haemorrhage CROSSES them, is boggy, shifts with head position and can hold a large proportion of the blood volume — that is the one to be frightened of, needing volume resuscitation, cross-match, coagulation screen, serial head circumference and neonatal unit care; a cephalohaematoma is managed CONSERVATIVELY and NEVER aspirated or incised, monitoring bilirubin because resorbing blood causes jaundice (★)

FAIL — Skipping hip INSPECTION and going straight to the manoeuvres, the single commonest fail in this station — creases and limb length come FIRST, then name each manoeuvre and what it is trying to achieve, because the naming is the mark: BARLOW flexes to ninety degrees with the thumb on the inner thigh, adducting and pushing posteriorly, one side at a time, TRYING TO DISLOCATE a hip that is in joint; ORTOLANI holds both thighs and abducts together like opening a book, lifting anteriorly, TRYING TO RELOCATE a hip that is already dislocated; be at the hips by 4:40, and know that a NORMAL examination does not exclude dysplasia — breech, female sex, first-born, family history and oligohydramnios all mean a hip ultrasound at about six weeks regardless (★)

FAIL — Skipping the opening because the stem has already given consent, or inspecting the genitalia from a metre away — say it anyway, because it costs eight seconds and it is scored (identity against the wristband, mother's consent, then observations, weight, head circumference, and whether he has fed, passed urine and passed meconium, which takes thirty seconds and frames every finding after it); and you must be SEEN TO PALPATE the scrotum from the inguinal canal down on each side, because the mannequin is a boy for exactly that reason — with the meatus at the tip excluding hypospadias and epispadias, and a patent, normally sited anus; this is also the one station where you INTRODUCE YOURSELF TO THE EXAMINER, who is the only other person in the room (★)

SAY — Read the word INSTRUMENTS and say so up front, because three lines show that you did: the FONTANELLE not bulging (a bulging fontanelle after an instrumental delivery raises intracranial haemorrhage), the CLAVICLES intact with no step or crepitus, and the MORO symmetrical (asymmetry suggests a brachial plexus injury or a fractured clavicle); AUSCULTATE FIRST, before he cries, using two positions on a chest smaller than your diaphragm — and remember respiratory distress is an INSPECTION finding (grunting, nasal flaring, tracheal tug, intercostal and subcostal recession), said while you are looking rather than listening; examine the UMBILICAL STUMP because he is SIX HOURS OLD, the item only a newborn stem can test and the one candidates forget because the doll has no cord (clean and dry, three vessels, no surrounding redness suggesting omphalitis); the red reflex is done FROM A DISTANCE looking THROUGH the instrument rather than fundoscopy up close, and an absent or white reflex means congenital CATARACT or RETINOBLASTOMA, both needing same-day ophthalmology; name the two neck lumps rather than 'looking for lumps' (midline THYROGLOSSAL duct cyst, lateral BRANCHIAL cyst); it is RADIO-FEMORAL delay with weak femoral pulses that indicates COARCTATION, not radio-radial, which indicates a subclavian origin lesion; floppy is HYPOTONIA, while hypertonia is the stiff, extended, fisted baby with scissoring legs; RESERVE THE LAST FORTY SECONDS for a structured summary with a plan — measurements plotted in the state child health record, vitamin K and hepatitis B confirmed, the newborn bloodspot screen at 48 to 72 hours, the hearing screen, pulse oximetry with pre- and post-ductal saturations, and handover for a six-week check — because running to the bell and offering nothing is worth less than one extra reflex; cover the baby and wash your hands before you summarise; and Version B, the SIX-WEEK CHECK with the mother at the bedside, changes everything except your hands — obtain consent yourself, and CONTRACT FOR A SUMMARY AT THE END rather than promising to explain as you go, because forty translations means you never reach the hips, with only three mid-examination reassurances (after the chest, after the eyes, after the hips) and sixty seconds of lay-terms closing with questions invited and a safety net

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional GP, Wallaroo. TWO EXAMINATIONS IN ONE STATION, so consent to BOTH in one sentence and NAME THE REPOSITIONING UP FRONT. THE HINGE IS AT 4:00: if you are still at the head at five minutes you will not finish the cardiovascular examination, and if you never lie him back you have done half the task. SAY THE REASON ALOUD AS YOU REPOSITION — it converts a sequence into reasoning. And never leave without asking about sleepiness at the wheel.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo. Michael Docherty, 40, with DAYTIME SLEEPINESS; his partner complains he SNORES LOUDLY. Known hypertensive on treatment. BP 158/96 — HR 78 regular — RR 14 — SpO2 96% RA — 108 kg, 178 cm, BMI 34. 8 minutes, no history required.
tasks: Perform a relevant focused physical examination with a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient and what your examination was looking for
time: CONSENT TO BOTH EXAMINATIONS AND THE REPOSITIONING in one opening · GENERAL APPEARANCE IN THREE SENTENCES naming the SHORT THICK NECK inside the first thirty seconds · hands, pulse, and MEASURE THE BLOOD PRESSURE YOURSELF WITH A LARGE CUFF, because an undersized cuff over-reads in an arm this size and the sphygmomanometer was put on the trolley to see whether you use it · ASK FOR FUNDOSCOPY UNPROMPTED and read the photograph in a FIXED ORDER: DISC, then VESSELS, then BACKGROUND · THE NOSE with the tip lifted and a torch, then THE THROAT: 'open wide and poke your tongue right out · WITHOUT MAKING A SOUND', because saying aah or using a tongue depressor lifts the palate and gives a falsely reassuring Mallampati · grade the MALLAMPATI and the TONSILS confidently · ASK FOR NECK CIRCUMFERENCE, waist and BMI, the request itself being the mark · THE HINGE AT 4:00: 'that completes the airway. I'm now going to lay the bed back to about forty-five degrees and examine your heart, BECAUSE SLEEP APNOEA AND BLOOD PRESSURE TRAVEL TOGETHER' · CVS at 45 degrees screening for HEART FAILURE (JVP, hepatojugular reflux, bases, liver, ankles) · then sit him up, ask what he already thinks, name it, explain the mechanism in plain words, EXPLAIN WHY YOU TOUCHED THE CHEST, and finish with the driving question.

back.dx: OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNOEA — daytime sleepiness and loud snoring in an obese hypertensive man with a short thick neck, BMI 34, MALLAMPATI III with a crowded oropharynx, large tongue and slightly receding jaw, no nasal obstruction and tonsils grade 1 — plus GRADE 3 HYPERTENSIVE RETINOPATHY WITH SHARP DISCS and no clinical evidence of heart failure. THE MECHANISM IN PLAIN WORDS: when you fall asleep the muscles at the back of your throat relax and go floppy; in a narrow airway that tissue closes over, you stop breathing for a few seconds, your body notices the oxygen dropping and wakes you just enough to open it again — dozens of times an hour, all night. You never remember waking, but you never get proper deep sleep, which is why you are exhausted all day. PLAN: a SLEEP STUDY, usually at home; weight loss as the single biggest lever; NO ALCOHOL FOR THREE TO FOUR HOURS BEFORE BED; side rather than back; CPAP if moderate or severe, a mandibular advancement splint if mild; and urine dipstick for protein, ECG, TSH, HbA1c and lipids. Then THE DRIVING SENTENCE: 'have you ever felt sleepy at the wheel? Until this is measured and treated you must not drive if you feel sleepy' — and for a commercial driver, the standards are stricter and there is a reporting obligation in South Australia, framed as 'this is not me taking your licence; it is us getting you treated so you keep it safely'. Safety-net morning headaches, chest pain, ankle swelling, or falling asleep in the day without warning. IF THE DISC MARGIN IS BLURRED: grade 4, accelerated hypertension — recheck the BP now, dipstick the urine, renal bloods, SAME-DAY assessment rather than routine review.
plan: CONSENT TO BOTH, and name the repositioning now: '...I have been asked to examine you today. I will be doing TWO THINGS: first looking at your nose and the back of your throat, because that is the airway you breathe through at night; then examining your heart — looking, feeling and listening to your chest. I need you sitting up to start, and LATER I WILL LAY YOU BACK TO ABOUT FORTY-FIVE DEGREES, so I will need your chest exposed for that part. Any pain anywhere? Happy for me to go ahead?' → 'what's my throat got to do with being tired?' → 'that is where the airway narrows when you are asleep — I will explain at the end.' (Consenting only to 'an ENT examination' boxes you in.)

THREE SENTENCES, then move: 'on general inspection this is an alert, comfortable, OVERWEIGHT middle-aged man with a SHORT, THICK NECK. He is not cyanosed, not in respiratory distress, there is no audible stridor and he is not mouth-breathing at rest. From the chart the blood pressure is 158 over 96, heart rate 78 and regular, saturations 96% on room air.' Then hands and pulse: 'no clubbing, no peripheral cyanosis, no nicotine staining, no tendon xanthomata. Pulse 78, regular, normal volume and character. I WOULD NOW LIKE TO CHECK THE BLOOD PRESSURE MYSELF, USING A LARGE ADULT CUFF — IN AN ARM THIS SIZE A STANDARD CUFF OVER-READS.' (If told to skip it: 'thank you — I would want it in both arms with the correct cuff size', then move on immediately. The cuff-size sentence is the cheapest distinguishing mark in the station.)

FUNDOSCOPY, ASKED FOR UNPROMPTED, then read in a fixed order: 'Examiner, in a patient with known hypertension I would like to perform fundoscopy on both eyes in a darkened room, looking for hypertensive retinopathy.' → photograph → LOOK AT IT FOR THREE SECONDS, then DISC first: 'the DISC MARGINS ARE SHARP. The ARTERIOLES are narrowed with copper wiring and there is arteriovenous nipping. In the BACKGROUND there are blot haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and hard exudates. This is hypertensive retinopathy — GRADE 3 with sharp discs; it would be grade 4 if the disc were swollen, which would make this accelerated hypertension needing same-day management.' (Naming findings in a random order and never mentioning the disc is the trap: a swollen disc described and then followed by a routine referral is an automatic fail.)

NOSE, THEN THROAT — the two scored findings: 'Michael, could you look up at the ceiling?' (lift the tip, torch) 'the mucosa is pink and not boggy, I cannot see NASAL POLYPS, there is no septal deviation visible anteriorly, no turbinate hypertrophy and no discharge. Both nostrils are patent when I occlude each in turn.' Then: 'now OPEN YOUR MOUTH AS WIDE AS YOU CAN AND POKE YOUR TONGUE RIGHT OUT — WITHOUT MAKING A SOUND. Examiner, I am assessing the MODIFIED MALLAMPATI SCORE: I can see the soft palate and the base of the uvula only, so this is CLASS III, a crowded oropharynx. The TONSILS ARE GRADE 1, within the pillars, with no visible adenoidal tissue. The tongue is large relative to the oral cavity and the mandible is slightly receding.' → 'why not the ears?' → 'because the question is the upper airway. I would examine the ears if he had ear symptoms, but they will not change my diagnosis here.'

MEASUREMENTS, THEN THE HINGE: 'to complete the airway assessment I would like to measure the NECK CIRCUMFERENCE — the most useful single measurement here — the waist circumference, and his height and weight for a BMI.' → 'there is no tape measure' → 'understood — I would want a neck circumference above 43 cm and a waist above 94 cm as supporting features.' Then: 'THAT COMPLETES THE AIRWAY. Michael, I am now going to lay the bed back to about forty-five degrees and examine your heart, BECAUSE SLEEP APNOEA AND BLOOD PRESSURE TRAVEL TOGETHER. Could you slip your shirt off for me?' (This is the moment the station is won or lost.)

CARDIOVASCULAR AT 45 DEGREES, aimed at heart failure: 'turn your head slightly to the left — the JVP is not raised. Pressing over the right upper quadrant, a transient rise that falls back: hepatojugular reflux negative. Trachea central, no goitre — I WOULD CHECK A TSH, as hypothyroidism worsens this. No carotid bruits. Chest: no scars or deformity, apex not displaced, no parasternal heave, no thrills at the four areas. Bell then diaphragm at the apex, then tricuspid, pulmonary and aortic: S1 and S2 normal, no murmur, no third or fourth sound, P2 not loud. Both sides anteriorly and out to the axillae: no bibasal crepitations. Right iliac fossa to costal margin: no palpable liver edge. No ankle or sacral oedema. To complete: urine dipstick for protein, an ECG and an EPWORTH SLEEPINESS SCALE.' → 'why are you listening to the lungs in an ENT station?' → 'I am screening for heart failure — bases, liver, ankles — because untreated sleep apnoea and hypertension both damage the heart.' (A full respiratory examination earns nothing here and costs you the explanation task.)

SIT HIM UP, ASK WHAT HE THINKS, NAME IT, EXPLAIN THE MECHANISM: 'before I tell you what I think — had you any idea what might be causing the tiredness?' → 'getting old and fat, I reckon' → 'from what you have described and what I have found, I think you have a condition called OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNOEA.' Then the plain-words mechanism (see dx) → 'so I actually stop breathing?' → 'briefly, yes — your body restarts it every time; it is the interruption that causes the tiredness.' → 'is it going to kill me?' → 'untreated it raises your blood pressure and your risk of heart problems and stroke — which is why we treat it. It is very treatable.'

WHY YOU EXAMINED THE HEART, THE PLAN, AND THE DRIVING SENTENCE: 'let me tell you what I was doing. First I was checking your AIRWAY — the back of your throat, to see how much room there is, and inside your nose for anything blocking it, like polyps or a bent partition. Then I examined your HEART: sleep apnoea and heart disease travel together, and uncontrolled blood pressure strains the heart and damages the small vessels in the eyes and kidneys. The good news is that your heart examination was normal today.' Then the sleep study, weight, alcohol, position, CPAP or a dental splint — and: 'ONE IMPORTANT THING: HAVE YOU EVER FELT SLEEPY AT THE WHEEL?' → (pause) 'once or twice on the Copper Coast road' → 'then this matters more than the tiredness. Until it is measured and treated, you must not drive if you feel sleepy. I am not taking anything off you — I am getting you treated so you stay safe.' Safety-net morning headaches, chest pain, ankle swelling. (Explaining sleep apnoea beautifully and never explaining why you touched the chest answers only half of task 2.)

'Open wide, tongue out, WITHOUT MAKING A SOUND.' / 'Modified Mallampati class III; tonsils grade 1, within the pillars.' / 'I would measure the neck circumference, waist and BMI.' / 'That completes the airway — I am laying you back to forty-five degrees.' / 'I am screening for heart failure — bases, liver, ankles.'

'The muscles at the back of your throat go floppy and close the airway over.' / 'I examined your heart because sleep apnoea and blood pressure travel together.' / 'HAVE YOU EVER FELT SLEEPY AT THE WHEEL?' / 'This is not me taking your licence; it is us getting you treated so you keep it safely.'

VARIANTS: BLURRED DISC MARGIN → 'there is disc swelling — GRADE 4 hypertensive retinopathy, or accelerated hypertension. My urgency changes: recheck the blood pressure now, dipstick the urine, bloods for renal function, and arrange SAME-DAY assessment, not a routine review.' / 'I DRIVE A TRUCK FOR THE GRAIN CO-OP' → 'the standards for commercial driving are stricter. Until this is measured and treated you must not drive if you feel sleepy, and in South Australia I have a reporting obligation... I will chase the sleep study urgently.' / 'IT'S ONLY SNORING — MY WIFE'S THE ONE COMPLAINING' → 'the snoring is the noise; the problem is underneath it. Your airway is closing over and interrupting your sleep, and untreated that pushes your blood pressure up and raises your risk of heart problems, stroke and crashes.'

MORE: 'WHAT IF THE SLEEP STUDY IS NORMAL?' → 'then look elsewhere — hypothyroidism, poorly controlled diabetes, anaemia, depression, insufficient sleep or shift work, alcohol and sedating medications — and if it persisted, referral for narcolepsy assessment.' / ANKLE SWELLING AND CRACKLES GIVEN → 'raised JVP, bibasal crepitations and pitting oedema — that is heart failure. ECG, BNP and echocardiogram, and consider CENTRAL apnoea with a Cheyne-Stokes pattern.' If he starts at 45 degrees, do the airway there and continue straight on.
pefe: Role-player: Michael Docherty, 40, machinery operator and TRUCK DRIVER for the grain co-op at Wallaroo; married to Deb, two kids; 108 kg and 178 cm, up about 15 kg in four years; perindopril taken 'most days' with a gap last month when the script ran out; four or five stubbies most nights in front of the TV; smoked until 30; father had a stroke at 61. Exhausted every afternoon, asleep in the chair by seven; DEB SLEEPS IN THE SPARE ROOM because of the snoring and says he STOPS BREATHING THEN GASPS; dry mouth and a dull headache two or three mornings a week. HIDDEN AGENDA: HE NODDED OFF AT THE WHEEL ON THE COPPER COAST ROAD a couple of months ago and drifted onto the gravel — it frightened him badly, HE HAS TOLD NOBODY INCLUDING DEB, and he is afraid of losing his licence and his job. Flat, dry, a bit fatalistic, not hostile; he MINIMISES ('it's just the snoring') until the doctor takes it seriously. Asked directly about driving or sleepiness at the wheel he pauses, looks away, and tells them; if never asked he volunteers it at about seven and a half minutes. He pushes once at the throat: 'what's my throat got to do with it?' If given false reassurance he says 'so it's not serious then?' and lets them dig the hole.

Numbers: neck over 43 cm in men and 41 cm in women, with STOP-BANG using 40 cm or more; waist 94 cm or more in men, 80 cm or more in women; BMI 34 in this stem. Mallampati I-IV, with III-IV predicting OSA; tonsils Brodsky 1-4. AHI 5-14 mild, 15-29 moderate, 30 or more severe. Epworth over 10 is excessive sleepiness (8 or more for referral criteria). An apnoea is 10 seconds or more. No alcohol within 3-4 hours of bed. A 10% weight loss cuts AHI by about a quarter. The cuff bladder should cover at least 80% of the arm. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450, PATS for travel.

Mark them on: consented to BOTH examinations and named the repositioning up front; said SHORT THICK NECK in the first thirty seconds; measured or asked for the blood pressure WITH CUFF SIZE; asked for fundoscopy unprompted and DESCRIBED THE DISC FIRST; graded Mallampati and tonsils without asking for 'aah' or using a blade; asked for neck circumference, waist and BMI; REPOSITIONED TO 45 DEGREES BY FOUR MINUTES and examined the heart; screened for heart failure with JVP, bases, liver and ankles; explained the mechanism in plain words with no jargon; EXPLAINED WHY THE HEART WAS EXAMINED; named a sleep study, weight, alcohol, position and CPAP; ASKED ABOUT SLEEPINESS AT THE WHEEL and gave clear advice; and finished the explanation within the eight minutes.

FAIL — Walking past the sphygmomanometer, which was put on the trolley to see whether you use it, and never mentioning CUFF SIZE — the cheapest distinguishing mark in the station: 'I'd like to check the blood pressure myself, using a LARGE ADULT CUFF, because in an arm this size a standard cuff over-reads' (the bladder should cover at least 80% of the arm); if told to skip it, 'thank you — I'd still want it in both arms with the correct cuff size', then move on without arguing (★)

you stop breathing for a few seconds, your body notices the oxygen dropping and wakes you just enough to open the airway again, and that can happen dozens of times an hour; you never remember waking, but you never get proper deep sleep either, which is exactly why you're exhausted all day' — then 'I examined your heart because sleep apnoea and heart disease travel together, and uncontrolled blood pressure strains the heart and damages the small vessels in the eyes and kidneys'; ask for the NECK CIRCUMFERENCE as the most useful single measurement, plus waist and BMI, because the request itself is the mark (over 43 cm in men, waist 94 cm or more, BMI 34 here); screen for heart failure rather than examining the chest generically — JVP, hepatojugular reflux, bases, liver, ankles — and offer a urine dipstick for protein, an ECG and an EPWORTH SLEEPINESS SCALE; Epworth over 10); safety net — morning headaches, chest pain, ankle swelling, or falling asleep during the day without warning; and if the sleep study is NORMAL, look elsewhere: hypothyroidism, poorly controlled diabetes, anaemia, depression, insufficient sleep or shift work, alcohol and sedating medications, with narcolepsy assessment if it persists

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — rural GP, mannequin, FIVE MINUTES FOR THE EXAMINATION AND THEN A PROMPT. THE MARKS LIVE IN THE SEVEN CHARACTERISTICS, in order, with consistency tested ON TWO AXES and mobility in TWO STEPS — and TENDERNESS IS THE ONE YOU CANNOT FEEL, SO YOU HAVE TO ASK. When you find a lump, DO NOT STOP: finish both breasts first, because in the bilateral version the PATTERN is the diagnosis. Three sentences fail this station: 'yes, there is a lump' and nothing further; 'I'm sure it's nothing to worry about'; and 'I'll refer you to BreastScreen for a mammogram'.
stem: VERSION A: rural South Australian practice. Jenny Harding, 28, felt a LUMP IN HER RIGHT BREAST three weeks ago; otherwise well, no discharge, no fevers. A mannequin is provided. Tasks: examine both breasts and the regional nodes with commentary (5 minutes, prompted), RECORD THE FINDINGS ON THE DIAGRAM, give the diagnosis and differentials to the patient, and explain the investigations. 8 minutes total.
VERSION B: Melissa Grant, 35, BILATERAL BREAST PAIN for months, worse premenstrually, on the combined pill — and YOU WILL FIND MULTIPLE LUMPS IN BOTH BREASTS.

The carcinoma mannequin: skin PUCKERING in the right upper outer quadrant most obvious on leaning forward, NIPPLE RETRACTION, a 3 x 2 cm lump — irregular border, bumpy surface, HARD AND STONY on two axes, fixed and TETHERED TO PECTORALIS on contraction, non-tender — plus a single 1 cm firm mobile node in the right central axillary group.

Record your findings on the diagram provided

time: WIPE IN 45-60 SECONDS, AND DO NOT RUSH THE SECOND HALF OF IT: the steps explained before touching, CONSENT TAKEN TWICE, privacy and a sheet, a stop signal, and A CHAPERONE OFFERED WITHOUT STALLING OVER WHO · name a nurse and move · INSPECTION: give all THREE POSITIONS in one run (hands in lap, hands on hips pushing in, hands behind head leaning forward), THEN ONE COMMENTARY covering SKIN, NIPPLE and DISCHARGE · PALPATION: temperature with the backs of the fingers, then the systematic sweep with the FLAT PADS compressing against the chest wall, in VERTICAL STRIPS from clavicle to inframammary fold, sternum to mid-axillary line, INCLUDING UNDER THE NIPPLE AND THE AXILLARY TAIL, starting on the NORMAL SIDE · and if she declines to lie down, adapt to a BIMANUAL technique with one hand supporting the breast · CHARACTERISE BY 4:00, the seven in order · NODES: five axillary groups named with the arm supported, then supraclavicular BOTH SIDES · then the diagram narrated aloud, the diagnosis, and the TRIPLE TEST in lay language.

back.dx: THE SEVEN CHARACTERISTICS, in order: SITE (quadrant), SIZE, BORDER (rub around it), SURFACE (rub across it), CONSISTENCY ON TWO AXES (stabilise between finger and thumb and press on two axes), MOBILITY IN TWO STEPS (freely mobile within the breast, and does it move on PECTORAL CONTRACTION — tethering), and TENDERNESS, which you must ASK about. FIBROADENOMA: solitary, ~1.5 cm, regular border, smooth surface, RUBBERY, freely mobile, no tethering, non-tender — the commonest breast lump in a young woman — but say honestly that a cyst, fibrocystic change, fat necrosis or A BREAST CANCER cannot be excluded by feel, which is exactly why you do not stop at examination. CARCINOMA: hard and stony, irregular, fixed, tethered, with skin puckering or nipple retraction and possibly a node. THE TRIPLE TEST, in lay terms: (1) the examination just done; (2) IMAGING — ULTRASOUND IF UNDER 35, ultrasound PLUS MAMMOGRAM from 35; (3) a CORE BIOPSY, because feel and scan can both be wrong and the only way to be certain is to look at the cells. Together they pick up over 99 in 100 cancers, and the test is POSITIVE IF ANY ONE COMPONENT IS INDETERMINATE OR WORSE, even if the other two are benign. BREASTSCREEN IS FOR ASYMPTOMATIC WOMEN AND WILL TURN HER AWAY — she needs the diagnostic pathway. Core biopsy over FNA because it gives architecture, invasive versus in situ, grade, and hormone and HER2 receptor status. Supraclavicular nodes are never optional: an ipsilateral node is N3c, stage IIIC, still treated with curative intent but a completely different plan; a contralateral one is M1. Safety-net: come back if it grows, the skin or nipple changes, discharge appears, or the breast becomes red and hot.
plan: THE SENSITIVE WIPE — and the second half is the part candidates rush: '...I have been asked to examine your breasts today, and I want to tell you exactly what that involves before we start. I will LOOK at both breasts while you move your arms into three positions; then I will FEEL both breasts with the flat of my fingers; and at the end I will feel UNDER YOUR ARMS AND ABOVE YOUR COLLARBONES. Are you happy for me to go ahead?' → 'do you have to look at both? It's only the right one' → 'I DO, AND I'LL START WITH THE NORMAL SIDE — comparing the two is the only way I can tell what is different.' Then: 'I will step outside and give you privacy to undress from the waist up. There is a sheet to cover yourself, and I will only uncover what I need to. If anything feels uncomfortable at any point, tell me and we will stop. WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE PRESENT?' → 'yes' → 'of course — I will ask one of our nurses to join us.' (Stalling over who the chaperone would be, or asking the examiner to act as one, loses the mark. If she declines: 'that's fine — I'll document that I offered.') Then hands washed, gloves, and CONSENT A SECOND TIME.

INSPECTION — three positions in one run, then ONE commentary: 'first, hands resting on your lap, relaxed. Second, hands on your hips and PUSH IN FIRMLY. Third, hands behind your head, elbows back, and now LEAN FORWARD towards me.' Then: 'Examiner, on inspection of both breasts in all three positions — SKIN: symmetrical in size and contour, no visible mass, no dimpling, no puckering, no peau d'orange, no rash, redness or scars. NIPPLE: both everted and at the same level, no retraction, ulceration or eczematous change. DISCHARGE: none visible. Jenny, could you squeeze the nipple for me? ... Of course, I'll do it — no discharge expressed from either side.' (If the examiner cuts in with 'don't tell me what you're looking for, tell me what you SEE' — stop, look properly, and NAME THE SIGN: puckering in the right upper outer quadrant, most obvious on leaning forward, with nipple retraction.)

PALPATION — temperature first, then the sweep: 'first just the backs of my fingers to check the temperature — no difference between the two breasts; I am screening for an inflammatory process such as mastitis or an abscess.' Then position: 'when I examine each side, please put that arm behind your head' → if she declines to lie down: 'that's completely fine. While you stay sitting I will place ONE HAND UNDERNEATH YOUR BREAST TO SUPPORT IT and feel with the other.' Then: 'Examiner, I am palpating with the FLAT PADS of my fingers, COMPRESSING THE TISSUE AGAINST THE CHEST WALL, in VERTICAL STRIPS from the clavicle down to the inframammary fold, between the sternum and the mid-axillary line, INCLUDING UNDER THE NIPPLE AND THE AXILLARY TAIL. The left breast is soft with no discrete lump and no tenderness. Moving to the right — EXAMINER, I HAVE FOUND A LUMP. I WILL COMPLETE MY PALPATION OF BOTH BREASTS AND THEN COME BACK TO CHARACTERISE IT.' (The moment you feel something, the temptation is to stop and describe — in Version B there are five more lumps and the pattern is the diagnosis.)

CHARACTERISATION — the seven, in order, where the marks live: 'in the right breast, UPPER OUTER QUADRANT, there is a SOLITARY lump roughly THREE BY TWO CENTIMETRES. Rubbing AROUND it, the BORDER is irregular; rubbing ACROSS it, the SURFACE is bumpy. Stabilising it between finger and thumb and PRESSING ON TWO AXES, the CONSISTENCY is hard and stony. It is NOT MOBILE within the breast. Jenny, could you SQUEEZE YOUR CHEST MUSCLES for me — press your palms together? — the lump MOVES ON PECTORAL CONTRACTION, indicating TETHERING to pectoralis major. Jenny, IS IT SORE when I press on it? — non-tender, with overlying skin puckering.' (Checking consistency on one axis and skipping the pectoral-contraction step are two separate named marks; and tenderness is the one characteristic you cannot feel — guessing it is a fail.)

NODES AND COMPLETION — 45 seconds, and explicitly in the task: 'Jenny, I'm going to feel under your arm now, and I'll SUPPORT YOUR ARM so the muscles relax. Examiner, supporting the right arm with my right hand and examining with my left, I am palpating the APICAL, CENTRAL, PECTORAL, SUBSCAPULAR and LATERAL groups: there is a single firm, mobile 1 cm node in the central group. Jenny, shrug your shoulders — no SUPRACLAVICULAR lymphadenopathy on either side. To complete, I would take a full history including family history, attempt transillumination if a torch were available, and examine the chest, abdomen and spine for metastatic disease.'

THE DIAGRAM, NARRATED ALOUD: 'Examiner, I'll record this on the diagram. I am MARKING the lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, DRAWING an irregular outline for an irregular border and bumpy surface. Beside it I am WRITING: 3 by 2 cm; hard and stony; fixed and tethered to pectoralis on contraction; non-tender; overlying skin puckering and nipple retraction. One palpable right central axillary node; left breast, left axilla and both supraclavicular fossae clear.' (Writing in silence loses the reasoning credit and ninety seconds. DRAW site, border, surface — WRITE size, consistency, mobility, tenderness. And if you genuinely cannot find the lump, say so and prove you know what you would have done, then proceed to the triple test anyway, because a normal examination does not exclude malignancy.)

DIAGNOSIS TO THE PATIENT — concerned, honest, with a plan: 'Jenny, you can cover up. I want to be straight with you. The lump is about three centimetres. It feels HARD, its edge is IRREGULAR, it does not move freely, and there is a DIMPLE in the skin above it. [PAUSE] Those are features that CONCERN me, and I have to tell you that one of the possibilities is BREAST CANCER. I can't tell you today that it is, and I can't tell you that it isn't — but I am not going to wait to find out. I will arrange everything urgently. Is there someone who can come with you to the appointment?' (False reassurance and blurting out cancer as a fact are the twin failures. Say concerned, name the possibility, and give a plan with a timeframe. If she becomes distressed, LET THE SILENCE SIT for two seconds before speaking.)

THE TRIPLE TEST IN LAY LANGUAGE, then the safety-net: 'there is a standard way we check any breast lump in Australia. It is called the TRIPLE TEST, and it has three parts. ONE — the examination I have just done. TWO — a scan: because you are under 35 that means an ULTRASOUND, which is painless; from 35 onwards we add a MAMMOGRAM. THREE — a sample: we numb the skin and take a small piece of tissue with a needle, a CORE BIOPSY, so a specialist can look at the actual cells. We do all three even when a lump feels harmless, because together they pick up over 99 out of 100 cancers, and no single one is good enough on its own.' Then: 'should I just go to BreastScreen?' → 'BreastScreen is for women with NO symptoms. Because you have found something, you need the diagnostic pathway instead — they would turn you away.' Then referral urgently with a phone call rather than a letter, PATS for travel, a breast care nurse, someone to come with her, and the safety-net: growth, skin or nipple change, discharge, or a red hot breast — plus 'ring us anyway if you haven't heard within a week.'

VERSION B — MULTIPLE BILATERAL LUMPS: 'Examiner, I have found multiple lumps — three in the right breast and four in the left. RATHER THAN CHARACTERISE EACH IN TURN, I WILL REPORT THEM AS A GROUP. They are all of similar size, roughly one to two centimetres, with regular borders and smooth surfaces. On two axes all feel rubbery. All are mobile, none moves on pectoral contraction, and they are tender, which fits. IMPORTANTLY, NONE FEELS HARDER, LARGER OR MORE FIXED THAN THE OTHERS, and there is no lymphadenopathy.' SAMENESS IS A FINDING — say it. / IF ONE LUMP IS DIFFERENT: 'six of these are rubbery, mobile and tender and feel identical. HOWEVER, the lump in the left upper outer quadrant is FIRMER, its border less distinct and it is less mobile. I will characterise that one fully... while the overall pattern is fibrocystic, THE ODD ONE OUT NEEDS A TRIPLE TEST IN ITS OWN RIGHT.' (Averaging — folding the different lump into 'they all feel the same' — misses the case.)

MORE VARIANTS: A RED HOT BREAST IN A NON-LACTATING WOMAN with peau d'orange and induration, no discrete lump, TWO WEEKS OF ANTIBIOTICS WITHOUT IMPROVEMENT → 'in a non-lactating woman, erythema and peau d'orange that has failed to respond to antibiotics is INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER until proven otherwise. I would refer urgently for imaging with SKIN PUNCH BIOPSY and core biopsy, AND I WOULD NOT PRESCRIBE ANOTHER COURSE OF ANTIBIOTICS.' / STRONG FAMILY HISTORY SURFACING → two separate actions: 'they do not change what we do about this lump — that is the triple test either way. Second, they mean I would like you assessed separately for your ongoing risk... I would refer you to a FAMILIAL CANCER CLINIC.' / SHE IS PREGNANT OR BREASTFEEDING → 'being pregnant does not change the plan... breast tissue is denser and lumpier in pregnancy, which makes it HARDER, not easier, to be reassuring — so I am going to be MORE careful, not less. Ultrasound is completely safe, a mammogram can be done with shielding, and a core biopsy is safe in both.' ('Let's wait until after the baby is born' is why pregnancy-associated breast cancer is diagnosed late.)
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Harding, 28, primary-school teacher in Kadina, living with her partner Tom; non-smoker, six standard drinks a week, on the combined pill for six years; no children, never breastfed; menarche at 12, periods regular. Felt the lump three weeks ago in the shower, unchanged, painless, no discharge, no fevers or weight loss, never had a mammogram ('I thought you couldn't have one at my age'). MOTHER HAD BREAST CANCER AT 52 and is alive and well; MATERNAL AUNT HAD OVARIAN CANCER in her sixties — volunteered only if asked, or at the very end. HIDDEN AGENDA: frightened it is cancer AND frightened of the biopsy needle, said only to an open question such as 'what has been worrying you?', otherwise in the last minute: 'doctor — am I going to die?' HOW SHE PLAYS IT: undresses only after being offered privacy, and if examined without it says 'sorry — here? Now?'; says YES to a chaperone then asks 'who, though?' once, to see whether they stall; REFUSES THE NIPPLE SQUEEZE ('could you do it, doctor?'); DECLINES TO LIE DOWN ('I'd rather stay sitting'), which is the bimanual-technique test; looks blank the first time she is asked to squeeze her chest muscles; and PUSHES AT TWO MINUTES: 'you've found it, haven't you. Is it cancer?' — a good candidate acknowledges, defers briefly and gives a timeframe. She becomes emotional only when the word cancer is used, then goes quiet — and does not rescue the silence.

Numbers: 8 minutes total with the examination prompt at 5:00 and 3 minutes for the rest; WIPE 45-60 s; palpation 30-45 s per breast; CHARACTERISE BY 4:00. THREE positions by THREE boxes (skin, nipple, discharge). SEVEN characteristics. Consistency on TWO axes, mobility in TWO steps. The index first phalanx is about 2-2.5 cm for sizing. FIVE axillary groups — CLIPS: central, lateral, infraclavicular/apical, pectoral, subscapular — plus supraclavicular both sides. Triple test sensitivity over 99%, POSITIVE IF ANY ONE PART IS INDETERMINATE OR WORSE. Imaging: ultrasound under 35, ultrasound plus mammogram from 35. BreastScreen SA 13 20 50, invited 50-74, eligible from 40, annual from 40 with a strong family history — NOT for symptoms. Cancer Council SA 13 11 20, TIS 131 450, PATS, healthdirect 1800 022 222.

EXAMINER VIVA: why not simply aspirate — FNA gives cytology only, while a core biopsy gives architecture, invasive versus in situ, grade, and hormone and HER2 receptor status; FNA has a role in a simple cyst where clear fluid and complete resolution is the answer. What makes the triple test positive — any one component indeterminate, suspicious or malignant, even if the other two are benign. Why check temperature — breast abscess is on the differential for a painful lump, and it costs five seconds. What tethering to pectoralis tells you — local invasion beyond the breast parenchyma, raising the T stage and making malignancy considerably more likely than any benign cause. Why supraclavicular nodes — an ipsilateral node is N3c, stage IIIC, still curative intent but a completely different plan; a contralateral node is M1. PEAU D'ORANGE — dermal lymphatic obstruction causes skin oedema; the skin swells but stays tethered at the hair follicles, so it pits like orange peel.
Discharge — None expressed from either side
Axilla — A single FIRM, MOBILE, 1 cm node in the RIGHT CENTRAL group; left axilla clear
Supraclavicular fossae — Clear, both sides

Testing consistency on one axis, skipping the pectoral-contraction step, or GUESSING tenderness rather than asking — three separate named marks
Rushing the second half of the WIPE: privacy, a sheet, a stop signal, the second consent, and a chaperone offered without stalling over who

Running the clock down and skipping the nodes when they are explicitly in the task and take 45 seconds; writing on the diagram in silence; and averaging in Version B so the one lump that feels different is folded into 'they all feel the same'

must: FAIL — Reporting 'yes, there is a lump' and nothing further — one of the three sentences that fail this station, along with 'I'm sure it's nothing to worry about' and 'I'll refer you to BreastScreen for a mammogram'; the marks live in the SEVEN CHARACTERISTICS, in order: SITE, SIZE, BORDER (rubbing around it), SURFACE (rubbing across it), CONSISTENCY tested ON TWO AXES, MOBILITY in two steps (within the breast, and on PECTORAL CONTRACTION), and TENDERNESS (★)

FAIL — Stopping to characterise the moment you feel something instead of finishing both breasts — in the bilateral version there are five or six more lumps and THE PATTERN IS THE DIAGNOSIS: 'Examiner, I have found a lump; I will complete my palpation of both breasts and then come back to characterise it'; and start on the NORMAL side, because comparing the two is the only way to tell what is different (★)

FAIL — Testing consistency on ONE axis, skipping the PECTORAL-CONTRACTION step, or GUESSING tenderness rather than asking — three separate named marks; stabilise the lump between finger and thumb and press on two axes; ask her to squeeze her chest muscles (rephrasing as 'press your palms together in front of you' when she looks blank) to test for TETHERING; and tenderness is the one characteristic you cannot feel, so you have to ASK (★)

FAIL — Rushing the second half of the WIPE: privacy, a sheet, a stop signal, the SECOND consent, and a chaperone offered WITHOUT STALLING over who it would be — name a nurse, say you will arrange it, and carry on, and if she declines, say aloud that you will document that it was offered; and when she asks 'do you have to look at both? It's only the right one', the answer is yes, starting with the normal side (★)

FAIL — Running the clock down and skipping the NODES when they are explicitly in the task and take forty-five seconds — support the arm so the muscles relax and palpate the five axillary groups by name (CLIPS: central, lateral, infraclavicular or apical, pectoral, subscapular), then shrug the shoulders for SUPRACLAVICULAR nodes on BOTH sides, which are never optional, because an ipsilateral supraclavicular node is N3c and stage IIIC while a contralateral one is M1 (★)

SAY — Give the diagnosis with the possibility named and a plan attached, avoiding both false reassurance and announcing cancer as fact: for benign-feeling findings, 'those features fit a FIBROADENOMA, the commonest breast lump in women your age… but I also want to be honest about what else it could be — a cyst, fibrocystic change, fat necrosis, or, and I can't rule this out just by feeling it, a breast cancer; that is exactly why I'm not going to stop at an examination'; for the carcinoma mannequin, 'the lump is about three centimetres, it feels hard, its edge is irregular, it doesn't move freely, and there's a dimple in the skin above it… those features CONCERN me, and I have to tell you that one of the possibilities is BREAST CANCER — I can't tell you today that it is, and I can't tell you that it isn't, but I'm not going to wait to find out', pausing after the word and not rushing to fill the silence; when she asks mid-palpation 'you've found it, haven't you — is it cancer?', acknowledge, defer briefly and give a timeframe rather than saying 'don't worry' or blurting a diagnosis; then the TRIPLE TEST in lay terms, all three parts — the examination, IMAGING (ultrasound under 35, ultrasound PLUS mammogram from 35), and a CORE BIOPSY rather than a fine-needle aspirate, because core gives architecture, invasive versus in situ, grade and receptor status — 'together they pick up over 99 in 100 cancers, and no single one is good enough on its own', with the test POSITIVE if ANY ONE component is indeterminate or worse; BreastScreen is for ASYMPTOMATIC women and will turn her away, so this is the diagnostic pathway; narrate the proforma out loud while you draw it (site, border and surface drawn; size, consistency, mobility and tenderness written), because writing in silence loses ninety seconds and the reasoning cannot be credited; check temperature with the backs of your fingers to screen for mastitis or abscess; adapt to a BIMANUAL technique if she declines to lie down, supporting the breast with one hand and palpating with the other; safety net — the lump growing, skin or nipple change, any discharge, or the breast becoming red and hot — with a timeframe and a request that she ring if she has not heard within a week; variants — MULTIPLE bilateral lumps are reported as a GROUP with sameness named as a finding, but if ONE feels firmer, less distinct or less mobile, that one is characterised fully and needs a triple test in its own right, because averaging misses the case; a RED, HOT breast in a NON-LACTATING woman with peau d'orange and induration that has failed two weeks of antibiotics is INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER until proven otherwise, needing urgent imaging with skin punch and core biopsy rather than a second course of flucloxacillin; a strong FAMILY HISTORY changes nothing about the lump but earns a separate familial cancer clinic referral; and PREGNANCY does not delay investigation, because ultrasound and core biopsy are both safe and 'let's wait until after the baby is born' is why pregnancy-associated cancer is diagnosed late

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — rural GP, male chest. THE WHOLE STATION IS ONE SENTENCE: is there a firm, rubbery, DISC-LIKE PLAQUE OF GLANDULAR TISSUE beneath the nipple, and is it CONCENTRIC OR ECCENTRIC? Concentric disc = true gynaecomastia; no disc, fat only = pseudogynaecomastia; ECCENTRIC HARD MASS = you are in a cancer station. The peripheral sweep gets NINETY SECONDS MAXIMUM — the completeness reflex is the commonest reason candidates never reach the breast. Offer a chaperone even though you are both men. Three sentences fail it: 'it's just the nandrolone, nothing to worry about'; 'no, men don't really get breast cancer'; and 'I ran out of time for the breast examination'.
stem: VERSION B: rural South Australian practice. Josh Tanner, 25, concerned about ENLARGEMENT OF HIS BREASTS, using NANDROLONE from the gym (2023 recall: ramipril for hypertension). Observations normal. A mannequin, or a real obese role-player who will not lie down. Tasks: examination with running commentary, then diagnosis and differentials to the patient. 8 minutes.
VERSION A: John Meredith, 40, with A LUMP in his breast — exclude carcinoma.

The harder run: a firm rubbery CONCENTRIC subareolar disc bilaterally, 4 cm right and 3 cm left, mobile and mildly tender — PLUS, in the right breast at 2 o'clock and 3 cm from the nipple, a separate 2 x 2 cm ECCENTRIC lump, irregular, bumpy, hard on two axes, immobile and TETHERED, non-tender, with a 1 cm right central axillary node.
tasks: Perform a physical examination with running commentary to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: WIPE IN 45 SECONDS with the steps named, consent taken TWICE, privacy and a stop signal, a choice of lying or sitting, AND A CHAPERONE OFFERED · then, if he is embarrassed, ONE sentence and move on · THE PERIPHERAL SWEEP IN NINETY SECONDS: general appearance, hands (acropachy, clubbing, palmar erythema, leuconychia, TREMOR), eyes (exophthalmos, lid retraction, scleral icterus), spider naevi · then SAY YOU ARE MOVING ON and will return to the other systems at the end · INSPECTION IN THREE POSITIONS, identical to the female station, reporting SKIN, NIPPLE and DISCHARGE, and commenting on SYMMETRY rather than just presence, because gynaecomastia is commonly asymmetrical and asymmetry alone is not a red flag · PALPATION: temperature, then BIMANUAL with one hand supporting and lifting the tissue, flat pads, vertical strips, clavicle to inframammary fold, INCLUDING THE AXILLARY TAIL · THEN THE DISC SENTENCE, and if there is an eccentric mass, characterise all seven features · NODES with the arm supported, five groups plus supraclavicular · OFFER thyroid, abdomen, TESTES and visual fields with fundoscopy, and ACCEPT EVERY SKIP with 'thank you, Examiner' · then the diagnosis, the differential list ACROSS SYSTEMS, and the non-judgemental steroid line.

back.dx: TRUE GYNAECOMASTIA — a firm, rubbery, disc-like plaque of GLANDULAR tissue CONCENTRIC to the areola with a distinct edge against the surrounding fat, mobile and often tender — most likely DRUG-INDUCED here (anabolic steroids are aromatised to oestrogen). But name the whole list ACROSS SYSTEMS: liver disease, kidney disease, thyrotoxicosis, an hCG- or oestrogen-secreting TESTICULAR or adrenal tumour, a PROLACTINOMA — and MALE BREAST CANCER, about 1% of all breast cancers, which stays on the list until the tests are back. THE FINAL COMMON PATHWAY for every cause is a shifted OESTROGEN-TO-ANDROGEN RATIO. PSEUDOGYNAECOMASTIA is adipose tissue only with no palpable disc — and the ABSENCE of the disc is a positive diagnostic statement, not a 'normal examination'. AN ECCENTRIC HARD MASS is cancer until proven otherwise: for a MAN that is MAMMOGRAM AND ULTRASOUND AT ANY AGE — the under-35 ultrasound-first rule is a female-station rule — then CORE BIOPSY. Bloods: LFT, U&E, TSH and free T4, MORNING testosterone, LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin, beta-hCG, and a karyotype if the testes are small and firm (Klinefelter carries a 20-50 fold increase in breast cancer). Duration matters: under 6 months and tender is potentially reversible; OVER 12 MONTHS IT IS FIBROTIC and may need surgery. Remove the cause and review at three months. NEVER unilaterally stop a prognostic drug — spironolactone in heart failure is discussed with the prescriber, not ceased by you. And fibroadenoma essentially does not occur in men, so any discrete male breast lump gets the triple test.
plan: WIPE with the chaperone offered — four seconds, and it is an assessed item even between two men: '...I have been asked to examine your chest and breasts today, and I want to tell you exactly what that involves. I will LOOK at both sides while you move your arms into three positions; then I will FEEL both sides with the flat of my fingers; and at the end I will feel UNDER YOUR ARMS AND ABOVE YOUR COLLARBONES. Are you happy for me to go ahead? I'll need your shirt off. If anything is uncomfortable, tell me and we'll stop. WOULD YOU PREFER TO LIE ON THE COUCH OR STAY SITTING? WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE PRESENT? I'll wash my hands. Still happy for me to proceed?' → 'bit embarrassing, this' → ONE sentence: 'for what it's worth, this is common and you're right to have it checked — that's the sensible thing to do, not the awkward thing.'

THE NINETY-SECOND SWEEP, ONE OR TWO SIGNS PER SYSTEM, THEN STOP: 'on general inspection Josh is a well-looking young man, not cachectic, not jaundiced, dressed appropriately for the weather. Could I see your hands? — no thyroid acropachy, no clubbing, no palmar erythema, no leuconychia, and no fine tremor. Look straight ahead for me, and now look down — no exophthalmos or lid retraction, and no scleral icterus. There are no spider naevi on the upper chest. EXAMINER, I WOULD LIKE TO MOVE ON TO THE BREAST EXAMINATION NOW, AND I WILL RETURN TO THE THYROID, ABDOMEN, TESTES AND VISUAL FIELDS AT THE END.' (Listing ten thyroid signs and eight liver signs feels impressive and is the single commonest reason candidates never reach the breast. If he asks why you are looking at his eyes: 'because a few conditions elsewhere in the body can cause this, and the eyes and hands give them away quickly. I'll be thirty seconds.')

INSPECTION IN THREE POSITIONS — do not skip them because he is a man, since they test pectoral contraction and gravity, not female anatomy: 'hands on your lap, relaxed... hands on your hips and push in firmly... hands behind your head, elbows back, and lean forward.' Then: 'SKIN: symmetrical apart from slightly greater fullness on the right; no visible discrete mass, no dimpling, no puckering, no peau d'orange, no rash or scars. NIPPLE: both everted and level, no retraction, ulceration or eczematous change. DISCHARGE: none visible — Josh, could you squeeze the nipple? ... Of course, I'll do it — no discharge expressed either side.' (Comment on SYMMETRY, not just presence: gynaecomastia is commonly asymmetrical and can be genuinely unilateral; asymmetry alone is not a red flag, but a unilateral hard eccentric mass is.)

PALPATION AND THE DISC SENTENCE — the whole station: 'checking temperature with the backs of my fingers — no difference between the two sides. Josh, while you stay sitting I'll place ONE HAND UNDERNEATH TO SUPPORT AND LIFT THE TISSUE and feel with the other. Examiner, I am performing a BIMANUAL palpation with the flat pads of my fingers, compressing the tissue against the chest wall in vertical strips from the clavicle to the inframammary fold, sternum to mid-axillary line, including the axillary tail. BENEATH THE RIGHT NIPPLE I CAN FEEL A FIRM, RUBBERY, DISC-LIKE PLAQUE OF GLANDULAR TISSUE, CONCENTRIC TO THE AREOLA, approximately 4 cm across, with A DISTINCT EDGE AGAINST THE SURROUNDING FAT. It is mobile and mildly tender. There is no eccentric hard mass, no skin tethering and no nipple retraction. The same is present on the left, approximately 3 cm.' (A generic breast commentary that never uses the word GLANDULAR misses the one sentence the examiner is waiting for.)

IF THERE IS AN ECCENTRIC MASS, characterise it in full and do not let the gynaecomastia distract you: 'however, in the right breast at the 2 o'clock position, approximately 3 cm from the nipple, and therefore ECCENTRIC to the areola, there is a SEPARATE discrete lump. I'll complete my palpation and then characterise it... it measures approximately 2 by 2 cm, the border is irregular and the surface is bumpy, on two axes the consistency is HARD, it is NOT MOBILE, and on pectoral contraction it MOVES, indicating TETHERING. Josh, is it sore when I press? — non-tender, and the overlying skin is normal.' If he asks 'what have you found?', defer briefly with a timeframe: 'there's a separate lump on the right that I want to look at properly before I say anything. Give me one minute.'

NODES, THEN THE OFFERS: 'I'm going to feel under your arms — I'll support your arm so the muscles relax. Palpating the apical, central, pectoral, subscapular and lateral groups: there is a single firm, mobile 1 cm node in the right central group; the left axilla is clear. Josh, shrug your shoulders — no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy either side. Examiner, to complete my examination I would like to examine the THYROID, the ABDOMEN for stigmata of chronic liver disease, THE TESTES for a mass or atrophy, and VISUAL FIELDS with fundoscopy for a prolactinoma.' → 'skip, skip, skip, skip' → 'THANK YOU, EXAMINER' and move straight on. (If told to do the thyroid: twenty seconds, inspection and palpation only, then name what you are leaving out — percussion, bruit, Pemberton's — and go.)

THE DIAGNOSIS, in order of importance: 'behind each nipple I can feel a firm disc of ACTUAL BREAST GLAND — not just fat. That condition is called GYNAECOMASTIA, and it is common. The most likely reason in your case is the nandrolone: anabolic steroids get converted in the body into oestrogen, and oestrogen makes breast tissue grow. BUT I DON'T WANT TO STOP THERE. Other things can cause this: liver disease, kidney disease, an overactive thyroid, a hormone-producing growth in a testicle or an adrenal gland, or a small growth on the pituitary gland in the head. And although I found nothing today to suggest it, MEN DO GET BREAST CANCER — about one in a hundred breast cancers happens in a man — so I keep that on my list until the tests are back.' If there IS an eccentric lump, lead with it: 'the second is the part I'm more concerned about... it feels hard, it doesn't move, it seems attached to the muscle, and there's a small gland under your arm. [PAUSE] I have to be straight with you: one of the possibilities there is breast cancer.' → 'blokes don't get breast cancer' → LET THE SILENCE SIT, then: 'they do — about one in a hundred. It's uncommon, and it gets found late for exactly the reason you just said.'

THE PLAN AND THE NON-JUDGEMENTAL LINE: 'two parts. Blood tests to check the liver, the kidneys, the thyroid and your hormone levels, including a pregnancy-type hormone that some testicular tumours produce — those go this morning, and TESTOSTERONE HAS TO BE AN EARLY SAMPLE. And I want to EXAMINE YOUR TESTICLES, because occasionally a growth there shows up first as breast tissue. If I had found a firm lump off to one side I would also arrange a mammogram AND an ultrasound and a needle biopsy — AND FOR A MAN THAT'S BOTH SCANS, WHATEVER THE AGE.' Then: 'I'M NOT HERE TO LECTURE YOU. What I do want you to know is that the same thing causing the breast tissue also shrinks the testicles and lowers sperm counts, and it pushes up your blood pressure and your cholesterol. I can help you come off it safely and check all of that. Would that be useful?' Then review in three months, with the honest caveat that beyond about a year it becomes scar-like and may need a surgeon. (Moralising loses you the rest of the history — including the supplements he has not mentioned yet.)

ask: 'Would you like a chaperone present?' (yes, to a man too) / 'Would you prefer to lie on the couch, or stay sitting? That's completely fine.' / 'Examiner, I'd like to move to the breast examination now and return to the other systems at the end.' / 'While you stay sitting I'll place one hand underneath to support and lift the tissue and feel with the other.'

'Beneath the nipple I can feel a firm, rubbery, disc-like plaque of GLANDULAR tissue, CONCENTRIC to the areola.' / 'There is no eccentric hard mass, no tethering, no nipple retraction and no discharge.' / 'Josh, press your palms together hard in front of you.' / 'To complete, I'd examine the thyroid, the abdomen, the testes, and visual fields with fundoscopy.' / 'Thank you, Examiner' — to every skip, without hesitation.

'That's real breast gland, not just fat — that's what gynaecomastia means.' / 'Men do get breast cancer — about one in a hundred breast cancers — so it stays on my list.' / 'For a man that's a mammogram AND an ultrasound, whatever the age.' / 'I'm not here to lecture you — I want to help you come off it safely.'

VARIANTS: A REAL OBESE ROLE-PLAYER WITH NO DISC → 'palpating bimanually on both sides, I can feel SOFT, UNIFORM ADIPOSE TISSUE extending right up to the areola with NO DISTINCT EDGE and NO PALPABLE DISC of glandular tissue beneath either nipple... THAT ABSENCE IS THE FINDING: this is PSEUDOGYNAECOMASTIA rather than true gynaecomastia.' (Saying 'normal examination' misses it — the absence of the disc is a positive diagnostic statement.) / A 14-YEAR-OLD BOY WITH HIS MOTHER → 'a small, tender, concentric subareolar disc bilaterally, about 2 cm, no eccentric mass, no lymphadenopathy, mid-puberty. This is PUBERTAL gynaecomastia, which occurs in a majority of boys and resolves spontaneously, usually within 18 months to 2 years. Reassurance and review rather than investigation — but I would still ask about medications and substances, check growth and pubertal development, and EXAMINE THE TESTES.' / A 62-YEAR-OLD ON SPIRONOLACTONE FOR HEART FAILURE → 'the onset three months after a dose increase makes spironolactone the most likely cause. PLEASE DO NOT STOP IT YOURSELF — it is doing important work for your heart. I'll talk to your cardiologist about switching.'

EXAMINER VIVA: true versus pseudo — proliferation of glandular tissue giving a firm rubbery CONCENTRIC disc with a distinct edge, versus adipose tissue only with no palpable disc. Gynaecomastia versus cancer clinically — CONCENTRIC versus ECCENTRIC: symmetrical around the nipple, rubbery, mobile and often tender, against eccentric, hard, fixed, usually unilateral and painless with possible nipple retraction, skin change or bloody discharge. Why chronic liver disease causes it — reduced hepatic clearance of oestrogens and altered sex-hormone binding globulin shift the oestrogen-to-androgen ratio, which is the final common pathway for every cause. Which drugs — SPIRONOLACTONE, digoxin, ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, cimetidine and PPIs, ketoconazole, metronidazole, risperidone and other antipsychotics, antiretrovirals, bicalutamide and finasteride, plus anabolic steroids, alcohol, cannabis and opioids. Why examine the testes — an hCG- or oestrogen-secreting tumour can present with gynaecomastia before the mass is noticed, and small firm testes suggest Klinefelter. Can you reassure a man with a benign-feeling mobile lump — NO: fibroadenoma essentially does not occur in men, so any discrete male breast lump gets the triple test. When is surgery indicated — beyond about 12 months when the tissue is fibrotic and will not regress, or when it causes significant distress.
pefe: Role-player: Josh Tanner, 25, fitter and turner at the Wallaroo grain terminal, living with his girlfriend, training five days a week. His chest has been getting fuller over about eight months, RIGHT BIGGER AND TENDER; he wears loose shirts and has stopped taking his top off at the beach. No discharge, no skin change noticed, no weight loss or fevers. THE BIT HE DOES NOT LEAD WITH: he has been INJECTING NANDROLONE through a mate at the gym for about a year, plus three or four supplements he cannot name — he will admit it IF ASKED OPENLY AND WITHOUT JUDGEMENT about supplements, substances or anything he takes for training; IF THE DOCTOR IS PREACHY HE BECOMES GUARDED AND SAYS 'JUST PROTEIN'. Six to eight beers on a weekend, non-smoker, occasional cannabis, no prescribed medications. If asked: his TESTICLES ARE A BIT SMALLER than they used to be and his SEX DRIVE HAS DROPPED OFF. HIDDEN AGENDA: terrified this means he is 'turning into a woman' and worried his girlfriend has noticed — given only to an open question such as 'what's been worrying you about it?'

How he plays it: embarrassed but cooperative, short answers at first, warming up if the doctor is matter-of-fact; DECLINES a chaperone but NOTICES whether it was offered; DECLINES to lie down, which is the bimanual-technique test; REFUSES the nipple squeeze ('you do it, doc'); looks blank the first time he is asked to squeeze his chest muscles. THE FINDINGS ARE RATIONED BY TECHNIQUE: a 4 cm concentric rubbery tender disc behind each nipple — and if the candidate palpates properly, ALSO the 2 cm hard immobile eccentric lump at 2 o'clock on the right with a 1 cm axillary node. IF THEY PALPATE FOR LESS THAN TWENTY SECONDS A SIDE, REPORT ONLY THE DISCS AND MARK THE MISS. He pushes at the discovery ('what? What have you found?'), says 'blokes don't get breast cancer' when cancer is named and then GOES QUIET WITHOUT RESCUING THE SILENCE, and finishes with 'are you going to have a go at me about the gear?' and 'will it go back to normal?'

Numbers: 8 minutes — WIPE 45 s, peripheral sweep 90 s MAXIMUM, breast examination 3 min, nodes 45 s, offers and skips 45 s, diagnosis 2 min. Male breast cancer about 1% of all breast cancers; Klinefelter carries a 20-50 fold increase; BRCA2 is the commonest inherited link. Concentric rubbery disc = gynaecomastia; no disc = pseudogynaecomastia; eccentric hard mass = cancer until proven otherwise. Under 6 months and tender = potentially reversible; over 12 months = fibrotic and surgical. Bloods: LFT, U&E, TSH and free T4, MORNING testosterone, LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin, beta-hCG, karyotype if small firm testes. IMAGING IN A MAN: MAMMOGRAM AND ULTRASOUND AT ANY AGE, then core biopsy; triple test sensitivity over 99%. Nodes CLIPS plus supraclavicular. findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — 'It's just the nandrolone, nothing to worry about' — a drug in the stem is the MOST LIKELY CAUSE, not the differential list; name the drug AND keep the list: liver disease, kidney disease, thyrotoxicosis, a hormone-producing testicular or adrenal tumour, a pituitary prolactinoma — and male breast cancer (★)

FAIL — Agreeing with 'men don't get breast cancer' — in Version A that is an automatic fail, and he says it to test you: 'they do — about ONE IN A HUNDRED breast cancers happens in a man; it's uncommon, and it gets found late for exactly the reason you just said'; then let the silence sit rather than rushing to fill it (★)

FAIL — Giving a generic breast commentary that never uses the word GLANDULAR, or never saying whether the disc is CONCENTRIC or ECCENTRIC — the examiner is waiting for one sentence, and that distinction decides everything: a firm, rubbery, DISC-LIKE PLAQUE OF GLANDULAR TISSUE CONCENTRIC to the areola with a distinct edge against the surrounding fat is TRUE GYNAECOMASTIA; soft, uniform adipose tissue with NO palpable disc is PSEUDOGYNAECOMASTIA, and that ABSENCE is a positive diagnostic statement rather than a 'normal examination'; and an ECCENTRIC HARD MASS puts you in a cancer station, characterised in full with all seven features (★)

FAIL — The completeness reflex: ten thyroid signs and eight liver signs in the peripheral sweep, so the breast examination never happens — or 'I ran out of time for the breast examination'; cap the sweep at NINETY SECONDS with one or two signs per system (hands for acropachy, clubbing, palmar erythema, leuconychia and tremor; eyes for exophthalmos, lid retraction and scleral icterus; upper chest for spider naevi), then 'Examiner, I'd like to move on to the breast examination now, and I'll return to the thyroid, abdomen, testes and visual fields at the end'; be at the breast by about 1:30, say 'thank you, Examiner' to every skip without hesitating, and if the thyroid is NOT skipped, give it twenty seconds of inspection and palpation only, then name what you are leaving out and go (★)

FAIL — Skipping the chaperone offer because you are both men — it is an assessed item, it takes four seconds, and the male chest is a sensitive area; the same sensitive WIPE applies as in the female station (explain the three positions, the palpation and the nodes before touching, offer privacy and a stop signal, ask whether he would rather lie down or stay sitting, take consent TWICE, and document a declined chaperone); do ALL THREE inspection positions, because they test pectoral contraction and gravity rather than female anatomy, and ADAPT to a BIMANUAL technique when he declines to lie down — one hand underneath supporting and lifting the tissue, the other palpating with flat pads in vertical strips (★)

SAY — Be NON-JUDGEMENTAL about the steroids, because moralising loses you the rest of the history including the supplements he has not mentioned: 'I'm not here to lecture you; what I do want you to know is that the same thing causing the breast tissue also shrinks the testicles and lowers sperm counts, and it pushes up your blood pressure and your cholesterol — I can help you come off it safely and check all of that; would that be useful?'; explain gynaecomastia as REAL BREAST GLAND rather than fat ('anabolic steroids get converted in the body into oestrogen, and oestrogen makes breast tissue grow'); investigations in two parts — BLOODS for liver, kidneys, thyroid and hormones including morning TESTOSTERONE, LH, FSH, OESTRADIOL, PROLACTIN and BETA-hCG, with a karyotype if the testes are small and firm, and EXAMINING THE TESTES, because an hCG- or oestrogen-secreting tumour can present with breast tissue before the testicular mass is noticed and small firm testes suggest KLINEFELTER, which carries a 20- to 50-fold increase in breast cancer risk; stopping the causative drug is the single most useful step, with review at three months, and gynaecomastia present beyond about TWELVE MONTHS becomes fibrotic and will not regress, at which point it is a surgical conversation; if there IS a discrete lump the triple test applies, and IN A MAN THAT IS MAMMOGRAM AND ULTRASOUND AT ANY AGE, because the under-35 ultrasound-first rule is a female-station rule and male breast tissue is not dense — then a core biopsy, with over 99% sensitivity; fibroadenoma essentially does not occur in men, so even a mobile, benign-feeling lump still gets the triple test; ask what is worrying him, because he is terrified he is 'turning into a woman' and that his girlfriend has noticed, and he will not volunteer it; safety net — the lump growing, skin or nipple change, any discharge, and ringing if he has not heard within a week; variants — a 14-year-old with small, tender, concentric discs at mid-puberty is PUBERTAL gynaecomastia needing reassurance and review rather than investigation, though you still ask about medications and substances and examine the testes, reconsidering if it is unilateral and hard, over 4 cm, or persisting beyond two years; and SPIRONOLACTONE in heart failure is one of the commonest drug causes, but never tell him to stop it himself — substitute in discussion with the prescriber

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — rural ED, unconscious patient. FOUR AUTOMATIC FAILS: no painful stimulus given at all; a score announced that was never derived; SUPRAORBITAL OR NAIL-BED PRESSURE IN A HEAD INJURY; and the patient never spoken to. THE ROLE-PLAYER GIVES NOTHING TO A STIMULUS SHORTER THAN A SECOND — hold the trapezius squeeze for a full one to two seconds and watch the face and BOTH arms at once. Say EMERGENCY DOCTRINE, not Good Samaritan. And the discussion is SIGNIFICANCE, not management: airway and imaging belong there as implications of the number, phrased as what the score TELLS you to do.
stem: Emergency department, rural hospital; you are the HMO. A 30-year-old man after a FALL FROM HIS BICYCLE with a head injury. Primary and secondary surveys complete, haemodynamically stable. HIS GCS ON ARRIVAL WAS 10. On the trolley: a neurological observation chart, a pen and a pen torch. Recent versions add 'you are only required to perform a GCS assessment and nothing else'. 8 minutes.
tasks: Perform a Glasgow Coma Scale assessment
Score it on the chart provided
Discuss the clinical significance of the GCS score with the examiner
time: APPROACH FROM HIS RIGHT, INTRODUCE YOURSELF TO THE PATIENT even though he is unconscious, then to the examiner: 'my patient is unconscious and cannot consent. I am PROCEEDING UNDER THE EMERGENCY DOCTRINE, because the assessment is necessary and cannot reasonably be delayed. I would like to wash my hands and I will wear gloves. Are there any injuries or precautions I should know about?' · THE VERBAL STIMULUS, COWS, AS FOUR SEPARATE ATTEMPTS WITH A PAUSE AFTER EACH: 'can you hear me?' ... 'open your eyes' ... 'what is your name?' ... then PLACE YOUR FINGERS INTO HIS PALM and 'squeeze my fingers' · THE PAINFUL STIMULUS, warned first, TRAPEZIUS SQUEEZE OR STERNAL RUB ONLY, held ONE TO TWO SECONDS, watching eyes, listening for sound, and watching BOTH ARMS · if you missed it, ANNOUNCE THAT YOU ARE REPEATING IT, which is safer than guessing · SCORE ON THE CHART OUT LOUD, ONE COMPONENT AT A TIME, each as NUMBER, WORD, BEHAVIOUR · the one-sentence offer of pupils, plantars and CSF discharge, then STOP IF REFUSED · then the four-minute discussion in THREE BLOCKS: what it is and its four properties, three management implications, and prognosis with THIS patient's trend.

back.dx: VERSION A: E3 V2 M3 = 8 out of 15, DOWN FROM 10 ON ARRIVAL — a two-point deterioration, which concerns you more than the absolute value. E3 because his eyes were CLOSED on arrival and opened TO VOICE, not spontaneously; V2 because he made sounds with no identifiable word; M3 because on a sustained central stimulus his elbows flexed inwards and HIS HANDS NEVER REACHED THE SOURCE — abnormal flexion. THE DISCUSSION IN THREE BLOCKS. (1) WHAT IT IS AND ITS FOUR PROPERTIES: a standardised tool for assessing and communicating conscious level, 3 to 15 across eye opening, verbal response and best motor response — QUANTITATIVE, so conscious level becomes a number; OBJECTIVE, so a different doctor should reach the same score; A COMMON LANGUAGE, so you hand over one figure rather than a description; and REPEATABLE, so it detects improvement or deterioration. (2) THREE MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS: it grades severity into mild, moderate and severe; A SCORE OF 8 OR LESS MEANS THE AIRWAY IS UNLIKELY TO BE PROTECTED, so definitive airway management; and it drives imaging, with moderate and severe injuries needing a CT head. (3) PROGNOSIS: the lower the score at presentation the worse the outcome, and THE MOTOR COMPONENT CARRIES MOST OF THE PROGNOSTIC WEIGHT — and here the fall from 10 to 8 is the finding. LIMITATIONS, the commonest add-on question: poor inter-rater reliability for the verbal component; not testable in an intubated, aphasic or facially swollen patient; confounded by alcohol, drugs, sedation and hypoglycaemia; it says nothing about brainstem reflexes or pupils; and the same total can arise from very different component combinations. VERSION B: E3 V2 M2 = 7 — EXTENSION is the more ominous posture, suggesting a lower brainstem lesion, and you escalate now. VERSION C: E2 V3 M5 = 10, unchanged — the hand CROSSED THE MIDLINE to the source, so he is LOCALISING.
plan: APPROACH, INTRODUCE, AND GET CONSENT RIGHT: gloves on, stand on his right. 'Hello, my name is Doctor -, I am one of the doctors here in the emergency department. I am going to examine you now to check your level of consciousness. I WILL BE GENTLE AND I WILL TELL YOU BEFORE I DO ANYTHING.' Then to the examiner: 'my patient is unconscious and cannot consent. I AM PROCEEDING UNDER THE EMERGENCY DOCTRINE, because the assessment is necessary and cannot reasonably be delayed. I would like to wash my hands, and I will wear gloves. Are there any injuries or precautions I should know about before I begin?' (Saying GOOD SAMARITAN is wrong — that covers assistance outside your employment, not a hospital doctor in their own department. And do not hunt for a hand sanitiser that has been removed from the room: say the words, take no action, move on.)

THE VERBAL STIMULUS — COWS, FOUR SEPARATE ATTEMPTS WITH A PAUSE AFTER EACH: 'James, CAN YOU HEAR ME?' ... 'James, OPEN YOUR EYES.' ... 'WHAT IS YOUR NAME?' ... then PLACE TWO FINGERS INTO HIS PALM: 'SQUEEZE MY FINGERS.' (Asking all four in one breath means you never see the answer to each. Asking for a hand squeeze from two metres away gets nothing — the fingers must be in his palm. AND EVEN THE FAINTEST SQUEEZE IS M6 AND ENDS THE MOTOR ASSESSMENT.)

THE PAINFUL STIMULUS, warned and SUSTAINED: 'James, I AM GOING TO SQUEEZE YOUR SHOULDER NOW — THIS MAY BE UNCOMFORTABLE.' Squeeze the trapezius firmly and HOLD FOR TWO SECONDS, watching his eyes, listening for any sound, and watching BOTH ARMS. If you did not see it clearly: 'James, I am sorry, I need to do that once more. Examiner, I DID NOT OBSERVE THE RESPONSE CLEARLY, SO I AM REPEATING THE STIMULUS.' (A stimulus lasting a fraction of a second produces NO finding, and you cannot score what you did not see — the role-player is briefed to give nothing. Repeating once, announced, is far safer than guessing. NO supraorbital pressure in a head injury, and NO nail-bed pressure, which produces spinal reflex withdrawal you cannot separate from M4.)

SCORE THE CHART OUT LOUD, ONE COMPONENT AT A TIME, each as NUMBER, WORD, BEHAVIOUR: 'his eyes were CLOSED when I arrived and OPENED WHEN I SPOKE to him, so eye opening is 3, TO SPEECH. He made sounds to the painful stimulus but I could not identify any words, so his best verbal response is 2, INCOMPREHENSIBLE SOUNDS. On a sustained squeeze his elbows FLEXED INWARDS and his hands did not reach my hand, so that is ABNORMAL FLEXION, motor 3. E3, V2, M3 — A TOTAL OF 8 OUT OF 15. HIS GCS ON ARRIVAL WAS 10, SO THIS IS A TWO-POINT DETERIORATION.' (Announcing a total without the components is a trap: two patients with a GCS of 8 can have completely different injuries.)

THE ONE-SENTENCE OFFER, then stop if refused: 'Examiner, I would also like to check the PUPILS for size, symmetry and reaction, and the PLANTAR RESPONSES, and to look for CLEAR DISCHARGE FROM THE NOSE OR EARS suggesting a base-of-skull fracture. Would you like me to?' → 'no, stick to your task' → 'thank you' and move on INSTANTLY. (Arguing costs marks. If allowed: pupils equal at 4 mm and reactive, right plantar upgoing, glucose 6.2.)

BLOCK 1 — WHAT IT IS AND THE FOUR PROPERTIES: 'the Glasgow Coma Scale is a standardised tool for assessing and communicating conscious level, scored from 3 to 15 across eye opening, verbal response and best motor response. Its value is that it is QUANTITATIVE, so I can express conscious level as a number; OBJECTIVE, so a different doctor examining the same patient should reach the same score; A COMMON LANGUAGE, so I can hand over one figure rather than a description; and REPEATABLE, so it lets me detect improvement or deterioration.'

BLOCK 2 — THREE MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS: 'it has three management implications. It GRADES HEAD INJURY SEVERITY into mild, moderate and severe. A SCORE OF 8 OR LESS MEANS THE AIRWAY IS UNLIKELY TO BE PROTECTED, so I would arrange definitive airway management. And IT DRIVES THE DECISION TO IMAGE — moderate and severe injuries need a CT head.' (Phrase these as what the score TELLS you to do. If asked 'should you intubate?': 'a GCS of 8 or less means the airway is unlikely to be protected, so definitive airway management would be indicated — but my task is the assessment and its significance, so I would hand that decision to the senior team.')

BLOCK 3 — PROGNOSIS AND THIS PATIENT: 'finally it is PROGNOSTIC: the lower the score at presentation, the worse the outcome, and THE MOTOR COMPONENT CARRIES MOST OF THAT PROGNOSTIC WEIGHT. In this man the score has fallen from 10 to 8, WHICH IS A DETERIORATION AND CONCERNS ME MORE THAN THE ABSOLUTE VALUE.' Then have the extras ready, because the examiner has four minutes and this takes ninety seconds: the LIMITATIONS (see dx); why the chart is not enough ('the chart records the score; it does not make the judgement — deciding between withdrawal and localising has to come from the behaviour I observed'); and justifying any single score in the same shape every time — THE NUMBER, THE WORD, THE BEHAVIOUR: 'two — incomprehensible sounds — because I heard noise but no word.'

Open your eyes. What is your name? Squeeze my fingers.' / 'I am going to squeeze your shoulder now — this may be uncomfortable.'
