back.dx: MALIGNANT PAROTID TUMOUR WITH FACIAL NERVE PALSY — a five-year painless swelling that has grown over three months, firm to hard with an irregular border and poor mobility, DISPLACING THE EAR LOBE, with WEAKNESS OF ALL BRANCHES OF THE IPSILATERAL FACIAL NERVE INCLUDING THE FOREHEAD. THE SENTENCE THAT EARNS THE STATION: 'forehead involvement makes this a LOWER MOTOR NEURONE lesion, and WITH AN IPSILATERAL PAROTID MASS THAT IS MALIGNANT INFILTRATION UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.' THE SINISTER TRIAD: PAINLESS, RECENT GROWTH, FACIAL PALSY. TO HIM, HONEST WITHOUT OVER-CLAIMING: 'when a lump that's been there for years starts to grow, and the nerve running through it stops working properly, THAT MAKES ME CONCERNED THIS COULD BE A CANCER. I can't be certain today — that needs a scan and a sample. BUT I'M NOT GOING TO PRETEND I'M NOT WORRIED.' DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN WORDS: a non-cancerous growth of the gland, which can sit there for years; an inflamed or infected gland, unlikely with no pain and no fever; a gland of the immune system inside the parotid (lymphoma); and A SKIN CANCER THAT HAS SPREAD INTO IT, which is why you examine the scalp and ears. MANAGEMENT: SCAN, SAMPLE, SURGERY — ultrasound of the gland, then ULTRASOUND-GUIDED FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION OR CORE BIOPSY by the specialist service, then parotidectomy with radiotherapy if indicated VERIFY — referred URGENTLY, TODAY. NEVER an incisional biopsy in primary care: it risks TUMOUR SEEDING and compromises the definitive operation. AND A NORMAL FACIAL NERVE DOES NOT EXCLUDE CANCER — palsy is HIGHLY SPECIFIC BUT INSENSITIVE, and most parotid cancers present with an intact nerve, so image and refer anyway. Surgical risks to name if asked: FACIAL NERVE INJURY, numbness of the ear lobe from the greater auricular nerve, FREY SYNDROME, salivary fistula, haematoma and infection — leaving detailed consent to the surgeon. Support: PATS for travel from a country town, Cancer Council SA 13 11 20. Safety-net: rapid growth, skin breakdown over the lump, or the face getting weaker.
plan: TEMPERATURE FIRST, WITH THE REASON: 'Examiner, before I begin, MAY I HAVE THE TEMPERATURE? SIALADENITIS AND PAROTITIS ARE ON MY DIFFERENTIAL LIST, so that is the vital sign that matters here.' → 36.8. Then THE STRUCTURED REQUEST: 'could you please tell me the features of the swelling: its SITE AND SIZE, its SHAPE AND SURFACE, its CONSISTENCY, its BORDER, whether it is TENDER, whether it is MOBILE OR FIXED to the skin or the underlying tissue, and whether it is FLUCTUANT OR PULSATILE?' (Asking in a random order, or asking only for size and tenderness, misses what is being marked — a SYSTEM — and consistency, border and fixation are the three that separate benign from malignant.)

IF GIVEN A SHORT HISTORY, one question per turn — and the one that sets up the station: 'how long has the lump been there? Has it changed recently? Is it painful at all? DOES IT SWELL OR HURT WHEN YOU EAT? Have you had any fevers? HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY WEAKNESS OR CHANGE IN THE MOVEMENT OF YOUR FACE? Any trouble opening your mouth or swallowing? Any lumps elsewhere, weight loss or night sweats? HAVE YOU EVER HAD A SKIN CANCER ON YOUR SCALP, EAR OR FACE?' → five years, bigger over three months, no pain, no change with eating, no fevers, HIS WIFE SAYS HIS SMILE LOOKS CROOKED, no trismus, no other lumps, and SKIN CANCERS CUT OFF HIS FOREARMS YEARS AGO.

INSPECTION: 'there is a swelling in the LEFT PAROTID REGION, in front of and below the ear, LIFTING AND DISPLACING THE LEFT EAR LOBE OUTWARDS. The overlying skin shows no redness, ulceration, tethering or scars. Looking at the FACE AT REST, I am comparing both sides for asymmetry, ptosis, loss of the nasolabial fold and drooping of the corner of the mouth, and inspecting the ear and canal for vesicles.'

THE MOUTH: 'Gordon, could you open your mouth as wide as you can? There is NO LIMITATION OF JAW OPENING. The SOFT PALATE IS SYMMETRICAL with no pharyngeal asymmetry or medial bulging. I am looking at the opening of STENSEN'S DUCT, OPPOSITE THE UPPER SECOND MOLAR, for bulging, redness, a stone or purulent discharge — it appears normal.'

PALPATION AND NODES: 'TEMPERATURE with the backs of my fingers ON BOTH CHEEKS — no local rise. Gordon, I'm going to feel the lump; tell me if it's tender. It is about 3 by 4 centimetres, FIRM TO HARD, NON-TENDER, with an IRREGULAR BORDER and a NODULAR SURFACE, and it is POORLY MOBILE in both planes with no fixation to the skin. Not fluctuant, not pulsatile.' Then from behind: 'PRE-AURICULAR, POST-AURICULAR, OCCIPITAL, SUBMENTAL, SUBMANDIBULAR, ANTERIOR AND POSTERIOR CERVICAL CHAINS AND THE SUPRACLAVICULAR FOSSA — no lymphadenopathy.'

THE SPECIAL TEST: 'MY SPECIAL TEST IS THE FACIAL NERVE. Gordon, COPY WHAT I DO AND HOLD AGAINST ME: raise your eyebrows and wrinkle your forehead; screw your eyes shut and don't let me open them; puff out your cheeks; show me your teeth; purse your lips and tense your neck.' → weakness of all branches including the forehead → THE SENTENCE: 'there is weakness of ALL BRANCHES of the left facial nerve, INCLUDING THE FOREHEAD. Forehead involvement makes this a LOWER MOTOR NEURONE lesion, and WITH AN IPSILATERAL PAROTID MASS THAT IS MALIGNANT INFILTRATION UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.' Then completion: 'I would MASSAGE THE GLAND ALONG THE DUCT, perform a BIMANUAL INTRAORAL PALPATION, examine the other salivary glands, and EXAMINE THE SKIN OF THE SCALP, EARS AND FACE FOR A PRIMARY SKIN CANCER.' (Testing the smile only, or finding the weakness and never saying what it means, are both common and both cost the station.)

WARNING SHOT, THEN THE HONEST ANSWER: 'Gordon, I've found something I need to be straight with you about. Is now a good time? The lump is in your PAROTID GLAND — the big saliva gland in front of your ear. The important part is that the LEFT SIDE OF YOUR FACE ISN'T MOVING NORMALLY, and THE NERVE THAT CONTROLS YOUR FACIAL MUSCLES RUNS STRAIGHT THROUGH THAT GLAND.' → 'is it cancer?' → 'when a lump that's been there for years starts to grow, and the nerve running through it stops working properly, THAT MAKES ME CONCERNED THIS COULD BE A CANCER. I can't be certain today — that needs a scan and a sample. But I'm not going to pretend I'm not worried.' (Answering 'is it cancer?' with either 'yes it is' or 'no, I'm sure it's fine' fails: the first is not supportable on examination alone, the second is dishonest and unsafe.)

DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN WORDS, THEN SCAN, SAMPLE, SURGERY (see dx), then support and safety-net: 'there's a scheme called PATS that helps with travel and accommodation to get to Adelaide, and CANCER COUNCIL SOUTH AUSTRALIA ON 13 11 20 can help with information and support. I'll see you again this week. COME BACK SOONER IF THE LUMP GROWS QUICKLY, IF THE SKIN OVER IT BREAKS DOWN, OR IF YOUR FACE GETS WEAKER. What questions do you have?'

THE URGENT REFERRAL TO DICTATE BEFORE HE LEAVES: a five-year history of a painless left parotid swelling that has increased over three months; a 3 by 4 cm firm-to-hard non-tender mass with an irregular border and reduced mobility, DISPLACING THE EAR LOBE; and CRITICALLY a complete left lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy INVOLVING THE FOREHEAD. No fever, no local temperature rise, no skin ulceration or tethering, no trismus, symmetrical palate and pharynx, normal duct orifice with no pus, and no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. pefe: Role-player: Gordon Whitely, 55, shearing contractor on the Yorke Peninsula, married thirty years, PRACTICAL, DRY, NOT A COMPLAINER, and he has not seen a doctor in four years. His wife made the appointment. The lump has been there ABOUT FIVE YEARS and he always ignored it BECAUSE IT HAS NEVER HURT — but over the last THREE MONTHS it has clearly got bigger. HIDDEN AGENDA, NOT SAID FIRST: his wife has been telling him HIS SMILE HAS GONE CROOKED and that he DRIBBLES TEA from the left side of his mouth — he thinks she is fussing. ONLY MENTION IT IF THE DOCTOR ASKS ABOUT HIS FACE, OR ASKS WHAT HIS WIFE HAS NOTICED. Background: ex-smoker, gave up at 40 after about 20 a day; four or five beers on a Friday; SEVERAL SKIN CANCERS CUT OFF HIS FOREARMS AND ONE OFF HIS EAR, said if asked; no fevers, no weight loss, no night sweats, no other lumps; HIS FATHER DIED OF THROAT CANCER AT 61 AND IT WAS A BAD DEATH. He is frightened but will not say so unless asked about concerns or until cancer is named — then quietly: 'IS IT CANCER?' and 'HOW LONG HAVE I GOT BEFORE I KNOW?' Understated, dry humour early, quieter once the doctor becomes serious — and if the doctor is honest: 'THANKS FOR BEING STRAIGHT WITH ME.'

ON EXAMINATION: open the mouth fully with no difficulty; THE LEFT FOREHEAD DOES NOT MOVE; the left eye does not close fully; air escapes from the left on puffing; THE SMILE PULLS TO THE RIGHT and the left corner does not move. THREE MISTAKES ROLE-PLAYERS MAKE: VOLUNTEERING THE CROOKED SMILE — wait to be asked, because it is the question that carries the station; MOVING THE LEFT SIDE OF THE FACE — keep the forehead, eye, cheek and mouth still; and BECOMING TEARFUL — Gordon is understated, and going quiet is more useful to the candidate than crying, because it tests whether they notice.

and his father died of throat cancer at 61, which he will not raise unless you ask about concerns; variants — an intact nerve is reassuring but changes nothing; a tender, warm, diffusely swollen gland with a fever of 38.4 and PUS AT THE DUCT on massage is ACUTE BACTERIAL SIALADENITIS, needing a swab of the pus, antibiotics, rehydration, sialagogues and gland massage, with imaging if an abscess is suspected and review in 24 to 48 hours; and pain and swelling that come on WITH EATING and settle afterwards is a SALIVARY DUCT STONE, examined by bimanual palpation along the duct and referred for ultrasound and consideration of sialendoscopy

setting: HISTORY THEN EXAMINATION — rural GP, a photograph of a red linear rash, A THERMOMETER AND A TIMER ON THE DESK. YOU ARE PROMPTED AT THREE MINUTES, so ask ONE QUESTION PER TURN: bundle four into a breath and the role-player answers only the last, and you lose THE DIRECTION OF SPREAD, WHICH IS THE DIAGNOSIS. Two palpation failures live in this station: palpating landmarks and NEVER ONCE PRESSING THE RASH, and going to the axilla while SKIPPING THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE — the node the forearm actually drains to, and the special test the examiner is waiting for.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo. Alex Brennan, 32, with A RASH ON HIS RIGHT FOREARM. A photograph shows a RED LINEAR RASH; a thermometer and a timer are on the desk; VITAL SIGNS AVAILABLE FROM THE EXAMINER ON REQUEST. 8 minutes, PROMPTED AT THREE MINUTES.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient — you will be prompted at three minutes
Perform a relevant physical examination, giving a running commentary
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: ASK THE EXAMINER ABOUT STABILITY FIRST · but do NOT ask for the full vital signs yet, because the task is a history and starting to examine collapses your structure into examine, history, examine again · THEN AN OPEN QUESTION AND SILENCE, then ONE QUESTION PER TURN: when, WHERE IT STARTED, IS IT SPREADING AND IN WHICH DIRECTION, first time, ITCHY OR PAINFUL, warm, discharge · THE PORTAL OF ENTRY: 'what were you doing in the couple of days before it started?' and then NARROW IT · scratches, thorn pricks, bites, gloves, cannulas or injections · because GARDENING IS THE CONTEXT AND THE SCRATCH IS THE FINDING · SYSTEMIC SCREEN WITH FEVER FIRST, since fever changes management and atopy does not · THEN THE EXAMINATION: general appearance, and NOW ask for the full vital signs and USE THE TIMER AND THE THERMOMETER, reading both aloud · INSPECTION IN FIVE PARTS (site, colour, primary morphology, secondary morphology, borders) PLUS THE ENTRY POINT · PALPATION: temperature with the backs of the fingers ON THE RASH AND COMPARED WITH THE OTHER ARM, capillary refill, radial pulse, THEN PRESS THE RASH, then elevation, surface and BLANCHING HANDLED HONESTLY · THE ELBOW, because the rash crosses it · THEN THE SPECIAL TEST: EPITROCHLEAR NODE FIRST, then the axilla, AFFECTED SIDE ONLY · then name it, answer the blood-poisoning fear, give plain-word differentials, and DRAW THE LINE.

back.dx: LYMPHANGITIS OF THE RIGHT FOREARM — a well-defined LINEAR erythematous patch running PROXIMALLY from a portal of entry at the wrist, warm and tender, with a REACTIVE EPITROCHLEAR NODE and no systemic upset. TO HIM IN ONE SENTENCE: 'under the skin there are small drainage channels called LYMPHATIC VESSELS. Bacteria have got in through a small break in the skin — most likely from the gardening — and THEY'RE TRAVELLING ALONG ONE OF THOSE CHANNELS, which is why it looks like A LINE RATHER THAN A PATCH.' THEN ANSWER THE FEAR DIRECTLY: 'IT'S NOT BLOOD POISONING, and it's very treatable with tablets. But it CAN turn into a more serious infection if it's left, which is exactly why I want to see you again in two days AND WHY I'VE DRAWN THAT LINE ON YOUR ARM.' DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN WORDS — and keep them to this consultation: CELLULITIS, the same sort of infection but spread over an AREA instead of a line; INFLAMMATION OF A VEIN, which usually gives a FIRM TENDER CORD you can feel, and there isn't one; A PLANT REACTION, which would be ITCHY AND BLISTERY rather than sore; AN INSECT BITE; and A CLOT IN THE DEEP VEINS OF THE ARM, which usually swells THE WHOLE arm. (Listing meningococcaemia, HSP, ITP, lymphoma and viral exanthems belongs in a lecture on rashes, not here — it frightens the patient for no clinical gain.) HOW LYMPHANGITIS DIFFERS FROM CELLULITIS: SHAPE. Cellulitis spreads LATERALLY with a POORLY DEFINED margin; lymphangitis travels IN A CHANNEL and gives a WELL-DEFINED LINE running toward the draining node. WHY THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE: it is the FIRST DRAINING NODE FOR THE FOREARM, a reactive node there SUPPORTS a lymphatic infection, and involvement of the node itself is LYMPHADENITIS. MANAGEMENT: flucloxacillin 500 mg orally six-hourly for five days, or cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly VERIFY; TETANUS if over five years VERIFY; DRAW A LINE AT THE TOP OF THE REDNESS WITH TODAY'S DATE; review at 24-48 hours; and come straight back IF THE REDNESS PASSES THAT LINE, if fevers or shakes develop, IF THE PAIN GETS MUCH WORSE THAN IT LOOKS, or if the elbow becomes painful to move.
plan: STABILITY FIRST, BUT NOT THE FULL VITALS: 'Examiner, IS MY PATIENT STABLE ENOUGH FOR ME TO PROCEED WITH THE HISTORY?' → 'yes, please proceed.' (Asking for the full set of vital signs here is the trap: you have been asked to take a history, the examiner will LET you start examining, and your structure collapses into examine, history, examine again.) Then WIPE and AN OPEN QUESTION FOLLOWED BY SILENCE: 'Alex, CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT THIS RASH?'

ONE QUESTION PER TURN, IN THIS ORDER: 'when exactly did it start?' — 'WHERE ON THE ARM DID IT START?' — 'IS IT SPREADING, AND IN WHICH DIRECTION?' — 'has this ever happened before?' — 'IS IT ITCHY, OR IS IT PAINFUL?' — 'does it feel warm to touch?' — 'is there any oozing or discharge?' → Monday, near the wrist, MOVING UP TOWARD THE ELBOW, never before, SORE NOT ITCHY, warm, no discharge. (Bundling four questions into one breath means the role-player answers ONLY THE LAST, and you lose the direction of spread — which IS the diagnosis.)

THE PORTAL OF ENTRY — and then narrow it: 'WHAT WERE YOU DOING IN THE COUPLE OF DAYS BEFORE IT STARTED?' → 'I was out in the garden on Sunday, cutting the roses back.' → 'DID YOU NOTICE ANY CUTS, SCRATCHES OR THORN PRICKS? Any insect or spider bites? Were you wearing gloves? Any recent injections, drips or blood tests in that arm?' → a scratch on the wrist he barely noticed, no gloves, no cannula. (ACCEPTING 'I WAS GARDENING' AND MOVING ON IS THE TRAP: gardening is the CONTEXT, the SCRATCH is the FINDING. And gardening also opens contact dermatitis and, if it were nodular and slow, sporotrichosis — so the same answer serves three differentials.)

SYSTEMIC SCREEN, FEVER FIRST: 'HAVE YOU HAD ANY FEVERS, CHILLS OR SHIVERING EPISODES? Do you feel generally unwell in yourself? Any swelling of the whole arm, or heaviness? Have you been doing any repetitive overhead work with that arm? Any history of eczema, hay fever or asthma, in you or your family? Any new soaps, creams, lotions or sunscreens? Any injury to the arm? What do you do for work?' (IF THE PROMPT IS COMING, ASK FEVER FIRST AND DROP THE ATOPY QUESTIONS — fever changes management, atopy does not.)

GENERAL APPEARANCE AND THE VITALS, NOW: 'Examiner, the patient is alert and orientated, comfortable at rest, WITH NO RIGORS. AS THIS IS AN INFECTIVE RASH I WOULD LIKE THE FULL VITAL SIGNS.' → a thermometer and a timer are handed over → USE THEM AND READ THE NUMBERS ALOUD: 'pulse 82, regular, normal volume. Temperature 37.2. HE IS AFEBRILE AND HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE.'

INSPECTION IN FIVE PARTS, PLUS THE ENTRY POINT: 'SITE — flexor aspect of the right forearm, wrist to antecubital fossa, about 15 by 2 centimetres, UNILATERAL. COLOUR — erythematous. PRIMARY MORPHOLOGY — flat and larger than a centimetre, so A PATCH, IN A LINEAR DISTRIBUTION running proximally. SECONDARY MORPHOLOGY — no vesicles, no scratch marks, no erosions, no discharge, no scale, AND NO VISIBLE VENOUS CORD. BORDERS — WELL DEFINED. There is no swelling of the whole limb. I AM ALSO LOOKING FOR AN ENTRY POINT — a bite, scratch, thorn prick or injection mark — and I can see a small linear abrasion at the wrist.'

PALPATION — and PRESS THE RASH: 'TEMPERATURE with the backs of my fingers, ON THE RASH AND COMPARED WITH THE OTHER FOREARM — there is a local rise. CAPILLARY REFILL under two seconds. RADIAL PULSE present. Alex, I'M GOING TO PRESS GENTLY ALONG THE LINE — tell me if it hurts.' → he winces → 'thank you, I'll be gentle. TENDER TO LIGHT PALPATION, consistent with infection. The lesion is NOT ELEVATED and the surface is SMOOTH. I am pressing to CHECK FOR BLANCHING — I WOULD EXPECT THIS TO BLANCH; THE APPLIED COLOURING LIMITS MY INTERPRETATION, so I am not relying on it.' (Asserting a NON-BLANCHING rash and then treating it as lymphangitis is an automatic fail — handle blanching honestly.)

THE ELBOW, THEN THE SPECIAL TEST: 'THE RASH CROSSES THE ELBOW, SO I WANT TO EXCLUDE JOINT INVOLVEMENT. The joint line is not tender and there is no effusion. Alex, bend and straighten your elbow, and turn your palm up and down.' → full pain-free movement → 'no evidence of septic arthritis. MY SPECIAL TEST IS THE REGIONAL NODES ON THE AFFECTED SIDE: THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE, ABOUT THREE CENTIMETRES ABOVE THE MEDIAL EPICONDYLE, then the axilla — apical, central, anterior, posterior and lateral chains.' → a single tender mobile epitrochlear node, axilla clear → 'A TENDER, MOBILE NODE IS REACTIVE and consistent with infection — a hard, fixed or matted node would make me think about malignancy. To complete, I would MEASURE BOTH FOREARMS AT THE SAME LEVEL for a size difference, given upper limb DVT is on my list.'

NAME IT, ANSWER THE FEAR, GIVE THE DIFFERENTIALS, DRAW THE LINE (see dx). → 'is that blood poisoning? That's what my mate reckoned.' → 'IT ISN'T, and it's very treatable with antibiotic tablets. But it can become a more serious infection if it's left, which is why I want to see you again in two days.' Then: 'I'll start you on antibiotics, and I'VE DRAWN A LINE AT THE TOP OF THE REDNESS WITH TODAY'S DATE. COME STRAIGHT BACK IF THE REDNESS PASSES THAT LINE, if you get fevers or shakes, IF THE PAIN GETS MUCH WORSE THAN IT LOOKS, or if your elbow becomes painful to move.'
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute run, with the history prompt at three minutes
ask: 'Examiner, is my patient stable enough for me to proceed with the history?' / 'Can you tell me more about this rash?' / 'Where did it start, and is it spreading?' / 'Is it itchy, or is it painful?' / 'What were you doing in the day or two before it came up?' / 'Have you had any fevers, chills or shivering?'

'As this is an infective rash, may I have the full vital signs?' / 'Site, colour, primary morphology, secondary morphology, borders.' / 'A linear erythematous patch with well-defined borders, running proximally.' / 'Temperature with the backs of my fingers, on the rash, compared with the other side.' / 'I am pressing to check for blanching — I would expect this to blanch.'

'The rash crosses the elbow, so I want to exclude joint involvement.' / 'My special test is the epitrochlear node, then the axilla, affected side only.' / 'I've drawn a line at the top of the redness with today's date on it.' EXAMINER CHALLENGES: 'did the rash blanch?' → 'it did not blanch on my testing, BUT THE RASH HAS BEEN APPLIED TO THE SKIN, so I do not think that finding is interpretable. Clinically, lymphangitis blanches, and nothing else in the examination suggests a purpuric process.' / 'Why the epitrochlear node?' → 'it is the FIRST DRAINING NODE FOR THE FOREARM. A reactive node there supports a lymphatic infection, and involvement of the node itself is LYMPHADENITIS.' / 'How do you tell this from cellulitis?' → 'SHAPE. Cellulitis spreads laterally and gives an AREA with a poorly defined margin. Lymphangitis travels in a channel and gives a WELL-DEFINED LINE running toward the draining node.'

VERSION B — FEBRILE AND TACHYCARDIC: INTERRUPT YOURSELF. 'Examiner, I want to STOP AND FLAG that the temperature is 38.6 and the pulse is 108. I AM TREATING THIS AS SEPSIS FROM A SKIN AND SOFT TISSUE SOURCE. I would like large-bore intravenous access, BLOOD CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS, FBE, CRP, UEC, glucose and lactate, intravenous fluids, and INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS NOW. I would then complete my examination.' (Continuing a calm examination in the febrile, tachycardic variant without recognising sepsis is an automatic fail.)

THE PAIN-OUT-OF-PROPORTION MOMENT — ask, then escalate: 'Alex, IS THE PAIN MUCH WORSE THAN THE RASH LOOKS? Does the skin feel NUMB anywhere over it? And how fast has it changed — over days, or over HOURS?' → if yes, yes, hours → 'Examiner, PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION, ALTERED SENSATION OVER THE RASH AND SPREAD OVER HOURS make me concerned about NECROTISING FASCIITIS. THIS IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS AND A SURGICAL EMERGENCY — I would resuscitate, give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and CALL THE SURGICAL REGISTRAR IMMEDIATELY RATHER THAN ARRANGE IMAGING.' / THE NODULAR VARIANT, when the line is made of LUMPS and has evolved over WEEKS: 'the lesions are NODULES ARRANGED IN A LINE rather than a continuous streak. That pattern is NODULAR OR SPOROTRICHOID LYMPHANGITIS. I would ask specifically about ROSE THORNS AND SPHAGNUM MOSS, which points to SPOROTHRIX, and about FISH TANKS OR FISH HANDLING, which points to MYCOBACTERIUM MARINUM. It needs a BIOPSY WITH TISSUE CULTURE, and I would TELL THE LABORATORY WHAT I SUSPECT so the cultures are held long enough.'
pefe: Role-player: Alex Brennan, 32, works at the Wallaroo grain terminal, lives with his partner and a four-year-old, plays footy on Saturdays and almost never sees a doctor. Two days ago he noticed a red mark near his right wrist; it is now a RED LINE RUNNING HALFWAY UP THE FOREARM, SORE NOT ITCHY, hot, with nothing coming out of it. WHAT HE DID: on Sunday he spent the afternoon CUTTING BACK THE ROSES WITHOUT GLOVES and got scratched a few times, thinking nothing of it — ONLY VOLUNTEER THIS IF ASKED WHAT HE WAS DOING. No medications or allergies, non-smoker, six to eight beers a week; no eczema, hay fever or asthma in him or the family; no cannulas, injections or blood tests; no overhead work; no new soaps or creams; last tetanus probably at school. HIDDEN AGENDA: HIS MATE AT WORK TOLD HIM THIS WAS 'BLOOD POISONING' and that people lose arms from it — he is more worried than he is letting on. Raise it WHEN THE DOCTOR NAMES THE DIAGNOSIS, or in the last minute if they never ask about concerns, AND NOT IN THE FIRST THREE MINUTES. Practical, cheerful, slightly embarrassed to be here, not distressed.

THE MOST IMPORTANT CUE: IF THE DOCTOR PRESSES ON THE RASH, WINCE AND SAY IT IS TENDER — and IF THEY NEVER PRESS THE RASH, DO NOT PROMPT THEM. Move the elbow freely when asked: 'that's fine, no pain.' THREE MISTAKES ROLE-PLAYERS MAKE: VOLUNTEERING THE GARDENING — wait to be asked, because it is the single most discriminating question in the history; ANSWERING A BUNDLED QUESTION FULLY — if four questions arrive at once, ANSWER ONLY THE LAST, which is what a real patient does; and FORGETTING TO WINCE, when tenderness is a physical sign the candidate has to elicit and report.

Scored out of 20: washed hands, introduced, consented; ASKED THE EXAMINER ABOUT STABILITY FIRST; used an open question and let him answer; ASKED WHERE IT STARTED AND ESTABLISHED THE DIRECTION; asked itchy versus painful; ASKED WHAT HE WAS DOING BEFOREHAND; asked about scratches, thorns or bites; asked about cannulas or injections; ASKED ABOUT FEVER AND CHILLS; asked for the FULL VITAL SIGNS AND USED THE EQUIPMENT; described site, colour, primary and secondary morphology and borders; COMPARED TEMPERATURE WITH THE OTHER ARM; PRESSED THE RASH FOR TENDERNESS; commented on elevation and surface; HANDLED BLANCHING WITHOUT ASSERTING NON-BLANCHING; EXAMINED THE ELBOW by palpation and movement; EXAMINED THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE AND THE AXILLA; gave a shaped differential with reasons in plain words; and gave a safety net with named reasons to return. Numbers: capillary refill under 2 s; PATCH flat and 1 cm or more, MACULE flat and under 1 cm, PLAQUE raised and 1 cm or more, PAPULE raised and under 1 cm; VESICLE under 5 mm, BULLA 5 mm or more; epitrochlear node about 3 cm above the medial epicondyle; 5 axillary chains; flucloxacillin 500 mg PO six-hourly for 5 days or cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly VERIFY; review 24-48 h; tetanus if over 5 years VERIFY; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.
Entry point — A small LINEAR ABRASION at the wrist

must: FAIL — Continuing a calm examination in the febrile, tachycardic variant without recognising SEPSIS — INTERRUPT YOURSELF: 'Examiner, I want to STOP AND FLAG that the temperature is 38.6 and the pulse is 108; I am treating this as SEPSIS FROM A SKIN AND SOFT TISSUE SOURCE — large-bore intravenous access, BLOOD CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS, FBE, CRP, UEC, glucose and lactate, intravenous fluids, and intravenous antibiotics now; I would then complete my examination' (★)

FAIL — Never asking about FEVER at all — it is the single most discriminating question in the history, and he is briefed to wait to be asked; if the three-minute prompt is coming, ASK FEVER FIRST and drop the atopy questions, because fever changes management and atopy does not (★)

FAIL — Never examining the JOINT the rash crosses: 'the rash crosses the elbow, so I want to exclude joint involvement' — palpate the joint line for tenderness and effusion, then active movement in both planes ('bend and straighten your elbow, and turn your palm up and down'), reporting 'full pain-free active movement with no joint-line tenderness, so no evidence of septic arthritis' (★)

FAIL — Asserting a NON-BLANCHING rash and then treating it as lymphangitis anyway — the rash has been APPLIED to the skin, so the finding is not interpretable and you must say so rather than claim it: 'I am pressing to check for blanching — I would expect this to blanch; the applied colouring limits my interpretation, so I am not relying on it', and if challenged, 'clinically, lymphangitis blanches, and nothing else in the examination suggests a purpuric process' (★)

FAIL — Sending him away with no REVIEW and no SAFETY NET, palpating landmarks and never once PRESSING THE RASH, or going to the axilla and skipping the EPITROCHLEAR node — that node sits about 3 cm above the medial epicondyle, it is the FIRST DRAINING NODE for the forearm, and it is the special test the examiner is waiting for ('a tender, mobile node is REACTIVE and consistent with infection; a hard, fixed or matted node would make me think about malignancy'); then antibiotics, a LINE DRAWN at the top of the redness WITH TODAY'S DATE, review in 24 to 48 hours, tetanus if it has been over five years, and named reasons to return — redness passing the line, fevers or shakes, pain much worse than it looks, or the elbow becoming painful to move (★)

SAY — Ask the examiner about STABILITY before the history ('is my patient stable enough for me to proceed with the history?'), then ONE QUESTION PER TURN, because bundling four into one breath gets you the last answer only and you lose the DIRECTION OF SPREAD, which IS the diagnosis: when it started, WHERE ON THE ARM it started, whether it is spreading and IN WHICH DIRECTION, ever before, itchy or painful, warm, any discharge; then find the PORTAL OF ENTRY, because 'I was gardening' is the CONTEXT and THE SCRATCH IS THE FINDING — ask specifically about cuts, scratches and thorn pricks, insect or spider bites, gloves, and recent injections, drips or blood tests in that arm; describe the rash in FIVE PARTS (site with dimensions and laterality; colour; PRIMARY morphology — flat and over a centimetre is a PATCH, in a LINEAR distribution; SECONDARY morphology, with no vesicles, scratch marks, erosions, discharge, scale or visible venous cord; and well-defined BORDERS), looking for the entry point as you go; on palpation compare TEMPERATURE with the backs of your fingers ON the rash against the same level on the other arm, check capillary refill and the radial pulse, then press gently ALONG the line for tenderness, which is the physical sign he is briefed to give you; name it and explain in ONE sentence ('under the skin there are small drainage channels called lymphatic vessels, and bacteria have got in through that scratch and are travelling ALONG one of those channels, which is why it looks like a LINE rather than a patch'); answer the BLOOD POISONING fear directly, because his mate told him people lose arms from it ('it's not blood poisoning, and it's very treatable with tablets — but it can turn into a more serious infection if it's left, which is exactly why I want to see you again in two days'); give the differentials in PLAIN WORDS and not a lecture, because meningococcaemia, Henoch–Schönlein purpura, ITP, lymphoma and viral exanthems frighten the patient for no clinical gain — cellulitis (the same infection spread over an AREA with a poorly defined margin rather than a line), inflammation of a vein (which usually gives a firm tender cord you can feel), a plant reaction (itchy and blistery rather than sore), an insect bite, and a clot in the deep veins of the arm (which swells the WHOLE arm, and his isn't swollen), offering to measure both forearms at the same level; flucloxacillin or cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly for five days (VERIFY); variants — PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION with altered sensation over the rash and spread over HOURS rather than days raises NECROTISING FASCIITIS, a CLINICAL diagnosis and a surgical emergency, so resuscitate, give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and call the surgical registrar IMMEDIATELY rather than arranging imaging; and NODULES arranged in a line, evolving over WEEKS, is nodular or sporotrichoid lymphangitis, so ask specifically about ROSE THORNS AND SPHAGNUM MOSS for Sporothrix and about FISH TANKS OR FISH HANDLING for Mycobacterium marinum, arranging a biopsy with TISSUE CULTURE and telling the laboratory what you suspect so the cultures are held long enough

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION REQUEST, EXPLANATION AND MANAGEMENT — general practice, and THE FRAMEWORK STATION FOR EVERY PAEDIATRIC HISTORY. THE FOUR WELL-BABY QUESTIONS ARE THE SPINE: alertness and appearance, DRINKING (not just eating), WET NAPPIES QUANTIFIED, and bowel motions. Do NOT recite the whole of BINDSMA — birth history in a healthy 18-month-old with gastroenteritis is worth almost nothing and costs the ninety seconds you need for tasks 3 and 4. FOUR AUTOMATIC FAILS: never establishing hydration status or stating a grade; never asking whether the vomit was GREEN; discharging with no specific safety-netting; and prescribing antibiotics or an antidiarrhoeal because the mother pressed for it.
stem: General practice, Port Augusta; you are the GP registrar, Saturday morning. RILEY CHAPMAN, 18 MONTHS, brought by his mother Danielle with VOMITING AND LOOSE STOOLS FOR TWO DAYS.
Weight today 10.8 kg — WEIGHT AT THE 16-MONTH CHECK 11.4 kg — T 37.9 — HR 148 — RR 32 — central capillary refill 2 s — SpO2 98% RA — ALERT BUT CLINGY. 8 minutes with the patient, 2 minutes reading.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the mother (about five minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your most likely diagnosis and the differentials you considered, in plain language
Outline your immediate management and safety-netting advice
time: OPEN QUESTION AND THIRTY SECONDS UNINTERRUPTED · almost everything is in her first answer · VOMITING: how many, WHAT COLOUR AND IS ANY OF IT GREEN, blood, forceful or not · DIARRHOEA: how many, how loose, BLOOD OR MUCUS OR JELLY, and DOES HE GO PALE AND PULL HIS KNEES UP IN EPISODES, which is what separates gastroenteritis from intussusception at exactly this age · EXCLUDE THE OTHERS: fever measured, RASH AND WHETHER IT BLANCHES UNDER A GLASS, ears, cough, offensive urine, POLYURIA AND POLYDIPSIA for diabetes, and access to medicines or chemicals · THEN THE FOUR WELL-BABY QUESTIONS, said as 'these matter most to me' · TARGETED BINDSMA ONLY: immunisations including rotavirus, SICK CONTACTS at home and daycare, medications and allergies, and a one-line development check · CONCERNS, then SUMMARISE BACK before you examine · REQUEST THE EXAMINATION including a BEDSIDE GLUCOSE AND KETONES and a CLEAN-CATCH URINE · GRADE THE DEHYDRATION OUT LOUD as a percentage · explain with the exclusions NAMED IN PLAIN WORDS · then the rehydration TECHNIQUE, what NOT to give, and SIX SPECIFIC RETURN TRIGGERS in writing with review in 24 hours.

back.dx: ACUTE VIRAL GASTROENTERITIS WITH CLINICAL DEHYDRATION of about 5% in an 18-month-old — vomiting first then watery diarrhoea, TWO CHILDREN AT DAYCARE WITH THE SAME THING and a partner unwell midweek, alert but flat and clinging, drinking only sips, and WET NAPPIES DOWN FROM THREE OR FOUR A DAY TO ONE. GRADE IT OUT LOUD: 11.4 to 10.8 kg is 600 g, about 5.3% of body weight, and it is all fluid. THE EXCLUSIONS, NAMED IN PLAIN WORDS RATHER THAN LISTED: green vomit would mean a BLOCKAGE needing surgery — it isn't; screaming in episodes going pale would mean the bowel TELESCOPING — he isn't; ears, throat and chest are clear so nothing else is driving it; THE URINE IS CLEAR, which matters because a urine infection in a toddler looks exactly like this; sugar and ketones are normal so it is not DIABETES; and there is no rash, so this is not MENINGOCOCCAL. MANAGEMENT: antibiotics do not help and make the diarrhoea worse. ORAL REHYDRATION SOLUTION — Hydralyte or Gastrolyte — as ABOUT A TEASPOON EVERY FIVE MINUTES by syringe, because a whole cup comes straight back; four hours then RE-WEIGH. NO juice, cordial, sports drinks or lemonade — too sugary and they worsen the diarrhoea; water alone is not ideal because he is losing salts; keep milk going and let him eat as soon as he wants. IF HE CANNOT MANAGE BY MOUTH THE NEXT STEP IS A NASOGASTRIC TUBE, NOT A DRIP — it works better than a drip for this — and intravenous fluid is for the child who becomes really unwell. SAFETY-NET WITH SIX SPECIFIC TRIGGERS: floppy or hard to wake; FEWER THAN THREE WET NAPPIES IN A DAY; nothing kept down over six hours; VOMIT TURNS GREEN; blood in the vomit or the nappy; a rash that does not fade under a glass — plus 'or you are simply worried, because you know him better than I do'. In writing, review in 24 hours regardless, and PATS covers travel for country families.
plan: OPEN AND LET HER TALK: '...you must be Danielle, and this must be Riley. Hello, mate. I can see he's had a rough couple of days. I'd like to ask you some questions, then examine him, then we'll make a plan together. TELL ME, IN YOUR OWN WORDS, WHAT'S BEEN HAPPENING.' THEN DO NOT INTERRUPT FOR THIRTY SECONDS — onset, sequence, behaviour change and her own worry are all in that first answer.

THE VOMITING, quantified and coloured: 'how many times in the last twenty-four hours? What does it look like — is it milk, is it food, OR IS ANY OF IT GREEN? Any blood? Does it just come up, or does it SHOOT RIGHT OUT?' (If the answer is 'a funny colour', DISAMBIGUATE: 'GREEN LIKE GRASS OR SPINACH, OR YELLOW LIKE CURDLED MILK?' Green is malrotation until excluded and it ends the outpatient conversation.)

THE DIARRHOEA, and the one question that separates the diagnoses: 'how many times a day, and how loose? Any blood or mucus, anything like JELLY? DOES HE GO PALE AND PULL HIS KNEES UP IN EPISODES?' (That question separates gastroenteritis from INTUSSUSCEPTION at exactly this age, and there is a mark for it.)

EXCLUDE THE OTHER CAUSES: fever measured; ANY RASH, and does it fade under a glass; ears, cough, hard breathing; offensive urine; DRINKING AND WEEING FAR MORE THAN USUAL over the last week; access to medicines or chemicals → 'he did tug his ear a bit yesterday' → DO NOT DISCARD IT: 'that's worth knowing, I'll make sure I look in his ears' — parenteral diarrhoea from otitis media is genuine, and the ear-pulling is deliberate misdirection.

THE FOUR WELL-BABY QUESTIONS, flagged as important: 'now some questions about how well Riley is in himself — THESE MATTER MOST TO ME. Is he ALERT AND ACTIVE AND PLAYFUL as usual, or drowsy? IS HE DRINKING as he normally would, and what about eating? HOW MANY WET NAPPIES would he normally have, and how many today? Any other change in his bowel motions?' (Asking only about EATING loses the mark — it is attached to DRINKING. And 'not many wet nappies' must be QUANTIFIED, because the numbers are what let you grade the dehydration.)

TARGETED BINDSMA ONLY — immunisations including ROTAVIRUS, SICK CONTACTS at home and daycare, medicines and allergies, one line on growth and development. Then CONCERNS: 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' → tearful: 'my sister's little boy ended up in hospital on a drip for three days. I keep thinking I've left it too long' → NAME IT AND HOLD IT: 'it sounds like watching that was really frightening. YOU HAVE NOT LEFT IT TOO LONG — he is alert and still taking fluid, and those are the two things that matter most.' Then SUMMARISE BACK before examining.

REQUEST THE EXAMINATION — the marks are in the hydration assessment and the deliberate search for another source: weight undressed; full observations with CENTRAL capillary refill; HYDRATION SIGNS — eyes, membranes, tears, turgor, fontanelle; full abdomen and HERNIAL ORIFICES; EARS, THROAT AND CHEST; full skin inspection; BEDSIDE GLUCOSE AND KETONES; CLEAN-CATCH URINE. Then GRADE IT ALOUD: 'that is CLINICAL DEHYDRATION, NOT SHOCK... with a 600 gram loss I'd put him at about FIVE PER CENT.'

EXPLAIN, WITH THE EXCLUSIONS IN PLAIN WORDS: 'the good news first: I think this is a tummy bug — gastroenteritis — almost certainly the virus going round his daycare... I did think about some other things, and I want you to know I've checked for them' — green vomit, telescoping bowel, ears and chest, the urine, sugar and ketones, the rash. (Listing differentials as NAMES loses the mark. And do not say 'he'll be fine': say what you are watching and what would change your mind.)

MANAGEMENT AND SIX TRIGGERS: antibiotics declined WITH A REASON, then the TECHNIQUE — 'tiny amounts, very often: about a teaspoon every five minutes, by syringe. If you give him a whole cup he'll bring it straight back' — four hours then re-weigh; the explicit NOT-list; nasogastric before intravenous; the six return triggers IN WRITING; review in 24 hours; PATS so cost never stops her coming in. ('Come back if he gets worse' is scored as ABSENT safety-netting.)

pefe: Role-player: Danielle Chapman, 29, receptionist in Port Augusta; partner Josh is FIFO and home this week; Riley is her first child, born 39 weeks by normal delivery at 3.4 kg, ALL IMMUNISATIONS UP TO DATE INCLUDING ROTAVIRUS, no medicines or allergies, never in hospital, walking since 13 months with about ten words. Anxious and slightly apologetic after two nights without sleep, HALF-CONVINCED SHE SHOULD HAVE COME IN YESTERDAY — cooperative and articulate, not hostile, TEARFUL ONLY ONCE, about her sister's son. HIDDEN AGENDA: her sister's boy had the same illness, was admitted three days on a drip, and she found it terrifying; she is quietly terrified of being judged, and does NOT volunteer it unless asked about her concerns.

HOW SHE PLAYS IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED — do not offer the EAR-PULLING, the DAYCARE OUTBREAK or the NAPPY NUMBERS unless a question opens the door. IF THE DOCTOR ASKS ONLY ABOUT EATING, ANSWER ONLY ABOUT EATING AND SAY NOTHING ABOUT DRINKING. To an open question, give a good 20-30 second answer then stop. PUSH ONCE at about four minutes: 'DOES HE NEED ANTIBIOTICS?' — accept a clear explanation, press once more if it is vague. Become emotional only when asked about concerns, or volunteer it by minute six: 'can I just tell you what I'm scared of?' If the doctor uses jargon, say 'sorry — what does that mean?' once, which is a deliberate test. IF THE DOCTOR SAYS 'COME BACK IF HE GETS WORSE' WITHOUT SPECIFICS, ASK 'WORSE HOW? WHAT AM I LOOKING FOR?'

Numbers: DEHYDRATION under 4% none, 4-6% clinical, 7% or more shock — AND BLOOD PRESSURE FALLS LATE. Bolus 20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride IV or IO. Oral rehydration 0.5-1 mL/kg every 5 minutes. Deficit about 50 mL/kg over 4 hours for 4-6%. Ongoing losses 10 mL/kg per watery stool and 2 mL/kg per vomit. Maintenance 100/50/20 mL/kg/day, so 10.8 kg is about 1040 mL/day. Paracetamol 15 mg/kg 4-6 hourly, maximum 60 mg/kg in 24 hours. RILEY: 11.4 to 10.8 kg = 600 g = 5.3% deficit. Return criteria: under 3 wet nappies a day, nothing kept down for 6 hours, green vomit, blood, non-blanching rash, floppy. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, Poisons 13 11 26, CARL 13 14 78.
Other sources — EARS, THROAT AND CHEST ALL NORMAL — the ear-pulling was misdirection, but you had to look
What it adds up to — CLINICAL DEHYDRATION, NOT SHOCK — dry membranes, sunken eyes and reduced turgor WITH a normal central refill and warm peripheries, plus a 600 g loss = about 5%

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION CARD AND MANAGEMENT — rural general practice. THE CASE IS BUILT TO TEMPT 'VIRAL URTI, GO HOME': the card shows a mildly red throat and nothing else, and A MILDLY RED THROAT DOES NOT EXPLAIN A DROWSY CHILD. Interpret the vitals ALOUD as abnormal for age — the interpretation is the mark, not the reading. FOUR AUTOMATIC FAILS: diagnosing tonsillitis or a viral illness and discharging; agreeing to oral antibiotics at home; sending the child by private car without discussion; and NEVER SAYING THE WORD SEPSIS.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo (nearest ED five minutes, the Women's and Children's in Adelaide two hours by road). NOAH, 18 MONTHS, brought for an urgent appointment by his father with FEVER AND VOMITING FOR 24 HOURS — and the father says he has been 'UNRESPONSIVE'.

Vitals on request: T 39.4 — HR 168 — RR 38 — SpO2 96% air — CAPILLARY REFILL 3 SECONDS — weight 11 kg. History six minutes with a prompt, then the examination card, then two minutes on investigations and management.

back.dx: SEPSIS UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE in an 18-month-old — fever 39.4 with tachycardia at 168 (the limit is about 150 between one and four years), tachypnoea, CAPILLARY REFILL OF THREE SECONDS, drowsy and floppy with poor eye contact and a WEAK HIGH-PITCHED CRY, not drinking, and only TWO WET NAPPIES SINCE LAST NIGHT. THE SENTENCE THAT CARRIES THE STATION: 'I am very concerned that Noah has SEPSIS — a serious infection that has spread into his blood and is affecting his whole body. The reasons are his high fever, that he is drowsy and floppy, his heart is racing, his circulation is slow, and he isn't drinking or passing much urine. THE SLIGHTLY RED THROAT DOES NOT EXPLAIN HOW UNWELL HE IS. This needs the hospital, now.' THE PLAN IN FOUR PARTS, NAMING ACTIONS RATHER THAN A REFERRAL: (1) MY NURSE IS CALLING AN AMBULANCE NOW — ring the emergency department so they are ready, and if he needs Adelaide THE RETRIEVAL TEAM COMES TO HIM; (2) the work-up: blood count, INFECTION MARKERS AND A BLOOD CULTURE, a urine sample, possibly a chest X-ray, and ONCE HE IS STABLE possibly a lumbar puncture; (3) ANTIBIOTICS INTO A VEIN WITHIN THE HOUR — AND IF THE AMBULANCE IS DELAYED, THE FIRST DOSE HERE AS AN INJECTION — plus intravenous fluids because he is dry and cannot drink, and paracetamol for comfort; (4) continuous monitoring by the paediatric team. Then honestly: 'he is seriously unwell, but WE'VE CAUGHT IT AND WE'RE STARTING TREATMENT NOW, which is what matters most.' Ask him to ring the mother to meet them there, and stay with the child until the ambulance arrives. IF THE CARD SHOWS PURPURIC SPOTS: meningococcal disease until proven otherwise — CEFTRIAXONE 50 mg/kg INTRAMUSCULARLY RIGHT NOW, BEFORE the ambulance, notify SA Health today, and household contacts need clearance antibiotics. THE FEBRILE CONVULSION AT 14 MONTHS IS A DECOY: there are no seizure features today — say so out loud and STAY ON SEPSIS.
plan: VITALS FIRST, AND INTERPRET THEM: 'could I have Noah's observations? ... 39.4, heart rate 168, breathing 38, oxygen 96, capillary refill 3 seconds. HIS HEART RATE AND CIRCULATION ARE ABNORMAL FOR AN 18-MONTH-OLD, so I'll be quick and thorough.' Then the open question: 'tell me what's been happening.' → 'fever and vomiting for two days and now he's floppy and won't look at me. I THINK IT'S GASTRO. CAN YOU GIVE HIM SOMETHING?' (Reading the numbers without saying they are abnormal loses the mark.)

TIMING OF ALL THREE, SEPARATELY: 'when did the fever, the vomiting and the floppiness EACH start — and is it getting worse?' Then 'have you measured the temperature? Paracetamol — did it help?' Then THE VOMIT: 'any green? Any blood? Is he keeping anything down?'

CLARIFY 'UNRESPONSIVE' — three options, then the seizure questions: 'when you say unresponsive — is he SLEEPY AND HARD TO WAKE, FLOPPY AND NOT RESPONDING, or has he been FITTING?' → 'sleepy and floppy, wakes when I pick him up, cries and shuts his eyes.' Then 'sudden or gradual?' and 'any JERKING? EYES ROLLING UP? WET OR SOILED himself?'

THE FEVER SPINE, hunting the source: ears, runny nose, DROOLING, CHANGE IN THE CRY OR VOICE, neck lumps → 'his cry has gone WEAK AND SQUEAKY'. RASH: 'any spots that don't fade under a glass?' Chest: cough, noisy or fast breathing, recession → 'no cough, but he's breathing fast'. Contacts and travel. GI: diarrhoea, blood, drawing the legs up. URINARY: crying on weeing, smelly urine. MENINGISM WITHOUT THE JARGON: 'does he DISLIKE BEING PICKED UP? Does he turn away from the light? Is his neck stiff?' → 'HE CRIES WHEN I PICK HIM UP.'

WELL-BABY WITH NUMBERS, then the rest: 'is he drinking? HOW MANY WET NAPPIES IN THE LAST TWELVE HOURS? Bowels? Alert or drowsy?' → 'two, and he won't drink.' Then joints and limping, then KAWASAKI features — red eyes, cracked lips, swollen hands or feet. Then targeted BINDSMA: term birth, IMMUNISATIONS UP TO DATE, growth, medicines and allergies, PREVIOUS FITS, who is at home → 'he had a fit with a fever at 14 months' → NAME IT AND MOVE ON: 'that was a febrile convulsion; there are NO seizure features today, so this is different.'

READ THE CARD BACK IN ONE LINE: 'so he is DROWSY, whimpers on handling, hot and dry with a capillary refill of three seconds; the only source is a MILDLY RED THROAT; no rash, no neck stiffness, chest and abdomen clear.'

THE DIAGNOSIS SENTENCE, said plainly to the father (see dx) — fever, drowsiness, racing heart, slow circulation, not drinking or weeing, AND THE RED THROAT DOES NOT EXPLAIN IT. → 'sepsis? He's only got a cold. CAN'T YOU GIVE HIM ANTIBIOTICS HERE?' → 'the antibiotics he needs go INTO A VEIN, with fluids and monitoring, and that needs the hospital team.'

THE FOUR-PART PLAN IN ORDER (see dx), then CONSENT AND CLOSE: 'is that okay with you? Could you ring his mum and ask her to meet you there? I'LL STAY WITH NOAH UNTIL THE AMBULANCE ARRIVES. Do you have any questions?' → 'is he going to die?' → 'he is seriously unwell, but we've caught it and we're starting treatment now, which is what matters most.' (Opening with 'I'll refer him to a paediatrician' is the trap — NAME THE ACTIONS; the referral is how they happen.)

Fever two nights (39 on the ear thermometer, Panadol helps for an hour), vomiting since yesterday six times, milky then clear, NO green and NO blood, NOTHING KEPT DOWN SINCE THIS MORNING, and DROWSY AND FLOPPY SINCE 6 AM, crying when picked up, with A WEAK SQUEAKY CRY. TWO WET NAPPIES SINCE LAST NIGHT, not drinking. Runny nose a few days ago, no cough but breathing fast, no rash, no diarrhoea. Term, fully immunised including the 18-month shots last month, growing well, no medicines or allergies, ONE FEBRILE CONVULSION AT 14 MONTHS, daycare three days a week. ANXIOUS BUT UNDERESTIMATING — he thinks it is gastro and wants a script, and gets frightened when the doctor says sepsis: 'is he going to die?' HIDDEN AGENDA: he does not want to go to hospital because he cannot get hold of Jess and the ute is loaded for a job — HE SAYS 'I'LL DRIVE HIM' if the ambulance is raised, and backs down if the risk is explained.

How he answers: WET NAPPIES AND DRINKING ONLY IF ASKED. If the doctor starts without vitals, answer normally and mark it missing. If the doctor says 'tonsillitis' or 'viral, go home': 'okay... BUT WHY IS HE SO FLOPPY?' and mark it a fail. If the doctor never mentions fluids: 'HE WON'T DRINK — WHAT ABOUT THAT?'

setting: HISTORY AND EXPLANATION — general practice, A KNOWN ASTHMATIC. The stem already says he has asthma, so the condition you have to name is POORLY CONTROLLED ASTHMA, with the FOUR REASONS said out loud. The pass/fail behaviour is THE FOUR CONTROL QUESTIONS, asked with NUMBERS rather than adjectives. And the clinical error the station is built around is ESCALATING TREATMENT FOR A CHILD WHO MAY NOT BE TAKING — OR CORRECTLY USING — THE MEDICINE HE ALREADY HAS. FOUR AUTOMATIC FAILS: never grading the asthma; saying only that he 'has asthma'; prescribing without asking about adherence and technique; and starting a long-acting beta agonist alone or removing the reliever when adding a preventer.

back.dx: POORLY CONTROLLED ASTHMA in a 9-year-old ON RELIEVER ALONE, with adherence unverified and inhaler technique NEVER CHECKED. NAME IT AND GIVE THE FOUR REASONS: he coughs at night ALMOST EVERY NIGHT; he cannot exercise normally and HAS GIVEN UP FOOTBALL; he has daytime symptoms on MOST DAYS, well over two a week; and he needs his reliever on MOST DAYS, again well over two. WELL-CONTROLLED ASTHMA MEANS NO NIGHT SYMPTOMS, NO LIMITATION ON EXERCISE, AND SYMPTOMS AND RELIEVER USE ON NO MORE THAN TWO DAYS A WEEK — he fails all four. MANAGEMENT, AND THE ORDER MATTERS. FIRST, ADHERENCE AND TECHNIQUE: 'if the medicine isn't reaching his lungs, ADDING A SECOND ONE WON'T HELP EITHER' — watch him use it now WITH A SPACER, which he does not own: shake it, ONE PUFF into the spacer, FOUR TO SIX NORMAL BREATHS, then repeat for the second puff, ONE PUFF AT A TIME AND NEVER TWO TOGETHER. SECOND, STEP UP, explaining the two kinds of puffer: a RELIEVER opens the airways when symptoms come and is used as needed; a PREVENTER is taken every day whether he feels well or not and stops the airways becoming narrowed in the first place. Add a LOW-DOSE INHALED CORTICOSTEROID twice daily — AND HE KEEPS THE VENTOLIN. Then walk the rest of the ladder so the examiner hears the sequence: next is MONTELUKAST 5 mg at night on top; after that a COMBINATION INHALER containing a preventer and a long-acting reliever. NON-DRUG MEASURES: the smoking, addressed with a realistic fallback ('if that's not realistic right now, SMOKING ENTIRELY OUTSIDE would still make a real difference'); the carpet and dust mite; the cat out of the bedroom; and GET HIM BACK TO FOOTBALL, because 'NOT BEING ABLE TO PLAY IS A SIGN THE ASTHMA ISN'T CONTROLLED, NOT A REASON TO STOP'. Then a WRITTEN ASTHMA ACTION PLAN, review in FOUR TO SIX WEEKS with technique rechecked at every visit, step down only after THREE MONTHS STABLE, and two sets of red flags — chronic (night symptoms return, sport affected, reliever more than a couple of days a week) and acute (sudden worsening, real difficulty breathing, CANNOT SPEAK IN FULL SENTENCES, or the reliever stops lasting).
plan: VITALS FIRST, THEN OPEN: 'before I begin, could I have Liam's vital signs — RESPIRATORY RATE AND OXYGEN SATURATION PARTICULARLY, plus heart rate and temperature.' Then: 'what's been happening? And is there anything in particular that's worrying you today?' → 'he's had asthma for years, but THE PUFFER DOESN'T SEEM TO BE DOING ANYTHING ANY MORE. I'm worried we need something stronger.'

THE COUGH — TWO MINUTES, NOT A FULL DIFFERENTIAL: 'is it dry, or is he bringing anything up? Any wheeze? IS IT WORSE AT NIGHT? IS IT WORSE WHEN HE'S RUNNING AROUND OR PLAYING SPORT? And how is it affecting him — at school, at home, with his friends?' → dry, wheezy, WORST AT NIGHT, and HE HAS STOPPED GOING TO FOOTY TRAINING. (Running croup, pertussis, post-nasal drip and reflux here is the trap — this is a KNOWN-CONDITION station.)

THE FOUR KNOWN-ASTHMA QUESTIONS: 'when was he diagnosed? WHAT TREATMENT IS HE ON at the moment? AND IS HE TAKING IT AS PRESCRIBED? HAS ANYONE EVER WATCHED HIM USE HIS INHALER AND CHECKED HIS TECHNIQUE? Is he having regular reviews, with a GP or a specialist? Has he ever been admitted to hospital, the emergency department, or INTENSIVE CARE because of his asthma?' → 'just the blue one, Ventolin' ... 'HONESTLY? I'M NOT SURE. I give it to him but I don't stand over him' ... 'NO. NEVER.' → ACKNOWLEDGE IT WITHOUT BLAMING: 'thank you for being straight with me — that's genuinely useful AND IT CHANGES WHAT I'D DO NEXT.' (Asking what treatment he is on and STOPPING THERE loses the mark: it lives in adherence and technique, and her uncertainty is the planted finding.)

THE FOUR CONTROL QUESTIONS — the stated pass/fail item: 'now four questions I ask everyone with asthma, to work out how well controlled it is. ONE, any symptoms at night? TWO, any limitation with exercise? THREE, HOW MANY DAYS A WEEK does he cough or wheeze during the day? FOUR, HOW MANY DAYS A WEEK does he need his Ventolin?' She answers vaguely first — 'a fair bit', 'quite often' — SO PUSH FOR NUMBERS: 'five or six days' and 'nearly every day'. (Questions three and four have a THRESHOLD; the other two do not, and any night symptoms or exercise limitation counts.)

TRIGGERS AND THE LAST TWO DIFFERENTIALS: 'does anyone smoke at home? Pets, carpet, a recent move? Does he have eczema or hay fever, and is there asthma or allergy in the family?' → HIS DAD SMOKES IN THE KITCHEN WITH THE WINDOW OPEN, they moved six months ago to a fully carpeted house, and there is an indoor cat. Then, quickly: 'HAS HE EVER HAD AN EPISODE OF CHOKING? Has he had a lot of chest infections, and any concerns about his growth or development?' (Those two questions are what stop you being the candidate who never considered an inhaled foreign body or cystic fibrosis.)

EXPLAIN THE CONDITION — and the condition is NOT 'asthma': 'you already know Liam has asthma... BUT THE IMPORTANT THING I WANT TO TELL YOU TODAY IS THAT HIS ASTHMA IS CURRENTLY POORLY CONTROLLED. And I want to tell you exactly why I say that' — then the four reasons, then the definition of good control. 'Any one of those would tell me his asthma isn't well controlled. HE HAS ALL FOUR.' → 'I thought the puffer was supposed to fix it' → 'the puffer he's on is a RELIEVER — it opens the airways when symptoms come, but it doesn't stop them coming. That's the gap we need to close.'

ADHERENCE AND TECHNIQUE BEFORE ANY PRESCRIPTION: 'two things have to happen, AND THE ORDER MATTERS. The first is making sure he is actually getting the medicine he already has... IF THE MEDICINE ISN'T REACHING HIS LUNGS, ADDING A SECOND ONE WON'T HELP EITHER. So I'd like to watch him use it right now, WITH A SPACER' — then the concrete steps, and supply one today. (Reaching for the prescription pad first is the clinical error the station is built around. And offering to check technique WITHOUT KNOWING THE STEPS is worse than not offering.)

STEP UP, WALK THE LADDER, THEN THE REST: reliever versus preventer explained in plain words, ADD A DAILY PREVENTER while KEEPING THE VENTOLIN, then name montelukast and then the combination inhaler so she can see there is a sequence. Then the smoking with a realistic fallback, carpet and cat, BACK TO FOOTBALL, a WRITTEN ACTION PLAN, review at FOUR TO SIX WEEKS with technique rechecked, step down only after three months stable, and both sets of red flags. (Finishing on the drug is the common failure — the action plan, review interval, smoking conversation and red flags are all separately marked, so PROTECT THE LAST NINETY SECONDS.)

VARIANT B — ALREADY ON A PREVENTER, TAKING IT PROPERLY, TECHNIQUE ALREADY CHECKED: say so explicitly — 'THIS IS NOT ANYTHING YOU'VE DONE WRONG. He's taking it, he's taking it correctly, and it still isn't enough. That means the treatment needs to go up a level rather than anything needing fixing at home.' Add MONTELUKAST once daily in the evening on top, keeping both puffers — WITH THE BEHAVIOURAL COUNSELLING: it can occasionally affect MOOD, SLEEP OR BEHAVIOUR (vivid dreams, irritability, anxiety), so stop it and ring if anything changes — and name the step after, a combination inhaler. / VARIANT C — A FOUR-YEAR-OLD ALREADY AT STEP 3, and the mother asks for the combination puffer her niece uses: 'in an older child that would be exactly the next step. BUT HE'S FOUR, and in this age group I'M NOT GOING TO START A COMBINATION PUFFER CONTAINING A LONG-ACTING RELIEVER FROM GENERAL PRACTICE. That decision belongs to a paediatrician.' REFER TODAY, and in the meantime re-check technique with A SPACER AND MASK, confirm the montelukast is given nightly, and revisit triggers. (Starting a LABA in a preschool child is an automatic fail.)

VARIANT D — THE STEROID-AVERSE PARENT: 'I'd much rather talk that through than talk you out of it. Can I tell you what I know, and then we decide together?' The inhaled dose is small and goes STRAIGHT INTO THE AIRWAYS, quite different from steroid tablets; AT LOW DOSES THE EFFECT ON GROWTH IS SMALL — the honest position, not 'no effect' — and it must be weighed against what UNCONTROLLED asthma does: broken sleep, missed school, giving up sport, emergency visits. Rinsing the mouth deals with most local side effects. THEN OFFER THE GENUINE ALTERNATIVE: montelukast, not a steroid, generally a bit less effective, with its own mood and sleep caveat — 'both are reasonable places to start. WHICH WOULD YOU RATHER TRY, and I'll review him in four to six weeks either way?' VERIFY current wording on inhaled corticosteroids and growth before quoting figures.
pefe: Role-player: Sarah Doyle, 37, works part-time at a childcare centre in Mount Gambier; husband Mark works at the timber mill; Liam is 9 with a 13-year-old sister. Diagnosed at about four, ON SALBUTAMOL ALONE, NO SPACER — he puffs it straight into his mouth — NO preventer, repeats collected from the pharmacy without seeing a doctor, ONE emergency department visit last year for a nebuliser, never intensive care. Eczema as a baby, father has hay fever, otherwise healthy and growing normally, NO choking episodes, no recurrent chest infections. Home: moved six months ago to a fully carpeted house, one indoor cat, and MARK SMOKES IN THE KITCHEN WITH THE WINDOW OPEN. Tired and mildly frustrated, convinced the medication has stopped working and here to ask for SOMETHING STRONGER — not hostile, and she softens once someone finally explains what is happening.

HOW SHE PLAYS IT — the withheld findings: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED. If asked what treatment he is on, say 'just the blue one, Ventolin' — AND ONLY IF ASKED WHETHER HE IS TAKING IT does she admit 'honestly? I'm not sure. I give it to him but I don't stand over him.' The SPACER only comes up if technique is asked about. The SMOKING only if asked — and if the doctor lectures, become slightly defensive: 'he's trying to cut down.' ON THE CONTROL QUESTIONS, GIVE VAGUE ANSWERS FIRST — 'sometimes', 'a fair bit' — AND ONLY GIVE NUMBERS IF THE DOCTOR ASKS SPECIFICALLY HOW MANY DAYS A WEEK. Push once at about minute six: 'IS THAT A STEROID? I'm not sure about a child being on steroids.' If the doctor finishes early, ask 'how long before it works?' and 'will he be on it forever?' If jargon is used — corticosteroid, exacerbation, adherence, bronchodilator — say 'sorry, what does that mean?' once.

Numbers: CONTROL THRESHOLD is MORE THAN 2 DAYS A WEEK of daytime symptoms or reliever use; ANY night symptoms or exercise limitation counts. Good control means all four favourable; poor means three or four adverse; TREAT PARTIAL THE SAME AS POOR. STEPS AT 6-11 YEARS: reliever as needed, then add LOW-DOSE INHALED CORTICOSTEROID twice daily, then add MONTELUKAST, then an ICS/LABA COMBINATION. STEPS AT 1-5 YEARS: identical to step 3, but STEP 4 IS REFERRAL, NOT A LABA. NEVER a LABA alone; NEVER remove the reliever. Review after stepping up at 4-6 weeks; three months stable before stepping down; step back up if control slips. Salbutamol 100 micrograms per actuation, 1-2 puffs via spacer as needed. Fluticasone low dose 100-200 micrograms a day. Montelukast 5 mg at night for 6-14 years. UNDER 12 MONTHS IT IS NEVER ASTHMA. At 1-5 years, response to treatment replaces spirometry; at 6-11 years spirometry confirms. A SPACER FOR EVERY CHILD, with a MASK under 4-5 years, and RINSE THE MOUTH after the preventer.
Everything else — NO examination findings are provided beyond the vitals — this is a history and explanation station
Why you ask anyway — You do not know this is chronic rather than an exacerbation until you have the respiratory rate and saturation, AND ASKING IS A SCORED ITEM

THE DISCRIMINATING MOMENT IS THE THUMB: over the radial head, then HYPERPRONATE, or supinate and fully flex — and SAY THE TWO-ATTEMPT RULE AND THE X-RAY INDICATIONS BEFORE THE FINDINGS ARRIVE, so the examiner knows you were not simply lucky. THE TRAP IS VERSION B, which hands you a TENDER, SWOLLEN elbow: any candidate who is already demonstrating the manoeuvre has failed. findings: NO swelling, NO bruising, NO deformity
NO TENDERNESS of clavicle, humerus, elbow, radial head, forearm or wrist
DISTRESSED ON ATTEMPTED SUPINATION — otherwise tolerates the arm being still

back.dx: PULLED ELBOW — RADIAL HEAD SUBLUXATION — in a 2-year-old after a classic traction mechanism, with the arm held pronated and slightly flexed, NO tenderness anywhere from clavicle to wrist, distress ONLY on attempted supination, and normal distal neurovascular status. TO THE MOTHER IN LAY WORDS: 'the good news is I don't think anything is broken. One of the forearm bones, the radius, has a ROUNDED HEAD held in the elbow by a BAND called a ligament. A sudden pull on the hand stretches that band and THE HEAD SLIPS PARTLY OUT FROM UNDER IT. A SMALL SLIP — NOT A TRUE DISLOCATION, NOT A FRACTURE — and it only hurts when the elbow moves, which is why he keeps it so still.' NEVER SAY 'DISLOCATED' ON ITS OWN. ANSWER THE GUILT DIRECTLY: 'thousands of children a year get this — a quirk of the joint at his age, not something you did wrong.' THE MANOEUVRE, DESCRIBED WORD FOR WORD: he sits ON HIS MOTHER'S LAP FACING YOU; support the right elbow in your LEFT hand with YOUR THUMB OVER THE RADIAL HEAD — outside the elbow, just below the crease; your right hand on his wrist, ELBOW AT NINETY DEGREES; then FIRMLY HYPERPRONATE the forearm — palm down and beyond — in ONE SMOOTH MOVEMENT, FEELING FOR A CLICK UNDER YOUR THUMB. If that fails, the second option is SUPINATE FULLY THEN FLEX THE ELBOW COMPLETELY, hand to shoulder. Then LET GO, STEP BACK AND OFFER A TOY ABOVE HEAD HEIGHT. Success is normal use within FIVE TO THIRTY MINUTES. THE RULES SAID OUT LOUD BEFORE THE FINDINGS ARRIVE: TWO FAILED ATTEMPTS, or ANY change on examination, means an X-RAY; an injury over twelve hours old can take a day or two to recover; NO SLING once he is using it. PREVENTION: lift under the arms, NOT by the hands, and no swinging — RECURRENCE IS ABOUT ONE IN FOUR while he is small. SAFETY-NET: back tomorrow, or to hospital, if he is not using it normally, if it swells, or if the hand goes pale or cold. VERSION B: 'tenderness and swelling — I AM CONCERNED ABOUT A FRACTURE AND WILL NOT ATTEMPT REDUCTION.' Paracetamol 15 mg/kg (about 180 mg at 12 kg) and a sling, ELBOW AP AND LATERAL today looking for a SUPRACONDYLAR FRACTURE, a POSTERIOR FAT PAD and the ANTERIOR HUMERAL LINE, pulse and hand rechecked before he leaves; normal film, consider reduction; fracture, orthopaedic registrar and PATS if transfer is needed.
plan: OPEN AT THE CHILD'S LEVEL, AND DISARM THE GUILT EARLY: 'hello, I'm Dr -, one of the GPs here. Sarah? And this is Oliver — hi mate.' [CROUCH, HANDS TO YOURSELF] 'I can see you're worried; we'll sort it out together.' → 'I THINK I'VE BROKEN HIS ARM' (tearful) → 'let's find out. Tell me exactly what happened — how did you lift him?' → 'he pulled towards the road, I yanked him back up by the hand and he screamed' → 'THAT'S THE MOST COMMON WAY THIS HAPPENS — NOT YOUR FAULT.' (Letting her guilt run the consultation costs you the history.)

THE INCIDENT AND THE ARM: 'when was it? Was there a POP OR CLICK? DID HE FALL, or bump his head?' → a little click, no fall. Then: 'since then, is he using it AT ALL, or not at all? Is he UPSET WHEN IT'S STILL, OR ONLY WHEN IT'S MOVED?' → 'not at all. He's happy if I leave it alone. HE SCREAMS IF I TRY TO BEND IT.' (Not asking about a fall or head knock is a named trap.)

RED FLAGS IN FOUR GROUPS — fifteen seconds that separate this from a supracondylar fracture: 'any swelling, redness or bruising around the elbow? Does it look different from the other side — any bend or deformity? DOES HE LET YOU TOUCH THE ELBOW? Has the hand changed colour — pale, blue or cold? Is he moving his fingers? Any fever?' → everything normal; he let her hold it in the car and is picking at his shoe with that hand. (Skipping the vascular and neurological questions because 'it's just a pulled elbow' is the trap.)

NAI SCREEN, NORMALISED, THEN THE WRAP-UP: 'questions I ask every family: who was with him, who's at home, how are things at home? Any previous injuries, fractures or hospital visits? Has this happened before?' Then: 'is he alert and himself — not drowsy or vomiting? Any medical problems, medicines, allergies? Immunisations up to date? And is there anything else worrying you?' → 'IS IT BROKEN? DOES HE NEED AN X-RAY?' → NOT A FLAT NO: 'if the examination is as I expect we usually don't need one — I'll explain why. IF ANYTHING DOESN'T FIT, WE WILL.'

ASK FOR THE EXAMINATION, NAMING THE PARTS — you get exactly what you ask for: 'Examiner, could I have general appearance and observations, then the right upper limb: INSPECTION for swelling, bruising or deformity; PALPATION FROM THE CLAVICLE through humerus, elbow and RADIAL HEAD, forearm and wrist; posture and tolerated movement; and DISTAL NEUROVASCULAR STATUS — RADIAL PULSE, capillary refill, hand colour and finger movement.' (Asking for 'an elbow examination' means the clavicle and the pulse never appear.)

EXPLAIN IN LAY WORDS, THEN ANSWER THE GUILT (see dx) → 'SO I DID THIS TO HIM' → 'thousands of children a year get this — a quirk of the joint until about five, NOT something you did wrong.' (Saying 'dislocated' on its own gets you 'DISLOCATED?! SHOULDN'T HE BE IN HOSPITAL?')

CONSENT AND WARN OF THE CRY: 'I can put it back right now — it takes a few seconds. I hold his elbow and turn his forearm in one quick movement. HE'LL PROBABLY CRY FOR A MOMENT, then within minutes to half an hour he should be using the arm normally. Painkillers usually aren't needed — THE MOVEMENT TAKES THE PAIN AWAY — but I can give paracetamol first if you'd prefer. Happy for me to go ahead?' → 'yes — can I hold him?' → 'please, on your lap, facing me.'

DEMONSTRATE THE MANOEUVRE, NARRATED TO THE EXAMINER (see dx) — thumb over the radial head, elbow at ninety, ONE SMOOTH HYPERPRONATION feeling for the click, then the supination-and-full-flexion alternative, then LET GO, STEP BACK AND OFFER A TOY ABOVE HEAD HEIGHT. → 'you feel a click; after a few minutes the child reaches for a toy with the right hand.' → [to Oliver] 'all done, mate. HIGH FIVE?'

THE RULES, PREVENTION AND THE SAFETY-NET — these are separate marks and candidates end at the click: 'had he not used it within half an hour I'd re-examine and TRY ONCE MORE; TWO FAILED ATTEMPTS, or any swelling or tenderness, means an X-RAY. NO SLING — once he's using it, let him. It can recur while he's small, ABOUT ONE IN FOUR, so LIFT HIM UNDER THE ARMS, NOT BY THE HANDS, and no swinging.' Then written information, and: 'come back, or go to hospital, if he isn't using it normally by tomorrow, if it swells, or if the hand goes pale or cold.' Then summarise and invite questions.

Normal film, consider reduction; fracture, orthopaedic registrar with PATS if transfer is needed.

VARIANT C — NO PULL REMEMBERED (about half of real cases): do NOT abandon the diagnosis, but widen the screen — fall, head knock, fever, and the NAI questions carry more weight. 'SHOULD I KEEP IT IN A SLING?' → 'no — once he's using it, let him.' If concerns are never asked, she volunteers in the last minute: 'WAS IT MY FAULT?' pefe: Role-player: Sarah, 31, part-time bookkeeper in Kadina, Oliver's mother. Oliver is 2, fully immunised, no medical history, allergies or medicines, NEVER IN HOSPITAL; lives with her and his father Tom, a farm mechanic — a stable, happy home. AN HOUR AGO he lunged towards the road, she had his RIGHT HAND and yanked him up off the ground; he screamed, cried a few minutes, settled, and has held the arm still since. SHE FELT A SMALL CLICK. NO fall, NO head knock. REGISTER: guilty and frightened, CONVINCED SHE HAS BROKEN HIS ARM and half expecting to be told off — tearful early, relaxing if the doctor is kind and clear. HIDDEN AGENDA: 'DID I DO THIS TO HIM?' and 'DOES HE NEED AN X-RAY?' — she asks the X-ray question herself at about three minutes if it has not been raised. Oliver is a doll on her lap: happy at rest, plays with the LEFT hand, screams ONLY if the elbow is moved.

HOW SHE PLAYS IT: tearful for the first minute; PUSH THE X-RAY QUESTION ONCE — 'wouldn't it be safer to just X-ray it?'; become emotional at 'SO I DID THIS TO HIM'; PROTEST IF THE ARM IS GRABBED WITHOUT EXPLANATION; and if concerns are never asked, volunteer 'was it my fault?' in the last minute. If told 'dislocated' with no explanation, ALARM: 'dislocated?! Shouldn't he be in hospital?' VERSION B: report puffiness and screaming on touch, and the examiner gives swelling and significant tenderness — THE DOCTOR MUST NOT DEMONSTRATE A REDUCTION.

Scored out of 20: WIPE and greets Oliver; exact mechanism; pop or click, fall, head knock; arm use — immediate, at all versus on and off, rest versus movement; swelling, bruising, deformity; 'DOES HE LET YOU TOUCH IT?'; hand colour and fingers; fever; NAI screen, normalised; alert, past history, medicines, allergies, immunisations; ASKS FOR CLAVICLE-TO-FINGERS EXAMINATION AND THE PULSE; names pulled elbow with a lay explanation and 'not your fault'; STATES X-RAY INDICATIONS BEFORE THE FINDINGS; consent and warns of the cry; THUMB ON THE RADIAL HEAD, correct manoeuvre, and the second manoeuvre; success in 5-30 minutes; the TWO-ATTEMPT RULE; prevention and recurrence; safety-net and written information; summary and invites questions.
Posture — Right arm PRONATED and SLIGHTLY FLEXED, held against the body
Version B — Swelling over the elbow with significant tenderness — otherwise as above. Do not attempt reduction
Version C — No pull remembered by the parent — about half of real cases have no recalled traction
After a successful reduction — You feel a CLICK; after a few minutes the child REACHES FOR A TOY with the right hand
What you must ask for — You get EXACTLY what you request — the clavicle and the radial pulse will NOT appear unless you name them
fails: ★ Attempting or demonstrating a reduction in Version B, where the elbow is tender and swollen
★ Being unable to describe the manoeuvre — 'I'd manipulate the elbow' is not an answer, and the thumb has to be somewhere specific
Skipping the vascular and neurological questions because 'it's just a pulled elbow'
Asking for 'an elbow examination' rather than clavicle to fingers with the radial pulse — you get exactly what you ask for

Letting her guilt run the consultation; saying 'dislocated' without explaining it is a small slip; a flat 'no' to the X-ray question; presenting paracetamol as mandatory when the reduction is the analgesic; and ending at the click, so the two-attempt rule, prevention and safety-net never happen

NO vitals given. History 4 minutes, examination findings from the examiner 2 minutes, explanation 2 minutes.

back.dx: VERSION A — TRANSIENT SYNOVITIS, AN IRRITABLE HIP, AS A PROVISIONAL, HIGHER-PROBABILITY DIAGNOSIS. To the mother: 'the lining of the hip joint has become inflamed, usually caused by a virus. THE KNEE PAIN IS ACTUALLY COMING FROM THE HIP; IN CHILDREN HIP PROBLEMS OFTEN SHOW UP AS KNEE PAIN.' THREE REASONS: he can still stand and walk even though he is limping; he had a cold two weeks ago; and on examination THE HIP WAS THE ONLY SORE THING, with a positive log roll. FIVE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH A REASON: SEPTIC ARTHRITIS OR OSTEOMYELITIS — no fever, well in himself, joint not hot or swollen, BUT IT IS THE ONE THAT CANNOT WAIT; PERTHES DISEASE — less likely because he still weight-bears and this followed a cold, BUT ONLY AN X-RAY EXCLUDES IT, so if it has not settled in two weeks we do one; BLOOD OR BONE CANCER — nothing points there today; FRACTURE OR INJURY; and CHILDHOOD ARTHRITIS. PLAN: rest, paracetamol 15 mg/kg or ibuprofen 10 mg/kg with food, no sport this week, REVIEW IN TWO DAYS, X-ray at two weeks if unresolved, and THE THREE-ITEM RETURN LIST — FEVER, CANNOT WEIGHT-BEAR AT ALL, or the leg becomes HOT, RED OR SWOLLEN. Growing pains do not cause a limp — say so if she raises it. VERSION B — PERTHES DISEASE. EXPLAIN THE X-RAY NORMAL SIDE FIRST: 'white is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air. This long bone is the thigh bone; at the top it has a rounded head that sits in the hip bone like A BALL IN A CUP. Look at the normal side first: the head is ROUND, like a ball. Now the other side: THE HEAD IS FLAT, IT HAS LOST ITS CURVE, and it doesn't match the other side.' Then: 'the head of the thigh bone is damaged because ITS BLOOD SUPPLY WAS CUT OFF FOR A TIME; we don't know why it happens, AND IT'S NOTHING YOU DID.' Never say sclerosis, epiphysis or avascular necrosis to a parent, and NEVER POINT AT THE ABNORMAL HIP FIRST. Then the same differential list, then referral to the children's orthopaedic service, no running or jumping, and pain relief.
plan: OPEN AND NORMALISE WHAT IS COMING: 'you must be Emma, and this is Jack? Hi Jack. How can I help you both today?' → limping since Saturday, now says his knee hurts → 'I can hear how worried you are, and A LIMP IN A CHILD IS SOMETHING I TAKE SERIOUSLY, so I'm going to ask quite a few questions, SOME ABOUT SERIOUS THINGS I ASK EVERY PARENT.' Then the two separate questions: 'CAN HE PUT ANY WEIGHT ON THE LEG AT ALL? IS HE STILL WALKING?' (Accepting 'limping' without asking about weight-bearing is the trap — the examiner is listening for both.)

THE LIMP AND THEN THE PAIN: constant or on and off, getting worse, morning versus evening, rest versus activity, anything that helps. Then: 'is he in any pain? WHERE EXACTLY — show me on your own leg. ANYWHERE ELSE? WHAT ABOUT THE HIP? The ankle? Out of ten? Dull ache or sharp? Does it travel anywhere? AND DOES IT WAKE HIM AT NIGHT?' → 'just his knee. He only says his knee.' (Do NOT argue that it is really the hip — note it and examine the hip. And do not skip night pain because the child looks well: it is the malignancy question.)

THE THREE RED-FLAG BOXES, IN ORDER: MSK first — swelling, redness, rash, stiffness. INFECTION — 'any fever or chills? Is the joint hot, red or swollen? Has he been unwell in himself?' MALIGNANCY — 'any weight loss? Lumps or bumps? Unusually tired or pale? Bruising easily?' → she goes slightly sharp: 'WHY, WHAT ARE YOU THINKING?' → 'these are questions I ask EVERY child with leg pain, to be sure I'm not missing something rare. NOTHING YOU'VE TOLD ME POINTS THAT WAY.' FRACTURE AND NAI — 'any falls, injuries or knocks? Does he play sport? HOW ARE THINGS AT HOME? And childcare — any problems or bullying?' → 'I'm not sure, he might have fallen at childcare, nobody said anything.' (That is NOT an admission and NOT a red flag on its own — it tests whether you ask the social questions calmly and without accusation.)

THE VIRAL QUESTION AND THE REST — number seven, but it must be reached: 'any recent flu-like illness, a cold, or a virus?' → 'yes, a cold about two weeks ago.' Then other joints and family arthritis (her mother's hand osteoarthritis is a distractor), rashes, tummy pain, diarrhoea or blood in the stool, waterworks, pregnancy and birth, THE SIX-WEEK CHECK, and the well-child wrap-up.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, IN A FIXED ORDER, TEMPERATURE FIRST: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, any rash? CAN HE BEAR WEIGHT, and if so I'd like to observe his gait. Vital signs: TEMPERATURE FIRST, then heart rate and blood pressure. May I see his growth chart? Then LOWER LIMB — HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE, comparing both sides: inspection for swelling, redness, deformity or abnormal posture; palpation for local warmth and tenderness; active and passive movement for pain and restricted range; TRUE LEG LENGTH measured and compared; SPECIAL TEST, THE LOG ROLL; and an abdominal examination, with a urine dipstick if there is time.' (Asking for 'a knee examination' gets you a normal knee and nothing else.)

DIAGNOSIS WITH THREE REASONS: 'Jack's knee is actually fine; THE SORENESS IS COMING FROM HIS HIP, and in children hip problems very often show up as knee pain. I think he MOST LIKELY has transient synovitis, sometimes called an irritable hip...' then the three reasons. → 'is it serious?' → 'usually not; it settles on its own in one to two weeks. BUT LET ME TELL YOU WHAT ELSE I CONSIDERED, BECAUSE SOME OF THOSE MATTER.'
FIVE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH A REASON (see dx), leading with septic arthritis as the one that cannot wait and naming the honest limit on Perthes — only an X-ray excludes it.

PLAN, SAFETY-NET, CONCERNS, SUMMARY: rest, paracetamol or ibuprofen with food, no soccer this week, REVIEW IN TWO DAYS, and 'come straight back, or go to the emergency department AT ANY HOUR, if he develops A FEVER, if he CAN'T PUT ANY WEIGHT ON THE LEG AT ALL, or if the leg becomes HOT, RED OR SWOLLEN.' Then ask what worried her → 'I thought it might be growing pains, or that he'd broken something' — and her hidden fear, a colleague's child with leukaemia → 'GROWING PAINS DON'T CAUSE A LIMP, so I wouldn't put it down to that.' Summarise and WRITE IT DOWN. (Closing without the return-immediately list is where the septic-joint mark is lost.)
