THE FEBRILE CHILD (the hard version of A) — examiner gives T 38.8 and a hip he will not let you move: 'I'M STOPPING HERE. A fever with a hip he won't let anyone move is AN INFECTION IN THE JOINT UNTIL WE PROVE OTHERWISE, and that can damage the joint WITHIN HOURS. He needs the emergency department TODAY for blood tests, an ultrasound and the bone doctors; I'M RINGING THEM NOW.' / THE PALE, TIRED CHILD — 'pale, tired and leg pain worse at night is a combination I NEVER LEAVE: we'll do a blood count TODAY, before anything else.' / THE STORY THAT DOES NOT FIT — a fall on Wednesday presenting Saturday with bruises on the back: 'whenever a child has an injury nobody saw, I ask every family the same questions, and I'll need to examine him all over. Because the injury doesn't quite fit the story, I'm also obliged to involve the child protection team; THAT'S A LEGAL DUTY FOR EVERY DOCTOR IN SOUTH AUSTRALIA, NOT A JUDGEMENT ABOUT YOU.' (CARL 13 14 78)

'DOES HE NEED AN X-RAY TODAY?' in Version A → 'not today: he's well, no fever, he can stand on it, and the story fits an irritable hip after a virus. An X-ray is the right test IF HE ISN'T BETTER IN TWO WEEKS, or sooner if anything changes.' pefe: Role-player (Version A): Emma Harper, 34, part-time bookkeeper; partner Dan is a plumber; daughter Mia is 2. Jack is 5, at childcare three days a week, plays Saturday soccer; no medicines, no allergies, fully immunised, normal pregnancy and birth, SIX-WEEK CHECK DONE. Her own mother has osteoarthritis of the hands — A DISTRACTOR, mentioned only if family history of arthritis is asked. HIDDEN AGENDA: she is frightened it is 'SOMETHING IN THE BONE' because a work colleague's child had leukaemia, and she half-wonders whether he fell at childcare and nobody told her. Worried but composed; she becomes slightly sharp — 'WHY, WHAT ARE YOU THINKING?' — when asked about weight loss and lumps, and softens if the doctor explains why they ask. She volunteers the leukaemia fear ONLY if asked what worries her, or in the last minute if never asked.

HOW SHE PLAYS IT: SAY 'KNEE' EVERY TIME, and only concede the hip if asked directly — and even then, 'he only ever says his knee'. NEVER VOLUNTEER THE COLD TWO WEEKS AGO; answer it only if asked about viral illness. 'I'M NOT SURE IF HE FELL AT CHILDCARE' is the answer to any injury question — DO NOT ELABORATE. If the doctor says 'definitely synovitis' or 'just a virus', ask 'BUT HOW DO YOU KNOW IT ISN'T SOMETHING IN THE BONE?' If they never give a safety-net, ask 'AND WHAT IF HE GETS WORSE TONIGHT?' in the final thirty seconds. IF THEY EXAMINE ONLY THE KNEE, DO NOT CORRECT THEM — the examiner reports normal knee findings and nothing else.

Mark them on: asked weight-bearing AND walking as separate questions; asked about the hip when she said knee; asked fever and chills, and REQUESTED TEMPERATURE FIRST in the examination; asked night pain, weight loss, lumps and bruising; asked home and childcare; asked recent viral illness; requested HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE plus leg length, log roll and abdomen; said 'MOST LIKELY' transient synovitis with reasons; NAMED AND EXCLUDED SEPTIC ARTHRITIS; named Perthes with the X-ray limit; gave at least three further differentials; gave the THREE-ITEM RETURN LIST and a review time; asked what worried her and addressed the leukaemia fear directly; and finished with a summary inside eight minutes.

back.dx: A SEIZURE CAUSED BY A HEAD INJURY — a MILD HEAD INJURY WITH RISK FACTORS. NAME IT IN PLAIN WORDS: 'a seizure is a burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain, and a knock to the head can set that off. The jerking of all four limbs, the eyes rolling and the drowsiness afterwards are what tell me it was a seizure.' THEN CATEGORISE IT, AND THIS IS THE SENTENCE THE STATION IS BUILT ON: 'we grade head injuries by HOW AWAKE AND ALERT a child is. Liam is FULLY ALERT, so this is a MILD head injury. But because he was KNOCKED OUT and then HAD A FIT, we count those as RISK FACTORS — things that make us more careful — so we call it A MILD HEAD INJURY WITH RISK FACTORS.' Calling it moderate because of the seizure is an automatic fail. THEN SAY WHAT YOU EXCLUDED: normal sugar, no fever, no medications, no previous seizures, normal examination — 'so I'm not finding any sign of bleeding inside the head or a neck injury RIGHT NOW.' AND WHEN SHE ASKS 'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING?': 'I CAN'T PROMISE THAT YET — THAT'S EXACTLY WHY WE WATCH HIM.' It is not epilepsy; it was a one-off fit triggered by the knock, though a small number of children have another fit in the first week. VERIFY MANAGEMENT: (1) OBSERVE AT LEAST FOUR HOURS with regular neurological observations — conscious level, pupils, strength — half-hourly for two hours then hourly; (2) IMAGING WITH THREE NAMED TRIGGERS, because a CT is radiation to a growing brain and most mild injuries do not need one — SCAN IF HE BECOMES DROWSY OR HARD TO WAKE, VOMITS REPEATEDLY, OR HIS HEADACHE WORSENS — and discuss him with the paediatric NEUROSURGEON so the decision is made together; (3) paracetamol 15 mg/kg for the headache, an antiemetic if needed, and the NECK PROTECTED until fully examined; (4) HOME ONLY IF HE STAYS WELL, with a WRITTEN SHEET OF WARNING SIGNS — repeated vomiting, worsening headache, hard to wake, confusion, another fit, weakness, or fluid from the nose or ears — A RESPONSIBLE ADULT OVERNIGHT, GP review in two to three days, and NO CONTACT SPORT UNTIL SYMPTOM-FREE AND CLEARED. 'Should I keep him awake tonight?' — no: let him sleep, check every few hours, and make sure he ROUSES NORMALLY. VERIFY
plan: STABILITY, GLUCOSE, THEN OPEN: 'may I confirm the primary survey is complete, and have his vitals, GCS and a BEDSIDE GLUCOSE?' → 5.6. Then: 'hello Lily, I'm Dr -. LIAM IS IN SAFE HANDS. Can you tell me what happened?' → 'he was tackled and went down head-first. He just lay there, and then he started shaking all over. I THOUGHT HE WAS DYING.' → ADDRESS IT AND EXPLAIN THE QUESTIONS: 'that sounds absolutely terrifying, and YOU DID THE RIGHT THING calling the ambulance. I'm going to ask a lot of questions — they help me work out HOW SERIOUS this is, and that decides what we do next.'

THE INCIDENT: 'when did this happen? Was it a DIRECT BLOW to the head, or a FALL ONTO HIS HEAD OR NECK? How hard, roughly — was he running at full pace? Any other injuries or pain anywhere else? ANY NECK PAIN?'

THE RED-FLAG BOX — twelve questions, and the two durations kept separate: 'when he hit his head, did he LOSE CONSCIOUSNESS COMPLETELY, or was he awake and aware? HOW LONG? And SEPARATELY, the shaking — were his arms and legs jerking? ALL FOUR LIMBS, or one side? Eyes rolling up? Tongue bite? Frothing? Did he wet himself? HOW LONG DID THE SHAKING LAST? Any vomiting since? Was he CONFUSED OR DROWSY when he woke — BETTER NOW OR WORSE? Any problems with vision, weakness, numbness, speech or walking? DOES HE REMEMBER what happened? Is he complaining of headache — IS IT GETTING WORSE? Any FLUID OR BLOOD FROM HIS NOSE OR EARS?' (Hearing 'seizure' and stopping is the trap: the marks are in the other ten.)

THE CAUSES OF THE SEIZURE — the half candidates drop: 'what was he doing just before? Did he complain of anything — feeling sick or dizzy — BEFORE the tackle? HAD HE MISSED ANY MEALS? Any fever or rash in the last few days? Is he on any medications, or could he have taken anything?' → guiltily: 'HE SKIPPED BREAKFAST — we were running late. DOES THAT MATTER?' → 'it can, because a low sugar can cause a fit — THAT'S WHY I CHECKED IT, AND IT'S NORMAL.' (Missed breakfast is planted: it is not the cause, but the examiner marks whether you asked AND whether you checked the glucose.)

BACKGROUND: 'any blood thinners, or does he bruise or bleed easily? Any seizures before? Any concerns about his development? HOW ARE THINGS AT HOME — who lives there, any stress? How's school, any bullying? Any family history, especially of seizures? Immunisations up to date?' (Nothing about non-accidental injury is planted here — you still ask about home.)

READ THE CARD ALOUD AND INTERPRET IT, THEN ADD: 'GCS 15, normal neurology, no neck tenderness, normal glucose. THAT PLACES LIAM IN THE MILD CATEGORY, and it excludes a current deficit and hypoglycaemia. I'd like to ADD: pupils and fundoscopy, a look at the scalp for a BOGGY SWELLING, BEHIND THE EARS and AROUND THE EYES for bruising, and a check of the EARDRUMS FOR BLOOD.' (Treating the card as the end of the examination is the trap — base-of-skull signs are the classic omission.)

NAME IT, CATEGORISE IT, SAY WHAT YOU EXCLUDED (see dx) → 'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING?' → 'I can't promise it isn't yet — and that's exactly why he's staying with us. But everything I can see is reassuring.'

THE PLAN, AND NEVER A BARE YES OR NO ON THE CT: four hours of observation with regular neurological checks; the THREE named scan triggers with the reason a CT is not automatic; the neurosurgeon informed; paracetamol and neck protection; then home only if he stays well, WITH THE WRITTEN WARNING SHEET, a responsible adult overnight, GP in two to three days, and no contact sport until cleared. → 'SHOULDN'T YOU JUST DO A SCAN?' → answer with the radiation reason and the three triggers. Then summarise and invite questions.

VERSION C — THE CARD SHOWS GCS 13 AND A RIGHT PUPIL 5 mm AND SLUGGISH: 'Lily, Liam's examination HAS CHANGED and I need to act quickly. He is less alert than he was and ONE PUPIL IS LARGER, which can mean PRESSURE INSIDE THE HEAD from bleeding. THIS IS NOW A MODERATE HEAD INJURY. He's going for a CT scan IMMEDIATELY, I'm calling the neurosurgeon and the retrieval team NOW, and we'll protect his airway and neck. I'll come back and explain everything as soon as he is safe.' (Continuing the history while the child deteriorates, or 'observe another hour', is the fail. Name MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.)

VERSION B — A 4-YEAR-OLD, 'FELL OFF THE COUCH', with a boggy scalp swelling and BRUISES OF DIFFERENT AGES: 'can I ask exactly what time that was, and who was with him?' [note the delay and who answers] 'I'd like to examine him fully, INCLUDING UNDRESSED, which is routine for any child with a head injury.' Then: 'I'm going to be straightforward with you. THE INJURIES I'M SEEING ARE MORE THAN I WOULD EXPECT FROM A FALL OFF A COUCH, and some of the bruises look older. Whenever we see that in a child, we have to make sure he is safe, and BY LAW I HAVE TO INVOLVE our child-protection team and the Child Abuse Report Line. I'm also arranging a CT scan of his head now, and he'll be admitted under the paediatric team.' In South Australia notification is MANDATORY — YOU NOTIFY ON REASONABLE SUSPICION, YOU DO NOT INVESTIGATE. Never accuse; never let the child leave; never discharge on 'observation' with a GCS of 14 and a boggy swelling. CARL 13 14 78.
pefe: Role-player: Lily, 38, part-time at the Wallaroo IGA; married to Ben, a grain farmer; daughter Ruby, 6. Liam is a healthy, sporty boy — no medicines, no allergies, immunisations up to date, normal development, NEVER HAD A FIT, and nobody in either family has epilepsy. SHE WATCHED THE TACKLE FROM THE SIDELINE: he went down head-first with another boy on top, LAY STILL FOR ABOUT A MINUTE, then ALL FOUR LIMBS JERKED AND HIS EYES ROLLED BACK FOR ABOUT A MINUTE. No tongue bite, no incontinence. Groggy and confused in the ambulance, clearer now; MILD STEADY HEADACHE, feels sick but has NOT vomited, no fluid from nose or ears, no neck pain, DOESN'T REMEMBER THE TACKLE. HE SKIPPED BREAKFAST because they were late. No fever, no rash, no medicines. Home is fine; he loves school.

REGISTER: frightened, a little guilty about the breakfast, and FIXED ON 'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING?'. She wants a scan AND wants to go home — both. If the doctor is calm and explains the four hours, she settles. IF THEY SAY 'HE'S FINE', PUSH: 'HOW DO YOU KNOW?' If concerns are never asked, at minute five volunteer: 'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING? CAN'T YOU JUST SCAN HIM?'

Score them on: vitals, GCS and glucose requested; concern addressed; mechanism asked with options; other injuries; neck; LOC AND DURATION; seizure features including all four limbs; vomiting; confused or drowsy; at least three deficit questions; amnesia; headache; fluid from nose or ears; warning before; MISSED MEALS; fever or rash; medications; blood thinners; previous seizures; development; home and school; family history; NAMES 'MILD WITH RISK FACTORS'; excludes other causes aloud; observe four hours with neurological observations; THREE CT TRIGGERS; neurosurgeon or senior involved; analgesia; written advice with a responsible adult and no sport; summary and invites questions. Numbers: GCS 14-15 mild, 9-13 moderate, 3-8 severe — OBSERVE 4 HOURS, neurological observations half-hourly for 2 hours then hourly — ANY loss of consciousness is a risk factor and OVER 5 MINUTES IS HIGH RISK — A SEIZURE LASTING OVER 5 MINUTES IS TREATED (midazolam 0.15 mg/kg, maximum 10 mg) — paracetamol 15 mg/kg — ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg — A FALL OVER 1 METRE IS A DANGEROUS MECHANISM — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, CARL 13 14 78.
Scalp — A small left temporal scalp haematoma, no laceration

What you must add aloud — Pupils and FUNDOSCOPY — the scalp for a BOGGY SWELLING — BEHIND THE EARS and AROUND THE EYES for bruising — and the EARDRUMS for blood. Base-of-skull signs are the classic omission

Version B — A 4-year-old, 'Fell off the couch': GCS 14, a boggy scalp swelling, and bruises on the back and upper arms of different ages

setting: HISTORY, EXPLANATION AND MANAGEMENT — GP clinic. THE CUE IS NON-VERBAL: the mother cradles a doll with THREE BRUISES ON THE FACE AND CHEEK, and NOBODY WILL POINT THEM OUT. If you do not look at the doll you will not find the case. Notice them, say nothing, and use them at the right moment. THE SECOND-COMMONEST REASON CANDIDATES FAIL IS FORGETTING THE ACUTE INJURY: a bruised, crying infant needs an INTRACRANIAL INJURY EXCLUDED TODAY, not deferred to child protection. Excluding the medical causes of crying is a SEPARATELY SCORED TASK — skipping it fails you even if you name the abuse.
stem: GP clinic, metropolitan Adelaide, late afternoon. A 4-MONTH-OLD BOY brought by his mother JENNY for EXCESSIVE CRYING. NO physical examination is given; the role-player holds a doll, cradled as she would hold her baby.

History about five minutes, then diagnosis and management in about three. 8 minutes. VERSION B (online): the same stem with WRITTEN examination findings replacing the doll — multiple bruises OF DIFFERING AGES on the cheeks, buttocks and inner thighs, child otherwise alert with normal vitals.

back.dx: SUSPECTED NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY in a 4-month-old presenting with excessive crying — facial bruising in an infant who is not yet rolling, a history of REPEATED DROPS by a partner who is NOT the biological father, arguing at home, increasing alcohol use, financial stress and a flat, exhausted mother. THE ORDER IS: ACUTE INJURY, THEN NOTIFY, THEN ED, THEN DOCUMENT. FIRST NAME WHAT YOU EXCLUDED, ALOUD AND TO HER: 'I was looking for causes of the crying — an infection like an ear or urine infection, a problem in the tummy such as reflux or a blockage — AND I HAVEN'T FOUND ANYTHING TO SUGGEST THOSE TODAY.' THEN RAISE IT WITHOUT THE WORD ABUSE FIRST: 'what I am concerned about is HIS SAFETY. You've told me about the falls, you've told me how hard things have been, and I CAN SEE BRUISES ON HIS CHEEK. Bruises like that in a baby who isn't yet rolling over are unusual, and I have to take them seriously. I'm worried about the possibility of a NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY — an injury that wasn't caused by an accident.' THEN THE RESCUE LINE, WORD FOR WORD: 'JENNY, I WOULD NEVER ACCUSE YOU OR YOUR PARTNER OF DOING SUCH A THING. I can see how overwhelming things have been for you. MY JOB IS SIMPLY TO MAKE SURE YOUR SON IS SAFE, and to make the safest decisions in his best interest. That is all this is.' THEN THE NOTIFICATION: 'I am LEGALLY REQUIRED to let the child protection service know. EVERY DOCTOR HAS TO DO THIS — it isn't a choice I'm making about you, and it isn't a punishment.' ANSWER 'WILL THEY TAKE MY BABY AWAY?' BEFORE SHE ASKS IT: no — what they do is A FULL ASSESSMENT; they talk with you, see him, speak with your family and look at what supports you need, and MOST OF THE TIME CHILDREN STAY WITH THEIR FAMILY with services in place. Do not guarantee an outcome: 'I can't promise you what they'll decide, but removal is NOT what a notification automatically means.' THEN THE PART CANDIDATES FORGET: 'because he has bruising to his face and he's been crying, I'm worried about AN INJURY OR BLEEDING INSIDE HIS HEAD. THAT HAS TO BE CHECKED TODAY, so I'm sending you both to the children's emergency department NOW' — ring ahead. THEN SUPPORT HER: normalise the frustration, give the SAFE-PLACE-AND-WALK-AWAY advice — put him down somewhere safe like his cot, leave the room, ring someone — offer the Parent Helpline and child health nurse, review her own mood, and screen for family violence. FINALLY DOCUMENT in her words and record where the bruises are. CARL 13 14 78, mandatory notifier, and the threshold is SUSPICION ON REASONABLE GROUNDS — YOU NOTIFY, YOU DO NOT INVESTIGATE.
plan: OBSERVATIONS, THEN AN OPENING THAT NAMES HER EXHAUSTION: 'could I have his observations, please?' Then: 'hello Jenny, I'm Dr -. You must be Jenny, and this must be the little man. I CAN SEE HE'S BEEN GIVING YOU A HARD TIME. Crying that goes on for hours is EXHAUSTING and it can be really OVERWHELMING. Is it alright if I ask a few questions so I can work out why he's crying, and then we'll make a plan together?' NOTE THE BRUISES AND SAY NOTHING YET.

THE CRYING, INCLUDING HER: 'when did it start? Constant or in episodes? Getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse? What have you been doing to settle him — AND HOW ARE YOU COPING WITH IT?' → three weeks, evenings worst, hours at a time, nothing works, 'I'M EXHAUSTED, HONESTLY.'

THE MEDICAL DIFFERENTIALS — A SEPARATELY SCORED TASK, so do not skip it even though you have seen the bruises. INFECTION: fever, cough or runny nose, ear pulling, crying with nappy changes or offensive urine, rash, feeding, unusual sleepiness. GI AND SURGICAL: 'any vomiting — ANY GREEN IN IT? Does he arch his back with feeds? Any blood or REDCURRANT-JELLY stool? Constipated? ANY LUMP IN THE GROIN OR SCROTUM? ANY HAIR WRAPPED ROUND A FINGER OR TOE? Any red, watery eye?' Then feeding, wet nappies and weight gain.

OPEN THE ACCIDENTAL DOOR AND DETAIL IT: 'has he had any falls, knocks or head injuries lately?' → 'my partner dropped him the other day while he was changing his nappy.' → 'THAT MUST HAVE BEEN FRIGHTENING. Tell me exactly what happened — how far did he fall, what did he land on, did he cry straight away, was he floppy, did he vomit or go drowsy afterwards?' → change table onto floorboards, screamed, seemed alright, SHE WASN'T IN THE ROOM.

THE PIVOT — one question, asked flatly: 'HAS ANYTHING LIKE THAT HAPPENED BEFORE?' → 'a couple of times, I think. He's dropped him three or four times now', delivered casually. DO NOT REACT VISIBLY. Keep your voice level and keep going.

THE HOUSEHOLD, ASKED NEUTRALLY: 'can I ask who lives at home with you? ... AND IS HE YOUR SON'S BIOLOGICAL FATHER? ... How are things between you two at the moment, and how is he coping with the crying?' → not the father, they separated before the birth, HE HAS BEEN ASKING ABOUT THAT, there is arguing, and he gets frustrated with the noise.

THE THIRD-PERSON QUESTION AND THE SAFETY SCREEN: 'Jenny, looking after a baby who cries for hours is really hard, and SOME PARENTS GET SO FRUSTRATED THAT THEY SHAKE OR SMACK THE BABY. Has that ever happened with you or your partner?' → a firm denial, and YOU STILL GET THE MARK FOR ASKING IT SAFELY. Then: 'how are things financially? HOW HAS YOUR OWN MOOD BEEN? Does anyone at home use alcohol or other drugs? Who supports you? And DO YOU EVER FEEL UNSAFE AT HOME?' → money tight, flat and crying a lot, he drinks more than he used to, and 'no, I'm fine' said quickly.

NAME WHAT YOU EXCLUDED, THEN RAISE THE CONCERN, THEN THE RESCUE LINE (see dx) → she pulls the doll closer and looks away: 'ARE YOU SAYING I DID THIS?' → SLOW DOWN, LOWER YOUR VOICE, AND DO NOT RETREAT FROM THE CONCERN. (Saying 'your son has child abuse', leading with the word abuse, arguing back when she becomes defensive, or DROPPING THE CONCERN ALTOGETHER WHEN SHE CRIES are the four ways this goes wrong.)

NOTIFICATION, AND ANSWER THE REMOVAL QUESTION BEFORE SHE ASKS IT (see dx), then THE ACUTE INJURY: 'there's something JUST AS IMPORTANT. Because he has bruising to his face and he's been crying, I'm worried about the possibility of an injury or BLEEDING INSIDE HIS HEAD. That has to be checked TODAY, so I'm sending you both to the children's emergency department NOW. They'll examine him, and they may do a scan. The child protection team can talk with you there too.' → 'today? Right now?' → 'yes, straight from here. I'LL RING AHEAD so they're expecting you.'

SUPPORT HER, SAFETY-NET, DOCUMENT, SUMMARISE: 'and I HAVEN'T FORGOTTEN YOU. What you're doing is exhausting, and it's normal to feel frustrated — THAT'S NOT A FAILING. If it ever gets to the point where you feel you can't cope, PUT HIM DOWN SOMEWHERE SAFE LIKE HIS COT, WALK OUT OF THE ROOM, AND RING SOMEONE.' Parent Helpline and child health nurse, review of her own mood, family-violence support. Then: 'I'll write down what you've told me in his notes, IN YOUR WORDS, and record where the bruises are.' Then the four-part summary and questions.

THE HARD MOMENTS: SHE STANDS UP ANGRY → 'Jenny, please — I'm not accusing you of anything, and I'm not going anywhere. Sit with me for one more minute. Everything I've said is about keeping him safe, and I want you to hear it FROM ME rather than from someone else later.' / SHE REFUSES ED → 'I'm worried enough about a possible head injury that I CAN'T LET THIS WAIT — that's a MEDICAL decision, separate from anything else we've discussed. Can I ring them now? If getting there is the problem, we'll sort that out.' / 'CAN'T WE JUST LEAVE IT?' → 'I'm afraid I can't. This is one of the few things doctors are LEGALLY OBLIGED to report — I don't have the discretion to keep it between us. What I can do is make sure they hear the full picture.' / 'WILL I LOSE HIM?' → 'there will be a record of the notification and the assessment. I can't promise you an outcome. What I can tell you is that they work with families far more often than they separate them, and ENGAGING WITH THEM IS THE SINGLE BEST THING YOU CAN DO.'

IF THE PARTNER IS IN THE ROOM: 'would it be alright if I speak with Jenny on her own for a few minutes? I DO THAT WITH EVERY PARENT — IT'S ROUTINE.' NEVER conduct the safeguarding or family-violence questions with the suspected person present. OLDER-CHILD VARIANT: 'children do get bruises when they're running around — usually on the SHINS, KNEES AND FOREHEAD. What's unusual here is that they're on BOTH EARS AND THE BUTTOCKS, and those aren't places children bruise by falling.' Numbers: CARL 13 14 78 (SA, 24 hours) — mandatory notifier — the threshold is SUSPICION ON REASONABLE GROUNDS — TEN-4-FACESp — ANY bruise in an infant under about five months — 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise' — ED work-up: skeletal survey, CT or MRI head, fundoscopy, FBC and coagulation screen — CaFHS 1300 733 606, Parent Helpline 1300 364 100, 1800RESPECT 1800 737 732.
pefe: Role-player: Jenny, 22, second-year university student; her partner is also a student and money is very tight. PROPS: HOLD A DOLL THROUGHOUT, cradled as a baby, WITH THREE BRUISES ON THE FACE AND CHEEK — DO NOT POINT THEM OUT, but hold it so they are visible. The baby is formula fed three-hourly, posits after feeds, no fever, vomiting, blood in stool, groin lump or rash; nappies fine; weighed once at the child health nurse a while ago and was fine; immunisations probably due. CRYING for three weeks, worst in the evenings, sometimes hours, nothing settles him. THE INJURY STORY: her partner dropped him from the change table onto floorboards a few days ago — he screamed, seemed fine after, AND SHE WASN'T IN THE ROOM. IF ASKED WHETHER IT HAS HAPPENED BEFORE, SAY YES — THREE OR FOUR TIMES — AND SAY IT CASUALLY, AS IF IT'S CLUMSINESS.

HOUSEHOLD: she lives with her partner, who is NOT the baby's biological father — she separated from the father before the birth, and her partner HAS RECENTLY BEEN ASKING WHETHER THE BABY IS HIS. There is arguing; he drinks more than he used to; he gets very frustrated with the crying. She is flat, tearful and exhausted, and says she feels safe at home — BUT ANSWERS THAT ONE QUICKLY AND MOVES ON. HIDDEN AGENDA: she is frightened of losing the baby, and will not raise it until the doctor mentions child protection.

HOW TO PLAY IT: volunteer the drop ONLY when asked about falls or injuries; volunteer the REPETITION only when asked whether it has happened before; volunteer the BIOLOGICAL-FATHER fact only when asked directly. THE MOMENT THE DOCTOR SAYS 'CHILD PROTECTION', BECOME DEFENSIVE — hide the doll behind your arm, stop making eye contact, answer in short sentences: 'we'd never do that, we're not those kind of people.' RECOVER ONLY if they use non-accusatory, safety-focused language. IF THE DOCTOR ACCUSES, INTERROGATES, OR ASKS 'DID YOUR PARTNER HIT HIM?', SHUT DOWN COMPLETELY and answer in one word. If the doctor does not answer it first, ask 'WILL THEY TAKE MY BABY AWAY?' — that is the marked moment. IF THE DOCTOR NEVER MENTIONS THE HEAD INJURY OR THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT, ASK AT THE END: 'SO WE JUST GO HOME?' If the doctor never asks how you are, DO NOT VOLUNTEER IT.
The cue — The doll has THREE VISIBLE BRUISES ON THE FACE AND CHEEK — nobody points them out, and if you never look at the doll you never find the case
Why the bruises matter — A 4-month-old is NOT YET ROLLING OVER — 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise'; ANY bruise in an infant under about five months is unusual
Older-child variant — Bruises on BOTH EARS and the BUTTOCKS — not the shins, knees and forehead where children bruise from falling
What ED will do — Skeletal survey — CT or MRI head — FUNDOSCOPY — full blood count and coagulation screen
fails: ★ Never looking at the doll, so the bruises — the entire cue — are never noticed
★ Notifying but not sending the child to the emergency department today: bruising plus crying means an intracranial injury must be excluded now

back.dx: CONJUGATED HYPERBILIRUBINAEMIA — 60 of 200, nearly a third — with BILIARY ATRESIA at the top of the list. EXPLAIN THE RESULT IN PLAIN WORDS FIRST: 'bilirubin is the yellow pigment made when old red blood cells break down; the liver processes it and sends it out in the bile into the bowel. Harry's total is 200, and 60 of that is the PROCESSED type. When the processed type builds up, IT MEANS IT CAN'T DRAIN OUT OF THE LIVER PROPERLY. The pale poos and the dark wee tell me exactly the same thing.' THEN NAME IT WITH THREE REASONS: biliary atresia, A BLOCKAGE OF THE TUBES THAT CARRY BILE FROM THE LIVER TO THE BOWEL — because of the PALE STOOLS AND DARK URINE, because HE ISN'T GAINING WEIGHT, and because of the HIGH PROCESSED FRACTION. Alternatives at that level: hepatitis, or a CHOLEDOCHAL CYST. THE FULL DIFFERENTIAL IN ORDER, CONJUGATED FIRST: infection in the liver or bloodstream, a blocked-duct cyst, GALACTOSAEMIA; then the unconjugated causes — HYPOTHYROIDISM, blood-group INCOMPATIBILITY, BRUISING from birth, and INADEQUATE INTAKE; and LAST, physiological and breast-milk jaundice, which are harmless and common BUT DO NOT CAUSE PALE STOOLS OR THIS BLOOD PATTERN. MANAGEMENT IN TWO PARTS: TREAT THE BILIRUBIN — plotted on a chart for his age, PHOTOTHERAPY if above the line, exchange transfusion in rare severe cases; and TREAT THE CAUSE — liver and CLOTTING bloods, ULTRASOUND of the liver and bile ducts, a bile-flow scan, and sometimes a LIVER BIOPSY. IF IT IS BILIARY ATRESIA, THE KASAI PROCEDURE connects the bowel directly to the liver so bile can drain, AND IT WORKS BEST BEFORE ABOUT SIXTY DAYS OF AGE — which is why you ring the children's hospital NOW and send them TODAY. SAY 'KEEP BREASTFEEDING — THERE IS NOTHING WRONG WITH YOUR MILK', and 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS'. SAFETY-NET: drowsy, feeding poorly, fever, or THE YELLOW REACHING PALMS AND SOLES. Referral without urgency — 'see the paediatrician next month' — is the fail.
plan: OBSERVATIONS FIRST, BECAUSE SEPSIS IS ON EVERY JAUNDICE LIST: 'may I have Harry's observations — temperature, heart rate, breathing rate, and is he alert?' → 36.8, 140, 40, alert. THE JAUNDICE AND THEN THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES THE STATION: 'when did you first notice it — WAS IT THERE ON THE FIRST DAY? Which parts are yellow — face, chest, tummy, arms, legs, PALMS? Constant, or coming and going? Getting worse?' Then: 'HAVE YOU NOTICED HIS WEE BEING DARK, OR HIS POOS PALE, WHITE OR CHALKY?' → 'yes — the wee's a dark yellow-brown, and the poos went pale, like putty, over the last three or four days.' → SAY IT BACK: 'THAT'S THE MOST IMPORTANT THING YOU'VE TOLD ME — it tells me the bile isn't getting through.'

PREGNANCY: 'any infections or fevers during the pregnancy? DID YOU HAVE THE GROUP B STREP SWAB — and antibiotics in labour? High blood sugar or blood pressure? Medicines, alcohol, drugs? Were your antenatal blood tests and scans normal — DO YOU KNOW YOUR BLOOD GROUP, AND WHETHER YOU HAD ANTIBODIES?' → all clear, GBS negative, A positive with no antibodies.

DELIVERY AND AFTER: 'term or early — how many weeks? Vaginal or caesarean? Long labour, FORCEPS OR VACUUM? ANY BRUISING OR A LUMP ON HIS HEAD? Did he need resuscitation? WAS THE HEEL-PRICK TEST DONE AND NORMAL? Vitamin K given?' → 39 weeks, normal delivery, no instruments, no bruising, cried straight away, heel-prick normal on day three, vitamin K given.

FEEDING IN SIX QUESTIONS, NOT ONE LINE: 'breast or formula? How many feeds in 24 hours? How long on each side? Any problems — pain, attachment, cracked nipples? DO YOU FEEL YOU HAVE ENOUGH MILK — is he satisfied? What was his birth weight, AND WHAT IS HE NOW — is he on his growth chart?' → breastfed eight times a day, fifteen minutes each side, no problems, satisfied — BUT 3.4 kg AT BIRTH AND 3.1 kg YESTERDAY, and the nurse said he should be climbing by now.

SEPSIS, WELL-BABY, THYROID AND FAMILY: 'any fever, or feeling hot or cold? Any rash? Is he alert and active, or drowsy and hard to wake? Fewer wet nappies? Any DRY SKIN, HOARSE CRY, CONSTIPATION? Thyroid problems in the family? ANYONE IN THE FAMILY JAUNDICED AS A BABY FOR WEEKS, or with a blood disorder like G6PD DEFICIENCY OR SPHEROCYTOSIS?' → no to all.

READ THE RESULT ALOUD IN PLAIN WORDS, THEN NAME IT WITH THREE REASONS (see dx) → 'IS IT MY FAULT? Did I do something in pregnancy?' → 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS.' Then the full differential list, conjugated first, with physiological and breast-milk jaundice explicitly at the bottom AND WHY.

MANAGEMENT — TREAT THE BILIRUBIN, TREAT THE CAUSE, REFER TODAY (see dx) → 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' → the Kasai, and THE SIXTY-DAY WINDOW, which is why you are ringing the hospital now. Then 'PLEASE KEEP BREASTFEEDING — there is nothing wrong with your milk', the safety-net, travel support, written information, and a four-line summary.

EXPLAIN THE FILMS KNEE FIRST: 'bone is white, soft tissue grey, air black. This is the knee — IT'S COMPLETELY NORMAL, so the knee isn't the problem. This is his hip. The hip is a BALL-AND-SOCKET joint. ON THE RIGHT, the round head of the thigh bone sits NEATLY ON TOP of its growth plate. ON THE LEFT, THE HEAD HAS SLIPPED OFF THE GROWTH PLATE — it's sitting lower and further back.' Never mention Klein's line or say 'epiphysis' to the mother without translating it. THEN NAME IT AND REMOVE THE BLAME: 'in growing boys, particularly around Ethan's size and during the growth spurt, THE GROWTH PLATE IS WEAKER and the head can slip off it. IT'S NOT BROKEN, AND BASKETBALL DIDN'T CAUSE IT — it just showed up during the game.' THEN THE TWO BULLET POINTS, IN THIS ORDER: (1) FROM NOW ETHAN MUST NOT WALK ON THAT LEG AT ALL — A WHEELCHAIR, NOT CRUTCHES — AND NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK until the surgeon has seen him; (2) PHONE THE CHILDREN'S ORTHOPAEDIC TEAM NOW, because this needs an operation soon to PIN THE HEAD OF THE BONE IN PLACE. THE REASON FOR THE RUSH: 'EVERY STEP RISKS THE HEAD SLIPPING FURTHER AND DAMAGING ITS BLOOD SUPPLY, which can permanently damage the joint — that's why it's a wheelchair and an ambulance rather than the car.' THE OTHER HIP: slips are bilateral in about one in five, and the second is often silent, so the surgeon may pin both. AFTERCARE: about six weeks on crutches, physiotherapy, NO BASKETBALL UNTIL THE SURGEON CLEARS HIM — never promise a return date — X-rays until the growth plates close, and weight management later, once he has recovered. UNSTABLE SLIP — cannot weight-bear at all: the risk to the blood supply is much higher (AVN up to about 50%), so he stays exactly where he is, ambulance and orthopaedic registrar now, nil by mouth, MedSTAR Kids if there is any delay. THE ATYPICAL PATIENT — younger, shorter, or bilateral: screen for an underlying cause with THYROID FUNCTION, RENAL FUNCTION AND A GROWTH-HORMONE ASSESSMENT alongside the orthopaedic management.

THE OTHER HIP, AFTERCARE, EXPECTATIONS: the screw across the growth plate; pinning the other side because it happens bilaterally in about one in five; six weeks of crutches, physiotherapy, X-rays until the growth plates close; weight worked on later; and NO BASKETBALL UNTIL THE SURGEON CLEARS HIM — never a return date. Then analgesia now, written information, and questions. → 'CAN HE PLAY IN THE FINALS?' asked at about 6:30 if you never asked what she was hoping for.

VARIANT — OSGOOD-SCHLATTER (one finding changed: tender swollen tibial tuberosity, hips normal, BMI 19, both films normal): 'with normal hips and normal films, this is OSGOOD-SCHLATTER DISEASE — the tendon from the kneecap pulls on the growing bump of bone below the knee, which gets inflamed with jumping. IT SETTLES AS HE FINISHES GROWING. Cut back the jumping sports for a few weeks, ice after activity, paracetamol or ibuprofen, and thigh stretches — HE CAN KEEP PLAYING AS PAIN ALLOWS. He stays exactly where he is; ambulance and orthopaedic registrar now, nothing to eat or drink, and MedSTAR Kids if there's any delay.'

VARIANT — 'WHAT ABOUT THE OTHER HIP?': 'slips are bilateral in about one in five, AND THE SECOND SLIP IS OFTEN SILENT, so I'd ask the surgeon about PROPHYLACTIC PINNING of the right hip — particularly if there's an endocrine cause or if follow-up from the country is difficult. If it isn't pinned, we watch it with X-rays and a low threshold for review.' / VARIANT — THE ATYPICAL PATIENT, 9 years old, short, both hips: 'he's younger and shorter than the typical patient and both hips are affected, so I'd SCREEN FOR AN UNDERLYING CAUSE — thyroid function, renal function, and a growth-hormone assessment through paediatric endocrinology — alongside the orthopaedic management.' / 'CAN HE JUST TAKE ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES AND REST?': 'I understand why that sounds reasonable, BUT REST DOESN'T PUT THE HEAD BACK OR STOP IT SLIPPING FURTHER — only pinning does, and DELAY IS WHAT DAMAGES THE JOINT.'
pefe: Role-player: Sharon, 44, works at the Kadina supermarket; partner Mick is a farm contractor; Ethan, 12, is the youngest of three. No family history of hip problems; Mick had a knee reconstruction from football. Ethan: normal birth, immunised, no medical problems, medicines or allergies; ALWAYS 'A BIG BOY', and he HAS PUT ON A LOT OF WEIGHT AND GROWN FAST IN THE LAST YEAR; basketball three times a week, FINALS IN THREE WEEKS. Two weeks ago his LEFT KNEE started aching during a game — NO FALL, NO TWIST — limping since and worse, and yesterday he could barely walk on it.

WHAT TO WITHHOLD: LEAD WITH THE KNEE AND BASKETBALL. DO NOT VOLUNTEER THE HIP, THE OUT-TOEING OR THE EARLIER EPISODE UNLESS ASKED DIRECTLY. The hip is sore too — only if asked about hip, groin or thigh. The foot points outward — only if asked about the foot or leg. A SORE HIP TWO MONTHS AGO THAT WENT AWAY — only if asked about previous episodes. No fever, no night pain, no weight loss, no other joints, no rash, no injuries; home and school fine; Ethan says no testicular pain, embarrassed. Ethan answers symptom questions in short sentences; Sharon fills in the background.

REGISTER: practical, slightly impatient; SHOCKED AND THEN TEARFUL WHEN 'OPERATION' IS SAID, recovering if the doctor explains why and what happens next. HIDDEN AGENDA: she wants him fit for the finals and is hoping for 'rest and physio' — ASK 'CAN HE PLAY IN THE FINALS?' at about 6:30 if the doctor never asks what she is hoping for. IF THE DOCTOR OFFERS CRUTCHES OR 'REST AND REVIEW', ACCEPT HAPPILY — THAT IS THE FAIL. If the doctor says wheelchair and ambulance, PUSH BACK ONCE: 'can't we just drive him?' If they say Klein's line or 'epiphysis' without explaining, LOOK BLANK: 'what does that mean?'

THE OTHER FOUR RECALLS: (B) 9 years, months of headache WITH WEIGHT LOSS, BLURRED VISION AND MORNING VOMITING. back.dx: VERSION A — TENSION-TYPE HEADACHE. 'It's a stress-related headache — we think it comes from tightening of the muscles around the head and neck.' FOUR REASONS: REAL STRESS AT SCHOOL WITH THE BULLYING; THE HEADACHES ONLY HAPPEN ON SCHOOL DAYS; SHE STILL PLAYS AND EATS THROUGH THEM; and the examination is COMPLETELY NORMAL. THEN ANSWER THE TUMOUR QUESTION WITH HER OWN NEGATIVES: 'I know your neighbour's diagnosis frightened you. I DON'T THINK THIS IS A BRAIN TUMOUR: no night headaches, no morning vomiting, no weight loss, no weakness or numbness, no vision problems, and THE BACK OF HER EYES AND HER NERVES ARE NORMAL.' Then at least four more differentials WITH REASONS — migraine (no nausea, no photophobia, no aura, no family history), infection of ears, throat, sinuses or teeth (no fever, all normal), and eye strain (vision fine). MANAGEMENT: 'A SCAN WOULDN'T HELP HER and isn't needed with a normal examination — AND I'LL TELL YOU WHAT WOULD CHANGE THAT.' The treatment IS the bullying: with permission, write to the SCHOOL'S WELLBEING LEADER; child psychologist or school counsellor; regular sleep, meals, water, less screen time; PARACETAMOL ONLY OCCASIONALLY, BECAUSE DAILY USE CAUSES HEADACHES ITSELF; a headache diary; review in two weeks; and return for night or morning headache, vomiting, vision change, weakness or drowsiness. VERSION B — A BRAIN TUMOUR: 'in Emily's case, I AM CONCERNED ABOUT THE POSSIBILITY OF A GROWTH IN THE BRAIN.' [PAUSE.] Reasons: weight loss, vision problems, MORNING VOMITING, and on examination HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE WITH A SLOW PULSE, which happens when the pressure around the brain is raised, plus SWELLING AT THE BACK OF THE EYES. 'I CAN'T TELL YOU TODAY WHAT IT IS OR HOW SERIOUS — ONLY A SCAN CAN. What I can promise is that this happens FAST': urgent MRI — better than CT and NO RADIATION — urgent neurosurgical and paediatric referral, and because the pulse and blood pressure show the pressure is already high, PHONE THE ON-CALL PAEDIATRICIAN NOW and transfer today. PATS covers travel; call 000 for drowsiness, repeated vomiting or a fit. VERSION C — BENIGN INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION, most likely TRIGGERED BY THE DOXYCYCLINE: STOP IT TODAY, urgent MRI FIRST because a growth must still be excluded, URGENT OPHTHALMOLOGY because untreated pressure on the optic nerve can damage sight, and paediatric neurology, who may do a lumbar puncture to measure the pressure ONCE THE SCAN IS CLEAR. VERSION D — MIGRAINE, and stress is the TRIGGER, NOT A SECOND DIAGNOSIS: ibuprofen 10 mg/kg at the first sign, water, a dark quiet room, a trigger diary, and a paediatrician about preventers if they become frequent. VERSION E — VIRAL URTI: redness WITHOUT PUS and a temperature of 38.3, so antibiotics will not shorten it but can cause diarrhoea and rashes; paracetamol 15 mg/kg four to six hourly, fluids, home from school, review at 48 hours, and return immediately for NECK STIFFNESS, A RASH THAT DOES NOT FADE UNDER A GLASS, drowsiness, floppiness, stopping drinking, or a climbing fever. E-HARD: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM or IV NOW, MedSTAR, AND DO NOT DELAY FOR A LUMBAR PUNCTURE.
plan: VITALS, OPEN QUESTION, AND ACKNOWLEDGE WITHOUT REASSURING: 'Examiner, before I start, could I have Emily's blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature?' Then: 'Karen, tell me about Emily's headaches from the beginning.' → six months, Panadol doesn't help, 'OUR NEIGHBOUR WAS JUST DIAGNOSED WITH A BRAIN TUMOUR AND I'M TERRIFIED IT'S THAT.' → 'I can hear how frightening that is, especially with what happened next door. I'M GOING TO ASK A LOT OF QUESTIONS, INCLUDING SOME SPECIFICALLY ABOUT THE SERIOUS CAUSES, AND THEN I'LL TELL YOU EXACTLY WHAT I THINK.' (Saying 'I'm sure it's nothing' before the red flags is the trap — she will come back with 'BUT HOW CAN YOU BE SURE?')

SICORA AND IMPACT: where, one side or both, out of ten, THROBBING OR DULL AND PRESSING, on and off or constant, GETTING WORSE, does it spread, what helps or worsens it, WORSE WHEN SHE RUNS AROUND, and how it affects her at home and at school. → right side mostly, five or six, mixed quality, not worsening, nothing helps, SHE CAN STILL PLAY, and she has MISSED NEARLY A DAY A WEEK OF SCHOOL. (Deciding migraine or tension from 'right-sided' and 'throbbing' is the trap — the recall deliberately mixes site and quality.)
The weekend question: 'Does she get the headaches on weekends and in the holidays too?' → [pause] 'No. Now that you say it — it's only ever school days.'

THE EIGHT RED FLAGS, IN WORDS, EVEN THOUGH SHE HAS SAID SIX MONTHS AND NOTHING SERIOUS: 'does it WAKE HER AT NIGHT? Headache or VOMITING FIRST THING IN THE MORNING? Worse when she COUGHS, SNEEZES OR STRAINS? Any BLURRED OR DOUBLE VISION? WEAKNESS in an arm or leg? NUMBNESS or pins and needles? Any change in her SCHOOL WORK, SPEECH OR WALKING? Any HEAD INJURY, even months ago? Losing weight, off her food, unusually tired, any lumps?' THEN MEDICATIONS BY NAME: 'is she on any regular medicines — anything for SKIN OR ACNE, VITAMIN A TREATMENTS, THE PILL, STEROIDS?'

THE MIGRAINE FIVE: 'when she has it — does she feel SICK OR VOMIT? Is she LIGHT AND NOISE SENSITIVE? Does she see SPARKLING OR FLASHING LIGHTS before it, or hear buzzing? Does ANYONE IN THE FAMILY get migraines? Does it come on with certain FOODS, MISSED MEALS, POOR SLEEP OR STRESS?'

HOME AND SCHOOL — AND GO DEEP ONCE BULLYING APPEARS: 'how are things at home? How does she get on with you and her brother? And school — any bullying that you know of? How is her school performance?' → [quieter] 'there's a group of girls. It started about six months ago — leaving her out, saying things. She cries about it. I'VE TOLD THE TEACHER, BUT NOTHING'S REALLY CHANGED.' → DO NOT MOVE ON: 'has it affected her mood, her sleep, her wanting to go to school? HAS SHE EVER SAID ANYTHING ABOUT HURTING HERSELF?' Then the quick sweep: fever, sore throat, earache, toothache, stiff neck, rash, neck lumps, SQUINTING AT THE BOARD, well-child questions, growth, development, immunisations, allergies.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, BY SYSTEM, WITH FUNDOSCOPY NAMED: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, dehydration, rash, limb posture, PTOSIS. Vital signs. Neurological examination: CRANIAL NERVES AND SPECIFICALLY FUNDOSCOPY; upper and lower limbs for power, sensation and reflexes. ENT: tympanic membranes, nose, throat for redness, swelling or exudate, SINUS TENDERNESS, teeth. NECK: STIFFNESS, pain on movement, lymph nodes. AND THE GROWTH CHART.' (Not saying 'fundoscopy' in Versions B and C is an automatic fail — and in C it is deliberately left off the card.)
One diagnosis, with reasons, then the tumour answered with negatives, then four more differentials (see dx). → 'So it's the bullying? Are you sure she doesn't need a scan?'

MANAGEMENT — AND FOR VERSION A THE TREATMENT IS THE BULLYING (see dx): the school wellbeing leader, psychology, sleep and meals, ANALGESIC CAUTION because daily paracetamol causes headaches itself, a diary, review in two weeks, and the red-flag safety-net. Then invite questions. (If the tumour question was never answered explicitly, she asks it at the end: 'SO YOU DON'T THINK IT'S A TUMOUR?')

[bilateral disc swelling] → 'most likely Chloe has BENIGN INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION — raised pressure of the fluid around the brain, MOST LIKELY TRIGGERED BY THE DOXYCYCLINE. (Labelling BIH without imaging first is the trap.) / VERSION D, the mother pushes for 'stress headache': 'I understand why stress seems the answer — IT'S THE TRIGGER, BUT THE HEADACHE ITSELF IS MIGRAINE: nausea, flashing lights, a throbbing pain SHE CAN'T PLAY THROUGH, and it runs in the family.' (Saying 'migraine AND tension' is the fail.)

VERSION E, the mother asks for antibiotics: 'I hear you — AND I'D GIVE ANTIBIOTICS IF THEY WOULD HELP. With redness and NO PUS, and a temperature of 38.3, this is almost certainly a virus; antibiotics won't shorten it but can cause diarrhoea and rashes. Paracetamol 15 mg/kg four to six hourly, fluids, home from school, review in 48 hours' — then the meningitis safety-net. E-HARD: 'a febrile child with headache, NECK STIFFNESS, A NON-BLANCHING RASH AND DROWSINESS is MENINGITIS until proven otherwise. IM or IV CEFTRIAXONE 50 mg/kg NOW, call MedSTAR, AND DO NOT DELAY FOR A LUMBAR PUNCTURE.' / VERSION B, examiner asks 'why not the emergency department?': 'the priority is SAME-DAY IMAGING AND NEUROSURGICAL REVIEW. Here, with a Cushing response and papilloedema, I'd speak to the on-call paediatrician NOW and transfer through MedSTAR rather than book an outpatient scan.'
pefe: Role-player (Version A): Karen, 38, dental receptionist in Wallaroo; married to Dave, a grain-truck driver; son Liam is 6. HOME IS SETTLED — no separation, no deaths, no moves. Emily is 9, bright and sensitive, in Year 4. THE HEADACHES: six months, right side mostly but sometimes both, five or six out of ten, sometimes throbbing and sometimes a squeezing pressure, ON AND OFF, NOT WORSENING, no spread, nothing helps, SHE CAN STILL PLAY. Never at night, never in the morning, no vomiting, not worse on coughing. No vision problems, weakness, numbness or injuries. Eating well, weight fine, no lumps, not tired. NO medications and no creams. No nausea, no light or noise sensitivity, no flashing lights, no family migraine. NEVER ON WEEKENDS OR HOLIDAYS — BUT YOU HAVE NOT NOTICED THIS UNTIL ASKED.

HIDDEN AGENDA: your neighbour, 44, was diagnosed with a brain tumour two months ago and you are convinced Emily has one — MENTION THE NEIGHBOUR IN YOUR OPENING, and if the doctor never comes back to it, ASK 'SO YOU DON'T THINK IT'S A TUMOUR?' at the end. THE REAL STORY: a group of girls has been excluding and taunting Emily since the start of the year; her marks have slipped, she dreads Mondays, she cries about it. You told the teacher once and nothing changed, AND YOU FEEL GUILTY THAT YOU DIDN'T PUSH HARDER. VOLUNTEER THIS ONLY WHEN ASKED ABOUT SCHOOL — if asked about home first, say home is fine. REGISTER: anxious and talkative, quick to relief; TALK FAST FOR THE FIRST THIRTY SECONDS; GO QUIET AND TEARFUL ON THE BULLYING; brighten quickly once reassured WITH REASONS. IF THE DOCTOR REASSURES BEFORE ASKING THE RED FLAGS, SAY ONCE: 'BUT HOW CAN YOU BE SURE?'

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION REQUEST AND EXPLANATION — regional ED. ONE STRUCTURE, AND ONE QUESTION DECIDES WHICH STATION YOU ARE IN: 'WHAT WAS HE DOING IN THE SECONDS JUST BEFORE — DID ANYTHING HURT OR UPSET HIM?' A jammed finger and a scream make it a BREATH-HOLDING SPELL; nothing at all makes it a BRUE. Work it BEFORE, DURING AND AFTER — that is how you tell it from a seizure. THREE AUTOMATIC FAILS: calling Version B a BRUE because the trigger was never asked; giving a diagnosis with NO differentials excluded; and reassuring that 'it was nothing' before the screen and the examination.
stem: Emergency department, regional South Australia. OLIVER, 7 MONTHS, brought in by his mother MARY after an EPISODE OF UNRESPONSIVENESS about thirty minutes ago. HE LOOKS WELL NOW. Vitals on request. History 4 minutes with a prompt, examination findings 2 minutes, then diagnosis and differentials 2 minutes.

VERSION A — BRUE: no fever, no seizure features, NO TRIGGER, no head injury, normal social history; he 'went floppy and blank for a few seconds, then came back to normal'. VERSION B — BREATH-HOLDING SPELL: getting into the car, HIS MOTHER JAMMED HIS FINGER IN THE DOOR, he cried, went pale, stopped breathing and went floppy for a few seconds, then suddenly back to normal and NOT drowsy.

back.dx: VERSION B — A BREATH-HOLDING SPELL. 'When a young child gets a SUDDEN PAIN OR FRIGHT, they cry hard, and AT THE END OF THE CRY THE BREATH CATCHES — they stop breathing for a few seconds, go pale or blue, and go limp. IT LOOKS DREADFUL, BUT IT IS A REFLEX. It is not dangerous, IT DOES NOT DAMAGE THE BRAIN, and children grow out of it by school age.' THEN NAME THE EXCLUSIONS, WHICH IS A SEPARATE MARK: not a seizure — no jerking, alert straight afterwards; not a serious infection — no fever, well; not a bowel problem, not a head injury, not a heart rhythm problem, not low sugar; and the examination is completely normal. VERSION A — A BRIEF RESOLVED UNEXPLAINED EVENT, AND TRANSLATE THE WORDS: 'BRIEF — it lasted seconds. RESOLVED — he came back to normal on his own. UNEXPLAINED — after asking about seizures, infection, bowel problems, injury, heart problems and low sugar, and examining him, WE HAVE FOUND NO CAUSE. It is a diagnosis we reach ONLY AFTER RULING OUT THE SERIOUS THINGS, and he is in the LOWEST-RISK GROUP.' MANAGEMENT. BREATH-HOLDING: check a FULL BLOOD COUNT AND IRON, because LOW IRON MAKES SPELLS MORE LIKELY AND IS EASY TO FIX; and if any spell is ever WITHOUT A TRIGGER, LASTS OVER A MINUTE, OR HAPPENS WITH EXERCISE, do an ECG. IF IT HAPPENS AGAIN: 'LAY HIM FLAT ON HIS SIDE, STAY CALM, DON'T SHAKE HIM, DON'T PUT ANYTHING IN HIS MOUTH — IT STOPS ITSELF.' Come back or call 000 if he does not recover within a minute, if there is fever or drowsiness, or if there is any jerking. LOWER-RISK BRUE: observation on a monitor for a couple of hours if she would like, TEACH INFANT CPR, review tomorrow — NO TESTS ARE NEEDED TODAY, AND HOME MONITORS ARE NOT RECOMMENDED. GP review in 48 hours and written information. AND ADDRESS THE GUILT IN ONE SENTENCE WHEN IT APPEARS, THEN KEEP GOING: 'that was an accident, and what happened next is A KNOWN REFLEX IN SOME CHILDREN, NOT AN INJURY TO HIS BRAIN — I'll explain it properly in a moment.' Do not stop the screen to comfort her at length.
plan: OBSERVATIONS BEFORE YOU SIT: 'could I have Oliver's observations first, please?' → all normal, alert. → 'ALL NORMAL AND HE LOOKS WELL — THAT'S REASSURING. Mary, I'm Dr -. THIS MUST HAVE BEEN TERRIFYING. Tell me what happened.' → 'he went floppy and wasn't breathing, his lips went blue. I THOUGHT HE WAS DEAD.' → 'I'm so sorry. He's well right now, which is the most important thing. I'm going to ask a lot of small questions about the seconds BEFORE, DURING AND AFTER, because that is how we work out what it was.'

DURING — timing and the three seizure questions: 'when did it happen, and how long did it last? First time? While he was floppy, WAS THERE ANY JERKING of his arms or legs? DID HIS EYES ROLL UP? DID HE WET OR SOIL HIMSELF?' → half an hour ago, about twenty seconds, never before, no jerking, no eye rolling, nappy dry.

DURING — colour, breathing, tone, choking: 'did he go PALE OR BLUE? Did his BREATHING STOP or change? FLOPPY OR STIFF? Any choking, gagging or coughing — anything he could have swallowed?' → Version B: white first, then bluish round the mouth, not breathing at all, FLOPPY LIKE A DOLL, no choking.

BEFORE — THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES THE STATION: 'what was he doing in the seconds just before? DID ANYTHING HURT OR UPSET HIM JUST BEFORE — A BUMP, A FRIGHT, A JAMMED FINGER?' → [tearful] 'I SHUT HIS FINGERS IN THE CAR DOOR. He screamed, and then it happened. IT'S MY FAULT.' → ONE SENTENCE OF COMFORT, THEN CONTINUE THE SCREEN: 'that was an accident, Mary, and what happened next is a known reflex in some children, NOT AN INJURY TO HIS BRAIN. I'll explain it properly in a moment. A few more questions first.' Then: missed feeds, fever, rash or illness this week, falls or bumps to the head, anything he could have got into.

AFTER: 'did he come back SUDDENLY OR GRADUALLY? Was he DROWSY afterwards, or straight back to himself?' → suddenly, smiling before she got him out of the seat, NOT DROWSY. (That answer is what separates this from a seizure with a postictal phase.)

THE EXCLUSION SCREEN, FAST: infection — cough, snuffles, vomiting, diarrhoea, sick contacts at home, immunisations. GI — GREEN VOMIT, BLOOD IN THE POO, DRAWING HIS LEGS UP, LUMPS IN THE TUMMY OR GROIN. SOCIAL — 'how are things at home? Who lives with you? WHO WAS WITH HIM? Any stress? Childcare?' CARDIAC AND FAMILY — 'HAS ANYONE IN THE FAMILY DIED SUDDENLY OR YOUNG, FAINTED WITH EXERCISE, OR BEEN DEAF FROM CHILDHOOD? Any seizures in the family?' Then well-baby and birth: alert and active, feeding, wet nappies, term, growth and development, medicines and allergies.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, BY SYSTEM: 'general appearance — alert, interactive? Hydration? Any rash, AND ANY BRUISING ANYWHERE, INCLUDING BEHIND THE EARS? Vitals including temperature. Growth chart. FONTANELLE, FUNDOSCOPY, PUPILS, TONE IN ALL FOUR LIMBS, symmetrical movement, REFLEXES. Chest — work of breathing, air entry, added sounds. HEART SOUNDS, MURMUR, FEMORAL PULSES. Abdomen — distension, mass, HERNIAL ORIFICES. And A BEDSIDE GLUCOSE.'

THE DIAGNOSIS, WITH THE EXCLUSIONS NAMED (see dx) → 'SO YOU'RE NOT GOING TO CHECK ANYTHING?' if you named the spell without the exclusion list, or 'WHAT DOES THAT MEAN?' if you said BRUE without translating the words.

PLAN AND SAFETY-NET: blood count and iron, the ECG triggers, and 'IF IT HAPPENS AGAIN: LAY HIM ON HIS SIDE, STAY CALM, DON'T SHAKE HIM, DON'T PUT ANYTHING IN HIS MOUTH — IT STOPS BY ITSELF.' Then the 000 criteria, GP review in two days, and the fact sheet. → 'I really thought I'd hurt him.' → 'YOU DIDN'T. YOU DID EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING BRINGING HIM IN.'

'Any bruising anywhere, INCLUDING BEHIND THE EARS — and fundoscopy.' / 'Has anyone in the family died suddenly or young, fainted with exercise, or been deaf from childhood?' / 'I would still assess tone, symmetry and reflexes.' / 'And a bedside glucose.'

HE STAYS FOR THE ECG BEFORE GOING HOME.'

HIGHER-RISK BRUE — a 6-week-old ex-31-weeker, NO trigger, 40 seconds: 'because he is UNDER TWO MONTHS and was BORN EARLY, this sits in the HIGHER-RISK group. Numbers: BRUE is under 12 months and under 1 minute — LOWER-RISK requires over 60 days old and 32 weeks or more gestation — breath-holding spells run from 6 months to 5 years — review at 24-48 hours — call 000 if over a minute, fever, drowsiness or jerking.
pefe: Role-player: Mary, 29, part-time bookkeeper; first child Oliver, 7 months; partner Dave, a plumber. Term normal birth, breastfed then formula, immunisations up to date, SITTING WITH SUPPORT, a happy baby. VERSION B: this morning, getting into the car, SHE SHUT HIS FINGERS IN THE DOOR. He screamed, went WHITE THEN BLUE ROUND THE MOUTH, stopped breathing, went limp 'LIKE A DOLL' for about twenty seconds, then SUDDENLY SMILED. NOT DROWSY. Snuffle last week, gone; nobody sick at home; NO family history of sudden death, seizures or deafness; no medicines in reach, no falls; home is stable. VERSION A is identical EXCEPT there was no door — he was in his bouncer, nothing happened, and she is NOT SURE ABOUT THE COLOUR.

Register: frightened and fast-talking at first; if the doctor asks the trigger question, go tearful and say 'It's my fault.' Hidden agenda: she is afraid it is epilepsy and that she caused brain damage — volunteer 'Is it epilepsy? Did I hurt his brain?' Late, if never asked about concerns. If the doctor starts without asking for observations, answer normally and mark it missing. If they say 'Breath-holding spell' without the exclusion list, ask 'So you're not going to check anything?' if they say 'Brue' without explaining the words, ask 'What does that mean?' if they say 'It's nothing' before examining, ask 'How can you know that?'

Score out of 18, 13 to pass: asked for observations first; empathy plus early reassurance about NOW; timing, duration, first episode; THREE SEIZURE QUESTIONS; colour, breathing, tone, choking; ASKED WHAT HAPPENED IMMEDIATELY BEFORE AND ABOUT A PAINFUL TRIGGER; missed feeds, fever or rash, head injury; SUDDEN VERSUS GRADUAL AND DROWSINESS; infection screen; GI screen; social history for non-accidental injury; FAMILY HISTORY OF SUDDEN DEATH OR SEIZURES; well-baby and birth; examination requested by system INCLUDING BRUISING, FUNDI, TONE AND REFLEXES, AND GLUCOSE; correct diagnosis for the version; NAMED THE EXCLUDED SERIOUS DIFFERENTIALS; what to do if it recurs and when to call 000; and follow-up with blood count and ferritin or 24-hour review, plus written information.
The bait — If told 'you can't do reflexes in a baby', say 'I WOULD STILL ASSESS TONE, SYMMETRY AND REFLEXES' and move on

TO THE FATHER: 'a hernia is A POUCH THAT BULGES OUT THROUGH A WEAK SPOT IN THE TUMMY WALL — in his case in the groin. A LOOP OF BOWEL HAS SLIPPED INTO THAT POUCH AND GOT STUCK, which is why he's in pain and vomiting. I'm confident because the lump CAN'T BE PUSHED BACK and IS PAINFUL TO TOUCH.' THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST HAS SIX OR SEVEN ITEMS AND 'INTUSSUSCEPTION, GASTRO, COLIC' SCORES TWO: intussusception, TESTICULAR TORSION, reflux disease, his brother's gastroenteritis, a urinary or ear infection or serious infection, food allergy, a head injury, and simple colic — each named and then excluded on the examination. MANAGEMENT, AND THE FIRST SENTENCE CARRIES THE MARK: 'HE NEEDS TO GO TO HOSPITAL NOW, BY AMBULANCE — THIS NEEDS AN OPERATION.' Then: the surgeons will give pain relief and sedation and TRY TO EASE THE BOWEL BACK; if it will not go, they OPERATE TODAY to free the bowel and close the pouch. NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK from now, A DRIP FOR FLUIDS, and analgesia. Ring the retrieval service and the children's surgeon NOW. AND ADDRESS THE GUILT UNASKED: 'THIS ISN'T SOMETHING YOU MISSED — IT'S HIDDEN UNDER A NAPPY.' DO NOT ATTEMPT REDUCTION YOURSELF IN THE ROOM, and if the father says he tried, ask him not to try again. If the bell goes after 'I'd give him paracetamol and some fluids', the task is failed — SURGERY FIRST, ALWAYS. STRANGULATION: red or dusky skin, a tense lump, a distended abdomen with absent bowel sounds and green vomit — 'this is a STRANGULATED hernia with obstruction: nil by mouth, NASOGASTRIC TUBE, intravenous fluid bolus, analgesia, and IMMEDIATE RETRIEVAL FOR EMERGENCY SURGERY.' TORSION: a sudden swollen, tender, HIGH-RIDING testis with no cough impulse — 'a twisted testicle until proven otherwise, a surgical emergency WITHIN HOURS, AND I WON'T DELAY FOR AN ULTRASOUND.' A REDUCIBLE HERNIA IN A WELL BABY: it still needs repair, referred today for surgery in the next few weeks, with return criteria if it will not go back, goes red, or he screams and vomits.
plan: VITALS, OPEN QUESTION, AND DO NOT ADOPT THE GASTRO THEORY: 'Examiner, the vital signs please.' Then: 'hello John, I'm Dr -. Tell me what's been happening with him.' → 'he's been screaming on and off since last night, he's thrown up twice, AND HIS BROTHER'S GOT A TUMMY BUG SO I FIGURED IT'S THAT — BUT HE'S NEVER SCREAMED LIKE THIS.' → 'it's frightening to watch. Let's work out what's going on together — I'll ask you some specific questions.' ('I figured it's that' is the bait: acknowledge it and keep all four buckets open.)

THE VOMIT, THEN THE SCREAMING: onset, how many, pattern, worsening, COLOUR, blood, volume, FORCEFUL, smell, better or worse with anything, position, relation to feeds. Then: 'when did the screaming start? HOW OFTEN? HOW LONG DOES EACH BOUT LAST? IS HE SETTLED IN BETWEEN? IS THIS THE FIRST TIME, OR HAS HE HAD CRYING SPELLS LIKE THIS FOR MONTHS?' → every fifteen to twenty minutes, a couple of minutes each, grizzly in between, NEVER LIKE THIS BEFORE. THE GI BUCKET AND THE GROIN QUESTION: 'when did he last open his bowels? Passing wind? Diarrhoea? ANY BLOOD IN THE NAPPY? Is his tummy bloated?' Then THE INTUSSUSCEPTION TRIO: 'does he GO PALE when he screams? Does he DRAW HIS KNEES UP? ANY RED JELLY-LIKE POO? Any cold recently? Any vaccinations in the last few weeks?' → he goes RED not white, he pulls his legs up, no jelly stool, a cold two weeks ago. Then the GORD block: vomiting only after feeds, refusing feeds, arching, WEIGHT GAIN, sleep.

THE INFECTION LADDER AND THE REST: fever and whether it was measured, anything given; travel; runny nose, cough, DROOLING; pulling at his ears; crying with nappy changes and offensive urine; rash. Then well-baby — alert or drowsy, drinking, wet nappies; falls or knocks to the head; how things are at home; new foods and a rash around the mouth; immunisations.

I'D NOW LIKE TO EXAMINE THE INGUINAL REGION AND THE SCROTUM — IS THERE ANY LUMP OR SWELLING?' → the photograph is handed over.

(Do NOT attempt reduction yourself in the room, and do NOT say 'strangulated' with no skin change or toxicity — say INCARCERATED, AT RISK OF STRANGULATION.)
The diagnosis with reasons, then six or seven grouped differentials (see dx) → 'Stuck? Is that dangerous?' / 'Can't you just push it back?' / 'Is it because I didn't notice?'

TWO THINGS FAIL THIS STATION: ASSESSING ONLY THE DOMAIN NAMED IN THE STEM, and SAYING 'GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY' WITHOUT A STRUCTURED LIST OF CAUSES AFTER IT. back.dx: GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY — significant delay in TWO OR MORE DOMAINS — CAUSE NOT YET KNOWN. DEFINE IT RATHER THAN ANNOUNCE IT: 'what we've found is called GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY. That means TWO OR MORE AREAS of her development are behind where we'd expect at nine months. For Ruby it's her MOVEMENT — she isn't sitting and she isn't holding her head — and her HAND SKILLS, because she isn't passing a toy between her hands, which most babies do by about seven months. HER UNDERSTANDING, HER HEARING AND HER SOCIAL SIDE ARE DOING WELL, which is genuinely good news.' THEN BE STRAIGHT: 'GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY DESCRIBES WHAT WE'RE SEEING, IT DOESN'T TELL US WHY, and today I can't tell you which cause applies to Ruby. What I can do is tell you the groups we look at.' THE SIX GROUPS, EACH WITH A NAMED EXAMPLE — THE HIGHEST-SCORING THIRTY SECONDS OF THE STATION: GENETIC, of which Down syndrome is the best known; HORMONE AND METABOLIC, where AN UNDERACTIVE THYROID IS THE IMPORTANT ONE BECAUSE IT IS TREATABLE; CONDITIONS AFFECTING THE BRAIN, mainly cerebral palsy; INJURY TO THE BRAIN from a difficult birth, an infection or a head injury — and nothing in her history suggests that; NERVE AND MUSCLE conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy or a muscle disease; and HEARING OR VISION PROBLEMS, WHICH CAN LOOK EXACTLY LIKE THIS — the hearing screen was normal but both get checked formally. THE HONEST ANSWER TO 'WILL SHE BE NORMAL? WILL SHE WALK?': 'I can't promise you that, AND I'D BE DOING YOU NO FAVOURS IF I PRETENDED OTHERWISE. What I can say is that WE'VE FOUND IT EARLY, that SOME OF THESE CAUSES ARE TREATABLE, and that THE THERAPY HELPS WHATEVER THE CAUSE TURNS OUT TO BE.' PLAN: formal HEARING AND VISION testing; bloods including THYROID FUNCTION, CREATINE KINASE and a CHROMOSOMAL MICROARRAY WITH FRAGILE X; MRI brain if the specialist thinks it is needed; referral to a developmental paediatrician; AND PHYSIOTHERAPY STARTED NOW — 'WE DON'T WAIT FOR A DIAGNOSIS TO START HELPING HER.' Safety-net: loss of any skill, a fit, or stopping feeding. Then: 'IS THERE ANYONE YOU'D LIKE WITH YOU AT THE NEXT APPOINTMENT?'
plan: OPEN AND ANNOUNCE THE STRUCTURE: 'you must be Ruby's mum — and hello Ruby. Tell me what's been worrying you.' → 'she's nine months and she still can't sit up. EVERYONE ELSE'S BABY WAS SITTING AGES AGO... I keep thinking I'm being silly.' → 'YOU'RE NOT BEING SILLY AT ALL — YOU KNOW HER BEST, and I'm glad you came. I'm going to ask about ALL the areas of her development, not just the sitting, then about her birth and her health, and then I'll tell you what I think.' (Diving straight into the sitting is the trap — announcing the structure buys her patience and shows the examiner where you are going.)

GROSS MOTOR, BACKWARDS DOWN THE LADDER: 'can she sit WITH support — with a cushion or your hands?' → 'no. NOT EVEN WITH SUPPORT.' 'When you pick her up, does she hold her head up, OR DOES IT FLOP?' → 'it flops.' 'Can she roll over? On her tummy, does she lift her head and shoulders? Does she take weight on her legs if you stand her up?' → rolls onto her side, doesn't push up, legs buckle. THEN SAY THE LEVEL: 'HEAD CONTROL IS A SKILL WE EXPECT AT AROUND FOUR MONTHS — that tells me how far behind she is.' (Accepting 'she can't sit' and moving on throws away every scored backward step.)

THE OTHER THREE DOMAINS — WHERE THE CASE IS WON. FINE MOTOR AND VISION: 'can she hold a toy AND PASS IT FROM ONE HAND TO THE OTHER? Does she reach? ARE HER HANDS OPEN, OR CLENCHED IN FISTS? DOES SHE USE ONE HAND MORE THAN THE OTHER? Does she follow you with her eyes?' → grabs but does not transfer, HANDS OFTEN FISTED, eyes fine. COMMUNICATION AND HEARING: 'is she babbling WITH TWO PARTS — ba-ba, ma-ma? Does she turn to your voice or startle at a loud noise? DID SHE PASS THE NEWBORN HEARING SCREEN? Does she wave?' → ma-ma-ma all day, turns, screen fine. SOCIAL: 'does she SHARE HER EXCITEMENT with you — smiling, laughing? Does she know you from a stranger? Does she like peekaboo?' → a happy baby who belly-laughs at her brother. (Never leaving the presenting domain is THE fail: two affected domains is what makes it GLOBAL, and if you do not ask, you cannot say it.)

RED FLAGS: 'HAS SHE LOST ANY SKILL SHE USED TO HAVE? Any fits or funny turns? IS HER HEAD GROWING ALONG ITS LINE ON THE CHART?' → never gone backwards, no fits, head always on the smaller side but the nurse was not worried.

BIRTH HISTORY IN THREE ZONES — a scored block, and where cerebral palsy is supported or excluded: PREGNANCY — illness, blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid, infections, medicines, alcohol, smoking, drugs, scans and growth. DELIVERY — term, mode, LONG LABOUR, FORCEPS OR VACUUM, birth weight, DID SHE BREATHE STRAIGHT AWAY OR NEED HELP. POSTNATAL — special care, JAUNDICE NEEDING TREATMENT, feeding problems, fits, infections, AND THE HEEL-PRICK TEST.

CAUSES BY SYSTEM, THEN THE MOTHER: BRAIN — meningitis, head injury, seizures. THYROID — constipated, dry skin, HOARSE OR UNUSUAL CRY. NERVE AND MUSCLE — 'DOES SHE FEEL FLOPPY WHEN YOU PICK HER UP, OR STIFF?' plus weak cry, feeding, coughing or choking → 'SHE IS FLOPPY — LIKE A RAG DOLL WHEN I LIFT HER' (only if asked). GENES AND SENSES — family history of a developmental or genetic condition, ARE YOU AND HER FATHER RELATED BY BLOOD, and any concerns about hearing or sight. Then well-baby, immunisations, AND 'HOW ARE YOU GOING — WHO'S AT HOME TO HELP?' (Forgetting the mother costs nothing to ask and is scored — and she is about to be told her baby has a developmental delay.)

READ THE CARD ALOUD AND INTERPRET IT, INCLUDING WHAT IS MISSING (see findings and dx) — low tone fitting the history, the head circumference trajectory, the absence of dysmorphism, and THE REFLEXES AS THE FINDING YOU MOST WANT AND DO NOT HAVE. (Reading the card silently throws away marks worth as much as the history.)

NAME IT, DEFINE IT, THEN THE SIX GROUPS (see dx) → 'SO WHAT'S CAUSING IT?' → 'I'm going to be straight with you...' → 'WILL SHE BE NORMAL? WILL SHE WALK?' → the honest answer, then the plan: hearing and vision, thyroid, CK and genetic testing, MRI if the specialist wants it, developmental paediatrician, AND PHYSIOTHERAPY STARTED NOW. Then the safety-net and 'is there anyone you'd like with you at the next appointment?'

pefe: Role-player: Kate, 29, at home with Ruby and her 3-year-old brother; Ruby's father works away on a fortnightly roster. RUBY, 9 MONTHS: cannot sit without support AND, IF ASKED, NOT EVEN WITH SUPPORT; her head flops when picked up; she rolls onto her side sometimes, does NOT push up on her arms, and her legs buckle if stood up. HANDS: she grabs a toy but DOES NOT PASS IT HAND TO HAND, and HER HANDS ARE OFTEN IN FISTS — SAY THIS ONLY IF ASKED. She follows with her eyes and uses both hands equally. TALKING AND HEARING FINE: ma-ma-ma all day, turns to your voice, passed the newborn screen. SOCIALLY LOVELY: smiles, belly-laughs at her brother, knows you from a stranger. NO loss of skills, NO fits; head 'always on the smaller side' but the nurse was not worried. BIRTH: 39 weeks, normal delivery, 3.2 kg, cried straight away, no special care, no jaundice treatment, normal heel-prick, uncomplicated pregnancy. HEALTH: no meningitis, head injury or seizures; not constipated, normal skin and cry; feeding, nappies and immunisations fine; no family history, parents not related.

HOW TO PLAY IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED, in one or two sentences, AND MAKE THE DOCTOR WORK FOR THE DETAIL. DO NOT VOLUNTEER THE FISTING OR THE 'RAG DOLL' LINE — the one word you offer if asked how she feels to hold is 'FLOPPY — LIKE A RAG DOLL.' IF THE DOCTOR ONLY ASKS ABOUT SITTING AND NEVER ABOUT HANDS, SPEECH OR SOCIAL, SAY NOTHING ABOUT THEM — THAT IS THE TRAP. REGISTER: apologetic and self-doubting at first ('I'm probably being silly'); open up if taken seriously; become QUIETLY FRUSTRATED if only asked about sitting; GET UPSET if told 'she'll grow out of it' — 'THAT'S WHAT EVERYONE KEEPS TELLING ME.' HIDDEN AGENDA: she has been told twice that she is worrying over nothing and is frightened of being dismissed again. PUSH ONCE: 'what's causing it?' and once more: 'WILL SHE BE NORMAL? WILL SHE WALK?' If they never ask how she is coping, do not raise it.

Score them on: introduced and gained permission; SAID THEY WOULD ASSESS ALL AREAS; sitting with support; head control; rolling, prone push-up and weight bearing; FINE MOTOR — TRANSFERRING A TOY (auto-fail if missed); fisting or one-sidedness; babble, response to voice and the hearing screen; SOCIAL INTERACTION AND SHARED ENJOYMENT; LOSS OF SKILLS; seizures; head growth; pregnancy history; delivery history INCLUDING RESUSCITATION; postnatal history INCLUDING THE HEEL-PRICK; screened brain, thyroid, muscle, genetic and sensory causes; family history and CONSANGUINITY; ASKED HOW THE MOTHER IS COPING; READ THE CARD ALOUD AND INTERPRETED IT INCLUDING THE MISSING REFLEXES; SAID GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY AND DEFINED IT; GAVE A STRUCTURED DIFFERENTIAL LIST BY GROUP (auto-fail if missed); avoided promising she would be normal or grow out of it; arranged hearing and vision testing; and REFERRED AND STARTED THERAPY WITHOUT WAITING FOR A DIAGNOSIS.

back.dx: A MILD ALLERGIC REACTION TO FOOD — most likely the peanut butter, WITH THE NEW SUNSCREEN ALSO ON THE LIST because it went on exactly where the rash is. SAY ONE LABEL AND PROVE IT WITH THE NEGATIVES: 'I want to tell you WHY I'M CONFIDENT IT'S THE MILD KIND. I WAS DELIBERATELY LOOKING FOR THE SIGNS OF A SEVERE REACTION: swelling of the tongue, tightness in the throat, a change in his voice, noisy or difficult breathing, drooling, dizziness or drowsiness. HE HAS NONE OF THEM. His oxygen level is normal, his blood pressure and heart rate are NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD, and his chest is clear. The rash itself is HIVES — itchy and dramatic-looking, but it settles.' WHEN HE ASKS 'ARE YOU SURE?', DO NOT HEDGE INTO ANAPHYLAXIS — ANSWER WITH THE PLAN: 'I'm confident on what I can see now, AND THAT IS EXACTLY WHY I WANT TO KEEP HIM HERE AND WATCH HIM rather than send him home.' MANAGEMENT IN FOUR PARTS: (1) an ANTIHISTAMINE — cetirizine — for the hives and the itch; (2) OBSERVE HIM HERE FOR A FEW HOURS with observations, because a reaction can occasionally come back; (3) NAMED WARNING SIGNS HANDED TO THE FATHER IN PLAIN WORDS — tongue swelling, voice change, noisy or difficult breathing, drooling, or going floppy or dizzy — tell us immediately; (4) NO PEANUT BUTTER AND NO MORE OF THAT SUNSCREEN until we know more. BEFORE HOME: an ALLERGY ACTION PLAN — not an anaphylaxis action plan — referral to the ALLERGY CLINIC for skin-prick or blood testing, WHICH IS WORTH DOING BECAUSE CAKE AND BISCUITS CAN CONTAIN EGG, MILK, WHEAT AND NUT ALL AT ONCE, and GP review. THE PEN, REFUSED WITH A REASON AND A PATHWAY, NEVER A FLAT NO: 'not from today, and let me explain why rather than just say no. ADRENALINE PENS ARE FOR CHILDREN WHO HAVE HAD A SEVERE REACTION, OR WHO THE ALLERGY SPECIALIST DECIDES ARE AT HIGH RISK. Ryan has had a mild one. IF I GAVE A PEN TO EVERY CHILD WITH A MILD REACTION, ALMOST EVERY FAMILY WOULD HAVE ONE AND IT WOULD STOP MEANING ANYTHING. What I'm doing instead is referring him to the allergy clinic, and if they find he needs one, THEY will prescribe it — that decision belongs with them, not with a single visit here.' AND THE HONEST CLOSE: 'I CAN'T PROMISE IT WILL NEVER HAPPEN AGAIN, BUT I CAN TELL YOU EXACTLY WHAT TO DO IF IT DOES.'
plan: WIPE, ACKNOWLEDGE, SIGNPOST — before any questions: 'I'm Dr -, one of the emergency doctors. Are you Ryan's dad? I CAN SEE THE RASH AND I CAN SEE YOU'RE WORRIED — YOU DID THE RIGHT THING BRINGING HIM STRAIGHT IN. I'm going to ask some questions, then examine him, then tell you what I think.' → he interrupts once, early: 'IS IT SERIOUS?' → answer it properly by promising an answer in a couple of minutes; answering with a diagnosis before examining gets 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW ALREADY?'

THE RASH, WITH THE INTERVAL PINNED IN MINUTES: 'when did he have breakfast, AND HOW LONG AFTER THAT DID THE RASH COME UP? Is it spreading? WHEREABOUTS ON HIS FACE — AROUND THE EYES, OR THE LIPS? Is it raised or flat? Itchy or painful?' → fifteen to twenty minutes later, cheeks then chest, raised and bumpy, very itchy. ('On his face' is NOT an answer — accepting it means you never establish that THE LIPS ARE SPARED.)

THE SIX RED FLAGS, SIGNPOSTED AS A BLOCK — the scored block, and the examiner is counting: 'I'm going to run through a short list of specific things I need to check for. JUST YES OR NO. Any swelling of his LIPS OR TONGUE? Any DROOLING, or trouble swallowing his saliva? Any NOISY BREATHING — a wheeze, or a harsh sound breathing in? Any DIFFICULTY BREATHING or shortness of breath? Has his VOICE OR CRY CHANGED — gone hoarse? Any NAUSEA OR VOMITING? Has he been DIZZY, FLOPPY OR DROWSY, or passed out?' → all negative. (Asking three of six and moving on is the fail; asking them as a named block is what makes it audible as a SYSTEM rather than luck. And if you ask 'any other symptoms?' as one vague question, the father answers 'no'.)

THE TRIGGER HUNT — and say out loud that you are not assuming the food: 'what exactly did he eat? WAS THAT THE FIRST TIME HE'S HAD IT? Any new medicine recently, EVEN ONE DOSE? Any chance of an insect bite or sting? ANYTHING NEW ON HIS SKIN — SOAP, BODY WASH, CREAM, SUNSCREEN? Has this ever happened before?' → toast with peanut butter, FIRST TIME, no medicines, no stings — 'OH — I DID PUT A NEW SUNSCREEN ON HIM THIS MORNING, ON HIS FACE AND HIS CHEST.' → 'that's useful, thank you — IT WENT ON EXACTLY WHERE THE RASH IS, SO IT GOES ON MY LIST TOO.'

ATOPY AND FAMILY — a distractor to note, not to escalate on: family food allergy or anaphylaxis; asthma, eczema or hay fever in him or the family; normally well, medicines, immunisations, behaving normally. → bronchiolitis as a baby, mother has hay fever, sister has asthma. → note that it SLIGHTLY RAISES HIS BACKGROUND RISK, and DO NOT let it change your severity label.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, IN ORDER: 'general appearance and level of consciousness — alert or drowsy? ANY AUDIBLE STRIDOR OR WHEEZE? FULL VITAL SIGNS PLEASE, INCLUDING OXYGEN SATURATION. Is there a rash, and IS IT RAISED WITH WELL-DEFINED MARGINS? Any swelling of the lips or tongue? Any hoarseness? Respiratory examination — air entry equal, added sounds? Heart sounds and murmurs? Abdomen — any tenderness?' Then INTERPRET: 'thank you — AND THOSE OBSERVATIONS ARE NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD.' (Announcing shock because the blood pressure is not 120/80 is a named fail.)

ONE LABEL, PROVED WITH NAMED NEGATIVES (see dx) → 'SO IT'S NOT THE SERIOUS KIND? But it looks so bad — are you sure? MY FRIEND'S SON HAD SOMETHING LIKE THIS AND HE STOPPED BREATHING.' → answer with the plan, not with a hedge.

THE FOUR-PART MANAGEMENT, THE PEN REFUSED WITH A REASON AND A PATHWAY, AND THE ALLERGY ACTION PLAN (see dx) → 'SHOULD HE HAVE ONE OF THOSE EPIPENS? A boy at his school carries one.' → the scripted refusal. Then the specific red flags handed to him in plain words, the observation period, the clinic referral and GP review, and 'how does that sound?'
