back.dx: IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA — BUT THAT IS THE RESULT, NOT THE DIAGNOSIS. THE CAUSE IS TWO THINGS TOGETHER: (1) EXCESSIVE COW'S MILK — 'cow's milk is A POOR SOURCE OF IRON — there is almost none in it. And drinking SEVEN OR EIGHT GLASSES A DAY FILLS HIM UP, so he isn't hungry for solid food. It's good for protein and calcium, but it isn't giving him iron AND IT'S CROWDING OUT THE FOOD THAT WOULD'; and (2) LOW IRON IN THE SOLIDS — 'biscuits and chips have NO IRON in them either. Some foods are much higher in iron, RED MEAT ESPECIALLY, and I couldn't find any red meat in his diet.' THEN THE TEN-SECOND DIFFERENTIAL SENTENCE: 'I did also consider other causes of low iron — BLOOD LOSS, and ABSORPTION PROBLEMS such as COELIAC DISEASE or A COW'S MILK ALLERGY — but there's nothing in his history to suggest those.' EXPLAIN THE RESULTS IN SIXTY SECONDS, FOUR NUMBERS, ONE SENTENCE EACH: 'red blood cells carry oxygen using HAEMOGLOBIN, and the main building block of haemoglobin is IRON. His HAEMOGLOBIN is low. The MCV — THE SIZE of the red cells — is low, so they're smaller than they should be. The MCH and MCHC — HOW MUCH HAEMOGLOBIN IS INSIDE EACH CELL — are also low. And his FERRITIN, WHICH IS HIS BODY'S IRON STORE, is low as well.' MANAGEMENT IN TWO COMPONENTS, AND ONE ALONE IS A FAIL. FIX THE DEFICIT: ORAL IRON SYRUP, 3-6 mg/kg/day elemental VERIFY, with the side effects given up front — CONSTIPATION, BLACK STOOLS WHICH ARE HARMLESS, and TOOTH STAINING, so USE A STRAW AND BRUSH AFTERWARDS; better absorbed WITH ORANGE JUICE OR VITAMIN C AND NOT WITH MILK; REPEAT THE BLOOD TEST IN A MONTH, because if the haemoglobin is not rising he may not be absorbing it; and CONTINUE AT LEAST THREE MONTHS AFTER THE COUNT IS NORMAL to refill the stores. FIX THE SOURCE: 'this matters just as much, OTHERWISE THE STORES EMPTY AGAIN IN SIX MONTHS. CUT THE COW'S MILK BACK TO ONE OR TWO GLASSES A DAY — I'M NOT ASKING YOU TO STOP IT. And I need IRON-RICH SOLIDS, RED MEAT PARTICULARLY, plus variety and fewer biscuits and chips' — with A DIETITIAN, because diet advice for a toddler is genuinely hard. AND NO BLAME: 'a toddler who loves his bottle is completely normal, and THIS IS ONE OF THE COMMONEST PROBLEMS WE SEE. It's very fixable.' IRON IN CHILDREN IS ORAL — offering an infusion or a transfusion here is wrong. VERSION B — COELIAC: 'his bowel is SENSITIVE — NOT EXACTLY ALLERGIC — to a protein called GLUTEN, found in wheat, barley, rye and often oats. That sensitivity DAMAGES THE LINING OF THE BOWEL, so he can't absorb iron and other nutrients — which explains BOTH the greasy stools AND the low iron. Your sister having it fits, BECAUSE IT RUNS IN FAMILIES.' THEN THE GLUTEN RULE: 'PLEASE KEEP GLUTEN IN HIS DIET — DON'T TAKE IT OUT YET.' Coeliac serology is ANTI-tTG ANTIBODY WITH A TOTAL IgA; if positive, paediatric gastroenterology for a SMALL BOWEL BIOPSY; and ONLY WHEN CONFIRMED does the lifelong gluten-free diet start, with a dietitian.
plan: CLOSE THE FLU IN ONE QUESTION: 'your colleague arranged a blood test when you were here last week — the results are back and I'd like to go through them with you. FIRST, JUST TO CHECK: HAS HE RECOVERED FROM THAT CHEST INFECTION?' → 'yes, completely.' → 'good, we can set that aside.' (Keep asking about fever, cough and sore throat and the role-player will keep saying he is better — every one of those questions is a wasted second and signals you have not recognised the case.)

THE PALLOR AND ANAEMIA SYMPTOMS: 'does he look pale to you? When did you first notice it? Has it got worse? Would you say he's tired, or looks tired? DOES HE GET SHORT OF BREATH OR STRUGGLE WHEN HE'S ACTIVE?'

BOX 1 — INTAKE, THE HEART OF THE STATION. Open first: 'PLEASE DESCRIBE HIS DIET FOR ME' and let her talk. Then: 'have you started solids? Are you giving him A VARIETY of solids, INCLUDING RED MEAT? Is he drinking cow's milk?' → 'yes — A FEW GLASSES A DAY.' → THE QUESTION THAT UNLOCKS THE STATION, ASKED UNHURRIED: 'HOW MANY GLASSES IS A FEW?' → 'um... SEVEN OR EIGHT, PROBABLY. He asks for the bottle all day.' Then: 'any rash around his mouth after cow's milk?' (If you ask 'is his diet healthy?' she answers 'yes, he eats well' — MAKE HER ANSWER ABOUT SOLIDS AND RED MEAT.)
BOX 2 — LOSS: 'has he had any bleeding episodes recently? Any recent surgery? ANY BLOOD IN HIS STOOLS?' → no to all.

BOX 3 — ABSORPTION, ASKED IN EVERY VERSION: 'have you noticed GREASY STOOLS — ONES THAT STICK TO THE PAN, FLOAT ON THE WATER, HARD TO FLUSH? Any rash? Any diarrhoea or blood in the stool?' — and in an older child, TUMMY PAIN, JOINT PAINS, MOUTH ULCERS, LIMPING — then 'ANY FAMILY HISTORY OF ANAEMIA, COELIAC DISEASE OR INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE?' (Thirty seconds, and in the five-year-old it IS the entire diagnosis.)

WELL CHILD, GROWTH, DEVELOPMENT: alert and active, eating, drinking, passing urine; happy with growth and weight gain; concerns about development or behaviour; birth, immunisations, medications, allergies.

THE RESULTS IN SIXTY SECONDS — FOUR NUMBERS, ONE SENTENCE EACH (see dx), with the page turned so she can see. → 'WHAT ABOUT THE OTHER NUMBERS?' → 'THEY WERE ALL NORMAL — THE RED CELLS ARE THE PART THAT MATTERS TODAY.' (If you are explaining white cells, platelets or reticulocytes, the examiner will ask what you were explaining.)

THE CONDITION, THEN THE TWO CAUSES, THEN THE DIFFERENTIAL SENTENCE (see dx) → 'HAVE I BEEN DOING SOMETHING WRONG? He just loves his bottle, I couldn't stop him.' → 'NOT AT ALL — a toddler who loves his bottle is completely normal, and this is one of the commonest problems we see. IT'S VERY FIXABLE.' (Do not let the explanation become an accusation.)

MANAGEMENT IN TWO COMPONENTS — and one alone is a fail (see dx): the iron syrup with dose, side effects, absorption advice, the one-month recheck and the three-month continuation; THEN the diet, the milk cut to one or two glasses WITHOUT STOPPING IT, red meat and variety, and a dietitian. → 'HE'LL SCREAM IF I TAKE THE BOTTLE AWAY' → you are not taking it away, you are cutting it back.

pefe: Role-player: Emma, 29, mother of Jack, 18 months. He had a CHEST INFECTION TEN DAYS AGO AND IS COMPLETELY BETTER. The doctor noticed he LOOKED PALE and did a blood test. FEEDING: breastfed to six months, then formula; COW'S MILK SINCE TWELVE MONTHS — SEVEN OR EIGHT GLASSES A DAY, BUT YOU FIRST SAY 'A FEW GLASSES' AND ONLY GIVE THE NUMBER IF ASKED DIRECTLY. REFUSES SOLIDS; eats biscuits and chips; WILL NOT EAT RED MEAT. No rash around the mouth. NEGATIVES: no bleeding, no surgery, no blood in stool, bowels normal, NO greasy stools, no family history of anaemia, coeliac or bowel disease. Growth fine on the chart, immunised, no medicines or allergies, A BIT GRIZZLY LATELY. REGISTER: cooperative, SLIGHTLY GUILTY. HIDDEN AGENDA: 'HAVE I DONE SOMETHING WRONG?' — raised after the cause is explained.

How to play it: say 'A few glasses' and stop — give 'Seven or eight' only if asked how many. If asked 'Is his diet healthy?', answer 'Yes, he eats well' — make them ask about solids and red meat. If the doctor asks flu questions, keep saying 'He's completely better' — do not help them. If they never ask about red meat, ask at the end: 'So is it just the milk?' if they offer only iron and no diet advice, ask 'So the medicine fixes it?' and mark them down. Version B, the five-year-old: answer yes to greasy stools that stick, float and are hard to flush, and say your sister has coeliac disease — only when asked.

Score them on: CLOSED THE INFECTION IN ONE QUESTION; pallor timing and anaemia symptoms; an OPEN diet question; solids and variety; RED MEAT BY NAME; QUANTIFIED THE COW'S MILK; rash around the mouth; the LOSS box; the COELIAC AND INFLAMMATORY BOWEL box; family history; growth, development and behaviour; FOUR NUMBERS EXPLAINED IN SIXTY SECONDS OR LESS; BOTH CAUSES NAMED; iron dose plus side effects plus follow-up plus duration; MILK CUT TO ONE OR TWO GLASSES plus iron-rich solids plus a dietitian; and NO BLAME. FAIL IF: they chased the flu, accepted 'a few', gave one cause, gave one treatment, or told a coeliac family to stop gluten.

Ask them all, audibly, so the examiner can tick them: IRON, THALASSAEMIA, LOSS, MALABSORPTION, HAEMOLYSIS, MALIGNANCY. And in VERSION B, WHERE ONLY PALLOR AND A BIG SPLEEN ARE GIVEN, 'DEFINITELY SPHEROCYTOSIS' IS A FAIL SENTENCE — you cannot confirm it without a blood test TODAY.
stem: VERSION A: general practice, regional South Australia. A 5-YEAR-OLD BOY brought in by his father, who is worried that THE CHILD LOOKS PALE. History five minutes, then a card is given, then diagnosis and differentials.

THE VERSION A CARD: PALLOR — SPLENOMEGALY — Hb LOW — RETICULOCYTE COUNT INCREASED — BLOOD FILM: SPHEROCYTES SEEN — BILIRUBIN INCREASED. VERSION B (current format): the same stem, but the card gives ONLY 'the child is pale, there is splenomegaly, NO INVESTIGATIONS AVAILABLE' — and the third task adds WHAT YOU WOULD DO NEXT.

IRON: describe his diet, DOES HE EAT RED MEAT, cow's milk AND HOW MUCH. THALASSAEMIA: family history of anaemia or thalassaemia, AND MAY I ASK YOUR FAMILY'S ETHNIC BACKGROUND. back.dx: HEREDITARY SPHEROCYTOSIS. EXPLAIN IT IN SIXTY SECONDS, THREE MOVES, AND DRAW IT: 'in the blood there are red cells that carry oxygen. NORMALLY THEY'RE SHAPED LIKE A DOUGHNUT. In your son's blood film we saw that many are SHAPED LIKE A SPHERE — A BALL. Those round cells CAN'T SQUEEZE THROUGH THE TINY BLOOD VESSELS IN THE SPLEEN, so they get trapped and broken down there — WHICH IS WHY THE SPLEEN IS ENLARGED, AND WHY HE LOOKED YELLOW AFTER HIS COLD. To keep up, THE BONE MARROW PUMPS OUT YOUNG, IMMATURE RED CELLS CALLED RETICULOCYTES — and we can see a high number of those. Overall the HAEMOGLOBIN, the oxygen-carrying part, is LOW — THAT IS ANAEMIA.' SHAPE, SPLEEN, RETICULOCYTES — three moves, and no white cells or platelets. THE DIAGNOSIS WITH ITS REASONS: pale and tired; WENT YELLOW AFTER A COLD; spleen enlarged; SPHERE-SHAPED CELLS ON THE FILM; young red cells high; AND THE GRANDFATHER'S SPLENECTOMY, BECAUSE IT RUNS IN FAMILIES. THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH A REASON FOR BEING LESS LIKELY: IRON DEFICIENCY — his diet is good; THALASSAEMIA — no family history, and the film doesn't fit; BLEEDING — none; ABSORPTION problems like coeliac — bowels normal; OTHER HAEMOLYTIC conditions such as G6PD DEFICIENCY; LEUKAEMIA — no weight loss, lumps, bruising or fevers, and no abnormal white cells on the film; and B12 OR FOLATE DEFICIENCY. NEXT STEPS: blood tests TODAY — full blood count, film, reticulocytes, breakdown markers and a DAT — then a specific test for spherocytosis; referral to paediatric haematology; A DAILY FOLIC ACID TABLET; checking the family; and THE SAFETY-NET THAT MATTERS: 'urgent review if he becomes SUDDENLY VERY PALE OR UNWELL AFTER A VIRAL ILLNESS, because HIS MARROW CAN BRIEFLY STOP — THAT'S AN EMERGENCY.' VERSION B, WHERE ONLY PALLOR AND SPLENOMEGALY ARE GIVEN: 'THREE THINGS ARE AT THE TOP OF MY LIST, AND I WANT TO BE HONEST THAT I CAN'T CONFIRM ANY OF THEM WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST. Most likely SPHEROCYTOSIS, because of the paleness, the yellow episode and your father-in-law's history. I also have to consider other conditions where red cells break down, like G6PD DEFICIENCY. And A CANCER OF THE BLOOD, LEUKAEMIA — though he has had no weight loss, lumps, bruising or fevers, WHICH MAKES IT LESS LIKELY. BECAUSE THE SPLEEN IS ENLARGED I WANT THE BLOOD TEST DONE TODAY, and I'll speak to the children's hospital.' THE ORDER OF THE THREE DOES NOT MATTER; LEAVING ONE OUT DOES. AND WHEN HE ASKS 'IS IT CANCER?': 'no — I LOOKED FOR THAT SPECIFICALLY, and nothing on the history or the film points to it. This is a manageable, inherited condition.'
plan: ACKNOWLEDGE, THEN TIMING AND SYMPTOMS: 'paleness is definitely something we need to look into properly, and I'm glad you came. When did you first notice it? Is it there all the time? Getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse?' Then: 'is he tired, or does he look tired? DOES HE GET PUFFED OR STRUGGLE WHEN HE RUNS AROUND WITH OTHER CHILDREN?' → two months, constant, slightly worse, tired and puffed on the trampoline. (Listen here for 'HE LOOKED YELLOWISH AFTER A COLD LAST MONTH' — if you never follow it up under haemolysis, the examiner notes it.)

GROUP 1, IRON: 'can you describe his diet? DOES HE EAT RED MEAT? Does he drink cow's milk — HOW MUCH?' (Ask 'how's his diet?' alone and he answers 'healthy' — you get the detail only by asking specifically.) GROUP 2, THALASSAEMIA: 'any family history of anaemia or thalassaemia? MAY I ASK YOUR FAMILY'S ETHNIC BACKGROUND?' → 'MY FATHER-IN-LAW HAD HIS SPLEEN OUT AS A YOUNG MAN — something with his blood.' → 'thank you, that's useful' — AND KEEP GOING. (Closing on the splenectomy and stopping the remaining groups is the fail — the marks are in the groups.)

GROUP 3, LOSS: 'any recent surgery? Regular medications? Any bleeding — nosebleeds, blood in stool or urine?' GROUP 4, MALABSORPTION: 'GREASY STOOLS THAT STICK, FLOAT, OR ARE HARD TO FLUSH? Rashes? Diarrhoea? Blood in the stool? JOINT PAIN OR MOUTH ULCERS? Family history of coeliac disease or bowel inflammation?'

GROUP 5, HAEMOLYSIS — and this is where the opening clue gets captured: 'HAS HE EVER HAD A YELLOW TINGE TO HIS SKIN OR EYES? DARK URINE? Any new medicines, OR BROAD BEANS? ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WITH JAUNDICE, GALLSTONES, OR THEIR SPLEEN REMOVED?' → yellow eyes after the cold, dark urine for two days, no new medicines, no broad beans.

GROUP 6, MALIGNANCY — and skipping it leaves leukaemia unscreened: 'has he lost weight — are you happy with his growth? Appetite? ANY LUMPS OR BUMPS? NIGHT SWEATS? EASY BRUISING, BONE OR LEG PAIN, FEVERS?' → all negative. Then the leftovers: alert and active, eating, drinking, passing urine; birth, immunisations, medical problems, medicines, allergies.

THE CARD, THEN THE EXPLANATION IN SIXTY SECONDS — SHAPE, SPLEEN, RETICULOCYTES — with a doughnut and a ball drawn for him (see dx). (Going past sixty seconds steals the time you need for the differentials, and explaining white cells or platelets wastes it.)
THE DIAGNOSIS WITH ITS REASONS, THEN EVERY DIFFERENTIAL WITH A REASON FOR BEING LESS LIKELY (see dx). → 'SO WHAT'S IT CALLED?' → spherocytosis, inherited, which fits the grandfather.

NEXT STEPS AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'IS IT CANCER?' → 'no — I LOOKED FOR THAT SPECIFICALLY, and nothing on the history or the film points to it.' → 'WILL HE NEED HIS SPLEEN OUT LIKE HIS GRANDFATHER?' → that is a specialist decision, generally deferred until after about six years of age and with vaccination first. pefe: Role-player: Mark, 38, electrician, father of Oliver, 5. OLIVER: pale for TWO MONTHS — the teacher and his wife noticed — always present, slightly worse; tired, GETS PUFFED ON THE TRAMPOLINE. GOOD EATER — red meat two or three nights a week, one glass of milk. AFTER A COLD LAST MONTH HIS EYES WENT YELLOW AND HIS URINE WAS DARK FOR TWO DAYS. Bowels normal. No surgery, medicines, bleeding, rashes, ulcers or joint pain. NO weight loss, growing well, no lumps, sweats, bruising, bone pain or fever. Normal birth, immunised, no allergies. FAMILY: HIS FATHER-IN-LAW HAD HIS SPLEEN REMOVED AS A YOUNG MAN 'FOR A BLOOD THING'; Scottish-Irish background. REGISTER: practical, slightly anxious. HIDDEN AGENDA: 'IS IT CANCER?' — asked after the diagnosis, or earlier if the doctor mentions leukaemia without softening it.

How to play it: volunteer the yellow-after-a-cold line only under haemolysis questions — or in the opener if the doctor asks an open question and then waits. Volunteer the splenectomy only when asked about family history of anaemia or blood conditions. Answer 'Healthy' to 'How's his diet?' — give the meat and milk detail only if asked specifically. If the doctor closes on spherocytosis after the family history and stops asking groups, ask 'Is that it?' and mark them down. Version B: the examiner gives pallor and splenomegaly only — if the doctor says 'Definitely spherocytosis', ask 'How do you know?'

Score them on: acknowledged the concern; timing and anaemia symptoms; IRON — red meat AND milk quantity; THALASSAEMIA — family history and ethnicity; LOSS — surgery, medicines, bleeding; MALABSORPTION — greasy stools and the bowel questions; HAEMOLYSIS — jaundice, dark urine, triggers and family history; MALIGNANCY — weight, lumps, bruising, fever; well-child and BINDSMA leftovers; EXPLAINED SHAPE, SPLEEN AND RETICULOCYTES IN SIXTY SECONDS OR LESS; diagnosis with reasons; DIFFERENTIALS EACH WITH A REASON; and in Version B, 'NEEDS CONFIRMATION TODAY'. FAIL IF: they gave the diagnosis before completing the six groups, never screened for malignancy, or said 'definitely' in Version B.
The opening clue — 'He looked yellowish for a few days after a cold last month' — often volunteered early, and if you don't follow it up under haemolysis the examiner notes it
Under haemolysis — YELLOW EYES AFTER THE COLD AND DARK URINE FOR TWO DAYS — no new medicines, NO broad beans
The family history — HIS FATHER-IN-LAW HAD HIS SPLEEN OUT AS A YOUNG MAN, 'SOMETHING WITH HIS BLOOD' — given when you ask about family history of anaemia or blood conditions
Iron group — GOOD EATER — red meat two or three nights a week, ONE glass of milk. Ask 'how's his diet?' and he just says HEALTHY
Loss and malabsorption — ALL NEGATIVE — no surgery, medicines or bleeding; bowels normal; no rashes, ulcers or joint pain

Malignancy screen — ALL NEGATIVE — no weight loss, growing well, no lumps, no night sweats, NO BRUISING, no bone pain, NO FEVERS. Skipping these leaves leukaemia unscreened, and in Version B that is the difference between 'less likely' and 'cannot comment'
Ethnicity — Australian, Scottish and Irish — which argues against thalassaemia
fails: ★ Closing on the grandfather's splenectomy and stopping the remaining groups — the marks are in the six groups
★ Saying 'definitely spherocytosis' in Version B, where only pallor and splenomegaly are given
Never screening for malignancy — no weight loss, lumps, bruising, bone pain or fever questions leaves leukaemia unscreened
Hearing 'he went yellow after a cold' in the opening and never recapturing it under haemolysis

back.dx: BENIGN FAMILIAL SHORT STATURE, with CONSTITUTIONAL GROWTH DELAY as the alternative. EXPLAIN IN THIS ORDER. (1) NAME IT: 'the most likely explanation is BENIGN FAMILIAL SHORT STATURE — BENIGN MEANING THERE IS NO DISEASE BEHIND IT.' (2) THE ARITHMETIC: 'a child usually ends up near THE AVERAGE OF HER PARENTS' HEIGHTS, CORRECTED FOR BEING A GIRL. For you two that is ABOUT 148 TO 149 CENTIMETRES, give or take eight either way. Amelia is tracking toward that — AND SHE'S BEEN ON THE SAME LINE SINCE SHE WAS FIVE, which is reassuring: SHE'S GROWING AT A NORMAL RATE, JUST ON A LOW LINE.' (3) THE ALTERNATIVE: 'CONSTITUTIONAL GROWTH DELAY — a TEMPORARY delay, where growth and puberty both come late AND SHE CATCHES UP to her expected height.' (4) NAME THE TEST: 'to tell those two apart we do AN X-RAY OF HER HAND AND WRIST to measure her BONE AGE. IF IT MATCHES HER AGE IT'S THE FAMILIAL PATTERN; IF IT'S BEHIND, THERE IS CATCH-UP TO COME.' (5) LIST THE EXCLUSIONS: bowel conditions like coeliac and inflammatory bowel disease, lung conditions like cystic fibrosis, THYROID AND GROWTH HORMONE problems, poor nutrition, and rarer causes including blood cancers, kidney disease and genetic conditions — 'nothing points to any of them, but I'll confirm with blood tests.' (6) SAFETY-NET AND FOLLOW-UP: RE-MEASURE IN SIX MONTHS, because THE GROWTH RATE TELLS YOU MORE THAN ANY SINGLE MEASUREMENT; return sooner for MORNING HEADACHES OR VOMITING, VISUAL CHANGE, tummy symptoms, weight loss, or if she seems to stop growing. AND THE KARYOTYPE, WITH THE REASON: 'I don't think she has TURNER SYNDROME — she has none of the usual features. BUT IT'S THE ONE CONDITION WHERE BEING SHORT CAN BE THE ONLY SIGN, AND IT'S TREATABLE, SO WE TEST EVERY GIRL WITH UNEXPLAINED SHORT STATURE rather than only the ones who look like they have it.' Also write to the school about the netball and the teasing — THAT PART MATTERS TOO. VERSION B — PALE FLOATING STOOLS AND TUMMY PAIN: that changes the thinking to COELIAC DISEASE, 'common, OFTEN SILENT APART FROM POOR GROWTH, and completely manageable once we know' — coeliac antibodies WITH A TOTAL IgA, AND KEEP HER EATING GLUTEN UNTIL THE TESTS ARE DONE. VERSION C — FALLING CENTILES from the 50th to the 3rd over two years: 'what concerns me most ISN'T WHERE SHE SITS TODAY — IT'S THAT SHE HAS FALLEN ACROSS THE LINES. A child who has always been small is usually normal; A CHILD WHO IS DROPPING ACROSS THE LINES HAS SOMETHING SLOWING HER DOWN.' And if HEIGHT FALLS WHILE WEIGHT RISES, that points to A HORMONE CAUSE — hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency or excess steroid — because IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT MALNUTRITION AND BOWEL DISEASE DO. VERSION D — THE MOTHER ASKING FOR GROWTH HORMONE: it is a specialist treatment for PARTICULAR DIAGNOSES with strict funding criteria, NOT for healthy short children growing normally for their family. VERIFY
plan: OPEN AND UNPACK 'SMALLER': 'tell me what you've noticed.' → 'she looks smaller than all of her classmates.' → 'WHEN YOU SAY SMALLER — DO YOU MEAN SHORTER, OR SMALLER ALL OVER, LIGHTER AND THINNER AS WELL?' → 'shorter. SHE EATS LIKE A HORSE.' (Accepting 'smaller' without unpacking it is the first trap: height alone and height-plus-weight are two different differentials.)

THE TIMELINE AND THE IMPACT: 'HAS SHE ALWAYS BEEN THE SMALLEST, or have you only noticed it recently?' → always, since reception. Then: 'and HOW IS IT AFFECTING HER — at home and at school? IS ANYONE TEASING HER?' → 'THEY CALL HER SHORTY. She says she doesn't mind but SHE'S STOPPED WANTING TO GO TO NETBALL.' AND SPEAK TO AMELIA: 'do you mind being the shortest, or is it mostly Mum who worries about it?' (Skipping the impact drops a scored item, and it is usually why the family came.)

THE BENIGN DIFFERENTIAL: 'CAN I ASK HOW TALL YOU ARE, AND HOW TALL HER FATHER IS? WAS EITHER OF YOU A LATE DEVELOPER, growing later than your friends?' → 150 and 160, neither a late developer. Then: 'any concerns about her weight, now or in the past? AND HAS SHE SHOWN ANY SIGNS OF PUBERTY — any breast development, or hair under her arms or in the pubic area?' (Not asking about puberty because she is only eight is the trap — ASK IT ANYWAY, because both precocious and delayed puberty change the whole reading.)

THE PATHOLOGICAL SCREEN — WHERE THE MARKS ARE, run aloud so the examiner can tick each system: DIET in detail; GUT — 'any PALE, GREASY OR BULKY STOOLS — ones that FLOAT or are HARD TO FLUSH? Diarrhoea, blood, mouth ulcers, tummy pain, joint pains? ANY FAMILY HISTORY OF COELIAC DISEASE, CROHN'S OR COLITIS?'; CHEST — 'recurrent chest infections, long-term cough or wheeze? WAS HER NEWBORN HEEL-PRICK NORMAL?'; MEDICINES — 'any medicines, PARTICULARLY STEROID PUFFERS OR STEROID TABLETS?'

AND THE PART THAT SEPARATES A STRUCTURED CANDIDATE FROM A LUCKY ONE: THYROID — 'does she FEEL THE COLD more than other people? Any CONSTIPATION, DRY SKIN, or is she more tired or SLOWED DOWN?'; MALIGNANCY — 'has she lost weight, or had LUMPS, NIGHT SWEATS OR UNUSUAL BRUISING?'; INTRACRANIAL — 'any HEADACHES, ESPECIALLY IN THE MORNING, any VOMITING ON WAKING, or any CHANGE IN HER VISION?' Then birth and birth weight, pregnancy, development, and 'WHAT WERE YOU HOPING WE COULD DO TODAY?'

PLOT IT, AND SAY WHAT YOU SEE: 'her height at 117 cm is ON THE 3RD CENTILE. Her weight at 23 kg is on the 25th to 50th. SO HER WEIGHT IS BETTER PRESERVED THAN HER HEIGHT — which points AWAY from undernutrition and chronic illness, because those take the weight first.' Then: 'EXAMINER, ARE THERE ANY PREVIOUS MEASUREMENTS — from the child health record, the school or her GP? I want to know WHETHER SHE HAS BEEN TRACKING ALONG THIS LINE OR CROSSING CENTILES, WHICH MATTERS MORE THAN WHERE SHE SITS TODAY.' Then the arithmetic OUT LOUD: (150 + 160 — 13) / 2 = 148.5 cm, range about 140 to 157. (Averaging 150 and 160 to 155 is the error — THE 13 cm SEX CORRECTION IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A CORRECT AND AN INCORRECT TARGET.)

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST: height, weight, HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE and BMI plotted, AND THE PARENTS' HEIGHTS; general appearance including DYSMORPHIC FEATURES, pallor, jaundice, rash, bruising, clubbing and mouth ulcers; BODY PROPORTION — ARM SPAN VERSUS HEIGHT AND UPPER-TO-LOWER SEGMENT RATIO; THE THYROID; TANNER STAGING WITH A CHAPERONE; chest and heart with blood pressure; abdomen for distension, tenderness and organomegaly; joints and spine; lymph nodes; AND FUNDI AND VISUAL FIELDS given the growth concern. (The parents' heights and the charts are handed over if you ask and withheld if you do not.)

SHOULD I BE WORRIED?' → 'I don't think she has it... but IT'S THE ONE CONDITION WHERE BEING SHORT CAN BE THE ONLY SIGN, AND IT'S TREATABLE.'

AMELIA HAS ALWAYS BEEN THE SMALLEST since her first year of school; she has NOT suddenly fallen behind. IT IS HER HEIGHT, NOT HER WEIGHT — she eats well and is not thin. DANA IS 150 cm AND HER PARTNER IS 160 cm, NEITHER A LATE DEVELOPER — GIVE THESE NUMBERS READILY IF ASKED, BUT DO NOT VOLUNTEER THEM. No puberty signs. EVERYTHING ELSE NORMAL: bowels, no greasy stools, no blood, no mouth ulcers, no joint pain or rash, no chest infections or cough, NO MEDICINES OR PUFFERS, normal heel-prick, no cold intolerance or constipation, no weight loss, lumps or night sweats, NO HEADACHES, MORNING VOMITING OR VISUAL CHANGE. back.dx: VERSION B — TYPE 1 DIABETES. 'The most likely explanation is DIABETES — which means THE SUGAR LEVEL IN HIS BLOOD IS TOO HIGH. The reasons I think that: he's been DRINKING MUCH MORE than usual, he's PASSING MUCH MORE URINE AND HAS STARTED WETTING THE BED AGAIN, he's LOST A LITTLE WEIGHT, and he's tired. WHEN THE SUGAR IN THE BLOOD IS HIGH, THE BODY GETS RID OF THE EXTRA SUGAR IN THE URINE, AND THAT PULLS WATER OUT WITH IT — so he passes more urine and gets thirsty.' WHEN SHE SAYS 'DIABETES? HE'S FIVE': 'I know that's a shock. IT DOES HAPPEN AT THIS AGE — it's the type where THE BODY STOPS MAKING INSULIN, AND IT ISN'T CAUSED BY ANYTHING YOU DID OR BY WHAT HE EATS.' VERSION A — OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNOEA: 'when he sleeps, THE MUSCLES IN HIS THROAT RELAX AND BECOME FLOPPY, and his TONSILS AND ADENOIDS narrow the airway — so THE AIRWAY BLOCKS OFF FOR SHORT PERIODS. That's what causes the snoring and the gasping, IT INTERRUPTS HIS SLEEP OVER AND OVER WITHOUT WAKING HIM PROPERLY, and that's why he's tired all day and struggling at kindy.' THE FULL DIFFERENTIAL LIST, AND A LONG LIST IS CORRECT HERE, NOT PADDING — THREE IS NOT ENOUGH AFTER A SIX-MINUTE HISTORY: an UNDERACTIVE THYROID; CANCERS OF THE BLOOD such as leukaemia; INFECTIONS, particularly viral ones LIKE GLANDULAR FEVER that leave children tired for weeks; ANAEMIA; LOW MOOD or something happening at kindy; COELIAC DISEASE; HEART PROBLEMS he might have been born with; and SLEEP APNOEA — 'nothing you've told me points to those; the pattern here fits this much better.' NEXT STEPS, VERSION B: 'I'd like to do A FINGER-PRICK TEST RIGHT NOW to check his sugar level, AND A TEST FOR KETONES. If the sugar is high, HE NEEDS TO GO TO THE CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL TODAY so they can start treatment and teach you both how to manage it. I know that sounds frightening — IT IS A SERIOUS CONDITION, BUT IT IS VERY TREATABLE, AND CHILDREN WITH DIABETES LIVE COMPLETELY NORMAL LIVES.' AND THE SAFETY-NET: if he becomes DROWSY, STARTS VOMITING, OR HIS BREATHING LOOKS DEEP AND SIGHING, that is an emergency and you arrange retrieval. NEXT STEPS, VERSION A: paediatrician and ENT referral plus A SLEEP STUDY; for most children it is LARGE TONSILS AND ADENOIDS and removing them fixes it; return if he becomes very sleepy during the day, stops growing well, or the behaviour worsens. KETOACIDOSIS: 'he's dehydrated, drowsy, and his breathing is DEEP AND SIGHING — that suggests DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS, WHICH IS AN EMERGENCY. Drip in now, glucose, ketones and bloods, fluids started, and RETRIEVAL — PLEASE DON'T DRIVE HIM YOURSELVES.' To the examiner: cautious fluid resuscitation, INSULIN AFTER FLUIDS per the paediatric DKA protocol, HOURLY NEUROLOGICAL OBSERVATIONS FOR CEREBRAL OEDEMA, senior paediatric involvement throughout. VERIFY

He used to run around all day and now he just sits.' (Skip this and you can spend six minutes chasing fatigue in a child with a sleep disorder, or the reverse.)
TIMING AND PATTERN: how long, every day or on and off, worse at a particular time of day, getting worse, anything that makes it better or worse, AND IS IT AFFECTING HIM AT KINDY OR AT HOME.

E — ENDOCRINE, ASKED EARLY AND AS TWO SEPARATE QUESTIONS: 'HAS HE BEEN MORE THIRSTY THAN USUAL — DRINKING MORE THAN HE USED TO?' [PAUSE FOR THE ANSWER] → water bottle everywhere, drinks in the night. Then SEPARATELY: 'HAVE YOU NOTICED HIM PASSING MORE URINE, OR WETTING THE BED AGAIN?' → 'HE'S STARTED WETTING THE BED AGAIN. HE'D BEEN DRY FOR OVER A YEAR — I THOUGHT IT WAS THE NEW KINDY.' Then cold intolerance, constipation, and family history of diabetes or thyroid disease. (Ask 'any thirst?' as a throwaway and move on before the answer lands, and you can miss the entire diagnosis. And parents often answer only the first of a doubled question.)

M — MALIGNANCY: 'has he lost weight — are you happy with his growth and weight gain? Any change in appetite? ANY LUMPS OR BUMPS? NIGHT SWEATS? EASY BRUISING, BONE OR LEG PAINS, OR UNEXPLAINED FEVERS?' → trousers looser and eating less, everything else negative.

I — INFECTION AND A — ANAEMIA: fever or chills, travel, rashes, RECENT FLU-LIKE ILLNESS OR SORE THROAT; then 'does he look pale to you? Can you describe his diet — DOES HE EAT RED MEAT, and HOW MUCH COW'S MILK? Any YELLOW TINGE to his skin or eyes, or DARK URINE?'

D, C AND O: mood, sleep, home stressors, kindy and BULLYING; then GREASY STOOLS that stick, float or are hard to flush, diarrhoea, blood; cough or difficulty breathing, PUFFED OR BLUE WHEN RUNNING; then the sleep block — 'DOES HE SNORE? ANY GASPING OR PAUSES IN HIS BREATHING? Sleepy in the mornings? Recurrent infections? Any new behavioural problems?' → Version B: 'NO SNORING AT ALL.'

SAY THE RECOVERY LINE AND KEEP MOVING: 'THANK YOU — THAT MAKES A SLEEP PROBLEM MUCH LESS LIKELY. LET ME ASK ABOUT SOME OTHER CAUSES.' Then the well-child and BINDSMA leftovers: alert or drowsy, eating and drinking, passing urine; development; birth, immunisations, medications, allergies; family history of thyroid disease, diabetes or coeliac. (Freezing when the negatives arrive is what the station is designed to catch.)
NAME IT AND EXPLAIN THE MECHANISM IN PLAIN WORDS (see dx) → 'DIABETES? HE'S FIVE.' → the shock acknowledged, the type explained, AND THE BLAME REMOVED before she asks.

EIGHT OR MORE DIFFERENTIALS BY NAME, EACH DISMISSED AGAINST THE HISTORY (see dx), then the bedside glucose and ketones IN THE ROOM, the hospital TODAY, the honest 'serious but very treatable', and the ketoacidosis safety-net. → 'IS IT BECAUSE OF WHAT HE EATS?' → NO, and do not blame her.

VERSION A — THE SLEEP BLOCK: 'does he snore?' → 'every night, you can hear him through the wall.' → 'have you noticed him GASPING, OR PAUSES in his breathing?' → 'yes — he stops, then takes a big gasp.' → then morning sleepiness, recurrent throat infections and behavioural change, and the OSA explanation. Management: paediatrician and ENT, A SLEEP STUDY, and for most children it is LARGE TONSILS AND ADENOIDS, where removing them fixes it.

KETOACIDOSIS VARIANT — vomiting, drowsy, sighing breathing: 'he's dehydrated, drowsy, and his breathing is DEEP AND SIGHING — that suggests DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS, WHICH IS AN EMERGENCY. I'm putting a drip in now, checking his glucose, ketones and bloods, starting fluids, and calling for RETRIEVAL. PLEASE DON'T DRIVE HIM YOURSELVES.' To the examiner: cautious fluid resuscitation, INSULIN AFTER FLUIDS per the paediatric DKA protocol, HOURLY NEUROLOGICAL OBSERVATIONS FOR CEREBRAL OEDEMA, senior paediatric involvement throughout VERIFY. / LEUKAEMIA VARIANT — bruising and bone pain: 'I'm concerned enough to arrange A BLOOD TEST TODAY RATHER THAN NEXT WEEK... I want that either confirmed or excluded now. I'll phone the children's hospital while you're here.' / IF THE STEM SAYS 'TIRED AND NOT PAYING ATTENTION AT SCHOOL' — THAT IS A DIFFERENT STATION: approach it through the BEHAVIOUR pathway — ADHD, autism, ABSENCE SEIZURES, hearing impairment, sleep apnoea — because THE STRUCTURE IS AIMED AT THE STEM, NOT AT THE DIAGNOSIS.
pefe: Role-player: Kate, 33, mother of Noah, 5. He is 'ALWAYS TIRED' — LOW IN ENERGY, NOT SLEEPY; six weeks, every day, GETTING WORSE; HAS STOPPED JOINING IN AT KINDY. POSITIVES, GIVEN ONLY WHEN ASKED: drinking much more, CARRIES A WATER BOTTLE, asks for drinks at night; WETTING THE BED AGAIN AFTER A YEAR DRY, which she has blamed on the new kindy; TROUSERS LOOSER; eating less. NEGATIVES: NO snoring, gasping or pauses; no recurrent infections; no fever, travel or rash; not pale, eats meat, one glass of milk; no jaundice or dark urine; mood and kindy fine, no bullying; bowels normal, no greasy stools; no cough, NEVER BLUE. Normal birth, immunised, no medicines or allergies. GRANDMOTHER HAS AN UNDERACTIVE THYROID.

How to play it: if the doctor asks only 'Any thirst?' and moves straight on, answer 'Maybe a bit' — make them ask properly. Give the bedwetting only if asked about urine or bedwetting specifically. If the doctor asks sleep questions, answer 'No snoring at all' flatly — and see whether they recover or keep pushing. If they land on the diagnosis, react: 'Diabetes? He's five.' then ask 'Is it because of what he eats?' — a good candidate says no and does not blame you. Register: calm at first, shocked at the word diabetes. Version A: swap the answers — snoring every night, gasping, worse in the mornings, recurrent sore throats, grumpy behaviour, and no thirst or urine changes.

Score them on: DEFINED SLEEPY VERSUS LOW ENERGY; timing, pattern and effect on function; THIRST; URINE AND BEDWETTING; thyroid; MALIGNANCY — weight, lumps, sweats, bruising, bone pain; infection and glandular fever; anaemia and diet; mood, home, kindy and bullying; coeliac; cardiopulmonary; THE OSA BLOCK; well-child and BINDSMA; NAMED THE DIAGNOSIS WITH REASONS; EIGHT OR MORE DIFFERENTIALS; bedside glucose and ketones with hospital today; and DID NOT BLAME THE DIET. findings: NARROWING OF THE AIRWAY behind the nose and throat, caused by LARGE TONSILS AND A LARGE ADENOID
LARGE TONSILS on throat examination, MOUTH-BREATHING AT REST — consistent with the airway narrowing on the film

back.dx: OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNOEA. THE X-RAY IN FOUR SENTENCES, POINTING AS YOU SPEAK: 'this is an X-ray of the side of his neck. On it I can see NARROWING OF HIS AIRWAY — the tube air travels down behind his nose and throat. The narrowing is because of LARGE TONSILS AND A LARGE ADENOID, WHICH IS A GLAND AT THE BACK OF THE NOSE AND THROAT. A narrow airway HAS A MUCH HIGHER CHANCE OF BLOCKING WHILE HE SLEEPS, and that is what causes the snoring and the gasping you've described.' NO COLOUR LECTURE. THE SLEEP STUDY, BASELINE THEN ABNORMAL, WITH THE THRESHOLD SAID: 'while he was asleep we measured THE OXYGEN LEVEL IN HIS BLOOD through the night. NORMALLY IT STAYS HIGH WITH ONLY TINY DIPS. On his trace I can see MULTIPLE DROPS, AND THEY GO BELOW 90 PER CENT. WHEN THAT HAPPENS MORE THAN TWO OR THREE TIMES IN A NIGHT IT IS SIGNIFICANT.' THE DIAGNOSIS WITH MECHANISM AND REASONS: 'Liam has OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNOEA. In his case THE LARGE TONSILS AND ADENOID NARROW THE AIRWAY. WHEN HE SLEEPS THE MUSCLES IN THE THROAT BECOME FLOPPY, THE NARROWED AIRWAY BLOCKS, AND HE SNORES, PAUSES, AND THEN GASPS TO OPEN IT AGAIN. I'm confident because of what you've told me — the snoring, the gasping and pauses, mouth breathing, tiredness in the mornings, THE CHANGE IN BEHAVIOUR AND THE BEDWETTING — and because BOTH TESTS CONFIRM IT: the X-ray shows the blockage and the sleep study shows his oxygen dropping.' MANAGEMENT: 'it's COMMON AND TREATABLE.' Referral to a paediatrician AND an ENT surgeon; THE USUAL TREATMENT IS AN OPERATION TO REMOVE THE TONSILS AND ADENOID, AND CHILDHOOD IS THE RIGHT TIME; if surgery is not suitable, CPAP — 'a small mask worn during sleep that provides a constant flow of air to keep the airway open'. Also CHECK HIS HEARING AND DEVELOPMENT, treat the blocked nose, and review. SAFETY-NET: 'IF YOU EVER SEE HIM GO BLUE OR GREY DURING A PAUSE, CALL 000.' NEVER PROMISE SURGERY OR A DATE — THE SURGEON DECIDES; YOU REFER AND SAFETY-NET. VERSION B — THE TIRED, INATTENTIVE 7-YEAR-OLD: park the school fight ('YOU'VE MENTIONED THE FIGHT; I'LL COME BACK TO IT. FIRST I WANT TO UNDERSTAND THE TIREDNESS, BECAUSE A TIRED CHILD CAN'T PAY ATTENTION'), then run the OSA block, then ADHD, then ASD, then THE CHEAP DIFFERENTIALS THAT SEPARATE A FULL LIST FROM A RECALL: ABSENCE SEIZURES — 'any episodes where he STARES BLANKLY for a few seconds and isn't with you?'; DIABETES — passing more urine, drinking more, weight loss; thyroid; vision and hearing; sleep hygiene and SCREENS IN THE BEDROOM; head injury; and MOOD. THE VERSION B DIAGNOSIS: OSA, with reasons — tired and sleepy WORST IN THE MORNINGS AND BETTER AFTER A LONG SLEEP, snoring AND MORE IMPORTANTLY GASPING AND PAUSES, THE BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, and LARGE TONSILS on the card — then ADHD excluded (no hyperactivity or impulsivity, and CONCENTRATION IMPROVES WHEN HE'S RESTED), autism excluded (social skills, speech and play typical), absence seizures (no staring spells), diabetes (no thirst or polyuria, AND A FINGER-PRICK SUGAR TODAY), thyroid, iron, vision, hearing, head injury and low mood.
plan: OPEN AND ACKNOWLEDGE WITHOUT REASSURING: 'I can hear that the snoring is worrying you. LET'S WORK TOGETHER: I'll find out what is causing it and we'll make the best plan for him.' (Reassuring at the door — 'lots of children snore' — before you have asked a single question is the first trap. ACKNOWLEDGE, DON'T REASSURE. And the father pushes back once: 'MY WIFE SAYS ALL KIDS SNORE.')
THE SNORING: when did you first notice it, every night or on and off, IS IT GETTING WORSE, anything that makes it better or worse — colds, lying on his back.

The apnoea question, asked twice in two forms: 'Have you ever noticed him gasping or choking during his sleep?' ... 'And does he ever stop breathing for a few seconds — any pauses in his breathing?' then: 'Does he breathe through his mouth? Is he restless, sweaty, sleeping with his head tipped back?' (Asking only 'Does he gasp?' Loses it — some parents describe pauses, not gasps.)

DAYTIME AND BEHAVIOUR: 'how is he in the mornings — tired, HARD TO WAKE? Sleepy during the day? Any trouble CONCENTRATING at kindy? ANY CHANGE IN HIS BEHAVIOUR — more aggressive, hyperactive, harder to manage?' → grumpy mornings, asleep in the car every afternoon, AND HITTING OTHER CHILDREN AT KINDY.

THE TEN-SECOND MARKED ITEMS THAT CANDIDATES SKIP: 'ANY BEDWETTING, OR HAS HE STARTED WETTING AGAIN? Does he get a lot of runny noses or colds? ANY EAR INFECTIONS? Any worry about HIS HEARING OR HIS SPEECH? Any concerns about his growth or development?' → dry and now wetting again, permanent runny nose, two ear infections this year.

BINDS, COMPRESSED, THEN SUMMARISE: pregnancy and birth, immunisations, medical problems, medicines, allergies, AND FAMILY HISTORY OF SNORING, SLEEP APNOEA, ASTHMA OR HAY FEVER. Then: 'so to summarise: six months of loud nightly snoring with gasping and pauses, mouth breathing, tired grumpy mornings, bedwetting and lots of colds. LET ME SHOW YOU THE TESTS.'

THE X-RAY IN FOUR SENTENCES — POINT, NAME, LINK TO OBSTRUCTION (see dx). → 'SO THE ADENOID — IS THAT THE SAME AS TONSILS?' → a gland at the back of the nose and throat. (The colour lecture eats a minute you do not have.)

THE OXIMETRY — BASELINE, THEN THE ABNORMAL, WITH THE THRESHOLD STATED (see dx). → 'IS THAT DANGEROUS?' → 'it's not dangerous tonight, BUT IT DOES NEED FIXING.' (Describing the waveform without stating the threshold or its meaning loses the mark — it is for 'BELOW 90%, THREE OR MORE, SIGNIFICANT'.)

THE DIAGNOSIS: name it, the mechanism, the reasons from his own history, AND BOTH TESTS (see dx). If the examination card is handed over: 'large tonsils and mouth breathing at rest — BOTH CONSISTENT WITH THE AIRWAY NARROWING ON THE X-RAY.'

MANAGEMENT AND SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'WILL HE NEED THE OPERATION FOR SURE?' → the surgeon decides; you refer. → AND THE HIDDEN AGENDA IF YOU ASKED: 'COULD HE JUST... NOT WAKE UP?' → answer it directly, and give the blue-or-grey safety-net.

THE VERSION B DIAGNOSIS runs: OSA named with mechanism and reasons, then ADHD, autism, absence seizures, diabetes WITH A FINGER-PRICK SUGAR TODAY, thyroid, low iron, vision, hearing, head injury and low mood — each dismissed against the history — then paediatrician, ENT, a sleep study and review.
pefe: Role-player: Mark, 34, FIFO electrician, home this week; father of Liam, 3, who attends kindy three days a week; NEW BABY SISTER, 4 MONTHS. Mark SNORED AS A CHILD AND HAD HIS TONSILS OUT AT 6; his wife has hay fever. Liam: normal pregnancy and birth at 39 weeks, immunisations up to date, no medicines or allergies, GROWING ON THE 15TH CENTILE. REGISTER: practical, SLIGHTLY EMBARRASSED THAT HIS WIFE THINKS HE IS FUSSING, and warms when the doctor takes it seriously. PUSH BACK ONCE: 'MY WIFE SAYS ALL KIDS SNORE.'

Hidden agenda: he is secretly worried the child could stop breathing and not start again. Volunteer it only if asked 'Is there anything you're particularly worried about?' — or at the very end if never asked: 'Could he just... Not wake up?' How to play it: answer only what is asked. Give vague answers first and detail on the follow-up. Become quietly emotional if the doctor names the breathing pauses as real.

back.dx: PRIMARY MONOSYMPTOMATIC NOCTURNAL ENURESIS. NAME IT, DEFINE IT, NORMALISE IT: 'Oliver has what we call PRIMARY NOCTURNAL ENURESIS — bedwetting. PRIMARY because HE'S NEVER BEEN DRY, NOCTURNAL because IT ONLY HAPPENS AT NIGHT. Most children learn to hold on at night somewhere between FIVE AND SEVEN; some — OFTEN DEEP SLEEPERS, AND OFTEN WHERE A PARENT WAS THE SAME — get there a bit later. HIS BRAIN DOESN'T YET WAKE HIM WHEN HIS BLADDER IS FULL, and at night the kidneys make more urine than the bladder can hold. IT'S NOT LAZINESS AND IT ISN'T HIS FAULT — AND IT ISN'T YOURS.' THEN LIST WHAT YOU EXCLUDED: 'from the questions, the examination and the two tests, I've ruled out A URINE INFECTION, DIABETES, CONSTIPATION, SLEEP APNOEA, AND ANY PROBLEM WITH HIS NERVES OR HIS BLADDER — that's why we can treat this as simple bedwetting.' MANAGEMENT, AND THE ALARM COMES FIRST: 'the most effective treatment, AND THE ONE THAT LASTS, is A BEDWETTING ALARM. A small sensor goes under the sheet or clips to his pyjamas; THE MOMENT THE FIRST DROPS OF WEE TOUCH IT, THE ALARM GOES OFF AND WAKES HIM. HE GETS UP, SWITCHES IT OFF HIMSELF, and finishes in the toilet. Over SIX TO EIGHT WEEKS — sometimes a few months — his brain learns to wake to a full bladder, and then to hold on without waking. IT'S HIS ALARM — you may need to help him wake at first, BUT HE SWITCHES IT OFF.' ALONGSIDE: DRINK WELL THROUGH THE DAY — NO FLUID RESTRICTION — but NO CORDIAL, COKE OR CAFFEINATED DRINKS, especially in the evening, and no big drinks in the last hour before bed; wee before bed; TELL ME IF HE GETS CONSTIPATED, because that makes wetting worse; NO TELLING OFF OR LOSING SCREEN TIME FROM NOW — HE CAN'T HELP IT — and instead A STAR CHART FOR THE THINGS HE CAN CONTROL: drinking well in the day, using the alarm, HELPING CHANGE THE SHEETS; and a waterproof mattress protector. DESMOPRESSIN, AND ITS ONE INDICATION HERE: 'there is a medicine that reduces how much urine the kidneys make overnight. IT'S NOT THE TREATMENT — IT ONLY WORKS ON THE NIGHTS HE TAKES IT — but FOR THE CAMP NEXT TERM, or a sleepover, we can use a tablet or a wafer under the tongue for those ONE OR TWO NIGHTS, with limited drinks that evening. WE DON'T USE THE NASAL SPRAY ANY MORE.' REVIEW IN FOUR TO SIX WEEKS, and return sooner for DAYTIME WETTING, pain, fever or smelly urine, THIRST, or SOILING; if the alarm has not worked after a few months, or he is still wetting at seven, involve the children's continence clinic. VARIANTS: DAYTIME WETTING TOO — this is NOT simple bedwetting, an alarm will not fix it, and it needs urine testing, a renal tract ULTRASOUND and the continence clinic. SECONDARY ENURESIS WITH THIRST AND WEIGHT LOSS — CHECK FOR DIABETES RIGHT NOW with a finger-prick glucose and urine for glucose and ketones. SNORING AND GASPING — blocked breathing at night can cause bedwetting on its own; look at the tonsils and refer to ENT. SECONDARY ONSET AFTER A FAMILY CHANGE IN A WITHDRAWN CHILD — ask Oliver separately whether anything is worrying him or anyone is making him feel unsafe, and be honest that you are obliged to report a concern.
plan: ACKNOWLEDGE BIG, AND SPEAK TO THE CHILD: 'washing the bed linen every day — I CAN HEAR HOW TIRED AND FRUSTRATED YOU ARE. Thank you for coming in. I'll ask a lot of questions, INCLUDING ABOUT HIS WEE DURING THE DAY, examine him, and then we'll make a plan that helps you both. OLIVER — LOTS OF KIDS YOUR AGE WET THE BED. IT'S NOT YOUR FAULT, AND WE'RE GOING TO HELP.' (A token 'I understand' for a big opening, or 'he'll grow out of it' before the history, are the two early traps.)

THE TWO KEY QUESTIONS, IN THE FIRST MINUTE: 'how long has this been happening? HAS HE EVER BEEN DRY AT NIGHT FOR MORE THAN SIX MONTHS? How many nights a week — more than once a night? Getting worse? AND — IMPORTANTLY — DOES HE WET HIMSELF DURING THE DAY AT ALL, EVEN DAMP PANTS? Anything that makes it better or worse?' → never dry, five or six nights a week, NEVER in the day, worse after a big drink before bed.

EVERY LUTS BY NAME, SIGNPOSTED: 'I'm going to run through a list about his wee, day and night. Any PAIN OR BURNING? Does he need to go MORE OFTEN than other kids? Does he get a SUDDEN DESPERATE URGE and have to run? Any DRIBBLING AFTER HE'S FINISHED, damp pants? Is the STREAM WEAK, OR DOES IT STOP AND START? Does he STRAIN or take a while to get going? Any BLOOD in the urine? Any URINE INFECTIONS in the past? Does he pass LARGE AMOUNTS?' THEN SAY THE CONCLUSION ALOUD: 'SO NO DAYTIME OR OTHER URINARY SYMPTOMS — THAT'S IMPORTANT.' (Asking only dysuria and infections is an automatic fail — the mother volunteers nothing.)

THE PSYCHOSOCIAL BLOCK — the second automatic fail if skipped: 'how are things at home? HOW DO YOU REACT WHEN IT HAPPENS — HAVE YOU PUNISHED HIM? How's school? Any teasing? DOES IT STOP HIM GOING ON SLEEPOVERS? OLIVER, HOW DO YOU FEEL ABOUT IT? How does he sleep — IS HE A VERY DEEP SLEEPER? Does he sleep on his own — HOW FAR IS THE TOILET FROM HIS BED?' → she has told him off and taken screen time, he refuses sleepovers, THERE IS A CAMP NEXT TERM HE IS DREADING, and he sleeps like a log with the toilet down the hall.

THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH A MARKED ITEM: 'does he drink a lot during the day? WHAT DOES HE DRINK IN THE EVENING — CORDIAL, FIZZY OR CAFFEINATED DRINKS?' → CORDIAL AND COKE WITH DINNER AND BEFORE BED, the one modifiable positive. Then: 'any CONSTIPATION — hard or infrequent poos? Does he ever SOIL himself? Has he been unusually THIRSTY? PASSING LARGE VOLUMES? Lost weight, tired? DOES HE SNORE? Any GASPING OR PAUSES? Tired in the mornings? Any trouble WALKING, NUMBNESS OR WEAKNESS IN THE LEGS, BACK PROBLEMS, A DIMPLE ON HIS LOWER BACK?'

BINDS, GROWTH, MEDICINES AND FAMILY HISTORY: pregnancy and birth, ANY KIDNEY OR SPINE PROBLEMS FOUND AS A BABY, immunisations, other problems, regular medicines, growth and development, AND 'DID EITHER PARENT OR A SIBLING WET THE BED AS A CHILD — UNTIL WHAT AGE?' → HIS DAD WET THE BED UNTIL ABOUT EIGHT. Then SUMMARISE and transition.

The examination request, naming the two tests: general appearance and hydration; growth chart; abdomen for a palpable bladder or faecal masses and the renal angles; genitalia and the position of the meatus; perianal inspection and anal wink; spine for a sacral dimple, hair tuft or scoliosis; lower-limb tone, power, reflexes, sensation and gait; tonsils and mouth-breathing; and a urine dipstick — glucose, protein, blood, leucocytes, nitrites — and a fingerprick blood glucose.
The diagnosis: name, define, normalise, and list the exclusions (see dx). → 'So why are his friends dry? Is there a tablet?'

MANAGEMENT, ALARM FIRST, AND PROTECT THE LAST NINETY SECONDS (see dx): the alarm explained with HE SWITCHES IT OFF HIMSELF; fluids through the day WITHOUT RESTRICTION and no evening caffeine; no punishment and a star chart; the mattress protector; DESMOPRESSIN FOR THE CAMP ONLY, with the nasal spray no longer used; review in four to six weeks; and the red flags. → she pushes once: 'THAT SOUNDS LIKE A LOT OF WORK — CAN'T HE JUST HAVE TABLETS?' → 'it IS more work for the first few weeks — AND IT'S THE ONLY TREATMENT THAT TEACHES HIS BODY TO STAY DRY AFTER IT STOPS.'

pefe: Role-player: Emma, 34, works at the Wallaroo bakery; partner Josh works at the port; two younger children. EXHAUSTED, AND EMBARRASSED THAT OLIVER 'ISN'T LIKE HIS FRIENDS'. Oliver, 6: normal pregnancy and birth, nothing found as a baby, immunised, no medical problems, no medicines, growing well, started school this year and doing fine. WETS 5-6 NIGHTS A WEEK, ONCE A NIGHT, AND ALWAYS HAS — NEVER DRY FOR A WEEK, LET ALONE SIX MONTHS. NEVER WETS IN THE DAY. NO urinary symptoms at all — no burning, frequency, urgency or dribbling, strong stream, no blood, never an infection, normal amounts. Drinks little during the day; CORDIAL AND COKE WITH DINNER AND BEFORE BED, ONLY IF ASKED ABOUT EVENING DRINKS. Bowels fine, no soiling. Not thirsty, no weight loss. No snoring. Walks fine, no back problems. DEEP SLEEPER — 'LIKE A LOG'. Own room, TOILET DOWN THE HALL. JOSH WET THE BED UNTIL ABOUT EIGHT — volunteered only when family history is asked.

HOW TO PLAY IT: open with the sheets and 'ALL HIS FRIENDS ARE DRY'. ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED. IF THE DOCTOR ASKS JUST 'ANY BURNING OR INFECTIONS?', ANSWER 'NO' AND SAY NOTHING MORE — DO NOT VOLUNTEER THE OTHER LUTS. IF THE DOCTOR DOESN'T ASK ABOUT DAYTIME WETTING, DON'T MENTION IT. You have TOLD HIM OFF AND TAKEN SCREEN TIME — volunteer that only when asked how you react. He REFUSES SLEEPOVERS and there is A SCHOOL CAMP NEXT TERM HE IS DREADING. HIDDEN AGENDA: YOU WANT A TABLET, because a friend's child 'got one and was fixed' — ask 'IS THERE A TABLET?' when the diagnosis is explained, AND AGAIN if the doctor only talks about the alarm. IF THE DOCTOR OFFERS DESMOPRESSIN AS THE MAIN PLAN, ACCEPT HAPPILY — THAT IS THE FAIL. If they recommend the alarm, PUSH ONCE: 'THAT SOUNDS LIKE A LOT OF WORK — CAN'T HE JUST HAVE TABLETS?' REGISTER: frazzled and a little defensive; softens when told it isn't his fault or hers; relieved with a concrete plan. OLIVER says 'I DON'T LIKE IT' if asked how he feels; otherwise silent.

back.dx: ENCOPRESIS FROM FUNCTIONAL CONSTIPATION, WITH OVERFLOW. NAME IT AND EXPLAIN THE MECHANISM: 'Liam has a condition called ENCOPRESIS, AND IT'S CAUSED BY CONSTIPATION. HARD STOOL HAS BUILT UP AND GOT STUCK AT THE END OF THE BOWEL. BEHIND THAT BLOCKAGE, LIQUID STOOL BUILDS UP, AND AFTER A WHILE IT LEAKS AROUND THE HARD LUMP — that's the runny stool in his pants. BECAUSE THE BOWEL IS STRETCHED, HE GENUINELY CAN'T FEEL IT COMING, SO HE CAN'T STOP IT. IT ISN'T NAUGHTINESS.' THE FOUR REASONS: the soiling is RUNNY AND SMALL, which is the liquid leaking around a blockage; he has been constipated for years with HARD MOTIONS EVERY FOUR OR FIVE DAYS; IT STARTED AFTER A PAINFUL, BLEEDING MOTION AT SEVEN, and since then he has HELD ON, WHICH MAKES THE STOOL HARDER AND THE CYCLE WORSE; his diet is LOW IN FIBRE AND WATER; and ON EXAMINATION YOU COULD FEEL THE STOOL IN HIS TUMMY. Then the reassurance with reasons: 'HE DOESN'T WET, WALKS NORMALLY AND IS GROWING WELL, SO I'M NOT WORRIED ABOUT A NERVE OR GLAND PROBLEM.' MANAGEMENT IN THREE STEPS, IN ORDER. STEP ONE — EMPTY THE BOWEL: 'because the cause is that blockage, THE VERY FIRST THING WE DO IS CLEAR IT OUT COMPLETELY. A laxative powder, MACROGOL, IN BIGGER DOSES FOR A FEW DAYS — it HOLDS WATER IN THE STOOL so it comes out soft — and if that doesn't shift it, A SMALL ENEMA. FOR A FEW DAYS THE SOILING MAY ACTUALLY GET WORSE — THAT'S THE OLD STOOL COMING OUT. THAT'S THE SIGN IT'S WORKING.' STEP TWO — KEEP IT SOFT FOR MONTHS: 'a smaller dose every day, adjusted until he has ONE SOFT, EASY POO A DAY. He'll need it FOR MONTHS. IT ISN'T ABSORBED, IT ISN'T HABIT-FORMING AND IT WON'T MAKE HIS BOWEL LAZY. STOPPING EARLY IS THE COMMONEST REASON THIS COMES BACK, so we wean it slowly when I say.' STEP THREE — RETRAIN: 'sit on the toilet FOR FIVE MINUTES AFTER BREAKFAST, AFTER SCHOOL AND AFTER DINNER — WITH A FOOTSTOOL SO HIS KNEES ARE HIGHER THAN HIS HIPS, which opens things up. A STAR CHART FOR SITTING, NOT FOR RESULTS. More fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, a water bottle at school, MILK TO ABOUT TWO CUPS A DAY, less junk, and run around every day. And NO PUNISHMENT FROM NOW — HE CAN'T CONTROL IT, AND FEAR MAKES HIM HOLD ON. I'll write a letter so school lets him use the toilet and keeps a change of clothes, and we'll deal with the teasing.' REVIEW IN TWO WEEKS to check the clear-out worked and adjust the dose, then monthly; return sooner for BLOOD, WORSENING, WETTING, VOMITING OR A SWOLLEN TUMMY. TIMELINE IF SHE ASKS: the clear-out takes a few days, the soiling settles over the following weeks, AND THE BOWEL TAKES MONTHS TO SHRINK BACK TO NORMAL. VARIANTS: HE WETS TOO — bowel AND bladder together means CHECK THE NERVES TO THE BOTTOM, and an abnormal back or legs needs SPINAL IMAGING before treating this as simple constipation. 'AREN'T LAXATIVES BAD FOR KIDS?' — macrogol HOLDS WATER, IS NOT ABSORBED AND DOES NOT ACT ON THE BOWEL MUSCLE, SO IT CANNOT CAUSE DEPENDENCE. 'JUST DO THE DIET' — diet and water matter BUT WILL NOT SHIFT A BLOCKAGE THAT IS ALREADY THERE. NEW SOILING WITH FEAR — ask the child alone whether anyone is hurting him, involve paediatrics, and be honest about the obligation to report.
plan: ACKNOWLEDGE BIG AND ADDRESS THE CHILD: 'I can hear how EXHAUSTING this has been — washing his clothes every day and not knowing why. I'm going to ask a lot of questions to find the cause, AND THEN WE'LL MAKE A PLAN THAT FIXES IT — FOR HIM AND FOR YOU. LIAM, some of these questions might feel a bit embarrassing; LOTS OF KIDS HAVE THIS PROBLEM AND IT'S FIXABLE.' (A one-line 'I understand' for a massive opening, or siding with 'he's doing it on purpose', are the two early traps.)

BOX 1, TIMING: how long, how often, DAYTIME, NIGHT-TIME OR BOTH, getting worse, and is this the first time or did it happen before and settle. → six months, every day, DURING THE DAY, worse, with a brief episode at five.

BOX 2, DESCRIBE THE SOILING: 'what does he soil with — HARD LUMPS, OR WATERY STOOL? Have you ever noticed ANY BLOOD? Is it a LARGE AMOUNT OR SMALL SMEARS? DOES HE KNOW IT'S HAPPENING — CAN HE FEEL IT? AND DOES HE ALSO WET HIMSELF — DAY OR NIGHT?' → runny, small, he cannot feel it, no blood, NO WETTING. (Hearing 'runny' and thinking diarrhoea is the trap: LIQUID PLUS SMALL VOLUME PLUS CANNOT FEEL IT EQUALS OVERFLOW. And the wetting question is the neurological screen — it is not optional.)

BOX 3, BOWEL MOTIONS: 'does he usually have diarrhoea or constipation? HOW OFTEN DOES HE OPEN HIS BOWELS PROPERLY? Are the stools hard and lumpy, or DO THEY EVER COME OUT IN A RIBBON SHAPE? Any blood or mucus? Does he STRAIN, or sit for ages?' → every four or five days, HARD AS ROCKS, blocks the toilet, strains.
DIET, WATER AND EXERCISE: a typical diet, fruit and vegetables, HOW MUCH WATER — and milk and fizzy drinks — and any exercise or sport. → junk, barely any water, ABOUT A LITRE OF MILK, no sport.

BEHAVIOUR AND THE TRIGGER — the origin of the cycle: 'does he refuse to go to the toilet, or AVOID THE TOILETS AT SCHOOL? Have you noticed him CROSSING HIS LEGS, STANDING ON TIPTOE, DANCING AROUND — HOLDING IT IN? HAS HE EVER HAD A REALLY PAINFUL OR FRIGHTENING BOWEL MOTION, OR BLEEDING WHEN HE WENT?' → never goes at school, crosses his legs, AND AT SEVEN A MOTION THAT MADE HIM SCREAM WITH BLOOD ON THE PAPER. (Not asking the painful-motion question loses the key to the whole explanation.)

The differentials: tummy pain, nausea, vomiting, bloating; pale, greasy, hard-to-flush stools and family coeliac or type 1 diabetes; feeling the cold, dry skin, tiredness; trouble walking, back pain, numbness or weakness in the legs, a dimple or tuft of hair on the back; and regular medicines.

BINDS, GROWTH, HOME AND SCHOOL: 'DID HE PASS HIS FIRST BOWEL MOTION IN THE FIRST DAY OR TWO?', immunisations, other problems, growth. Then: 'LIAM, HOW DO YOU FEEL ABOUT ALL THIS?' → quietly, 'I HATE IT. THE KIDS CALL ME STINKY.' Then: 'Jane, how are things at home — HOW DO YOU REACT WHEN IT HAPPENS? HAVE YOU PUNISHED HIM? How's school — is he being teased?' → she has yelled and taken the iPad, and is not proud of it. (Judging her for punishing is the trap — NOTE IT AND ADDRESS IT IN THE PLAN WITHOUT BLAME.)
Summarise, request the examination, then name it and give the four reasons (see dx) → 'So he's not doing it on purpose? I feel terrible.' → 'Most parents feel that way until someone explains it.'

MANAGEMENT IN ORDER — EMPTY, MAINTAIN FOR MONTHS, RETRAIN (see dx), then no punishment, THE SCHOOL LETTER, review in two weeks then monthly, and the red flags. → 'HOW LONG BEFORE IT STOPS?' → a few days for the clear-out, weeks for the soiling, AND MONTHS FOR THE BOWEL TO SHRINK BACK. (Promising two weeks of treatment, or referring to the emergency department, are the two management errors.)

pefe: Role-player: Jane, 38, single parent, shifts at the hospital kitchen; Liam's father lives in Adelaide and sees him monthly. TIRED, FRUSTRATED, EMBARRASSED. Liam, 10: normal birth, MECONIUM DAY ONE, immunised, no medical problems, no medicines, growing well on the 50th centile; toilet-trained at three with a battle; brief soiling at five that settled. SIX MONTHS OF DAILY DAYTIME SOILING — small amounts of RUNNY stool, comes home from school stained, AND HE SAYS HE CAN'T FEEL IT. NO blood. DOES NOT WET. ALWAYS CONSTIPATED: bowels every four or five days, HARD AS ROCKS, blocks the toilet, strains; no ribbon stools, no blood or mucus; tummy ache before he goes. AT SEVEN, A SCREAMING, BLEEDING MOTION — AND SINCE THEN HE REFUSES TO GO, especially at school, and crosses his legs. Diet: chips, nuggets, white bread, a banana; cordial and ABOUT A LITRE OF MILK; barely any water; iPad, no sport. No coeliac or diabetes in the family; not cold; skin fine; walks fine; no back pain or dimple.

How to play it: open big — 'I'm at the end of my tether... Washing his clothes every day' — and only relax if the doctor acknowledges properly. Volunteer 'Runny like diarrhoea' readily; volunteer the constipation only when asked about his bowel motions. The painful motion at seven and the leg-crossing come out only when asked directly. If the doctor says 'Laxatives' without 'Clear it out first', ask: 'But why is it runny if he's constipated?' if the doctor says two weeks of treatment, ask 'And then it's fixed?' Hidden agenda: you think he's doing it on purpose and feel guilty for punishing him — if not asked how you react, say at about 4:30: 'I've been punishing him — is that wrong?' Register: exasperated at the start; guilty and tearful when the mechanism is explained; relieved with a plan. Liam speaks only when addressed, and says 'I hate it, they call me stinky' if asked how he feels.

back.dx: Picky eating in a normally growing toddler, driven by fluid and snack displacement plus unstructured mealtimes. The counselling: 'Sam is growing well, he's active and healthy, and nothing you've told me suggests a medical cause. This is picky eating, which is very common at his age.' then the three explanations: 'A toddler's appetite goes up and down with how fast he's growing, and growth slows after the first year. Some children learn that refusing food gets attention. And the milk, juice and snacks are filling his small stomach so there's no room for meals — a litre of milk is about double what he needs and can make him low in iron.' then the sentence that carries the station: 'Children eat when they're hungry. Your job is what and when; his job is how much.' Three prioritised actions, not twenty tips: (1) regular mealtimes — three meals and two small snacks, nothing in between; (2) cap the milk at about two cups a day, swap the juice for water, and phase out the night bottle; (3) at meals — small portions, two or three choices, thirty minutes with the TV off, then take the plate away without a fuss. Then the rest in writing: keep offering new foods, because it can take ten tries; eat with him when you can; let him help in the kitchen; and no bribes, no punishments, and no second dinner. When she asks 'What if he just won't eat? Won't he be hungry?': 'He will — and hunger is exactly what brings him to the table. He won't starve himself with food on offer at regular times.' Investigation and safety-net: check a blood count and iron because of the milk volume; 'The one thing that would change my mind is his weight — if he stops gaining, or you notice pallor, tiredness, loose stools or cough, come back sooner'; review in four to six weeks with the blue book; and the child health nurse can help with routines. Version B — the chart shows a drop: 'Thank you — that changes how I think about this. A picky eater keeps growing; a child who crosses two centile lines has faltering growth, and I need to look for a cause before we talk about behaviour. Could I see the chart? I'd like to go through what goes in, what comes out, his health from birth, and how things are at home' — then the faltering growth structure, examination, investigations (Full blood count, ferritin, coeliac serology, electrolytes, liver function and urine), and paediatric review. If she pushes back — 'I've tried all that, it doesn't work': 'Most parents have tried pieces of it. What usually fails is doing it for two days, or doing it while the milk and snacks continue. Let's pick the two changes you can hold for four weeks, and I'll see you with the blue book to check his weight, so you're not doing this alone.'
plan: OPEN, ADDRESS THE FRUSTRATION, AND DEFINE THE COMPLAINT: 'I can hear this is frustrating. I'll ask what he eats and how mealtimes go, then some health questions, and then we'll make a plan together. WHAT DO YOU MEAN BY POOR EATING — DOES HE REFUSE FOOD, OR EAT LESS THAN YOU'D EXPECT? All foods or particular ones? Since when?' → refuses most meals, eats chips, sausages and biscuits, since about eighteen months. ('HE'S FUSSY' IS THE BAIT — say 'let me check a few things first' and keep going.)

THE DIET IN DETAIL — AND THE VOLUMES ARE WHERE THE CAUSE LIVES: 'walk me through A TYPICAL DAY'S FOOD. Any fruit, vegetables, meat, eggs, bread, rice, pasta? DOES HE DRINK COW'S MILK — HOW MANY CUPS OR BOTTLES A DAY? Juice, cordial, soft drink, flavoured milk? WHAT DOES HE SNACK ON, AND HOW OFTEN? DOES HE STILL HAVE A BOTTLE, ESPECIALLY AT NIGHT?' → FOUR OR FIVE BOTTLES, ABOUT A LITRE; juice at breakfast and a popper at kindy; biscuits, chips and muesli bars whenever he asks; a bedtime bottle and sometimes overnight. (Stopping after 'what does he eat' misses the entire cause.)

MEALTIME BEHAVIOUR: 'how long does a meal take? How many meals and snacks a day? REGULAR TIMES — does the family eat at the table? Any tantrums, throwing, spitting, leaving the table? IS THE TV OR TABLET ON? Do you end up making a SEPARATE MEAL? Any BRIBES OR REWARDS?' → an hour of battle, no set times, EATS ALONE IN FRONT OF THE TV, throws food and screams, she makes chips instead, and she has tried chocolate.

THE MOST IMPORTANT QUESTION, ASKED BEFORE YOU LABEL ANYTHING: 'HAS ANYONE BEEN CONCERNED ABOUT HIS WEIGHT GAIN? HOW IS HIS GROWTH ON THE CHART IN THE BLUE BOOK?' → Version A: 'the nurse said he's RIGHT ON HIS LINE.' Then development: talking, running, playing with others. (Labelling him fussy before asking about weight or growth is the fail, and she will say nothing.)

THE ORGANIC SCREEN: 'how are his bowel motions — LOOSE, GREASY, PALE OR SMELLY? Any chronic cough or infections that keep coming back? DOES HE EVER GO BLUE OR GET PUFFED with running, playing or eating? Any lumps, pallor, bruising or fevers? Vomiting, constipation, snoring?' → all negative apart from occasional constipation and a little snoring.

THE PARENTS AND HOME — because HE EATS WHAT HE'S GIVEN: 'he eats what he's given, so a little about you: WHAT'S YOUR OWN DIET LIKE, and do you have regular family mealtimes? HOW'S YOUR MOOD BEEN? Any money worries — IS THERE ALWAYS ENOUGH FOOD? Alcohol or drugs at home? Who's at home, and how are things generally?' → she skips meals and is exhausted, money is tight but there is food, stable home.
Ask what worries her most → 'That there's something wrong with him. And that I'm doing it wrong.' → answer both HALVEs.

COUNSEL: growing well, no medical cause, picky eating, AND THE THREE EXPLANATIONS — appetite, attention, and displacement by milk, juice and snacks — then 'CHILDREN EAT WHEN THEY'RE HUNGRY. YOUR JOB IS WHAT AND WHEN; HIS JOB IS HOW MUCH.'

THREE PRIORITISED ACTIONS WITH NUMBERS, THEN THE REST IN WRITING (see dx) → 'WHAT IF HE JUST WON'T EAT? WON'T HE BE HUNGRY?' → 'HE WILL — AND HUNGER IS EXACTLY WHAT BRINGS HIM TO THE TABLE.' Then the blood count and iron, the weight-based safety-net, review in four to six weeks WITH THE BLUE BOOK, and the child health nurse. (Delivering twenty tips as a list is the counselling trap — she pushes back with 'I'VE TRIED ALL THAT.')

How to play it: do not volunteer the milk volume, the snacks or the growth result — make the doctor ask. If the doctor labels him fussy before asking about weight or growth, say nothing and mark it as a fail. Hidden agenda: you are worried something is medically wrong and that it is your fault — reveal it only when asked about your concerns: 'Is something wrong with him? Am I doing it wrong?' Register: frustrated, defensive if blamed, relieved by a plan. If the advice is delivered as a long list, push back once: 'I've tried all that — it doesn't work.'

back.dx: OBESITY IN A NORMALLY GROWING 12-YEAR-OLD — lifestyle in origin, with a parental exercise ban as the modifiable driver. EXPLAIN THE CHART IN FOUR MOVES. ORIENT: 'these are Sophie's growth charts — one for height, one for weight and one for BODY MASS INDEX. BMI is just a number we get from her weight and her height together; it's A BETTER GUIDE TO BODY SIZE THAN WEIGHT ALONE.' DEFINE THE PERCENTILE: 'IF YOU IMAGINE 100 TWELVE-YEAR-OLD GIRLS LINED UP, being on the 90th percentile means her number is HIGHER THAN 90 OF THOSE 100.' WALK THE TREND: 'HER HEIGHT HAS SAT ON THE 50TH LINE for years and still does — THAT'S GOOD. Her weight and BMI were also in the middle when she was younger, but FROM ABOUT AGE TEN THEY'VE CLIMBED THROUGH THE LINES, and now they're ABOVE THE 97TH.' CONCLUDE WITHOUT SHAME: 'because her BMI is above the 97th line WE CLASSIFY THIS AS OBESITY. THAT WORD JUST MEANS HER WEIGHT IS ABOVE THE HEALTHY RANGE FOR HER AGE AND HEIGHT — IT'S ABOUT THE NUMBER, NOT ABOUT SOPHIE, and the good news is that IT'S VERY TREATABLE WHEN WE CATCH IT AT TWELVE.' 'IS IT MY FAULT?' → 'NO. LOTS OF THINGS ADD UP; WHAT MATTERS IS WHAT WE DO FROM HERE, TOGETHER.' MANAGEMENT: 'the main treatment at her age is CHANGES TO EVERYDAY HABITS — and it works best WHEN THE WHOLE FAMILY DOES IT TOGETHER, WITH A TEAM HELPING YOU.' DIET: more vegetables and fruit, less takeaway and chips, WATER OR MILK INSTEAD OF SOFT DRINK, and snacks swapped for fruit, nuts or yoghurt — WITH A DIETITIAN. ACTIVITY AND THE BAN, WHICH IS THE CENTRE OF THE STATION: 'regular activity every day THAT SHE ENJOYS, and a limit on screens of about two hours. AND ABOUT THE ASTHMA: WELL-CONTROLLED ASTHMA IS NO BARRIER TO EXERCISE — BEING ACTIVE IS ONE OF THE BEST THINGS FOR HER LUNGS. If she gets tight when she runs, TWO PUFFS OF THE RELIEVER THROUGH A SPACER ABOUT FIFTEEN MINUTES BEFORE SPORT PREVENTS IT' — plus an EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGIST to design something safe and fun. 'I DIDN'T KNOW SHE WAS ALLOWED. I THOUGHT I WAS PROTECTING HER.' → 'YOU WERE DOING WHAT ANY PARENT WOULD. NOW YOU HAVE THE RIGHT INFORMATION.' TEAM, SCREENING AND REVIEW: the children's weight-management service; BLOODS FOR SUGAR, LIPIDS AND LIVER; review in four to six weeks; AND ASK TO SEE SOPHIE HERSELF NEXT TIME SO SHE HAS A SAY IN THE PLAN. THE IMPLICATIONS AND SAFETY-NET: extra weight strains HIPS AND KNEES, affects SLEEP AND BREATHING AT NIGHT, raises the risk of DIABETES, and CAN AFFECT MOOD AND CONFIDENCE, ESPECIALLY WITH TEASING — so return for a LIMP OR HIP OR KNEE PAIN, SNORING WITH TIREDNESS, DRINKING A LOT, or if she seems SAD, NOT SLEEPING, OR HAS ANY PROBLEM WITH EATING. NO STRICT DIETS — 'we want her weight to stay steady WHILE SHE GROWS INTO IT' — and no weight-loss drugs at her age. VERSION B — STRIAE: everything above applies, PLUS 'because of the pink stretch marks and how quickly he's gained, I want to RULE OUT A HORMONE PROBLEM — CUSHING SYNDROME, where a gland above the kidney makes too much of a stress hormone called CORTISOL. It's uncommon but easy to check: A SALIVA SAMPLE AT BEDTIME, or a tablet at night and a blood test in the morning.'

back.dx: SPASTIC HEMIPLEGIC CEREBRAL PALSY. TO THE EXAMINER, IN THIS ORDER. FIRST LOCALISE: 'the card shows INCREASED TONE AND HYPERREFLEXIA ON THE LEFT WITH REDUCED MUSCLE BULK, and a normal right side. INCREASED TONE WITH BRISK REFLEXES IS AN UPPER MOTOR NEURONE PATTERN, which localises the lesion TO THE BRAIN OR SPINAL CORD rather than to nerve, muscle or joint. The distribution is UNILATERAL, so this is A HEMIPLEGIC PATTERN.' THEN COMMIT, WITH THE EXCLUSION IN THE SAME BREATH: 'my most likely diagnosis is SPASTIC HEMIPLEGIC CEREBRAL PALSY. I CAN CALL IT CEREBRAL PALSY RATHER THAN A PROGRESSIVE CONDITION BECAUSE HE HAS NEVER LOST A SKILL HE HAD ALREADY GAINED, and the other three developmental domains are normal.' THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH A REASON: AN ACQUIRED BRAIN INJURY — no history of meningitis, head injury or prolonged seizure; A NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDER — but he is STIFF WITH BRISK REFLEXES, NOT FLOPPY; CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM — heel-prick normal, no hoarse cry or constipation, THOUGH I WOULD STILL CHECK THYROID FUNCTION; A GENETIC SYNDROME — less likely with three normal domains and normal growth; and A MUSCULOSKELETAL CAUSE such as developmental dysplasia of the hip — BUT THAT WOULD NOT CAUSE HYPERTONIA OR HYPERREFLEXIA, AND THE ARM IS INVOLVED. TO THE MOTHER: 'cerebral palsy is A MOVEMENT AND POSTURE DISORDER CAUSED BY AN INJURY TO THE DEVELOPING BRAIN — the part that sends signals to the muscles. THE IMPORTANT THING IS THAT THE INJURY ISN'T GETTING WORSE. IT HAPPENED ONCE. But as he grows, THE WAY IT SHOWS UP CHANGES, which is why we treat it actively.' ON CAUSE, BE HONEST AND REMOVE THE BLAME: 'it can happen during pregnancy, around the time of birth, or in the first couple of years. In Mason's case there are two things that MAY have contributed: THE FEVER YOU HAD IN PREGNANCY, and THE DIFFICULT DELIVERY when he didn't breathe straight away. I want to be honest that WE OFTEN CAN'T PIN IT TO ONE THING.' THEN, WHEN SHE SAYS 'SO IT WAS THE FEVER, I SHOULD HAVE GONE TO THE DOCTOR': 'I want to say this clearly: NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS, AND THERE IS NOTHING YOU COULD REASONABLY HAVE DONE TO PREVENT IT. Most people don't see a doctor for three days of fever, and WE CAN'T SAY THE FEVER CAUSED IT — only that it's one of several possibilities.' AND WHEN SHE ASKS 'WILL HE WALK?': 'I CAN'T TELL YOU THAT TODAY, AND I'M NOT GOING TO GUESS. Children with his pattern have A WIDE RANGE OF OUTCOMES. What I can tell you is that STARTING THERAPY EARLY MAKES A REAL DIFFERENCE.' THE PLAN: an MRI BRAIN to look for the cause; THYROID FUNCTION, because that is the treatable condition you always exclude; REFERRAL TO THE CHILD DEVELOPMENT TEAM AND TO PHYSIOTHERAPY AND OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY TODAY — 'WE DON'T WAIT FOR THE SCAN'; REGULAR HIP SURVEILLANCE; and early childhood funding support. SAFETY-NET: return if he STARTS LOSING SKILLS HE HAS NOW, has any FITS, becomes unwell, or she is simply worried — and close with 'CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT YOU'LL SAY TO HIS DAD TONIGHT?'
plan: OPEN, ACKNOWLEDGE, AND PIN IT DOWN: 'A CHILD NOT USING ONE ARM AND ONE LEG IS DEFINITELY NOT NORMAL, AND YOU WERE RIGHT TO BRING HIM IN. We'll work out the cause together.' Then the four pinning questions: when did you first notice, IS IT CONSTANT OR DOES IT COME AND GO, DOES HE USE THAT SIDE LESS OR NOT MOVE IT AT ALL, IS IT STIFF OR FLOPPY WHEN YOU PICK HIM UP, and IS THE RIGHT SIDE COMPLETELY NORMAL — PLUS 'IS HE IN ANY PAIN WHEN YOU MOVE IT?', because pain sends you down a completely different branch.

THE EXCLUSION QUESTION, ASKED IN WORDS: 'HAS HE EVER BEEN ABLE TO DO SOMETHING AND THEN STOPPED BEING ABLE TO DO IT?' → 'no. HE'S NEVER GONE BACKWARDS.' (Without this you cannot safely say cerebral palsy, and the role-player scores zero on that item if it is never asked.)

THE FOUR DOMAINS, OPEN THEN STEP DOWN THE LADDER. GROSS MOTOR: 'describe what movements he can do. Can he stand WITHOUT holding on? Can he stand HOLDING furniture? Does he crawl or roll? Can he sit on his own? CAN HE HOLD HIS HEAD UP?' FINE MOTOR: 'I know the left hand isn't working — TELL ME ABOUT THE RIGHT. Does he scribble? Can he pick up something small BETWEEN THUMB AND FINGER? Does he pass a toy hand to hand? ARE HIS HANDS EVER ALWAYS CLENCHED?' COMMUNICATION AND SOCIAL: clear words, babble in strings, understands a simple request; plays with other children, peekaboo, shares a smile.

BIRTH HISTORY IN THREE PHASES — THE BLOCK THAT HANDS YOU THE ANSWER. PREGNANCY: 'any complications — high blood pressure, diabetes, ANY INFECTIONS OR FEVERS? Any medications, alcohol or drugs?' → 'I HAD A FEVER AROUND FIVE MONTHS... I NEVER WENT TO THE DOCTOR.' → EXPLORE IT NEUTRALLY: 'thank you for telling me. How long did it last, and were you unwell with it?' (Reacting with anything that sounds like 'you should have gone to a doctor' makes her defensive and withdrawn — and 'was the birth normal?' as a single question throws the block away.)

DELIVERY AND AFTER: 'was he born on time or early? Vaginal or caesarean? Long or complicated? DID THEY NEED FORCEPS OR A VACUUM? Birth weight?' Then: 'DID HE CRY AND BREATHE NORMALLY STRAIGHT AWAY? DID HE NEED ANY RESUSCITATION, OR OXYGEN? ANY FITS OR SEIZURES IN THOSE FIRST DAYS? Was the heel-prick done and normal? Did he go yellow, and did that need treatment? HOW LONG DID HE STAY IN HOSPITAL?' → forceps, HE DIDN'T CRY, oxygen at the resuscitation table, five days in hospital.

CAUSES, ONE OR TWO QUESTIONS EACH: BRAIN — meningitis, encephalitis, head injury, a long seizure; THYROID — constipation, dry skin, HOARSE OR HARSH CRY; NERVE AND MUSCLE — deformities, SCISSORING OF THE LEGS when held up, AND ANY DIFFERENCE IN THE SIZE OF THE MUSCLES BETWEEN THE TWO SIDES → 'NOW THAT YOU ASK — THE LEFT SIDE DOES LOOK SMALLER.'

The general screen, and follow the emotion: vision and hearing, sleep, coughing or choking on food, family history of developmental or muscle problems, and 'How are things at home — how are you coping with all this?' → 'Honestly? I'm scared. I keep wondering if I did something wrong.' → stop the checklist for one sentence: 'That's a very natural thing to be feeling, and I'm going to tell you everything I know.' It costs five seconds and it is a marked item.

THE CARD — LOCALISE BEFORE YOU NAME, THEN COMMIT WITH THE EXCLUSION, THEN FOUR DIFFERENTIALS WITH REASONS (see dx). (Announcing cerebral palsy without ever saying UPPER MOTOR NEURONE, and without saying NO SKILLS HAVE BEEN LOST, is the automatic fail.)

EXPLAIN IT TO THE MOTHER (see dx): what cerebral palsy is, THAT THE INJURY HAPPENED ONCE AND ISN'T GETTING WORSE, the honest account of possible causes, THE BLAME REMOVED EXPLICITLY, NO PROGNOSIS INVENTED, and the plan — MRI, thyroid, CHILD DEVELOPMENT TEAM AND THERAPY TODAY WITHOUT WAITING FOR THE SCAN, hip surveillance and funding support. Then the safety-net, and 'CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT YOU'LL SAY TO HIS DAD TONIGHT?'

VARIANT — THE CARD SAYS HYPOTONIA AND REDUCED REFLEXES, WHICH CHANGES THE WHOLE ANSWER: 'the card shows REDUCED TONE WITH DEPRESSED REFLEXES AND WASTING. THAT IS A LOWER MOTOR NEURONE OR MUSCLE PATTERN, so I MOVE AWAY FROM CEREBRAL PALSY and towards A NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDER, A SPINAL CORD LESION, or CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM — WHICH IS THE TREATABLE ONE AND THE ONE I WOULD EXCLUDE FIRST, with TSH and free T4 and by CHECKING THE NEWBORN SCREENING RESULT. I would also send a CREATINE KINASE, and examine the back for A SACRAL DIMPLE OR HAIR TUFT.' (This is the single most dangerous misdiagnosis available in the station.) MILESTONES: at 18 months — walks alone, one clear word, scribbles, plays with others; at 12 months — stands holding on, babbles phrases, PINCER GRIP, peekaboo; at 9 months — sits unsupported, two-part babble and gestures, transfers a toy. Moro gone by about 6 months, ATNR by 6-7 months, and HAND PREFERENCE BEFORE 12 MONTHS IS ABNORMAL.
pefe: Role-player: Kate, 29, married, one child, works part-time in administration; supportive partner, no money worries. SHE HAS BEEN QUIETLY WORRIED FOR MONTHS AND TOLD HERSELF SHE WAS IMAGINING IT — since Mason started trying to walk it has become obvious. THE PROBLEM: he barely moves the left arm and left leg, IT IS STIFF NOT FLOPPY, it has always been like this, HE HAS NEVER LOST A SKILL, and he is NOT in pain. MILESTONES: sits well, good head control, pulls to stand but CANNOT STAND ALONE, SHUFFLES rather than crawls; THE RIGHT HAND IS EXCELLENT — scribbles and pincer grip — and THE LEFT IS ALWAYS IN A FIST; says mama, dada and two other words, understands 'no' and 'come here'; very smiley, loves peekaboo, plays with others.

PREGNANCY: A FEVER AT ABOUT FIVE MONTHS — three days of aches and temperature — SHE NEVER SAW A DOCTOR AND FEELS GUILTY ABOUT IT. No medications, alcohol or drugs. DELIVERY: on time, A VERY LONG LABOUR, FORCEPS, 3.5 kg. AFTER BIRTH: HE DID NOT CRY STRAIGHT AWAY, was taken to the resuscitation table AND GIVEN OXYGEN, and stayed in hospital ABOUT FIVE DAYS; no jaundice, no seizures, heel-prick normal. Everything else normal — no meningitis, head injury or seizures; bowels normal; cry normal; sees and hears well; sleeps well; no choking; no family history.

HOW TO PLAY IT: start worried but composed — YOU HAVE REHEARSED SAYING THIS IN YOUR HEAD. ONLY MENTION THE FEVER IF ASKED ABOUT THE PREGNANCY, and when you do, LOOK AWAY AND ADD 'I NEVER WENT TO THE DOCTOR.' THE FORCEPS AND 'HE DIDN'T CRY' DETAILS ARE THE GOLD — GIVE THEM ONLY WHEN ASKED, BUT GIVE THEM FULLY, WITH FEELING: 'IT FELT LIKE FOREVER.' Only mention the smaller muscles on the left IF ASKED ABOUT A DIFFERENCE IN MUSCLE SIZE. If asked how you are coping: 'I'M SCARED. I KEEP WONDERING IF I DID SOMETHING WRONG' — and if never asked, VOLUNTEER IT AT ABOUT 5:30. WHEN THE DIAGNOSIS IS GIVEN, GO QUIET, THEN SAY 'SO IT WAS THE FEVER. I SHOULD HAVE GONE TO THE DOCTOR' AND BECOME TEARFUL. THEN ASK THE HARD QUESTION: 'WILL HE WALK?' — SETTLE ONLY IF THE CANDIDATE DECLINES TO GUESS AND OFFERS A CONCRETE PLAN, AND STAY DISTRESSED IF THEY PROMISE HE WILL BE FINE. IF THE CANDIDATE IMPLIES YOU SHOULD HAVE SEEN A DOCTOR, BECOME DEFENSIVE AND WITHDRAW.
