back.dx: VERSION A — AN INFECTED THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST. THE LAY MECHANISM: 'the thyroid is a gland at the front of the neck. BEFORE BIRTH IT FORMS AT THE BASE OF THE TONGUE AND MOVES DOWN TO THE LOWER NECK. Sometimes PART OF THAT PATH STAYS OPEN AND FORMS A SMALL SAC — that's the cyst. IT CAN SIT QUIETLY FOR YEARS; then it gets inflamed or infected — OFTEN AFTER A COLD, LIKE HIS — and becomes bigger, warm and sore, WHICH IS WHY YOU'VE ONLY NOTICED IT NOW.' THE REASONS: 'it is EXACTLY IN THE MIDLINE, it MOVES UP WHEN HE SWALLOWS AND WHEN HE POKES HIS TONGUE OUT — THAT'S THE GIVEAWAY FOR THIS SAC — and it is WARM AND SORE, which is the inflammation.' THE SPECIFIC DIFFERENTIALS: other THYROID problems — an enlarged thyroid, a nodule, or ECTOPIC THYROID TISSUE; then LYMPH NODES swelling with infection — ear infections, tonsillitis, a sore throat, a runny nose, DENTAL infections, SKIN infections, a chest infection, or a node that simply stays up for weeks after a virus; then, BECAUSE OF YOUR WORRY, CANCERS OF THE BLOOD — LEUKAEMIA AND LYMPHOMA, WHICH ARE RARE IN CHILDREN; and at the bottom, A BRANCHIAL CYST, WHICH SITS ON THE SIDE OF THE NECK, and a DERMOID CYST. THEN CLOSE THE CONCERN EXPLICITLY: 'I know you were worried about lymphoma. I DON'T THINK THAT'S WHAT THIS IS: the lump is IN THE MIDDLE, it MOVES WITH HIS TONGUE, it's SORE AND WARM RATHER THAN PAINLESS AND HARD, he has NO weight loss, tiredness, sweats, bruising or other lumps, and HE'S GROWING WELL.' THE PLAN: examine him today, ULTRASOUND OF THE NECK AND A THYROID BLOOD TEST, AN ANTIBIOTIC for the infection with analgesia, REVIEW IN TWO DAYS, and referral to a paediatric ENT surgeon — 'the usual treatment is A SMALL OPERATION TO REMOVE THE SAC ONCE THE INFECTION HAS SETTLED, SO IT DOESN'T KEEP COMING BACK.' VERSION B — POST-VIRAL LYMPHADENOPATHY: 'lymph nodes are GLANDS IN THE NECK, PART OF THE IMMUNE SYSTEM; they get bigger when the body fights an infection — HIS FLU A MONTH AGO — and IT'S NORMAL FOR THEM TO STAY UP FOR A FEW WEEKS AFTER THE INFECTION HAS GONE, EVEN THOUGH HE'S WELL.' Close the concern with BOTH the history negatives AND the examination: THE GLAND HAS NORMAL FEATURES — SOFT, MOBILE, NOT STUCK DOWN OR HARD — NO OTHER ENLARGED GLANDS, NO SPLENOMEGALY, AND HE ISN'T PALE. PLAN: reassure and observe — 'it's been three weeks; I'D EXPECT IT TO SETTLE BY SIX. I'll see him again in THREE WEEKS, and if the gland is still there we'll examine him again and decide about tests.' RETURN SOONER IF: it grows, new lumps appear, or he loses weight, looks pale, gets tired, or has fevers, sweats or bruising — WRITTEN DOWN.
plan: ACKNOWLEDGE THE COUSIN EARLY: 'I can understand how frightening that is, with what happened to his cousin. IT'S A VERY FAIR WORRY AND WE'LL WORK IT OUT TOGETHER.' ('I'm sure it's nothing' at the door is the first trap — acknowledge, PROMISE TO RETURN TO IT, AND RETURN TO IT.)

SITE AND TIMING — AND THE QUESTION THAT SPLITS THE DIAGNOSIS: 'where exactly is it — can you show me? IS IT IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NECK OR OFF TO ONE SIDE?' → she says 'IN THE NECK' until you ask. → 'in the middle, just below his chin.' Then: when did you first notice it, IS THIS THE FIRST TIME, IS IT GETTING BIGGER.

CHARACTER, TAKEN AS HISTORY AND PREFACED HONESTLY: 'some of these are things I'd normally check by examining him, BUT YOU KNOW THE LUMP BEST. HOW BIG IS IT — A PEA, A GRAPE, A WALNUT? Is it HARD OR SOFT? Is it PAINFUL when you touch it? DOES IT MOVE FREELY, OR FEEL STUCK UNDER THE SKIN? Any REDNESS OR CHANGE IN THE SKIN over it? IS IT WARM TO TOUCH?' → a grape, not sure about consistency or mobility, sore, slightly pink, WARM.

THYROID — AND THE DISCRIMINATOR: 'does he feel the heat or the cold more than other people? Any diarrhoea or constipation? DOES THE LUMP MOVE WHEN HE SWALLOWS? AND WHEN HE STICKS HIS TONGUE OUT?' → yes to both. (Skipping the tongue question because swallowing was already positive is the named trap — TONGUE PROTRUSION IS THE DISCRIMINATOR.)

THE INFECTION SCREEN, REGION BY REGION: fever or chills; RECENT FLU-LIKE ILLNESS; sore throat, runny nose, ear pain; cough or shortness of breath; RASHES OR SKIN INFECTIONS ON THE HEAD, NECK OR SCALP; TOOTHACHE OR DENTAL PROBLEMS; and RECENT TRAVEL, SICK CONTACTS OR ANIMALS — CATS. → a cold two weeks ago, everything else negative.

THE MALIGNANCY SCREEN — and this is what lets you close her fear with evidence: 'any WEIGHT LOSS? Loss of appetite? ANY OTHER LUMPS OR BUMPS ANYWHERE? More tired than usual — ANY DROP IN SCHOOL PERFORMANCE? NIGHT SWEATS? BONE PAIN, OR BLEEDING OR BRUISING EASILY?' Then growth and development, and the well-child questions.
BINDSMA, BRIEFLY: pregnancy, immunisations, other medical problems, medicines, allergies, and anything else in the family.
NAME IT WITH THE LAY MECHANISM AND WHY NOW, THEN THE THREE REASONS (see dx) → 'WHY DIDN'T I SEE IT FOR ELEVEN YEARS?' → because the sac sits quietly until it gets inflamed.

THE SPECIFIC DIFFERENTIALS, THEN CLOSE THE CANCER CONCERN WITH ITS OWN REASONS, THEN THE PLAN (see dx) → 'SHOULDN'T HE HAVE A BLOOD TEST TODAY?' → 'I understand why you'd want that. I'm arranging AN ULTRASOUND AND A THYROID BLOOD TEST, because those answer the question THIS lump is asking. A blood test looking for leukaemia isn't needed on what I've found today — HE HAS NONE OF THE WARNING SIGNS — BUT IF ANYTHING CHANGES, WE DO IT STRAIGHT AWAY.'

VARIANTS: IF THE EXAMINER REPORTS A RED FLAG — a HARD, FIXED node with A SPLEEN 3 cm BELOW THE COSTAL MARGIN: 'thank you. THAT CHANGES MY PLAN... the gland and the spleen AREN'T WHAT I'D EXPECT AFTER A VIRUS, so I want TESTS TODAY rather than waiting: a BLOOD COUNT AND FILM, and I'm going to speak to the children's hospital NOW about seeing him urgently. I'M NOT SAYING IT'S CANCER — I'M SAYING IT NEEDS LOOKING AT PROPERLY AND QUICKLY.' / A TENDER, WARM LATERAL LUMP WITH FEVER AND A SORE THROAT: 'most likely A GLAND FIGHTING A BACTERIAL INFECTION — a LYMPHADENITIS. Examine the throat and ears, start an antibiotic, review in two days; IF IT BECOMES FLUCTUANT IT MAY NEED DRAINING.' VERIFY / IF SHE MENTIONS CATS: 'that's useful — CATS CAN CAUSE A GLAND TO SWELL FOR WEEKS FROM A SCRATCH, called CAT-SCRATCH DISEASE. It usually settles on its own; I'll check for a scratch mark and, if the gland persists, a blood test can confirm it.'
pefe: Role-player (Version A): Michelle, 41, teacher's aide, mother of Oliver, 11. Oliver is WELL — plays football, thriving at school, normal pregnancy, immunised, no medicines, no allergies. HER NEPHEW, OLIVER'S 14-YEAR-OLD COUSIN, WAS DIAGNOSED WITH HODGKIN LYMPHOMA LAST YEAR, AND THE FIRST SIGN WAS A NECK LUMP. Oliver had A COLD TWO WEEKS AGO. She noticed the lump TEN DAYS AGO: IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NECK BELOW THE CHIN, GRAPE-SIZED, WARM, SORE TO PRESS, SLIGHTLY PINK, MOVES UP ON SWALLOWING AND ON POKING HIS TONGUE OUT, and UNCHANGED IN SIZE. REGISTER: FRIGHTENED AND A LITTLE CLIPPED, softening when the cousin is acknowledged.

How to play it: say 'It's in the neck' until asked middle or side. Answer 'I'm not sure' to hard-or-soft and to mobility. Hidden agenda: you have been googling and think he needs a scan and blood tests today — volunteer it if asked about your concerns, otherwise late: 'Shouldn't he have a blood test?' and if the doctor never mentions cancer at the end, ask: 'But are you sure it's not cancer?'

back.dx: VERSION A — NEPHROTIC SYNDROME. TO THE FATHER, IN PLAIN WORDS: 'THE KIDNEYS WORK LIKE A VERY FINE FILTER — THEY LET WASTE OUT AND KEEP PROTEIN IN. In this condition THE FILTER BECOMES LEAKY AND PROTEIN ESCAPES INTO THE URINE. PROTEIN IS WHAT HOLDS FLUID INSIDE THE BLOOD VESSELS, so when it drops THE FLUID SEEPS OUT INTO THE TISSUES — AND IT SHOWS FIRST WHERE THE SKIN IS THINNEST, AROUND THE EYES.' Never say albumin, oncotic pressure or proteinuria to a parent — the role-player looks blank and says 'sorry, I didn't follow that'. THE REASONS, WHICH THE TASK EXPLICITLY DEMANDS: A LARGE AMOUNT OF PROTEIN AND NO BLOOD on the dipstick; the swelling is BILATERAL AND WORSE IN THE MORNING; there is FLUID IN THE ABDOMEN AND AT BOTH LUNG BASES; and THE BLOOD PRESSURE IS NORMAL, WHICH ARGUES AGAINST THE OTHER KIDNEY CONDITION. THE DIFFERENTIALS IN THREE GROUPS, NOT AS A LIST: (1) THE EYE — ORBITAL CELLULITIS, excluded because the eye is white with FULL PAINLESS MOVEMENTS and he is afebrile; PRESEPTAL CELLULITIS, for the same reasons; and a STYE OR CHALAZION, which would be ONE LID, NOT FOUR. (2) ALLERGY — a reaction or ANGIOEDEMA, against which there is NO TRIGGER, NO ITCH AND NO RASH, and you screened for anaphylaxis. (3) FLUID RETENTION — renal, and within that NEPHROTIC SYNDROME, POST-STREPTOCOCCAL GLOMERULONEPHRITIS and IgA NEPHROPATHY; then CARDIAC FAILURE, CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE, HYPOTHYROIDISM and PROTEIN-LOSING ENTEROPATHY. MANAGEMENT AND REASSURANCE: 'IT ISN'T ANYTHING YOU DID. It is serious enough that HE NEEDS TO COME INTO HOSPITAL, but the common form in four-year-olds — ABOUT NINE IN TEN — USUALLY RESPONDS WELL TO STEROID TREATMENT.' Confirm with a URINE PROTEIN:CREATININE RATIO on a first-morning sample, SERUM ALBUMIN and bloods, with nephrology involved today. VERSION A2 — POST-STREPTOCOCCAL GLOMERULONEPHRITIS: 'after a throat infection with a particular bacterium, THE IMMUNE SYSTEM MAKES ANTIBODIES, and A COUPLE OF WEEKS LATER those can INFLAME THE FILTERS in the kidney. That's why there's BLOOD in the urine, why he's PASSING LESS, why his BLOOD PRESSURE IS UP, and why he's swollen.' Investigations: urine microscopy for RED CELL CASTS, electrolytes, C3 LOW WITH NORMAL C4, ASOT or anti-DNase B, throat swab. Management: SALT AND FLUID RESTRICTION, DAILY WEIGHTS, blood pressure monitoring, a diuretic if overloaded — most children recover fully, and RECHECK C3 AT EIGHT WEEKS. VERSION B — ORBITAL CELLULITIS: 'I'm concerned about AN INFECTION IN THE TISSUES BEHIND THE EYE. It usually STARTS IN THE SINUSES AND SPREADS THROUGH A VERY THIN PIECE OF BONE into the eye socket. The reasons are that it is ONLY ONE EYE, the eye itself is RED, he has A FEVER, and ABOVE ALL IT HURTS HIM TO MOVE IT — THAT IS WHAT TELLS ME THE INFECTION IS BEHIND THE EYE RATHER THAN IN THE LID.' Admit; IV ANTIBIOTICS STARTED NOW, NOT AFTER THE SCAN; urgent CT ORBITS AND SINUSES WITH CONTRAST; blood cultures and inflammatory markers; ophthalmology and ENT today; HOURLY ACUITY, COLOUR VISION AND PUPIL CHECKS; and surgery for an abscess or no improvement at 24-48 hours. VERSION B-MINUS — PRESEPTAL: 'this is an infection of THE EYELID TISSUE IN FRONT OF THE EYE, NOT BEHIND IT. I can say that because HIS EYE MOVES FREELY AND IT DOESN'T HURT HIM TO MOVE IT, his vision is normal and THE EYE ITSELF ISN'T RED' — oral antibiotics, review tomorrow, NO SCAN, and return sooner if it spreads, the eye becomes red or painful to move, vision changes, or he becomes febrile. BEING ABLE TO SEPARATE THOSE TWO OUT LOUD, WITH THE REASON ATTACHED, IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE THIRTY SECONDS IN THE STATION.
plan: FRAME THE THREE BUCKETS — it costs eight seconds: 'I can see his eyes are puffy. SWELLING AROUND A CHILD'S EYE COMES FROM ONE OF THREE PLACES — A PROBLEM IN THE EYE OR THE EYELID ITSELF, AN ALLERGIC REACTION, OR FLUID THE BODY IS HOLDING ONTO — so I'm going to ask about each of those in turn, then examine him, then tell you what I think.'

CHARACTERISE, AND ASK LATERALITY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: 'when did it start? Has it happened before? Is it getting worse? IS IT ONE EYE OR BOTH? IS IT ONE EYELID OR BOTH EYELIDS? IS IT WORSE AT ANY PARTICULAR TIME OF DAY?' → both eyes, all four lids, WORST FIRST THING IN THE MORNING and better by the afternoon. (Taking a full history without ever establishing laterality is the first trap — those two questions delete most of the differential in ten seconds.)

BUCKET 1, THE EYE — NEVER SKIPPED: 'any blurring of his vision, or bumping into things? ANY PAIN IN THE EYE? ANY PAIN WHEN HE MOVES HIS EYE OR LOOKS AROUND? Any redness — IN THE LIDS, AND IN THE EYE ITSELF? Any discharge, or stuck shut in the mornings? Are they itchy? ANY FEVER OR CHILLS? Any blocked nose, headache or pain in the face?' (Skipping straight to the kidney is what examiners have watched candidates do for years — and in the orbital cellulitis version it is the difference between a pass and a miss.)

BUCKET 2, ALLERGY — forty-five seconds that buy you an explicit anaphylaxis screen AND one of the three differential groups: 'what was he doing just before it started? Any new food or medicine? ANY INSECT BITE OR STING? Any known allergies, asthma, eczema or hay fever? Any rash anywhere? ANY SWELLING OF HIS LIPS OR TONGUE? ANY NOISY BREATHING?'

BUCKET 3, FLUID — RENAL FIRST, AND ASKED PRECISELY: 'any change in HOW MUCH WEE he's passing? IS IT FROTHY OR BUBBLY? IS IT DARK, OR BLOODY — LIKE COLA OR TEA? Has he had A SORE THROAT OR ANY SKIN SORES recently — AND HOW LONG BEFORE THE SWELLING STARTED? Did he see a doctor or take antibiotics for it?' → he is going less, AND IT'S BEEN REALLY BUBBLY — given only because you asked. (Accepting 'his wee's a funny colour' without splitting FROTHY from DARK is the named trap: frothy is protein and nephrotic, cola is blood and glomerulonephritis — different diseases, different treatments.)

THE REST OF BUCKET 3: 'any swelling of his legs or feet? Any chest pain or breathlessness when he runs and plays? DOES HE EVER GO BLUE? Any yellowing of his eyes or skin? Any pale stools or dark urine? Is he bothered by the cold? Constipated? Dry skin? Any tummy pain, vomiting or diarrhoea? HAS HIS TUMMY LOOKED SWOLLEN?' → ankles puffy in the evening, AND HIS TUMMY HAS LOOKED BLOATED FOR A FEW DAYS — the second withheld finding.

THE EXAMINATION, AND THE ORDER IS THE POINT: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, any rash, ANY STRIDOR, and his growth? ALL THE VITAL SIGNS, PARTICULARLY THE BLOOD PRESSURE AND THE TEMPERATURE. I'D LIKE TO EXAMINE THE EYE FIRST: any redness, any discharge, ANY PROPTOSIS? VISUAL ACUITY? Pupils? ARE THE EYE MOVEMENTS FULL, AND IS THERE PAIN ON MOVEMENT? Thyroid. Respiratory — equal air entry, added sounds, ANY DULLNESS AT THE BASES? Cardiovascular. Abdomen — distension, tenderness, organomegaly, ballotable kidneys, SHIFTING DULLNESS? Lower limbs for PITTING OEDEMA. AND A URINE DIPSTICK.' → 'WHAT WERE YOU LOOKING FOR ON THE DIPSTICK?' → 'TWO THINGS: PROTEIN AND BLOOD.' (Asking for the abdomen before the eye, or reciting every dipstick pad, both lose marks. And missing the blood pressure leaves you unable to separate nephritic from nephrotic.)
THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS, WITH SUPPORTING AND EXCLUDING REASONS (see dx) → 'IS THAT SERIOUS? IS IT SOMETHING WE DID?' → no, and the hospital admission with the nine-in-ten steroid response.
THE DIFFERENTIALS IN THREE GROUPS, NOT AS A LIST (see dx), each with the reason it is excluded. → and late, if never invited: 'SHOULD I HAVE BROUGHT HIM IN EARLIER?'

VERSION A2 — PSGN: 'this is a different kidney condition. After a throat infection with a particular bacterium, THE IMMUNE SYSTEM MAKES ANTIBODIES, and a couple of weeks later those can INFLAME THE FILTERS in the kidney. That's why there's BLOOD in the urine, why he's passing less, WHY HIS BLOOD PRESSURE IS UP, and why he's swollen.' Investigations: urine microscopy for RED CELL CASTS, electrolytes, C3 AND C4, ASOT or anti-DNase B, throat swab. Management: SALT AND FLUID RESTRICTION, DAILY WEIGHTS, blood pressure monitoring, diuretic if overloaded, and RECHECK C3 AT EIGHT WEEKS. TIMING: PSGN follows a sore throat by 1-2 WEEKS and a skin infection by 3-6 WEEKS — whereas IgA NEPHROPATHY gives haematuria 1-2 DAYS INTO THE ILLNESS, so calling a two-day post-viral haematuria post-streptococcal is wrong.

VERSION B — ORBITAL CELLULITIS: 'THIS CHANGES THINGS' — then the explanation (see dx), then ADMIT, IV ANTIBIOTICS NOW NOT AFTER THE SCAN, urgent CT ORBITS AND SINUSES WITH CONTRAST, blood cultures, ophthalmology and ENT today, HOURLY ACUITY, COLOUR VISION AND PUPIL CHECKS, and surgery for an abscess or no improvement at 24-48 hours. / VERSION B-MINUS — PRESEPTAL: oral antibiotics, review tomorrow, NO SCAN, with return criteria. / IF ASKED FOR INVESTIGATIONS INSTEAD OF DIFFERENTIALS, ANSWER THE WHOLE CHILD: 'bedside — urine dipstick, A URINE PROTEIN:CREATININE RATIO ON A FIRST-MORNING SAMPLE, microscopy and culture. Bloods — electrolytes and creatinine, SERUM ALBUMIN, full blood count, lipids, C3 AND C4, ASOT or anti-DNase B, liver function, TSH, AND HEPATITIS AND VARICELLA SEROLOGY BEFORE ANY STEROID. Imaging — renal ultrasound if there is renal impairment or an atypical picture. AND A KIDNEY BIOPSY IS NOT FIRST-LINE IN A TYPICAL FOUR-YEAR-OLD — it is for atypical features or steroid resistance, and that decision belongs with nephrology.'
pefe: Role-player: Daniel, 36, works in logistics; partner at home with the baby; father of Sam, 4. He has brought Sam in because HIS EYES HAVE BEEN PUFFY FOR ABOUT A WEEK AND THE CHILDCARE CENTRE COMMENTED ON IT. REGISTER: CALM, COOPERATIVE, SLIGHTLY PUZZLED RATHER THAN FRIGHTENED — HE HALF EXPECTS TO BE TOLD IT IS AN ALLERGY, and becomes concerned ONLY WHEN THE DOCTOR MENTIONS HOSPITAL. HIDDEN AGENDA: he is quietly worried he missed something, because it has been a week and he did not come sooner — raised late: 'SHOULD I HAVE BROUGHT HIM IN EARLIER?'

THE DETAILS HE HOLDS BACK — THE TWO FINDINGS THAT MAKE THE CASE: THE BUBBLY URINE AND THE BLOATED TUMMY. DO NOT VOLUNTEER EITHER. Give the urine detail ONLY if asked whether it is FROTHY OR BUBBLY; give the tummy ONLY if asked about ABDOMINAL SWELLING OR TUMMY PAIN. IF ASKED A VAGUE 'ANYTHING ELSE?', SAY NO. If asked 'is his urine normal?', say 'I THINK SO' — and only if they ask frothy or bubbly do you say yes. Background: Sam is otherwise well, MILD ECZEMA, immunised, no medicines or allergies, growing normally, NO family history of kidney disease; he had a runny nose and cough a fortnight ago, NO sore throat, NO skin sores.

HOW TO PLAY IT: answer only what is asked, and answer briefly. IF THEY ASK ABOUT THE EYE AT ALL, BE CLEARLY REASSURING — no pain, no redness, normal vision, normal movements. IF THEY NEVER ASK A SINGLE QUESTION ABOUT THE EYE ITSELF, SAY NOTHING AND MARK THEM DOWN. IF THEY USE WORDS LIKE ALBUMIN, ONCOTIC PRESSURE OR PROTEINURIA, LOOK BLANK AND SAY 'SORRY, I DIDN'T FOLLOW THAT.' When they mention hospital, become worried: 'HOSPITAL? IS IT SERIOUS?' Ask 'IS IT SOMETHING WE DID?' once the diagnosis is given, and close with 'WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?' MARK OUT OF 10: framed the history naming the three groups; ONE EYE OR BOTH AND ONE LID OR BOTH; AT LEAST FOUR EYE QUESTIONS INCLUDING PAIN ON EYE MOVEMENT; asked whether THE EYE ITSELF was red, separately from the lids; screened allergy INCLUDING LIPS, TONGUE AND NOISY BREATHING; ASKED WHETHER THE URINE WAS FROTHY AND FOUND IT; ASKED ABOUT ABDOMINAL SWELLING AND FOUND IT; asked for THE EYE EXAMINATION FIRST plus blood pressure and temperature; asked for a dipstick AND NAMED PROTEIN AND BLOOD; and gave the diagnosis WITH REASONS AND EXCLUDED THE ALTERNATIVES OUT LOUD. AUTOMATIC FAIL: asked nothing about the eye itself; never asked for a urine dipstick; named a diagnosis with no supporting reasons; or in Version B, did not recognise orbital cellulitis or sent the child home on oral antibiotics.
The preceding illness — A runny nose and cough a fortnight ago — no sore throat, no skin sores

The two findings the father withholds — THE URINE IS REALLY BUBBLY IN THE TOILET, given ONLY if you ask frothy or bubbly; and HIS TUMMY HAS LOOKED BLOATED FOR A FEW DAYS, given ONLY if you ask about abdominal swelling

time: Open and address the concern, then signpost three parts · the patches: how long, first time, spreading, do they WIPE off and is the skin red underneath, feeding, fever, dribbling, unusual crying · source and other sites: other rashes including the nappy area and skin folds; breast, bottle or both; any pain, cracking, shininess or white patches on your nipples; dummy or bottle teats; and any thrush or discharge around the time of birth · drugs: any antibiotics recently, for him or for you while breastfeeding; steroid creams, puffers or medicines · then the immune screen, which is the pass/fail block, prefaced honestly: 'I'd like to ask about his general health, because thrush sometimes shows up when the body's defences are lower. back.dx: ORAL CANDIDIASIS — oral thrush — with chronic pale greasy diarrhoea that must be linked and screened. Explain it in plain words: 'Sam most likely has oral thrush. It's a yeast called candida that lives harmlessly in most people's mouths; in babies it sometimes overgrows because their immune system is still maturing. The creamy patches that don't WIPE off, with a red base, are typical. It's common, it's not caused by anything you've done — it's not about cleanliness — and it's treatable.' then the two additions that carry the station. First, treat both: 'Thrush passes back and forth between a baby's mouth and mum's nipples, so I'd treat you both.' Second, link and screen — and the examiner's checklist item reads links the thrush to the chronic diarrhoea and names the screen: 'And this is why I asked so many questions. Thrush is more likely when the body's defences are a little lower. He's had loose, greasy stools for a month; with the thrush, I'd like to check his gut is absorbing food properly and his immune system is working: confirm his newborn screening result, a sweat test for cystic fibrosis, and some blood tests. Most babies I check are completely fine.' On its own the diarrhoea would be watched — together with the thrush it is checked. When she asks 'Cystic fibrosis — isn't that really serious?': 'It is serious, which is exactly why I'd rather check than assume; his normal heel-prick makes it unlikely, but the test isn't perfect, and the check is simple.' Note that coeliac cannot be assessed yet, because he started solids only last week. The plan: antifungal drops or gel after feeds for one to two weeks, continued a couple of days past clearing; antifungal cream for her nipples after each feed; antifungal cream for the nappy rash; boil the dummy daily and sterilise teats; and keep breastfeeding. Review in two weeks — sooner if he stops feeding, has a fever, is drowsy or has fewer wet nappies — and if it keeps returning or his weight drops, refer to the children's hospital. Version B — antibiotics and no diarrhoea: 'That's the likely trigger — antibiotics knock back the friendly bacteria and let the yeast overgrow. His bowels are normal, he's growing well, no unusual infections, so I'm not concerned about his immune system' — treat, sterilise the teats, review in two weeks. Harder variant — growth has dropped: 'That changes things. I'll weigh him today, arrange the sweat test and bloods this week, and phone the paediatric team today.' and if she declines the tests — 'He's fine, I just want the cream': 'You'll have the treatment today regardless; the tests are simple, and if they're normal we can both stop worrying.'
plan: OPEN, ADDRESS THE CONCERN, AND SIGNPOST: 'I can see that's worrying. Let me ask some questions about the patches, THEN ABOUT HIS HEALTH GENERALLY, and then I'll explain what I think is going on.' Then the patches: how long, first time, spreading, DO THEY WIPE OFF, IS IT RED UNDERNEATH, feeding, fever, dribbling, unusual crying. → two weeks, spread from tongue to cheeks, DOESN'T WIPE OFF AND LOOKED RED AND RAW UNDERNEATH. (Stopping to explain after three questions is the trap — THE DIAGNOSIS IS NOT THE POINT, THE SCREEN IS.)

SOURCE AND OTHER SITES: 'any other rashes or white patches — NAPPY AREA, NECK FOLDS? Breast, bottle or both? ANY PAIN, CRACKING, SHININESS OR WHITE PATCHES ON YOUR NIPPLES? Dummy or bottle teats? Any thrush or discharge around the time of his birth?' → a nappy rash that won't clear, fully breastfed, AND — only because you asked — 'MY NIPPLES HAVE BEEN STINGING AFTER FEEDS AND LOOK SHINY.' (Treating the baby and not the mother is the named trap, and the role-player mentions the nipples ONLY if asked.)
DRUGS: 'any antibiotics recently — FOR HIM OR FOR YOU WHILE BREASTFEEDING? Any steroid creams, puffers or medicines? Any regular medicines at all?'

THE IMMUNE SCREEN — THE PASS/FAIL BLOCK, PREFACED SO IT MAKES SENSE: 'I'd like to ask about his general health, BECAUSE THRUSH SOMETIMES SHOWS UP WHEN THE BODY'S DEFENCES ARE LOWER. HOW ARE HIS BOWEL MOTIONS?' → 'he's actually had LOOSE POOS FOR ABOUT A MONTH.' → THEN EXPLORE IT PROPERLY: 'how long has that been going on? Every day or on and off? Getting worse? WHAT DO THEY LOOK LIKE — WATERY, GREASY, PALE, BULKY, SMELLY? Any blood or mucus? How many a day?' → four or five a day, PALE AND GREASY, quite smelly, no blood. (Hearing 'loose poos for a month' and moving on is the fail — THE MARKS ARE IN EXPLORING IT AND LINKING IT.)

THE REST OF THE SCREEN: 'WAS HIS HEEL-PRICK TEST DONE AND NORMAL? Has he had MANY INFECTIONS, OR ANY THAT WERE SERIOUS? Has he STARTED SOLIDS — ANYTHING WITH WHEAT? Any lumps or bumps, pale colour, easy bruising?' → heel prick fine, one cold, rice cereal started last week.

WELL-BABY, ANTENATAL AND GROWTH: alert and active, drinking, wet nappies; 'ANY INFECTIONS IN THE PREGNANCY? WERE ALL YOUR ANTENATAL BLOOD TESTS AND SCREENING NORMAL?'; term, special care; immunisations and development; 'IS HE GAINING WEIGHT AS EXPECTED ON THE GROWTH CHART?'; family history of immune problems, cystic fibrosis, coeliac or bowel disease; and who is at home and how she is coping. (Asking 'DO YOU HAVE HIV?' COLD is the trap — USE THE ANTENATAL-SCREEN ROUTE, and if she asks why, explain honestly.)
Explain the thrush in plain words, and remove the blame (see dx) → 'Did I give it to him?' → 'No — the yeast is normal, it's not about cleanliness.'

THE TWO ADDITIONS: TREAT BOTH OF THEM, THEN LINK THE DIARRHOEA AND NAME THE SCREEN (see dx) → 'CYSTIC FIBROSIS? ISN'T THAT REALLY SERIOUS?' → soften it with the normal heel-prick and the low likelihood, WITHOUT pretending the test is perfect. (Explaining thrush fluently and never saying the word DIARRHOEA is how this station is failed.)

THE PLAN AND SAFETY-NET (see dx): antifungal for him after feeds, ANTIFUNGAL CREAM FOR HER NIPPLES, the nappy rash, BOIL THE DUMMY DAILY, keep breastfeeding, review in two weeks, and return sooner if he stops feeding, has a fever, is drowsy or has fewer wet nappies. Then a one-line summary: THRUSH, TREAT YOU BOTH, AND A FEW CHECKS BECAUSE OF THE DIARRHOEA.

HER CONCERN: the white patches are 'SOMETHING BAD', AND SHE MAY HAVE CAUSED THEM BY NOT CLEANING HIS MOUTH. HIDDEN AGENDA: she has had STINGING, SHINY NIPPLES FOR TWO WEEKS AND IS EMBARRASSED TO MENTION IT — REVEAL ONLY IF ASKED ABOUT NIPPLES OR BREASTFEEDING PROBLEMS. How to play it: answer only what is asked. Do not volunteer the diarrhoea or the nipple pain. setting: History, examination findings and explanation — regional GP. Age adaptation must be audible: no pain questions to a 15-month-old — the mother looks puzzled and says 'He can't tell me, he's one'. The timing question replaces pain: has the limp been there since his very first steps. And the AUTO-FAIL is the birth history: she says 'A caesarean' and will not say breech unless you ask — then breech must chain immediately to hip ultrasound, the six-week check and family history. A normal six-week check does not exclude DDH. And never promise a brace — a 15-month-old is past that window.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. JAYDEN, 15 MONTHS, brought in by his mother KELLY: 'HE'S NOT WALKING PROPERLY — HE LIMPS.' Well child, afebrile, immunisations up to date. He PULLED TO STAND AT 12-13 MONTHS and took INDEPENDENT STEPS ABOUT A MONTH AGO, AND SHE HAS NOTICED THE LIMP SINCE HE STARTED WALKING.

History FIVE MINUTES, then the examiner HANDS YOU A CARD OF EXAMINATION FINDINGS AND AN X-RAY, then explain the most likely diagnosis WITH YOUR REASONS to the mother. 8 minutes. IN THE FACE-TO-FACE FORMAT you ask the examiner for the findings instead.

Read the card of physical examination findings and the X-ray — or, face to face, ask the examiner for the findings
Explain the most likely diagnosis, with your reasons, to the mother
time: WIPE, open and acknowledge without reassuring · do not agree with grandma, because a limp from first steps in a well child is a structural hip until proven otherwise · explore the limp: can he stand and bear weight on both legs, which leg does he favour, when did he pull to stand and take his first steps, has the limp been there since those very first steps or did it start later, is it getting worse, anything better or worse · then what she sees and the septic-hip screen: swelling or redness at hips, knees or ankles; deformity, a foot turning in, a leg that looks shorter; does he cry when you change his nappy or move the leg; fever; has there ever been a time he wouldn't weight-bear at all; recent illness · then the birth history, signposted and deep: 'Because this has been there since his first steps, I need to go back to when he was born' · pregnancy, medications, delivery, forceps or vacuum, was he breech, was he your first, term, special care, was he swaddled tightly, did he have his six-week check and was anything said about his hips, did he ever have a hip ultrasound, and anyone in the family with hip problems as a child · then the other three domains in thirty seconds: pincer grip, babble and words, stranger awareness and peekaboo, plus floppy or stiff as a baby and when he sat · then trauma, NAI, growth and binds · then summarise, read the findings aloud and translate them, and explain ball and socket with the normal side first.
findings: LEFT LEG 2 cm SHORTER — THIGH CREASES ASYMMETRIC — LEFT HIP ABDUCTION RESTRICTED — AFEBRILE, NO WARMTH OR TENDERNESS — Barlow and Ortolani NEGATIVE — neurology and spine normal — weight 50th centile
The right hip is normal; on the left the femoral head sits high and lateral to a shallow socket, and Shenton's line is broken

back.dx: Developmental dysplasia of the left hip. Read the findings aloud and translate them: 'The left leg is 2 centimetres shorter, the thigh creases are asymmetric and left hip abduction is restricted, in an afebrile child with no warmth or tenderness. On the x-ray the right hip is normal; on the left the ball sits high and outside a shallow socket, and the smooth curve we call Shenton's line is broken.' then explain it, normal side first, in plain words: 'The hip is a ball-and-socket joint — the round TOP of the thigh bone sits in a cup in the pelvis. In Jayden's left hip the cup didn't form deeply enough, so the ball has slipped up and out of it. That's why his left leg is shorter, why the skin folds on his thighs don't match, and why that hip doesn't open out as far — and it's why he LIMPS.' The reasons and the blame removed: 'Being breech, being a first baby and having a family history all make it more likely — none of that is anything you did. It's called developmental because the hip can look normal early on and slip out later as the baby grows, so it can be missed at six weeks even by a careful examiner. What matters is that we've found it now, while treatment is still straightforward.' What happens next, with honest expectations: x-ray today, phone the children's orthopaedic team so he is seen quickly, and PATS for travel. 'At his age the usual treatment is to put the ball back into the socket under a short anaesthetic and hold it there with a plaster cast for a few months; sometimes an operation is needed' — never 'He'll grow out of it' and never 'The brace will fix it', because a 15-month-old is past the brace window. Safety-net: 'If he gets a fever, stops walking on the leg, or the hip becomes hot or swollen, bring him straight in — that would be something different and urgent.' then offer to write it down for his father. Variants: bilateral DDH in a waddling girl — 'Because both hips can be affected, symmetrical creases don't reassure me': ask whether abduction is restricted on both sides, whether there is a waddling gait with a pronounced lower-back curve, and x-ray both hips — 'Both sockets are shallow, so both balls sit out of place, which is why she rocks from side to side rather than limping on one leg.' The examiner pushes on the x-ray: 'A horizontal line through the growth cartilage of the pelvis and a vertical line from the edge of the socket — a normal head sits in the lower-inner quadrant; here it's upper-outer. And Shenton's line, the curve from the femoral neck to the pubic bone, is broken on the left. I'm not measuring angles — that's for orthopaedics.' Febrile and refusing to weight-bear — the case flips: 'A febrile toddler who won't bear weight has a septic hip until proven otherwise' — temperature, the position he holds the hip in, warmth and tenderness, same-day bloods and ultrasound, phone the orthopaedic registrar, and MedSTAR kids if he is unwell. And when she says her mother told her not to fuss: 'I understand — and a family history of hip problems actually makes it more likely, not less. This is one where waiting makes the treatment bigger.'
plan: WIPE, OPEN, ACKNOWLEDGE — AND DO NOT AGREE WITH GRANDMA: 'that does sound worrying, especially when he's only just started walking. I'll ask you a number of questions, INCLUDING ABOUT HIS BIRTH AND DEVELOPMENT, and then we'll work out what's going on.' (Reassuring before the history is the first trap — and if you do, she pushes back: 'SO WHY IS THE LEG SHORTER?')

EXPLORE THE LIMP: 'can he stand and put weight on both legs? WHICH LEG DOES HE FAVOUR? When did he first pull to stand, and when were his first steps? HAS THE LIMP BEEN THERE SINCE THOSE VERY FIRST STEPS, OR DID IT START LATER? Is it getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse?' → left, FROM THE VERY FIRST STEPS, unchanged. (Asking 'where does it hurt?' or 'is the pain sharp or dull?' of a 15-month-old is what the examiner listens for — THE TIMING QUESTION REPLACES PAIN.)

WHAT SHE SEES, AND THE SEPTIC-HIP SCREEN: 'any swelling or redness around his hips, knees or ankles? ANY DEFORMITY — A FOOT TURNING IN, A LEG THAT LOOKS SHORTER? DOES HE SEEM IN PAIN — CRYING WHEN YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY OR MOVE THE LEG? ANY FEVER? HAS THERE EVER BEEN A TIME HE WOULDN'T PUT WEIGHT ON THE LEG AT ALL? Has he been unwell recently?' → the left leg does look shorter when she changes him.

THE BIRTH HISTORY — SIGNPOSTED, EARLY AND DEEP, AND THIS IS THE AUTO-FAIL BLOCK: 'because this has been there since his first steps, I NEED TO GO BACK TO WHEN HE WAS BORN. How was the pregnancy? Any medications, alcohol or drugs? The delivery — was it long, forceps or vacuum, WAS HE BREECH? WAS HE YOUR FIRST? Born at term? Any special care? WAS HE SWADDLED TIGHTLY? DID HE HAVE HIS SIX-WEEK CHECK — WAS ANYTHING SAID ABOUT HIS HIPS, AND DID HE EVER HAVE A HIP ULTRASOUND? ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WITH HIP PROBLEMS AS A CHILD?' → BREECH, caesarean, first baby, swaddled, six-week check normal, NO SCAN, AND HER SISTER WORE A BRACE. (Hearing 'breech' and not chaining to the ultrasound, the six-week check and the family history is the fail — and hearing 'normal six-week check' and dropping DDH is the other one, because A NORMAL EARLY CHECK DOES NOT EXCLUDE A DEVELOPMENTAL DISLOCATION.)

THE OTHER THREE DOMAINS IN THIRTY SECONDS: 'walking is one part of his development — a few quick questions on the rest. Can he pick up small things like A SULTANA WITH HIS THUMB AND FINGER? Does he babble, any words? Does he notice strangers, play peekaboo, roll a ball back? AS A BABY WAS HE FLOPPY OR STIFF? WHEN DID HE SIT?'

TRAUMA, NAI, GROWTH AND BINDS — fifteen seconds that are marked even though the mother seems lovely: 'any falls or injuries to the legs — DID ANYONE SEE THEM HAPPEN? Any bruises you couldn't explain? How are things at home? WHO LOOKS AFTER HIM — does he go to childcare? Any stress at home lately? Is he growing and gaining weight as expected? Any pallor, or waking at night crying? Immunisations, other problems, medicines, allergies?'

SUMMARISE AND TRANSITION: 'so: A PAINLESS LIMP ON THE LEFT SINCE HIS FIRST STEPS A MONTH AGO, in a well boy who was BREECH AND FIRST-BORN, with a normal six-week check BUT NO HIP SCAN, other development on track, no injury or fever. I'd like to examine him now.'

THE CARD AND THE X-RAY — READ THEM ALOUD AND TRANSLATE (see dx). IN THE FACE-TO-FACE VERSION, REQUEST BY NAME: general appearance, temperature and growth chart; WATCH HIM STAND AND WALK — weight-bearing, and is the gait A LIMP, A WADDLE OR OUT-TOEING; inspection of both legs INCLUDING WHETHER THE THIGH AND GLUTEAL CREASES ARE SYMMETRICAL; palpation for warmth or tenderness; movement, SPECIFICALLY HIP ABDUCTION WITH HIPS AND KNEES FLEXED; TRUE LEG LENGTH, ASIS TO MEDIAL MALLEOLUS; BARLOW AND ORTOLANI, NOTING THEY ARE UNRELIABLE AFTER THREE MONTHS; tone and reflexes; and the spine for a dimple or hair tuft. (A generic 'lower limb examination' request gets 'normal' and loses creases, length and abduction — THE THREE MARKED FINDINGS.)

NAME IT, BALL AND SOCKET, NORMAL SIDE FIRST, THEN THE REASONS AND THE BLAME REMOVED (see dx) → 'IS THAT BECAUSE HE WAS BREECH? DID I DO SOMETHING WRONG?' and 'WHY DIDN'T THEY PICK IT UP AT THE CHECK?' (Become tearful at the words 'developmental dysplasia' if no plain-language explanation follows within fifteen seconds.)

THE PLAN, THE HONEST EXPECTATIONS AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' → it depends on what the specialist finds: cast, sometimes an operation — NOT A BRACE. Then offer to write it down for his father.

'Does he cry when you change his nappy or move the leg? Any fever? HAS HE EVER REFUSED TO WALK?' / 'Walking is one part of his development — can he pick up a sultana, does he babble, does he play peekaboo?' / 'Who looks after him during the day? How are things at home?'

VARIANT — BILATERAL DDH, a waddling girl where 'both sides look the same': 'BECAUSE BOTH HIPS CAN BE AFFECTED, SYMMETRICAL CREASES DON'T REASSURE ME. I'd like to know whether ABDUCTION IS RESTRICTED ON BOTH SIDES, whether she has A WADDLING GAIT WITH A PRONOUNCED LOWER-BACK CURVE, and I'd X-RAY BOTH HIPS.' Explaining it: 'both hip sockets are shallow, so both balls sit out of place — THAT'S WHY SHE ROCKS FROM SIDE TO SIDE RATHER THAN LIMPING ON ONE LEG.' / THE EXAMINER PUSHES ON THE X-RAY — 'what lines are you using?': 'a horizontal line through the growth cartilage of the pelvis and a vertical line from the edge of the socket — A NORMAL HEAD SITS IN THE LOWER-INNER QUADRANT; HERE IT'S UPPER-OUTER. And SHENTON'S LINE is broken on the left. I'M NOT MEASURING ANGLES — THAT'S FOR ORTHOPAEDICS.'

VARIANT — FEBRILE AND REFUSING TO WEIGHT-BEAR, WHERE THE CASE FLIPS: 'THIS CHANGES EVERYTHING: A FEBRILE TODDLER WHO WON'T BEAR WEIGHT HAS A SEPTIC HIP UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. I need a temperature, THE POSITION HE HOLDS THE HIP IN, warmth and tenderness, and I'd send him for SAME-DAY BLOODS AND AN ULTRASOUND — I'd phone the orthopaedic registrar and, from here, MedSTAR Kids if he's unwell.' / VARIANT — 'MY MUM SAYS DON'T FUSS, HIS DAD WALKED LIKE THAT': 'I understand — AND A FAMILY HISTORY OF HIP PROBLEMS ACTUALLY MAKES IT MORE LIKELY, NOT LESS. This is one where WAITING MAKES THE TREATMENT BIGGER, so I'd like him seen soon. Can I explain what I found?'
pefe: Role-player: Kelly, 27, part-time hairdresser who stopped work when Jayden was born; partner Dean drives trucks and is away a lot; money is tight. JAYDEN: FIRST CHILD, BREECH, ELECTIVE CAESAREAN AT 39 WEEKS, 3.4 kg, home day 3, SWADDLED, breastfed then formula, immunisations up to date, no illnesses except a cold two months ago. Sat 7 months, crawled 9, stood 12-13 months, FIRST STEPS 4-5 WEEKS AGO — AND HE LIMPED ON THE LEFT FROM THE FIRST STEP. NO pain, NO fever, NEVER REFUSED TO WALK. HIS LEFT LEG LOOKS SHORTER WHEN SHE CHANGES HIM — volunteer only if asked about deformity or leg length. SIX-WEEK CHECK 'NORMAL', NO HIP ULTRASOUND. HER SISTER WORE A HIP BRACE AS A BABY — volunteer only when family history is asked. No falls, no bruises. HER MOTHER AND DEAN BOTH SAY 'DON'T FUSS'.

How to play it: answer only what is asked. If the doctor asks 'Any problems with the birth?', say 'No, it was a caesarean' — do not volunteer breech unless they ask about breech or why the caesarean. If pain questions are asked, look puzzled: 'He can't tell me, he's one.' if the doctor reassures early — 'Probably nothing' — push: 'So why is the leg shorter?' Become tearful at 'Developmental dysplasia' if no plain-language explanation follows within fifteen seconds. Hidden agenda: you fear he will need surgery and that you caused it by swaddling or by the breech birth — raise it late as 'Did I do something wrong?' Unless the doctor asks what worries you most; if never asked, at 6:30 say 'Will he need an operation? Was it the swaddling?' Register: anxious, slightly defensive — 'I'm not overreacting' — and visibly relaxing when the doctor explains without blame.

back.dx: AN UNDISPLACED SPIRAL FRACTURE OF THE DISTAL TIBIA — a toddler's fracture. Name the film precisely to the examiner: 'A fine spiral lucency in the distal third of the tibial shaft, undisplaced, fibula intact.' Do not explain the film to the mother — it is not a task — and never say 'Normal'. To the mother, in plain words: 'Noah has a broken bone: a fine spiral crack in the lower part of his shin bone, the tibia. The bone hasn't moved out of place. We call it a toddler's fracture because it happens in children his age who are new walkers, from a twist of the leg, often on a slide or when a foot gets caught, and very often nobody sees it. So please don't feel you missed something.' then the differentials, each excluded with its reason — the task says diagnosis and differentials, so this half is not optional: 'An infection in the bone or joint — he has no fever, he's well, his hip moves freely, so that doesn't fit. A blood problem like leukaemia — good colour, no bruising, no night pain, so no. An irritable hip after a cold — no recent cold, and the hip is fine. Joint inflammation — no rash or swollen joints. And, as I ask every family, nothing about how this happened worries me.' when she asks 'Did his sister push him?': 'Nothing suggests that; a twist on the slide is enough. His sister didn't do anything wrong either.' Management is not a task — one sentence if asked: 'Pain relief and a plaster from above the knee for some weeks, with the bone doctors reviewing him. Children's bones heal fast and completely; he will walk normally again.' then summarise and close with 'What is worrying you most?' → 'Just that I didn't see it' → 'That's the usual story with this fracture. You brought him in within a day, which is exactly right.' Version B — the film is reported normal: 'The x-ray doesn't show a break, but a well child who is tender over the shin bone and won't bear weight has a toddler's fracture until proven otherwise; the crack is often invisible for the first week or two. We treat it as a fracture with a plaster and repeat the x-ray in ten to fourteen days, when the healing bone shows.' Version C — febrile with a hip held still, and the station stops: 'Emma, I'm going to stop here. A fever with a hip he won't let anyone move is an infection in the joint until we prove otherwise, and that can damage the joint within hours. He needs blood tests, an ultrasound of the hip and the bone doctors today; I'm arranging that now' — and name the Kocher criteria. The pale child: 'Pale, tired and now leg pain is a combination I never leave: we do a blood count today, before anything else.' Bruises of different ages on the back: 'Bruises on the back at different ages in a three-year-old are unusual. I'll ask the children's team to see him today and do a full check of his bones; I'm required to speak with the child protection service, and I'll keep you informed.'
plan: VITALS INCLUDING TEMPERATURE, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE: 'Examiner, may I have his vital signs INCLUDING TEMPERATURE?' → 36.9, HR 110. Then: 'Emma, tell me what's been happening with his leg.' → 'since yesterday afternoon HE WON'T WALK. NOBODY SAW HIM FALL, and now I'm worried something's really wrong.' → 'THAT'S FRIGHTENING WHEN THERE'S NO OBVIOUS REASON, AND IT'S EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING TO BRING HIM IN.'

DEFINE THE LIMP: 'when you say he won't walk — CAN HE PUT ANY WEIGHT ON IT AT ALL, OR DOES HE WALK WITH A LIMP? When did it start, and was it sudden? Is it getting better or worse? Worse in the morning or the evening? Anything that helps?' → NO WEIGHT AT ALL, sudden at about 3 pm, same or a bit worse, happy sitting. (NON-WEIGHT-BEARING IS A KOCHER CRITERION — register it. And do NOT suggest a mechanism yet.)

THE PAIN AND THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SWEEP: 'WHERE IS THE PAIN — HIP, THIGH, KNEE, SHIN, ANKLE OR FOOT? CAN HE POINT? Constant or does it come and go? Does it go anywhere? DOES IT WAKE HIM AT NIGHT? How bad? Any swelling, redness, warmth, bruising or change in the shape of the leg? ANY OTHER JOINTS SORE OR SWOLLEN?' → lower shin, sometimes the ankle, slept okay, nothing visible. (KNEE PAIN IS HIP PAIN UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, so at least ask where — and NIGHT PAIN WOULD MOVE MALIGNANCY UP THE LIST.)

THE DIFFERENTIALS IN ORDER — THE PASS MARK. INFECTION: 'any fever? Is he unwell, off his food? ANY RECENT COLD, EAR INFECTION OR SKIN INFECTION?' BLOOD PROBLEMS: 'has he been PALE, TIRED, BRUISING EASILY, LOSING WEIGHT, SWEATING AT NIGHT?' ONLY THEN INJURY, AND OPEN FIRST: 'WHAT WAS HE DOING YESTERDAY? Any fall, twist, jump, trampoline, SLIDE, FOOT CAUGHT IN A COT OR A FENCE? WHO WAS WITH HIM? Any injuries or broken bones before?' IRRITABLE HIP: 'any cold or tummy bug in the last couple of weeks?' JOINT INFLAMMATION: 'any rash, red eyes, swollen joints, STIFF IN THE MORNINGS?' (Asking trauma first because the stem smells of fracture is exactly what this station tests.)

THE NAI BLOCK, FRAMED AS ROUTINE BEFORE SHE CAN TAKE IT PERSONALLY: 'and AS I ASK EVERY FAMILY: WHO WAS LOOKING AFTER HIM YESTERDAY? Who lives at home? Any brothers or sisters? Any stresses at the moment? Does he go to childcare?' → 'WHY ARE YOU ASKING ABOUT HOME?' → 'BECAUSE WHEN A CHILD HAS AN INJURY THAT NO ONE SAW, I ASK EVERY FAMILY THE SAME QUESTIONS. IT PROTECTS HIM, AND IT'S ROUTINE.' Then: walking on time, growth and development, birth and WERE HIS HIPS CHECKED, immunisations, medicines, allergies, AND ANY HIP OR BONE PROBLEMS IN THE FAMILY.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST — HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE EVERY TIME: 'general appearance — well or unwell, alert, colour, growth chart? WILL HE STAND OR WEIGHT-BEAR? With BOTH LEGS EXPOSED: any swelling, redness, bruising, deformity, rash, OR BRUISES ANYWHERE ELSE ON HIS BODY? FEEL: the hip, the knee, the ankle, THEN BONE BY BONE ALONG THE TIBIA, AND THE SOLE OF THE FOOT; any warmth? MOVE: hip range of movement AND A LOG ROLL TEST; knee; ankle? Leg lengths equal? Spine and abdomen? LYMPH NODES, PALLOR, BRUISING?' (A candidate who palpates the tibia only has not run the limping examination — and SAY 'LOG ROLL' BY NAME.)

pefe: Role-player: Emma, 29, works part-time at the supermarket; partner Dan is a farmhand; daughter Ruby is 5. NOAH, 3: walked at 13 months, normal birth, HIPS CHECKED, fully immunised, no medicines, no allergies, well, eating normally. YESTERDAY AFTERNOON he was playing in the backyard with Ruby, RUNNING AND USING THE SLIDE, while she hung washing. AROUND 3 PM HE SAT DOWN CRYING AND HAS REFUSED TO STAND SINCE. NO ONE SAW A FALL. HE POINTS TO THE LOWER SHIN. He slept normally. No fever, not pale, no bruising or weight loss, no recent colds, no rash or stiff joints, no previous fractures, no family bone problems.

If the doctor never asks who was there or about home, do not volunteer it. If pushed on stresses, add 'Dan's been working long hours with harvest.' Close by asking 'Will he need a cast? Will he walk again?'

WHITE IS BONE, GREY IS SOFT TISSUE, BLACK WOULD BE AIR, AND THERE'S NONE HERE. The hand, finger and wrist bones ALL LOOK NORMAL. These are the two forearm bones: THE ULNA on the little-finger side, WHICH IS FINE, and THE RADIUS on the thumb side. Just above the wrist on the radius you can see A SMALL BULGE, A BUMP IN THE EDGE OF THE BONE, HERE ON BOTH PICTURES. THAT'S THE INJURY.' When he says the nurse thought it looked normal: 'IT'S EASY TO MISS.' NEVER SAY 'NORMAL' AND NEVER SAY 'STRESS FRACTURE'. THEN THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS: 'this is called A BUCKLE FRACTURE. When he landed on his outstretched hand, THE SOFT BONE JUST ABOVE THE WRIST WAS SQUASHED AND BUCKLED OUTWARDS, LIKE A DENT IN A CAN, RATHER THAN SNAPPING. It's THE MILDEST AND ONE OF THE COMMONEST FRACTURES IN CHILDREN, because THEIR BONES ARE SOFTER THAN OURS. IT HASN'T MOVED AND IT DOESN'T NEED TO BE PUT BACK INTO PLACE. IT HEALS IN ABOUT THREE WEEKS.' THEN ANSWER THE TWO THINGS HE IS ACTUALLY ASKING: 'NOTHING YOU'VE TOLD ME SUGGESTS WEAK BONES OR ANYTHING YOU DID WRONG: TWO WITNESSED FALLS IN AN ACTIVE FOUR-YEAR-OLD, NORMAL GROWTH, NO BONE PAIN. TWO BREAKS IN FOUR MONTHS WITH A GOOD STORY EACH TIME IS NOT UNUSUAL.' MANAGEMENT IS NOT A TASK — one sentence if he asks: 'pain relief, and A SPLINT OR A HALF-PLASTER ON THE BACK OF THE ARM FOR ABOUT THREE WEEKS, with a GP check-up. HE WON'T NEED ANOTHER X-RAY unless something changes — and come back sooner if his fingers go PALE OR NUMB or the pain gets worse in the splint.' Then summarise and CLOSE WITH A CONCERN CHECK: 'is there anything worrying you?' THE EXAMINATION EXPLAINED TO THE FATHER, IN LAYMAN'S TERMS AND UNDER TWO MINUTES — do NOT list radial, median and ulnar nerves to a parent: 'I'll LOOK at both hands and forearms for swelling, bruising, cuts and any difference in shape. I'll GENTLY FEEL them: compare the warmth, CHECK THE PULSE AT THE WRIST, PRESS THE NAILS TO CHECK THE BLOOD FLOW, and press along each bone to find where it's sore. I'll ask him to MOVE his fingers, wrist and elbow. Then I'll CHECK THE NERVES with a piece of cotton wool and a few hand shapes. I'll wash my hands first.' VERSION C — THE STORY CHANGES: 'James, I NEED TO BE HONEST. THE STORY HAS CHANGED A LITTLE BETWEEN TELLINGS, and IT'S BEEN TWO DAYS, and THIS IS HIS SECOND FRACTURE IN FOUR MONTHS. FOR EVERY CHILD IN THAT SITUATION I'M OBLIGED TO LOOK FURTHER. I'M NOT ACCUSING YOU. The children's doctors will see him TODAY and may do EXTRA X-RAYS AND BLOOD TESTS TO CHECK HIS BONES, and I'LL BE SPEAKING WITH THE CHILD PROTECTION TEAM, WHICH IS MY LEGAL DUTY. I'll keep you informed.' 'HE BRUISES EASILY': 'WHERE, AND HOW OFTEN? Any NOSEBLEEDS, BLEEDING GUMS, or FAMILY BLEEDING PROBLEMS? I'll examine his skin all over and CHECK A BLOOD COUNT.' A DEFORMITY ON THE FILM — AN ANGULATED GREENSTICK RATHER THAN A BUCKLE: 'THIS ONE HAS BENT AND CRACKED ON ONE SIDE; IT NEEDS TO BE STRAIGHTENED UNDER SEDATION AND PUT IN A PLASTER BY THE BONE DOCTORS TODAY.'
plan: OPEN, REASSURE, SIGNPOST: 'I can see you're worried about Oliver's arm. HIS OBSERVATIONS ARE NORMAL AND HE'S HAD SOME PAIN RELIEF. I'd like to hear exactly what happened, then LOOK AT THE X-RAY WITH YOU. Tell me what happened.' (The father starts standing and anxious, and sits once reassured.)

THE INJURY IN DETAIL — and the lecture's own phrase is THE MORE QUESTIONS YOU ASK ABOUT THE INJURY, THE HAPPIER THE EXAMINER: 'can you take me through it STEP BY STEP? What was he doing, HOW DID HE FALL, AND HOW DID HE LAND? WAS HIS HAND OUT FLAT, AND WAS THE WRIST BENT BACK? HOW HIGH WAS HE, AND ONTO WHAT SURFACE? YOU SAW IT YOURSELF? WHAT TIME WAS IT, AND WHAT DID YOU DO THEN?' (A one-line fall is not a history — and TIMING MATTERS, because a story that fits, promptly presented, IS the first NAI screen.)

Head and other injuries — before the pain questions, because head injury outranks the wrist: 'Did he hit his head? Did he lose consciousness at all, even briefly? Has he vomited since? Any other injuries — swelling, redness, bruises anywhere else on his body? Is he limping, or complaining of pain anywhere else?'

THE PAIN AND ALL THREE SYSTEMS — BONES, BLOOD SUPPLY, NERVES: 'where exactly is the pain — the wrist or further up? How bad is it, and IS HE USING THE HAND AT ALL? Does it go anywhere else? HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY DIFFERENCE IN SHAPE COMPARED WITH THE OTHER ARM? Any pain or difficulty moving the arm, the wrist, the fingers? ANY CHANGE IN COLOUR OF THE HAND — PALE, BLUE, BLOTCHY? IS IT COLD? ANY PINS AND NEEDLES, or not using his fingers?' (A selective SOCRATES — site, severity, radiation only — is the trap, and DEFORMITY MEANS DISPLACEMENT AND A DIFFERENT FILM.)
The previous fracture, explored: 'The notes say he broke the same arm four months ago. Can you tell me more about that? What happened, who saw it, where was the break and what treatment did he have?'

Home and bone, framed as routine — and 'Happy family' is scripted to see whether you stop: 'Tell me about home: who lives with you? Any siblings? Any recent stresses or problems at home — work, money, relationships? Does he go to childcare or kindy — any concerns there? Who else looks after him?' → 'We're a happy family, doctor. Why all the questions?' → 'When a child has had two breaks in a few months I ask every family these questions; sometimes the reason is in the bones, and it protects him.' then: 'Any concerns about his growth or weight? Has he ever complained of bone pain, or does anyone in the family break bones easily?' → 'My brother has brittle bones, he's broken heaps. Does that matter?' (Given only if you ask — and it is his hidden worry.)
The x-ray — normal landmarks first, then point on both views (see dx) → 'I thought the x-ray was normal, the nurse said it looked fine' → 'It's easy to miss.'
THE EXAMINATION EXPLAINED IN LAYMAN'S TERMS, UNDER TWO MINUTES (see dx) — look, gently feel, move, check the nerves, hands washed first.

THE DIAGNOSIS — A DENT IN A CAN, SOFTER BONES, HASN'T MOVED, HEALS IN THREE WEEKS — THEN ANSWER THE WEAK-BONES AND THE FAULT QUESTIONS (see dx), one sentence of management if asked, a summary, and a concern check.

ask: 'TAKE ME THROUGH IT STEP BY STEP: HOW DID HE FALL AND HOW DID HE LAND?' / 'Was his hand out flat, and was the wrist bent back? How high, and onto what surface?' / 'DID HE HIT HIS HEAD? ANY BLACKOUT? VOMITING SINCE?' / 'Any other injuries, swelling or bruises anywhere else?'

'ANY DIFFERENCE IN SHAPE COMPARED WITH THE OTHER ARM?' / 'Any change in colour or warmth of the hand? Pins and needles?' / 'Tell me more about the fracture four months ago: WHAT HAPPENED, WHO SAW IT, WHAT WAS DONE?' / 'Tell me about home: who lives with you? Any recent stresses?' / 'WHEN A CHILD HAS HAD TWO BROKEN BONES IN A FEW MONTHS I ASK EVERY FAMILY THE SAME QUESTIONS.' / 'Any concerns about his growth? ANY BONE PAIN? ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WHO BREAKS BONES EASILY?'

'WHITE IS BONE, GREY IS SOFT TISSUE, BLACK WOULD BE AIR.' / 'A SMALL BULGE IN THE EDGE OF THE BONE: A BUCKLE FRACTURE, LIKE A DENT IN A CAN.' / 'Softer bones, SO IT BUCKLES RATHER THAN SNAPS; it hasn't moved and HEALS IN THREE WEEKS.' / 'I'll LOOK, GENTLY FEEL, ASK HIM TO MOVE, THEN CHECK THE NERVES.' / 'Nothing you've told me suggests weak bones or anything you did wrong.'

VERSION C — THE STORY CHANGES BETWEEN TELLINGS, A TWO-DAY DELAY, THE MOTHER UNCONTACTABLE: 'James, I NEED TO BE HONEST. The story has changed a little between tellings, and it's been two days, and this is his second fracture in four months. FOR EVERY CHILD IN THAT SITUATION I'M OBLIGED TO LOOK FURTHER. I'M NOT ACCUSING YOU. The children's doctors will see him today and may do EXTRA X-RAYS AND BLOOD TESTS TO CHECK HIS BONES, and I'LL BE SPEAKING WITH THE CHILD PROTECTION TEAM, WHICH IS MY LEGAL DUTY. I'll keep you informed.' NAME THE CONCERN, DO NOT CONFRONT, AND FOLLOW THE MANDATORY REPORTING DUTY.

'HE BRUISES EASILY': 'WHERE, AND HOW OFTEN? Any NOSEBLEEDS, BLEEDING GUMS, or FAMILY BLEEDING PROBLEMS? I'll examine his skin all over and CHECK A BLOOD COUNT.' / A DEFORMITY ON THE FILM — AN ANGULATED GREENSTICK: 'THIS ONE HAS BENT AND CRACKED ON ONE SIDE; IT NEEDS TO BE STRAIGHTENED UNDER SEDATION AND PUT IN A PLASTER BY THE BONE DOCTORS TODAY.' / IF MANAGEMENT IS ASKED: 'pain relief, a REMOVABLE SPLINT OR A HALF-PLASTER on the back of the arm for about THREE WEEKS, GP review, NO REPEAT X-RAY. Back sooner for pain, swelling, or PALE OR NUMB FINGERS.' Numbers: HEALS 3 WEEKS — splint or backslab 3 weeks — SPORT AT 6 WEEKS — NO REPEAT FILM — capillary refill under 2 seconds — paracetamol 15 mg/kg, ibuprofen 10 mg/kg — SKELETAL SURVEY IF UNDER 2 — CARL 13 14 78. VERIFY
pefe: Role-player: James, 36, diesel mechanic; wife Sarah is a teacher; OLIVER HAS TWO SISTERS, 7 AND 2. Oliver is fit, TALL, fully immunised, no medicines, no allergies, kindy three days a week, GRANDPARENTS BABYSIT. FOUR MONTHS AGO he fell off a slide at the park WITH SARAH and had a forearm cast for a few weeks. LAST NIGHT AT 7 PM you saw him TRIP ON THE RUG CHASING HIS SISTER and land PALM-DOWN, WRIST BENT BACK, ONTO FLOORBOARDS; you iced it, he slept, and this morning he would not use the hand.

Register: standing and anxious at the start, sitting when reassured. Mildly defensive when asked about home — 'Why all the questions?' — and settling if the doctor explains it is routine for every family. Guilty near the end: 'Is it our fault?' Hidden agenda: you are worried the two fractures mean his bones are weak, because your brother has 'Brittle bones' — but you only mention the brother if asked about family bone problems, and if never asked by 5:00 you ask 'Is his bone weak?' At the x-ray. At the film, say 'The nurse thought it looked normal.' if pushed once more on stresses, add 'Money's a bit tight, like everyone.' Version C: first say he fell off the couch, later say he tripped in the yard; it happened two days ago; Sarah is away and uncontactable; become quiet and defensive rather than angry.

Mark them against: reassured you and signposted the plan; MECHANISM IN DETAIL — how he fell, landing, wrist position, height, surface, witnessed, time, delay; HEAD INJURY, LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS, VOMITING; other injuries, bruises, limping; site, severity, radiation, DEFORMITY, movement, COLOUR, PINS AND NEEDLES; THE PREVIOUS FRACTURE EXPLORED IN DETAIL; home, who lives there, siblings, stresses, CHILDCARE, OTHER CARERS, framed as routine; GROWTH AND BONE PAIN, AND ASKED ABOUT FAMILY BONE PROBLEMS — FINDING THE BROTHER; the X-ray with THREE COLOURS, NORMAL STRUCTURES FIRST, THEN THE BULGE ON BOTH VIEWS, NAMED A BUCKLE FRACTURE, AND NEVER CALLED NORMAL OR A STRESS FRACTURE; explained a buckle in plain words and that it heals in three weeks; the examination explained in layman's terms in under two minutes; and a summary with a concern check.
Everything else on the film — The HAND, FINGER AND WRIST BONES all normal; THE ULNA IS FINE — so orient on the normal structures before you point at the bulge
What the nurse said — 'IT LOOKED FINE' — the father will quote that back, so the line is 'IT'S EASY TO MISS'

The mechanism — Chasing his sister, TRIPPED ON THE RUG, HAND OUT FLAT, PALM DOWN, WRIST BENT BACK, from standing onto FLOORBOARDS, WITNESSED, about 7 pm — iced, slept, and this morning he would not use it
Head injury screen — NO head strike, NO loss of consciousness, NO vomiting — and no other injuries, bruises or limp
The previous fracture — FELL OFF THE SLIDE AT THE PARK, WITNESSED BY HIS MOTHER, forearm, cast for a few weeks
Home — Father, mother, Oliver and TWO SISTERS — 'WE'RE A HAPPY FAMILY' — kindy three days a week, grandparents babysit, NO stresses (and if pushed once more, 'money's a bit tight, like everyone')
The family history he withholds — HIS BROTHER HAS BRITTLE BONES AND HAS BROKEN HEAPS — given ONLY if you ask about family bone problems, and it is his hidden worry

VERSION C — the concern variant — The story CHANGES BETWEEN TELLINGS — first off the couch, later tripped in the yard — IT HAPPENED TWO DAYS AGO, THE MOTHER IS AWAY AND UNCONTACTABLE, and he says 'HE BRUISES EASILY'
fails: ★ A one-line fall instead of a step-by-step mechanism — the more questions about the injury, the happier the examiner
★ Asking about the head injury as an afterthought, or not at all — it outranks the wrist and comes before the pain questions
Stopping at 'we're a happy family' instead of continuing through childcare, other carers, growth and bone pain
Calling the film normal, or calling it a stress fracture — and the father will quote the nurse's 'it looked fine' back at you

A selective SOCRATES with no deformity, colour or pins-and-needles questions; never asking about family bone problems, so the brother with brittle bones is never found; listing radial, median and ulnar nerves to a parent; and spending the station on management, which is not a task
numbers: BUCKLE FRACTURE HEALS IN ABOUT 3 WEEKS · splint or backslab for 3 weeks · SPORT AT 6 WEEKS · NO REPEAT FILM · capillary refill under 2 seconds · paracetamol 15 mg/kg, ibuprofen 10 mg/kg VERIFY

A SKELETAL SURVEY IS INDICATED UNDER AGE 2 · deformity on the film means an ANGULATED GREENSTICK needing reduction under sedation, not a buckle · VERSION C: story changed between tellings, TWO-DAY DELAY, second fracture in four months · CARL 13 14 78

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION REQUEST AND MANAGEMENT — regional GP, AND THE DIAGNOSIS IS GIVEN TO YOU. DO NOT SPEND FOUR MINUTES RE-DERIVING IT. TWO BLOCKS ARE THE PASS MARK: THE IMMUNE STATE, WHICH DECIDES THE ANTIVIRAL, AND THE COMPLICATIONS SCREEN — BRAIN, EYE, CHEST, SKIN. SAY THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION AND ITS REASON IN ONE SENTENCE: 'we could give aciclovir' WITHOUT A DECISION HAS NOT ANSWERED THE TASK. The mother wants a prescription in the first thirty seconds — acknowledge, promise pain relief, and KEEP THE HISTORY MOVING. And COUNT THE WEES: two today is the measurable red flag you hand back to her.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. LIAM, 5 YEARS, brought by his mother MARY. He has presented with LESIONS IN THE MOUTH AND HAS BEEN DIAGNOSED WITH HERPETIC GINGIVOSTOMATITIS. A PHOTOGRAPH OF THE MOUTH IS PROVIDED.

Take A FURTHER RELEVANT HISTORY from the mother (about 4 minutes), ASK THE EXAMINER FOR THE RELEVANT PHYSICAL EXAMINATION FINDINGS, then EXPLAIN YOUR MANAGEMENT. 8 minutes. VERSION B: the same child but ON MAINTENANCE PREDNISOLONE for nephrotic syndrome, or with TYPE 1 DIABETES, or post-chemotherapy. VERSION C: a VESICLE ON THE THUMB if you ask about rash elsewhere.
tasks: Take a further relevant history from the mother (about 4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings
Explain your management to the mother
time: ASK FOR THE VITALS BEFORE YOU START, acknowledge her exhaustion, AND PROMISE PAIN RELIEF · THE LESIONS: when first noticed, FIRST TIME, getting worse, WHERE EXACTLY · gums, tongue, lips, the skin around the mouth, WERE THERE BLISTERS FIRST, any pus or discharge, painful or itchy · GENERAL FEATURES AND SOURCE: fever and whether anything helped, tired or flat, ANY RASH ANYWHERE ELSE · ON HIS HANDS OR FINGERS, lumps in the neck, and ANYONE AT HOME OR SCHOOL WITH COLD SORES · THEN THE IMMUNE BLOCK, WHICH IS THE PASS MARK, PREFACED SO IT MAKES SENSE: 'some questions about his general health, BECAUSE THEY CHANGE HOW I TREAT THIS' · any long-term medical conditions, DOES HE GET INFECTIONS MORE OFTEN OR TAKE LONGER TO GET OVER THEM, ANY REGULAR MEDICINES PARTICULARLY STEROIDS LIKE PREDNISOLONE OR ANYTHING FOR HIS IMMUNE SYSTEM, growth and weight, AND ANY DIABETES, KIDNEY OR BLOOD PROBLEMS · THEN THE COMPLICATIONS BY NAME: BRAIN · headache, drowsy or hard to wake, vomiting, blurred vision, unusual behaviour, FITS; EYE · RED EYE, SPOTS ON THE EYELIDS, discharge, PHOTOPHOBIA; CHEST · cough or fast breathing; SKIN · ECZEMA AND WHETHER IT IS FLARING · THEN HYDRATION: DROOLING, HOW MUCH IS HE DRINKING COMPARED WITH NORMAL, HOW MANY WEES TODAY, bowels, alert and playing or flat · then BINDSMA and home · then the examination in order, and management with THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION STATED.
findings: ALERT, MISERABLE, DRY LIPS, CAPILLARY REFILL 2 SECONDS, growth on the 50th centile
As in the photograph — and when the examiner says 'AS YOU CAN SEE', NAME WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR ANYWAY — discharge, extent, tonsils — then move on
Several tender enlarged nodes both sides
THREE DAYS, first time, gums, inside the lips, a few on the tongue and CRUSTY BITS ON THE LIP — LITTLE BLISTERS ON THE LIP FIRST, then they popped — no pus, PAINFUL

back.dx: HERPETIC GINGIVOSTOMATITIS IN AN IMMUNOCOMPETENT CHILD WITH MILD DEHYDRATION — supportive care, no antivirals, and the reason said aloud. Explain it: 'Liam has herpetic gingivostomatitis: a viral infection, the herpes simplex virus, in his mouth, on his gums and tongue and around his lips. It's very common in young children, this first episode is always the worst, and it runs its course over about one to two weeks. Antibiotics don't work on viruses. The treatment is pain relief so that he can drink.' The pain ladder, which is the whole point: paracetamol every four to six hours, no more than four times a day; ibuprofen with food; and a numbing gel, lignocaine, dabbed on the sores with a cotton bud about ten minutes before he drinks or eats. Then fluids: small sips often, cool drinks, icy poles, oral rehydration like Hydralyte, water or milk rather than juice, which stings. Then the antiviral decision in one sentence with its reason: 'There is an antiviral, but because Liam has no condition and no medicine that weakens his immune system, he doesn't need it; his own immune system will clear this, and the tablets make little difference in a healthy child. If he were on steroids or had diabetes, I'd give it.' then exclusion and hygiene: home from school until the sores have dried, wash hands, no sharing cups, and no kissing the baby. Review in a day or two. The red flags, including a measurable urine-based one: 'Come straight back or go to the emergency department if he becomes drowsy or hard to wake, complains of headache, vomits, has a fit, gets a red or sore eye or blisters on the eyelid, or if he stops drinking or has no wee for eight hours. Count the wees: fewer than three a day, or none for eight hours, or too drowsy to drink — bring him straight in and we'll give fluids through a tube or a drip.' then summarise and ask what worries her most. Version B — prednisolone or another immunocompromising condition: 'Because Liam is on prednisolone his immune system is weaker, so this infection can spread further and last longer. I'm going to start an antiviral, aciclovir, five times a day for a week, and I'll speak to the children's team today. If he can't keep fluids down he needs to come in.' Version C — the whitlow: 'The blister on his thumb is the same virus, spread from his mouth when he sucks it. It's painful but it heals by itself; we don't cut it. Keep it covered and wash hands, so it doesn't spread to his eyes.' The red eye: 'A red, sore eye with this infection can be the virus on the surface of the eye. That needs an eye specialist today, with a dye test and antiviral drops. Please don't use any leftover eye drops at home.' Drowsy and vomiting: 'Drowsiness and vomiting with this infection can mean the virus has reached the brain. I'm stopping here and arranging the emergency department now; he'll need a drip and an antiviral through the vein.'
plan: VITALS, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE AND PROMISE: 'Examiner, may I have Liam's vital signs?' → 38.4, HR 118. Then: 'I've read that Liam has a herpes infection in his mouth AND I CAN SEE HOW SORE IT IS. I'd like to ask how he's been, examine him, and then go through the plan.' → 'he's screaming when he eats, he's not sleeping, and now he won't drink either. CAN'T YOU GIVE HIM SOMETHING?' → 'THAT SOUNDS MISERABLE FOR BOTH OF YOU, AND YES, THERE'S A LOT WE CAN DO FOR HIS PAIN. Let me ask a few things first.' (She wants a prescription now — acknowledge, promise, and keep moving. And do NOT spend the four minutes re-deriving a diagnosis you were given.)

THE LESIONS: 'when did you first notice the sores? IS THIS THE FIRST TIME? Getting worse? WHERE EXACTLY — gums, tongue, lips, the skin around the mouth? WERE THERE BLISTERS FIRST? Any pus or discharge? Painful, or itchy?'

GENERAL FEATURES AND SOURCE: 'any fever or chills? Did you give anything, and did it help? Is he tired or flat? ANY RASH ANYWHERE ELSE, ON HIS HANDS OR FINGERS? Any lumps in his neck? Anyone at home or at school with cold sores or something similar?' (A NEGATIVE CONTACT HISTORY IS NORMAL — most sources shed without symptoms — so do NOT chase the source at the cost of the immune block.)

The immune block — the pass mark: 'Now some questions about his general health, because they change how I treat this. Does he have any long-term medical conditions? Does he get infections more often than other children, or take a long time to get over them? Is he on any regular medicines, particularly steroids like prednisolone, or anything for his immune system? Any concerns about his growth or weight? Any diabetes, kidney or blood problems?'

THE COMPLICATIONS SCREEN, BY SYSTEM AND BY NAME: 'HIS BRAIN: any headache? Is he DROWSY OR HARD TO WAKE? Vomiting? Blurred vision or unusual behaviour? ANY FITS? HIS EYES: any RED EYE? SPOTS ON THE EYELIDS? Discharge? DOES LIGHT BOTHER HIM? HIS CHEST: any cough or fast breathing? HIS SKIN: DOES HE HAVE ECZEMA, AND IS IT FLARING?'

HYDRATION, WITH NUMBERS: 'is he DROOLING? HOW MUCH IS HE DRINKING COMPARED TO NORMAL? HOW MANY WEES TODAY? Bowels? Alert and playing, or flat?' → drooling, half of normal in small sips of juice, TWO WEES TODAY. (JUICE STINGS — swap to water, milk, oral rehydration or icy poles. And TWO WEES IN A DAY IS YOUR MEASURABLE MARKER TO HAND BACK TO HER AS A RED FLAG.) Then birth and development, immunisations, allergies, home and school.

THE EXAMINATION, IN ORDER: 'general appearance — is he alert, and how does he look? HYDRATION — mucous membranes, tears, skin turgor, CAPILLARY REFILL? Growth chart? MOUTH — site of the ulcers, any blisters, any discharge, tonsils? CERVICAL LYMPH NODES? EYES — conjunctival redness, LID VESICLES, discharge, visual acuity, fundi? NEUROLOGICAL — conscious level, NECK STIFFNESS, cranial nerves, limbs, gait? CHEST — air entry, added sounds? SKIN AND HANDS — ANY VESICLES OR ECZEMA?' (Do not lead with a urine dipstick or blood sugar; if you mention ketones, do it last.)

MANAGEMENT: the virus explained, ANTIBIOTICS DON'T WORK, the pain ladder with LIGNOCAINE GEL TEN MINUTES BEFORE DRINKS, and fluids in small sips WITHOUT JUICE (see dx) → 'SO NOTHING TO MAKE IT GO AWAY?'

THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION IN ONE SENTENCE WITH ITS REASON, THEN EXCLUSION, REVIEW AND THE RED FLAGS (see dx) → 'HOW DO I KNOW IF HE'S GETTING DEHYDRATED?' → COUNT THE WEES. Then summarise and ask what worries her most. ('We could give aciclovir' with no decision has not answered the task.)

pefe: Role-player: Mary, 34, WORKS IN THE LOCAL PHARMACY, so she knows Panadol and WANTS 'SOMETHING STRONGER'. Liam is her only child, in reception. Normal birth, fully immunised, no allergies, NO MEDICAL CONDITIONS, NO MEDICINES (VERSION B: ON PREDNISOLONE FOR NEPHROTIC SYNDROME — SAY IT ONLY IF ASKED ABOUT MEDICINES OR CONDITIONS). Her husband works away on a mine roster and SHE HAS HAD THREE NIGHTS WITHOUT SLEEP. THE STORY: three days of sores on the gums, inside the lips, a few on the tongue and crusty bits on the lip, WITH LITTLE BLISTERS FIRST; no pus; painful enough that he screams; FEVER UP TO 39 with Panadol helping for a few hours; flat but played a bit this morning; no other rash; NECK LUMPY BOTH SIDES; no known cold-sore contacts.

REGISTER: FRAYED AND A LITTLE SHARP AT THE START — 'CAN'T YOU JUST GIVE HIM SOMETHING?' — softening when the doctor promises to deal with the pain, and TEARFUL ONCE when asked what worries her most. HIDDEN AGENDA: SHE IS FRIGHTENED HE IS DEHYDRATED BECAUSE HE HAS ONLY DONE TWO WEES TODAY, BUT SHE DOES NOT SAY THE NUMBER UNLESS ASKED ABOUT WEES OR DRINKING — AND IF NOT ASKED BY 3:30 SHE VOLUNTEERS 'HE'S HARDLY WEED TODAY'. UNDERLYING BELIEF: that ANTIBIOTICS would fix it faster — push once, then accept a clear explanation. Ask 'ISN'T THERE A TABLET TO KILL IT?' after the antibiotic answer, and 'HOW DO I KNOW IF HE'S DEHYDRATED?' if no urine-based red flag has been given.

Mark them against: ASKED THE EXAMINER FOR VITALS and acknowledged your exhaustion; characterised the lesions — site, blisters, discharge, pain; fever, tiredness, RASH ELSEWHERE, neck lumps, contacts; THE IMMUNE STATE — conditions, recurrent infections, MEDICINES OR STEROIDS, which is the pass mark; COMPLICATIONS BY NAME — BRAIN, EYE, CHEST, SKIN; drooling, drinking, WEES, bowels, alertness, and BINDSMA; examination in order — general and hydration, mouth, nodes, eyes, neurology, chest, skin; explained A VIRUS, NO ANTIBIOTICS, FIRST EPISODE WORST, 1-2 WEEKS; paracetamol, ibuprofen, LIGNOCAINE GEL BEFORE DRINKS, cool fluids, small sips, ORS, NO JUICE; STATED THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION WITH THE REASON; exclusion until dry, hygiene and a review time; and RED FLAGS INCLUDING A URINE-BASED ONE, a summary, and asking what worries you most.
Immune block — VERSION A — NO conditions, no recurrent infections, NO MEDICINES, growing fine — which is exactly why he does NOT get an antiviral
Immune block — VERSION B — ON PREDNISOLONE FOR NEPHROTIC SYNDROME, or TYPE 1 DIABETES, or FINISHED CHEMOTHERAPY LAST YEAR — given only if you ask about conditions or medicines
Inhaled steroids — If she mentions a puffer, ask whether it is a steroid preventer and whether he has had oral steroid courses — inhaled steroids alone do not make him immunocompromised
Complications screen — ALL NEGATIVE — tired but wakes easily, no vomiting or fits, EYES FINE, no cough, NO ECZEMA
HYDRATION — the numbers — DROOLING — DRINKING ABOUT HALF OF NORMAL, IN SMALL SIPS OF JUICE — AND TWO WEES TODAY. She is frightened about this and volunteers it at 3:30 if you have not asked
Version C — A VESICLE ON THE THUMB — a herpetic whitlow, from sucking it — found only if you ask about rash on the hands or fingers
fails: ★ Saying 'we could give aciclovir' without making a decision — the antiviral decision and its reason belong in one sentence
★ Skipping the immune block, which is the pass mark and the only thing that changes the treatment

back.dx: VULVOVAGINITIS — non-specific vulval erythema — in a well, happy 4-year-old, with no feature of abuse on history or examination. Explain it: 'Jenny, I completely understand why you were worried. Having gone through everything with you and examined Mia, I believe the likely cause is a condition called vulvovaginitis — an inflammation of the skin of the private parts. It's very common in young girls, because the skin there is thin and sensitive and gets irritated easily by moisture, urine, soaps and bubble bath.' then give the reasoning before she asks for it — this is a required item: 'Let me tell you why I don't think this is abuse. The skin is simply red — there is no bruising, no tears, no discharge, no blisters or sores, and those are the things I specifically look for. She's happy, sleeping well and keen to see her dad. And the pattern fits the daily bubble bath and the leggings. I did consider other skin irritations and infections, and I found nothing else.' The management, and in mild cases no tests are needed: keep the area clean and dry; WIPE front to back; wash with water or a soap-free cleanser; stop the bubble bath and any scented WIPEs; about half a cup of white vinegar in a shallow bath for ten minutes; loose cotton underwear, no leggings for now, and nothing at night; a mild moisturiser and a zinc barrier cream to the red skin; and if she is itchy or it is not settling, a thin layer of one-percent hydrocortisone twice a day for about a week. Sort out the constipation. Review in one to two weeks. Safety-net: 'If anything changes — bruising, discharge, bleeding, or a change in how she's behaving — I want to see her straight away.' and when she says 'How can you be sure?' — re-explain once, then offer the pathway, never argue: 'I can't give you a guarantee, but I've looked specifically for every sign of abuse and found none, and she's happy in herself. If you still have concerns, we can involve the child protection team at the women's and children's for a more complete assessment. I expect they'll say the same, but I'd rather you felt sure. Would you like me to make that call?' The variant — the card shows blisters and inner-thigh bruising: 'Jenny, what I found on examination concerns me. There are blisters and bruising, and I'm not able to call this a simple skin irritation. I need to involve the child protection team at the women's and children's today so Mia is properly assessed and kept safe. I am required to report this, and I will support you through every step. Please don't question Mia about it yourself — the team are trained to do that gently.' back.dx: BALANITIS — inflammation of the skin at the tip of the penis and the foreskin, with a non-retractile foreskin that is normal for age and a negative dipstick. Explain it: 'Liam has a condition called balanitis. In plain words, it's inflammation of the skin at the tip of the penis and the foreskin. That skin is thin and sensitive, and under a nappy it sits in moisture and urine; bubble bath and WIPEs irritate it further, and sometimes a yeast joins in. It's the boy's version of nappy rash, and very common.' then kill the UTI idea explicitly: 'It hurts when he wees because urine stings the irritated skin — it doesn't mean he has a urine infection, and his dipstick is clear.' then the foreskin: 'His foreskin not pulling back is normal at his age — please don't force it; it loosens by itself over the next few years.' Management, conservative and specific: keep it clean and dry — change nappies often, nappy-free time, wash with water or a soap-free cleanser, and stop the bubble bath and scented WIPEs; a warm salt-water bath once or twice a day, then Pat dry; a mild steroid cream with an antifungal — hydrozole from the pharmacy — a thin layer two or three times a day for up to a week; and paracetamol if he's sore. Review in three to five days. The red-flag safety-net, which is a required item: 'Come back straight away if he can't pass urine, if the tip swells or goes dark, if the redness spreads up the shaft with fever, or if he becomes unwell.' The three questions he will ask: 'Is it because I pulled it back?' → 'That may have added a little irritation, but this happens in boys who've never been touched — please just don't force it again.' 'Does he need antibiotics?' → 'No — antibiotics don't help skin inflammation; the cream does.' 'Should he be circumcised?' → 'No. Circumcision is only considered for repeated problems or a scarred, tight foreskin that doesn't respond to cream.' Variants: febrile at 38.8 with redness onto the shaft, warmth and pus at the meatus — 'This is more than balanitis — a cellulitis, and I must exclude a urine infection. Urine culture first, oral antibiotics today, review in twenty-four hours; drowsy, vomiting or not improving means the children's hospital.' VERIFY the foreskin stuck back with a purple tip — 'That's paraphimosis and it's urgent — the foreskin is acting like a tight ring and cutting off the blood supply. I'll give him pain relief and try to reduce it now; if I can't, he goes to the children's surgeons today.' The changed social history — a new partner, weekends with his mother, bedwetting again and nightmares: go deeper on supervision, who bathes him, bruising and disclosures, then 'Thank you for telling me. I'd like advice from the child protection team at the women's and children's — a routine step to make sure Liam is safe.'
