Well, afebrile, growth normal — MOUTH BREATHING — CLEAR BILATERAL DISCHARGE — PALE, SWOLLEN, CONGESTED NASAL MUCOSA WITH SWOLLEN PALE INFERIOR TURBINATES — ears, throat, chest and skin normal
'WE BOTH SMOKE — INSIDE, YES.' Register it neutrally now and act on it in management

back.dx: VERSION B — recurrent viral upper respiratory tract infections at a normal frequency, with immunodeficiency excluded on history and examination. 'Archie is having recurrent upper respiratory tract infections — colds. For a two-year-old at childcare, eight to twelve a year is normal — roughly one a month, more in winter.' The differentials are marked one by one, so name four with reasons: 'Allergies in the nose, which his examination doesn't show; a long-standing sinus infection; something stuck up his nose, which gives a one-sided smelly discharge; and conditions that weaken the immune system — cystic fibrosis, coeliac disease, very rarely a blood cancer, or medicines that suppress immunity. Nothing in his story or examination points to any of those.' Stopping at 'Colds' loses the task. When she pushes: 'It's the number that frightens you, and I understand that. What tells me his immune system is working is how he gets sick: short, mild colds, over in a few days, never in hospital, never needing antibiotics, and growing beautifully in between. Children with a weak immune system look very different.' The two refusals, each with reasons: antibiotics — 'Not today, because this cold is viral and antibiotics don't work on viruses. But it isn't never: each time he's unwell, bring him in; if he has signs of a bacterial infection — high fever, ear infection, chest signs — we'll treat it.' Blood test — 'Not today either, for three reasons: no warning signs in his history, he's growing well with a normal examination, and these are the mild colds we expect at childcare. A normal blood count in a well child wouldn't change anything.' then say what would change your mind — the red flags: 'More than ten to twelve a year, infections that drag on or are severe — pneumonia, joint or skin infections, needing hospital — poor weight gain, lumps, or thrush that won't go. If any of those happen we test straight away.' Management, four things, and the first is the only one that will actually reduce the colds: 'The biggest one is the smoke: children in smoking households get more and longer colds and more ear infections. Smoking outside helps; stopping helps most, and I can refer you both to Quitline on 13 7848 or start you on something today.' then the flu vaccine each Autumn, free under five; for each cold fluids, rest, saline drops, paracetamol if uncomfortable, and no cough-and-cold medicines under six; and a fact sheet with review in a month to check his growth. And when she says she didn't want to be fobbed off: 'You're not being fobbed off — you've asked the right question and I've looked for the answer properly. The door is open.' Version A — allergic rhinitis: 'Most likely Noah has allergic rhinitis — an allergic reaction in the lining of the nose to things he breathes in, like dust or pollen — and I think that because the discharge is clear and constant, the lining of his nose looks the way allergy looks, and he mouth-breathes. He doesn't have the sneezing or itchy eyes some children get; many his age don't.' and when the father offers 'So it's just childcare then?': 'Childcare certainly spreads colds, but colds come and go with fevers and coughs, and Noah's nose runs clear every day even when he's well. I want to look at his nose before I tell you what it is.' The two other variants: the history reveals the package — two pneumonias, one needing a drip, and weight down two centile lines: 'That changes things. I'm not reassured, and I'm going to test today: a full blood count and film, immunoglobulin levels, an HIV test with your consent, a sweat test for cystic fibrosis and coeliac antibodies, and I'll speak to the paediatric immunologists.' A green, one-sided discharge: 'A smelly discharge from one nostril in a toddler usually means something has been pushed up there. I'm going to look now with a TORCH. If I can see it and it's soft we can try the parent's kiss technique; if not, he needs ENT the same day — and if there's any chance it's a button battery, that's an emergency.'
plan: Vitals, acknowledge, and ask the agenda question early: 'What's been worrying you?' → 'He just gets sick all the time. Cold after cold. I'm worried something's wrong with him.' → 'That sounds exhausting and worrying, and I'm glad you've come. Was there something in particular you were hoping for today?' → 'Antibiotics to knock it on the head, and a blood test to make sure his immune system is ok.' → 'Noted — I'll come back to both once I understand what's been happening.'

THE COMPLAINT IN SEVERITY TERMS, NOT COUNT: 'HOW MANY COLDS IN THE LAST TWELVE MONTHS? HOW LONG DOES EACH ONE LAST? HAS HE EVER BEEN ADMITTED TO HOSPITAL FOR AN INFECTION? EVER NEEDED ANTIBIOTICS? ANYTHING THAT WASN'T JUST A COLD — CHEST, EARS, JOINTS, SKIN? What does a typical one look like? Is he having one now?' → THEN SAY IT ALOUD: 'SO THEY'RE SHORT AND MILD.' ('Eight' is not the finding — the duration, the absent admissions and the absent antibiotics are.)

The immunodeficiency box, before anything else — this order is the concept of the case: 'Any infections during the pregnancy — were HIV and hepatitis tested? Born at term? Was the newborn heel-prick done and normal? Any long-term diarrhoea or greasy, pale stools? Any concerns about his growth or weight gain? Any lumps or bumps, or unusual bruising? Anyone in the family with a weak immune system? Any regular medicines — steroids? Any thrush in his mouth that won't clear?' → and when the sister comes up, one question only: 'Has she ever been admitted, or been given a diagnosis?' then move on.

Allergic rhinitis, then immunisation and childcare: itchy nose or rubbing, sneezing, red itchy watery eyes, wheeze, itchy rashes; mouth breathing, dark shadows under the eyes; snoring or gasping at night, daytime tiredness, ear infections, hearing or speech worries; anyone smoke at home or in the car, carpets, pets, dust, asthma, eczema or hay fever in the family; immunisations, childcare, eating, drinking, wet nappies. → 'We both smoke — inside, yes.' → register it neutrally.

THE CARD — READ IT ALOUD IN ONE SENTENCE AND SAY WHAT THE GROWTH CHART MEANS: 'normal ENT examination, clear chest, no nodes or thrush, AND A NORMAL GROWTH CHART — THAT'S THE MOST REASSURING FINDING.' (Silence while you read is wasted marks.)

Name it, give the normal frequency, then four differentials each with a reason (see dx) → 'But eight colds — that can't be normal. His sister was never this bad.' → answer with how he gets sick, not how often.
The two refusals with reasons, then the red flags that would change your mind (see dx). (Refusing flatly earns 'So you're fobbing me off'.)

MANAGEMENT — FOUR THINGS, SMOKE FIRST (see dx): the smoke addressed WITHOUT BLAME and with Quitline or medication offered; the FLU VACCINE, free under five; cold care with NO COUGH-AND-COLD MEDICINES UNDER SIX; and a fact sheet with review in a month. → 'I JUST DIDN'T WANT TO BE FOBBED OFF.' → 'YOU'RE NOT. YOU ASKED THE RIGHT QUESTION AND WE'VE LOOKED PROPERLY. THE DOOR IS OPEN.' Then summarise.

pefe: Role-player (Version B): JANE, 31, works part-time at the IGA; partner Dean drives trucks. Two children: ARCHIE (2) and RUBY (5). ARCHIE GOES TO CHILDCARE THREE DAYS A WEEK. In the last year he has had ABOUT EIGHT COLDS, each a runny nose, a bit of a cough, maybe a bit warm, OVER IN TWO OR THREE DAYS. NEVER IN HOSPITAL, NEVER HAD ANTIBIOTICS, NEVER ANYTHING WORSE THAN A COLD. Mild runny nose today. Eats and sleeps well, GROWING FINE. Normal pregnancy with all tests normal, term, HEEL PRICK NORMAL, immunised. Normal stools, no lumps or bruising, NO THRUSH, no medicines or allergies. YOU AND DEAN BOTH SMOKE, MOSTLY INSIDE — you know you shouldn't and WILL GET DEFENSIVE IF LECTURED, BUT WILL ENGAGE IF OFFERED HELP. RUBY 'GETS CHEST INFECTIONS' — if asked: two courses of antibiotics for bronchitis last winter, NEVER ADMITTED, NO DIAGNOSIS.

Agenda and register: you want antibiotics and a blood test — volunteer both if asked 'Anything specific?' In the first minute; if never asked, raise them at about six minutes. You are tired and a little defensive, not hostile. Push once on 'Eight can't be normal — his sister was never like this'. Soften only if the doctor gives reasons, not just a refusal; if refused flatly, say 'So you're fobbing me off'. If the doctor lectures about smoking, fold your arms; if offered Quitline or help, say 'Maybe — I've tried before'.

VERSION A CARD — MARK, father of NOAH (3): a CLEAR, WATERY RUNNY NOSE FROM BOTH NOSTRILS ALMOST EVERY DAY FOR ABOUT FIVE MONTHS. Fine today. No fever, cough, sore throat or ear pain with it. NO sneezing, NO itchy or watery eyes, no rashes, no wheeze. Doesn't snore. Ears, hearing and speech fine. HE DOES BREATHE THROUGH HIS MOUTH IF ASKED. NO SMOKERS, no pets, no carpet in his room. NO FAMILY ATOPY. Heel prick normal, term, normal growth, no admissions, no medicines, immunised. GOES TO CHILDCARE AND 'PICKS UP EVERYTHING' — VOLUNTEER THIS AROUND FOUR MINUTES TO TEMPT THE DOCTOR INTO 'RECURRENT INFECTIONS'. You are frustrated: 'we've tried everything from the chemist'. Score them on: vitals; frustration acknowledged; AGENDA ASKED EARLY; the complaint explored properly; the infection screen; allergic symptoms, signs, complications, triggers and family; THE IMMUNE BOX — pregnancy, heel prick, stools, growth, lumps, admissions, family, medicines; IN VERSION B, THE IMMUNE BOX BEFORE ALLERGY; immunisation, childcare and SMOKE; THE CARD READ ALOUD; in Version A, THE DIAGNOSIS FROM THE CARD WITH THREE REASONS AND NOT CLOSED EARLY; in Version B, RECURRENT URTI NAMED with FOUR DIFFERENTIALS AND WHY NOT; ANTIBIOTICS DECLINED WITH THE 'ASSESS EACH TIME' LINE; BLOODS DECLINED WITH THREE REASONS; THE IMMUNODEFICIENCY RED FLAGS STATED; SMOKE ADDRESSED WITH HELP; FLU VACCINE; fact sheet; review; and summary.
Which finding matters most — THE NORMAL GROWTH CHART — say so aloud: 'that's the most reassuring finding'
VERSION B — the severity answers — About eight colds in the year — two or three days each — never in hospital — never had antibiotics — nothing worse than a cold
The immunodeficiency box — ALL NEGATIVE — normal pregnancy with all tests fine, term, HEEL-PRICK NORMAL, normal stools, GROWING FINE, no lumps or bruising, no medicines, NO THRUSH
The sister — 'HIS SISTER GETS CHEST INFECTIONS BUT SHE'S HEALTHY OTHERWISE' — A DISTRACTOR. Explore in ONE question — any diagnosis, any admissions — then leave it
VERSION A — the discharge — FIVE MONTHS, ALMOST EVERY DAY, CLEAR AND WATERY, BOTH NOSTRILS, no blood or smell, NO SYMPTOMS TODAY — and he DOES breathe through his mouth if asked
Version A — the tempting line — 'He goes to childcare and picks up everything' — volunteered around four minutes to tempt you into 'Recurrent infections'

setting: History, mental state examination and management — general practice, and the framework card for all of psychiatry. The station is won on the follow-up question, not the first one. Five AUTOMATIC FAILS: suicide never asked, or asked only in euphemism; a positive answer accepted without follow-up; no confidentiality statement; reassurance offered before the risk assessment; and no safety plan or crisis contact. The first answer is deliberately vague — 'I've been feeling out of sorts' — and accepting it is how the station is lost in ninety seconds.

8 minutes: take a focused psychiatric history, present your mental state examination to the examiner, then give the most likely diagnosis, the differentials and immediate management. FOUR VARIANTS: THE BURIED TRAUMA; THE UNINTERRUPTIBLE PATIENT; THE SILENT PATIENT; AND THE HOSTILE PATIENT.

back.dx: A moderate major depressive episode. Present it with the features attached: 'Two months of low mood and anhedonia with early-morning waking, appetite and weight loss, guilt, impaired concentration, functional decline, and passive suicidal ideation without plan, intent or preparation. There are no psychotic features and no past manic episode.' The differentials, each with its reason: adjustment disorder — 'There is a clear stressor, but the symptom count and duration meet depressive criteria'; bipolar disorder — 'I screened negative for past elevated mood'; and an organic cause, particularly thyroid disease, plus substance use. The mental state examination, presented in order: 'A young man who looks his stated age, casually but adequately dressed, mildly unkempt, sitting with a stooped posture and poor eye contact, with psychomotor slowing. Speech is slow, quiet and monotonous with poverty of speech. He describes his mood as low and empty; affect is restricted in range, minimally reactive, and congruent. No hallucinations or illusions. Thought form is linear; content shows over-valued guilt and passive suicidal ideation with no plan, means or intent, and no homicidal ideation. Insight is intact, judgement is normal on the fire question, and he is alert and oriented.' Management — and finishing on the diagnosis is marked down even when the diagnosis is right: agree a safety plan with him; establish who is at home tonight and where he sleeps; ask permission to involve a support person — his mother; arrange a mental health treatment plan with psychological therapy; take bloods including TSH; and review within a week. The plan must say where he sleeps tonight and who is with him. The four variants. The buried trauma — he offers only an argument and a cut: 'Tell me more about the argument' → 'She was wearing a pink dress and I got angry' → 'That doesn't sound like something that would usually make you angry. Did the dress remind you of anything?' → the childhood abuse. Then nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance, hypervigilance, duration over a month, and the function of the self-injury — relief, not intent to die. The uninterruptible patient — 'I'm sorry to interrupt — that's really helpful and I want to make sure I cover a few important things in the time we have. Can I bring you back to your sleep for a moment?' — and add the mania criteria: reduced need for sleep, grandiosity, distractibility, overspending, increased goal-directed activity, hypersexuality, plus the extended delusion set. The silent patient — 'Take your time, there's no rush' and 'Would it help if I asked some shorter questions and you just tell me yes or no?' — shorten every question, tolerate silence, and the examiner is scoring whether you keep the structure without becoming brusque. The hostile patient at the psychosis screen — 'Not at all, and I'm sorry, I should have explained better. These are questions I ask everybody who comes to see me about how they're feeling. Some of them do sound odd. Would it be all right to carry on?' — do not abandon the screen; re-signpost and continue, because that recovery is itself the scored behaviour.
plan: CONFIDENTIALITY WITH ITS LIMITS, BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: 'I'm here to help you, and EVERYTHING WE TALK ABOUT IS CONFIDENTIAL AND STAYS BETWEEN US, UNLESS THERE'S A RISK OF HARM TO YOU OR TO SOMEONE ELSE. IS THAT OKAY WITH YOU?' (Delivering it AFTER the first open question is the trap — candidates then skip the open question because it feels as though it has already been asked.)

TWO OPEN QUESTIONS, MINIMUM: 'so James, HOW CAN I HELP YOU TODAY?' → 'I've been feeling out of sorts.' → WAIT, DO NOT FILL THE SILENCE → 'CAN YOU TELL ME A LITTLE MORE ABOUT THAT? WHAT DOES OUT OF SORTS FEEL LIKE FOR YOU?' → the story. (Accepting the vague first answer and moving to a symptom checklist is the commonest way this station is lost in the first ninety seconds.)
The three ts: 'How long have you been feeling like this — and is it getting worse? Did anything happen before it started? How is it affecting your life — your study, your day to day?'

GROUP ONE, WITH A FOLLOW-UP ON EVERY ABNORMAL ANSWER: 'how has your mood been? How has your sleep been? IS THAT TROUBLE FALLING ASLEEP, OR WAKING EARLY AND NOT GETTING BACK? How's your appetite? Any change in your weight? Energy and concentration?'

The risk question, direct and without euphemism: 'James, have you ever had thoughts of harming or killing yourself, or anyone else?' → 'Sometimes... I've thought everyone would be better off without me.' → then the staircase, and this is the scored moment of the entire station: 'Thank you for being honest — that's important. Have you ever tried to act on it before? Do you have a plan? Have you made any preparations, or thought about when? And any thoughts of harming anyone else?' (Accepting 'Sometimes' and moving on is the fail — and you say the answer out loud when you present.)

Signpost, then the psychosis screen: 'I'm going to ask a few questions that sound a bit strange — I ask them of everyone. Is that okay? Do you ever see, hear or feel things that other people don't? Do you have any thoughts or ideas that other people find strange? Do you feel guilty about anything? Do you feel you have any special powers? Does anyone seem to be trying to control you, follow you, or harm you?' (Skipping this in an obvious depression case means you cannot exclude major depression with psychotic features, and the examiner will say so.)

HEADSS AND THE REST: 'who do you live with, how are things between you, any stress at home? What are you studying — any stress there? ARE YOU STILL ENJOYING THE THINGS YOU USED TO? Any recreational drugs? HOW MUCH ALCOHOL IN A USUAL WEEK? HAVE YOU EVER TAKEN MEDICATION FOR YOUR MENTAL HEALTH? Any change in your sex life? ANY PREFERENCE FOR HOT OR COLD WEATHER?' (Ask medication as EVER, not present tense — 'are you on anything?' gets a bare no.)

Insight, judgement, past and family: 'Do you think you need medical help with this? This is just an imaginary question: if a large fire broke out in this room, what would you do? Have you ever had a mental health problem before, or been admitted for one? Has anyone in your family had a mental illness?'

SUMMARISE BACK AND OPEN THE DOOR: 'let me summarise: for about two months you've felt flat and lost interest, you're waking at four, eating less and losing weight, you're behind at university, and you've had thoughts that people would be better off without you — WITHOUT ANY PLAN. HAVE I GOT THAT RIGHT? IS THERE ANYTHING WORRYING YOU THAT I HAVEN'T ASKED ABOUT?'

back.dx: A MENTAL STATE EXAMINATION CONSISTENT WITH A MODERATE DEPRESSIVE EPISODE — presented as an examination, not a diagnosis. Open by naming the structure: 'Examiner, I'll present my mental state examination under nine headings: appearance, behaviour, speech, emotion, perception, thought, insight, cognition and judgement.' Appearance: 'I assessed facial expression, eye contact, clothing, grooming and posture, and looked for evidence of alcohol or drug use. A 34-year-old woman who looks her stated age, casually dressed in clothing appropriate for the setting but creased, hair unbrushed, mildly unkempt. She sits with a stooped posture, makes poor eye contact, and her facial expression is tearful. No flushing, tremor or other evidence of intoxication.' Describing the clothing colour and stopping is the trap — colour is not a finding; appropriateness, grooming and self-neglect are. Behaviour: 'Overall behaviour, attitude towards the interviewer, and abnormal movements. Cooperative but withdrawn; attitude engaged although slow to respond; marked psychomotor retardation, with no tremor, tics, abnormal facial movements or mannerisms.' Speech: 'Rate, quantity, quality and volume. Rate slow with increased latency of response, poverty of speech with largely monosyllabic answers, quality clear with no slurring, stuttering or echolalia, volume low and monotonous.' Emotion: 'She described her mood, in her own words, as just empty. Her affect was restricted in range, minimally reactive — it did not lift when she spoke about her children — and congruent with the mood she described.' Giving one word for affect is the trap: three terms are expected — range, reactivity, congruence. Perception: 'Hallucinations and illusions. She denied seeing, hearing or feeling anything others do not, and there was nothing on observation to suggest she was responding to internal stimuli.' Thought: 'Form was linear but with poverty of ideas. Taking content in order of importance: on risk, she has passive suicidal ideation — she said her family would be better off without her — with no previous attempt, no plan, no preparation and no chosen date, and no thoughts of harming anyone else. She holds over-valued guilt about the breakdown of her marriage, which she partly concedes may be unfair. There were no delusions, obsessions, compulsions, phobias or hypochondriacal thoughts.' Risk is thought content, it comes first, and it is stated either way — leaving it to the end or omitting it because it was negative is the trap. Insight, cognition and judgement: 'Her insight is intact — she came at her sister's insistence but told the doctor she thinks something is wrong and wants help. On cognition she was alert with no clouding of consciousness. She addressed the doctor by title and referred to attending the clinic, so she is oriented to person and place; orientation to time was not tested, and no formal memory testing was performed. Judgement was not formally tested, but there was nothing in the consultation to suggest impairment.' Saying 'Insight not assessed' and 'Not oriented' is the trap — both were demonstrated indirectly, and saying so is the difference between a candidate who understands that the MSE is observation and one who is waiting to be handed answers. The summary and the two findings: 'A 34-year-old woman with psychomotor retardation, poverty of speech, a restricted and congruent affect, and passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent. The two findings I would act on are her suicidal ideation, which needs a full risk assessment and a safety plan today, and her functional decline. This is consistent with a moderate depressive episode.' The variants. The intoxicated man: 'A dishevelled man who looks older than his stated age, flushed, with a smell of alcohol and a coarse tremor — evidence of intoxication. Behaviour: initially drowsy, rousing to hostility, attitude uncooperative and at times threatening. Speech slurred, loud and rambling. Affect labile. On cognition: drowsy with clouding of consciousness, and disoriented to time' — and clouding of consciousness is the finding that makes this medical before it is psychiatric. The psychotic man: 'Unkempt with evidence of self-neglect, attitude distracted, appearing to respond to internal stimuli; thought form showed loosening of association and thought blocking; in content he reports third-person auditory hallucinations — and I would specifically want to know whether they carry command content — and a persecutory delusion that his neighbours are monitoring him. Insight is impaired.' The incongruent affect: 'She described her mood as happy, honestly fine. Her affect, however, was tearful and restricted, and therefore incongruent with the stated mood. Given that incongruence, I would not accept the denial of low mood at face value and would want a collateral history.' The cognitive video, where the doctor performs an MMSE and the task is still to present an MSE: 'Appearance, behaviour and speech as observed; mood was not asked — on affect I observed a shallow but reactive affect; perception and thought could not be assessed, since no questions were put to him; on cognition he was alert and oriented to place and person, with impaired registration and recall indicating short-term memory loss, and a minor error in attention.'

THE TERMS YOU MUST NOT FUMBLE: DELUSION — a fixed, firm belief, UNSHAKEABLE by evidence or rational argument. OVER-VALUED IDEA — the same shape, less strength; THE PATIENT CONCEDES IT MAY BE UNTRUE. PREOCCUPATION — prominent and recurrent, NOT FIXED, NOT UNWANTED. OBSESSION — intrusive, unwanted, RESISTED, anxiety-provoking, AND THE RELIEVING ACT IS THE COMPULSION. HALLUCINATION — a perception WITH NO STIMULUS. ILLUSION — a MISINTERPRETATION OF A REAL STIMULUS. MAGICAL THINKING — an action IRRATIONALLY LINKED to an unlikely outcome.

AND THE FORM DISTINCTIONS: CIRCUMSTANTIAL ARRIVES; TANGENTIAL DOES NOT. FLIGHT OF IDEAS STAYS RELEVANT; LOOSENING OF ASSOCIATION DOES NOT. ECHOLALIA is repetition of the examiner's words. THOUGHT BLOCKING is when speech stops and the thought is gone.
pefe: Role-player: SARAH MILTON, 34, primary school teacher, TWO CHILDREN AGED 6 AND 9, SEPARATED FOUR MONTHS AGO. You live with the children; YOUR SISTER CHECKS ON YOU AND MADE THIS APPOINTMENT. No medical conditions, no medications, no alcohol or drugs, no past psychiatric history. YOUR MOTHER HAD POST-NATAL DEPRESSION.

How to play it — this matters more than the answers: sit heavily and keep your coat on. Look at your hands, not at the doctor. Leave a three to four second pause before every answer. Speak quietly, slowly, on one note. Give single words unless pushed. Do not move your hands at all. WIPE your eyes twice. When you talk about your children, do not brighten — your face should not change. If the doctor rushes, become slower and quieter; if kind and waiting, give one extra sentence. If asked about hallucinations without warning, look up sharply: 'Why would you ask me that?'

SCORE THE PRESENTATION: named ALL NINE HEADINGS IN ORDER; named the SUB-COMPONENTS under appearance, behaviour, speech and affect; stooped posture; poor eye contact; tearful expression; mildly unkempt; NO EVIDENCE OF INTOXICATION; PSYCHOMOTOR RETARDATION; slow rate with INCREASED LATENCY; POVERTY OF SPEECH; low monotonous volume; MOOD QUOTED IN HER OWN WORDS; AFFECT AS RANGE, REACTIVITY AND CONGRUENCE; perception addressed; thought form named; RISK STATED FIRST UNDER CONTENT with plan, means and intent; GUILT CALLED AN OVER-VALUED IDEA, NOT A DELUSION; INSIGHT CALLED INTACT WITH THE REASON; alertness and orientation; SAID WHICH ITEMS WERE NOT TESTED rather than 'not assessed'; and a CLOSING SUMMARY NAMING WHAT TO ACT ON.
The nine headings — A B s E P T I C J — appearance, behaviour, speech, emotion, perception, thought, insight, cognition, judgement
Mood, in her own words — 'JUST EMPTY' — after a long pause
Affect — Restricted in range — minimally reactive, because it did not lift when she spoke about her children — and congruent
Risk — 'I've thought they'd be better off without me' — no previous attempt, no plan, no preparation, no date, and no thoughts of harming anyone else
The guilt — 'The marriage ending was my fault... My sister says it wasn't. I suppose she might be right. I just can't feel it' — an over-valued idea, not a delusion
Insight — 'I THINK SOMETHING'S WRONG, DOCTOR. I CAME TO YOUR CLINIC BECAUSE I WANT IT TO STOP' — intact, and that sentence also gives person and place
What was NOT tested — ORIENTATION TO TIME — FORMAL MEMORY TESTING — AND JUDGEMENT. Say which items were NOT TESTED rather than 'not assessed'
If the doctor asks about hallucinations without warning — She looks up sharply: 'Why would you ask me that?'

VARIANT — the intoxicated man — Flushed with a coarse tremor and a smell of alcohol, drowsy rousing to hostility, slurred loud rambling speech, labile affect — and clouding of consciousness with disorientation to time, which makes it medical before it is psychiatric

VARIANT — the incongruent affect — She says her mood is 'Happy, honestly fine' while her affect is tearful and restricted — the variant exists to test whether you know mood and affect are two different observations

What the video shows you — She sits down heavily and does not take her coat off — looks at her hands throughout — WIPEs her eyes twice — takes several seconds to begin each answer — does not move her hands at all

How each becomes a finding — The pause length gives you latency — the head-shake with no change in expression gives you reactivity — the concession about her sister's view converts a guilt delusion into an over-valued idea — and 'I came to your clinic, doctor' gives you insight, person and place without a single direct question

back.dx: IMPAIRED REGISTRATION AND RECALL WITH A MINOR ATTENTIONAL DEFICIT — isolated short-term memory impairment, most likely alcohol-related, with hyperglycaemia contributing. The closing explanation, in order: normal first — 'Most of it was normal. You knew the date, where we were, and what floor we're on. Your language was fine — you named things, read and followed the instruction, wrote a sentence, followed a three-part command and repeated the phrase. And you copied the drawing well.' then the two abnormalities, described rather than scored: 'When I gave you three words to remember, it took a few goes before you had them; and when I asked for them a few minutes later, you could give me one of the three. There was also a small error when you spelled the word backwards.' then the interpretation in plain words: 'What that means is that you're having some difficulty with your short-term memory, and a minor difficulty with concentration.' then the screening limitation, which you already set up at the start: 'This is a screening test, so it can't tell us on its own why that is. It tells us there's something worth looking into.' then the likely cause and the hope: 'Given how much you've been drinking over the last few years, alcohol is the most likely explanation, and the good news is that some of this can improve now you've stopped. Your blood sugar today is also very high, and that can affect memory and concentration too.' then the next step: 'Blood tests, start you on a vitamin called thiamine, sort out your insulin, and see you again to repeat this in a few weeks. Does that make sense? What questions do you have?' Three sentences fail the station: 'This shows dementia', 'You're a bit confused', and 'Your long-term memory is poor' — and so does the opposite error, 'You did quite well, nothing to worry about'. When he asks 'So have I got dementia?': 'That's a very understandable question, and the honest answer is that this test can't tell us that. It's a screening test — it tells us there's something worth looking into, not what's causing it.' and one more thing before he goes: 'I'd like to talk about driving at your next visit, and it would help me a great deal if your daughter could come with you.' The variants. Present to the examiner instead: 'This patient had impaired registration — three trials to learn three words — and impaired recall, one of three retained, with a single-letter error spelling world backwards indicating a minor attentional deficit. Orientation, naming, repetition, reading, writing, the three-stage command and construction were normal. The pattern is isolated short-term memory impairment. Given sustained heavy alcohol use, the most likely cause is alcohol-related brain injury. I would not label this wernicke-korsakoff syndrome on these findings alone, since that requires more than memory impairment.' The interrupter: redirect without explaining — 'I'll explain everything in a few minutes when we're finished. If we could just carry on — we're almost done.' The incomplete chart, with no place questions and no writing task: say nothing about it and do the examination in full from memory — and if the examiner asks afterwards, 'I noticed the chart didn't include the ORIENTATION-TO-PLACE items or the writing task, so I completed those from the standard structure.' This is the reason the six steps are memorised — it is a deliberate discriminator. The management version: 'Parenteral thiamine before any glucose-containing fluid; check ketones and HbA1c; bloods including B12, folate, thyroid function, liver function, calcium and electrolytes. A collateral history, a medication review, support and monitoring of abstinence, his insulin adherence, driving against the national fitness-to-drive standards, and repeat cognitive assessment after a period of sobriety and better glycaemic control. I'd involve his family with his consent, and refer for formal cognitive assessment if the deficit persists.'
plan: INTRODUCE AND EXPLAIN IT IN PLAIN LANGUAGE: 'I've been asked to explain a test called a MINI-MENTAL STATE EXAMINATION and then do it with you. IT'S A SIMPLE BEDSIDE TEST. We use it to check YOUR SHORT-TERM MEMORY, YOUR THINKING, YOUR COMMUNICATION, AND HOW YOUR BRAIN IS WORKING OVERALL.' (Using the word COGNITION to a patient is the trap — break it into the three plain terms first.)

THE SCREENING-TEST BOX — the sentence that protects you at the end: 'IT'S A SCREENING TEST, WHICH MEANS IT CAN'T BE USED ON ITS OWN TO MAKE A DIAGNOSIS. BUT IF IT COMES BACK ABNORMAL, IT RAISES THE POSSIBILITY — AND THE CONCERN — THAT THERE MIGHT BE A PROBLEM, AND WE'D THEN ARRANGE SOME FURTHER TESTS TO LOOK INTO IT PROPERLY.' (Skip this and the closing interpretation gets much harder and the critical error much easier.)

THE STEPS, CONSENT AND THE GROUND RULE: 'a few simple steps — questions about the time and the place; a few words to remember and recall later; reading, writing and repeating a phrase; and copying a drawing. I'D LIKE YOU TO CONCENTRATE AS BEST YOU CAN — ARE YOU HAPPY TO GO THROUGH THIS WITH ME? IF ANYTHING ISN'T CLEAR, TELL ME AND I'LL REPEAT IT. BUT QUESTIONS ABOUT WHAT I'M FINDING AND WHAT IT MEANS, I'LL ANSWER ONCE WE'RE FINISHED.'

ORIENTATION — FIVE AND FIVE: 'what year is it? What season? What month? What's the date today? What day of the week?' then 'what country are we in? What state? What town? What building are we in? WHAT FLOOR ARE WE ON?'

Registration: 'I'm going to say three words. Repeat them back, and please try to remember them because I'll ask you again in a few minutes. Ball... Car... Man.' — said slowly, about a second apart, with about ten seconds between trials, up to three to five trials — and scored on the first.

ATTENTION: 'now I'd like you to SPELL A WORD BACKWARDS. The word is WORLD — W, O, R, L, D. Can you spell it backwards for me?' → D, L, R, W, O. A SINGLE TRANSPOSITION IS A MINOR ERROR, NOT IMPAIRMENT.

RECALL — ONCE ONLY, NO PROMPTING: 'a few minutes ago I gave you three words. CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT THEY WERE?' → 'ball... that's all I've got.' → ACCEPT IT AND MOVE ON. (Re-asking or giving a clue converts a scored finding into an unscoreable one.)

Language, five parts: 'What is this called? And this?' — then 'Please read this and do what it says' with close your eyes written out — then 'Please write a complete sentence on this paper' — then 'Take this paper in your hand, fold it in half, and put it on your lap' — then 'Please repeat after me: no ifs, ands or buts.' then construction: 'Here are two shapes that overlap. Please copy this drawing as accurately as you can.'

The closing explanation — normal first, then the two abnormalities described, then the plain-words interpretation, then the screening limitation, the likely cause and the next step (see dx) → 'So have I got dementia?' → the honest answer, then the driving-and-daughter line before he leaves.

pefe: Role-player: Ken Harding, 60, retired truck driver, lives alone since his wife died three years ago. Type 2 diabetes on insulin which he often skips. Four glasses of wine every night for four years; stopped two weeks ago because his daughter asked him to. His daughter says he has become forgetful and unreliable — he does not think it is a problem.

How to play it — this is the whole brief: be cooperative but uninterested, and do not be helpful. Do what you are asked; do not volunteer anything. Answer only the specific question you were asked. Flat tone, unhurried, slightly bored. Do not offer information about your drinking or your memory unless asked a direct question — and if they start taking a history, answer briefly and let them realise it is not their task. The three interruptions, spread through the test: 'What did you say?', 'Why are we doing this?', and 'Is this because of my daughter?' if the doctor explains or gets drawn into conversation, keep going with another question. If they redirect politely and repeat the task, accept it and comply. At the very end, ask 'So have I got dementia?' — their answer is the most important thing you will score.

stem: Medical officer, mental health ward of a regional hospital, 10:00. James Whitfield, 22, brought in by ambulance and police at 02:00 after his housemate rang 000: four nights without sleep, spending money he does not have, rapid speech, believes he has been chosen for a special purpose. Assessed overnight as a first episode of mania with psychotic features. He refused admission and refuses medication, and is on a level 1 inpatient treatment order.

HR 96 — BP 128/78 — T 36.8 — RR 16 — SpO2 99% — BSL 5.4. Settled but irritable. His father has arrived, is shouting at the nurses' station, and is threatening to call a lawyer and take his son home. 8 minutes. The examiner may ask you to state the criteria in the last minute. Version B: the gp-room patient who refuses transfer. Version C: an Aboriginal patient with a fearful family.
tasks: Take a brief further history from the father, relevant to this presentation
Explain why his son is being kept and treated without consent
Explain the legal framework, its criteria and its safeguards
Explain his son's rights and the father's own options
Respond to his concerns and answer his questions
time: Acknowledge the emotion before explaining anything, and ask what he has been told · then open the collateral wide: 'You know James better than any of us · tell me what you've seen over the last week or two' · then the three questions that change management: has anything like this happened before, even milder; has he been using anything · alcohol, cannabis, ice, prescription tablets; and has he ever talked about harming himself or anyone else · then name the illness before the law, and say that the illness has taken away his ability to recognise he is unwell · then the consent sentence: normally nobody can treat an adult without consent, not me, not you, and there is one exception in law for exactly this situation · then correct 'Locked up' immediately and without defensiveness · then the four criteria in order, the order's name, its length and its 24-hour review by a different psychiatrist · then volunteer the four rights before he asks: a second opinion arranged today, appeal to the tribunal with free legal representation, a carer or advocate present at meetings, and his own legal advice · then his questions, and protect the last thirty seconds for the summary by watching the clock at six minutes.

back.dx: A FIRST PRESENTATION OF MANIA WITH PSYCHOTIC FEATURES, TREATED UNDER A LEVEL 1 INPATIENT TREATMENT ORDER — and the station is about explaining it to a terrified father. Name the illness before the law: 'James has become unwell with a condition that changes how he thinks and how he sees the world. One of the cruellest parts of it is that it takes away his ability to recognise that he's unwell — so he can't make this treatment decision for himself at the moment.' then the consent sentence: 'Normally nobody can treat an adult without their consent — not me, not you. There is one exception in law and it exists for exactly this situation, where an illness has taken away the ability to decide.' then the correction, immediately and without defensiveness: 'He's not under arrest and he hasn't done anything wrong. He is in hospital receiving treatment, and the door is locked to keep him safe while he's unwell, not to punish him.' The four criteria, in order, and all four true: 'One, he has a mental illness. Two, he needs treatment to protect him from harm. Three, his illness has impaired his ability to make this decision. Four, there is no less restrictive way — we did try to do it voluntarily first.' The order, its length and its check — and the examiner is listening for a number: 'It's a level 1 inpatient treatment order. It lasts up to seven days. A psychiatrist — a different one from whoever made it — has to review it within 24 hours. If he improves, it can be lifted the same day. If he needs longer, that decision goes to a psychiatrist, and beyond that to a tribunal, not to me.' Saying 'Indefinitely' or 'Until he's better' is the trap. Then the four rights, volunteered — 'And you should know what you can do, because you have real options': 'You can ask for a second opinion from another psychiatrist — say the word and I'll arrange it today. James, or you on his behalf, can appeal to the tribunal, and legal representation for that appeal is free. He's entitled to have a carer, family member or advocate with him for meetings about his care, and I'd like that to be you. And you can take your own legal advice whenever you like. Nothing here is hidden.' His five questions, answered: 'Can I take him home if I watch him?' → 'I can't let you do that today, and I'm sorry. What I can do is get him reviewed quickly, and if he improves the order comes off.' 'What have you given him?' → 'An antipsychotic — it settles the racing thoughts and lets him sleep. I'll go through the side effects with you both.' 'What did he say about me?' → 'I can't share what James has told me without his agreement. I can listen to anything you want me to know.' 'Is it my fault?' → 'No. This is an illness. Nothing you did caused it, and you are the reason he got here at all.' 'I'm going to sue you.' → 'That's your right, and there is a free legal service for exactly this. I'll write the details down for you.' The closing summary, last thirty seconds, every time: 'James is unwell with an illness that's treatable. He's here under an order that lasts up to seven days and gets reviewed within 24 hours. You can ask for a second opinion, you can appeal with free legal help, and you can be with him. I'll find you after the psychiatrist has seen him. Is there anything I've not answered?' Version B — the patient who refuses transfer: 'Jenny, a plan, a time and preparations — that tells me you are not safe to go home this evening. I'm not going to let that happen, and it isn't a punishment.' and when she stands: 'I won't physically stop you, and I won't pretend this is fine either. If you walk out I will ring an ambulance and the police, because I believe you will die tonight if I don't. I'd much rather sit here and do this together.' Hold the line without a threat. Version C — an Aboriginal patient and a fearful family, and cultural safety is explicitly assessed: say it early, not after being prompted — 'Would you like an Aboriginal health practitioner or a family member with us while we talk? I can also arrange 13yarn, and I'd like to know if there is anyone in the community you want involved in his care.'
plan: Acknowledge before explaining, and ask what he has been told: 'Mr Whitfield? I'm Dr -, one of the doctors looking after James. Can we sit down in here — it's quieter.' → 'I don't want to sit down. I want my son. You've got him locked in there like a criminal.' → 'I can see you're upset, and honestly I would be too. I've got about eight minutes and I want to use them properly. Can I hear what you've been told so far, and then I'll explain exactly what's happening and what your options are?' → 'A nurse said he's been detained. That's all anyone will tell me.' → 'That's not enough, and I'm sorry. Let me start with James rather than the paperwork.'
The collateral, opened wide: 'You know him better than any of us. What have you seen over the last week or two?' → the 3 a.m. Calls, no sleep, four thousand dollars.

The three questions that change management: 'Has anything like this happened before, even milder?' → the month in bed two years ago. 'Has he been using anything — alcohol, cannabis, ice, prescription tablets?' → 'That's what this is, isn't it?' → neither accept nor reject it. 'Has he ever talked about harming himself, or anyone else?'

Name the illness, then the consent sentence, then correct 'Locked up' (see dx) → 'He seems fine to me. He's just tired.' / 'So you decide for him.' (Answering 'Why is he here' with the legislation first is the named trap — illness first, then the law as the thing that permits the treatment.)

The four criteria in order, then the order's name, length and 24-hour review (see dx) → 'Who decided that? One doctor can just do that? What if you're wrong?' → and he presses hard for a number: 'How long? Days? Weeks? Give me a number.'

Volunteer the four rights before he asks — the discriminating issue of the station: 'And you should know what you can do, because you have real options' (see dx) → he sits down: 'Nobody said any of that.' → 'Then I'm glad we sat down. The order isn't there to take his rights away — it's the thing that lets us treat him and gives him a review, a tribunal and a lawyer.'

HIS QUESTIONS (see dx) — taking him home, the medication, confidentiality, the licence, and the lawsuit threat met without defensiveness. → and if you have been warm, quietly: 'IS IT MY FAULT? I TOLD HIM TO PULL HIMSELF TOGETHER.'

The closing summary — protect it by watching the clock at six minutes (see dx): illness, duration and review, second opinion, appeal with free legal help, and his place beside his son — then 'Is there anything I've not answered?' and if the examiner asks: 'Mental illness; treatment needed for protection from harm to self or others; impaired decision-making capacity about that treatment; and no less restrictive means available.'

I can also arrange 13yarn, and I'd like to know if there is anyone in the community you want involved in his care.' Offering it early is the difference.
pefe: Role-player: RAY WHITFIELD, 54, A SHEARING CONTRACTOR FROM KADINA. His son James is 22, HIS ONLY CHILD, in a share house in town. HIS WIFE DIED SIX YEARS AGO. HE HAS NOT SLEPT — the housemate rang at 4 a.m. and he drove straight in. HE HAS BEEN TOLD ALMOST NOTHING: a nurse used the word 'DETAINED' and walked off, and he has been standing in a corridor for two hours.

WHAT HE KNOWS: 3 a.m. calls with business ideas, no proper sleep for days, ABOUT $4,000 SPENT ON EQUIPMENT. TWO YEARS AGO A MONTH WHERE HE WOULD NOT GET OUT OF BED. He smokes cannabis. NO VIOLENCE, EVER. No previous psychiatric contact. Apprentice diesel mechanic, missed work all week. FAMILY HISTORY, ONLY IF ASKED: 'MY BROTHER WAS IN AND OUT OF HOSPITAL. NOBODY TALKED ABOUT IT.'

Hidden agenda and register: he is not really angry — he is terrified and guilty, because he told James a fortnight ago to 'Pull himself together'. He says it only near the end, and only if the doctor asks what is worrying him or is kind. Start at 8/10 anger, standing, loud. Drop to 4/10 the moment the doctor acknowledges your feelings before explaining anything. Sit down when rights are volunteered without you asking. If the doctor leads with legislation or policy, go up to 9/10 and threaten to call the police. If rights only come when demanded: 'I had to drag that out of you' — and stay hard. Push 'Can I take him home if I watch him?' Twice before accepting no, and test confidentiality once with 'What did he say about me?'
What he has been told — Almost nothing — a nurse used the word 'Detained' and walked off, and he has been standing in a corridor for two hours
The collateral — Ringing him at 3 a.m. With business ideas — no proper sleep for days — spent about $4,000 on equipment he doesn't need — missed work all week

The previous episode — 'TWO YEARS AGO HE WENT THE OTHER WAY. WOULDN'T GET OUT OF BED FOR A MONTH. WE THOUGHT IT WAS THE BREAK-UP' — which is what makes this bipolar rather than a first psychotic episode
Substances — 'HE SMOKES A BIT OF WEED. THAT'S WHAT THIS IS, ISN'T IT? IT'S THE DRUGS' — the father trying to hand you a diagnosis
How to handle that — Do not accept it and do not reject it: 'That's an important thing to check, and we are checking it. Even if cannabis is part of it, what we're seeing today still needs treating'
Risk and family history — Never any violence, 'He's a gentle kid' — and, only if asked, 'My brother was in and out of hospital. Nobody talked about it'

His emotional register — Starts at 8 out of 10 anger, standing, loud — drops to 4 the moment you acknowledge his feelings before explaining anything — sits down when rights are volunteered without him asking
If you lead with the law — He goes up to 9 out of 10 and threatens to call the police: 'Don't give me paperwork. That's my son'
If rights are only given when demanded — 'I had to drag that out of you' — and he stays hard

The hidden agenda — He is not really angry — he is terrified and guilty, because he told James a fortnight ago to 'Pull himself together'. He says it only near the end, and only if you ask what is worrying him or are kind to him

The questions he will push — 'Can I take him home if I watch him?' — pushed twice before accepting no — 'What have you given him?' — 'What did he say about me?' To test confidentiality — 'Will this follow him? His job needs a licence' — and 'How long? Days? Weeks? Give me a number'
fails: ★ Waiting to be asked about rights — rights volunteered at minute six pass, rights extracted at minute eight do not
★ Accepting the father's consent to treat his son, or disclosing what James said without his agreement
Being unable to state the four criteria, or never giving a duration — saying 'indefinitely' or 'until he's better' when the examiner is listening for a number
Promising discharge, or becoming defensive and dismissive when threatened with legal action

Answering 'why is he here' with the legislation first, when illness comes before law; failing to correct 'locked up' immediately; accepting or flatly rejecting the father's 'it's the drugs'; and running out of time and skipping the closing summary, which carries marks for orientation, plan and the invitation to ask
numbers: Four criteria: mental illness · treatment needed for protection from harm · impaired decision-making capacity · no less restrictive means. Level 1 inpatient treatment order up to 7 days, reviewed within 24 hours by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner who did not make it VERIFY

Level 2 ito 42 days, extendable once · level 3 ito 12 months, 6 months for a child, by SACAT · community treatment order 42 days or 12 months VERIFY · SA mental health triage 13 14 65 · Lifeline 13 11 14 · Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636 · 13yarn 13 92 76 · CARL 13 14 78

must: FAIL — Accepting the father's consent to treat James, or disclosing what James said without his agreement — AUTOMATIC FAILS, and he tests both; 'what did he say about me?' → 'I can't share what James has told me without his agreement; I can listen to anything you want me to know' (★)

FAIL — Being unable to state the criteria, or never giving a duration, or saying 'indefinitely' or 'until he's better' — AUTOMATIC FAILS and the examiner is listening for a number; all four criteria in order: he has a mental illness; he needs treatment to protect him from harm; his illness has impaired his ability to make this decision; and there is no less restrictive way — we did try voluntarily first; Level 1 inpatient treatment order, up to seven days, reviewed by a different psychiatrist within 24 hours, then psychiatrist and tribunal, not you (VERIFY current SA durations) (★)

FAIL — Waiting to be asked about rights — the discriminating issue of the station: rights volunteered at minute six pass, rights extracted at minute eight do not; 'before you ask me, you have real options' — a second opinion from another psychiatrist arranged today, an appeal to the tribunal by James or by you on his behalf with FREE legal representation, a carer, family member or advocate with him for meetings about his care, and your own legal advice whenever you like; 'nothing here is hidden'

FAIL — Leading with the legislation, promising discharge, or becoming defensive or dismissive when threatened with legal action — AUTOMATIC FAILS; fathers do not hear law, they hear bureaucracy, so illness first and the law second as the thing that permits treatment: 'James has become unwell with a condition that changes how he thinks and how he sees the world, and one of the cruellest parts is that it takes away his ability to recognise that he's unwell'; 'I'm going to sue you' → 'that's your right, and there is a free legal service for exactly this — I'll write the details down for you' (★)

DO — Acknowledge the emotion before explaining anything — 'I can see you're upset, and honestly I would be too' — he starts at 8/10 standing and loud, drops to 4/10 the moment you do this and escalates to 9/10 if you lead with paperwork; then the collateral history and the three questions that change management: anything like this before even milder (a month in bed two years ago), alcohol, cannabis, ice or prescription tablets, and ever talked about harming himself or anyone else; 'it's the drugs, that's all this is' is neither accepted nor rejected → 'that's an important thing to check, and we are checking it; even if cannabis is part of it, what we're seeing today still needs treating'

SAY — Correct 'locked up' immediately and protect the last thirty seconds: 'he's not under arrest and he hasn't done anything wrong — he is in hospital receiving treatment, and the door is locked to keep him safe while he's unwell, not to punish him'; 'normally nobody can treat an adult without their consent — not me, not you; there is one exception in law and it exists for exactly this situation'; 'is it my fault?' → 'no, this is an illness; nothing you did caused it, and you are the reason he got here at all'; then the summary — illness, order length, 24-hour review, second opinion, appeal with free legal help, you can be with him — and 'is there anything I've not answered?'

setting: Brief history, explanation and a full management plan — rural general practice, no examination. The discriminating issue: buy the tablet time, and pay for it the same day. 'Give it four weeks' and nothing else is the commonest fail, because another four weeks of nothing is exactly what she is afraid of. Six AUTOMATIC FAILS: never asking directly about suicidal thoughts; never screening for a past manic episode; missing or dismissing the ST John's wort; changing or stopping the medication without checking adherence; no crisis plan; and no review date.
stem: GP, rural South Australian practice, standard 15-minute appointment. Rebecca Ellis, 34, a teacher, diagnosed with major depressive disorder at her last visit and started on citalopram 20 mg daily seven days ago. She has come back early, frustrated, saying the tablets are doing nothing and she wants to stop them.

Observations normal. Mood still low, sleep still poor. She has not started psychology. Her aunt has told her to try a herbal tablet instead. 8 minutes. Version B: no response at four weeks. Version C: the switch and serotonin syndrome. Version D: she is 12 weeks pregnant.
tasks: Take a brief further history relevant to her non-response
Explain why the medication has not worked yet
Explain your full management plan — medication, therapy and support
Address her concerns and answer her questions
time: Open with her experience, not your explanation · 'I'm glad you came back rather than just stopping them. Tell me what it's actually been like this week' · then adherence asked so it cannot be dodged: how many days in the last week did you miss a tablet · then the four screening questions: have you had any thoughts of ending your life; has there ever been a week where you needed far less sleep than usual and felt unstoppable, or were spending far more than normal; how much are you drinking and is there anything else; and is there anything else at all you're taking · vitamins, supplements, anything from the chemist or health food shop · then the timeframe in her language: two weeks for a first change, four weeks to judge it, eight weeks or more for the full effect, and finish the first box before deciding · then the answer to 'So I just wait?', which is the mark: waiting on its own isn't a plan, and everything else starts today · then side effects normalised but not dismissed, with the warning not to stop suddenly · then name the three boxes before detailing any of them: medication, therapy and lifestyle, and support · then the crisis plan, which is never optional, the duration in months, and a review booked before she goes.

back.dx: NON-RESPONSE AT SEVEN DAYS — which is too early to judge — complicated by partial adherence, nightly alcohol, no psychology, and a planned switch to ST John's wort. The timeframe, in her language: 'Seven days is genuinely too early to judge this. These tablets aren't like a painkiller — they don't work on the day you take them. You might notice something around two weeks, four weeks is when we can properly judge it, and the full effect can take eight weeks or more. I tell people to finish the first box before deciding.' then the sentence that is the mark: 'No. Waiting on its own isn't a plan. The tablet needs time, but everything else starts today — the psychologist, the sleep, and a plan for the bad days. So you're not sitting at home for a month with nothing.' Side effects, normalised but not dismissed: 'The nausea is common in the first week and it almost always settles. Take it with food. If it hasn't settled by next week, ring me — don't just stop, because stopping suddenly can make you feel shaky and anxious.' The three boxes, named before any is detailed: 'There are three parts to treating this: the medication, the therapy and lifestyle side, and the support around you.' Therapy: 'A psychologist for cognitive behavioural therapy. It has two HALVEs — the cognitive part finds the thoughts that keep you stuck and challenges them, and the behavioural part gives you strategies to cope. I'll write a mental health treatment plan today so the sessions are subsidised.' Lifestyle: 'Exercise has the best evidence of anything here — a walk most days is enough to start. Cut the alcohol right down; a couple of glasses a night is making both the mood and the sleep worse.' plus a sleep hygiene sheet. Support: 'Beyond Blue, 1300 22 4636, has free coaching sessions and forums; and if you'd rather do something privately, online CBT programs — MoodGYM and this way up.' The crisis plan, never optional: 'If you start having thoughts of ending your life: in hours, ring me and we'll see you the same day. After hours, go to the emergency department. If neither is possible, ring Lifeline on 13 11 14 — you can phone, chat online or text.' Duration and review, said out loud: 'If it works, we stay on it at least six months after you feel well — usually six to twelve months — then we reassess together. I'll see you in four weeks, and I'll book it before you go.' The ST John's wort answer: 'I'm really glad you mentioned it. ST John's wort isn't harmless — it genuinely works, and it works on the same system as your tablet, so together they can make you seriously unwell, with shaking, sweating, a racing heart and confusion. It also stops the contraceptive pill and some other medicines working properly. Please don't start it, and tell me before you start anything new.' Her other questions: addictive — 'No. They're not addictive and they're not sedatives. But we do come off them slowly, over about a month, so your body isn't startled.' Change who I am — 'No. They lift the illness off you — people usually say they feel more like themselves, not less.' Weight and sex drive — 'Some people notice changes in sexual function, and some notice weight change over time. Both are worth telling me about rather than quietly stopping.' if this one doesn't work — 'Then we change it. These medicines are a family — if one doesn't suit you, another often does. It doesn't mean you can't be treated.' Do I have to see a psychologist — 'You don't have to. But the tablet and the talking do different jobs, and the evidence is strongest together.' Version B — no response at four weeks, and the seven checks spoken as one breath: 'Before I change anything I want to check a few things. Are you taking it most days? Is the dose high enough and has it had long enough? Could something else be causing this — your thyroid, your iron, your sleep? Is the alcohol still there? Has anything happened at home or at work that we haven't talked about? And has there ever been a high period I should know about?' then the decision: 'Everything checks out, so the next step is to increase the dose rather than change the tablet.' Version C — the switch: 'The safest way is to bring the first one down gradually, leave a short gap, then start the new one and build it up. I'll write the schedule out and see you through the gap.' and volunteer the complication, which is the mark: 'One thing to watch for while we change over. If you get shakiness, sweating, a racing heart, muscle twitching or confusion, stop the tablets and go to hospital. It's uncommon, it's called serotonin syndrome, and it's treatable — but it needs to be seen the same day.' Version D — 12 weeks pregnant: do not stop an effective antidepressant on her own, because untreated depression carries real risk to both; discuss risks and benefits and involve the obstetric team — 'This is a decision we make with the obstetric team — not one you make alone at home tonight.'
plan: OPEN WITH HER EXPERIENCE, NOT YOUR EXPLANATION: 'Rebecca, come in. I'M GLAD YOU CAME BACK RATHER THAN JUST STOPPING THEM. TELL ME WHAT IT'S ACTUALLY BEEN LIKE THIS WEEK.' → 'honestly? Nothing. A week of tablets and I feel exactly the same. I DON'T SEE THE POINT.' → 'THAT'S A HORRIBLE PLACE TO BE IN. Can I ask a few quick questions about how the week has actually gone, and then I'll explain what I think is happening and what I'd like us to do?'

ADHERENCE, ASKED SO IT CANNOT BE DODGED: 'HOW MANY DAYS IN THE LAST WEEK DID YOU MISS A TABLET?' → 'maybe two. It made me feel sick in the mornings.' (Ask 'are you taking it?' and she says yes and volunteers nothing — THE NUMBER IS THE QUESTION.) Then normalise the nausea and say to take it with breakfast.

The four screening questions — two of them are single-item fails if skipped: 'Have you had any thoughts of ending your life?' 'Has there ever been a week where you needed far less sleep than usual and felt unstoppable, or were spending far more than normal?' 'How much are you drinking, and is there anything else — cannabis, anything?' 'Is there anything else at all you're taking — vitamins, supplements, anything from the chemist or health food shop?' → and the last one produces the ST John's wort. (Skipping the risk screen because she 'Just' has non-response, and skipping the mania screen because the diagnosis is already made, are both single-item fails.)
The timeframe in her language — two, four, eight, and finish the box (see dx) → 'Four weeks? Nobody told me that.' / 'So I just wait another month feeling like this?'
The answer that is the mark: 'No. Waiting isn't a plan. The tablet needs time, but everything else starts today.' then the side-effect advice with don't just stop — ring me first.

NAME THE THREE BOXES, THEN DETAIL THEM (see dx): medication continued; THERAPY with CBT explained in its two halves AND A MENTAL HEALTH TREATMENT PLAN WRITTEN TODAY; LIFESTYLE with exercise as the best evidence, the alcohol cut right down, and a sleep sheet; and SUPPORT with Beyond Blue and online CBT. (Naming the tablet and stopping is the trap — THREE BOXES, A CRISIS PLAN, A DURATION AND A BOOKED REVIEW ARE SEPARATE MARKS.)
The ST John's wort, answered properly and not brushed off (see dx) → 'I had no idea. She meant well.' → 'She did, and you did exactly the right thing telling me.'
THE CRISIS PLAN, THE DURATION IN MONTHS, AND THE REVIEW BOOKED BEFORE SHE LEAVES (see dx) — in hours ring me, after hours the emergency department, otherwise Lifeline 13 11 14.

HER REMAINING QUESTIONS AND THE CLOSING SUMMARY (see dx): keep the tablet and finish the box, psychology and care plan today, walk most days, less wine, sleep sheet, Beyond Blue, the three crisis routes, and four weeks — then 'WHAT HAVEN'T I COVERED?'

pefe: Role-player: REBECCA ELLIS, 34, A PRIMARY SCHOOL TEACHER in a country town, lives with her partner, no children. DIAGNOSED WITH DEPRESSION A WEEK AGO AND STARTED ON CITALOPRAM 20 mg. back.dx: AN ACUTE MANIC EPISODE — in bipolar mood disorder. Name it, explain it in plain words, count the criteria aloud, and account for the missing pole: 'Alex, from what you've told me, what you're experiencing is an acute manic episode. That means a period where your mood is unusually high, you have a great deal of energy, you need far less sleep than normal, and you may do things you wouldn't usually do — spending large amounts of money, or having unprotected sex with several partners. The reasons I think this: your mood has been high for six months; you're managing on an hour's sleep and still feel energetic; you feel you're the most capable person in your class; you've been spending well beyond what you normally would; you have several partners at once; and you're speaking very quickly and moving quickly between topics. This usually happens as part of a condition called bipolar mood disorder, where people move between high periods like this one and low periods. I haven't been able to find a period of low mood in your history, which is why I'm calling it a manic episode today.' The differentials — the same mood-disorder list, reordered: 'Bipolar mood disorder — the most likely context. Drug-induced — stimulants can produce exactly this, so I'd like to check a urine sample. Schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder — less likely; you've no hallucinations, and your thinking is fast rather than disorganised. Depression with psychotic features — your mood is high, not low. A physical cause — an overactive thyroid, a head injury, an infection of the brain; nothing in your history suggests these, but I'd check a thyroid test. And the effects of alcohol, which you've told me you drink a good deal of.' if time allows: 'I also considered whether this could be a long-standing pattern rather than an episode — but you've described a clear change over six months.' when he pushes back — 'So you think there's something wrong with me? I've never felt better' — do not argue: 'I can hear that this feels like the best you've been. And I'm not going to argue with you about how you feel. What concerns me is what's happening around it — the sleep, the money, the conflict at university, and the risk to your sexual health. Those are the things I'd like us to look after.' then the plan, which names a real next step: 'I'd like to arrange for you to be seen by the mental health team today, and to do a urine test and some blood tests. I'd also ask you not to drive until we've sorted this out. Would it be alright if I spoke to someone in your family?' Version B — the depressive pole is positive, and no hedging is needed: 'Thank you, that's important. It means what you're experiencing now is almost certainly part of a condition called bipolar mood disorder — periods of low mood like the one you had at seventeen, and high periods like this one. You're currently in the high, or manic, phase.' The irritable variant: 'I can see you're frustrated, and I'm not here to argue with you. I'd just like to understand what's been happening. Would you be willing to answer a few questions?' — and the count changes: if the mood is irritable rather than elevated or expansive, you need four of seven symptoms, not three — say so when you present. Name, gesture, acknowledge, quantify the time, ask permission — and if he still will not yield, ask the two questions anyway, because the examiner is scoring whether they were asked. Name it and explain it in one paragraph, because management carries the marks: 'James, I think you have a condition called serotonin syndrome. All the antidepressants we use work by increasing a chemical in your brain called serotonin. When there is too much serotonin, it becomes toxic to the body — and that produces exactly what you have: fever, a fast heart rate, sweating, agitation, shaking and stomach cramps. It usually happens when a dose is increased, or when a second antidepressant is added or swapped in, because the effects overlap. In your case you've been taking two medicines that both act on serotonin.' then name the confirming sign rather than listing symptoms back: 'When I examined you I found some signs that confirm it — your reflexes are very brisk and your ankles show a repetitive jerking movement we call clonus, which is quite specific to this condition.' The differentials, ten seconds: 'Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — a similar reaction, but it happens with antipsychotic medicines over days rather than hours, and the reflexes are reduced rather than brisk. An anticholinergic reaction — but those patients are dry, and you're sweating. Meningitis or encephalitis — you have no headache or neck stiffness, but we'll keep watching. Withdrawal from sedatives or alcohol, and illicit stimulants — neither fits your history, but we'll send a urine test.' Management as headings, not paragraphs, and the first line is the one that passes you: 'The first and most important thing: we need to stop both of your antidepressants now. The pushback: 'I understand, and I'm not leaving you without treatment. But this condition can become dangerous, and the medicine is what's causing it. So we stop it now, we treat this, and once you're better the psychiatry team and I will make a plan with you.' and refuse the half-dose. The blame question: 'No — this isn't anyone's fault. This reaction is unpredictable. It can happen at a normal dose, in someone who has taken the medicine safely before, and there's no test that tells us in advance who it will affect. We do know the risk rises when a dose goes up or two medicines are combined, which is why we warn people about the symptoms — and you did exactly the right thing by coming in today.' if he presses on making a complaint, tell him how and offer to help — do not argue him out of it, and do not criticise the colleague. The five culprit versions. The dose increase — found by 'Has the dose of anything been changed?', not by 'Has anything new been started?': 'There's no dose that is completely safe from this reaction, but the risk does rise when we increase a dose.' Fluoxetine to sertraline — prozac to zoloft, and the trap is the missing washout, not the choice of drug: 'Fluoxetine stays in the body far longer than the others — for weeks after the last tablet — so when a new one is started straight away, both are working at once.' Tramadol, the commonest non-antidepressant cause and the one examiners most like to ask about: 'Tramadol also acts on serotonin, which most people don't realise. We'll stop the tramadol and use a different painkiller.' Nothing changed on the script — ST John's wort, serotonergic, available without a script, a strong enzyme inducer, and almost never volunteered. And extra tablets taken last night, which makes it an overdose and a self-harm presentation — poisons information 131 126, and he does not leave unaccompanied. The severe version: T 41.2, rigid and drowsy means intensive care, intubation and paralysis, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — sedate, never restrain.
plan: STABILISE FIRST — ONE SENTENCE, AND IT IS FREE MARKS: 'James, BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — I CAN SEE YOU'RE UNWELL, SO I'D LIKE TO MOVE YOU THROUGH TO THE TREATMENT ROOM, PUT YOU ON A MONITOR AND CHECK YOUR PULSE, BLOOD PRESSURE AND TEMPERATURE TO MAKE SURE YOU'RE STABLE. IS THAT ALRIGHT?' Then confidentiality briefly, the open question, and 'I UNDERSTAND HOW WORRYING THIS MUST BE. LET ME ASK YOU SOME QUESTIONS, EXAMINE YOU, FIND THE CAUSE AND MAKE A PLAN FOR YOU.' (Skipping the stability statement in a febrile, tachycardic, hypertensive patient is the same error as taking a leisurely history from a chest-pain patient in the waiting room.)

Timing and the missing symptoms: 'When exactly did this start? Have the symptoms come on over hours, or over days? Are they getting worse? Is this the first time?' then 'Any diarrhoea? Any shakiness in your hands, or shivering? Any flushing? Any dizziness? Any anxiety or irritability?'

THE MEDICATION HISTORY — THE BODY OF THE STATION, NINE QUESTIONS, AND DO NOT RUSH IT (see the run sheet). THE MARK IS IN THE DATES: 'WHEN DID YOU STOP THE FIRST ONE? WHEN DID YOU START THE NEW ONE? WAS THERE ANY MEDICINE-FREE GAP IN BETWEEN?' → 'I DIDN'T. NOBODY TOLD ME TO. I'VE BEEN TAKING BOTH.' → DO NOT REACT, AND DO NOT STOP ASKING: 'thank you — that's very helpful. So there was no gap?' Then adherence, then the named supplement question, then illicit drugs. ('Any supplements?' gets a no — NAME ST JOHN'S WORT, because patients do not classify it as a medicine.)

Risk and the two closing questions: 'Some of my patients, when they're feeling low, have thoughts of harming themselves or that life isn't worth living. Has that happened to you? Have you ever tried to harm yourself in the past?' then 'Has the medication been helping your mood at all? Have you noticed any other side effects?' (Not optional for two reasons: a depressed patient holding a bottle of antidepressants has the means already in his hand, and a deliberate overdose is one of the ways this presents — so the answer changes both your differential and your disposition.)

The card, then the diagnosis in one paragraph with clonus named as the confirming sign, then ten seconds of differentials (see dx). (Do not spend ninety seconds explaining serotonin — you have a large management plan to deliver and the marks live there.)

MANAGEMENT AS HEADINGS, FIRST LINE FIRST: 'WE NEED TO STOP BOTH OF YOUR ANTIDEPRESSANTS NOW' — then monitoring, cooling and fluids, diazepam, cyproheptadine if severe, bloods with a muscle marker and an ECG, AMBULANCE TRANSFER TO HOSPITAL, and PSYCHIATRY REVIEW (see dx). (A candidate who explains cooling in detail and never reaches transfer, psychiatry or the bloods scores less than one who names all eight in forty seconds.)

The two pushbacks, both scored (see dx) → 'But what about my depression? I need those tablets' → hold the line, and refuse the half-dose compromise. → 'Was it your colleague's fault?' → answer without defending or accusing, and finish with 'You did exactly the right thing by coming in today.'
