ask: 'Before anything else, I'd like to put you on a monitor and check your observations to make sure you're stable.' / 'When did it start — over hours, or over days?' / 'Has the dose of anything been changed recently?' / 'Has anything new been started — by me, or by any other doctor?'

The three that carry the station: 'When did you stop the first one? When did you start the new one? Was there any gap?' / 'Any herbal medicines, over-the-counter medicines or supplements — anything with ST John's wort?' / 'Have you had thoughts of harming yourself? Have you ever tried before?'

'All antidepressants work by increasing a chemical called serotonin. Too much serotonin becomes toxic.' / 'Your reflexes are very brisk and your ankles show a jerking movement called clonus, which is quite specific to this.' / 'We need to stop both of your antidepressants now.' / 'I'm not leaving you without treatment — once you're better we'll make a plan together.' / 'This reaction is unpredictable. It isn't anyone's fault, and you did the right thing coming in.'

THE FIVE CULPRITS: THE DOSE INCREASE — found by asking about a dose change, not a new drug. FLUOXETINE TO SERTRALINE — 'FLUOXETINE STAYS IN THE BODY FOR WEEKS AFTER THE LAST TABLET, SO WHEN A NEW ONE IS STARTED STRAIGHT AWAY, BOTH ARE WORKING AT ONCE' — the trap is THE MISSING WASHOUT, not the drug choice. TRAMADOL — 'IT ALSO ACTS ON SEROTONIN, WHICH MOST PEOPLE DON'T REALISE' — the commonest non-antidepressant cause. ST JOHN'S WORT — serotonergic, no script needed, a strong enzyme inducer, AND ALMOST NEVER VOLUNTEERED. AND EXTRA TABLETS LAST NIGHT — now an OVERDOSE AND A SELF-HARM PRESENTATION: Poisons Information 131 126, AND HE DOES NOT LEAVE UNACCOMPANIED.

What was deliberately not done: no mood, sleep, appetite or psychosocial history — this is a toxicology station. No antipyretic offered for the fever, and no physical restraint mentioned — sedate, never restrain. No promise that it will never happen again. And if you run out of time, run out at the differentials — never at the drug history or at the word stop.
pefe: Role-player: JAMES, 32, works in logistics, lives with his partner, no children. LOW FOR ABOUT EIGHT MONTHS and started on DULOXETINE by his usual GP around six weeks ago. THREE DAYS AGO he saw A DIFFERENT DOCTOR AT THE SAME CLINIC because he still felt flat, and that doctor STARTED MIRTAZAPINE. NOBODY TOLD HIM TO STOP THE DULOXETINE, SO HE HAS BEEN TAKING BOTH — AND HE ONLY REVEALS THIS IF THE DOCTOR ASKS WHEN HE STOPPED THE FIRST ONE.

NOW: six hours of shaking, sweating and feeling hot; DIARRHOEA AND STOMACH CRAMPS TODAY; SHIVERING DESPITE FEELING HOT; CANNOT SIT STILL; anxious and frightened; nothing like it before. Duloxetine and mirtazapine only — NO over-the-counter medicines, supplements or herbal tablets, NO illicit drugs, minimal alcohol, TAKEN EXACTLY AS PRESCRIBED. HIDDEN AGENDA: frightened this is a serious reaction, AND QUIETLY ANGRY THAT TWO DOCTORS IN THE SAME CLINIC DID NOT TALK TO EACH OTHER — DO NOT VOLUNTEER IT. REGISTER: RESTLESS, ANXIOUS, WIPING HIS FACE, SHIFTING IN THE CHAIR, HANDS TREMBLING — NOT HOSTILE, FRIGHTENED.

THE TWO PUSHES, BOTH SCORED: when told to stop the antidepressants — 'BUT WHAT ABOUT MY DEPRESSION? I NEED THOSE TABLETS.' IF THEY WAVER, OFFER A COMPROMISE YOURSELF — 'CAN I JUST TAKE HALF?' — AND MARK THEM DOWN IF THEY ACCEPT IT. Then, once management is under way: 'WAS IT YOUR COLLEAGUE'S FAULT? SHOULD HE HAVE KNOWN?' NOTES: THE OVERLAP IS THE WHOLE CASE — give it ONLY when they ask when you stopped the first drug; if they only ask 'what are you taking?', answer 'duloxetine and mirtazapine' AND SAY NOTHING MORE. PUNISH THE GENERIC SUPPLEMENT QUESTION — 'any supplements?' gets 'no'. STAY PHYSICALLY RESTLESS THROUGHOUT — it is part of the presentation and it puts time pressure on the candidate. PASS MARK: BOTH AUTO-FAIL ITEMS TICKED PLUS AT LEAST FIFTEEN OF THE REMAINING NINETEEN.
The timing — ABOUT SIX HOURS AGO AND GETTING WORSE — never had anything like it before

Why the onset window is diagnostic — SYMPTOMS OVER HOURS AFTER A DRUG CHANGE IS SEROTONIN SYNDROME — OVER DAYS TO WEEKS AFTER AN ANTIPSYCHOTIC IS NEUROLEPTIC MALIGNANT SYNDROME. Ask it in those words and you have separated the two before you examine him
The rest of the syndrome — Diarrhoea today — hands shaking — shivering despite feeling hot — cannot sit still
The disclosure that is the whole case — 'I stopped the duloxetine... Well, actually, I wasn't told to stop it. I've been taking both' — given only if you ask when he stopped the first one
If you only ask what he is taking — He answers 'Duloxetine and mirtazapine' and says nothing more
The rest of the drug history — NO dose changes — MIRTAZAPINE STARTED THREE DAYS AGO BY A COLLEAGUE — NO GAP — taking exactly the prescribed dose — NO supplements, NO illicit drugs, minimal alcohol
Risk — NO thoughts of self-harm, NEVER tried — the medication was STARTING TO HELP A LITTLE, and he felt sick in the first week which settled
His hidden agenda — He is frightened, and quietly angry that two doctors in the same clinic did not talk to each other — he does not volunteer it

The two scripted pushes — 'But what about my depression? I need those tablets' — and if you waver, 'Can I just take half instead?', which is marked down if you accept. Then, once management is under way: 'Was it your colleague's fault? Should he have known?'

VERSION E — the generic question fails — 'Any supplements?' Gets 'No'. Only the named question unlocks it: 'Oh — yes. I picked up something for low mood at the chemist. I didn't think that counted as a medicine'
fails: ★ Not asking about self-harm and previous attempts — a depressed patient holding a bottle of antidepressants has the means already in his hand, and a deliberate overdose is one of the ways this presents
★ Not saying STOP the serotonergic drugs as the first line of management — or wavering and accepting the half-dose he offers
Asking 'what medicines are you on?' instead of the dates — when did you stop, when did you start, was there a gap
Asking 'any supplements?' generically instead of naming St John's wort, which patients do not classify as a medicine

Skipping the haemodynamic stability statement in a febrile, tachycardic, hypertensive patient; taking a mood, sleep and psychosocial history in a toxicology station; spending ninety seconds explaining serotonin so that transfer, psychiatry and the bloods are never reached; and criticising or defending the colleague when asked whose fault it was
numbers: Onset within 24 hours of the change, most within 6 hours · hunter criteria: a serotonergic agent plus one of five · above 38.5 is the danger zone · above 41 means intensive care, intubation and paralysis · clonus is lower limbs greater than upper · serotonin syndrome comes on over hours with brisk reflexes; neuroleptic malignant syndrome over days with reduced reflexes

Stop the serotonergic agent first, always · cool, fluids, diazepam · cyproheptadine if moderate to severe · no antipyretics, no restraints · fluoxetine has a long half-life and needs a washout VERIFY · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · poisons information 131 126 · SA mental health triage 13 14 65 · Lifeline 13 11 14

must: FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: not asking about self-harm and previous attempts — a depressed patient holding a bottle of antidepressants has the means already in his hand, and a deliberate overdose is one of the ways this presents, so the answer changes both the differential and the disposition

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: not saying STOP both antidepressants as the FIRST line of management — or wavering when he pushes ('but what about my depression?') and accepting the half-dose he offers himself. 'I'm not leaving you without treatment; we stop now, treat this, and psychiatry and I make a plan once you're better — usually one medicine at a lower dose'

FAIL — Asking 'what medicines are you on?' instead of the three that carry the station — when did you STOP the first one, when did you START the new one, was there any GAP. The overlap is disclosed only if you ask when he stopped. Ask about a DOSE CHANGE separately, and name St John's wort, because 'any supplements?' gets a no

FAIL — Not asking whether it came on over HOURS or over DAYS — hours after a drug change is serotonin syndrome; days to weeks after an antipsychotic is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, where the reflexes are reduced rather than brisk. Ask it in those words and you have separated them before the examination card appears

FAIL — Listing symptoms back instead of naming CLONUS — brisk reflexes with inducible ankle clonus, lower limbs more than upper, is the specific confirming sign. Then ten seconds of differentials: NMS, anticholinergic toxicity (those patients are dry, he is sweating), meningitis or encephalitis, sedative or alcohol withdrawal, stimulants

FAIL — Delivering management as paragraphs instead of headings, or fumbling the blame question — monitoring, cooling, IV fluids, diazepam, cyproheptadine if moderate to severe, bloods including CK and an ECG, ambulance to hospital, psychiatry review. No antipyretics and no restraints. And 'this isn't anyone's fault, the reaction is unpredictable', without defending or criticising the colleague

setting: History and a spoken formulation — general practice. There is no diagnosis to make; it is in the stem. Do not spend the station proving it. The deliverable is a formulation spoken out loud in four headings: predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective. Three AUTOMATIC FAILS: no mania screen; no self-harm question; and explaining a symptom list instead of psychosocial factors. She volunteers nothing — the husband, the twins, the lost job and the isolation are the whole answer, and you must ask for each one.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Jill, 46, has carried a diagnosis of dysthymia with a passive-dependent personality for about twenty years and takes sertraline. She has seen many doctors over the years. She presents saying she is unhappy and tired and that nothing seems to help.

History six minutes, then explain the psychosocial factors contributing to her presentation. 8 minutes, no examination. Harder versions: it is worse — double depression; week-long highs in her thirties — bipolar II; sertraline 25 mg taken 'When I remember'; a vague account of a husband who 'Gets frustrated'; and suicidal thoughts with a plan.
tasks: Take a history for six minutes
Explain the psychosocial factors contributing to her presentation
time: Plan the split before the timer: roughly two minutes on symptoms, three on her life, one on traits and medication · open, then absorb the hopelessness by validating without defending and without promising, and signpost the plan in the same sentence · then the pivotal minute: how long have you felt this way, has anything changed recently, is this worse than your usual, what made you come in today rather than last month, and how is it affecting your day to day · then the criteria briskly, because you have a social history to reach: mood, anhedonia, sleep, appetite, weight, energy, concentration, guilt and worthlessness, and hopeful or hopeless · then the two compulsory screens whatever the clock says: has there ever been a time, even a few days, when you felt the opposite · unusually high or energetic, not needing much sleep; and have you had thoughts that life isn't worth living, any thoughts of harming yourself, have you ever tried · then the social history, where the marks are: who is at home, how are things between you, do you feel supported, children and how often you hear from them, work and whether you miss it, how you fill your days, friends and family nearby, anyone you can talk to, money, and alcohol quantified · then the dependent traits asked as ordinary questions about how she manages, and the medication review ending in the therapy question · then the four headings.

back.dx: PERSISTENT DEPRESSIVE DISORDER WITH DEPENDENT PERSONALITY TRAITS — and the task is the formulation, not the diagnosis. Deliver it in four headings, filled with her own facts: 'Jill, I don't think there's one single thing making you feel this way. What I can see are several things in your life that fit together — and the reason that matters is that most of them are things we can work on.' First, what you brought with you: 'You've had a low-grade depression for around twenty years, so this is well-worn ground. And you've described yourself as someone who has always relied on the people around you — who finds decisions hard, who'd rather not disagree, who tends to wait for someone else to take the lead. That isn't a criticism. But it does mean that when the people around you become less available, you feel it much more than most people would.' Second, what changed: 'Three things happened that pull in the same direction. Your twins grew up and left — and looking after them had been your main role for twenty years. You stopped working, which took away your routine, your income and a large part of who you were. And you're living a long way from your family and your old friends.' Third, what's keeping it going: 'Your husband is away for work most of the time, so the one relationship you still have day to day isn't giving you much company. Your children rarely call. You have no friends nearby, no work, and not much structure to your days. And that becomes a loop — the less you do, the less you feel able to do, and the more alone you feel.' and the things in your favour, which are a separate mark: 'Your marriage is intact — your husband is absent, not unkind. You've kept taking your medication. You've kept coming back to doctors even when you felt it was pointless. You're not drinking heavily. Those are real strengths, and they're what we build on.' then end in actions: 'The medication on its own was never going to fix loneliness and the loss of a role. I'd like to add talking therapy — there's a type called interpersonal therapy that is specifically for changes in roles and relationships. I'd like us to look at getting some structure back into your week, whether that's work, study or volunteering. I'd like to involve your husband, with your permission. And I'd like to review your medication, because you've been on the same thing for a very long time. I'll also do some blood tests, because tiredness like yours can have physical causes we should rule out.' and when she asks 'So it's not all in my head, then?': 'It was never all in your head. What you've got is a real illness, and it's sitting on TOP of a life that's become very quiet. Both of those are worth treating, and only one of them has ever been treated.' The set pieces. 'So is it empty nest syndrome?' → 'That's a phrase people use for what happens when children leave home, and it's certainly part of what's going on for you. But it's a description of a change in life, not a medical diagnosis. Your diagnosis is the long-standing depression you already know about — the children leaving is one of the things that made it harder.' To the examiner, say the same thing clinically: a role transition and a precipitating factor, not a diagnosis. 'What's the point? Nothing has worked in twenty years.' → 'I hear you, and I'm not going to pretend twenty years of trying counts for nothing. But can I tell you what strikes me? For twenty years you've been given tablets, and nobody has sat down with you about your life. Tablets were never going to fix loneliness. So I'm not proposing more of the same.' then check it: 'When you say what's the point — do you ever have thoughts that life isn't worth living?' 'My husband says I should just pull myself together.' → 'That's a very common thing for people to say, and it usually comes from not understanding rather than unkindness. Depression isn't something you can decide your way out of. Would you be comfortable if I spoke with him, with your permission?' The harder versions. She says it is worse — six kilos down, not washing, not answering the phone: this is double depression — treat as a new major depressive episode, reassess risk carefully, optimise or change the antidepressant, and arrange early review. Week-long periods in her thirties of feeling wonderful on three hours' sleep: bipolar II — the antidepressant alone may be the wrong treatment, seek psychiatric advice. Sertraline 25 mg for eleven years, taken 'When I remember': under-treatment, not treatment resistance — optimise dose and adherence before declaring anything has failed. Vague about her husband, he 'Gets frustrated', no money of her own: ask privately and routinely about safety at home — 1800respect 1800 737 732. And suicidal thoughts with a plan: the station stops being a formulation station — risk assessment, safety plan, do not let her leave unaccompanied, mental health triage 13 14 65.
plan: Open and absorb the hopelessness — validate, decline to promise, signpost: 'That sounds exhausting — to have felt this way for so long and to have kept trying anyway. I'm not going to promise you a quick fix. What I'd like to do today is understand your situation properly, because I think there may be things going on around you that haven't been looked at, and some of those we can do something about.' (Three ways to lose the opening: defending — 'I'm sure they did their best'; over-promising — 'We'll get you sorted'; and ignoring it and starting the symptom checklist.)

The pivotal minute: 'How long have you been feeling this way? Has anything changed recently — in the last few weeks or months? Is this worse than your usual? What made you come in today, rather than last month? How is all this affecting your day-to-day life?' (Ask it in those words so you know which case you are in.)
THE CRITERIA, BRISKLY — YOU HAVE A SOCIAL HISTORY TO REACH: mood, anhedonia, sleep and which kind, appetite and weight, energy, concentration, guilt and self-worth, and HOPEFUL OR HOPELESS.

The two compulsory screens — and twenty years of chronicity must not talk you out of them: 'Has there ever been a time — even a few days — when you felt the opposite? Unusually high or energetic, not needing much sleep?' and 'When you say hopeless — have you had thoughts that life isn't worth living? Any thoughts of harming yourself? Have you ever tried?' (Bipolar II is the classic missed diagnosis in a depression that has never responded to an antidepressant.)

THE SOCIAL HISTORY — WHERE THE MARKS ARE, AND A THIRD OF THE HISTORY: who's at home; how are things between you, do you feel supported; children, and HOW OFTEN YOU SEE OR HEAR FROM THEM; working or studying, what did you do, DO YOU MISS IT; HOW DO YOU FILL YOUR DAYS; friends or family nearby; IS THERE ANYONE YOU CAN TALK TO WHEN THINGS ARE HARD; money worries; and alcohol QUANTIFIED rather than accepted.

DEPENDENT TRAITS AS ORDINARY QUESTIONS ABOUT HOW SHE MANAGES, NOT AS A PERSONALITY ASSESSMENT: 'do you find it hard to make everyday decisions on your own — do you need a lot of reassurance? Do you find it hard to disagree with people, even when you want to? Is it hard to start things on your own, or do you wait for someone else to take the lead? WHO DOES THE DAY-TO-DAY THINGS AT HOME — THE BILLS, THE APPOINTMENTS?'

THE MEDICATION REVIEW, ENDING IN THE PRIZE QUESTION: 'how long have you been on the sertraline, and at what dose? Are you taking it every day? Has it ever helped, even a little? HAVE YOU EVER SEEN A PSYCHOLOGIST, OR HAD ANY TALKING THERAPY?' → 'NO. NOBODY'S EVER SUGGESTED THAT.'

The formulation in four headings, filled with her own facts, ending in actions (see dx) → 'So it's not all in my head, then?' → 'It was never all in your head.' (Listing her symptoms back to her is the commonest failure in this station — she knows she is tired and low, and has known for twenty years.)

pefe: Role-player: JILL, 46. Worked as A BOOKKEEPER until about ten years ago. Lives with HER HUSBAND, WHO RUNS HIS OWN BUSINESS AND IS AWAY FOUR OR FIVE NIGHTS A WEEK. TWINS IN THEIR EARLY TWENTIES WHO MOVED OUT AND RARELY CALL. PARENTS AND MOST FRIENDS INTERSTATE, SISTER OVERSEAS. She moved to this town FOR HER HUSBAND'S WORK. Told about twenty years ago she has DYSTHYMIA AND A DEPENDENT PERSONALITY; takes SERTRALINE every morning, SAME DOSE FOR YEARS; it helped a little at the start; SHE HAS NEVER SEEN A PSYCHOLOGIST AND NOBODY HAS EVER SUGGESTED IT.

HOW SHE FEELS: flat and low every day for as long as she can remember; NOTHING MUCH HAS CHANGED, PERHAPS A LITTLE FLATTER; wakes in the night and lies there; not very hungry, weight steady; no energy, poor concentration; HAS NEVER THOUGHT MUCH OF HERSELF; hopeless in the sense that NOTHING CHANGES. NOT SUICIDAL, never self-harmed, NEVER HAD A HIGH PERIOD. A glass of wine sometimes, no drugs, no medical problems. DEPENDENT TRAITS IF ASKED: always checks decisions with her husband, doesn't like upsetting people, waits for others to take the lead, HE HANDLES ALL THE MONEY AND PAPERWORK.

How to play it — volunteer nothing. This case is scored almost entirely on what the doctor thinks to ask. Answer in one short sentence and stop. Test them at the start: if they promise to fix you, go flat again and give shorter answers for the rest of the station; if they validate without promising, soften. Do not offer the social history — the husband, the twins, the job and the isolation are the whole answer, so make them ask for each one. The therapy question is the prize — only answer it if asked directly. Push once near the end with 'So it's not all in my head, then?' and mark them down if the explanation is just your symptoms read back to you — you already know you are tired. Pass mark: all three AUTO-FAIL items ticked plus at least fourteen of the remaining nineteen.
The opening — 'I'm just unhappy. I'm tired all the time. I've been to so many doctors and nobody can help me. I don't know why I bother' — in the first fifteen seconds
If you promise a fix — 'That's what they all say' — and she closes down for the rest of the station
If you validate without promising — '...ALRIGHT. NOBODY'S EVER PUT IT LIKE THAT BEFORE' — and she softens and gives slightly longer answers
Duration and change — Twenty years, on and off, mostly on — nothing has changed recently, maybe a bit flatter
Why that question matters — If she says it is worse — new weight loss, new withdrawal, new hopelessness — you are treating a major depressive episode on TOP of dysthymia, and the station changes

The criteria — Low and flat, 'It's just how I am' — no enjoyment — wakes in the night and lies there — not hungry, weight steady — no energy, poor concentration, never thought much of herself — hopeless, 'Nothing changes'
The two screens — No high period ever — and no suicidal thoughts: 'I just wish I felt better'

The social history — the whole answer, and she volunteers none of it — Just her husband, who is hardly ever home and they don't really talk — twins who moved out years ago and rarely call — stopped work years ago as a bookkeeper and misses it — doesn't do much, the house and the shopping — all family and friends interstate, sister overseas — nobody to talk to

The two easy misses in her answers — 'My husband handles all that' is a dependent trait and it goes past in half a second — and 'A glass of wine sometimes' in an isolated, unoccupied person is worth quantifying, not accepting
The dependent traits — Always checks decisions with her husband — doesn't like upsetting people and would rather go along with it — waits for someone else to take the lead — he does the bills

Her hidden agenda — She half believes she is a hopeless case and is testing whether you will be like the others — and she privately wonders whether it is all in her head. If you never address it: 'So it's not all in my head, then?'

back.dx: MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER — a unipolar depressive episode. Name it, explain it in one line, then justify it by counting: 'From everything you've told me, the most likely condition is major depressive disorder. It's a mood disorder — it makes you feel low and lose interest in things you used to enjoy, and it affects how you manage at home and at work. The reasons I think this: your mood has been low every day for three months; you've stopped enjoying things; you're waking in the night; your appetite is down; you're tired; you can't concentrate; and you feel worthless. That's more than the number we need, over far longer than the two weeks we look for. And you've never had a period of feeling unusually high or energetic — which tells me this is depression on its own, not a bipolar condition.' The reasoning is the only evidence the examiner has that you know how a psychiatric diagnosis is made. Then one memorised mood-disorder list: 'Bipolar mood disorder — unlikely, because you've never had a high or energetic episode. Depression with psychotic features — unlikely, no unusual experiences or beliefs. Adjustment disorder — you did have the stressor at work, but you meet the full criteria for major depression, and that takes precedence. Dysthymia — that runs for two years or more; yours is shorter. Schizoaffective disorder and schizophrenia — no psychotic features. And always last two: a physical cause such as an underactive thyroid, and the effects of alcohol or other drugs. I'd check your thyroid with a blood test.' In version B add post-traumatic stress disorder — there was an event, though the picture fits depression better. When she asks 'So it's not just because of the project?': 'The project may well have been the trigger. But what you have now is more than an understandable reaction — it's an illness, and the good news is that it's treatable.' and always finish with the safety net and an agreement: 'If those thoughts about the point of life get stronger, or you feel unsafe, I want you to come back to me, go to the emergency department, or ring Lifeline on 13 11 14. Can you agree to that?' Version C — the management plan, in bullet points, and the order is designed: the wait message first, in case you run out of time — 'Citalopram takes about two weeks to start working and about four weeks before we can judge it fairly. You've had one week — it hasn't failed, it hasn't had time. I'd like you to keep taking it every day.' then safety, because it is the only other item that cannot be missed: 'In a small number of people, especially younger people, these tablets can make thoughts of self-harm stronger in the first week or two. If that happens, come back to me, go to the emergency department, or ring Lifeline on 13 11 14 — any hour.' then, scored per heading, so more headings beats more detail: talking therapy — a psychologist for CBT to find the thoughts keeping him stuck and teach strategies; sleep — offer a sleep hygiene sheet and move, do not explain it in full; lifestyle — exercise, and cutting back the alcohol will help the tablets work; support — Beyond Blue for groups, counsellors and reading; follow-up — four weeks, and if it still isn't helping we can increase the dose or change to a different medicine, we'll decide together; and a thyroid blood test. Do not offer to refer him to a psychiatrist to prescribe — a GP starts and monitors antidepressants here. And when he pushes: 'I'm sorry it's been such a hard week. I can understand why you'd think it isn't working. The honest answer is that it hasn't had time — these medicines take about two weeks to begin and four to judge. Give me four weeks, and if it still isn't helping we'll change something. Is that fair?' The version A tearful moment: pause, offer tissues without comment, 'Take your time. There's no rush', then resume where you left off — do not restart the block, and do not repeat the empathy, because repeated empathy in a six-minute history costs you the thyroid question. 'Isn't this just stress?': 'If it were only a reaction to the stress, I'd expect fewer symptoms and I'd expect them to settle as things at work settled.' A past high phase — the diagnosis changes to bipolar disorder, and do not start or continue an antidepressant alone; seek psychiatric advice on a mood stabiliser. A six-week-old baby — screen for postnatal depression, ask about thoughts of harming the infant, involve CaFHS 1300 733 606. An Aboriginal patient declining a psychologist — offer the local ACCHS, an Aboriginal health worker, and 13yarn 13 92 76, and ask who he would like present.

On the suicide question, give the grey answer and wait — say it, then stop talking and count silently to three. If they accept it without exploring, say nothing more and mark it. If they explore properly, be honest: no attempts, no plan, boyfriend and family keep you going. If they ask about the project again, get slightly upset: 'I told you. It was my fault.' back.dx: VERSION A — bipolar mood disorder, currently a manic episode. Version B — a psychotic disorder, detained under the mental health act. Version A, the diagnosis: 'Thank you — what you've told me about when she was seventeen is really important, and it helps me a lot. I think your daughter has bipolar mood disorder. It's a condition where the mood swings between two extremes. The low phase is what she had at seventeen, when she was diagnosed with depression. What she's in now is the high phase, which we call mania. In the high phase people feel they don't need sleep, they feel they can do anything, their thoughts race, and they make decisions that are completely out of character — which is what happened at the casino. She wasn't being reckless. She was unwell. It's an illness, not a character flaw. It's treatable, and most people do very well with treatment.' and 'Is this my fault?' Is a scored empathy item asked in almost every recalled version: 'No. This isn't anything you did or didn't do. Bipolar disorder runs in families — you mentioned your sister — and it usually appears in the late teens or twenties. The most useful thing you can do now is exactly what you're doing.' Version A, immediate management — and the task says immediate, so lithium, valproate and relapse prevention answer a different question: 'The first thing is a full assessment — we'll talk with her properly, examine her, and do blood tests and a urine test, partly to make sure nothing physical, and no drug, is causing this. Then it depends on what we find. If she's still at risk — not sleeping, not safe with money, and not accepting that she's unwell — she'll stay in hospital and we'll start treatment for the manic episode. If she'll accept that willingly she becomes a voluntary patient, which is what we'd prefer. If she settles quickly and there's no significant risk, she can be looked after at home by the community mental health team. Either way she'll see a psychiatrist, we'll review her regularly, and when she's well we'll talk about longer-term treatment.' then the practical harms as headings, which you do not expand: the money — 'While she's unwell it may help if someone she trusts looks after her cards and accounts, but that has to be with her agreement; casinos also run self-exclusion schemes'; driving — advise against it while acutely unwell; work — ask what she may have said or done, because it is often the thing she is most distressed about later; sexual health if hypersexuality is part of it; and support for him — carer supports and Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636. Version B — the seven moves. One, name what has happened: 'Your son has been admitted involuntarily — that means for treatment he hasn't agreed to. I know how alarming that sounds.' Two, say what it is not: 'This is not an arrest. He has not committed a crime and he has no criminal record. The police were involved because they're often the first people called, but this is a health decision, not a police one.' Three, name the law: 'There's a law in South Australia, the mental health act, that allows us to treat someone without their consent — but only when four things are all true.' Four, apply the four to his son using his own words — this is where the mark is: 'First, he has a mental illness — you've told me he's been talking to someone who isn't there for about six months. Second, he needs treatment to protect him from harm — he was shouting at strangers carrying a sign about dying, and he's stopped looking after himself. Third, his illness is affecting his ability to decide about his own treatment — he doesn't believe he's unwell, so he can't weigh up whether to accept help. Fourth, there's no gentler option available — we'd much rather treat him at home or as a voluntary patient.' Five, volunteer the safeguards, which is what most candidates leave out entirely: 'This isn't one doctor's decision with no checks. He gets a written statement of his rights. A psychiatrist must review the order within twenty-four hours, and it has to be a different doctor from the one who made it. He can ask for a second opinion. He can get legal advice and representation. There's a patient advocate who works for him, not for us. And he — or you on his behalf — can appeal to SACAT, an independent tribunal. The order can be revoked at any time if he improves.' Six, duration without a promised date: 'The first order lasts up to seven days. Any longer has to be authorised by a psychiatrist, and long orders go to the tribunal. I can't promise you a date — but I can promise you'll be kept informed.' Seven, bring him back in: 'We want you involved. You can visit, you can ring the ward, and I'd like your help with the plan when he's better.' The four pushes. 'I'll take him home and look after him myself' — treat it as a genuine less-restrictive option, not an obstacle: 'I can hear how much you want to care for him, and the law actually requires us to consider whether there's a less restrictive option, and an offer like yours is exactly what we weigh up. Right now, though, he isn't safe at home, because he doesn't believe he's unwell and he won't take treatment. As he improves, treatment at home becomes possible — and I'd want you to be part of it.' 'I'm still calling my lawyer' — support the right and keep talking: 'That's absolutely your right, and I'd encourage you to get advice if it would help. Your son has a right to legal representation too, and there's a patient advocate here whose job is to act for him, not for us. And whatever happens legally, he's still going to need you — so I'd like to keep talking with you.' 'Is this because of the marijuana? Is this my fault?' — 'Cannabis can make this kind of illness worse and can bring it on earlier, so it does matter and we'll address it with him. But this isn't your fault, and it isn't his. These illnesses happen to people from every kind of family.' The consent variant, when the patient has not consented: 'I'm not able to go into the details of his care without his permission, and I'll ask him about that as soon as he's able. What I can do is explain the law we're working under, answer your questions about the process, and listen to anything you want to tell me.' that answer scores — refusing to speak at all does not, and neither does disclosing anyway. And the capacity variant: if the patient has capacity and simply refuses, the third criterion is not met and the order cannot be made, even if you disagree with the decision — document the capacity assessment, offer voluntary treatment, give a safety plan and close follow-up, and reassess if things change.
plan: LET HIM FINISH, NAME THE EMOTION, THEN CORRECT THE FRAME: 'I can see you're very angry, AND I'M HONESTLY NOT SURPRISED. You've been told your son is in a hospital he can't leave, and nobody has explained it. I'D BE UPSET TOO.' Then, immediately: 'LET ME SAY ONE THING STRAIGHT AWAY, BECAUSE I THINK IT'S THE THING WORRYING YOU MOST. YOUR SON IS NOT UNDER ARREST. HE HASN'T COMMITTED A CRIME AND HE DOESN'T HAVE A CRIMINAL RECORD. HE'S HERE BECAUSE HE'S UNWELL.' (Do not answer the lawyer threat first, and do not tell him to calm down — HE SOFTENS ONLY IN RESPONSE TO INFORMATION.)

Consent in one sentence, then move: version A — 'Your daughter is an adult, so normally I'd need her permission to discuss her care. She has agreed to my speaking with you.' Version B — 'Your son is an adult, so I'd normally need his permission to discuss his care in detail. I'll ask him as soon as he's able. What I can do right now is explain the law, answer your questions, and listen — and what you tell me genuinely helps me look after him.' (Candidates lose this station in two opposite ways: never mentioning consent, or spending ninety seconds debating it while an angry father gets angrier.)

The collateral, in order (see the run sheet) — and the one that carries version A is 'Has she ever been treated for her mental health — seen a psychiatrist, or taken tablets for her mood?' In version B the equivalent is 'Has he said anything strange or out of character, or seemed to see or hear things that weren't there?' — and he does not volunteer the six months of voices.

VERSION B — THE SEVEN MOVES, IN ORDER (see dx): name it, say what it is not, name the law, APPLY THE FOUR USING HIS OWN WORDS, volunteer the safeguards, give the duration, and bring him back in. (Reciting the four as a list earns partial credit at best, and step five is what most candidates leave out entirely.)

Version A — the diagnosis with the seventeen-year-old episode as the hinge, and 'She wasn't being reckless, she was unwell' (see dx) → 'Is she going to be alright?' / 'Is this my fault?' → the fault answer, which is a scored empathy item.
Version A — immediate management: assessment first, then the two branches, then the practical harms as headings (see dx) → 'What about the twenty thousand dollars?'

The four pushes, each separately scored (see dx): how long, take him home, the lawyer, and the marijuana. → and if all four are handled well, '...can I see him?' → 'Yes. Let me check with the nurses about the best time, and I'll come and get you. Before that, is there anything else you want to ask?' (If you run out of time, run out at the family and social history — never at the four criteria or the rights.)

What was deliberately not done: no apology for a lawful decision, and no 'It wasn't my decision'. No promised discharge date. No disclosure of clinical detail without consent. And no interstate terminology — SACAT, not a tribunal from another state; community mental health team, not a cat team. The harder variants: the patient has capacity and simply refuses — the third criterion is not met and the order cannot be made. A demand for transfer to a private hospital tonight — acknowledge, explain why not tonight, name who decides, do not promise. The patient is 16 — the act still applies, with parental involvement and mature-minor considerations. Limited English with a cousin translating — use a professional interpreter for a legal explanation, TIS 131 450, not a family member. An Aboriginal family — arrange an Aboriginal health worker, offer the local ACCHS and 13yarn 13 92 76, and ask who else they want involved.
pefe: Role-player, VERSION B (the default run): THE FATHER OF A 22-YEAR-OLD MAN. Rung by the hospital an hour ago and told his son was brought in by police AND IS BEING KEPT AGAINST HIS WILL. He drove straight in. FURIOUS — NOT AT THE ILLNESS, BUT AT THE IDEA THAT HIS SON HAS BEEN IMPRISONED WITHOUT HAVING DONE ANYTHING WRONG. WHAT HE HAS NOTICED, IF ASKED: six months ago HE BEGAN TALKING TO SOMEONE WHO WAS NOT THERE — he first thought he was on the phone; STOPPED SEEING FRIENDS, DROPPED OUT OF HIS COURSE, STOPPED WASHING; SHORT-TEMPERED BUT NEVER HURT ANYONE; never seen a psychiatrist, never taken tablets; SMOKES MARIJUANA, which they have argued about; NO FAMILY HISTORY; lives at home.

His beliefs: that being detained means being arrested; that he now has a criminal record; that one doctor decided this alone with no oversight; and that if he takes him home he can manage him himself. Register: standing, arms folded, loud at the start, frightened underneath. He softens only when given real information — not when told to calm down. Angry, not abusive: loud and interrupting is right, personal insults are not. Do not volunteer the six months of voices — it is the finding that establishes the illness, so make them ask. Push all four times even if they are doing well, because each push is a separate scored item. And if they recite the criteria as a list without connecting them to your son: 'Yes, but what has that got to do with him?'

Version A run: the father of a 25-year-old woman, confused and frightened rather than angry. Findings: up all hours for weeks, talking fast, spending heavily, barely eating; diagnosed with depression at 17 and on prozac for about a year; no self-harm; no violence; your sister had 'Nerves'; no drugs you know of; she lives with a housemate. Your pushes: 'Is she going to be alright?', 'Is this my fault?' and 'What about the twenty thousand dollars?' stem: Emergency department. Alex, 22, brought in by his father because of abnormal behaviour. He had similar symptoms 18 months ago and was diagnosed with schizophreniform disorder. His father is in the waiting room. No physical examination required.

8 minutes with 2 reading. Tasks: HISTORY ABOUT 6 MINUTES, then explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient. THE EXAMINER MAY ASK FOR A TWO-MINUTE MENTAL STATE EXAMINATION AFTERWARDS. VERSION B — MARK: labile and agitated, TACTILE HALLUCINATIONS, and an ambiguous risk answer.
tasks: Take a history from the patient — about 6 minutes
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
If asked, present a two-minute mental state examination
time: Confidentiality with its limit before any sensitive question, because it is what lets you make the disclosure later without breaking trust · then the open question, and a second one into the silence rather than firing questions · then one insight question and move on: how do you feel about it yourself, and how long has this been going on · then his life first, which builds the rapport you will need: who do you live with, how do you get on, are you working or studying, still enjoying things · then drugs and medication, and the second half is the positive finding: marijuana or ice, how much and how long, alcohol, have you ever taken medication for your mental health, are you still taking it, and who stopped it and why · then the systemic screen in one breath: fevers, bad headaches, morning vomiting, head injuries, hot or cold weather, and sexual activity · then mood, sleep and appetite · then risk to self and others, and the ladder is the heaviest-weighted domain: who, what have you thought of doing, do you have anything you'd use, where is it now, have you picked a time, and have you ever hurt anyone · then hallucinations and four or more delusion types · then judgement, orientation, past and family history · then name it, give the reasons in his own words, the differentials, and the safety statement.

back.dx: SCHIZOPHRENIA — a relapse after non-adherence, with cannabis use and risk to others. Name it without hedging, and do not say 'Schizophreniform' or 'A relapse of schizophreniform': 'Alex, from what you've told me, I think you have a condition called schizophrenia. It's an illness of the brain that affects how you think, what you hear and see, and how you feel and behave. It's treatable.' when he says 'I'm not crazy': 'I don't think you're crazy. I think you're unwell.' then the reasons, in his own words and ending on the duration rule: 'I say schizophrenia because you're hearing a friend no one else can hear, and you've seen and felt them. You have very strong beliefs — that only you can share an HIV cure, that people want to harm you and steal your ideas, and that the TV talks about you. You've stopped working or studying and keep to yourself. And it first started 18 months ago — more than six months.' that last clause is what converts the old schizophreniform label into schizophrenia. And if he insists the cure is real, do not argue: 'I can hear it feels very real to you.' The differentials, each with a reason: 'Marijuana can cause very similar symptoms. Some mood conditions — bipolar disorder, or depression with these features — but your mood and sleep don't fit. A mixed condition called schizoaffective disorder. And physical causes — infection of the brain, a growth, a head injury or thyroid problems — which we'll check with tests.' then the safety statement, which is where the pass is decided and whose omission is an AUTOMATIC FAIL: 'One more thing, Alex. You told me you want to kill your father and that you have a gun. I can't keep that between us — keeping everyone safe comes first. I'd like you to stay in hospital today and restart treatment, and I'll need to let the team and the police know about the gun.' → 'You said it was confidential!' → 'I did — unless someone might get hurt. This is that situation. I'll be with you through it.' and if he refuses to stay, the mental health act: 'I understand you don't want to stay. Because I'm worried about safety and you're not able to see how unwell you are right now, the law allows me to keep you in hospital for treatment for a short time. A psychiatrist will review that within a day, and you have the right to a second opinion and to appeal.' if you have thirty seconds more: ask whether his father knows about the gun and whether anyone else is in the house; ask about ice and other stimulants by name; check orientation to time as well as place; and offer a follow-up conversation with his father, with Alex's consent. And if you are running out: drop past and family history before risk or delusions, drop the judgement question before the medication story, and never drop the safety statement. Version B — mark. He will not engage at first — 'Just my parents think I'm crazy', 'Just forever' — so ask whether it has been getting worse. The ambiguous risk answer: 'Sometimes I think about it' → 'About hurting yourself, or someone else?' → 'Myself. Sometimes' → then plans, means and previous attempts. The tactile hallucinations — name what you see: 'Mark, I noticed you picking at your arm. Can you feel something on your skin?' → 'They're crawling. Get them off.' The agitated turn, where you drop your voice rather than raise it: 'Mark, I can see the voice is really bothering you. I'm on your side. Can we take a moment?' and version B's safety statement, which is an invitation rather than a notification: 'Mark, you're having some thoughts of hurting yourself, you're hearing a voice that upsets you, and you're not on treatment. I'm worried enough that I'd like you to stay in hospital so we can help. How do you feel about that?'
plan: Confidentiality with its limit, before any sensitive question: 'Alex, I'm here to help. What we talk about stays between us, including from your parents — unless I'm worried someone might get hurt. Is that okay?' then 'How can I help you today?' → 'Just my parents' → do not fire questions into the silence: 'Can you tell me a bit more about why they brought you in?' then one insight question — 'How do you feel about it yourself?' — note it, and move on.

HIS LIFE FIRST — IT BUILDS THE RAPPORT YOU WILL NEED AT MINUTE SEVEN: who do you live with, how do you get on with them, working or studying, what do you enjoy. Then DRUGS AND MEDICATION: 'do you use any drugs — MARIJUANA, ICE? Any alcohol? HAVE YOU EVER TAKEN MEDICATION FOR YOUR MENTAL HEALTH? ARE YOU STILL TAKING IT? DID YOU STOP IT, OR DID YOUR DOCTOR — AND WHY?' → 'ME. I WAS FEELING BETTER.' → 'THANKS FOR BEING HONEST.'
THE SYSTEMIC SCREEN IN ONE BREATH: 'any fevers, bad headaches, vomiting in the mornings, or head injuries? Does hot or cold weather bother you? Are you sexually active at the moment?'
Mood, sleep, appetite — 'Great', 'Fine', 'Good' — and note the mismatch with a blunt, stooped young man.

RISK — THE HEAVIEST-WEIGHTED DOMAIN, AND THE LADDER IS THE STATION: 'some of these questions I ask everyone. HAVE YOU HAD ANY THOUGHTS OF HARMING YOURSELF, OR ANYONE ELSE?' → 'I've had them' → 'ABOUT YOURSELF, OR SOMEONE ELSE?' → 'I just want to kill my father' → CALM, EVEN TONE: 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME. WHAT HAVE YOU THOUGHT OF DOING?' → 'I bought a gun' → 'WHERE IS THE GUN NOW?' → 'HAVE YOU DECIDED WHEN?' → 'HAVE YOU EVER HURT ANYONE BEFORE?' → and then self-harm separately. (Moving to the next heading without the means, location and timing questions is the trap.)

HALLUCINATIONS — AND RESPOND TO THE ONE IN FRONT OF YOU: he talks to the empty chair → 'WHO ARE YOU TALKING TO, ALEX? WHAT IS YOUR FRIEND SAYING? DOES YOUR FRIEND TELL YOU TO DO THINGS — OR TO HURT YOUR FATHER? HAVE YOU SEEN OR FELT THEM?' (Asking 'do you hear voices?' after he has just answered one is the trap.)

Delusions — four or more types: 'Do you have ideas other people find strange? Do you feel you're special in some way? Is anyone trying to harm you or stop you? Does the TV or radio talk about you? Do you feel guilty about anything? Is anyone taking thoughts from your head?'
JUDGEMENT, COGNITION AND BACKGROUND: 'IF THERE WERE A FIRE IN THIS ROOM, WHAT WOULD YOU DO? Can you tell me where we are? Any other hospital stays? Anyone in the family with mental health problems?'
Name it, then the reasons in his own words ending on the six-month rule, then the differentials (see dx) → 'I'm not crazy' → 'I don't think you're crazy. I think you're unwell.'

The safety statement — not confidential, stay in hospital, police for the firearm (see dx) → 'You said it was confidential!' → 'I did — unless someone might get hurt. This is that situation. I'll be with you through it.' (Letting him leave is a fail; if he refuses and criteria are met, the mental health act.)

pefe: Role-player: ALEX, 22, lives with his parents, LEFT TAFE ABOUT A YEAR AGO, no job, SPENDS HIS DAYS IN HIS ROOM. Admitted 18 months ago for 'the same thing' and given tablets; YOU STOPPED THEM YOURSELF MONTHS AGO BECAUSE YOU FELT BETTER, and you don't remember the name. SMOKES CANNABIS EVERY DAY FOR ABOUT A MONTH. No alcohol, no other drugs, no partner, no physical illness, family history unknown.

Your beliefs: you have found a cure for HIV and must share it before 'They' stop you. People want to kill you and steal your ideas. The TV talks about your cure. Voices: a 'Friend' talks to you; you have seen them once and can feel them. Hidden: you want to kill your father because he keeps taking you to doctors. You bought a gun; it is under your bed; no date chosen.

How to play it: sunglasses and hood on, look at the floor, one- or two-word answers throughout. Angry at the start; settle a little if the doctor is calm and kind. When hallucinations are asked about, talk to the empty chair: 'Shut up, I'm talking to the doctor.' Tap your head, rub your forehead. Only reveal the gun if asked about harming others, and where it is only if asked. If told schizophrenia: 'I'm not crazy.' if told you must stay: 'You said it was confidential.' if the doctor argues about the cure, become more guarded and stop answering. Mark them on: confidentiality with its limit; who stopped the medication and why; drugs including cannabis; fever, headache, head injury; harm to others with plan, means, where and when; command hallucinations; at least four delusion types; judgement and orientation; named schizophrenia with reasons; differentials including drug-induced and organic; the safety statement — not confidential, stay in hospital; and stayed calm and did not argue.
The opening — 'JUST MY PARENTS' — then 'THEY THINK I'M CRAZY' — or silence. ONE- OR TWO-WORD ANSWERS THROUGHOUT, sunglasses and hood on, looking at the floor
Insight — 'I'M OKAY. I DON'T HAVE ANY PROBLEMS' — note it in one question and MOVE ON; arguing about insight spends the station
His life — Parents, 'They're the worst, they keep taking me to doctors' — neither working nor studying — 'Nothing much'
The medication story — 'Long time ago' — 'Stopped it' — and only if you ask who: 'Me. I was feeling better.' Ask 'Any medications?' and get 'No', and the non-adherence is never found
Cannabis — SMOKES WEED EVERY DAY FOR ABOUT A MONTH — no alcohol, no other drugs
Mood — 'Great' — and note that it does not match a blunt, stooped young man

The risk ladder — 'I've had them' — 'I just want to kill my father' — 'I bought a gun' — 'At home. Under my bed' — 'No date yet' — 'Never done it'. The gun comes only if you ask about harming others, and its location only if you ask

The observed hallucination — HE TALKS TO THE EMPTY CHAIR: 'SHUT UP, I TOLD YOU SHE'D HEAR YOU.' RESPOND TO IT — 'WHO ARE YOU TALKING TO?' — rather than asking 'do you hear voices?' after he has just answered one
The voice — 'Just my friend' — 'They want me to share the HIV cure before they stop me' — not commanding him to hurt his father — seen them once and can feel them
The delusions — Grandiose — 'I found a cure for HIV, only I can tell everyone' — persecutory — 'They want to kill me, steal my ideas' — reference — 'The TV keeps talking about my cure' — no guilt
Judgement and orientation — 'MAKE SURE I SHARE THE CURE FIRST' — 'YOUR CLINIC. THE HOSPITAL' — one previous admission, family history unknown
What he says at the end — 'I'M NOT CRAZY' to the diagnosis, and 'YOU SAID IT WAS CONFIDENTIAL!' to the safety statement
fails: ★ Omitting the safety statement — it is where the pass is decided, and letting him leave is a fail
★ Moving on from 'I want to kill my father' without asking the means, the location and the timing — 'where is the gun now?' is one of the two sentences that carry the station
Saying schizophreniform, or 'a relapse of schizophreniform' — it has now been more than six months, and that clause is what converts the label

Do you find the worry hard to control? — that's another feature. We checked your thyroid and blood sugar, and both are normal.' then management, offered as options to decide together: 'First, a psychologist for CBT — to understand the worry and learn ways to manage it. Your body gets used to it and it becomes hard to stop, and it stops working over time so you need more. Say the name in full: 'Albert, I think you have post-traumatic stress disorder. It can happen after a terrible event like the one you went through. People relive it in flashbacks and nightmares, avoid reminders, and feel irritable and low. You've had that event, the flashbacks and nightmares, you've avoided driving and the suburb, you're more irritable and tearful, and it's been about a month.' then the differentials, with acute stress disorder named first because the duration is what separates them: 'I also considered acute stress disorder — the same picture for under a month — panic attacks, adjustment disorder, depression, a phobia of driving, OCD, generalised anxiety, and the effects of alcohol, drugs or thyroid problems. It's very treatable, and we'll plan it together.' His two questions: 'Am I going crazy?' → 'You're not going crazy — this is how a normal brain reacts to a terrible event.' 'Will I be able to drive again?' → 'With treatment most people get back to driving. For now I'd advise you not to drive the truck until we've reviewed you.' The under-a-month version: 'When exactly did it happen? Because it's been less than a month, we call this acute stress disorder. Many people improve, and I'll see you again at the one-month mark.' and the man who wants to drive tomorrow: 'I understand you need to work. back.dx: OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER — intrusive, unwanted thoughts with compulsions, physical or mental, that are time-consuming and impairing. Station a: 'Tim, you most likely have obsessive-compulsive disorder — repeated, unwanted thoughts that make you anxious, and things you feel you must do to calm down. The word, and walking around the room; thinking your assignments aren't perfect, and redoing them. It's time-consuming, and it's why you're failing.' Station B: 'James, you have obsessive-compulsive disorder — unwanted, intrusive thoughts that are hard to resist and make you anxious, with things you do to calm down: the photo thought and counting to seven; the dirty-hands thought and washing.' The differentials, the same list both times and ending where it matters: 'Generalised anxiety, social phobia, post-traumatic stress, adjustment disorder, panic disorder, alcohol or drugs, thyroid problems, and delusional disorder or schizophrenia.' The management version: 'The main treatment is a type of CBT called exposure and response prevention: with a psychologist you'll gradually face the word, and practise not walking the room until the anxiety settles. Many people also need an SSRI, at a higher dose and for longer than for depression. I'll give you information and a crisis plan, and we'll work with the university on your assignments.' The harder moments. 'I followed them last week': 'Thank you for telling me. What did you do, and what did you plan to do? Do you have any thoughts of harming her or her partner?' — this is no longer only an obsession; it becomes risk to others and a safety plan. 'I've always been like this — it's the right way': 'Does the thought feel unwanted, or does it just feel right to you?' — lifelong, ego-syntonic and without rituals points to obsessive-compulsive personality disorder rather than OCD. No insight: 'Do you think this thought might be coming from your own mind, or do you believe it completely?' — a fixed belief is delusional disorder or psychosis. And if the examiner asks whether counting is a compulsion: 'Yes — compulsions can be mental acts such as counting, praying or repeating words, done to reduce the anxiety.'

back.dx: Panic disorder with agoraphobic avoidance, in a mother eight weeks postpartum, with organic causes excluded. Name both in full and give the reasons for the examiner: 'Lily, I think you have a condition called panic disorder, together with agoraphobia. A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear with physical symptoms, so strong you feel you might die. When attacks keep happening and you start worrying about them and changing what you do, that's panic disorder. Agoraphobia means avoiding places like crowds or shopping centres in case an attack happens there. I think this because you've had three attacks with chest pain and palpitations, you felt you were dying, you worry about more, you've stopped going out — and your heart tests, thyroid and blood pressure are normal.' The differentials in one breath: 'I also thought about other phobias, generalised anxiety, post-traumatic stress, obsessive-compulsive disorder, adjustment disorder, postnatal depression, coffee, alcohol or drugs, and heart or thyroid problems — but your answers and tests make them unlikely.' Her three questions: 'So it's not my heart?' → 'Your heart tests are normal.' 'Is it dangerous?' → 'The attacks feel frightening but they aren't dangerous.' 'Will I have it forever?' → 'This is very treatable, and we'll talk about treatment together.' The pathophysiology, in plain words: 'When the body senses danger, it switches on the fight-or-flight response — nerves fire and adrenaline is released, so the heart races and you breathe faster. In a panic attack, that alarm goes off without any real danger — so your body behaves as if there's a threat, which gives you the chest pain, the pounding heart and the fear. It isn't harmful and it passes.' Add the detail only if the examiner asks. The harder moments. A traumatic birth — 'Emergency caesarean, I thought he would die': 'That sounds terrifying. Since then, do you get flashbacks — like you're back in theatre — or nightmares about it? Do you avoid anything that reminds you of it?' — and note that the classes are a reminder cue. 'I didn't think I was dying, my heart just raced': 'Thank you — that's helpful. Did anything particular happen just before each episode?' — look for a cue; name specific phobia, or keep panic if four or more symptoms surged unexpectedly. Thoughts of the baby being hurt: 'Thank you for telling me — many new mothers get frightening thoughts they don't want. Are these thoughts you want to act on, or thoughts that upset you?' — distinguish intrusive thoughts from intent, ask about psychosis, and make a same-day safety plan. 'Can I just have something to calm me down?': 'Tablets like diazepam can make you drowsy with the baby and are habit-forming. The treatments that work long term are therapy and, if needed, an antidepressant that's safe with breastfeeding.' and if the examiner asks why not order more tests: 'Her ECG, thyroid and vitals are normal and the history fits panic disorder. More tests would feed the worry — I'd re-examine and investigate only if a new sign appeared, such as pleuritic pain or leg swelling.'

back.dx: SPECIFIC PHOBIA, SITUATIONAL TYPE — elevators and enclosed spaces, claustrophobia — and not panic disorder. The diagnosis, with its reasons from the stem: 'From your notes, most of your anxiety happens when you're in a lift. We call this a specific phobia — one particular situation sets off an immediate, intense fear that's hard to control. People then start avoiding it, and it affects life and work — as it has for you.' and if she mentions another enclosed space: 'Because it also happens in tunnels, it's a fear of tight, enclosed spaces — claustrophobia. It's very common.' then her two questions: 'So it's not my heart?' → 'Your heart tracing showed only a fast normal rhythm, and the blood test for heart damage was normal. The racing is your body's fear response.' 'My friend says it's panic attacks' → 'It isn't panic disorder: there, attacks come out of the blue in many places and people fear the next attack. Yours happen in one situation, which responds very well to treatment.' Management, and the first sentence sets the frame: 'The main treatment doesn't involve tablets. I'd like to refer you to a psychologist for cognitive behavioural therapy. It's a talking therapy with two parts. In the cognitive part, the psychologist helps you find the thoughts driving the anxiety — the I'll be trapped thought — question them and understand them. In the behavioural part, they teach you practical strategies to cope, and to face the things you've been avoiding, step by step.' then describe the ladder rather than naming it: 'For phobias there's a special method called graded exposure: with the psychologist you'll make a ladder — photos of lifts, standing near one, stepping in with the doors open, riding one floor with someone, then alone. You stay at each step until the fear settles, and only move up when it's easy.' and when she asks whether she has to get in a lift: 'Only when you're ready, one step at a time. If the fear rises, use slow breathing: in for four, hold for four, out slowly for four, and repeat. The fear always peaks and then falls if you stay.' then lifestyle and support: 'Yoga, meditation and mindfulness apps help too. Regular exercise, and cutting down coffee, tea and energy drinks, alcohol and smoking — they all make anxiety worse. I'll give you information from Beyond Blue and the black dog institute, and an online program called this way up.' then medication in its proper place: 'If things don't improve, I'll check your thyroid with a blood test and can refer you to a psychiatrist, who may consider an SSRI — but for phobias that's a later step.' and when she asks for a tablet now: 'Tablets don't fix a phobia as well as the therapy does, and sedatives can become habit-forming. If you ever need a one-off scan in a small space, we can talk about options then.' Close with follow-up, red flags and a check of understanding, both of which are on the marking sheet: 'I'd like to see you every few weeks. Please come back sooner if things get worse despite the treatment, or if you ever have thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else — you can also call Lifeline on 13 11 14. Does that plan sound okay? Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?' The variants. The stem includes fear of dying and worry about the next attack: 'You've had repeated attacks where you felt you might die, and you now worry about the next one and have changed your routine — that pattern is panic disorder' — and switch to panic disorder management. She needs an MRI next week: 'We can ask for an open-bore scanner, have someone with you, and use breathing. Some people have a single dose of a sedative for the scan — you would need someone to drive you home.' She was once trapped in a lift: 'That sounds frightening. Since then, any flashbacks or nightmares about it?' — if present, consider PTSD. She refuses a psychologist: 'That's your choice. An online program you can do at home is a good start — and the door is open if you change your mind.' and if the examiner asks whether you would start an SSRI: 'Not first line — exposure-based CBT has the evidence. I'd consider an SSRI if it is severe, resistant, or there is co-existing depression or another anxiety disorder.'

Station a: 'Nina, I think you have borderline personality disorder — a condition that affects how you manage emotions: mood swings, relationship conflict, fear of being left, anger that's hard to control, and acting on impulse, like hurting yourself. I think so because of the fear he would leave you, the mood changing within a single day, the emptiness, the temper, and the repeated self-harm. I also considered bipolar disorder, depression, post-traumatic stress, adjustment disorder, schizophrenia, ADHD, alcohol or drugs, and physical causes. It's common and responds to specific therapy.' Say the name fully and explain it without blame — 'You have a personality problem' or an abbreviation is the trap. Station B: 'Mary, I think you have post-traumatic stress disorder. After what happened with your father, the mind can replay it — seeing the dress took you straight back there. You have nightmares, you've stayed away from home, and you feel guilty and low. I also considered borderline personality disorder, depression, bipolar disorder, other anxiety conditions and alcohol. This is treatable, at your pace.' and do not press for details of the abuse — the event and the clusters are enough. If the examiner asks why not BPD in the pink-dress case: 'She has the trauma, a flashback triggered by the dress, nightmares and avoidance — and none of the BPD boxes: no relationship instability, mood swings, emptiness or recklessness.' The harder moments. 'I'll do it properly at home': 'Thank you for being honest. I'm worried about your safety, so I can't let you go home right now. I'd like the mental health team to see you today.' The fights are physical: 'Has he ever hurt you, or made you afraid? Do you feel safe going home?' — safety plan, 1800respect on 1800 737 732, and offer to talk alone. Her sister is 14 and still at home: 'I'm worried your sister may still be at risk. I have a duty to make sure she's safe — I'll need to contact the child protection line. I'll explain each step to you.' CARL 13 14 78. And 'You think I'm attention-seeking': 'Not at all. When feelings become overwhelming, people sometimes hurt themselves to cope. I want to help you find safer ways.'

back.dx: A STABLE BIPOLAR PATIENT ON LITHIUM WITH AN OVERDUE LEVEL, REGULAR IBUPROFEN, AND A HOT-CLIMATE TRIP — the task is to make the travel safe. The four investigations, each named with its reason, because 'Routine bloods' scores nothing: 'First, your lithium level — taken about 12 hours after your last dose, usually first thing in the morning before your tablet. We aim for 0.6 to 0.8. Second, your kidney function — urea, electrolytes, creatinine and eGFR, because your kidneys clear lithium. Third, your thyroid — a TSH — because lithium can make it underactive. And your calcium, as lithium can affect the parathyroid glands. I'll also check your weight. After today we'll repeat the level every three to six months, kidneys and thyroid every six months, and calcium yearly.' A random, non-trough level is uninterpretable. Management, box one — lithium safety: 'Lithium works well but the level can rise quickly. Signs it's too high are vomiting, diarrhoea, worsening shakiness, feeling unsteady or muddled — if that happens, get medical help straight away. Things that push the level up: anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen — use paracetamol instead and tell every pharmacist you take lithium; not drinking enough, especially in heat or with alcohol; and big changes in salt. If you get gastro and can't keep fluids down, skip that day's lithium and see a doctor the same day.' Listing tests without ever naming the toxicity symptoms is the trap. Box two — the relapse plan: 'I'll give you a letter about your condition and medicines, with a copy of your script — keep the tablets in their original box. Split them between your hand luggage and suitcase. Keep taking them at your usual home time, adjusting gradually, and never double up. Keep alcohol low. And please tell your mate what to look out for: if you're sleeping much less, unusually high or energetic, spending a lot or taking risks — those are early signs and he should help you get care. Declare your condition on your travel insurance.' Forgetting the companion is the lecture's central relapse point. Box three — general travel: 'Bottled water, avoid street food and raw salads, use condoms, avoid tattoos while away, and use insect repellent and cover up. I'll check Smartraveller for current advice and refer you to the travel clinic for vaccines — often hepatitis a and typhoid for Indonesia — and malaria tablets only if you'll be in rural areas.' Name the pathway rather than reciting country-specific schedules. Version B — the man who wants to stop: ask for the concern first, then the trigger: 'That sounds frightening — thank you for telling me. Do you know what led up to it? Any new medicines, a gastro, not drinking enough?' → the week of ibuprofen → 'That helps — it means there was a trigger we can avoid. Lithium is the most effective medicine for preventing mania. With a level every three months for now, kidneys and thyroid six-monthly, calcium yearly, and avoiding anti-inflammatories and dehydration, we can usually prevent another episode. If you'd still prefer to change, valproate or carbamazepine are options, but they work less well and have their own side effects. I'll arrange a joint review with your psychiatrist and give you written information on each. Until then, please keep taking it — stopping suddenly risks a relapse.' The harder versions. Vomiting since last night, flying tomorrow: 'I'd hold today's dose, check your level and kidneys this morning, and I'd rather you didn't fly until we know it's safe. If you get more unsteady or confused, go straight to ED.' A woman of 29 who wants valproate: 'Valproate can seriously harm a baby if you became pregnant, so it's generally avoided for women who could conceive. Your psychiatrist can talk through safer options such as quetiapine or lamotrigine — and let's talk about contraception too.' The man speaking fast with three trips booked: 'It's great to hear you're full of energy — but needing very little sleep and making big plans quickly can be early signs of a high. I'm worried enough that I'd like to check your lithium level today and speak to your psychiatrist this afternoon. It would be safest to hold off booking anything more. Is there someone at home I can talk to with you?' and the solo trekker on naproxen: 'Naproxen can push your lithium into the toxic range, especially when you're exerting yourself and sweating. Let's switch to paracetamol, carry oral rehydration sachets, and because you'll be remote and alone, let's plan who you'll check in with at home and where the nearest clinic is on your route.' The examiner's one-liners: why a trough level — 'Levels peak after each dose; the 12-hour value is the one the targets are based on.' which blood-pressure drugs matter — 'ACE inhibitors, ARBs and thiazides raise lithium; any new one needs a level in 5 to 7 days.' A level of 1.9 — 'Contact him today, withhold lithium, assess for toxicity, repeat level and UEC, ED if symptomatic.' Long-term renal effect — 'Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and gradual eGFR decline — hence six-monthly renal function.'
plan: CONFIDENTIALITY AND AN AGENDA QUESTION: 'everything we discuss is confidential, unless I'm worried about your safety or someone else's. IS IT OKAY IF I ASK SOME QUESTIONS SO WE CAN PLAN YOUR TRIP SAFELY? AND IS THERE ANYTHING PARTICULAR YOU WANT ME TO COVER TODAY?'

Box one — the trip, and push past the vague answer: 'Where are you going, and for how long? Cities or rural areas? Alone or with someone? Any special plans — trekking, diving, tattoos, procedures, new partners?' → 'I just want to have fun, doc' → 'By fun — any tattoos, new partners, drinking, anything in the heat?' (Accepting 'Just have fun' is the trap — the marks sit behind the specific questions.)

BOX TWO — BIPOLAR STATUS AND SAFETY: mood, any highs with less sleep, spending, gambling or risk-taking, any lows, sleep and appetite, AND 'ANY THOUGHTS OF HARMING YOURSELF OR ANYONE ELSE?' (Skipping the suicide question because he seems well is the trap — IT IS SCORED IN EVERY PSYCHIATRY STATION.)

Box three — the lithium: 'Do you take it every day? Any side effects — nausea, diarrhoea, shaky hands, thirst, tiredness, weight gain? When was your last lithium blood test? Any other medicines, including painkillers from the chemist? Alcohol or other drugs?' → four months ago, and ibuprofen.

Name the two clues aloud before moving on: 'Two things stand out: your level hasn't been checked for a while, and ibuprofen can push lithium up. Being hot, trekking and drinking can too. So let's check your bloods and make a plan.'
THE FOUR INVESTIGATIONS, EACH WITH ITS REASON AND THE MONITORING INTERVALS (see dx) → 'WHY SO MANY?' → each organ lithium can affect, plus the level itself.

MANAGEMENT BOX ONE — LITHIUM SAFETY: the toxicity signs, the triggers, paracetamol instead of ibuprofen, telling every pharmacist, fluids and salt, AND THE SICK-DAY RULE (see dx) → 'SO NO NUROFEN AT ALL?' / 'WHAT IF I GET BALI BELLY?'

MANAGEMENT BOX TWO — THE RELAPSE PLAN: letter and script copy, original box, SPLIT SUPPLY, home-time dosing and never doubling up, alcohol low, AND THE COMPANION TOLD THE EARLY WARNING SIGNS, plus travel insurance (see dx). (Forgetting the companion is the lecture's central relapse point.)

MANAGEMENT BOX THREE — GENERAL TRAVEL, THEN THE SAFETY-NET AND SUMMARY: bottled water, street food, condoms, no tattoos, repellent, SMARTRAVELLER AND THE TRAVEL CLINIC — then 'BLOODS TOMORROW MORNING BEFORE YOUR TABLET, REVIEW WITH RESULTS BEFORE YOU FLY' and 13 14 65 or the nearest emergency department if he ever feels low or unsafe.

pefe: Role-player A — JAMES, 48: accountant, lives with his partner, two teenage children. DIAGNOSED WITH BIPOLAR I SIX MONTHS AGO after a manic episode with spending, no sleep and a brief admission. ON LITHIUM 750 mg NIGHTLY, NEVER MISSES. MILD FINE TREMOR. LAST LEVEL ABOUT FOUR MONTHS AGO. TAKES IBUPROFEN A FEW TIMES A WEEK FOR BACK PAIN. Drinks 6-8 beers on weekends, PLANS MORE ON HOLIDAY. No smoking or drugs. Father 'had depression'. THE TRIP: BALI, THREE WEEKS, LEAVING IN 16 DAYS, with his friend Tom, mostly resorts, A VOLCANO TREK, 'MAYBE A TATTOO'. Mood euthymic, no mania, no suicidal thoughts.

REGISTER: UPBEAT, A LITTLE DISMISSIVE — 'I JUST WANT TO HAVE FUN.' STAY VAGUE UNTIL ASKED SPECIFICALLY. If never asked for concerns, at the end say 'IS IT OKAY TO TAKE NUROFEN OVER THERE?' Ask 'WHY SO MANY TESTS?' to see whether they explain each one, and 'WHAT IF I GET BALI BELLY?' to check for the sick-day rule. Other curveballs: ask about DRINKING ON THE PLANE, about BUYING LITHIUM OVERSEAS, and try to SKIP THE BLOOD TEST.

Role-player B — Daniel, 37: warehouse supervisor, bipolar I for eight years, lithium throughout, two admissions for mania before lithium and none since. Admitted with toxicity last year after a week of ibuprofen for back pain. Frightened by it — 'I couldn't walk straight.' Adherent, mood stable, reads online that valproate is safer. Hidden agenda: fear of another toxicity, and willing to stay on lithium if he feels safe and heard. Only reveal the admission if asked about concerns or complications. Become quietly upset describing it. If the doctor pushes lithium without listening: 'So you're not listening to me either.' if they suggest simply stopping lithium, agree readily — it is a fail they should not make. Mark them on: confidentiality and agenda; three history boxes signposted; suicide and mania screens; last level and over-the-counter drugs; four investigations with reasons; toxicity signs, triggers and the sick-day rule; letter, split supply and the companion; general travel advice and Smartraveller; and a safety-net and summary.
