back.dx: BIPOLAR I, STABLE ON LITHIUM, NEWLY PREGNANT AT SIX WEEKS — with a high relapse risk from two admissions, a failed valproate trial and a maternal postpartum illness. The first thing you say, before any risk figure: 'Please don't stop your lithium suddenly — that makes a relapse much more likely, which is risky for you and the baby. Take tonight's dose as usual.' then the risk in absolute numbers, which is what calms her: 'Lithium early in pregnancy slightly raises the chance of a heart problem, from about one in a hundred to about two in a hundred; the rare one people mention, ebstein's anomaly, is about one or two in a thousand. Most babies exposed are born healthy, and we'll check the heart in detail at the 20-week scan.' Saying 'It's safe' or 'It causes heart defects' without numbers is the trap — and if you mention defects without figures she asks 'Have I already hurt the baby?' then the options, with the decision placed where it belongs: 'I'd like you seen this week by your psychiatrist and the obstetric team, and I'll coordinate. Because you've had two admissions, valproate didn't work, and your mum was unwell after birth, your risk of relapse is high — so continuing lithium at the lowest effective dose may well be safest. The other option, if the specialists agree, is a gradual reduction with an alternative such as quetiapine, restarting lithium later. You won't be making this decision alone.' Making the decision yourself, or offering valproate, are both errors. Then monitoring through to postpartum, because ending at delivery loses a scored item: 'If you continue, we'll check levels every four weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks. Your 18 to 20 week scan will include a detailed heart check. You'll give birth in hospital; lithium is paused in labour and the baby is checked by the paediatricians. Breastfeeding on lithium is generally not recommended — we'll plan feeding. After birth is the riskiest time for relapse, so we'll have a plan in place.' and when she says she really wanted to breastfeed: acknowledge it, defer to the specialist discussion, and note that formula or expressed alternatives let her partner share night feeds — which protects her sleep and is itself relapse prevention. Today: 'Folic acid 5 mg, pregnancy bloods, lithium level, kidney and thyroid tests, and I'll call your psychiatrist.' The safety-net: 'If you're vomiting and can't keep fluids down, feel shaky or unsteady, or notice your mood going high or low, contact us straight away or call 13 14 65.' Version B — first mania in pregnancy. To the examiner: 'Her symptoms — a week of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, pressured speech and grandiosity with no previous episodes — fit a manic episode. I'd exclude organic causes: thyroid, drugs, steroids, and I'd check for psychosis and risk.' To the patient: 'This is a condition called a manic episode. At ten weeks, the safest treatment is usually an antipsychotic such as quetiapine or olanzapine, chosen by the psychiatrist. Lithium isn't used this early, but later in pregnancy it may be the best way to prevent another episode. You'd be seen today by the mental health team, and possibly admitted to keep you and the baby safe.' The harder moments. Hyperemesis at nine weeks, still taking lithium: 'Vomiting can push your lithium level up quickly. I'd like a level and kidney test now; hold today's dose until we have the result, and if you feel unsteady or confused, go straight to the emergency department.' Unsure about continuing the pregnancy: 'That's okay — you don't have to decide today. I can talk through all your options, including continuing or ending the pregnancy, without judgement, and whatever you choose we'll keep you well.' The partner answering for her: 'Thanks — I routinely see everyone on their own for part of the visit. Would you mind waiting outside for a few minutes?' Preconception planning: see the psychiatrist together before stopping contraception; a slow taper while still contracepting, or staying on the lowest effective dose; folate 5 mg now, level, kidneys and thyroid, and a written plan for pregnancy, birth and the months afterwards. Already pregnant on valproate: 'Valproate can affect a baby's spine and development, so I'd like you seen by your psychiatrist and an obstetrician in the next day or two. Please don't stop it on your own today — stopping suddenly can bring on a relapse.' The examiner's one-liners: why the postpartum period is dangerous — 'Hormonal shift, sleep loss and falling lithium clearance; postpartum psychosis risk is highest in bipolar I.' Neonatal problems — 'Floppy baby, poor feeding, lethargy, hypothyroidism or goitre — hence paediatric review.' Why weekly levels near term — 'Clearance changes and delivery fluid shifts make toxicity more likely around birth.'
plan: FEELINGS FIRST, THEN CONFIDENTIALITY, THEN THE QUESTION THAT FINDS THE HIDDEN PROBLEM: 'I understand you've had a positive pregnancy test — HOW ARE YOU FEELING ABOUT IT?' → 'happy, but I've been panicking about the lithium.' → 'Everything's confidential unless I'm worried about your safety. HAVE YOU CHANGED ANYTHING WITH YOUR LITHIUM SINCE YOU FOUND OUT?' → 'I DIDN'T TAKE IT THIS MORNING.' (Assuming the pregnancy is welcome, and missing that she may have already stopped, are the two opening traps.)

BOX ONE — THE BOOKING HISTORY, SIGNPOSTED: last period and cycles; bleeding, pain or vomiting; first pregnancy; FOLIC ACID; other medicines and allergies; smoking, alcohol, drugs; LAST CERVICAL SCREENING; and WHO'S AT HOME AND DO YOU FEEL SAFE THERE. (Skipping the booking history entirely is a named trap — THE LECTURE STRESSES BOTH HALVES OF THIS STATION.)

BOX TWO — THE BIPOLAR AND LITHIUM HISTORY: when diagnosed, how many episodes and admissions; WHAT MEDICINES HAVE YOU TRIED, AND DID THEY WORK; dose, adherence and last level; mood now, highs, lows, sleep; ANY THOUGHTS OF HARMING YOURSELF; 'DID ANYONE IN YOUR FAMILY BECOME UNWELL AFTER HAVING A BABY?'; and who supports you. → valproate failed, AND HER MOTHER WAS HOSPITALISED AFTER HER BIRTH. THE TWO OPTIONS AND THE TEAM DECISION (see dx) — the relapse risk named from her own history, continuing at the lowest effective dose as probably safest, a gradual reduction with quetiapine as the alternative, AND 'YOU WON'T BE MAKING THIS DECISION ALONE.'

MONITORING, BIRTH, FEEDING AND POSTPARTUM (see dx): levels 4-weekly then weekly from 36 weeks, THE FETAL ECHO AT 18 TO 20 WEEKS, hospital birth with lithium paused in labour and paediatric review, breastfeeding generally not recommended, AND THE POSTPARTUM PLAN. → 'I REALLY WANTED TO BREASTFEED' → acknowledge, defer to the specialists, and note that shared night feeds PROTECT HER SLEEP AND PREVENT RELAPSE. (Ending at delivery is the trap — THE POSTPARTUM PLAN IS SCORED.)

TODAY'S ACTIONS, THE SAFETY-NET AND THE SUMMARY (see dx): FOLIC ACID 5 mg, pregnancy bloods, lithium level, kidney and thyroid tests, and a call to her psychiatrist — then vomiting, tremor or mood change means contact us or 13 14 65.

pefe: Role-player: SARAH, 32, primary-school teacher, lives with her supportive partner Tom. BIPOLAR I DIAGNOSED AT 25; TWO MANIC ADMISSIONS at 25 and 28, NONE SINCE. VALPROATE FIRST — WEIGHT GAIN AND A RELAPSE; switched to LITHIUM 900 mg NIGHTLY, WELL FOR FOUR YEARS. Last level three months ago, 'fine'. POSITIVE HOME TEST TODAY, LAST PERIOD SIX WEEKS AGO, regular cycles. Mild nausea, no vomiting. NO FOLATE. No smoking, stopped alcohol when trying — THE PREGNANCY WAS SEMI-PLANNED. YOUR MOTHER HAD A 'BREAKDOWN' AND A HOSPITAL STAY AFTER YOUR BIRTH — ONLY SAY IF ASKED ABOUT FAMILY HISTORY. HIDDEN: YOU SKIPPED THIS MORNING'S LITHIUM OUT OF FEAR.

Register: anxious and teary at first, calmer once risk is explained in numbers. Ask 'Should I just stop it?' Early. Ask 'Have I already hurt the baby?' if they mention heart defects without numbers. If never asked about changes to your lithium, say at the end: 'I didn't take it this morning — was that okay?' Ask about breastfeeding if they don't raise it. If they tell you to stop lithium today, agree readily — it's their error to catch. Other curveballs: your partner wants you off all medicines; ask about ibuprofen for headaches; ask about future pregnancies.

MARK THEM ON: FEELINGS FIRST; ASKED ABOUT CHANGES TO THE LITHIUM; the booking history — LMP, symptoms, obstetric, folate, medicines, screening, SAFETY AT HOME; the bipolar course INCLUDING FAILED TREATMENTS; mood, mania and suicide; FAMILY POSTPARTUM HISTORY; 'DON'T STOP SUDDENLY'; ABSOLUTE RISK IN NUMBERS; MDT WITH BOTH PATHWAYS; the levels schedule; FETAL ECHO AT 18 TO 20 WEEKS; hospital birth and paediatric review; BREASTFEEDING DISCUSSED; THE POSTPARTUM RELAPSE PLAN; FOLATE 5 mg AND BOOKING BLOODS; and a safety-net with a summary.
How she feels — 'HAPPY, BUT TERRIFIED ABOUT THE LITHIUM' — and the pregnancy was SEMI-PLANNED, so assuming it is unwelcome is a trap in both directions

The hidden finding — 'I haven't taken it today — I didn't know if I should.' Given only if you ask whether she has changed anything, and otherwise volunteered at the end as 'I didn't take it this morning — was that okay?'

Booking history — Six weeks, regular cycles — some nausea, no vomiting — first baby — no folate yet — lithium only, no allergies — no smoking, stopped drinking — screening two years ago, normal — partner Tom, and she feels safe

back.dx: ECT FOR SEVERE MAJOR DEPRESSION WITH SUICIDAL IDEATION — explained to a frightened son, with the South Australian consent pathway. The procedure, in plain words: 'ECT stands for electroconvulsive therapy. Your mum will have a short general anaesthetic so she's fully asleep, and a medicine to relax her muscles so her body barely moves. The doctor places two pads on her head and gives a brief electrical pulse, which causes a short, controlled seizure in the brain — usually under a minute — that we monitor. She wakes a few minutes later. It takes about half an hour, and it's a course: two or three times a week, usually six to twelve treatments.' How it works and why her: 'We're not completely sure how it works — it seems to rebalance brain chemistry involved in depression. We use it for severe mental illness, when other treatments haven't worked, or when we need a quick response. Your mum's depression is severe and she's had thoughts of ending her life, so waiting weeks for tablets to work is risky.' Say 'Severe, resistant, or urgent' and then link it to her — reading out a list of diagnoses is the trap. Advantages: 'It's one of the most effective treatments for severe depression, and it often works faster than medication — which matters when someone is at risk. It's done in hospital with close monitoring, and many people start to improve after a few treatments' — often within one to three weeks. Do not promise a cure; relapse is common without ongoing medication. Disadvantages, and the memory answer is the one that wins the communication marks: 'The common side effects are headache, aching muscles, nausea and feeling muddled for a while after waking. The one people worry about most is memory: during the course she may find it harder to remember new things, and she may have patchy memories of the weeks around the treatment. For most people that improves over the weeks after the course; a few gaps can remain. She won't forget who she is or who you are. Rarely, there can be dental injury, a heart rhythm problem or an anaesthetic complication — that's why we do a full check first: heart, lungs, brain, teeth, bloods and a heart tracing.' The myth, acknowledged then corrected: 'I can understand why you've heard that — ECT has had a bad reputation from old films. Modern ECT doesn't damage the brain or change someone's personality. When severe depression lifts, families usually tell us their mum is back to her old self.' The consent pathway, which is the legal core of the station: 'We always ask your mum first — we assume she can decide unless it's clear she can't. If she agrees, she signs; if she understands and says no, we wouldn't give it. If her illness means she can't decide, someone she appointed in an advance care directive can consent for her; if there's no one, the psychiatrist applies to a tribunal called SACAT. Without that appointment you can't legally consent or refuse — but your views really matter, we'll involve you, and you can attend the hearing.' and if he asks whether you would do it even if he said no: 'If SACAT agrees it's the least restrictive way to treat her safely, yes — and we'd make sure your concerns are heard.' then close: continuation medication after the course, possible outpatient completion once she is safe to go home, written information, a meeting with her psychiatrist, and a summary. The variants. The daughter is the appointed decision-maker: 'If the psychiatrist finds your mum can't make this decision herself, you can give written consent on her behalf — or decline. The law asks you to decide as she would have wanted, based on her values.' The patient has capacity and refuses: 'Your mum understood what we explained and has decided she doesn't want ECT. Because she's able to make that decision, we won't give it. We'll keep treating her with medication and support, keep her safe on the ward, and if her ability to decide changes, we'll reassess.' Postpartum psychosis, the best example of a rapid-response indication: 'With postpartum psychosis, waiting weeks puts your wife and the baby at risk. ECT often works much faster, which is why the team recommends it.' The angry son — 'You're experimenting on her': 'I can hear how angry and scared you are, and it makes sense — you're watching your mum go through something awful. ECT isn't experimental; it's one of the oldest and best-studied treatments in psychiatry, and it's recommended because we're worried about her safety. Would it help if we sat down with her psychiatrist together?' — and mention the community visitor scheme. 'Will she need it forever?': 'Most people have one course. Afterwards she'll continue medication to stop the depression coming back. A small number who relapse despite medication have occasional maintenance ECT, but that's decided later, with her.' The examiner's one-liners: why reduce benzodiazepines — 'They raise the seizure threshold, making ECT less effective.' Unilateral versus bitemporal — 'Right unilateral has fewer cognitive effects; bitemporal may act faster in very severe illness.' after the course — 'Continuation antidepressant with or without lithium, or maintenance ECT; relapse is otherwise common.' Absolute contraindication — 'None; relative ones are raised intracranial pressure, recent myocardial infarction or stroke, an unstable aneurysm, and high anaesthetic risk.'

back.dx: VERSION A — an anniversary grief reaction. Version B — major depressive disorder with psychotic features. The counting rule first, silently: fewer than five MDD criteria after a death is grief; five or more is depression; plus persistent psychosis is depression with psychotic features. Jane has four; Tim has seven. Version A, the diagnosis with its reasons: 'Jane, I think this is an anniversary grief reaction. Grief is the natural response to losing someone you love, and it can come back around special dates. I say this because your low mood, broken sleep, tiredness and poor concentration started as the anniversary approached, you've been well for two years, you still enjoy the gym, you're eating normally and you have no thoughts of harming yourself. Hearing mum call you once is common in grief.' The differentials: 'I thought about depression, but you don't have enough of its features; a longer, stuck kind of grief, but you were well until recently; a stress reaction called PTSD; and thyroid problems, which we can check if things don't settle.' then the management that answers the referral rather than obeying it: 'I don't think you need an antidepressant — they treat an illness, and grief isn't one. What helps is support: keep seeing your counsellor, who can focus on grief; look after sleep and keep the gym going; think about a way to mark the anniversary; and I can write to the university about extensions. I'd like to see you in two to three weeks. If your mood gets worse, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, come back sooner or call Lifeline on 13 11 14.' and when she says her counsellor said she needed tablets: 'She was right to send you. With your permission, I'll let her know my thinking.' Starting sertraline to satisfy the referral is the trap. Version B — Tim, 17. Confidentiality is phrased for a minor: 'Tim, what you tell me stays between us, even from family, unless I'm worried about your safety or someone else's. If that happens, I'll talk to you first.' Characterise the perception: 'How often do you see her? Every day? What does she say?' → 'She wants me to know I'm guilty' → and then the question that is the version B trap if missed: 'Why would you be guilty? She had a car crash' → 'I don't know. It's my fault.' then: 'Tim, I think you have depression with psychotic features. Your mood has been very low for three months, you've lost interest, you're not eating or sleeping well, you're exhausted and can't concentrate. Seeing and hearing your mum constantly, and feeling you're to blame, are psychotic features. It's treatable. I'd like the youth mental health team to see you this week. A psychiatrist will probably recommend an antidepressant and an antipsychotic together, and a psychologist will help with the grief. I'll check some bloods, see you often, and if you're not safe or not eating, we may need hospital. Can we talk about who could support you at home?' and the sentence that names the difference for him: 'What you're going through is more than grief.' Variant C — Tim was in the crash: 'Were you there, or involved in the crash? Do you have flashbacks, or avoid cars or roads?' — if yes, PTSD moves to the TOP of the list. And the Jane variant: 'It's her birthday next week, not the anniversary' — which changes nothing about the reasoning.

You told me you have no thoughts of that and have never tried. That's good.' Starting with the risk factors is the named trap. Step two — the risk factors, named from his own answers: 'But I'm worried. You're hearing and seeing God, and you believe you've been chosen and that people want to stop you — those are symptoms of your illness. You stopped your medication. You're living on the street, using marijuana and alcohol, you don't feel you need help, and you hadn't noticed the wound on your foot.' Step three — the protective factors, and the point is that there are none: 'Right now I can't find the supports around you that would keep you safe — a home, family, or a team you see regularly.' Step four — so what: 'So I'm worried you can't look after your basic needs at the moment. I'd like you to stay in hospital so we can treat your illness and your foot, and help with somewhere to live. How do you feel about that?' → 'I have to go. I have a mission' / 'God will look after me' → 'I hear that. I'd still like to look after you here for a while. A psychiatrist will see you today.' Letting him leave is the fail — and if he refuses and the criteria are met, the mental health act applies, with a level 1 order lasting up to seven days and a psychiatrist review within 24 hours. I'm a doctor here and I'm on your side. If you'd rather not answer something, that's okay.' Echolalia — he repeats your question back word for word: note it, then rephrase once. He falls asleep: 'David, can I wake you for a second? I know you're tired. There are just a few more questions, and then you can rest. Can you stay with me?' — note the drowsiness for the mental state examination and think delirium, head injury or intoxication. Name it in plain words, say why, and remove the blame: 'You have a condition called postpartum depression with psychotic features. It's a serious but treatable mental health condition that affects some mothers after birth. It happens because of the big changes your body and mind go through, and the exhaustion of caring for a newborn. It is not your fault.' Never say 'Baby blues'. Then the two parts: 'One part is depression — feeling low, not sleeping or eating, and sometimes thoughts of harming yourself or the baby. The other part is psychotic features — losing touch with reality, hearing things that aren't there, or strong beliefs that aren't true. Does that make sense?' then her own symptoms, and the reassurance that is a separate mark because the guilt is the delusion: 'You've told me your mood is low, you can't sleep or eat and you've lost weight. You hear a voice saying you're a horrible mother, you feel very guilty, and you've had thoughts of harming your baby. I want you to know you're doing a good job — that voice is the illness, not the truth.' and add the question the stem does not cover: 'Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself as well?' then the admission, led by safety: 'I'm extremely concerned about the safety of you and your baby. That's why I'd like you to be admitted to hospital today — ideally a unit where mothers and babies are cared for together. How do you feel about that?' Offering outpatient review is the trap. Then the sentence she is waiting for: 'This doesn't mean we're separating you. Your baby will stay with your husband for now, and you'll have time together every day with staff there to help, so you're both safe.' then treatment: 'A psychiatrist will see you in hospital and decide on treatment. There are two main options: medicines — an antidepressant for the low mood and an antipsychotic for the voice — or ECT, done under a short anaesthetic, which works faster than tablets, and that matters with a new baby.' and the breastfeeding answer: 'Usually yes — we'll choose medicines that suit feeding, and not treating you is a much bigger risk than the small amount that reaches your milk. But I have to be honest: because you have an illness, there's a serious risk to your baby and to you, and there's no safer way to treat you right now, if you decided not to come in I would have to arrange admission under the mental health act. We'll repeat the memory test in a few months, because it often improves.' Step two — once we know: 'If the assessments show a condition like dementia, I'd refer you to a geriatrician, who may consider a medicine for some types; arrange an aged-care assessment through my aged care for help at home; and put you and your family in touch with dementia Australia. We'd talk about an advance care directive and choosing someone to make decisions if you ever can't. And we'd review driving safety.' Leading with donepezil is the trap — medication follows a diagnosis, and does not suit alcohol-related impairment. Her questions: 'Will I lose my licence?' → 'Only if the assessment shows it isn't safe; we'd discuss it first.' 'Will my memory come back?' → 'Often it improves, sometimes a lot. I can't promise how much, but stopping gives it the best chance — and we'll track it together.' The variants. Signs of Wernicke's: 'She's confused, unsteady and has nystagmus — that's Wernicke's encephalopathy until proven otherwise. I'd give parenteral thiamine urgently, before any glucose, and transfer her to hospital.' The daughter demanding a diagnosis: 'I understand you want an answer. This test shows a short-term memory problem, and alcohol may be part of it. We need blood tests, a scan and a more detailed assessment — with your help, because your view of how she manages day to day is really valuable.' Results six months later: 'Your memory tests are better than six months ago, which fits alcohol-related memory problems improving with abstinence. Let's keep going — and keep taking the thiamine.' and the curveballs: mid-test 'What's the point of this?' → 'It checks different parts of memory — I'll explain everything at the end', then continue. Refusing to write a sentence → encourage once, then note it as not completed and move on. The daughter answering for her → 'I'd like to hear Helen's own answers for this part — thank you.' 'Am I going mad?' → 'No — this shows a short-term memory problem, and we'll find out why.' A drink this morning → note possible intoxication, retest when sober, thiamine, and revisit abstinence support. Insisting on driving → assessment first, and if unsafe, South Australian doctors must notify the registrar — discussed openly. The examiner's one-liners: why thiamine before glucose — 'Glucose can precipitate Wernicke's in thiamine-deficient patients.' What korsakoff's is — 'A chronic amnestic syndrome, anterograde amnesia with confabulation, after thiamine deficiency.' when dementia is diagnosed — 'Cognitive decline affecting daily function, after excluding delirium, depression, medicines and physical causes.'

back.dx: GENDER DYSPHORIA IN A TRANS MAN SEEKING GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE — and being trans is not a mental illness. Affirm before advising: 'Thank you for sharing all that with me. Being trans isn't a mental illness or a problem. What matters is how you're feeling — the distress you've described about your chest and with your mum is what we can support.' and if he asks why the psychologist called it dysphoria: it describes the distress, not him. Agreeing that he has 'A disorder' is the trap. Then hormones, with the three things candidates forget — permanence, fertility and contraception: 'I can start testosterone here using an informed-consent approach, or refer you to the adult gender diversity health service at Modbury. Testosterone deepens your voice and increases hair — permanent changes — stops periods and changes body shape. We monitor your blood count, liver and cholesterol. It's not contraception, and it can affect fertility, so we'll talk about storing eggs first if you might want children. Cervical screening still matters. For TOP surgery, I'd refer you to a surgeon.' Do not promise a start date or public surgery — be honest that TOP surgery is limited in the South Australian public system. Then the practical steps, which carry marks and are what most candidates omit in favour of emotional support alone: 'I'd like you to keep seeing a psychologist experienced in gender. If you'd like, I can meet with your mum, and PFLAG supports parents. I'll update your records with your name and pronouns today. You can change your name and gender on your licence and birth certificate — you don't need surgery or hormones.' and binding safety: 'Take breaks, don't bind overnight or while exercising hard, never use tape, and come in if you get pain or breathlessness.' Close with a safety-net and a review: 'If your mood drops or those dark thoughts come back, call me, QLife on 1800 184 527, or Lifeline on 13 11 14. Let's book a review in a few weeks.' The variants. He is already injecting testosterone bought online: 'Thank you for telling me — I'm not here to judge. Online products can be the wrong strength or contaminated, and without monitoring there are risks like a high blood count. I'd like to check your bloods and, if you're happy, prescribe it properly so we can monitor you safely. Are you using clean needles?' A non-binary patient who does not want hormones: 'Thank you for telling me — I'll use they/them. Care is about your goals, and not everyone wants medical treatment. Let's update your records, talk about support at work or study, and I can help with documents if you'd like.' The mother, upset — 'I just want my daughter back': 'I can hear how much you love Alan, and how hard this is for you. Many parents feel a sense of loss at first. What helps young people most is family support — it's strongly protective for their mental health. PFLAG connects parents with others who've been through this. Would you like to come back together?' The examiner's one-liners: monitoring on testosterone — 'Haematocrit, liver function, lipids, blood pressure and weight, at baseline and then regularly in the first year.' Cervical screening — 'Yes, if he has a cervix; offer self-collection.' Fertility before hormones — 'Testosterone can reduce fertility, and preservation is best before starting.'

back.dx: POST-CONCUSSION SYNDROME — the symptoms of a head injury lasting longer than expected, with a normal CT and without major depression. Give the label with its three reasons, because a label without reasons is explicitly scored down: 'The most likely explanation is post-concussion syndrome — when the symptoms of a head injury last longer than expected. The reasons: you had a clear head injury a week ago; since then you've had headaches, tiredness, poor concentration, poor sleep and low mood, and feel slowed down; and the CT has ruled out a bleed, fracture or structural damage.' then the sentence that answers 'Am I going mad?': 'Concussion affects how the brain works for a while, not its structure — so what you feel is real.' then name the depression trap and explain it away by timing: 'Some of it can look like depression, but it started with the injury and has only been a week, so I think it's part of the concussion.' then the prognosis, which is also scored: 'The outlook is good: most people recover within a few weeks. I'll see you regularly, and if symptoms drag on beyond about four weeks, there's specialist rehab help.' The return to play, step by step: 'Gentle activity, back to work first, then training once you've been symptom-free for two weeks, and no competitive games for at least three weeks from the injury.' and the red-flag safety-net: 'If your headache gets worse, you vomit, get drowsy, confused, weak or have a seizure, go straight to ED.' His other question: 'Should I have another scan?' → only if there are red flags or he is worsening. The variants. A 62-year-old on apixaban with a worsening headache and confusion: 'I'm worried there may be slow bleeding under the skull that wasn't there on the first scan. You need an urgent repeat CT today — I'll arrange transfer to ED now.' Acute stress symptoms — 'I keep reliving the tackle, I can't go near the ground': 'That sounds really distressing. After a frightening event, the mind can replay it for a while — when it's within the first month, we call it an acute stress reaction. Talking therapy with a psychologist helps a lot, and I'll check how it's going at each visit.' Still unwell at six weeks: 'I'd like to get you more help: a concussion clinic or sports physician, a vestibular physio for the dizziness, and a psychologist. We'll also look at your mood and sleep specifically, and plan a gradual return to work.' The curveballs: he demands another scan — only for red flags or worsening, and explain why it would not change management now. He asks for stronger painkillers — avoid opioids and daily analgesia because of medication-overuse headache; use pacing and sleep. The coach has cleared him — a minimum of 21 days before competitive contact, with a graded return and review. He drinks to get to sleep — alcohol slows recovery; sleep hygiene and a mood review. 'Is this permanent?' — 'Very unlikely; most people recover within weeks.' and he needs a work certificate — yes, with a graded return to duties. The examiner's one-liners: why not strict rest — 'Prolonged rest delays recovery; symptom-limited activity after 24 to 48 hours helps.' Second impact syndrome — 'Rare catastrophic brain swelling after a second head injury before recovery, which is why early return is dangerous.' Repeating the CT — 'Only with red flags or worsening, not for stable persisting symptoms.'
plan: OPEN QUESTION, EMPATHY, CONFIDENTIALITY, AND 'HOW ARE YOU FEELING NOW?': 'I'm sorry — THAT SOUNDS FRUSTRATING. I'll ask some questions; everything's confidential unless I'm worried about your safety. HOW ARE YOU FEELING NOW?' (Jumping to 'the scan was normal' before exploring is the opening trap — HE HAS ALREADY BEEN TOLD THAT, AND IT IS WHY HE IS HERE.)

The incident and the red flags: 'What exactly happened? Did you lose consciousness? Do you remember before and after? Vomiting? Blurred or double vision, trouble speaking? Weakness or numbness? Neck pain? What did ED tell you? Any blood thinners?' (Skipping these because the CT was normal is the trap — a delayed bleed is the must-not-miss.)

The full post-concussion symptom list — and this is where the diagnosis comes from: 'Tell me about the headaches — where, how bad, what kind, what helps or worsens them, how many painkillers? Dizziness — lightheaded or spinning? Tiredness? Memory or concentration? Is noise or light bothering you?' (Stopping at the headache is the named trap — most candidates never ask the full list.)

MOOD, SLEEP, APPETITE AND RISK: 'HOW'S YOUR MOOD? SLEEP — GETTING TO SLEEP, WAKING, NIGHTMARES? APPETITE? ANY THOUGHTS OF HARMING YOURSELF OR ANYONE ELSE?' (Missing the suicide question because this is a 'medical' station is the trap.)

PSYCHOSOCIAL AND THE PTSD SCREEN: who's at home, work, back to your usual activities and still enjoying them — then 'SINCE THE INJURY, ANY FLASHBACKS OR NIGHTMARES ABOUT IT, AVOIDING FOOTBALL, FEELING ON EDGE OR ANGRY?' Then smoking, alcohol, drugs, medicines, PREVIOUS CONCUSSIONS and family history.
The diagnosis with its three reasons, and the 'Am I going mad?' Sentence (see dx) → 'Why do you think that?' if you gave no reasons.
The depression trap named and explained away by timing, then the prognosis (see dx) → 'So it's in my head?' → 'Concussion affects how the brain works, not its structure — so what you feel is real.'

Return to activity and sport, then the red-flag safety-net and a review (see dx) → 'How long till I can play?' → gentle activity, work first, training after two weeks symptom-free, and no competitive games for at least three weeks from the injury.

pefe: Role-player: TOM, 25, ELECTRICIAN, lives with his supportive girlfriend, plays community Australian rules. A WEEK AGO: HEAD CLASH IN A TACKLE, KNOCKED OUT FOR A FEW SECONDS by his teammates' account, NO MEMORY OF THE TACKLE ITSELF. VOMITED ONCE IN ED. CT NORMAL, OBSERVED FOUR HOURS, DISCHARGED.

Since then: frontal dull headache daily, 5 out of 10, worse by evening, paracetamol most days; lightheaded on standing, no spinning; exhausted; can't concentrate at work; noise bothers him; trouble falling asleep; mood flat; 'I've slowed down'. No suicidal thoughts. No flashbacks or avoidance. A few beers on weekends, no drugs, no medicines. One concussion at 18, recovered in a week.

How to play it: frustrated — 'They said I'm fine, but I'm not.' Give the full symptom list only if asked each item. If the doctor says 'Depression', ask 'So it's in my head?' Ask 'When can I play again?' Near the end. If the doctor gives no reasons for the diagnosis, ask 'Why do you think that?' if never asked about mood, say 'Honestly, I'm pretty down.' setting: Counselling a mother — GP, three days after she walked in on her 16-year-old. The counselling needs both HALVEs: normalise the curiosity and name the risks. Catastrophising and dismissing are both marked down. The safety question — did anyone send it to her or show her — is answered reassuringly, but you only know that if you ask. Five messages must be given, and consent and the illegality of an adult showing porn to a minor are named pass items. And educate rather than punish, without criticising her for taking the laptop.
stem: GP clinic. Karen, 42, has come about her 16-year-old daughter Emily, whom she found watching pornography at home. Task: talk to the mother — take a history and counsel her regarding her concerns.

Findings: the daughter is well, good at school, has no boyfriend and is not sexually active; the mother is upset. Harder versions: an adult sent it; problematic use; the mother is not coping; religious parents; and Emily attends later on her own.

Counsel her regarding her concerns

back.dx: Normal adolescent sexual curiosity in a well 16-year-old, with an upset mother who does not know how to start the conversation — and the task is to coach her. The counselling needs both HALVEs: 'It's normal for teenagers to be curious about sex — they're learning and exploring their sexuality. But porn has risks: unrealistic expectations, a negative body image, distressing content if it's violent, and for a few young people, problematic use where they can't stop even though they want to, and it affects school or friends.' Catastrophising — 'This is harmful' — and dismissing — 'Boys will be boys' — are both marked down. And one episode is not addiction; describe the features to watch for instead. Then coach the conversation with a concrete opener, rather than telling her to confront Emily: 'Pick a calm, private moment. Start from something you've seen together on TV, then ask something like, some people your age come across porn — has that happened to you or your friends? Stay calm and honest, keep your own feelings to one side, and ask without shaming or accusing. Educating her works much better than punishing — punishment tends to make it secretive.' and on the laptop, without criticising her: 'It's an understandable reaction. But punishment tends to make things secretive; talking is what protects her.' then the five messages, and consent and the law are named pass items: 'What she sees isn't real life; safe sex matters and condoms are a normal part of real sex; consent is essential; real bodies don't look like bodies in porn; and it's illegal for an adult to show porn to someone her age — if that ever happens, she can tell you.' then the plan: 'If she ever feels she can't stop, bring her to me — she can see me on her own — or we can have a family meeting. I'll give you the eSAFETY parents' guide. And if this keeps weighing on you, I can help you too.' On blocking: 'Filters can help with accidental exposure but aren't the answer on their own.' The harder versions. An adult sent it — a man in his thirties from a gaming chat: 'Thank you for telling me — this changes things. An adult sending sexual material to a 16-year-old is grooming and a criminal offence. Please keep the messages but don't confront him. I'd like to see Emily today, and I have a legal duty to report this to child protection; we should also contact the police, and eSAFETY can help. None of this is Emily's fault.' Problematic use — every night until 2 a.m., grades dropping, can't stop: 'I'd like to see him — on his own for part of the visit — check his mood and wellbeing, and link him with a psychologist. Meanwhile, devices out of the bedroom at night can help sleep, as part of a plan you make together rather than a punishment.' The mother not coping: 'It sounds like this has hit you hard — sometimes a stressful event leads to what we call an adjustment reaction. I'd like to support you too: a follow-up with me, and a referral to a psychologist under a mental health treatment plan. Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?' Religious parents who cannot say the words: 'I respect that, and your values are part of what you can share with her. You don't need to use any words you're uncomfortable with — the key is that she hears the safety messages from someone she trusts. I'm happy to see her myself, or a school nurse or counsellor could help, and I can give you written material you can hand her.' and Emily attending alone: 'What you tell me stays between us. The only exception is if I'm worried you or someone else is at serious risk of harm — then I'd talk with you first about who needs to know. At 16 in South Australia you can make your own decisions about your health care.' The curveballs: the husband thinks she is overreacting — both reactions are understandable, and a calm, united approach agreed before talking to Emily is best. 'Should I check her phone?' — secret monitoring damages trust; agree online rules openly, though safety concerns are different and warrant action. 'What if she says it's none of my business?' — respect her privacy, keep the door open, and she can see a GP confidentially. And a request to test her for STIs — only with Emily's own consent. The examiner's one-liners: when to report — 'Reasonable suspicion of abuse or exploitation, for example an adult sending material or requesting images, to CARL on 13 14 78.' Is porn addiction a diagnosis — 'Not in dsm-5-tr; icd-11 has compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, and the principle is loss of control with harm to function.' if she is sexually active — 'See her confidentially: contraception, condoms, STI testing, consent and relationship safety.'
plan: EMPATHY AND CONFIDENTIALITY BEFORE ANY ADVICE: 'I CAN SEE HOW UPSETTING THIS HAS BEEN. I'll ask some questions and we'll make a plan together — is that okay? Everything we discuss is confidential, unless someone's safety is at risk.' (Rushing to advice before hearing the story is the opening trap — EMPATHY AND THE INCIDENT ARE MARKED FIRST.)

The incident: 'Can you tell me more about what happened? Is this the first time? How did you react — and how did she? Have you talked about sex before? Did you punish her?' → the yelling, the laptop, and 'We've never really talked about sex.'

EMILY THROUGH HER MOTHER, PLUS THE SAFETY QUESTIONS: who's at home; her relationship with you and her siblings; school, grades and friends; boyfriend or girlfriend; DO YOU KNOW IF SHE'S SEXUALLY ACTIVE, AND WHETHER SHE KNOWS ABOUT SAFE SEX; mood, sleep and eating; past mental health problems; AND 'DO YOU KNOW HOW SHE CAME ACROSS IT — DID ANYONE SEND IT OR SHOW HER? ANYONE ONLINE YOU DON'T KNOW?' (Forgetting the safety questions is the trap — THE ANSWER IS REASSURING, BUT ONLY IF YOU ASK.)
Karen herself — a separate box: 'How are you coping? Mood, sleep, appetite? Any stress or anxiety since? Who supports you?' → 'My husband says I'm overreacting.'
Normalise and name the risks — both HALVEs (see dx) → 'So it's normal? It doesn't feel normal.' / 'Is she addicted?' → one episode is not addiction; describe what problematic use looks like.

Coach the conversation with a concrete opener, and address the punishment without criticising her (see dx) → 'I wouldn't know what to say.' / 'Should I take her phone too?' (Telling her to confront Emily with 'I know what you did' is the trap.)

THE FIVE MESSAGES (see dx) — not real life, safe sex and condoms, CONSENT, real bodies, AND THE ILLEGALITY OF AN ADULT SHOWING PORN TO SOMEONE HER AGE. (Omitting consent or the illegality message loses named pass items.)

THE PLAN AND THE SUMMARY: offer to SEE EMILY ON HER OWN OR HOLD A FAMILY MEETING, the eSAFETY PARENTS' GUIDE, and support for Karen herself. → 'SHOULD I BLOCK THE WEBSITES?' → filters help with accidental exposure BUT AREN'T THE ANSWER ON THEIR OWN. → 'CAN YOU TALK TO HER?' → offer both: coaching now, AND seeing Emily yourself.

pefe: Role-player: Karen, 42, office manager, married, two children — Emily 16 and Josh 12. Three days ago she walked into Emily's room and saw pornography on her laptop. She shouted and left, and took the laptop. Emily has been quiet with her since. She has never talked with Emily about sex — her own parents never did. Emily is a strong student with many friends, no boyfriend, and she does not believe Emily is sexually active. No mental health history. Karen is upset and embarrassed, sleeping okay, not depressed. Her husband thinks she is overreacting. Her real agenda: 'How do I even talk to her about this?'

How to play it: start tearful and a bit embarrassed; relax as the doctor normalises. Ask 'Should I take her phone too?' To test the punishment point. Ask 'Is she addicted?' if the doctor mentions addiction. If the doctor lectures or moralises, go quiet and defensive. If never asked about your own coping, say 'I've been so stressed about this.' Do not volunteer any adult involvement — there is none; answer 'I think she just searched it.' At the end, ask 'Can you talk to her?'

setting: History then a spoken mental state examination — two versions, and the risk ladder is climbed rung by rung, out loud. Version A's trap is stopping at the gun: its location and who can remove it are the management, so ask now. Version B's two deciding questions are 'Did you want to die?' and 'Any thoughts of hurting anyone, now or in the past?' — the second surfaces a homicidal plan she would otherwise never mention. back.dx: VERSION A — severe major depression with mood-congruent psychotic features and active suicidal intent with prepared means: a psychiatric emergency. Version B — self-harm without suicidal intent on a background of borderline personality traits. The model MSE for Julianne, read aloud: 'Appearance: a woman in dark clothing, with a sad, withdrawn expression, poor eye contact and a stooped posture. Behaviour: withdrawn but cooperative, with psychomotor retardation. Speech: slow, quiet and monotonous, with poverty of speech. Emotion: mood broken; affect flat, restricted and congruent. Perception: auditory hallucinations — whispering voices calling her a traitor. Thought: poverty of ideas. Content: active suicidal ideation with intent, a plan using a firearm she has already bought, and a date within the next week; no note. A delusion of guilt about losing the project. Insight impaired — she sees ending her life as the only solution. Cognition: alert and oriented. Judgement impaired — she said a fire would help her die sooner. This is a psychiatric emergency.' and the safety sentence said to her before the presentation: 'Julianne, I'm very worried about your safety. I don't want you to go home today. I'd like you to stay here with me while I arrange for you to be seen at the hospital, and we need to make sure the gun is removed from your home.' The model MSE for Maria: 'Appearance: a young woman wearing a heavy coat and long sleeves on a very hot day — inappropriate for the weather — with glasses, poor eye contact, a stooped, tense posture and an angry, upset expression. Behaviour: withdrawn but cooperative, repeatedly picking at her skin, hair and eyebrows. Speech: slow, quiet, monotonous, unclear at times. Emotion: mood okay; affect irritable, restricted and incongruent. Perception: none. Thought: linear. Content: no current suicidal intent; self-harm today and eight times before; past homicidal ideation towards a friend, none now; preoccupation with abandonment, jealousy, chronic emptiness and an inflated self-image. Insight partially assessed. Cognition: alert and oriented. Judgement not assessed.' The risk statement templates, filled aloud: suicide — 'She has passive or active suicidal ideation, with or without a plan, has or has not prepared means, timeframe, note, previous attempts, protective factors.' Self-harm — 'Self-harm without suicidal intent, this many previous episodes, function to manage distress, long-term risk elevated.' Others — 'No, past or current homicidal ideation towards whom, with or without a plan; no current thoughts.' where each woman goes: Julianne does not go home — admission, voluntarily or under a level 1 order, and the firearm removed through her partner or the police; treatment is an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic, or ECT. Maria goes home with a safety plan and follow-up if safe — wound care and tetanus, a check on her safety in the relationship, and referral for a structured therapy such as dbt, with her GP as the consistent point of contact. The variants. She refuses admission: 'I hear that you don't want to go. Because of the plan and the gun, I'm not able to let you leave today — I'd like to arrange this with your agreement, but if needed I can use the mental health act to keep you safe.' The voices give commands: 'You said the voices call you a traitor. Do they ever tell you to do anything — to hurt yourself, or anyone else? Do you feel you have to obey them?' — if yes, add command hallucinations to the MSE and the risk statement. Maria asks you not to tell her boyfriend: 'What we discuss stays between us. The only time I'd share anything is if I was worried about your safety or someone else's — and if that happened I'd talk to you first.' and 'I'll just do it again': 'Thank you for being honest. When the urge comes, what helps you get through it? Let's write down three things you can do and two people you can call, and I'll give you the crisis numbers. I'd like to see you again this week.' The examiner's follow-ups: why not start an antidepressant and review next week — 'Because she has a plan, the means and a timeframe within that week, with psychotic features — she needs to be safe today, and the firearm needs to be removed.'

back.dx: A PSYCHOTIC ILLNESS WITH ACTIVE SUICIDAL IDEATION AND A PREVIOUS ATTEMPT — and the task is the mental state examination, with two sentences that must not be dropped: 'Active suicidal ideation with a plan and a previous attempt', and 'Engaging with auditory hallucinations'. The model for Alex, read aloud: 'Appearance: a young man in a dark T-shirt wearing sunglasses indoors and two necklaces, a cross and a sword. Stooped, poor eye contact, withdrawn expression; hair dishevelled by the end. Behaviour: initially uncooperative, then agitated and irritable when he appeared to respond to voices, telling them to be quiet; tapping his forehead, a head tremor and fidgeting. Speech: slow, quiet, monotonous, with long pauses. Emotion: mood good; affect flat, restricted and incongruent. Perception: auditory hallucinations — a single voice; no visual. He also described depersonalisation — a screen between himself and the world. Thought: poverty of ideas. Content: active suicidal ideation with a plan, a previous attempt two years ago, no date or note. Persecutory delusion about his parents; grandiose — he must save the world and everyone is jealous of him. No passivity. Insight impaired. Cognition: alert and oriented. Judgement intact on testing.' The model for Bruce: 'Appearance: a young man in a blue hoodie and glasses, unshaven with unkempt hair, holding his hands in front of his face in a prayer position throughout; no eye contact; stooped; withdrawn. Behaviour: withdrawn and initially uncooperative, cooperative towards the end; catatonic — he did not move for the whole consultation, with posturing of his hands. Speech: slow, quiet and monotonous, mostly monosyllabic, with pauses and perseveration on I slept bad last night. Emotion: mood great; affect blunted, restricted and incongruent. Perception: visual and auditory hallucinations — he sees God, who commands him to save everyone. Thought: loosening of associations. Content: a grandiose delusion that he can save everyone by closing his eyes; a persecutory delusion about his parents; suicide and homicide risk not assessed — I'd assess it now, given the command hallucinations. Insight impaired. Cognition: alert but disoriented to place and person — he thought he was in a park; time not established. Judgement impaired. His catatonia and disorientation need an organic cause excluded.' The model for max: 'Appearance: a man in a dark T-shirt with a headset and glasses, unkempt with a beard; tense and stooped, no eye contact, an anxious, fearful expression; sniffing. Behaviour: uncooperative and increasingly agitated, talking back to a voice; rocking with a head tremor — psychomotor agitation. Speech: normal to fast, low volume, stuttering, mumbling and monosyllabic, with poverty of speech. Emotion: mood on TOP of the world; affect restricted and incongruent. Perception: auditory hallucinations — a voice that agrees with his plan. Thought: poverty of ideas. Content: homicidal ideation with a plan to kill a named public figure, endorsed by the voice, and he wants to leave today to act on it; a persecutory delusion that the fbi is trying to harm him; delusions of reference — the TV and radio talk about him; no suicidal ideation. Insight impaired. Cognition: alert, oriented to place and person; time not answered. Judgement not assessed. He is a serious risk to others.' The variant moments. Bruce gives irrelevant answers — 'Bad. I slept bad last night. I walk': one gentle redirect — 'That sounds hard. When you say you slept badly, what kept you awake?' — then move on and report loosening of associations. Bruce's command hallucination: 'You said God wants you to save people. Does God ever tell you to hurt yourself or anyone else? Do you feel you have to do what he says?' and then the question the lecture's candidate forgot: 'Have you had any thoughts of ending your life?' MAX'S homicidal plan: 'You said you need to kill the president. Tell me more — how would you do it? Do you have anything to do it with? When?' and then: 'I'm worried about the safety of other people. I'm not able to let you leave today, and I'll need to share this with the team and the police who brought you in.' and when max mumbles through the fire question: 'I know you're upset, max, and you want to go. I'll be quick. If there were a fire in this room, what would you do?' The examiner's follow-up, what would you do now: 'Alex has active suicidal ideation with a plan, a previous attempt and psychotic symptoms, so he isn't safe to go home. I'd offer voluntary admission; if he declines and meets the criteria, a level 1 inpatient treatment order. I'd arrange an organic screen and urine drug screen, a collateral history from his parents with his consent, and referral to the early psychosis service.'

WHAT BRINGS YOU IN TODAY?' → 'my parents think I'm crazy.' → 'WHAT ARE YOUR PARENTS WORRIED ABOUT? WHAT HAVE THEY NOTICED?' (Accepting 'I'm okay' and moving on is the trap — THE RE-OPEN IS WHAT CONVERTS A DENIAL INTO A HISTORY.)

Context and substances: 'How are things at home? Do you study or work? Still enjoy things? Do you smoke, drink, use cannabis or anything else — how much?' (Do not lecture on safe drinking limits mid-station.)

Mood, sleep, appetite and risk — and take the risk to its end: 'How's your mood? Sleep? Appetite? Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else? Ever tried? Any plan now? Prepared anything — a date, a note?' (Stopping at 'Yes' is the trap — the mark is plan, preparation, timing, past attempts and harm to others.)

Does it tell you to do things?' then: 'Do you feel people are against you? Is anyone trying to harm you? Any special powers? Any guilt? Are thoughts being put into or taken out of your mind, or broadcast?' → and catch the screen answer as depersonalisation.

pefe: Role-player: Alex, early 20s. Lives with his parents; he has never worked. He smokes cigarettes and cannabis — 'Whatever I have' — and drinks. For months he has heard one voice that comments on him and interrupts. He believes his parents want to harm him, that he must save the world, and that everyone is jealous of him. Sometimes he feels unreal, as if behind a screen. Two years ago he tried to end his life; recently he has thought about how he would do it, but has not set a date or written a note.

How to play it: wear sunglasses and two necklaces. Flat, slow, few words; uncooperative at first. At about minute four snap at the voice — 'I told you to shut up when I'm talking to the doctor!' — and become agitated; tap your forehead; shake your head; run your hand through your hair so it's messy. Say nothing about the voice or suicide unless asked.

Score the doctor on: re-opened after 'I'm okay'; context and substances; mood, sleep and appetite; suicide — ideation, plan, preparation and past attempt, and it is an AUTO-FAIL if not asked; harm to others; the voice explored; the full delusion set; depersonalisation noticed; insight, orientation and judgement; and in the MSE — the necklaces and sunglasses, engaging with voices, incongruent affect, poverty of ideas, and the risk described.
The opening denial — 'My parents think I'm crazy' / 'I'm okay, doctor' — and accepting it and moving on is the trap. Ask what they have noticed
Context and substances — Bad at home, not getting along with his parents — never worked — 'I'm not sure' about enjoyment — smokes and drinks — 'Weed, whatever I have'
Why you do not lecture — A lecture on safe drinking limits mid-station is a named trap — offer it at follow-up and move on
Mood and sleep — 'GOOD' — 'GREAT, NINE HOURS' — NO CHANGE IN APPETITE. All incongruent with how he looks

The risk, taken to its end — 'Yes... I did it once, two years ago' — 'I've thought about how I'd do it' — no date, no note. Stopping at 'Yes' is the trap; the mark is plan, preparation, timing and past attempts, plus harm to others
The moment at minute four — He snaps aside: 'I told you to shut up when I'm talking to the doctor!' → 'Who were you speaking to just then?' → 'It's just this voice'
The answer routinely missed — 'Sometimes I think I'm not real — like there's a screen in front of me' — depersonalisation, and it belongs under perception as a separate finding
The delusions — 'THEY'RE JUST JEALOUS OF ME' — 'I NEED TO SAVE THE WORLD', though he doesn't know from what — 'MY PARENTS WANT TO HARM ME' — NO passivity phenomena
Insight and judgement — 'I'M OKAY, DOCTOR' — and to the fire question, 'I'LL JUST RUN AWAY'. Oriented to place, time and person
Why insight is impaired — 'Insight intact because he answered' is the trap — he denies any problem, so it is impaired. But judgement here is intact on testing
What he is wearing — SUNGLASSES INDOORS AND TWO NECKLACES, A CROSS AND A SWORD — and by the end his hair is dishevelled from running his hand through it
Version C — max — A homicidal plan against a named public figure, endorsed by a voice, and he wants to leave today to act on it
fails: ★ Accepting 'I'm okay, doctor' and moving on instead of asking what his parents have noticed, which is what opens the story
★ Stopping the risk at 'yes' — the mark is plan, preparation, timing and previous attempts, plus harm to others, and not asking about suicide at all is an auto-fail
Missing 'I'm not real, like there's a screen in front of me' — that is depersonalisation and it belongs under perception as a separate finding
Calling insight intact because he answered the questions, when he denies any problem

Not asking who he was speaking to when he snapped at the voice; running an incomplete delusion set that omits passivity phenomena; lecturing on safe drinking limits mid-station; and in Bruce's version, never assessing suicide or homicide despite command hallucinations

back.dx: BENZODIAZEPINE DEPENDENCE AFTER SIX MONTHS OF DIAZEPAM STARTED FOR SITUATIONAL ANXIETY — and the answer to task 2 is yes, but gradually. The decision, said in words: 'Linda, I think this is a very good time to stop. Your son is doing well, you're feeling better, you're motivated, and you have a supportive partner. So yes — but we'll do it gradually, so it's safe.' then the plan, in six parts. Dependence: 'Diazepam is a medicine your body gets used to. Over time you need a higher dose for the same effect — that's why it went up. And if it's stopped suddenly, the body reacts: anxiety, poor sleep, headaches, and very rarely a fit. That's why we go slowly.' The taper, with its numbers: 'We'll reduce it over about four to eight weeks. Every one to two weeks we'll take off about a quarter of the dose — so from ten milligrams to seven and a half first. Towards the end we'll go in smaller steps and then stop. If you get symptoms, we'll stay on that step a little longer rather than go back up.' The supply rules: 'I'll write small scripts, and I'd like you to fill them at one pharmacy you choose, and get them only from me. That helps us keep to the plan together.' The red flags: 'If you have a severe headache, vomiting, confusion, see or hear things that aren't there, feel faint, or have a fit — call 000 and go to hospital. For milder symptoms, call me.' The support: 'I'd also like you to see a psychologist for cognitive behavioural therapy — it helps with the anxiety and with coming off the tablets. Relaxation, mindfulness and regular exercise help, and it's best to keep coffee and alcohol low. If the anxiety comes back, there are non-addictive medicines like an SSRI. Your partner is welcome at the next visit.' and the follow-up: 'Let's meet again in one to two weeks. Does this plan sound okay?' plus the driving advice, since she drives daily: best not to drive if she feels drowsy or unwell during the taper. Her questions: 'What if I can't sleep?' → 'That's common in the first couple of weeks and settles. Keep a regular wake-up time, no screens in bed, and we'll review at each step.' 'Can I just stop when I feel ready?' → 'Stopping suddenly after six months can cause withdrawal and, rarely, fits. Going down in steps is safer — and you're in control of the pace.' The variants. She drinks heavily: 'Drinking alcohol with diazepam is dangerous, and both affect the plan. I'd like to involve the drug and alcohol team so we can do this safely together.' She is low with suicidal thoughts: 'I'm worried about how you're feeling. Before we change the diazepam, I'd like to look after your mood and your safety first.' She is on temazepam rather than diazepam: 'First we'll switch the temazepam to an equal dose of diazepam, which lasts longer in the body and makes withdrawal gentler — then we'll reduce that slowly.' and she wants to stop tomorrow: 'I love your determination. But stopping all at once can cause withdrawal and, rarely, seizures. A few weeks of reducing is the safest way to get there.'

The medication, with the three scored boxes: 'What dose are you taking, and how often? Who prescribes it? Have you had to increase the dose to get the same effect? Have you ever tried stopping, or missed it for a day or two — how did you feel? On a scale of one to ten, how motivated are you to stop? What worries you most about stopping?' (Skipping motivation or withdrawal because she is obviously motivated is the trap.)
Mood and safety: 'How's your mood now? Sleep? Appetite? Are you still feeling anxious? Any thoughts of harming yourself?'

Substances, support and background — and ask alcohol early: 'Do you drink alcohol? Smoke? Any other drugs, or other medicines like sleeping tablets or painkillers? Coffee? Who's at home — how's the support? Do you drive? Any mental health problems in the past? Seizures? Could you be pregnant?' (Leaving substances until the end and running out of time is the trap — alcohol with a benzodiazepine changes the plan.)

The plan, part one: dependence explained, then the taper with its numbers (see dx) — four to eight weeks, about a quarter off every one to two weeks, ten milligrams to seven and a half first, smaller steps at the end, and staying on a step longer rather than going back up.
The plan, part two: supply rules — small scripts, one pharmacy, one prescriber — then the red flags and 000, and the driving advice.

The plan, part three: a psychologist for CBT, relaxation, mindfulness and exercise, coffee and alcohol kept low, an SSRI as a non-addictive option if the anxiety returns, her partner welcome next visit — then review in one to two weeks and 'Does this plan sound okay?'

The examination confirms genuine dental disease without spreading infection. My assessment is that she is at high risk of substance misuse: she has a history of heroin dependence and is on methadone 70 mg, and she smokes cannabis nightly with tolerance and withdrawal. I'm concerned about interactions — another opioid on TOP of methadone risks oversedation and overdose, and tramadol risks serotonin toxicity. She took four paracetamol in one go, so I'd quantify her total intake. She has depression and has stopped treatment, with no suicidal thoughts today. And she has financial barriers to seeing a dentist.' The plan, if asked: 'I wouldn't prescribe an opioid. I'd arrange urgent dental care through SA dental service, give regular ibuprofen and paracetamol within safe limits, contact her methadone prescriber with her consent, and follow up her depression and cannabis use.' and the sentence that makes the refusal land: 'The tooth itself needs treating — that's what will stop the pain.' The combination of ibuprofen and paracetamol actually works better for tooth pain, and I'll help you get to a dentist quickly.' Facial swelling and trismus: 'This swelling and trouble opening your mouth worry me — the infection may be spreading. I'd like you to go to the emergency department today.' She is on an SSRI and asks for tramadol: 'Tramadol with your antidepressant and methadone can cause a dangerous reaction called serotonin toxicity. It isn't safe for you.' and her two questions: 'Why won't you trust me?' → 'I do believe you're in pain. With your methadone, another opioid could be dangerous — I want to treat the pain in a way that's safe for you.' 'Can I take extra methadone?' → 'Please don't change your dose yourself — that can cause an overdose. I'll talk to your prescriber about the pain.' back.dx: VERSION A — quetiapine-induced weight gain with lifestyle contribution, organic causes excluded. Version B — schizophrenia with command hallucinations and high risk. Version A's plan, in four parts. The cause: 'The most likely cause of your weight gain is a side effect of quetiapine. Your diet and not getting much exercise are also contributing.' The investigations: 'I'd like to check your weight, waist and blood pressure, and do blood tests for your sugar, cholesterol and liver, plus a thyroid test and a pregnancy test to be thorough.' The lifestyle: 'The first step is lifestyle. A healthier diet with more vegetables and fruit, fewer takeaways and no sugary drinks — I'll refer you to a dietitian. Aim for at least 150 minutes of activity a week, like 30 minutes on five days. Cutting down smoking will help your health too, and Quitline can support you.' and the next steps, which are psychiatrist-led: 'If that isn't enough, I'll talk to your psychiatrist about switching to a medicine from the same family with fewer weight side effects, such as aripiprazole. There's also a diabetes tablet called metformin that can help some people. Please don't stop quetiapine on your own — the voices could come back. I'll give you some reading and see you again in four to six weeks.' Saying 'I'll change your medication' is the trap — GPs do not switch antipsychotics alone. Her questions: 'Will the weight come off if I switch?' → 'Often some does, but not always. Diet and exercise help whichever medicine you're on, so let's start those now.' 'Can I take a diet pill?' → 'Let's start with diet, exercise and a dietitian. If needed, metformin has the best evidence for antipsychotic weight gain, and I'd discuss it with your psychiatrist.' and if she wants to stop: 'Stopping suddenly risks the illness coming back. Let's try the other steps first, and talk to your psychiatrist together.' Version B's diagnosis, to the examiner: 'The most likely diagnosis is schizophrenia. My reasons: auditory hallucinations — a voice commanding her to stop medication and to kill herself; a persecutory delusion that doctors want to harm her; disorganised, irritable behaviour; and functional decline — isolated, not working, reversed sleep — over years, with a previous involuntary admission. She is misusing her late mother's quetiapine and is not taking her diabetes medication. Differentials are schizoaffective disorder, bipolar or depression with psychotic features, substance-induced psychosis, and organic causes including hypoglycaemia. Her risk is high, and she needs same-day psychiatric assessment.' The things to say to Anne. To the demand: 'I understand your frustration, and I'm sorry you've had to repeat yourself. I can't prescribe this without a proper history — that's our procedure, and it keeps you safe. I'll make it quick.' To 'Why do you need my history? It's just a script': 'Because it's a medicine that has to be prescribed for you specifically, and I need to make sure it's safe and right for you.' To 'You doctors want to harm me': 'I can hear that you don't trust doctors, and I'm sorry you feel that way. I'm here to help you stay safe' — and do not argue with the belief. And if she is on her phone or drinking coke throughout: 'I can see you're busy with your phone. This will only take a few minutes, and it really matters for your safety — can I have your attention for a moment?' The examiner's probes: what if she walks out — 'Contact mental health triage on 13 14 65 and, if she meets the criteria, consider a level 1 inpatient treatment order; police assistance if she is at immediate risk.' Why ask about her periods in version A — 'Pregnancy, PCOS and hypothyroidism all cause weight gain in a young woman. Quetiapine rarely raises prolactin, so irregular periods point towards PCOS, thyroid disease or pregnancy rather than the drug.'

Respect and permission: 'Thanks for being honest with me, Josh. I understand you're not ready to stop, and it's your decision. Can I share a few things, so you can make an informed choice?' The benefits, framed in his own life rather than in health abstractions: 'Stopping would help with dad and your brother, with money, with keeping a job, and with avoiding trouble with police and driving. It's better for your lungs, memory and mood too.' The dependence and the psychosis risk: 'Cannabis causes dependence. Your body gets used to it — that's why one cone became two — and when you stop you get withdrawal: anxious, poor sleep, feeling low. It passes in a week or two. Seeing and hearing things when you're high worries me — in some people cannabis can trigger a serious illness like schizophrenia.' The plan: 'If you decide to stop, we'd choose a quit date and I'd see you in the first week to help with any withdrawal. The best treatment is talking with a psychologist — cognitive behavioural therapy — to handle cravings and stress. There's marijuana anonymous, and the alcohol and drug information service on 1300 13 1340. If you're happy, we could sit down with your dad and brother and make a plan together. Please don't drive after using. Exercise and cutting down alcohol and cigarettes help too.' and the door left open, which is its own mark: 'The first person who can help you is you — and whenever you're ready, I'm here. Could we meet again next week, even just to talk?' The variants. Version 2, where he has cut down: 'That's a good step. Can I ask — when you cut down, did you notice any symptoms? And do you need more now to get the same effect when you do use?' — the same tolerance and withdrawal questions still apply. The father insists on staying: 'I'll talk with you both in a moment. Because Josh is an adult, I'd like to hear from him first — then we'll bring you in to make a plan together.' Voices when not using: 'Hearing voices even when you haven't used concerns me. I'd like you to see a specialist team who help young people with these experiences.' Motivation rises during the chat: 'That's great. Let's pick a quit date in the next week or two, and I'll see you in the first week to help with any withdrawal.' His pushbacks: 'It's natural — it's harmless' → 'Lots of people think that. For some people, especially young adults, it affects memory, mood and motivation, and it can trigger psychosis.' HEADSS before any drug question: 'Who do you live with? How are things with your parents? What happened with your brother — was anyone hurt? Are you studying or working?' (Opening with 'How much marijuana do you smoke?' Is the trap — he is told to shut down.)

The dependence assessment: 'Have you needed more to get the same effect? Have you ever stopped, or gone a few days without — what happened, and why did you start again? On a scale of zero to ten, how motivated are you to stop? Does it annoy you when your parents criticise it? Do you feel guilty about it? Do you use first thing in the morning?'

The consequences: 'Any money problems from buying it? Problems at work? Any fights or trouble with police while high? Do you drive after using — any fines or accidents? Any cough or breathlessness? Memory problems?'

Mood, risk, psychosis and other substances: 'How's your mood, sleep and appetite? Any thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else? Do you ever hear, see or feel things others don't — only when you're high? Does anyone want to harm or control you? Do you drink? Smoke? Any other drugs?' back.dx: ALCOHOL USE DISORDER — and the differentials are psychiatric. The diagnosis with its reasons, in DSM terms and plain words: 'James, the most likely diagnosis is a condition called alcohol use disorder. You're drinking large amounts over a long time, you get cravings, you spend a lot of time getting alcohol, and it's affecting your home, your work and your licence. Most importantly, your body has become dependent: you need more for the same effect, and you get shakes and sweats when you stop — and you have a drink in the morning to settle them.' The differentials: 'Drinking and mental health often go together — heavy drinking can cause low mood and anxiety, and conditions like depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety or PTSD can lead people to drink. As you've been feeling low and not sleeping, I'd like to look into depression and anxiety as well. Other substance use, like smoking, is also linked.' The counselling, version A — the daily drinker, where the aim is abstinence and the withdrawal is planned: 'I'm concerned about your drinking. It affects your physical health — your liver, heart and stomach — your mental health, and your home, work and driving. Your body has become dependent on alcohol: that's the tolerance and the shakes. I'd like to do some blood tests — blood count, liver, kidneys, sugar, vitamin B12 — and a heart tracing. Because your body is used to alcohol, stopping suddenly on your own can be dangerous — fits or severe confusion. So we'll plan it: I'll check your risk, and either help you withdraw at home with a medicine called diazepam and daily check-ins, or through drug and alcohol services in a residential unit. I'll also give you thiamine — a vitamin heavy drinkers run low on.' then relapse prevention: 'Afterwards, medicines like acamprosate or naltrexone help you stay off alcohol. Disulfiram is another — but you must not drink at all on it, or you get a very severe reaction. A psychologist can help with cravings and relapse. I'll refer you to alcoholics anonymous and the alcohol and drug information service on 1300 13 1340. Healthy diet, exercise; we'll talk about smoking at another visit. I'd like to meet with your wife too. The first person who can help you is you — and I'll support you every step.' The counselling, version B — the weekend drinker, where the aim is safe limits: 'Fifteen beers in one day is binge drinking and it's harmful, even if you don't drink during the week. The guideline is no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day. Alternate with water or soft drinks, eat before and while you drink, avoid the pub with the mates who lead to big nights, never drive after drinking, and I'll see you again to see how you're going.' The variants. A previous withdrawal seizure: 'Because you've had a fit when stopping before, it isn't safe to stop at home. I'd like to arrange admission through drug and alcohol services so you're monitored.' not motivated: 'That's your decision, and I respect it. Can I share my concerns and some information, and we'll talk again? In the meantime, please don't drive after drinking.' A doctor, pilot or truck driver: 'Because your job involves other people's safety, I need to talk about whether it's safe for you to work while we get this under control.' and children at home with violence: 'I need to ask about the children's safety — has anyone been hurt? If I'm worried a child is at risk, I have to involve child protection.'

The counselling, in six parts. Praise and benefits: 'Thank you again. Stopping will help your health, your marriage, your son, your money and your work.' The condition: 'Heroin causes dependence. Praise and benefits: 'Thank you for considering stopping. It'll help your asthma, protect your son's ears and lungs, and save you a lot of money.' The quit date: 'The best approach is to choose a quit date in the next week or two and stop completely on that day.' The withdrawal, named before it happens: 'You'll likely get withdrawal — irritability, poor sleep, cravings, feeling hungrier. It's worst in the first week and settles over a few weeks. Our aim is to control those symptoms.' The tools: 'Nicotine is what your body depends on. Nicotine replacement gives it to you without the smoke: patches, gum, lozenges, an inhalator or a mouth spray — and because you smoke first thing, a patch plus gum or lozenges works best. Patches are subsidised. Or there are tablets: varenicline — started a week or two before the quit date; the main side effect is nausea, so take it with food. Bupropion is another option, but not for people with seizures. I'll give you some reading so you can choose.' The support and follow-up: 'I'll refer you to Quitline — 13 7848 — they have counsellors and a callback service. A psychologist can help with cravings and relapse prevention. Avoid your triggers for a while — the pub and drinking. I'll see you a week after your quit date.' The four handbook questions. 'Is it too late — is the damage already done?' → 'No. The damage done so far can't be undone completely, but stopping now prevents further damage — your lungs and heart start benefiting within weeks.' 'Should I stop suddenly or cut down?' → 'Stopping on a set day works best. If that feels impossible, we can cut down with nicotine replacement towards a quit date.' 'Do hypnotherapy or acupuncture work?' → 'There isn't good evidence they work, so I'd rather you use what does — nicotine replacement or tablets, and Quitline.' 'Do I need a course or support group?' → 'Support doubles your chances. Quitline on 13 7848 is free, and there's quitcoach online and the my QuitBuddy app.' The variants. His father has lung cancer: 'I'm so sorry about your dad. It makes sense that it's made you think about your own health — and this is the single most powerful thing you can do.' not motivated: 'That's okay — it's your decision. Can I leave you with some information, and if you change your mind I'm here to help? Would you be open to cutting down in the meantime?' Worried about weight gain: 'Some weight gain is common, but it's far less harmful than smoking. Regular exercise and a healthy diet help, and nicotine replacement can reduce it.' A history of seizures: 'Because of your seizures, bupropion isn't suitable, but nicotine replacement or varenicline are.' and his two other questions: 'Can I use the patch and still smoke?' → 'It's safe, but the aim is to stop completely on your quit date. If you slip, keep the patch on and get back on track.' 'Won't the tablets make me depressed?' → 'Most people have no mood problems. If you notice low mood or unusual thoughts, stop the tablets and call me.'
