time: Open, confidentiality, and acknowledge the decision · then the usage and the four questions that carry a three-minute history: how long have you been vaping, how often through the day, do you know the nicotine strength, where do you vape and who with · then is it hard not to vape in places where it's banned, and how soon after you wake up do you have your first vape · then have you increased how much you vape to get the same effect, have you ever tried stopping, and have you ever gone a few days without it · then other substances, mood and motivation: do you smoke cigarettes as well, alcohol, any drugs or anything else in the vape such as cannabis, how is your mood and sleep, and on a scale of one to ten how motivated are you · then counselling in its three named parts: the effects with the social benefits, the nicotine dependence explained from his own history, and the strategies · a quit date, the medicines, named support and a review.

back.dx: NICOTINE DEPENDENCE FROM VAPING, IN A HIGHLY MOTIVATED YOUNG MAN — and task 2 is delivered in the three parts it names. Part one, the effects, with honesty about what is not known: 'Vaping irritates your mouth and throat and causes coughing; it can cause nausea, dizziness and headaches, and it can damage the lungs. The liquid is poisonous if swallowed or spilt on skin, and devices can overheat. Because vapes are new, we don't yet know the long-term effects — they may be less harmful than smoking, but they aren't safe. People who vape are also more likely to start smoking.' and the social benefits: 'You'll save a lot of money, and you won't be sneaking off at work.' Part two, the dependence, explained from his own history: 'The substance in the vape your body depends on is nicotine — the same as in cigarettes. Over time your body gets used to it: you need more for the same effect — that's tolerance — and when you stop, you get withdrawal: irritability, poor sleep, trouble concentrating, feeling hungrier, cravings. That's what happened on your camping trip. It's worst in the first week and settles over a few weeks.' Part three, the strategies: 'The best approach is to choose a quit date in the next week or two and stop completely on that day. To control the withdrawal, nicotine replacement works well — a patch, plus gum or lozenges for cravings, because you vape first thing in the morning. Or a tablet called varenicline, which you start a week or two before your quit date; the main side effect is nausea. These are smoking medicines that we also use for vaping. I'll refer you to Quitline — 13 7848 — they support people quitting vaping as well as smoking, and the my QuitBuddy app can help. A psychologist can teach you to manage cravings and avoid relapse. Tell your mates you're quitting, avoid situations where everyone vapes for a while, keep beer to a minimum, and exercise. I'll see you a week after your quit date.' His questions. 'Is it worse than smoking?' → 'Probably not as harmful as cigarettes, but it isn't safe, and we don't know the long-term effects yet. Quitting nicotine altogether is best.' 'Can't I just go to lower-strength ones?' → 'Some people do cut the strength down over a few weeks, but it keeps you vaping — with a quit date and nicotine replacement you have the best chance.' 'Will the patches work if I vaped, not smoked?' → 'Yes — it's the nicotine your body depends on, and patches give you nicotine without vaping. They're used off-label for vaping, and they work.' 'What if I slip up?' → 'Slips are common. Don't give up — get rid of the device, call Quitline, and we'll adjust the plan at your review.' 'How long will the cravings last?' → 'The worst is the first few days to a week. They get less frequent over two to four weeks, and each one passes in a few minutes.' 'Will I put on weight?' → 'Some people do, a little. Regular exercise, healthy snacks and nicotine replacement help.' 'Can my mates help?' → 'Tell them you're quitting and ask them not to vape around you for a while.' 'Is it expensive?' → 'Quitting saves you money. Some nicotine replacement is subsidised with a script, and Quitline is free.' The variants. He also smokes: 'Since you smoke as well, let's plan to stop both on the same date — nicotine replacement covers both, and Quitline can help with both.' not motivated: 'That's okay — it's your decision. Can I give you some information, and if you change your mind, come back and we'll make a plan?' The six-minute version: add the full substance structure — CAGE, effects at home, work, money, legal and health, a fuller psychiatric history, and other substances. He asks about pharmacy vapes: 'Pharmacists can now supply lower-strength nicotine vapes to adults, but they're meant as a quitting aid, not a long-term habit. Proven medicines and support are still the best route.' and the examiner's probe on why a quit date rather than tapering: 'He is motivated and sick of vaping. The RACGP recommends a quit date first; tapering is an option if abrupt stopping fails.'
plan: Open, confidentiality and acknowledge the decision: 'I really appreciate that you're considering stopping, and that you've come in for help. Is it okay if I ask a few questions so I can assist you better?'
The usage: 'How long have you been vaping? How often through the day? Do you know the nicotine strength? Where do you vape, and who with?'

THE TWO DEPENDENCE QUESTIONS: 'IS IT HARD NOT TO VAPE IN PLACES WHERE IT'S BANNED? HOW SOON AFTER YOU WAKE UP DO YOU HAVE YOUR FIRST VAPE?' → sneaking it at work, AND BEFORE HE IS OUT OF BED — which is what makes a patch PLUS gum or lozenges the right choice.

Tolerance and withdrawal: 'Have you increased how much you vape to get the same effect? Have you ever tried stopping? Have you ever gone a few days without it?' → 'Not really' → then the camping trip. (Accepting 'Not really' and moving on is the trap.)

Other substances, mood and motivation: 'Do you smoke cigarettes as well? Alcohol? Any drugs — anything else in the vape, like cannabis? How is your mood and sleep? On a scale of one to ten, how motivated are you to stop?' (Check dual use before the CAGE questions.)
Counselling part one — the effects, with the social benefits and honesty about the unknown long-term picture (see dx).

COUNSELLING PART TWO — NICOTINE DEPENDENCE, EXPLAINED FROM HIS OWN HISTORY (see dx): the same nicotine as cigarettes, tolerance because he goes through pods faster, AND THE CAMPING TRIP AS HIS OWN WITHDRAWAL.

COUNSELLING PART THREE — THE STRATEGIES (see dx): A QUIT DATE in the next week or two and stop completely; A PATCH PLUS GUM OR LOZENGES because he vapes first thing, or VARENICLINE STARTED A WEEK OR TWO BEFORE; QUITLINE ON 13 7848 AND MY QUITBUDDY; a psychologist; telling his mates and avoiding the vaping crowd and the beer; AND REVIEW A WEEK AFTER THE QUIT DATE.

Answer his questions and close: 'Is it worse than smoking?' and 'Can't I just use weaker ones?' (see dx) — then 'Is there anything else you'd like to ask? I'll see you a week after your quit date, and Quitline is on 13 7848 any time.'

pefe: Role-player: Andrew, 25, apprentice electrician, lives with two housemates. Vaping three years, having switched from cigarettes, which he quit then. Nicotine 20 mg/mL pods, all day, every half hour or so. First vape before getting out of bed. He goes through pods much faster now. Never properly tried to stop — but his charger broke on a camping trip and two days left him cranky, sleepless, unable to focus and constantly eating.

HIS OTHER ANSWERS: he vapes EVERYWHERE and ALL HIS MATES VAPE; HE SNEAKS IT AT WORK AND IN PUB TOILETS; a few beers on weekends, NO drugs and nothing else in the liquid; mood fine and sleep okay; MOTIVATION TEN; HIS GIRLFRIEND HATES IT AND HE FEELS A BIT GUILTY.

How to play it: fed up, motivated, a bit embarrassed. Hidden agenda: worried quitting will make you snappy at work and your boss will notice. Ask 'Is it worse than smoking?' and 'Can't I just use weaker ones?' if the doctor doesn't cover them. Mark them on: acknowledgement; the first vape; banned places; tolerance; withdrawal via days without; cigarettes; alcohol and drugs; mood; motivation; the effects; dependence; a quit date; nicotine replacement; varenicline or bupropion; Quitline named; CBT; and follow-up.
The opening — 'I'M SICK OF VAPING, DOC. I WANT TO QUIT' — fed up, motivated, a bit embarrassed
The usage — About three years — all day, every half hour or so — twenty milligrams per mL — everywhere, and all his mates vape
The two dependence questions — 'I sneak it at work and in the toilets at the pub' — and 'It's the first thing I grab, before I'm out of bed'
Tolerance — 'Yeah, I go through a pod way faster now'

The withdrawal, behind a 'No' — 'Not really' to ever trying to stop — but: 'My charger broke on a camping trip — two days. I was so cranky, couldn't sleep, couldn't focus, kept eating.' Accepting 'Not really' and moving on is the trap
Dual use, checked early — 'I QUIT SMOKES WHEN I STARTED VAPING' — a few beers on weekends, NO drugs and nothing else in the liquid
Mood and motivation — Mood fine, sleep okay — and 'Ten, I'm over it'
The CAGE answers — His girlfriend hates it, and he feels a bit guilty
His hidden agenda — He is worried quitting will make him snappy at work and his boss will notice
The two questions he will ask — 'IS IT WORSE THAN SMOKING?' AND 'CAN'T I JUST USE WEAKER ONES?' — asked if you do not cover them

What the law now says — Since 1 October 2024, pharmacists can supply nicotine vapes of 20 mg/mL or less to adults without a prescription; higher strengths and anyone under 18 still need one, and no other retailer may sell any vape
Why that matters here — It changes nothing about the counselling — it only matters if he asks whether he can just buy a weaker vape

setting: A seven-minute history and a one-minute impression to the examiner — and the request is not the problem. Saying 'Your BMI is 23, you don't need it' in the first minute ends the station before it starts: explore four lanes first — the request, the eating-disorder screen, mood and risk, and the relationship. 'He just wants me to be healthy' is defended until you ask how he goes about pushing her. The pattern that emerges is coercive control — family violence without hitting — and the impression must name its domains rather than describe the partner.
stem: Version 1 — general practice. A 27-year-old woman seeks advice on using Ozempic. The practice nurse has noted that her partner is exerting pressure on her weight-loss seeking. BMI 23; BP, pulse and temperature normal.

Version 2 — a 24-year-old woman attends for a vaccination; the nurse refers her because she asked about Ozempic and thinks her partner wants her to lose weight. BMI 23 to 24. Tasks: take a relevant history — 7 minutes — then outline your findings and impression to the examiner — 1 minute. Variants: the eating-disorder screen is positive; she discloses choking; the child has seen violence; and 'Can you just give me a script?'
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient — 7 minutes
Outline your findings and impression of the patient's condition to the examiner — 1 minute
time: Four lanes, in order. Lane one, the request: tell me more about your weight and how you feel about it, what is your weight and height, any recent change, what have you tried, and whose idea was the injection · lane two, the eating-disorder screen, six questions, asked even though the BMI is normal: are you afraid of gaining weight, what do you see in the mirror, what do others say, have you cut down your eating or exercised a lot or vomited or used laxatives, any times of eating a lot and losing control, and is your self-esteem linked to your weight · lane three, mood and risk: mood, sleep, appetite, enjoyment, energy, concentration, guilt, the mania screen, and thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else · lane four, the relationship: tell me about your partner, how does he push you, does he control other things like money, friends or your phone, are you ever afraid of him, has he ever hurt or threatened you or choked you, and anything sexual you didn't want · then the child, safety and heads · then the impression in four named domains.

back.dx: A HEALTHY-WEIGHT WOMAN REQUESTING SEMAGLUTIDE UNDER PARTNER PRESSURE — with low mood and coercive control, and a negative eating-disorder screen. Semaglutide is not indicated. The impression, in four named domains and one minute: 'Lily is a 24-year-old woman of healthy weight, BMI 23, requesting Ozempic under pressure from her partner. Eating disorder: no fear of weight gain, no body-image disturbance, no binge eating or purging, though her partner restricts her diet. Mood: low mood, broken sleep, reduced enjoyment and fatigue for a month — I would count the remaining criteria for major depression; no manic episodes. Risk: no suicidal or homicidal thoughts, no psychosis; she feels safe at home and her son is safe. Relationship: restriction of food and alcohol, isolation from friends and monitoring — coercive control, a form of family violence. Semaglutide is not indicated. Plan: safety plan and domestic violence services, mood treatment, review in a week.' A long description of the partner with no named domains is the trap. And if the examiner asks what you would do about the partner: 'Nothing directly — I support her, keep her safe and document; I don't contact him.' The variants. The eating-disorder screen is positive: 'You've told me you're frightened of gaining weight, you see yourself as bigger than others do, and you've been cutting right down on food. Those are signs of an eating disorder. An injection that suppresses appetite could make that much worse. I'd like to check some bloods and a heart tracing, and get you support from a psychologist and dietitian.' She discloses choking: 'Thank you for telling me — that is serious, and it isn't your fault. Being choked is one of the strongest warning signs that someone could be badly hurt. Can we make a plan today for how you'd stay safe? I can call the DV crisis line with you now.' The child has seen violence: 'Children who see violence at home can be harmed by it, even if they aren't hit. I have a legal duty to let the child abuse report line know, and I'll tell you what I'm doing and why. The aim is support for you both.' and 'Can you just give me a script?': 'I understand you want this to work. At your weight the injection isn't safe or recommended, so I can't prescribe it. If you'd like, we can talk about eating well in a way that feels good for you — not for anyone else.'
plan: LANE ONE — THE REQUEST, EXPLORED BEFORE IT IS REFUSED: 'what we discuss is confidential unless someone's safety is at risk. HOW CAN I HELP?' → 'I want Ozempic to lose weight.' → 'TELL ME MORE ABOUT YOUR WEIGHT AND HOW YOU FEEL ABOUT IT. CAN I CHECK YOUR WEIGHT AND HEIGHT? ANY RECENT CHANGE? WHAT HAVE YOU TRIED? WHOSE IDEA WAS THE INJECTION?' (Saying 'your BMI is 23, you don't need it' in the first minute is the trap.)

Lane two — the six eating-disorder questions, asked despite a normal BMI: 'Are you afraid of gaining weight? What do you see in the mirror? What do others say? Have you cut down your eating, exercised a lot, vomited or used laxatives? Times of eating a lot and losing control? Is your self-esteem linked to your weight?' (Skipping it because the BMI is normal is the trap — it is marked.)

Lane three — mood and risk: 'How has your mood been? Sleep, appetite? Still enjoying things? Energy, concentration? Guilt? Ever felt very high? Any thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else?' → a month of low mood, broken sleep, lost enjoyment and fatigue. (Not asking about suicide or homicide is an AUTOMATIC FAIL.)

Lane four — the relationship, and the question that opens it: 'Tell me about your partner. How does he push you?' → the diet, the wine, the friends, the phone. Then: 'Does he control other things — money, friends, your phone? Are you ever afraid of him? Has he ever hurt or threatened you, or choked you? Anything sexual you didn't want?' (Accepting 'He wants me healthy' without asking how is the trap.)

The child, safety and heads: 'Do you have children? Has your son seen any arguments? Has anyone ever hurt him? Do you feel safe going home? Work, money, drugs, alcohol? Hot or cold weather? Past or family mental health?' (Forgetting the child in version 2 is the trap.)

THE IMPRESSION, IN FOUR NAMED DOMAINS AND ONE MINUTE (see dx) — eating disorder, mood, risk, relationship — THEN 'SEMAGLUTIDE IS NOT INDICATED', AND THE PLAN: SAFETY PLAN AND DV SERVICES, MOOD TREATMENT, REVIEW IN A WEEK. (A long description of the partner with no named domains is the trap.)

pefe: Role-player: Lily, 24, hairdresser, separated from her husband, with a son aged 6 who lives with her. A new partner of nine months who doesn't live with her but is there most days. He puts her on his diet: no takeaway, no wine, he checks what she eats, he doesn't like her eating out with friends, and he sometimes checks her phone. He has never hit her. 64 kg, 167 cm, no weight change.

Her answers: mood low for about a month; sleep broken; she doesn't enjoy going out any more; tired; concentration okay; no guilt; no highs; no suicidal thoughts. All eating-disorder questions negative. No drugs, and she has stopped drinking because of him. No past mental illness. Her son is safe and has never seen violence, and she feels safe going home.

How to play it: open with 'I want to try Ozempic to lose weight.' Defend him at first — 'He just wants me to be healthy' — and give examples of control only if asked how he pushes you or what else he controls. Become tearful if the doctor says 'It isn't your fault'. If the doctor tells you to leave him, become defensive and quiet. Mark them on: weight and height; change, what she tried, and whose idea; the six eating questions; mood with the criteria counted; mania; suicide and homicide, which is an AUTO-FAIL; 'How does he push you?'; control, fear, violence and choking; the child asked; safe to go home; heads and thyroid; an impression naming eating disorder, mood, risk and coercive control; and the injection not indicated.

setting: History, diagnosis and differentials in six minutes, then management in two — and this case has a high failure rate because the stem says bulimia and the findings do not. back.dx: ANOREXIA NERVOSA, BINGE-EATING AND PURGING TYPE — not bulimia, despite the vomiting the stem leads with. The diagnosis, given with its criteria in her own words: 'Tasha, I think you have a condition called anorexia nervosa. You've told me you're afraid of becoming fat, you see yourself as bigger than others do, you go without food and exercise a lot, and your periods have stopped. You also binge and then make yourself sick, which is called the binge-purge type, and it's what has damaged your teeth. I also considered bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder, depression, thyroid problems and pregnancy.' Telling her it is bulimia because she vomits is the trap — and so is delivering 'You're underweight' as a verdict. When she says 'But I'm not skinny': 'I hear that it doesn't feel that way to you — that's part of the condition. Could I explain how we can help?' The management, built round a team and a physical check: 'This is treatable, and we'll work as a team — me, a psychologist who'll help with the thoughts about weight and food, a dietitian for a regular eating plan, and a psychiatrist if needed. Today I'd like to check your weight, pulse, blood pressure and temperature, do a heart tracing and blood tests — vomiting can lower your potassium, which affects the heart — and a pregnancy test. A special eating-disorder plan gives you medicare-funded sessions. The butterfly foundation helpline is 1800 33 4673. If you ever faint, have chest pain or feel unsafe, go to the emergency department. Can I see you next week?' Leaving out the ECG and the potassium is a trap, and so is promising she will never need hospital. Her two questions: 'Do I have to tell my parents?' and 'Will I have to go to hospital?' → 'You're an adult, so it's your choice who we involve — many people find family support really helps. Most people are treated outside hospital. We only admit if your heart, blood tests or safety become a concern.' The variants. The older recall, which is true bulimia — normal weight, no fear of fatness, no distorted body image: 'You have times of eating a lot and losing control, and afterwards you make yourself sick several times a week. How you feel about your body affects how you feel about yourself. You're not underweight and you're not restricting, so this is bulimia nervosa.' She has fainted and is medically unstable: 'Your pulse is very slow and your blood pressure drops when you stand. That tells me your heart is under strain. I need to send you to hospital today so we can keep you safe while we correct your blood tests and start eating safely.' She refuses everything: 'That's ok — you don't have to agree to everything today. Could we start with just a blood test and a heart tracing, so we know your body is safe? And could we meet again next week?' and she asks you not to tell her mother: 'You're 19, so I won't share anything without your permission — unless I thought your life was in danger. back.dx: TWO LABELS, NOT ONE: TENSION-TYPE HEADACHE PLUS SOMATIC SYMPTOM DISORDER — or, in version B, irritable bowel syndrome plus somatic symptom disorder. The explanation: 'I believe your headaches are real. They're most likely tension-type headaches — headaches brought on by stress and muscle tension — and the MRI has ruled out anything serious in the brain. I also think the worry about them has become so big that it's taking over your life: you think about them all the time, it makes you anxious, and you're seeing lots of doctors. That's called somatic symptom disorder. With your divorce, the children and your job, that's very understandable. I thought about generalised anxiety, panic disorder, depression, illness anxiety and painkiller-related headache, but these fit less well. It is treatable, and I'd like us to work on it together.' Giving only one label, or saying 'There's nothing wrong with you', is the trap. And when she asks whether you think she is making it up: 'Not at all. The pain is real. Stress and worry turn up the volume on pain — that's how the nervous system works — so treating the stress and the worry is part of treating the headaches.' The plan that follows: regular scheduled reviews with one GP rather than visits only when it is bad, a psychologist for the stress and the worry, painkillers kept to a few days a week, and no repeat testing unless something new appears. The variants. Version B, where she is angry that 'They all say it's in my head': 'I'm sorry you've been made to feel that way. Your pain is real. Can I ask a few questions to understand it — and what's been happening around it?' and the version B explanation: 'I agree it's irritable bowel syndrome: the pain eases after opening your bowels, you get bloating and changes in your stools, and the tests have ruled out coeliac disease, liver problems and cancer. Stress affects the bowel. The pain has also taken over your thoughts — that's somatic symptom disorder. We can treat both.' Her stressors in version B are hating her job, suspecting her boyfriend is cheating, money problems, few friends, trouble falling asleep, and drinking and smoking. 'I want another mri': 'I understand wanting certainty. Another scan wouldn't tell us anything new, and each normal result only settles the worry for a little while. If anything changes — new symptoms or new findings — I'll arrange tests straight away.' and illness anxiety, where there are no symptoms at all: 'You don't have symptoms of bowel cancer and your tests are normal, but the fear of having it is taking over your life. That's called illness anxiety disorder, and a psychologist can really help.'

The diagnosis, with a reason attached to every differential: 'Gina, I thought about a condition called body dysmorphic disorder, but you don't have repeated thoughts you can't control, you don't check or compare, and your breasts are genuinely large. What I think is happening is an adjustment disorder — your mood has been low and your sleep broken since your relationship ended three months ago. I also considered depression, but you're still enjoying things and your energy and concentration are fine; obsessive-compulsive disorder — no other unwanted thoughts; an eating disorder — no weight worries; generalised anxiety and panic — you're not a worrier and have no attacks; and thyroid problems or substances — nothing to suggest them.' Listing differentials without a reason for each is the trap, and so is saying 'Mdd' or 'Ocd' as abbreviations to the patient. The referral, which is the point of the station: 'Yes, I can. You're entitled to discuss it with a surgeon. I'll be honest: surgery may not change how you're feeling right now, and big decisions are easier when your mood has settled. Alongside the letter, I'd like us to support you — a psychologist, and a check-in with me in a couple of weeks.' Refusing is not patient-centred; promising surgery will fix things is the opposite error. The variants. Version A, classic body dysmorphic disorder: 'I appreciate your concern about your breasts, but I'm more concerned about the thoughts and feelings you have about them. You think about them most of the day, check the mirror and compare yourself, and it's affecting your work and relationship. That fits body dysmorphic disorder. It's treatable — with a psychologist, sometimes a medicine, and a psychiatrist's input.' and if she asks whether the surgeon will operate: 'I'll refer you for a second opinion. Surgeons now check for body dysmorphic disorder before operating, and I think they'll agree surgery isn't the answer — many people who have it still feel the same afterwards.' Symptomatic macromastia: 'The back and neck pain, the grooves and the rash are caused by the weight of your breasts. A breast reduction is a recognised treatment for that, so I'll refer you to a plastic surgeon and meanwhile suggest a professionally fitted bra, physiotherapy and treatment for the rash.' and a passive death wish in version A: 'Thank you for telling me. Have you thought about how? Have you ever acted on it? What stops you? I'd like to make a safety plan with you today, and if things get worse the mental health line is 13 14 65, day or night.'

back.dx: SEVERE SELF-NEGLECT IN A HOMELESS MAN WITH AN ULCER HE CANNOT SEE — and the answer is that he does not go back out today. The plan, said to him: 'Gary, I'm worried about you. You have a serious wound on your leg that you weren't aware of, you've stopped your blood pressure tablets, and you don't have a safe place to live. I don't think it's safe for you to go back out today. I'd like you to stay in hospital so we can clean and dress the wound every day, do blood tests — including for infection and diabetes — a test of the circulation in your legs, and an x-ray if it's deep, and restart your blood pressure treatment. I'd also like a mental health doctor to see you, and a social worker to help with housing, money and food.' and the sentence that makes the psychiatric referral land without offending him: 'Not noticing a wound like this can be a sign your mind or memory needs some help.' when he says he wants to leave, the honest version rather than a threat: 'I hear you, and I don't want to keep you here against your will. But I'm really worried this wound could become badly infected. Could you stay tonight so we can make a start? If you tried to leave, I'd need to talk with the team about how to keep you safe — sometimes that means using the mental health act for a short time, and a psychiatrist would review that quickly.' Threats — 'We'll lock you up' — and giving in and discharging are the two ways to fail the second task. The ulcer work-up to name: full blood count, CRP, electrolytes, HbA1c and lipids; an ankle-brachial index; a swab if infected; an x-ray if deep; tetanus; and daily dressings. The variants. He hears voices: 'Thank you for telling me. I think the voices may be part of an illness that is making it hard to look after yourself and your leg. I'd like a psychiatrist to see you today. Because I'm worried about your safety, if you tried to leave we may need to keep you under the mental health act for a short time while we start treatment.' He gets up to leave: 'Gary, please wait — I'm not trying to trap you. I'm worried the leg could get infected and make you very sick. Can we sit for five minutes and I'll get the mental health team to talk with you now?' Diabetes found, with a neuropathic ulcer: 'Your sugar is very high, which means you have diabetes. It has damaged the nerves in your feet, which is why the ulcer doesn't hurt and you didn't notice it. We'll take pressure off the foot, treat the diabetes, and get a foot specialist involved.' and if he has capacity and declines: 'You understand the risks and you've made your choice, and I respect that. Can I at least dress the wound now, give you antibiotics, and arrange a nurse to see you tomorrow? You can come back any time.'

Since then he hasn't been able to work, which takes away routine and confidence, and he's been drinking heavily every day, which makes all of it worse. Does that fit with what you've seen?' No jargon — not 'Frontal disinhibition', not 'Organic', not 'Cognitive deficits'. The trigger, which is the precipitating group: 'The other thing is what happened last night. At the moment he's also having some beliefs that make him feel people are against him, or talking about him. Someone called him a name — psycho — and to him that wasn't just an insult, it felt like a threat. That, with the alcohol, was the spark.' The strengths, which are the protective group and the part most often omitted: 'It's just as important to say what he has going for him. He has you — family who care and who came straight in. He worked hard in rehabilitation before, so we know he can engage with help. And he has no other serious illness.' and when he asks for the diagnosis — neither invent nor stonewall: 'That's exactly the right question, and the psychiatry team will answer it properly once they've assessed him. What I can tell you today is what seems to have contributed — the head injury, the alcohol, losing his work, and the beliefs he's having at the moment. They will talk with you about what it is and what treatment can help. Can I check — does what I've explained make sense? What else would you like to ask?' and on prognosis: 'I can't promise, and it wouldn't be fair of me to guess before he's been properly assessed. What I can say is that people do improve with the right support, and cutting back the drinking makes a real difference to memory and temper.' The five Ps, for when the formulation goes to an examiner instead: presenting is the complaint; predisposing is the past; precipitating is the trigger; perpetuating is what keeps it going; protective is what is on his side — and the grid check is four Ps across against biological, psychological and social down. The online version, spoken to the examiner after a history: 'My formulation is: predisposing — severe traumatic brain injury with coma, resulting cognitive impairment, chronic heavy alcohol use and loss of his work role; precipitating — the verbal provocation, alcohol on the night and his current persecutory and grandiose beliefs; perpetuating — continued daily drinking, untreated symptoms, absent insight and no daily structure; protective — an involved father, previous engagement with rehabilitation and no other major illness.' The variants. The angry father: 'I can hear how angry you are, and I'd be worried too if it were my son. Can I tell you what we think has led to this? And then I want to hear what you've noticed, because you know him far better than we do.' The guilty father: 'I want to be clear about one thing: this isn't your fault. A head injury like his changes the way the brain works, and that isn't something a parent causes or could have prevented.' and 'Is he going to be charged?': 'I don't know what the police will decide — that isn't something I can influence. What I can do is make sure his health is assessed properly, and the team can provide information about his condition if it's needed.'

pefe: Role-player: Peter, the father. His son is 30. Five years ago he had a motor vehicle accident and was in a coma for two weeks, then spent a long time in rehabilitation. Since then he has not worked or studied. He drinks heavily — 'A carton lasts him two days'. He has changed: short-tempered, forgetful with names and conversations, says people watch him and talk about him, and is convinced his girlfriend is cheating — she is not. The police rang tonight about a fight at the pub, and he has never been violent before.

How to play it: open worried, not hostile — 'The police rang me. What's going on?' Offer the details about the beliefs, the drinking and the forgetfulness only when asked. Halfway through, ask 'So it's the accident that did all this?' Near the end, press once: 'So what is it? Is he mentally ill?' and then 'Will he get better?' You are worried and a little guilty, supportive, and will do anything to help.

If the doctor names a diagnosis or starts describing treatment, accept it — and mark it as a fail. Mark them on: confirmed relationship; permission to share; 'What have you been told?'; your main worry; collateral — onset, good days, alcohol, past violence; signposted three parts; predisposing — head injury, cognition, alcohol, lost role; precipitating — the insult, the beliefs, alcohol; protective — the father named; plain English with no jargon; no blame; no diagnosis; no management; checked understanding; and invited questions.

stem: General practice. A community disability worker attends to discuss his client and to collect a repeat prescription. The client, Travis, has epileptic seizures and takes carbamazepine and sodium valproate. He had a motor vehicle accident at age 12 resulting in an acquired brain injury. The worker reports a recent change in behaviour.

Tasks: take a history from the disability worker — the bulk of the station — then explain the possible causes of the change in behaviour, and explain your supportive management. Variants: the carer discloses a concern about another staff member; a toxicity picture; and the friend who moved out.

time: Confirm the legal carer and consent before any detail · then describe the change: what do you mean by a change in his behaviour, when did it start, is it constant or intermittent, is it getting worse, were there any events or changes before it started, how is it affecting his usual level of function, and what makes it better or worse · then the epilepsy and the medication: is he taking his tablets regularly and since when, when was his last seizure, any long vacant or confused episodes, any dose changes or new medicines, any drowsiness or unsteadiness or shaking, and any recent weight gain · then the seven-area systemic screen: pain in the teeth, ears or tummy; weight loss, lumps or low energy; fever, chills or rash; urinary symptoms or smell; constipation; thirst and polyuria; weather preference; and falls or injuries · and then the abuse question, asked plainly · then the psychiatric screen and risk · then family, friends, carers and substances · then the causes as a list, and a management plan that tests and sees the patient.

back.dx: A NEW BEHAVIOUR IN A MAN WHO CANNOT TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG — and the task asks for causes, not a diagnosis. The causes, given as a list and in plain words: 'There can be a number of reasons. Travis can't easily tell us what's wrong, so it shows up in his behaviour. It could be physical — pain such as a tooth, an infection like a urine or dental infection, constipation, his thyroid, or diabetes, which can go with his medicines. It could be his tablets — he's stopped them, and that can bring on seizures and affect his mood and thinking. It could be something that has upset or frightened him, including being hurt or treated badly. And it could be a mental health problem such as depression or anxiety, which often shows as mood and behaviour rather than words — particularly when family can't visit and a close friend has moved out.' Giving one cause is a trap, and so is naming the brain injury as the cause. And when he asks which one it is: 'I can't say yet, and I don't want to guess. The way we find out is to test and to see him.' The supportive management, in four parts. The tests: 'Blood count and inflammatory markers, kidneys and sodium, liver, thyroid, blood sugar, and the levels of his epilepsy medicines, plus a urine test.' Seeing the patient: 'I'd like to see Travis and examine him — teeth, ears, chest, tummy and skin.' The treatment: 'Get him back on his medication with whatever support helps, and involve neurology about the seizure. If it's his mood, a psychologist can help, and I'd get psychiatry advice before any medicine. I'd also like a meeting with his mum and sister, by video if needed.' and the safeguarding: 'Because of the new night staff, I need to make sure he's safe.' Ending with advice and no investigations, or managing him without ever seeing him, are the two management traps. On the scripts: 'Yes — I'll do the repeats today. But I don't want the tablets to be the only thing that happens, because he isn't taking them and something has changed. Let's book him in this week.' The variants. The carer discloses a concern about another staff member: 'Thank you for telling me — that took courage, and you've done the right thing. My first job is to make sure Travis is safe, which means he shouldn't be alone with that person while this is looked into. I'll examine him carefully and document everything, and I'll help you contact the adult safeguarding unit and your provider's safeguarding process. If anything happened recently, we may need the police involved so evidence isn't lost.' A toxicity picture: 'The drowsiness and unsteadiness make me think the medicine levels may be too high — valproate can push up the active part of carbamazepine, and carbamazepine can drop the sodium in the blood. I'll check both today before we change anything.' and the friend who moved out: 'Losing someone he lived with for years is a real bereavement, even if it doesn't look like grief from the outside. That, with his family not visiting, is enough to explain low mood and a change in behaviour — but I still want to rule out the physical causes first.'
plan: Consent before content: 'Can I confirm your name? How can I help today?' → the scripts and the worry. → 'Before we go further — can I confirm that you are Travis's legal carer and have consent to discuss his health with me?' (Discussing the client first is an AUTOMATIC FAIL.)

Describe the change: 'What do you mean by a change in his behaviour? When did it start? Is it there all the time or does it come and go? Is it getting worse? Were there any events or changes before it started? How is it affecting his usual level of function?' (Accepting 'He's just difficult' and moving on is the trap.)

Epilepsy and medication: 'Is he taking his tablets regularly? Since when? When was his last seizure? Any long vacant or confused episodes? Any dose changes or new medicines? Any drowsiness, unsteadiness or shaking? Any recent weight gain?' → refusing for weeks, and a fit a fortnight ago.

The systemic screen, seven areas: pain — teeth, ears, tummy; weight loss, lumps, low energy; fever, chills, rash; urinary pain or smell; constipation; thirst and polyuria; weather preference; and falls or injuries. → the jaw, the straining, and the water.

The abuse question, asked plainly and without accusing: 'I ask this of everyone — is there any chance he could have been physically or sexually harmed, by anyone at the house, another resident or a visitor?' → the new night casual. (Skipping it because it feels rude is an AUTOMATIC FAIL.)

The psychiatric screen and risk: 'How would you describe his mood? Sleep — trouble falling asleep or waking early? Appetite or weight change? Is he still enjoying what he used to? Has he ever harmed himself, or anyone else? Does he ever seem to see or hear things that aren't there?'

Home, friends, carers and substances: 'Tell me about his family — do they visit? How is he with his friends at the house — has anyone moved out? How does he get on with his carers? Does he do any work or programs? Any chance of alcohol, drugs or smoking?' → Joe, and the family who don't visit.
The causes as a list — physical, medication, distress or harm, and psychiatric (see dx) → 'So which one is it?' → 'I can't say yet. The way we find out is to test and to see him.'

Supportive management (see dx): the bloods and urine, seeing and examining Travis this week, getting him back on his medication with neurology input, a psychologist with psychiatry advice before any medicine, a video meeting with his mum and sister, and the safeguarding. → 'Can I still get his scripts?' → yes, today — but not as the only thing that happens.

stem: The four history steps: introduction under 45 seconds — explore the pain with CICORA, finished — the differential sweep, one specific question each — then a good closure. Step 3 is the only thing that separates you: everyone does an open question, CICORA and a closure.

The order within step 3: your provisional diagnosis first, with every key point — five or six questions over two minutes, no apology — then the space-occupying lesion red flags in full — then the rest of the list, one question each. Do not run a head-to-toe list of associated symptoms: an examiner marking forty candidates a day recognises it instantly, and a medical student can do it.

dx: **One headache structure for every headache station** — acute or chronic, adult or adolescent. The context of the case makes minor changes; it does not make a second structure.

**Three things pass this station: differentials, structure, key points.** ‘Infections’ earns nothing — **meningitis, sinusitis, dental abscess** earns three ticks. As many as you can, as specific as you can, and all of them good.
**Step 1 — intro, under 45 seconds.** Vitals at the door (**blood pressure, pulse, temperature, respiratory rate**), open question then **stop talking**, acknowledge the concern once, promise a plan.

**Step 2 — CICORA, finished**: **site · intensity out of ten · character · onset, pattern and progression · radiation · aggravating and relieving · affect on life.** In **nine out of ten** headache stations the provisional diagnosis falls out here. The exception is **giant cell arteritis**, where CICORA gives you nothing.

**Step 3 is the only thing that separates you** — everyone does an open question, CICORA and a closure. Order within it: **provisional diagnosis key points first** (five or six questions, **two minutes, no apology**) → **space-occupying lesion red flags in full** → the rest of the list, **one specific question each**.

**Step 4 — closure**: past medical history then family history; **SADMA last and least.** If you run out of time before SADMA you have lost nothing — anything in it that mattered was already asked as a key point.

**The thirteen, in memorised order**: **space-occupying lesion · migraine · tension-type · cluster · trigeminal neuralgia · subarachnoid haemorrhage · other intracranial haemorrhage · benign intracranial hypertension · meningitis, encephalitis, abscess · sinusitis · dental · cervicogenic · glaucoma.** Plus **TMJ dysfunction, medication-overuse headache**, and **giant cell arteritis only if over 50**.

**Glaucoma, not refractive error.** By the time you reach the eye you have asked about vision four times — for tumour, aura, arteritis and deficit. **‘Have you had a red eye?’** is a question you have not asked, and it is specific.

**Diagnosis in 90 seconds, three moves**: name it, explain it in five seconds, **reason it from your key points** → **answer the stated concern by name, with the negatives** → reason three or four differentials, then **list the rest until the bell.** Every named condition is a tick; an eloquent explanation of differential two is two ticks you did not collect.

**Context switches**: over 50 → add giant cell arteritis · sudden and severe → subarachnoid to the top · fever → meningitis and encephalitis · young woman, raised BMI, acne treatment → benign intracranial hypertension · any fall at any age → intracranial haemorrhage, chronic subdural in the elderly · under 25 → drop arteritis.
plan: Door
**‘Examiner, before I start — can you tell me the blood pressure, pulse rate, temperature and respiratory rate?’** One sentence, before you sit down.
**‘Hello, I’m one of the doctors here. How can I help you today?’** Then **stop talking** and let the opening statement land.

Address the concern — this is where approach-to-patient is scored: **‘I understand why that is worrying you. Let me ask you some questions, examine you, and we’ll work out the cause together and make a plan. Does that sound alright?’** Then **‘are you in any pain now?’** — almost always no.

**CICORA, finished.** **‘Show me where it is — one side or both?’ · ‘Out of ten, ten being the worst pain of your life?’ · ‘Throbbing or pulsating, or dull, or sharp?’ · ‘How long? On and off or constant? Getting worse?’ · ‘Does it travel anywhere?’ · ‘Anything make it better or worse?’ · ‘How is it affecting your life?’** The **progression** question is the one that gets skipped.
**Key points of the provisional diagnosis** — five or six questions, two minutes, **no apology for the depth**. Knowing the recall is not the same as asking the key points.

**Space-occupying lesion red flags, probing depth, every one**: **‘Any weight loss? Loss of appetite? Lumps or bumps? Feeling tired?’ · ‘Does the pain wake you at night?’ · ‘Any early-morning headache with vomiting?’ · ‘Any blurring of vision? Weakness? Numbness or pins and needles? Trouble walking?’ · ‘Is it worse when you cough, sneeze or bend forward?’**

**The sweep — one specific question each.** Tension: **home and work separately**. Meningitis: **fever, sore neck, rash**. Subarachnoid: **sudden onset, worst ever**. Cluster: **watery eye or runny nose on that side**. Trigeminal: **set off by talking, smiling, shaving, touching the cheek**. Sinusitis: **secretions down the back of the throat**. Dental: **toothache, last dentist**. BIH and overuse: **medications, painkiller days a month**. Haemorrhage: **injury, trauma or fall**. Glaucoma: **red eye**. Cervicogenic: **neck pain**.
Closure
PMHx, then FHx, **SADMA last**. Never ask SADMA twice — under stress it becomes a comfort ritual, and those are the seconds that were meant for the aura question.
Bell → +2:00

**PEFE, hard stop at 2:00.** General appearance → **all four vitals** → cranial nerves → **fundoscopy asked separately** → limbs → neck → **ENT and dental** → chest and heart in ten seconds. A thin examination does not fail; running past the bell does.
Last 90s

**Name it and reason it → answer the stated concern with its negatives → three reasoned differentials, then list the rest.** Never two diagnoses, never a scan to reassure, never ‘infections’ as a differential.
pefe: **The five-step spine, every PEFE, every cluster**: general appearance (three or four relevant items, **not the PRICCLED ritual**) → **all four vital signs, every time** → the core system in depth → the other systems fast, **two questions each** → office tests **only if genuinely relevant**.
**Headache core = neurological examination + ENT + neck.** Most candidates forget the ENT.
General appearance in a headache case: **alert or drowsy · any rash · any ptosis · if over 50, a visible or thickened temporal artery.**

Cranial nerves, in these words: **‘are the pupils symmetrical and the light reflexes normal? Are the eye movements full? Is sensation over the three divisions of the face normal? Are the facial movements symmetrical?’** — pupils, III/IV/VI together, trigeminal, facial. Skip the rest.

**Fundoscopy, always, and asked separately: ‘do I see any papilloedema?’** The single highest-yield request in the cluster. Asked inside ‘cranial nerves’ you will simply be told ‘normal’ and lose the finding.
Limbs: **power in the myotomes, sensation, and the reflexes.** Reflexes and coordination if time; **skip tone and inspection**.
Neck: **tenderness over the spinous processes or paraspinal muscles · painful movements · neck stiffness** — cervicogenic, spondylosis, metastasis, and meningism.

**ENT and dental — the part almost everyone drops**: **‘any dental caries, or redness and swelling of the gums? Any post-nasal drip? Is there sinus tenderness?’** Three questions, fifteen seconds, three differentials closed.
Office tests: **blood glucose and dipstick are not relevant and earn ‘unavailable’ and no marks.** A **urine pregnancy test** is defensible in a woman of reproductive age.

**Conditional add-ons only on a positive finding** — meningism → **Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s**; over 50 → **temporal tenderness, thickened or pulseless artery, girdle tenderness**; raised pressure → fundoscopy, then **blood pressure and pulse again for a Cushing response**. Asking them unprompted tells the examiner you are reciting.

CORRECTION — polymyalgia rheumatica is often taught as ‘proximal myopathy’. It causes **pain-limited movement with preserved power**, not true weakness. If pressed: **‘I would expect tenderness and restriction from pain, with power preserved — true weakness would make me think of an inflammatory myopathy instead.’**
ddx: **Space-occupying lesion — always first, all ages**
Progressive headache, night waking, early-morning headache with vomiting, focal deficit, known primary cancer

**Probing, not screening — ask all of them**: weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness · wakes at night · morning vomiting · vision, weakness, numbness, gait · **worse on cough, sneeze or bending** (raised intracranial pressure)
**AUTO-FAIL if never named.** Normal neurology and fundoscopy; **CT or MRI if any flag is positive**
Migraine
Unilateral, throbbing, worse on routine activity, nausea, photophobia

**‘Any nausea or vomiting with it?’ · ‘Sensitive to light and noise?’ · ‘Flashing or sparkling lights before it?’ · ‘Does alcohol set it off? Any food — cheese, bananas?’ · ‘Are you on the contraceptive pill?’ · ‘Anyone in the family?’**
Five key points. **The pill question is why this recall is almost always a woman** — ‘changes in the blood vessels and nerves of the brain’
Tension-type headache
Bilateral, pressing or tightening, mild to moderate, not worse on activity
**‘Tell me about home — any stress there? And what do you do for work, any stress there?’** — asked separately
One AMC version hid **bullying at work** behind an initial ‘stress is fine’. ‘A stress headache — the scalp and neck muscles tighten’

Strictly unilateral periorbital, excruciating, in bouts, patient restless
**‘Do you get a watery eye or a runny nose on that side when the pain comes?’**
**Autonomic features are the discriminator, not severity**
Trigeminal neuralgia
Brief electric-shock facial pain
**‘Is the pain set off by sudden movements of your face — talking, smiling, shaving, or just touching your cheek?’**
Coughing, sneezing and chewing trigger it too, but you have asked those already

Thunderclap, peaks in seconds, neck stiffness, vomiting
**‘Did the pain start suddenly?’ · ‘Is this the worst headache of your life?’**
**The only place the ‘sudden’ question belongs.** Thunderclap = sudden **and** worst ever. Emergency
Other intracranial haemorrhage — subdural, extradural
Older patient, fall, anticoagulant, fluctuating symptoms
**‘Any recent injury, trauma or fall?’** — in an older patient say **falls** specifically, and over months
Urgent imaging
Benign intracranial hypertension · medication-overuse headache
Young woman, raised BMI, visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus; or headache on most days with frequent analgesia
**‘Are you on any medication?’ · ‘Any painkillers — and how many days a month?’**
Trigger set is the **acne treatments: isotretinoin, doxycycline, minocycline, the pill, vitamin A**. Overuse ≈ **15+ days a month** VERIFY

**‘Any fever or chills?’ · ‘Any soreness in your neck?’ · ‘Any rash?’**
**‘Sore neck’ beats ‘neck stiffness’** — patients understand it. The rash question also screens shingles. Emergency
Sinusitis
Facial pressure, blocked nose, worse bending forward
**‘Any secretions running down the back of your throat?’**
Better than ‘facial pain’ — you already asked site. ‘An infection in the air cavities inside your skull’
Dental infection · TMJ dysfunction
Pain on chewing, toothache, joint clicking
**‘Any toothache? When did you last see a dentist?’**
**‘Worse on chewing’ was already asked under arteritis** and covers this and TMJ

Neck pain precedes the headache, provoked by posture, side-locked
**‘Any neck pain?’**
Already half-covered by ‘sore neck’ and by radiation
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Severe unilateral headache with a red painful eye, haloes, vomiting
**‘Have you had a red eye?’**
**Vision has been asked four times already; redness has not.** Emergency
Giant cell arteritis — **only if over 50**
New headache over 50; scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, girdle stiffness
**‘A painful cord on the side of your head?’ · ‘Any blurring of vision?’ · ‘Worse on chewing, or combing your hair?’ · ‘Any shoulder or hip pain or stiffness?’**
In the AMC recall **the first three are negative and the last is positive — do not stop at three.** Under 25, drop it entirely

dx: **Migraine with aura in a 30-year-old woman** — recurrent unilateral throbbing headache, **4–72 hours** untreated, worse on routine activity, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, relieved by sleep in a dark quiet room, triggers and a family history. VERIFY

**The stem is deliberately bare** — no timeline, no severity, nothing acute or chronic — precisely so the whole diagnosis has to come out of your history. **Build the history, do not chase the recall.**

**Aura is present in around one third** of migraine sufferers; typically **5–60 minutes**, resolving as the headache begins. VERIFY Do not let the aura answer contaminate the red-flag vision answer — **clarify which one she means.**

The reasoning sentence: **‘Most likely you have migraine, and specifically migraine with aura. It happens because of changes in the blood vessels and nerves of the brain. I’m saying that because your headache is one-sided and throbbing, you get flashing lights before it starts, you’re sensitive to light and noise, you feel sick with it, wine sets it off, and your mother had the same thing.’**

**Aura plus the combined oral contraceptive pill is the management point of the whole station** — migraine with aura raises ischaemic stroke risk and the combined pill compounds it. **Stop the pill today** and replace the method. VERIFY

Acute attack: **aspirin or ibuprofen or paracetamol, taken early and at an adequate dose**, plus an **antiemetic — metoclopramide or an ondansetron wafer**, which also improves absorption of the analgesic. If that fails, a **triptan (sumatriptan, rizatriptan)** as tablet, wafer or nasal spray. VERIFY

**Avoid opioids and codeine-containing compounds** — they worsen nausea and drive overuse. **Cap acute analgesia below roughly 15 days a month** (10 for triptans or combination analgesics) to prevent medication-overuse headache. VERIFY

**No imaging, and say why**: **‘a scan wouldn’t tell us anything your story and examination haven’t already told us. If any of those warning signs appear, we scan the same day.’** Ordering an MRI to reassure teaches her the scan, not your assessment, is the answer.

Non-drug and prevention: **headache diary — date, duration, what she ate, what she was doing, medication taken**; identify and avoid the triggers it actually shows; dark quiet room, ice pack, gentle neck stretches; **sleep regularity, meals, hydration, graded aerobic exercise**. Prevention at roughly **4 or more disabling attacks a month**: **propranolol, amitriptyline, candesartan or topiramate**. VERIFY

SA — **SHINE SA** or the practice for progesterone-only or non-hormonal contraception; neurology via **Country Health Connect** telehealth with **PATS** travel support, no transfer needed for routine migraine; **healthdirect 1800 022 222** after hours; **TIS National 131 450**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap** PBS co-payment; sudden severe headache at home → **000**, remote → **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**.
plan: Door: **‘Examiner, before I begin — blood pressure, pulse rate, temperature and respiratory rate?’** Then **‘Hello, I’m one of the doctors here. How can I help you today?’** and stop talking. **A second open question buys you ‘no, nothing else’ and costs ten seconds.**

Acknowledge once: **‘I can see this has been getting to you. Let me ask you some questions, and by the end I’ll tell you what I think is going on and what we do about it.’** Then **‘are you in any pain right now?’**

**CICORA, finished** — **‘one side or both?’ · ‘out of ten?’ · ‘throbbing or pulsating, or dull or sharp?’ · ‘how long — on and off or constant — and are they getting worse?’ · ‘does it travel?’ · ‘better or worse with anything?’ · ‘how is it affecting your life?’** Ninety seconds and the provisional diagnosis is made. **Do not stop once you ‘have it’ — the progression question is the one that separates migraine from a tumour.**

**The five key points, immediately, no exceptions**: **‘Do you get nausea or vomiting with it?’ · ‘Are you sensitive to light and to noise?’ · ‘Do you see flashing or sparkling lights before it starts?’ · ‘Does alcohol set it off? Any food — cheese, chocolate, bananas?’ · ‘Are you on the contraceptive pill?’ — here, not in SADMA · ‘Does anyone in your family get migraines?’**

**Every tumour red flag, probing depth**: **‘Any weight loss? Loss of appetite? Lumps or bumps? Unusual tiredness?’ · ‘Does the headache wake you at night?’ · ‘Any early-morning headache with vomiting?’ · ‘Any blurring of vision, weakness, numbness, pins and needles, trouble walking?’ · ‘Is it worse when you cough, sneeze or bend forward?’**

**The sweep, one specific question each** — tension (**home and work separately**) · meningitis (**fever, sore neck, rash**) · subarachnoid (**sudden, worst ever**) · cluster (**watery eye or runny nose**) · trigeminal (**talking, smiling, touching the face**) · sinusitis (**post-nasal secretions**) · dental (**toothache, last dentist**) · BIH and overuse (**medications, painkiller days a month**) · haemorrhage (**injury or fall**) · glaucoma (**red eye**) · cervicogenic (**neck pain**). **Not giant cell arteritis — she is 30, and naming it costs credibility.**
Closure if the clock allows: **PMHx, then FHx, SADMA last** — the two items that mattered, the pill and analgesic use, are already asked.
Bell

**Diagnosis with reasons**, then **answer the tumour concern by name before she raises it**: **‘I don’t think this is a brain tumour: it doesn’t wake you at night, there’s no morning vomiting, no weight loss, no weakness or numbness, no change in vision, and it doesn’t get worse when you cough or strain.’**

**Differentials — reason three, then list the rest until the bell.** Tension (one-sided, throbbing, vomiting — not tension) · cluster (no watery eye or blocked nose) · subarachnoid (not sudden, not worst ever) · then **meningitis, raised brain pressure, medication-overuse, sinusitis, dental, TMJ, cervicogenic, glaucoma, trigeminal neuralgia.** Every named condition is a tick.

**The pill, before she leaves**: **‘because you get aura and you’re on the combined pill, I’d like to stop that pill today and talk about a different method — the combination slightly raises the risk of stroke.’** Then the safety-net: **sudden worst-ever headache, weakness or trouble speaking → 000.**
pefe: **Version A has no examination task.** The only examiner interaction is the **haemodynamic check at the door — blood pressure, pulse, temperature, respiratory rate** — asked as one sentence before you sit down.
**No imaging.** Migraine with a normal examination and no red flags does not need a scan, and the station scores you for saying so **and giving the reason**.
The diagnosis is **clinical, on criteria**, with a **normal examination between attacks**.

If she asks for a scan: **‘a scan wouldn’t tell us anything your story and examination haven’t already told us. If any of those warning signs appear, we scan the same day.’** Agreeing to imaging to make the conversation easier is scored against you — **the role-player accepts it happily and marks you down.**
What would change that: **a new headache, a changed headache, or any neurological deficit — that is imaging, not reassurance.**
In Version B the **MRI has already been done and is normal** — that is AMC telling you the red flags are excluded for you. **Ask the key points only.**

dx: **Tension-type headache in a 45-year-old man whose brother has just been diagnosed with a brain tumour** — bilateral, pressing or tightening, **4–5/10**, not aggravated by routine activity, radiating into the neck, relieved by simple analgesia, with **work stress as the key point**.

**The commonest headache in the population, and the commonest headache the AMC dresses up as something frightening.** At most **one** of photophobia or phonophobia, and **no vomiting** — or it is not tension-type. VERIFY
**The discriminating issue is answering the brother out loud, with reasons, before he asks.** Reassurance without reasons is not reassurance; it is a guess the patient is asked to trust.

The sentence that wins it: **‘Jacob, you came in worried about a brain tumour, so let me answer that directly. I do not think you have one, and these are my reasons: the headache doesn’t wake you at night, you have no early-morning headache or vomiting, no weight loss or appetite change, no weakness, numbness or change in vision, and it doesn’t get worse when you cough or bend. Your neurological examination is completely normal, and I looked into the back of your eyes — the pressure signs we’d expect with a tumour are not there.’**

Then commit: **‘What I think you do have is a tension-type headache — a stress-related headache, where the muscles of the scalp and neck tighten up. I’m saying that because it’s on both sides, it’s a dull tightening ache rather than a throbbing one, it’s four or five out of ten, it runs down into your neck, paracetamol helps, and it started when work got very stressful.’**

**Name the trigger as the treatment target — the work stress, not the headache.** Address the stressor: workload, hours, and **the bullying if it is disclosed**. Screening for it and then not acting on it is worse than never asking.

Management: **simple analgesia used sparingly** VERIFY · sleep, regular meals, hydration, aerobic exercise, **screen and posture breaks** · **physiotherapy or neck and shoulder stretching** if there is a postural component · **psychological therapy and a mental health treatment plan** if indicated VERIFY · **cap analgesia below roughly 15 days a month** VERIFY · **review in 4–6 weeks with a headache diary**.

**No imaging, and justify it**: a normal neurological examination, no red flags and no papilloedema. **‘A scan wouldn’t tell us anything your story and examination haven’t already told us, and a normal scan wouldn’t stop the headaches.’**
**Never the word ‘just’.** ‘It’s just tension’ dismisses six months of real pain, and reads as dismissal to both the patient and the examiner.

SA — **SafeWork SA** and **ReturnToWorkSA** for workplace stress or bullying; psychology via a **GP mental health treatment plan** with telehealth through **Country Health Connect**; **Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636**, **Lifeline 13 11 14**; **TIS National 131 450**; ACCHS with **Closing the Gap** PBS co-payment; urgent imaging through the regional hospital in Yorke and Northern LHN, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for retrieval if a red flag emerges.
plan: Door: **‘Examiner, before I start — blood pressure, pulse rate, temperature and respiratory rate, please?’** Then **‘Hello Jacob, I’m one of the doctors here. How can I help you today?’**

The concern, **once**: **‘I’m very sorry to hear about your brother. How is he doing? … I understand why this is worrying you. Let me ask you some questions, examine you, and we’ll find the cause and make a plan together.’** **Do not follow the brother down the rabbit hole** — his staging and treatment earn nothing and cost you the sweep.

**CICORA** — **‘one side or both?’ · ‘out of ten?’ · ‘throbbing or pulsating, or dull or sharp?’ · ‘how long, on and off or constant, getting worse?’ · ‘does it travel anywhere?’ · ‘better or worse with anything?’ · ‘how many days a month are you taking painkillers?’ · ‘how is it affecting your life?’** Ninety seconds and the provisional diagnosis is made.

**Go deeper on stress than you would elsewhere — it is the key point.** **‘Who do you live with at home, and how are things going there? Any stress at home?’** then separately **‘What do you do for work — and is there any stress there?’** If the first answer is a flat no: **‘Any problems at work — with colleagues, or with your manager?’** Then **‘and how has your mood been?’** — one question, no more.

**Every tumour red flag, out loud, prefaced**: **‘You’re worried about a brain tumour, so I’m going to ask you every question I’d ask to look for one.’** Weight loss · appetite · lumps and bumps · tiredness · **wakes at night** · **early-morning headache with vomiting** · vision · weakness · numbness · gait · **worse on coughing, sneezing or bending forward**.

**Screening until the bell — you will not finish the list, and that is expected.** Migraine (**nausea, light and noise, flashing lights**) · infection (**fever, sore neck, rash**) · sinusitis (**post-nasal secretions**) · dental (**toothache, chewing, last dentist**) · cluster (**watery eye or runny nose**) · then if time TMJ, painkiller days, head injury or fall, red eye. **Not giant cell arteritis — he is 45.**

**Four tasks in eight minutes: roughly 4:00 history · 1:30 examination · 1:15 diagnosis and differentials · 1:15 management.** The station is failed by the clock, not by the medicine — **if you never say the word ‘hospital’, the first three tasks do not matter.**
**AMC role-players rarely say ‘I have a fever’. They say ‘I’ve been feeling hot’.** The moment you hear it, move straight into the meningitis block.
**Exclude the bleed first — two questions and ten seconds**: not sudden in onset, not the worst headache of her life. **Saying that out loud is a mark.**

Management, **starting with the disposition**: **‘Amanda, I’m not able to let you go home. I’m calling an ambulance now.’** Then **two sets of blood cultures before any antibiotic if that causes no delay · dexamethasone with or just before the first dose · empirical IV antibiotics — ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, plus benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover in the appropriate groups, with vancomycin where resistant pneumococcus is a concern.** VERIFY

**CT head before lumbar puncture if: reduced conscious state, focal deficit, seizure, papilloedema or immunosuppression.** VERIFY Otherwise LP for **cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture and PCR**, with paired serum glucose, blood PCR and throat swab.

DIVERGENCE — CORRECTION: older teaching (Murtagh) withholds antibiotics until the LP so as not to sterilise the CSF. **Therapeutic Guidelines is explicit that treatment must not be withheld where there will be any significant delay** — which from a rural SA site is essentially always. The safe answer: **‘blood cultures, then dexamethasone and empirical antibiotics without delay, because delaying treatment to obtain CSF increases mortality and CSF PCR remains informative after antibiotics. In a metropolitan department with an immediate LP available I would take the CSF first.’** VERIFY

**If there is a purpuric rash or any feature of sepsis — give benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone immediately, in your room, before the ambulance leaves. Do not wait for anything.** Yes, it may compromise the cultures, and you do it anyway — **say that reasoning out loud; it is the mark.**

**Notifiable.** Invasive meningococcal and pneumococcal disease are notifiable in South Australia; **clearance antibiotics for household and intimate contacts are arranged through the public health unit.** VERIFY Audiology follow-up after pneumococcal meningitis. VERIFY

SA — no on-site CT or laboratory out of hours from an MM5 site: **regional hospital plus MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**, retrieval consultant early; **SA Health Communicable Disease Control Branch** for contact tracing; **healthdirect 1800 022 222** for the family; **TIS 131 450**; ACCHS and Aboriginal Liaison Officer, noting the **higher burden of invasive meningococcal disease in some remote communities** when counselling household contacts.

Is it alright if I ask you a few questions first — just so I can give you the right advice with it? It won’t take long.’** **Do not hand over the certificate, and do not ask questions over her.**
**CICORA at speed** — all over the head, eight out of ten, dull, since this morning, constant and **getting worse**, nothing helps. **Skip the effect-on-life question in an acute case.**

**Exclude the bleed**: **‘Did it start suddenly, like a switch?’** → no, built over an hour or two. **‘Is this the worst headache of your life?’** → no. Both negative — remember to say so in the differential run.

**The meningitis block** — **‘Any fever or chills?’** → *‘I’ve been feeling hot.’* Then **nausea or vomiting · sensitive to light · is your neck sore** (the most important question in the station) **· any rash anywhere, even a few small spots · anyone around you unwell, any recent travel, are your immunisations up to date.**

**Short screens until the bell**: cluster · migraine · tension · sinusitis · dental · trigeminal · medications and painkiller days. **No giant cell arteritis — she is 25.**

**Diagnosis, then the differentials as a LIST, not a lecture**: **‘I’ll be quick because there’s something important I need to tell you about next.’** Every name is a tick; explaining three richly and hearing the bell is a fail.

**Ask for the rash explicitly, and for the sepsis check** — cool peripheries, capillary refill, hypotension. **A purpuric rash changes the management completely**, and **purpura can appear over minutes**, so re-examine the whole skin.

**‘Any tenderness over the spinous processes and paraspinal muscles?’** → no. Say out loud that **the absence of muscle tenderness supports meningeal rather than muscular irritation** — it is a free mark.

Since this morning he has been confused and saying inappropriate things to family and friends. He then had a seizure and was brought in by ambulance. He is confused — you are talking to the father.

Tasks: explain the physical examination findings and the investigation results to the father — explain your diagnosis and your differentials — and explain the implications of this condition. dx: **Delirium caused by viral encephalitis — herpes simplex until proven otherwise.** **Name both layers.** The syndrome the father watched is **delirium: an acute change in mental state with confusion and disordered behaviour.** The cause is **encephalitis — inflammation of the brain tissue itself.** Saying only ‘encephalitis’ leaves him without a name for what he actually saw.

**This looks like an infectious-diseases case and is scored as a communication case.** The medicine is straightforward; the marks are in **consent, pacing, plain language, checking understanding, and honesty about implications without minimising or catastrophising.**

**The one-sentence explanation: ‘Meningitis is the covering of the brain. Encephalitis is the brain tissue itself. That’s why his neck isn’t stiff.’** Explain the absent neck stiffness rather than ignoring it.

**IV aciclovir empirically — started now, not when the PCR returns.** VERIFY Say it early and unprompted: **‘we’ve already started the antiviral — we haven’t waited for the final virus test, because starting early makes a real difference to the outcome. If the test comes back negative, we’ll stop it.’**

Add **empirical antibacterial cover until bacterial meningitis is excluded** if there is any doubt. VERIFY **Blood cultures, FBC, UEC, LFT, glucose, coagulation profile.** Manage the seizure: **airway, oxygen, a benzodiazepine if it recurs, a loading antiepileptic if seizures continue.** VERIFY

Translating the CSF rather than reciting it: **‘there are more white cells than there should be, and nine out of ten are the type that go up with a virus rather than a bacterium. The sugar is normal and the protein only slightly raised — again a viral picture.’** Bacterial CSF by contrast is **neutrophil-predominant with low glucose and markedly raised protein.** VERIFY

**The guilt and contagion questions, answered directly and before he has to ask twice**: **‘This is a very rare complication of an extremely common virus. It isn’t anyone’s fault, he didn’t catch it from you, and encephalitis itself isn’t passed from person to person. Your other children are not at risk from him.’**

Implications, **honestly**: **‘Most people recover well — around six in ten with no lasting problems** VERIFY **. But some are left with difficulties with memory, concentration, speech, personality or mood, and some develop seizures needing long-term treatment. I can’t tell you today which group he’ll be in.’** Then what is in his favour, and **the rehabilitation team — occupational therapy, speech therapy, neuropsychology.**

**Quote prognosis as a range with uncertainty, not a single number** — outcome in HSV encephalitis turns on **how quickly aciclovir was started.** Untreated HSV encephalitis is far worse than the general viral-encephalitis figure.

**Driving**: he must not drive after a seizure — **Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive** and the reporting duty under the **Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (SA)**. VERIFY SA — from a rural site this needs a metropolitan centre: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**, and **give the first dose of aciclovir before transfer**. **TIS 131 450**; Aboriginal Liaison Officer early for families facing metropolitan transfer.
plan: **Introduction and role**: **‘Hello, are you Mark? I’m one of the doctors in the emergency department and I’m looking after your son today.’**

**Consent — the box almost everyone misses, and it takes six seconds**: **‘Before we start — your son isn’t well enough to take this in himself at the moment. Is it alright with you if I go through his results with you? Are you his next of kin?’**

**‘Can I ask what you’ve been told so far, and what you understood from it? That way I won’t repeat things or leave gaps.’** Then acknowledge, once and genuinely: **‘That must have been terrifying to watch.’**
**Warning shot and signpost**: **‘Some of what I’m going to say is serious, and I’ll go through it slowly. I’ll cover what we found, what we think it is, and what it means. Stop me at any point.’**

**Task 1 — findings, one at a time, pausing.** Mild temperature · confused and disorientated, speech not making sense · **‘his neck was not stiff — I’ll come back to why that matters’** · drowsy after the fit. Then bloods · normal glucose and biochemistry · **the CT: ‘no abscess, no bleed, no tumour — but it doesn’t show inflammation itself’** · the spinal fluid. **Pause after the scan and after the fluid** — the father cannot absorb five results in one breath, and the examiner is watching for whether you noticed.

**Task 2 — the diagnosis in two layers.** **‘What you’ve been watching has a name — delirium, a sudden change in how the brain is working. Delirium always has a cause, and we think his cause is encephalitis — inflammation of the brain tissue itself, almost always from a virus, most commonly the cold sore virus.’** Then **the neck-stiffness explanation**, then **the contagion and guilt answer before he asks twice**.

**Differentials — name them, do not lecture.** Bacterial meningitis (soft neck, mild fever, viral CSF pattern) · abscess, tumour, bleed (**excluded by the normal CT**) · metabolic causes — low sugar, sodium, liver or kidney failure (**excluded by the bloods**) · drugs, alcohol or withdrawal · prolonged post-ictal state · **autoimmune encephalitis, neurosyphilis, HIV if the PCR is negative.**

**Task 3 — implications, two minutes, and it is a third of the marks.** **Treatment already started, first.** Then the honest proportions, then **‘I can’t tell you today which group he’ll be in’**, then what is in his favour, then **the rehabilitation team by name**.

**The practical one**: **‘because he’s had a seizure, he won’t be able to drive for a period, and that will be reviewed by the specialists. I know that’s a small detail today, but it’s better you hear it from me now.’**
**‘Is that making sense so far? What questions do you have?’** Pause after each block rather than talking for eight minutes straight — **no check of understanding is its own fail risk.**
pefe: **There is no history-taking and no examination task** — the findings and the results are handed to you, and the whole station is explaining them.

**The findings you are given**: mild temperature (**not the 39–40°C of bacterial meningitis**) · confused, disorientated, inappropriate speech · **no neck stiffness** · post-ictal after a witnessed seizure · no rash, no focal deficit.

**The investigations you are given**: raised WCC, ESR and CRP; **normal glucose and remaining bloods**; **normal CT brain**; **CSF with raised white cells, 90% lymphocytes, normal glucose and mildly elevated protein.**
**The normal CT excludes abscess, bleed and tumour — and nothing else.** ‘Good news, the scan is clear’ is a fail risk; it does not show the inflammation.

**What you would add**: **CSF PCR for HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV** · **MRI brain**, classically temporal lobe change VERIFY · **EEG** if seizures recur or the conscious state does not improve · blood cultures, FBC, UEC, LFT, glucose, coagulation.
**A repeat lumbar puncture may be needed if the first was taken very early and is normal** — a normal CSF does not exclude encephalitis.

**Version C — mosquito exposure**: recent time in rural south-eastern Australia, camping near waterbirds, or work around piggeries adds **Japanese encephalitis virus** — notifiable, vaccine for at-risk groups, **no specific antiviral, management supportive** VERIFY . **Aciclovir is still started empirically until HSV is excluded.** Also consider Murray Valley and West Nile/Kunjin.
