dx: **Benign intracranial hypertension (idiopathic intracranial hypertension, pseudotumour cerebri) in a 16-year-old girl** — raised CSF pressure **without a mass lesion**. The package: **young, female, raised BMI, on acne treatment, headache with visual symptoms and nausea.**

**It is called pseudotumour because it behaves exactly like a tumour** on history and examination — chronic headache, blurred and double vision, visual obscurations, tinnitus, papilloedema — **and then the scan comes back normal.**

**The pivot is the medication question.** **Doxycycline, minocycline, isotretinoin, vitamin A derivatives, the combined pill and corticosteroids all cause it**, and combining them multiplies the risk — **which is why isotretinoin and doxycycline are not given together.** VERIFY

**Correct the word ‘benign’ explicitly**: **‘Benign only means there’s no tumour. If this isn’t treated, the pressure can permanently damage her sight. That’s why I want her eyes examined properly within a day or two, not in a few weeks.’**

**The order of investigation, said out loud**: **‘We’ll do a scan of her brain first, including the veins, to be certain there’s nothing there. Only after that would we measure the pressure with a needle in the back — doing it the other way round can be dangerous if there turns out to be something pressing on the brain.’**

**Same-day or next-day ophthalmology: visual acuity, formal visual fields and documented fundoscopy. Vision is what is at stake.** Then serial visual field monitoring, and **surgical options — optic nerve sheath fenestration, shunting, venous stenting — if vision deteriorates.** VERIFY

**Stop the doxycycline after discussion with whoever prescribed it**, and **arrange an alternative acne plan** — the combined pill is permitted at 16 and can be part of it, **though it also appears on the causative list, so this is a specialist conversation.** VERIFY **Paediatric or neurology referral; acetazolamide is first-line medical therapy and specialist-initiated.** VERIFY

**Weight management, sensitively framed** — sustained weight loss is **disease-modifying** in this condition VERIFY . **Do not discuss weight bluntly in front of a 16-year-old**: frame it as part of treatment, privately, without moralising.

**‘My wife says I twitch in my sleep’ is a seizure until proved otherwise** — not restless legs, not a sleep habit. **Nocturnal twitching reported by a partner in an adult with a progressive headache** is red flag number two, and it arrives in the opening statement.

**Read the film in two sentences**: **‘I can see a space-occupying lesion. And there is a midline shift, which tells me the mass is large enough to be pushing the brain across — and that would explain his seizures.’** Mass, and shift. Nothing more.

**The shift in register**: in every other headache station you say ‘most likely’. **Here you have seen the mass — saying ‘possibly’ now sounds evasive.** Use **‘I am concerned about’**, then give the reasons.

Giving it: **‘Mark, I’ve looked at your scan, and I need to tell you what it shows. I’m concerned about a brain tumour, or a spread of your melanoma to the brain.’** — **pause, let it land, do not fill the silence** — **‘How are you feeling? … Is it alright if I explain a bit more?’**

**The honesty about which**: **‘On this scan I can’t tell whether it’s a tumour that started in the brain or a spread from the melanoma. stem: Your next patient is a 55-year-old man who presents to your general practice complaining of difficulty in walking, which has been getting worse. He has a specific concern: he is worried he is having a stroke. Tasks: take a very complete six-minute history — this is the predominant assessment area — then explain your diagnosis, and explain your differentials.

A gait stem carries one of the widest differential lists in the whole exam — brain, cord, nerve, muscle, cerebellum, vestibular apparatus, joints, eyes and drugs. The station appeared in 2022 and 2023 and very few candidates passed it even knowing the recall, because the marks are in the breadth of the list rather than the diagnosis. Variants: no trauma at all with a normal CT; and a new focal deficit appearing.

dx: **Chronic subdural haematoma in a 55-year-old man** — a fall three months ago, apparently trivial at the time, with **a slow venous collection that only became symptomatic weeks later.**

**The trap is arithmetic.** Candidates hear ‘three months ago’ and strike intracranial haemorrhage off, reasoning that a bleed would have declared itself on the day. **That is exactly how chronic subdurals are missed in real practice.** Symptoms may not appear for weeks, and when they do they are **vague, fluctuating and non-focal**: headache, lightheadedness, unsteadiness, cognitive change, seizures.
**Risk factors: age, alcohol, cerebral atrophy and anticoagulation — and a ‘trivial’ fall is the usual history.** CT appearance: **a crescentic collection, often hypodense, ± midline shift.**

Explaining the mechanism when he disbelieves you: **‘It sounds wrong, and it’s exactly how this one behaves. A small vein tears when you hit your head, and it bleeds very slowly — so slowly that nothing happens for weeks. Then the collection gets big enough to press on the brain. Being on a blood thinner makes it a good deal more likely, because the bleeding doesn’t stop as readily.’**

**Answering the stroke concern by name, with reasons**: **‘I don’t think this is a stroke. A stroke comes on suddenly, usually in minutes, and then stays the same or improves. Yours has come on gradually over a month, is getting worse, and varies from day to day — and you’ve had no slurred speech, no weakness down one side, no numbness and no loss of vision.’**
**Urgent CT head — today, not next week.** Then **bloods: FBC, UEC, LFTs, coagulation profile and INR, glucose and B12.** Assess and document any focal deficit and conscious state.

**Review the anticoagulant with the treating team** — it will likely need to be withheld or reversed depending on the findings, and **reversal is discussed with the receiving team before any agent is given.** VERIFY **Neurosurgical referral if a collection is confirmed — many chronic subdurals are drained via burr holes, with good outcomes.** VERIFY

**If the CT is normal**: MRI cervical spine for **myelopathy** and MRI brain, plus the metabolic screen. **Cervical myelopathy is easily missed and a common real cause of gait change at this age** — neck pain, clumsy hands, bladder symptoms.

**He should not drive until this is sorted** — a progressive gait disturbance of unknown cause. VERIFY Then **physiotherapy and occupational therapy assessment, a gait aid, a home falls-hazard review, a medication review (sedatives, antihypertensives) and a postural blood pressure.**

SA — **CT from an MM5 site means the regional hospital, arranged today rather than as an outpatient**; discuss with the **neurosurgical registrar** at the receiving metropolitan unit and arrange transfer, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if he deteriorates; **PATS** for travel; community physio and OT through **Country Health Connect**; **My Aged Care 1800 200 422** if he needs home supports; driving under the **Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (SA)** and **Austroads — document the advice you give**; **TIS 131 450**; ACCHS.
plan: **Vitals are optional here** — there is no subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis on a gait list. Asking costs ten seconds and is never penalised; **skipping it to buy differential time is also defensible.** Then the open question.

Acknowledge the stated fear **and make a mental note to answer it**: **‘I understand why a stroke is on your mind — that’s a reasonable thing to worry about. Let me ask you some questions and I’ll tell you directly what I think by the end.’**

**‘Tell me what you mean by difficulty walking — is it weakness, stiffness, balance, pain, or your legs not doing what you tell them?’** **Weakness, imbalance, stiffness and pain lead to four different groups, and the answer redirects the whole history.** Then: how long · getting worse · does it come and go · have you fallen because of it · **‘is it worse at the end of the day when you’re tired?’** · effect on life.

**Group 1 — upper motor neuron.** The deficit block, which does double duty for everything in this group: **blackouts or fainting · slurred speech · blurring of vision · weakness in arms or legs · numbness or pins and needles.** Then tumour: **long-standing headaches · early-morning headache or vomiting · weight loss.**

**The question over the right time frame**: **‘Have you had any trauma, injury or fall — not just recently, but at any point over the last few months?’** **‘Any recent falls?’ invites a no, because three months does not feel recent to the patient.**

**The fall, explored — do not move on.** **‘Describe the fall for me — what happened, and what did you hurt? Did you hit your head? Did you lose consciousness, even briefly? Did you vomit afterwards? Did you see a doctor at the time — did you have a scan?’** Then **‘Are you on any blood thinners — aspirin, warfarin, apixaban, clopidogrel?’** and **‘How much alcohol do you drink?’**

**Groups 2–3 — lower motor neuron, muscle, extrapyramidal.** Parkinson’s: **shakiness in the hands · taking longer to do things.** Myasthenia: **the end-of-day question, plus drooping eyelids, double vision, difficulty chewing or swallowing.** Neuropathy causes: **diabetes, alcohol.** Myopathy: **rising from a chair, stairs, thyroid, statin.** Cord: **back or neck pain · numbness around the back passage · bowel or bladder control.**

**Groups 4–5 — cerebellar and vestibular.** **Balance overall · difficulty saying some words · shakiness reaching for things** · then **hearing loss · buzzing or ringing · spinning · nausea with it.**

**Group 6 — antalgic and the non-neurological risk factors.** **Pain in legs, hips, knees or feet on walking · vision and hearing · sleeping tablets or sedatives, new blood pressure medications · dizziness on standing · other recent falls.** Then closure: PMHx, FHx, smoking, alcohol.

**Name it and explain the delayed mechanism → answer the stroke concern by name with the negatives → deliver the differential list BY GROUP** — brain, cord, extrapyramidal, nerve and muscle, cerebellar and vestibular, antalgic and non-neurological. Then **CT today, not next week**, and **don’t drive.**

**Version B — no trauma at all, and the CT is normal**: the leading diagnoses become **cervical myelopathy**, **normal pressure hydrocephalus** (the triad of **gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline** — a magnetic, shuffling gait), **Parkinson’s disease**, and **peripheral neuropathy.** VERIFY

**Version C — a new focal deficit appears**: a weak arm, a drooping face, drowsiness or confusion makes this **a 000 and an ambulance, not a CT booking.** Reverse the anticoagulant in discussion with the receiving team, speak to neurosurgery immediately, consider retrieval — **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**

**Cross-reference**: the cerebellar examination, ITPRSC and gait-pattern content sit in the **Unsteady Gait — Cerebellar Examination** pair, and the tremor questions in **Tremor and Parkinsonism.** **This document is the history station only.**

dx: **Pelvic fracture in a 26-year-old footballer — most consistent with an injury involving the ischium**, given **tenderness over the ischial tuberosity, posterior thigh bruising, restricted hip movement and equal true leg lengths.**

**Why not ‘hip fracture’?** The hip is a joint built from **the acetabulum (ilium, ischium and pubis) and the femur**, so ‘hip fracture’ does not tell the examiner what you think is broken. **A proximal femoral fracture classically shortens and externally rotates the leg** — **here the true lengths are equal**, which points away from the femur and towards the pelvis.

**Your differential list is built for the complaint, not for what you find.** You make the list for ‘difficulty walking’ **before you know anything**. The history then **reorders** it — acute and traumatic pushes fracture and infection up, degenerative causes down — **but the list itself does not change, and you still rule the others out.**

**This case appeared two months after the chronic subdural gait station.** Candidates walked in expecting a bleed, heard ‘I had a fall’, and stopped thinking — **then a full page of musculoskeletal findings arrived on the card.**

**Read the card correctly, out loud**: **‘The power is reduced, but the card tells me that is limited by pain rather than true weakness — and with normal tone, sensation and reflexes I would not call that a neurological deficit.’**

**When an AMC role-player volunteers a paragraph, it is scripted, and it is the answer.** Here: **pushed from the left, landed on the right hip, unable to walk properly since.** Mine it — direction of force, landing point, **could she get up, could she weight-bear at the time.**

Naming it precisely: **‘Most likely you have a fracture in your pelvis — the ring of bone your hip joint sits in. I’m saying pelvis rather than hip because there is bruising at the back of your thigh and tenderness right over the sitting bone, your hip doesn’t move through its full range, and importantly both your legs are the same length — a break in the top of the thigh bone usually makes one leg shorter.’**

**Pelvic X-ray today, with CT pelvis if the plain film is equivocal or a ring injury is suspected.** VERIFY **Analgesia; non-weight-bearing until imaging is reviewed, with crutches and instruction.** **Assess haemodynamic stability — an unstable pelvic ring injury can bleed litres.** VERIFY **Orthopaedic referral — same day if she cannot weight-bear or the ring may be involved.**

**Most isolated, stable pelvic fractures are managed conservatively**: analgesia, protected weight-bearing, physiotherapy. **Unstable ring injuries or displaced acetabular fractures require operative fixation.** VERIFY **VTE prophylaxis if mobility is significantly reduced** VERIFY ; work certificate and modified duties; **if it turns out to be a hamstring avulsion, surgical repair is time-sensitive.** VERIFY

**Skip the geriatric falls assessment** — vision, hearing, home hazards and polypharmacy belong to the 65-year-old with recurrent falls, not a 26-year-old tackled at football. **Say so if challenged; it shows you are reasoning, not reciting.** SA — plain films locally, **CT pelvis at the regional centre with PATS travel**; discuss with the **orthopaedic registrar** before sending her; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if unstable; community physio via Country Health Connect; **ReturnToWorkSA** only if it happened at work; **TIS 131 450**; ACCHS.
plan: Open question, then the framing line that works for any gait case: **‘I’m going to ask about quite a few different systems — walking involves the brain, the nerves, the muscles, the joints and the balance organs, so some questions will sound unrelated.’**

**‘Tell me what you mean by difficulty walking — is it pain, weakness, stiffness, balance, or your leg not doing what you tell it?’** → **pain**. Then: how long · getting worse · **can you weight-bear at all** · better or worse · worse at the end of the day · effect on life.

**Vascular and infective, asked EARLY in an acute presentation** — **before** the trauma answer arrives. **Calf pain on walking that eases with rest · swelling, warmth or pain in one calf · on the pill, long flights, recent immobility · fever or chills · rash on the legs · any hot, swollen, red joint.** **Skipping the fever question because the story is obviously traumatic is how a septic hip gets missed.**

**‘Have you had any recent injuries, trauma or falls?’** → yes, football. Then **the mechanism, in full**: **‘Can you describe the fall for me? Which way were you pushed, and what did you land on? Could you get up afterwards? Could you weight-bear at the time?’**

**The head-injury screen that follows EVERY fall**: **‘Did you hit your head? Did you lose consciousness or faint, even for a few seconds? Did you vomit afterwards? Any headaches since? Did anyone look at you at the time — a trainer, a doctor? Any imaging?’** **The marks for asking are there whether or not the answer is positive.**

**Neurological deficit, head to toe, after any injury**: **blurring of vision · slurred speech · weakness moving the leg · numbness or pins and needles · headaches since · weight loss** (intracranial haemorrhage and tumour are still on the list).

**The cauda equina screen — two questions, ten seconds, and it belongs in every acute gait case**: **‘Any back or neck pain since the injury? Any numbness around the back passage or inner thighs? Any change in bowel or bladder control?’**

**Groups 4–6, asked anyway** — because the examiner is marking whether you rule out differentials **for the complaint**. Cerebellar: **balance, difficulty saying words.** Vestibular: **hearing loss, buzzing, spinning, nausea.** Myopathy and endocrine: **thyroid, rising from a chair, statin.** Drugs: **any medications including the pill, sleeping tablets.**
Closure: PMHx, FHx, medications, smoking and alcohol. **Then say what you are skipping and why** — the geriatric falls assessment does not belong to a 26-year-old.

**Build the list for the complaint — VISION LOSS — not for ‘transient and recurrent’.** That list includes **retinal detachment, central retinal artery and vein occlusion, optic neuritis, glaucoma and tumour — none of which recover** — and you **name them and then explain why the recovery excludes them.** **The recovery is a discriminator you use, not a filter you apply before thinking.**

**Why it is urgent despite feeling well**: **‘I know everything feels back to normal, and that’s exactly what makes this worth acting on today. back.dx: LYMPHOMA — reached through a head and neck examination rather than a systemic one. The warning shot, the word, then the reasons: 'David, thank you for waiting. I am afraid what I have found does concern me.' Pause. 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.' Pause and let it land. 'The lump you can feel is an enlarged gland, and there are three of them. They feel rubbery, they do not move, and they are not sore — and glands from an infection are usually tender and move freely. I also found your spleen is bigger than it should be, and I noticed the scratch marks on your skin. Your thyroid gland is normal, so this is not a thyroid problem.' The euphemism and the reassurance are both AUTOMATIC FAILS here — 'Probably just a gland' and 'Let's try another course of antibiotics' — and so is delivering a differential list instead of a diagnosis. When he asks if it is the smoking: 'Smoking causes several cancers of the head, neck and lungs, and those are on my list — but lymphoma is not usually caused by smoking. Either way, stopping now would be the single best thing you could do for whatever we find, and I will help you with that.' then the three groups with named members, because group names with no members score nothing and the rule is specificity. Thyroid problems — a cancer, a nodule or a cyst, or a goitre; less likely, because the gland felt normal and this lump does not move on swallowing. Infections — in the skin, such as impetigo or cellulitis; in the teeth; in the throat and ears, such as tonsillitis; and longer-standing infections like glandular fever, tuberculosis and HIV, which need blood tests and his permission. Other cancers — skin cancers on the head and neck, cancers of the nose, mouth or throat, of the food pipe or stomach, and lung cancer. 'That is why I looked at so many areas today.' The investigations, in order of priority and delivered slowly: one, full blood examination. Two, blood film. Three, an excisional biopsy of one of the cervical nodes, because lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture. Four, PET-CT for staging, or CT of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis. Then for the other differentials: TSH and a neck ultrasound for the thyroid group; nasendoscopy and laryngoscopy for a pharyngeal or laryngeal primary; a chest x-ray; gastroscopy if there is any dysphagia; and ESR, CRP with EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, HIV and syphilis serology and an IGRA for the infective group. The answer that separates you, when the examiner asks why not a fine-needle aspirate: 'Suspected lymphoma means excisional biopsy, because we need nodal architecture and tissue for immunophenotyping — an aspirate gives cells without architecture. Suspected metastatic squamous cell carcinoma means fine-needle aspiration plus nasendoscopy to find the primary, and I would avoid an open biopsy of the neck before ENT assessment.' The safety-net: 'I will organise the blood tests today and speak to the specialist myself. Come back or go straight to hospital if you develop difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, trouble swallowing, swelling of your face or neck, or a fever. I will phone you with the blood results personally. Cancer council SA on 13 11 20 can help with information and with travel. Is there someone at home with you?' The variants. A stony hard fixed node with a non-healing lateral tongue ulcer and referred ear pain in a smoker over forty: metastatic squamous cell carcinoma is the leading diagnosis, not lymphoma — urgent ENT referral for nasendoscopy and fine-needle aspiration, CT neck and chest, and no open neck biopsy first. A midline lump that rises both on swallowing and on tongue protrusion: movement on tongue protrusion is the discriminator, so it is a thyroglossal duct cyst — ultrasound and TSH to confirm normal thyroid tissue elsewhere before any excision. And a temperature of 38.3 with a tender mobile node, red overlying skin and a broken molar with gingival swelling: reactive cervical lymphadenitis from dental sepsis — urgent dental review and drainage, antibiotics, and review in 48 hours; and if the node has not settled once the dental source is treated, it still needs investigating.

'Separately, I would like a full thyroid examination' — with the follow-up loaded for 'What are you looking for?': inspection for a visible mass and engorged veins, palpation for size, nodularity and tenderness, and percussion over the manubrium for retrosternal extension. (Sip-and-swallow, tongue protrusion, auscultation and Pemberton's are all correct and all optional — if the first three are normal, stop, because you need the time for the skin check.)

Chest and abdomen, each with its reason said aloud: 'Air entry equal, any added sounds? I'm asking because lung cancer is on my list.' 'Inspection for swelling, distension or redness; then tenderness, masses, and hepatomegaly or splenomegaly? I'm asking because gastric carcinoma is on my list.'
The skin check: 'Finally, a full skin check — are there any suspicious skin lesions or moles on the head and neck?'
Stop asking. Turn the chair fully towards him and lower your voice — then the warning shot, the word lymphoma, a pause, and the reasons from what you found (see dx).
The three groups with named members (see dx) — then the investigations in order of priority, the excisional-versus-fna answer ready, and the safety-net with someone at home confirmed.

ask: The thirteen lines, one to seven: 'With a lump in the neck my differentials fall into three groups — thyroid, infection, and malignancy.' / 'Vital signs, and the temperature first.' / 'A full ENT examination, and I will go region by region.' / 'Any caries, and any swelling or redness of the gums?' / 'A full lymph node examination, all chains, over the whole body.' / 'Consistency, mobility or fixation, tenderness, and the overlying skin.' / 'Separately, I would like a full thyroid examination.'

Eight to thirteen: 'Inspection, palpation, and percussion for retrosternal extension.' / 'A full skin check — any suspicious skin lesions or moles on the head and neck?' / 'I am afraid what I have found does concern me.' / 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.' / 'Your thyroid gland is normal, so this is not a thyroid problem.' / 'Suspected lymphoma: excisional. Suspected metastatic squamous cell carcinoma: fine-needle aspiration plus nasendoscopy.'

If the examiner asks 'Do you need to examine them separately?' — this is a check that you understand the anatomy: 'Yes — I asked for the lymph nodes specifically and the thyroid specifically, because a neck lump is one or the other. The answers tell me this is a node.'

The discriminators to hold: a neck lump is one of two structures, lymph node or thyroid — movement on swallowing means thyroid, and movement on tongue protrusion means a thyroglossal duct cyst — four node characters, four ENT sub-requests, three differential groups — and tender and mobile is lymphadenitis while rubbery, fixed and non-tender is a malignant pattern.

The first four investigations in order: full blood examination, blood film, excisional biopsy of a cervical node, and PET-CT for staging. Cancer council SA 13 11 20 — TIS National 131 450 — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.
pefe: The ENT examination as four separate asks, because a summary request invites 'What are you looking for?': 'Throat — any redness or exudate? Are the tonsils enlarged? Mouth — any ulcers? Dental — any caries, and any swelling or redness of the gums? Nose — any discharge, or any abnormal growth in the nasal cavity?'

Role-player: David Nowak, 45, a grain handler at the Wallaroo terminal, living with his partner with two adult children. Twenty-five a day since he was twenty, six to eight beers on Friday and Saturday, no regular medications, no allergies. A lump on the right side of his neck for about three months, slowly bigger, painless, unchanged by two courses of antibiotics. Weight loss with his belt two holes tighter and a poor appetite. Itching all over for weeks with scratching in his sleep. No sore throat, toothache, dysphagia, hoarseness, cough beyond a smoker's morning cough, or noticed night sweats — though his wife says he is hot at night. He is outdoors all day and has never had his moles checked.

How to play it: stoic, understated, slightly gruff, minimising everything — 'It's probably nothing.' You are mostly a witness for the first five minutes while the doctor talks to the examiner; do not interrupt, but watch them. One interruption is allowed — at around four minutes, if they have not looked at you once, say 'Are you going to tell me what it is?' when the word cancer is said, go still, then flatly: 'Cancer? I've had two lots of antibiotics for this. Nobody said cancer.' Push once with 'Is it because I smoke?' Become emotional only if they rush past your reaction without a pause — then go quiet and say 'My dad had throat cancer.' if they use jargon, say 'In English, doc?' Do not volunteer the itching, the weight loss, the smoking or your father unless asked.

Score them out of ten: did they greet you before turning to the examiner (1); ask for cachexia and the temperature (1); ask the ENT regions separately — throat, mouth, dental, nose (2); ask for all four node characters (1); ask for the thyroid as a separate examination (1); ask for a full skin check of the head and neck (1); say the word lymphoma to you (1); give differentials in three groups with named members (1); and give investigations in order (1).
The four characters — Rubbery — fixed — non-tender — largest about 3 cm, with normal overlying skin. That is a malignant pattern, and say so
Why you ask about tenderness — To separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy — say the reason aloud as you ask

The best line in the station — The full skin check — no suspicious lesions, with scratch marks over the trunk and limbs. Melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck drain to exactly these nodes, almost nobody asks, and it costs eight seconds

What he tells you — Three months, slowly bigger from a PEA to a grape, never painful — two courses of antibiotics that made no difference — his belt two holes tighter without trying — and itching all over for weeks, scratching himself raw in his sleep. 25 a day since he was twenty

His hidden agenda — 'My dad died of throat cancer at fifty-eight. I watched it happen. I've been telling myself this is just a gland' — given only if you ask what he is worried about, or after you say the word cancer

What he does in the room — He is a witness for the first five minutes while you talk to the examiner — and at about four minutes, if you have not looked at him once, he says 'Are you going to tell me what it is?' if you use jargon he says 'In English, doc?'

Asking for the ENT examination as a summary rather than four separate regions, which invites 'what are you looking for?' and wastes the time you need
Never asking for the full skin check — melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck drain to exactly these nodes, almost nobody asks, and it costs eight seconds

Giving group names with no members, since 'infections' scores nothing while impetigo, dental infection and tonsillitis score the item; gold-plating the thyroid with optional manoeuvres when the first three are normal; never asking for the thyroid separately; and never turning to the patient until he asks whether you are going to tell him what it is

findingsLabel: What the examiner gives back, and what he never volunteers
must: FAIL — Opening with 'a full lymph node examination' instead of DECLARING THE THREE GROUPS — that is the previous case's sequence, and the groups are what LICENSE every unusual request that follows: 'Examiner, this man has a lump in the neck, so my examination is built around THREE GROUPS — thyroid disease, infection, and malignancy of the head, neck and chest; may I have the general appearance, cachexia, pallor and scratch marks, and the vital signs, TEMPERATURE FIRST?' (★)

FAIL — Softening it into 'probably just a gland' or offering another course of antibiotics — both are automatic fails here, and so is delivering a DIFFERENTIAL LIST instead of a DIAGNOSIS; warning shot, the word, then the reasons, pausing after each: 'David, I am afraid what I have found does concern me… I am concerned about the possibility of a CANCER OF THE LYMPH GLANDS, called LYMPHOMA… the lump you can feel is an enlarged gland, and there are three of them; they feel RUBBERY, they do NOT MOVE, and they are NOT SORE — and glands from an infection are usually tender and move freely; I also found your spleen is bigger than it should be, and I noticed the scratch marks on your skin; your thyroid gland is normal, so this is not a thyroid problem' (★)

FAIL — Asking for the ENT examination as a SUMMARY rather than FOUR SEPARATE REGIONS, which invites 'what are you looking for?' and burns the clock — THROAT (any redness or exudate, and are the tonsils enlarged), MOUTH (any ulcers), DENTAL (any caries, and any swelling or redness of the gums — never 'tell me the dental hygiene') and NOSE (any discharge, or any abnormal growth in the nasal cavity); every answer comes back negative, and every negative is a differential you exclude out loud later (★)

FAIL — Group names with no members — 'infections' scores nothing, while 'skin infections such as impetigo or cellulitis, dental infection, and ENT infections such as tonsillitis' scores the item, and the rule is SPECIFICITY; the three groups given to the PATIENT are thyroid problems (a cancer, a nodule or a cyst, or a goitre — less likely, because the gland felt normal and this lump does not move when you swallow), infections (in the skin, in the teeth, in the throat and ears, and the longer-standing ones: glandular fever, tuberculosis and HIV, which need blood tests and his permission) and other cancers (skin cancers on the head and neck, cancers of the nose, mouth or throat, of the food pipe or stomach, and lung cancer) — closing with 'that is why I looked at so many areas today' (★)

FAIL — Never asking for the FULL SKIN CHECK of the head and neck — the best line in the station, because melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck drain to EXACTLY these nodes, almost nobody asks, and it costs eight seconds; likewise ask for the THYROID as a SEPARATE examination with the follow-up already loaded, because the examiner is likely to ask 'what are you looking for?' first ('on inspection, a visible mass and any engorged veins; on palpation, the size of the gland, any nodularity and any tenderness; and PERCUSSION over the manubrium for RETROSTERNAL EXTENSION') — but do not gold-plate it, because sip-and-swallow, tongue protrusion, auscultation and Pemberton's sign are all correct and all OPTIONAL, and if inspection, palpation and percussion are normal you stop, since you need the time for the skin check; ask for all FOUR NODE CHARACTERS after the chains (consistency, mobile or fixed, tender — 'I am asking about tenderness to separate LYMPHADENITIS from LYMPHADENOPATHY' — and the overlying skin), and stop asking for findings at 5:15

SAY — Give the investigations IN ORDER and slowly: FULL BLOOD EXAMINATION, BLOOD FILM, an EXCISIONAL BIOPSY of one of the cervical nodes, and PET–CT for staging (or CT of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis) — then, for the other differentials, TSH and a neck ultrasound; nasendoscopy and laryngoscopy for a pharyngeal or laryngeal primary; a chest X-ray; gastroscopy if there is any dysphagia; and ESR, CRP with EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, HIV and syphilis serology and an IGRA; the answer that separates you is WHY — 'suspected LYMPHOMA means an EXCISIONAL biopsy, because lymphoma is classified on NODAL ARCHITECTURE and an aspirate gives cells without architecture, and an excised node also provides tissue for immunophenotyping; suspected METASTATIC SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA means FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION plus NASENDOSCOPY to find the primary, and I would avoid an open biopsy of the neck before ENT assessment'; the discriminators to hold — a neck lump is one of TWO STRUCTURES, LYMPH NODE OR THYROID; movement ON SWALLOWING means thyroid, and movement ON TONGUE PROTRUSION means a THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST; and asking for the nodes and the thyroid SEPARATELY is what lets you say which; ask for the chest ('lung cancer is on my list') and the abdomen ('gastric carcinoma is on my list') with the reason attached; GREET the patient before you turn to the examiner, and turn the chair fully towards him when you name it, because he is briefed to ask 'are you going to tell me what it is?' at about four minutes if you have not looked at him once; answer 'is it because I smoke?' honestly ('smoking causes several cancers of the head, neck and lungs, and those are on my list — but lymphoma is not usually caused by smoking; either way, stopping now would be the single best thing you could do for whatever we find, and I'll help you with that'); translate every piece of jargon, because he will say 'in English, doc?'; his father died of throat cancer at 58 and he watched it, which he will not volunteer unless you ask what he is worried about; safety net — difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, trouble swallowing, swelling of the face or neck, or a fever — with Cancer Council SA on 13 11 20, a personal phone call with the results, and 'is there someone at home with you?'; variants — a STONY HARD fixed node with a non-healing lateral tongue ulcer and referred ear pain in a smoker over forty makes METASTATIC SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA the leading diagnosis rather than lymphoma; a MIDLINE lump rising on BOTH swallowing and tongue protrusion is a THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST, needing an ultrasound and a TSH to confirm normal thyroid tissue elsewhere before any excision; and a TENDER, MOBILE node with red overlying skin, a temperature of 38.3 and a broken molar with gingival swelling is REACTIVE CERVICAL LYMPHADENITIS FROM DENTAL SEPSIS — urgent dental review and drainage, antibiotics, review in 48 hours, and if the node has not settled once the dental source is treated, it STILL needs investigating

stem: Your next patient is a 32-year-old man who has come to you complaining of low back pain. Tasks: take a focused history for six minutes — at six minutes you are handed a card with the physical examination findings, which you do not perform and do not read aloud — then explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient. 8 minutes total.

The clock rule: still exploring the pain at three minutes? Stop and move to the red flags. You can pass with an incomplete SICORA. You cannot pass having never asked about saddle numbness. Variants: the card shows no deficit, which is non-specific mechanical back pain; and he volunteers a cauda equina symptom at about three minutes.
tasks: Take a focused history for six minutes
Read the physical examination card silently at six minutes
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: Normal, or mild PARASPINAL tenderness — muscle, not midline bone

40° ON THE RIGHT, 60° ON THE LEFT. That is a CROSSED STRAIGHT LEG RAISE — raising the unaffected leg reproduces pain on the affected side. Less sensitive, considerably MORE SPECIFIC for a disc-related radiculopathy. Read it as CONFIRMATION, not confusion. Positive window 30–60° VERIFY
KNEE JERK ABSENT — or ankle jerk reduced on the affected side VERIFY
REDUCED OVER THE MEDIAL CALF AND FOOT — or over the sole
How the card is handed over

At six minutes, and you DO NOT EXAMINE and DO NOT READ IT ALOUD. Ten seconds, silent, take what you need and move on. Recall variation: some recalls report the LEFT leg — take the side from the role-player and stay consistent
VARIANT A — the card shows NO deficit

Tender over the paravertebral muscles, movements restricted by pain, NEUROLOGY NORMAL, SLR NEGATIVE → non-specific mechanical low back pain. THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST IS IDENTICAL — do not shorten it because the diagnosis is benign
VARIANT B — he volunteers a cauda equina symptom

‘I’ve been wetting myself a bit for two days, and the inside of my thighs feels odd when I wipe.’ STOP THE HISTORY. Same-day MRI and neurosurgical referral; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 and the RAH spinal service from MM5. DELAY HERE IS THE AUTOMATIC FAIL

dx: **Lumbar radiculopathy from a disc protrusion in a 32-year-old storeman** — **pain, sensory change or weakness in the distribution of a single lumbosacral nerve root**, caused by compression or irritation of that root as it leaves the spinal canal.

**Say radiculopathy, not sciatica.** ‘Sciatica’ names a symptom; **radiculopathy names the mechanism.** Use the correct term with the examiner and **plain English with the patient**: **‘one of the nerves that leaves your spine and runs down your leg is being squeezed.’**

**Nobody fails for missing the diagnosis — it is written on the card.** They fail because **the differential list is short, generic, or delivered as an undifferentiated stream.** ‘Fractures’ scores nothing; **‘osteoporotic and pathological vertebral fractures’ scores.** **Name the group before its members**, and **aim for fifteen names.**
**The four groups, every back and neck station in this cluster**: **red flags · spinal · arthritis · referred** — and inside red flags, **cancer · cauda equina · infection · myeloma.**

**The three planted distractors — statin, past kidney stones, father's aneurysm — do not change the diagnosis.** They exist so you can **name each and dismiss it with a reason**, which is exactly where the marks sit: **‘You’re on a cholesterol tablet and those can cause muscle aching — but yours is focal and runs into one leg, not a general ache. You’ve had kidney stones — but no burning, no blood in the urine, no fever. And your father’s aneurysm — a swelling of the main blood vessel in the tummy can cause back pain, so I’ll examine your tummy, but nothing in your story suggests it today.’**

**Three reasons drawn from this patient — one from the pain, one from the history, one from the card**: **the sharp radiating pain below the knee is nerve pain not muscle pain · the same leg feels numb, so the nerve is under pressure rather than irritated · lifting the leg reproduced the pain and one reflex was absent.**

**Management: regular paracetamol ± NSAID if not contraindicated** VERIFY **· stay active, advise against bed rest · physiotherapy and graded return · a Work Capacity Certificate with SPECIFIC RESTRICTIONS — no heavy lifting — rather than blanket unfitness · review at 4–6 weeks.** Most improve substantially within **six weeks, with leg pain often the last to go.**

**No imaging in the first six weeks of an uncomplicated radiculopathy — and say so out loud; it is a mark, not an omission.** **‘It does not change management, frequently shows incidental findings, and plain films expose him to unnecessary gonadal radiation and will not show a disc. I would image for red flags, a progressive deficit, or failure of conservative care.’** **Avoid bed rest, opioids first-line, and surgical referral without a progressive deficit.** Evidence for **pregabalin and gabapentin in radiculopathy is weak and Australian guidance has moved away from routine use.** VERIFY

**The safety net, verbatim and named**: **‘Come back immediately, or go to an emergency department, if you get numbness around your back passage or private parts, if you can’t pass urine or start leaking, if the leg becomes weak, or if you develop fevers.’** **Four named symptoms — ‘any questions?’ is not a safety net.**

SA — suspected cauda equina from MM5: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** and spinal services at the **Royal Adelaide Hospital**; **PATS** for metropolitan appointment travel; a work-related injury goes to **ReturnToWorkSA** with a Work Capacity Certificate carrying specific restrictions; **ACCHS** and Aboriginal Liaison Officer with **Closing the Gap** PBS co-payment; **TIS National 131 450.**
plan: **WIPE, open question FIRST** — the role-player is briefed to deliver **two free lines only in response to an open question.** Ask a closed question first and you never get them, **and the examiner watched you not ask.** Then acknowledge and reassure.

**The analgesia offer — eight seconds, not a consultation.** **‘Are you in pain right now? Would you like something for it? I’ll organise some now, and we can keep talking while it’s being arranged.’** No allergies, no what-have-you-tried, no doses.

**SICORA.** **Point to exactly where · out of ten · dull ache or SHARP AND STABBING · when did it start, constant or intermittent, getting worse, IS THIS THE FIRST TIME · does it TRAVEL anywhere, into the buttock, down either leg · anything better or worse · WORSE SITTING OR STANDING · WORSE WHEN YOU COUGH OR SNEEZE · how is it affecting work, sleep and daily life.**

**Pattern of the pain, and the MSK screen — fifteen seconds.** **Night pain, does it wake you · worse in the morning or at the end of the day · worse after resting or after being active · any swelling, any RASH over the back, any stiffness, any injury.** **The rash question is not a throwaway — shingles causes severe unilateral back pain for two to three days before the rash appears.**

**Group 1 — red flags, the block you never sacrifice.** Malignancy and myeloma: **weight loss · appetite · lumps or bumps · more tired · ever treated for a cancer, or anyone in the family · repeated infections · unusually thirsty.**

**The two you never skip**, normalised: **‘Two questions I ask everyone with back pain. Any numbness or pins and needles in your private parts, around the saddle area? And any loss of control of your bladder or your bowels?’** Then infection: **‘Any fevers, chills or night sweats?’**

**Group 2 — spinal, the most commonly dropped questions.** **‘Any numbness or pins and needles in your legs? Any weakness — does the leg give way, or do you catch your toe?’** **You cannot claim a nerve root is under pressure if you never asked whether anything is numb or weak.** Then **occupation and heavy lifting**, and **‘any leg pain when you walk that eases when you stop or lean forward?’**

**Group 3 — arthritis, four questions in one breath**: other joints · family history of arthritis · **rashes, scaly patches on elbows, knees or scalp** · painful red eye · **recent diarrhoea or blood in the stools** · **recent discharge** — reactive arthritis follows a urogenital or GI infection by **one to four weeks.**

**Group 4 — referred; drop this group first if you are behind.** **Burning passing urine · going more often · blood in the urine · tummy pain · nausea or vomiting.** Then **one question, three differentials**: **‘Are you on any medications? In particular any blood thinners, any steroids, or a cholesterol tablet?’** — retroperitoneal haemorrhage, osteoporotic fracture and spinal infection, statin myopathy.
6:00 — card

**Read it silently.** Then **thirty seconds maximum** on the diagnosis in plain English, **three reasons**, **the three distractors named and dismissed**, **the grouped list**, then **plan and the four named return symptoms.** **Over-explaining the disc is how candidates lose the larger mark.**
pefe: **You do not examine — the findings arrive on a card at six minutes, and you must not read it aloud.** Ten seconds, silent.

**The crossed straight leg raise is the line that panics candidates.** ‘SLR 40° right, 60° left’ is **not** bilateral radiculopathy and **not** canal stenosis: **raising the unaffected leg reproduces pain on the affected side.** If asked: **‘it is less sensitive than the standard test but considerably more specific for a disc-related radiculopathy, so it strengthens the diagnosis rather than confusing it.’**

**Root patterns worth recognising**: **L3/L4 — medial calf, knee jerk · L5 — dorsum and big toe, reflexes normal · S1 — sole, ankle jerk.** VERIFY You are **not required to announce a nerve root level** — but recognising that **the deficit matches the symptomatic leg** converts ‘I think it’s a disc’ into a defended diagnosis.

**What you would examine yourself**: **cauda equina screen — saddle sensation, bladder and bowel function, and if concerned anal tone and post-void residual** · **full lower limb neurology — tone, power, reflexes, sensation, gait, plantars** · **abdominal examination including the aorta and the renal angles**, given the distractors in this history.

**Investigations**: **MRI lumbosacral spine** for red flags, progressive deficit or failed conservative care — **the test of choice for cauda equina and for infection.** **FBE, CRP, ESR** if infection or malignancy is suspected; **calcium, ALP, EUC, LFT, EPG and free light chains** for myeloma; **urine dipstick and MSU** given the stone history; **CK only if statin myopathy is genuinely in play** — diffuse aching, not focal back pain.

**Do not miss**: **progressive or bilateral neurological deficit · saddle anaesthesia · urinary retention with overflow · fever with focal midline tenderness · a pulsatile abdominal mass.** **Any one of these turns the station from a consultation into an emergency transfer.**

stem: Version A: a 32-year-old man with low back pain. Version B: a 65-year-old man presenting to general practice with low back pain. Both: take a focused history for six minutes — receive the examination findings on a card — then explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient. 8 minutes total.

The version A card: normal inspection, tenderness over the paravertebral muscles, movements restricted by pain, normal neurology and straight leg raise. The version B card: normal inspection, tenderness over the T10 spinous process, painful thoracic and lumbar movements, normal neurology and straight leg raise. dx: **One stem, two patients.** **Version A — a 32-year-old with a lifting injury: non-specific mechanical low back pain. Version B — a 65-year-old: spinal malignancy.** What separates them is **one answer on history — unintentional weight loss — and one line on the examination card — where the tenderness is.**

**Version A is not an easier station. It is the same station with a reassuring answer, and it is only reassuring because you asked.** **Run the full six-minute structure for both; let the answers, not the patient's age, decide which diagnosis goes on top.**

**A ‘yes’ is the start of a question, not the end of one.** Every positive red flag gets the follow-up ladder: **how many kilos · over what period · were you trying to.** Here: **four to five kilograms over the last few months, unintentional, at 65.**

**The prostate questions move forward in version B.** In a 65-year-old man with weight loss and back pain, **prostate is one of the three commonest primaries to metastasise to bone** — so **stream, nocturia and dribbling** go inside the red flag block rather than waiting for referred pain at the end, **which in a six-minute history you may never reach.** His answer — **up twice a night, poor stream** — turns the list from a recital into **‘prostate first, because of what you told me about your waterworks.’**

**The six primaries, plus myeloma**: **breast · lung · prostate**, then **thyroid · kidney · melanoma**, plus **multiple myeloma — a primary marrow cancer, not a metastasis.** Name all of them; **‘cancer, infection, fracture’ scores nothing.**

**Breaking it — four moves, thirty seconds. Signpost, warn, say it, justify, then stop talking and let him speak.** **‘I’ve asked you a lot of questions and examined your back, and I’ve been thinking about a number of causes. I’m afraid what I have to say isn’t straightforward.’** [pause — two full seconds] **‘I’m concerned there may be a cancer in your spine, or a cancer somewhere else in the body that has spread to it.’**

**Answering ‘are you sure?’**: **‘I’m not certain, and that’s an honest answer. What I am certain of is that this needs sorting out quickly, and I’m not prepared to wait and see. The tests will tell us.’** Then **two reasons**: **the four to five kilos lost without trying, and the tenderness over one particular bone, which points at the bone itself rather than the muscles.**

**Version A — reassure with a timeframe, not a shrug.** ‘It’s nothing to worry about’ is dismissal. **‘What you have is non-specific mechanical back pain — the muscles and small joints beside your spine have been strained and are in spasm. Three things tell me that: the pain stays in your back and doesn’t run down your leg; there’s no numbness or weakness; and the tenderness was in the muscles beside your spine, not on the bones. It is the commonest cause of back pain and most people are much better within four to six weeks.’** **Three negatives are a positive finding — say all three out loud.**

**Version B plan**: **full examination looking for the primary — breast, chest, abdomen, lymph nodes, skin, thyroid, and prostate on rectal examination** · **assess for cord compression — any neurology, any bladder or bowel change** · bloods as above · **MRI whole spine** · **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis** · **urgent referral to a service that can biopsy and stage, telephoned today rather than posted.** Then: **‘Is there someone at home with you — would you like your wife to come in so we can go through this together?’**

**The cord compression safety net, verbatim**: **‘If you develop any weakness or numbness in your legs, any numbness around your back passage, or you can’t pass urine or start leaking — go straight to an emergency department, day or night. Do not wait for the scan.’** **Metastatic spinal cord compression converts an urgent referral into a same-day emergency: MRI whole spine within hours, dexamethasone, and immediate oncology or neurosurgical discussion.** VERIFY SA — **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for time-critical transfer, **PATS** for planned appointments, tertiary oncology and spinal services at the **RAH** and **Flinders**; **ACCHS** and Aboriginal Liaison Officer with **Closing the Gap** co-payment; **TIS National 131 450.**
plan: **Opening — identical in both versions.** WIPE, **open question first**, acknowledge, **offer analgesia.** Version B opens with **‘it’s not shifting’** and **‘my wife made me come in.’**

**SICORA and pattern — ninety seconds, and do not redesign the history because the patient is older.** Site · severity · **dull ache or sharp** · onset, constant, getting worse, first time · **does it travel — into the buttock, down either leg** · better or worse, sitting or standing, coughing · effect on life · **pain at night** · morning or evening · **after rest or after activity.**

**Two version-B answers that should already have your attention, offered BEFORE any red flag question**: **‘Nothing much helps — it’s there whatever I do’** (mechanical pain has a position that eases it; **unremitting pain does not**) and **‘it’s worse at night’** (a classic red flag). **Pick both up out loud when you justify the diagnosis later.**

**The red flag block — where the two versions separate. Seventy seconds, never shortened.** **Lost any weight without trying · appetite · lumps or bumps · more tired · ever been treated for a cancer, or anyone in the family · repeated infections · unusually thirsty · fevers, chills or night sweats** · then **the two you ask everyone: saddle numbness, and bladder or bowel control.**

**Version B: the ‘yes’ arrives — DO NOT MOVE ON. QUANTIFY.** **‘Thank you for telling me — that’s important. How many kilos, roughly? Over what period? And were you trying to lose it — dieting, exercising more?’**

**Version B only — hunting the primary, forty seconds and worth every one.** **Long-standing cough or coughing blood · lumps anywhere including chest or breast · WATERWORKS: stream slower, dribbling at the end, up at night · change in bowel habit or blood in the motions · moles or skin spots that have changed · lumps in the neck or trouble swallowing.**

**Spinal, arthritis and referred, as in the master structure** — leg numbness and weakness, claudication eased by leaning forward, other joints, rashes, eyes, diarrhoea, discharge, urinary symptoms, tummy pain, **medications including blood thinners, steroids and a statin.**
6:00 — card
**Read it silently.** **The palpation line is the discriminator**: paraspinal muscles = mechanical; **one spinous process = bone.** **Neurology normal in both — it separates nothing.**

**Version A**: reassurance **that is earned** — three reasons, **then say that you asked about weight, fevers, cancer and waterworks and they were all clear, ‘which is what lets me tell you this confidently.’** No imaging, and say why. Work certificate with **specific restrictions.** Review **4–6 weeks.**

**Version B**: **signpost → warn → say cancer → two reasons → stop.** Then the differential list **led by the prostate**, then **bloods, MRI whole spine, urgent telephoned referral**, then **the cord compression safety net**, then **‘is there someone at home with you?’**

**‘Neurological examination normal’ appears on both cards and separates nothing.** In version A it is reassuring; **in version B it is irrelevant**, because a deposit that has not yet reached cord or root gives exactly this picture.

**Version B — full examination looking for the primary**: **breast, chest, abdomen, lymph nodes, skin, thyroid, and prostate on rectal examination where appropriate.** Plus **assessment for cord compression — any neurology, any bladder or bowel change.**

Plain films are insensitive early — a normal film does not exclude a deposit.** VERIFY Then **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis** to identify the primary. **Version A gets no imaging in the first six weeks, and saying so is a scored decision, not an omission.**

MODIFIED SCHÖBER 16 cm. Baseline is 15 cm, so this is AN INCREASE OF 1 cm. NORMAL IS 5 cm OR MORE. READ THE INCREASE, NOT THE FINAL NUMBER — ‘16 cm’ means nothing until you subtract the baseline
VERSION A — say the test's name correctly
It is the MODIFIED SCHÖBER TEST. Transcribed recalls render it as the ‘shoulder test’ — THERE IS NO SUCH SPINAL TEST, and using the transcription error in front of the examiner is a fail risk
VERSION B — what you must REQUEST, half one

‘This presented as back pain, so I would still perform a FULL SPINE EXAMINATION.’ General appearance (alert or drowsy, lying still or RESTLESS), all four vitals particularly the TEMPERATURE, inspection, palpation over the SPINOUS PROCESSES, PARASPINAL MUSCLES and SACROILIAC JOINTS, movements, SLR, and lower limb neurology
VERSION B — what you must REQUEST, half two
‘I would then examine the abdomen — palpation for tenderness or masses, and specifically over the kidneys: tender, ballotable?’ MY TWO KEY POINTS ARE RENAL ANGLE TENDERNESS AND A URINE DIPSTICK
VERSION B — what the examiner then gives you
THE SPINE EXAMINATION IS NORMAL. HE IS AFEBRILE. RENAL ANGLE TENDERNESS POSITIVE ON THE RIGHT. URINE DIPSTICK SHOWS BLOOD
A CLEAR DIPSTICK DOES NOT EXCLUDE A STONE — the dipstick-negative proportion is quoted around 10–15 per cent VERIFY
VERSION B — the card that is NOT colic

TEMPERATURE 38.9°C WITH RIGORS, and the dipstick shows blood, LEUCOCYTES AND NITRITES. That is pyelonephritis or an INFECTED OBSTRUCTED SYSTEM — a urological emergency needing DECOMPRESSION, not analgesia and a scan next week. Let the findings choose, not the recall
VERSION C — no examination at all

NO PHYSICAL EXAMINATION IS PROVIDED. The finding that would settle it has been DELIBERATELY WITHHELD — no weight loss, no neurological deficit, a normal mammogram. You are marked on the breadth of the history and on YOUR WILLINGNESS TO COMMIT, not on being right
VERSION C — what you would arrange

Spine and lower limbs including SLR and neurology · PLAIN FILMS OF THE THORACOLUMBAR SPINE given the possibility of a crush fracture · FBE, ESR, CALCIUM and ALP · urine dipstick given the stone history · MRI if the films are normal and you remain concerned · and a BONE DENSITY SCAN with a fracture-risk review

dx: **Three versions of one stem, and what changes is which single element is being examined**: **version A — reading a special test** (ankylosing spondylitis); **version B — requesting the right examination** (renal colic); **version C — committing to an answer** (deliberately unresolved).

**Version B is the one candidates fail — and they fail it AFTER getting the diagnosis right.** They worked out renal colic and were then asked what examination they would perform, and **asked only for the abdomen and kidneys.** **It is still a back pain presentation. Ask for one and you land on a three.**

**Version A — ankylosing spondylitis.** A chronic seronegative spondyloarthropathy causing **inflammatory back and buttock pain with progressive restriction of spinal movement, typically beginning before 45.** **Ten years of recurrent back pain in a young man is chronic inflammatory disease until proven otherwise — chronicity is the clue, not the comfort.**

**The inflammatory pattern, asked in full**: **worse in the morning · how long before you loosen up (over 30 minutes) · worse after resting or sitting still · better with exercise · buttock pain that swaps sides · wakes him in the second half of the night.** **Night pain is not one thing** — in A it is inflammatory and **improves once he gets up and moves**; in C it is a red flag, **unremitting and not relieved by position.** **Ask what happens when he gets up.**

**Version A management: exercise IS the treatment, not an adjunct** — daily spinal extension and mobility work, and physiotherapy experienced in spondyloarthritis — **with regular NSAIDs first-line.** VERIFY Bloods **FBE, CRP, ESR, HLA-B27** (supports, does not confirm — common in healthy people and absent in a minority); **sacroiliac X-ray first, MRI SIJ if the X-ray is normal and suspicion is high, because radiographic change lags years behind symptoms.** Biologics for inadequate response. **Smoking cessation — smoking accelerates radiographic progression, Quitline 13 7848.** **Safety net: a painful red eye with blurred vision or photophobia is acute anterior uveitis and needs same-day ophthalmology, not chloramphenicol.**

**Version B — renal (ureteric) colic.** Four minutes only, so **the order must change.** **Say the redirect out loud**: **‘The way you’ve described that — one-sided, coming in spasms, and travelling to your flank and groin — makes me want to ask about your waterworks first.’** That tells the examiner you reshuffled **deliberately** rather than by accident.

**Version B management**: **analgesia is the priority — an NSAID first-line unless contraindicated**, opioid if insufficient VERIFY · antiemetic · **urine dipstick and MSU; FBE, EUC, CRP, calcium and urate** · **non-contrast CT KUB is the first-line imaging test** (ultrasound first in pregnancy and children) · **strain the urine and send any stone for analysis.** **Urgent urology — do not manage in the community: fever with obstruction, a solitary or transplanted kidney, bilateral obstruction, acute kidney injury, or pain not controlled by adequate analgesia.**

**Version C — the grey zone.** **The most defensible top diagnosis is lumbar radiculopathy, with osteoporotic vertebral fracture a strong second — and any of several answers passes provided it is reasoned.** **‘I can’t say without examining her’ fails. So does four diagnoses with equal weight.**

**Version C's extra block, which nobody asks**: **‘When did you have your last period? Any flushes or sweats around that time? Have you ever taken hormone replacement? Ever had a bone density scan, or been told your bones are thin? Have you lost any height? Any steroid tablets, ever? Do you smoke?’** **A post-menopausal woman who never took HRT, whose pain began as she stood up from gardening, is the classic candidate for an osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture — minimal force, sudden onset.**

**Committing, the script**: **‘Back pain can come from a number of different places, and I want to be honest with you that I can’t be certain today. But if you ask me what I think is most likely, it is a lumbar radiculopathy — a nerve leaving the lower spine that is being irritated or pressed on. I say that because the pain travels down one leg, and that pattern is typical of a nerve rather than a muscle.’** Then **name and dismiss the rest — the standing-up mechanism and post-menopausal bone loss, the past kidney stones, the mother's breast cancer with her own normal mammograms.**
plan: **Opening — identical in all three versions.** WIPE, **open question first**, acknowledge, offer analgesia. **Version B explicitly briefs the role-player to voice concern — reflect it back before you start asking questions.** It is a scored communication item and **costs eight seconds even in a four-minute station.**

**Version A — the answer that should change your track in the first sentence**: **‘On and off for about ten years now — it's nothing new for me.’** **Stop racing through SICORA and move the arthritis group forward.**

**The inflammatory pattern block, in full** — morning stiffness and its duration, worse after rest, better with exercise, **alternating buttock pain**, second-half-of-the-night waking. **Ask them even if the recall reports the stiffness question answered vaguely — you are marked on asking.**

**The trigger and the extra-articular screen**: **painful red eye or blurred vision · scaly rashes on elbows, knees or scalp · diarrhoea or blood in the stools · pain in the heel or sole · family history of arthritis or psoriasis.**

**Version B — SICORA, fast.** The three answers that redirect you: **site ‘right side of my mid to low back’ · character ‘it's a spasm-like pain’ · radiation ‘to my right flank’ / ‘to my groin’.** Then **name the redirect out loud.**

**KUB block, moved to the FRONT of the queue**: **burning or stinging passing urine · passing urine more often or up at night · blood in the urine, pink, red or tea-coloured · difficulty starting or dribbling at the end · FEVERS, CHILLS OR SHAKES · nausea or vomiting · ever had a kidney stone.**

**Then the rest in priority order, whatever time is left**: **malignancy including renal cancer** given where the pain is · infection (covered by the fever question) · **cauda equina — two questions, thirty seconds, never dropped however short the station** · radiculopathy — leg numbness and weakness · mechanical and arthritis last.

**‘What physical examination would you like to perform?’ — the single highest-value 45 seconds in this pair.** **Spine first, then abdomen and KUB, and say why you want both.** If you are running out of time, **say the two halves as headings with the key points inside each — that alone earns the mark.** If the bell goes mid-list: **‘I'd have gone on to ask about the arthritis group and the remaining referred causes.’** Naming what you would have asked salvages part of the mark; silence salvages nothing.

**Version C — the standard structure, then the trigger.** **‘Was there anything that started it off?’** → she stood up after gardening. **‘Have you had back pain before, and how does this compare?’** → worse this time. **‘Does it affect your sleep?’** → not letting her sleep at night.

**The menopause and bone-health block — ask it in every older woman with back pain, and only in older women.** Then **the two planted items to name and dismiss: past kidney stones, and her mother's breast cancer with her own normal mammograms.** Then **commit, with a reason beside it, and name the rest.**
pefe: **Version A — read the card, do not recite it.** The **modified Schöber**: mark a line joining the **posterior superior iliac spines**, a point **5 cm below** and a point **10 cm above**, giving a **15 cm baseline**; on full forward flexion that distance should **increase by at least 5 cm.** **An increase of 1 cm is markedly restricted lumbar flexion.** VERIFY

**Version B — the discriminating issue of this entire pair is the examination request.** **Half one: a full spine examination.** **Half two: abdomen and KUB.** **Two key points, verbatim: renal angle tenderness, and a urine dipstick.** If you name nothing else in the abdominal half, name those two.

**Renal colic or pyelonephritis?** **Colic: colicky, cannot lie still, AFEBRILE, dipstick blood only.** **Pyelonephritis: constant loin ache, FEBRILE AND RIGORING, renal angle tenderness, dipstick blood + leucocytes + nitrites.** **Restlessness is characteristic of colic — a patient with peritonitis lies rigidly still.**

**Version A investigations**: **FBE, CRP, ESR, HLA-B27**; **plain X-ray of the sacroiliac joints first, MRI sacroiliac joints if the X-ray is normal and clinical suspicion is high.** Rheumatology referral. **Screen for osteoporosis despite the stiff spine, and for cardiovascular risk.**

Pain across the lower back, worse on bending and by the end of the day, eased by lying down. No leg pain, numbness or weakness. No trauma, fever, weight loss, bladder or bowel change, or cancer history. Tasks: explain the most likely diagnosis to the patient — and discuss your management with the patient.

Examination: afebrile with normal observations, lumbar paraspinal tenderness with painful restriction of flexion, negative straight leg raise and normal lower limb neurology. Variants: lumbar radiculopathy; six weeks on and still off work; and the cauda equina emergency.

dx: **The seven bullets, in order: reassure · stay active · pain relief · physiotherapy · NO IMAGING, and say why · work with modified duties · review at 2–4 weeks with a named safety net.** **Ninety seconds. Bullets five and six are the two candidates omit, and they are the two the examiner is waiting for.**

**THE discriminating issue: never say ‘rest’ without ‘but keep doing your usual daily activities’ in the same breath.** **‘Rest from the thing that set it off — so no heavy lifting for now — but I want you up and moving and doing your usual day-to-day things.’** **Practise the two halves as one unbreakable sentence so they cannot be separated under pressure.**

**Reassurance is the treatment, not the preamble.** **‘The problem is in the muscles, ligaments and small joints of your back — it is not a problem with the bones, and I've specifically checked for and ruled out the serious causes. Backs are strong. HURTING IS NOT THE SAME AS HARMING. And this will get better.’** **Never ‘it's JUST a muscle strain’** — *just* is heard as dismissal by a man in pain who is frightened for his job.

**The two clocks, not to be mixed**: **mechanical — conservative 4–6 weeks before reassessing. Radiculopathy — conservative 6–8 weeks before considering surgical referral. BOTH — review the patient at 2–4 weeks regardless.** Escalate immediately at any point for a **progressive deficit or cauda equina symptoms.**

**Drugs**: **NSAID first line — ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food, short course** VERIFY (check renal function, blood pressure, peptic ulcer disease and asthma). **Paracetamol optional — Australian randomised evidence found no benefit over placebo in acute low back pain**, so offer it but do not present it as effective. VERIFY **Heat is cheap, safe and modestly effective — recommend it.**

**AVOID opioids — Australian randomised evidence found them no better than placebo for acute low back and neck pain, with more harm.** VERIFY **AVOID pregabalin and gabapentin — no benefit over placebo in sciatica with substantial adverse effects.** VERIFY **Muscle relaxants rarely: limited evidence, sedation, dependence risk.** If he asks for something stronger: **‘there's good Australian research showing opioids are no better than a dummy tablet for back pain like yours, and they cause drowsiness, constipation and dependence. What actually shifts this is keeping moving and the physio.’**

**CORRECTION on certificates — the source teaches a medical certificate and time off at home, which contradicts the stay-active advice given in the same breath.** **Time away from work is one of the strongest predictors of long-term disability in back pain, and the risk rises with the duration of absence.** The evidence-based instrument is **a work capacity certificate specifying what he CAN do**, not a sickness certificate. **Total incapacity is reserved for jobs that cannot be modified at all, and then for days.**

**The safety net is a marked item, not a formality**: **‘Come back the same day, or go to the emergency department, if you get numbness between your legs or around your back passage; trouble passing urine, or not feeling when you need to go; any loss of control of your bowels; weakness in both legs; a fever; or if the pain suddenly becomes much worse.’** **Cauda equina is the one outcome here where a delay of hours produces permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.**

**Five versions, same seven bullets, differently loaded.** **B — radiculopathy: same plan, 6–8 weeks, add an image-guided epidural corticosteroid injection as an option and name the spinal surgical service as the escalation.** **C — demands a scan: the incidental-findings explanation, then the criteria that would change your mind.** **D — not better at six weeks: re-check red flags, screen yellow flags, address fear-avoidance, graded return to work, and only now consider imaging.** **E — the red flag: cauda equina. Immediate transfer, urgent MRI, emergency surgical referral, nil by mouth.** VERIFY

SA — **ReturnToWorkSA**: a lifting injury at work is a claim; complete a work capacity certificate specifying **capacity, not incapacity**, and engage the employer's return-to-work coordinator early. **SafeWork SA** if the workplace manual handling is generating injuries. **MM5: MRI is not available locally — book through the regional service or refer to Adelaide with PATS; suspected cauda equina is a TRANSFER, not a booking — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.** CORRECTION — **both neurosurgical and orthopaedic spinal services manage lumbar disc disease in Australia; refer to whichever spinal service your region uses rather than assuming one specialty.** **ACCHS** and Aboriginal Liaison Officer with **Closing the Gap** co-payment; **TIS 131 450.**
plan: **The diagnosis first, 25 seconds — as a MECHANISM, not as ‘just a strain’.** Muscles, ligaments and small joints; not the bones; serious causes specifically checked for and ruled out; **hurting is not the same as harming**; and it will get better.
**Bullet 1 — signpost.** **‘Let me tell you what I'd like to do about it — there are a few parts to the plan.’** Signposting buys you structure and stops the task becoming a lecture.

**Bullet 2 — STAY ACTIVE, one unbreakable sentence.** Rest from the trigger, **but keep doing your usual day-to-day things — walking, the shopping, getting out. Not lying in bed or on the couch.** Then defend it when he pushes: **‘It's the opposite of what most people expect, and it used to be what doctors said. Lying still stiffens you up, weakens the muscles that support your back and prolongs the pain. Moving hurts a bit at first — that's expected, and it isn't doing damage.’**
**Bullet 3 — pain relief.** **NSAID with food, short course** · paracetamol as an option **with the honest caveat** · **heat** · and **decline anything stronger with the reason**, not just a refusal.

**Bullet 4 — allied health.** Physiotherapy for **stretching, strengthening and the confidence to move** — **the part with the best evidence, both for getting better and for preventing recurrence.** Massage or manual therapy is reasonable **alongside the exercise, not instead of it.**

**Bullet 5 — NO IMAGING, said OUT LOUD.** **‘If we scanned the backs of everyone in this waiting room — including the people with no pain at all — we'd find bulging discs, worn joints and little tears in nearly all of them. It's a normal part of getting older, a bit like grey hair. So a scan would very likely show something, that something probably wouldn't be causing your pain, and it wouldn't change what we do — but it might leave you frightened of your own back.’** Then **name what WOULD make you scan.**

**Hold the line when he pushes**: **‘How do you know mine isn't serious without looking?’** → **‘Because of what you've told me and what I found examining you. The things that would worry me are a fever, weight loss, a history of cancer, numbness between the legs, trouble with your waterworks or weakness in your legs. You have none of them, and your nerve examination is completely normal.’**

**Bullet 6 — work.** **‘I'd rather keep you at work than sign you off, because staying at work is part of getting better.’** A certificate for **modified duties — no heavy lifting, the chance to change position — for the next couple of weeks.** If the employer can't manage it, review. **And the ReturnToWorkSA claim, done today.**

**The hidden agenda.** His father **hurt his back at the abattoir and never worked again**, and he is frightened the same thing is happening. **Ask what is worrying him — or he volunteers it after the work discussion.** Then **separate his situation from his father's**: no nerve damage, no serious cause, and **the single best thing for keeping him in work long term is staying in it now, in some form.**

**Bullet 7 — review at 2–4 weeks, then the safety net in plain English, then STOP.** **‘Does that all make sense — anything you'd like me to go over?’** Write it down for him. **Running over means losing the safety net, and the safety net is the marked item.**

**The rule, in one paragraph**: **do not image mechanical, non-specific low back pain — not an X-ray, not a CT, not an MRI.** It does not improve outcomes, delivers radiation for no benefit with plain films and CT, and **reliably produces findings that are present in asymptomatic people of the same age.**

**Do not image lumbar radiculopathy early either.** If the history and examination have established a root lesion, **an early scan does not change management, which is conservative for six to eight weeks.** **Image when surgery is genuinely on the table** — the scan is then a **surgical planning tool rather than a diagnostic one.**

**When you DO image**: **any red flag** — suspected cauda equina, malignancy, infection or fracture · **a progressive or severe neurological deficit** — a worsening foot drop, not a stable patch of numbness · **failure of conservative management at the end of the window**, where the patient would accept surgery or an injection · **diagnostic uncertainty that genuinely changes the plan.**

**The honest test**: **what would I do differently on Monday if the scan were abnormal? If the answer is nothing, it is not an investigation.** **MRI is the modality where imaging is indicated**, because it shows the disc, the root and the cord; **CT is the alternative where MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, and is the test for suspected fracture.**

**The reassessment at 4–6 weeks is not just ‘extend the certificate’.** **Re-check the red flags — they were negative ten days ago, they are not negative forever; a malignancy or an infection can declare itself between visits.** Then **screen the yellow flags formally — they predict chronicity better than any imaging finding, and they are treatable.**

**Version B adds an image-guided epidural corticosteroid injection** for persisting severe radicular pain — short-term benefit, referred and performed under image guidance. VERIFY **Surgery comes late, for specific indications, and most people never need it — do not promise it.**
