dx: **Acute right C6 cervical radiculopathy, most likely a lateral disc protrusion at C5/6**, in a 40-year-old teacher two days after a weekend painting ceilings overhead. **The label follows the deficit, not the recall.**

**The premature-closure trap this case was built to punish**: old recalls record the answer as ‘cervical spondylosis’, and candidates say it even when the card in their hand describes **a numb thumb and weak elbow flexion.** CORRECTION — **spondylosis is simply osteoarthritis of the spine and is a fine diagnosis for mechanical neck pain with normal neurology. It is the WRONG diagnosis when there is an objective root-level deficit.** If challenged: **‘degenerative change may well be present and may even be the underlying cause of the foraminal narrowing, but the diagnosis I have to act on is the radiculopathy, because that is what the sensory loss over the thumb and the weak elbow flexion demonstrate.’**

**Localise the root — the only table you need.** **C5 lateral shoulder · shoulder abduction · biceps jerk. C6 THUMB · ELBOW FLEXION and wrist extension · BICEPS AND SUPINATOR. C7 middle finger · elbow extension and wrist flexion · triceps. C8 little finger · finger flexion · no reliable reflex. T1 medial upper arm · finger abduction.** **The sentence that scores is the one that joins them: ‘those two findings belong to the same single nerve root.’**

**Radicular versus referred**: radicular pain **travels below the elbow in a band and comes with numbness, tingling or weakness.** Referred pain from a facet joint or muscle is **a diffuse ache over the shoulder and upper arm with no neurological symptoms and no clear border.** **Naming that distinction out loud is worth more than any single question.**

**THE discriminating issue: screen for cervical myelopathy OUT LOUD, then cite the negative when you explain.** It is **the neck equivalent of saddle anaesthesia in low back pain**, it costs fifteen seconds, and **its absence is visible to the examiner twice — when you fail to ask, and again when your differential cannot say why myelopathy is unlikely.**

**Three corrections to how myelopathy is usually taught**: **(1) it is usually NOT acute and usually NOT a disc** — the commonest cause is **degenerative cervical myelopathy** developing over months to years; **(2) the legs are usually numb and clumsy, NOT painful** — leg pain is a radiculopathy or claudication feature; **(3) LOSS OF HAND DEXTERITY is the earliest and most useful symptom, earlier than bladder involvement, which is a LATE sign.** **Asking only about bladder and bowel will miss the diagnosis you are screening for.**

**Explaining it to her, plain English first**: **‘One of the nerves that leaves your spine in the neck and runs down your arm is being squeezed. The usual cause is a small tear in one of the cushions between the bones — a disc — where some of the softer centre bulges out and presses on the nerve as it comes out. Two days of painting with your head back is exactly the sort of thing that sets it off.’** **Never say the jargon version to Jenny — that is a sentence for the examiner.**

**Management**: **analgesia offered at minute one, not at the end** · **NSAID, ibuprofen 400–600 mg up to three times daily with food, shortest effective course** VERIFY · **keep the neck moving rather than resting it** · **NO COLLAR — it relieves briefly, then deconditions** · physiotherapy and graded return · **review at two weeks.** **AVOID pregabalin and gabapentin — Australian randomised evidence found no benefit over placebo in radicular pain with substantial adverse effects.** VERIFY **Most are much better within about six weeks; the great majority settle within three months without an operation.** VERIFY

**No imaging in the first six weeks without red flags or a progressive deficit — say it out loud, it is a marked point.** **‘A scan now would show wear and tear that nearly everyone over forty has. It wouldn't change what we do, and it can leave people frightened of a picture rather than reassured by how they're feeling.’** **MRI cervical spine is the test if imaging becomes indicated** — red flags, progressive or severe deficit, myelopathic features, or failure at six weeks. **Plain films only for suspected fracture, instability, or before manipulation in rheumatoid arthritis.**

**The hidden agenda: her mother's breast cancer went to her bones and her neck.** **Answer it with the specific negatives you elicited, not with blanket reassurance**: **‘Nothing you've told me points that way — no weight loss, no lumps, no pain waking you at night, and you've never had cancer yourself. A relative's breast cancer doesn't cause a spread in you.’** **Never ‘it's definitely not cancer’ — say that and add a review date.** SA — **MM5: MRI not available locally, book through the regional service or refer to Adelaide with PATS; urgent MRI means transfer, not a waiting list.** Cord compression → **RAH neurosurgical service, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.** **Significant upper limb weakness affects vehicle control — advise against driving and document it** (Motor Vehicles Act 1959 SA). **ACCHS**, Closing the Gap, **TIS 131 450.**
plan: **WIPE and open question**, then **acknowledge the distress before questioning.** **Then the analgesia offer — ten words, one mark, and it changes the tone of the whole consultation**: **‘Before we start — are you in pain right now? Would you like something for it?’**

**SICORA, SITE FIRST — ‘is it at the FRONT of your neck or the BACK?’** **The answer changes the entire differential structure**, and in version C this one question saves the station. Then severity, character, onset and what she was doing, constant or intermittent, getting better or worse, ever before.

**The question that makes the diagnosis**: **‘Does the pain travel anywhere — into your shoulder, your arm, your hand? WHICH FINGERS? Any pins and needles, numbness or weakness in that arm?’** **‘My hand tingles’ localises nothing. ‘Thumb and index’ is C6 and it makes the diagnosis for you.**

**Pattern of pain — three questions, never skipped**: **wakes you at night · worse in the morning or the end of the day · worse with activity or worse after rest · morning stiffness and how long.** Then **say what you just learned**: **‘so it's worse with activity and eases with rest, and the stiffness is short — that fits a mechanical pattern.’** The examiner hears you reasoning, not collecting.

**General MSK screen, four quick questions**: swelling · redness or rash · **stiffness AND ITS DURATION — the highest-yield of the four, separating mechanical from inflammatory in one question** · any injury, even minor.

**Red flag block one — malignancy.** Weight loss · appetite · lumps · unusually tired · **ever diagnosed with any cancer, anyone in the family** · cough or haemoptysis · **tailored: ‘ever had a breast lump, or been called back from a mammogram?’** · smoking. CORRECTION — in a man ask about **a known prostate diagnosis or a previous PSA**, not nocturia, which is non-specific BPH.

**Red flag block two — infection, then meningitis in the same breath.** Fevers, chills, night sweats · recent infections, skin infections, dental work · diabetes · steroids · injecting drug use. Then **headache, nausea or vomiting, photophobia, rash.** **Neck stiffness is not neck pain — meningitis gives painful resistance to passive flexion with fever and systemic illness.**

**Red flag block three — CERVICAL MYELOPATHY, four questions word for word.** **‘Have you had any problems with your walking — any unsteadiness or falls? Any loss of control of your bladder or bowel? Have your hands become clumsy — buttons, keys, handwriting, dropping things? When you bend your neck forward, do you get any electric-shock feeling down your back?’** If she asks why: **‘there's a more serious condition where the pressure is on the spinal cord itself rather than a single nerve, and your answers tell me that isn't what's happening.’**

**Spine group, then arthritis, then referred.** Occupation, desk or overhead work, **anything out of the ordinary in the last week** — *she painted the ceilings, so repeat it back so the examiner hears you registered it.* Then other joints, family arthritis, scaly rash and nail changes, diarrhoea or blood in stools, dysuria or discharge. Then **headaches and stress, EXERTIONAL CHEST PAIN OR BREATHLESSNESS, shoulder and hip girdle stiffness.**

**SADMA, then ideas concerns and expectations — this is where the hidden agenda lives.** **You will not run out of time in this station**: neck pain has a shorter differential than low back pain and most candidates finish the nine blocks at about 5:30. **Spend the spare thirty seconds on ‘anything you were particularly worried this might be?’** Then at 6:00 **ask for the card, read it silently, and say what it MEANS before you say what it IS.**

**Read the card out loud before you speak to her, and say the meaning first**: **‘a sensory deficit in the thumb and weak elbow flexion — the same nerve root.’** Candidates who skim the card and announce a diagnosis lose the reasoning mark.

**If the examiner notes the card never said Spurling was positive**: **‘it described restriction of rotation and lateral flexion by pain, which is the position Spurling's test reproduces. The finding I am relying on is the objective root-level deficit.’** **Spurling is specific ~90%, sensitive ~30–60%.** VERIFY

**Say you would complete the neurological examination and the myelopathy screen yourself even when the findings arrive on a card**, and **document the root — the dermatome, the myotome and the reflex.**

**Investigations — version B asks for them explicitly, and the answer is CONDITIONAL, not ‘none’**: **‘In an uncomplicated first presentation I would not image today. If imaging were indicated — red flags, a progressive or severe deficit, myelopathic features, or failure at six weeks — the investigation of choice is MRI cervical spine, because it shows the disc, the nerve root and the cord. A plain X-ray has a limited role — suspected fracture or instability. If red flags were present I would add FBE, ESR, CRP, calcium, ALP and protein electrophoresis.’** **A shopping list including rheumatoid factor, ANA, HLA-B27 and nerve conduction studies reads as uncertainty.**

**Never manipulate the neck** where there is **myelopathy, suspected dissection, or rheumatoid arthritis with possible atlanto-axial instability** — and **ask about RA before any manipulation or intubation.**

**The safety net, in her words**: **‘Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if the weakness in your arm gets worse, if you start dropping things, if your walking becomes unsteady, if you have any trouble controlling your bladder or bowel, if you develop a fever, or if the pain becomes severe and sudden with a headache. I'll see you in two weeks regardless.’**

**The sweep, seven groups, two or three questions each.** **Prostate** — nocturia and how many times, difficulty starting, weak stream, dribbling, incomplete emptying, haematuria. **Lung** — cough or breathlessness beyond baseline, haemoptysis, **smoking in pack-years (here 20 a day for 30 years = 30 PACK-YEARS, quit 12 years ago)**, **and occupation now AND before retirement** — on Yorke Peninsula that earns its keep: **the Moonta and Wallaroo copper mines and smelters, farm chemicals, asbestos in older sheds, silos and fibro housing.** Add **‘were you ever around asbestos or dust at work?’**

**Thyroid** — neck swelling, voice change, trouble swallowing, heat or cold intolerance. **Kidney** — haematuria, loin pain. **Skin** — a changing mole, a skin cancer cut out, sun exposure. **Bowel** — pain, change in habit, blood or black motions, **the screening kit.** **Blood** — bone pain elsewhere, recurrent infections, **thirst, constipation, confusion** (hypercalcaemia).

**Background, only if the clock allows — thirty seconds.** **‘Your COPD and anaemia — when were you diagnosed, what treatment, who reviews them, any admissions?’** **They are not scenery**: unexplained anaemia with a bone lesion points at **marrow infiltration, myeloma, or occult GI blood loss**, and **a COPD patient can still develop lung cancer** with breathlessness blamed on the wrong disease for years. **If you are behind, skip it and tell the examiner you would have taken it.**
**Task 2 — explain the report.** Name the test, then the finding, in plain words. Then **warning shot → pause → the word → ‘this is not a diagnosis’ → stop talking.**
**Task 3 — the most likely diagnosis with THREE REASONS, then the differentials in plain English**, including **at least one benign and one infective cause.**

**Task 4 — the operation FIRST, with two reasons and a pain plan.** Then **how we confirm it and what each test is for**: today — examination including DRE and the neck lump, bloods including **PSA, calcium and a myeloma screen**; this week — **MRI spine, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bone scan**; then **a sample, most likely from the neck lump.** Then **urgent urology and medical oncology, and an MDT.**

**The last thirty seconds carry marks.** **Red flags** — leg weakness or numbness, trouble passing urine or holding on, saddle numbness, **a band of pain around the chest** → same day. **Written information with the practice number and Cancer Council SA 13 11 20** · **PATS for Adelaide** · **‘is there someone you'd like with you next time? I'm happy to go through it again with Beryl’** (*‘I haven't told her anything yet’* → **‘then let's do it together’**) · **review in a week.** **And no moralising about the smoking.**
pefe: **No film and no examination findings are given — the report is on the desk.** What is scored is **what you would examine and what you would order**, and both must look for **spread**.

**Examine: the cord compression screen first** — power, sensation, reflexes, plantars, **saddle sensation and anal tone** — then **for the primary**: DRE, **cervical and supraclavicular nodes**, breasts, **full skin survey including the back**, chest, abdomen, testes.

**CORRECTION — do not overclaim the neck node.** The source concludes from a left-sided node that this is prostate. **A left supraclavicular (Virchow) node classically drains the abdomen and chest — stomach, pancreas, lung, lymphoma — and only uncommonly prostate.** If challenged: **‘I used the node as evidence of systemic malignancy rather than of prostate specifically. A left supraclavicular node would push me to look hard at the abdomen and chest as well — and it is the most accessible site to biopsy.’**

**Analgesia today** — regular paracetamol, add an opioid for significant bone pain; **avoid NSAIDs by reflex in an anaemic, comorbid 72-year-old.** And **cancel the theatre booking and tell the surgical unit yourself.**

**Do not miss**: **metastatic spinal cord compression** (new weakness, a sensory level, sphincter change or band-like pain = **same-day MRI and same-day discussion with neurosurgery or radiation oncology**, with high-dose corticosteroid on specialist advice VERIFY ) · **hypercalcaemia of malignancy** — corrected calcium today · **impending long-bone fracture** — ask about hip and thigh pain, a painful femoral deposit may need prophylactic fixation · **infection dressed as tumour** — fever and rigors mean **blood cultures before antibiotics.**

**If the examiner pushes**: *‘why not do the hip and investigate afterwards?’* → **‘an undiagnosed malignancy raises anaesthetic and thrombotic risk, the T5 lesion is a hazard during positioning, and treatment may need to start before the joint is addressed.’** *‘What if the PSA is normal?’* → **‘that makes prostate less likely but does not exclude it, and does not remove the need for tissue. I'd broaden the search, not stop it.’** VERIFY

**If the role-player gives you nothing** — some briefs are written with every answer negative — **do not invent a primary**: **‘I haven't found a clear source today, which happens. We then look with scans, and if we still can't find it we take a sample from the abnormal area itself.’** **Then still answer the operation question — that decision does not depend on knowing the primary.**

SA — Wallaroo is **Yorke and Northern LHN, MM5**: imaging beyond plain film and specialist review mean travel, so **arrange PATS at this visit, not later**; tertiary referral to **RAH, TQEH or FMC** by unit; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** and the RFDS for retrieval; **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20**; **TIS 131 450**; Aboriginal Liaison Officer or ACCHS and Closing the Gap. Advance care planning is right to raise **later, once a diagnosis exists** — in SA that is an **Advance Care Directive under the Advance Care Directives Act 2013.**

stem: Your general practice, regional South Australia. Daniel Hartley, 38, presents complaining of headache and neck pain. Temperature 36.7, heart rate 74, BP 132/84, respiratory rate 14, saturations 99 per cent — and he looks tired. Tasks: take a history for six minutes — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings on a card, with no further questions afterwards — then explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient.

8 minutes. Variants: a thunderclap episode three days ago, which is subarachnoid haemorrhage; sudden one-sided neck pain with a droopy eyelid after chiropractic manipulation, which is arterial dissection; daily Nurofen plus, which is medication-overuse headache; and a woman over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw claudication, which is giant cell arteritis.
tasks: Take a history for six minutes
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings on the card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: What to ASK FOR, by name

Blood pressure AND FUNDOSCOPY — both free, both marked, both routinely omitted · cranial nerves · limbs and gait · TEMPORAL ARTERIES · and for the neck: RANGE OF MOVEMENT, PARAVERTEBRAL AND TRAPEZIUS TENDERNESS, and WHETHER PRESSURE OVER THE UPPER CERVICAL SPINE REPRODUCES HIS HEADACHE. After the card, NO FURTHER QUESTIONS to the patient
NORMAL — NO PAPILLOEDEMA. This is the finding that answers his father's brain tumour
Tone, power, reflexes and coordination normal. GAIT NORMAL
NORMAL AND PULSATILE. He is 38 — in the 68-year-old version this row reads THICKENED, TENDER AND PULSELESS
FULL RANGE OF MOVEMENT with discomfort at end range · MARKED TENDERNESS OF THE PARAVERTEBRAL AND TRAPEZIUS MUSCLES BILATERALLY · NO MIDLINE BONY TENDERNESS · no lymphadenopathy · NO MENINGISM
Interpret the card BEFORE you name the diagnosis

‘So the only abnormality is tender neck muscles. The fundi, cranial nerves, limbs and gait are all normal, and there is no meningism and no bony tenderness. That combination excludes the serious causes and points to a muscular origin.’

B — NECK STIFFNESS, PHOTOPHOBIA, DROWSY BUT ROUSABLE, no focal deficit → subarachnoid haemorrhage. C — PTOSIS AND MIOSIS on the painful side, NO ANHIDROSIS, otherwise normal → internal carotid dissection. D — normal examination with mild paravertebral tenderness → medication-overuse headache. E — THICKENED, TENDER, PULSELESS TEMPORAL ARTERY with proximal girdle tenderness → giant cell arteritis with polymyalgia rheumatica

dx: **Tension-type headache** — bilateral, **pressing or tightening**, mild to moderate, **not aggravated by routine physical activity**, without vomiting, with **at most one of photophobia or phonophobia.** **Pericranial muscle tenderness is the physical sign, and it is exactly what the card describes.**

**A simple diagnosis wrapped in a deliberately awkward stem. The marks are not in the answer — almost everyone says tension headache — they are in whether you worked BOTH lists.** The neck pain was added because the plain headache version was too easy.

**The two complaints are not coincidental; they are the same problem seen from two ends.** **Cervicogenic headache is a GROUP, not a diagnosis — every cause of neck pain sits inside it** — and tension-type headache **arises from sustained contraction of the very neck muscles you are being asked about.**

**SAY THE WORD CERVICOGENIC OUT LOUD.** It is **the single word that tells the examiner you understood why both complaints were in the stem.** The patient-facing differential run, serious first: **‘a bleed around the brain — that comes on like a thunderclap, yours builds up slowly; a tear in one of the arteries in the neck — sudden one-sided neck pain and often a droopy eyelid, you have neither; an infection of the lining of the brain — but you have no fever, rash or light sensitivity; pressure inside the head, from a growth for example — that would be worse on waking or coughing, with vomiting or a change in vision, and the backs of your eyes are normal.’** Then **‘migraine, which throbs, worsens with activity and makes you feel sick; and cluster, which sits around one eye and makes it water.’** Then **‘headaches coming from the neck itself — we call those cervicogenic: wear and tear in the neck joints, arthritis, a trapped nerve. Your neck moves fully, no other joints are involved and you have no arm symptoms — but the muscular cause I've described sits at the mild end of that same group.’**

**The two red flags that live in the overlap.** **(1) Subarachnoid haemorrhage** — headache with neck pain is its signature, because blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the meninges. **CORRECTION — the source drops SAH from this list because tension headache is likelier. Likelihood is not safety. It stays on the list.** **(2) Cervical artery dissection** — sudden unilateral neck pain with headache after minor trauma, heavy lifting or **neck manipulation**, with **Horner syndrome on the painful side.** It is **a leading cause of stroke in the under-fifties.**

**One question decides whether this is a GP problem or an emergency**: **‘How quickly did it come on — how long from feeling normal to the worst it got?’** **Duration tells you the pattern; SPEED OF ONSET is what finds the bleed.** **Severity alone does not do it — plenty of tension headaches are described as the worst ever.** If asked about severity: **‘the question is the speed of onset. If that is under a minute I would treat it as a subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.’**

**The three questions that separate the primary headaches**: **worse on routine activity?** yes → migraine, no → tension-type · **vomiting?** → migraine, raised pressure or an emergency, not tension-type · **worse on coughing, straining or bending?** → raised intracranial pressure.

**The explanation IS the treatment, and ‘it's just stress’ undoes it** — *just* is heard as ‘there's nothing wrong with you’. Give the mechanism: **‘When we're under pressure, and when we sit for hours with the head held forward and still, the muscles at the back of the neck and across the shoulders hold a low-grade contraction all day. Those muscles get tender — which is exactly what I found when I pressed on them — and the pain from them is felt as a tight band around the head. So your two complaints are one problem: THE NECK IS WHERE IT COMES FROM, THE HEAD IS WHERE YOU FEEL IT.’**

**Answer the brain tumour fear with your FINDINGS, not with comfort**: **‘The features that would make me worry about something inside the head are a headache worse first thing in the morning or on coughing, vomiting, a change in vision, weakness, numbness or fits — and swelling at the backs of the eyes. You have none of them and your examination is normal. That is why I'm not scanning you today, and I'll tell you exactly what would change my mind.’**

**Management**: **address the stressor** — hours, workload, sleep, desk breaks, and ask what he can actually change · **physiotherapy, posture and workstation review** (*‘those screens being low is worth fixing’*), stretching, regular aerobic exercise · **simple analgesia for individual bad days with an EXPLICIT cap, in these words: ‘no more than a couple of days a week — painkillers most days turn an occasional headache into a daily one’** VERIFY · **headache diary** — days affected, medication days, triggers · **relaxation or CBT, and a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan with sessions with a psychologist** where stress or mood is the driver · **low-dose amitriptyline nocte** as the usual first preventive for frequent or chronic tension-type headache VERIFY · **review at four weeks with the diary.** SA — **SafeWork SA** duties if the workload is a workplace hazard, **ReturnToWorkSA** for a psychological injury claim, and **a certificate for modified duties rather than blanket time off**; **MM5: CT is at the base hospital but MRI and angiography mean transfer — suspected dissection or SAH is a transfer, not an outpatient booking, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**; **TIS 131 450.**
plan: WIPE, open question, acknowledge, **offer analgesia** — then **SIGNPOST THE SPLIT, the cheapest structural mark in the station**: **‘You've mentioned two things, so I'm going to ask about the headache first and then about the neck, and then some questions to make sure I'm not missing anything serious.’**

**SICORA of the headache — ONSET FIRST.** **‘How quickly does it come on — how long from feeling normal to the worst it gets?’** Then side, character, severity, duration and frequency, radiation, **‘worse when you move about, climb stairs, bend over or cough?’**, aggravating and relieving. **If the answer to onset is seconds to a minute, STOP — you are in version B and the station is now a subarachnoid haemorrhage.**

**SICORA of the NECK, separately — do not blend the two into one muddled account.** Front or back · **‘which came first, the headache or the neck pain?’** · out of ten · dull or sharp · **radiation into the shoulder or down the arm, pins and needles, numbness** · wakes you at night · morning or end of day · worse with activity or after rest · **stiffness and how long** · any injury.

**Say what you have learned — the examiner hears you reasoning**: **‘So the neck ache and the headache rise together through the day, and neither wakes you — that fits a muscular, mechanical pattern rather than anything inflammatory or sinister.’** **Neck pain PRECEDING and provoking the headache points to cervicogenic; rising together points to tension-type.**

**The overlap red flags, one block.** **Thunderclap** — a single episode, worst ever, maximum within a minute, anything on exertion or straining. **Dissection** — sudden one-sided neck pain · **any injury, heavy lifting, or neck manipulation — a chiropractor or physiotherapist** · **drooping eyelid, double vision or blurring** · weakness, numbness or difficulty speaking down one side.

**Meningitis and raised pressure** — fevers, chills, rashes · nausea or vomiting **particularly first thing in the morning** · bright lights · **worse lying down or on waking** · vision, weakness, numbness, fits, **personality change others have noticed.** **Malignancy and the neck-specific ones** — weight loss, appetite, lumps, previous cancer · **unsteadiness or falls, and loss of bladder or bowel control.** **Say out loud that one neurological screen covered brain tumour, dissection, myelopathy and radiculopathy together.**

**The headache group.** **‘How are things at work and at home — any particular pressures at the moment? How is your sleep, and your mood?’** **DO NOT POUNCE.** The moment the boss is mentioned the temptation is *‘so it's stress then’* — **the stressor is the answer, but the EXPLORATION is the mark**: hours, sleep, mood, alcohol, home, plus **two depression screening questions.** Then **migraine** — aura, nausea, light and noise, family history — and **cluster** — watering or red eye, blocked or running nostril.

**THE NECK BLOCK — the block that decides the station, and it costs twenty seconds.** **‘What do you do for work, and how is your desk and screen set up? How many hours a day is your head forward and still? Any unaccustomed activity, a new pillow, an awkward sleeping position? Any pain or swelling in other joints? Any family history of arthritis, any scaly rashes, any recent diarrhoea or urinary symptoms? Any pain or stiffness across the shoulders in the morning?’**

**Analgesia frequency — almost always dropped.** **‘What have you been taking, and HOW MANY DAYS IN A TYPICAL MONTH? Anything with codeine? How much coffee, tea or energy drink — and does a missed coffee give you a headache?’** Then closure: PMHx **particularly blood pressure**, medicines, allergies, smoking, alcohol, and **‘is there anything you were particularly worried this might be?’** — the agenda arrives here, or is volunteered at 5:30 regardless.

**Ask for the card, naming fundoscopy and blood pressure.** Then **interpret it before you name the diagnosis** → **the diagnosis linking both complaints** → **the four reasons** → **both differential lists, serious first, and say CERVICOGENIC** → **decline imaging with the reason, cap the analgesia frequency, and give the safety net.**
pefe: **Ask for blood pressure and fundoscopy BY NAME.** Both are free, both are marked, and both are routinely omitted. **Add the temporal arteries**, and for the neck: **range of movement, paravertebral and trapezius tenderness, and whether pressure over the upper cervical spine reproduces his headache.**

**Read the card and interpret it before naming anything.** The only abnormality is tender neck muscles; everything that would indicate a serious cause is normal — **and saying that combination out loud is what converts a guess into a defended diagnosis.**

**Investigations: NONE in a typical tension-type headache with a normal examination.** **CT head only for thunderclap onset, focal deficit, seizure, papilloedema, immunosuppression, or a headache that has changed character.** **CT or MR angiography if dissection is suspected.** **ESR and CRP in ANY patient over 50 with a new headache.** **Blood pressure in everyone.**

**The scripted imaging answer**: **‘I would not image him. His headache has no warning features, his neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal, and imaging in that setting does not change management. It also has a real cost: an incidental finding in a worried man becomes a second problem. I would review him in four weeks, and I would image if the pattern changed, if he developed any neurological sign, or if the headache became worse on waking, coughing or straining.’**
**Never manipulate the neck where dissection is possible.** In version C: **‘please don't have your neck manipulated again.’**

**Separating tension-type from cervicogenic, if challenged**: **‘Cervicogenic headache is typically side-locked, preceded by neck pain, and reproduced by neck movement or upper cervical pressure. His is bilateral and rises WITH the neck ache rather than after it. In practice they overlap, and the management — posture, physiotherapy and the stressor — is much the same.’**

**Version D — medication overuse**: acute headache medication on **10–15+ days a month for three months or more** turns an episodic headache into a daily one, and **no preventive works until the offending drug is withdrawn.** VERIFY Simple analgesics have the higher threshold; **opioid, combination and triptan preparations the lower.** **Warn about 1–2 weeks of rebound and that the rebound is expected, not evidence you are wrong.** It is **the single most treatable cause of chronic daily headache in Australian general practice, and almost no candidate asks.**

**Version E — over 50 with a new headache**: add **scalp tenderness on brushing hair, jaw claudication on chewing, transient visual change, and girdle stiffness.** **Start corticosteroid immediately — do not delay for the biopsy** — with urgent ESR and CRP, temporal artery biopsy and same-day ophthalmology. VERIFY **And the household question once: carbon monoxide, if everyone at home has a headache that is better away from the house.**

setting: The task is 'Describe', not 'Diagnose' — and launching into 'This is psoriasis' before a single descriptive word throws the station away. stem: Version A: general practice, Wallaroo. Daniel, 34, a builder, with three months of a scaly, mildly itchy rash on both elbows that is spreading slowly. Well, no joint pain volunteered, normal vitals. A photograph is provided and a medical student is present. Tasks: describe the rash to the medical student and tell them how you would examine it — perform a focused examination for associated features, with no history — and tell the examiner your most likely diagnosis and one key differential. 2 minutes reading, 8 minutes.

Version B: rural ED. Mia, 6, with her mother — a rash on both legs and buttocks for two days, a week after a cold. Afebrile, alert and playing, with HR 96, BP 100/62 and temperature 36.9. Tasks: describe the rash to the examiner — perform a focused physical examination — and give your provisional diagnosis and the differentials you must exclude.
tasks: Describe the rash, and say how you would examine it
Perform a focused examination for associated features
Give your most likely diagnosis and your key differential
time: WIPE, consent to look and then feel, and frame it for the student: I'll describe it in the standard order, inspection first and then palpation · then the seven inspection headings, each named out loud: primary morphology; size, site and shape; borders; discrete or confluent; colour; secondary morphology, with what is present and what is absent; and distribution, including the sites you would go on to look at · then the four palpation headings: temperature with the backs of the fingers against normal skin beside it, tenderness with the patient warned, surface, and blanching with a glass slide and an explanation of what it means · then the special sign if there is one, and the sentence that closes the block: that completes the rash · then the focused examination for associated features · then the diagnosis with its reasoning and one argued differential, the explanation in plain words, and the safety net.
findings: Plaques, raised and larger than a centimetre — the largest about 4 by 3 cm over the extensor surface of the left elbow, oval, with a smaller lesion below — borders well-defined — the two larger plaques becoming confluent and the satellite discrete — salmon-pink to red with a silvery-white surface — scale present and no crust, lichenification, fissuring, erosion, ulceration, vesicles or pustules

Not warm compared with the skin beside it — not tender — rough, scaly and slightly raised — and it blanches, so the blood is still within the vessels. Then lift the edge of one scale → pinpoint bleeding, which is a positive auspitz sign
Nail pitting on three fingers of the right hand — ignoring the nails misses the finding the examiner has scripted. Similar plaques over both knees; joints normal
What you see in Version B

Pinpoint petechiae and larger purpuric patches up to 2 cm — most look macular — over both buttocks and the backs of both thighs and calves, symmetrical and dependent, sparing trunk and face — small lesions sharply defined and larger patches irregular — red-purple — and no scale, crust, vesicles, ulceration or bullae

Not warm, not tender — the larger lesions very slightly raised, so palpable purpura — and under the slide the colour does not fade: non-blanching, because the blood has leaked out of small vessels into the skin

back.dx: VERSION A IS CHRONIC PLAQUE PSORIASIS: 'MY MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS IS CHRONIC PLAQUE PSORIASIS — well-defined, salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale over an extensor surface, with nail pitting and a positive auspitz sign. The key differential is discoid eczema, which is itchier, more exudative and less sharply defined; I would also consider tinea corporis, which is annular with an active scaly edge and a clearing centre — a skin scraping would exclude it.' One well-argued differential beats a list of five with no reasoning. If asked what the auspitz sign is: 'Pinpoint bleeding when a psoriatic scale is lifted, because the thinned epidermis over dilated dermal capillaries is torn. It supports psoriasis; it is not needed for the diagnosis.' The focused examination for associated features: nails for pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop discolouration and subungual hyperkeratosis; scalp, hairline and behind the ears; knees, umbilicus and natal cleft; joints for swollen tender small joints, dactylitis and back stiffness; feet and flexures for the tinea and eczema differentials; and weight and blood pressure, because psoriasis carries cardiometabolic risk. Do not run a full musculoskeletal screen and run out of time. The explanation in plain words: 'This looks like psoriasis — a common, non-contagious condition where the skin renews itself too quickly and builds up into scaly patches. It tends to come and go. It's not caused by anything you've done, and we can control it well.' and to the hidden concern: 'It is not infectious at all — you cannot pass it to anyone. If a mate comments, the honest answer is that it's a skin condition like eczema.' Management: emollient with a potent topical corticosteroid once daily for four weeks, with or without calcipotriol; screening for psoriatic arthritis and cardiovascular risk; review in six weeks; and dermatology through PATS if it fails to respond or covers more than ten per cent of his skin. The safety net: come back sooner if it spreads quickly, becomes red all over, pus spots appear, or the joints swell or stiffen. Version B is henoch-schonlein purpura — IgA vasculitis — with early renal involvement. The examination, and why: 'The systems HSP involves, and the alternatives I must exclude. Abdomen for tenderness, a mass or intussusception; testes in a boy; joints — ankles and knees for swelling; blood pressure and a urine dipstick for nephritis; mouth and gums for mucosal bleeding; lymph nodes, liver and spleen and pallor for leukaemia; neck stiffness and conscious state for meningococcal disease; and a full skin survey for bruises of different ages in unusual sites, because non-accidental injury must be considered.' then: 'She is well and afebrile, so meningococcaemia is unlikely, but I'll send an FBC and film to exclude thrombocytopenia and leukaemia, U&E and a formal urine protein-creatinine ratio.' To the mother: 'This is a condition where small blood vessels become inflamed after a viral illness; the rash is bleeding into the skin, not an infection, and it usually settles over a few weeks. The thing we watch is the kidneys, so we'll check her urine and blood pressure weekly for a month and then monthly until six months. Bring her straight back — or call 000 — if she gets a fever with the rash spreading, severe tummy pain or vomiting, blood in the stool, swelling, or if she becomes drowsy. If there is protein in the urine or the pressure rises, she'll see the paediatric team at the women's and children's.' The version B traps: reassuring before a temperature and a urine dip; calling purpura the primary morphology; and describing for four minutes and never reaching the abdomen and urine, which is where the marks are.
plan: WIPE, consent to look and then feel, and frame it: '[to the student] I'll describe it in the standard order: inspection first, then palpation.'

Inspection, heading one and two: 'Primary morphology: these are plaques — raised, palpable lesions larger than one centimetre. Size, site and shape: the largest is about four by three centimetres, over the extensor surface of the left elbow, roughly oval.'

Headings three to five: 'Borders: well-defined — I could draw a line round each one. Discrete or confluent: the two larger plaques are merging, so confluent; the small satellite is discrete. Colour: salmon-pink to red, with a silvery-white surface.' (Colour is never worth an argument.)

Heading six, with what is absent as well as present: 'Secondary morphology: there is scale; there is no crust, no lichenification, no fissuring, no erosion or ulceration, and no pustules or vesicles.'

Heading seven, without inventing what you cannot see: 'Distribution: from this view localised to the extensor elbow; I would look at the other elbow, both knees, the scalp, behind the ears, the umbilicus and the natal cleft.'

Palpation, all four headings, now and not later: temperature with the backs of the fingers against adjacent normal skin; tenderness, warning him first; surface; and blanching with a glass slide — 'The redness fades and returns, so it blanches: the blood is still within the vessels.'
The special sign, then close the block: 'I'll gently lift the edge of one scale — pinpoint bleeding beneath it would be the auspitz sign.' → positive. 'That completes the rash.'

The focused examination for associated features (see dx) — nails first, because that is the scripted finding, then scalp and hidden sites, knees, joints and dactylitis, feet and flexures, and weight and blood pressure.
The diagnosis with its reasoning and one argued differential (see dx) — then the explanation in plain words, the management, and the safety net.
Answer the hidden concern clearly — it is not infectious at all — and summarise: the description, the associated features, the diagnosis, the differential and the plan.
back.planNote: Version A's eight minutes, with the description block closed before the associated features
ask: 'I'll describe it in the standard order — inspection, then palpation.' / 'The primary morphology is a ___ — flat or raised, smaller or larger than a centimetre.' / 'Size, site and shape: ___ centimetres, over the ___, oval or round or annular.' / 'Borders are well-defined — I could draw a line round it' or 'Ill-defined — I cannot say where it ends.'

'The lesions are discrete' / 'Becoming confluent.' / 'Secondary changes: ___ present; no crust, scale, lichenification, fissure, erosion or ulcer.' / 'Distribution: localised, symmetrical, generalised, flexor, extensor, dermatomal or photodistributed.'

'Now I'll feel it: temperature, tenderness, surface, and whether it blanches.' / 'Pressing with a glass slide — the colour fades, so it blanches' or 'The colour persists: non-blanching, the blood has leaked out of the vessel.' / 'That completes the rash. I'll now examine the features that go with it.'

The definitions the examiner may ask for: 'Crust is dried fluid; scale is dead tissue.' / 'A nodule is raised with a solid or cystic core beneath it.' / 'I can see a purpuric rash; its primary morphology is macular.' / 'I describe what I see, then reconcile it with the diagnosis.'

The purpura framework: petechiae under 2 mm, purpura 2 mm to 1 cm, ecchymosis over 1 cm — and the causes as hit me: HSP and HUS, ITP, trauma, meningococcaemia, plus coagulopathy, viral, leukaemia and drugs. Fever plus purpura means ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg to a maximum of 2 g VERIFY and then MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33. Child protection is CARL 13 14 78.
pefe: The seven inspection headings: primary morphology — size, site and shape — borders — discrete or confluent — colour — secondary morphology — distribution. The four palpation headings: temperature — tenderness — surface — blanching. The three never to omit: primary, secondary and borders. The 1 cm cut separates macule from patch, papule from plaque, and vesicle from bulla, though some texts use 0.5 cm for vesicles. The five secondary changes: lichenification, scale, crust, fissure, and erosion or ulcer. The seven distributions: localised, symmetrical, generalised, flexor, extensor, dermatomal, photodistributed.

Role-player: Daniel, 34, a builder, with a scaly rash on both elbows for three months and now on the knees too, flaking on his work shirt. Mildly itchy, not painful, with little bleeding spots if he picks it. The left elbow first, then the right, then the knees. No joint pain, back stiffness or nail complaints — he has not noticed the pits. Some flakes in his hair he thought were dandruff. No sore throat, no medicines, work has been stressful. Ten cigarettes a day, weekend drinking, BMI about 29, no allergies. His father had scalp psoriasis. A chemist moisturiser didn't do much.

How to play it: matter-of-fact and a little embarrassed. Do nothing during the description — that is where they are marked — and do not help. If they press and ask about pain, say 'No, it doesn't hurt'; if they never press, say nothing and mark it. If they say 'This is psoriasis' before describing, ask once: 'How can you tell?' if they call it symmetrical without asking to see the other elbow, show mild surprise: 'You haven't looked at the other one.' Volunteer the family history late, during the joint questions. Ask 'Is it catching?' Only if they give a diagnosis — and if they never do, ask it in the last minute.

Mark them on: naming a primary morphology in the first descriptive sentence; saying well-defined and naming the secondary change and what was absent; palpating for temperature, tenderness, surface and blanching with an explanation; examining nails, scalp, knees and joints without fabricating distribution; giving a diagnosis with reasoning, one argued differential and a safety net; and answering 'Is it catching?' Clearly.

The distribution trap — Inventing 'Symmetrical' from a photograph that shows one elbow. Call it localised for now and say where you would look next — and if you call it symmetrical without asking, he says 'You haven't looked at the other one'
What he volunteers late — 'MY DAD HAD SOMETHING LIKE THIS ON HIS SCALP' — given during the joint questions — AND 'SOME FLAKES IN MY HAIR, I THOUGHT IT WAS DANDRUFF' if you ask about the scalp

His hidden concern — 'Is it catching? I work on site with a crew' — he thinks it might be contagious and his crew have started to comment. Asked only if you give a diagnosis, and in the last minute if you never do

VERSION B — the mother's first question — 'It came up two days ago and it's spreading — is it meningitis?' → 'That is exactly the thing I check for first. Mia is alert, playing, and has no fever, and her heart rate and blood pressure are normal — that reassures me, but I'll look carefully'

The rule the source insists on — If it looks flat, say macular with reasoning — do not announce 'Palpable purpura' because the textbook says so. 'I describe what I see, then reconcile it with the diagnosis'

Where the Version B marks are — Abdomen and urine. Describing for four minutes and never reaching them loses the station — and the examiner gives: abdomen soft, ankles mildly swollen, BP 100/62, urine dipstick blood 2+ and protein trace, spleen not palpable
What he does if you diagnose too early — If you say 'This is psoriasis' before describing, he asks once: 'How can you tell?' and if you never press on the rash, he says nothing and marks it
fails: ★ Launching into the diagnosis before a single descriptive word — the task is describe, and the diagnosis is the third task
★ Deferring palpation until after the examination, when the rash is palpated now — and pressing with a slide without saying what blanching or non-blanching means
Saying 'red rash' and stopping, omitting borders, or inventing 'symmetrical' from a photograph that shows one elbow
Ignoring the nails, which is the finding the examiner has scripted — or running a full musculoskeletal screen and running out of time

Naming five differentials with no reasoning when one well-argued differential beats a list; and in Version B, reassuring before a temperature and a urine dip, calling purpura the primary morphology, announcing 'palpable purpura' because the textbook says so when it looks flat, or describing for four minutes and never reaching the abdomen and urine
numbers: 2 steps: inspect then palpate · 7 inspection headings · 4 palpation headings · 3 never to omit: primary, secondary, borders · the 1 cm cut separates macule from patch, papule from plaque and vesicle from bulla, though some texts use 0.5 cm for vesicles · 5 secondary changes and 7 distributions

Petechiae under 2 mm, purpura 2 mm to 1 cm, ecchymosis over 1 cm · causes as hit me: HSP and HUS, ITP, trauma, meningococcaemia, plus coagulopathy, viral, leukaemia and drugs · fever plus purpura: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg to a maximum of 2 g VERIFY then MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · HSP follow-up: urine and BP weekly for 4 weeks then monthly to 6 months · CARL 13 14 78 · TIS National 131 450

source: Describing_a_Rash.pdf (an inspection and palpation framework for every rash station, worked through two cases — Daniel, 34, with three months of scaly elbow plaques, which is chronic plaque psoriasis; and Mia, 6, with a purpuric rash on legs and buttocks a week after a cold, which is Henoch-Schonlein purpura; the seven inspection headings and four palpation headings each named out loud, the rash palpated immediately rather than deferred, blanching explained rather than just stated, distribution never invented from a photograph showing one side, the nails examined because that is the scripted finding, one argued differential preferred to a list of five, and in the paediatric version the abdomen and the urine dipstick reached because that is where the marks are)

findingsLabel: What you see, what you feel, and what each version withholds
must: FAIL — Launching into the diagnosis before a single descriptive word — the task is DESCRIBE, and the diagnosis is the THIRD task; frame it for the student first ('I'll describe it in the standard order — INSPECTION, then PALPATION'), and he is briefed to ask 'how can you tell?' once if you name it early (★)

FAIL — Saying 'red rash' and stopping, omitting BORDERS, or inventing 'symmetrical' from a photograph that shows one elbow — SEVEN inspection headings, every heading NAMED: PRIMARY MORPHOLOGY ('these are PLAQUES — raised, palpable lesions larger than one centimetre'), SIZE, SITE and SHAPE, BORDERS ('well-defined — I could draw a line round each one', against 'ill-defined — I cannot say where it ends'), DISCRETE OR CONFLUENT, COLOUR, SECONDARY MORPHOLOGY naming what is present AND what is absent (scale, crust, lichenification, fissuring, erosion or ulceration, pustules or vesicles), and DISTRIBUTION; if you can see only one side, say LOCALISED FOR NOW and name the sites you would check, because he is briefed to show mild surprise at 'you haven't looked at the other one' (★)

FAIL — Deferring palpation until after the examination, when the rash is palpated NOW — and pressing with a slide without saying WHAT BLANCHING MEANS; FOUR palpation headings: TEMPERATURE with the backs of your fingers on the lesion AND on the normal skin beside it, TENDERNESS asked rather than assumed, SURFACE, and BLANCHING with the interpretation attached — 'the redness fades and returns, so it BLANCHES: the blood is still WITHIN the vessels', or 'the colour does not fade: NON-BLANCHING — the blood has LEAKED OUT of small vessels into the skin' — then 'that completes the rash; I'll now examine the features that go with it' (★)

FAIL — Ignoring the NAILS, which is the finding the examiner has scripted — or running a full musculoskeletal screen and running out of time; nails for PITTING, ONYCHOLYSIS, oil-drop discolouration and subungual hyperkeratosis; scalp, hairline and behind the ears; knees, umbilicus and natal cleft; joints asked about and looked at for swollen tender small joints and DACTYLITIS, with back stiffness asked; feet and flexures for the differentials; and weight and blood pressure, because psoriasis carries cardiometabolic risk (★)

FAIL — Naming five differentials with no reasoning, when ONE WELL-ARGUED DIFFERENTIAL BEATS A LIST: 'my most likely diagnosis is chronic plaque psoriasis — well-defined, salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale over an extensor surface, with nail pitting and a positive Auspitz sign; the key differential is DISCOID ECZEMA, which is itchier, more exudative and less sharply defined; I would also consider TINEA CORPORIS, which is annular with an active scaly edge and a clearing centre, and a skin scraping would exclude it' — the AUSPITZ SIGN being pinpoint bleeding when a psoriatic scale is lifted, because the thinned epidermis over dilated dermal capillaries is torn: supportive, but not needed for the diagnosis (★)

SAY — Answer the hidden concern, because he thinks it is contagious and his crew have started commenting, and he will only ask if you have given him a diagnosis: 'it is NOT infectious at all — you cannot pass it to anyone; if a mate comments, the honest answer is that it's a skin condition like eczema'; explain it in plain words ('a common, non-contagious condition where the skin renews itself too quickly and builds up into scaly patches; it tends to come and go, it's not caused by anything you've done, and we can control it well'), with an emollient and a potent topical corticosteroid once daily, with or without calcipotriol, psoriatic arthritis and cardiovascular screening, review at six weeks, and dermatology if it fails to respond or covers more than ten per cent of his skin; safety net — spreading quickly, becoming red all over, pus spots, or joints swelling or stiffening; the size cut is ONE CENTIMETRE for macule/patch, papule/plaque and vesicle/bulla; the five secondary changes are lichenification, scale, crust, fissure and erosion or ulcer; the seven distributions are localised, symmetrical, generalised, flexor, extensor, dermatomal and photodistributed; CRUST IS DRIED FLUID and SCALE IS DEAD TISSUE, and a nodule is raised with a solid or cystic core beneath it; and in VERSION B, the purpuric rash in a child, the traps shift — do not reassure before a TEMPERATURE and a URINE DIP; do not call PURPURA the primary morphology, because 'I can see a purpuric rash; its primary morphology is MACULAR' is the correct shape, and if it looks flat you say macular WITH REASONING rather than announcing 'palpable purpura' because the textbook says so (petechiae under 2 mm, purpura 2 mm to 1 cm, ecchymosis over 1 cm); and do not describe for four minutes and never reach the ABDOMEN and the URINE, where the marks are — the examination covers the abdomen for tenderness, a mass or intussusception, the testes in a boy, the ankles and knees, blood pressure and a urine dipstick for nephritis, the mouth and gums for mucosal bleeding, nodes, liver, spleen and pallor for leukaemia, neck stiffness and conscious state for meningococcal disease, and a full skin survey for bruises of different ages in unusual sites, because NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY must be considered (fever with purpura means ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg to a maximum of 2 g and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; HSP follow-up is urine and blood pressure weekly for four weeks then monthly to six months; CARL 13 14 78 for child protection)

setting: Gynaecology is the most structurally repetitive block in the AMC. The complaint changes; the history does not. Every station is the same three moves — explore the complaint, run the five Ps, then ask the pelvic PEFE — with a short list of differentials driving which extra questions you squeeze in. The differentials are the only part you have to memorise separately. The one-line rule: where is the problem? Almost always the pelvis — so you ask one fixed set of questions and examine one fixed area, and what changes between stations is the key points you squeeze into that fixed frame.
stem: The repeatable skeleton behind every gynaecology station: the opening, the five Ps in their adult, menopausal and teenage versions, the differential spine by complaint, and the word-for-word physical examination request. Learn this once and every later station becomes the same history with a different set of key points squeezed in.

The six station types: a period problem — heavy, painful, absent or between periods. A bleeding problem — post-coital, postmenopausal, or on a mirena. A discharge or vulval problem — discharge, itch, a lump down below, pain on sex. A urinary problem — leaking, frequency, retention. A counselling station — a result, a device, a hormone, a vaccine or a screening programme, with no history or a short one. And a result interpretation — her screening test, hormone profile or ultrasound handed to you.
tasks: Open, acknowledge, and name confidentiality before the personal questions
Run the five Ps in the version the stem calls for, adding the key points the differential list demands
Request the pelvic PEFE word for word, with consent and a chaperone said aloud
time: The opening and the permission sentence · then the five Ps, two questions per P, which is the fixed spine · periods, partner, pills, pregnancy, pap · then whatever the differential list for this complaint demands on TOP · then the pelvic PEFE ladder, headlining each step out loud before asking for the finding: general appearance and vitals, the abdomen, then consent and chaperone, then inspection, speculum, bimanual and the office tests · then the diagnosis in plain words with a named next test. If the stem already gives you the history, everything shifts left and the explanation gets the extra three minutes.
findings: Cervical motion tenderness is PID in gynaecology and ectopic in obstetrics — a bulky irregular uterus is fibroids, a bulky smooth uterus is adenomyosis — an adnexal mass is ovarian pathology, and adnexal tenderness is PID

back.dx: The framework, not a diagnosis. The opening, word for word: 'Good morning, my name is Dr ___, I am one of the doctors here in the practice. I understand you have come in about ___ — can you tell me a little more about what has been happening?' then acknowledge before you interrogate: 'That sounds uncomfortable and I can see it has been worrying you. I would like to ask you a series of questions, some of them quite personal, so that I can work out what is going on. Everything you tell me stays confidential. Is that alright?' In a gynaecology station the role-player is briefed to be embarrassed, and the marks for rapport are earned in that sentence — it costs ten seconds. If the examiner asks why you said it: 'Sexual and menstrual history is intrusive. Consent and confidentiality up front improve disclosure and are expected practice.' The name correction: the lecture and most study notes still say 'Pap smear', but it is the cervical screening test — a primary HPV test on a self-collected or clinician-collected sample, five-yearly from 25 to 74 for anyone with a cervix who has ever been sexually active. Say cervical screening to the patient; 'Pap smear' is only a memory hook for the fifth P. If challenged: 'The programme changed to primary HPV testing; cytology is now reflex, done on the same sample only if HPV is detected.' The pregnancy correction, which is not optional: in any woman of reproductive age presenting with abnormal bleeding, pelvic pain or amenorrhoea, a urine or serum beta-hCG is a required step, because a stated last menstrual period does not exclude an ectopic pregnancy. If she says her period was last week: 'A reported recent bleed can occur with an ectopic pregnancy, so I would still confirm with a beta-hCG before I move on.' The abdominal correction: candidates rush to the speculum, but the uterus is a pelvic organ and is barely palpable abdominally when normal — which is exactly why an abdominally palpable mass matters. Two questions only, tenderness and mass, then the lower-border question: a mass whose lower border you cannot reach is arising from the pelvis. The South Australian teenage law, for the adolescent version: the age of consent in South Australia is 17. Sexual activity under that age, or any age gap or coercion concern, triggers a child protection assessment via the child abuse report line on 13 14 78. A young person under 16 may still consent to their own treatment if they are gillick competent and you document that assessment, and the consent to medical treatment and palliative care act 1995 lets a 16-year-old consent as an adult. If asked what you would do with a sexually active 15-year-old: 'Assess her competence, ask about the partner's age and whether the relationship is consensual and free of coercion, offer confidential contraception and STI screening, and make a child protection report if there are any concerns.' HPV vaccination: the national programme now uses the nine-valent vaccine given in school, and a single dose is the standard schedule for immunocompetent people aged 9 to 25, with more for the immunocompromised. And the rural South Australian closing to have ready in any station: pathology and imaging via country health connect, with PATS travel subsidy for metropolitan gynaecology appointments; interpreters through TIS National 131 450, offered rather than using family; sexual health advice, contraception and STI management through SHINE SA; the local ACCHS and closing the gap PBS co-payment for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval; and healthdirect 1800 022 222 after hours.
plan: THE OPENING AND THE PERMISSION SENTENCE (see dx) — CONFIDENTIALITY NAMED AND PERMISSION ASKED BEFORE ANY PERSONAL QUESTION. (Launching into a sexual history cold is the fail behaviour here.)

P ONE, PERIODS: last period, cycle length, days of bleeding, excessive pain or heavy bleeding, and any pain or bleeding between periods — WITH THE PAIN QUESTION ASKED AS 'BAD ENOUGH TO STOP YOUR NORMAL DAY?' RATHER THAN 'ARE THEY PAINFUL?'

P TWO, PARTNER: sexually active and ever been, stable relationship, safe sex and condoms, multiple partners or a previous STI — AND THEN THE TWO THAT ARE ALWAYS FORGOTTEN: PAIN DURING OR AFTER SEX, AND BLEEDING AFTER SEX.
P THREE, PILLS: which contraception and for how long — because it is both cause and cure in this block.
P FOUR, PREGNANCY: how many, how delivered, and any chance she could be pregnant now.
P FIVE, CERVICAL SCREENING: up to date, and were the results normal.

Whatever the differential list for this complaint demands on TOP — the five Ps are fixed, and the list is what earns the marks. If you cannot recall the list for the complaint in front of you, you will not ask the questions and you will not be scored for them.

The PEFE ladder (see PEFE) — general appearance and vitals, then the abdomen with the lower-border question, then consent and chaperone said aloud, then inspection, speculum, bimanual and the office tests.
The diagnosis in plain words with a named next test: 'Everything I have found so far points towards ___, and the test that will confirm it is ___.'
The closing — investigations, the management options in outline, any overdue screening picked up as an item, and the rural South Australian supports where relevant (see dx).
back.planNote: the document's eight-minute budget - shift everything left if the stem hands you the history
ask: The phrase bank: 'Some of these questions are personal — everything stays between us.' / 'Is the bleeding heavy enough to soak through a pad in an hour, or to make you plan your day around it?' / 'I would like to examine you internally. I will explain each step, and I will have a chaperone with us. You can stop me at any time.' / 'Everything I have found so far points towards ___, and the test that will confirm it is ___.'

How to spend the extra questions — three worked stems. A 32-year-old with heavy periods: add clot size and flooding, pads or tampons per day, double protection and days off work; bruising, gum bleeding and family bleeding history; tiredness, breathlessness and pica; cold intolerance and weight change — and do not leave out ferritin and a full blood count, or endometrial assessment if the bleeding is irregular at her age.

A 54-year-old with one bleed since menopause: add exactly how long since the last period, how many bleeds and how heavy; MHT or tamoxifen use; weight, diabetes and hypertension; and family history of endometrial, ovarian or bowel cancer — because postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until excluded, which means transvaginal ultrasound and referral, always.

A 15-year-old who has not had a period: add the puberty sequence and its timing, the growth spurt, cyclical abdominal pain suggesting outflow obstruction, sense of smell, exercise and weight and eating pattern, and chronic illness — and ask for secondary sexual characteristics and a height and weight plot, because this station is scored on the sequence rather than the diagnosis.

The numbers: cervical screening 25 to 74, five-yearly, with self-collection available VERIFY — menopause is diagnosed after 12 months of amenorrhoea — heavy bleeding means clots over 2.5 cm, flooding, double protection and iron deficiency — uterine size is described in weeks, as in pregnancy — HPV vaccine is nine-valent, single dose for immunocompetent people aged 9 to 25 VERIFY — and the SA age of consent is 17, with CARL 13 14 78.
pefe: The PEFE ladder, headlining each step before asking for findings. First the general appearance — conscious state, pallor, cachexia and BMI — and vital signs with a postural blood pressure. Then the abdomen: tenderness and any mass, and if there is a mass, whether the lower border is palpable.

Then the sentence that is the most reliably scored in gynaecology, and the one most often lost in the rush: 'I would like to perform a pelvic examination. I would explain it, obtain her consent, and have a chaperone present.' Examining without consent or chaperone is treated as a professionalism breach rather than a knowledge gap.

INSPECTION — THREE FIXED BOXES ASKED EVERY TIME, SKIN, LUMPS AND DISCHARGE: 'ON INSPECTION OF THE VULVA AND PERINEUM — ANY SKIN CHANGES SUCH AS REDNESS, RASH OR ULCERS? ANY LUMPS OR SWELLINGS? ANY DISCHARGE OR BLEEDING?' You are looking for a Bartholin swelling, prolapse at the introitus, lichen sclerosus, warts or an ulcer.

SPECULUM — AND THE VAGINAL WALL QUESTION IS THE ONE THAT UNLOCKS ATROPHIC VAGINITIS: 'ON SPECULUM — IS THE CERVIX NORMAL? SPECIFICALLY ANY LESION, MASS OR ABNORMAL GROWTH, ANY CONTACT BLEEDING OR DISCHARGE FROM THE OS? AND CAN YOU DESCRIBE THE VAGINAL WALLS?' Cervical cancer is an irregular, friable, bleeding lesion; an ectropion is a smooth red ring around the os, which is the AMC's favourite finding.

THE ADNEXA: ANY MASS OR TENDERNESS?' THEN 'URINE DIPSTICK, AND A URINE PREGNANCY TEST.' An examiner who does not hear the step will not give you the finding — and a finding you were never given cannot be used in your diagnosis.

P one — periods — 'When was your last period?' — asked in every case whether or not it matters. 'How many days is your cycle?' 'How many days do you bleed for?' 'Do you get excessive pain, or heavy bleeding, with your periods?' 'Any pain or bleeding in between your periods?' — intermenstrual bleeding opens polyps, cervical pathology and malignancy

Which one, and for how long?' — contraception is both cause and cure in this block: the implant and the injection cause irregular bleeding, the mirena treats heavy bleeding, and the pill masks and mimics. It also tells you her pregnancy risk without asking twice

Were the results normal?' — prior abnormality changes the whole risk calculation in post-coital and intermenstrual bleeding, and if she is overdue that is a management item for your closing

dx: **Constitutional delay of puberty — a DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION, and you are not marked on the diagnosis. You are marked on the exclusions.** Candidates fail this station having said 'constitutional delay' correctly, because they never asked about exercise, eating, galactorrhoea, visual symptoms, cyclical pain or family history — **so they had no grounds to exclude anything. An exclusion you did not perform is not an exclusion.**

**Definitions, stated exactly. Primary amenorrhoea: no menarche by 13 in a girl with NO breast development, or no menarche by 15 (some references say 16) when puberty has otherwise progressed normally. Secondary amenorrhoea: previously regular periods absent for 3 months, or previously irregular periods absent for 6 months.** VERIFY — either 15 or 16 is defensible if you explain your reasoning.

**The vertical map generates the entire differential list, and LH/FSH is its pivot. LOW LH and FSH — the brain is not driving**: hypothalamic (stress, exercise, eating), pituitary disease, prolactinoma, constitutional delay, chronic illness. **HIGH LH and FSH — the brain is shouting and the ovary is not answering**: Turner syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis, premature ovarian insufficiency. **NORMAL** — outflow obstruction, PCOS, or constitutional delay.

CORRECTION — **'premature ovarian failure' is now premature ovarian INSUFFICIENCY**, and the change matters clinically: ovarian function and even pregnancy can be intermittent, so 'failure' misinforms the patient.

CORRECTION — the source repeatedly says **'hyperpituitarism'. The pituitary cause of amenorrhoea is HYPOpituitarism** — the gland underproducing LH and FSH. Excess is relevant only as **hyperprolactinaemia**. If challenged — 'which pituitary problem causes amenorrhoea?' — **'either hypopituitarism, or a prolactin-secreting adenoma suppressing gonadotrophins.'**

CORRECTION — **offer her time alone.** The source treats the mother's presence as settled. Australian practice is to offer the young person part of the consultation without her parent, and to explain confidentiality and its limits: **'Mrs Ellis, I usually spend a few minutes with young people on their own — it's routine, and it helps them ask anything they might not want to ask in front of a parent.'** If challenged: **adolescents disclose sexual activity, substance use and mental health concerns far more reliably alone.**

CORRECTION — **how to talk about the hymen.** The source asks whether it is 'intact' and uses the word 'virgin'. **Do neither. The hymen is NOT a marker of sexual activity, and inspecting to establish virginity is condemned practice.** The clinical question is whether it is **imperforate** — whether menstrual blood has an outlet. Say: **'I am inspecting the introitus to exclude an imperforate hymen or a vaginal septum.'**

CORRECTION — the source says not to ask about alcohol and drugs in a 17-year-old **because it is not legal at that age. Legality is not a reason to skip a question — prevalence is why you would ask, and time is why you might not.** In eight minutes differentials come first; a single screening line is appropriate and safe if there is room.

**ADDED — two things the source leaves out. Ask about the SENSE OF SMELL: amenorrhoea with anosmia is Kallmann syndrome, and one question is the only way you will ever get it.** And **haematocolpos is not a review-in-six-months problem** — it can obstruct the urinary tract and cause retention, and retrograde flow causes endometriosis. **Cyclical pain without bleeding is obstructed menstruation until proven otherwise**, needing imaging and gynaecology referral.

**Investigations, in order: β-hCG first in anyone who could conceivably be pregnant · LH and FSH — the pivot of the algorithm · prolactin · TSH · pelvic ultrasound (uterus present? ovaries? haematocolpos? polycystic morphology — a structural answer in one test) · oestradiol · karyotype when LH and FSH are high or stature is short · androgens and 17-OHP if hirsute or virilised · MRI pituitary for high prolactin, headache or field loss.** SA: adolescent gynaecology and endocrinology through the **Women's and Children's Hospital**, with **PATS** from a rural site; **SHINE SA** for confidential youth health and contraception; **headspace** for youth mental health; **National Alliance for Eating Disorders** helpline and local CAMHS; **Child Abuse Report Line 13 14 78** for any safeguarding concern; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: WIPE. **Open, never closed** — the role-player has three scripted lines and a closed question loses all of them: **'I can see you have some concerns about your periods — tell me more about that.'**

**Acknowledge, empathise, reassure — approach is separately scored and this is where it is won**: **'I can understand how worrying that is when all your friends have started. I want to reassure you that we'll work through this together, find the cause, and sort out a plan. Can I ask you some questions?'**

**Offer time alone**: **'Mrs Ellis, I usually spend a few minutes with young people on their own — would you mind stepping out briefly?'** Then to Jenny: **'everything you tell me is confidential.'** If the mother stays, the sexual-activity answer comes with a glance at her and a mumbled no.

**Confirm, then the three puberty questions — the key point of the station**: **'have you ever had a period, or any bleeding down below at all?'** then **'any change in the size of your breasts?' · 'any hair growth in your armpits or private parts?' · 'have you had a growth spurt — a sudden increase in your height?'** **Puberty present means the hormonal axis is working**, which shifts you toward outflow obstruction or constitutional delay.

**The teenage five Ps.** **Partner** — 'I ask all my patients some personal questions, is that alright? Are you sexually active, or have you ever been?' **Pills** — 'any contraception, tablets, an implant, an injection?' The implant and the injection cause amenorrhoea. **Pregnancy slot becomes** 'any operations on your tummy or your womb?' **Screening slot becomes** 'have you had your Gardasil vaccination at school?'

**Hypothalamic**: **'how are things at home? Any stress? How about school — any bullying or pressure?' · 'do you exercise regularly, how much on a usual day?' · 'tell me about your eating — any crash dieting? Have you ever made yourself sick or used laxatives?'** **Over an hour a day of training starts to matter; several hours clearly does — quantify it.**
**Pituitary — the prolactinoma triad in one breath**: **'any headaches? Any blurring or loss of side vision? Any milky discharge from your nipples?'**
**Thyroid**: **'do you feel the cold or the heat more than others? Any change in weight, bowels or energy? Any thyroid problems in the family?'**
**Ovary**: PCOS — **'any acne? Any excessive hair growth, particularly on your face? Any recent weight gain?'** Then POI — **'any hot flushes or night sweats?'**
**Genetic and family**: **'any genetic conditions in the family? When did your mother and sisters start their periods?'** — **Mum was nearly 17, and she gives this only if asked.**

**Outflow — the auto-fail question**: **'do you get a regular monthly lower tummy pain, even though you're not bleeding?'** Then close the history: **'any medications? Any medical conditions?'** and the one the source omits — **'can you smell normally — perfume, coffee?'**

**PEFE, key point first**: **'Examiner, I'd like the Tanner staging — breast development and pubic hair.'** Then **height, weight and BMI, and on inspection any acne, hirsutism or features of Turner syndrome — short stature, webbed neck. Vital signs. Visual fields to confrontation and fundoscopy. A thyroid examination. Abdomen for tenderness or a lower abdominal mass.**

**The pelvic request, word for word**: **'a pelvic examination with consent and a chaperone. On inspection: skin changes, lumps or swellings, discharge or bleeding. Is the development of the external genitalia normal? And with the labia separated, is the hymen imperforate?'** Then decline the speculum out loud and say why.

**Name it in plain words first**: **'what Jenny has is called primary amenorrhoea, which simply means her first period is late.'** Then **constitutional delay — 'periods starting later than usual with nothing wrong underneath'**.

**Give the three reasons — this is what converts a lucky guess into a pass**: **'your puberty has gone through normally, your examination today is completely normal, and your mum started at nearly 17 herself, which often runs in families.'**

**When she asks 'so there's definitely nothing wrong?' — do NOT accept the certainty**: **'it's the most likely answer, but it's a diagnosis we make by ruling other things out, so I want to do that properly.'** Then the differentials **as a line from brain to womb**: stress, heavy exercise or eating problems · a small growth in the pituitary · the thyroid · PCOS or ovaries stopping early · the womb not formed in the usual way, or the opening blocked.

**The plan, named**: **LH and FSH, prolactin, TSH, and a pelvic ultrasound**, results in about two weeks with both of them. Safety-net: **monthly pain, headaches, vision changes or nipple discharge — come back sooner.** Answer her real worry if she voices it — **'does this mean I won't be able to have children?'**

**General**: height, weight and BMI; on inspection **acne or hirsutism**; **features of Turner syndrome — short stature, webbed neck**. Then vital signs.
**Pituitary: visual fields to confrontation, and fundoscopy.** This is the examination half of the prolactinoma screen.
**Thyroid examination.** Then **abdomen — any tenderness, any mass, particularly in the lower abdomen** (haematocolpos).
