**You are given NO examination and NO investigations. The history has to do all the work** — which is why the discharge must be re-characterised in full even though the stem already told you the colour. **The answer is greyish, not white.**

**THE REPORTED CRITICAL ERROR: telling the patient this is a sexually transmitted infection**, and triggering a full STI screen off the back of it. **Taking swabs here is LOOKING FOR THE CAUSE of an undiagnosed discharge, which is a different thing — and worth saying in those words**: **'I'm taking swabs to find out what's causing this, not because I think you have a sexually transmitted infection.'**

**The explanation**: **'normally the vagina has a balance of bacteria, mostly one friendly type that keeps things slightly acidic. In bacterial vaginosis that balance is upset and other bacteria overgrow — particularly one called Gardnerella. It is common, it is not something you have caught from someone, and it is not your fault.'**

**The three reasons — and the second and third are the design of the stem**: the discharge is **thin and greyish with a fishy smell**; there is **no itch or soreness**, which you would expect with thrush; and **she has already had an antibiotic covering chlamydia and a treatment for thrush, and neither worked.** **'The fact that neither treatment worked is itself a clue.'**

**The honest caveat, which is a strength rather than a weakness**: **'I can't be completely certain without the swab, and I'll test for gonorrhoea and chlamydia as well. But the pattern points most strongly to bacterial vaginosis.'**

**Amsel criteria — three of four: 1. thin, homogeneous, grey-white discharge · 2. vaginal pH greater than 4.5 · 3. positive whiff test, a fishy odour on adding potassium hydroxide · 4. clue cells on microscopy.** Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria so the cell border becomes indistinct. **If you have thirty spare seconds, this is the thing to say.**
**Dose: metronidazole 400 mg BD for 7 days.** Compare: **PID 14 days · trichomonas 2 g stat.** **Avoid alcohol during and for a day after** — metallic taste is common. VERIFY

**The douching and scented washes are a genuine cause AND a management item** — they strip out the protective flora and make it worse. **'Plain water is all that area needs.'** She volunteers this only if asked.

**Three things worth knowing: do not treat asymptomatic BV** outside pregnancy or before gynaecological instrumentation · **in pregnancy BV is associated with preterm birth and late miscarriage, and symptomatic women are treated** (VERIFY the preferred regimen) · **recurrence within 6–12 months is common — say so in advance, so a relapse brings her back rather than convincing her the diagnosis was wrong.** **The wider picture, if the examiner asks**: BV is strongly associated with sexual activity, and recent Australian trial evidence supports **treating male partners** to reduce recurrence in recurrent disease — **but that is not the same as calling it an STI.** SA: **SHINE SA**, pathology through **Country Health Connect**, ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**, **healthdirect 1800 022 222**.

CORRECTION — **the modern name is the genitourinary syndrome of menopause**, because oestrogen deficiency affects the bladder and urethra as well as the vagina — **urgency, frequency, dysuria and recurrent urinary tract infections** alongside dryness, discharge and dyspareunia. Using the newer term **and asking the urinary questions** shows you understand the whole syndrome. If asked why she keeps getting urinary infections: **'the same oestrogen deficiency affects the urogenital epithelium, which is why vaginal oestrogen also reduces recurrent urinary tract infection.'**

**THE TRAP IS THE WORD BROWN. A brown discharge in a woman eleven years past menopause is OLD BLOOD until excluded, and any bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhoea is postmenopausal bleeding — endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.** Ask about blood explicitly, twice if necessary.

CORRECTION — **do not close the case on the vaginal walls alone. Atrophic vaginitis is the commonest benign cause of postmenopausal discharge and bleeding, and finding it does not exclude cancer. Both coexist — and an atrophic vagina is exactly the setting in which an endometrial carcinoma bleeds.** If challenged — 'her walls are atrophic, isn't that your answer?' — **'it's the most likely cause, but atrophy and endometrial cancer coexist, and postmenopausal bleeding is investigated on its own account.'**

**The closing sentence that passes the station**: **'the most likely explanation is atrophic vaginitis, but because there may be blood in this discharge I'm not going to stop there — I'll arrange a co-test, an ultrasound to measure the lining of the womb, and a sample of the lining if it's thickened.'**

**The explanation and its three reasons**: oestrogen falls after the periods stop, the vaginal lining becomes thinner, drier and more fragile, and a thin lining gets irritated and produces a discharge sometimes containing old blood. **Reasons: periods stopped eleven years ago with flushes at the time · she feels dry and sex has become painful · the walls are thin, pale and dry on examination.**

**What changes in an older woman: P1 becomes 'when did your periods stop, and have you had ANY bleeding since?' · P2 is STILL a full sexual history — older women have sex and acquire sexually transmitted infections — plus dryness and pain with sex · P3 becomes hormone replacement and tamoxifen · P4 adds urinary leakage and prolapse, because some women describe leakage as discharge · P5 is cervical screening AND mammogram. Do NOT ask about Gardasil — she was well past school age when the programme began — and skip tampons.**

**Management. Non-hormonal first: vaginal moisturisers used regularly, lubricants for sex, avoid soaps and scented products. Topical vaginal oestrogen — cream or pessary — is the effective treatment, systemic absorption is low, and it also reduces recurrent urinary tract infections. Systemic menopausal hormone therapy is NOT needed for isolated vaginal symptoms, particularly when the flushes settled years ago. In a woman with a history of breast cancer, topical oestrogen is a specialist decision, particularly on an aromatase inhibitor.** VERIFY
**Do not forget lichen sclerosus** — common in this age group, **white plaques, fissures, loss of labial architecture — and a vulval cancer risk** requiring treatment and follow-up.

**Numbers: menopause = 12 months of amenorrhoea · postmenopausal endometrium greater than 4–5 mm → sample · around 1 in 10 women with postmenopausal bleeding has endometrial cancer · cervical screening to age 74, and symptomatic women get a CO-TEST, not a screening test · BreastScreen invitations 50–74.** VERIFY. **She will ask 'so it's just the change of life?' — and this is where the station is won or lost**: **'it's the most likely explanation... but I want to be honest with you. Because the discharge is brownish and that may be old blood, and because any bleeding after menopause has to be taken seriously, I'm not going to stop here.'**

**When she asks 'you think it's something worse?'**: **'I don't think so, and the examination is reassuring. But thinning of the lining and a cancer of the womb can exist together, and the only way to be sure is to look.'** Then the work-up: **co-test, ultrasound for endometrial thickness, and a sample of the lining if it's thicker than it should be.**

**Treatment for the dryness, which you CAN start today**: moisturisers regularly, lubricant for sex, **topical low-dose vaginal oestrogen — very little absorbed, and it helps the bladder symptoms too.** **Arrange the overdue mammogram.** Safety-net: **frank bleeding, pain, or feeling unwell — come back sooner.**
pefe: **'And can you describe the vaginal walls?' — this is the single most important sentence in the station.** It is the **only** place in the entire pelvic examination where the examiner will not volunteer the answer. Ask 'is the cervix normal?' and you get 'yes' and no diagnosis.

**Inspection matters as much as the speculum here**: skin changes, **white plaques, fissures or ulcers**, and **any loss of the labial architecture** — that is lichen sclerosus, common in this age group and a vulval cancer risk.
**General and vitals including temperature; abdomen for tenderness, any mass and the lower border if there is one.**
**Swabs — high vaginal for microscopy and culture, endocervical for chlamydia and gonorrhoea — and a urine dipstick. Take them; her age does not exempt her.**

**If there is ANY suggestion of blood, the work-up is: CO-TEST (not a screening test — she is symptomatic) · transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness · endometrial sampling if the endometrium is above threshold or the bleeding recurs.**
**Postmenopausal endometrial thickness greater than 4–5 mm → sample.** VERIFY the local threshold.
**Around 1 in 10 women with postmenopausal bleeding has endometrial cancer** — which is why atrophic walls do not close the case.

**Treatment: vaginal moisturisers regularly, lubricants for sex, avoid soaps and scented products. Topical vaginal oestrogen — cream or pessary — is the effective treatment, with low systemic absorption, and it reduces recurrent urinary tract infections.** VERIFY doses.

**Systemic menopausal hormone therapy is not indicated for isolated vaginal symptoms**, particularly when the flushes settled years ago. **In a woman with a history of breast cancer, topical oestrogen is a specialist decision**, particularly on an aromatase inhibitor.
**Arrange the overdue mammogram** — BreastScreen invitations run 50–74, and you have just discovered she has let it slip.

High vaginal and endocervical swabs. Treat per organism

**A real differential in this age group.** Remove it

stem: Your general practice, rural South Australia. Your next patient is a 32-year-old woman presenting with vaginal discharge. She has had three similar episodes in the last three months and this is the fourth. A previous swab confirmed candidiasis, and she was treated with Nystatin.

Tasks: take a history — ask the examiner for physical findings — explain your further investigations and management. 8 minutes. Her opening: 'I have got thrush again. This is the fourth time in three months and I am sick of it.'
tasks: Take a history
Ask the examiner for physical findings
Explain your further investigations and management
findings: No pallor, no cachexia, no lymphadenopathy, NO ORAL CANDIDIASIS — you asked, which is what matters
ERYTHEMA with FISSURING and EXCORIATION; thick white curdy discharge. No white plaques or ulcers on the vulva
ADHERENT WHITE PLAQUES on the vaginal walls. Cervix normal — no lesion, ectropion or polyp
Normal — no cervical motion tenderness, normal uterus and adnexae
GLUCOSE ++. THE FINDING THAT MAKES THE STATION — and you only get it if you ask for glucose on the dipstick BY NAME
Dipstick negative for glucose, no family history, no thirst — but she is on PREDNISOLONE for asthma and has had FOUR courses of antibiotics this year
Everything negative and she has ALREADY completed six months of weekly fluconazole. Culture and speciate — think Candida glabrata

dx: **Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis with newly suspected diabetes — and the diagnosis is HANDED to you in the stem. Everything you are scored on sits behind it: why does a healthy 32-year-old get four episodes in three months?** **A candidate who takes a beautiful discharge history and then says 'I'll give you fluconazole' has answered the wrong question.**
**Definition: four or more symptomatic episodes in twelve months, with at least some microbiologically confirmed.** She meets it several times over. VERIFY

**The cause hunt IS the history, and it runs in this order: drugs (antibiotics, steroids, immunomodulators) · oestrogen (a new or changed pill, pregnancy) · diabetes · malignancy and HIV · the organism species · and LAST, weight and local factors.** **Leading with tight clothing is the named error — it is real but least important, and organic causes come first.**

**This patient has THREE contributors and gives two of them only if asked**: **antibiotics for a chest infection four months ago · started the combined pill around the same time · and thirst, nocturia, tiredness, weight gain and a father with type 2 diabetes.** **The diabetes answers are the reward questions.**

**ADDED — the cause the lecture does not mention. Non-albicans Candida, particularly Candida glabrata, causes a meaningful minority of recurrent cases and responds POORLY to fluconazole.** That is why the swab must be **a culture with SPECIATION, not just microscopy** — and why a woman failing standard therapy needs the species known before the next prescription. If challenged — 'she's completed six months of weekly fluconazole and it's back' — **'I'd culture and speciate. If it's a non-albicans species such as glabrata, azoles are often ineffective and it needs specialist advice on alternative topical treatment.'**

**TWO SETS of investigations, and saying 'two sets' out loud is the structure the task is asking for. Set 1, for the discharge: high vaginal swab for microscopy, culture AND SPECIATION · endocervical NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea · CO-TEST (HPV plus cytology), because this is a persistent unexplained discharge in a symptomatic woman · urine pregnancy test.**

**Set 2, for an underlying cause: blood glucose and HbA1c · full blood examination · HIV serology with consent · coeliac serology if supportive features · ESR and CRP if systemic illness is suspected · iron studies and thyroid function if the history suggests them.**

**Management: induction fluconazole 150 mg on days 1, 4 and 7, THEN 150 mg weekly for SIX MONTHS.** **The six-month maintenance course is the single most commonly omitted item in this station — say the dose, the days and the duration.** Simple single episode by comparison: **clotrimazole 1% × 6 nights, 2% × 3 nights, or 10% stat; or fluconazole 150 mg stat.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **two prescribing points. Nystatin is second line and now little used; it is less effective than the azoles, and the fact that she was given it is part of the case design. And oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy** — if she is or may be pregnant, use a **topical imidazole for 7 nights**, since candidiasis in pregnancy is harder to clear.

**ADDED — the partner question, said BEFORE she asks: routine partner treatment is not indicated. Treat a male partner only if he has symptomatic candidal balanitis.** Then the advice, last and briefly: plain water only, no washes or scented products, cotton underwear, out of gym gear and wet swimwear promptly. **And address the cause — if diabetes is confirmed, treating it will do more than any cream; and discuss whether the oestrogen-containing pill is contributing, since there are options without oestrogen.** SA: pathology through **Country Health Connect**; HIV testing with pre- and post-test discussion, **SHINE SA**; **Diabetes SA**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; gynaecology or sexual health with **PATS** if she fails maintenance.
plan: WIPE, open question. **'This is the fourth time in three months and I'm sick of it.'** Answer with the station's own thesis: **'that's genuinely wearing, and four episodes in three months is not something to just keep treating — I want to work out WHY it keeps coming back.'**

**Explore briefly — confirm the picture is still candida**: **'when did the first episode start? How many altogether? What is the discharge like — colour, consistency, any smell? Any itch?'** White, thick, curdy, no smell, **unbearable itch**. **A change of pattern would mean a change of diagnosis.**

**The treatment history — four questions, and the commonest reason for apparent 'recurrence' is inadequate treatment**: **'what treatment were you given each time? Did you complete the full course? Did it work, and for how long? Have you had any follow-up?'** Creams twice, then **nystatin** — second line and less effective than an azole.

**Cause hunt 1 — DRUGS**: **'have you had any antibiotics recently — even short courses? Any steroids, in any form — tablets, inhalers, creams? Any medications for arthritis, bowel disease or any immune condition?'** Antibiotics for a chest infection four months ago.
**Cause hunt 2 — OESTROGEN**: **'have you started the contraceptive pill recently, or changed it? Any chance you're pregnant?'** Started the pill four months ago — **one of the recalled positives.**

**Cause hunt 3 — DIABETES, and this is where the station is won**: **'have you ever been told your blood sugar was high? Any diabetes in the family? Are you passing more urine than usual, or drinking more, or losing weight?'** Father has diabetes; thirsty; up at night. **She gives all of this only if asked.**

**Cause hunt 4 — MALIGNANCY AND HIV**: **'any weight loss, loss of appetite, lumps or bumps, unusual tiredness? Any night sweats? Any recurring infections, mouth ulcers, or thrush in the mouth?'** **Night sweats and oral candidiasis are the additions that mark you out.**

**Cause hunt 5 — weight and local factors, asked LAST**: **'any recent weight gain? Do you wear tight or synthetic underwear or gym clothes for long periods? Do you use soaps, washes, douches or scented products?'**

**Full sexual history — it is still a vaginal discharge case**: partners, condoms, type of sex, previous STI. Then **cervical cancer**: **'any bleeding after sex? Pain during sex? Cervical screening up to date and normal?'** — **a previous candida swab does not immunise her against a cervical lesion.** Then **PID**: fever, lower tummy pain, nausea, vomiting.
**PEFE — short and mostly confirmatory, but two items carry it**: **'height, weight and BMI. Any pallor, cachexia, lymphadenopathy, or ORAL CANDIDIASIS?'** Then all four vital signs and the abdomen.

**Pelvic with consent and a chaperone**: inspection for **vulval erythema, swelling, fissuring, excoriation, satellite lesions**, white plaques or ulcers, and the character of the discharge. Speculum for the cervix, **the vaginal walls, and any adherent white plaques**. Bimanual as usual.

**The office tests, and ask for glucose BY NAME**: **'swabs, a urine pregnancy test, and a urine dipstick — INCLUDING FOR GLUCOSE.'** Glucose ++. **Glycosuria hands you the diagnosis, and you only get it if you asked.**

**Name it, then pivot immediately to the why**: **'you have recurrent thrush. But the important point today is that healthy people don't usually get four episodes in three months, so I've been looking for a reason — and I think I've found more than one.'**

**Give the reasons as a set**: **sugar in the urine, plus thirst, nocturia, tiredness, her father's diabetes and recent weight gain — which makes me suspect diabetes, and high blood sugar is one of the commonest reasons thrush keeps returning.** **On top of that, antibiotics four months ago and the pill started around the same time, both of which encourage thrush.**

**Say 'two sets of tests' and name them.** Set 1 about the discharge — **swab to confirm AND identify which type, because some types don't respond to the usual tablets**; chlamydia and gonorrhoea; a test from the cervix. Set 2 about **why** — blood sugar and HbA1c, full blood count, and **with her agreement an HIV test**.

**The regimen, with numbers**: **fluconazole 150 mg on days one, four and seven to clear it, then one tablet weekly for six months to stop it coming back. That long course is the part that actually prevents recurrence.** Then **'if the blood tests confirm diabetes, treating that will make a bigger difference than any cream'**, and raise the pill.

**Pre-empt the partner question** — not routinely, only if he has symptoms. Then the advice briefly, and the safety-net: **bleeding, pain, fever, or if this stops looking like thrush — come back.** Review at the end of the first week.
pefe: **Ask for the urine dipstick INCLUDING GLUCOSE, by name.** Glycosuria hands you the diagnosis, and the examiner will not volunteer it if you just say 'a dipstick'.

**Ask for BMI, lymphadenopathy and ORAL CANDIDIASIS** — you are looking for an immunocompromised state and for weight gain, and oral thrush is the finding that would redirect you toward HIV or haematological malignancy.

**Inspection: vulval erythema, swelling, FISSURING, excoriation, satellite lesions**; white plaques or ulcers; the character of the discharge. **Speculum: the cervix, the vaginal walls, and adherent white plaques.**

**SET 2 — for an underlying cause: blood glucose and HbA1c · full blood examination · HIV serology with consent · coeliac serology if supportive features · ESR and CRP if systemic illness suspected · iron studies and thyroid function if indicated.**

**Speciation is not optional. Non-albicans species, particularly Candida glabrata, respond poorly to fluconazole** — and a woman who fails standard therapy needs the species known before the next prescription.
**The co-test is needed because this is a persistent unexplained discharge in a symptomatic woman** — a previous candida swab does not exclude a cervical lesion.
**Induction: fluconazole 150 mg on days 1, 4 and 7. Maintenance: 150 mg weekly for 6 months.** Simple single episode: **clotrimazole 1% × 6, 2% × 3, or 10% stat; or fluconazole 150 mg stat.** VERIFY
**In pregnancy, avoid oral fluconazole — use a topical imidazole for 7 nights**, because candidiasis in pregnancy is harder to clear.
**Routine partner treatment is not indicated** — treat a male partner only for symptomatic candidal balanitis. **Say it before she asks.**

setting: A cluster with a high failure rate, because candidates walk in with one diagnosis. They recognise the recall — prolapse in an older woman, Bartholin abscess in a younger one — reach the right answer, and still fail, because they never showed the examiner a differential list. The task says 'And your differentials' for exactly that reason. The second failure is anatomical narrowness: 'Down below' includes the groin and the back passage, so a hernia, an inguinal node, a perianal abscess, a thrombosed haemorrhoid and a rectal prolapse are all lumps in a woman's private parts.
stem: Your general practice, rural South Australia. Your next patient is a 52-year-old woman who presents complaining of a lump down below.

Tasks: take a history for six minutes — explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient. 8 minutes. This is the structure behind every 'Lump down below' stem, and behind the Bartholin and prolapse stations that follow.
tasks: Locate the lump before characterising it — vagina, back passage, or groin
Run prolapse and dermatological causes in whichever order the age dictates
Explain the diagnosis AND a grouped differential list, red flags included
time: Locate it first — vagina, back passage or groin — because everything after that question is cheaper · then characterise: when, painful, skin changes, reducible, posture, impact · then, in an older woman, prolapse first — symptoms, then bowel and urinary, then obstetric and pressure risk factors — followed by skin with red flags · in a younger woman with pain, start with skin and infection — red flags first, then skin changes, then fever and systemic features — then run prolapse anyway because it collects the bowel and urinary questions · then the five Ps in the version her age calls for · then the PEFE with Valsalva asked twice and the inguinal nodes examined · then the diagnosis and the grouped differential list.
findings: 'Any change in the skin over it — redness, ulceration, bleeding, discharge?' REDNESS AND HEAT → infection · ULCERATION OR SURFACE BLEEDING → MALIGNANCY. 'Can you push it back in?' REDUCIBLE → prolapse, hernia, haemorrhoid · NOT REDUCIBLE → cyst, abscess, tumour

back.dx: THIS IS A STRUCTURE, NOT A SINGLE DIAGNOSIS — AND THE MARKS ARE IN THE GROUPED DIFFERENTIAL LIST SAID OUT LOUD. YOU DO NOT NAME EVERY ENTITY IN THE ROOM; YOU NAME THE GROUP HEADINGS AND ONE OR TWO FROM EACH, AND THE EXAMINER HEARS A STRUCTURE: PROLAPSE — anterior, posterior, apical · BARTHOLIN — cyst and abscess, and the carcinoma in an older woman · SKIN, BENIGN — cysts, lichen sclerosus, hidradenitis, urethral caruncle · SKIN, INFECTIVE — warts, herpes, abscess · SKIN, MALIGNANT — vulval carcinoma · GROIN — inguinal or femoral hernia, lymphadenopathy · BACK PASSAGE — perianal abscess, fistula, haemorrhoids, rectal prolapse, anal carcinoma. CORRECTION — THE VULVAL LUMP THAT HAS BEEN TREATED FOR MONTHS. Vulval cancer is characteristically diagnosed late, because a lump or an ulcer gets treated as thrush, dermatitis or irritation, repeatedly, for months. THE RULE THAT PREVENTS THIS: ANY VULVAL LUMP OR ULCER THAT PERSISTS, THAT DOES NOT RESPOND TO TREATMENT, OR THAT OCCURS IN A POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMAN NEEDS A BIOPSY — NOT ANOTHER CREAM. EXAMINER CHALLENGE, 'Her GP has given her three lots of antifungal already' → 'THAT IS EXACTLY THE PATTERN IN WHICH VULVAL CANCER IS MISSED. I WOULD EXAMINE IT AND REFER FOR BIOPSY RATHER THAN PRESCRIBE AGAIN.' DESCRIBING A LESION SO THE EXAMINER CAN HEAR YOU THINKING — site, size, consistency, tenderness, skin, edge: 'A firm, 2 cm, non-tender swelling at the posterior introitus on the left, with overlying erythema and no ulceration.' It takes five seconds and it is the difference between a candidate who examined and a candidate who guessed. THE DRILL SET, ONE SENTENCE EACH: 58 with a painless bulge worse by evening after four vaginal deliveries and a forceps → PELVIC ORGAN PROLAPSE, staged by compartment; pelvic floor physiotherapy, pessary, surgery, and treat the constipation and the cough · 24 with an exquisitely painful red swelling at the posterior introitus, febrile, cannot sit → BARTHOLIN ABSCESS; incision and drainage, Word catheter, analgesia, swab, antibiotics if cellulitis or systemic features · 30 with a painless smooth 2 cm swelling present for months → BARTHOLIN CYST; conservative if asymptomatic, drainage if it bothers her · 68 with an irregular ulcerated labial lesion that bleeds, two years of itch and 5 kg weight loss → VULVAL CARCINOMA until biopsied; urgent gynae-oncology referral and examine the groin nodes · 45 with itchy white crinkled plaques, fissuring and loss of the labia minora → LICHEN SCLEROSUS; potent topical steroid, long-term follow-up, and biopsy any persistent lump because of the cancer risk · 22 with multiple small painless cauliflower-like lumps → GENITAL WARTS; treatment options, screening, vaccination, condoms · 19 with crops of painful ulcers preceded by tingling, fever and tender groin nodes → PRIMARY GENITAL HERPES; PCR swab, oral antiviral, analgesia, counselling · 35 with a groin lump that appears on standing and reduces on lying with a cough impulse → INGUINAL OR FEMORAL HERNIA; surgical referral, urgent if irreducible or tender · 40 with severe perianal pain, fever and a tender fluctuant swelling beside the anus → PERIANAL ABSCESS; surgical incision and drainage, check for diabetes, consider Crohn disease · 55 with a lump visible only on straining and leakage on coughing → PROLAPSE WITH STRESS INCONTINENCE; Valsalva and cough stress test, physiotherapy first line · 70 with everything protruding, ulcerated at the tip and difficulty passing urine → PROCIDENTIA with decubitus ulceration and possible obstruction; urgent gynaecology, post-void residual, consider pessary and topical oestrogen · 48 with recurrent painful lumps in the groin and axillae that discharge and scar → HIDRADENITIS SUPPURATIVA; dermatology, smoking cessation, weight, long-term management · 62 with a small red fleshy lump at the urethral opening that bleeds a little → URETHRAL CARUNCLE, usually benign and oestrogen-related, biopsy if atypical · 33 with a non-reducible painful bluish lump at the anal margin after straining → THROMBOSED EXTERNAL HAEMORRHOID; analgesia, conservative or excision within the first 72 hours. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN LOCALISATION: PELVIC FLOOR PHYSIOTHERAPY IS FIRST-LINE for prolapse and stress incontinence, and access is limited rurally — name telehealth options and the National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66 VERIFY; pessary fitting through a gynaecology clinic or a trained GP; urgent gynaecology or gynae-oncology referral for a suspicious vulval lesion with PATS travel support; the local emergency department for an abscess needing drainage, and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if septic; local ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; interpreters through TIS National 131 450.
plan: OPEN, THEN LOCATE IT BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: 'Can you show me or describe where it is — is it around the vagina, around the back passage, or up in the groin?' This is the cheapest question in the station and it deletes two thirds of the list.

CHARACTERISE IN SIX MOVES — when first noticed, constant or intermittent, getting bigger · PAINFUL TO TOUCH · skin changes, ulceration, bleeding, discharge · CAN SHE PUSH IT BACK IN · worse standing and better lying · and the impact on her day-to-day life.

OLDER WOMAN: PROLAPSE SYMPTOMS — dragging or heaviness, dyspareunia, difficulty passing urine, leaking, difficulty with stools and having to press, recurrent urinary infections. YOUNGER WOMAN WITH PAIN: skin and infection first, then run this block anyway.

PROLAPSE RISK FACTORS — the obstetric history with the bad-history questions (large babies, long labour, forceps or vacuum, tears or stitches) · menopause · PREVIOUS HYSTERECTOMY · chronic cough, constipation, heavy lifting, obesity · connective tissue disorders.

THE RED FLAG BLOCK, OUT LOUD — weight, appetite, tiredness, AND LUMPS IN THE GROIN · skin changes with ULCERATION AND BLEEDING · itch and how long it has been there. Then infection: fever, chills, feeling unwell, nausea.
SEXUAL HISTORY AS A SCREEN unless something turns up · BOWEL QUESTIONS — pain on passing stools, blood, discharge from the back passage · HOST FACTORS — diabetes, smoking, immunosuppressants.
THE FIVE Ps IN THE VERSION HER AGE CALLS FOR — the menopausal version for a 52-year-old, with the hormone and mammogram questions rather than contraception and Gardasil.

HISTORY CLOSES. PEFE: BMI, cachexia, pallor · all four vital signs with temperature · abdomen AND THE INGUINAL REGIONS FOR MASSES OR LYMPHADENOPATHY · CONSENT AND CHAPERONE · inspection with skin changes, white plaques, loss of architecture, and the lump described properly · VALSALVA · COUGH STRESS TEST · speculum AND VALSALVA AGAIN · bimanual · dipstick, with a post-void residual if she describes incomplete emptying.

THE DIAGNOSIS NAMED IN PLAIN WORDS WITH COMPARTMENT AND STAGE IF IT IS PROLAPSE, THEN THE GROUPED DIFFERENTIAL LIST BY HEADINGS (see dx) — this is the part candidates omit and the reason they fail with the right answer.

dx: **Bartholin gland abscess — and this is the most reliably failed station in the gynaecology block, for a documented reason: candidates reach the right diagnosis with no differentials and no red flags.** They walk in with one diagnosis in mind, take a competent history, say 'Bartholin abscess', and fail. **Being right is not the same as being safe, and the marking sheet tests the second thing.**

**The three Bartholin diagnoses, because candidates are asked. CYST — the duct outlet is blocked, secretions accumulate, NOT infected: a smooth, PAINLESS swelling, no redness, no fever, often noticed incidentally. BARTHOLINITIS — infection of the gland WITHOUT a collection: tender, enlarged, no fluctuant swelling and no pus to drain. ABSCESS — the obstructed gland becomes infected and fills with pus: painful, tense, red, hot; she often cannot sit; fever and malaise. This is the recalled case.**

**Anatomy you must be able to state: the Bartholin (greater vestibular) glands sit at the 4 o'clock and 8 o'clock positions of the posterior vaginal introitus, with ducts opening just outside the hymenal ring, secreting mucus for lubrication.** So the expected swelling is at **the lower part of the vaginal opening, to one side.**

**The explanation**: two small glands at the lower part of the vaginal opening, one each side, that make fluid for lubrication; **if the outlet of one becomes blocked, fluid builds up, and if that becomes infected it forms an abscess — a sac full of pus.** **Reasons: the lump is exactly where those glands sit, it is very painful, the skin over it is red, and she has had a fever.**

**The differentials, said in this order, six minimum, grouped**: **Bartholin cyst without infection** (painless) · **Bartholin gland carcinoma — rare, but the reason we take a persistent lump seriously** · a boil or skin abscess · a perianal abscess · herpes or warts · a sebaceous or epidermoid cyst · hidradenitis suppurativa · vulval skin cancer · and less likely, a hernia, a thrombosed haemorrhoid, or a prolapse.

**DRAINAGE IS THE TREATMENT.** **'An abscess does not settle on tablets alone, because antibiotics do not get into pus well.'** Local anaesthetic, a small incision, let the pus out — **she should feel dramatically better almost immediately** — then **a WORD CATHETER, a small tube with a tiny balloon, left in for 2–4 weeks so a new outlet forms and it does not simply refill.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **antibiotics are not the reflex answer.** The lecture says 'definitely give antibiotics'. **For an uncomplicated, adequately drained abscess in a well, non-pregnant, non-diabetic woman, drainage alone is often sufficient.** The better answer: **'drainage is the treatment; I would add antibiotics if there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy, diabetes or a positive swab.'**

CORRECTION — **where drainage happens.** The lecture routes every abscess to the emergency department. **In practice a Bartholin abscess is frequently drained under local anaesthetic in general practice, and Word catheter insertion is a GP-level skill.** Say what you actually mean: **'this needs to be drained today. I can do that here under local anaesthetic with a Word catheter, or if that isn't available I'll arrange it at the hospital — but it is not something to wait on.'** **Refer if she is septic, if the anatomy is unclear, or if malignancy is suspected.**

**Swab the pus for microscopy and culture, AND take chlamydia and gonorrhoea swabs** — gonorrhoea can occasionally be involved. **Analgesia and warm baths.** **For recurrence: marsupialisation**, where the edges are stitched open so the gland drains permanently.

**THE OVER-40 RULE: biopsy any Bartholin-area mass in a woman over about 40**, or any persistent mass. **A painless Bartholin-area swelling present for months in an older woman is not an abscess — it is a biopsy.** That rule is what connects this version to Version B. SA: drainage locally where possible; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if septic; gynaecology or gynae-oncology with **PATS**; **SHINE SA** for sexual health swabs; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**.
plan: WIPE, open question. **'I've got a lump down below and it's really sore. I can hardly sit down.'** Acknowledge, then locate it.

**Explore the lump — and the first question is location, because it splits the differential**: **'where exactly — is it around the vagina, around the back passage, or up in the groin?'** Then **'when did you notice it? Is it getting bigger? Is it painful to touch? Any change in the skin over it? Can you push it back in? Is it worse standing?'**
**Characterise the pain**: **'what is the pain like — burning, throbbing, a dull ache? How bad out of ten? Anything that makes it better or worse?'** Throbbing, eight out of ten, worst on sitting.

**RED FLAGS — asked FIRST, not last, and this is the block candidates omit**: **'have you lost any weight? Any change in appetite? Are you unusually tired? ANY LUMPS IN YOUR GROIN?'** All negative — **and the negatives are what make your benign diagnosis defensible.**

**Skin**: **'any redness or rash? Any ulcers or blisters? Any bleeding from it? Any discharge? Any long-standing itch?'** Red and shiny, no ulceration, no bleeding. **The long-standing itch question is the one that would open lichen sclerosus.**
**Infection — the block that separates abscess from cyst**: **'any fever or chills? Do you feel unwell? Any nausea?'** Shivery last night.

**Prolapse block, quickly — it collects the bowel and urinary questions and covers the perianal differentials**: **'any dragging or heaviness? Difficulty passing urine, or leaking? Difficulty or pain passing stools, or blood?'**
**Sexual history — a screen here, not a full one**: sexually active, condoms, new partners, previous STI, pain during sex. **Dyspareunia is expected with an abscess — do not over-read it.**

**Before prescribing**: **'when was your last period? Any chance you could be pregnant? Any allergies, particularly to antibiotics? Any diabetes? Up to date with cervical screening?'** **Diabetes predisposes to abscess, and both allergy and pregnancy must precede any drug.**

**Ask to see the photograph and DESCRIBE IT OUT LOUD**: **'there is a tense swelling at the lower part of the vaginal opening on the left, with redness of the overlying skin and no ulceration.'** **If the skin is dark: 'erythema is difficult to assess in this skin tone, so I would rely on warmth, tenderness and fluctuance.'**
**Name it and explain the mechanism** — the two glands, the blocked outlet, the infected collection. **Then the four reasons: the site, the pain, the redness, the fever.**

**The differentials — six, grouped, and she will ask 'could it be anything else?'**: cyst without infection, boil or skin abscess, perianal abscess, herpes or warts, sebaceous cyst, hidradenitis — **and rarely a cancer of the vulval skin or of the gland itself, 'which is why I asked about weight, tiredness and lumps in the groin, and why I'd want to look again once this settles if anything remains.'**
**Management — drainage first, and say why tablets alone will not do it**: local anaesthetic, small incision, immediate relief, **then a Word catheter for a few weeks so a new outlet forms.**

**When she asks about antibiotics — qualify, do not reflex**: not necessarily; **if the surrounding skin is infected, if she is unwell, or if the swab grows something.** **Send the pus for culture, and take chlamydia and gonorrhoea swabs.** Regular analgesia, warm baths.

**When she asks whether it can come back**: yes, and **marsupialisation** for repeated episodes. Safety-net: **fever, spreading redness, worsening pain, or the lump returning.** Review after drainage and again when the swabs are back.

dx: **Vulval carcinoma, or rarely a Bartholin gland carcinoma — and this version exists to prove why the red flags in Version A are not optional. In Version A the red flags make a confident benign diagnosis defensible. HERE THEY ARE THE DIAGNOSIS. The same four questions carry both.**

**What the stem gives you, and what each item means: a lump around the vagina getting WORSE over four months — progressive, not self-limiting · PAIN present in some recalls and absent in others — painlessness is NOT reassuring · BROWNISH DISCHARGE — old blood · SPOTTING — surface bleeding from a friable lesion · and a photograph of an irregular, ugly lesion with superficial bleeding.**

**You are not expected to recognise the photograph.** The candidates who sat this case could not match it to any image they had seen. **That is the point. You are expected to know that irregular plus bleeding plus progressive equals cancer until biopsied.**

**How to say it — concern, honesty, reasons, urgency, and no false certainty**: **'I need to be honest with you about what I'm thinking. When I look at this area I can see an irregular growth with some bleeding on its surface, and it has been getting worse rather than better. That combination makes me concerned about the possibility of a cancer — either a skin cancer of the vulva, or, rarely, a cancer of the Bartholin gland itself.'**

**Then the sentence that keeps you honest**: **'I want to be clear that I cannot tell from looking. The only way to know is to take a small sample of it, and I am going to arrange that urgently with a specialist.'**

**Give your reasons**: the appearance, the progression over four months, the bleeding and the discharge, **the painlessness if that is the version you have**, and the red flags she gave you — **the weight loss and the tiredness.**

**ADDED — what you should know about vulval cancer. Mostly squamous cell carcinoma. TWO PATHWAYS: HPV-related (younger women, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, smoking, immunosuppression) and NON-HPV related (older women, arising in LICHEN SCLEROSUS).** Her **two-year unresolved itch is the lichen sclerosus clue**, and recognising it is on the marking sheet.
**It spreads FIRST to the INGUINAL LYMPH NODES** — which is why you examine the groin and why 'any lumps in your groin?' is in the history at all.
**Diagnosis is by BIOPSY. Management is surgical, by a gynaecological oncology service, with sentinel node assessment or groin node dissection. Referral is URGENT.** VERIFY

**And whichever version you get, the task says 'and your differentials'. Say six of them, grouped, before you move to management** — Bartholin cyst or abscess, Bartholin gland carcinoma, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, lichen sclerosus, a chronic ulcer from herpes or syphilis, hidradenitis, and a sebaceous cyst. **Naming them is scored even when you are confident.** SA: **urgent** gynae-oncology referral with **PATS**; **BreastScreen SA** and **National Cancer Screening Register** if screening has lapsed; ACCHS, Aboriginal Health Worker, **Closing the Gap PBS**; **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20**; **TIS National 131 450**.

**Do NOT be reassured by the painlessness — say so to yourself and keep going.** Malignancy is classically painless until late, and this is where a candidate running the abscess script goes wrong.

**RED FLAGS, asked first and in full — here they ARE the diagnosis**: **'have you lost any weight? Any change in appetite? Are you unusually tired? Any lumps in your groin?'** **About four kilos without trying, and tired.** She gives these only if asked.

dx: **THREE diagnoses, not two: uterine prolapse · a fungal or irritant rash · and NEW DIABETES. Everyone asks why the examiners put a blood sugar in a prolapse case. The answer: a random glucose of 12 mmol/L with symptoms meets the threshold for diabetes mellitus, and undiagnosed diabetes is WHY she keeps getting a fungal rash in her groin.** VERIFY the criteria.

**The complete answer, said in three parts**: **'First, you have a prolapse of the womb. Second, the rash is most likely a fungal or irritant rash, and I'll take a scraping and treat it. And third — and this may be the most important thing today — your blood sugar is high enough to suggest diabetes, which is very likely why this rash keeps coming back. I want to confirm that with further blood tests.'**
**If asked why the diabetes matters here**: **'it explains the recurrence, it will not settle until the glucose is controlled, and it needs managing in its own right.'**

CORRECTION — **the recalls call this rash candida, and the reasoning does not hold.** Look at what you were actually given: **a VERY ITCHY, RECURRENT rash in the groin, with incontinence keeping the skin wet, and a blood sugar of 12.**

**The four candidates, with their discriminating features. CANDIDAL INTERTRIGO — beefy red, moist, in the skin folds, with SATELLITE LESIONS beyond the main area; itch usually moderate, soreness and burning more typical. TINEA CRURIS — an ANNULAR patch with a RAISED SCALY ACTIVE EDGE and CENTRAL CLEARING, spreading onto the thighs, and characteristically VERY ITCHY. CONTACT OR IRRITANT DERMATITIS — ill-defined erythema matching the area in contact with urine, pads or a new product, and intensely itchy. FLEXURAL PSORIASIS — well-demarcated, glazed red plaques in the folds WITHOUT scale.**

**The defensible exam answer is not to pick one blindly**: **'the rash is most likely an irritant contact dermatitis from urinary leakage, or a fungal infection — TINEA CRURIS fits an intensely itchy recurrent rash better than candida. I'd look for a raised scaly edge with central clearing versus satellite lesions, take skin scrapings for fungal microscopy and culture, and treat accordingly.'** **That answer survives whichever way the marking sheet is written.**

**Explore the rash properly, in four blocks: WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE — just redness, or ulcers or blisters? colour? discharge, scaling or weeping? where exactly — skin folds, labia, spreading to the thighs? HOW IT FEELS — itchy or painful? COURSE — how long, first time or recurrent, anything better or worse, creams tried and did they help? CONTACT AND MOISTURE — leaking urine onto the skin? new soaps, wipes, pads, washing powder or creams?**
**Then the HOST FACTORS question, which is the one that connects to the BSL of 12**: **'do you have diabetes, or has your sugar ever been high? Any steroids? Any recent antibiotics?'**

**The prolapse half is unchanged and still fully scored: Valsalva twice, the risk factor blocks, the red flags, and grouped differentials.** Do not let the rash consume the station — **a candidate who solves the rash and never asks for Valsalva has still failed the prolapse.**

**Management is also three-part: prolapse — physiotherapy first, treat constipation and cough, weight and lifting, vaginal oestrogen, pessary, surgery, managed by bother · rash — skin scrapings, then topical antifungal or barrier and steroid as indicated, plus keeping the skin dry and managing the incontinence · diabetes — confirm with fasting glucose and HbA1c, then full diabetes assessment and management.** SA: **Diabetes SA** and practice diabetes education; pelvic floor physiotherapy and **National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66**; gynaecology with **PATS**; **Quitline 13 7848**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.

dx: **A gynaecology station wearing a urology coat. The examiners have rotated the diagnosis THREE times off the same one-word complaint — stress incontinence, urge incontinence, and atrophic change — so you cannot prepare by memorising the answer. The pass is in the structure.**

**And before it is a gynaecology case it is a KIDNEY–URETER–BLADDER case. You will not pass by reaching the right menopausal diagnosis if you never excluded bladder cancer and infection in a 62-year-old with urinary symptoms.**

**TWO SWEEPS, IN THIS ORDER. The KUB sweep — haematuria, weight loss, fever, dysuria, stones, glucose. Then the MENOPAUSAL sweep — dryness, prolapse, leaking on coughing, and the prolapse risk factors. MISS THE FIRST AND YOU FAIL WITH THE RIGHT DIAGNOSIS. MISS THE SECOND AND YOU NEVER REACH IT.**

**STEP 1 — make her define the word, because 'frequency' means four different things to four patients. Going more often with normal volumes → overactive bladder, infection, small-capacity bladder, atrophy. Passing LARGER amounts (polyuria) → diabetes, diabetes insipidus, diuretics, excess fluid or caffeine. Waking at night (nocturia) → overactive bladder, heart failure, sleep apnoea, polyuria. Going often to manage leakage → incontinence.**

**Then sweep EVERY urinary symptom once, as a block: dysuria, urgency, hesitancy, poor stream, incomplete emptying, incontinence, haematuria.** Half your differential shares these — collect them in one pass and stop coming back.
**The single question that sorts the two commonest versions**: **'when you leak, is it a FEW DROPS or a LARGE AMOUNT?'** **Stress = a few drops on effort. Urge = a large volume with a sudden need.**

CORRECTION — **two things the versions can hide. MIXED INCONTINENCE is the commonest pattern in this age group** — if she describes both leaking on coughing AND urgency, **say so; the answer is not one or the other.** **OVERFLOW INCONTINENCE is the dangerous one to miss**: frequency, small volumes, poor stream, straining and incomplete emptying in a woman with a large prolapse or on anticholinergics is **chronic retention**, and **treating it as an overactive bladder makes it worse. Ask for a post-void residual whenever there are voiding symptoms.**

CORRECTION — **painless visible haematuria is NOT part of a continence work-up.** In a 62-year-old it is **bladder cancer until proven otherwise** and needs **urgent urological referral for cystoscopy and upper tract imaging, regardless of whatever else you find.** Smoking and occupational exposure to aromatic amines are the classic risk factors. If challenged — 'her dipstick shows blood and she has a positive cough test' — **'she has two problems. I'd treat the incontinence, but the haematuria needs its own urgent work-up. I'm not attributing it to the prolapse.'** VERIFY referral criteria.

**If she is too embarrassed to say what is wrong** — an older recall opens with **'I've been having some problems and I'm a bit embarrassed to talk about them'** — **that is a cue, and the response is a confidentiality statement**: **'everything you tell me stays between us. Whatever it is, I promise you it's something I hear often and it's almost always treatable — take your time.'** **Candidates who pressed on with closed questions never got the history.**

**Management: behavioural FIRST in both common types, and saying so is worth more than naming a drug. Stress — supervised pelvic floor training for at least three months, plus treating constipation, caffeine reduction and weight. Urge — bladder training, caffeine reduction, then antimuscarinics WITH their risks named: confusion, falls, constipation and retention in older women. Atrophic — topical vaginal oestrogen.** **Numbers: normal voiding roughly 4–7 times daily · a 3-DAY BLADDER DIARY is the single most useful investigation and the one candidates never mention.** VERIFY. SA: pelvic floor physiotherapy and continence nurse services are limited rurally — **name telehealth and the National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66**; **Continence Aids Payment Scheme**; urology and urogynaecology with **PATS**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: WIPE, open question. **'I've been having some problems and I'm a bit embarrassed to talk about them.'** **Do NOT push on with closed questions — offer confidentiality**: **'whatever it is, everything you tell me stays between us. I promise you it's very likely something I hear often and can help with. Take your time.'** She then opens up.

**STEP 1 — define the word**: **'is it that you go more often, or that you're passing a larger amount each time?'** More often, normal volume. Then **'how many times a day, and do you wake at night to go?'** Eight or nine, once at night.

**KUB sweep 2 — INFECTION AND STONES**: **'any fever or chills? Any burning? Any lower tummy or back pain? Any nausea or vomiting? Any smell to the urine? How often have you had urine infections? Any history of kidney stones, in you or the family? Any loin pain?'**

**MENOPAUSAL sweep — and all three recalled answers live here**: **'when did your periods stop? Any hot flushes? Any dryness in the vagina, or pain with sex? Do you leak when you cough? Have you felt any lump or bulge down below?'**

**The prolapse risk factors, because they become your explanation**: **'how many pregnancies, and how did you deliver? Any large babies, long labours, forceps, tears? Any operations down below? Any chronic cough, constipation, or heavy lifting? And your weight?'** Four vaginal deliveries, two large babies, one forceps, constipation, BMI 31.

**Neurological screen**: **'any back pain, weakness or numbness in the legs, or any change in bowel control?'** Then **drugs and habits**: **'any water tablets or other medications? **Name it with the mechanism**: **'you have stress incontinence. You leak a small amount whenever the pressure inside your tummy rises — coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting. It happens because the pelvic floor muscles and the gateway of the bladder have become weakened, so they can't hold against that pressure.'**

**'Why has it happened?' — reasons from her own history**: four vaginal deliveries including two large babies and a forceps delivery; menopause thinning the tissues; constipation and straining; extra weight. **Then the examination: anterior wall descent, and she leaked when she coughed.**

**SAY THE RED-FLAG EXCLUSIONS OUT LOUD — this is the sentence that separates a pass from a fail with the right diagnosis**: **'I also checked there was no blood in your urine, no infection and no sugar, because at your age I wouldn't want to miss a bladder problem or diabetes hiding behind this.'**

**'Can anything be done?' — behavioural FIRST**: **'the first treatment is not a tablet or an operation. Supervised pelvic floor exercises with a physiotherapist, done properly for at least three months, work well for this.'** Plus constipation, caffeine, weight, and **topical vaginal oestrogen**. Then support devices and surgery if needed.
**Safety-net**: **blood in the urine, fever, pain, or any weakness in the legs — come back.** Offer a **three-day bladder diary** to bring to the review.

dx: **Genital herpes causing acute urinary retention — and the station is DESIGNED to catch the candidate who knows the recall.** Everyone knows the answer is herpes. The marks are for **a full differential sweep, a proper pain assessment, and the decision not to catheterise through active lesions.**

**Do NOT catheterise before taking the history.** Ask yourself: **what is causing the retention, before you have asked anything or looked at anything?** **Acknowledge the urgency without abandoning the task**: **'I can see you're in a lot of pain. I'm going to ask a nurse to prepare some pain relief now and to set up to empty your bladder — and while that happens, I need to ask you a few questions quickly so I use the right method. Is that alright?'** **Ten seconds, and it shows urgency, safety and sequence.**

**ADDED — THE DIAGNOSIS THAT MUST NOT BE MISSED. Cauda equina syndrome: retention WITH back pain, saddle (perineal) numbness, bilateral leg weakness or sciatica, or loss of bowel control — a surgical emergency requiring immediate MRI and neurosurgical referral. Urinary retention is one of its cardinal features.** The question belongs in **every** retention history and takes ten seconds. If challenged on why you asked: **'because painless retention with saddle anaesthesia would be cauda equina syndrome, which needs an MRI the same day.'**
**Worth knowing: herpes itself can cause retention through SACRAL NERVE INVOLVEMENT as well as through pain — sometimes called Elsberg syndrome.**

**Acute retention is uncommon in young women and therefore ALWAYS has a cause.** Six differential groups: **cancer and pelvic mass · fibroids and a gravid retroverted uterus · infection · local lesions such as herpes · neurological, including cauda equina · trauma and drugs.** **Say the six headings and the examiner hears a differential, not a recall.**

**Anchor the infection questions to BEFORE the retention began** — you cannot ask about dysuria in someone who is not passing urine. **'Before this started, were you passing urine more often, or was it burning?'**

**Describe the photograph rather than naming a diagnosis straight away**: **'there are multiple shallow, round ulcers with erythematous margins on the labia bilaterally, with surrounding oedema — consistent with ruptured herpetic vesicles.'**

**The explanation**: **'you most likely have genital herpes. It's a sexually transmitted infection caused by a virus, and it causes very painful blisters and ulcers. The pain is severe enough that the bladder outlet closes up — and that's why you haven't been able to pass urine.'** **Reasons: the appearance of the ulcers, the severity of the pain, the timing, and the sexual history.**

CORRECTION — **aspiration empties a bladder once; retention may need ongoing drainage.** The recalled answer is **suprapubic aspiration** and it is accepted, **but retention caused by herpes often persists for days, so what is usually needed is a suprapubic CATHETER left in until she can void.** Say the principle and you cannot be wrong: **'I would avoid passing a catheter through ulcerated skin, so I'd drain the bladder suprapubically, and leave drainage in place until she can void comfortably.'** VERIFY local practice.

**TWO PROBLEMS, NOT ONE. The retention: analgesia, suprapubic drainage, lignocaine gel, warm bath or shower to void. The herpes: valaciclovir 500 mg BD for 5–10 days in a first episode (famciclovir 250 mg, aciclovir 400 mg — shorter for recurrences) VERIFY · HSV PCR swab from the BASE of an ulcer · a full STI screen, because they travel together · and counselling on recurrence, asymptomatic shedding, condoms, suppression and pregnancy.** **Herpes is NOT notifiable; chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV are.** SA: bladder ultrasound and drainage locally, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if retrieval is needed; **SHINE SA** with **Let Them Know** and **Better to Know** for anonymous notification; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **Acknowledge and act, in one sentence** — pain relief and drainage set in motion, then permission for a few quick questions **'because they decide how I do it safely.'** **She will interrupt with 'can you just put a tube in?' — if you do not acknowledge the pain, she becomes insistent and answers poorly.**

**Timing**: **'when did you last pass urine? Has this ever happened before? Did it come on suddenly, or build up gradually?'** Eighteen hours, never before, built up over a day. **Sudden points to an acute local cause; gradual points to obstruction or a neurological process.**

**Pain assessment — the candidate who knows the recall skips this, and it is scored**: **'where is the pain? What is it like? How bad out of ten? Does it go anywhere? Anything that makes it better or worse?'** **It also distinguishes suprapubic bladder pain from vulval pain.**

**Group 1 — cancer and mass**: **'any weight loss? Appetite change? Any lumps or bumps? Unusual tiredness? Any family history of cancer? Any bloating, or change in your bowels?'** **Bloating and bowel change are the vague symptoms of ovarian cancer.**

**Group 2 — fibroids, periods and pregnancy**: **'when was your last period? Any heavy or painful periods? Any pressure or heaviness in your lower tummy? Any chance you could be pregnant?'** **A fibroid uterus or a gravid retroverted uterus can obstruct the outlet.**

**Group 3 — infection, anchored to before the retention**: **'BEFORE this started, were you passing urine more often, or was it burning? Any blood in the urine? Any fever or chills?'** Burning for two days, hot and achy.

**Group 4 — the rash, asked in SEQUENCE and not first**: **'have you noticed any rash or sores down below? Can you describe them — is it redness, blisters, or open sores? Any discharge? Are they painful?'** Started as blisters, now open and raw.

**Group 5 — full sexual history, where the recalled positives sit**: **'are you sexually active? A stable relationship, or more than one partner? Do you use condoms? Any new partner recently? Have you or a partner ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection?'**

**Group 6 — NEUROLOGICAL, non-negotiable, ten seconds**: **'any back pain? Any numbness between your legs or in the saddle area? Any weakness in your legs? Any change in bowel control?'** All negative here — **and the mark is for asking.**

**Group 7 — trauma and drugs**: **'any injury to the back or the private parts? Any recent surgery? Any medications — antihistamines, strong painkillers, antidepressants?'** **Common and reversible causes.** Then **'any allergies? Any chance you're pregnant?'**

**PEFE**: general appearance and distress; **all four vital signs including TEMPERATURE**; abdomen for tenderness and **a palpable bladder**; **inspection of the vulva and perineum with consent and a chaperone**; **a brief neurological assessment of perineal sensation and leg power**; and **a bladder scan for residual volume**.
**Describe the photograph before naming it**: multiple shallow round ulcers with erythematous margins on both labia, with surrounding oedema — **'consistent with ruptured herpetic vesicles.'**

**Name it with reasons** — appearance, severity of pain, timing, sexual history — **then the differentials in one breath**: a pelvic mass such as an ovarian cyst or fibroid pressing on the bladder, a urinary infection, a stone, a problem with the nerves in the lower spine, and severe inflammation from another cause.

**Problem one — the bladder, and SAY WHY you are avoiding the urethra**: **'because you have open sores, I don't want to pass a tube up through the urethra — it would be extremely painful and it risks carrying infection inside. Instead I'll drain the bladder through the lower part of your tummy, under local anaesthetic and using ultrasound to guide me.'** **Leave drainage in until she can void.**

**Problem two — the herpes**: **valaciclovir twice daily for up to ten days**; **strong analgesia and lignocaine gel**, which also makes voiding bearable; **salt baths, and voiding in a warm bath or shower because the water dilutes the urine**; **swab the base of an ulcer for HSV PCR**; and **a full STI screen — chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV — because they travel together.**

**Counselling, three sentences that turn a diagnosis into care**: **the virus stays in the body and can recur, but later episodes are almost always much milder and shorter** · **it can be passed on even with no visible sores, so condoms help but don't remove the risk** · **and if she ever becomes pregnant she must tell her midwife or doctor, because it matters around the time of delivery.** Mention **daily suppression** for frequent recurrences.

**Partners and follow-up**: herpes is not notifiable, but partners are worth telling, and **if the other tests are positive there are confidential and anonymous ways to notify.** Safety-net: **still unable to pass urine after drainage, fever, or worsening pain.**

dx: **The second great contraception counselling station. It is passed on TWO contraindication lists — because you are inserting both a device AND a hormone — and on the practical aftercare block. If you only run the hormonal list, you have counselled her for a progestogen-only pill.**

**Open with the question that gives you three things at once**: **'what do you already know about the Mirena? And can I ask what's made you want to change from the pill — any side effects or problems?'** **It gives you her side effects, her adherence and her expectations in one answer.**

**Mechanism, said simply — TWO things: it thickens the cervical mucus so sperm cannot get through, and it thins the lining of the womb so a pregnancy cannot implant.** In some women it also suppresses ovulation, **but that is not its main action — mention it only if you have time.**

**LIST 1 — because it is a DEVICE IN THE UTERUS: current pelvic inflammatory disease · current sexually transmitted infection, symptomatic or not · unexplained vaginal bleeding — investigate it first · distorted uterine cavity (large fibroids, congenital anomaly) · current puerperal or post-abortion sepsis · gestational trophoblastic disease · endometrial cancer · cervical cancer awaiting treatment · known or suspected pregnancy.**

**LIST 2 — because it contains a PROGESTOGEN: current or past breast cancer · severe liver disease or hepatic tumour · ischaemic heart disease or stroke (for continuation if it develops on treatment) · systemic lupus with antiphospholipid antibodies.** **Note how much shorter this list is than the combined pill's — a Mirena is often the answer for a woman who cannot take oestrogen: migraine with aura, previous clot, smoker over 35, enzyme-inducing medication.**

**TWO EXCLUSIONS BEFORE INSERTION, said out loud as part of the plan. 1 — PREGNANCY: inserting a device into a pregnant uterus is the disaster this station guards against. Last period, recent unprotected sex, urine test. 2 — SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTION: inserting through an infected cervix seeds the upper tract. Sexual history, and screen for chlamydia and gonorrhoea under 30, or over 30 with risk factors.** **And note what you do NOT do: antibiotic prophylaxis is never indicated for IUD insertion.**

**Facts the lecture omits that a patient will ask. Duration: licensed for contraception up to 8 years, and 5 years for heavy menstrual bleeding or endometrial protection with MHT. Effectiveness: over 99%. Periods: irregular spotting for 3–6 months, then much lighter, with about 1 in 5 having no periods at all by a year — normal and harmless, but she MUST be told in advance or she will think something is wrong. Fertility returns immediately on removal. Other uses: first-line for heavy menstrual bleeding, useful in adenomyosis and endometriosis, and for endometrial protection including hyperplasia without atypia.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **do NOT tell her it will not hurt.** The lecture says it is like a cervical screening test and 'is not going to be painful'. **That is untrue for many women, and it is both a consent problem and a credibility problem the moment the tenaculum goes on.** **Insertion commonly causes strong cramping, and a significant minority — particularly those who have never given birth vaginally — find it severely painful.** Discuss pain openly and **offer analgesia: an NSAID beforehand, local anaesthetic to the cervix where appropriate, and a clear agreement that she can ask you to stop at any point.** VERIFY local protocols.

CORRECTION — **timing is not restricted to days 1–5.** Traditional teaching inserts in the first five days, when pregnancy is effectively excluded and no extra cover is needed. **In current practice a Mirena may be inserted at ANY point in the cycle provided pregnancy can reasonably be excluded, with seven days of additional contraception. It can also be inserted immediately after delivery or after a termination, and is safe while breastfeeding.** VERIFY

**ADDED — the sulfur allergy, answered properly. Two moves. FIRST, characterise it** — 'what did you take, what did it do, and how quickly did it come on?' — **a rash hours later is a different matter from anaphylaxis in minutes.** **SECOND, know what the device contains: the frame holds BARIUM SULFATE, which makes it visible on X-ray. Barium sulfate is an inert inorganic salt, immunologically distinct from sulfonamide antibiotics and from sulfites; cross-reactivity is not expected, and no Australian source lists sulfur allergy as a contraindication to a Mirena.** SA: insertion in general practice by trained GPs and through **SHINE SA** — **check who locally inserts and what the wait is before promising a date**; ultrasound and gynaecology with **PATS** if the device is lost; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: WIPE, open question. **'I want to talk about getting a Mirena, and ideally get it done.'** Then **'what do you already know about it? And what's made you want to change from the pill — any side effects or problems?'**

**P1 Periods, and the sub-question that can stop the whole procedure**: **'when was your last period? Are they regular? Any heavy bleeding or excessive pain? AND ANY BLEEDING OR PAIN BETWEEN PERIODS?'** **Unexplained abnormal bleeding is investigated BEFORE a device goes in, not treated with one.**

**P2 Partner — risk factors AND symptoms**: **'are you sexually active? In a stable relationship, or have there been multiple partners? Do you use condoms? Ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection?'** Then **'any vaginal discharge? Any lower tummy pain? Any fever? Any pain during sex or bleeding after sex?'** **Dyspareunia and post-coital bleeding also cover the cervix.**

**P3 Pills**: **'which pill, for how long, and what side effects have you had?'** Microgynon fifteen years, nausea and headaches in the pill-free week — **and this is your chance to say the Mirena avoids those particular problems.**

**P4 Pregnancy — and the reward question sits here**: **'how many pregnancies? How did you deliver — ANY CAESAREAN SECTIONS? Any surgery on the womb, such as fibroid removal? Any chance you could be pregnant now?'** One caesarean. **A scar on the uterus raises the risk of perforation, and examiners ask why you asked.**

**P5 Screening**: **'are you up to date with cervical screening, and was it normal?'** Then **past history, covering the progestogen list**: **'any history of breast cancer? Any liver disease or liver lumps? Any heart attack or stroke? Any other cancers — of the womb or cervix? Any medications?'**

**Allergies — and CHARACTERISE, do not just note**: **'any allergies?'** *'I'm allergic to sulfur.'* **'Can you tell me what happened — what did you take, what did it do, and how quickly did it come on?'** A delayed rash to an antibiotic, no swelling, no breathing difficulty.

**PEFE, short and each item purposeful**: **'height, weight and BMI; blood pressure and the other vital signs INCLUDING TEMPERATURE; a cardiovascular examination; an abdominal examination for hepatomegaly and right upper quadrant tenderness.'**

**The pelvic examination — NOT optional here, and say why**: **'with consent and a chaperone — inspection, speculum for the cervix and any discharge, and bimanual for uterine SIZE, POSITION and tenderness, and for cervical motion tenderness.'** Then **'and a urine pregnancy test, and swabs where indicated.'**

**Block 1 — what it is and how it works**: a small T-shaped device releasing levonorgestrel; **thickens the secretions at the mouth of the womb, and thins the lining**; **lasts years, over 99% effective, and you don't have to remember anything — which is exactly what she was after.**

**Block 2 — minor side effects, and the one everybody must be warned about**: headache, mood changes, breast tenderness, weight change — **then 'irregular spotting and unpredictable bleeding for the first three to six months. It settles. After that most women have much lighter periods, and about one in five stop having periods altogether — which is normal and harmless.'**

**Block 3 — three serious risks, named**: **infection in the womb, particularly in the first few weeks · the device can be pushed out without her realising · and rarely, at insertion, it can make a hole in the wall of the womb and move outside, needing an operation to retrieve.** **Link the last one to her caesarean: 'because you've had a caesarean, there's a scar on the womb, which slightly raises that risk — so I'll be careful and I'll check afterwards.'**

**Block 4 — before insertion, said aloud as part of the plan**: **'I'll make sure you're not pregnant, and check there's no infection — a swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea.'** Add that it is usually done in the first few days after a period **but can be done at other times if pregnancy can be excluded.**

**Block 5 — the procedure, honestly**: starts like a cervical screening test, speculum, then the device through the neck of the womb with a fine applicator. **'Most women get strong period-type cramping and some find it quite painful, so I'd recommend an anti-inflammatory beforehand, we can use a local anaesthetic, and you can tell me to stop at any point.'** Some feel faint, so she stays lying down a few minutes.

**Block 6 — THE AFTERCARE BLOCK, four items, all on the sheet**: **nothing inside the vagina for 48 HOURS — no sex, tampons, cups, swimming or baths · it takes SEVEN DAYS to start working, so condoms until then · CHECK THE THREADS herself regularly · and review at THREE TO SIX WEEKS.**

**Block 7 — red flags and the STI line**: **unusual or offensive discharge, tummy pain, fever, abnormal bleeding, or if she cannot feel the threads.** Then **'and this does not protect you against sexually transmitted infections — condoms do that.'**

**Answer the sulfur question directly**: not a reason to avoid a Mirena; **the device contains barium sulfate, which makes it show up on X-ray, and that is a completely different substance from the sulfur-containing antibiotics people react to** — and her reaction was a delayed rash. **'I'm happy to go ahead, and if you develop a rash, itching, swelling or trouble breathing afterwards, come straight back and we can remove it.'**
