findings: Alternate runs — the two that change everything

INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER: two weeks of pain in ONE breast which is RED, SWOLLEN AND WARM WITH AN ORANGE-PEEL LOOK, NO FEVER, and a course of antibiotics from another doctor that did nothing → DO NOT PRESCRIBE MORE ANTIBIOTICS; refer urgently for imaging and biopsy · CHEST WALL: unilateral sharp pain REPRODUCED BY PRESSING ON THE COSTAL CARTILAGE and worse on twisting, with no lump, discharge or skin change → COSTOCHONDRITIS

back.dx: TWO DIAGNOSES, GIVEN IN ORDER, WITH REASONS FOR EACH — THAT IS THE PASS. FIRST, THE MOST LIKELY: 'Most likely you have a condition called FIBROCYSTIC CHANGE. That means the breast tissue develops multiple small cysts — little sacs of fluid — along with some thickening and scarring of the tissue around them, and that causes pain and lumpiness. I say that because you have MANY SMALL LUMPS RATHER THAN ONE, they are in BOTH BREASTS, and they are TENDER — which is the typical pattern. It is very common and it is not a disease as such.' SECOND, THE CONCERN YOU ARE NOT PREPARED TO DISMISS: 'But I want to be honest about my second concern, which is THE POSSIBILITY OF A BREAST CANCER. Your mother had breast cancer at 50, which raises your own risk, and you have some nipple discharge. So even though I think fibrocystic change explains most of this, ONE LUMP AMONG MANY CAN STILL BE SOMETHING DIFFERENT, and I am not going to assume.' THEN THE REST OF THE LIST: 'I also considered an infection in the breast, though you have no fever or redness; scarring after the knock you described, which we call FAT NECROSIS; hormonal causes including the pill; pain from the CHEST WALL, RIBS OR SPINE; and CYCLICAL BREAST PAIN, which many women get before their periods.' PICKING ONE DIAGNOSIS AND IGNORING THE REST FAILS EITHER WAY — a confident benign answer ignores the family history, and a cancer-only answer ignores twenty bilateral tender lumps. EXPLAINING THE DISCHARGE IS ITS OWN MARK: 'Brown discharge from both sides, from several spots, only when you squeeze, with no blood in it, is usually a benign condition of the milk ducts called DUCT ECTASIA. The pattern that worries us is discharge from ONE SPOT ON ONE SIDE that appears ON ITS OWN and has BLOOD in it — and that is not what you have.' THE PLAN: an ultrasound of both breasts, and IF THERE IS A LUMP THAT STANDS OUT FROM THE REST, that one is assessed properly with a TRIPLE TEST. For the pain itself, a well-fitted supportive bra and simple analgesia genuinely help, with a pain diary against the cycle and review. THE SAFETY NET, WHICH IS SPECIFIC RATHER THAN GENERIC: come back for A NEW LUMP THAT FEELS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHERS, ANY BLOOD IN THE DISCHARGE, or ANY CHANGE IN THE SKIN OR NIPPLE. WHAT THIS STATION ADDS TO THE LUMP STATION: the differential leaves the breast. CHEST WALL — costochondritis, reproducible tenderness over the costal cartilage, worse on twisting · SPINE — cervical or thoracic radiculopathy, with radiation into the arm or through to the back · LUNG AND PLEURA — with cough or breathlessness · plus HORMONAL causes including a recently started pill, and PREGNANCY, because breast tenderness is an early sign and the question takes two seconds. NAME THOSE GROUPS AND THE EXAMINER HEARS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A PAIN STATION AND A LUMP STATION. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN LOCALISATION: breast ultrasound through the regional service or by referral, with PATS travel support where the trip is metropolitan; urgent breast surgical referral for a dominant lump with an abnormal or discordant triple test; BreastScreen SA for screening age only, remembering it does not apply at 27 and does not replace assessment of a symptomatic breast; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 for family-history concerns and information; local ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; interpreters through TIS National 131 450.
plan: OPEN AND ACKNOWLEDGE THE WORRY SHE NAMED — she said she is worried. Then: ONE BREAST OR BOTH, and whereabouts exactly — nearer the nipple, out towards the armpit, or more over the ribs.

SEVERITY, QUALITY, ONSET AND COURSE — out of ten, aching or burning or sharp, when it started, constant or intermittent, getting worse. Two years of intermittent bilateral ache is a different story from two weeks of unilateral sharp pain.
The two discriminating questions — does it radiate into the arm, back or neck, and is it worse in the days before her period.

LUMPS — 'CAN YOU FEEL ANY LUMPS?' and then characterise them fully: how many, one side or both, how big, painful, hard or rubbery, SMOOTH OR IRREGULAR, and whether they MOVE. The role-player is briefed to answer all of it.
DISCHARGE, CHARACTERISED IN FIVE DIMENSIONS — colour, ANY BLOOD, one side or both, ONE SPOT OR SEVERAL, and spontaneous or only on squeezing.
SKIN AND NIPPLE CHANGE — dimpling, puckering, redness, peau d'orange, rash; nipple retraction, ulceration, eczema · THEN FAMILY HISTORY OF BREAST AND OVARIAN CANCER, who and at what age.
General cancer questions after the specific ones — weight, appetite, tiredness, and lumps in the armpit.
INFECTION AND TRAUMA — breastfeeding, fever, chills, redness, heat, cracked nipples · AND ANY KNOCK TO THE BREAST OR PREVIOUS SURGERY, which is where the netball elbow lives.
OUTSIDE THE BREAST — back or neck pain, cough or breathlessness, and whether the pain is worse on movement or on pressing the ribs.
HORMONES AND THE FIVE Ps — recently started pill or hormone treatment, other medications, last period, ANY CHANCE OF PREGNANCY, cervical screening.
HISTORY CLOSES. DIAGNOSIS ONE — FIBROCYSTIC CHANGE, explained in plain words with the three reasons: many small lumps rather than one, bilateral, and tender (see dx).
DIAGNOSIS TWO — THE CANCER CONCERN, NAMED HONESTLY WITH ITS OWN REASONS: the family history, and the discharge. Then the rest of the differential list including the causes outside the breast.

EXPLAIN THE DISCHARGE PATTERN AND WHY IT IS REASSURING · the plan: bilateral ultrasound, triple test for any dominant lump, supportive bra and analgesia · AND THE SPECIFIC SAFETY NET: a new lump that feels different, blood in the discharge, or skin or nipple change.

ask: The three questions that carry this station: 'Can you feel any lumps?' · 'Does the pain go anywhere else — into the arm, back or neck?' · 'Is it worse in the days before your period?'
THE RANKING SENTENCE: 'MOST LIKELY THIS IS FIBROCYSTIC CHANGE — BUT I WANT TO BE HONEST ABOUT MY SECOND CONCERN.' Two diagnoses, in order, each with its own reasons.

'The pattern that worries us is discharge from one spot on one side, on its own, with blood in it' — and then say plainly that hers is not that. / 'Pain on its own is rarely the way breast cancer shows itself — but because you also have lumps and a family history, I am not going to leave it there.'

EXAMINER CHALLENGES: 'So is it cancer?' → the ranked answer, not a yes or no · 'Does fibrocystic change raise her risk?' → 'ORDINARY FIBROCYSTIC CHANGE DOES NOT; ONLY PROLIFERATIVE LESIONS WITH ATYPIA DO, AND THOSE ARE DIAGNOSED ON BIOPSY.' · 'She has milky discharge and is not breastfeeding' → 'CHECK PROLACTIN AND THINK OF A PROLACTINOMA.' · 'Her one breast is red and swollen with no fever and antibiotics did nothing' → 'INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER UNTIL EXCLUDED — IMAGING AND BIOPSY, NOT MORE ANTIBIOTICS.'

THE DRILLS: characterise the pain in six dimensions in 30 seconds · characterise a lump and a discharge fully in 30 seconds each · give two ranked diagnoses with reasons in 45 seconds · name the causes outside the breast in 15 seconds · then run the cyclical mastalgia and costochondritis variants and say what changes.
pefe: THERE IS NO EXAMINATION TASK, WHICH IS WHY THE HISTORY CARRIES EVERYTHING — and the role-player is briefed to answer examination-type questions about her lumps. Ask them of the patient: how many, where, how big, tender, hard or rubbery, smooth or irregular, mobile. IF AN EXAMINATION WERE OFFERED, it would be the standard breast examination with consent and a chaperone, including the axillary and supraclavicular nodes and the opposite breast.

Role-player: NICOLE FARRAR, 27, NO CHILDREN, ON THE COMBINED PILL FOR SEVERAL YEARS. Two years of heavy aching pain in both breasts, five or six out of ten, worse over recent months, slightly worse premenstrually but present most of the time. MANY SMALL LUMPS IN BOTH BREASTS — painful, edges feel irregular to her, and they move. BROWN DISCHARGE FROM BOTH NIPPLES ON SQUEEZING, NO BLOOD. No skin or nipple change, no fever or redness. MOTHER HAD BREAST CANCER AT 50. AN ELBOW TO THE LEFT BREAST AT NETBALL a few months ago, sore for weeks. Last period two weeks ago, screening two years ago normal.

How to play it: give the trauma only if asked — it is a reward answer — and the same for the family history. After the diagnosis ask 'So it is nothing to worry about?', then 'What else could it be?', then 'And the discharge?'. Mark down any candidate who never asks about lumps, any who reassures without addressing the family history, and any who gives a single diagnosis when the case points several ways.

MARKING PROMPTS: pain characterised — side, site, severity, quality, onset, course · RADIATION ASKED · CYCLICAL RELATIONSHIP ASKED · LUMPS ASKED AND FULLY CHARACTERISED · DISCHARGE ASKED WITH COLOUR, BLOOD, LATERALITY, DUCT AND SPONTANEITY · skin and nipple changes · FAMILY HISTORY OF BREAST AND OVARIAN CANCER · general cancer questions with axilla · infection questions · TRAUMA · NON-BREAST CAUSES — spine, chest wall, lung · hormones and medications · PREGNANCY · TWO DIAGNOSES GIVEN IN RANKED ORDER WITH REASONS · full differential list · DISCHARGE PATTERN EXPLAINED · triple test for any dominant lump · practical advice for the pain · safety net.

The question that discriminates most — 'IS THERE ANYTHING THAT MAKES IT BETTER OR WORSE — IN PARTICULAR, IS IT WORSE IN THE DAYS BEFORE YOUR PERIOD?' BILATERAL PREMENSTRUAL PAIN THAT SETTLES WITH THE PERIOD IS CYCLICAL MASTALGIA. In the recalled case it is a bit worse before but present most of the time, which is not pure cyclical pain

The question that leaves the breast — 'DOES THE PAIN GO ANYWHERE ELSE — INTO THE ARM, THE BACK, THE NECK?' Radiation to the arm or through to the back IS NOT BREAST TISSUE. The differential in this station reaches outside the breast — CHEST WALL, SPINE AND LUNG — which the lump station does not, and naming those is what separates the two

The other breast symptoms come as a set — PAIN, LUMP AND DISCHARGE. In a pain station candidates forget to ask about lumps, AND THE WHOLE CASE TURNS ON THE ANSWER. If she says yes, characterise them exactly as in a lump station: how many, one side or both, how big, painful, HARD OR RUBBERY, SMOOTH OR IRREGULAR EDGE, and DO THEY MOVE

What Nicole gives you — TWO YEARS OF HEAVY ACHING PAIN IN BOTH BREASTS, five or six out of ten, worse over recent months, present most of the time · NO radiation · MANY SMALL LUMPS IN BOTH BREASTS, painful, edges feel irregular to her, and they MOVE · BROWN DISCHARGE FROM BOTH NIPPLES ONLY ON SQUEEZING, NO BLOOD · no skin or nipple change · no fever or redness, not breastfeeding, no children

The two answers she only gives if asked — 'MY MUM HAD BREAST CANCER. SHE WAS 50, I THINK' — the finding that stops you settling on a benign answer · AND 'ACTUALLY YES — I TOOK AN ELBOW AT NETBALL A FEW MONTHS AGO, RIGHT ON THE LEFT BREAST', which raises FAT NECROSIS and is a reward answer for asking about trauma

How to weigh what she gave you — TWO YEARS, BOTH SIDES → long-standing and bilateral, pointing to benign hormonal or fibrocystic change · MANY SMALL BILATERAL TENDER LUMPS → the signature of FIBROCYSTIC CHANGE; it would be extraordinary for twenty of them to be cancers · IRREGULAR BORDERS → concerning in a single lump, much less so across twenty small bilateral ones · BROWN, NO BLOOD, BOTH SIDES, ONLY ON EXPRESSION → typical of DUCT ECTASIA · THE FAMILY HISTORY → the reason you do not close the case

Discharge, decoded — REASSURING: bilateral · several ducts · ONLY ON EXPRESSION · green, brown or milky · NO BLOOD. CONCERNING: unilateral · SINGLE DUCT · SPONTANEOUS · BLOOD-STAINED · clear and watery · or with a lump. AND MILKY DISCHARGE IN A NON-LACTATING WOMAN → check prolactin and think of a PROLACTINOMA VERIFY

Fibrocystic change is not simply 'Lots of cysts' — CORRECTION — it is a SPECTRUM OF BENIGN CHANGE — cysts, fibrosis and adenosis — occurring in response to cyclical hormones, common enough to be regarded as A NORMAL VARIANT RATHER THAN A DISEASE. Explaining it as 'small sacs of fluid plus some thickening of the tissue' is accurate and understandable. AND IMPORTANT FOR HER: ORDINARY FIBROCYSTIC CHANGE DOES NOT ITSELF INCREASE BREAST CANCER RISK — only certain proliferative lesions with atypia do, and those are diagnosed on biopsy VERIFY

The reassurance you are entitled to give — ADDED — BREAST PAIN ALONE IS AN UNCOMMON PRESENTATION OF BREAST CANCER, and the great majority of women with pain, no lump, no skin change and normal imaging have a benign cause VERIFY. That does not excuse you from assessing, but your closing can be genuinely reassuring rather than evasive: 'PAIN ON ITS OWN IS RARELY THE WAY BREAST CANCER SHOWS ITSELF — BUT BECAUSE YOU ALSO HAVE LUMPS AND A FAMILY HISTORY, I AM NOT GOING TO LEAVE IT THERE'

Management if you are asked for it — ANY DISCRETE OR DOMINANT LUMP STILL GETS A TRIPLE TEST · multiple bilateral tender lumps at 27 are usually imaged with ULTRASOUND · the brown discharge is documented and reviewed. FOR THE PAIN ITSELF: A WELL-FITTED SUPPORTIVE BRA including for exercise and at night if severe · simple analgesia or a topical anti-inflammatory · A PAIN DIARY AGAINST THE CYCLE to establish whether it is cyclical · REASSURANCE, WHICH IS ITSELF EFFECTIVE TREATMENT · and review. Evening primrose oil is widely used with weak evidence; danazol and tamoxifen are reserved for severe refractory mastalgia under specialist care VERIFY

Alternate run — cyclical mastalgia — Bilateral pain CONFINED TO THE WEEK BEFORE THE PERIOD and settling once it starts, NO LUMPS, no discharge, no family history → diagnose cyclical mastalgia, reassure that pain alone is rarely cancer, and advise a supportive bra, analgesia and a pain diary

setting: An old recall that has returned, and the stem has already done the diagnostic work for you — scans clear, no recurrence — precisely so the station can test explanation and management instead. It is won on why it happens, said in plain words, and on a management plan with no drugs in it: education, skin care, exercise, massage, compression, and knowing when to worry. Diuretics do not work in lymphoedema and should not be offered.
stem: Your general practice, rural South Australia. A 55-year-old woman with a known history of breast cancer, treated with mastectomy and chemotherapy and now taking tamoxifen, presents with swelling of one arm. Her follow-up scans are clear with no evidence of recurrence. A photograph shows a markedly swollen arm on the side of the mastectomy.

Tasks: explain your diagnosis and differentials — explain why this has happened — explain your management plan. 8 minutes. Her opening: 'It is my left arm. It has swollen up and it feels heavy and tight. I want to know why it is happening and what can be done.'
tasks: Explain your diagnosis and differentials
Explain why this has happened
Explain your management plan
time: Ask for her own concern first, because she is frightened the cancer is back and will not say so unless asked · then a short focused history: onset and course, infection features, recurrence red flags, and the treatment history including whether she had radiotherapy · then address the recurrence fear directly, with reasons · then the mechanism in plain words — nodes removed, drainage disturbed, fluid collects · then the differentials, with recurrence named even though the scans are clear · then the honest sentence about it being lifelong · then the five components of complex decongestive therapy · then the cellulitis safety net, the clinical-procedure advice, and follow-up.
findings: Component 1 and 2 — education and skin care

EDUCATION: lifelong, controllable, reading material, and referral to a lymphoedema association for information and support · SKIN CARE, WHICH IS MORE IMPORTANT THAN IT SOUNDS: MOISTURISE THE ARM EVERY DAY BECAUSE DRY SKIN CRACKS AND CRACKS LET INFECTION IN · treat any cut or scratch promptly · GLOVES FOR GARDENING AND WASHING UP · avoid sunburn, tight jewellery, and very hot days or saunas, BECAUSE HEAT MAKES THE SWELLING WORSE

MANUAL LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE — a specific light massage that moves fluid towards working lymph glands, done by a practitioner and taught to her as self-massage · COMPRESSION — A GARMENT THAT IS MEASURED AND FITTED by a lymphoedema practitioner, not bought off a shelf. TOGETHER THE FIVE COMPONENTS ARE CALLED COMPLEX DECONGESTIVE THERAPY, and naming it shows you know the package

back.dx: LYMPHOEDEMA OF THE ARM FOLLOWING MASTECTOMY WITH AXILLARY NODE REMOVAL. THE STEM TELLS YOU THE SCANS ARE CLEAR AND THERE IS NO RECURRENCE — THAT IS DELIBERATE, BECAUSE IT REMOVES THE DIAGNOSTIC UNCERTAINTY SO THE STATION CAN TEST EXPLANATION AND MANAGEMENT. YOU STILL NAME RECURRENCE AS A DIFFERENTIAL; YOU JUST DO NOT NEED TO CHASE IT. THE STATION HAS FOUR PARTS AND ALL FOUR ARE MARKED. ONE, ELICIT AND ANSWER HER REAL CONCERN — she is frightened the cancer is back and will only say so if you ask, and the answer is reasons first, then reassurance, then what to watch for (see findings). TWO, THE MECHANISM IN PLAIN WORDS: a second drainage system carrying lymph, glands in the armpit removed with the breast, drainage channels disturbed, fluid collects. THREE, THE DIFFERENTIALS — lymphoedema, venous insufficiency, arm DVT, cellulitis, RECURRENCE, and systemic causes which would give bilateral rather than unilateral swelling. FOUR, THE MANAGEMENT, WHICH IS ENTIRELY NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL AND HAS FIVE COMPONENTS: EDUCATION · SKIN CARE · EXERCISE · MANUAL LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE · COMPRESSION — together, COMPLEX DECONGESTIVE THERAPY, with SURGERY AS A LAST RESORT if swelling remains severe despite all of it. DIURETICS DO NOT WORK FOR LYMPHOEDEMA AND SHOULD NOT BE OFFERED, and saying so explicitly is worth a mark. THE HONESTY THAT CARRIES THE STATION: 'I want to be honest with you first, because it matters for how we approach this. LYMPHOEDEMA IS A LIFELONG CONDITION. WE CANNOT CURE IT. But we can control the swelling and the symptoms well, and the things that work are not tablets — in fact water tablets do not help this at all.' A candidate who implies it will resolve has set her up to lose faith in a plan that requires daily effort for the rest of her life. THE SKIN CARE DETAIL IS NOT PADDING — IT IS THE PREVENTION OF THE COMPLICATION THAT CAUSES REAL HARM: moisturise daily because dry skin cracks and cracks let infection in; treat cuts promptly; gloves for gardening and washing up; avoid sunburn, tight jewellery and heat. AND THE EXERCISE CORRECTION MATTERS BOTH WAYS — using the arm is good for it, the old advice to rest it was wrong, and deconditioning makes lymphoedema worse. WHAT TO SAFETY-NET: CELLULITIS FIRST — red, hot, newly painful, rapidly increasing swelling, fever or chills means come straight back, because the threshold to treat is low and every episode damages the lymphatics further · RECURRENCE, even with clear scans — unintended weight loss, new lumps in the breast area, axilla or neck, bone pain, breathlessness, or a sudden change in the swelling · AND DVT — sudden swelling with pain and prominent veins, rather than the gradual swelling of lymphoedema. FOLLOW-UP: reading material, referral to a lymphoedema service, and regular review with you, BECAUSE THIS IS A CONDITION SHE WILL MANAGE FOR THE REST OF HER LIFE. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN LOCALISATION: referral to a lymphoedema clinic or ACCREDITED LYMPHOEDEMA PRACTITIONER, which from rural South Australia may mean a metropolitan service with PATS travel support or telehealth review with a local physiotherapist; the AUSTRALASIAN LYMPHOLOGY ASSOCIATION maintains a practitioner register and the LYMPHOEDEMA ASSOCIATION OF AUSTRALIA provides patient information and support VERIFY current names and contacts; compression garments may attract subsidy, so check the current SA scheme; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 for support and information; local ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; interpreters through TIS National 131 450.
plan: OPEN, ACKNOWLEDGE WHAT THE ARM LOOKS LIKE, AND ASK FOR HER CONCERN: 'Before I explain — is there anything else in particular you are worried about?' This is where the whole station turns.

A SHORT FOCUSED HISTORY — when the swelling started and whether it came on GRADUALLY OR SUDDENLY · is the arm painful, red or hot, any fever or feeling unwell · any weight loss, new lumps, bone pain or breathlessness · and when the last scans were.
CLARIFY THE TREATMENT HISTORY — mastectomy, AXILLARY NODES REMOVED, chemotherapy, tamoxifen, AND WHETHER SHE HAD RADIOTHERAPY, because it adds scarring in the same area.
ADDRESS THE RECURRENCE FEAR DIRECTLY AND WITH REASONS (see findings) — clear scans, no red flags, gradual onset, the expected arm. Then promise to keep watching and to tell her what to look for.
NAME THE DIAGNOSIS AND EXPLAIN THE MECHANISM IN PLAIN WORDS — lymph, glands in the armpit, removed with the breast, drainage disturbed, fluid collects (see dx).

THE DIFFERENTIALS — venous insufficiency, arm DVT which comes on suddenly and painfully, cellulitis which would be red and hot, RECURRENCE, and systemic causes which give bilateral swelling not one arm.
The honest sentence — lifelong, not curable, but controllable — and that the treatments are not tablets, with diuretics named as not helping.

COMPONENTS 1 AND 2 — education with reading material and a lymphoedema association, then SKIN CARE IN DETAIL: daily moisturiser and why, prompt treatment of cuts, gloves, sunburn, tight jewellery, heat.
COMPONENT 3 — referral to a LYMPHOEDEMA PHYSIOTHERAPIST for graded exercise, with the explicit correction that USING THE ARM IS GOOD FOR IT, plus elevation at night.
COMPONENTS 4 AND 5 — manual lymphatic drainage taught as self-massage, and a MEASURED AND FITTED COMPRESSION SLEEVE. Name the package: COMPLEX DECONGESTIVE THERAPY.
SURGERY AS A LAST RESORT if swelling remains severe despite the full package — a referral, not a starting point.

THE SAFETY NETS — CELLULITIS FIRST, with the explanation that each infection makes the lymphoedema worse · THE CLINICAL-PROCEDURE ADVICE, use the other arm · RECURRENCE red flags · and regular review with you.

ask: THE QUESTION THAT UNLOCKS THE STATION: 'IS THERE ANYTHING ELSE IN PARTICULAR YOU ARE WORRIED ABOUT?' — she is frightened the cancer is back and will not volunteer it.
'No — I do not think this is the cancer coming back, and here is why.' / 'This is a lifelong condition. We cannot cure it, but we can control the swelling and the symptoms well.'

'Dry skin cracks, and cracks let infection in.' / 'Using the arm is good for it — the old advice to rest it was wrong.' / 'Tell any nurse or doctor to use the other arm for blood pressure, blood tests, drips and injections.'

Examiner challenges: 'Should she avoid using that arm?' → 'No — graded supervised exercise improves lymphatic flow; what she avoids is skin injury, infection and overheating.' · 'Would you give a diuretic?' → 'No, they do not work in lymphoedema.' · 'Her scans were clear three months ago, do you need to think about recurrence?' → 'I still name it as a differential, and if she develops weight loss, new lumps, bone pain or a sudden change in the swelling I would image her whatever the last scan showed.' · 'The arm is now red and hot' → 'Cellulitis in a lymphoedematous limb — antibiotics promptly, low threshold, and prophylaxis if episodes recur.'

THE DRILL: name the five components in 20 seconds, then expand each to one sentence in 60 · say the mechanism in plain words in 30 seconds · give the differentials in 20 · then run the three alternate runs — cellulitis, DVT and recurrence — and say what changes in each.
pefe: THERE IS NO EXAMINATION TASK — the photograph gives you the swollen arm. IF AN EXAMINATION WERE OFFERED, the things that would change your answer are: REDNESS, WARMTH AND TENDERNESS suggesting cellulitis · SUDDEN SWELLING WITH PROMINENT SUPERFICIAL VEINS suggesting DVT · and NEW LUMPS IN THE AXILLA, SUPRACLAVICULAR FOSSA OR CHEST WALL suggesting recurrence. Objective monitoring is by ARM CIRCUMFERENCE MEASUREMENT OR BIOIMPEDANCE.

Role-player: JENNY KALISCH, 55. Two years ago, breast cancer treated with LEFT MASTECTOMY AND AXILLARY NODE REMOVAL, then chemotherapy; now on TAMOXIFEN. Most recent scans three months ago WERE CLEAR. Over the last few months the left arm has swollen GRADUALLY and feels HEAVY AND TIGHT RATHER THAN PAINFUL. No redness, heat or fever. No weight loss, new lumps, bone pain or breathlessness. NO RADIOTHERAPY.

How to play it: her hidden concern is that the cancer is back, and she gives it only if the doctor asks whether anything else is worrying her. If they never ask, stay anxious and preoccupied and ask at the very end: 'But it is not the cancer, is it?' During the explanation ask 'So it is not the cancer?', then 'Then why has it happened?', then 'Could it be anything else?'; during management, 'So what can you do about it?', then 'I had no idea about the heat', then 'And if none of that works?'; and at the end, 'Is there anything I should watch for?'

MARKING PROMPTS: open question · HIDDEN CONCERN ELICITED AND ADDRESSED DIRECTLY · onset and character of the swelling · infection features asked · recurrence red flags asked · treatment history clarified · diagnosis named · MECHANISM EXPLAINED IN PLAIN WORDS · DIFFERENTIALS INCLUDING RECURRENCE, DVT, CELLULITIS, VENOUS INSUFFICIENCY AND SYSTEMIC CAUSES · 'LIFELONG BUT CONTROLLABLE' SAID HONESTLY · SKIN CARE with moisturiser, injury, gloves, sunburn and heat · EXERCISE FRAMED AS BENEFICIAL · elevation · manual lymphatic drainage · FITTED COMPRESSION GARMENT · surgery as last resort · NO DIURETICS · USE THE OTHER ARM FOR PROCEDURES · CELLULITIS RED FLAGS · recurrence red flags · reading material and support group · regular review.

Ask for her concern, or you will never hear it — 'Before I explain — IS THERE ANYTHING ELSE IN PARTICULAR YOU ARE WORRIED ABOUT?' → 'HONESTLY? I AM WORRIED THE CANCER IS BACK.' If you never ask, she stays anxious and preoccupied and asks at the very end — 'BUT IT IS NOT THE CANCER, IS IT?' — with no time left to answer properly

Why it happens, word for word — 'Your body has a drainage system alongside the blood vessels, carrying fluid called LYMPH. That fluid travels up the arm and passes through glands — LYMPH NODES — in the armpit. When the breast was removed, SOME OF THOSE GLANDS WERE TAKEN AS WELL, and the drainage channels were disturbed. Because that drainage route is damaged, the fluid cannot get away as easily, so it collects in the arm and causes the swelling.' IF SHE ALSO HAD RADIOTHERAPY: 'radiotherapy to the armpit causes scarring in the same area and adds to it'

The differentials to name — 1 LYMPHOEDEMA — the diagnosis · 2 VENOUS INSUFFICIENCY · 3 DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS OF THE ARM, particularly with a previous port or line · 4 CELLULITIS, which both causes and complicates lymphoedema · 5 TUMOUR RECURRENCE obstructing lymphatic drainage — ALWAYS NAMED, EVEN WHEN THE SCANS ARE CLEAR · 6 SYSTEMIC CAUSES — heart, kidney or liver failure, hypothyroidism — BUT THOSE CAUSE BILATERAL OR GENERALISED SWELLING, NOT ONE ARM

How to address the recurrence fear — 'Your scans are clear, you have no weight loss, no new lumps and no other symptoms, and the swelling has come on GRADUALLY in exactly the arm and the way we would expect after your surgery. SO NO — I DO NOT THINK THIS IS THE CANCER COMING BACK. I will still keep an eye out for it, and I will tell you what to watch for.' Reasons, then reassurance, then the safety net

The two sentences she needs to hear — The honest one: 'This is a lifelong condition. We cannot cure it, but we can control the swelling and the symptoms well.' Candidates who imply it will resolve are setting her up to lose faith in the plan · the infection one: 'If the arm becomes red, hot or painful, or you develop a fever, come straight back — infections in this arm need treating quickly'

Component 3 — exercise is treatment, not a risk — CORRECTION — women were historically told to avoid lifting and exertion with the affected arm. THAT ADVICE HAS BEEN REVERSED: SUPERVISED, GRADED RESISTANCE AND AEROBIC EXERCISE IS SAFE AND IMPROVES LYMPHOEDEMA, and deconditioning makes it worse VERIFY. Add ELEVATION on a pillow at night. EXAMINER CHALLENGE, 'Should she avoid using that arm?' → 'NO. GRADED EXERCISE UNDER THE GUIDANCE OF A LYMPHOEDEMA PHYSIOTHERAPIST IMPROVES LYMPHATIC FLOW. WHAT SHE SHOULD AVOID IS SKIN INJURY, INFECTION AND OVERHEATING'

The clinical-procedure advice, said explicitly — 'One practical thing to tell any health worker who sees you: USE THE OTHER ARM. No blood pressure cuffs, no blood tests, no drips, no injections and no vaccinations on the affected side, and take care with any skin procedure on that arm.' VERIFY — this is long-standing, widely taught precautionary advice; the evidence for absolute avoidance is weaker than its reputation and some services individualise it. IN THE EXAM, SAY IT

The red flag that matters most — CELLULITIS. A limb with poor lymphatic drainage INFECTS EASILY, and infection in turn damages the lymphatics further — EACH EPISODE MAKES THE LYMPHOEDEMA WORSE. Teach her to return for REDNESS, INCREASING WARMTH, NEW PAIN, RAPID INCREASE IN SWELLING, FEVER, CHILLS OR FEELING UNWELL. The threshold to start antibiotics is low, and women with recurrent episodes may be offered PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS VERIFY

The investigations, if asked — MOSTLY TO EXCLUDE THE DIFFERENTIALS RATHER THAN CONFIRM THE DIAGNOSIS, WHICH IS CLINICAL: VENOUS DOPPLER ULTRASOUND for DVT and venous insufficiency · FULL BLOOD COUNT, ESR AND CRP for infection · thyroid, renal and liver function if the picture is not clearly unilateral · IMAGING OF THE AXILLA AND CHEST IF RECURRENCE IS SUSPECTED CLINICALLY, WHATEVER THE LAST SCAN SHOWED · and arm circumference measurements or bioimpedance for objective monitoring VERIFY

Alternate runs — CELLULITIS: the arm became RED, HOT AND PAINFUL over two days and she feels shivery and unwell → recognise cellulitis in a lymphoedematous limb, START ANTIBIOTICS PROMPTLY, and explain that each infection worsens the lymphoedema · DVT: swelling came on SUDDENLY over two days, the arm aches, veins over the shoulder are prominent, and she had a port → URGENT DOPPLER ULTRASOUND · RECURRENCE: swelling worsening quickly, 6 kg LOST WITHOUT TRYING, and A LUMP ABOVE THE COLLARBONE → urgent imaging and referral back to oncology REGARDLESS OF THE PREVIOUS CLEAR SCAN

stem: Your general practice, rural South Australia. Your next patient is a young woman who has been trying to conceive. Her opening: 'My partner and I have been trying for a baby and it is just not happening. We are starting to get worried.'

Tasks: take a history for six minutes — the physical examination is given on a card and is normal — explain your diagnosis. 8 minutes. Version A: her husband is fly-in fly-out and home about one week a month. Version B: frequency is fine but untimed, with an appendicectomy at ten.

time: A human opening that acknowledges the stress before any question · then explore the complaint — how long, ever pregnant, does he have children, and how is it affecting her · then the partner and the sex, early rather than last: has he been checked, does she know the fertile period, how often, and any difficulties · then the five Ps with cycle length, previous STI, the depot injection, and abdominal or pelvic surgery · then the differential sweep TOP to bottom as in amenorrhoea — hypothalamic, pituitary, thyroid, ovary, endometriosis, systemic · then the card, the diagnosis framed as a cause rather than a label, the fertile window explained with her own cycle length, and a plan that includes him.

back.dx: IN BOTH RECALLED VERSIONS THERE IS NO ORGANIC CAUSE, AND THE ANSWER IS THE SEX — HOW OFTEN, AND WHEN. THE EXPLANATION, WORD FOR WORD: 'The good news is I have not found anything to suggest something is wrong with either of you. I think the most likely reason is that you are having sex relatively infrequently, and not at the time in your cycle when the chance of pregnancy is highest.' Then the fertile window, calculated with HER cycle length, then the tracking methods, then the every-two-to-three-days advice that removes the arithmetic (see findings). IN VERSION B, NAME BOTH CONTRIBUTORS: untimed intercourse, AND possible tubal adhesions after the childhood appendicectomy — explained in plain words as scar tissue after abdominal surgery that can interfere with the tubes carrying the egg from the ovary to the womb — with TUBAL PATENCY TESTING and a SEMEN ANALYSIS arranged. THE INVESTIGATIONS, WHICH STILL APPLY EVEN WHEN THE ANSWER IS 'MORE SEX, BETTER TIMED'. FEMALE: CONFIRM OVULATION with a MID-LUTEAL PROGESTERONE taken about 7 DAYS BEFORE THE EXPECTED PERIOD, which is day 21 of a 28-day cycle · FSH and LH early follicular, days 2 to 5 · TSH · PROLACTIN · AMH with the caveat above · PELVIC ULTRASOUND for uterus, ovaries and polycystic morphology · CHLAMYDIA TESTING and cervical screening · RUBELLA AND VARICELLA IMMUNITY, plus full blood count and ferritin · TUBAL PATENCY by hysterosalpingogram or HyCoSy, usually arranged by the specialist · androgens if PCOS is suspected. MALE, AT THE SAME TIME: SEMEN ANALYSIS — volume, concentration, motility and morphology, after 2 TO 5 DAYS OF ABSTINENCE, repeated if abnormal. ORDERING IT AT THE FIRST VISIT RATHER THAN AFTER MONTHS OF INVESTIGATING HER IS A MARK OF GOOD PRACTICE AND AN EASY THING TO SAY ALOUD; if abnormal, repeat, then refer for hormonal assessment and urology or andrology review. THE PLAN SHE LEAVES WITH, IN FOUR PARTS: ONE, the timing advice or simply sex every two to three days · TWO, PRECONCEPTION CARE — FOLIC ACID STARTED NOW, before pregnancy rather than after, and RUBELLA AND VARICELLA IMMUNITY CHECKED because those vaccines must be given beforehand, plus smoking, alcohol and weight · THREE, HIS SEMEN ANALYSIS AND HER BASELINE BLOODS · FOUR, EMOTIONAL SUPPORT OFFERED EXPLICITLY, because she told you it is straining the relationship and counselling is genuinely useful and commonly used. REFERRAL CRITERIA, SAID ALOUD: 12 MONTHS UNDER 35 · 6 MONTHS AT 35 TO 39 · IMMEDIATELY AT 40 OR WHERE A CAUSE IS ALREADY KNOWN VERIFY. THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST TO GIVE HER, WHICH IS THE AMENORRHOEA MAP WITH ADDITIONS: male factor · hypothalamic — stress, exercise, low weight · pituitary — prolactinoma · thyroid in either direction · ovarian — PCOS and premature ovarian insufficiency · TUBAL — previous chlamydia or abdominal surgery · UTERINE — fibroids, Asherman · endometriosis · and systemic disease, medications and lifestyle. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN LOCALISATION: fertility specialist services are metropolitan, so referral with PATS travel support, AND BE HONEST ABOUT COST — Medicare covers part of assisted reproduction but out-of-pocket expenses are significant; preconception and sexual health support through SHINE SA; counselling through a fertility counsellor or the practice psychologist under a Mental Health Treatment Plan; local ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; interpreters through TIS National 131 450.
plan: THE HUMAN OPENING BEFORE ANY QUESTION — acknowledge the stress, warn that some questions are personal, and promise a plan together (see findings). This is a scored item, not a courtesy.

EXPLORE THE COMPLAINT — how long have you been trying · EVER BEEN PREGNANT, including a pregnancy that did not continue · DOES YOUR PARTNER HAVE CHILDREN FROM A PREVIOUS RELATIONSHIP · and HOW IS THIS AFFECTING YOU AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP.

THE PARTNER AND THE SEX, EARLY: 'HAS YOUR PARTNER BEEN CHECKED OR HAD A SPERM TEST?' · 'DO YOU KNOW ABOUT THE FERTILE PERIOD?' · 'CAN I ASK HOW OFTEN YOU HAVE SEX?' · and any difficulties — pain for her, erectile or ejaculatory difficulty for him.
P1 PERIODS — last period, CYCLE LENGTH, regularity, excessive pain or heavy bleeding, bleeding between. Regular cycles suggest ovulation, and cycle length is what you need to calculate her window.
P2 PARTNER — stable and supportive, PREVIOUS STI IN EITHER OF THEM, dyspareunia, post-coital bleeding · P3 PILLS — what contraception she has used, AND SPECIFICALLY THE THREE-MONTHLY INJECTION.

P4 PREGNANCY AND SURGERY — previous pregnancies or terminations, AND ANY SURGERY ON THE ABDOMEN OR PELVIS INCLUDING APPENDIX, ovarian or bowel, any uterine instrumentation, ANY CONE BIOPSY · P5 screening.

THE DIFFERENTIAL SWEEP, TOP TO BOTTOM — hypothalamic: stress, exercise, dieting or fasting · pituitary: headaches, visual change, milky discharge · thyroid: temperature preference, weight and bowel change.

SWEEP CONTINUED — ovary: flushes and night sweats for premature ovarian insufficiency, acne, hirsutism and weight gain for PCOS · endometriosis: dysuria or dyschezia around the period, blood in urine or stool · systemic: conditions, medications, rashes, joint pains, smoking, alcohol.
READ THE CARD AND SAY WHAT IT MEANS — BMI, thyroid, abdominal and pelvic examination all normal. 'The good news is I have not found anything to suggest something is wrong with either of you.'
The diagnosis framed as a cause, not a label, and the fertile window explained using her own cycle length (see dx). Never say 'You are infertile'.
NORMALISE IT — 'almost nobody is taught this, and it is one of the commonest reasons couples take longer than they expect' — then the tracking methods and the every-two-to-three-days alternative.

THE FOUR-PART PLAN: timing or frequency · PRECONCEPTION CARE with folic acid and rubella and varicella immunity · HIS SEMEN ANALYSIS AND HER BASELINE BLOODS · AND SUPPORT OFFERED EXPLICITLY. Then the referral criteria if it still has not happened.

pefe: THE EXAMINATION IS GIVEN ON A CARD AND IS NORMAL: BMI normal · thyroid examination normal · breast examination normal · abdominal examination normal · PELVIC EXAMINATION ENTIRELY NORMAL · all vital signs normal. READ IT ALOUD AND SAY WHAT IT MEANS rather than skipping it — a normal examination is the finding that makes the timing explanation the answer rather than a guess.

Role-player: JANE CORRIGAN, 29. Trying EXACTLY TWELVE MONTHS. Neither has children. Periods REGULAR EVERY 30 DAYS, not heavy or painful, last one two weeks ago. HER HUSBAND WORKS FLY-IN FLY-OUT AT A MINE AND IS HOME ABOUT ONE WEEK A MONTH; they have sex a few times during that week and not otherwise. SHE DOES NOT KNOW WHAT THE FERTILE PERIOD IS. No sexual difficulties, no infections, NO ABDOMINAL OR PELVIC SURGERY, never had the injection, screening up to date, no stress, exercise or diet issues, no PCOS or thyroid symptoms, non-smoker.

HOW TO PLAY IT: if asked about impact — 'IT IS HARD. EVERY MONTH I GET MY HOPES UP AND THEN THEY COME CRASHING DOWN. WE SNAP AT EACH OTHER.' Her questions: 'I HAD NO IDEA. I FEEL A BIT STUPID.' · 'THEN WHY IS IT NOT HAPPENING?' · 'COULD IT BE SOMETHING ELSE AS WELL?' · 'SO WHAT DO WE DO NOW?'. VERSION B: sex every day or two but UNTIMED, stopped the pill exactly a year ago, one previous partner, APPENDIX REMOVED AT AGE 10, partner never checked, examination card normal.

MARKING PROMPTS: EMPATHIC OPENING ACKNOWLEDGING THE STRESS · duration asked · previous pregnancies · partner's children · IMPACT ON HER AND THE RELATIONSHIP · PARTNER INVESTIGATED? · FERTILE PERIOD KNOWN? · FREQUENCY OF INTERCOURSE · sexual difficulties · full period history INCLUDING CYCLE LENGTH · STI history · CONTRACEPTION INCLUDING THE INJECTION · ABDOMINAL AND PELVIC SURGERY · cervical procedures and screening · hypothalamic block · prolactinoma · thyroid · POI and PCOS · endometriosis · systemic and lifestyle · DIAGNOSIS FRAMED WITHOUT THE WORD INFERTILE · FERTILE WINDOW EXPLAINED WITH HER OWN CYCLE LENGTH · tracking methods including ovulation kits · differentials INCLUDING MALE FACTOR WITH A FIGURE · SEMEN ANALYSIS ARRANGED · PRECONCEPTION CARE — folic acid, rubella and varicella · lifestyle advice · EMOTIONAL SUPPORT OFFERED · referral criteria stated.

The definition, and why it decides version A — INFERTILITY IS FAILURE TO CONCEIVE AFTER 12 MONTHS OF REGULAR UNPROTECTED INTERCOURSE UNDER 35, OR 6 MONTHS AT 35 OR OVER VERIFY. THE WORDS THAT MATTER ARE REGULAR AND UNPROTECTED — a woman who sees her partner three days a month and has intercourse twice HAS NOT MET THE DEFINITION however long she has been trying, and that is the entire point of Version A. PRIMARY = never conceived; SECONDARY = previously conceived, now unable

Say something human before you start asking — 'Thank you for coming in to talk about this. I UNDERSTAND HOW STRESSFUL THIS CAN BE FOR BOTH OF YOU, and I am here to help. I am going to ask a series of questions, some of them quite personal, so we can work out what is going on — and then we will make a plan together.' THEN ASK AGAIN LATER: 'HOW IS ALL OF THIS AFFECTING YOU, AND YOUR RELATIONSHIP?' The psychosocial question is a scored item

The two questions that solve both versions — 'DO YOU KNOW ABOUT THE FERTILE PERIOD — the days in your cycle when the chance of conceiving is highest?' — IN BOTH RECALLED VERSIONS THE ANSWER IS NO · AND 'HOW OFTEN DO YOU HAVE SEX?' — ask it plainly, because hedging makes it more awkward, not less. ASK THEM EARLY, NOT LAST

About forty per cent of causes are male — ADDED — roughly a third to 40% male, a third female, the rest mixed or unexplained VERIFY. That single statistic justifies everything else: THE MALE PARTNER IS INVESTIGATED AT THE SAME TIME, NOT AFTERWARDS, and a SEMEN ANALYSIS is the cheapest, quickest and least invasive test in the whole work-up. EXAMINER CHALLENGE, 'Why are you asking about him? She is your patient.' → 'BECAUSE INFERTILITY IS A PROBLEM OF THE COUPLE, AND AROUND 40% OF CAUSES ARE MALE. INVESTIGATING BOTH TOGETHER AVOIDS PUTTING HER THROUGH INVASIVE TESTS FOR A PROBLEM A SEMEN ANALYSIS WOULD HAVE FOUND IN A WEEK'

Version A — what she tells you — Trying exactly 12 months · periods REGULAR EVERY 30 DAYS, not heavy, not painful, nothing between · HER HUSBAND WORKS FLY-IN FLY-OUT AND IS HOME ABOUT ONE WEEK A MONTH, with sex a few times during that week and nothing in between · SHE DOES NOT KNOW WHAT THE FERTILE PERIOD IS · everything else negative, examination card NORMAL. THE DIAGNOSIS IS INFREQUENT AND UNTIMED INTERCOURSE — there is no organic cause, AND THAT IS THE ANSWER, NOT A FAILURE TO FIND ONE

Do not tell her she is infertile — Saying 'you have infertility' to a woman who has been trying for a year is unkind and unhelpful. PHRASE IT AROUND THE CAUSE OF NOT CONCEIVING YET: 'I think the most likely reason you have not conceived so far is that you are having sex relatively infrequently, and not at the time in your cycle when the chance of pregnancy is highest. THAT IS A VERY FIXABLE THING, AND IT DOES NOT MEAN ANYTHING IS WRONG WITH EITHER OF YOU'

The fertile window, explained with her own cycle — 'In each cycle there is only a short window. THE EGG IS RELEASED ABOUT HALFWAY THROUGH — for a 30-day cycle that is around DAY 15, counting the first day of bleeding as day one. Sperm survive for several days, so the fertile window is roughly THE FIVE DAYS BEFORE OVULATION PLUS THE DAY ITSELF.' TRACKING: a calendar or phone app is simplest · OVULATION PREDICTOR KITS from the pharmacy are the most accurate and tell you the day · temperature and mucus changes are described but NOT RELIABLE ENOUGH TO PLAN AROUND

The advice that removes the timing problem altogether — ADDED — if timing is stressful or a roster makes it impractical, the simplest evidence-based advice is INTERCOURSE EVERY TWO TO THREE DAYS THROUGHOUT THE CYCLE. That covers the fertile window without anyone calculating anything, and AVOIDS TURNING SEX INTO A SCHEDULED TASK, which is itself a common source of distress. Also worth saying: MOST LUBRICANTS IMPAIR SPERM MOTILITY, so a fertility-friendly product should be used if one is needed

The history items that are easy to miss — THE DEPOT INJECTION — depot medroxyprogesterone CAN DELAY RETURN OF FERTILITY FOR MANY MONTHS after the last dose, while implants and devices do not · ABDOMINAL AND PELVIC SURGERY including APPENDIX, ovarian and bowel — adhesions · UTERINE INSTRUMENTATION — Asherman · CONE BIOPSY — cervical stenosis · and PREVIOUS CHLAMYDIA, which is the commonest cause of tubal damage

What AMH does and does not tell her — CORRECTION — AMH is a marker of OVARIAN RESERVE and predicts RESPONSE TO OVARIAN STIMULATION in assisted reproduction. IT IS NOT A GOOD PREDICTOR OF NATURAL FERTILITY, and a low result in a woman with regular cycles should NOT be used to tell her she cannot conceive, nor a normal result to reassure her she has plenty of time. Women increasingly request it after seeing it advertised — SAY WHAT IT MEANS BEFORE ORDERING IT VERIFY

Would you investigate the version A woman? — A fair examiner question with a nuanced answer: 'She has not strictly met the definition, because the intercourse has not been regular. So I would correct that first, start preconception care, and arrange a semen analysis, which is simple. If she has not conceived after a few months of well-timed, regular intercourse, I would investigate her fully and refer'

back.dx: RECURRENT PREGNANCY LOSS — TWO OR MORE LOSSES BEFORE 24 WEEKS — AND IN THIS WOMAN, TWO FIRST-TRIMESTER LOSSES PLUS A SECOND-TRIMESTER LOSS, A PREVIOUS CALF CLOT, A CURETTAGE, A SISTER WITH LOSSES, AND AN AGE OF 37. THE STATION IS PASSED BY THREE MOVES. ONE, RE-ORIENT OUT LOUD IN THE FIRST TEN SECONDS: 'I am very sorry. Three losses is a great deal to have gone through. SO THE DIFFICULTY IS NOT FALLING PREGNANT — IT IS THAT THE PREGNANCIES HAVE NOT CONTINUED. THAT IS A DIFFERENT PROBLEM, AND I WANT TO LOOK AT IT DIFFERENTLY.' TWO, GIVE THE TWO HONEST STATEMENTS BEFORE THE TESTS, NOT AFTER: 'Even after a full set of tests, in ABOUT HALF OF COUPLES we never find a specific cause. And — more importantly — MOST WOMEN IN YOUR POSITION DO GO ON TO HAVE A SUCCESSFUL PREGNANCY. That is not me being kind; it is what the evidence shows.' THREE, PAIR EVERY TEST WITH ITS DIFFERENTIAL. 'Because I am thinking about A GENETIC CAUSE — where one of you carries a rearrangement of chromosomes without being affected by it — I would arrange CHROMOSOME TESTING FOR BOTH OF YOU; and if there is ever a future loss I would want THE TISSUE TESTED, because that is the most informative test of all.' 'Because I am thinking about THE SHAPE AND STRUCTURE OF THE WOMB — fibroids, a differently shaped womb, or SCARRING INSIDE IT WHICH CAN FOLLOW A CURETTAGE LIKE THE ONE YOU HAD — I would arrange A TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND, and a more detailed scan or hysteroscopy if that raises a question.' 'Because I am thinking about ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME, an immune condition that causes clots and also causes pregnancy loss by affecting the placenta, I would test LUPUS ANTICOAGULANT, ANTICARDIOLIPIN AND ANTI-β2-GLYCOPROTEIN I ANTIBODIES. YOUR CLOT AND YOUR LATER LOSS BOTH POINT THAT WAY. IT MATTERS ENORMOUSLY BECAUSE IT IS TREATABLE — aspirin and heparin injections in the next pregnancy substantially improve the chance of a live birth — and the test is repeated twelve weeks later to confirm it.' Then thyroid with antibodies, glucose, prolactin, and rubella and varicella immunity corrected BEFORE she conceives rather than during. AND THE SECOND-TRIMESTER LOSS GETS ITS OWN SENTENCE: 'A loss at that stage, with fluid loss and very little pain, can be due to the neck of the womb opening early — CERVICAL INSUFFICIENCY. It cannot be tested for now, but in a future pregnancy it means watching the cervical length on scans, and there are treatments including a stitch.' WHAT NOT TO ORDER: A ROUTINE INHERITED THROMBOPHILIA SCREEN (see findings) and ROUTINE TORCH SEROLOGY. EXAMINER CHALLENGE, 'Would you screen her for factor V Leiden?' → 'NOT ROUTINELY. I WOULD SCREEN FOR ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME IN EVERYONE, BUT INHERITED THROMBOPHILIA SCREENING HAS NOT BEEN SHOWN TO CHANGE OUTCOMES AND I WOULD RESERVE IT FOR A PERSONAL OR FAMILY HISTORY OF CLOTS.' THE MANAGEMENT SHE LEAVES WITH: the tests arranged · SPECIALIST REFERRAL, because at 37 after four years you refer rather than observe · PRECONCEPTION CARE — folic acid now, alcohol out, caffeine reduced · SUPPORTIVE CARE IN EARLY PREGNANCY, with early scans and a team who know her history, which genuinely improves outcomes · AND BEREAVEMENT SUPPORT OFFERED EXPLICITLY, because losing three pregnancies is a bereavement and this is the step candidates omit and the one she will remember. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN LOCALISATION: referral to an early pregnancy assessment service or recurrent pregnancy loss clinic, which is metropolitan and therefore with PATS travel support; genetic counselling through the SA Clinical Genetics Service; bereavement support through Red Nose Grief and Loss 1300 308 307 and SANDS, with counselling under a Mental Health Treatment Plan; preconception and sexual health support via SHINE SA; local ACCHS, Aboriginal Health Worker and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; interpreters through TIS National 131 450. VERIFY current services and contacts.
plan: The empathic opening, then the pivot within ten seconds of her statement — say you are sorry, name that three losses is a great deal, and state out loud that this is a different problem from not conceiving.
EXPLORE THE LOSSES — HOW MANY, and AT WHAT GESTATION EACH ONE HAPPENED. This single question splits the differential into first-trimester and second-trimester groups.
HOW EACH PRESENTED — bleeding and pain, or found on a scan · AND DID SHE NEED A CURETTAGE · WAS THE TISSUE TESTED · HAS SHE EVER CARRIED TO TERM · any other uterine, cervical or abdominal surgery.

THE IMPACT QUESTION, ASKED PROPERLY — 'How is all of this affecting you, and your relationship?' She is frightened to try again and her husband does not know what to say. Acknowledge it before moving on.
P1 AND P2 — periods, cycle length, heavy or painful bleeding, bleeding between · stable supportive relationship, previous STI, dyspareunia or post-coital bleeding.

THE ENDOCRINE BLOCK — temperature preference, weight and bowel change, family thyroid disease · acne, hirsutism, weight gain · headaches, visual change, milky discharge · DIABETES, thirst and polyuria.

The immune and thrombophilia block, where the case is won — joint pains or rashes · 'Have you ever had a clot in your leg or lung?' · 'Has anyone in your family had clots — or recurrent pregnancy losses?'
LIFESTYLE AND CLOSE — smoking, alcohol, CAFFEINE, other drugs, stress at home and work · medical conditions and all medications including over-the-counter and herbal · pets · cervical screening.
NAME THE CONDITION AND GIVE THE TWO HONEST STATEMENTS FIRST — about half remain unexplained, and most women in her position go on to have a successful pregnancy (see dx).

THE PAIRED INVESTIGATIONS, IN THE FIXED FORM — genetic, then uterine, then ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID WITH HER CLOT NAMED AS THE REASON AND THE TREATMENT STATED, then thyroid, glucose and prolactin, then immunity.
THE SECOND-TRIMESTER LOSS ADDRESSED SEPARATELY AS POSSIBLE CERVICAL INSUFFICIENCY, with surveillance and a suture named as future-pregnancy management.

CLOSE — SPECIALIST REFERRAL because she is 37 after four years · folic acid, alcohol and caffeine · SUPPORTIVE EARLY-PREGNANCY CARE WITH EARLY SCANS · AND BEREAVEMENT COUNSELLING OFFERED, not as an afterthought.

ask: The pivot sentence: 'So the difficulty is not falling pregnant; it is that the pregnancies are not continuing. That is a different problem and I want to look at it differently.'

The two questions that decide the station: 'At what stage of pregnancy did each one happen?' and 'Have you ever had a clot in your leg or lung? Has anyone in your family had clots, or recurrent pregnancy losses?'

The two honest statements, given before the tests: 'In about half of couples we never find a specific cause' and 'Most women in your position do go on to have a successful pregnancy — that is not me being kind, it is what the evidence shows.'

Examiner challenges: 'Would you screen her for factor V Leiden?' → 'Not routinely — antiphospholipid antibodies in everyone, inherited thrombophilia only with a personal or family clot history.' · 'What is the treatable cause?' → 'Antiphospholipid syndrome — aspirin and low molecular weight heparin in the next pregnancy.' · 'Would you do TORCH serology?' → 'No — infection causes sporadic but rarely recurrent loss.' · 'She is 37 and has been trying four years' → 'That argues for referral rather than further waiting.'

THE DRILLS: state the definition and the word to use with the patient in 10 seconds · say the pivot sentence cold · give six investigations each paired with its differential in 60 seconds · explain antiphospholipid syndrome, its testing rule and its treatment in 30 seconds · then change the losses to three first-trimester ones and say what drops off the list.
pefe: THERE IS NO EXAMINATION TASK IN THIS STATION — the six minutes are history and the last two are the paired investigations. IF AN EXAMINATION WERE OFFERED, the relevant elements would be BMI, blood pressure, thyroid, and a pelvic examination with cervical screening status, but the diagnosis here is made from the pattern of the losses rather than from findings.

Role-player: ANNA DELANEY, 37, FOUR YEARS OF TRYING AND THREE LOSSES — the first two at about EIGHT AND NINE WEEKS with bleeding and cramping, the third AT SIXTEEN WEEKS where she started LOSING FLUID and it happened quickly WITH VERY LITTLE PAIN. A CURETTAGE AFTER THE SECOND. NO TISSUE TESTING. Never carried to term, no other surgery. Periods regular at 28 days. No endocrine symptoms, no joint pains or rashes. Stopped smoking two years ago, very little alcohol, THREE COFFEES A DAY. No medications, no pets, screening normal.

How to play it: quiet and controlled at first, but visibly upset if the doctor is warm. If the doctor launches straight into questions without acknowledging the losses, answer flatly and do not volunteer the clot or your sister's history even when asked directly the first time. Her questions: 'Really?' after the prognosis · 'Nobody has mentioned any of this before' · 'And the clot?' · 'So there might be something we can actually do' · 'What about the one at sixteen weeks?' · 'So what happens now?'. The two things that decide the station: does the doctor ask the gestation of each loss, and do they connect the clot to antiphospholipid syndrome.

The pivot, and the sentence that shows you made it — The stem reads like infertility and you will walk in with an infertility structure. THE SWITCH HAPPENS ON ONE QUESTION YOU ALREADY ASK: 'HAVE YOU EVER BEEN PREGNANT BEFORE?' Ask it early and the case declares itself. THEN SAY IT: 'SO THE DIFFICULTY IS NOT FALLING PREGNANT; IT IS THAT THE PREGNANCIES ARE NOT CONTINUING. THAT IS A DIFFERENT PROBLEM AND I WANT TO LOOK AT IT DIFFERENTLY'

The definition, and the word to use — RECURRENT PREGNANCY LOSS IS TWO OR MORE PREGNANCY LOSSES BEFORE 24 WEEKS. The older threshold was three; most current guidance uses two VERIFY. Guidelines moved from 'recurrent miscarriage' to RECURRENT PREGNANCY LOSS deliberately, because of how the word lands on women living it. USE PREGNANCY LOSS WITH THE PATIENT — AND NEVER SAY 'FAILED PREGNANCY', 'INCOMPETENT CERVIX' OR 'ABORTION' TO HER FACE

The most useful question in the history — 'AT WHAT STAGE OF PREGNANCY DID EACH ONE HAPPEN?' FIRST-TRIMESTER LOSSES point to CHROMOSOMAL AND ENDOCRINE causes · SECOND-TRIMESTER LOSSES raise ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME, UTERINE ANOMALY AND CERVICAL INSUFFICIENCY. It changes the entire differential, and it is one of the two things that decide this station

How each loss presented — 'Was there bleeding and pain, or was it found on a scan? DID YOU NEED A PROCEDURE AFTERWARDS, SUCH AS A CURETTAGE?' PAINLESS DILATATION AND RUPTURE OF MEMBRANES IN THE SECOND TRIMESTER SUGGESTS CERVICAL INSUFFICIENCY · AND A CURETTAGE RAISES ASHERMAN SYNDROME as a cause of the later losses. Also ask whether THE TISSUE WAS TESTED — genetic testing of the products of conception is the single most informative test, and in the exam the answer is usually no

What Anna gives you — THREE LOSSES: the first two at ABOUT EIGHT AND NINE WEEKS with bleeding and cramping; the THIRD AT SIXTEEN WEEKS, where she started LOSING FLUID and it happened very quickly WITH VERY LITTLE PAIN · A CURETTAGE AFTER THE SECOND · no tissue testing · never carried to term · no other surgery · regular 28-day cycles · no endocrine symptoms

The two reward answers she gives only if asked — 'I had a clot in my calf after a long flight about six years ago' · and 'My sister has had two losses as well'. Clots plus losses is antiphospholipid syndrome until excluded, and a family history of losses raises a balanced translocation. Connecting the clot to antiphospholipid syndrome is the second thing that decides this station

The answer has a fixed shape — The task is not 'list tests' — it is INVESTIGATIONS WITH REASONS, so every line has the form: 'BECAUSE I AM THINKING ABOUT ___, I WOULD DO ___.' Said in that order, the examiner hears your differential list AND your investigation list at the same time

The treatable one — ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME — an immune condition causing clots in the placenta. TEST: LUPUS ANTICOAGULANT, ANTICARDIOLIPIN ANTIBODIES AND ANTI-β2-GLYCOPROTEIN I ANTIBODIES, AND IT REQUIRES A POSITIVE RESULT ON TWO OCCASIONS AT LEAST 12 WEEKS APART. TREATMENT IS ASPIRIN PLUS LOW MOLECULAR WEIGHT HEPARIN in the next pregnancy, which substantially improves the chance of a live birth VERIFY

Do not order a routine thrombophilia screen — CORRECTION — the lecture lists factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene and protein C and S alongside antiphospholipid antibodies. SEPARATE THEM. Antiphospholipid syndrome is an accepted, testable and TREATABLE cause and is screened for in everyone. INHERITED THROMBOPHILIA SCREENING IS NOT RECOMMENDED ROUTINELY in recurrent first-trimester loss: the association is weak, treatment based on it does not improve live birth rates, and a positive result creates anxiety and unnecessary anticoagulation. Reserve it for a personal or strong family history of VTE, or second-trimester loss, preferably with specialist input VERIFY

The rest of the paired list — GENETIC — KARYOTYPING OF BOTH PARTNERS, and genetic testing of the PRODUCTS OF CONCEPTION if there is a future loss, with genetic counselling if abnormal · UTERINE — TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND first, with three-dimensional ultrasound, saline infusion sonography, hysteroscopy or MRI if an anomaly is suspected · THYROID — TSH AND THYROID PEROXIDASE ANTIBODIES, because thyroid autoimmunity is associated with loss even when the TSH is normal · DIABETES AND PCOS — HbA1c or fasting glucose, androgens and ultrasound if suspected · PROLACTIN · GENERAL — full blood count, ferritin, coeliac serology where suggested, and RUBELLA AND VARICELLA IMMUNITY corrected BEFORE the next pregnancy

Two more things not on the lecture's list — ADDED — CERVICAL INSUFFICIENCY for second-trimester losses described as painless dilatation, ruptured membranes and rapid delivery without contractions: IT IS DIAGNOSED FROM THE HISTORY, and managed with CERVICAL LENGTH SURVEILLANCE in the next pregnancy and consideration of a CERVICAL SUTURE — naming it in a woman whose loss was at 16 to 22 weeks is a strong answer · AND ROUTINE TORCH SCREENING IS NOT RECOMMENDED, because infection causes sporadic but rarely RECURRENT loss: a single infection does not usually recur

Three things she needs to hear, and the examiner wants to hear — ADDED — ONE: AROUND HALF REMAIN UNEXPLAINED even after a complete work-up, and saying so IN ADVANCE prevents normal results from feeling like a failure · TWO: THE PROGNOSIS IS BETTER THAN SHE FEARS — most women with unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss go on to have a successful pregnancy, which is true, evidence-based, and the kindest thing you will say VERIFY · THREE: AGE IS THE STRONGEST SINGLE FACTOR, and at 37 after four years that argues for REFERRAL RATHER THAN FURTHER WAITING

setting: The recall has been endometriosis almost every time, which is exactly why the station is failed: candidates arrive with the answer and skip the red flags. The marking sheet is built the other way round — it rewards four key differentials, endometrial cancer, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease and endometriosis, and the red flags that separate them. The case turns on one question in the history — the pain's relationship to the bleeding — and one request at the end of the examination.
stem: Your general practice, rural South Australia. A 28-year-old woman presents with severe period pain. Her opening: 'My periods have become unbearable. The pain goes on for days and nothing touches it. I cannot keep taking time off work.'

Tasks: take a history — ask the examiner for physical findings — explain your diagnosis and differentials — explain your investigations. 8 minutes. An alternate run hands you an ultrasound report instead.

time: An empathic opening, because women with dysmenorrhoea are commonly dismissed before they reach you · then the pain assessment, which everyone does · then the block almost nobody does: before or after the bleeding, worse once bleeding starts, how many days, does analgesia help · then the impact · then the five Ps with heaviness, intermenstrual bleeding, deep dyspareunia and her pregnancy plans · then the four key differentials by block: cancer · fibroids and pressure · endometriosis with its urinary and bowel questions · PID with fever and discharge · then the PEFE with the temperature and the rectal examination requested by name · then diagnosis, four differentials, and two investigations in order.
findings: No cachexia, no pallor · AFEBRILE, observations normal · abdomen soft, mildly tender suprapubically, no mass · inspection and speculum NORMAL · bimanual: NO cervical motion tenderness, uterus normal size with a regular border, non-tender, mobile, no adnexal mass · RECTAL EXAMINATION, ONLY IF REQUESTED: TENDERNESS AND NODULARITY

back.dx: ENDOMETRIOSIS — REACHED THROUGH THE OTHER THREE, NOT INSTEAD OF THEM. THE EXPLANATION, WORD FOR WORD: 'Most likely you have a condition called endometriosis. Tissue very similar to the lining of the womb grows OUTSIDE the womb — on the ovaries, the ligaments behind the womb, and sometimes on the bladder or bowel. That tissue responds to your hormones each month just as the lining does, WHICH IS WHY THE PAIN FOLLOWS YOUR PERIODS.' THEN THE REASONS, BUILT FROM WHAT SHE TOLD YOU: 'The pain is severe, it lasts far longer than a normal period pain, IT GETS WORSE ONCE THE BLEEDING STARTS, and painkillers are not touching it. You have pain during sex DEEP INSIDE. You have pain opening your bowels and blood in your urine around your period, which suggests deposits near the bladder and bowel. You have been trying to conceive for a year without success. And on examination I found TENDERNESS AND SMALL NODULES BEHIND THE WOMB, which is characteristic.' THEN THE FOUR DIFFERENTIALS, NAMED EVEN THOUGH YOU ARE CONFIDENT: a CANCER OF THE WOMB OR OVARY — which is why you asked about weight, appetite and family history, and nothing pointed that way · FIBROIDS · PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE, excluded by no fever and no discharge · ADENOMYOSIS, where the same tissue grows into the muscle of the womb itself · and less likely, bowel conditions, urinary causes or referred back pain. INVESTIGATIONS, TWO, IN THIS ORDER: ONE, TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND — first line, looking for endometriomas, fibroids, adenomyosis and ovarian masses, and far more accurate than a transabdominal scan. SAY EXPLICITLY THAT A NORMAL SCAN DOES NOT RULE THIS OUT. TWO, LAPAROSCOPY — visualises deposits directly and allows EXCISION OR ABLATION IN THE SAME PROCEDURE, diagnostic and therapeutic together. GUIDED BY THE DIFFERENTIAL: swabs if PID is possible, A PREGNANCY TEST, midstream urine, hysteroscopy for suspected adhesions, and MRI for deep disease or adenomyosis. NOT CA125. AND SAY THE TREATMENT CAN START NOW: 'I do not want you waiting months in this much pain for a test to confirm what your history already shows.' THE MANAGEMENT, ADJUSTED TO HER PREGNANCY PLANS (see findings): normally an NSAID STARTED A DAY OR TWO BEFORE the pain begins, then continuous combined pill or a Mirena — BUT THOSE ARE CONTRACEPTIVE, and she is trying to conceive, so for her it is the NSAID approach now plus EARLIER GYNAECOLOGY REFERRAL, because surgical treatment can also improve the chance of pregnancy. AND CLOSE THE CHRONIC-PAIN LOOP: pain this severe for this long takes a toll, she has told you about work and her relationship, so name pelvic pain physiotherapy, support organisations and counselling — dysmenorrhoea of this severity is a chronic pain condition and deserves to be treated as one. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN LOCALISATION: transvaginal ultrasound locally where available; gynaecology and laparoscopy by referral with PATS travel support; persistent pelvic pain services and pelvic floor physiotherapy are metropolitan, so consider telehealth; ENDOMETRIOSIS AUSTRALIA and QENDO for patient information and peer support, with the National Action Plan for Endometriosis underpinning current Australian care and funded specialist endometriosis clinics VERIFY; local ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; interpreters through TIS National 131 450.
plan: THE EMPATHIC OPENING, WHICH IS SCORED: 'I am sorry you have been going through this — severe period pain is exhausting and it is often not taken seriously. Let me ask some questions, find the cause, and we will make a plan together.'
THE PAIN ASSESSMENT — site, severity out of ten, character, when the painful periods started and whether they are worsening, radiation, aggravating and relieving factors.
The block that decides the case — before or after the bleeding · worse once bleeding starts · how many days · pain at other times · what analgesia she has tried and whether it helps.
THE IMPACT — work or study, relationship, mood. Days off every month is itself a measure of severity, and it is a scored item.

THE FIVE Ps — last period, cycle length, days of bleeding, HEAVINESS with clots or flooding, INTERMENSTRUAL BLEEDING · sexual history with STI questions AND DEEP DYSPAREUNIA · contraception including a copper coil · previous pregnancy, uterine or cervical surgery, AND WHETHER SHE IS HOPING TO CONCEIVE · screening.

DIFFERENTIAL 1, CANCER — weight loss, appetite, tiredness, lumps, and family history of uterine, ovarian, breast or bowel cancer · DIFFERENTIAL 2, FIBROIDS — pressure or heaviness, abdominal swelling, urinary frequency or constipation.
Differential 3, endometriosis — pain passing urine or opening bowels, particularly around her period, and blood in urine or stool · differential 4, PID — fever, chills, unusual discharge, nausea.
THE REST IF TIME — persistent bloating and bowel habit change for ovarian cancer, urinary symptoms, and back pain.

The diagnosis in plain words with the mechanism, then the reasons assembled from her own answers (see dx).
THE FOUR DIFFERENTIALS NAMED, PLUS ADENOMYOSIS AND THE NON-GYNAECOLOGICAL CAUSES — with the reason you asked the red flag questions made explicit.

The request the examiner is waiting for: 'I would also like to perform a rectal examination, to feel the uterosacral ligaments and the pouch of douglas for tenderness and nodularity.'

'A normal scan does not rule this out.' / 'Take the anti-inflammatory a day or two before the pain begins, not once it has taken hold.' / 'I do not want you waiting months in this much pain for a test to confirm what your history already shows.'

Examiner challenges: 'Do you need a laparoscopy to diagnose it?' → 'Not any more — a normal ultrasound does not exclude it and empirical treatment can start on clinical grounds.' · 'Would you order a CA125?' → 'No — it is raised in endometriosis, fibroids, PID, pregnancy and menstruation, and is not diagnostic.' · 'The scan shows a 1.9 cm cyst' → 'Small, unilocular, thin-walled and mid-cycle — a normal follicular cyst, not an endometrioma.' · 'She wants to conceive' → 'Hormonal treatment is contraceptive, so she needs the NSAID approach and earlier specialist referral.'

pefe: THE FULL REQUEST, WITH THE TWO ITEMS CANDIDATES SKIP: general appearance for CACHEXIA and PALLOR · all four vital signs and PARTICULARLY THE TEMPERATURE, because PID is one of the four key differentials · abdomen for tenderness, any mass and its lower border · CONSENT AND CHAPERONE · inspection · speculum for the cervix, vaginal walls and the POSTERIOR FORNIX where deep deposits may be visible as nodules · bimanual for cervical motion tenderness, uterine SIZE, BORDER, TENDERNESS AND MOBILITY — A FIXED RETROVERTED UTERUS IS A CLASSIC ENDOMETRIOSIS SIGN — and adnexal mass or tenderness · AND THE RECTAL EXAMINATION, REQUESTED BY NAME.

Role-player: RUBY MARSH, 28. Periods fine as a teenager; painful for THREE YEARS and steadily worsening. Eight or nine out of ten, deep cramping, radiating to lower back and thighs. STARTS A DAY OR TWO BEFORE BUT MUCH WORSE ONCE BLEEDING STARTS, LASTS SEVEN OR EIGHT DAYS, with a dragging ache at other times. Analgesia barely helps. TWO OR THREE DAYS OFF WORK EVERY MONTH. Cycle 28 days, bleeds six, fairly heavy with clots, no intermenstrual bleeding. One partner four years, no infections, NO CONTRACEPTION AND TRYING TO CONCEIVE FOR A YEAR.

HOW TO PLAY IT: THE THREE REWARD ANSWERS — deep dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia with haematuria, and the year of trying — ARE GIVEN ONLY IF ASKED. Her questions: 'WHY DO YOU THINK THAT IS WHAT IT IS?' · 'COULD IT BE SOMETHING ELSE?' · 'SO WHAT HAPPENS NOW?' · 'WHAT TREATMENT?'. IF THE DOCTOR DOES NOT ASK FOR THE RECTAL EXAMINATION, SAY NOTHING — THIS IS THE FINDING THE STATION IS BUILT AROUND. ALTERNATE RUNS: the ultrasound version with the 1.9 cm cyst; a 54-year-old with new pain, 7 kg lost and postmenopausal bleeding, which is endometrial carcinoma until excluded; and a PID version with five days of pain, fever, offensive discharge and a new partner, treated empirically today.

Primary or secondary — the four questions that define the case — 'DOES THE PAIN START BEFORE THE BLEEDING OR AFTER IT? DOES IT GET WORSE ONCE THE BLEEDING STARTS? HOW MANY DAYS DOES IT LAST? DO PAINKILLERS HELP?' PRIMARY: starts before bleeding, lasts 2 to 3 days, eases. SECONDARY: WORSENS ONCE BLEEDING STARTS, LASTS 7 TO 8 DAYS OR LONGER, and analgesia barely touches it. Everyone does the pain assessment; almost nobody does this

The four differentials that decide the station — ENDOMETRIAL CANCER · FIBROIDS · PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE · ENDOMETRIOSIS. Name all four even when you are confident of the last one — the whole reason this station is failed is that candidates who know the recall never exclude anything

The RANZCOG red flags in dysmenorrhoea — Weight loss · rectal bleeding · new-onset pain, particularly in an older woman · pain after menopause · a palpable pelvic mass · post-coital bleeding · and suicidal ideation from the burden of chronic pain. Each one changes the urgency VERIFY

The single most important line in the document — 'I WOULD ALSO LIKE TO PERFORM A RECTAL EXAMINATION, TO FEEL THE UTEROSACRAL LIGAMENTS AND THE POUCH OF DOUGLAS FOR TENDERNESS AND NODULARITY.' THE PELVIC EXAMINATION IN THIS STATION IS NORMAL — if you stop at the bimanual you leave with nothing and you are guessing. Deposits sit behind the uterus where a vaginal examination reaches poorly and a rectal one reaches well, AND THE EXAMINER GIVES THE FINDING ONLY IF YOU ASK

What Ruby gives you — Periods fine as a teenager, PAIN STARTED THREE YEARS AGO AND STEADILY WORSENED · low across the abdomen, EIGHT OR NINE OUT OF TEN, deep cramping radiating to lower back and thighs · STARTS A DAY OR TWO BEFORE BUT MUCH WORSE ONCE BLEEDING STARTS · SEVEN OR EIGHT DAYS, with a dragging ache at other times · paracetamol and ibuprofen BARELY TAKE THE EDGE OFF · TWO OR THREE DAYS OFF WORK EVERY MONTH

The three reward answers she gives only if asked — 'SEX HAS BECOME PAINFUL — DEEP INSIDE, NOT AT THE ENTRANCE' — deep dyspareunia is the second cardinal symptom · 'IT HURTS TO OPEN MY BOWELS DURING MY PERIOD, AND I HAVE SEEN BLOOD IN MY URINE A COUPLE OF TIMES AROUND THEN' — cyclical dyschezia and haematuria mean deposits near bowel and bladder · AND 'WE HAVE BEEN TRYING TO CONCEIVE FOR ABOUT A YEAR WITHOUT LUCK', which both supports the diagnosis and DETERMINES THE TREATMENT

Endometriosis and adenomyosis are related, not identical — CORRECTION — ENDOMETRIOSIS is deposits OUTSIDE the uterus, typically ovaries, uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas; classically a younger woman with dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, dyschezia and subfertility · ADENOMYOSIS is endometrial tissue WITHIN THE MYOMETRIUM; classically an older, parous woman with a BULKY, GLOBULAR, TENDER UTERUS and heavy painful periods, suggested on ultrasound and best characterised on MRI. THEY FREQUENTLY COEXIST VERIFY

The management the lecture does not cover — ADDED — FIRST LINE: NSAIDs — mefenamic acid or ibuprofen — STARTED BEFORE THE PAIN BEGINS rather than once it is established, which works far better, plus simple analgesia and heat · HORMONAL: the combined pill CONTINUOUSLY or in extended cycles to skip withdrawal bleeds, a LEVONORGESTREL INTRAUTERINE SYSTEM, or oral progestogens; specialist options include GnRH analogues with add-back · SURGICAL: laparoscopic excision or ablation; hysterectomy only in carefully selected cases with completed childbearing · ALONGSIDE ALL OF IT: PELVIC FLOOR PHYSIOTHERAPY, A CHRONIC PAIN APPROACH AND PSYCHOLOGICAL SUPPORT

Ask about her pregnancy plans first — HORMONAL TREATMENT IS CONTRACEPTIVE, so a woman trying to conceive needs a different plan and EARLIER SPECIALIST REFERRAL — and surgical treatment of endometriosis can itself improve the chance of pregnancy. In this case she has been trying for a year, so the NSAID timing advice plus early gynaecology referral is the answer rather than the pill

The ultrasound version — the cyst that is not the answer — The scan is done MID-CYCLE, TWO WEEKS BEFORE THE PERIOD, and reports a 1.9 cm UNILOCULAR THIN-WALLED CYST in the left ovary with a normal endometrial lining. SMALL — a simple follicular cyst below about 3 cm is physiological · UNILOCULAR AND THIN-WALLED — an endometrioma has THICK WALLS and low-level ground-glass echoes · AND MID-CYCLE IS EXACTLY WHEN THE DOMINANT FOLLICLE IS LARGEST. DO NOT CALL IT AN ENDOMETRIOMA BEFORE TAKING THE HISTORY — that tells the examiner you memorised the recall. Report it as a normal follicular cyst, find the endometriosis clinically, then say the cyst is incidental

Laparoscopy is no longer required to diagnose it — CORRECTION — the lecture presents laparoscopy as the diagnostic endpoint. CURRENT GUIDANCE HAS MOVED: A NORMAL ULTRASOUND DOES NOT EXCLUDE ENDOMETRIOSIS, and EMPIRICAL MEDICAL TREATMENT MAY BE STARTED ON CLINICAL GROUNDS WITHOUT LAPAROSCOPIC CONFIRMATION VERIFY. This matters because the average delay to diagnosis has been AROUND SEVEN YEARS, much of it spent waiting for surgery. 'I WOULD START TREATMENT NOW RATHER THAN MAKE HER WAIT FOR A LAPAROSCOPY TO CONFIRM WHAT THE HISTORY ALREADY SHOWS' is a strong, current answer. AND CA125 IS NOT A DIAGNOSTIC TEST — it is raised in endometriosis, fibroids, PID, pregnancy and menstruation
