'I would gently touch the vestibule with a moistened cotton swab to map where the pain is and whether light touch provokes it.' POSITIVE IN PROVOKED VESTIBULODYNIA — localised tenderness at the vestibule with a NORMAL-LOOKING VULVA VERIFY. And if she tolerates a single finger, ASSESS PELVIC FLOOR MUSCLE TONE, which is increased in vaginismus

back.dx: VAGINISMUS — A LOCALISED, PROVOKED FORM OF VULVODYNIA — REACHED LAST, AFTER THE ORGANIC CAUSES ARE EXCLUDED. THE ORDER IS THE STATION: cancers, infection, endometriosis, dryness, skin, trauma, and THEN the diagnosis of exclusion. Raising it in the first minute is the single clearest marker of a memorised recall. VALIDATE FIRST, ALWAYS: 'I want to be clear about something. YOUR PAIN IS REAL. I am not telling you it is imagined. It is caused by the muscles in that area tightening involuntarily, and that is a real, physical thing — and it is treatable.' THEN THE EXPLANATION, WORD FOR WORD: 'What you have is a condition called vaginismus, which is a form of a broader condition called vulvodynia. The muscles of the pelvic floor tighten involuntarily when penetration is attempted, which makes entry painful or impossible.' THEN THE REASONS, WHICH ARE THE FOUR DISCRIMINATORS: 'The pain happens RIGHT AT THE START of penetration rather than deep inside. It STOPS COMPLETELY when intercourse stops. TOUCHING THE AREA ITSELF IS NOT PAINFUL. And you have described TENSING UP AND FEELING ANXIOUS BEFOREHAND, which sets up a cycle — anticipating pain makes the muscles tighten, which makes it hurt, which increases the fear.' THEN THE DIFFERENTIALS IN FIVE SECONDS: 'This is a diagnosis we reach by excluding other causes, and the ones I was most concerned about were A CANCER OF THE CERVIX, AN INFECTION IN THE PELVIS, AND ENDOMETRIOSIS — and nothing in your history or examination points to any of them.' THE MANAGEMENT IS THREE STRANDS, AND THE DRUGS ARE ADJUNCTS RATHER THAN THE TREATMENT. ONE, THE MUSCLES: referral to a PELVIC FLOOR PHYSIOTHERAPIST who will teach her where those muscles are and, importantly, HOW TO RELAX THEM, then retrain the response step by step. TWO, VAGINAL TRAINERS: a graded set of smooth inserts starting very small, USED BY HER, AT HER OWN PACE, ENTIRELY IN HER CONTROL — and saying that last part is what makes the offer acceptable. THREE, THE FEAR CYCLE: a psychologist for COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY, and a SEX THERAPIST who can work with her and her partner together if they would both like that. ALONGSIDE: lubricants continued even though they have not solved it, a TOPICAL LOCAL ANAESTHETIC GEL before intercourse, plain water only with no soaps or washes, and NEUROPATHIC PAIN AGENTS held in reserve if needed later — starting with physiotherapy and therapy because those treat the cause. THEN REVIEW IN A FEW WEEKS. THE SENSITIVE QUESTION IS NOT OPTIONAL: after establishing confidentiality, ask whether sex has ever been forced or whether she has experienced sexual abuse, WITH A SUPPORTIVE RESPONSE READY. If she discloses, respond supportively, do not interrogate for detail, affirm that it was not her fault, and offer support and referral rather than moving back to the checklist. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN LOCALISATION: pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychosexual therapy are largely metropolitan, so from a rural site consider telehealth and check what the local women's health physiotherapy service offers; psychology under a Mental Health Treatment Plan; sexual and reproductive health support and counselling through SHINE SA; gynaecology referral with PATS travel support; IF SEXUAL ASSAULT IS DISCLOSED, 1800RESPECT 1800 737 732 AND YARROW PLACE, South Australia's sexual assault service; local ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; interpreters through TIS National 131 450.
plan: THE SENSITIVE OPENING WITH CONFIDENTIALITY: 'Thank you for sharing this with me — I know it is not an easy thing to bring up. It must be distressing, and I am here to help. I will need to ask some sensitive questions, and everything we discuss is confidential. Is that alright?'
QUESTION 1 AND 2 — SUPERFICIAL OR DEEP, and DOES THE PAIN CONTINUE AFTER SEX STOPS or occur at other times. These two split the differential and separate vulvodynia from vaginismus.
SEVERITY AND QUALITY — out of ten, BURNING or a DEEP DULL ACHE · then onset and course: when it started, every time or intermittent, SAME WITH PREVIOUS PARTNERS, getting worse.

MODIFIERS — do LUBRICANTS help, is it painful to TOUCH the area or insert a TAMPON, is it worse in particular positions · THEN THE IMPACT, ASKED EARLY: 'How is this affecting you, and your relationship?'

RED FLAGS FIRST, ALL THE CANCERS — weight loss, appetite, tiredness, lumps, family history · CERVIX: POST-COITAL BLEEDING, unusual discharge, SCREENING STATUS · uterus and ovary: heavy or intermenstrual bleeding, pressure, bloating, bowel change.

ENDOMETRIOSIS — very painful periods, pain passing urine or opening bowels around the period, blood in urine or stool · PID — fever, discharge, lower abdominal pain between periods, plus a screening sexual history.
DRYNESS, SKIN AND TRAUMA — dryness, breastfeeding, hormones · rash, redness, ITCHING, ulcers, blisters, splits, lumps · recent delivery with tear or episiotomy, any surgery or procedure.

ONLY NOW THE DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION — is penetration possible at all, can she use a tampon or a finger · THE FEAR QUESTION: 'Do you feel anxious or fearful about sex — do you find yourself tensing up beforehand?'
THE PSYCHOSOCIAL BLOCK — relationship stress, mood and sleep, AND THE ABUSE QUESTION ASKED SENSITIVELY, with permission not to answer and a supportive response ready.

THE EXAMINATION AND CARD: vulval inspection in detail, THE COTTON-SWAB TEST, speculum ONLY IF POSSIBLE — and if not, that refusal is a finding · pelvic floor tone if a single finger is tolerated · INVESTIGATIONS ADAPTED to what she can tolerate (see findings).

THE REASONS, WHICH ARE THE FOUR DISCRIMINATORS, THEN THE THREE DIFFERENTIALS YOU EXCLUDED — cervical cancer, pelvic infection, endometriosis.

THE THREE STRANDS OF TREATMENT — PELVIC FLOOR PHYSIOTHERAPY · VAGINAL TRAINERS AT HER OWN PACE AND IN HER CONTROL · CBT AND SEX THERAPY — plus lubricant, topical anaesthetic, plain water only, and review in a few weeks.

ask: THE SENTENCE THAT COMES BEFORE ANY EXPLANATION: 'YOUR PAIN IS REAL. I AM NOT TELLING YOU IT IS IMAGINED.' One sentence, and it is the difference between a patient who engages with physiotherapy and one who never comes back.

The four discriminators as questions: 'Does it happen right at the beginning, or deeper inside?' · 'Does the pain carry on after sex stops?' · 'Is it painful just to touch the area, or to insert a tampon?' · 'Do you find yourself tensing up beforehand?'
'YOU USE THEM YOURSELF, AT YOUR OWN PACE, ENTIRELY IN YOUR CONTROL.' — said about the vaginal trainers, and it is what makes the offer acceptable to a woman who feels her body is not hers to command.

Superficial or deep — the organising question — SUPERFICIAL, AT THE ENTRANCE ON ENTRY: vaginismus and vulvodynia · VAGINAL DRYNESS — atrophic, lactational, hormonal contraception, reduced arousal, anti-oestrogen therapy · DERMATOLOGICAL — contact or allergic dermatitis, LICHEN SCLEROSUS, lichen planus, psoriasis · INFECTION — candidiasis, herpes, vulvovaginitis · BARTHOLIN cyst or abscess · TRAUMA — tear, episiotomy, surgery, female genital cutting · VULVAL CARCINOMA. DEEP, ON DEEP PENETRATION: ENDOMETRIOSIS AND ADENOMYOSIS, the commonest organic cause · PID · PELVIC MASSES including OVARIAN AND UTERINE CARCINOMA · CERVICAL CARCINOMA and cervicitis · adhesions · retroverted uterus · interstitial cystitis and irritable bowel

The four questions that place her — 1 'Does the pain happen at the beginning, as penetration starts — or deeper inside?' · 2 'Does the pain continue after sex stops? Do you have pain when you are not having sex at all?' — the after-sensation, which points to vulvodynia rather than vaginismus · 3 'Is penetration possible at all? What about a tampon, or a finger? Is it painful just to touch the area?' — touch-provoked pain again suggests vulvodynia · 4 'Has this been there since you first had sex, or is it new? Was it the same with previous partners?' — lifelong versus acquired, generalised versus situational

Vaginismus versus vulvodynia — VAGINISMUS: involuntary spasm of the pelvic floor on attempted penetration · triggered by penetration — intercourse, tampon, finger, speculum · LIGHT TOUCH USUALLY NOT PAINFUL · NO AFTER-SENSATION, stop and the pain stops · FEAR IS PROMINENT in a fear-avoidance cycle. VULVODYNIA: chronic vulval pain of AT LEAST THREE MONTHS without an identifiable cause, a pain-regulation disorder · PROVOKED or SPONTANEOUS · LIGHT TOUCH OF THE VESTIBULE PROVOKES IT · AFTER-SENSATION PRESENT · fear present but less central. VAGINISMUS IS WIDELY REGARDED AS A FORM OF LOCALISED PROVOKED VULVODYNIA, which is exactly why the two overlap

The answer that cannot be marked wrong — ADDED — DSM-5 merged vaginismus and dyspareunia into GENITO-PELVIC PAIN/PENETRATION DISORDER, while gynaecological classification still separates them and describes vulvodynia by three axes: LOCALISED OR GENERALISED, PROVOKED OR SPONTANEOUS, PRIMARY OR SECONDARY VERIFY. SAY: 'This is a chronic vulval pain condition. Given that the pain occurs only on attempted penetration, stops when intercourse stops, and there is a clear fear component, I WOULD CALL IT VAGINISMUS — WHICH IS GENERALLY REGARDED AS A LOCALISED, PROVOKED FORM OF VULVODYNIA. Both are diagnoses of exclusion and both are managed the same way.' That names both, explains the relationship, and commits

What Tess gives you — RIGHT AT THE BEGINNING — 'IT FEELS LIKE HITTING A WALL' · sharp, tearing, burning, EIGHT OUT OF TEN · NO PAIN ONCE THEY STOP AND NONE OTHERWISE · TOUCHING THE AREA DOES NOT HURT · CANNOT INSERT A TAMPON · lubricant makes no difference · first relationship, painful EVERY TIME since starting three months ago · periods normal, no discharge, no itch, no rash, one partner with condoms, on the pill, no pregnancy or surgery

The reward answer and the sensitive one — FEAR: 'YES. COMPLETELY. I START DREADING IT HOURS BEFORE, AND I CAN FEEL MYSELF GOING RIGID' — the core of vaginismus and the target of treatment, given only if asked · AND THE ABUSE QUESTION, ASKED AFTER CONFIDENTIALITY IS ESTABLISHED AND WITH A SUPPORTIVE RESPONSE READY: 'Has sex ever been forced, or have you ever experienced sexual abuse?' Adapt the investigations to what she can tolerate — CORRECTION — the reflex answers are transvaginal ultrasound and endocervical swabs, and NEITHER IS REALISTIC in a woman who cannot tolerate a speculum. USE INSTEAD: a TRANSABDOMINAL PELVIC ULTRASOUND — less sensitive but achievable — and a SELF-COLLECTED VAGINAL SWAB OR FIRST-VOID URINE for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, which perform well and need no speculum. SAY IT EXPLICITLY: 'BECAUSE AN INTERNAL EXAMINATION IS PAINFUL FOR HER, I WOULD USE A SCAN THROUGH THE TUMMY AND A SELF-COLLECTED SWAB RATHER THAN INSISTING ON A SPECULUM'

If your explanation lands as 'the pain is in your mind', you have lost the patient and the station. THE FIRST SENTENCE AFTER THE DIAGNOSIS: 'I want to be clear about something. YOUR PAIN IS REAL. I am not telling you it is imagined. It is caused by the muscles in that area tightening involuntarily, and by the nerves there becoming oversensitive — AND BOTH OF THOSE ARE TREATABLE'

time: The organising question first — inside or outside, and if outside, whereabouts · then timing, course, night-time itch, and what creams have already failed · then the impact · then the red flags before anything else: weight, appetite, tiredness, groin nodes, a non-healing lesion or bleeding from the skin, and any bleeding since the periods stopped · then the dermatitis group — the rash characterised, atopy, contact exposures, and autoimmune history · then the vaginitis group — discharge, infection, sexual history, dryness and urinary symptoms, diabetes and antibiotics · then the menopausal five Ps · then the PEFE in three inspection layers, with the vaginal walls and a suspicious lesion requested by name.
findings: Candidates expect CHALK WHITE and are thrown when it is not. LOOK FOR PALLOR AND SHINE rather than pure white, a WRINKLED, CRINKLED OR CIGARETTE-PAPER TEXTURE, and THE FIGURE-OF-EIGHT DISTRIBUTION encircling vulva and anus. IN DARKER SKIN the pallor may be subtle or appear as HYPOPIGMENTATION — rely on TEXTURE, DISTRIBUTION AND LOSS OF ARCHITECTURE. FISSURES, PURPURA AND BRUISE-LIKE AREAS ARE PART OF THE CONDITION, not evidence of trauma, and should not distract you
The three-layer inspection, and the layer nobody asks for

'With consent and a chaperone: FIRST, any rash or erythema? SECOND, any ulcers, blisters, fissures or excoriation? THIRD, ANY SUSPICIOUS LESION SUGGESTIVE OF MALIGNANCY — irregular, raised, bleeding? AND IS THERE ANY LOSS OF THE NORMAL ARCHITECTURE?' Ask 'is there a rash?' and you get 'yes'. ASK FOR COLOUR, SITE AND DISTRIBUTION, AND MORPHOLOGY and you get white, vulval and perianal, plaque — which is the diagnosis. RESORPTION OF THE LABIA MINORA OR BURYING OF THE CLITORIS IS SPECIFIC

back.dx: LICHEN SCLEROSUS IN THE WORKED VERSION — AN AUTOIMMUNE VULVAL DERMATOSIS THAT SPARES THE VAGINA. THE EXPLANATION, WORD FOR WORD: 'You have a condition called lichen sclerosus. It is an AUTOIMMUNE condition — your own immune system is attacking the skin in that area and causing long-term inflammation. That inflammation is what causes the itch, the change in the skin, and over time the scarring.' THEN THE FOUR REASONS: THE APPEARANCE AND DISTRIBUTION of the rash, pale, shiny and wrinkled in a ring around the vulva and back to the anus · THE INTENSE, LONG-STANDING ITCH · THE PAIN WITH SEX from scarring · AND THE FACT THAT BOTH AN ANTIFUNGAL AND AN OESTROGEN CREAM FAILED, which rules out the two things she was treated for · PLUS HER GRAVES DISEASE, because autoimmune conditions cluster. DIAGNOSIS AND BIOPSY: the diagnosis is CLINICAL in a typical case. A PUNCH BIOPSY is taken when the appearance is atypical, when it does not respond to adequate treatment, or when any lesion looks suspicious for malignancy — and in the exam, offering one is reasonable and safe: 'I can take a small sample of skin to confirm the diagnosis and make sure there is nothing more worrying in it.' WHAT IS NOT DONE IS ROUTINE REPEAT BIOPSY AS SURVEILLANCE — SURVEILLANCE IS CLINICAL EXAMINATION, with biopsy of anything that changes. THE TREATMENT, AND THE CORRECTION THAT CARRIES IT: HYDROCORTISONE WILL NOT TREAT THIS, AND UNDER-TREATMENT IS THE USUAL ERROR. The instinct in genital skin is to reach for the mildest steroid because thin skin atrophies; in lichen sclerosus that instinct is wrong, because IT IS THE UNTREATED INFLAMMATION — NOT THE STEROID — THAT SCARS THE SKIN AND CARRIES THE CANCER RISK. Use CLOBETASOL PROPIONATE 0.05% OINTMENT NIGHTLY FOR ABOUT 12 WEEKS, then maintenance TWO TO THREE NIGHTS A WEEK LONG TERM VERIFY. Patients commonly under-apply out of fear, so say it explicitly: 'I know it sounds strong, and people often worry about steroid creams thinning the skin. IN THIS CONDITION IT IS THE OPPOSITE — USING IT PROPERLY PROTECTS THE SKIN, AND USING TOO LITTLE IS WHAT CAUSES DAMAGE.' AND SAY IT IS LIFELONG: 'WE CONTROL IT RATHER THAN CURE IT' — or she will stop the maintenance when the itch settles and return years later with scarring. SKIN CARE ALONGSIDE: plain water and a soap substitute only, no soaps, wipes or scented products; a simple moisturiser as a barrier; loose cotton underwear. AND THE PART THAT IS THE CANCER PLAN: REVIEW EVERY SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS TO EXAMINE THE SKIN, WITH RED FLAGS FOR EARLIER RETURN — a new lump, a sore or ulcer that does not heal, bleeding from the skin, or the cream ceasing to work. THE OTHER VERSIONS: CANDIDIASIS treated as in the recurrent candidiasis station, with the reassurance that thrush is an overgrowth rather than something caught · ATROPHIC VAGINITIS treated with vaginal moisturisers, lubricants and TOPICAL VAGINAL OESTROGEN, with the answer to 'is this just old age?' being that it is a treatable consequence of oestrogen loss rather than something to endure · AND THE CARCINOMA VERSION, which is urgent gynae-oncology referral for biopsy with the inguinal nodes examined. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN LOCALISATION: dermatology or vulval clinic referral for atypical or refractory disease with PATS travel support; URGENT GYNAE-ONCOLOGY REFERRAL FOR ANY SUSPICIOUS LESION; potent topical steroids are PBS-listed, so check current authority requirements; continence support for the contact dermatitis cases through the National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66; local ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; interpreters through TIS National 131 450. VERIFY all regimens and durations against current guidance.
plan: ACKNOWLEDGE SIX MONTHS OF FAILED TREATMENT — 'that sounds miserable, and I understand why you are worried' — THEN THE ORGANISING QUESTION: inside the vagina, or on the skin outside, and if outside, whereabouts.
TIMING AND COURSE — how long, constant or intermittent, getting worse, AND IS IT WORSE AT NIGHT. Constant and progressive suggests a dermatosis; intermittent suggests infection or irritant exposure.

THE CASE-DESIGN QUESTION — 'WHAT HAVE YOU TRIED, AND DID ANYTHING HELP?' A failed antifungal and a failed oestrogen cream are two diagnoses excluded by history · THEN THE IMPACT ON SLEEP, WORK AND HER RELATIONSHIP.
Red flags first — weight, appetite, tiredness, lumps in the groin · a lump, ulcer or sore that does not heal, or bleeding from the skin · and any vaginal bleeding since the periods stopped.
THE DERMATITIS GROUP — the rash characterised by COLOUR, site, discharge, ULCERS BLISTERS OR SPLITS, and itchy versus painful · atopy in her or the family.

CONTACT AND AUTOIMMUNE — new soap, wash, wipes, pads, laundry powder, underwear, douching, URINE LEAKING ONTO THE SKIN · AND AUTOIMMUNE CONDITIONS: thyroid disease, vitiligo, coeliac disease, type 1 diabetes.

THE VAGINITIS GROUP — discharge characterised fully · fever, abdominal pain, nausea · a screening sexual history · DRYNESS INSIDE, DYSPAREUNIA AND URINARY SYMPTOMS · diabetes, recent antibiotics or steroids.
THE MENOPAUSAL FIVE Ps — last period, flushes, ANY BLEEDING SINCE THEY STOPPED, dyspareunia and post-coital bleeding, hormone therapy, deliveries, leaking urine and any lump, SCREENING AND MAMMOGRAM.

PEFE: cachexia and RASHES ELSEWHERE INCLUDING THE MOUTH · temperature · abdomen AND THE INGUINAL REGIONS · consent and chaperone · THE THREE-LAYER INSPECTION with a suspicious lesion and loss of architecture requested by name.
ASK FOR THE RASH BY COLOUR, SITE AND DISTRIBUTION, AND MORPHOLOGY — and ASK FOR THE VAGINAL WALLS at the speculum, because Version 2 is handed over there and nowhere else.
THE DIAGNOSIS WITH ITS FOUR REASONS, INCLUDING THE TWO FAILED CREAMS AND THE AUTOIMMUNE HISTORY (see dx) — and name the differentials from both groups plus the red flag.
WHY IT MATTERS — the untreated inflammation scars the skin and a small number of women develop a skin cancer on that background. Then the biopsy offered to confirm and exclude.

Treatment: clobetasol nightly for about three months then two to three nights a week · the steroid fear addressed directly · skin care · 'We control it rather than cure it' · and six to twelve monthly examination with red flags for earlier return.

ask: THE QUESTION THAT PICKS THE VERSION: 'IS IT ON THE SKIN OUTSIDE, OR INSIDE THE VAGINA?' — and then, if outside, exactly where, because perianal extension in a figure-of-eight is the diagnosis.
'HAVE YOU TRIED ANY CREAMS — AND DID THEY HELP?' A failed antifungal and a failed oestrogen cream exclude two diagnoses before you have examined anything.

To the examiner, by name: 'Do I see any suspicious lesion suggestive of malignancy, and is there any loss of the normal architecture?' · 'Can you describe its colour, its site and distribution, and its morphology?' · 'And can you describe the vaginal walls?'

The sentence that gets the cream used: 'I know it sounds strong, and people often worry about steroid creams thinning the skin. In this condition it is the opposite — using it properly protects the skin, and using too little is what causes damage.' and: 'We control it rather than cure it.'

Examiner challenges: 'Would hydrocortisone do?' → 'No — under-treatment is the usual error, and it is the untreated inflammation that scars the skin and carries the cancer risk.' · 'Do you need a biopsy?' → 'The diagnosis is clinical in a typical case; I would biopsy an atypical appearance, a failure to respond, or any suspicious lesion.' · 'How is she followed up?' → 'Clinical examination every six to twelve months, not routine repeat biopsies.' · 'She has vaginal erosions and mouth ulcers' → 'That is lichen planus rather than sclerosus — lichen sclerosus spares the vagina.'
pefe: THE FULL REQUEST: general appearance for cachexia AND RASHES ELSEWHERE — elbows, knees, scalp, wrists AND THE MOUTH, because rashes elsewhere reframe the whole case into psoriasis, eczema or lichen planus · TEMPERATURE for infection and secondary bacterial infection of excoriated skin · abdomen AND THE INGUINAL REGIONS FOR LYMPHADENOPATHY, the drainage field of the vulva · CONSENT AND CHAPERONE · THE THREE-LAYER INSPECTION (see findings) · the rash described by COLOUR, SITE AND DISTRIBUTION, AND MORPHOLOGY · speculum for the cervix AND THE VAGINAL WALLS · bimanual, swabs, and a URINE DIPSTICK INCLUDING GLUCOSE.

THE FINDINGS IN VERSION 3: no cachexia, NO RASHES ELSEWHERE AND MOUTH NORMAL · afebrile · abdomen normal, NO INGUINAL LYMPHADENOPATHY · WHITE, SHINY, WRINKLED PLAQUE IN A FIGURE-OF-EIGHT AROUND THE VULVA EXTENDING TO PERIANAL SKIN, with fissuring and a few purpuric areas and PARTIAL RESORPTION OF THE LABIA MINORA · NO ULCER AND NO SUSPICIOUS LESION, but only said if asked specifically · CERVIX AND VAGINAL WALLS NORMAL, which is what separates it from lichen planus · bimanual normal, dipstick negative.

Role-player: BEVERLEY NASH, 60. Six months of constant worsening itch ON THE SKIN OUTSIDE, extending back towards the anus, WAKING HER AT NIGHT. Rash PALE, ALMOST WHITE, SHINY AND CRINKLED. Skin splits sometimes with a little bleeding but heals; no lump, no ulcer. SEX HAS BECOME PAINFUL so they have stopped. TWO DOCTORS HAVE ALREADY TREATED HER — oestrogen cream for 'dryness from the change', no difference; antifungal for thrush, no difference. GRAVES DISEASE treated for years. No atopy, no new products, no incontinence, no discharge or dryness inside, no urinary symptoms, no bleeding since menopause eight years ago, screening and mammogram up to date.

HOW TO PLAY IT AND WHAT TO WITHHOLD: IF ASKED SIMPLY 'IS THERE A RASH?', ANSWER ONLY 'YES' — give the colour, distribution and morphology ONLY IF ASKED FOR THEM SPECIFICALLY, and the same for the absence of a suspicious lesion. Her questions: 'WHY DO YOU THINK THAT, WHEN TWO OTHER DOCTORS DID NOT?' · 'IS IT SERIOUS?' · 'SO WHAT IS THE TREATMENT?' · 'A STRONG STEROID? ON SKIN LIKE THAT? I THOUGHT STEROIDS THINNED THE SKIN.' · 'ANYTHING ELSE?'. The organising question — 'Can you describe what you mean — IS THE ITCH ON THE SKIN OUTSIDE, OR DOES IT FEEL LIKE IRRITATION INSIDE THE VAGINA? And if it is outside, whereabouts — near the opening, on the lips, in the groin, around the back passage?' INSIDE POINTS TO VAGINITIS. OUTSIDE POINTS TO DERMATITIS. That one answer halves your list and tells you which version you are in — and PERIANAL INVOLVEMENT IN A FIGURE-OF-EIGHT is characteristic of lichen sclerosus

The question that is the case design — 'Have you tried any creams — and did they help?' An antifungal that failed argues against candida; an oestrogen cream that failed argues against atrophy. In version 3 she has tried both, and that is the whole point of the stem

The red flags, asked before anything else — WEIGHT LOSS, APPETITE, TIREDNESS, AND LUMPS PARTICULARLY IN THE GROIN, because vulval carcinoma drains to the inguinal nodes · 'HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY LUMP, ULCER OR SORE THAT DOES NOT HEAL? ANY BLEEDING FROM THE SKIN?' — the question that finds a vulval cancer · AND ANY VAGINAL BLEEDING SINCE THE PERIODS STOPPED, which is never explained away by an itch. EVERYONE ASKS ABOUT THRUSH; ALMOST NOBODY ASKS ABOUT CANCER

Version 1 — candidiasis — 28-year-old, two weeks of itch, and a discharge that when characterised is WHITE, THICK, CHEESY, NON-SMELLY, NO BLOOD · urinary frequency but no dysuria · unremarkable sexual history · NO RASH. 'Most likely you have a vaginal infection, and from the characteristics of the discharge — thick, white, curd-like and without a smell — I think it is a fungal infection called thrush.' She asks 'IS IT AN INFECTION I HAVE CAUGHT?'

Version 2 — atrophic vaginitis — 60-year-old, THE ITCH IS FELT INSIDE RATHER THAN ON THE SKIN, WITH DRYNESS, likely dyspareunia and urinary symptoms if asked, NO RASH. THE FINDING IS HANDED OVER ONLY IF YOU ASK ABOUT THE VAGINAL WALLS: THIN, PALE AND DRY. Reasons: the site is internal, she reports dryness, and the walls are thin and pale. She asks 'IS THIS JUST OLD AGE?'

Lichen sclerosus versus lichen planus — CORRECTION — the lecture treats 'different versions of lichen' as one group. THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS: LICHEN SCLEROSUS SPARES THE VAGINA — vulval and perianal skin only · EROSIVE LICHEN PLANUS INVOLVES THE VAGINA, causing erosions, adhesions and a purulent discharge, AND OFTEN THE MOUTH, with lacy white striae on the buccal mucosa. Both carry squamous cell carcinoma risk and both are treated with potent topical steroids, but VAGINAL INVOLVEMENT PLUS ORAL LESIONS MEANS LICHEN PLANUS VERIFY

Why the AMC keeps setting it — BECAUSE UNTREATED, IT BECOMES CANCER. Nobody dies of eczema or contact dermatitis; lichen sclerosus scars the vulval skin and a proportion of women develop VULVAL SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA on that background VERIFY the quoted lifetime risk. That single fact drives the whole management answer: TREAT IT PROPERLY, AND WATCH IT FOR LIFE

Two things worth knowing — ADDED — LICHEN SCLEROSUS OCCURS IN PREPUBERTAL GIRLS, presenting with vulval itch, soreness, splitting and constipation, AND THE BRUISE-LIKE PURPURA IT CAUSES HAS BEEN MISTAKEN FOR INJURY — recognising the characteristic appearance matters diagnostically · AND NIGHT-TIME ITCH raises scabies and threadworm, which is worth one question when the pattern fits

Characterise the rash like a discharge — 'Is there a rash or redness? WHAT COLOUR? Where exactly? Any discharge from it? ANY ULCERS, BLISTERS, SPLITS OR CRACKS? And is it ITCHY OR PAINFUL?' COLOUR MATTERS MOST — most rashes are red; A PALE, WHITE, SHINY ONE IS LICHEN SCLEROSUS. Then atopy — eczema, asthma, hay fever · contact exposures — new soap, wash, wipes, pads, laundry powder, underwear, douching, AND URINE LEAKING ONTO THE SKIN · and AUTOIMMUNE HISTORY, because lichen sclerosus clusters with thyroid disease, vitiligo, coeliac disease and type 1 diabetes

Version 3 — lichen sclerosus, the worked case — 60-year-old, SIX MONTHS OF CONSTANT WORSENING ITCH ON THE SKIN OUTSIDE extending to the perianal area, WAKING HER AT NIGHT · rash PALE, ALMOST WHITE, SHINY AND CRINKLED · the skin SPLITS with a little bleeding but heals · SEX HAS BECOME PAINFUL · ANTIFUNGAL CREAM DID NOT HELP, OESTROGEN CREAM DID NOT HELP · PAST HISTORY OF GRAVES DISEASE, which is a planted clue

Version 4 — the one that turned into cancer — 72-year-old with TWO YEARS OF ITCH TREATED REPEATEDLY WITH CREAMS, and now a RAISED ULCERATED LESION ON THE LEFT LABIUM THAT BLEEDS, plus 5 kg WEIGHT LOSS and A LUMP IN THE GROIN → CANCER UNTIL BIOPSIED, urgent referral. This is the natural history of the untreated Version 3, and it is why the red flag block is asked in every vulval itch station

setting: The sentence the examiner is waiting for is 'This is mild croup — which is why…'. Grade the child out loud, then let the grade choose the drug. Naming prednisolone without grading is a guess, and it is marked as one. Ask for the observations in the first fifteen seconds, because the examiner is holding them and without a saturation you will choose a treatment with no severity behind it.
stem: Your general practice, regional South Australia. Noah Whitfield, 15 months, is brought in by his mother Kate, concerned about a cough that keeps coming back and now noisy breathing. Weight 10 kg. Vital signs and examination findings are available from the examiner on request.

findings: Barking cough confirmed on history, and the mother has a recording of it · SpO2 98% on room air · respiratory rate normal for age · temperature 37.9 · miserable but alert on his mother's lap · inspiratory stridor, louder when he cries · occasional widespread wheeze · no respiratory distress, no cyanosis · throat deliberately not examined
Read the card out loud and agree with the throat

'Saturations 98% on room air, respiratory rate normal for age, temperature 37.9, alert, no recession and no tracheal tug, and an inspiratory stridor louder when he cries. THE THROAT HAS DELIBERATELY NOT BEEN EXAMINED — I AGREE WITH THAT, BECAUSE EXAMINING THE THROAT OF A CHILD WITH STRIDOR RISKS WORSENING THE OBSTRUCTION. Putting behaviour, accessory muscle use, respiratory rate, saturation and stridor together, THIS IS MILD CROUP.' READING THE CARD SILENTLY CLAIMS NOTHING — every line on it is a mark you take only by saying it

back.dx: MILD CROUP — VIRAL LARYNGOTRACHEOBRONCHITIS — GRADED OUT LOUD BEFORE ANY DRUG IS NAMED. THE EXPLANATION, IN LAY WORDS: 'Kate, most likely Noah has a condition called CROUP. It is A VIRUS THAT SETTLES IN THE MAIN AIRWAY AND MAKES IT SWELL AND NARROW — and that narrow airway is what gives him the barking cough and the noise when he breathes in.' THEN TWO REASONS: 'First, THE SOUND OF HIS COUGH — that barking is very typical. Second, the noise he makes breathing in is a particular sound we call STRIDOR, and it tells me THE NARROWING IS HIGH UP, NOT DEEP IN THE LUNGS.' THEN THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH THE REASON IT IS UNLIKELY, IN ONE BREATH: 'a chest infection; whooping cough; asthma; something small caught in his airway; and a more serious infection of the flap at the top of the windpipe. His story and my examination do not fit any of those — HE IS NOT DROOLING, HE IS SWALLOWING FINE, HE IS FULLY IMMUNISED, AND THERE WAS NO CHOKING EPISODE.' TWO FAILURE MODES SIT HERE: reciting 'laryngotracheobronchitis with subglottic oedema' at a frightened parent, and listing differentials without saying why each is unlikely. THE ANTIBIOTIC REFUSAL, WHICH SHE WILL ASK FOR ONCE: 'No — and I know that can feel like we are not doing enough. ANTIBIOTICS WORK ON BACTERIA AND THIS IS A VIRUS, so they would not help him and can upset his tummy. THE STEROID IS THE THING THAT ACTUALLY WORKS HERE.' THE NUMBERS: PREDNISOLONE 1 mg/kg ORALLY, ONE SINGLE DOSE · dexamethasone equivalent 0.15 mg/kg orally as the hospital alternative · NEBULISED ADRENALINE 1:1000, 0.5 mL/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 5 mL, UNDILUTED, for severe disease, working in minutes and wearing off in about two hours so the child is observed · paracetamol 15 mg/kg four to six hourly to a maximum of four doses in 24 hours · ibuprofen 10 mg/kg six to eight hourly with food · OXYGEN ONLY BELOW SpO2 92%, AND ONLY IF IT DOES NOT DISTRESS HIM · croup runs 6 MONTHS TO 6 YEARS with a peak at 1 to 3, lasts 3 TO 5 DAYS and is WORSE AT NIGHT · and the bronchiolitis and asthma cut-offs are both 12 MONTHS VERIFY all doses against current Therapeutic Guidelines and the local paediatric pathway. IF THE EXAMINER CHALLENGES THE STEROID DOSE: 'I would give a single dose of prednisolone 1 mg/kg, which is what Therapeutic Guidelines recommends and what most children need. In severe croup some hospital protocols use a larger first dose and a repeat the following evening BECAUSE CROUP RELAPSES OVERNIGHT — I would follow the local paediatric protocol, and in a severe child that decision would be made with the receiving team.' ONE MORE YOU MAY MEET: RECURRENT OR UNDER-SIX-MONTH STRIDOR — a 4-month-old with noisy breathing since birth, worse lying down and with feeding, thriving and afebrile, is LARYNGOMALACIA, not croup; reassure, monitor growth and refer to paediatric ENT. RECURRENT CROUP-LIKE EPISODES IN THE SAME CHILD warrant ENT review for subglottic stenosis or haemangioma. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: forty minutes from the hospital with a car available is what makes home observation reasonable here; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for paediatric retrieval and 000 for an emergency ambulance.
plan: WIPE, THEN ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS BEFORE ANY HISTORY: 'Before I start, could I please have his respiratory rate and oxygen saturation first, then temperature, heart rate and weight?' Then to the mother: 'I'll leave him on your lap where he's comfortable — I won't upset him.'

OPEN QUESTION, EMPATHY, AGENDA AND CONCERNS — 'Tell me what's been happening' · 'that sounds frightening, especially in the middle of the night' · signpost the shape of the consultation · AND 'IS THERE ANYTHING IN PARTICULAR YOU'RE WORRIED IT MIGHT BE?', which is where the asthma agenda arrives.

THE COUGH — when it started, worse at any time especially at night · THEN THE SOUND: barking like a dog or a seal, or wet and chesty · whooping at the end of a fit. LISTEN TO THE RECORDING AND NAME IT ALOUD.
THE NOISY BREATHING — ask her to describe it, then GIVE THE MENU, then in or out, then at rest or only when upset · then the brothers: working hard, ribs sucking in, blue around the lips.

THE SWEEP BY BUCKET, WITHOUT PAUSING — fever and what was given · runny nose · ears · DROOLING AND SWALLOWING · change in cry · rash and neck lumps · travel, sick contacts, childcare · CHOKING EPISODE · vomiting after coughing, diarrhoea · family atopy · smoking at home.

WELL-BABY — alert or drowsy, eating and drinking, WET NAPPIES, bowels · THEN BINDS: birth and special care, ever a breathing tube, IMMUNISATIONS, allergies, medicines, AND DISTANCE FROM HOSPITAL AND TRANSPORT.
ASK FOR THE CARD, READ IT ALOUD, AGREE THE THROAT SHOULD NOT BE EXAMINED, AND STATE THE GRADE (see findings). The grade is the hinge of the whole station.
THE DIAGNOSIS IN LAY WORDS WITH TWO REASONS — the barking cough, and stridor telling you the narrowing is high up.
THE DIFFERENTIALS WITH A REASON EACH, AND THE ASTHMA CONCERN ANSWERED EXPLICITLY — whistling out from deep in the chest versus stridor in from higher up, and no asthma label at fifteen months.
'BECAUSE THIS IS THE MILD FORM' — THEN THE FOUR BULLETS: prednisolone one single dose now · antipyretic · fluids in small frequent sips · keep him calm. NO ANTIBIOTICS, with the reason.
DISPOSITION — watch him here for twenty minutes after the steroid, then home; worse at night before it improves over three to five days.
The safety net with the word ambulance and four red flags, then a summary and 'Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?'

ask: The opening fifteen seconds: 'Before we start, could I have his respiratory rate and oxygen saturation?' — and 'I'll leave him on your lap where he's comfortable, I won't upset him.'

The question that makes the diagnosis: 'This may sound like an odd question, but what does the cough sound like — is it barking, like a dog or a seal?' and for the noise: 'Is it whistling, rattling, or a harsh crowing sound — and is it breathing in or out?'
THE TWO EXCLUSION QUESTIONS: 'IS HE DROOLING, OR HAVING ANY TROUBLE SWALLOWING?' AND 'HAS HE HAD ANY CHOKING EPISODE?' — then use both as relevant negatives in your presentation.

The three sentences that carry the station: 'The throat has deliberately not been examined — I agree with that, because examining the throat of a child with stridor can worsen the obstruction.' · 'Putting behaviour, accessory muscles, respiratory rate, saturation and stridor together, this is mild croup.' · 'Because this is the mild form, he needs a steroid called prednisolone — one single dose, not a course.'

EXAMINER CHALLENGES: 'Why not examine the throat?' → risk of precipitating complete obstruction · 'She reports a wheeze, is it asthma?' → 'STRIDOR OUTRANKS WHEEZE, AND CROUP IS LARYNGOTRACHEOBRONCHITIS — A WIDESPREAD WHEEZE DOES NOT UNSEAT IT.' · 'Justify the steroid dose' → the prednisolone answer in full (see dx) · 'He is drowsy with stridor at rest and sats of 90' → 'SEVERE CROUP — NEBULISED ADRENALINE AND A STEROID NOW, OXYGEN IF TOLERATED, AMBULANCE, AND I TREAT HIM HERE WHILE WE WAIT RATHER THAN SIMPLY REFERRING.'
pefe: ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS FIRST AND THE CARD SECOND. THE FINDINGS: respiratory rate 30, SATURATION 98% ON ROOM AIR, temperature 37.9, heart rate 130, weight 10 kg · alert and miserable on his mother's lap · NO RECESSION AND NO TRACHEAL TUG · INSPIRATORY STRIDOR LOUDER WHEN HE CRIES · occasional widespread wheeze · NO CYANOSIS · THROAT DELIBERATELY NOT EXAMINED. DO NOT ASK TO EXAMINE THE THROAT — IT IS A SINGLE-ITEM AUTOMATIC FAIL.

Role-player: KATE WHITFIELD, 34, a teacher in a regional town FORTY MINUTES FROM THE NEAREST HOSPITAL, with a car. Noah is 15 months, her first child, born at term, no special care, never a breathing tube, FULLY IMMUNISED, no allergies or medicines, at childcare three days a week. Two days of runny nose, then at 2 am a harsh cough and noise on breathing in. Temperature 38 last night, Panadol helped. GRIZZLY BUT WATCHING EVERYTHING, off his food but drinking, NAPPIES NORMAL. Dad had eczema; dad smokes but outside.

HOW TO PLAY IT: VOLUNTEER NOTHING — answer only what is asked, two sentences to an open question then stop. THE PHONE RECORDING IS PRODUCED ONLY IF THE DOCTOR ASKS WHAT THE COUGH SOUNDS LIKE. HER HIDDEN AGENDA IS HER SISTER'S ASTHMA CLAIM, RAISED ONLY IF ASKED WHAT SHE IS WORRIED ABOUT — otherwise she raises it at the end of the explanation. Push once at three minutes with 'DOCTOR, IS THIS SERIOUS?', ask for antibiotics once during management, and IF THE DOCTOR REACHES TOWARDS NOAH'S MOUTH, PULL HIM AWAY. If they never safety-net, ask 'SO WHAT DO I DO IF HE GETS WORSE TONIGHT?' and mark that item as prompted.

THE 14-ITEM CHECKLIST: respiratory rate and saturation asked BEFORE choosing treatment · ASKED WHAT THE COUGH SOUNDS LIKE and elicited barking · asked her to describe the noise AND GAVE A MENU · established the noise is on breathing IN and only when upset · ASKED ABOUT DROOLING AND SWALLOWING · ASKED ABOUT A CHOKING EPISODE · asked about immunisation · well-baby: behaviour, drinking, WET NAPPIES · READ THE CARD ALOUD AND AGREED THE THROAT SHOULD NOT BE EXAMINED · SAID 'THIS IS MILD CROUP' OUT LOUD · explained croup in lay words with two reasons · differentials each with a reason, and the asthma concern answered · MANAGEMENT TIED TO THE GRADE: prednisolone single dose, fluids, antipyretic, calm, no antibiotics · SAFETY NET WITH RED FLAGS AND THE WORD AMBULANCE, PLUS REVIEW. AUTOMATIC FAIL: asking to examine the throat · choosing treatment without ever obtaining severity · ignoring drooling in the harder version · sending the child home with no red flags · prescribing antibiotics · saying 'refer to hospital' in the severe variant without treating first.

The question the station turns on — 'This may sound like an odd question, but WHAT DOES THE COUGH SOUND LIKE? Is it a harsh, BARKING cough — like a dog or a seal? Or a wet, chesty cough? Does he make a WHOOPING noise at the end of a coughing fit?' 'Tell me about the cough' gets you 'he has been coughing a lot'. AND SHE HAS A RECORDING ON HER PHONE, PRODUCED ONLY IF YOU ASK WHAT IT SOUNDS LIKE — listen to it and say out loud 'that is a barking cough'

Give her a menu for the noise — Lay parents cannot name a noise — she will say 'I don't know how to describe it, just noisy'. SO OFFER THE MENU: 'Is it a WHISTLING sound, a RATTLING sound, or a HARSH CROWING noise when he breathes in? Do you hear it BREATHING IN, OR OUT, OR BOTH? Is it there ALL THE TIME, OR ONLY WHEN HE IS UPSET?' Then the brothers: working hard, ribs sucking in, any blue around the lips

The two questions that are scored negatives — 'IS HE DROOLING, OR HAVING ANY TROUBLE SWALLOWING?' and 'HAS HE HAD ANY CHOKING EPISODE — anything small he might have put in his mouth?' These exclude EPIGLOTTITIS and an INHALED FOREIGN BODY, and their absence is a scored relevant negative in your presentation. Skipping them because 'it is obviously croup' is the trap

The rest of the sweep, run without pausing — Fever and whether measured, anything given · runny nose · pulling at ears · CHANGE IN CRY OR VOICE — his is husky · rash or neck lumps · travel · sick contacts and childcare · vomiting, and whether he vomits after a coughing fit · diarrhoea · FAMILY ASTHMA, ECZEMA OR HAY FEVER · and whether anyone smokes at home or in the car

The well-baby block and the background — Alert and active or unusually tired, floppy or drowsy · eating and drinking normally · ANY DROP IN WET NAPPIES · bowels · THEN: born at term, any special care, EVER NEEDED A BREATHING TUBE · IMMUNISATIONS UP TO DATE · allergies and regular medicines · AND HOW FAR FROM THE HOSPITAL, AND IS THERE A CAR TONIGHT — forty minutes out, which is what changes your disposition threshold in regional South Australia

The management, four bullets tied to the grade — 'BECAUSE THIS IS THE MILD FORM, here is the plan — four things. ONE, PREDNISOLONE, a steroid that brings the swelling down, ONE SINGLE DOSE HERE IN THE ROOM NOW, NOT A COURSE. TWO, paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and misery. THREE, FLUIDS — small sips as often as he will take them, and do not worry about food for a few days. FOUR, KEEP HIM CALM, because upset makes the breathing worse.' NO ANTIBIOTICS — it is a virus. Watch him for twenty minutes, then home

The safety net, which carries the most marks per second — 'It is usually WORSE AT NIGHT before it gets better, over THREE TO FIVE DAYS. CALL AN AMBULANCE ON TRIPLE ZERO if he is STRUGGLING TO BREATHE, if his LIPS OR FACE TURN BLUE, if he becomes DROWSY OR FLOPPY or you cannot wake him properly, or if he STOPS DRINKING OR HAS NO WET NAPPIES. Otherwise bring him back to me tomorrow.' Say it even if the bell is about to go

Variant — severe croup — Drowsy, leaning on mother, STRIDOR AT REST, tracheal tug and intercostal recession, SpO2 90%, not drinking. GRADE IT THEN ACT: NEBULISED ADRENALINE 1:1000, 0.5 mL/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 5 mL, UNDILUTED, driven with oxygen · CORTICOSTEROID AS WELL, not omitted because you gave adrenaline · oxygen if tolerated · emergency ambulance and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 in a regional setting. ADRENALINE WORKS IN MINUTES AND WEARS OFF IN ABOUT TWO HOURS, SO HE MUST BE OBSERVED. THE COMMONEST WAY THIS VARIANT IS FAILED IS 'THIS IS SEVERE, I WILL SEND HIM TO HOSPITAL' AND NOTHING ELSE

Variants — epiglottitis and foreign body — EPIGLOTTITIS: 4 years, NOT IMMUNISED, six hours of high fever, DROOLING, muffled voice, SITTING FORWARD, almost no cough, toxic → DO NOT EXAMINE THE THROAT, DO NOT LIE HIM FLAT, DO NOT CANNULATE; upright on the parent, oxygen only if tolerated, emergency ambulance, and alert the receiving anaesthetic and ENT teams so the airway is secured in theatre, with a third-generation cephalosporin AFTER the airway is safe · FOREIGN BODY: 2 years, completely well until this afternoon, sudden cough while eating peanuts, NO CORYZA AND NO FEVER → THE PRODROME IS THE DISCRIMINATOR, croup has two days of runny nose behind it and a foreign body has nothing; keep him calm and upright, no blind finger sweeps, urgent transfer for rigid bronchoscopy

The reported wheeze is deliberate misdirection — She says his chest sounds a bit whistly, and her sister has told her it sounds like ASTHMA. CROUP IS LARYNGOTRACHEOBRONCHITIS — A WIDESPREAD WHEEZE DOES NOT UNSEAT IT, AND STRIDOR OUTRANKS WHEEZE. The answer to the sister: 'ASTHMA MAKES A WHISTLING NOISE BREATHING OUT, FROM DEEP IN THE CHEST. NOAH'S NOISE IS BREATHING IN, FROM HIGHER UP, AND IT COMES WITH A BARKING COUGH. We also would not put an asthma label on a child of fifteen months'
fails: ★ Asking to examine the throat of a child with stridor — a single-item automatic fail, and the card already tells you it was deliberately not examined
★ Choosing a treatment without ever obtaining the severity — ask for observations in the first fifteen seconds, and let the grade choose the drug
Reading the card silently instead of aloud, or never saying 'this is mild croup' — everything on that card is a mark you claim only by saying it
Never asking what the cough sounds like, or accepting 'just noisy' without offering a menu; and abandoning croup because a wheeze was reported, when stridor outranks wheeze
Skipping drooling and choking because it is obviously croup; prescribing antibiotics; and running out of time before the safety net, which carries the most marks per second in the station
numbers: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg oral, one single dose · dexamethasone equivalent 0.15 mg/kg oral · nebulised adrenaline 1:1000, 0.5 mL/kg, max 5 mL, undiluted — works in minutes, wears off in about 2 hours, so observe · paracetamol 15 mg/kg 4 to 6 hourly, max 4 doses in 24 h · ibuprofen 10 mg/kg 6 to 8 hourly with food · oxygen if SpO2 under 92% and only if not distressing · VERIFY all

Croup 6 months to 6 years, peak 1 to 3 · course 3 to 5 days, worse at night · bronchiolitis and asthma cut-off both 12 months · anaphylaxis adrenaline IM 10 micrograms/kg 1:1000 to the thigh · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · ambulance 000 · her case: SpO2 98%, temperature 37.9, weight 10 kg, 40 minutes from hospital

SAY — 'This may sound like an odd question, but WHAT DOES THE COUGH SOUND LIKE — is it barking, like a dog or a seal?' When she says 'just noisy', offer the menu: whistling, rattling or harsh crowing, in or out

setting: There are two ways to fail this station. Naming any medication — puffer, steroid, adrenaline, antibiotic. Or reaching the right diagnosis but never grading the severity out loud, so the ambulance looks unjustified. The findings are released only on specific request, so ask for the observations in the first twenty seconds and ask whether the wheeze is generalised or localised — because in the variant it is in the right middle zone only, and that is a foreign body.
stem: Your general practice, regional South Australia. A 4-month-old boy, Jack, is brought in by his mother with breathing difficulty. His birth was uneventful at term and his immunisations are up to date.

Tasks: take a focused history for 4 minutes — ask the examiner for relevant physical examination findings, and you will only be given what you ask for specifically — explain your diagnosis to the mother with your reasons, differentials not asked for — explain your management. 8 minutes.
tasks: Take a focused history for four minutes
Ask the examiner for relevant physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis to the mother with your reasons
Explain your management
time: Observations before you sit down, then the open question about her concern · then unpack the words 'Breathing difficulty' by offering three options · then the cough and the noise characterised · then the three key questions: recession, apnoea, cyanosis · then the differential sweep in one rapid pass · then the well-baby block, which is how you earn the word dehydrated · then the examination requested item by item, including generalised or localised · then the diagnosis with three reasons, five seconds of unasked differentials, the severity grade with four features, ambulance, oxygen, the three-step fluid ladder, the not-giving list, red flags and a summary.
findings: The examination findings, released only on specific request

SpO2 91% in room air · respiratory rate 62 · heart rate 160 · afebrile · alert but tired and miserable · mild to moderate respiratory distress with subcostal recession · not cyanosed · dehydrated, capillary refill just over 2 seconds · no apnoea observed · generalised expiratory wheeze in all zones with fine inspiratory crackles · heart sounds dual, no murmur, femorals present

back.dx: SEVERE BRONCHIOLITIS IN A 4-MONTH-OLD — A VIRAL LOWER RESPIRATORY INFECTION NARROWING THE SMALLEST AIRWAYS, GRADED OUT LOUD AND MANAGED WITH NO MEDICATIONS AT ALL. THE STATION HAS TWO SINGLE-ITEM FAILURES AND BOTH ARE AVOIDABLE: NAMING ANY DRUG, AND REACHING THE DIAGNOSIS WITHOUT GRADING THE SEVERITY SO THAT THE AMBULANCE LOOKS UNJUSTIFIED. THE SHAPE OF THE ANSWER: DIAGNOSIS WITH THREE REASONS → five seconds of unasked differentials → SEVERITY WITH FOUR FEATURES → ambulance and emergency department → oxygen → THE THREE-STEP FLUID LADDER → THE NOT-GIVING LIST WITH REASONS → red flags → summary and questions (all scripted in the findings panel). WHAT THE HOSPITAL WILL ACTUALLY DO, EXPLAINED SIMPLY: monitor his breathing and oxygen closely; oxygen by mask or prongs; and fluid in steps — oral first, then nasogastric, then intravenous only if that is not enough. 'THAT IS REALLY ALL HE NEEDS.' HOLDING THE LINE WHEN SHE PUSHES: 'I believe you, and I understand why that makes antibiotics sound like the answer. BABIES WITH THIS ILLNESS GET BETTER IN THAT SORT OF TIMEFRAME ANYWAY, which is often why it looks as though the antibiotic worked. Here, antibiotics would not touch the virus and they carry side effects such as diarrhoea and rash. What will actually help him is oxygen and fluid, and that is what we are going to do. IF ANYTHING CHANGES AND I THINK A BACTERIAL INFECTION HAS DEVELOPED ON TOP, I WILL TREAT IT STRAIGHT AWAY AND I WILL TELL YOU WHY.' THE LINES THAT RESCUE AN AWKWARD MOMENT: 'I can see this is a shock — let me explain why I am being careful.' · 'That is a very reasonable thought, and here is why I think differently.' · 'I would rather he was watched on the way than not.' · 'DOING NOTHING MEDICINE-WISE IS THE RIGHT TREATMENT HERE, AND I WILL EXPLAIN WHY THAT IS NOT THE SAME AS DOING NOTHING.' THE RED FLAGS, GIVEN EVEN THOUGH HE IS GOING BY AMBULANCE, BECAUSE THEY APPLY TO ANY FUTURE EPISODE OR A MILD CASE MANAGED AT HOME: worsening breathing · STOPPING BREATHING EVEN BRIEFLY · TURNING BLUE · TAKING LESS THAN HALF HIS FEEDS OR FEWER THAN HALF HIS USUAL WET NAPPIES · BECOMING DROWSY OR FLOPPY — that is an emergency, call an ambulance. THE NUMBERS: UNDER 12 MONTHS is the age that makes it bronchiolitis, PEAK 3 TO 6 MONTHS · KEEP SpO2 AT OR ABOVE 92%, with 90 TO 92% MODERATE and UNDER 90% SEVERE VERIFY the local threshold · his saturation is 91% · RESPIRATORY RATE 30 TO 60 IS NORMAL AT THIS AGE, OVER 60 SIGNIFICANT · CAPILLARY REFILL OVER 2 SECONDS IS DELAYED · FEEDS OR WET NAPPIES BELOW HALF OF USUAL IS A RED FLAG, AS IS FEWER THAN FOUR WET NAPPIES IN 24 HOURS · DAYS 3 TO 5 ARE THE PEAK AND THE COUGH MAY LAST 2 TO 4 WEEKS · nasogastric or intravenous fluid is TWO-THIRDS MAINTENANCE, ISOTONIC · UNDER 8 WEEKS, PREMATURITY OR COMORBIDITY MEANS A LOWER ADMISSION THRESHOLD · AND THE NUMBER OF INDICATED MEDICATIONS AND INVESTIGATIONS IS ZERO. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: she is 90 minutes from the nearest base hospital and her partner has the car, which is part of why the ambulance is the right call rather than a convenience; MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33 for paediatric retrieval, and in the apnoea variant speak with the retrieval service before he travels.
plan: WIPE AND SIT AT HER LEVEL, THEN ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — saturation, respiratory rate, temperature, heart rate and blood pressure. IF THE EXAMINER DECLINES, ASK AGAIN IN TASK 2.
SIGNPOST THE CONSULTATION, THEN THE OPEN QUESTION: 'WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST TODAY?' — and acknowledge the answer before moving on.
UNPACK 'BREATHING DIFFICULTY' WITH THREE OPTIONS (see findings) — struggling, noisy, or mostly coughing.

THE COUGH AND THE NOISE — when it started and whether it is worsening, dry or wet, vomiting or gasping after coughing, worse at night or with feeds · AND IS THE NOISE A WHISTLE, A RATTLE, OR HARSH ON BREATHING IN.
THE THREE KEY QUESTIONS — RECESSION around the neck, ribs or tummy · APNOEA, even for a few seconds, how long and how many times · CYANOSIS of lips, tongue or skin.

THE DIFFERENTIAL SWEEP IN ONE PASS — fever and whether measured · runny nose, ear pulling, drooling, trouble swallowing feeds · change in cry · rash or neck lumps · vomiting or diarrhoea · SICK CONTACTS ESPECIALLY A LONG COUGH · travel · CHOKING OR GAGGING · any new food or medicine.
THE WELL-BABY BLOCK — alert or drowsy · WHAT PROPORTION OF FEEDS · HOW MANY WET NAPPIES COMPARED WITH NORMAL · then prematurity, heart or lung problems, and IMMUNISATIONS.

THE EXAMINATION REQUESTED ITEM BY ITEM — vitals · general: alert or drowsy, distress, cyanosis, HYDRATION, CAPILLARY REFILL, APNOEIC EPISODES · respiratory: nasal flaring, tracheal tug, recession, grunting, expansion, tracheal position, percussion, air entry and added sounds, AND WHETHER ANY WHEEZE IS GENERALISED OR LOCALISED · cardiovascular: heart sounds, murmurs, femoral pulses.
Turn fully to the mother and give the diagnosis with three reasons, then the asthma answer if she raises it, then five seconds of differentials (see findings).
THE SEVERITY GRADE WITH ITS FOUR FEATURES — low oxygen, visible work of breathing, dehydration, and being tired and not himself.
Ambulance and emergency department, said plainly — then pause when she reacts and acknowledge it before continuing. Then oxygen, and the three-step fluid ladder.
THE NOT-GIVING LIST WITH A REASON FOR EACH ITEM — no antibiotics, no puffers, no steroids or adrenaline, no X-rays or blood tests.
RED FLAGS, THEN THE SUMMARY: diagnosis, why it is severe, where he is going and how, what they will do, and that no medicines are needed. 'Is there anything I have not covered?'
back.planNote: the stem gives four minutes of history within eight minutes, and the not-giving list and red flags have to survive the clock
ask: The opening twenty seconds: 'Before we start, could I please have his oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, temperature, heart rate and blood pressure?' Followed by 'What is worrying you most today?'

The three key questions, asked as a set: 'Any pulling in around his neck, ribs or tummy when he breathes?' · 'Has he ever stopped breathing, even for a few seconds?' · 'Has he turned blue at any time?'
THE WORDS THAT CATCH THE VARIANT: 'AND IS ANY WHEEZE GENERALISED OR LOCALISED?' — asked in the examination request itself, not as an afterthought.

The grade, said out loud: 'This is a severe bronchiolitis, and I am saying severe for four reasons: his oxygen is low at 91 per cent, he is visibly working hard to breathe, he is dehydrated, and he is tired and not himself.'

Examiner challenges: 'The mother wants a puffer' → 'Babies this age do not have the airway muscle for a puffer to work on, and we do not diagnose asthma under twelve months.' · 'Would you x-ray him?' → 'No — it would not change what we do.' · 'The wheeze is in the right middle zone only' → 'That is a localised finding and suggests an inhaled foreign body — urgent hospital, expiratory film and bronchoscopy, nothing by mouth, and a normal x-ray would not settle it.' · 'He is 6 weeks old, born at 34 weeks, with two brief apnoeas and sats of 94' → 'Admit whatever the saturation — apnoea, age under 8 weeks and prematurity each independently mean admission.'
pefe: REQUEST IT IN FULL AND BY NAME, BECAUSE YOU ARE GIVEN ONLY WHAT YOU ASK FOR: vitals — SATURATION IN ROOM AIR, respiratory rate, heart rate, temperature, blood pressure · general — alert or drowsy, respiratory distress, central cyanosis, DEHYDRATION, CAPILLARY REFILL TIME, AND ANY APNOEIC EPISODES · respiratory — nasal flaring, tracheal tug, intercostal, subcostal or sternal recession, grunting, chest expansion, tracheal position, percussion, air entry and added sounds, AND WHETHER ANY WHEEZE IS GENERALISED OR LOCALISED · cardiovascular — heart sounds, murmurs and femoral pulses.

Role-player: SARAH, 29, mother of JACK, 4 months, in a regional town ABOUT 90 MINUTES FROM THE NEAREST BASE HOSPITAL, with her partner at work and the car. A 3-year-old daughter started day care two weeks ago and has a cold. Jack: born at term, no medical problems, BREASTFED ONLY, immunisations complete, no allergies, nobody smokes. THREE DAYS OF RUNNY NOSE, dry cough since yesterday and worse today, WHISTLING NOISE WORSE AT NIGHT AND WITH FEEDS, TUMMY SUCKING IN, ABOUT HALF HIS USUAL FEEDS, TWO WET NAPPIES SINCE THIS MORNING INSTEAD OF FIVE OR SIX, sleepy and grizzly, temperature 37.8 last night.

HOW TO PLAY IT: GIVE ONLY WHAT IS ASKED — do not volunteer the wet nappies, the recession or the reduced feeding. HER HIDDEN AGENDA IS HER SISTER'S ASTHMA CLAIM AND A BELIEF THAT ANTIBIOTICS FIX CHEST INFECTIONS; SHE WILL PUSH TWICE FOR A PUFFER OR ANTIBIOTICS once treatment is mentioned and will accept only a clear reason. BECOME EMOTIONAL AT THE WORD AMBULANCE, and settle if the doctor pauses and acknowledges it. If nothing has been asked about her concerns by six minutes, volunteer the asthma agenda.

SCORING — 25 ITEMS, 20 OR MORE WITH NO AUTOMATIC FAIL IS A COMFORTABLE PASS: hands and introduction · SATURATION AND RESPIRATORY RATE ASKED · open question about her concern · 'BREATHING DIFFICULTY' CLARIFIED · cough and noise characterised · RECESSION · APNOEA · CYANOSIS · fever · sick contacts · choking · new food or medicine · alertness, feeding, WET NAPPIES · immunisation · GENERALISED OR LOCALISED WHEEZE · bronchiolitis named · THREE REASONS · SEVERITY GRADE WITH FOUR FEATURES · ambulance and emergency department · oxygen explained · THREE-STEP FLUID LADDER · NOT-GIVING LIST · red flags · summary and questions invited · plain language throughout. AUTOMATIC FAIL: prescribing or promising salbutamol, steroids, adrenaline or antibiotics · diagnosing asthma or croup · sending this child home · giving no safety net at all.

The three key questions — 'Have you noticed ANY PULLING IN AROUND HIS NECK, BETWEEN HIS RIBS OR UNDER HIS TUMMY when he breathes?' · 'HAS HE EVER STOPPED BREATHING, EVEN FOR A FEW SECONDS — how long, and how many times?' · 'HAS HE EVER TURNED BLUE — lips, tongue or skin?' OMITTING APNOEA IS THE TRAP: the role-player may be briefed to disclose an apnoeic episode ONLY ON DIRECT QUESTIONING, and it changes the disposition

Wheeze under twelve months is not asthma — Hearing 'wheeze' and jumping to asthma is the commonest error. UNDER 12 MONTHS THIS IS BRONCHIOLITIS UNTIL THE WHEEZE TURNS OUT TO BE LOCALISED. The answer to the sister: 'A very reasonable thought, because the noise sounds similar. BUT WE DO NOT DIAGNOSE ASTHMA UNDER TWELVE MONTHS — at his age this pattern is bronchiolitis'

The well-baby block is how you earn the word dehydrated — 'Is he ALERT AND ACTIVE as usual, or tired and drowsy? Is he FEEDING AND DRINKING as usual — roughly what proportion? HOW MANY WET NAPPIES in the last day compared with normal?' → SLEEPY AND GRIZZLY, ABOUT HALF HIS FEEDS, TWO WET NAPPIES SINCE THIS MORNING INSTEAD OF FIVE OR SIX. Without this block you cannot say he is dehydrated, and dehydration is one of the four features that make this severe

The diagnosis with three reasons — 'Most likely Jack has a condition called BRONCHIOLITIS. It is a viral chest infection that causes SWELLING AND NARROWING OF THE SMALLEST BREATHING TUBES in the lungs, which is why the air makes a whistling noise on its way through and why he is working harder to breathe. I am saying this for THREE REASONS: THE COUGH he has had, THE NOISY BREATHING THROUGHOUT BOTH HIS LUNGS, and the fact that this condition happens specifically IN BABIES UNDER TWELVE MONTHS'

Five seconds of differentials, unasked — Differentials are not a task, but add them briefly anyway: 'I did also think about SOMETHING BEING BREATHED IN, a PNEUMONIA, WHOOPING COUGH and a SEVERE ALLERGY — but the noise is throughout both lungs, he has no fever or coughing fits, he is fully immunised, and there was no choking or new food'

The severity grade with four features — 'This is a SEVERE bronchiolitis, and I am saying severe for FOUR REASONS: his OXYGEN LEVEL IS LOW AT 91 PER CENT, he has VISIBLE DIFFICULTY BREATHING, he is DEHYDRATED and has lost fluid, and he is TIRED AND MISERABLE rather than his usual self.' Without this the ambulance looks unjustified, and that is one of the two ways to fail

Disposition and the three-step fluid ladder — 'He needs to go to the emergency department NOW, and I want him taken BY AMBULANCE rather than in the car, so he is MONITORED ON THE WAY. You will go with him.' PAUSE AND ACKNOWLEDGE WHEN SHE REACTS. Then: oxygen through a mask or prongs because his level is low, and FLUID IN STEPS — FIRST BY MOUTH, THEN A FINE NASOGASTRIC TUBE IF HE CANNOT FEED, AND ONLY THEN A DRIP IN A VEIN

The not-giving list, with reasons — 'I want to be clear about what we will NOT give, so it does not look as though something is being missed. NO ANTIBIOTICS — this is a virus. NO PUFFERS — babies this age do not have the muscle in their airways for a puffer to work on. NO STEROIDS AND NO ADRENALINE — those are for a different condition called croup. AND NO X-RAYS OR BLOOD TESTS, because they would not change anything we do. THIS ILLNESS GETS BETTER ON ITS OWN; our job is to support his oxygen and his fluids while it does.' SHE WILL PUSH TWICE — agreeing even as a 'trial' is a single-item fail

The four variants — LOCALISED WHEEZE → foreign body: ask about a sudden cough or gag, then urgent hospital for expiratory-phase chest X-ray and bronchoscopy, NOTHING BY MOUTH, AND A NORMAL FILM DOES NOT SETTLE IT · MILD, SpO2 96% and feeding → home with red flags and oral rehydration solution, warning that DAYS THREE TO FIVE ARE WORST and cough lasts 2 TO 4 WEEKS, reviewed in 24 to 48 hours · APNOEA IN A 6-WEEK-OLD BORN AT 34 WEEKS → ADMIT WHATEVER THE SATURATION, because apnoea, age under 8 weeks and prematurity each independently mean admission · AND THE MOTHER WHO INSISTS ON ANTIBIOTICS because her friend's baby got them

Unpack 'Breathing difficulty' by offering options — 'When you say breathing difficulty, DO YOU MEAN HE IS STRUGGLING TO BREATHE, OR THAT HE IS MAKING A NOISE WHEN HE BREATHES, OR IS IT MOSTLY COUGHING?' Accepting a vague symptom and building a history on it is the trap — THE OFFERED OPTIONS ARE WHAT TURN THIS INTO A RESPIRATORY PRESENTATION, and they have already answered your shortness-of-breath question

Ask generalised or localised, every time — Asking 'is there a wheeze?' and stopping there is the trap. IN THE VARIANT THE ANSWER IS YES — BUT ONLY IN THE RIGHT MIDDLE ZONE, WITH REDUCED AIR ENTRY ON THAT SIDE, AND THAT IS AN INHALED FOREIGN BODY. Use the words generalised or localised in the request itself

stem: GP registrar, general practice, regional South Australia. Liam Whitfield, 6 years, brought by his mother Kate. Coughing for five weeks, seen twice already — told 'A virus' at week one and given amoxicillin at week two, with no improvement. T 36.8 · HR 92 · RR 20 · SpO2 99% RA · weight 21 kg on the 50th centile · nkda · no regular medications.

findings: The normal examination is the bait

Growth on the 50th centile, afebrile, saturations 99%, ENT normal, RESPIRATORY EXAMINATION NORMAL, cardiovascular normal, no lymphadenopathy, NO SUBCONJUNCTIVAL HAEMORRHAGES, and he did not cough during the consultation. DO NOT SAY 'IN THAT CASE IT IS PROBABLY JUST A POST-VIRAL COUGH'. SAY: 'A NORMAL EXAMINATION IS WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IN PERTUSSIS — CHILDREN ARE TYPICALLY WELL BETWEEN PAROXYSMS — SO IT DOES NOT CHANGE MY DIAGNOSIS'

back.dx: PERTUSSIS — WHOOPING COUGH — IN A FULLY VACCINATED SIX-YEAR-OLD, DIAGNOSED CLINICALLY FROM THE STORY DESPITE A NORMAL EXAMINATION AND TWO FAILED COURSES OF AMOXICILLIN. NAME IT IN PLAIN WORDS AND WARN FIRST: 'Kate, I think I know what this is, and I do not think it is asthma or anything sinister. I think Liam has an infection called WHOOPING COUGH — the medical name is PERTUSSIS.' THEN GIVE HER YOUR REASONING BACK, THREE THINGS: 'THE LENGTH — five weeks, when an ordinary cough is settling by two. THE FITS OF COUGHING with him being completely well in between. AND MOST OF ALL, THE VOMITING AT THE END OF A COUGHING SPELL — that is really characteristic.' THEN ANSWER THE TWO QUESTIONS SHE HAS NOT ASKED YET — the clear chest and the failed antibiotic (see findings) — AND THE TWO SHE WILL: the vaccine and the missing whoop. THE PLAN, SAID PLAINLY: A NASOPHARYNGEAL SWAB FOR PCR, THOUGH AFTER FIVE WEEKS IT IS OFTEN NEGATIVE AND WILL NOT CHANGE WHAT YOU DO — PCR IS USEFUL IN THE FIRST TWO TO THREE WEEKS AND SEROLOGY BEYOND THAT · A MACROLIDE, NOT AMOXICILLIN: AZITHROMYCIN 10 mg/kg DAILY FOR 5 DAYS IN INFANTS UNDER SIX MONTHS, OR 10 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 500 mg ON DAY 1 THEN 5 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 250 mg FOR FOUR DAYS AT SIX MONTHS AND OVER; CLARITHROMYCIN 7.5 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 500 mg TWICE DAILY FOR 7 DAYS FROM ONE MONTH; trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole 4+20 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days from two months as the alternative VERIFY against current Therapeutic Guidelines · SCHOOL EXCLUSION UNTIL FIVE DAYS OF ANTIBIOTIC, OR 21 DAYS FROM COUGH ONSET, WHICHEVER IS SOONER · NOTIFICATION TO PUBLIC HEALTH, framed as routine and as how babies are protected · AND THE HOUSEHOLD: THE FATHER NEEDS SEEING AND TREATING, AND BECAUSE THE SISTER HAS A THREE-MONTH-OLD, HER FAMILY SHOULD SEE THEIR GP ABOUT PREVENTIVE ANTIBIOTICS BEFORE THE NEXT VISIT. PROPHYLAX THE WHOLE HOUSEHOLD IF ANY INFANT UNDER SIX MONTHS LIVES THERE, AND ALSO COVER THIRD-TRIMESTER PREGNANCY AND CHILDCARE OR HEALTH WORKERS CARING FOR INFANTS, WITHIN 14 DAYS OF EXPOSURE. THE SAFETY NET: return or go to the emergency department if Liam STRUGGLES TO BREATHE, GOES BLUE, STOPS BREATHING, CANNOT KEEP FLUIDS DOWN, OR DEVELOPS A FEVER. THEN THE TEACH-BACK, WHICH CLOSES THE STATION: 'That was a lot. WHAT WILL YOU TELL LIAM'S DAD TONIGHT ABOUT WHAT HE HAS GOT AND WHAT HE NEEDS TO DO?' THE NATURAL HISTORY WORTH CARRYING: incubation 7 TO 10 DAYS, range 4 to 21 · a CATARRHAL PHASE OF 1 TO 2 WEEKS WHICH IS THE MOST INFECTIOUS · a PAROXYSMAL PHASE OF 2 TO 6 WEEKS · then convalescence over weeks to months · INFECTIOUS FOR 21 DAYS FROM COUGH ONSET OR UNTIL 5 DAYS OF ANTIBIOTIC · anything over FOUR WEEKS is a chronic cough in a child and always needs an explanation · a WHITE CELL COUNT OVER 50 × 10⁹/L IN AN INFANT MEANS SEVERE DISEASE · and the vaccine schedule is DTPa AT 2, 4, 6, 18 MONTHS AND 4 YEARS, dTpa IN YEAR 7, AND dTpa AT 20 TO 32 WEEKS OF EVERY PREGNANCY, with immunity waning over 6 to 10 years. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: notifiable to SA Health, SA CDCB 1300 232 272, and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for infant retrieval.
plan: WIPE, GREET THE CHILD, AND NAME THE FRUSTRATION WITHOUT DEFENDING THE PRACTICE — this is her third visit for the same cough. Signpost the consultation, then 'BEFORE I START, WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST?'
OPEN AND LET HER TALK FOR THIRTY SECONDS — 'take me back to the very start, how did it begin and how has it changed?' Hear the coryzal prodrome and the class flu WITHOUT closing on post-viral cough.
Characterise the paroxysms — odd coughs or long runs where he cannot get a breath in · worse at night.
THE DISCRIMINATING QUESTION IN FULL, AND RE-ASK IT IF YOU GET A NO (see findings). This is the pivot of the entire station.
WHOOP, APNOEA, COLOUR CHANGE AND THE WELL INTERVAL — and do not let a missing whoop unseat the diagnosis.
THE FOUR-QUESTION SWEEP, ONE BREATH EACH — CHOKING EPISODE · wheeze, exercise and cold air triggers, family atopy · fevers, weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis · travel and TB contact.

CONTACTS AND HOUSEHOLD — anyone else coughing at home or school · IMMUNISATION STATUS · AND WHO ELSE LIVES IN THE HOUSE, ANY BABIES, ANYONE PREGNANT. This is where the father's cough and the sister's three-month-old live.
IMPACT AND ICE — school, sleep, work, AND 'WHAT WERE YOU WORRIED IT MIGHT BE?' Close the history here.

THE STRUCTURED EXAMINATION REQUEST — appearance and growth, full vitals with saturations, complete respiratory examination looking for wheeze, crackles or asymmetry, ENT, cardiovascular, lymph nodes, AND SPECIFICALLY SUBCONJUNCTIVAL HAEMORRHAGES OR FACIAL PETECHIAE AND WHETHER HE COUGHED DURING THE CONSULTATION.
Say that a normal examination is expected in pertussis and does not move you off the diagnosis — do not take the bait.
WARN, THEN NAME IT, THEN GIVE THE THREE REASONS BACK (see dx). Lead with 'I do not think this is asthma or anything sinister'.
Pre-empt the clear chest and the failed amoxicillin, and answer the vaccine and whoop challenges without dismissing her.
The differentials in plain English with a reason each, finishing by naming her fear of asthma explicitly.
THE PLAN — swab, MACROLIDE, five days off school, NOTIFICATION with its reason, THE FATHER AND THE SISTER'S BABY — then the honest six-to-ten-week timeline, the safety net, and the TEACH-BACK.

ask: The question the station turns on, asked in full: 'When he has one of those long coughing spells — does he ever vomit at the end of it? Bring up food, or thick stringy mucus?' and if you got a no to the generic version, 'Can I ask it a slightly different way, because it really matters…'
THE PUBLIC-HEALTH QUESTION: 'WHO ELSE LIVES IN THE HOUSE WITH YOU — ARE THERE ANY BABIES, OR IS ANYONE PREGNANT?' — plus 'is anybody else at home or at school coughing?' and the immunisation status.

'A normal examination is what I would expect — pertussis is a clinical diagnosis and children are well between paroxysms.' / 'Amoxicillin is a good antibiotic but it does not cover this bug — we need a macrolide.' / 'The cough can take another six to ten weeks — some call it the hundred-day cough.'

EXAMINER AND PARENT CHALLENGES: 'But he is vaccinated, and he does not whoop' → the vaccine and whoop answer in full (see findings) · 'So were the other doctors wrong?' → 'IN THE FIRST WEEK THIS LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE A COLD; IT IS ONLY THE PATTERN OF COUGHING SINCE THAT HAS MADE IT CLEAR.' · 'The chest X-ray is normal' → READ IT SYSTEMATICALLY, SAY IT IS NORMAL, AND SAY THAT A NORMAL FILM IS CONSISTENT BECAUSE PERTUSSIS DOES NOT SHOW ON X-RAY · 'Will the antibiotic fix the cough?' → 'IT MAINLY STOPS HIM PASSING IT ON.'

THE DRILLS: ask the post-tussive vomiting question cold, then re-ask it after a no · run the four-question safety sweep in 20 seconds · give the three reasons in 15 seconds · deliver the five differentials in plain English with a reason each in 45 seconds · state the exclusion rule and the prophylaxis rule in 20 seconds.
pefe: ASK FOR IT STRUCTURED AND IN FULL: general appearance and GROWTH PARAMETERS · full vitals INCLUDING SATURATIONS · a complete respiratory examination — work of breathing, chest shape, percussion, auscultation for WHEEZE, CRACKLES OR ASYMMETRY · ENT for nose, throat and eardrums · cardiovascular for murmurs · lymph nodes · AND SPECIFICALLY SUBCONJUNCTIVAL HAEMORRHAGES OR FACIAL PETECHIAE, AND WHETHER THE CHILD COUGHED DURING THE CONSULTATION. EVERYTHING COMES BACK NORMAL, AND THAT IS THE POINT.

Role-player: KATE WHITFIELD, 34, in a regional South Australian town, working part-time at the pharmacy. HUSBAND STEVE IS A SHEARER AND A SMOKER WITH A NAGGING COUGH FOR ABOUT FOUR WEEKS who refuses to see anyone. Liam is 6, otherwise healthy, FULLY IMMUNISED INCLUDING HIS FOUR-YEAR-OLD BOOSTERS. HER SISTER AMY LIVES TWENTY MINUTES AWAY WITH A THREE-MONTH-OLD DAUGHTER, VISITED MOST WEEKENDS. SHE WAS NOT VACCINATED AGAINST PERTUSSIS IN PREGNANCY and does not remember being offered it.

HOW TO PLAY IT: START FRUSTRATED AND SLIGHTLY COOL — this is the third visit — and soften if the doctor acknowledges how hard five weeks has been. BECOME TEARFUL ONCE, BRIEFLY, when asked about impact. BECOME DEFENSIVE IF THE DOCTOR IMPLIES SHE SHOULD HAVE COME SOONER. TO THE GENERIC 'DOES HE VOMIT?' ANSWER 'NO' AND SAY NOTHING MORE — DO NOT HELP. Her hidden agenda is a fear of asthma and an explanation for the failed antibiotics, raised herself at about six minutes if never asked. Challenge once after the diagnosis with 'BUT HE IS VACCINATED. AND HE DOES NOT WHOOP.'

SCORE THE CANDIDATE: WIPE, consent, spoke to the child · elicited her concern in the first minute · ASKED THE POST-TUSSIVE VOMITING QUESTION SPECIFICALLY · ASKED ABOUT A CHOKING EPISODE · asked whoop, apnoea and the well interval · screened asthma, TB and systemic red flags · ASKED WHO ELSE IS AT HOME AND ABOUT BABIES · asked immunisation status · requested a structured examination · SAID A NORMAL EXAMINATION IS EXPECTED IN PERTUSSIS · named the diagnosis in plain words · EXPLAINED WHY THE AMOXICILLIN FAILED · explained vaccine failure without dismissing her · gave differentials in plain English with reasons · NAMED A MACROLIDE, NOT AMOXICILLIN · mentioned NOTIFICATION AND SCHOOL EXCLUSION · ACTED ON THE FATHER AND THE BABY · honest about the six-to-ten-week timeline · safety-netted and used teach-back. AUTOMATIC FAIL: never asking about post-tussive vomiting · never asking about a choking episode · diagnosing post-viral cough and reassuring her home · prescribing amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate · never asking who else is in the household · saying the vaccine means he cannot have pertussis · inventing abnormal findings on a normal examination or film.

The discriminating question — do not shorten it — 'WHEN HE HAS ONE OF THOSE LONG COUGHING SPELLS — DOES HE EVER VOMIT AT THE END OF IT? BRING UP FOOD, OR THICK STRINGY MUCUS?' → 'Actually — yes. Twice. He coughed and coughed and then brought his dinner straight back up. I thought he had a tummy bug that night.' ASK THE GENERIC VERSION AND SHE SAYS NO AND STOPS. If you get a no, RE-ASK IMMEDIATELY with the specific wording

The prompt that earns it — 'Is it the odd cough here and there, or DOES HE GET LONG RUNS OF COUGHING ONE AFTER ANOTHER WHERE HE CANNOT GET A BREATH IN?' → ten or fifteen coughs in a row, BRIGHT RED IN THE FACE, then it stops and he is fine. WORSE AT NIGHT, waking the whole house

The coryzal prodrome is a decoy — It started five weeks ago LIKE A NORMAL COLD with a runny nose, and there was 'a flu going round his class'. Those are planted to make you close on POST-VIRAL COUGH — but A CATARRHAL PRODROME IS ALSO EXACTLY HOW PERTUSSIS STARTS. Do not close yet

Whoop, apnoea and the well interval — 'At the end of a spell, does he make a big gasping or whooping noise sucking air back in? Does he ever GO BLUE OR STOP BREATHING? And IN BETWEEN THE FITS, IS HE COMPLETELY HIS NORMAL SELF?' → a big gasp sometimes but she would not call it a whoop, never blue, and COMPLETELY FINE IN BETWEEN. THE CLASSIC WHOOP IS OFTEN ABSENT, PARTICULARLY IN VACCINATED AND OLDER CHILDREN — do not use 'no whoop' to exclude pertussis

The four-question safety sweep — ONE, at the time this started, WAS THERE ANY MOMENT WHERE HE SUDDENLY CHOKED OR SPLUTTERED on food or a small toy · TWO, any wheezing, cough worse with running or cold air, eczema, hay fever or asthma in the family · THREE, any FEVERS, WEIGHT LOSS, NIGHT SWEATS OR HAEMOPTYSIS · FOUR, overseas travel or TB contact. OMITTING THE CHOKING QUESTION IS A SINGLE-ITEM FAIL IN ANY PAEDIATRIC CHRONIC COUGH STATION, even when the answer is pertussis

The public-health questions she only answers if asked — 'Is anybody else at home or at school coughing? Is Liam up to date with all his immunisations? AND WHO ELSE LIVES IN THE HOUSE WITH YOU — ARE THERE ANY BABIES, OR IS ANYONE PREGNANT?' → HER HUSBAND HAS HAD A COUGH FOR A MONTH and blames his smoking · Liam is fully vaccinated including his four-year-old boosters · AND HER SISTER HAS A THREE-MONTH-OLD THEY VISIT MOST WEEKENDS. If you never ask, she never tells you, and half the sheet is gone

The two questions she is about to ask — pre-empt them — 'WHY IS HIS CHEST CLEAR? Because whooping cough does not show up when we listen, and IT DOES NOT SHOW UP ON X-RAY — we make the diagnosis from the story.' · 'WHY DID THE AMOXICILLIN NOT WORK? Because it is a good antibiotic but IT DOES NOT COVER THIS PARTICULAR BUG. The right ones are a different family called MACROLIDES'

The challenge — 'But he is vaccinated, and he does not whoop' — 'Both very fair points. THE WHOOP IS ACTUALLY UNCOMMON, especially in vaccinated and older children. And THE VACCINE DOES NOT STOP YOU CATCHING IT — what it does is stop you getting severely unwell, and its protection FADES OVER SEVERAL YEARS. So being vaccinated is exactly why he has the mild version rather than being in hospital'

The honest timeline, set now — 'The cough can take ANOTHER SIX TO TEN WEEKS to fully settle — some people call it THE HUNDRED-DAY COUGH. THE ANTIBIOTIC MAINLY STOPS HIM PASSING IT ON RATHER THAN STOPPING HIS COUGH QUICKLY.' Promising a quick cure brings her back angry in a week

The differentials, in plain English with a reason each — An ordinary lingering cough after a virus — POSSIBLE, BUT THOSE GET BETTER WEEK BY WEEK AND DO NOT MAKE YOU VOMIT · ASTHMA, which she is frightened of — no wheeze, no family history, not triggered by running or cold air, and a breathing test if you are wrong · SOMETHING STUCK IN HIS AIRWAY — starts suddenly with choking and the chest sounds different on one side · PNEUMONIA — no fever and a clear chest · TUBERCULOSIS — no weight loss, night sweats or contact. NAME HER FEAR EXPLICITLY, because that is a communication mark

The variants — THE NORMAL CHEST X-RAY RECALL — read the film systematically out loud and SAY IT IS NORMAL WITH CONVICTION; candidates invented pneumonia and hilar enlargement rather than report a normal film, and a normal X-ray is entirely consistent because PERTUSSIS DOES NOT SHOW ON X-RAY · THE VACCINATED CHILD WITH A 10-WEEK-OLD SIBLING — treat the whole household including the well, notify, and give the infant red flags: THEY OFTEN DO NOT COUGH OR WHOOP AT ALL, THEY JUST STOP BREATHING, GO PALE OR BLUE, OR GO OFF FEEDS · THE INFANT AS PATIENT — a 3-week-old with apnoeas needs HOSPITAL TODAY via MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, and prescribing and discharging is a single-item automatic fail
