back.dx: PERTUSSIS IN A FOUR-YEAR-OLD WITH A FOUR-MONTH-OLD BROTHER AT HOME — AND THE BABY, NOT ETHAN, IS WHAT THE STATION IS ABOUT. FOUR AUTOMATIC-FAIL CONDITIONS, ALL AVOIDABLE: NEVER IDENTIFYING THE FOUR-MONTH-OLD AS THE PERSON AT RISK OR NEVER OFFERING HIM PROTECTION · NOT OFFERING PROPHYLAXIS TO THE HOUSEHOLD, OR OFFERING IT ONLY TO THOSE WITH SYMPTOMS · NEVER ASKING WHETHER ANYONE ELSE LIVES AT HOME, SO THE GRANDMOTHER IS MISSED · AND STATING THAT TREATMENT WILL BE WITHHELD UNTIL THE TEST RESULT RETURNS. THE SHAPE OF THE ANSWER IS FIVE BOXES AND THEY ARE ALL SCRIPTED IN THE FINDINGS PANEL: TREAT · EXCLUDE · NOTIFY · CONTACTS · EDUCATE. THE PROPHYLAXIS RULE, WHICH IS CONDITIONAL RATHER THAN AUTOMATIC: TREAT THE WHOLE HOUSEHOLD IF AN INFANT UNDER SIX MONTHS OR A WOMAN IN HER LAST MONTH OF PREGNANCY LIVES THERE · TREAT AN INDIVIDUAL IF THEY ARE AN INFANT UNDER SIX MONTHS EXPOSED TO A CASE, IN THE LAST MONTH OF PREGNANCY, OR THEIR WORK BRINGS THEM INTO CONTACT WITH INFANTS UNDER SIX MONTHS · PROPHYLAXIS IS THE IDENTICAL DRUG, DOSE AND DURATION AS TREATMENT, GIVEN WITHIN 14 DAYS OF EXPOSURE. THE DOSES: AZITHROMYCIN 10 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 500 mg DAILY FOR 5 DAYS · CLARITHROMYCIN 7.5 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 500 mg TWICE DAILY FOR 7 DAYS · AND UNDER ONE MONTH OF AGE, AZITHROMYCIN AND NEVER ERYTHROMYCIN, BECAUSE OF PYLORIC STENOSIS VERIFY against current Therapeutic Guidelines. THE TESTING WINDOW: PCR IN THE FIRST 21 DAYS OF COUGH, SEROLOGY BEYOND THAT — and the recall picks exactly three weeks to put you on the boundary, so say why you are ruling the swab out rather than simply ordering it. EXCLUSION: UNTIL FIVE DAYS OF ANTIBIOTICS ARE COMPLETED, OR 21 DAYS FROM ONSET IF UNTREATED. PROGNOSIS: THE COUGH MAY PERSIST UP TO THREE MONTHS — THE HUNDRED-DAY COUGH. VACCINATION: dTpa FOR ADULTS NOT VACCINATED IN TEN YEARS, AND A MATERNAL DOSE IN EVERY PREGNANCY AT 20 TO 32 WEEKS, which is the single best way to protect a newborn. THE COMMUNICATION MOVES THAT CARRY THIS STATION: the opening two questions before any explanation · an empathy statement that names how hard the last few weeks have been · REASONS BEFORE THE LABEL · defending the previous GP with a clinical reason rather than a shrug · framing complications as the argument for what follows rather than as a list · giving notification a reason so it does not sound punitive — 'not at all, it is how we protect other people's babies, and one day it is how somebody else's notification protects yours' · being honest that the antibiotic will not stop the cough · asking about her antenatal dTpa and his father's booster rather than assuming · offering a written parent information sheet · and closing with a summary and a check of understanding. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: notifiable to SA Health; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for infant retrieval to the Women's and Children's Hospital; and in Whyalla the childcare centre contact and any exposed infants are traced by public health rather than from the consulting room.
plan: INTRODUCE, CONFIRM WHO SHE IS, AND ASK THE TWO OPENING QUESTIONS — 'what has happened so far?' and 'is there anything in particular you are worried about today?' THIS IS WHERE THE VACCINE QUESTION ARRIVES.

THE EMPATHY STATEMENT AND THE PROMISE — name the stressful few weeks, say you will make the best plan you can, AND SAY EXPLICITLY THAT YOU WILL COME BACK TO HER VACCINE QUESTION BECAUSE IT DESERVES A PROPER ANSWER.
FOUR REASONS, THEN THE LABEL — three weeks of cough, POST-TUSSIVE VOMITING, the whooping sound, and the father coughing. Then name pertussis AND whooping cough, and describe it in lay terms.
'So the other doctor got it wrong?' — defend the colleague with a clinical reason (see findings).
Investigations in three points — clinical diagnosis and treatment does not wait · PCR swab in the first three weeks · serology beyond, which is where Ethan now sits, with the reason.

COMPLICATIONS, DELIVERED AS THE ARGUMENT FOR THE PLAN — severe chest infection, apnoea, rarely seizures and brain injury; exhausting rather than dangerous at four, BUT LIFE-THREATENING UNDER SIX MONTHS.
BOX 1, TREAT — azithromycin daily for five days, started today, the right drug for this bug, AND HONEST THAT IT WILL NOT SWITCH THE COUGH OFF.
BOX 2, EXCLUDE — no childcare, school or contact with other children until five days of antibiotic are finished, and specifically away from pregnant women and infants under six months.
BOX 3, NOTIFY — with the reason attached, and reframed if she asks whether she is in trouble.

BOX 4, CONTACTS — the whole household treated, same drug, same dose, same five days, even though they are well · THEN 'IS THERE ANYONE ELSE LIVING AT HOME?' AND ADD THE GRANDMOTHER'S PRESCRIPTION WHEN SHE APPEARS.
Box 5, educate — red flags for Ethan, then the separate infant red flags including apnoea, colour change and poor feeding, said as an emergency rather than a phone call.
CHECK THE VACCINATIONS — her antenatal dTpa, and whether Dad has had one in the last ten years — AND THEN ANSWER THE VACCINE QUESTION IN FULL (see findings).
Offer a written information sheet, summarise all five boxes including the grandmother, and check understanding — 'Is there anything I have not covered?'
back.planNote: the stem gives eight minutes for two counselling tasks - the five boxes need the second half, so the reasons and investigations are delivered briskly
ask: The question the station is built around: 'Is there anyone else living at home? Grandparents, an aunt or uncle, anyone at all?' — the grandmother exists only if you ask.

The prophylaxis sentence: 'Everyone in the household gets treated — same antibiotic, same dose, same five days — even though you are well. We are not treating you because we think you are sick; we are doing it to stop the baby catching this.'

'The diagnosis is based on symptoms and signs — we do not wait for a test before we treat.' / 'It stops him being infectious, but it will not switch the cough off.' / 'Babies his age often do not whoop at all — watch for pauses in breathing, colour change, or not feeding.'

THE THREE PUSHES SHE IS BRIEFED TO MAKE: 'Are we in trouble?' when notification comes up → 'NOT AT ALL — IT IS HOW WE PROTECT OTHER PEOPLE'S BABIES, AND ONE DAY IT IS HOW SOMEBODY ELSE'S NOTIFICATION PROTECTS YOURS.' · 'Why do we all need antibiotics? None of us are sick' → the prophylaxis sentence in full. · 'So he got it wrong then?' about the previous GP → the catarrhal-phase defence, without doubling down.

THE DRILLS: run the five boxes from memory in 90 seconds · say the three investigation points in 30 seconds · answer the vaccine question in 30 seconds · state the conditional prophylaxis rule — household, individual, and the work-exposure trigger — in 30 seconds · then run the four variants and say who gets antibiotics in each.
pefe: THERE IS NO EXAMINATION TASK — the diagnosis is given in the stem and the eight minutes are counselling. WHAT REPLACES IT IS THE HOUSEHOLD ASSESSMENT: who lives at home, ages, anyone pregnant, anyone working with young infants, and everyone's vaccination status. TREAT THAT AS THE EXAMINATION AND ASK IT AS SYSTEMATICALLY.

Role-player: MARY MARSH, 33, in Whyalla, on maternity leave from a school administrative job. Household: her, husband DAN a fitter at the steelworks, ETHAN 4, BABY NOAH 4 MONTHS — AND HER MOTHER, WHO MOVED IN WHEN NOAH WAS BORN AND WHO SHE DOES NOT MENTION UNLESS ASKED. Ethan: runny nose three weeks ago, told it was a virus, now coughing fits and HAS VOMITED TWICE at the end of a bout, with a gasp at the end and completely well in between, NO FEVER. DAN STARTED COUGHING ABOUT A WEEK AGO. Ethan fully vaccinated; Noah has had his six-week and four-month vaccines and is WELL WITH NO COUGH; Ethan goes to kindergarten three mornings a week. SHE HAD dTpa IN PREGNANCY WITH NOAH; SHE DOES NOT KNOW ABOUT DAN.

HOW TO PLAY IT: tired, slightly frustrated and QUIETLY WORRIED SHE HAS DONE SOMETHING WRONG — not hostile, and warming noticeably once the vaccine question is answered properly. OPEN WITH THE VACCINE QUESTION when asked about concerns, and ASK IT AGAIN AT ABOUT MINUTE SEVEN if the doctor never returns to it. RELEASE THE GRANDMOTHER ONLY IF ASKED WHETHER ANYONE ELSE LIVES AT HOME — if they list 'you, your husband and the baby', DO NOT CORRECT THEM. Ask 'are we in trouble?' at notification, push once with 'why do we all need antibiotics? None of us are sick', and ask the prognosis by minute six if none has been given.

THE CHECKLIST: introduced and confirmed who she is · ASKED WHAT HAS HAPPENED SO FAR BEFORE EXPLAINING · asked about specific concerns · empathy statement · REASONS BEFORE THE LABEL, all four of them · named pertussis AND whooping cough · lay terms without jargon · DID NOT BLAME THE PREVIOUS GP · said the diagnosis is clinical and treatment does not wait · EXPLAINED PCR AND ITS THREE-WEEK LIMIT · EXPLAINED SEROLOGY BEYOND THREE WEEKS · complications with emphasis on young infants · BOX 1 macrolide named with a duration · said it will not stop the cough · BOX 2 exclusion until five days done, and away from pregnant women and infants · BOX 3 notification WITH A REASON · BOX 4 IDENTIFIED THE FOUR-MONTH-OLD AS AT RISK · OFFERED PROPHYLAXIS TO EVERY HOUSEHOLD MEMBER · ASKED WHETHER ANYONE ELSE LIVES AT HOME · same drug, dose and duration · BOX 5 red flags for Ethan · SEPARATE INFANT RED FLAGS INCLUDING APNOEA · asked about her antenatal vaccination · offered dTpa to adults unvaccinated in ten years · offered written information · ANSWERED THE VACCINE QUESTION FULLY · honest prognosis · summarised and checked understanding.

The opening a counselling station still needs — 'Before I explain anything — CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT HAS HAPPENED SO FAR? … AND IS THERE ANYTHING IN PARTICULAR YOU ARE WORRIED ABOUT TODAY?' → 'He has had ALL HIS VACCINATIONS, every one on time. SO WHY HAS HE STILL GOT THIS?' THAT IS THE SCRIPTED CONCERN, AND IT IS SEPARATELY MARKED. Acknowledge it, promise to return to it, and then actually return to it

Four reasons before the label — 'Let me tell you why I think what I think. FIRST, three weeks of coughing — this condition typically causes a long-lasting cough. SECOND, THE VOMITING AT THE END OF A COUGHING BOUT is very suggestive. THIRD, THE WHOOPING SOUND at the end of a run of coughs. AND FOURTH, HIS DAD IS COUGHING TOO — we usually find another family member with the same thing.' THE REASONING IS SEPARATELY MARKED FROM THE LABEL, so give it first

Defend the previous GP — 'So the other doctor got it wrong?' → 'NO — THAT WAS A COMPLETELY REASONABLE CALL AT THE TIME. IN THE FIRST WEEK WHOOPING COUGH LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE A COMMON COLD. It is only the pattern of coughing since then that has made it clear.' Criticising the colleague is a professionalism error and she will push if you seem defensive

Investigations — all three points, because the task asks for them — One, the diagnosis is clinical — based on symptoms and signs, we do not always need a test and we do not wait for one before starting treatment · two, in the first three weeks of coughing a nasopharyngeal swab for PCR looks for the bacterium itself · three, Ethan is at three weeks, and beyond that the bacterium is generally gone even though the cough continues, so the swab would probably be negative — so instead pertussis serology, a blood test looking for his body's response. Answering 'It is clinical' and stopping loses the task

Complications, framed as the argument for the plan — 'This condition can cause serious complications, PARTICULARLY IN VERY YOUNG BABIES. It can lead to a SEVERE CHEST INFECTION, to DIFFICULTY BREATHING AND PAUSES IN BREATHING, and rarely to SEIZURES AND PROBLEMS AFFECTING THE BRAIN. For Ethan at four it is mostly going to be exhausting and unpleasant rather than dangerous. BUT IN A BABY UNDER SIX MONTHS IT CAN BE LIFE-THREATENING — and that is exactly why I want to talk about your four-month-old.' Listing them abstractly wastes them; they exist to make the prophylaxis conversation obviously necessary

Box 1 — treat — AZITHROMYCIN ONCE A DAY FOR FIVE DAYS, STARTED TODAY WITHOUT WAITING FOR THE BLOOD TEST. 'It is not the antibiotic we would normally use for a chest infection, but it is the right one for this bug.' AND BE HONEST: IT STOPS HIM BEING INFECTIOUS, BUT IT WILL NOT SWITCH THE COUGH OFF — that can go on for weeks yet

Box 2 and box 3 — exclude and notify — EXCLUSION: no childcare, no school, NO CONTACT WITH OTHER CHILDREN UNTIL HE HAS FINISHED FIVE DAYS OF ANTIBIOTIC — and specifically away from PREGNANT WOMEN and ANY BABY UNDER SIX MONTHS · NOTIFICATION with its reason attached: 'partly for statistics, but MAINLY FOR INFECTION CONTROL — they can contact the childcare centre and find any babies under six months who need protecting. That is something I cannot do from this room.' Vague exclusion advice and unexplained notification are both marked down

Box 4 — the question the station is built around — 'Everyone in the household is treated — NOT JUST ETHAN. The baby, you, and Ethan's dad all get THE SAME ANTIBIOTIC, AT THE SAME DOSE, FOR THE SAME FIVE DAYS, even though you are all well. We are not treating you because we think you are sick; we are doing it TO STOP THE BABY CATCHING THIS. CAN I ASK — IS THERE ANYONE ELSE LIVING AT HOME? Grandparents, an aunt or uncle, anyone at all?' → 'Just us four… oh — WELL, MY MUM LIVES WITH US. She moved in when the baby was born. Does she count?' SHE DOES, AND SHE IS RELEASED ONLY IF YOU ASK

Box 5 — red flags, two sets — FOR ETHAN: difficulty breathing, a high fever, or becoming drowsy → emergency department · FOR THE BABY, BE QUICKER: 'BABIES THIS AGE OFTEN DO NOT WHOOP AT ALL, so watch for PAUSES IN BREATHING, ANY CHANGE IN COLOUR, OR HIM NOT FEEDING. If any of that happens, THAT IS AN EMERGENCY, NOT A PHONE CALL'

The vaccine question, answered in full — 'The honest answer is that THE WHOOPING COUGH VACCINE IS NOT ONE HUNDRED PER CENT PROTECTIVE, unlike some others. WHAT IT DOES VERY WELL IS PROTECT AGAINST SEVERE DISEASE AND SERIOUS COMPLICATIONS. It gives less protection against catching a milder coughing illness like this one. SO THE VACCINE HAS NOT FAILED HIM — IT IS VERY LIKELY THE REASON HE HAS THIS RATHER THAN SOMETHING FAR WORSE.' Then check: DID SHE HAVE dTpa IN PREGNANCY, and HAS DAD HAD ONE IN THE LAST TEN YEARS — she had hers, she does not know about his

Variant — no vulnerable contact, the restraint answer — No baby under six months, nobody heavily pregnant, no work contact with infants → 'GOOD NEWS — NO. The rest of you do not need antibiotics, and I would rather not give medication that is not going to help you.' Exclusion still applies. PRESCRIBING TO FIVE PEOPLE BECAUSE YOU MEMORISED 'TREAT THE HOUSEHOLD' IS THE TRAP — THE RULE IS CONDITIONAL, and saying explicitly that you are NOT prescribing, and why, scores better than silence

Variants — pregnancy, work exposure, and the coughing infant — 37 WEEKS PREGNANT → treat the whole household so nobody is carrying it when the baby arrives, AND OFFER dTpa TODAY even at 37 weeks, without judgement about the missed antenatal dose VERIFY current timing · MOTHER WORKS IN THE BABIES' ROOM AT CHILDCARE WITH NO INFANT AT HOME → TREAT HER BUT NOT HER HUSBAND, because WORK EXPOSURE IS A SEPARATE TRIGGER FROM HOUSEHOLD COMPOSITION · THE BABY HAS STARTED COUGHING AND WENT FLOPPY AND BLUE FOR A FEW SECONDS → STOP THE SCRIPT: that is APNOEA, a medical emergency, and he needs assessment in hospital NOW rather than a prescription, with MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval
fails: ★ Never identifying the four-month-old as the person at risk, or never offering him any protection — the station exists to test exactly this
★ Never asking whether anyone else lives at home, so the grandmother is missed — or offering prophylaxis only to those with symptoms
Saying treatment will be withheld until the test result returns, when the diagnosis is clinical and the antibiotic starts today
Answering 'it is clinical' and stopping when the task explicitly asks you to explain the investigations — the recall picks three weeks to put you on the PCR-to-serology boundary

Launching into the explanation without the opening two questions, criticising the previous GP, stating notification without a reason so it sounds punitive, promising the antibiotic will stop the cough, or leaving the vaccine question unanswered
numbers: Under 6 months is the number the whole station turns on · PCR in the first 21 days of cough, serology beyond · azithromycin 10 mg/kg (Max 500 mg) daily × 5 days · clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg (Max 500 mg) BD × 7 days · under 1 month use azithromycin, never erythromycin, because of pyloric stenosis · prophylaxis is the identical drug, dose and duration

Exclusion until 5 days of antibiotics completed, or 21 days from onset if untreated · treat the whole household if an infant under 6 months or a woman in her last month of pregnancy lives there · treat an individual for work contact with infants under 6 months · DTPa for adults not vaccinated in 10 years and every pregnancy at 20 to 32 weeks · cough may last up to 3 months · notifiable to SA health · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · VERIFY all

setting: This station opens with terror, not with a symptom — she believed her daughter was dying an hour ago, and one sentence of acknowledgement costs four seconds and is a scored item. The diagnostic pivot is the duration: parents almost universally overestimate, she will say ten minutes, and she concedes two only if you ask whether anyone looked at a clock. And the counselling pivot is her guilt — she thinks she caused it by not giving enough Panadol, and she will leave believing it unless you release her explicitly.
stem: Emergency department, Port Augusta hospital, regional South Australia. You are the emergency registrar. Mia trenaman, 16 months, brought in by ambulance with her mother Kate after a generalised shaking episode at home lasting about two minutes during a fever. She is now awake. Temp 38.9 · HR 152 · RR 32 · SpO2 98% RA · capillary refill 2 s · BGL 5.1 · weight 10.5 kg · alert, crying, consolable.

Tasks: take a focused history from the mother, about four minutes — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings — explain to the mother what has happened and answer her concerns — outline your management, follow-up and safety-netting. 8 minutes.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain what has happened and answer her concerns
Outline management, follow-up and safety-netting
time: Name the fear before any clinical question · then the seizure in three parts — before, during, after — with the duration anchored to something measured · then hunt the fever source · then exclude infection around the brain, including the antibiotic and immunisation questions · then the well-baby block, development and family history — and stop there rather than running all of BINDSMA · then her concerns and a summary back · then the examination request including glucose and an undressed skin inspection · then classify it simple out loud with the six reasons, answer her three questions, correct the antipyretic myth, and replace it with a first-aid plan.
findings: Alert, interactive, playing with a toy · temp 38.7, HR 148, RR 30, refill 2 seconds, GLUCOSE 5.1 · RIGHT TYMPANIC MEMBRANE RED AND BULGING · throat mildly injected · chest clear, abdomen soft · NO NECK STIFFNESS, FONTANELLE CLOSED, NO PHOTOPHOBIA · SKIN FULLY EXPOSED, NO RASH · normal tone, symmetrical movement, NO FOCAL DEFICIT

back.dx: SIMPLE FEBRILE CONVULSION IN A 16-MONTH-OLD WITH A RIGHT ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA AS THE FEVER SOURCE — CLASSIFIED OUT LOUD, WITH THE MENINGITIS EXCLUSIONS MADE VISIBLE. THE EXPLANATION: 'What Mia had is called A FEBRILE CONVULSION — a fit brought on by a fever. It happens to ABOUT THREE CHILDREN IN EVERY HUNDRED, usually between SIX MONTHS AND SIX YEARS, and it is the commonest kind of fit in young children. A young child's brain is still developing and it is sensitive to a temperature climbing quickly — IT IS THE SPEED OF THE RISE THAT MATTERS MORE THAN HOW HIGH IT GETS. Her brain effectively short-circuited for a couple of minutes and then reset itself.' THEN THE SIX REASONS AND THE EXCLUSIONS (see findings), WHICH IS WHY NO LUMBAR PUNCTURE IS NEEDED HERE. THEN HER THREE QUESTIONS, ALL THREE, PROPERLY. BRAIN DAMAGE — NO: simple febrile convulsions do not cause brain damage and do not affect learning, memory or behaviour, and that is well established. EPILEPSY — ALMOST CERTAINLY NOT: any child has ABOUT A ONE PER CENT CHANCE of developing epilepsy, and after a simple febrile convulsion it is ABOUT ONE TO TWO PER CENT, barely different from any other child. AND DID SHE CAUSE IT — ABSOLUTELY NOT: 'This is the part I most want you to hear. YOU COULD NOT HAVE PREVENTED THIS, AND GIVING PANADOL EARLIER WOULD NOT HAVE STOPPED IT.' THEN THE HONEST PART: IT CAN HAPPEN AGAIN — ABOUT ONE CHILD IN THREE HAS ANOTHER, usually within the next year — 'that is not a sign of anything getting worse, it just means she is a child who does this while she is in this age range, and SHE WILL GROW OUT OF IT, ALMOST ALWAYS BY ABOUT SIX.' THEN THE ANTIPYRETIC CORRECTION (see findings), AND IMMEDIATELY REPLACE THE REMOVED JOB WITH A REAL ONE — THE FIRST-AID PLAN: 'PUT HER ON HER SIDE, ON THE FLOOR, AWAY FROM ANYTHING HARD. NOTE THE TIME — look at a clock, because it always feels longer. DO NOT HOLD HER DOWN, AND DO NOT PUT ANYTHING IN HER MOUTH. Most stop by themselves within a couple of minutes.' AND THE AMBULANCE TRIGGERS: MORE THAN FIVE MINUTES · A SECOND FIT STRAIGHT AFTER · GOING BLUE OR STOPPING BREATHING · NOT WAKING UP PROPERLY AFTERWARDS · OR A RASH THAT DOES NOT FADE UNDER A GLASS. FOR TODAY: TREAT THE EAR, paracetamol for comfort, AND NAME THE TESTS YOU ARE DELIBERATELY WITHHOLDING AND WHY — no bloods, no scan, no EEG, because they would not tell us anything here and you would rather not put her through them. Restraint stated as a decision reads as confidence rather than omission. GP REVIEW IN THE NEXT DAY OR TWO, WRITTEN INFORMATION, AND THE IMMUNISATION SENTENCE: 'PLEASE KEEP HER IMMUNISATIONS GOING — THE ILLNESSES WE VACCINATE AGAINST CAUSE MUCH HIGHER FEVERS AND FAR WORSE FITS THAN THE VACCINES DO.' Both take ten seconds and both are scored. THE NUMBERS: age window 6 MONTHS TO 6 YEARS with a peak at 12 TO 18 MONTHS · 3 IN 100 CHILDREN · SIMPLE MEANS UNDER 15 MINUTES, GENERALISED, SINGLE IN 24 HOURS AND RECOVERY WITHIN AN HOUR · RECURRENCE ABOUT 1 IN 3, UP TO 75% WITH THREE OR MORE RISK FACTORS · EPILEPSY 1% POPULATION, 1 TO 2% AFTER SIMPLE, 4 TO 6% AFTER COMPLEX · MIDAZOLAM 0.15 mg/kg IV OR IM, OR 0.3 mg/kg BUCCAL OR INTRANASAL TO A MAXIMUM OF 10 mg, TWO DOSES MAXIMUM · second line levetiracetam 40 mg/kg to a maximum of 3 g, or phenytoin 20 mg/kg over 20 minutes · hypoglycaemia 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose IV · PARACETAMOL 15 mg/kg FOUR TO SIX HOURLY TO A MAXIMUM OF 60 mg/kg PER 24 HOURS, FOR COMFORT ONLY VERIFY. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the Women's and Children's Hospital, Poisons 13 11 26, CARL 13 14 78.
plan: WIPE, LOOK AT THE CHILD FIRST, SIT AT THE MOTHER'S LEVEL — AND NAME THE FEAR BEFORE ANY CLINICAL QUESTION (see findings). Then the open question: 'can you talk me through exactly what happened, from the start?'
BEFORE — hot first, or only afterwards · DURING — stiff, jerking or both, ONE SIDE VERSUS BOTH, eye position, colour change.
ANCHOR THE DURATION TO SOMETHING MEASURED — the ambulance call, a clock, a phone — and normalise the overestimate as you ask. Then AFTER: how long to full recovery, and moving all four limbs.
THE FEVER SOURCE — cough, runny nose, sore throat · EAR PULLING · vomiting, diarrhoea, offensive urine · rash · sick contacts. ACKNOWLEDGE THE EAR ALOUD.

EXCLUDE CNS INFECTION — non-blanching rash, floppy or hard to wake, irritable on handling, photophobia or neck arching, RECENT ANTIBIOTICS, AND IMMUNISATION STATUS INCLUDING THE TWELVE-MONTH VACCINES.
WELL-BABY — alert and playful, drinking, eating, WET NAPPIES · then DEVELOPMENT and any lost skill · FAMILY HISTORY of fits or epilepsy · medicines and allergies. Then stop.
'WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST ABOUT THIS?' — take all three questions, NOTE THEM AND PROMISE THEM rather than answering now. Then summarise the history back and ask what you have missed.
The examination request in full, including the bedside glucose and the undressed skin inspection (see findings).
CLASSIFY IT OUT LOUD — 'a simple febrile convulsion with an identified source and no indication for a lumbar puncture' — then explain what a febrile convulsion is, and the six reasons.
Say the meningitis exclusions explicitly, so the reassurance is earned rather than asserted.

THE THREE ANSWERS — no brain damage · 1 to 2 per cent epilepsy against a 1 per cent background · AND THE GUILT RELEASED DIRECTLY. Then the honest recurrence figure and that she grows out of it by about six.
THE ANTIPYRETIC CORRECTION WITHOUT HEDGING, AND NO SPONGING, FANS OR COOL BATHS — THEN IMMEDIATELY THE FIRST-AID PLAN, because you have just removed her job and must replace it.

THE FIVE AMBULANCE TRIGGERS · treat the ear and give paracetamol for comfort · NAME THE TESTS NOT BEING DONE AND WHY · GP review in a day or two · KEEP THE IMMUNISATIONS GOING · written information, and a summary.
back.planNote: the stem gives about four minutes of history within eight - the counselling tasks carry the marks, so BINDSMA is compressed rather than run in full
ask: The first sentence: 'She is awake and settled now, and that is genuinely a good sign. What you have been through would frighten anyone.'

The question that decides simple versus complex: 'Did anyone look at a clock or a phone? Parents almost always remember it as longer than it was.' plus 'Was she hot before the shaking started, or only afterwards?' and 'Was one side different from the other at any point?' and 'How long until she was properly herself?'

The two exclusion questions that justify not doing a lumbar puncture: 'Has she had any antibiotics in the last week or two?' and 'Are her immunisations up to date, particularly the twelve-month ones?'

The three sentences that carry the counselling: 'Simple febrile convulsions do not cause brain damage, and they do not affect learning, memory or behaviour.' · 'Panadol will not prevent this happening again. Give it for comfort. You cannot prevent this, and it is not your job to.' · 'On her side, on the floor, note the time, nothing in her mouth — ambulance if it passes five minutes.'

EXAMINER AND PARENT CHALLENGES: 'So should I give her Panadol regularly to stop it happening again?' → a plain no, because agreeing or hedging is an automatic fail · 'Does she need a lumbar puncture?' → 'NOT HERE, AND I WOULD TELL YOU IF IT WERE NEEDED' with the exclusions named · 'The fit lasted twenty-five minutes and her right arm moved more' → NOT SIMPLE: cultures and IV antibiotics first, LP when stable, paediatric team and retrieval · 'He shook first and was hot afterwards, and his teacher says he goes blank' → NOT A FEBRILE CONVULSION — paediatric referral and an EEG, plus first-seizure safety advice about bathing, swimming and heights.
pefe: REQUEST IT IN FULL: general impression — well or toxic, and conscious state now · full observations INCLUDING TEMPERATURE AND CENTRAL CAPILLARY REFILL, AND CONFIRM THE BEDSIDE GLUCOSE · a focused search for the fever source: EARS, throat, chest, abdomen · MENINGISM SPECIFICALLY — neck stiffness, fontanelle if still open, photophobia · A FULL SKIN INSPECTION UNDRESSED FOR ANY NON-BLANCHING RASH · a brief neurological assessment for tone, symmetry of limb movement and focal deficit · AND A CLEAN-CATCH URINE IF NO SOURCE IS FOUND.

Role-player: KATE TRENAMAN, 31, in Port Augusta, a dental assistant three days a week; husband Dan drives trucks. MIA IS 16 MONTHS, born at 40 weeks, 3.6 kg, normal delivery, ALL IMMUNISATIONS UP TO DATE INCLUDING THE TWELVE-MONTH ONES, no medicines or allergies, never in hospital, WALKING SINCE 12 MONTHS WITH ABOUT FIFTEEN WORDS. HER BROTHER HAD FITS WITH FEVERS AS A SMALL BOY and is a healthy adult — mentioned only if asked about family history.

HOW TO PLAY IT: BEGIN VISIBLY SHAKEN AND TEARFUL — she genuinely believed Mia was dying an hour ago — frightened rather than hostile, settling noticeably once things are explained. SAY THE SEIZURE 'FELT LIKE TEN MINUTES', AND CONCEDE TWO MINUTES ONLY IF THE DOCTOR ASKS WHETHER ANYONE TIMED IT OR LOOKED AT A CLOCK. DO NOT OFFER THE EAR-TUGGING OR THE FAMILY HISTORY UNLESS A QUESTION OPENS THE DOOR. HER HIDDEN AGENDA IS THAT SHE CAUSED IT BY NOT GIVING ENOUGH PARACETAMOL, raised only when asked what is worrying her, or volunteered at about minute six. PUSH ONCE: 'SO SHOULD I BE GIVING HER PANADOL REGULARLY TO STOP IT HAPPENING AGAIN?' If the doctor agrees or hedges, that is a fail. If told 'just bring her back if she is worse', ask 'WORSE HOW? WHAT AM I ACTUALLY LOOKING FOR?'

AUTOMATIC-FAIL CONDITIONS: telling her regular paracetamol or ibuprofen will PREVENT another febrile convulsion, or hedging when pushed · reaching the diagnosis and reassuring her WITHOUT EVER ASKING ABOUT IMMUNISATION STATUS, RECENT ANTIBIOTICS, RASH OR RECOVERY · ACCEPTING 'TEN MINUTES' AS THE DURATION AND STILL CALLING IT SIMPLE, or missing a complex feature offered in a variant · SENDING HER HOME WITH NO FIRST-AID INSTRUCTIONS AND NO SPECIFIC AMBULANCE TRIGGER. THE CHECKLIST ALSO SCORES: fear named in the first minute · before-versus-after asked · focality asked · eye deviation and colour · duration anchored · time to full recovery · recurrence today · fever source hunted · non-blanching rash · meningism · antibiotics · immunisation · well-baby · development and skill loss · family history · concerns elicited · summary back · glucose and observations requested · UNDRESSED SKIN INSPECTION · classified simple with reasons · no-LP reasoning · no brain damage · the epilepsy figure · the recurrence figure · GUILT RELEASED · antipyretics do not prevent · first aid · the five-minute trigger · immunisations continue · tests withheld with reasons · written information and review.

The opening sentence, which is scored — 'Before anything else — SHE IS AWAKE AND SETTLED NOW, AND THAT IS GENUINELY A GOOD SIGN. WHAT YOU HAVE JUST BEEN THROUGH WOULD FRIGHTEN ANYONE.' She will say 'I THOUGHT SHE WAS DYING. I HONESTLY DID.' Moving straight to clinical questions without acknowledging that loses a mark and closes her down

The seizure in three parts — BEFORE — 'HAD SHE FELT HOT BEFORE THE SHAKING STARTED, OR ONLY AFTERWARDS?' → hot first, since this morning · DURING — stiff, jerking or both · BOTH SIDES THE SAME OR ONE SIDE MORE · WHICH WAY WERE HER EYES LOOKING · did she go blue → stiff then jerking, SYMMETRICAL, EYES ROLLED UP NOT DEVIATED, lips a bit dusky · AFTER — what was she like and HOW LONG UNTIL SHE WAS PROPERLY HERSELF, and was she moving all four limbs → floppy and sleepy for fifteen to twenty minutes, then normal

Anchor the duration — the diagnostic pivot — She says it FELT LIKE TEN MINUTES. 'DID ANYONE LOOK AT A CLOCK OR A PHONE? Parents almost always remember it as much longer than it was, and that is completely normal — I just need something measured.' → 'Dan said it was ABOUT TWO MINUTES from when it started to when he called. So I suppose it was not ten.' THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN TWO MINUTES AND TWENTY IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SIMPLE AND COMPLEX, AND BETWEEN DISCHARGE AND ADMISSION

The fever source, buried mid-answer — Runny nose since Thursday and a bit of a cough — AND 'SHE HAS BEEN TUGGING AT HER RIGHT EAR THE LAST TWO DAYS, ACTUALLY.' Given only if you ask about ear pulling. ACKNOWLEDGE IT ALOUD — 'that is useful, I will make sure I look in her ears' — so the examiner sees you caught it. Also ask vomiting and diarrhoea, OFFENSIVE URINE, rash, and sick contacts

Excluding infection around the brain — 'A few questions to make sure this is not an infection around the brain.' NON-BLANCHING RASH ON THE GLASS TEST · unusually floppy, hard to wake, or unusually irritable when picked up · bothered by light or arching the neck · 'HAS SHE HAD ANY ANTIBIOTICS IN THE LAST WEEK OR TWO?' · AND ARE HER IMMUNISATIONS UP TO DATE, PARTICULARLY THE TWELVE-MONTH ONES. PARTIALLY TREATED BACTERIAL MENINGITIS MIMICS A SIMPLE FEBRILE CONVULSION PERFECTLY, AND IN VERSION B THE ANTIBIOTIC ANSWER IS YES

Do not run the whole of BINDSMA — Birth history in a developmentally normal sixteen-month-old with a viral illness EARNS NOTHING AND COSTS THE COUNSELLING TIME YOU NEED. Take IMMUNISATION, DEVELOPMENT INCLUDING ANY LOST SKILL, FAMILY HISTORY OF FITS OR EPILEPSY, MEDICATIONS AND ALLERGIES — then stop. HER BROTHER HAD FITS WITH FEVERS AS A CHILD, given only if asked

Her three questions, noted and promised — 'Will she have brain damage?' · 'Does this mean she has epilepsy?' · and the one candidates leave unanswered: 'I keep thinking I should have given her more Panadol, or given it sooner. Did I cause this?' Note them, promise them, examine, and then deliver all three — answering them out of order before examining is the trap

The six reasons it is simple — WHOLE BODY EVENLY RATHER THAN ONE SIDE · ABOUT TWO MINUTES RATHER THAN FIFTEEN OR MORE · ONLY ONE FIT · BACK TO HERSELF WITHIN TWENTY MINUTES · SIXTEEN MONTHS, RIGHT IN THE USUAL AGE RANGE · AND DEVELOPING COMPLETELY NORMALLY. Plus the source found. AND SAY THE MENINGITIS EXCLUSIONS OUT LOUD: no neck stiffness, no rash, fully immunised, NO ANTIBIOTICS THAT COULD MASK IT, and completely back to normal — the reassurance lands because the work is visible, not because you assert it. NEVER SAY 'IT IS JUST A FEBRILE CONVULSION'

The antipyretic correction, said without hedging — 'GIVING PANADOL OR NUROFEN DOES NOT PREVENT ANOTHER FEBRILE CONVULSION. That has been properly tested, and it does not work. So DO use them if she is miserable and they make her comfortable — I would give them for her ear — but PLEASE DO NOT SET ALARMS THROUGH THE NIGHT, and please do not feel you have failed if this happens again despite them. YOU CANNOT PREVENT THIS. IT IS NOT YOUR JOB TO.' And no sponging, fans or cool baths. HEDGING LEAVES HER DOING EXACTLY WHAT YOU WERE TRYING TO STOP

The variants — 9-MONTH-OLD, 25 MINUTES, RIGHT ARM MORE THAN LEFT, STILL DROWSY AN HOUR ON, AMOXICILLIN ON THURSDAY AND BEHIND ON THE TWELVE-MONTH VACCINES → NOT SIMPLE: blood cultures and IV ANTIBIOTICS FIRST, lumbar puncture once stable, paediatric team and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — delaying antibiotics for the LP is the trap, and meningeal signs are unreliable at nine months · THIRD EPISODE WITH AN EXHAUSTED MOTHER → a plan, not a vigil, and buccal midazolam IS worth discussing when they are two hours from a paediatric hospital, but never a daily prophylactic anticonvulsant · 5-YEAR-OLD WHO SHOOK FIRST AND WAS HOT AFTERWARDS, WITH STARING EPISODES AT SCHOOL → NOT A FEBRILE CONVULSION, and the 1 to 2% epilepsy figure is actively misleading

The examination request, and the part candidates forget — General impression and conscious state · full observations AND CONFIRM THE BEDSIDE GLUCOSE · a focused search for the source: EARS, throat, chest, abdomen · MENINGISM — neck stiffness, fontanelle, photophobia · A FULL SKIN INSPECTION UNDRESSED FOR A NON-BLANCHING RASH, requested explicitly, because a rash on the back or buttocks in a clothed toddler is missed · tone, symmetry and focal deficit · and a clean-catch urine if no source is found
fails: ★ Telling her regular paracetamol will prevent another febrile convulsion, or hedging when she pushes — it has been tested and it does not work, and hedging leaves her setting alarms all night

★ Accepting 'about ten minutes' as the duration and still classifying it as simple — anchor it to something measured, because two versus twenty separates simple from complex and discharge from admission
Reaching the diagnosis and reassuring her without ever asking about immunisation status, recent antibiotics, rash or recovery — the reassurance has to be earned visibly
Leaving the guilt unaddressed when she has told you she thinks she under-treated the fever, or answering her three questions out of order before examining

Sending her home with no first-aid plan and no specific ambulance trigger; requesting a neurological examination but forgetting the undressed skin inspection; or saying 'it is just a febrile convulsion'
numbers: Age window 6 months to 6 years, peak 12 to 18 months · 3 in 100 children · simple = under 15 minutes, generalised, single in 24 hours, recovery within 1 hour · recurrence about 1 in 3, up to 75% with three or more risk factors · epilepsy 1% population, 1 to 2% after simple, 4 to 6% after complex

Midazolam 0.15 mg/kg IV or IM, 0.3 mg/kg buccal or intranasal, max 10 mg, two doses maximum · levetiracetam 40 mg/kg (Max 3 g) or phenytoin 20 mg/kg over 20 minutes · hypoglycaemia 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose IV · paracetamol 15 mg/kg 4 to 6 hourly, max 60 mg/kg per 24 h, comfort only · ambulance: over 5 minutes, second fit, blue, not waking, non-blanching rash · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · VERIFY all

setting: Three places this station is lost. The label — announcing 'A parapneumonic effusion' instead of 'A pneumonia that has caused fluid around the lung'. The clock — four minutes spent lovingly describing the film, and the differentials never delivered. And the severity — a complete infection history that never asks whether he is alert, drinking or passing urine, so there is no basis for admitting him. The x-ray explanation is sixty seconds, rehearsed with a stopwatch.

Two complaints in the stem means both must be explored, and the last three minutes carry as many marks as the first five.

findings: The x-ray in sixty seconds — the three colours

'This is an X-ray of Joseph's chest. On an X-ray we generally see three shades. WHEREVER YOU SEE WHITE, THAT IS USUALLY BONE. GREY IS USUALLY SOFT TISSUE. AND WHEREVER YOU SEE BLACK, THAT MEANS THERE IS AIR — which is what I would expect to see in the lungs'
'So there is water on his lung?'

'CLOSE — IT IS AROUND THE OUTSIDE OF THE LUNG RATHER THAN INSIDE IT, in the space between the lung and the chest wall. That space normally has just a tiny film of fluid in it. Here it has filled up, and THAT IS SQUASHING THE LUNG A LITTLE, WHICH IS PART OF WHY HE IS BREATHING FASTER'
Three reasons — child first, film last

'Three days of a chesty cough WITH A HIGH FEVER THAT KEEPS COMING BACK after the Panadol · HE HAS BEEN TIRED AND NOT HIMSELF AND OFF HIS FOOD, which tells me this is a significant infection rather than a simple cold · AND THE X-RAY SHOWS FLUID AROUND THE LUNG, which is a complication we see with pneumonia.' LEADING WITH THE X-RAY IS THE TRAP — child first, film last, because PNEUMONIA IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS and the film added the complication

back.dx: PNEUMONIA WITH A PARAPNEUMONIC EFFUSION — AND THE ORDER OF THOSE TWO WORDS IS THE STATION. THE DIAGNOSIS IS CLINICAL; THE FILM ADDED THE COMPLICATION. WHAT HAPPENS NOW, BRIEFLY: 'That does mean he needs to COME INTO HOSPITAL, so we can give ANTIBIOTICS INTO A DRIP, keep his FLUIDS up, and LOOK AT THAT FLUID MORE CLOSELY WITH AN ULTRASOUND. This is treatable and children generally do well — but it needs treating properly.' THEN CLOSE BY CHECKING RATHER THAN SUMMARISING AT LENGTH: 'What questions do you have? — and just so I know I have explained it clearly, HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE IT TO JOSEPH'S MUM?' THE SEVERITY FRAMEWORK THAT JUSTIFIES ADMISSION: MILD means home on oral amoxicillin · MODERATE is the grey zone · SEVERE means SATURATIONS UNDER 90%, MARKED DISTRESS, DROWSY OR NOT DRINKING, and means admission, oxygen and intravenous antibiotics. Joseph sits at 93% with marked lethargy and an effusion, so he is admitted. ANTIBIOTICS: AMOXICILLIN 25 TO 30 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 1 g ORALLY EIGHT-HOURLY FOR 5 DAYS for the child going home; BENZYLPENICILLIN 50 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 1.2 g INTRAVENOUSLY SIX-HOURLY for severe disease VERIFY. AND THE RULE THAT DRIVES THE VARIANTS: FEVER BEYOND 48 TO 72 HOURS OF ANTIBIOTICS IS A COMPLICATION UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, AND THE NEXT TEST IS A CHEST ULTRASOUND. PNEUMONIA IS CLINICAL — X-RAY, BLOODS AND MICROBIOLOGY ARE NOT ROUTINE, and are reserved for severe illness, non-response, or a suspected complication. Claiming that pneumonia requires an X-ray to diagnose is an automatic fail, and DECLINING AN X-RAY WITH A REASON SCORES BETTER THAN ORDERING ONE TO KEEP A PARENT HAPPY: 'Pneumonia is diagnosed on the examination and the story. An X-ray would not change what I do today, and it does involve radiation. Where I WOULD X-ray is if she were much more unwell, if I thought there was a complication, or if she had not improved after a couple of days on the antibiotic.' THE OTHER THREE VARIANTS RUN ON THE SAME HABIT — TREATING THE EPISODE IN FRONT OF YOU AND STOPPING THERE. STILL FEBRILE ON DAY FOUR: expect real improvement by 48 to 72 hours, so ongoing fevers mean something more rather than the wrong antibiotic — the commonest reason is infected fluid, AN EMPYEMA, and the test that answers it is A CHEST ULTRASOUND showing whether the fluid is thin and free-flowing or thick and loculated; thin fluid often settles with antibiotics, pocketed fluid usually needs drainage, sometimes with fibrinolytics and occasionally surgery. THE TUMMY ACHE REFERRED AS QUERY APPENDIX: 'The nerves that supply the bottom of the lungs also supply the top of the abdomen, so a chest infection in the lower lung very often causes tummy pain in children — sometimes that is the only thing they complain of' — while saying plainly that you are not dismissing the abdomen and will reassess if the pain localises or he develops guarding. THE FOURTH EPISODE THIS YEAR: look for why rather than prescribing again — CYSTIC FIBROSIS with a sweat test, IMMUNE DEFICIENCY, ASPIRATION, and BRONCHIECTASIS from repeated infection, with paediatric referral, because the earlier a cause is found the more lung function is protected. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33 for paediatric retrieval, and Quitline 13 7848 for the grandfather who smokes outside.
plan: Before sitting down — ask the examiner for stability and observations, particularly respiratory rate, saturations and temperature. This shows you are triaging rather than interviewing.
OPEN QUESTION TO THE FATHER, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE THE WORRY AND SIGNPOST — 'I can absolutely understand why you are worried, and I am taking it seriously.'

THE COUGH — how long, continuous or intermittent, getting worse, dry or chesty · THEN THE THREE SOUND WORDS: BARKING, HONKING, WHOOPING · then worse at night, worse on exertion, shortness of breath, noisy breathing.
THE FEVER — measured and how high, what was given, DOES IT WORK AND HOW LONG BEFORE IT CLIMBS AGAIN.
UPPER RESPIRATORY SCREEN IN ONE BREATH — ear pain, runny nose, sore throat, drooling, voice change, difficulty swallowing, neck lumps, rashes.

EXPOSURE AND THE SPECIFIC DISEASES — travel, sick contacts at home or school, VOMITING AFTER A COUGHING BOUT, any children at home under six months, ever wheezy or used puffers, family atopy, CHOKING EPISODE, and smoking at home or in the car.
GASTROINTESTINAL — vomiting apart from with the coughing, diarrhoea, AND TUMMY PAIN, which you keep rather than discard.
THE WELL-CHILD QUESTIONS — ALERT AND ACTIVE OR DROWSY · EATING, AND THEN DRINKING AS A SEPARATE QUESTION · AND URINE OUTPUT. This is the severity assessment and the basis for admitting him.
BIND-SMA COMPRESSED TO THIRTY SECONDS — immunisations, birth and newborn screening, growth and development, medications and allergies, who is at home.
The film is handed over. Three colours · four landmarks · the normal side · then the other side and name the fluid once (see findings). Sixty seconds, pointing rather than saying left or right.
ANSWER 'WATER ON HIS LUNG' PRECISELY — around the outside rather than inside, squashing the lung, which is part of why he is breathing faster.
The diagnosis with the label the right way round — pneumonia first, effusion as its complication — then the three reasons, child first and film last.
WHAT HAPPENS NOW IN TWO SENTENCES — admission, intravenous antibiotics, fluids, ultrasound — then THE FIVE DIFFERENTIAL GROUPS WITH ONE EXCLUDING CLAUSE EACH, AND CLOSE BY ASKING HIM TO SAY IT BACK.
back.planNote: the stem gives five minutes of history and hands over the film at five minutes whether or not you have finished
ask: The first line, before sitting down: 'Before I start — is he haemodynamically stable? May I have his respiratory rate, saturations and temperature?'

The two questions that are most often merged and must not be: 'His appetite I would expect to drop — but is he still drinking? And is he passing less urine?' plus 'How has he been in himself — still alert and active, or drowsy and tired?'

The film, verbatim: 'White is usually bone, grey is soft tissue, and black means air.' · 'This is the shadow of his heart, these are his collarbones, this is his spine, and this is his main airway in the middle.' · 'On this side you can see the normal lung — dark, because it is full of air.' · 'On the other side there is this white shadow at the bottom — fluid collected around the outside of his lung.'

The label sentence: 'Most likely Joseph has pneumonia, an infection in the lung, and that infection has caused the fluid.' and the close: 'So I know I have explained it clearly — how would you describe it to Joseph's mum?'

EXAMINER AND PARENT CHALLENGES: 'Do you not need an X-ray to diagnose pneumonia?' → 'NO — IT IS DIAGNOSED ON THE EXAMINATION AND THE STORY; AN X-RAY WOULD NOT CHANGE WHAT I DO TODAY AND INVOLVES RADIATION.' · 'He is still febrile on day four of antibiotics' → 'I WOULD EXPECT IMPROVEMENT BY 48 TO 72 HOURS, SO THIS IS A COMPLICATION UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE — THE NEXT TEST IS A CHEST ULTRASOUND FOR AN EMPYEMA.' · 'They referred him as query appendicitis' → the shared innervation explanation, without dismissing the abdomen · 'This is his fourth chest infection this year' → sweat test, immune workup, aspiration and bronchiectasis, with paediatric referral.
pefe: There is no examination task — the observations are requested from the examiner at the start and the film is handed over at five minutes. The numbers that matter: temperature 39.2 · respiratory rate raised for age · saturations 93% on room air · heart rate 140 · blood pressure normal. Saturations and work of breathing decide disposition, and 93% with lethargy and an effusion means admission.

Role-player: MARK ELLISON, 38, a diesel mechanic in a regional South Australian town, father of Joseph 5 and a daughter of 8. Joseph is normally EXTREMELY ENERGETIC and has never been in hospital; immunisations up to date, no medications or allergies, normal birth and development. HIS OWN FATHER SMOKES BUT OUTSIDE. Worried and slightly impatient after a two-hour wait, not aggressive, and FRIGHTENED MORE BY HOW FLAT AND SLEEPY JOSEPH HAS BECOME THAN BY THE COUGH.

How to play it: hold back the two answers that decide the case — 'Sleeping all the time' and 'Still drinking' — until asked directly. Answer 'Eating and drinking?' with appetite only, and make them ask about drinking as its own question. Say 'Sorry, what does that mean?' At every piece of jargon, without exception. If the doctor calls it 'A parapneumonic effusion' and never says pneumonia, look blank and ask 'So what is actually wrong with him?' His hidden concern is a nephew who went to intensive care with a chest infection two years ago, revealed only if asked about worries, or volunteered at about 6:30. Call the clock at five minutes and hand over the film whether or not the history is finished, and time the x-ray explanation — past 90 seconds is the commonest failure here.

SCORE THEM, 14 MARKS: asked stability and observations before starting · open question then acknowledged the worry · EXPLORED BOTH COMPLAINTS · ASKED THE SOUND OF THE COUGH · asked the fever response to antipyretic · complete upper respiratory screen · asked contacts and travel · asked pertussis, asthma, foreign body and smoking · ASKED TUMMY PAIN · ASKED ALERT OR DROWSY · ASKED DRINKING SEPARATELY FROM EATING · ASKED URINE OUTPUT · asked immunisation · X-RAY EXPLAINED IN PLAIN LANGUAGE, NORMAL BEFORE ABNORMAL, INSIDE 90 SECONDS. AUTOMATIC FAIL, ANY ONE: named the effusion as the diagnosis and NEVER SAID PNEUMONIA · NEVER REACHED THE DIFFERENTIALS · no well-child questions at all · used radiological jargon throughout with the father · said the child could go home · claimed pneumonia requires an X-ray to diagnose.

Stability first, before you sit down — 'Before I start — IS JOSEPH HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE? May I have his vital signs, PARTICULARLY THE RESPIRATORY RATE, OXYGEN SATURATION AND TEMPERATURE, along with heart rate and blood pressure?' → stable, TEMPERATURE 39.2, RESPIRATORY RATE RAISED FOR AGE, SATURATIONS 93% ON ROOM AIR, heart rate 140, blood pressure normal. RESPIRATORY RATE AND SATURATIONS ARE WHAT DECIDE WHETHER THIS CHILD GOES HOME

The three sound words — 'Is the cough dry or chesty? AND WHAT DOES IT SOUND LIKE — IS THERE A BARKING SOUND, A HONKING SOUND, OR A WHOOPING NOISE AT THE END OF A BOUT?' Accepting 'chesty' and moving on is the trap. THE THREE WORDS TAKE TEN SECONDS AND RULE OUT CROUP, PERTUSSIS AND HABIT COUGH — ask them even when the age does not fit

The fever is the second complaint, not a detail — 'Have you measured it — how high? Have you given him anything? DOES IT BRING THE TEMPERATURE DOWN, AND HOW LONG BEFORE IT CLIMBS AGAIN?' → 39.5 at home, Panadol brings it down BUT AFTER A FEW HOURS IT IS RIGHT BACK UP. A FEVER THAT REBOUNDS WITHIN HOURS IN AN UNWELL CHILD IS A BACTERIAL PATTERN

The tummy pain is not a distraction — 'He said his tummy hurt yesterday, but it seems alright today.' DO NOT DISMISS IT — A LOWER LOBE PNEUMONIA IN A CHILD FREQUENTLY PRESENTS AS ABDOMINAL PAIN, SOMETIMES AS THE ONLY COMPLAINT. It supports your diagnosis rather than confusing it

The well-child questions are the severity assessment — 'HOW HAS HE BEEN IN HIMSELF — STILL ALERT AND ACTIVE, OR DROWSY AND TIRED?' → 'THAT IS WHAT HAS WORRIED US MOST. He is normally a very playful kid and HE HAS JUST BEEN SLEEPING ALL THE TIME FOR TWO DAYS' — given only if asked · THEN DRINKING AS A SEPARATE QUESTION FROM EATING, because every sick child eats less: 'his appetite is gone completely… BUT YES, HE IS STILL DRINKING' · AND URINE OUTPUT: fewer wet trips than usual. ALERTNESS IS THE SEVERITY MEASURE; DRINKING AND URINE ARE THE DEHYDRATION MEASURES

Normal landmarks, then the normal side, then the abnormal — 'Before I show you anything that is not right — THIS IS THE SHADOW OF HIS HEART, THESE ARE HIS COLLARBONES, THIS IS HIS SPINE running down the middle, and THIS IS HIS MAIN AIRWAY, sitting in the centre where it should be.' · 'On THIS SIDE you can see the normal shadow of the lung — nice and dark, because it is full of air.' · 'But compare it with THE OTHER SIDE — you can see THIS WHITE SHADOW AT THE BOTTOM. That is FLUID COLLECTED AROUND THE OUTSIDE OF HIS LUNG, BETWEEN THE LUNG AND THE CHEST WALL. We call that a pleural effusion.'

The label, the right way round — 'Most likely Joseph has a condition called PNEUMONIA — AN INFECTION IN THE LUNG. THAT INFECTION HAS CAUSED THE FLUID to build up around his lung that we just looked at. When fluid collects because of a pneumonia we call it A PARAPNEUMONIC EFFUSION — but THE UNDERLYING PROBLEM, AND THE THING WE TREAT, IS THE CHEST INFECTION.' Naming the effusion as the diagnosis and never saying pneumonia is an automatic fail

Five differential groups, one excluding clause each — INFECTIONS HIGHER UP — throat, tonsils, nose or sinuses with mucus dripping down, but no sore throat or runny nose, and those do not cause fluid on an X-ray · SPECIFIC CHEST INFECTIONS — whooping cough or tuberculosis, but no whooping sound, no vomiting with the coughing, no travel and no contacts · SOMETHING INHALED — but no choking episode and this came on gradually with a fever · ASTHMA — but he has never wheezed and there is no family history · AND OTHER COMPLICATIONS OF PNEUMONIA such as a lung abscess, which the ultrasound will help rule out. FIVE GROUPS WITH ONE CLAUSE EACH BEATS FIFTEEN NAMES, AND FITS THE NINETY SECONDS YOU ACTUALLY HAVE

Three traps in the film task — THE CLOCK — this task is worth roughly a third of the station, and four minutes here means the differentials never happen; rehearse it with a stopwatch until it runs in sixty seconds · RIGHT AND LEFT — the film is reversed relative to you, SO SAY 'THIS SIDE' AND 'THE OTHER SIDE' AND POINT, because nobody has ever lost a mark for avoiding the words · JARGON — no costophrenic angle, no meniscus, no opacification, no silhouette sign. IF THE FATHER COULD NOT REPEAT YOUR SENTENCE TO HIS WIFE, REWRITE IT

back.dx: A VIRAL LOWER RESPIRATORY INFECTION THAT HAS TRIGGERED AN ASTHMA FLARE — TWO DIAGNOSES, EACH WITH ITS OWN REASONS, IN A CHILD WHOSE SATURATION OF 90% MAKES THIS SEVERE DESPITE LOOKING COMFORTABLE. THE SATURATION BANDS THAT DECIDE EVERYTHING: ABOVE 94% MILD TO MODERATE · 90 TO 94% SEVERE · BELOW 90% LIFE-THREATENING · AND GIVE OXYGEN TO KEEP IT AT OR ABOVE 92%. So 'no gross respiratory distress' and 'speaking in full sentences' are reassuring findings inside a severe episode, not a reason to downgrade it. THE FULL PLAN, DELIVERED IN ORDER: OXYGEN NOW · SALBUTAMOL SIX PUFFS BY SPACER AND MASK, one puff at a time with four to six breaths after each, repeated every twenty minutes for the first hour — TWELVE PUFFS IF SIX YEARS OR OVER · IPRATROPIUM FOUR PUFFS UNDER SIX, EIGHT IF SIX OR OVER, EVERY TWENTY MINUTES FOR THE FIRST HOUR ONLY · ORAL PREDNISOLONE 1 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 50 mg DAILY FOR THREE DAYS, NO WEANING · AND AMBULANCE TRANSFER SO HE IS MONITORED EN ROUTE. OBSERVE FOR AT LEAST ONE HOUR AFTER THE LAST SALBUTAMOL BEFORE ANY DISCHARGE, AND SPIROMETRY IS NOT FEASIBLE UNDER SIX YEARS SO THE DIAGNOSIS HERE IS CLINICAL VERIFY doses locally. WHAT MAKES THIS STATION DIFFERENT FROM A PURE WHEEZE CASE IS THAT YOU ARE MAKING A CHRONIC DIAGNOSIS FOR THE FIRST TIME IN A FAMILY THAT HAS NEVER HEARD IT — 'ASTHMA? NOBODY HAS EVER SAID THAT' — so the four reasons have to be given as a positive case rather than as a list of exclusions, and the family atopy question is what earns the fourth. THE SMOKING IS HANDLED TACTFULLY RATHER THAN AVOIDED: thank him for being straight, raise Quitline later without blame, and name it as something that makes asthma worse rather than as the cause. AND THE CHRONIC-DISEASE PACKAGE IS NOT OPTIONAL — action plan, spacer teaching, review in one to two days and then four to six weeks for a preventer discussion, trigger control and written red flags. THE LINES THAT RESCUE AN AWKWARD MOMENT: 'He looks well, and that is reassuring — BUT THE OXYGEN LEVEL IS THE MEASUREMENT I TRUST MOST.' · 'I would rather treat him properly now than wait and see.' · 'Thank you for being straight with me about the smoking.' · 'Most children respond quickly to this treatment.' · 'I would not want to promise you either way today — let us see the pattern when he is well.' AND THE ANTIBIOTIC REFUSAL WHEN HE CITES A PREVIOUS COURSE: 'I believe you, and I understand why that makes antibiotics look like the answer. MOST OF THESE INFECTIONS SETTLE IN ABOUT THAT TIME WHATEVER WE DO, which is often why it looks as though the antibiotic worked. Here there are no signs of a bacterial pneumonia, antibiotics would do nothing for the wheeze, and they carry side effects. What will actually help him is the reliever, the steroid and the oxygen — and if focal signs or a persistent high fever appear, I will treat him with antibiotics straight away and tell you exactly why.' SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: Quitline 13 7848, MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33 for paediatric retrieval, and an ambulance rather than a private car for a hypoxic child in a regional practice.
plan: WIPE AND ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — saturation, respiratory rate, temperature, heart rate, blood pressure. Then 'WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST TODAY?' and acknowledge it.
THE COUGH ON TWO TIMESCALES — how long ALTOGETHER, and WHAT CHANGED IN THE LAST FEW DAYS. Say both halves back to him.
CHARACTER AND SOUND — constant or intermittent, dry or chesty, BARKING, WHOOPING OR HONKING · then WORSE AT NIGHT, WORSE ON RUNNING, shortness of breath, and A WHISTLING SOUND ON BREATHING OUT.
THE FEVER — measured, how high, what was given, DID IT WORK AND DOES IT COME BACK. Interpret the response as a viral pattern rather than just recording it.
PACE — pertussis questions · THEN FAMILY ATOPY AND ANY PREVIOUS PUFFER, which is the most efficient question in the station · croup questions · CHOKING, SMOKING, PETS, CARPET, WOOD HEATER.
THE QUICK SCREEN — runny nose, sore throat, ear pain, drooling or trouble swallowing, voice change, rash, neck lumps, vomiting, diarrhoea, tummy pain, RECURRENT CHEST INFECTIONS, travel.
WELL-CHILD AND BACKGROUND — alert and active or drowsy, eating and drinking, urine · birth and NEWBORN HEEL PRICK, immunisations, growth and development.
THE EXAMINATION REQUEST IN FULL — including CAN HE SPEAK IN FULL SENTENCES, audible wheeze or stridor, work of breathing, AND WHETHER ANY WHEEZE IS GENERALISED OR LOCALISED.
GRADE IT OUT LOUD — 'generalised wheeze, no crackles, and a saturation of 90 per cent, WHICH PUTS THIS IN THE SEVERE CATEGORY EVEN THOUGH HE LOOKS COMFORTABLE'.
THE TWO-PART DIAGNOSIS — infection first, then the asthma flare it triggered, WITH THE FOUR REASONS FOR ASTHMA AND THE THREE FOR INFECTION.
Say the severity to the father and hold it when he pushes back (see findings).
THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH ONE EXCLUDING REASON — pneumonia, croup, pertussis, foreign body, a cold alone, cystic fibrosis, and the allergy and smoke contributors.

The plan — oxygen, six puffs by spacer every twenty minutes, oral prednisolone, ambulance · no antibiotics with the reason and the trigger for changing · then the package: action plan, spacer teaching, review, Quitline, red flags, and a summary.

ask: The first request: 'Could I please have his oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, temperature, heart rate and blood pressure?' — and then read the saturation back as a grade.

The two-timescale questions: 'How long has he been coughing altogether?' and 'What changed in the last few days?' plus the most efficient question in the station: 'Does anyone in the family have asthma, eczema or hay fever?'

'A saturation of 90 per cent puts this in the severe category, even though he looks comfortable.' / 'There are two things going on, and they fit together.' / 'Six puffs through a spacer with a mask, one puff at a time, with a few breaths after each.'

EXAMINER AND PARENT CHALLENGES: 'Severe? He is sitting there talking to me' → validate, then hold the grading on the oxygen level · 'Does he need antibiotics?' → no, with the reason and the trigger for changing your mind · 'His chest is quiet now' → 'A SILENT CHEST WITH POOR AIR ENTRY IS LIFE-THREATENING, NOT IMPROVEMENT' · 'He already has a blue puffer and it does nothing' → no spacer and sprayed into the mouth, so the delivery has failed rather than the drug — demonstrate and watch him.

THE DRILLS: ask the two timescales and the four asthma reasons in 30 seconds · state the saturation bands in 10 seconds · give seven differentials with one clause each in 45 seconds · say the acute treatment with puff counts and the steroid dose in 30 seconds · then run the pneumonia and silent-chest variants and say what changes.
pefe: REQUEST IT IN FULL, BECAUSE FINDINGS COME ONLY ON SPECIFIC REQUEST: vitals — SATURATION IN ROOM AIR, respiratory rate, heart rate, temperature, blood pressure · general appearance — alert or drowsy, distressed, cyanosed, dehydrated, AND CAN HE SPEAK IN FULL SENTENCES · AUDIBLE WHEEZE OR STRIDOR · work of breathing — nasal flaring, tracheal tug, recession, grunting · ENT and cervical nodes · respiratory — expansion, tracheal position, percussion, air entry and added sounds, AND IS ANY WHEEZE GENERALISED OR LOCALISED · cardiovascular — heart sounds and murmurs.

Role-player: DANIEL, 35, a diesel mechanic in a regional town, father of LIAM 3½ and a daughter of 7 WHO HAS ASTHMA. His wife Steph has eczema AND SMOKES INSIDE THE HOUSE; he has hay fever. There is a dog and carpet throughout. Liam: born at term, normal heel prick, FULLY IMMUNISED, no allergies or medicines, NEVER HAD A PUFFER, never in hospital, growing well, at child care three days a week WHERE SEVERAL CHILDREN HAVE BEEN UNWELL.

How to play it: give only what is asked — never volunteer the family atopy, the smoking, or the night and exercise pattern. If asked 'How long has he had the cough?', say 'A long time' and wait to be asked how long. Push back once at the word severe or ambulance — 'Severe? He is sitting there talking to me' — and settle if the saturation is explained. Ask for antibiotics once. If they never ask about family history but announce asthma, say 'What makes you say asthma?'

SCORING — 38 ITEMS, 30 OR MORE WITH NO AUTOMATIC FAIL IS A COMFORTABLE PASS. AUTOMATIC FAIL: GIVING ONLY ONE DIAGNOSIS · PLANNING HOME MANAGEMENT DESPITE A SATURATION OF 90% · OMITTING THE ORAL STEROID IN A SEVERE FLARE · PRESCRIBING ORAL ANTIBIOTICS WITH NO FOCAL SIGNS. The checklist also scores: saturation and respiratory rate requested · open question about concern · TOTAL DURATION AND WHAT CHANGED · dry or chesty and the cough sound · WORSE AT NIGHT AND ON EXERCISE · wheeze · fever measured and its response · pertussis questions · FAMILY ATOPY · previous puffer · croup questions · CHOKING · SMOKING AT HOME · pets and exposures · ENT and GI screens · recurrent infections and growth · well-child questions · immunisation · GENERALISED OR LOCALISED AND FULL SENTENCES REQUESTED · SEVERITY GRADED OUT LOUD · BOTH DIAGNOSES NAMED · FOUR REASONS FOR ASTHMA · reasons for infection · five or more differentials with reasons · oxygen · SALBUTAMOL BY SPACER WITH THE CORRECT PUFF COUNT · ORAL PREDNISOLONE · ambulance and emergency department · ANTIBIOTICS DECLINED WITH A REASON · action plan and spacer teaching · review date · smoking cessation offered without blame · red flags · summary.

The number that grades the station — SpO2 90% IN ROOM AIR · temperature 38 · heart rate and blood pressure normal for age · ALERT, SPEAKING IN FULL SENTENCES · NO GROSS RESPIRATORY DISTRESS · not cyanosed, not dehydrated · ENT: clear rhinorrhoea, throat unremarkable · CHEST: GENERALISED EXPIRATORY WHEEZE BOTH FIELDS, NO CREPITATIONS, trachea central, resonant · heart sounds normal. HEARING 'NO DISTRESS' AND RELAXING IS THE TRAP — READ THE SATURATION BACK: 'NINETY PER CENT, SO THIS IS A SEVERE EXACERBATION'

The cough on two timescales — 'HOW LONG HAS HE BEEN COUGHING ALTOGETHER?' → MONTHS, REALLY · 'AND WHAT CHANGED IN THE LAST FEW DAYS?' → MUCH WORSE FOR TWO DAYS, WITH A TEMPERATURE. RECORDING ONE TIMESCALE IS THE TRAP: two days alone gives you a viral illness with no asthma, months alone gives you asthma with no trigger, AND THE EXAMINER WANTS BOTH HALVES

The four reasons for asthma — Months of cough rather than days · wheeze · worse at night and worse when he runs about · and a strong family history — mother's eczema, father's hay fever, sister's asthma. Night plus exercise plus wheeze is three of them; the family atopy question is the fourth and the single most efficient question in the station — one question, three positives — and he volunteers none of it

The three reasons for infection — THE FEVER · THE OUTBREAK AT CHILD CARE, which the stem planted for you to quote · AND EVERYTHING WORSENING OVER THE LAST TWO DAYS. And the fever pattern itself is evidence: 38.5 with PARACETAMOL BRINGING IT DOWN FOR A FEW HOURS AND THEN IT CLIMBS AGAIN is a normal viral pattern — interpret it rather than record it

The pace sweep — P — coughing fits one after another, VOMITING AT THE END OF A BOUT, any whoop · A — FAMILY ASTHMA, ECZEMA OR HAY FEVER, Liam's own eczema or allergies, HAS HE EVER BEEN GIVEN A PUFFER AND DID IT HELP · C — barking cough or a harsh noise breathing in, hoarseness · E — ANY CHOKING EPISODE, smoking at home or in the car, pets, carpets, dust, a wood heater · then the quick screen: runny nose, sore throat, ear pain, drooling, voice change, rash, neck lumps, vomiting, diarrhoea, tummy pain, RECURRENT CHEST INFECTIONS, travel

The two-part diagnosis, acute problem first — 'There are TWO things going on, and they fit together. FIRST, Liam has picked up A CHEST INFECTION. SECOND, THAT INFECTION HAS SET OFF A FLARE-UP OF ASTHMA — a condition where the small airways in the lungs are sensitive and narrow down, and that narrowing is what causes the whistling sound and the cough.' THEN THE FOUR REASONS. AND THEN THE PART HE NEEDS NOW: 'HIS OXYGEN LEVEL IS 90 PER CENT, WHICH IS LOWER THAN I AM COMFORTABLE WITH. THAT MAKES THIS A SEVERE FLARE-UP.' Explaining the chronic diagnosis at length while a hypoxic child sits in front of you is the trap

'Severe? He is sitting there talking to me' — He pushes back once, and the answer holds the grading without dismissing him: 'He is, and that is genuinely reassuring. But the oxygen level is the measurement we trust most, and it tells me to treat him properly now rather than wait and see. Most children respond quickly to treatment'

The differentials, each with a reason — PNEUMONIA — sounds spread evenly through both lungs with NO CRACKLES · CROUP — no barking cough and no harsh noise breathing in · WHOOPING COUGH — no coughing fits, no vomiting afterwards, fully immunised · SOMETHING INHALED — no choking episode and the wheeze is in BOTH lungs rather than one spot · AN ORDINARY COLD ALONE — would explain the fever but not the wheeze or the months of coughing · CYSTIC FIBROSIS — never had a chest infection and growing well · AND ALLERGIES WITH POST-NASAL DRIP, AND THE CIGARETTE SMOKE AT HOME, which are not the main cause but make asthma worse

The acute treatment — Oxygen · six puffs of salbutamol through a spacer with a mask, one puff at a time with four to six breaths after each, repeated every twenty minutes for the first hour · oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg · then ambulance to the emergency department so he is monitored on the way. Ipratropium 4 puffs under 6 years every 20 minutes for the first hour only. Omitting the oral steroid in a severe flare is an AUTOMATIC FAIL VERIFY doses locally

No antibiotics, with the trigger for changing your mind — 'There are no signs pointing to a bacterial pneumonia, and this looks viral. Antibiotics would not help the wheeze and they do carry side effects. IF FOCAL SIGNS OR A PERSISTENT HIGH FEVER APPEARED, I WOULD CHANGE MY MIND AND TREAT STRAIGHT AWAY.' He asks once, and may cite a previous course that 'worked'

The package that is forgotten at the end — Five easy marks in ninety seconds: a WRITTEN ASTHMA ACTION PLAN · SPACER TECHNIQUE TAUGHT AND WATCHED · REVIEW IN A DAY OR TWO, then a preventer discussion · TRIGGER CONTROL, including the smoking raised WITHOUT BLAME — 'thank you for being straight with me about that', and Quitline 13 7848 · AND RED FLAGS: breathing worse, GOING QUIET, blue lips, THE RELIEVER NOT LASTING FOUR HOURS, or stopping drinking

The variants — PNEUMONIA — four days only with no previous cough, fever 39.5 with rigors, FOCAL CRACKLES AND BRONCHIAL BREATHING AT THE RIGHT BASE, dull to percussion → that one DOES need an antibiotic, and FOCAL SIGNS REWRITE THE STATION · THE SILENT CHEST — SpO2 86%, drowsy, cyanosed, MINIMAL AIR ENTRY WITH NO WHEEZE AUDIBLE → LIFE-THREATENING, and a quiet chest is not improvement: high-flow oxygen, continuous nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium, IV steroid, consider IV magnesium, 000 and MedSTAR Kids · THE PUFFER THAT 'DOES NOT WORK' — no spacer, sprayed straight into the mouth → THE MEDICINE HAS NOT FAILED, IT HAS NOT BEEN GETTING THERE; demonstrate and watch him do one

setting: A ten-minute station with no patient in the room and a form on the desk. The thing that separates a pass from a fail is the reliever ladder: 1–2 → 4–12 → 12, with the preventer identical in all three boxes, and never '4, 4, 4'. The second is translation — 'Obstruction' means narrowing, said in the same breath. And the third is that you narrate every box as you write it, because silent writing is dead air and is marked.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. John citizen, 10 years, 30 kg, several months of cough and wheeze. The GP arranged spirometry. His mother Kate attends for the results; John is not in the room. Afebrile, uses Ventolin only as needed, no preventer, no other history, no allergies. The spirometry report and a blank national asthma council action plan are on the desk.

The report: predicted FEV1 2.10 L, FVC 2.45 L, predicted ratio 0.86 with an LLN of 0.80. Pre-bronchodilator FEV1 1.30 L (62% pred), FVC 2.20 L (90% pred), ratio 0.59. Post-bronchodilator FEV1 1.85 L (88% pred), FVC 2.35 L, ratio 0.79. Change in FEV1 +42%. Tasks: explain the spirometry result — explain the diagnosis — complete the asthma action plan, explaining each section as you fill it in. 10 minutes.
