time: An open question before any numbers, then signpost the three parts · then what spirometry is and how it is done · then the three numbers in order — FVC, FEV1, the ratio — with obstruction translated as narrowing · then the reversibility test and the actual percentage · then the diagnosis in plain words, and the three questions she will ask answered in one go · then teach-back before you touch the form · then the plan box by box, narrated while writing: ID, green, orange, red, danger signs · then spacer technique, two copies, review date and a second teach-back.

back.dx: ASTHMA, CONFIRMED ON SPIROMETRY WITH SIGNIFICANT BRONCHODILATOR REVERSIBILITY — AND THE STATION IS THE TRANSLATION AND THE FORM, NOT THE DIAGNOSIS. THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS: 'Asthma is a LONG-TERM LUNG CONDITION WHERE THE AIRWAYS BECOME INFLAMED AND NARROW. That causes cough, wheeze — a whistling, noisy sort of breathing — and shortness of breath, and it is classically WORSE AT NIGHT AND WITH EXERCISE, and worse with colds, cold air, smoke and pollen. It is common, it is very treatable, and AS HIS TEST JUST SHOWED, THE NARROWING IS REVERSIBLE.' THE NUMBERS BEHIND THE REPORT: SPIROMETRY IS USABLE FROM ABOUT AGE SIX · THE NORMAL PAEDIATRIC FEV1/FVC RATIO IS 0.85 TO 0.90, AND THE ADULT 0.70 CUT-OFF IS NEVER USED IN A CHILD · the bronchodilator challenge is SALBUTAMOL 400 MICROGRAM VIA SPACER WITH REPEAT SPIROMETRY AT 10 TO 15 MINUTES · significant reversibility is AT LEAST 12% FROM BASELINE on the paediatric criterion, or OVER 10% OF PREDICTED on ATS/ERS 2021 · AND NO REVERSIBILITY DOES NOT EXCLUDE ASTHMA. THE RELIEVER LADDER, WHICH IS THE SINGLE THING THIS STATION IS BUILT TO TEST — SALBUTAMOL 100 MICROGRAM PUFFS VIA SPACER, ONE PUFF AT A TIME WITH FOUR BREATHS AFTER EACH: AGE 6 AND OVER — 1 TO 2 WHEN WELL, 4 TO 12 IN A FLARE, 12 IF SEVERE · AGE 1 TO 5 — 1 TO 2, THEN 2 TO 6, THEN 6 · REPEAT EVERY 20 MINUTES IF NEEDED · AND THE PREVENTER DOSE IS IDENTICAL IN ALL THREE BOXES. WRITING THE SAME RELIEVER NUMBER IN ALL THREE BOXES, OR INCREASING THE PREVENTER FOR A FLARE, IS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL. PREDNISOLONE 1 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 50 mg EACH MORNING FOR THREE DAYS — 30 mg for a 30 kg child, 16 mg for 16 kg — which is the Australian Asthma Handbook primary-care dose, while RCH and many hospital guidelines load with 2 mg/kg then 1 mg/kg daily, SO NAME WHICH ONE YOU ARE USING VERIFY. ESCALATION: RELIEVER NEEDED MORE OFTEN THAN EVERY THREE TO FOUR HOURS MEANS A DOCTOR THAT DAY; RELIEVER NEEDED AGAIN WITHIN THREE HOURS IS THE RED ZONE. FIRST AID IS 4 PUFFS, WAIT 4 MINUTES, 4 PUFFS, WAIT 4 MINUTES, THEN CALL 000 AND CONTINUE. PEAK FLOW IS NOT RECOMMENDED UNDER TWELVE. REVIEW ANNUALLY IF WELL CONTROLLED, THREE TO SIX MONTHLY IF NOT. SPACER WASHED MONTHLY IN WARM SOAPY WATER AND AIR-DRIED WITHOUT RUBBING, BECAUSE RUBBING MAKES IT STATIC. THE SPACER TECHNIQUE, NARRATED IN SEVEN STEPS: assemble and check it is clean and dry · cap off, hold upright and SHAKE WELL · push the puffer into the open end · mouthpiece between the teeth without biting, lips sealed · PRESS ONCE FOR ONE PUFF · four normal breaths through it, or one slow deep breath held about five seconds · remove, SHAKE AGAIN, and repeat. NEVER FIRE TWO PUFFS IN TOGETHER, because the medicine sticks to the walls and he gets less. THE STEROID-AND-GROWTH VARIANT IS ANSWERED BY VALIDATING RATHER THAN DISMISSING: inhaled steroids DO slow growth a little, mostly in the first year or two, with a small effect on final adult height of around a centimetre — and the other half that does not get said is that POORLY CONTROLLED ASTHMA ALSO SLOWS GROWTH and costs sleep, school and sport; montelukast is an alternative but CAN CAUSE SLEEP DISTURBANCE, NIGHTMARES, AGITATION AND MOOD CHANGES, so watch closely and stop if they occur; and either way use the lowest effective dose and PLOT HIS HEIGHT AT EVERY VISIT. AND DOUBLING THE PREVENTER IN A BAD WEEK DOES NOT WORK, because it acts over days to weeks — which is exactly why the preventer line is identical in all three boxes. THE FOUR-YEAR-OLD VARIANT CHANGES TWO THINGS: SPIROMETRY IS NOT RELIABLE UNDER ABOUT SIX so the diagnosis is clinical and documented as such, and THE DOSES HALVE to 1 to 2, then 2 to 6, then 6, with prednisolone 16 mg for 16 kg and a spacer with a face mask held on for six breaths.
plan: OPEN BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN — 'tell me what has been happening with John so far, and what you are hoping to get from today' — THEN SIGNPOST THE THREE PARTS and ask whether anything is worrying her in particular.
WHAT SPIROMETRY IS AND HOW IT IS DONE — a small tube, the biggest breath in he can take, then blow out as hard and as long as possible, measuring how much air comes out and how fast.
The three numbers in order — FVC normal so lung size is fine · FEV1 lower than it should be · the ratio 0.59 against an expected 0.86 — and translate obstruction as narrowing in the same breath.
The reversibility test, which is also the answer to 'Is the narrowing permanent?' — Ventolin, fifteen minutes, repeat, more than 12% confirms it in a child, and his went up by 42%.
Name the diagnosis and describe asthma in plain words (see dx), including the classic night and exercise pattern and the family tendency.
ANSWER HER THREE QUESTIONS IN ONE GO — growing out of it, sport, and heredity — then TEACH-BACK BEFORE TOUCHING THE FORM.
Explain what the plan is and that it is colour-coded like traffic lights, then the ID box — name, date, twelve-month review, your details — and hand her the pen for the emergency contact.
GREEN — what 'well' looks like, PREVENTER AS USUAL, RELIEVER 1 TO 2 PUFFS UP TO FOUR-HOURLY AND BEFORE SPORT, and 'NONE — RELIEVER ONLY' written in with a flag to review it.
Orange — what 'Not well' looks like, preventer unchanged, reliever 4 to 12 puffs repeatable every twenty minutes, and the three-to-four-hour escalation trigger said and written.
Answer the twelve-puff safety challenge, including tremor and tachycardia and the one-puff-at-a-time rhythm.
Red — severe features, preventer still unchanged, reliever 12 puffs every twenty minutes, and prednisolone 30 mg each morning for three days, doctor the same day.
Danger signs and 000 with the words 'Asthma emergency', sit him upright and keep giving the reliever · and leave the peak flow boxes blank, explaining why.

SPACER TECHNIQUE IN FULL, THEN TWO COPIES — FRIDGE AND SCHOOL OFFICE WITH A SPARE PUFFER AND SPACER — a fortnight to check technique, annual review, AND A CLOSING TEACH-BACK: 'what would you do if he needed the puffer twice in two hours?'
back.planNote: the stem gives ten minutes across three tasks - the form is the largest of them and every box is narrated aloud while writing
ask: The translation the examiner is listening for: 'When the ratio is low we call it an obstruction — and obstruction means narrowing in the airways.'
The ladder, said and written: 1 to 2 puffs when well · 4 to 12 in a flare · 12 if severe · and 'The preventer dose stays exactly the same in all three sections.'

The escalation trigger and the emergency line: 'If he needs the puffer more often than every three to four hours, see a doctor that day.' · 'Blue lips, cannot speak, or the puffer is not helping — call triple zero and say asthma emergency.'
The two teach-backs: 'Can you tell me back in your own words what the test showed?' before the form, and 'Can you tell me what you would do if he needed the puffer twice in two hours?' At the end.

CHALLENGES: 'Narrowing? Is that permanent?' → the reversibility result is the answer · 'Twelve puffs? Isn't that dangerous?' → safe medicine, guideline dose, tremor and tachycardia expected, and never twelve at once · 'Is that Flixotide a steroid? They stunt growth' → validate and quantify rather than calling it a myth (see dx) · 'Should I double the preventer in a bad week?' → no, it works over days to weeks, which is why the line is identical in all three boxes · 'Is 10% or 12% the threshold?' → different denominators, and his result is significant on either.
pefe: There is no examination and no child in the room — the report and the blank form are the station. What to do with the report: read the FVC, the FEV1 and the ratio against predicted, note the pre- and post-bronchodilator values, and quote the percentage change in FEV1 out loud. Never apply the adult 0.70 ratio cut-off to a child, and never invent peak flow numbers for a ten-year-old.

Role-player: KATE CITIZEN, 38, a school admin officer in a regional town. JOHN IS 10, 30 kg, plays junior football. COUGHING ABOUT FOUR MONTHS, WHEEZES WHEN HE RUNS, WAKES COUGHING TWO OR THREE NIGHTS A WEEK, using a blue puffer THREE OR FOUR TIMES A WEEK. NO SPACER, AND NOBODY HAS EVER SHOWN HIM HOW TO USE IT — given only if asked. No other medication, no allergies. HER SISTER HAS ASTHMA and was admitted as a teenager. Nobody smokes indoors but there is a wood heater in winter.

HOW TO PLAY IT: start anxious and rushed, relaxing once things are explained clearly. PUSH AT THREE MOMENTS — at the word OBSTRUCTION, ask whether the narrowing is permanent · at the reliever dose, challenge 'TWELVE PUFFS?' · and if a preventer is mentioned, raise the STEROID-AND-GROWTH fear and press it. STAY QUIET WHILE THEY WRITE, AND IF THEY WRITE IN SILENCE FOR MORE THAN ABOUT FIFTEEN SECONDS, MARK IT — BUT DO NOT RESCUE THEM. Her hidden agenda is that this means lifelong medication and giving up football, volunteered at about seven minutes only if never asked about concerns.

AUTOMATIC FAIL: WRITING THE SAME RELIEVER DOSE IN ALL THREE BOXES · INCREASING THE PREVENTER DOSE FOR A FLARE-UP · never giving an escalation trigger or 000 advice · NEVER TRANSLATING 'OBSTRUCTION' INTO PLAIN ENGLISH · firing several puffs into the spacer at once · inventing peak-flow numbers for a ten-year-old · calling a non-reversible obstruction 'COPD' in a child · dismissing the steroid concern as a myth. THE CHECKLIST ALSO SCORES: open question before any numbers · three parts signposted · concerns elicited early · what spirometry is and how it is done · FVC then FEV1 then the ratio, in that order · the Ventolin challenge and the 12% threshold · THE ACTUAL 42% QUOTED · asthma named and described in plain words · TEACH-BACK BEFORE THE FORM · EVERY BOX NARRATED WHILE WRITING · THE PEN HANDED OVER for emergency contacts · prednisolone 30 mg each morning for three days · one puff and four breaths explained · PEAK FLOW LEFT BLANK WITH A REASON · danger signs and 000 · TWO COPIES AND A REVIEW DATE.

The three numbers, in order, in plain words — FVC — 'the TOTAL AMOUNT OF AIR he can blow out after that big breath in. His is NORMAL, so the size of his lungs is fine' · FEV1 — 'how much of that air he gets out IN THE VERY FIRST SECOND. That is the number that matters in asthma, and John's is LOWER THAN IT SHOULD BE' · THE RATIO — 'the machine compares the two and we check it against what is expected for a boy his age and height. His is 0.59 when we would expect about 0.86'

Translate obstruction in the same breath — 'When that happens we call it AN OBSTRUCTION, and what that means in plain terms is NARROWING IN HIS AIRWAYS — the air cannot get out as fast as it should.' USING 'OBSTRUCTION' AND STOPPING IS THE TRAP; THE EXAMINER IS SPECIFICALLY LISTENING FOR THE TRANSLATION, and she is briefed to ask 'NARROWING? IS THAT PERMANENT?'

The reversibility test answers her fear — 'We gave him a few puffs of Ventolin, WAITED ABOUT FIFTEEN MINUTES and repeated the whole test. In asthma we expect a big improvement in that first-second measurement — IN A CHILD, AN IMPROVEMENT OF MORE THAN 12% CONFIRMS ASTHMA. HIS WENT UP BY 42%. The narrowing opened right up.' The reversibility result IS the answer to 'is it permanent?'

The 10 versus 12 per cent argument — Do not get drawn in. THE TWO NUMBERS USE DIFFERENT DENOMINATORS — GINA and the Australian Asthma Handbook use 12% OF BASELINE, the ATS/ERS 2021 standard uses 10% OF PREDICTED and is not restricted to over-12s, and the 2005 rule was 12% AND 200 mL. QUOTE WHAT YOU CAN SEE: '42% FROM BASELINE, 26% OF PREDICTED — SIGNIFICANT ON EITHER CRITERION.' Then move on

Her three questions, answered together — 'Will he grow out of it? Will he have it forever? Can he still play footy? My sister has asthma — is it hereditary?' → 'MANY CHILDREN IMPROVE A LOT AS THEY GROW, though it can come back. HE ABSOLUTELY CAN PLAY SPORT — well-controlled asthma should not stop him doing anything, and a couple of puffs before a game helps if he needs it. And YES, IT DOES RUN IN FAMILIES, which fits with your sister'

Teach-back before you touch the form — 'That was a lot of new words. Can you tell me back in your own words what the test showed?' Move on only when she can say 'His airways were narrow and the puffer opened them up'

The ID box, and the pen — Name, today's date, NEXT CHECK-UP AT TWELVE MONTHS since he is otherwise well, and your details as his doctor. THEN HAND HER THE FORM FOR THE EMERGENCY CONTACT BOX — filling it yourself is the trap, because it is her contact and PASSING THE PEN IS A VISIBLE MARK OF SHARED DECISION-MAKING. TWO COPIES: ONE FOR HOME, ONE FOR THE SCHOOL

Green — when well — No night-time cough or wheeze, only the odd daytime symptom, only occasional reliever, and he can do everything he normally does. PREVENTER EXACTLY AS USUAL; RELIEVER 1 TO 2 PUFFS AS NEEDED UP TO EVERY FOUR HOURS, AND 1 TO 2 PUFFS BEFORE SPORT. HE IS ON NO PREVENTER, SO WRITE 'NONE — RELIEVER ONLY' RATHER THAN LEAVING IT BLANK, and say you will review it because his symptoms are frequent enough that he likely needs one

Orange — when not well, and the escalation trigger — Waking at night, symptoms first thing, needing the reliever more than usual, or asthma getting in the way. PREVENTER UNCHANGED; RELIEVER 4 TO 12 PUFFS, REPEATABLE EVERY TWENTY MINUTES. AND THE LINE YOU SAY AND WRITE: 'IF HE NEEDS THE BLUE PUFFER MORE OFTEN THAN EVERY THREE TO FOUR HOURS, SEE A DOCTOR THAT SAME DAY. THAT IS YOUR WARNING LIGHT'

Red — severe flare — Increasing wheeze and difficulty breathing, waking often at night, AND NEEDING THE PUFFER AGAIN WITHIN THREE HOURS. PREVENTER STILL UNCHANGED; RELIEVER 12 PUFFS REPEATED EVERY TWENTY MINUTES; AND PREDNISOLONE 30 mg EACH MORNING FOR THREE DAYS, which is 1 mg/kg for his 30 kg. See a doctor the same day

'Twelve puffs? That sounds like an enormous amount' — 'It does sound like a lot. IT IS A SAFE MEDICINE and this is the dose the national asthma guidelines recommend for a child his age in a flare-up. It may make him A BIT SHAKY OR GIVE HIM A FAST HEARTBEAT for a while — that is expected and it settles.' AND HOW TO ACTUALLY GIVE IT: 'TWELVE PUFFS DOES NOT MEAN TWELVE AT ONCE. One puff into the spacer, FOUR NORMAL BREATHS, then the next puff, shaking the puffer each time'

Danger signs, peak flow, and the close — 'If his symptoms get worse very quickly, if he is SO SHORT OF BREATH HE CANNOT SPEAK COMFORTABLY, if his LIPS LOOK BLUE, or if THE BLUE PUFFER IS NOT HELPING — CALL TRIPLE ZERO AND SAY ASTHMA EMERGENCY. Sit him upright, stay with him, keep giving the reliever until the ambulance arrives.' · LEAVE THE PEAK FLOW BOXES BLANK ON PURPOSE AND SAY WHY: PEAK FLOW IS NOT RECOMMENDED UNDER TWELVE YEARS · then two copies, a fortnight to check technique, annual review, and a closing teach-back

numbers: Spirometry usable from about age 6 · normal paediatric FEV1/FVC 0.85 to 0.90, never the adult 0.70 · challenge with salbutamol 400 microgram via spacer and repeat at 10 to 15 minutes · reversibility at least 12% from baseline, or over 10% of predicted · no reversibility does not exclude asthma · his: ratio 0.59 to 0.79, FEV1 +42%

Reliever ladder age 6+: 1 to 2 / 4 to 12 / 12, repeat every 20 minutes · age 1 to 5: 1 to 2 / 2 to 6 / 6 · preventer identical in all three boxes · prednisolone 1 mg/kg, max 50 mg, each morning for 3 days · escalate if reliever needed more often than 3 to 4 hourly; red zone if needed again within 3 hours · first aid 4 puffs, wait 4 minutes, 4 puffs, wait 4 minutes, then 000 · peak flow not under 12 years · review annually if controlled, 3 to 6 monthly if not · VERIFY all

setting: Two ways to fail. Naming a psychogenic cough before sweeping the differentials — you will recognise the honk in the first ninety seconds and must not say it for another four minutes. Or explaining it in words that tell a frustrated mother her daughter is imagining the cough. She opens angry after six months and two failed treatments, and the first fifteen seconds decide whether she gives you the social history the diagnosis lives in.
stem: Your general practice, regional South Australia. A 12-year-old girl, Mary, is brought in by her mother, having coughed for six months. A previous GP prescribed asthma inhalers and antibiotics; neither helped. The mother is angry that no one has found a cause.

Tasks: take a focused history for 6 minutes — physical examination findings will be handed to you on a card at 6 minutes — explain your diagnosis to the parent — explain your differential diagnoses and why each is less likely.

Read the examination card
Explain your diagnosis to the parent
Explain your differentials and why each is less likely
time: Defuse before you assess — let her finish, validate, and set out a plan · then characterise the cough including its sound · then the two positive questions: does she cough once asleep, and does it settle when she is absorbed in something · then the impact · then the ten-differential sweep, two questions each, said out loud · then the social history, where the diagnosis lives, asked gently and twice · then the well-child block and an offer to see Mary alone · then read every line of the card · then reassure about structure first, name it, explain both mechanisms, link it to her specific stressors, and give three reasons · then the differentials, deprescribing, the technique, and red flags.
findings: GROWTH ON THE 50TH CENTILE AND TRACKING · vitals normal, afebrile, SpO2 99% · no respiratory distress · NO FINGER CLUBBING · ENT normal, NO POST-NASAL SECRETIONS · CHEST CLEAR, EQUAL AIR ENTRY, NO ADDED SOUNDS · cardiovascular normal. READ EVERY LINE BEFORE YOU SPEAK — in the variant recall the card carries CLUBBING OR A FALLING CENTILE, and that single line rewrites the entire station

back.dx: PSYCHOGENIC COUGH — HABIT COUGH — A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION, REACHED IN THAT ORDER AND EXPLAINED WITHOUT EVER IMPLYING THE COUGH IS IMAGINED. THE DIFFERENTIALS, GIVEN TO THE PARENT IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH A REASON EACH SO SHE CAN SEE IT WAS NOT A GUESS: ASTHMA — no wheeze, no night or exercise pattern, no family or personal atopy, and a properly used inhaler with a spacer for six weeks did nothing · A LINGERING POST-VIRAL COUGH — possible at the start, but SIX MONTHS IS TOO LONG · WHOOPING COUGH — no coughing fits, no vomiting afterwards, fully immunised · TUBERCULOSIS — no travel, no contacts, no night sweats or weight loss · CYSTIC FIBROSIS OR BRONCHIECTASIS — a DRY rather than chesty cough, no chest infections, normal newborn screening, and growing beautifully · POST-NASAL DRIP FROM ALLERGY OR SINUS DISEASE — no nasal symptoms or facial pain · SOMETHING INHALED — no choking episode and both sides of the chest are clear · REFLUX — no heartburn or acid taste · A HEART PROBLEM — she keeps up with her friends at netball with no breathlessness or chest pain · AND IRRITANTS AT HOME — no smoke, dust or pets. THE ADOLESCENT-SPECIFIC MOVE THAT IS SEPARATELY MARKED: 'I USUALLY OFFER YOUNG PEOPLE A FEW MINUTES ON THEIR OWN, so they can raise anything they would rather say privately. WOULD THAT BE ALL RIGHT WITH YOU BOTH?' And if she does speak alone — 'I hate going to Dad's, I do not tell Mum because she cries' — the response is confidentiality with its limits stated plainly, then a screen of mood, sleep, appetite, SELF-HARM AND SAFEGUARDING, and thanks for the courage it took. THE NUMBERS: CHRONIC COUGH IN A CHILD IS OVER FOUR WEEKS, against eight in adults · this cough is SIX MONTHS, far beyond post-viral · TEN differentials swept with TWO questions each before naming a psychogenic cause · THREE reasons given to the parent · growth ON THE 50TH CENTILE AND TRACKING is the finding that supports you · REVIEW AT 2 TO 4 WEEKS · and the count that matters most, ZERO INVESTIGATIONS REQUIRED IN A CLASSIC CASE AND ZERO NEW PRESCRIPTIONS. AND THE RULE THAT OVERTURNS EVERYTHING: A CHRONIC WET COUGH OVER FOUR WEEKS IN A CHILD IS ALWAYS PATHOLOGICAL — think protracted bacterial bronchitis and bronchiectasis — AND IS NEVER A HABIT COUGH. THE THREE VARIANTS RUN OFF SINGLE LINES: THE WET COUGH with clubbing, coarse basal crackles and weight on the 10th centile needs a chest X-ray, sputum, spirometry, a SWEAT TEST and paediatric respiratory referral, with a longer targeted antibiotic course rather than another short one · THE UNDER-TREATED ASTHMATIC — worse at night and with netball, wheeze after sport, eczema as a toddler, salbutamol alone with no spacer and poor technique — where 'the treatment has not failed, SHE HAS NOT YET HAD THE RIGHT TREATMENT': watch the technique, add a spacer, start a preventer, do pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry, and give a written action plan · AND THE MOTHER WHO REFUSES the diagnosis and demands a scan and a specialist, where the answer is to negotiate rather than cave or dig in: 'I will arrange a chest X-ray and breathing tests as a baseline — NOT BECAUSE I EXPECT THEM TO SHOW ANYTHING, BUT BECAUSE YOU DESERVE TO SEE IT FOR YOURSELF', happily refer to a paediatrician, AND STILL PRESCRIBE NOTHING, because 'MORE ANTIBIOTICS WOULD NOT BE KINDNESS TO MARY'. THE LINES THAT RESCUE AN AWKWARD MOMENT: 'A normal examination is not me finding nothing — it is me ruling things out.' · 'I am not dismissing the cough; I am telling you where it is coming from.' · 'If anything changes in the way I have described, I will rethink this completely.' SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: SA Child Abuse Report Line 13 14 78 and Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800 for the adolescent conversation, and a school liaison and psychology referral as part of the plan rather than as an afterthought.
plan: WIPE, SIT AT HER LEVEL, AND LET HER VENT — then validate, apologise for the experience without blaming colleagues, and set out what you will do (see findings).
CHARACTERISE THE COUGH — constant or intermittent, getting worse, DRY OR CHESTY, AND THE SOUND: barking, whooping, or a loud honk. Note the honk and show no reaction.
PATTERN AND THE TWO POSITIVES — worse at night or with exercise · DOES SHE COUGH ONCE ASLEEP · DOES IT SETTLE WHEN DISTRACTED · then the impact on school and home.
THE SWEEP, PART ONE — asthma with the FULL INHALER INTERROGATION · post-viral onset · tuberculosis · pertussis · allergic rhinitis.

THE SWEEP, PART TWO — sinusitis and post-nasal drip · cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis with GREASY STOOLS AND THE HEEL PRICK · cardiac and exercise tolerance · foreign body · reflux and irritants including smoking, pets and a wood heater.
THE SOCIAL HISTORY — 'HOW ARE THINGS AT HOME?' THEN STOP TALKING. Ask again when she says 'not that good'. Then who she lives with, stresses, and SCHOOL AND BULLYING.
WELL-CHILD AND BACKGROUND — alert and active, eating and drinking, bowels and urine, WEIGHT LOSS · birth, heel prick, immunisations, growth and development.
OFFER TO SEE MARY ALONE FOR A FEW MINUTES, framed as something you do with all young people her age.
ASK FOR THE CARD AND READ EVERY LINE — growth centiles, vitals and saturation, distress, CLUBBING, ENT, full respiratory and cardiovascular examination.
Reassure about structural disease first, then name it, then explain both mechanisms (see findings).
LINK IT TO HER SPECIFIC STRESSORS BY NAME — the separation with the pattern around visits, and the tummy pains during last year's bullying — THEN GIVE THE THREE REASONS.
Handle 'So it is all in her head?' with the rescue line, then the differentials in plain English with a reason each.
THE PLAN — DEPRESCRIBE, the breathing and sipping technique, stop remarking on the cough, back to school and netball, address the stressor, REVIEW IN 2 TO 4 WEEKS, and RED FLAGS.

ask: The opening that buys the rest of the station: 'Before anything else — tell me what has been happening.' then 'I can hear how frustrating this has been, and you were right to keep bringing her back.'

The three questions that make the diagnosis positive rather than residual: 'What does the cough sound like — barking, whooping, or more of a honk?' · 'Does she cough once she is asleep?' · 'Does it settle when she is absorbed in something?'
The question that unlocks the social history: 'How are things at home?' — and then stop talking. Followed by 'How are things going at school? Has there ever been any bullying?'

'I have found no structural or physical problem in her lungs or airways.' / 'Some children cough when they are under stress, and that cough is completely real, not imagined.' / 'She is not pretending and she cannot simply stop.' / 'I am going to stop the puffers and the antibiotics, and here is why.'

CHALLENGES: 'So it is all in her head?' → the rescue line, keeping the cough real · 'Should we try a stronger antibiotic, or see a specialist?' → refer willingly, investigate reasonably, prescribe nothing · 'How can you say that? You have not asked me a single thing about our life' → which is what she says if you name it without the social history · 'The card shows clubbing and crackles' → A CHRONIC WET COUGH IS NEVER A HABIT COUGH; X-ray, sputum, spirometry, sweat test and respiratory referral.
pefe: ASK FOR IT IN FULL AND READ EVERY LINE: GROWTH PARAMETERS AND CENTILES · vital signs and OXYGEN SATURATION · general appearance and any respiratory distress · FINGER CLUBBING · ENT INCLUDING POST-NASAL SECRETIONS · a full respiratory examination with air entry and added sounds · and a cardiovascular examination. Glancing at it, seeing 'normal' and moving on is the trap, because the variant card carries clubbing or a falling centile.

Role-player: KAREN, 41, a school administration officer in a regional town, SEPARATED FROM MARY'S FATHER ABOUT FOUR MONTHS AGO with Mary staying with him every second weekend; a son of 8; nobody smokes, no pets. MARY IS 12, born at term, normal heel prick, FULLY IMMUNISED, no medical problems or allergies, ALWAYS ON THE 50TH CENTILE, plays netball, NO FAMILY HISTORY OF ATOPY. The cough is six months old, possibly after a mild cold, DRY, ALL DAY, LOUD LIKE A HONK, never during sleep, quieter when distracted, and she has missed a lot of school.

HOW TO PLAY IT: OPEN HOT — sharp and interrupting for the first thirty seconds — AND SOFTEN ONLY IF THEY VALIDATE THE FRUSTRATION FIRST; if they answer anger with a clinical question, stay cold and give short answers. NEVER VOLUNTEER THE SLEEP PATTERN, THE SEPARATION OR THE BULLYING. MAKE THEM ASK TWICE ABOUT HOME — 'NOT THAT GOOD, DOCTOR' and then silence. CHALLENGE THE DIAGNOSIS ONCE WITH 'SO IT IS ALL IN HER HEAD?' and push for more treatment. AND IF THEY NAME A PSYCHOGENIC COUGH WITHOUT EVER ASKING ABOUT HOME OR SCHOOL, SAY: 'HOW CAN YOU SAY THAT? YOU HAVE NOT ASKED ME A SINGLE THING ABOUT OUR LIFE.'

AUTOMATIC FAIL: NAMING A PSYCHOGENIC COUGH BEFORE SWEEPING THE DIFFERENTIALS · saying the cough is IMAGINARY, MADE UP OR 'JUST STRESS' · MISSING A RED FLAG ON A VARIANT CARD · prescribing another antibiotic or escalating the inhaler. SCORE 30 OR MORE OF 39 WITH NO AUTOMATIC FAIL: validated the frustration · cough timing, dry or wet, SOUND · night and exercise · SLEEP · DISTRACTION · impact · breathlessness · asthma INCLUDING INHALER TECHNIQUE AND SPACER · post-viral · TB · pertussis · rhinitis · sinusitis · cystic fibrosis · cardiac and exercise tolerance · foreign body · reflux · irritants and smoking · HOME AND SEPARATION · SCHOOL AND BULLYING · well-child questions · growth, immunisation, development · asked for the findings · REASSURED ABOUT STRUCTURAL DISEASE FIRST · named it in plain words · EXPLAINED BOTH MECHANISMS · LINKED IT TO HER SPECIFIC STRESSORS · three reasons · six or more differentials with reasons · STOPPED THE INHALERS AND ANTIBIOTICS · gave a cough-suppression technique · addressed the stressor or school · OFFERED TO SEE MARY ALONE · red flags and review · summarised.

Defuse first — the first fifteen seconds — 'Before anything else — TELL ME WHAT HAS BEEN HAPPENING.' Let her finish. Then: 'I CAN HEAR HOW FRUSTRATING THIS HAS BEEN. Six months of coughing, two lots of treatment, and still no answer — I WOULD FEEL EXACTLY THE SAME, AND YOU WERE RIGHT TO KEEP BRINGING HER BACK.' Opening with 'how long has the cough been there?' when the stem and the mother have both already said six months reads as not listening, AND SHE STAYS COLD IF YOU ANSWER HER ANGER WITH A CLINICAL QUESTION

The sound — recognise it and say nothing — 'What does it sound like — A BARKING SOUND, A WHOOPING SOUND AT THE END OF A BOUT, OR MORE OF A LOUD HONKING NOISE?' → 'It is loud. HONESTLY, IT IS LIKE A HONK, LIKE A GOOSE. You can hear it from the other end of the house.' YOU NOW KNOW THE ANSWER AND MUST NOT ANNOUNCE IT — make a note, show no reaction, and keep going

The two positive questions — 'DOES SHE COUGH ONCE SHE IS ASLEEP?' → she pauses, surprised — 'NO. ACTUALLY, NO, NEVER. I HAD NOT THOUGHT ABOUT THAT' · 'DOES IT SETTLE WHEN SHE IS ABSORBED IN SOMETHING — A FILM, A GAME?' → yes. THESE ARE THE STRONGEST POSITIVE EVIDENCE YOU WILL GET, and without them your diagnosis rests on absence of disease alone

The ten-differential sweep, two questions each — 1 ASTHMA — wheeze, family and personal atopy, AND WHICH INHALER, WHAT TECHNIQUE, WITH A SPACER, FOR HOW LONG · 2 POST-VIRAL — did it start after a cold · 3 TB — travel, contacts with a long cough, night sweats, fevers, weight loss · 4 PERTUSSIS — coughing fits, VOMITING AT THE END OF A BOUT, whoop · 5 ALLERGIC RHINITIS — runny nose, sneezing, itchy eyes · 6 SINUSITIS AND POST-NASAL DRIP — secretions down the back of the throat, facial pain · 7 CYSTIC FIBROSIS AND BRONCHIECTASIS — recurrent chest infections, LOOSE GREASY STOOLS, newborn heel prick · 8 CARDIAC — cyanosis, chest pain, exercise tolerance versus peers · 9 FOREIGN BODY — any choking episode · 10 REFLUX AND IRRITANTS — heartburn, sour taste, smoking, pets, dust, mould, wood heater

Failed treatment is not excluded disease — 'The inhaler did not work' does NOT exclude asthma. ASK WHICH ONE, WHAT TECHNIQUE, WITH A SPACER, HOW OFTEN AND FOR HOW LONG. Here the answer is a blue puffer used properly with a spacer for six weeks — which genuinely helps you. IN THE UNDER-TREATED VARIANT IT IS SALBUTAMOL ALONE, NO SPACER, POOR TECHNIQUE AND NO PREVENTER, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE STATION

The social history, asked gently and twice — 'Some questions about life in general now, because a long-standing cough can be affected by what else is going on. HOW ARE THINGS AT HOME?' THEN STOP TALKING. She says only 'NOT THAT GOOD, DOCTOR' and waits to be asked again. 'Thank you for telling me. CAN YOU TELL ME A LITTLE MORE?' Then: who does she live with, stresses at home, anyone unwell, AND HOW SHE IS GETTING ON AT SCHOOL AND WHETHER THERE HAS EVER BEEN BULLYING

The two gifts — A current stressor with a temporal link — 'My partner and I separated a few months ago, and she coughs much more around the times she goes to her dad's' · and a previous physical symptom in response to stress — 'She had bullying at school last year, and she had a lot of tummy pains then, and they stopped once the teacher dealt with it'. Both go into your explanation by name

Reassure about structure before you name anything — 'The most important thing I can tell you is that I HAVE FOUND NO STRUCTURAL OR PHYSICAL PROBLEM IN MARY'S LUNGS OR AIRWAYS. Her growth is normal, her chest is completely clear, and ALL MY QUESTIONS ABOUT THE SERIOUS CAUSES CAME BACK NEGATIVE.' A normal examination is not you finding nothing — IT IS YOU RULING THINGS OUT, and saying so converts it into a positive finding

The two mechanisms, then the three reasons — Mechanism one: 'Some children cough when they are under stress — the body expresses stress physically, and that cough is entirely real, not imagined' · mechanism two: 'It often begins after an ordinary viral infection — the child coughs for weeks, the infection clears, but the coughing has become a habit the body has not switched off' · then three reasons: the sound and the fact it stops in sleep · the stressors and the pattern around the visits · and a completely normal examination and growth with no warning signs

'So you are saying she is putting it on?' — The rescue line: 'Not at all, and I want to be clear about that. She is not pretending and she cannot simply stop. The cough is real — what is different is that it comes from a habit and a stress response rather than from disease in her lungs. And the good news is that it is very treatable, which is more than I could say if this were scarring in the lung'

The plan — four separate marks, all easy — ONE, STOP THE PUFFERS AND THE ANTIBIOTICS, because they are not treating anything and they have side effects · TWO, THE TECHNIQUE: when she feels the urge, SLOW BREATHS AND SIPS OF WATER INSTEAD OF COUGHING, with the clear message that this will settle · THREE, AT HOME AND SCHOOL STOP DRAWING ATTENTION TO EACH COUGH, and she returns to full school and netball · FOUR, ADDRESS THE STRESS ITSELF — a word with the school, and a psychologist if that would help · THEN REVIEW IN 2 TO 4 WEEKS and RED FLAGS: a chesty cough or haemoptysis, weight loss, breathlessness or fever
fails: ★ Naming a psychogenic cough before sweeping the differentials — you will hear the honk in the first ninety seconds and must not say it for another four minutes
★ Explaining it in words that tell her the cough is imaginary, made up, or 'just stress' — she is not pretending and she cannot simply stop
Opening with a clinical question instead of letting her vent, which costs the rapport marks in the first fifteen seconds and closes off the social history the diagnosis lives in
Treating 'the inhaler did not work' as excluding asthma without asking which drug, what technique, with a spacer, for how long

Ending on reassurance without deprescribing, without a technique, without addressing the stressor and without red flags — four separate marks, all easy; and glancing at a card that in the variant carries clubbing or a falling centile

setting: The station is the travel history. 'Have you been overseas?' Followed by 'Yes, malaysia' and then moving on will fail you no matter how good the rest is — the mosquito bites and the pre-travel vaccination are released only if the specific questions are asked. The second trap is converging on gastroenteritis because he has vomited and has diarrhoea, when the cough, sore throat and body aches make that cluster an atypical pneumonia pattern.
stem: General practice, Whyalla, regional South Australia. You are the GP registrar. David chen, 7 years, with fever and dry cough for 24 hours. The family returned three days ago from a one-month trip to malaysia. Temp 38.0 measured at home. COVID rapid antigen test negative. Further vital signs from the examiner on request. His mother Jane has come to talk to you.

Tasks: take a focused, relevant history from the mother — you have six minutes for this — explain your most likely diagnosis and the differentials you have considered. No physical examination in this station. 8 minutes.

time: Vital signs from the examiner before you sit, then one sentence answering her stated worry · then the cough in full, including character and sound even though the stem already says dry · then the travel box, signposted and asked in seven headings · then the widened screen across the whole body, because infections picked up overseas do not stay in the lungs · then close the cough list with pertussis, foreign body, atopy and smoke · then four well-child questions and immunisation · then the diagnosis in lay terms with three reasons, two separately named differential lists, the alarm managed, and specific safety-netting.
findings: The widened screen — some infections do not stay in the lungs

Fever and what was given · ENT: ear pain, runny nose, SORE THROAT, drooling, voice change, neck lumps · GASTROINTESTINAL: VOMITING, DIARRHOEA, tummy pain · MUSCULOSKELETAL: JOINT PAINS OR ACHING ALL OVER · RASH ANYWHERE, which is the question that catches dengue · MENINGITIS: headache, stiff neck, photophobia · AND JAUNDICE of skin or eyes

back.dx: ATYPICAL PNEUMONIA IN A SEVEN-YEAR-OLD RETURNED TRAVELLER — DIAGNOSED ON HISTORY ALONE, BECAUSE THERE IS NO EXAMINATION IN THIS STATION. THE PLAN: BLOODS TODAY INCLUDING MALARIA TESTING · START AZITHROMYCIN NOW RATHER THAN WAITING — 10 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 500 mg DAILY FOR 3 DAYS, avoiding doxycycline under eight years for this indication · PARACETAMOL FOR THE FEVER · PLENTY OF FLUIDS · AND REVIEW IN A DAY OR TWO, SOONER IF ANYTHING CHANGES. THE SAFETY NET, WHICH MUST SURVIVE THE CLOCK — even with fifteen seconds left, give three specific triggers: DROWSY OR HARD TO ROUSE · WORKING HARD TO BREATHE · UNABLE TO KEEP FLUIDS DOWN · A RASH THAT DOES NOT FADE UNDER A GLASS · A STIFF NECK OR DISLIKE OF LIGHT · BLEEDING FROM NOSE OR GUMS · OR TURNING YELLOW. AND IF HE IS NOT CLEARLY IMPROVING IN 48 HOURS, REVIEW REGARDLESS. THE CLINICAL PATTERNS THAT SEPARATE THE TWO PNEUMONIAS: ATYPICAL — DRY COUGH, FEVER AROUND 38, BODY ACHES AND SORE THROAT, VOMITING AND DIARRHOEA, SCHOOL-AGED · TYPICAL — ABRUPT ONSET, PRODUCTIVE COUGH, FEVER 39 TO 40 WITH RIGORS, FOCAL CHEST SIGNS. THE TRAVEL-INFECTION NUMBERS WORTH CARRYING: MALARIA IS EXCLUDED ONLY AFTER THICK AND THIN FILMS PLUS A RAPID ANTIGEN TEST, THREE SETS 12 TO 24 HOURS APART · DENGUE INCUBATES 3 TO 14 DAYS AND TAKES NO ASPIRIN AND NO IBUPROFEN · TYPHOID GIVES A DRY COUGH, A STEPWISE FEVER AND RELATIVE BRADYCARDIA · AND TB MEANS A COUGH OVER THREE WEEKS WITH NIGHT SWEATS OR WEIGHT LOSS. NOTIFIABLE IN SOUTH AUSTRALIA: MALARIA, DENGUE, TYPHOID, TUBERCULOSIS, LEGIONELLOSIS, Q FEVER AND MEASLES. THE COMMUNICATION MOVES THAT CARRY THIS STATION: asking the examiner for THE SATURATION AND RESPIRATORY RATE BEFORE SITTING DOWN, so you are not eight minutes into a consultation without knowing whether the child is hypoxic · ONE SENTENCE ANSWERING HER STATED WORRY rather than a clinical question — 'I can hear how worried you are, and that is completely understandable' · SIGNPOSTING THE TRAVEL BLOCK AND EXPLAINING WHY IT MATTERS · asking the cough character and the barking and whooping sounds even though the stem and the age argue against them · naming BOTH differential groups explicitly · and holding a frightening list without leaving the parent inside the fear it created. THE TELEHEALTH VARIANT IS MARKED ON DIFFERENT BEHAVIOURS ENTIRELY: confirming identity and a callback number in case the call drops, stating plainly that you cannot examine him and what you will do if concerned, USING THE PARENT AS YOUR EXAMINER — counting a full minute of breathing, describing work of breathing, photographing the chest and back for a rash — and defining explicitly what would trigger an in-person review. QUARANTINE ALSO MATTERS CLINICALLY, BECAUSE IT CONSTRAINS HOW QUICKLY THE CHILD CAN BE SEEN, SO THE SAFETY-NETTING MUST BE MORE SPECIFIC, NOT LESS. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 and the Women's and Children's Hospital in North Adelaide for escalation from Whyalla, and notification to SA Health for any of the listed travel infections.
plan: ASK THE EXAMINER FOR VITAL SIGNS BEFORE SITTING — SATURATION AND RESPIRATORY RATE PARTICULARLY, plus heart rate and blood pressure. Then introduce yourself and confirm both names.
OPEN QUESTION, THEN ONE SENTENCE OF EMPATHY ANSWERING HER STATED WORRY — not a clinical question on top of it.
THE COUGH — exact onset, continuous or intermittent, progression, DRY OR PRODUCTIVE CONFIRMED ALOUD, BARKING, HONKING OR WHOOPING, aggravating factors, and breathlessness or noisy breathing.
SIGNPOST THE TRAVEL BLOCK AND EXPLAIN WHY — then DURATION AND DESTINATION, and ACTIVITIES including jungle, caves, farms and freshwater swimming.
BITES — ASKED SPECIFICALLY — THEN FOLLOWED UP WITH DAY VERSUS EVENING BITING · contacts with unwell people, animals or birds · street food and drinking water.
'DID YOU SEE A GP BEFORE YOU TRAVELLED?' — then name the likely hepatitis A and typhoid pair, AND ASK SEPARATELY ABOUT DAILY MALARIA PROPHYLAXIS.
THE WIDENED SCREEN, SIGNPOSTED — fever and what was given · ENT · GASTROINTESTINAL · BODY ACHES AND JOINT PAINS · RASH · meningitis screen · JAUNDICE.
CLOSE THE COUGH LIST — pertussis, foreign body, family atopy, smoke at home — asked out loud rather than filtered by age.
WELL-CHILD AND IMMUNISATION — alert or drowsy, eating and drinking, urine output, AND VACCINATION STATUS, which covers pertussis, pneumococcus and measles and links back to the pre-travel question.
Name atypical pneumonia in lay terms and give the three reasons, ending with the antibiotic difference (see findings).
THE FIRST GROUP — other causes of cough and fever, with the negative COVID test and the TB duration point made explicitly.
THE SECOND GROUP — travel-related infections, with MALARIA AT THE TOP and typhoid's dry cough named as genuinely relevant.
RE-ANCHOR AND JUSTIFY THE MALARIA TEST WITHOUT LEAVING HER IN THE FEAR · then the plan — bloods, azithromycin now, paracetamol, fluids, review — AND THE SPECIFIC SAFETY-NET TRIGGERS, WRITTEN DOWN.
back.planNote: the stem gives six minutes for the history and two for both differential lists - the travel box and the widened screen are where the marks concentrate
ask: The question the station is built on: 'Did he get any insect or mosquito bites?' — followed by whether they were daytime or evening. And the second: 'Did you see a GP before you travelled? And was he given anything daily for malaria?'

The signposts: 'I would like to ask about the trip in some detail, because where he has been changes what I need to think about.' · 'Now some questions about the rest of his body, not just his chest.' · 'There are two groups of things I have considered.'

The diagnosis and its reasons: 'Pneumonia is a lung infection. Atypical means the bug causing it is one of the unusual ones.' · 'Three reasons: the cough is dry, the fever is mild grade, and the vomiting, diarrhoea and body aches fit the atypical pattern.' · 'The usual antibiotic, amoxicillin, does not cover these bugs — so I would use azithromycin.'

The malaria lines: 'Any fever in someone back from the tropics has to be tested for malaria, regardless of how well everything else fits.' and 'I do not think he has malaria. But it is the one we test for rather than assume.'

CHALLENGES: 'He has vomiting and diarrhoea, is this gastro?' → the cough, sore throat and body aches make it an atypical cluster · 'Why not just do a chest X-ray?' → the diagnosis is clinical and the bloods including malaria are what change management here · 'His fever is 39.6 with pain behind the eyes and bleeding gums' → DENGUE WITH A WARNING SIGN: paracetamol only, NO IBUPROFEN OR ASPIRIN, platelets today · 'The cough has actually been four weeks and Grandma has coughed for months' → tuberculosis, notifiable, contact tracing and isolation.
pefe: THERE IS NO PHYSICAL EXAMINATION IN THIS STATION — WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY THE VITAL SIGNS MUST BE REQUESTED FROM THE EXAMINER BEFORE YOU SIT DOWN: SATURATION 98% ON ROOM AIR, RESPIRATORY RATE 22, HEART RATE 104, BLOOD PRESSURE 100/62, TEMPERATURE 38.1. Those numbers are what let you say the reassuring sentence — his oxygen and breathing rate are normal — rather than guessing.

Role-player: JANE CHEN, 38, an office manager in Whyalla; husband Wei was born in Malaysia and his family still lives there. ONE MONTH IN MALAYSIA, mostly Kuala Lumpur with about ten days up north with family, RETURNED THREE DAYS AGO. Normal tourist activities, NO caves, farms or river swimming. DAVID IS 7, healthy, no medicines or allergies, ALL IMMUNISATIONS UP TO DATE, nobody smokes, and his father had asthma as a child.

HOW TO PLAY IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED — THIS IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE STATION. THE MOSQUITO BITES ARE THE KEY WITHHELD FINDING and are released only on a specific question about insect or mosquito bites; if asked 'did anything happen on the trip?' say 'NOT REALLY'; if asked only 'have you been overseas?' say 'YES, MALAYSIA' AND NOTHING MORE. THE PRE-TRAVEL GP VISIT IS THE SECOND WITHHELD FINDING. Sore throat, body aches, vomiting and diarrhoea are all present but VOLUNTEERED ONLY WHEN THAT SPECIFIC SYSTEM IS ASKED ABOUT. REACT WITH ALARM IF MALARIA IS MENTIONED. If the doctor never asks about the trip in detail, DO NOT RESCUE THEM — at about minute seven you may say only 'SO WHAT DO YOU THINK IT IS?'

AUTOMATIC FAIL: TAKING NO TRAVEL HISTORY BEYOND 'HAVE YOU BEEN OVERSEAS?', so the bites and the pre-travel vaccination are never elicited · DIAGNOSING GASTROENTERITIS on the vomiting and diarrhoea while discarding the cough, sore throat and body aches · GIVING ONLY ONE DIFFERENTIAL LIST, either a pure respiratory list that ignores the travel or an exotic list with no respiratory diagnoses in it · REACHING A CONFIDENT DIAGNOSIS AND DISCHARGING WITHOUT EVER MENTIONING MALARIA TESTING IN A FEBRILE RETURNED TRAVELLER. The checklist also scores: vital signs requested before starting · empathy statement · exact onset · continuous versus intermittent and progression · DRY VERSUS PRODUCTIVE CONFIRMED · barking, honking and whooping · aggravating factors · breathlessness · TRAVEL HISTORY SIGNPOSTED AND OPENED · duration and destination · activities · BITES · contacts · food and water · PRE-TRAVEL GP · MALARIA PROPHYLAXIS · ENT · gastrointestinal · BODY ACHES · RASH · meningitis screen · jaundice · pertussis · foreign body · atopy and smoke · well-child questions · immunisation · ATYPICAL PNEUMONIA NAMED AND EXPLAINED IN LAY TERMS · THREE REASONS · BOTH LISTS NAMED SEPARATELY · MALARIA TESTING JUSTIFIED CALMLY · specific safety-netting and review.

The travel box — seven headings, signposted — 'I would like to ask about the trip in some detail now, BECAUSE WHERE HE HAS BEEN CHANGES WHAT I NEED TO THINK ABOUT.' DURATION AND DESTINATION · ACTIVITIES — bushwalking, jungle, caves, farms, swimming in rivers or lakes · BITES · CONTACTS with unwell people, animals or birds · FOOD AND WATER — street food, bottled water · AND DID YOU SEE A GP BEFORE YOU TRAVELLED. In a child skip the Drugs and Exposure headings

Follow the bites and the shots — 'WERE THEY MOSTLY DURING THE DAY OR IN THE EVENING? DAYTIME BITING MOSQUITOES CARRY DIFFERENT INFECTIONS FROM THE NIGHT-TIME ONES' → both, more in the evenings eating outside · AND 'that is usually hepatitis A, often with typhoid. WAS HE GIVEN ANYTHING TO TAKE EVERY DAY WHILE YOU WERE AWAY, FOR MALARIA?' → NO, NOTHING DAILY, JUST THE INJECTIONS. Using a positive finding rather than filing it is what the examiner is watching for

What she gives you — Cough started EXACTLY YESTERDAY, constant, worse today, COMPLETELY DRY, no barking or whooping, no day-night pattern, NOT SHORT OF BREATH · a bit of a runny nose and A SORE THROAT · VOMITED TWICE AND DIARRHOEA SINCE THIS MORNING · BODY ACHES, ESPECIALLY HIS LEGS · no rash, no headache or stiff neck, no jaundice · quieter than usual but up and about, off his food but drinking, urine normal · FULLY IMMUNISED

The cluster that is not gastroenteritis — Hearing vomiting and diarrhoea and quietly converging on gastro is the trap. THIS CHILD HAS A COUGH, A SORE THROAT AND BODY ACHES AS WELL, AND THAT COMBINATION IS AN ATYPICAL PNEUMONIA PATTERN. The other trap is dropping the rash question, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT CATCHES DENGUE

The diagnosis in lay terms — 'I think David most likely has something called ATYPICAL PNEUMONIA. PNEUMONIA IS A LUNG INFECTION. The reason we call this one atypical is that THE BUG CAUSING IT IS ONE OF THE LESS COMMON, UNUSUAL ONES — not the bugs that usually cause a chest infection. They still cause a genuine lung infection; they just behave a bit differently.' Saying 'atypical pneumonia' and stopping loses the mark — 'LUNG INFECTION CAUSED BY UNUSUAL BUGS' IS THE PHRASE TO HAVE READY

The three reasons for atypical over typical — One, his cough is dry — the usual bacterial pneumonias give a chesty, productive cough · two, his temperature is 38, a mild-grade fever — the typical bugs usually push it to 39 or 40 · three, everything else he has — the vomiting, diarrhoea, aching and sore throat — is characteristic of the atypical bugs. And the practical difference is the antibiotic: amoxicillin does not cover these, so azithromycin instead

Two differential lists, named as groups — SAY THE WORDS 'THE FIRST GROUP' AND 'THE SECOND GROUP' SO THE EXAMINER HEARS THE STRUCTURE. GROUP ONE, OTHER CAUSES OF COUGH AND FEVER: typical bacterial and viral pneumonia with the negative COVID test noted · TUBERCULOSIS, considered seriously in any returned traveller though TB usually causes weeks of cough rather than a day · throat and tonsil infections · pertussis · something inhaled · asthma. GROUP TWO, TRAVEL-RELATED: MALARIA AT THE TOP · dengue · TYPHOID, WHICH CLASSICALLY CAUSES A DRY COUGH so it is genuinely relevant · glandular fever · Q fever · Legionnaires' disease · and the mosquito-borne infections affecting the lining of the brain. ONE LIST ONLY IS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL EITHER WAY

Manage the alarm you just created — 'MALARIA? DO YOU THINK HE HAS MALARIA?' → 'NO — I DO NOT. His story fits a chest infection much better. BUT MALARIA IS THE ONE CONDITION WHERE THE RULE IS ABSOLUTE: ANYONE WITH A FEVER WHO HAS BEEN IN THE TROPICS GETS TESTED, because it is the one that can turn dangerous fastest. It is a blood test, and it is how we make sure RATHER THAN ASSUME.' Name the alternatives, then IMMEDIATELY RE-ANCHOR to the main diagnosis

The variants — TELEHEALTH IN HOTEL QUARANTINE — confirm identity and a callback number, state the limitation of remote assessment, USE THE PARENT AS YOUR EXAMINER by having her count the respiratory rate for a full minute and photograph the chest and back, and define what would trigger in-person review · DENGUE-WEIGHTED — 39.6, RETRO-ORBITAL HEADACHE, a BLANCHING rash, AND BLEEDING GUMS as a warning sign → PARACETAMOL ONLY, NO IBUPROFEN AND NO ASPIRIN, platelet count today, and still test for malaria · THE FOUR-WEEK COUGH — weight loss, night sweats, and a grandmother who has coughed for months → TUBERCULOSIS, notifiable, with contact tracing and respiratory isolation while it is worked up

The two withheld findings — 'Did he get any insect or mosquito bites?' → 'Oh — yes. He got a lot of mosquito bites, actually. All over his hands' · and 'Did you see a GP before you travelled?' → 'Yes, he gave them some hepatitis shots'. Both are released only on the specific question. If you ask 'Did anything happen on the trip?' She says 'Not really'

Ask pertussis and foreign body anyway — Omitting them because the child is seven is the trap — PERTUSSIS HAS NO AGE GROUP AND ASKING IT IS A MARKED ITEM. Whooping, vomiting after a long run of coughing, any choking episode, family atopy, and smoking at home. SAY THEM OUT LOUD RATHER THAN FILTERING BY AGE. The same applies to asking the cough character when the stem already says dry — THE EXAMINER IS MARKING WHETHER YOUR STRUCTURE IS COMPLETE, NOT WHETHER YOU CAN READ THE STEM

Converging on gastroenteritis because of the vomiting and diarrhoea, when the cough, sore throat and body aches make that cluster an atypical pneumonia pattern

Dropping the rash question, which is the one that catches dengue; omitting pertussis and foreign body because the child is seven; or finishing with 'come back if he gets worse' instead of three specific triggers
numbers: Travel box: duration and destination, then activities · bites · contacts · food and water · pre-travel GP — skip drugs and exposure in a child · atypical clues: dry cough, fever about 38, body aches and sore throat, vomiting and diarrhoea, school-aged · typical clues: abrupt onset, productive cough, fever 39 to 40 with rigors, focal chest signs

Azithromycin 10 mg/kg (Max 500 mg) daily for 3 days · avoid doxycycline under 8 years for this indication · malaria: thick and thin films plus rapid antigen, 3 sets 12 to 24 hours apart before exclusion · dengue incubates 3 to 14 days, no aspirin and no ibuprofen · typhoid: dry cough, stepwise fever, relative bradycardia · TB: cough over 3 weeks with night sweats or weight loss · notifiable in SA: malaria, dengue, typhoid, TB, legionellosis, Q fever, measles · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: Four lines pass this station: 'Is it worse when he feeds?' · 'Is it worse lying on his back?' · 'Blood pressure in all four limbs, please.' · 'Are the femoral pulses palpable?' The examiner volunteers nothing, and never requesting four-limb blood pressure or femoral pulses is the AUTOMATIC FAIL. A mother brings a five-week-old in with a cough and you have to leave with a cardiac diagnosis.
stem: Emergency department, a regional South Australian hospital. A five-week-old boy is brought in by his mother, worried about cough and noisy breathing. Triage: temperature 36.8 · heart rate 178 · respiratory rate 68 · SpO2 93% right hand in air · weight 3.65 kg against a birth weight of 3.40 kg.

Tasks: take a focused history from the mother, 4 minutes — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings, 2 minutes, nothing is volunteered — explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the mother, 2 minutes.

time: WIPE, keep the baby on her lap, and get the agenda out in the first thirty seconds · then characterise the cough and the noise, and ask both pivot questions — position and feeding — whichever answer you expect · then colour change, sweating, feed duration and completion, and the unwell-baby screen · then forty seconds of birth history, immunisation, contacts and family history · then the examination request with four-limb blood pressure and femoral pulses first · then the diagnosis in plain words with its reasons, the guilt answered before the logistics, the differentials, and the safety net.
findings: The weight is a cardiac sign

3.65 kg AT FIVE WEEKS AGAINST A BIRTH WEIGHT OF 3.40 kg — 250 g IN FIVE WEEKS AGAINST AN EXPECTED 150 TO 200 g PER WEEK. Recognising failure to thrive as a sign of cardiac failure rather than as a feeding problem is the difference between collecting numbers and interpreting them. Wet nappies are down to about four a day

Alert but tachypnoeic and pale, subcostal recession, capillary refill three seconds · right arm 136/91, left arm 124/82, left leg 67/45, right leg 58/41 · femoral pulses not palpable, radio-femoral delay and a radio-radial difference · saturations 93% right hand and 86% right foot · fine bibasal crackles, no wheeze or stridor · apex displaced and heaving, systolic murmur in the left infraclavicular area radiating to the back, gallop rhythm · liver 3 cm below the costal margin

'IT IS WORSE WHENEVER I PUT HIM DOWN IN HIS COT. IF I HOLD HIM UPRIGHT OR ON HIS TUMMY HE IS MUCH QUIETER. HE FEEDS BEAUTIFULLY AND HE HAS PUT ON 200 GRAMS A WEEK.' STILL ASK FOR FOUR-LIMB PRESSURES AND FEMORALS — they are normal. Then: the tissues at the top of the voice box are soft and get drawn inwards ON BREATHING IN, which is exactly why it is worse on his back and better held upright. Very common, not dangerous in itself, RESOLVES BY 12 TO 24 MONTHS. Weigh regularly, feed upright in smaller more frequent feeds, smoke-free house, review in 2 to 4 weeks — AND KEEP SLEEPING HIM ON HIS BACK. ENT referral if apnoea, cyanosis, feeding difficulty, faltering growth or recession

back.dx: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA PRESENTING AS COUGH AND NOISY BREATHING IN A FIVE-WEEK-OLD — AND THE WHOLE STATION IS WHETHER YOU ASK FOR FOUR-LIMB BLOOD PRESSURE AND FEMORAL PULSES. THE ONE SENTENCE TO LEAVE THE ROOM HAVING SAID: 'MAY I HAVE HIS BLOOD PRESSURE IN ALL FOUR LIMBS, AND ARE THE FEMORAL PULSES PALPABLE?' It costs eight seconds and the mark sheet is built around it. THE NUMBERS THAT INTERPRET THE FINDINGS: AN ARM-TO-LEG SYSTOLIC GRADIENT OVER 20 mmHg IS SIGNIFICANT COARCTATION · normal infant systolic is 65 TO 95 mmHg AND THE LEG SHOULD BE EQUAL TO OR HIGHER THAN THE ARM · A PRE- TO POST-DUCTAL SATURATION DIFFERENCE OVER 3% IS DIFFERENTIAL CYANOSIS · coarctation occurs in about 1 IN 2500 LIVE BIRTHS and 5 TO 8% OF CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE · A BICUSPID AORTIC VALVE ACCOMPANIES IT IN 50 TO 85% · weight gain should be 150 TO 200 g PER WEEK with at least 4 TO 6 WET NAPPIES A DAY · and FEVER AT OR ABOVE 38 UNDER THREE MONTHS MEANS A SEPTIC SCREEN AND ADMISSION. DRUGS: ALPROSTADIL 5 TO 10 nanogram/kg/min INTRAVENOUSLY, TITRATED, WATCHING FOR APNOEA; FRUSEMIDE 1 mg/kg; FLUID BOLUSES 10 mL/kg CAUTIOUSLY VERIFY ALL. THE EXAMINER CHALLENGES AND THEIR ANSWERS. 'THOSE BLOOD PRESSURES ARE NOT POSSIBLE IN A NEONATE' → 'You are right that I have taken the readings at face value. THE FINDING I AM ACTING ON IS THE DIRECTION OF THE GRADIENT. An upper-limb systolic more than 20 mmHg above the lower limb with impalpable femorals is coarctation until echocardiography says otherwise, and I would recheck with a correctly sized cuff.' 'WOULD YOU EXPECT RIB NOTCHING?' → 'No. RIB NOTCHING DEPENDS ON YEARS OF COLLATERAL INTERCOSTAL FLOW AND IS RARELY SEEN BEFORE ABOUT FIVE YEARS. In a neonate I would expect cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion instead.' 'WHY NOT CROUP?' → 'Croup is essentially a diagnosis from around six months to three years; it would be very unusual at five weeks and does not explain the pulses or the liver.' 'WHY ARE YOU CAUTIOUS WITH OXYGEN?' → 'OXYGEN IS A PULMONARY VASODILATOR AND ENCOURAGES DUCTAL CLOSURE. In a duct-dependent systemic lesion both effects worsen systemic perfusion, so I would correct hypoxia but avoid unrestricted high flow and target saturations on cardiology advice.' 'WHAT LESIONS TRAVEL WITH COARCTATION?' → 'BICUSPID AORTIC VALVE IN ROUGHLY 50 TO 85%, VENTRICULAR SEPTAL DEFECT, PATENT DUCTUS, SHONE COMPLEX, TURNER SYNDROME IN A GIRL, AND BERRY ANEURYSMS OF THE CIRCLE OF WILLIS.' THE TIMING DISCIPLINE THIS STATION DEMANDS: WIPE AND AGENDA BY 0:30 · cough and the describe-the-noise questions by 1:30 · THE TWO PIVOT QUESTIONS AND THE FEEDING BLOCK BY 2:15 · screening by 3:00 · birth history, immunisation and family by 4:00 · EXAMINATION REQUESTS FROM 4:00 TO 6:00 WITH FOUR-LIMB PRESSURES AND FEMORALS FIRST · diagnosis, guilt, differentials and escalation to 7:30 · safety net and summary to 8:00. IF YOU ARE BEHIND AT FOUR MINUTES, ABANDON THE REMAINING HISTORY, SAY 'I WOULD NORMALLY ALSO COVER THE BIRTH HISTORY AND IMMUNISATIONS', AND MOVE TO THE EXAMINATION — NEVER SACRIFICE THE EXAMINATION REQUEST TO FINISH THE HISTORY. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT: MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the Women's and Children's Hospital in North Adelaide, PATS for country family travel and accommodation, and a social worker involved the same day — this family is three hours from Adelaide, the husband is on shift and there is a four-year-old at home.
plan: WIPE AND CONSENT, KEEP THE BABY ON HER LAP AND SAY SO, THEN THE OPEN QUESTION — AND GET THE AGENDA OUT: 'WAS THERE SOMETHING IN PARTICULAR YOU WERE WORRIED IT MIGHT BE?' She is convinced this is bronchiolitis because her sister's baby went to intensive care.
THE COUGH — onset and course, dry or wet and rattly, comes in bursts, EVER COUGHED UNTIL HE VOMITED, ever gone blue or stopped breathing during a fit.
THE NOISE — describe it: A WHISTLE, A RATTLE, OR A HARSH CROWING SOUND · in or out · constant or intermittent.
BOTH PIVOT QUESTIONS — WORSE LYING ON HIS BACK, AND WORSE WHEN HE FEEDS. Ask both whichever answer you expect.
The feeding block, which is the infant's exercise test — colour change and when · sweating on the forehead · how long a feed takes and whether he finishes. Acknowledge it aloud.
THE UNWELL-BABY SCREEN — alert or drowsy, drinking as usual, WET NAPPIES, vomiting, bowels, fever, runny nose, drooling, ear pulling, rash.

BIRTH HISTORY IN FORTY SECONDS — pregnancy infections, diabetes, hypertension, scans · term, delivery, breathing at birth · NEWBORN HEEL PRICK AND WHETHER OXYGEN LEVELS WERE CHECKED IN HANDS AND FEET BEFORE DISCHARGE · AND BIRTH WEIGHT.

IMMUNISATION, CONTACTS AND FAMILY — vaccines so far, MATERNAL PERTUSSIS VACCINE IN THIS PREGNANCY, anyone at home with a cough lasting weeks, smoking, family heart disease. Acknowledge the brother's pertussis and KEEP IT ON THE LIST RATHER THAN CLOSING ON IT.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST — GENERAL APPEARANCE, THEN FOUR-LIMB BLOOD PRESSURE AND FEMORAL PULSES AND RADIO-FEMORAL DELAY FIRST, then pre- and post-ductal saturations, ENT, respiratory, cardiovascular and HEPATOMEGALY.
SIT DOWN, OFFER HER A CHAIR, AND EXPLAIN THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS WITH THE FIVE REASONS (see findings). Pause for her reaction rather than moving straight on.
ANSWER THE GUILT FIRST, THEN THE PROGNOSIS WITHOUT PROMISING AN OUTCOME, THEN THE LOGISTICS — retrieval, PATS, the social worker, and someone to be with her.
The differentials in plain words, then back to the finding that decides the plan — the impalpable femoral pulses.
THE SAFETY NET, THE SUMMARY, AND AN INVITATION TO ASK QUESTIONS — plus the call to the paediatric team and retrieval made now rather than after she leaves.
back.planNote: the stem splits the eight minutes four, two and two - never sacrifice the examination request to finish the history
ask: The four lines that pass the station: 'Is it worse when he feeds?' · 'Is it worse lying on his back?' · 'Examiner, may I have his blood pressure in all four limbs?' · 'Are the femoral pulses palpable, and is there a radio-femoral delay?'

The sentence that shows you registered the pivot: 'Thank you, that is important — it tells me I need to check his heart as well as his lungs.' and the one that opens the consultation: 'Please keep holding him — that is the best place for him.'

The explanation and the guilt: 'There is a narrowing in the main blood tube that carries blood from the heart to the body.' · 'This is not something you caused. You did the right thing bringing him in.' · 'It is serious, but it is fixable — and there is a medicine we can start here to take the strain off his heart while he travels.'
EXAMINER CHALLENGES: the blood pressures, rib notching, croup, cautious oxygen, and associated lesions — all answered in full on the back (see dx).

THE DRILLS: run the eight-minute timing with a stopwatch and close the history at four minutes whatever is left · say the examination request in 20 seconds with four-limb pressures first · give the five reasons in 20 seconds · answer the guilt question cold · then run Version B and say what changes when the noise is positional rather than feeding-related.
pefe: NOTHING IS VOLUNTEERED — EVERY FINDING HAS TO BE REQUESTED BY NAME, AND THE ORDER IS THE MARK. Four-limb blood pressure and femoral pulses come FIRST, before observations and before the chest, because they are what make the diagnosis and because a candidate who runs out of time still has them. THE RADIO-RADIAL DIFFERENCE MATTERS TOO — it suggests the narrowing involves the origin of the left subclavian.

Role-player: SARAH, 29, in a regional town ABOUT THREE HOURS FROM ADELAIDE, on maternity leave, husband a shift worker at the abattoir and AT WORK NOW, AND A FOUR-YEAR-OLD AT HOME WITH WHOOPING COUGH diagnosed last week. JACK IS FIVE WEEKS, born at 39 weeks by normal delivery, BIRTH WEIGHT 3.4 kg, cried immediately, heel prick normal, HEPATITIS B IN HOSPITAL AND NOTHING SINCE. SHE HAD dTpa AT 28 WEEKS. Breastfeeding, exhausted, up most nights for three weeks.

How to play it: start anxious and talking quickly, convinced this is bronchiolitis because her sister's baby ended up in intensive care. Do not volunteer the blue colour, the sweating, the poor weight gain or the older son's whooping cough unless a question opens the door. If concerns are never asked about, interrupt at about six minutes with 'Sorry — is he going to be alright? Is this the same as what my sister's baby had?' At the diagnosis become tearful, ask 'Is it something I did?' and then 'How am I supposed to get to Adelaide?', and push back once if the doctor is vague — 'But you are not actually sure, are you?'

AUTOMATIC FAIL: NEVER REQUESTING FEMORAL PULSES OR FOUR-LIMB BLOOD PRESSURE · reassuring her it is a virus and planning discharge · FAILING TO ESCALATE TO PAEDIATRICS OR RETRIEVAL · telling her the baby will 'DEFINITELY BE FINE' · IGNORING THE CYANOSIS ON FEEDING. The checklist also scores: introduction and consent · open question before closed · CONCERN ELICITED IN THE FIRST MINUTE · cough explored including paroxysms and post-tussive vomiting · NOISE DESCRIBED, INSPIRATORY OR EXPIRATORY · WORSE LYING DOWN · WORSE ON FEEDING · COLOUR CHANGE, SWEATING AND FEED DURATION · fever, ENT, GI, contacts, choking · unwell-baby screen INCLUDING WET NAPPIES AND WEIGHT · birth history and newborn screen · IMMUNISATION AND MATERNAL PERTUSSIS VACCINE · FOUR-LIMB BLOOD PRESSURE · FEMORAL PULSES AND RADIO-FEMORAL DELAY · HEPATOMEGALY · diagnosis without jargon and with reasons · GUILT ANSWERED BEFORE LOGISTICS · safety-net and summary.

The two pivot questions — ask both, every time — 'IS IT WORSE IN ANY PARTICULAR POSITION — WORSE WHEN YOU LAY HIM ON HIS BACK?' AND 'IS IT WORSE WHEN HE FEEDS?' THE STATION IS BUILT SO THAT ONLY THE QUESTION YOU ASK GETS ANSWERED. Here position is negative and FEEDING IS POSITIVE; in the laryngomalacia version it is the other way round

The moment the station turns — 'Does he turn blue at any point — around his lips or his tongue? When does that happen?' → he goes blue around the mouth when he feeds and settles when she stops · 'Does he sweat on his forehead while he feeds?' → sweaty all over his head · 'How long does a feed take, and does he finish it?' → half an hour or more and he gives up halfway. Say it out loud — 'Thank you, that is important; it tells me I need to check his heart as well as his lungs' — so the examiner sees you registered it. Feeding is the infant's exercise test

The examination request — order matters — General appearance, distress, cyanosis, capillary refill and hydration · THEN 'BLOOD PRESSURE IN ALL FOUR LIMBS, PLEASE' · 'ARE HIS FEMORAL PULSES PALPABLE, AND IS THERE A RADIO-FEMORAL DELAY?' · observations with PRE-DUCTAL SATURATIONS IN THE RIGHT HAND AND POST-DUCTAL IN A FOOT · ENT · full respiratory examination · cardiovascular: APEX BEAT DISPLACED OR HEAVING, murmur, GALLOP RHYTHM · AND HEPATOMEGALY

The explanation in plain words — 'THE AORTA IS THE MAIN BLOOD TUBE THAT CARRIES BLOOD AWAY FROM THE HEART TO THE REST OF THE BODY. In his case THERE IS A NARROWING IN THAT TUBE. Blood gets to his head and arms easily, but IT STRUGGLES TO GET PAST THE NARROWING down to his tummy and legs. That is why his blood pressure is much higher in his arms than his legs, and why I cannot feel the pulses in his groin. And because his heart is pushing hard against that narrowing IT IS GETTING TIRED, which is what is causing the fast breathing, the cough, and the trouble feeding'

The five reasons, given to her — The cough is worse when he feeds · he goes blue when he feeds · the blood pressure is much lower in his legs · I cannot feel his leg pulses · and his liver is larger than it should be. No jargon — not 'Juxtaductal coarctation with a pressure gradient'

Her three questions, answered in this order — GUILT FIRST: 'THIS IS NOT SOMETHING YOU CAUSED. IT HAPPENS AS THE HEART FORMS VERY EARLY IN PREGNANCY AND NOTHING YOU DID OR DID NOT DO BRINGS IT ON. YOU DID EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING BRINGING HIM IN' · PROGNOSIS SECOND, WITHOUT FALSE PROMISES: 'I cannot promise you an outcome, but this is a condition children's heart surgeons repair regularly, and most babies do very well afterwards' · LOGISTICS THIRD: retrieval team, PATS for country families, the social worker today, AND 'IS THERE SOMEONE I CAN CALL TO BE WITH YOU?'

The differentials, without frightening her further — WHOOPING COUGH — her older boy has it and this baby has not had his own vaccine, so swab and treat · A CHEST INFECTION OR BRONCHIOLITIS — less likely with no fever, no runny nose, and weeks of symptoms · A FLOPPY VOICE BOX — makes babies noisy but does not affect the pulses or the liver · ANOTHER HEART PROBLEM SUCH AS A HOLE IN THE HEART, which the ultrasound will also show. THEN BRING IT BACK: 'WHOOPING COUGH DOES NOT EXPLAIN WHY I CANNOT FEEL THE PULSES IN HIS LEGS — THAT IS THE FINDING TAKING US TO ADELAIDE TODAY'

The plan and the safety net — TRANSFER TO THE WOMEN'S AND CHILDREN'S TODAY FOR ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY · ALPROSTADIL STARTED HERE to keep the duct open and take the strain off his heart while he travels, WITH SOMEONE ABLE TO MANAGE HIS AIRWAY AT THE BEDSIDE BECAUSE APNOEA IS THE EXPECTED ADVERSE EFFECT · MedSTAR Kids retrieval · AND THE RED FLAGS: blue or grey, stopping breathing even briefly, working hard to breathe, refusing feeds, FEWER THAN FOUR WET NAPPIES A DAY, floppy or hard to wake, OR ANY FEVER — because at this age any fever needs same-day assessment

The harder variants — THE COLLAPSED NEONATE at ten days, mottled and cool, femorals absent, capillary refill five seconds, lactate 7, foot saturations 88% → SHOCKED, DUCT-DEPENDENT LEFT HEART LESION AS THE DUCT CLOSES: senior help now, access, gas and lactate, CULTURES AND ANTIBIOTICS BECAUSE SEPSIS CANNOT BE EXCLUDED, ALPROSTADIL 5 TO 10 nanogram/kg/min, FLUID IN 10 mL/kg ALIQUOTS ONLY, CAUTIOUS OXYGEN RATHER THAN HIGH FLOW because oxygen encourages ductal closure · THE PERTUSSIS DECOY, where she asks for the antibiotic and to go home → swab and treat, but INFANTS UNDER SIX MONTHS ARE THE ONES WHO STOP BREATHING so he stays regardless, and the impalpable femorals are what decide the transfer
fails: ★ Never requesting four-limb blood pressure or femoral pulses — the examiner volunteers nothing, and this is the behaviour the mark sheet is built around
★ Reassuring her it is a virus and planning discharge, or ignoring the cyanosis on feeding and carrying on down the respiratory track
Asking only one of the two pivot questions — position and feeding are both asked in every infant with noisy breathing, whichever answer you expect
Failing to escalate to paediatrics and retrieval, or telling her the baby will definitely be fine, which is not yours to promise

Closing on the brother's pertussis instead of keeping it on the list; skipping the birth history because time ran out; or delivering the diagnosis and moving straight to logistics without answering the guilt
numbers: Arm-to-leg systolic gradient over 20 mmHg is significant coarctation · normal infant systolic 65 to 95 mmHg, leg equal to or higher than arm · pre- to post-ductal saturation difference over 3% is differential cyanosis · coarctation 1 in 2500 live births and 5 to 8% of congenital heart disease · bicuspid aortic valve in 50 to 85%

Alprostadil 5 to 10 nanogram/kg/min IV, titrated, watch for apnoea · frusemide 1 mg/kg · fluid boluses 10 mL/kg cautiously · weight gain 150 to 200 g per week, wet nappies 4 to 6 a day minimum · fever at or above 38 under 3 months means septic screen and admission · first pertussis vaccine at 6 weeks, maternal dose 20 to 32 weeks · laryngomalacia resolves 12 to 24 months, 10 to 15% need supraglottoplasty · MedSTAR kids 1300 13 12 33 · VERIFY all
