setting: The structure card for every paediatric cough station, run on a four-year-old with three weeks of coughing fits. Four positives are buried and each is released only by its exact question — the whoop, the post-tussive vomiting, the father's month-long cough, and the six-week-old sister at home. You can get the diagnosis, the swab and the antibiotic right and still fail, because ruby is the person at genuine risk in this room.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Mrs Mary Delaney brings her 4-year-old son Ethan, who has been coughing. She is worried. Ethan is not in the room.

Tasks: take a focused history from the mother, 4 minutes — ask the examiner for your physical examination findings — state your most likely diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the examiner — explain your management to the mother. 8 minutes.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother, four minutes
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
State your diagnosis and differentials to the examiner
Explain your management to the mother
time: Vital signs before you sit, and they must include respiratory rate and saturations · then a genuinely open question that lets the three-line opening statement arrive, then empathy with its second half · then the cough: timing, dry or chesty, and the three sounds named · then difficulty breathing and noisy breathing · then the differential sweep — fever chain, ENT, rash, GI, travel and contacts, then pace · then three well-baby questions and immunisation · close the history at four minutes even if it feels incomplete, because half the marks sit after it ends · then the named examination list, the examiner-facing diagnosis with reasons, and two minutes of management.
findings: Vital signs first, and the two that matter

'Examiner, before I start, may I have Ethan's vital signs — SPECIFICALLY HIS RESPIRATORY RATE AND OXYGEN SATURATION, and also his heart rate, temperature and blood pressure?' → RR 24, SpO2 98% ON AIR, HR 96, TEMP 36.9, BP 95/60. Asking for blood pressure and temperature but NOT respiratory rate and saturations is the trap — every severity judgement in this cluster rests on those two numbers

General appearance and WHETHER HE LOOKS TOXIC · work of breathing — recession, tracheal tug, grunting, nasal flaring · STRIDOR AT REST · chest findings and WHETHER ANY ARE FOCAL · hydration and capillary refill · ears, nose and throat · RASH · cardiovascular including murmurs · AND GROWTH PARAMETERS PLOTTED ON A CHART

Alert and well between bouts, NOT TOXIC · no increased work of breathing, NO STRIDOR · CHEST CLEAR with good air entry · well hydrated · ENT normal, no rash · cardiovascular normal · tracking on the 50th percentile · AND 'YOU MAY NOTE SOME SUBCONJUNCTIVAL HAEMORRHAGES'. THOSE AND FACIAL PETECHIAE ARE CAUSED BY THE PRESSURE OF VIOLENT PAROXYSMS, AND A CLEAR CHEST BETWEEN BOUTS IN A WELL-LOOKING CHILD IS EXACTLY THE PERTUSSIS PICTURE — say both out loud, because recognising them is worth a mark each

back.dx: PERTUSSIS IN A PARTIALLY IMMUNISED FOUR-YEAR-OLD — BUT THE STATION IS ABOUT THE SIX-WEEK-OLD SISTER, AND THE HISTORY STRUCTURE THAT FINDS HER. THE CLOCK IS FIXED AND WORTH INTERNALISING: 0:00 TO 0:20 VITAL SIGNS · 0:20 TO 0:50 OPEN QUESTION AND EMPATHY · 0:50 TO 1:40 THE COUGH INCLUDING THE SOUND · 1:40 TO 1:55 DIFFICULTY AND NOISY BREATHING · 1:55 TO 3:40 THE DIFFERENTIAL SWEEP · 3:40 TO 4:00 WELL-BABY AND IMMUNISATION · 4:00 TO 5:00 EXAMINATION FINDINGS · 5:00 TO 6:00 DIAGNOSIS AND DIFFERENTIALS TO THE EXAMINER · 6:00 TO 8:00 MANAGEMENT TO THE MOTHER. CLOSE THE HISTORY AT FOUR MINUTES EVEN IF IT FEELS INCOMPLETE, BECAUSE HALF THIS STATION'S MARKS SIT AFTER THE HISTORY ENDS. THE MANAGEMENT EXPLANATION, WORD FOR WORD: 'I think Ethan has whooping cough — a bacterial infection called pertussis. That whoop, the fits, and being sick afterwards are very typical, and it explains why it has dragged on for three weeks. I will take a swab from the back of his nose to confirm it, and start him on an antibiotic. I WANT TO BE HONEST WITH YOU — THE ANTIBIOTIC MAINLY STOPS HIM PASSING IT TO OTHER PEOPLE. It will not switch the cough off quickly; that can take weeks to settle, WHICH IS WHY IT IS SOMETIMES CALLED THE HUNDRED-DAY COUGH. He will need to stay away from kindy UNTIL HE HAS HAD FIVE DAYS OF ANTIBIOTICS. Whooping cough is a notifiable illness, so I will let the health department know and they will help with contact tracing. NOW THE MOST IMPORTANT PART. Ruby is six weeks old, and whooping cough is genuinely dangerous in babies that young — THEY CAN STOP BREATHING RATHER THAN WHOOP. I would like to see her today. She and the rest of the household will need preventive antibiotics, and I want to check your own vaccination in pregnancy and get everyone's immunisations up to date, including Ethan's.' THEN TWO SETS OF RED FLAGS AND A TEACH-BACK: for Ethan, going blue or stopping breathing during a fit, being unable to catch his breath, stopping drinking or fewer wet nappies, or becoming floppy or drowsy; FOR RUBY, ANY PAUSE IN BREATHING, ANY COLOUR CHANGE OR POOR FEEDING IS AN AMBULANCE, NOT AN APPOINTMENT — 'CAN YOU TELL ME BACK WHAT YOU WOULD WATCH FOR IN RUBY?' THE NUMBERS: ACUTE COUGH IS UNDER TWO WEEKS AND CHRONIC IS OVER FOUR, WITH RCH USING THREE · BRONCHIOLITIS IS UNDER 12 MONTHS · PERTUSSIS EXCLUSION IS FIVE DAYS OF ANTIBIOTICS OR 21 DAYS FROM ONSET IF UNTREATED · THE PERTUSSIS DANGER AGE IS UNDER SIX MONTHS · MATERNAL dTpa IS GIVEN IN THE THIRD TRIMESTER, AROUND 20 TO 32 WEEKS · CROUP TAKES DEXAMETHASONE 0.15 mg/kg ORALLY AS A SINGLE DOSE AT ALL SEVERITIES · ASTHMA TAKES SALBUTAMOL 6 PUFFS UNDER SIX YEARS AND 12 PUFFS AT SIX AND OVER VIA SPACER, WITH PREDNISOLONE 1 mg/kg DAILY FOR THREE DAYS · TACHYPNOEA IS ROUGHLY OVER 40 A MINUTE AT ONE TO FIVE YEARS AND OVER 30 AT FIVE TO TWELVE · AND THERE ARE THREE WELL-BABY QUESTIONS AND THREE COUGH SOUNDS VERIFY ALL. THE FIVE VARIANTS RUN OFF THE SAME STRUCTURE: CROUP at two years, sudden onset this evening, barking with stridor — dexamethasone as a single dose, keep him calm on the parent's lap, AND DO NOT EXAMINE THE THROAT · ASTHMA at six years with wheeze and a family full of atopy — salbutamol by spacer, prednisolone, action plan and inhaler technique before they leave · BRONCHIOLITIS at seven months, feeding poorly — no medicine shortens it, and NOT PRESCRIBING SALBUTAMOL BECAUSE THERE IS A WHEEZE IS THE TRAP · THE TEENAGER ALONE with four months of a loud single explosive cough that NEVER HAPPENS WHILE ASLEEP — habit cough, asked about school and bullying, explained as real and not deliberate, with no further testing because testing makes it stick · AND THE FOREIGN BODY at 18 months, well until yesterday, playing with Lego — sudden onset after choking with reduced air entry, where A NORMAL CHEST X-RAY WOULD NOT EXCLUDE IT and the answer is rigid bronchoscopy, with MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval from a regional site.
plan: VITAL SIGNS FROM THE EXAMINER BEFORE YOU SIT — AND NAME RESPIRATORY RATE AND SATURATIONS SPECIFICALLY, not just heart rate, temperature and blood pressure.
INTRODUCE, CONFIRM WHO SHE IS, AND ASK A GENUINELY OPEN QUESTION — 'TELL ME MORE ABOUT ETHAN'S COUGH' — so the three-line opening statement arrives.
EMPATHY WITH BOTH HALVES: name the emotion, then say what you are going to do about it. Then move on.
THE COUGH — constant or in bouts, getting worse, dry or chesty · THEN NAME ALL THREE SOUNDS: BARKING, A LOUD SINGLE HONK, AND A WHOOP AT THE END OF A FIT.
TRIGGERS — anything better or worse, worse on running, WORSE AT NIGHT.
The two safety questions before any differential — difficulty breathing or gasping, and any noisy breathing.
THE FEVER CHAIN AND ENT — fever, measured, treated, helping · runny nose, ears, throat, swallowing, neck lumps, voice · AND RASH.
GI AND CONTACTS — vomiting, diarrhoea, tummy pain · travel · AND ANYONE SICK AT HOME OR AT KINDY, which is where the father's month-long cough lives.
PACE — 'HAS HE VOMITED AFTER A COUGHING SPELL?' AND 'IS THERE A BABY AT HOME, ANYONE UNDER SIX MONTHS?' · family atopy · harsh or barking noise on inspiration · choking episode and smoking.
Three well-baby questions and immunisation — alert and playful, eating and drinking, wet nappies, and vaccination status. Close the history at four minutes whatever is left.
THE NAMED EXAMINATION LIST (see findings) — and say the SUBCONJUNCTIVAL HAEMORRHAGES and the CLEAR CHEST BETWEEN BOUTS out loud when they come back.
THE EXAMINER-FACING PRESENTATION — the pattern, the contact, the incomplete immunisation, THE SIBLING, and the findings — then the four differentials each with its reason.

MANAGEMENT TO THE MOTHER — swab and antibiotic with the honest expectation, exclusion, notification, THEN RUBY: same-day review, household prophylaxis, maternal vaccine checked, catch-up immunisation · TWO SETS OF RED FLAGS AND TEACH-BACK ON RUBY'S.
back.planNote: the source gives an exact clock for this station - half the marks sit after the history ends, so four minutes is a hard stop
ask: The four questions that unlock the case, in these words: 'Do you hear a whooping sound at the end of a coughing fit?' · 'Has he been sick after a coughing spell?' · 'Has he been in contact with anyone who is sick — at home or at kindy?' · 'Is there a baby at home — anyone under six months?'

The opening: 'Examiner, before I begin — may I have his respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, and his heart rate, temperature and blood pressure?' then 'Mary, can you tell me more about Ethan's cough?'

The three sounds asked individually: 'Does it bark? Is it a loud single honk? Do you hear a whoop at the end of a fit?' — and the safety pair: 'Has he had any difficulty breathing? Have you heard any noisy breathing?'

The honest management line: 'The antibiotic mainly stops him passing it on — it will not switch the cough off quickly.' and the one that matters most: 'Babies that young can stop breathing rather than whoop — any pause in breathing, any colour change, or poor feeding means an ambulance, not an appointment.'

THE DRILLS: run the fixed clock with a stopwatch and stop the history dead at four minutes · name the three cough sounds in five seconds · ask the four buried-positive questions in their exact wording · give the examiner-facing presentation with four differentials and their reasons in 45 seconds · then run the croup, asthma, bronchiolitis, habit-cough and foreign-body variants off the same structure.
pefe: REQUEST IT AS A NAMED LIST RATHER THAN 'the examination findings': general appearance AND WHETHER HE LOOKS TOXIC · work of breathing — recession, tracheal tug, grunting, nasal flaring · STRIDOR AT REST · chest on auscultation AND WHETHER ANY FINDINGS ARE FOCAL · hydration and capillary refill · ENT · RASH · cardiovascular including murmurs · AND GROWTH PARAMETERS PLOTTED. The subconjunctival haemorrhages are offered unprompted, and ignoring them wastes a mark.

Role-player: MARY DELANEY, 33, in Berri, with ETHAN 4 — NOT IN THE ROOM — and RUBY, SIX WEEKS, AT HOME WITH HER MOTHER. Three weeks of cough beginning with a runny nose, now in fits with a well period between, worse at night, no fever since the first few days. HER HUSBAND DAVE HAS COUGHED FOR ABOUT A MONTH and they assumed it was a lingering cold. Nobody smokes, no pets, no travel. ETHAN HAD HIS EARLY NEEDLES BUT THEY FELL BEHIND AFTER MOVING HOUSE, and she is vague about which were missed and cannot remember whether she had a pertussis vaccine in pregnancy with Ruby.

How to play it: frightened and tired rather than tearful, settling noticeably once there is an explanation and a plan. Give the full three-line opening statement only to a genuinely open question, and only fragments to a closed one. The four buried positives are released only in their exact wording (see findings). If the doctor never asks about ruby, do not volunteer her — at about seven minutes say once 'Should I be worried about the baby?' and mark that as a fail.

AUTOMATIC FAIL: NOISY BREATHING NEVER ASKED · VITAL SIGNS NEVER REQUESTED · THE INFANT SIBLING NEVER IDENTIFIED · NO MANAGEMENT GIVEN · NO SAFETY-NETTING. The 25-item checklist: vital signs before the history AND respiratory rate and saturations specifically · a genuinely open question that elicits the full opening statement · empathy then moving on · duration and bouts · dry versus chesty WITHOUT RUNNING CCVO · ALL THREE SOUNDS NAMED · night and exercise triggers · DIFFICULTY AND NOISY BREATHING · fever chain · ENT block · RASH · GI · travel and sick contacts · VOMITING AFTER A COUGHING SPELL IN THAT PHRASING · choking, smoking, family atopy · A BABY UNDER SIX MONTHS AT HOME · immunisation status · three well-baby questions · A NAMED EXAMINATION LIST · pertussis committed to with reasons · three or more differentials each excluded · swab, antibiotic, notification, exclusion · SAME-DAY REVIEW AND PROPHYLAXIS FOR THE INFANT · named safety-net symptoms and teach-back.

The four buried positives, and the exact wording that releases them — 'DOES HE MAKE A WHOOPING SOUND AT THE END OF A FIT?' — ask only 'what does the cough sound like?' and she says 'just a cough, really' · 'HAS HE VOMITED AFTER A COUGHING SPELL?' — ask 'has he been vomiting?' and the answer is NO · 'IS ANYONE AT HOME OR AT KINDY SICK?' → HER HUSBAND HAS COUGHED FOR A MONTH · AND 'IS THERE A BABY AT HOME — ANYONE UNDER SIX MONTHS?' → RUBY, SIX WEEKS OLD

The open question and the second half of empathy — 'HOW LONG HAS HE BEEN COUGHING?' IS A CLOSED QUESTION; 'TELL ME MORE ABOUT ETHAN'S COUGH' IS NOT — and only the second gets you the three-line opening statement. THEN EMPATHY WITH ITS SECOND HALF: 'I completely understand why you are worried — three weeks of watching him cough like that is exhausting and frightening. LET ME ASK YOU SOME QUESTIONS SO I CAN WORK OUT WHAT IS GOING ON AND MAKE THE BEST PLAN FOR ETHAN.' Then stop being empathic and start taking a history

Noisy breathing is an AUTOMATIC FAIL if missed — 'HAS HE HAD ANY DIFFICULTY BREATHING, OR SEEMED TO BE GASPING FOR AIR?' AND 'HAVE YOU HEARD ANY NOISY BREATHING — ANY WHEEZE, OR A HARSH NOISE WHEN HE BREATHES IN?' Both asked BEFORE any differential, and the structure gives you three chances to remember it

The sweep — fever chain, ENT, rash, GI, then pace — FEVER CHAIN: any fever, HAVE YOU MEASURED IT, have you given anything, IS IT HELPING · ENT: runny nose, ear pain or pulling, sore throat, swallowing, NECK LUMPS, voice change · RASH, which catches scarlet fever in the sore-throat versions · GI: vomiting, diarrhoea, tummy pain · TRAVEL AND SICK CONTACTS · THEN PACE: PERTUSSIS — post-tussive vomiting AND A BABY UNDER SIX MONTHS AT HOME · ASTHMA — family atopy · CROUP — harsh or barking noise on breathing in · EXPOSURE — choking episode and smoking at home

What she gives you — THREE WEEKS, started with a runny nose · COMES IN FITS — he goes red and cannot stop, then is COMPLETELY FINE FOR HOURS · worse at night · dry · NOT BARKING, NOT HONKING, BUT A WHOOP WHEN HE FINALLY CATCHES HIS BREATH · struggles during a fit but NORMAL BETWEEN THEM, no wheeze, nothing noisy · no fever since the first few days, no rash, no travel · AND IMMUNISATIONS INCOMPLETE BECAUSE THEY FELL BEHIND AFTER MOVING

The differentials, each with its reason — POST-VIRAL COUGH — less likely with the whoop and post-tussive vomiting · ASTHMA — less likely without wheeze, an exercise pattern or family atopy · MYCOPLASMA OR ANOTHER ATYPICAL PNEUMONIA — less likely with a clear chest and no fever · FOREIGN BODY — excluded, no choking episode. THE REASON IS THE MARK, not the name

The management, and where it actually lands — Swab and antibiotic, with the honest line that it mainly stops him passing it on rather than switching the cough off — weeks to settle, the hundred-day cough · exclusion from kindy until five days of antibiotics · notification and contact tracing · then the most important part: ruby is six weeks old and babies that age stop breathing rather than whoop — see her today, prophylax the household, check the maternal pregnancy vaccine and catch everyone up · and two sets of red flags, with teach-back on ruby's: any pause in breathing, any colour change, or poor feeding means an ambulance, not an appointment

The three cough sounds, named individually — BARKING = CROUP · A LOUD SINGLE HONK = HABIT COUGH · A WHOOP AT THE END OF A FIT = PERTUSSIS. THREE DIAGNOSES HIDING IN TEN SECONDS OF QUESTIONING, and skipping them because the cough is 'dry' is the trap. REPLACE CCVO ENTIRELY — asking the mother of a four-year-old what colour the phlegm is wastes the slot where the sound question belongs

The examiner-facing presentation — 'A 4-year-old with A THREE-WEEK PAROXYSMAL COUGH, WITH AN INSPIRATORY WHOOP, POST-TUSSIVE VOMITING, AND A WELL PERIOD BETWEEN BOUTS. His father has a month-long cough, HIS IMMUNISATIONS ARE INCOMPLETE, AND THERE IS A SIX-WEEK-OLD SIBLING AT HOME. On examination he is well, afebrile, with a clear chest and SUBCONJUNCTIVAL HAEMORRHAGES.' MENTION THE SIBLING HERE AND AGAIN IN THE MANAGEMENT — it demonstrates you have grasped where the danger sits
fails: ★ Never asking whether there is a baby under six months at home — you can get the diagnosis, the swab and the antibiotic right and still fail, because the six-week-old is the person at genuine risk
★ Never asking about noisy breathing, or never requesting vital signs, both of which are automatic fails in this cluster
Asking 'has he been vomiting?' and accepting no, when the question that finds the case is 'has he vomited after a coughing spell?' — a different question to her

Giving the diagnosis without reasons, listing differentials without saying why each is less likely, leaving the sibling out of the presentation, or overrunning the history so the management and safety-netting never happen

setting: Nothing is volunteered. The whole station turns on five words inside the general appearance request — 'And is there any noisy breathing?' Ask for distress and cyanosis but not that, and the examiner says nothing about the stridor, and there is no other route to the diagnosis. stem: After-hours clinic, regional South Australia, 11 pm. Archie Lawson, 2 years, brought by his mother with two days of runny nose and now a harsh barking cough that woke him and is frightening her.

No findings are volunteered; everything comes from what you ask. Version B is a 7-year-old with three days of cough and wheeze, adding 'What further testing would you arrange?'

findings: Ask for the weight with the vitals

'Vital signs please — SPECIFICALLY THE RESPIRATORY RATE AND THE OXYGEN SATURATION ON ROOM AIR. Also heart rate, temperature, capillary refill, AND HIS WEIGHT' → RR 34, SpO2 96% ON ROOM AIR, HR 130, TEMP 37.9, CRT UNDER 2 SECONDS, WEIGHT 12 kg. The weight is what lets you dose in mg/kg AND in milligrams later
The throat, and the condition under which you refuse it

Examine it here — he is not drooling and not toxic — but SAY THE CONDITION OUT LOUD UNPROMPTED, BECAUSE IT IS WORTH A MARK: 'I am comfortable examining his throat because he is not drooling and does not look toxic. IF HE WERE, I WOULD HAVE AVOIDED IT BECAUSE OF EPIGLOTTITIS.' And if the examiner instead describes a toxic, drooling child: STOP, DO NOT EXAMINE THE THROAT, DO NOT LIE HIM DOWN, leave him upright on his mother's lap, oxygen if tolerated, and call anaesthetics and ENT immediately
Four other children, each failed by a reassuring finding

EPIGLOTTITIS — toxic, sitting forward, drooling, muffled voice, NO COUGH, incomplete immunisation: THE MARK IS THE REFUSAL, said out loud · BRONCHIOLITIS at five months with wheeze and fine crackles: supportive only, and GIVING SALBUTAMOL OR STEROIDS IS THE FAIL · INHALED FOREIGN BODY at 18 months after peanuts: UNILATERAL SIGNS, and A NORMAL CHEST X-RAY DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT because most nuts are radiolucent, so rigid bronchoscopy regardless · THE SILENT CHEST in a known asthmatic who has gone quiet with drowsiness and saturations of 88%: LIFE-THREATENING ASTHMA, NOT IMPROVEMENT, because there is too little airflow to generate a wheeze

back.dx: MODERATE CROUP — AND THE STATION IS THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, NOT THE DIAGNOSIS. THE SEQUENCE, SIGNPOSTED ONCE AT THE START AND THEN FOLLOWED: GENERAL APPEARANCE — conscious state, hydration, distress by named signs, cyanosis, NOISY BREATHING · VITAL SIGNS — respiratory rate and saturations first, plus heart rate, temperature, capillary refill and WEIGHT · UPPER TRACT — ears, nose, throat, nodes · LOWER TRACT — inspection and palpation, percussion, auscultation, VOCAL RESONANCE · HEART — sounds, murmurs, HEPATOMEGALY · AND TO COMPLETE, GROWTH PLOTTED ON A CENTILE CHART AND IMMUNISATION HISTORY. SPIROMETRY ONLY FROM ABOUT FIVE OR SIX YEARS, AND SAYING 'NOT APPROPRIATE AT THIS AGE' IS ITSELF AN ANSWER. THE INTERPRETATION IS COMPRESSED, NOT READ BACK AS A LIST: 'Archie is an alert, well-hydrated two-year-old with mild intercostal recession and INSPIRATORY STRIDOR AT REST, a mildly raised respiratory rate for age, normal saturations on room air, and a low-grade fever. His ears, nose and throat are unremarkable apart from clear coryza, and HIS CHEST IS ENTIRELY CLEAR — symmetrical, resonant, equal air entry, no wheeze or crackles, normal vocal resonance. His heart is normal.' THEN THE LOCALISING SENTENCE, THEN THE NAME, THEN THE GRADE. IF YOU MISSED SOMETHING, SAY SO: 'I REALISE I HAVE NOT ASKED ABOUT PERCUSSION — MAY I HAVE THAT NOW?' costs three seconds and one mark; PRESENTING A FINDING YOU NEVER REQUESTED COSTS THE EXAMINER'S TRUST IN EVERYTHING ELSE YOU SAY. NEVER INVENT A NORMAL. DISPOSITION, WHICH IS WHERE DISTANCE MATTERS: discharge once he has NO STRIDOR AT REST AND IS DRINKING; admit or transfer for PERSISTENT STRIDOR AT REST, HYPOXIA, POOR ORAL INTAKE, A SECOND DOSE OF ADRENALINE, OR A FAMILY WHO LIVE TOO FAR TO GET BACK EASILY — the mother is briefed to say 'we are forty minutes out of town, is that a problem?' precisely to test whether distance changes your answer. MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33 early if he is deteriorating. VERSION B, THE WHEEZY SEVEN-YEAR-OLD, RUNS THE SAME STRUCTURE TO A DIFFERENT PLACE: 'THE SIGNS ARE ALL EXPIRATORY WITH HYPERINFLATION, SO THIS IS A LOWER AIRWAY PROBLEM: ACUTE ASTHMA, MODERATE. THE HARRISON SULCUS TELLS ME IT SITS ON CHRONIC, POORLY CONTROLLED DISEASE.' Differentials: bronchiolitis, which would be under 12 months · an inhaled foreign body, but her wheeze is WIDESPREAD AND POLYPHONIC rather than monophonic and unilateral · pneumonia, but there are no focal signs or fever · and cardiac failure, but her heart is normal with no hepatomegaly. Her findings: RR 30, SATURATIONS 94%, WEIGHT 24 kg, HYPER-RESONANT AND EQUAL, AIR ENTRY REDUCED BUT EQUAL WITH WIDESPREAD EXPIRATORY WHEEZE, AND SPIROMETRY SHOWING AN OBSTRUCTIVE PATTERN WITH REVERSIBILITY. THE NUMBERS: OXYGEN AND ADMISSION BELOW ABOUT 92% ON ROOM AIR · CROUP — DEXAMETHASONE 0.15 mg/kg ONCE OR PREDNISOLONE 1 mg/kg, WITH NEBULISED ADRENALINE 1:1000 0.5 mL/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 5 mL AND FOUR HOURS OF OBSERVATION FOR REBOUND, AND NO NECK X-RAY · ASTHMA — SALBUTAMOL BY SPACER, 6 PUFFS UNDER 6 YEARS AND 12 PUFFS FROM 6, EVERY 20 MINUTES FOR THE FIRST HOUR, WITH PREDNISOLONE 1 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 50 mg FOR 3 DAYS · BRONCHIOLITIS UNDER 12 MONTHS IS SUPPORTIVE ONLY · PNEUMONIA — AMOXICILLIN 25 mg/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 1 g EIGHT-HOURLY · SPIROMETRY FROM ABOUT 5 TO 6 YEARS VERIFY ALL. THE PATTERN ACROSS EVERY VARIANT IS WORTH NAMING TO YOURSELF BEFORE YOU WALK IN: EACH ONE IS FAILED BY A REASSURING-SOUNDING FINDING — A QUIET CHEST, A NORMAL X-RAY, A CHILD WHO IS NOT WHEEZING, A SETTLED TODDLER. THE EXAMINATION SEQUENCE PROTECTS YOU BECAUSE IT FORCES YOU TO ASK ABOUT SYMMETRY, SATURATIONS AND CONSCIOUS STATE BEFORE YOU FORM AN IMPRESSION.
plan: INTRODUCE, CONFIRM BOTH NAMES, AND ASK PERMISSION — 'I'LL KEEP HIM ON YOUR LAP SO HE STAYS SETTLED', which in croup is a scoring item rather than politeness. THEN SIGNPOST THE SEQUENCE ONCE.
GENERAL APPEARANCE IN ONE REQUEST — alert or drowsy · hydration by named signs · DISTRESS BY NAMED SIGNS · central cyanosis · AND NOISY BREATHING. This is where the diagnosis is hiding.
Vital signs led by respiratory rate and saturations, plus weight — then interpret the rate against age in one line.

UPPER TRACT — otoscopy for a red or bulging drum, discharge or perforation · nasal discharge and its character · throat for redness, exudate and tonsil size or asymmetry · CERVICAL NODES. And state the epiglottitis condition unprompted.
LOWER TRACT IN FOUR REQUESTS — movement and CHEST WALL SHAPE and tracheal position · PERCUSSION · auscultation · VOCAL RESONANCE.
HEART AND COMPLETION — first and second sounds, murmurs, HEPATOMEGALY · then growth plotted and immunisation history.
THE INTERPRETATION, COMPRESSED RATHER THAN READ BACK (see dx) — and if you skipped something, ask for it now rather than inventing it.
THE LOCALISING SENTENCE — all inspiratory with a clear chest means upper airway, not lower airway or parenchyma.
NAME IT AND GRADE IT — croup, moderate, with the four features that would make it severe held ready.
THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH THE FEATURE THAT EXCLUDES IT — epiglottitis first, because it is the one that kills.
Management in order — minimal handling first, then dexamethasone in mg/kg and in milligrams, then what would escalate to adrenaline, then oxygen only if saturations fall.
Decline the neck x-ray with a reason if asked, then disposition — discharge criteria, admission criteria, and the distance question answered.

THE SAFETY NET IN THE MOTHER'S LANGUAGE, THEN THE ONE-SENTENCE EXPLANATION SHE ACTUALLY WANTS: the swelling is at the top of his windpipe, which is why the noise is on breathing in and why the cough barks.

ask: THE FIVE WORDS THAT MAKE THE DIAGNOSIS AVAILABLE: 'AND IS THERE ANY NOISY BREATHING?' — asked inside the general appearance request, unprompted.
The vitals request: 'Vital signs please — specifically the respiratory rate and the oxygen saturation on room air. And his weight.' then interpret: 'A rate of 34 is mildly raised for a two-year-old.'

The four-part lower tract request, including the two people skip: 'On percussion, is the note normal, dull or hyper-resonant, and equal on both sides?' and 'Is vocal resonance normal, increased or decreased?'

The three sentences that carry the second half: 'The abnormal signs are all inspiratory with a clear chest, which localises this to the upper airway.' · 'Before any drug — keep him calm on his mother's lap with minimal handling, because distress worsens the obstruction.' · 'Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose — 1.8 mg for 12 kilograms.'

EXAMINER CHALLENGES: 'Would you order a neck X-ray?' → 'NO — CROUP IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS, AND SENDING A CHILD WITH A NARROWED AIRWAY TO RADIOLOGY DELAYS TREATMENT WITHOUT CHANGING IT.' · 'What would make you call it severe?' → the five features (see findings) · 'He is toxic and drooling' → THE REFUSAL, said out loud, with anaesthetics and ENT called · 'The asthmatic's chest has gone quiet' → 'A SILENT CHEST WITH DROWSINESS AND HYPOXIA IS LIFE-THREATENING ASTHMA, NOT IMPROVEMENT.'
pefe: THE EXAMINER GIVES NOTHING THAT IS NOT EXPLICITLY ASKED FOR. To an open request — 'I would like to examine the respiratory system' — the reply is only 'WHAT ARE YOU LOOKING FOR?' If noisy breathing is never asked about, THE STRIDOR IS NEVER MENTIONED, EVEN AT THE END. Answers come in short factual sentences with no hints and no encouragement, and anything not listed is 'normal' — BUT ONLY IF IT WAS ASKED FOR BY NAME.

Version B findings, the wheezy seven-year-old: alert, speaking in short phrases, well hydrated · subcostal recession and accessory muscle use, no cyanosis · widespread expiratory wheeze · RR 30, SpO2 94% on air, HR 120, afebrile, weight 24 kg · ears, nose and throat normal, no nodes · symmetrical but hyperinflated with a Harrison sulcus, trachea central · hyper-resonant and equal · air entry reduced but equal with widespread expiratory wheeze · vocal resonance normal · heart normal · 25th centile · spirometry available, showing an obstructive pattern with reversibility.

The 14-mark checklist: introduces and keeps the child with the parent · signposts a sequence · asks conscious state · asks hydration · asks distress by named signs · asks noisy breathing · asks respiratory rate and interprets it for age · asks oxygen saturation · asks weight · completes ears, nose, throat and nodes · asks percussion and vocal resonance, not just air entry · examines the heart · localises to the upper airway before naming croup · correct management order with dexamethasone dosed in mg/kg and a parent-language safety net. AUTOMATIC FAIL, any one: never asked about noisy breathing · never asked oxygen saturation · examined the throat in the epiglottitis variant · gave salbutamol or steroids in the bronchiolitis variant · presented a finding never requested · no safety net or disposition at all.

The five words the station turns on — 'On general appearance: IS HE ALERT OR DROWSY? IS HE DEHYDRATED — mucous membranes, capillary refill, skin turgor? IS THERE ANY RESPIRATORY DISTRESS — nasal flaring, tracheal tug, intercostal or subcostal recession, grunting? ANY CENTRAL CYANOSIS? AND IS THERE ANY NOISY BREATHING?' → 'Alert, well hydrated, no cyanosis. MILD INTERCOSTAL RECESSION. YES — HE HAS INSPIRATORY STRIDOR AT REST, AND A HOARSE BARKING COUGH.' Ask everything except the last five words and you get 'no, nothing abnormal'

The four you never miss — DISTRESS AND CYANOSIS · NOISY BREATHING · RESPIRATORY RATE · OXYGEN SATURATION. Asking for blood pressure and temperature while omitting saturations is THE SINGLE MOST-FORGOTTEN OBSERVATION IN EVERY RESPIRATORY CASE — and it is an automatic fail here

Interpret the number immediately, in one line — 'Thank you — a rate of 34 is mildly raised for a two-year-old, and his saturations are normal, so he is not hypoxic at rest.' Collecting numbers and never interpreting them is the trap. Normal ranges: neonate 40 to 60 · under 1 year 30 to 40 · 1 to 2 years 25 to 35 · 2 to 5 years 25 to 30 · 5 to 12 years 20 to 25 · over 12 years 15 to 20

The lower tract in four requests, not two — INSPECTION AND PALPATION — symmetrical movement, CHEST WALL SHAPE with hyperinflation, barrel chest, HARRISON SULCUS or pectus, tracheal position · PERCUSSION — normal, dull or hyper-resonant, and equal · AUSCULTATION — air entry equal and any added sounds · AND VOCAL RESONANCE. Most candidates ask only about air entry and added sounds. PERCUSSION, CHEST WALL SHAPE AND VOCAL RESONANCE ARE EACH SEPARATE MARKS, AND VOCAL RESONANCE IS WHAT SEPARATES AN EFFUSION FROM CONSOLIDATION

The localising sentence — this is the mark — 'THE ABNORMAL SIGNS ARE ALL INSPIRATORY, AND THE CHEST ITSELF IS CLEAR. THAT LOCALISES THE PROBLEM TO THE UPPER AIRWAY RATHER THAN THE LOWER AIRWAYS OR THE LUNG PARENCHYMA.' Jumping straight from 'stridor' to 'croup' skips the reasoning step the examiner is marking. LOCALISE, THEN NAME

Name it, then grade it — 'My diagnosis is croup — laryngotracheobronchitis. I would grade it as moderate: he has stridor at rest with mild recession, but he is not hypoxic, not agitated or drowsy, and not exhausted.' What would make it severe: increasing stridor at rest with marked recession, agitation or drowsiness, exhaustion with a falling respiratory rate, hypoxia, or a silent chest with poor air entry

Differentials, each with the feature that argues against it — EPIGLOTTITIS — not toxic, NOT DROOLING, fully immunised, and HE DOES HAVE A COUGH · INHALED FOREIGN BODY — possible at two, but the onset was GRADUAL WITH A CORYZAL PRODROME rather than sudden, and air entry is equal · BACTERIAL TRACHEITIS — would give a higher fever and a toxic child · ANAPHYLAXIS — no exposure, urticaria or angioedema · RETROPHARYNGEAL ABSCESS — would usually give neck stiffness or refusal to move the neck · ASTHMA OR BRONCHIOLITIS — would give EXPIRATORY, NOT INSPIRATORY, noise. Three names with no exclusions score far less than three names each followed by its reason

Management — lead with the thing that is not a drug — FIRST: 'KEEP HIM CALM ON HIS MOTHER'S LAP WITH MINIMAL HANDLING — no cannula, no throat examination, no unnecessary observations — BECAUSE DISTRESS WORSENS UPPER AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION AND CAN TURN MODERATE CROUP INTO SEVERE CROUP' · SECOND: ORAL DEXAMETHASONE 0.15 mg/kg AS A SINGLE DOSE, WHICH IS 1.8 mg FOR 12 kg, AND EVERY CHILD WITH CROUP GETS A STEROID INCLUDING MILD CASES; prednisolone 1 mg/kg if unavailable · THIRD: if he worsens, NEBULISED ADRENALINE 1:1000, 0.5 mL/kg TO A MAXIMUM OF 5 mL — about 6 mL for him, SO CAPPED AT 5 — which WORKS IN MINUTES BUT WEARS OFF IN TWO TO THREE HOURS, SO AT LEAST FOUR HOURS OF OBSERVATION FOR REBOUND · oxygen only if saturations fall, given in the least distressing way. NO NECK X-RAY: it is a clinical diagnosis and sending a child with a narrowed airway to radiology delays treatment

The safety net in the mother's words — 'Come straight back, or call an ambulance, IF HE HAS NOISY BREATHING WHILE HE IS RESTING OR ASLEEP, IF YOU CAN SEE THE SKIN SUCKING IN AROUND HIS RIBS OR AT THE BASE OF HIS NECK, IF HIS LIPS OR FACE LOOK BLUE OR GREY, IF HE BECOMES DROWSY OR FLOPPY, OR IF HE WILL NOT DRINK. IT IS OFTEN WORSE AT NIGHT — THAT IS EXPECTED — BUT THOSE THINGS ARE NOT.' 'Return if there is increased work of breathing' means nothing to a frightened parent at midnight

Given in the stem: 20-week scan showed the placenta 5 cm from the internal os · vital signs stable · symphysio-fundal height 29 cm · a bruise on the abdomen · she has already been admitted.

Tasks: take a focused history from Nicole — explain the most likely diagnosis, with your reasons, and give your differential diagnoses. 8 minutes. No investigations, no management, no physical examination.

back.dx: PLACENTAL ABRUPTION SECONDARY TO TRAUMA — AND THE TRAUMA IS FAMILY VIOLENCE, WHICH IS WHAT THE STATION IS ACTUALLY ABOUT. THE THREE WAYS TO LOSE IT ARE ALL IN THE SAME PART OF THE CONSULTATION: asking a violence question WITH SOMEONE ELSE IN THE ROOM · opening with 'DID HE DO THIS TO YOU?' instead of a normalised screening question · and stopping at her WITHOUT EVER ASKING ABOUT THE CHILDREN. WHY SHE STAYS IN, SAID TO HER: 'The bleeding has stopped and you're stable, which is good. BUT AN ABRUPTION CAN BLEED AGAIN WITHOUT WARNING, AND IT CAN BLEED INWARDS WHERE WE CANNOT SEE IT — which is exactly why you are staying in, so we can watch you and the baby closely.' THE SAFETY CONVERSATION MUST HAPPEN, BRIEFLY: while she is here she is safe · social work before discharge · AND A PLAN — somewhere she could go, a bag with documents and clothes, a working phone, and someone who knows what is happening. THE NUMBERS TO GIVE HER: 1800RESPECT ON 1800 737 732, twenty-four hours, AND THE SOUTH AUSTRALIAN DOMESTIC VIOLENCE CRISIS LINE ON 1800 800 098 — either can be rung whether or not she wants police involved. AND THE POLICE ANSWER, GIVEN HONESTLY: 'That is entirely your decision and I will support you either way. I AM NOT OBLIGED TO REPORT VIOLENCE AGAINST AN ADULT, AND I WILL NOT DO IT WITHOUT YOU. WHAT I DO HAVE A DUTY ABOUT IS CHILDREN — so if I were worried about your two, I would have to act, AND I WOULD TELL YOU BEFORE I DID ANYTHING.' On notification more fully: family violence against an adult is not a mandatory notification, but CHILDREN LIVING WITH FAMILY VIOLENCE ARE AT RISK EVEN WHEN THEY ARE NOT STRUCK, so assess that specifically; in South Australia AN UNBORN CHILD CONCERN can be raised so supports are in place before birth VERIFY; and DOCUMENT CONTEMPORANEOUSLY AND IN HER OWN WORDS, because the notes may later be evidence. THE NUMBERS: APH IS BLEEDING FROM THE GENITAL TRACT FROM 20 WEEKS TO BIRTH · PRAEVIA COVERS THE OS AND LOW-LYING IS AN EDGE WITHIN 2 cm, SO 5 cm IS NORMAL · ONLY 60 TO 80% OF ABRUPTIONS BLEED VAGINALLY · SYMPHYSIO-FUNDAL HEIGHT EQUALS GESTATION PLUS OR MINUS 2 TO 3 cm AND A RISING FUNDUS MEANS A CONCEALED BLEED · CORTICOSTEROIDS UNDER 34 TO 35 WEEKS AND MAGNESIUM SULFATE UNDER 34 WEEKS VERIFY. THE UNSTABLE VARIANT — pulse 126, blood pressure 86/50, A WOODY EXQUISITELY TENDER UTERUS, and the fundal height risen 3 cm in an hour — is a CONCEALED ABRUPTION WITH MATERNAL SHOCK AND AN OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: two large-bore cannulae, FULL BLOOD COUNT, COAGULATION PROFILE WITH FIBRINOGEN, CROSS-MATCH AND KLEIHAUER, fluid resuscitation and the MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL, continuous CTG, NO DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION, obstetric team and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — though at 31 weeks and that unstable, the decision is likely IMMEDIATE DELIVERY WHERE SHE IS rather than transfer. THE PAINLESS BRIGHT RED VARIANT points to praevia, and the essential point is NO DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION UNTIL PRAEVIA IS EXCLUDED — a finger through a praevia can cause catastrophic haemorrhage; a gentle speculum is safe and transvaginal ultrasound is the test. AND IF SHE ASKS WHETHER THE BABY IS DAMAGED: 'Your baby is well protected inside the womb, surrounded by fluid, and I HAVE NO REASON AT ALL TO THINK HE HAS BEEN INJURED DIRECTLY. What the blow has done is disturb the join between the afterbirth and the wall of the womb — which is why we are monitoring him now.' THINGS NEVER TO SAY: 'I would do a vaginal examination to assess the cervix' · 'Did he do this to you?' as an opening · 'Are you sure that is how you got the bruise?' · 'Why don't you just leave him?' · 'I won't tell anyone anything, I promise' · 'The scan was normal, so it isn't an abruption' · and 'I'll refer you to White Ribbon', WHICH IS AN AWARENESS CAMPAIGN, NOT A REFERRAL SERVICE.
plan: WIPE AT EYE LEVEL, CHECK SHE IS STABLE BEFORE ANY QUESTIONS — pain, dizziness — AND TELL HER SHE WAS RIGHT TO COME IN. Agreeing that it was probably nothing is the trap; she is minimising more than the bleeding.
THE BLEEDING — onset, still happening or stopped, VOLUME IN PADS, COLOUR, clots, tissue · any trigger, RECENT INTERCOURSE, earlier bleeding this pregnancy.
THE PAIN QUESTION — CONSTANT OR COMES AND GOES — then tenderness, does the tummy GO HARD AND SOFTEN, tightenings, LEAKING FLUID, back pain.
THE BABY — moving as much as usual, when last felt · THEN THE 20-WEEK SCAN, AND INTERPRET THE 5 cm OUT LOUD.
Establish privacy and state confidentiality with the child exception, then name the bruise without accusing (see findings).
DO NOT CHALLENGE THE TABLE STORY — NORMALISE AND SCREEN. Then wait through the pause and respond with the four sentences.
RISK — previous episodes, escalation, WEAPONS, STRANGULATION, HEAD INJURY, other injuries, alcohol and drugs.
THE CHILDREN — ages, whether they have witnessed it, whether he has hurt them, WHERE THEY ARE NOW · then supports, money, phone, somewhere to go.
OBSTETRIC HISTORY — parity, previous deliveries, PREVIOUS CAESAREAN, previous bleeding or abruption.
THIS PREGNANCY — booking bloods, blood pressure, PRE-ECLAMPSIA SYMPTOMS, SMOKING, alcohol and drugs, vitamins and the social context behind them.
The diagnosis in plain words, then the three reasons (see findings).
The differentials, one clause each with the reason each does not fit.
Why she stays in — can rebleed, can bleed inwards — then the safety plan, the social worker, the two numbers, and the honest police answer.
back.planNote: 8 minutes with no investigations, no management and no examination - the history is long, so the diagnosis and differentials need the last two minutes protected
ask: The three lines the station is built on: 'Is the pain constant, or does it come and go?' · 'Is there anyone waiting outside for you?' · 'I noticed a bruise on your tummy — can you tell me how that happened?'

The screening question, which must be normalised rather than accusatory: 'Can I ask you something I ask everyone, because it is common and because it matters so much in pregnancy? Do you ever feel frightened of anyone at home?'

The four sentences after disclosure: 'Thank you for telling me. That took courage. I believe you. None of this is your fault.' and the one that is separately marked: 'Are there other children at home? Are they safe?'

'You absolutely should have come in.' / 'Five centimetres from the opening is a normal position.' / 'A small part of the afterbirth has come away from the wall of the womb.' / 'An abruption can bleed inwards, where we cannot see it.' / 'A normal ultrasound does not exclude an abruption.'

CHALLENGES: 'Is the baby all right?' → he is moving and she is stable, and she is admitted for continuous monitoring · 'Has he hurt the baby? Is the baby brain-damaged?' → the answer in full on the back · 'You won't call the police, will you?' → her decision, no mandatory report for an adult, BUT THE CHILD EXCEPTION STATED PLAINLY · 'Why do I have to stay if it has stopped?' → rebleeding and concealed bleeding · and the examiner's 'she asks you not to tell anyone — what are your obligations?'
pefe: THERE IS NO EXAMINATION TASK IN THIS STATION — and the trap is offering one anyway. NEVER OFFER A DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION IN ANTEPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE UNTIL PRAEVIA IS EXCLUDED; a speculum is what is safe. The findings you are given are in the stem and are meant to be used: STABLE OBSERVATIONS, SFH 29 cm AT 31 WEEKS, THE 5 cm SCAN RESULT, AND THE BRUISE.

Role-player: NICOLE VAUGHAN, 29, 31 weeks, THIRD PREGNANCY, two children aged four and eighteen months, DOUBLE SHIFTS AT THE ROADHOUSE with all the money in her partner's account, mother an hour away, LIVES 45 MINUTES FROM THE HOSPITAL. Smokes five a day, cut down from fifteen; two previous normal births, NO CAESAREAN, no previous bleeding; booking bloods and 20-week scan normal; COULD NOT AFFORD THE PREGNANCY VITAMINS.

THE TRUTH SHE DOES NOT VOLUNTEER: her partner punched her in the abdomen last night after taking drugs; it has happened twice before and is worse when he uses; NEVER A WEAPON, NEVER STRANGULATION, NEVER A HEAD INJURY, AND HE HAS NEVER TOUCHED THE CHILDREN, who were asleep. HOW SHE PLAYS IT: quiet, minimising, apologetic, arms across the bump; SAYS THE TABLE STORY A BEAT TOO FAST; CLOSES DOWN AND GIVES SHORT ANSWERS IF CHALLENGED; discloses after a long pause IF NORMALISED, and becomes tearful. IF THE DOCTOR NEVER MENTIONS THE BRUISE, SHE SAYS NOTHING AND LETS THEM FAIL IT.

THE CHECKLIST: checked she was stable first · said she was right to come in · QUANTIFIED THE BLEED · ASKED CONSTANT VERSUS COMES AND GOES · uterine tenderness and contractions · fluid loss · FETAL MOVEMENTS · INTERPRETED 5 cm CORRECTLY AND OUT LOUD · CHECKED SHE WAS ALONE · ASKED ABOUT THE BRUISE AT ALL · AVOIDED CHALLENGING THE TABLE STORY · USED A NORMALISING SCREENING QUESTION · said 'I believe you' and 'not your fault' · ASSESSED ESCALATION, WEAPONS, STRANGULATION AND HEAD INJURY · ASKED ABOUT THE OTHER CHILDREN AND THEIR SAFETY · asked about supports, money, phone and somewhere to go · asked about PREVIOUS CAESAREAN · asked about SMOKING · NAMED PLACENTAL ABRUPTION IN PLAIN WORDS · GAVE THREE REASONS · gave differentials with why each does not fit · EXPLAINED WHY SHE STAYS IN · offered social work and a named support line · ANSWERED THE POLICE QUESTION HONESTLY INCLUDING THE CHILD EXCEPTION · AND AVOIDED OFFERING A DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION.

The pain question — one question, four differentials — 'Have you had any pain in your tummy? And is the pain constant, or does it come and go?' → 'Sore all day. Constant, like a deep ache. Not in waves.' Constant = abruption or rupture · comes and goes = labour · painless = praevia. Asking 'Any pain?' and stopping is the trap

Do not be reassured by a small bleed — Spotting, less than half a pad, DARK AND OLD-LOOKING, no clots, stopped after an hour. ONLY 60 TO 80% OF ABRUPTIONS BLEED VAGINALLY, AND A SMALL REVEALED BLEED CAN SIT ON TOP OF A LARGE CONCEALED ONE. The dark colour is itself evidence — blood that sat behind the placenta before it came out

Establish privacy before you ask anything — 'Before I go on — IS THERE ANYONE WAITING OUTSIDE FOR YOU? I would like us to have a few minutes on our own. Everything we talk about here is confidential. THE ONE EXCEPTION IS IF I AM EVER WORRIED ABOUT A CHILD'S SAFETY, AND IF THAT CAME UP I WOULD TALK TO YOU ABOUT IT FIRST.' If the partner is in the room, make the request routine and non-negotiable — 'I need to go through some questions we ask everybody' — and IF HE REFUSES TO LEAVE, THAT IS ITSELF INFORMATION: do not ask, find another moment

Name the bruise without accusing, then normalise — 'I noticed a bruise on your tummy. Can you tell me how that happened?' → 'I walked into the corner of the table. I am so clumsy' — said a beat too quickly. Do not challenge the story, because she closes down and gives short answers for the rest of the station. Instead: 'That is easily done. Can I ask you something I ask everyone, because it is common and because it matters so much in pregnancy? Do you ever feel frightened of anyone at home? Has anyone ever hit you, pushed you, or hurt you?'

The disclosure, and the four sentences — Long pause, then quietly: 'IT WAS MY PARTNER. He had taken something — he gets like that when he's used. He hit me. He's not always like it.' THE RESPONSE, UNHURRIED: 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME. THAT TOOK COURAGE. I BELIEVE YOU. NONE OF THIS IS YOUR FAULT. NOBODY HAS THE RIGHT TO HURT YOU, AND I AM GLAD YOU ARE HERE BECAUSE I CAN HELP'

The risk assessment — Has this happened before · is it getting more frequent or more severe · has he ever used a weapon, or put his hands around your neck · have you been hit on the head or knocked out · any other injuries · does he use alcohol or drugs. Her answers: twice before, worse when he is using, no weapon, no strangulation, no other injuries

The children — stopping at her is one of the three ways to lose this — 'ARE THERE OTHER CHILDREN AT HOME? HOW OLD? HAVE THEY EVER SEEN THIS HAPPEN? HAS HE EVER HURT THEM? ARE THEY SAFE RIGHT NOW, AND WHO IS WITH THEM?' → two, FOUR AND EIGHTEEN MONTHS, asleep at the time, never touched, her mother has them today. Then SUPPORTS AND MEANS: who else knows, somewhere to stay, YOUR OWN MONEY AND A WORKING PHONE, somewhere to go tonight — 'only my mum, an hour away; I have a phone; THE MONEY IS ALL IN HIS ACCOUNT'

The rest of the history in ninety seconds — OBSTETRIC: which pregnancy, previous problems or deliveries, ANY PREVIOUS CAESAREAN, any previous bleeding or abruption · THIS PREGNANCY: booking bloods, blood pressure, HEADACHES, VISUAL CHANGES OR RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT PAIN, SMOKING, alcohol and drugs, folic acid and vitamins. She smokes five a day — AN INDEPENDENT RISK FACTOR FOR ABRUPTION, worth naming later — and could not always afford the vitamins, which is answered with 'that is very common and it is not a criticism'

The diagnosis in plain words — 'The afterbirth — the placenta — is the organ attached to the wall of your womb that carries oxygen and food to your baby. I THINK A SMALL PART OF IT HAS COME AWAY FROM THE WALL OF THE WOMB. We call that A PLACENTAL ABRUPTION. When it separates IT BLEEDS FROM BEHIND, and some of that blood has found its way out'

The three reasons — the task asks for them — ONE, A BLOW TO THE ABDOMEN, one of the commonest causes — 'the womb is stretchy but the afterbirth isn't, so a sudden force can shear it away' · TWO, THE PAIN IS CONSTANT RATHER THAN COMING IN WAVES — waves would be labour · THREE, THE BLOOD WAS DARK RATHER THAN BRIGHT RED, so it had been sitting behind the afterbirth. And you may add that SMOKING MAKES AN ABRUPTION MORE LIKELY

The differentials, one clause each — PLACENTA PRAEVIA OR LOW-LYING PLACENTA — the scan put it 5 cm away, and that bleeding is USUALLY PAINLESS · EARLY LABOUR — pain that COMES AND GOES IN WAVES and gets stronger · UTERINE RUPTURE — very rare WITHOUT A PREVIOUS CAESAREAN, and she would be far more unwell · A LOCAL CERVICAL CAUSE — a polyp or inflammation, checked BY SPECULUM. Explaining each one fully is the trap; one clause each with the reason it does not fit, then stop

Interpret the scan number out loud — 'FIVE CENTIMETRES FROM THE OPENING IS A NORMAL POSITION. It is NOT low-lying, which is under 2 cm, and it is NOT a praevia, where the afterbirth covers the opening. So I can set that aside.' The number is in the stem TO BE INTERPRETED, NOT TO MISLEAD YOU — and hearing 'placenta' and 'scan' and reaching for praevia is the trap
fails: ★ Never mentioning the bruise, or asking about it with someone else in the room — and she will not raise it for you
★ Stopping at her and never asking about the other children, or challenging the table story so she closes down for the rest of the station
Asking 'any pain?' without asking whether it is constant or comes and goes — that single question sorts abruption, labour and praevia
Being reassured by a small dark bleed, or hearing 'placenta' and 'scan' and reaching for praevia instead of interpreting 5 cm as normal out loud

Offering a digital vaginal examination; giving the diagnosis without three reasons; explaining each differential at length instead of one clause each; or promising 'I won't tell anyone anything' when the child exception exists
numbers: APH = bleeding from the genital tract from 20 weeks to birth · praevia covers the os, low-lying = edge within 2 cm, 5 cm from the os is normal · only 60 to 80% of abruptions bleed vaginally · SFH = gestation ± 2 to 3 cm and a rising fundus means a concealed bleed · corticosteroids under 34 to 35 weeks, magnesium sulfate under 34 weeks

1800respect 1800 737 732 · SA domestic violence crisis line 1800 800 098 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · unstable abruption: 2 large-bore cannulae, FBC, coagulation with fibrinogen, cross-match, Kleihauer, massive transfusion protocol, continuous CTG, no digital vaginal examination · VERIFY all

Do you ever feel frightened of anyone at home? Has anyone ever hit you, pushed you or hurt you?'

setting: Six boxes, and the first is the one everyone used to fail: she does not go home and she does not stay in the level 4 hospital — she is transferred to a level 6 unit today. Then Kleihauer and anti-D because she is Rh-negative, steroids, a planned caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks, serial scans looking for accreta, and red flags to the end of the pregnancy. There is no history task — drifting into one gets 'Stick to your task'.
stem: Emergency department of a rural hospital, 250 km from the tertiary hospital — a level 4 maternity service with an adult ICU. Jess, 30, 34 weeks pregnant, presented with vaginal bleeding that has now stopped. Haemodynamically stable.

Given: transvaginal ultrasound — single live fetus, cephalic, normal growth, normal liquor, normal fetal heart, placenta praevia grade 4 completely covering the internal os · previous caesarean in her first pregnancy · blood group O negative · BP 118/74, HR 84, afebrile. Tasks: explain the ultrasound findings — explain the other tests and investigations — explain your diagnosis — explain your management plan until the end of the pregnancy. 8 minutes.
tasks: Explain the ultrasound findings
Explain the other tests and investigations
Explain your diagnosis
Explain your management plan until the end of the pregnancy
time: Thirty seconds of opening with an open question, not a lecture · ninety seconds on the scan, normal findings first and the praevia second · ninety seconds on the investigations in three groups, with the Kleihauer first and its reason given · forty-five seconds on the diagnosis and its risks, which are what justify the transfer · then three and a half minutes on the six boxes in order, absorbing her interruptions · then red flags, support and a summary.
findings: Normal findings first, then the praevia

'THE GOOD NEWS FIRST: the fluid around the baby is normal, the heartbeat is normal, THE BABY IS GROWING WELL AND IS HEAD DOWN. Now the placenta — THINK OF IT AS A BRIDGE BETWEEN THE BABY AND YOUR WOMB. Normally it sits at the top. YOURS HAS FORMED AT THE BOTTOM AND IS COMPLETELY COVERING THE OPENING OF THE WOMB. We call that PLACENTA PRAEVIA, and the biggest concern is SEVERE BLEEDING, especially at the birth'

back.dx: MAJOR — GRADE 4 — PLACENTA PRAEVIA WITH A RESOLVED ANTEPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE AT 34 WEEKS, IN A RHESUS-NEGATIVE WOMAN WITH A SCARRED UTERUS, PRESENTING TO A RURAL LEVEL 4 SERVICE 250 km FROM THE TERTIARY HOSPITAL. THE NUMBERS: GRADE 4 IS A COMPLETE PRAEVIA AND 20 mm IS THE LOW-LYING THRESHOLD · KLEIHAUER AFTER 20 WEEKS, WITH ANTI-D 625 IU INTRAMUSCULARLY WITHIN 72 HOURS · BETAMETHASONE 11.4 mg INTRAMUSCULARLY TWICE, 24 HOURS APART, ROUTINE UNDER 35 WEEKS AND CONSIDERED TO 36+6 · LEVEL 6 UNITS ARE THE WOMEN'S AND CHILDREN'S AND FLINDERS, WITH MedSTAR ON 1300 13 12 33 · 24 HOURS OF MONITORING, WITH DISCHARGE ONLY NEAR THE TERTIARY UNIT · CAESAREAN AT 36 TO 37 WEEKS FOR PRAEVIA AND 38 TO 39 FOR A PERSISTENT LOW-LYING PLACENTA · SCANS EVERY 2 TO 3 WEEKS · ACCRETA IN 10 TO 25% WITH ONE PRIOR CAESAREAN · TWO CANNULAE AND 2 TO 4 UNITS CROSS-MATCHED · AND PATS FOR COUNTRY PATIENT TRAVEL, WITH TIS ON 131 450 IF AN INTERPRETER IS NEEDED VERIFY ALL. THE EXAMINER CHALLENGES AND THEIR ANSWERS. 'WHY NOT OBSERVE HER HERE? YOU HAVE AN ICU' → 'An adult ICU does not provide 24-hour obstetric theatre or neonatal intensive care; A RECURRENT BLEED AT 34 WEEKS NEEDS BOTH WITHIN MINUTES.' 'WHY STEROIDS AT 34 WEEKS?' → 'She is under 35 weeks and may need delivery before 37; BENEFIT PERSISTS TO 36+6 FOR A PLANNED CAESAREAN.' 'SHE ALREADY HAD ANTI-D AT 28 WEEKS' → 'PROPHYLACTIC DOSING DOES NOT COVER A SENSITISING BLEED; the Kleihauer guides an additional dose.' 'WHEN WOULD YOU DELIVER IF SHE BLEEDS AGAIN?' → 'HEAVY OR RECURRENT BLEEDING MEANS CAESAREAN THEN, AT ANY GESTATION FROM VIABILITY; otherwise 36 to 37 weeks.' THE VARIANTS. BLEEDING CONTINUES WITH HR 118 AND BP 92/60 → act now: TWO DRIPS, FLUIDS AND BLOOD, OXYGEN, CONTINUOUS FETAL MONITORING, call the retrieval team and the obstetrician, AND IF THE BLEEDING CANNOT BE CONTROLLED THE BABY IS DELIVERED BY CAESAREAN AS SOON AS IT IS SAFE — HERE WITH THE SURGEON IF SHE CANNOT BE MOVED IN TIME — and stay with her. A LOW-LYING PLACENTA AT 32 WEEKS WITH A SMALL BLEED IN A RHESUS-POSITIVE WOMAN → still admit, bloods and CTG and steroids, but MANY LOW PLACENTAS MOVE UP SO RESCAN AT 36 WEEKS; if still low, caesarean at 38 TO 39 weeks, with vaginal birth discussable if it moves further away; NO ANTI-D NEEDED. ACCRETA CONFIRMED ON THE REPEAT SCAN → the placenta has grown into the scar and WILL NOT SEPARATE NORMALLY, so the birth is planned in the city with a big team — obstetrician, anaesthetist, blood bank, sometimes urology and interventional radiology — CAESAREAN AT 34 TO 36 WEEKS, with honesty that THERE IS A REAL CHANCE THE WOMB HAS TO BE REMOVED, discussed with the specialist and with her husband present. AND IF SHE REFUSES TRANSFER → respect the right to refuse, but ensure she is deciding with the full picture, SOLVE THE THINGS STOPPING HER — social work for the children, PATS for the costs, her husband travelling with her — and if she still declines, DOCUMENT IT, KEEP HER ON THE WARD WITH BLOOD CROSS-MATCHED, AND KEEP THE RETRIEVAL TEAM INFORMED. THE LOGISTICS ARE PART OF THE MARK, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: social work for the two children aged four and two, PATS for travel and accommodation, and her husband coming with her — because her hidden agenda is that she wants to go home to the children and Ben cannot get time off.
plan: WIPE, CONFIRM NAME AND DATE OF BIRTH, AND OPEN WITH A QUESTION RATHER THAN A LECTURE — 'how are you feeling now, tell me what has happened' — THEN SIGNPOST THE FOUR PARTS.
THE SCAN — NORMAL FINDINGS FIRST: liquor, fetal heart, growth, cephalic presentation.
Then the praevia with the bridge analogy, the scar as the likely cause, and a clear 'It will not move' at 34 weeks with a complete praevia.
Investigations in three groups — Kleihauer first with its reason, then FBC, iron studies and cross-match, then CTG.
Answer the 28-week anti-D question: a bleed is a separate sensitising event and needs its own dose.

The diagnosis and its risks — vaginal birth impossible, severe bleeding, transfusion, and accreta with possible hysterectomy — then pause and reassure when she becomes tearful without retracting the information.
BOX ONE — TRANSFER TODAY TO A LEVEL 6 UNIT, WITH THE REASON: blood bank, 24-hour theatre, neonatal intensive care.
Box two — 24 hours of monitoring, then staying near the city rather than coming back · box three — caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks, earlier if bleeding returns.
Box four — steroids today and in 24 hours · box five — anti-D per Kleihauer · box six — scans every 2 to 3 weeks looking specifically for accreta.
Absorb the two pushes — 'Can't I go home' and 'Why can't I stay here, you have an icu' — with the answers on the front, and offer social work, PATS and her husband travelling with her.
Red flags to the end of the pregnancy, no sex until after the birth, then the full summary written down, and invite questions.
back.planNote: 8 minutes across four explaining tasks and no history - the management box is three and a half minutes of it, and ending at transfer loses the rest
ask: The critical investigation, explained rather than listed: 'Because you are O negative, a bleed can mix the baby's blood with yours and sensitise you — a problem for a future pregnancy. The Kleihauer test measures how much mixing has happened so I can give the right dose of anti-D.'

The transfer lines: 'We need to transfer you to a more equipped hospital, in preparation for the complications of this condition.' · 'Today's bleed was a warning, and the next one could be sudden and heavy.' · 'We have an adult ICU, but not the newborn intensive care.'

The explanation lines: 'The placenta is like a bridge between the baby and your womb. Normally it sits at the TOP.' · 'This makes it impossible to plan a vaginal birth.' · 'I will ask the radiologist to look for placenta accreta — the placenta growing into the caesarean scar.'
The red flags: 'Any bleeding, pain, tightenings, fewer movements or feeling faint — call 000.'

CHALLENGES: 'Will it move?' → not at 34 weeks with a complete praevia · 'Is it because of my caesarean?' → yes, and it is nothing she did · 'Remove my womb? Is that likely?' → uncommon, most women with praevia do not need it, and you are telling her so it can be looked for and planned · 'Can Ben come with me? Who looks after the kids?' → social work and PATS, answered as part of the plan · and any history question → answer briefly but do not drift off task.
pefe: There is no examination and no history task — the scan report is the station's data. Read back the normal findings before the abnormal one: single live fetus, cephalic, normal growth, normal liquor, normal fetal heart — then grade 4 praevia completely covering the internal os. The other facts that decide management are all in the stem: previous caesarean, O negative, 34 weeks, 250 km from the tertiary unit, level 4 service with an adult ICU.

Role-player: JESS, 30, a farm bookkeeper living 250 km from the city with her husband Ben and CHILDREN AGED FOUR AND TWO, non-smoker. FIRST BIRTH WAS AN EMERGENCY CAESAREAN FOR FETAL DISTRESS. This pregnancy uncomplicated until today; booking bloods normal, O NEGATIVE, ROUTINE ANTI-D AT 28 WEEKS; the 20-week scan reported 'placenta low, rescan later' WHICH SHE FORGOT ABOUT. Today: SUDDEN BRIGHT RED BLEEDING that soaked a pad and her jeans, NO PAIN, no contractions, baby moving, stopped by arrival.

How she plays it: frightened but coherent, interrupting at the natural points. Tearful at 'Remove the womb' — and the mark is whether the doctor pauses and reassures without retracting the information. Her hidden agenda is wanting to go home to the children, raised when management is discussed and pushed twice. The two traps she sets: if the doctor says 'Admit here for observation' she accepts it quietly, and if they say 'You can go home' she says 'Great' and stops asking — both are marked down.

The checklist: opened with a question not a lecture · normal findings first · the bridge analogy · named placenta praevia with severe bleeding as the risk · linked it to the caesarean scar · Kleihauer with its reason · anti-D · FBC, iron, cross-match · CTG · vaginal birth impossible · risks including transfusion and hysterectomy or accreta · transfer to a level 6 hospital, not home and not here · 24-hour monitoring then staying near the city · caesarean 36 to 37 weeks, earlier if bleeding · steroids today · repeat scans and accreta · red flags to the end of pregnancy · family and social support · and stuck to the tasks with no history.

Link it to the scar, and do not promise migration — 'THE MOST LIKELY REASON IS YOUR PREVIOUS CAESAREAN — the placenta tends to attach near the scar. It is nothing you did.' AND WHEN SHE ASKS WHETHER IT WILL MOVE: 'AT 34 WEEKS AND COMPLETELY COVERING THE OPENING, IT WILL NOT MOVE OUT OF THE WAY.' Telling her it may still migrate is the trap

The Kleihauer is the critical investigation — 'The most important: YOU ARE O NEGATIVE. When you bleed, SOME OF THE BABY'S BLOOD CAN MIX WITH YOURS and your body can BECOME SENSITISED to the baby's blood group, which causes problems in a future pregnancy. We prevent that with AN ANTI-D INJECTION — but THE DOSE DEPENDS ON HOW MUCH MIXING THERE HAS BEEN, so we do a blood test called A KLEIHAUER that measures the baby's cells in your blood.' LISTING FBC, ULTRASOUND AND CTG AND MISSING THE KLEIHAUER IS A CRITICAL ERROR

'I had anti-D at 28 weeks — do I need another?' — 'Yes. The 28-week dose is a routine one; a bleed is a separate event and needs its own dose, sized by the Kleihauer.' Put to the examiner: prophylactic dosing does not cover a sensitising bleed
The other two groups — Second: full blood count, iron studies, and cross-matched blood so it is ready · third: a CTG, a trace of the baby's heart, to check the baby is not distressed

The diagnosis and its risks — the risks justify the transfer — 'The placenta is covering the opening of the womb. THAT MAKES A VAGINAL BIRTH IMPOSSIBLE. The risks are SEVERE BLEEDING, often needing A BLOOD TRANSFUSION, and in the severe form — WHERE THE PLACENTA GROWS INTO THE WALL OF THE WOMB, ESPECIALLY INTO A CAESAREAN SCAR — AN OPERATION TO REMOVE THE WOMB may be needed to stop the bleeding. That is rare, and we plan for it.' Softening it into 'a low placenta' or omitting the transfusion and hysterectomy risk is the trap

Box one — transfer today — 'Because of the risk of heavy bleeding and of needing to deliver early, WE TRANSFER YOU TODAY TO A CITY HOSPITAL — A LEVEL 6 UNIT WITH A BLOOD BANK, THEATRE AROUND THE CLOCK AND A NEWBORN INTENSIVE CARE UNIT. The retrieval team will take you.' THIS IS THE BOX EVERYONE USED TO FAIL, AND THE ROLE-PLAYER PUSHES TWICE

Boxes two and three — TWO: MONITORED AT LEAST 24 HOURS for bleeding, contractions and the fetal heart; if there is no further bleeding SHE MAY LEAVE THE HOSPITAL BUT STAYS CLOSE TO IT — accommodation nearby, NOT back to the rural town · THREE: THE BIRTH IS BY CAESAREAN, PLANNED AT 36 TO 37 WEEKS, EARLIER IF BLEEDING RETURNS

Boxes four, five and six — Four: a steroid injection today and another in 24 hours to mature the baby's lungs — betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly, twice, 24 hours apart · five: the anti-D injection, dose per the Kleihauer · six: scans every two to three weeks to check the baby and the placenta, and ask the radiologist specifically to look for the placenta growing into the scar — accreta

'Can't I just go home now it has stopped?' — 'I understand, and I am sorry — no. TODAY'S BLEED WAS A WARNING, AND THE NEXT ONE COULD BE SUDDEN AND HEAVY. You need to be somewhere that can TRANSFUSE BLOOD, DO AN URGENT CAESAREAN AND CARE FOR A PREMATURE BABY WITHIN MINUTES. That is the city hospital, NOT HOME AND NOT HERE. We will help with the children and the travel'

'Why can't I stay here? You have an icu' — 'WE HAVE AN ADULT ICU, BUT NOT THE NEWBORN INTENSIVE CARE OR THE ROUND-THE-CLOCK OBSTETRIC SURGICAL TEAM a 34-week baby with this condition would need. IT IS SAFER TO MOVE YOU NOW WHILE YOU ARE STABLE THAN IN AN EMERGENCY.' Accepting 'admit here for observation' or 'you can go home' is the marked trap, and she accepts either quietly to see whether you say it

Red flags and the close — 'Any time from now: BLEEDING, PAIN OR TIGHTENINGS, FEWER MOVEMENTS, FEELING FAINT — straight to hospital, CALL 000. NO SEX UNTIL AFTER THE BIRTH.' Then the summary: praevia caused by the scar; Kleihauer, anti-D, bloods and CTG now; steroids; TRANSFER TODAY; caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks; SCANS LOOKING FOR ACCRETA; and she stays near the city — WRITTEN DOWN FOR HER. Ending at transfer is the trap, because the wording is 'UNTIL THE END OF THE PREGNANCY'
fails: ★ Admitting her here for observation, or sending her home — she does not stay in a level 4 service and she does not go home; she is transferred to a level 6 unit today
★ Listing FBC, ultrasound and CTG and missing the Kleihauer in a rhesus-negative woman who has bled — a critical error
Ending the plan at transfer when the task says 'until the end of the pregnancy' — the timing of the caesarean, serial scans, accreta, red flags and where she lives until then are all marked
Telling her the placenta may still migrate at 34 weeks with a complete praevia, or starting with the praevia and never giving the normal findings
Softening the diagnosis into 'a low placenta', omitting the transfusion and hysterectomy risks that justify the transfer, or drifting into a history the station did not ask for

Caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks for praevia, 38 to 39 for persistent low-lying · scans every 2 to 3 weeks · accreta 10 to 25% with one prior caesarean · 2 cannulae and 2 to 4 units cross-matched · level 6 units: women's and children's, Flinders · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS for country travel, TIS 131 450 · VERIFY all

setting: A telephone station. Candidates do not fail it for forgetting carboprost — they fail it for starting on drugs, jumping back to airway, remembering the catheter late, and running out of time before the speculum. Announce the three phases out loud — resuscitate, then gather information, then manage all four T's — and name the drugs, because 'Some medication to help the uterus contract' does not pass.
stem: You are the HMO in a rural hospital. You receive a call from the birth suite. The midwife tells you a 29-year-old woman delivered by normal vaginal delivery 15 minutes ago, a 3.7 kg baby, is having severe vaginal bleeding, and has already lost 1.5 litres of blood. You are five minutes away from the birth suite.

There is a telephone in the middle of the station. Pick it up and begin. Tasks: talk to the midwife and take a history, which here includes asking her for examination findings — advise her on the management steps to take between now and your arrival. 8 minutes.
tasks: Talk to the midwife and take a history, including examination findings
Advise her on the management steps to take before you arrive
time: Thirty seconds to open and identify her · a minute and a half of resuscitation instructions · two and a half minutes gathering information, including the examination through her hands · three minutes of management across all four T's plus theatre · and thirty seconds to read the whole plan back as a closed loop.
findings: Phase 2 — the examination through her hands

'FEEL THE FUNDUS — what size is it, IS IT FIRM OR LAX, and is it tender?' → AT THE UMBILICUS, TWENTY WEEKS' SIZE, LAX AND SOFT, NOT TENDER · 'INSPECT THE PERINEUM — any tears or lacerations?' · 'PLEASE PASS A SPECULUM and tell me if there are tears of the cervix or the vaginal walls'

Empty the bladder with the catheter, remove clots, and rub up the fundus until it contracts · oxytocin 5 units IV slowly or 10 units IM, then an infusion of 40 units in a litre over four hours · if bleeding continues, ergometrine 250 micrograms IM — she is not hypertensive — with an antiemetic · then misoprostol or carboprost as next line · and if still uncontrolled, bimanual compression kept on until you arrive

back.dx: PRIMARY POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE WITH SHOCK, MOST LIKELY UTERINE ATONY — MANAGED DOWN A TELEPHONE FROM FIVE MINUTES AWAY, WHICH IS WHY THE STRUCTURE MATTERS MORE THAN THE DRUG LIST. THE NUMBERS: PRIMARY PPH IS 500 mL OR MORE WITHIN 24 HOURS, OR 1000 mL AT CAESAREAN · MAJOR IS OVER 1000 mL AND MASSIVE IS OVER 1500 mL, WHICH TRIGGERS THE MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL · OXYTOCIN 5 IU IV SLOWLY OR 10 IU IM, WITH AN INFUSION OF 40 IU IN 1 LITRE OVER 4 HOURS · ERGOMETRINE 250 MICROGRAMS IM OR SLOW IV, NOT IN HYPERTENSION OR PRE-ECLAMPSIA · MISOPROSTOL 800 TO 1000 MICROGRAMS PER RECTUM · CARBOPROST 250 MICROGRAMS IM EVERY 15 MINUTES TO A MAXIMUM OF 8 DOSES, NOT IN ASTHMA AND NEVER INTRAVENOUSLY · TRANEXAMIC ACID 1 g IV, BEST WITHIN 3 HOURS OF THE BLEEDING STARTING · CRYSTALLOID UP TO ABOUT 2 LITRES WHILE BLOOD IS ARRANGED · AND ANTI-D WITHIN 72 HOURS IF RHESUS D NEGATIVE, BUT ONLY AFTER THE FOUR T'S VERIFY ALL AGAINST THERAPEUTIC GUIDELINES AND LOCAL PROTOCOL. THE VARIANTS EACH MOVE A DIFFERENT T TO THE FRONT. CONTROLLED CORD TRACTION WITH A SNAPPED CORD AND RETAINED PLACENTA → 'pass a speculum, CAN YOU SEE THE CORD? If you can, CLAMP IT — that alone will slow the bleeding — then gentle controlled traction on the clamp. If it delivers, check it is complete. If it does not, call the consultant for MANUAL REMOVAL IN THEATRE UNDER ANAESTHESIA. And still work through all four T's: A RETAINED PLACENTA IS ITSELF A RISK FACTOR FOR ATONY.' BLEEDING WITH A WELL-CONTRACTED UTERUS → 'A FIRM UTERUS WITH CONTINUING BLEEDING IS TRAUMA UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. Speculum now — cervix and vaginal walls — and check the episiotomy if one was done.' SHOCKED WITH LITTLE VISIBLE BLOOD, PREVIOUS CAESAREAN, TENDER ABDOMEN → 'SHOCK OUT OF PROPORTION TO THE VISIBLE LOSS means she is bleeding somewhere I cannot see — RUPTURED UTERUS OR A BROAD LIGAMENT HAEMATOMA. Resuscitate, and she needs the consultant and URGENT LAPAROTOMY — WE DO NOT WAIT FOR IMAGING.' BLOOD NOT CLOTTING WITH OOZING FROM THE CANNULA SITE → tranexamic acid now, urgent coagulation screen with fibrinogen, FFP AND PLATELETS THROUGH THE PROTOCOL, and haematology. AND IF THE MIDWIFE SAYS 'MY NOTES SAY A SPECULUM IS CONTRAINDICATED' — THAT IS WRONG, AND THE ANSWER IS TO DISAGREE POLITELY: 'I have a clear indication — I need to see the cervix and vaginal walls, because A TEAR THERE IS A TREATABLE CAUSE I WOULD OTHERWISE MISS.' THE RURAL VARIANT: at an MM5 site with no on-site obstetrician, CALL MedSTAR ON 1300 13 12 33 IMMEDIATELY for advice and urgent retrieval, CHECK EMERGENCY O-NEGATIVE STOCK, involve the on-call obstetrician and anaesthetist by phone, and KEEP BIMANUAL COMPRESSION GOING WHILE WAITING — with the Aboriginal Family Birthing Program and an Aboriginal Liaison Officer where relevant, and TIS National 131 450 for interpreting. THE ROLE-PLAYER SETS FOUR TRAPS DELIBERATELY: the intact-perineum question · 'should I wait for the coags before the tranexamic acid?' · 'WHICH MEDICATION, DOCTOR?' if you say only 'give her something for the uterus' · and at about six minutes, 'DO YOU WANT ME TO PREPARE HER FOR THEATRE?' if you have not said it. If you never mention the woman herself, she ends with 'WHAT SHALL I TELL HER AND HER HUSBAND?'
plan: Identify yourself, identify her by name and role, and ask what has happened — before any instruction.
Announce the structure out loud, then phase 1: alert and responsive · send for help, registrar and consultant · airway, breathing, high-flow oxygen.
Observations, then say the shock out loud · two large-bore cannulas with bloods as she goes · warmed saline · catheter with output measured.
Activate the massive transfusion protocol at 1.5 litres, get o-negative up, and keep her warm.
PHASE 2, THE BLEEDING — colour, pouring or oozing, clots, IS IT CLOTTING AND WHY YOU ASK, blood group.
THE DELIVERY HISTORY AS FOUR T'S — labour length and baby size, instruments and episiotomy, previous caesarean, PLACENTA DELIVERED AND COMPLETE, bleeding disorder and anticoagulants.
The examination through her hands — fundus size, tone and tenderness, then perineum, then insist on the speculum with the reason.
State the working diagnosis honestly — atony most likely, all four treated together because the phone cannot exclude the others.
TONE — bladder, clots, FUNDAL MASSAGE, OXYTOCIN WITH THE DOSE, then ergometrine, then misoprostol or carboprost, then BIMANUAL COMPRESSION.
TISSUE — recheck placenta AND MEMBRANES, and name manual removal and uterine exploration if anything is missing.
TRAUMA — speculum findings and direct pressure on any tear, with rupture named if she stays shocked without visible loss.
THROMBIN — TRANEXAMIC ACID 1 g IV NOW WITHOUT WAITING FOR COAGS, and the three blood tests by name.
The fifth T — theatre prepared now, anaesthetist informed, and someone talking to her and her partner.
Read the whole plan back as a closed loop and ask what you have not covered.
