ask: The opening two: 'Who am I speaking with?' and 'Can you tell me what has happened so far?' — then 'Resuscitate first, then questions, then a plan.'

The resuscitation lines: 'Please send for help now — registrar and consultant.' · 'Two large-bore cannulas, bloods as you go, warmed saline immediately.' · 'She has lost more than 1500 mL — activate the massive transfusion protocol.'
The two questions that are not in the volume: 'Is the blood clotting on the floor?' and 'Has the placenta delivered — and is it complete?'

The line that is the critical error if missed: 'An intact perineum does not exclude a cervical or vaginal tear.' and the one she will test: 'Tranexamic acid one gram IV now — don't wait for the coags.'

THE DRILLS: say the full resuscitation block in 45 seconds without notes · name the four T's with one question each in 30 seconds · give the uterotonic ladder with doses in 20 seconds · then run the snapped-cord, firm-uterus, concealed-rupture and coagulopathy variants and say what changes in each.
pefe: There is no patient and no examiner findings card — you examine through the midwife's hands, and the order is fundus, then perineum, then speculum. What comes back: uterus at the umbilicus, twenty weeks' size, lax and soft, not tender · perineum intact · and on speculum, no tears of the cervix or vaginal walls. The negative speculum is not a wasted question — it is what lets you say atony with confidence.

Role-player: JANE, a midwife in the birth suite of a small rural hospital, CAPABLE BUT STRETCHED AND ALONE WITH A BLEEDING WOMAN. She is BUSY, NOT HYSTERICAL — brisk, professional, a little urgent. She does what she is told promptly and reports back, BUT ONLY GIVES WHAT IS ASKED FOR. Observations given once: 80/50, PULSE 120, SATS 98.

Her set-pieces: 'The perineum's intact, doctor — do you still want a speculum?' · 'Should I wait for the coags before the tranexamic acid?' · 'Which medication, doctor?' if the instruction is vague · at six minutes, 'Do you want me to prepare her for theatre?' · and at the end, 'What shall I tell her and her husband?' if the woman has never been mentioned.

THE CHECKLIST, WITH FIVE MARKED AUTO-FAILS: INTRODUCED THEMSELVES AND IDENTIFIED HER BEFORE GIVING ORDERS · announced the structure · ★SENT FOR HELP, REGISTRAR AND CONSULTANT · two cannulas, warmed fluids, oxygen, catheter, continuous observations · RECOGNISED SHOCK OUT LOUD AND ACTIVATED THE PROTOCOL AT 1.5 L · named GROUP AND CROSS-MATCH FIRST with FBE and coagulation screen · asked whether the blood was clotting AND SAID WHY · asked uterine size, tone and tenderness · ★INSISTED ON THE SPECULUM DESPITE THE INTACT PERINEUM · ★CONSIDERED RETAINED TISSUE AND UTERINE EXPLORATION DESPITE A COMPLETE PLACENTA · ★NAMED THE DRUGS · gave tranexamic acid without waiting for coags · PREPARED HER FOR THEATRE · and mentioned the woman and her partner and closed the loop.

Open by identifying her, not by giving orders — 'Hello, this is Dr [name], I'm the HMO on tonight. WHO AM I SPEAKING WITH? … Thanks for calling. CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT HAS HAPPENED SO FAR?' Opening with 'check her blood pressure' READS AS PANIC, loses the rapport marks, and means you miss the detail the role-player is scripted to add beyond the stem

Phase 1 — the resuscitation instructions, in this order — 'I'm going to do three things: resuscitate first, then ask questions, then give you a full plan' · is she alert and responsive · send for help now and call the obstetric registrar and consultant · airway patent, breathing, high-flow oxygen · blood pressure, pulse and saturations monitored continuously · two large-bore cannulas, bloods as you go, warmed normal saline immediately · indwelling catheter with urine output measured · activate the massive transfusion protocol and get o-negative up while waiting for cross-match · and keep her warm

Say the number back as a grade — BP 80/50, PULSE 120, SATS 98, awake but PALE AND CLAMMY → 'EIGHTY OVER FIFTY WITH A PULSE OF A HUNDRED AND TWENTY — SHE IS SHOCKED, AND WITH 1.5 LITRES THIS IS A MASSIVE OBSTETRIC HAEMORRHAGE.' Naming the shock out loud is a mark, and it explains to the examiner why you are activating the protocol

Phase 2 — the bleeding itself — Bright red or dark · POURING OR OOZING · any clots · IS THE BLOOD CLOTTING ON THE FLOOR · do we know her blood group. Asking about pads or asking her to estimate millilitres is the trap — YOU ALREADY KNOW THE VOLUME; what you need is whether it is ongoing and whether it clots. AND SAY WHY YOU ARE ASKING: 'if it isn't clotting I'm thinking about a coagulopathy'

Phase 2 — the delivery history, where every question is a T — HOW LONG WAS THE LABOUR and how big the baby → TONE · INSTRUMENTS OR EPISIOTOMY → TRAUMA · PREVIOUS CAESAREAN OR UTERINE SURGERY → RUPTURE · HAS THE PLACENTA DELIVERED AND IS IT COMPLETE → TISSUE · BLEEDING DISORDER OR ANTICOAGULANTS → THROMBIN. Say the link out loud once and the examiner knows you are not reading a list. Her answers: 18-HOUR LABOUR, no instruments, single baby, no previous surgery, PLACENTA COMPLETE, no bleeding disorder

The set-piece — 'The perineum's intact, do you still want a speculum?' — Yes, and say why: 'An intact perineum does not exclude a cervical or vaginal tear, and I need to know before she goes to theatre.' Accepting 'The perineum is intact' and moving on is the named critical error of the handbook case

The diagnosis, stated honestly — 'She has a PRIMARY POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE AND SHE IS SHOCKED. The most likely cause is UTERINE ATONY, because the uterus is LAX AND SOFT and she had a LONG LABOUR AND A BIG BABY. BUT I CANNOT EXCLUDE THE OTHERS DOWN A TELEPHONE, SO I AM GOING TO ASK YOU TO TREAT ALL FOUR CAUSES TOGETHER.' If the examiner asks for the diagnosis, THE MARKED ANSWER IS NOT A SINGLE CONFIDENT WORD — it is atony as most likely, with all four T's assessed and treated at once because it is too urgent to work through them one at a time

Tissue and trauma — TISSUE: 'lay the placenta out again and RUN THE MEMBRANES THROUGH YOUR FINGERS' — if anything is missing, or if bleeding continues, MANUAL REMOVAL AND UTERINE EXPLORATION UNDER ANAESTHESIA · TRAUMA: perineum and SPECULUM for cervix and vaginal walls, DIRECT PRESSURE on any tear, repaired on arrival or in theatre if high · AND IF SHE STAYS SHOCKED WITHOUT MUCH VISIBLE BLOOD, THINK RUPTURED UTERUS

Thrombin, and the fifth T — TRANEXAMIC ACID 1 GRAM IV NOW — 'WE DO NOT WAIT FOR THE COAGULATION SCREEN', and she is scripted to ask whether she should wait · BLOODS: GROUP AND CROSS-MATCH FIRST, FULL BLOOD EXAMINATION, AND A COAGULATION SCREEN WITH INR, APTT AND FIBRINOGEN · packed cells, FFP and platelets through the protocol, HAEMATOLOGY if it continues · THE FIFTH T IS THEATRE: tell the registrar and consultant she will likely need EXAMINATION UNDER ANAESTHESIA AND UTERINE EXPLORATION, prepare her now, tell the anaesthetist — AND EXPLAIN TO HER AND HER PARTNER WHAT IS HAPPENING

The closed loop — do not skip it — 'LET ME READ THAT BACK, JANE. Help called, oxygen, two cannulas, warmed fluids, catheter, MTP activated, O-negative up. Bloods: group and cross-match, full blood count, coagulation screen. Fundal massage and clots out, oxytocin and tranexamic acid now, ergometrine if it continues, bimanual compression if it does not settle. Speculum for tears, placenta and membranes rechecked, and prepare her for theatre. ANYTHING YOU'RE WORRIED ABOUT THAT I HAVEN'T COVERED? I'M WALKING DOWN NOW'

★ Not naming the drugs — 'some medication to help the uterus contract' does not pass, and she will ask 'which medication, doctor?'
Failing to send for help and call the registrar and consultant, or never activating the massive transfusion protocol despite 1.5 litres
Opening with an order instead of identifying yourself and her; or letting the three phases collapse into each other so you run out of time before the speculum and theatre
Dropping retained tissue because the placenta 'looked complete', waiting for the coagulation screen before tranexamic acid, or never mentioning theatre, the anaesthetist, or the woman and her partner

Carboprost 250 mcg IM every 15 min, max 8 doses, not in asthma and never IV · tranexamic acid 1 g IV, best within 3 hours · crystalloid up to about 2 L while blood is arranged · bloods: group and cross-match, FBE, coagulation screen with fibrinogen · anti-D within 72 h if Rh d negative, after the four T's · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450 · VERIFY all

setting: The shape of a pass is four findings as reasons, then four differentials. Candidates who reach 'Endometritis' and stop there do not pass. The single most useful question is 'Does it have a bad smell?' — she is embarrassed and will not volunteer it, and if you never ask she never offers it, which is the whole point of the station. Ask for the temperature in your first sentence and you have 38.5 at twenty seconds.
stem: Your next patient is Mary, a 25-year-old woman, who has presented to the emergency department complaining of bleeding. She delivered a 3.9 kg baby by normal vaginal delivery 10 days ago. She had a long labour and an episiotomy. She is on the bed, and the examiner is in the room and will hand you examination findings when you ask for them.

Tasks: take a history from the patient — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings — explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient. 8 minutes. A management task is sometimes added.

findings: Ask for the temperature in your first sentence

'Examiner, BEFORE I BEGIN — may I have her observations, INCLUDING HER TEMPERATURE?' → TEMPERATURE 38.5, BP 110/70, PULSE 88, RR 16, SATS 99. Leaving the temperature until the examination block is the trap; getting it at twenty seconds LETS YOU STEER THE WHOLE HISTORY TOWARD INFECTION while still covering the other four causes

INSPECTION: is the episiotomy healing or bleeding, any discharge, swelling, redness or bruising · SPECULUM: IS THE OS OPEN OR CLOSED — SAY THE OS BEFORE blood, discharge, lesions or tears · BIMANUAL: CERVICAL MOTION TENDERNESS, uterine SIZE, TENDERNESS and border regularity, adnexal tenderness or masses

Temperature 38.5, BP 110/70, pulse 88 · alert, not pale, uncomfortable · lower abdominal tenderness, a suprapubic mass, and the lower border cannot be felt · episiotomy healing with no bleeding from it · speculum: the os is open with blood coming through it, no tears or lesions · bimanual: cervical motion tenderness present, uterus ten weeks' size, tender, regular border, adnexae normal

back.dx: ENDOMETRITIS CAUSING A SECONDARY POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE AT DAY TEN — AND THE STATION IS PASSED BY GIVING FOUR FINDINGS AS REASONS AND THEN FOUR DIFFERENTIALS, NOT BY NAMING THE DIAGNOSIS. THE ANATOMY AND TIMELINE THAT MAKE THE FINDINGS MEAN SOMETHING: PRIMARY PPH IS WITHIN 24 HOURS AND SECONDARY IS FROM 24 HOURS TO 12 WEEKS, WITH NO AGREED VOLUME THRESHOLD FOR SECONDARY · THE FUNDUS IS AT THE UMBILICUS AT BIRTH AND DESCENDS ABOUT ONE FINGER-BREADTH A DAY, SO IT SHOULD BE BEHIND THE SYMPHYSIS BY DAY 10 TO 14 AND NORMAL SIZE BY SIX WEEKS — WHICH IS WHY A TEN-WEEK-SIZE UTERUS WITH AN UNREACHABLE LOWER BORDER AT DAY TEN IS ABNORMAL · THE CERVICAL OS CLOSES WITHIN ONE TO TWO DAYS, SO OPEN AT DAY TEN IS ABNORMAL · AND LOCHIA RUNS RED FOR A FEW DAYS, THEN BROWN, THEN PALE, OVER TWO TO SIX WEEKS. THIS CASE: 38.5 °C, BP 110/70, PULSE 88, UTERUS TEN WEEKS' SIZE. ANTI-D WITHIN 72 HOURS IF RHESUS D NEGATIVE VERIFY. THE VARIANTS SHIFT WHICH CAUSE LEADS BUT RARELY CHANGE THE TREATMENT. AFEBRILE, CORD SNAPPED AT DELIVERY, OS OPEN → retained products leads: ultrasound and a short procedure, BUT STILL START ANTIBIOTICS, BECAUSE WHEN TISSUE IS LEFT BEHIND THERE IS ALMOST ALWAYS SOME INFECTION WITH IT. DAY 4, NO FEVER, BRUISING AND NOSEBLEEDS → a clotting problem, possibly congenital and only now revealed: full blood count, clotting studies, and HAEMATOLOGY INVOLVED. FEVER 39.2, PULSE 128, BP 88/52, CONFUSED → THIS IS SEPSIS AND NOT A HISTORY STATION ANY MORE: move her to resuscitation, high-flow oxygen, TWO LARGE-BORE CANNULAS, fluids, BLOOD CULTURES AND LACTATE, INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS WITHIN THE HOUR, escalate to senior and gynaecology immediately — AND THINK ABOUT GROUP A STREPTOCOCCUS, WHICH CAN DETERIORATE VERY FAST. PAINFUL SWELLING BESIDE THE EPISIOTOMY → a haematoma or wound breakdown, WHICH NEEDS LOOKING AT RATHER THAN JUST PALPATING THE ABDOMEN, and may need draining or re-suturing. DAY 30, WELL, BOTTLE FEEDING SINCE WEEK ONE → the first period returning is plausible, BUT ONLY AFTER EXCLUSION: still examine and still scan. AND AT AN MM5 RURAL SITE WITH NO ULTRASOUND TODAY, YOU STILL TREAT — cultures and swabs and the first dose of IV antibiotics given locally, discussed with on-call gynaecology, TRANSFER ARRANGED FOR THE SCAN WITH PATS SUPPORT, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if she becomes unstable, Country Health Connect for follow-up, and TIS National 131 450 for an interpreter. THE HUMAN PART IS SEPARATELY MARKED: 'YOU WERE RIGHT TO COME IN' near the start, asking HOW THE BABY IS AND HOW SHE IS COPING during the history, and ANSWERING HER TWO QUESTIONS — breastfeeding continues, and the baby is not at risk from her infection. If you use jargon she says 'sorry, what does that mean?', and if nothing has been said about the baby by seven minutes she asks 'WHO'S GOING TO LOOK AFTER HIM?' AND FOR MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT IN THE POSTNATAL PERIOD, PANDA IS 1300 726 306.
plan: Sanitise hands where the examiner can see, then ask for observations including the temperature before you greet her.
INTRODUCE YOURSELF, ASK HOW YOU CAN HELP, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE HER WORRY AND SAY SHE WAS RIGHT TO COME IN — then signpost history, examination, explanation.
THE BLEEDING — onset, constant or intermittent, worsening, COLOUR, CLOTS, DISCHARGE, PAD COUNT AND WHETHER SOAKED.
THE SMELL QUESTION, THEN NAME ITS SIGNIFICANCE OUT LOUD · then dizziness, tiredness and breathlessness as symptoms of the loss.
THE DELIVERY — mode and term, LABOUR LENGTH, instruments, THE CUT AND WHETHER IT IS HEALING, PROBLEMS WITH THE AFTERBIRTH, immediate postnatal bleeding, parity.
INFECTION — abdominal pain, FEVER, CHILLS AND SHIVERING, and anything introduced: sex, tampons, a coil.
CLOTTING AND BACKGROUND — bruising, nosebleeds, previous menstrual history, FAMILY BLEEDING HISTORY, anticoagulants · CERVICAL SCREENING AND BLOOD GROUP.
THE BABY AND HOW SHE IS COPING — separately marked, and she will raise it herself at seven minutes if you do not.
Examination — general, then abdominal inspection and palpation, including whether the lower border of the mass can be felt.
Pelvic with consent and a chaperone — episiotomy, then speculum with the os first, then bimanual.
Name endometritis in plain words and give the four reasons as findings she can follow.
The four differentials in plain English, each with what would settle it.
If management is asked — admit, cultures and swabs, IV antibiotics before the scan, ultrasound, possible theatre — then answer the breastfeeding and baby questions.

ask: The first sentence: 'Examiner, before I begin — may I have her observations, including her temperature?'
The question the station is built on: 'Does it have a bad smell?' — followed by 'That's important, because a smell like that points towards an infection.'
The two examination questions that are separately marked: 'Can I feel the lower border of that mass?' and 'Is the os open or closed?'
The four reasons, said as plain findings: fever · a womb bigger than expected at day ten · a tender womb · and an os still open when it should have closed within a day or two.

HER QUESTIONS AND THE CHALLENGES: 'Is that serious?' → treatable, but treated promptly because infections after birth can spread · 'CAN I STILL FEED HIM?' → yes, with antibiotics safe in breastfeeding · 'Is my baby at risk?' → no, but someone needs to be with him · 'Sorry, what does that mean?' if you use jargon · and 'WHO'S GOING TO LOOK AFTER HIM?' if the baby is never mentioned.
pefe: Request the findings in the right order, because the order is the mark: general appearance · abdominal inspection · abdominal palpation with the lower-border question · then pelvic with consent and a chaperone, with the os asked before anything else on speculum. Going to the pelvis first loses the finding that makes the diagnosis — a suprapubic mass whose lower border you cannot reach is the uterus, not a bladder or a cyst.

Role-player: MARY, 25, FIRST BABY TEN DAYS AGO — a boy, 3.9 kg, normal delivery AFTER A VERY LONG LABOUR, WITH AN EPISIOTOMY. Tired, sore and worried, HOT AND COLD WITH SHIVERS LAST NIGHT. She plays it FLAT AND EXHAUSTED, NOT DRAMATIC, and does not cry or volunteer a diagnosis.

HER SET-PIECE: SHE IS EMBARRASSED ABOUT THE SMELL AND REVEALS IT ONLY IF ASKED DIRECTLY — IF THE DOCTOR NEVER ASKS, SHE NEVER OFFERS IT. On the afterbirth she says 'I WASN'T WATCHING' and does not help. After the diagnosis she asks 'IS THAT SERIOUS?' then 'CAN I STILL FEED HIM?'; she asks what jargon means; and at seven minutes, if nothing has been said about the baby, 'WHO'S GOING TO LOOK AFTER HIM?'

THE CHECKLIST, WITH FIVE MARKED AUTO-FAILS: asked for observations INCLUDING TEMPERATURE early · acknowledged her worry first · ★ASKED EXPLICITLY WHETHER THE BLEEDING SMELLED · colour, clots, pad count and whether soaked · dizziness and tiredness · WHETHER THE EPISIOTOMY WAS HEALING · PROBLEMS DELIVERING THE AFTERBIRTH · clotting screen by history · cervical screening · EXAMINED THE ABDOMEN BEFORE THE PELVIS · ★ASKED WHETHER THE LOWER BORDER OF THE MASS COULD BE FELT · mentioned CONSENT AND A CHAPERONE · ★ASKED WHETHER THE OS WAS OPEN OR CLOSED · uterine size, tenderness and cervical motion tenderness · ★NAMED ENDOMETRITIS WITH FOUR FINDINGS AS REASONS · ★GAVE FOUR DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN ENGLISH · said ANTIBIOTICS BEFORE THE SCAN · and asked about the baby and how she is coping.

The smell question — the set-piece — Asked in plain words: 'DOES IT HAVE A BAD SMELL?' → 'YES. IT SMELLS AWFUL, ACTUALLY. I WAS TOO EMBARRASSED TO SAY.' THEN NAME THE SIGNIFICANCE OUT LOUD: 'THAT'S IMPORTANT, BECAUSE AN OFFENSIVE SMELL POINTS TOWARDS AN INFECTION.' It is the most useful question in the station and the one most often skipped

The bleeding — When it started — THREE DAYS AGO, ten days postpartum · CONSTANT AND GETTING HEAVIER · BRIGHT RED · a few clots · SOME DISCHARGE WITH IT · FIVE OR SIX PADS A DAY, SOAKED THROUGH · the smell · AND THE SYMPTOMS OF LOSS: light-headed on standing, EXHAUSTED

The delivery history — ask about the episiotomy even though it is in the stem — Vaginal or caesarean and at term · HOW LONG THE LABOUR — nearly a whole day · instruments · 'DID THEY HAVE TO MAKE A CUT? IS IT HEALING WELL?' — sore but closing up · 'WERE YOU AWARE OF ANY PROBLEMS DELIVERING THE AFTERBIRTH?' — 'I WASN'T WATCHING', and she will not help you · did she bleed heavily straight after the birth · first baby. THE STEM SAYS THE EPISIOTOMY EXISTS; ONLY YOU CAN ASK WHETHER IT IS HEALING AND HAVE IT INSPECTED

Infection, clotting and the rest — Tummy pain — a low dragging ache · fever, chills or shivering — hot and cold, shivers last night · sex, tampons, or anything put inside like a coil — no · bruising, nosebleeds, heavy periods before pregnancy, family bleeding history, blood thinners — all negative · cervical screening and blood group — screening fine two years ago, O positive · and how is the baby, and how are you coping

Why you keep asking after you already know — You had the diagnosis at twenty seconds. THE REMAINING FOUR MINUTES ARE HOW YOU EARN THE DIFFERENTIALS MARK — every block is a cause you will name later, and THE EXAMINER IS WATCHING WHETHER YOU ACTIVELY EXCLUDED THEM OR SIMPLY LISTED THEM AT THE END

The four differentials, in plain English — RETAINED TISSUE — 'a small piece of the afterbirth or its membranes left behind in the womb; that is common, and WE CAN ONLY REALLY TELL WITH A SCAN' · A TEAR — in the neck of the womb or the vagina, OR THE CUT BLEEDING AGAIN · A CLOTTING PROBLEM — one she was born with that has shown up now, or one that has developed · AND CAUSES UNRELATED TO THE PREGNANCY — a fibroid, a cervical polyp, RARELY A CANCER, and THE FIRST PERIOD RETURNING, which can be early and heavy especially if breastfeeding has stopped

If a management task is added — ADMIT · BLOODS, BLOOD CULTURES AND SWABS · BROAD-SPECTRUM IV ANTIBIOTICS STARTED STRAIGHT AWAY, because 'WE DO NOT WAIT FOR THE SCAN — IF THERE IS TISSUE LEFT BEHIND THERE IS ALMOST ALWAYS INFECTION WITH IT' · THEN ULTRASOUND, and theatre for a short procedure if products are seen · fluids, analgesia, and close observation of temperature and blood pressure. HER TWO QUESTIONS: 'CAN I STILL BREASTFEED?' → YES, with antibiotics safe in breastfeeding, and feeding is good for both · 'IS MY BABY AT RISK?' → NO, this is an infection in her womb, not something that passes to him, BUT SOMEONE NEEDS TO BE WITH HIM WHILE SHE IS IN HOSPITAL. DO NOT QUOTE A REGIMEN YOU ARE UNSURE OF — 'broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines' IS A COMPLETE ANSWER

The four reasons — said back to her as findings — 'The most likely cause is ENDOMETRITIS — AN INFECTION OF THE LINING OF THE WOMB. I say that FOR FOUR REASONS. FIRST, YOU HAVE A FEVER — 38.5. SECOND, YOUR WOMB IS LARGER THAN I WOULD EXPECT TEN DAYS AFTER BIRTH — it should have shrunk back behind your pubic bone by now. THIRD, IT IS TENDER WHEN I PRESS ON IT. AND FOURTH, THE OPENING OF THE WOMB IS STILL OPEN, when it should have closed within a day or two of the birth. THE BAD SMELL FITS WITH THAT TOO'

The examination request — abdomen before pelvis — GENERAL: alert or drowsy, pale, in pain, dehydrated · ABDOMEN INSPECTION: distension, scars, movement with respiration · ABDOMEN PALPATION: tenderness, A MASS, AND CAN I FEEL THE LOWER BORDER OF THAT MASS · THEN PELVIC WITH CONSENT AND A CHAPERONE. Going to the pelvis first is the trap — THE UTERUS IS FOUND ON THE ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION, AND 'CAN I GET BELOW IT?' IS THE QUESTION THAT TURNS A MASS INTO A DIAGNOSIS
fails: ★ Never asking whether the bleeding smells — she is too embarrassed to volunteer it, and the station is built around the question
★ Naming endometritis and stopping there, without four findings as reasons and four differentials in plain English
Going to the pelvis before the abdomen, or never asking whether the lower border of the suprapubic mass can be felt — that question is what turns a mass into a uterus
Failing to ask whether the os is open or closed, or leaving the temperature until the examination block instead of the first sentence

Skipping the episiotomy because it is in the stem; quoting an antibiotic regimen you are unsure of instead of 'broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines'; or waiting for the ultrasound before starting antibiotics
numbers: Primary PPH < 24 hours; secondary 24 hours to 12 weeks, with no agreed volume threshold · fundus at the umbilicus at birth, descending about one finger-breadth a day · behind the symphysis by day 10 to 14 and normal size by 6 weeks · cervical os closes within 1 to 2 days, so open at day 10 is abnormal · lochia red for a few days, then brown, then pale, over 2 to 6 weeks

This case: 38.5 °C, BP 110/70, pulse 88, uterus 10 weeks' size, os open with blood through it · anti-D within 72 hours if Rh d negative · sepsis variant: blood cultures and lactate with IV antibiotics within the hour, thinking group A streptococcus · PANDA 1300 726 306 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450 · VERIFY all

setting: A telephone call twenty minutes after delivery, and the only information you are given is one blood pressure reading. The two special questions are what medications she has had — named, because 'Any medications?' Gets 'The usual for the third stage' — and how much IV fluid. The explanation must be a list with the most likely first and postpartum pre-eclampsia kept open, not one cause.
stem: You are the doctor on duty in a rural South Australian maternity unit, with the obstetric registrar and consultant reachable by phone and MedSTAR for retrieval. The midwife calls: a 32-year-old woman delivered 20 minutes ago and her blood pressure is 190/100. She was diagnosed with gestational hypertension at 39½ weeks, had an induction for it, and has lost 250 mL of blood.

You have one reading and nothing else until you ask. Tasks: talk to the midwife and take a history, including the examination findings you direct her to obtain — explain the reason for the high blood pressure and the likely causes — explain your management plan. 8 minutes.
tasks: Talk to the midwife and take a history, including directed examination findings
Explain the likely causes of the high blood pressure
Explain your management plan
time: Thirty seconds to introduce and ask an open question · ninety seconds of resuscitation checklist · two and a half minutes across four history boxes and the directed examination · a minute on the causes, most likely first · and two and a half minutes of management, the consultant call, monitoring and a closed-loop read-back.
findings: What comes back, and the grade you say out loud

Awake, talking, HOLDING THE BABY · RR 18, SATS 98 · PULSE 88, TEMP 37.1 · TWO READINGS FIVE MINUTES APART, 190/100 AND 186/102 · cannula already in from the induction. SAY IT: 'SO THIS IS SEVERE HYPERTENSION.' THE CUFF VARIANT EXISTS — one reading only, and on a large cuff it repeats at 148/92
The directed examination, through her hands

Is she fully alert · any rash or bruising · are you able to do fundoscopy — she cannot · right upper quadrant tenderness · the uterus, firm and tender or not · 'Please check her reflexes and for ankle clonus' — normal, no clonus · a urine dipstick for protein when she next passes urine · and the cord blood group, because she is O negative
Bloods and the antihypertensive, by name and dose

Bloods from the cannula: UEC with creatinine and eGFR, full blood count with platelets and haemoglobin, liver function, and a spot urine protein as well as the dipstick · then labetalol 20 mg IV over two minutes; if still above 160/110 at ten minutes, 40 mg, then 80 mg · if labetalol is unavailable or she is asthmatic, hydralazine 5 to 10 mg IV repeated every 20 minutes · aiming below 160/110 first, then towards 110–140/80–85. Doses without a repeat interval is the trap, and she will ask 'What do you want me to give, doctor?' if you are vague

back.dx: SEVERE POSTPARTUM HYPERTENSION ON A BACKGROUND OF GESTATIONAL HYPERTENSION, DRIVEN BY PAIN, DRUGS AND FLUID — WITH POSTPARTUM PRE-ECLAMPSIA NOT YET EXCLUDED. THE NUMBERS: HYPERTENSION IS 140/90 OR ABOVE AND SEVERE IS 160 SYSTOLIC AND/OR 110 DIASTOLIC OR ABOVE, WITH A TARGET OF 110–140 OVER 80–85 · LABETALOL 20 THEN 40 THEN 80 mg IV AT TEN-MINUTE INTERVALS TO A MAXIMUM OF 300 mg · HYDRALAZINE 5 TO 10 mg IV EVERY 20 MINUTES · NIFEDIPINE 10 TO 20 mg ORALLY · PARACETAMOL 1 g · MAGNESIUM SULFATE 4 g OVER 15 TO 20 MINUTES THEN 1 g PER HOUR, WITH TOXICITY MONITORED BY REFLEXES, A RESPIRATORY RATE UNDER 12 AND URINE OUTPUT UNDER 100 mL IN 4 HOURS, AND CALCIUM GLUCONATE 10% 10 mL AT THE BEDSIDE · BLOODS ARE UEC AND eGFR, URINE PROTEIN, FBE WITH PLATELETS AND HAEMOGLOBIN, AND LFTs · OBSERVATIONS EVERY 15 MINUTES UNTIL BELOW 160/110 · ANTI-D 625 IU WITHIN 72 HOURS IF THE BABY IS RHESUS POSITIVE · FOLLOW-UP IN 3 TO 7 DAYS AND WITH THE GP AT 6 WEEKS · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 VERIFY ALL. NOTE ALSO THAT 250 mL IS NOT A POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE — PPH IS 500 mL OR MORE — WHICH IS WHY THE FLUID QUESTION MATTERS AND WHY A BOLUS IS WRONG HERE. THE VARIANT CARDS CHANGE THE STATION COMPLETELY. CLONUS: 'she has just told me her head is pounding and she is seeing flashing lights; reflexes are brisk and there are THREE BEATS OF CLONUS' → 'THEN THIS IS PRE-ECLAMPSIA WITH SEVERE FEATURES UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE AND SHE IS AT RISK OF A SEIZURE. MAGNESIUM SULFATE NOW — 4 g IV OVER 20 MINUTES THEN 1 g AN HOUR — and the labetalol as planned. Check reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output hourly, CALCIUM GLUCONATE AT THE BEDSIDE. Consultant now, and I am calling MedSTAR for retrieval. DIM THE LIGHTS, ONE-TO-ONE CARE, KEEP THE BABY WITH A SUPPORT PERSON.' THE SOFT UTERUS: 'actually it is not stopping — the uterus feels boggy and she has soaked another pad' → 'Then we have A POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE ON TOP OF THE HYPERTENSION. Fundal massage now, empty the bladder, OXYTOCIN 10 UNITS IV — NO ERGOMETRINE WITH THIS PRESSURE — second cannula, bloods including group and hold, WEIGH THE PADS, and I am coming now. If it reaches a litre we activate the massive transfusion protocol.' AND DAY FIVE AT HOME, called by the community midwife with a BP of 165/105 and a headache → 'DAY THREE TO SIX IS THE PEAK FOR POSTPARTUM PRE-ECLAMPSIA. She needs to come to hospital now — BY AMBULANCE IF THE HEADACHE IS SEVERE OR SHE HAS VISUAL SYMPTOMS — for bloods, urine protein and IV treatment. PLEASE DO NOT MANAGE THIS AT HOME.' WHAT THE EXAMINER IS ASSESSING, STATED PLAINLY IN THE SOURCE: a structured telephone assessment with each phase announced · WHETHER YOU ASK THE TWO SPECIAL QUESTIONS — medications by name and how much fluid · whether you ask about PAIN and whether the BLEEDING HAS STOPPED · whether you KEEP POSTPARTUM PRE-ECLAMPSIA ON THE LIST and screen for it with symptoms, reflexes, urine and bloods · and whether you NAME SEVERE HYPERTENSION, GIVE AN IV ANTIHYPERTENSIVE BY NAME, AND CALL THE CONSULTANT. AND THE LAST TRAP IS THE EASIEST ONE TO FALL INTO: 'I'LL COME AND SEE HER' IS NOT A PLAN — THE PLAN IS WHAT HAPPENS BEFORE YOU ARRIVE.
plan: Introduce yourself, ask who you are speaking with, and ask what has happened — then announce the three phases.
Alert and responsive · send for help and notify registrar and consultant · airway, breathing, respiratory rate and sats.
Pulse and temperature · how many BP readings and repeat it on the correct cuff · IV access, and no fluids for now.
Say 'This is severe hypertension' out loud, then signpost the history: pregnancy, delivery, baby.
The pregnancy box — complications, when the hypertension was diagnosed and how treated, the pre-eclampsia screen, previous pregnancies.
THE DELIVERY BOX — route, term, duration, instruments, tears · THEN ERGOMETRINE OR SYNTOMETRINE AND NSAIDs BY NAME · AND HOW MUCH IV FLUID.
Pain and anxiety · has the bleeding stopped and is the uterus firm · then the baby and the apgar.
THE PRE-ECLAMPSIA SYMPTOM SWEEP — headache, vision, dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness, RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT PAIN, nausea.
THE DIRECTED EXAMINATION — alertness, rash, fundoscopy, RUQ tenderness, uterus, REFLEXES AND CLONUS, DIPSTICK, AND CORD BLOOD GROUP.
Explain the causes as a list, most likely first, with pre-eclampsia kept open (see findings).
Bloods named, then labetalol with dose and repeat interval and the target, with hydralazine as the alternative.
Treat the causes — paracetamol 1 g, hold the NSAID, no ergometrine, repair the tear with good local, no further boluses.
Call the consultant and raise magnesium sulfate · then monitoring: 15-minutely BP, neuro obs, strict fluid balance, fundus and lochia, baby stays.
MedSTAR if uncontrolled or severe features develop · ask her to explain it to the woman · and ask her to read the plan back.

ask: The two special questions, asked by name: 'Was she given ergometrine or Syntometrine for the third stage? Any NSAIDs — ibuprofen, diclofenac?' and 'How much IV fluid has she received?'
The two that are easy to forget entirely: 'Is she in pain right now?' and 'Has the bleeding stopped — is the uterus firm?'
The one-line formulation: 'She has severe hypertension on a background of gestational hypertension, most likely driven by pain, drugs and fluid; pre-eclampsia isn't excluded yet.'

The drug line with its ladder and target: 'Labetalol 20 mg IV over two minutes, then 40, then 80 if needed — aiming below 160 over 110.' and the non-drug half: 'Paracetamol 1 g; no NSAIDs, no ergometrine.'

CHALLENGES: 'give her something for the pressure' → she will ask WHAT do you want me to give · 'so should I hold the diclofenac?' → yes, and no ergometrine · 'do you want to know what she's had?' at 4:30 if you never asked about drugs · brisk reflexes with THREE BEATS OF CLONUS → magnesium now and retrieval · a BOGGY UTERUS AND ANOTHER SOAKED PAD → PPH on top, oxytocin NOT ergometrine · and DAY FIVE AT HOME WITH 165/105 AND A HEADACHE → hospital now, not managed at home.
pefe: There is no patient in front of you — the examination is directed through the midwife, and the sequence is alertness, rash, fundi, right upper quadrant, uterus, reflexes and clonus, dipstick. She cannot do fundoscopy, and saying so is part of the script rather than a failure of the request. The cord blood group is asked for because she is O negative.

Role-player: SARAH, a midwife with ten years' experience, CALM AND COMPETENT. Her patient is 32, FIRST BABY, normal vaginal birth at 40 weeks AFTER A 14-HOUR INDUCTION for gestational hypertension diagnosed at 39½ weeks at 150/95, with oral labetalol started and A NEGATIVE PRE-ECLAMPSIA SCREEN. SYNTOMETRINE AT THE BIRTH, DICLOFENAC TEN MINUTES AGO for a second-degree tear, ABOUT 2.5 LITRES OF IV FLUID IN LABOUR. Loss 250 mL and stopped, uterus firm. Baby 3.5 kg, Apgars 9 and 9. MOTHER O NEGATIVE.

How she plays it: she answers only what is asked, volunteers the stem sentence and nothing more. If asked 'Any medications?' Without names she says 'The usual for the third stage' and waits. If drugs have not come up by 4:30 she prompts: 'Do you want to know what she's had?' She pushes back once on a vague plan — 'What do you want me to give, doctor?' — and will read the plan back accurately if asked.

THE CHECKLIST: introduced self and asked who, with an open question · ANNOUNCED THE THREE PHASES · responsiveness, then help, then airway and breathing, then pulse, sats and temperature, then REPEAT BP, then IV · asked whether the hypertension was TREATED and whether she was SCREENED FOR PRE-ECLAMPSIA · delivery route, duration, instruments, tears · ASKED ERGOMETRINE AND NSAIDs BY NAME · ASKED HOW MUCH FLUID, WHETHER SHE IS IN PAIN, AND WHETHER THE BLEEDING HAS STOPPED · asked about the baby and Apgar · SYMPTOM SWEEP FOR PRE-ECLAMPSIA · DIRECTED EXAMINATION INCLUDING REFLEXES AND CLONUS · EXPLAINED CAUSES WITH THE MOST LIKELY FIRST AND PRE-ECLAMPSIA KEPT OPEN · BLOODS NAMED AND IV DRUG NAMED WITH DOSE · paracetamol given and the offending drugs stopped · CALLED THE CONSULTANT AND DISCUSSED MAGNESIUM · monitoring plan and CLOSED-LOOP READ-BACK.

Open, then announce the three phases — 'Hello, this is Dr [name], the doctor on duty. WHO AM I SPEAKING WITH? … Thanks for calling, Sarah. CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT HAS HAPPENED SO FAR? … I'M GOING TO DO THREE THINGS: MAKE SURE SHE IS SAFE RIGHT NOW, ASK YOU SOME QUESTIONS, THEN GIVE YOU A PLAN.' Launching into drugs is the trap — the opening earns rapport and the extra detail the role-player is scripted to add

Phase 1 — resuscitation, in this order — IS SHE ALERT AND RESPONSIVE · SEND FOR HELP, NOTIFY THE REGISTRAR AND CONSULTANT · airway, breathing, RESPIRATORY RATE AND SATURATION · PULSE AND TEMPERATURE · 'HOW MANY TIMES HAS THE BLOOD PRESSURE BEEN CHECKED? PLEASE REPEAT IT NOW, CORRECT CUFF SIZE' · AND DOES SHE HAVE IV ACCESS — 'if not, put one in now. NO FLUIDS FOR THE MOMENT.' Acting on one reading, or ordering a fluid bolus for a bleed that has stopped, is the trap

The pregnancy box — Complications — blood pressure, sugars, kidney problems · when was the hypertension diagnosed and was she treated · was she investigated for pre-eclampsia — urine protein, kidney function, liver tests · previous pregnancies and any high blood pressure in them, especially after the birth. Answers: uncomplicated until 39½ weeks at 150/95, started on oral labetalol and booked for induction, pre-eclampsia screen negative, first baby

The delivery box — the two special questions live here — Route, term, how long the labour, instruments, cuts · then: 'What medications has she had? Was she given ergometrine or Syntometrine for the third stage? Any NSAIDs — ibuprofen, diclofenac?' · and 'How much IV fluid has she received?' Ask vaguely and she says 'The usual for the third stage' and waits. Ask by name and you get Syntometrine at the birth and diclofenac ten minutes ago for the tear, plus about 2.5 litres of IV fluid

The two questions people forget to ask at all — 'Is she in pain right now? Is she anxious or worried about anything?' → the tear is sore and she has afterpains, 6 out of 10, and she is a bit shaky · and 'You said 250 mL — has the bleeding stopped? Is the uterus firm?' → stopped, firm and contracted below the umbilicus

The baby and the pre-eclampsia symptom sweep — How is the baby, WHAT WAS THE APGAR — 3.5 kg, 9 AND 9, skin to skin · THEN: HEADACHE, BLURRED VISION, DIZZINESS · CHEST PAIN OR BREATHLESSNESS · ABDOMINAL PAIN ESPECIALLY UNDER THE RIGHT RIBS · NAUSEA. All negative here apart from the afterpains

The explanation — a list, not one cause — 'She ALREADY HAS GESTATIONAL HYPERTENSION AND IT HAS BECOME SEVERE — 190 systolic. The most likely reasons it has spiked now are PAIN AFTER A LONG LABOUR AND A TEAR, THE FLUID SHE HAD IN LABOUR, AND THE ERGOMETRINE AND ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES, WHICH BOTH PUSH BLOOD PRESSURE UP. I CANNOT YET EXCLUDE PRE-ECLAMPSIA DEVELOPING AFTER THE BIRTH — IT CAN SHOW UP FOR THE FIRST TIME POSTPARTUM — which is why we are checking symptoms, reflexes, urine and bloods. Thyroid or adrenal causes are possible but much less likely today.' Explaining only pre-eclampsia, or only pain, is the trap

Treat the causes you just named — Paracetamol 1 g for the pain now, oral or IV · no more NSAIDs until you have kidney function and platelets, and no ergometrine · get the tear repaired with good local anaesthetic · and no further fluid boluses. She asks 'So should I hold the diclofenac?' and the answer is yes

The consultant, monitoring and the close — 'I am calling the consultant now, and I will discuss magnesium sulfate with them — with a pressure this high it may be indicated even without pre-eclampsia features, and it becomes mandatory if she develops headache, visual symptoms or clonus' · blood pressure every 15 minutes until below 160/110, then half-hourly · neuro observations · strict fluid balance with no boluses · keep checking fundus and lochia · baby stays with her · MedSTAR if it cannot be controlled · and 'Please tell her what we are doing and why — I am on my way.' then ask her to read it back

back.dx: Two stations from one source, with four AUTOMATIC FAILS between them. Version A fails if the OGTT is never named or the safety question is never asked. Version B fails if the breastfeeding is never discovered, or if galactocele or abscess is given as the TOP diagnosis with the family history ignored. Version C is the mastitis management variant, explained to the patient in three parts: 'You have mastitis — an infection in the breast tissue. It started because milk wasn't draining well, probably from the cracked nipple and the way he's attaching. There is nothing wrong with your breast or your milk. First, antibiotics: flucloxacillin, one capsule four times a day for at least five days — it is safe while feeding. Second, pain relief — paracetamol and ibuprofen — with a warm pack before each feed to help the milk flow and a cold pack afterwards for the swelling. Third, and this is the important one: keep feeding from the sore side, and start each feed on that side. If it is too painful, express with a pump instead. Emptying the breast is treatment.' and when she asks whether the milk is safe: 'It is safe. Stopping is the worst thing to do — the breast fills, and that is how an abscess forms.' Add a lactation consultant or child health nurse to watch a feed and fix the attachment, the Australian breastfeeding association helpline, rest and fluids, and review in two days. The examiner challenges on that variant: 'Would you order an ultrasound today?' → 'No — mastitis is a clinical diagnosis and there is no discrete lump. The two triggers for ultrasound are a lump on presentation, or no response to antibiotics at 48 hours.' 'She has a severe penicillin allergy' → 'Clindamycin 450 mg 8-hourly; cephalexin if the allergy were mild.' 'Can she have a mammogram while breastfeeding?' → 'Yes — ultrasound first because lactating tissue is dense, but mammography is safe; feed or express beforehand.' 'Why continue feeding with mastitis?' → 'Milk stasis drives the infection; the milk is safe for the baby; stopping causes engorgement and abscess.' The numbers: 75 g OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks, then every 1 to 3 years · combined pill from 6 weeks if breastfeeding, or day 21 if not and no risk factors · lactational amenorrhoea is about 98% effective if exclusive, amenorrhoeic and under 6 months · epds 13 or more, and any positive on question 10 · flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly for at least 5 days, with cephalexin 500 mg 6-hourly or clindamycin 450 mg 8-hourly as alternatives · review at 48 hours with ultrasound if a lump or no response · endometritis takes amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily · mammogram from age 35 or if suspicious, with ultrasound first when lactating VERIFY all. South Australian numbers: Australian breastfeeding association 1800 686 268 · PANDA 1300 726 306 · CaFHS 1300 733 606 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33. 'Please give me her observations — blood pressure, pulse, temperature, respiratory rate and saturations' → 118/70, pulse 88, temperature 36.9, RR 16, sats 98. Then say why it mattered: 'That matters, because her membranes have been ruptured ten hours and I need to know she isn't febrile'

back.dx: ARREST IN THE ACTIVE PHASE OF THE FIRST STAGE OF LABOUR — named in three keywords, with the reasoning for why neither augmentation option is available. The numbers that make the diagnosis defensible: full dilatation is 10 cm and the latent phase becomes active at 4 to 5 cm · active-phase progress is about 0.5 cm per hour, and delay is less than 2 cm in 4 hours · arrest is 6 cm or more with no change for 4 hours despite adequate contractions, or 6 hours if contractions were inadequate and oxytocin has been given — so ten hours at 8 cm with four in ten is well beyond it · adequate contractions are 3 to 5 in 10 minutes lasting 40 to 60 seconds · normal fetal baseline is 110 to 160 · engaged is two-fifths or less palpable, and this case is three-fifths at station minus one · the usual upper limit of the active first stage is about 18 hours nulliparous and 12 multiparous VERIFY · prolonged rupture of membranes is over 18 hours · caesarean category 1 means 30 minutes and category 2 means 75 minutes · and cefazolin 2 g IV before skin incision VERIFY. The variants change either the diagnosis or the urgency. The delay: 7 cm four hours ago, 8 cm now, membranes intact, contractions two in ten → 'This is a delay in the active phase — she is still progressing, just slower than half a centimetre an hour. I'd like to discuss three options with her: artificial rupture of the membranes, oxytocin, or waiting. It is her decision. Before any oxytocin I need the presentation confirmed, a reassuring CTG, obstruction and disproportion excluded, and no previous caesarean scar.' The abnormal CTG with late decelerations → the diagnosis is unchanged but the urgency is not: 'Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency. This is now a category 1 caesarean — decision to delivery within thirty minutes. Obstetric emergency call, left lateral position, oxygen if indicated, stop any oxytocin, and get her to theatre.' The infection: temperature 38.2, maternal pulse 112, fetal baseline 175, offensive liquor → 'This is chorioamnionitis' and it must be named before the arrest: blood cultures and a full septic screen, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics now, paracetamol, fluids, expedite delivery, and alert the neonatal team for early-onset sepsis review VERIFY the local regimen. The previous caesarean with constant pain between contractions → 'Constant pain between contractions in a woman with a uterine scar makes me worry about uterine rupture. Absolutely no oxytocin. Obstetric emergency call, two cannulas, cross-match, and prepare for immediate laparotomy.' and if the woman refuses: 'Thank you for telling me — that is important. I'll come and talk to her and her partner myself. I'll explain why her labour has stopped, why the things we would normally use to help it along will not work here, and what the risks are of continuing. It remains her decision, and I'll make sure she has the information to make it.' The two free marks sitting at the end of this station are the words 'Emergency caesarean section' and the closed-loop read-back — both are lost by simply finishing.
plan: Introduce, ask who you are speaking with, check the mother is stable and the fetal heart is normal, then one open question — and signpost mother, baby, pelvis, plan.
Obstetric history — first pregnancy, any complications including hypertension, diabetes and a large baby on scan, and when labour started.
The contractions in four parts — how many in ten minutes, how long each lasts, whether the intervals are shortening, and whether they are getting stronger.
THE SYMPTOMS BLOCK — MEMBRANES AND WHEN, MECONIUM, bleeding, FETAL MOVEMENTS, bladder, analgesia and exhaustion.
OBSERVATIONS WITH THE TEMPERATURE NAMED — and say out loud why it matters after ten hours of ruptured membranes.
Abdominal palpation — lie, presentation, position and engagement in fifths · then the fetal heart rate.
The last vaginal examination — dilatation, effacement, consistency, cervical position, station — and when the dilatation last changed.
THE BABY — CTG BASELINE AND VARIABILITY, THE TYPE OF DECELERATION, and the estimated fetal weight.
THE PELVIS — CEPHALOPELVIC DISPROPORTION ASSESSMENT, and confirm no previous caesarean or uterine surgery.
Name the diagnosis in three keywords and explain why oxytocin and amniotomy are both unavailable.
Refuse the oxytocin when offered, with the hyperstimulation reason.
Escalate first — registrar and consultant, then theatre, anaesthetics and the neonatal team.
MONITORING — continuous CTG, continuous contraction monitoring, OBSERVATIONS INCLUDING TEMPERATURE, AND NO EXTRA VAGINAL EXAMINATIONS.
PREPARE FOR THEATRE — two cannulas, FBE and group and hold, nil by mouth, fluids, CATHETER — AND SAY 'EMERGENCY CAESAREAN SECTION, CATEGORY 2, WITHIN 75 MINUTES'.
Ask for the read-back, say you will consent her yourself, and give the three things that should trigger an immediate call.

ask: The four contraction questions, because 'Is she contracting?' Gets 'Yes' and nothing more: 'How many in ten minutes? How long do they last? Are the intervals shortening? Are they getting stronger?'

The three examination requests by name: 'Observations please — including the temperature.' · 'Lie, presentation, position and engagement in fifths.' · 'Dilatation, effacement, consistency, position and station.'
The CTG question that carries the mark: 'Are the decelerations early, late or variable?' — not 'Is the CTG normal?'

The diagnosis and its logic: 'This is an arrest in the active phase of the first stage.' · 'A delay is slow progress. This is no progress.' · 'Oxytocin has nothing to add and there is nothing left to rupture.'

CHALLENGES: 'Should I start some oxytocin while you come over?' → no, with the reason · 'so what do I tell her family?' if you finish early · vague answers to vague questions — ask 'how is the CTG?' and she says 'it looks fine' and makes you ask again · plus the four variants: the delay, late decelerations, chorioamnionitis, and a uterine scar with constant pain.

Do not ask for a speculum and do not order repeat vaginal examinations with membranes ruptured ten hours.

The contraction frequency is the evidence that kills oxytocin — 'IS SHE CONTRACTING?' → 'YES' AND NOTHING MORE · 'HOW MANY IN 10 MINUTES?' → FOUR IN TEN · 'HOW LONG IS EACH ONE LASTING?' → ABOUT FIFTY SECONDS · 'ARE THEY GETTING STRONGER?' → STRONG, AND THEY HAVE NOT WEAKENED. Accepting 'yes, she's contracting' and moving on is the trap — YOU MUST EXTRACT THE FREQUENCY AND THEN SAY IT BACK, because it is what makes augmentation pointless

The membranes, and the infection blind spot — HAVE THE MEMBRANES RUPTURED AND WHEN → EXACTLY TEN HOURS AGO · IS THE LIQUOR MECONIUM STAINED → clear · any vaginal bleeding → no · IS SHE STILL FEELING THE BABY MOVE → yes · has she passed urine or is there a catheter · what analgesia and IS SHE EXHAUSTED → gas and an epidural, pretty tired. TEN HOURS OF RUPTURED MEMBRANES AND NO TEMPERATURE QUESTION IS THE BLIND SPOT THE CASE IS BUILT AROUND — you get one chance, inside the observations

The baby — ask the type of deceleration — 'Are you running a CTG? What is the baseline and the variability? Are there any decelerations — early, late or variable?' → continuous CTG, baseline 150, normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations. 'Is the CTG normal?' Is not the question — the mark is for asking the type. Then the estimated fetal weight — about 3 kg, no concerns

The pelvis — the last block — 'Has she been assessed for CEPHALOPELVIC DISPROPORTION? Any concern about the pelvis?' → assessed, NO CONCERNS. And confirm NO PREVIOUS CAESAREAN OR UTERINE SURGERY, because that changes the whole station

The diagnosis in three keywords — 'This is AN ARREST — AN ARREST IN THE ACTIVE PHASE OF THE FIRST STAGE OF LABOUR. She is BEYOND 6 CENTIMETRES, HER MEMBRANES ARE RUPTURED, and there has been NO CERVICAL CHANGE AT ALL IN TEN HOURS DESPITE CONTRACTIONS OF FOUR IN TEN. THAT IS NOT A DELAY. A DELAY IS SLOW PROGRESS; THIS IS NO PROGRESS. Because the contractions are already adequate, OXYTOCIN HAS NOTHING TO ADD, and because the membranes are already ruptured, THERE IS NOTHING TO RUPTURE. She will most likely need a caesarean'

Refusing the oxytocin, with the reason — 'Should I start some oxytocin while you come over?' → 'No, please don't. With contractions already at four in ten and no change in ten hours, oxytocin will not deliver this baby, and it risks hyperstimulation and fetal compromise. Here is what I need instead.' if you agree, she says 'Okay doctor', writes it down and does not rescue you

Escalate first, then monitor — 'First and most importantly, notify the obstetric registrar and consultant now and tell them I have diagnosed an arrest in the active phase of the first stage' · alert the anaesthetist and theatre and give the neonatal team a heads-up · 'I'm coming to see her now' · then continuous CTG and continuous contraction monitoring · maternal observations including temperature every 15 to 30 minutes · and 'Please do not do extra vaginal examinations — her membranes have been ruptured ten hours'

Prepare for theatre, and close the loop — Two large-bore cannulas, full blood examination and group and hold · nil by mouth with maintenance fluids · indwelling catheter for an empty bladder and urine output · 'Prepare her for an emergency caesarean section. This is a category 2 — I want her in theatre well within 75 minutes' · 'I'll consent her myself when I arrive' · 'Can you read that plan back to me?' · and call me immediately if the CTG changes, if she spikes a temperature, or if she develops constant abdominal pain

The abdominal examination, by name — 'Please do an abdominal palpation — Leopold's. Tell me the lie, the presentation, the position and the engagement in fifths' → longitudinal, cephalic, occipito-anterior, three-fifths palpable. Engaged is two-fifths or less, so three-fifths is not engaged

The vaginal examination — ask for the one she has already done — 'From the last vaginal examination — how many centimetres dilated, what is the effacement, the consistency, the position of the cervix, and the station of the head?' → 8 cm, fully effaced, soft, anterior, station minus one · 'And when did that dilatation last change?' → ten hours, no change at all. Asking for 'A speculum to check the dilatation' is the trap — dilatation and station are digital findings, and with ruptured membranes you do not request extra examinations
fails: ★ Agreeing to start oxytocin when contractions are already four in ten and nothing has changed in ten hours — she offers it deliberately and will not rescue you
★ Hedging the diagnosis — 'possibly some sort of prolonged labour' scores nothing; it is arrest, active phase, first stage, in one sentence
Accepting 'yes, she's contracting' without extracting the frequency, or never asking the temperature after ten hours of ruptured membranes
Asking 'is the CTG normal?' instead of the type of deceleration, or requesting a speculum for a dilatation that is a digital finding
Finishing without saying the words 'emergency caesarean section', without escalating to the consultant first, or without a closed-loop read-back — all free marks
numbers: Full dilatation 10 cm; active phase from 4 to 5 cm · active-phase progress about 0.5 cm/h; delay is <2 cm in 4 hours · arrest = 6 cm or more with no change for 4 hours with adequate contractions, or 6 hours if inadequate and oxytocin given · adequate contractions 3 to 5 in 10 minutes, 40 to 60 seconds · normal fetal baseline 110 to 160

Engaged = 2/5 or less palpable; this case 3/5 and station −1 · usual upper limit of active first stage 18 h nulliparous, 12 h multiparous VERIFY · prolonged rupture of membranes >18 hours · caesarean category 1 = 30 minutes, category 2 = 75 minutes · cefazolin 2 g IV before skin incision VERIFY · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

setting: You never say yes and you never say no. The mark is for exploring why she wants it, asking the three eligibility questions, giving both sides of both options, saying 'About 1 in 200' out loud, and building the emergency caesarean into the plan for a vaginal birth. If you give a flat yes she looks relieved and stops asking questions — that is the trap. If you list only disasters she becomes tearful and asks whether you are saying she shouldn't.
stem: General practice, antenatal clinic. Jane, 25, is early in her second pregnancy at her booking visit in the first trimester. Her first baby was born by caesarean section. Today she tells you she wants a vaginal birth this time. Observations normal, pregnancy so far uncomplicated, no bleeding and no pain.

Tasks: take a focused history from Jane, about 3 minutes — counsel her regarding her request, covering benefits, risks, contraindications and the plan for the pregnancy, about 4 to 5 minutes. 8 minutes.

Counsel her on benefits, risks and contraindications
Give the plan for the pregnancy
time: Sixty seconds to open and explore the agenda — why she wants it and what worries her, which is marked separately and is the whole station in version B · then the three deciding questions about the last caesarean · then ninety seconds on this pregnancy and the rest · then four to five minutes of balanced counselling in six steps · and a plan with dates, not 'Come back if you have questions'.
findings: The skin scar is not the uterine incision

'That's reassuring — that usually means the cut in the womb was the modern lower one, which heals strongest. I'LL REQUEST THE OPERATION REPORT TO BE SURE.' Ask about the skin scar, THEN SAY YOU WILL GET THE OPERATION REPORT — because the two do not always match, especially when the caesarean was done very early

back.dx: A REQUEST FOR PLANNED VAGINAL BIRTH AFTER ONE PREVIOUS LOWER-SEGMENT CAESAREAN — and the whole station is balanced counselling without a verdict. The numbers, said plainly rather than softened: rupture is about 1 in 200 with one lower-segment scar in spontaneous labour, but 2 to 9% with a classical scar · about 3 in 4 planned VBACs succeed, rising to 85 to 90% if she has had a previous vaginal birth · about 1 in 4 need an intrapartum caesarean · two or more caesareans is usually advised against · an interval under 18 months raises the rupture risk · the discussion timeline is 26 to 28, 32 and 36 weeks · and the birthing unit must have a 30-minute decision-to-delivery capability VERIFY all. The examiner challenges. 'Can she VBAC after two caesareans?' → 'RANZCOG regards it as a specialist, individualised decision; most units advise a planned repeat caesarean; I would not promise it and would refer.' 'Can she be induced?' → 'Yes, but prostaglandins raise the rupture risk; a balloon catheter or cautious oxytocin under obstetric supervision is preferred, or a planned caesarean.' 'Where does a rural woman birth?' → 'A unit with 24-hour theatre and obstetric, anaesthetic and paediatric cover, with accommodation nearby from 37 weeks.' The variants. The vertical scar — 'Up and down from my belly button, an emergency at 29 weeks, the placenta came away' → 'A vertical scar on the skin sometimes means the cut in the womb was also the vertical, old-style one — that is more likely when a caesarean is done very early. If it was, we would not plan a vaginal birth, because that type of scar has a much higher chance of tearing. I don't know yet — I'll request the operation report and we'll discuss it with the obstetrician. Whatever it shows, I'll support you and we'll make the safest plan together.' Failure to progress as the original indication — 'I was 6 centimetres for hours and it just stopped' → 'When a caesarean is done because labour didn't progress, there is a higher chance the same thing could happen again, so the odds of success are a bit lower — perhaps closer to 6 in 10 rather than 3 in 4. It doesn't rule it out, and many women in your situation do go on to birth vaginally.' 'My partner wants a caesarean' → 'It's good that he is involved, and I'd be happy to see you both together so he hears the same information. The decision is yours, and I'll support it.' and a low placenta on the 20-week scan at a later visit → rescan at 32 weeks, because most move up; if it stays low or over the exit a vaginal birth would not be safe regardless of the old scar — and because there is a scar, ask the sonographer to check the placenta has not grown into it. Version B is the same station with a hidden agenda: last time she got a wound infection and 'Nobody explained anything — I had no say'. She volunteers it only if asked about concerns, and if never asked she says at minute six: 'I just don't want it to be like last time.' that is why the agenda question is marked separately from the counselling — in that version it is the entire case.
plan: WIPE, confirm name and date of birth, congratulate her, and ask an open question.
Explore the agenda — why she prefers a vaginal birth, and whether anything about the last caesarean or about birth worries her. Marked separately from the counselling.
The three deciding questions — why the caesarean was done, planned or emergency, horizontal or vertical scar, other uterine surgery or rupture — and say you will request the operation report.
Complications afterwards, and whether she has ever had a vaginal birth.

THIS PREGNANCY AND THE REST — age of the first child, booking bloods and dating scan, BLOOD GROUP, bleeding or pain, previous hypertension or diabetes, MOOD AND PARTNER SUPPORT, smoking, alcohol and drugs, AND SAFETY AT HOME.
Step one — acknowledge, empower, and say explicitly that your job is not to say yes or no.
Step two — the benefits of a vaginal birth.
Step three — the risks, with rupture first and '1 in 200' said out loud, then the 1 in 4 intrapartum caesarean, then the ordinary risks of vaginal birth.
Step four — both sides of the planned repeat caesarean, including the future-pregnancy placental risk.
Step five — the contraindications, and that none of them apply to her.
Step six — build the emergency caesarean into the plan before she asks.
The timeline — 26 to 28, 32 and 36 weeks — plus the birth setting, reading material, and time to decide with her partner.
Safety net for bleeding or pain before then, and close with 'Whatever you choose, I'm here to support you.'

ask: The two agenda questions, marked separately: 'Can I ask what makes you prefer a vaginal birth this time?' and 'Is there anything about the last caesarean, or about birth, that worries you?'

The three that decide eligibility: 'Why was the caesarean done last time?' · 'Is the scar on your tummy across, or up and down?' · 'Any other surgery on your womb, or were you ever told it tore or ruptured?' — plus 'I'll request the operation report so we know exactly what type of cut was made in the womb.'
The two numbers said plainly: 'In about 1 in 200 women the scar can tear during labour — rare, but serious.' and 'About 1 in 4 women who try will need a caesarean during labour.'

The stance, and the plan: 'I support you, and I'll be here whatever you decide. My job is not to say yes or no.' · 'Even with a plan for a vaginal birth, there are moments where we may need to change to a caesarean.' · 'We'll talk again at 26 to 28 weeks, at 32, and finalise at 36.'

CHALLENGES: 'So can I or can't I?' → she pushes once, and will not accept a quiet yes or no · 'How likely is the tearing, really?' · 'What if I go over my due date?' · 'What if it goes wrong in labour?' asked at minute six if you have not said it · plus the examiner on two previous caesareans, induction, and where a rural woman should birth.
pefe: There is no examination in this station — the observations are given as normal and the pregnancy is uncomplicated. The 'Findings' are the three history answers that decide eligibility: why the caesarean was done, the orientation of the skin scar, and whether there has been other uterine surgery or rupture — and the operation report is what converts the skin scar into knowledge of the uterine incision.

Role-player: JANE, 25, A CHILDCARE WORKER living with her partner Tom and their son Max, aged two. Non-smoker, no alcohol or drugs, FEELS SAFE AT HOME. LAST BIRTH: PLANNED CAESAREAN AT 39 WEEKS FOR BREECH, BIKINI-LINE SCAR, NO COMPLICATIONS, HOME ON DAY THREE — but she found THE RECOVERY SLOW AND FELT SHE MISSED OUT. THIS PREGNANCY: 9 WEEKS, booking bloods normal, O POSITIVE, dating scan done, no bleeding or pain, no medical problems.

How she plays it: warm and hopeful, wants a yes. She gives short answers and does not volunteer the breech reason until asked why. She pushes once — 'So can I or can't I?' — and will not accept a quiet verdict: 'That's a relief' if yes, 'Why not?' if no. If the doctor gives a flat yes she looks relieved and stops asking questions, which is the trap. If the doctor lists only disasters she becomes tearful: 'So you're saying I shouldn't?'

The checklist: introduced and confirmed identity with an open question · asked why she wants a vaginal birth · asked about concerns and the last birth experience · asked the reason for the caesarean · asked horizontal versus vertical and mentioned the operation report · asked other uterine surgery, rupture and previous vaginal birth · gave the benefits of VBAC · named rupture as about 1 in 200 · named the chance of caesarean in labour · gave pros and cons of the repeat caesarean · listed the contraindications · explained an emergency caesarean may still be needed · gave the 26–28 / 32 / 36 timeline · offered reading material and time to decide · said 'I support your decision' without giving a verdict · and addressed the hidden agenda in version B.

Explore before you counsel — 'CAN I ASK WHAT MAKES YOU PREFER A VAGINAL BIRTH THIS TIME? … AND IS THERE ANYTHING ABOUT THE LAST CAESAREAN, OR ABOUT BIRTH GENERALLY, THAT'S WORRYING YOU?' → she felt she MISSED OUT, and THE RECOVERY WAS SLOW — she could not lift her son for weeks. COUNSELLING BEFORE EXPLORING IS THE TRAP: the examiner marks 'explores reasons and concerns' as a separate item, AND IN VERSION B THE CONCERN IS THE WHOLE STATION

The three deciding questions — 'Why was the caesarean done last time?' → breech, planned at 39 weeks, never laboured — a reason that will not necessarily happen again · 'Is the scar on your tummy horizontal — across — or vertical, up and down?' → across, low, bikini line · 'Any other surgery on your womb, or were you ever told it tore or ruptured?' → no to both. Asking 'Was it a classical caesarean?' Is the trap — she cannot know

The rest of the history, in ninety seconds — How old is her first · BOOKING BLOODS AND DATING SCAN, BLOOD GROUP · any bleeding or pain this pregnancy · ANY BLOOD PRESSURE OR SUGAR PROBLEMS LAST TIME · how she has been in herself since the last birth and WHETHER HER PARTNER IS SUPPORTIVE · smoking, alcohol and drugs · AND WHETHER SHE FEELS SAFE AT HOME. Spending three minutes on generic antenatal questions and running out of time for the counselling — WHICH CARRIES MOST OF THE MARKS — is the trap

Step one — acknowledge and empower — 'Jane, I SUPPORT YOU, AND I'LL BE HERE WHATEVER YOU DECIDE. MY JOB ISN'T TO SAY YES OR NO — it's to give you the good and the not-so-good about a vaginal birth after a caesarean, AND ABOUT A PLANNED REPEAT CAESAREAN, so you can make an informed choice'

Step two — the benefits of a vaginal birth — SHORTER STAY AND FASTER RECOVERY · NO MAJOR SURGERY, so none of its bleeding, infection, clot and anaesthetic risks · BETTER CHANCE OF BREASTFEEDING · AND EASIER BIRTHS IN FUTURE

Step three — the risks, with the big one first and the number said plainly — 'There is a scar on your womb, and in about 1 in 200 women it can tear in labour. Rare, serious, and the reason we monitor you continuously in a hospital with a theatre ready' · second, about 1 in 4 women who try end up needing a caesarean in labour, and an emergency one is riskier than a planned one · third, the usual risks of vaginal birth — tears, later bladder leakage or prolapse — and a very small increase in risk to the baby

Step four — both sides of the repeat caesarean too — 'A planned caesarean is PREDICTABLE AND PROTECTS THE PELVIC FLOOR, BUT IT IS SURGERY: slower recovery, more risk of BLEEDING, INFECTION AND CLOTS, and EACH ONE MAKES THE NEXT PREGNANCY RISKIER BECAUSE THE PLACENTA CAN GROW LOW OR INTO THE SCAR. Babies can have A LITTLE MORE BREATHING TROUBLE AT FIRST.' Giving only the VBAC side is half a station

Step five — the contraindications, and that none apply — 'We would not plan a vaginal birth if the old cut was the vertical type, if the womb had ruptured before, after other womb surgery, after two or more caesareans, or if anything in this pregnancy needs a caesarean — the placenta over the exit, or a breech baby. None of that applies from what you've told me'

Step six — build the emergency caesarean into the plan — 'AND IF IT GOES WRONG IN LABOUR?' → 'THEN WE CHANGE THE PLAN FOR YOUR SAFETY AND THE BABY'S — if labour stalls, if the baby's heart rate worries us, or if there is any sign from the scar, we would move to a caesarean. I'D RATHER YOU HEAR THAT TODAY THAN BE SURPRISED ON THE DAY.' She asks this herself at about six minutes if you have not said it

The plan with dates, not 'Come back if you have questions' — 'IT'S EARLY, SO WE DON'T DECIDE TODAY. We'll meet again AT 26 TO 28 WEEKS WITH THE OBSTETRICIAN AND MIDWIFE, AGAIN AT 32, AND AT 36 WEEKS WE'LL FINALISE THE PLAN — including what happens if labour doesn't start by itself. YOU'D BIRTH IN A HOSPITAL WITH A 24-HOUR THEATRE. HERE'S SOME READING; think it over, TALK WITH YOUR PARTNER, and bring your questions back. And if you have any bleeding, pain or worries before then, come straight in. WHATEVER YOU CHOOSE, I'M HERE TO SUPPORT YOU'

Her three interruptions — 'SO YOU'RE SAYING I CAN HAVE ONE?' → 'I'M SAYING NOTHING SO FAR RULES IT OUT, AND MOST WOMEN IN YOUR POSITION WHO TRY DO SUCCEED — ABOUT THREE IN FOUR. But it's your decision, and I want you to make it knowing the risks as well as the benefits' · 'HOW LIKELY IS THAT TEARING THING, REALLY?' → about 1 in 200, HALF OF ONE PERCENT · 'WHAT IF I GO OVER MY DUE DATE?' → 'we prefer labour to start on its own. If it doesn't, the obstetrician will talk with you about the safest way to start it, BECAUSE SOME INDUCTION MEDICATIONS RAISE THE RISK TO THE SCAR, or about a planned caesarean instead. WE'LL SETTLE THAT AT 36 WEEKS'

setting: The commonest cause is a sleeping baby, and that is never a reason to send her home. Warn her, then reassure her, then investigate her anyway — and in that order, because reassurance before assessment buys nothing and costs the mark. She is braced to be told she is being silly: if you open with 'Try not to worry' she gets more anxious and asks 'But how do you know?'

back.dx: REDUCED FETAL MOVEMENTS AT 32 WEEKS — ASSESSED FULLY WHATEVER THE RISK STATUS, BECAUSE THE COMMONEST CAUSE BEING BENIGN IS NOT A REASON TO SEND HER HOME. THE EXAMINATION CARD, IF OFFERED: BP 116/72 · PULSE 84 REGULAR, TEMPERATURE 36.8 · ABDOMEN SOFT AND NON-TENDER WITH NO PALPABLE CONTRACTIONS · SYMPHYSIO-FUNDAL HEIGHT 32 cm, APPROPRIATE FOR DATES · LONGITUDINAL, CEPHALIC · FETAL HEART PRESENT AT 144 · NO VAGINAL LOSS · AND NO PROTEIN ON DIPSTICK. THE NUMBERS: MOVEMENTS ARE FIRST FELT AROUND 20 WEEKS AND BECOME MAXIMAL AND ESTABLISHED AT 28 WEEKS · A SLEEP CYCLE IS 20 TO 40 MINUTES AND RARELY OVER 90 · THERE IS NO THRESHOLD COUNT, WITH A NORMAL RANGE OF 4 TO 100 PER HOUR, THOUGH RACGP CITES 10 IN 2 HOURS VERIFY · ASSESSMENT SHOULD HAPPEN WITHIN 2 HOURS · THE CTG RUNS AT LEAST 20 MINUTES AND IS EXTENDED TO 40 IF UNREACTIVE · AN ACCELERATION IS 15 bpm FOR 15 SECONDS AND YOU WANT 2 IN 20 MINUTES · BASELINE 110 TO 160 WITH VARIABILITY 5 TO 25 · SFH EQUALS GESTATION PLUS OR MINUS 2 TO 3 cm · AND REVIEW IS IN 1 WEEK IF ALL IS REASSURING. THINGS NEVER TO SAY: 'IT'S PROBABLY JUST THE BABY SLEEPING' as your opening or as your plan · 'COUNT TEN MOVEMENTS OVER TWO HOURS AND RING IF THERE ARE FEWER' · 'YOU'RE LOW RISK, SO I'M NOT WORRIED' · 'I'M SURE YOUR BABY IS FINE' · 'COME BACK TOMORROW IF IT HASN'T IMPROVED' · AND 'CLAY-HOWARD TEST', WHICH IS KLEIHAUER–BETKE. THE VARIANTS. NO MOVEMENTS AT ALL AND NO FETAL HEART ON DOPPLER → 'Mary, I'M HAVING DIFFICULTY PICKING UP THE HEARTBEAT WITH THIS DEVICE. I don't want you to read too much into that yet — these hand-held machines can miss a heartbeat depending on the baby's position. BUT I'M NOT PREPARED TO GUESS. I'M ARRANGING AN ULTRASOUND SCAN RIGHT NOW, AND I'M GOING TO STAY WITH YOU. IS THERE SOMEONE YOU'D LIKE ME TO CALL TO BE WITH YOU?' — and to the examiner, an immediate ultrasound to confirm viability, the obstetric team called now, MedSTAR from a rural site, NOT LEAVING HER ALONE AND NOT OFFERING REASSURANCE YOU CANNOT SUPPORT. If fetal death is confirmed it becomes a breaking-bad-news consultation: WARNING SHOT, PLAIN WORDS — 'DIED', NOT 'LOST' — SILENCE, A SUPPORT PERSON, SENIOR OBSTETRIC INVOLVEMENT, AND NO DISCUSSION OF DELIVERY METHOD UNTIL SHE IS READY. THE SAME STORY AT 24 WEEKS → 'Formal guidance applies FROM 28 WEEKS, because that is when movements become maximal and established and a fall from her own baseline becomes interpretable. Between 20 and 28 weeks the evidence does not support specific advice. THAT IS NOT A REASON TO DO NOTHING — I would still take a history, examine her, confirm the fetal heart and arrange an ultrasound, AND BE HONEST THAT THE MONITORING IS LESS INFORMATIVE AT THIS GESTATION.' RECURRENT PRESENTATIONS → 'this is your third visit in a fortnight, AND THAT CHANGES MY THINKING. RECURRENT REDUCED MOVEMENTS IS A STRONGER WARNING SIGN THAN A SINGLE EPISODE, AND REPEATING A NORMAL CTG EACH TIME IS NOT ENOUGH. I want a GROWTH SCAN WITH LIQUOR VOLUME AND UMBILICAL ARTERY DOPPLER, and I'm referring you for obstetric review rather than sending you home again' — and if the fundal height is 31 cm at 35 weeks, SAY OUT LOUD THAT IT IS SMALL FOR DATES. AND ON THE KLEIHAUER: it detects FETAL RED CELLS IN THE MATERNAL CIRCULATION, so it identifies a FETOMATERNAL HAEMORRHAGE, one recognised cause of reduced movements. IT IS NOT ROUTINE — considered when the CTG is abnormal or fetomaternal haemorrhage is suspected — and it has a second role in a RHESUS-NEGATIVE WOMAN, QUANTIFYING THE BLEED AND THEREFORE THE ANTI-D DOSE.
