ask: The opening mark: 'You did exactly the right thing coming in.' and the question that shapes everything after it: 'Is he moving less than usual, or is there no movement at all?'
The quantifying pair and the timing question: 'How many would he normally do in an hour? And how many now?' · 'When did you first become concerned?'
The three that catch abruption: 'Any bleeding? Any leaking of fluid? Any tummy pain or tenderness?' and the gentle one: 'Did you deliver a healthy baby?'
The two sentences that carry the counselling: 'A present heartbeat tells me he is alive; the CTG tells me he is well.' and 'We want at least two rises in his heart rate in twenty minutes.'

CHALLENGES: 'Is my baby going to be all right?' → 'I CAN'T PROMISE YOU AN OUTCOME, BUT I CAN TELL YOU EXACTLY WHAT WE'RE GOING TO DO' — and if you over-promise she looks unconvinced and asks how you can know · 'And if it's not normal?' after you mention the CTG, testing whether you have a next step · 'So I just go home and wait?' if you offer a kick chart · and near the end, if concerns were never explored, 'MY COUSIN'S BABY DIED AT 36 WEEKS. IS THAT WHAT'S HAPPENING?'
pefe: ASK FOR IT BY NAME EVEN THOUGH THE STATION IS MOSTLY HISTORY AND COUNSELLING: BLOOD PRESSURE AND TEMPERATURE · AN ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION FOR FUNDAL HEIGHT, UTERINE TENDERNESS AND UTERINE ACTIVITY · AND THE FETAL HEART RATE ON HAND-HELD DOPPLER. Then interpret it out loud rather than collecting it: the fundus is appropriate for dates, the uterus is not tender and not contracting, AND THE HEART RATE BEING PRESENT PROVES LIFE BUT NOT WELLBEING.

Role-player: MARY DOHERTY, 27, 32 WEEKS IN HER FIRST PREGNANCY, working full time in a supermarket bakery ON HER FEET FROM SEVEN IN THE MORNING. Her partner works away, SHE LIVES 50 MINUTES FROM THE HOSPITAL AND DOES NOT DRIVE — her sister brought her in. No medical problems, PREGNANCY MULTIVITAMIN ONLY, non-smoker, no alcohol or drugs, ALL ANTENATAL CARE NORMAL INCLUDING A NORMAL 20-WEEK SCAN WITH A NORMALLY SITED PLACENTA.

How she plays it: frightened and slightly tearful, hands on the bump, having poked her belly all morning trying to get a response. She half expects to be told she is being silly and is braced for it. If told she did the right thing she visibly relaxes; if reassured before being assessed she gets worse and asks 'But how do you know?' She does not volunteer 'Less rather than none' unless asked directly.

HER HIDDEN AGENDA: HER COUSIN HAD A STILLBIRTH AT 36 WEEKS TWO YEARS AGO AND IT IS ALL SHE HAS THOUGHT ABOUT SINCE THIS MORNING. SHE DOES NOT VOLUNTEER IT — only if asked what she is worried about, or near the end if never asked. THE CHECKLIST: said she did the right thing EARLY · asked LESS VERSUS NONE · QUANTIFIED BEFORE AND NOW · asked when she first became concerned and whether it was the first episode · EXPLORED HER DAY · asked smoking, medications, sedatives, drugs, alcohol and FEVER · REVIEWED THE CURRENT PREGNANCY INCLUDING THE 20-WEEK SCAN, BLOOD PRESSURE, SUGARS AND WEIGHT GAIN · ASKED BLEEDING, FLUID LOSS AND ABDOMINAL PAIN · the pre-eclampsia set · previous pregnancies · ASKED ABOUT HER CONCERNS · requested the fetal heart, uterine tenderness and activity and fundal height · WARNED BEFORE REASSURING · explained the sleep cycle WITH A DURATION · named the four concerns briefly · NAMED THE CTG AND EXPLAINED A REACTIVE TRACE · arranged an ultrasound and said what it checks · gave one-week follow-up and a RETURN-IMMEDIATELY SAFETY NET · AND AVOIDED A KICK CHART AND AVOIDED PROMISING AN OUTCOME.

The opening sentence that earns the mark — 'I'M REALLY GLAD YOU CAME IN, MARY — THAT WAS EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING TO DO, AND WE ALWAYS TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY. I understand how frightening it is. Can I ask you some questions, and then I'll examine you and tell you exactly what we're going to do?' OPENING WITH 'TRY NOT TO WORRY' OR 'IT'S PROBABLY FINE' REASSURES BEFORE YOU HAVE ASSESSED, AND YOU CANNOT GET THAT MARK BACK

Less, or none at all — then quantify — 'Can you describe what you mean by kicking less? Specifically — is he moving less than usual, or is there no movement at all?' → still moving, much less · 'How many times would he normally kick or move in an hour? And how many now?' → normally ten or fifteen, most in the evening; now about once every few hours. She answers 'Less than usual' only if asked directly

Ask when she first became concerned, not when it started — 'WHEN DID YOU FIRST BECOME CONCERNED? … Has it been constant, or has he had spells of moving normally? … IS THIS THE FIRST TIME THIS HAS HAPPENED IN THIS PREGNANCY?' → this morning, ONE BURST AROUND LUNCHTIME, first episode. ASKING 'WHEN DID IT START?' IS THE TRAP — SHE CANNOT KNOW

The mother's day — explains, but does not excuse — 'Tell me about your day today — what have you been doing?' → on her feet at work since seven, non-stop · then smoking today, medications including anything to help her sleep, alcohol and other drugs, and any fever or feeling unwell. Finding a plausible explanation and stopping is the trap — 'She was busy, so that explains it' is reasoning towards the discharge you want. It explains, and you still investigate

The current pregnancy — the forgotten block — Booking bloods · dating scan · down syndrome screening · the 18 to 20 week scan, were they happy with growth and with the placenta · the glucose tolerance test at 26 to 28 weeks · any high blood pressure or high sugars · and has weight gain been as expected. Skipping this because 'The case is about kicking' is the trap — growth restriction, hypertension, diabetes and placental problems all live here, and they are the things that reduce movement

The three symptoms that must be asked — Any vaginal bleeding · any leaking of fluid · any abdominal pain, or has your tummy felt tender or tight — plus nausea and vomiting. Placental abruption presents exactly like this, and missing all three is an AUTOMATIC FAIL

The pre-eclampsia set — Headaches · visual change — blurring, flashing lights, spots · dizziness · swelling of legs, hands or face · chest pain or shortness of breath · and passing less urine than usual. All negative here

Previous pregnancies, and the phrasing that matters — If not her first: did anything like this happen before, any complications in pregnancy or delivery, AND 'DID YOU DELIVER A HEALTHY BABY?' — WHICH IS HOW YOU ASK ABOUT STILLBIRTH AND NEONATAL DEATH WITHOUT SAYING THE WORDS COLD. If the answer is that she lost a baby: STOP, ACKNOWLEDGE IT PROPERLY, and note that PREVIOUS STILLBIRTH SUBSTANTIALLY RAISES RECURRENCE RISK AND LOWERS YOUR THRESHOLD FOR ADMISSION AND OBSTETRIC REVIEW

Counselling step 1 and 2 — warn before you reassure — WARN: 'I want to be straight with you. WHEN A MOTHER TELLS US HER BABY IS MOVING LESS, WE ALWAYS TAKE IT SERIOUSLY, BECAUSE REDUCED MOVEMENTS CAN BE A SIGN THAT THE BABY ISN'T DOING AS WELL AS WE'D LIKE. That is why we never brush it off' · THEN NORMALISE: 'ONE OF THE COMMONEST REASONS IS SIMPLY THAT THE BABY IS ASLEEP. Babies have SLEEP CYCLES — USUALLY ABOUT 20 TO 40 MINUTES, SOMETIMES UP TO AN HOUR — and during one they move much less. It's also very common for a mother to have had such a busy day that she hasn't noticed movements that were actually happening.' REVERSING THESE TWO STEPS COSTS THE MARK

Step 3 — the concerns, one clause each — 'But we do need to make sure there's no risk to your baby, because reduced movements can be linked with A GROWTH PROBLEM IN THE BABY, A PROBLEM WITH THE PLACENTA — the tissue that connects you to your baby and carries his oxygen and food — LESS FLUID AROUND HIM, AN INFECTION IN THE WOMB, OR OCCASIONALLY EARLY LABOUR.' FOUR CLAUSES, THEN STOP — explaining each one is the trap

Step 4 — the CTG, explained properly — 'I'll listen with a small hand-held ultrasound first, and then we'll put you on a monitor for A CTG, OR NON-STRESS TEST, for about twenty minutes. WHAT WE WANT TO SEE IS AT LEAST TWO RISES IN HIS HEART RATE OVER THAT TIME — A BABY'S HEART RATE GOES UP WHEN HE MOVES, so those rises tell us he's moving and coping well. IF WE DON'T SEE THEM IN THE FIRST TWENTY MINUTES, THAT OFTEN JUST MEANS HE'S ASLEEP, SO WE SIMPLY RUN IT LONGER.' AND SAY THE DISTINCTION OUT LOUD: 'A PRESENT HEARTBEAT TELLS ME HE IS ALIVE; THE CTG TELLS ME HE IS WELL'

The scan, the follow-up, and the thing not to offer — An ultrasound today, checking three things: growth, the amount of fluid, and the placenta · if both are normal, review in a week with a fact sheet · and the safety net: 'If it happens again, come straight back — every time. Don't wait, don't count at home for hours first, and don't ever worry you're bothering us.' Ending with 'Count ten movements over two hours and ring if there are fewer' is the trap — kick charts are not recommended VERIFY
fails: ★ Reassuring before assessing — 'try not to worry' or 'it's probably just the baby sleeping' as your opening, or the sleep cycle given before the warning
★ Omitting bleeding, fluid loss and abdominal pain, because placental abruption presents exactly like this
Finding a plausible explanation in her busy day and stopping there — it explains, and you still investigate
Skipping the current-pregnancy block because 'the case is about kicking', when growth restriction, hypertension, diabetes and placental problems all live there
Ending with a kick chart, sending her home to count, promising the baby will be fine, or having no next step when she asks what happens if the CTG is not normal
numbers: Movements first felt about 20 weeks; maximal and established at 28 weeks · sleep cycle 20 to 40 minutes, rarely over 90 · no threshold count, range 4 to 100 per hour, RACGP cites 10 in 2 hours VERIFY · assessment within 2 hours · CTG at least 20 minutes, extended to 40 if unreactive

Acceleration = 15 bpm for 15 seconds; want 2 in 20 minutes · baseline 110 to 160, variability 5 to 25 · SFH = gestation ± 2 to 3 cm · review in 1 week if reassuring · Kleihauer–Betke detects fetomaternal haemorrhage and sizes the anti-D dose in a rhesus-negative woman · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · VERIFY all

setting: No rash is the whole clue, and the question belongs in the first minute because the answer routes everything after it. Say what it means out loud — no rash moves you away from the skin and towards the liver. The failure mode of this station is explaining cholestasis beautifully, prescribing a cream and an antihistamine, and never saying planned birth.
stem: Antenatal clinic, rural South Australian general practice. The midwife has referred Jenny Marsh, 29, who is 36 weeks pregnant in her second pregnancy, because of recent itchiness and tiredness. Antenatal visits to date have been normal.

Examination findings already on the card: pale striae on the abdomen · symphysio-fundal height 35 cm, appropriate for dates · longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation · engagement 4/5 · fetal heart rate normal. Tasks: take a history in 6 minutes — investigation results will be provided at six minutes — state and explain your diagnosis. 8 minutes.

Interpret the investigation results handed to you
State and explain your diagnosis
time: Twenty seconds of empathy, then move — this station's marks are in the structure · timing and course, then the rash question in the first minute · then site, which is most of the diagnosis · then the pre-eclampsia set, forty seconds · then the cholestasis block including the tiredness in one question · then four short non-pregnancy blocks · then the obstetric history with fetal movements never omitted · then read the results in order and explain it to her.
findings: The results, read in this order

'Her bile acids are raised — that is the diagnostic result and the one I was looking for. Her transaminases are mildly raised, which fits. Her bilirubin is normal, which does not argue against the diagnosis at all — most women with cholestasis are never jaundiced. Her alkaline phosphatase is mildly raised, but I would interpret that cautiously, because ALP rises two to fourfold in normal pregnancy from placental isoenzyme, and her GGT is normal, which supports a placental rather than a biliary source.' 'There's a cholestatic picture, so I'd scan for gallstones' is the trap — the ALP is a red herring created by pregnancy physiology

back.dx: INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS OF PREGNANCY AT 36 WEEKS — diagnosed on itch without rash, palms and soles, worse at night, and confirmed by raised serum bile acids. The differentials, given to the examiner with the reason each is out: pre-eclampsia and acute fatty liver of pregnancy — both excluded on symptoms, a normal blood pressure and this biochemistry · polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, pemphigoid gestationis and atopic eruption — all excluded by the absence of a rash · and scabies — no burrows, no web-space itch, no itchy contacts. The investigations to name before the results are handed over: serum bile acids, liver function tests, full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, a coagulation profile, blood pressure with urine dipstick, and a CTG. The numbers: bile acids 10 µmol/L or above are diagnostic, 40 or above is moderate and 100 or above is severe VERIFY · planned birth at 36 to 37 weeks, earlier if bile acids are very high VERIFY · ALP rises two to fourfold physiologically in pregnancy while GGT does not · permethrin 5% is safe in pregnancy for scabies and all contacts are treated · pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks at 140/90 or above · fetal heart 110 to 160 and SFH plus or minus 2 to 3 cm · and engagement of 4/5 means not yet engaged, since engaged is 2/5 or less. The rest of the plan: obstetric referral the same day for repeat bloods, fetal monitoring and birth planning · for the itch, nails short, loose cotton, cool compresses and plenty of moisturiser, with menthol helping some women · and a safety net that includes reduced fetal movements, bleeding or fluid loss, contractions, becoming yellow, or headache, visual change or rib pain. Her two other questions: 'Will it happen again next time?' → 'It often does — it recurs in a large proportion of later pregnancies, and it runs in families, which fits with your mum. That means we watch for it early next time rather than waiting for you to be miserable' VERIFY · 'Can I still breastfeed?' → 'Yes, absolutely. The condition resolves within days of the birth and it doesn't affect breastfeeding.' The variants. The photograph of the abdomen showing itchy red papules and plaques on the striae with periumbilical sparing → describe then diagnose: 'Urticarial papules and plaques arising on the abdominal striae, with a clear zone of periumbilical sparing. In a primigravida in the late third trimester that is polymorphic eruption of pregnancy' — harmless to mother and baby, settles within days to weeks of birth, treated with a mild steroid cream, moisturiser and an antihistamine, and it does not change when or how she delivers, which is the difference from the liver condition VERIFY. In that version she has known eczema and gestational diabetes on insulin, both there to make you anchor — so ask whether this is the same as her usual eczema or different. If the umbilicus is involved rather than spared, with tense vesicles and bullae on urticarial plaques, it is pemphigoid gestationis — autoimmune, needing dermatology and a skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence, and carrying a higher risk of growth restriction and preterm birth. If she is unwell — vomiting for four days, very thirsty, yellow sclerae and a glucose of 2.9 → 'That changes everything. Itch with vomiting, malaise, thirst, jaundice and hypoglycaemia in the third trimester is acute fatty liver of pregnancy until proven otherwise. This is an obstetric emergency: resuscitate, correct the glucose, take a coagulation profile, and arrange immediate transfer — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33. The treatment is urgent delivery.' and if the itch is between the fingers and on the wrists, worse at night and after a hot shower, with the children scratching too → scabies: permethrin 5%, everyone in the house treated on the same day whether they itch or not, bedding and clothes washed hot, and the itch can continue for two to four weeks after successful treatment without meaning failure. Things never to say: 'There's no rash, so it's probably nothing' · 'Your bilirubin is normal, so it isn't your liver' · 'The ALP is up, so I'd scan for gallstones' · 'I'll give you an antihistamine and see you in two weeks' · 'This medicine will protect your baby' of ursodeoxycholic acid · and 'Let's just wait for labour to start naturally'.

The rash question, in the first minute — and say out loud what the answer means.
SITE — WHERE EXACTLY — AND REACT TO PALMS AND SOLES · then night waking, HOT SHOWER, ITCHY CONTACTS, WEB SPACES · then fever and weeping skin.

THE CHOLESTASIS BLOCK — RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT PAIN, nausea, appetite, THE TIREDNESS IN ONE QUESTION, jaundice, DARK URINE AND PALE STOOLS, past liver disease.
The family history question that buries the clue — liver problems, or itching in pregnancy.
FOUR SHORT BLOCKS — travel, contacts and pets · new creams and detergents · new medicines, foods, wheeze and lip swelling · atopy and psoriasis.
THE OBSTETRIC HISTORY — booking bloods, scans, GTT, THE 35 TO 37 WEEK SWAB · AND FETAL MOVEMENTS, BLEEDING AND FLUID LOSS · then the first pregnancy and whether she itched then.

ask: The question that routes the station, asked in the first minute: 'Have you noticed any rash, or any redness of the skin?' — followed by 'No rash moves me away from the skin and towards the liver.'
The one that makes the diagnosis: 'Where exactly do you feel itchy?' — and the scabies pair: 'Is it worse after a hot shower? Is anyone else at home itchy?'
The buried clue: 'Did anyone in your family have itching in pregnancy?' and the request that names the disease: 'Examiner — I'd like serum bile acids with liver function tests.'
The two interpretation lines: 'ALP rises two to fourfold in normal pregnancy — her GGT is normal.' and 'The only thing that cures it is delivering the baby, so we plan the birth.'

CHALLENGES: 'My liver? I don't drink.' · 'Is the baby all right?' asked tearfully the moment risk is mentioned · 'Have I done something wrong?' · the examiner's 'HER BILIRUBIN IS NORMAL, DOES THAT NOT GO AGAINST IT?' and 'WHY DOES IT MATTER?' · and if you stop at creams and tablets she asks what happens next, which is the test of whether you reach planned birth.
pefe: The examination findings are given on the card at the start and are meant to be used: pale striae with no rash · SFH 35 cm at 36 weeks, appropriate for dates · longitudinal, cephalic · engagement 4/5, which is not yet engaged · and a normal fetal heart rate. The one thing to add is blood pressure and a urine dipstick, which come back 128/78 with no protein and exclude pre-eclampsia.

The results handed over at six minutes: ALT and AST mildly raised · GGT normal · alkaline phosphatase mildly raised · bilirubin normal · serum bile acids raised · full blood count, urea, electrolytes and creatinine normal. The bile acids are the answer, and you are not to be thrown by the normal bilirubin or the mildly raised ALP.

Role-player: Jenny Marsh, 29, 36 weeks in her second pregnancy, one daughter aged three born at term with no itching in that pregnancy. Works in a childcare centre, supportive partner, lives 90 minutes from the nearest maternity unit. No medical or skin conditions, pregnancy multivitamin only, non-smoker, no alcohol, all antenatal tests normal. Ten days of relentless itching, palms and soles, much worse at night, with no rash — only scratch marks — plus exhaustion, reduced appetite, an intermittent right rib ache and slightly darker urine.

How she plays it: tired and frustrated rather than distressed — she has been told it is 'Just a pregnancy thing'. She volunteers 'There's nothing to see' when asked about rash, with puzzlement, but does not volunteer the palms and soles or her mother unless asked. She becomes frightened and tearful the moment risk to the baby is mentioned and asks 'Is the baby all right?' — settling if the doctor is honest and gives a plan, and staying frightened if they are vague or over-reassuring. Her hidden worry is that she has done something wrong — eaten something, used the wrong cream.

The rash question belongs in the first minute — 'Have you noticed any rash, or any redness of the skin? Any blisters?' → 'No rash at all. Just the marks where I've been scratching. That's what's so odd about it.' Leaving it until minute four is the trap — the answer routes the entire rest of your history. Ask it early and say what it means: 'No rash moves me away from the skin conditions and towards the liver'

Site is most of the diagnosis — 'Where exactly do you feel itchy?' → 'My palms, and the soles of my feet. Mostly there.' She does not volunteer it. Asking 'Where is it?' and not acting on 'Palms and soles' is the trap — that answer, with no rash, is the diagnosis, and you say it back to her

The scabies discriminators, asked in one breath — IS IT WORSE AT NIGHT AND DOES IT WAKE YOU → terrible at night, awake for hours · IS IT WORSE AFTER A HOT SHOWER → no difference · IS ANYONE ELSE AT HOME ITCHY → no · ANY ITCHING BETWEEN YOUR FINGERS → no · then SECONDARY INFECTION ONCE: any fever, any weeping, crusting or discharge where she has scratched

The pre-eclampsia set — forty seconds, not skipped — Headaches · visual change — blurring, flashing lights, spots · dizziness · swelling of legs, hands or face · chest pain or breathlessness · passing less urine. Deciding this is a skin case and skipping the set is the trap — pre-eclampsia can itch, and it is the diagnosis you cannot miss in any woman beyond 20 weeks

The cholestasis block — Pain under the ribs on the right → an ache, on and off · nausea, vomiting, appetite → gone off her food · the tiredness in one question: 'Are you sleepy, or low in energy?' → wiped out, partly from not sleeping · yellowing of skin or eyes → no · dark urine or pale stools → urine might be a bit darker · past liver problems or gallstones · and the buried clue: 'Anyone in the family with liver problems, or with itching in pregnancy?' → her mother, when pregnant with her brother
Do not open a tiredness workup — Thyroid, sleep, mood, weight and cancer screening are the wrong turn. THE CONTEXT TELLS YOU THIS IS ITCH WITH TIREDNESS, NOT TIREDNESS WITH ITCH. ONE QUESTION

Four short non-pregnancy blocks — SCABIES AND FUNGAL — recent travel, close contact with anyone itchy, PETS · CONTACT DERMATITIS — any new cream, soap, body wash, laundry powder or perfume · URTICARIA — new medicines, new foods, ANY WHEEZE OR SWELLING OF LIPS OR TONGUE · ATOPY AND PSORIASIS — eczema, asthma, hay fever, psoriasis or any other skin condition in her or the family. All negative

The obstetric history, and the two never omitted — Booking bloods, dating scan, screening, THE 18 TO 20 WEEK SCAN WITH BABY AND PLACENTA, the glucose tolerance test, THE SWAB AT 35 TO 37 WEEKS · AND NEVER OMIT: 'IS THE BABY KICKING AS MUCH AS USUAL? ANY BLEEDING OR LEAKING OF FLUID?' · then the first pregnancy — straightforward, AND NO ITCHING THEN

The explanation, in plain language — 'The itching is on your palms and soles, it's worse at night, and there's no rash — and that combination points away from a skin problem and towards your liver. Your liver makes a fluid called bile, which normally drains away into the gut. In pregnancy the hormones can slow that drainage down, so the salts in the bile build up in your bloodstream — and those salts are what make your skin itch so intensely. Your blood test confirms it. It only happens in pregnancy, and it goes away completely once the baby is born.' She challenges once: 'My liver? I don't drink'

The honest answer about the baby — 'I'm going to be straight with you. THE ITCHING IS MISERABLE BUT IT ISN'T DANGEROUS TO YOU. THE REASON WE TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY IS THE BABY. Cholestasis carries A SMALL BUT REAL INCREASE IN THE RISK OF STILLBIRTH, and that risk goes up as the bile acid level goes up' — also SPONTANEOUS PRETERM BIRTH AND MECONIUM-STAINED LIQUOR

The thing the station is actually testing — planned birth — 'The only thing that cures it is delivering the baby. So we monitor your blood levels and the baby closely, and we plan the birth rather than waiting for labour to start on its own — usually around 36 to 37 weeks. You're 36 weeks now, so this is a conversation about the next week or two, not the next month.' Refer to the obstetric team today. And be honest about ursodeoxycholic acid: it makes her more comfortable, but the evidence does not show it reduces the risk to the baby — the thing that does that is planning the birth VERIFY

back.dx: Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy, with thalassaemia trait kept alive as the differential until the ferritin returns. The numbers: anaemia in pregnancy is Hb under 110 in the first and third trimesters and under 105 in the second VERIFY · MCV under 80 is microcytic and MCH under 27 is hypochromic · plasma volume rises 50% while red cell mass rises 25%, which is the dilution — and physiological anaemia is normocytic, which is the whole point · the Mentzer index is MCV divided by red cell count, with over 13 favouring iron and under 13 favouring thalassaemia trait · reticulocytes rise at about a week and haemoglobin by about 10 g/L in three to four weeks VERIFY · recheck at four weeks and continue iron for three months after the haemoglobin normalises VERIFY · and two carriers means 1 in 4 affected per pregnancy. The variants. The ferritin comes back normal — 'A ferritin of 84 with a red cell count of 5.8 and a Mentzer index below 13 makes thalassaemia trait far more likely than iron deficiency. I would stop the iron, request haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, and if a trait is confirmed I would test the partner and refer for genetic counselling. At 15 weeks there is still time for prenatal diagnosis if both are carriers' — and to her: 'Your iron stores are actually fine, so iron isn't the answer, and I'm going to stop those tablets, because iron you don't need can build up.' She has not responded to iron at 24 weeks after eight weeks of daily tablets — 'Non-response after adequate adherence means I re-diagnose, not escalate the dose. I would check the ferritin and reticulocyte count — a flat reticulocyte count means she is not responding at all. I would reconsider coexisting thalassaemia trait, ongoing blood loss, coeliac disease and anaemia of chronic disease, and I would ask how she is taking it, because taking iron with tea or with food substantially reduces absorption.' Severe anaemia late — 35 weeks, Hb 78, MCV 69, ferritin 4, breathless on one flight — 'This is severe symptomatic iron deficiency with insufficient time for oral iron to work before delivery. I would give intravenous iron rather than tablets, discuss her with the obstetric team, ensure her blood group and antibody screen are available, plan active management of the third stage, and make sure she delivers where blood products are available. Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or very severe anaemia close to delivery' VERIFY. And if the examiner asks why not just give iron to everyone — 'Because iron given to someone with thalassaemia trait does not help and, given long enough, risks iron overload. It also delays the diagnosis that actually matters for the pregnancy — carrier status, and therefore the need to test the partner. A ferritin is cheap, can be added to an existing sample, and answers the question in days.' if she asks whether the baby has been harmed: 'Your baby takes iron from you before you take it for yourself — which is part of why you feel so worn out. At this level, and this early, I have no reason to think your baby has come to harm. Treating it now protects both of you: untreated anaemia is associated with a smaller baby and early birth, and it makes bleeding at delivery more dangerous for you.' Things never to say: 'It's just the anaemia of pregnancy' · 'Your MCV and MCH are low with a raised rdw' to the patient · 'You need to eat more red meat' to a vegetarian without asking why · 'It's really important that you take the tablets' after she has said she cannot afford them · 'I'll just give you iron and see you in three months' · and 'Thalassaemia is nothing to worry about' without mentioning the partner. The cost, acknowledged not lectured — 'Have you been taking your pregnancy vitamins and folic acid?' → '(Quietly, looking down) I stopped them — I couldn't afford them on TOP of everything.' Hearing that and replying 'It's really important that you take them' is the trap. Acknowledge the cost, then solve it

The thalassaemia block — it keeps the fork open — 'Where is your family from?' → bangladesh · 'Has anyone in your family been told they have a blood condition, or thalassaemia?' → her mother has always been told she is anaemic · 'Has anyone needed regular transfusions?' → no · 'Have you ever been told your blood count was low before, even when you felt well?' → a bit low last pregnancy · and the partner: 'Where is his family from? Has he ever been tested?' → bangladeshi, never tested. Raising thalassaemia and then dropping it is the trap — the risk to this baby depends on him

Rungs 1 to 3 — and rung 3 is the one that matters — 'Your blood count is low — that's what we call being ANAEMIC. Your haemoglobin is 96, and at this stage we'd want it ABOVE ABOUT 105' · 'HAEMOGLOBIN IS THE SUBSTANCE IN YOUR RED BLOOD CELLS THAT CARRIES OXYGEN AROUND YOUR BODY — AND TO YOUR BABY' · THEN RUNG 3: 'The test also measures HOW BIG YOUR RED CELLS ARE, and yours are SMALLER AND PALER than they should be. PREGNANCY ON ITS OWN DOES DROP THE COUNT A LITTLE, since you make a lot more fluid in your bloodstream and it dilutes things. BUT THAT KIND OF ANAEMIA LEAVES THE CELLS A NORMAL SIZE. YOURS ARE SMALL. SO THIS ISN'T JUST THE PREGNANCY — THERE'S A REASON, AND WE SHOULD FIND IT'

Rungs 4 and 5 — the two causes and the one test — 'There are two common reasons for small pale red cells. The commonest by a long way is a lack of iron. The other is an inherited condition of the blood called thalassaemia — more common in families from South Asia, the Mediterranean, the middle east, africa and South-East Asia. It isn't something you catch or develop; you're born with it' · 'One extra blood test tells us which. It's called a ferritin, and it measures your iron stores. I've asked the lab to add it to the sample they already have, so you won't need another needle'

'Would the baby have it?' — 'CARRYING THE TRAIT CAUSES VERY LITTLE TROUBLE FOR YOU — a permanently slightly low blood count and nothing else. IT ONLY MATTERS FOR A BABY IF BOTH PARENTS CARRY IT. So if your ferritin comes back normal, we'd do a second test to confirm it, AND WE'D TEST YOUR PARTNER. YOU'RE 15 WEEKS, SO WE HAVE PLENTY OF TIME.' Two carriers means 1 IN 4 AFFECTED PER PREGNANCY

Rung 6 — connect it to her life, and handle 'It's my fault' — 'Your periods were always heavy. You bled heavily after your daughter and never really replaced what you lost. She's only 14 months old, so two pregnancies close together, and you're still breastfeeding — three separate demands on your iron at the same time. And you don't eat meat, so the iron in your diet is harder to absorb.' when she says 'So it's my fault for not eating properly': 'Not at all. Pregnancy roughly doubles what your body needs, and you've had two close together while feeding a toddler. Almost anyone would be low in that situation' · then one specific change: move the tea away from meals and add vitamin C at dinner · and the ice: 'You're not going mad. It's called pica and it's a recognised sign of low iron'

Rung 7 — the plan, the side effects, the cost and the next birth — Start iron today rather than wait for the ferritin, because you are confident and she is symptomatic · recheck blood count and ferritin at about four weeks · anticipate the side effects: constipation and dark stools, expected and harmless, and alternate-day dosing often works as well and is better tolerated VERIFY · solve the cost: prescribe the cheapest option that works, have the practice nurse check eligibility for help, and 'Please don't stop it because of money without telling me first' · and flag the next birth: 'Because you bled heavily last time, and because you're anaemic now, I want your blood count properly corrected before you deliver'
fails: ★ Never naming serum ferritin as the single test, or never saying that physiological anaemia of pregnancy is normocytic so a low MCV always has another reason
★ Raising thalassaemia and then dropping it — without ethnicity, family history and the partner, the differential is decorative and the baby's risk is never assessed
Asking about periods and stopping, so the previous postpartum haemorrhage — the single biggest item in the history — is never found
Responding to 'I couldn't afford them' with 'it's really important that you take them', or agreeing when she says it is her fault
Skipping pica and restless legs; telling a vegetarian to eat more red meat without asking why she doesn't; or giving iron and reviewing in three months with no ferritin and no four-week recheck
numbers: Anaemia in pregnancy: Hb <110 in first and third trimesters, <105 in the second VERIFY · MCV <80 microcytic, MCH <27 hypochromic · plasma volume +50% and red cell mass +25%, so physiological anaemia is normocytic · Mentzer index = MCV / RBC, >13 iron and <13 thalassaemia trait · two carriers = 1 in 4 affected per pregnancy

Reticulocytes rise at about 1 week; Hb up about 10 g/L in 3 to 4 weeks VERIFY · recheck at 4 weeks and continue iron for 3 months after Hb normalises VERIFY · alternate-day dosing often as effective and better tolerated · IV iron if severe and late, with transfusion reserved for haemodynamic compromise · haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC if ferritin is normal · VERIFY all

must: SAY — 'Your red cells are SMALLER AND PALER than they should be. Pregnancy dilution leaves the cells a NORMAL SIZE — yours are small, so this isn't just the pregnancy' — a low MCV is never the physiological anaemia of pregnancy

DO — Name SERUM FERRITIN as the one test — 'added to the sample they already have, no extra needle' — and keep THALASSAEMIA TRAIT alive: where the family is from, any blood condition or transfusions, ever told the count was low, and 'has your PARTNER ever been tested?' — two carriers is 1 in 4 per pregnancy

FAIL — Asking about periods and stopping, so the previous POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE — a drip and an extra day — is never found; it is the biggest item in the history and the reason to correct her Hb before this delivery

DO — Ask the questions nobody asks: PICA ('do you ever crave ice, dirt, chalk?') and restless legs · tea or coffee with meals · the age of her first child and whether she is still BREASTFEEDING · whether she is taking her pregnancy vitamins

FAIL — Answering 'I couldn't afford them' with 'it's really important that you take them', or agreeing or lecturing when she says 'so it's my fault' — acknowledge the cost, prescribe the cheapest option, and 'please don't stop it because of money without telling me'

DO — Start oral iron today without waiting for the ferritin, one concrete change (tea between meals, vitamin C with dinner), warn about constipation and dark stools and offer alternate-day dosing, recheck Hb and ferritin at 4 WEEKS — never 'I'll give you iron and see you in three months'

setting: Two things must both be done or you fail: counsel the low-lying placenta — rescan at 32 weeks, nine in ten resolve, caesarean at 38 to 39 if it stays — and find and address the hidden agenda, which is fear of labour pain, with the full five-rung menu. No yes, no no. And if you say 'You'll probably need a caesarean anyway', she looks relieved and says 'Great, so we'll book it' — that is the trap.
stem: General practice. Jenny, 27, is 20 weeks pregnant and here to discuss her morphology scan. The report: low-lying placenta with the edge within 2 cm of the internal os; fetal anatomy normal; liquor normal. She tells you she wants a caesarean section. Observations normal, first pregnancy, no bleeding and no pain.

Tasks: take a history from the patient, about 2.5 minutes — explain the ultrasound result to her, about 1.5 minutes — counsel her regarding her request for a caesarean section, about 4 minutes. 8 minutes.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Explain the ultrasound result to her
Counsel her regarding her request for a caesarean section
time: Seventy-five seconds to open and find the agenda — why she wants it, and what she already knows about pain relief · two minutes of obstetric history with bleeding never omitted · ninety seconds on the scan, normal findings first · then four minutes of counselling budgeted deliberately: placenta 60 seconds, caesarean pros and cons 75, the pain menu 90, and the close 30.
findings: Normal findings first, then the placenta

'THE GOOD NEWS FIRST: THE BABY HAS FORMED WELL — brain, heart, spine, kidneys, limbs all normal — AND THE FLUID IS NORMAL. Now, the placenta. IT'S A PIECE OF TISSUE LIKE A BRIDGE BETWEEN THE BABY AND YOUR WOMB; the baby's oxygen and food come across it. NORMALLY IT SITS TOWARDS THE TOP OF THE WOMB. In your case it's IN THE LOWER PART, CLOSE TO THE OPENING THE BABY COMES OUT THROUGH — WITHIN ABOUT TWO CENTIMETRES. We call that A LOW-LYING PLACENTA. IT IS NOT COVERING THE OPENING, AND AT 20 WEEKS IT'S COMMON.' Jargon — 'internal os', 'placental edge distance' — or skipping the normal findings is the trap

back.dx: A LOW-LYING PLACENTA AT 20 WEEKS, WITH A MATERNAL REQUEST FOR CAESAREAN DRIVEN BY FEAR OF LABOUR PAIN — and the station is failed by doing either half without the other. The numbers: 20 mm is the low-lying threshold, over the os is praevia, and 5 cm is normal · transvaginal rescan at 32 weeks, and again at 36 if persistent · 9 in 10 resolve and 1 in 10 stay low · planned caesarean at 38 to 39 weeks for a persistent low-lying placenta, against 36 to 37 for a praevia · 39 weeks is the earliest for a maternal-request caesarean · morphine onset 20 to 30 minutes with a 2 to 4 hour duration · five rungs on the pain ladder · and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, with 000 for bleeding at home VERIFY all. The examiner challenges. 'Why not caesarean now for the placenta?' → 'Nine in ten low-lying placentas at 20 weeks resolve; decisions are made on the 32 to 36 week transvaginal scan.' 'She insists on a caesarean at 36 weeks with a normal placenta.' → 'After full counselling she may choose it; I'd involve the obstetrician, offer a second opinion, and it would be booked at or after 39 weeks.' 'Which pain option is safest for the baby?' → 'Non-pharmacological and nitrous oxide; opioids can cause neonatal drowsiness; epidural is safe for the baby with maternal blood pressure managed.' What the role-player is briefed to do: open firmly with 'I want a caesarean' and only reveal the pain fear when asked why · if the doctor says she will probably need one anyway, look relieved and say 'Great, so we'll book it' · if pain relief is never mentioned, ask at minute six how bad the pain really is · if the epidural is listed without side effects, ask whether it hurts or can paralyse · push once at minute seven with 'So can I have it or not?' and accept 'Too early, your decision, we'll review' · and if the normal findings are not given first, ask 'Is the baby ok?' She is marked down against: no 'Why', no pain menu, a verdict given, no rescan plan, and no bleeding red flag. The wider point this card is worth remembering for: a request station is never about the request. The marks are in why it was made, what she already knows, both sides of both options, and a decision deferred with a date attached.
plan: WIPE, confirm name and date of birth, and ask an open question.
Find the agenda — why she would prefer a caesarean — and then ask what she already knows about pain relief. Two separate marked items.
THE PREGNANCY — booking bloods and blood group, scans and screening · ANY VAGINAL BLEEDING AT ALL · pain or tightenings · FETAL MOVEMENTS.
Parity and surgery — first pregnancy, previous caesarean or any uterine surgery including a curette or termination · smoking · pre-eclampsia symptoms · partner, mood and safety at home.
The scan — normal findings first, then the bridge analogy and the words 'Low-lying', with 'Not covering the opening' said explicitly.
Half one — rescan at 32 weeks, nine in ten resolve, caesarean at 38 to 39 if it stays, and the bleeding red flag.
Half two a — the caesarean, good side then downside, including the next-pregnancy risks and the neonatal ones.
Half two B — acknowledge the fear, then all five rungs of the pain menu with the epidural caveats given unprompted.
The close — too early to decide, reading on all three topics, a longer visit with her partner, the bleeding red flag repeated, and support whatever she chooses.
back.planNote: the stem splits it 2.5 minutes history, 1.5 explanation, 4 counselling - and the counselling is itself budgeted 60 / 75 / 90 / 30 so the pain menu survives
ask: The two agenda questions, scored separately: 'Can you tell me why you'd prefer a caesarean?' and 'How much do you know about the options for pain relief in labour?'
The symptom question that is easy to skip with a scan in front of you: 'Have you had any vaginal bleeding at all?' — and the red flag it earns: 'Any bleeding at all — go straight to the hospital.'
The explanation: 'The placenta is like a bridge between the baby and your womb. Normally it sits at the TOP.' · 'We'll repeat the scan at around 32 weeks. In nine out of ten women it has moved up.'
The two sentences that carry the counselling: 'Less pain during the birth, but more pain and a slower recovery afterwards.' and 'You would not be left alone with it — there's a menu of options.'

CHALLENGES: 'Is the baby OK?' if you start with the placenta · 'Do I need a caesarean because of the placenta?' · 'BUT MY FRIENDS SAID A CAESAREAN IS LESS PAINFUL' · 'DOES AN EPIDURAL HURT? CAN IT PARALYSE YOU?' · 'SO CAN I HAVE IT OR NOT?' pushed once at minute seven · and 'what if I bleed?' if no red flag was given.
pefe: THERE IS NO EXAMINATION — THE SCAN REPORT IS THE DATA, AND THE MARK IS FOR READING IT IN THE RIGHT ORDER: FETAL ANATOMY NORMAL AND LIQUOR NORMAL FIRST, THEN THE PLACENTAL POSITION. The number that matters is THE EDGE WITHIN 2 cm OF THE INTERNAL OS, WHICH IS LOW-LYING BUT NOT PRAEVIA — and saying 'it is not covering the opening' explicitly is what stops her hearing the worst.

Role-player: JENNY, 27, A PRIMARY SCHOOL TEACHER IN HER FIRST PREGNANCY AT 20 WEEKS, with a supportive partner Mark. Non-smoker, no alcohol, no medical problems, PREGNANCY MULTIVITAMIN ONLY, O POSITIVE. NO BLEEDING, NO PAIN, FLUTTERS FELT THIS WEEK, AND NO PREVIOUS SURGERY OF ANY KIND. She read the word 'low' on the report and is worried about it — BUT THE REAL DRIVER IS FEAR OF PAIN.

Her hidden agenda: terrified of labour pain after friends' stories, believing a caesarean 'Hurts less', and knowing nothing about pain relief. She volunteers the fear only when asked why — and if never asked, says at minute five 'I just can't face the pain.' Anxious and a little defensive, softening once the fear is acknowledged and the options explained.

The checklist: asked why she wants a caesarean · asked what she knows about pain relief · asked about bleeding · asked about pain and movements · asked previous caesarean and uterine surgery · explained normal findings first · placenta as a bridge, normally at the TOP, hers low and under 2 cm · rescan at 32 weeks · nine in ten resolve · caesarean 38 to 39 weeks if it stays, with the bleeding risk named · the bleeding red flag · caesarean pros and cons · acknowledged the fear of pain · listed all five pain-relief options · gave the epidural caveats · said it is too early to decide, with reading, the partner and a review · and gave no verdict.

Find the agenda before the scan — 'Before we go through the report — is there a particular concern about the birth you'd like to talk about? Can you tell me why you'd prefer a caesarean?' → 'I'm really scared of the pain. My friends said it's awful and that a caesarean hurts less' · then the second half: 'How much do you know about the options we have for pain relief in labour?' → 'Not much, really. Nothing.' Going straight to the scan is the trap — the examiner ticks 'Explores reason for request' and 'Assesses knowledge of pain relief' as separate items

The obstetric history, with the one that is easy to skip — Booking bloods and BLOOD GROUP, dating scan, screening · 'HAVE YOU HAD ANY VAGINAL BLEEDING AT ALL?' · any tummy pain or tightenings · HAVE YOU STARTED FEELING THE BABY MOVE · first pregnancy · ANY PREVIOUS CAESAREAN, OR ANY SURGERY ON THE WOMB — FIBROIDS, A CURETTE, A TERMINATION · smoking · headaches, vision changes or swelling · partner support, mood, AND SAFETY AT HOME. OMITTING BLEEDING IS THE TRAP — IT IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT SYMPTOM QUESTION WITH A LOW PLACENTA, AND IT IS EASY TO SKIP BECAUSE 'THE SCAN ALREADY TOLD ME'

Half one — the placenta plan in four parts — We repeat the scan at about 32 weeks · as the womb grows the placenta is carried upward, and in nine out of ten women it is no longer low · in one in ten it stays low, and then there is a higher risk of heavy bleeding at the birth, so we would usually recommend a planned caesarean at around 38 to 39 weeks · and the red flag: 'Between now and then, any bleeding or pain — go straight to the hospital'

Half two a — the caesarean, both sides — The good: no labour pain, a set date, fewer tears, less risk of leaking urine or prolapse later · the downside: it is major surgery — more bleeding, infection, injury to bladder or bowel, clots, anaesthetic risks, a very small risk of death or of losing the womb · more pain afterwards and a slower recovery, four to six weeks · and it raises the risks in the next pregnancy — a low placenta again, the placenta growing into the scar, the scar tearing in labour · plus more breathing trouble at first and a bit more asthma later for the baby

'But my friends said a caesarean is less painful' — 'They're right that you don't feel the birth itself. But afterwards there's a wound to recover from, so there's usually more pain in the days after and a slower recovery — weeks rather than days. Whereas in labour we have very good ways to manage the pain, which I'll go through'

Half two B — acknowledge the fear, then the five rungs — 'I understand labour pain can feel frightening. You would not be left alone with it — there's a menu.' One: breathing, relaxation, moving, warm water, massage, a support person · two: a tens machine — pads on the back, gentle tingling pulses · three: the gas — nitrous oxide through a mask, takes the edge off, wears off in seconds · four: a morphine injection — works in 20 to 30 minutes, can make you nauseated and the baby sleepy, so we use it less · five: an epidural — a fine tube next to the spinal cord in the lower back, numb from the waist down, the most effective

The epidural caveats, given unprompted — It can drop your blood pressure, so you would have a drip · it occasionally causes a headache afterwards · and we would monitor the baby's heart continuously. If she asks whether it hurts or can paralyse: 'There's a small sting of local anaesthetic first, then pressure. Serious nerve injury is extremely rare — the common side effects are the blood pressure drop and the headache. The anaesthetist can see you in a clinic before the birth to talk it through'

The close — no verdict, and a date to come back — 'SO CAN I HAVE THE CAESAREAN OR NOT?' → 'IT'S YOUR DECISION, AND IT'S TOO EARLY TO MAKE IT. THE PLACENTA MAY DECIDE IT FOR US. Read the information, TALK WITH YOUR PARTNER, and come back — IF YOU STILL WANT A CAESAREAN THEN, WE'LL DISCUSS IT WITH THE OBSTETRICIAN.' Book a longer visit with the partner, give reading on all three topics, repeat the bleeding red flag, AND CLOSE WITH 'WHATEVER YOU CHOOSE, I'LL SUPPORT YOU'

The budget that protects the pain menu — Placenta 60 seconds · caesarean pros and cons 75 seconds · pain menu 90 seconds · close 30 seconds. Ending the station without the pain menu because time ran out on the caesarean risks is the commonest way to lose this — and if you never mention pain relief she asks at minute six 'So how bad is the pain, honestly?'

The variants that change the scan — PLACENTA 5 cm FROM THE OS → 'that is A NORMAL POSITION — it isn't low and it isn't covering anything. SO THE PLACENTA DOESN'T AFFECT HOW YOU GIVE BIRTH. That leaves the question you came with, and I'd like to understand it properly' · PREVIOUS CAESAREAN PLUS A LOW PLACENTA → one extra thing at the 32-week scan: ASK THE SONOGRAPHER TO CHECK THE PLACENTA HAS NOT GROWN INTO THE OLD SCAR — ACCRETA — because if it were there the birth would be planned in a large hospital with the full team

The variants that change the station — BLEEDING AT 30 WEEKS → 'with a low placenta ANY BLEEDING HAS TO BE CHECKED IN HOSPITAL TODAY, not in the clinic. They'll check your blood pressure and pulse, DO A SPECULUM LOOK BUT NO INTERNAL EXAMINATION, check the baby's heart trace, and BECAUSE YOU'RE RH-NEGATIVE they'll do a blood test AND GIVE ANTI-D. At 30 weeks they'll also GIVE A STEROID INJECTION' · A PREVIOUS TRAUMATIC BIRTH DRIVING THE REQUEST → 'what you went through sounds GENUINELY TRAUMATIC, AND WANTING TO AVOID IT IS A REASONABLE RESPONSE, NOT A WEAKNESS': obstetric referral for both options with a clear birth plan, PERINATAL MENTAL HEALTH SO THE FEAR ITSELF IS TREATED, and CONTINUITY OF MIDWIFERY CARE — with a caesarean supported at 39 weeks if that is her choice
fails: ★ Doing only one half — counselling the placenta without ever finding the fear of pain, or addressing the fear without the rescan plan and the caesarean-if-it-stays
★ Giving a verdict, or saying 'you'll probably need a caesarean anyway' — she immediately says 'great, so we'll book it' and the counselling never happens
Never asking why she wants a caesarean, or never asking what she already knows about pain relief — they are scored as two separate items
Omitting the bleeding question and the bleeding red flag, which are the most important symptom and the most important safety-net with a low placenta
Running out of time on the caesarean risks so the five-rung pain menu never happens, or listing the epidural without its side effects
numbers: 20 mm is the low-lying threshold; over the os is praevia; 5 cm is normal · transvaginal rescan at 32 weeks, and 36 if persistent · 9 in 10 resolve, 1 in 10 stay low · planned caesarean 38 to 39 weeks for persistent low-lying, 36 to 37 for praevia · 39 weeks is the earliest for a maternal-request caesarean

Five rungs: breathing and movement, tens, nitrous oxide, opioid, epidural · morphine onset 20 to 30 minutes, duration 2 to 4 hours · caesarean recovery 4 to 6 weeks · epidural caveats: blood pressure drop needing a drip, occasional headache, continuous fetal monitoring · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, 000 for bleeding at home · VERIFY all

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Doing only one half — counselling the placenta without ever finding the FEAR OF LABOUR PAIN, or treating the fear without the placenta plan; both halves must be done or you fail
DO — The two agenda questions, scored separately, before the scan: 'Can you tell me WHY you'd prefer a caesarean?' and 'How much do you know about the options for PAIN RELIEF in labour?'

FAIL — Omitting the BLEEDING question in the history and the bleeding red flag in the plan — 'any bleeding at all, go straight to the hospital' — or never asking about a previous caesarean or womb surgery

SAY — Normal findings first, no jargon: 'the placenta is like a bridge, normally at the top — yours is within about two centimetres of the opening. We REPEAT THE SCAN AT 32 WEEKS; in NINE IN TEN it has moved up; if it stays low we'd recommend a planned caesarean at 38 to 39 weeks'

FAIL — Giving a verdict, or saying 'you'll probably need a caesarean anyway' — she says 'great, so we'll book it' and the counselling never happens; close with 'it's too early to decide', reading, bring your partner, a longer review, 'whatever you decide, I'll support you'

DO — Budget the time so both lists happen: caesarean pros AND cons (more pain and a slower recovery afterwards, a low placenta or accreta next time) then the FIVE-RUNG PAIN MENU — breathing and movement, TENS, gas, morphine, EPIDURAL with its side effects (BP drop and a drip, headache, continuous monitoring)

setting: The stem says 'Trying for six years without success' and does not mention the four miscarriages. Three infertility questions — ovulation tracking, timing, semen analysis — and the station is lost, because she answers briefly, looks puzzled and does not correct you. The pivot line is 'So you can fall pregnant, but the pregnancies aren't continuing', and the answer to the investigation task is one word: karyotype.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo. Sarah Whitlock, 33, married, a primary-school teacher. 'Sarah has come to see you because she and her husband have been trying for a baby for six years without success. She is otherwise well. Vital signs normal. BMI 27.'

What the stem does not say: she has conceived four times and lost every pregnancy at 7, 9, 8 and 11 weeks, and she only volunteers this to an open question. Tasks: take a focused history, 6 minutes — tell the examiner your differential diagnoses with reasons — outline the investigations you would arrange for this couple. 8 minutes, no examination.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Give your differential diagnoses to the examiner, with reasons
Outline the investigations you would arrange for this couple
time: Sixty seconds to open, catch the pivot and acknowledge it · seventy-five seconds on the losses themselves · forty-five seconds on periods, partner and screening, and no longer · two and a quarter minutes sweeping the buckets — endocrine, immune and clotting, infection, environment and lifestyle · forty-five seconds summarising to her · then two minutes of differentials by bucket and investigations to the examiner.

back.dx: RECURRENT PREGNANCY LOSS — four first-trimester losses presented as six years of infertility, where the station is won by hearing it, restructuring it aloud, and saying karyotype. The numbers: the definition is two or more losses under 24 weeks · chromosomal losses are mostly under 10 weeks while APS and uterine causes tend to be 10 weeks or later · antiphospholipid antibodies must be positive twice, twelve weeks apart · APS treatment is aspirin 100 mg plus enoxaparin 40 mg daily · caffeine under 200 mg per day · folate 0.5 mg, or 5 mg if high risk · about 50% remain unexplained, with a live birth rate next time of about 60 to 75% · a translocation carrier is found in 2 to 5% of couples · and red nose is 1300 308 307 with TIS on 131 450 VERIFY all. The investigation-card version hands you: FBC normal, TSH 1.8, HbA1c 5.3%, prolactin normal, anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant negative, pelvic ultrasound normal — and asks what is missing. 'Two things stand out. There is no karyotype for either partner — a balanced translocation gives a normal person and recurrent early loss, so I'd arrange chromosome analysis for both, and cytogenetics on the tissue at any future loss. And the antiphospholipid results are a single set without ANTI-β2-GLYCOPROTEIN I; the syndrome is defined by persistence at twelve weeks, so I'd complete and repeat them. The ultrasound doesn't fully define the cavity after her curette, so I'd consider hysteroscopy.' and if the karyotypes are normal too → 'Then this is unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss, which is about half of couples. I'd be honest about that, and equally honest that her chance of a live birth next time is still around two in three. I'd refer her to a recurrent pregnancy loss clinic, arrange an early scan at six to seven weeks next pregnancy, use vaginal progesterone if she bleeds, optimise folate, caffeine and alcohol, and make sure she has psychological support.' The examiner challenges: 'Why not a TORCH screen?' → 'Those infections cause sporadic loss, not recurrent; guidelines don't recommend routine TORCH serology. I'd screen for STIs and rubella immunity.' 'Thrombophilia screen?' → 'Antiphospholipid testing for everyone; inherited thrombophilia only with a personal or family clot history, as guidelines differ.' 'And management?' → 'Find the cause and treat it — surgery for a septum, aspirin and heparin for antiphospholipid syndrome, thyroxine, genetic counselling. If nothing is found, supportive care in an early pregnancy clinic, folate, lifestyle change, and I would tell her that most couples still go on to have a baby.' and if she asks for a tablet to stop it happening: 'I understand why you'd want one. Without a specific cause, aspirin and heparin don't help and I wouldn't start them. What does help is being looked after closely from the very start of the next pregnancy, folate, and progesterone if there is any bleeding — and the honest truth is that most women in your position do have a baby.' Prescribing aspirin or heparin 'Just in case' is an examiner target. And if you say 'We'll definitely find the cause', she asks 'You promise?'
plan: OPEN WITH A GENUINELY OPEN QUESTION — 'tell me what's been happening' — AND LET HER GIVE YOU THE LOSSES.
Acknowledge the loss in one sentence, then say the reframe out loud: this is not infertility, and it has its own checklist.
The losses — how many, at what gestation each, was the tissue tested, have you ever completed a pregnancy, and any curette or uterine surgery.
Periods, partner and screening in forty-five seconds — including whether periods are lighter since the d&C.
ENDOCRINE BUCKET — thyroid, diabetes, PCOS, prolactin.
Immune and clotting bucket — joints, rashes, ulcers, personal clot history, and family history of loss or clots.
INFECTION AND ENVIRONMENT — cats and fevers · smoking, alcohol, CAFFEINE · medications and FOLATE.
The impact question — how is this affecting you — then acknowledge, ask about safety, and promise to return to it.
SUMMARISE TO HER — the pattern, the six areas, the honest half-unexplained figure with hope attached, and the three things to start today.
Differentials to the examiner, by bucket, each with the reason it is on the list.
Investigations — karyotype of both parents first, then products of conception, cavity assessment, APS antibodies with the twelve-week repeat, TSH, HbA1c, prolactin, and baseline bloods.
Referral to a recurrent pregnancy loss clinic, psychological support, and review in two weeks with results.

ask: The pivot line: 'So you are able to fall pregnant, but the pregnancies aren't continuing — that's a different problem from infertility.' and the safety net if she does not volunteer it: 'Have you ever had a positive pregnancy test?'

The four loss questions, including the wording that matters: 'At what stage of pregnancy did each one happen?' · 'Was the tissue ever sent to the lab?' · 'Have you ever completed a pregnancy?' · 'Any procedures down below — a curette, a termination, surgery on the womb?'
The family question and the impact question: 'Any family history of miscarriages, stillbirths or clots?' and 'How is all of this affecting you?'

The two sentences for the examiner: 'Karyotype of both partners, and the products of conception next time.' and 'Antiphospholipid antibodies need to be positive twice, twelve weeks apart.' plus the one for her: 'In about half of couples no cause is found — and most still go on to have a baby.'

CHALLENGES: 'Why karyotype both? She's the one miscarrying.' · 'Why not a TORCH screen?' · 'Thrombophilia screen?' · 'Everything is normal — what is missing?' · 'IS THIS BECAUSE OF THE COFFEE? IS IT ME?' · 'IS THERE A TABLET I CAN TAKE TO STOP IT HAPPENING?' · and 'YOU PROMISE?' if you say you will definitely find the cause.
pefe: There is no physical examination in this station. The 'Findings' are the pattern of the losses — four, at 7, 9, 8 and 11 weeks, the last with a heartbeat, one curettage, no completed pregnancy, a sister with two losses, high caffeine and no clot history — and the mark is for converting that pattern into which causes lead the list.

THE INVESTIGATION CARD, IF THE SECOND VERSION IS RUN: FBC NORMAL · TSH 1.8 · HbA1c 5.3% · PROLACTIN NORMAL · ANTICARDIOLIPIN AND LUPUS ANTICOAGULANT NEGATIVE · PELVIC ULTRASOUND SHOWING A NORMAL UTERUS AND OVARIES. THE ANSWER TO 'WHAT IS MISSING?' IS KARYOTYPE — plus the incomplete and single-time-point APS testing, and a cavity that ultrasound does not fully define after a curette.

Role-player: Sarah Whitlock, 33, a primary-school teacher in Kadina, married to Tom for eight years. Six years trying, four miscarriages at 7, 9, 8 and 11 weeks, the last with a heartbeat seen at nine weeks · d&C after the second · periods regular but slightly lighter since · never completed a pregnancy · no thyroid, diabetes, PCOS or prolactin symptoms, no clots, joints or rash · her sister had two miscarriages then two healthy boys · non-smoker, wine most nights, five or six coffees, and she stopped folate after the last loss.

How she plays it: controlled, tired, close to tears at the start, warming up if the doctor is kind and structured. Her hidden agenda is that she fears it is her fault and she is low — some days she does not want to get up, with no thoughts of self-harm. If the doctor asks infertility questions she answers briefly and looks puzzled but does not correct them. If they never acknowledge the losses she becomes flat and monosyllabic. The AUTOMATIC FAILS are: an infertility history throughout · no karyotype · and no acknowledgement of the loss at all.

The pivot, and the safety net if she does not volunteer it — An open question gets: 'Six years. I do get pregnant — four times — but I lose them every time, around two months in. Nobody has ever explained why.' if she does not volunteer it, the safety-net question is: 'In those six years, have you ever had a positive pregnancy test?' then say the reframe out loud: 'So you are able to fall pregnant, but the pregnancies aren't continuing — that's a different problem from infertility, and it has its own checklist of causes'

The acknowledgement takes eight seconds — 'I'm so sorry. That is a lot of loss, and the fear of trying again makes complete sense.' Skipping it because 'There isn't time' is the trap — and if the losses are never acknowledged at all she becomes flat and monosyllabic for the rest of the station

The losses — four questions, and the wording of the fourth — How many altogether → four · at what stage did each one happen → seven, nine, eight, and the last at eleven weeks, which had a heartbeat on the scan · was the tissue from any of them sent to the laboratory → no, nobody offered · and 'Have you ever completed a pregnancy?' — not 'Do you have any children?', which is the trap with a woman who has had four losses · then any procedures: a curette, a termination, surgery on the womb → a d&C after the second

Use the pattern, do not just collect it — 'THE EARLY LOSSES POINT TOWARD A CHROMOSOMAL CAUSE; THE ELEVEN-WEEK LOSS AND THE CURETTAGE MAKE ME ALSO CONSIDER ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME AND THE UTERINE CAVITY.' THAT SENTENCE IS TASK TWO DONE WELL — chromosomal losses are mostly under 10 weeks, while APS and uterine causes tend to be 10 weeks or later

Periods, partner, screening — forty-five seconds, do not expand — Last period and regularity · heavy or painful, any bleeding in between — and whether they are lighter than they used to be, because 'Much lighter since the d&C, barely a day' is Asherman's · is your husband supportive · any STI, post-coital bleeding or pain with sex · cervical screening. Asking about contraception is the trap — she is conceiving, and it tells the examiner you are on autopilot

Bucket one — endocrine — THYROID: do you prefer hot or cold weather, any change in WEIGHT, ENERGY OR BOWELS · DIABETES: PASSING MORE URINE OR DRINKING MORE THAN USUAL · PCOS: EXTRA HAIR ON THE FACE OR BODY, ACNE, RECENT WEIGHT GAIN · PROLACTIN: MILKY DISCHARGE FROM THE NIPPLES, HEADACHES, CHANGE IN VISION. All negative apart from some weight gain since the losses

Bucket two — immune and clotting — Any joint pains, rashes, mouth ulcers · have you ever had a blood clot in the leg or lung, or a stroke · and 'Is there any family history of miscarriages, stillbirths or clots?' → her sister had two miscarriages before her boys. In the APS variant she answers: 'I had a clot in my calf on the pill when I was 24'

Buckets three and four — infection and environment — Pets at home, cats in particular, and any fevers or rashes around the pregnancies — a dog, no fevers · then smoking, alcohol and caffeine → no smoking, a glass of wine most nights, five or six coffees · and medications and supplements including folate → she stopped the folate after the last loss

The question that must not be skipped — 'HOW MUCH STRESS IS THERE AT HOME AND WORK, AND HOW IS ALL OF THIS AFFECTING YOU?' → 'IT'S TAKEN OVER EVERYTHING. I DREAD PREGNANCY ANNOUNCEMENTS. SOME DAYS I DON'T WANT TO GET UP.' ACKNOWLEDGE IT, ASK ABOUT SAFETY, AND SAY YOU WILL COME BACK TO IT BEFORE SHE LEAVES. Her hidden fear is that IT IS HER FAULT — the coffee, the wine, working too hard — and she asks 'IS THIS BECAUSE OF THE COFFEE? IS IT ME?' at about five minutes if you have not asked how she is coping

The differentials by bucket, with reasons — Genetic — a parental balanced translocation is the leading concern given early losses and a family history · immune and clotting — antiphospholipid syndrome, given a later loss with a heartbeat · uterine — a septum, fibroid, or adhesions after her curettage, made more likely by lighter periods · endocrine — thyroid disease, PCOS or diabetes, and hyperprolactinaemia, though her history doesn't suggest them · infection is low yield · and modifiable factors — caffeine and alcohol. Listing tests before differentials is the trap

The investigations — and the one word the station turns on — Karyotype of both partners · cytogenetics on the products of conception at any future loss · pelvic ultrasound, ideally 3d, with hysteroscopy or hsg if the cavity needs defining · antiphospholipid antibodies — anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant and ANTI-β2-GLYCOPROTEIN I, repeated at twelve weeks if positive · TSH · HbA1c · prolactin · baseline bloods with an STI screen and rubella immunity · and inherited thrombophilia testing only if a clot history emerges. 'Why karyotype both? She's the one miscarrying' → 'Because a balanced translocation can sit in either parent, gives a normal person, and only shows up as an unbalanced conceptus'

The summary to her, before the examiner tasks — 'Four losses between seven and eleven weeks, one needing a curette, a sister with losses, and otherwise you're well. This is RECURRENT PREGNANCY LOSS, and we look for causes in SIX AREAS: THE WOMB, HORMONES, IMMUNE AND CLOTTING PROBLEMS, INFECTION, GENETICS, AND LIFESTYLE. IN ABOUT HALF OF COUPLES NO CAUSE IS FOUND — AND EVEN THEN, MOST GO ON TO HAVE A BABY. Today I'd like to organise the tests, RESTART FOLATE, and cut the coffee to two a day and the wine while trying'
fails: ★ Running an infertility history — ovulation tracking, timing, semen analysis — because the stem said 'trying for six years without success'; she will not correct you
★ Never saying karyotype, or never acknowledging the losses at all
Asking 'do you have any children?' instead of 'have you ever completed a pregnancy?', or never asking whether the tissue was sent to the laboratory
Listing investigations before differentials, reflexly offering a TORCH screen, or prescribing aspirin and heparin 'just in case' for unexplained loss
Skipping 'how is all of this affecting you?' when she has given you low mood, or promising that the cause will definitely be found
numbers: Definition: two or more losses under 24 weeks · chromosomal losses mostly under 10 weeks; APS and uterine causes 10 weeks or later · APS antibodies: two tests, twelve weeks apart · APS treatment: aspirin 100 mg plus enoxaparin 40 mg daily · caffeine under 200 mg a day · folate 0.5 mg, or 5 mg if high risk

Unexplained in about 50% of couples, with a live birth rate next time of about 60 to 75% · translocation carrier in 2 to 5% of couples · early scan at 6 to 7 weeks next pregnancy, with vaginal progesterone if she bleeds · inherited thrombophilia testing only with a personal or family clot history · red nose 1300 308 307 · TIS 131 450 · VERIFY all

She stays irritable and clipped until that is addressed and softens once it is — so the communication domain is won or lost in the first fifteen seconds. Then one question sorts the case: 'When you wake up in the morning, is the swelling still there?'
stem: Your general practice, rural South Australia, routine antenatal clinic. Karen Whitmore, 37, is 36 weeks pregnant, gravida 3 para 2, attending a scheduled visit. Presenting complaint: swelling of both legs. Antenatal care has been uncomplicated and today's observations are on the card in the room.

Tasks: take a focused history from Karen, six minutes — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings — explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to Karen. 8 minutes. No investigation task and no management task.

Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings

time: Answer the emotional line before any question · then explore the swelling, with the morning question asked as its own question · then the other sites, including face and hands · then the pre-eclampsia set at about two minutes, not five · then clotting and the four organ failures · then a short obstetric history that is never skipped · then request the card by naming findings, read it back aloud, and explain one mechanism covering four problems.
findings: BP 118/76 — normal · pulse 88, temp 36.7 · bilateral pitting oedema to the mid-thigh, symmetrical · varicose veins both calves · oedematous vulva with vulval varicosities · haemorrhoids · ankle clonus, one beat · calves soft, non-tender, no asymmetry · SFH 35 cm, longitudinal, cephalic, FHR 142 · and no urine dipstick provided

back.dx: PHYSIOLOGICAL OEDEMA OF LATE PREGNANCY — not pre-eclampsia — in a woman whose sister had pre-eclampsia and who is frightened this is the same thing. The numbers: sustained clonus is more than 3 beats · hypertension in pregnancy is 140/90 or above, severe at 160/110 · the treated target is under 135/85 · significant proteinuria is a protein-creatinine ratio of 30 mg/mmol or more VERIFY · fetal heart 110 to 160 · SFH equals gestation plus or minus 2 to 3 cm · the GBS swab is at 35 to 37 weeks · and aspirin prophylaxis is started before 16 weeks VERIFY. The safety net she leaves with: come back or go to hospital if the swelling is still there on waking, if it spreads to the face or hands, if there is headache or flashing lights, pain under the ribs, any bleeding or fluid loss, or reduced fetal movements — 'And you have five weeks to go, not fifteen'. The variants. The numbers change — BP 156/98 repeated, four beats of sustained clonus, and oedema of the face and hands → 'Sustained clonus beyond three beats with hypertension makes this pre-eclampsia with severe features. I would want a urine protein-creatinine ratio, full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests with LDH, urate and a coagulation profile, plus a CTG and an ultrasound for growth, liquor and umbilical artery doppler' — and to her: 'I'm sending you to hospital now, and I'll speak to the obstetric team while you're on your way. They'll monitor the baby, start a medicine to bring your blood pressure down, and very likely give you magnesium to protect you from a seizure. At 36 weeks, the treatment that cures pre-eclampsia is delivering the baby.' From a rural site, discuss in-utero transfer with MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33 rather than retrieving a sick newborn afterwards. Unilateral swelling — a left calf 4 cm larger, warm and tender → 'Asymmetrical, tender calf swelling in a pregnant woman is a deep vein thrombosis until proven otherwise, and pregnancy alone is a risk factor. I would arrange a compression ultrasound today, and if there is any delay I would discuss starting therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin in the interim with the obstetric team. D-dimer is not useful in pregnancy because it is physiologically raised' VERIFY. And when she demands induction — 'I understand completely, and I'm not dismissing it. But at 36 weeks your baby is still doing important growing — particularly the lungs and the feeding reflexes — and bringing labour on early without a medical reason carries real risks for the baby and raises your chance of a caesarean. Right now I don't have a medical reason to deliver you early, and that's actually good news. What I can do is take the discomfort seriously and treat it properly.' Things never to say: 'Pelvic congestion syndrome' · 'I'll give you a fluid tablet' · 'Try cutting down your salt' · 'It's just normal, don't worry about it' before excluding · and 'She has clonus so this is pre-eclampsia'.
plan: Sanitise, sit at eye level slightly to her side, offer left-lateral positioning — and answer her opening line before asking anything.
THE SWELLING — onset, constant or intermittent, GETTING WORSE, ONE LEG OR BOTH, HOW FAR UP.
THE MORNING QUESTION, ASKED SEPARATELY AND FLAGGED AS IMPORTANT · then worse standing, better with feet up.
Other sites — vulval swelling, then face, eyes and hands · pain, itch, rash, varicose veins, haemorrhoids.
THE PRE-ECLAMPSIA SET IN FULL — headache, vision, dizziness, RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT PAIN, nausea, chest pain and breathlessness, REDUCED URINE.
CLOTTING — calf pain, travel, bed rest, surgery, PERSONAL AND FAMILY CLOT HISTORY, cough or haemoptysis.
Heart, kidney, liver and thyroid — and clarify why she sleeps propped up.
THE OBSTETRIC HISTORY — antenatal tests including THE GBS SWAB · FETAL MOVEMENTS AND BLEEDING OR FLUID LOSS · previous pregnancies AND ANY PRE-ECLAMPSIA · medications and allergies.
Request the examination card by naming findings, including the number of beats of clonus and a dipstick.
Read the findings back aloud — normal blood pressure first, symmetrical pitting oedema with soft calves against a clot, and one beat of clonus as normal.
Answer the missing-dipstick and clonus challenge.
Bracket the news with acknowledgement, name it as normal for this stage, and give the single mechanism covering all four findings.
Name the clonus before anyone else does · the seven differentials in one clause each · practical help with no diuretic and no salt restriction · and the safety net.
