ask: The question the case turns on, asked alone: 'Is the swelling still there when you first wake up in the morning?' and its companion: 'Any swelling around your eyes, your face, or your hands?'

The examination request that shows you know the threshold: 'Examiner — is there ankle clonus, and how many beats?' — followed by 'One beat is normal. Clonus only concerns us when it is sustained beyond three beats.'
The two that always score in an obstetric history: 'Is the baby kicking as much as usual?' and 'Any bleeding or leaking of fluid?'
The explanation sentences: 'That one thing explains all four of your problems.' and 'I'm not saying nothing is wrong — I'm saying nothing is dangerous.'

CHALLENGES: the opening 'I just want this pregnancy to be over' · 'NORMAL? HAVE YOU SEEN MY LEGS?' · 'CAN'T YOU JUST INDUCE ME?' raised once near the end · 'IS THIS THAT PRE-ECLAMPSIA THING? MY SISTER HAD IT' volunteered late if you never ask her concerns · and the examiner on the missing dipstick and the clonus.
pefe: Ask for the card by naming the finding you are hunting, not the region — 'I'd like to examine the cardiovascular system' repeated three times earns nothing. The items that matter: blood pressure repeated after rest · whether the oedema is pitting, symmetrical and how far it extends · whether either calf is tender or asymmetrical · the number of beats of clonus · and a urine dipstick, which is deliberately not provided.

Read it back as you receive it: the normal blood pressure is the most important finding · bilateral, pitting, symmetrical oedema with soft non-tender calves argues strongly against a deep vein thrombosis · one beat of clonus is within normal limits · and fundal height and fetal heart rate are normal.

Role-player: KAREN WHITMORE, 37, THIRD PREGNANCY AT 36 WEEKS, two children aged 6 and 4 BOTH BORN NORMALLY WITH NO COMPLICATIONS. Works part-time on supermarket checkouts, ON HER FEET FOR SIX-HOUR SHIFTS. HER PARTNER WORKS AWAY MONDAY TO FRIDAY AND SHE LIVES 40 MINUTES FROM THE HOSPITAL. No medical problems, PREGNANCY MULTIVITAMIN ONLY, all antenatal tests normal with the GBS swab pending.

How she plays it: opens irritable, flat and short with arms folded, exhausted and feeling nobody has taken her seriously — and softens noticeably if acknowledged in the first or second sentence, staying clipped if not. She is embarrassed about the vulval swelling and relaxes if it is handled matter-of-factly. She pushes back once when told it is normal. Her hidden agenda is that her sister had pre-eclampsia and was rushed in for an emergency caesarean at 34 weeks — volunteered only if asked about concerns, or late if never asked — and she raises induction once near the end.

The opening line is not about the legs — 'I just want this pregnancy to be over. I can't take this any more.' → 'I'm really sorry you're feeling like that, Karen. Thirty-six weeks is hard work, and you're doing a great job carrying this baby. I'm here to help. Tell me what's been troubling you most — we'll go through it properly and make a plan together.' Opening with 'So, tell me about the swelling' and ignoring the line is the trap: she is briefed to stay clipped until it is addressed and to soften visibly once it is

The red-flag question, asked as its own question — 'This one matters — when you wake up in the morning, is the swelling still there?' → 'No. It's much better in the mornings. It builds up over the day and by night it's awful.' Burying it inside 'Anything make it better or worse?' Is the trap — ask it separately, and she does not offer the morning answer unless asked directly

The other sites — and the one that would change the diagnosis — 'Have you noticed swelling anywhere else?' → around her private parts, swollen and uncomfortable and embarrassing · 'What about around your eyes, your face, or your hands and fingers?' → no, my rings still fit. Non-dependent oedema is the finding that would change the diagnosis, and you must be heard to look for it · then pain, itch, rash, varicose veins and haemorrhoids. Flinching at the vulval swelling loses her

The pre-eclampsia set — asked at two minutes, not five — Headaches · visual change, blurring, flashing lights, spots or floaters · dizziness · pain under the ribs on the right · nausea or vomiting · chest pain or breathlessness · passing less urine. Running out of time before you get here is the trap, and every recall of a failed attempt at this station has the same cause

Clotting, then the four organ failures — Clotting: calf pain or tenderness, long travel or bed rest, recent surgery, personal or family clot history, cough or haemoptysis · heart: exertional breathlessness, chest pain, orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea · kidney: reduced urine, known kidney problem · liver: jaundice, itching, dark urine, pale stools · thyroid: cold intolerance

Clarify 'I sleep propped up' — 'Is that because you can't breathe lying flat, or because of the reflux?' → the reflux and the bump. Accepting it as orthopnoea without asking is the trap — at term, a splinted diaphragm and reflux both do this, and saying so out loud is what shows you know

The obstetric history — short, but never skipped — Booking bloods, dating scan, screening, THE 18 TO 20 WEEK SCAN WITH BABY AND PLACENTA, the glucose tolerance test, THE GBS SWAB AT 35 TO 37 WEEKS · THE TWO THAT ALWAYS SCORE: 'IS THE BABY KICKING AS MUCH AS USUAL?' AND 'ANY BLEEDING OR LEAKING OF FLUID?' · AND THE PREVIOUS PREGNANCIES INCLUDING ANY HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE OR PRE-ECLAMPSIA. 'Uncomplicated' in the stem gives you permission to be quick, NOT PERMISSION TO OMIT

The clonus challenge — the answer that passes this station — 'THERE IS NO DIPSTICK AVAILABLE. AND SHE HAS CLONUS. DOES THAT NOT CONCERN YOU?' → 'CLONUS IS ONLY A SIGN OF CORTICAL IRRITABILITY WHEN IT IS SUSTAINED — MORE THAN THREE BEATS. ONE OR TWO BEATS OCCURS IN NORMAL PEOPLE AND IN NORMAL PREGNANCY. With a normal blood pressure and no neurological, hepatic or renal symptoms, I CAN EXCLUDE PRE-ECLAMPSIA CLINICALLY WITHOUT THE DIPSTICK — although I would still do one today, because it is free and it is part of every antenatal visit'

One mechanism, four findings — 'Towards the end of pregnancy the womb and the baby become very large and heavy, and they press back on the big blood tubes at the back of your tummy. The blood coming up from your legs has to work harder to get past, so the pressure backs up and pushes fluid out into the tissues. That one thing explains all four of your problems — the legs, the swelling down below, the veins on your calves, and the piles. And it's why it's worse by evening and better in the morning: gravity.' Explaining them as four separate problems is the trap

The pushback, the differential in twenty seconds, and what not to prescribe — 'Normal? Look at my legs!' → 'I'm not saying nothing is wrong — I'm saying nothing is dangerous' · then seven differentials, one clause each: pre-eclampsia excluded on a normal blood pressure and no symptoms · kidney · heart · liver including a pregnancy-specific liver condition · underactive thyroid · a clot in the leg · and cellulitis · then practical help: left lateral rest, feet up, avoid prolonged standing, graduated compression stockings, normal fluids, and do not cut salt — and deliberately no diuretic, because they reduce blood supply to the baby

Request the card by naming findings, not regions — Blood pressure repeated after rest, pulse, temperature · is the oedema pitting, symmetrical, and how far does it extend · is either calf tender or asymmetrical · varicose veins, vulval swelling, haemorrhoids · 'Is there ankle clonus, and how many beats?' · SFH, lie, presentation, fetal heart rate · and a urine dipstick for protein. Asking for the number of beats is what shows you know the threshold exists

time: Two minutes to open, welcome the wish and dig through three layers for the agenda · two minutes of focused obstetric and home history · three and a half minutes of counselling in four boxes — acknowledge, your two concerns, pros and cons with 'Too early', then the patient-centred close · and thirty seconds of next steps.

back.dx: A REQUEST FOR HOME BIRTH THAT IS NOT LOW RISK — two previous retained placentas and a postpartum haemorrhage, in a woman 40 minutes from a level 2 service that is itself 400 km from the tertiary centre. The numbers and rules: she is 25 and 20 weeks, with four minutes for the history · the final plan is made at 36 weeks, with a third-trimester hospital visit and a 36-week home visit · eligibility is a single, cephalic, term pregnancy at 37 to 42 weeks with no previous caesarean, no uterine surgery and no previous complications · attendants are two ahpra-registered midwives · transfer triggers are a request for pain relief, slow progress, or concern for mother or baby · and active management of the third stage is oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly VERIFY. Supports: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS for country travel · TIS 131 450 · healthdirect 1800 022 222. The older recall version changes the agenda to a previous caesarean and a miscarriage, with bad treatment by hospital staff — and the discriminating line changes with it: 'After a caesarean, the scar on the womb needs to be watched closely in labour, with continuous monitoring of the baby, and if there is any sign it is giving way we need a theatre within minutes. That is the one thing that can't be done at home — and it is why the home-birth programs can't take women with a previous caesarean.' The offer that follows matters as much as the refusal: 'What we can do is plan a vaginal birth after caesarean in a hospital, with the same things you want — your family, your music, minimal intervention — and a team who explain everything this time.' Two other variants. A low placenta on today's report → 'A low-lying placenta at 20 weeks often moves up as the womb grows, so we repeat the scan at around 32 weeks. If it is still covering the opening at term, the baby can only be born safely by caesarean, and home is off the table for that reason alone. Let's wait for that scan before we decide anything.' and the unsafe home — 'Dan drinks a bit, we've only got the one car and he's usually out' → 'I'm glad you told me. For a home birth we need someone sober who can drive you at three in the morning, a phone that works, and a house that is calm and safe. From what you're describing, that plan isn't safe yet — a birth centre gives you the same feel with all of that taken care of. And if things at home are ever frightening, I want you to tell me.' What the examiner is assessing, stated plainly: whether you find the agenda behind the candles · whether you take an obstetric history at all, which is the most commonly missed component · whether you name her two specific risks in plain language · whether you give a genuine patient-centred answer rather than a verdict either way · and whether you know who is eligible and what a transfer plan is.
plan: Open, let her give the whole list, and answer it with warmth and an offer to support her decision.
Layer one and two — why home, and any concerns about the delivery itself.
Layer three — bad experiences with previous births — then acknowledge it properly before asking anything else.
THE CURRENT PREGNANCY — bloods, scans, screening, THE PLACENTA POSITION ON THE 20-WEEK SCAN, and fetal movements.
PREVIOUS PREGNANCIES — how many, mode of birth, problems during them — AND THEN PROBLEMS WITH THE BIRTH ITSELF, THE PLACENTA, AND BLEEDING AFTERWARDS.
TRANSFUSION AND THEATRE · medical problems, medicines and allergies.
THE HOME — who she lives with, SUPPORT, stress, coping, DISTANCE, CAR AND PHONE RECEPTION — then ask permission to share your thinking.
Box one — full support and a strong acknowledgement of what she went through.
Box two — concern one, the placenta again · and concern two, the rural service and the 400 km — said back from the stem.
Answer 'I want it to come by itself' without arguing twice.
Box three — the genuine pros, the honest cons, and 'Too early, we plan at 36 weeks'.
Box four — eligibility criteria, the transfer plan, the birth centre alternative, and the offer to introduce a midwife.
Reading material, a second meeting with her partner, and close on 'It is your decision and I'll support you'.

ask: The three layers: 'Can I ask why you've decided to deliver at home?' · 'Do you have any concerns or worries about the delivery itself?' · 'Have you had any bad experiences with previous births?'

The obstetric question that finds the case: 'Any problems with the birth itself — bleeding afterwards, trouble with the placenta?' and the one people never ask: 'Can you describe your home situation for me?'

The two concerns, named as two: 'There is a higher chance we will face difficulty delivering the placenta this time.' and 'The services here might be insufficient to deal with a severe bleed — we may not be able to do an urgent operation.'

The honest pros: 'Lower risk of tears, less use of instruments, lower chance of an urgent caesarean; risk to the baby is the same.' and the close: 'Whatever you decide, it's your decision and I'll support you.'

CHALLENGES: 'I just want to, doctor' to the first why · 'THAT'S WHY I WANT IT TO COME BY ITSELF' · 'WELL, IT WASN'T GENTLE LAST TIME' · 'SO YOU'RE SAYING I CAN'T' → which is never answered with a verdict · 'I KNOW ALL THAT' to the pros and cons · 'I'VE NEVER HEARD OF A BIRTH CENTRE — IS IT LIKE A HOSPITAL?' · and 'ONE MIDWIFE… MAYBE. NOT A DOCTOR.'
pefe: There is no examination and no data in the stem — everything you know, you ask for. The two pieces that decide the counselling are her obstetric history and her geography, and the second is handed to you in the stem: a level 2 maternity service 400 km from the tertiary centre. Saying that number back to her is a marked item.

Role-player: KAREN, 25, THIRD PREGNANCY AT 20 WEEKS, with two children aged 4 and 2 BOTH BORN VAGINALLY AT THIS RURAL HOSPITAL. BOTH TIMES THE PLACENTA WOULD NOT COME AND WAS PULLED OUT; AFTER THE SECOND SHE BLED HEAVILY AND WAS GIVEN BLOOD. SHE FELT HANDLED ROUGHLY, NOBODY EXPLAINED ANYTHING, AND SHE WAS TERRIFIED. She lives on a property 40 MINUTES FROM TOWN with her partner Dan, who is supportive and WAS THERE BOTH TIMES. No medical problems; scans and bloods normal with a normally sited placenta.

How she plays it: bright and determined at first, refusing each suggestion once — 'No doctors', 'Not the hospital', 'It comes by itself'. She softens only if the doctor is warm, apologises for her experience, and does not argue. She volunteers the placenta story only if asked about previous births or bad experiences — and if not asked by 3:30 she says 'You haven't asked me why I don't want doctors.' if told she can't or must go to hospital she shuts down: 'Then we're done here.'

The scoring sheet: welcomed the wish before anything else · asked why, concerns and bad experience, and found the placenta story · took current and previous pregnancy history including problems after the birth · asked about the home · acknowledged strongly · named concern one and concern two including the 400 km and the absence of urgent surgery · gave pros and cons · said it is too early and the plan is made at 36 weeks · offered reading, a second meeting, a midwife or obstetrician, a birth centre and a transfer plan · never said 'You can't' or 'Go ahead' · and never argued a point twice.

Welcome the wish before anything else — Her list: home, the whole family there, music, candles, no doctors, no midwives, and the placenta to come out by itself · your first response: 'That's a really exciting decision, Karen. I want you to know I'm here to support you to make the best decision about your birth. Is it ok if I ask you a few questions so I understand what matters to you?' Responding to the wish with a concern is the trap — she softens only to warmth

Three layers to break the agenda — One: 'Can I ask why you've decided to deliver at home?' → 'I just want to, doctor' — designed to be deflected · two: 'Do you have any concerns or worries about the delivery itself?' → 'I just don't want to be in a hospital' · three: 'Have you had any bad experiences with previous births — with the hospital, or with doctors or midwives?' → 'Yes. I had problems in my previous pregnancies. That's why I don't want any doctors or midwives involved.' Stopping at 'I just want to' is the trap. If you have not asked by 3:30 she says 'You haven't asked me why I don't want doctors'

Acknowledge properly before moving on — 'I'M SO SORRY TO HEAR THAT. I CAN IMAGINE HOW DIFFICULT THAT EXPERIENCE MUST HAVE BEEN.' The source is explicit that the acknowledgement here should be STRONGER THAN USUAL, because she has a real reason

The previous-pregnancy block that finds the story — How many, vaginal or caesarean, problems during the pregnancies — then the question that matters: 'Any problems with the birth itself — a long labour, instruments, bleeding afterwards, any trouble with the placenta?' → 'Both times they had trouble getting the placenta out — they had to pull it out. After the last one I had a massive bleed. They said it was a postpartum haemorrhage. That's why I want it to come out by itself this time — nobody pulling' · then did you need a blood transfusion, did they take you to theatre → blood the second time

Do not let the retained placenta make you directive — Taking it as a reason to abandon the counselling and start instructing her is the trap. IT IS THE REASON TO COUNSEL WELL — and if you say 'you can't' or 'you must go to hospital' SHE SHUTS DOWN WITH 'THEN WE'RE DONE HERE'

The current pregnancy, and then the home — Booking bloods, dating scan, screening, the 18 to 20 week scan especially the position of the placenta, fetal movements · then: 'Because you're planning to give birth at home — can you describe your home situation for me? Who do you live with? Are they supportive? Any stress at home? How are you coping? How far is the nearest hospital, and do you have a reliable car and phone reception?' → a property 40 minutes out, a ute, and patchy reception in the back paddock

Box one — acknowledge and support — 'Karen, first of all I want to tell you that I FULLY SUPPORT YOUR DECISION, and I understand how difficult your previous births have been — AND HOW THAT HAS MADE THIS A BAD EXPERIENCE FOR YOU. I'd like to talk a bit more about home birth, SO YOU CAN MAKE AN INFORMED DECISION based on the pros and cons'

Box two — your two concerns, named early — 'Overall, I have two main concerns in your case. Concern one: because you've had difficulty delivering the placenta twice, there is a higher chance we will face difficulty delivering the placenta this time. Concern two: you live in a rural area, and the services at our hospital might be insufficient to deal with complications such as a severe bleed or a stuck placenta. We may not be able to do an urgent operation here — we are 400 kilometres from the tertiary centre.' Leaving concern two to the last minute, or never linking it to the stem, is the trap — the 400 km is in the stem so that you say it back

Answering 'I want it to come by itself' — 'We usually expect the placenta to deliver by itself. If it doesn't, we can gently pull on the cord to remove it. Sometimes that can cause bleeding and other complications — and I think that is what happened to you.' She answers 'Well, it wasn't gentle last time', and the answer is not to argue it twice

Box three — pros and cons, then 'Too early' — The pros, given honestly: lower risk of tears, less use of instruments, a lower chance of needing an urgent caesarean, and the risk to the baby is the same as in hospital · the cons: transfer may be challenging — someone has to drive her, at whatever hour, on whatever road — and some pain relief such as an epidural is not available at home · then: 'You are 20 weeks and it is a little early to finalise plans — we usually make the delivery plan around 36 weeks'

Box four — eligibility, transfer plan, and the alternative — Who is eligible: a single pregnancy, no previous caesarean or uterine surgery, and the baby head down close to the birth · and a transfer plan — who drives, and how long it takes · then the alternative that keeps what she wants: 'A birth centre or birthing suite close to the tertiary hospital. They are very similar to home — your family can be there, you can have your music — but help is minutes away' · and the midwives: 'We usually do these births with two midwives. I know you've had bad experiences; if you like, I can introduce you to a midwife, you can hear them out, and then decide'

The last sentence — 'Whatever you decide, it is your decision, and I'll support you. Let's book the next visit' — with reading material and a second meeting with her partner and family. Ending with 'So I really think you should…' is the trap, and the scoring sheet says explicitly: never said 'You can't' or 'Go ahead' — the decision stayed mine, and never argued a point twice

Did they take you to theatre to remove it?'; and ask the whole block, because the history is what licenses the counselling — how many pregnancies, vaginal or caesarean, any problems DURING them, then the birth itself; plus the CURRENT pregnancy (booking bloods, dating scan, screening, the 20-week scan and specifically the PLACENTAL POSITION, fetal movements) and the HOME (who she lives with, whether they are supportive, stress at home, how she is coping, and the distance, the car and the phone reception)

FAIL — Leaving the RURAL concern to the last minute or never linking it to the stem — the 400 km is written there so that you SAY IT BACK, and concern two is 'you live in a rural area, and the services at our hospital might be insufficient to deal with complications such as a severe bleed or a stuck placenta; we may not be able to do an urgent operation here — we are 400 kilometres from the tertiary centre'; concern one comes first and is specific to her: 'because you've had difficulty delivering the placenta twice, there is a HIGHER CHANCE we will face difficulty delivering the placenta this time' — and when she says 'that's why I want it to come by itself', the reply is 'we usually expect the placenta to deliver by itself; if it doesn't, we can gently pull on the cord to remove it, and sometimes that can cause bleeding and other complications — I think that is what happened to you' (★)

DO — Give the PROS honestly before the cons, because a balanced answer is what makes the counselling credible: at home there is a LOWER risk of tears, LESS use of instruments, a LOWER chance of an urgent caesarean, and the RISK TO THE BABY IS THE SAME as in hospital; the cons are that transferring in a complication may be challenging — someone has to drive her, at whatever hour, on whatever road — and that some pain relief such as an epidural is not available; then the pressure-release line that buys the decision time: 'you are 20 weeks and it is a little early to finalise plans — we usually make the delivery plan around 36 WEEKS', with the complications that would change it named (a low-lying placenta, a breech baby, an abnormal fetal heart rate); close with reading material, a second meeting WITH HER PARTNER, an offer to involve an obstetrician or midwife, the ELIGIBILITY criteria stated plainly (a single baby, head down near the birth, no previous caesarean or uterine surgery, term 37 to 42 weeks, with TWO AHPRA-registered midwives), a TRANSFER PLAN (who drives, and how long it takes), and the safer alternative offered rather than imposed — a BIRTH CENTRE close to the tertiary hospital, 'very similar to home: your family can be there, you can have your music, but help is minutes away'; never argue a point twice, and never end with 'so I really think you should'; variants — VERSION B substitutes a PREVIOUS CAESAREAN, which is an absolute exclusion because the scar needs continuous monitoring in labour and a theatre within minutes, so the offer becomes a VBAC in hospital with the same things she wants; a LOW-LYING placenta at 20 weeks often resolves, so repeat the scan at about 32 weeks before deciding anything; and an UNSAFE HOME — a partner who drinks, one car, patchy reception — is named gently as a reason the plan is not safe YET, with the door left open ('if things at home are ever frightening, I want you to tell me')

setting: 'Are you compliant?' Gets 'Yes'. The role-player answers the question asked, and the trigger is only released by the words 'Has he missed any doses recently, even one?' The other two things this station is built on: a full abdominal examination despite an obvious diagnosis, and a dipstick where you say 'Glucose and ketones' — because the examiner asks what you are looking for and gives only what you name.
stem: Emergency department, Wallaroo hospital, Yorke Peninsula (MM5). Nearest paediatric ICU is the women's and children's in Adelaide, about 160 km, with retrieval via MedSTAR kids. Liam, a 4-year-old boy, is brought in by his father mark with two days of vomiting and diarrhoea. He is a known type 1 diabetic diagnosed 18 months ago, on insulin.

Triage observations are stable and do not need repeating: HR 112, RR 26, BP 96/58, temp 37.4, SpO2 99% on air, weight 16 kg. Tasks: take a focused history from the father, about 4 minutes — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings, given only if you ask specifically, about 2 minutes — explain the most likely diagnosis and your reasons to the father, about 2 minutes.

time: Twenty seconds to open, using the observations you have already been given rather than repeating them · then vomiting and diarrhoea · then the four diabetes questions with missed doses asked in words, plus polyuria and polydipsia · then the GI differentials and the gastroenteritis screen · then DKA symptoms, well-child questions and triggers · then the infection box · then a full examination request including the abdomen and groin · then three layers, reasons, the trigger without blame, and differentials anyway.
findings: The two bedside tests, and the trick inside them

'A finger-prick blood glucose and a urine dipstick' → glucose 18, and then the examiner asks 'What are you looking for on the dipstick?' → 'Glucose and ketones' → glucose 4+, ketones 3+, and blood ketones 4.2 if you ask. Listing blood, protein, leucocytes and nitrites — everything except ketones — is the trap

Alert but tired · pink, no rash · breathing slightly deep · dry lips, capillary refill two seconds, eyes not sunken · throat mildly red, ears normal, no neck stiffness · chest clear · abdomen soft with mild generalised tenderness, no guarding, no masses, normal bowel sounds · no hernia

back.dx: Diabetic ketoacidosis in a 4-year-old with established type 1 diabetes, triggered by two missed insulin doses with an intercurrent gastroenteritis — and the station is decided by the wording of the compliance question, a full abdomen despite an obvious diagnosis, and naming ketones on the dipstick. The numbers: bedside glucose 18 to 19 · dipstick glucose 4+ and ketones 3+, with blood ketones 4.2 · DKA is glucose over 11 plus ketones 3 or more plus a pH under 7.3 or bicarbonate under 15 · severity is pH under 7.3 mild, under 7.2 moderate, under 7.1 severe · fluids are 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline only if shocked, with the deficit replaced over 48 hours and potassium at 40 mmol/L · insulin is 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h started an hour after fluids, with no bolus · cerebral oedema occurs 4 to 12 hours in · and MedSTAR kids is 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the women's and children's VERIFY all. If the examiner asks for immediate management: 'IV access; venous gas, glucose, blood ketones, electrolytes and full blood count; weigh him; call the paediatric team and MedSTAR kids. If he is shocked, 0.9% saline 10 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes; otherwise rehydrate over 48 hours with potassium added once I have a level; insulin infusion 0.05 to 0.1 units per kilo per hour starting an hour after fluids, no bolus; hourly glucose and neuro observations for cerebral oedema.' The variants. Version B hides the diabetes — the stem says only vomiting and diarrhoea, and it appears in past history if you ask: 'Does Liam have any medical conditions, or take any regular medicines?' → 'He's diabetic — on insulin' → and you pivot: 'That's very important, so let me ask about it properly' and run all four questions plus polyuria and polydipsia. The drowsy-child version — 'He's really sleepy, I can hardly wake him' → severity moves the examination to the front: 'I'm going to examine him straight away and ask the nurse to call the paediatric team and MedSTAR kids now. Examiner: consciousness, breathing pattern, capillary refill, blood glucose and ketones first' — and the explanation shortens to one line: DKA, serious, retrieval. If the examiner challenges the abdomen — 'Vitals are stable and you know it's DKA, do you really need it?' → 'Yes. Vomiting with abdominal pain in a child can be appendicitis, intussusception or a strangulated hernia, and DKA can mask or mimic them — so a full abdominal examination and the groin, and I'd re-examine after treatment starts.' and if the father asks to go home — 'I understand; hospital with a small child is hard. But his blood is acidic and he can't keep fluids down; giving insulin at home now, without fluids and monitoring, can be dangerous. He needs the drip today. I'll arrange PATS if he's transferred to Adelaide.' and the close that is worth the last ten seconds: sick-day rules discussed once he is better, not while his father is frightened.
plan: Open in twenty seconds — use the triage observations rather than repeating them, say they are reassuring, and ask what has been happening.
VOMITING — onset, frequency, worsening, COLOUR INCLUDING GREEN AND BLOOD, forceful, AND WHETHER HE IS KEEPING FLUIDS DOWN.
DIARRHOEA BRIEFLY — days, frequency, watery, BLOOD OR MUCUS, amount.
The four diabetes questions — with missed doses asked in words — then polyuria and polydipsia.
ABDOMINAL PAIN, THEN THE SURGICAL SCREEN — screaming in bouts, distension, GROIN LUMP, RED JELLY STOOL.
THE GASTROENTERITIS SCREEN — food reactions, SICK CONTACTS, travel, new foods, tank water.
Well-child and triggers — alert versus drowsy, diet change and sweets, deep or fast breathing, headache, new medicines including steroids.
THE INFECTION BOX AND THE CLOSE — fever, ENT, ear pain, URINE, rash, recent vaccination · allergies, immunisations, birth and development, FAMILY HISTORY, who is at home.
THE EXAMINATION REQUEST — consciousness, colour, BREATHING PATTERN, hydration, ENT and neck, chest.
The full abdomen and the groin — inspection, palpation for tenderness guarding rigidity and masses, auscultation, and a hernia check.
The two bedside tests, and say 'Glucose and ketones' when asked what you are looking for.
The three-layer explanation, then the five reasons.

Name the trigger without blame, answer 'Is this my fault?', give the differentials anyway, and state the disposition — hospital today, fluids and insulin by drip, and a call to the Adelaide specialists.

ask: The wording that unlocks the case: 'Are you giving it as instructed — and has he missed any doses, even one?' not 'Are you compliant?'

The two active-symptom questions: 'More thirsty than usual? Passing more urine, wetting the bed?' and the one that is both feature and differential: 'Has he complained of tummy pain — where, constant or in waves?'

The examination lines: 'A full abdominal examination — inspection, palpation for tenderness, guarding, rigidity, masses; auscultation; the groin.' and 'A finger-prick blood glucose and a urine dipstick — glucose and ketones.'

The explanation spine: 'DKA — a complication of the diabetes he already has.' · 'Not enough insulin — sugar builds up — the body burns fat and makes ketones — ketones make the blood acidic.' · and 'Easy to do — the point is what we do now.'

CHALLENGES: 'SO THIS IS MY FAULT?' when the trigger is named · 'CAN WE JUST GO HOME WITH FLUIDS AND I'LL GIVE HIS INSULIN TONIGHT?' · the examiner on whether the abdomen is really needed · 'WHAT IS YOUR IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT?' · and the drowsy-child version, where the examination moves to the front.
pefe: The examiner gives a finding only if you ask for it specifically, and the dipstick is a trap inside a trap: ask for one and you are asked what you are looking for, and you receive only what you name. Say glucose and ketones. The other deliberate omission is the abdomen — cutting it to 'Soft' because the diagnosis is obvious is exactly what the case is testing.

Role-player: mark, 34, a grain farmer near Wallaroo. Liam, 4, is his eldest, with type 1 diabetes diagnosed 18 months ago on twice-daily long- and short-acting insulin, reviewed every three months by the WCH diabetes team. They were camping at the weekend, ran out of insulin, and he missed the last two doses; his cousin had a vomiting bug there.

How he plays it: worried and guilty about the insulin. He says 'We're always careful' and only admits the missed doses if asked directly about missed doses. He answers only what is asked, in short answers. He raises 'So this is my fault?' when the trigger is named, pushes once for going home with fluids, and becomes quiet and looks at the floor if blamed. If the doctor is doing well but has not asked by 3:30 he says 'His tummy's been sore too.'

THE CHECKLIST: open question with NO VITALS REPEAT · vomiting explored · diarrhoea explored briefly · WHEN DIAGNOSED · TREATMENT · MISSED DOSES ASKED SPECIFICALLY · follow-up and complications · POLYURIA AND POLYDIPSIA · ABDOMINAL PAIN · hernia, intussusception and allergy questions · gastroenteritis contacts and travel · ALERT VERSUS DROWSY · diet change · STEROIDS AND NEW MEDICINES · fever, ENT, urinary symptoms, rash · past history, allergies, immunisations and family history · EXAMINATION COVERING CONSCIOUSNESS, HYDRATION, TEMPERATURE, ENT, CHEST, A FULL ABDOMEN AND THE GROIN · BLOOD GLUCOSE ASKED · DIPSTICK WITH 'GLUCOSE AND KETONES' NAMED · DKA NAMED AS A COMPLICATION OF EXISTING DIABETES · THREE-LAYER EXPLANATION WITHOUT A LECTURE · REASONS LISTED · TRIGGER NAMED WITHOUT BLAME · DIFFERENTIALS STATED · AND HOSPITAL TODAY WITH SPECIALIST INVOLVEMENT.

The question that releases the trigger — 'Are you giving it as instructed — and has he missed any doses recently, even one?' → 'We're always careful…' and then, only if missed doses are asked about directly: 'We were camping on the weekend and ran out. He missed the last two doses.' Asking 'Are you compliant?' Gets 'Yes' and nothing else

The four diabetes questions, plus the active symptoms — When was he diagnosed — 18 months ago · what treatment, which insulin, how given — twice daily long-acting and short · given as instructed and any missed doses · regular follow-up and previous complications or admissions — WCH every three months, never admitted · then: 'More thirsty, drinking a lot? Passing more urine, wetting the bed?' → drinking heaps and wet the bed twice, which he never does

The vomiting and diarrhoea, briefly — VOMITING: onset, frequency, GETTING WORSE, COLOUR AND ANY GREEN OR BLOOD, FORCEFUL, after food, KEEPING FLUIDS DOWN → two days, four or five a day, worse today, NO GREEN OR BLOOD, not keeping much down · DIARRHOEA: days, frequency, WATERY, BLOOD OR MUCUS, large amounts → since yesterday, three or four watery, nothing abnormal. Chronic-diarrhoea questions on a two-day history waste time

The abdominal pain question — both a DKA feature and the surgical differential — 'Has he complained of tummy pain? Where — constant or in waves?' → all over, sort of constant · then irritable or screaming in bouts, tummy swollen, any lump in the groin, any red jelly-like stool. Forgetting abdominal pain entirely is the trap — and if you are doing well but have not asked by 3:30, the father says 'His tummy's been sore too'

The gastroenteritis screen and the food questions — Any rash around the mouth or reaction after certain foods · anyone at home or kindy with the same → his cousin had a vomiting bug at the campsite · any travel, new foods, tank water. The cousin is a second trigger, not a reason to stop

WHEN THERE ISN'T ENOUGH INSULIN, SUGAR CAN'T GET INTO THE CELLS AND BUILDS UP IN THE BLOOD; THE BODY SWITCHES TO BURNING FAT, WHICH MAKES A WASTE CHEMICAL CALLED KETONES; AND KETONES MAKE THE BLOOD ACIDIC. That's what's causing the vomiting, the tummy pain, the thirst and the tiredness.' A pancreas lecture, or naming only one layer, is the trap

And when she pushes back in version A — 'Can't we just do the Hydralyte thing at home? That's what they did with his sister' → 'For his sister, who was alert and drinking, that was right. Liam is drowsy and not keeping fluids in, and at this level a baby can get worse very quickly.' The variants. The ED setting → 'Supervised oral rehydration now: ondansetron, then 5 mL of ORS every minute by syringe with the nurses recording it; if he is not tolerating that within an hour we move to a nasogastric tube at 50 mL/kg over four hours; I'd check a glucose and electrolytes, and if he is shocked at any point, a 20 mL/kg bolus of normal saline. Reassess and REWEIGH at four hours.' The unvaccinated version — 'He hasn't had any vaccinations' → 'Thank you for telling me. Unvaccinated babies can get more severe rotavirus gastro, which fits with today. Once he's better I'd like to talk about catch-up immunisation — the rotavirus drops have an age limit, so we'll check what's still possible. Is there something that's held you back that I can help with?' Do not lecture: note it, link it to severity, and offer the conversation later — judgement here is an approach-to-patient mark. And her hidden agenda is guilt — she believes she gave him the bug by not washing her hands after looking after his sister, and she mentions it only if asked how she is coping, or at the end. back.dx: TESTICULAR TORSION IN A 13-YEAR-OLD PRESENTING AS GROIN PAIN — twisting of the spermatic cord on its axis, cutting venous then arterial supply, with a peak incidence at 12 to 18 years and a second peak in neonates, affecting about 1 in 4,000 males under 25. The bell-clapper deformity, where the tunica vaginalis completely surrounds the testis, predisposes to it and is usually bilateral — which is why both sides are fixed at surgery. Pain is often felt in the groin or lower abdomen, and the AMC gives 'Groin' deliberately. The numbers: onset two hours ago against a window of about six · salvage about 90% under 6 hours and under 10% beyond 24 · an absent cremasteric reflex is the most useful sign but is preserved in 10 to 30% of torsions, so it does not exclude · Doppler sensitivity is about 85 to 95% · intranasal fentanyl 1.5 mcg/kg to a maximum of 100 mcg, or IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg · manual detorsion is 'Open book', medial to lateral · consent covers orchidopexy plus or minus orchidectomy with contralateral fixation · and MedSTAR is 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the women's and children's VERIFY all. The red flags in any groin-pain history: sudden severe pain in a teenager with nausea or vomiting · onset with exertion, sleep or cold · previous brief episodes that resolved, which is intermittent torsion · pain that has improved after hours, which may be infarction rather than recovery · and any groin pain in a boy where the scrotum has not been examined. Version B is the harder one: ten hours of lower abdominal and groin pain that woke him at 3 am, two vomits, and previous self-limiting episodes months ago — intermittent torsion — with an embarrassed adolescent minimising in front of his father. The opening that works: 'I can see this is uncomfortable to talk about, and I'll keep it quick. Sometimes a problem with the testicle is felt in the tummy — so I need to ask: is there any pain or swelling in the testicles or scrotum? And has this ever happened before, even for a few minutes, and then gone away?' → 'Yeah. It's the right one. It happened twice before, a few months ago — it went away after about half an hour, so I didn't say anything.' The harder explanation: 'It sounds like it has twisted briefly before and untwisted itself. This time it hasn't. Because it's been about ten hours, the chance of saving it is lower than it would have been at two hours, but not zero, and the only way to know is for the surgeon to look. Even if it can't be saved, the other one will be stitched so it can never twist, and one testicle is enough. You did nothing wrong by not mentioning the earlier episodes — but from now on, pain there is something to tell someone straight away.' The examination card in that version adds scrotal oedema and erythema with a reactive hydrocele, and a horizontal lie on the left too — the bell-clapper. And the investigation principle does not change: surgery now, a Doppler only if the surgeon wants it and it does not delay theatre, bloods for the anaesthetist on the way.

Mark, the father, 44, an electrician, is worried, assumes a pulled muscle, asks 'An operation tonight?' and 'Can't you scan it first?', and steps out if asked politely. Three weeks sits between acute, which is under 14 days, and chronic, which is usually over four weeks — so both acute and chronic causes stay on the list. The management, if asked, is six numbered items: juice, cordial and soft drink down to less than half a cup a day or none, with water to drink · whole fruit instead · a bit more fat — full-cream milk and yoghurt, cheese, avocado — and restart the dairy, since it was not the milk · total drinks to about a litre a day · a barrier cream for his bottom · and review in two weeks with a note of how many motions a day, coming sooner for blood, night-time motions, stopping eating or drinking, or seeming unwell. Difficile is treated with oral vancomycin and not tested under 12 months VERIFY all. Version B adds a recent antibiotic course, and the examiner is checking that the differential list did not change and that both findings were used: 'Two things are contributing. He's finished the course, he's well, there's no blood or fever, so I'd expect it to settle with the juice change. If it doesn't, or if blood or fever appear, we'll send a stool sample for that bug and treat it if it's there.' Omitting the antibiotic when the mother has handed it to you is a missed finding — and so is dropping the juice because the antibiotic is 'More medical'. If the mother asks for a CT — 'I understand wanting certainty. A CT wouldn't add anything here — there are no features pointing to a structural problem, and it carries radiation. And the sentence that decides whether she accepts the diagnosis is not the mechanism but the one before it: 'The pain is real — she is not making it up.' The normality is the evidence, and it only counts if you asked for the right things.

Role-player: Karen, 38, a primary-school teacher. Ellie is 8, in year 3, with a brother Tom aged 5 and a farmer father Dan. Six months of pain — all over, dull, 4 to 5 out of ten, on and off, never at night, never worsening, nothing helps. About 20 days of school missed, some mornings she will not get out of bed, and weekends are better — which Karen only notices when asked.

How she plays it: frustrated and brisk at the start, softening when the doctor examines carefully and says the pain is real, and tearful when her mother is mentioned. Two doctors have said 'Probably stress' and she felt they were calling her daughter a liar — so if the doctor says 'Just stress' without explanation she asks 'That's what the others said — so she's making it up?'

She volunteers the grandmother only if asked openly about recent stress — and in version B, if asked 'Has her grandmother died?', she says 'No — why would you ask that?' Her hidden agenda is a fear of leukaemia after a colleague's child, raised only if invited, plus guilt that her own grief has made her less available to Ellie. The child is in the room, and speaking to her — 'Ellie, you're not making it up' — is part of the explanation.

The open stress question — and the recall question that fails — 'Has there been any stress in the family in the last six months or so — illness, a death, a move, separation?' → a pause, then the grandmother. Asking 'Has her grandmother died?' Fails version B outright — 'No, why would you ask that?' — and reveals the recall in version A. Ask it by 3:15, because the psychosocial screen is what runs out of time

The two timing questions that discriminate — 'DOES IT EVER WAKE HER FROM SLEEP?' → NEVER — SHE SLEEPS FINE · 'DOES SHE GET IT ON WEEKENDS AND HOLIDAYS AS MUCH AS SCHOOL DAYS?' → '…NOW YOU MENTION IT, WEEKENDS ARE BETTER.' Both must be asked by name — she does not notice the weekend pattern until asked

The pain and its functional impact — 'Can she point with one finger, or is it all over?' → all over, sometimes here, sometimes there · 4 or 5 out of ten · dull · on and off for six months and not worsening · no radiation · nothing makes it better or worse, including food, dairy, position and opening her bowels · and the impact: about twenty days of school missed, some mornings she will not get out of bed, and she has stopped netball

The red-flag block, asked as a block — 'Some quick important questions' — weight loss or stopped growing · blood in her poo · vomiting, any green · persistent diarrhoea · fever · pain or difficulty swallowing · mouth ulcers, rashes, sore joints or limping, red eyes · pale, bruising easily, lumps in the neck or tummy, unusually tired · pain passing urine. All negative — and that is the point

Ask constipation properly — How often does she open her bowels, are they hard, does she strain, any soiling → daily, normal, no straining, no soiling. 'Bowels okay?' Misses the commonest organic cause of chronic abdominal pain in a child

The rest of the GI group, by name — Bloating and wind · travel or sick contacts · greasy stools that float or stick · anyone in the family with coeliac disease, Crohn's or colitis, or stomach ulcers · any lump in the groin · heartburn, or pain when hungry or after meals · and does dairy or any food set it off, with any rash around the mouth

Home, school and mood — 'I'd like to ask about things outside her tummy, because they matter for tummy pain in children' · how are things at home, who lives with her, how does she get on with everyone · then the stress question · then school — friends, teachers, any bullying · does she seem worried, sad or tearful · how is she sleeping → school fine and no bullying, but clingier, quieter, and broken sleep

What she tells you, and how to receive it — Version B: 'My mum was diagnosed with cancer about six months ago. She's still with us, but she's having chemo. She was very close to her. She cried a lot when we told her, and she's been quieter since' · version A: 'My mum died six months ago. They were very close' · the response: 'Thank you for telling me — I'm sorry about your mum; that's a lot for the whole family, and for her especially. That's very relevant to what's going on, and I'll come back to it'

The diagnosis — name it, and say the pain is real — 'I've examined her carefully and asked about all the warning signs, and I'M CONFIDENT THERE IS NO DISEASE OR STRUCTURAL PROBLEM in her bowel, her stomach or anywhere else. What she has is called NON-ORGANIC ABDOMINAL PAIN — some doctors say functional or stress-related pain. I WANT TO BE VERY CLEAR: THE PAIN IS REAL. SHE IS NOT MAKING IT UP. THE NERVES IN THE GUT AND THE BRAIN ARE CLOSELY CONNECTED, and when a child is under emotional strain THE GUT'S NERVES BECOME OVER-SENSITIVE AND SEND PAIN SIGNALS EVEN THOUGH NOTHING IS DAMAGED' · THEN THE SIX REASONS: PAIN ALL OVER RATHER THAN IN ONE PLACE · NEVER WAKES HER · BETTER ON WEEKENDS · GROWING NORMALLY · EXAMINATION NORMAL · NO WARNING SIGNS · AND IT BEGAN AT THE SAME TIME AS A BIG UPSET IN THE FAMILY

Differentials by group, then the plan — Bowel — a lingering gut infection, constipation, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, ulcers or reflux, a hernia, and food problems like lactose intolerance or allergy · urinary — infection or stones · gynaecological — she has not started her periods, but some girls have pain from a blockage before their first period · musculoskeletal — hip or spine problems referring pain · malignancy — leukaemia or lymphoma, with no pallor, bruising, lumps or weight loss · and abdominal migraine · then the plan: school every day with a letter you write, regular meals, sleep and sport, a chance to talk about her grandmother at home and with the school counsellor, a child psychologist, and review in two weeks

The examination request — say pallor, rash and lymph nodes — General appearance — alert, comfortable, pallor, bruising, rash, mouth ulcers · vitals and growth chart · lymph nodes — cervical, axillary, inguinal · abdomen — distension, masses, tenderness, guarding, faecal loading, liver and spleen, bowel sounds, hernial orifices, perianal inspection · hip and spine screen · urine dipstick and finger-prick glucose. Those three words are the marks that show you looked for leukaemia and IBD, not just a tummy

numbers: Rome IV: episodic or continuous pain at least 4 times a month for at least 2 months, not explained by another condition · prevalence 10 to 15% of school-age children, peaks at 4 to 6 and 7 to 12 years · this case: 6 months, 4 to 5 out of ten, no night pain, about 20 school days missed, 50th centiles tracking

setting: She came about one harmless thing and leaves with two surgical problems and a thyroid test — without panic and without blaming the doctor who did the six-week check. There is no history task, and the examiner will say 'Stick to your task' if you start asking questions. Navel first, because it is what she came for — then the groin hernia, then the testis.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo, Yorke Peninsula (MM5), with the nearest paediatric surgery at the women's and children's in Adelaide about 160 km away. Noah, a 7-month-old boy, is brought in by his mother Jenny, who is worried about a swelling at his belly button. He is well, feeding and growing normally, fully immunised, born at term.

Your examination is already done: a 1.5 cm umbilical hernia, soft, easily reducible, skin normal · a small right inguinal hernia, reducible and non-tender · only the left testis palpable in the scrotum, with the right felt in the groin and not bringable down. This was not picked up at the 6-week check. Tasks, 8 minutes and no history taking: explain the findings and diagnoses in plain language — explain the risks and complications of each — explain your management plan including referral, timing and safety-netting.

time: Twenty seconds to open with one open question and an acknowledgement — not a history · two and a half minutes on the three findings in her order, each as finding, name, one-sentence meaning · ninety seconds on risks — incarceration weighted correctly, then the four testicular risks · then three minutes of management: three timetables, one operation, referral, red flags, the thyroid test, named reading and review · and check understanding last, if there is time.
findings: The four risks of the undescended testis

One, it can be injured in the groin · two, it can twist on itself, which is painful and an emergency · three, the groin is warmer than the scrotum, and a testicle needs to be cool to work properly, so fertility can be affected · four, over a lifetime there is a higher risk of testicular cancer. 'Bringing it down early lowers that risk — not to zero — and it also lets the testicle be checked easily later on.' Naming only fertility, or promising no cancer risk after surgery, is the trap

back.dx: Three diagnoses in one well 7-month-old: a 1.5 cm umbilical hernia, a right indirect inguinal hernia, and a right undescended — canalicular — testis. The definitions that keep the explanation plain: a hernia is a sac of abdominal contents protruding through a weakness in the wall · an umbilical hernia goes through the navel ring and closes spontaneously in most · an infant inguinal hernia is indirect, through a patent processus vaginalis, does not close, and needs surgery · an undescended testis has not reached the scrotum by term and cannot be brought down. The key differentials: a retractile testis can be milked into the scrotum and stays, which is normal and needs no surgery · a hydrocele transilluminates, you cannot get above it, and it usually resolves by 12 to 18 months · an ectopic testis · and bilateral impalpable testes, especially with hypospadias, which is a disorder of sex development and urgent. The numbers: the 6-2 rule is under 6 weeks to 2 days, 6 weeks to 6 months to 2 weeks, and over 6 months within 2 months · orchidopexy at 6 to 12 months and before the first birthday, with descent not expected after about 6 months · the umbilical hernia is observed to 4 years with about 95% closing by 2 to 3, and its 1.5 cm size does not change the plan · four testicular risks, one operation, two weeks to review · and TSH with free T4 VERIFY all. Supports: WCH paediatric surgery, PATS for over 100 km, MedSTAR kids 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450. The variants. Version B, where she is angry and asks whether to complain — 'I understand why you'd ask, and you're entitled to. At six weeks a testicle can be genuinely hard to feel, and some that were in the scrotum move up later, so I honestly can't tell you it was missed. What I can promise is that we're inside the best window now. If you'd like to raise it, I can note your concern and the practice manager can talk it through with you — and I'll make sure today's plan isn't delayed by any of that.' A three-week-old with an inguinal hernia sits in the first band of the rule — 'The surgeons want to fix this within about two days; the younger the baby, the more likely a hernia is to get stuck. I'm phoning the paediatric surgical registrar now.' if she returns at ten days with a hard red groin lump, vomiting and screaming — 'This is the trapped hernia we talked about. I'm not going to push on it. Hospital today: nil by mouth, a drip, pain relief, and MedSTAR kids for retrieval. The surgeons will try to settle it under sedation and repair it within a day or two — or operate straight away if the bowel is at risk.' if neither testis is palpable, or there is hypospadias with an impalpable testis — 'That changes the plan. This needs urgent review today by the children's hormone and surgical teams, and an ultrasound is not the answer': the disorder-of-sex-development pathway, where you do not reassure, do not circumcise, and check for a salt-losing crisis. And if the TSH comes back high — congenital hypothyroidism, very treatable with a daily tablet, seen by paediatric endocrinology that week, and the surgery still goes ahead. Her hidden agenda is that she secretly fears the missed finding means he will be infertile — raised only if you invite concerns, and otherwise at 6:30 as 'So will he be able to have kids?'
plan: Open with one question and one acknowledgement, ask what she was worried it might be, and say the headings you will cover — then take no history.
THE UMBILICAL HERNIA — HER CONCERN FIRST: finding, name, one-sentence meaning, AND THE WORDS 'NOT DANGEROUS'.
THE INGUINAL HERNIA — the canal that should have sealed, AND THAT IT WILL NOT CLOSE BY ITSELF.
THE UNDESCENDED TESTIS — THE DESCENT STORY AND 'STUCK IN THE CANAL' — then the no-blame answer about the six-week check.
Incarceration and strangulation in plain words, with the risk weighted: high for the groin, very rare for the navel.
The four testicular risks — injury, torsion, fertility, cancer — with the risk lowered, not removed.
Soften the cancer word and answer the fertility question before she has to ask it.
The umbilical plan — observe to four, 95% close by two to three, and no tape, coins or strapping.
The 6-2 rule applied to his age, with 'Breathing room, not a wait' — and the 6 to 12 month orchidopexy window.
One operation fixes both, under general anaesthetic, usually day surgery.
Referral to the women's and children's today, with PATS for the travel.
The red flags for the waiting period, given as specific signs.
The thyroid drop and why the heel-prick was only a screen · then RCH fact sheets by name, review in two weeks, and check understanding last.

ask: The three plain-language definitions: 'A hernia is a small sac from inside the tummy poking through a weak spot in the tummy wall.' · 'The inguinal canal is a passage from the tummy to the scrotum that should seal before birth.' · 'The testicles form inside the tummy and travel down that canal near birth; one got stuck.'

The weighting sentence: 'Much more likely with the groin hernia, very rare with the belly-button one — so we treat them differently.' and the four risks in four words: injured, twist, fertility, cancer.

The timing, said as a rule: 'Under six weeks, two days; six weeks to six months, two weeks; over six months, within two months.' and 'Best window for the testicle is six to twelve months — so now, with the hernia, in one operation.'

The no-blame line and the red flags: 'I can't say it was missed; what matters is we've found it in time.' · 'Bigger, hard, red, won't push back, screaming, vomiting, no poo or wind — emergency department.'

Challenges: 'Nobody told me at the six-week check' and 'Should I complain?' · 'Could that happen tonight?' · 'Cancer?! He's a baby' · 'Mum was going to tape a coin on it' · 'Two months seems long if it can get stuck' · 'Will he be put to sleep?' · 'Adelaide? That's a long drive' · 'Thyroid? He had the heel-prick — wasn't it normal?' · and 'So will he be able to have kids?'
pefe: The examination is already done and handed to you in the stem — there is no history task and no examination task, and asking questions earns 'Please stick to your task'. The findings to explain: a 1.5 cm umbilical hernia, soft and easily reducible with normal skin · a small right inguinal hernia, reducible and non-tender · and a right testis palpable in the groin that cannot be brought down.
THE SIZE IS A DISTRACTION: 1.5 cm DOES NOT CHANGE THE UMBILICAL PLAN. WHAT CHANGES MANAGEMENT IS SITE, NOT SIZE — the navel is watched and the groin is operated on, and saying why is the mark.

Role-player: Jenny, 29, a teacher's aide in Wallaroo with a partner working FIFO. Noah, 7 months, is her first baby, born at term, breastfed and thriving. She came about the belly-button lump that pops out when he cries; her mother says it is harmless and to tape a coin over it. She did not know about anything in the groin.

How she plays it: calm at first, with a flash of anger at 'Nobody told me' about the six-week check — settling to a no-blame explanation and escalating to 'Should I complain?' if the other doctor is blamed. She becomes tearful if cancer is mentioned bluntly, pushes once on the two-month timing, and asks about the coin if it is not pre-empted. She expects a named source for the reading material, and her secret fear is infertility, raised at 6:30 if never invited.

Open, then do not take a history — 'What brought you in today?' → THE BELLY-BUTTON LUMP THAT POPS OUT WHEN HE CRIES · 'I understand — a swelling on your baby is stressful. I'VE EXAMINED HIM CAREFULLY AND I'LL EXPLAIN EXACTLY WHAT I FOUND, WHAT IT MEANS, AND WHAT WE'LL DO. IS THERE ANYTHING SPECIFIC YOU WERE WORRIED IT MIGHT BE?' → whether it is dangerous, and whether he needs an operation. SLIDING INTO HISTORY — 'any vomiting? was he premature?' — GETS 'PLEASE STICK TO YOUR TASK'

The navel first, because it is her concern — 'That swelling is an umbilical hernia. A hernia is when a small sac from inside the tummy pokes out through a weak spot in the tummy wall. Here the weak spot is the ring at the belly button, which hasn't fully closed yet. It's very common, it's soft, it goes back in easily and it is not dangerous.' Explaining the groin before the navel is the trap — as is an anatomy lecture on direct versus indirect and the processus vaginalis

'Nobody told me at the six-week check' — 'I can hear that's upsetting. A testicle can be hard to feel at six weeks, and some move up later, so I can't say it was missed. What matters is we've found it now — and seven months is still the ideal time to fix it. Nothing has been lost for Noah.' Blaming the other doctor makes her ask 'Should I complain?' and keep pushing

'Cancer?! He's a baby' — 'I know that's a frightening word. THE RISK IS IN ADULT LIFE, IT'S SMALL, AND TREATING IT NOW IS EXACTLY HOW WE REDUCE IT. WITH ONE NORMAL TESTICLE AND THE OTHER BROUGHT DOWN EARLY, MOST BOYS HAVE NORMAL FERTILITY.' She becomes tearful if cancer is mentioned bluntly without this softening

The umbilical plan — and pre-empt the coin — 'For the belly button WE DO NOTHING EXCEPT WATCH. ABOUT 95% CLOSE ON THEIR OWN BY TWO TO THREE YEARS, SO WE'RE HAPPY TO WAIT UNTIL HE'S FOUR. If it's still there at four, A SIMPLE DAY-SURGERY CLOSES IT. IT MAY LOOK A BIT BIGGER OVER THE NEXT FEW MONTHS AS HE GROWS — THAT'S EXPECTED. And please: NO TAPE, NO COINS, NO STRAPPING — IT DOESN'T HELP AND CAN HURT THE SKIN.' Her mother has told her to tape a coin on it, and she will ask if you do not pre-empt it

The 6-2 rule, as reasoning not a memorised date — 'Surgeons time hernia repair by age: under six weeks, within about two days; six weeks to six months, within two weeks; over six months — Noah — within the next two months. That doesn't mean we wait two months; it means we have a little breathing room and the surgeon books the youngest babies first.' She pushes once: 'Two months seems a long time if it can get stuck'

One operation fixes both — 'The groin hernia and the testicle both need an operation — and it's one operation, in the groin, that fixes both. For the testicle the best window is six to twelve months, so seven months is ideal — both are done together, before his first birthday.' and yes, a general anaesthetic, usually day surgery, with the surgeon going through it

Referral, red flags, the thyroid drop, and the close — Refer today to the paediatric surgeons at the women's and children's, who will re-examine and set the date, with PATS organised for the travel · red flags to the emergency department: the groin lump bigger, hard, red or won't push back, or screaming, vomiting, or not passing poo or wind · then the drop: 'When I see more than one hernia together with an undescended testicle, I like to check the thyroid, a gland in the neck that controls growth. He had the heel-prick as a newborn — that's a screen; a simple blood test today confirms it' · and close with the Royal children's hospital fact sheets named, review in two weeks, and 'What questions do you have?'

The inguinal hernia — 'I also found TWO OTHER THINGS I NEED TO EXPLAIN. The first is A SECOND, SMALLER HERNIA IN THE GROIN — AN INGUINAL HERNIA. It forms in or around a little passage called THE INGUINAL CANAL, WHICH RUNS FROM THE TUMMY DOWN TO THE SCROTUM. That passage is MEANT TO SEAL BEFORE BIRTH; in Noah it has stayed open, so a small sac can slip into it. UNLIKE THE BELLY-BUTTON ONE, IT WON'T CLOSE BY ITSELF'

The undescended testis, with the descent story — 'I can feel only one testicle in the scrotum. The other is sitting up in the groin — an undescended testis. Before birth the testicles form inside the tummy and, near birth, travel down that same canal into the scrotum. Sometimes one doesn't finish the journey and gets stuck in the canal.' and when she asks whether it will come down: 'At seven months it won't come down on its own — after about six months we don't expect it to'

Incarceration — and the weighting is the mark — 'With any hernia the worry is that a loop of bowel slips into the sac and gets trapped — an incarcerated hernia — and if the blood supply is cut off, a strangulated hernia. The baby gets very upset, vomits, and the lump goes hard, tender and red. This is much more likely with the groin hernia and very rare with the belly-button one — which is why we treat them differently.' if she asks how she would know, park it: 'I'll give you the exact signs before you go'

setting: Tramadol is charted in two places — a regular order on page 3 and a PRN order on the back — and nobody will tell you the regular one is there. Candidates who went straight to the back page ceased the PRN, charted oxycodone, and never saw it. Open every face of the chart before the pen touches it. And opioids, antiemetics and relievers are PRN unless the stem says 'Regular'.

findings: The reason, written on the chart
'Ceased — serotonin syndrome risk with citalopram — date — signature'. The examiner reads both pages for when it was stopped, who stopped it, and why

back.dx: A prescribing and documentation station with no role-player, testing three separable skills: the PRN box, ceasing an order properly in every place it is written, and a concise interaction explanation. The numbers: tramadol IV or IM 50 to 100 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 600 mg in 24 hours — so 50 mg IV 6 hourly PRN with 600 mg as the maximum · oxycodone subcut 7.5 to 12.5 mg every 2 hours for this age band — so 10 mg subcut 2 hourly PRN, maximum 120 mg, or 7.5 mg giving 90 mg · paracetamol, in the older version of this case, is 1 g orally 6 hourly with a maximum of 4 g in 24 hours, and never 'Qid' in the hourly-frequency box · and the sedation score runs 0 alert, 1 easy to rouse, 2 rousable but cannot stay awake, 3 difficult to rouse — with the dose held at 2 VERIFY all against the AMH and local protocol. The marking brief is blunt about what fails outright: ceasing only the PRN tramadol while the regular entry stays live · ceasing with a scribble that obliterates the order · omitting the reason, date or signature on either cease · writing 'Sc' for the route · charting the opioid as a regular order · and writing a range such as '7.5–12.5 mg' instead of one dose. Amber items, two of which together also fail: 'D/c' instead of ceased · 'Tds' in the hourly-frequency box · an empty maximum for the oxycodone · and dates written into the PRN administration record, which is the nurse's column. Choosing morphine passes, because the stem allowed either. The habit being trained, and separately noted by the marker, is the re-check before leaving: both tramadol entries ceased, reason and date and signature on both, route written as subcut, and a maximum in the box. The variants: if tramadol is charted in only one place, cease that one — but still open every face and say to yourself 'One entry only' · if the stem says 'Regular oxycodone', it becomes a page 3 order with a frequency word and times from the margin guide, which is the only time an opioid leaves the PRN box · and if you chart the new opioid in the wrong box, you cease it as 'Written in error' and re-chart rather than obliterating. The deeper point this card is worth remembering for: a chart is a legal document read by people who are not in the room. The administration record stays empty — NOTHING GOES IN THE ADMINISTRATION GRID — THE NURSE WRITES IT WHEN A DOSE IS GIVEN. For a REGULAR order you date the columns; FOR A PRN THE DOCTOR WRITES NO DATES AT ALL. Writing today's date in the record is the trap

Ceasing — the six things, in both places — One diagonal line through the order box, so the original stays legible · two lines crossing the administration grid · the word 'Ceased' — not D/C, not 'Stopped' · the reason · the date · and your signature. Then repeat it exactly on the other page. 'D/c' is ambiguous between discharge and discontinue, which is why ceased is the recommended word

Never obliterate, never overwrite — Scribbling the order out is a fail, and so is changing the dose on TOP of an existing order. If you needed a different dose you would cease and re-chart. The same applies to your own mistakes: one line, two lines, 'Ceased — written in error', date, sign, and re-chart in the correct box — the examiner sees a correct correction

The oxycodone PRN box — Date · medicine oxycodone · route subcut — written out, because 'Sc' is a non-approved abbreviation and a fail, even though the AMH itself abbreviates it · dose 10 mg · hourly frequency 2 hourly · max PRN dose 120 mg · indication pain · signature, print, contact · and fill the year on the PRN page. The AMH band for this age is 7.5 to 12.5 mg every 2 hours subcutaneously

The maximum where the book gives none — THE AMH GIVES NO 24-HOUR MAXIMUM FOR OXYCODONE AND NO FORMAL AUSTRALIAN RULE EXISTS. THE EXAMINER ACCEPTS MULTIPLICATION — 10 mg × 12 DOSES = 120 mg, OR 7.5 mg × 12 = 90 mg — OR A SEDATION-SCORE LIMIT, OR A RESPIRATORY-RATE LIMIT. A CHOSEN NUMBER BEATS AN EMPTY BOX. If you use 'sedation score < 2' it barely fits, so write it small and legibly or multiply instead

The serotonin syndrome answer, in forty seconds — 'This patient takes citalopram, an SSRI. Tramadol also increases serotonin, and the combination carries a significant risk of serotonin syndrome — agitation, tremor, clonus, sweating, hyperthermia, which can be life-threatening. So I have ceased tramadol, both the regular and the as-required orders, documented the reason, dated and signed it, and charted oxycodone 10 mg subcutaneously 2 hourly as required with a maximum of 120 mg in 24 hours'

'Why oxycodone rather than morphine?' — 'Both are appropriate and the stem allowed either. I chose oxycodone for its more predictable subcutaneous absorption and fewer active metabolites in a patient whose renal function I have not been given. I would ask nursing staff to check a sedation score before each dose and to hold the dose and call me if the score is 2 or more, or the respiratory rate is below 12'

back.dx: A ONCE-ONLY PRESCRIBING STATION — the first stat order the AMC has set — testing three things at once: that you know which box a stat dose lives in, that you can dose per kilogram within a renal band, and that the housekeeping boxes are still completed when the stem is silent. The numbers: gentamicin at CrCl above 60 is 5 to 7 mg/kg, and at CrCl 30 to 60 it is 4 to 5 mg/kg · eGFR 60 is treated as CrCl 60 for the exam · 5 mg/kg × 60 kg = 300 mg IV · the once-only box is on the front page · and the weight of 60 kg goes in the ID box VERIFY all against the AMH and local protocol. The marking brief's outright fails: charting gentamicin in the regular box for one day, which is the 2025 failing move · writing '5 mg/kg' or '300' with no unit · writing your own name as the patient · missing the ID box on the back · and leaving the VTE box blank. Omitting the weight is amber to some examiners and a fail to others, and filling in 'Given by' or 'Time given' is amber. Both 'Stat' and a date with an approximate time pass. Choosing 4 mg/kg for 240 mg, or 7 mg/kg for 420 mg, passes if the band is defensible and you can justify it — so know why you picked your number. And if you ask the examiner whether eGFR equals CrCl, they are briefed to shrug and say nothing. The variants. eGFR 45 at 80 kg puts you in the 30 to 60 band — 5 × 80 = 400 mg, or 4 × 80 = 320 mg, and you write the milligrams. 'Chart gentamicin daily for three days' makes it a regular order on page 3 with a daily frequency, a time such as 0800, three dated columns and the rest blocked — a course needing levels could sit in the variable-dose box, but for the exam a fixed daily dose for three days is regular. If you chart it as regular by mistake, the correction is one line, two lines, 'Ceased — written in error', date and signature, then re-chart in the once-only box — do not panic, because the examiner sees a correct correction. And for a one-word slip such as IM written for IV, a single line through the wrong word, initialled, with the correct word beside it is enough — full re-ordering is for anything larger. The principle underneath this station, which generalises to every chart: the box you choose is itself a clinical decision. A stat dose in the regular section reads as a course; a course in the once-only box reads as one dose; and the person who has to interpret it is not in the room with you.

back.dx: A PRESCRIBING STATION BUILT AROUND THE MEDICINES-TAKEN-PRIOR-TO-PRESENTATION BOX — the first time the AMC used it — plus transcribing home medicines as regular orders from pharmacy stickers, generic names, and withholding one drug around surgery. The numbers: perindopril 8 mg orally daily · atorvastatin 20 mg orally daily, with Lipitor on the box and the generic on the chart · aspirin 100 mg orally daily, blocked today and on the surgery day · 0800 mane and 2000 nocte · and the surgeon's rule, aspirin withheld seven days pre-operatively. The AMH maximums — perindopril 8 mg a day and atorvastatin 80 mg a day — are ceilings, not this patient's dose VERIFY all. The marking brief's outright fails: skipping the medicines-prior box · writing 'Lipitor' anywhere · charting the three only in the prior box so no inpatient orders exist · leaving aspirin open today and tomorrow, which is the point of the case · and missing the ID box on the back. Amber items, two of which together also fail: blocking aspirin for the next seven days, which is a misread worth discussing afterwards · never looking at the boxes and charting AMH maximums · writing 'Htn' or 'Ihd' instead of the indication in full · and entering no administration times. Writing 'Withhold' rather than crossing out passes, and so does also blocking perindopril and atorvastatin on the surgery day. The variants. If the stem gives the doses in words and there are no boxes, chart exactly the doses stated, and put a duration in the prior box only if one is given — 'Four years' becomes '4 years'. If a fourth drug is 'Ventolin as needed', the prior box gets salbutamol with dose and frequency blank if not given, the regular page gets nothing, and the PRN page gets salbutamol 100 micrograms by metered aerosol 4 hourly as required for asthma — or nothing at all if no dose is given and you are unsure, because you do not invent one. And if the patient is post-operative today, aspirin restarts on the surgeon's instruction only — withhold today and note 'Withhold — surgeon to review' — while VTE prophylaxis becomes a live question, with enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily in the VTE box if the stem asks VERIFY. The principle underneath this one: a medication chart has to survive the handover. The prior box tells the pharmacist what he takes at home; the regular orders tell the nurse what to give; and the blocked columns tell both of them what not to give tomorrow morning when nobody who wrote the chart is on the ward.

Why you block anything at all — The surgeon said withhold seven days before surgery, and the patient stopped at home — you cannot chart the past. What you control is today and the surgery day. Blocking nothing because 'He stopped it seven days ago at home' is the failing move, and blocking the next seven days is a misread — the instruction was seven days before surgery, and surgery is tomorrow

The other two on the surgery day — Blocking perindopril and atorvastatin on the surgery day because he is nil by mouth is reasonable and is not marked either way — the stem does not ask. The emphasis of the whole case is aspirin

Set up the grid before the orders — WRITE THE YEAR AND THE DATES ACROSS THE TOP OF PAGE 3 — TODAY IS COLUMN ONE AND TOMORROW, COLUMN TWO, IS THE SURGICAL DAY. Doing this first is what makes the aspirin blocking unambiguous to the nurse reading it

The re-check — 'Prior box — three drugs, signed. Three regular orders — generic names. Aspirin — today and tomorrow blocked. Times — entered. ID back — yes.' The marker notes whether you re-checked before leaving

Your patient has been admitted with an acute exacerbation of asthma — or COPD. Tasks: chart prednisolone — chart Ventolin. The recall wording is incomplete, so assume the patient is past the initial emergency loading.

findings: The prednisolone order, field by field

Date · prednisolone · PO · 50 mg · daily · indication asthma, or COPD exacerbation · signature, print, contact · times 0800 in days one to five, because morning dosing is conventional · and days six onward crossed out. Leaving the course open-ended — a steroid with no stop date — is the fail
The salbutamol order, field by field

Date · salbutamol · MA · 100 micrograms — 200 micrograms for two puffs is also defensible · hourly frequency 4 hourly, or 1 to 4 hourly, which is accepted for salbutamol · indication asthma · signature, print, contact · and the year on the PRN page · with the administration record left completely empty

back.dx: A two-order prescribing station where the easy half is a fixed-dose steroid course and the hard half is an inhaler — generic name, metered-aerosol route, micrograms written in full, a chosen hourly frequency, the PRN box, and an honestly empty maximum. The numbers: prednisolone for asthma is 37.5 to 50 mg daily for 5 to 10 days and for COPD 40 to 50 mg daily for 5 to 14 days, with therapeutic guidelines giving 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg — so 50 mg orally daily for 5 days · salbutamol is 100 micrograms per puff, with 4 to 12 puffs, or 400 to 1200 micrograms, via spacer every 20 minutes acutely and then every 1 to 4 hours — so 100 micrograms by metered aerosol 4 hourly as required · and no 24-hour maximum for salbutamol exists VERIFY all. The marking brief's outright fails: writing 'Ventolin' · writing 'Mcg' or 'Ug' · charting salbutamol as a regular order · leaving prednisolone open-ended when the stem gave a duration · missing the ID box on the back · and leaving the VTE box blank. Amber items: putting prednisolone in the variable-dose box, which the examiner will ask about · writing 'Inh' or 'Mdi' as the route · and writing 'Every 20 min' as '20 minly'. Things that pass and are worth knowing pass: '1 puff' as the dose, which is common practice though less formal than 100 micrograms · '1 to 4 hourly' as the frequency · and an empty maximum PRN dose. The variants. A COPD exacerbation takes the same two orders with the indication changed, a course that may run to 14 days though five remains the taught default, and any antibiotic as a separate regular order with its own duration blocked. If asked to chart the acute regimen in emergency: salbutamol, MA, 1200 micrograms for 12 puffs via spacer, 'Every 20 minutes for 3 doses' written in words, for asthma — in the PRN box, or the once-only box if a single loading dose is asked — and then hand over to the 4-hourly PRN order. If a nebuliser is ordered, the route is neb and the adult dose is 5 mg, still salbutamol and still PRN unless told regular VERIFY. And if he has a maintenance inhaler at home such as budesonide with formoterol, it goes in the prior box under its generic names and on the regular page twice daily at 0800 and 2000 if the stem gives the dose — with the route as MA, or written in words for a dry-powder device, since dpi has no single approved abbreviation VERIFY. The two sentences worth having ready for the examiner: 'Salbutamol is a reliever, so it is as-required' and 'The AMH gives no maximum for salbutamol, so I have left the box empty'. And the generalisable point: the unit and the box are both clinical decisions. 'Mcg' misread as mg is a thousand-fold overdose, and a reliever in the regular section is a drug given on a schedule to someone who may not need it.
