DO — Ask what he was hoping for, early — he wants a scan or a treadmill to prove his heart is fine and is frightened of leaving his children without a father; if you never ask he raises it at about seven minutes as you wrap up

DO — Give every domain a number or a named referral, never an adjective — under 10 standard drinks a week, no more than 4 in a day, 2 free days; 150 minutes as 5 × 30; BMI under 25, waist under 94 cm; Quitline 13 7848, dietitian, exercise physiologist — and push past 'my diet's alright' to vegetables, fried food and salt

setting: Read the stem for numbers in the reading minute, because that is what tells you which station you are in. Two versions circulate: with no blood pressure, lipids or glucose you explain the process and order the tests; here the assessment is already done at 12% over five years, and explaining how risk assessment works wastes half the station. And 'Normal for the lab' is not normal for a high-risk man — his targets are tighter.
stem: General practice. Mr James Whitcombe, 50, has come in because his brother, 54, had coronary artery bypass surgery two weeks ago. He is anxious about his own heart. He smokes 15 a day and is otherwise well. 8 minutes.

Results: BP 148/94 (Average of two seated in-clinic readings) · BMI 29 · waist 102 cm · total cholesterol 6.8, LDL 4.6, HDL 0.9, triglycerides 2.6 · fasting glucose 5.2 and HbA1c 5.5%, normal · eGFR 82 · ECG sinus rhythm.
Cardiovascular risk assessment already calculated: 12% over five years.
tasks: Take a focused history
Explain the investigation results to the patient
Explain your management plan
Answer the examiner's questions
time: The plan has three limbs and all three are marked: medicines with monitoring · lifestyle · services and dated review · and every drug is a package — choice, side effect, monitoring, target, and when I see you
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Limb one — both drugs, each as a complete package

High risk with both the blood pressure and the fats up means two tablets, not one. An ACE inhibitor: the thing to know is a dry, tickly cough, and if it happens you switch to a closely related tablet that doesn't — with a blood test at two weeks for potassium and kidney function. A statin such as atorvastatin: the side effect is muscle aches, and most aches people get aren't the tablet, but if the pain or weakness is genuinely bad, come back for a creatine kinase. Then give him the targets, because people work towards numbers: total cholesterol under 4 · the bad type under 2 · stored fat under 2 · the good type above 1 · blood pressure consistently under 140/90 · and repeat lipids at three months

back.dx: High cardiovascular risk at 12% over five years, with the numbers already in the stem. Limb two, lifestyle, with the smoking first and without lecturing: 'The biggest single thing on this list is the smoking. Stopping would do more for that 12% than either tablet. Is that something you'd consider?' — ask permission, ask what he has tried, and offer something concrete: Quitline, and patches or a tablet, which roughly doubles the chances of it sticking. Food: more vegetables, fish, wholegrains, olive oil instead of butter, less red meat, and the salt is worth tackling — under a teaspoon a day and none at the table. Alcohol: no more than 10 standard drinks a week, no more than 4 in a day, and a couple of alcohol-free days. Activity: 150 minutes a week of something that gets him a bit puffed, which is thirty minutes on five days, plus resistance work twice a week. And on weight: 'Any weight you lose is a win — I'm not going to give you a target you'll hate.' Do not repeat the smoking message three times — if you lecture him he shuts down with 'Yeah, I know'. Limb three, services and review: a dietitian who will build an actual eating plan rather than a leaflet · an exercise physiologist who will write a programme for someone who has not exercised in a while · set up under a GP management plan so the visits are subsidised · heart foundation reading and today's plan written down · two weeks for the blood test and to check how he is going on the tablets, and three months to recheck the fats. And the principle worth saying: 'We don't need to keep recalculating that percentage — you're in the high group, so we just treat it.' Red flags: chest pain or tightness, pain into the jaw or arm, sudden breathlessness, or sudden weakness, numbness or slurred speech — ring 000, don't drive yourself. Then close the loop on the question he came in with: 'You came in asking whether you're next. You're not where your brother was — he already had blockages when they operated, and nothing today suggests you do. What you've got is a set of risks we've caught while there's still time to change them.' What a failing run looks like, with every fact correct: explains how a risk assessment is performed when the stem already gives 12% · never asks about chest pain · reads the lipid numbers aloud without translating them · gives the percentage bare · starts a statin only · names two drugs with no side effects, no bloods, no targets and no review dates · no referrals · recommends aspirin because the brother is on it · and never returns to 'Am I next?'. The harder moments, scripted: 'Can I just try the diet first and see how I go?' → 'I'm all for the diet, and it will do more than people expect. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I let you leave thinking diet alone will take a cholesterol of 6.8 down under 4. How about this: we start the lifestyle changes and the smoking work today, start one tablet, and I'll see you in two weeks — then you decide about the second with the numbers in front of you.' 'My cholesterol's only 5.6 — the lab says that's in range' → 'The lab range describes the general population. It doesn't describe what's safe for someone in the high risk group. It's not that your result is abnormal for everyone — it's that it's not low enough for you.' and the examiner's hardest question, 'He declines both tablets, have you failed?' → 'No — provided the refusal is informed. I would document that I explained his high-risk category, the recommended treatment and the reasoning, and that he declined. I would secure what he has agreed to — here, smoking cessation, which is the single highest-yield intervention available — arrange review in two weeks, and leave the offer open. A patient who leaves feeling heard is far more likely to come back and reconsider than one who has been argued at.' This station can be passed with the patient declining medication and failed with the patient accepting it — what is marked is whether the results were explained, the risk translated, the plan given in three limbs with dates attached, and the decision shared.
plan: WIPE AND CONSENT, open question, THEN NAME THE BROTHER BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — going straight into questions reads as a checklist and loses the empathy and agenda marks in thirty seconds.
Cardiovascular symptoms, before any risk factor question.

RISK FACTORS TICKED OFF AUDIBLY: cigarettes per day and years, and whether he has ever stopped · BP or cholesterol ever high · diabetes · THE BROTHER'S EXACT AGE AND OTHER RELATIVES WITH AGES · diet and salt · alcohol · exercise · kidneys and mood.
SAY 'PREMATURE CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE' OUT LOUD when you hear 54 — then ask what he was hoping you would say today.
THE LIPIDS AS FOUR FATS IN PLAIN ENGLISH — total, bad, good, stored.
The normal glucose given genuinely as good news, then the blood pressure, then back to the three things that are not fine.
TRANSLATE THE 12% AS 12 IN 100 OVER FIVE YEARS — then benchmark it when he minimises, and answer 'but I feel fine'.
LIMB ONE, MEDICINES: ACE inhibitor with the cough and the two-week potassium and kidneys · statin with muscle aches and creatine kinase · THE TARGETS · lipids at three months.
The aspirin question, answered with the primary-versus-secondary reason.
LIMB TWO, LIFESTYLE: smoking first, by permission, with Quitline and pharmacotherapy — then salt, alcohol and activity with numbers.
LIMB THREE, SERVICES: dietitian, exercise physiologist, GP management plan, written plan — AND TWO DATED REVIEWS.
Red flags with 000, close the loop on 'Am I next?', and invite him to disagree.
back.planNote: four tasks in eight minutes; the three limbs of the plan are each separately marked, so none can be dropped
ask: THE OPENING AND HISTORY SET: 'I'm sorry about your brother — and coming in to get yourself checked is exactly the right response.' · 'First I need to be sure your heart is healthy right now — any chest tightness on exertion, or cramping in the calves when you walk?' · 'YOUR BROTHER — HOW OLD IS HE EXACTLY?' · 'Before I go through the results — what were you hoping I'd say today?'

THE RESULTS SET: 'The total is the overall amount of fat in the blood, and yours is high.' · 'THERE'S A BAD TYPE THAT BUILDS UP AND BLOCKS THE TUBES SUPPLYING THE HEART — yours is high.' · 'There's a good type that clears the build-up away — we want it above 1.' · 'YOUR SUGAR IS NORMAL, AND THAT'S GENUINELY GOOD NEWS.' · 'IF WE IMAGINE 100 PEOPLE THE SAME AGE, SAME SEX AND SAME CIRCUMSTANCES AS YOU, 12 OF THEM WILL HAVE A HEART ATTACK OR A STROKE IN THE NEXT FIVE YEARS.' · 'For a man of 50 that number should be nearer 2 or 3. IT ISN'T A PREDICTION — IT'S A MEASURE OF WHAT'S STILL CHANGEABLE.' · 'FEELING WELL DOESN'T MEAN WE'RE SAFE. IT MEANS WE'VE GOT TIME.'

THE PLAN SET: 'THREE PARTS: MEDICINES, LIFESTYLE, AND SUPPORT.' · 'I'll see you in two weeks for a blood test to check your potassium and your kidneys.' · 'ASPIRIN IS FOR PEOPLE WHO ALREADY HAVE THE DISEASE. In someone who doesn't, the bleeding risk cancels out the benefit.' · AND THE CLOSING LOOP: 'You're not where your brother was — he already had blockages when they operated, and nothing today suggests you do.'
pefe: Everything is in the stem and the task is to translate it: BP 148/94 as the average of two seated readings · BMI 29, waist 102 cm · total cholesterol 6.8, LDL 4.6, HDL 0.9, triglycerides 2.6 · fasting glucose 5.2 and HbA1c 5.5%, both normal · eGFR 82 · ECG sinus rhythm · and a calculated five-year risk of 12%.

WHAT HE GIVES ON HISTORY: 15 CIGARETTES A DAY FOR 30 YEARS, stopped for a fortnight once · nobody has ever mentioned blood pressure or cholesterol · no diabetes · BROTHER PAUL IS 54, and his father died at 78 of cancer · MEAT AND POTATOES, REGULAR TAKEAWAY, AND HE SALTS EVERYTHING · six or seven beers across a weekend · NO EXERCISE BEYOND BEING ON HIS FEET AT WORK · kidneys and mood fine · AND WHAT HE ACTUALLY WANTS IS TO BE TOLD HE IS ALRIGHT. He does not volunteer the salt, the alcohol, his brother's exact age, or his expectations unless asked directly.

He is briefed to say 'But I feel fine' at least twice and to stay unconvinced if it is never addressed · to latch onto the normal sugar and try to treat the whole visit as reassuring · to test the number with 'So 88 out of 100 don't, that's not terrible, is it?' and disengage if you simply agree · and to ask for aspirin because his brother is on it.

Symptoms first, and the brother's age is the mark — Chest pain or tightness on exertion · pain into the jaw, neck or arm · breathlessness on exertion, lying flat, or waking him · calf cramping that eases when he stops · palpitations, dizziness, blackouts · weakness, numbness or trouble speaking, even briefly. Then: 'Your brother — how old is he exactly?' A first-degree relative with coronary disease before 55 is premature cardiovascular disease, and his brother at 54 qualifies — say it out loud. It does not change this man's management because he is already high risk, but in an intermediate patient it is exactly the reclassification factor that pushes them into treatment

Explain the lipids as four fats, not as a list of numbers — 'THE TOTAL AMOUNT is the overall figure, and yours is high — 6.8. Inside that there's A BAD TYPE — THAT'S THE ONE THAT BUILDS UP ON THE WALLS AND BLOCKS THE TUBES SUPPLYING THE HEART, THE SAME PROCESS YOUR BROTHER HAD. Yours is high. There's also A GOOD TYPE, WHICH HELPS CLEAR THAT BUILD-UP AWAY — we want it as high as possible and AT LEAST ABOVE 1; yours is 0.9. And a fourth, TRIGLYCERIDES, WHICH IS FAT YOUR BODY STORES — that's a bit high too.' RECITING 'LDL 4.6, HDL 0.9, TRIGLYCERIDES 2.6' IS NOT EXPLAINING

Give the good news honestly, then bring him back — 'YOUR SUGAR IS NORMAL, AND THAT'S GENUINELY GOOD NEWS — it means you don't have diabetes, WHICH WOULD HAVE MADE ALL OF THIS CONSIDERABLY HARDER.' Do not bury it: one piece of real good news MAKES THE REST LAND BETTER. But he will latch onto it and try to treat the whole visit as reassuring — SO BRING HIM BACK TO THE THREE THINGS THAT ARE NOT FINE: THE SMOKING, THE BLOOD PRESSURE AT 148/94, AND THE FATS

Translate the 12% — the sentence the guideline asks for — 'If we imagine 100 people the same age as you, the same sex, and in the same circumstances, 12 of those 100 will have a heart attack or a stroke in the next five years. That puts you in the high risk group.' He will minimise it — 'So 88 are fine? That doesn't sound too bad' — and do not simply agree. Benchmark it: 'For a man of 50 that figure should be around 2 or 3. Twelve is high — and it isn't a prediction, it's a measure of how much of this is still changeable.' and when he says 'But I feel fine': 'The furring-up builds silently over years — your brother felt fine too, until he didn't. Feeling well doesn't mean we're safe. It means we've got time'

The aspirin question, and the 'Normal for the lab' question — 'Should I be on aspirin? He's on aspirin.' → 'Aspirin is for people who already have the disease, like your brother. In someone who doesn't, the extra bleeding risk cancels out the benefit, so we don't use it routinely.' and from the examiner — 'His total cholesterol is 5.6 and his BP 140/95, still treat?' → 'Yes. Those figures sit inside the laboratory reference range but they are not target for a high-risk patient. The question is never whether a number is normal — it is whether it is normal for this patient's risk category'

numbers: Risk 12% over 5 years, high — bands <5 low, 5–10 intermediate, ≥10 high · lipid targets for high risk: total cholesterol <4, LDL <2, triglycerides <2, HDL >1 · BP target <140/90, lower if tolerated · ACE inhibitor: dry cough means switch to an ARB, review at 2 weeks with potassium and creatinine, and a fall in kidney function of more than about 25% prompts review · statin: muscle aches, creatine kinase if severe, repeat lipids at 3 months · aspirin is not for primary prevention VERIFY

Snap: Quitline 13 7848 · salt under 5 g a day · alcohol ≤10 standard drinks a week, ≤4 in a day, 2 alcohol-free days · activity ≥150 minutes a week plus resistance training twice weekly · BMI <25, waist <94 cm in men and <80 cm in women · premature family CVD is a first-degree relative before 55 · do not repeat the risk score in a high-risk patient, repeat the monitoring instead · if challenged on a number, say you would confirm against current lipid and hypertension guidance VERIFY

setting: There is no complaint in the stem — there is an agenda. Within the first minute he will tell you, in some form, that he has stopped his cholesterol tablet because it was giving him muscle aches. That sentence is the case, and it surfaces out of your open question or your concerns question — if you ask neither, it may never surface at all.
stem: Your general practice. John Reid, 55, attending for a vaccination. Known hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, on perindopril and atorvastatin. Family history of ischaemic heart disease.
Presenting complaint: none stated. 2 minutes reading, 8 minutes in the room.
In version A he volunteers it with the flu jab request. In version B he does not volunteer it at all, and only the concerns question — or a drug-by-drug compliance question — will catch it.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Counsel him regarding his cardiovascular risk and management
time: Five things are being paid for: finding the agenda · validating it rather than arguing · exploring the pain with the four discriminating questions · restarting the statin with the ladder ready · and an explicit benefit-versus-risk conversation that ends by handing the decision back

back.dx: STATIN-ASSOCIATED MUSCLE SYMPTOMS AND NON-ADHERENCE IN A MAN WITH HYPERTENSION, HYPERCHOLESTEROLAEMIA AND A FATHER WHO HAD A HEART ATTACK AT 58. THE EDUCATION THAT TARGETS THE ACTUAL HEALTH BELIEF: 'it's from a group called STATINS, and its job is to lower the fats in your blood. That matters because high fat levels increase your risk of a heart attack, a stroke and other heart disease — AND THEY CAUSE NO SYMPTOMS AT ALL, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY THEY'RE SO EASY TO IGNORE. You said you feel completely fine, AND YOU DO — BUT THE RISK IS BUILDING QUIETLY IN THE BACKGROUND. And in your case there's MORE THAN ONE THING STACKING UP: having high blood pressure as well increases that risk further, and YOUR FATHER HAD A HEART ATTACK AT 58. By controlling both, we bring that risk down together.' THEN OPEN THE DOOR TO OTHER CAUSES BEFORE BLAMING THE DRUG: JOINT PROBLEMS LIKE ARTHRITIS, AN UNDERACTIVE THYROID, LOW VITAMIN D, FIBROMYALGIA, OR SIMPLY DOING MORE PHYSICALLY THAN USUAL — 'so before we decide the tablet is the culprit, WE NEED TO BE SURE THE PAIN REALLY IS COMING FROM IT.' THE BENEFIT-VERSUS-RISK ANALYSIS, SAID IN THESE TERMS: 'THE BENEFIT is that it lowers your chance of a heart attack, a stroke, or developing heart disease — SERIOUS, LIFE-CHANGING EVENTS, AND ONES WE WOULD FAR RATHER PREVENT. THE RISK is muscle aching. It's uncomfortable, and I'M NOT DISMISSING IT — but IT IS NOT LIFE-THREATENING, AND IT GOES AWAY WHEN WE STOP. ON BALANCE, THE BENEFITS CLEARLY OUTWEIGH THE RISK. That's why I'd like you back on it — AND IT'S WHY I'VE GOT A STEP-BY-STEP PLAN IF IT DOES HAPPEN AGAIN, RATHER THAN JUST TELLING YOU TO PUT UP WITH IT.' THE LADDER, IN ORDER: RESTART → IF ACHES RETURN, CHECK THE CK → IF RAISED, STOP FOR A FEW WEEKS TO LET THE MUSCLES SETTLE → THEN RESTART AT A LOWER DOSE, OR SWITCH WITHIN THE FAMILY, ATORVASTATIN TO ROSUVASTATIN → IF IT RECURS, CHECK CK AGAIN AND TRY INTERMITTENT DOSING, EVERY SECOND DAY OR TWICE A WEEK, BECAUSE TAKING SOME IS MUCH BETTER THAN TAKING NONE → AND ONLY THEN A DIFFERENT CLASS ALTOGETHER, EZETIMIBE. 'SO THERE'S A LOT OF ROAD BEFORE WE GIVE UP ON PROTECTING YOU' VERIFY. THEN LIFESTYLE WITH NUMBERS AND REFERRALS — diet with a DIETITIAN for a Mediterranean pattern · 150 MINUTES A WEEK with an EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGIST built around the driving · alcohol UNDER 10 STANDARD DRINKS A WEEK, ≤4 IN A DAY, TWO FREE DAYS · BMI UNDER 25 AND WAIST UNDER 94 cm. THE CLOSING BLOCK HAS TWO TRAPS IN IT: ENDING WITH 'SO YOU'LL RESTART IT THEN' INSTEAD OF HANDING THE DECISION BACK — 'BUT I WANT TO BE CLEAR, THIS IS YOUR DECISION, NOT MINE. Take the Heart Foundation reading home, have a think, and come back and we'll make the plan together. THERE'S NO PRESSURE FROM ME — I'D JUST RATHER WE DECIDED IT DELIBERATELY THAN BY ACCIDENT' — AND RUNNING THE WHOLE CONSULTATION WITHOUT EVER GIVING HIM THE VACCINATION HE ACTUALLY CAME IN FOR. Bloods in two weeks: cholesterol, kidneys and liver, PLUS A THYROID TEST AND VITAMIN D GIVEN THE ACHING, because both cause muscle pain in their own right. SAFETY-NET: GO STRAIGHT TO HOSPITAL IF THE PAIN BECOMES SEVERE, IF REAL WEAKNESS DEVELOPS, OR IF THE URINE TURNS DARK. THE VARIANTS: B, HE NEVER VOLUNTEERS IT — the compliance question drug by drug is what catches it, and if you never ask he mentions it at about six minutes as you wrap up. C, COST IS THE REAL BARRIER — 'I lost the depot job in March, I've been stretching the blood pressure ones too, taking them every other day.' DO NOT MOVE ON: STRETCHING THE ANTIHYPERTENSIVES IS RISKIER THAN THE MUSCLE ACHES, SO FIX THAT FIRST — both are on the PBS, a GENERIC BRAND is often considerably cheaper, a CONCESSION CARD lowers the copayment, the PBS SAFETY NET drops it further once reached, and a PHARMACIST MEDICATION REVIEW goes through the whole list. NON-ADHERENCE RARELY STOPS AT ONE DRUG. D, THE RED FLAG — weakness on the stairs and urine 'like Coke' for two days, still taking the tablet: STOP EVERYTHING, THIS IS NO LONGER A COUNSELLING STATION. 'Muscle pain with weakness and dark urine can mean THE MUSCLE IS BEING DAMAGED AND RELEASING A SUBSTANCE THAT CAN HARM THE KIDNEYS — that's RHABDOMYOLYSIS, and it needs sorting out TODAY. STOP THE STATIN NOW — THIS IS ONE SITUATION WHERE STOPPING IS EXACTLY RIGHT.' Urgent CK, kidney function and urine test, possible fluids in hospital, DON'T DRIVE YOURSELF — AND WE WOULD NOT SIMPLY RESTART THIS TABLET AFTERWARDS. And if weakness is PROGRESSIVE AND PERSISTS WEEKS AFTER STOPPING WITH A VERY HIGH CK, think IMMUNE-MEDIATED NECROTISING MYOPATHY — specialist referral, ANTI-HMGCR ANTIBODIES, AND DO NOT RECHALLENGE VERIFY. E, HE REFUSES OUTRIGHT — 'THAT'S YOUR RIGHT, AND I'M NOT GOING TO PUSH YOU. Everything we said about lifestyle matters MORE, NOT LESS. PLEASE KEEP TAKING YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE TABLET; THAT'S DOING HALF THE JOB ON ITS OWN. I'll arrange the blood tests anyway and see you in a fortnight. AND THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.' A COMPETENT REFUSAL IS NOT A FAILED STATION — WHAT FAILS IS PRESSURING HIM, OR LETTING THE REFUSAL COLLAPSE THE REST OF THE PLAN.
plan: OPEN QUESTION — he says he is here for the flu jab. THEN ASK THE CONCERNS QUESTION ANYWAY.
ACKNOWLEDGE AND VALIDATE: thank him for raising it rather than stopping quietly, and confirm the side effect is recognised.
THE TWO CONDITIONS: when diagnosed · what he takes for each · COMPLIANCE WITH THE PERINDOPRIL TOO · cough and postural dizziness · follow-up and bloods.
COMPLICATIONS SCREEN IN TWENTY SECONDS: chest pain or breathlessness on exertion · leg pain on walking · blurred vision.
THE FOUR DISCRIMINATING PAIN QUESTIONS: side · muscle or joint · dull or sharp · TIMING AFTER STARTING.
THEN: did it settle on stopping · WEAKNESS · morning stiffness · DARK URINE · any new medicine including from the chemist.
THE ADHERENCE SCREEN: what he understands the tablet is for · memory · AND COST.
Risk factors briskly — a B C d E F s, including the father's heart attack at 58.
EDUCATE: what a statin is, what it prevents, THAT THE RISK IS SILENT, and that the two conditions compound.
Other causes of muscle pain, then the rechallenge and why a ck today would be meaningless.
The explicit benefit-versus-risk comparison, then the ladder in order.
Lifestyle with numbers, dietitian and exercise physiologist.
HAND THE DECISION BACK · reading material · bloods including THYROID AND VITAMIN D · review in two weeks · SAFETY-NET FOR SEVERE PAIN, WEAKNESS AND DARK URINE · AND GIVE THE VACCINATION.
back.planNote: the agenda usually surfaces in the first minute; the rest is a working split
ask: THE FINDING AND VALIDATING SET: 'Before we do that — IS THERE ANYTHING ELSE ON YOUR MIND, or anything you were hoping to raise while you're here?' · 'Thank you for telling me that, and for being honest with me. I'M GLAD YOU RAISED IT RATHER THAN JUST STOPPING QUIETLY.' · 'YOU'RE RIGHT THAT THESE TABLETS CAN CAUSE MUSCLE ACHES — THAT'S A RECOGNISED SIDE EFFECT.'

THE FOUR QUESTIONS: 'Where do you feel it — and is it on one side of your body, or both?' · 'IS IT THE MUSCLES THAT ARE SORE, OR THE JOINTS THEMSELVES?' · 'Is it a dull ache, or a sharp, stabbing pain?' · 'HOW LONG AFTER YOU STARTED THE TABLET DID IT BEGIN?' PLUS: 'Did your GP explain why you needed this medication?'

THE MANAGEMENT SET: 'I'd like you to start it again. YOU'RE ALREADY OFF IT, SO A BLOOD TEST NOW WOULD BE NORMAL NO MATTER WHAT — IT WOULDN'T TELL US ANYTHING.' · 'If the aches come back, I'll check a CREATINE KINASE.' · 'Let's weigh up the benefits against the side effects… ON BALANCE, THE BENEFITS OUTWEIGH THE RISK.' · 'TAKING IT TWICE A WEEK IS MUCH BETTER THAN NOT TAKING IT AT ALL.' · 'BUT THIS IS YOUR DECISION, NOT MINE. Take the reading home, have a think, and come back and we'll make the plan together.'
pefe: No examination — the pain history is the examination. What he gives: both shoulders, both hips and the TOPs of both thighs, bilateral · the muscle, 'The meat of the shoulder, not the joint' · a dull ache, 'Like I've overdone it at the gym, except I haven't been near a gym' · about a month after starting · much better since stopping three weeks ago · no weakness, he can do everything · ten minutes of morning stiffness · urine normal · no new medicines.

THE REST OF THE PICTURE, ONLY IF ASKED: perindopril taken every morning without fail, NO COUGH AND NO DIZZINESS · GP once or twice a year and BLOODS NOT FOR A GOOD WHILE · no chest pain, claudication or visual blurring · two beers most nights and four on a Friday · SERVO FOOD AND TAKEAWAY BECAUSE HE DRIVES · little exercise, quit smoking ten years ago · AND HIS FATHER'S HEART ATTACK AT 58, GIVEN ONLY IF YOU ASK ABOUT FAMILY HISTORY AND THE AGE.

The starred items on the scoring sheet: asked whether there was anything else on his mind and found the agenda · asked all four pain questions · restarted the statin and explained why a ck today would be useless · gave an explicit benefits-versus-risks comparison · and handed the decision back.

Ask the concerns question even if he has already told you — 'Of course, we'll get that sorted. BEFORE WE DO — IS THERE ANYTHING ELSE ON YOUR MIND, OR ANYTHING YOU WERE HOPING TO RAISE WHILE YOU'RE HERE?' A candidate who opens with 'so you're here for a vaccination and you have high blood pressure and cholesterol, tell me about your risk factors' MAY NEVER DISCOVER THE CASE AT ALL. And in a station with a medication in the stem, THE SECOND NET IS ALWAYS COMPLIANCE DRUG BY DRUG: 'you're on one for blood pressure and one for cholesterol — ARE YOU TAKING BOTH OF THEM AS PRESCRIBED?'

Acknowledge before you investigate — and never defend the drug — 'Thank you for telling me that, and for being honest with me — I'm really glad you raised it rather than just stopping quietly. You're right that these tablets can cause muscle aches; that's a recognised side effect.' He is braced for a telling-off and says so. 'Statins don't really do that' loses the consultation in one sentence, and the examiner will hear it — he goes cool and short and says 'So you don't believe me either'

The four discriminating questions — the block everyone forgets — 'Where exactly do you feel it — and is it on one side of your body, or both? Is it the muscles that are sore, or the joints themselves? Is it a dull ache, or a sharp, stabbing pain? And how long after you started the tablet did it begin?' His answers fit: both shoulders, hips and thighs, bilateral · the muscles, not the joint · a dull ache · about a month in. Accepting the patient's own diagnosis without asking these means you have agreed the statin is the cause without testing it — and you will have no answer when the examiner asks how you excluded arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica or a radiculopathy

Three more, including the two that separate this from a different station — 'Did it settle once you stopped? IS IT PAIN, OR IS THERE REAL WEAKNESS — any trouble getting up out of a chair or climbing stairs? Any morning stiffness, and how long does it last? AND — HAS YOUR URINE BEEN DARK AT ALL? Have you started any new medicines recently, including anything from the chemist?' WEAKNESS AND URINE COLOUR ARE THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT SEPARATE THE STANDARD STATION FROM THE RHABDOMYOLYSIS VARIANT, WHERE THE RECHALLENGE LOGIC THAT EARNS THE MARKS BECOMES DANGEROUS. ASK THEM EVERY TIME

Why he really stopped — keep screening after the first reason — 'Did your previous GP explain why you needed that tablet? What's your understanding of what it does?' → 'Not really. They just handed me a script. I don't see the point — my cholesterol's high but I feel completely fine.' that is a second, entirely separate barrier, and it is the one your education is going to fix. Then the rest of the adherence screen: trouble remembering, and — 'I ask everyone this' — any difficulty affording them

Restart it — and explain why a blood test today would be useless — 'I'd like you to start the tablet again. And here's why I'm not just doing a blood test today: you're already off it, so a test now would come back normal no matter what. It wouldn't tell us anything. So: restart it. If the aches come back, come straight back to me and I'll do a creatine kinase — ck. That tells us whether the muscle really is being affected by the tablet, and it decides what we do next.' Ordering the ck today and calling the normal result reassuring is one of the clearest single-item fails in this station

numbers: Creatine kinase, checked only if the aches recur on rechallenge · atorvastatin → rosuvastatin as the in-family switch · ezetimibe second line and last · the pattern that fits a statin: bilateral, proximal, muscle rather than joint, dull, beginning weeks to months after starting · washout a few weeks before rechallenge · intermittent dosing alternate days or twice weekly VERIFY

Perindopril side effects to ask about: dry cough and postural dizziness · lifestyle: 150 minutes a week · under 10 standard drinks a week, ≤4 in a day, 2 free days · BMI under 25 and waist under 94 cm · bloods at two weeks including thyroid and vitamin d · heart foundation 13 11 12 · and give the vaccination

setting: The sentence the station turns on: 'I'd like some tests, for three purposes — to look for damage to your organs, to look for an underlying cause, and to check your other risk factors.' then name every test. The run that fails is 'Full blood count, ESR, CRP, liver function, kidney function, thyroid function and refer him to a specialist' — no structure, no named tests, no reasoning. Name the organ or the condition first, then the test.
stem: General practice. Michael Doherty, 42, has returned to discuss the results of his 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. No examination. 8 minutes.
Results: 24-hour ABPM average 150/100 · clinic reading today 170/100 · and a fundus photograph showing silver and copper wiring, AV nipping and early disc blurring.
Aim roughly two minutes on the results, two on the risks, and four on the investigations.
tasks: Explain the significance of the results, including the retinal findings
Explain the risks and consequences of hypertension
Explain the further investigations you would arrange and why
time: Two / two / four minutes — the investigation task is the one that decides the station and it gets half the time · missing any of the three starred items fails: announcing the three purposes · a specific test named for every secondary cause · and eGFR plus urine ACR for the kidneys, not just electrolytes
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Honest reassurance about the eyes, and the safety decision inside it

'Your sight is fine now, and these early changes can settle once the pressure is controlled. That is exactly why I want to act rather than watch. If the swelling at the nerve is confirmed, I'd want you seen the same day rather than in a few weeks — I'll arrange that.' Grade 3 or 4 retinopathy is accelerated hypertension and means same-day review, with controlled reduction rather than a rapid drop

back.dx: Long-standing hypertension confirmed on ambulatory monitoring, with hypertensive retinopathy already present at 42. Purpose three, the cardiovascular risk factors, and the closing line: 'Whatever else we find — a fasting blood sugar, because diabetes is another major risk factor, and a fasting lipid profile. I'll look at your LDL and at your total cholesterol to HDL ratio, which is the one that best reflects risk. I'll also take baseline electrolytes and creatinine before we start any treatment. Because you are 42, I won't be calculating a formal cardiovascular risk score — those apply from 45 onwards — but these are still important risk factors in their own right. So: tests for organ damage, tests for an underlying cause, and tests for your other risk factors.' His two hidden worries: a stroke, because his father had one at 55 and never walked properly again, and being on tablets for the rest of his life. When he says 'So that's the stroke then, like dad': 'I'd put it the other way round — your father's stroke is part of why we've found this now instead of in ten years, and treating blood pressure is one of the most effective things we do in medicine for preventing exactly that.' and on tablets: answer honestly and briefly, and defer the detail to the next visit — with a pressure at this level and changes already in the eyes it is likely he will need medication, often long term, but it is safe, usually one tablet a day, and it is what prevents the events discussed. Two things he will not volunteer and that reward asking: the snoring and witnessed apnoeas, and the daily ibuprofen for his back plus a pseudoephedrine decongestant in hay-fever season — NSAIDs and decongestants lift blood pressure themselves and are a reversible contributor. His background: 10 cigarettes a day since his twenties · six to eight standard drinks over a weekend · no regular exercise · around 100 kg with a takeaway-heavy, salty diet · mother on blood pressure tablets. Safety-net: severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, sudden visual change, or any weakness or numbness — come straight in or call an ambulance. Then a teach-back, because the station expects it. The variants: one, the patient is 52 rather than 42 — 'Because you are over 45, I also want to work out your overall risk of a heart attack or stroke in the next five years', which guides how hard you push the blood pressure down and whether a cholesterol tablet is needed, so the sugar and cholesterol tests do double duty. Two, unmistakable papilloedema with small haemorrhages — 'I need to be straight with you. Your blood pressure is not only high, it is causing active damage right now. This changes my plan: rather than giving you test forms and seeing you next week, I want you assessed today.' that is grade 4 retinopathy and accelerated hypertension — same-day assessment, urgent bloods and urinalysis, and controlled BP reduction rather than a rapid drop. Three, potassium 3.1 on earlier bloods — 'A low potassium is a clue. There is a hormone made by a small gland above the kidney that controls salt and water, and if there is too much of it, it drives the blood pressure up and pushes the potassium down. The test is the aldosterone–renin ratio.' Correct the potassium first, and ideally take the sample before starting interfering antihypertensives, particularly spironolactone. Four, 'I don't want any tablets' — 'I hear you, and nothing gets prescribed today without your agreement. At this level, and with changes already in your eyes, lifestyle alone is unlikely to be enough — but it does make a genuine difference and it makes any medication work better. How about this: we do the tests, you start on the salt, the walking and cutting back the cigarettes, and we sit down together with the results and decide. Would that feel fair?'
plan: INTRODUCE, OPEN QUESTION, AND ELICIT CONCERNS BEFORE READING OUT A SINGLE NUMBER — the father's stroke surfaces here if you ask.
The clinic reading, then the ABPM average — and the sentence about ambulatory monitoring being the most accurate method, with both thresholds.
The retina: silver wiring · AV nipping · disc swelling — each named and translated, then the chronicity inference.
Honest reassurance on the sight, and same-day eye assessment if the disc swelling is confirmed.
RISKS GROUP ONE: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE — the biggest treatable risk factor for heart attack and stroke.
RISKS GROUP TWO: END-ORGAN DAMAGE, ORGAN BY ORGAN — eyes, kidneys, legs, coronary arteries, heart muscle. Then causes: genes, lifestyle, and sometimes a specific condition.
Announce the three purposes of investigation before naming a single test.
PURPOSE ONE, END-ORGAN DAMAGE: ECG and echocardiogram · eGFR AND URINE ACR · ankle–brachial index · eyes already done.

PURPOSE TWO, SECONDARY CAUSES: condition named before each test — thyroid, renal artery, coarctation, cortisol, kidneys, phaeochromocytoma, aldosterone, MEDICATIONS, SLEEP APNOEA. Ask about snoring and about over-the-counter medicines here.
PURPOSE THREE, RISK FACTORS: fasting glucose, fasting lipids with the TC:HDL ratio, and baseline electrolytes and creatinine before treatment — and why no formal risk score at 42.
Answer the tablets question honestly and briefly, deferring the detail to the next visit.
SAFETY-NET, FOLLOW-UP, AND TEACH-BACK: 'can you tell me back what you understood, so I know I've explained it clearly?'
back.planNote: the station's own aim is two minutes on results, two on risks and four on investigations
ask: THE RESULTS SET: 'I have your blood pressure results with me — IS THERE ANYTHING WORRYING YOU BEFORE I GO THROUGH THEM?' · 'The monitor checked your pressure roughly every 30 minutes across a full day and night.' · 'IT IS THE MOST ACCURATE AND RELIABLE WAY WE HAVE OF MEASURING BLOOD PRESSURE.'

THE RETINA SET: 'The blood tubes look shiny — we call that SILVER WIRING.' · 'Where the arteries and veins cross, the artery presses on the vein — AV NIPPING.' · 'There is swelling where the nerve attaches to the back of the eyeball.' · 'CHANGES LIKE THESE DO NOT HAPPEN IN DAYS OR WEEKS — YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE HAS BEEN HIGH FOR A LONG TIME.'

THE INVESTIGATION SET: 'I'd like some tests, AND THEY HAVE THREE PURPOSES.' · 'For your kidneys, TWO SPECIFIC TESTS — AN eGFR AND A URINE ALBUMIN-TO-CREATININE RATIO.' · 'A special ultrasound that shows blood flow — a RENAL ARTERY DOPPLER.' · 'You take a tablet at night and we check the hormone the next morning.' · AND THE CLOSE: 'CAN YOU TELL ME BACK WHAT YOU'VE UNDERSTOOD, SO I KNOW I'VE EXPLAINED IT CLEARLY?'
pefe: No examination — the findings are the two readings and the fundus photograph: clinic 170/100, ABPM average 150/100, and silver or copper wiring, AV nipping and early disc blurring. The retinopathy grades: 1 silver wiring · 2 AV nipping · 3 haemorrhages and exudates · 4 papilloedema, with grade 3 to 4 meaning accelerated hypertension and same-day review.

The history that rewards asking, none of which he volunteers: loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas and mid-afternoon exhaustion · daily ibuprofen for his back and a pseudoephedrine decongestant in hay-fever season · and his father's stroke at 55. He is otherwise completely asymptomatic — no headaches, no chest pain, no breathlessness, no visual problems and he is surprised his eyes are involved, no muscle cramps or weakness, and no episodes of pounding headache, sweating or palpitations.

He starts slightly dismissive — 'I feel completely fine' — pushes once at the eye findings with 'My vision is perfect, how can my eyes be damaged?', and says 'I've lost you' if you rattle off test names without explaining what they are for. If you say it is nothing to worry about he challenges you: 'Then why are you doing all these tests?'

The ABPM sentence that costs eight seconds and is a marked point — 'That machine measured your blood pressure ROUGHLY EVERY 30 MINUTES ACROSS A FULL DAY AND NIGHT, and gave an average of 150 over 100. I want to explain why that test matters: IT IS THE MOST ACCURATE AND MOST RELIABLE WAY WE HAVE OF MEASURING BLOOD PRESSURE, because it TAKES AWAY THE EFFECT OF BEING NERVOUS IN A DOCTOR'S ROOM and shows what your pressure is doing while you go about your normal day AND WHILE YOU SLEEP. So the 24-hour result ON ITS OWN IS ENOUGH FOR ME TO MAKE THE DIAGNOSIS — I DON'T NEED TO KEEP RE-CHECKING.' THRESHOLDS: HIGH ABOVE 130/80 ON A 24-HOUR MONITOR, ABOVE 140/90 IN THE CLINIC

The retina — describe, translate, then state the conclusion — 'The blood tubes LOOK SHINY RATHER THAN DULL — we call that SILVER WIRING. Where the arteries and the veins cross over each other, THE ARTERY IS PRESSING ON THE VEIN AND PINCHING IT — that's AV NIPPING. And there is SOME SWELLING WHERE THE NERVE ATTACHES TO THE BACK OF THE EYEBALL, at the OPTIC DISC.' THEN THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST: 'CHANGES LIKE THESE DO NOT HAPPEN IN A FEW DAYS OR A FEW WEEKS. THEY TAKE A LONG TIME TO DEVELOP. SO THIS TELLS ME YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE HAS BEEN HIGH FOR QUITE A WHILE — WE HAVE ONLY JUST FOUND IT.' Saying 'there's some hypertensive retinopathy' and stopping is the trap

Risks in two groups, organ by organ — GROUP ONE, CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE: 'high blood pressure is THE BIGGEST TREATABLE RISK FACTOR WE HAVE for a heart attack and a stroke, and for heart failure.' GROUP TWO, END-ORGAN DAMAGE: THE EYES, already seen · THE KIDNEYS, leading to chronic kidney disease · THE BLOOD TUBES IN THE LEGS, causing peripheral arterial disease · THE BLOOD TUBES OF THE HEART, causing coronary artery disease · AND THE HEART MUSCLE ITSELF, causing heart failure — 'WHICH MEANS THE HEART CANNOT PUMP BLOOD AROUND YOUR BODY AS WELL AS IT SHOULD.' On cause: a mixture of THINGS YOU CAN'T CHANGE, like genes and family history, and THINGS YOU CAN — smoking, alcohol, weight, salt, activity — and SOMETIMES A SPECIFIC UNDERLYING MEDICAL CAUSE

Purpose one — end-organ damage, with the kidney tests named separately — HEART: an ECG, 'a simple tracing of the heart's electrical activity, which shows WHETHER THE MUSCLE HAS THICKENED, whether the rhythm is irregular, and whether there has been PREVIOUS DAMAGE' — and an ECHOCARDIOGRAM if that raises anything. KIDNEYS, TWO SPECIFIC TESTS: AN eGFR, a blood test of how well the kidneys are filtering, AND A URINE ALBUMIN–CREATININE RATIO, IDEALLY ON THE FIRST URINE OF THE MORNING, LOOKING FOR PROTEIN LEAKING INTO THE URINE. LEGS: THE ANKLE–BRACHIAL INDEX, comparing the pressure in the arm and the ankle. EYES: already done today

Purpose two — secondary causes, condition named before each test — Thyroid → TSH · narrowing of the arteries to the kidneys → renal artery Doppler ultrasound · narrowing of the main artery from the heart → Doppler echocardiogram · excess cortisol → dexamethasone suppression test, 'Where you take a tablet at night and we check the hormone the next morning' · kidney disease → the eGFR and urine ACR already named · a rare adrenal tumour → plasma metanephrines · an excess of a salt-controlling hormone → aldosterone–renin ratio with potassium · medications → a careful review including anti-inflammatories and decongestants · and sleep apnoea → a sleep study. He snores, his wife says he stops breathing, and he is exhausted by mid-afternoon — ask, and the sleep study moves up the list rather than down

setting: Add a second class, do not double the first. Doubling the amlodipine to 10 mg is the intuitive move, it is what most candidates say, and it is the single thing this station was designed to detect. And note the wording of the task: lifestyle advice is correct medicine and will not score here — the marks are in why the current tablet isn't working, confirming the reading, adding a second class, naming real drugs at real doses, the monitoring plan, and the target and review interval.
stem: General practice. Mr James Corrigan, 50, has attended for a shingles vaccination. The practice nurse checked his blood pressure and it was 160/100, and it remained elevated on a second measurement.
He is a known hypertensive already on treatment: amlodipine 5 mg daily. Blood tests six months ago, including the screen for secondary causes, were all normal.
Task 1 is four minutes of focused history; task 2 is a medication-focused management plan, as the stem specifies.

Explain your management plan — the stem specifies a medication-focused plan
time: Four minutes of history, three and a half on the medication plan, thirty seconds to close · if you spend more than about thirty seconds on lifestyle he looks at his watch and says 'Yes, I've heard all that before' — and the role-player is briefed to mark it

back.dx: HYPERTENSION ABOVE TARGET ON MONOTHERAPY — CONFIRM IT, FIND THE REASON, ADD A SECOND CLASS, MONITOR, REVIEW. THE SINGLE-PILL COMBINATION POINT, WHICH SHOWS CURRENT PRACTICE: FROM 1 APRIL 2026 PBS RESTRICTIONS CHANGED SO THAT DUAL-THERAPY FIXED-DOSE COMBINATIONS MAY BE PRESCRIBED AS INITIAL TREATMENT FOR HYPERTENSION — 30-day items as Unrestricted Benefit listings, 60-day items as Restricted Benefit for stable patients. Before that, subsidised therapy COULD NOT BE STARTED with a combination pill. For a man who already takes amlodipine and needs a second agent, A PERINDOPRIL–AMLODIPINE COMBINATION KEEPS HIM ON ONE TABLET A DAY, which is easier to remember and usually cheaper — BUT IT DOES NOT CHANGE THE UNDERLYING DECISION, WHICH IS STILL TO ADD A SECOND CLASS RATHER THAN UPTITRATE THE FIRST VERIFY. THE COMPLICATIONS SCREEN, BY ORGAN: EYES — blurring or change in vision · HEART — chest pain or tightness walking uphill, breathlessness lying flat or waking him · KIDNEYS — passing less urine, frothy urine, nocturia, itching · BRAIN — weakness, numbness, speech trouble, blank episodes · LEGS — calf cramping on walking that eases with rest. THE VARIANTS, SCRIPTED: ONE, HE IS NOT ACTUALLY TAKING IT — 'I probably miss three or four days a week, I feel fine so I forget.' 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME — THAT CHANGES WHAT I'D DO. IT WOULD BE THE WRONG MOVE TO ADD A SECOND TABLET ON TOP OF ONE THAT ISN'T BEING TAKEN; I'D BE TREATING THE WRONG PROBLEM AND YOU'D BE ON TWO TABLETS YOU DON'T NEED. What gets in the way — remembering, the cost, the trip to the chemist, or that it's hard to take something for a problem you can't feel?' Link it to a daily habit, set an alarm, arrange a repeat script, and RECHECK IN FOUR WEEKS WITH HIM ACTUALLY ON THE TABLET. TWO, A DAILY ANTI-INFLAMMATORY — 'anti-inflammatories PUSH BLOOD PRESSURE UP IN THEIR OWN RIGHT AND BLUNT THE EFFECT OF BLOOD PRESSURE TABLETS, so part of the reason your reading is high MAY BE SITTING IN YOUR MEDICINE CUPBOARD. And there's a second reason to be careful: an ACE inhibitor plus later a water tablet WHILE STILL TAKING AN ANTI-INFLAMMATORY IS THE TRIPLE WHAMMY, WHICH CAN DAMAGE THE KIDNEYS, particularly with dehydration.' Manage the back differently — regular paracetamol, a topical anti-inflammatory, physiotherapy — stop the tablets, and RECHECK BEFORE ADDING ANYTHING. THREE, SWOLLEN ANKLES ON AMLODIPINE — 'that's a known effect and IT GETS WORSE WITH HIGHER DOSES, WHICH IS ANOTHER REASON NOT TO DOUBLE IT. ADDING PERINDOPRIL HELPS TWICE OVER: it lowers the pressure, AND IT TENDS TO REDUCE THAT ANKLE SWELLING RATHER THAN ADD TO IT. WHAT I WOULD NOT DO IS TREAT THE SWELLING WITH A WATER TABLET, BECAUSE THAT ISN'T WHAT'S CAUSING IT.' FOUR, STILL UNCONTROLLED AT SIX WEEKS AT 154/96 — recheck adherence, technique and home readings, re-ask about anti-inflammatories and alcohol, then ADD THE THIRD CLASS, A THIAZIDE-LIKE DIURETIC SUCH AS INDAPAMIDE 1.5 mg DAILY, rather than pushing either existing drug up, with electrolytes again a week or two later. IF HE REMAINS ABOVE 140/90 ON THREE AGENTS INCLUDING A DIURETIC AT MAXIMALLY TOLERATED DOSES, THAT MEETS THE DEFINITION OF RESISTANT HYPERTENSION — add SPIRONOLACTONE 12.5 TO 25 mg DAILY with close potassium monitoring, RE-SCREEN FOR SECONDARY CAUSES INCLUDING SLEEP APNOEA AND PRIMARY ALDOSTERONISM, and refer to a nephrologist or hypertension clinic. FIVE, THE EXAMINER ASKS ABOUT CHANGING GUIDANCE — 'I would treat to under 140 over 90 in line with current Australian guidance, WHILE ACKNOWLEDGING THAT THE NATIONAL GUIDELINE IS BEING REVISED: the 2026 Australian hypertension guideline is a HEART FOUNDATION, STROKE FOUNDATION AND HYPERTENSION AUSTRALIA COLLABORATION due in the second half of this year, and its authors have signalled BETTER MEASUREMENT STANDARDS, LOWER TARGETS AND GREATER USE OF COMBINATION THERAPY. If a lower target is adopted I would apply it with the same caution about POSTURAL SYMPTOMS IN OLDER PATIENTS' VERIFY. HIS HIDDEN AGENDA: he is worried about BEING ON TABLETS FOREVER, and had privately assumed one tablet meant the problem was HANDLED. He asks at the end whatever happens — answer honestly rather than reassuringly: possibly long term, BUT IT ISN'T A ONE-WAY STREET, and if weight, alcohol and activity change substantially the dose can sometimes be reduced. HIS FATHER HAD A HEART ATTACK AT 55, AND HE SAYS IT AND PAUSES TO SEE WHETHER YOU NOTICE.
plan: WIPE, open question, ACKNOWLEDGE THAT THIS ISN'T WHAT HE CAME IN FOR — and promise the vaccination.
When diagnosed and with what numbers · what he takes now and at what dose.
The four-part probe: adherence · side effects including ankle swelling · understanding · other medicines including over-the-counter.
Follow-up and home readings, then the complications screen by organ.
The two causes with no blood test: sleep apnoea, and substances or energy drinks.
RISK FACTORS FAST: alcohol, smoking, diet and salt, activity, FAMILY HISTORY WITH THE AGE, diabetes, kidneys, cholesterol, allergies.
CONFIRM THE READING BEFORE COMMITTING — one more check here or at home, while planning on the basis that it is real.
STATE THE TARGET, THEN ADD RATHER THAN DOUBLE — WITH THE REASON. Expect the push and answer the mechanism.
Two named options at real doses with honest trade-offs — then ask his preference.
MENTION THE SINGLE-PILL COMBINATION as a way to keep him on one tablet a day.
Dose · blood test at 1–2 weeks with the thresholds · review at 4–6 weeks · adherence emphasis · safety-net.
One sentence on lifestyle, the vaccination, and the summary.

ask: THE PROBE SET: 'A lot of people find it hard to take a daily tablet for something they can't feel — ROUGHLY HOW MANY DO YOU MISS IN A FORTNIGHT?' · 'HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY SWELLING OF YOUR ANKLES?' · 'Anything you buy yourself — ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES, COLD AND SINUS TABLETS, HERBAL REMEDIES?' · 'Has anyone told you that you snore, OR STOP BREATHING IN YOUR SLEEP?'

The decision set: 'You came in expecting a needle, and nerves can push the pressure up — I'd like one more check.' · 'We're aiming to keep it under 140 over 90.' · 'The best next step is to add a second tablet rather than double the one you're on.' · 'Adding a small dose of a different tablet lowers the pressure more than doubling the first — and causes fewer side effects, because side effects come with higher doses.' · 'Most people with blood pressure like yours end up on two tablets. That's normal.'

THE DRUG SET: 'Perindopril also PROTECTS THE HEART AND THE KIDNEYS — the two organs blood pressure damages over time.' · 'About one in ten people get a dry cough; if that happens WE SWAP TO A CLOSELY RELATED TABLET.' · 'I'd want a blood test ONE TO TWO WEEKS AFTER YOU START, to check your kidney function and your potassium.' · 'The tablet takes FOUR TO SIX WEEKS to reach full effect.' · 'IF YOU FEEL DIZZY, RING ME RATHER THAN JUST STOPPING THE TABLET.'
pefe: NO EXAMINATION — THE READING IS GIVEN AS 160/100 ON TWO MEASUREMENTS, AND THE HISTORY IS THE ASSESSMENT. IN VERSION A THERE IS NOTHING HIDDEN: he takes the amlodipine every morning beside the kettle, HAS NO SIDE EFFECTS, TAKES NOTHING ELSE AT ALL, snores but has never been told he stops breathing, and feels completely well. THE STATION IS TESTING THE PRESCRIBING DECISION RATHER THAN THE DETECTIVE WORK.

WHAT HE GIVES ON BACKGROUND: diagnosed three years ago at a work medical around 155/95 · NO GP REVIEW FOR ABOUT A YEAR AND NO HOME MACHINE · two or three beers most nights, FIFTEEN TO TWENTY A WEEK · quit smoking eight years ago · plenty of takeaway and HE SALTS HIS FOOD · desk job with almost no exercise · FATHER'S HEART ATTACK AT 55 · no diabetes, kidney or cholesterol problems, no allergies.

The role-player marks it a fail if you: double the amlodipine · name no drug or no dose · start a beta blocker · never mention a blood test after starting the ACE inhibitor · spend more than about thirty seconds on lifestyle · or never come back to the vaccination.

The four-part probe on the existing tablet — ADHERENCE, ASKED WITHOUT JUDGEMENT: 'a lot of people find it hard to take a daily tablet for something they can't actually feel — ROUGHLY HOW MANY DOSES WOULD YOU SAY YOU MISS IN A FORTNIGHT? Do you ever run out before you get to the chemist?' SIDE EFFECTS, NAMING THE RIGHT ONE: 'anything since you started it, particularly ANY SWELLING OF YOUR ANKLES, flushing, headaches or dizziness?' UNDERSTANDING: 'has anyone explained why we treat blood pressure and what it protects you from?' OTHER MEDICINES: 'including things you buy yourself — ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES LIKE IBUPROFEN, COLD AND SINUS TABLETS, STEROIDS, or any herbal remedies?' TWO FAILURES LIVE HERE — ESCALATING THERAPY IN A MAN WHO TAKES HIS TABLET THREE DAYS A WEEK, AND MISSING A DAILY NSAID BEFORE YOU ADD AN ACE INHIBITOR

What 'Investigations normal' does not exclude — The stem says the secondary screen was normal, which reasonably excludes renal, endocrine and thyroid causes. IT DOES NOT EXCLUDE THE TWO COMMONEST REVERSIBLE CONTRIBUTORS, BECAUSE NEITHER HAS A BLOOD TEST: DRUGS AND SUBSTANCES, AND OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNOEA. 'HAS ANYONE TOLD YOU THAT YOU SNORE LOUDLY, OR STOP BREATHING OR GASP IN YOUR SLEEP? Do you wake up unrefreshed or feel sleepy during the day?' — plus recreational drugs and energy drinks. Asking both, briefly, SHOWS YOU UNDERSTOOD WHAT THE PHRASE MEANS

Confirm before you commit — fifteen seconds, and it costs nothing — 'YOU CAME IN EXPECTING A NEEDLE, AND NERVES CAN PUSH THE PRESSURE UP. So I'd like one more check — either here in a week, or with a machine at home over the next week — SO THAT WE'RE CHANGING YOUR TREATMENT FOR THE RIGHT REASON. But your reading is high enough that I'd plan on the basis that it is real.' The whole hypertension cluster rests on NOT ACTING ON SINGLE READINGS, and saying it even when the stem has given you two SHOWS THE EXAMINER YOU HOLD THE PRINCIPLE RATHER THAN RECITING A RECALL

The sentence the station exists for — 'We're aiming to get you under 140 over 90, and you're well above that on one tablet. The best next step is to add a second tablet rather than double the one you're already taking. I know that sounds like the wrong way round — but adding a small dose of a different tablet usually brings the pressure down more than doubling the first one, and it causes fewer side effects, because side effects tend to come with higher doses. Most people with blood pressure like yours end up on two tablets, and that's normal rather than a sign anything has gone wrong.' He pushes once — 'Why can't I just take two of the ones I've got?' — and you must explain the mechanism, naming ankle oedema, not just assert it

Two named options with honest trade-offs, then ask his preference — Perindopril, an ACE inhibitor — preferred because as well as lowering the pressure it protects the heart and the kidneys, the two organs high blood pressure damages over time. Downsides: about one in ten get a dry, tickly cough, and then you swap to a closely related tablet that doesn't cause it · and a blood test one to two weeks after starting for kidney function and potassium, where a small change in both is expected, but if eGFR drops by more than about a quarter or the potassium goes above range, stop and rethink. Or a thiazide such as indapamide — downsides are low potassium, gout if he is prone, a nudge up in blood sugar, and postural light-headedness. If he mentions gout, the thiazide is out

Close with the four items that make it a plan rather than a gesture — THE DOSE — perindopril 5 mg once daily alongside the amlodipine · THE BLOOD TEST at one to two weeks · THE REVIEW INTERVAL at four to six weeks, BECAUSE THAT IS HOW LONG THE TABLET TAKES TO REACH FULL EFFECT · AND THE TARGET, under 140/90. Then: 'the most important thing is to take both tablets every day at the same time — MISSING DOSES IS THE COMMONEST REASON BLOOD PRESSURE STAYS UP. If you feel dizzy, RING ME RATHER THAN JUST STOPPING THE TABLET.' AND GIVE HIM THE SHINGLES VACCINATION HE CAME IN FOR

setting: You must find the one specific reason this patient stopped, and your management must solve that reason. A flawless generic lecture on why blood pressure matters, delivered to a patient who simply cannot afford the tablets, is a fail. The role-player brief carries six interchangeable barriers — cost, memory, education, a life event, a side effect, or a belief — and you do not decide which it is until she tells you.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Mary Doyle, 40, attending for her influenza vaccination. 8 minutes.
Essential hypertension diagnosed two years ago; prescribed perindopril; has recently stopped taking it. Today BP 165/100, asymptomatic. Recent renal function, LFTs, lipids and glucose all normal.

Before anything else: read the blood pressure and ask about headache and dizziness. At 165/100 with no symptoms you are in this station. At over 180/110 with symptoms you are in its twin, and everything below is the wrong answer.

back.dx: ESSENTIAL HYPERTENSION WITH MEDICATION NON-ADHERENCE — FIND THE BARRIER, THEN DISMANTLE IT. THE PHARMACIST IS THE MOST COMMONLY MISSED SCORED ITEM IN ADHERENCE STATIONS: 'I'd like to BRING THE PHARMACIST ONTO OUR TEAM. I can arrange a MEDICATION REVIEW — here we call it a HOME MEDICINES REVIEW. They'll go through your medicines with you properly, EXPLAIN THEM BETTER THAN I CAN IN A SHORT APPOINTMENT, and follow you up. YOU SEE THEM MONTHLY FOR SCRIPTS, SO THEY'RE A FAR BETTER SAFETY NET THAN I AM. They can TEXT YOU REMINDERS when a script is due, and MANY PHARMACIES WILL DELIVER TO YOUR DOOR. If tablets ever get confusing, they can make you a WEBSTER PACK.' If she bristles at the Webster pack, NORMALISE IT — IT IS AN OPTION, NOT A VERDICT. LIFESTYLE WITH NUMBERS, BECAUSE 'EAT HEALTHY AND EXERCISE MORE' SCORES NOTHING: SALT UNDER ABOUT 5 TO 6 GRAMS A DAY, which mostly means less processed and takeaway food · a diet high in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and low-fat dairy · ALCOHOL UNDER 10 STANDARD DRINKS A WEEK AND NO MORE THAN 4 IN ONE DAY · 150 TO 300 MINUTES OF MODERATE ACTIVITY A WEEK PLUS RESISTANCE WORK TWICE A WEEK · AND EVEN 5 TO 10 PER CENT WEIGHT LOSS MAKES A REAL DIFFERENCE · QUITLINE 13 7848 if she smokes. IF SHE SAYS IT IS A LOT, PICK ONE WITH HER RATHER THAN PRESSING ALL FIVE. THEN THE 4 Rs AND THE CLOSE: referrals to a DIETITIAN AND EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGIST under a CHRONIC CONDITION MANAGEMENT PLAN so they are subsidised · HEART FOUNDATION reading · REVIEW IN FOUR WEEKS to check she has restarted, see how she is tolerating it and recheck the pressure, with home or pharmacy readings in between · RED FLAGS: bad headaches, dizziness, blurred vision, chest pain, breathlessness, or weakness or numbness · AND THE INFLUENZA VACCINATION SHE ACTUALLY ATTENDED FOR, WHICH COSTS ONE SENTENCE AND READS AS GENUINE PATIENT-CENTREDNESS. THE SIX BARRIERS AND THEIR MATCHING SOLUTIONS: COST — prescribe the GENERIC BRAND, explain the PBS SAFETY NET and how to track it, check CONCESSION CARD ELIGIBILITY and Centrelink support, and write a LONGER SCRIPT so the dispensing fee comes round less often. MEMORY — 'forgetting is very common', and do two things: CHECK THE MEMORY PROPERLY with a short cognitive test plus the routine bloods, AND MAKE IT EASIER with a Webster pack, phone alarms and a family member checking in. DO NOT LAUNCH INTO DEMENTIA MANAGEMENT — INITIAL ASSESSMENT ONLY. EDUCATION — the education block itself is the solution. LIFE EVENT — 'life gets in the way and that's very human. I CAN'T GIVE YOU MORE HOURS, BUT I CAN MAKE THIS TAKE FEWER OF THEM': a longer script, pharmacy text reminders, and DELIVERY, WHICH MATTERS WHEN YOU'RE FORTY MINUTES OUT OF TOWN. DO NOT SYMPATHISE WITHOUT OFFERING A SINGLE PRACTICAL FIX. SIDE EFFECT, THE COUGH — 'that dry cough is a WELL-KNOWN EFFECT OF THAT PARTICULAR CLASS, it happens to ABOUT ONE IN TEN PEOPLE, IT'S NOT IN YOUR HEAD, AND IT ISN'T SOMETHING YOU HAVE TO PUT UP WITH. It usually settles within a few weeks of stopping, and we have SEVERAL OTHER CLASSES THAT LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE JUST AS WELL AND DON'T CAUSE IT.' DO NOT PERSUADE HER TO PERSEVERE — SWITCH THE DRUG. BELIEF — 'I'd like to understand what you've been using and what appeals to you about it, and I do need to check nothing interacts. I'M NOT GOING TO PRETEND THE EVIDENCE IS EQUAL, BUT I'D MUCH RATHER WORK WITH YOU THAN ARGUE WITH YOU. Could we do this: KEEP DOING WHAT YOU'RE DOING, ADD THE TABLET, AND MEASURE YOUR PRESSURE OVER THREE MONTHS. IF THE NUMBERS SAY WE DON'T NEED IT, I'LL BE THE FIRST TO SAY SO.' DO NOT DISMISS TRADITIONAL MEDICINE OUTRIGHT, AND OFFER AN INTERPRETER IF LANGUAGE IS A FACTOR. AND THE VARIANT WHERE IT TURNS INTO ITS TWIN: mid-consultation she says 'ACTUALLY, I HAVE BEEN GETTING HEADACHES, AND I FELT DIZZY THIS MORNING', and you recheck at 186/118. 'THANK YOU FOR MENTIONING THAT — I NEED TO STOP AND TAKE IT SERIOUSLY BEFORE WE GO ANY FURTHER.' Characterise the headaches, ask about blurring, weakness, numbness, speech trouble, chest pain and vomiting, RECHECK THE PRESSURE YOURSELF — then: 'your reading is very high AND YOU HAVE SYMPTOMS WITH IT. That's a HYPERTENSIVE URGENCY, and it needs ASSESSMENT IN HOSPITAL TODAY rather than a script from me. I'm going to arrange an ambulance now — I DON'T WANT YOU DRIVING YOURSELF. We'll come back to the tablets once you're safe.' THIS IS THE AUTOMATIC FAIL IF MISSED. ON THE TARGET, IF CHALLENGED: 'below 140 over 90 as a minimum, and BELOW 130 OVER 80 IF SHE TOLERATES IT AND HER ABSOLUTE CARDIOVASCULAR RISK IS HIGH. Guidance differs a little between bodies on how low to push, so I'd INDIVIDUALISE IT AND AVOID SYMPTOMATIC HYPOTENSION' VERIFY.

SHE IS COMPLETELY ASYMPTOMATIC AND SAYS SO CLEARLY: no headache, dizziness, blurred vision, chest pain, breathlessness, calf pain, weakness, numbness or speech trouble — 'I FEEL COMPLETELY FINE, THAT'S HALF THE PROBLEM, ISN'T IT.' She stopped SIX TO EIGHT WEEKS AGO, has HAD NO GP REVIEW FOR ABOUT A YEAR, and HAS NEVER CHECKED HER OWN PRESSURE. Non-smoker, two or three standard drinks a week, no other medicines, no allergies.

SHE PUSHES ONCE WITH 'BUT I FEEL COMPLETELY FINE, SO WHY DOES IT MATTER?' AND ONLY ACCEPTS THE ANSWER IF YOU EXPLAIN THAT IT IS SILENT AND THE DAMAGE IS IRREVERSIBLE. She warms up if you thank her for being honest, and goes quiet and defensive if you lecture or sound disapproving. At the end she asks 'AM I GOING TO BE ON THIS FOREVER?' or 'HAVE I ALREADY DONE DAMAGE?' — and the honest answer to the second is that her recent bloods and lack of symptoms are reassuring, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY RESTARTING NOW MATTERS.

Elicit the concern early, and do not react to it — 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME THAT SO OPENLY — A LOT OF PEOPLE WOULDN'T, and it's really useful to know. And of course we'll do the flu vaccination as well. IS THERE ANYTHING IN PARTICULAR ABOUT THE MEDICATION THAT'S BEEN WORRYING YOU?' If you ask in the first two minutes she gives the barrier; IF YOU NEVER ASK SHE HOLDS IT BACK UNTIL ABOUT FIVE MINUTES AND MARKS YOU DOWN. And she becomes quiet and defensive if you lecture, say 'you must', or sound disapproving

Three boxes — doctor, medication, patient — DOCTOR AND SYSTEM: 'DID ANYONE EXPLAIN TO YOU WHY WE TREAT HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE? And did anyone tell you what can happen if it isn't treated? Did you feel you got the chance to ask questions?' — framed NEUTRALLY, because you are checking her understanding, NOT AUDITING A COLLEAGUE. MEDICATION: side effects, AND SPECIFICALLY A DRY COUGH IN SOMEONE ON AN ACE INHIBITOR, plus postural dizziness and whether once-daily dosing is manageable. PATIENT: FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY · other medicines including over-the-counter and herbal · HOW DO YOU FEEL ABOUT TAKING BLOOD PRESSURE MEDICATION GENERALLY · memory · who she lives with and support · ANYTHING SIGNIFICANT CHANGED RECENTLY · AND ARE YOU TRYING ANYTHING ELSE INSTEAD

Ask, then wait — the highest-yield question in the station — Firing all seven patient-factor questions as a checklist is the trap. Ask, then wait: the one she hesitates on is usually the real answer. And 'How do you feel about taking blood pressure medication?' Is the highest-yield question here — give it silence

Continuity of care, and the pair that separates the two stations — 'Have you been having regular follow-ups with a GP for this? Any regular blood tests? And do you ever check your blood pressure yourself, at home or at the chemist?' — THIS IS WHAT TURNS 'SHE STOPPED HER TABLETS' INTO 'SHE FELL OUT OF CARE', AND IT DIRECTLY GENERATES YOUR FOLLOW-UP PLAN. THEN THE COMPLICATIONS SCREEN, ENDING WITH THE PAIR YOU CANNOT SKIP BECAUSE SHE LOOKS WELL: 'AND — IMPORTANTLY — ANY HEADACHES OR DIZZINESS?'

Lead the education with silent, not with the scary list — 'High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms at all. You can feel completely well and still have it — which is exactly why it's dangerous. We're not treating you to make you feel better today, because you already feel fine. We're treating you to prevent damage.' then the organs and the killer word: heart, kidneys, eyes, brain and the blood vessels in the legs, plus heart attack and stroke — 'And here's the part that matters most: once that damage happens, we can't reverse it.' if she doesn't accept that a symptomless condition can be harmful, the complication list lands as scaremongering. Then check understanding

Name her barrier back and solve it — the moment the examiner is listening for — 'Now, you told me at the start that [the cost was the problem / you'd been forgetting / nobody explained it / the cough was unbearable], and I want to make sure we actually deal with that rather than talk around it.' then the matching solution. If that moment never comes, the station is lost however good everything else was. And restart with a choice: 'If the perindopril suited you we can go back to it; if it didn't, we have several other classes — I'd rather we pick something you'll actually take than something that looks best on paper'

back.dx: HYPERTENSIVE URGENCY — severe hypertension with symptoms but no clinical evidence of acute end-organ damage, the last phrase being scored and only earned by having asked. The management, in order. First, the sentence that saves the station: 'I'm going to arrange an ambulance now and send you to the emergency department. I don't want you driving yourself — you're dizzy, and if things change on the way I'd rather you were with paramedics. Is there someone I can call to meet you there?' He resists once — 'Can't I just drive over myself?' — and agreeing is a fail, as is never saying the word ambulance at all: 'Go to hospital sometime today' does not score as escalation. Second, what will happen there, named rather than vague: an ECG · blood tests for kidney function and a heart enzyme · a urine sample for protein or blood · probably a chest x-ray · a CT brain if there is any concern · and fundoscopy, because the pressure shows there. 'They'll do some tests' scores nothing — ECG and kidney function are the core. Third, treatment and why it is slow: 'In your situation we use tablets rather than a drip — usually one called amlodipine — and we bring it down gradually, over a day or two. That sounds counter-intuitive, but dropping the pressure too fast is as dangerous as leaving it high: your brain, heart and kidneys have adapted to this pressure, and if it falls suddenly they don't get enough blood.' Promising rapid IV treatment is a knowledge error — IV therapy and intensive care belong to an emergency, where there is acute organ damage. Fourth, restart his usual antihypertensive once the pressure is controlled and the symptoms have settled — never returning to it at all is half a management plan. Fifth, and only now, ninety seconds of adherence work: high blood pressure normally causes no symptoms at all, so it is very easy to feel there's no point taking something daily — but it damages heart, kidneys, eyes, brain and the vessels in the legs, raises the risk of heart attack and stroke, and once that damage happens we can't reverse it. 'That's why we treat it: to prevent, not to fix.' then a pharmacist medication review on discharge with script reminders and a webster pack if remembering is the issue, salt, alcohol, activity, weight and smoking, and review shortly after he gets home. Sixth, red flags before the ambulance arrives: if the headache suddenly becomes much worse, if vision changes, if he feels weak or numb, if speech is affected, if he gets chest pain or starts vomiting — tell the paramedics straight away. If the bell is close, prioritise ambulance → ECG and bloods → slow reduction → red flags, and let the lifestyle content go. The variants: a, thunderclap — 'It hit me all at once an hour ago, like being struck on the back of the head', with vomiting, tinnitus and neck stiffness at 192/118: 'The way that headache came on — suddenly and at full force — is something we always take very seriously, because it can mean bleeding around the brain. That's not something I can rule out here. I'm calling an ambulance now: you need an urgent CT scan of your head, and if that's clear they may still need to do a lumbar puncture. The high blood pressure may well be a consequence of what's happening in your head rather than the cause, so we won't be rushing to lower it.' B, hypertensive emergency at 224/138 with confusion, vomiting, blurred vision and papilloedema: 'Your pressure is extremely high and it's already affecting you — your vision, your thinking, and the changes I can see at the back of your eyes. We call that a hypertensive emergency.' Hospital immediately, high-dependency or intensive care, IV medication through a drip with continuous monitoring, and consider MedSTAR retrieval from a rural site. C, pain-driven at 188/112 with agonising renal colic and no headache: 'Your blood pressure is very high, but I think the pain is a large part of why. Severe pain pushes blood pressure up, and the right first treatment here is strong pain relief, not a blood pressure tablet. Let's get on TOP of the pain, then recheck the pressure and see where we really stand.' Whichever version you get, every one opens with a known hypertensive who stopped his tablets — and that fact is never the answer on its own. Get the number, get the symptoms, screen for deficit, look for a cause, and only then decide whether you are writing a script or calling an ambulance.

WE CALL THAT A HYPERTENSIVE URGENCY.' · 'Pressure this high can start to damage organs quickly — particularly your brain.' · 'I'M GOING TO ARRANGE AN AMBULANCE NOW AND SEND YOU TO THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT.' · 'I DON'T WANT YOU DRIVING YOURSELF — YOU'RE DIZZY, AND THINGS CAN CHANGE.' · 'WE BRING IT DOWN GRADUALLY — DROPPING IT TOO FAST IS AS DANGEROUS AS LEAVING IT HIGH.'
pefe: Ask for the observations by name and repeat the pressure yourself: pulse 88 regular, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, BSL 6.1, BP 184/118 right and 182/116 left, alert and orientated.

HE DOES NOT VOLUNTEER THE REASSURING NEGATIVES — MAKE HIM ASK FOR EACH ONE. HE HAS NO visual change, weakness, numbness, slurred speech, gait difficulty, witnessed confusion, fits, chest pain, TEARING BACK PAIN, breathlessness, orthopnoea, vomiting, tinnitus, neck stiffness, photophobia, other pain or urinary retention · NO NEW MEDICINES, NSAIDs, DECONGESTANTS, STEROIDS OR RECREATIONAL DRUGS. Background: hypertension eight years on perindopril 5 mg, STOPPED TWO MONTHS AGO BECAUSE HE FELT WELL AND THE PACKET RAN OUT, no side effects, no cost or memory problem, NOBODY EVER EXPLAINED WHY HE NEEDED IT, 10 cigarettes a day for 30 years, a few beers at weekends, AND REDUNDANCIES ANNOUNCED AT WORK LAST MONTH.

THE ESCALATION SWITCH FOR A SECOND RUN CHANGES THREE ANSWERS: THE HEADACHE IS 10/10 AND CAME ON SUDDENLY AN HOUR AGO · HE HAS VOMITED TWICE · HIS VISION HAS BEEN BLURRED SINCE · AND 'MY WIFE SAYS I KEEP REPEATING MYSELF'. That is subarachnoid haemorrhage or hypertensive encephalopathy, and the management shifts to URGENT CT BRAIN, IV THERAPY AND INTENSIVE CARE rather than oral amlodipine.

Park the tablets — he offers them in his first sentence — 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME — WE'LL DEFINITELY COME BACK TO THE TABLETS. FIRST I WANT TO UNDERSTAND THIS HEADACHE PROPERLY, BECAUSE THAT'S WHAT'S BROUGHT YOU IN.' He is briefed to cooperate happily if you start asking compliance questions early AND LET YOU DIG YOURSELF IN. He also asks 'IS IT BECAUSE I STOPPED THE TABLETS?' at about three minutes

The headache in full — and onset is the question that matters — Site · WHEN IT STARTED AND WHETHER IT CAME ON SUDDENLY OR BUILT UP GRADUALLY · character · radiation into the neck · severity out of ten · constant or intermittent and whether it is worsening · and modifiers — bright light, noise, coughing, bending forward. His answer: forehead and back, BUILT UP SINCE TUESDAY WITH NOTHING SUDDEN, dull pressure, about six out of ten, slowly worsening, paracetamol helps. FAILING TO ASK ABOUT ONSET IS THE TRAP: SUDDEN THUNDERCLAP ONSET MEANS SUBARACHNOID HAEMORRHAGE UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, AND CHANGES YOUR MANAGEMENT FROM AMBULANCE-FOR-ASSESSMENT TO AMBULANCE-FOR-URGENT-CT

Pin down 'Dizzy', then run the deficit screen — 'DO YOU FEEL LIGHTHEADED, AS THOUGH YOU MIGHT FAINT — OR IS THERE A SPINNING SENSATION, AS IF THE ROOM IS MOVING AROUND YOU?' The word covers PRESYNCOPE, VERTIGO, DISEQUILIBRIUM AND GENERALISED WEAKNESS, EACH WITH A DIFFERENT DIFFERENTIAL, and offering two options is the fastest way to pin it down. THEN THE DEFICIT AND ENCEPHALOPATHY SCREEN: vision · weakness or numbness in face, arm or leg · slurred speech or word-finding · gait · HAS ANYONE SAID YOU SEEM CONFUSED · fits, blackouts or lost time. A POSITIVE ANSWER HERE CONVERTS AN URGENCY INTO AN EMERGENCY AND CHANGES THE WHOLE DISPOSITION

The causes block everyone omits — say out loud that you are looking — 'I ALSO WANT TO MAKE SURE NOTHING ELSE IS PUSHING YOUR PRESSURE UP LIKE THIS.' Chest pain, tightness or breathlessness · TEARING PAIN THROUGH TO THE BACK · orthopnoea or PND · nausea or vomiting · TINNITUS · neck stiffness or photophobia · PAIN ANYWHERE ELSE IN THE LAST FEW DAYS — back, joints, tummy, teeth · recent stressful events · URINARY RETENTION · anything new including ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES, DECONGESTANTS OR STEROIDS · and 'I ask everyone this — ANY RECREATIONAL DRUGS SUCH AS AMPHETAMINES OR COCAINE?' IF HE REPORTS PAIN, ANALGESIA BECOMES YOUR FIRST-LINE ANTIHYPERTENSIVE

Name it plainly, in the honest register — 'Your blood pressure today is very high — 185 over 120 — and you're having symptoms with it. That combination has a name: we call it a hypertensive urgency. It means I'm not comfortable managing it here with a prescription. Pressure this high can start to damage organs quite quickly — particularly your brain, but also your heart, kidneys and eyes. The tests for that are in the hospital, not in this room. Most people in your situation do well — but it needs to be checked today.' Neither extreme: 'You're about to have a stroke' is frightening and unjustified, 'It's probably nothing' is unsafe. The register is serious, checkable, today, and most people do well

At her follow-up you recorded a high blood pressure, arranged repeated clinic and home readings, and the average is consistent with hypertension at around 160/100 mmHg. She is generally healthy, eats well, exercises regularly, and her BMI is 23.
