back.dx: COMBINED ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE-INDUCED HYPERTENSION — 'The pill contains a hormone called oestrogen, and in a small number of women, around one in twenty, that hormone pushes blood pressure up. It usually appears in the first few months, which fits exactly, and it usually settles within two to three months of stopping. That's the main reason we check blood pressure at the three-month visit after starting the pill.' The differentials as a seventy-five-second list: an overactive thyroid · kidney disease, or a narrowing of the vessel supplying a kidney · a narrowing of the main vessel from the heart, coarctation · too much cortisol or too much aldosterone · a rare tumour of a gland above the kidney that releases hormones in bursts · other medicines or substances including a lot of caffeine · and sleep apnoea. 'If we look for all of those and find nothing, and the pressure stays up after stopping the pill, we'd call it essential high blood pressure, which just means no single cause is found.' then the honesty line and the reassurance line, both marked: 'I'm not certain your blood pressure was normal before I started the pill, so part of what we're doing is finding that out' · and 'These are things I'm checking for, not things I expect to find', because she looks alarmed at the list and asks whether she might have a tumour. The management, three initial steps. First and discriminating: stop the combined pill today and replace it the same day. 'Because that's your contraception, I don't want you walking out of here without cover — that's a bigger risk to you over the next month than the blood pressure is. The progestogen-only pill, the implant and the hormonal IUD all work perfectly well with high blood pressure, so I'd like us to start one of those today, and use condoms for the first week while it takes effect. Have you had any unprotected sex in the last few days?' 'Stop the pill and come back another day to talk about alternatives' is what the recall says and it is not safe — a sexually active 23-year-old left without contraception for a fortnight is the most likely harm in this entire consultation. And if she asks about restarting the combined pill: 'I need to be straightforward: no. Once blood pressure has gone up on a combined pill we avoid that whole group for good, even if the numbers come back to normal — the risk of stroke and heart attack stays higher. But that's the only door that closes. The mini-pill, the implant, both types of IUD and the injection all stay open to you, and most of them are more reliable than the pill you were on.' Second: investigations — kidney function and a urine test, thyroid function, blood sugar and cholesterol, a blood count, and an ECG — plus the examination today: blood pressure in both arms, the pulses in the groin and legs, and auscultation of the abdomen and back. Third: keep measuring — home readings continued, review at two to four weeks, then again at two to three months, by which point you should know whether the pressure has come down. Safety-net: same-day review for severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, blurred vision, weakness or trouble speaking — plus the one small thing that helps whatever the cause, which is going easy on salt and on those energy drinks. The variants: one, the pressure predated the pill — a work medical two years ago called it borderline. 'That changes how I think about this. It means your blood pressure was probably already drifting up before the pill, and the pill has made it worse rather than caused it from nothing. Practically the plan is the same, but my expectation is different — I'd expect the pressure to come down some after stopping, not necessarily all the way to normal. If it stays up we'd be treating hypertension in her own right, and at 23 that makes it more important to look carefully for a cause rather than accept it.' Two, unprotected sex this week — deal with it first: emergency contraception if within five days, either an oral tablet or a copper IUD, which is the most effective and gives ongoing contraception straight away, solving two problems at once — plus a pregnancy test today, because being already pregnant changes everything about the medication side. Three, she blames you — 'You put me on this, why didn't you check my blood pressure before?' → 'That's a completely fair question, and I'm not going to talk around it. Blood pressure should be checked before starting a combined pill, and I can see from your record that it wasn't — I'm sorry about that, and I'll make sure it's documented. What I'd say is this: we did check at three months, which is exactly when this shows up, we've found it early, you have no damage from it, and it is very likely to settle once we stop.' Four, still 158/98 at three months off the pill with a negative screen — that makes essential hypertension the working diagnosis with the pill as an aggravator. Confirm with home readings, complete outstanding testing including an aldosterone-to-renin ratio, which is more interpretable now she is off the oestrogen, and treat, since Australian guidance treats at or above 160/100 regardless of calculated risk. In a 23-year-old woman the drug choice matters: avoid an ACE inhibitor or ARB because of fetal risk unless contraception is reliable and pregnancy plans have been discussed explicitly — a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as controlled-release nifedipine, or labetalol, is safer if pregnancy is possible VERIFY.

ask: The framing and key-question set: 'It may well be the pill, and we'll come to that — but several things can push blood pressure up at your age, and I'd like to go through them properly rather than assume.' · 'Had anyone ever told you your blood pressure was high, even borderline, before I started you on the pill?'

The trackpads set: 'Do you feel the heat more than other people?' · 'Do you get episodes of throbbing headache with flushing, sweating and your heart pounding, all together and out of nowhere?' · 'Has anyone told you that you snore, or gasp or stop breathing in your sleep?' · and for the pill: 'Do you get migraines — and do you ever get a visual warning first, like zigzag lines?' · 'How important is it to you not to become pregnant at the moment?'

The explaining and managing set: 'The pill contains oestrogen, and in about one in twenty women it pushes blood pressure up.' · 'It usually settles within two to three months of stopping — that's why we check at the three-month visit.' · 'These are things I'm checking for, not things I expect to find.' · 'I'm not certain your blood pressure was normal before I prescribed, so part of what we're doing is finding that out.' · 'We stop the combined pill today — and I don't want you leaving here without cover.' · 'Once blood pressure has risen on a combined pill we avoid that group for good — but that's the only door that closes.'
pefe: The diagnosis is already confirmed by repeated clinic and home readings averaging around 160/100 — do not offer to confirm it again. What you do plan is the examination that looks for the two causes with no history questions: blood pressure in both arms and in a leg · femoral pulses for radio-femoral delay · an abdominal bruit · and an interscapular murmur.

Her history is entirely negative and that is the point: no symptoms at all, 'I feel completely normal, which is the weird part' · blood pressure never checked before this year · mother on tablets in her fifties · non-smoker, two or three drinks on a weekend · the pill taken every day without missing one, condoms before · no other side effects · no migraine and no aura, no clot history · last period two weeks ago with no chance of pregnancy. The two things she gives only if asked: three or four coffees a day plus an energy drink before late shifts, and how important it is that she does not become pregnant.

SHE PUSHES HARD ON WHAT SHE USES INSTEAD OF THE PILL AND WILL NOT LET IT GO — IF YOU SAY 'WE'LL DISCUSS ALTERNATIVES AT ANOTHER APPOINTMENT' AND SHE LEAVES WITH NO CONTRACEPTION, SHE MARKS IT A FAIL. She also marks it a fail if you never ask whether her pressure was high before the pill, never ask about migraine with aura, TELL HER SHE CAN RESTART THE COMBINED PILL LATER, or run out of time before the management plan. And she asks at around four minutes if you have not: 'IF I STOP THE PILL, WHAT AM I SUPPOSED TO DO? I REALLY CAN'T GET PREGNANT RIGHT NOW.'

Set the frame instead of agreeing — 'IT MAY WELL BE THE PILL, AND WE'LL COME TO THAT. BUT SEVERAL THINGS CAN PUSH BLOOD PRESSURE UP AT YOUR AGE, AND I'D LIKE TO GO THROUGH THEM PROPERLY RATHER THAN ASSUME. Let me ask you some questions, then I'll tell you what I think and what I'd like to do first.' She is genuinely frightened — SHE HAS LOOKED THE NUMBERS UP ONLINE — and settles quickly if you are calm

The question that justifies everything afterwards — 'Had anyone ever told you before this year that your blood pressure was high, or even borderline? Do you remember it being checked before I started you on the pill?' Her answer in version A: it has never been checked. If her pressure was never measured before the prescription, 'The pill caused it' is an assumption — and saying that out loud later is marked, because it is what justifies your investigation plan. Also screen symptoms and end-organ features: headache, dizziness, visual change, chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, ankle swelling

Ask for the risk factors the stem did not give you — The notes already say she eats well and exercises, so DO NOT GO OVER THAT. What you do not have: SMOKING OR VAPING · alcohol · COFFEE, TEA AND ENERGY DRINKS · stress at work and home · family history of heart attack or stroke WITH AGES · and diabetes, kidney trouble or cholesterol. SHE DRINKS THREE OR FOUR COFFEES A DAY AND AN ENERGY DRINK BEFORE LATE SHIFTS, AND SHE MENTIONS IT ONLY IF ASKED — A REAL CONTRIBUTOR THE STEM DOES NOT SUPPLY

Trackpads as one fluent block, under ninety seconds — THYROID — do you feel the heat more than other people, any tremor, weight loss or loose bowels · KIDNEY — ever told you have kidney problems, any change in urine, FROTHY OR BLOODY URINE, swelling of legs or face · PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA — 'DO YOU GET EPISODES OF THROBBING HEADACHE WITH FLUSHING, SWEATING AND YOUR HEART POUNDING, ALL TOGETHER AND OUT OF NOWHERE?' · CUSHING'S — central weight gain, PURPLE STRETCH MARKS, easy bruising, steroid use · ALDOSTERONISM — muscle weakness or cramps · DRUGS — ibuprofen, cold and sinus tablets, steroids, herbal remedies, recreational · SLEEP APNOEA — snoring, gasping, witnessed apnoeas, unrefreshed sleep. IN VERSION A THIS BLOCK IS ENTIRELY NEGATIVE, AND THAT IS THE POINT: A NEGATIVE SCREEN YOU ACTUALLY PERFORMED IS WORTH MARKS; ONE YOU ASSUMED IS WORTH NONE

Name the two causes with no history questions — Say it to the examiner as you finish the block: 'Two of the secondary causes have no useful history questions — renal artery stenosis, which in a woman of this age would be fibromuscular dysplasia, and coarctation of the aorta. I would look for those on examination: femoral pulses for radio-femoral delay, blood pressure in both arms and in a leg, and auscultation for an abdominal bruit and an interscapular murmur'

The pill history — and the three questions candidates skip — Adherence, previous method and why she changed, and other side effects. Then: 'Do you get migraines — and do you ever get a visual warning beforehand, like flashing lights or zigzag lines?', which is an absolute contraindication in its own right · calf pain or swelling, pleuritic chest pain, and family history of clots · and 'When was your last period, is there any chance you could be pregnant, and how important is it to you not to become pregnant at the moment?' that last one determines whether your management plan is safe, because you are about to take her contraception away

setting: The decision to treat is made by the calculated absolute cardiovascular risk and by excluding secondary causes — never by the cholesterol number alone. Every candidate reaches 'Start a statin'. The pass belongs to the one who gets there the right way, out loud. The stem is loaded with smoking, wine, BMI 30 and diabetes: read it as a cardiovascular risk station, not a cholesterol station.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. James Bennett, 50, here to discuss his blood test results. No history taking and no physical examination required. 8 minutes.
Known type 2 diabetes on metformin 2 g daily. Smoker. Two glasses of wine every night. Exercises twice a week. BMI 30.
Results: total cholesterol 6.3 (Range <5.5) · LDL 3.9 (<3.4) · HDL 1.5 (>1.0) · triglycerides 2.9 (<1.7) · total cholesterol to HDL ratio 5.7 (<4.5) · HbA1c 6.5% or 48 mmol/mol, target under 7.0%.
tasks: Explain the blood test results to the patient
Discuss your management plan with the patient
time: Three beats. Ninety seconds on the results · two minutes on the two things everyone forgets, secondary causes and absolute risk · three minutes on drug, lifestyle, referrals, kidney and review · if you are still in beat one at three minutes, cut to the ratio and move
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: The statin, pros then cons — and his mate's leg pains

Atorvastatin taken at night: it lowers the fats, lowers the chance of heart attack or stroke, and is the most effective medication we have for this. The main downside is muscle aches and pains, sometimes with tenderness or weakness — 'Common and usually manageable, and if it happens we check a blood test and adjust rather than just abandoning treatment.' Rarely, more severe muscle inflammation: bad widespread muscle pain, very dark urine, or feeling really unwell means come straight back. When he raises his mate, validate first, then give the stepwise approach — never 'That won't happen to you'

back.dx: MIXED DYSLIPIDAEMIA IN A 50-YEAR-OLD MAN WITH TYPE 2 DIABETES — explain the results, then negotiate the plan. Targets and review: 'Once you're on it I'm aiming for total cholesterol under 4, the bad cholesterol and triglycerides under 2, and the good one above 1. So I'll repeat the bloods and see you again in about six weeks to three months. If we haven't reached those numbers I'll increase the dose, and if we still can't get there we can add a second tablet.' Worth pre-empting: he will feel no different on it, which is exactly why adherence lapses. Snap with actual numbers: smoking — stopping is the single biggest thing he can do for his heart, with Quitline 13 7848 and patches or medication · diet — more vegetables, fruit and fibre, olive oil instead of butter, oily fish twice a week, less saturated fat, less red meat, less salt · alcohol — 'There's no completely safe level, and two glasses a night is about 14 a week; I'd like you under 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 in one sitting' · exercise — twice a week is a good start, aim for 150 minutes a week plus weights twice a week · weight — with a BMI of 30, even 5 to 10 per cent would improve these numbers. He has tried quitting before and it didn't stick: affirm the attempt — 'Most people need a few goes, that's normal' — negotiate rather than dictate on the wine, and offer walking rather than a gym. Then the closing block, which is where time is lost: allied health — a dietitian for a proper eating plan, an exercise physiologist, and a diabetes educator, 'They get a full hour with you, which I never do', all arranged under a chronic condition management plan so they are subsidised · the CKD screen, which is specific to this patient: 'Because you have diabetes and high fats together, you're at higher risk of chronic kidney disease, so I'd like to screen — an eGFR and a first-morning urine sample for protein. It also matters for your metformin, because the 2-gram dose needs your kidneys to be working well' · heart foundation reading · safety-net for bad muscle pain, dark urine, chest pain or breathlessness · and the shared decision with a review date. If the bell is close, compress to: 'Kidney screen, dietitian and diabetes educator, heart foundation reading, and I'll see you in six weeks.' The variants: a, familial hypercholesterolaemia — TC 8.4, LDL 5.6, HDL 0.9, ratio 9.3, father died of an MI at 42: 'Your cholesterol is high enough that I'm not going to wait for a calculator — above 7.5 total, or a bad cholesterol above 5, we treat regardless of the overall score. Your father dying that young also raises the possibility of an inherited high-cholesterol condition. I'd like to look at your eyes and Achilles tendons for two specific signs, start a stronger statin today, refer you to a specialist lipid service, and arrange cholesterol tests for your children and siblings — about half of close relatives may carry it.' B, the refuser with a calculated high risk who declines medication: 'It's absolutely your decision, and I'm not going to push a tablet on you. What I'd suggest is a proper trial — three months of the diet, activity and alcohol changes with the dietitian's help, and I'll repeat the bloods. If the bad cholesterol comes down below 2 we keep going as we are. If it hasn't moved, I'd like us to revisit the tablet then. Would you be comfortable with that as a plan?' The trap is capitulating with no review date, or coercing — negotiate a threshold and a date. C, muscle aches on atorvastatin 40 mg for eight weeks, bilateral thigh and shoulder ache, stopped himself: 'First I want to be sure it's the tablet — statin pain is usually both sides, in the big muscles, and comes on weeks after starting, which fits. But I'll also check your thyroid and vitamin d and think about arthritis. I'll check a ck. We'll stop it for a few weeks to settle, then try again — a lower dose, or a different statin, or even just twice a week. Statins are important enough that we work around the side effect rather than giving up on them.' His background, given only if asked: 15 cigarettes a day since 20, one patch attempt five years ago that lasted three weeks · two glasses of red most nights, more at weekends · takeaway two or three nights a week · walks the dog twice a week for half an hour · father had a heart attack at 68 and survived, mother has type 2 diabetes, and nobody died young. If he mentions any family cardiac event, note the age — premature CVD in a first-degree relative is a reclassification factor and, with very high numbers, a pointer to FH.

ask: THE EXPLAINING SET: 'I'll go through the results first, then what we do about them — AND WE'LL DECIDE TOGETHER.' · 'HbA1c shows your average sugar over the last three months.' · 'LDL IS THE BAD TYPE — IT BLOCKS THE BLOOD TUBES IN YOUR HEART AND CAUSES HEART ATTACKS.' · 'HDL IS THE GOOD TYPE — IT PREVENTS THE BLOCKING, SO WE WANT IT HIGH, ABOVE 1.' · 'Triglyceride is the form your body stores spare fat in.' · 'THE RATIO TELLS US THE OVERALL RISK THESE NUMBERS CARRY FOR HEART DISEASE.'

The two key points: 'Before we treat, I want to check nothing else is pushing these fats up.' · 'An underactive thyroid can raise your fats — that's a simple test called a TSH.' · 'I don't just look at the cholesterol number — I work out your risk of a heart attack or stroke over the next five years.'

The closing set: 'The main side effect is muscle aches, pains and sometimes weakness.' · 'I'll give you some reading material, you have a think, and we'll make a plan together.' · 'Come back sooner with bad muscle pain, dark urine, chest pain or breathlessness.'
pefe: No history taking and no examination are asked for, but the observations matter because the risk calculator needs a blood pressure: BP 142/88, pulse 78 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C. The printed numbers are the findings — TC 6.3, LDL 3.9, HDL 1.5, triglycerides 2.9, ratio 5.7, HbA1c 6.5%.

He starts relaxed and slightly jokey, goes quieter and flat when told the fats are high, and warms again if you reassure him that the problem is changeable. He pushes at the HDL explanation and stays confused unless you re-explain it, pushes once on the tablet with 'Can't I just fix it with diet?', and raises his mate's leg pains. If you are cold or rushed he goes quiet and says 'So I'm heading for a heart attack then.'

THERE IS NO SCRIPTED HIDDEN AGENDA, WHICH IS WHY CANDIDATES SKIP THE CONCERNS QUESTION — IT IS STILL A SCORED ITEM. If you never ask, at about six minutes he volunteers either 'IS THIS GOING TO AFFECT MY TRUCK LICENCE?' or 'HOW MUCH DO THESE TABLETS COST?', and you are then obliged to weave it into the plan.

Signpost, then the sugar — and do not slide into a diabetes consultation — 'I'll go through the results first, then we'll talk about what we do about them — AND WE'LL MAKE THE PLAN TOGETHER.' HbA1c SHOWS THE AVERAGE SUGAR OVER THE LAST THREE MONTHS; his is 6.5% against a target under 7, SO THE DIABETES IS WELL CONTROLLED. ACKNOWLEDGE, CONGRATULATE, MOVE ON — THIS STATION IS NOT ABOUT DIABETES CONTROL. And when he asks 'is that bad?' during the cholesterol, DO NOT ANSWER YET: 'let me take you through all of them and then I'll tell you what it means overall', or you will explain the risk three separate times and lose two minutes

The deliberate misdirection is HDL — pause and check — LDL is the bad type: 'It builds up inside the blood tubes that feed your heart and blocks them, and that's what causes a heart attack.' HDL is the good type: 'It actually helps prevent the blocking — it clears fat away. So with this one, unlike the others, we want the number as high as possible, ideally above 1. Yours is 1.5, which is a good level.' He is briefed to be genuinely confused — 'Hang on, so high is good for that one?' — and to stay confused unless you re-explain: 'I know it sounds back-to-front — one blocks, one clears. Does that make sense?'

The ratio is the commonest task 1 omission — TRIGLYCERIDE IS 'THE FORM YOUR BODY USES TO STORE SPARE FAT' — and if he asks whether it comes from the wine, FLAG IT BRIEFLY AND BANK IT FOR LATER rather than starting SNAP counselling mid-task. THEN THE RATIO: 'the last number is the balance between your total cholesterol and your good cholesterol. IT GIVES US THE OVERALL RISK THESE NUMBERS CARRY FOR HEART DISEASE — IT'S ABOUT THE BALANCE BETWEEN THE FATS, NOT JUST ONE NUMBER. We like it under 4.5; yours is 5.7.' AND RESIST FALSE REASSURANCE — 'DON'T WORRY, YOUR GOOD ONE IS FINE' IS A SCORED ERROR WHEN THE RATIO IS 5.7

Key point one — secondary causes, the highest-value omission in the station — 'THE FIRST THING I WANT TO DO IS CHECK THERE ISN'T ANOTHER CONDITION PUSHING THESE FATS UP. DIABETES IS ONE OF THEM — you have that, but it's well controlled. THE OTHER COMMON ONE IS AN UNDERACTIVE THYROID: the gland at the front of your neck not working properly CAN RAISE THE FATS IN YOUR BLOOD. THAT'S A SIMPLE BLOOD TEST CALLED A TSH, AND I'LL ADD IT TO YOUR FORM TODAY. ALCOHOL AND KIDNEY PROBLEMS CAN ALSO RAISE THEM.' One sentence of explanation, NAME THE TEST, MOVE ON — do not lecture on thyroid physiology

Key point two — show what goes into the risk calculation — 'I don't just look at the cholesterol number — I work out your overall risk of a heart attack or stroke over the next five years, using a calculator. For that I'll check your blood pressure today; I have your sugar and fat results; I'll ask your age, whether you smoke, your postcode, your background, and how long you've had diabetes; and I'll add a kidney function test.' Saying 'I'll do a risk assessment' and stopping scores nothing, and postcode is a genuine input as a socioeconomic index — answer it confidently. Then the bands: 10% or more is high and we start a tablet · 5 to 10% usually means lifestyle first with review · under 5% is lifestyle alone. Say 'Likely', not 'Definitely' — do not promise a result you haven't calculated

stem: General practice. Ken Docherty, 58, attended last week for an unrelated matter and his blood pressure was 156/96. You asked him to start monitoring it at home, and he has since bought an automated upper-arm machine. He has come back to be shown how to use it.
Counselling only — no examination and no investigations to order. 8 minutes.

His three planted errors, given only if you ask: he checks it right after his morning walk · he sits at the kitchen bench with the radio on, chatting to his wife · and it is his wife's machine, she is much smaller than him, and it is several years old. He has been getting frightening numbers, one as high as 178.
tasks: Explain how he should measure his blood pressure at home, and how to make the readings reliable
Explain what you will do with the results
Answer his questions
time: One minute to greet and elicit · forty-five seconds on why and the single-reading principle · the technique block from 1:45 to 5:45, which carries most of the marks · then thresholds and what happens next, and a final minute for safety-net, teach-back and written information

back.dx: TEACHING HOME BLOOD PRESSURE MONITORING AFTER A SINGLE RAISED CLINIC READING. WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, IN THREE OUTCOMES: 'IF THE AVERAGE COMES OUT NORMAL, it was probably the clinic pushing it up, AND WE'LL JUST KEEP AN EYE ON IT. IF IT'S CLEARLY HIGH, I'll do some BLOOD TESTS, A URINE TEST AND A HEART TRACING, work out your OVERALL HEART RISK, and we'll talk about whether treatment is worth it — LIFESTYLE CHANGES, TABLETS, OR BOTH. AND IF THE READINGS ARE BORDERLINE OR DON'T ADD UP, I might arrange A 24-HOUR MONITOR — a small machine you wear for a day that checks it ABOUT EVERY HALF HOUR, INCLUDING OVERNIGHT. THAT'S THE MOST ACCURATE TEST WE'VE GOT.' ON THE TABLETS QUESTION, HONEST WITHOUT OVER-PROMISING: 'POSSIBLY, BUT NOT NECESSARILY — and that's a decision we'd make TOGETHER, NOT SOMETHING I'D IMPOSE. Plenty of people get their blood pressure down with salt, weight, exercise and alcohol changes alone. And to be straight with you: HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE MATTERS BECAUSE OVER YEARS IT DAMAGES THE HEART, BRAIN, KIDNEYS AND EYES — BUT IT'S SLOW, AND IT'S VERY TREATABLE. THERE'S NO EMERGENCY HERE.' THE SAFETY-NET HAS TWO HALVES AND BOTH ARE SCORED: 'DON'T PANIC AT A SINGLE HIGH NUMBER. If you get one, SIT QUIETLY FOR TEN MINUTES AND DO IT AGAIN — and please don't change anything based on one reading. BUT IF A READING IS VERY HIGH, SAY OVER 180 ON THE TOP NUMBER, AND YOU ALSO FEEL UNWELL WITH IT — a severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, blurred vision, or weakness or trouble speaking — THAT COMBINATION NEEDS SEEING STRAIGHT AWAY. CALL AN AMBULANCE ON TRIPLE ZERO. A HIGH NUMBER ON ITS OWN WITH NO SYMPTOMS ISN'T AN EMERGENCY; A HIGH NUMBER WITH THOSE SYMPTOMS IS.' THEN CLOSE PROPERLY: TEACH-BACK — 'CAN YOU TELL ME BACK HOW YOU'LL DO IT TOMORROW MORNING?' — IS A SCORED COUNSELLING ITEM AND TAKES FIFTEEN SECONDS, and so does BOOKING THE FOLLOW-UP AND ASKING HIM TO BRING THE MACHINE SO YOU CAN CALIBRATE IT, WHICH SHOWS YOU THOUGHT PAST THE CONSULTATION. Add printed instructions and a Heart Foundation sheet, and book two weeks. HIS HIDDEN AGENDA: HIS FATHER HAD A STROKE AT 61 AND HE IS QUIETLY FRIGHTENED THE SAME IS COMING. He does not volunteer it; ask about concerns, or be warm, and he says so — and if you never ask, he raises it in the last minute. THE VARIANTS: ONE, THE FRIGHTENED PATIENT with 200/110 on Tuesday — 'A SINGLE HIGH READING, ON ITS OWN, IN SOMEONE WHO FEELS COMPLETELY WELL, IS NOT AN EMERGENCY. Blood pressure spikes for all sorts of reasons — a rush, a coffee, stress, a full bladder, OR SIMPLY A CUFF THAT'S THE WRONG SIZE. What matters is the average over time, not one number.' TWO, WHITE-COAT HYPERTENSION — clinic 165/100 on three occasions, home diary averaging 128/78: 'that pattern has a name, WHITE-COAT HYPERTENSION. To be certain I'd arrange a 24-HOUR MONITOR. If that confirms it, YOU MAY WELL NOT NEED ANY TREATMENT AT ALL — BUT I'D STILL WANT TO KEEP AN EYE ON IT, BECAUSE WHITE-COAT HYPERTENSION CAN PROGRESS OVER TIME.' THREE, MASKED HYPERTENSION, THE MIRROR IMAGE — clinic 132/82, home 148/92: 'THIS IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT I EXPECTED, AND IT'S ACTUALLY MORE IMPORTANT. IF WE'D ONLY EVER MEASURED IT IN THIS ROOM, WE'D HAVE MISSED IT ENTIRELY. THE RISK TO YOUR HEART AND BLOOD VESSELS IS MUCH THE SAME AS IF IT WERE HIGH ALL THE TIME.' Confirm with ABPM, then assess end-organ damage and absolute risk and treat accordingly. FOUR, THE CONTRACEPTIVE PILL VERSION in a 26-year-old at 152/96 four months after starting — stop the combined pill, recheck over a couple of months, AND COVER HER CONTRACEPTION IN THE SAME CONSULTATION with a progestogen-only pill, an implant or an IUD. FIVE, THE EXAMINER ASKS ABOUT AMBULATORY MONITORING — patient version: 'a small monitor on a belt with a cuff on your arm, INFLATING ABOUT EVERY HALF HOUR FOR A DAY AND A NIGHT, INCLUDING WHILE YOU'RE ASLEEP. Go about your normal day, but KEEP YOUR ARM STILL WHEN IT INFLATES, and keep a short diary.' Technical version: TWO MEASUREMENTS PER HOUR GIVING AT LEAST 40 READINGS · daytime, night-time and 24-hour averages, with hypertension supported by a 24-HOUR AVERAGE OF 130/80 OR ABOVE · AND THE NOCTURNAL DIP, WHICH NORMALLY FALLS BY AT LEAST 10% OVERNIGHT, WITH FAILURE TO DIP AN ADVERSE PROGNOSTIC SIGN IN ITS OWN RIGHT. AND IF ASKED ABOUT THE MANUAL TECHNIQUE: PALPATE THE RADIAL PULSE, INFLATE UNTIL IT DISAPPEARS, DEFLATE SLOWLY — THE RETURN OF THE PULSE GIVES THE APPROXIMATE SYSTOLIC · FULLY DEFLATE AND WAIT BEFORE REINFLATING, AND NEVER REINFLATE A PARTLY DEFLATED CUFF · THEN AUSCULTATE OVER THE BRACHIAL ARTERY FOR THE KOROTKOFF SOUNDS, FIRST SOUND SYSTOLIC AND DISAPPEARANCE DIASTOLIC, DEFLATING AT ABOUT 2 mmHg PER SECOND.

WHY HOME MONITORING AT ALL, AND THE SINGLE-READING PRINCIPLE — plus two occasions a week or more apart.
THE MACHINE: validated upper-arm, calibration against the practice's — THEN CUFF SIZE WITH THE MECHANISM, AND THE COST CONVERSATION.
PREPARATION: caffeine, smoking, exercise, meal, BLADDER, not when stressed or in pain, AND FIVE MINUTES SEATED.
POSTURE: back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed, ARM AT HEART LEVEL, BARE SKIN, AND NO TALKING.
Three readings one to two minutes apart, discard the first, average the second and third.
Both arms on the first occasion, then morning and evening for at least a week, discarding day one — and record everything.
The three thresholds, with the reason the home bar is lower.
The three possible outcomes and what each leads to, including what a 24-hour monitor is.
The tablets question answered honestly, with shared decision-making and no over-promising.
Safety-net in both HALVEs, teach-back, written information, and book two weeks — bringing the diary and the machine.

ask: THE OPENING SET: 'BEFORE I GO THROUGH ANYTHING — HAVE YOU HAD A GO WITH IT YET, AND HOW HAVE YOU BEEN DOING IT?' · 'Blood pressure isn't one fixed number — it moves around all day.' · 'ONE READING NEVER MAKES A DIAGNOSIS.' · 'To diagnose it I need raised readings ON AT LEAST TWO SEPARATE OCCASIONS, A WEEK OR MORE APART.'

The technique set: 'A cuff that's too small squeezes harder and reads falsely high; one that's too big reads falsely low.' · 'No caffeine or smoking for a couple of hours, empty your bladder, and don't measure it when you're stressed or in pain.' · 'Sit quietly for five minutes before you press the button — five, not one.' · 'Feet flat on the floor, arm resting at heart level, cuff on bare skin — and don't talk while it's running.' · 'Take three readings one to two minutes apart, throw the first one away, and average the second and third.' · 'The very first time, measure both arms — then use the arm that reads higher.'

THE CLOSING SET: 'At home we call it high if the average is 135 OVER 85 OR MORE — that's lower than the 140 over 90 we use in the clinic, BECAUSE HOME READINGS ARE MORE RELIABLE.' · 'Don't panic at a single high number — BUT IF IT'S OVER 180 ON TOP AND YOU FEEL UNWELL WITH IT, CALL AN AMBULANCE.' · 'CAN YOU TELL ME BACK HOW YOU'LL DO IT TOMORROW MORNING?'
pefe: No examination and nothing to order — the findings are what he tells you about his technique, and he gives them only if asked: measuring right after his morning walk · kitchen bench, radio on, chatting to his wife · his wife's several-year-old machine with a cuff that is 'A bit tight, now you mention it' · no rest beforehand, coffee usually, just one reading, always the left arm, and not writing them down — 'I just remember the bad ones'.

THE REST OF THE PICTURE IF YOU ASK: no medications, NON-SMOKER BUT FOUR OR FIVE BEERS MOST NIGHTS, IBUPROFEN FOR HIS BACK NOW AND THEN, a lot of takeaway and salt on everything, walks the dog most mornings, NO SYMPTOMS AT ALL — AND HIS FATHER'S STROKE AT 61, WHICH IS THE HIDDEN AGENDA.

HE PROBES YOUR PRECISION: if you say 'take a couple and average them' he asks 'HOW MANY EXACTLY? AND DO THEY ALL COUNT?' · if you quote 140/90 for home he asks 'IS THAT THE SAME NUMBER FOR AT HOME?', giving you ONE CHANCE TO CORRECT YOURSELF · if you use jargon he asks what it means · AND HE SAYS 'I'VE BEEN DOING HALF OF THAT WRONG, HAVEN'T I', WHERE AGREEING BLUNTLY MAKES HIM GO QUIET AND DEFENSIVE.

The principle the station exists to test — 'Blood pressure ISN'T ONE FIXED NUMBER — it moves around all day. It goes up when you're rushing, when you've had a coffee, when you're stressed, EVEN WHEN YOU'RE TALKING. And for a lot of people it's higher in a doctor's room than anywhere else — WE CALL THAT THE WHITE-COAT EFFECT. So the single most important thing: ONE READING NEVER MAKES A DIAGNOSIS. NOT THE 156 I GOT LAST WEEK, AND NOT THE 178 YOU GOT AT HOME. TO ACTUALLY DIAGNOSE HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE I NEED RAISED READINGS ON AT LEAST TWO SEPARATE OCCASIONS, A WEEK OR MORE APART.' TEACHING FLAWLESS TECHNIQUE AND NEVER STATING THIS IS THE TRAP — SAY IT EARLY AND REPEAT IT IN THE SUMMARY

The cuff — and get the direction right — A validated upper-arm machine, not a wrist one, and bring it in so you can check it against the practice's, because they drift. Then: 'If the cuff is too small, it has to squeeze harder and you get a reading that's falsely high. If it's too big, you get one that's falsely low.' Anchor it to the mechanism so you don't reverse it. His wife's machine with her smaller cuff could alone explain the high readings. And address cost rather than ignoring it: a larger cuff is sold separately and is not expensive, some pharmacies loan machines, and the practice has one he could borrow for a fortnight

Preparation and posture, with a reason attached to each rule — No cigarettes, coffee, tea, energy drinks, exercise or a big meal beforehand — ideally no caffeine or smoking for a couple of hours · empty the bladder, because a full bladder raises it · not when in pain or upset, 'Because you'll just be measuring that' · sit quietly for five minutes, not one or two · a chair with a back, feet flat, legs uncrossed, arm resting so the cuff is level with the heart · cuff on bare skin, not over a sleeve · and the one nearly everyone breaks: don't talk while it's running and turn the radio off, because talking alone can add several points. 'That's probably why you got 178' is far better received than 'You've been doing it wrong'

The two most commonly dropped items in the whole station — 'Take three readings, about one to two minutes apart. Then throw the first one away — it's nearly always the highest, because your body hasn't fully settled. Average the second and third.' and: 'Just for the first time you use it, measure both arms. A small difference between sides is normal. If one arm is consistently higher, use that arm from then on — and let me know, because a big difference between arms is something I'd want to look into.' 'Take a couple and average them' does not score

When, for how long, and recording everything — Morning before breakfast and before any tablets, and again in the evening · every day for at least a week, ideally two · and ignore the whole of the first day, because everyone's first day is unrepresentative. 'Write every single reading down — or use the machine's memory — and bring the whole lot in. Don't leave out the high ones or the odd ones; I want to see all of it. And if something unusual was going on — a rough night, a stressful day, feeling unwell — just note it beside that reading'

The threshold changes with the method — 'At home we call it high if the average is 135 OVER 85 OR MORE. That's a bit lower than the number we use here in the clinic, WHICH IS 140 OVER 90 — AND THE REASON THE BAR IS LOWER AT HOME IS THAT HOME READINGS ARE MORE RELIABLE, SO WE DON'T NEED AS MUCH MARGIN.' The 24-hour average is 130/80. QUOTING 140/90 FOR HOME READINGS IN A STATION EXPLICITLY ABOUT HOME MEASUREMENT IS CONSPICUOUS, and he is briefed to give you one chance to correct yourself: 'IS THAT THE SAME NUMBER FOR AT HOME?'

setting: Two single-item AUTOMATIC FAILS sit in this station. Omitting the rest-pain and ulcer questions, because in the harder version she answers yes to both and a candidate who never asked will confidently deliver a routine chronic-disease plan to a patient with a threatened limb. And never mentioning the propranolol — the planted misdirection, a beta blocker that worsens claudication and is not first-line for hypertension in Australia anyway.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. You are the GP registrar. Lily Harrison, 68. 8 minutes.
Pain in the right leg, getting worse. Brought on by walking, worse uphill, settles with rest. Past DVT right leg 10 years ago. Hypertension, on propranolol. Smokes 20 cigarettes per day.
Already performed: ankle–brachial index 0.7, with a normal range of 0.9 to 1.3.

Her hidden agenda: her neighbour Mary had 'Leg trouble' and lost her foot eighteen months ago. She is frightened the same will happen and has told nobody. If you don't ask in the first minute, she raises it at 7:30 as you try to close.
tasks: Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Explain the differential diagnoses
Request further investigations and explain them
Explain your management plan
Explain the complications of this condition
time: Five tasks in eight minutes · watch the clock at 7:00, because red flags, review, summary and teach-back are each separately scored and they are the four things candidates lose when they run over
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Supervised exercise, and the foot care that gets dropped

'I know this sounds odd given that walking is what hurts, but supervised walking is one of the most effective treatments we have.' The three words that earn the mark are individualised, supervised and gradually increased — an exercise physiologist finds where her pain starts at 250 metres and builds from there. Then the feet, via a podiatrist and four things at home: check both feet daily including between the toes and underneath, with a mirror or someone's help · well-fitting shoes and never barefoot · toenails cut gently and straight across · and skin moisturised, because 'Dry skin cracks, and a crack is where an ulcer starts'. And do not reach for compression stockings because you heard 'Previous dvt' — compression is contraindicated at an ABI of 0.7

back.dx: Peripheral arterial disease with intermittent claudication, ABI 0.7. Investigations, framed before they are listed: 'This condition shares its risk factors with heart disease, so some tests look at the leg and the rest check those risk factors.' The leg: an arterial ultrasound scan — painless, gel and a probe — with CT or MRI angiography only if planning a procedure. Say arterial, not just 'Doppler' or 'Ultrasound', because you already have a venous differential on your list and radiology will send the request back. The risk factors: fasting glucose, lipids, renal function, urine ACR and FBC — plus repeating the ABI at reviews. Management in three blocks, signposted. Block one, medicines: aspirin 100 mg daily, 'It makes the blood a little less sticky and protects your heart and brain as well as your leg' · a statin, and if she says her cholesterol is normal, 'We use this tablet in this condition even when the cholesterol reading looks normal, because it does more than lower the number — it helps stabilise the narrowed areas' · and the propranolol switch. Block two, exercise and feet. Block three, risk factors led by smoking: 'Of everything we've talked about, stopping smoking will do the most for your leg. I don't expect you to do that alone' — Quitline 13 7848, nicotine replacement, and a separate appointment so it gets the time it deserves. She has failed twice: 'Most people who succeed have tried several times first — that's not failure, that's practice.' Moralising without offering a practical support is the trap — instruction is not intervention. Then diet with a dietitian, alcohol up to ten standard drinks a week and no more than four in a day, and weight. Referrals: vascular surgeon — 'Not because you need an operation now, you don't, but so the team knows you and can step in quickly if things ever change', with telehealth where possible — plus podiatrist, dietitian and exercise physiologist under a care plan. When she infers surgery, correct it immediately. The second complication is beyond the leg: 'This condition tells us the arteries elsewhere are affected too, so it raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. That's the real reason for the aspirin, the cholesterol tablet and stopping smoking — we're protecting your heart and your brain, not just your calf.' Red flags in three tiers: any sore, cut, crack, blister or redness on the foot — come straight in · rest pain, night pain or a rapidly shortening walking distance — see me promptly and repeat the ABI · and the emergency: a leg that suddenly becomes severely painful, pale, cold or numb — ambulance or emergency department, plus 000 for chest pain or sudden weakness or speech trouble. Then review in two to three weeks for the new tablet, heart foundation written information, a structured summary, teach-back, and a return to the two things she asked at the start. The examiner's questions: would you still stop the beta blocker if she had heart failure? — 'No. Beta blockers are not contraindicated in pad — they can worsen claudication, so we avoid them when a better option exists, which is the case here where the only indication is hypertension. But in heart failure a beta blocker is a cornerstone of treatment and the morbidity and mortality substantially outweigh the effect on claudication. The same reasoning applies to atrial fibrillation needing rate control.' Do we screen for pad in Australia? — no routine population screening, though a low threshold for measuring the ABI in symptomatic or high-risk patients. When would you think about surgery? — revascularisation for lifestyle-limiting claudication that fails optimal medical therapy and supervised exercise, and urgently for critical limb-threatening ischaemia; a progressive fall towards 0.3 to 0.4 would prompt preparation for intervention. Compression stockings after her DVT? — not at an ABI of 0.7 VERIFY. The variants: B, critical limb-threatening ischaemia — burning forefoot pain at night that she hangs out of bed, a six-week non-healing toe sore, ABI 0.35: name the change of gear immediately, call the vascular surgical team today not in a few weeks, keep the foot clean and protected, no pressure, no heat packs and absolutely no compression — and answer the amputation question honestly: 'The leg is genuinely at risk now — that's precisely why we're moving today rather than next month. I can't promise an outcome, but I can promise you won't be waiting.' Running the version A script here — supervised exercise, routine referral, review in three weeks — is an AUTOMATIC FAIL, because exercise therapy is for claudication, not for a threatened limb. C, pad plus heart failure on a beta blocker — keep it, and say the principle out loud: weigh the total burden of disease, not one organ at a time. D, the masked presentation — 'I don't get pain walking, but then I don't really walk anywhere, my knees stop me first': arthritis, gout, back pain and angina all limit walking before the claudication distance is reached, so examine the feet and measure the ABI regardless of symptoms.

The six clarifying questions, including rest pain, night pain and foot sores.
THE DIAGNOSIS NAMED, THREE REASONS GIVEN, THEN CHUNK AND CHECK — and separate arteries from veins if she asks about the clot.
DIFFERENTIALS BY GROUP WITH A REASON EACH IS LESS LIKELY — and recover properly after the word growth.
INVESTIGATIONS, FRAMED FIRST: arterial duplex for the leg, then the risk-factor bloods and urine.
Block one — aspirin, statin, and the propranolol switch with the four-part explanation.
Block two — supervised graduated walking, then podiatry and the four foot-care rules.
Block three — smoking with real support, then diet, alcohol and weight briskly. Then the referrals and care plan.

ask: THE OPENING AND SCREENING SET: 'Before I tell you what I think is going on — IS THERE ANYTHING PARTICULAR THAT'S WORRYING YOU?' · 'Does it ever hurt when you're not walking — SITTING, OR IN BED AT NIGHT?' · 'ANY SORES, CUTS, CRACKS OR BLACK AREAS ON YOUR FOOT OR TOES?' · 'When you're at the supermarket, DOES LEANING ON THE TROLLEY MAKE ANY DIFFERENCE?'

The explaining set: 'I think you have a condition called peripheral arterial disease.' · 'There are three reasons I think that.' · 'I compared the blood pressure at your ankle with the one in your arm. They should be about the same — yours at the ankle is lower.' · 'The clot you had was in a vein. This is in the arteries. Different pipes, different problem.' · 'That was a lot at once — how are you going with that so far?'

The management and honesty set: 'Your tablet hasn't done anything wrong — we simply have a better option for your situation now. How does that sit with you?' · 'I know it sounds odd given that walking is what hurts, but supervised walking is one of the most effective treatments we have.' · 'Dry skin cracks, and a crack is where an ulcer starts.' · 'Of everything we've talked about, stopping smoking will do the most for your leg — and I don't expect you to do it alone.' · 'That can happen in severe cases, and I won't pretend otherwise. But you are at an early stage, and that's the stage at which treatment works best.'
pefe: THE ABI IS ALREADY DONE AT 0.7 AND THE HISTORY IS THE ASSESSMENT. SHE VOLUNTEERS NOTHING — not the claudication distance, not the absence of rest pain, not the dry skin. WHAT SHE GIVES WHEN ASKED: 250 m flat and under 100 m uphill · settles in two to three minutes standing · NO REST OR NIGHT PAIN AND NO SORES, JUST DRY HEELS THAT CRACK IN SUMMER · LEANING DOESN'T HELP, IT'S THE STOPPING · no back pain, no chest pain, no neurological symptoms · propranolol twice daily for eight years, started by a cardiologist she saw once · A PACK A DAY SINCE 19, TWO FAILED QUIT ATTEMPTS · father died of a heart attack at 64, mother had a stroke · AND SHE CAN'T EASILY SEE THE SOLES OF HER FEET ANY MORE.

In version B she answers yes to the two critical questions: burning forefoot pain at night that she hangs out of bed, and a six-week non-healing sore on her little toe. That is a threatened limb and a completely different station.

She pushes back once on the propranolol, once on the exercise — 'But walking is what sets it off' — reacts to the word growth, and asks at least once 'Do I have to go to Adelaide for that?', which deserves a real answer about local organisation and travel assistance. If you say 'Don't worry, you'll be fine' she stays flat: 'That's what Mary's doctor said.'

The sixty-second clarification that makes the rest safe — 'How far can you walk before the pain starts?' — 250 m flat, under 100 m uphill · 'And when you stop, what happens?' — gone in two or three minutes · 'Does it ever hurt when you're not walking — sitting, or in bed at night? Have you ever hung your leg out of bed to settle it?' · 'Any sores, cuts, cracks or black areas on your foot or toes that haven't healed?' · 'When you're at the supermarket, does leaning on the trolley make any difference?' · and back pain, numbness, pins and needles, chest tightness on that hill. The third and fourth are the critical ones

Name the diagnosis and give three reasons — 'Peripheral arterial disease. In plain terms, the blood tubes — the arteries — carrying blood down into your leg have become narrowed. So when you walk, your calf muscles ask for more blood, they can't get enough, and that's the cramping ache.' Three reasons: the pattern — walking, worse uphill, gone within minutes of stopping · the test — 'I compared the blood pressure at your ankle with the blood pressure in your arm. They should be about the same — yours at the ankle is lower' · and the risk factors. Saying 'Poor circulation' and moving on is the trap. And when she asks about her old clot: 'The clot you had was in a vein, which carries blood back up. This is in the arteries, which bring blood down. Different pipes, different problem'

Differentials by group, each with why it is less likely — and recover from 'Growth' — Nerve, the strongest alternative: spinal canal narrowing, which usually eases on leaning forward and is worse downhill as well as up — and she has told you leaning doesn't help. Vein, using her own history: post-thrombotic syndrome, which causes heaviness and swelling worse standing at the end of the day and better with the leg up, rather than pain with exercise. Then joint, soft tissue, a growth in the bone — 'Though that typically causes pain at night that doesn't settle' — and medications. She sits forward at 'Growth': 'You mean cancer?' The recovery is scored: 'I'm sorry — I've worried you. It's on my list only because it's my job to think of it, not because I think you have it. Are you all right for me to keep going?' You score the bucket, not the list

back.dx: PROXIMAL DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS — soleal and gastrocnemius veins extending into the popliteal vein — provoked by immobility, a combined oral contraceptive and a possible familial tendency. Breaking it: 'You have a condition called a deep vein thrombosis — in plain terms, there's a clot in one of the deep blood tubes in your leg.' Pause. 'I know that sounds alarming. It is something we take seriously, but it is very treatable.' She asks immediately whether it is the thing that goes to your lungs: 'You're right that that's what we're preventing. You have none of those symptoms and your observations are normal — and starting treatment today is exactly what stops it happening.' Treatment as options, not a prescription. Option one, the preference: a NOAC, apixaban — it starts working within hours, needs no regular blood monitoring, and has fewer interactions; the catch is that it cannot be used if kidney function is poor. Option two, warfarin — 'It takes three to four days to work, so we can't give it alone: warfarin and an injectable blood thinner together, then blood tests, and once the INR is above two we stop the injections.' Downsides are regular blood tests, food and drug interactions and a higher bleeding risk, and you would choose it if the kidneys were impaired or if the tests showed antiphospholipid syndrome. Option three, for a very large clot, is catheter-directed removal or thrombolysis — not needed here. The bridging explanation is a commonly dropped mark. Duration, with the reasoning said out loud: 'It depends on two things. Whether something triggered it — yes, the flight and the pill. And where the clot is — yours reaches the vein behind your knee, which makes it a proximal clot. Putting those together, three to six months, and we'll review along the way.' Practical advice: take the exact dose at the same time every day · tell any doctor, dentist or pharmacist you're on a blood thinner, especially before a procedure · avoid contact sports. Two sets of red flags, both scored. Bleeding: nosebleeds that won't stop, bleeding gums, black stools, blood in the urine, much heavier periods, unusual bruising — and note that heavier periods are quite common on these medicines, so tell us rather than putting up with it. And the clot travelling: 'If you become short of breath, get chest pain on breathing in, or feel dizzy or faint — come straight back or call an ambulance on triple zero. Don't wait it out.' then teach-back on that specifically. Future flights, which she will worry about: 'Get up and walk regularly, stretch your legs, stay hydrated, go easy on alcohol because it dehydrates you. Compression stockings help. And see your GP before you travel — for some people we give a dose of blood thinner before a long flight. You can absolutely still travel, you just do it with a bit of preparation.' The items most often dropped in task 3: the investigations, the warfarin bridging explanation, post-thrombotic syndrome, future travel advice, and arranging alternative contraception. The variants: one, she names a progestogen-only pill — 'Microlut is a progestogen-only pill, no oestrogen. That type isn't a problem after a clot, so you can safely continue it' — and the immobility and family history become the main factors. Two, a distal clot with the popliteal not involved — the less concerning pattern, and with a clear trigger you would usually treat for about six weeks rather than months. Three, she develops breathlessness mid-station — stop counselling immediately: observations including saturations, oxygen if hypoxic, IV access, ECG and chest x-ray, an urgent CTPA, and escalate to your senior. Four, known chronic kidney disease — 'The newer tablets aren't safe for you, your kidneys clear them and they'd build up. So we'd use warfarin, with an injectable blood thinner to start', aiming for an INR of two to three, with frequent blood tests at first and care with alcohol, certain foods and medicines. If you finish early, fill the time with announced components — warfarin counselling on dietary vitamin K consistency and monitoring, NOAC counselling on why adherence matters more with a short half-life and the limited reversal agents, post-thrombotic syndrome and compression stockings, or when to consider testing her sister VERIFY.

stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town (MM5). You are the GP. Jenny Marsden, 55, a primary school teacher, with right hip pain for three months that is not settling.
Given to you: temp 36.7°C · HR 74 · BP 126/78 · RR 14 · BMI 29. She walked in unaided. No investigations available. No physical examination is available and no findings will be provided.
8-minute station, 2 minutes reading. History in six minutes, then diagnosis and differentials.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient (6 minutes)
Tell the patient your most likely diagnosis in plain language, and give her the reasons you have reached it
Give your differential diagnoses to the examiner

dx: **Greater trochanteric pain syndrome** — **gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy with or without trochanteric bursitis.** **The triad: LATERAL SITE + WORSE ON WALKING AND STAIRS + WORSE LYING ON THAT SIDE AT NIGHT.** Peak **40–60 years, female:male about 4:1.**

**The two components, and saying this is what separates a good candidate from a passable one**: **worse with activity tells you there is a TENDON component; worse lying on it tells you there is a BURSA component.** **Both together are why you call it greater trochanteric pain syndrome rather than plain bursitis.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: there is no examination and no investigations, so you must commit to a diagnosis on history alone and justify it feature by feature.** **‘I think it's bursitis, we'll get an X-ray’ leaves a scored task unanswered. Naming it, then saying BECAUSE three times, passes.**

**Translate it, no jargon**: **‘On the outer side of your hip there's a bony bump, and the tendons of your buttock muscles attach onto it. Sitting between them is a small fluid-filled cushion called a bursa, which stops the tendons rubbing on the bone. In this condition both the tendons and that cushion become irritated and inflamed. Some doctors still call it trochanteric bursitis — it's the same thing.’** **Bump, tendon, cushion, inflamed, loaded — never tendinopathy, abduction, enthesis or iliotibial band.**

**The three reasons, quoting her own answers back to her**: **‘First, you pointed to the OUTER SIDE of your hip — that's exactly where the bump, the tendons and the cushion sit. Second, it's WORSE WHEN YOU WALK AND ON STAIRS — that's the tendons being loaded. Third, it's WORSE WHEN YOU LIE ON THAT SIDE at night — that's pressure on the cushion, so the bursa is involved too.’** Then **close the loop on what you excluded** — fevers, weight loss, pain unchanged by movement, numbness or weakness, steroid tablets.

**Answer the hidden agenda with a SPECIFIC CONTRAST, not general comfort.** Her mother had a hip replacement at 60 and she is dreading the same: **‘No, this isn't the arthritis your mother had. Hip arthritis is wear INSIDE the joint and usually causes deep GROIN pain with stiffness and grinding. Yours is on the OUTSIDE, in the tendons and the cushion. It doesn't damage the joint and it doesn't lead to a hip replacement.’**

**Night pain is not one thing, and the distinction is the mark.** **POSITIONAL night pain — only when lying on that side — is a bursa.** **Night pain present regardless of position and unrelieved by rest is malignancy or infection.** **Ask which one it is** rather than hearing ‘yes’ and treating it as a red flag.

**Management — load advice IS the treatment**: **avoid standing on one leg, avoid crossing the legs sitting or standing, avoid sleeping on the painful side, a PILLOW BETWEEN THE KNEES at night, avoid long strides and steep stairs while it settles.** **Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily, maximum 4 g in 24 hours** · **topical NSAID, e.g. diclofenac 1% gel three to four times daily** · a short oral NSAID course if not contraindicated (**ibuprofen 200–400 mg tds with food**) — **checking renal function, BP, GI and cardiovascular risk, and avoiding it in the elderly or anyone on the ‘triple whammy’ of ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic.** **Weight reduction where BMI is raised — hers is 29.**

**Physiotherapy for education and a graded gluteal strengthening programme is the most important part** — **education plus exercise beats corticosteroid injection at both 8 weeks and 12 months.** VERIFY **Reserve an injection for failure of 6–8 weeks of load management; repeated injections risk tendon harm and give no long-term benefit.** **Review 4–6 weeks. Realistic timeframe: weeks to months, in some patients up to 12 months.** **Keep walking the dog — shorter and flatter, built back up as the physio guides.**

**Imaging is not required to make this diagnosis.** X-ray pelvis if hip joint pathology is suspected; **ultrasound if unclear or an injection is planned; MRI for red flags, suspected AVN, or suspected occult or stress fracture.** SA — **physiotherapy through the local LHN, or private with a GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangement giving up to five subsidised allied health visits per calendar year** VERIFY ; **telehealth rheumatology and orthopaedics through the regional LHN, PATS for Adelaide travel**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for a septic hip or displaced fracture needing retrieval; **ReturnToWorkSA and SafeWork SA** if the work is aggravating it; **ACCHS and Closing the Gap**.
plan: **WIPE with consent and confidentiality — scored in every station and it takes eleven seconds.** Then the open question, **acknowledge, check comfort**, and **SIGNPOST**: **‘I'll start with questions about the pain itself, then some questions about your general health, and finally a few to make sure I'm not missing anything serious.’** **Signposting is not politeness, it is insurance** — when you later ask about bowels, periods and urine in a hip station, the examiner has already been told why.

**Site — OPEN, THEN CLOSED.** **‘Where exactly do you feel the pain?’** → *‘My right hip.’* and she stops there. **‘My right hip’ is not an answer.** **‘Is it the front of the hip, the side, or the back?’** → *‘The outer side.’* **Candidates who never ask the closed question spend the remaining five minutes with a fourteen-item list they cannot narrow.**

**The rest of SOCRATES**: out of ten · dull ache or sharp · when did it start · constant or intermittent · **getting worse** · does it travel · better or worse with anything · **worse standing and walking** · **‘how is this affecting your day-to-day life, at home and at work?’** — that last one **scores functional impact, gives you her occupation, and opens the door to her concerns. Never drop it for time.**

**The four pattern questions — the station is won here.** **‘Does the pain wake you at night?’ · ‘Worse in the morning or the end of the day?’ · ‘Worse after rest, or after activity?’ · ‘IS IT WORSE WHEN YOU LIE ON THAT SIDE AT NIGHT?’** Register it silently, **keep going, and do not close the diagnosis until the red-flag block is done.**
**Lower-limb add-ons — ask BOTH, in the same breath**: **‘Have you been limping, or is walking painful?’ · ‘Are you able to put your full weight on that leg?’**

**General MSK screen, five questions in one breath**: swelling · redness · rash · change in the shape of the joint · **stiffness, and HOW LONG IT LASTS in the morning** · **any injury or trauma, even minor.** **Stiffness is the one that earns marks — over 30–45 minutes points to inflammatory disease; under 30 minutes eased by moving points to osteoarthritis.**

**Red flags, ANNOUNCED and always first among the differentials.** **‘I'm going to ask a few questions I ask everybody with this problem, to make sure nothing serious is being missed.’** Weight · appetite · lumps or bumps · more tired than usual. **Then the metastasis screen if any is positive or she is over about 50**: cough or haemoptysis · **women: a lump in the breast** · **men: difficulty passing urine or nocturia.** Then **fevers, sweats or chills.**

**Bone and joint.** Osteoarthritis: **occupation — standing, squatting, lifting · exercise · cracking or grinding.** Inflammatory: **pain in any other joints — and if no, NAME ONE: ‘any pain or stiffness in your shoulders?’** (that is your PMR screen) · family arthritis · rashes or psoriasis · red meat or alcohol trigger · recent diarrhoea or blood in stools · recent genital discharge.

**AVN — the block you must not skip.** **‘What medications are you taking, including anything from the chemist? HAVE YOU EVER TAKEN STEROID TABLETS SUCH AS PREDNISOLONE — for asthma, bowel problems, or anything else?’** · **statins too, which cause a proximal myopathy in exactly these muscle groups** · **‘have you ever fractured or dislocated this hip?’** · **alcohol per week.**

**Soft tissue, neurovascular and referred, fast**: back pain · pins and needles or numbness · weakness · colour or temperature change · tummy pain · **last period, heavy or painful** · burning or frequency passing urine. **Then closure — but do NOT repeat SADMA items already asked inside the differential blocks.** **At 6:00 stop, whatever is unasked**: **‘I'm conscious of our time, so let me tell you what I think is going on.’**
pefe: **No physical examination is available in this station and no findings will be provided.** The diagnosis must be reached, named and defended **on history alone** — that is the whole point of the case.

**If the examiner asks what you WOULD examine**: **focal tenderness over the greater trochanter · pain on resisted hip abduction · a positive Trendelenburg or 30-second single-leg stand · and NORMAL, PAINLESS PASSIVE INTERNAL ROTATION — the finding that separates GTPS from hip joint pathology**, where internal rotation is restricted and painful.

**‘Would you image her today?’** → **‘Not to make the diagnosis — it is clinical. I would image if there were red flags, if I suspected hip joint pathology such as osteoarthritis or avascular necrosis, if she failed six to eight weeks of load management, or if an injection were being planned, in which case ultrasound would be the test.’**
**Bloods only if red flags**: FBE, CRP and ESR, calcium, ALP, EUC, LFT, and where indicated **PSA, urate or a myeloma screen.**

**‘Isn't this just trochanteric bursitis?’** → **‘Both terms are in use and the references differ. Murtagh still lists trochanteric bursitis; Talley and O'Connor and current Australian rheumatology practice prefer greater trochanteric pain syndrome, because imaging shows gluteal tendinopathy is present far more often than isolated bursal inflammation, and pure bursitis is uncommon. I would answer GTPS and note the older term describes the same clinical problem.’** VERIFY

**‘The X-ray is normal but you are still worried about a fracture — now what?’** → **‘MRI. A normal plain film does not exclude an occult or stress fracture of the neck of femur, and it does not exclude early avascular necrosis. dx: **Meniscal tear (version A) or anterior cruciate ligament tear (versions B, C, D).** **Meniscus** — a C-shaped fibrocartilage cushion between femur and tibia, torn by **a twisting force on a semi-flexed, weight-bearing knee.** **ACL** — the central rope-like ligament preventing the tibia sliding forward, torn by **sudden deceleration and change of direction, awkward landing, or hyperextension.**

**Candidates fail this station for two reasons only**: they cannot separate a meniscal from a cruciate tear so they **hedge, list five things and commit to nothing**; or they take a generic pain history and **never explore the injury itself.** **You have six full minutes — there is no excuse of ‘no time’.**

**THE SWELLING CLOCK is the single most useful number in the station.** **Under 30 minutes = tense immediate swelling = HAEMARTHROSIS — ACL in the great majority, also osteochondral fracture, patellar dislocation, peripheral meniscal tear.** **6–24 hours = gradual = REACTIVE EFFUSION — meniscal tear, collateral sprain, soft tissue.** **Days later or none = simple sprain or contusion.**

**Say the clock out loud in the room — that one sentence is worth several ticks**: **‘The fact the knee swelled within about half an hour suggests bleeding inside the joint rather than simple swelling.’** VERIFY If challenged on figures, say **‘the majority’** rather than quoting a percentage.

**MURTAGH'S RULE OF THREE — a meniscal tear can be diagnosed clinically with THREE OR MORE of**: **a twisting mechanism · joint effusion · locking or catching · medial or lateral joint line tenderness · inability to fully extend · pain on hyperextension or hyperflexion · pain on rotation of the lower leg · weak or wasted quadriceps.** **Version A gives you four — COUNT THEM OUT LOUD.** VERIFY If challenged: *‘this is Murtagh's composite — no single test is diagnostic, so I am combining features.’*

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE is not which label you pick.** Candidates who name the right diagnosis still fail. **It is whether you can take the mechanism, the timing of the swelling and the findings on the card and hand them back to the patient AS THE REASONS.** **Hedging without committing fails; committing without a caveat is unsafe.**

**The three-part formula**: **name it simply in plain English → explain what that structure does in one sentence → give THREE NUMBERED REASONS drawn from mechanism, then symptoms, then findings.** The phrase that passes: **‘There are three reasons I think this: the mechanism of your injury, how quickly the knee swelled, and what I found when I examined you.’**

**Jargon translator** — *meniscus* → **‘a cushion-like pad of cartilage inside the knee’** · *anterior cruciate ligament* → **‘a rope-like band in the middle of the knee that keeps it stable’** · *haemarthrosis* → **‘bleeding inside the joint’** · *effusion* → **‘fluid inside the knee’** · *reduced extension* → **‘you can't straighten it all the way’** · *arthroscopy* → **‘keyhole surgery to look inside the knee’.**

**Management: analgesia — paracetamol 1 g four times daily, max 4 g/24 h; ibuprofen 200–400 mg tds with food if not contraindicated** VERIFY · **neurovascular check** · **POLICE, which has replaced strict RICE — Protect, Optimal Loading, Ice, Compression, Elevation; ice 15–20 minutes every 2–3 hours for 48 hours, never directly on skin** · **crutches and partial weight-bearing, a knee immobiliser or hinged brace for instability** · **X-ray if Ottawa positive** · **physiotherapy early** — the mainstay for meniscal tears and pre-habilitation before ACL reconstruction · **early orthopaedic or sports physician referral for a suspected ACL** · **review in 5–7 days, when the swelling settles and the special tests become reliable — and SAY SO.**

**A truly locked knee is a same-week orthopaedic referral, not a physiotherapy trial** — usually a bucket-handle tear. **MRI is the investigation of choice for meniscal and cruciate injury**; a GP may request MRI knee after acute trauma where there is inability to extend suggesting a meniscal tear, or findings suggesting an ACL tear, within the age eligibility. VERIFY **If unsure, say ‘I would request an MRI and check my eligibility to order it directly, otherwise refer.’** SA — **MRI and orthopaedics are largely metropolitan; PATS for travel, regional LHN telehealth for review** · **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for a knee dislocation with vascular compromise · **ReturnToWorkSA and a work capacity certificate** if injured at work — **ask the occupation before you plan anything** · **no driving in an immobiliser or non-weight-bearing on crutches, and document it** · **name the out-of-pocket cost of private MRI versus public waiting times.**
plan: **WIPE, open question, and STOP — let him give the injury story unprompted.** Then **empathy and analgesia, which is a mark in nearly every acute-pain station**: **‘That sounds really uncomfortable, and I can see you're worried about it. Are you in pain right now? Would you like something for the pain before we go on?’** The usual answer is *‘no, I took Panadol’* — **you still get the mark.** Then the agenda.

**Box 1 — the pain, SIQORA not SOCRATES, 75 seconds maximum.** **‘Where exactly is the pain — the INNER part of the knee, the OUTER part, or the BACK?’** (inner → medial meniscus or MCL · outer → lateral meniscus or LCL · back → Baker's cyst, PCL, hamstring) · out of ten · dull or sharp, one breath · **when did it start — immediately at the moment of injury?** · constant or intermittent, getting worse · radiation · **‘is it worse when you stand or walk on it?’ — the Ottawa rule in disguise** · effect on stairs, work, walking.

**Box 2 — EXPLORE THE INJURY. The scoring block. Start semi-open, then close down question by question EVEN IF HE HAS ALREADY TOLD YOU THE STORY — the examiner scores the questions asked, not the information obtained.** **‘I'd now like to go through the injury itself in detail. Can you describe exactly what happened?’** Let him talk for a full minute.

**Then the seven closed questions.** **‘Did you TWIST the knee?’** (meniscus) · **‘Did you land awkwardly, or suddenly change direction or stop?’** (ACL) · **‘Was there a DIRECT BLOW, and from which side?’** (valgus → MCL · hyperextension → ACL · dashboard → PCL) · **‘Did you hear or feel a POP or a snap?’** (ACL, also patellar dislocation and patellar tendon rupture) · **‘How soon after the injury did the knee SWELL — within minutes, or later that day?’** · **‘Were you able to stand and put weight on it straight after — AND CAN YOU NOW?’** · **‘Did you injure anything else — and IN PARTICULAR, DID YOU HIT YOUR HEAD?’** **Never skip the last one, even when he clearly did not fall — a head injury outranks the knee entirely.**

**Box 3 — the three key knee questions, rehearsed as a single 20-second block.** **‘Does your knee ever LOCK or get stuck, so you have to wiggle it to free it?’** — the single most commonly forgotten question · **‘Does it ever GIVE WAY or buckle under you?’** · **‘Are you able to FULLY BEND AND FULLY STRAIGHTEN it?’** — **ask it that way, not ‘is it moving freely’, which gets a vague answer and loses the best meniscal clue.** **Plus weight-bearing, already asked. Locking, giving way, extension, weight-bearing — these four are what the examiner ticks.**

**Box 4 — general MSK screen, one breath each.** Swelling, and is it still increasing · redness or warmth · bruising · deformity · stiffness and how long in the morning · **fevers, sweats, feeling unwell** · any previous injury or surgery to this knee. **This is an acute traumatic case — a single screening sweep is enough; the in-depth infection, malignancy and inflammatory work belongs to the chronic knee station.**

**Box 5 — the other two compartments, plus referred and background.** **Bone and ligament are covered; now NERVE: ‘any pins and needles or numbness in the leg or foot? Any weakness moving the foot or ankle?’** and **VESSEL: ‘any colour change, or the leg or foot feeling cold?’** Then **REFERRED: ‘any pain in your hip or lower back?’** — a disc lesion radiates to the knee, and **hip pathology presents AS knee pain.**

**Occupation and sport — not for diagnosis, for the plan.** *Apprentice electrician, on his knees half the day* is the reason he gets a light-duties certificate. Then background briefly. Then **‘was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?’** — **the cousin's cruciate and the fear of losing the apprenticeship. One sentence of acknowledgement; do not open a counselling consultation.**
**Request the examination in a structured twenty seconds, take the card, and READ IT ALOUD.**

**Commit to ONE diagnosis with three numbered reasons → a RANKED differential where every name is followed by ‘less likely because’ → Ottawa status and the X-ray decision → the plan → answer the cousin question directly → safety-net with the four specific warning signs and a review date.** **If he asks ‘are you sure?’**: **‘I'm confident enough to start treating it this way, but not certain. In an acutely swollen knee the specific tests aren't reliable, so I'll know much more when I see you again next week — and a scan would settle it if there's any doubt.’**
pefe: **You do not examine — the findings arrive on a card at six minutes, and you get about twenty seconds to read it.** Since 2018–19 this station has never asked the candidate to perform the examination.

**OTTAWA KNEE RULES — X-ray if ANY ONE is present**: **age 55 or older · isolated tenderness of the patella · tenderness at the head of the fibula · unable to flex to 90° · UNABLE TO BEAR WEIGHT (four steps) BOTH IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE INJURY AND AT ASSESSMENT.** **Criterion 5 is the one to ask twice** — once as an aggravating factor, once in the injury block. **A completely negative rule lets you safely omit the X-ray.** VERIFY

**The named tests, if the examiner asks you to describe them**: **Lachman — ACL, knee 20–30°, stabilise the femur and pull the tibia anteriorly; positive is increased translation with a soft end point, and it is the most sensitive test that still works in an acutely painful swollen knee.** **Anterior drawer — ACL at 90°, less sensitive acutely because hamstring spasm splints the knee.** **Posterior drawer and sag sign — PCL at 90°.** **Valgus and varus stress — MCL and LCL at 0° and 30°; laxity at 0° means a severe combined injury.** **McMurray, Apley and Thessaly — menisci, rotation under load; positive is joint line pain, a click or catching.** **Patellar apprehension — previous or recurrent dislocation.** **Always add: ‘and I would compare with the other knee.’**

**Do not miss**: **a truly locked knee** (bucket-handle — same-week orthopaedics, not physio) · **tense haemarthrosis** (ACL, osteochondral fracture or patellar dislocation until proven otherwise) · **fracture, particularly tibial plateau in an older patient who can still walk** · **neurovascular injury after a knee dislocation, INCLUDING ONE THAT REDUCED SPONTANEOUSLY and looks deceptively benign — ABI <0.9 means CT angiography and immediate referral** · **extensor mechanism rupture — test the straight-leg raise** · **head, cervical spine or other injury from the same fall** · **septic arthritis in a hot febrile joint** · **in an adolescent, SUFE, physeal injury, and non-accidental injury where the mechanism does not fit.**

**Avoid**: calling it ‘just a sprain’ and discharging without follow-up · **treating ‘special tests not performed’ as a negative result** · **forcing McMurray's or Apley's on an acutely painful guarded knee** · promising surgery, timelines or a return-to-sport date · **ordering an MRI for every acute knee, or before an X-ray when Ottawa is positive** · aspirating a joint in general practice without clear indication and aseptic technique · **NSAIDs without checking renal function, ulcer history and other medicines.**
**Lipohaemarthrosis — a fat–fluid level on a horizontal-beam lateral — means an INTRA-ARTICULAR FRACTURE.** X-ray views: **AP, lateral, and skyline if you suspect patellar pathology.**

**The curveballs a partner can add**: **‘I fell afterwards and banged my head, but I'm fine’** → stop and screen for loss of consciousness, vomiting, amnesia and anticoagulants · **‘my foot's gone a bit numb on the top’** → common peroneal nerve, examine and escalate · **‘it happened at work, on site’** → ReturnToWorkSA claim and a work capacity certificate, and ask whether it was reported · **‘I'm playing in a grand final on Saturday’** → be honest, do not negotiate a return · **‘I drove here in my manual ute’** → advise against driving while unable to control the pedals safely.

**The safety net — say all four**: **‘Come back or go to the emergency department straight away if the knee LOCKS and you cannot straighten it, if the leg or foot becomes NUMB, COLD OR PALE, if you develop FEVER with a hot red swollen knee, or if the PAIN BECOMES MUCH WORSE despite the tablets.’** Then **the review date at 5–7 days, the interim advice, and written information.**
