time: Absorb the barrage without interrupting and without answering · acknowledge, collect anything else, ask permission · then three minutes in four blocks — medications, bleeding risk with the kidney question asked twice, clotting risk with the valve question, diabetes and surgical basics · then team framing, her cardiologist, bleeding versus clotting, the NOAC plan, and the SGLT2 plan as its own numbered item · and reserve the last forty-five seconds to go back through every concern by name

back.dx: PERIPROCEDURAL MANAGEMENT OF A DIRECT ORAL ANTICOAGULANT AND AN SGLT2 INHIBITOR, WRAPPED IN A CONCERNS BARRAGE — two named key points and everything else communication. The numbers: stop before a low bleeding risk procedure, apixaban and rivaroxaban 24-48 h, dabigatran 24-72 h and up to 96 h with poor renal function · high bleeding risk such as major bowel surgery 48-72 h, longer for dabigatran · minimal risk procedures such as dental, cataract or a diagnostic scope often need no interruption at all · restart is surgeon-decided, about 24 h after low or moderate risk and 2-3 days after high risk · SGLT2 inhibitor stops at least 3 days before and restarts when eating and drinking normally · bridging is never used for a NOAC · eGFR roughly 30-50 lengthens the interruption for apixaban and rivaroxaban, and dabigatran extends earlier and further VERIFY all. The examiner questions and their answers. 'Would you bridge her?' → 'No. Bridging is not recommended when interrupting a direct oral anticoagulant, because these agents have a rapid onset on restarting, so there is no therapeutic gap to cover. Bridging is a warfarin concept, where the delay to therapeutic effect creates that gap. Her clotting risk is low in any case.' 'If her eGFR came back at 35?' → 'The interruption lengthens — for apixaban at a low bleeding risk procedure, from around 24 hours to about 48. On dabigatran, which is substantially more renally cleared, it could extend to 72 or even 96 hours and I'd seek specialist advice. I'd also review her anticoagulant dose longer term, be cautious about perioperative nephrotoxins, and be cautious about restarting metformin until renal function returned to baseline.' 'Why stop the dapagliflozin three days before rather than on the morning like the metformin?' → 'Because SGLT2 inhibitors carry a risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis, precipitated by fasting, dehydration and surgical stress. The glucose can be normal or only mildly elevated, so the usual warning sign is absent and the diagnosis is easily missed. The effect on ketogenesis persists beyond a single dose, so omitting it only on the morning is not sufficient.' 'She is having a colonoscopy with bowel preparation instead?' → 'For the SGLT2 inhibitor, no change — bowel preparation causes significant dehydration and the same risk applies. For the anticoagulant it depends: a purely diagnostic colonoscopy is low bleeding risk, but if polypectomy is anticipated I'd plan as for a low-to-moderate risk procedure and discuss it with the proceduralist.' The variants. B, sigmoid resection — a higher bleeding risk procedure, so 48-72 hours rather than 24-48, and the surgeon most likely waits 2-3 days to restart; the colostomy question is answered with the emergency-versus-planned distinction and deferred to the surgeon, never with a flat promise. C, dabigatran — widen to 24-72 hours and the kidney point gets stronger still. E, a mechanical valve or a mini-stroke six weeks ago disclosed in the history — change gear and escalate: 'That changes how we approach this. NOACs are not used for mechanical valves and bridging does apply here. This isn't a decision I'd make on my own today — I'll discuss it with your cardiologist and the surgical team before anything is changed, and please don't stop any medication on your own.' Recognising that you are outside the routine algorithm is the mark.
plan: WIPE, confirm identity and preferred name, then an open question — and let the barrage run without interrupting and without answering.
Acknowledge, reserve, collect anything else, count them back, and ask permission to take the history (see findings).

BLOCK ONE, MEDICATIONS — how long she has had the AF and diabetes · talk me through your medicines and are you taking them regularly · WHEN DID YOU LAST TAKE THE BLOOD THINNER · side effects, unusual bruising or bleeding · GP reviews and recent bloods · AND ANYTHING OVER THE COUNTER, FISH OIL, ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES OR HERBAL.

BLOCK TWO, BLEEDING RISK — high blood pressure · THE KIDNEY QUESTION ASKED AS TWO SEPARATE QUESTIONS · liver problems · stroke or TIA · ANY SERIOUS BLEED, ULCER, BLOOD IN URINE OR BOWELS · alcohol per week. Answer the 'why my kidneys' question there and then.
BLOCK THREE, CLOTTING RISK — is the AF constant or paroxysmal · previous clot, stroke or TIA · HAVE YOU EVER HAD A HEART VALVE REPLACED · heart failure, heart attacks or leg circulation problems.

BLOCK FOUR, DIABETES AND SURGICAL BASICS — usual sugars and home monitoring, hypos, any admission or ketones · WHEN IS THE OPERATION and has she been told when to stop eating and drinking · allergies and previous anaesthetic trouble · and who is at home.
Team framing first, because it pre-answers two of her concerns — then her own cardiologist, with the promise, the fallback and the check.
The framework — bleeding if we keep it going against clotting if we stop it — then her actual scores on each side.

The NOAC plan — quick offset in one sentence · the eGFR decides · 24 to 48 hours with the exact day confirmed by phone and in writing · no bridging, and hold that line if she pushes · and the surgeon restarts, usually about 24 hours after, with 'Please don't restart it yourself'.

The SGLT2 plan as its own numbered item — three days, the reason in plain words, hydration, glucose monitoring and insulin cover, and when to restart — then the remaining tablets, which continue to the day with the morning oral glucose-lowering dose omitted.
BACK THROUGH EVERY CONCERN BY NAME — bleeding, stroke, the surgeon, the cardiologist, the neighbour, the brother-in-law (see findings). She raised them; the examiner wrote them down.

Safety-net — bleeding that won't stop, black or bloody motions, blood in urine or unusual bruising → contact us or ED · sudden weakness, face droop, trouble speaking or chest pain → triple zero · and feeling unwell, nauseated, vomiting or breathless in the days around surgery even with a normal sugar → ring us. Then summarise, ask her to tell it back, and offer a family meeting.
back.planNote: 3 minutes of history in four blocks, and the last 45 seconds reserved for the concerns — the commonest way to lose this station is to run out of time before returning to what she raised at the start
ask: The control line, learned whole: 'I appreciate you sharing your concerns with me and I can hear how worried you are... Before I start — is there anything else you're worried about? Tell me now, so I know to cover everything. Is it okay if I ask you a few questions first, so that when I answer them my answers are actually about you?'

The two key points, said plainly: 'I'll need to check your kidney function, with a test called the eGFR, to decide exactly when we stop it — your kidneys are how this medicine leaves your body.' and 'The dapagliflozin we stop three days before, because around an operation it can cause a build-up of acid in the blood even when your sugar looks normal.'
The bridging refusal, kindly: 'You won't need any injections in the gap. Yours starts working within hours, so there's nothing to cover.' Explain the warfarin difference; never concede.

The honest-reassurance line, which is the hardest thing here to get right: 'On a planned operation we have time to prepare — bloods, medication decisions, getting you in the best shape. That's why it carries less risk than emergency surgery. It doesn't mean no risk, and I won't tell you it does.'

Challenges: 'Am I going to bleed to death?' · 'But you're still stopping it — that's when the stroke happens, isn't it?' · 'Why do you keep asking about my kidneys?' · 'Can't you just tell me a day? I need to write it on the calendar.' · 'My friend had injections in her stomach — why don't I need those?' · 'Insulin? I don't want to end up on needles for good.' · and 'That's what they told my neighbour' if you reassure without a reason.
pefe: There is no examination, and the one number that decides the plan is deliberately withheld from the stem: the eGFR. The correct response is to name the test, give the range, order it today and commit to ringing with the exact date — not to invent a day to sound decisive.

Role-player: Jane Whitcombe, 60, a retired bookkeeper living with her husband Ken. Paroxysmal AF for about six years, type 2 diabetes for about twelve. Apixaban twice daily, dapagliflozin, metformin, atorvastatin, atenolol — taken reliably, last apixaban last night, paracetamol occasionally and nothing else. Blood pressure always normal, no kidney or liver problems, no stroke or TIA, no clots, no valve replacement, no heart failure, never a serious bleed, a little arm bruising she has always had, two glasses of wine at weekends, sugars seven or eight, no hypos, no allergies, a gallbladder out years ago. Surgery is a week on Thursday and nobody has told her anything about her tablets.

How she plays it: frightened underneath, coming out as sharp and demanding — not rude for its own sake; she feels ignored and unprepared. She delivers four or five concerns in one breath and does not let the doctor in until she runs out. She holds the cardiologist back for 'Anything else?' and drops it mid-explanation if never asked. She interrupts the history once with 'But you still haven't told me if I'm going to bleed to death' — and if the doctor abandons the history to answer, she keeps interrupting so they never get through it. She asks why the kidneys keep coming up, pushes for one fixed date, pushes for the injections, and panics about insulin. She softens only in response to specific answers — 'Don't worry' or 'You'll be fine' gets 'That's what they told my neighbour.' She accepts a family meeting warmly.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE, WITH FIVE FLAGGED CRITICAL: let her finish the barrage without interrupting · acknowledged before answering any of them · ASKED WHETHER THERE WAS ANYTHING ELSE · asked permission before the history · completed a structured history despite the interruption · ASKED ABOUT KIDNEY FUNCTION TWICE, AS TWO SEPARATE QUESTIONS (CRITICAL) · liver, previous bleeding, alcohol and other drugs · ASKED ABOUT A PROSTHETIC VALVE (CRITICAL) · previous clots or strokes · diabetes control and the operation date · explained the team decision · PROMISED TO TRY HER OWN CARDIOLOGIST WITH A FALLBACK AND CHECKED SHE AGREED · low bleeding risk procedure and no HAS-BLED factors · clotting risk low and why · the quick offset explained · SAID THE eGFR DECIDES EXACTLY WHEN TO STOP IT (CRITICAL) · GAVE A 24-48 HOUR RANGE RATHER THAN AN INVENTED DATE · SAID NO BRIDGING AND DID NOT AGREE TO ARRANGE INJECTIONS (CRITICAL) · surgeon restarts at about 24 hours · IDENTIFIED THE DAPAGLIFLOZIN AND SAID STOP 3 DAYS BEFORE (CRITICAL) · explained why, plus hydration, monitoring, insulin cover and restart · other medications and the omitted morning dose · reframed insulin as short-term · answered the surgeon concern without simply defending him · ANSWERED THE NEIGHBOUR CONCERN HONESTLY AND DID NOT PROMISE ZERO RISK · safety-netting and a written plan · summary and teach-back · CAME BACK TO EVERY CONCERN RAISED AT THE START · offered a family meeting.

The opening barrage — do not start answering — 'I'm on a blood thinner — am I going to bleed to death? And if you stop it, am I going to have a stroke? My brother-in-law had a stroke after an operation. My neighbour went in for a routine operation and she never came home. I don't know your surgeon from a bar of soap' — five in one breath, with 'I want to speak to my cardiologist, not one of yours' held back for 'Anything else?'

The line that takes control without dismissing her — 'I appreciate you sharing your concerns with me, and I can hear how worried you are — those are all reasonable things to be thinking about. I'll be doing my best to address every one of them and we'll make the best plan together. Before I do — is there anything else you're worried about? Tell me now, so I know to cover everything. Then, is it okay if I ask you a few questions first?' Counting them back — 'That's five, I've got all five' — is itself scored

If she interrupts the history — ONE LINE, THEN CONTINUE: 'THAT'S IMPORTANT AND I PROMISE I'LL ANSWER IT PROPERLY IN A MOMENT — CAN I JUST FINISH THESE FEW QUESTIONS SO MY ANSWER IS A GOOD ONE?' If you abandon the history to answer her, she is briefed to keep interrupting and you never get through it

Key point one — ask the kidney question twice, as two questions — 'HAVE YOU EVER HAD AN ABNORMAL KIDNEY FUNCTION TEST?' AND, SEPARATELY, 'HAS ANYONE EVER TOLD YOU THAT YOU HAVE CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE?' Buried once in a list, or not at all, is a single-item automatic fail

'Why do you keep asking about my kidneys?' — a gift, take it — 'That's a really good question and I'm glad you noticed. Your kidneys are how this particular blood thinner leaves your body. So how well they're working decides exactly how long before surgery we need to stop it. It's the single most important piece of information I need' — the examiner hears the reasoning twice

The valve question rules out a different station — 'Have you ever had a heart valve replaced?' → no. A mechanical valve would mean a NOAC is not the right drug at all, bridging would apply, and the whole plan changes. One question rules it out

Lead with the team, which pre-answers two concerns — 'This decision isn't made by one person — we make it as a team: your surgeon, your regular GP, the anaesthetist and a cardiologist, and I'll make sure they're all talking to each other'

Bleeding versus clotting, with her actual scores — Bleeding: a keyhole hernia repair is a low bleeding risk procedure, and on HAS-BLED her blood pressure is fine, no previous bleed, no kidney or liver problem, not over 65, no anti-inflammatories — no risk factors at all · clotting: diabetes counts for a point, but no heart failure, no hypertension, not 75, no previous clot or stroke and no artificial valve — low, which is what makes a short planned gap safe

The pharmacology in one sentence — 'Your blood thinner has a quick offset of action — the effect wears off within a few hours of stopping it, and it starts working again just as fast when you restart. That's quite different from warfarin, which hangs around for days'

The timing — give the range, name the test, commit to confirming — 'Most likely 24 to 48 hours before your surgery, and I'll confirm the exact day once I have the eGFR.' when she presses for one day: 'I'd rather give you an accurate answer than a quick one. I'll organise the blood test today and ring you with the exact date and put it in writing.' Naming a single invented day to sound decisive is the trap

No bridging — and do not be talked into it — 'My friend had injections in her stomach before her hip replacement. Why don't I need those?' → 'Your friend was almost certainly on warfarin, which takes days to start working again, so there's a real gap to cover. Yours starts working within hours, so there isn't one. Adding injections wouldn't make you safer — it would only add bleeding risk.' Agreeing to arrange bridging is an AUTOMATIC FAIL

Key point two — the planted tablet — 'There's one other tablet and this one's important — the dapagliflozin. We stop that one three days before. Around an operation, when you're not eating or drinking, it can cause a serious build-up of acid in the blood — and it can happen even when your sugar reading looks perfectly normal, so it's easy to miss.' Lumping it in with 'Your diabetes tablets stop on the morning' is a single-item AUTOMATIC FAIL

The three things that go with it — One, keep drinking plenty of fluids while she is still taking it, because dehydration is what sets it off · two, closer glucose monitoring once it stops, with insulin if sugars run high · three, restart it once she is eating and drinking normally. And if she panics about insulin: 'This would only be short-term cover around the operation, if your sugars needed it — not a permanent change'

Going back through the concerns by name — The surgeon — ask what specifically worries her, then offer a sit-down with him before the operation rather than defending him · the neighbour who died — 'With a planned operation we have time to prepare... That's why planned surgery generally carries lower risk than emergency surgery. It doesn't mean there's no risk, and I won't tell you it does' · the brother-in-law's stroke — his situation may be quite different; speak to her numbers · and in the bowel-surgery version, the colostomy question

Her cardiologist — promise, fallback, then check she agrees — 'I will do my best to get hold of him and speak to him directly. If I can't reach him before your surgery, I'll ask one of our experienced cardiologists to come and see you, so the decision is still made properly and you still get to ask your questions. How does that sound — are you happy for me to do that?' 'We have our own cardiologists here' reads as brushing her off; the check is what converts it into shared decision-making
fails: ★ Never asking about kidney function, or burying it once in a list — the eGFR is what decides the interruption, and it is the named key point of the case
★ Lumping the dapagliflozin in with 'your diabetes tablets stop on the morning of surgery' instead of stopping it three days before and explaining euglycaemic ketoacidosis
★ Agreeing to arrange bridging injections to keep her happy — bridging is never used when interrupting a direct oral anticoagulant

Nurse's observations: temp 38.6°C · HR 104 regular · BP 126/78 · RR 18 · SpO2 97% on air · BGL 6.8. No physical examination is required and no examination findings will be provided.

dx: **Septic arthritis of the right hip — and because a prosthesis is in place, a PROSTHETIC JOINT INFECTION.** Specifically a **LATE ACUTE HAEMATOGENOUS infection, six years after a well-functioning replacement, seeded from a recent dental procedure.** **The organism forms a BIOFILM on the metal that antibiotics alone cannot penetrate — so cure normally needs SURGERY PLUS antibiotics, not antibiotics alone.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE, in one sentence: THE DIAGNOSIS IS NOT THE MARK. The audible, grouped exclusion of the other four differential groups AFTER you already have the answer is the mark.** **Nearly every candidate finds the fever and says septic arthritis. A large proportion still fail.** What separates them is the three minutes after the fever: **the passing candidate announced a switch and worked through kidney, bowel, genital and skin systematically; the failing candidate either closed early into past medical history, or kept asking more detailed questions about the same hip. Both read as PREMATURE CLOSURE — the single commonest reason this station is failed.**

**THE SWITCH LINE, verbatim, at about three minutes**: **‘Thank you — the temperature is important and I'll come back to it in a moment. Before I do, I want to make sure I'm not missing anything else that causes pain in this area. I'll ask about the hip itself, then your waterworks, then your tummy, then some private questions, then the skin. A lot of these will be a no — that's exactly what I'm checking.’**

**THE FIVE GROUPS, named out loud before the questions inside them**: **1 HIP AND MUSCULOSKELETAL — septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, the arthritides, AVN, PMR, greater trochanteric pain syndrome, implant loosening, fracture · 2 KIDNEY, URETER, BLADDER · 3 ABDOMEN AND PELVIS · 4 GENITAL · 5 SKIN AND LYMPH NODE.** Plus **neurological (L1/L2 radiculopathy) and vascular (femoral aneurysm, iliofemoral DVT)** if time allows. **Two groups is a fail even with the right diagnosis.**

**WHY THERE IS NO SWELLING OR REDNESS — and candidates hesitate because of it.** **The hip is a DEEP joint, encased in muscle on every side — iliopsoas and pectineus in front, the glutei behind, the adductors medially.** A septic knee is red, hot and visibly swollen because it sits under skin. **A septic hip shows you almost nothing: what you get instead is FEVER, SEVERE PAIN ON ANY MOVEMENT, and COMPLETE REFUSAL TO WEIGHT-BEAR.** **ABSENCE OF REDNESS ARGUES FOR A DEEP JOINT, NOT AGAINST INFECTION.**

**THE WEIGHT-BEARING LOGIC IS THE CENTRAL PLANK OF THE EXPLANATION**: **‘If this were a boil in the skin, a swollen gland, or a strain, you could still stand. NOT BEING ABLE TO LOAD THE LEG TELLS ME THE PROBLEM IS INSIDE THE JOINT.’** **Do not accept ‘it hurts to walk’ — ask ‘can you put ANY weight on it at all?’**

**THE SECOND DISCRIMINATING LAYER — THE PROSTHESIS.** Two candidates both say ‘septic arthritis’. One adds: **‘and because there is an artificial joint in there, this is a PROSTHETIC JOINT INFECTION — which usually needs an OPERATION as well as antibiotics, so I'm not going to start antibiotics here.’** **Ask WHY the hip was replaced, WHEN, and HOW IT HAS BEEN SINCE — and say the words prosthetic joint infection out loud.**

**Explaining it to him, in plain words and with the reasoning**: **‘The most likely cause of your pain is an infection inside the hip joint itself — septic arthritis. And because you have an artificial hip, we give it a specific name, a prosthetic joint infection. First, you have a temperature that isn't settling with paracetamol, so there is an infection somewhere. Second — and this is the important part — you can't put any weight on that leg at all. Third, germs travelling in the bloodstream can settle on artificial joints. That tooth extraction three weeks ago is ONE POSSIBLE WAY germs could have got in — I can't say for certain, and NOTHING WAS DONE WRONGLY.’** **Never say ‘haematogenous seeding’ or ‘biofilm’ to him.**

**The dental prophylaxis question he will ask** VERIFY : **current Australian guidance — Therapeutic Guidelines and the Australian Dental Association — is that routine antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is NOT recommended solely because a patient has a prosthetic joint.** **Answer honestly and WITHOUT BLAME: ‘nothing was done wrongly, and we also can't be certain the tooth is the source — it's one possibility among several.’** **Blaming the dentist is an error of both fact and manner.**

**The hidden agenda, raised at six minutes if you never ask**: **‘Doctor, be straight with me — is this cancer? My BROTHER had SOMETHING in his bones and it STARTED like this.’** **Answer it DIRECTLY, with the specific negatives**: **‘I did think about it, which is why I asked about weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats and blood in your urine and bowels. Everything you told me was reassuring, and a three-day illness with a fever is much more likely to be infection. I'm not dismissing it, and the tests in hospital will look at that too.’** **IGNORING OR EVADING a directly asked question about cancer is an automatic fail.** And on the implant: **‘sometimes the surgeon can wash the joint out and keep the replacement, changing only some parts; sometimes it does need replacing. The surgeon will tell you once they've looked — I don't want to promise you either way.’**
plan: **WIPE, then comfort first — he is in pain and febrile.** **‘I can see you're in a lot of discomfort, so I'll be as quick as I can. Are you in pain right now?’** Then **THE AGENDA SENTENCE, which is what makes the next five minutes read as a plan rather than a fishing trip**: **‘Groin pain can come from a few different places — the hip joint, the kidneys and bladder, the tummy, the private parts, or the skin and glands. I'm going to go through each area in turn so we don't miss anything. Some questions won't seem related — please bear with me.’**

**The pain — nine questions, NINETY SECONDS, then move on.** Point with ONE finger · out of ten now and at worst · **dull ache or sharp and stabbing, does it come in WAVES** · when and sudden or gradual · constant or intermittent, better, worse or the same · **does it travel — down the leg, into the back, into the private parts** · better or worse with anything, and **has what you've taken helped** · effect on sleeping, washing, getting to the toilet.

**RED FLAGS, ANNOUNCED AND UNCONDITIONAL.** **Malignancy**: weight loss, appetite, lumps anywhere, unusually tired, **night sweats soaking the sheets**, long-standing cough, **blood in urine or bowel motions.** **A 60-year-old with new hip and groin pain has BONE, BOWEL, PROSTATE AND BLADDER malignancy on the list — there is no version of this station where you may skip this block.** **Infection**: fevers, **‘any SHIVERING AND SHAKING — rigors?’**, **‘have you taken anything for it, and is it bringing the temperature down?’** — *38.6 since FRIDAY and paracetamol is not SHIFTING it, which means an ESTABLISHED infection rather than a transient viral temperature* — recent infections — skin, chest, urine, teeth — **and RECENT PROCEDURES, OPERATIONS OR DENTAL WORK.**

**THE FEVER LANDS HERE AND MOST CANDIDATES STOP. DO NOT STOP. Say the switch line.** Then **GROUP 1 — HIP**: occupation and lifting · other joints · family arthritis · rash on elbows, knees or scalp, nail changes · **diarrhoea or urethral discharge** (which doubles as a bowel and genital screen) · **medications, and EVER had steroid tablets or injections** · alcohol · **previous hip surgery, fracture or dislocation → WHY, WHEN, AND HOW HAS IT BEEN SINCE** · painful to lie on that side · **shoulder stiffness, new headache, tender scalp, jaw ache on chewing.**

**GROUP 2 — KIDNEY, URETER, BLADDER. ‘Now your waterworks.’** Burning passing urine · frequency or urgency · **blood in the urine** · **getting up at night, and has the stream changed — slow, dribbling, hard to start** (worth adding in a man over 50; it also picks up prostate pathology, which refers to the groin and perineum).

**GROUP 3 — ABDOMEN AND PELVIS. ‘Now your tummy and bowels.’** **A lump or bulge in the groin, especially on coughing or straining** · tummy pain · vomiting · **passing wind and opening bowels normally** · constipation, diarrhoea, blood · overall change in bowel habit. **Pain plus vomiting plus no flatus is obstruction or strangulation — a surgical emergency.** **In a woman add: last period, heavy or painful periods, bleeding between periods or after menopause, and any chance of pregnancy.**

**GROUP 4 — GENITAL. Ask permission first: ‘I need to ask a few personal questions — is that alright?’** Testicular pain, swelling or lump · discharge, ulcers, blisters or sores · sexual activity and STI risk. Then **GROUP 5 — SKIN AND NODES. ‘Last area.’** **Boils, cuts, ulcers or infected hair follicles — ESPECIALLY IF HE SHAVES THERE** · **a band of rash, blisters or burning skin round to the back** · rash, redness, swelling or a break in the skin anywhere on that leg or foot · **tender lumps in the groin creases.** **Nodes have now been asked three times — deliberately.**

But NEVER drop the final open question: the hidden concern lives there and task 2 is marked partly on whether you answer it.**

**Diagnosis with the reasoning → differentials BY GROUP, each with a reason it is less likely → the plan.** **‘This needs to be sorted out today, in hospital — not next week. I'm going to ring the orthopaedic doctor on call now and arrange an ambulance. Please don't eat or drink anything from now, in case they need to take you to theatre.’** Then **safety-net: ‘if you feel confused or drowsy, if the temperature climbs, or if you feel much worse in any way, tell the staff straight away.’** **If the bell goes before you finish, get the three words out — HOSPITAL TODAY, BY AMBULANCE.**

C, THE HIP: the same 22-year-old and the same basketball, but the hip aches, is stiff, he is limping AND CANNOT PUT WEIGHT THROUGH IT → 'THE HIP SITS DEEP, WRAPPED IN MUSCLE, SO A PROBLEM THERE OFTEN SHOWS UP AS FULLNESS IN THE GROIN RATHER THAN ANYTHING VISIBLE' — examine the hip, X-ray and ultrasound; ADD A FEVER AND IT IS SEPTIC ARTHRITIS UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, WHERE THE ABSENCE OF VISIBLE REDNESS ARGUES FOR A DEEP JOINT RATHER THAN AGAINST INFECTION. D, THE MALIGNANT NODE: hard, fixed, growing over two months with SIX KILOGRAMS OF UNINTENTIONAL WEIGHT LOSS AND DRENCHING NIGHT SWEATS → urgent bloods, imaging and biopsy; EXAMINE THE WHOLE DRAINAGE TERRITORY INCLUDING THE SOLES AND BETWEEN THE TOES FOR A MELANOMA AND THE PENILE, SCROTAL AND ANAL SKIN, AND INSIST ON A CORE OR EXCISIONAL BIOPSY RATHER THAN FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION IF LYMPHOMA IS POSSIBLE, BECAUSE ARCHITECTURE IS NEEDED FOR CLASSIFICATION VERIFY. E, STRANGULATION: out since yesterday, irreducible, tender, with abdominal pain and vomiting → STOP AND ACT — nil by mouth, IV access, analgesia, surgical team now, likely theatre today, with MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval coordination from a regional site. F, THE FEMORAL HERNIA IN AN OLDER, THINNER WOMAN: small, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, EASILY MISSED, AND WITH A MUCH HIGHER STRANGULATION RISK BECAUSE THE FEMORAL CANAL IS NARROW AND RIGID — so repair is recommended even if asymptomatic and the safety-net becomes more emphatic, not less VERIFY.
plan: INTRODUCE, CONFIRM IDENTITY, OPEN QUESTION — AND ACKNOWLEDGE THE WORRY THE PATIENT VOLUNTEERS BEFORE ASKING ANYTHING ELSE. Eight seconds, a scored item, and the stem gives them the worry precisely so you have something to respond to.

THE CHARACTER BLOCK, WHICH IS THE EXAMINATION YOU ARE NOT ALLOWED TO DO: WHEREABOUTS — CLOSER TO THE HIP OR TO THE PRIVATE PARTS · HOW BIG · 'WHEN YOU PRESS IT, DOES IT FEEL SOFT, OR FIRM AND RUBBERY, OR HARD?', because the three options force a discriminating answer where an open question gets 'like a lump' · tender, red or warm · duration · CONSTANT OR COMES AND GOES · GETTING BIGGER · AND 'IS IT WORSE WHEN YOU STAND, COUGH OR STRAIN, AND DOES IT GO WHEN YOU LIE DOWN?' Follow the patient's own words — 'when it's out' tells you it is intermittent before you ask.
BUCKET ONE, SKIN — fever and chills, redness or rash, discharge, boils, and whether he shaves or waxes there. Forty seconds, and the fever question also serves the node bucket.

BUCKET TWO, HERNIA — groin pain separate from the lump, abdominal pain, THEN THE OBSTRUCTION SCREEN IN FIFTEEN SECONDS: VOMITING, BOWELS OPENING, PASSING WIND, AND 'HAS IT EVER GOT STUCK AND BEEN IMPOSSIBLE TO PUSH BACK?' Never skip it because the lump has been painless for two months — that is exactly the patient who returns strangulated. Then the risk factors: CONSTIPATION AND STRAINING · CHRONIC COUGH AND SMOKING · STRAINING TO PASS URINE AND NOCTURIA · OCCUPATION AND HEAVY LIFTING, INCLUDING WHAT HE DID BEFORE HE RETIRED · PREVIOUS ABDOMINAL SURGERY · AND WEIGHT.

BUCKET THREE, HIP — hip pain, stiffness, limp, WEIGHT-BEARING, and trauma. Thirty seconds, and it closes a bucket that 'swelling' makes people skip because it reads as a lump rather than a joint. One recalled version turns entirely on it.

BUCKET FOUR, LYMPH NODES — FIRST THE DRAINAGE TERRITORY: cuts, ulcers, rashes or infections on that leg or foot, athlete's foot or an ingrown toenail · rash, blisters or ulcers on the penis or genitals · scrotal swelling or pain · DISCHARGE OR BURNING PASSING URINE · anorectal symptoms.

THE SEXUAL HISTORY, WITH THE NORMALISING PREAMBLE AND ASKED OF EVERYONE: sexually active · ARE YOUR PARTNERS MEN, WOMEN OR BOTH · condoms always, sometimes or not usually · number of partners in the last six months · ever diagnosed with an STI · AND, ONCE RISK EMERGES, THE TWO FOLLOW-UPS: EVER TESTED FOR HIV OR USED PrEP, AND WHETHER CONTACT HAS BEEN ORAL OR ANAL, WHICH DECIDES WHETHER YOU SWAB THROAT AND RECTUM AS WELL AS TESTING URINE. Ask it flatly, without commentary, and never react.
The constitutional block — unintentional weight loss, appetite, fatigue, night sweats soaking the sheets, lumps elsewhere in the neck or armpits, changing moles on the legs, and recent travel.

COMMIT TO A LEADING DIAGNOSIS, EXPLAIN IT WITH A MECHANISM THE PATIENT COULD REPEAT, AND JUSTIFY IT FROM WHAT THEY ACTUALLY SAID (see dx). Describing the anatomy without committing, or naming it without explaining it, both lose the mark.

The differentials as four groups, with the node group subdivided into infective and malignant, local and generalised — and one clause of why-not on each, referencing the history so the examiner can tell you listened.

A NEXT STEP AND A SAFETY-NET EVEN THOUGH MANAGEMENT WAS NOT ASKED. VERSION A: examine to confirm, surgical referral for repair, and WORK ON THE DRIVERS — constipation, cough, smoking, and the urinary symptoms in their own right — PLUS THE STRANGULATION WARNING: 'IF THAT LUMP EVER BECOMES STUCK AND PAINFUL, OR YOU GET ABDOMINAL PAIN AND VOMITING, THAT'S AN EMERGENCY — COME STRAIGHT TO HOSPITAL, DON'T WAIT.' VERSION B: urine sample, swabs, and bloods including HIV and syphilis, WITH SHINE SA OFFERED AS A CONFIDENTIAL ALTERNATIVE TO HIS USUAL PRACTICE.
back.planNote: six minutes feels generous, which invites a leisurely hernia history — it is exactly enough for four buckets and only if you start immediately
ask: The two sentences that carry the station: 'My differentials fall into four groups — a hernia; a skin or soft tissue problem; a hip problem; and enlarged lymph nodes, which I'd divide into infective and malignant, each local or generalised.' and 'I ask everyone these questions, because infections in that area are a common cause of swelling in the groin.'
The consistency question in three options: 'Soft, or firm and rubbery, or hard?' — and the posture pair, 'Worse when you stand, cough or strain?' and 'Does it go when you lie down?'
The obstruction screen, asked even of a painless two-month lump: vomiting · bowels · passing wind · 'Has it ever got stuck and been impossible to push back?'

THE SEXUAL HISTORY BLOCK, LEARNED VERBATIM AND ASKED FLATLY: 'ARE YOU SEXUALLY ACTIVE?' · 'ARE YOUR PARTNERS MEN, WOMEN, OR BOTH?' — never 'do you have a girlfriend?' · 'DO YOU USE CONDOMS — ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, OR NOT USUALLY?', where the three options make an honest answer easier · number of partners · previous STI · THEN HIV TESTING AND PrEP, AND SITES OF EXPOSURE.

CHALLENGES: 'IS IT CANCER?' · 'IT DOESN'T HURT — CAN'T WE JUST LEAVE IT?', answered with the strangulation risk without frightening him · 'DOES THIS GO ON MY RECORD? MY FAMILY USE THIS CLINIC' → confidentiality plus SHINE SA as an alternative · 'DO I HAVE TO TELL MY PARTNERS?' → contact tracing framed as supported and often anonymous, not as his burden alone · and 'AM I GOING TO BE ALL RIGHT?' → 'I'd rather test broadly now than treat a guess.'
pefe: THERE IS NO EXAMINATION AND NO INVESTIGATIONS — THE CHARACTER BLOCK IS THE EXAMINATION. Rushing it because there is nothing to anchor to leaves you with nothing to reason from, and every conclusion in task two has to be built from the words the patient chose.

Brief A: James Corbett, 50, a retired bricklayer of thirty years, married thirty years to one partner, in a regional South Australian town. A soft swelling in the right groin for two months, about half a golf ball when it is out, squishy and reducible, painless, worse by the end of the day and on coughing, gone by morning. Given only if asked: straining with constipation most days · a smoker's cough, twenty a day since eighteen · a slow stream, hesitancy and twice-nightly nocturia · thirty years of heavy lifting and the previous occupation · an appendicectomy on the same side · and that he is overweight. His concern, only if asked what is on his mind: 'I've been worried it might be something serious. Cancer.'

Brief B: Daniel Nguyen, 22, a university student working in hospitality, who noticed a grape-sized right groin lump playing basketball though it has probably been there a couple of months. Firm, mildly tender, present all the time and unchanged by standing, coughing or lying flat — which alone should move you off hernia. All hernia risk factors and all hip questions negative. Given only when asked about discharge or burning: stinging when passing urine, said as if he had not thought it relevant, and a little morning discharge only if asked directly. Partners are men, condoms not usually, three or four partners in six months, one previous STI he cannot name, never tested for HIV, never heard of PrEP, both oral and anal exposure. He is embarrassed and hopes he will not be asked much, but answers honestly if asked directly and without judgement — and if the candidate becomes awkward or moralises, he becomes brief and closed for the rest of the station. His concern: 'Does this go on my record? My family use this clinic.'

Mark them against these, scored the same way for both briefs: an open question and the concern acknowledged before proceeding · the full character block including consistency in three options and the posture questions · skin bucket including fever · hernia bucket with the obstruction screen and all six risk factors · hip bucket including weight-bearing · node territory in full · the sexual history asked at all, with a normalising preamble, and handled without awkwardness or moralising · constitutional block including changing moles and travel · a leading diagnosis committed to and justified from the history · differentials as four groups with the nodes subdivided · a next step and a safety-net · understanding checked and finished on time.
fails: ★ Never taking a sexual history in either brief — the commonest single reason candidates failed the recalled version
★ Never asking the obstruction screen in a patient with a groin lump, which is the safety element of the station
★ Diagnosing inguinal hernia in Brief B despite a firm, constantly present lump that does not change with posture and no risk factors at all

Responding to the disclosure of a male partner with visible discomfort, moralising or a change in manner — or reassuring without investigation where the node is hard and fixed with constitutional symptoms

Giving direct, indirect, femoral and incisional hernia as four differentials when that is one bucket; skipping the hip block because 'swelling' reads as a lump; rushing the character block because there is no examination to anchor to; or stopping dead at the differential list with no next step or safety-net
numbers: The six-minute budget: 40 s opening · 80 s characterising · 40 s skin · 80 s hernia · 30 s hip · 70 s lymph nodes · 20 s to close · four buckets run in every version without exception · the obstruction screen takes 15 seconds · the sexual history is six questions plus two follow-ups

Six hernia risk factors in brief A: chronic cough and smoking · constipation and straining · urinary straining with a slow stream and nocturia · thirty years of heavy lifting · previous ipsilateral abdominal surgery · excess weight · femoral hernias are commoner in women, small and easily missed, sit below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and carry a much higher strangulation risk, so repair is recommended even if asymptomatic VERIFY

If lymphoma is possible, core or excisional biopsy rather than fine-needle aspiration, because architecture is needed for classification · sites of exposure decide whether to swab throat and rectum as well as testing urine · SHINE SA for confidential sexual health testing · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval if a hernia strangulates at a regional site · VERIFY all

Full detail — FAIL — Never asking the obstruction screen in a patient with a groin lump — the safety item of the station, fifteen seconds, asked even of a painless two-month lump ('that is exactly the patient who returns obstructed'): 'any pain in the groin itself, separate from the lump? any pain in your abdomen? any nausea or vomiting? are your bowels normal, and are you passing wind normally? and has the lump ever got stuck — been impossible to push back?'; the safety net verbatim: 'if that lump ever becomes stuck and painful, or you get abdominal pain and vomiting, that's an emergency — come straight to hospital, don't wait'; 'it doesn't hurt, can't we just leave it?' → watching is sometimes reasonable, 'but occasionally the contents get trapped and the blood supply is squeezed — that's an emergency and needs surgery within hours, so even if we watch it you need to know the warning signs' (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Never taking a sexual history in either brief, or responding to 'men' with visible discomfort, moralising or a change in manner — skipping the sexual history was the single commonest reason candidates failed the June version; ask it in the married 50-year-old too — it finds nothing, and that is the point: a candidate who asks only when they already suspect will miss the case where the suspicion has to come from the question; the normalising preamble verbatim: 'I'd like to ask a few questions about sexual health — I ask everyone, because infections in that area are a common cause of swelling in the groin; is that all right?'; then six questions flatly — active? 'are your partners men, women, or both?' (not 'do you have a girlfriend?'), 'condoms — always, sometimes, or not usually?', how many partners in six months, previous STI, ever tested for HIV or used PrEP; once risk emerges, two follow-ups — HIV testing and PrEP, and 'has any contact been oral or anal — I ask because it changes where we need to test' (throat and rectal swabs as well as urine); never react — he is briefed to close down if you become awkward (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Diagnosing 'inguinal hernia' in the 22-year-old despite the absence of every supporting feature — a firm, constantly present, mildly tender grape-sized lump that does not vary with standing, coughing or lying flat is not a reducible hernia; that answer alone should move you off hernia; consistency asked in three options ('soft, or firm and rubbery, or hard?' — an open 'what does it feel like?' gets 'like a lump'); and reassuring without investigation in a variant with a hard fixed growing node, six kilos lost and drenching sweats — 'I need to rule out conditions affecting the lymph glands themselves, such as a lymphoma, or a cancer somewhere in the area these glands drain; blood tests, a scan, and most likely a biopsy of the gland — urgently'; examine the whole drainage territory incl. the soles and between the toes; a core or excisional biopsy, not FNA, if lymphoma is possible (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Listing direct, indirect, femoral and incisional hernia as four differentials — that is one bucket and is marked as one; the two sentences that carry the station: 'my differentials fall into four groups — a hernia; a skin or soft tissue problem; a hip problem; and enlarged lymph nodes, which I'd divide into infective and malignant, each local or generalised' and 'I ask everyone these questions, because infections in that area are a common cause of swelling in the groin'; why each other group is less likely in one clause referencing the history

Full detail — DO — Acknowledge the stated worry before asking anything (eight seconds, scored); the character block IS the examination — site oriented ('closer to your hip, or closer to your private parts?'), size ('the size of a coin, or bigger?' — half a golf ball), consistency, tenderness, redness or warmth, duration, constant or intermittent, enlarging, 'worse when you stand up, cough or strain? gone when you lie down?' (follow the patient's own 'when it's out'); the four buckets in every version without exception — skin (fever and chills, redness or rash, discharge, boils, shaving), hernia (pain, the obstruction screen, then risk factors — 'you mentioned constipation, do you have to strain? a long-standing cough? do you smoke? difficulty passing urine — strain, up at night? occupation and heavy lifting — and what did you do before you retired? (a bricklayer for thirty years — the previous occupation only if asked) any operations on your abdomen? (an appendicectomy on that side) your weight?'), hip ('any pain in the hip itself? stiffness? limping — can you put your full weight through that leg? injury or fall?' — 'swelling' reads as lump rather than joint, and one recalled version turns entirely on it; the basketball is held until the hip block closes it), lymph nodes (the drainage territory — leg or foot infection, athlete's foot, ingrown toenail; genital rash, blisters, ulcers; scrotal swelling or pain; urethral discharge or 'burning when you pass urine?' → 'it does sting a bit, now you mention it'; anorectal symptoms; the sexual history; constitutional — weight, appetite, tiredness, night sweats 'soaking the sheets', lumps in neck or axillae, changing moles on the legs, travel); budget — 40 s opening, 80 characterising, 40 skin, 80 hernia, 30 hip, 70 nodes, 20 to close

Full detail — SAY — Brief A: 'the most likely explanation is an inguinal hernia; the wall of your abdomen is a sheet of muscle holding everything in, and in the groin there's a naturally weaker point; over time that point can stretch, and a small sac of the lining of your abdomen — sometimes with a bit of fat or bowel in it — pushes out through the gap; that bulge is what you're feeling; two reasons: how it behaves — soft, pushes back in, comes out when you stand or cough, gone by morning; and the things you've told me that push the pressure up inside your abdomen against that weak point — a long-standing cough, straining with constipation, straining to pass urine, thirty years of bricklaying, and some extra weight'; next — examine to confirm, surgical referral, work on the drivers (constipation, cough, smoking, and the waterworks in their own right); 'is it cancer?' → the specific negatives plus 'I'd still want to examine you to confirm'; Brief B: 'that lump is most likely a swollen gland, a lymph node; glands are part of your immune system, and the ones in your groin drain the skin of your legs and your genital area; when there's an infection anywhere in that territory, the gland that drains it swells and becomes tender — the gland doing its job; putting that together with the stinging when you pass urine and what you've told me about your sexual health, the most likely cause is an infection passed on through sex; I'm not going to guess which one, because the treatment depends on it — but they're all treatable, and I'd test for the others at the same time'; urine, swabs (throat and rectum too), HIV and syphilis serology; 'does this go on my record? my family use this clinic' → confidential, not shared, and SHINE SA as an alternative service; 'do I have to tell my partners?' → contact tracing is supported and often anonymous, 'you don't have to do that alone'; Variant C (hip aching since the game, stiff, limping, can't weight-bear) → the hip, not a lump — examine, X-ray, ultrasound; add fever → septic arthritis until proven otherwise; Variant E (out since yesterday, can't reduce it, tender, abdominal ache, vomited) → stop and act — NBM, a drip, analgesia, surgical team, 'you may well need an operation today'; a femoral hernia in an older thinner woman (small, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle) → repair even if asymptomatic, the safety net more emphatic

FAIL — Calling a firm, constant, tender lump that doesn't change with coughing or lying flat a HERNIA — ask consistency in options; a hard, fixed, growing node with weight loss and night sweats needs urgent bloods, scan and biopsy for lymphoma

DO — Acknowledge the worry first, characterise the lump ('worse standing or coughing, gone lying down?'), then all four buckets every time: skin, hernia with its drivers (cough, straining, heavy lifting, past bricklaying), hip, and the node drainage territory incl. stinging on passing urine

setting: Every candidate reaches diabetic neuropathy. The line the whole station turns on is 'You have a sensory neuropathy — and there are two things driving it.' The second cause is alcohol, and it is lost by asking 'Do you drink?' and accepting 'Socially'. Quantify it neutrally every time, and clear the vascular group by name even though you already know the answer — skipping it is a starred fail and, in one variant, a missed limb.
stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town. James Whitfield, 60, a storeman, with burning pain in both feet.
On the door: BP 148/86 · HR 78 regular · T 36.8°C · RR 14 · BMI 31 · random capillary glucose 12.4 mmol/L. Not in acute distress.

8-minute station with a bell at 6 minutes. History 6 minutes · ask the examiner for the findings, which come on a card, and do not examine the patient · explain the diagnosis in language he understands · explain the other diagnoses and why they are less likely.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings — you will be handed a card
Explain the most likely diagnosis to the patient in language he can understand
Explain the other diagnoses you considered and why they are less likely
time: Forty-five seconds to open, offer analgesia and ask for his concerns — which is where the amputation fear is won or lost · the pain, site first then quality, to 2:30 · then five headings said out loud: red flags, vascular, neurological, soft tissue, restless legs · hard stop at 6:00 whatever is unasked · request the card by naming the systems, read it back in one interpretive sentence · then the syndrome, both causes, the fear answered directly, five grouped differentials and the foot-care safety-net
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Vascular — and this is the reassuring half
Warm, well-perfused feet. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial palpable bilaterally, capillary refill under 2 seconds, no elevation pallor or dependent rubor
Dry skin with callus over both first and fifth metatarsal heads. No ulcer, erythema, swelling or interdigital maceration. Nails thickened

Reduced light touch and pinprick in a stocking distribution to mid-shin bilaterally. 10 g monofilament not felt at 6 of 10 sites per foot. Vibration absent at both great toes and present at the tibial tuberosities. Proprioception impaired at the great toes
Power 5/5 throughout with no wasting. Knee jerks present, ankle jerks absent bilaterally, plantars downgoing. Romberg positive, gait mildly broad-based

back.dx: A LENGTH-DEPENDENT SENSORY NEUROPATHY WITH TWO AETIOLOGIES WORKING TOGETHER — CHRONIC HYPERGLYCAEMIA AND ALCOHOL — IN A MAN WHOSE FATHER LOST A LEG TO DIABETES. TO HIM, IN PLAIN WORDS: 'THE NERVES THAT CARRY SENSATION FROM YOUR FEET UP TO YOUR BRAIN HAVE BEEN DAMAGED. DAMAGED NERVES MISFIRE, AND YOU FEEL THAT AS BURNING AND PINS AND NEEDLES — AND WHERE THEY'VE STOPPED WORKING ALTOGETHER, YOU FEEL NUMBNESS. THAT'S THE THICK-SOCK FEELING.' THEN BOTH CAUSES: 'THE FIRST IS YOUR BLOOD SUGAR — RUNNING HIGH OVER YEARS DAMAGES THE SMALL NERVES AND THE TINY VESSELS THAT FEED THEM. THE SECOND IS THE ALCOHOL — SIX TO EIGHT DRINKS MOST NIGHTS IS DIRECTLY TOXIC TO NERVES AND ALSO AFFECTS THE VITAMINS NERVES NEED.' AND THE HONEST FRAME: THE DAMAGE ALREADY DONE IS HARD TO REVERSE, BUT IT CAN BE STOPPED FROM PROGRESSING AND THE PAIN CAN BE TREATED — AND BECAUSE HIS FEET CANNOT FEEL, HE MAY NOT NOTICE AN INJURY, WHICH IS THE REAL RISK. FIVE GROUPED DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH ITS DISCRIMINATING REASON: SERIOUS — foot or bone infection and CHARCOT NEUROARTHROPATHY, excluded by no fever, redness, swelling or skin break, and malignancy with nothing to suggest it; VASCULAR — arterial narrowing, against no claudication, no rest pain and strong pulses, and venous disease, against no swelling or staining; OTHER NEUROPATHY CAUSES — B12 DEFICIENCY, WHICH METFORMIN ITSELF CAN CAUSE, hypothyroidism, renal and hepatic disease, and drug causes, all checked on bloods, plus a lumbar root which would be unilateral with back pain and TARSAL TUNNEL which would be one foot; FOOT ITSELF — MORTON'S NEUROMA, which is forefoot pain easing as soon as the shoe comes off; AND RESTLESS LEGS, an urge to move relieved by walking, often from low iron, which is why the ferritin goes on the form anyway. THE PLAN: bloods covering GLUCOSE AND HbA1c, B12, THYROID, RENAL, LIVER AND IRON · PODIATRY for pressure areas, sensation and footwear · restart the metformin and re-enter diabetes review · AMITRIPTYLINE AT NIGHT for the neuropathic pain · and a conversation about the drinking with support offered. THE THREE FOOT-CARE INSTRUCTIONS: LOOK AT THE FEET DAILY INCLUDING THE SOLES, USING A MIRROR · NEVER BAREFOOT AND NEVER A HOT WATER BOTTLE OR HEATER, BECAUSE HE WILL NOT FEEL A BURN · AND SAME-DAY REVIEW FOR ANY SKIN BREAK, BLISTER, REDNESS, SWELLING, BLACK AREA OR FEVER, WITH A SUDDENLY COLD, PALE, PAINFUL FOOT GOING STRAIGHT TO EMERGENCY. THE VARIANTS. B, A 45-YEAR-OLD WOMAN WITH FOREFOOT PAIN: 'right at the front, on the ball of my right foot, like a stone in my shoe, with electric shocks into the third and fourth toes' AND GONE WITHIN A MINUTE OF TAKING THE SHOE OFF, WORST IN WORK HEELS, with a POSITIVE MULDER'S CLICK and normal sensation and reflexes → MORTON'S NEUROMA: wider flatter shoes with a low heel and roomy toe box and a METATARSAL PAD first, ultrasound if uncertain, then corticosteroid injection, surgery last. THE VERSION B TRAP IS HEARING 'BURNING FOOT PAIN' AND TAKING A DIABETES HISTORY FROM SOMEONE WITHOUT DIABETES — the forefoot location and the relief on removing the shoe are the discriminators. C, A 68-YEAR-OLD SMOKER: pain WORST LYING FLAT AT NIGHT, RELIEVED BY SITTING ON THE EDGE OF THE BED WITH THE LEG HANGING DOWN, claudication at EIGHTY METRES and shortening, with a cool hairless foot, ABSENT PEDAL PULSES, ELEVATION PALLOR AND AN ABI OF 0.32 → CRITICAL LIMB ISCHAEMIA: vascular surgical discussion TODAY, urgent arterial duplex, KEEP THE FOOT DOWN RATHER THAN ELEVATED, protected and warm but never with direct heat, aspirin and a statin, and smoking cessation as the thing that decides whether revascularisation holds. TREATING REST PAIN AS NEUROPATHIC AND PRESCRIBING A GABAPENTINOID IS THE FAILING MOVE — NIGHT PAIN RELIEVED BY DEPENDENCY IS ISCHAEMIC UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.
plan: WIPE, ASK WHAT HE LIKES TO BE CALLED, SIGNPOST THE SHAPE OF THE EIGHT MINUTES — THEN TWO QUESTIONS IN THE FIRST FORTY-FIVE SECONDS: 'ARE YOU IN ANY PAIN RIGHT NOW, WOULD YOU LIKE SOMETHING FOR IT?' AND 'IS THERE ANYTHING IN PARTICULAR YOU'RE WORRIED THIS MIGHT BE?' The role-player is briefed to hold the amputation fear until 7:30 if you do not ask, when there is no time to answer it.

CHARACTERISE THE PAIN, SITE BEFORE QUALITY: 'WHEREABOUTS IN THE FOOT EXACTLY — THE BALL, THE HEEL, THE WHOLE FOOT, OR BETWEEN THE TOES? ONE FOOT OR BOTH?' Then onset and course, the description, AND 'DO YOU GET PINS AND NEEDLES OR NUMBNESS WITH IT?' — name that combination as significant out loud. Then radiation from the back, the day-night and rest-activity pattern, severity, and the effect on sleep and work.

RED FLAGS, HEADING SAID ALOUD — fever, chills or sweats · spreading redness, warmth or swelling · ANY BREAK IN THE SKIN, ULCER OR BLACK AREA · weight loss or night sweats · AND THE CAUDA EQUINA SCREEN: leg weakness, foot drop, bladder or bowel change, saddle numbness.

VASCULAR, BY NAME, IN SIX QUESTIONS AND FORTY-FIVE SECONDS EVEN THOUGH YOU ALREADY KNOW THE ANSWER: CALF CRAMPING ON WALKING AND HOW FAR, ESPECIALLY UPHILL · does it settle standing still · REST OR NIGHT PAIN AND WHETHER HANGING THE LEG OUT OF BED HELPS · colour change and cold feet · hair loss and non-healing sores · smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol, sugar, and any heart attack, stroke or angina.

NEUROLOGICAL, AND THIS IS WHERE THE SECOND CAUSE LIVES. Weakness and unsteadiness, back pain radiating down the leg · DIABETES IN FOUR QUESTIONS AND THEN STOP: when diagnosed, what treatment, HOW OFTEN HE ACTUALLY TAKES IT, and when last reviewed with the HbA1c · complications — vision, kidneys, postural dizziness, erectile difficulty · thyroid, renal and hepatic screen · THEN THE ALCOHOL QUESTION ASKED NEUTRALLY AND QUANTIFIED: 'ON A DAY WHEN YOU DO DRINK, ROUGHLY HOW MANY WOULD YOU HAVE, AND WHAT SORT?' · then diet and vegetarianism, gastric surgery, long-term reflux tablets, AND OTHER DRUGS INCLUDING PAST TREATMENT FOR INFECTION, ARRHYTHMIA, TB OR CHEMOTHERAPY.

SOFT TISSUE AND RESTLESS LEGS — tight or narrow shoes, WORSE WITH SHOES ON AND BETTER OFF, A PEBBLE-UNDER-THE-FOREFOOT FEELING, occupation and standing, injury · AND 'DO YOU GET AN URGE TO MOVE YOUR LEGS AT REST, AND DOES WALKING RELIEVE IT?' Then the closing open question.

HARD STOP, WHATEVER IS UNASKED — AN INCOMPLETE HISTORY WITH A COMPLETE EXPLANATION SCORES FAR BETTER THAN THE REVERSE. REQUEST THE CARD BY NAMING THE SYSTEMS: vitals and BMI · a vascular assessment with both pedal pulses, capillary refill, temperature, hair distribution and BUERGER'S · inspection of both feet including between the toes and the soles · a neurological assessment with light touch, pinprick, 10 g MONOFILAMENT AT TEN SITES, 128 Hz VIBRATION, proprioception, power, ankle and knee reflexes, ROMBERG AND GAIT · lumbar spine with straight leg raise · AND MULDER'S CLICK AND TINEL'S AT THE TARSAL TUNNEL. Naming them earns the marks allocated to the examination you are not allowed to perform.
Read the card back in one interpretive sentence, then ask what he already understands before explaining anything — then name the syndrome and both causes (see dx and findings).

Answer the amputation fear directly and specifically: 'You are not in that position today. Your circulation is good, your pulses are strong, and there's no ulcer or infection. What happened to your father is not inevitable for you — it is largely preventable, and the three things that make the difference are the sugar, the alcohol, and looking after the skin on your feet.'

The five grouped differentials with a discriminating reason each, then the plan, the three foot-care instructions, the safety-net and a two-week review with results — and ask permission to return to the drinking then.

The line the station turns on: 'You have a sensory neuropathy — and there are two things driving it.' not 'Diabetic neuropathy'.

The three site-and-pattern questions that split the list: 'Whereabouts in the foot exactly?' · 'Do you get pins and needles or numbness with the burning?' · and 'Do you get an urge to move your legs at rest, and does walking relieve it?'

Challenges: 'Am I going to lose my foot, doctor? My father did' · 'The drink? Nobody's ever said that' · 'I thought it was just getting older' · 'So it's just the sugar then, is it?' pefe: YOU DO NOT EXAMINE HIM — YOU NAME THE SYSTEMS AND RECEIVE A CARD, SO THE EXAMINATION MARKS ARE ENTIRELY IN THE WORDING OF THE REQUEST AND IN READING THE CARD BACK. The three items candidates leave out are BUERGER'S TEST, THE 10 g MONOFILAMENT AT TEN SITES, AND THE TWO SPECIAL TESTS — MULDER'S AND TINEL'S — which are exactly what let you exclude Morton's neuroma and tarsal tunnel out loud at the end.

Role-player: James Whitfield, 60, a storeman at a regional produce depot, married to Denise for 31 years, in a country town two hours from Adelaide — practical, understated, not a complainer, and here because Denise made the appointment. Six to seven months of gradually worsening burning in both feet, whole foot and worst in the toes, constant and unchanged by walking or resting, with pins and needles and patches of numbness like a thick sock, about six out of ten, waking him some nights and the sheets on his feet unpleasant. Type 2 diabetes for ten years on metformin, missed most days, no review for two years and he does not know his HbA1c. Ex-smoker, twenty a day, stopped fifteen years ago. Ordinary meat-containing diet, no gastric surgery, no reflux tablets, no other medicines.

The hidden items and how they come out: the alcohol is six to eight stubbies most nights plus a couple of scotches on Saturday, and is never volunteered — to 'Do you drink?' He says 'A few, socially' and stops, and gives the real amount only to a quantifying question asked in a neutral tone. The amputation fear — his father was diabetic and had a below-knee amputation — is offered whenever concerns are asked about, and otherwise raised at about 7:30 when there is barely time to answer. He pauses before the embarrassing answers, is visibly relieved by a direct answer about his foot, and mildly deflated by 'Nothing to worry about'. He pushes once if you close early: 'So it's just the sugar then, is it?'

The sentence that interprets it — 'Reduced sensation in a stocking pattern with absent vibration and absent ankle jerks, but normal pulses and no ulceration — that fits a sensory nerve problem rather than a circulation problem, which is reassuring in one important respect.' ★ Never asking any vascular question — claudication, rest or night pain, colour change, ulcers — which in the ischaemic variant is a missed limb
★ Telling him it is 'just the diabetes' or 'nothing to worry about', which is wrong on both counts

numbers: 10 g monofilament at 10 sites, and failure at any site means loss of protective sensation · 128 Hz tuning fork at the great toe · ABI under 0.40 critical ischaemia, 0.40-0.90 pad, 0.91-1.30 normal, over 1.30 falsely high from calcification · toe-brachial index under 0.70 is abnormal and is the number to use in diabetes · a difference of more than 2°C between feet supports active Charcot neuroarthropathy

NHMRC alcohol: no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day · a 375 mL full-strength stubby is about 1.4 standard drinks, so six to eight most nights is roughly 50 to 70 a week — five to seven times the limit

Amitriptyline 10 mg nocte increasing by 10 mg every 1-2 weeks to 25-75 mg · duloxetine 30 mg daily for a week then 60 mg · pregabalin 25-75 mg nocte up to 150-300 mg daily in two doses, renally adjusted · thiamine 100 mg orally daily, higher and parenteral if Wernicke's is a risk · hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM alternate days × 5 then 3-monthly · HbA1c around 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) individualised, BP under 140/90 · DASSA 1300 13 1340 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · VERIFY all

Full detail — FAIL — Never asking about alcohol, or asking but never quantifying it — 'do you drink?' → 'a few, socially' → move on is the commonest way the second cause is lost; quantify every time, neutrally: 'on a day when you do drink, roughly how many would you have, and what sort?' → 'most nights, six or eight stubbies, a couple of scotches on a Saturday; the wife has said something' (given only to a quantifying question in a neutral tone — sound disapproving and he says 'not that much really'); a full-strength stubby is ~1.4 standard drinks, so 50–70 a week against a limit of 10; the line the station turns on: 'you have a sensory neuropathy — and there are two things driving it' — the blood sugar AND the alcohol; 'diabetic neuropathy' alone is the crowd (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Never asking any vascular question — one of the two starred fails; six questions, forty-five seconds: 'now I'd like to check the blood supply to your legs — cramping in the calves when you walk, especially uphill, and how far? does it settle standing still? pain in the foot at rest or at night in bed — does hanging your leg out of the bed help? colour change — pale, blue, dusky? cold feet? hair loss, sores that won't heal? smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol, heart attack or stroke?'; Version C (a 68-year-old smoker sitting on the edge of the bed at three in the morning with the leg hanging down, eighty metres before cramping, a cool hairless foot with absent pulses and ABI 0.32) → 'this is more urgent than a nerve problem — the blood supply to your foot is severely reduced; gravity is doing the work your arteries can't' — vascular today, arterial duplex, keep the foot down, aspirin and a statin, stop smoking; treating rest pain as neuropathic with a gabapentinoid and a routine review is the fail (★)

Full detail — FAIL — 'It's just your diabetes, nothing to worry about' — wrong on both counts; and explaining in jargon without checking understanding; start with 'what do you already understand about why your feet might be burning?' ('I thought it was just age' — 'it isn't age'); 'you have a condition called a sensory neuropathy; in plain terms, the nerves that carry sensation from your feet up to your brain have been damaged; when nerves are damaged they misfire, and you feel that as burning and pins and needles — and where they've stopped working altogether, you feel numbness; that's why parts of your feet feel like they're wrapped in a thick sock; does that make sense so far?'; then both causes ('the first is your blood sugar — when it runs high over years it damages the small nerves and the tiny blood vessels that feed them; the second is the alcohol — six to eight drinks most nights is directly toxic to nerves, and it also affects the vitamins nerves need'); he pushes once — 'so it's just the sugar then, is it?' — see whether you reconsider (★)

Full detail — FAIL — No foot-care advice and no safety net for an insensate foot — loss of protective sensation (monofilament not felt at 6 of 10 sites, callus over the metatarsal heads) is the real risk, not just a symptom: 'because your feet can't feel properly, you may not notice an injury — that's the thing we most need to protect against; three things: look at your feet every day, including the soles — use a mirror or ask your wife; never walk barefoot, and never use a hot water bottle or heater on your feet, because you won't feel a burn; and if you see any break in the skin, blister, redness, swelling or black area, or you get a fever, come in that same day; if the foot ever becomes suddenly cold, pale and painful, that's an emergency — go straight to the emergency department'; a podiatry referral ('more than nails — pressure areas, sensation, proper footwear — the single best way to protect a foot that can't feel'); the amputation fear (his father lost his leg — offered if you ask concerns in the first 45 seconds; otherwise volunteered at 7:30 when you have no time) answered straight: 'you are not in that position today; your circulation is good, your pulses are strong, and there's no ulcer or infection; what happened to your father is not inevitable for you — it is largely preventable; the three things that make the difference are getting the sugar down, cutting the alcohol back, and looking after the skin on your feet' (★)

setting: Two things decide this station and neither is the diagnosis. He says 'I did it in years ago' and will never say the word fracture unless you ask what the diagnosis was — three questions, in order: what happened, what were you told it was, what treatment did you have. And the card makes the diagnosis, so read it back in three findings — deformity, pain in all four planes, reduced range — in those words.
stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town (MM5). James Whitcombe, 58, runs a hardware store and is on his feet most of the day. Right heel pain for four months.
Also in the stem: he injured that same ankle about ten years ago. Given to you: temp 36.6°C · HR 72 · BP 132/80 · RR 14 · BMI 30. He walked in unaided.
8-minute station. History in 6 minutes, then the examination findings on a card when you ask, then the diagnosis and differentials explained to the patient in plain language with your reasons.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings, provided on a card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient, in plain language, with the reasons you have reached them
time: Forty seconds to open and signpost, because you are about to ask a man with heel pain about diarrhoea, psoriasis and antibiotics · SOCRATES and the pattern, including the first-step pair, to 2:40 · the MSK screen and the old injury in three questions to 4:00 · red flags then bone and joint, soft tissue, nerve and vessel, and the fluoroquinolone question, to 5:20 · request the card as a structure and read it aloud to 6:20 · then the diagnosis with three reasons, differentials excluded in plain words, the joint-replacement fear answered, plan, safety-net and summary
findingsLabel: The card makes the diagnosis — read three findings back in these words: deformity, all four planes, reduced range
findings: Afebrile. Weight-bearing with a mild antalgic gait on the right. The right heel appears widened compared with the left — a deformity, and one he had already noticed himself. No redness, rash, skin break or ulcer
No local rise in temperature. Pedal pulses present, capillary refill under 2 seconds. Ankle joint line tenderness — and no tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle or the Achilles insertion
Movement — the finding that localises it

Painful in all four directions, with dorsiflexion 20°, plantarflexion 20° against a normal 30-50, inversion 20° and eversion 10° against a normal 15-25. A tendon or ligament hurts in one direction; a joint hurts in all of them
Power, sensation and reflexes intact. Windlass negative, Thompson negative, no laxity on anterior drawer or talar tilt

back.dx: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the right ankle, following a fracture ten years ago. To him: 'A joint has a smooth cushion of cartilage on the ends of the bones so they glide over each other. When a fracture involves a joint it disturbs those surfaces and the way the joint lines up, and over the years that means more wear and tear — the cushion thins, the bone underneath thickens, and the joint gets stiff and sore. It has been going on quietly since your injury and it has now caught up with you.' Never say intra-articular, congruity or degenerative change to a shopkeeper. Three reasons, which are the scored half: the pain is mechanical — worse walking, better resting, which is how a worn joint behaves; the right heel is wider than the left, which he had noticed himself, so the shape has changed; and the movements are painful in every direction and reduced, which points at the joint rather than a tendon or ligament — all sitting on TOP of the fracture. Differentials in plain words with their reasons, never as a list of names: infection — no fever, skin intact; something sinister like a growth — no weight loss, no rest pain; other arthritides, rheumatoid or gout — no other joints, no family history, no rashes, no food trigger; the soft tissues — the band under the heel (Plantar fasciitis), the Achilles behind it, and the bursae, with today's tests negative; the ligaments from the old injury — 'Your ankle is stiff rather than loose', which is his own phrase used back as evidence; and the nerves and circulation, both normal. The plan: a weight-bearing x-ray and an ultrasound for soft tissues and ligaments · paracetamol 1 g QID to a maximum of 4 g in 24 hours plus a topical anti-inflammatory · supportive shoes with a stiff or rocker sole · physiotherapy and podiatry · weight reduction, which takes load through the ankle at every step · and a stool behind the counter so he is not on concrete all day. The safety-net: fever, a red hot swollen foot, skin breakdown, inability to weight-bear, or pain that becomes constant and stops easing with rest — otherwise review at 4 to 6 weeks with the x-ray. And the agenda answered: 'Almost certainly not a new ankle, not now. Most people are managed with footwear, exercises, weight and simple pain relief. Surgery — fusing the joint or replacing it — is kept for people whose pain stays severe despite all of that. We're a long way from that conversation.' The variants. B, plantar fasciitis (45 F, BMI 32, standing job): 'Right under the heel. The first few steps out of bed are agony, then it loosens off after a couple of minutes, and by the end of a shift it's back' → calf and sole stretching, a cushioned heel cup, supportive shoes, less standing, weight loss and simple analgesia, with the honest timeframe of months not weeks and most settling without any procedure. C, Achilles tendinopathy (52 m, new runner): pain behind the heel with tendon tenderness, and the history only appears if you ask the drug question — 'I had a course of ciprofloxacin for a prostate infection a month ago, and I'd just started running again' → stop any remaining course and speak to the prescriber, rest from running, a small heel raise, a physio-guided loading programme, never inject steroid around the tendon because it can rupture, and return at once for a sudden snap or inability to push off. D, the septic heel (68 F, diabetes, an ulcer over the heel, fever, struggling to weight-bear) → fever plus a skin break plus diabetes can mean infection that has reached the bone: bloods and x-ray now, hospital referral today, MRI as the definitive scan, and no weight-bearing meanwhile.
plan: WIPE, CONFIRM IDENTITY AND DATE OF BIRTH, STATE CONFIDENTIALITY, AND OPEN — THEN SIGNPOST, BECAUSE YOU ARE ABOUT TO ASK THIS MAN ABOUT DIARRHOEA, PSORIASIS AND ANTIBIOTICS IN A CONSULTATION ABOUT HIS HEEL: 'I'LL ASK ABOUT THE PAIN, THEN SOME GENERAL QUESTIONS, THEN A FEW TO MAKE SURE NOTHING SERIOUS IS BEING MISSED.' Tell him now and none of it seems strange when you get there. This is the same history you already run for ankle and foot pain — only the top of the differential list changes, so do not abandon your structure.

SITE — OPEN, THEN THE THREE-WAY CLOSED QUESTION, BECAUSE HE GIVES ONLY 'MY RIGHT HEEL' UNTIL YOU ASK: 'IS IT UNDER THE HEEL, BEHIND THE HEEL, OR ALL OVER THE HEEL AND ANKLE?' Then the rest of SOCRATES — severity, dull or sharp, onset and course, radiation, aggravating and relieving, worse standing and walking, effect on work.

The pattern, including the plantar fasciitis pair asked even though you have decided it is arthritis, because the negative is worth as much as a positive: night waking · morning versus evening and how long the stiffness lasts, quantified — 'A bit stiff' is not an answer, and fifteen minutes is mechanical while over thirty is inflammatory · worse after rest or after activity · 'Are the first few steps out of bed painful?' and 'Does it ease off after a few minutes of walking?'

THE MSK SCREEN — swelling, redness or rash · ANY CHANGE IN THE SHAPE OF THE HEEL OR ANKLE, which is where he offers 'it looks a bit thicker than the other one' before you ever see the card · limping and full weight-bearing · AND ANY TRAUMA OR INJURY TO THAT ANKLE.

THE THREE INJURY QUESTIONS, IN THIS ORDER, AND THE CASE TURNS HERE: 'CAN YOU DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENED?' · 'WHAT WERE YOU TOLD IT WAS — WHAT WAS THE DIAGNOSIS?' · 'AND WHAT TREATMENT DID YOU HAVE?' → off a ladder ten years ago, TOLD HE HAD FRACTURED IT, six to eight weeks in a cast then physiotherapy, settled fine at the time. Without the middle question you never get the word fracture and cannot use the word post-traumatic or explain the mechanism.

Red flags, announced — fevers, sweats or chills · any break in the skin, sore or ulcer on the foot · diabetes · weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness · and pain present all the time at rest and at night that does not change with movement.

BONE AND JOINT THEN SOFT TISSUE, NERVE AND VESSEL — occupation and standing, exercise · other joints, family history of arthritis, RASHES OR PSORIASIS, red meat, seafood or alcohol triggers, RECENT DIARRHOEA OR URETHRAL DISCHARGE · 'DOES THE ANKLE EVER GIVE WAY OR FEEL UNSTEADY ON UNEVEN GROUND?' — 'IT'S STIFF RATHER THAN WOBBLY' IS A GIFT, SO USE IT LATER AGAINST LIGAMENT INSTABILITY · back pain, paraesthesiae, numbness, burning, weakness · claudication and colour or temperature change.

DRUGS AND CLOSURE — medications including over the counter · 'HAVE YOU HAD ANY ANTIBIOTICS RECENTLY — ANYTHING LIKE CIPROFLOXACIN?', which is the question that saves the Achilles variant · steroid tablets · other conditions, operations, allergies, smoking, mood · AND THE CONCERN QUESTION, because if you never ask it the fear arrives in the last thirty seconds.

REQUEST THE CARD AS A STRUCTURE, NOT A WISH: general appearance, weight-bearing and gait · vitals PARTICULARLY THE TEMPERATURE · inspection for swelling, redness, rash, skin break, ulcer AND DEFORMITY · palpation for local temperature, PEDAL PULSES AND CAPILLARY REFILL, and tenderness over the plantar heel, the Achilles and its insertion, the malleoli and the joint line · movement in all four planes with pain and range · A BRIEF NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION OF THE FOOT · and the special tests, WINDLASS, THOMPSON, ANTERIOR DRAWER, TALAR TILT AND TINEL'S. Naming pulses and neurology is what puts vascular and neurological causes on your list.

READ THE CARD ALOUD IN THREE DECISIVE FINDINGS, IN THOSE WORDS — DEFORMITY, PAIN IN ALL FOUR PLANES, REDUCED RANGE — WITH THE NORMAL RANGES QUOTED (see findings). Taking the card and going silent is how the reasoning mark is lost.
Turn your chair to the patient, name the diagnosis and translate it, then give the three reasons and the differentials in plain words with why each is excluded (see dx).
Answer the new-ankle fear, then the plan, the safety-net, a four-to-six-week review with the x-ray, and a summary checked back with him.
