ask: The three injury questions, in order, and the middle one is the station: 'Can you describe what happened?' · 'What were you told it was — what was the diagnosis?' · 'And what treatment did you have?'

The closed site question and the plantar fasciitis pair: 'Is it under the heel, behind the heel, or all over the heel and ankle?' · 'Are the first few steps out of bed painful — and does it ease after a few minutes of walking?'
The drug question that saves the Achilles variant: 'Have you had any antibiotics recently — anything like ciprofloxacin?'

Reading the card and the three reasons: 'A deformity, pain in all four planes, and a reduced range — that localises the problem to the joint.' · 'Mechanical pain, a heel that is wider on that side, and movements painful in every direction and reduced.'

Challenges: 'Am I going to end up needing a new ankle? My father had both knees replaced and it wasn't pretty' · 'How do you know that?' if you give a diagnosis with no reasons · 'Sorry, what does that mean?' Every time you use jargon · and 'So what about all the other things it could have been?'
pefe: THE CARD IS HANDED OVER WHEN YOU ASK, AND IT IS THE CARD RATHER THAN THE HISTORY THAT MAKES THE DIAGNOSIS — WHICH IS WHY THE HISTORY SHOULD ESTABLISH THAT THE PAIN IS MECHANICAL AND THEN SAY SO OUT LOUD RATHER THAN COMMITTING EARLY. 'Worse walking, better resting' keeps bone, joint and loaded soft tissue in play and pushes inflammatory, infective and malignant causes down; it does not choose between them.

Role-player: James Whitcombe, 58, who runs a hardware store and is on concrete all day. Non-smoker, one blood pressure tablet, no antibiotics for years, no steroids, no diabetes, BMI 30. Four months of right heel pain, all around it and deep inside rather than on the bottom — but he says only 'My right heel' until asked the three-way question. About six out of ten, a deep ache that is sharp if he twists on it, gradually worse, worse the more he is on it and better sitting down, hobbling by closing time. It does not wake him. Fifteen minutes of morning stiffness. The first steps are not especially bad and walking makes it worse, not better. He offers that the heel 'Looks a bit thicker than the other one — wider', and that the ankle is 'Stiff rather than wobbly'.

The injury and the agenda: ten years ago he came off a ladder at the shop and twisted the right ankle badly. He says 'I did it in years ago' and nothing more — the ladder comes only if asked what happened, the word fracture only if asked what the diagnosis was, and the cast and physiotherapy only if asked about treatment. His father had both knees replaced and it went badly, and he is frightened of ending up with a replaced ankle — not volunteered unless asked about concerns, and otherwise raised in the last thirty seconds of the history, where talking over it to finish your list costs the easiest communication marks in the station. Practical, matter-of-fact, a bit fed up; if you use jargon he asks what it means, and if you give a diagnosis with no reasons he asks how you know.

Full detail — SAY — To the patient, chair turned, no jargon (no 'intra-articular', 'congruity', 'degenerative change'): 'James, the most likely diagnosis is osteoarthritis of your ankle joint, and because it has followed your old fracture we call it post-traumatic osteoarthritis; a joint has a smooth cushion of cartilage on the ends of the bones so they glide over each other; when a fracture involves a joint, it disturbs those smooth surfaces and the way the joint lines up; over the years that means more wear and tear — the cushion thins, the bone underneath thickens, and the joint gets stiff and sore; it has been going on quietly since your injury and has now caught up with you'; three reasons (mechanical — worse walking, better resting; the heel wider than the other side, which he had noticed himself; movements painful in every direction and reduced — the joint, not a tendon or ligament; all on top of the fracture ten years ago); differentials excluded in plain words (infection — no fever, skin intact; a growth — no weight loss, no rest pain; rheumatoid or gout — no other joints; the band under the heel, the Achilles, the bursae — today's tests negative; the ligaments — stiff rather than loose; nerves and circulation — fine); 'a new ankle like Dad's knees?' → 'almost certainly not yet; most people are managed with footwear, exercises, weight and simple pain relief; surgery — fusing the joint or replacing it — is kept for people whose pain stays severe despite all of that; we're a long way from that conversation'; a weight-bearing X-ray and an ultrasound, paracetamol 1 g qid max 4 g plus an anti-inflammatory gel, supportive shoes with a stiff or rocker sole, physio and podiatry, some weight off, a stool behind the counter; safety net (fever, red hot swollen, skin breakdown, can't weight-bear, pain becomes constant); review 4–6 weeks with the X-ray; Version B (45 F, BMI 32, standing job, 'right under the heel, the first few steps out of bed are agony then it loosens off') → plantar fasciitis — calf and sole stretches, a cushioned heel cup, supportive shoes, less standing, weight loss, 'slow — months, not weeks — but most settle without any procedure'; plantar fascia >4 mm on ultrasound

Pain at the first MTP with a reduced range of movement, no redness and no deformity → 'Stiffness without inflammation and without deformity makes hallux rigidus, which is osteoarthritis of the first MTP joint, the most likely diagnosis'

The joint is red, warm and swollen, painful on palpation and movement with a restricted range, no deformity and no fever → acute gouty arthritis, with septic arthritis as the critical differential because it is clinically indistinguishable and can coexist, so aspirate for gram stain, culture and polarised-light microscopy. If the card gives you a fever, this is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — urgent aspiration, blood cultures and same-day referral, not colchicine

back.dx: CARD A IS HALLUX VALGUS — A BUNION. TO HER: 'IT'S A CHANGE IN THE SHAPE OF THE JOINT AT THE BASE OF THE BIG TOE. OVER YEARS THE BIG TOE GRADUALLY LEANS ACROSS TOWARDS THE OTHER TOES AND THE BONE BEHIND IT DRIFTS THE OTHER WAY, SO A BUMP FORMS ON THE INNER SIDE OF YOUR FOOT. BECAUSE THAT BUMP STICKS OUT, IT PRESSES INSIDE YOUR SHOE — WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY IT'S WORSE IN SHOES AND FINE BAREFOOT. THE HARD PATCH OF SKIN OVER IT IS FROM THAT RUBBING. IT TENDS TO RUN IN FAMILIES, WHICH FITS WITH YOUR MOTHER.' THREE REASONS, EACH TIED TO THE DIAGNOSIS IT EXCLUDES: THE SHAPE HAS CHANGED · THE JOINT MOVES COMPLETELY NORMALLY AND PAINLESSLY, WHICH ARGUES AGAINST OSTEOARTHRITIS OF THAT JOINT, WHERE YOU WOULD EXPECT STIFFNESS PARTICULARLY BENDING UPWARDS · AND THERE IS NO REDNESS, HEAT OR SUDDEN OVERNIGHT ONSET, WHICH ARGUES AGAINST GOUT OR SEPTIC ARTHRITIS — PLUS RED MEAT AND ALCOHOL MAKE NO DIFFERENCE AND SHE HAS NEVER HAD AN ATTACK. THE OTHER DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH ITS REASON: RHEUMATOID OR PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS — no other joints, no prolonged morning stiffness, no rash or nail change; MORTON'S NEUROMA — her pain is at the joint, not burning between the toes; A STRESS FRACTURE — nothing has changed in her activity and the tenderness is not over the other bones. THE PLAN: FOOTWEAR IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING — WIDE, DEEP, SOFT-FRONTED SHOES WITH A LOW HEEL · A BUNION PAD · SIMPLE ANALGESIA · PODIATRY FOR THE HARD SKIN AND AN INSOLE · AND THE HONEST SENTENCE: SPLINTS AND EXERCISES WILL NOT STRAIGHTEN AN ESTABLISHED BUNION, AND SURGERY IS RESERVED FOR PAIN THAT LIMITS WHAT SHE CAN DO DESPITE ALL OF THIS, NOT FOR APPEARANCE. Safety-net for a joint that becomes red, hot and much more painful, for fever, or for skin breakdown, and review in six to eight weeks. CARD B, HALLUX RIGIDUS: the discriminating history question is 'IS THE PAIN WORSE WHEN YOU PUSH OFF AS YOU WALK, OR GOING UPHILL OR UP STAIRS? IS IT HARDER TO BEND THE BIG TOE UPWARDS? AND HAS THE SHAPE CHANGED?' → worst on push-off, stairs miserable, cannot bend it up, SHAPE UNCHANGED, WITH A HARD RIDGE ON TOP OF THE JOINT. Say both names and translate the Latin — 'HALLUX RIGIDUS JUST MEANS A STIFF BIG TOE, AND IT IS OSTEOARTHRITIS' is a scoring sentence. Management: A SHOE WITH A STIFF OR ROCKER SOLE, OR A FIRM INSERT UNDER THE BIG TOE, so the joint does not have to bend as she walks · activity modification, topical anti-inflammatory and simple analgesia · physiotherapy · a STEROID INJECTION if that is not enough · and surgery — cheilectomy to shave the spur, or fusion if wear is advanced. CARD C, ACUTE GOUT: the history changes completely — ONSET OVERNIGHT, WAKING AT THREE IN THE MORNING UNABLE TO BEAR THE WEIGHT OF THE SHEET, WORST WITHIN HOURS, FLARING AFTER A BARBECUE AND BEER, AND A SIMILAR ATTACK IN THE SAME TOE A YEAR AGO. Treatment of the attack is ONE anti-inflammatory approach — an NSAID, or colchicine, or a short course of steroid — with rest and ice; then RECHECK THE URATE AT TWO TO FOUR WEEKS BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN MISLEADINGLY NORMAL DURING AN ATTACK, and start allopurinol and titrate if levels are high or attacks recur, alongside alcohol, sugary drinks, weight, blood pressure and renal function.
plan: WIPE, CONFIRM HER NAME, STATE CONFIDENTIALITY, ASK IF SHE IS IN PAIN NOW AND OFFER SOMETHING FOR IT — four seconds, and it is on the mark sheet in almost every pain station.

THE SITE QUESTION, WHICH IS THE HIGHEST-YIELD QUESTION IN THE STATION: 'CAN YOU SHOW ME, OR TELL ME, WHERE EXACTLY IN THE FOOT? IS IT THE FRONT OF THE FOOT, THE MIDDLE, THE HEEL, OR THE ANKLE?' Then 'IS IT ONE SPOT OR SPREAD OUT?' AND 'ONE FOOT OR BOTH?' — bilateral points to a systemic or biomechanical cause, a single hot joint to crystal or septic arthritis. Without the site you cannot prioritise, cannot justify, and will run the wrong half of the structure.

EXPLORE THE PAIN — how long, SUDDEN OR GRADUAL, any injury before it started, dull ache versus sharp versus burning, radiation, severity, aggravating and relieving, EFFECT ON WORK AND DAILY LIFE — AND 'IS IT WORSE WHEN YOU WEAR YOUR SHOES?' Then split the two diagnoses that share that answer: 'DO YOU WEAR TIGHT OR NARROW SHOES? IS IT A BURNING PAIN BETWEEN THE TOES, OR AN ACHE AT THE BUMP?' Gradual over years, worse in shoes and better barefoot is a mechanical pressure problem, which makes gout unlikely before you see the card.

PATTERN, WEIGHT-BEARING AND FOOTWEAR — night pain or waking · morning versus end of day · REST VERSUS ACTIVITY · FULL WEIGHT-BEARING AND LIMPING, which are compulsory in every lower-limb station · WHAT SORT OF SHOES, NARROW ACROSS THE FRONT, HEELS, which is both a clue and the first line of treatment · AND WORSE PUSHING OFF OR WALKING UPHILL, which is the hallux rigidus question. Worse with activity, better with rest and worse at the end of the day is MECHANICAL; inflammatory disease is the reverse, with prolonged morning stiffness — say which pattern you found when you present.

RED FLAGS AND THE DIFFERENTIAL SWEEP, ANNOUNCED: 'SOME QUESTIONS WILL SOUND UNRELATED BUT I ASK THEM OF EVERYONE.' Fever, chills or sweats · lumps · unintentional weight loss · NIGHT PAIN · any break in the skin, ulcer or infection · then BONE AND JOINT: occupation and standing, other joints, family history of arthritis, MORNING STIFFNESS AND HOW LONG, RASHES, SCALY PATCHES OR NAIL CHANGES · 'DOES RED MEAT OR BEER BRING THE PAIN ON?', which is the discriminating question — 'do you eat red meat?' lures you towards gout because almost everyone says yes · previous attacks · recent diarrhoea, vaginal discharge, or red or painful eyes.

SOFT TISSUE, NEUROVASCULAR, SKIN AND NAILS — heel pain with the first steps in the morning · BURNING OR ELECTRIC PAIN BETWEEN THE TOES OR A PEBBLE-IN-THE-SHOE FEELING · claudication and cold feet · numbness, paraesthesiae or burning especially at night · back pain radiating down the leg, weakness or tripping · AND INGROWN TOENAIL, CORN, CALLUS, WART, ULCER OR ITCHING AND PEELING BETWEEN THE TOES.

SADMA AND CLOSURE — smoking, alcohol and what kind, recreational drugs · MEDICATIONS ASKED BY NAME FOR THE ONES THAT MATTER: DIURETICS AND LOW-DOSE ASPIRIN · CONTRACEPTION, which matters not as a gout risk factor but because it tells you she is PREMENOPAUSAL, AND PRIMARY GOUT IS UNCOMMON BEFORE THE MENOPAUSE BECAUSE OESTROGEN IS URICOSURIC · allergies · diabetes, hypertension or renal disease · operations · family history · AND 'IS THERE ANYTHING I HAVEN'T ASKED ABOUT THAT YOU WERE HOPING TO DISCUSS?', where the surgery question lives.

Take the card and read it as a pattern, not a list — synthesise: 'A mechanical, gradually progressive forefoot problem, aggravated by footwear, with a structural deformity but a normal painless range of movement and no inflammation' (see findings).
Name it and translate it, then give the three reasons, then the differentials with why each is excluded (see dx).
The plan, the honest sentence about splints and surgery, the answer to her mother's operation, the safety-net and a six-to-eight-week review.

ask: The question that HALVEs the list, asked in the first thirty seconds: 'Where exactly in the foot — the front, the middle, the heel or the ankle? Can you point to it?' and 'Is it one foot or both?'
THE DISCRIMINATING FOOD QUESTION: 'DOES RED MEAT OR BEER BRING THE PAIN ON?' — not 'do you eat red meat?', which almost everyone answers yes to and which pulls you towards gout.

The two questions that split the shoe answer: 'Do you wear tight or narrow shoes?' and 'Is it a burning pain between the toes, or an ache at the bump?' — plus the hallux rigidus question, 'Is it worse pushing off or going up stairs, and is it harder to bend the big toe upwards?'

The scoring sentences: 'There is deformity with a normal range of movement and no redness.' · 'A bunion — the medical name is hallux valgus — is a change in the shape of the joint, not an arthritis.' · 'Hallux rigidus just means a stiff big toe — it is osteoarthritis.' · and 'Splints and exercises will not straighten an established bunion. We reserve surgery for pain that limits function — not for appearance.'

Challenges: 'Is it arthritis?' · 'Will I need an operation like mum did?' · 'Can you straighten it?' · and, if you say gout on card A, she looks puzzled and says 'But there's no redness and it's been like this for two years?'
pefe: The card is handed over at the prompt and there is no examination to perform — the marked moment is the synthesis, with each of three findings tied to the diagnosis it excludes, said in one breath. Practise it aloud until it runs as a single sentence.

Role-player: Jenny, 40, who works in retail and is on her feet all day, married and otherwise well. Pain at the base of the big toe, right mainly with the left starting, about two years, gradually worse, a dull ache five or six out of ten. Much worse in shoes and fine barefoot at home, worse at the end of the day and with activity, relieved by rest, not waking her. She weight-bears and does not limp but has stopped walking the dog. The big toe leans across towards the others with a bump on the inner side and a hard patch of skin over it where the shoe rubs — no redness, no heat, about five minutes of morning stiffness. Non-smoker, a couple of wines at weekends, no medications except the oral contraceptive pill, no fluid tablets and no aspirin, no diabetes, hypertension or renal disease.

How she plays it: pleasant, practical, a bit worn down by it, not hostile. Her first answer is 'It's my foot' and nothing more — she gives 'The base of my big toe' only if asked where or asked to point, and if the site is never asked she keeps saying 'My foot' and 'It just hurts' for the whole station. To 'Do you eat red meat?' She answers 'Yes, and I have a drink' and stops there; only the trigger question gets 'No, it makes no difference at all.' She volunteers nothing about fever, weight loss, night pain, numbness, burning between the toes, calf pain, heel pain, other joints, rashes or nail changes — all negative. Her mother had the same bumps on both feet and had surgery on both, and her hidden agenda is whether she will end up needing an operation too — raised in the last minute if concerns are never asked about.

Mark them against these, one mark each out of ten: introduced, confirmed her name, asked whether she was in pain · asked where in the foot in the first minute and asked her to point · asked sudden versus gradual and about injury · asked 'Is it worse in shoes?' and about her footwear · asked weight-bearing and limping · asked all the red flags — fever, weight loss, lumps, night pain, skin breakdown · asked whether red meat or beer brings the pain on, not just whether she consumes it · covered soft tissue, neurovascular and skin and nail causes rather than only the big toe · explained it in plain English, gave the medical name, and justified it from her own findings — deformity, normal movement, no redness · addressed the surgery question honestly, gave a footwear and podiatry plan, and safety-netted.

The sentence that scores — 'There is deformity with a normal range of movement and no redness — that makes a bunion far more likely than osteoarthritis or gout.' A candidate who says 'Bunion' and a candidate who says that sentence score very differently. Do not recite the card item by item, and do not say 'Examination is normal' — it is not, there is a deformity

Full detail — SAY — 'Jenny, I think the pain is coming from a bunion; the medical name is hallux valgus; it's a change in the shape of the joint at the base of the big toe: over years the big toe gradually leans across towards the other toes, and the bone behind it drifts the other way, so a bump forms on the inner side of your foot; because that bump sticks out, it presses inside your shoe — which is exactly why you told me it's worse in shoes and fine barefoot; the hard patch of skin over it is from that rubbing; it does tend to run in families, which fits with your mother'; 'a change in the shape of the joint, not an arthritis'; differentials with reasons — hallux rigidus (your joint isn't stiff), gout (no redness or heat, gradual not overnight, food and alcohol don't trigger it), infection (no fever, well), rheumatoid or psoriatic (no other joints, no prolonged stiffness, no rash or nails), a trapped nerve between the toes (pain at the joint, not burning between the toes), a stress fracture (nothing changed, tenderness not over the other bones); the plan — 'the most important thing is footwear: wide, deep, soft-fronted shoes with a low heel', a bunion pad, simple pain relief, a podiatrist for the hard skin and an insole; the surgery question honestly — 'splints and exercises will not straighten an established bunion; surgery works well, but we reserve it for when pain is limiting what you can do despite all of this — not for appearance'; safety net (red, hot and much more painful, fever, skin breaks down); review 6–8 weeks

Full detail — DO — Card B (hallux rigidus): the separating question 'is the pain worse when you push off, or going uphill or up stairs? is it harder to bend the big toe upwards? has the shape changed?' → 'worst as I push off, stairs are miserable, I can't bend it up like the other one, the shape hasn't changed but there's a hard ridge on top'; card: reduced range, no redness, no deformity → 'stiffness without inflammation and without deformity makes hallux rigidus, which is osteoarthritis of the first MTP joint, the most likely diagnosis'; say both names and translate the Latin — 'hallux rigidus just means a stiff big toe — it is osteoarthritis, wear and tear of that joint; small bony spurs form along the top — that ridge you can feel; it hurts most when you push off and go up stairs because those are the moments the toe has to bend upwards'; a shoe with a stiff or rocking sole or a firm insert under the big toe, activity modification, a rub-on anti-inflammatory, physio, a steroid injection, then cheilectomy or fusion if advanced; Card C (gout): 'it came on overnight — I woke at three and couldn't bear the sheet; worst within hours; whenever I've had a barbecue and a few beers it flares; something similar a year ago; no fever' → 'the joint is red, warm and swollen, painful on palpation and movement with a restricted range, no deformity, no fever; abrupt overnight onset peaking within hours and a clear trigger — acute gouty arthritis; my critical differential is septic arthritis, clinically indistinguishable and able to coexist, so I would aspirate the joint for Gram stain, culture and polarised-light microscopy'; to the patient — 'tiny crystals of a waste product called uric acid form inside a joint and set off sudden, intense inflammation'; an NSAID, colchicine or a short steroid course plus rest and ice; check urate 2–4 weeks after ('often misleadingly normal during an attack'), target <0.36 (<0.30 with tophi), allopurinol built up if high or recurrent; alcohol, sugary drinks, weight, BP, kidneys; a fever on the card changes the answer — septic arthritis until proven otherwise: urgent aspiration, blood cultures, same-day referral, not colchicine

stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town (MM5). You are the GP. Marion Deakin, 50, with pain and swelling in the right lower leg for two days.
Given to you: temperature 39.0°C. Other observations available on request.
8-minute station. History in four minutes only, then the examination findings, then explain the most likely diagnosis and the differentials to the patient.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Four minutes is about twenty-five questions, and anything you have not planned you will not ask — budget six on the pain and swelling, six vascular, four neurogenic, and the rest on musculoskeletal, red flags and the infection detail · then the examination requested as a named structure and the observations read aloud · then both diagnoses, the differentials, and a disposition stated without softening it
findingsLabel: Two abnormal sets of findings — the observations and the pulses. Both are there to be named
findings: Confluent poorly demarcated erythema over the right shin and calf extending to just below the knee. No bullae, discharge or dusky areas. Hair loss over the shin. Skin cracked and scaly between the fourth and fifth toes. No joint swelling

Warm and tender over the erythema, and the tenderness does not extend beyond it, which is reassuring against necrotising infection. No crepitus. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial absent on the right, popliteal weak, femoral present. Capillary refill 4 seconds. No calf circumference difference. Non-pitting
Knee and ankle move fully and painlessly, which excludes a septic joint out loud. Tender right inguinal nodes. Sensation intact. Buerger's positive on the right

back.dx: TWO DIAGNOSES IN ONE LEG, PUT THERE DELIBERATELY — CELLULITIS OF THE RIGHT LOWER LEG WITH SYSTEMIC FEATURES, ON A LIMB WITH PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE. EXPLAINING ONLY THE CELLULITIS MEANS HALF THE CASE IS MISSED EVEN THOUGH THE LABEL WAS RIGHT. TO HER: 'THE FIRST IS WHY YOU'RE UNWELL TODAY — AN INFECTION OF THE SKIN AND THE TISSUE JUST UNDER IT. BACTERIA THAT NORMALLY LIVE HARMLESSLY ON THE SKIN HAVE GOT IN THROUGH A BREAK — MOST LIKELY THAT SCRATCH, AND THE CRACKED SKIN BETWEEN YOUR TOES — AND ARE SPREADING THROUGH THE TISSUE.' THEN: 'THE SECOND I FOUND WHILE EXAMINING YOU, AND IT HAS BEEN BUILDING FAR LONGER. I CAN'T FEEL THE PULSES IN YOUR RIGHT FOOT, THE SKIN IS COOL AND THE HAIR HAS WORN AWAY OVER YOUR SHIN. THAT FITS WITH NARROWED ARTERIES — THE PIPES CARRYING BLOOD DOWN TO THE FOOT HAVE FURRED UP — AND IT EXPLAINS THE CRAMP YOU GET AFTER TWO HUNDRED METRES. IT MATTERS TODAY BECAUSE A LEG WITH A POOR BLOOD SUPPLY HEALS MORE SLOWLY.' THE DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN WORDS: DVT — usually swells the calf without this rash, but it can coexist with infection so it stays in mind; A SEPTIC JOINT — the knee and ankle move freely and painlessly; NECROTISING FASCIITIS — the pain matches how the leg looks, there are no blisters, and THE TENDERNESS STOPS WHERE THE REDNESS STOPS; A LUMBAR ROOT — no back pain, numbness or weakness; GOUT — no single joint involved. THE DISPOSITION, SAID WITHOUT SOFTENING IT: 'YOUR TEMPERATURE IS 39, YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE IS 90 OVER 60 AND YOUR HEART IS RUNNING AT 110. THAT TELLS ME THE INFECTION IS AFFECTING YOUR WHOLE BODY, NOT JUST THE LEG. I'M NOT GOING TO SEND YOU HOME WITH TABLETS' — IV access, BLOOD CULTURES, LACTATE, FLUIDS, INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS AND HOSPITAL TODAY. THEN MARK THE MARGIN: DRAW A LINE AROUND THE REDNESS AND DATE IT, elevate the leg, paracetamol, fluids. AND THE THREE THINGS AFTERWARDS: A CREAM FOR THE TINEA BETWEEN THE TOES, BECAUSE THAT IS THE DOORWAY FOR THE NEXT INFECTION AND ALMOST NOBODY ASKS ABOUT IT · AN ANKLE-BRACHIAL INDEX · AND SMOKING CESSATION, WHICH IS THE SINGLE BIGGEST THING FOR THOSE ARTERIES. THE VARIANTS. B, SEPTIC ARTHRITIS (62 M, diabetic): 'MY KNEE'S SWOLLEN TOO AND ANY MOVEMENT IS AGONY' → a swollen joint where every movement hurts is INFECTION INSIDE THE JOINT UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, needing ASPIRATION IDEALLY BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS, and hospital now. C, NECROTISING FASCIITIS (44 M, injecting drug use): twelve hours, PAIN FAR OUT OF PROPORTION, SPREADING WHILE YOU WATCH, EARLY BLISTERS, DUSKY SKIN, VOMITING AND HYPOTENSION → ambulance and the surgical team now, operation as well as intravenous antibiotics, AND YOU DO NOT WAIT FOR SCANS. D, DVT (58 F, five days after knee replacement): unilateral calf swelling and tenderness WITH NO RASH and a low-grade temperature → risk score and ultrasound today; antibiotics would not treat this. E, VENOUS ECZEMA (71 F on her third course of antibiotics this year): BOTH legs, red scaly and itchy for MONTHS, varicose veins, ankles swelling by evening, AFEBRILE → 'cellulitis is nearly always in one leg, comes on over days and causes fever; yours is in both legs, has been months, and you have no temperature' — moisturiser, a short course of steroid ointment and compression, BUT CHECK THE ARTERIES FIRST BECAUSE COMPRESSION IS ONLY SAFE IF THEY ARE HEALTHY.
plan: Open fast and signpost the speed — 'I'm going to ask a series of quick questions, then examine you. Some will seem to have nothing to do with your leg; they help me rule other things out. Short answers are fine.' and park the bait: 'Thank you — I'll come back to the rash, I promise. First, a few questions about the leg itself.'

THE PAIN AND THE SWELLING IN SIX QUESTIONS — site, severity, onset and how quickly, WHETHER IT IS SPREADING BY THE HOUR OR BY THE DAY, aggravating and relieving, worse walking and WEIGHT-BEARING · then the swelling, WHICH IS IN THE PRESENTING COMPLAINT AND THEREFORE ON THE MARK SHEET: WHERE AND HOW FAR UP · ONE LEG OR BOTH · did it come with the pain or before it · AND DOES IT SETTLE OVERNIGHT. 'Spread since yesterday' is days not hours, which argues against necrotising fasciitis, and 'I can still get about' argues against a septic joint — notice both and quote them back.

THE VASCULAR BLOCK, WHICH IS THE WHOLE REASON THE STATION EXISTS: 'BEFORE THIS STARTED, DID YOU GET CRAMPING IN THE CALF AFTER WALKING A CERTAIN DISTANCE? HOW FAR — AND DOES IT SETTLE IF YOU STAND STILL?' Ask the symptom, not the label; patients do not know they have arterial disease, they know they get a cramp walking to the shops. Then night pain relieved by hanging the foot out of bed · pale or cold foot · slow-healing sores · smoking, diabetes, blood pressure, cholesterol · THEN THE VENOUS SIDE: recent long trips, surgery or immobility, previous clots, the pill or hormone therapy, any cancer.

Neurogenic in four — back pain · paraesthesiae or numbness · weakness · bladder or bowel change. Vascular claudication is a predictable distance relieved by standing still within minutes; neurogenic is a variable distance relieved only by sitting or leaning forward, usually with back pain and paraesthesiae.

JOINTS AND RED FLAGS — any injury · IS ANY JOINT SWOLLEN, AND DOES IT HURT TO MOVE IT · ever had gout · THEN THE SAFETY QUESTIONS: IS THE PAIN FAR WORSE THAN THE LEG LOOKS · IS IT SPREADING BY THE HOUR · ANY BLISTERS · faint, confused or very unwell in herself · chest pain or breathlessness · weight loss or night sweats.

ONLY NOW, THE INFECTION DETAIL — the rash, when it started, whether it is spreading, blisters or discharge · fevers or shakes · ANY BREAK IN THE SKIN: A SCRATCH, BITE, CUT, GARDENING OR BUSHWALKING · AND THE ONE ALMOST NOBODY ASKS: CRACKING OR ITCHING BETWEEN THE TOES, which is the second portal of entry and the thing you treat to stop this recurring · leg ulcers · previous cellulitis in this leg · other conditions and medications · AND ALLERGIES, PARTICULARLY PENICILLIN AND WHAT HAPPENED, because a childhood rash and an anaphylaxis lead to different drugs · tetanus · who is at home.

REQUEST THE EXAMINATION AS A NAMED STRUCTURE — general appearance and conscious level, BMI · ALL VITAL SIGNS INCLUDING BLOOD PRESSURE, PULSE, RESPIRATORY RATE, SATURATIONS AND BLOOD SUGAR · inspection: morphology, discharge, BULLAE, site, extent AND WHETHER THE EDGE IS SHARPLY DEMARCATED, pallor, ulcers, breaks in the skin, BETWEEN THE TOES, hair loss, joint swelling · palpation: local temperature, tenderness AND WHETHER TENDERNESS EXTENDS BEYOND THE REDNESS, CREPITUS, PEDAL, POPLITEAL AND FEMORAL PULSES, CAPILLARY REFILL, calf tenderness and circumference, pitting · movement of knee and ankle · AND SPECIAL TESTS: INGUINAL NODES, A SENSORY EXAMINATION AND BUERGER'S. You named vascular and neurological differentials, so leaving pulses, refill and sensation out is an internal contradiction the examiner will notice.
READ THE NUMBERS AND THE PULSES ALOUD — BOTH ABNORMAL SETS, NAMED (see findings). Taking the findings and moving straight to 'so this is cellulitis' is how both marks are lost at once.
Explain both diagnoses in plain words, then the disposition without softening it, then the differentials with their reasons (see dx).

Answer 'Am I going to lose the leg?' — 'No, I don't think so. But I'm being careful for two reasons: the infection is making you unwell all over, and the circulation in that leg isn't as good as it should be. Treating it properly now is exactly how we avoid the outcome you're worried about.' then mark and date the margin, the interim measures, the three things afterwards, and the safety-net: back to emergency if the redness passes the line, if the pain becomes much worse than the leg looks, if blisters appear, or if she feels faint or confused.

pefe: The examiner gives what you name, and the card contains two separate abnormal sets — the observations and the pulses. Reading the observations aloud and saying they change your management is scored, and so is naming the absent pulses, the four-second refill, the hair loss and the positive Buerger's. A systolic of 90 with a pulse of 110 and a temperature of 39 in a diabetic with a spreading skin infection is not an oral antibiotic consultation.

Role-player: Marion Deakin, 50, with two days of pain, redness and swelling of the right lower leg and fevers and shakes. Type 2 diabetes, a cholesterol tablet, fifteen cigarettes a day, no allergies, tetanus up to date, husband at home. She volunteers freely that the leg is red, hot, swollen and that she is shivery, offers it repeatedly and steers back to it if the doctor moves on — she is the bait.

What she gives only if asked: that for about a year she has had cramp in that calf after two hundred metres, relieved by standing still for a minute, which she put down to getting older · that the foot sometimes feels cold · that the skin between her toes has been cracked and itchy for ages · and that she scratched her shin on a branch bushwalking at the weekend. Her hidden agenda is a fear of losing the leg because her uncle had an amputation, raised only when the diagnosis is explained or in the last thirty seconds.

Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Forty seconds to open and acknowledge the stated concern · the pain with the site offered in four options to 1:50 · the pattern, where the theatre sign lives, to 2:50 · MSK screen and the injury question to 3:20 · red flags to 3:50 · the six key knee questions to 4:20 · differentials by bucket to 5:30 · closure and ice to 6:00 · then the card, then commit with three reasons

Version B card — chronic meniscal tear
INSPECTION NORMAL, PALPATION NORMAL, McMURRAY'S TEST POSITIVE — in a knee that LOCKS and has an untreated twisting injury fifteen years ago
Genu varum · quadriceps wasting · crepitus · reduced flexion · medial joint line tenderness · no warmth, no erythema

back.dx: CHONDROMALACIA PATELLAE — PATELLOFEMORAL PAIN SYNDROME — WITH PREPATELLAR BURSITIS AS THE CLOSE SECOND. TO HIM: 'THE CARTILAGE ON THE BACK OF YOUR KNEECAP HAS BECOME DAMAGED. CARTILAGE IS THE SMOOTH COATING THAT LETS THE KNEECAP GLIDE OVER THE BONE UNDERNEATH; WHEN IT'S WORN, THE KNEECAP RUBS INSTEAD OF GLIDES, AND THAT HURTS.' THREE REASONS: THE SITE — THE PAIN IS EXACTLY ON THE KNEECAP · IT IS WORSE ON STAIRS, SQUATTING AND AFTER SITTING FOR A LONG TIME, ALL OF WHICH PRESS THE KNEECAP AGAINST THE BONE · AND ON EXAMINATION PRESSING THE KNEECAP WAS PAINFUL WHILE THE KNEE OTHERWISE LOOKED COMPLETELY NORMAL. THE RANKED SECOND: PREPATELLAR BURSITIS, 'a small cushion in front of the kneecap that can become inflamed, usually in people who kneel a lot' — less likely because there is NO VISIBLE SWELLING OR REDNESS, HE IS AT A DESK AND DOES NOT KNEEL, AND A BURSITIS DOES NOT USUALLY WORSEN ON STAIRS. THEN THE WIDER LIST BY BUCKET RATHER THAN FIVE ARTHRITIDES: OSTEOARTHRITIS AND THE INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIDES — against him, morning stiffness of a minute or two rather than an hour, one joint only, no swelling, heat or redness, and no family history of the inflammatory types; SOFT TISSUE — bursitis, patellar tendinopathy, a Baker's cyst; NEUROVASCULAR AND REFERRED — the lumbar spine and the hip; AND THE SERIOUS ONES CHECKED DELIBERATELY — a bone tumour and septic arthritis, with nothing pointing that way, which is itself reassurance worth saying out loud. ANSWERING 'IS IT ARTHRITIS?' WITH 'NO, DON'T WORRY' IS THE FAILURE — GIVE HIM THE REASONS, AND ADD THE HONEST LIMIT: 'I CAN'T BE CERTAIN FROM ONE VISIT, AND IF YOU DON'T IMPROVE I'D RECONSIDER AND WE'D LOOK AT AN X-RAY OR A SPECIALIST OPINION. BUT I DON'T THINK YOU'RE HEADING FOR YOUR FATHER'S KNEE AT 45.' THE PLAN: PHYSIOTHERAPY FOR QUADRICEPS AND HIP STRENGTHENING, WHICH IS THE MAINSTAY AND NOT REST · CUT BACK THE AGGRAVATING LOADS — STAIRS, SQUATTING, DEEP LUNGES, AND DO NOT RAMP THE RUNNING BACK UP TOO FAST · PARACETAMOL OR A TOPICAL ANTI-INFLAMMATORY · IMPROVEMENT OVER WEEKS RATHER THAN DAYS, AND MOST PEOPLE GET BACK TO SPORT · REVIEW AT 4 TO 6 WEEKS · AND THE SAFETY-NET: A HOT, RED OR SWOLLEN KNEE OR A FEVER, LOCKING SO HE CANNOT STRAIGHTEN IT, PAIN WAKING HIM AT NIGHT, OR UNINTENDED WEIGHT LOSS. IF THE EXAMINER ASKS WHAT YOU WOULD DO IF HE DOES NOT IMPROVE: 'I WOULD REASSESS THE DIAGNOSIS RATHER THAN REPEAT THE SAME PLAN — check adherence to the physiotherapy programme, re-examine including Clarke's test, the hip and the lumbar spine, then consider a weight-bearing X-ray. If inflammatory features had emerged I'd send FBE, ESR, CRP, urate, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP and refer to rheumatology. MRI I'd reserve for genuine mechanical symptoms.' THE VARIANTS. B, CHRONIC MENISCAL TEAR: the knee LOCKS AND HAS TO BE WIGGLED FREE, and there was a TWISTING INJURY AT FOOTBALL FIFTEEN YEARS AGO — which must then be explored properly: what happened, was there a twist, was there a pop, could he weight-bear afterwards, what treatment, did it ever fully settle. Reasons: the locking, the untreated twisting injury, and a POSITIVE McMURRAY'S. THE TRAP IS REFERRING STRAIGHT FOR ARTHROSCOPY — in a middle-aged knee with a degenerate tear and no true mechanical block, PHYSIOTHERAPY COMES FIRST AND SURGERY IS FOR THE GENUINELY LOCKED KNEE. C, OSTEOARTHRITIS: aching after being on his feet, worse downstairs, TEN MINUTES OF MORNING STIFFNESS, grinding and clicking → reasons are age over 45 with activity-related pain relieved by rest, mechanical-length morning stiffness, and the card's varus alignment, quadriceps wasting, crepitus and medial joint line tenderness with no warmth. IT IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS AND YOU WOULD NOT ROUTINELY X-RAY, SINCE RADIOLOGICAL CHANGE CORRELATES POORLY WITH SYMPTOMS; exercise and weight management are first-line, NOT REST, with a structured programme such as GLA:D, topical anti-inflammatory, simple analgesia and a walking aid if needed, and surgery for those significantly limited despite all of it. THE CURVEBALLS A PARTNER CAN ADD: GOUT — flares after a barbecue and beers, red and hot, on a thiazide → aspiration for crystals is definitive, urate may be normal during the attack, review the diuretic. RHEUMATOID — over an hour of morning stiffness, both hands, exhausted → switch buckets, FBE, ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, EARLY REFERRAL BECAUSE DELAY COSTS JOINTS. SEPTIC JOINT — swollen and febrile → stop the differential list, urgent aspiration and same-day hospital referral. RED FLAG — night pain and five kilos lost → complete the malignancy screen, examine for masses and nodes, X-ray and urgent review. RUPTURED BAKER'S CYST — sudden calf pain and bruising round the ankle → ultrasound, which confirms the cyst and excludes the DVT it mimics. ADOLESCENT — a 14-year-old with a normal knee and a limp → EXAMINE THE HIP, because it is SUFE until proven otherwise, and night pain with weight loss means think osteosarcoma.
plan: WIPE, confirm name and age, and acknowledge the stated concern in the opening statement: 'Six months is a long time to be putting up with something, and I can hear you're worried about it. I'm here to help.' then signpost the shape and ask whether he is in pain now.

THE PAIN — AND OFFER THE FOUR SITES EVERY TIME, BECAUSE 'IN MY KNEE, DOCTOR' IS WHAT YOU GET OTHERWISE: 'IS IT ON THE FRONT OF THE KNEE, THE INNER OR OUTER SIDE, OR THE BACK?' Then severity, dull or sharp, duration and whether it is constant or intermittent and worsening, radiation, aggravating and relieving factors, worse on standing and walking, AND THE EFFECT ON HIS LIFE AT HOME AND AT WORK.

THE PATTERN, WHICH IS THE DISCRIMINATOR: NIGHT PAIN THAT WAKES HIM, which is your malignancy and infection screen for the joint and separates severe osteoarthritis from a patellofemoral problem · MORNING VERSUS END OF DAY AND HOW LONG THE MORNING STIFFNESS LASTS · WORSE AFTER REST OR AFTER ACTIVITY, WHICH IS WHERE THE THEATRE SIGN ARRIVES — 'IF I'VE BEEN SITTING A LONG TIME, LIKE AT THE CINEMA OR IN THE CAR, IT'S STIFF AND SORE WHEN I FIRST STAND UP' · then limping and weight-bearing.

MSK SCREEN AND THE INJURY QUESTION — swelling, redness or rash, stiffness beyond a couple of minutes, AND 'HAVE YOU EVER INJURED THIS KNEE, EVEN YEARS AGO?' If that answer becomes yes you must switch modes and explore it properly, because that single answer converts the station into the chronic meniscal version.

RED FLAGS, SIGNPOSTED AS ROUTINE AND ASKED IN FULL — unintended weight loss · appetite · lumps or bumps · unusual tiredness · night sweats · fevers or chills · AND EVER TREATED FOR CANCER. The examiner is not scoring your probability estimate that six months excludes infection and malignancy; they are scoring whether you asked, and this is the commonest single reason candidates fail.

The six key knee questions — does it lock or get stuck so he has to wiggle it free · does it give way · can he fully bend and fully straighten it · clicking or grinding · worse up or down stairs and squatting · and worse after prolonged sitting. These build a case; they do not close it, because osteoarthritis is also worse on stairs.

DIFFERENTIALS BY BUCKET, NOT BY LIST. JOINT — other joints, family history of arthritis, rashes or nail changes, SUDDEN RED HOT ATTACKS OR TRIGGERS FROM RED MEAT OR ALCOHOL, recent diarrhoea, blood in the stool or urethral discharge. SOFT TISSUE — KNEELING OR DIRECT PRESSURE AT WORK, jumping sport or a recent increase in training load, A LUMP BEHIND THE KNEE. NEUROVASCULAR — back pain now or previously, paraesthesiae or weakness, colour change or coldness in the foot. REFERRED — HIP OR GROIN PAIN, and recent or recurrent sore throats.

CLOSURE — occupation and sport, medical conditions and regular medicines INCLUDING FLUID TABLETS, allergies, smoking and alcohol — AND THE ICE QUESTION, WHICH IN THIS STATION IS SCORED BECAUSE THE CONCERN IS IN THE STEM: 'WAS THERE ANYTHING IN PARTICULAR YOU WERE WORRIED THIS MIGHT BE?'

REQUEST THE EXAMINATION AS A STRUCTURE: inspection for swelling, redness, deformity, alignment AND QUADRICEPS WASTING, compared with the other side · palpation for warmth, AN EFFUSION, JOINT LINE TENDERNESS, TENDERNESS OVER THE PATELLA AND AT ITS INFERIOR POLE, and the popliteal fossa · active and passive range and crepitus · CLARKE'S PATELLAR GRIND TEST, McMURRAY'S AND THE LIGAMENT STRESS TESTS · AND THE HIP, THE LUMBAR SPINE, GAIT AND NEUROVASCULAR STATUS, because in a knee station the referred causes are examined and not just asked about, and it costs one sentence.
Read the card back, commit to one diagnosis, translate it, and give the three reasons — then the ranked second differential with why it is less likely (see dx and findings).
Answer the arthritis fear with evidence from his own history, not blanket reassurance — then the plan, the safety-net and a four-to-six-week review.
back.planNote: the card comes at 6:00 whatever you have or have not asked — the red-flag block sits at 3:20 for a reason, because candidates who leave it late never reach it
ask: THE SITE, IN FOUR OPTIONS, EVERY TIME: 'IS THE PAIN ON THE FRONT OF THE KNEE, THE INNER OR OUTER SIDE, OR THE BACK?' — he answers 'in my knee, doctor' and waits otherwise.

THE THEATRE SIGN, WHICH HE WILL NOT VOLUNTEER: 'IS IT WORSE AFTER SITTING FOR A LONG TIME — IN THE CAR, OR AT THE CINEMA?' It is the highest-value clue in the station and it is earned by asking about rest versus activity or prolonged sitting.

The three pattern questions: 'Do you get any pain at night that wakes you?' · 'Is it worse in the morning or at the end of the day — and how long does the morning stiffness last?' · 'Worse after rest, or after activity?'
The question that would change the station: 'Have you ever injured this knee — even years ago?'

Challenges: 'Do you think it's arthritis, doctor?' Pushed once at about four minutes · 'But it's not arthritis? That's what I came in about' · 'Will I need a knee replacement like dad?' · 'Can I still play hockey?' · and 'Sorry, what does that mean?' Every time you use jargon.
pefe: THE CARD ARRIVES AT SIX MINUTES WHETHER YOU ARE READY OR NOT, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY ALMOST EMPTY: A NORMAL-LOOKING KNEE WITH TENDERNESS OVER THE PATELLA. THE SKILL IS USING THE NORMAL FINDINGS AS POSITIVE EVIDENCE — no swelling ranks bursitis second, no heat or redness argues against inflammatory arthritis, and no deformity or wasting argues against established osteoarthritis.

Role-player: James Whitlock, 45, an accounts manager with a desk job and no kneeling, who plays club field hockey on Saturdays and runs two or three times a week — and increased his running sharply before the season started. Six months of left knee pain, gradually worse, on and just under the kneecap, a dull ache five to six out of ten. Worse on stairs in both directions, squatting, and after sitting still. Flat walking is fine. No swelling, no redness, no locking, no giving way, an occasional click, a slight limp after stairs. Morning stiffness one to two minutes. Everything else negative — no night pain, no fevers, no weight loss, no lumps, no night sweats, no other joints, no rashes, no bowel or urinary symptoms, no back, hip or groin pain, no paraesthesiae, and no injury to this knee ever. Non-smoker, four or five drinks a week, no medicines, no diuretics, no allergies. Father had osteoarthritis and a knee replacement at 60, with no rheumatoid in the family.

How he plays it: matter-of-fact and a little impatient — he has put up with this for six months — warming up if the doctor acknowledges the six months and the hockey, and going briefly flat when the arthritis fear comes up. His opening line is general. If asked 'Where is the pain?' with no options he says 'In my knee' and waits. He withholds the theatre sign until asked about rest versus activity or prolonged sitting — make them earn it. He pushes once at about four minutes with 'Do you think it's arthritis?', and a good candidate acknowledges it and finishes the history first. His hidden agenda — that he is convinced he is heading for his father's knee replacement and is quietly grieving the hockey — is raised as the doctor starts explaining if concerns were never asked about.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE: acknowledged the stated concern IN THE OPENING STATEMENT · OFFERED THE FOUR SITE OPTIONS · SIQORA completed without over-running · effect on life · NIGHT PAIN · morning versus evening and the DURATION of stiffness · rest versus activity · limping and weight-bearing · swelling, redness and stiffness screened · ASKED WHETHER THE KNEE HAD EVER BEEN INJURED · ALL THE RED FLAGS — weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, night sweats, fever, previous cancer · LOCKING · GIVING WAY · full flexion and extension · THE THEATRE SIGN · stairs and squatting · clicking · ALL FOUR BUCKETS · occupation and sport used in the plan · ICE ELICITED · EXAMINATION REQUESTED IN A STRUCTURED WAY INCLUDING HIP AND LUMBAR SPINE · COMMITTED TO ONE DIAGNOSIS WITH THREE EXPLICIT REASONS · a ranked second differential with why it is less likely · A WIDER LIST ACROSS BUCKETS RATHER THAN FIVE ARTHRITIDES · THE ARTHRITIS FEAR ANSWERED WITH EVIDENCE · plan and safety-net with a review date.

Say it back, and use the normal as evidence — 'SO A NORMAL-LOOKING KNEE WITH NO SWELLING OR REDNESS, AND TENDERNESS ON DIRECT PRESSURE OVER THE PATELLA ITSELF.' The absent swelling is what ranks prepatellar bursitis second, and the absent heat and redness is what argues against inflammatory arthritis
fails: ★ Not asking the red flags — no malignancy screen and no infection screen — on the reasoning that six months excludes them
★ Running the acute traumatic knee structure and spending six minutes on a mechanism that never happened
★ Ignoring the stated concern about arthritis, or answering it with 'don't worry', or promising it is 'definitely not arthritis'
Never asking about locking or giving way; or the patient discloses an old injury and it is never explored
Giving a diagnosis with no reasons; accepting 'my knee' as the site; promising a cure or a return-to-sport date; or finishing with no safety-net and no review plan
numbers: Six months in the stem is the word that tells you which knee station you are in · six minutes of history with the card at 6:00 · morning stiffness under 30 minutes is mechanical and over 30-60 is inflammatory — his is one to two minutes · age over 45 supports a clinical diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis

Four sites — front, inner, outer, back, always offered · five buckets — red flags, bone and joint, soft tissue, neurovascular, referred · six key questions — locking, giving way, full range, prolonged sitting, stairs, clicking · paracetamol 1 g QID to a maximum of 4 g/24 h · ibuprofen 200-400 mg TDS with food, with a topical NSAID preferred in older patients · review at 4-6 weeks · VERIFY all

must: FAIL — Not asking the red flags — the commonest single reason candidates fail this station; reasoning that six months rules out infection and malignancy so the questions are unnecessary — the examiner is not scoring your probability estimate, they are scoring whether you asked: 'there are a few questions I ask everyone with long-standing joint pain — any weight loss you didn't intend? change in appetite? lumps or bumps? unusual tiredness, night sweats? fevers or chills? ever been treated for cancer?'; and night pain is one question and is your malignancy and infection screen for the joint (★)

FAIL — Never asking about locking or giving way, or not exploring a disclosed old injury — 'does it ever lock or get stuck, so you have to wiggle it free? does it ever give way? can you fully bend and fully straighten it? any clicking or grinding?'; 'have you ever injured this knee — even years ago?' → 'no, never' (Version B: 'I twisted it playing football fifteen years ago' → switch modes and explore it — what happened, a twist, a pop, weight-bearing afterwards, treatment, did it ever fully settle → the chronic meniscal tear: locks, an untreated twisting injury, McMurray's positive; physiotherapy first — arthroscopy is for the genuinely locked knee, not a middle-aged degenerate tear) (★)

FAIL — Giving a diagnosis with no reasons, ignoring the arthritis concern or answering it 'don't worry', or promising 'definitely not arthritis', a cure or a return-to-sport date — the concern is written into the stem; acknowledge it in the opening statement ('I can understand why you're worried') or the communication marks are gone before you've asked a question, and answer it specifically at the end with evidence: 'I thought hard about that, because of your dad; against arthritis: your morning stiffness lasts a minute or two rather than an hour, only one joint is involved, there's no swelling, redness or heat, and no family history of the inflammatory types; I also deliberately checked for the serious causes — a growth in the bone and an infection in the joint — and nothing points that way; I can't be certain from one visit, and if you don't improve I'd reconsider — but I don't think you're heading for your father's knee at 45' (★)

FAIL — Running the acute traumatic knee structure — six minutes on a mechanism that never happened; 'six months' in the stem is the word that tells you which knee station you are in; and accepting 'in my knee' as the site — offer the four options every time ('the front of the knee, the inner or outer side, or the back?' → a palm over the kneecap) — the answer sets up the entire differential

DO — SIQORA without over-running; the pattern is the discriminator — night pain (no), 'worse in the morning or the end of the day, and how long does the morning stiffness last?' (a minute or two — <30 min mechanical, >30–60 inflammatory), 'worse after rest or after activity?' → the theatre sign, delivered casually and withheld until asked ('if I've been sitting a long time — the car, the cinema — it's stiff and sore when I stand up and I have to stretch it out' — the highest-value clue in the station), limping and weight-bearing; the MSK screen; the key knee questions incl. 'worse climbing or going down stairs, or squatting?' ('both directions, squatting is horrible' — but osteoarthritis is also worse on stairs; these build a case, they don't close it); differentials by bucket, not five arthritis questions called five differentials — joint (other joints, family history — 'Dad had arthritis in his knees and had one replaced', rashes or nails, red-hot attacks or red meat and alcohol, diarrhoea or discharge), soft tissue (kneeling or direct pressure at work, jumping sport or a recent training increase — 'I ramped my running up before hockey season', a lump behind the knee), neurovascular (back pain, paraesthesiae, weakness, colour change), referred (hip or groin pain, recent sore throats); closure with occupation, sport, medicines incl. fluid tablets, ICE ('I'm worried it's arthritis — Dad had a knee replacement at 60 and I'm 45; I don't want to give up hockey'); the examination requested in structure incl. Clarke's patellar grind, McMurray's, ligament stress tests, AND the hip and lumbar spine — referred causes are examined, not just asked about; read the card aloud and use 'normal' as positive evidence ('a normal-looking knee with no swelling or redness, and tenderness on direct pressure over the patella')

SAY — 'James, the most likely explanation is a condition called chondromalacia patellae — also known as patellofemoral pain syndrome; in plain terms, the cartilage on the back of your kneecap has become damaged; cartilage is the smooth coating that lets the kneecap glide over the bone underneath; when it's worn, the kneecap rubs instead of glides, and that hurts'; three reasons ('the pain is right on the kneecap; it's worse on stairs, squatting, and after sitting for a long time — all of those press the kneecap against the bone; and pressing the kneecap was painful, and the knee otherwise looked completely normal'); the ranked second — 'a bursitis, a small cushion in front of the kneecap that can become inflamed, usually in people who kneel a lot; less likely here because there's no swelling or redness, you don't kneel at work, and a bursitis doesn't usually get worse on stairs'; then the wider list by bucket; the plan — physiotherapy for thigh and hip strengthening ('the mainstay, not rest'), cut back the aggravating loads (stairs, squatting, deep lunges, don't ramp the running), paracetamol or an anti-inflammatory gel, 'most people get back to their sport — improvement over weeks, not days'; review 4–6 weeks; safety net (hot, red or swollen or a fever; locking so it won't straighten; pain waking him; weight loss); 'what if he doesn't improve?' → reassess rather than repeat — adherence, re-examine incl. Clarke's, hip and spine, a weight-bearing X-ray; inflammatory features → FBE, ESR, CRP, urate, RF, anti-CCP, rheumatology; MRI reserved for genuine mechanical symptoms; Version C (aches after standing, worse downstairs, ten minutes of stiffness, grinds and clicks; genu varum, quadriceps wasting, crepitus, reduced flexion, medial joint line tenderness, no warmth) → osteoarthritis — a clinical diagnosis over 45, no routine X-ray, exercise and weight management first-line (GLA:D), topical gel, simple analgesia; curveballs — a barbecue-and-beers flare on a thiazide = aspirate for crystals; over an hour of stiffness with both hands and exhaustion = switch buckets, early rheumatology; a swollen feverish knee = stop the list, aspirate, hospital same day; night pain and five kilos lost = the malignancy screen, masses and nodes, X-ray, urgent review; a limping 14-year-old with a normal knee = examine the hip, SUFE until proven otherwise

setting: The history and examination are already done — this is an explain, investigate and manage station, and trying to take a full history is not the task and will be stopped. The single most important sentence is naming septic arthritis first, saying why it matters and saying how you will exclude it. And the management is six components, not one: treating the flare and stopping there is a fail.
stem: General practice. James Corrigan, 40, with left knee pain for two weeks and similar episodes before that settled without treatment. No fever. No injury.
A known hypertensive taking hydrochlorothiazide. Non-smoker, four standard drinks of beer daily, an accountant, otherwise well, no other past or family history.

Examination already performed: the knee is swollen and red, warm and tender on palpation. Temperature normal. Tasks: explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials — request further investigations and explain them — explain your immediate management.
