'I'd inspect, palpate and move the joint' RETURNS NOTHING, because the examiner answers only what you ask for by name. ASK FOR: alert or drowsy and systemically unwell, BMI AND WAIST CIRCUMFERENCE · TEMPERATURE FIRST, then BP, pulse and respiratory rate · inspection for swelling, redness, GENU VARUM OR VALGUM, VISIBLE TOPHI and intact skin · palpation for local temperature and tenderness · pain and restriction on active and passive movement · A PATELLAR TAP OR SWEEP TEST FOR AN EFFUSION · THE JOINT ABOVE AND BELOW, THE FIRST MTP JOINTS, AND TOPHI AT THE EAR HELIX, OLECRANON AND ACHILLES · a brief cardiovascular examination · AND OFFICE TESTS: BLOOD GLUCOSE AND URINE DIPSTICK
Version 6 — office tests asked for by name

A capillary blood glucose, saying whether fasting or random · a urine dipstick, saying what you are looking for — glucose, ketones, protein, blood, and nitrites and leucocytes for infection · blood pressure · height, weight, BMI and waist · and temperature. Answering an office-test task with pathology requests is the trap

back.dx: GOUTY ARTHRITIS. EXPLAIN IT IN TWO LAYERS AND THEN LINK THEM: 'ARTHRITIS SIMPLY MEANS INFLAMMATION IN A JOINT — AND WHEN A JOINT IS INFLAMED IT GOES RED, IT SWELLS UP, AND IT BECOMES PAINFUL. THAT'S EXACTLY WHAT I FOUND IN YOUR KNEE. GOUT IS THE CAUSE OF THAT INFLAMMATION. THERE'S A NATURAL SUBSTANCE IN YOUR BLOOD CALLED URIC ACID; WHEN THERE'S TOO MUCH OF IT, IT FORMS TINY CRYSTALS THAT SETTLE INSIDE THE JOINT, AND YOUR BODY REACTS TO THEM WITH THIS INTENSE INFLAMMATION.' THREE NUMBERED REASONS, SAID AS 'THERE ARE THREE REASONS' SO THE EXAMINER CAN TICK THEM: THE PATTERN — SUDDEN ATTACKS IN A SINGLE JOINT THAT HAVE COME AND GONE BY THEMSELVES BEFORE · THE APPEARANCE — RED, WARM, SWOLLEN AND TENDER · AND THE RISK FACTORS THAT PUSH URIC ACID UP — FOUR BEERS A DAY AND ONE OF HIS BLOOD PRESSURE TABLETS. THE DIFFERENTIAL THAT MUST COME FIRST: 'THE ONE I'M MOST CONCERNED TO RULE OUT IS AN INFECTION INSIDE THE JOINT — SEPTIC ARTHRITIS. IT LOOKS ALMOST IDENTICAL: A RED, HOT, SWOLLEN, PAINFUL JOINT. IT'S SERIOUS, BECAUSE AN INFECTED JOINT CAN BE DAMAGED QUICKLY. IN YOUR FAVOUR YOU HAVE NO FEVER AND YOU'RE NOT UNWELL IN YOURSELF — AND THE FLUID SAMPLE WILL SETTLE IT DEFINITIVELY.' THEN THE REST: PSEUDOGOUT, a different crystal causing the same picture; RHEUMATOID, REACTIVE OR PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS, which usually affect several joints, often symmetrically, with long morning stiffness; OSTEOARTHRITIS, which does not usually go this red and hot; PREPATELLAR BURSITIS; CELLULITIS OF THE SKIN OVER THE JOINT; and nothing to suggest referred pain from back or hip, or a DVT. INVESTIGATIONS, TWO THEN TWO, EACH WITH A REASON — NEVER A SHOPPING LIST, WHICH IS EXPLICITLY A FAIL. SERUM URATE for a baseline before long-term treatment, WITH THE CAVEAT SAID ALOUD THAT IT CAN BE NORMAL DURING AN ATTACK SO A NORMAL RESULT WOULD NOT CHANGE YOUR MIND. JOINT ASPIRATION under ultrasound guidance and local anaesthetic, sent for POLARISED LIGHT MICROSCOPY to confirm the crystals and CULTURE to exclude infection. THEN RENAL FUNCTION, because urate is renally cleared and it decides the doses, AND GLUCOSE AND LIPIDS, because they travel with gout and matter for his heart. THE NEEDLE RELUCTANCE IS ANSWERED WITH TWO REASONS AND A BONUS: it is the only way to be certain there is no infection, it confirms a diagnosis before you ask him to take a lifelong tablet, AND YOU CAN INJECT STEROID AT THE SAME TIME. THE SIX MANAGEMENT COMPONENTS: ONE, THE FLARE — OFFERED AS THREE OPTIONS RATHER THAN PRESCRIBED: an NSAID with food, a steroid either oral or intra-articular, or colchicine — plus rest, keeping weight off it, ice and elevation; when he says anti-inflammatories give him heartburn, having offered options lets you switch immediately. TWO, CONFIRMATION by aspirate. THREE, LIFELONG ALLOPURINOL, started low and titrated every two to four weeks TO TARGET, because a dose that never reaches target is not doing its job, and it is A TREATMENT, NOT A CURE. FOUR, FLARE PROPHYLAXIS WITH COLCHICINE FOR ABOUT SIX MONTHS, because starting allopurinol can itself trigger an attack — omit this and he stops the tablet at the first flare. FIVE, TRIGGERS AND REVERSIBLE CAUSES — red meat, offal and seafood framed as 'not none, but as little as you can manage'; ALCOHOL WITH NO SAFE LIMIT ENDORSED AND BEER THE WORST; sugary drinks; hydration, because dehydration brings attacks on; GRADUAL weight loss, because crash dieting can trigger an attack; AND THE HYDROCHLOROTHIAZIDE, WHICH MAKES THE KIDNEYS HOLD ON TO URATE — SUBSTITUTE IT FOR AN ACE INHIBITOR OR CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKER AND RECHECK THE BLOOD PRESSURE, NEVER SIMPLY STOP IT. SIX, CARDIOVASCULAR RISK ASSESSMENT. THE RASH WARNING IS NON-NEGOTIABLE: IF HE DEVELOPS A RASH, STOP THE TABLET AND CONTACT YOU STRAIGHT AWAY. AND TOPHI, WHICH IS HIS UNCLE'S HANDS, ARE DEPOSITS OF URIC ACID AFTER YEARS OF UNCONTROLLED ATTACKS — NOT INEVITABLE, AND EXACTLY WHAT THIS PLAN PREVENTS. THE EXAMINER FOLLOW-UPS: 'WHAT IF THE CULTURE GROWS AN ORGANISM?' → septic arthritis until proven otherwise, urgent referral, blood cultures, IV antibiotics AFTER cultures, joint washout — AND THE TWO CAN COEXIST. 'HIS eGFR IS 34?' → avoid NSAIDs, reduce the colchicine dose, PREFER A CORTICOSTEROID for the flare; allopurinol still applies but start lower, titrate more slowly and watch for hypersensitivity. 'WOULD YOU TREAT A URATE OF 0.49 IN A MAN WITH NO ATTACKS?' → NO — ASYMPTOMATIC HYPERURICAEMIA IS NOT TREATED; address the cardiovascular risk factors instead.
plan: One open question, then the agenda, then ice — and neither lecture nor take a history: 'Just so I've heard it from you, what's been happening with the knee? … I've reviewed your notes and examined it and I have a good idea what's going on. I'd like to explain what I think it is, go through the tests I want to arrange, then talk about treatment. Before I start — is there anything specific you're worried about, or hoping I'll cover today?'
The diagnosis in two layers — what arthritis is, then what gout is — and then link them into 'Gouty arthritis'. Check understanding before moving on.
The three numbered reasons: the pattern, the appearance, and the risk factors (see dx).
Differentials with septic arthritis named first, why it matters, and how you will exclude it — then the rest by bucket.

INVESTIGATIONS RANKED — TWO THAT MATTER MOST, THEN TWO MORE, EACH WITH THE REASON ATTACHED. Handle the needle reluctance with two reasons and the offer of intra-articular steroid rather than an instruction.

The flare, offered as three options rather than prescribed — 'I'll start you on indomethacin' is doctor-centred; 'We have three options' earns the communication mark and lets you demonstrate you know when NSAIDs are unsafe. Add rest, weight off it, ice and elevation.

Triggers and the thiazide — diet, alcohol with no safe limit offered, sugary drinks, hydration and gradual weight loss · then the substitution: 'Your blood pressure tablet makes the kidneys hold on to uric acid — I'd like to swap it, not just stop it', with the blood pressure rechecked afterwards.

THE LONG-TERM PLAN — ALLOPURINOL, WHY IT MATTERS (fewer attacks means less joint damage, no tophi, and a lower risk of urate stones), THEN THE THREE THINGS HE MUST KNOW: TREAT-TO-TARGET WITH TITRATION EVERY TWO TO FOUR WEEKS · IT IS A TREATMENT AND NOT A CURE, SO STOPPING IT BRINGS THE ATTACKS BACK · AND STARTING IT CAN TRIGGER AN ATTACK, SO COLCHICINE RUNS ALONGSIDE FOR ABOUT SIX MONTHS. THEN THE RASH WARNING. When he asks whether diet alone would do, be honest: diet helps and you want the changes, BUT THE TABLET DOES THE HEAVY LIFTING.

THE FOUR Rs AND THE SUMMARY — RISK ASSESSMENT pulling blood pressure, sugar, cholesterol and renal function together · READING, specifically a food and drink fact sheet, which is the part patients find most useful · REVIEW in a week or two for the flare then every few weeks while titrating · AND RED FLAGS: fever or feeling unwell, a rapidly worsening joint, or a rash on the new tablet.
back.planNote: the management content is identical across all five recall versions — what changes is which slice of it you are asked to deliver, so know all six components and give the ones the task names
ask: The sentence the station turns on: 'The one I'm most concerned to rule out is an infection inside the joint — septic arthritis. It looks almost identical, and an infected joint can be damaged quickly. The fluid sample will settle it definitively.'

The two-layer explanation and the caveat: 'Arthritis means inflammation in a joint — it goes red, it swells, and it hurts.' · 'Too much uric acid forms tiny crystals that settle in the joint.' · 'The uric acid level can be normal during an attack, so a normal result wouldn't change my mind.'

The three lines that protect the long-term plan: 'We start low and increase every two to four weeks until the level is below target — a dose that never reaches target isn't doing its job.' · 'Starting it can trigger an attack at first, so I'll give you colchicine alongside it for about six months.' · 'If you develop a rash, stop the tablet and contact me straight away.'

The thiazide line: 'Your blood pressure tablet makes the kidneys hold on to uric acid — I'd like to swap it, not just stop it.' and the alcohol line: 'No alcohol is best, and the less you drink the fewer attacks — beer is the worst of them.'

Challenges: 'A needle in my knee? Is that really necessary?' · 'Anti-inflammatories give me shocking heartburn' · 'I've read two drinks a day is fine, though?', where agreeing is marked down · 'Can I just stop the blood pressure tablet then?' · 'Forever? Can't I just watch my diet instead?' · 'So the tablet might make it worse at first — why would I take it?' · and 'Am I going to end up like my uncle?'
pefe: The examination is already done in version 1, which is why the whole station is explaining, investigating and managing — but know the version 2 request by heart, because the examiner there answers only what you name and a generic 'Inspect, palpate and move' returns nothing and scores three out of ten while feeling fine (see findings). The contributing-factors task that follows it is: diet, alcohol at four beers daily, sugary drinks, the thiazide, obesity if the BMI is raised, dehydration, and recurrent pressure or trauma including footwear.

Role-player: James Corrigan, 40, an office-based accountant, married with two young children, not sporty. The left knee has been swollen, red and painful for two weeks, coming on over about a day, after three or four similar episodes in two years — once in the big toe, twice in this knee — each settling by itself in about a week, which is why he never came in. Crucially negative: no fever, chills or sweats, he feels well in himself, no injury, no weight loss, no lumps, no rashes, no other joints, no morning stiffness, no bowel or urinary symptoms. Hypertension for three years on hydrochlorothiazide, which he calls 'A fluid tablet for my blood pressure'. No allergies and no kidney or stomach problems — but anti-inflammatories give him bad heartburn and he says so if they are offered. Non-smoker, four cans of beer every evening, red meat most days and he loves prawns.

How he plays it: practical and a bit blunt to start — he wants an answer, not a chat — softening if the doctor acknowledges the pain and asks about his worries, and becoming noticeably quieter when the uncle comes up. His hidden agenda is the richest mark in the station and he withholds it until asked about concerns: his uncle had severe gout, his hands ended up covered in chalky lumps and he could barely hold a cup. He pushes back once on the needle, mentions the heartburn only if NSAIDs are offered, tests the alcohol advice with 'I've read two drinks a day is fine, though?', and tests adherence with 'Do I have to take this forever?' if jargon is used — urate, birefringent, arthrocentesis — he looks blank and asks what it means.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE: one open question rather than a lecture or a full history · AN AGENDA SET · ICE ASKED · arthritis explained in lay terms · gout and urate crystals explained in lay terms · THE TWO LINKED INTO GOUTY ARTHRITIS · THREE EXPLICIT REASONS · SEPTIC ARTHRITIS NAMED, WITH WHY IT MATTERS AND HOW IT WILL BE EXCLUDED · further differentials across more than one bucket · SERUM URATE WITH A REASON AND THE NORMAL-DURING-ATTACK CAVEAT · ASPIRATION WITH A REASON, NAMING POLARISED MICROSCOPY AND CULTURE · needle reluctance handled with reasons, not instruction · renal function, glucose and lipids each with a reason · NO UNRANKED SHOPPING LIST · THREE FLARE OPTIONS OFFERED RATHER THAN ONE PRESCRIBED, AND ADAPTED WHEN HEARTBURN WAS MENTIONED · rest, ice and elevation · diet framed as less is better · NO SAFE ALCOHOL LIMIT ENDORSED · THE THIAZIDE IDENTIFIED AND SUBSTITUTED RATHER THAN STOPPED · LIFELONG URATE-LOWERING THERAPY WITH TREAT-TO-TARGET · FLARE PROPHYLAXIS WITH ITS REASON · THE RASH WARNING · CARDIOVASCULAR RISK ASSESSMENT · THE UNCLE AND TOPHI ANSWERED SPECIFICALLY · reading, review, red flags and summary · understanding checked at least twice.

Given in the stem — THE KNEE IS SWOLLEN AND RED, WARM AND TENDER ON PALPATION. TEMPERATURE NORMAL — and 'no fever, and you're not unwell in yourself' is what you quote back when you explain why septic arthritis is less likely, without ever saying it is excluded

Version 3 — the crystal report, with two traps in it — 'JOINT ASPIRATE: URIC ACID CRYSTALS SEEN, NEGATIVELY BIREFRINGENT. LEUCOCYTES PRESENT. CULTURE NEGATIVE.' NEGATIVELY BIREFRINGENT IS NOT A NEGATIVE RESULT — it is how urate crystals look under polarised light, and it is the fingerprint that confirms gout. PSEUDOGOUT CRYSTALS ARE RHOMBOID AND WEAKLY POSITIVELY BIREFRINGENT. AND THE LEUCOCYTES ARE EXPECTED IN ANY INFLAMED JOINT — IT IS THE NEGATIVE CULTURE THAT EXCLUDES SEPSIS. Confirmed already means you skip 'we need to confirm it' and go straight to lifelong allopurinol
fails: ★ Never mentioning septic arthritis as a differential — or naming it in passing without saying why it matters and how you will exclude it
★ Omitting long-term urate-lowering therapy and treating only the flare, or omitting flare prophylaxis so he stops the allopurinol at the first attack
★ Telling him to stop the thiazide with no replacement and no blood pressure plan, or endorsing a 'safe' alcohol limit as acceptable for a gout patient
Giving an unranked shopping list of investigations with no prioritisation, or quoting colchicine in grams rather than milligrams

Ignoring the uncle and tophi concern or answering it with blanket reassurance; lecturing for the whole station with no pause and no check of understanding; or missing the rash warning and the cardiovascular risk assessment
numbers: Target serum urate under 0.36 mmol/L, and under 0.30 if tophaceous · allopurinol start 50 mg daily, lower in renal impairment, titrated by 50 mg every 2-4 weeks · colchicine flare prophylaxis 500 micrograms once or twice daily for at least 6 months · colchicine for an acute flare 1 mg then 500 micrograms at one hour — milligrams, never grams VERIFY

Review 1-2 weeks after a flare, then urate monitoring 6 to 12 monthly once at target · urate-lowering therapy is lifelong · asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is not treated · if eGFR is 34: avoid NSAIDs, reduce colchicine, prefer a corticosteroid, and start allopurinol lower and slower · gout crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent; pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent · VERIFY all

Full detail — FAIL — Never mentioning septic arthritis as a differential, or naming it in passing without saying why it matters and how you will exclude it — the single most important sentence in the station: 'I do have to consider other possibilities, and there's one I'm most concerned to rule out — an infection inside the joint; it looks almost identical to gout: a red, hot, swollen, painful joint; it's serious, because an infected joint can be damaged quickly, so we don't take chances with it; in your favour, you have no fever and you're not unwell in yourself — and when we take a sample of the fluid from the joint, that will settle it definitively'; septic arthritis and gout can coexist; 'if the culture grows an organism' → septic until proven otherwise, urgent referral, blood cultures, IV antibiotics after cultures, washout (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Omitting long-term urate-lowering therapy — treating the flare and stopping fails the station; 'once we've confirmed this with the joint fluid, I'd recommend a tablet called allopurinol; it lowers the uric acid, and that means fewer attacks — which matters, because repeated inflammation over the years can damage the joint permanently, cause those chalky lumps, and it reduces your risk of uric acid kidney stones; three things: we start at a low dose and increase every two to four weeks, checking the blood level, until the uric acid is below a target — a dose that never reaches target isn't doing its job; it's a long-term tablet — a treatment, not a cure; if you stop it the uric acid climbs and the attacks come back; and when we first start it, it can trigger an attack, so I'll give you colchicine alongside it for about six months to prevent that; the one side effect to watch for is a rash — stop the tablet and contact me straight away'; 'can't I just watch my diet?' → 'diet genuinely helps, but on its own it usually lowers the uric acid only modestly; the tablet does the heavy lifting'; no flare prophylaxis and the patient stops allopurinol at the first attack; target <0.36 (<0.30 with tophi); allopurinol 50 mg starting, 50 mg every 2–4 weeks, lower in renal impairment (★)

Full detail — FAIL — An unranked shopping list of investigations ('FBE, ESR, CRP, UEC, LFT, TFT, X-ray, uric acid, calcium') — explicitly a fail; two, then two, each with a reason: 'the first is a blood test for the uric acid level — a baseline before long-term treatment; worth knowing: it can be normal during an attack, so a normal result wouldn't change my mind — we'd repeat it once things settle; the second is a sample of fluid from the joint, with ultrasound to guide the needle, sent for polarised light microscopy, which looks for the uric acid crystals and confirms the diagnosis, and a culture, which is how we make certain there is no infection'; then 'kidney function, because uric acid is cleared by the kidneys and it affects which doses I can use; and blood sugar and cholesterol, because those travel with gout and matter for your heart'; 'a needle in my knee? is that really necessary?' → two reasons ('the only way to be certain there's no infection; and it confirms the gout — which matters because I'm going to recommend a tablet you'd take long term, and I'd rather be sure before asking that of you') and offer the steroid injection at the same time (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Endorsing a 'safe' alcohol limit, stopping the thiazide with no replacement, quoting colchicine in grams, or answering the uncle with blanket reassurance — 'I've read two drinks a day is fine, though?' → 'no alcohol is best, and the less you drink the fewer attacks — beer is the worst of them' (four a day is well above what I'd want anyway); 'your blood pressure tablet, hydrochlorothiazide, makes the kidneys hold on to uric acid, so it may be contributing; there are three main groups — ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, and thiazides like yours; I'd like to swap you to one of the other groups; I won't stop it without a replacement, and I'll check your blood pressure after the change' ('can I just stop it then?' → substitute, then recheck); colchicine 1 mg then 500 micrograms at one hour for a flare, 500 micrograms once or twice daily for prophylaxis — milligrams, never grams; the uncle's hands (withheld until you ask concerns — the single richest mark) → 'those lumps are called tophi — deposits of uric acid that build up after years of attacks that weren't controlled; they're not inevitable, and they're exactly what we're going to prevent; controlled gout doesn't damage joints; the two things that get you there are keeping the uric acid at target and staying on the treatment' (★)

Full detail — DO — One open question, then the agenda and the ICE question — not a lecture, not a full history (the examiner will stop you); the diagnosis in two layers then linked ('arthritis simply means inflammation in a joint — red, swollen, painful — that's exactly what I found; gout is the cause: a natural substance in your blood called uric acid; when there's too much it forms tiny crystals that settle inside the joint, and your body reacts with this intense inflammation; too much uric acid, crystals in the knee, a hot swollen painful joint — does that make sense so far?'); three reasons numbered aloud (the pattern — sudden attacks in a single joint that have come and gone before; the appearance — red, warm, swollen, tender; the risk factors — the beer and one of your blood pressure tablets); differentials killer first, then by bucket (pseudogout, rheumatoid, reactive, psoriatic — several joints, symmetrical, long morning stiffness; OA — not this much heat; prepatellar bursitis; cellulitis; the back or hip; a DVT); the flare offered as three options, not prescribed ('an anti-inflammatory with food for a short course; a steroid — prednisolone tablets or an injection into the knee at the same time as the fluid sample; or colchicine, particularly if anti-inflammatories aren't suitable' — 'anti-inflammatories give me terrible heartburn' → switch immediately to the steroid; rest, off-load, ice, elevate); triggers ('cut back red meat and offal, and seafood — not none, but as little as you can manage; avoid sugary soft drinks; plenty of water — dehydration brings attacks on; gradual weight loss — crash diets can trigger an attack'); the four Rs to close — a cardiovascular risk assessment ('gout travels with blood pressure, kidney, sugar and cholesterol problems'), reading material and a food-and-drink fact sheet, review in 1–2 weeks then every few weeks while titrating, red flags (fever or unwell, rapidly worse, a rash on the new tablet); chunk and check twice; no doses unprompted; asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is not treated; eGFR 34 → avoid NSAIDs, reduce colchicine, prefer a steroid, start allopurinol lower and slower

Full detail — DO — Version 2 (request the examination): 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, systemically unwell? BMI and waist; the temperature first, then BP, pulse, RR; the knee — swelling, redness, deformity, visible tophi, skin intact; a local rise in temperature, tenderness; pain on active and passive movement, restricted range; a patellar tap or sweep for an effusion; the hip and ankle, the first MTP joints, tophi at the ear helix, olecranon and Achilles; a brief CVS; glucose and a dipstick' — 'I'd inspect, palpate and move' returns nothing; Version 3 (the crystal report): 'negatively birefringent uric acid crystals' is the fingerprint that confirms gout — not a negative result, not pseudogout (rhomboid, weakly positive); leucocytes are expected in any inflamed joint; the negative culture is what excludes sepsis — go straight to lifelong allopurinol; Version 4 (known gout on prednisolone, now nocturia, BMI 34): three investigation boxes — the gout (urate, aspiration), cardiometabolic risk (HbA1c, lipids, eGFR, ACR, a formal risk assessment), the nocturia ('prednisolone raises glucose, glucose spills into the urine and drives an osmotic diuresis' — glucose, urine MCS, discuss a PSA); Version 5 (five flares in 18 months, stopped allopurinol six months ago because 'the uric acid came back normal so I thought I was fixed') → 'it was normal because the tablet was working — a treatment, not a cure'; BOTH halves: treat this attack AND restart, baseline urate, titrate, six months of colchicine cover — the April 2025 cohort restarted allopurinol and forgot the flare; Version 6 (polyuria a month after a steroid-treated flare): office tests are what you do in the room — capillary glucose (fasting or random), a dipstick naming what you look for (glucose, ketones, protein, blood, nitrites, leucocytes), BP, BMI, waist, temperature → 'your blood sugar is high and it's spilling into the urine; the most likely cause is the prednisolone — a form of diabetes brought on by the medication, which often settles; I don't want to label you diabetic on one test' — plus the other causes (a UTI, diabetes unmasked, kidneys, the prostate, evening fluids, alcohol, caffeine), ketones → blood ketones and a VBG, and don't forget the smoker, the BMI, and the gout itself

setting: Two audiences in one station, and the mark is level, letter, consequence — then hand the decision over. The report must chain the fracture's level to the Weber letter to syndesmotic risk to ankle instability, and the management must present surgery as probable while attributing the decision to orthopaedics. Candidates who commit to a definitive plan of their own fail this station regardless of which plan they pick.
stem: Emergency department. Mark, 30, has attended after trauma to his leg with pain on movement of the ankle. He has been examined: no neurovascular injury, closed fracture.
An ankle x-ray is displayed. Tasks: explain the x-ray to the examiner, with a prompt at three minutes — explain the diagnosis to the patient — explain your management plan.
8 minutes. The structure invites you to walk past the patient to get to the film. Do not.

SILENCE IN AN OSCE FEELS CATASTROPHIC AND CANDIDATES FILL IT BY INVENTING FINDINGS THEY CANNOT DEFEND. DELIVER THE SIX STEPS, SUMMARISE IN ONE SENTENCE, AND STOP — candidates report being told to move on after about a minute. If pushed, offer what you would REQUEST: three views, and CT to assess the syndesmosis if non-operative management were being contemplated

back.dx: A DISPLACED OBLIQUE WEBER C FRACTURE OF THE DISTAL FIBULA, MANAGED AS AN UNSTABLE ANKLE INJURY. TO THE PATIENT, WITH THE BRACKET-AND-HINGE IMAGE DOING THE HEAVY LIFTING: 'THERE ARE TWO BONES IN THE LOWER LEG. THE THICK ONE IS THE TIBIA, YOUR SHIN BONE, AND THAT'S THE ONE THAT CARRIES YOUR WEIGHT. THE THINNER ONE ON THE OUTSIDE IS THE FIBULA, AND THAT'S THE ONE YOU'VE BROKEN. AT THE BOTTOM THEY FORM THE SOCKET OF YOUR ANKLE JOINT — THE ANKLE BONE SITS BETWEEN THEM, A BIT LIKE A HINGE SITTING IN A BRACKET. FOR THAT TO WORK, THE TWO BONES HAVE TO STAY EXACTLY THE RIGHT DISTANCE APART, AND WHAT HOLDS THEM THERE IS A STRONG BAND JUST ABOVE THE ANKLE — THE SYNDESMOSIS.' THEN WHY THE LEVEL MATTERS: 'IF THE FIBULA BREAKS LOW DOWN, BELOW THAT BAND, THE BAND IS USUALLY FINE AND THE ANKLE STAYS STABLE. YOUR BREAK IS ABOVE IT — AND FOR THE BONE TO BREAK UP THERE, THE FORCE HAS USUALLY TRAVELLED THROUGH THE BAND ON ITS WAY. SO THE BAND MAY WELL BE TORN, AND THE TWO BONES CAN DRIFT APART SO THE ANKLE BONE STOPS SITTING PROPERLY IN ITS SOCKET.' ONCE HE UNDERSTANDS THE SOCKET HAS A CORRECT WIDTH, INSTABILITY AND SURGERY BOTH EXPLAIN THEMSELVES. THE MANAGEMENT: IMMEDIATE CARE FIRST — ANALGESIA, A BELOW-KNEE BACKSLAB RATHER THAN A CIRCUMFERENTIAL CAST BECAUSE THE ANKLE WILL SWELL, NON-WEIGHT-BEARING WITH CRUTCHES, ELEVATION AND ICE, AND NIL BY MOUTH PENDING THE ORTHOPAEDIC DECISION. THEN ORTHOPAEDIC REVIEW BEFORE DISPOSITION, STATED AS A REFERRAL TO BE SEEN HERE AND NOT A CLINIC LETTER. THEN BOTH PATHWAYS, CORRECTLY WEIGHTED: PLATE AND SCREWS WITH SOMETIMES AN EXTRA SCREW ACROSS TO HOLD THE TWO BONES AT THE CORRECT WIDTH WHILE THE BAND HEALS, AS THE MORE LIKELY OUTCOME — AND A SMALLER CHANCE OF CAST MANAGEMENT IF THE ANKLE PROVES GENUINELY STABLE AND UNDISPLACED, WHICH MAY NEED EXTRA VIEWS OR CT. AROUND SIX WEEKS IMMOBILISED AND NON-WEIGHT-BEARING, THEN PHYSIOTHERAPY. NO DRIVING. RED FLAGS: TINGLING OR NUMBNESS IN THE TOES, COLOUR CHANGE, PAIN NOT SETTLING DESPITE ANALGESIA, A SLAB THAT FEELS TOO TIGHT — AND AFTER SURGERY, FEVER OR WOUND DISCHARGE. THE VARIANTS. A, WEBER A: transverse, BELOW the joint line and syndesmosis, ligaments usually intact and GENERALLY A STABLE INJURY with a congruent mortise — symptomatic treatment, a boot or backslab, weight-bearing as tolerated in many cases, and routine fracture clinic rather than acute review; THE REASONING YOU SAY ALOUD IS THE SCORED ITEM, NOT THE DISPOSITION VERIFY. B, WEBER B, THE GENUINELY UNCERTAIN ONE THAT EXAMINERS LIKE FOR THAT REASON: at the level of the syndesmosis, typically spiral, and stability turns on TWO QUESTIONS YOU MUST NAME OUT LOUD — IS THERE DISPLACEMENT AND IS THE MORTISE CONGRUENT, CHECKING THE MEDIAL CLEAR SPACE; AND IS THERE A MEDIAL-SIDE INJURY, EITHER A MEDIAL MALLEOLAR FRACTURE OR MEDIAL TENDERNESS SUGGESTING A DELTOID TEAR, BECAUSE A LATERAL MALLEOLAR FRACTURE PLUS A MEDIAL-SIDE INJURY IS A FUNCTIONALLY BIMALLEOLAR UNSTABLE ANKLE EVEN WITH ONE BONE BROKEN. Undisplaced with a congruent mortise and no medial injury is often non-operative; displaced or with medial injury is usually surgical, and weight-bearing or gravity stress views are worth naming as something to ask orthopaedics about VERIFY. C, BIMALLEOLAR OR TRIMALLEOLAR: a second fracture of the medial malleolus makes it BY DEFINITION UNSTABLE and unambiguously surgical, with the lateral view checked for a posterior malleolar fragment — the mark here is simply SEEING the second fracture, which requires having looked. D, TALAR SHIFT OR DISLOCATION: THE ONLY TIME-CRITICAL VERSION — a talus out of the mortise puts skin and neurovascular structures at risk and needs URGENT REDUCTION, usually under procedural sedation, before definitive imaging or referral discussions, with neurovascular status reassessed before and after and a post-reduction film. DO NOT DELIVER A LEISURELY SIX-STEP REPORT WHILE THE FOOT IS DISLOCATED. F, THE DESK WORKER: same five return-to-work beats, different content — no driving in the slab so transport or working from home, swelling if the leg is down all day so elevation at the desk and breaks, and a return within a few weeks realistic BUT CONFIRMED AT REVIEW RATHER THAN PROMISED TODAY.
plan: GREET MARK BEFORE THE EXAMINER, ACKNOWLEDGE THE PAIN AND PRE-COMMIT TO ANALGESIA: 'I'M GOING TO HAVE A GOOD LOOK AT YOUR X-RAY WITH MY COLLEAGUE FOR A MINUTE OR TWO, THEN I'LL COME STRAIGHT BACK AND TAKE YOU THROUGH EVERYTHING. I'LL SORT SOME PAIN RELIEF THE MOMENT I'M BACK.' Twenty-five seconds that convert an awkward two-audience structure into a courtesy the examiner can score — and that protect you if the film takes longer than expected.

The report in six steps — orientation · the fracture named and sited · the classification chain · the pattern · displacement, angulation and the mortise · exclusion of other injuries — then a summary sentence that does the examiner's job for them by converting findings into a management-relevant conclusion (see findings).

Back to the patient and ask the pain score before any anatomy — a confirmed painful fracture with no analgesia offered is the easiest mark in the station to drop, and it is dropped constantly by candidates arriving from the radiology exchange still in radiology mode.

THE DIAGNOSIS — NAME THE BONE AND SHOW HIM ON THE FILM, THEN THE TWO BONES AND THE SOCKET, THEN THE SYNDESMOSIS IN PLAIN ENGLISH, THEN WHY THE LEVEL MATTERS AND THE WORD WEBER C — AND CHECK UNDERSTANDING BEFORE MOVING ON (see dx). When he says it sounds worse than he thought, ACKNOWLEDGE THEN REFRAME: 'it's a significant injury, but it's a very treatable one' — do not minimise.

Immediate care, in order and with reasons — analgesia · a backslab rather than a full cast, with the reason · non-weight-bearing with crutches and how to use them · elevation and ice · and nil by mouth in case he needs theatre today.

Orthopaedic review before he goes anywhere, with the sentence that converts humility into a scoreable statement: 'This is a fracture where the decision needs to be theirs, not mine.' then both pathways with surgery weighted as more likely, and the timeframe.

OUTCOME QUESTION ANSWERED HONESTLY — most people walk normally because the bone heals well WHEN IT IS HELD IN THE RIGHT POSITION, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE OPERATION, but stiffness and swelling take months, WHICH IS WHY PHYSIOTHERAPY MATTERS AS MUCH AS THE SURGERY. Then no driving, and the red flags.

THE RETURN-TO-WORK QUESTION — AND ASK THE OCCUPATION BEFORE ANSWERING IT, BECAUSE 'ABOUT SIX WEEKS' IS A WRONG ANSWER TO A QUESTION THAT IS OCCUPATIONAL, NOT ORTHOPAEDIC. THE FIVE BEATS: NAME THE OBSTACLES — the non-weight-bearing period and ongoing swelling on a long shift · A CERTIFICATE NOW covering the next few weeks · REVIEW, to see how he is actually functioning rather than just how the bone looks · MODIFIED DUTIES as an intermediate step, written to the employer · AND FULL DUTIES once he is functioning normally and the specialists are happy, with physiotherapy running alongside.

When he discloses it happened at work — a deliberate late twist — absorb it rather than unpick an earlier guess: this is a workplace injury going through ReturnToWorkSA, so a work capacity certificate rather than an ordinary medical certificate, with the return-to-work plan built with the employer — which makes modified duties easier to arrange, not harder.

RECAP IN ONE BREATH — pain relief now, backslab, no weight on that leg, orthopaedics seeing him here, most likely a plate and screws, around six weeks, then physiotherapy, no driving, and the red flags — THEN INVITE QUESTIONS.
back.planNote: the examiner prompt comes at three minutes but the film needs about eighty seconds — the spare time belongs to the patient, not to inventing findings
ask: The two sentences that carry the station: 'The fracture is above the joint line and the syndesmosis, so this is a Weber C, with a high risk of syndesmotic injury and therefore an unstable ankle joint.' and 'The most likely plan is surgery — but that decision belongs to the orthopaedic team, and I want them to see you before you go anywhere.'

THE HONEST HEDGE THAT SIDESTEPS BOTH TRAPS ON DISPLACEMENT: 'THERE IS DISPLACEMENT AND I THINK A DEGREE OF ANGULATION — I'D WANT THE OTHER VIEWS TO QUANTIFY IT.' Defensible whatever the true answer, unlike asserting 'no displacement' or refusing to state any finding.

The lay translations: 'A strong band holding the two leg bones exactly the right distance apart, just above the ankle.' · 'The two bones can drift apart, so the ankle bone stops sitting properly in its socket.' · 'A plaster splint along the back of your leg rather than a full cast — it leaves room for the swelling.' · 'An extra screw going across from one bone to the other, holding them at the right width while the band heals.'
The question asked before the work answer: 'What's your job, and what does it involve physically?'

Challenges: 'Is it broken, or just sprained?' · 'Can't you just plaster it and let me go home? I've got a shift tomorrow' · 'Just tell me straight — do I need surgery or not?' · 'Will I be able to walk on it normally afterwards?' · 'How am I supposed to get to appointments?' · 'Will I get paid?' · and from the examiner: 'Is it displaced?', 'Would you send him home in a backslab?', and 'What would you do if you were the orthopaedic surgeon?'
pefe: This station needs two people to rehearse — one taking the examiner role with the film, one playing mark. The examiner prompts are: 'Please describe this x-ray for me' · 'Anything else?' Once only, if you stop after naming the fracture · 'That's fine, you can move on' if you finish early · then the three challenges · and 'Summarise the case for me' if time allows.

Role-player: mark deloitte, 30, a baggage handler at the airport — lifting, bending, on his feet the whole shift — living with his partner in a regional South Australian town. Two hours ago he slipped on a wet loading ramp at work and twisted his right ankle going down, heard a crack, could not weight-bear, and a workmate drove him in. Pain seven or eight out of ten, worse on any movement. Fit and well, no medications, no allergies, non-smoker. Toes normal colour and sensation, no wound, no other injuries. He drives a manual and had assumed he would drive himself to appointments. He is worried mainly about work and money.

How he plays it: his opening line is 'G'day doc. I did my ankle at work — they said you'd have the X-ray' and nothing more. He does not volunteer his occupation, and gives that it happened at work only near the end, after the return-to-work discussion has started — which is why candidates who asked the job early absorb it smoothly and candidates who guessed 'Six weeks' now have two errors to unpick. If no analgesia is offered by four minutes he says once: 'Sorry doc — is there anything I can have for this?' He applies two pressure tests — asking to be plastered and sent home for tomorrow's shift, and demanding to be told straight whether he needs surgery — and he does not develop numbness, colour change or a wound, because the stem states the fracture is closed and neurovascularly intact.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE: GREETS AND ORIENTS THE PATIENT BEFORE TURNING TO THE EXAMINER · orients to the film and names three views · identifies the distal fibular fracture · STATES IT LIES ABOVE THE JOINT LINE AND SYNDESMOSIS · CLASSIFIES IT AS WEBER C · STATES THE CONSEQUENCE — SYNDESMOTIC RISK AND INSTABILITY · describes the pattern · comments on displacement and angulation WITHOUT FALSE CONFIDENCE IN EITHER DIRECTION · NAMES THE MORTISE ASSESSMENT · EXPLICITLY EXCLUDES OTHER FRACTURES AND DISLOCATION · MENTIONS MAISONNEUVE · summarises with a management-relevant conclusion · ASKS ABOUT PAIN AND OFFERS ANALGESIA BEFORE EXPLAINING · names the fibula using the film · explains the two bones and the socket · EXPLAINS THE SYNDESMOSIS IN LAY TERMS · explains why the level matters · checks understanding · BACKSLAB NOT A CIRCUMFERENTIAL CAST, WITH A REASON · non-weight-bearing with crutches, elevation and ice · NIL BY MOUTH · REFERS TO ORTHOPAEDICS FOR REVIEW BEFORE DISPOSITION · presents surgery as more likely AND non-operative as a smaller possibility · ATTRIBUTES THE DECISION TO ORTHOPAEDICS · gives the six-week timeframe · fracture clinic and physiotherapy · ADVISES NOT DRIVING · gives the red flags · ASKS THE OCCUPATION BEFORE ANSWERING THE WORK QUESTION · does not give a fixed number of weeks · names the obstacles · certificate now and review · MODIFIED DUTIES BEFORE FULL DUTIES · AND RECOGNISES THE WORKPLACE INJURY AND THE WORK CAPACITY CERTIFICATE.

Orientation, which is free marks — 'THIS IS A PLAIN RADIOGRAPH OF THE ANKLE. IDEALLY I'D BE REVIEWING THREE VIEWS — AP, LATERAL AND MORTISE — AND I'D CONFIRM THE PATIENT'S IDENTITY AND THE DATE OF THE FILM FIRST.' Diving straight to the fracture leaves these on the table and invites the examiner to ask what else you would want

The chain — the highest-value sentence available — 'There is a fracture of the distal fibula. It lies above the level of the ankle joint line and the syndesmosis, which makes this a Weber type C — and that matters because a fracture at this level carries a high risk of syndesmotic injury and therefore a high risk that the ankle joint is unstable.' The letter on its own is worth nothing; the consequence is the mark

Pattern, displacement and the mortise — The pattern looks oblique — four seconds, and it is omitted entirely by most · displacement of the distal fragment with some angulation, 'Perhaps ten to fifteen degrees, though I'd want the other views to quantify it' · and the mortise assessment named: medial clear space, which should be under 4 mm, for talar shift, and tibiofibular clear space and overlap for syndesmotic widening

Exclusions, and the twelve-second sentence — No other fracture — tibia, medial malleolus, posterior malleolus and talus all intact — and no dislocation · then: 'I'd palpate the fibula up to the knee to exclude a maisonneuve injury', which is the injury this presentation most commonly hides
fails: ★ Discharging the patient without orthopaedic discussion, or stating he can go home in plaster as a settled plan, or permitting weight-bearing on an unstable ankle fracture
★ Reporting the film without identifying that the fracture is above the syndesmosis, and therefore treating it as a stable injury
★ Committing to a definitive management decision of your own — 'you'll definitely need surgery' or 'we'll just cast it and send you home' — when the decision belongs to orthopaedics
Applying a circumferential cast to an acutely swelling ankle and sending him away, or offering no analgesia at any point in the station

Saying 'Weber C' without saying what it implies; inventing findings to fill three minutes; answering the return-to-work question with a number instead of asking the occupation; or omitting the red flags for tingling, colour change, worsening pain and a tight slab
numbers: Weber a is below the syndesmosis and generally stable · Weber B is at the level and stability turns on displacement, mortise congruence and a medial-side injury · Weber C is above it and carries a high risk of syndesmotic injury and instability · medial clear space should be under 4 mm · tibiofibular clear space and overlap are the other two mortise measures VERIFY

Around 6 weeks immobilised and non-weight-bearing, then physiotherapy · three views — AP, lateral and mortise — and CT to assess the syndesmosis if non-operative management is contemplated · palpate the fibula to the knee for a maisonneuve injury · a lateral malleolar fracture plus a medial-side injury is functionally bimalleolar · ReturnToWorkSA work capacity certificate for a workplace injury · PATS for country travel to fracture clinic · VERIFY all

Full detail — FAIL — Reporting the film without identifying that the fracture is above the syndesmosis, and therefore treating it as a stable injury — the classification chain said as one sentence: 'the fracture lies above the level of the ankle joint line and the syndesmosis, which makes this a Weber type C; that's the important finding, because a fracture at this level carries a high risk of injury to the syndesmosis, and therefore a high risk that the ankle joint is unstable'; the letter is worth nothing on its own — the consequence is the mark; Weber A (below the syndesmosis — ligaments usually intact, generally stable, boot or backslab, often weight-bear as tolerated); Weber B (at the level — genuinely uncertain: is there displacement and is the mortise congruent? is there a medial-side injury — a medial malleolar fracture or deltoid tenderness? a lateral malleolar fracture plus a medial-side injury is a functionally bimalleolar unstable ankle); bimalleolar or trimalleolar = unambiguously surgical (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Discharging without orthopaedic discussion, stating he can go home in plaster as a settled plan, permitting weight-bearing, or applying a circumferential cast to an acutely swelling ankle — 'can't you just plaster it and let me go home? I've got a shift tomorrow' → 'I can't do that with this particular break; because it's above that band the ankle may not be stable, and if we plaster an unstable ankle and send you home it can shift out of position; I need the bone surgeons to look at it before you go anywhere'; 'I'll book you into fracture clinic' is discharging an unstable ankle without a specialist opinion; a below-knee backslab 'rather than a full cast, because the ankle will swell over the next day or two and a slab gives it room'; non-weight-bearing with crutches, elevation, ice, nil by mouth in case of theatre today (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Committing to a definitive plan of your own — 'you'll definitely need surgery' or 'we'll just put you in a cast' both fail regardless of which is picked; both pathways, correctly weighted, with the decision handed over: 'I want to be straight with you about what they're likely to say: because of the level of this break and the risk to that band, we treat it as unstable, so the most likely plan is an operation — a metal plate and screws on the outside of the bone, and sometimes an extra screw going across to hold the two bones apart at the correct width while the band heals; there's a smaller chance that if they're satisfied the ankle is genuinely stable and the bones are in a good position they'd manage it in a cast; they may want extra X-rays or a CT'; 'just tell me straight — do I need surgery or not?' → 'the honest answer is that it's most likely, and I'd plan on it — but I'd be misleading you if I said it was certain, because that call belongs to the orthopaedic team'; 'what would you do if you were the surgeon?' is a standard challenge — rehearse it (★)

Full detail — FAIL — No analgesia at any point — the easiest mark in the station, dropped constantly by candidates arriving from the radiology exchange in radiology mode; greet the patient BEFORE the examiner ('I'm going to have a good look at your X-ray with my colleague for a minute or two first, then come straight back' — 'it's pretty sore, though' → 'I'll sort some pain relief the moment I'm back'); then 'first things first — how's the pain out of ten?' → seven or eight → strong analgesia now; if none by four minutes he asks once; and answering the return-to-work question with a number — 'about six weeks' is a wrong answer to a question that is occupational, not orthopaedic: 'what's your job, and what does it involve physically?' → a baggage handler, lifting, on his feet all shift (never volunteered) → the five beats — the obstacles (non-weight-bearing for weeks; the ankle swells for months on a long shift), a certificate now, review, modified duties ('something seated for a few weeks instead of the lifting'), full duties once functioning normally and the specialists are happy, physio alongside; 'it happened at work — I slipped on the ramp' (volunteered late) → ReturnToWorkSA, a Work Capacity Certificate not an ordinary sick certificate, the plan built with the employer; a desk worker → the same five beats, different content (can't drive, elevate at the desk, a return within weeks realistic but confirmed at review) (★)

Full detail — DO — The six-step report in about seventy seconds then stop — silence invites invented findings: orientation ('a plain radiograph of the ankle; ideally three views — AP, lateral and mortise — and I'd confirm the patient and date'), the fracture sited, the classification chain, the pattern (oblique), displacement and angulation described honestly then hedged ('displacement of the distal fragment and a degree of angulation — perhaps ten to fifteen degrees, though I'd want the other views to quantify it' — neither false confidence in 'undisplaced' nor refusing to commit), the mortise named ('the medial clear space, which should be under four millimetres, for talar shift; the tibiofibular clear space and overlap for syndesmotic widening'), other injuries excluded (tibia, medial malleolus, posterior malleolus, talus, dislocation), a summary sentence that does the examiner's job ('a displaced oblique Weber C fracture of the distal fibula, which I'd manage as an unstable ankle injury'), and the Maisonneuve line ('I'd palpate the fibula to the knee to exclude a Maisonneuve injury' — twelve seconds, the injury this presentation most commonly hides); talar shift or a dislocation on the film is the only time-critical version — urgent reduction under sedation, neurovascular check before and after, splint, post-reduction film — not a leisurely report

Full detail — SAY — To the patient, using the film: 'there are two bones in the lower part of the leg; this thick one is the tibia — your shin bone, the one that carries your weight; this thinner one on the outside is the fibula, and that's the one you've broken; these two bones sit side by side, and at the bottom they form the socket of your ankle joint — the ankle bone sits in between them, a bit like a hinge sitting in a bracket; for that to work the two bones have to stay exactly the right distance apart, and what holds them there is a strong band of tissue connecting them just above the ankle — the syndesmosis'; 'did I break that band too?' → 'that's exactly the right question, and it's why where the bone broke matters so much; if the fibula breaks low down, below that band, the band is usually fine; but your break is above the band — and for the bone to break up there, the force has usually travelled through the band on its way; so yes, the band may well be torn; we call this a Weber type C; the two bones can drift apart and the ankle bone stops sitting properly in its socket — that's not something we can leave to chance'; 'sounds worse than I thought' → 'a significant injury, but a very treatable one'; check understanding before management; timeframe (around six weeks immobilised and non-weight-bearing, then physiotherapy — 'the stiffness and swelling can hang around for months, which is why the physio matters as much as the surgery'); 'will I walk normally?' → most people do; no driving in the slab (a manual ute, PATS for country travel); red flags (pins and needles or numbness in the toes, colour change, pain worsening despite painkillers, a slab that feels too tight; after surgery, fever or wound discharge); recap and 'what questions do you have?'

setting: The clock and the compression gate. This is a results station wearing a history station's clothes, and the explanation is genuinely harder than usual — two tests, two vascular systems, one anatomical junction — which is exactly why it invites you to spend three minutes on it. Ninety seconds. And the ankle-brachial index must be named as the reason compression is safe, not merely reported as a normal result.
stem: General practice. A 50-year-old presented with pain and itchiness in both legs and was investigated. He has returned for results.
Ankle-brachial index 0.9 left, 1.0 right. Venous duplex ultrasound: incompetence of the sapheno-femoral junction and the perforating veins.
Tasks: explain the investigations and the diagnosis — take a history, five minutes — explain your management plan. 8 minutes total.
tasks: Explain the investigations and the diagnosis
Take a history (five minutes)
Explain your management plan
time: Twenty-five seconds to open with one question that surfaces the fear · the explanation in four beats and ninety seconds, with the fear answered before the physiology · then three pre-loaded history blocks — symptoms and complications, risk factors, function and home — finishing in four minutes rather than five · move to management at 5:30 whatever is unfinished, mid-sentence if you must · five named management blocks each with its reason · then safety-net, written information and review
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: 0.9 left, 1.0 right — 'A test comparing the blood pressure at your ankle with the blood pressure in your arm. That one looks at the arteries, and yours came back essentially in the normal range — so blood is getting down into your feet properly. That matters for treatment, and I'll come back to it.' Flagging it here lets you close the loop inside the compression paragraph without re-explaining

back.dx: CHRONIC VENOUS INSUFFICIENCY — and the condition must be named out loud with each word translated, because explaining the mechanism beautifully and never giving it a name leaves the patient unable to tell anyone what he has: 'Venous means the veins, insufficiency just means they're not quite doing enough of their job. It's very common, it's long-term, so we manage it rather than cure it — but there's a great deal we can do.' Answer the fear before the physiology: 'It is not a clot, and it is not cancer' first, because an anxious patient processes nothing until the fear is addressed. The two goals stated before the plan, because without the reason adherence collapses and so does the communication score: prevent progression, and prevent ulceration. The five management blocks, each with its reason attached. One, compression as the cornerstone — firm stockings tightest at the ankle easing up the leg, which narrows the stretched veins so the flaps can meet again, stops fluid leaking into the tissues and helps push blood back up · on before rising, before the swelling builds, and off at night · measured for fit · and explicitly linked to the arterial result: 'We can only use firm compression safely if the arteries are supplying the leg properly, and yours are — that's why we checked before prescribing.' Two, podiatry with content rather than a bare referral — daily emollient, daily inspection of the lower legs and between the toes, and what infection looks like so he knows when to come back; plus a short course of steroid cream for the venous eczema alongside the moisturiser, and a warning against scented or medicated over-the-counter creams, which this skin reacts to. Three, elevation above the level of his heart — pillows under the ankles, not a footstool, which does not remove the hydrostatic column — and movement breaks and a footrest given ten hours on concrete. Four, supervised exercise with a physiotherapist or exercise physiologist and calf-pump exercises, because the calf muscles are the pump doing the job the valves are not — his legs hurt, so unsupervised generic advice is not a plan. Five, the background factors connected to their mechanisms — weight with a dietitian, because weight around the middle presses on the veins returning from the legs · smoking pushed hardest with Quitline 13 7848, because it slows healing and healing is the whole game · alcohol · and occupational modification. Escalation named: vascular surgery if symptoms progress despite conservative treatment or an ulcer develops, with endovenous ablation through a small puncture rather than open surgery — offered as escalation, never as the primary treatment. The variants. B, a clinical photograph in the stem: describe it aloud, which earns marks and saves history time — brownish staining is iron from leaked blood cells, dry scaly skin is the itch, thickened tight low leg is lipodermatosclerosis, and the skin is still intact, which is what you want to keep; stage it silently as c4a for pigmentation and eczema and c4b for the thickening. C, an active venous ulcer, which changes the plan in four ways: multilayer compression bandaging rather than stockings while the ulcer is open, with stockings later for maintenance VERIFY · community nursing through country health connect, not optional in a man who cannot reach his own feet · early vascular referral now rather than deferred, because treating the superficial reflux early improves ulcer healing VERIFY · and selective swabbing with an HbA1c, swabbing only if there are clinical signs of infection, because every chronic ulcer is colonised and treating the swab drives resistance. D, history first with results at the end, where you must generate the diagnosis rather than explain it: say the differential groups aloud — venous, arterial, lymphatic, systemic oedema, dermatological, neurological and systemic causes of itch — then request findings explicitly including pulses and capillary refill, the distribution of oedema and whether it pits, toe and dorsum involvement, gaiter skin changes, ulceration, stemmer sign, temperature and asymmetry, sensation with monofilament and vibration, abdominal and cardiac examination if bilateral, and BMI — then investigations with reasons attached. E, the recombination rules, because this cluster is recombined every sitting: always establish arterial status before committing to compression, whatever the venous findings say · bilateral, gradual, itchy and gaiter-distributed is venous, while unilateral, acute, hot and tender is infective or thrombotic, and if both pictures are present treat the acute one first and say so · and anyone with chronic leg disease gets an HbA1c and a sensation check, because neuropathy is the layer that turns a manageable leg into an ulcerated one and it is the layer candidates forget.
plan: INTRODUCE, CONFIRM IDENTITY, ORIENT HIM TO THE PURPOSE — THEN ONE OPEN QUESTION BEFORE ANY EXPLANATION: 'BEFORE I TAKE YOU THROUGH THEM — WHAT'S BEEN GOING THROUGH YOUR MIND ABOUT IT?' Twenty-five seconds that hand you his fear and his family history for free, both of which you would otherwise have to ask for in the risk block.

The explanation in four beats and ninety seconds — the fear answered first, then the two-system model, then the arterial test with 'I'll come back to it', then the duplex with the one-way flaps and the pooling — and finally the name, translated (see findings and dx). One check for understanding, then move.

SIGNPOST THE TRANSITION, THEN BLOCK A, SYMPTOMS AND COMPLICATIONS: pain character and duration · THE TWO HIGHEST-YIELD QUESTIONS — WORSE STANDING, AND BETTER ON ELEVATION, BECAUSE THE ARTERIAL PATTERN IS THE EXACT REVERSE AND A 'YES' TO THAT WOULD SEND YOU BACK TO THE LEFT ABI OF 0.9 RATHER THAN TO A STOCKING · swelling and whether it settles overnight · ULCERS, SORES OR ANY BREAK IN THE SKIN SLOW TO HEAL, which is the complication the whole plan exists to prevent and is scored in every version · skin colour, rash and dryness · numbness · AND THE NINE-SECOND SCREEN FOR CELLULITIS AND DVT: 'DOES EITHER LEG EVER SUDDENLY GO HOT, RED, VERY PAINFUL, OR MUCH MORE SWOLLEN THAN THE OTHER?'

BLOCK B, RISK FACTORS — TIER ONE ASKED INDIVIDUALLY AND BY NAME BECAUSE THOSE ARE THE SCORED ONES: PREVIOUS CLOT OR DVT OR BLOOD THINNERS · VARICOSE VEINS · PROLONGED STANDING AT WORK · FAMILY HISTORY OF VARICOSE VEINS OR ULCERS. THEN THE CARDIOVASCULAR SWEEP BUNDLED INTO A SINGLE QUESTION TO SAVE FORTY SECONDS — smoking and how much, alcohol, heart disease, diabetes, blood pressure, cholesterol, weight and diet. Spending ninety seconds on cholesterol and never asking about a previous DVT is the wrong way round here.

BLOCK C, FUNCTION AND HOME — THE BLOCK THAT IS ALWAYS CUT AND WHERE THE GENERAL-PRACTICE MARKS ARE: impact on work, sleep and the things he enjoys · falls or unsteadiness · activities of daily living AND 'CAN YOU COMFORTABLY REACH YOUR OWN FEET, TO PUT A SOCK ON OR HAVE A PROPER LOOK AT THEM?' · and support at home. That one question changes the plan — a donning aid, and the daily skin check becomes his wife's job or the community nurse's, and you must say so.

Move to management now, mid-sentence if you must — state the two goals first, and make the ulcer argument concrete with his own evidence: 'You told me a graze on your ankle took three weeks to heal — that's the early warning. Once the skin properly breaks down it can take months, it can get infected, and it's hard to get back. That's your mother's leg.'

The five blocks in order, each with its reason — compression with the ABI link · podiatry with content · elevation above heart level · supervised exercise with calf pumping · and the background factors connected to their mechanisms (see dx). Tailor it to what he actually said: the donning aid and the wife trained in the skin check.

Escalation criteria and vascular surgery named — then the safety-net, which in a station about preventing ulceration is close to an AUTOMATIC FAIL if omitted: any break in the skin that isn't healing, spreading redness, a hot or much more painful leg, or fever — come back straight away, don't wait. Written information, stocking measurement organised, review in four to six weeks, and questions invited.

ANSWER 'ARE THE STOCKINGS FOREVER?' HONESTLY RATHER THAN COMFORTABLY: 'REALISTICALLY, YES, LONG-TERM — THEY'RE MANAGING THE PROBLEM RATHER THAN FIXING IT. BUT THEY WORK, AND WE'LL FIND A PAIR YOU CAN ACTUALLY LIVE WITH.' That last clause is what keeps the stocking in use at week six when the legs are better but not perfect.
back.planNote: the stem says five minutes of history and four is enough — the minute you save is what buys the management plan, and running out of time here leaves the station with no plan at all
ask: The sentence that is the discriminating item of the station: 'That's why we checked your arteries before prescribing compression — and yours are fine, so it's safe for you.'

THE TWO HIGHEST-YIELD HISTORY QUESTIONS: 'IS IT WORSE WHEN YOU'RE STANDING?' AND 'DOES IT EASE OFF WHEN YOU PUT YOUR FEET UP?' — gravity-dependent pain relieved by elevation is venous, and the arterial pattern is the exact reverse.
The question that changes the plan: 'Can you comfortably reach your own feet?' and the one that must never be skipped: 'Any ulcers, sores, or any break in the skin that's been slow to heal?'

The lay translations: 'Little one-way flaps inside the veins that aren't sealing any more, so blood falls back down.' · 'The brown staining — that's iron from blood cells leaking into the skin over time.' · 'Your calf muscles are the pump that pushes blood back up out of your legs.' · and the elevation phrase that is scored: above the level of your heart.

CHALLENGES: 'IS IT A CLOT, DOCTOR?' · 'IS THAT WHAT MY MOTHER HAD?' · 'AREN'T THOSE STOCKINGS FOR OLD LADIES? I'M FIFTY.' · 'MY NEIGHBOUR HAD A WATER TABLET FOR HER SWOLLEN LEGS — CAN'T I JUST HAVE ONE OF THOSE?', answered by explaining that the problem is local pressure in the leg rather than too much fluid in the body · 'HOW MUCH ARE THESE STOCKINGS GOING TO COST ME?', answered honestly rather than pretending they are free · 'MY MATE JUST HAD HIS VEINS DONE, WHY CAN'T I?' · AND 'DO I HAVE TO WEAR THEM FOREVER?'
pefe: There is no examination in the spine version — the two results are the data, and the skill is translating them rather than reporting them. In variant D, where the order is reversed and you must generate the diagnosis, the examination is requested explicitly and the items that separate the groups are pedal pulses and capillary refill, whether the oedema pits and whether it involves the toes and dorsum, the gaiter skin changes, stemmer sign, and sensation with monofilament and vibration.

Role-player: David Whitmore, 50, a loading dock supervisor married to Karen, in a regional South Australian town, back for scan results and anxious at the start. Eight or nine months of heavy aching pain in both lower legs — 'By the end of a shift they feel like they weigh a tonne' — worse standing and much better with the feet up. Swelling that is fine in the morning and builds through the day until his socks leave a ring. Brown discolouration around both ankles, dry flaky skin that itches worst at night so his wife says he scratches in his sleep. No numbness and no sudden unilateral change. Bulging veins behind the left calf for years. Ten-hour shifts on concrete, four days a week. Fifteen cigarettes a day since twenty, four or five beers most nights, overweight, blood pressure 'A bit up' two years ago with nothing done.

What he gives only if asked, and each must be earned: the three-week graze from catching his ankle on a tow bar, given only to a question about ulcers, sores or slow healing · the varicose veins · the family history, where his mother had varicose veins and a leg ulcer and his sister has the veins · the standing at work · and that reaching his feet is a struggle, with his wife cutting his toenails. His fear is given if asked what is worrying him: a workmate had a clot that went to his lung, and his mother's ulcer never healed. He relaxes visibly once told it is not a clot, and he does not develop a hot red leg, because there is no acute complication in this case.

Venous duplex — Incompetence of the sapheno-femoral junction and the perforating veins — 'An ultrasound of the veins. Veins have little one-way flaps inside them; every time your calf muscle squeezes it pushes blood up through them towards the heart, and the flaps stop it falling back. The scan shows that at a major junction up at your groin, and in some small connecting veins in your calves, those flaps aren't sealing any more.' Reading the report aloud is a report, not an explanation

The two-system model, stated before either test — 'THE ARTERIES BRING BLOOD DOWN FROM THE HEART INTO THE LEGS. THE VEINS TAKE IT BACK UP — WHICH IS THE HARDER JOB, BECAUSE IT'S UPHILL, AGAINST GRAVITY. TWO DIFFERENT SYSTEMS, AND WE TESTED BOTH.' Without the model nothing that follows is intelligible and the patient stops listening

The left 0.9 is a second consultation — A borderline left ankle-brachial index alongside an untreated blood pressure and fifteen cigarettes a day is worth naming and booking separately — it is safe for compression, but it is not nothing

Full detail — FAIL — Reading the report aloud instead of explaining it — 'incompetence at the sapheno-femoral junction and the perforators' is a report, not an explanation; four beats in ninety seconds: the fear answered first ('it is not a clot, and it is not cancer' — his mate's PE and his mother's ulcer, surfaced by 'what's been going through your mind about it?'), the two-system model ('the arteries bring blood down; the veins take it back up — the harder job, uphill against gravity; two systems, and we tested both'), the ABI ('compared the blood pressure at your ankle with your arm — that looks at the arteries; essentially normal, so blood is getting down into your feet properly'), the duplex ('an ultrasound of the veins; veins have little one-way flaps like valves; every time your calf squeezes it pushes blood up through those flaps, and they stop it falling back; the scan shows that at a major junction up here at your groin, and in some small connecting veins in your calves, those flaps aren't sealing any more, so blood falls back and pools in your lower legs; that pooling and the pressure it builds up is what's causing the aching and the itch'), then the name ('chronic venous insufficiency — venous means the veins, insufficiency just means they're not quite doing enough of their job; very common, long-term, so we manage it rather than cure it — but there's a great deal we can do'); one check for understanding, then move — three check-backs and a re-explanation burns the station

Full detail — DO — Three history blocks pre-loaded, signposted; symptoms (pain — eight or nine months, both legs, heavy and aching, 'by the end of a shift they weigh a tonne'; the two highest-yield questions — 'worse standing? better with your feet up?' — gravity-dependent pain eased by elevation is venous; the arterial pattern is the reverse and would send you back to the left ABI of 0.9; swelling that builds through the day, 'socks leave a ring by four'; ulcers or slow healing; skin — brown around the ankles, dry, flaky, itches at night; numbness; 'does either leg ever suddenly go hot, red, very painful, or much more swollen than the other?' — screens cellulitis and DVT in nine seconds, ask it in every version); risk factors tier one by name (previous DVT or blood thinners, varicose veins — behind the left calf for years, prolonged standing — a loading dock supervisor, ten hours on concrete, family history — mother's veins and ulcer, sister's veins), then the cardiovascular sweep bundled into one question (fifteen a day since twenty, four or five beers most nights, BP 'a bit up' two years ago untreated, overweight, 'diet's whatever's quick'); function (impact — poor sleep from the itch, stopped walking the dog; falls; 'can you comfortably reach your own feet, to put a sock on or have a proper look at them?' → 'my wife cuts my toenails' — changes the plan: a donning aid, the wife trained in the daily skin check, or community nursing; support at home) — the block candidates always cut, and where the general-practice marks are

Full detail — SAY — The two goals before the plan ('to stop it getting worse — left alone it tends to progress; and, the bigger one for you, to prevent an ulcer'); five named blocks each with its reason: compression ('firm elastic stockings, tightest at the ankle, easing off up the leg; that squeeze narrows the stretched veins so the flaps can meet again, stops fluid leaking, and helps push blood back up' — measured for fit, on first thing before you get out of bed and before the swelling builds, off at night; 'aren't those for old ladies?' → 'the single most effective treatment we have, and there are options that look like sports socks — a stocking in the drawer does nothing'; cost acknowledged honestly), podiatry with content (daily emollient, teach him and his wife to check the lower legs and between the toes daily, what infection looks like), elevation ABOVE the level of the heart ('pillows under the ankles, not just a footstool' — a footstool doesn't remove the hydrostatic column) and movement breaks and a footrest at the dock, supervised exercise (physio or exercise physiologist, calf-pump exercises — 'your calf muscles are the pump that drives blood out of your legs, so working them deliberately does the job your valves aren't doing'; walking the dog as the goal), risk factors with the mechanism (weight — abdominal pressure on the veins returning from the legs, dietitian; smoking — 'slows healing, and healing is the whole game here', Quitline 13 7848, 'I've tried twice' → 'most people who succeed have tried several times first'; alcohol; the untreated BP as a separate consultation); escalation named ('if things get worse despite all that, or an ulcer that isn't healing, a vascular surgeon — procedures to close off the faulty veins, mostly through a small puncture; but we start here'; 'my mate just had his veins done' → compression first, procedure if not enough — not the other way round); safety net (any break in the skin not healing, spreading redness, hot or much more painful, feverish), written information, review at four weeks; Variant C (an active ulcer) → multilayer compression BANDAGING not stockings while open, community nursing (Country Health Connect) for a patient who can't reach his feet, EARLY vascular referral now, HbA1c, swab only with clinical signs of infection; the recombination rules — bilateral, gradual, itchy, gaiter-distributed is venous; unilateral, acute, hot, tender is infective or thrombotic — treat the acute one first and say so; anyone with chronic leg disease gets an HbA1c and a sensation check

back.dx: CASE A IS SEROPOSITIVE RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS — symmetrical small-joint inflammatory polyarthritis with positive rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP and a first-degree family history. Reason to it rather than announcing it: symptoms, then family history, then the two tests, then 'Putting all of that together, I'm afraid this does look like rheumatoid arthritis' — then stop talking. 'That's a lot to take in. How are you feeling about that?' and wait; examiners mark the pause, and her answer — 'Scared. I've seen what it did to mum's hands' — is the doorway to her agenda, so walk through it: 'Tell me what happened to your mum's hands.' then correct the health belief with a fact: treatment has changed enormously since her mother was diagnosed, and that is exactly why you want to move quickly. Cause and course: an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the joint lining — but not only a joint disease, because the same process affects eyes, lungs, heart and blood vessels and nerves · the cause is genes plus environment with smoking the one we know most about, and it is not anything she did or ate · it settles and flares, and it is the repeated flares that damage joints, and that damage does not reverse · no cure, but very treatable, and the goal is remission. Never say 'There's no treatment for this' — inaccurate, cruel and marked down. The management in two HALVEs: symptom control with an NSAID and a steroid bridge, naming the steroid harms — blood pressure, blood sugar, weight, bone thinning · and the half that passes the station: an urgent rheumatology referral for a DMARD, usually methotrexate, which does not mask symptoms but calms the immune system and stops joint damage — and the earlier it starts, the less damage there is. When she asks whether methotrexate is chemotherapy: yes at much higher doses for cancer, but for arthritis it is a low dose once a week working by calming the immune system, with folic acid and regular bloods. Then the pregnancy question, which changes the drug choice and is a serious safety miss if omitted: methotrexate cannot be used in pregnancy or while trying, but that means planning rather than not having children, and hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are considered safe. Then the team — physiotherapy, hand therapy and splints, psychology — lifestyle including smoking, which makes the disease worse and the medicines work less well — and support through arthritis Australia. Her hidden agenda is that she is a professional pianist, and the piano question is never answered yes or no: 'I can't give you a straight answer because it depends on how the condition behaves and how your hands respond. If we get you onto the right treatment with a physiotherapist and a hand therapist, there is a real chance you'll keep playing. I'm not promising, and I'm not writing it off' — plus avoid playing through a flare, and the offer of a letter to her employer about a suitable role rather than losing the career. Case B is a de-escalation station. Let him finish without interrupting, then concede before explaining anything. The three-part cancer answer, spoken in direction of effect and uncertainty rather than invented numbers: one, rheumatoid arthritis itself increases the risk of certain cancers, particularly lymphoma — that is the disease, not the drug · two, methotrexate may add a small amount and I am not going to tell you it doesn't · three, in someone with both we cannot separate them, and because methotrexate controls the inflammation that drives the risk it may actually lower it — 'What we are certain about are the risks of leaving the arthritis uncontrolled.' then side effects sandwiched with folic acid, the monitoring the task actually asks for, the three practical rules, the safety-net, and the decision handed back. Examiner questions: 'What is treat to target?' → setting a defined target of remission or low disease activity and escalating at regular reviews until it is reached, judged on symptoms, swollen joints and inflammatory markers. 'Can you force him to take it?' → no — he has capacity, and the obligation is to inform him fully, offer alternatives and continue caring for him whatever he decides.
plan: OPEN BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN — 'I DO HAVE YOUR RESULTS BACK. BEFORE WE GET TO THEM, CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT HAS HAPPENED SO FAR? AND IS THERE ANYTHING IN PARTICULAR YOU'RE WORRIED ABOUT TODAY?' Opening with 'I've got your results, they're positive' loses rapport and you never find out that her mother's deformed hands are the picture in her head.

Reason it out, then name it — symptoms, family history, the screening test, the specific test, then the diagnosis (see findings). Then pause and acknowledge, and explore what happened to her mother's hands rather than talking past it.

Cause and course — what it is, that it is not only a joint disease, why it happened with blame removed, and flares with irreversible damage — then 'No cure, but very treatable, and the goal is remission' (see dx).
Symptom control — another NSAID with its gastric and renal watch points, and a steroid bridge named as a bridge with its harms.

The half that passes the station, and say all four words: 'I'm going to refer you to a rheumatologist, and I want that soon. They'll start a disease-modifying medicine — a DMARD — and the usual first one is methotrexate. The earlier they're started, the less damage there is, and damage doesn't come back once it's done.' Answer the chemotherapy question honestly and reframe the dose and mechanism.

THE PREGNANCY QUESTION, ASKED BEFORE THE DRUG IS SETTLED: 'BEFORE WE GO FURTHER, THERE'S SOMETHING I NEED TO ASK BECAUSE IT CHANGES WHAT WE CHOOSE. ARE YOU PLANNING A PREGNANCY IN THE FORESEEABLE FUTURE, AND WHAT ARE YOU USING FOR CONTRACEPTION?' — then the safe alternatives, and the promise that the rheumatologist will know from the first appointment.

The team, lifestyle and support — physiotherapy, hand therapy with splints and aids, psychology at 25 · exercise, diet and weight, smoking and alcohol · written material and arthritis Australia. Stopping at the drugs fails a task that says management plan.
The agenda — if she has not raised the piano, ask about work and hands a second time; if she has, answer it properly rather than quickly (see dx). Then summarise, safety-net and book two weeks.

Let him finish the thirty-second burst without interrupting, nod, and do not respond to the threat of legal action — do not defend the rheumatologist, do not mention complaints processes, and never say 'Calm down' or 'That's not true'. Then concede: 'I completely understand why you're angry, and I want to be honest — you are pointing at something real. I'd be worried too. Can I take you through the condition and the medication, and then we'll make a plan together?'

Task one is the management of rheumatoid arthritis, not of methotrexate — two irreversible consequences if it is uncontrolled, joints and organs · then the whole package: NSAIDs and short steroid courses for symptoms, other DMARDs including injected and biological ones if this does not suit him, physiotherapy, hand therapy and splints, psychology, exercise, weight, smoking and support organisations. Spending all eight minutes on methotrexate fails task one.
The three-part cancer answer, verbatim and without numbers you cannot defend (see dx).

SIDE EFFECTS SANDWICHED — nausea, mouth ulcers, tiredness, dry skin and hair thinning; the liver and blood count watched with bloods; rarely lung inflammation — AND THE GOOD NEWS THAT FOLIC ACID REDUCES MUCH OF IT.

The monitoring the task is actually asking for: full blood count, liver function and kidney function — every two to four weeks for the first few months and after any dose change, then every one to three months, with three the longest you would leave it · plus vaccinations up to date and hepatitis B and varicella immunity checked, ideally before starting, because live vaccines cannot be given once he is on it and his response to any vaccine is weaker. Saying 'Full blood count and liver function' and stopping leaves out the kidneys, and methotrexate is renally cleared.

The three rules he must not break — once a week, one dose, the same day each week, with the day written on the box because daily dosing by mistake is dangerous · alcohol low or none, because both it and the drug work on the liver · and tell any doctor or pharmacist he is on it, because trimethoprim can cause a serious drop in blood counts in combination.
Safety-net for same-day review — fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers · unusual bruising or bleeding · yellow eyes or dark urine · a new dry cough or breathlessness.

Hand the decision back: written information, a joint appointment with his rheumatologist so he can put these questions directly, and alternatives if he still wants to stop — 'My job is to make sure whatever you choose is an informed choice. Does that sound fair?' You are not there to win, and pushing for a commitment before he leaves is the error.
