The pause and the doorway: 'That's a lot to take in. How are you feeling about that?' — then wait — then 'Tell me what happened to your mum's hands.'

THE SENTENCE THAT DE-ESCALATES CASE B, SAID BEFORE ANY CONTENT: 'I COMPLETELY UNDERSTAND WHY YOU'RE ANGRY, AND YOU ARE POINTING AT SOMETHING REAL.' The role-player's anger drops audibly at that line and stays up all station if you say 'that's not true'.

The honest framing lines: 'There's no cure, but it is very treatable — the goal is remission.' · 'Possibly a small added risk — and the risks of leaving the arthritis uncontrolled are ones we're far more certain about.' · 'My job is to give you the whole picture so that whatever you choose is an informed choice.'

CHALLENGES: 'LIKE MUM' said quietly after the diagnosis · 'ARE YOU SURE? IT'S JUST ONE BLOOD TEST' · 'ISN'T METHOTREXATE CHEMOTHERAPY?' · 'SHOULD I STOP PLAYING?' at about six minutes · 'WE'VE BEEN TRYING FOR A BABY FOR SIX MONTHS', which changes the drug now and means a pregnancy test before the first dose · 'I'M GOING TO SUE YOU PEOPLE' · 'SO YOU ADMIT IT — THEN WHY WOULD ANYONE TAKE IT?' · AND 'I'VE MADE UP MY MIND, I'M STOPPING IT AND TRYING HERBAL MEDICINE INSTEAD', answered by explaining what stopping means, asking what preparation he plans to take because some affect the liver or interact, and asking him to keep the reviews and bloods going whatever he decides.
pefe: There is no examination in either case — these are explaining stations, and the data are the two antibodies in case A and what Gary discloses in case B. If the examiner asks what else you would order, the baseline set before immunosuppression is in the findings panel.

Brief A — Jane Whitfield, 25, a professional pianist with a symphony orchestra, living with her partner Sam. Non-smoker, occasional wine, no other problems or medications. Four months of pain and swelling in both hands, mainly the knuckles and middle finger joints, with about an hour of morning stiffness that eases once she gets moving, plus some tiredness and sore feet under the toes. No rash, mouth ulcers, dry eyes, chest symptoms, fevers or weight loss. Her mother was diagnosed in her thirties and has badly deformed hands — that is the image in her head. Composed, articulate and a little guarded; she does not cry unless the doctor is blunt or cold, and opens up if they are warm. After the diagnosis she goes quiet and says 'Like mum' — a good candidate pauses. She becomes emotional only if told there is no treatment or if the doctor moves straight to management without acknowledging. She does not volunteer the piano unless asked about work, hobbies, hands or concerns a second time — and otherwise releases it at about six minutes. She does not volunteer pregnancy plans either: 'Not right now, but we do want kids.'

Brief B — Gary Nolan, 45, a self-employed builder, married with three children, diagnosed eight months ago and started on methotrexate three months ago by his rheumatologist. Angry, loud and fast at the start, not abusive but forceful and interrupting, opening with a thirty-second burst about suing. He has decided to stop the drug unless someone treats him like an adult. If the doctor interrupts, defends or says 'Calm down' he escalates — 'Don't tell me to calm down, just answer the question.' if the doctor concedes the point he de-escalates noticeably, sits back and lowers his voice: 'Right. Go on then.' and if the doctor says methotrexate does not cause cancer he stands up, says 'Then you haven't read what I've read', and stays hostile for the rest of the station.

back.dx: Nodal hand osteoarthritis at annual review, with three things that have changed and are the actual content of the station: pain risen from four to seven out of ten over the year · an oral anti-inflammatory that is working less and causing dyspepsia in a 74-year-old · and declining function with minimal social support. To her, in plain words: 'The smooth lining that lets the small joints glide has worn thin, and the bone around it has thickened — those are the firm lumps you can feel at your fingertips. It is common with age and slowly progressive, but there is a lot we can do about the pain and about keeping your hands working.' and the correction she needs: 'Resting them completely actually makes it worse — the muscles waste and the joints stiffen. Keeping them moving, with the right aids and a splint, is a large part of the treatment.' The differentials each get a reason rather than being recited: rheumatoid — the knuckles are spared and the stiffness is ten to fifteen minutes, not over an hour · psoriatic — no rash, no nail pitting or onycholysis · gout — no acute hot red attacks and no tophi · and septic or inflammatory causes — nothing hot or red. The three-part plan. One, the tablets: stop the ibuprofen, because it is causing the heartburn and is not helping much any more, and switch to a topical anti-inflammatory gel with paracetamol, checking kidneys and blood pressure. Two, the hands: hand therapy for a thumb-base splint, exercises and aids — jar openers, tap turners, thicker handles — which make a real difference to jars and buttons. Three, help at home: with her daughters interstate, my aged care for an assessment for shopping and housework, and an occupational therapist to look at the kitchen. When she says 'I don't want to be a bother': 'You are not a bother — these services exist precisely for this. And I would rather sort it out now than after a fall or a month of poor meals.' if she still deflects, start small — just the hand therapist and a couple of gadgets, and look at more later. Safety-net for hot red joints, black bowel motions or stomach pain, and falls, with review in three months after the medication change. Things never to say: 'It's just wear and tear at your age' · 'There's not much we can do for arthritis' · 'Rest your hands as much as possible' · 'Just keep taking the ibuprofen' · and Heberden's at the proximal joints. The variants. One, the hybrid, where task 2 becomes a description of how you would examine — headlines in ninety seconds, and the trap is starting a real examination and narrating each step. Two, she has no complaint at all — 'Even so, a yearly review is a chance to check how the treatment is working, whether it is causing any trouble, and how you are managing at home', then run the same structure, because there is always enough to fill four minutes. Three, the pattern has changed — knuckle swelling with a couple of hours of morning stiffness is a change in pattern rather than simply worse osteoarthritis, and means inflammatory markers, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP and a rheumatology referral. Four, the examiner challenges — 'Why differentials when the stem gives the diagnosis?' → 'Because a label carried for eight years deserves re-checking at review; if the pattern had moved to the knuckles or stiffness had lengthened, I'd be considering a second diagnosis on TOP.' and 'Would you x-ray her hands?' → 'Not routinely — hand osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis and the x-ray would not change my management. I'd image if the presentation were atypical, if I suspected erosive disease, or for surgical planning.'
plan: WIPE, confirm identity, and ask an open question — which gets 'I'm just here for my yearly check' and nothing more.

The second open question, which is where the station is won: 'Tell me how things have been going with your hands since I last saw you.' → 'Since you ask, they've got worse. The tablets aren't doing much any more, and I can't open jars at all now.' then acknowledge the loss rather than stepping over it: 'Having to ask for help with something you have always done yourself is hard.'

THE PAIN IN SIXTY SECONDS, WITH THE COMPARISON THAT MAKES IT AN ANNUAL REVIEW: which joints · OUT OF TEN TODAY, AND WHAT WOULD YOU HAVE SAID A YEAR AGO · constant or not · better or worse with what · night pain · use versus rest · morning versus evening AND HOW MANY MINUTES OF STIFFNESS. Then a quick joint screen — swelling, redness or warmth, crepitus, change in shape, other joints.

THE TREATMENT REVIEW IN FIVE QUESTIONS: when diagnosed · WHAT ARE YOU TAKING AND HOW OFTEN · are you able to take it as prescribed · IS IT HELPING AS MUCH AS IT USED TO · AND SIDE EFFECTS BY NAME — INDIGESTION, HEARTBURN, STOMACH PAIN, BLACK BOWEL MOTIONS, ANKLE SWELLING. When she says heartburn, ACT: screen for melaena, dizziness and tiredness, ask about over-the-counter medicines, and say you will change the drug today. A 74-year-old on daily ibuprofen with dyspepsia is a gastrointestinal bleed waiting to happen.

Function — the scored block, and every limitation comes out only because the tasks are named: 'Who cooks for you?' · can you wash and shower yourself · can you dress yourself, buttons and zips · can you open a jar, turn a tap, turn a key · are you still driving, and can you grip the wheel. Never accept 'I manage'.

Role-player: Nancy Pearce, 74, a retired schoolteacher widowed four years ago and living alone in a country town, with two daughters in queensland who ring on Sundays. Pain up from about four to about seven over the year, worst at the fingertips and both thumb bases, worse by evening after using them, ten to fifteen minutes of morning stiffness, aching at night now and then. Knobbly cracking joints, nothing hot or red, and knees that ache on the stairs. Ibuprofen two or three times most days plus paracetamol and blood pressure tablets, with antacids bought from the chemist for heartburn and no black motions or dizziness.

What she gives only if the tasks are named: she cannot open jars or tins at all · buttons take an age so she buys pull-on clothes · showering is fine · she still drives but turning the key hurts · and she mostly heats frozen meals because chopping is too hard, having eaten tea and toast and a frozen dinner yesterday. Polite, understated and a little proud, she minimises with 'I manage' and 'I don't want to be a bother'. Her hidden agenda is that she had to ask a neighbour to open a jar last week and hated it, and she wants to know whether her hands will stop working altogether — volunteered at about three minutes if nobody has asked about daily activities. She becomes briefly tearful only if asked about her husband or about loneliness, and she resists home help once before accepting.

The fixed order — DISTRIBUTION → NAMED SIGNS → DEFORMITY → WASTING → SKIN AND NAILS. Saying 'this is osteoarthritis' first and then describing loses the observation mark

Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings

time: Open, acknowledge the lost work and ask the concern question early · the site question — front, back or whole elbow · pain and the three pattern questions · the general screen and two trauma questions, not ninety seconds of mechanism · then the five groups said out loud — red flags, joint and bone, soft tissue, nerve, referred · then SADMA · the card at six minutes, read aloud · then the diagnosis with its two causes and grouped differentials
findingsLabel: The card at six minutes — say the two findings that decide the case out loud
findings: Afebrile and systemically well. Left elbow: a discrete, tender, fluctuant swelling over the olecranon, about 5 cm across. Overlying skin warm and pink — no spreading erythema, no lymphangitis, no skin break

back.dx: Non-septic olecranon bursitis, with two causes that must both be named: the direct trauma three weeks ago, and his gout. To him: 'A bursa is a small cushion that sits between the skin and the bony point of your elbow and stops them rubbing. Yours has become inflamed and filled with fluid. Two things explain it: the knock on the door, and your gout — crystal problems inflame these cushions as well as joints. Kneeling and leaning on the elbow all day keeps it going.' Connecting crystal disease to bursitis is the discriminating step. The differentials are grouped and each gets its reason, because the bare word scores nothing: septic bursitis — unlikely, afebrile with no cellulitis and no skin break, but not excluded by the absence of fever alone; olecranon fracture or triceps avulsion — excluded by intact active extension; gouty or inflammatory bursitis, rheumatoid nodules, psoriatic disease — no other joints, no rash, no nail change; septic arthritis of the elbow itself — the joint line is not tender and movement is preserved; soft tissue causes including epicondylitis — wrong site, since his pain is posterior on the point rather than at either epicondyle; upper-limb DVT — the whole arm is not swollen; and referred pain from the neck or chest — no neck symptoms, no paraesthesiae, no chest pain or cough. The plan: no operation · rest from leaning on it, an elbow pad, ice and a short course of an anti-inflammatory · ultrasound to confirm · and aspiration if the swelling is tense or there is any doubt, sending the fluid for four tests — cell count, gram stain, culture and crystals. A work capacity certificate for modified duties, because kneeling and leaning are the problem rather than the work itself, and a ReturnToWorkSA claim since this is work-related. Safety-net: back straight away if the elbow becomes hot and red, if redness spreads up the arm, or if he gets fevers or shakes — and review in a week. Things never to say: 'It's just a bursitis, nothing to worry about' · 'You're a carpenter, so this is tennis elbow' · 'I'll give you some antibiotics to be safe' without aspirating · and 'We'll inject some steroid into it today'. The variants. One, the 2025 swelling version — only the opening block changes: 'Where exactly is the swelling — the whole elbow, the back of it, or one side? Is it one side or both? Any swelling anywhere else in your body?' then the full pain sequence, and add one line to the presentation: 'Because swelling was the complaint, I gave extra weight to upper-limb DVT and asked whether the whole arm was involved.' Two, the septic version — up over two days, hot, shivery, with a graze last week: 'This looks infected rather than simply inflamed. I'd like to draw a sample of the fluid off with a needle and send it to the laboratory, take blood tests and blood cultures, and start antibiotics straight after the sample is taken' — with intravenous antibiotics in hospital if he were more unwell. Three, the examiner challenges: 'Why not just inject it with steroid?' → 'Not at first presentation. Infection has not been excluded, and the skin over the olecranon tolerates steroid poorly — atrophy, chronic pain and a higher rate of secondary infection are described.' 'He's afebrile, so it isn't septic?' → 'Fever is absent in a substantial proportion of septic bursitis, so I do not rely on it — I use speed of onset, warmth, spreading erythema, a skin break, tenderness out of proportion, and host factors such as diabetes or immunosuppression. If any were present I would aspirate.' 'Is trauma a differential?' → 'Trauma is a mechanism rather than a diagnosis, but it obliges me to exclude an olecranon fracture and a triceps avulsion, which I did by testing active extension against gravity.' Four, the locking elbow — true locking points to something mechanical inside the joint, a loose body or osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum, needing an x-ray, orthopaedic assessment and MRI if the film is normal.
plan: WIPE, confirm identity, ask about pain now, and open — then respond to what he tells you rather than diving into questions: he says he is self-employed and losing days on site, so name it: 'Three weeks is a while, and I can hear it is costing you work, which is stressful.' then ask the concern question early, because it is where the surgery fear lives.
THE SITE QUESTION, WHICH THE CASE TURNS ON: 'IS IT THE FRONT OF YOUR ELBOW, THE BACK, OR THE WHOLE ELBOW?' He says 'my left elbow' and waits, and most candidates never ask.

PAIN AND PATTERN — severity, dull ache versus sharp electric, onset and course, radiation, aggravating and relieving, effect on life — AND THE THREE PATTERN QUESTIONS THAT SPLIT MECHANICAL FROM INFLAMMATORY AND ARE SCORED: NIGHT PAIN · REST VERSUS ACTIVITY · MORNING VERSUS EVENING.

THE GENERAL SCREEN AND THE TRAUMA IN TWO QUESTIONS — swelling, redness or rash, stiffness, any knock or injury — THEN 'HOW DID YOU HIT IT?' AND 'CAN YOU STRAIGHTEN THE ELBOW FULLY YOURSELF?' Two questions is the whole yield; ninety seconds on the mechanism is wasted, but active extension is your fracture screen and must not be skipped.

GROUP ONE, RED FLAGS — weight loss, appetite, lumps elsewhere, tiredness, night sweats · FEVERS, CHILLS OR SHAKES · ANY BREAK OR GRAZE IN THE SKIN OVER THE ELBOW · IS THE WHOLE ARM SWOLLEN OR JUST THE ELBOW · recent repeated overhead work, painting or sport · AND CLOTS IN HIM OR THE FAMILY.

GROUP TWO, JOINT AND BONE — what his work involves, sport, other painful joints, family history of arthritis, RASHES ON ELBOWS, KNEES OR SCALP, FLARES WITH RED MEAT OR ALCOHOL, AND 'HAVE YOU EVER BEEN TOLD YOU HAVE GOUT?', plus recent diarrhoea, blood in the stool or urinary burning or discharge. WHEN HE GIVES YOU THE GOUT, EXPLORE IT — how often, when the last attack was, and whether he is on a preventer — because it is half the explanation.

GROUPS THREE TO FIVE, TEN SECONDS EACH — SOFT TISSUE: does the elbow lock or catch · NERVE: neck pain, numbness, paraesthesiae or weakness in the arm · REFERRED: any chest pain or cough. Dropping these because 'it's only an elbow' loses the mark that shows you thought beyond the joint.

SADMA AND CLOSURE — smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, medications including over the counter, allergies, and other conditions INCLUDING DIABETES, RENAL DISEASE AND ANYTHING AFFECTING THE IMMUNE SYSTEM, because those are the host factors that change the septic-bursitis threshold.

ASK FOR THE CARD AS A STRUCTURE — inspecting for swelling, redness and skin breaks, palpating for SITE, TEMPERATURE AND FLUCTUANCE, testing active and passive movement, checking the joint above and below, and a neurovascular assessment — THEN READ THE TWO DECIDING FINDINGS OUT LOUD (see findings).
Explain it to him in plain words with both causes, then give the differentials to the examiner in groups, leading with red flags and finishing with referred causes, each with its reason (see dx).

THE PLAN, THE CERTIFICATE AND THE SAFETY-NET, THEN A SUMMARY TO THE EXAMINER — a 30-year-old carpenter with three weeks of localised posterior elbow swelling after direct trauma on a background of gout, with a fluctuant olecranon swelling and preserved joint movement, most likely non-septic olecranon bursitis, with infection, fracture, inflammatory arthritis, upper-limb thrombosis and referred pain excluded.
back.planNote: six minutes for a lump on an elbow — the five groups exist to fill it, and running out of questions before four minutes is itself an automatic fail
ask: The question the case turns on: 'Is it the front of your elbow, the back, or the whole elbow?'
The two that cost ten seconds and are routinely dropped: 'Is the whole arm swollen, or just the elbow?' and 'Any chest pain or cough?'
The fracture screen and the infection screen: 'Can you straighten the elbow all the way yourself?' and 'Any fevers, chills or shakes with this?', plus 'Any break or graze in the skin over it?'
The explanation: 'A bursa is a small cushion between the skin and the bone that stops them rubbing.' and 'Two things explain it: the knock, and your gout.'

CHALLENGES: 'MY MATE SAID IT MIGHT NEED AN OPERATION' · 'AM I GOING TO NEED SURGERY? I CAN'T AFFORD TO BE OFF', volunteered at about four minutes if you never ask what worries him · 'SO IT'S NOT INFECTED?' · 'HOW LONG AM I OFF WORK?' · and the golf, which is misdirection towards epicondylitis and should be noted rather than chased.
pefe: The card and a photograph come at six minutes. The station is not testing whether you recognise a bursa — it is testing whether six minutes of history was spent on five named groups, and whether you interpret the card rather than recite it.

Role-player: James Whitfield, 30, a self-employed carpenter, married with two young children, in a country town. He bangs and leans on his elbows all day laying floors. Three weeks ago he clipped his left elbow on a doorframe carrying a door, and a lump came up over the following days and has slowly got bigger and sorer — six out of ten, eight if he knocks it, a dull ache that does not spread, worse leaning or kneeling, not waking him, no difference morning to night. He can straighten it, sore at the end. He gets gout in his right big toe once or twice a year, last attack four months ago, taking ibuprofen when it flares and never on a preventer. Non-smoker, about six beers on a weekend, no allergies, no diabetes or immune problems. Father has 'Arthritis' of unknown type.

How he plays it: practical, slightly impatient, not distressed — worried about money rather than cancer, and he mentions the lost work in his opening line. If asked a vague question he gives a vague answer: 'My left elbow', and waits to be asked which part. He reveals the gout only if asked about other joints, arthritis, family history, or red meat and alcohol triggers. His hidden agenda — whether he needs an operation and when he can get back on the tools — is volunteered at about four minutes if never asked for. He mentions golf, which is misdirection.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE: introduction and identity · ASKED ABOUT PAIN BEFORE STARTING · open question first · ACKNOWLEDGED THE IMPACT ON WORK · ASKED WHAT HE WAS WORRIED ABOUT BEFORE HE VOLUNTEERED IT · ASKED FRONT, BACK OR WHOLE ELBOW · full pain characterisation · NIGHT PAIN · REST VERSUS ACTIVITY · MORNING VERSUS EVENING · swelling, redness, stiffness · ASKED ABOUT TRAUMA · TESTED THAT HE CAN STRAIGHTEN IT · ASKED ABOUT FEVER · cancer screen · ASKED WHETHER THE WHOLE ARM WAS SWOLLEN · DVT questions · occupation explored · other joints · ELICITED THE GOUT AND EXPLORED IT · family history of arthritis · rash and nail questions · reactive arthritis questions · asked about locking · neck, numbness and weakness · CHEST PAIN AND COUGH · SADMA · DID NOT CHASE THE GOLF · named the diagnosis in plain words · explained a bursa without jargon · LINKED BOTH THE TRAUMA AND THE GOUT TO THE CAUSE · GROUPED DIFFERENTIALS OUT LOUD · SAFETY-NET FOR INFECTION · OFFERED A WORK CERTIFICATE · and asked if he had questions.

The movement — the other half of the answer — Flexion and extension restricted at the end of range by pain only, and the joint line itself is not tender. Neurovascular examination intact, right elbow normal, no other swollen joints

The sentence that interprets it — 'The two findings that matter to me are that the swelling is fluctuant and sits on the olecranon, and that the joint still moves — which places the problem outside the joint, in the bursa.' Reading the card in silence loses the interpretation mark

The fracture screen you do in the history — 'Can you straighten the elbow all the way yourself?' — active extension against gravity is what excludes an olecranon fracture and a triceps avulsion, and it takes one question
fails: ★ Never asking about fever, or never asking about trauma
★ Proposing antibiotics or a steroid injection without aspiration — the skin over the olecranon tolerates steroid poorly and infection has not been excluded
★ Running out of questions before four minutes, which is what happens when the five groups are not used
Accepting 'my left elbow' without asking which part, or being pulled towards epicondylitis by the golf and the carpentry

Listing differentials with no reason attached; reading the card in silence instead of naming the fluctuance and the preserved movement; or missing the gout because other joints, family history and food triggers were never asked about

setting: This station's failure mode is finishing early, not running out — you will have spare time, and it belongs to the differential sweep. Explain in four layers, take the history you would have taken if the scan had never existed, say the other diagnoses out loud, and offer a process rather than a verdict. Never say 'Three of your four muscles are torn' — name each tendon separately and finish on the normal one.
stem: General practice in regional South Australia, 8 minutes. Jack Brennan, 62, an office manager, has come to discuss the ultrasound of his right shoulder. His physiotherapist referred him after two months of physiotherapy failed to settle the pain. The report is available to you.
Tasks: explain the ultrasound findings to the patient — take a further focused history. You are not required to examine the patient.
The shape of the eight minutes: 0:00 open · 0:30 to 3:15 explain · 3:15 to 6:00 history · 6:00 to 7:15 the sweep · 7:15 to 8:00 impact, plan and close.
tasks: Explain the ultrasound findings to the patient
Take a further focused history from the patient
time: Open before you explain, ask what he understands and ask permission · then the four explanation layers — the joint, the four muscles, what partial and full mean, then the result one tendon at a time · frame it, check it, transition · then pain, shoulder function with the word overhead, work and sport and hand dominance, trauma and what has already been tried · then signpost and run the five-group sweep · then impact, mood and support, the agenda, the plan, the safety-net and a summary
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Subscapularis: full-thickness tear · supraspinatus: partial-thickness tear · infraspinatus: partial-thickness tear · teres minor: normal · no subacromial-subdeltoid bursitis, no calcific tendinopathy, no significant effusion, long head of biceps intact and located, no acromioclavicular abnormality

back.dx: A CHRONIC DEGENERATIVE ROTATOR CUFF TEAR — full-thickness subscapularis with partial supraspinatus and infraspinatus tearing. The explanation runs in four layers and every sentence builds towards why torn tendons matter: the joint — 'A ball and socket, but the socket is very shallow, a bit like a golf ball on a tee, which gives you a huge range of movement but means the joint relies on the muscles around it to hold it in place' · the four muscles, named once and lightly, which move the shoulder and hold the ball centred, together called the rotator cuff · what partial and full mean · then the result (see findings). The five-group sweep is the pass point and must be signposted and spoken, because running it silently in your head scores nothing: neck — pain or stiffness, paraesthesiae, weakness or dropping things · girdle — the other shoulder, hips and thighs, morning stiffness duration, fatigue and weight loss, then without pausing the giant cell arteritis screen: new headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing, visual change — compulsory over 50 with girdle symptoms · joint — grinding, catching or locking, other joints, family history · chest — 'A routine one I ask about any shoulder or arm pain — any chest pain or tightness, any breathlessness, especially on exertion?' · lung and systemic — smoking, cough, haemoptysis, hoarseness, fevers, night sweats, previous cancer. A run of negatives is the point; you are marked for asking. The surgery question is never answered yes or no: 'Most tears like yours are managed without surgery to begin with, and many people get their function back that way. Whether an operation would help you depends on how limiting this is and how you go with a proper rehabilitation programme. If we get there, it will be a decision you make with the specialist — not something that happens to you.' The plan: analgesia better than paracetamol, but check renal function before regular anti-inflammatories because of the blood pressure, the borderline diabetes and the Nurofen he is already taking — commenting on that combination is a free mark · a plain x-ray to look at the bone, which ultrasound cannot see · and a structured physiotherapy programme with a written goal rather than a sheet of exercises, asking first what the physio actually had him doing and whether he kept it up, because adherence is the answer here. Review at four to six weeks, with orthopaedic referral if he fails it. Safety-net: sudden much worse pain, inability to lift the arm at all, fever with a hot swollen shoulder, numbness or weakness in the hand — and 'If you ever get chest pain or breathlessness, that's not the shoulder, that's an emergency.' if the examiner asks why not MRI: 'The ultrasound has already answered the diagnostic question — I would reserve MRI for surgical planning or genuine diagnostic doubt.' The variants. One, the traumatic tear at work — 'It went three weeks ago lifting a pallet and I couldn't lift my arm afterwards' → that changes things in a good way: a sudden tear in someone who uses the arm all day is referred early rather than after three months, with an x-ray today, a work capacity certificate, a ReturnToWorkSA claim and a letter about modified duties with no overhead lifting. Two, the girdle patient — both shoulders, both hips, stiff until eleven in the morning → polymyalgia rheumatica, treated completely differently, with inflammatory markers today and the head and eye symptoms flagged as a same-day problem rather than wait-and-see. Three, the angry expectation-loaded patient — 'So that's it, I'm stuffed, when do I get the operation?' → validate, ask what makes him feel it is finished, then give a straight answer rather than a comfortable one: the tendons do not knit back together on their own, but the pain and what he can do are not the same thing as the picture on the scan, surgery needs months of rehabilitation itself and is not guaranteed, and a proper trial with a review date is the offer. Matching his frustration with defensiveness, or capitulating and promising a referral you cannot justify, both fail.
plan: WIPE, ASK WHICH NAME HE PREFERS, AND PUT THE REPORT FACE DOWN — THEN OPEN BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN: 'I DO HAVE THE RESULTS OF YOUR SHOULDER SCAN WITH ME. BUT BEFORE WE GET TO THOSE, CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT HAS HAPPENED SO FAR?' Walking in and talking costs you rapport, his agenda and any idea of what he already understands.

Acknowledge the two months of work, ask the concern question, ask what he was told the scan was looking for, and ask permission: 'Would it be alright if I take you through it step by step, so it makes sense?' You have the time — this station fails by finishing early.
The four explanation layers — the joint, the four muscles, the definitions, then the result one tendon at a time ending on the normal one (see findings and dx).

Frame it as age-related wear, check understanding, and ask permission to take a history. When he asks about surgery at three minutes, defer it explicitly and promise to answer: 'That's exactly the right question, and I'll answer it properly — but let me ask you a few things first so my answer is worth something.'

THE PAIN IN FULL — site pointed to with one finger, radiation, character, severity, constant or intermittent, course, aggravating and relieving — AND NIGHT PAIN AND WHETHER HE CAN LIE ON IT. Then 'HOW IS IT AFFECTING YOUR LIFE?' as its own question rather than tacked on.

THE SHOULDER ITSELF — stiffness · anything he simply cannot do · AND THE DISCRIMINATING FUNCTIONAL QUESTION, SAID WITH THE WORD OVERHEAD: 'WHAT ABOUT REACHING ABOVE YOUR HEAD — A HIGH SHELF, HANGING WASHING, AN OVERHEAD CUPBOARD?' · reaching behind his back for a pocket or seatbelt · weakness · giving way or feeling like it might pop out · clicking, catching or locking.

WORK, SPORT AND HAND DOMINANCE — and ask specifically about reaching above shoulder height, because 'office job' does not mean no overhead load. THEN TRAUMA AND WHAT HAS ALREADY BEEN TRIED: previous injury, dislocation or accident at work; previous scans, injections or surgery; AND WHAT THE PHYSIO ACTUALLY HAD HIM DOING AND WHETHER ANY OF IT HELPED EVEN A LITTLE.

Signpost the sweep and run it out loud: 'The scan explains a lot of what you've told me. Even so, shoulder pain occasionally comes from somewhere other than the shoulder, and I don't want to miss anything — can I ask a few quick questions that may sound unrelated?' then neck, girdle with the giant cell arteritis screen, joint, chest, and lung and systemic (see dx).

IMPACT, MOOD AND SUPPORT — how he is coping, mood, sleep beyond the shoulder waking him, who is at home, anything difficult with work, money or relationships — AND THE CONCERN QUESTION A SECOND TIME, WHICH IS WHERE THE BROTHER'S FAILED SHOULDER SURGERY COMES OUT. Then a rapid SADMA, noticing the Nurofen alongside the blood pressure tablet and the borderline diabetes.

SUMMARISE WITH THE NEGATIVES YOU ELICITED, GIVE THE PLAN, ANSWER THE AGENDA WITH A PROCESS RATHER THAN A VERDICT, AND SAFETY-NET (see dx). The summary is where a scrappy consultation is rescued, because it demonstrates the sweep.
back.planNote: eight minutes with only two tasks — you will have spare time, and it belongs to the sweep, not to silence
ask: The opening that protects everything else: 'I do have your results — but before we get to those, can you tell me what has happened so far?'
The definitions before the findings, and the last thing he hears about the scan being something intact: 'And the fourth one is completely normal.'
The discriminating functional question, with the word examiners listen for: 'What about reaching above your head — a high shelf, hanging washing?'

The sweep signpost and the two questions inside it that are AUTOMATIC FAILS if missed: 'Any chest pain or tightness, or breathlessness especially on exertion?' and, over 50 with girdle symptoms, 'Any new headaches, tenderness on the scalp, pain in the jaw when you chew, or any change in your vision?'

CHALLENGES: 'THAT SOUNDS LIKE A LOT OF DAMAGE', said quietly with a pause — name the emotion · 'SO DO I NEED AN OPERATION?' at about three minutes and again at seven · 'I'VE JUST DONE TWO MONTHS OF PHYSIO' if you re-refer without asking what it involved · AND 'MY BROTHER HAD A SHOULDER DONE AND HE WAS OFF WORK FOR MONTHS AND HE STILL CAN'T THROW A BALL', which is the hidden agenda and comes out only if you ask about concerns a second time or about mood and coping.
pefe: You are not required to examine him — the report is the data, and the history is the one you would have taken if the scan had never existed. The temptation is to let the scan do the work and finish at six minutes; the sweep is what the spare time is for.

Role-player: Jack Brennan, 62, an office manager at a farm-machinery dealership, married to Denise, right-handed and living in a country town, who plays lawn bowls on Saturdays or did until this. Pragmatic, dry, not dramatic — not angry, just tired and a bit deflated, giving short answers unless asked properly. Six months of aching over the outer right shoulder radiating to about the elbow and never into the hand, six at worst and three now, worse reaching overhead, with nights the worst — he cannot lie on that side and wakes two or three times. Ten minutes of morning stiffness. Cannot get anything off the TOP shelf, twists to do the seatbelt, feels weak lifting, no giving way and no locking. No injury ever. Mostly desk work but he stacks files on high shelves.

What he gives only if asked: ex-smoker from 18 to 40, giving up about twenty-two years ago · four or five beers a week · a blood pressure tablet, Panadol most days and Nurofen when it's bad · high blood pressure and 'Borderline diabetic' last year · father with bad hand arthritis · and that the physiotherapy was a sheet of band exercises he tailed off after about six weeks because it wasn't helping — admitted only if asked directly whether he kept them up. He offers no negatives: he says 'No' only when asked, and the whole point of the station is whether you ask. His hidden agenda is his brother's failed shoulder reconstruction and a fear of losing his job, released on the second concern question or at about seven minutes. After the findings he says 'That sounds like a lot of damage' and goes quiet for two seconds — a good candidate names the emotion — and he becomes emotional only if told bluntly that three of his four muscles are torn.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE, OUT OF 20: hand hygiene, introduction, name check · OPEN QUESTION BEFORE THE RESULTS · concerns asked early · checked what he already understood · explained the ball-and-socket joint · named the four muscles as the rotator cuff · DEFINED PARTIAL VERSUS FULL-THICKNESS BEFORE THE FINDINGS · GAVE THE FINDINGS ONE TENDON AT A TIME, ENDING ON THE NORMAL ONE · REFRAMED AS COMMON AGE-RELATED WEAR WITHOUT CATASTROPHISING · checked understanding at least once · asked permission before the history · full pain characterisation INCLUDING NIGHT PAIN · ASKED ABOUT OVERHEAD ACTIVITY · asked about reaching behind the back · asked about trauma, work, sport and dominant hand · ★SIGNPOSTED AND RAN THE DIFFERENTIAL SWEEP · ★ASKED ABOUT CHEST PAIN AND BREATHLESSNESS · ★SCREENED FOR GIANT CELL ARTERITIS · asked about mood, sleep, coping and support · ★DID NOT PROMISE SURGERY OR SAY NOTHING COULD BE DONE · summarised, gave a plan and safety-netted.

Then frame it, because he will go quiet — 'I want to be straight with you: this is wear and tear that has built up over years, not something you did last week, and it is very common at your age. Plenty of people have changes like these and manage very well. It does not mean your shoulder is finished.'

Define the words before the result — 'PARTIAL MEANS PART OF THE TENDON IS TORN BUT SOME OF IT IS STILL ATTACHED AND STILL WORKING. FULL-THICKNESS MEANS IT'S TORN RIGHT THE WAY THROUGH, SO THAT MUSCLE IS NO LONGER PULLING ON THE BONE THE WAY IT SHOULD.' Give the findings first and define afterwards and he stops listening the moment he hears 'torn'

Deliver it one tendon at a time, ending on the normal one — 'THE MUSCLE AT THE FRONT, SUBSCAPULARIS, HAS A FULL-THICKNESS TEAR. TWO OF THE MUSCLES AT THE BACK HAVE PARTIAL TEARS — DAMAGED, BUT STILL PARTLY ATTACHED AND STILL DOING SOME WORK. AND THE FOURTH ONE, TERES MINOR, IS COMPLETELY NORMAL' — then the reassuring negatives: no inflammation of the cushion, no calcium build-up, biceps tendon exactly where it should be. NEVER CATASTROPHISE BY ARITHMETIC
fails: ★ Omitting the chest-pain question, or omitting the giant cell arteritis screen in a patient over 50 with girdle symptoms
★ Telling him he needs surgery, or telling him nothing can be done
★ Running the differential sweep silently in your head — if it is not signposted and spoken, it earns nothing
Giving the findings in jargon and never checking understanding, or catastrophising by arithmetic with 'three of your four muscles are torn'

Walking in and talking instead of asking what has happened so far; defining partial and full-thickness after giving the result; hearing 'physio didn't work' and re-referring without asking what it was or whether he did it; or missing the Nurofen alongside the blood pressure tablet and borderline diabetes
numbers: 4 rotator cuff muscles — supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis, with three inserting on the greater tuberosity and subscapularis on the lesser · partial means part of the tendon thickness and full-thickness means joint surface to bursal surface · 5 differential groups to sweep: neck, girdle, joint, chest, lung

Conservative trial of about 3 months before considering surgery VERIFY · review at 4-6 weeks with a written functional goal · paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily, max 4 g/24 h VERIFY · the giant cell arteritis screen is compulsory over 50 with girdle symptoms · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Quitline 13 7848 · PATS for country travel · VERIFY all

Full detail — FAIL — Omitting the chest-pain question, or omitting the GCA screen in a patient over 50 with girdle symptoms — the differential sweep is the section that passes the station; signpost it and say it out loud ('the scan explains a lot of what you've told me; even so, shoulder pain occasionally comes from somewhere other than the shoulder, and I don't want to miss anything — can I ask a few quick questions that may sound unrelated?'): neck (pain, stiffness, numbness or pins and needles, weakness — dropping things, buttons), girdle (the other shoulder, hips or thighs, morning stiffness duration, tiredness, weight loss — then without pausing: 'any new headaches, tenderness on the scalp, pain in the jaw when you chew, or any change in your vision?'), joint (grinding, catching, locking, other joints, family arthritis), chest ('a routine one I ask about any shoulder or arm pain — any chest pain or tightness, any breathlessness, especially on exertion?'), lung and systemic (smoking, cough, haemoptysis, hoarseness, fevers, sweats, cancer); a run of negatives is the point — you are marked for asking; run it silently and you get nothing (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Giving the findings in jargon and never checking understanding, or catastrophising by arithmetic — never 'three of your four muscles are torn' (he sits back: 'so my shoulder's wrecked then'); four layers before the result: open before you explain ('I do have your results — but before we get to those, can you tell me what has happened so far?'), what he understands and permission, the joint ('a ball and socket; unlike your hip the socket is very shallow — like a golf ball on a tee; huge range of movement but naturally unstable, so it relies on the muscles around it'), the four muscles ('together they're called the rotator cuff' — names lightly, once), define partial vs full BEFORE the result ('partial means part of the tendon is torn but some is still attached and still working; full-thickness means it's torn right the way through, so that muscle is no longer pulling on the bone the way it should'), then one tendon at a time finishing on the normal one ('subscapularis at the front — a full-thickness tear; two of the muscles at the back — partial tears, still partly attached and still doing some work; and the fourth, teres minor, is completely normal; no inflammation of the cushion, no calcium, your biceps tendon is exactly where it should be'); 'that sounds like a lot of damage' → name the emotion ('I can see that's a lot to take in') then reframe ('wear and tear that has built up over years, not something you did last week, very common at your age; plenty of people have changes like these and manage very well; it does not mean your shoulder is finished'); 'does that make sense so far?' setting: Read the task list twice. This is an older online-exam format: diagnosis only with no differentials asked for, and then the course of the disease, with management explicitly excluded. Candidates lose it by delivering a management plan nobody asked for and running out of time before the course. If you are asked for the course, give the course — and offer management rather than assuming it.
stem: General practice in regional South Australia. James Doyle, 26, a storeman who played country football until a few years ago. The stem says 'A problem with his shoulder' or 'Shoulder pain' — but his opening line is not about pain: 'My shoulder keeps falling out.'
Afebrile · HR 70 · BP 122/76 · walks in unaided, no sling.

back.dx: ANTERIOR SHOULDER INSTABILITY DUE TO A LABRAL TEAR, WITH INFERIOR CAPSULAR LAXITY AS AN ADDITIONAL COMPONENT — following a documented traumatic anterior dislocation sustained playing football six years ago. The explanation runs in five steps: name it · describe the joint — 'A ball-and-socket joint, but unlike the hip the socket is very shallow, more like a saucer than a cup, which lets you move your arm in every direction but makes it the least stable joint in the body' · name the two stabilisers — the labrum, 'A rim of firm gristle around the edge of the socket that deepens it', and the rotator cuff, 'Muscles that wrap around the joint and pull the ball into the socket' · say which tore — 'When you were tackled and landed on it, the ball came out, and as it came out it tore that rim' · and connect it to his symptom — 'With the rim torn, the socket is shallower than it should be, and the ball slips out again. That's exactly why it keeps happening.' Saying 'You have a labral tear' and stopping is a failed explanation — define the labrum in the same breath. Then the course, in four sentences: the tear itself does not heal, because that rim has a poor blood supply, so once torn it stays torn and the socket stays shallow · this is long-term and recurrent, and the shoulder will keep coming out · it happens with less and less force over time, which is exactly what he has described — the first time took a football tackle, now it goes turning over in bed · and each episode can do a little more damage to the rim and to the bone at the edge of the socket, which is one reason not simply to put up with it. Then close well and offer rather than deliver: 'I know that's not the easiest thing to hear. It is manageable, and there are good options — would you like me to go through the treatment options?' Only if invited: physiotherapy to strengthen the cuff so the muscles compensate for the torn rim, avoiding the provocative position of abduction with external rotation, and surgical repair if it keeps dislocating or in a young person returning to contact sport — with an orthopaedic opinion and imaging given his job and frequency VERIFY. If he asks about football: 'Contact sport with an unstable shoulder means it will keep coming out, and each time risks a bit more damage. I wouldn't tell you never — I'd tell you it's the single strongest reason to see a surgeon about repairing it.' Things never to say: 'You've got recurrent shoulder dislocation syndrome', which describes the symptom rather than the pathology and is not a term in the standard references · 'You have a labral tear' without defining the labrum · 'It'll heal up with rest' · 'There's nothing much to be done' · and a management plan when the task asked for the course. The variants. One, a first dislocation over 40 — a 58-year-old who fell three weeks ago and now cannot lift the arm and feels weak: in someone over forty a first dislocation carries a high chance of an associated rotator cuff tear, and weakness rather than instability is the clue — examine the cuff specifically and arrange ultrasound or MRI VERIFY. Two, atraumatic multidirectional instability — both shoulders loose, never injured, always double-jointed: generalised capsular laxity rather than a traumatic labral tear, with a bilaterally positive sulcus sign, managed with structured physiotherapy and surgery as a last resort that does less well VERIFY. Three, posterior dislocation — came out during a seizure, held by the side and unable to externally rotate: classically missed on a single anteroposterior film, so request an axillary or scapular y view and involve orthopaedics urgently. Four, the examiner challenges: 'What does the sulcus sign tell you?' → inferior capsular laxity, and not evidence of the labral tear itself — the apprehension test is what points to anterior instability, and a positive sulcus alongside it suggests a multidirectional component, which matters because it makes you more cautious about a purely anterior surgical repair. 'What imaging?' → plain films first including an axillary view, which may show a hill-sachs defect or a bony bankart, but plain films are often normal between dislocations, so for a suspected labral tear the investigation of choice is mr arthrography VERIFY. Five, he asks for a certificate — write him onto modified duties rather than off altogether, because staying at work in a restricted role gives better outcomes: no overhead work and a lifting limit, and a ReturnToWorkSA claim if it started at work.
plan: Open, ask about pain now, and let the long rambling account run — the bed, the door frame, the footy injury, all in one go. He is testing whether you can take control politely: acknowledge first — 'That sounds really unsettling, and having to put your own shoulder back is not something anyone should be doing' — then structure it.

Make him describe it, because everything after this depends on the answer: 'Can you describe exactly what you mean by falling out? Do you feel the joint pop out of place, or is it more a weakness, or stiffness?' then 'Does it go back on its own, or do you have to put it back?' and whether anything goes numb or tingles while it is out.

TIME IT AND GRADE IT — how long, how often now, WHAT BRINGS IT ON, and the question that gives you the natural history: 'IS IT HAPPENING WITH LESS AND LESS FORCE?' → 'IT USED TO TAKE A PROPER KNOCK; NOW IT GOES REACHING FOR A SEATBELT, OR TURNING OVER IN BED.' Then the effect on work, sport and sleep.

THE ORIGINAL INJURY IN FULL — what he was doing and how he landed · swelling or bruising at the time · A POP · whether he saw a doctor · ANY X-RAYS OR SCANS AND WHAT HE WAS TOLD, which is what makes this DOCUMENTED TRAUMATIC INSTABILITY RATHER THAN ATRAUMATIC LAXITY · how it was reduced · and sling and physiotherapy afterwards.

THE SHOULDER SWEEP — AND ASK ABOUT PAIN EVEN THOUGH HE NEVER RAISED IT, BECAUSE THE STEM SAID SHOULDER PAIN: pain · locking or catching · stiffness · can he get it all the way up · swelling · redness or rash · clicking or grating · weakness · numbness or paraesthesiae.

FUNCTION AND CLOSURE — occupation and what it involves · sport · OVERHEAD ACTIVITIES, WHERE NORMAL STRENGTH IS WHAT EXCLUDES A CUFF TEAR · other joints and morning stiffness over half an hour · neck pain · and a rapid SADMA.
Ask for the card as a structure, then interpret all three findings out loud rather than reading it silently (see findings).
The five-step explanation — name it, the joint, the two stabilisers, which tore, and the link to his symptom (see dx).

THE COURSE IN FOUR SENTENCES — IT DOES NOT HEAL · LONG-TERM AND RECURRENT · LESS AND LESS FORCE · EACH EPISODE DOES A LITTLE MORE DAMAGE. If you find yourself saying 'so we'd start with physiotherapy', STOP — that was not the task.

CLOSE WELL AND OFFER MANAGEMENT RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT — THEN, IF INVITED, GIVE IT BRIEFLY. Summarise to the examiner: a 26-year-old storeman with six years of recurrent right shoulder dislocation following a documented traumatic anterior dislocation, now occurring with minimal force and with self-reduction, no neurological symptoms, preserved power and overhead function, full range with a positive apprehension test and a positive sulcus sign.

Role-player: James Doyle, 26, a storeman who stacks, lifts and reaches all day, living with his partner in a country town, otherwise fit and well. About six years ago he was tackled from the side playing country football and landed on his right shoulder with the arm stretched out. It came up in a lump and swelled, he felt a pop, he went to hospital that night, they x-rayed it, said it was dislocated and put it back under sedation, and he wore a sling for about three weeks. Physiotherapy was mentioned but he never went. Since then it pops out roughly every couple of months — he feels it go and sees the shape change, and he puts it back himself, usually by hooking it on a door frame.

How he plays it: matter-of-fact, a bit fed up, slightly embarrassed about relocating it on a door frame, and not distressed. He opens with a long rambling account — the bed, the door frame, the footy injury, all in one go — which tests whether the doctor can take control politely; if interrupted rudely he becomes terse, and if let finish and then structured he engages fully. He does not mention pain unless asked, and then only 'It aches for a day or two after it goes back'. It aches only afterwards, with no locking, no stiffness, full movement, no swelling, no weakness and never any numbness. Overhead reaching is strong and he only avoids it because he is afraid. He has stopped football, is careful lifting at work, and is not sleeping because he is afraid of rolling onto it. His hidden agenda is whether it will ever heal and whether he will end up unable to work, asked near the end.

back.dx: POLYPHARMACY — six regular medicines plus over-the-counter ibuprofen — with a clinically significant drug interaction that is already symptomatic, a benzodiazepine to deprescribe, and an adherence problem that may be cognitive. The interaction, translated: 'His cholesterol tablet and the new heart tablet don't sit well together. The heart tablet slows down how the body clears the cholesterol tablet, so the level builds up higher than it should — and at high levels those tablets can damage muscle, which causes aching and weakness and very occasionally something more serious that can affect the kidneys.' then connect it to the aching legs the son has just given you. What you do: ask about muscle symptoms today and, if present, stop the statin and check creatine kinase and renal function · either lower the simvastatin to the dose considered safe with diltiazem or switch to a statin not affected by that pathway · keep the diltiazem, because the cardiologist added it deliberately · write to the cardiologist · and check liver and kidney function and repeat the lipids. The safety-net is specific: 'If he gets aching, tenderness or weakness in his muscles — especially the thighs or shoulders — or if his urine goes dark like tea, I want him to stop the cholesterol tablet and contact us that day.' The temazepam: 'It works well for a few weeks, but after that the body gets used to it and it stops helping the sleep — while it keeps causing drowsiness, unsteadiness, falls and problems with memory.' and then the safety point that is non-negotiable: 'We don't stop it suddenly. Stopping a tablet like this abruptly can cause serious withdrawal, including fits. We bring it down slowly, in small steps, over weeks to months, at a pace he's comfortable with — and only if he agrees.' Treat the sleep rather than just the tablet: ask what the problem actually is — getting off, staying asleep, early waking — and screen for depression, pain, sleep apnoea, nocturia, alcohol, caffeine and restless legs, with sleep hygiene and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, which is more effective than a hypnotic and without the harms VERIFY. The dose administration aid is the one that solves what the son described: 'Each day of the week has its own row, and morning, lunch and night each have their own sealed compartment. You just pop out the compartment — and if a compartment is still full, you know a dose has been missed.' What else a good review covers: is anything missing for his ischaemic heart disease · is anything doubled up across prescribers · allopurinol dose against renal function and whether the gout is actually controlled · the total daily paracetamol and whether anything else contains it · aspirin continued for secondary prevention with reflux and bleeding asked about · and stopping the over-the-counter NSAID, which does not sit well with aspirin, gout or cardiac disease. And the person rather than the list: cognition if he is muddling tablets — assess it rather than assuming age · falls on a benzodiazepine and a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker · driving · who supports him and whether they need support · cost and a home medicines review · and a written medication list for both to carry. The pressure points, scripted. 'Can't you just stop the sleeping tablet?' → 'No — and this is important. Stopping a tablet like that suddenly can cause serious withdrawal, including fits.' 'Should he stop the new heart tablet?' → 'No. The cardiologist added it deliberately and it's doing an important job. It's the cholesterol tablet I'll change, and I'll write to them.' 'He won't agree to any of this' → 'Then we go at his pace. These are suggestions, not orders, and the one I'd least like to leave is the tablet combination, because that one can actually hurt him.' and if the son asks you to stop telling his father things because it only worries him — explore the concern, but the patient's right to information stands; negotiate how, not whether.
plan: WIPE, THEN CONSENT IN FIFTEEN SECONDS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: 'MR AZIZ — AND YOU MUST BE HIS SON? BEFORE WE START: MR AZIZ, ARE YOU HAPPY FOR ME TO DISCUSS YOUR MEDICINES WITH YOUR SON HERE?' If the patient is not present or not able to answer, ask the son whether he has his father's consent or is the substitute decision-maker — and if only the examiner is available, ask the examiner. THE MARK IS FOR RECOGNISING THAT CONFIDENTIALITY APPLIES.

FIND OUT WHY THEY CAME, AND — SEPARATELY — WHY THE SON CAME: 'WHAT MADE YOU COME IN FOR A MEDICATION REVIEW?' AND 'CAN I ASK WHAT PROMPTED YOU TO COME ALONG TODAY?' The second answer is the clinical information the stem has deliberately left out. Then signpost the shape of the consultation.

THE THREE-MINUTE HISTORY, USING THE MEDICINES AS THE STRUCTURE BECAUSE THERE IS NO PRESENTING COMPLAINT. WHO AND HOW: who looks after the tablets · HOW DOES HE KEEP TRACK OF WHAT TO TAKE WHEN · does he ever miss doses or take them twice · DOES HE GET THEM ALL FROM THE SAME PHARMACY. You already have the list — what you need is how he takes it.

Side effects, with the one that matters most: 'Any muscle aches, pains or weakness — particularly since the new heart tablet was started?' · 'Any dark or tea-coloured urine?' · falls, dizziness or daytime drowsiness · and any recent slowing of the pulse or feeling faint, given newly added diltiazem.

COMPLETENESS AND CONTEXT — 'ANYTHING OVER THE COUNTER: ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES, VITAMINS, HERBAL THINGS?', which is never on the list and always in the cupboard · allergies · anything changed recently, new specialists or new tablets · HOW IS HIS MEMORY · how is he sleeping and how long has he been on the temazepam · who picks the tablets up and is cost a problem · does he live alone, does he drive, does he drink.
Ask the examiner for the report out loud, then read it back in your own words (see findings).
Action one, the interaction — explain it in lay terms, connect it to the aching legs, say what you will change and what stays, and give the safety-net sentence (see dx).
Action two, the temazepam — why it should come down, then the safety point that it is never stopped abruptly, then negotiate rather than announce. Deprescribing without agreement does not happen.

ACTION THREE, THE DOSE ADMINISTRATION AID, EXPLAINED PRACTICALLY — AND THEN THE REST OF THE REVIEW: stopping the Nurofen, assessing his memory properly rather than assuming age, and checking the allopurinol against renal function.

Close: 'So: three changes. I'll change the cholesterol tablet because of the interaction, start bringing the sleeping tablet down slowly if he agrees, and organise a pack from the pharmacy that sorts everything by day and time. I'll do blood tests today and write to the cardiologist. Come back straight away for muscle aches, weakness or dark urine, and I'll see you both in two weeks.' and speak to the patient directly at least once rather than letting the son answer everything.

stem: General practice. Your next patient is a 40-year-old woman recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Her HbA1c is 7.5%.

A glucometer is provided — on screen in the online format, on the desk in a face-to-face station. If it is on the desk, pick it up and demonstrate while narrating, then hand it to her and ask her to show you.

back.dx: NEWLY DIAGNOSED TYPE 2 DIABETES AT 7.5% — diagnostic, but only modestly above target, which is exactly why a lifestyle-first approach is reasonable and why this consultation matters. She is at risk of large-vessel disease — heart attack, stroke, peripheral arterial disease — and small-vessel disease of the eyes, kidneys and nerves, and lifestyle addresses both. The advice, with a number on every item. Food, asked about first: more vegetables at two meals a day, wholegrain cereals and breads, one and a half to two serves of dairy daily, fish twice a week, legumes and nuts, and olive oil as the main fat · less sugary drinks, which are the single biggest easy win, less saturated fat, smaller and less frequent red and processed meat, less takeaway and smaller portions · and alcohol within national guidelines. Frame it as swaps and additions and keep 'Nothing is completely banned' in the script, because a prohibition list is the failure mode. Exercise, after the cardiac question: 150 minutes a week of moderate to vigorous activity — enough to make her puff, so a gentle stroll does not count — spread over at least three days with never more than two consecutive days off, plus two or three resistance sessions totalling about an hour. Weight and waist: 5 to 10 per cent weight loss meaningfully improves glucose and cardiovascular risk — about five kilos for her — and waist under 80 cm for women and 94 cm for men. BMI under 25 is the ideal, not the starting target, and setting it as one is demotivating. Then the domains candidates forget: smoking cessation as the highest-value single change with Quitline 13 7848 · sleep, asking about snoring and daytime sleepiness because obstructive sleep apnoea is common and worsens control · daily foot checks including the soles and between the toes, never barefoot, well-fitting shoes · optometry at diagnosis · influenza and pneumococcal vaccination · driving, and never driving below 5 mmol/L · a sick day plan — keep taking medication, test more often, keep fluids up, seek help if vomiting · and mood, because diabetes distress and depression are common at diagnosis. The negotiation is the marked behaviour, not comprehensiveness: 'Of everything we've discussed — the drink, the bread, the vegetables, the walking — which two would you be willing to start this week?' and 'Two changes you keep beat twelve you abandon.' Hypoglycaemia — teach the rule of 15 but put it in context, because a patient on lifestyle or metformin alone is at very low risk: symptoms, then check, and if below 4.0 take 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate — half a glass of juice or regular soft drink, three teaspoons of sugar or honey, six or seven jelly beans, or glucose tablets — wait 15 minutes, recheck, repeat if still below 4, then a longer-acting snack or meal. Before exercise aim above 5, and watch for delayed lows after prolonged exercise. The team, named: credentialled diabetes educator, who gives her an hour you cannot · dietitian · exercise physiologist or physiotherapist · optometrist and podiatrist · pharmacist · under a GP management plan with team care arrangements. Baseline screening at diagnosis: eyes, feet with pulses and monofilament, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR, lipids, blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, liver function, mood and dental. Review in two to four weeks to see how the changes are going, repeat HbA1c at three months, NDSS registration for subsidised strips, and red flags: very thirsty, passing lots of urine, losing weight, blurred vision, or a foot wound that is not healing. What else to consider: do not assume type 2 at 40 — a lean, rapidly symptomatic, ketotic patient is type 1 or lada and needs antibodies and c-peptide VERIFY · steroid-induced hyperglycaemia · and a misleading HbA1c in anaemia, recent transfusion, iron therapy or chronic kidney disease, where fasting glucose or an OGTT is used instead VERIFY.
plan: Open by asking rather than telling: 'Before I go through them — what do you already know about diabetes? And is there anything in particular worrying you?' Her mother's diabetes is the frame she hears everything through, and it must be addressed early: 'Your mother's diabetes is not your diabetes. Hers was probably found late; yours has been found early and is only a little above target.' and to 'I feel completely fine': 'That's the difficulty with diabetes — it does its damage quietly for years before anyone feels anything. That's exactly why acting now works.'
Explain the number and the condition in one paragraph, then signpost the three things you will cover (see findings).

THIRTY SECONDS OF DIETARY AND ACTIVITY HISTORY BEFORE ADVISING: 'TALK ME THROUGH A NORMAL DAY'S EATING. BREAKFAST, LUNCH, DINNER, SNACKS, DRINKS.' AND 'WHAT ACTIVITY DO YOU DO NOW?' It makes everything afterwards specific and credible instead of generic — and it is how you find the two or three cans of Coke a day.
Dietary advice built out of her answers, leading with her biggest single win — the soft drink — then the specifics, and 'Nothing is completely banned' (see dx).

The cardiac question before prescribing exercise: 'Before I ask you to push yourself — do you get any chest tightness, pressure or breathlessness when you exert yourself? I ask everyone, because diabetes raises the risk of heart disease and can make it silent.' if yes: examination, ECG, and consider stress testing before recommending vigorous activity VERIFY. Then the prescription with its numbers.

NEGOTIATE RATHER THAN REPEAT. When she says she has two kids and a full-time job and it is not happening, DO NOT SAY THE TARGET AGAIN LOUDER — she becomes resigned and stops engaging. 'THEN LET'S NOT START WITH THE GYM. WHAT ABOUT A TEN-MINUTE WALK AFTER DINNER, AND THE STAIRS AT WORK?' Then ask which two she will start this week.

WEIGHT, WAIST AND THE REMAINING DOMAINS — a realistic 5 to 10 per cent rather than an unreachable BMI target, waist, alcohol, smoking, sleep and snoring, daily foot checks, eyes, vaccination and driving (see dx).
PROTECT THE LAST TWO MINUTES AND TEACH THE METER, NARRATING ALL NINE STEPS — then TEACH-BACK, and correct the deliberate error when she says she would use the pad of her finger (see findings).
How often to test, answered honestly — then the rule of 15 with the risk put in context, so she is not frightened of something she is not yet at risk of.

The team, the baseline screening, NDSS registration, a review in two to four weeks, repeat HbA1c at three months and the red flags. And if she asks about tablets or remission: 'If you do need metformin, that isn't you failing — diabetes is progressive and the medication is a tool, not a punishment' and 'Some people with early type 2 get their sugar back into the normal range with weight loss and activity — we call that remission. I can't promise it, and it isn't a cure, but it is a real possibility' VERIFY.

HbA1c 7.5% — explain it in one breath — 'The test is called HbA1c. It tells us your average blood sugar over about three months. Below 6 is normal. 6.5 and above means diabetes. Yours is 7.5. Check the strips are in date, take one out and close the pot · 3. Put the strip in the meter, which turns itself on · 4. New lancet, set the depth, and prick the side of a fingertip not the pad — less painful and more blood — rotating fingers · 5. Let a drop form without squeezing hard, which dilutes the sample · 6. Touch the drop to the edge of the strip and let it draw in · 7. Wait for the reading · 8. Write it down with the time · 9. Lancet into a sharps container, not the bin

setting: You have been sent to tell a daughter that her father is dying. The clinical content is small and the communication content is the whole station. The single commonest failure is letting 'Palliative care' sound like 'We are stopping treatment'. And do not open with 'How can I help you?' — you asked to see her, about her dying father.
stem: Hospital ward. You are the treating junior doctor. A 90-year-old man admitted with lower lobe pneumonia and started on antibiotics has been having episodes of hypoxia and hypotension.

He has an advance care directive for no CPR and no enteral feeding. The consultant has suggested palliative care and asked you to discuss this with the family. His daughter is here and wishes to discuss his condition.
Tasks: explain the measures being taken — what is happening with her father — and explain what further can be done for the patient.

Explain what further can be done for the patient
time: The opening shape is memorised, not improvised — introduce as her father's doctor, express sorrow, offer a seat · then two questions in the first minute, both separately marked: what do you already know, and are you his substitute decision-maker · then the story in order so the conclusion arrives as something she can see coming · then the directive as his voice · then palliative care, defined properly · then the person, the family, the supports and the meeting

back.dx: A 90-year-old dying of severe pneumonia that is not responding to full treatment, with a valid advance care directive. The story is built in order so the conclusion arrives as something she can see coming: what he has → how serious → what we are doing → how he is responding → what we are worried about → what he himself asked for → what we propose. By the time you say the words palliative care, she should already be most of the way there. The warning shot and the reassurance belong together, in that order: 'He is not responding as well as we had hoped. He has had further episodes of low blood pressure and low oxygen' — pause — 'We are concerned his condition may get worse, and we will keep doing everything we can for him. He is not going to be left without care.' when she asks whether he is dying, answer it: 'I think he may be. He isn't responding to the treatment and I'm worried he will get worse rather than better. I can't tell you how long and I won't guess — but I'd rather you knew exactly where we stand.' then stop talking; silence after bad news is part of the answer, not dead air. The directive is handed back to her rather than used against her: 'That was his decision, made when he could make it, and we will respect it. Did the two of you ever talk about what he wanted?' then the three sentences the whole station is built around, and all three must be said: 'Palliative care is not giving up.' · 'It runs alongside what we are already doing, not instead of it — the antibiotics, the oxygen and the fluids carry on as long as they help him.' · 'What changes is what we are aiming for — comfort, rather than cure at any cost. Nothing is being taken away from him.' then be concrete, because detail is what makes palliative care sound like care rather than withdrawal: symptom medicines charted ready in advance for pain, breathlessness, nausea, secretions and restlessness, so nobody waits while he is uncomfortable · stopping medicines that cannot help him now, like the cholesterol tablets · mouth care, positioning and gentle nursing · fewer needles, observations and blood tests that will not change anything · and a quiet room with unrestricted visiting. The second half of the discriminating issue is not making her decide — she is the substitute decision-maker, not the person who must authorise her father's death: 'The medical recommendation is ours to make, and I don't want you carrying that. Your role is to help us understand who your dad is and what he would have wanted' — often the most relieving sentence in the station. Then the person and the family: what mattered most to him · was he religious and is there anyone to call · any cultural things to get right · did he ever say where he would want to be · who else needs to be here · and how is she, sleeping, eating, working, and is anyone else depending on her. The supports: specialist palliative care and the hospital social worker today · pastoral care · carer gateway 1800 422 737 with centrelink carer allowance and carer payment VERIFY · country health connect and community palliative care if home becomes the plan · bereavement support offered in advance rather than afterwards · an Aboriginal liaison officer where relevant, because practices and language around dying differ and must be led by the family · and TIS National 131 450, never using a family member to interpret an end-of-life discussion. And the plan: a family meeting with the consultant and the palliative care team, documented goals of care consistent with the directive, and overnight contact arrangements with her best number. Before concluding he is dying, still review the reversible: culture results and antibiotic cover, fluid status and heart failure, empyema, pulmonary embolism, and delirium — which is distressing, treatable and frequently missed at the end of life.
plan: THE OPENING, WHOSE SHAPE IS MARKED: 'HELLO, I'M DR [NAME], ONE OF THE DOCTORS LOOKING AFTER YOUR FATHER. ARE YOU SAMANTHA? I'M SO SORRY TO HEAR YOUR FATHER HAS BEEN UNWELL. PLEASE, TAKE A SEAT.' Introduction, your relationship to the patient, an expression of sorrow, a seat — and then her understanding before yours.

THE TWO QUESTIONS, BOTH SEPARATELY MARKED: 'BEFORE I SAY ANYTHING — CAN YOU TELL ME HOW MUCH YOU ALREADY KNOW ABOUT YOUR FATHER'S CONDITION?' AND 'CAN I CHECK — ARE YOU NAMED AS HIS SUBSTITUTE DECISION-MAKER?' Then ask whether there is anything in particular she wants covered, and signpost the three things you will do.

The situation in four short blocks, pausing after each — what he has · how serious, and why low oxygen and low blood pressure make it severe · what you are doing, which she needs to hear before she can hear that it is not working · and how he is responding, with the reassurance sentence attached (see dx).

Answer 'Are you telling me he's dying?' Honestly and directly — then stop, offer tissues, and let her react. 'Take whatever time you need. This is an enormous thing to be told.' Continuing the explanation while she is crying is the error.

The advance care directive, brought in respectfully as his voice in the room and then handed back to her — and if she says he signed it years ago and didn't mean this: 'That's a fair thing to raise. The directive isn't a rule that overrides you — it's his voice in the room. Tell me what you think he'd say if he could.'
If she asks about the ventilator, answer it in terms of benefit and burden rather than of what the document does or does not list (see findings).

NAME WHO ASKED, DEFINE PALLIATIVE CARE, AND THEN SAY ALL THREE CORRECTING SENTENCES — NOT GIVING UP, ALONGSIDE NOT INSTEAD OF, NOTHING BEING TAKEN AWAY. When she says 'so you're giving up on him', that is the moment the station turns.

What it looks like in practice, concretely — the anticipatory medicines, the medicines stopped, the mouth care, the reduced needles and the open visiting (see dx). And make clear the decision is not hers to carry alone.

THE PERSON AND THE FAMILY — what mattered most to her dad, whether he was religious and who to call, cultural needs, who else needs to be here, and how SHE is. Four separately marked items live in this last stretch, and candidates end on the definition of palliative care and never reach them.
Supports, the family meeting with the consultant and the palliative care team, overnight contact with her best number, and a summary that ends on 'Nothing is being taken away from him.'
