ask: The opening shape, which is marked: 'I'm one of the doctors looking after your father.' · 'I'm so sorry to hear your father has been unwell.' · 'Can you tell me how much you already know?' · 'Are you named as his substitute decision-maker?'

The three sentences that prevent the misunderstanding the station is built on: 'Palliative care is not giving up.' · 'It runs alongside what we're doing, not instead of it.' · 'Nothing is being taken away from him.'
The honest answer and the relieving one: 'I think he may be dying. I can't tell you how long, and I won't guess.' · 'The medical recommendation is ours to make — I don't want you carrying that.'

The ones that reach the person: 'His directive is his voice in the room — did the two of you ever talk about it?' · 'What mattered most to your dad?' · 'We don't wait for him to be uncomfortable before we treat it.' · 'If anything changes overnight, the ward will call you.'

Challenges: 'Are you telling me he's dying?' · 'So you're giving up on him' · 'Can't you just put him on a ventilator?' · 'He signed that form years ago — he didn't mean this' · 'Are you going to stop his antibiotics?' · 'Will he be in pain?' · 'Can we take him home?' · 'It's my decision then?' · and 'My brother will want everything done.'
pefe: There is no examination and no history task — but two questions must still be asked in the first minute and both are separately marked: what she already knows, and whether she is the substitute decision-maker. Discussing treatment decisions with a relative of unconfirmed standing is the procedural failure here.

Role-player: Samantha Hobbs, 58, a school administrator whose father Ronald, 90, was admitted three days ago. She has visited daily, nobody has updated her since Tuesday, and she has been waiting outside the ward all morning — not aggressive, but frightened, tired and slightly aggrieved at the lack of communication. Ronald lived independently until this admission, was widowed six years ago, and is devoutly catholic — he would want the priest. He completed the directive about four years ago after a friend died badly in intensive care, and told her plainly that he had had a good innings and did not want to be kept alive by machines — said only if asked whether they ever discussed it.

How she plays it: she listens quietly to the explanation, then goes silent when told he is not responding and asks directly whether he is dying. If answered honestly she cries, accepts tissues and recovers in about thirty seconds; if evaded she asks again more sharply — 'I need you to tell me straight.' She asks once about the ventilator. When palliative care is mentioned she says flatly 'So you're giving up on him' and waits — and if it is not corrected clearly she becomes upset and hostile for the rest of the station, while a good 'Alongside, not instead of' settles her visibly and she starts asking practical questions. She has a brother Greg interstate who will want everything done and whom she dreads telling — raised only if asked who else needs to be involved. She has not eaten or slept properly in three days, said only if asked. Her hidden fear, volunteered late or if asked what worries her most, is that he will be in pain and will die alone while she is at home. If the doctor never asks about her father as a person or about her, she does not volunteer the priest or the brother.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE: INTRODUCED AS ONE OF HER FATHER'S DOCTORS AND OFFERED HER A SEAT · EXPRESSED SORROW RATHER THAN SAYING 'HOW CAN I HELP YOU' · ASKED WHAT SHE ALREADY KNEW BEFORE EXPLAINING · CONFIRMED SHE WAS THE SUBSTITUTE DECISION-MAKER · explained the pneumonia and why it was severe · explained the antibiotics, oxygen and fluids · GAVE A CLEAR WARNING SHOT · SAID EXPLICITLY THEY WOULD KEEP DOING EVERYTHING THEY COULD · ANSWERED 'IS HE DYING?' HONESTLY · PAUSED AND LET HER REACT, OFFERING TISSUES · raised the directive as HIS WISHES and asked whether they had discussed it · ADDRESSED THE VENTILATOR IN TERMS OF BENEFIT AND BURDEN · SAID PALLIATIVE CARE IS NOT GIVING UP · SAID IT RUNS ALONGSIDE AND NOTHING IS BEING TAKEN AWAY · DESCRIBED SYMPTOM CONTROL CONCRETELY · MADE CLEAR THE DECISION WAS NOT HERS TO CARRY ALONE · asked about her father as a person and about his spiritual needs · ASKED HOW SHE WAS AND ABOUT OTHER FAMILY · offered a family meeting, palliative care team and social worker · and gave a clear overnight contact plan and closing summary.

The clinical picture — Lower lobe pneumonia on intravenous antibiotics, with episodes of hypoxia and hypotension — which is what makes it a severe pneumonia, and it is failing to respond to appropriate therapy in a 90-year-old

The directive — No CPR and no enteral feeding. It does two things: records refusals of specific treatments, which are legally binding when valid, and appoints a substitute decision-maker. It does not replace a conversation with the family, it never means withdrawal of comfort care, and it is not a document to hide behind — never say 'He signed a form'

The intubation question — where the obvious reasoning is wrong — The directive says nothing about intubation, and it is tempting to conclude that intubation is therefore the next step. That is unsafe: a directive lists what a person refuses, and does not oblige you to provide everything they did not think to refuse. Clinicians are not obliged to offer treatment that is not clinically indicated VERIFY

So say this instead — 'If he continues to worsen, the only remaining option would be a breathing tube and intensive care. His directive doesn't mention that specifically — so the question is whether it would help him, and whether it fits what he would have wanted. In someone of 90 whose pneumonia isn't responding, it is very unlikely to give him more good time, and it would almost certainly mean he died in intensive care rather than with you'

South Australian terminology — Under the advance care directives act 2013 the appointed person is a substitute decision-maker — not a 'Medical decision maker', which is Victorian, and not 'Next of kin', which has no decision-making status in law. Ask: 'Are you named as your father's substitute decision-maker in his advance care directive?' VERIFY

setting: It looks like a dermatology station and it is not. Acne cases are designed around the psychosocial impact, and the role-player will show you — poor eye contact, a quiet voice, a story about school. A candidate who counts spots and lists side effects and never asks how he is coping has missed the station. And note the task wording: the impact of the condition is a marked task, not a throwaway phrase.
stem: General practice. Your next patient is a 17-year-old boy who has had acne for about a year. He has already tried topical treatments and a course of oral antibiotics without success, and oral isotretinoin is now being considered.
Tasks: take a history from the patient — explain the impact of the condition and the treatment, including the side effects of retinoid therapy.
If he is accompanied, offer him part of the appointment alone and explain confidentiality in one sentence.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Explain the impact of the condition and the treatment, including the side effects of retinoid therapy
time: Open by letting him describe the skin in his own words, which is neutral ground and his area of expertise · classify it, including the scarring question · take a treatment history that asks how, not just what · then normalise and ask the question the station is built on · explore what he discloses and respond to it with named supports · then explain acne and de-blame it · then isotretinoin, benefit first and side effects in full
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Severity is not a lesion count

Any scarring means severe, whatever the count — and scars are permanent, which is why severe acne is treated aggressively and early VERIFY. And significant psychosocial impact is itself a recognised reason to escalate treatment, even when the skin looks moderate — so asking about it is taking a severity history, not being pastoral VERIFY

Mixed comedonal and inflammatory — blackheads and whiteheads plus deeper sore lumps · face mainly with some on the back and shoulders · and some spots on his cheeks have left small dents, which he mentions only if asked about marks or scars · he picks and squeezes them

back.dx: ACNE VULGARIS — mixed comedonal and inflammatory, with established atrophic scarring, which classifies it as severe irrespective of lesion count — on a background of inadequate rather than ineffective previous treatment, and with significant undisclosed psychosocial impact. Explain the condition and de-blame it in the same breath: 'Under the skin you have tiny oil glands. In your teens, hormones make them produce more oil. The opening gets blocked by dead skin, the oil builds up behind it, and bacteria that normally live on the skin multiply in there — which is what makes it red and sore. It is not caused by being dirty, and it is not caused by chocolate. It is hormones and genetics, and it is not your fault.' Scrubbing makes it worse; gentle wash twice daily, oil-free non-comedogenic moisturiser and sunscreen, and no picking, which causes scarring. Isotretinoin is indicated here on three separate grounds — scarring, failure of prior therapy, and psychological impact — and the other indications are severe or nodulocystic disease and frequent relapse VERIFY. Lead with the benefit because it is real: 'It is the most effective treatment we have — it shrinks the oil glands, and for many people a single course clears the acne for good. But it has real side effects, and you need to know them before you decide.' The common ones: dryness, especially the lips, in almost everyone — constant lip balm, moisturiser and artificial tears, and contact lenses may become uncomfortable · nosebleeds from a dry nose · sun sensitivity, with spf 50+, hat and shade · and it often gets worse before it gets better, with a flare in the first few weeks expected · muscle and joint aches, especially with heavy exercise · and night vision can be affected, which matters for driving. The ones requiring action rather than mention: blood tests before and during for liver enzymes and blood fats · pregnancy, where the drug is severely harmful to a developing baby and any patient who could become pregnant needs pregnancy testing and strict reliable contraception before, during and for a defined period after treatment, with explicit documented counselling VERIFY — mention it even for a male patient as part of explaining what the drug is · no blood donation during treatment or for a period afterwards · never with a tetracycline, because of raised pressure around the brain · and no waxing, laser or skin resurfacing during and for a period after. Sexual dysfunction is now noted in the Australian product information after a TGA review — mention it if asked and take a report seriously. The mood question is answered honestly and safely, and the honest position is neither 'There's no link' nor 'This drug causes depression': the Australasian college of dermatologists states that current evidence does not point to a causal relationship and that severe acne itself carries psychological risk, while the TGA concluded an association with psychiatric and sexual adverse effects could not be ruled out and had the product information updated as a precaution, with psychological monitoring recommended for anyone with a history of mental illness VERIFY. So: reported, not proven causal, taken seriously, actively monitored, report immediately. In Australia isotretinoin sits under appendix d of the poisons standard and is restricted to specialist dermatologists, with an RACGP application before the TGA to allow accredited GPs to prescribe — check whether that has changed before telling a patient what will happen VERIFY. PBS listing is for severe cystic acne unresponsive to other therapy, authority required streamlined VERIFY. And consider the other causes: drug-induced acne from anabolic steroids, corticosteroids, some anticonvulsants and lithium — abrupt, monomorphic, often truncal, and easily missed in a 17-year-old who trains · rosacea, which flushes and has no comedones · folliculitis, which is itchy and hair-follicle centred · and in a female patient, polycystic ovary syndrome with irregular periods, hirsutism or rapid weight change.
plan: Open and give him some control: 'Tell me about your skin, in your own words.' then, if a parent is present, offer privacy as routine: 'It's something I offer everyone your age — would you like some of this appointment on your own?' and confidentiality in one sentence — what he tells you stays between you, unless you were worried about his safety, and you would talk to him first.

CLASSIFY THE ACNE — how long · WHAT SORT OF SPOTS, BLACKHEADS AND WHITEHEADS OR THE DEEPER SORE LUMPS · where, face or chest and back too · is it getting worse · anything that makes it better or worse including stress, sweating, products, helmets or sports gear · DO YOU PICK OR SQUEEZE THEM · AND THE ONE THAT CHANGES THE PLAN: 'HAVE ANY OF THEM LEFT MARKS OR SCARS?'

THE TREATMENT HISTORY THAT ASKS HOW, NOT JUST WHAT: what have you tried · FOR HOW LONG EACH TIME · DID YOU PUT THE CREAM ON THE WHOLE AREA, OR JUST ON THE SPOTS · did you use it every day · did anything irritate your skin · how long were you on the antibiotic and did you take it every day. Then other causes — medications, ANYTHING FROM THE GYM INCLUDING SUPPLEMENTS AND PROTEIN, and family history.

Normalise, then ask — the single most useful sentence in the station and the difference between passing and failing: 'Can I ask you something a bit different? A lot of people your age find this really gets to them — how they feel about themselves, how school is. How much does it affect you?' Normalising is what converts a closed adolescent into an open one.

EXPLORE IT PROPERLY RATHER THAN ABSORBING IT AND MOVING ON — 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME, THAT TOOK SOMETHING' · what sort of things do they say · HOW OFTEN ARE THERE DAYS YOU DON'T GO IN · does anyone at school know · have you stopped doing things you used to do · HOW'S YOUR MOOD BEEN IN YOURSELF · still enjoying things · sleep and appetite · AND, IF THE PICTURE WARRANTS IT, WHETHER HE HAS FELT REALLY DOWN OR HOPELESS · plus who he talks to when things are tough.

RESPOND WITH ACTION, NOT SYMPATHY — 'NONE OF THIS IS YOUR FAULT, AND BEING TEASED ABOUT IT IS NOT SOMETHING YOU SHOULD HAVE TO JUST PUT UP WITH' · THEN NAMED SUPPORTS: THE SCHOOL COUNSELLOR, headspace, AND KIDS HELPLINE 1800 55 1800 ANY TIME · ENCOURAGE HIM TO TELL A TRUSTED ADULT AND OFFER TO SUPPORT THAT · AND A LONGER FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENT. If he discloses persistent low mood or hopelessness, ASSESS IT PROPERLY AND SUPPORT IT RATHER THAN PRESCRIBING AND MOVING ON — and say 'the two go together', because clearing the acne often lifts the mood and neither is a reason to ignore the other.
Explain acne and say explicitly that it is not his fault, then the everyday measures (see dx).

ISOTRETINOIN — WHY IT IS INDICATED FOR HIM SPECIFICALLY, THEN THE BENEFIT, THEN THE SIDE EFFECTS IN FULL (see dx). Listing them so alarmingly that he refuses an effective treatment is its own failure.

The mood question, answered honestly: 'Mood changes have been reported and we take that seriously. What that means in practice is that I'll ask about your mood before we start and at every single visit, and I want you — and your mum — to tell me straight away if anything changes, even a bit. We don't wait and see with that.' A flat 'No, that's a myth' leaves him unconvinced and is inaccurate.

CLOSE BY CONNECTING THE PLAN BACK TO WHAT HE DISCLOSED: dermatology referral for the tablet, baseline bloods, current treatment used properly in the meantime — whole area, every day, six weeks before judging it — AND A LONGER APPOINTMENT ABOUT SCHOOL. 'I WANT TO TREAT YOUR SKIN — AND I DON'T WANT TO TREAT ONLY YOUR SKIN.'

ask: The sentence that unlocks the station: 'A lot of people your age find this really gets to them — how much does it affect you?'

The one question that changes the severity classification: 'Have any of them left marks or scars?' and the one that changes the treatment history: 'Did you put the cream on the whole area, or just on the spots?'

The follow-ups that turn a disclosure into a plan: 'Are there days you don't want to go in?' · 'Does anyone at school know?' · 'Have you stopped doing things you used to do?' · 'How's your mood been in yourself?'

The de-blaming line and the honest one: 'It's not because you're dirty, and it's not chocolate. It's not your fault.' · 'Mood changes have been reported and we take that seriously — tell me straight away if anything changes, even a bit.'

Challenges: 'It's just spots. Mum made me come' · 'Isn't that how you do it?' About applying cream to the spots · 'So washing more won't fix it?' · 'That's a lot' at the side effects · 'Isn't that the one that makes you depressed?' · and, only if asked what worries him most, 'That I'll be left with scars and nothing will ever work.'
pefe: There is no examination task — the history is the assessment, and the scarring question is what stands in for grading the skin. The role-player's non-verbal behaviour is the other half of the data: poor eye contact, a flat quiet voice and short answers are cues, not scenery.

Role-player: Nathan Cullity, 17, in year 12, whose mother made the appointment and who is embarrassed to be there. He plays it quietly — little eye contact, short answers, looking at the floor or his hands — and volunteers nothing. If the doctor only asks about the skin he answers factually and reveals nothing about school. If the doctor normalises and asks how it affects him, he pauses and then opens up gradually — names first, then the days off school, then the football.

The two behaviours that tell you how you are doing: if the doctor responds warmly he makes eye contact for the first time. If the doctor moves straight from his disclosure to the medication, he closes down again and gives short answers for the rest of the station. He is not in crisis — he is worn down and lonely — and if the mood question is dismissed with 'No, that's a myth' he looks unconvinced and says 'Right.' At the end, if school has been asked about and support offered, he says: 'No one's asked me about any of that before.'

Mark them against these: spoke to him, not over him, and offered time on his own · explained confidentiality in a sentence · asked what sort of spots and where · asked whether any had left marks or scars · asked whether he picks or squeezes · asked what he had tried, and how he used it and for how long · explained that the cream goes on the whole area and takes six to eight weeks · asked about supplements or anything from the gym · family history · normalised and asked how much it affects him · asked about school and being teased · asked whether there were days he did not go in · asked whether he had stopped doing things · asked about his mood · thanked him and said it was not something to put up with · offered named support and encouraged telling a trusted adult · explained acne clearly and said explicitly that it is not his fault · explained the benefit as well as the side effects · covered dryness, sun sensitivity, early flare, aches, blood tests and pregnancy · and answered the mood question honestly with monitoring at every visit and follow-up for more than just his skin.

The treatment that did not fail — He applied the cream only to the visible spots rather than the whole area, and stopped at two weeks because his face went red. That is not treatment failure — topicals go on the whole affected area because they prevent the next spots rather than treat the visible ones, they need six to eight weeks, and early irritation is expected and settles VERIFY. Saying so is marked clinical reasoning

What he will not volunteer — Kids at school call him names · he misses about one day a week · he stopped playing football this year · nobody knows, not his mother and not a teacher · his mood is 'Alright — bit flat, I suppose' · and his hidden concern is that he will be left with scars and nothing will ever work. He takes protein powder, and his father had bad acne
fails: ★ Never asking about the psychosocial impact — a competent skin history and an accurate side-effect list, and nothing else
★ Eliciting the bullying and the missed school and then moving straight on to lip balm and blood tests — sympathy without action scores very little
★ Never asking about scarring, which is one question and is what justifies escalating treatment
Accepting 'the creams didn't work' at face value without checking how they were used and for how long, when most apparent failures are inadequate trials

Blaming him — washing, chocolate, diet; frightening him off an effective treatment with a relentless side-effect list and no benefit; omitting pregnancy counselling because the patient is male; answering the mood question with a flat 'that's a myth'; or conducting the consultation with the parent while he sits silent

back.dx: Multifactorial hyperactive delirium. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by an underlying physical problem, and the three features you give the family are: it comes on suddenly, it comes and goes through the day, and it is usually reversible once the cause is treated. The contrast that reassures must be said explicitly, because it is the question she actually asked: 'This is not dementia. Dementia comes on slowly over years and doesn't go away. This came on over hours, and we expect it to improve.' Be honest about the caveat too — it can take days to weeks, and cognition is rechecked afterwards because delirium can uncover or be followed by longer-term change VERIFY. Hypoactive delirium — quiet, withdrawn, drowsy — is commoner, carries a worse prognosis and is routinely missed, so quiet is not the same as better. The reasons, plural and applied to her: the chest infection itself · low oxygen at 93% even on oxygen, and the brain is very sensitive to that · the low salt level · the heart failure · her medications, reviewing the whole chart for anything sedating or anticholinergic and anything started or stopped on admission · withdrawal, including nicotine in a chronic smoker who has been in a smoke-free hospital for days, and alcohol or sedatives if relevant · pain, often untreated because she cannot tell you · a full bladder or constipation, both common and both easily fixed · and the environment — an unfamiliar place, no clock, no window, lights and noise at night, broken sleep, glasses and hearing aids not in, and not being able to understand or be understood. Say the mnemonic silently and the list out loud: drugs · electrolytes and endocrine · lack of drugs meaning withdrawal · infection · reduced sensory input · intracranial · urinary and faecal retention · myocardial and pulmonary · sleep, stress and environment — or pinch me: pain, infection, nutrition, constipation, hydration, medication, environment. Investigations, with reasons: bedside glucose first, always · observations and saturations · FBC, UEC, LFT, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, CRP · urine microscopy and culture, blood cultures if febrile · bladder scan for retention · chest x-ray · ECG, cheap and quick, for a silent infarct or arrhythmia · CT brain if there is a head injury, focal neurology, anticoagulation or no other explanation · thyroid function and B12 where relevant · medication review as an investigation in its own right · and a pain assessment using an observational tool if she cannot report it. Medical management: continue and review the antibiotics · optimise oxygen and treat the heart failure · correct the sodium carefully and slowly, guided by volume status · rationalise the drug chart · treat pain, constipation and retention · and nicotine replacement for a chronic smoker. The behavioural half, which is the evidence-based core of delirium care and is explicitly requested by the task: family at the bedside · glasses on and hearing aids in · orientation with a clock, a calendar, a window, and staff saying who they are and where she is at every interaction · day-night rhythm, with light and activity by day and dark and quiet at night, and not waking her for non-essential observations · early mobilisation, sitting out of bed, eating and drinking normally · removing tethers — unnecessary cannulas, catheters and monitoring leads · and an interpreter. Medication only if safety demands it: when she is a danger to herself or others, or so distressed that essential treatment is impossible — low dose, single agent, shortest course, reviewed daily, with an ECG for QT where practical, and benzodiazepines avoided except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal where they are the treatment VERIFY. Avoid physical and chemical restraint, because both worsen delirium and cause injuries. Safety: falls precautions with a low bed, close observation, a clear floor and the call bell in reach — an agitated 80-year-old who climbs out of bed can turn pneumonia into a fractured hip and a subdural. And the sentence that recruits the daughter: 'You are part of the treatment. Someone familiar sitting with her, holding her hand, telling her where she is — that does more for delirium than most of what we can prescribe.' In a small rural hospital where one-to-one nursing may not be available, family presence is not just kind, it is the practical alternative to restraint. Prognosis: most people recover, it can take days to weeks, it is often worse before it is better and worse at night, she may not remember much of it, and cognition is reassessed once she is physically well VERIFY.

back.dx: POORLY CONTROLLED CHRONIC ASTHMA WITH OVER-RELIANCE ON RELIEVER THERAPY — not an exacerbation. Control is not the same as severity: control describes how she is now and is assessed with four questions, while severity describes how much treatment she needs to achieve it. And frequent reliever use is a risk marker, not just a control marker — heavy short-acting beta-agonist use is associated with worse outcomes VERIFY. The contributing factors must be named individually and tied to her answers, not offered as 'Various triggers': her nose — perennial allergic rhinitis, blocked all year and never treated, because the nose and the chest are one airway and treating the nose often improves the chest VERIFY · the cat acquired in March, which matches her deterioration timeline exactly once you anchor it with 'And when did the symptoms start getting worse?' · her glaucoma eye drops, some of which are beta-blockers and can tighten the airways VERIFY · and simply that her preventer dose is not enough for how much asthma she has. The key explanation she needs: 'Your blue puffer is a reliever — it opens the airways for a few hours and then it wears off. It does nothing to the inflammation underneath. Your preventer treats that inflammation, but only if the dose is enough. So needing the reliever most days isn't you overusing it — it's the signal that the preventer needs to go up.' Telling her to cut down the reliever without increasing the preventer is both wrong and dangerous. The plan, in six parts: confirm the diagnosis with spirometry including reversibility if it has never been done VERIFY · watch her use the inhaler and spacer once anyway, saying so explicitly because it earns credit rather than losing it — 'I can see technique and adherence have been checked, I'd still watch you use it once, because it's the commonest reason for this and it takes twenty seconds' · treat the comorbidities with an intranasal corticosteroid for rhinitis, plus reflux, weight and sleep apnoea VERIFY · remove the triggers — cat out of the bedroom at minimum with weekly hot bedding washes, damp addressed, household smoke eliminated, and the eye drops reviewed with her ophthalmologist · step up the preventer — a higher-dose inhaled corticosteroid, or adding a long-acting bronchodilator, or a combination inhaler used as both preventer and reliever, selected against the current Australian asthma handbook rather than quoted from memory VERIFY · and a written action plan, influenza and pneumococcal vaccination, and review in four to six weeks, stepping down only after about three months of good control VERIFY. The action plan is written, on paper, in her hand — not 'I'll explain it' — and contains what to take when she is well, exactly what to increase when things slip, what to do when it is severe and to call the same day, and the emergency steps: four puffs of reliever through a spacer, one at a time, wait four minutes, repeat, call 000 VERIFY. Red flags for coming back sooner: the reliever not lasting the usual few hours or needed more often than every three to four hours · too breathless to speak in full sentences · waking repeatedly at night · not improving after reliever · and 000 for severe breathlessness, blue lips or drowsiness. And ask the question that reframes the whole station: 'Has anyone ever formally confirmed the asthma with breathing tests?' — because not everything that wheezes is asthma. Vocal cord dysfunction gives difficulty getting air in, throat tightness and no response to reliever, and needs a flow-volume loop and speech pathology rather than more asthma medication VERIFY · COPD or asthma-copd overlap in a smoker with incomplete reversibility · heart failure with orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea · bronchiectasis with chronic daily sputum · pulmonary embolism · and obesity, reflux or anxiety as contributors. Refer to a respiratory physician if control is not achieved despite a stepped-up regimen and treated comorbidities, if the diagnosis is uncertain, if she has had a life-threatening attack, or if she needs frequent oral corticosteroids.

back.dx: TYPE 1 DIABETES — autoimmune destruction of beta cells producing absolute insulin deficiency, requiring insulin for life, which is why 'I stopped my insulin because I wasn't eating' is dangerous rather than sensible. A 22-year-old is a different problem from a 60-year-old with type 2: he faces decades of injections and finger-pricks at the age when he is starting work, studying, drinking, driving and forming relationships, and psychological burden, diabetes distress and disordered eating are all commoner, with adherence the central clinical problem. The immediate management starts with his agenda, and for version A that means options rather than instructions: basal-bolus, which is the most flexible but has the most needles · a premixed pen twice daily, which is far fewer injections but requires regular meals and gives less fine control · and an insulin pump, a small device delivering insulin continuously through a tiny cannula changed every two or three days, usually paired with a sensor that reads glucose without finger-pricks — fewest needles and the best control, but worn all the time, and if it fails the sugar rises fast. Refer for pump assessment rather than promising a pump VERIFY. If he admits skipping doses, do not lecture — 'Thank you for telling me. What makes that one the hard one?' — and then change the regimen, because burden responds to redesign rather than repetition. The safety block is given in every version: hypoglycaemia and the rule of 15 — below 4, take 15 g of fast sugar, wait 15 minutes, recheck, then a proper snack — with glucagon for someone at home to use VERIFY · sick day rules, and this is the one that matters most: never stop insulin because he is not eating, because he usually needs more not less — test more often, check ketones, keep fluids up, and present if vomiting, drowsy or if ketones are climbing · driving — above 5 to drive, glucose in the car, and not within two hours of a severe hypo VERIFY · alcohol, which can drop the sugar several hours later and often overnight, so eat carbohydrate with it, check before bed and tell whoever he is with · and medical identification. The long-term plan: the team — an endocrinologist, because type 1 is specialist-led and his lapsed when he left paediatrics; a credentialled diabetes educator for technique, dose adjustment and carbohydrate counting; a dietitian; an optometrist and podiatrist — all under a GP management plan with team care arrangements. Annual screening: HbA1c three to six monthly with an individualised target · retinal examination · urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR · foot inspection with pulses and monofilament · lipids and blood pressure · and coeliac and thyroid screening, because other autoimmune conditions cluster with type 1 VERIFY. And the things easy to forget at 22: mood and diabetes distress, asked about directly · insulin omission for weight control, asked sensitively if there are clues · sexual health, contraception and preconception planning · work, study and disclosure · vaccination · travel letters and insulin storage · NDSS registration · and doing the script, because he came for it and it is both courteous and marked. On continuous glucose monitoring: a sensor worn on the skin giving real-time glucose and trend arrows without finger-pricks, with alarms, particularly valuable in type 1 and in hypoglycaemia unawareness. All people with type 1 can apply through the NDSS, with full subsidy for under-21s, concessional cardholders aged 21 and over, and in pregnancy, and a co-payment otherwise — and a GP cannot certify the access form, which must be signed by an endocrinologist or credentialled diabetes educator, which is another reason to refer VERIFY. back.dx: THREE PROBLEMS FEEDING EACH OTHER — osteopenia, recurrent falls and COPD with repeated glucocorticoid exposure — and the conceptual core of the station is one sentence: 'Soft bones on their own don't break. Soft bones plus falls do. That is why we treat both problems at once.' Contributing factors, given as two numbered groups rather than a vague 'It's multifactorial'. Why his bones are thin: repeated courses of oral prednisolone, which is the dominant factor VERIFY · long-term inhaled corticosteroid at higher doses · vitamin d deficiency at 30 · COPD itself through inactivity, low body weight, chronic inflammation and hypoxia · smoking and alcohol · and low dietary calcium with limited sun exposure. Why he is falling: breathlessness and deconditioning from COPD · steroid myopathy, meaning proximal muscle weakness from repeated courses · medications, particularly sedatives and antihypertensives · postural hypotension · and vision, footwear, home hazards and night-time toilet trips. The plan has three parts and is delivered as headings, not a pharmacology lecture. Bones: vitamin d replacement with colecalciferol, rechecked at about three months VERIFY · calcium from diet first, around three to four serves of dairy or equivalent daily, with supplements only if diet is inadequate · weight-bearing and resistance exercise · stopping smoking and limiting alcohol · and minimising oral steroid exposure by controlling the COPD better. If drug treatment is indicated, headlines only: alendronate weekly on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, upright for 30 minutes and separated from calcium and antacids · zoledronic acid yearly with renal function, corrected calcium and vitamin d checked first · denosumab six-monthly, where adherence is critical because delay beyond about four weeks risks rebound vertebral fractures and stopping it requires replacement with a bisphosphonate VERIFY · dental review before starting, for osteonecrosis of the jaw · and bisphosphonates reconsidered at five to ten years with a repeat DEXA at two years VERIFY. Falls: name the people, not just the idea — a physiotherapist for a supervised strength and balance programme, which is the single most effective falls intervention VERIFY · an occupational therapist for home hazards, rails, lighting and bathroom modifications · a podiatrist for feet and footwear · medication review and deprescribing, with the sleeping tablet weaned slowly rather than stopped abruptly · optometry, with caution about multifocals on stairs · postural blood pressure today · and a personal alarm, because he lives alone and that was his opening line. Chest — and this is a bone intervention: smoking cessation with Quitline 13 7848 and nicotine replacement · inhaler technique and adherence checked in the room · a written COPD action plan · pulmonary rehabilitation, which improves exercise capacity and so helps both the falls and the bones · influenza and pneumococcal vaccination · and reviewing whether an eight-day prednisolone course is needed, since shorter courses are standard for most exacerbations VERIFY. Two accuracy corrections the source flags against itself. First, calcium: it quotes 1300 mg daily for everyone, but Australian guidance is 1000 mg for adults generally, rising to 1300 mg for women over 50 and men over 70 on osteoporosis treatment — at 55 he needs 1000 mg, and 1300 is a supplementation threshold rather than his intake target VERIFY. Second, it is hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia: the risk before and during zoledronic acid and denosumab is a low calcium, which is exactly why calcium, vitamin d and renal function are corrected before the first dose VERIFY. And do not stop the inhaled steroid to protect his bones — that would worsen COPD control and lead to more oral prednisolone, which is far worse for bone. Watch for the things that change the station: a blackout before a fall makes this a syncope case needing an ECG, postural blood pressure, cardiac assessment and driving advice · back pain or height loss suggests an occult vertebral fracture needing a thoracolumbar x-ray, which would mandate treatment regardless of T-score · and a 55-year-old man is young for this diagnosis, so if the Z-score is low for age, screen for secondary causes with morning testosterone, LH and FSH, TSH, coeliac serology, parathyroid hormone and serum protein electrophoresis VERIFY.

The DEXA, explained in two minutes — 'It measures how dense and strong your bones are, at three places — spine, hip and the TOP of your thigh bone. It gives two numbers: a T-score comparing you to a healthy young man, and a Z-score comparing you to someone your own age and sex.' T above −1 is normal, −1 to −2.5 is osteopenia, and −2.5 or below is osteoporosis

The verdict, in plain words — 'Your T-score is between minus one and minus two and a half at all three sites. That means osteopenia — your bones are softer than they should be. It is not osteoporosis, which is when they become fragile and break easily. You are in between, and the point of today is to stop you going any further'

The question the whole station turns on — 'Have you ever broken a bone?' — then which one, and how much force. Hip or vertebral minimal trauma fracture → treat whatever the T-score is · any other minimal trauma fracture at 50 or over → presumptive osteoporosis, with frax run on the BMD where T sits between −1.5 and −2.5, treating if major fracture risk is 20% or more or hip 3% or more · no fracture → assess risk factors and use frax VERIFY. Without the answer you literally cannot produce a management plan

Which sites count — Minimal trauma means a fall from standing height or less, and the sites that count are vertebra, hip or proximal femur, distal radius, proximal humerus and pelvis. Fingers, toes, skull and face do not

back.dx: EPISODIC MIGRAINE WITHOUT AURA — a clinical diagnosis that the imaging was not required to make, and which you explain by showing your working rather than announcing a label: 'I don't want you to just take my word for it — let me show you how I know.' then what migraine actually is: 'It isn't just a bad headache. It's a condition of the brain and its blood vessels, where the nerve pathways that carry pain become over-sensitive and over-react to certain triggers. That's why the light hurts, why you feel sick, and why it knocks you out for hours. It is real, it is common, and it is treatable.' The management is delivered in three named parts and counted out loud, because a candidate who says the right drug names in the wrong shape has lost the structure mark. Part one, things she can do herself: a migraine diary started today, recording when, how bad, how long, what she ate and drank, how she slept and what she took · and the common triggers — missed or late sleep including sleeping in at weekends, skipped meals, dehydration, alcohol, caffeine both excess and withdrawal, stress and the let-down after stress, and hormonal timing around periods · plus a cold pack on the forehead, a warm pack on the neck, and a dark quiet room. Be honest about trigger avoidance rather than handing over a list of banned foods: triggers are usually cumulative, and the glass of wine that is fine on a well-slept Saturday causes an attack on a tired, dehydrated Thursday VERIFY. Part two, treating the attack: take it early, at the first hint, rather than waiting to see whether it turns into a bad one — the single most important thing about migraine treatment · a simple anti-inflammatory at a proper dose, because half a tablet will not touch it · then an antiemetic, explained properly or the mark is lost: 'It isn't only for the nausea. During a migraine your stomach almost stops emptying, so painkillers sit there and don't get absorbed. The anti-sickness tablet helps the painkiller actually get into you' · then triptans, which are migraine-specific and act on the process rather than dulling the pain, offered as a choice of tablet, wafer that dissolves on the tongue, or nasal spray that bypasses the stomach — and offering the three forms is the patient-centred mark, with the wafer being the answer to a woman who vomits her tablets. Triptans are serotonin agonists, so check for SSRIs and mao inhibitors, and they come in small packs on purpose so that overuse is noticed VERIFY. Avoid opioids — poorly effective in migraine and a major cause of overuse headache VERIFY. Part three, prevention: for roughly two to four or more attacks a month, or attacks disabling enough to cost days even if fewer — so at eight a year the honest answer today is not yet, and saying why is the useful part, because it tells her when to come back. If one is started it is taken daily whether or not she has a headache, given two to three months before judging it — impatience is the commonest reason preventers 'Fail' — and aimed at fewer and milder attacks rather than zero, with general-practice options including a beta-blocker, amitriptyline, pizotifen and candesartan, and pregnancy suitability checked first in a 25-year-old VERIFY. Then the two forgotten items. Medication overuse headache: 'If you take painkillers too often, they start causing headaches. Keep painkillers to fewer than 15 days a month, and triptans to fewer than 10. If you're needing them more often than that, come and see me — that means you need a preventer, not more painkillers' VERIFY. And the contraceptive pill: migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk, while migraine without aura is more nuanced — generally acceptable to initiate, with a lower threshold to stop if aura develops or vascular risk factors accumulate. Progestogen-only methods, the implant, the injection and both intrauterine devices are not restricted, so there is always an alternative and she is never left without contraception VERIFY. Red flags to give her explicitly, because the normal MRI does not cover future presentations: the worst headache of her life coming on in seconds · fever, neck stiffness or a rash · weakness, numbness, slurred speech or confusion · a headache that wakes her or is worse lying flat or on coughing · a change in pattern · headache after a head injury · and visual loss or double vision VERIFY. Review in six to eight weeks with the diary. And keep in mind the other things a young woman on the combined pill can have: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension with visual obscurations and pulsatile tinnitus VERIFY.

Role-player: Sarah Whitlock, 25, a primary school teacher with eight severe headaches in the past year — one-sided, throbbing, with nausea and light hurting her eyes so she has to lie in a dark room, often after a couple of glasses of red wine. Attacks last most of a day and she usually has to go home from work. No aura — no zigzags, flashing, blind spots or tingling. She is on the combined pill, said only if asked about contraception. She takes ibuprofen two or three hours in, once the headache is established, and it barely helps — and she has vomited tablets back up. She does not take painkillers on other days, so there is no overuse yet. She sleeps badly in term time, skips lunch, and drinks two or three coffees a day.

What did it show?' if the doctor starts taking a history she answers briefly and looks puzzled: 'I told the other doctor all this.' She is genuinely struck by the absorption explanation — 'That explains a lot, I thought they just didn't work on me' — and chooses the wafer if offered the three forms. If the doctor never asks about aura or contraception, she volunteers neither. Her hidden concern, given only if asked later, is that she will have to give up work.

stem: General practice. A 60-year-old man presents complaining of a rash. A photograph is provided, showing a vesicular rash in a unilateral, dermatomal distribution. On history it is extremely painful.

findingsLabel: Ask for a general examination, not a dermatological one — and name the reason as you ask
findings: What the examiner may hand back

Afebrile · BMI down from 25 to 22 · firm, non-tender lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular fossa and both axillae · spleen tip palpable · mouth clear · chest clear · rash confined to one dermatome — which changes the station, and you must be honest with him about it

back.dx: HERPES ZOSTER — reactivation of varicella zoster virus that has lain dormant in a sensory nerve root since chickenpox — and the real diagnosis is whatever let it reactivate. To him, in plain words: 'When you had chickenpox as a child, the virus didn't leave your body — it went to sleep in a nerve root next to your spine. Years later it can wake up, travel down that one nerve, and cause pain and a rash in exactly the strip of skin that nerve supplies. That's why it's a band on one side and stops in the middle.' then the part the task actually asks for: 'Why now? The virus is kept asleep by your immune system, so shingles appears when the immune system DIPs. Most often that is simply age — immunity to this virus fades as we get older, which is why it is common at 60. But sometimes there is another reason: diabetes, medicines that suppress immunity like steroids, a blood or other cancer, or an infection such as HIV. Physical or emotional stress and poor nutrition also play a part. That's why I asked all those questions, and it's why I want some blood tests.' Age is a diagnosis of exclusion, not a first answer. And the immune screen is not academic — it changes what you prescribe: in an immunocompetent patient antivirals are given within 72 hours of rash onset, while in an immunocompromised patient they are given regardless of how long the rash has been present, with a much lower threshold for admission and intravenous therapy VERIFY. The history is weighted accordingly. Malignancy: unintentional weight loss · drenching night sweats · lumps in the neck, axillae or groins · change in bowels or blood in urine or stool · cough or haemoptysis · and screening status. Diabetes and chronic disease: thirst and nocturia · recurrent infections or thrush · slow-healing wounds · renal or hepatic disease · family history. Drugs, HIV and lifestyle: steroids in tablet or strong inhaled form · methotrexate, azathioprine or biologics for arthritis, bowel disease or transplant · any chemotherapy ever · splenectomy · alcohol, smoking and injecting drug use · and sexual history, raised with framing rather than bluntly: 'One of the things that can allow shingles to happen is an infection that quietly weakens the immune system — including HIV. I ask everyone about this, and I'd like to include an HIV test in the bloods. Is that alright with you?' The treatment of the shingles itself: antiviral tablets started as soon as possible VERIFY · pain relief given regularly rather than as needed, with early consideration of a neuropathic agent, because under-treated pain is the commonest real-world failure in zoster VERIFY · skin care, keeping it clean, dry and covered with loose clothing and a non-stick dressing · contagion advice, because the fluid can give chickenpox rather than shingles to someone never infected, so keep it covered until every blister has crusted and avoid newborns, non-immune pregnant women and immunosuppressed people · review in two to three days · and vaccination once recovered, since shingles can recur VERIFY. Investigations in two groups. Group one, confirmation: the diagnosis is clinical — say so — with VZV PCR on a de-roofed vesicle only if atypical and never delaying treatment for the result, and fluorescein examination if there is any ocular involvement VERIFY. Group two, the cause: full blood count and film for lymphoma, leukaemia and cytopenias · blood glucose and HbA1c · HIV serology with consent · urea, electrolytes and creatinine, which are also needed for antiviral dosing · liver function · ESR or CRP, and LDH if lymphoma is a concern · chest x-ray for mediastinal nodes and lung malignancy · and hepatitis serology, protein electrophoresis and age-appropriate cancer screening depending on the history VERIFY. The complications that change the station: herpes zoster ophthalmicus, where involvement of the forehead, upper eyelid or tip of the nose means same-day ophthalmology and immediate antivirals, with tip-of-nose lesions predicting ocular involvement VERIFY · Ramsay hunt syndrome, with ear pain, canal vesicles, facial palsy, vertigo or hearing loss, needing urgent ENT VERIFY · disseminated zoster, with lesions well outside the dermatome or a systemically unwell patient, needing admission and intravenous therapy and implying significant immunosuppression · bacterial superinfection · and post-herpetic neuralgia, whose risk rises with age, severe acute pain and severe rash, and whose prevention includes treating the acute pain properly now VERIFY.
plan: Open and get the rash story fast — when it started, which fixes the 72-hour window · whether anything came before it · where exactly and whether it crosses the midline · whether it is spreading beyond the band · and the two same-day referral questions: any blisters near the eye or on the nose, and any in or around the ear with facial weakness or dizziness.
The pain — severity out of ten, character, whether light touch hurts, whether it is keeping him awake — and the systemic screen for fever, headache, neck stiffness or confusion.

Signpost the shift, or the next two minutes land as an interrogation: 'I'm fairly confident I know what this is, and I'll tell you in a moment. But I want to spend most of our time on why it has happened now, because that matters more than the rash itself. Some of my questions will seem unrelated — bear with me.'
THE IMMUNE SCREEN — MALIGNANCY, THEN DIABETES AND CHRONIC DISEASE, THEN DRUGS, HIV AND LIFESTYLE (see dx). This is the two and a half minutes that decide the station.
Request the general examination by name, with the reason attached — not a description of the rash (see findings).

Explain the diagnosis in plain words, then the causes — which is the half the task asks for and the half most candidates omit (see dx). If the examination has given you weight loss and lymphadenopathy, be honest: 'I'm not telling you what it is, because I don't know — but I'm not going to pretend I'm not concerned.'
Treatment today — antivirals started now rather than after the bloods, proper regular analgesia because nine out of ten is not something to put up with, skin care and contagion advice.
Investigations in two groups, saying that the diagnosis itself needs no test and that the second group is for the cause (see dx).

Safety-net and review — back sooner if it spreads well beyond the band, if the eye becomes red or painful, if he develops fever, headache or confusion, or if the pain is uncontrolled — with review in two to three days and urgent haematology referral if the film or count is abnormal.

ask: The sentence that carries the station: 'Shingles happens when the immune system drops its guard. At 60 that is usually just age — but I'd rather look for another reason than miss one.'

The signpost that makes the next two minutes acceptable: 'Some of my questions will seem unrelated — bear with me.' and the framing that makes the HIV question land: 'I ask everyone — there are infections that quietly weaken the immune system and are very treatable if we find them.'
The two same-day referral questions: 'Any blisters near your eye or on your nose?' and 'Any in or around the ear, or any weakness of your face?'

The examination request with its reason, and the contagion line: 'Because I'm looking for an underlying cause rather than examining the rash…' · 'The fluid can give chickenpox — not shingles — to someone who's never had it. Keep it covered until every blister has crusted.'

Can I give it to the grandkids?' · 'Will the pain go away?' · 'Cancer? … my brother had lymphoma' · and 'Thanks for not fobbing me off with a cream.'
pefe: The examination feels strange only if you have misread the station. Candidates ask the examiner to describe the rash and get told something they already know — the examination here is a general one looking for an underlying immunosuppressive illness, and naming the reason as you ask is what shows the examiner you understand that.

Role-player: Kevin Beattie, 60, a warehouse supervisor. Four days ago he developed a band of blisters around his left ribs, preceded by two days of burning. The pain is nine out of ten and he cannot bear his shirt touching it. He has come expecting a cream and is irritated that it is taking so long. He had chickenpox as a child. No blisters near the eye, nose or ear, no facial weakness, no fever or confusion. Medications: one blood pressure tablet, no steroids, no methotrexate, no chemotherapy ever. He smokes ten a day and drinks four or five beers most nights.

What he gives only if asked: about five kilos of unintentional weight loss over a few months, which he blames on stress at work · waking at night sweating, which he blames on the weather · and getting up at night to pass urine more than he used to. He is initially uncomfortable being asked about sexual health — 'What's that got to do with a rash?' — but answers if it is explained well. If the doctor spends the whole history on the rash he answers briefly and volunteers nothing; if they signpost that they want to know why it happened, he becomes cooperative. If cancer is mentioned he goes quiet and then says 'My brother had lymphoma' — which is his hidden concern, and he has been quietly frightened by the weight loss for weeks. If the doctor is honest about being concerned but has a clear plan, he is grateful rather than panicked.

Mark them against these: took a brief, focused rash history rather than an exhaustive one · asked about the eye, the nose and the ear · asked about severity and character of the pain including light touch · signposted that they wanted to explore why it had happened · asked about weight loss and night sweats · asked about lumps, bowels, blood and cough · asked about thirst and nocturia · asked about steroids and immunosuppressive medications · raised sexual health and HIV testing with a proper explanation · asked the examiner for a general examination, naming lymph nodes, spleen, weight and mouth · explained shingles as reactivation in a nerve, in plain words · explained why the rash is one-sided and stops at the midline · explained the causes — age, diabetes, medications, cancer, HIV · was honest about their concern given the weight loss and the glands · started antiviral treatment and did not wait for results · took the pain seriously and offered adequate analgesia · gave contagion advice · ordered investigations aimed at the cause · gave clear red flags and a review date · and responded to his brother's lymphoma with empathy rather than deflection.

How to ask — 'I'd like the examination findings, please. Because I'm looking for an underlying cause rather than examining the rash, I would specifically like: vital signs and temperature · weight · lymph nodes in the neck, axillae and groins · abdominal examination for hepatomegaly or splenomegaly · the mouth for oral candida · the chest · the skin generally for lesions outside the dermatome · and the eye, if there is any facial involvement'

What each finding would mean — Lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly → lymphoma or leukaemia · oral candida → significant immunosuppression · weight loss or cachexia → malignancy or chronic disease · lesions beyond the dermatome → disseminated zoster · red eye or corneal involvement → ophthalmic zoster · facial weakness → Ramsay hunt

The rash description — one line, then move on — 'I'd also confirm the rash is a grouped vesicular eruption in a single dermatome that does not cross the midline, and note whether the lesions are vesicular, pustular or crusted, which tells me how far through the illness he is.' that is all you need

setting: This is a framework card, not only a single case. The examiners can place an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient into any station — antenatal, chest pain, paediatric, palliative or emergency — and when they do, the same small set of behaviours earns marks and the same small set loses them. Whatever the tasks say, there is an additional unwritten task: demonstrate culturally safe practice, assessed through how you open, who you offer, what you assume and how you plan.
stem: Worked case — general practice, rural South Australia. A 45-year-old Aboriginal man has come because his sister told him he should get a check-up. He has not seen a doctor in several years and says he feels 'All right'.
His file records blood pressure 152/94 at a community screening event eighteen months ago, never followed up. No current medications. A family history of diabetes and kidney disease.
Tasks: take a history — explain what a health assessment involves and what you would check — discuss your management plan, including follow-up.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Explain what a health assessment involves and what you would check
Discuss your management plan, including follow-up
time: Spend the first minute earning the rest of the consultation — the identification question asked routinely so it is clearly not about him, then the offers · then the person before the organ · then the medical and family history · then risk factors asked neutrally and social and emotional wellbeing · then the access question · then the assessment explained and the blood pressure acted on · then the practical levers and the return negotiated

back.dx: Untreated hypertension with substantial undifferentiated cardiometabolic and renal risk, in a man with significant access barriers — and the most important clinical outcome of this consultation is the second consultation. Why the framework exists: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians experience a substantially lower life expectancy and a higher burden of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, respiratory disease, rheumatic heart disease and ear disease, with onset at younger ages VERIFY. The causes are structural rather than personal — dispossession, intergenerational trauma, racism, and inequitable access to housing, education, employment and health services — and if it comes up, say it correctly and never in a way that locates the problem in the patient. Say it to the examiner if asked; do not lecture the patient about his own community. What follows clinically: screening starts earlier and is repeated more often, access barriers must be actively removed rather than noted, and care works best when it is community-controlled, family-inclusive and continuous. The history takes the whole person: medical, including previous rheumatic fever or a heart murmur and the routinely under-asked ears, eyes, teeth and skin · social and emotional wellbeing — who is at home, what he does, where he is from because country and community matter, how he is travelling in himself, any sorry business or loss, housing, and who he goes to when things are hard · and risk factors asked neutrally and never assumed, in exactly the tone you would use with anyone. The wording that separates a pass from an offence: never 'I assume you'd be drinking a fair bit?', 'People in your community often…', 'Do you have a job at all?' or 'You people are at high risk of…'; instead 'Do you drink? If so, how much and how often?', 'Tell me about your situation at home', 'What do you do day to day?' and 'There are some things I'd check earlier for you than for others — can I explain why?' The health assessment, explained plainly as broader than a normal appointment and free: measure and examine — blood pressure, height, weight, waist · heart and chest, listening deliberately for a murmur · ears with otoscopy and hearing, because chronic ear disease is common and under-treated · eyes including vision and retinal screening · teeth and gums · skin, feet and pulses. Investigate — blood glucose and HbA1c · lipids and cardiovascular risk assessment commenced at a younger age than in the general population VERIFY · eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, which is the test that gets left off · full blood count and iron studies · sexually transmitted infection screening where appropriate · and age-appropriate bowel, cervical and breast screening. Prevent and support — immunisation per the indigenous schedule VERIFY · smoking cessation with Quitline 13 7848 and the Aboriginal Quitline where available · alcohol and other drug support if wanted · social and emotional wellbeing supports · hearing and dental referral · and the follow-up items attached to the assessment for nurse, health worker and allied health VERIFY. The blood pressure is acted on rather than repeating the last CLINICIAN'S omission, and acknowledging that failure honestly — 'That's not good enough and I'm sorry' — builds more trust than any reassurance. The enabling is where marks are won or lost, because noting a barrier scores nothing and removing it scores: cost → closing the gap PBS registration done today in the practice, bulk billing, generic options VERIFY · transport → one visit for everything, health worker transport, telehealth, PATS for specialist travel · time off work → batch the bloods and appointments · fear or past experience → an Aboriginal health worker, a support person, and continuity with one clinician · literacy → plain-language written information and checking understanding rather than asking 'Do you understand?' · distance → shared care with the local clinic and a named contact. And the follow-up is the treatment: 'What would make it easier for you to come back?' · 'Would you rather see me, or one of the Aboriginal health workers first?' · 'Is it alright if we ring you if we don't see you?' — with a recall set and named, one named contact at the practice, the next appointment booked before he leaves, everything batched into as few visits as possible, shared care with the ACCHS if he prefers, and family involved if he wants them. In hospital stations, ask about cultural obligations, family presence and practices around serious illness and dying — and let the family lead.
plan: Open, ask what brings him in, and then ask the identification question of everyone — framed as such, so it is clearly not about him: 'Before we go on, I ask everybody this: are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin?'

Explain why you asked, then make the offers — an Aboriginal health worker to sit in · a support person or family · an interpreter if a traditional language is preferred, through TIS National 131 450 and never a family member for clinical content · and a choice of clinician gender where the consultation involves men's or women's business. Offer once, accept the answer gracefully, move on.

Signpost and hand over some control: 'I'd like to hear about you first, then talk about a check-up that's available to you, then work out a plan together. Stop me any time, and tell me if there's something you'd rather not talk about today.'

THE PERSON BEFORE THE ORGAN — WHO IS AT HOME, WHAT HE DOES, WHERE FAMILY IS FROM, AND HOW HE IS TRAVELLING IN HIMSELF. Sixty seconds of genuine interest buys the rest of the consultation, and going straight to risk factors forfeits it.

Medical and family history — known problems, medications, allergies, immunisation · any rheumatic fever or heart murmur, which is a specific and important question in this population and changes your examination · and what runs in the family, which here is dialysis and diabetes and drives the testing.
RISK FACTORS ASKED NEUTRALLY AND SOCIAL AND EMOTIONAL WELLBEING ASKED USING THAT FRAMING — INCLUDING SORRY BUSINESS OR RECENT LOSS. Then WAIT after the question rather than rephrasing it three times.

THE ACCESS QUESTION, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT EXPLAINS THE LAST FIVE YEARS: 'HAS SOMETHING MADE IT HARD TO COME IN TO A DOCTOR BEFORE?' — then LISTEN, and do not defend the system or explain the experience away.

Explain the health assessment plainly and say what you would check and why — linking the kidney and sugar tests to his own family history (see dx). And answer 'I feel fine' honestly: 'A lot of these things don't make you feel anything until quite late. That's exactly why the check is worth doing.'
The blood pressure — repeated today, acted on, and the previous omission acknowledged honestly.

The practical levers, named and done rather than mentioned — closing the gap PBS registered today · a care plan for free allied health · health worker support with appointments · and shared care with the ACCHS if he prefers it.

Negotiate the return, book the next appointment before he leaves, set a recall and name a contact — because for a man who has not seen a doctor in years, the follow-up plan is the treatment and 'Come back if you're worried' is not one.

ask: The sentence to open with in any station: 'I ask everybody this: are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin? … thanks — the reason I ask is that it opens up some things that are there for you. Would you like one of our Aboriginal health workers to sit in?'

The questions that reach the person: 'Tell me a bit about you — who's at home, what you do, where family's from.' · 'How are you travelling in yourself?' · 'Has there been any sorry business or loss in the family?' · and 'Has something made it hard to come in to a doctor before?'

The two clinical questions specific to this population: 'Were you ever told you had rheumatic fever, or a murmur?' and the kidney screen that must include a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, not just a creatinine.

The enabling lines, said as actions rather than observations: 'There's a scheme that makes your medicines much cheaper or free — I can register you today.' · 'If you'd rather go through the Aboriginal health service, that's completely fine and I'll work with them.' · 'What would make it easier for you to come back?'

Challenges: 'My sister made me come' · 'I feel fine, but' · 'I don't really come to doctors' · 'My uncle went into hospital and never came home' · 'Nobody ever rang me' about the blood pressure · 'Can't afford the tablets anyway' · 'I'd have to get a lift into town' · and, only if asked what worries him most, 'Ending up on the machine like mum. And the grandkids.'
pefe: The examination is the health assessment itself and is deliberately broad — blood pressure and anthropometry, heart and chest with deliberate listening for a murmur, ears, eyes, teeth, skin, feet and pulses. The characteristic gaps are the ears and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and both are marked.

Role-player: Trevor Karpany, 45, who does fencing and seasonal farm work and lives with his partner and two grandchildren, with family from up the river. He has not seen a doctor in about five years and is here because his sister kept nagging him. Polite but reserved, he does not volunteer things. He does not know his blood pressure was high, because nobody rang him after the community screening day. His mother is on dialysis and his father had 'The sugar'. He may have had rheumatic fever as a child and is not sure. He smokes about ten a day and drinks on weekends, and food is expensive and limited at the local store.

How he plays it, and what it tells you: he takes pauses before answering and makes limited eye contact, which is normal for him rather than evasion. If the doctor fills his pauses or talks over him, he gives shorter answers for the rest of the station; if they wait, he gives a fuller answer. If the identification question is never asked he does not volunteer it; if it is asked routinely and explained he answers readily and warms slightly. If the doctor makes an assumption — 'I assume you'd be drinking a fair bit' — he goes flat and closed for the rest of the consultation. His brother died last year, mentioned only if asked how he is going or about loss, and only after a pause. He does not like hospitals because his uncle went in and never came home, mentioned only if asked whether something has made it hard to come in. He could not afford tablets in the past, which is the real reason he stopped going. His hidden concern, given only if asked what worries him most, is ending up on dialysis like his mother and the grandchildren being left without him.

What cultural safety actually means — It is defined by the recipient, not the provider — not a checklist you complete but whether the patient experiences the encounter as safe, respectful and free of judgement. Cultural awareness is knowing difference exists; cultural competence is having skills to work across it; cultural safety goes further and requires you to examine your own assumptions and the power imbalance in the room VERIFY

And the term to use — Social and emotional wellbeing is commonly preferred over 'Mental health' and is broader — connection to body, mind and emotions, family and kinship, community, culture, country and spirituality. Using the phrase signals that you understand health is not only individual VERIFY

stem: Version A, the current recall — Jenny, 28, 35 weeks pregnant, presents to your rural general practice or emergency department concerned about her pregnancy. In her opening statement she says she is leaking fluid from the vagina. Tasks: take a history (6 minutes) — physical examination findings are on a card, read them — explain the diagnosis to the patient.

Version B, the older recall — Jenny, 28, 33 weeks pregnant, complaining of passing fluid from the vagina since one hour ago. Tasks: take a history (4 minutes) — ask the examiner for physical examination findings — explain the diagnosis with reasons — explain your management plan.
In both: she had a LLETZ or cone for abnormal cells before this pregnancy, and at the 20-week scan the cervix was short so a cerclage was placed. On speculum the suture may be visible.

back.dx: Preterm pre-labour rupture of membranes at 33-35 weeks with a cervical cerclage in situ, no infection, no labour and GBS unknown. Explain it in lay words with the two reasons: 'Your waters have broken early, before 37 weeks and before labour. I think that because the fluid you describe — a gush, clear, no smell — is typical of the water around the baby, and because I could see it pooled in the vagina, and I've taken a sample to confirm. Importantly, you're not in labour and there's no sign of infection.' then the two risks that drive everything that follows: 'Infection can get into the fluid now the seal is broken, and labour can start any time, so the baby may come early — and early babies can have breathing trouble.' Investigations in three groups: bloods, swabs and a urine test for infection · an ultrasound for liquor volume and presentation · and a CTG for the baby. Treatment: prophylactic erythromycin 250 mg QID for ten days · betamethasone 11.4 mg IM twice, 24 hours apart, if under 35 weeks, which works within about 48 hours · magnesium sulphate if under 30 weeks · nifedipine tocolysis for 48 hours only and only with contractions, never with infection · and because the GBS swab has not been done, benzylpenicillin 3 g IV then 1.8 g four-hourly once labour starts VERIFY. Then the two choices, offered rather than dictated, because delivering a plan without options is the trap. Expectant versus active: wait with close monitoring — twice-weekly CRP, FBC and CTG, and four-hourly temperatures — until the end of 36 completed weeks and then induce, giving a more mature baby while watching for infection; or induce now, which at 35 weeks is also reasonable VERIFY. Hospital versus home: some women can go home after a couple of stable days, but she is an hour and a half away and the local hospital cannot care for a 35-week baby, so advise transfer to a hospital with a nursery — and say explicitly that it remains her decision. The avoid list and red flags: no sex, no tampons, no swimming · come straight back for fever, smelly or coloured fluid, tightenings, bleeding, or fewer movements. And the cerclage, which she will ask about: 'There's no single right answer — I'll discuss it with the obstetrician today. At 35 weeks they'll most likely take it out, because it's a source of infection and the lungs are mature enough.' The rule: remove above 32 weeks, or at any gestation for infection, bleeding or labour; below 32 weeks leave it while the steroids work VERIFY. Chorioamnionitis is diagnosed by temperature over 38, maternal heart rate over 100 and fetal heart rate over 160 — and if it is present you do not wait: intravenous antibiotics now, the stitch comes out, and the baby is born today, by induction if the trace is fine and by caesarean if it is not, with retrieval to a centre with paediatricians. Greenish fluid with reduced movements means meconium and possible fetal compromise — CTG now, and plan the birth today rather than wait if the trace is reassuring, or deliver urgently if it is not.
