Accepting 'Abnormal drums' is not enough: the explicit absence of redness, bulging, perforation and discharge is how you justify not prescribing an antibiotic

'Frequency is on the horizontal axis in hertz, and hearing level on the vertical axis in decibels, increasing downwards — so the lower the mark, the louder the sound needed to be. The normal range is 0 to 20 decibels.' then right ear: air conduction 45-50 dB, outside the normal band; bone conduction 5-10 dB, within it; an air-bone gap of roughly 40 dB. Then the left ear, same pattern. Only then name it

back.dx: BILATERAL OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION — glue ear — causing a bilateral moderate conductive hearing loss and consequent expressive language delay. To the mother, in plain English and without the terminology you already used with the examiner: 'Cooper has fluid sitting behind both of his eardrums. It is not an infection at the moment — there is no redness and he is not in pain — but the fluid is there. It is very common after repeated ear infections.' then the mechanism and the analogy: 'The eardrum has to be able to move to pass sound through to the hearing nerve. With fluid behind it, it cannot move properly, so everything he hears arrives muffled — as if he were listening from underwater.' then the reassuring half of the test: the part that goes through the eardrum is reduced, the part that goes straight to the hearing nerve is completely normal, so the problem is mechanical and mechanical problems can be fixed. And the link that explains why she came: 'Children learn to talk by hearing words clearly. If everything is muffled during the years they are learning language, speech falls behind. It is not that he is not bright, and it is not anything you have done.' The management has four parts and two referrals that go together rather than in sequence. First, ENT referral — because the fluid is bilateral, long-standing and affecting speech, he is likely to be offered grommets, tiny ventilation tubes that let the fluid drain and air back in, with hearing usually improving straight away and the tubes extruding themselves over six to twelve months. Second, and just as important, speech pathology — started today, not after the ears are fixed, because he has ground to make up. Third, repeat the hearing test after treatment. Fourth, review the rest of his development rather than just his talking. Then the antibiotic sentence, said explicitly and held under pressure: 'Antibiotics will not fix this, and neither will antihistamines, decongestants or steroid sprays. Those treat infection, and what cooper has now is fluid rather than infection. I know he has had a great deal of antibiotics over the last year, and I do not want you to think we are simply not trying.' if she pushes: they genuinely do not clear the fluid and each course carries side effects and resistance, but another acute infection with pain and fever is different and would be treated. Home advice: keep him away from cigarette smoke in the house and the car · get down to his level and have his attention before speaking · turn the television off when talking to him · read to him close up, face to face · and no bottle lying flat. The examiner's three follow-ups have set answers. Type B versus type C: type C is a peak shifted into negative pressure, meaning the Eustachian tube is not ventilating but there is air in there; type B is flat, the drum is not moving at all, and with a normal canal volume that means fluid — a large canal volume would suggest a perforation or a patent grommet instead. Why bone conduction is unaffected: the transducer sits on the mastoid and vibrates the skull directly, bypassing the canal, drum and ossicles, so it tests the cochlea and nerve alone. Could it be mixed: no — in a mixed loss the bone conduction line would also fall below the normal band. And if the audiogram is sensorineural instead, with air and bone together at 60-70 dB and no gap, the effusion does not explain it: ask about newborn hearing screening, family history of childhood deafness, meningitis, congenital CMV and ototoxic medication, and refer urgently — grommets are not the answer.
plan: GREET THE MOTHER FIRST AND BY NAME, BEFORE TURNING TO THE EXAMINER — AND VALIDATE HER IMMEDIATELY: 'YOU WERE ABSOLUTELY RIGHT TO BRING HIM IN.' It is true, and it pre-empts the guilt she will otherwise express at minute six.
The examination request, delivered as one continuous run — general, behaviour, growth, ears characterised, nose, palate and tongue tie, nodes, neurology and chest (see findings).

THE AUDIOGRAM — AXES FIRST, THEN RIGHT EAR AIR THEN BONE THEN THE GAP, THEN THE LEFT EAR, THEN THE CONCLUSION, THEN THE TYMPANOGRAMS. Saying 'bilateral conductive hearing loss' and stopping shows pattern recognition rather than interpretation.

TURN BACK TO HER — 'THANK YOU FOR WAITING' — AND EXPLAIN THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH THE UNDERWATER ANALOGY AND THE LINK TO HIS SPEECH (see dx). Expect her four questions: is he deaf, is it my fault, will he catch up, how bad is it.
The four-part plan — ENT for grommets, speech pathology in parallel, a repeat hearing test, and developmental review.
THE ANTIBIOTIC SENTENCE, SAID EXPLICITLY — AND HELD WHEN SHE ASKS FOR ANOTHER COURSE. Caving to satisfy her is the easiest way to lose the management domain.
Home advice, safety-net and summary: 'Come back sooner if he gets a painful ear, a fever, any discharge from the ear, if he seems to be hearing less than he was, or if he loses words he already had.'

The opening that pre-empts the tears: 'You were absolutely right to bring him in.' and the reassurance she is waiting for: 'His hearing is reduced, not absent, and the nerve itself is working perfectly.'

The line that must be said and held: 'Antibiotics will not fix this, and neither will antihistamines or decongestants.' and the pairing that is separately marked: 'ENT for grommets, and speech pathology — both today, not one after the other.'

The examination questions most often omitted: 'Are there any dysmorphic features? What are his growth centiles?' · 'Does he make eye contact and respond when his name is called?' · 'Is the palate intact? Is there a tongue tie?'

Challenges: 'So he is not deaf?' · 'Is it my fault? I did not realise' · 'Will he catch up?' · 'An operation? He is only two' · 'Can we not just try another course of antibiotics first?' · 'How long will we wait to see the specialist?' · 'Is there anything I can do at home?' · and, tearful at about minute six, 'I keep thinking I should have brought him in sooner.'
pefe: Role-player: cooper's mother. He is 2 years 9 months and uses about six words — mum, dad, more, no, ball, dog — never putting two together, pointing and pulling her by the hand instead. Normal pregnancy and birth, passed the newborn hearing check, walked at 13 months, happy and sociable with plenty of eye contact. About eight ear infections in the past year with antibiotics every time, the last six months ago. Childcare two days a week. His father smokes, mostly outside but sometimes in the car. English at home plus Vietnamese from his grandmother, and he says little in either.

What she has noticed and what she hides: he often does not turn when called from another room, which she assumed was toddler behaviour; he turns the television up; he is increasingly frustrated. Her hidden agenda is a fear that he is autistic, after her neighbour's son was diagnosed last year — raised only if the doctor asks whether anything in particular is worrying her, or mentions development. She also carries guilt about not coming sooner, and becomes tearful once at about minute six.

How she plays it: anxious, articulate and paying close attention. When surgery is mentioned she pushes back once — 'An operation? He is only two' — and then asks for another course of antibiotics. She accepts the plan only if the doctor explains why antibiotics will not work. If they simply prescribe antibiotics to please her, she accepts cheerfully and marks them down for it.

Mark them against these: greeted her before turning to the examiner · validated her concern early · asked about dysmorphic features and growth centiles · asked about eye contact and response to name · asked otoscopy of both ears and characterised the drums · explicitly excluded redness, bulging, perforation and discharge · asked about the palate and tongue tie · asked about tone and reflexes · explained the audiogram axes before interpreting · narrated air, then bone, then the gap, for the right ear, and the same for the left · named bilateral conductive loss after the narration · mentioned the tympanograms · explained glue ear in plain English with no jargon · used the underwater analogy · explained that the nerve is normal · linked the hearing loss to the speech delay · told her it was not her fault · handled the autism worry seriously if raised · referred to ENT for grommets · referred to speech pathology as well and in parallel · said antibiotics will not fix this and explained why · held that position when pushed · mentioned a repeat hearing test · mentioned smoke avoidance and home strategies · and safety-netted and summarised.

And the palate, which costs four words — Nose — septum, polyps, mucosa · mouth — is the palate intact, including submucous cleft or a bifid uvula, any tongue tie, tonsil size · cervical nodes · chest. A submucous cleft can be missed for years and presents with exactly this picture — nasal speech, recurrent middle ear disease and language delay

The conclusion, and the tympanograms — 'Bone conduction is normal in both ears, which tells me the cochlea and the auditory nerve are working. The deficit is therefore in the conducting apparatus. I am concluding this is a bilateral, moderate, conductive hearing loss.' plus type B tympanograms bilaterally with normal canal volumes, consistent with a middle ear effusion

back.dx: A SELF-LIMITING DIVERTICULAR BLEED THAT HAS STOPPED — but the clinical point the station is really testing is that fresh rectal bleeding in a 73-year-old is colorectal cancer until a lumen view says otherwise. A five-year-old colonoscopy showing diverticulosis does not exclude an interval cancer, and diverticular disease is so common that its presence proves nothing about the source of today's bleed VERIFY. Handing over 'Known diverticular bleed, settled, for discharge' without raising re-scoping closes a diagnosis on the telephone. The call: identify yourself by name and role, confirm who you are speaking to, and name the patient, the age and the bed. Situation in one sentence with your level of concern — 'He was admitted two days ago with fresh rectal bleeding, he has settled completely and he's stable. I'm calling because I think he's ready for discharge planning and I'd like your view on whether that happens today and what follow-up he needs.' Background: relevant only — the bleeding pattern, the five-year-old scope and the absence of a repeat, and the aspirin 100 mg named explicitly alongside the absence of any other agent that affects bleeding. Assessment: observations in a fixed order — temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, saturations, GCS — including the admission postural drop; the examination positives and relevant negatives; the haemoglobin with its trend and what you make of it; then your impression, which is the half candidates omit and where the marks are. Recommendation, which here has two parts: first a decision on discharge today after 48 stable hours with a stable haemoglobin, and second — the part that matters more — that he needs a colonoscopy, with an explicit ask about whether that is inpatient or booked as an outpatient before he leaves. Also flag the aspirin: the indication is not documented anywhere in the notes, and primary versus secondary prevention give different answers, so say you will check it rather than deciding blind added. His family history and screening status are also absent from the notes — saying so is better than assuming either way. Close with a read-back of the plan and the timeframe, and say who you will tell.
plan: READ THE NOTES BACKWARDS — the most recent progress note and observations tell you what you are handing over NOW; the admission note tells you how it started. Reading forwards through five pages means arriving at the current state with ninety seconds left.
PLAN THE CALL ON PAPER — one line per letter, and WRITE THE IMPRESSION AND THE ASK FIRST, because they are the two things you will otherwise leave out.
IDENTIFY — you, them, the patient, and the bed and ward. Ten to fifteen seconds, and do not apologise for calling.
SITUATION — one sentence, with your level of concern stated in words: stable, settling, ready for planning (see dx).
BACKGROUND — relevant only, with the aspirin and the absence of other bleeding agents said explicitly, and the five-year-old scope flagged.
ASSESSMENT — observations in order including THE ADMISSION POSTURAL DROP, examination, the haemoglobin trend with your reading of it, then YOUR IMPRESSION.
RECOMMENDATION — the two-part ask, with the colonoscopy as the substantive one, plus what has been done and what you will do meanwhile.
THE REGISTRAR'S QUESTIONS — expect three to five, answered in one sentence each.
READ BACK the plan and the timeframe, and state who you will tell.
back.planNote: a stable patient, so a conventional ISBAR run — the ask is held to the end here, unlike the ruptured aneurysm case
ask: THE SENTENCE THAT SEPARATES REPORTING FROM HANDING OVER: 'MY CONCERN IS THAT THIS IS A SELF-LIMITING DIVERTICULAR BLEED THAT HAS STOPPED, AND WHAT I WOULD LIKE IS…' — an impression followed by an ask. Everything before that sentence is data, and data alone is what a fax does.

The substantive ask: 'He's 73 with rectal bleeding and his last scope was five years ago, so I don't think we can put this down to diverticular disease without looking. I'd like to know whether you want that as an inpatient or booked as an outpatient before he leaves.'

The honest line about the numbers: 'Repeat haemoglobin today is 129 — that's three down from admission, which I read as stable rather than an ongoing bleed.' and the one about the aspirin: 'I don't have the indication documented, so I'll check that.'
The close: 'Can I read that back to make sure I've got it?'

Registrar challenges: 'How sick is he — do I need to come now?' · 'Is he still bleeding?' · 'What's his haemoglobin, and what was it before?' · 'He's got known diverticular disease — why does he need a scope?' · 'Do we stop the aspirin?' · 'Where is he?' · and 'What do you actually want from me?'
pefe: There is no examination task — the clinical notes are the data, and the skill is translating a document written in the order things happened into a call delivered in the order the listener needs them.

Role-player: the on-call surgical registrar — busy, not hostile, somewhere else in the hospital and unable to see the patient. Answers the phone with 'Surgical registrar.' and nothing else. Interrupts once early with 'Sorry — how sick is he? Do I need to come now?' and, if the candidate starts with the admission history rather than the current state, cuts in with 'Just tell me the obs first.'

How the registrar scores it in real time: if the candidate never gives an impression, ask 'So what do you think is going on?' and mark them down for having needed to be asked. If they never make a specific request, ask 'Ok — so what do you want me to do?' and mark them down. End with 'Anything else?' and wait to see whether they read back the plan.

The two traps in these numbers — THERE WAS A POSTURAL DROP ON ADMISSION — 120/80 LYING TO 100/70 SITTING IS A FALL OF 20 SYSTOLIC AND 10 DIASTOLIC, AT OR BEYOND THE USUAL THRESHOLD, AND THE ONE ABNORMAL NUMBER IN AN OTHERWISE REASSURING SET VERIFY. The Day 1 note is a statement about Day 1, not a correction of it — handing over 'his observations have been normal throughout' is wrong. AND Hb 132 TO 129 IS NOT A FALL: three grams per litre over 48 hours sits within assay and dilutional variation VERIFY, so say the numbers and say what you make of them

back.dx: Contained ruptured infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with haemorrhagic shock. Say the triad out loud, because it is what converts this from abdominal pain to a vascular emergency: pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass VERIFY. The call opens with identification and the request together: 'It's Dr [name], intern in the emergency department at [hospital]. I need you to come to resus now — I have a 65-year-old man with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound and he's hypotensive. Can I give you the details while you're on your way?' Situation: name, age, resus Bay, two hours of sudden severe central abdominal pain radiating to the back at 9 out of 10, now shocked, with an 8 cm infrarenal aneurysm and retroperitoneal blood on bedside ultrasound. Background: ex-smoker with twenty pack-years, hypertension on perindopril and atorvastatin, no anticoagulant and no antiplatelet said explicitly, no allergies, independent and well until two hours ago. Assessment: observations in order, the pallor and diaphoresis, the weak pulses and delayed capillary refill, the pulsatile mass, the lumbar tenderness, and the anuria since onset — then the impression stated as such. Recommendation, which is two questions rather than one: come and see him now, and tell me whether you are taking him straight to theatre or whether he needs retrieval to a vascular centre — followed by the list of what is already done so it is not repeated, and an explicit offer: 'Do you want me to activate the massive transfusion protocol and call MedSTAR while you're coming?' Two points the registrar may probe. First, resuscitation target: in ruptured AAA the aim before definitive repair is permissive hypotension — enough perfusion to maintain consciousness and urine output, not a normal blood pressure — because aggressive fluid loading raises pressure against a contained rupture, dislodges clot and worsens bleeding; say you would titrate to conscious state rather than to a number and confirm the current threshold against local protocol VERIFY. Second, rural reality: a rural site cannot repair this, so the call is actually two calls — the surgical or vascular registrar, and retrieval on MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — and saying that you have started the retrieval conversation in parallel rather than sequentially is the point, because time to theatre is the outcome determinant and a candidate who waits for permission before ringing retrieval has lost time they cannot get back added. Close with a read-back and say that you will update his family.

stem: You are the intern on the ward of a rural hospital. Read the clinical notes provided, then telephone the on-call registrar and hand over the patient using ISBAR.

A 50-year-old man presented to the emergency department yesterday with black, tarry stools over the preceding 24 hours — multiple dark stools with a characteristic offensive smell, consistent with melaena. Two episodes of dizziness on standing since onset, no loss of consciousness. No haematemesis, no coffee-ground vomiting, no bright red blood per rectum. No abdominal pain, though a background of intermittent epigastric discomfort consistent with known reflux.

Longstanding GORD; hypertension on regular treatment. Regular NSAIDs for the past three weeks, two to three times daily, for knee pain, with no gastroprotection. No anticoagulant or antiplatelet. Nkda. Lives independently. No bowel cancer screening to date; mother had bowel cancer. Tasks: hand over using a structured format — answer the registrar's questions — state clearly what you are asking them to do.

back.dx: Upper gastrointestinal bleed, most likely an nsaid-induced peptic ulcer, currently haemodynamically stable. The aetiology is the whole story and fits in one line: longstanding reflux plus three weeks of NSAIDs two to three times daily with no gastroprotection. Naming that link is the assessment. Stopping the NSAID is part of the handover rather than an afterthought — the cause of the bleed is still being administered unless someone stops it, and saying 'I've stopped his nsaid' out loud demonstrates that you have identified the cause and acted on it, which is a scored behaviour. The call: identify yourself and the patient with the bed; situation in one sentence — 24 hours of melaena and postural dizziness, stable, awaiting endoscopy, and you are ringing to ask when that should happen and whether it needs to be tonight. Background: the reflux, the hypertension, and the NSAIDs given the weight they deserve, with the explicit absence of anticoagulant and antiplatelet; the family history of bowel cancer in his mother and the absence of any screening are worth flagging as an incidental issue for later rather than as the acute problem. Assessment: observations in fixed order, the mild pallor, the epigastric tenderness, the rectal finding of black tarry stool with no fresh blood, the two episodes of postural dizziness with none since admission and no haematemesis at any point — then the missing haemoglobin named plainly: 'I don't have his haemoglobin back yet — the bloods went at [time] and I'll ring you the moment I have it' — then the impression. Inventing a number, or quietly skipping it and hoping the registrar does not ask, both fail. Recommendation: a decision on the timing of endoscopy — tonight's list or tomorrow morning's — followed by what is already in place (Pantoprazole 40 mg IV, nil by mouth, IV access with fluids, two-hourly observations, stool chart), the fact that the NSAID has been stopped, and explicit call-back criteria: if he drops his pressure, has haematemesis, or when the haemoglobin arrives. The registrar may ask about risk scores for upper GI bleeding — Glasgow-Blatchford and Rockall exist and stratify the need for intervention, and the honest answer is to name them and say you would confirm the cut-offs before quoting them VERIFY. A transcription note in the source: the document header names the patient mr tony stark while the body of the history refers throughout to mr Z — use one name consistently, because the discrepancy is an artefact of the source rather than a detail of the case correction.

stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Noah, 9 months, referred by the CaFHS nurse because his head circumference has crossed centiles — 50th at birth, 75th at 4 months, 97th at 8 months, and today 47.5 cm, above the 97th. Weight and length both track the 50th.
His mother Kate says he is a happy, sociable baby who sits, transfers objects and babbles. His father wears a size 62 hat.

back.dx: BENIGN FAMILIAL MACROCEPHALY — a large head crossing up to a familial centile, with normal development, a soft flat fontanelle, a normal neurological examination and a macrocephalic parent. Macrocephaly means an ofc above the 97th centile or more than 2 SD; concern is proportional to the rate of crossing and to symptoms, and crossing two major centile lines warrants assessment. To Kate, in plain English: 'Noah does have a big head and the nurse was right to check, because the serious cause is fluid building up inside the skull. I have looked for the signs of that — a tight bulging soft spot, vomiting, drowsiness, eyes turning down, losing skills — and none are there. His body is growing normally, his development is on track, and Dave's head is also above the TOP line. Big heads run in families, and babies with a family big head grow into it in the first year, crossing the lines exactly as Noah has.' Differentials, each with its discriminator: hydrocephalus, obstructive or communicating — bulging fontanelle, splayed sutures, sunset eyes, vomiting, irritability, rapid crossing, and a history of prematurity with IVH or past meningitis · benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces — often familial and self-limiting, with enlarged extra-axial spaces on ultrasound · subdural haematoma or effusion from non-accidental injury — irritability, retinal haemorrhages, bruises, an inconsistent history, and a mandatory report · intracranial mass or cyst — focal signs, regression, seizures · neurofibromatosis 1 — six or more cafe-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, family history · achondroplasia or skeletal dysplasia — short limbs, frontal bossing, short length · metabolic and storage disease such as glutaric aciduria or canavan — regression, hypotonia, dystonia · and overgrowth syndromes such as sotos — tall and large with developmental delay and facial features. Safety-netting is the other half of the diagnosis: return immediately for vomiting, drowsiness, irritability, a bulging soft spot, eyes turning down, a seizure, loss of skills, or a head growing faster than expected — and if the curve keeps diverging rather than running parallel, urgent paediatric review and MRI, with neurosurgery at WCH via MedSTAR if there is acute raised pressure.
plan: Open with the nurse's concern and the mother's own observations — 'The nurse asked me to see Noah about his head size; tell me what you have noticed.' She has noticed nothing, and saying so is itself a finding.

Raised ICP symptoms as a block: vomiting, particularly morning or projectile · irritability or a high-pitched cry · poor feeding · lethargy and sleepiness · seizures · eyes looking down · returning head lag.
Development in detail and in four domains — gross motor, fine motor, language, social — and then the question that matters most: has he lost any skills.
Birth and neonatal: gestation, birth weight and head circumference, instrumental or traumatic delivery, NICU, intraventricular haemorrhage if preterm, neonatal infection or meningitis, jaundice.
THE DECISIVE QUESTION: 'DO YOU OR HIS DAD HAVE BIG HEADS? WHAT HAT SIZE?' Then family history of hydrocephalus, neurofibromatosis, developmental delay or short stature.

Trauma and NAI screen without accusation — any falls or knocks, who cares for him during the day — plus skin birthmarks and cafe-au-lait spots, limb proportions, hearing and vision, immunisations and pregnancy exposures.
Ask for the chart and card and narrate them as a trajectory, ending on the father's 61 cm (see findings).

Diagnosis, differentials with reasons, and the four-part plan: measure both parents, serial ofc every 4-6 weeks with CaFHS, cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle, developmental surveillance at 12 and 18 months — then red flags, and ask her to repeat the plan back.

Her questions and the traps: she asks 'So nothing to worry about?' — and if told 'Nothing at all, no follow-up', she asks 'Shouldn't he have a scan?' if an urgent MRI or CT is ordered before the family history is taken, she HINTS at Dave and then asks about radiation and anaesthetic.

setting: An acute paediatric abdomen where the hallmark is the thing that looks like reassurance: the child is quiet and drowsy between the screaming episodes. Call it gastroenteritis and send him home on oral fluids and the station is lost — and so, in real life, is the bowel.

He has vomited twice and the last vomit was green. He had a cold last week. One nappy this morning had 'Jelly-looking' red mucus. Weight 8.6 kg · HR 150 · RR 34 · T 37.4 · CRT 3 seconds.

The rectal examination, which you have to ask for

back.dx: Ileocolic intussusception, peak incidence 6-18 months, with post-viral lymphoid hyperplasia as the lead point after last week's upper respiratory infection. The classic triad is intermittent colicky pain with pallor and drawing up the legs, vomiting that becomes bilious, and red-currant-jelly stool — but only about a third of children have all three, which is why the interval lethargy is the clue that actually discriminates. To Priya: 'Part of Oliver's bowel has slid into the next section, like a telescope. That explains the waves of pain when the bowel squeezes, the green vomit because the bowel is blocked, and the jelly-like blood because the trapped bowel oozes. His age and last week's cold fit — the glands in the bowel swell and act as the lead point.' Differentials with their discriminators: malrotation with midgut volvulus — bilious vomiting at any age, usually continuous pain without the episodic pattern, and a surgical emergency with the same first steps · incarcerated inguinal hernia — a groin lump, so always examine · acute gastroenteritis — no mass, no bile, watery stool rather than jelly · testicular torsion — scrotal swelling and tenderness in an inconsolable infant · meckel diverticulum — painless bleeding · henoch-schonlein purpura — purpuric rash and joint swelling, and itself a lead point · and sepsis, UTI or meningitis — lethargy and fever without the colic pattern. Management is a sequence, not a list: nil by mouth · IV access with FBE, UEC, glucose, venous gas and lactate, group and hold · a fluid bolus if compromised then maintenance with dextrose · nasogastric tube on free drainage if vomiting or distended · analgesia · urgent ultrasound for the target sign, which must not delay the referral · paediatric surgical referral now to WCH via MedSTAR · air (Pneumatic) enema reduction by radiology with the surgeon present as the definitive treatment · and operative reduction only if the enema fails or there is perforation, peritonitis or shock, in which case resuscitate, give broad-spectrum antibiotics and go straight to a theatre pathway. Safety-netting: observe 24 hours after reduction because about one in ten recur, and tell the mother explicitly that the same screaming episodes mean coming straight back.
plan: The episode pattern first — onset, frequency, duration, what he does during them (Screams, knees up, pallor) and, decisively, what he is like in between: playing, or floppy and drowsy.
Vomit and stool, asked for specifically: how many vomits and what colour — milk turning bile-stained · last normal stool, diarrhoea, and any blood or mucus.
Hydration and intake: last feed tolerated, wet nappies in 12 hours, tears · then recent URTI or gastro in the last two weeks, and fever now.
Red flags for the other causes — groin or scrotal swelling, rash, trauma, ingestion — and background: birth, growth, development, previous abdominal surgery, rotavirus vaccine timing, family history.

The examination request as one run: appearance and hydration between episodes, vitals, abdomen for the mass and the empty right iliac fossa, peritonism, hernial orifices, testes, rectal examination, skin (see findings).
Name the diagnosis with three reasons and give the differentials in one breath each — volvulus and incarcerated hernia as the must-excludes (see dx).
Management in order: NBM · IV fluids and bloods · analgesia · NGT · ultrasound without delaying referral · the surgeon at WCH via MedSTAR · air enema with the surgeon present · theatre if it fails.

Explain the transfer to the mother — retrieval flies them both and she stays with him — then the 24-hour observation, the one-in-ten recurrence and the instruction to return immediately if the episodes restart.

ask: THE QUESTION THAT MAKES THE DIAGNOSIS: 'WHAT IS HE LIKE IN BETWEEN THE EPISODES?' Floppy and sleepy, not himself — and that is the answer that separates this from colic and from gastroenteritis.
The two that must be asked by name: 'Has he vomited, and what colour was it?' and 'Has there been any blood or mucus in the nappy?'

The explanation that lands: 'Like a telescope — one part of the bowel slides inside the next.' and the treatment in her words: 'Air is gently pumped through the bottom under x-ray and it pushes the bowel back into place; it works in most children without an operation.'
The safety-net that is separately marked: 'It can happen again in about one in ten children — if you see the same screaming episodes, come straight back.'

Challenges: 'Is it dangerous?' · 'Do we have to go to Adelaide?' · and, if you say gastro or suggest oral fluids at home, the line that is handing you the diagnosis back — 'But he is so floppy in between, is that normal?'

Two vomits, the second green. One wet nappy today and he refused the bottle. A cold last week. No fever, no groin swelling, no rash, no falls, term baby, all vaccines, no operations, nothing in the family.

What she withholds: the red jelly mucus in the nappy, volunteered only if asked about blood or stool. She is anxious but cooperative; her partner is a truck driver and away tonight, which matters for the transfer conversation.

The child between episodes — Lethargic, pale, mildly dehydrated with dry lips and a capillary refill of 3 seconds, HR 150. The lethargy between episodes is not the child settling — it is a hallmark, and saying so is where the mark is

dx: **Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction — ABO incompatibility from a MIS-IDENTIFIED UNIT.** **Fever, rigors, hypotension, loin or back pain and haemoglobinuria WITHIN THE FIRST 15–30 MINUTES.** **DIC and acute kidney injury follow.**

**THE FIRST SENTENCE MUST BE ‘STOP THE TRANSFUSION’ — before questions, before examination.** Then, in order, to the nurse: **‘Disconnect the giving set and KEEP THE PACK AND SET — don't discard them.’ · ‘Keep the cannula, flush with saline and start 0.9% saline VIA A NEW GIVING SET.’ · ‘ABC: oxygen if saturations under 94, full obs every 15 minutes, call the registrar and notify the blood bank.’ · ‘Check the patient's wristband against the blood pack label and the compatibility form WITH ME NOW.’**

**The three discriminators, in order**: **(1) STOP, first sentence. (2) CHECK THE IDENTITY of unit and patient and recognise the mismatch as the cause. (3) OPEN DISCLOSURE — tell Helen plainly that THE WRONG UNIT WAS GIVEN, rather than hiding behind ‘a reaction’.**

**THE FIVE REACTIONS** VERIFY — **ACUTE HAEMOLYTIC (ABO)**: fever, rigors, hypotension, loin or back pain, haemoglobinuria, oozing, identity mismatch. **FEBRILE NON-HAEMOLYTIC**: fever rise ≥1°C, chills, **no hypotension, otherwise well.** **ALLERGIC (mild)**: urticaria and itch, no systemic features. **ANAPHYLAXIS**: wheeze, stridor, angioedema, hypotension within minutes. **BACTERIAL CONTAMINATION (especially platelets)**: high fever, rigors, shock. **TACO**: dyspnoea, **HYPERTENSION**, raised JVP, crackles, elderly or cardiac. **TRALI**: hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates, fever, hypotension within 6 hours.
**TIME COURSE sorts them**: **haemolytic and anaphylaxis — MINUTES** · FNHTR — during or within 4 hours · **TACO and TRALI — within 6 hours** · **delayed haemolytic — 3 to 14 days.**

**RENAL PROTECTION, QUANTIFIED — this is a scored item, not a gesture.** **IV 0.9% saline bolus 500 mL to 1 L, then an infusion to maintain URINE OUTPUT ABOVE 1 mL/kg/h** — free haemoglobin is what damages the kidney. **Catheter and HOURLY urine measures.** **Consider furosemide 40 mg IV ONLY if oliguric DESPITE adequate filling.** VERIFY

**Escalate and report**: registrar and physician, **ICU or HDU review**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if deteriorating at a rural site; haematology advice via the blood service. **DIC — FFP, cryoprecipitate and platelets UNDER HAEMATOLOGY GUIDANCE ONLY.** **Notify the blood bank and Australian Red Cross Lifeblood, RETURN the unit and set, file an incident report, and expect a root-cause analysis of the identification error.**

**DO NOT RESTART ANY BLOOD until a full investigation is complete.** Re-crossmatch new units when needed. **Treat the anaemia later with correctly crossmatched blood or IV iron, and manage the menorrhagia that caused it.**

**OPEN DISCLOSURE, in these words**: **‘Helen, I need to explain what's happened. The blood you were being given was NOT the unit matched for you — the label has a different hospital number. Your immune system is breaking down those blood cells, which is causing the fever, the back pain and the dark urine. We've stopped it, we're giving you fluid to protect your kidneys, and we'll watch your blood counts, clotting and kidney function closely with the senior team. I'M SORRY THIS HAS HAPPENED; IT'S AN ERROR, AND IT WILL BE FULLY INVESTIGATED AND YOU'LL BE TOLD THE FINDINGS.’**

**Answering ‘Am I going to be all right?’**: **‘Most people recover with the treatment we've started, and we've caught it early. The next hours matter, so you'll be closely monitored, possibly in the high-dependency unit. No more blood will be given until everything has been re-checked. Would you like us to call your husband?’** **Then document, and inform next of kin with consent.**
plan: 0:00 — to the NURSE, before anything else

**‘Helen, I'm Dr ___. We've stopped the blood. Tell me what you're feeling.’** Let her give the sequence: **hot and shivery, then the back ache, then the pounding head, and she is frightened.**

**The anaphylaxis screen in one question**: **‘Any chest tightness, trouble breathing, itching or hives, swelling of the lips?’** → no. **That is TACO, TRALI and anaphylaxis screened in a single breath.**

**Timing and the first unit**: **‘How far into this unit did it start? How was the first unit?’** → about half an hour; the first was fine. **The first unit being uneventful is what makes a unit-specific problem likely.**

back.dx: RH(D) ALLOIMMUNISATION — a sensitised Rh-negative mother with an anti-D titre of 1:16 at 12 weeks, following an unprotected sensitising event in the previous pregnancy, and a fetus at risk of haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn if it is Rh positive. The mechanism, explained in her words: 'Your blood group is O negative, which we knew. What is new is that your blood contains antibodies against the d factor. Some of your first baby's blood — probably at that fall or at the birth — mixed with yours, and your immune system learned to make antibodies against it. In a normal Rh-negative pregnancy we give an anti-D injection to prevent exactly this. Once the antibodies exist, the injection cannot undo them.' then the risk, graded and not catastrophised: 'If this baby is also Rh positive, those antibodies can cross the placenta and break down some of the baby's red cells. Mildly, that means jaundice after birth; more seriously, the baby can become anaemic before birth. Your level is the level at which we watch closely — and we have very good ways of monitoring and, if needed, treating this before birth. Most babies do well.' The pathway, in order: refer to maternal-fetal medicine at WCH today rather than waiting for the next titre · establish the fetal Rh status with cell-free fetal DNA RhD genotyping on maternal blood, with the paternal group as a supplementary check — if the fetus is Rh negative there is no risk and care returns to routine · serial titres four-weekly to 28 weeks then two-weekly · MCA peak systolic velocity Doppler from 18-20 weeks once the titre is critical, where a mom above 1.5 indicates moderate to severe fetal anaemia · intrauterine cordocentesis transfusion in the tertiary centre if the fetus is anaemic · delivery planned at the tertiary centre around 37-38 weeks with the neonatal team, cord blood group, DAT, Hb and bilirubin, and phototherapy or exchange transfusion if needed. anti-D immunoglobulin is not indicated and is the common error this station exists to catch correction. The rest of the plan is rural and forward-looking: PATS for travel and accommodation, country health connect, social work, partner testing, written information, and the warning that each subsequent rh-positive pregnancy is usually more severe, so any future pregnancy needs MFM planning from before conception.

The sequence is the station: warning shot — 'Frank, I have the scan and blood results, and I am afraid it is serious news, not what either of us hoped for' · invitation — 'Would you like Maureen in the room?' · then the word itself: 'The scan shows a growth in the head of the pancreas, and with the jaundice, the weight loss and the blood marker I am almost certain this is cancer of the pancreas' · then stop. Silence, tissues, 'I am so sorry. Take your time.' Only then chunk and check: what the pancreas does and why his sugar Rose and he lost weight · why he is yellow and itchy, because the growth is blocking the bile duct · what the scan shows about spread, in plain words — wrapped around a large vein, with two small liver spots not yet certain · and what happens next. The pathway in patient order: confirm the diagnosis with EUS-guided fine needle aspiration and stage with a CT chest · take it to the multidisciplinary team at RAH or FMC, who are the decision-makers on surgery, not you · relieve the jaundice with an ERCP and a metal stent, which fixes the itch and makes him well enough for treatment · keep him strong with pancreatic enzyme replacement at every meal, a dietitian, diabetes optimisation and analgesia that actually works, with a coeliac plexus block later if needed · and involve palliative care now, framed explicitly as symptom expertise rather than surrender, because people seen early live better and often longer. Chemotherapy — folfirinox or gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel if he is fit — is the MDT's discussion VERIFY. The practical layer: INR and vitamin K before any procedure · a glucose plan · paracetamol then a low-dose opioid with a laxative and no NSAIDs VERIFY · driving advice while opioids are adjusted · smoking cessation, which genuinely improves treatment tolerance · Trousseau DVT awareness · a mood and risk check · carer support, centrelink and financial counselling · advance care planning over time · a cancer nurse, cancer council SA 13 11 20, PATS for Adelaide travel · and GP review within days, sooner for fever or rigors.

back.dx: MILD VIRAL UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION, ALREADY IMPROVING — and a hidden agenda: a backdated certificate for an exam missed before the illness began, which he missed because of exam panic. The rule, which must be said plainly: a medical certificate is a legal document, so you certify the date you saw him, the findings you made, and your opinion on fitness from today — and you never backdate the date of examination or state as fact anything you did not observe (Ahpra good medical practice and medical board guidance on certificates) VERIFY. What you can write: a certificate dated today stating you examined him today and found a mild viral illness, unfit for study for a day or two from today · a clearly labelled line of reported history — 'Mr Reid reports that he has been unwell since Thursday with sore throat and fatigue' · and a factual letter for the special-consideration panel setting out his account and today's findings. What you cannot: certify unfitness on a day you did not see him as fact, backdate the consultation, invent findings, or retrospectively certify 'Unfit for exam'. How to say it: 'I can only certify what I have seen — I saw you today. What I cannot do is write, as if I had examined you, that you were unfit on Tuesday. That is not me doubting you — it is the rule every doctor works under, and a backdated certificate can void your application and get us both in trouble.' then the thing that turns a refusal into help: an honest letter about exam panic is a legitimate ground for special consideration and is often stronger than a cold. Differentials for the illness itself: infectious mononucleosis — exudative tonsillitis, posterior nodes, splenomegaly, weeks of fatigue · streptococcal pharyngitis — fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough · influenza or COVID — fever, myalgia, cough, test if in window · and the real differential for the missed exam, which is exam-related anxiety, panic or depression, or a substance-related night. back.dx: SPASTIC DIPLEGIC CEREBRAL PALSY SECONDARY TO PERIVENTRICULAR LEUKOMALACIA OF PREMATURITY — legs more than arms, velocity-dependent hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, scissoring and persistent primitive reflexes, with motor delay but preserved social, visual and communication milestones. The explanation, in plain words: 'Cerebral palsy is the name for a group of conditions that affect movement and posture, caused by an injury to the developing brain — in Liam's case the areas that control the legs, damaged around the time of his very early birth by the bleeding and the fragile blood supply premature brains have. The MRI shows exactly that pattern.' then the three sentences the examiner is listening for: 'It happened once and it does not get worse — it is not a disease that spreads. What changes is how it shows up as he grows, which is why the stiffness is more obvious now than at three months.' · 'Spastic means the muscles are tight; diplegic means mainly the legs, with the arms much less affected — and children with this pattern usually have normal or near-normal thinking, which his smiling, babbling and reaching support.' · 'This is nobody's fault — nothing you did or did not do in pregnancy or since caused this.' On walking, honest and bounded: most children with diplegia do walk — some independently, some with a frame or sticks and a wheelchair for distance — the picture is clearer by two to three years, and sitting unaided by two is a good predictor and exactly what therapy targets now VERIFY. What to exclude: hereditary spastic paraplegia or leukodystrophy — progressive with regression and a family history · a spinal cord lesion such as a tethered cord — legs only with sphincter or back signs · dopa-responsive dystonia — diurnal variation, worth a levodopa trial · global developmental delay or a genetic syndrome — all domains delayed, dysmorphism · and muscular dystrophy — weakness and hypotonia rather than spasticity, check ck. Any loss of skills means this is not cerebral palsy and needs urgent neurology. The team and the plan: paediatrician as coordinator with paediatric neurology and rehabilitation at WCH, and SA cp register notification · physiotherapy for goal-directed task-specific practice, positioning, standing frames and ankle-foot orthoses when standing · occupational therapy for hand function, equipment and home adaptations · speech pathology for feeding and later communication · NDIS early childhood approach for under-sixes as the funding route, applied for today, with novita or kids plus, country health connect, telehealth therapy and PATS for Adelaide trips · spasticity management later with botulinum toxin to calves and adductors from about two years, casting, and oral baclofen if generalised · orthopaedic hip surveillance, because spastic hips sublux silently · and comorbidity surveillance across ophthalmology for the esotropia, audiology, epilepsy vigilance, growth and nutrition, reflux, constipation, dental, sleep and pain. And the family is part of the plan: written information, carer gateway, carer allowance, a separate appointment for Sarah's own sleep and mood, and an offer to go through it all again with her husband present.

dx: **Acute periapical (dentoalveolar) abscess of the lower left first molar, with LOCALISED BUCCAL-SPACE CELLULITIS, systemic features and MILD TRISMUS.**

**THE THREE DISCRIMINATORS**: **(1) check the airway-threatening spread — floor of mouth, tongue elevation, drooling, dysphagia, voice change, stridor, severe trismus = LUDWIG'S ANGINA or a deep neck space infection, and that is an emergency.** **(2) Recognise that THE GP CANNOT CURE A DENTAL ABSCESS — antibiotics are an adjunct; definitive treatment is DRAINAGE or EXTRACTION by a dentist.** **(3) SOLVE THE ACCESS PROBLEM — public dental emergency pathway, cost, transport, PATS.**

**‘Candidates who write amoxicillin and “see a dentist” fail on BOTH counts.’** Say the negatives of the airway screen out loud, then say plainly that the dentist is the treatment, **and show him how he gets there.**

**Explaining it**: **‘You have an abscess — a pocket of pus — at the root of that broken tooth, and the infection has spread into the cheek. The tooth is DEAD and infected, and ANTIBIOTICS ALONE WON'T FIX IT: the pus has to be drained and the tooth root-treated or, more likely, taken out by a dentist. What I can do today is get the infection under control, get you pain relief that's safe, and get you to a dentist quickly and affordably. The one thing I've checked carefully is that the infection hasn't spread under your tongue or into your neck, because that can block the airway — yours hasn't.’**

**ANALGESIA — the combination, and it beats either alone for dental pain**: **paracetamol 1 g QID PLUS ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food.** VERIFY **Warn of the paracetamol maximum of 4 g a day — he is taking ten tablets daily.** **AVOID escalating opioids.**

**ANTIBIOTICS AS ADJUNCT, because of the spreading swelling and fever**: **amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days PLUS metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5 days.** VERIFY **NO ALCOHOL with metronidazole.** **Clindamycin 300 mg 8-hourly if penicillin allergic.** **IV benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin AND admission if systemic toxicity, more than moderate trismus, or deep space involvement.**

**THE ACCESS PLAN, which is half the station**: **Health Care Card → eligible for SA DENTAL SERVICE EMERGENCY CARE. PHONE THE REGIONAL COMMUNITY DENTAL CLINIC NOW for an urgent appointment within 24–48 hours.** Explain the private alternative and its cost. **PATS if referred to the Adelaide Dental Hospital.** Aboriginal dental programs where applicable. **ASK ABOUT TRANSPORT — community transport, or family.** *His brother can drive him.*

**Also**: warm salt-water mouth rinses, soft diet, fluids, keep hygiene up · **if fluctuant and accessible intra-orally, incision and drainage can be done under local anaesthetic; otherwise extraction IS the drainage** · **review in 48 hours, or by phone** · **medical certificate.**

**THE RED FLAGS, given verbatim**: **‘Go straight to emergency, day or night, if the swelling moves UNDER YOUR TONGUE or INTO YOUR NECK, you CAN'T SWALLOW YOUR SPIT, you DROOL, your VOICE CHANGES, you CAN'T OPEN YOUR MOUTH TWO FINGERS, the swelling reaches your EYE, or you get SHAKING CHILLS.’**

**Prevention, raised without moralising**: **smoking cessation (Quitline 13 7848) — ‘the smoking is the biggest thing for your gums, when you're ready’** · sugar reduction · brushing and fluoride · regular dental checks.
plan: **The pain** — site, character (throbbing, **worse lying down and at night**, hot or cold sensitivity), duration, previous episodes, **the broken tooth history**, and **the over-the-counter analgesia with doses.**
**The swelling** — onset, **spread: cheek, under the jaw, neck, eye** · **trismus in finger widths** · bad taste or discharge, which means spontaneous drainage.

**THE AIRWAY AND DEEP-SPACE SCREEN, asked as the SECOND question of the consultation**: **‘Any trouble swallowing your spit? Any drooling? Any muffled or “hot potato” voice? Does your tongue feel pushed up? Any neck stiffness? Any difficulty breathing, or lying flat?’**
**Systemic**: fever, rigors, malaise, appetite. *He was hot and sweaty last night.*
**Dental history and the barriers**: last visit, hygiene, other bad teeth, dentures — **and then the barriers explicitly: cost, distance, fear.** *Ten years, cost, and 90 km.*

**Medical**: **diabetes, immunosuppression** · **heart valve disease or a prosthetic valve** for endocarditis considerations · **bleeding disorders or anticoagulants**, because extraction is coming · allergies, particularly penicillin · medications.

**Social and habits**: smoking, alcohol, sugar-sweetened drinks, **methamphetamine — ‘meth mouth’** · **Health Care Card status for public dental eligibility** · transport · work impact · living alone.

**Ask for the examination, naming the airway items**: **‘I'd like the facial and intra-oral findings, SPECIFICALLY the floor of the mouth, tongue position, trismus, swallowing, voice, and any neck or periorbital swelling, plus vitals and a fingerprick glucose.’**
**Name it, state the airway negatives out loud, and say plainly that antibiotics won't cure it.** Then the differentials.
**The access plan — phone the clinic in the room** — then the analgesia correction, the antibiotics, the rinses, the bloods, the 48-hour review, and the red flags.

back.dx: LARYNGOMALACIA — the commonest cause of chronic infant stridor, where soft supraglottic tissues collapse inward on inspiration: onset at 2-4 weeks, inspiratory, positional, in a thriving infant, self-resolving by 12-24 months. To Bec: 'The tissue at the TOP of the voice box is soft and floppy in the first months, so when he breathes in — especially on his back, feeding or upset — it gets sucked inward and makes that squeak. It is not an infection, it is not croup, and it is not his windpipe collapsing. He is feeding beautifully, gaining weight, pink, and the noise vanishes when he is upright or asleep. The tissue stiffens as he grows — it usually peaks around six to eight months and is gone by his first or second birthday.' The differentials, dismissed with reasons rather than listed: tracheomalacia — present from birth, expiratory or biphasic, rattly with a washing-machine cough · croup — acute, febrile, barking cough in a 6-month to 3-year-old, not a chronic noise from two weeks of age · vascular ring — biphasic with feeding difficulty, dysphagia and recurrent chest infections · subglottic haemangioma — biphasic and worsening between one and three months, with a cutaneous haemangioma in the beard distribution in about half · vocal cord palsy — from birth, weak or hoarse cry, aspiration, after forceps or cardiac surgery · subglottic stenosis — biphasic after neonatal intubation · foreign body — sudden onset in an older infant · and epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis — acute, toxic, drooling, an emergency. The diagnosis is clinical; flexible nasolaryngoscopy by ENT confirms it with an omega-shaped epiglottis and prolapsing arytenoids, and imaging or bronchoscopy is for atypical features only. Management: no treatment today, but warn that the noise usually gets louder before it improves and is worse with colds, which is expected rather than deterioration · feeding upright and paced, smaller and more frequent if he tires, frequent burping and 20-30 minutes upright afterwards · conservative reflux measures, with acid suppression only for clear GORD VERIFY · safe sleep, which is the second scoring point: on his back in his own cot despite the noise, because prone sleeping on a parent's chest is a SIDS risk — said with empathy, acknowledging why she does it · fortnightly weights with CaFHS · ENT referral for poor weight gain or feeding difficulty, apnoea or cyanosis, stridor with retractions at rest, worsening beyond expectations, cough or aspiration, hoarse cry, any haemangioma, or parental anxiety, with supraglottoplasty for the roughly 10% who are severe VERIFY · and red flags straight to emergency: blue or grey colour, pauses in breathing, sucking in at the ribs or neck when calm, fast breathing at rest, refusing feeds, fever with a barking cough, drooling or lethargy. back.dx: BLUNT LEFT RENAL TRAUMA — contusion or laceration — with gross haematuria in a haemodynamically stable patient, plus probable left lower rib fractures and a splenic injury still to exclude. To Tom: 'You landed hard on your left side and there is bruising over the left kidney, tenderness over the kidney, and blood in your urine. That tells me the kidney has been bruised or torn. You are stable, which is reassuring, but blood in the urine after this kind of injury always needs a CT with contrast dye — it shows how deep any tear goes, whether the drainage system is leaking urine, and whether the spleen next door is injured.' The investigation must be named precisely: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast, arterial and portal venous plus a 10-minute delayed excretory phase to detect collecting-system or ureteric leak, with a chest x-ray and CT chest if rib fractures are suspected. Ultrasound or non-contrast CT as the definitive test is a marked error. Differentials with discriminators: splenic injury — left upper quadrant tenderness, referred left shoulder tip pain, tachycardia or hypotension, positive fast · rib fractures with pneumothorax or haemothorax — rib tenderness, crepitus, reduced air entry · bladder or urethral injury — pelvic fracture, blood at the meatus, inability to void, perineal bruising · hollow viscus injury — peritonism, evolving pain, free air · and musculoskeletal contusion alone, which does not produce gross haematuria and so does not excuse skipping imaging. Immediate management: two IV cannulas with FBE, UEC, group and hold, coags and a venous gas and lactate · urinalysis · nil by mouth until the CT is reviewed · analgesia with IV paracetamol and titrated opioid, avoiding NSAIDs while bleeding and renal injury are in play · tetanus status for the abrasions. Disposition by grade: stable grades i-iii are managed non-operatively with admission, bed rest until the gross haematuria clears, serial haemoglobin, hourly to two-hourly observations, repeat examination and urology notification · grades iv-v, haemodynamic instability or an expanding haematoma mean resuscitation, massive transfusion if needed, and urology with interventional radiology for angioembolisation or laparotomy, transferred to the RAH trauma service via MedSTAR. Discharge advice when the time comes: no contact sport or heavy lifting for 4-6 weeks, return for increasing flank pain, fever, recurrent haematuria or dizziness, follow-up imaging for grade III and above, and a blood pressure check at follow-up for post-traumatic hypertension VERIFY.

findings: THE PHOTOGRAPH — describe it with the formula, do not say ‘red itchy rash’
SITE → DISTRIBUTION → MORPHOLOGY (macule/papule/plaque) → COLOUR → SURFACE (scale, crust, excoriation, lichenification) → BORDER → SECONDARY CHANGE → ASSOCIATED FEATURES

‘SYMMETRICAL, BILATERAL ANTECUBITAL FOSSAE. ILL-DEFINED ERYTHEMATOUS PLAQUES with LICHENIFICATION — thickened skin with accentuated markings — multiple LINEAR EXCORIATIONS, and on the left several HONEY-COLOURED CRUSTS suggesting SECONDARY BACTERIAL INFECTION. No vesicles, pustules or scale, no punched-out erosions. In keeping with chronic flexural atopic dermatitis with impetiginisation’
Flexural lichenified plaques with excoriations. A FEW HONEY-COLOURED CRUSTS on the LEFT antecubital fossa. NO VESICLES. No pustules
The negatives that exclude the differentials
NAIL PITTING ABSENT · NO SCALY SCALP · PALMS CLEAR · NO BURROWS IN THE WEB SPACES. Those four exclude psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis and scabies in one sweep
TEMPERATURE 36.8, NO LYMPHADENOPATHY — she is not systemically unwell
What you are LOOKING FOR and did NOT find
NO MONOMORPHIC PUNCHED-OUT VESICLES OR EROSIONS. That is ECZEMA HERPETICUM, and excluding it explicitly is part of the description
The treatment history — ask exactly what, how much, how often, how long
A SUPERMARKET MOISTURISER ‘when I remember’ and 1% HYDROCORTISONE ‘when it's bad’. THAT IS UNDER-TREATMENT, and it is why it ‘never works’. You cannot diagnose under-treatment without asking HOW MUCH
‘How do you feel about steroid creams?’ → ‘I've read they thin your skin.’ If you do not ask, she will not tell you, and she will not use what you prescribe
HAIRDRESSER — WET HANDS ALL DAY, rarely gloves. Long hot showers. Irritant and allergic contact overlap, and a patch-test question
SWAB THE CRUSTED AREA FIRST, then treat. No routine bloods

dx: **Adult atopic dermatitis — flexural, lichenified — with likely SECONDARY STAPHYLOCOCCAL INFECTION (impetiginisation) of the left elbow.**

**THE FIVE DISCRIMINATORS**: **(1) describe the rash SYSTEMATICALLY; (2) recognise the atopic triad and the FLEXURAL pattern; (3) treat with the RIGHT-POTENCY topical steroid, NOT 1% hydrocortisone, plus a proper emollient regimen; (4) spot the IMPETIGINISED patch and treat it; (5) the OCCUPATIONAL trigger — wet work as a hairdresser.**

**THE EXAMINER IS LISTENING FOR POTENCY.** **Naming a MODERATE–POTENT steroid for the body and a MILD one for the face, used DAILY UNTIL CLEAR, alongside a QUANTIFIED emollient regimen.** **Candidates who prescribe ‘hydrocortisone cream and moisturiser’ repeat the failed plan.**

**Explaining it**: **‘Eczema is a condition where the SKIN BARRIER IS LEAKY and the immune system in the skin OVER-REACTS — it isn't an infection or an allergy to one thing. It runs with hay fever and asthma. It's CONTROLLED RATHER THAN CURED, and the two pillars are restoring the barrier with moisturiser and calming the flare with the right-strength steroid cream used properly.’**

**PILLAR ONE — EMOLLIENT, QUANTIFIED**: thick, fragrance-free (sorbolene with glycerine, or an ointment), **twice daily to the WHOLE BODY and after every wash — 250 to 500 g PER WEEK for an adult.** VERIFY **Soap substitute, short lukewarm showers, pat dry, cotton clothing.** To her: **‘a 500-gram tub should last about a week or two.’**

**PILLAR TWO — POTENCY MATCHED TO SITE**: **TRUNK AND LIMBS — moderate/potent: methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% or mometasone 0.1% ONCE DAILY.** **FACE, EYELIDS AND NECK — mild to moderate: hydrocortisone 1% or desonide.** VERIFY **Use ENOUGH — a fingertip unit — daily for one to two weeks until clear, then TWICE-WEEKLY ‘weekend’ maintenance on trouble spots.** **1% hydrocortisone on lichenified elbows is too weak, and that is why it never works.**

**Answering steroid phobia with a SPECIFIC safety explanation, not reassurance**: **‘Skin thinning happens with STRONG steroids used CONTINUOUSLY on THIN skin for MONTHS. Used this way — to clear a flare and then stopped — it's safe, and the untreated scratching does more damage.’**

**THE INFECTION**: the crusted left elbow — **swab first, then flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 7 days** VERIFY **(cephalexin if penicillin allergic).** **Dilute bleach baths twice weekly for recurrent infection.** VERIFY

**The rest**: **sedating antihistamine at night SHORT TERM — for sleep, NOT for the itch itself** · keep nails short · **wet wraps for a severe flare** · **face and eyelids: if a steroid is needed beyond two weeks, a calcineurin inhibitor — pimecrolimus 1% or tacrolimus** VERIFY · **OCCUPATION: nitrile gloves with COTTON LINERS for wet work, hand emollient at every break, consider occupational advice, and PATCH TESTING via dermatology for PPD, fragrance and preservatives.**

**Step-up via dermatology**: phototherapy, methotrexate or ciclosporin, **dupilumab under PBS criteria.** VERIFY **Give a WRITTEN ECZEMA ACTION PLAN and review in 2 weeks.** **RED FLAGS — same day: fever, a rapidly spreading painful rash, CLUSTERS OF SMALL BLISTERS OR PUNCHED-OUT SORES (eczema herpeticum), and eye involvement.**
plan: **The rash** — onset, **sites over time**, **itch severity and timing**, **sleep loss**, bleeding or weeping, **any blisters**, **fever or feeling unwell** (herpeticum).
**The atopic background** — childhood eczema, asthma, hay fever, food allergy, **family atopy.** *Baby eczema, spring hay fever, mother has asthma.*
**Triggers** — heat, sweat, wool, soaps, **hot showers**, stress, seasonal — **and the occupation: hairdresser, wet work, shampoos, dyes, gloves?**

**TREATMENTS — EXACTLY what, HOW MUCH, HOW OFTEN, HOW LONG.** *Supermarket moisturiser ‘when I remember’, 1% hydrocortisone ‘when it's bad’.* **That answer IS the diagnosis of under-treatment.** Also emollient type and frequency, over-the-counter or ‘natural’ remedies, previous steroid courses.
**Infection** — crusting, oozing, pain, spreading redness, **cold sores in the household.**
**Impact and background** — work, relationships, mood, cost · PMHx, medications, allergies, **pregnancy plans, because they affect therapy choice** · smoking and alcohol.

**Steroid phobia, asked directly**: **‘How do you feel about steroid creams?’** → *‘I've read they thin your skin.’* **Surface it now, answer it in the management block — do not discover it after you have prescribed.**
**Describe the photograph to the examiner using the formula**, then ask for the rest of the skin examination and vitals.
**State the diagnosis with the differentials and their discriminators**, including **‘I've looked for eczema herpeticum and not found it.’**

**The barrier explanation → emollient with a QUANTITY → the right-potency steroid with the phobia answered → the infection → the occupation → written action plan → the herpeticum red flag → ‘what's your plan when you get home?’**

**The four negatives that clear the field in one sweep**: **no burrows in the web spaces** (scabies) · **no nail pitting and no scaly scalp** (psoriasis) · **palms clear** · **no monomorphic punched-out vesicles** (eczema herpeticum).

dx: **Erythema nodosum — a SEPTAL PANNICULITIS — as an EXTRA-INTESTINAL MANIFESTATION of NEW INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE.** Bloody diarrhoea, urgency, left lower quadrant pain, weight loss, an oral ulcer and peripheral arthritis **favour ulcerative colitis (or Crohn's colitis).**

**THE EXAMINER IS SCORING WHETHER YOU TREAT THE SHIN LUMPS AS A SIGN, NOT A DIAGNOSIS.** The bowel history must be taken **PROACTIVELY**, and the EN cause list run through. **The second scoring point is INFECTION BEFORE IMMUNOSUPPRESSION — stool cultures and C. difficile before steroids — and a SEVERITY ASSESSMENT to decide outpatient versus admission.**

**THE THREE-LAYER DIFFERENTIAL — think in this order.** **WHAT ARE THE LUMPS?** erythema nodosum · cellulitis (unilateral, spreading) · superficial thrombophlebitis or DVT · **nodular vasculitis / erythema induratum (POSTERIOR calves, they ULCERATE, TB)** · insect bites · other panniculitis. **WHY HAS SHE GOT EN?** **IBD · streptococcal pharyngitis · sarcoidosis · drugs (OCP, sulfonamides) · TB · PREGNANCY · mycoplasma, Yersinia, Campylobacter · Behçet · lymphoma · IDIOPATHIC in up to half.** **WHAT IS THE BOWEL DISEASE?** ulcerative colitis · Crohn's colitis · infective colitis · coeliac · microscopic colitis · colorectal cancer · **and IBS does NOT bleed or cause weight loss.**

**The description, word for word**: **‘Bilateral, symmetrical, tender, warm, erythematous subcutaneous nodules 2 to 4 cm in diameter on the anterior shins, poorly demarcated, non-ulcerated, some evolving to a bruise-like yellow-purple colour — the appearance of erythema nodosum. Combined with three months of bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, an aphthous ulcer and peripheral arthritis, the likely underlying cause is inflammatory bowel disease, probably ulcerative colitis.’**

**Explaining it to Zoe**: **‘The lumps on your shins are called erythema nodosum — inflammation of the fat under the skin. They're NOT DANGEROUS THEMSELVES and they fade like bruises over a few weeks, but they're A SIGNAL THAT SOMETHING IS INFLAMED ELSEWHERE, and the bowel symptoms you've described are the likely reason. Three months of bloody diarrhoea with urgency, weight loss, mouth ulcers and joint pains fits inflammatory bowel disease — most likely ulcerative colitis, where the lining of the large bowel becomes inflamed. IT'S A LONG-TERM CONDITION BUT VERY TREATABLE, and people live full lives with it.’**

**SEVERITY TODAY, out loud**: six stools a day with blood, **but HR 88 and T 37.6 → MODERATE.** **Check Hb, CRP and albumin.** **ADMIT if severe criteria are met: ≥6 bloody stools PLUS HR >90, T >37.8, Hb <105, or raised CRP/ESR.** VERIFY **Ask the severity questions directly: nocturnal stools, fever, dizziness on standing, inability to keep fluids down.**

**DO NOT START STEROIDS before infection is excluded and gastroenterology is contacted, unless she is severe.** **Initial UC treatment after diagnosis is usually ORAL PLUS RECTAL 5-ASA (mesalazine), with ORAL PREDNISOLONE 40 mg for moderate–severe flares** VERIFY **— and that can begin on gastro advice once the stool tests are back.**

**THE NSAID TRAP, and it is specific to this case**: **NSAIDs are usually first line for erythema nodosum — but AVOID THEM HERE, because they worsen IBD.** **Stop her ibuprofen, use paracetamol, and manage the EN with REST, LEG ELEVATION and COMPRESSION STOCKINGS. The EN settles as the colitis is treated.**

**Before immunosuppression — a whole block candidates forget**: **vaccination review (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID, hepatitis B, HPV, varicella status), TB and hepatitis screening, contraception counselling, and document the smoking status.** **Smoking is PROTECTIVE in UC and HARMFUL in Crohn's — ask.** **Iron replacement (IV if intolerant or severe) once the bleeding is controlled. Dietitian — and AVOID RESTRICTIVE DIETS.**

**Support and safety-net**: **Crohn's & Colitis Australia**, a work certificate, a mental-health check, and an explanation of the **chronic flare–remission course and later cancer surveillance.** **Review in 1 week with results, sooner if worse.** **RED FLAGS TO ED: fever, more than 8 stools a day, severe pain or distension, dizziness, heavy bleeding.** SA — gastroenterology via **RAH or FMC outpatients or telehealth, with PATS.**

‘Have you ever had a BLACK HENNA TATTOO on holiday, or a reaction to any dye, rubber or sunscreen?’ → A BLACK HENNA TATTOO IN BALI TWO YEARS AGO THAT BLISTERED. That paste is NEARLY PURE PPD and it is what SENSITISED her

dx: **Allergic contact dermatitis to PARA-PHENYLENEDIAMINE (PPD) in permanent hair dye — a DELAYED (TYPE IV) HYPERSENSITIVITY.** **Sensitisation can occur after YEARS of tolerance.**

**THE DISCRIMINATOR, in one line: name PPD, explain delayed allergy and PERMANENT sensitisation, treat with a moderate-potent topical steroid to the neck and ears and a mild one to the eyelids (or a short oral prednisolone course if the facial oedema is severe), and give a LIFELONG AVOIDANCE PLAN with patch testing and cross-reactors.**
**‘The candidate who treats it as “a rash — hydrocortisone and antihistamine” and lets her use a different brand next time FAILS THE PREVENTION TASK.’**

**Explaining it**: **‘This is an allergic reaction to a chemical in permanent hair dye called PPD. It's a DELAYED allergy — your immune system reacts ONE TO THREE DAYS after contact — which is why it came on after the dye, and why you could use it for years and then suddenly react. ONCE SENSITISED, IT STAYS FOR LIFE. The pattern along the hairline, ears and neck, WHERE THE DYE RUNS OFF, is typical. Your eyelids react because the skin there is thin and you've transferred it with your hands.’**

**TREATMENT, BY SITE** VERIFY : **wash residual dye out with a mild shampoo; COOL COMPRESSES to weeping areas; saline wet soaks for crusts.** **Moderate–potent steroid — methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% or mometasone 0.1% — to HAIRLINE, EARS AND NECK, once to twice daily for 7–14 days.** **MILD — hydrocortisone 1% — to the EYELIDS for 5–7 days only.** **A lotion formulation for the scalp.**

**SYSTEMIC STEROID, justified by the eyelid oedema**: **if severe facial or periorbital oedema, or more than about 20% body surface — oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg (25–50 mg) daily for 5–7 days THEN TAPER OVER 2 WEEKS.** VERIFY **A short course that stops abruptly REBOUNDS.**

**Plus**: non-sedating antihistamine by day, sedating at night for sleep — **it helps the itch only modestly, and it is NOT the main treatment** · emollient to settled areas · avoid fragranced products until healed · **review in 3–5 days, earlier if worsening** · **medical certificate — she works at a bank and can't go in like this.**

**PREVENTION — the half of the station candidates skip.** **PERMANENT AVOIDANCE of PPD and related dyes: check ingredients for p-phenylenediamine, TOLUENE-2,5-DIAMINE (PTD) and p-aminophenol.** **‘PPD-FREE’ DYES MAY CONTAIN CROSS-REACTORS.** **Refer for PATCH TESTING via dermatology to confirm PPD and identify what else she reacts to.**

**THE CROSS-REACTORS, and one of them matters to an anaesthetist**: **azo textile dyes · BLACK RUBBER · sulfonamides · BENZOCAINE and PABA sunscreens · some LOCAL ANAESTHETICS.** **Document the allergy in the record, give a WRITTEN ALLERGY CARD, and note the benzocaine cross-reaction for future anaesthesia.**

**Answering ‘can I just use a different brand?’ — this is the scored moment**: **‘No — that's the key message. Every permanent dye contains PPD or close relatives like PTD, and “PPD-free” products often contain cousins that cross-react. You'll need to avoid permanent and most semi-permanent dyes FOR LIFE. Pure henna in red-orange is generally safe, and highlights that don't touch the scalp are lower risk, but NOTHING IS GUARANTEED. And never have a black henna tattoo again.’**

back.dx: BILATERAL CHRONIC OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION — glue ear — causing a moderate conductive hearing loss with speech and language delay, with adenoidal obstruction feeding it. To Jess: 'After her ear infections, thick fluid has stayed behind the eardrums instead of draining. The eardrum cannot vibrate properly, so sound reaches her muffled — about the level of hearing through earplugs. That is why she says what, turns the TV up, and why her words are unclear: she is learning speech from muffled sound. The hearing nerve itself is normal, which is the good news — when the fluid goes, hearing returns.' Differentials: sensorineural loss, where bone conduction is also reduced — congenital CMV, genetic causes, post-meningitis, ototoxicity, and a failed newborn screen · mixed loss with both components · cholesteatoma or chronic suppurative otitis media — discharge, perforation, an attic retraction pocket · wax or foreign body on otoscopy · autism spectrum or global delay, where the response is inconsistent and social communication is abnormal while hearing may be fine · and adenoid hypertrophy with obstructive sleep apnoea, which coexists here and shapes the surgery. The pathway VERIFY: she meets criteria for ENT referral for ventilation tubes now — bilateral effusion, present more than three months, hearing loss at or above 25-30 dB and speech delayed — with adenoidectomy considered given the snoring and mouth breathing. Watchful waiting for three months is right only for shorter, milder, unilateral effusions without language impact. Speech pathology is referred now, not after surgery. Hearing strategies at home and kindy are separately marked: face her and get her attention first, reduce background noise, sit her at the front, speak clearly rather than loudly, repeat and check understanding — and write to the kindy. Repeat audiology after grommets, or three-monthly if waiting. Reduce risk with a smoke-free home, treating nasal congestion, no bottle in bed and up-to-date pneumococcal and influenza vaccination. There is no evidence for antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants or steroids in OME VERIFY, though autoinflation may help older children. And if speech does not track once hearing is restored, reassess for language disorder or autism. Rurally: ENT via PATS and WCH or a visiting service, Aboriginal ear health programs where relevant, and grommet aftercare advice.

The ear and nose burden: number of infections and antibiotic courses, discharge or perforation, ear pulling, balance or clumsiness — then snoring, mouth breathing, apnoeas, chronic rhinorrhoea and sleep quality.

back.dx: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 31 weeks complicated by umbilical cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia — an obstetric emergency whose definitive treatment is emergency caesarean, not 'Transfer and see'. The three nevers: never perform a digital vaginal examination in PPROM without cord prolapse · never push the cord back in or handle it, keeping it warm and moist in the vagina if it is outside · never leave the patient to make phone calls. The sequence, said in the order you act: declare it and call for help — a second doctor, senior midwife, theatre notified if there is local caesarean capability, and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 simultaneously for retrieval and obstetric advice · relieve cord compression physically: knee-chest position or steep left-lateral Trendelenburg, with manual elevation of the presenting part by two gloved fingers, the hand staying in until delivery, or the bladder filled with 500 mL of saline via an indwelling catheter and clamped for transfer VERIFY · high-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulas, FBE, group and hold, coags and IV fluids · tocolysis to buy time with subcutaneous terbutaline if delivery is not immediate VERIFY · continuous fetal monitoring, and if the heart rate recovers with positioning, maintain it and transfer · antenatal corticosteroids with betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now, which benefit even if birth is within hours, and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection discussed with MedSTAR at this gestation VERIFY · erythromycin for the PPROM, with benzylpenicillin for GBS prophylaxis if she is in labour VERIFY · anti-D if she is rhesus negative, nil by mouth, times documented and the partner contacted. The disposition decision: if a surgeon and anaesthetist can operate locally, proceed to caesarean here with the MedSTAR neonatal team coming to you; if not, retrieve with the presenting part elevated and the bladder filled, left-lateral, on oxygen and continuously monitored. And the PPROM pathway without prolapse, which is the variant and must not be the answer here: admit, sterile speculum without a digital examination, high vaginal and GBS swabs, MSU, FBE and CRP, CTG and ultrasound · betamethasone two doses 24 hours apart from 23+0 to 34+6 weeks · erythromycin for 10 days or until labour · magnesium sulfate if birth is expected under 30 weeks · expectant management with 4-hourly observations, daily bloods, twice-weekly CTG and weekly liquor volume · and delivery at 37 weeks or earlier for chorioamnionitis, abruption, fetal compromise or labour, with transfer to a unit with neonatal care for the gestation VERIFY.
