back.dx: POLYMORPHIC ERUPTION OF PREGNANCY — PEP, also called PUPPP — in a primigravida in the third trimester: striae-based urticarial papules and plaques with the umbilicus spared, no blisters, and normal LFTs and bile acids. It is benign for mother and baby and resolves within days to a few weeks of birth. To Amy: 'It happens in about one in 160 pregnancies, usually first pregnancies in the last few weeks, and it typically starts in the stretch marks as the skin is pulled. It is uncomfortable, but it is harmless: it does not affect the baby, it does not affect the birth or breastfeeding, and it clears after the baby arrives.' The two differentials that matter, each excluded out loud: intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — itch without a primary rash, worst on palms and soles and at night, with raised bile acids and ALT, carrying fetal risk and needing ursodeoxycholic acid, serial bile acids, fetal surveillance and planned early birth VERIFY · and pemphigoid gestationis — periumbilical urticarial plaques evolving into tense blisters in the second or third trimester, autoimmune, carrying preterm and small-for-gestational-age risk and needing biopsy with immunofluorescence, dermatology and systemic steroids. The rest of the list: atopic eruption of pregnancy, which comes earlier and is flexural with an atopic history · scabies, with burrows, web spaces and itchy contacts · drug eruption or viral exanthem, with a temporal link, fever or mucosal involvement · and urticaria, whose wheals migrate and last under 24 hours. Treatment, with the pregnancy-safety said explicitly because she expects to be refused VERIFY: emollient thickly and often, cool showers, light cotton clothing, cold compresses and oatmeal or bicarbonate baths · a moderate-potency topical corticosteroid such as betamethasone valerate 0.02-0.05% or methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% once to twice daily for one to two weeks, which is safe in pregnancy at these amounts · an oral antihistamine, loratadine or cetirizine by day and sedating chlorphenamine at night for sleep, all considered safe · and a short course of oral prednisolone 20-30 mg daily tapering over one to two weeks after obstetric discussion if the itch is severe and unresponsive. Nothing else changes: the antenatal plan stands, birth at term as planned, breastfeeding is fine, the rash resolves post-partum and recurrence in later pregnancies is uncommon. Safety-net: return if blisters appear, if the itch spreads to palms or soles, if there is jaundice or dark urine — repeating LFTs and bile acids — or for reduced fetal movements, headache, visual change, swelling or fever. Review in one to two weeks and at routine antenatal visits, with written information.

The reassurance, which must be specific rather than general: 'Harmless for you and the baby — same birth plan, same checks, and it clears after birth.'

The treatment sentence she is waiting for: 'A moderate-strength steroid cream in this amount is safe in pregnancy' — and 'Loratadine by day and chlorphenamine at night to help you sleep; both are fine.'

Challenges: 'Can I use anything? I thought nothing was safe in pregnancy' and, if you refuse everything, 'I haven't slept in a week' · 'And the baby?' — she becomes anxious if risk is mentioned without immediate clarification · and she will not volunteer the blister or palm and sole information unless asked.
pefe: Role-player: Amy Lawson, 32, first pregnancy, 36 weeks. Ten days ago itchy bumps started in the stretch marks below her belly button and spread to her thighs and bottom; the itch keeps her awake. The belly button itself is clear. No blisters, palms and soles fine, no dark urine or yellow eyes. Nothing new used and nobody else itchy. Baby moving well, mild ankle swelling only. She had bloods last week and knows only that the liver was normal.

How she plays it: she assumes nothing is safe in pregnancy and asks what she can use; if refused everything she says she has not slept in a week. She asks about the baby and becomes anxious if risk is raised without immediate clarification. She does not volunteer the absence of blisters or palm and sole itch unless asked.

Mark them against these: asked where it started and whether the umbilicus is involved · asked about blisters · asked about palm and sole itch and itch without rash · ran the full cholestasis screen and confirmed the bile acids were checked · asked about drugs, contacts, atopy and previous pregnancies · checked fetal movements and pre-eclampsia symptoms · described the rash systematically · stated the three discriminators · named polymorphic eruption of pregnancy · excluded cholestasis and pemphigoid gestationis with reasons · offered a moderate-potency topical steroid rather than withholding treatment · offered antihistamines day and night · said explicitly that each is safe in pregnancy · kept prednisolone as the reserve after obstetric discussion · reassured specifically that the baby and the birth plan are unaffected · and gave the blister, palm-sole and jaundice safety-net with a review date.
Discriminator one — the umbilicus — Periumbilical skin spared. Pemphigoid gestationis starts around the umbilicus, so saying this out loud is how you exclude it
Discriminator two — no blisters — No vesicles and no bullae anywhere · face, palms, soles and mucosae all spared. Tense blisters would mean pemphigoid gestationis and a different pregnancy altogether

DO — The reassurance, which must be SPECIFIC rather than general: 'harmless for you and the baby — same birth plan, same checks', with the condition named and explained ('polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, also called PUPPP; it happens in about one in 160 pregnancies, usually FIRST pregnancies in the last few weeks, and it typically starts IN THE STRETCH MARKS as the skin is pulled'); then the safety net by symptom, which is what converts the reassurance into safe practice — return if BLISTERS appear, if the itch spreads to PALMS OR SOLES, if the urine goes dark or the eyes yellow (repeat the LFTs and bile acids), if fetal movements drop, or if she develops headache, visual change, marked swelling or fever — with review in one to two weeks and written information; variants — bile acids of 45 with palm and sole itch and NO primary rash is INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS, needing obstetric referral, ursodeoxycholic acid, weekly bile acids and LFTs, fetal surveillance and planned birth (VERIFY); periumbilical urticaria progressing to tense blisters at 30 weeks is PEMPHIGOID GESTATIONIS, needing urgent dermatology and obstetrics with growth surveillance and the possibility of a neonatal rash; and a twin pregnancy with rapid weight gain makes PEP MORE likely, with management unchanged

back.dx: Thin superficial spreading melanoma, stage ia, breslow 0.45 mm, not ulcerated, completely excised with clear margins. The bad-news sequence, compressed: warning shot — 'Josh, I have your results with me. I am afraid they are not what we hoped for, and I really wish I had better news for you today' · invitation — 'Is there anyone you would like to have with you?' · diagnosis in one sentence with the word said plainly — 'The results show a condition called melanoma, which is a type of skin cancer' · then stop talking. The explanation that task two is marked on: 'A melanoma is an uncontrolled, cancerous growth in a special pigment cell in the skin called a melanocyte. The single most important factor for how this behaves is its depth — how far down into the skin it has grown. The good news is we picked yours up early: it is less than one millimetre deep, it has not spread deep into the skin, and the whole thing was removed with clear edges.' then five management points in order. One, wide local re-excision: a further rim of normal skin, 1 cm all round at this depth, referred to dermatology or plastics because a forehead lesion may need a small flap — and if he asks why it was not all taken at once, because a wide first cut disrupts lymphatic mapping and makes sentinel node biopsy unreliable. Two, sentinel lymph node biopsy, discussed at that operation: dye is injected, the first draining gland is sampled, and only if it contains cancer cells do CT or PET scans follow — at 0.45 mm without ulceration this is a discussion rather than a mandate, but you still raise it. Three, a full skin check today, because one melanoma raises the risk of another about ten-fold — scalp, behind the ears, eyelids, trunk, limbs, palms, soles and the backs of the legs, undressed to underwear in good light with a dermatoscope. Four, sun protection explained rather than chanted: spf 30 or higher broad-spectrum applied thickly 20 minutes before going out and reapplied two-hourly and after sweating or swimming · avoiding peak uv around 10 am to 3 pm and checking the uv index · clothing, a broad-brimmed hat rather than a cap, sunglasses and shade · and the occupational version for a farmer, with long sleeves and cabin shade. Five, review and family: annual skin checks for a thin stage I melanoma, monthly self-examination, and first-degree relatives asked to see their own GP because their risk is about four-fold. Close with red flags — any spot growing, changing colour, itching or bleeding on touch, come back promptly — plus dermatology or plastics referral with PATS for travel, cancer council SA 13 11 20 and the cancer nurse line, written information, and a teach-back rather than 'Any questions'.
plan: Sit down, introduce, and open: 'Can you tell me what has happened so far?' — then perception: 'Did my colleague tell you what we were looking for and why we took the sample?' He was only told it looked a bit odd.

The emotional phase, one empathy statement at a time, each paired with an object or with silence: tissues, then water, then ten seconds of saying nothing. Talking over the crying is what keeps it going.
The hard stop that rescues the clock: 'Would you like me to go on, or would you prefer we continue in another appointment?' He settles and says go on.
Task two, which is the one most often skipped: what a melanocyte is, that depth is the most important prognostic factor, and the good-news sandwich that follows it immediately.
Management points one and two: re-excision with a 1 cm margin and why it is a second operation · sentinel node biopsy explained in plain words, with scans only if the node is positive.
Points three, four and five: the full skin check today · sun protection explained component by component for a farmer · annual review, self-examination and first-degree relatives.
Red flags, cancer council and written information, then the teach-back: 'What will you tell your wife when you get home?'

Nobody told him clearly what they were looking for. He has never used sunscreen and wears a cap, not a broad-brimmed hat. His father had 'A few things burnt off'. Two children, 19 and 22.

How the crying works: he breaks down at the word melanoma or cancer, asks whether he is going to die and raises the mate who died within a year. He keeps crying through the first two empathy statements and settles only after a third, or after silence, or when offered another consultation — and he does not settle at all if the doctor talks over him.

stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Ray Fowler, 62, type 2 diabetes for 10 years on metformin 1 g BD and gliclazide mr 60 mg mane, plus perindopril and atorvastatin.

Yesterday at the supermarket he had a 'Funny turn' — sweating, shaking, pounding heart, blurred vision and confusion for about 15 minutes. A staff member gave him a lemonade and he recovered fully within 10 minutes. He drives a delivery van. Last HbA1c 6.2%. Today's vitals normal, clinic BSL 6.1 mmol/L.
Tasks: take a focused history (5 minutes) — state the most likely diagnosis with reasons and the differentials — explain your immediate management and advice to the patient, including driving.

findings: EXAMINATION NORMAL. BP 128/78 LYING, 122/76 STANDING — NO postural drop. HR 72 REGULAR. NO FOCAL NEUROLOGY. NO CAROTID BRUIT. FINGERPRICK GLUCOSE 6.1 mmol/L. ECG SINUS RHYTHM, NO ISCHAEMIA
WHIPPLE'S TRIAD — establish it explicitly, it IS the diagnosis

(1) SYMPTOMS consistent with hypoglycaemia · (2) a LOW GLUCOSE at the time · (3) RELIEF WITH CARBOHYDRATE. He had all three: sweating and shaking, then confusion, and full recovery within 10 minutes of a lemonade
The symptom SEQUENCE — and the order matters
ADRENERGIC FIRST: sweating, tremor, palpitations. THEN NEUROGLYCOPENIC: confusion, blurred vision, slurred speech. That order is what makes it a hypo rather than an arrhythmia or a TIA
The exclusions, asked in one question
NO blackout · NO tongue biting · NO incontinence (seizure) · NO chest pain · NO focal weakness (ACS, TIA). Full recovery with sugar excludes both
THE MECHANISM — timing of tablet versus meal
TOOK THE TABLETS AT 7 am WITH A COFFEE AND SKIPPED BREAKFAST, then walked around the shops. GLICLAZIDE PUSHES INSULIN OUT WHETHER OR NOT HE HAS EATEN. Two beers the night before add to it
THE OVER-TREATMENT — the number that names the cause
HbA1c 6.2% ON A SULFONYLUREA in a 62-year-old commercial driver. The target here is about 7–7.5%, NOT 6.2 VERIFY. He is not badly controlled — he is OVER-controlled
The warning signs he already had
SEVERAL MID-MORNING SHAKY SPELLS THIS MONTH, fixed with a biscuit. A HOME READING OF 3.6 LAST WEEK. Ask about home BSL records and any reading under 4 — he will not volunteer them

LEVEL 1 <3.9 · LEVEL 2 <3.0 · LEVEL 3 = NEEDS THIRD-PARTY ASSISTANCE = SEVERE VERIFY. A checkout worker sat him down and gave him lemonade — BY DEFINITION THIS IS A SEVERE HYPO, and that is what triggers the driving rules
UEC and eGFR — RENAL DECLINE PROLONGS GLICLAZIDE · HbA1c · LFTs · REVIEW INTERACTING DRUGS, particularly a new SULFONAMIDE ANTIBIOTIC or a BETA-BLOCKER MASKING warning symptoms
LIGHT RIGID — A COMMERCIAL LICENCE. Stricter Austroads rules, and he DROVE HOME AFTERWARDS. Ask the licence class and whether he has had a hypo while driving

dx: **Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia in an OVER-TREATED older patient — Whipple's triad, HbA1c 6.2% on gliclazide.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE IS TWO SENTENCES**: **‘Your diabetes is OVER-TREATED — we will reduce the gliclazide’** and **‘You must NOT DRIVE until we've reviewed you and the lows have stopped.’** **A candidate who treats the hypo but leaves the sulfonylurea and the licence untouched fails the management task.**

**Explaining it**: **‘That was a hypo — low blood sugar. Your sugar control is VERY TIGHT, an HbA1c of 6.2, and gliclazide works by pushing your pancreas to release insulin WHETHER OR NOT YOU'VE EATEN. Skipping breakfast and then walking around the shops dropped your sugar. The good news is the fix is straightforward: less of the tablet that causes lows, a slightly relaxed target, and a plan for spotting and treating lows early.’**

**THE MEDICATION CHANGE — the first half of the answer** VERIFY : **STOP the gliclazide, or halve it to 30 mg with a plan to cease.** **CONTINUE METFORMIN — it does not cause lows.** **Individualise the target to about HbA1c 7–7.5%.** **If more glucose lowering is needed later, prefer agents WITHOUT hypo risk — a DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist.**

**THE RULE OF 15, given concretely — ‘generic eat regularly’ is the named trap**: **if BSL under 4 or symptomatic — 15 g of FAST carbohydrate (6–7 jellybeans, half a glass of juice or soft drink, or glucose tablets) — RECHECK IN 15 MINUTES — REPEAT if still under 4 — THEN a longer-acting snack (a sandwich, or biscuits with milk).** **Carry a hypo kit and a glucose meter ALWAYS, especially in the van.**

**THE DRIVING BLOCK — the second half, and the automatic fail if omitted** VERIFY : **a SEVERE hypoglycaemic event (one needing another person's help) means DO NOT DRIVE until assessed and cleared. The minimum period off driving is generally SIX WEEKS, and for a COMMERCIAL licence an ENDOCRINOLOGIST review and demonstrated hypo-free control are expected before return.**

**On returning to driving — ‘DON'T DRIVE UNDER FIVE’**: **check the BSL before EVERY drive and treat if below 5 · carry carbohydrate in the vehicle · if symptoms occur, PULL OVER, REMOVE THE KEYS, treat, recheck at 15 minutes, and only resume once the BSL is above 5, AT LEAST 30 MINUTES HAVE PASSED, and he feels well · commercial drivers must also KEEP A GLUCOSE RECORD.**

**The legal duties, said plainly and without losing him**: **he has a duty to notify the licensing authority of a condition affecting driving, and in South Australia a doctor has a MANDATORY REPORTING DUTY under the Motor Vehicles Act 1959 if he drives against advice.** **Deliver it with: ‘I know, and the aim is to get you back safely and quickly — stopping the gliclazide is the main fix.’**

**Education that prevents the next one**: **NEVER skip meals on a sulfonylurea · alcohol WITH FOOD only · TEACH A FAMILY MEMBER to recognise a hypo and where the jellybeans are · medical alert identification.** **Home monitoring: fasting and BEFORE DRIVING for the next fortnight, recording every reading under 4.**

**Then**: **work certificate**, discussion with the employer, vocational advice if needed · **diabetes educator** · **GP management plan and annual cycle of care** · **review in 1–2 weeks with the BSL diary.** SA — **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for a rural retrieval if recurrent and severe; telehealth endocrinology via Country Health Connect; **PATS** for Adelaide specialist review.
plan: **The event, in sequence** — **‘Tell me about yesterday.’** Let him give the order: sweating, shaking, racing heart, then unable to read the labels, then muddled. **Duration; witnesses.**

**The exclusions in one question**: **‘Did you black out, bite your tongue, wet yourself, get chest pain, or have weakness in an arm or your face?’** → no to all. **That covers seizure, ACS and stroke in a single breath.**

**THE MECHANISM**: **‘What had you eaten that morning, and WHEN DID YOU TAKE YOUR TABLETS?’** → *tablets at seven with a coffee, skipped breakfast, running late for deliveries.* Then **‘Any alcohol the night before? More exercise than usual? Any new medicines including antibiotics?’**
**Recovery — completing Whipple's triad**: **‘And you were fully better within minutes of the lemonade?’** → yes, ten minutes.

**Previous episodes and HYPO AWARENESS**: **‘Have you had turns like this before? Do you get warning symptoms? Do you check your sugars at home — any readings under 4? Any night sweats or nightmares?’** → *several shaky spells this month; a 3.6 last week.*
**Medications in detail**: doses, **recent changes**, **a new sulfonamide antibiotic**, **a beta-blocker masking warnings**, over-the-counter, adherence, **who packs the Webster pack.**
**Renal and systemic**: **last eGFR**, weight loss, appetite, intercurrent illness. Then comorbids — heart disease, epilepsy, previous stroke — **alcohol quantity, and does he live alone.**

**DRIVING**: **‘What licence class do you hold? When did you last drive? Have you ever had a hypo while driving?’** → *light rigid for the van, and he DROVE HOME afterwards.* Then **the concern: ‘I'm worried about my job.’**
**Ask for the examination, the fingerprick glucose AND the ECG.** Then **name it with Whipple's triad and the over-treatment as the cause**, and say what you excluded.

**Stop the gliclazide → the relaxed target → bloods → the rule of 15 and the hypo kit → home monitoring → THE DRIVING RULES AND THE REPORTING DUTY → certificate → educator → review 1–2 weeks → teach-back.**

back.dx: POSTMENOPAUSAL BLEEDING WITH A 14 MM HETEROGENEOUS ENDOMETRIUM ON AN UNOPPOSED-OESTROGEN BACKGROUND — most likely endometrial hyperplasia, and the only question that matters is whether there is atypia, which only tissue answers. The rule, said plainly: any postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise and requires endometrial assessment, however light or brief. To Denise: 'After menopause that lining should be thin — under about four millimetres — because the monthly hormone cycle has stopped building it up. Yours measured fourteen. The commonest cause is an overgrowth of the lining called hyperplasia, driven by oestrogen — after menopause body fat is the main place oestrogen is still made, and with no pregnancies and periods starting young, your lining has had a lot of oestrogen without the balancing hormone. But in about one in ten women, bleeding after menopause turns out to be a cancer of the lining, and the scan cannot tell the difference — only a sample of the tissue can. That is why the next step is a biopsy in the next couple of weeks, not months.' not to miss: endometrial carcinoma · cervical cancer, since screening does not exclude a visible lesion · vulval and vaginal lesions · urinary or bowel sources · tamoxifen or unopposed oestrogen HRT · Lynch syndrome · anticoagulants · a retained pessary · and atrophic vaginitis, which is a diagnosis of exclusion only. Investigations VERIFY: endometrial sampling with a pipelle in rooms if available and tolerated, remembering that a negative or insufficient pipelle does not exclude cancer when the endometrium is thickened or bleeding persists · hysteroscopy with dilatation and curettage as the gold standard here given 14 mm and a heterogeneous appearance, which also finds polyps and focal lesions · FBE and ferritin, UEC and LFT, HbA1c and lipids, with CA-125 only if ovarian pathology is suspected · colposcopy if any visible cervical abnormality · MRI pelvis with CT if cancer is confirmed, to a gynae-oncology MDT · and Lynch screening by immunohistochemistry on the specimen given the family history. The histology fork, which is task three: normal or atrophic endometrium — treat the atrophy with vaginal oestrogen and re-investigate any recurrence, always · endometrial polyp — hysteroscopic polypectomy with histology · hyperplasia without atypia, which progresses in only about 1-3% over twenty years — levonorgestrel intrauterine device first line for at least six months and usually five years, or continuous oral medroxyprogesterone or norethisterone, plus weight loss, with repeat sampling at 6 and 12 months then six-monthly until two consecutive negatives, and hysterectomy if it persists, progresses or bleeding continues · atypical hyperplasia, where 25-40% harbour or develop carcinoma — total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in a postmenopausal woman, with the LNG-IUD and three-monthly sampling reserved for those unfit or refusing surgery, or fertility-sparing in younger women · and endometrial carcinoma — surgical staging through a gynae-oncology MDT with adjuvant therapy by stage and Lynch testing. Around it: urgent category 1 gynaecology referral with PATS for travel · weight and blood pressure managed as part of treatment rather than blame, with a dietitian and a diabetes and sleep apnoea screen that also matters for anaesthesia · anaemia checked and treated · a safety-net for heavy bleeding, pain, fever or offensive discharge and for any future recurrence · a stated timeline so she can plan · and the doctor chasing the result personally rather than leaving it to her.

back.dx: Probable adult ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, with lifelong symptoms and clear functional impairment — provisional, not confirmed, today. The counselling needs three statements. First, the diagnostic requirements: onset before 12, pervasive across two or more settings, and causing impairment. Second, why there is no script today, said without closing the door: 'I cannot confirm it today, because low mood, anxiety, poor sleep, thyroid problems, low iron and some substances can look identical and the treatment differs. Since February 2026, GPs in South Australia who have completed the extra ADHD training can diagnose and prescribe without a psychiatrist referral — for adults and for children aged 8 and over. I have not done that training, so I will do the groundwork and refer you to a colleague who is accredited, or to a psychiatrist' VERIFY. Saying flatly that only a psychiatrist can diagnose ADHD in SA is now out of date and is marked as such. Third, what she can do this week. Differentials and comorbidities: major depression, which is episodic with concentration following mood · anxiety, where distractibility is worry-driven and onset can be later · bipolar disorder, episodic with reduced sleep need, where stimulants are hazardous · substance use, sleep deprivation and OSA, all temporally related and recent in onset · hypothyroidism and anaemia · PTSD and trauma · autism spectrum disorder · and personality disorder, which may also coexist. The workup to do today VERIFY: asrs V1.1 as the adult screener, plus k10, phq-9, gad-7, AUDIT and a bipolar screen · bloods for TSH, FBE, ferritin, UEC, LFT and glucose · baseline blood pressure, heart rate and weight, with an ECG if there is cardiac history or before stimulants · and collateral: primary school reports, a parent's account of childhood and a partner or colleague perspective, which whoever assesses her will want. Diva-5 is the structured interview at specialist level. The prescriber will consider stimulants — methylphenidate, dexamfetamine or lisdexamfetamine — or non-stimulants such as atomoxetine or guanfacine, with side effects on appetite, sleep, blood pressure, heart rate and anxiety, and stimulants remain schedule 8 with state authority and scriptchecksa applying VERIFY. Non-pharmacological management starts today and is the other half of the station: psychoeducation that ADHD is a difference in attention regulation rather than laziness or low intelligence, which reframes the 'Didn't apply herself' story she has carried since school · externalised organisation with one calendar and alarms for everything, tasks broken into 25-minute blocks, a two-minute rule, a single written list, visual boards and body-doubling · environment with noise-cancelling headphones, single-tasking, the phone in another room, agendas in advance and notes or recordings of meetings · workplace adjustments if she chooses to disclose, with written instructions, chunked deadlines and a quiet space, and a GP letter offered · sleep hygiene on a fixed schedule, regular aerobic exercise, and limits on alcohol and cannabis · adhd-focused CBT or coaching through a mental-health treatment plan, which also treats the anxiety · and peer support through ADHD Australia. Safety: no stimulants bought online or borrowed — unregulated, dangerous, and they would muddy the assessment — plus caffeine limits and a contraception discussion. Review in two to three weeks with the results and questionnaires.

stem: Surgical ward, day of surgery. You are the HMO. Your next patient is a 35-year-old woman who had a thyroidectomy four hours ago and is now complaining of shortness of breath.

Initial information: vital signs stable · oxygen saturation 97% on room air · she is sitting up in bed with a dressing over the neck wound and is frightened. There is no history task and no formal examination task.
Tasks: explain the cause of her breathlessness to the patient — explain your immediate management, the procedure step by step — some recalls add: name the equipment you would need.
tasks: Explain the cause of her breathlessness to the patient
Explain your immediate management — the procedure, step by step
Name the equipment you would need (added in some recalls)
time: Thirty seconds to introduce, acknowledge the fear and promise not to leave · ten seconds of rapid assessment narrated out loud, skipped entirely if she is stridulous · the diagnosis and the word urgent inside the first two minutes · escalation named before the procedure is described · then the equipment, SCOOP in five plain steps with its reason, theatre, and the last twenty seconds protected for questions and consent
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: A firm, tense swelling under the wound with the wound edges intact · and the drain bottle is empty. A drain can block — an empty drain does not rule out a haematoma, and saying so is a scored line

An emergency box kept at the bedside of every thyroidectomy patient — not in the treatment room: clip remover or stitch cutter to open the skin · scissors for the dressing and deeper sutures · a blade · artery forceps · sterile gauze packs · gloves · and the printed SCOOP card VERIFY

back.dx: POST-THYROIDECTOMY WOUND HAEMATOMA — bleeding into the closed space deep to the strap muscles, compressing the airway first by direct tracheal pressure and then by venous and lymphatic obstruction causing supraglottic and laryngeal oedema, which is why the airway can still be lost after the clot is released. Most occur within six hours and the great majority within 24 VERIFY. Of all thyroidectomy complications only haematoma is rapid, life-threatening and reversible at the bedside. The explanation, in order: name it and call it urgent in the first sentence — 'I am concerned about a rare but serious and urgent complication of thyroid surgery, and it is called a haematoma' · then what it is, in one breath — 'Bleeding underneath the surgical wound. The blood gets trapped and forms a collection, and that collection presses on your windpipe. That is why you feel short of breath' · then, if she asks why it is dangerous, the mechanism: the neck is a closed space, so as pressure rises it squeezes the windpipe and blocks drainage from the voice box so the tissues swell · and why it happened, without blame: a recognised complication in an area full of small vessels, not a mistake and not something she did. Escalation comes before the procedure description and is separately marked: surgical registrar, anaesthetics because they own the airway, senior nurse, theatre prepared — and say the words post-thyroidectomy neck haematoma. Then SCOOP, in plain words: expose the skin by taking the dressing off · cut the sutures and remove the clips · open the skin · open the strap muscle layers with a finger · pack with sterile gauze and move to theatre — with the sentence that earns the mark attached: 'By opening everything up we create extra space for that collection of blood, and that takes the pressure off your windpipe. I am not trying to remove the blood here — only to release the pressure.' Alongside: sit her upright, high-flow oxygen, monitoring and IV access · then theatre for exploration and haemostasis, FBE, coagulation screen and group and hold, a review of anticoagulants and the operative record, and a corrected calcium and magnesium. Differentials, each with why it is not this: bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy — stridor from the moment of extubation with a normal-looking wound, needing nasendoscopy and the airway team rather than an open neck · laryngeal or supraglottic oedema after difficult intubation — stridor without a tense wound, treated with steroids and nebulised adrenaline VERIFY · hypocalcaemic laryngospasm — perioral tingling, cramps, Chvostek and Trousseau, more often day 1-3 · tracheomalacia after a large retrosternal goitre · pulmonary embolism, with hypoxia out of proportion and a clear neck, CT only once the airway is secure · anaphylaxis · and seroma, which is soft and non-tense. One correction the source flags against itself: the calcium after thyroidectomy falls, it does not rise — the parathyroids sit on the back of the thyroid and may be bruised, devascularised or removed, so the complication is hypocalcaemia correction, which is why these patients get calcium and why the pins-and-needles station exists. Consent is asked for, and if she refuses you explain the consequence without arguing — and if she loses capacity with an immediate risk to life, treatment may proceed under the consent to medical treatment and palliative care act 1995 (SA) VERIFY. Rurally, at an MM5 site with no overnight surgeon or anaesthetist, you still decompress at the bedside — the geography does not change the first step — then MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval and phone advice while you work, with TIS National 131 450 if English is not her first language.
plan: WIPE, sit at eye level, and open with 'How are you feeling right now?' — not 'How can I help you', because the ward called you. Then the two sentences that buy you the room: 'I am taking this very seriously, and I am not going to leave you.'

Signpost once — what I think is causing this, what I am doing right now, what happens in theatre — then narrate the ten-second assessment: saturation, listening for stridor, dressing down, feeling either side of the wound (see findings). Skip it entirely if she is stridulous, and say that you are skipping it.
Name it and call it urgent in the same sentence, then explain a haematoma in one breath — bleeding, trapped, collection, pressing on the windpipe (see dx).

CALL FOR HELP BEFORE DESCRIBING ANYTHING: SURGICAL TEAM NOW, ANAESTHETICS BECAUSE THEY LOOK AFTER THE BREATHING, THEATRE BEING PREPARED. Describing SCOOP first and mentioning the surgeon last is a scored failure.
The equipment, each item tied to its job, and the point that the box lives at the bedside — 'Everything I need is in this room, which is why we can do this immediately.'

SCOOP in five plain steps with the purpose sentence attached — extra space, pressure off the windpipe — and the honest pain answer: 'I am not making a new cut, I am opening the one that is already there. It will feel like pressure, and we can give you more pain relief straight away.'

The urgency sentence, said once and plainly, and the refusal to image — then what happens in theatre: find the bleeding, stop it, wash out, close, with the anaesthetist minding her breathing throughout.

Protect the last twenty seconds: 'Do you have any questions? Are you happy for me to go ahead?' — then a short closing summary, an offer to call her husband, and the ward safety-net that the box stays at her bedside and what nursing staff should call you for.
back.planNote: eight minutes with no history and no examination task — the clock is spent on naming it early, escalating before describing, and leaving room at the end for consent
ask: The opening pair: 'How are you feeling right now?' and 'I am taking this seriously and I am not going to leave you.'

The diagnosis sentence, with both words in it: 'A rare but serious and urgent complication called a haematoma' — then 'Bleeding under the wound, trapped, forming a collection, pressing on your windpipe.'

The sentence the whole procedure is marked on: 'This creates extra space for the blood and takes the pressure off your windpipe' — and 'I am not making a new cut, I am opening the one that is already there.'

The two refusals to delay: 'A scan wouldn't change what I do, and the delay is the dangerous part' and, when offered the normal observations, 'Normal observations are reassuring but they do not exclude this, and they change late.' plus 'A drain can block — an empty drain does not rule this out.'

Challenges: 'Am I going to die?' · 'Did the surgeon do something wrong?' · 'Here? In the bed? You're joking.' · 'Is it going to hurt?' · 'Can't you wait for my surgeon?' — and from the examiner, 'Would you like an ultrasound of the neck?' and 'The surgeon is in another operation for twenty minutes', neither of which changes anything.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Whitcombe, 35, a primary school teacher whose whole thyroid was removed this morning for a large goitre. She woke fine and expected to go home tomorrow. Over the last thirty minutes her neck has felt tight and she cannot get a full breath. She speaks in short phrases with a hand near her throat, voice a little croaky since waking, and something like a lump on swallowing. The nurse checked her twenty minutes ago and said the observations were all fine, which is part of why she is confused.

How she plays it: she does not know what a haematoma is and looks blank if the word is used unexplained · she says 'Sorry, I don't understand' at any jargon and does not help the candidate out · if the doctor hesitates, talks about waiting or mentions a scan she becomes more distressed — 'But it's getting worse, can't you do something now?' · she pushes once on pain and once on refusal at about six minutes, accepting a kind explanation of the consequence but not being talked over · and if consent is never asked for, she does not offer it.

The hidden agenda, given late or if asked what is worrying her most: her mother died during an operation when she was nineteen. She also wants her husband Dan called, and asks whether she will still be able to talk afterwards.

Mark them against these: introduced, washed hands and asked how she was feeling rather than 'How can I help' · acknowledged her fear and said they were not leaving · narrated a rapid assessment before explaining · said haematoma and urgent within two minutes · explained it in lay words as bleeding, trapped, collection, pressure · called both the surgical and anaesthetic teams and said so early · named the emergency box and at least four items with purposes · gave all five SCOOP steps in order in plain language · said why the wound is opened · stated the urgency and refused imaging · answered the pain question honestly without over-promising · explained theatre · asked for questions and for consent · handled the refusal without arguing · picked up the hidden agenda · offered to call her husband · left no jargon untranslated · and stayed calm, with the urgency in the plan rather than the voice.

The numbers, which are a trap — Saturation 97% on room air with stable blood pressure and pulse — entirely compatible with an airway about to close. Desaturation is a late sign and it falls fast. Say that out loud when the examiner offers you the normal observations

The airway signs that mean open it now — Stridor · voice change · difficulty swallowing · a feeling of choking or neck tightness · distended neck veins · and agitation, because anxiety in a post-operative neck is an airway sign until proven otherwise. She says her neck feels tight, which is the classic pre-stridor description

★ Being reassured by normal observations and choosing to observe and review in an hour
★ Failing to decompress a threatened airway, or waiting for the consultant before acting
★ Never calling for help, or naming the surgeon only in the final sentence after describing the whole procedure

Describing SCOOP without the purpose sentence; never asking for consent; leaving jargon like strap muscles, evacuate and decompress untranslated; jumping to a bedside tracheostomy as the first manoeuvre; sedating an agitated patient with a narrowing airway; calling the calcium complication hypercalcaemia
numbers: Four hours post-operative, with most haematomas inside 6 hours and the great majority inside 24 VERIFY · SpO2 97% on room air with stable vitals, neither of which excludes it · zero investigations before decompression · SCOOP is five steps: skin, cut, open skin, open muscle, pack

After theatre: FBE, coagulation screen, group and hold, and a corrected calcium and magnesium — the post-thyroidectomy risk is hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia correction, with perioral and fingertip paraesthesia, cramps, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and at the severe end laryngospasm, seizures and a prolonged QT, treated with IV calcium gluconate VERIFY · adrenaline 0.5 mg IM 1:1000 for the anaphylaxis differential VERIFY · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450 · VERIFY all

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: being reassured by normal observations and choosing to observe and review in an hour — 97% on room air is entirely compatible with an airway about to close, because desaturation is a LATE sign; and an empty drain does not exclude it, because drains block

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: never calling for help, or naming the surgeon only in the final sentence after describing the whole procedure — escalation is the FIRST item after the diagnosis, and you name both teams: surgical and anaesthetics

FAIL — Describing SCOOP without the purpose sentence — the five steps in plain words (dressing off; cut the stitches and open the skin; separate the muscle layers with a finger; gauze over the wound; straight to theatre) and then WHY: 'opening it creates extra space for the blood and takes the pressure off your windpipe'

FAIL — Finishing on the procedure and never asking for consent, or leaving jargon untranslated — bleeding, collection, pressure, windpipe, muscle layers; not evacuate, decompress or strap muscles. And if the examiner asks about calcium, it FALLS after thyroidectomy, not rises

setting: A high-failure station for one reason: the photograph is persuasive. Candidates recognise continuous colitis and deliver a flawless ulcerative colitis consultation — and fail, because the mark sheet is built around knowing both conditions and not over-calling ahead of histology. Write one line before you go in: IBD — both. Biopsy confirms.
stem: General practice, post-colonoscopy results consultation. Your next patient is a 24-year-old man who has had chronic diarrhoea and has undergone a recent colonoscopy to investigate it. For the previous six months he has been passing bloody stools six to seven times per day, without mucus or slime.

He was told he has inflammatory bowel disease but could not remember any specific names. The specialist gave him copies of the photographs taken of the colon and said the appearance was similar throughout the whole large bowel. The photographs show ulceration and diffuse erythema of the mucosa. The histopathology report is not yet available.
Tasks: explain the colonoscopy findings to the patient — counsel him regarding inflammatory bowel disease: what it is, the two types and how they differ, their complications, and the management.
tasks: Explain the colonoscopy findings to the patient
Counsel him regarding inflammatory bowel disease — what it is, the two types and how they differ, their complications, and the management
time: A perception check and the concern question inside the first minute, because what he names there must be answered inside the consultation rather than in the last ten seconds · about a minute on the photograph, which is task one and is routinely skipped · then the two-types sentence and the comparison done attribute by attribute · treatment with real drug names · and twenty seconds protected for the long-term block, which is three separately marked items
findingsLabel: The photograph, the severity check, and the bloods that go today
findings: The photograph, narrated with your finger on it

'This is the inside lining of your large bowel. Normally it is smooth, pale pink and shiny, with small blood vessels you can see through it. Yours is red and inflamed, the vessels have disappeared, and here — and here — the lining has broken down into ulcers, which are raw patches. That is where the bleeding is coming from.' Holding the picture and pointing turns a monologue into a shared activity
What the histology will show, if the examiner asks

Ulcerative colitis — inflammation limited to mucosa and submucosa, crypt abscesses, crypt architectural distortion, goblet cell depletion · Crohn disease — transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas, skip lesions, deep fissuring ulcers VERIFY

back.dx: INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE — chronic, relapsing and remitting immune-mediated inflammation of the gut, comprising ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, with the endoscopic appearance here favouring ulcerative colitis and the histology pending. In roughly one in ten colitis cases the two cannot be separated initially — IBD unclassified. The three clauses that are the station: 'There are two types — ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease. The appearance on your pictures points towards ulcerative colitis, but the samples taken during the test are what confirm which one it is, and those results are not back yet. So let me tell you about both.' if those are not said, the candidate has almost certainly failed however good the rest is. The comparison, delivered attribute by attribute rather than as two monologues: ulcerative colitis affects only the large bowel, starts at the rectum and spreads proximally continuously with no gaps, and involves only mucosa and submucosa · Crohn disease can affect anywhere from mouth to anus, characteristically the terminal ileum, in patches with normal bowel between, and goes through the whole thickness of the wall — which is why it produces strictures, fistulae and abscesses. Complications follow from the depth: colitis flares, toxic megacolon with severe pain and fever, and a bowel cancer risk building over many years, which is why surveillance colonoscopy exists · Crohn flares, narrowing and obstruction from transmural scarring, fistulae tunnelling to skin or other organs, and perianal disease with ulcers, tears and abscesses · and both can involve joints, eyes, skin and the liver and bile ducts, with primary sclerosing cholangitis particularly in ulcerative colitis, so tell him to report a red painful eye or new joint swelling. Treatment must name real drugs in families: prednisolone for induction, fast and effective but not for maintenance · 5-aminosalicylates, mesalazine and sulfasalazine, as oral or rectal preparations and mainstays in ulcerative colitis specifically, with much less role in Crohn disease correction · immunomodulators, where the usual first agent is a thiopurine — azathioprine or mercaptopurine — rather than methotrexate, which is used mainly in Crohn disease correction · biologics such as infliximab and adalimumab for refractory disease · and surgery for failure or complication, which cures ulcerative colitis at the cost of a stoma or a pouch but never cures Crohn disease VERIFY. The pre-immunosuppression block is explicitly expected and is one sentence: 'Before we start any medicine that DAMPS down the immune system, we test for tuberculosis and hepatitis, check whether you are immune to chickenpox, and give vaccinations first, because some cannot be given once you are on these medicines' — plus HIV, thiopurine methyltransferase testing before azathioprine, skin checks and cervical screening VERIFY. And the long-term block, three separately marked items: iron and nutrition after six months of bleeding, with B12, folate and a dietitian and no blanket exclusion diets · bone health, because both the disease and steroids thin bone, with calcium, vitamin d, weight-bearing exercise and baseline densitometry where indicated · and surveillance colonoscopy from about eight years after symptom onset in extensive colitis at risk-stratified intervals of one to five years, not the flat two-yearly interval the source quotes correction VERIFY. Close with Crohn's and colitis Australia, written information, a mental health check, a work or study letter, PATS for Adelaide infusions and telehealth gastroenterology, and red flags: fever, severe or swollen tender abdomen, much more bleeding with faintness or palpitations, vomiting with no wind passing, perianal pain or discharge, a red painful eye.
plan: PERCEPTION FIRST: 'WHAT WERE YOU TOLD ON THE DAY, AND WHAT HAVE YOU BEEN TOLD SINCE?' — then acknowledge that six months of bleeding without a name is a long time and that this is frightening to read about online.

THE CONCERN QUESTION, EARLY ENOUGH TO ANSWER INSIDE THE CONSULTATION: 'WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST?' He will say the bag first and cancer second. Answer the cancer one immediately — no, this is not cancer — and promise to come back to the bag properly.
Signpost the shape in one line: what the pictures show, what the condition is, the two types and how they differ, the treatments, and what we keep an eye on long term.
TASK ONE — THE PHOTOGRAPH, HELD UP AND POINTED AT (see findings). Skipping it to get to disease education loses a whole task.
Name it, explain autoimmune in one sentence, say it is not his diet and not anything he did — then the two-types sentence, word for word, and hold that position when he pushes (see dx).

The comparison by attribute — site, pattern, depth — then the complications of each, reframing cancer the moment it lands: not now, not soon, a risk that builds over years and the reason surveillance exists.
The severity check, which fits here and is the commonest omission: fevers, heart racing, faintness on standing, weight — and bloods and stool cultures today.

Treatment by families with at least one real drug in each, then the pre-immunosuppression sentence, then the long-term block — iron, bones, surveillance — the red flags, Crohn's and colitis Australia, follow-up tied to the biopsy, and an invitation for questions.
back.planNote: eight minutes where the photograph is a whole task, the two-types sentence is the pass mark, and the last twenty seconds belong to iron, bones and surveillance
ask: The sentence the station is built around: 'There are two types — ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease. The appearance points towards colitis, but the biopsy is what confirms it. So let me tell you about both.'

The answer when he pushes — and he will: 'Because the appearance and the microscope don't always agree, and which one it is changes the treatment, the complications we watch for and the follow-up. I'd rather tell you about both today and be certain next week than be confident now and wrong.'

The comparison in two lines: 'Colitis — large bowel only, from the back passage, continuous, surface layers.' · 'Crohn — anywhere from mouth to anus, in patches, through the whole wall.' and the translation that lands: 'Fistulas are tunnels from the bowel that can open onto the skin.'

The two reframes: on cancer, 'Not now and not soon — it is a risk that builds over years, and that is why we watch' · on the bag, 'Most people never need one, and not everyone who has surgery ends up with a permanent bag.'

Challenges: 'It looks like colitis though, doesn't it? Why won't you just say so?' — and if you do say so, he accepts it readily with 'Right, so that's confirmed then', which is how the examiner sees the over-call · 'Is this cancer?' · 'Will I end up with a bag?' · 'Steroids? Don't they make you blow up?' · 'TB? I haven't got TB.' · 'So this is for life then.' · and, only at the very end, 'Will I still be able to have kids?'
pefe: Role-player: Sam Toohey, 24, an apprentice electrician. Six months of bloody loose stools six or seven times a day with urgency, a few kilos lost and constant tiredness. He had a colonoscopy last week, was given photographs and told something about inflammatory bowel disease while groggy, and has been frightening himself online since. No fever, no night sweats, not dizzy standing — he is not acutely unwell today. Five cigarettes a day, weekend drinking, occasional mouth ulcers, no family history, no travel, antibiotics or sick contacts.

How he plays it: he pushes once on the diagnosis and accepts a proper explanation of why the biopsy decides — but if told outright that he has ulcerative colitis he accepts that readily and says 'Right, so that's confirmed then', which is the trap closing. He says 'You've lost me' at any jargon and does not help the candidate out. He reacts hard to the word cancer and waits to see whether it is reframed.

What he withholds: his two hidden concerns, given only if asked what is worrying him most — the bag first, then cancer · that he has had to leave jobsites urgently and his boss has started making comments · and, right at the end or if asked whether anything else is on his mind, whether he will still be able to have children.

Mark them against these: asked what he had been told and what worried him most · explained the photograph in plain words · named inflammatory bowel disease and explained autoimmune simply · said it was not his fault and not his diet · said there are two types and named both · did not confirm ulcerative colitis and explained that the biopsy decides · held that position when pushed · compared site, pattern and depth · gave complications of each including toxic megacolon and cancer for uc and fistulae and obstruction for Crohn · reframed the cancer risk · asked about fever, palpitations and dizziness to exclude acute severe colitis · named actual drugs in at least three families · explained the TB, hepatitis, varicella and vaccination checks · covered iron, bones and surveillance colonoscopy · was honest about surgery without catastrophising · gave red flags and when to go to hospital · offered written information and a support organisation · tied follow-up to the biopsy · and left no jargon untranslated.

The severity check everyone forgets while counselling — He has six to seven bloody stools a day, which is at the threshold — so ask for the rest: fever, palpitations, dizziness on standing, weight. Six or more bloody stools with fever, tachycardia, anaemia or a raised inflammatory marker is acute severe colitis and needs admission today. In this stem he is not acutely unwell — but not asking is the failure

What goes off today — Full blood count, iron studies, CRP and ESR, UEC, LFT, B12, folate and vitamin d — six months of bleeding means iron deficiency until proven otherwise · and stool microscopy, culture and C. Difficile toxin, because infection must be excluded before any immunosuppression
fails: ★ Counselling only about ulcerative colitis — an accurate, well-structured UC consultation that never mentions Crohn disease
★ Confirming the diagnosis before the histology: 'you have ulcerative colitis'
★ Never explaining the photograph, which is task one
★ Missing acute severe colitis because everyone is busy counselling — six or more bloody stools a day with systemic upset means admission

Saying 'immunosuppressants' and naming no actual drug; omitting the TB, hepatitis and varicella screening; running out of time before iron, bones and surveillance; leaving transmural, mucosa, skip lesions and biologic untranslated; promising cure or catastrophising about a bag

Surveillance colonoscopy from about 8 years after symptom onset in extensive colitis, at risk-stratified intervals of 1-5 years rather than a flat two-yearly schedule correction VERIFY · pre-immunosuppression: TB with quantiferon and chest x-ray, hepatitis B and C, HIV, varicella immunity, and vaccination before starting, plus thiopurine methyltransferase testing before azathioprine VERIFY · drug families: prednisolone · mesalazine or sulfasalazine in uc · azathioprine or mercaptopurine, with methotrexate mainly in Crohn · infliximab or adalimumab · surgery VERIFY · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · PATS · VERIFY all

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: confirming the diagnosis before the histology — 'you have ulcerative colitis' is the commonest way to fail this station. Say the three clauses: there are two types, the biopsy confirms which, so let me tell you about both. He pushes once, so hold the line: the appearance and the microscope don't always agree, and which one it is changes the treatment, the complications and the follow-up

And send stool cultures and C. difficile toxin, because infection must be excluded before any immunosuppression

Ask his concerns early, because the bag, the cancer and fertility are what he is actually frightened of

setting: It looks like an osteoarthritis case and it is not one — task three is an instruction, not a hint. The source ends with 'We have decided not to proceed as the risks outweigh the benefits', and that sentence on its own fails the station twice: a decision announced at him rather than made with him, and clinically wrong, because most of what makes him high risk is modifiable.
stem: General practice, referred back by the anaesthetist. Your next patient is a 67-year-old man scheduled for a knee replacement for osteoarthritis. He is a known case of COPD, ischaemic heart disease and mild chronic kidney disease. At his pre-operative assessment the anaesthetist reported that surgery carries a high risk and referred him back to you.

Medications: aspirin, an ACE inhibitor, a statin, a beta-blocker, inhalers for COPD, and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Investigations: chest x-ray and spirometry consistent with established COPD · haemoglobin is low · other results unremarkable.
Tasks: take a history regarding the osteoarthritis and his other conditions — discuss the risks and benefits of surgery with the patient — do not discuss alternative management of the osteoarthritis.
tasks: Take a history regarding the osteoarthritis and his other conditions
Discuss the risks and benefits of surgery with the patient
Do not discuss alternative management of the osteoarthritis
time: Five to six minutes of history in four blocks — a short osteoarthritis block weighted entirely to function, falls and severity · control rather than diagnosis for chest, heart and kidneys · ninety seconds of functional capacity · and six anaesthetic questions most candidates never ask · then two to three minutes of risk communication that must still fit benefits, the reframe, four named actions, a meeting, a review date and a pain appointment

back.dx: HIGH PERIOPERATIVE RISK FOR ELECTIVE TOTAL KNEE REPLACEMENT, DRIVEN BY THE THREE CS — coronary artery disease giving perioperative myocardial infarction risk, COPD giving postoperative pulmonary complications, and chronic kidney disease giving acute-on-chronic injury, anaemia and independently raised cardiovascular morbidity — compounded by a functional capacity under 4 mets, which is the dominant predictor. The explanation is framed first: 'Before any operation we do an assessment, because surgery puts your body under a lot of stress — you lose some blood, you are given strong medicines and fluids, and you are asleep for a while. To get through that safely we need the heart, the lungs and the kidneys all working reasonably well.' then the verdict and the reasons, in his own words rather than in generic terms: the heart — narrowed arteries and chest pain after one block, so the stress of surgery raises the chance of a heart attack during or after it · the lungs — COPD with four flare-ups this year, so a higher chance of parts of the lung collapsing down or a chest infection afterwards · the kidneys — adding strain to the heart, likely to worsen after surgery, and the reason his blood count is low, leaving less reserve if he bleeds. The benefits must be named because the task says risks and benefits: a new knee would very likely take away most of the pain, restore walking and sleep, and reduce his falls. Then the reframe that carries the station: 'This is not no, never. It is not safe yet — and here are the four things we can change before we ask the question again.' Those four: smoking cessation, targeting at least four weeks smoke-free before surgery, with nicotine replacement and Quitline VERIFY · COPD optimisation with inhaler technique and adherence, a written action plan, pulmonary rehabilitation and influenza and pneumococcal vaccination · cardiology and medication review, with further cardiac testing only if it would change management VERIFY · and investigating and correcting the anaemia. Alongside them: a perioperative medication plan with the SGLT2 inhibitor stopped at least three days before surgery because of euglycaemic ketoacidosis risk, ACE inhibitor handling decided, aspirin continued in most joint replacements for established ischaemic heart disease and the beta-blocker continued VERIFY · prehabilitation with physiotherapy, nutrition and dental review · ECG today with FBE, iron studies, B12, folate, UEC and eGFR · a multidisciplinary meeting including him, the surgeon, the anaesthetist and the cardiologist · and review in six to eight weeks. What stops the elective pathway altogether: unstable, rest or crescendo angina, new breathlessness, syncope or palpitations · an active COPD exacerbation · and a family history of malignant hyperthermia, which is hyperthermia not hypothermia correction — an inherited hypermetabolic reaction to volatile agents and suxamethonium causing rigidity, rising end-tidal CO2, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and arrhythmia, treated with dantrolene, and mandating specialist assessment and a trigger-free technique VERIFY. On egg and soy allergy: ask, because it is on every form, but do not tell a patient it rules out propofol — the evidence does not support that VERIFY. And do not leave him without a pain plan: the stem forbids discussing alternative osteoarthritis management, it does not permit sending a man in pain away with nothing — 'I am not going through the treatments for the knee today, because that deserves its own appointment, but I am booking you in this week specifically for your pain.'
plan: Acknowledge before asking: eighteen months is a long time to wait in pain, and being turned away with an unexplained letter would frustrate anyone — then contract, with the phrase that buys you five minutes of questions: 'Then I can explain what the report actually means and what we can do about it.'

Osteoarthritis, short and weighted to complications: when diagnosed, what he takes — then function (Shopping, stairs, showering, sleep), falls, and pain severity out of ten. No SOCRATES, no treatment ladder.
COPD by control: smoking asked neutrally and first, current breathlessness, cough and wheeze, flare-ups in twelve months, admissions, home oxygen or ICU.

Heart and kidneys: chest pain on exertion and at what workload, previous infarct or stent, orthopnoea, ankle oedema, palpitations or blackouts — and critically 'Has any of this changed recently?' · then who looks after the kidneys, last checked, diuretics and anti-inflammatories, and whether he knows he is anaemic or has had black stools.
Functional capacity, open then closed then the follow-up that decides it (see findings).
The anaesthetic block — six questions, ninety seconds, routinely omitted (see findings).
Frame why the assessment exists, say the words high risk, then give the three reasons using his own answers back to him (see dx).

Benefits, then 'Not no — not yet', then the four modifiable factors, the MDT meeting with him in it, a six-to-eight-week review, and the pain appointment this week — all separately marked and all routinely lost to poor time control.
back.planNote: five to six minutes of history and two to three of explanation — and the last ninety seconds carry six separately marked items, so the osteoarthritis block has to stay short
ask: The contract that makes him cooperate: 'Is it alright if I ask you some questions first? Then I can explain what it means and what we can do about it.'
The closed functional questions and their follow-up: 'Can you climb two flights without stopping? Can you walk four blocks?' and 'What stops you first — the knee, your breathing, or the chest pain?'

The framing and the verdict: 'Surgery puts the body under a lot of stress — we need the heart, lungs and kidneys all working reasonably well' then 'You are at high risk of complications during and after surgery, and it is not one thing.'

The sentence that carries the station: 'This isn't no. It's not yet — and here are the four things we can change before we ask the question again.' plus 'This is your decision as much as ours' and 'I'm booking you back this week just about the pain.'

Challenges: 'Is it because of my smoking?' · 'So that's it then. No operation.' Said flatly, and he does not soften it · 'So I just have to live with it, then' if you only say no · 'And if I do all that?' if you say not yet · 'I'm 67, I'd rather take the risk' · and 'What am I supposed to do about the pain?'
pefe: Role-player: ray Aspinall, 67, a retired grain-handler from a country town, eighteen months on the waiting list for a right knee replacement. He travelled to Adelaide last week, the anaesthetist saw him briefly, said it was too high risk and sent him back with a letter he did not understand. He is disappointed and indignant rather than aggressive, assumes this is about his smoking and is braced for a lecture.

The history he holds: knee pain 8/10 most days, sleeping in the recliner, his wife doing the shopping, two falls in the yard this year · ten cigarettes a day down from thirty, one previous patch attempt · breathless most days, four steroid-requiring flare-ups, one week in hospital two years ago · chest tightness at one block relieved by spray and unchanged for a year · ankles swelling by evening · told he is 'A bit anaemic' with kidneys 'Down a bit'.

What he withholds: the difficult intubation and the two days of vomiting after his 1998 hernia repair, both only if asked · and the hidden concern, given late or if asked what worries him most or about home: his wife Val has early dementia and he is her carer — if he cannot walk, she goes into a home. If the doctor lectures him about smoking he becomes defensive and gives less for the next minute.

Mark them against these: acknowledged the disappointment before starting · asked permission and explained why · asked about function, falls and pain severity · did not spend the station on arthritis treatments · asked about smoking neutrally and got a number · asked flare-up count and admissions · asked at what workload the chest pain comes and whether it has changed · asked about orthopnoea and ankle swelling · asked about the kidneys and the anaemia · asked two flights and four blocks specifically · asked what stops him first · asked the six anaesthetic questions · explained that surgery stresses heart, lungs and kidneys · said the words high risk and broke it into three using his own answers · named the benefits · framed it as not yet · named at least three modifiable factors with practical smoking help · offered an MDT meeting and said the decision was his too · gave a review date · arranged a separate pain appointment · and did not moralise at any point.

Functional capacity, the single best predictor — Ask it open then closed: 'Can you climb two flights of stairs without stopping? Can you walk four blocks on the flat?' He stops halfway up one flight — under 4 mets, which is the conventional threshold and the backbone of your explanation VERIFY. 'Not very active' is not assessable

The discriminating follow-up almost nobody asks — 'What stops you first — the knee, your breathing, or chest pain?' if the knee is the limit, his cardiorespiratory reserve is untested and may be fine, which is an argument for operating. Here it is the breathing, then the chest — so the report is right, and say which one you found

Control, not diagnosis — COPD — still smoking about ten a day, breathless most days, four exacerbations this year all needing steroids, one week-long admission two years ago · heart — exertional chest pain at about one block relieved by spray, unchanged for a year, ankles swelling by evening · kidneys — 'Down a bit' and 'A bit anaemic'. The 'Has it changed recently?' Question is what separates stable from crescendo angina

The anaesthetic block, six questions and ninety seconds — Previous surgery — a hernia in 1998 · a previously difficult intubation, which he mentions only if asked · two days of post-operative vomiting · allergies including latex and egg, soy or peanut · and a family history of a severe anaesthetic reaction with a dangerously high temperature. The first two each change the anaesthetic plan and are separately marked

Why the low haemoglobin is in the stem — It is not decoration — CKD causes anaemia through reduced erythropoietin, and pre-operative anaemia independently predicts transfusion, complications and death. Iron studies, B12 and folate, and in a 67-year-old man with iron deficiency, the bowel needs investigating, not just treating VERIFY
