setting: You cannot detain a competent adult, so this is not a persuasion station. It is about finding why she wants to leave and solving that, then informing her and handing the decision back. The documented reason candidates fail it is reaching for 'I'll ask my registrar' instead of counselling — you were never the one deciding, she was.
stem: Surgical ward, post-operative day 2. You are the HMO. Your next patient is a 27-year-old woman admitted with a ruptured appendix who underwent surgery the day before yesterday. The surgeon has recommended 72 hours of observation before discharge. She is currently on heparin, intravenous antibiotics and intravenous fluids.
Today is her second day after surgery and the patient wants to go home. Provided to you: her vital sign observation chart, her physical examination findings and a urine dipstick.
Tasks: take a history from the patient — explain the vital sign chart to your patient — counsel her regarding the discharge plan.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Explain the vital sign chart (the observation chart) to your patient
Counsel her regarding the discharge plan
time: Ninety seconds on the agenda — why she wants to go, can I help, and what she already understands, all three separately marked · then a tight abdominal screen and the five ws, with the history capped at about three and a half minutes · the chart explained as a trend · and the last three minutes protected for the three reasons, the handback, the red flags and the safe exit
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Version A — the harder one, everything normal

No symptoms on history · observation chart normal with no fever · dipstick normal · abdomen normal. You have no clinical lever at all: she is well and she wants to go, and the only things between her and the door are the 72-hour plan and your ability to explain it. Use the normal chart as evidence rather than hurrying past it
Version B — the repeated one, a urinary tract infection

Afebrile on day 1, today running a temperature approaching 38 · slight burning on passing urine, volunteered only if asked · dipstick nitrites positive, leucocytes 1+, blood 1+ · mild tachycardia at about 96 with normal respiratory rate, saturation and blood pressure. You now have a named reason to recommend staying, but the approach does not change

After a perforated appendix, a positive dipstick does not exclude an intra-abdominal or pelvic collection — classically day 5-7 but it can declare earlier, with worsening rather than settling pain, swinging fevers, diarrhoea or tenesmus, anorexia and a tender mass. Say you would send an MSU but also want inflammatory markers and a low threshold for CT VERIFY

back.dx: Post-operative day 2 after appendicectomy for a perforated appendix, requesting discharge against a planned 72-hour observation period — and in version B, a new low-grade fever with a positive dipstick suggesting a urinary tract infection. The clinical background: perforation means peritoneal contamination, which is why the plan is 72 hours of intravenous antibiotics and observation rather than early discharge VERIFY — the window exists to confirm the bowel is working, that no infection is developing, and that she can eat, drink and take oral antibiotics. The legal position is the spine of the station: a competent adult may leave at any time, you cannot force her and should not try — what you can do is make the decision informed, remove the obstacle driving it, and make leaving as safe as possible. The passing pattern, in order: 'Can I ask why?' · 'Is there any way I can help with that?' with a named, concrete offer · 'Do you know why we'd like to keep you and what we're watching for?' · then the risks in three plain headings, each arriving attached to its treatment so that staying feels purposeful rather than arbitrary. One, the bowel: 'We operated inside your tummy, so we need to be sure the bowel is working — eating, drinking, passing wind and opening your bowels, and being off the drip.' Two, infection: 'Your appendix had burst, so there was infection in the tummy — that is what the drip antibiotics are for, and we watch the wound, the chest, the waterworks and the drip site, because an infection that starts here is much easier to catch than one that starts at home.' Three, clots: 'After an operation there is a higher risk of clots in the legs that can travel to the lungs — that is what the blood-thinning injection is for, along with getting you up and walking.' In version B add a fourth, named in plain words: an untreated urinary infection can ascend to the kidneys and into the bloodstream — urosepsis to the examiner, 'Get into the bloodstream and make you very unwell' to her — so send an MSU for culture before changing anything, review the intravenous cover she is already on, check inflammatory markers and reassess in the morning, without committing to a specific oral antibiotic in a woman already on broad cover for a perforated appendix VERIFY. Then hand the decision back explicitly — patient-centred is not a tone, it is a sentence said out loud — and if she still goes, four things every time: red flags spelled out (Fever or shivers, worsening pain, vomiting, no wind or bowels, wound redness or discharge, a painful swollen calf, chest pain or breathlessness, faintness — back to emergency any hour) · practical cover with oral antibiotics, analgesia, wound advice and a booked review · the DAMA form explained as a record rather than a punishment · and documentation of capacity, what was explained, what was offered and what she declined, with a letter or call to her GP. The differential for a day-2 fever runs through the five ws — wind at day 1-2, water at 3-5, wound at 5-7, walking from day 5, and wonder drugs any day VERIFY — plus line sepsis, antibiotic-associated diarrhoea or C. Difficile, venous thromboembolism despite prophylaxis, and sepsis itself, where rigors, tachycardia out of keeping, hypotension or confusion stop the conversation and start a pathway. Rurally, ask how far she lives and who is at home — if she is returning to a farm two hours away with nobody there, the risk calculation changes and you should say so — and use country health connect for district nursing, PATS for follow-up travel, healthdirect 1800 022 222 after hours, and the Aboriginal liaison officer before a discharge against advice rather than after it.
plan: Open with 'How are you feeling today?' rather than 'How can I help' — she is an inpatient and you came to her — then name why you are there and ask the question the station hangs on: 'I've been told you'd like to leave earlier than your surgeon recommended. Can I ask why?'

OFFER TO SOLVE IT, CONCRETELY AND WITH A TIMEFRAME — A SOCIAL WORK REFERRAL TODAY FOR HER MOTHER, A MEDICAL CERTIFICATE NOW, A PHONE CALL TO A RELATIVE. Vague 'support' scores nothing; she will ask what that actually means.

The third agenda question, which most candidates never ask and which is separately marked: 'Do you know why we'd like to keep you a bit longer, and what we're watching for?' Her answer tells you how much explaining is left.

The abdominal screen, all five: pain better or worse than yesterday · fever or shivers · nausea or vomiting · eating and drinking · and passing wind and opening bowels, which is the practical discharge criterion and the most concrete thing you can offer her.

The five ws, one question each: cough or breathlessness and whether the analgesia is working · burning or frequency on passing urine · wound redness or discharge · calf pain or swelling and whether she has been up walking · cannula site, rash and diarrhoea.
Ask for the chart and findings, then explain the chart as a pattern rather than a list of numbers (see findings).
The three reasons, each tied to what is being done about it — and in version B the fourth, with the ascending-infection risk named plainly (see dx).

Hand the decision back out loud, offer her time and invite any concern she has not mentioned — then the safe exit either way: red flags with 'Any hour', scripts and wound advice, a booked review, the DAMA form described without menace, and 'The door is open and you can come back at any time'.
back.planNote: the history is capped at about three and a half minutes because the counselling is where the marks are — and the agenda has to be out and answered before a single word about risk
ask: The three open questions that do most of the work: 'How are you feeling today?' · 'Why do you want to leave — and is there any way I can help?' · 'Do you know why we'd like to keep you a bit longer?'

The sentence that carries the station: 'I can't keep you here and I wouldn't try — this is your decision. My job is to make sure you're making it with the whole picture, and to sort out whatever is pulling you home.'

The chart, oriented before it is read: 'Each column is a time and each row is a measurement — the pattern matters more than any one dot.' then 'Yesterday it was normal; today it's come up to just under 38.'

The DAMA sentence, said without menace: 'It just records that we talked about the risks and you chose to go. It isn't a punishment and it doesn't stop you coming back.' and the close: 'We respect your decision. The door is open, any hour.'

Challenges: 'You can't actually keep me here, can you?' · 'But I feel fine — couldn't I just take tablets at home?' · 'A form? Am I in trouble?' · and if you offer only vague support, 'What does that actually mean?' — while if you lead with risks before asking why, she goes polite and immovable and gives you nothing for the rest of the station.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Okafor, 27, an administrative assistant, two days after appendicectomy for a burst appendix, on a drip with antibiotics and fluids and a daily blood-thinning injection. She feels much better and wants to go home today. Polite and reasonable rather than hostile, but determined, and quietly stubborn if she feels lectured. She lives 40 minutes away and her partner works away.

The agenda, given only if asked why: her mother is 80, lives alone, and she does everything — medications, meals, shopping — and nobody has checked on her since Tuesday. Her brother is two hours away and never answers his phone, and she has not actually tried today. If she is never asked, she never mentions her.

How she plays it: if the doctor leads with risks she becomes polite but immovable — 'I hear you, but I've made up my mind' — and gives minimal information from then on · if asked why and listened to, she is visibly relieved · if offered a social worker today or a call to her brother, she softens and offers to stay the night · if told she is not allowed to leave she pushes back firmly · and if the form is used as a threat she becomes anxious about being in trouble. In version B the stinging on passing urine is mentioned only if asked directly, because she thinks it is nothing.

Mark them against these: opened with how she is feeling rather than how can I help · named why they had come · asked why within ninety seconds · offered concrete help with a named service and a timeframe · asked what she already understood · asked about pain, fever, nausea and eating · asked about wind and bowels · asked about chest, urine, wound, calves and drip site · explained the chart as a pattern and pointed out the abnormal row · gave three clear reasons each linked to its treatment · explained the ascending-infection risk in version B · said explicitly that they could not keep her and that the decision was hers · offered time and invited further concerns · gave specific red flags with return at any hour · offered antibiotics, analgesia and a review if she left · explained DAMA without making it a punishment · said the door was open · and never lectured.

How to read the chart out loud — Orient her first — 'Each column is a time and each row is a measurement; what matters is the pattern across the page, not any one dot' · name the rows in lay terms including 'The two arrows are the TOP and bottom numbers' · describe the trend · point at the abnormal row and say what it means · then say what you will do. Reciting numbers scores nothing

★ Telling her she cannot leave, or implying the surgeon's plan overrides her decision
★ Letting her go with no antibiotics, no red flags, no follow-up and no documentation

Finding the agenda and not solving it, or offering vague 'support' with no named service; skipping flatus and bowels; reading the chart as numbers; anchoring on the dipstick and never considering a pelvic collection; presenting the DAMA form as a threat; never explicitly returning the decision to her

setting: A specificity station — you either say the specific things or you do not pass, and fluency will not save you. 'We'll vaccinate him and give him antibiotics' is the borderline answer that fails, and the role-player is scripted to push: say vaccinations and she asks 'Against what?', say antibiotics and she asks 'Which one, for how long?'
stem: Emergency department, metropolitan hospital. Ryan Mercer, 24, was brought in after a motor vehicle accident a few hours ago. On arrival he was haemodynamically stable and the decision was made to manage him conservatively. He is now complaining of chest and abdominal pain.

CT chest and abdomen: fractures of the left lower ribs, a grade II splenic laceration, and a small volume of free fluid in the abdominal cavity. Observation chart: blood pressure falling from 120/80 on arrival to 100/70, with a rising heart rate — not shocked, but the trend is downward. He is alert and orientated. His mother Jane is in the department and has asked to speak to you. She has not yet been told what the scan showed.
Tasks: explain the condition to the mother — explain the immediate management — explain the long-term management — answer her questions.
tasks: Explain the condition to the mother
Explain the immediate management
Explain the long-term management
Answer her questions
time: Thirty seconds to introduce, confirm consent, ask an open question and give empathy and reassurance as one twenty-second block · ninety seconds on the findings and what the spleen is · a minute on why theatre now · then two and three quarter minutes on the four key points, where the station is decided · thirty seconds for the ribs · and the last minute for MedicAlert, follow-up, her questions and a teach-back

back.dx: GRADE II SPLENIC LACERATION FAILING NON-OPERATIVE MANAGEMENT — ongoing haemorrhage with a falling blood pressure and free intraperitoneal fluid — heading for theatre and most likely splenectomy, with left lower rib fractures alongside. Immediate management: two large-bore cannulae, group and hold and crossmatch, FBE, coagulation and lactate, with the massive transfusion protocol if he deteriorates · serial observations and serial haemoglobin · fasted and consented for theatre · analgesia and oxygen · tranexamic acid if within three hours of injury VERIFY · surgical and anaesthetic review · and, rurally, resuscitate and activate MedSTAR rather than sitting on a bleeding spleen. If he stabilises, splenic preservation, repair or angioembolisation by interventional radiology are established alternatives, and mentioning embolisation is what makes the answer sound current VERIFY. Say early, before she has to ask: people live completely normal lives without a spleen — work, sport, travel, family — with some specific precautions. Those precautions are the four key points, and each needs its specifics. One, vaccination against the encapsulated organisms the spleen normally clears: pneumococcal, both conjugate and polysaccharide in sequence · meningococcal, both ACWY and B, which are different vaccines and both must be said · Haemophilus influenzae type B, which is a bacterium and not the flu vaccine, a confusion that catches candidates every sitting · plus annual influenza, a virus, given because flu predisposes to secondary bacterial infection, and the routine schedule and COVID-19 kept up to date VERIFY. Timing is the number the examiner waits for: elective splenectomy means completing vaccines at least two weeks before surgery; an emergency splenectomy means at least two weeks after — but if follow-up is doubtful, vaccinate before discharge, because a vaccine given early beats a vaccine never given VERIFY. Two, daily prophylaxis: amoxicillin 250 mg once daily or phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg twice daily for at least three years, longer or lifelong where risk is higher — not the commonly taught 500 mg, and not 'Six months to two years' correction VERIFY — with once-daily preferred because adherence over years is the whole game. Three, the emergency standby supply and the fever rule, which is the highest-yield thing said in the station: amoxicillin 2 g stat, four 500 mg capsules, continued at 1 g eight-hourly if review is delayed, or cefuroxime 500 mg for non-severe penicillin hypersensitivity with ID advice for severe allergy VERIFY — and the rule given as an instruction: any fever, shivers, shakes or chills means take it immediately and go straight to an emergency department, not wait and see, not ring for an appointment — and yes, even though he is on the daily tablet, because that is a small preventive dose and will not treat a serious infection. The justification: overwhelming post-splenectomy infection begins non-specifically and can progress to septic shock and death within hours, with risk lifelong but front-loaded — about 30% of infections in year one and about 50% within two years VERIFY. Four, travel, animal bites and malaria: a pre-travel consultation, malaria chemoprophylaxis where indicated and rigorous bite avoidance because asplenic patients get more severe malaria · any dog or cat bite or scratch breaking the skin needs prompt review and antibiotics, typically amoxicillin-clavulanate, for capnocytophaga canimorsus, with tick bites mattering too VERIFY · travel insurance declared · and every doctor, dentist and pharmacist told. Then the wrap-around that turns a borderline pass into a clear one: a MedicAlert bracelet or card plus a phone medical ID, with its reason — if he is ever brought in drowsy, whoever finds him needs to know in five seconds · a vaccination card and everything on the Australian immunisation register · educating the family, not just the patient, because a septic patient may be too confused to act · and surgical and GP follow-up with boosters and a recall. One South Australian point almost nobody makes: spleen Australia registration is not open to South Australians — the register covers victoria, Western Australia, queensland and tasmania — so use its patient materials and vaccination cards, but the ongoing recall system in SA is the GP, the air and a practice recall correction VERIFY.
plan: Confirm consent in ten seconds, then open properly: 'Can you tell me what you've been told so far, and how you're doing?' — then empathy and reassurance together as one twenty-second block, not repeated into padding.
The three scan findings in plain words, then what the spleen is and does — before any talk of removing it (see findings).

Why theatre now: the plan was to watch, but the blood pressure is drifting down and there is blood in the abdomen, so the bleeding has not settled — preservation or embolisation if he stabilises, otherwise splenectomy.

Answer the question before she asks it: people live completely normal lives without a spleen — then the caveat that sets up the rest: a few specific serious infections, and four straightforward precautions.

Key points one and two with their numbers: the four vaccine groups with Hib distinguished from influenza and meningococcal split into ACWY and B, plus the timing rule · then amoxicillin 250 mg daily for at least three years (see dx).
Key point three, given as an instruction and held when she pushes — the standby supply, the fever rule, and why the daily tablet is not enough.
Key point four — travel, malaria and animal bites — then the ribs in thirty seconds (see findings).

pefe: Role-player: Jane Mercer, 51, Ryan's mother, rung ninety minutes ago and drove straight in. She has seen him briefly — awake, in pain, told her to talk to the doctors — and nobody has told her anything about the scans. Ryan is 24, an apprentice electrician who plays local football and lives at home, healthy, no allergies, no medications. She is frightened and holding it together, asking rapid-fire questions, and becomes tearful at the words operation or remove.

What she holds back: the dog at home and Ryan's Bali trip in October, raised only if the candidate mentions travel or animals or asks about concerns. Her agenda is 'Is he going to be alright?' and, once surgery is mentioned, 'Can he live without it?' — and what she wants to leave with is something concrete she can do, so she visibly relaxes when the fever rule is given clearly.

How she tests them: she makes them be specific — categories get 'Against what?' and 'Which one, for how long?' · if they use 'Grade ii' she asks whether two out of five is good · if they hedge on living without a spleen she asks again · if they talk over her tears she goes quiet and withdrawn, and recovers only if they pause · if they never ask about consent she says nothing and marks it.

Mark them against these: confirmed the patient's consent to discuss with his mother · open question then about twenty seconds of empathy and reassurance · explained the three scan findings in plain English · explained what the spleen is before discussing removing it · justified theatre by the falling BP and free fluid rather than the grade · mentioned preservation or embolisation · said clearly that people live normal lives without a spleen · named pneumococcal · named both meningococcal ACWY and B · named Hib and distinguished it from influenza · named annual influenza · gave the timing rule · named the daily antibiotic with dose and duration · gave the standby supply as a separate thing · stated the fever rule as an instruction and held it when pushed · explained why prophylaxis does not replace the standby dose · covered travel and malaria · covered animal bites · gave MedicAlert with a reason · arranged a vaccination card and recall · educated the family · addressed the rib fractures · and finished with teach-back of the fever rule.

The ten seconds that must not be skipped — Ryan is 24 and an adult, so his information is confidential to him: 'Before we start — because Ryan is an adult, I just need to confirm he's happy for me to discuss his condition with you. Have you been able to speak with him?' She says yes. Tick it and move on. If the candidate never asks, the role-player says nothing and marks it as a fail

Why he is going to theatre — Grades I and II are usually managed non-operatively, so the grade is not the decision — the physiology is. A falling blood pressure with free intraperitoneal fluid means the bleeding has not settled: failed non-operative management. Say 'The grade doesn't decide the operation — his blood pressure does'

The rib fractures, which almost every candidate ignores — They do not need an operation — ribs heal over six to eight weeks and you cannot cast a chest. The point is analgesia, because pain means shallow breathing, atelectasis and then pneumonia — so proper pain relief, deep-breathing exercises, physiotherapy, and watching for air or blood around the lung. Thirty seconds, and she asks about them at seven minutes if you do not

The three scan findings, said in plain words — Broken ribs on the left · a tear in the spleen · blood collecting inside the abdomen. Do not lead with 'Grade ii' — it means nothing to her, and if you say it she asks whether two out of five is good

What the spleen is, before you talk about removing it — 'An organ about the size of a fist, sitting in the upper left part of the tummy, tucked up under the ribs — which is why a blow to that side can injure it. It is part of the immune system: its main job is helping the body fight off certain serious infections in the blood.' Saying 'Under the ribs' ties the two injuries together for free

setting: The diagnosis is easy, which is exactly why the failure rate is high. Candidates say 'It's viral, it's self-limiting, take paracetamol and fluids' and stop. She will say 'My throat really hurts' up to three times — she is not asking for a diagnosis, she is asking for relief, and the mark is the lignocaine spray used before she eats and drinks.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Jane Whitmore, 19, a university student, saw your colleague two days ago with a severe sore throat, a cough and marked tiredness. She has returned today for the results and still feels unwell.

Examination two days ago: redness and exudate on both tonsils · multiple tender cervical lymph nodes, soft on palpation · no rash · mild splenomegaly and mild hepatomegaly. Results: FBE shows a raised white cell count with lymphocytosis and atypical lymphocytes, Hb and platelets normal · EBV IgM positive · CMV IgG positive · LFTs show a mild rise in AST and ALT under three times the upper limit, bilirubin normal.

findings: The liver function tests, which are there deliberately

A mild rise in the enzymes under three times the upper limit with a normal bilirubin — mild EBV hepatitis, expected, settling, and not liver damage. It sets up two practical things: no alcohol until it settles, and repeat bloods at review. Skipping it because it is the least dramatic result loses a marked item
If the examiner probes the serology

Monospot is quick but insensitive in the first week, so a negative does not exclude EBV · ebv-specific serology is more reliable, with VCA IgM positive and EBNA IgG absent indicating acute infection, because EBNA IgG only appears at 6-12 weeks · and naming HIV seroconversion, CMV, toxoplasmosis and acute viral hepatitis shows you have not anchored VERIFY

back.dx: ACUTE EPSTEIN-BARR VIRUS INFECTION PRESENTING AS INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS — glandular fever — with mild hepatitis and mild splenomegaly. Use the syndrome name with the patient and mention EBV as the virus behind it, then map the features onto her rather than reciting them into the air: severe exudative sore throat, fever, tender swollen neck glands, marked and prolonged tiredness, enlarged spleen and inflamed liver — 'You have almost the full picture, which is why I am confident rather than going on one blood test.' 'Implications' means three blocks — complications, prognosis, and what it means for her life over the next few weeks — and candidates who do only the first lose marks. Frame before naming: most people recover completely, and these are mentioned so she knows when to seek help — the spleen, which can tear if it takes a knock · tonsillar swelling enough to obstruct the airway · rarely neurological, cardiac or haematological involvement · and the fatigue that genuinely drags for weeks and sometimes a couple of months. On the cancer link: do not lead with it and do not hide it — 'There is a very small, long-term association between this virus and some rare blood and throat cancers. To put that in perspective, the large majority of adults carry this virus for life and never have any problem from it.' Management is where the station is won, and 'Supportive' is a list with numbers on it. The throat first, because it is her agenda: paracetamol 1 g four times daily to a maximum of 4 g in 24 hours, taken regularly rather than when unbearable · ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food if not contraindicated · codeine added if that is not enough · and the item that actually helps, a lignocaine or benzydamine throat spray or gargle used a few minutes before eating and drinking so she can swallow — which is the point, because it keeps fluids going · plus cool fluids, ice blocks, soft food and saline gargles VERIFY. Then hydration with oral rehydration solution and small sips, rest while febrile and then graded activity rather than a month in bed. Then the spleen, specific and with a duration: no contact or collision sport and no heavy lifting for at least four weeks from symptom onset, walking and light activity fine, and clinical review before return — individualised, with longer for persistent splenomegaly or high-impact sport, and no routine serial ultrasound because it does not predict rupture VERIFY. Then what you are not doing, each with a reason: no antibiotics, because it is viral — and critically because amoxicillin or ampicillin causes a florid morbilliform rash in the large majority of acute EBV, which is not a true penicillin allergy and must be documented as such, with phenoxymethylpenicillin preferred if a bacterial tonsillitis genuinely needs treating · no antivirals, because aciclovir reduces shedding without improving outcomes · and no routine corticosteroids — not because they 'Trigger the malignant associations of ebv', which is a theoretical concern rather than the reason correction, but because there is no demonstrated benefit in uncomplicated disease and there are risks, reserving them for impending airway obstruction from tonsillar hypertrophy or severe haemolysis or thrombocytopenia VERIFY. Then transmission and life admin: saliva spread, so no kissing or sharing drink bottles, cutlery, toothbrushes or lip products while symptomatic · no work, school or university exclusion, because shedding continues for months and exclusion is pointless — she returns when she feels well enough · no alcohol while the enzymes are raised · blood donation deferred · a medical certificate · and missed-pill rules if she has been vomiting on the combined pill VERIFY. Red flags with actions: inability to swallow saliva, drooling, voice change or noisy breathing — airway · inability to keep fluids down or minimal urine — dehydration · severe abdominal pain, especially left-sided, or pain at the left shoulder tip, or faintness — the spleen, and that is a triple-zero call · severe headache, neck stiffness, confusion or seizure · chest pain or palpitations · jaundice or dark urine · and new petechiae or bleeding gums. Review in one week with repeat LFTs, a spleen check and written information.
plan: Open with 'How are you feeling today?' and let her describe the throat — then validate it honestly: 'This is one of the sorest throats there is, and I'm going to make that the first thing we deal with.' then permission, signpost, and the first concern check.
The results in a building sequence — infection, then viral, then this virus, then the liver — chunking and checking after each (see findings).
Name the syndrome and the virus, say it spreads by saliva and is extremely common, then map its features onto her own findings so the diagnosis is evidenced rather than asserted.

Implications as a framed block: most people recover fully, then the spleen, the airway, the rare neurological, cardiac and haematological ones, and the fatigue — each attached to when to seek help, not left as frightening nouns.

Management led by the throat: regular paracetamol, an NSAID, a step up if needed, and the lignocaine spray before eating and drinking — then fluids with oral rehydration and small sips, and rest with graded return.
The spleen with its duration and the pre-return review — and hold it when she pushes about finals, with empathy and a reason rather than a lecture.
What you are not giving and why — no antibiotics with the amoxicillin rash named, no antivirals, no routine steroids — plus transmission, no exclusion from university, no alcohol and a certificate.

Red flags each with an action including the left shoulder-tip pain and the triple-zero call · review in one week with repeat liver tests · written information · second concern check and a teach-back of the sport advice and the red flags.

pefe: Role-player: Jane Whitmore, 19, a second-year university student in a share house who plays Saturday netball, unwell about five days. The worst sore throat she has ever had — swallowing feels like swallowing glass — with fevers and sweats, sore neck glands, exhaustion after fourteen hours' sleep, and a dry cough. She has barely eaten in three days and is drinking much less because it hurts, though she is not vomiting and is still passing urine. On the combined pill, taking one paracetamol 'When I remember', no allergies, six standard drinks on a Saturday, has a boyfriend. Flat and miserable rather than anxious.

Her two agendas: the throat, said early and repeated if nothing better than paracetamol is offered — this is the engine of the station · and netball finals in three weeks, which she fully intends to play and pushes back on once. The worry she voices only if asked about concerns is that she googled 'Atypical lymphocytes' last night and read about leukaemia, and she asks the cancer question at about five minutes if complications were mentioned and it was skipped.

How she scores it: she warms noticeably when the lignocaine spray is offered · she accepts the sport advice if given a clear reason, and accepts it enthusiastically if softened to please her, which is marked as a fail · and she asks what any unfamiliar word means rather than helping the candidate out.

Mark them against these: acknowledged the throat before the results · checked concerns twice · explained the FBE including 'Atypical' and defused it · gave IgM versus IgG as a principle · explained CMV as past infection only · explained the liver result with the alcohol advice and repeat testing · named glandular fever and the virus · mapped the features onto her · delivered complications framed with actions attached · answered the cancer question honestly and proportionately · gave paracetamol dose and frequency with an NSAID and a step-up · offered the lignocaine spray before eating and drinking · gave hydration advice with oral rehydration and small sips · gave the spleen advice with a duration and a pre-return review · held it when pushed · stated no antibiotics and why including the amoxicillin rash · stated no antivirals and when steroids are used · gave transmission advice and said there is no exclusion period · named red flags with actions including left shoulder-tip pain · arranged a one-week review with repeat bloods and a certificate · and closed with teach-back.

The full blood count — 'Your white cells — the cells that fight infection — are higher than normal. The type that is raised is called lymphocytes, and that pattern usually points to a virus rather than a bacteria. Some of them look bigger and different from usual — we call them atypical, and that is a very typical finding in this infection, not something sinister.' Defuse 'Atypical' the moment you say it — she googled it last night and read about leukaemia

The antibodies, and the CMV distractor — Give the principle first: IgM is the early one and means recent or current; IgG is the later one, stays for years and means past. So EBV IgM positive is the infection she has now, and CMV IgG positive means she met that virus at some point and it healed — it is not causing today's illness. 'EBV now, CMV in the past'

The paracetamol question candidates freeze on — Yes — therapeutic doses for a short course are safe. Mildly raised transaminases from EBV are not a contraindication; the concern is overdose and chronic high-dose use. Do not exceed 4 g in 24 hours, avoid combination products that double-dose, and avoid alcohol VERIFY

findings: Well, comfortable, afebrile, no pallor or jaundice · hands on photograph: flat erythema involving both hands and fingers roughly symmetrically — a patch rather than raised plaques — with mild scaling and some crusting and no purulent discharge · scalp: small papules and vesicles, no discharge · no burrows in the web spaces · no lymphadenopathy and no supraclavicular nodes · thyroid normal · no hepatosplenomegaly · dipstick normal

back.dx: ALLERGIC CONTACT DERMATITIS TO HAIR DYE — a type IV delayed hypersensitivity, most often to para-phenylenediamine, in the exact distribution of contact. The reasoning given out loud, in three parts: she has an itchy rash, so the problem is inflammation in the skin rather than elsewhere · it is confined to two areas rather than being all over, and when itch is that localised something has usually touched those places · and those two places are exactly where the dye went — the scalp, and the ungloved fingers that applied it — with an onset 24 to 72 hours later, which is the timing of delayed hypersensitivity rather than an immediate reaction. The point candidates fold on: previous uneventful use does not exclude it — sensitisation develops over time, and it is the second and subsequent exposures that react. She pushes once with 'But I've used it for years', and a candidate who changes diagnosis has failed the point. The differentials, each with why it fits less well: irritant contact dermatitis — same distribution but burns rather than itches, needs no prior sensitisation, often coexists, and patch testing separates them · atopic dermatitis — no personal or family atopy, no flexural involvement, first episode with an obvious trigger · pompholyx — deep-seated vesicles on palms and finger sides, recurrent, and would not explain the scalp · scabies — no burrows, no itchy contacts, and in adults it characteristically spares the head and neck, which hers does not · psoriasis — a flat patch rather than a thickened silvery plaque, normal nails, no family history · tinea — symmetrical and not annular, with scrapings if it fails to respond · urticaria — wheals are raised, individually resolve within 24 hours and migrate, whereas hers is flat, fixed and contact-shaped · lichen planus — violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules · herpetic whitlow — usually one digit, painful more than itchy · secondary bacterial infection — afebrile with crusting but no purulence, though worth rechecking · and drug eruption — no new medications and the wrong distribution. Then the systemic group, said briefly but said: lymphoma and leukaemia, cholestatic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, thyroid disease, coeliac disease and iron deficiency — none supported by the history or examination, and with the clinching general point that a systemic cause almost always causes itch all over rather than in two specific spots. Management is brief but should not be omitted: stop and wash off the product · a moderate to potent topical corticosteroid such as methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% or mometasone 0.1% to hands and scalp, as a lotion or foam in hair, with a mild steroid only if face or eyelids are involved VERIFY · emollient and a soap substitute · a sedating antihistamine at night, which helps sleep more than itch · oral prednisolone only for severe or extensive disease or significant facial swelling VERIFY · swab and flucloxacillin if pustules or honey-coloured crust appear VERIFY · dermatology patch testing once the acute episode settles, to confirm PPD and map cross-reactors · and review in three to five days. Prevention is parked and then answered properly when she asks whether she can ever dye her hair again: lifelong avoidance of PPD and its relatives p-phenylenediamine, toluene-2,5-diamine and p-aminophenol, with 'Ppd-free' not guaranteed because cross-reactors exist — azo textile dyes, black rubber, sulfonamides, and benzocaine and paba sunscreens and local anaesthetics, which is worth documenting for future dental and surgical work · never a black henna tattoo · the box's 48-hour patch test is unreliable once sensitised and can itself provoke a reaction · and an allergy card with the record documented VERIFY.
plan: Open, empathise with the itch and ask about concerns — then the framing sentence that shows you have a system before you have an answer: 'I divide the causes into problems in the skin itself and problems elsewhere in the body that show up as itch, and then I ask whether there is a rash, because that splits it further.'

The itch: onset, first episode or recurrent, all over or localised, severity out of ten, does it wake her at night, and is it worse after a hot shower — the last two are the scabies pair and both are expected.
'Is there a rash?' — then explore it rather than ticking it: where exactly, what colour, any blisters, any discharge, painful as well as itchy, symmetrical.

The contact history, which solves it: new soaps, shampoos and conditioners · creams, makeup, nail and hair products — 'Have you dyed or treated your hair recently?' · then 'Did you wear gloves?' and 'Have you used that product before?' · plus perfumes, clothes, washing powder, jewellery, occupation and hobbies.

Differential-specific questions — atopy and family history, family psoriasis, travel or new accommodation and whether contacts are itching, new medications, recent viral illness — then the systemic red-flag screen even though you already know the answer: weight loss, night sweats, lumps, jaundice or dark urine, kidney problems, heat intolerance and tremor, chronic diarrhoea.
Ask the examiner in the fixed sequence, naming what you are looking for (see findings).

pefe: Role-player: Lily Barnett, 24, a university student who works part-time in a bookshop and lives in a share house, normally very healthy. Four days of itch at 8/10 in her fingertips and across her scalp and nowhere else, waking her at night, with red flaky hands and tiny blisters on the scalp, no pus and no pain. She scratches her hands and head throughout, and is fed up and practical rather than frightened.

The key fact and when she gives it: she dyed her own hair at home on the weekend with a permanent box dye and did not wear the gloves, having used that brand for years without a problem, which is why she does not believe it could be the cause. The itch started the next day or the day after. She volunteers it only if asked about new products, cosmetics, hair products or contacts — and if nobody asks, she offers it at about six minutes.

Everything else is negative: no atopy in her or her family, no family psoriasis, no travel or new accommodation, nobody else itchy, no new medications or herbal products, no recent illness, no weight loss, night sweats, lumps, jaundice, dark urine, bowel symptoms, heat intolerance or joint pains, not pregnant, no known allergies. Her hidden worry, given only if asked about concerns, is that her aunt had lymphoma.

Mark them against these: opened with empathy and asked about concerns · established timing and that it was a first episode · established that the itch is localised · asked about severity and night waking · asked about hot showers · asked 'Is there a rash?' · took a mini rash history · took a contact history including hair products · asked about gloves and previous use · asked about occupation and hobbies · asked atopy and family history · asked the scabies questions about travel, accommodation and itchy contacts · asked about new medications and recent viral illness · ran the systemic red-flag screen · asked for general appearance and temperature · asked for a full skin examination · specifically asked for the web spaces, wrists and axillae · asked for lymph nodes including supraclavicular · asked for thyroid and abdomen · described the rash with primary and secondary morphology and negatives · named contact dermatitis with reasons · explained that prior tolerance does not exclude allergy · gave differentials with reasons, skin and systemic · and finished with a brief plan, patch testing, safety-net and teach-back.

Ask in sequence and say what you are looking for — General appearance — cachexia, pallor, jaundice · vital signs, particularly temperature for secondary infection · a full skin examination · the hands and scalp, and specifically the web spaces, wrists, axillae and waistline for scabies burrows, plus the nails · a full lymph node examination including supraclavicular · thyroid · abdomen for hepatosplenomegaly · and a urine dipstick. Asking for 'A general examination' and waiting costs thirty seconds

Describing it to formula — Site and distribution · primary morphology — flat patch, so not urticaria which is raised and oedematous, and not psoriasis which is a thickened plaque · secondary morphology — scale and crust · then the negatives that matter: no purulent discharge, no burrows, no nail pitting · then interpret

Do not be thrown by the vesicles — Candidates learn that dermatitis is flat, then hear 'Papules and vesicles on the scalp' and abandon the diagnosis. Acute contact dermatitis is vesicular, weeping and crusted; the flat scaly lichenified picture is the chronic phase, and both can coexist

The history detail the case turns on — She dyed her own hair at home a few days ago and did not wear gloves. She has used that brand for years without trouble. The itch began 24 to 48 hours later, confined to scalp and fingertips — exactly where the dye touched her. She volunteers it only if asked about new products or hair products

POSITIVE — ask for it BY NAME, even after a general tenderness question. Some examiners answer 'no tenderness' generally and then give you a positive renal angle only when you name it
Trap on the card — the blood
Blood on the dipstick does NOT mean a stone. Infection causes haematuria. Do not switch to renal colic
Trap on the card — the protein
1+ protein does NOT mean pre-eclampsia when the blood pressure is normal and there are no neurological features. Infection causes proteinuria too. NITRITES are what confirm the urinary tract

dx: **Acute pyelonephritis at 20 weeks.** Say it with the reasons attached: **the pain is on the right and drags downward, which is the pattern kidney pain follows · burning on passing urine and going more often · a fever · nitrites on the dipstick, which come from bacteria · and tenderness when I tapped over your kidney at the back**.

CORRECTION — **cystitis does not usually cause fever.** Systemic upset — **fever, rigors, vomiting, loin pain** — is what moves you from the lower tract to the upper. **Fever with urinary symptoms in pregnancy is pyelonephritis until proven otherwise.**

**The two dipstick traps.** **Blood does not mean a stone** — infection causes haematuria, and switching to renal colic is a named fail. **1+ protein does not mean pre-eclampsia** when the blood pressure is normal and there are no neurological features — infection causes proteinuria too. **Nitrites are what tie this to the urinary tract.**
**This is not managed in general practice.** Transfer to the emergency department for **admission**. It is a different disease in pregnancy.

**Urine for microscopy, culture and sensitivity BEFORE the first dose.** Then **intravenous antibiotics, continued until she is clinically improving** — **not a single stat dose, and not oral**. VERIFY the current first-line agent against Therapeutic Guidelines; **do not memorise a combination**.
**Analgesia and antipyretics safe in pregnancy, and intravenous fluids.** **Bloods including FBE and inflammatory markers. CTG to monitor the baby.**
**Post-treatment culture**, and **consider prophylaxis for the remainder of the pregnancy**. **Significant bacteriuria is 10⁵ CFU/mL on culture.**

Keep screening after you know the answer — say the bridging sentence out loud: **'That does sound like a urine infection, and I'll come back to it. Before I do, I need to check a few things about the pregnancy itself — any bleeding? Any leaking of fluid? Is the baby moving normally?'**

Deliver the differentials **in named groups, three Ps leading**: **the pregnancy-related causes — pre-eclampsia, the labour starting early, the afterbirth separating** · other kidney and bladder causes — cystitis, a stone · gastrointestinal causes · liver and gallbladder causes. **Seven names in four groups beats twelve recited flat.**

The numbers and the SA plan: **20 weeks is the line above which pre-eclampsia exists at all · 140/90 hypertension, 160/110 severe · fetal heart rate 110–160 · CTG from about 26–28 weeks** VERIFY. From an MM5 site this is **stabilise and transfer** — Wallaroo and Kadina do not manage it; receiving units are the **WCH, Lyell McEwin or FMC**. **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if she is unstable. **PATS** for the partner's travel, said aloud. **TIS National 131 450** — never a family member.
plan: **'Examiner, could I have her vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?'** In this version the **temperature is the station** — 39 °C.
Open question, then acknowledge the concern in one sentence and signpost.

The pain: **where exactly · out of ten · what sort of pain · when did it start · constant or coming and going · does it radiate · anything better or worse**. Here: right-sided, **dragging down to the right lower abdomen**, two days, on and off then constant, getting worse.

The bridging sentence, out loud, the moment the answer appears: **'that does sound like a urine infection, and I'll come back to it. Before I do, I need to check a few things about the pregnancy itself.'** **The marks are for exclusion, not arrival.**
General gastrointestinal screen: **any nausea or vomiting · bowels normal · passing wind · any bloating · any fevers or chills · any change in appetite**.

The obstetric block, the three Ps, asked even though the pain is urinary: **any bleeding from down below · any discharge or leaking of fluid · is the baby moving as much as usual, when did you last feel it**.

**Preterm labour specifically: does the pain come in waves that last longer and arrive closer together?** **Abruption specifically: is the pain constant, and is the uterus tender?** One question each.

The pre-eclampsia set in full: **headaches · change in vision, blurring, flashing lights, spots · swelling in your legs, hands or face, and is it there when you wake · pain up under the ribs on the right · yellowing of the skin · chest pain or breathlessness · passing less urine**.
Routine antenatal history, briskly: **routine bloods, dating scan, the 18–20 week scan, the sweet drink test · previous pregnancies and any problems**.

Gastrointestinal rule-outs: **appetite · any lump in the groin · worse after fatty meals · aspirin or anti-inflammatories**. Then kidney and bladder: **burning on passing urine · going more often · blood in the urine**.
Travel, social history, and **'what were you most worried this might be?'** — deliberately last, and deliberately brief.

Ask for the card, in order: **general appearance · vital signs including temperature · neurological, fundoscopy, reflexes and specifically ankle clonus · chest · abdomen, distension and tenderness over the liver and the uterus · then the uterus: fundal height, fetal heart rate, tenderness, palpable contractions · bowel sounds · RENAL ANGLE TENDERNESS BY NAME · inguinal orifices and a rectal examination · speculum with consent and a chaperone — os open or closed, blood or fluid · lower limbs · urine dipstick**.

Give the diagnosis **with the reasons attached**: the site and pattern of the pain, the dysuria and frequency, the fever, **the nitrites**, and **the positive renal angle**. Explain nitrites as **'a chemical that comes from bacteria'**.

Handle the two dipstick traps **before the examiner raises them** — the blood is from the infection, not a stone; the protein is from the infection, not pre-eclampsia, because the blood pressure is normal.

Differentials **in named groups**, three Ps first, then kidney and bladder, then gastrointestinal, then liver and gallbladder. Close with the six-bullet plan in thirty seconds: **transfer and admit · culture before antibiotics · IV antibiotics until improving · analgesia, antipyretics and fluids · bloods and CTG · post-treatment culture and consider prophylaxis.**

dx: **Constipation at 28 weeks, with iron as the contributor.** Say it with the mechanism attached: **'iron commonly causes constipation, and it can also upset the stomach lining. The pain dragging to your left lower side fits with loaded bowel on that side, and everything else I've examined is normal.'**

**Why a normal card is not an anticlimax.** A normal examination **is a finding**. It moves the benign diagnosis to the top and tells you the marks are elsewhere. **Delivering a benign diagnosis with reasons is a marked skill, not a consolation prize.**

The sentence that earns it: **'a normal examination is itself a finding — it lets me tell you this with confidence rather than as a guess.'** Then list what was normal: examination, urine, blood pressure, fetal movements, non-tender uterus.

The mechanism, in her words: **'pregnancy hormones slow the bowel down, and the iron tablets you're taking for your anaemia slow it further — that combination is one of the commonest causes of pain in pregnancy.'**

**Do not simply stop the iron.** **'Not without replacing it — the anaemia matters for you and the baby.'** Options: **alternate-day dosing**, or **a different preparation**. **Change how she takes it rather than stopping it.** VERIFY current iron regimens.

The six-bullet plan: **reassure with a named diagnosis · increase fluid and fibre · review the iron — alternate-day dosing or a different preparation · an OSMOTIC laxative is preferred in pregnancy · treat the anaemia, do not simply stop the iron · safety-net and review in a week.** VERIFY laxative choice in pregnancy.

Keep screening after the iron appears: **'that's useful, thank you. Iron can certainly do that. Let me still work through the rest, because I don't want to settle on the simplest explanation too early.'**

**Travel is in the stem in this version, which is your cue to open that door — at the END, not the beginning.** A forty-second mini travel history, compressed into the last twenty-five seconds. **A candidate who spends two minutes on street food and never asks about bleeding has failed.**

The travel additions, **added to the four usual groups and never substituted for them**: **hepatitis A** (street food, jaundice, dark urine, pale stool — serology) and **malaria** (cyclical fever, rigors, anaemia, endemic destination — **thick and thin films × 3** or rapid antigen test; **severe in pregnancy, admit**). back.dx: Acute viral hepatitis, most likely B or C, acquired through a shared needle. The naming: 'Gary, most likely you have acute hepatitis — that means your liver is inflamed — and it is most likely caused by a virus you picked up when you shared the needle. Given that route, the likely ones are hepatitis B or C. My reasons: the tummy pain, nausea and loss of appetite, the yellowing of your skin and eyes — and on examination an enlarged, tender liver and bilirubin in your urine, which should not be there.' if he asks which type: 'It matters more than you'd think. If it is hepatitis B we can vaccinate the people around you. If it is hepatitis C there is no vaccine — but it is now curable with tablets, usually over two to three months.' The history is identical across all three versions and the card decides the answer. The spine: acknowledge the fear he voices in his first sentence · signpost three blocks — the unwellness, the trip, the heroin · define 'Unwell' (Low energy, sleepy or feverish), then timing and impact · the travel history in full by mnemonic, because 'Just having fun with mates' is not a travel history · the heroin in three steps and in order — 'Can you tell me more about that?', then 'How did you use it?', then 'Did you share needles?', because opening with the needle question loses the guilt, the first-time detail and whether use has continued · all three blood-borne virus boxes every time — hepatitis, HIV, injection-related — so the negatives let you exclude the other two versions out loud · go back for the sexual history after he says no to sex overseas, because the brief tells him to say no once and answer fully the second time · pick up 'I feel so guilty', said at least three times, and screen mood and self-harm · and interrogate the card for what it does not mention — jaundice, organomegaly, murmur, injection sites, dipstick. Confidentiality is qualified: these are notifiable infections and contact tracing is done sensitively without naming him. Harm reduction — needle and syringe services and take-home naloxone — is offered without judgement. Differentials, grouped: the other blood-borne infections — HIV seroconversion, which the absent rash and lymphadenopathy argue against but which is still tested · infective endocarditis, which the absent murmur argues against · hepatitis a from street food, despite the vaccine, and hepatitis E · travel infections — malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis · glandular fever and CMV, which can cause a hepatitis · syphilis · drug- or alcohol-related liver injury · and, given the guilt, depression and anxiety. The plan: LFTs, HbSAg with anti-HBc IgM and anti-HBs, HCV antibody with HCV RNA, HIV and syphilis serology with specific consent for the HIV test, hepatitis a and E serology, FBE, coagulation, malaria films · referral to sexual health and hepatology or ID · notification and sensitive contact tracing · no alcohol, no paracetamol beyond therapeutic doses · harm reduction · a mood review next week · and red flags: confusion or drowsiness, which is hepatic encephalopathy, bleeding, or rapid deterioration — emergency department or 000.

A week of being drained and feverish, worse each day, unable to get out of bed for two days. Three weeks in Indonesia, back two weeks, 'Just fun with mates, beach and bars' until pressed. My reasons: fever, chest pain, the racing of your heart — and on examination an abnormal heart sound and signs your heart is struggling to pump. Those are a complication, not a separate illness. Hospital today.' if the examiner challenges: 'Endocarditis stays primary because acute valvular regurgitation from the infection explains the failure. Heart failure alone would miss the treatable cause and delay cultures and antibiotics.' The history is identical across all three versions and the card decides the answer. (twenty seconds, one of them self-harm) (★)

findings: Normal — but only given if you ask for it, and if you never ask for an ECG that is a fail on its own regardless of the total. A potassium of 6.1 is moderate and cannot be ignored even in a well patient

back.dx: PSEUDOHYPERKALAEMIA — potassium released from red cells during collection, not a true elevation — but only concluded after a normal ECG, normal observations and a haemolysed-sample report, and only confirmed by a clean repeat. The opening sentence: 'A potassium of 6.1 is in the moderate range and I cannot ignore it. Even though she is well, I would obtain an ECG and review her observations before I decide anything. I would also ask the laboratory whether the sample was haemolysed, whether there was a delay in processing, and what her platelet and white cell counts were.' then, with a normal ECG and a haemolysed report: 'The most likely explanation is pseudohyperkalaemia. I would repeat the sample with a wider-bore needle, avoiding a prolonged tourniquet and fist clenching, and get it to the laboratory promptly. I would not treat, and I would not cancel her procedure, until I have a clean result. If the repeat is also high, then it is real and I work through renal function, medications and adrenal causes.' The causes to state: sample haemolysis from a small needle, a tight or prolonged tourniquet, fist pumping, or vigorous tube handling · delayed separation or processing, particularly in a cold sample · marked thrombocytosis or leukocytosis releasing potassium in the tube · contamination from an edta tube drawn first · and, if the repeat is genuinely high, the true causes — renal impairment, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, salt substitutes, acidosis, and Addison's disease. The contrast with version A is the whole point: there, a potassium of 7.2 with ECG changes in a man with stage 4 CKD on ramipril and spironolactone is protect, shift, remove — calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose and salbutamol, then dialysis. Here, nothing is given, because treating a false value with insulin in a well woman causes the hypoglycaemia that was the only danger in the room. To the patient: 'One of your blood tests has come back with a high level of a salt called potassium. When that is genuine it can affect the heart's rhythm, which is why I have checked your heart tracing — and it is normal. The laboratory has told me the sample was damaged when it was collected, which releases potassium from the blood cells and makes the result read falsely high. The most likely explanation is that the result is not real, but I am not going to assume that — I would like to repeat the test now, taken more carefully, and your procedure stays on the books unless the repeat says otherwise.'
plan: First sentence: the level is moderate and cannot be ignored — ECG and observations before any conclusion, even though she is well.
The laboratory questions: haemolysis, processing delay, platelet and white cell counts.
Read the ECG systematically — rate, P, PR, QRS, T — and state that it is normal, which is what licenses the next step.
Name pseudohyperkalaemia as the most likely explanation, with the mechanism, and list the sample-related causes.
Management: repeat the sample properly, do not treat, do not cancel the procedure — and say what you would do if the repeat is also high, including a medication and renal review.
Explain to the patient in plain words — the effect, not the number — without false reassurance or alarm, and with the repeat and the procedure decision made clear.

The three laboratory questions: 'Was the sample haemolysed, was there a delay in processing, and what were her platelet and white cell counts?'
The conclusion, in its place: 'The most likely explanation is pseudohyperkalaemia. I would not treat, and I would not cancel her procedure, until I have a clean result.'
The conditional that shows judgement: 'If the repeat is also high, then it is real and I work through renal function, medications and adrenal causes.'

Examiner challenges: 'She is well — why do you want an ECG?' · 'The lab says haemolysed — so it's nothing?' · and 'Would you give calcium?' — no, there are no ECG changes and the value is unconfirmed.
pefe: Role-player and examiner: a well 44-year-old woman who came in for routine bloods before a planned procedure and has been called back. The examiner hands over only the phoned result, holds the ECG until it is requested, and holds the haemolysis comment until the laboratory is asked. If the ECG is never requested it is never given, and that is marked as a fail.

As the patient she is well and slightly alarmed at being called back. She asks whether her procedure will be cancelled and whether something is wrong with her heart. If the number is quoted at her she looks blank and asks 'Is that bad?'

Mark them against these: asked for an ECG and observations in the first response · asked whether the sample was haemolysed · asked about processing delay and the cell counts · read the ECG systematically · named pseudohyperkalaemia with the mechanism · described the repeat technique · did not treat and did not cancel the procedure · stated what a high repeat would trigger · explained the effect rather than the number to the patient · and neither falsely reassured nor alarmed her.

The laboratory — The specimen was reported as haemolysed — held back until you ask. The questions to put to them: was the sample haemolysed, was there a delay in processing, and what were her platelet and white cell counts

Why haemolysis does this — Red cells contain potassium at many times the plasma concentration, so even modest haemolysis during collection raises the measured value substantially. Marked thrombocytosis or leukocytosis do the same in the tube, which is why the counts matter
The repeat, done properly — A wider-bore needle, no prolonged tourniquet, no fist clenching, and prompt delivery to the laboratory — with the ECG already done

FAIL — If it is real, not knowing the three jobs with the drug that does each — PROTECT: calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL IV over two to three minutes on the monitor, repeated at five minutes if the ECG has not improved — 'this does not lower the potassium; it stabilises the myocardium for 30 to 60 minutes; it must always be given alongside something that shifts or removes, never instead of it' (the question asked almost every time); SHIFT: ten units of short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% glucose over 15–30 minutes with hourly blood glucose for at least six hours, said unprompted — 'hypoglycaemia is the commonest complication and is often delayed'; plus salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised (additive); sodium bicarbonate if acidotic, evidence weak; REMOVE: dialysis is definitive in oliguric renal failure — involve renal and retrieval early, not after failed medical therapy; withhold ramipril, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim; recheck the potassium at one to two hours on continuous monitoring (★)

DO — Read the ECG systematically in order — rate, P, PR, QRS, T: 'the rate is 52 and bradycardic; I cannot clearly identify P waves — flattened and of low amplitude; the PR interval is prolonged; the QRS is broad at around 130 ms without a typical bundle branch morphology; the T waves are tall, narrow-based, symmetrical and peaked, most marked in the mid-precordial leads; taken together these are the changes of severe hyperkalaemia'; 'could the T waves be ischaemic?' → hyperacute T waves of infarction are broad-based and asymmetrical — the combination with flat P waves, a long PR and a wide QRS makes hyperkalaemia the explanation; in Version A read the panel as AKI on CKD (urea 24, creatinine 312, eGFR 16, a prerenal component), metabolic acidosis (HCO3 16 — shifts potassium out of cells), mild hyponatraemia fitting volume depletion; causes are multifactorial — name all four (stage 4 CKD as the baseline; AKI from gastroenteritis and poor intake; ramipril plus spironolactone — additive potassium retention; acidosis) and ask specifically about over-the-counter anti-inflammatories (ibuprofen for his knee, admitted only if asked), recent trimethoprim and potassium-based salt substitutes; 'his ECG had been normal — would you still have treated?' → yes at this level; the well dialysis patient at 6.9 with a normal ECG — chronic tolerance is not permission to wait: monitor, treat, bring dialysis forward

SAY — To the patient, explain the effect, never the number (quote 7.2 and he says 'is that bad?'): 'your blood tests show a salt called potassium is much higher than it should be; potassium helps your nerves and muscles work, but when it gets too high it upsets the electrical rhythm of your heart — and your heart tracing is already showing that; that is why I am treating it now rather than waiting; three things: calcium first — it does not lower the potassium, it protects your heart while the rest works; then insulin with sugar, which pushes the potassium back into your cells; and a nebuliser that helps do the same; then we work on clearing it from your body — and because your kidneys are not doing that well, you may need dialysis, which means transferring you; two of your tablets — the blood pressure one and the fluid one — hold potassium in; I am stopping both today; please do not restart them until you are reviewed'; 'am I going to have a heart attack?' → 'not a heart attack in the usual sense — this affects the rhythm rather than blocking an artery; but I don't want to understate it: at this level the rhythm can become dangerous, which is exactly why you're on a monitor'; 'is it something I did?' → 'you have not done anything wrong'; 'do I have to go to Adelaide?' → 'possibly — I'm arranging that conversation now rather than waiting; is there someone you'd like me to call?'

DO — Variants: the sine wave (K 8.4, QRS merging with T, drowsy, hypotensive) → peri-arrest — calcium immediately and repeated, insulin–dextrose and salbutamol simultaneously not sequentially, call for help and the arrest trolley, emergency dialysis; digoxin toxicity (K 6.4, nausea, yellow-green vision) → hyperkalaemia is a marker of severity and the indication for digoxin-specific antibody fragments — avoid calcium as a reflex, discuss with toxicology; DKA (K 5.9, glucose 28, ketones 5.2, pH 7.12) → total body potassium is depleted despite the high serum level — once insulin and fluids start it falls rapidly; follow the DKA protocol and replace potassium once below 5.5 and passing urine — 'the one hyperkalaemia you treat with potassium'; the angry patient ('you lot gave me those tablets — now they nearly killed me?') → 'a fair thing to be upset about; both were prescribed for good reasons — they protect your heart and kidneys; what has changed is that your kidneys have taken a hit from being unwell, and at that point the same tablets become a problem; not the wrong choice — they need reviewing when things change; I'm stopping them today and we'll work out a safer plan together'

versions.doorStem: A results-interpretation station: a potassium result is handed to you. Tasks are the same in both versions — interpret the results and any further investigation to the examiner → state the likely causes → outline immediate management → explain the situation to the patient. The two versions land on DIFFERENT answers.
rows: A · the sick one

68-year-old man, CKD stage 4, rural ED, two days of lethargy and generalised muscle weakness after gastroenteritis last week, drinking little. On ramipril, spironolactone, metformin, atorvastatin. BP 104/62, PR 52. K⁺ 7.2, urea 24.1, creatinine 312, eGFR 16, bicarbonate 16. ECG: bradycardic, flat P, long PR, broad QRS, peaked T.

SEVERE HYPERKALAEMIA with ECG changes — MULTIFACTORIAL: CKD sets the floor, acute illness and dehydration precipitate, ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone are additive, acidosis shifts K⁺ out of cells. Treat now.
B · the well one

44-year-old woman, entirely well, routine bloods before a minor procedure. Lab phones K⁺ 6.1. No symptoms, no relevant medications, normal renal function, lab comments 'specimen haemolysed'. ECG normal.
PSEUDOHYPERKALAEMIA — repeat the sample properly. But get the ECG FIRST and confirm it is normal before concluding the result is spurious, not after.
versions.note: The trap in version B splits candidates two ways and both fail: treating a haemolysed sample with insulin–dextrose in a well patient, or dismissing it as artefact with no ECG and no repeat. ECG first, repeat second, treat only if confirmed. Severity: mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe ≥6.5 · ANY level with ECG change = severe, and that row overrides the rest. A normal ECG at 7.2 is not reassurance. Practice cards in the source (crush injury/rhabdomyolysis, Addison, trimethoprim interaction, tumour lysis, dialysis patient with broad-complex tachycardia) are partner drills, not recalls.

findings: The results, read for her — and for the examiner

Transaminases under twice the upper limit is a mild rise — inflammation, not severe. Raised triglycerides above 1.7 and cholesterol above 5.5 are the positive ground. AST:ALT under one favours fatty liver, where a ratio above two would have favoured alcohol

back.dx: NON-ALCOHOLIC FATTY LIVER DISEASE — steatosis with mild steatohepatitis — on a background of dyslipidaemia and a sedentary, high-sugar diet, with the right upper quadrant pain needing its own explanation. The results explained: 'We checked your liver enzymes, which are chemicals that leak out of liver cells when the liver is irritated. Yours are up, but only mildly — less than twice what we expect — so there is inflammation, but not a severe one. We also checked the fat in your blood, cholesterol and triglycerides, and both are higher than we would like. When there is a lot of fat circulating, some of it is stored in the liver, and that stored fat causes the irritation. That condition is called fatty liver.' The reasons spoken: no alcohol at all, so the commonest cause is excluded · dyslipidaemia and a diet and activity pattern that produce it · a mild transaminase rise with AST below ALT, which is the fatty liver pattern · and the other causes excluded on history — no viral risk factors, no medications or supplements, no family history. Differentials: viral hepatitis B and C · drug-induced liver injury including over-the-counter, herbal and gym supplements · autoimmune hepatitis · haemochromatosis and wilson disease · alcohol, excluded but quantified · coeliac disease and thyroid disease as quiet causes of a mild rise · biliary disease · and malignancy kept in mind. For the pain, separately: gallstones and biliary colic, peptic ulcer disease, reflux, and musculoskeletal causes. The plan: hepatitis B and C serology, iron studies, autoimmune screen, fasting glucose or HbA1c, a full lipid profile, TSH, coeliac serology, FBE for platelets, and an abdominal ultrasound that looks for steatosis and for gallstones · staging with a non-invasive fibrosis score such as FIB-4, and transient elastography where available, because enzyme levels do not indicate fibrosis · cardiovascular risk assessed, because that is what kills people with fatty liver · and the lifestyle intervention that is the treatment — gradual weight loss of seven to ten percent, soft drinks out, a dietitian, 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, alcohol kept at none, and statin therapy for the lipids if indicated by risk, which is safe in fatty liver VERIFY. Review in six to twelve weeks with repeat LFTs, and safety-net for jaundice, abdominal swelling, bruising, black stools or confusion.
plan: Bridge from 'I'm here for my results' to the history: 'May I ask a few questions first, so the results make more sense when we get to them?'
Liver symptoms and red flags: jaundice, itch, dark urine, pale stools, weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, family history of bowel, liver, pancreatic or stomach cancer.
The pain characterised on its own — site, onset, character, relation to fatty meals, radiation, nocturnal, relation to food and posture — because it will need a separate explanation.

The alcohol question quantified even though the answer is none, then the risk-factor screen: antibiotics, transfusions, tattoos, injected drugs, travel, occupation and needle-stick, sexual history, medications including over-the-counter, herbal and gym supplements, operations, fever.

The lifestyle block, demanding a typical day — what he actually eats and drinks from morning to night, sugary drinks, takeaway, exercise, weight trend, family history of diabetes and heart disease, snoring.
The examination requested by name (see findings).

Explain the results pad by pad, name fatty liver with its reasons, give the differentials for the liver and separately for the pain, then the investigations, the lifestyle treatment, review and safety-net.

The lifestyle question that actually scores: 'Can you describe your diet on a typical day — what you actually eat and drink from morning to night? Any sugary drinks or takeaway? And do you exercise regularly?'
The explanation: 'When there is a lot of fat circulating, some of it is stored in the liver, and that stored fat causes the irritation.'

The separation that answers the examiner's challenge: 'Fatty liver is usually asymptomatic and is not a recognised cause of abdominal pain — so I would treat the steatosis on its own merits and keep looking for a separate explanation for the pain.'

Examiner challenges: 'Fatty liver does not cause abdominal pain — explain yourself' · 'Why did you not ask about lifestyle in the alcohol version?' — because there the ratio and the drinking had already identified a cause · and 'How would you stage this patient?' — FIB-4 and elastography, because enzymes do not indicate fibrosis.
pefe: Role-player: a 35-year-old man with some right upper quadrant discomfort who has come back for his blood results. He drinks no alcohol at all and says so plainly. No viral risk factors, no medications or supplements, no family history of liver disease or cancer. He describes his diet as 'Pretty healthy and balanced' and only gives the pastry, the takeaway, the late dinner, the soft drinks and the absent exercise if pressed for a typical day.
His questions: 'Is my liver damaged?' · 'Is the pain from the fatty liver?' · and 'Do I need tablets for the cholesterol?' He closes down if lectured about his weight or diet.

Mark them against these: bridged from results to questions · asked liver symptoms and red flags · characterised the pain separately · quantified alcohol despite the answer · ran the full risk-factor screen including supplements · refused 'Healthy and balanced' and got a typical day · asked exercise and weight trend · requested stigmata, BMI, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, shifting dullness, Murphy's sign and dipstick by name · explained the results in plain words · named fatty liver with reasons including the ratio · gave differentials for the liver and separately for the pain · ordered the exclusion bloods and an ultrasound · mentioned staging and cardiovascular risk · gave a concrete lifestyle plan without moralising · and reviewed and safety-netted.

The answer that scores nothing — 'My diet is pretty healthy and balanced, doctor.' Accept that and the block is empty. Press for a typical day and you get coffee and a pastry, takeaway at lunch, a big late dinner, two or three soft drinks a day, and no exercise — 'No time'

The pain, held separate — Fatty liver is usually asymptomatic and is not a recognised cause of abdominal pain. Treat the steatosis on its own merits and keep looking for the pain — biliary disease, peptic ulcer, reflux — rather than assuming the two findings are connected

What to ask the examiner for, by name — General appearance — jaundice, cachexia, scratch marks, oedema, stigmata of chronic liver disease such as spider naevi and palmar erythema · vital signs with temperature · BMI and waist circumference · abdomen for distension, scars, tenderness, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, shifting dullness · Murphy's sign given the pain · urine dipstick for bilirubin

Staging with FIB-4 from age, transaminases and platelets, and transient elastography where available VERIFY · treatment is 7-10% gradual weight loss, sugary drinks out, 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and statins if indicated by cardiovascular risk, which are safe in fatty liver VERIFY · review with repeat LFTs at 6-12 weeks · TIS 131 450 · VERIFY all
