must: FAIL — Not quantifying alcohol, or getting the arithmetic wrong — 'do you drink?' 'a drink most nights, I own a restaurant' and moving on is a fail (he does not help you); 'what do you drink, roughly how much on those nights, and how many nights a week? and how long at that level?' → 'a bottle of wine; most nights; probably every night, if I'm honest; twenty years'; convert it out loud without judgement: 'a bottle of wine is about seven to eight standard drinks, so that's roughly fifty in a week; the recommended maximum for a healthy adult is ten a week and four in a day; I'm not saying that to make you feel bad — it's directly relevant to the result I'm about to show you' (a 750 mL bottle at 13% is about 7.7 standard drinks, not 12–14; a standard drink is 10 g); Version B is the reverse trap — 'my diet is pretty healthy and balanced' scores nothing if accepted; 'describe what you actually eat and drink from morning to night' → coffee and a pastry, takeaway lunch, a big late dinner, two or three soft drinks a day, no exercise (★)

FAIL — Moralising, or 'you need to stop drinking' without asking how he feels about it — he closes down and gives one-word answers; non-judgemental, specific follow-up gets honesty; the hidden agenda ('my wife says I drink too much — is that what this is?') surfaces only if you are non-judgemental or ask what he is worried about; the brief intervention: 'the most useful thing I can offer today is help to stop; because you've been drinking heavily for a long time, I don't want you to stop suddenly on your own — withdrawal can be dangerous; let's plan it together, and I can involve a service that supports people through it'; thiamine; 'how do you feel about what we've discussed?' (★)

FAIL — Naming the diagnosis without the three spoken reasons including magnitude and ratio — Version A (AST ~95, ALT ~40–50, GGT up, ALP and bilirubin near normal): 'the amount and duration — about fifty standard drinks a week for twenty years; I've ruled out the other causes — no viral risk factors, no medications, no gallbladder symptoms, no travel, no family history; and the pattern of the test itself: a mild rise, which is what alcohol does, with a ratio above two — a viral hepatitis would have given a far larger rise' (mild = under 5× the limit, marked = over 10×; AST:ALT >2 favours alcohol; ratio here ~2.4); Version B (35, RUQ pain, AST and ALT under twice the limit, raised triglycerides and cholesterol, no alcohol) → fatty liver / non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and the extra task to explain the results: 'we measured your liver enzymes — chemicals that leak out of liver cells when the liver is irritated; yours are up, but only mildly — less than twice what we expect — so there is inflammation, but not a severe one; we also checked the fat in your blood — cholesterol and triglycerides — and both are higher than we'd like; when there's a lot of fat circulating, some is stored in the liver, and that stored fat causes the irritation' (★)

FAIL — Assuming fatty liver explains the abdominal pain — 'fatty liver does not cause abdominal pain; explain yourself' → 'correct, and I agree; fatty liver disease is usually asymptomatic and not a recognised cause of abdominal pain; I'd treat the steatosis on its own merits but continue to look for a separate explanation for the pain — biliary disease, peptic ulcer disease or reflux — rather than assume the two findings are connected'; 'why no lifestyle history in Version A?' → fatty liver is a diagnosis of exclusion at the bottom of the list; the alcohol history and the ratio already identified a cause; in Version B there is no alcohol and dyslipidaemia is in the stem, so lifestyle becomes the only positive ground (★)

DO — Bridge a station with no complaint ('I do have your results here and I will go through them with you; before I do, may I ask a few questions so the results make more sense when we get to them?'); liver symptoms and red flags (yellowing, itching, dark urine, pale stools; weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness; family history of bowel, liver, pancreatic or stomach cancer); the alcohol block; the rest of the risk factors then fever — ABP FIT NO SEX (antibiotics, blood transfusion, piercings/tattoos, food, IV drugs, travel, needle-stick/occupation, sexual history and condoms, medications incl. over-the-counter, herbal and gym supplements), pain after fatty meals, operations, fever or chills; the examination requested by name — general appearance (jaundice, cachexia, scratch marks, oedema, stigmata of chronic liver disease — spider naevi, palmar erythema), temperature, abdomen (distension, scars, tenderness, masses, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, shifting dullness, bowel sounds), a dipstick for bilirubin; investigations — hepatitis B and C serology, iron studies, an autoimmune screen, lipids and glucose, an ultrasound; staging if asked — enzyme levels don't indicate fibrosis: FIB-4 (age, transaminases, platelets) and transient elastography; low platelets, low albumin, a rising INR or splenomegaly suggest cirrhosis and change follow-up to variceal and HCC surveillance

SAY — 'We measured your liver enzymes — chemicals that leak out of liver cells when the liver is irritated; yours are up, but only mildly; there's a second thing I look at: the relationship between two of those enzymes; in your case one is more than twice the other, and that pattern is very characteristic of alcohol; the condition is alcoholic hepatitis — inflammation of the liver caused by drinking; in the long run, if the inflammation continues, it leads to scarring — cirrhosis — and at that point the liver stops working properly'; 'is my liver damaged?' → 'a warning rather than a catastrophe; at the stage you're at it is largely reversible if the alcohol stops — that's genuinely good news'; the differentials with a test for each ('fatty liver from cholesterol and weight can look identical; viral hepatitis B and C; medications incl. over-the-counter and herbal; autoimmune; inherited — iron overload or a copper problem; gallstone disease and blockage of the drainage tubes; and I always keep cancers of the liver, gallbladder and pancreas in mind'); safety net ('turn yellow, tummy swells, bruise or bleed easily, vomit blood or black stools, confused'); review in a fortnight; a summary — 'your liver is inflamed, alcohol is the most likely cause, we'll check for the others, and the plan is supported reduction with review in two weeks'; Version B plan — diet and exercise specifics, weight, lipids and glucose, ultrasound, cardiovascular risk

setting: Version A of the presyncope station — the older recall, identical history to the silent MI version, but the ECG is normal and the first aider's glucose was 2.7. Candidates do not fail this one by missing the diagnosis. They fail by announcing 'It's a hypo' and offering nothing else — the differential is marked even when the answer is obvious.
stem: You are the GP. Mrs Anita Rowe, 44, has come to your practice from the shopping centre. She was shopping this morning, felt unwell and was about to fall. She is a known diabetic on insulin. Her vital signs are stable.
Tasks: take a focused history (5 minutes) — interpret the ECG for your examiner — explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient.
tasks: Take a focused history (5 minutes)
Interpret the ECG for your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Five minutes of history on the same spine as the silent MI version — presyncope treated as syncope, before, during and after, the full diabetes block, the system screen · a systematic ECG hand-over that ends in 'Normal' · then the diagnosis with a structured differential and a plan that fixes today and prevents the next one
findingsLabel: What the examiner gives, and what the history contains
findings: 'The ECG shows sinus rhythm at 78 with no acute ST or T wave change. The capillary glucose taken at the shopping centre by a first aider was 2.7.' Read the ECG systematically anyway — rate, rhythm, P, PR, QRS, axis, ST, T, Q — and state that it is normal, because the marks are in the order, not the announcement

back.dx: HYPOGLYCAEMIA IN AN INSULIN-TREATED DIABETIC — insulin given, breakfast missed, hours of unaccustomed activity — with a normal ECG, and with probable hypoglycaemia unawareness given the absent prodrome and the microvascular changes. Said to her: 'The most likely explanation is a low blood sugar. You take insulin, you skipped breakfast and had only an apple, and then walked for several hours — more activity than usual burns through sugar and makes a low far more likely. But I don't want to stop at the obvious answer, so let me tell you what else I have considered.' The differential, structured and spoken even though the answer is obvious: a heart rhythm or coronary problem — her tracing is normal, which is reassuring, and in a diabetic with a father who had an infarct at 58 it was the thing to exclude first · a drop in blood pressure on standing · dehydration · a mini-stroke · a seizure · infection · anaemia · a salt disturbance · and any medication effect. The plan: something to eat now, with a repeat glucose · bloods today — FBE, UEC, HbA1c, lipids, and renal function · a review of her insulin regimen, meal timing and snacks, particularly on days she will be on her feet for hours, with the diabetes educator · the hypoglycaemia rule taught and checked — under 4.0, 15 g of fast carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes, then a longer-acting snack · glucagon at home and the family shown how to use it · hypoglycaemia unawareness named and managed, with less tight targets for a period to restore the warning symptoms · the complication screen completed — feet, eyes, kidneys, cardiovascular risk · and the driving conversation, which is not optional: she drove here, she has had a severe hypoglycaemic episode with impaired awareness, and under Austroads she should not drive until reviewed and stable, with a glucose check before driving and a supply of fast carbohydrate in the car thereafter VERIFY. Safety-net for recurrence, confusion or collapse, and review within the week. The contrast with version B is the point of learning both: identical history, and the ECG decides whether this is a hypo or a silent inferior STEMI — which is why the ECG is read as if the history never happened.
plan: Introduce, confirm, check she is all right now, signpost — and ask for a bedside glucose while you talk.

Explore the episode: loss of consciousness or awareness throughout, jerking or one-sided twitching, incontinence, duration, first episode — and stay on the syncope spine when she says she didn't actually black out.
Context, before and after: what she was doing, heat, standing, posture change, upsetting news, any warning, missed meals and fluids, head knock, fever, and afterwards — confusion, injury, pallor.

The diabetes block: diagnosis, compliance and whether insulin was taken today, dose changes, new or herbal medicines, diet and snacks, home monitoring and warning symptoms, regular review — then the complication screen.
The system screen: neurological, chest pain even slight, breathlessness, palpitations, oedema, GI, SADMA, stress, exertion, cardiovascular risk factors and family history, driving and who is at home.
The ECG hand-over, systematic, ending in 'Normal' (see findings).

Name hypoglycaemia with its reasons, then the structured differential, then the plan — food now, bloods, insulin and meal review, the hypo rule, glucagon, unawareness, the complication screen, and the driving conversation.
back.planNote: the same five-minute history as the silent MI version — this one is lost after the diagnosis, by a candidate who names the hypo and stops
ask: The one thing to ask for at the start: 'Could I please have a bedside blood glucose while we talk?'
The question that separates syncope from a fall: 'Did you lose consciousness completely, or were you aware of your surroundings?'
The prodrome question that reveals unawareness: 'Did you get any warning at all — light-headed, sweaty, shaky, hungry?'
The sentence that passes this version: 'The most likely explanation is a low blood sugar — but I don't want to stop at the obvious answer, so let me tell you what else I have considered.'

Challenges: 'It's just my sugar, isn't it? I skipped breakfast' at two minutes — agree it is possible and keep going · 'Can I still go to the party? My car's outside' — she has had a severe hypo with no warning, and the driving answer is not yet.
pefe: Role-player: Anita Rowe, 44, part-time retail administration, married with two teenagers, diabetes for about two years on insulin and conscientious about it, mildly offended by any suggestion otherwise. Blood pressure and cholesterol a bit up, father's infarct at 58, non-smoker. Feet tingle at night and the optometrist noted early changes — mentioned only if asked. This morning she woke late, skipped breakfast bar an apple, took her insulin, and walked the shopping centre for three hours for tonight's party before feeling unwell and nearly falling — seconds, aware throughout, no warning, no injury.

How she plays it: brisk and slightly dismissive, here only because her friends insisted. She pushes at two minutes with 'It's just my sugar, isn't it?' and she always finishes with the party and the car. In this version the examiner gives a normal ECG and the first aider's glucose of 2.7.

Mark them against these: full WIPE, consent, open question and acknowledgement · asked for a bedside glucose · kept the syncope structure despite 'I didn't black out' · covered before, during and after including the absent prodrome · took the full diabetes block · screened complications and linked them to unawareness · screened CNS, CVS, GI, SADMA and psychogenic causes · read the ECG systematically and called it normal · named hypoglycaemia with reasons · gave a structured differential rather than a single answer · taught the hypo rule and arranged glucagon · reviewed insulin, meals and snacks · addressed driving · offered to call family and summarised.

The history that explains it — Insulin taken as prescribed this morning · breakfast skipped, only an apple · three hours of walking, far more activity than usual · no dose change, no new medicines or herbal products · a few seconds, fully aware, no jerking, no injury, first episode

The finding that still matters — She reports no warning at all — no sweating, shaking or hunger. In a woman with tingling feet and early retinal changes that is hypoglycaemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy, and it changes her insulin plan and her driving advice

Why the diabetes block still earns its marks — Compliance, recent dose change, new or herbal medicines, diet and snacks, home monitoring, and the complication screen — feet, eyes, kidneys, postural dizziness, early satiety — are what let you explain why today happened and why she had no warning
fails: ★ Announcing 'it's a hypo' and offering no differential — the differential is marked even when the answer is obvious
★ Switching to a falls assessment because she didn't actually black out
★ Not reading the ECG systematically because it is normal, or not reading it at all
★ Letting her drive home after a severe hypoglycaemic episode with no warning symptoms
Not asking for a bedside glucose; skipping the diabetes block; missing the absent prodrome and what it means; no hypo rule, no glucagon, no review of insulin and meal timing
numbers: Hypoglycaemia under 4.0 mmol/L: 15 g of fast carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes, then a longer-acting snack; unconscious — glucagon 1 mg IM or 50 mL of 50% glucose IV VERIFY · the first aider's reading was 2.7 · ECG read in order: rate, rhythm, P, PR, QRS, axis, ST, T, Q

Driving after severe hypoglycaemia or with impaired awareness is deferred until medical review and stability under Austroads, with a glucose check before driving and fast carbohydrate in the car VERIFY · STEMI criteria for the contrast: new ST elevation of at least 1 mm in two contiguous leads, inferior II, III and aVF with reciprocal I and aVL · VERIFY all

Full detail — FAIL — Reading the ECG correctly and then keeping counselling — no aspirin, no ambulance, and a patient who drives home: the single most common fail; 'I'd like you to chew this aspirin (300 mg) now; I'm calling an ambulance, and you'll go straight to a hospital that can open the blocked vessel — the sooner that's done, the more heart muscle we save; I'll put a drip in, keep you on a monitor with a defibrillator available, stay with you until they arrive, and send your tracing ahead so the team is ready'; she always finishes with 'can I still go to the party? my car's outside — I'll drive myself' → 'I'm sorry — tonight isn't possible, and you must not drive: not today, and not until the specialist clears you (about two weeks after successful PCI); your car can stay here; is there someone I can call — your husband?'; agree, hesitate, or fail to arrange the ambulance and it's a fail; she refuses → 'part of your heart muscle is losing its blood supply right now and every minute counts; it must be an ambulance rather than your car because the most dangerous moments are the first hours, when the rhythm can go wrong very suddenly — the paramedics carry the equipment to fix that; you can decline, and I'll respect it, but I'd be failing you if I didn't tell you plainly it would be a very dangerous choice' (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Announcing the diagnosis without the systematic run-through, or missing the reciprocal change — one continuous hand-over: 'a 12-lead ECG; rate approximately 70; regular sinus rhythm — a P wave before every QRS; PR normal, no heart block; QRS narrow; axis normal; ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in aVL and lead I; no established Q waves; T waves upright; I'd examine V1–V3 for posterior extension and obtain right-sided leads, particularly V4R, before giving any nitrate; my interpretation is an acute inferior STEMI, and I'd treat this as a time-critical emergency'; the reciprocal change is what distinguishes infarction from pericarditis or early repolarisation; 'which artery?' → the right coronary in about 80% of inferior infarcts (ST elevation taller in III than II), the circumflex in the rest; 'why no chest pain?' → diabetic autonomic neuropathy impairs the afferent pain pathway — painless infarction is well described in diabetes, women and older patients (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Switching to a falls assessment because 'I didn't actually black out' — presyncope carries the same differential and the same risk as syncope; stay on the spine: LOC or aware ('I could still hear everything'), jerking or one-sided twitching, incontinence, duration, first time; context (walking the centre for hours, not hot, no sudden standing, no bad news); 'did you get any warning at all — light-headed, sweaty, shaky, hungry, heart racing, vision greying?' → 'none at all — it just came over me' — say it to yourself: no prodrome is DISCORDANT, argues against a simple faint and puts cardiac causes higher; missed meals ('skipped breakfast — only an apple'), fluids, head injury, fever, rash; afterwards (confusion, injury, pallor); and 'no chest pain at all' said firmly is a clue in a diabetic, not a closed door (★)

Full detail — FAIL — Announcing 'it's a hypo' and offering nothing else (Version A — ECG normal, first-aider glucose 2.7) — the differential is marked even when the answer is obvious: 'the most likely explanation is a low blood sugar — insulin, a skipped breakfast, hours of walking; but I don't want to stop at the obvious answer: a heart rhythm or artery problem, a drop in blood pressure on standing, dehydration, a mini-stroke, a seizure, an infection, anaemia, a salt disturbance, a medication effect; your tracing is normal, which is reassuring; bloods today, something to eat now, and we'll review your insulin, meal timing and snacks — particularly on days you'll be on your feet for hours'; ask for a bedside glucose in the first minute ('vitals stable' is given — don't re-ask them, but a woman on insulin who nearly fainted needs a capillary glucose); at two minutes she pushes 'it's just my sugar, isn't it?' → agree it's possible and keep going (★)

Full detail — DO — The diabetes block (when diagnosed, compliance — 'exactly as prescribed' said slightly defensively, taken today, any dose change, new or over-the-counter or herbal medicines, diet and snacks, home readings 'in the sevens', regular review) and the complications screen linked out loud to mechanism — 'numbness, tingling or burning in the feet, ulcers; vision changes and the last eye check; kidneys; dizzy on standing, full quickly after meals, bladder trouble' → tingling feet at night, early retinal changes (only if asked) → 'she has evidence of microvascular disease, which supports both autonomic neuropathy and painless ischaemia'; the system screen (CNS — headache, weakness, numbness, speech, vision, unsteadiness; CVS — chest pain 'even a little', breathlessness, palpitations, ankle swelling; GI; SADMA; psychogenic — breathing fast, stress; exertion — 'more activity than usual'); risk factors (BP and cholesterol 'a bit up', father's MI at 58); 'do you drive, and who's at home?' → she drove herself — needed for the closing; STEMI criteria — new ST elevation ≥1 mm in two contiguous leads; ECG within 10 minutes; ticagrelor 180 mg or clopidogrel 300–600 mg loading; GTN 300–600 µg SL not in RV infarct, hypotension, bradycardia or PDE5 inhibitor within 24–48 h; morphine 2.5–5 mg IV titrated; oxygen only if SpO2 <93%; primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact (120 if transfer), otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 minutes and angiography at 3–24 hours

Full detail — SAY — The warning shot then plain English: 'Mrs Rowe, I need to tell you something important, and I'd like you to hear all of it before you react; your heart tracing shows that you are having a heart attack right now'; 'that's not possible — I don't have any chest pain' → the two-part diabetes explanation: 'diabetes does two separate things here; first, over years it damages the small blood vessels that supply the heart muscle — if one suddenly blocks, that part of the muscle stops getting blood, and that is a heart attack; second, the same diabetes damages the nerves — including the nerves that carry pain from the heart; so instead of the chest pain most people get, the only thing you felt was being unwell and about to fall; we call that a silent heart attack, and it's why the tracing tells us more than how you feel'; 'am I going to die?' → 'this is serious, and it is also very treatable — the safest possible thing is what we're doing right now' (never jargon like 'an inferior STEMI with reciprocal change', never false comfort like 'a small issue with your tracing'); the differential still given (hypoglycaemia 'may still be part of the picture', hyperglycaemia, arrhythmia or valve, PE, TIA, seizure, electrolytes, dehydration, anaemia, medication); Variant 3 (BP 82/54, pulse 46 after the ECG) → right ventricular involvement — lie flat, withhold nitrates, avoid morphine, right-sided leads, a cautious saline bolus (preload-dependent), atropine 600 µg and pacing ready, escalate; rural SA more than two hours from a cath lab → MedSTAR or RFDS activated in parallel, the ECG transmitted, pre-hospital tenecteplase within 30 minutes under the SA STEMI pathway after checking contraindications, then transfer for angiography at 3–24 hours

Carded separately from MED-99, which is Version B, the inferior STEMI)

must: FAIL — Reading the STEMI correctly and then carrying on counselling — no 300 mg ASPIRIN, no AMBULANCE, or letting her drive to the party (the commonest fail): 'tonight isn't possible, and you must not drive'; if she refuses, tell her plainly it would be very dangerous

FAIL — Announcing the diagnosis without a systematic read, or missing the RECIPROCAL change — ST elevation in II, III and aVF with depression in aVL and I, right-sided leads before any nitrate — 'an acute inferior STEMI, a time-critical emergency'

FAIL — Switching to a falls assessment because 'I didn't actually black out' — presyncope carries the same risk; 'any warning at all — light-headed, sweaty, shaky, heart racing?' gets none, and NO PRODROME is discordant, so cardiac causes move up

FAIL — In the normal-ECG version (glucose 2.7), saying 'it's a hypo' and nothing else — give the differential anyway, ask for a bedside glucose in the first minute, feed her, and review insulin, meals and snacks for active days

DO — Link the complications screen to mechanism — tingling feet and retinal changes mean microvascular disease, so autonomic neuropathy and painless ischaemia are plausible — and ask 'do you drive, and who's at home?' (she drove herself)

SAY — Warning shot, then 'your heart tracing shows you are having a HEART ATTACK right now'; answer 'but I have no chest pain' in two parts — diabetes blocks the small vessels AND damages the nerves that carry the pain: 'a silent heart attack — serious, and very treatable'

setting: An easy station with a low recalled pass rate, and the reason is narrow. Every candidate lists painkillers, breathing exercises and red flags. The pass is decided by whether you say out loud that pain causes shallow breathing, shallow breathing causes collapse, and collapse causes pneumonia — and then hang every part of the plan off that chain. The role-player asks 'But how do painkillers help my ribs heal?' even if you have already explained it, to see whether you can say it a second way.
stem: Emergency department, regional South Australia, 21:40. Jenny Kowalski, 42, came off her bicycle at speed onto her left side about three hours ago. She wore a helmet, did not hit her head and did not lose consciousness. She is fully alert and haemodynamically stable throughout.

Chest x-ray and CT chest: fractures of the left 4th, 5th and 6th ribs, all minimally displaced · mild pulmonary contusion of the left lower lobe · no pneumothorax and no haemothorax. Observations: BP 128/76, HR 84, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8, GCS 15. Abdomen soft and non-tender. The ED consultant has reviewed her, cleared her for discharge, and has asked you to speak to her.

Tasks: explain the x-ray and CT findings and the diagnosis — explain the discharge plan including analgesia and breathing care — explain the red flags and when she must return — address her questions and concerns. No examination required.
tasks: Explain the X-ray and CT findings and the diagnosis to the patient
Explain the discharge plan, including analgesia and breathing care
Explain the red flags and when she must return
Address the patient's questions and concerns
time: Forty-five seconds on WIPE, name, 'How are you feeling' and an offer of analgesia · fifteen seconds on the first agenda check · two minutes translating the three imaging findings · a minute on the chain, which is where the station is decided · two minutes on analgesia, breathing numbers, cough splinting and mobilising · a minute on red flags with actions and follow-up · and the last minute on the two agendas and teach-back

back.dx: UNCOMPLICATED MULTIPLE RIB FRACTURES — left 4th to 6th, minimally displaced — with a mild left lower lobe pulmonary contusion, no pneumothorax and no haemothorax, haemodynamically stable and dischargeable. Rib level is the whole point of the stem: 4–6 sits below the great vessels (Ribs 1–3) and above the solid organs (Ribs 9–12), so aortic, cardiac, splenic and hepatic injury are argued away by position rather than ignored. The defensive differential, grouped: rs — pneumothorax, haemothorax, atelectasis, pneumonia, flail chest (≥ 3 contiguous ribs in ≥ 2 places, not present here) · CVS — blunt cardiac and aortic injury · GI — splenic, hepatic and diaphragmatic injury · MSK — sternal, scapular, clavicular and thoracic spine injury · CNS — head and C-spine · other — was the fall itself syncope, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia or alcohol. The three that can still declare themselves after discharge are delayed pneumothorax, delayed haemothorax and a progressing contusion — that is what the safety-net is built around. Management is multimodal analgesia, then breathing, then mobilising, in that order because each depends on the one before: paracetamol 1 g QID by the clock (Max 4 g/24 h) · ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food where not contraindicated · a short small supply of oxycodone IR 5 mg 4–6 hourly PRN with a laxative started the same day · regional blocks (Serratus anterior, erector spinae, intercostal) named as the next step if pain stops her breathing deeply · incentive spirometry · cough with pillow splinting · early mobilisation with no bed rest and no chest binders · chest physiotherapy referral named · written handout, work certificate, smoking cessation, and review at about one week in fracture clinic or with the GP, often by telephone. Repeat imaging is symptom-driven, not routine. VERIFY all doses. The discharge decision should be said out loud as reasoned rather than inherited: stable, normoxic, mobile, pain controlled orally, someone at home — if any one of those fails, she stays.
plan: WIPE, name and role, then 'How are you feeling right now?' and — before any content — offer another dose of pain relief. Ten seconds, and it is a free empathy mark. Then permission and signpost.
First agenda check: 'Before I go through the plan — is there anything in particular worrying you?' Ask again before you close; the bike question usually only comes the second time.
The three imaging findings in plain English, chunked, with a check after each (see findings).
The chain, unprompted — pain → shallow breathing → collapse → pneumonia — so the agenda question is already answered when it arrives.
Screen before you prescribe: allergies, ulcer, renal, asthma, pregnancy, other medicines, driving or caring for small children. Then the drugs with names, doses and side effects (see dx).

Breathing with numbers: ten slow deep breaths, hold 3–5 seconds, every 1–2 hours while awake, incentive spirometer if available · cough hugging a pillow · short walks from day one, no bed rest, no binders · chest physio referral.
Red flags, each paired with its action · then follow-up, written information, work certificate, smoking, and who is at home — a rural address changes the threshold.
The two agendas: painkillers do not heal bone, they buy back the deep breath · the bike answered by principle then range then safety, never a bluffed number · then teach-back.
back.planNote: generous time for the content — the risk is running dry at five minutes, so bank the teach-back, written information, smoking, work certificate and second agenda check for the tail
ask: The chain, verbatim: 'Pain makes you breathe shallowly; shallow breathing lets parts of the lung collapse; collapse plus phlegm is how a chest infection starts.' and its companion: 'The painkillers are not to heal the bone — they are so you can take a deep breath and cough. That is the treatment.'

The breathing prescription, which is the sentence the examiner is listening for: 'Ten slow deep breaths, hold each for three to five seconds, every one to two hours while you are awake.' plus 'Hug a pillow against your ribs when you cough — it hurts less and the cough is stronger. Please do cough.'

Red flags with actions: sudden or worsening breathlessness · chest pain suddenly much worse or different · coughing blood, or green phlegm with fever or shivers · dizziness, faintness or racing heart · pain the tablets are not touching so she cannot breathe deeply · any tummy pain or left shoulder-tip pain → straight back to ED or 000; healthdirect 1800 022 222 if unsure.

The bike answer, without a bluffed number: 'There is no fixed number of weeks — it depends on your healing, not the calendar. Once you have no pain at rest and can take a deep breath and cough, build back up gradually — for most people with three broken ribs that is around six to eight weeks for proper riding.' then helmet, not while on the stronger tablets, and not if unwell — and the same for driving a car, which is the free mark candidates drop.

Challenges: 'It really hurts when I breathe in' · 'How do painkillers help my ribs heal?' Asked even after you have explained it · 'A bruised lung? Is that serious?' · 'Will I get addicted?' · 'Every one to two hours? Even at work?' · 'Coughing is going to be agony' · 'I live forty minutes out — can I drive myself in?' · 'My friend was back on after two weeks — is that definite?' · and, if you moralise about cycling, 'It is how I get to work. I am not giving it up.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Kowalski, 42, a primary school teacher in a country town who commutes by bike. Pain 7/10 at rest and 9/10 on deep breathing, visibly guarding and breathing shallowly throughout — that is the visual cue the candidate is meant to notice. Stoic, slightly impatient, wants a plan; she only goes quiet if the candidate is dismissive.

What she volunteers only if asked: smokes five a day, two wines most weekends, on the oral contraceptive pill only, no allergies, not pregnant, no past history, helmet worn, no dizziness or blackout before the fall, partner at home forty minutes out of town.

Her hidden agenda is that she fears being told to give up cycling. She will not raise it until asked about concerns; if the candidate never asks, she raises it herself at about six and a half minutes. She pushes the painkiller question once even if it has been answered, and asks what any jargon means every time.

Mark them against these: asked how she feels and offered analgesia first · permission and signposting · asked about concerns twice · explained the fractures, the negatives and the contusion in plain English including the 1–3 day worsening · explained the chain · screened before prescribing · named drug, dose and frequency · added a laxative and the no-driving advice · gave the breathing numbers · pillow splinting · mobilise, no bed rest, no binder · chest physio · red flags each with an action · named the follow-up · answered both agendas · smoking, written information and work certificate · teach-back at the close.

Variants to rehearse: a 74-year-old ex-smoker with COPD and SpO2 91% — the hidden discriminator is that he may not be safely dischargeable and you must say so · ribs 9–11 — add the delayed splenic rupture warning with left shoulder-tip pain · an anticoagulated patient — drop the NSAID and lower the return threshold · refusal of opioids — structured shared decision-making, not persuasion · a rural patient ninety minutes out with no reception and alone — the discharge is not safe as written.

The fractures — 'Three of your ribs are broken — the fourth, fifth and sixth on the left. The broken ends are still lined up.' that matters because lined-up ribs heal themselves over six to eight weeks — nothing to pin or plate, and you cannot cast a chest. Minimise the treatment, never the injury: 'Only three ribs' is a trap

The contusion — the one candidates skip — 'A small part of your left lung is bruised — exactly like the bruise on your skin where you landed, a little bleeding and swelling in the tissue. It is not a hole and it is not an infection.' It evolves over 24–72 hours and then settles over about a week — which is the honest justification for the safety-net, and the answer if the examiner asks why a mild contusion needs red flags at all

The chain — the single most important thirty seconds — 'When a rib is broken, a deep breath hurts, so people breathe shallowly and avoid coughing. But the bottom of the lung needs a deep breath to stay open. Without it small areas collapse and the phlegm sits there — and that is how a chest infection starts. So the painkillers are not there to heal the bone. They are there so you can take a deep breath and cough. That is the treatment'

The mechanism question almost nobody asks — 'Did you feel unwell, dizzy or black out before you came off?' A syncopal fall is a different presentation entirely. Also worth asking: helmet and head injury, alcohol, whether this is a workcover or third-party matter, and who is at home tonight

The reassuring negatives — 'There is no air leaking around the lung and no blood collecting around it — the two things we look hardest for, and neither is there.' Plain phrase first, the words pneumothorax and haemothorax second, never the other way round
fails: ★ Never explaining why analgesia matters — a fluent list of drugs, then no answer when she asks how painkillers help her ribs heal
★ No red flags, or red flags with no action attached ('come back if you feel unwell')
★ Prescribing an NSAID or an opioid without screening for allergy, ulcer, renal impairment, asthma and pregnancy

Vague breathing advice with no numbers; skipping the contusion because it is awkward to explain; jargon first and plain English second; never asking about concerns; bluffing a number for the bike; forgetting the driving warning on a sedating opioid; recommending chest strapping or a binder; not offering analgesia at the start; no named follow-up; and running out of material at five minutes
numbers: Left ribs 4–6, minimally displaced · bony union 6–8 weeks · contusion evolves over 24–72 hours and resolves over about a week · flail chest = ≥ 3 contiguous ribs fractured in ≥ 2 places · breathing: 10 breaths, hold 3–5 seconds, every 1–2 hours while awake · higher risk: age ≥ 65, ≥ 3 rib fractures, pre-existing lung disease, smoking, obesity, anticoagulation, contusion VERIFY

Paracetamol 1 g QID, max 4 g/24 h · ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food · oxycodone IR 5 mg 4–6 hourly PRN, small supply · laxative from day one with any opioid · codeine has been prescription-only in Australia since February 2018 correction · judicious not liberal IV fluid in a contused lung added · review at 1 week · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Quitline 13 7848 · PATS if fracture-clinic review means over 100 km · VERIFY all

source: Rib_Fracture_Discharge_Counselling_Notability.pdf (Jenny Kowalski, 42, bicycle fall, left ribs 4–6 minimally displaced with a mild LLL contusion, cleared for discharge — a counselling station where the pass turns on saying the pain-to-pneumonia chain out loud and hanging the whole plan off it, and on answering the painkiller and the bike agendas without bluffing)
drive: AMC Clinical Notability › Counselling › Rib_Fracture_Discharge_Counselling_Notability.pdf
must: FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: never explaining why analgesia matters — say the chain out loud, unprompted: pain makes you breathe shallowly, shallow breathing lets parts of the lung collapse, collapse plus trapped phlegm is how pneumonia starts. The painkillers do not heal the bone; they buy back the deep breath, and THAT is the treatment

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: no red flags, or red flags with no action attached ('come back if you feel unwell') — name the symptom AND the action: sudden or worsening breathlessness, pain that suddenly changes, coughing blood or green sputum with fever, dizziness, pain the tablets do not touch, abdominal or LEFT SHOULDER-TIP pain — straight back, or triple zero

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: prescribing an NSAID or an opioid without screening for allergy, ulcer, renal impairment, asthma and pregnancy — ten seconds before any drug name; then paracetamol 1 g four times daily BY THE CLOCK, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food, a small opioid supply WITH a laxative, and no driving, riding or alcohol on it

FAIL — Vague breathing advice with no numbers — ten slow deep breaths, hold each three to five seconds, every one to two hours while awake; cough on purpose hugging a pillow against the ribs; keep walking, no bed rest, and NO chest binder, which does the opposite of what she needs

FAIL — Skipping the contusion because it is the awkward one to explain — it is the finding the examiner most wants translated: a bruise in the lung, like the bruise on her skin, which can feel slightly WORSE over the first day or two before settling over about a week. That is the honest justification for the safety-net

FAIL — Bluffing a number for the bike — there is no guideline; give the principle (no pain at rest, deep breath and cough without it stopping you, then graded return, roughly six to eight weeks), then the safety conditions. And offer analgesia in the first thirty seconds rather than leaving her in pain for eight minutes

setting: Almost every candidate knows the number six. This station separates those who know the number from those who know what the six months is counted from. Both clocks — time on treatment and time seizure-free — started four months ago, so the answer is two months, not six. The role-player is briefed to ask 'So six months from today?' Precisely to give you the chance to get it right or wrong.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Julie Nguyen, 28, a university student, comes to see you to discuss her driver's licence. She had a seizure four months ago and was diagnosed with epilepsy. Her neurologist started her on anti-seizure medication. She wants to know when she can drive again.
Tasks: take a focused, relevant history from the patient (4 minutes, prompted) — counsel the patient appropriately regarding her driving licence.

Some recent sittings hand you a printed extract of the fit to drive standards table in the stem. If so, read it with her and point to the row that applies — that is better counselling than reciting from memory. The marks are still in the history and in applying the criteria.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient (4 minutes, prompted)
Counsel the patient appropriately regarding her driving licence
time: Forty seconds on introduction, open question, the agenda and empathy · three and a quarter minutes of focused history, where four AUTO-FAIL items live · thirty seconds on empathy again and the public-safety reason · seventy-five seconds explaining the three criteria as criteria · forty-five seconds applying them to her · fifty seconds on compliance, triggers, contraception and non-driving safety · and the last forty seconds on the reporting duty, reading, the neurologist letter, review and teach-back

back.dx: EPILEPSY TREATED FOR THE FIRST TIME — fitness-to-drive assessment, private vehicle, in a non-adherent patient with three modifiable seizure triggers. The standard that applies is the first-time-treatment variation (Treatment started within the preceding 18 months), not the default: a conditional licence with at least annual review may be considered if she has been treated for at least 6 months, has had no seizures in the preceding 6 months, any seizures after starting treatment were only in the first 6 months and not the last 6, and she follows medical advice including adherence. She is four months in and seizure-free, so she is two months away. The other private standards worth holding: default 12 months seizure-free · first seizure 6 months, with an unconditional licence possible after 2 years seizure-free and 12 months off medication · breakthrough seizure in previously well-controlled epilepsy 4 weeks if there is an identified, reliably avoidable provoking factor that has not caused seizures before, otherwise 3 months · acute symptomatic seizures 6 months · sleep-only seizures 12 months, or 2 years if there were previous awake seizures · no driving during a medication taper or switch and for 3 months after the last dose · unconditional licence again after 5 years seizure-free and 12 months off medication · commercial default 10 years seizure-free plus EEG, specialist-led, with no reductions. Three rules override the table: adherence is a licence condition and a patient who refuses medical advice should be assessed as not fit to drive, with periodic drug levels available as a condition where there is doubt · a crash caused by a seizure removes every reduction · and if more than one standard could apply, the longest non-driving period wins. Two corrections: sleep deprivation is clinically a major trigger but is explicitly not accepted as a licensing provoking factor because it cannot be reliably avoided, so it cannot shorten a period to four weeks; and weight gain is not a carbamazepine effect — that is valproate, gabapentin and pregabalin. Carbamazepine causes drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, diplopia, nausea, rash and hyponatraemia, with rare blood dyscrasias and severe cutaneous reactions, and hla-b*1502 screening is recommended before starting it in people of han Chinese, Thai and other South-East Asian ancestry added. Take her actual side effects at face value and discuss them with the neurologist rather than assuming a class effect. VERIFY all figures against Austroads assessing fitness to drive.
plan: Open question, acknowledge the agenda, empathy for the lost independence — then permission: 'Is it alright if I ask a few questions first, so what I tell you is actually right for your situation?' Do not answer the licence question yet.
The four key questions, asked explicitly and separately (see findings), then the rest of the history.
Empathy again, then the reason before the rule: not a punishment — a seizure at the wheel could hurt her and others.

The three criteria explained as criteria: six months on treatment so we know it is working · no seizures in those six months · taking it as prescribed, which is written into the standard as a licence condition.
Apply them: four months in, seizure-free — two months away, not six. Then conditional licence, annual review, and that the licensing authority decides, not you.

Fix the adherence problem rather than naming it: letter to the neurologist about the side effects, possible dose or drug change, phone alarm, pill box or blister pack — and the honest blocker that missed doses mean she does not meet the standard even at six months.
Triggers with numbers not disapproval · contraception and pre-conception folate on an enzyme-inducing teratogen · non-driving safety and seizure first aid for flatmates · seizure diary.
Her duty to notify and the SA mandatory reporting duty, stated calmly as information and never as leverage · reading material · review in two months · teach-back of the three criteria.
back.planNote: keep the criteria explanation tight — the safety, women's health and legal blocks are all marked items and they are what candidates run out of time for
ask: The four questions, verbatim: 'And when was your last seizure?' · 'Are you able to take it every day exactly as prescribed — and what gets in the way?' · alcohol, drugs, sleep, other medicines and herbal products · 'Do you drive a private car only, or do you drive for work — truck, bus, taxi or rideshare?'

The answer that decides the station: 'Your six months started when your treatment started. You are two months away, not six.' then 'It is called a conditional licence and it needs a medical review every year' and 'I do not issue the licence — the licensing authority decides, based on what I send them. What I can promise is that if those three things are true, I will support it.'

The compliance move: 'That is a real problem, not an excuse — I will write to your neurologist about the drowsiness, because sometimes the dose can be adjusted and sometimes a different medication suits better.' plus the honest line: 'If you are missing doses you do not meet the standard even at six months, and if there is doubt the authority can require periodic blood-level checks.'

The two things almost nobody says: 'Carbamazepine can make the contraceptive pill less reliable' — the combined pill, mini-pill and implant are affected, an IUD or depot generally is not; and 'If you were ever thinking about pregnancy, come and see me first — there is a high-dose folate we start beforehand and any change is planned by your neurologist, never stopped abruptly.' Note that a drug switch itself triggers the three-month non-driving period.

Challenges: 'I just want my licence back' · 'So six months from today?' — the scripted opening for the key answer · 'What does conditional mean?' · 'Every year? Forever?' · 'Are you definitely going to give it to me?' — saying yes is a fail · 'They would actually test me?' · 'Nobody told me that about the pill — could I have got pregnant?' · 'Are you going to report me?' · and if you lecture her, 'I know. It is just not that simple' and one-word answers thereafter.
pefe: Role-player: Julie Nguyen, 28, a third-year university student in a share house with casual cafe shifts. First seizure four months ago — a witnessed convulsion at home — diagnosed with epilepsy, saw the neurologist once, started on carbamazepine, has not driven since. Frustrated and deflated rather than hostile; she brightens if the candidate is warm about how hard the two-hour bus trip has been, and goes quiet and monosyllabic if lectured.

She misses two or three doses a week. She wants a yes today and expects to be told six months. The worry she voices only if asked about concerns is that she will never be allowed to drive again and will have to defer her degree.

How she tests them: she volunteers nothing about the last seizure unless asked directly, and marks it as a fail if the question never comes · she admits non-adherence but gives the reasons only if asked why · she does not mention rideshare unless asked whether she drives for work · she asks 'So six months from today?' after the criteria, and marks six months as a fail and two months as a pass · she marks any promise of the licence as a fail · and if threatened with reporting she goes cold.

Mark them against these: empathy and agenda acknowledged · permission before the history · asked the last-seizure date separately from the diagnosis date · asked about adherence and then why · alcohol with quantity, drugs, sleep, other medicines and supplements · private versus commercial vehicle · neurologist follow-up · mood and psychosocial impact · the public-safety reason before the rules · the three criteria explained before being applied · the correct answer of two months · conditional licence explained · annual review · the authority decides, not the doctor · a concrete plan for the side effects · trigger counselling with a figure for alcohol · contraception and pre-conception folate · non-driving safety and seizure first aid · both legal duties stated factually · review, reading and a neurologist letter · teach-back.

Variants: last seizure two weeks ago — six months runs from that seizure, so about five and a half months, and the treatment needs review now · long-standing epilepsy seizure-free 20 years with one seizure after six beers — four weeks, because alcohol is identified, avoidable and novel; if the trigger was an all-nighter it is three months because sleep deprivation does not count · rideshare driver — commercial, specialist-led, handle the livelihood conversation · she says she will drive anyway — not fit to drive, explore, document, involve the neurologist, disclose the duty without threatening · neurologist weaning the drug — no driving during the taper and for three months after · crash caused by the seizure — full twelve months, no reductions.

Are you taking it as prescribed — and what gets in the way — 'Not really, I miss it a fair bit.' The mark is in the second half: 'It makes me feel dopey in the mornings, I have put on weight, and I forget when I am busy.' if you just say 'You must take it' she goes quieter and marks it

What increases your risk of a seizure — Alcohol five or six wines on a Saturday · sleep up until 2 or 3 am most nights with assignments · ST John's wort daily for stress, which induces enzymes and lowers her drug level · no recreational drugs · plus missed doses, illness and fever

What do you drive — private or commercial — 'Just my own car.' In the variant she has started driving for a rideshare app and only says so if you ask whether she drives for work — which is commercial, specialist-led, ten years seizure-free with an EEG, and no first-time-treatment reduction

The rest of the history, not optional — Seizure description and any subtle episodes since · sleep-only or time-of-day pattern · neurologist follow-up (Seen once, not since), EEG and MRI · contraception and pregnancy plans — she is on the combined pill · home safety — she has baths most nights · mood, study and stigma · SADMA, past history and family history

When was your last seizure — not when were you diagnosed — 'Four months ago — that was the one. Nothing since.' The whole clock hangs off this date and she volunteers nothing unless asked directly. In the harder recall variant she answers 'Actually… two weeks ago', and the seizure-free clock restarts from then
fails: ★ Never asking when the last seizure was, and taking the four-month diagnosis date as the seizure date
★ Asking about compliance but never asking why — 'are you taking it? no? well, you need to'
★ Never establishing the vehicle type, and assuming private because she is a young student
★ 'Wait six months from today' — the commonest wrong answer in this station

Telling her the plan before explaining the criteria; never saying conditional licence or annual review; promising the licence; skipping triggers; using the reporting duty as a threat; missing contraception and pregnancy on an enzyme-inducing teratogen; no non-driving safety advice; no empathy before the regulation; and blaming her for the non-adherence
numbers: Private standards: default 12 months seizure-free · first seizure 6 months · epilepsy treated for the first time (Treatment started within 18 months) 6 months treated and 6 months seizure-free — this case · breakthrough in previously well-controlled epilepsy 4 weeks with an identified avoidable provoking factor, 3 months without · acute symptomatic 6 months · sleep-only 12 months, or 2 years after previous awake seizures · taper or switch: no driving during and for 3 months after · unconditional again after 5 years seizure-free and 12 months off medication · commercial default 10 years plus EEG, first seizure 5 years, no reductions · two or more seizures in 24 hours count as one · Austroads assessing fitness to drive 2022, paraphrased — VERIFY

SA is the jurisdiction detail that decides the station: reporting is mandatory under the motor vehicles act 1959 section 148 — a health professional who believes a licence holder's condition makes driving likely to endanger the public must inform the registrar in writing and then tell the person that the report was made and what was in it · most other states are discretionary · the patient also has her own duty to notify service SA · for a private licence the GP may liaise with the authority, for commercial only a specialist may · folic acid 5 mg daily pre-conception · people with epilepsy are around twice as likely to be in a crash added · telehealth neurology supported rurally, PATS over 100 km, TIS National 131 450 · VERIFY all

source: Epilepsy_Driving_Licence_Counselling_Notability.pdf (Julie Nguyen, 28, epilepsy treated for the first time four months ago, non-adherent on carbamazepine, private vehicle — four history questions decide the station and the correct answer is review in two months, not six, with a conditional licence and annual review)
drive: AMC Clinical Notability › Counselling › Epilepsy_Driving_Licence_Counselling_Notability.pdf
must: FAIL — Never asking when the LAST SEIZURE was, and taking the four-month DIAGNOSIS date as the seizure date — the whole clock hangs off that one date, and without it every number you quote afterwards is invented: 'I know you were diagnosed four months ago; when was the most recent seizure you had?'; she volunteers nothing, and in the harder variant the answer is TWO WEEKS AGO, which restarts the seizure-free clock and changes the entire answer (★)

FAIL — Asking about compliance but never asking WHY — 'are you taking it? no? well, you need to' scores the first half and loses the second, because you cannot fix what you have not named: 'what gets in the way of taking it?' → side effects, forgetting, cost, denial of the diagnosis, not wanting to be 'on tablets', fear of dependence; she is briefed to go quieter and say 'I know, it's just not that simple' if you simply tell her to try harder (★)

FAIL — Never establishing the VEHICLE TYPE, and assuming private because she is a young student — 'do you drive a private car only, or do you drive for work: a truck, bus, taxi or rideshare?'; she mentions the rideshare app ONLY if asked, and rideshare and taxi driving are COMMERCIAL, where the first-time-treatment reduction does not apply at all, the default is TEN YEARS seizure-free with an EEG, and the assessment must come from a SPECIALIST rather than from you (★)

FAIL — 'Wait six months from today' — the commonest wrong answer in this station, and what separates candidates who know the number from those who know WHAT THE SIX MONTHS IS COUNTED FROM: both clocks started when TREATMENT started, so she is TWO MONTHS AWAY, NOT SIX; explain the criteria AS CRITERIA before applying them, because the examiner is marking the explanation — and she is briefed to ask 'so six months from today?' precisely to give you the chance to get it right or wrong (★)

DO — The three criteria, in this order, for EPILEPSY TREATED FOR THE FIRST TIME on a PRIVATE licence: treated for AT LEAST SIX MONTHS, so the medication has had time to show it works; NO SEIZURES in those six months; and TAKING THE MEDICATION AS PRESCRIBED, because adherence is WRITTEN INTO THE STANDARD as a condition of the licence — then 'your six months started when your treatment started, and you've had no seizures since, so you're TWO MONTHS away, not six'; name CONDITIONAL LICENCE and explain it (you can drive, but the licence carries a medical condition and needs review EVERY YEAR rather than the ten-year licence most people have), and say explicitly that THE LICENSING AUTHORITY DECIDES, NOT YOU ('I can't promise the outcome; I can promise I'll support the application if those three things are true'); give the public-safety reason BEFORE the rules and the empathy before both, because she has lost her independence on top of a diagnosis she did not ask for; other private standards — 12 months seizure-free by default; 6 months after a first seizure; 4 WEEKS for a breakthrough seizure in previously well-controlled epilepsy IF there is an identified, reliably avoidable provoking factor that has not caused seizures before, and 3 MONTHS if no cause is found; 6 months for acute symptomatic seizures; and NO DRIVING during a medication taper or switch AND FOR THREE MONTHS AFTER THE LAST DOSE (VERIFY against Austroads); three rules override the table — compliance is a licence condition, a crash caused by a seizure removes every reduction, and where more than one standard could apply THE LONGEST NON-DRIVING PERIOD WINS

DO — The compliance move: 'that is a real problem, not an excuse — I will write to your neurologist about the drowsiness, because sometimes the dose can be adjusted and sometimes a different medication suits better', with practical aids (a phone alarm, a weekly pill box, a pharmacy blister pack) and the honest blocker named ('if you're missing doses you don't meet the standard even at six months, and if there's doubt the authority can attach a condition that we check the drug LEVEL in your blood'); then the blocks candidates run out of time for — TRIGGERS with numbers rather than disapproval (no alcohol is safest and certainly not five or six in a night; a regular sleep pattern matters almost as much as the tablets, though SLEEP DEPRIVATION IS NOT ACCEPTED AS A LICENSING 'PROVOKING FACTOR' because it cannot be reliably avoided; and tell every doctor and pharmacist about the epilepsy medication, because ST JOHN'S WORT induces enzymes and lowers her drug level); CONTRACEPTION AND PREGNANCY, which almost nobody raises — carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces the effectiveness of the combined pill, the mini-pill and the implant while an IUD or depot is generally unaffected, and it is teratogenic, so pre-conception FOLIC ACID 5 MG DAILY with any change planned by the neurologist and never stopped abruptly (VERIFY); NON-DRIVING SAFETY in thirty seconds (showers not baths, never swim alone, care on ladders and around the stove, seizure first aid for flatmates — protect the head, do not restrain, nothing in the mouth, recovery position, call 000 if over five minutes or she does not wake), plus a seizure diary and medical identification; and the LEGAL part stated calmly as information and NEVER as a threat — her own duty to notify the licensing authority, and in SOUTH AUSTRALIA a MANDATORY doctor's duty to report under the Motor Vehicles Act 1959 s148, with 'that's not something I'm doing today, and I'd always tell you if I did'; do not say WEIGHT GAIN is a carbamazepine side effect if challenged, because that belongs to valproate, gabapentin and pregabalin, while carbamazepine causes drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, diplopia, nausea, rash and hyponatraemia, with HLA-B*1502 screening recommended before starting it in people of Han Chinese, Thai and other South-East Asian ancestry; close with teach-back

setting: The varicose vein is scenery. This is ANZCOR first aid for bleeding delivered down a phone line to a frightened husband, and the clinical content is first-aid level. The failing candidate hands the crisis back — tells a panicking 71-year-old to hang up and ring triple zero himself, then delivers a correct list into a phone nobody is listening to. The passing candidate takes the emergency off him in the first minute, gives one instruction at a time in kitchen words, and does not hang up.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Your next case is a telephone appointment. It concerns a 68-year-old woman who is a known case of varicose veins. She has just cut her leg on broken glass and is bleeding. Her partner is on the telephone and both of them are at home.
Tasks: take a history / assessment from the partner — explain your immediate management to the partner.

Some recalls give task 1 as 'Take a history' and others as 'Do an assessment' — they are the same instruction. You are on a telephone, so the assessment is the history, asked of a frightened third party. The station may be converted to face-to-face mid-station; say nothing down the phone you would not say in the room. Stem reconstructed from 2024 recalls.
tasks: Take a history / assessment from the partner
Explain your immediate management to the partner
time: Ten seconds for his name · twenty seconds addressing the panic properly, once · twenty seconds stating that you are arranging the ambulance · two and a half minutes of closed binary questions in order · three and a half minutes of instructions, one action each, each closed with 'Tell me when that is done' · and the last minute on monitoring, the three do-nots, what the crew will do, and reassurance — not on vein education

back.dx: Bleeding varicosity of the lower leg after a glass laceration, managed by telephone through a panicking third party. The varicosity exists in the stem only to make prolonged, non-self-limiting bleeding plausible — incompetent valves leave the superficial venous system under sustained high pressure and the overlying skin is thin and poorly nourished, so a minor knock opens a vein that is already hypertensive and it flows faster the longer the leg stays dependent. It changes nothing you do. The sequence is DRSABCD adapted to a phone: danger from the glass · response, with 'She is talking' said aloud as a positive airway and breathing finding · then haemorrhage control. Firm direct pressure on or around the wound is the fastest, easiest and most effective measure and everything else is an adjunct to it or a consequence of it failing: lie her flat · any clean cloth, folded, both hands, press harder than feels polite and do not let go · if it soaks through, a second pad on TOP and never lift the first, because lifting strips the clot · stacking pads is not pressure — absorbent layers feel productive while the pressure at the bleeding point falls, so the answer is a firmer more focused push and a bandage over the TOP added · embedded glass stays in and he presses either side of it, because the fragment may be plugging the vessel it cut and blind removal can extend the injury to vessels, tendons and nerves · blanket on for warmth, because cold blood clots badly · nothing by mouth · and she does not stand, because standing puts the venous pressure straight back up. Elevation is the one place the common teaching needs resolving correction: ANZCOR does not recommend routine elevation for bleeding in general — no evidence of benefit and potential for pain or injury — while the vascular literature for a bleeding varicosity specifically does recommend lying flat and raising the leg above heart level with a compression bandage not removed until review, because this bleeding is pressure-driven. The exam position: pressure first always, elevation as an adjunct added after pressure is on, never interrupting it, and not if fracture is suspected. The tourniquet is last resort only — life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure has failed to control — and must be described properly: a belt or folded strip, 5–10 cm above the wound, not over a joint, not over the wound, not covered by clothing, tightened until the bleeding stops and then left alone, time written down and handed over, and keep pressing anyway — because an improvised band that is too loose occludes venous return only and makes the bleeding worse added. Commercial windlass tourniquets outperform improvised ones; say so. Afterwards: paramedic pressure dressing, haemostatic dressing or tourniquet if uncontrolled, IV access and fluids, analgesia, oxygen, transport · ED assessment for blood loss and shock, FBC and group and hold, wound exploration and glass removal with imaging if retained fragments are suspected, closure · tetanus booster if the last dose was over 5 years ago for a tetanus-prone wound, 10 years for a clean minor one, with immunoglobulin if the primary course is incomplete or uncertain · and venous duplex then endovenous ablation, sclerotherapy or surgery, with graduated compression and skin care meanwhile — a bled varicosity recurs if the reflux is not treated, so this is a referral, not a reassurance. VERIFY all.
plan: 'Who am I speaking with?' — get his name and use it. Then address the fear once, properly: 'Ben, I can hear how frightening this is and you have done exactly the right thing ringing. Stay with me — I will tell you exactly what to do and I am not going to hang up.' Do it well and he cooperates for the rest of the call.

Help first, history second: 'Before anything else — I am getting an ambulance to you now. My nurse is dialling triple zero on the other line while we talk. She has your address. You do not have to make that call.' Pre-empts the scripted objection.

Closed binary questions in order — response, danger, timing and trajectory, lay quantity, oozing or spurting, glass in the wound, shock signs, anticoagulants, comorbidities, address and access (see findings). No SADMA, no pulse count, no blood pressure.
Danger first: clear patch of floor, do not kneel in the glass. Then lie her down flat and keep her still.

Cleanest cloth, folded, straight on the cut, both hands, press hard, do not let go — speakerphone or phone on the floor. Then: soaked means a second on TOP, never lift the first. Glass stays in, press either side.
Pillow or folded coat under the calf without interrupting the pressure · blanket on · nothing to eat or drink · she does not stand.

The tourniquet, labelled as last resort as you say it, with placement and the time noted (see dx). Then the three do-nots said out loud, including the explicit refusal of the car when he offers it at about six minutes.

Monitoring instructions — tell me if she stops answering, if her breathing changes, or if she goes grey and sweaty · what the crew will do · reassurance that most bleeds like this stop with the pressure he is already applying · tetanus and vascular referral flagged for later · and you stay on the line.
back.planNote: eight minutes is generous for first-aid content — candidates fail on sequence and on losing the caller, not on time; spend any spare minute on monitoring and reassurance rather than vein education
ask: The four rules of a panic call: one instruction per sentence, then stop and let him do it · kitchen words not clinical words — tea towel not compress, press hard not apply firm digital pressure · close the loop with 'Tell me when you have the towel on it' · and address the fear once, properly, at the start.

The five scripted obstacles and their answers. 'I called you — why should I ring triple zero?' → 'You do not have to. My nurse is dialling right now. Your job is your wife's leg, nothing else.' · 'How can I press on it while I am talking to you?' → 'Put me on speakerphone, or put the phone down on the floor next to you. Both hands on the leg.' · 'I am on my own, I cannot do all that' → 'Then do one thing: press on it and do not let go. Everything else can wait for the ambulance.' · 'I have got the car — should I just drive her in?' → 'No. If you drive, nobody is pressing on that leg, and she can faint on the way. Stay where you are and keep pressing.' · he goes quiet or repeats himself → 'Ben, you are doing this right. Take one breath with me. Now — both hands, press hard. Tell me what you can see.'

The three do-nots, said out loud: do not drive her to hospital · do not remove embedded glass · do not lift the pad to check. Plus no creams or ointments, nothing to eat or drink, and she does not stand up.

The examiner challenge on elevation — 'Why did you elevate? ANZCOR does not recommend it.' → 'You are right that ANZCOR does not recommend routine elevation for bleeding in general. I raised this leg because the bleeding is venous and pressure-driven, so lowering the venous pressure reduces flow at the bleeding point, and there was no suspected fracture. I did it only after direct pressure was on, and it did not interrupt the pressure.'

Traps to name before they happen: launching into questions before saying the ambulance is coming · treating 'Take a history' as an invitation to a full SADMA · letting him dodge a question instead of asking it again shorter — 'Ben, just yes or no. Is she talking to you?' · forgetting that 'She is talking' is a positive airway and breathing finding · offering the tourniquet early because it sounds decisive · giving the whole list in one breath · and ending the call.
pefe: Role-player: Ben Halloway, 71, a retired shearer, at home with his wife Marge, 68, who has bad varicose veins on her right shin and has just dropped a glass jar and cut her leg. He is frightened and not thinking clearly. He opens fast and loud, talking over the doctor: 'My wife's bleeding, there's blood everywhere, you have to help me.'

How he plays it: he avoids the first question he is asked, answering a different one or just repeating that she is bleeding · if the doctor uses clinical words like compress, elevate or apply pressure to the wound site he says 'I don't understand what you're telling me to do' · if the doctor does not arrange the ambulance and tells him to call 000 he gets cross: 'I've called you for help and you want me to make another call?' · he objects once about holding the phone, says once that he is on his own, and at about six minutes offers to drive her in · he settles as soon as he is named, told to breathe, and given one clear instruction at a time.

What he reports if asked: she is awake and talking, scared · it started about five minutes ago and has not stopped · a soaked tea towel and a puddle on the floor · steady dark red, not spurting · glass on the floor and he thinks a bit is in the cut · no blood thinners, just a fluid tablet · blood pressure, nothing else · she is a bit pale and says she feels funny · tetanus unknown.

Mark them against these: got his name and used it · addressed the panic before instructing · arranged the ambulance themselves · asked about danger from the glass · confirmed she was awake and talking · asked about blood thinners · had her lie down · cloth and firm pressure with both hands · second pad on TOP and never lifted the first · left the glass in and pressed around it · explicitly refused the car · gave monitoring instructions · described the tourniquet as a last resort · used words he could understand · one instruction at a time, confirmed · and stayed on the line at the end.

Variants: she slumps and stops answering — leave the bleeding, look listen and feel, compressions if not breathing normally · bright red and spurting — arterial, harder more focused pressure and a much lower tourniquet threshold, tell the crew · she takes apixaban for AF — it will not self-arrest, continuous pressure to handover and she goes to hospital whether or not it stops · 'It has stopped, can we stay home?' — no, the dressing stays on until review and a bled varicosity rebleeds added · a neighbour rings with a forearm cut on a circular saw — identical sequence, plus any amputated part goes dry in a sealed bag and that bag on ice, never directly on ice or in water added · 'What would you do if you were there?' — same order, upgraded tools.

Danger — the written-in hazard — 'Is there broken glass on the floor where you are?' — 'There is glass everywhere, she dropped a jar.' Danger to him as much as to her: find a clear patch of floor, do not kneel in it

Characterising the bleed — Started about five minutes ago, has not stopped, looks worse · quantity in lay terms — 'A soaked tea towel and a puddle on the floor', never ask a frightened man for millilitres · 'Oozing steadily or spurting?' — steady dark red, so venous as expected; bright red spurts would be arterial and a much lower tourniquet threshold

The answers that change what you say — Glass: he thinks there is a bit in the cut — so it stays in and he presses around it · shock: she is a bit pale and says she feels funny · anticoagulants: no, just a fluid tablet — if she were on apixaban or warfarin this would not stop on its own and pressure is continuous until handover · other conditions: blood pressure only · address and front-door access, worth ten seconds rurally · tetanus: he has no idea, and that is a question for the end, not the third slot

The branch you must be able to take — If she slumps or stops answering, leave the bleeding: 'Look at her chest — is it rising and falling? Put your ear close to her mouth and tell me if you can hear or feel any air.' Occasional gasping is not normal breathing — chest compressions now, hard and fast in the centre of the chest, and upgrade the ambulance. Circulation to the brain comes before haemorrhage control

Response, airway and breathing — 'Is she awake? Is she talking to you?' — 'Yes, she is talking, she is scared.' Say out loud that this tells you her airway is clear and she is breathing; that is how the examiner sees you doing a and B without ever saying DRSABCD down the phone
fails: ★ Telling him to hang up and ring 000 himself, and leaving it there
★ Agreeing to private-car transport, or failing to rule it out when he offers
★ Instructing removal of embedded glass, or offering a tourniquet as the first or second step

★ Missing danger entirely — no mention of the broken glass on the floor — or, in the unresponsive variant, controlling the bleeding on a patient who is not breathing normally instead of starting compressions

★ Ending the call before help arrives. Borderline: clinical jargon he cannot follow; stacking the whole list into one speech; arguing with him; running a full past history; leaving tetanus, monitoring or the vascular referral unmentioned
numbers: Direct pressure is the single most effective measure · pad soaked → add another on TOP, never lift the first · glass stays in, press around it · tourniquet 5–10 cm above the wound, not over a joint, not covered, time noted, for life-threatening limb bleeding pressure has failed to control — harm reported with prolonged application in the order of hours VERIFY · tetanus booster if over 5 years for a tetanus-prone wound, 10 years for a clean minor wound VERIFY · definitive care: venous duplex then ablation, sclerotherapy or surgery

In an MM5 rural town the responding SA ambulance crew may be volunteer and the response long — plan instructions for a caller who has to keep pressing for 20–30 minutes, not 5 · 000 SA ambulance · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval and coordination from a small country hospital · healthdirect 1800 022 222 for the after-hours version of this call · TIS National 131 450, a credible extra mark in a station built around a caller who cannot follow instructions · country health connect for ongoing wound and compression dressings · PATS for the later vascular outpatient appointment · VERIFY all
