DO — The pressure sequence, in kitchen words: lie her down, cleanest cloth straight on the cut, both hands, press hard, DON'T LET GO. Soaking through means a second cloth ON TOP — never lift the first, because lifting strips the clot. Pillow under the calf only after pressure is on, blanket over her, nothing by mouth, and tell me if she stops answering you

setting: Version C of the dysphagia station — the same 57-year-old woman, every red flag subtracted. The swallowing history is identical, so the candidate who has drilled version A delivers the cancer speech and is wrong; the candidate who answers 'Gord' is also wrong, and that is an AUTOMATIC FAIL. The answer is a peptic stricture, with cancer still named second and not ruled out without the scope.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo, South Australia (MM5). Endoscopy and ENT services are in Adelaide. Susan Hartley, 57, presents with new difficulty swallowing.

Version C: solids stick in the chest, but there are no red flags at all — no weight loss, no appetite change, not tired, and it is not progressive. What she does have is heartburn, a metallic taste, water brash and a lot of spicy food.
Tasks: take a focused history (6 minutes) — explain your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons — give your differential diagnoses.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons, to Susan
Give your differential diagnoses
time: Forty seconds on the opening, with the reply matched to what she actually said · ninety seconds defining and placing the symptom — hard or painful, initiation or sticking, throat or chest, solids or solids and liquids · three minutes on general GI and the six differential groups, with the four cancer sites asked in full even though they will all come back negative · then two minutes on the diagnosis with reasons, the grouped differentials, and the safety-net

back.dx: OESOPHAGEAL PEPTIC STRICTURE SECONDARY TO CHRONIC GORD — fibrous narrowing that has developed as a complication of years of acid reflux. The answer is not 'Gord': GORD is the underlying condition and does not itself cause dysphagia — it causes heartburn, regurgitation and oesophagitis. Saying GORD is a listed AUTOMATIC FAIL. Oesophageal cancer stays on the list as differential two and is not ruled out by the absence of red flags — a malignant stricture can look benign, so it is biopsied either way. The six differential groups, delivered as groups and not as twelve diagnoses: cancers at four sites — oesophageal, oropharyngeal, thyroid causing extrinsic compression, and lung or mediastinal · strictures and reflux disease · infections of the throat and oesophagus · motility and neurological causes — stroke, multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, diabetes, achalasia · autoimmune — scleroderma, Sjögren's · and medications. First investigation is gastroscopy with biopsy in every version; barium first only if a pharyngeal pouch is suspected, where blind intubation risks perforation. Management once confirmed: a proton pump inhibitor, endoscopic dilatation where the stricture is tight, and reflux measures — weight, meal size and timing, elevating the bed head, and cutting the spicy food, alcohol and coffee. VERIFY PPI dosing, category-1 endoscopy timeframes and PATS eligibility. Rurally: category referral to an Adelaide upper GI unit with PATS travel and accommodation paperwork started at this visit.
plan: Introduce, then match the reply to what she actually said — no canned 'I understand your concern' to a patient who never voiced one. Signpost and ask permission.
★ 'Is it hard to swallow, or painful to swallow?' — odynophagia is a different list. Then ★ Initiation versus sticking, ★ Throat versus chest, and ★ Solids only versus solids and liquids.

Duration, pattern, progression, aggravating and relieving foods, and the impact on eating. In version C the 'Not progressive' answer is the one that shifts the diagnosis — ask it explicitly rather than assuming it.

General GI, then the generic red flags quantified, then the four site-specific cancer sets — sore throat, ear pain and voice change; haematemesis and melaena; neck lump and weather preference; cough and haemoptysis. Ask them all even when they come back negative; asking is the mark.

Reflux, motility and drug blocks — heartburn, metallic taste, water brash, what she takes and whether it still works · neurological and autoimmune screens · medications · 'Have you ever smoked?' · alcohol, spicy food and coffee · past and family history.

The diagnosis with reasons: a narrowing of the food pipe — a stricture — scarring from years of acid, which is why solids catch and liquids do not. Name the reflux burden and the absence of progression as the reasons.

Cancer named second, honestly: still on the list, not ruled out, the warning signs are absent which is reassuring, and the camera test is what settles it. Then the remaining groups at about nine seconds each.

Plan and safety-net: gastroscopy with biopsy, PPI, reflux measures, PATS paperwork · and go straight to ED if she cannot swallow her own saliva, if food becomes completely stuck, or if she vomits blood.
back.planNote: the history is identical to Versions A and B — only the answers differ, so the time budget does not change; what changes is the last two minutes
ask: The three lines that decide the station in every version: 'Is it hard to swallow, or painful to swallow?' · 'Does it happen with solid food only, or with liquids as well?' · and, where it applies, 'A normal examination does not rule out a cancer.'

The version C diagnosis, verbatim: 'The most likely cause is a narrowing of the food pipe — a stricture. These are scars caused by long-term inflammation from acid coming up, and they narrow the pipe so solid food catches.' then, without being asked: 'A cancer of the food pipe is still on my list and I haven't ruled it out. You don't have the warning signs I look for, which is reassuring, but the camera test is what tells us for certain.'

If challenged with 'Isn't this just GORD?': 'GORD is the underlying condition, but it does not itself cause dysphagia — it causes heartburn, regurgitation and oesophagitis. The swallowing difficulty is caused by a peptic stricture, fibrous narrowing that has developed as a complication of years of reflux. I would still biopsy it, because a malignant stricture can look benign.'

Other examiner challenges: 'Why not a barium swallow first?' → barium obtains no tissue; endoscopy sees and biopsies in one sitting, and barium comes first only for a suspected pharyngeal pouch · 'What does solids-only tell you?' → obstructive rather than motility, with the caveat that a very advanced obstruction eventually affects liquids too, so progression and red flags outrank the pattern · 'How does being in Wallaroo change your plan?' → category referral to an Adelaide upper GI unit, PATS started today, country health connect, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if she obstructs completely or aspirates.

Her pushback: 'Am I going to be alright?' Asked once at the end — scored on whether you falsely reassure. And, if you asked about concerns, 'My sister-in-law died of cancer of the gullet. That's what's been in my head.'
pefe: Role-player: Susan Hartley, 57, works part-time in the front office of a transport yard in Kadina and lives in Wallaroo with her husband ray. Composed and practical but tense — frightened and covering it. She answers only what is asked.

Version C answers: no weight loss, appetite fine, not tired, and the problem is not getting worse · heartburn for years with a metallic taste and a sudden rush of saliva · 'I eat a lot of spicy food' · two glasses of wine most nights · no regular medicines beyond Mylanta · mother had bowel cancer at 70 · ex-smoker, twenty a day, quit ten years ago — but only if asked 'Have you ever smoked?'

Scoring domains: defining the symptom out of 4 — dysphagia versus odynophagia, initiation versus sticking, throat versus chest, solids versus solids and liquids · exploring it out of 3 — duration and progression, aggravating and alleviating including the antacid, impact · red flags out of 6 — the generic four quantified plus the four site-specific sets · differential groups out of 6 · diagnosis out of 4 — correct for the version run, named sensitively, 'Not confirmed' said, reasons given · differentials out of 2 — delivered as groups, with cancer named second · communication out of 3.

Sibling cards: med-130 is Versions A and B of this station — the same stem and the same history, landing on oesophageal cancer, with version B adding a completely normal examination card that half the recalled cohort let talk them down to 'Stricture'. Run the two cards back to back: the point of the pair is that the swallowing history is identical and only the red-flag answers move.

The swallowing history — unchanged from version A — Hard, not painful · no coughing or choking at initiation · goes down then catches mid-sternum · solid food only, liquids fine. So the lesion is still obstructive and still in the oesophagus — that part of the history does not discriminate between the versions and is not what you hang the answer on

The red flags — all negative — No weight loss · appetite unchanged · not tired · no night sweats · no lumps · no haematemesis or melaena · no sore throat, ear pain or voice change · no neck lump or weather preference · no cough or haemoptysis · and, crucially, it is not getting worse
What she does have — Heartburn for years · a metallic taste · a sudden rush of saliva (Water brash) · and 'I eat a lot of spicy food'. The reflux burden is the positive finding, not an incidental
The smoking trap, still live — 'Do you smoke?' Gets a flat no and nothing else. Only 'Have you ever smoked?' Gets 'Twenty a day, gave up ten years ago'. It is scored in every version

Her hidden agenda, unchanged — Her sister-in-law died of oesophageal cancer four years ago and it is why she put off coming in. She volunteers it only if asked what she is worried about — or, if never asked, drops it at the very end. In version C this matters more, because the reassurance you give has to be honest rather than flat

★ Never asking whether it is solids only, or never asking any cancer-specific question
★ Delivering the Version A cancer speech because the swallowing history sounded familiar, without having asked whether it is progressive or checked a single red flag

Dropping cancer from the differential entirely because the red flags are negative; not offering the scope because the picture looks benign; giving twelve separate diagnoses instead of six groups; missing the ex-smoker history by asking only 'do you smoke?'; canned empathy to a patient who voiced no concern; no safety-net

Management once confirmed: PPI, endoscopic dilatation for a tight stricture, and reflux measures — weight, meal size and timing, bed-head elevation, spicy food, alcohol and coffee VERIFY · category-1 endoscopy timeframes and PATS eligibility VERIFY · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450 · country health connect · dietitian and texture-modified diet if intake is compromised

must: FAIL — Answering 'GORD' in Version C — GORD is the underlying condition but does not itself cause dysphagia; it causes heartburn, regurgitation and oesophagitis; 'the most likely cause is a narrowing of the food pipe — a stricture; these are scars caused by long-term inflammation from acid coming up, and they narrow the pipe so solid food catches'; a peptic stricture is a fibrous narrowing that has developed as a complication of years of reflux — 'I would still biopsy it, because a malignant stricture can look benign'; and cancer is named SECOND, not dropped: 'a cancer of the food pipe is still on my list and I haven't ruled it out; you don't have the warning signs I look for, which is reassuring, but the camera test is what tells us for certain' (★)

FAIL — Never asking whether it is solids only — the three lines that decide the station: 'is it hard to swallow, or painful to swallow?' (a patient with odynophagia uses the same words — painful swallowing points to infection, ulceration, pill oesophagitis or an ulcerated tumour, a different list), 'is it hard to start the swallow — do you cough or choke as you begin? or does it go down and then get stuck — in your throat or your chest?' (goes down then catches at mid-sternum), and 'does it happen with solid food only, or with liquids as well?' (only solids — bread and meat the worst, on soft food); solids only = obstructive, solids and liquids = motility; those two answers place the lesion on both axes and carry more weight than the rest of the history combined; caveat if asked — a very advanced obstruction eventually affects liquids too, so progression and red flags outrank the pattern (★)

FAIL — Never asking any cancer-specific question, or asking only the generic four red flags — four site-specific sets: oesophageal/gastric ('ever vomited blood, or had black tarry stools?'), pharyngeal ('a sore throat that won't settle, any pain in your ear, any change in your voice?' — ear pain and voice change are the two candidates almost never ask), thyroid ('any lump in your neck? do you prefer hot or cold weather more than you used to?'), lung ('any cough that won't go, or ever coughed up blood?'); the generic four quantified (weight loss — how many kilos over what period; appetite; lumps; tiredness; night sweats); and the smoking trap: 'do you smoke?' gets a flat 'no' — 'have you EVER smoked?' → 'twenty a day, gave up ten years ago' (★)

FAIL — Downgrading the diagnosis because the examination was normal (Version B — half the cohort answered 'stricture' and failed) — to the examiner, aloud: 'I note the examination is entirely normal; a normal examination does not exclude an oesophageal malignancy and my concern is unchanged'; to her, after the compulsory pushback 'but you said the examination was normal?': 'you're right, and I want to be honest with you; I examined you and could not find anything abnormal; but a normal examination does not rule out a cancer — early tumours very often produce no physical signs at all; my concern comes from your symptoms, and it has not changed' — soften or backtrack and it's a fail; 'am I going to be alright?' is asked at the end — no false reassurance; 'are you sure?' → 'the only investigation that removes cancer from the top of my list is a normal endoscopy' (★)

DO — Respond to what she actually said rather than a canned 'I understand your concern' to someone who voiced none (examiners penalise it); duration, first time, every day or on and off, progression, aggravating foods, impact ('soft and mashed food, not enjoying eating'); the general GI screen; then the six differential groups in the history — cancers at four sites, reflux ('heartburn? metallic or bitter taste? a sudden rush of saliva? have you taken anything for it — is it still working?' → 'Mylanta used to help; it doesn't do anything now' — delivered with emphasis, marked as missed if you move straight past it: 'thank you — that change matters'), infection, neurological motility (weakness, numbness, blurred or double vision, droopy eyelids, tremor, stroke, diabetes), autoimmune (rashes, joint pains, tight skin on the hands, dry eyes or mouth), medications; alcohol (two glasses most nights), spicy food and coffee, family history (mother's bowel cancer at 70); the hidden agenda (her sister-in-law died of oesophageal cancer — 'what are you worried about?'); first investigation gastroscopy with biopsy — 'why not barium first?' → 'barium obtains no tissue; endoscopy lets me see the lesion and biopsy it in the same sitting; barium first only for a suspected pharyngeal pouch, where blind intubation risks perforation'

SAY — Versions A and B: 'Susan, I've been thinking about a number of conditions that cause difficulty swallowing; in your case I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer in the food pipe; it is not confirmed, and that is exactly why I want to arrange a test; my reasons: reflux for a long time and the Mylanta that used to help has stopped working; it is getting worse; you have lost six kilograms without meaning to; and it happens only with solid food, which suggests something is physically blocking the way rather than a problem with the muscle movement'; the differential in GROUPS, nine seconds each — 'other cancers that can press on the food pipe — in the throat, the thyroid gland or the lung; narrowing from long-standing reflux, a stricture; infections in the throat; problems with movement of the food pipe — nerve conditions like stroke, MS, myasthenia and diabetes, immune conditions like scleroderma, and achalasia; and some medications; the camera test sorts between them'; the Wallaroo plan — category 1 referral to an Adelaide upper GI unit, PATS travel and accommodation paperwork started today, Country Health Connect, the dietitian (texture-modified diet, oral supplements, weight monitoring; speech pathology if any aspiration features); safety net — 'if you cannot swallow your own saliva, if food becomes completely stuck, or if you vomit blood, go straight to the emergency department' (complete obstruction and aspiration are real risks in someone already on soft food); MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if she obstructs

setting: Version B of the sewer station — the same patient, the same six-minute history, and a different examination card. The candidate who has rehearsed the hepatitis answer still delivers it after being handed a normal liver and a normal dipstick, and that is a listed AUTOMATIC FAIL. The card is the whole point of the version: read it, say what it rules out, and change your mind out loud.
stem: General practice. Jane Whitmore, 30, has come in feeling unwell. She reports there has been an incident at work. No further detail is given. T 38.1, HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
Version B examination card: no jaundice · no hepatomegaly · mild lower abdominal tenderness · urine dipstick normal.
Tasks: take a focused history (6 minutes) — you will be given the examination findings on screen or card — explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient.

Ask for and read the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: Thirty seconds on the opening and the concern question · forty-five seconds exploring 'Unwell' in four questions · twenty-five seconds opening the incident with an open question and saying the exposure back · thirty-five seconds on the four exposure questions · two minutes on the three infection groups · forty-five seconds on the psychological screen · a minute on the rest · then ask for the findings by name and spend the last two minutes on the diagnosis and the differential list

back.dx: GASTROENTERITIS — a sewage-borne bowel infection acquired by swallowing contaminated material when she fell in, fitting the fever, the low abdominal pain, the nausea and the loose stools, and confirmed as the answer by what the card does not show: no jaundice, no tender hepatomegaly, no bilirubinuria. Name the likely organisms rather than the category — viral: rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus · bacterial: salmonella, shigella, E. Coli, campylobacter · protozoal: giardia, cryptosporidium, Entamoeba. The differential list, delivered out loud and in order: acute viral hepatitis a or E, which the card has just argued against but which serology still covers · leptospirosis from RAT urine in sewers — she has no calf pain and no conjunctival suffusion, but it is treatable so it is tested · liver abscess, which cannot be separated from hepatitis without imaging · the psychological consequence of the incident — acute stress reaction now, post-traumatic stress disorder only if symptoms persist beyond a month · then, further down and said as a list she is not meant to be alarmed by, glandular fever, CMV, HIV and syphilis, travel-related infection, haematological malignancy, thyroid disease and diabetes, anaemia, coeliac disease and autoimmune conditions. Plan: stool sample for culture and parasites, bloods including liver function and renal function, hepatitis and leptospirosis serology · oral rehydration, rest, no alcohol · no empirical antibiotics and no anti-diarrhoeals while a shiga-toxin-producing organism is possible · hand hygiene and household precautions · work exclusion until 48 hours after symptoms settle, longer for some occupations VERIFY · notification where the organism is notifiable — salmonellosis, shigellosis, campylobacteriosis and shiga-toxin E. Coli are, alongside hepatitis a and E and leptospirosis · ReturnToWorkSA for the claim and SafeWork SA for the confined space · review in two days with results and a deliberate return to the dreams at four weeks · return immediately if she cannot keep fluids down, passes blood, becomes confused or drowsy, or goes yellow.
plan: Open, confirm her name, signpost the shape of the consultation — and ask what she is particularly worried this might be. It is a scored item and costs eight seconds.
Explore 'Unwell' in four questions only — what kind of unwell, how long, getting worse, how it is affecting her. Do not spend two minutes here.

★ 'You mentioned an incident at work — can you tell me more about that?' not asking is the single commonest reason candidates fail. React like a person, then say the exposure back: 'So you were exposed to urine and faeces.'
★ The four exposure questions: PPE · fluid into eyes or mouth · incident report · head injury or other injury (see findings).

The three infection groups — hepatitis (Jaundice, site of pain, nausea, urine and stool colour) · gastroenteritis (Diarrhoea consistency, blood or mucus, fever and chills) · water contact and rarer (Rash, lymph nodes, calf aches, red eyes). In version B the answers shift to low pain and loose stools four or five times a day.
★ The psychological screen, not just 'How is your mood?' — coping, sleep, nightmares, avoidance of work, other stress. If she answers everything flatly, prompt it explicitly before the end.
The rest, fast: weight loss, lumps, travel, sexual history, chest symptoms, past history, medications, allergies, alcohol, smoking, and hepatitis vaccination for work.

Ask for the findings by name including the dipstick, read the card, and change your mind out loud: not hepatitis, because the liver is normal and the dipstick is clear. Then the diagnosis, the named-organism differential list, the plan and the safety-net, ending with a teach-back.
back.planNote: the six minutes of history are identical to Version A — the version only declares itself when the card is handed over, which is why the last two minutes carry all the discrimination
ask: The version B diagnosis, said without hedging: 'Jane, the examination changes what I think, so let me be clear. You are not yellow, your liver is not enlarged or tender, and your urine test is normal — so this is not hepatitis. What you have is gastroenteritis: an infection of the bowel, most likely from a bug you swallowed when you fell in.'

The four exposure questions and the line that precedes them: 'That sounds horrible. Thank you for telling me — that changes what I need to check for. So you were exposed to urine and faeces.' The global question the role-player is asked is whether she felt like a person who had just fallen into a sewer or like a checklist.

The psychological prompt if she never raises it: 'One more thing before we finish. That was a frightening thing to happen. Some people find afterwards that they replay it, or dream about it, or feel uneasy going back. Has any of that happened to you?' then normalise it, offer a four-week review specifically for it, and book it.

The antibiotic line if there is blood in the stool: 'I am deliberately not giving you antibiotics or anti-diarrhoeal tablets yet — with some of these bacteria, antibiotics can make things worse by triggering a serious kidney complication, so we wait for the result.'

Challenges: 'Cancer? Do you think I've got cancer?' when the long list is read — answer plainly that it is on the list you work through and nothing points that way · 'Am I infectious — will my little boy catch it?' · and, in the notification variant, 'If this goes to public health I'll lose my job' — agreeing not to notify is an AUTOMATIC FAIL; the notification is what supports her ReturnToWorkSA claim.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Whitmore, 30, a sampling technician for the regional water utility, living with her partner and a three-year-old son. Five days ago she slipped on the ladder climbing into a sewer access to take routine samples and fell into the sewage up to her chest, in full protective equipment, and filed an incident report the same day.

Emotional register: embarrassed and a little disgusted, trying to be matter-of-fact, and underneath frightened about what she has caught and about losing shifts. If the doctor is warm she softens and volunteers the dreams; if the doctor is brisk and clinical she keeps them to herself.

Her hidden agenda: she has not been back into a sewer since, has dreamt about it twice, and is quietly worried she will not be able to do her job any more. She becomes tearful on the avoidance question. If the doctor never asks about coping, sleep, mood or work, she drops it at the very end with 'Doctor, can I ask you something else?'

Mark them against these: introduced and confirmed her name · asked her concerns · explored the unwellness in four questions · opened the incident with an open question · named the exposure aloud · asked all four exposure questions · asked jaundice, pain site, nausea, urine and stool colour · asked diarrhoea consistency and blood · asked fever and chills · asked rash and lymph nodes · asked calf pain and red eyes · asked coping, mood, sleep, nightmares and avoidance · asked weight loss, travel and a sexual history · asked past history, medications, allergies, alcohol and smoking · asked for the findings by name including the dipstick · named a single most likely diagnosis · gave named organisms · named leptospirosis · named a psychological differential · plain English · safety-netted · checked understanding.

Sibling card and harder variants: MED-84 is version A, the same stem and history with tender hepatomegaly and bilirubinuria on the card, landing on acute hepatitis a or E. Also rehearse: the card showing jaundice, calf tenderness and creatinine 210 — leptospirosis, treat today and admit · she asks you not to notify · she never mentions the dreams · and bloody diarrhoea with a high fever.

What the version B card says — No jaundice · no hepatomegaly · mild lower abdominal tenderness · urine dipstick normal. Say out loud what that rules out: no tender liver and no bilirubinuria means this is not hepatitis. In version A the same card reads tender hepatomegaly, right upper quadrant tenderness and a dipstick positive for bilirubin

The history answers that differ — Abdominal pain is low and across the bottom of the abdomen, not right upper quadrant · diarrhoea yes — loose, four or five times a day, no blood or mucus · fever and chills · nauseated but not vomiting · no jaundice, urine and stools normal in colour

The four exposure questions — same in both versions — Was she wearing protective equipment? — yes, full kit · did fluid get into her eyes or mouth? — 'I don't know, it happened so fast' · did she file an incident report? — yes · did she hit her head or hurt herself? — no, she landed on her side. Missing the eyes-and-mouth question or the head-injury question is an AUTOMATIC FAIL in either version

The leptospirosis screen and the psychological screen — Severe calf aches and red or sore eyes — both negative, and asking them earns the mark anyway · coping, mood, sleep, nightmares and avoidance — she has dreamt about it twice and has not been back down a sewer, but only volunteers it if the doctor is warm and asks properly

Ask for the findings by name, not 'An abdominal examination' — General appearance and hydration · jaundice in the sclerae and under the tongue · vital signs · lymph nodes · abdominal tenderness and its site · liver size and tenderness · splenomegaly · calf tenderness and conjunctival suffusion · any rash · and a urine dipstick. Asking for a summary and stopping costs the mark and the dipstick is the item the version turns on

must: FAIL — Never asking about the incident — the lead point of the stem and the single commonest reason candidates fail: 'you mentioned there was an incident at work — can you tell me more about that?' → 'I collect samples from the sewer; I slipped climbing in and fell into the sewage'; react ('that sounds horrible — thank you for telling me; that changes what I need to check for') and name the exposure aloud — 'so you were exposed to urine and faeces'; then the four exposure questions: 'were you wearing protective equipment?' (full kit), 'did any of the fluid get into your eyes or your mouth?' ('I don't know — it happened so fast'), 'did you file an incident report?' ('good — that matters, because it protects you if you need time off'), 'did you hit your head, or hurt yourself anywhere else?' — never asking about fluid in the eyes or mouth, or about a head injury, is an automatic fail (★)

FAIL — Still diagnosing hepatitis after the normal Version B card, or hedging 'it might be early hepatitis' — it reads as an unwillingness to let go of the recall: 'Jane, the examination changes what I think, so let me be clear: you are not yellow, your liver is not enlarged or tender, and your urine test is normal — so this is not hepatitis; what you have is gastroenteritis — an infection of the bowel, most likely from a bug you swallowed when you fell in; that fits your fever, the lower tummy pain, the nausea and the diarrhoea' (Version B history: lower abdominal pain, loose stools four or five times a day, no blood, fever and chills, nauseated) (★)

FAIL — Never screening mood, sleep and coping — 'falling into a sewer would shake anyone; how have you been coping since it happened? how has your mood been? how is your sleep — any nightmares or flashbacks? have you found yourself avoiding going back to work?' — the nightmare and avoidance questions are what make it a PTSD-directed screen ('I keep replaying it; I've dreamt about it twice; I haven't been back down there and I don't want to' — volunteered only to a warm doctor; if never asked she drops it at the very end); 'a very normal reaction in the first few weeks, and it usually settles; if it's still there in a month I'd want to see you about it specifically' — PTSD needs symptoms beyond one month, before that an acute stress reaction; a psychological differential must be named (★)

FAIL — Agreeing not to notify — 'if this goes to public health I'll lose my job' → 'I understand why that worries you, and I'm not going to pretend I have a choice — hepatitis A is a notifiable infection and I have to report it; but the notification is what protects you: it confirms this came from work, it supports your ReturnToWorkSA claim, and it gets your workmates checked; it is not a complaint about you' (notifiable in SA: hepatitis A and E, leptospirosis, salmonellosis, shigellosis, campylobacteriosis, Shiga-toxin E. coli); and asking for 'an abdominal examination' and stopping — name the findings you want: appearance and hydration, jaundice in the sclerae and under the tongue, temperature and vitals, lymph nodes, abdominal tenderness and its SITE, liver size and tenderness, spleen, calf tenderness and conjunctival suffusion, rash, and a urine dipstick (★)

DO — The concern question first ('is there anything you're particularly worried this might be?' — eight seconds, scored); explore 'unwell' in four questions then move (feverish, achy, night sweats, no appetite, five days, worse); the three infection groups — hepatitis (yellowing, tummy pain and WHERE — right under the ribs in A, across the bottom in B; nausea or vomiting; dark urine or pale stools), gastroenteritis ('any diarrhoea — loose, or completely watery? any blood or mucus? fever or chills?'), water contact and rarer (rash, lumps in the neck, armpits or groin, 'any severe muscle aches, particularly in your calves? any red or sore eyes?' — the leptospirosis screen; a negative answer still earns the mark); the rest fast — weight loss, appetite, lumps, travel, 'any new sexual partners — I ask everyone', chest pain or breathlessness, PMH, medications, allergies, alcohol, smoking, 'have you had a hepatitis vaccination?' ('shots for work, not certain'); Version A card — no jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, RUQ tenderness, dipstick positive for bilirubin: 'acute hepatitis — inflammation of the liver — most probably hepatitis A or a close relative, hepatitis E; both are picked up by swallowing something contaminated with sewage; you are not yellow yet, but the urine test shows the pigment is already building up, and that comes first' (bilirubinuria precedes visible jaundice at ~40–50 µmol/L; hepatitis A incubation 15–50 days, E 15–60; neither becomes chronic in an immunocompetent adult; 'will my little boy catch it?' → infectious through the bowel — handwashing, vaccinate the household)

SAY — The differential aloud with named organisms: 'first, other infections you can catch from contact with urine and faeces — gastroenteritis, which can be viral (rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus), bacterial (Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Campylobacter) or protozoal (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba); second, leptospirosis, from rat urine in sewers — you don't have the severe calf pain or red eyes, but it's treatable so I want to test for it; third, a liver abscess, which I can't tell apart from hepatitis without a scan; fourth, the effect of the incident on your mind — post-traumatic stress or an adjustment reaction; then further down glandular fever, CMV, HIV and syphilis, travel infections, blood cancers, thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, coeliac and autoimmune conditions' ('cancer?' → 'no — I'm not worried about that at all here; I mention it because it's on the list I work through'); the plan — LFTs and clotting, hepatitis and leptospirosis serology, liver ultrasound (Version B: stool MCS, fluids, work exclusion until 48 hours after symptoms settle), rest, fluids, no alcohol, notify, household vaccination, a letter to the employer, review in two days, 'we'll talk properly about the dreams then'; safety net ('confused or drowsy, bruise or bleed, cannot keep fluids down, go yellow'); teach-back ('what will you tell your partner tonight?'); variants — jaundice, calf tenderness and creatinine 210 = leptospirosis (doxycycline or benzylpenicillin today, admit); bloody diarrhoea with high fever = bacterial colitis — stool sample, kidney function, deliberately NO antibiotics or anti-diarrhoeals yet (HUS risk with Shiga-toxin E. coli)

setting: Version B of the MDD station. Two things are built into this patient that the other two do not have. The first open question yields 'I've been feeling out of sorts' and nothing usable — only the second open question converts it into a mood presentation. And she hands you a stressor, the lost project, which is the commonest trap in the mood block: label it adjustment disorder and you will be defending that while she ticks seven of nine criteria.
stem: General practice. Jane, 25, a project worker who lives with her boyfriend, has been 'Feeling out of sorts' for a month. She is flat and slowed rather than tearful, sits slowly, and answers a beat late.
Tasks: take a history (6 minutes) — explain your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons — give your differential diagnoses.

Explain the most likely diagnosis, with your reasons

time: Forty-five seconds to open, offer confidentiality with the harm exception, and ask the second open question · a minute on the three ts — how long, every day or coming and going, getting worse, any trigger, what it is doing to her life · one and three quarter minutes on the six psychological questions · seventy-five seconds on the mania gate then risk · seventy-five seconds on a four-question psychosis screen, HEADSS and the organic question · then two minutes on the diagnosis with the criteria counted aloud, the differentials and the safety net

back.dx: MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER — a unipolar depressive episode, seven of nine criteria over three to four months with both core symptoms present, no past manic or hypomanic episode and no psychotic features. The work stressor is the trigger, not the diagnosis. The differential is one memorised mood-disorder list, each with its reason: bipolar mood disorder — unlikely, no high or energetic episode ever · depression with psychotic features — unlikely, no unusual experiences or beliefs · adjustment disorder — she did have the stressor, but she meets the full criteria for major depression and that takes precedence · dysthymia — runs two years or more, hers is shorter · post-traumatic stress disorder — added in this version because there was an event, though the picture fits depression better · schizoaffective disorder and schizophrenia — no psychotic features · and always last two, a physical cause such as hypothyroidism, and the effects of alcohol or other drugs, with thyroid function checked on a blood test. Naming the diagnosis without the reasons loses this station while appearing to pass it: the counted criteria are the only evidence the examiner has that you know how a psychiatric diagnosis is made. Finish with a safety net naming a service and get her agreement to it. If the station continues into management: psychology referral for CBT under a mental health treatment plan, consideration of an SSRI with the two-week onset and four-week review explained, the activation warning in the first week or two, sleep hygiene, exercise, cutting the nightly alcohol, Beyond Blue, and thyroid function tests.
plan: Open, ask how she would like to be addressed, and offer confidentiality with the harm exception. Then the open question — and, whatever she says, the second open question.
The three ts plus the trigger and the impact on her life. Note the project; do not pursue it.
The six psychological questions in order — mood, sleep with the initiation-versus-maintenance follow-up, appetite then weight, anhedonia, concentration, energy, guilt and worthlessness.
★ The mania gate, closed before the word depression is used — ever a few days unusually high, extremely good about herself, not needing sleep, out of character.
★ Risk, and the ladder when the grey answer comes: acted on it, plan, anything prepared, what stops her, thoughts of harming others.

Psychosis in four questions only, then HEADSS — who is at home and is he supportive, work stress, alcohol and drugs, previous psychiatric medication, sex drive — then the organic question about cold tolerance.
Name it, one line of explanation, then count the seven criteria out loud with the duration. Add that she has never had a high, which is what makes this unipolar.

The mood-disorder differential list with a reason each, ending in organic and substance causes · answer 'So it's not just because of the project?' · then the safety net with Lifeline named and her agreement obtained.

ask: The second open question, which is the whole reason this version exists: 'Can you tell me a little more about what you mean by that?'
The sleep follow-up that separates candidates: 'Disturbed' is not an answer — 'Is it trouble getting off to sleep, or do you wake in the night and can't get back?'

The mania gate and the risk ladder, verbatim: 'Has there ever been a time, even a few days, when you felt unusually high or energetic, extremely good about yourself, didn't need much sleep, or did things out of character?' · 'Some of my patients, when they feel this low, have thoughts of harming themselves, or that life isn't worth living. Has that happened to you?' · then 'Have you ever acted on it? Do you have a plan? What has stopped you?'

The answer to 'Isn't this just stress?': 'The project may well have set this off. But what you have now goes beyond a reaction to it — you meet the full criteria for major depression, and that means it needs treating in its own right. If it were only a reaction to the stress, I'd expect fewer symptoms and I'd expect them to settle as things at work settled.'

The close: 'If those thoughts about the point of life get stronger, or you feel unsafe, I want you to come back to me, go to the emergency department, or ring Lifeline on 13 11 14. Can you agree to that?' — the named service and the agreement are both scored.
pefe: Role-player: Jane, 25, works in a project team at a mid-sized company and lives with her boyfriend of three years. No children. She moved cities for this job two years ago and her family are interstate — so the support Network is thinner than it looks.

Emotional register: flat and slowed rather than tearful. She answers a beat late, gives short answers, and volunteers nothing unless asked. If the doctor is warm she softens slightly. The case is scored on what the doctor asks, not on what she tells them.

AUTO-FAIL items on the role-player's sheet: screened for a past manic episode · asked about self-harm and explored the grey answer · gave a safety net with a named service. The pass mark applied is both AUTO-FAIL items plus at least twelve of the remaining fifteen behaviours.

The other fifteen: a second open question before moving on · confidentiality with the harm exception · timing, trigger and impact · mood, sleep and appetite with the sleep answer followed up · concentration, tiredness and guilt · anhedonia asked explicitly · a plan and protective factors · hallucinations and delusions in four questions or fewer · alcohol, drugs and previous psychiatric medication · at least one organic screening question · the diagnosis named with the criteria counted aloud · a mood-disorder differential list with reasons · organic and substance causes at the end · finished within eight minutes.

Sibling cards: PSYCH-09 is version A, Lily, 22, tearful and quiet with no trigger at all — she cries during the sleep question and the test is one line of empathy, tissues without comment, and resuming where you left off rather than restarting the block. PSYCH-59 is version C, max, 30, where the history is compressed to four minutes and the marks move into a management plan. Harder variants across all three: a disclosed plan · a volunteered past high phase · a six-week-old baby · and an Aboriginal patient declining a psychologist.

The opening — and why the second question exists — 'I've just been feeling out of sorts this last month. I'm not feeling well.' that is unusable. 'Can you tell me a little more about what you mean by that?' Converts it in ten seconds to 'I'm just sad. All the time'

The three ts — Three to four months — not the one month the stem implies, so ask rather than assume · every day · 'I don't know' to whether it is worsening · still dragging herself to work · arguing a lot with her boyfriend

The trigger, and the trap — 'We lost a project at work. I think it was all my fault the company lost it.' Given with feeling and only when asked about a trigger. Log it as a branch to close later; do not pursue it and do not diagnose off it. If you go back to it she gets slightly upset: 'I told you. It was my fault'

The seven criteria she gives — Mood low and sad all the time · sleep 'Disturbed' — and on follow-up, both initiation and maintenance, waking at four · appetite down with about two kilograms lost, which is the one version that gives a number · anhedonia — no longer going out with friends · cannot focus at work · tired all the time · guilt, 'It was all my fault'. Seven of nine, well over two weeks

The grey answer — the pivot — Mania gate first: 'No. Never.' then risk: 'I sometimes think what's the point of life' — and she stops talking and counts silently to three. That is not a no. Climb it: ever acted on it, any plan, anything prepared, what stops her, any thoughts of harming anyone else. She answers no, no plan, 'It's not that serious', and protective factors are her boyfriend and her family. If you accept the grey answer and move on, she says nothing more and marks it

Psychosis, social and organic — Four questions close the psychosis box and all are negative — she may say 'Apart from the guilt about the project, no' · boyfriend at home, fighting a lot, 'He tries' · working, hard since the project · a glass of wine most nights, no drugs, never any psychiatric medication · no cold intolerance · mother had 'Nerves'

Her hidden agenda, pushed once and late — She is frightened she is going mad and ashamed she cannot pull herself together. At about six minutes, if nobody has asked about her concerns: 'Doctor — am I going crazy?' A good candidate answers it in one sentence and carries on. She also asks 'So it's not just because of the project?'

back.dx: MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER PRESENTING AS IRRITABILITY — the same unipolar diagnosis as the other two versions, reached through a presentation designed to look like anxiety or PTSD, in a man one week into an SSRI started by someone else. The differential list is the same memorised mood-disorder list with reasons: bipolar disorder — excluded only because the mania gate was closed, and it is a listed reason an antidepressant fails · depression with psychotic features · adjustment disorder — no trigger here · dysthymia · schizoaffective disorder and schizophrenia · and, last two always, organic causes such as hypothyroidism and the effects of alcohol or other drugs. The management plan, delivered as headings rather than paragraphs because more headings beats more detail: first and always first, the wait message — citalopram takes about two weeks to start working and about four weeks before it can be judged fairly, so one week is not a failed trial, and he should keep taking it every day. Second, safety: in a small number of people, especially younger people, these tablets can make thoughts of self-harm stronger in the first week or two — if that happens, come back, go to the emergency department, or ring Lifeline on 13 11 14 at any hour added. Then, in order: psychology referral for cognitive behavioural therapy, described in one sentence as finding the thoughts that keep him stuck, challenging them and learning strategies · a sleep hygiene sheet offered rather than explained in full · lifestyle — exercise, and cutting back the alcohol because it will help the tablets work · support — Beyond Blue for groups, counsellors and reading · and follow-up at four weeks with an explicit shared decision: if it still is not helping, increase the dose or change the medicine, decided together. Check thyroid function. A GP starts and monitors antidepressants here — do not offer to refer him to a psychiatrist to prescribe. VERIFY dosing and review intervals against therapeutic guidelines.

ask: The wait message, said first: 'Citalopram takes about two weeks to start working and about four weeks before we can judge it fairly. You've had one week — it hasn't failed, it hasn't had time. I'd like you to keep taking it every day.'

The answer to his frustration, which concedes before it explains: 'I'm sorry it's been such a hard week. I can understand why you'd think it isn't working. The honest answer is that it hasn't had time — these medicines take about two weeks to begin and four to judge. Give me four weeks, and if it still isn't helping we'll change something. Is that fair?'

The activation warning, which is what turns a prescription into a management plan: 'In a small number of people, especially younger people, these tablets can make thoughts of self-harm stronger in the first week or two. If that happens, come back to me, go to the emergency department, or ring Lifeline on 13 11 14 — any hour.'

The early medication questions, brought forward in this version only: 'I can see you've been started on citalopram. Have you been taking it every day as prescribed? Have you had any side effects or problems with it?'
If he volunteers a past high phase: the diagnosis becomes bipolar disorder, you do not start or continue an antidepressant alone, and you seek psychiatric advice on a mood stabiliser.
pefe: Role-player: max, 30, lives alone. Short, frustrated and interrupts. He has been unwell many months, is not going to work and is not seeing friends. He is taking the citalopram as prescribed and is angry that nothing has changed in a week.

How he tests them: he pushes once with 'It's been a week and nothing — why should I keep taking it?' and marks whether the answer concedes before it explains · he gives the grey suicide answer and waits · he says 'I haven't checked my weight' to see whether the candidate wastes time chasing a number · and he lives alone, which should show up in the safety plan.

Scored the same way as the other versions on the three AUTO-FAILS — the mania screen, the explored risk answer, and a safety net with a named service — plus, in this version, whether the management task actually got its time. The source's own warning: do not explain sleep hygiene in full, offer the sheet and move; and do not offer to refer him to a psychiatrist to prescribe.

Sibling cards: PSYCH-09 is version A, Lily, 22, tearful and quiet with no trigger, where the test is one line of empathy and resuming without restarting the block. PSYCH-58 is version B, Jane, 25, where the first open question yields nothing and the lost project is the adjustment-disorder trap. Harder variants across all three: a disclosed plan · a volunteered past high phase · a six-week-old baby, where you screen for postnatal depression, ask about thoughts of harming the infant and involve CaFHS · and an Aboriginal patient declining a psychologist, where you offer the local ACCHS, an Aboriginal health worker and 13yarn, and ask who he would like present.

The opening — built to misdirect — 'I'm irritable and I suddenly start crying. Your colleague gave me this tablet a week ago and it isn't helping.' The word 'Outbursts' is designed to pull you toward anxiety or PTSD. The second open question protects you

The three ts and the medication questions, brought forward — Many months · getting worse · no trigger · not going to work, not seeing friends. Ask early: 'Have you been taking it every day as prescribed? Any side effects or problems with it?' — 'I've been taking it, it's just not working'

The criteria, compressed — Mood low · sleep disturbed, followed up as initiation versus maintenance · appetite down, and 'I haven't checked my weight' — which is not a negative, appetite change alone ticks the criterion, and chasing the number costs you the thyroid question · anhedonia · poor concentration · tired · worthless

The mania gate — why it is never skipped here — 'No, never.' but undiagnosed bipolar disorder is a listed reason the citalopram is not working, so the gate is not a formality in this version — it is part of the answer to his question. If he does volunteer a past high phase, the diagnosis changes and you do not continue an antidepressant alone

Risk — 'Sometimes it comes to my mind' — the grey answer again. No attempts, 'It's never been that serious', no plan. Climb it anyway and ask what stops him and whether he has thoughts of harming anyone else

Social and organic, whatever survives — Lives alone — which matters for the safety plan · work 'Always stressful, nothing new' · wine sometimes · citalopram is the only medication he has ever taken for his mental health · psychosis screen negative on four questions · no cold intolerance

His pressure — 'It's been a week and nothing. Why should I keep taking it?' — asked shortly, with interruptions. The answer is not defensive: apologise for the week, agree it feels like failure, then give the timeline and ask for four weeks

setting: Version B of the dizziness station — the 2023 re-skin. The stem is identical and the word on the door is still 'Dizzy', but the answer to the defining question is not spinning. stem: General practice, South Australia. A 60-year-old man has come in complaining of dizziness. The reception note reads 'Dizzy spells, 5 days'. Information on the door: HR 78 regular · BP 132/80 sitting · RR 14 · SpO2 98% RA · T 36.7 · BGL 5.8 · GCS 15.
At the defining question he says: 'It's not spinning. I go light-headed and grey when I stand up out of the chair, and twice my legs have gone from under me.'

back.dx: ORTHOSTATIC (POSTURAL) HYPOTENSION WITH FALLS — most likely drug-induced or drug-worsened, on antihypertensive and prostate medication, in a man whose presenting word was 'Dizzy'. This is a falls and medication-review station wearing a vertigo costume, and the entire ear block is irrelevant to it. The differential spans the groups the original stem sets up, each with a reason: drug causes — antihypertensives, alpha blockers for the prostate, diuretics, nitrates, antidepressants, anything recently started or up-titrated · volume depletion — poor intake, diarrhoea, vomiting, bleeding · cardiac — arrhythmia, bradycardia, aortic stenosis and ischaemia, which is why the ECG and the pulse rhythm are asked for · autonomic failure — diabetes, Parkinson's disease, other neurodegenerative causes · endocrine — adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism · anaemia · and the vestibular group, which is excluded by the answer to the defining question rather than ignored. Management is a medication review first and a drug second: review and reduce or reschedule the culprits rather than adding treatment · rise in stages and sit on the edge of the bed for several seconds before standing · adequate fluid and, if not contraindicated, liberalised salt · compression stockings · avoid large hot meals, alcohol and hot showers, all of which worsen it · a home falls assessment — loose rugs, cords, lighting, stairs, grab rails, footwear and a night light on the path to the bathroom · vision checked · physiotherapy for strength and balance · bloods including full blood count, electrolytes and renal function, glucose and HbA1c, and an ECG · and review in one to two weeks with a repeat postural blood pressure. Driving still has to be addressed — he has had two episodes where his legs gave way, and in South Australia the doctor carries a mandatory duty to notify the registrar where a patient is unfit and continues to drive. VERIFY thresholds and any drug treatment against current guidelines.
plan: Confirm haemodynamic stability before a word is spoken — the stem word could be hiding a stroke, an arrhythmia or a bleed. Then WIPE, open question, acknowledge, signpost.

Switch structure out loud, then run the postural and falls history: timing after standing, warning symptoms, awareness throughout versus blackout, injuries, number and circumstances of falls.
Every medication with dose and timing, anything recently started or increased, over-the-counter and herbal · fluid intake, diarrhoea, vomiting, bleeding · alcohol.

The cardiac and systemic blocks — chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, ankle swelling · diabetes, parkinsonism, numb feet · tiredness, weight loss · then the geriatric and social screen: memory, mood, who is at home, ADLs, home hazards, vision, footwear, and driving.

Hard stop. Name the examination items — lying and standing BP at one and three minutes, pulse rhythm, gait and balance, falls-risk assessment, medication review, plus glucose and ECG — then interpret the drop aloud against the threshold.

The diagnosis with the number given back to him, the grouped differentials, the medication review as the main treatment, the rise-in-stages and home-safety advice, driving, review in one to two weeks, and a safety-net — then teach-back.

ask: The defining question, which must come before any ear question: 'Dizziness means different things to different people — do you mean a spinning sensation, feeling light-headed as if you are about to faint, or being off-balance?' then 'Have you had any fainting or blacking out?' and 'And any falls?'

The switch, said out loud: 'Thank you — that tells me something different is going on, so let me change the questions I am asking. Does it happen specifically when you stand up from sitting or lying? How quickly after standing? Did you black out at all, or were you aware throughout? Tell me about all your medications and when you take them.'

The examiner request, named rather than summarised: 'A lying and standing blood pressure at one and three minutes, pulse rate and rhythm, gait and balance, a full falls-risk assessment including vision and footwear, and a medication review.'

The explanation, with the number: 'Your blood pressure is dropping when you stand — it fell from 138 to 106 today. That is very likely being caused or worsened by your blood pressure and prostate tablets. I would like to review those doses, and I want to talk about preventing falls, because that is what worries me most.'

The safety-net and the driving line, both separately scored: come back or call an ambulance for slurred speech, one-sided weakness or numbness, double vision, trouble swallowing, severe headache or new neck pain, a blackout, chest pain or a racing heart, or an injury from a fall · and 'While you are still having these episodes you should not drive' — with the SA notification duty stated as information, never as leverage.
pefe: Role-player: the same 60-year-old man as the standard version — a retired diesel fitter in a country town, widowed, living alone in a single-storey house, with a daughter nearby and a grandson he drives to school on Thursdays. Guarded and slightly gruff, understates things, warms up if the doctor is warm.

He is briefed to be deliberately unhelpful on the open 'What makes it better or worse?' and to give the positional detail only when the position is named for him. In this version the detail that must be named is standing up from a chair, not rolling over in bed.

His hidden agenda is unchanged: his brother had a stroke at 62 and he is convinced this is the same thing. He will not say so unless asked about ideas and concerns; if nobody has asked by about six minutes he interrupts with 'Doctor, just tell me straight — is this a stroke?' if reassured without reasons he stays unconvinced and says 'But how do you know?'

The driving line is planted in every version: 'I drive, and I take my grandson to school on Thursdays. Should I be doing that?' if the candidate never asks about driving he raises it late, and an answer that is not ready costs both the safety and the professionalism mark.

The source's own study method is to run the stem once, then re-run it with a version the partner does not name — the second run is the one that predicts the exam, because it punishes anchoring.

The triage triad — ask it before anything else — 'Dizziness means different things to different people. Do you mean a spinning sensation — the room going round? Or light-headed, as if you are about to faint? Or more that you are off-balance and unsteady?' then 'Any fainting or blacking out, even for a second?' and 'Any falls?' The second and third questions are what catch this version

Switch structure openly when the answer comes — 'Thank you — that tells me something different is going on, so let me change the questions I am asking.' Saying it aloud is the mark; silently redirecting looks like a candidate who has lost the thread

The questions that replace the ear block — Does it happen specifically on standing from sitting or lying, and how quickly after standing? · any warning before the falls? · did he black out, or was he aware throughout? · any injuries? · and every medication with the times he takes them — the dose schedule matters as much as the list

The other four variants of this stem, for contrast — Unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus — hearing loss abolishes the benign diagnosis; audiometry, MRI of the internal auditory canals, ENT · continuous vertigo with ataxia and slurred speech — posterior circulation stroke, ambulance now, not a Dix–Hallpike · head injury twelve days ago on apixaban — urgent CT for subdural haematoma · and the standard version A, posterior-canal BPPV, which is med-101

Urine dipstick: blood ++, nitrites negative, leucocytes negative. A non-contrast CT KUB has been done and the film is on your desk. No stone size is reported.

back.dx: URETERIC COLIC — an obstructing calculus at the vesicoureteric junction, confirmed on non-contrast CT KUB, with a dipstick showing blood but no evidence of infection. The diagnosis is given with its reasons: the stone is visible on the scan, and the story fits it exactly — pain starting in the flank and travelling to the groin, coming in waves, with blood in the urine. Management is two pathways and both must be given. Small stone, around 5 mm or less: most pass spontaneously and he is managed at home — an NSAID first, ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food or indometacin 100 mg PR, with oxycodone 5 mg orally if that is not enough · an antiemetic, ondansetron 4–8 mg wafer · tamsulosin 400 microgram daily as medical expulsive therapy, with postural light-headedness as the side effect to warn about · strain the urine and catch the stone for analysis · drink normally, enough not to be thirsty — explicitly do not force large volumes to 'Flush it out', which does not work and worsens the pain · review in 48 hours to 3 days, and urology if it has not passed by four weeks. Large stone, above about 7 mm: unlikely to pass, so urology referral — ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy, which suits a stone sitting low like this one · extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy · percutaneous nephrolithotomy for large stones inside the kidney · or a stent if the kidney needs relieving quickly — with analgesia and tamsulosin continuing while he waits. 5–7 mm is the grey zone. Long term: 2.5–3 L of fluid a day, which matters particularly for a man working in a hot shed · reduce salt · keep dairy and calcium normal, because cutting calcium out increases stone risk — a counterintuitive point worth saying explicitly · and stone analysis plus calcium, phosphate, PTH and urate, with a 24-hour urine for calcium, oxalate, citrate and urate. VERIFY all doses and size thresholds. The one picture that changes everything is fever or rigors with positive nitrites and leucocytes — an infected obstructed kidney, which is a urological emergency needing IV fluids, blood cultures, IV antibiotics and urgent decompression by stent or nephrostomy, and from a rural site a MedSTAR retrieval conversation.
plan: Open properly even though the task is explanation — name, check who you are speaking to, acknowledge the morning he has had, then signpost: 'I have your scan here, so let me take you through what it shows, then what it means, then what we do about it.'
The film: orient with bladder and hip bones, build the ureters, then reveal the stone at the junction (see findings).

The diagnosis in plain words — a kidney stone on the move, with the pain coming from pressure against the wall of the tube — and the three reasons: the stone is visible, the pain migrated flank to groin in waves, and there is blood in the urine.

★ The fork sentence and the two exclusions — urine culture for infection behind the blockage, and a UEC for kidney function — said before 4:15, with the reasoning that a stone plus infection means hospital the same day.
★ The small-stone pathway in five parts: NSAID first, antiemetic, tamsulosin with its warning, strain the urine, and drink normally rather than forcing fluids.

★ The large-stone pathway: urology, and the four options named in plain language — laser via a fine telescope from below, shock waves from outside, a small cut in the back for stones in the kidney, and a stent if the kidney needs relieving.
Prevention: fluid volume with the hot-shed context, low salt, normal calcium said explicitly because it surprises people, and stone analysis with metabolic bloods.
Safety-net — fever or shakes, uncontrollable pain, not passing urine, or vomiting so much he cannot keep fluids down — then review in two to three days, and teach-back.
back.planNote: Version A is a four-minute history with a hard stop; Version B has no history at all, so the whole eight minutes is explanation and the risk is finishing early with one pathway given
ask: The orientation sequence, in order: slice and viewpoint → hip bones → bladder → the two ureters → the bright dot. Never the dot first.

The fork, verbatim: 'What we do next depends on how big the stone is — but before any of that, I need to be certain there is no infection and to check your kidney function.' and the reason attached: 'A stone and an infection together is the one combination that means hospital the same day.'

The two counterintuitive instructions that are separately marked: 'Drink normally — enough that you are not thirsty. Please do not force large amounts of water; it will not push the stone out and it makes the pain worse.' and 'Keep your dairy and calcium normal — cutting calcium out actually makes stones more likely.'
'Strain your urine and catch the stone, so we can analyse what it is made of' — and the tamsulosin warning: light-headedness on standing, so get up slowly.

Challenges: 'How big is it, doctor?' — answered with both pathways, never an estimate off the film · 'Panadol's useless, just give me the Endone' — 'I am not going to leave you in pain. The most effective drug for this particular pain is actually an anti-inflammatory rather than a strong painkiller, so I will start there. If that is not enough I will add something stronger — a short course, and you must not drive or operate the forklift while you are taking it' · and 'How long till it comes out? Can I still go to work? Will it happen again?'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitmore, 40, a storeman at the grain terminal outside Wallaroo, married with two children, driving a forklift all day in a hot shed and drinking almost no water at work. Ten cigarettes a day, four to six beers on a weekend, no regular medications, no allergies, never had a stone, two working kidneys. His father had kidney stones twice in his forties.

His hidden agenda carries into this version: an uncle died of bladder cancer at 58, and he saw pink urine this morning and is convinced it is the same thing. He has told nobody, not even his wife. He releases it only if asked about concerns; if nobody asks, he interrupts at about six minutes with 'Doctor — can I ask you something? Is this cancer?'

False reassurance is marked down every time: 'It is definitely not cancer' gets 'How can you know that without a scan?' In version B you do have the scan, so the honest answer is available — the stone is visible and explains both the pain and the blood — but it still has to be said rather than assumed, and the fear still has to be elicited.

Version B's own AUTOMATIC FAILS, listed separately on the marking sheet: answered with only one management pathway · never mentioned excluding infection. The shared ones still apply: telling him to drink as much water as possible to flush the stone out · telling him to cut out calcium or dairy · and false reassurance about cancer.

Sibling card and variants: med-163 is version A — the four-minute history, examination request and investigation station from the same stem, where the AUTOMATIC FAILS are never saying the word fever and never requesting the dipstick. Also rehearse the febrile patient (Infected obstructed kidney, retrieval), the opioid request, the pregnant patient (Ultrasound not CT, avoid NSAIDs, involve obstetrics and urology early), and the solitary kidney with a rising creatinine, where size is irrelevant and decompression is today.

Orient before you point — 'This is a slice through your lower tummy, looking from your feet upward. These bright white shapes on either side are your hip bones. This big grey circle in the middle is your bladder.' Pointing at the stone in the first sentence is the trap — the image means nothing to him until he knows what he is looking at

Build the structure, then reveal — 'There are two narrow tubes carrying urine from your kidneys down into the bladder — the ureters. Now, this small bright dot here is a stone. It is sitting in one of those tubes, right at the point where the tube joins your bladder.' Give the plain version first and vesicoureteric junction second

The fork sentence — say it before 4:15 — 'What we do next depends on how big the stone is. But before any of that, there are two things I have to sort out. First, I need to be certain there is no infection sitting behind the blockage — so I am sending your urine for a culture. A stone and an infection together is the one combination that means hospital the same day. Second, a blood test to check your kidney function.' Going straight from 'You have a stone' to 'Here are your painkillers' is an AUTOMATIC FAIL

No size is reported — and he will ask — 'How big is it, doctor?' The answer is not an estimate off the film: 'The report doesn't give me a measurement, and I am not going to guess from the picture. What I can do is tell you both possibilities, so nothing surprises you.' Giving only one pathway is the other AUTOMATIC FAIL

What the dipstick already tells you, said aloud — Blood ++ fits a stone scraping its way down · nitrites and leucocytes both negative means no current evidence of infection — which is why this is a general practice problem today rather than a same-day urological emergency. Say that reasoning out loud rather than assuming it

back.dx: FREQUENCY AND POLYURIA EXPLAINED BY DELIBERATE EXCESSIVE FLUID INTAKE — about six large glasses of water a day taken on health advice — in a man with no lower urinary tract symptoms of obstruction and no red flags, whose real presenting problem is a fear of prostate cancer. The explanation is built from named negatives rather than from reassurance: when the prostate is the problem you expect difficulty starting, a weak stream, stopping and starting, dribbling, a feeling of not emptying and waking at night — he has none of them, has seen no blood, lost no weight and has no pain. The differentials, each with a reason: benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer — excluded by the absent voiding symptoms and absent red flags, not by optimism · urinary tract infection and prostatitis — no dysuria, no fever, no perineal pain · diabetes mellitus — no polydipsia beyond the deliberate drinking, no weight loss, no blurred vision, but worth a glucose or HbA1c · hypercalcaemia · diabetes insipidus · diuretics and other drugs · caffeine and alcohol · overactive bladder · and bladder pathology, which is why haematuria is asked. The management is a behavioural experiment rather than a test: cut back to natural thirst for a fortnight and keep a simple bladder diary, and the symptom is expected to settle — with an MSU and a glucose as a low-cost backstop. When he pushes for certainty, the answer is neither a guarantee nor a reflex test: name PSA, say plainly that it has real benefits and real drawbacks including false alarms and unnecessary biopsies, and offer a separate appointment to go through it properly so he can decide. A digital rectal examination is offered as part of that assessment rather than sprung on him. Safety-net on the things that would change the answer: blood in the urine, a weaker stream, waking at night, weight loss or bone pain — come straight back. VERIFY PSA thresholds and current Australian screening guidance before quoting them.
plan: Open, confirm his name, and answer the fear he has already named: 'Thank you for telling me straight away that you are worried about prostate cancer — that is exactly what I want to know. I am going to ask a series of questions so I can work out what is causing this, and then I will come back to your concern and answer it properly.'
Define the symptom before diagnosing it: how long, constant or intermittent, worsening, count per day, nocturia number, and — the one that turns the station — large or small volume each time.

The storage package: urgency, urge incontinence, dysuria, suprapubic pain. Then the voiding package: hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining, terminal dribble, incomplete emptying. Ask them all even though they will all be negative.
★ Haematuria unprompted, then the rest of the red flags — weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, fever and rigors, loin pain, bone or back pain, and a one-line cauda equina screen.

★ The fluid and polyuria block — water, tea, coffee, cola, alcohol, diuretics and any recent medication change, then thirst, weight loss and blurred vision. The water answer is the diagnosis (see findings).
Past history, medications, allergies, smoking and family history — particularly prostate cancer in a father or brother, which changes the screening conversation you are about to have.
The explanation, built out of the negatives you asked for — name what prostate disease would look like, then say he has none of it, then give the six glasses as the sufficient explanation.
The two-week experiment and the diary, the grouped differentials with reasons, the PSA shared-decision offer as a separate appointment, and the safety-net — then check what he is taking away.
back.planNote: the negatives are the work — a candidate who skips the voiding package has nothing to build the explanation from and is left with bare reassurance, which scores nothing
ask: The opening move: thank him for naming the fear, park it explicitly, and promise to return to it — then actually return to it. Parking without returning is as bad as never asking.

The explanation, verbatim and built from negatives: 'Prostate cancer is very unlikely here, and I want to give you my reasons rather than just ask you to trust me. When the prostate is the problem, we expect difficulty starting, a weak stream, stopping and starting, dribbling, a feeling of not emptying, and getting up at night. You have none of those. You have seen no blood, lost no weight and have no pain.'

The diagnosis and the experiment: 'What you do have is around six large glasses of water a day. Anyone drinking that much would be in the toilet frequently — that alone explains it. If you would like, cut back to your natural thirst for a fortnight and keep a simple diary, and I expect it will settle.'

When he pushes — 'Are you sure it is not cancer?': 'I cannot give you a hundred per cent guarantee about anything, and I would be wrong to pretend otherwise. What I can say is that nothing in your story points that way. If you would like certainty about your prostate, there is a blood test called PSA — it has real benefits and real drawbacks, including false alarms and unnecessary biopsies. I would be very happy to book a separate appointment to go through that properly so you can decide.'
The safety-net that closes it honestly: 'And if anything changes — blood in the urine, a weaker stream, waking at night, weight loss — come straight back.'
pefe: Role-player: James, 62, who has watched a television programme about prostate cancer and has come in convinced. Unlike version A he is not guarded — he volunteers the fear immediately, which is its own test: the candidate has to park it without dismissing it and still take a six-minute history.

His answers: good volumes each time · no dysuria, no urgency, no leaking · every voiding symptom negative · no blood, no weight loss, no bone pain, no fever · and, when asked, about six big glasses of water a day because he read it was good for him.

He pushes once for certainty — 'Are you sure it is not cancer?' — and is not satisfied by 'Don't worry'. He is satisfied by named negatives, an honest refusal to guarantee, and an offer to discuss PSA properly. A candidate who orders the PSA reflexively to close the conversation is penalised just as heavily as one who reassures blankly.

Sibling card: med-170 is version A — Jane Whitcombe, 50, four days of frequency with a cystocele and an HbA1c of 6.1%, where a dipstick card is handed over at six minutes and has to be explained pad by pad, and where the hidden agenda is pink on the paper and an aunt with bladder cancer. The shared spine of both versions is the same: define the symptom with a count, a nocturia number and a volume; run both symptom packages; ask haematuria unprompted; and answer the cancer fear with reasons.

Two further recalled variants of the stem: a woman who volunteers incontinence — add bladder training and pelvic floor physiotherapy to the plan explicitly, treat the infection first because it worsens urgency, and do not promise surgery · and a patient who opens with frank polyuria — the structure is unchanged, but thirst, weight loss and blurred vision come earlier and the thinking is diabetes, hypercalcaemia and diabetes insipidus before cystitis.

The volume question — 'When you go, are you passing a large amount, or only a small amount each time?' — 'A good amount each time, actually.' that is polyuria, not frequency of small voids, and it points away from cystitis and away from outflow obstruction before you have asked anything else

The fluid question — this is the whole diagnosis — 'Roughly how much water do you drink in a day?' — 'About six big glasses. I read that it is good for the kidneys, so I have made myself do it.' Asked as small talk, it is missed; asked as routine history, it answers the station

The voiding package — every answer negative, and that is the point — Hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining, terminal dribble, incomplete emptying — all no. The negatives are not wasted time: they are the material the explanation is built from, and you cannot name them back to him if you never asked them

The red flags — also negative — No haematuria even on the paper · no weight loss · no bone or back pain · no fever or rigors · no loin pain. The haematuria question is the single-item AUTOMATIC FAIL of this station in both versions and must be asked unprompted

The polyuria screen that has to run alongside — Extra thirst, weight loss and blurred vision for diabetes · constipation, bone pain and low mood for hypercalcaemia · diuretics, lithium and any recent medication change · and how much alcohol, tea, coffee and cola. A genuine polyuria opening is its own recalled variant, and there the thinking is diabetes, hypercalcaemia and diabetes insipidus before cystitis
