setting: Version A of the tired child — the older recall. The stem is word for word identical to the diabetes version and only the answers change, which is the entire point of the pair: a memorised script for either version dies in the first minute. One sentence splits them — sleepy all the time, or low in energy? Here the answer is sleepy, worst in the mornings, and the teacher raised it.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother, who says he is always tired. The kindergarten teacher raised it.

What emerges on history: tired all day but worst in the mornings · snoring every night, audible through the wall, with pauses and gasps · waking at night · recurrent sore throats, four or five a year · grumpy and hard to manage · kindy performance affected. No thirst, no increased urine, no bedwetting.
Tasks: take a history (6 minutes) — explain the diagnosis and your differentials to the parent. No physical examination and no investigations are provided.
tasks: Take a history from the mother (6 minutes)
Explain the diagnosis and your differentials to the parent
time: Forty-five seconds to introduce, empathise and define sleepy versus low in energy · forty-five seconds on timing, pattern and effect on function · three and a quarter minutes running every letter of the mnemonic audibly — endocrine, malignancy, infection, anaemia, mood, coeliac, cardiopulmonary and the sleep block · forty-five seconds on the well-child questions · thirty seconds on birth, immunisations, medications, allergies and family history · then two minutes on the diagnosis with its mechanism, eight or more named differentials, and the referral plan

back.dx: Obstructive sleep apnoea in a 5-year-old, most likely from adenotonsillar hypertrophy, presenting as daytime tiredness and behavioural change. The mechanism has to be explained, not just named: during sleep the throat muscles relax and become floppy, and enlarged tonsils and adenoids narrow the airway, so it blocks off for short periods — that causes the snoring and the gasping, interrupts his sleep over and over without waking him properly, and leaves him exhausted and struggling at kindy. The recurrent sore throats fit the same anatomy and are worth saying back to her. The full differential list is marked item by item and three is not enough after a six-minute history: hypothyroidism · haematological malignancy, particularly leukaemia · infection, especially epstein–barr virus, which leaves children tired for weeks · anaemia, including iron deficiency from excessive cow's milk · low mood or something happening at kindy · coeliac disease · congenital heart disease · type 1 diabetes, which is the other version of this very stem and must be named and dismissed with its negatives · and obstructive sleep apnoea itself. The plan: referral to a paediatrician and to ENT, with a sleep study to quantify how often his breathing stops — for most children this is driven by large tonsils and adenoids and adenotonsillectomy is curative. Safety-net on excessive daytime sleepiness, faltering growth and worsening behaviour. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy peaks between about 2 and 8 years VERIFY. Note what this station is not: a stem reading 'Tired and not paying attention at school' is a different station run through the behavioural pathway — ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, absence seizures, hearing impairment and sleep apnoea — because the structure is aimed at the stem, not at the diagnosis.
plan: Introduce, empathise without padding — 'That must be worrying; you did the right thing bringing him in' — then ★ The defining question: sleepy all the time, or low in energy?

Timing and pattern: how long, every day or intermittent, worse at any time of day, getting worse, better or worse with anything, and the effect at kindy and at home. 'Worst in the mornings' is a finding, not scenery.
Endocrine first and early — thirst, then urine and bedwetting as a separate question with a pause, then cold intolerance, constipation and family history of diabetes or thyroid disease.
Malignancy, then infection, then anaemia with the diet questions — each as a named block so the examiner hears the structure (see findings).

Mood, home, kindy and bullying · coeliac · cardiopulmonary · then ★ The sleep block: snoring, gasping or pauses, morning sleepiness, recurrent infections, new behavioural problems — which in this version is where everything lands.
Well-child: alert or drowsy, eating and drinking, urine output, developmental concerns · then birth, immunisations, medications, allergies and family history of thyroid, diabetes and coeliac disease.
Name obstructive sleep apnoea and explain the mechanism in plain words — floppy throat muscles, large tonsils and adenoids, airway blocking, sleep broken repeatedly without waking him.

Eight or more differentials by name, each dismissed against the history — including diabetes, because it is the other version of this stem · then paediatrician and ENT referral, a sleep study, the likely adenotonsillectomy, and the safety-net.
back.planNote: every letter of the mnemonic must be audibly covered inside six minutes — the marking sheet ticks the blocks, not the conclusion
ask: The defining question, which is one sentence and splits the differential in half: 'Do you mean he is sleepy all the time, or low in energy — not playing and running around like other children?'

The sleep block, asked as four separate questions: 'Does he snore? Any gasping or pauses in his breathing? Is he sleepy in the mornings? Does he get recurrent throat or ear infections? Any new behavioural problems?'

The mechanism, verbatim: 'When he sleeps, the muscles in his throat relax and become floppy, and his tonsils and adenoids narrow the airway — so the airway blocks off for short periods. That is what causes the snoring and the gasping, it interrupts his sleep over and over without waking him properly, and that is why he is tired all day and struggling at kindy.'
The recovery line for when a block comes back empty: 'That makes a sleep problem less likely — let me ask about some other causes.' Same sentence, other direction, in the diabetes version.

The plan and safety-net: 'I will refer him to a paediatrician and to an ear, nose and throat specialist, and arrange a sleep study to see how often his breathing stops. For most children this is caused by large tonsils and adenoids, and removing them fixes it. In the meantime, tell me straight away if he becomes very sleepy during the day, stops growing well, or the behaviour gets worse.'

The question that decides which station you are in — 'When you say he is tired, do you mean he is sleepy all the time, or that he is low in energy — not playing and running around like other children?' Version A: 'Sleepy — his kindy teacher says he nods off, and he is worst first thing in the morning.' Version B: 'Low in energy.' One sentence, and it HALVEs the differential

The sleep block — where version A lives — 'Does he snore?' — 'Every night, you can hear him through the wall.' · 'Any gasping or pauses in his breathing?' — 'Yes, he stops, then takes a big gasp.' · sleepy in the mornings · recurrent throat infections, four or five a year · and new behavioural problems — grumpy and hard to manage

The endocrine block — negative here, but still asked early and separately — Thirst normal · no increase in urine, no return of bedwetting · no cold intolerance or constipation. Ask the thirst and the urine questions as two separate questions with a pause — parents answer only the first, and in the other version that habit loses the entire diagnosis

The rest of the mnemonic, run in full — Malignancy — weight and growth, appetite, lumps, night sweats, easy bruising, bone or leg pains, unexplained fevers · infection — fever, travel, rash, recent flu-like illness · anaemia — pallor, red meat and cow's milk volume, jaundice, dark urine · mood, home and kindy including bullying · coeliac — greasy stools that float or stick, diarrhoea, blood · cardiopulmonary — cough, breathlessness, getting puffed or blue on running

The recovery line, which belongs to whichever version you are not in — When a whole block comes back negative, say it aloud and keep moving: 'That makes a sleep problem less likely — let me ask about some other causes.' Freezing when the rehearsed script dies is exactly what this pair is designed to catch

'Well child, growth normal; mouth breathing; clear discharge both sides; and the nasal lining is pale, swollen and congested with swollen inferior turbinates.' The pale, swollen, congested mucosa is what allergy looks like and it is the finding the whole card exists for. Silence while you read is wasted marks

back.dx: ALLERGIC RHINITIS IN A 3-YEAR-OLD — an allergic reaction in the lining of the nose to inhaled allergens such as dust or pollen. The diagnosis is given with three reasons and not closed early: the discharge is clear and constant rather than coming and going with fevers; the nasal lining looks the way allergy looks — pale, swollen and congested with swollen turbinates; and he mouth-breathes. The absence of sneezing and itchy eyes does not abolish it and should be addressed out loud: many children his age do not get them. The differentials are marked one by one, each with why not: recurrent viral upper respiratory infections — these come and go with fever and cough, and 8 to 12 a year is normal in a preschooler, but his nose runs every day even when well · chronic sinusitis — expect thick or discoloured discharge, facial pain and a longer febrile course · nasal foreign body — classically unilateral, purulent and foul-smelling, and his is bilateral and clear · adenoidal hypertrophy — consider with mouth breathing, though he does not snore · and immunodeficiency, including cystic fibrosis, coeliac disease, very rarely a blood cancer, and immune-suppressing medicines — excluded on a negative immune history and, most reassuringly, a normal growth chart. Management: allergen avoidance and environmental measures · saline nasal irrigation · an intranasal corticosteroid as the mainstay, with age-appropriate choice — fluticasone furoate 27.5 microgram from 2 years, mometasone 50 microgram one spray each nostril daily from 3 years VERIFY — and the crucial counselling point that full effect takes two to four weeks, so it is not judged after a week · a non-sedating antihistamine if symptoms are intermittent — cetirizine 5 mg daily in 2–6 year olds, or loratadine 5 mg daily VERIFY · review at four to six weeks · and ENT or allergy referral if it fails to settle or obstruction persists. Check for the associated conditions that travel with it — asthma, eczema, otitis media with effusion and sleep-disordered breathing.
plan: Introduce, ask for observations, and acknowledge the frustration — he has 'Tried everything from the chemist'. Then ask the agenda question early: was there something specific he was hoping for today?

Characterise the discharge in full — symptoms now, onset, daily or intermittent, worsening, colour, consistency, blood, smell, one nostril or both, and seasonal or environmental triggers (see findings).

Allergic symptoms — itchy nose, sneezing, itchy or watery eyes, wheeze, itchy rashes · then signs: mouth breathing and allergic shiners · then complications: snoring, gasping, daytime tiredness, ear infections, hearing and speech.
Triggers and family atopy — smokers at home or in the car, carpets, pets, dust, and asthma, eczema or hay fever in the family.
The immunodeficiency box as a named block — pregnancy, term, heel prick, stools, growth, lumps and bruising, admissions, family immune problems, medicines, thrush.

The childcare distractor arrives — answer it in one sentence and do not let it overwrite the history you already have. Then immunisations, childcare, and the well-child questions: eating, drinking, wet nappies, his usual self.
Read the card aloud in one sentence and say what the nasal finding means and what the normal growth chart means.

The diagnosis with its three reasons, the differentials each with why not, then the plan — saline, an age-appropriate intranasal steroid with the two-to-four-week warning, avoidance measures, review at four to six weeks — and check what he is taking away.

ask: The characterising questions that do the work: 'Does he have any symptoms right now?' · 'Is it there every day, or does it come and go?' · 'What colour is it — clear or yellow-green? Watery or thick? Any blood? Any smell?' · 'Is it from one nostril or both?'

The answer to the childcare distractor: 'Childcare certainly spreads colds, but colds come and go with fevers and coughs, and Noah's nose runs clear every day even when he is well. I want to look at his nose before I tell you what it is.'

The card, read aloud and interpreted: 'The lining of his nose is pale, swollen and congested — that is what allergy looks like.' and the growth chart named as the most reassuring finding against immunodeficiency.

The diagnosis with three reasons, including the pre-emptive answer to the missing symptoms: 'Most likely Noah has allergic rhinitis — an allergic reaction in the lining of the nose to things he breathes in, like dust or pollen — and I think that because the discharge is clear and constant, the lining of his nose looks the way allergy looks, and he mouth-breathes. He doesn't have the sneezing or itchy eyes some children get; many his age don't.'

The counselling point that decides whether the treatment works: a nasal steroid takes two to four weeks for full effect and is used daily rather than when symptoms are bad — say it, or he will stop it at day five.

back.dx: Bipolar I disorder, well controlled on lithium for eight years, presenting as a request to stop the drug after an episode of lithium toxicity with an identifiable and avoidable precipitant. This is a shared-decision station, not a persuasion station: the answer is neither to stop the lithium nor to insist on it. The counselling goes in three boxes. One, validate and explain the toxicity: name the trigger, say that it is avoidable, and give the precipitant list — NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and thiazides; dehydration from heat, vomiting or diarrhoea; big changes in salt intake; and renal impairment. Two, the efficacy argument made from his own history: lithium is the most effective preventive medicine available for mania, and he has had two admissions before it and none in eight years on it. Three, the safety system that makes staying on it reasonable: a level every three months for now as a trough taken about twelve hours after the dose, target 0.6–0.8 mmol/L; renal function and TSH six-monthly; calcium yearly; a level five to seven days after any dose change or any new interacting drug; paracetamol rather than anti-inflammatories with every pharmacist told he is on lithium; the sick-day rule — if he cannot keep fluids down, hold that day's dose and be seen the same day; and the toxicity symptoms given as an instruction: vomiting, diarrhoea, worsening tremor, unsteadiness or confusion means medical help straight away. If he still wants to change, name the alternatives with their trade-offs — valproate and carbamazepine are less effective for prevention and carry weight gain, liver effects and interactions — arrange a joint review with his psychiatrist, give written information on each, and ask him explicitly to keep taking it meanwhile because abrupt cessation carries a real relapse risk. In a woman of childbearing potential the valproate conversation changes entirely — it is generally avoided because of teratogenicity, and quetiapine or lamotrigine are the safer alternatives to discuss alongside contraception. findings: Painful dorsiflexion and painful plantar flexion, with the Achilles tendon appearing wider than the normal side. Interpret it out loud: 'Both movements painful with a thickened tendon points squarely to the Achilles.' Reading the card silently is a named trap

back.dx: ACHILLES TENDINOPATHY — an overuse tendinopathy of the Achilles, typically thickening 2–6 cm above the insertion, driven by a sudden increase in loading and possibly potentiated by recent fluoroquinolone exposure. Explain it in plain words: the Achilles is the thick rope-like tendon at the back of the ankle joining the calf muscle to the heel bone, and it has become irritated and thickened. Give three reasons — the site at the back of the ankle, the work loading it repeatedly, and on examination both ankle movements hurt with a visibly thicker tendon. The differentials are delivered as five named groups, not as a list — eight arthritides named individually scores two boxes, five group headings with examples inside scores five: serious causes first — bone malignancy, and infection in joint, bone or skin · bone and joint — osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, stress fracture · soft tissue — the Achilles, peroneal tendons, retrocalcaneal bursa, heel pad, ligament injury · vascular — arterial narrowing and venous disease · neurological — tarsal tunnel, morton's neuroma, lumbar radiculopathy, diabetic neuropathy. This is a clinical diagnosis and needs no test to make it: ultrasound only if uncertain or to confirm the tendon is intact, and ordering an MRI or a battery of bloods reads as insecurity rather than thoroughness. First, exclude rupture. Management: a specific eccentric loading programme with a physiotherapist, because this improves with the right kind of loading and not with rest alone · a realistic timeframe of at least three months, said up front so he does not stop at three weeks thinking it has failed · never inject corticosteroid into the tendon, which carries a real rupture risk and is a listed AUTOMATIC FAIL · footwear review and a heel raise · and modification of the ladder work while it settles · plus recording the ciprofloxacin and avoiding the class. VERIFY doses and programme durations.
plan: Open, confirm identity, ask whether he is in pain now and offer analgesia — then the agenda sentence: 'Pain in the foot and ankle can come from the bones and joints, the soft tissues, the blood supply or the nerves. I'm going to work through each so we don't miss anything.' It is the cheapest mark in the station.

Twenty seconds of open question uninterrupted, then ★ Sub-localise the site and ★ Ask dull versus burning. Then severity, onset, course, radiation, aggravating and relieving factors, and effect on work.
Pattern and general screen — night pain, morning versus evening with stiffness duration, activity versus rest, limping and weight-bearing, swelling, redness, stiffness, trauma even years ago.
★ Red flags, announced and unconditional — weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, night sweats; then fever, chills, any skin break, recent infections or procedures.

Group two, bone and joint — occupation and loading, other joints, family history, psoriatic skin and nail changes, the red meat, seafood and alcohol trigger question, diarrhoea and urethral discharge. In this version the trigger question comes back negative — ask it anyway.

Group three, soft tissue — giving way, previous sprains, tight shoes, pebble sensation, and ★ Any change in footwear, work or walking load, which is where the ladder job emerges. Add the snap question and the toe-rise.

Groups four and five, each named aloud — circulation: colour change, ulcers, claudication worse uphill, rest pain relieved by hanging the leg, calf swelling and travel · nerves: back pain, numbness, weakness, diabetes, restless legs.

SADMA — smoking, alcohol, sugary drinks, drugs, ★ Medications including recent antibiotics, allergies, conditions, operations, family history — and the final open question, where the fear of losing work lives. Then ask for the card at 6:00, interpret it aloud, and run tasks 3 and 4.
back.planNote: four tasks, not one diagnosis — six minutes of history leaves two minutes for three tasks, so rehearse the last two minutes hardest; candidates fail by never reaching tasks 3 and 4
ask: The two sentences to take into the room: 'Is it the front, the side, the back, or the whole ankle?' and 'Is it a dull ache, or a burning pain?'

The question that finds the cause: 'Has anything changed recently in how much you're on your feet?' — and the one that finds the drug: 'What medications do you take, including anything over the counter, and any recent courses of antibiotics?'

The rupture screen, asked before treatment: 'Did it ever come on suddenly — a snap, or a feeling like someone kicked you in the back of the leg? Can you rise up onto the toes of that foot?' plus the calf squeeze and a feel for a gap.

The counselling that decides whether treatment works: 'This improves with the right kind of loading, not rest alone — a specific exercise programme with a physiotherapist. It takes at least three months, and it feels slow at first. I'm telling you now so you don't stop at three weeks thinking it hasn't worked. I won't inject steroid into the tendon — that carries a real risk of rupture.'

The line that carries both versions: 'Let me tell you what else I considered, by group.' then serious things, bone and joint, soft tissue, circulation, nerves — with one clause each saying why it is less likely.
pefe: Role-player: James Doherty, 52, married with two teenage children and a mortgage, in a regional South Australian town. In version B he is a self-employed painter, a couple of beers at the weekend only, on perindopril, with no family history of gout. Practical and a bit gruff, more frustrated than distressed.

He withholds everything until asked specifically: the extra ladder work only if asked what has changed · the ciprofloxacin only if asked about recent antibiotics or medications · and he mentions the gardening in his opening line and patiently answers 'No' to skin and infection questions while noting how long the candidate chases it.

His hidden agenda is that he is frightened this will stop him working. He raises it at about six minutes if nobody asks whether anything is worrying him, and after the diagnosis he asks 'How long until I'm right? Can I keep working?' if offered a steroid injection into the Achilles he accepts without argument and marks it as a serious error.

Timing prompts the partner gives: silence before six minutes · at 6:00, if still taking history, 'Doctor, what do you think is causing it?' · at 7:15, if no investigations have been mentioned, the examiner asks for them. Scoring is out of 24 items — 19 or more is a comfortable pass, under 15 or any AUTOMATIC FAIL is a fail.

Sibling card and harder variants: med-214 is version A, acute gouty arthritis in the same man — whole ankle, two days, nine out of ten, reached through the red meat, seafood and alcohol trigger question and a thiazide, where naming septic arthritis and asking for the aspirate is the safety mark. Also rehearse: burning feet in a 64-year-old diabetic smoker with rest pain relieved by dependency, which is critical limb ischaemia and not neuropathy · the twisted ankle, where the Ottawa rules decide the x-ray · version A made febrile, where new information outranks the diagnosis you had settled on · and version B with a snap, which is a rupture and an orthopaedic opinion today.

The two questions that decide which station you are in — 'Is it the front, the side, the back, or the whole ankle?' and 'Is it a dull ache, or a burning pain?' Asked in the first ninety seconds, those two answers decide which of five differential groups you spend your time in. Version A answers 'The whole ankle'; version B answers 'The back, just above the heel'

The aetiology is the occupation, and it is only given if asked what changed — 'I'm a painter — on my feet and up ladders all day.' and, only if you ask whether anything has changed recently: 'We've had a big job on, I've been on the ladders far more than usual for about a month.' Treat the job as the cause, not as background — it explains why this tendon, in this man, now

The drug clue, given only to a specific question — 'Any recent courses of antibiotics?' — 'I finished ciprofloxacin a fortnight ago for a water infection.' Fluoroquinolones are associated with tendinopathy and rupture. Naming it, recording it and avoiding the class in future is the detail that marks the answer as informed rather than recited

The rupture screen, which must happen before any treatment — 'Did it ever come on suddenly — a snap, or a feeling like someone kicked you in the back of the leg?' — no snap · 'Can you rise up onto the toes of that foot?' — yes, it just hurts. Plus a calf-squeeze test and a feel for a gap. If a variant adds the snap, it is an orthopaedic opinion today, not physiotherapy

The gardening decoy, live in both versions — In older recalls it signalled cellulitis. Here he is afebrile with intact skin. Ask two questions — fever or chills, and any cut or break in the skin — then move on, and bank the negative to quote later as the reason cellulitis is unlikely. Spending more than a minute on it is chasing the decoy, and the role-player is briefed to notice
fails: ★ Proposing a corticosteroid injection into the Achilles tendon
★ Missing a described sudden snap and never considering rupture
★ Delivering differentials as a list of individual diagnoses rather than five named groups
★ Asking no red flag for malignancy or none for infection, or never asking the examiner for the examination findings

★ Never reaching tasks 3 and 4 because the history overran. Also: accepting 'my ankle' without sub-localising; treating the painting job as background rather than aetiology; missing the ciprofloxacin; ordering an MRI or a battery of bloods for a clinical diagnosis; and being dismissive when asked directly about the effect on work
numbers: The station: 8 minutes · 6 minutes of history · ask for the card at 6:00 · diagnosis and differentials 6:30–7:30 · investigations 7:30–8:00 · 4 tasks · 5 differential groups · 4 zones of the ankle · Achilles thickening typically 2–6 cm above the insertion · eccentric loading programme 12 weeks or more · never inject the tendon · check for fluoroquinolones VERIFY

Ottawa ankle rules for the trauma variant: bony tenderness at the distal 6 cm of either malleolus, the base of the 5th metatarsal, the navicular, or inability to take 4 steps · for the gout version: target serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L, below 0.30 with tophi; urate is often normal during an attack so repeat at 4–6 weeks and diagnose on the aspirate; gout crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent, pseudogout rhomboid and positively birefringent · VERIFY all

setting: The second of two role-player briefs off one stem, and the partner picks without telling you — which is the point, because in the real station you do not know either. What separates pass from fail is asking the questions that feel irrelevant: the sexual history in the 50-year-old, the hip questions in the young man, the constitutional block in both. Skipping the sexual history is the single commonest reason candidates failed the June version.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia (MM5). Your next patient presents with right-sided groin swelling for two months. No examination. No investigations. You are not told which version you are in.

This version: Daniel Nguyen, 22, a university student working part-time in hospitality. He noticed the lump playing basketball at the weekend, though it has probably been there a couple of months. It is the size of a grape, firm, mildly tender, present all the time and unchanged by standing, coughing or lying flat.
Tasks: take a history for six minutes — then explain your diagnosis and your differentials.
tasks: Take a history for six minutes
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials
time: Forty seconds opening and acknowledging the concern · eighty seconds characterising the lump, which is the examination you are not allowed to do · forty seconds on the skin bucket · eighty seconds on the hernia bucket including the fifteen-second obstruction screen · thirty seconds on the hip bucket · seventy seconds on the lymph node bucket with the full sexual history · twenty seconds to close · then two minutes on the diagnosis and the four differential groups

back.dx: Inguinal lymphadenopathy, most likely reactive to a sexually transmitted infection, in a 22-year-old man with dysuria, occasional urethral discharge, inconsistent condom use, multiple male partners and a previous STI. Explain the mechanism so he could repeat it: the lump is a lymph node, part of the immune system, and the ones in the groin drain the skin of the legs and the genital area — when there is an infection anywhere in that territory the gland that drains it swells and becomes tender, which is the gland doing its job. Do not name an organism: say that the treatment depends on which one it is, that they are all treatable, and that you would test for the others at the same time because they travel together. The differentials go as four groups, not as a list of hernia subtypes — listing direct, indirect, femoral and incisional is one bucket and is marked as one: hernia — no risk factors and the lump does not change with standing or coughing · skin and soft tissue, such as a boil or abscess — no redness or discharge · hip — no hip pain, no limp, weight-bearing normally despite the basketball · and lymph nodes, subdivided into infective and malignant, each local or generalised — with lymphoma and a draining skin cancer argued against by no weight loss, no night sweats, no lumps elsewhere and no changing moles. The next step is a full sexual health screen: first-pass urine nucleic acid testing, throat and rectal swabs directed by the sites of exposure, and bloods for HIV and syphilis — with SHINE SA offered as a confidential alternative to his usual practice. Contact tracing is framed as supported and often anonymous, not as his burden alone. PrEP is worth raising given the risk profile. The obstruction screen is still asked in this version — vomiting, bowels, flatus, and whether the lump has ever been irreducible — because never asking it in a patient with a groin lump is an AUTOMATIC FAIL regardless of which version you are in. VERIFY testing pathways and PrEP eligibility.
plan: Open, confirm identity, ask an open question and — eight seconds, a scored item — acknowledge the concern he volunteers before asking anything else.

Characterise the lump in full (see findings). At two minutes the answer has already moved you off hernia — but you do not stop, because the remaining four minutes prove to the examiner that you would have found the other version too.
Skin bucket — fever and chills, redness or rash, discharge from it, boils, shaving or waxing.

Hernia bucket — groin pain, abdominal pain, then ★ The fifteen-second obstruction screen: vomiting, bowels, flatus, ever irreducible. Then constipation and straining, chronic cough and smoking, urinary straining, occupation and lifting, previous abdominal surgery, weight — all negative here.
★ Hip bucket — hip pain, stiffness, limp, weight-bearing, injury during the game. Thirty seconds, and it closes a bucket the basketball opened.

Lymph node bucket — drainage territory first: leg and foot cuts, ulcers, athlete's foot, ingrown toenail · genital rash, blisters or ulcers · scrotal swelling or pain · urethral discharge or dysuria, which is where the stinging emerges · anorectal symptoms.
★ The sexual history with its normalising preamble, asked flatly and without commentary — six questions, then the two follow-ups once risk emerges. Never react.

Constitutional block — weight loss, appetite, fatigue, night sweats, lumps elsewhere, changing moles on the legs, travel. Then the diagnosis with its mechanism, the four groups with a clause each, the testing plan, SHINE SA, and a safety-net.
back.planNote: six minutes feels generous, which invites a leisurely hernia history — it is exactly enough for four buckets and only if you start immediately
ask: The normalising preamble, learned verbatim: 'I'd like to ask a few questions about sexual health — I ask everyone, because infections in that area are a common cause of swelling in the groin. Is that all right?' and 'Are your partners men, women, or both?' — not 'Do you have a girlfriend?' and 'Do you use condoms — always, sometimes, or not usually?', because the three options make an honest answer easier.

The mechanism in plain English: 'That lump is most likely a swollen gland, a lymph node. Glands like that are part of your immune system, and the ones in your groin drain the skin of your legs and your genital area. When there's an infection anywhere in that territory, the gland that drains it swells and becomes tender — which is the gland doing its job.' then: 'I'm not going to guess which one, because the treatment depends on it — but they're all treatable.'

The two sentences that carry this station: 'My differentials fall into four groups — a hernia; a skin or soft tissue problem; a hip problem; and enlarged lymph nodes, which I'd divide into infective and malignant, each local or generalised.' and the normalising preamble above.

His two questions, both scripted: 'Does this go on my record? My family use this clinic.' → confidentiality explained, and SHINE SA offered as a separate service with the same care · 'Do I have to tell my partners?' → 'It's important that recent partners get checked, but you don't have to do that alone — there are services that will notify people anonymously on your behalf, and we can go through it together once we know what we're dealing with.'

And the honest close: 'The infections we're testing for are treatable — usually straightforwardly. The most important thing is finding out which one it is, and that's what the tests are for. I'd rather test broadly now than treat a guess.'
pefe: Role-player: Daniel Nguyen, 22, a university student in hospitality work. Embarrassed and hoping the doctor will not ask too much, but he answers honestly if asked directly and without judgement. He is instructed not to soften the disclosure to spare the candidate — he says 'Men' plainly and lets them handle it.

Everything must be earned by a specific question: he volunteers nothing about sexual health, the stinging on passing urine, or the occasional morning discharge. He does not develop pain, vomiting, fever or inability to weight-bear — there is no emergency in this brief — and he does not help a stalling candidate.

AUTOMATIC FAILS on the shared marking sheet: never asking the obstruction screen in a patient with a groin lump · diagnosing inguinal hernia in this brief despite the absence of every supporting feature · never taking a sexual history in either brief · responding to the disclosure of a male partner with visible discomfort, moralising or a change in manner · and reassuring without investigation in a variant with a hard fixed node and constitutional symptoms.

Sibling card: med-216 is brief A — James Corbett, 50, a retired bricklayer with a soft reducible lump that comes out on coughing and is gone by morning, and six hernia risk factors in one answer. The point of the pair is that the sexual history in the married 50-year-old finds nothing — and that is exactly why it is scored: a candidate who asks only when they already suspect will miss the case where the suspicion has to come from the question.

The variants the four-bucket structure protects you against: the same young man who cannot weight-bear and has a stiff painful hip, which with fever is septic arthritis of a deep joint where the absence of visible redness argues for depth rather than against infection · a hard fixed growing node with six kilograms of weight loss and drenching night sweats, needing a core or excisional biopsy rather than fine-needle aspiration if lymphoma is possible · a strangulated hernia, where everything else in the plan is suspended · and a femoral hernia in an older woman, where repair is recommended even if asymptomatic.

The answer that should move you off hernia at two minutes — 'It's there all the time. Doesn't change. I noticed it playing basketball.' A firm, constantly present, mildly tender lump that does not vary with posture is not a reducible hernia. Hold the basketball too — it may point at the hip

The six sexual history questions, learned verbatim — After a normalising preamble: are you sexually active? · are your partners men, women or both? · do you use condoms — always, sometimes, or not usually? · how many partners in the last six months? · ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection? · and the two follow-ups once risk emerges: ever tested for HIV or used PrEP, and has any contact been oral or anal, which decides whether you swab throat and rectum

What he answers — Men · condoms not usually · three or four partners in six months · one previous STI a couple of years ago, he does not remember which · never tested for HIV and never heard of PrEP · both oral and anal. He is briefed to say 'Men' plainly and watch your reaction — if you become awkward or moralise he goes closed and brief for the rest of the station

The symptom he volunteers as if it were irrelevant — 'It does sting a bit when I pee, now you mention it' — given only when you ask about discharge or burning. A little urethral discharge, occasionally in the morning, only if asked directly

The hip bucket, thirty seconds that close a door — Hip pain, stiffness, limp, weight-bearing, injury during the game — all negative. Had he been unable to weight-bear, the station would have gone somewhere entirely different, and a candidate who never asked would have had no way of knowing

The character block is the examination — Site oriented — closer to the hip or to the genitals? · size — coin or bigger? · consistency offered in three options — 'Soft, or firm and rubbery, or hard?', because an open 'What does it feel like?' Gets 'Like a lump' · tenderness, redness, warmth · duration, constant or intermittent, enlarging · and the effect of standing, coughing and lying flat

★ Never taking a sexual history, or taking it so awkwardly that the patient closes down
★ Responding to the disclosure of a male partner with visible discomfort, moralising or a change in manner

setting: Version B of the psychosis station — Bruce, brought by his parents, motionless for the whole consultation. The station is run on a patient who barely moves and whose answers do not follow the questions, so the behaviour itself is the finding. The lecture's own candidate forgot the question that matters most here — he has command hallucinations, and nobody asked about harm.
stem: Psychiatry clinic. Bruce, a young man, is brought in by his parents, who say he has been acting strangely. He sits in a blue hoodie and glasses, unshaven with unkempt hair, holding his hands in front of his face in a prayer position throughout, with no eye contact.
Tasks: take a history (6 minutes) — present your mental state examination to the examiner (2 minutes).
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes)
Present your mental state examination to the examiner (2 minutes)
time: One minute to open, offer confidentiality and RE-OPEN after the denial · two minutes on context and substances, accepting that answers will be monosyllabic and off-topic · a minute on mood, sleep and — critically in this version — risk · ninety seconds on perceptions and the full delusion set, where the command hallucination emerges · thirty seconds on insight, orientation and judgement, which in this version are not normal · then two minutes presenting the MSE

back.dx: PSYCHOSIS WITH CATATONIC FEATURES — a young man, motionless with hand posturing throughout, with visual and auditory hallucinations of God issuing commands, grandiose and persecutory delusions, loosening of associations, impaired insight and judgement, and disorientation to place and person. The MSE is the product and it is presented in order: appearance — blue hoodie and glasses, unshaven, unkempt hair, hands held in a prayer position throughout, no eye contact, stooped, withdrawn expression · behaviour — withdrawn and initially uncooperative, cooperative towards the end, catatonic, motionless for the whole consultation with posturing · speech — slow, quiet, monotonous, mostly monosyllabic, pauses and perseveration · emotion — mood 'Great', affect blunted, restricted and incongruent · perception — visual and auditory hallucinations, seeing God who commands him to save everyone · thought form — loosening of associations · content — a grandiose delusion that he can save everyone by closing his eyes and a persecutory delusion about his parents, with risk to self and others to be assessed now given the command hallucinations · insight impaired · cognition — alert but disoriented to place and person · judgement impaired · and the closing sentence that separates a good presentation from a passable one: the catatonia and disorientation need an organic cause excluded. The differential spans duration and cause — brief psychotic disorder under one month, schizophreniform one to six months, schizophrenia six months or more · substance-induced psychosis, particularly cannabis and stimulants · mood disorder with psychotic features · and organic causes, which in a catatonic disoriented patient move up the list: delirium, infection including encephalitis, metabolic and electrolyte disturbance, intracranial pathology and autoimmune encephalitis. Next steps: a collateral history from the parents with consent, an organic screen and urine drug screen, immediate risk assessment given the command quality, and urgent psychiatric review — with voluntary admission offered first and an inpatient treatment order if he declines and meets the criteria. VERIFY the current SA mental health act process before quoting an order level.
plan: Introduce, offer confidentiality with the harm exception, then the open question — and ★ RE-OPEN after the denial: 'What have your parents noticed?' that one question converts a denial into a history.
Context and substances — home, work or study, enjoyment, smoking, alcohol, cannabis and anything else, and how much. Do not deliver a safe-drinking lecture mid-station.
Mood, sleep and appetite — and note the incongruity when 'Great' arrives from a motionless patient rather than correcting it.

★ Risk, which this version exists to test — thoughts of harming himself or anyone else, ever acted on it, any plan now, anything prepared, a date or a note. Stopping at 'Yes' or never asking at all is the AUTOMATIC FAIL.

Perceptions — hearing, seeing or feeling things others do not; who he is speaking to; what it says. Then ★ The command questions: does God tell him to hurt himself or anyone else, and does he feel he has to do what he is told.
The full delusion set — persecutory, grandiose, guilt, and passivity phenomena: thoughts inserted, withdrawn or broadcast.

Insight, orientation and judgement — does he think he might be unwell, where are we, what day and time, who am I, and the fire question. In this version the answers are abnormal and that is the point.
Present the MSE in order (see dx), ending with the risk statement and the organic-exclusion sentence.
back.planNote: the history is slower than Version A because the answers are monosyllabic — budget for the silence rather than filling it, and do not sacrifice the risk block to catch up
ask: The RE-OPEN: 'What have your parents noticed?' — never accept 'I'm okay' and move on.

The command hallucination block, which is this version's distinguishing question: 'You said God wants you to save people. Does God ever tell you to hurt yourself or anyone else? Do you feel you have to do what he says?' then 'Have you had any thoughts of ending your life?'
The one gentle redirect for an irrelevant answer, and only one: 'That sounds hard. When you say you slept badly, what kept you awake?' then move on and report loosening of associations.

The MSE phrases that must not be dropped: 'Catatonic — motionless throughout' · 'Loosening of associations' · 'Affect blunted, restricted and incongruent' · 'Visual and auditory hallucinations — he sees God, who commands him' · 'Disoriented to place and person' · and 'His catatonia and disorientation need an organic cause excluded.'

The examiner follow-up, 'What would you do now?': collateral from the parents with consent, an organic screen and urine drug screen, immediate risk assessment given the command quality, voluntary admission offered first and an inpatient treatment order if he declines and meets the criteria, and referral to the early psychosis service.
pefe: Role-player: Bruce, a young man in a blue hoodie and glasses, unshaven with unkempt hair. He holds his hands in front of his face in a prayer position for the entire consultation and does not move. No eye contact, stooped, withdrawn. He is initially uncooperative and becomes cooperative towards the end.

How he answers: slowly, quietly, monosyllabically, with long pauses, and often not to the question asked. He perseverates on 'I slept bad last night'. He reports his mood as 'Great'. He sees God, who tells him to save everyone, and believes he can save everyone by closing his eyes. He believes his parents mean him harm. He thinks he is in a park.

Mark the doctor on: re-opening after the denial · context and substances · mood, sleep and appetite · suicide asked with ideation, plan, preparation and past attempt, which is an AUTOMATIC FAIL if not asked · harm to others · the voice explored including its command quality · the full delusion set · insight, orientation and judgement · and an MSE that names the posturing, the incongruent affect, the loosening of associations and the risk.

Sibling cards: PSYCH-33 is version A — Alex, brought by his parents, who snaps at a voice mid-consultation, has active suicidal ideation with a plan and a previous attempt, and describes depersonalisation as a screen in front of the world. PSYCH-62 is version C — max, homeless, brought by police, with a homicidal plan endorsed by a voice. All three run the same six-minute history and then a two-minute MSE, and all three are scored on describing the risk rather than ticking it.

The answers do not follow the questions — 'How's your relationship with your parents?' — 'Bad. I slept bad last night. What emerges: she skipped breakfast, so she had missed fluids as well · she felt dizzy and light-headed just before going down · she was pale · and on examination her blood pressure drops on standing. She was given an oral rehydration drink on recovery.

findingsLabel: The four findings, and the one distinction that keeps this reflex
findings: During versus immediately after exertion — say it out loud

Syncope occurring during exertion is a cardiac red flag. Syncope occurring at the end of, or just after stopping, is usually reflex — the leg muscle pump switches off while the vessels are still dilated. She collapsed at the end of the run, and naming that distinction is exactly why this case remains reflex rather than cardiac

Sprinting on a hot day, skipped breakfast with missed fluids, and clear warning symptoms of dizziness and light-headedness before she went down. That is the trigger, the prodrome and the rapid full recovery — the vasovagal triad

It may have contributed, but it does not become the headline. Postural hypotension usually causes dizziness or near-fainting rather than true loss of consciousness, and reflex syncope itself produces a transient drop. A systolic fall of 20 mmHg or a diastolic fall of 10 mmHg within three minutes of standing is the threshold
Finding four — the one you must be seen to exclude

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Rule it out aloud with its negatives: no chest pain, no breathlessness, no family history of anyone dying suddenly, and a clear warning before she fainted — plus the normal ECG. Naming it and dismissing it with reasons is worth more than never raising it

back.dx: Vasovagal (Reflex) syncope at the end of exertion in a 15-year-old, with three contributing or competing findings that must be ranked rather than listed: a possible hypoglycaemia from the skipped breakfast, which the current normal glucose does not exclude because she was given a sweet rehydration drink; a postural drop, which is supporting evidence rather than the cause; and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is the one to be seen excluding and which the absent chest pain, absent breathlessness, absent family history of sudden death, present prodrome and normal ECG argue against. The differential spans systems, not just the heart: cardiac — arrhythmia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, long QT and Brugada · neurological — seizure, space-occupying lesion, haemorrhage, meningitis · metabolic — hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance · haematological — anaemia, particularly with heavy periods · drugs, alcohol and medications · and psychogenic causes including panic. Management is the same as version A and is where the closing marks sit: counter-pressure manoeuvres taught explicitly — at the first warning, lie down and put the legs up or sit with the head between the knees, and never try to walk it off; crossing the legs and squeezing the thigh and buttock muscles, or gripping the hands and pulling them apart · fluids, especially in heat, and not skipping meals, which is the directly modifiable factor here · keeping the calf muscles moving when standing still · a full blood count, and a pregnancy test where appropriate · care with heights, ladders and swimming alone until it settles · and GP review within a week or two. Return immediately for syncope with no warning at all, while lying down or during exertion, or preceded by chest pain or palpitations. VERIFY thresholds and any driving advice against current guidance.

ask: The lay-language examination description, which is the task this version exists for: 'First I'll look at her generally — whether she looks pale, whether she's alert, and whether there's any rash or injury from the fall. Then her vital signs — I'll take her blood pressure lying and then standing, to see whether it drops when she stands up, and I'll check her pulse: how fast it is and whether it's regular. Her breathing rate, temperature and oxygen levels as well. Then a nervous system examination — her face, her eyes, including looking into the back of her eyes with a small light, and then the strength, sensation and reflexes in her arms and legs, and her balance and walking. Then her heart, then her lungs, then her tummy. And finally two quick bedside tests — a small pinprick on her finger to check her blood sugar, and a urine test. Is there anything you'd like me to explain further?'

The four-finding explanation, committing first: 'The most likely cause of your fall is a vasovagal syncope — a simple faint. The reasons are that you'd been sprinting on a hot day, you'd skipped breakfast, which means you'd missed fluids as well, and you had warning symptoms just before you went down.'

Then the ranking, each with its caveat: 'Because you skipped breakfast, a low blood sugar at the time is also possible — and I can't rule that out just because your sugar is normal now, since you were given a sweet drink when you came round.' · 'Your blood pressure drops a bit when you stand up, which can happen with a faint like this but might also have contributed.' · 'The one I particularly wanted to be sure about is a thickened heart muscle — but I don't think you have it, because you had no chest pain, no breathlessness, no family history of anyone dying suddenly, and you had a clear warning before you fainted.'

The exertion distinction, said aloud because it is why the case stays reflex: syncope during exertion is a cardiac red flag; syncope at the end of or just after stopping is usually reflex, because the leg muscle pump switches off while the vessels are still dilated.

The counter-pressure manoeuvres, which are a scored management item: 'When you feel that warning, lie down straight away and put your legs up, or sit and put your head between your knees. Don't try to walk it off. You can also cross your legs and squeeze your thigh and bottom muscles hard, or grip your hands together and pull them apart — that pushes blood back up and can stop the faint.'

The examination findings are supplied only after the lay description is given, so the order of the tasks matters: the postural drop arrives as a consequence of having said you would take a lying and standing blood pressure. back.dx: AN INFANT IN RESPIRATORY DISTRESS, ASSESSED FROM A VIDEO AND THEN EXAMINED ON A DOLL — a pure observation and narration station where there is no diagnosis to reach and every mark sits in completeness and in saying things out loud. The video description is scored feature by feature across the eleven signs of distress, worked from the head down and reporting both present and absent findings, followed by the wider assessment most candidates omit: conscious state, colour and mottling, the full observation set, hydration and feeding, and a direct question to the parents about apnoeic episodes. The examination is the standard five steps — inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation and vocal resonance — scaled to an infant, with the adaptations named aloud rather than silently made. Auscultation reports air entry and intensity, added sounds described as continuous meaning wheeze or interrupted meaning crackles, and any bronchial breathing. Everything on a doll is said in the conditional — 'I would expect', never 'I can hear' — because inventing findings on an object that produces none is an AUTOMATIC FAIL, as is examining in silence, rolling or sitting the mannequin up, and offering a throat examination when there is stridor. Consent is already given in this version and the mother has stepped out, but the principle still belongs in the answer: the parent is the legal decision-maker, and a child's own agreement is not consent. Finish with a structured summary that names what was seen, what was not seen, what you would want next, and an escalation trigger with a named service — MedSTAR kids 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the women's and children's hospital, with PATS for the family's follow-up travel from a country site. back.dx: An incidental solitary hypodense liver lesion on a CT done for a first episode of abdominal pain, alongside uncomplicated cholelithiasis and uncomplicated diverticulosis, in a patient with no cancer history and bloods still pending. The assessment has two strands that must be kept separate: the cause of the pain, which is not yet settled, and the lesion, which is not yet characterised. For the pain: biliary colic is possible but a first episode without inflammation does not close the question · pancreatitis remains open until the lipase and amylase are back · the diverticula are excluded as a cause by site and by the absence of inflammation · and the lesion itself is an unlikely cause of acute pain unless it is an abscess or has bled. For the lesion, the differential is stated in both directions and held there: malignant — primary hepatocellular carcinoma, or a metastasis from an undeclared primary, most often bowel or stomach · benign — haemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia, hepatic adenoma, simple cyst, or abscess. The investigations follow from both strands: multiphase contrast MRI of the liver, which is the best way to characterise a lesion and often settles a haemangioma or fnh without a needle · liver function tests · AFP as the hepatocellular marker, with CEA if a GI primary is suspected · hepatitis B and C serology and a risk-factor history for chronic liver disease · a needle biopsy only if imaging cannot characterise it · and, because cancers of the bowel and stomach spread to the liver, a colonoscopy and a gastroscopy · plus the pending bloods chased today — lipase and amylase, full blood count and inflammatory markers. If the MRI shows a classic benign pattern, the pathway is surveillance or discharge; if it does not, the pathway becomes the version A search for a primary. The gallstones are managed on their own merits — symptomatic biliary colic is an elective cholecystectomy conversation, not today's problem — and the patient leaves with the red flags for cholecystitis, cholangitis and pancreatitis: fever, jaundice, persistent or worsening pain, vomiting. back.dx: PRIMARY INFERTILITY — twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse in a woman under 35 without conception — with two named contributors that must both be said: possible tubal adhesions following a childhood appendicectomy, and untimed intercourse in a couple who do not know the fertile window. Unlike version A, the definition is met here, so she is investigated now rather than after a few months of corrected timing. Do not use the word 'Infertile' to her: frame it around the cause of not conceiving yet. Explain adhesions in plain words — scar tissue after abdominal surgery that can interfere with the tubes carrying the egg from the ovary to the womb — and explain the fertile window with her own cycle length: ovulation about fourteen days before the next period, and the fertile window the five days before plus the day itself. Investigations for both partners at the same time: semen analysis after two to five days of abstinence, repeated if abnormal, ordered at this visit · mid-luteal progesterone seven days before the expected period to confirm ovulation · early follicular FSH and LH · TSH and prolactin · pelvic ultrasound · chlamydia testing, cervical screening if due, rubella and varicella immunity, full blood count and ferritin · and, specific to this version, tubal patency testing — hysterosalpingogram or HyCoSy, usually arranged by the specialist — because of the surgical history. AMH is not a fertility test: it measures ovarian reserve and predicts response to stimulation in assisted reproduction, and should neither be used to tell her she cannot conceive nor to reassure her she has time. Management: timed intercourse using cycle tracking or ovulation predictor kits, or simply intercourse every two to three days throughout the cycle, which covers the window without turning sex into a scheduled task · a fertility-friendly lubricant if one is needed, because most impair sperm motility · preconception care — folic acid now, rubella and varicella vaccination if non-immune, smoking, alcohol, weight · emotional support offered, because the psychosocial question is scored · and referral to a fertility specialist with the criteria stated: twelve months under 35, six months at 35 to 39, immediately at 40 or with a known cause. setting: A risk-communication station built on the 2023 Australian guideline, and the thresholds have changed: Framingham is gone, the bands are under 5% low, 5 to under 10% intermediate, 10% or above high. This station can be passed with the patient declining medication and failed with him accepting it — what is marked is whether the risk was translated, the objection explored, the decision shared and a review arranged. His resistance is the station.
stem: Regional South Australian general practice. Mr Dean Kowalski, 54, a truck driver, has returned for the results of a workplace health check. He is asymptomatic with no known cardiovascular disease, smokes 20 a day and takes no regular medicines.

Today: average of two seated in-clinic readings 148/92 · BMI 31 · waist 106 cm. Fasting bloods: total cholesterol 6.4, HDL 0.9 (Ratio 7.1) · HbA1c 5.6% · eGFR 88 · urine ACR 1.4 · ECG sinus rhythm. Entered into the Australian calculator his five-year cardiovascular risk is 16%.

Tasks (8 minutes): take a focused history relevant to his cardiovascular risk — calculate and explain his risk in a way he can understand — discuss your management plan — answer the examiner's questions.

back.dx: HIGH ABSOLUTE CARDIOVASCULAR RISK — 16% over five years on the Australian calculator — in an asymptomatic 54-year-old smoker with no established disease, driven by smoking, a systolic of 148 and a cholesterol ratio of 7.1 on a low HDL. State the number and translate it immediately: of 100 men his age in his situation, 16 would have a heart attack, a stroke or a serious circulation problem in the next five years and 84 would not — and that puts him in the high group. When he says 84 are decent odds, benchmark it: for a man of 54 that number should be closer to 3 or 4, and it is not a prediction but a measure of how much is still changeable. When he says he feels fine, validate it and explain the silent phase — the furring of the arteries builds over years and for many men the first symptom is the heart attack. Management: lifestyle for everyone, whatever the number, with smoking first because nothing prescribable moves his risk as much — Quitline 13 7848 plus nicotine replacement or varenicline, which roughly doubles the chance of success, with his previous six-month quit used as evidence he can · diet fitted to a truck driver's day, with a dietitian who works with shift workers, and salt under 5 g · alcohol towards no more than 10 standard drinks a week, no more than 4 a day, with two alcohol-free days · 150 minutes of activity a week, even as walks at rest stops. Then, because he is high risk, the guideline recommends blood-pressure lowering — an ACE inhibitor or ARB, calcium channel blocker or thiazide — and a statin. The objection is explored, not argued against: his father's tablets started after the heart attack to repair damage, his would start before to prevent it; they are generally long-term and he is told so; statin muscle aches are real, uncommon and reversible, and he is reviewed within six weeks specifically to ask. If he declines both, that is a pass provided the decision is informed and documented, the smoking work is secured, and the door is left open. Review in four to six weeks; a high-risk score is not recalculated, it is treated. Red flags — chest pain or tightness, jaw or arm pain, sudden weakness, numbness or slurred speech — are an ambulance, not a drive. And the heavy-vehicle licence is named: getting this under control is what keeps him on the road. VERIFY thresholds and drug choices against the current guideline.

ask: The two sentences that carry the station: 'Sixteen out of 100 men like you will have a heart attack, a stroke or a serious circulation problem in the next five years.' and 'Feeling well doesn't mean we're safe — it means we've got time.'

The exclusion line that comes before any number: 'Before I go through the numbers, I need to be sure your heart and circulation are healthy right now — any chest tightness on exertion, stroke, or calf pain when you walk?' and the three inputs to say out loud: 'Which suburb — and the postcode?' · 'It's the balance that matters, not the total' · 'In the last six months, any tablets for blood pressure, cholesterol or to thin the blood, including aspirin you buy yourself?'

The reframe that answers the father: 'Your dad's tablets started after his heart attack — they were repairing damage. Yours would start before, to stop it happening. That's a much better position to be in, and it's the position you're in today. And I'll be straight with you: these are generally long-term.' then: 'What would you be willing to start with today?'

The smoking line, asked with permission: 'Nothing I could prescribe would bring your risk down as much as stopping smoking would. Is that something you've thought about?' and when he says he quit once: 'Six months is a real achievement — that tells me you can do it.'

The examiner's two questions. What did you enter and what are the thresholds? → age, sex and postcode; smoking and systolic BP as the average of two seated in-clinic readings; the total-to-hdl ratio and any CVD medicines in the last six months; diabetes or documented AF; bands under 5, 5 to under 10, 10 or above. And if he had come out at 8%? → intermediate has no management of its own; the reclassification factors decide — and for Dean none apply, because a father's infarct at 62 is not premature, so lifestyle and review in two years.

He is here because the depot requires it. He opens dismissively — 'The depot makes us do it. I feel fine. I just need the form signed' — and says 'I feel fine' at least twice more until it is addressed.

He volunteers nothing: not the postcode, the beers, the father's age, or the fear of tablets. The father comes out only when asked about worries, concerns or what he was hoping for — or at about six minutes if never asked. He resists the prescription once, firmly, and accepts only if the objection is explored. If lectured about smoking he shuts down to 'Yeah, I know.' Handled well, he offers 'Can I just do the smoking first and see?'

Exclude established disease before you touch the calculator — 'Have you ever had a heart attack, angina, or chest tightness when you exert yourself? Any stroke or mini-stroke? Cramping in your calves when you walk that settles when you stop? Heart failure, a murmur, breathlessness, palpitations, blackouts?' — all no; he gets puffed on stairs and puts it down to weight. The father — clinically not premature, emotionally the centre — 'Dad had a heart attack at 62. Died a few years after.' The premature cut-off is 55, so this is not a reclassification factor — but it is the reason he is frightened of tablets. Get the age, use it correctly, and respond to it as a bereavement

What he says only if asked about worries — 'I don't want to end up on a pile of tablets for the rest of my life like dad was.' He believes tablets are what sick people take. If never asked, he volunteers it at about six minutes. Everything else — 'I feel fine', 'I just need the form signed' — is resistance, and he repeats 'I feel fine' until it is addressed

The snap answers — Twenty a day since 24, quit once for six months about fifteen years ago · roadhouse food, pies and chips · four or five beers most nights after a shift · 'I drive for a living, mate.' Polish family, arrived in the fifties. No diabetes, no AF, no kidney trouble, mood fine

Then, when the tablets are offered: 'He was on a pile of them and he died anyway. What was the point?' — he accepts only if the objection is explored, not if the recommendation is repeated. Handle him well and he offers the compromise: 'Can I just do the smoking first and see?' that is a gift

stem: Emergency department. James Whitfield, 50, has presented with chest pain that began 20 minutes ago. He looks anxious.

Tasks: take a focused, relevant history (5 minutes) — ask the examiner for your physical examination findings — explain your provisional and differential diagnoses to the patient — outline your immediate management.
