Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
Explain your provisional and differential diagnoses to the patient
Outline your immediate management
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Ask for the vitals FIRST — and name oxygen saturation

‘Blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature, and OXYGEN SATURATION.’ SpO2 is the one most often left off and it directly changes management. Add RADIO-RADIAL DELAY and BP IN BOTH ARMS for dissection
RESPIRATORY DISTRESS · CYANOSIS · PALLOR (the MI patient may look pale and grey) · LEVEL OF CONSCIOUSNESS, alert or drowsy. NOT ‘is he in pain’ — you already know that
Cardiovascular — EXPAND it, do not reduce it to ‘S1, S2, any murmurs’

INSPECTION: raised JVP? visible apex? PALPATION: displaced apex? parasternal heave? AUSCULTATION: S1 and S2 normal? murmurs? ADDED SOUNDS — and when the examiner asks WHICH added sound, the answer is ‘A PERICARDIAL FRICTION RUB, FOR PERICARDITIS’
‘Is air entry equal bilaterally, and are there any added sounds?’ Keep it brief; you have several respiratory differentials but the marks are elsewhere
Chest wall and skin — KEPT SEPARATE ON PURPOSE
‘Any RASH on the chest? Any TENDERNESS on palpation of the chest wall?’ Keeping this out of the cardiovascular block makes it explicit that you are testing the MSK and shingles differentials

‘Any tenderness? Any masses — SPECIFICALLY HEPATOMEGALY?’ (expect ‘which mass?’ — the answer is the LIVER). Then ‘any oedema, any DIFFERENCE IN CALF SIZE, any calf tenderness?’ — the DVT screen feeding back to PE
THE ECG — every chest pain patient gets one, and read it IN ORDER
RATE → RHYTHM → AXIS → P WAVES → PR → QRS → ST/T. RATE AND RHYTHM BEFORE ST SEGMENTS, because the commonest exam disaster is an SVT at 180 reported as an MI
THE CARD in the anchor case

2 mm ST ELEVATION IN II, III AND aVF with RECIPROCAL ST DEPRESSION IN I AND aVL = ACUTE INFERIOR STEMI. Then ask for RIGHT-SIDED LEADS, PARTICULARLY V4R — because RV involvement changes whether you can safely give nitrates
Signs and what each should make you say

RADIO-RADIAL DELAY or BP differential → DISSECTION · FRICTION RUB → pericarditis · HYPER-RESONANCE with absent breath sounds → pneumothorax, and if hypotensive with tracheal deviation, TENSION — DECOMPRESS BEFORE IMAGING · RAISED JVP + CLEAR LUNGS + HYPOTENSION → RV infarction, tamponade or massive PE, and DO NOT GIVE NITRATES · ejection systolic murmur to the carotids with a slow-rising pulse → aortic stenosis · unilateral calf swelling → DVT then PE · dermatomal vesicular rash → zoster

TROPONIN (serial, on a 0/1-h or 0/3-h pathway) · FBC — DO NOT SKIP IT, it is the test that catches the ANAEMIA-INDUCED ANGINA case · UEC, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, TFTs · CXR · D-dimer ONLY if pre-test probability is low · CTPA or CT AORTOGRAM — chosen by the history, they answer different questions · ECHO for wall motion, effusion, valve lesion, RV strain

dx: **Chest pain stations should be easy passes. Candidates fail them THREE WAYS: differentials bunched into one system, SICORA left half-finished, and cardiovascular risk factors forgotten.** Fix those three and the case is yours.

**TIER 1 — LIFE-THREATENING, and they go FIRST. Mnemonic MPAP**: **M**yocardial infarction / ACS · **P**ericarditis (± myocarditis, ± tamponade) · **A**ortic dissection · the two respiratory P's — **P**neumothorax and **P**ulmonary embolism. **Add OESOPHAGEAL RUPTURE (Boerhaave) as the sixth.** **If the examiner's mark sheet lists five or six differentials, there is a high chance ALL of them come from this group.**

**TIER 2 — FIVE SYSTEMS, and choose differentials that GENERATE A NEW QUESTION. A differential that adds no question adds nothing.** **CVS**: angina, heart failure (gives you orthopnoea, PND, oedema), **aortic stenosis (gives you EXERTIONAL SYNCOPE)**. **RESP**: pneumonia (fever, cough, sputum), **lung malignancy (the red-flag block)**. **GI**: **GORD (acid brash and water brash — questions nobody else asks)**, peptic ulcer, biliary, pancreatitis, oesophageal spasm. **MSK/SKIN**: costochondritis and **shingles — two questions cover the group.** **PSYCH**: panic — **legitimate, but ALWAYS LAST.**

**SICORA, not SOCRATES — and the structural reason matters**: in SICORA **associated symptoms do not come up early**, which keeps them where they belong, **in step 3, doing the work of ruling differentials in and out.**

**THE FOUR ALLEVIATING/AGGRAVATING PROBES — the most diagnostically productive part of SICORA, and about 95% of role-players answer ‘I don't know’ to the general question because they are told not to volunteer**: **(1) EXERTION AND REST — ‘worse with activity, better with rest?’ AND ‘do you get any pain AT REST?’** · **(2) POSITION — ‘better leaning forward?’ (pericarditis)** · **(3) BREATHING — ‘worse on a deep breath?’ (pleuritic)** · **(4) FOOD — ‘any relationship to eating?’ (GORD, ulcer, biliary).**

**THE ENTIRE PURPOSE of characterising the pain is to reach ONE FORK: TYPICAL or ATYPICAL. If you finish SICORA and cannot say which, you have not done SICORA — you have asked six questions.** **TYPICAL: central, an AREA not a point, crushing/heavy/tight, radiates to jaw, neck, left or both arms, worse on exertion and relieved by rest, minutes to a couple of hours, with sweating, nausea and breathlessness.** **ATYPICAL: a single finger-point, sharp or burning, pleuritic, reproduced by movement or palpation, lasting seconds or continuous for days.**
**LEVINE'S SIGN — a patient with genuine ischaemic pain rarely puts one fingertip on a spot. They put a CLOSED FIST over the centre of the chest.** Worth naming when you summarise.

**THE KEY POINT OF THE ENTIRE CLUSTER — CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS, ASKED EARLY, INSIDE THE CVS BLOCK, IN EVERY CHEST PAIN CASE — INCLUDING THE ONES THAT TURN OUT TO BE REFLUX, because at the time you ask you don't yet know.** **Six**: **family history of MI or STROKE (premature = male under 55, female under 65)** · **diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol NAMED SPECIFICALLY** · **smoking with pack-years** · **alcohol in standard drinks** · **weight.** **A generic ‘any past medical history?’ at the end scores nothing, because it shows you don't know WHY those questions exist.**

**THE ANAEMIA TWIST, and it is a known AMC case**: **black tarry stools from an occult GI bleed → anaemia → reduced oxygen-carrying capacity UNMASKS fixed coronary disease → angina.** **That is why ‘any black, tarry motions?’ sits inside your ACS block, and why FBC is not an optional blood test.** Same logic covers **thyrotoxicosis, tachyarrhythmia, sepsis, hypoxia and severe aortic stenosis — type 2 MI.**

**THE MONA TRAP — read the task.** In an OSCE **history-taking** station, opening with cannulas, oxygen and MONA burns 90 seconds and examiners have cut candidates off mid-request. **A brief haemodynamic-stability statement ticks the safety box; anything more is over-doing it.** **And it is clinically wrong too: give a nitrate in an inferior MI with RV infarction and you drop preload in a preload-dependent ventricle.** **Inferior ST elevation → right-sided leads (V4R) → WITHHOLD NITRATES if RV infarction.**
plan: **Ask for the vital signs INCLUDING SATURATION**, make **ONE** haemodynamic-stability statement, then **WIPE and an open-ended question.** **Online format: make it a CLOSED STATEMENT to the patient — ‘I'll check your vital signs to make sure you're stable, then we'll proceed’ — and do not wait for numbers.**

**ONE memorised empathy sentence, then let it go.** **‘I can see this has frightened you. That's completely understandable. Let me ask some focused questions so I can work out what's causing it and get you the right treatment.’** **Empathy is a BOX, not a THEME — candidates who sprinkle it through every answer run out of clock.**

**SICORA — START IT, FINISH IT, DO NOT INTERLEAVE.** **S**: ‘show me where’ + **‘one point, or an area?’** · **I**: one to ten · **Q**: **offer options** — sharp, crushing, or something else · **O**: when, constant or intermittent, **getting worse** · **R**: does it travel · **A**: general question, **then all four probes.**
**Make the call out loud in your head: TYPICAL or ATYPICAL.** Then **work every system anyway.**

**CVS block.** Associated symptoms — **breathlessness, nausea, sweating, palpitations** — then **‘any black, tarry bowel motions?’** — then **THE SIX RISK FACTORS.** Then **pericarditis (fever, recent viral illness), heart failure (orthopnoea, pillows, PND, ankle oedema), aortic stenosis (exertional syncope), and dissection (‘was it at its absolute WORST from the very first second?’, ‘does it go through to your back between the shoulder blades?’).**

**RESPIRATORY — the two P's first.** PE: **calf swelling or pain · recent long-haul travel or immobility · personal or family clotting history.** Pneumothorax: **chest trauma.** Pneumonia: **fever, cough, sputum, noisy breathing.** Malignancy: **weight loss, appetite, lumps, HAEMOPTYSIS.**

**GI.** General: tummy pain, vomiting. **GORD — the two questions that win the case: ACID BRASH (‘an acidic or bitter taste in your mouth’) and WATER BRASH (‘a sudden rush of saliva filling your mouth when you're not eating’).** Peptic ulcer: **related to food**, NSAIDs, aspirin. Biliary and pancreatitis if the story fits.

**MSK and SKIN — two questions cover the group**: **‘Any rash on your chest?’** and **‘Is the pain worse when you move, or when you press on your chest?’** **Shingles pain PRECEDES the rash, so a negative rash question does not exclude it — ask about a BURNING BAND of skin hypersensitivity.**

**PSYCH, last**: **‘Any stressors at home or work? How has your mood been?’** **Never tell a patient they have had a panic attack before PE and MI are excluded.** Then **closure: ALLERGIES BEFORE YOU PROPOSE ASPIRIN, medications, occupation and driving.**

**The examination request in structure → the ECG read in order → diagnosis in plain language with the fear acknowledged → differentials across FIVE SYSTEMS → immediate management with the reperfusion clock.**
pefe: **Explaining a STEMI in plain language**: **‘Your heart is a muscle, and like any muscle it needs its own blood supply through small pipes called coronary arteries. One of those pipes has become blocked by a clot, so part of your heart muscle isn't getting oxygen. That's what we call a heart attack, and your tracing confirms it. The good news is we've caught it very early, we have excellent treatments to open that artery back up, and you're in exactly the right place.’**

**Answering ‘am I going to die, like my dad?’**: **‘That fear makes complete sense, and I'm not going to dismiss it. Treatment now is very different from what was available to your father. You came in within half an hour, which is the single most important thing. Our whole focus in the next hour is opening that artery, and the sooner we do it the more heart muscle we save. I'll stay with you through it.’**

**IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT of a STEMI** VERIFY : **resuscitation area, continuous cardiac monitoring, defibrillator available, senior help now** · **ABC, IV access ×2, OXYGEN ONLY IF SATURATIONS FALL BELOW 92–94% — routine oxygen in a normoxic patient is not beneficial** · **ASPIRIN 300 mg CHEWED plus a second antiplatelet per local protocol** · **IV morphine titrated with an antiemetic; NITRATE ONLY AFTER V4R EXCLUDES RV INFARCTION and if not hypotensive** · **REPERFUSION: primary PCI if deliverable within 120 MINUTES of first medical contact, otherwise thrombolysis after screening contraindications** · bloods and serial ECGs.

**INFARCT TERRITORIES**: **INFERIOR — II, III, aVF, usually RCA → DO V4R, no nitrates if RV infarct, watch for bradyarrhythmia and heart block** · **ANTEROSEPTAL — V1–V4, LAD, largest territory, highest risk of cardiogenic shock** · **LATERAL — I, aVL, V5, V6** · **POSTERIOR — TALL R WITH ST DEPRESSION V1–V3, do posterior leads V7–V9, the ‘mirror image’ trap.**

**EIGHT ECG PATTERNS worth recognising instantly**: STEMI · NSTEACS (dynamic ST depression or T inversion in a coronary distribution) · **pericarditis — WIDESPREAD CONCAVE ‘saddle’ elevation with PR DEPRESSION, PR ELEVATION IN aVR, and NO reciprocal change** · **PE — sinus tachycardia is commonest by far; S1Q3T3, right axis, RBBB, T inversion V1–V4** · **SVT — regular narrow ~150–200, P waves buried** · AF · **hyperkalaemia — tall peaked T → flat P → wide QRS → sine wave** · **WELLENS and DE WINTER — critical proximal LAD, treat as high risk DESPITE no ST elevation.**

**PRESENTING AN ECG — same script every time**: **‘This is a 12-lead ECG belonging to [name], taken on [date]. Calibration is standard at 25 mm/sec and 10 mm/mV. The rate is ___, the rhythm is ___, the axis is ___. P waves ___, PR ___, QRS ___. There is ___ in leads ___, with reciprocal change in ___. My overall interpretation is ___.’** It buys thinking room and shows structure even when the diagnosis is hard.

**RED FLAGS THAT STOP THE HISTORY**: drowsy, cyanosed or in distress → resuscitation cubicle · **systolic under 90 → shock, cautious fluids, WITHHOLD NITRATES** · ST elevation → reperfusion clock · **tearing pain with unequal pulses → CT aortogram, and NO antiplatelets or anticoagulation until excluded** · **tracheal deviation with hyper-resonance and hypotension → needle decompression BEFORE imaging** · **raised JVP + muffled sounds + hypotension → tamponade, urgent echo** · syncope with the pain · **fever with severe pain after vomiting → oesophageal rupture.**

**THE FOUR PARTNER CARDS**: **A — 61 F, worse lying down, better leaning forward, ‘bad flu’ ten days ago → PERICARDITIS; the mark is asking POSITION, recent VIRAL ILLNESS, and requesting a FRICTION RUB.** **B — 58 M, exertional tightness, DARK STICKY STOOLS for three weeks, daily ibuprofen, pale → ANGINA FROM IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA; the mark is asking black stools and requesting an FBC.** **C — 34 F, sharp right-sided pleuritic pain, flew from London four days ago, achy swollen calf, on the pill → PE.** **D — 44 M, burning, worse lying flat after dinner, ACID BRASH and WATER BRASH, settled by peppermint tea → GORD — and MISSING THE RISK FACTORS HERE IS STILL A FAIL EVEN THOUGH THE ANSWER IS REFLUX.**

back.dx: This is the scaffold, not a diagnosis. The differentials are delivered groups first and diagnoses second, in one breath: 'I'll group these by system. Gastrointestinal — my most likely is [x], and I'd also consider bowel cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis and obstruction. Renal tract — ureteric colic, pyelonephritis and a lower urinary tract infection. Genital and pelvic — in a woman of reproductive age, ectopic pregnancy is the one I must exclude first, with pelvic inflammatory disease and ovarian torsion. Because the pain is upper abdominal I've also considered liver and biliary — biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis. And from other systems, acute coronary syndrome, a lower lobe pneumonia and a leaking aortic aneurysm.' The rural sentence for every acute abdomen in a smaller centre: 'I'd make the transfer decision early rather than late, take bloods and a dipstick here, discuss with MedSTAR, and move while the work-up is still running.' South Australian localisation to say out loud: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval, RFDS for fixed-wing, tertiary destinations RAH, Flinders, Lyell McEwin, QEH, and the women's and children's for paediatric and obstetric cases, PATS offered before the patient asks, country health connect for community nursing, ACCHS and the closing the gap co-payment for an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient, TIS National 131 450 rather than a family member, and ReturnToWorkSA if the pain is work-related. The self-audit after every practice run: stability handled in the first fifteen seconds · the open question not interrupted · all nine pain items · 'Has it moved?' Asked · every applicable group named aloud before its questions · cancer screened regardless of age or duration · pregnancy asked where relevant · every red flag covered before SADMA · previous abdominal surgery asked · no question carried more than two barrels · every positive probed for amount and duration · summary, concern and safety-net all delivered.

pefe: This is a drill card — run it against a carded abdominal pain station with a partner holding that station's role-player brief, and score the structure, not the diagnosis. The source is the companion to an 'Approach document 01' that is not in drive; the drill card stands alone.

The AUTOMATIC FAILS it lists: stability neither asked for nor read off the stem in an acute abdomen · last menstrual period and pregnancy not asked in a woman of reproductive age · the cancer screen skipped because the pain seemed acute · a diagnosis reached without the questions that support it · a volunteered positive left unprobed · an examiner's direct question not answered out loud · groin and scrotum not requested where hernia or torsion is in the differential · a finding claimed that was never sought.

Stations to drill it on: appendicitis med-116 · central abdominal pain and young chronic abdomen · epigastric pain · RUQ biliary pain and obstructive jaundice med-148 · LLQ pain · RLQ pelvic pain and PID med-159 · ureteric colic med-163 · and the pregnancy versions in og-26. The companion flow sheet for the diagnoses themselves is med-254.
The one thing to remember on the day: name the group out loud before asking its questions, and screen every group the site switches on.

Box one — open, verbatim — Stability: 'Examiner, before I begin I'd like to confirm my patient is haemodynamically stable — could you give me the vital signs?' or 'I can see from the stem that the observations are stable, so I'll move straight to the history.' then greet, open, acknowledge, and signpost: 'Because this is abdominal pain I'm going to work through it by system — the bowel first, then the urinary tract, then because the pain is [low down / high up] the [gynaecological / liver and gallbladder] causes, and finally the chest'

Box two — nine items, and what each one moves — Site ('Point with one finger') switches groups on and off · onset in seconds means perforation, rupture, torsion or stone · character: colic is bowel, ureter or biliary tree · radiation is the single highest-yield question · timing separates colic from inflammation · worse on movement is peritonism · better leaning forward is pancreatitis · pain out of proportion is mesenteric ischaemia · progression: 'Has it moved from where it began?' — central to right iliac is appendicitis

Box three — the bowel, with cancer screened in every case — 'A few questions about your bowels.' Cancer every time: change in habit, blood or black in the stool, weight loss quantified, appetite · obstruction: wind, last motion, vomiting and its colour · IBD: bloody diarrhoea with slime, mouth ulcers, red eyes, joints, rashes · gastroenteritis: contacts, travel, takeaway · pancreatitis: through to the back, alcohol per week, gallstones · IBS: relieved by opening the bowels, bloating, how long

Box three continued — the groups the site switches on — Waterworks: burning, frequency, urgency, blood, cloudy, fevers and rigors, loin pain, hesitancy and stream · low down: first day of the last period, was it normal, any chance of pregnancy, has a test been done; bleeding, discharge, dyspareunia, STI risk; in men the testicles; in both a groin lump that grows on coughing · high up: jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch, fever with shaking chills (Fever plus jaundice plus RUQ pain is cholangitis), fatty food, heartburn, NSAIDs · chest: pain to jaw or arm, breathlessness, sweating, cough, pleuritic pain, a rash over the painful area, thirst and polyuria

Box four and five — SADMA, then a close that is never cut — Alcohol quantified per week, never 'Socially' · drugs probed for NSAIDs, steroids, opioids, anticoagulants · 'Any operations on your tummy?' For adhesions · family history of bowel cancer, IBD, gallstones · women: periods, contraception, previous pregnancies, previous ectopic or pelvic infection. Then twenty seconds: summarise in three sentences, 'Have I missed anything?', 'Was there anything you were worried this might be?', and the safety-net said aloud

dx: **STEP 0, BEFORE YOU NARROW ANYTHING**: **A to E, observations, IV access, and ANALGESIA OFFERED EARLY AND OUT LOUD.** Then the **three moves that are marked every time**: **URINE βhCG in every woman of reproductive age · ECG in anyone over 40 with upper abdominal pain · HERNIAL ORIFICES AND EXTERNAL GENITALIA in every patient, because TESTICULAR TORSION REFERS TO THE LOWER ABDOMEN.** **Bloods: FBE, UEC, LFT, LIPASE, CRP, LACTATE, glucose, group and hold. Erect CXR if peritonitic.**

**THE KILL LIST — decide these in the first five minutes. Every one of them kills through DELAY, not through diagnostic difficulty.** **Rigid silent abdomen, shock, free gas → PERFORATION.** **Pulsatile expansile mass, back pain, collapse, man over 65 → RUPTURED AAA — bedside USS, and DO NOT SEND AN UNSTABLE PATIENT TO CT.** **Pain far out of proportion to a soft abdomen, AF or vascular disease, rising lactate → MESENTERIC ISCHAEMIA.** **Positive βhCG with pain, faintness, shoulder-tip pain → RUPTURED ECTOPIC — resuscitate and theatre, NOT a formal scan.** **Irreducible tender groin lump with obstruction → STRANGULATED HERNIA — STOP attempting reduction.** **Fever, hypotension, delirium with an abdominal source → INTRA-ABDOMINAL SEPSIS: cultures then antibiotics WITHIN THE HOUR, and source control.**

**RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA — in a woman this is a GYNAECOLOGICAL problem until the pregnancy test AND the ovary have been cleared.** Central pain migrating to the RIF with anorexia, low fever and rebound at McBurney → **appendicitis** (Alvarado or AIR score; **USS first in young women and pregnancy**, CT if inconclusive). Sudden severe unilateral pain in waves with an adnexal mass, afebrile → **ovarian torsion — and NORMAL DOPPLER FLOW DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT.** Bilateral low pain with discharge, deep dyspareunia and cervical excitation → **PID: treat EMPIRICALLY, don't wait for swabs.**

**LEFT ILIAC FOSSA**: pain, fever, altered habit, over 50, previous identical episodes → **diverticulitis** (CT, Hinchey grade, **colonoscopy at 6–8 weeks**). Guarding, rigidity or free gas → **perforated diverticulitis.** **Blood MIXED THROUGH stool with weight loss and iron deficiency → COLORECTAL CANCER.** Older patient with AF, sudden pain then bloody diarrhoea that settles → **ischaemic colitis.** **Pain reproduced with the abdominal wall TENSED → ABDOMINAL WALL PAIN, Carnett sign positive — stop investigating the viscera.**

**EPIGASTRIC — character and what relieves it separates the four.** Boring through to the back, better leaning forward, alcohol or gallstones → **pancreatitis (lipase >3× ULN).** Gnawing burning eased by food or antacid → **peptic ulcer.** **Pressure with sweating and nausea, exertional, risk factors → INFERIOR MI — ECG WITH POSTERIOR AND RIGHT-SIDED LEADS.** Hard infrequent stool on opioids or iron → constipation, **and exclude overflow on PR.**

**RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT — DURATION OF THE EPISODE IS THE DISCRIMINATOR.** **Settles fully within 6 hours, no fever → BILIARY COLIC.** **Constant beyond 6 hours with fever and a positive Murphy → CHOLECYSTITIS** (USS wall >3 mm, pericholecystic fluid; **surgery same admission**). **Pain + fever + JAUNDICE → ASCENDING CHOLANGITIS; add confusion and hypotension for the pentad — ERCP drainage within 24–48 h.** And **fever with pleuritic pain and cough, especially a child → RIGHT BASAL PNEUMONIA: chest examination and CXR, antibiotics not laparotomy.**

**LOIN TO GROIN — ask about FEVER. That one answer separates an analgesia problem from a DECOMPRESSION EMERGENCY.** Sudden colic, **restless and unable to lie still**, dipstick haematuria → **ureteric colic** (non-contrast CT KUB; **USS first in pregnancy**). **Colic PLUS rigors and hypotension with a stone → OBSTRUCTED INFECTED SYSTEM: a urological emergency needing NEPHROSTOMY OR STENT — ANTIBIOTICS ALONE FAIL.** **First episode of loin and back pain in a man over 60 → LEAKING AAA: do not anchor on renal colic.**

**CENTRAL AND DIFFUSE — and the MEDICAL MIMICS that get taken to theatre.** Colicky central pain, vomiting, absolute constipation, distension, previous surgery → **bowel obstruction.** **DKA — vomiting, thirst, polyuria, deep sighing breathing: bedside ketones and a venous gas, FLUIDS AND INSULIN, NOT THEATRE.** **Hypercalcaemia** — confusion, constipation, thirst, bone pain. **Adrenal crisis** — postural hypotension, pigmentation, hyponatraemia, steroid withdrawal: **hydrocortisone BEFORE the result.** **RUQ pain with hypertension and proteinuria over 20 weeks → PRE-ECLAMPSIA or HELLP.**

**UPPER GI — the ALARM features decide who gets scoped and when**: **A**naemia · **L**oss of weight · **A**norexia · **R**ecent onset and progressive · **M**elaena or haematemesis · **S**wallowing difficulty · **age over 55.** Any one, or persistent vomiting, an epigastric mass or a family history → **urgent gastroscopy rather than another PPI script.** **Iron deficiency anaemia in a man or a postmenopausal woman is investigated at BOTH ENDS.** **A gastric ulcer is biopsied AND re-scoped — they can be malignant.**

**LOWER GI — two rules govern the whole page.** **An abdominal examination without a PR here is INCOMPLETE — offer it, with a chaperone, and document that you offered.** And **separate functional from organic on the red flags: weight loss, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, fever, a mass, onset after 50, or a family history of bowel or ovarian cancer. Any one of them and this is NOT irritable bowel.** **SYMPTOMS ALWAYS TRUMP SCREENING — never use a faecal occult blood test to reassure a symptomatic patient.**
plan: PAGE 1 · site

**Acute abdominal pain clustered by WHERE IT HURTS.** Step 0 first, then the kill list, then the six site clusters: **RIF · LIF · epigastric · RUQ · loin-to-groin · central and diffuse with the medical mimics.**
PAGE 2 · upper GI

**Dyspepsia, swallowing, vomiting, bleeding.** Alarm features → scope. **DYSPHAGIA opens on two questions: SOLIDS ONLY or solids AND liquids from the start, and TROUBLE STARTING the swallow versus food STICKING AFTER it.** **Obstruction biochemistry is a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with AKI.**
PAGE 3 · lower GI

**Diarrhoea, bleeding, bowel habit, perianal.** **Describe the blood precisely — on the paper, dripping into the pan, or mixed through the stool — then EXAMINE.** Perianal: **consent, chaperone, left lateral with knees drawn up, good light. INSPECT BEFORE YOU TOUCH — most of this is diagnosed on inspection. NEVER force a PR on a fissure.**
PAGE 4 · liver, pelvis, whole patient

**Jaundice opens on urine colour, stool colour and itch.** **Liver bloods: NAME THE PATTERN before ordering anything.** **Pelvic pain: urine βhCG BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.** **Girth and weight: documented weights, then percuss for shifting dullness.**
The jaundice split

**Urine and stool colour split it into thirds; then ask the ultrasound ONE question — ARE THE BILE DUCTS DILATED?** Dilated with pain, fever and rigors → **stone with cholangitis.** **Dilated, PAINLESS, weight loss, palpable non-tender gallbladder → PANCREATIC HEAD CANCER.** Not dilated with raised ALP and GGT in a middle-aged woman with itch → primary biliary cholangitis.
Liver function versus liver injury

**ALT and ALP describe INJURY. INR, ALBUMIN and BILIRUBIN describe FUNCTION — and only those change management urgently.** **AST:ALT above 2 with high GGT and macrocytosis → alcohol-related.** **ALP up with a NORMAL GGT → BONE, NOT LIVER.**
Girth — six causes

**FAT · FLUID · FLATUS · FAECES · FETUS · a MASS.** **Any woman of reproductive age with rising girth gets a βhCG before anything else.** **New persistent bloating with early satiety and urinary urgency in a woman over 50 → OVARIAN CANCER — the classic trap, and it is NOT irritable bowel.**
Weight loss — divide by appetite
**REDUCED appetite → malignancy, chronic infection, psychosocial.** **PRESERVED appetite → thyrotoxicosis, diabetes, malabsorption.** Full examination including **breast, testes, nodes and PR.**
Telehealth format

**A recurring station shape. Duration 4-5 months, so DSM's six months is not yet met — say 'most likely' rather than pretending the criterion is satisfied. Differentials, each with its discriminator: agoraphobia — fear of being unable to escape or get help, and she is comfortable in crowds · specific phobia — confined to a single object or situation, not to being observed · panic disorder — unexpected attacks out of the blue plus worry about the next one, whereas hers are cued only by speaking · generalised anxiety disorder — worry across many domains most days, but she is fine when there is no meeting · post-traumatic stress disorder — a traumatic event with re-experiencing and hyperarousal, absent here · adjustment disorder — the temptation, because of the project; it does not explain a trigger that is specifically being watched and evaluated · major depression — pervasive low mood and anhedonia, absent · substance and caffeine-related anxiety, and thyrotoxicosis — named even though the TFT is normal, because naming them is what is scored.

back.dx: Non-reactive non-stress test at 34 weeks in a woman presenting with reduced fetal movements — a reactive trace needs two accelerations of 15 beats lasting 15 seconds in 20 minutes, and this has none, with reduced variability as well. The most likely explanation is a fetal sleep cycle, which can last up to 40 minutes, and that is precisely why the answer is to extend the trace rather than either reassure and discharge or deliver on this strip. Other causes of reduced variability to name: opioids or sedation, prematurity, fetal anaemia, and — the one that matters — hypoxia. Reduced fetal movements is itself an independent risk marker for stillbirth and fetal growth restriction, so the presentation does not become benign just because the trace is only non-reactive.

Two things follow. Clinically, the airway is the problem: a GCS that swings between 9 and 14 will not reliably be protected, and the management is supportive in primary-survey order rather than any antidote. Dispositionally, this is not a recreational overdose to be slept off — it requires a mental health assessment before discharge. Flumazenil is avoided: reversing the benzodiazepine in a mixed sympathomimetic overdose can precipitate seizures.

back.dx: Osgood-Schlatter disease — traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity at the patellar tendon insertion in a skeletally immature athlete. Everything points one way: activity-related anterior knee pain over weeks in a 13-year-old in a jumping sport, tenderness confined to a prominent tuberosity, pain on resisted extension and single-leg loading, and a normal joint, ligament, meniscal and hip examination with no systemic features. Differentials, each with its discriminator: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson — tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella, not the tuberosity · patellar tendinopathy — mid-tendon tenderness, older adolescents and adults · patellofemoral pain — diffuse retropatellar pain, positive on squatting and stairs, no tuberosity tenderness · SLIPPED CAPITAL FEMORAL EPIPHYSIS — knee pain is the classic presentation, and the hip examination is what finds it · septic arthritis or osteomyelitis — fever, effusion, warmth, refusal to bear weight · bone tumour, osteosarcoma around the knee in exactly this age group — night pain, rest pain, a mass, systemic symptoms · tibial tuberosity avulsion fracture — acute jumping injury with sudden inability to straighten the knee, an urgent orthopaedic problem. Imaging is not routine: X-ray only for the atypical picture — trauma, night or rest pain, systemic symptoms, a mass, an effusion, or inability to extend.

Feel: tibial tuberosity, inferior and superior patellar poles, patellar tendon, medial and lateral joint lines, temperature compared with the other side.
Move: active then passive flexion and extension, resisted knee extension, and a single-leg squat or hop to reproduce the pain under load.
★ Examine the HIP — internal rotation above all — and screen the ligaments and menisci. A normal hip is the finding that keeps SCFE out of the diagnosis, and the examiner is listening for it.

Explain to the mother in her words: the tendon pulls on a growth plate at the top of the shin that has not yet hardened, so the bone there becomes sore and prominent. It is not a joint injury, it does not damage the knee, and it does not cause arthritis later. It settles as he finishes growing; the bump may stay.

Management, all of it load-based: keep playing but modify the load rather than stopping sport altogether — cut jumping volume and training frequency to the level where pain stays mild and settles within 24 hours · ice after sport · a short course of simple analgesia, paracetamol or ibuprofen, for bad days VERIFY · quadriceps and hamstring stretching and progressive eccentric quadriceps work through physiotherapy · a knee pad for kneeling · no corticosteroid injection into the apophysis.

Safety-net explicitly and review at 6 weeks: fever, a hot swollen knee or inability to weight bear · pain at night or at rest, or pain that wakes him · a lump or unexplained weight loss · a sudden inability to straighten the knee after a jump. FAIL — Not clearing NIGHT PAIN, REST PAIN, FEVER and EFFUSION before settling on a benign apophysitis — the must-not-miss list is SCFE, SEPTIC ARTHRITIS or osteomyelitis, BONE TUMOUR or LEUKAEMIA, and referred TESTICULAR TORSION: fever in an unwell child who holds the hip still and will not let you move it is a septic joint needing same-day bloods and ultrasound with possible aspiration; pain that WAKES HIM AT NIGHT, a mass, weight loss, pallor or bruising means an X-ray of the painful part with a full blood count and film TODAY; and groin or thigh pain with vomiting means examining the scrotum, because torsion refers to the groin and thigh (★)

DO — LOCALISE the tenderness to the TIBIAL TUBEROSITY and REPRODUCE the pain, because that is what converts 'anterior knee pain' into a diagnosis: point tenderness and swelling over the tuberosity, pain on RESISTED KNEE EXTENSION or single-leg loading, a normal joint line, no effusion, full pain-free passive range, stable ligaments, negative meniscal tests and NORMAL HIPS — then name it: OSGOOD–SCHLATTER DISEASE, a traction apophysitis in which the patellar tendon pulls repeatedly on the growing apophysis at the top of the shin, in an active 10- to 15-year-old

DO — Give a LOAD-MODIFICATION plan, not total rest and not a routine X-ray — it is a CLINICAL diagnosis, and imaging is normal or shows fragmentation of the apophysis without changing what you do; reduce the jumping and kneeling load rather than stopping sport altogether, ice after activity, simple analgesia, and QUADRICEPS AND HAMSTRING STRETCHING with a graded return as symptoms allow, reviewed rather than left open-ended; image only if there are red flags, a single acute injury, or the picture does not fit

SAY — 'He hasn't damaged the joint, and it won't cause arthritis; the bump may stay' — the three things the family actually want to know, because the visible lump frightens parents more than the pain does: it is a growth-plate irritation rather than joint damage, it SETTLES WITH SKELETAL MATURITY as the growth plate closes, and the bony prominence often remains permanently without causing trouble, though kneeling on it may stay uncomfortable; answer the sport question honestly rather than promising the finals, and be explicit that pain during and after activity which settles within a day is expected, while pain that changes character is not

DO — SAFETY-NET a sudden inability to straighten the knee after a jump as an urgent TIBIAL TUBEROSITY AVULSION needing same-day orthopaedic assessment, and give the four returns by name — FEVER, INABILITY TO WEIGHT-BEAR, NIGHT PAIN, or HIP PAIN — all same day; keep Osgood–Schlatter on the list, but keep SCFE on it too until the hip has actually been examined; and name the local pathway if escalation is needed — Women's and Children's Hospital paediatric orthopaedics, MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33 for advice or retrieval from country SA, Country Health Connect for physiotherapy, and PATS for travel to Adelaide reviews

setting: A counselling-weighted neurology station where the diagnosis is handed to you in the stem, so none of the marks are in working it out. Task one is an ASKED examination — you request findings from the examiner rather than performing them. The whole station turns on whether the patient leaves believing that you believed him. First sitting ran as a performed examination in the morning and was switched to an asked one that afternoon; some recalls name it functional neuropathy.
stem: You are the intern (HMO) covering the ward at a metropolitan hospital.

James Whitfield, 37, has come to the Emergency Department today because he is unable to walk. He has had weakness of the right lower limb since a motor vehicle accident two months ago. He was assessed at the time and examination and all imaging were normal.
The neurologist has already reviewed him today and has diagnosed a functional neurological disorder.
Tasks: ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings — explain the diagnosis to the patient — explain your management plan. Eight minutes.
tasks: Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Explain the management plan
time: Thirty seconds to introduce yourself and tell him you will examine first — never three minutes of examiner dialogue with an ungreeted patient · two and a half minutes on the examination request in six blocks · turn back by 3:00 · two and a half minutes on the explanation, which is where the marks are · two minutes on the team · the last thirty seconds on reading material, safety-net and teach-back. Spare time goes to the explanation, never to extra tests.
findingsLabel: Ask the examiner — the findings you are given
findings: Alert and oriented, comfortable at rest. Wheelchair at the bedside.
RIGHT ANKLE HELD FIXED and stiff, resisting movement.
Unable to walk unaided. Cannot heel-walk or toe-walk.
No wasting, no fasciculation, no tremor.
INCREASED AT THE RIGHT ANKLE; normal elsewhere.
Reduced at the right ankle and VARIABLE on repeat testing.
Normal and symmetrical, arms and legs.
NO CLONUS. PLANTARS DOWNGOING. NO DRIFT.
POSITIVE — or 'not tested'. Asking for it by name is what is scored.
must: FAIL — Explaining the cause as stress or the mind-body connection — the role-player is briefed to go cold, and the station is lost at that sentence
FAIL — Telling him nothing is wrong, or hedging when he asks 'do you believe me?' instead of answering with the word YES first
FAIL — Declaring the nerves undamaged without asking for CLONUS, PLANTAR and DRIFT after being told there is hypertonia — and never asking for HOOVER'S SIGN or fundoscopy by name
FAIL — Introducing yourself only to the examiner — three minutes of examiner dialogue with your back to him reads as dismissal; sit down and greet him first, then turn away for two minutes

SAY — All five, counted off: your symptoms are real · you are not imagining them · I see a lot of people with this · because there is no damage there is a real chance of getting better · this is not your fault

SAY — 'The hardware of your body is intact; it is the software that is not running properly at the moment' — then the plan: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychology for the DISTRESS not the cause, neurology and GP review, social work, and decline repeat imaging with a reason

back.dx: FUNCTIONAL NEUROLOGICAL DISORDER — altered voluntary motor function with positive clinical evidence of incompatibility between the symptom and recognised neurological disease, causing significant functional impairment. Diagnosed on POSITIVE SIGNS (Hoover, distractibility, give-way weakness, entrainment, midline sensory splitting), not by exclusion, and current criteria no longer require an identifiable psychological stressor — which is why 'your symptoms are real' is clinically accurate rather than merely kind. Here: fixed dystonic posture at the right ankle with increased tone, variable power and a positive Hoover, against normal reflexes, downgoing plantars, no clonus, no drift, normal sensation, coordination, cranial nerves and fundoscopy. Differentials to be seen excluding on the way: spinal cord compression or cauda equina (sensory level, retention, saddle anaesthesia, upgoing plantars), stroke (sudden onset, upper motor neurone pattern, drift), Guillain-Barré (ascending, areflexic, bulbar or respiratory), multiple sclerosis (relapsing, optic or brainstem involvement), radiculopathy or common peroneal palsy (dermatomal sensory loss, flaccid foot drop), and complex regional pain syndrome as a coexisting rather than alternative diagnosis. FND is NOT malingering or factitious disorder — symptoms are not consciously produced; know the distinction, never voice it, and be especially careful here because the index event was an MVA with a likely open CTP claim. Management is people, not prescriptions: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychology for CBT, neurologist and GP review, social work. No repeat imaging and no nerve conduction studies. VERIFY DSM-5-TR wording, MBS item caps and the SA reporting duty.
plan: Sanitise, sit at eye level, introduce yourself: 'I'm going to check your nerves and muscles first, then come straight back and explain everything. Two minutes.' Do not apologise, and do not skip this to save time.

The examination request in six blocks (see findings): general appearance → gait including heel and toe walking → ITPRSC in upper and lower limbs → cranial nerves, and ask for fundoscopy by name even if told cranial nerves are normal → clonus, plantar and drift, because hypertonia was reported → Hoover's sign.

Turn back and sit. 'Before we discuss it — is there anything worrying you?' Then the six beats: purpose of the examination → what you found → name the diagnosis → the disorders he does NOT have (no stroke, no bleed, no tumour, no injury from the accident) → hardware intact, software not running → the five statements, counted.
Answer the belief question the moment it comes, with yes as the first word. If it never comes, it will surface at the end — ask for questions before moving to the plan.

The team, one sentence each: physiotherapist (retrain movement, balance, flexibility) · occupational therapist (home review, aids, daily activities) · psychologist (CBT for the distress, which makes the condition harder to treat — never for the cause) · neurologist and GP (regular review) · social worker (income, work, disability supports).
Decline repeat imaging with a reason. Written information — FND Australia Support Services, neurosymptoms.org. Safety-net. Teach-back: 'How would you explain this to your partner?'
ask: The examination request is spoken in blocks, and blocks 5 and 6 are what separate you from a candidate reciting a generic neurological examination. If told 'cranial nerves are normal', still ask: 'Could I confirm fundoscopy specifically?' — papilloedema is the one bedside finding that would make your reassurance false.

Hoover's sign, by name: 'Hip extension tested alone, then again while the patient flexes the opposite hip.' Positive = extension that is weak on direct testing and becomes strong once attention moves to the other leg.
The six explanation beats in order: purpose → findings → name it → what he does not have → hardware and software → the five statements. Never lead with the negatives.
Never say: mind and body are connected · it's stress · there's nothing wrong · it's psychological · conversion disorder · a promised timeframe for recovery.
Mobility aids are genuinely contested — dependence versus deconditioning. Safe position: provide one as a bridge alongside active physiotherapy, with a plan to wean it.
Fitness to drive: a fixed ankle affecting pedal control must be assessed against Assessing Fitness to Drive, with a reporting duty in SA under the Motor Vehicles Act 1959. VERIFY
pefe: Role-player: James Whitfield, 37, warehouse supervisor, currently off work. Lives with his partner and a nine-year-old daughter; four steps at the front door. Mother had a stroke at 61 and he is quietly frightened this is the same thing. Starts flat, guarded and slightly impatient — he has told this story to four doctors. Warms only if told his symptoms are real; goes cold and monosyllabic if stress or his mind is offered as the cause.

Hidden agenda — he is convinced the doctors think he is faking it for the insurance claim. If asked about concerns early he raises it then; otherwise he interrupts mid-explanation with 'Do you actually believe me?', or says it at the close: 'You think I'm making this up for the insurance, don't you?' It is said in every run.
His questions: how long will this take · do I need another scan · will I need a wheelchair · what about my job · why do I need a psychologist if it's a nerve problem.

Recall versions — A: ask the examination (current, most common). B: perform it, with cotton wool and a tendon hammer, first sitting morning only; prioritise gait, tone, power, reflexes, plantar and Hoover if short of time. C: named 'functional neuropathy' — same station, use the correct term yourself. D: the belief question as an explicit hidden agenda. E: opens angry, having been dismissed elsewhere — acknowledge without defending the previous clinicians, then run the same six beats.

Recall discrepancy: the source describes the ankle as held in dorsiflexion while also saying he cannot dorsiflex or heel-walk, which cannot both be true. Fixed functional ankle dystonia is characteristically plantarflexion with inversion. Describe back whatever the examiner gives and call it 'a fixed, stiff posture at the ankle' rather than committing to a direction.
fails: ★ Explaining causation psychologically — stress, or the mind-body axis
★ Telling him nothing is wrong, or that all the tests are normal and leaving it there
★ Failing to answer 'do you believe me?' with a clear yes
★ Telling him he is imagining or exaggerating the symptoms

Reassuring that the nerves are undamaged without asking for clonus, plantar and drift after being told about hypertonia; never greeting the patient before three minutes of examiner dialogue; omitting Hoover's sign; ordering repeat imaging or a nerve conduction study to fill an awkward silence; saying conversion disorder; delivering two of the five reassurance statements and moving on; promising a recovery timeframe; running out of time so the plan becomes a rushed list of five professions
